entries.shortExplanation: 오전 means "morning / AM" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 오전 (ojeon) means "morning / AM". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오전에 ("in the morning"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오전 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: attaches the time particle 에 for 'during the AM'
period word comes BEFORE the clock time
오전 directly modifies the following noun, no 의
내내 stresses the whole stretch of the AM

examples.en: I have a meeting in the morning.
examples.note: basic: 에 marks the time-when

examples.ko: 저는 보통 오전 열 시에 일어나요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun botong ojeon yeol sie ireonayo.
examples.en: I usually get up at 10 AM.
examples.note: everyday: period 오전 + hour 열 시 + 에 together

examples.en: I'll get in touch sometime during the morning.
examples.note: real-situation: 오전 중(으로) = 'within the AM', polite work register

entries.nuance: 오전 is the Sino-Korean clock label for the AM half of the day, literally 午前 'before noon' (午 = noon, 前 = before), and its mirror is 오후 午後 'after noon'. The key contrast learners blur is 오전 vs 아침: 아침 is the FELT early part of the day (sunrise to mid-morning, and also breakfast), while 오전 is the neutral clock span from midnight-ish to 12:00 used on schedules, tickets, and timetables. So you say 아침에 커피를 마셔요 (lived experience) but 오전 9시 출발 (a printed departure). It is more formal/factual than 아침 and pairs habitually with clock times (오전 9시), 회의/수업/근무, and 오전 중. The classic English-speaker pitfall is word order: AM attaches AFTER the number in English ('9 AM'), but in Korean the period leads, so it must be 오전 9시, never 9시 오전. Also do not reach for 오전 when you simply mean the breakfast-time feel of 'morning' — use 아침.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오전 시간이에요 when you mean the cozy early morning feel — that idea is 아침; 오전 is the neutral clock-span AM and sounds like a timetable.
Putting the period after the hour, e.g. 아홉 시 오전 — Korean fixes the order as 오전 아홉 시 (period first, then clock time).
Dropping 에 in 오전 회의 있어요 — to mark 'during the morning' you need 오전에 회의가 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 오후 means "afternoon / PM" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "afternoon / PM" is 오후 (ohu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오후에 ("in the afternoon"). Watch the particle attached to 오후 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: time particle 에 = 'during the PM'
period precedes the clock number
오후 modifies the noun directly
day word + 오후 stack with no particle between

examples.en: I meet a friend in the afternoon.
examples.note: basic: 에 marks time-when

examples.en: I have an appointment at 2 PM.
examples.note: everyday: 오후 + 두 시 + 에 in sequence

examples.ko: 오후 늦게 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: ohu neutge biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: It looks like it'll rain late in the afternoon.
examples.note: real-situation: 오후 늦게 = 'late in the PM', a fixed phrase

entries.nuance: 오후 is the Sino-Korean PM label, literally 午後 'after noon' (午 noon, 後 after), the exact counterpart of 오전 午前. It covers every PM hour from 12:00 until evening, where it hands off to 저녁. The contrast to watch is 오후 vs 저녁: 오후 is the neutral clock-PM you write on schedules (오후 3시 회의), while 저녁 is the lived early-evening AND the dinner meal; so a 6 p.m. plan can be 오후 6시 on a timetable but 저녁 when you talk about eating. 오후 collocates with clock times (오후 3시), 수업/회의/근무, and the fixed 오후 늦게 'late in the afternoon'. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is order: 'PM' follows the number in English but the period LEADS in Korean — say 오후 5시, never 5시 오후. A second trap is treating 오후 as a greeting-time word like 'good afternoon'; Korean has no clock-based greeting, so you still say 안녕하세요, not anything built on 오후.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 다섯 시 오후 — Korean order is period-then-time, so it must be 오후 다섯 시.
Using 오후 for an early-evening dinner plan — for the dinner-time feel switch to 저녁 (저녁 여섯 시), since 오후 is the neutral daytime-PM span.
Trying to greet someone with a phrase based on 오후 like English 'good afternoon' — Korean uses the all-purpose 안녕하세요 regardless of the hour.

entries.shortExplanation: 아침 means "morning; also breakfast" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아침 (achim) = "morning; also breakfast". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아침에 ("in the morning") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아침, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: time + 에 for the time-when reading
here 아침 is the meal, so it takes object 을
매일 + 아침 = habitual time phrase
아침 + adverb 일찍, a set collocation

examples.en: I drink coffee in the morning.
examples.note: basic: 아침에 = the time slot

examples.en: I don't eat breakfast.
examples.note: everyday: 아침 + 을 shows it's the MEAL, object of 먹다

examples.ko: 아침 일찍 출발하면 길이 안 막혀요.
examples.romanization: achim iljjik chulbalhamyeon giri an makyeoyo.
examples.en: If we leave early in the morning, traffic won't be jammed.
examples.note: real-situation: 아침 일찍 set phrase + conditional 면

entries.nuance: 아침 is a native Korean word that does double duty: the early part of the day (roughly sunrise to mid-morning) and the breakfast meal — the same way English 'morning' differs from the meal but Korean merges the breakfast sense into the time word. The grammar disambiguates: with 에 (아침에) it's the time, with 을 (아침을 먹다) it's the food. Contrast 아침 vs 오전: 아침 is the felt, lived early morning, while 오전 午前 is the neutral clock-AM you put on timetables — so 아침에 일어나요 (waking life) but 오전 9시 회의 (a scheduled item). Habitual partners: 아침에 일어나다/운동하다, 아침을 먹다/거르다 ('skip breakfast'), 아침 일찍, 매일 아침. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 오전 for the breakfast meal — 오전 is only the clock period and can never name food, so 'eat breakfast' must be 아침을 먹다, never 오전을 먹다. Also don't force 에 onto the meal sense: you eat 아침을, you don't 'eat at morning'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오전을 먹어요 for 'eat breakfast' — 오전 is only the clock-AM span; the meal is 아침, so it must be 아침을 먹어요.
Marking the breakfast meal with 에 (아침에 먹어요 meaning the food) — as a meal-object it needs 을: 아침을 먹어요. 아침에 먹어요 only means 'eat (something) in the morning'.
Assuming 아침 always equals clock-morning like 오전 — on schedules and tickets Koreans switch to 오전 9시; 아침 is the lived, informal morning.

entries.shortExplanation: 점심 means "lunch / noon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 점심 (jeomsim) means "lunch / noon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 점심을 먹어요 ("eat lunch"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 점심 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: meal sense → object 을
time sense → 에
fixed compound (often written closed)
점심 modifies the noun directly

examples.en: Let's have lunch together.
examples.note: basic: object 을 is often dropped in casual speech → just 점심 먹다

examples.en: What are you going to eat for lunch?
examples.note: everyday: 점심에 = the time slot + future 을 거예요

examples.en: Have you eaten lunch (yet)?
examples.note: real-situation: a routine greeting that means 'how are you', not a literal question

entries.nuance: 점심 is Sino-Korean, literally 點心 — 點 'a dot/spot' + 心 'heart/center', an old phrase for a small 'touch-the-heart' midday bite that came to mean both the noon-time and the lunch meal. Like 아침/저녁, grammar splits the senses: 점심을 먹다 (the meal) vs 점심에 (the time). Note the near-synonym 정오 正午 'exactly noon' is the precise clock point 12:00, while 점심 is the looser lunch-time/meal — you'd never say 정오를 먹다. Habitual partners: 점심을 먹다, 점심시간, 점심 약속, 점심 메뉴, and the ritual greeting 점심 먹었어요?. Two English-speaker pitfalls: (1) translating 'lunch break' word-for-word — Korean uses the set compound 점심시간, not 점심 휴식; (2) reading 점심 먹었어요? literally and giving a detailed menu report — like 'how's it going', it's mostly phatic, and 네, 먹었어요 is enough. Also remember the meal is an object (점심을 먹다), so don't say 점심에 먹다 when you mean eating the lunch itself.

Saying 정오를 먹어요 for 'eat lunch' — 정오 is the clock instant 'noon (12:00)'; the meal is 점심, so use 점심을 먹어요.
Coining 점심 휴식 for 'lunch break' — the natural fixed word is 점심시간.
Answering 점심 먹었어요? with a long literal report — it's a routine greeting like 'how are you'; a simple 네, 먹었어요 fits.

entries.shortExplanation: 저녁 means "evening; also dinner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "evening; also dinner" is 저녁 (jeonyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저녁을 먹어요 ("eat dinner"). Watch the particle attached to 저녁 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: meal sense → object 을
time sense → 에
식사 'a meal' makes the dinner sense explicit & polite
day word + 저녁 with no particle between

examples.en: I watch a movie in the evening.
examples.note: basic: 저녁에 = the time slot

examples.en: What should we eat for dinner?
examples.note: everyday: meal 을 dropped in casual speech + 을까요 suggestion

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 시간 괜찮으면 같이 식사해요.
examples.romanization: oneul jeonyeoge sigan gwaenchaneumyeon gachi siksahaeyo.
examples.en: If you're free this evening, let's eat together.
examples.note: real-situation: 저녁에 (time) + polite invitation 식사하다

entries.nuance: 저녁 is a native Korean word covering the early-night period AND the dinner meal, mirroring 아침/점심: 저녁을 먹다 is the food, 저녁에 is the time. The fine line is 저녁 vs 밤: 저녁 is the social early evening — dusk through dinner, when people are still out — whereas 밤 is true late night when it's dark and quiet; so a 7 p.m. dinner is 저녁, but 11 p.m. is 밤. 저녁 also contrasts with the clock label 오후, which ends as 저녁 begins. Habitual partners: 저녁을 먹다, 저녁 식사, 저녁 약속, 저녁 메뉴, 저녁에 만나다. The main English-speaker pitfall is using 밤 for the dinner meal because 'night' feels close — but 'eat dinner' is 저녁을 먹다, never 밤을 먹다 (밤 can't name a meal, and 밤 also happens to mean 'chestnut'). A second trap: don't mark the dinner-meal with 에; you eat 저녁을, while 저녁에 means 'in the evening (do something)'.

Saying 밤을 먹어요 for 'eat dinner' — 밤 names late-night, not a meal (and also means 'chestnut'); the dinner meal is 저녁을 먹어요.
Using 저녁 for genuinely late night (e.g. midnight) — past dinner into the dark, quiet hours it becomes 밤; 저녁 is the early, social evening.
Marking the meal with 에 (저녁에 먹어요, meaning the food) — the dinner-as-object needs 을: 저녁을 먹어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 밤 means "night" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 밤 (bam) = "night". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 밤에 ("at night") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 밤, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: time + 에 for 'during the night'
fixed adverb, written closed: 밤+늦게
compound; note the inserted ㅅ (사이시옷): 어제+밤
period word + late clock hour

examples.en: I read books at night.
examples.note: basic: 밤에 = the time slot

examples.en: I worked until late at night.
examples.note: everyday: set adverb 밤늦게 + 까지 'until'

examples.en: I couldn't sleep well last night.
examples.note: real-situation: 어젯밤 (note 사이시옷) + 잘 못 자다 'can't sleep well'

entries.nuance: 밤 is a native word for true night — the dark, quiet hours after 저녁, peaking around bedtime and past midnight. The contrast to fix is 밤 vs 저녁: 저녁 is the social early evening (dusk to dinner) while 밤 is deep night, so 7 p.m. is 저녁 but 11 p.m. or 1 a.m. is 밤. A spelling point: 'last night' is 어젯밤 with an inserted ㅅ (사이시옷) and is preferred over the looser 어제 밤; 'tomorrow night' is 내일 밤. Habitual partners: 밤에 자다, 밤늦게, 밤새(우다) 'stay up all night', 어젯밤, 깊은 밤 'the dead of night'. The English-speaker pitfall: 밤 only names the time of night and can NEVER mean the dinner meal — that's 저녁; and beware the homograph 밤 also means 'chestnut', so context (밤에 vs 밤을 굽다 'roast chestnuts') keeps them apart. Finally, like other pure time words 밤 takes 에 for 'at night' (밤에), so don't drop it when stating when something happens.

Using 밤 for the dinner meal — 밤 is only night-time (and separately 'chestnut'); the evening meal is 저녁: 저녁을 먹어요.
Calling early evening (around dinner) 밤 — 7 p.m. when people are still out is 저녁; 밤 is the dark, quiet late hours.
Writing 'last night' as 어제밤 — the standard form inserts 사이시옷: 어젯밤.

entries.shortExplanation: 요일 means "day of the week" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 요일 (yoil) means "day of the week". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무슨 요일 ("what day of the week"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ask with 무슨, not 어느/어떤
specific day name + 에
요일 + 별로 'sorted per day'
요일 + 마다 'each day'

examples.en: What day of the week is it today?
examples.note: basic: the standard way to ask the weekday

examples.en: What day of the week is the class on?
examples.note: everyday: 무슨 요일 + 에 to ask the time-when

examples.en: I switch the workout by the day of the week.
examples.note: real-situation: 요일마다 = 'each day-of-week', a habitual pattern

entries.nuance: 요일 is the Sino-Korean suffix that builds weekday names, 曜日 — 曜 'celestial body/light' + 日 'day', the same East-Asian system that names days after the sun, moon, and five elements: 일(日)요일 Sun, 월(月)요일 Moon, 화(火)요일 Fire/Mars, 수(水)요일 Water, 목(木)요일 Wood, 금(金)요일 Metal/Gold, 토(土)요일 Earth. By itself 요일 means 'day of the week' as a category. The key usage point is the question word: to ask which weekday you MUST use 무슨 요일이에요?, because 무슨 asks 'what kind/which of a known set'; 어느 요일 or 어떤 요일 sound unnatural here. Habitual partners: 무슨 요일, 요일마다, 요일별, 주말/평일 요일. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'which day → 어느', producing 어느 요일이에요?; Korean idiom locks this to 무슨 요일. entries.nuance: 주말 is Sino-Korean, 週末 — 週 'week' + 末 'end', literally 'week-end', and its opposites are 평일 平日 'weekday' and 주중 週中 'midweek'. It refers to Saturday and Sunday as a block. A second subtlety: for 'this weekend' use 이번 주말 (이번 = the current instance), not 오늘 주말; and 다음 주말 'next weekend' vs 다음 주 주말 can differ, so keep 다음 주말 for the upcoming Sat–Sun.

entries.nuance: 어제 is a native deictic time word meaning 'yesterday', sitting in the set 그저께(엊그제) 'day before yesterday' – 어제 – 오늘 'today' – 내일 'tomorrow' – 모레 'day after tomorrow'. Its defining grammar quirk is that, like 오늘 and 내일, it normally takes NO 에: you say 어제 만났어요, never 어제에. (The particle reappears only when 어제 combines with a sub-period, e.g. 어제 아침에, where 에 attaches to 아침.) 어제 naturally pairs with past tense — 았어요/었어요 — so it's a reliable signal that the verb should be past. Habitual partners: 어제 아침/저녁, 어제부터, 어제 일 'yesterday's matter', 어제 본/한/간 + noun. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-marking with 에 by analogy to 'on' or to other time nouns like 주말에; bare 어제 is correct. A second trap is pairing 어제 with present or future tense; because it's firmly past, 어제 가요 is wrong — it must be 어제 갔어요.

Adding 에: 어제에 만났어요 — the bare time words 어제/오늘/내일 drop 에; say 어제 만났어요.
Using present/future with 어제 — 어제 갔어요 (past) is required, not 어제 가요.
Reaching for 그저께/엊그제 to mean plain 'yesterday' — those mean 'the day before yesterday'; simple yesterday is 어제.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. examples.note: basic: noun–number–counter, object 를 often dropped when ordering

entries.nuance: 개 is the Sino-Korean general counter for inanimate objects, 個/箇, the catch-all you use when no more specific counter fits (it won't do for people, animals, or flat/long things, which have their own counters). The headline English-speaker pitfall is using Sino numbers with 개 — 일 개, 이 개 is wrong; counters like 개/명/마리 take native numbers (한 개), even though money/minutes take Sino. A second trap is English order: don't say 세 사과 개 or 개 세 사과; it's 사과 세 개. Note the contrast with 명/분 (people) and 마리 (animals): 개 is strictly for things.

Copying English order (세 사과 / three-apples) — Korean is noun + number + counter: 사과 세 개.

entries.nuance: 명 is the Sino-Korean counter for people, 名 'name/person', and like all counters it takes native numbers: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 (with the usual shortening 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무). Using neutral 명 for respected guests or elders — switch to the honorific counter 분: 손님 세 분, 할머니 한 분.
Using Sino numbers: 이 명, 삼 명 — the counter 명 takes native numbers: 두 명, 세 명.

entries.nuance: 원 is the Korean currency unit (the symbol is ₩) and, like all money and clock-number words, it REQUIRES Sino-Korean numbers: 일·이·삼·사·오·육·칠·팔·구·십·백·천·만 (so 천 원, 만 원, 오천 원). The single biggest stumbling block for English speakers is the 만 'ten-thousand' place: Korean groups large numbers by 10,000, not 1,000, so 만 원 = 10,000 won (not 1,000), 십만 = 100,000, 백만 = 1,000,000. Reading prices therefore means re-chunking — 30,000 is 삼만 (3×10,000), 15,000 is 만 오천. Habitual partners: 얼마예요?, 만 원짜리 'a 10,000-won bill/item', ~원만 'just ~won', 거스름돈 'change'. The headline pitfall, beyond the comma-grouping, is using NATIVE numbers with 원 (한 원, 두 원) — money never takes native numbers; it's 천 원, 만 원. Contrast this with counters like 개/명, which take native numbers — Korean splits the two systems, and 원 firmly sits on the Sino side. Also note 원 is read after the full number, e.g. 사천오백 원, with no 'and'.

entries.nuance: 가족 is the Sino-Korean word 家族 ('house' 家 + 'clan/group' 族), so it names the whole family unit as a collective, never a single relative — for one member you must say 가족 한 명 or name the relationship (형, 누나). The near-synonym 식구 also means family but literally means 食口 'mouths to feed', stressing the people who live and eat under one roof, so 식구 feels warmer and more domestic ('우리 식구 다섯이에요') while 가족 is the neutral standard term that also covers relatives living apart. Register is neutral and safe in any setting. The big English-speaker trap is two-fold: 'big/small family' is 가족이 많다/적다 (many/few), never 가족이 크다 (that sounds like physically large bodies); and Koreans say 우리 가족 ('our family') where English forces 'my family', so the 우리 is idiomatic, not a mistake.

Using 가족 to point at one person ('그 가족이 제 형이에요') — 가족 is a group word; for a single relative say 가족 중 한 명 or just 제 형.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 + the built-in honorific 님 = the polite default
use 계시다, the honorific of 있다, to match 님
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테, required by 님
댁 is the honorific of 집 (house)

examples.en: I live with my parents.
examples.note: 살다 (to live/reside) drops its ㄹ before some endings but keeps it in 살아요

examples.en: I call my parents every day.
examples.note: 드리다 is the humble form of 주다/하다 — you 'give' the call up to elders

examples.en: My parents are in Busan right now.
examples.note: 계세요 (honorific 있어요) is obligatory because the subject is 부모님

entries.nuance: 부모님 is Sino-Korean 父母 ('father' 父 + 'mother' 母) plus the honorific suffix 님, so the respect is baked into the word itself and it is the everyday polite default — there is no need to add anything to make it courteous. The bare root 부모 exists but is abstract and institutional ('부모의 역할' the role of parents, '부모 교육' parenting education); aimed at a real person it sounds cold, so for your own or anyone's parents you say 부모님. Because 님 marks the referent as worthy of respect, every verb around it must climb to its honorific tier: 있다→계시다, 주다→드리다, 집→댁, 에게→께, and the topic/subject can even take 께서. The classic English-speaker pitfall is pairing 부모님 with plain verbs ('부모님이 있어요', '부모님한테 줬어요'); grammatically the words exist, but to a Korean ear it clashes like saying 'Her Majesty ate fast' — you must use 계세요 and 드렸어요/께.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 부모 instead of 부모님 for an actual person ('제 부모는…') — without 님 it sounds blunt and textbook-like; always use 부모님 for real parents.
Using plain 있어요/없어요 with 부모님 ('부모님이 있어요') — the honorific subject demands 계세요/안 계세요.
Writing 부모님한테 or 부모님에게 — with the honorific 님 the dative must rise to 부모님께.

entries.shortExplanation: 엄마 means "mom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 엄마 (eomma) = "mom". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 엄마 ("my mom") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 엄마, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is the natural possessive even for one's own mother
엄마 takes 가 as the thing-liked with 좋다
돕다 is ㅂ-irregular: 돕 + 아요 → 도와요
한테 is the casual dative that suits this intimate word

examples.en: My mom cooks well.
examples.note: 잘하다 = 잘 (well) + 하다, written as one word

examples.en: I really like my mom.
examples.note: 좋아하다 (verb, takes 를) acts on 엄마, unlike adjective 좋다 (takes 가)

examples.en: Yesterday I gave mom a present.
examples.note: 주다 + 었어요 contracts to 줬어요; 한테 marks the recipient

entries.nuance: 엄마 is the warm, intimate nursery word for 'mother', the everyday home register you use speaking to her directly or about her among family and friends — emotionally it is exactly English 'mom/mommy'. Its formal counterpart is 어머니, the respectful word for polite or public settings (introducing her, speaking to in-laws, addressing a friend's mother as 어머니); think of the pair as a sliding scale, 엄마 (intimate) → 어머니 (formal/respectful). Unlike 부모님, 엄마 has no honorific 님 built in, so it stays in the casual zone, though you still naturally use it with polite -요 endings ('엄마가 와요'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 엄마 as a neutral all-purpose 'mother': calling a stranger's mother 엄마, or saying 엄마 to your boss when reporting on a parent, feels childish or over-familiar — switch up to 어머니 the moment the situation turns formal, just as English shifts from 'my mom' to 'my mother'.

Using 엄마 in formal or public speech ('저희 엄마께서…' in a job interview) — it sounds childish there; use 어머니 for respectful contexts.
Pairing 엄마 with 좋아하다 but keeping the adjective particle ('엄마가 좋아해요' to mean 'I like mom') — 좋아하다 needs the object 엄마를 좋아해요; 가 belongs with adjective 좋다.
Calling someone else's mother 너희 엄마 to her face — address her directly as 어머니, the polite vocative.

entries.shortExplanation: 아빠 means "dad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아빠 (appa) means "dad". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 아빠 ("my dad"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 아빠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is the idiomatic possessive for one's own father
멋있다 (cool/stylish) takes the subject 가
닮다 takes an object with 를, not 와
한테 is the casual, affectionate dative

examples.en: My dad works at a company.
examples.note: 다니다 means to attend/commute to regularly; pairs with 에

examples.en: I look a lot like my dad.
examples.note: 닮다 uses 를 + past 았어요; the resemblance is stated as completed

examples.en: On weekends I work out with my dad.
examples.note: 하고 (casual 'with') + 같이 doubles the togetherness, very natural

entries.nuance: 아빠 is the affectionate home word for 'father', the casual nursery register matching English 'dad/daddy', used to him directly and about him in relaxed company. Its formal partner is 아버지, the respectful term for public or polite situations — introductions, talking to elders, a friend's father — so the pair runs 아빠 (intimate) → 아버지 (formal), exactly mirroring 엄마 → 어머니. Like 엄마, it carries no honorific 님, so it lives in the casual zone but still combines with polite -요 endings. A frequent and very Korean collocation is 닮다 'to resemble' — 아빠를 닮다 'take after dad' — and note it takes the object particle 를, where English-speakers often wrongly reach for 'with' (와/하고). The bigger pitfall is register: dropping 아빠 into a formal report or addressing a stranger's father as 아빠 sounds childish; climb to 아버지 the instant the setting turns respectful, just as English moves from 'my dad' to 'my father'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 아빠를 닮았어요 but using 와/하고 ('아빠하고 닮았어요') — 닮다 takes the object particle, so it must be 아빠를 닮았어요.
Using 아빠 in a formal context ('저희 아빠는 의사세요' to a stranger) — it sounds childish; use 아버지 for respectful or public speech.
Treating 아빠 as the only word for 'father' and never learning 아버지 — you will sound like a small child when the situation calls for formality.

entries.shortExplanation: 형 means "older brother (male speaker)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "older brother (male speaker)" is 형 (hyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 형 ("my older brother"). Watch the particle attached to 형 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a male; the word itself signals the speaker is male
있다 = 'have/exist'; 형 takes 가→이 after a consonant
한테 is the casual dative used among close family
친 (親, 'blood/real') distinguishes him from a 사촌 or 의형

examples.en: I have one older brother.
examples.note: 명 counts people; one says 한 명, never 일 명

examples.en: I play games with my older brother.
examples.note: 하고 (casual 'with') + 같이 is the everyday combo for 'together with'

examples.en: My older brother is taller than me.
examples.note: 보다 = 'than'; literally 'than me, height is big' = taller

entries.nuance: 형 (Sino-Korean 兄 'elder brother') is the word a MALE uses for an older brother, and crucially it is also a warm address term a younger man uses for any slightly-older male he is close to — an older friend, schoolmate, or colleague — so '민수 형' can mean 'Minsu, my big-brother-figure', not a blood relative. The matched set is gendered by speaker: a female says 오빠 for the same older-brother relationship, while 누나/언니 cover older sisters — so the single word leaks the speaker's gender, something English's flat 'older brother' never does. Register is casual-but-respectful: 형 is itself an honorific address (you call him 형, never his bare name), and you speak up to him. The dominant English-speaker pitfall is gender: a woman must never call her older brother 형 — that is 오빠 — and second, don't assume 형 always means kin; in daily life it is most often the affectionate title for an older male friend.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A female speaker using 형 for her older brother — women say 오빠; 형 is strictly male-to-male.
Assuming 형 only ever means a blood brother — a younger man also calls a close older male friend 형 (e.g. 동수 형).
Calling your older brother by his bare first name instead of 형 — Korean requires the title 형 as both address and reference for elders.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 누나, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a male; the word marks the speaker as male
있다 'have'; 누나 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
한테 is the casual dative for close family
친 (親 'real/blood') marks her as a full sister, not 사촌

examples.en: I have two older sisters.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 두 명 = two (people)

examples.en: My older sister often helps me.
examples.note: 도와주다 (돕다 + 주다, ㅂ-irregular) = do the favor of helping

examples.en: I go to a cafe with my older sister.
examples.note: 하고 'with' + 같이; 에 marks the destination 카페

entries.nuance: 누나 is the word a MALE uses for an older sister, and like 형 it doubles as a warm address title a younger man uses for any older woman he is close to — an older female friend, senior student, or, famously, a beloved older woman ('누나' in K-pop). Its gendered partner is 언니, which a FEMALE uses for the very same older-sister relationship, so 누나 vs 언니 is split purely by who is speaking, and the word betrays the speaker's gender in a way English 'older sister' cannot. Register is casual but deferential: 누나 is itself a respectful address (you call her 누나, not her name) and you speak up to her with -요 forms. A very natural collocation is 도와주다 'help (as a favor)'. The headline English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나 and a woman 언니 for an older sister — swapping them is an immediate giveaway — and remember 누나 is also how a younger man fondly addresses an older woman, not only a sibling.

A female speaker using 누나 for her older sister — women say 언니; 누나 is strictly used by males.
Confusing 누나 (male→older sister) with 언니 (female→older sister) — the choice depends entirely on the SPEAKER's gender, not the sister's.
Addressing your older sister by her bare name rather than 누나 — Korean expects the kinship title 누나 for someone older.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 오빠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a female; the word signals the speaker is female
있다 'have'; 오빠 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
한테 is the casual dative among close people
친 (親 'real') separates him from a boyfriend or cousin called 오빠

examples.en: I have one older brother.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 한 명 = one (person)

examples.en: My older brother is coming to pick me up.
examples.note: 데리러 오다 = come in order to fetch a person; -러 marks purpose

examples.en: I watch a movie with my older brother.
examples.note: 보다 'watch' → 봐요; 하고 같이 = 'together with'

entries.nuance: 오빠 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older brother, and it is the most socially loaded kinship term in Korean: a woman also calls a close older male friend, a senior, or especially a boyfriend 오빠, so '오빠' on its own can mean 'my big brother', 'my guy friend', or 'babe' depending on context — hence 친오빠 exists to specify the actual sibling. Its gendered counterpart is 형, used by a MALE for the same older-brother relationship, so 오빠 vs 형 splits by speaker, and the word instantly reveals the speaker is a woman. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 forms, and 오빠 is itself the address term (never his bare name). The major English-speaker pitfall is gender — a man must say 형, never 오빠 — and the cultural trap: because 오빠 also means 'boyfriend' in romantic use, calling a male friend 오빠 can imply flirtation, so learners should know the connotation before using it freely.

A male speaker using 오빠 for his older brother — men say 형; 오빠 is used only by females.
Not realizing 오빠 can mean 'boyfriend' — a woman calling any older man 오빠 may signal romantic interest, so use it knowingly.
Saying 친오빠 when you mean a boyfriend — 친오빠 specifically means a blood older brother; for a boyfriend just say 남자친구.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a female; the word marks the speaker as female
있다 'have'; 언니 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
한테 is the casual dative for close family
친 (親 'real') distinguishes her from a cousin or older female friend

examples.en: I have two older sisters.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 두 명 = two (people)

examples.en: My older sister often lends me clothes.
examples.note: 빌려주다 (빌리다 + 주다) = lend; the favor flows from her to me

examples.en: I go shopping with my older sister.
examples.note: 쇼핑을 하다 = to shop; 하고 같이 = 'together with'

entries.nuance: 언니 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older sister, and it extends warmly to any close older woman — an older female friend, a senior at school or work — and is also the friendly way younger women address a female shopkeeper or restaurant server ('언니, 여기요!'), so it ranges from blood sister to polite stranger. The chief English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나, never 언니, for an older sister; and don't be surprised to hear women call a saleswoman 언니 — it is friendly social lubricant, not a claim of kinship.

Thinking 언니 always means a relative — women also use 언니 to address an older female friend or even a shop assistant.

entries.shortExplanation: 동생 means "younger sibling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동생 (dongsaeng) = "younger sibling". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 동생 ("my younger sibling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동생, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: works for a younger brother OR sister, any speaker
있다 'have'; 동생 ends in a consonant so it takes 이
남 (男 'male') specifies the sex of the sibling
여 (女 'female') specifies the sex of the sibling

examples.en: I have one younger sibling.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 동생 doesn't reveal the sex on its own

examples.en: I often take care of my younger sibling.
examples.note: 돌보다 'look after' → 돌봐요; 동생 takes object 을 here

examples.en: My younger brother is tall.
examples.note: 키가 크다 = 'height is big' = tall; 남동생 makes the sex explicit

entries.nuance: 동생 (Sino-Korean 同生 'born of the same' parents) means a younger sibling and, unlike the older-sibling words, is NOT split by speaker gender and does NOT itself reveal whether the sibling is male or female — to specify you prepend 남 (男) for 남동생 'younger brother' or 여 (女) for 여동생 'younger sister'. entries.explanation: 남편 (nampyeon) means "husband". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 남편 ("my husband"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 남편 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is idiomatic even for one's own husband

usagePhrases.en: I have a husband / I'm married
usagePhrases.note: 있다 'have'; a common way to say one is married
하고 is the casual 'with'; 과 is the formal version
분 raises it to honor another person's husband

examples.en: My husband is an office worker.
examples.note: 이에요 'is' after a consonant; 회사원 = company employee

examples.en: I travel with my husband.
examples.note: 여행을 가다 = to go on a trip; 하고 같이 = 'together with'

entries.nuance: 남편 (Sino-Korean 男便, lit. 'male side') is the standard, neutral word for 'husband', used for your own husband and, in plain speech, anyone's. The decisive English-speaker pitfall is the boyfriend/husband line: 남편 means a legally married spouse only, so a girlfriend's partner is 남자친구, NOT 남편 — English casually says 'my man/my partner', but in Korean 남편 firmly implies marriage. usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is the natural possessive for one's own wife

usagePhrases.en: I have a wife / I'm married
usagePhrases.note: 있다 'have'; 아내 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
하고 casual 'with'; 과 is the bookish form
two nouns stacked; 의 is omitted naturally

Its near-synonyms divide cleanly: 와이프 (from English 'wife') is very common in casual male conversation but too informal for formal writing; 부인 (夫人) is the POLITE word for ANOTHER man's wife ('사장님 부인') and sounds odd for your own; and 집사람/안사람 are older, humble self-references ('the person of the house') now fading and faintly old-fashioned. A second trap is calling your own wife 부인; reserve 부인 for politely referring to someone else's wife.

entries.shortExplanation: 아이 means "child" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아이 (ai) = "child". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 아이 ("my child") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is idiomatic; can mean 'my kid'
있다 'have'; 아이 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
명 counts people; native number 두 + 명
키우다 'raise/bring up' takes the object 를

examples.en: I have one child.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 한 명 = one (person)

examples.en: My child goes to school.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination 학교 with the motion verb 가다

examples.en: I really love my child.
examples.note: 사랑하다 (verb) acts on 아이, which takes the object particle 를

entries.nuance: 아이 means 'child' in the broad sense — your own kid or any young person — and is routinely contracted to 애 in casual speech ('우리 애가…'), which is natural but a touch more colloquial. Pin down the age band against its neighbors: 아기 (or 애기) is a baby/infant who can't yet walk or talk; 아이/애 is a child roughly from toddler through pre-teen; 어린이 is the more formal, respectful 'child' used on signs and in institutions (어린이날 Children's Day, 어린이 보호구역 school zone); and 자녀 is the formal Sino-Korean word for one's offspring used on forms ('자녀가 몇 명이세요?'). So 아이 sits in the middle, neutral-casual. The main English-speaker pitfall is mixing 아이 with 아기: English 'kid/child/baby' overlap loosely, but calling a 10-year-old 아기 sounds like babying them, and calling a newborn 아이 understates how tiny they are — match the word to the age.

Confusing 아이 (child) with 아기 (baby) — 아기 is a pre-walking infant; a school-age kid is 아이, not 아기.
Using 아이 on a formal document or sign where 어린이/자녀 is expected ('아이 보호구역') — the public/formal word is 어린이 (어린이 보호구역).

entries.shortExplanation: 머리 means "head; also hair" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 머리 (meori) means "head; also hair". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리가 아파요 ("my head hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 머리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the single most common '머리' complaint; 가 marks the body part
하다 sense of 'hair'; say this at a salon, not 머리카락을 자르다
감다 is the dedicated verb for hair only, never 씻다
fixed idiom 'good head' = clever; opposite is 머리가 나쁘다

examples.en: My head hurts.
examples.note: survival sentence; learn 가 + 아프다 as one chunk

examples.en: My hair is long.
examples.note: here 머리 = hair; the adjective 길다 forces the 'hair' reading

examples.en: I got a haircut and dyed it at the salon too.
examples.note: real situation; 자르다 + 염색하다 are the salon collocations

entries.nuance: 머리 covers both the head and the hair on it, and only context (the verb or adjective) tells them apart: 머리가 아프다 = head hurts, but 머리가 길다 / 머리를 감다 = hair. The strict word for a single strand is 머리카락, yet in speech Koreans almost always shorten it to 머리, so 'cut my hair' is 머리를 자르다, not 머리카락을 자르다. The pitfall for English speakers is the washing verb: hair takes 감다 (머리를 감다), never the 씻다 you use for hands or face, so 머리를 씻다 sounds childish or wrong. Also note 머리가 좋다/나쁘다 is a fixed idiom for being smart/dim, not a comment on hair quality, and the body part is always marked with 가 (머리가 아파요), not 을.

Saying 머리를 씻다 for washing hair — hair uses the special verb 감다, so the natural form is 머리를 감다.
Saying 머리카락을 자르다 at a salon — it is technically correct but stiff; native speakers just say 머리를 자르다.
Using 머리를 아파요 — a body-part ache marks the part with 가, so it must be 머리가 아파요.

entries.shortExplanation: 눈 means "eye" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "eye" is 눈 (nun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 눈이 아파요 ("my eyes hurt"). Watch the particle attached to 눈 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: common complaint; 가 marks the body part
vision is 좋다/나쁘다, never 강하다/약하다
감다 here means 'close', distinct from washing hair
go-to compliment about appearance

examples.en: My eyes hurt.
examples.note: survival sentence; 눈 stays singular even for both eyes

examples.en: My older sister has really big eyes.
examples.note: appearance; 크다 describes facial features

examples.en: My eyesight is bad so I go around wearing glasses.
examples.note: real situation; 눈이 나쁘다 + 안경을 쓰다 collocate

entries.nuance: 눈 is the eye, but the identical spelling also means 'snow'; the two are split by pitch (eye = short/low, snow = long/high) and above all by context, so listeners rarely confuse them. Korean treats the pair of eyes as one uncountable 눈, so you never pluralize it. The big English-speaker trap is eyesight: vision is rated with 좋다 (good) and 나쁘다 (bad) — 눈이 좋아요 / 눈이 나빠요 — never with 'strong/weak' (강하다/약하다), which would sound bizarre. Note that 눈을 감다 uses the same 감다 as washing hair but means 'close', and the related verb 보다 ('see/look') is what the eye does, while 만나다 ('meet') is for people, so don't blend them.

Pluralizing as 눈들이 아파요 — the pair of eyes stays singular, so say 눈이 아파요.

entries.shortExplanation: 코 means "nose" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 코, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the standard cold symptom; 막히다 = be blocked
for snot use the compound 콧물 (코+물), not just 코
풀다 'release'; never 코를 불다 (that is whistling/blowing air)

usagePhrases.en: to have a high nose bridge
usagePhrases.note: appearance compliment; opposite 코가 낮다

examples.en: My nose is stuffy.
examples.note: survival sentence; learn 막히다 as the blocked-nose verb

examples.en: I keep having a runny nose because of a cold.
examples.note: everyday; 콧물 + 나다 is the runny-nose collocation

examples.en: Blowing your nose with a tissue is the polite thing to do.
examples.note: real situation; 코를 풀다 = blow nose

entries.nuance: 코 is the nose, but cold symptoms split into precise collocations English speakers must memorize: a blocked nose is 코가 막히다 (막히다 = be blocked) and a runny nose is 콧물이 나다, where 콧물 literally stitches 코(nose)+물(water) into 'nose-water' = snot. To blow your nose is 코를 풀다 (풀다 'to release/undo'); beware 코를 불다, which means to blow air out like a whistle and sounds absurd here. For looks, a tall nose bridge (admired in Korea) is 코가 높다, with 코가 낮다 as the flat-bridge opposite, paralleling how 키가 크다 works for height.

Saying 코를 불다 for blowing your nose — 불다 is blowing air out; the correct verb is 풀다, so 코를 풀다.

entries.shortExplanation: 입 means "mouth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 입 (ip) means "mouth". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 입을 벌리다 ("to open one's mouth wide"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 입 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 벌리다 = spread apart; what the dentist asks
fixed food idiom, not literal 'fits in mouth'
idiom 'short mouth'; eats little or fussily
다물다 = close lips; also 'be quiet'

examples.en: Open your mouth wide.
examples.note: survival sentence; 벌리다 is the open-mouth verb

examples.en: This kimchi stew really suits my taste.
examples.note: everyday; 입에 맞다 judges flavor, not size

examples.ko: 우리 아이는 입이 짧아서 골고루 안 먹어요.
examples.romanization: uri aineun ibi jjalbaseo golgoru an meogeoyo.
examples.en: My kid is a picky eater so doesn't eat a variety.
examples.note: real situation; 입이 짧다 = fussy eater

entries.nuance: 입 is the mouth, but its most useful expressions are idioms that won't survive word-for-word translation. 입에 맞다 means food 'suits your taste' (lit. 'fits the mouth') — it judges flavor, so 'this fits in my mouth' is a beginner mistranslation. 입이 짧다 ('short mouth') describes a picky or light eater, while 입이 무겁다 ('heavy mouth') means tight-lipped/discreet and 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth') means a blabbermouth — none are about physical size. To physically open the mouth is 입을 벌리다 (벌리다 = spread apart), as a dentist commands; do not use 열다 ('open' a door/box) for the mouth. Note also that 입 (mouth, the organ) is different from 말 (speech/words), so 'watch your mouth' as in language is 말조심하다, not anything with 입.

Saying 입을 열다 for opening your mouth at the dentist — 열다 is for doors/boxes; the body uses 입을 벌리다.
Reading 입이 무겁다 as a heavy/big mouth — it idiomatically means discreet and tight-lipped, the opposite of talkative.

entries.nuance: 귀 is the ear, and the key English-speaker pitfall is the verb of hearing. So 'I can't hear' is 귀가 안 들려요 with the passive 들리다 — using 못 듣다 implies you deliberately didn't listen, which is rude when talking about someone's deafness. entries.nuance: 손 is the hand, and the first thing to fix is the washing verb: hands take 씻다 (손을 씻다), in deliberate contrast to hair, which uses 감다 — mixing them (손을 감다) is a classic beginner slip. entries.nuance: 발 is specifically the foot — the part below the ankle — and Korean keeps it strictly separate from 다리 (the leg, the whole limb above), so pointing at your ankle and saying 다리 is wrong; that is the core mix-up for English speakers who blur 'leg/foot'. Useful collocations: 발을 다치다 (injure the foot, with 다치다 taking 을/를) and 발이 붓다 (the foot swells), where 붓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb that drops ㅅ before a vowel → 부어요, 부었어요, not 붓어요. Idiomatically 발이 넓다 ('wide foot') means well-connected with a broad social network, never literally big feet (for that you'd say 발이 크다). When you cause an injury yourself, prefer the active 다치다 (발을 다쳤어요) over a passive construction.

Conjugating 붓다 as 붓어요 — it is ㅅ-irregular, so the swelling form is 부어요 / 부었어요.

entries.nuance: 배 means the belly/stomach (the body region), and the same syllable also means 'pear' and 'boat/ship' — three homonyms split only by context. entries.nuance: 다리 is the leg — the whole limb from hip to ankle — and must be kept apart from 발 (the foot only); calling the foot 다리 is the classic English-speaker error since English loosely says 'leg'. For looks, 다리가 길다 (long legs) is a strong compliment, mirroring 키가 크다 for height. Note a leg ache is marked with 가 (다리가 아파요), while an action done to the leg takes 을/를 (다리를 다쳤어요).

entries.nuance: 감기 (感氣, 'feeling/affecting + air/energy') is the Sino-Korean word for a common cold, the everyday illness with cough, runny nose, and sore throat — distinct from the heavier 독감 (毒感, 'poison-cold' = influenza/the flu), which is a serious, feverish illness, so don't call the flu just 감기. The critical grammar point is the particle: you 'catch' a cold with 감기에 걸리다, using 에, because 걸리다 ('get caught by/hung on') takes a location-like target — 감기를 걸리다 with 을 is the number-one English-speaker error. Cold medicine is taken with 먹다 (감기약을 먹다, lit. 'eat medicine'), never 마시다 ('drink'), even for liquid syrup. The phrase 감기 조심하세요 ('be careful of cold') is a warm, very common parting line when the weather turns cold, much like 'stay warm / don't catch a cold.'

Describing a high fever as 열이 커요 — fever level uses 높다, so it is 열이 높아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 밥 means "cooked rice; a meal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 밥 (bap) means "cooked rice; a meal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 밥을 먹어요 ("I eat rice / I eat a meal"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 밥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I eat rice / I eat a meal
usagePhrases.note: object marker 을; the all-purpose word for having any meal
subject marker 이 spotlights the rice itself
drops the particle in casual speech; works as a friendly greeting
밥하다 = make rice/a meal, not 만들다

examples.en: I eat rice in the morning.
examples.note: simple daily routine with object 을

examples.en: If you're done eating, let's head out together.
examples.note: casual 반말; 밥 here = the whole meal, particle dropped

examples.ko: 식사 나오기 전에 밥부터 좀 주세요.
examples.romanization: siksa naogi jeone bapbuteo jom juseyo.
examples.en: Before the meal comes, could you give us some rice first?
examples.note: real restaurant line; 밥(rice) vs 식사(the meal) used side by side

entries.nuance: 밥 literally is the bowl of cooked white rice, but by extension it is the default word for 'a meal' — which is why 밥 먹었어요? functions as a real greeting like 'how are you?', not a literal question about rice. Contrast it with 식사(食事), the polite Sino-Korean word for 'a meal': you offer an elder 식사하셨어요?, never the blunt 밥 먹었어요?. The verb is 먹다(eat), and to cook rice you say 밥을 하다 or 밥을 짓다, not 밥을 만들다. The big English-speaker pitfall is hearing 밥 only as 'rice' and missing that 밥 먹자 means 'let's grab a bite', and that to a boss you must upgrade to 식사 to stay polite.

Saying 밥을 만들어요 for 'I make rice' — Korean fixes this verb as 밥을 해요 (or 밥을 지어요); 만들다 sounds like manufacturing.
Greeting an elder with 밥 먹었어요? — too blunt; use the honorific 식사하셨어요? instead.
Hearing 밥 only as 'rice' and so misreading 밥 먹자 — it actually means 'let's eat / let's grab a meal'.

entries.shortExplanation: 국 means "soup (clear/broth, eaten with rice)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "soup (clear/broth, eaten with rice)" is 국 (guk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국을 먹어요 ("I eat soup"). Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을; note 먹다, never 마시다 for a rice-side soup
subject marker 이 to warn about temperature
하고 = and; the two together are the base of a Korean meal
끓이다 = boil/cook soup, the set verb here

examples.ko: 한국 사람은 밥에 국을 같이 먹어요.
examples.romanization: hanguk sarameun babe gugeul gachi meogeoyo.
examples.en: Koreans eat soup together with rice.
examples.note: simple cultural habit; 국 paired with 밥

examples.ko: 국이 좀 식었는데 다시 데워 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: gugi jom sigeonneunde dasi dewo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: The soup has cooled a bit — shall I reheat it for you?
examples.note: everyday service line; 식다(cool down) vs 데우다(reheat)

examples.ko: 찌개 말고 그냥 맑은 국으로 주세요.
examples.romanization: jjigae malgo geunyang malgeun gugeuro juseyo.

examples.note: real ordering line that draws the 국 vs 찌개 line

entries.nuance: 국 is a light, broth-based soup with plenty of liquid that you spoon up alongside rice at nearly every meal. The near-synonym to separate it from is 찌개: a 찌개 (jjigae) is thicker, saltier, more concentrated and simmered right in a communal pot (된장찌개, 김치찌개), whereas 국 (미역국, 콩나물국) is milder and served in your own bowl. There is also 탕, a heartier long-boiled soup-stew (갈비탕). The set verb is 끓이다(boil/make), and Koreans 먹다(eat) soup with a spoon. The classic English-speaker mistake is reaching for 마시다(drink) because in English we 'drink' or 'have' soup — in Korean you 먹다 국, and calling a thick 찌개 a 국 will sound off to a native ear.

Using 마셔요 (drink) for soup — even broth is 먹어요 in Korean because you spoon it with rice.
Calling a thick simmered 찌개 a 국 — 국 is the thin, individually-served broth; 찌개 is the concentrated shared pot.
Saying 국을 만들어요 — the natural verb is 국을 끓여요 (to boil).

entries.shortExplanation: 김치 means "kimchi (fermented vegetable side dish)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 김치 (gimchi) = "kimchi (fermented vegetable side dish)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 김치를 먹어요 ("I eat kimchi") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가 to describe the taste

usagePhrases.en: please give a bit more kimchi
usagePhrases.note: 반찬 refills are free; 좀 softens the request
담그다 = ferment/pickle, the proper verb for kimchi

examples.en: I really like kimchi.
examples.note: simple preference statement

examples.ko: 이 김치가 잘 익어서 더 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: i gimchiga jal igeoseo deo masisseoyo.
examples.en: This kimchi is well fermented, so it's even tastier.
examples.note: everyday remark; 익다 = ripen/ferment, a key kimchi word

examples.en: Kimchi is a side dish, so you can get refills.
examples.note: real-situation note on the 반찬 (banchan) system

entries.nuance: 김치 is salted, seasoned, lactic-acid-fermented vegetable — most often napa cabbage (배추김치) but also radish (깍두기), cucumber, and more — eaten as a 반찬(side dish), never as the main. The word to contrast is 반찬, the umbrella term for all the little shared side dishes: 김치 is one specific 반찬. The native-feeling verb is 담그다(to put up / ferment), and as it ages people say it 익다(ripens). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 김치 like a single countable food and giving it a main-course slot; another is using 만들다 — Koreans say 김치를 담그다. Note too that fresh, just-made kimchi (겉절이) and well-aged sour kimchi (묵은지) are different enough to have their own names.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 김치 as a main dish — it is a 반찬 (side dish) that accompanies rice and is refilled for free.
Saying 김치를 만들어요 — the set verb is 김치를 담가요 (to ferment/put up).
Assuming all 김치 is cabbage — 깍두기 (radish) and 오이김치 (cucumber) are kimchi too; the word names the method, not one vegetable.

entries.shortExplanation: 고기 means "meat (esp. pork or beef)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고기 (gogi) means "meat (esp. pork or beef)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고기를 먹어요 ("I eat meat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가 to describe texture
-고 싶다 = want to; attaches to 먹다
굽다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 구워요; the verb for Korean BBQ

examples.en: I want to eat meat tonight.
examples.note: simple desire with -고 싶어요

examples.ko: 고기가 좀 질긴데 더 익혀 주세요.
examples.romanization: gogiga jom jilginde deo ikyeo juseyo.
examples.en: The meat is a bit tough — please cook it more.
examples.note: everyday line; 질기다(tough) vs 부드럽다(tender)

examples.ko: 우리 회식인데 소고기로 구울까, 돼지고기로 할까?
examples.romanization: uri hoesiginde sogogiro guulkka, dwaejigogiro halkka?
examples.en: It's our team dinner — shall we grill beef, or go with pork?
examples.note: real situation; 소고기 vs 돼지고기 specified for clarity

entries.nuance: In everyday speech 고기 by default means red land meat — usually 돼지고기(pork) or 소고기(beef) — so 고기 먹으러 가자 implies a BBQ, not seafood. To be specific you compound the animal onto 고기: 닭고기(chicken), 소고기(beef), 돼지고기(pork). The words to contrast are 생선(fish as food) and 해산물(seafood), which Koreans do NOT file under 고기; chicken sits on the edge, so people usually say 닭고기 rather than bare 고기 for it. The set cooking verb is 굽다, a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 구워요/구웠어요 (not 'gubeoyo'). The English-speaker pitfall is the English umbrella sense of 'meat' that includes fish and poultry — in Korean, unmarked 고기 leans strongly toward pork/beef, and you should name the animal when you mean otherwise.

Assuming bare 고기 covers fish or chicken — Koreans say 생선 for fish and usually 닭고기 for chicken; unmarked 고기 ≈ pork/beef.
Conjugating 굽다 as 'gubeoyo' regularly — it is ㅂ-irregular: 굽다 → 구워요, 구웠어요.
Using 고기 for seafood at a restaurant — order 회 (raw fish) or 해산물 (seafood); 고기 sets up the wrong dish.

entries.shortExplanation: 생선 means "fish (as food)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을
subject marker 이; 싱싱하다 = fresh (of produce/fish)
topic marker 은 sets fish up as the contrasted topic
굽다 → 구워요; grilled fish is a classic side dish

examples.en: I eat fish often.
examples.note: simple eating habit

examples.ko: 이 생선 진짜 싱싱한데 회로 드실래요?
examples.romanization: i saengseon jinjja singsinghande hoero deusillaeyo?
examples.en: This fish is really fresh — would you like it as sashimi?
examples.note: everyday market/restaurant line; 회 = raw sliced fish

examples.ko: 살아 있는 건 물고기, 접시에 오르면 생선이에요.
examples.romanization: sara inneun geon mulgogi, jeopsie oreumyeon saengseonieyo.
examples.en: While it's alive it's 물고기; once it's on the plate it's 생선.
examples.note: real-situation rule contrasting the two 'fish' words

entries.nuance: 생선 is 生鮮 — 生 'live/raw' + 鮮 'fresh' — literally 'fresh(-caught) thing', i.e. fish as FOOD, on the market stall or the dinner table. The essential contrast is 물고기, the live fish swimming in water (a pet goldfish, fish in a pond): same creature, but 물고기 is the animal and 생선 is the ingredient. Sliced raw for eating it becomes 회(sashimi), and dried fish is 건어물. 싱싱하다/신선하다(fresh) is its habitual partner adjective, and you 굽다(grill) or 조리다(braise) it. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'fish' covers both the live animal and the food, so learners say 물고기 when ordering at a restaurant — ask for 생선 (or the specific dish) instead, and never call the fish you're about to eat 물고기.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 물고기 when ordering fish to eat — 물고기 is the live animal; food fish is 생선.
Forgetting raw fish has its own word — sliced sashimi is 회, not 생선회 in casual ordering (e.g. 회 먹으러 가자).
Pairing 생선 with the wrong 'fresh' word — use 싱싱하다/신선하다, not 새롭다 (which means 'new', not 'fresh').

entries.shortExplanation: 야채 means "vegetables" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 야채 (yachae) = "vegetables". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 야채를 먹어요 ("I eat vegetables") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: object marker 를; no plural -s needed
subject marker 가; 신선하다 = fresh
도 = also/too; 좀 softens the request
다듬다 = clean and trim produce before cooking

examples.en: I eat a lot of vegetables.
examples.note: simple healthy habit; mass noun, no plural ending

examples.ko: 고기만 말고 야채도 같이 싸 드세요.
examples.romanization: gogiman malgo yachaedo gachi ssa deuseyo.
examples.en: Don't just eat meat — wrap some vegetables with it too.
examples.note: everyday BBQ line; 쌈 culture, 도 adds vegetables

examples.ko: 메뉴에 채소 이름으로 적혀 있는데, 야채랑 같은 말이에요.
examples.romanization: menyue chaeso ireumeuro jeokyeo inneunde, yachaerang gateun marieyo.
examples.en: On the menu it's written as 채소, but that's the same word as 야채.
examples.note: real-situation note on the 야채 vs 채소 register

entries.nuance: 야채 means 'vegetables' as an uncountable mass — you never add a plural ending, even for a whole pile. Its near-twin is 채소(菜蔬): the two overlap almost completely, but 채소 is the more 'proper', Sino-Korean and slightly bookish term you'll see on menus, packaging, and nutrition labels, while 야채 is the everyday, conversational word (the 野 in 야채 is 'field', 菜 'vegetable'). For raw leaves you eat fresh, there's also 쌈채소/상추류. Habitual partners are 신선하다(fresh) and the prep verb 다듬다(trim). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: adding a plural like 'vegetables' (야채들 sounds wrong here), and over-using 야채 in formal writing where 채소 reads better. When unsure in writing, 채소 is the safe, neutral choice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding a plural marker (야채들) because English says 'vegetables' — 야채 is a mass noun and stays unmarked.
Assuming 야채 and 채소 are different foods — they're the same; 채소 is just the more formal/written word.
Using 야채 on a formal menu or label — 채소 is the expected, neutral term there.

entries.shortExplanation: 과일 means "fruit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 과일 (gwail) means "fruit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 과일을 먹어요 ("I eat fruit"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 과일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을; mass noun, no plural
subject marker 이; 달다 = sweet (ㄹ-stem)
깎다 = peel with a knife, the set verb for apples/pears
박스/상자 counter; you count by container, not by 'fruits'

examples.en: I eat fruit every day.
examples.note: simple daily habit; 과일 stays singular

examples.en: Shall I peel some fruit for dessert?
examples.note: everyday home line; 깎다 + 후식 (dessert) collocation

examples.ko: 선물용으로 과일 한 상자 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: seonmuryongeuro gwail han sangja pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: Please pack a box of fruit as a gift.
examples.note: real-situation line; 과일 counted by 상자, gift culture

entries.nuance: 과일 is the mass category 'fruit'; like English 'fruit' used generally, it takes no plural ending, and when you mean specific items you name them (사과 apple, 배 pear, 딸기 strawberry) and count with 개 or by container (한 상자). Note 과일 is native-Korean-feeling and general; the parallel formal/technical term you'll meet on labels is 과실(果實) or in compounds 과(果). Its signature partner verb is 깎다(to peel) — Koreans peel apples and pears for guests — and its taste adjectives are 달다(sweet) and 시다(sour). The English-speaker pitfall is forcing a plural (과일들 for 'fruits' is unnatural as a generic) and using 자르다(cut) where 깎다(peel) is expected; another is treating 과일 as a dessert by default — in Korea cut fruit is itself the classic 후식.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pluralizing as 과일들 for generic 'fruits' — 과일 is a mass noun; keep it unmarked and name specific fruits when needed.
Saying 과일을 잘라요 for peeling an apple — the set verb is 깎다 (peel); 자르다 just means cut into pieces.
Counting fruit with the wrong unit — use 개 for pieces or 상자/박스 for boxes, not a plural of 과일.

Treating 과일 as a dessert by default fits Korea, where cut fruit is itself the classic 후식.
과일 is native-Korean-feeling and general; the parallel formal/technical term you'll meet on labels is 과실(果實) or in compounds 과(果).
Its signature partner verb is 깎다(to peel) — Koreans peel apples and pears for guests — and its taste adjectives are 달다(sweet) and 시다(sour).

entries.shortExplanation: 사과 means "apple" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "apple" is 사과 (sagwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사과를 먹어요 ("I eat an apple"). Watch the particle attached to 사과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가; 빨갛다 → 빨개요 (ㅎ-irregular)
깎다 = peel; apples are peeled before serving
개 counts items; numbers use native Korean 두

examples.en: I eat an apple every morning.
examples.note: simple daily habit; -마다 = every

examples.ko: 이 사과 좀 시지 않아요? 다른 거 주세요.
examples.romanization: i sagwa jom siji anayo? dareun geo juseyo.
examples.en: Isn't this apple a bit sour? Give me a different one.
examples.note: everyday market line; 시다 = sour

examples.ko: 사과 두 개 주세요. 빨간 걸로 골라 주세요.
examples.romanization: sagwa du gae juseyo. ppalgan geollo golla juseyo.
examples.en: Two apples, please. Pick the red ones for me.
examples.note: natural market line; 빨갛다 = red, 고르다 = to pick

entries.nuance: 사과 the fruit is 沙果/砂果 ('sand fruit'), while the homophone 사과 'apology' is a different hanja, 謝過 ('thank/decline' + 'fault') — identical sound and spelling, separated only by context. At a fruit stall or table it unambiguously means the apple; with verbs like 하다/받다/드리다 (사과를 하다 'to apologize') it means the apology. As fruit its partners are 깎다(peel), 빨갛다(red, ㅎ-irregular → 빨개요), and tastes 달다/시다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the apple/apology mix-up, is the color verb: 빨갛다 is irregular, so 'the apple is red' is 사과가 빨개요, not 빨갛아요. Counting also trips learners — it's 사과 한 개/두 개 with native numbers, not Sino-Korean 일·이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 사과 the fruit with 사과 = apology — context and the verb decide; 사과하다 = apologize, never 'to apple'.
Saying 사과가 빨갛아요 — 빨갛다 is ㅎ-irregular, so it becomes 사과가 빨개요.
Counting with Sino-Korean numbers (사과 이 개) — use native numbers with 개: 사과 두 개.

entries.shortExplanation: 빵 means "bread (and baked goods generally)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 빵 (ppang) = "bread (and baked goods generally)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 빵을 먹어요 ("I eat bread") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빵, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을
subject marker 이; 부드럽다 → 부드러워요 (ㅂ-irregular)

usagePhrases.en: I buy it at the bakery
usagePhrases.note: 빵집 = 'bread house' = bakery; 에서 marks the place of the action
굽다 → 구워요; same verb as grilling/baking

examples.en: I eat bread in the morning.
examples.note: simple breakfast habit

examples.en: It's freshly baked bread, so it's still warm.
examples.note: everyday bakery line; 갓 구운 = freshly baked

examples.ko: 케이크도 빵집에서 파니까 빵 사러 갈 때 같이 보자.
examples.romanization: keikeudo ppangjibeseo panikka ppang sareo gal ttae gachi boja.
examples.en: They sell cake at the bakery too, so let's look when we go to buy bread.
examples.note: real-situation note that 빵/빵집 covers cakes and pastries

entries.nuance: 빵 is a broad word covering essentially all baked, leavened wheat goods — loaves, rolls, pastries, even cake-ish items — not just sliced sandwich bread; that's why a bakery is 빵집, literally 'bread house', and a pastry-loving person is a 빵순이/빵돌이. The word itself isn't Sino-Korean; it came via Portuguese pão through Japanese, which is why it's written in the native-feeling single syllable 빵. The contrast to keep straight is 케이크(cake) and 과자(cookies/snacks/crackers): 과자 is dry, crunchy snack food, NOT 빵. Habitual partners: 굽다(bake), 부드럽다(soft, ㅂ-irregular → 부드러워요), 바삭하다(crispy crust). The English-speaker pitfall is narrowing 빵 to 'loaf bread' and so being surprised that a croissant or 단팥빵 (red-bean bun) is also 빵 — and that you 'eat' (먹다) bread, never 'drink' it even when it's soft.

Limiting 빵 to sliced loaf bread — it covers buns, pastries, and most baked goods; a 단팥빵 (sweet-bean bun) is still 빵.
Calling cookies or crackers 빵 — dry, crunchy snacks are 과자, a separate category.
Conjugating 부드럽다 regularly as 부드럽어요 — it's ㅂ-irregular: 부드러워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 우유 means "milk (cow's milk)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 우유 (uyu) means "milk (cow's milk)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우유를 마셔요 ("I drink milk"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 우유 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 마시다 = drink, the correct verb for any liquid
subject marker 가; 차갑다 → 차가워요 (ㅂ-irregular)
topic marker 는 marks milk as the contrasted topic
잔 counts glasses/cups of a drink

examples.en: I drink milk every day.
examples.note: simple daily habit; 마시다, not 먹다

examples.en: The milk smells a little off — it might have gone bad.
examples.note: everyday line; 상하다 = go bad/spoil

examples.ko: 커피에 넣게 우유 좀 데워 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: keopie neoke uyu jom dewo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you warm up some milk to put in the coffee?
examples.note: real-situation café request; 데우다 = warm up

entries.nuance: 우유 is 牛乳 — 牛 'cow' + 乳 'milk' — so it specifically means cow's milk; for other kinds you compound, e.g. 두유(豆乳, soy milk) or 분유(粉乳, powdered/baby formula). As a liquid it strictly takes 마시다(drink), not 먹다 — though, importantly, casual Korean does allow 먹다 for consuming food/drink generally (밥을 먹다, 약을 먹다), so you will hear 우유 먹어 to a child; still, the clean textbook verb is 마시다. The near-contrast is 요구르트(yogurt) and 치즈(cheese), which are 유제품(dairy) but not 우유. Habitual partners: 차갑다/시원하다(cold), 데우다(warm up), 상하다(spoil). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 먹다 from 'have milk', and forgetting the counter — milk is counted in 잔(glass) or 팩/병(carton/bottle), never with 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 먹어요 as the default for 우유 — the textbook verb is 마셔요 (drink); 먹다 is only loose/casual.
Counting milk with 개 — use 잔 (a glass), 팩 (a carton), or 병 (a bottle).
Assuming 우유 covers all milk — it's cow's milk; soy milk is 두유 and powdered/formula milk is 분유.

entries.shortExplanation: 식당 means "restaurant; eatery; cafeteria" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "restaurant; eatery; cafeteria" is 식당 (sikdang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식당에서 먹어요 ("I eat at the restaurant"). Watch the particle attached to 식당 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place where an action happens
에 marks the destination of movement
subject marker 이; 깔끔하다 = neat, clean
단골 = a place one frequents

examples.en: Let's eat lunch at this restaurant.
examples.note: simple line contrasting place-of-action 에서

examples.en: I'll go to that restaurant and grab a table first.
examples.note: everyday line; movement 에 then 가서

examples.ko: 회사 구내식당이 싸고 빨라서 점심은 거기서 해결해요.
examples.romanization: hoesa gunaesikdangi ssago ppallaseo jeomsimeun geogiseo haegyeolhaeyo.
examples.en: The company cafeteria is cheap and fast, so I handle lunch there.
examples.note: real-situation use; 구내식당 = staff cafeteria

entries.nuance: 식당 is 食堂 — 食 'eat' + 堂 'hall' — an 'eating hall', i.e. an ordinary, everyday place to have a meal: a neighborhood eatery, a noodle shop, or a 구내식당(cafeteria). The register contrast is 레스토랑, the loanword reserved for fancier, often Western, sit-down dining; you'd call a humble 백반집 a 식당, never a 레스토랑, and a candlelit Italian place a 레스토랑, not a plain 식당. The crucial grammar point is particle choice: use 에서 for an action done there (식당에서 먹어요 'eat AT the restaurant') but 에 for it as a destination (식당에 가요 'go TO the restaurant'). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 에/에서 split, since English 'at/to' don't map one-to-one; another is reaching for 레스토랑 as the default word for any restaurant when 식당 is the everyday term.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 에 instead of 에서 for an action — 식당에서 먹어요 (eat AT), but 식당에 가요 (go TO); the verb decides the particle.
Defaulting to 레스토랑 for any restaurant — everyday eateries are 식당; 레스토랑 implies an upscale/Western place.
Saying 식당으로 먹어요 — 으로 marks means/direction, not the location of an action; the location particle is 에서.

entries.shortExplanation: 메뉴 means "menu; a menu item / dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 메뉴 (menyu) = "menu; a menu item / dish". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 메뉴를 봐요 ("I look at the menu") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 메뉴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 = look at; 봐요 in 요-form
메뉴판 = the physical menu card; 주세요 polite request

usagePhrases.en: there are many menu items / choices
usagePhrases.note: subject marker 가; here 메뉴 = the dishes available
메뉴 = a specific offered dish, not the list

examples.en: Please show me the menu.
examples.note: simple polite request at a restaurant

examples.ko: 여기 제일 잘 나가는 메뉴가 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: yeogi jeil jal naganeun menyuga mwoyeyo?
examples.en: What's the most popular dish here?
examples.note: everyday ordering line; 메뉴 = a dish, 잘 나가다 = sell well

examples.ko: 메뉴 정하기 전에 메뉴판부터 다시 볼까요?
examples.romanization: menyu jeonghagi jeone menyupanbuteo dasi bolkkayo?
examples.en: Before we decide on a dish, shall we look at the menu card again?
examples.note: real-situation line using both senses: dish vs physical menu

entries.nuance: 메뉴 (loanword from 'menu') carries two senses Koreans switch between freely: (1) the printed list of offerings, and (2) an individual dish/order — so 무슨 메뉴 먹을까? means 'which dish shall we get?', and 메뉴 정했어? means 'have you decided what to order?'. When you specifically mean the physical card you hand over, Koreans often say 메뉴판 (menu-board) to disambiguate. The dish sense overlaps with 음식(food in general) and 요리(a cooked dish), but 메뉴 frames it as a selectable option on offer. Common partners: 메뉴를 정하다/고르다(decide/choose a dish), 메뉴가 다양하다(varied), 오늘의 메뉴(today's special). The English-speaker pitfall is locking 메뉴 to the printed-list meaning only, then being confused by 이 집은 메뉴가 맛있어요 — which praises the dishes, not the paper.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 메뉴 only means the printed list — it also means an individual dish, e.g. 이 메뉴 맛있어요 = 'this dish is tasty'.
Asking for the physical card as just 메뉴 when clarity matters — say 메뉴판 (the menu board/card).
Pairing 메뉴 with 마시다/읽다 oddly — you 보다 (look at) a menu and 정하다/고르다 (decide/choose) a dish.
