entries.shortExplanation: 빠르다 means "fast; quick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "fast; quick" is 빠르다 (ppareuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빨라요 ("it is fast"). Watch the particle attached to 빠르다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 르-irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ before 아요 (빠르 → 빨ㄹ + 아요)
modifier is regular: stem + ㄴ (빠르 → 빠른)
subject marked with 이/가
빠르 + 게 → adverb 'quickly', common with motion verbs

examples.en: This train is really fast.
examples.note: 르-irregular in action: 빠르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ → 빨라요, never 빠르어요.

examples.en: I was glad to get a quick reply.
examples.note: The modifier 빠른 is regular (빠르 + ㄴ) and sits before 답장.

examples.en: Please come just a little faster.
examples.note: The set adverb 빨리 ('quickly') is the form you'll hear most in daily speech.

The crucial synonym contrast is 이르다 ('early in time'): 빠르다 is about SPEED (how fast something moves), while 이르다 is about TIMING (how early on the clock/calendar) — '버스가 빨라요' means the bus is fast, but '아직 일러요' means 'it's still early'. entries.shortExplanation: 높다 means "high; tall" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 높다 (nopda) = "high; tall". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 높아요 ("it is high") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 높다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: last stem vowel ㅗ → 아요 by vowel harmony (높 → 높아요)
regular modifier: stem + 은 (높 → 높은)
subject marked with 이/가
높 + 게 → adverb 'high(ly)' with an action verb

examples.en: That mountain is very high.
examples.note: 요-form 높아요; the stem vowel ㅗ selects 아요, and the ㅍ links to give a '노파요' sound.

examples.en: I saw a tall building for the first time.
examples.note: The regular modifier 높은 (stem + 은) precedes 빌딩.

examples.en: The price was too high, so I didn't buy it.
examples.note: 높아서 marks the reason; note 가격이 높다 is the natural pairing for 'price is high'.

entries.nuance: 높다 means high or tall and also 'high in level' for abstractions — mountains and buildings (산이 높다, 빌딩이 높다), but also 가격이 높다 (price is high), 온도가 높다 (temperature is high), 소리가 높다 (pitch is high), and 가능성이 높다 (the likelihood is high). Conjugation is regular: vowel ㅗ takes 아요 (높아요), modifier is 높은. The key synonym boundary is with 크다 ('big/large') for people: a person's height is described with 키가 크다 (literally 'stature is big'), NOT 키가 높다 — 높다 is for objects rising from a base (a tower, a shelf), while a human's tallness is 키가 크다. Its opposites split too: 높다 ↔ 낮다 (low), but 크다 ↔ 작다 (small). It collocates with 산·건물·가격·온도·소리·확률·수준. English-speaker pitfall: 'a tall person' becomes 높은 사람 by direct translation, which sounds like 'a high-ranking/lofty person', not 'a tall one' — say 키가 큰 사람; reserve 높다 for things that stand high off the ground.

Using 높다 for a tall person (그 사람은 키가 높아요) — human height is 키가 크다: 키가 커요. 높다 is for objects rising from the ground.

entries.shortExplanation: 멀다 means "far" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 멀다 (meolda) means "far". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 멀어요 ("it is far"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 멀다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: stem 멀 + 어요 (the ㄹ stays before a vowel)
ㄹ-irregular: final ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ (멀 → 먼)
subject marked with 이/가
멀 → the set adverb 멀리 'far (away)', used with motion verbs

examples.en: My home is far from work.
examples.note: 요-form 멀어요; the reference point takes 에서 ('from'), as in 회사에서 멀다.

examples.en: I'm traveling to a faraway country.
examples.note: The modifier drops ㄹ before ㄴ → 먼 (not 멀은) before 나라.

examples.en: The station is far, so I take the bus.
examples.note: 멀어서 gives the reason 'because it's far'.

entries.nuance: 멀다 means far in distance (집이 멀다, 먼 길) and figuratively 'distant' in relationship or likelihood (사이가 멀어지다 = to grow apart; 거리가 멀다). It is the opposite of 가깝다 (near). Conjugation is ㄹ-irregular: the ㄹ stays before vowel endings (멀어요) but drops before the modifier ㄴ, so 'a far place' is 먼 곳, never 멀은 곳 — the same pattern as 길다→긴, 달다→단. The natural way to say the distance is FROM somewhere is with 에서: 여기에서 멀어요 ('it's far from here'). Note the set adverb is the irregular 멀리 ('far away', 멀리 가다), not 멀게. A subtle synonym point: for 'a remote/secluded place' Korean often prefers 외지다 or 외딴, while 멀다 is plain physical distance. It collocates with 집·학교·역·길·나라·거리·미래. Saying 멀은 곳 instead of 먼 곳 — 멀다 is ㄹ-irregular, so the ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ: 멀 → 먼.
Marking the reference point with 에 (회사에 멀어요) — 'far FROM X' uses 에서: 회사에서 멀어요.
Using 멀게 for 'far away' as an adverb — the idiomatic adverb is the irregular 멀리: 멀리 가다 (멀게 is grammatical but not what natives say for distance).

entries.shortExplanation: 가깝다 means "close; near" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "close; near" is 가깝다 (gakkapda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가까워요 ("it is close"). Watch the particle attached to 가깝다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가까워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가깝 → 가까운)
subject marked with 이/가
the set adverb 가까이 'near/close', used with motion verbs

examples.en: The subway station is close.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular in action: 가깝 + 어요 → ㅂ turns to 우 → 가까워요, not 가깝아요.

examples.en: I met a close friend after a long time.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가까운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 친구; note 가까운 친구 = a close (intimate) friend.

examples.en: Work is close, so I commute on foot.
examples.note: 가까워서 gives the reason 'because it's close'.

entries.nuance: 가깝다 means close or near in distance (집이 가깝다), and just as commonly 'close' in human relationships (가까운 사이 = an intimate relationship) and 'nearly equal' (백 명에 가깝다 = close to 100). It is the opposite of 멀다 (far). Its conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: the final ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel ending, so 가깝 + 어요 → 가까워요 and the modifier is 가까운 (never 가깝아요 or 가깝은) — the same shift as 무겁다→무거워, 어렵다→어려워. A useful synonym boundary: 가깝다 is the adjective ('is near'), while the place noun 근처 means 'the vicinity/nearby area' (역 근처에 = near the station) and the adverb 가까이 means 'closely/up near' (가까이 오세요) — they aren't interchangeable parts of speech. It collocates with 집·역·거리·사이·친구 and with the distance reference in 에서 (여기에서 가까워요). English-speaker pitfalls: writing 가깝아요 (ignoring the ㅂ-irregular), and confusing the adjective 가깝다 with the noun 근처 — 'there's a store nearby' is best as 근처에 가게가 있어요, not 가깝다 alone.

Using the adjective 가깝다 where a place noun is needed (가깝에 있어요) — for 'in the nearby area' use 근처: 근처에 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 깨끗하다 means "clean" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 깨끗하다 (kkaekkeutada) = "clean". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 깨끗해요 ("it is clean") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 깨끗하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다-verb: 하 + 여요 contracts to 해요 → 깨끗해요
하다-modifier: 하 + ㄴ → 한 (깨끗하 → 깨끗한)
subject marked with 이/가
깨끗하 + 게 → adverb 'cleanly/spotlessly' with an action verb

examples.en: This bathroom is clean.
examples.note: 하다-pattern: 깨끗하 + 여요 contracts to 깨끗해요 (the standard 해요-form).

examples.en: I drink clean water.
examples.note: The 하다-modifier 깨끗한 (하 + ㄴ) precedes 물.

examples.en: I tidied the room cleanly.
examples.note: The set adverb 깨끗이 (note spelling: -이, sounds '깨끄시') is the idiomatic 'cleanly/thoroughly'.

entries.nuance: 깨끗하다 means clean — free of dirt (깨끗한 방), but also 'pure/clear' for water and air (깨끗한 물·공기), 'fair/honest' for conduct (깨끗한 정치 = clean politics), and 'fully/completely' as the adverb 깨끗이 (깨끗이 잊다 = to forget completely). Being a 하다-adjective, it conjugates with the 해요-pattern: the 하 fuses with 여 to give 깨끗해요, and the modifier is 깨끗한 — there is no irregular drop here, just the regular 하다 contraction. Watch the synonym line with 맑다: 맑다 is 'clear/limpid' for water, sky, eyes, or sound (하늘이 맑다 = the sky is clear; 물이 맑다 = the water is transparent), whereas 깨끗하다 is 'free of dirt/impurity' (물이 깨끗하다 = the water is clean/sanitary). So a mountain stream can be both 맑다 (see-through) and 깨끗하다 (unpolluted), but a tidy desk is only 깨끗하다, never 맑다. It collocates with 방·옷·물·공기·손·거리. English-speaker pitfall: writing 깨끗하요 (forgetting the 하 → 해 contraction) and spelling the adverb 깨끗히 instead of the correct 깨끗이.

Saying 깨끗하요 instead of 깨끗해요 — 하다-adjectives contract 하 + 여요 into 해요: 깨끗하 → 깨끗해요.
Using 맑다 for a tidy, dust-free room (방이 맑아요) — that is 깨끗하다 (방이 깨끗해요); 맑다 is for see-through clarity of water, sky, or sound.

entries.shortExplanation: 무겁다 means "heavy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무겁다 (mugeopda) means "heavy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무거워요 ("it is heavy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무겁다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 무거워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (무겁 → 무거운)
subject marked with 이/가
무겁 + 게 → adverb 'heavily', also for atmosphere/mood

examples.en: This bag is too heavy.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 무겁 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 무거워요, never 무겁어요.

examples.en: I moved a heavy box by myself.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 무거운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 상자.

examples.en: My eyelids are heavy, so I'm sleepy.
examples.note: 무거워서 gives the reason; 눈꺼풀이 무겁다 is the idiomatic 'eyelids feel heavy (sleepy)'.

entries.nuance: 무겁다 means heavy in weight (무거운 가방, 짐이 무겁다), and metaphorically 'weighty/grave' for moods, responsibilities, and the body when tired — 분위기가 무겁다 (the atmosphere is heavy/tense), 책임이 무겁다 (the responsibility is heavy), 몸이 무겁다 (one's body feels sluggish), 입이 무겁다 (literally 'heavy-mouthed' = tight-lipped, can keep a secret). It is the opposite of 가볍다 (light). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel ending, giving 무거워요 and the modifier 무거운 — the same shift as 가깝다→가까워, 춥다→추워. Be careful with 무겁다 vs 어렵다: both can render English 'heavy' figuratively, but 무겁다 is 'weighty/somber', whereas 어렵다 is 'difficult' — a heavy (hard) exam is 어려운 시험, not 무거운 시험. It collocates with 가방·짐·몸·분위기·책임·마음. English-speaker pitfall: producing 무겁어요 instead of 무거워요, and over-extending 무겁다 to mean 'difficult' where 어렵다 is needed.

Saying 무겁어요 instead of 무거워요 — 무겁다 is ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ becomes 우 before the ending (무겁 + 어요 → 무거워요).
Using 무겁다 for a hard/difficult task (시험이 무거워요) — 'difficult' is 어렵다: 시험이 어려워요. 무겁다 is weight or somber mood, not difficulty.

entries.shortExplanation: 가볍다 means "light (in weight)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "light (in weight)" is 가볍다 (gabyeopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가벼워요 ("it is light"). Watch the particle attached to 가볍다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가벼워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가볍 → 가벼운)
subject marked with 이/가
가볍 + 게 → adverb 'lightly/casually'

examples.en: This laptop is really light.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 가볍 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.

examples.en: I bought one light bag.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가벼운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 가방.

examples.en: Today my heart feels much lighter.
examples.note: 마음이 가볍다 = to feel relieved/unburdened — a common figurative use.

entries.nuance: 가볍다 means light in weight (가벼운 가방), and figuratively 'light' in many senses: 마음이 가볍다 (heart is light/relieved), 가벼운 감기 (a mild cold), 가벼운 농담 (a light joke), 가볍게 운동하다 (to exercise lightly), and even negatively 입이 가볍다 ('light-mouthed' = can't keep a secret, the exact opposite of 입이 무겁다). It is the opposite of 무겁다 (heavy). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel ending, so 가벼워요 and the modifier 가벼운 — the same pattern as 무겁다→무거워, 춥다→추워. entries.shortExplanation: 새롭다 means "new" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 새롭다 (saeropda) = "new". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 새로워요 ("it is new/fresh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 새롭다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 새로워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (새롭 → 새로운)
subject marked with 이/가
새롭 + 게 → adverb 'newly/afresh'

examples.en: This restaurant is new.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 새롭 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 새로워요, not 새롭어요.

examples.en: I bought a new phone.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 새로운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 휴대폰 — the everyday way to say 'a new ~'.

examples.en: Seeing it again, that scenery feels fresh.
examples.note: Here 새롭다 means 'feels new/striking again', the emotional 'fresh' sense, not 'newly made'.

entries.nuance: 새롭다 means new in the sense of 'fresh, novel, renewed' — a new method, a fresh feeling, a renewed resolve (새로운 방법, 마음이 새롭다, 각오가 새롭다). Crucially it differs from the determiner 새 ('brand-new', placed directly before a noun): 새 (no conjugation) labels a physically new object — 새 차 (a brand-new car), 새 옷 (new clothes) — while 새롭다 is a full adjective expressing that something is novel or feels fresh, so '새 차' is a car just bought, but '느낌이 새로워요' means 'the feeling is fresh/novel'. Both translate as 'new', but you cannot say 새로운 차 to mean a factory-fresh car the way 새 차 does (새로운 차 leans 'a different/novel kind of car'). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, giving 새로워요 and the modifier 새로운 — the same shift as 가깝다→가까워, 무겁다→무거워. It collocates with 방법·기술·세상·마음·각오·디자인. Forgetting the modifier also takes the ㅂ-irregular and writing 새롭은 — it must be 새로운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ).

entries.shortExplanation: 의사 means "doctor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 의사 (uisa) means "doctor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 의사 선생님 ("doctor (polite address)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 의사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: add 선생님 when speaking to or about a doctor respectfully
받다 'receive' is the verb that pairs with 진료, not 하다
goal/result takes 가/이, never 을/를
에서 marks the place where an action happens

examples.en: I am a doctor.
examples.note: plain self-introduction; 예요 attaches after the vowel-final 의사

examples.en: If you catch a cold, you go to the doctor.
examples.note: 한테 = casual 'to (a person)'; note 감기에 걸리다 'be caught by a cold'

examples.ko: 할머니께서는 마을에서 오래 환자를 보신 의사세요.
examples.romanization: halmeonikkeseoneun maeureseo orae hwanjareul bosin uisaseyo.
examples.en: Grandmother is a doctor who long looked after patients in the village.
examples.note: 환자를 보다 'see patients' is the idiom for a doctor practicing

entries.nuance: 의사 is Sino-Korean 醫師 ('medicine' 醫 + 'master/teacher' 師), so the word literally frames a doctor as a master of medicine — which is why Koreans almost reflexively append 선생님 (의사 선생님) when addressing or referring to one, the way English keeps 'Doctor' as a title. Saying bare 의사 to or about a specific physician can sound flat or even slightly disrespectful, like calling them 'the doc'. Distinguish 의사 (the licensed physician) from 의자 'chair', which differs by a single vowel and trips up beginners constantly, and from 환자 'patient' and 간호사 'nurse', the other people in the room. The natural verb is 환자를 보다 ('see patients') or 진료를 보다/받다, never the English-style '의사를 하다'; a doctor 의사가 되다 ('becomes' a doctor), with the goal marked by 가, not 을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의사님 by analogy with other -님 titles; Koreans actually say 의사 선생님, treating 선생님 itself as the honorific.
Writing 의사를 되고 싶어요 with 를; the thing you become takes 가/이, so it must be 의사가 되고 싶어요.
Confusing 의사 'doctor' with the near-identical 의자 'chair' — one wrong vowel changes the whole sentence.

entries.shortExplanation: 간호사 means "nurse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "nurse" is 간호사 (ganhosa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 간호사 선생님 ("nurse (polite address)"). Watch the particle attached to 간호사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: like doctors, nurses are addressed with 선생님 in clinics
the fixed verb is 놓다 'place', not 주다 'give'
resultative goal marked with 가
에서 = location of the work activity

examples.en: I am a nurse.
examples.note: 예요 follows the vowel ending of 간호사

examples.en: The nurse kindly showed me the way.
examples.note: -아/어 주시다 adds the favor-plus-respect nuance

examples.en: My older sister is a nurse who works all night in the ER.
examples.note: 응급실 'emergency room'; 밤새 'all through the night'

entries.nuance: 간호사 is 看護師 ('watch over' 看 + 'protect' 護 + 'master' 師) — the picture is someone who watches over and protects the sick, a warmer image than the English 'nurse'. The crucial register point is that today 간호사 is fully gender-neutral and is the only respectful current term; the older 간호원 (with 員 'staff member') now sounds dated and faintly demeaning, much like 'stewardess' in English, so avoid it. Don't confuse 간호사 with 간병인, the paid caregiver who attends a patient's daily needs (eating, washing) but holds no nursing license. Beginners also overuse 주다 for injections — the locked collocation is 주사를 놓다 ('place a shot'), and you 'receive' one with 주사를 맞다, literally 'get hit by a shot'. As with all jobs ending in a vowel, the copula is 예요 (간호사예요), and one 간호사가 된다, not 를 된다.

Using the outdated, gendered-sounding 간호원 instead of the current neutral 간호사.
Saying 주사를 주다 'give a shot' by translating English; the set phrase is 주사를 놓다, and the patient side is 주사를 맞다.
Mixing up 간호사 (licensed nurse) with 간병인 (unlicensed bedside caregiver).

entries.shortExplanation: 경찰 means "police officer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 경찰 (gyeongchal) = "police officer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 경찰을 부르다 ("call the police") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 경찰, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 'summon' uses 부르다, the same verb as calling a person over
신고하다 takes 에 for the institution you report to
에 marks the destination 경찰서
에게 marks the human you direct a question to

examples.en: The police came.
examples.note: 이 after the consonant ending of 경찰

examples.en: If you get lost, ask a police officer.
examples.note: 한테 = colloquial 'to (a person)'; -(으)면 'if'

examples.ko: 사고가 나서 경찰관 두 명이 현장에 출동했어요.
examples.romanization: sagoga naseo gyeongchalgwan du myeongi hyeonjange chuldonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: Because there was an accident, two officers were dispatched to the scene.
examples.note: -아/어서 'because'; 출동하다 'be dispatched' is the news-register word

entries.nuance: 경찰 is 警察 ('warn/be alert' 警 + 'inspect/observe' 察) — literally 'to watch alertly', capturing policing as vigilant observation. The word is flexible: by context it can mean the police force as an institution ('경찰이 수사 중이다', the police are investigating) or a single officer on the street, so to single out one human being unambiguously Koreans prefer 경찰관 (官 'official'). Keep three look-alikes apart: 경찰 (police/officer), 경찰서 (the station building), and 경찰관 (one officer); beginners often say 'I went to the 경찰' when they mean 경찰서. Note the particle split — you 신고하다 (report) 경찰에 (to the institution), but you 물어보다 (ask) 경찰에게/한테 (to a person). Because 경찰 ends in a consonant, the copula is 이에요 (경찰이에요), not 예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 경찰 with 경찰서; 경찰서에 가요 means going to the station, while 경찰이 와요 means an officer is coming.
Saying 경찰예요 after a consonant; it must be 경찰이에요.
Using 경찰에게 신고하다 for reporting a crime; the institution-level idiom is 경찰에 신고하다 (에, not 에게).

entries.shortExplanation: 요리사 means "cook" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 요리사 (yorisa) means "cook". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 요리를 하다 ("cook / do the cooking"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요리사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the activity is 요리를 하다; the person is 요리사
에서 marks the workplace where cooking happens
goal of becoming marked with 가
만들다 'make' is the everyday verb for preparing dishes

examples.en: I am a cook.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 요리사

examples.en: The kimchi stew the cook made is really delicious.
examples.note: 만든 = past modifier of 만들다 describing the food

examples.ko: 제 꿈은 호텔에서 일하는 셰프가 되는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je kkumeun hotereseo ilhaneun syepeuga doeneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My dream is to become a chef working at a hotel.
examples.note: -는 거예요 nominalizes the goal; note 셰프 for a high-end chef

entries.nuance: 요리사 is 料理師 ('prepare/measure ingredients' 料 + 'arrange/manage' 理 + 'master' 師), so it frames cooking as the skilled craft of arranging ingredients. It refers to a professional who cooks for a living; the loanword 셰프 (chef) carries more prestige and a Western fine-dining flavor, while a traditional master cook may be called 조리사 (the term used on official culinary licenses) — overlapping but 조리사 sounds more institutional/cafeteria, 요리사 more general, 셰프 more upscale. The classic beginner slip is confusing the person 요리사 with the activity/dish 요리: '요리가 맛있어요' praises the food, '요리사가 친절해요' describes the person. Remember the activity is 요리를 하다 (do cooking), never '요리사를 하다'. Since the word ends in a vowel, it is 요리사예요, and one 요리사가 된다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 요리사 (the cook) with 요리 (the cooking/dish): 요리를 하다 'to cook' vs 요리사가 되다 'to become a cook'.
Saying 요리사를 하다 for 'to cook'; the verb attaches to the activity 요리, so it is 요리를 하다.
Assuming 셰프 and 요리사 are identical; 셰프 specifically implies a Western-style or head chef, often at a hotel or fine restaurant.

entries.shortExplanation: 가수 means "singer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "singer" is 가수 (gasu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 노래를 부르다 ("sing a song"). Watch the particle attached to 가수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the verb for singing is 부르다, the same as 'to call'
object of liking takes 를
resultative goal marked with 가
서다 'stand'; 에 marks where one stands

examples.en: I am a singer.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel of 가수

examples.en: I really like that singer.
examples.note: 를 marks 가수 as the object of 좋아하다

examples.ko: 동생은 데뷔를 준비하는 연습생이라 아직 가수는 아니에요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengeun debwireul junbihaneun yeonseupsaengira ajik gasuneun anieyo.
examples.en: My sibling is a trainee preparing to debut, so not yet a singer.
examples.note: 연습생 'trainee'; -(이)라 'being, since'; 데뷔 'debut'

entries.nuance: 가수 is 歌手 ('song' 歌 + 'hand/skilled person' 手), a Sino-Korean pattern where 手 turns an art into the person who does it (compare 선수 'player', 가수 'singer'). It means a professional or recognized singer who performs for an audience; merely singing in the shower is 노래하다 or 노래를 부르다, and you would never call yourself a 가수 for that — claiming it implies you do it as a career, so Koreans distinguish a 가수 from a 연습생 (idol trainee not yet debuted) or someone who just '노래를 잘해요'. Note that the act of singing uses 부르다 ('노래를 부르다'), the very same verb as calling someone, which surprises learners. The object you like takes 를 (가수를 좋아해요), the goal you become takes 가 (가수가 되다), and after the vowel the copula is 예요 (가수예요).

Calling yourself or anyone 가수 just for singing once; without a professional/performing sense, say 노래를 불러요 or 노래를 잘해요.
Saying 노래를 하다 and assuming it equals 부르다; the natural collocation for performing a song is 노래를 부르다.
Using 가수가 좋아해요 to mean 'I like the singer'; the singer is the object, so it must be 가수를 좋아해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 배우 means "actor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

나오다 'come out/appear'; 에 marks the work it appears in

examples.en: I am an actor.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 배우

examples.en: That actor acts really well.
examples.note: 연기를 잘하다 'be good at acting' is the set phrase

examples.ko: 이 드라마에는 유명한 배우들이 많이 나와요.
examples.romanization: i deuramaeneun yumyeonghan baeudeuri mani nawayo.
examples.en: Many famous actors appear in this drama.
examples.note: 나오다 'appear'; 들 pluralizes 배우

entries.nuance: 배우 is 俳優 (both 俳 and 優 historically meant 'performer/entertainer'), an old Sino-Korean compound that already covers actors of any gender in film, TV drama, and theater — so there is no need to mark gender, and the English loan 액터 is essentially never used in normal speech. The thing an actor does is 연기 'acting' (연기를 하다 / 연기를 잘하다), not '배우를 하다'; that 연기 vs 배우 split (craft vs person) mirrors 요리 vs 요리사 and trips learners up. Distinguish 배우 from 가수 'singer', 개그맨/코미디언 'comedian', and the broader 연예인 'celebrity/entertainer', which includes all of them. The verb 나오다 ('come out') is the idiomatic way to say an actor 'appears in' a film or show. After the vowel, the copula is 배우예요, and one 배우가 된다.

Saying 배우를 하다 for 'to act'; the activity is 연기, so use 연기를 하다 or 연기를 잘하다.
Confusing 배우 (actor) with the wider 연예인 (any entertainer/celebrity), which also includes singers and comedians.

entries.shortExplanation: 운동선수 means "athlete" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the activity 운동 takes 하다; the pro is 운동선수
attach the sport name + 선수 for a specialist
따다 'pick/win' is the verb for earning a medal
goal of becoming marked with 가

examples.en: I am an athlete.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel of 운동선수

examples.ko: 그 선수가 마지막에 골을 넣어서 이겼어요.
examples.romanization: geu seonsuga majimage goreul neoeoseo igyeosseoyo.
examples.en: That player scored at the end, so they won.
examples.note: 골을 넣다 'put in a goal' = to score; -아/어서 'so'

examples.ko: 형은 국가대표 야구 선수라서 훈련이 정말 많아요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeun gukgadaepyo yagu seonsuraseo hullyeoni jeongmal manayo.
examples.en: My brother is a national-team baseball player, so he has a lot of training.
examples.note: 국가대표 'national representative'; -(이)라서 'because (he) is'

entries.nuance: 운동선수 combines 운동 (運動 'movement/exercise') with 선수 (選手, '選 select' + '手 skilled hand' = a 'selected, skilled performer'), so it specifically means a chosen, competitive athlete — not just anyone who works out. That is the key contrast: 운동하다 / 운동을 하다 is what ordinary people do at the gym, whereas a 운동선수 competes professionally, and using 운동선수 for a casual exerciser sounds wrong. For a particular sport, swap in the sport name plus 선수: 축구 선수 (soccer), 야구 선수 (baseball), 수영 선수 (swimming); the bare 선수 is fine once context is clear ('그 선수가 빨라요'). Idiomatic partners include 메달을 따다 (win a medal) and 골을 넣다 (score a goal). Since the word ends in a vowel it is 운동선수예요, and one 운동선수가 된다, the goal marked by 가.

Calling a casual gym-goer a 운동선수; if they just exercise for health, say 운동을 해요, not 운동선수예요.
Saying 운동선수를 하다 for playing sports; the activity verb is 운동을 하다, and 선수 is the person.
Using 메달을 받다 'receive a medal' when the natural sporting idiom is 메달을 따다 'win a medal'.

usagePhrases.note: 에게 marks the person you consult
선임하다 is the formal verb for engaging counsel
goal of becoming marked with 가
사무실 'office'; the place a lawyer works

examples.en: I am a lawyer.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel of 변호사

examples.en: If a problem comes up, ask a lawyer.
examples.note: 한테 = casual 'to'; 생기다 'arise, come up'

examples.ko: 이 사건은 변호사를 선임해서 정식으로 대응하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: i sageoneun byeonhosareul seonimhaeseo jeongsigeuro daeeunghagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We decided to formally respond to this case by retaining a lawyer.
examples.note: 선임하다 'retain'; -기로 하다 'decide to'

entries.nuance: 변호사 is 辯護士 ('argue/plead' 辯 + 'defend/protect' 護 + 'professional/scholar' 士), literally 'one who pleads in defense' — the 護 'protect' element is why it feels like an advocate on your side. Crucially, keep the legal-profession trio straight, since they share the 士/事 family but are different jobs: 변호사 (lawyer who represents you), 판사 (判事, the judge who decides), and 검사 (檢事, the prosecutor who charges); beginners frequently swap 변호사 and 판사. Note the suffix difference too — 변호사 ends in 士 (a credentialed professional, like 회계사 accountant, 세무사 tax agent), whereas 판사/검사 end in 事. Saying 변호사를 되고 싶어요; the role you become takes 가, so it is 변호사가 되고 싶어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 기자 means "reporter" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기자 (gija) = "reporter". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기사를 쓰다 ("write an article") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: 기사 'news article' takes 쓰다; don't confuse with 기자 the person
취재 is the journalist's fieldwork; 하다 pairs with it
에서 marks the workplace
에게 marks the person questioned

examples.en: I am a reporter.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 기자

examples.en: The reporter asked the mayor a sharp question.
examples.note: 에게 marks 시장 as the person asked; 날카롭다 'sharp'

examples.ko: 선배는 십 년째 정치부에서 일하는 베테랑 기자예요.
examples.romanization: seonbaeneun sim nyeonjjae jeongchibueseo ilhaneun beterang gijayeyo.
examples.en: My senior is a veteran reporter who has worked the politics desk for ten years.
examples.note: -째 'for/into (a period)'; 정치부 'politics desk'

entries.nuance: 기자 is 記者 ('record/write down' 記 + 'person' 者), literally 'a person who records' — the 者 'person' suffix marks an agent (compare 학자 scholar, 독자 reader). It means a reporter/journalist who gathers and writes news; address one respectfully as 기자님. The pitfall is the near-homophone trap among 기자 (the reporter), 기사 (記事, the article they write — also 'driver' as in 택시 기사, a different word), and 작가 (作家, an author of books/scripts): you 기사를 쓰다 (write an article) but a 기자 is the human who does it, and a novelist is a 작가, not a 기자. Their core fieldwork verb is 취재하다 ('cover/gather news'), and they 인터뷰를 하다 (do interviews). Since 기자 ends in a vowel the copula is 기자예요, and questions to one take 에게/한테 (기자에게 질문하다).

Confusing 기자 (the reporter) with 기사 (the article, or a driver); you write 기사를 쓰다, but the person is the 기자.
Confusing 기자 with 작가; a journalist is 기자, but a book/screenplay author is 작가.
Saying 기자를 질문하다; you ask to someone, so it is 기자에게/한테 질문하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 군인 means "soldier" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 군인 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 지키다 'guard/protect'; the prototypical soldier's duty
군대 'the army (as an institution/service)'; 에 marks it
복무하다 is the formal verb for doing service; 으로 'as'
군 복무 is the standard phrase for the mandatory term

examples.en: I am a soldier.
examples.note: 이에요 after the consonant ending of 군인

examples.ko: 사촌 형은 지금 군대에서 군인으로 복무하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: sachon hyeongeun jigeum gundaeeseo gunineuro bongmuhago isseoyo.
examples.en: My cousin is now serving as a soldier in the military.
examples.note: 군대에서 'in the army'; -고 있다 'be (currently) doing'

examples.ko: 할아버지께서는 젊을 때 나라를 지킨 군인이셨어요.
examples.romanization: harabeojikkeseoneun jeolmeul ttae narareul jikin guninisyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandfather was a soldier who protected the country when he was young.
examples.note: -(으)셨- past honorific; 지킨 past modifier of 지키다

entries.nuance: 군인 is 軍人 ('army/military' 軍 + 'person' 人), the general word for any member of the armed forces. Distinguish three related terms learners blur: 군인 (a soldier, the person), 군대 (軍隊, the military as an institution or one's term of service — '군대에 가다' means to join up / do one's service), and 병사 (兵士, an enlisted rank specifically, more technical/military-register). In Korea, because of mandatory service, most young men 군대에 가다 and spend a stretch as a 군인, so '군 복무' (military service) is everyday vocabulary. The prototype verb is 나라를 지키다 ('protect the country'), and one serves 군인으로 복무하다 with the role-marking 으로. The critical grammar trap: 군인 ends in a consonant, so the copula is 이에요 (군인이에요) — never 군인예요.

Saying 군인예요 after a consonant; it must be 군인이에요.
Confusing 군인 (a soldier, the person) with 군대 (the military institution / one's service term): '군대에 가요' = go do military service.
Using 군인을 가다 for 'join the army'; you go to the institution, so it is 군대에 가다.

키우다 'raise/grow' for crops and animals

examples.en: I am a farmer.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 농부

examples.ko: 농부가 아침 일찍 밭에 나가서 일해요.
examples.romanization: nongbuga achim iljjik bate nagaseo ilhaeyo.

entries.nuance: 농부 is 農夫 ('farming/agriculture' 農 + 'man/laborer' 夫), and that 夫 'man' element historically skews male, though in practice 농부 is used broadly today; a more neutral, modern alternative is 농민 (農民, 'farming people', common in news and policy) or the polite 농사꾼. The activity is 농사 ('farming'), joined by the irregular collocation 농사를 짓다 — literally 'to build/make farming', the same 짓다 used in 밥을 짓다 'cook rice' and 집을 짓다 'build a house'; never say '농부를 하다'. examples.en: The hairdresser cut my hair nicely (for me).
examples.note: -아/어 주다 marks the service done for you; 예쁘게 'prettily'

examples.ko: 저 미용실 디자이너 선생님은 손님이 끊이지 않아요.
examples.romanization: jeo miyongsil dijaineo seonsaengnimeun sonnimi kkeuniji anayo.
examples.en: That salon's stylist never runs out of customers.
examples.note: 디자이너/선생님 are common in-salon address terms; 끊이지 않다 'never cease'

entries.nuance: 미용사 is 美容師 ('beauty' 美 + 'appearance/looks' 容 + 'master' 師) — literally a 'master of beautifying one's appearance', so it can cover hair, and historically skin/nails, though everyday use centers on hair. Don't confuse the worker with the workplace: the 미용사 works in a 미용실 (or the trendier loanword 헤어숍), so '미용실에 가요' means going to the salon, not the person. In real salons, customers and staff often address stylists as 디자이너(님) or 선생님 rather than the clinical-sounding 미용사, which is more of a job-category label; 미용사 vs 이발사 also matters — 이발사 is specifically a (traditionally men's) barber at a 이발소. The core verbs are 머리를 자르다 (cut hair) and 파마를 하다 (get a perm). After the vowel the copula is 미용사예요, and one 미용사가 된다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 미용사 (the worker) with 미용실 (the salon): '미용실에 가요' = go to the salon, while 미용사가 잘라요 = the hairdresser cuts.
Calling a traditional men's barber a 미용사; that role is 이발사, working at an 이발소.
Saying 머리를 깎다 for a haircut at a salon when 머리를 자르다 is the neutral choice (깎다 leans toward clippers/shaving very short).

entries.shortExplanation: 교실 means "classroom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교실 (gyosil) means "classroom". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교실에 ("to the classroom"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: destination 에: 교실에 가다 = go to the classroom
action-place 에서: 교실에서 공부하다
우리 here means 'my/our' group's room, very natural
넓다 = spacious; subject takes 이

examples.en: Where is the classroom?
examples.note: Simple location question; 이 marks the subject of 어디예요

examples.en: I chat with a friend in the classroom.
examples.note: 에서 = the place an action happens; 하고 = 'with'

examples.en: Class ended, so the students left the classroom.
examples.note: 나가다 takes 에서 (out from a place), never 에

entries.nuance: 교실 is Sino-Korean 教室 — 教 'teach' + 室 'room', literally 'teaching room', i.e. the single physical room where one class meets. The key contrast is 교실 vs 학교(學校 'school'): 학교 is the whole institution/campus, while 교실 is just one room inside it — so 'I'm at school' is 학교에 있어요, not 교실에 있어요 unless you literally mean the room. Also distinguish 교실 (the room) from 수업(授業, the lesson/class period that takes place in it). The everyday particle split is the trap for English speakers: use 에 when the room is a destination you move toward (교실에 들어가다 'enter the classroom'), but 에서 when you do an activity inside it (교실에서 발표하다 'present in the classroom'). English 'in the classroom' maps to 에서 only for actions; for static existence you say 교실에 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 학교 when you mean one room — 학교 is the whole school; the single room is 교실.
Using 에 for an action done inside (교실에 공부해요 ✗). An activity inside a place needs 에서: 교실에서 공부해요 ✓. Keep 에 only for going there or for 있다/없다.
Mapping English 'leave the classroom' to 교실에 나가다 ✗ — exiting a place uses 에서: 교실에서 나가다 ✓.

entries.shortExplanation: 숙제 means "homework" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "homework" is 숙제 (sukje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 숙제를 하다 ("do homework"). Watch the particle attached to 숙제 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The fixed verb is 하다, never 만들다; object takes 를
많다 = many/much; the amount is the subject, so 가
내다 = submit/turn in (also 제출하다, more formal)
Noun-noun compound; 숙제 takes the subject as a modifier

examples.en: Did you finish all your homework?
examples.note: Casual question; 다 = 'all/completely', a very common collocation with 하다

examples.en: Today there isn't much homework.
examples.note: 별로 + negative = 'not really/not much'; amount is the subject (가)

examples.en: I forgot the homework and didn't bring it.
examples.note: 깜빡하다 = 'absent-mindedly forget', the natural verb students use

entries.nuance: 숙제 is Sino-Korean 宿題 — 宿 'lodging/stay overnight' + 題 'topic/problem', literally a 'problem to take home overnight', i.e. work a teacher assigns to be done outside class. The verb is locked: Koreans say 숙제를 하다 'do homework', and 숙제를 내다 means a student turns it in (while a teacher 내다 a 숙제 means 'assign/set' it — context decides). Contrast 숙제 with 공부(工夫, 'study') and 과제(課題, 'assignment/coursework'): 공부하다 is the broad act of studying anything, whereas 숙제 is a specific assigned task, and 과제 is the more formal university word for a project or paper. The big English-speaker pitfall is translating 'do my homework' as 숙제를 만들다 'make homework' (✗ — that sounds like you created the assignment) or 숙제를 공부하다 (✗); the only natural pairing is 숙제를 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 숙제를 만들다 ('make homework') instead of 숙제를 하다 — 만들다 means create the task itself, not complete it.
Using 숙제를 공부하다 ✗. 공부하다 is general study; the set phrase to complete assigned work is 숙제를 하다.
Treating 숙제 as countable English plural and dropping the particle. You still need 를: 숙제를 했어요, not 숙제 했어요 in writing/formal speech.

entries.shortExplanation: 시험 means "exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 시험 (siheom) = "exam". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험을 보다 ("take an exam") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시험, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed verb is 보다 (literally 'see'), never 하다
Existence/scheduling; the exam is the subject, so 이
붙다 'stick' = pass, 떨어지다 'fall' = fail; both take 에
기말(期末) = end of term; cf. 중간 시험 = midterm

examples.en: Is there an exam tomorrow?
examples.note: Casual; 있어요 used for a scheduled event existing

examples.en: I took the Korean exam yesterday.
examples.note: 봤어요 = past of 보다; the set phrase 시험을 보다

examples.en: I studied hard so I passed the exam.
examples.note: Pass = 시험에 붙다; note the particle is 에, not 를

entries.nuance: 시험 is Sino-Korean 試驗 — 試 'try/test' + 驗 'examine', literally 'a trial examination'. The collocation English speakers must memorize is 시험을 보다 — Koreans 'see' an exam, they do not 'do' it, so 시험을 하다 is wrong. Passing and failing are vivid metaphors with the particle 에: 시험에 붙다 (literally 'stick to the exam') = pass, 시험에 떨어지다 ('fall off the exam') = fail — note these take 에, not 을. Contrast 시험 with 퀴즈(quiz, a small in-class test) and with 검사(檢査, an inspection/medical test like 건강 검사): a graded school test is always 시험, never 퀴즈 unless it is a tiny informal one. The classic 직역 trap is 'take an exam' → 시험을 가지다/취하다 ✗ (English 'take' never transfers); and learners often write 시험을 통과하다, which is understandable but bookish — the everyday word is 붙다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시험을 하다 instead of 시험을 보다. Koreans 'see/look at' an exam (보다); 하다 does not collocate with 시험.
Using 를 for pass/fail: 시험을 붙다 ✗. The verbs 붙다/떨어지다 take 에 — 시험에 붙다/떨어지다.
Translating 'take the exam' as 시험을 가지다 ('have/hold'). English 'take' is not literal here; the only natural verb is 보다.

entries.shortExplanation: 수업 means "class / lesson" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수업 (sueop) means "class / lesson". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수업을 듣다 ("take / attend a class"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수업 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 듣다 'listen' is the set verb for attending a class
Scheduling; the class is the subject, so 이
늦다 takes 에 for the event you're late to
Subject-noun modifier; cf. 수학 수업 'math class'

examples.en: Do you have class today?
examples.note: Casual schedule check; 있어요 for a class existing on the timetable

examples.en: I usually attend class diligently.
examples.note: 수업을 듣다 = attend; 열심히 = 'diligently', a habitual collocation

examples.en: I'm sorry for being late to class.
examples.note: 늦다 + 에 marks the event; -아서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 수업 is Sino-Korean 授業 — 授 'give/confer' + 業 'work/study', literally 'conferring instruction', i.e. the lesson or class session itself (the activity and time period). The set verb is 수업을 듣다 'listen to a class' = attend/take it; from the teacher's side it is 수업을 하다 'give/teach a class'. Three near-neighbors confuse learners: 수업 (the lesson event) vs 교실(教室, the room it happens in) vs 과목(科目, the subject like 'math' or 'history') vs 강의(講義, a university lecture). So 'I have three classes today' = 수업 세 개, but 'I take three subjects' = 과목 세 개. The English-speaker pitfall is using 하다 to mean 'take a class' (수업을 하다 actually means 'to teach', which is what a professor does) — as a student you 듣다 a class. Also, 'go to class' is 수업에 가다 (event as destination with 에).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A student saying 수업을 하다 to mean 'I take a class' — 수업을 하다 means to TEACH a class. Students say 수업을 듣다.
Confusing 수업 (lesson) with 교실 (room): you 'attend a 수업', but you 'sit in a 교실'.
Using 과목 and 수업 interchangeably. 과목 is the subject (math); 수업 is the actual class session. 'Math class' = 수학 수업, but 'How many subjects?' = 과목이 몇 개?

entries.shortExplanation: 공책 means "notebook" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "notebook" is 공책 (gongchaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공책에 쓰다 ("write in a notebook"). Watch the particle attached to 공책 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Surface/destination of writing takes 에
Object takes 를; everyday shopping verb 사다
Counter is 권 (for bound paper goods), not 개
새 is a pre-noun modifier; no 의 needed

examples.en: Do you have a notebook?
examples.note: Simple possession question; 있어요 = have/exist

examples.en: I organize vocabulary in my notebook.
examples.note: 에 marks the writing surface; 정리하다 = 'tidy up/organize'

examples.en: Please give me just one notebook.
examples.note: 권 counts bound books; 만 = 'just/only'; 주세요 = polite request

entries.nuance: 공책 is Sino-Korean 空冊 — 空 'empty' + 冊 'book/volume', literally an 'empty book', i.e. a blank bound notebook for writing in. Because it is a 冊, it is counted with the unit 권 (공책 한 권), exactly like 책 'book' — counting it with 개 is the classic foreigner slip. In real life Koreans very often just say the English loanword 노트 (from 'note'); 공책 sounds slightly more textbook/childlike, while 노트 is the casual everyday choice, and a 'notebook computer' is 노트북 — don't confuse the three. Contrast 공책 (paper to write in) with 교과서(教科書, 'textbook' you read from) and 수첩(手帖, a small pocket planner/memo book). The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (use 권, not 개) and assuming 'notebook' must be 공책 — in conversation 노트 is more natural, and never let 노트북 slip in when you mean the paper kind.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it with 개: 공책 한 개 ✗. Bound paper goods use 권: 공책 한 권 ✓.
Confusing 노트 (notebook) with 노트북 (laptop). 공책 = 노트; a laptop computer is 노트북.
Using 에서 for the writing surface: 공책에서 쓰다 ✗. Writing onto a surface takes 에: 공책에 쓰다 ✓.

entries.shortExplanation: 연필 means "pencil" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연필 (yeonpil) = "pencil". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연필로 쓰다 ("write with a pencil") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연필, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument/tool takes 로/으로
깎다 = shave/sharpen, the set verb for pencils
Counter 자루 for long thin sticks (pens, brushes)
色 'color' + 연필; a common compound

examples.en: Please lend me a pencil.
examples.note: 좀 softens the request; 빌려주다 = lend (to me)

examples.ko: 저는 시험 볼 때 연필로 써요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun siheom bol ttae yeonpillo sseoyo.
examples.en: I write with a pencil when taking exams.
examples.note: 로 marks the tool; -ㄹ 때 = 'when ~ing'

examples.en: The pencil is blunt, so I need to sharpen it.
examples.note: 연필을 깎다 = sharpen; -아야 하다 = 'have to'

entries.nuance: 연필 is Sino-Korean 鉛筆 — 鉛 'lead' + 筆 'writing brush/pen', literally 'lead pen', the wooden graphite pencil. The instrument particle 로/으로 is essential: you write 연필로 ('with/by means of a pencil'), and the matching verb for upkeep is 연필을 깎다 'shave the pencil' = sharpen it. The counter 자루 is used for long slender objects (pens, pencils, brushes, even umbrellas) — 연필 한 자루 — so don't default to 개. Contrast the writing tools clearly: 연필 (pencil, erasable) vs 볼펜(ballpoint pen) vs 샤프(mechanical 'sharp' pencil) vs 펜(pen, general). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle — 'write with a pencil' must be 연필로, not 연필을 (학생이 연필을 써요 means 'uses a pencil' as an object, fine, but 'by means of' is 연필로); and English 'sharpen' tempts learners toward a 'make sharp' calque, when the idiomatic verb is the everyday 깎다 (the same verb used for peeling fruit).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 to count: 연필 한 개 sounds off; long thin items take 자루 — 연필 한 자루.
Saying 연필을 쓰다 when you mean 'write WITH a pencil' as the means — that needs the tool particle: 연필로 써요.
Confusing 연필 (pencil) with 볼펜 (pen). They are different tools; a ballpoint is 볼펜, a mechanical pencil is 샤프.

entries.shortExplanation: 지우개 means "eraser" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 지우개 (jiugae) means "eraser". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지우개로 지우다 ("erase with an eraser"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 지우개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Tool particle 로 + the verb 지우다 it derives from
Existence/possession; subject takes 가
빌리다 = borrow (from someone); object takes 를
Small everyday item often counted with native 하나/한 개

examples.en: Do you have an eraser?
examples.note: Quick classroom ask; 있어요 = have

examples.en: I write with a pencil and erase with an eraser.
examples.note: Parallel 로 ... 로 for two tools; 지우개로 지우다

examples.en: Could you lend me an eraser?
examples.note: -ㄹ 수 있다 = 'can'; a polite, softer request than 주세요

entries.nuance: 지우개 is a pure native-Korean word (not Sino-Korean): the verb stem 지우- 'to erase/remove' + the productive suffix -개 'a tool/instrument for ~ing'. That -개 pattern is worth learning because it builds many tool nouns the same way — 베다→베개 'pillow (cutting-rest tool)', 덮다→덮개 'cover', 따다→따개 'opener' — so 지우개 transparently means 'erasing-tool'. It pairs naturally with 연필 (you erase pencil, 연필로 쓴 것을 지우개로 지우다) and the tool particle is 로: 지우개로 지우다. Watch the verb/noun split: 지우다 is the verb 'to erase' and 지우개 is the object; a beginner who says 지우개해요 for 'I erase' is mixing them — the verb is 지워요. Korean erasers are often called 고무지우개 ('rubber eraser') when emphasizing material, and a whiteboard eraser is 칠판지우개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing the noun and its verb: saying 지우개하다 for 'to erase' ✗. The verb is 지우다 (지워요); 지우개 is only the object.
Dropping the tool particle: 지우개 지우다 ✗ in careful speech — use 로: 지우개로 지워요.
Calling it a 'rubber' by direct calque (고무 alone) — 고무 just means rubber; the eraser is 지우개 (or 고무지우개 if the material matters).

entries.shortExplanation: 칠판 means "blackboard" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "blackboard" is 칠판 (chilpan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 칠판에 쓰다 ("write on the board"). Watch the particle attached to 칠판 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Surface/destination takes 에
보다 'look at'; object takes 를
지우다 = wipe/erase the board
Position noun 앞; 칠판 앞에 서다 'stand in front of the board'

examples.en: Please look at the board.
examples.note: Teacher's instruction; 보세요 = polite imperative

examples.en: The teacher wrote the answer on the board.
examples.note: 에 marks the writing surface; 썼어요 past of 쓰다

examples.en: I couldn't see the board, so I moved forward.
examples.note: 보이다 'be visible' (≠ 보다); -아서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 칠판 is Sino-Korean 漆板 — 漆 'lacquer/black paint' + 板 'board/plank', literally a 'lacquered (black) board', the writing board at the front of a classroom. The two everyday actions split by particle: write ON it = 칠판에 쓰다 (surface destination with 에), but look AT it = 칠판을 보다 (object with 를). Many modern rooms have a white 화이트보드 (whiteboard, written with markers) instead of a chalk 칠판, but 칠판 still serves as the generic word for 'the board'. A subtle contrast English speakers miss: 보다 'look at' the board is intentional looking, whereas 보이다 'the board is/ isn't visible' is the spontaneous can-see verb — '칠판이 안 보여요' = 'I can't see the board', not '칠판을 안 봐요' ('I'm not looking at the board'). The pitfall is keeping the particles straight: 에 for writing on, 을 for looking at, and reaching for 보이다 (not 보다) when the issue is visibility.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 을 for writing on it: 칠판을 쓰다 ✗ (that sounds like 'use the board'). Writing onto a surface needs 에: 칠판에 쓰다.
Saying 칠판을 안 봐요 to mean 'I can't see the board'. That means 'I'm not looking at it'. For visibility use 보이다: 칠판이 안 보여요.
Assuming any board is 칠판 — a marker whiteboard is 화이트보드; 칠판 is specifically the chalk(board).

entries.shortExplanation: 방학 means "school vacation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 방학 (banghak) = "school vacation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방학에 ("during the break") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방학, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Time point/period takes 에: 방학에 여행하다
School 'goes on vacation'; 하다 here = the break begins
Season + 방학; cf. 겨울 방학 'winter break'
끝나다 = come to an end; subject takes 이

examples.en: When is the break?
examples.note: Simple schedule question; 이에요 = 'it is'

examples.en: I want to go to Korea during the break.
examples.note: 에 marks the time; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: I worked a part-time job during the break.
examples.note: 동안 = 'for the duration of'; a very common time collocation

entries.nuance: 방학 is Sino-Korean 放學 — 放 'release/let go' + 學 'studies', literally 'releasing (from) studies', i.e. the official school break between terms (summer/winter). The crucial contrast is 방학 vs 휴가(休暇, 'leave/holiday'): 방학 belongs to the school calendar and applies to students/teachers, while 휴가 is the time off a worker takes from a job — a salaried adult on vacation is 휴가 중, never 방학 중. Also distinguish 방학 (a scheduled school break) from 휴일(休日, a single day off / public holiday like a national holiday) and 연휴(連休, a string of consecutive holidays). Note 방학을 하다 means '(the school) goes on break / break starts', an event, not 'I take a vacation'. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a working adult's trip 방학 (it must be 휴가), and forgetting that 'during vacation' uses the time particle 에 (방학에) or the duration noun 동안 (방학 동안), not 에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방학 for a working adult's time off — that is 휴가. 방학 is only the student/school-calendar break.
Saying 방학에서 for 'during vacation' ✗. A time period takes 에 (방학에) or 동안 (방학 동안); 에서 is for places/actions.
Confusing 방학 (a multi-week term break) with 휴일 (a single day off) or 연휴 (a holiday stretch).

structuredNuance.t: 방학 is the official school break between terms (summer/winter). Note 방학을 하다 means '(the school) goes on break / break starts', an event, not 'I take a vacation'.

entries.shortExplanation: 질문 means "question" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 질문 (jilmun) means "question". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 질문을 하다 ("ask a question"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 질문 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Set verb is 하다; 질문하다 is one word too
Existence; the question is the subject, so 이
답하다 takes 에 for the question being answered
받다 = receive; what a speaker does at Q&A

examples.en: Any questions?
examples.note: Standard classroom check; 있어요 = exist/have

examples.en: I asked the teacher a question.
examples.note: 께 = honorific 'to' (for a teacher); 질문을 하다 = ask

examples.en: Good question. Let's think about it together.
examples.note: 좋은 질문 is a fixed compliment; -아 보다 = 'try ~ing'

entries.nuance: 질문 is Sino-Korean 質問 — 質 'substance/inquire into' + 問 'ask', literally 'to inquire and ask', i.e. a question put to someone. The set verb is 질문을 하다 (or the single verb 질문하다); the person you ask takes 에게/한테 (or honorific 께 for a teacher): 선생님께 질문을 하다. Its natural partner is 대답/답(答) — a 질문 is answered by a 대답. The big redundancy trap for English speakers is 질문을 물어보다 ✗: 물어보다 already means 'to ask', so this literally says 'ask a question-asking' — say either 질문을 하다 or just 물어보다, never both. Distinguish 질문 (a question seeking information/an answer) from 문제(問題, a 'problem' or exam item) — '3 questions on the test' are 문제 세 개, but 'I have a question for you' is 질문이 있어요. Note answering takes 에: 질문에 답하다, not 질문을 답하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 질문을 물어보다 ✗ — 물어보다 already means 'ask', so it doubles up. Use 질문을 하다 OR 물어보다, not both.
Using 를 to answer: 질문을 답하다 ✗. 답하다 takes 에: 질문에 답하다 / 질문에 대답하다.
Using 질문 for an exam item. A test question/problem is 문제; 질문 is a question you ask a person for an answer.

entries.shortExplanation: 대답 means "answer / reply" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "answer / reply" is 대답 (daedap). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 대답을 하다 ("give an answer"). Watch the particle attached to 대답 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Set verb 하다; 대답하다 is the one-word form
The thing answered takes 에, not 를
No response; subject takes 이
듣다 = hear; what the asker does

examples.en: Why is there no answer?
examples.note: 대답이 없다 = no reply; 이 marks the subject

examples.en: The student answered loudly.
examples.note: 큰 소리로 = 'in a loud voice'; 대답하다 as one verb

examples.en: Please answer my question.
examples.note: 질문에 (에, not 를) + 대답하다; -아 주세요 = polite request

entries.nuance: 대답 is Sino-Korean 對答 — 對 'face/respond-to' + 答 'reply', literally 'a facing reply', i.e. the spoken/written response to a question or call. It is the natural partner of 질문(質問): a 질문 is met by a 대답, and the verb is 대답을 하다 / 대답하다. The sharp contrast to master is 대답 vs 정답(正答, 正 'correct' + 答): 대답 is simply 'a/the response someone gives' (it can be right or wrong), while 정답 is specifically 'the correct answer' to a problem — so on a quiz '정답은 3번이에요' = 'the correct answer is number 3', but 그 학생의 대답 = 'that student's response'. Also note 답 alone is a shorter everyday form of both. The particle pitfall mirrors 질문: you answer a question with 에 — 질문에 대답하다 / 질문에 답하다, NOT 질문을 대답하다. English 'answer the phone/door' does not use 대답 either — that is 전화를 받다 / 문을 열다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 를 for what is answered: 질문을 대답하다 ✗. The question takes 에: 질문에 대답하다.
Confusing 대답 (a response, right or wrong) with 정답 (the correct answer). A graded 'correct answer' is 정답.
Calquing 'answer the phone' as 전화를 대답하다 ✗. That is 전화를 받다 ('receive the call'); 대답 is replying to a question.

entries.shortExplanation: 사전 means "dictionary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사전 (sajeon) = "dictionary". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사전을 찾다 ("look something up in a dictionary") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사전, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: look something up in a dictionary
usagePhrases.note: Set verb 찾다 'search/find'; object takes 를
Source/location of the search takes 에서
Language + 사전; cf. 영어 사전 'English dictionary'
찾아보다 adds the 'try/check' nuance to 찾다

examples.en: Do you have a dictionary?
examples.note: Simple possession question; 있어요 = have

examples.en: I look up unknown words in the dictionary.
examples.note: 에서 marks where you search; 사전에서 찾다

examples.ko: 요즘은 종이 사전보다 앱을 더 많이 써요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jongi sajeonboda aebeul deo mani sseoyo.
examples.en: These days I use an app more than a paper dictionary.
examples.note: 종이 사전 = paper dictionary; -보다 = 'than'

entries.nuance: 사전 is Sino-Korean 辭典 — 辭 'words/diction' + 典 'canon/standard reference', literally a 'standard reference of words', i.e. a dictionary. The set verb is 사전을 찾다 — note 찾다 here means 'look up' (its other meaning is 'search for/find'), and the place you search takes 에서: 사전에서 단어를 찾다. The notorious pitfall for learners is the near-homophone pair 사전(辭典, dictionary) vs 사진(寫眞, photograph) — one letter apart (ㅓ vs ㅣ) but completely different; mixing them up ('I took a 사전' for a photo) is a classic slip. Also distinguish 사전 from 백과사전(百科事典, encyclopedia — note the different middle hanja 事 'matters') and from 단어장 (a personal vocabulary list/flashcards). Today most learners use a phone 사전 app rather than a 종이 사전 'paper dictionary'. English 'look up' transfers fine to 찾다, but remember to use 에서 for the dictionary as the place searched, while the word you seek takes 를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 사전 (dictionary) with 사진 (photo) — only ㅓ vs ㅣ differs, but the meanings are unrelated.
Using 에 instead of 에서 for the place you search: 사전에 찾다 ✗. Searching within a source takes 에서: 사전에서 찾다.
Saying 사전을 보다 'look at the dictionary' when you mean 'look it up' — the active 'look up' verb is 찾다 (사전을 찾다).

structuredNuance.t: 사전 is a dictionary. The set verb is 사전을 찾다 — note 찾다 here means 'look up' (its other meaning is 'search for/find'), and the place you search takes 에서: 사전에서 단어를 찾다. Today most learners use a phone 사전 app rather than a 종이 사전 'paper dictionary'.

entries.shortExplanation: 회의 means "meeting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 회의 (hoeui) means "meeting". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회의가 있어요. ("There is a meeting."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Existence with 있다 plus subject 이/가 — the default way to announce a meeting on the calendar.
회의에 들어가다 'enter a meeting' is the set phrase; use 에 here, not 에서, because you are moving in.
회의 takes 하다 to become a verb; 회의하다 = the act of meeting, distinct from the event noun.
Bare noun + 시간 forms a time phrase; no particle between 회의 and 시간.

examples.en: I have two meetings today.
examples.note: Counts meetings with 개; 회의가 (subject) is what 있다 describes.

examples.en: We decided a new plan in the meeting.
examples.note: 에서 marks the meeting as the place where the action happened — contrast with 에 for entering.

examples.ko: 부장님이 회의를 길게 끌어서 다들 지쳤어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimi hoeuireul gilge kkeureoseo dadeul jichyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The manager dragged the meeting out, so everyone got worn out.
examples.note: Real-office register: 회의를 끌다 'drag a meeting out' is the natural complaint collocation.

entries.nuance: 회의 (漢字 會議, 會 'gather' + 議 'discuss') is a formal, work-style meeting where people gather to discuss and decide something — a board meeting, a team sync, a planning session. The near-synonym learners reach for is 모임, but 모임 is a social get-together (a dinner, a club, friends meeting up) with no agenda, so calling drinks with friends a 회의 sounds robotic; conversely calling a budget review a 모임 sounds too loose. It pairs naturally with 회의를 하다 (hold), 회의에 들어가다 (go into), 회의가 길어지다 (run long). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you are *in* a meeting as a location, so the action takes 회의에서, but you *enter* a meeting with 회의에 들어가다 — and never confuse 회의 with the look-alike 회사 (company) or 회비 (membership fee).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 친구하고 회의했어요 for hanging out with friends — 회의 implies a formal agenda; for a casual gathering say 친구하고 모였어요 or use 모임.
Using 회의에 for where talking happens, as in 회의에 이야기했어요 — the location of an action needs 에서: 회의에서 이야기했어요. Reserve 회의에 for 들어가다/참석하다.
Mixing up 회의 with 회사; 회사에 가요 means go to the company/office, while 회의에 가요 means go to the meeting.

structuredNuance.t: 회의 is a formal, work-style meeting where people gather to discuss and decide something — a board meeting, a team sync, a planning session. It pairs naturally with 회의를 하다 (hold), 회의에 들어가다 (go into), 회의가 길어지다 (run long).

The near-synonym learners reach for is 모임, but 모임 is a social get-together (a dinner, a club, friends meeting up) with no agenda. Calling drinks with friends a 회의 sounds robotic; conversely calling a budget review a 모임 sounds too loose.
漢字 會議: 會 'gather' + 議 'discuss'.

The particle matters: you are *in* a meeting as a location, so the action takes 회의에서, but you *enter* a meeting with 회의에 들어가다. Never confuse 회의 with the look-alike 회사 (company) or 회비 (membership fee).

entries.shortExplanation: 서류 means "documents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "documents" is 서류 (seoryu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 서류를 작성하다. ("to fill out / draw up a document."). Watch the particle attached to 서류 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to fill out / draw up a document.
usagePhrases.note: 서류를 작성하다 is the formal verb for completing a form — more office-appropriate than just 쓰다.

usagePhrases.en: There is a lot of paperwork.
usagePhrases.note: 서류 is treated as a mass noun here; 많다 describes the pile, no plural marker needed.
제출하다 'hand in/submit' is the set partner for official forms (applications, reports).

usagePhrases.en: Please give me one copy of the document.
usagePhrases.note: Counter for a set/copy of papers is 부, not 개 or 장.

examples.en: Please take a look at this document.
examples.note: Everyday polite request; 좀 softens the ask, 봐 주세요 = 'look at it for me'.

examples.en: I gave the documents to the manager.
examples.note: Honorific recipient 께 + humble 드리다 because the boss outranks you.

examples.ko: 비자 신청 서류가 하나라도 빠지면 접수가 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: bija sincheong seoryuga hanarado ppajimyeon jeopsuga an dwaeyo.
examples.en: If even one visa application document is missing, they won't accept it.
examples.note: Real-life bureaucracy: 서류가 빠지다 'a document is missing' is the natural collocation.

entries.nuance: 서류 (漢字 書類, 書 'write' + 類 'kind/category') means official paperwork — forms, applications, reports, contracts — the documents you submit, sign, and file at work or a government office. It is not a casual word for any paper; a personal notebook is 공책, a book is 책, and a single loose sheet is 종이 (one sheet = 종이 한 장). 서류 usually behaves as a collective even when grammatically singular, so 서류가 많다 means 'there's a lot of paperwork.' It rides with 작성하다 (fill out), 제출하다 (submit), 처리하다 (process), 빠지다 (be missing). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 to count it — use 부 for a copy/set (서류 한 부) or 장 for individual sheets, and don't translate 'do the documents' as 서류를 하다; you 작성하다 or 처리하다 them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting with 개 (서류 한 개) — papers are counted with 장 (sheets) or 부 (a copy/set of a document): 서류 한 부.
Calling a personal book or notebook 서류 — 서류 is strictly official paperwork; a notebook is 공책/노트 and a book is 책.
Saying 서류를 해요 to mean 'I do the paperwork' — there is no 서류하다; use 서류를 작성하다 (fill out) or 서류를 처리하다 (handle).

structuredNuance.t: 서류 means official paperwork — forms, applications, reports, contracts — the documents you submit, sign, and file at work or a government office. It usually behaves as a collective even when grammatically singular, so 서류가 많다 means 'there's a lot of paperwork.' It rides with 작성하다 (fill out), 제출하다 (submit), 처리하다 (process), 빠지다 (be missing).
It is not a casual word for any paper: a personal notebook is 공책, a book is 책, and a single loose sheet is 종이 (one sheet = 종이 한 장).
漢字 書類: 書 'write' + 類 'kind/category'.
Don't reach for 개 to count it — use 부 for a copy/set (서류 한 부) or 장 for individual sheets. And don't translate 'do the documents' as 서류를 하다; you 작성하다 or 처리하다 them.

entries.shortExplanation: 이메일 means "email" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이메일 (imeil) = "email". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이메일을 보내다. ("to send an email.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이메일, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보내다 'send' is the core verb; the message takes 을/를 as the object.
Incoming mail is the subject of 오다; 이메일이 왔어요 = 'an email came.'
확인하다 'verify/check' is the standard verb for reading your inbox.
Compound noun; 주소 'address' attaches directly with no particle.

examples.en: What is your email address?
examples.note: Beginner exchange; 뭐예요? asks for the information directly.

examples.en: I sent an email to my coworker.
examples.note: Human recipient takes 에게 (written/neutral) — to a machine/place you'd use 에.

examples.ko: 참고로 아까 보낸 이메일에 자료 첨부했으니까 확인 부탁드려요.
examples.romanization: chamgoro akka bonaen imeire jaryo cheombuhaesseunikka hwagin butakdeuryeoyo.
examples.en: FYI, I attached the file to the email I sent earlier, so please check it.
examples.note: Workplace email register: 첨부하다 'attach', 확인 부탁드려요 'please check' are the real formulas.

entries.nuance: 이메일 is the everyday loanword (from English 'e-mail') for electronic mail, used freely at work and in daily life; the Sino alternative 전자우편 (電子郵便 'electronic post') exists but sounds stiff and bureaucratic, mostly seen on official forms. Crucially, 이메일 ≠ paper mail: a physical letter is 편지, and the postal-mail system is 우편, so 'I got your letter' about a posted envelope is 편지를 받았어요, not 이메일. It collocates with 보내다 (send), 받다 (receive), 확인하다 (check), 첨부하다 (attach a file), 답장하다 (reply). The English-speaker pitfall is the recipient particle — a person who receives mail takes 에게/한테 (동료에게 이메일을 보내요), and don't drag the English verb 'do' over: you 이메일을 보내다 or 쓰다, never 이메일하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이메일 for a posted paper letter — that is 편지 (a letter) or 우편 (postal mail); 이메일 is only the electronic kind.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 (동료를 이메일 보냈어요) — the person gets 에게/한테 and the email is the object: 동료에게 이메일을 보냈어요.
Saying 이메일했어요 to mean 'I emailed' — Korean doesn't verb it that way; say 이메일을 보냈어요 or 이메일을 썼어요.

structuredNuance.t: 이메일 is the everyday loanword (from English 'e-mail') for electronic mail, used freely at work and in daily life. It collocates with 보내다 (send), 받다 (receive), 확인하다 (check), 첨부하다 (attach a file), 답장하다 (reply).

entries.shortExplanation: 동료 means "coworker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동료 (dongnyo) means "coworker". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회사 동료 ("a company coworker."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 동료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 modifies 동료 directly; a frequent full phrase for 'colleague at my company.'
와/과 함께 'together with' is the bookish/neutral pairing; spoken Korean often uses 하고 같이.
돕다 (ㅂ-irregular: 도와요) takes the colleague as object with 을/를.
직장 'workplace' + 동료 is an extremely common fixed pairing, near-synonymous with 회사 동료.

examples.en: My coworker is really kind.
examples.note: Simple description; 참 'truly' adds warmth, 친절해요 describes character.

examples.en: I eat lunch together with a coworker.
examples.note: Spoken pairing 하고 같이; the everyday equivalent of 와/과 함께.

examples.ko: 새로 온 동료가 일을 빨리 배워서 팀에 큰 도움이 돼요.
examples.romanization: saero on dongnyoga ireul ppalli baewoseo time keun doumi dwaeyo.
examples.en: The newly arrived coworker learns fast, so it's a big help to the team.
examples.note: Real-office framing; 도움이 되다 'be of help' is the natural result clause.

entries.nuance: 동료 (漢字 同僚, 同 'same' + 僚 'fellow official/colleague') means a colleague — someone you work alongside, typically at a comparable level, with a neutral, slightly formal tone. The line learners blur is with rank words: a work senior is 선배 (or 상사 for a superior/boss), a junior is 후배, so once status is in play Koreans name the rank rather than say 동료. It is also strictly a *work* word — classmates at school are 친구 or 동급생, never 동료. Natural partners: 회사 동료, 직장 동료, 동료와 협력하다 (cooperate), 동료를 돕다. The English-speaker pitfall: 'colleague' in English can loosely include your boss, but Korean 동료 implies a peer — don't call 부장님 your 동료. Also note 동료 is the person; the human-recipient/companion particle is 하고/와, not 를, when you do something *with* them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling school classmates 동료 — that is 친구 (friend) or 동급생/반 친구; 동료 is specifically a work colleague.
Referring to your boss as 동료 — a superior is 상사 or by title (부장님); 동료 implies an equal-level peer.
Saying 동료를 점심 먹어요 for eating with a coworker — the companion takes 하고/와: 동료하고 같이 점심을 먹어요.

structuredNuance.t: 동료 means a colleague — someone you work alongside, typically at a comparable level, with a neutral, slightly formal tone. Natural partners: 회사 동료, 직장 동료, 동료와 협력하다 (cooperate), 동료를 돕다.
