entries.shortExplanation: 사장 means "company boss" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "company boss" is 사장 (sajang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사장님이 오시다. ("the boss comes (honorific)."). Watch the particle attached to 사장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 사장 almost always carries 님; the verb takes 시 honorific: 오시다 → 오셨어요.
께 is the honorific replacement for 에게/한테 when the recipient outranks you.
모시다 is the humble verb for serving a superior — far politer than 데리다.
Koreans say 우리 ('our') even for one's own boss/company — a collective-belonging idiom.

examples.en: The boss is not here right now.
examples.note: Honorific existence 계시다 → 계세요; negated for absence.

examples.en: Our boss really cares about the employees.
examples.note: 아끼다 'treasure/care for' + 시 honorific; 우리 for one's own company.

examples.ko: 사장님께 직접 보고드려야 하는 사안이라 좀 긴장돼요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimkke jikjeop bogodeuryeoya haneun saanira jom ginjangdwaeyo.
examples.en: It's a matter I have to report directly to the boss, so I'm a bit nervous.
examples.note: Real-workplace register; 보고드리다 'humbly report' + 께 to a superior.

entries.nuance: 사장 (漢字 社長, 社 'company' + 長 'chief/head') is the head/president/owner of a company. The crucial register fact: at work you virtually never say bare 사장 to or about your boss — it's 사장님, and the verbs go honorific (오시다, 계시다, 말씀하시다) while your own actions toward them go humble (드리다, 보고드리다, 모시다). Distinguish the rank ladder: 부장 is a department head (mid-level), 과장 a section chief, and 사장 sits at the top, with 회장 (chairman) above only in large groups. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 님 (사장 said to their face sounds blunt to the point of rude) and using plain verbs — 사장님이 왔어요 should be 사장님이 오셨어요. Bare 사장 without 님 mainly appears in neutral writing or when referring to a small-shop owner in the third person.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Addressing or referring to your own boss as plain 사장 — attach 님: 사장님. Bare 사장 to their face sounds disrespectful.
Using plain verbs for the boss (사장님이 말했어요) — superiors take honorific 시: 사장님이 말씀하셨어요 (말씀하시다 is the honorific of 말하다).
Saying 사장님에게 for 'to the boss' in polite speech — a superior takes the honorific particle 께: 사장님께.

entries.shortExplanation: 월급 means "monthly salary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 월급 (wolgeup) = "monthly salary". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 월급을 받다. ("to receive a salary.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 월급, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 'receive' is the core verb; the pay is the object with 을/를.
오르다 (르-irregular: 올라요) 'rise' takes the salary as subject — the happy collocation.
월급 + 날 'day' forms one compound noun: the day salary lands.
밀리다 'be pushed back/owed' is the standard verb when pay doesn't come on time.

examples.en: I got paid today.
examples.note: Plain everyday line; 월급 받다 'get one's salary' as the natural unit.

examples.en: My salary comes in on the 25th every month.
examples.note: 월급이 들어오다 'salary comes in (to the account)' + date with 에.

examples.ko: 첫 월급으로 부모님께 내복을 사 드렸어요.
examples.romanization: cheot wolgeubeuro bumonimkke naebogeul sa deuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: With my first paycheck I bought my parents long underwear.
examples.note: Cultural set phrase: 첫 월급으로 내복을 사 드리다 is a real Korean first-salary custom; 으로 = means.

entries.nuance: 월급 (漢字 月給, 月 'month' + 給 'pay/give') is pay received on a monthly cycle — the everyday word an ordinary worker uses for their paycheck. Distinguish the pay-period family sharply: 시급 (時給) is an hourly wage, 주급 (週給) weekly, and 연봉 (年俸) is annual salary — the figure you negotiate at hiring and quote when comparing jobs. So 'What's the salary?' for a part-time gig is 시급이 얼마예요?, but for a career offer it's 연봉이 얼마예요?; using 월급 there sounds slightly small-scale. Natural partners: 월급을 받다, 월급이 오르다, 월급이 밀리다 (be owed), 월급날, 월급이 들어오다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'salary' as one word — Korean splits it by period, so don't say 월급 when you mean the annual 연봉, and remember it's 받다 (receive), not 'earn-translated-literally.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 월급 for an hourly wage — a per-hour rate is 시급 (시급 만 원 = 10,000 won/hour); 월급 is strictly the monthly amount.
Quoting a job's pay as 월급 when you mean the yearly figure — career salaries are stated as 연봉 (annual): 연봉이 얼마예요?
Saying 월급을 벌어요 modeled on 'earn a salary' — the natural verb is 받다: 월급을 받아요. (벌다 fits 돈을 벌다 'make money' generally.)

entries.shortExplanation: 출근 means "going to work" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 출근 (chulgeun) means "going to work". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 출근하다 ("to go to work / clock in."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 출근 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to go to work / clock in.
usagePhrases.note: 출근 + 하다 makes the verb; describes heading to and arriving at the workplace.

usagePhrases.en: to go to work at nine.
usagePhrases.note: Clock time takes 에; states your start hour.
Bare compound; can mean rush hour or your designated start time.

usagePhrases.en: the way to work / one's commute.
usagePhrases.note: 출근 + 길 'road' = the journey in to work, as in 출근길에 'on the way to work.'

examples.en: I usually go to work at eight.
examples.note: 보통 'usually' sets a routine; 에 marks the clock time.

examples.en: Today I was late to work because of traffic.
examples.note: 출근이 늦다 'be late getting to work' + reason with 아서.

examples.ko: 내일 새벽같이 출근해야 해서 일찍 자려고요.
examples.romanization: naeil saebyeokgachi chulgeunhaeya haeseo iljjik jaryeogoyo.
examples.en: I have to get to work at the crack of dawn tomorrow, so I plan to sleep early.
examples.note: 새벽같이 출근하다 'go in at dawn' is a natural intensity collocation; ~려고요 states intention.

entries.nuance: 출근 (漢字 出勤, 出 'go out' + 勤 'attend to duty') is going to / showing up for work — both the leaving-home-for-the-job and the arriving/clocking-in sense. Its exact opposite is 퇴근 (退勤, 'withdraw from duty') = leaving work at day's end; the two are a fixed pair Korean learners must keep straight. Don't confuse 출근 (reporting to your job) with 통근 (通勤, the commute itself) or with 등교 (登校, a student going to school) — a pupil 등교하지 출근하지 않아요. Natural partners: 출근하다, 출근 시간, 출근길, 출근이 늦다, 정시 출근 (on-time arrival). The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 conjugation and particles: it's 출근해요 (not a separate verb 'go-work'), the time takes 에 (아홉 시에 출근해요), and the means of commuting takes (으)로 (지하철로 출근해요), never 'by'-translated-as-에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 출근 with 퇴근 — 출근 is arriving at work (morning), 퇴근 is leaving work (evening); they are opposites, so 여섯 시에 출근해요 said for going home is wrong.
Using 출근 for a student going to school — pupils 등교하다 (登校), not 출근하다; 출근 is only for a job.
Marking the means of commute with 에서 (지하철에서 출근해요) — the vehicle/means takes (으)로: 지하철로 출근해요.

structuredNuance.t: 출근 is going to / showing up for work — both the leaving-home-for-the-job and the arriving/clocking-in sense. Natural partners: 출근하다, 출근 시간, 출근길, 출근이 늦다, 정시 출근 (on-time arrival).

Its exact opposite is 퇴근 (退勤, 'withdraw from duty') = leaving work at day's end; the two are a fixed pair learners must keep straight. Don't confuse 출근 (reporting to your job) with 통근 (通勤, the commute itself) or with 등교 (登校, a student going to school) — a pupil 등교하지 출근하지 않아요.
漢字 出勤: 出 'go out' + 勤 'attend to duty'.

The 하다 conjugation and particles trip people up: it's 출근해요 (not a separate verb 'go-work'), the time takes 에 (아홉 시에 출근해요), and the means of commuting takes (으)로 (지하철로 출근해요), never 'by'-translated-as-에서.

entries.shortExplanation: 퇴근 means "leaving work" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "leaving work" is 퇴근 (toegeun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 퇴근하다 ("to leave work / clock out."). Watch the particle attached to 퇴근 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 퇴근 + 하다 makes the verb for finishing the day and heading home.
Sino 후 'after' + 에 marks the time slot; the set phrase for evening plans.
정시 (定時 'set time') + 퇴근 = clocking out exactly on schedule, a coveted thing.
퇴근 + 길 'road' = the commute home, as in 퇴근길에 'on the way home.'

examples.en: Today I want to leave work early.
examples.note: Desire with ~고 싶다; 일찍 퇴근하다 'leave early' is the everyday wish.

examples.en: We decided to grab a drink with coworkers after work.
examples.note: 퇴근 후에 + 한잔하다 'have a drink' — the classic after-work plan; ~기로 하다 'decide to.'

examples.en: Work is piled up, so leaving right on the dot is hopeless today too.
examples.note: Slang 칼퇴근 'knife-sharp on-time clock-out'; very natural colloquial office talk.

entries.nuance: 퇴근 (漢字 退勤, 退 'withdraw/retreat' + 勤 'duty') means leaving the workplace at the end of the working day — clocking out and heading home. Its hardwired opposite is 출근 (出勤) = going to work in the morning; the pair shares 勤 'duty,' with 出 'out (to)' versus 退 'withdraw (from).' Don't blur 퇴근 (going home after work today) with 퇴사 (退社, quitting the company for good) — 오늘 퇴근해요 means you're heading home, 회사를 퇴사해요 means you're resigning. Natural partners: 퇴근하다, 퇴근 후에, 퇴근길, 정시 퇴근, the slang 칼퇴근 (leaving exactly on time). The English-speaker pitfall: 'leave work' tempts a literal 일을 떠나요, but the single word is 퇴근하다; and the time still takes 에 (여섯 시에 퇴근해요), while 후에 attaches to 퇴근 for 'after work.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 퇴근 with 퇴사 — 퇴근 = leaving for the day, 퇴사 (退社) = quitting/resigning from the company permanently.
Translating 'leave work' literally as 일을 떠나다 — Korean uses the one verb 퇴근하다; 일을 떠나다 sounds like abandoning a task.

entries.shortExplanation: 휴가 means "vacation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 휴가 (hyuga) = "vacation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 휴가를 가다. ("to go on vacation.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 휴가, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 가다 'go' takes the leave as object with 을/를; the standard 'take a trip' framing.
내다 'put in/submit' is the office verb for filing for time off — 휴가를 내다 'put in for leave.'
中 'middle of' marks an ongoing state: 휴가 중이에요 'I'm on leave.'
여름 'summer' modifies 휴가 directly — the big annual leave most Koreans take.

examples.en: I'm going on vacation next week.
examples.note: Future-ish plan; 에 marks the time, 가요 the going.

examples.en: I'm taking leave this time and planning a trip to Jeju.
examples.note: 휴가(를) 내다 'request leave' (office sense) + ~려고요 intention; 다녀오다 'go and come back.'

examples.ko: 눈치 보여서 연차 휴가를 마음 편히 쓰기가 어려워요.
examples.romanization: nunchi boyeoseo yeoncha hyugareul maeum pyeonhi sseugiga eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: I feel self-conscious, so it's hard to use my annual leave with peace of mind.
examples.note: Real workplace culture: 연차(휴가)를 쓰다 'use one's annual leave' + 눈치 보이다 'feel watched.'

entries.nuance: 휴가 (漢字 休暇, 休 'rest' + 暇 'leisure/free time') is leave taken from a job — paid annual leave (연차 휴가), summer vacation (여름 휴가), or military/special leave. The boundary learners must guard is against 방학: 방학 is a *school* break (winter/summer holidays for students and teachers), so a worker says 휴가 while a student says 방학 — 회사원은 휴가, 학생은 방학. Also distinguish 휴일 (a single day off / public holiday) from 휴가 (a stretch of personal leave). Natural partners: 휴가를 가다 (go on), 휴가를 내다/쓰다 (take, in the office sense), 휴가 중, 연차 휴가. The English-speaker pitfall is using 휴가 for a school vacation (that's 방학) and reaching only for 가다 — to *request* time off at work you 휴가를 내다 or 휴가를 쓰다, which 'go on vacation' alone doesn't capture.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 휴가 for a student's school break — that is 방학 (방학 때 'during the school holidays'); 휴가 is leave from a job.
Confusing 휴가 (a span of personal leave) with 휴일 (a single day off / public holiday) — '5 days off' is 휴가 5일, but a national holiday is a 휴일.
Only ever saying 휴가를 가다 — to file for leave at work the verb is 내다 or 쓰다: 휴가를 냈어요 'I requested leave.'

entries.shortExplanation: 명함 means "business card" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 명함 (myeongham) means "business card". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 명함을 주고받다. ("to exchange business cards."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 명함 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 주고받다 'give-and-take' is the set verb for the two-way card swap at first meetings.

usagePhrases.en: to hand over a business card.
usagePhrases.note: 건네다 'pass/hand to' is more polished than 주다 for offering your card.
Flat cards are counted with 장 (sheets), not 개: 명함 한 장.

usagePhrases.en: to hand out one's cards around.
usagePhrases.note: 돌리다 'pass around' = distributing cards to several people, e.g. around a table.

examples.en: Please give me one of your cards.
examples.note: Polite request with counter 장; the everyday way to ask for someone's card.

examples.en: The job title is written on the card.
examples.note: Location with 에; 적혀 있다 'is written (and remains)' — passive resultative.

examples.ko: 처음 만나면 두 손으로 명함을 건네는 게 예의예요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum mannamyeon du soneuro myeonghameul geonneneun ge yeuiyeyo.
examples.en: When you first meet, handing your card with both hands is the polite thing.
examples.note: Cultural manners: 두 손으로 'with both hands' + 건네다; ~는 게 예의다 'it's etiquette to.'

entries.nuance: 명함 (漢字 名銜, 名 'name' + 銜 'title/rank') is a printed business card carrying your name, company, position, and contacts. In Korean work culture the *exchange* is a small ritual — you offer and receive 두 손으로 (with both hands), read the card a beat before pocketing it, and never write on someone's card in front of them. Don't confuse 명함 with 카드 (a generic card / credit card) or 신분증 (an ID card): 명함 is specifically the work introduction card. Natural partners: 명함을 주고받다, 명함을 건네다, 명함을 돌리다, 명함을 받다, 명함에 (직책이) 적혀 있다. The English-speaker pitfall is the counter — flat printed cards take 장 (명함 한 장), not the all-purpose 개; and the polite verb for offering one is 건네다/드리다, while the whole social act is captured by 주고받다, with no real English one-word equivalent.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting cards with 개 (명함 한 개) — thin flat cards use the counter 장: 명함 한 장.
Calling it 카드 — generic 카드 means a credit/ID/playing card; the work introduction card is specifically 명함.
Handing a card one-handed and saying 명함 줄게 to a senior — register and manners both matter; offer with both hands and the politer verb: 명함 드릴게요 / 명함 건네 드릴게요.

entries.shortExplanation: 사무실 means "office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "office" is 사무실 (samusil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사무실에 있다. ("to be in the office."). Watch the particle attached to 사무실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Static location of existence takes 에 with 있다: 사무실에 있어요.
An action's location takes 에서: 사무실에서 일해요 — contrast with 에 for mere existence.

usagePhrases.en: to move offices / relocate the office.
usagePhrases.note: 옮기다 'move/relocate' takes the office as object; said when the workplace changes location.
분위기 'mood' is a very common partner — 사무실 분위기가 좋다 'the office vibe is good.'

examples.en: Our office is on the third floor.
examples.note: Floor location with 에; 우리 'our' for one's own workplace.

examples.en: I'm in a meeting at the office right now.
examples.note: Action-location 에서 + 중이다 'in the middle of'; natural status update.

examples.en: The office is quiet, so I can concentrate well.
examples.note: Reason with 아서; 집중이 잘되다 'concentration goes well' — natural result.

entries.nuance: 사무실 (漢字 事務室, 事 'affair' + 務 'duty/task' + 室 'room') is literally the 'task-duty room' — the physical room or space where desk/clerical work is done. Keep it apart from 회사 (會社), which is the *company* as an organization/employer: you work 사무실에서 (in the office room) but you belong to a 회사 (the firm). Also distinguish 사무실 from 사무소 (an office/agency open to clients, e.g. 부동산 사무소 'real-estate office') and from the casual loan 오피스. Natural partners: 사무실에서 일하다, 사무실에 있다, 사무실을 옮기다, 사무실 분위기. The English-speaker pitfall is the 에 vs 에서 split: use 에 for simply being there (사무실에 있어요) but 에서 for doing something there (사무실에서 일해요) — and don't substitute 사무실 when you mean the company itself; that's 회사.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사무실 to mean the company/employer — the organization is 회사: 회사에 다녀요 'I work for a company,' but 사무실 is the physical room.
Saying 사무실에 일해요 for working there — an action's place takes 에서: 사무실에서 일해요. Reserve 사무실에 for 있다/가다.
Confusing 사무실 with 사무소 — 사무소 is a client-facing office/agency (e.g. 변호사 사무소 'law office'); 사무실 is an internal workroom.

entries.shortExplanation: 부장 means "department head" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부장 (bujang) = "department head". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부장님이 부르시다. ("the department head calls/summons (honorific).") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Title + 님 + honorific 시: 부장님이 부르세요 'the manager is calling you.'

usagePhrases.en: to report to the department head.
usagePhrases.note: Superior recipient takes 께; 보고하다 'report' often becomes humble 보고드리다.
Surname + title + 님 is the standard way to address/refer to a ranked superior.
Existence of a superior uses honorific 계시다: 부장님이 계세요.

examples.en: The department head is in a meeting right now.
examples.note: Honorific 중이시다; 시 attaches even to the status copula for a superior.

examples.en: Please take this document to the department head.
examples.note: 께 (to a superior) + humble 드리다 + 갖다 드리다 'take and give'; 으세요 command.

examples.ko: 부장님이 결재해 주셔야 다음 단계로 넘어갈 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimi gyeoljaehae jusyeoya daeum dangyero neomeogal su isseoyo.
examples.en: We can move to the next step only once the manager signs off.
examples.note: Workplace process: 결재하다 'approve/sign off' + 주시다 honorific benefactive; ~어야 'only if.'

entries.nuance: 부장 (漢字 部長, 部 'department/division' + 長 'chief/head') is a department head — a senior manager who runs a 부서 (department), ranking above 과장 (section chief) and 대리, and below executives and the 사장 (company president). Like all Korean rank titles it functions as an honorific address: you say 부장님 (with 님), and you can prefix a surname — 김 부장님. The whole speech frame goes honorific around them (부르시다, 계시다, 결재해 주시다) while your own actions toward them turn humble (보고드리다, 갖다 드리다). Don't confuse the title-as-address with a name — Koreans routinely call the person 부장님 rather than by given name at work. The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 사장: dropping 님 (bare 부장 to their face is rude), using plain verbs instead of honorific 시, and marking the recipient with 에게 instead of the honorific 께.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Addressing the department head as bare 부장 — attach 님: 부장님 (optionally 성 + 부장님, e.g. 김 부장님). Plain 부장 sounds curt.
Using plain verbs for a superior (부장님이 왔어요) — go honorific: 부장님이 오셨어요 / 부장님이 계세요.
Marking 'to the manager' with 에게/한테 (부장님에게 보고했어요) — a superior takes 께: 부장님께 보고드렸어요.

The whole speech frame goes honorific around them (부르시다, 계시다, 결재해 주시다) while your own actions toward them turn humble (보고드리다, 갖다 드리다). 漢字 部長: 部 'department/division' + 長 'chief/head'.
The trap mirrors 사장: dropping 님 (bare 부장 to their face is rude), using plain verbs instead of honorific 시, and marking the recipient with 에게 instead of the honorific 께.

entries.shortExplanation: 가격 means "price" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가격 (gagyeok) means "price". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가격이 비싸요 ("the price is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: with prices Korean says 비싸다/싸다 (expensive/cheap), never 높다/낮다
object marker 을 + 물어보다 'ask and see'
깎다 'to shave/cut' is the verb for haggling
drop the particle in speech; 좀 softens the request

examples.en: How much is the price of this?
examples.note: simple: point at an item with 이거 and ask

examples.en: These clothes are way too expensive.
examples.note: everyday: 너무 'too' + 비싸요, the default price adjective

examples.ko: 가격은 좀 비싼데 품질이 좋아서 살게요.
examples.romanization: gagyeogeun jom bissande pumjiri joaseo salgeyo.
examples.en: The price is a bit high, but the quality is good so I'll buy it.
examples.note: real situation: weighing 가격 against 품질 (quality) out loud

entries.nuance: 가격(價格) is Sino-Korean — 價 'value/price' + 格 'standard' — so it literally means the 'value-standard' set on a thing, the official posted price. Its native-Korean twin is 값, and the line is feel and register: 값 is shorter, warmer, and used in fixed everyday phrases (값이 싸다, 값을 치르다), while 가격 sounds more neutral and 'tag/system' (가격표 price tag, 가격 인상 price hike) and is what you read on signs. The biggest English-speaker trap is the adjective: a high price is 비싸요 (expensive), a low price is 싸요 (cheap) — Koreans do NOT say 가격이 높아요/낮아요 the way English says 'high/low price', so importing 'high' here sounds off. Note too that to ask a clerk you rarely say the noun at all: the natural line is just 얼마예요? ('how much?'). 가격 collocates with 비싸다, 싸다, 오르다 (rise), 내리다 (drop), and 깎다 (haggle down).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가격이 높아요 for 'the price is high' — that is a direct translation of English; Korean uses 비싸요 (expensive). Use 높다/낮다 only for height or numbers like temperature, not for prices.
Treating 가격 and 값 as freely swappable — they overlap, but you say 값을 치르다 (pay the price), not 가격을 치르다, and 가격표 (price tag), not 값표. Learn them as set phrases.
Asking a shopkeeper 가격이 뭐예요? ('what is the price?'). The natural question is 얼마예요? or 가격이 얼마예요?, never 뭐예요 for an amount.

structuredNuance.t: 가격 is the official posted price, the 'value-standard' set on a thing. It sounds neutral and 'tag/system' (가격표 price tag, 가격 인상 price hike) and is what you read on signs. It collocates with 비싸다, 싸다, 오르다 (rise), 내리다 (drop), and 깎다 (haggle down).
Its native-Korean twin is 값, and the line is feel and register: 값 is shorter, warmer, and used in fixed everyday phrases (값이 싸다, 값을 치르다), while 가격 sounds more neutral and system-like.
가격(價格) is Sino-Korean — 價 'value/price' + 格 'standard' — so it literally means the 'value-standard' set on a thing.

The biggest English-speaker trap is the adjective: a high price is 비싸요 (expensive), a low price is 싸요 (cheap) — Koreans do NOT say 가격이 높아요/낮아요 the way English says 'high/low price', so importing 'high' here sounds off. Note too that to ask a clerk you rarely say the noun at all: the natural line is just 얼마예요? ('how much?').

Watch the particle attached to 할인 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 할인 + 되다 'gets done'; the price-side passive, 'it is discounted'
받다 'receive' — you, the customer, are the receiver
할인하다 + 주다; what you actually say to bargain
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 'be able to' for asking if it's possible

examples.en: Is this discounted today?
examples.note: simple: 할인되다 as one verb, 'get discounted'

examples.en: Can students get a discount?
examples.note: everyday: 받다 puts the customer as receiver of the discount

examples.en: If you're a member, I'll give you 10 percent off.
examples.note: real situation: a clerk speaking up, using 해 드리다 (humble 'do for you')

entries.nuance: 할인(割引) is Sino-Korean — 割 'cut' + 引 'pull (down)' — literally 'cut and pull down', i.e. knock money off a price. The key contrast for learners is 할인 vs 세일: 할인 is the abstract act/amount of reducing a price on an item ('10% off', a discount), while 세일 (from English 'sale') names a store-wide selling event (백화점 세일 a department-store sale). So a 세일 contains many 할인s. Watch the voice carefully: from the price's point of view you say 할인이 되다/할인되다 ('it gets discounted'); from your point of view as buyer you say 할인을 받다 ('I receive a discount'); and to actively ask for one you say 할인해 주세요 ('please discount it for me'). The English-speaker pitfall is firing 할인해요 at a clerk hoping it means 'give me a discount' — bare 할인해요 just states 'someone discounts', so it lands as a flat description, not a request. Add 주세요/돼요 to make it work. Common partners: 할인되다, 할인받다, 할인 행사 (discount event), 할인 쿠폰.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 할인해요 to a clerk to mean 'please give me a discount'. Without 주세요 it is just a statement; the request form is 할인해 주세요 or the softer 좀 깎아 주세요.
Mixing up the receiver: customers say 할인을 받다 (receive a discount), shops say 할인을 해 주다 (give a discount). Saying 할인을 줘요 about yourself ('I give a discount') reverses the roles.
Using 세일 when you mean a discount on one item. 'This bag is 30% off' is 이 가방은 30퍼센트 할인이에요, not 세일이에요 — 세일 is the whole event, not the single markdown.

Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: (으)로 'by means of' is THE particle for payment method
계산하다 'settle/check out' — common at registers
만 'only' + 되다 'works/is OK'
현금 영수증 is the tax receipt clerks ask about

examples.en: I'll pay with cash.
examples.note: simple: 으로 marks the method, 낼게요 'I'll pay' shows your intention

examples.en: I'm a bit short on cash right now.
examples.note: everyday: 모자라다 'be short/lacking' is more natural here than 없다

examples.ko: 여기는 카드 안 되고 현금만 받아요.
examples.romanization: yeogineun kadeu an doego hyeongeumman badayo.
examples.en: They don't take card here, only cash.
examples.note: real situation: contrasting 카드 vs 현금 with 만 'only'

entries.nuance: 현금(現金) is Sino-Korean — 現 'present/actual' + 金 'gold/money' — literally 'actual money', i.e. physical notes and coins you hand over, as opposed to 카드 (card) or 계좌이체 (bank transfer). The crucial grammar point is the particle: payment method takes 으로/로 ('by means of'), so 'pay with cash' is 현금으로 내다/계산하다 — English speakers reach for 'with' and wrongly grab 와/하고 (which mean 'together with a person/thing') or 에 (location/time). 현금 is more specific than the umbrella word 돈 (money): 돈 covers wealth in general, but 현금 specifically means money in hand right now (you can have lots of 돈 in the bank but no 현금 in your wallet). A very useful real-life phrase is 현금 영수증 ('cash receipt') — a registered receipt for tax deduction that clerks routinely offer with 현금 영수증 해 드릴까요? Collocations: 현금으로 내다/계산하다/결제하다, 현금만 받다, 현금이 모자라다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 에 or 하고 for 'with cash' — 현금에 내요 or 현금하고 내요 are wrong. The means particle is 으로: 현금으로 내요. Reserve 하고/와 for accompaniment ('with a friend').
Treating 현금 and 돈 as identical. 돈이 없어요 can mean you're broke overall; 현금이 없어요 specifically means you have no physical cash on you (maybe you have a card). Pick the one you mean.
Forgetting that 되다 marks acceptability: 'is cash OK?' is 현금 돼요?, and 'cash only' is 현금만 돼요. Saying 현금 있어요? to ask a shop's policy asks whether the SHOP has cash, not whether they accept it.

(으)로 again marks the means of payment
개 is the counter for small objects: 동전 한 개, 두 개
바꾸다 'exchange/break (a bill)' into coins

examples.note: simple: 에 marks location (in the wallet), 많아요 'are many'

examples.ko: 동전 다섯 개로 자판기에서 음료를 샀어요.
examples.romanization: dongjeon daseot gaero japangieseo eumnyoreul sasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought a drink from the vending machine with five coins.
examples.note: everyday: counter 개 + 으로 for paying with coins

examples.ko: 주머니에 동전이 가득해서 걸을 때마다 짤랑거려요.
examples.romanization: jumeonie dongjeoni gadeukaeseo georeul ttaemada jjallanggeoryeoyo.
examples.en: My pocket is full of coins, so they jingle every time I walk.
examples.note: real situation: 가득하다 'be full' + the onomatopoeia 짤랑거리다 'jingle'

entries.nuance: 동전(銅錢) is Sino-Korean — 銅 'copper' + 錢 'coin/money' — literally 'copper money', the metal money minted as coins (10원, 100원, 500원). Its partner is 지폐(紙幣) 'paper currency' = bills; together 동전 + 지폐 make up 현금. So the dividing line is material: 동전 = metal coins, 지폐 = paper notes, and you must not call a 1,000원 note a 동전. A second word to keep separate is 잔돈, which means 'small change / leftover change' — 잔돈 is about the FUNCTION (the change you get back), and can be coins or small bills, whereas 동전 strictly names the coin object. The English-speaker pitfall is also the counter: coins are counted with 개 (동전 세 개 'three coins'), not with a 'piece' word you might invent, and the means particle for paying is 으로 (동전으로). Collocations: 동전을 모으다 (collect coins), 동전을 바꾸다 (break a bill into coins), 동전이 무겁다, 동전 지갑 (coin purse).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling paper money 동전. A 만원짜리 is a 지폐 (bill), not a 동전. 동전 is metal coins only; the cover term for both is 현금.
Confusing 동전 with 잔돈. When you want 'keep the change', say 잔돈은 괜찮아요, not 동전은 괜찮아요 — 잔돈 is the change you receive, which may include small bills, while 동전 just names coins as objects.

Watch the particle attached to 지갑 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 있다 'have'; 이 because it ends in a consonant
잃어버리다 = 잃다 + 버리다 'lose (completely, regretfully)'
두고 오다 'put down and came' — the set phrase for forgetting things

usagePhrases.en: I take a card out of the wallet
usagePhrases.note: 에서 'out of' + 꺼내다 'take out'

examples.en: My wallet is inside my bag.
examples.note: simple: 안에 'inside' locates 지갑 within 가방

examples.ko: 지갑을 집에 두고 와서 돈이 하나도 없어요.
examples.romanization: jigabeul jibe dugo waseo doni hanado eopseoyo.
examples.en: I left my wallet at home, so I have no money at all.
examples.note: everyday: 두고 오다 for forgetting + 하나도 없다 'not even one'

examples.ko: 지하철에서 누가 제 지갑을 훔쳐 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo nuga je jigabeul humchyeo gasseoyo.
examples.en: Someone stole my wallet on the subway.
examples.note: real situation: 훔쳐 가다 'steal and take away', a phrase you'd need in an emergency

entries.nuance: 지갑(紙匣) is Sino-Korean — 紙 'paper' + 匣 'small box/case' — historically a 'paper case', now the small folding holder for your money, cards, and ID. Don't confuse it with 가방, which is the larger bag/handbag/backpack you carry items in: a 지갑 typically goes INSIDE a 가방. Modern usage has stretched 지갑 to digital things too — your phone's payment app is a 모바일 지갑 ('mobile wallet') — but the core image is the physical billfold. A subtle pitfall is the verb of forgetting: English 'I forgot my wallet' becomes Korean 지갑을 두고 왔어요 ('I put it down and came'), NOT 지갑을 잊어버렸어요 — 잊어버리다 is for forgetting information/facts (a name, an appointment), while physically leaving an object behind is 두고 오다. For losing it irretrievably you use 잃어버리다. Collocations: 지갑을 열다 (open the wallet → spend), 지갑이 가볍다/두둑하다 (thin/fat wallet = broke/flush), 지갑을 챙기다 (grab your wallet), 동전 지갑 (coin purse).

Saying 지갑을 잊어버렸어요 for 'I forgot/left my wallet'. 잊어버리다 is for forgetting facts; for leaving a physical object behind, use 지갑을 두고 왔어요. To lose it for good, use 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.
Confusing 지갑 (wallet) with 가방 (bag). The small money holder is 지갑; the big carrier is 가방. 지갑 goes inside 가방, so they are not interchangeable.
Forgetting the particle when taking something out: it's 지갑에서 카드를 꺼내다 (out of the wallet), using 에서 for the source, not 지갑에 (which would mark a destination or static location).

Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 주다 'give' + 세요; the standard checkout request
필요하다 'be needed'; the thing needed takes 가/이

usagePhrases.en: please put it in a bag
usagePhrases.note: 에 'into' + 넣다 'put in' + 주세요
plastic bags are paid (봉투 값), a real-life detail in Korea

examples.en: Please give me one bag.
examples.note: simple: drop the particle in speech, 하나 'one' as a loose counter

examples.en: Please put them in separate bags.
examples.note: everyday: 따로따로 'separately' + 에 넣다, a real checkout request

examples.en: The bag costs 100 won — do you need one?
examples.note: real situation: a clerk asking, since paid bags are law in Korea

entries.nuance: 봉투(封套) is Sino-Korean — 封 'seal/close' + 套 'cover/case' — literally a 'sealing cover', i.e. a flat sleeve. That's why one word covers two things: the thin shopping bag a shop gives you (비닐봉투 plastic, 종이봉투 paper) AND a paper envelope for letters or money (편지봉투 letter envelope, and the cash gift envelopes used at weddings/funerals). Contrast it sharply with 가방, the sturdy bag with handles you own and reuse (backpack, handbag, suitcase): a 봉투 is flimsy and disposable, a 가방 is a possession. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'bag' maps onto BOTH, so learners say 봉투 when they mean a backpack — wrong; that's 가방/배낭. A useful cultural-practical note: in Korea store bags are not free, so 봉투 값 ('bag fee') and the clerk's question 봉투 드릴까요? / 봉투 필요하세요? are everyday phrases worth knowing. Collocations: 봉투에 넣다 (put in a bag), 봉투를 주다/받다, 비닐봉투, 종이봉투, 봉투 값.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 봉투 for a backpack or handbag. A reusable carry-bag is 가방 (or 배낭 backpack); 봉투 is the flimsy throwaway shopping bag or a paper envelope. Don't say 봉투를 메다 for wearing a backpack.
Forgetting that bags are paid items in Korea, so the clerk's 봉투 필요하세요? is a real cost question, not just politeness. Answer 네, 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요.
Mixing up the particle: you put things 봉투에 (into the bag), using 에 for destination. Saying 봉투에서 넣어요 reverses it to 'out of the bag', which is the opposite action.

examples.romanization: gyesandaemada juri neomu gireoseo selpeu gyesandaero gasseoyo.
examples.en: Every checkout had such a long line that I went to the self-checkout.
examples.note: real situation: 마다 'each' + 셀프 계산대 (self-checkout), a modern store reality

entries.nuance: 계산대(計算臺) is Sino-Korean — 計算 'calculation/reckoning' + 臺 'platform/stand' — literally the 'reckoning platform', the counter where the total is tallied and you pay. Keep three related words apart: 계산대 is the PLACE (the physical counter), 계산 is the ACT of paying/settling up (계산할게요 'I'll pay'), and 계산서 is the BILL/check that lists what you owe (common in restaurants). So you walk 계산대로 (to the counter), do the 계산 (paying), and may read a 계산서 (bill). The two direction-vs-location particles matter: heading toward it is 계산대로 가다 (으)로 for direction), but the paying happens 계산대에서 (에서 for the location of an action). The English-speaker pitfall is using 계산대 as if it were the action — 'I'll do the checkout' is 계산할게요 (verb 계산하다), not 계산대 할게요. In modern stores you'll also meet 셀프 계산대 (self-checkout) and 무인 계산대 (unmanned kiosk). Collocations: 계산대로 가다, 계산대에서 계산하다, 계산대 줄, 셀프 계산대.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 계산대 (the counter, a place) with 계산 (the act of paying). 'I'll pay' is 계산할게요, not 계산대 할게요. The -대 ending names the physical stand.
Mixing the particles: go 계산대로 (toward it, direction 로), but pay 계산대에서 (at it, action location 에서). Saying 계산대에 계산해요 misuses 에 for an action that needs 에서.
Saying 계산서 when you mean the counter. 계산서 is the itemized bill/check (mostly at restaurants); the counter you pay at is 계산대.

entries.shortExplanation: 손님 means "customer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "customer" is 손님 (sonnim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 손님이 많아요 ("there are many customers"). Watch the particle attached to 손님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 많다 'be many'; subject 이 after a consonant
object 을 + 기다리다 'wait for'
분 is the honorific counter for people, raising respect
모시다 is the humble verb for serving a respected person

examples.en: There are a lot of customers in the shop today.
examples.note: simple: 에 marks the location, 많아요 'are many'

examples.ko: 손님 한 분이 입구에서 기다리고 계세요.
examples.romanization: sonnim han buni ipgueseo gidarigo gyeseyo.
examples.en: One customer is waiting at the entrance.
examples.note: everyday: honorific 분 + 계시다 to respectfully describe the customer

examples.en: Sir/Ma'am, would you come this way?
examples.note: real situation: 손님 used as a direct address term by staff, with honorific -시-

entries.nuance: 손님 is native Korean — 손 'guest' + the honorific suffix -님 — so it builds 'guest' into a respectful form, and it covers BOTH a paying customer in a shop AND a guest visiting your home. That built-in 님 is why 손님 is inherently polite and why staff address you directly as 손님 (like English 'sir/ma'am'). Contrast it with the neutral 사람 'person' (too plain and even rude to call a customer) and with 고객, the more formal/corporate term banks, telecoms, and notices use (고객님, 고객 센터 customer center) — 손님 feels face-to-face and shop-floor, 고객 feels institutional. Because 손님 deserves respect, it's counted with the honorific 분 (손님 한 분, not 한 명) and described with honorific verbs (오시다 'come', 계시다 'be present', 기다리고 계세요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사람 ('a person came to the shop' → 사람이 왔어요 sounds cold); say 손님이 오셨어요. Collocations: 손님을 받다 (take/receive customers), 손님이 들다 (customers come in), 단골손님 (regular), 손님 접대 (hosting guests).

Using 사람 instead of 손님 for a customer or guest. 사람이 왔어요 ('a person came') sounds blunt; in a shop or home, say 손님이 왔어요/오셨어요 to show due respect.
Counting customers with 명 instead of the honorific 분. Say 손님 두 분, not 손님 두 명 — 분 raises the politeness that 손님 implies.
Treating 손님 and 고객 as identical in tone. Use 손님 face-to-face in shops and homes; use 고객(님) for formal/written/corporate contexts like 고객 센터 (customer service center).

entries.shortExplanation: 점원 means "store clerk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 점원 (jeomwon) = "store clerk". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 점원이 친절해요 ("the clerk is kind") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 점원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 친절하다 'be kind/courteous', a typical thing to say about staff
에게 'to (a person)' + 물어보다 'ask'
도와주다 = 돕다 + 주다 'help (for someone)'
부르다 'call'; in real life you'd say 저기요 to get attention

examples.en: The clerk at this shop is very kind.
examples.note: simple: describing staff with 친절하다

examples.en: I asked the clerk if there was another color.
examples.note: everyday: 에게 (to the clerk) + -는지 'whether' embedded question

examples.en: Excuse me, can I try this on?
examples.note: real situation: in practice you call out 저기요 to a clerk, not 점원!

entries.nuance: 점원(店員) is Sino-Korean — 店 'shop/store' + 員 'member/staff' — literally a 'shop staff member', the salesperson who works the floor and helps customers, the natural counterpart to 손님 (customer). Distinguish nearby words: 직원(職員) is the broader 'employee/staff' of any organization (office, bank, company), while 점원 specifically means a shop assistant; 사장(님) is the boss/owner; and 알바(생) is a part-timer. The single most important pitfall for English speakers is that 점원 is a descriptive label, not an address term — you never call out '점원!' to summon them the way English barks 'Clerk!'. To get a clerk's attention you say 저기요 ('excuse me') or 여기요, and to refer to them respectfully you can say 직원분 or 사장님. So 점원 mostly appears when you TALK ABOUT staff (점원이 친절했어요), and you switch to 저기요 when you TALK TO them. The person to ask takes 에게/한테 (점원에게 물어보다). Collocations: 점원이 친절하다, 점원에게 묻다/물어보다, 점원이 도와주다, 점원을 부르다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling out 점원! to get a clerk's attention. 점원 is a label, not a vocative. Say 저기요 or 여기요 to summon staff, and 사장님/직원분 to address them politely.
Confusing 점원 (shop clerk) with 직원 (employee in general). A bank or office worker is a 직원; a store salesperson is a 점원. They overlap but 점원 is shop-specific.
Using the wrong particle for the person you ask: it's 점원에게/점원한테 물어봐요 ('ask TO the clerk'), not 점원을 물어봐요, which would oddly mean 'ask about the clerk'.

entries.shortExplanation: 세일 means "sale" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 세일 (seil) means "sale". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 세일을 해요 ("there's a sale (on)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 세일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 세일 + 하다; the store 'does' a sale
중 'in the middle of' = currently running
끝나다 'come to an end'
기간 'period/duration' + 세일, e.g. 세일 기간에 'during the sale'

examples.en: Is there a sale on right now?
examples.note: simple: 중이에요 'is in progress', a quick question to a clerk

examples.en: The department store is having a sale this week.
examples.note: everyday: 세일을 하다 'hold a sale', the store as the doer

examples.ko: 세일 기간이라 평소보다 훨씬 싸게 샀어요.
examples.romanization: seil giganira pyeongsoboda hwolssin ssage sasseoyo.
examples.en: Since it was the sale period, I bought it much cheaper than usual.
examples.note: real situation: 기간이라 '(because) it's the period' + 싸게 사다 'buy cheaply'

entries.nuance: 세일 is a loanword from English 'sale', but Korean has narrowed it to mean specifically a store-wide markdown EVENT — a period when a whole shop or department store cuts prices (백화점 세일, 시즌 오프 세일). It is not the general word for 'selling': 'to sell' is the native verb 팔다, and a one-item price cut is 할인 (discount). So the sharp contrast is 세일 (the event/season) vs 할인 (the act/amount of discounting a given item): a bag inside a 세일 might have a 30% 할인. Grammatically 세일 pairs with 하다 (세일을 하다 'hold a sale') and lives in time phrases (세일 중, 세일 기간, 세일 때). The English-speaker pitfall is double: (1) don't use 세일 to mean 'sell' — 'I sold my phone' is 폰을 팔았어요, never 세일했어요; and (2) for a discount on a single product prefer 할인. Note also Korean keeps the borrowed -ㄹ sound, so it's 세일 (se-il), two syllables. Collocations: 세일을 하다, 세일 중이다, 세일 기간/때, 시즌 오프 세일.

Using 세일 to mean 'to sell'. 'They sell shoes here' is 여기서 신발을 팔아요, not 세일해요. 세일 only names a discount event; the verb 'sell' is 팔다.
Saying 세일 for a single item's discount. 'This is 20% off' is better as 이건 20퍼센트 할인이에요; 세일 refers to the whole store-wide event, 할인 to the markdown itself.
Forgetting 세일 takes 하다 and time words. 'There's a sale now' is 지금 세일 중이에요 / 지금 세일해요, not 세일이에요 alone, which sounds incomplete.

entries.shortExplanation: 환불 means "refund" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "refund" is 환불 (hwanbul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 환불을 받아요 ("I get a refund"). Watch the particle attached to 환불 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 'receive'; you, the buyer, get your money back
환불하다 + 주세요; what you say to request it
환불 + 되다 'be doable', about store policy
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 to ask if it's allowed

examples.en: Can I get a refund on this?
examples.note: simple: 환불되다 as one verb to ask about policy

examples.ko: 영수증이 있으면 환불 받을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yeongsujeungi isseumyeon hwanbul badeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you have the receipt, you can get a refund.
examples.note: everyday: -(으)면 'if' condition + 받을 수 있다 'can receive'

examples.ko: 사이즈가 안 맞아서 환불하러 왔는데요, 카드로 결제했어요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga an majaseo hwanbulhareo wanneundeyo, kadeuro gyeoljehaesseoyo.
examples.en: I came to get a refund because the size doesn't fit; I paid by card.
examples.note: real situation: -러 오다 'come in order to' + explaining 결제 (payment) method

entries.nuance: 환불(還拂) is Sino-Korean — 還 'return/give back' + 拂 'pay out' — literally 'pay back', i.e. returning the buyer's money for a returned item. The contrast learners must nail is 환불 vs 교환: 환불 = money back, 교환(交換 'exchange') = swap for a different item/size/color, no money returned. A related word is 반품(返品) 'returning the goods' — the physical act of sending the product back, which usually triggers a 환불. So you 반품 the item and receive a 환불. Voice matters as with 할인: from your side you say 환불을 받다 ('receive a refund'); to request it you say 환불해 주세요 ('refund it for me'); about whether it's allowed you say 환불이 되다/환불되다 ('a refund is possible'). The English-speaker pitfall is wanting an exchange but saying 환불 — if you actually want a different size, ask 교환돼요? / 교환해 주세요, because 환불 will give you cash back, not a swap. Note Korean also uses 결제 (결제하다) for 'make a payment/settle by card', often in the same conversation. Collocations: 환불을 받다, 환불해 주다, 환불되다, 환불 정책 (refund policy), 환불 규정.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 환불 when you want an exchange. 환불 returns your money; to swap for another size/color say 교환해 주세요 or ask 교환돼요?. They are different transactions.
Reversing the giver/receiver: customers say 환불을 받다 (receive a refund); shops say 환불해 주다 (give a refund). 환불을 줘요 about yourself wrongly casts you as the one paying back.

entries.shortExplanation: 영수증 means "receipt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 영수증 (yeongsujeung) = "receipt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영수증을 주세요 ("please give me the receipt") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 영수증, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 주다 + 세요; the basic checkout request
필요하다 'be needed'; the needed thing takes 가/이
받다 'receive', the customer's side
버리다 'throw away', a common follow-up action

examples.en: Could I have the receipt, please?
examples.note: simple: 좀 softens the request, particle dropped in speech

examples.en: You absolutely need the receipt to get a refund.
examples.note: everyday: -려면 'if you want to' + 꼭 'definitely' tying 영수증 to 환불

examples.en: Would you like the receipt, or shall I throw it away for you?
examples.note: real situation: the exact clerk's question, with humble 드리다 'give'

entries.nuance: 영수증(領收證) is Sino-Korean — 領 'receive' + 收 'collect' + 證 'proof/certificate' — literally a 'proof of receiving (payment)', the printed slip showing the shop got your money. Distinguish it from 계산서(計算書) 'the bill/check', which is the itemized statement of what you OWE (you read a 계산서 before paying, mostly at restaurants), whereas the 영수증 is issued AFTER you pay as proof. Also keep 영수증 apart from 현금 영수증, a specifically Korean tax-deduction receipt tied to your phone number that clerks ask about separately. Because clerks routinely offer it, you'll constantly hear the polite 영수증 드릴까요? ('shall I give you the receipt?', humble 드리다 raising you the customer), and the practical answer is 네, 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요. The English-speaker pitfall is mislabeling: don't call the receipt a 계산서 — that's the pre-payment bill — and remember a refund hinges on it (환불하려면 영수증이 필요해요). Collocations: 영수증을 주다/받다, 영수증이 필요하다, 영수증을 챙기다 (keep the receipt), 현금 영수증, 영수증을 버리다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 영수증 (proof-of-payment receipt, given after you pay) with 계산서 (the itemized bill you read before paying, common at restaurants). They sit on opposite sides of the payment.
Answering the clerk's 영수증 드릴까요? with the wrong move. 'Yes please' is 네, 주세요; 'no thanks' is 아니요, 괜찮아요. Saying just 네 without 주세요 can sound abrupt.
Forgetting the receipt is required for refunds. Throwing it away then asking 환불해 주세요 won't work; keep it (영수증을 챙기다) if you might return the item.

('shall I give you the receipt?', humble 드리다 raising you the customer), and the practical answer is 네, 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요. entries.shortExplanation: 기차 means "train" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기차 (gicha) means "train". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기차를 타요 ("I take the train"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: take a vehicle = 을/를 + 타다, never 에
로 marks the means of transport
getting off uses 에서 + 내리다
the departure schedule, not the clock

examples.en: The train is coming.
examples.note: Simple present; 가/이 marks the subject arriving.

examples.en: It takes three hours to Busan by train.
examples.note: 까지 = up to, 로 = by; everyday travel-time talk.

examples.ko: 기차표를 미리 예매하지 않으면 명절에는 자리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: gichapyoreul miri yemaehaji aneumyeon myeongjeoreneun jariga eopseoyo.
examples.en: If you don't book train tickets in advance, there are no seats during the holidays.
examples.note: Real situation: 예매 (advance booking) is essential for 명절 travel.

entries.nuance: 기차 (汽車, literally 'steam-vehicle') is an inter-city railway train you ride for longer trips between towns — Seoul to Busan, say — not the urban subway. The sharp dividing line learners must keep: 지하철 is the city subway/metro, 전철 is an above-ground commuter electric train, and the premium high-speed services have their own names (KTX, SRT) that Koreans use directly instead of 기차. Register is fully neutral, fine in any setting. It habitually pairs with 타다 (board), 표/기차표 (ticket), 예매하다 (book ahead), 출발하다/도착하다 (depart/arrive), and counts stations or hours of travel. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle on 타다: you 'get on' a train in English so people reach for 기차에 타요, but Korean treats the vehicle as a direct object — 기차를 타요. Also resist calling the subway 기차; inside a city it is almost always 지하철.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기차에 타요 because English 'get on the train' suggests 에 — Korean uses 기차를 타다 (vehicle as object), so the correct form is 기차를 타요.
Calling the city subway 기차 — within a city Koreans say 지하철; 기차 is reserved for inter-city rail, so use 지하철을 타요 for the metro.
Saying 기차에서 가요 for going by train — to express the means you need 기차로 가요; 에서 marks where you are, not how you travel.

entries.shortExplanation: 비행기 means "airplane" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "airplane" is 비행기 (bihaenggi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비행기를 타요 ("I take the airplane"). Watch the particle attached to 비행기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: board = 을/를 + 타다, not 에
로 marks the means of travel
항공권 is the formal ticket word
놓치다 = miss a departure

examples.en: The airplane flies high.
examples.note: Simple sentence; 날다 (to fly) is the verb that goes with it.

examples.ko: 인천에서 비행기로 두 시간이면 도쿄에 도착해요.
examples.romanization: incheoneseo bihaenggiro du siganimyeon dokyoe dochakaeyo.
examples.en: From Incheon it's two hours to Tokyo by plane.
examples.note: Everyday travel math: 에서 = from a starting point, 로 = by means.

examples.ko: 비행기가 연착돼서 환승 시간을 놓칠 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: bihaenggiga yeonchakdwaeseo hwanseung siganeul notchil ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: The flight was delayed so I almost missed my connection.
examples.note: Real situation: 연착 (delay), 환승 (transfer) — airport vocabulary.

entries.nuance: 비행기 (飛行機, literally 'fly-go-machine') is the everyday spoken word for an airplane — the aircraft you board for trips abroad or across the country. Its near-synonym 항공기 means the same machine but is a stiffer, technical/news register ('aircraft'), and the ticket has its own formal twin: spoken 비행기 표 vs. written/official 항공권. It collocates with 타다 (board), 표/항공권 (ticket), 예약하다 (reserve), 연착되다 (be delayed), 환승하다 (transfer), and 공항 (airport). As with all vehicles, the pitfall is the particle: 'get on the plane' tempts 비행기에 타요, but Korean wants the object marker — 비행기를 타요. A second subtle trap is 타다 vs 내리다: you board with 비행기를 타다 (object) but disembark with 비행기에서 내리다 (source), so the particle flips between getting on and getting off.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비행기에 타요 to mean 'board the plane' — Korean uses the object marker, so the natural form is 비행기를 타요.
Using 비행기에서 가요 for 'go by plane' — the means takes 로, giving 비행기로 가요; 에서 only marks the place you are in.
Treating 항공권 as casual speech — in conversation Koreans usually say 비행기 표; save 항공권 for booking sites and formal writing.

entries.shortExplanation: 자전거 means "bicycle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자전거 (jajeongeo) = "bicycle". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 자전거를 타요 ("I ride a bicycle") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 자전거, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ride = 을/를 + 타다
로 marks the means
도로 = dedicated cycle road
빌리다 = borrow/rent a share-bike

examples.en: I ride a bicycle.
examples.note: Core verb: 타다 covers bikes, cars, buses — anything you mount or board.

examples.en: Riding a bike along the Han River feels really refreshing.
examples.note: Everyday: 에서 marks the place of the activity; 한강 is the classic cycling spot.

examples.en: I rent a Ttareungi and commute to work by bike.
examples.note: Real situation: 따릉이 is Seoul's public share-bike; 출근하다 = commute to work.

entries.nuance: 자전거 (自轉車, literally 'self-turning-vehicle') is a human-powered two-wheeler for short trips or exercise, hugely popular along rivers and parks. Two near-neighbors trip learners up: its motorized cousin 오토바이 (a loanword scooter with an engine, no hanja) looks similar but is never called 자전거 since 자전거 has no motor; and 자동차 (自動車, 'self-moving-vehicle' = car) differs from 자전거 by just one hanja — 動 (move) vs 轉 (turn) — so the two written forms are easy to misread for each other. It pairs with 타다 (ride), 도로/길 (lane/path), 빌리다 (rent), 헬멧 (helmet), and brand-name share systems like 따릉이. The pitfall: English 'go by bike' and 'ride a bike' use different structures, and learners drop the right particle — for the means say 자전거로 가요 (instrumental 로), for the act of riding say 자전거를 타요 (object 를); never 자전거에 가요. Also note Koreans say 자전거를 타다, not a verb like 'pedal'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 자전거에 가요 for 'go by bike' — the instrument particle is 로, so it must be 자전거로 가요.
Confusing 자전거 (bicycle) with 자동차 (car); they share 自...車 but differ by 轉 (turn) vs 動 (move) — keep 자전거 for the pedal bike.
Inventing a verb like 자전거해요 — Korean has no such verb; you 'ride' it with 타다, giving 자전거를 타요.

entries.shortExplanation: 오토바이 means "motorcycle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 오토바이 (otobai) means "motorcycle". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오토바이를 타요 ("I ride a motorcycle"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오토바이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ride = 을/를 + 타다
로 marks the means
배달 = the food-delivery scooter
the engine roar

examples.en: The motorcycle is loud.
examples.note: Simple description; 시끄럽다 (noisy) is a ㅂ-irregular adjective.

examples.en: Delivery usually comes by motorcycle.
examples.note: Everyday: 로 marks the means; 배달 culture runs on scooters in Korea.

examples.en: Motorcycles are dangerous, so be sure to wear a helmet.
examples.note: Real situation: 위험하다 (dangerous) + 니까 (so) gives advice; 헬멧을 쓰다 = wear a helmet.

entries.nuance: 오토바이 is a loanword adapted from English 'auto-bi(ke)' (it is NOT Sino-Korean, so there is no hanja) and names an engine-powered two-wheeler — in Korea overwhelmingly the food-delivery scooter weaving through city traffic. The crucial contrast is with 자전거: same two-wheel shape, but 오토바이 has a motor and 자전거 does not, so never swap them. A textbook word 이륜차 ('two-wheeled vehicle') exists but is officialese for signs and law; in speech everyone says 오토바이. Heavier road bikes are sometimes called 바이크. It collocates with 타다 (ride), 배달 (delivery), 헬멧 (helmet), 시끄럽다/위험하다 (loud/dangerous). The pitfall is again the vehicle particle — say 오토바이를 타요 (object), not 오토바이에 타요 — plus, because it is a foreign loanword, English speakers tend to mispronounce it; keep all four syllables o-to-ba-i, not 'motorbike'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a 자전거 an 오토바이 — only the motorized scooter is 오토바이; the pedal bike is 자전거, so don't merge them.
Saying 오토바이에 타요 — board a vehicle with the object marker: 오토바이를 타요.
Pronouncing it like English 'motorbike' — it is the loanword 오토바이 (o-to-ba-i); using the English word will not be understood.

entries.shortExplanation: 자동차 means "car" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "car" is 자동차 (jadongcha). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 자동차를 타요 ("I ride in a car"). Watch the particle attached to 자동차 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: board = 을/를 + 타다
로 marks the means
교통사고 is the broader term
운전하다 = to drive

examples.en: There are a lot of cars.
examples.note: Simple sentence; 많다 describes quantity on the road.

examples.en: On weekends I go to the sea by car.
examples.note: Everyday: 로 = by means; a typical weekend-trip frame.

examples.ko: 요즘은 전기 자동차를 사는 사람이 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jeongi jadongchareul saneun sarami manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: These days more people are buying electric cars.
examples.note: Real situation: 전기 자동차 (EV), 많아지다 (to increase) — a current trend.

entries.nuance: 자동차 (自動車, literally 'self-moving-vehicle') is the full, slightly formal word for a car/automobile; in everyday speech Koreans clip it to plain 차 (e.g. 차 타고 가자 'let's go by car'), so 자동차 feels more like writing, signage, or careful speech while 차 dominates conversation. Note 차 is a homonym — it also means 'tea' — but context and collocation keep them apart. It differs from 자전거 by one hanja (動 move vs 轉 turn). Habitual partners: 타다 (ride), 운전하다 (drive), 사고 (accident), 막히다 (be jammed), 전기/중고 자동차 (electric/used car). Two pitfalls: first the means particle — 자동차로 가요, not 자동차에 가요; second, 타다 means 'ride in' generally, but to say you operate the car you need a different verb, 운전하다 (drive) — don't stretch 타다 to cover driving.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 자동차에 가요 for 'go by car' — the instrumental particle is 로: 자동차로 가요.
Using 타다 to mean 'drive' — 자동차를 타다 is 'ride in a car'; to say you drive it, use 자동차를 운전하다.
Forgetting 차 alone can mean 'tea' — rely on context/collocation (차 한 잔 = a cup of tea vs 차로 가다 = go by car) so the two readings don't clash.

entries.shortExplanation: 신호등 means "traffic light" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 신호등 (sinhodeung) = "traffic light". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 빨간 신호등 ("red light") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 신호등, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 빨간 modifies it; the stop signal
바뀌다 = the color turns
지키다 = keep/observe the signal

usagePhrases.en: I stop in front of the light
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place of stopping

examples.en: The traffic light is red.
examples.note: Simple sentence; 색 names the color directly.

examples.en: Cross when the light turns green.
examples.note: Everyday: 면 (when/if) gives a condition; 초록불 = green light.

examples.ko: 신호등을 안 지키고 건너면 정말 위험해요.
examples.romanization: sinhodeungeul an jikigo geonneomyeon jeongmal wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: It's really dangerous to cross without obeying the lights.
examples.note: Real situation: 지키다 here = obey a rule, a key collocation for signals.

entries.nuance: 신호등 (信號燈, literally 'signal-lamp', 信號 = signal + 燈 = lamp) is the colored traffic light that controls cars and pedestrians at a crossing. Keep it apart from the bare word 신호, which means the 'signal' itself (you can 신호를 기다리다 'wait for the signal'), whereas 신호등 is the physical lamp unit. The individual colors get -불 ('light/fire'): 빨간불 red, 노란불 yellow, 초록불/파란불 green — and note Koreans often call the green light 파란불 ('blue light') for historical color reasons, which surprises English speakers. It collocates with 바뀌다 (change), 켜지다 (light up), 지키다 (obey), 빨간/초록 (red/green), and 건너다 (cross). The pitfall: 지키다 with 신호등 does not mean 'protect the light' as the dictionary gloss 'keep' might suggest — it means 'observe/obey' the signal, an idiom that doesn't transfer literally from English.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 신호등을 지키다 as 'protect the traffic light' — here 지키다 means 'obey/observe', so it means following the signal, not guarding it.
Confusing 신호 (the signal) with 신호등 (the lamp) — say 신호를 기다리다 'wait for the signal' but 신호등이 바뀌다 'the light changes'.
Assuming the green light is always 초록불 — Koreans commonly say 파란불 ('blue light') for go, so don't be thrown when 파란불 means green.

信號燈, literally 'signal-lamp': 信號 = signal + 燈 = lamp.
지키다 with 신호등 does not mean 'protect the light' as the dictionary gloss 'keep' might suggest — it means 'observe/obey' the signal, an idiom that doesn't transfer literally from English.

entries.shortExplanation: 횡단보도 means "crosswalk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 횡단보도 (hoengdanbodo) means "crosswalk". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 횡단보도를 건너요 ("I cross at the crosswalk"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 횡단보도 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 건너다 takes 을/를 for the thing crossed
에서 marks the place
existence with 가/이 + 없다
앞 = the spot just before it

examples.en: Please cross at the crosswalk.
examples.note: Simple instruction; 로 marks the route you cross by.

examples.en: I cross the crosswalk when the light is green.
examples.note: Everyday: 일 때 (when it is) sets the timing; pairs naturally with the green light.

examples.ko: 여기는 횡단보도가 멀어서 무단횡단하는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: yeogineun hoengdanbodoga meoreoseo mudanhoengdanhaneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: The crosswalk here is far, so many people jaywalk.
examples.note: Real situation: 무단횡단 = jaywalking, the opposite behavior.

entries.nuance: 횡단보도 (橫斷步道, literally 'cross-cut-walk-path': 橫斷 = cross over + 步道 = footpath) is the striped pedestrian crossing painted on the road. Its functional opposite is 무단횡단 (無斷橫斷, 'crossing without permission' = jaywalking), and the verb that pairs with it is 건너다 (cross), not 가다. Don't confuse 횡단보도 (the painted crossing) with 인도/보도 (the sidewalk you walk along) or 육교 (the pedestrian overpass). It collocates with 건너다 (cross), 기다리다 (wait), 신호등 (the light beside it), 초록불 (green light). The pitfall is the verb-and-particle pairing of 'cross': English 'cross the street' makes learners want 길에 건너요, but 건너다 takes the object marker — 길을 건너요 / 횡단보도를 건너요 — and when you mean 'by way of the crosswalk' you switch to 횡단보도로 건너요 with instrumental 로. A four-syllable Sino-Korean word, it is easy to misspell, so lock in 횡단보도.

Mixing up 횡단보도 (crosswalk) with 인도/보도 (sidewalk) — the crosswalk spans the road; the 인도 runs alongside it.
Using 가다 instead of 건너다 — to 'cross' you need 건너다; 가다 only means 'go', so 길을 건너다 not 길을 가다 for crossing over.

entries.shortExplanation: 주차장 means "parking lot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "parking lot" is 주차장 (juchajang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주차장에 차를 세워요 ("I park the car in the lot"). Watch the particle attached to 주차장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I park the car in the lot
usagePhrases.note: 세우다 = bring to a stop/park

usagePhrases.en: I wait in the parking lot
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the activity place
넓다 describes its size
cost charged by time

examples.en: Where is the parking lot?
examples.note: Simple question; 가/이 marks the subject you're locating.

examples.en: I parked the car in the underground lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 에 marks the destination of parking; 지하 = underground.

examples.ko: 주말이라 백화점 주차장이 꽉 차서 한참 돌았어요.
examples.romanization: jumarira baekwajeom juchajangi kkwak chaseo hancham dorasseoyo.
examples.en: It's the weekend so the department-store lot was full and I circled for ages.
examples.note: Real situation: 꽉 차다 (be packed), 돌다 (circle looking for a spot).

entries.nuance: 주차장 (駐車場, literally 'park-car-place': 駐 = stay/park + 車 = car + 場 = ground/lot) is the lot or structure where cars are parked, sometimes free, sometimes charged by the hour. Distinguish it cleanly from the verb action 주차하다 ('to park') and from the related 場 words 정거장/정류장 (a vehicle stop) — they share the 'place' character 場 but mean very different sites, and learners blur 주차장 (cars sit) with 정거장 (vehicles pause). It collocates with 세우다 (pull in/park), 주차하다 (park), 요금 (fee), 넓다/좁다 (spacious/cramped), 지하/지상 (underground/above-ground), 만차/꽉 차다 (full). The pitfall is the directional particle: because it is a destination you 'go to', use 주차장에 가요 (static goal 에), NOT 주차장에서 가요 (에서 marks where action happens or a source) — a swap English speakers make constantly. Also park a car with 세우다 or 주차하다, not 만들다.

Writing 주차장에서 가요 to mean 'go to the parking lot' — going to a destination takes 에, so it's 주차장에 가요; 에서 marks where you do something or move out from.
Confusing 주차장 (where cars are parked) with 정거장 (where a bus/train stops) — both end in 場, but one is for parked cars, the other for boarding.
Saying 차를 주차장에 만들어요 for parking — to park you use 세우다 or 주차하다: 차를 주차장에 세워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 기름 means "gas / oil" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기름 (gireum) = "gas / oil". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기름을 넣어요 ("I put in gas") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기름, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = put in / fill up the tank
written solid; the cost of fuel
떨어지다 = run out / be used up
the proper word for kitchen oil

examples.en: There's no gas / oil.
examples.note: Simple existence sentence with 가/이 + 없다.

examples.en: I filled up the tank at the gas station.
examples.note: Everyday: 가득 = full; 주유소 = gas station, the place you 넣다 fuel.

examples.ko: 요즘 기름값이 너무 올라서 차를 잘 안 타게 돼요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gireumgapsi neomu ollaseo chareul jal an tage dwaeyo.
examples.en: Fuel prices have risen so much lately that I barely drive.
examples.note: Real situation: 기름값 (fuel price) + 오르다 (rise); a common complaint.

entries.nuance: 기름 is a native Korean word (no hanja) covering both car fuel and cooking/edible oil, so context decides whether it means gasoline or kitchen oil. The precise dividing lines: the formal/technical fuel word is 연료 (燃料, 'burn-material' = fuel in general) and the pump itself is 휘발유 (gasoline) or 경유 (diesel), while kitchen oil is properly 식용유 ('edible oil') or named by source (참기름 sesame oil, 올리브유 olive oil). So 기름 is the casual umbrella term; specialists narrow it down. It collocates with 넣다 (fill up), 값 (price → 기름값), 떨어지다 (run out), 가득 (full tank), 주유소 (gas station). The pitfall: don't say 기름을 채우다 by analogy with English 'fill up'; the idiomatic verb is 넣다 ('put in') — 기름을 넣다. And when you mean engine fuel specifically in formal contexts, English speakers reach for a loanword like 가솔린, but everyday Korean just says 기름.

Assuming 기름 only means car gasoline — it equally means cooking oil, so for the kitchen specify 식용유/참기름 to avoid 'I put gasoline in the pan'.
Saying 기름을 채워요 for 'fill up' — the natural verb is 넣다: 기름을 넣어요 (or 가득 넣다 to fill the tank).
Using a loanword like 가솔린 in casual speech — Koreans say 기름 for fuel at the pump; 가솔린/휘발유 sound technical or like a label.

entries.shortExplanation: 요금 means "fare / fee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 요금 (yogeum) means "fare / fee". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 요금을 내요 ("I pay the fare"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay a fee/fare
the metered charge
오르다 = rise
요금 covers utility charges too

examples.en: How much is the fare?
examples.note: Simple price question with 가/이 + 얼마.

examples.en: I paid the bus fare with a transit card.
examples.note: Everyday: 로 marks the means of payment; 내다 = pay.

examples.ko: 택시 요금이 기본요금보다 훨씬 많이 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: taeksi yogeumi gibonyogeumboda hwolssin mani nawasseoyo.
examples.en: The taxi fare came out much higher than the base fare.
examples.note: Real situation: 기본요금 (base fare), 나오다 (be tallied) — how charges 'come out'.

entries.nuance: 요금 (料金, literally 'charge-money': 料 = fee/materials + 金 = money) is the set, rate-based charge for using a service — a ride, phone line, utility, or hotel — fixed by a published tariff. Contrast it sharply with 값/가격 (the price of a physical thing you buy) and with 비용 (the broader 'cost/expense' you incur): you pay 요금 for a bus ride but 값/가격 for a bag, and you calculate total 비용 for a trip. Within transit it pairs as 버스/택시/지하철 요금 (fare), 기본요금 (base fare), 요금을 내다 (pay), 오르다/인상되다 (rise), 할인 (discount). The pitfall: English 'price' makes learners say 기차 값 for a fare, but a service charge is 요금 (기차 요금), and a ticket's price is 표 값 / 표 가격 — so the fare to ride and the price of the ticket are worded differently. Pay it with 내다, not 사다 (you don't 'buy' a fare).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기차 값 for a train fare — a service charge is 요금, so it's 기차 요금; reserve 값/가격 for the price of goods.
Using 사다 with 요금 — you 'pay' a fare with 내다 (요금을 내다), you don't 'buy' it; 사다 is for the ticket (표를 사다).
Confusing 요금 with 비용 — 요금 is the fixed rate for one service, while 비용 is overall cost/expense, so a whole trip's spending is 여행 비용, not 여행 요금.

entries.shortExplanation: 정거장 means "stop / station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "stop / station" is 정거장 (jeonggeojang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정거장에서 내려요 ("I get off at the stop"). Watch the particle attached to 정거장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I get off at the stop
usagePhrases.note: 내리다 = get off, with 에서
the upcoming one on the route
counts distance along a line
에서 marks the waiting place

examples.en: I get off at the next stop.
examples.note: Everyday: 에서 + 내리다 is the fixed pattern for getting off.

examples.en: My place is three stops from here.
examples.note: Counting stops as a distance measure — a very common usage.

examples.en: The bus stop's location changed when it was moved.
examples.note: Real situation: 정거장 as a fixed point whose 위치 (location) can change.

entries.nuance: 정거장 (停車場, literally 'stop-car-place': 停 = halt + 車 = vehicle + 場 = ground) is a stop where a vehicle pauses to let people on and off, and it doubles as a counting unit ('two stops away'). The near-synonyms split by formality and mode: 정류장 (停留場) is the standard modern word for a bus stop (버스정류장), 정거장 sounds slightly older/literary and is also used loosely for stations, while a big rail/subway terminal is a 역 (驛, 'station'). So for a bus today most Koreans say 정류장; 역 is for trains/subway lines. It collocates with 내리다 (get off), 다음/이번 (next/this), 버스 (bus), counting 한/두/세 정거장. Two pitfalls: getting off uses 에서 + 내리다 (not 를), and English speakers blur the 場-words — keep 정거장/정류장 (a pause-and-board point) apart from 주차장 (a place cars are parked) and from 역 (a rail station building).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 정거장을 내려요 — 'get off at' takes 에서 with 내리다, so it's 정거장에서 내려요; 내리다 doesn't take the object marker for the place.
Confusing 정거장/정류장 (a stop) with 역 (a station) — use 역 for subway/train terminals (서울역) and 정류장 for a bus stop.
Mixing up 정거장 with 주차장 — both end in 場 but 정거장 is where a vehicle pauses to board, 주차장 is where cars are parked; don't swap them.
