entries.shortExplanation: 교통 means "traffic / transit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교통 (gyotong) = "traffic / transit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교통이 복잡해요 ("traffic is heavy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 교통, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 복잡하다 = congested/complicated
buses + subway as a system
one card for fares
written solid; a road crash

examples.en: The traffic is heavy.
examples.note: Simple description; 복잡하다 is the go-to word for congestion.

examples.en: Public transit is really convenient in Seoul.
examples.note: Everyday: 대중교통 names the whole bus-and-subway system as a subject.

examples.ko: 출퇴근 시간에는 교통 체증이 심해서 지하철이 더 빨라요.
examples.romanization: chultoegeun siganeneun gyotong chejeungi simhaeseo jihacheori deo ppallayo.
examples.en: During rush hour the traffic jam is bad, so the subway is faster.
examples.note: Real situation: 교통 체증 (traffic jam), 출퇴근 (commute) — comparing modes.

entries.nuance: 교통 (交通, literally 'exchange-pass': 交 = cross/exchange + 通 = go through/communicate) is the broad abstract noun for the movement and flow of vehicles and people — the whole system of getting around, plus 'traffic' as in congestion. It is NOT a countable single vehicle: that is the pitfall — English 'a lot of traffic' is fine, but you can't use 교통 for 'a car' or 'a bus'; for those say 차/버스. Distinguish 교통 (the system/flow) from 교통수단 (交通手段, 'means of transport' = the specific modes) and from 길/도로 (the road itself). High-frequency compounds: 대중교통 (public transit), 교통카드 (transit card), 교통사고 (accident), 교통 체증/혼잡 (congestion), 교통편 (transport connection). When traffic is bad, Koreans say 교통이 복잡하다 or 길이 막히다 ('the road is blocked'); when it flows, 교통이 원활하다. Don't say 교통이 많다 for 'heavy traffic' — the natural adjective is 복잡하다 or 막히다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 교통 for a single vehicle — it means transit/traffic as a whole, not 'a car'; for one vehicle say 차, 버스, etc.
Saying 교통이 많아요 for 'heavy traffic' — the idiomatic phrasing is 교통이 복잡하다 or 길이 막히다; 많다 doesn't collocate here.
Confusing 교통 with 교통수단 — 교통 is the overall flow/system, while 교통수단 is the specific means (bus, subway, car), so 'which transport do you take?' is 무슨 교통수단, not 무슨 교통.

It is NOT a countable single vehicle: English 'a lot of traffic' is fine, but you can't use 교통 for 'a car' or 'a bus'; for those say 차/버스. And don't say 교통이 많다 for 'heavy traffic' — the natural adjective is 복잡하다 or 막히다.

entries.shortExplanation: 인터넷 means "internet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 인터넷 (inteonet) means "internet". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 인터넷이 빨라요 ("the internet is fast"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 인터넷 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + descriptive 빠르다
fixed phrase 안 되다 = not working
instrument 으로, not 에
noun + noun compound, no particle

examples.en: The internet at our place is fast.
examples.note: topic 은 sets the scene, 이 marks the real subject 인터넷

examples.en: I buy train tickets on the internet.
examples.note: 으로 = the means/channel you act through

examples.ko: 인터넷이 안 돼서 일을 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: inteonesi an dwaeseo ireul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: The internet was down so I couldn't work.
examples.note: 안 되다 + 아서 chains the cause to the result

entries.nuance: 인터넷 is the plain loanword (from English 'internet') for the network itself, and 'to go online' is normally 인터넷을 하다 — Korean turns the bare noun into an activity with 하다 rather than coining a separate verb. Do not confuse it with 와이파이 (the local wireless signal you connect to) or 데이터 (your phone's mobile data plan): you can have 인터넷 through either. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you search 인터넷으로 (by means of the internet), never 인터넷에 — 에 would wrongly treat the internet as a static location. Also, when it stops working Koreans say 인터넷이 안 돼요 (it doesn't function), not 인터넷이 없어요, which would mean the service literally doesn't exist there.

entries.explanation: "password" is 비밀번호 (bimilbeonho). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비밀번호를 입력해요 ("I enter the password"). Watch the particle attached to 비밀번호 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 + 입력하다 (type in)
casual 까먹다 in speech
subject 이 + 틀리다 (be incorrect)
object 을 + 바꾸다

examples.en: Please tell me the password.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 makes the request polite

examples.en: I forgot the password again.
examples.note: object 을; 까먹다 is casual for 잊어버리다

examples.en: This password is too easy.
examples.note: topic 는 contrasts this one against others

entries.nuance: 비밀번호 is Sino-Korean: 秘密 (비밀, 'secret') + 番號 (번호, 'number/code'), literally a 'secret number', so it naturally covers PINs and door-lock codes as well as login passwords. In casual speech almost everyone clips it to 비번, which is fine among friends but too slangy for a written form or a bank's formal prompt. The nearest neighbour is 암호 (暗號), which leans toward a cipher, secret signal, or military-style code; 비밀번호 is the ordinary everyday word you'll see on every signup screen. A common English-speaker slip is to assume you 'know' a password and reach for 알다, but for the action of typing it Korean prefers 입력하다 or 넣다 with the object marker: 비밀번호를 입력하다. Saying 비밀번호가 입력해요 for entering it. 입력하다 is a transitive verb, so the password is its object: 비밀번호를 입력해요.
Treating 비밀번호 and 암호 as identical. 암호 suggests a cipher/secret signal; for an everyday account login the standard word is 비밀번호.
Saying 비밀번호가 안 맞아요 when you mean you forgot it. 안 맞다 = 'it doesn't match'; if you simply can't recall it, say 비밀번호를 까먹었어요/잊어버렸어요.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 앱, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: colloquial 깔다 for installing
object 을 + 지우다 (erase)
subject 이 + 꺼지다 (shut off)
noun compound, no particle

examples.ko: 이 앱으로 음식을 시킬 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i aebeuro eumsigeul sikil su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can order food with this app.
examples.note: 으로 = via the app; -ㄹ 수 있다 = can

examples.en: I want to install a new app.
examples.note: -고 싶다 expresses the speaker's wish

examples.en: The app suddenly closed.
examples.note: subject 이; 꺼지다 = shut off by itself

entries.nuance: 앱 is the clipped loanword from English 'app' and is now the default spoken word for a mobile application; the older borrowing 어플 (from 'application') still appears but sounds slightly dated, and the full 애플리케이션 is reserved for formal or technical writing. Note the gentle contrast with 프로그램, which Koreans tend to use for desktop/PC software, while 앱 implies the phone. For installing, the idiomatic everyday verb is 깔다 ('to lay down/spread'); 설치하다 (設置) is the more formal equivalent you'd read in a manual. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle pair: you open or install the app with 을/를 (앱을 열어요), but when it crashes on its own it becomes the subject with 이/가 — 앱이 꺼졌어요, because 꺼지다 is intransitive (it shuts off) versus 끄다 (you turn it off).

Saying 앱이 열어요 for 'I open the app'. 열다 is transitive, so the app is the object: 앱을 열어요. (앱이 열려요 would mean 'the app opens (by itself)'.)
Calling a phone app 프로그램. Koreans reserve 프로그램 for PC software; for a smartphone app use 앱.
Using 설치하다 in casual chat. It's correct but stiff; friends say 앱을 깔다.

entries.shortExplanation: 화면 means "screen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 화면 (hwamyeon) means "screen". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 화면이 커요 ("the screen is big"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 화면 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + descriptive 크다
object 을 + 보다
subject 이 + intransitive 꺼지다
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: This screen is big.
examples.note: subject 이 with the adjective 크다

examples.en: If you watch the screen for a long time your eyes hurt.
examples.note: object 을; -(으)면 = conditional 'if/when'

examples.en: The screen suddenly went black.
examples.note: subject 이; 꺼지다 = goes off on its own

entries.nuance: 화면 is Sino-Korean: 畫 (화, 'picture/drawing') + 面 (면, 'surface/face'), literally a 'picture-surface', so it means the displayed image area of a phone, monitor, or TV — what you look at, not the hardware. Keep it apart from 액정 (液晶, 'liquid crystal'), the physical LCD glass panel that can crack, and from 모니터, the whole external monitor device; 화면 is the visual surface itself. A subtle near-synonym is 스크린, the loanword, which Koreans lean toward for a cinema/projector screen, whereas the everyday phone display is 화면. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb pairing: you watch the screen with 보다 and the object marker (화면을 보다), but the screen going dark uses the intransitive 꺼지다 with 이/가 (화면이 꺼지다); only a person 'turns it off' with the transitive 끄다.

Saying 화면이 봐요 for 'I look at the screen'. 보다 is transitive, so the screen is its object: 화면을 봐요.
Confusing 화면 with 액정. The crackable glass is 액정; the displayed image is 화면. 'My screen cracked' = 액정이 깨졌어요, not 화면이 깨졌어요.
Saying 화면을 꺼졌어요 when the display goes dark by itself. Use the intransitive subject form: 화면이 꺼졌어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 충전기 means "charger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "charger" is 충전기 (chungjeongi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 충전기가 있어요 ("there is a charger"). Watch the particle attached to 충전기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + existence 있다

usagePhrases.en: I charge it with the charger
usagePhrases.note: instrument 으로 + 충전하다
object 을 + 빌리다
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: I charge my phone with the charger.
examples.note: 으로 marks the tool; 휴대폰을 is the object

examples.en: There's a charger inside the bag.
examples.note: place 안에 + existence 있다

examples.en: I left the charger at home.
examples.note: -고 오다 = did it then came; object 을

entries.nuance: 충전기 is Sino-Korean: 充 (충, 'fill') + 電 (전, 'electricity') + 器 (기, 'device'), literally a 'fill-electricity device' — the same 充電 root gives the verb 충전하다 'to charge'. That 기 suffix consistently means 'instrument/machine' (compare 세탁기 washer, 청소기 vacuum). Distinguish the parts learners blur together: 충전기 is the brick/adapter, the 충전 케이블 is the cord, and the 보조 배터리 is a portable power bank — English 'charger' loosely covers all three but Korean separates them. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you charge a device 충전기로 (by means of the charger), never 충전기에; 에 would mark a destination. Note too that 충전 also means topping up a transit card or game credits, so 충전하다 stretches beyond batteries.

Saying 충전기에 충전해요 for 'charge with the charger'. The charger is the tool, so use 으로: 충전기로 충전해요. (휴대폰에 충전해요 'charge into the phone' is fine because the phone is the destination.)
Calling the cable a 충전기. The brick is 충전기; the cord is the 충전 케이블 (충전선).
Forgetting that 충전 covers more than batteries — 교통카드를 충전하다 means 'top up a transit card', not charge it electrically.

entries.shortExplanation: 와이파이 means "wifi" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 와이파이 (waipai) = "wifi". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 와이파이가 있어요 ("there is wifi") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 와이파이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + existence 있다
fixed phrase 안 되다
destination 에 + 연결하다
modifier 무료 + noun

examples.en: You can use the wifi here.
examples.note: place 에서; -ㄹ 수 있다 = can

examples.en: This cafe's wifi is free.
examples.note: topic 는 + subject 이 double-marking

examples.note: 안 되다 + 아서 links cause to feeling

entries.nuance: 와이파이 is the loanword for local wireless internet (the spoken form follows the English 'Wi-Fi'), and the key distinction English speakers must hold is 와이파이 vs 데이터: 와이파이 is the free signal you join from a router, while 데이터 is your paid mobile-data allowance — running out of one doesn't affect the other. It also differs from 인터넷, the network as a whole; 와이파이 is just one way to reach it. The pitfall is the connection particle: you connect 와이파이에 (to the wifi, a destination) with 연결하다, not 와이파이로, because here the wifi is where you're attaching, not a tool you act through. And like other tech that simply stops responding, a dead signal is 와이파이가 안 돼요 (it won't function), not 와이파이가 없어요, which claims there's no network at all.

Saying 와이파이로 연결해요 to mean 'connect to the wifi'. 연결하다 takes the destination 에: 와이파이에 연결해요. (You'd use 으로 only for the means, e.g. 와이파이로 영상을 봐요 'watch videos over wifi'.)
Mixing up 와이파이 and 데이터. If the router signal is gone you can still use 데이터; say 와이파이가 안 돼요, not 데이터가 안 돼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 영상 means "video" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 영상 (yeongsang) means "video". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영상을 봐요 ("I watch a video"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영상 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 + 보다
object 을 + 찍다 (shoot)
subject 이 + 길다
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: You can watch videos on your phone.
examples.note: 으로 = device; -ㄹ 수 있다 = can

examples.en: I watched a fun video today.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ adjective 재미있는 modifies 영상

examples.en: This video is too long.
examples.note: topic 은 contrasts this clip; 길다 = long

entries.nuance: 영상 is Sino-Korean: 映 (영, 'reflect/project') + 像 (상, 'image'), literally a 'projected image', and it means a video clip — the kind you watch online, on your phone, or record yourself. Draw the line carefully against 영화 (映畫, 'projected picture'), a full cinema movie: a YouTube clip is an 영상, never an 영화. It also contrasts with the casual loanword 비디오, which now sounds dated (it evoked old videotapes) and with 동영상 (動映像, 'moving image'), a near-identical, slightly more technical synonym you'll see on menus and settings. The verb pairing is the pitfall: you watch a video with 보다 + object (영상을 보다), and crucially you 'shoot/take' one with 찍다 — 영상을 찍다 — not 만들다 unless you mean editing/producing it. Saying 영상이 봐요 for 'I watch a video'. 보다 is transitive: 영상을 봐요.
Using 영상을 만들다 for simply recording on your phone. To capture footage use 찍다 (영상을 찍다); reserve 만들다 for producing/editing a finished video.

subject 이 + 재미있다
object 을 + 깔다

entries.nuance: 게임 is the loanword from English 'game' and in practice points to video and mobile games; for traditional board or playground games Koreans more often say 놀이 (as in 놀이터 'playground') or name the game directly. The crucial pitfall for English speakers is the verb: you 'play' a game with 하다, not 놀다 — 게임을 하다 is fixed, whereas 게임을 놀다 is ungrammatical because 놀다 ('to play/hang out') is intransitive and can't take 게임 as an object. (You can say 게임하고 놀다 'hang out playing games', but that's a different structure.) When you get addicted, the idiom is 게임에 빠지다 ('fall into the game'), taking 에. And to describe the game itself as enjoyable, it's the subject of the adjective 재미있다: 게임이 재미있어요.

Saying 게임을 놀아요 for 'I play a game'. The fixed verb is 하다: 게임을 해요. 놀다 can't take 게임 as a direct object.
Saying 게임이 해요 by mismatching the particle. 하다 needs the object marker: 게임을 해요.
Using 게임을 빠졌어요 for 'hooked on the game'. 빠지다 takes the destination 에: 게임에 빠졌어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 검색 means "search" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 검색 (geomsaek) = "search". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 검색을 해요 ("I do a search") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 검색, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 + 하다 (또는 검색하다)
subject 이 + 빠르다
noun compound 結果, no particle
-아/어 보다 = give it a try

examples.en: You can do a search on the internet.
examples.note: 으로 = via; -ㄹ 수 있다 = can

examples.en: I tried searching the restaurant name.
examples.note: -아/어 보다 = tried doing it

examples.en: There are too many search results.
examples.note: subject 이; 많다 = be many

entries.nuance: 검색 is Sino-Korean: 檢 (검, 'inspect/examine') + 索 (색, 'search/seek out'), so it's the act of looking information up, especially online, and it readily becomes the verb 검색하다. Distinguish it from everyday 찾다 ('to look for / find'): 찾다 is the broad native verb for searching for anything physical or abstract (찾다 a key, a person, a word), whereas 검색하다 specifically means querying a search engine or database. So 'I searched the internet' is 인터넷에서 검색했어요, but 'I'm looking for my keys' is 열쇠를 찾아요, not 검색해요. The English-speaker pitfall is double: first, 검색 as a noun needs 을/를 with 하다 (검색을 하다), and second, what you search appears as the object of 검색하다 (식당을 검색하다), so don't bolt on 에 thinking of the search engine as a place — the platform takes 에서 instead (구글에서 검색하다).

Saying 검색이 해요 for 'I search'. As a noun + 하다 it needs the object marker: 검색을 해요 (or just 검색해요).
Using 검색하다 to mean looking for a lost object. For physical searching use 찾다: 열쇠를 찾아요, not 열쇠를 검색해요.
Marking the search engine with 에. The platform you search on takes 에서: 네이버에서 검색해요, not 네이버에 검색해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 알림 means "notification" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 알림 (allim) means "notification". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 알림이 와요 ("a notification comes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 알림 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + 오다 (arrives)
subject 이 + 울리다 (rings)
object 을 + 끄다
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: Please turn off the notifications.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 = polite request

examples.en: Lots of notifications come starting from the morning.
examples.note: -부터 = starting from; 이 marks the subject

examples.en: The message notifications aren't coming.
examples.note: negation 안 + 오다; subject 이

entries.nuance: 알림 is a native Korean noun built from the verb 알리다 ('to inform/let know') plus the nominalizing 음/ㅁ, so it literally means 'a letting-know' — the app or phone alert that pops up. Contrast it with 공지 (公知, 'public notice'), a formal announcement a company or school posts, and with 알람 (the loanword 'alarm'), which Koreans reserve for a clock/timer alarm you set to wake up. So your phone's banner is an 알림, your morning wake-up is an 알람, and the official memo is a 공지. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb of arrival: a notification 'comes' with 오다 and takes the subject marker — 알림이 오다 — never 알림을 오다, because 오다 is intransitive (nothing arrives 'something'). You only switch to 을/를 when you act on it yourself: 알림을 끄다 (turn it off), 알림을 확인하다 (check it).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 알림을 와요 when one arrives. 오다 is intransitive, so the notification is the subject: 알림이 와요.
Confusing 알림 and 알람. The pop-up alert is 알림; the wake-up clock alarm is 알람. 'Set an alarm' = 알람을 맞추다, not 알림을 맞추다.
Using 공지 for a phone notification. 공지 is a formal public announcement; the app banner is an 알림.

entries.shortExplanation: 메시지 means "message" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "message" is 메시지 (mesiji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 메시지를 보내요 ("I send a message"). Watch the particle attached to 메시지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 + 보내다
object 을 + 받다
subject 이 + 오다 (arrived)
object 을 + 확인하다

examples.en: Please send me a message.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 = polite request

examples.en: I sent a message to my friend.
examples.note: recipient 한테 = to (a person)

examples.en: A message just came.
examples.note: 방금 = just now; subject 이 + 오다

entries.nuance: 메시지 is the loanword from English 'message' and covers chat/app messages broadly (a KakaoTalk message, a DM); the everyday near-synonym 문자 (literally 文字 'letters/characters') specifically means an SMS text, so '문자 보내' = 'text me' while '메시지' is the wider term. There's also 카톡, the verb-able brand shorthand for a KakaoTalk message, used constantly in real life (카톡 보낼게 'I'll Kakao you'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, the recipient is marked with 한테/에게 ('to a person'), not the English bare object — 친구한테 메시지를 보내다, where 친구한테 = 'to my friend' and 메시지를 is the thing sent; second, the message arriving uses intransitive 오다 with 이/가 (메시지가 오다), but you sending it uses 보내다 with 을/를 (메시지를 보내다). Don't carry the English 'send him a message' double-object pattern straight over.

Saying 메시지가 보내요 for 'I send a message'. 보내다 is transitive: 메시지를 보내요.
Marking the recipient with the object marker, e.g. 친구를 메시지를 보내요. The person who receives it takes 한테/에게: 친구한테 메시지를 보내요.
Treating 메시지 and 문자 as identical. 문자 specifically means an SMS text; for that, '문자 보낼게' is the natural phrase, while 메시지 is the broader word for any app message.

entries.shortExplanation: 키보드 means "keyboard" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 키보드 (kibodeu) = "keyboard". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 키보드로 써요 ("I type with the keyboard") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 키보드, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: instrument 으로 + 쓰다
object 을 + 치다 (hit keys)
subject 이 + 편하다
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: I write text with the keyboard.
examples.note: 으로 = the tool; 글을 = the object written

examples.en: This keyboard is very comfortable.
examples.note: subject 이 with the adjective 편하다

examples.en: I bought a new keyboard.
examples.note: 새로 = newly (adverb); object 을

entries.nuance: 키보드 is the loanword for a computer or on-screen typing keyboard; note that a piano-style musical keyboard is also called 키보드, but the bank of keys themselves is 건반 and the Korean character layout is the 자판. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the right verb-particle pair: when the keyboard is the tool you write with, use 으로 (키보드로 쓰다), but when you focus on striking the keys, Korean uses 치다 ('to hit/strike') with the object marker — 키보드를 치다 — the same 치다 used for 피아노를 치다 'play piano' and 타자를 치다 'type'. So 'typing' as an action is most idiomatically 타자를 치다 or 키보드를 치다, while 쓰다 emphasizes the text produced. Don't use 에 with the keyboard (키보드에 써요 is wrong for the instrument); 에 would mark a surface you write onto, like 종이에 쓰다 'write on paper'.

Saying 키보드에 써요 for 'type with the keyboard'. The keyboard is the instrument, so use 으로: 키보드로 써요. (Reserve 에 for the surface, e.g. 종이에 써요 'write on paper'.)
Saying 키보드가 쳐요 for tapping the keys. 치다 is transitive: 키보드를 쳐요.
Assuming 'keyboard' always means the computer kind. A musical keyboard is also 키보드; if you mean the keys specifically, that's 건반, and the character layout is the 자판.

entries.shortExplanation: 라면 means "instant ramen noodles" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 라면 (ramyeon) means "instant ramen noodles". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 라면을 끓이다 ("to cook/boil ramen"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 라면 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the default verb is 끓이다 'boil', not 만들다 'make'; you boil water and add the noodle block
붇다 (ㄷ-irregular → 불어요) is the specific verb for noodles swelling and going soft if you wait too long; do not confuse it with 불다 'to blow'
봉지 'bag/packet' counts the sealed package; 개 also works informally
prefix-style compound: instant ramen in a cup you just add hot water to

examples.en: I like ramen.
examples.note: simple statement of preference with 을 marking the object

examples.ko: 밤에 라면을 끓여 먹으면 너무 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: bame ramyeoneul kkeuryeo meogeumyeon neomu masisseoyo.
examples.en: Ramen tastes so good when you cook and eat it at night.
examples.note: 끓여 먹다 'boil-and-eat' is the natural verb chain; note the late-night-snack culture

examples.ko: 면 다 붇기 전에 빨리 드세요.
examples.romanization: myeon da butgi jeone ppalli deuseyo.
examples.en: Eat quickly before the noodles get all soggy.
examples.note: real-table urgency; 면 = noodles, base verb 붇다 keeps ㄷ before the consonant ending 기 (붇기), 드세요 is the polite imperative

entries.nuance: 라면 to a Korean means the cheap instant noodle block you boil at home in a small pot (양은냄비), eaten with kimchi at midnight — it is comfort food and student food, not a restaurant meal. The crucial dividing line is 라면 vs 라멘: 라멘 is the Japanese-restaurant bowl with rich tonkotsu/miso broth and chashu, while 라면 is the supermarket packet (신라면, 진라면). The word came in from Japanese ラーメン (itself from Chinese 拉麵 'pulled noodles'), but in Korea it shifted to mean the instant version specifically. Register is fully casual and neutral — anyone says it. The collocation trap: you 끓이다 'boil' ramen, you do not 만들다 'make' it, and the noodles 붇다 'swell/go soggy' (ㄷ-irregular → 불어요/불었어요, but 붇기 before a consonant) rather than 'get wet' — note 붇다 is a different verb from 불다 'to blow'. English speakers also wrongly assume 라면 covers fancy ramen-shop noodles; for that you must say 라멘.

Saying 라면을 만들어요 ('I make ramen') — Koreans say 라면을 끓여요 ('I boil ramen') because the whole act is defined by boiling water; 만들다 sounds like you assembled it from scratch.
Using 라면 to mean the Japanese ramen-shop dish — that is 라멘. Mixing them up makes a Korean picture a supermarket packet, not a restaurant bowl.
Describing soggy noodles as 라면이 젖었어요 ('the ramen got wet') — the correct verb is 불었어요 (from the ㄷ-irregular base 붇다, not 불다 'to blow'), the specific word for noodles swelling and softening.

entries.shortExplanation: 김밥 means "gimbap; seaweed rice roll" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "gimbap; seaweed rice roll" is 김밥 (gimbap). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 김밥을 싸다 ("to roll/make gimbap"). Watch the particle attached to 김밥 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the verb is 싸다 'wrap', because you roll the rice and fillings in seaweed; not 만들다 for the rolling act
줄 'line/strip' is the proper counter for a whole long roll; one 줄 is cut into bite pieces
compound naming by filling: 참치 'tuna' + 김밥; menus list 야채김밥, 치즈김밥 the same way
the famous cheap chain; shows 김밥 as everyday fast food you grab on the go

examples.en: One roll of gimbap, please.
examples.note: ordering at a shop; note the counter 줄, never 개, for a whole roll

examples.ko: 소풍 갈 때 엄마가 김밥을 싸 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: sopung gal ttae eommaga gimbabeul ssa jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: When we went on a picnic, my mom rolled gimbap for us.
examples.note: 싸 주다 'roll for someone' + honorific 주셨어요; picnic-and-gimbap is a core memory

examples.ko: 김밥은 식어도 맛있어서 들고 다니기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gimbabeun sigeodo masisseoseo deulgo danigi joayo.
examples.en: Gimbap is tasty even cold, so it is great to carry around.
examples.note: real reasoning with -아서; explains why it is the go-to portable food

entries.nuance: 김밥 is steamed rice and fillings (egg, pickled radish, carrot, spinach, ham) rolled in dried laver and sliced into bite-size pieces — cheap, portable, the definitive picnic and lunchbox food. The name transparently combines 김 'dried laver/seaweed' + 밥 'rice', so a learner can decode it. Do not confuse it with Japanese 김초밥/마키(스시): gimbap rice is seasoned with sesame oil and salt, not vinegar, and the fillings are cooked, so it is its own dish, not 'Korean sushi' (Koreans dislike that label). Two collocation points trip up English speakers: you 싸다 'wrap/roll' gimbap (the rolling motion), not 만들다; and you count a whole roll with 줄 'strip', so '두 줄' = two rolls, while 개 would wrongly count individual slices. Register is casual and universal.

Counting whole rolls with 개 — 김밥 두 개 sounds like two single slices. Use 줄: 김밥 두 줄 = two rolls.
Calling it 'Korean sushi' or equating it with 초밥 — the rice uses sesame oil and salt (not vinegar) and the fillings are cooked, so it is a distinct dish; many Koreans find the sushi comparison off.
Saying 김밥을 만들어요 for the act of rolling — the idiomatic verb is 싸다 (싸요), as in 김밥을 싸요, because you are wrapping/rolling it.

examples.en: Add the chili paste and mix it well before eating.
examples.note: real serving instruction; 비벼서 (from 비비다) + 드세요, the polite imperative

examples.ko: 채소가 많아서 비빔밥은 건강한 한 끼예요.
examples.romanization: chaesoga manaseo bibimbabeun geonganghan han kkiyeyo.
examples.en: Because it has lots of vegetables, bibimbap is a healthy meal.
examples.note: reasoning with -아서; 한 끼 'one meal' frames it as a full, balanced meal

entries.nuance: 비빔밥 is a bowl of warm rice topped with seasoned vegetables (나물), often an egg and a little meat, plus 고추장 chili paste, all stirred together right before eating. The name is pure native Korean and self-explaining: it is 비비다 'to mix/rub' turned into the noun 비빔 + 밥 'rice', literally 'mixed rice'. The whole point is the mixing, which sets up the key collocation 비비다 — you 비벼서 먹다 'mix-and-eat', and a learner who eats it in neat layers has missed the dish. Distinguish it from 덮밥 'rice topped with something' (a 덮밥 you eat as-is, scooping topping with rice; a 비빔밥 you must stir). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 섞다 'to mix' — 섞다 is for blending separate substances (mixing flour and water), but for stirring food in a bowl with utensils the idiomatic verb is 비비다. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Eating it in layers without stirring — by definition 비빔밥 must be 비벼서 (mixed) first; leaving it un-mixed defeats the dish and the name.
Using 섞다 instead of 비비다 ('비빔밥을 섞어요') — 섞다 is for combining separate ingredients; the in-bowl stirring of food is 비비다.
Forgetting the object particle in casual speech and over-correcting to 가/이 — it is 비빔밥을 먹어요/비벼요 (object 을), since the rice is what you act on.

structuredNuance.t: 비빔밥 is a bowl of warm rice topped with seasoned vegetables (나물), often an egg and a little meat, plus 고추장 chili paste, all stirred together right before eating. Register is neutral and everyday.

entries.shortExplanation: 불고기 means "bulgogi; grilled marinated beef" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 불고기 (bulgogi) means "bulgogi; grilled marinated beef". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불고기를 재우다 ("to marinate the bulgogi"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 불고기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 재우다 'let it rest/soak' is the cooking term for marinating the beef in sauce before grilling
양념 'seasoning mix'; 불고기 is defined by its sweet 간장(soy) base, unlike spicy dishes
백반-style set: 불고기 with rice and side dishes at a restaurant
굽다 'grill/roast'; note it is a ㅂ-irregular, so 굽다 → 구워요

examples.en: I like bulgogi.
examples.note: simple preference; 를 marks the object after a vowel

examples.en: I want to eat bulgogi tonight.
examples.note: -고 싶다 'want to'; a very natural dinner wish

examples.ko: 불고기는 양념이 달아서 아이들도 잘 먹어요.
examples.romanization: bulgogineun yangnyeomi daraseo aideuldo jal meogeoyo.
examples.en: Bulgogi has a sweet marinade, so even kids eat it well.
examples.note: reasoning with -아서; explains why this mild, sweet meat is family-friendly

entries.nuance: 불고기 is thin slices of beef marinated in a sweet soy-sauce mix (간장, sugar, garlic, sesame oil, often pear or onion) and grilled or pan-cooked, giving a tender, sweet-savory result rather than charred plain meat. The name is native Korean and decodes literally as 불 'fire' + 고기 'meat', i.e. 'fire-meat'. The sharpest contrast is 불고기 vs 갈비/삼겹살: 갈비 is short rib (also marinated, on the bone), 삼겹살 is fatty pork belly grilled plain and dipped after, while 불고기 is sliced, pre-marinated, sweet. So 불고기 is not a generic word for 'grilled meat' — that broader idea is 구이 or 고기구이. Collocation note for English speakers: you 재우다 'marinate' (let it soak) the meat, and you 굽다 'grill' it (ㅂ-irregular: 구워요). The pitfall is assuming any Korean BBQ meat is 불고기; if it is unmarinated pork belly it is 삼겹살, not 불고기. Register is neutral, used by everyone.

Using 불고기 for any grilled meat — it specifically means thin, sweet-soy-marinated beef. Plain grilled pork belly is 삼겹살; ribs are 갈비.
Conjugating 굽다 'grill' as regular (구버요) — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct form is 구워요 (불고기를 구워요).
Calling the sauce 소스 — the marinade for Korean meat is 양념, and 불고기 is 양념 고기 (seasoned meat); 소스 sounds like a Western dipping sauce.

entries.shortExplanation: 떡볶이 means "tteokbokki; spicy rice cakes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tteokbokki; spicy rice cakes" is 떡볶이 (tteokbokki). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 떡볶이 일 인분 ("one serving of tteokbokki"). Watch the particle attached to 떡볶이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 인분 'portion per person'; street tteokbokki is sold by the serving, not by piece
맵다 'spicy' (ㅂ-irregular → 매워요); spiciness is its defining trait
compound by style: 국물 'broth' version with more sauce to drink/dip in
볶다 'stir-fry' is the root verb; the cakes are cooked down in the sauce

examples.en: I like tteokbokki.
examples.note: plain preference statement

examples.en: One serving of tteokbokki at the snack shop, please.
examples.note: real ordering; 분식집 = snack bar, counter 인분 for the serving

examples.ko: 떡볶이가 너무 매워서 물을 많이 마셨어요.
examples.romanization: tteokbokkiga neomu maewoseo mureul mani masyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The tteokbokki was so spicy that I drank a lot of water.
examples.note: cause-result with -아서; 맵다 → 매워서 (ㅂ-irregular)

entries.nuance: 떡볶이 is chewy cylindrical rice cakes (떡) simmered in a sweet-spicy 고추장 red sauce, the iconic 분식 (snack-shop) street food eaten by students after school. The name is native Korean: 떡 'rice cake' + 볶이 from 볶다 'to stir-fry', so literally 'stir-fried rice cakes' (even though it is now more simmered than fried). The key collocation is the adjective 맵다 'spicy', a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 매워요/매워서 — spiciness is the whole identity of the dish, so expecting it to be sweet-only is the beginner's surprise. It is counted by 인분 'serving per person', not by individual cakes. Contrast 떡볶이 with plain 떡 (rice cake), which can be a chewy sweet snack like 가래떡; 떡볶이 specifically means the saucy spicy dish. English-speaker pitfall: do not call it 'rice cake' alone in a food context — that suggests the unseasoned 떡 or even a Western rice cracker; the dish is always the full word 떡볶이. Register is casual and youthful.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting it to be sweet and mild — 떡볶이 is fundamentally 매운 (spicy); the 고추장 sauce is its signature. Saying it sounds like dessert confuses Koreans.
Conjugating 맵다 as regular (맵어요) — it is ㅂ-irregular: 매워요 (떡볶이가 매워요).
Ordering by 개 ('떡볶이 두 개') — street tteokbokki is portioned, so use 인분: 떡볶이 이 인분 (two servings).

entries.shortExplanation: 치킨 means "Korean fried chicken" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 치킨 (chikin) = "Korean fried chicken". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 치킨을 시키다 ("to order fried chicken (delivery)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 치킨, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 시키다 'order (in)' is the go-to verb; 치킨 culture is built on delivery 배달
마리 counts whole animals; a full order is one 마리, half is 반 마리
compound: 양념 'seasoning' + 치킨; the saucy variety vs plain 후라이드
blend of 치킨 + 맥주; the beloved fried-chicken-with-beer combo

examples.en: I like fried chicken.
examples.note: simple preference

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 치킨 한 마리 시킬까요?
examples.romanization: oneul jeonyeoge chikin han mari sikilkkayo?
examples.en: Shall we order a whole chicken for dinner tonight?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ까요 suggestion; 시키다 for delivery, counter 마리

examples.ko: 치킨은 역시 맥주랑 같이 먹어야 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: chikineun yeoksi maekjurang gachi meogeoya masisseoyo.
examples.en: Fried chicken really tastes best when you eat it with beer.
examples.note: 역시 'as expected' + -아야 '(must/should)'; the 치맥 ritual

entries.nuance: 치킨 in Korea means deep-fried (or sauced) chicken that you order for delivery and share with friends or family over beer — a whole social ritual, not just a food. It is an English loanword (chicken), but its meaning narrowed: 치킨 = fried chicken the dish, while the live bird or raw meat is 닭 'chicken' / 닭고기 'chicken meat'. This is the central pitfall for English speakers: '닭/닭고기' for the ingredient, '치킨' only for the cooked fried dish — saying 치킨 for raw chicken in a recipe is wrong. Key collocations: you 시키다 'order' it (delivery culture), count it with 마리 (whole animal, so 한 마리 / 반 마리), and pair it as 치맥 (치킨+맥주). Contrast 후라이드(치킨) 'plain fried' vs 양념(치킨) 'sweet-spicy sauced' — the classic 'half-and-half' is 반반. Register is fully casual and ubiquitous.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 치킨 for raw or live chicken — that is 닭 (the bird) or 닭고기 (the meat). 치킨 only means the cooked fried dish.
Counting it with 개 — a whole order is one animal, so use 마리: 치킨 한 마리; a half order is 반 마리.
Saying 치킨을 만들어요 for ordering in — Koreans 시키다/주문하다 (order) chicken for delivery: 치킨 시켰어요 ('we ordered chicken').

entries.shortExplanation: 만두 means "dumplings" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 만두 (mandu) means "dumplings". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 만두를 빚다 ("to fold/shape dumplings"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 만두 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 빚다 'shape by hand' is the artisanal verb for folding dumplings (also used for 송편, pottery)
prefix by method: 군- (from 굽다 'fry') + 만두; cf. 찐만두 steamed, 물만두 boiled-in-water
개 counts individual dumplings; a plate/order may use 접시 or 인분
만두 in broth (note the 사이시옷: 만두+국 → 만둣국), a New Year dish with 떡국

examples.en: I like dumplings.
examples.note: plain preference; no plural ending in Korean

examples.en: On New Year's Day the family gathers and folds dumplings.
examples.note: 빚다 'fold/shape'; the communal New Year tradition

examples.en: Pan-fried dumplings are crispy and water-boiled ones are soft.
examples.note: contrasting cooking methods with -고; shows the prefix system

entries.nuance: 만두 are dough pockets filled with minced meat, tofu, vegetables, and glass noodles, which can be steamed (찐만두), pan-fried (군만두), or boiled in soup (물만두/만둣국) — one word covering all methods, so you prefix the style. It is Sino-Korean, written 饅頭 (literally 'steamed bun/stuffed head'), a word shared across East Asia. A learner should not equate it narrowly with Japanese 'gyoza': 교자(만두) is the thin-skinned pan-fried type, but 만두 is the broad category, including thick-skinned and soup versions. The grammar pitfall is the strongest one: Korean nouns are not pluralized, so 'dumplings' is still just 만두 (never 만두들 here) — you say 만두를 먹어요 for any number. The signature verb is 빚다 'to shape/fold by hand' (the same verb used for shaping 송편 rice cakes), which is more idiomatic than 만들다 for the folding craft. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding a plural -들 because English says 'dumpling-s' — Korean nouns are number-neutral; 만두 already covers one or many: 만두를 먹어요.
Assuming 만두 = gyoza only — 교자 is the thin-skin fried subtype; 만두 is the umbrella term covering steamed, fried, and soup versions.
Using only 만들다 for folding them — the idiomatic craft verb is 빚다 (만두를 빚다), the same verb for hand-shaping rice cakes.

entries.shortExplanation: 죽 means "rice porridge" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rice porridge" is 죽 (juk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 죽을 쑤다 ("to make porridge"). Watch the particle attached to 죽 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 쑤다 is the dedicated verb for cooking porridge/paste; more precise than 끓이다 or 만들다
compound by ingredient: 전복 'abalone' + 죽; also 호박죽 pumpkin, 닭죽 chicken
그릇 'bowl' is the counter; porridge is served and eaten by the bowl
먹다 'eat' (with a spoon), not 마시다 'drink', even though it is liquidy

examples.en: I like porridge.
examples.note: plain preference statement

examples.en: I caught a cold, so I ate porridge.
examples.note: cause with -아서; 죽 as the classic sick-day comfort food

examples.en: Grandma made abalone porridge for me.
examples.note: 쑤다 'cook porridge' + honorific 주셨어요; warmth and care

entries.nuance: 죽 is a soft, slow-simmered rice porridge eaten when you are sick, recovering, or want something gentle on the stomach — culturally it carries a strong 'comfort / convalescence / care' feeling, so bringing someone 죽 signals concern. It is Sino-Korean, written 粥 'congee/gruel'. Distinguish it along a thickness scale: 미음 is the thinnest (strained, for the very ill or babies), 죽 is the standard porridge, and 누룽지 is the toasted scorched-rice version — so 죽 is the middle, everyday term. The verb pitfall is double: first, although 죽 is liquidy, you 먹다 'eat' it (with a spoon), never 마시다 'drink' — Korean treats spoon-food as 'eaten'; second, the most idiomatic cooking verb is 쑤다 'to cook porridge', a special-purpose verb (죽을 쑤다), more precise than generic 끓이다. English speakers reaching for 'drink' because it is soupy will sound off. Register is neutral and warm.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 죽을 마셔요 ('drink the porridge') — you eat it with a spoon, so it must be 죽을 먹어요; Korean classifies spoon-eaten food as 먹다 regardless of how liquid it is.
Using 만들다 for cooking it — the precise idiomatic verb is 쑤다 (죽을 쑤다); 끓이다 'boil' is acceptable but 쑤다 is the natural choice.
Confusing it with 미음 — 미음 is the thin, strained gruel for the very sick or infants; standard porridge is 죽.

entries.shortExplanation: 반찬 means "side dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반찬 (banchan) = "side dish". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 반찬을 만들다 ("to make side dishes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 반찬, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 만들다 'make'; home cooks prepare several 반찬 ahead for the week

usagePhrases.en: please give me more side dishes
usagePhrases.note: the polite refill request; 반찬 are usually free and refillable at restaurants
밑- 'base' + 반찬: the keep-in-the-fridge standbys (장조림, 멸치볶음) that last days
가게 'shop'; ready-made 반찬 stores where busy people buy side dishes

examples.en: This place has a lot of side dishes.
examples.note: describing a restaurant's spread; 이 집 'this establishment'

examples.en: Please give me some more side dishes.
examples.note: real restaurant request for a free refill; 좀 softens it politely

examples.en: Mom makes side dishes in advance on Sundays.
examples.note: 미리 'in advance'; the weekly batch-cooking routine

entries.nuance: 반찬 are the small shared side dishes — kimchi, seasoned vegetables (나물), braised items, pickles — set out alongside rice and soup at every Korean meal; they are communal, usually free at restaurants, and refillable on request. It is Sino-Korean, written 飯饌, literally 'rice (飯) + prepared food (饌)', i.e. dishes that accompany rice — the etymology itself tells you they are companions to 밥, not standalone mains. The core contrast is 반찬 vs 주요리/메인 (main dish): a 반찬 is never what you 'order' as your meal; it supports the rice. Within 반찬, 밑반찬 are the long-keeping fridge staples. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 반찬 like a Western 'side' you order individually (a side of fries) — in Korea they come automatically with the meal and you ask for more with 반찬 좀 더 주세요, you do not order them à la carte. Another subtlety: 반찬 is generally an uncountable category; you talk about 반찬이 많다/적다 (many/few). Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 반찬 as a main dish you order on its own — 반찬 (literally 'food that goes with rice') accompanies the meal; the main is 주요리/메인 or the specific dish name.
Expecting to pay per side or order them individually like Western 'sides' — in Korea they usually come free with the meal and you simply ask 반찬 좀 더 주세요 for refills.
Pluralizing as 반찬들 to mean 'side dishes' — 반찬 is a number-neutral category noun; use 반찬이 많아요 ('there are many side dishes').

entries.shortExplanation: 간식 means "snack" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 간식 (gansik) means "snack". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 간식을 먹다 ("to have a snack"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 간식 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 'eat'; a light bite between meals to tide you over
시간 'time'; the set snack break, especially for children at school/home
-거리 'stuff/material for'; 간식거리 = snack items, things to nibble
으로 marks 'as/for' a snack; names what the snack is

examples.en: I like snacks.
examples.note: simple preference statement

examples.en: I'm hungry — shall we have a little snack?
examples.note: -는데 'since/and' background + -ㄹ까요 suggestion; everyday offer

examples.en: I prepared fruit as a snack for the kids.
examples.note: 으로 'as'; the caregiver context where 간식 is most used

entries.nuance: 간식 is a light snack eaten between meals to bridge hunger — fruit, rice cakes, cookies, bread — never a full meal in itself. It is Sino-Korean, written 間食, literally 'between (間) + eating (食)', i.e. 'eating in between', which pinpoints its meaning: food taken in the gap between regular meals. This sets up a precise three-way contrast you should master: 간식 = between-meal snack, 후식 (後食) = dessert right after a meal, 야식 (夜食) = late-night food. They are not interchangeable — fruit eaten at 3 p.m. is 간식, the same fruit eaten right after dinner is 후식, and fried chicken at midnight is 야식. The English-speaker pitfall is using 간식 for any non-main food including dessert; keep 간식 strictly for the between-meals bite and use 후식 for the end-of-meal sweet. Culturally, 간식 strongly evokes children's snack time. Register is neutral and everyday.

Confusing it with 야식 — late-night eating (after dinner, at night) is 야식 (夜食); 간식 is the daytime between-meals snack.

entries.shortExplanation: 후식 means "dessert" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "dessert" is 후식 (husik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 후식을 먹다 ("to have dessert"). Watch the particle attached to 후식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 'eat'; the sweet course taken right after the main meal
으로 'as/for'; Koreans often end a meal with coffee as the 후식
나오다 'come out/be served'; set menus include a 후식 that 'comes out' at the end
the English-based 디저트 is the trendy café synonym, especially for cakes/sweets

examples.en: I like dessert.
examples.note: plain preference statement

examples.en: After the meal we had ice cream for dessert.
examples.note: 식사 후에 'after the meal' + 으로 'as'; the textbook dessert frame

examples.en: 'Husik' is the same word as 'dessert'.
examples.note: 랑 'with/and' + 같은 말 'the same word'; pointing out the native/loanword pair

entries.nuance: 후식 is dessert — the sweet or finishing course eaten right after a meal, such as fruit, ice cream, tteok, or coffee. It is Sino-Korean, written 後食, literally 'after (後) + eating (食)', i.e. 'after-food', so the etymology directly encodes 'what you eat after the meal'. The key synonym pair is 후식 vs 디저트: they mean the same thing, but 후식 is the native Sino-Korean term that feels slightly more traditional/formal (a set-menu 'course' served as 후식), while 디저트 is the English loanword that dominates café culture and trendy sweets — you order 디저트 at a dessert café, but a Korean restaurant's set meal lists 후식. The sharp contrast to drill is 후식 (after-meal dessert) vs 간식 (間食, between-meals snack): an apple after lunch is 후식; an apple at 3 p.m. between meals is 간식. The English-speaker pitfall is lumping all sweet snacks as 'dessert/후식' — Korean separates the end-of-meal course (후식) from the between-meal nibble (간식). Register is neutral.

entries.shortExplanation: 라떼 means "latte" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 라떼 (ratte) = "latte". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 라떼를 마시다 ("to drink a latte") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 라떼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 마시다 'drink', not 먹다 — it is a beverage, so the drink verb is required
잔 'cup/glass' is the counter for drinks; one serving is 한 잔
아이스 (ice) + 라떼; 'iced' uses the loanword 아이스, ordered year-round
flavor + 라떼 compounding; 카페라떼, 녹차라떼 follow the same pattern

examples.en: I like lattes.
examples.note: simple preference statement

examples.en: One hot latte, please.
examples.note: real café order; 따뜻한 'hot/warm' + counter 잔 + the polite 주세요

examples.en: I like lattes more than (black) coffee.
examples.note: comparison with 보다 'than'; contrasting the milky latte with plain coffee

entries.nuance: 라떼 is a café latte — espresso with lots of steamed milk — and by extension flavored milk drinks like 녹차라떼 (green-tea latte) or 고구마라떼 (sweet-potato latte). It is a loanword from Italian latte ('milk'), which itself just means 'milk' in Italian; in Korean it has been clipped from 카페라떼 and now stands alone for the drink. The crucial grammar point is the verb: because it is a beverage you must use 마시다 'drink', not 먹다 'eat' — though casual speech sometimes stretches 먹다 to drinks, the safe, correct choice with a latte is 마시다. Count it with 잔 'cup/glass'. The synonym contrast worth knowing is 라떼 vs 아메리카노 vs 커피: 아메리카노 is espresso + water (black, no milk), plain 커피 is the umbrella word for coffee, and 라떼 specifically has milk — so a Korean who 'doesn't like coffee' may still drink 라떼 for the milky mildness. English-speaker pitfall: do not say 라떼를 먹어요 by default; use 마셔요. Register is fully casual and modern (café vocabulary).

Using 먹다 with it ('라떼를 먹어요') — a latte is a drink, so the correct verb is 마시다: 라떼를 마셔요. (Casual speech bends this, but 마시다 is the safe form.)
Counting it with 개 — drinks use 잔: 라떼 한 잔 (one cup of latte), not 라떼 한 개.
Treating 라떼 and 아메리카노 as interchangeable 'coffee' — 라떼 has steamed milk, 아메리카노 is black espresso-and-water; they are different orders.

entries.shortExplanation: 차 means "tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 차 (cha) means "tea". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 차를 마셔요 ("I drink tea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다 (drink); 차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를, not 을
the verb for letting tea leaves steep; 차를 끓이다 is to boil it
counter 잔 for cups/glasses of liquid; the number 한 (one) comes before the counter

usagePhrases.en: to serve tea to a guest
usagePhrases.note: 대접하다 is a polite, hospitable verb for offering food or drink to someone

examples.en: I drink tea in the morning.
examples.note: Basic habit sentence; 마셔요 is the 요-form of 마시다, which contracts 마시+어요 to 마셔요.

examples.en: Shall I give you a cup of warm tea?
examples.note: 드릴까요 is the humble offering form; note 따뜻한 (warm) modifying the noun directly before 차.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸렸을 때는 따뜻한 유자차를 마시는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gamgie geollyeosseul ttaeneun ttatteutan yujachareul masineun ge joayo.
examples.en: When you catch a cold, it's good to drink warm citron tea.
examples.note: Real-life advice register; 유자차 (citron tea) shows how a flavor word attaches in front of 차.

entries.nuance: 차 (茶) is the Sino-Korean word for 'tea,' the brewed leaf or herbal drink, and because it is a beverage it must pair with 마시다 (to drink), never 먹다 (to eat) — though casual speakers do say 차를 먹다 colloquially, learners should default to 마시다. The same syllable 차 (車) also means 'car/vehicle,' so only context separates 차를 마시다 (drink tea) from 차를 타다 (ride a car); they are written identically. Unlike English 'tea,' Korean 차 covers herbal and grain infusions too, so 보리차 (barley tea) and 옥수수차 (corn tea) are 차 even with no tea leaves. A common English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 먹다 by analogy with 'have some tea,' but in standard Korean a polite host says 차 드세요 (드시다 being the honorific of 마시다/먹다). Natural collocations include 차를 우리다 (steep tea) and 차 한 잔 하다 (literally 'do one cup of tea,' meaning to chat over tea).

Confusing 차 'tea' with 차 'car': 차를 타요 means 'I ride a car,' not 'I drink tea.' The verb (마시다 vs 타다) disambiguates the homonym.
Using 을 instead of 를: 차 ends in a vowel, so the object particle is 를 → 차를 마셔요, never 차을 마셔요.

entries.shortExplanation: 주스 means "juice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "juice" is 주스 (juseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주스를 마셔요 ("I drink juice"). Watch the particle attached to 주스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 주스 ends in a vowel, so 를 not 을
the fruit word goes directly in front; 사과 주스 (apple juice), 포도 주스 (grape juice)
짜다 means to press/squeeze; for fresh-squeezed juice you also hear 생주스 (fresh juice)
counter 잔 covers both cups and glasses of liquid in Korean

examples.en: The child likes juice.
examples.note: Simple preference; 좋아하다 takes 를 on its object, so 주스를 좋아해요.

examples.ko: 저는 아침마다 오렌지 주스를 한 잔 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun achimmada orenji juseureul han jan masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink a glass of orange juice every morning.
examples.note: 아침마다 = 'every morning' (마다 = each); the flavor word 오렌지 sits before 주스.

examples.ko: 여기 갓 짜낸 생주스가 정말 신선해요.
examples.romanization: yeogi gat jjanaen saengjuseuga jeongmal sinseonhaeyo.
examples.en: The freshly squeezed juice here is really fresh.
examples.note: Cafe register; 생주스 (fresh juice) contrasts with bottled 주스, and 갓 means 'just now / freshly.'

entries.nuance: 주스 is a direct loanword from English 'juice,' written in 한글 to fit Korean sounds (the English 'j' becomes ㅈ and the final cluster simplifies), and like all drinks it pairs with 마시다, not 먹다. Because it is borrowed, it carries no 한자 and behaves like any vowel-final noun, taking 를 as its object particle. A key boundary for learners: plain 주스 usually implies bottled or store juice, while 생주스 (생 'raw/fresh' + 주스) specifically means fresh-squeezed — ordering 생오렌지주스 at a cafe gets you the freshly pressed version. English speakers sometimes over-pluralize or add 'a' mentally ('a juice'), but Korean has no articles, so 주스를 마셔요 covers both 'I drink juice' and 'I drink a juice.' Habitual collocations: the flavor noun always precedes (오렌지 주스, 토마토 주스), and you can count it with 한 잔 (a glass) or, if bottled, 한 병 (a bottle).

Putting the flavor word after 주스 (주스 오렌지): Korean is modifier-first, so it must be 오렌지 주스, with the fruit in front.
Confusing 주스 (bottled/general juice) with 생주스 (fresh-squeezed): at a cafe, ask for 생주스 if you want it pressed on the spot.

entries.shortExplanation: 콜라 means "cola" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 콜라 (kolla) = "cola". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 콜라를 마셔요 ("I drink cola") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 콜라 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
counter 캔 (from English 'can') for canned drinks; use 한 병 for a bottle
톡 쏘다 is the set phrase for a sharp carbonated bite on the tongue

usagePhrases.en: to put ice in the cola
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination (into the cola); 넣다 = to put in

examples.en: Cola, please.
examples.note: Ordering minimal form; 주세요 (please give) is the everyday way to order at a counter.

examples.en: With pizza, cold cola really is the best.
examples.note: 에는 marks pairing ('with pizza'); 역시 = 'as expected / sure enough,' a very natural filler here.

examples.ko: 탄산 빠진 콜라는 맛이 없어서 안 마셔요.
examples.romanization: tansan ppajin kollaneun masi eopseoseo an masyeoyo.
examples.en: Flat cola tastes bad, so I don't drink it.
examples.note: Real-life complaint; 탄산 빠진 = 'with the fizz gone (flat),' and 안 마셔요 negates with 안.

entries.nuance: 콜라 is a loanword for 'cola,' transcribed so the English 'c' becomes ㅋ and 'la' becomes 라, and like any carbonated drink it takes 마시다 rather than 먹다. It functions as a near-generic term: Koreans say 콜라 for the brown fizzy soda regardless of brand, much as some English speakers say 'coke' generically, though 코카콜라 names the specific brand. A useful distinction is 콜라 vs the broader 탄산음료 (carbonated drink): 콜라 is one specific kind, while 탄산음료 is the whole category including 사이다 (note: Korean 사이다 is a clear lemon-lime soda like Sprite, not alcoholic cider — a classic false-friend trap). Because it carries fizz, the signature collocation is 톡 쏘다 (to have a sharp tingling bite). English speakers should remember there is no article and no plural marker, so 콜라 한 잔 더 주세요 ('one more glass of cola, please') uses the counter 잔, while a can is 한 캔.

English speakers should remember there is no article and no plural marker, so 콜라 한 잔 더 주세요 ('one more glass of cola, please') uses the counter 잔, while a can is 한 캔.

entries.shortExplanation: 맥주 means "beer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 맥주 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 counts glasses; a bottle is 한 병 and draft is 생맥주
따르다 (르 irregular: 따라요) is the verb for pouring a drink for someone
에 links the pairing; this combo is nicknamed 치맥 (치킨 + 맥주)

examples.en: How about a glass of beer?
examples.note: Casual invitation; 어때요? (how about?) is the standard way to suggest a drink.

examples.en: Draft beer is colder and fresher than bottled beer.
examples.note: Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 생맥주 (draft) vs 병맥주 (bottled) is a real distinction Koreans make.

examples.ko: 오늘 같은 날엔 치킨에 시원한 맥주 한잔 해야죠.
examples.romanization: oneul gateun naren chikine siwonhan maekju hanjan haeyajyo.
examples.en: On a day like today, you've gotta have chicken and a cold beer.
examples.note: Idiomatic 한잔 하다 ('have a drink'); 해야죠 = 'we really should,' a warm persuasive ending.

entries.nuance: 맥주 (麥酒) is Sino-Korean, literally 'barley(麥) + liquor(酒),' so the 한자 itself tells you it is a grain-based alcohol; as a beverage it takes 마시다, never 먹다 in careful speech. A core contrast for learners is 생맥주 vs 병맥주: 생 (raw/fresh) + 맥주 means draft beer on tap, while 병맥주 is bottled — bars list them separately, and 생맥주 is often shortened to 생맥. usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 소주 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
소주 is sold by the 병 (bottle); the shot glass serving is 한 잔
따르다 (르 irregular → 따라) + 주다 (do for someone); pouring for others is etiquette
에 links the food pairing; grilled 삼겹살 with 소주 is a classic combo

examples.en: One bottle of soju, please.
examples.note: Ordering form; soju comes by the bottle, so 한 병 is the natural count.

examples.ko: 어른께는 두 손으로 소주를 따라 드려야 해요.
examples.romanization: eoreunkkeneun du soneuro sojureul ttara deuryeoya haeyo.
examples.en: You must pour soju for elders with both hands.
examples.note: Etiquette sentence; 께 is the honorific 'to,' and 따라 드리다 is the humble 'pour for (a superior).'

examples.ko: 오랜만에 친구들이랑 소주 한잔하면서 옛날 얘기를 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane chingudeurirang soju hanjanhamyeonseo yennal yaegireul haesseoyo.
examples.en: I had soju with friends after a long time and talked about old times.
examples.note: Social register; 한잔하다 ('have a drink') is the natural casual verb for sharing a drink.

entries.nuance: 소주 (燒酒) is Sino-Korean, literally 'burn(燒) + liquor(酒)' — a nod to its distilled origin — and as an alcoholic beverage it pairs with 마시다, never 먹다 in standard speech. Contrast 소주 with 맥주 (beer) and the popular mix 소맥 (소주 + 맥주, a soju-beer bomb); all are 술 (alcohol). color word in front; white is 화이트 와인, sparkling is 스파클링 와인
따다 is to pop/open a sealed bottle; 와인을 따르다 is to pour it
잔 counts glasses; a bottle is 한 병

examples.en: Would you like a glass of wine?
examples.note: Polite invitation; 하실래요? is the honorific '~ㄹ래요?' offering form.

examples.ko: 이 레드 와인은 고기 요리랑 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: i redeu waineun gogi yorirang jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: This red wine goes well with meat dishes.
examples.note: Pairing language; 어울리다 ('to suit/match') + 랑 ('with') is how Koreans describe food-and-drink harmony.

examples.ko: 기념일이라서 분위기 좋은 곳에서 와인을 한 병 시켰어요.
examples.romanization: ginyeomiriraseo bunwigi joeun goseseo waineul han byeong sikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Since it was an anniversary, we ordered a bottle of wine at a nice place.
examples.note: Occasion register; 시키다 ('to order') and 한 병 (a bottle) fit a special-night context.

Natural collocations include 와인을 따다 (to uncork — note 따다, not 마시다, for opening) and 와인이 잘 어울리다 (the wine pairs well). entries.shortExplanation: 녹차 means "green tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 녹차 (nokcha) means "green tea". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 녹차를 마셔요 ("I drink green tea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 녹차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 녹차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 counts cups of liquid; 한 (one) precedes the counter
우리다 is to steep leaves; over-steeping makes it 떫다 (astringent/bitter)
녹차 also flavors desserts; 녹차 라떼 (green tea latte) is another common one

examples.en: I like green tea more than coffee.
examples.note: Comparison with 보다 ('than') + 더 ('more'); a simple preference sentence.

examples.en: If you steep green tea too long, it turns astringent.
examples.note: Conditional ~면; 떫어지다 ('become astringent') teaches the real taste vocabulary for over-brewed tea.

examples.ko: 식사 후에 따뜻한 녹차 한 잔이면 속이 편해요.
examples.romanization: siksa hue ttatteutan nokcha han janimyeon sogi pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: A warm cup of green tea after a meal settles the stomach.
examples.note: Wellness register; 속이 편하다 ('the stomach is at ease') is the idiomatic digestive phrase.

entries.nuance: 녹차 (綠茶) is Sino-Korean, literally 'green(綠) + tea(茶),' so the 한자 transparently names the color and the drink; as a beverage it takes 마시다, never 먹다. It is a specific type within the broad 차 family, contrasting with 홍차 (紅茶, 'red tea' = black tea), 보리차 (barley tea), and 옥수수차 (corn tea); note the Korean naming logic differs from English, since what English calls 'black tea' is 홍차 ('red tea') in Korean, matching the East Asian convention. A flavor note worth knowing: green tea steeped too long becomes 떫다 (astringent/puckery), a taste word distinct from 쓰다 (bitter), and Koreans will say 떫어요 about over-brewed tea. 녹차 also works as a dessert flavor (녹차 아이스크림, 녹차 라떼), where it doubles as 말차/matcha-style flavoring. English speakers should avoid the 먹다 reflex and remember the verb for steeping is 우리다 (not 끓이다, which is to boil); the natural counter is 한 잔.

Assuming 'black tea' is 검은차: in Korean it is 홍차 ('red tea'); 녹차 is green tea, and the color words follow the East Asian convention.
Describing over-steeped tea as 써요 (bitter) when you mean 떫어요 (astringent): green tea's harsh edge is 떫다, the puckery taste, not 쓰다.

entries.shortExplanation: 생수 means "bottled water" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

water is counted by the 병 (bottle); 한 통 for a large jug
sold at convenience stores (편의점); 사다 = to buy
통 counts large containers; 2리터 한 통 is a 2-liter jug

examples.en: I bought a bottle of water at the convenience store.
examples.note: Shopping past tense; 한 병 is the natural counter for a single bottle.

examples.ko: 수돗물 대신 생수를 마시는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: sudonmul daesin saengsureul masineun sarami manayo.
examples.en: Many people drink bottled water instead of tap water.
examples.note: Contrast with 대신 ('instead of'); pairs 생수 against 수돗물 (tap water).

examples.ko: 등산 갈 때는 생수를 넉넉히 챙겨 가세요.
examples.romanization: deungsan gal ttaeneun saengsureul neongneoki chaenggyeo gaseyo.
examples.en: When you go hiking, pack plenty of bottled water.
examples.note: Practical advice; 넉넉히 ('amply') + 챙겨 가다 ('pack and take along') is everyday usage.

entries.nuance: 생수 (生水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'raw(生) + water(水)' — 'raw' here means untreated/natural spring water sold in bottles — and as a drink it takes 마시다, not 먹다. The key contrast learners need is the three-way split among Korean 'water' words: 물 is the plain general word for water; 수돗물 (水道+물) is tap water from the faucet; and 생수 specifically means commercially bottled mineral/spring water. So you 'drink 물' generally, but you 'buy 생수' at a store. Another near term is 정수기 물 (water from a filter/purifier). The 生 in 생수 is the same 'raw/fresh' morpheme seen in 생맥주 (draft beer) and 생주스 (fresh juice). English speakers sometimes call all drinking water 생수, but if it came from the tap it is 수돗물, and if from a cooler it is 정수기 물. Natural collocations: 생수를 사다 (buy bottled water), counted as 한 병 (a bottle) or 한 통 (a big jug, e.g. 2리터).

Saying 생수를 먹어요: water is a drink → 생수를 마셔요 (먹다 is reserved for solids, though 약을 먹다 'take medicine' is a fixed exception).
Using 생수 for tap water: 생수 is bottled/commercial water; faucet water is 수돗물. Don't say '생수로 손을 씻어요' for tap water.
Counting water with 개: a bottle is 한 병, a big jug is 한 통 — 개 is the wrong counter for bottled water.

examples.en: If you add a slice of lemon to sparkling water, it's much more refreshing.
examples.note: Conditional ~면; 상큼하다 ('zesty/refreshing') is the natural taste adjective here.

entries.nuance: 탄산수 (炭酸水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'carbonic-acid(炭酸) + water(水),' i.e. carbonated water; as a drink it takes 마시다, never 먹다. The 탄산 morpheme ('carbonation/fizz') is the same one in 탄산음료 (carbonated soft drinks), so 탄산수 is unflavored fizzy water while 탄산음료 is the broad category of sweet sodas like 콜라 and 사이다. Contrast 탄산수 with 생수 (still bottled water): the difference is purely the bubbles — 탄산수 has 탄산 (fizz), 생수 does not. When the bubbles go flat, Koreans say 탄산이 빠지다 ('the fizz escapes'), and the lively bite is described as 톡 쏘다. English speakers sometimes conflate 탄산수 with 사이다, but 사이다 is sweet lemon-lime soda, whereas 탄산수 is plain carbonated water with no sugar. A natural way to dress it up is 탄산수에 레몬을 넣다 (add lemon), and the standard counters are 한 병 (a bottle) or 한 잔 (a glass).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 탄산수를 먹어요: sparkling water is a drink → 탄산수를 마셔요.
Confusing 탄산수 with 사이다: 사이다 is sweet lemon-lime soda; 탄산수 is unsweetened carbonated water. Ask for 탄산수 if you want no sugar.
Describing flat sparkling water as 탄산수가 죽었어요 literally-translated from English 'dead': Koreans say 탄산이 빠졌어요 ('the fizz escaped').

entries.shortExplanation: 음료수 means "beverage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 음료수 (eumnyosu) means "beverage". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 음료수를 마셔요 ("I drink a beverage"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 음료수 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 음료수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 for a glass; canned is 한 캔, bottled is 한 병
코너 (from 'corner') labels a store aisle; 음료 코너 is the shortened form
시원하다 ('cool/refreshing') is the habitual adjective for chilled drinks

examples.en: What would you like to drink? Shall I get you a drink?
examples.note: Host offering; 드릴까요? is the humble 'shall I give,' standard when serving a guest.

examples.ko: 저는 단 음료수보다 물을 더 자주 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun dan eumnyosuboda mureul deo jaju masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink water more often than sweet drinks.
examples.note: Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 단 ('sweet') modifies 음료수 to mean sugary drinks.

examples.ko: 회의 전에 음료수 좀 준비해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: hoeui jeone eumnyosu jom junbihae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you prepare some drinks before the meeting?
examples.note: Workplace request; 준비해 주시겠어요? is a polite '~해 주시겠어요?' favor-asking form.

entries.nuance: 음료수 (飮料水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'drink(飮) + material(料) + water(水),' a transparent label meaning 'a beverage,' and naturally it pairs with 마시다, not 먹다. It is the umbrella term for non-alcoholic drinks — sodas, juices, sweet drinks — but in everyday speech it leans toward soft drinks/sodas rather than water, tea, or coffee; if you ask '음료수 드릴까요?' a host will usually reach for juice or a soda, not plain water. Note the near-synonym 음료 (飮料): 음료 is the slightly more formal/written 'beverage' (seen on menus and labels as 음료 코너), while 음료수 is the spoken everyday word. Both contrast with 술 (alcoholic drinks), which 음료수 excludes. A pitfall for English speakers: 'beverage' in English can include coffee or tea, but Korean 음료수 in casual use rarely covers 커피 or 차 — those are named directly. Habitual collocations include 시원한 음료수 (a cold drink) and 음료수 한 잔/캔/병, plus the store sign 음료 코너 (beverage aisle).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 음료수를 먹어요: a beverage is a drink → 음료수를 마셔요.
Using 음료수 to mean plain water: 음료수 implies sodas/sweet drinks; for water say 물 or 생수. '음료수 주세요' likely gets you a soft drink.
Treating 음료수 as including alcohol: it covers non-alcoholic drinks only; alcoholic ones are 술 (e.g., 맥주, 소주).

entries.shortExplanation: 얼음 means "ice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ice" is 얼음 (eoreum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 얼음을 넣다 ("to put in ice"). Watch the particle attached to 얼음 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 얼음 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을; the verb is 넣다 (put in), not 마시다
녹다 ('to melt'); 얼음 takes subject 이 because it ends in a consonant
좀 ('a little/some') softens the request; 주세요 is the polite 'please give'
깨다 ('to break'); crushed ice for drinks is 잔얼음 or 분쇄 얼음

examples.en: Please put ice in the cola.
examples.note: Ordering request; 에 marks 'into the cola,' and 넣어 주세요 asks someone to add it for you.

examples.en: Since it's hot out, the ice melts quickly.
examples.note: Cause with ~니까; 금방 ('right away') + 녹다 ('melt') describes fast melting.

examples.ko: 아이스 아메리카노는 얼음을 가득 넣어야 제맛이에요.
examples.romanization: aiseu amerikanoneun eoreumeul gadeung neoeoya jemasieyo.
examples.en: Iced americano tastes right only when packed full of ice.
examples.note: Cafe register; 가득 ('full') + ~야 제맛이다 ('is only truly tasty when') is an idiomatic 'that's the way it should be.'

entries.nuance: 얼음 is a native Korean word (from the verb 얼다 'to freeze' + the noun-forming ending -음, literally 'the frozen thing'), so it carries no 한자, and unlike every drink in this set you do NOT 마시다 it — you put it in (넣다), it melts (녹다), or you crush it (깨다). This is the headline pitfall: English 'ice' in drinks tempts learners to treat it like a beverage, but 얼음 is a solid object, so 얼음을 마셔요 is wrong; instead you say 얼음을 넣어요 (put ice in) and then 마셔요 the drink itself. Grammatically, 얼음 ends in the consonant ㅁ, so it takes the subject particle 이 (얼음이 녹아요) and object particle 을 (얼음을 넣어요), not 가/를. A near-synonym distinction: 얼음 is ice cubes/chunks, while 성에 is frost on a window and 빙수 is shaved-ice dessert — don't mix them. Useful collocations: 얼음을 넣다 (add ice), 얼음이 녹다 (ice melts), 얼음을 깨다 (crush ice), and at a cafe 얼음 많이/적게 (lots of/less ice).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 얼음을 마셔요: ice is a solid you add to a drink, so the verb is 넣다 → 얼음을 넣어요; you 마시다 the drink, not the ice.
Using 가/를 with 얼음: it ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 이/을 → 얼음이 녹아요, 얼음을 넣어요 (never 얼음가/얼음를).
Confusing 얼음 (ice cubes) with 빙수 (shaved-ice dessert): if you want the dessert, say 빙수/팥빙수, not 얼음.
