entries.shortExplanation: 식혜 means "sikhye, sweet rice drink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 식혜 (sikye) = "sikhye, sweet rice drink". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 식혜를 마셔요 ("I drink sikhye") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 식혜, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 식혜 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
달다 ('to be sweet') is the signature taste; the ㄹ drops before some endings (단 식혜)
잔 counts glasses; served chilled with rice grains floating on top
traditionally made by fermenting cooked rice with 엿기름 (malt); 만들다 ㄹ-irregular

examples.en: Try a glass of sikhye.
examples.note: Offering; 드셔 보세요 ('please try [drinking]') uses honorific 드시다 + ~아 보다 'try doing.'

examples.ko: 식혜는 차갑게 해서 마셔야 더 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: sikyeneun chagapge haeseo masyeoya deo masisseoyo.
examples.en: Sikhye tastes better when you drink it chilled.
examples.note: Serving tip; 차갑게 해서 ('make it cold and then') + ~야 ('only if/must') explains the right way to serve it.

examples.ko: 명절에 한과랑 식혜를 함께 내면 분위기가 살아요.
examples.romanization: myeongjeore hangwarang sikyereul hamkke naemyeon bunwigiga sarayo.
examples.en: Serving sikhye with traditional sweets at the holidays sets a nice mood.
examples.note: Cultural register; 한과 (Korean confections) + 분위기가 살다 ('the atmosphere comes alive') is idiomatic.

entries.nuance: 식혜 (食醯) is a traditional sweet rice beverage made by fermenting steamed rice with malt water (엿기름), leaving tender rice grains floating in a cool, sweet liquid; as a drink it takes 마시다, not 먹다 — though because of the floating rice some people half-jokingly 먹다 it. Note the 한자 (食 'food/eat' + 醯, an old character for fermented liquid) and the spelling: it is 식혜 with ㅖ, not to be confused with 식해 (食醢), a completely different fermented-fish side dish from the east coast — a near-homophone (sikhye vs sikhae) but a savory food, a classic native-speaker spelling trap too. The signature taste adjective is 달다 (sweet), and it is always served 차갑게 (cold), especially after sauna visits and at 명절 (holidays) like Chuseok and Lunar New Year. A near comparison: 식혜 vs 수정과 (수정과 is a darker cinnamon-ginger punch with dried persimmon) — both are traditional sweet drinks but taste entirely different. English speakers should default to 마시다 and remember the counter 한 잔; to make it is 만들다 (a ㄹ-irregular verb).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 식해: 식해 (食醢) is a fermented-fish side dish; the sweet rice drink is 식혜 with the ㅖ vowel.
Saying 식혜를 먹어요 in careful speech: it is a beverage → 식혜를 마셔요 (the floating rice tempts 먹다, but 마시다 is standard).
Confusing 식혜 with 수정과: 식혜 is the malt-fermented sweet rice drink; 수정과 is the cinnamon-ginger persimmon punch — different drinks, different flavors.

entries.shortExplanation: 바나나 means "banana" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 바나나 (banana) means "banana". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 바나나를 먹어요 ("I eat a banana"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 바나나 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
노랗다 becomes 노래요 (ㅎ-irregular)
개 is the all-purpose counter for items
compound: noun + noun, no particle between them

examples.en: A banana, please.
examples.note: bare noun + 주세요 is the simplest way to ask for something

examples.en: I eat a banana every morning.
examples.note: 마다 means 'every'; 를 marks the thing eaten

examples.en: The banana got too ripe so it turned brown.
examples.note: real kitchen complaint; -아서 links cause to result

entries.nuance: 바나나 is a loanword (from English 'banana') written in Hangul, and unlike English it carries no plural form — one banana and a whole bunch are both just 바나나, with quantity shown by a number plus the counter 개 (바나나 세 개). Koreans give every syllable equal length and a flat, even rhythm (ba-na-na), without the stressed first syllable English speakers instinctively add. Note the spelling difference: the fruit is 바나나, but a near-look-alike loanword 바나 does not exist, so don't shorten it. It pairs naturally with 익다 (to ripen), 까다 (to peel), and the compound 바나나 우유 (the beloved banana-flavored milk). The classic English-speaker trap is adding an English-style plural ('바나나들' for 'bananas') — 들 is grammatically possible but sounds unnatural for fruit you'd buy or eat, so leave the noun bare and let context or a counter carry the number.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '바나나들을 먹어요' to mean 'I eat bananas' — Korean does not pluralize food nouns this way; 들 sounds forced. Use the bare noun: 바나나를 먹어요.
Stressing the first syllable like English BA-nana. Korean has no word stress; pronounce all three syllables evenly or you sound unnatural.
Writing the subject as '바나나는' when first introducing it in a sentence like 'the banana is yellow' — for a plain new fact use 바나나가 노래요; 는 adds a contrast nuance you may not intend.

entries.shortExplanation: 딸기 means "strawberry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "strawberry" is 딸기 (ttalgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 딸기를 먹어요 ("I eat strawberries"). Watch the particle attached to 딸기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the vowel 이
빨갛다 → 빨개요 (ㅎ-irregular adjective)
개 counts individual berries
flavor, not real fruit inside

examples.en: Do you like strawberries?
examples.note: drop the particle in casual speech: 딸기(를) 좋아해요

examples.en: These strawberries are really sweet and tasty.
examples.note: 달다 + 맛있다 linked with 고; 가 marks the topic being judged

examples.en: Strawberries are in season in spring so they're cheap.
examples.note: 제철 = peak season; -이라(서) gives the reason

entries.nuance: 딸기 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean and not a loanword), so it never takes a plural ending — a single berry and a whole carton are both 딸기. It is strongly tied to spring (봄), the season when it is 제철 (at its peak), and it is the default 'pink/sweet' flavor in Korea: 딸기 우유, 딸기 아이스크림, 딸기 케이크 all mean the flavor, with no actual berries guaranteed. Don't confuse 딸기 with 산딸기 — 산딸기 (literally 'mountain strawberry') is a wild raspberry, a different fruit. The English-speaker pitfall here is double: first, pluralizing ('딸기들') which sounds unnatural for fruit; second, mishearing the tense double consonant ㄸ at the start — it is a hard, unaspirated 'tt', not a soft English 'd', so 딸기 (ttalgi) is not 달기. It collocates with 달다 (sweet), 빨갛다 (red), 따다 (to pick), and 씻다 (to wash).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pronouncing 딸기 with a soft English 'd' (dalgi). The initial ㄸ is a tense consonant; say a tight, unaspirated 'tt' or the word sounds like a different one.
Using 딸기들 for 'strawberries'. Korean fruit nouns stay bare; the plural marker 들 is unnatural here. Say 딸기를 먹어요 for any amount.
Calling a raspberry 딸기. A wild raspberry is 산딸기 and a regular one is 라즈베리 — 딸기 alone always means the cultivated strawberry.

entries.shortExplanation: 포도 means "grapes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 포도 (podo) = "grapes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 포도를 먹어요 ("I eat grapes") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the vowel ㅗ
달다 → 달아요; 가 marks the subject
송이 counts clustered/blossom-like things
noun compound, no linking particle

examples.en: One bunch of grapes, please.
examples.note: 송이 is the natural counter, not 개

examples.ko: 이 포도가 씨가 없어서 먹기 편해요.
examples.romanization: i podoga ssiga eopseoseo meokgi pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: These grapes are seedless so they're easy to eat.
examples.note: 씨 = seed; -아서 gives the reason, 먹기 편하다 = easy to eat

examples.en: When autumn comes, grapes get really sweet.
examples.note: -아지다 shows a change of state (become sweet)

entries.nuance: 포도 is Sino-Korean, written 葡萄 (the two characters together simply name the fruit; neither is used alone in everyday Korean). It is grammatically a mass/group word, so it is never pluralized and a 'bunch' is counted with the counter 송이 (포도 한 송이), the same counter used for a cluster of flowers — using the all-purpose 개 here sounds childish or wrong. A single grape, if you must, is 포도 한 알 (알 = a small round unit, like a bead or pellet). Like 딸기, it doubles as a flavor word: 포도 주스, 포도 사탕, 포도 맛 candy. The English-speaker trap is treating 'grapes' as inherently plural and reaching for a plural marker, or saying 포도 한 개 — instead, learn the pair 송이 (bunch) and 알 (single grape). It collocates with 달다 (sweet), 시다 (sour), 씨 (seed/pip), and 따다 (to pick).

Counting grapes with 개 (포도 한 개). A cluster is 한 송이 and a single grape is 한 알; 개 is wrong for grapes.
Adding a plural like 포도들 because English 'grapes' is plural. 포도 is already a group noun — keep it bare.
Mixing up 송이 and 알: 송이 = a whole bunch, 알 = one individual grape. Asking for 포도 한 송이 at a store gets you a full bunch, not one grape.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 수박 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을 after the consonant ㄱ (받침)
크다 → 커요 (ㅡ drop); 이 after 받침
통 counts whole round/hollow things
조각 = a cut piece

examples.en: One whole watermelon, please.
examples.note: ask for a whole one with 통, not 개

examples.en: In summer we chill the watermelon and eat it.
examples.note: 차갑게 하다 = make cold; -아서 links the two actions

examples.en: Tap it to see if the watermelon is ripe.
examples.note: 익다 = ripen; -는지 봐요 = check whether

entries.nuance: 수박 is a native Korean word and the icon of Korean summer (여름) — eaten ice-cold in thick slices to beat the heat, often after a meal. The crucial point is counting: a whole melon is 수박 한 통 (통 is the counter for large hollow/rounded items, also used for buckets), while a cut wedge is 수박 한 조각 (조각 = piece). Using 개 for a whole watermelon sounds off; reserve 개 for smaller, ordinary objects. Don't confuse 수박 with 참외 — 참외 is the yellow Korean melon, a completely different summer fruit. The first character looks like 수(水, water) by coincidence of sound, but 수박 is native, not Sino-Korean, so don't over-analyze it. The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (defaulting to 개) and the 받침 particle choice: because 수박 ends in a consonant, the object marker is 을 (수박을) and the subject marker is 이 (수박이), not 를/가. It collocates with 익다 (ripen), 자르다 (to cut), 시원하다 (refreshing), and 통째로 (whole).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수박 한 개 for a whole watermelon. Use 수박 한 통 for a whole one and 한 조각 for a slice; 개 is unnatural here.
Using 를/가 after 수박: it ends in a 받침 (ㄱ), so the correct particles are 수박을 and 수박이.
Calling the yellow Korean melon 수박. That is 참외 — 수박 is specifically the green-striped, red-fleshed watermelon.

Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을 after the 받침 ㄹ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
개 is the everyday counter for tangerines
까다 = to peel by hand

examples.en: Five tangerines, please.
examples.note: 개 counts them; number goes before the counter

examples.ko: 겨울에 따뜻한 방에서 귤을 까 먹어요.
examples.romanization: gyeoure ttatteutan bangeseo gyureul kka meogeoyo.
examples.en: In winter we peel and eat tangerines in a warm room.
examples.note: 까 먹다 = peel-and-eat, a fixed cozy collocation

examples.ko: 귤이 너무 시면 아직 덜 익은 거예요.
examples.romanization: gyuri neomu simyeon ajik deol igeun geoyeyo.
examples.en: If the tangerine is too sour, it's not ripe yet.
examples.note: 시다 = sour; 덜 익다 = under-ripe

entries.nuance: 귤 is the small, loose-skinned citrus you peel by hand — closest to an English 'mandarin' or 'tangerine,' NOT an orange. The synonym line matters: 오렌지 (loanword 'orange') is the bigger, thick-skinned fruit you cut or juice, while 귤 is small and peels easily; calling a 귤 an 오렌지 marks you as a beginner. 귤 is deeply seasonal — winter (겨울), especially Jeju (제주) tangerines — and culturally tied to the image of lounging on a warm 온돌 floor peeling them one after another, captured in the verb phrase 까 먹다 (peel and eat). It is a single syllable ending in ㄹ, so the object particle is 을 (귤을) and subject is 이 (귤이). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: mapping it to 'orange' (use 오렌지 for that), and pronouncing the ㄹ-final syllable — say 'gyul' as one tight syllable, not 'gyu-eul.' It collocates with 까다 (peel), 달다/시다 (sweet/sour), and 한 박스 (a box of them, the way they're sold in winter).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 귤 as 'orange' and using 오렌지. 귤 = the small peel-by-hand tangerine/mandarin; 오렌지 = the large thick-skinned orange. They are different fruits in Korean.
Pronouncing 귤 as two syllables 'gyu-eul.' It is one syllable, gyul, with ㄹ as the final 받침.
Using 를/가 after 귤. Because it ends in ㄹ (a consonant), the right particles are 귤을 and 귤이.

entries.explanation: 토마토 (tomato) = "tomato". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 토마토를 먹어요 ("I eat a tomato") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 토마토, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅗ
빨갛다 → 빨개요 (ㅎ-irregular)
개 counts each tomato
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: One pack of cherry tomatoes, please.
examples.note: 방울토마토 = cherry tomato; 팩 = pack

examples.en: I just eat tomatoes like fruit.
examples.note: 과일처럼 = like fruit; 그냥 = just/plain

examples.en: The tomato is nicely ripe so its color is red.
examples.note: 익다 = ripen; -아서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 토마토 is a loanword (from 'tomato') written so that it reads the same forward and backward in Hangul — a fun fact Koreans themselves point out. Culturally, Korea treats the tomato more as a fruit (과일) than a cooked vegetable: people eat it raw, sometimes with sugar, or drink 토마토 주스, far more than they cook with it. A key sub-word is 방울토마토 (literally 'bell/droplet tomato') for cherry tomatoes, sold by the 팩 (pack). Like all loanwords, give each syllable even weight (to-ma-to) with no English stress on the first. The English-speaker pitfall is, again, the plural — don't say 토마토들; the bare noun covers any quantity. Also resist English word stress (toMAYto). It collocates with 익다 (ripen), 빨갛다 (red), 신선하다 (fresh), and 썰다 (to slice).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 토마토들 for 'tomatoes.' Korean keeps food nouns bare; use 토마토를 먹어요 regardless of number.
Applying English stress (to-MAY-to). Korean is syllable-timed: pronounce to-ma-to evenly and flatly.
Assuming a tomato is grouped with cooking vegetables and looking for a special word — in everyday Korean it's often eaten and spoken of as 과일 (fruit); the cherry kind is 방울토마토.

entries.explanation: 당근 (danggeun) means "carrot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 당근을 먹어요 ("I eat a carrot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당근 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을 after the 받침 ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
개 counts whole carrots
채 썰다 = cut into thin strips

examples.en: Two carrots, please.
examples.note: 개 counts them; the number precedes the counter

examples.en: I julienne the carrot and stir-fry it.
examples.note: 채 썰다 → -아서 → 볶다, a cooking sequence

examples.en: My kid dislikes carrots so I mince them small.
examples.note: 싫어하다 = dislike; 다지다 = mince

entries.nuance: 당근 is a native Korean word for the orange root vegetable, a staple in stir-fries, fried rice, 김밥, and soups — usually 채 썰다 (julienned) or 다지다 (minced) rather than eaten whole. There's a famous double meaning: in casual slang 당근(이지) means 'of course! / obviously!' (a pun, because 당근 sounds like 당연하지), but in any food context it is simply the carrot. Note the spelling 당근 with 받침 ㄴ on both syllables, so the object marker is 을 (당근을) and subject 이 (당근이). The English-speaker pitfall is the plural again (no 당근들) and the slang trap — if a friend says 당근! they mean 'duh, of course,' not the vegetable. It collocates with 썰다/다지다 (cut/mince), 볶다 (stir-fry), 달다 (sweet), and 신선하다 (fresh).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 당근들 to mean 'carrots.' Keep the noun bare: 당근을 먹어요 works for any amount.
Taking 당근! in conversation literally as 'carrot.' In slang it means '(absolutely) of course' — context tells you which.
Using 를/가 after 당근. It ends in 받침 ㄴ, so correct is 당근을 / 당근이.

entries.shortExplanation: 양파 means "onion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "onion" is 양파 (yangpa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 양파를 먹어요 ("I eat onion"). Watch the particle attached to 양파 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
맵다 → 매워요 (ㅂ-irregular)
개 counts each bulb
볶다 = stir-fry until soft/sweet

examples.en: Just one onion, please.
examples.note: 만 = only/just; softens the request

examples.en: When I cut onions, my eyes water.
examples.note: -(으)면 = when/if; 눈물이 나다 = tears come

examples.en: If you stir-fry onion a long time, it gets sweet.
examples.note: 볶다 + -(으)면; 단맛이 나다 = a sweet taste develops

entries.nuance: 양파 is the round bulb onion and is Sino-Korean-plus-native in feel: the prefix 양 (洋, 'Western/foreign') marks it as the 'Western' allium, distinguishing it from native 파 (green onion/scallion). That 양 prefix is the same one in 양배추 (cabbage, 'Western 배추') and 양식 (Western food) — a useful pattern: 양 + X often means the imported version. The vital contrast is 양파 (bulb onion) vs 파 (green onion/scallion): they are different plants used differently, and swapping them in a recipe is a real error. 양파 famously makes your eyes water (눈물이 나다) when cut, and turns sweet (단맛) when slow-cooked. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 양파 vs 파 mix-up, plus assuming 맵다 conjugates regularly — it's ㅂ-irregular, so 'the onion is pungent' is 양파가 매워요, not 맵어요. It collocates with 썰다 (slice), 볶다 (stir-fry), 다지다 (mince), and 까다 (peel).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 양파 (bulb onion) with 파 (green onion/scallion). They are distinct; 양파 = the round onion, 파 = the long green stalk.
Conjugating 맵다 regularly as 맵어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 양파가 매워요 is correct.
Adding a plural 양파들. Korean leaves the noun bare; 양파를 사요 covers one or many.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 감자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
맛있다 → 맛있어요; 가 marks the subject
개 counts each potato
삶다 → 삶아요 = to boil

examples.en: Three potatoes, please.
examples.note: 개 counts them; number before counter

examples.en: I boil the potatoes and mash them.
examples.note: 삶다 → -아서 → 으깨다 (mash)

examples.en: I prefer boiled potatoes to fries.
examples.note: A보다 B가 좋다 = prefer B over A; 삶은 = boiled (modifier)

entries.nuance: 감자 is a native Korean word for the starchy potato, boiled (삶다), fried as 감자튀김 (fries), or simmered in stews like 감자탕 and 감자조림. The single most important contrast is 감자 (potato) vs 고구마 (sweet potato): 고구마 is sweeter, often purple-skinned and orange/yellow inside, roasted as 군고구마 in winter — confusing the two is a classic beginner slip, and they are NOT interchangeable in recipes. The English-speaker pitfall is the 감자/고구마 mix-up and over-pluralizing — no 감자들; the bare noun is fine. The verb 삶다 looks tricky but conjugates to 삶아요 (boil). It collocates with 삶다 (boil), 튀기다 (fry), 으깨다 (mash), and 깎다 (to peel with a knife).

Saying 감자들 for 'potatoes.' Keep it bare: 감자를 사요 works for any quantity.
Using 깎다 vs 까다 for peeling: a potato is peeled with a knife/peeler → 감자를 깎다, whereas soft-skinned fruit like 귤 is 까다 (peel by hand).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 오이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

시원하다 = cool/refreshing; 가 marks subject
개 counts each cucumber

usagePhrases.en: I season the cucumber (as a side dish)
usagePhrases.note: 무치다 = dress/season into 무침

examples.en: Two cucumbers, please.
examples.note: 개 counts them

examples.en: I slice the cucumber thin and dress it.
examples.note: 얇게 썰다 = slice thin; 무치다 = make into a seasoned side

entries.nuance: 오이 is the crisp, watery cucumber, eaten raw, pickled (오이지), or seasoned as 오이무침 / 오이소박이 (a stuffed cucumber kimchi). Its hallmark adjective is 시원하다 — here meaning 'cool and refreshing' (the same word used for refreshing soup or cold water), not literally 'cold,' which is 차갑다; 오이가 시원하다 captures that fresh, hydrating crunch. Culturally, 오이 is a famous love-it-or-hate-it food: some people are sensitive to its smell, so liking or disliking 오이 is a common conversation topic. entries.shortExplanation: 마늘 means "garlic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "garlic" is 마늘 (maneul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마늘을 먹어요 ("I eat garlic"). Watch the particle attached to 마늘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을 after the 받침 ㄹ
맵다 → 매워요 (ㅂ-irregular)
쪽 counts a single clove
다지다 = mince finely

examples.en: Please add just a little garlic.
examples.note: 조금만 = only a little; 넣다 = put in

examples.en: A lot of garlic goes into Korean food.
examples.note: 들어가다 = go in/be included; 가 → here 이 after 받침

examples.en: I mince the garlic and stir-fry it in oil.
examples.note: 다지다 → -아서 → 볶다, a base step in Korean cooking

entries.nuance: 마늘 is a native Korean word for garlic, and few foods are more central to Korean cooking — it's the aromatic base (with 양파 and 파) of countless dishes, eaten raw with grilled meat, pickled, or 다지다 (minced) into almost everything. Conjugating 맵다 as 맵어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 마늘이 매워요.
Using 를/가 after 마늘. It ends in ㄹ, so the correct particles are 마늘을 / 마늘이.

entries.shortExplanation: 배추 means "napa cabbage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배추 (baechu) = "napa cabbage". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 배추를 사요 ("I buy napa cabbage") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배추, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅜ
싱싱하다 = fresh/crisp; 가 marks subject
포기 counts whole leafy heads/plants

usagePhrases.en: I make kimchi with napa cabbage
usagePhrases.note: -로 = with/using; 김치를 담그다 = make kimchi

examples.en: One head of napa cabbage, please.
examples.note: 포기, not 개, for a whole head

examples.ko: 이 배추가 아주 싱싱하고 속이 꽉 찼어요.
examples.romanization: i baechuga aju singsinghago sogi kkwak chasseoyo.
examples.en: This napa cabbage is very fresh and tightly packed inside.
examples.note: 속이 차다 = the inside is full/dense (a quality cabbage)

examples.en: In autumn we make a big batch of winter kimchi with napa cabbage.
examples.note: 김장 = the annual kimchi-making; 배추로 = using cabbage

entries.nuance: 배추 is a native Korean word for napa (Chinese) cabbage — the tall, pale, leafy head that is THE base of kimchi, not the round Western head cabbage, which is 양배추 (literally 'Western 배추,' with the 양 = 洋 'foreign' prefix seen also in 양파). Keep 배추 (napa) and 양배추 (round green cabbage) distinct: they look and taste different and are used in different dishes. A whole head is counted with the special counter 포기 (배추 한 포기 / 두 포기), the counter for leafy clumped plants — 개 is wrong here. 배추 is bound up with 김장 (the seasonal mass kimchi-making) and the verb 담그다 (to make/ferment kimchi, 김치를 담그다). The English-speaker pitfall is using 개 instead of 포기, confusing 배추 with 양배추, and pluralizing (no 배추들). It collocates with 절이다 (to salt/brine), 싱싱하다 (fresh), 속이 차다 (dense inside), and 다듬다 (to trim).

Counting cabbage with 개. A whole head of napa cabbage is 배추 한 포기; 개 is unnatural for it.
Confusing 배추 (napa cabbage for kimchi) with 양배추 (round green/Western cabbage). They are different vegetables.
Saying 배추들 for 'cabbages.' Use the bare noun with the counter 포기: 배추 두 포기.

entries.shortExplanation: 고양이 means "cat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고양이 (goyangi) means "cat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고양이가 있어요 ("there is a cat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고양이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 고양이 ends in a vowel, so the subject marker is 가, not 이
키우다 (to raise/keep a pet) is the natural verb, paired with object 를
animals are counted with 마리, never with 개 (which is for objects)
길 (street) + 고양이; a very common compound you will see on signs and news

examples.en: The cat is cute.
examples.note: simple: subject 가 + the high-frequency adjective 귀엽다

examples.en: I want to keep a cat.
examples.note: everyday: object 를 with 키우다 + -고 싶어요 'want to'

examples.ko: 우리 고양이는 사람을 별로 안 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: uri goyangineun sarameul byeollo an joahaeyo.
examples.en: Our cat doesn't really like people.
examples.note: real situation: topic 는 to introduce the cat, then 별로...안 'not really'

entries.nuance: 고양이 is the plain, everyday noun for a cat, neutral in register and usable from the classroom to the news. A kitten is 새끼 고양이 or affectionately 아기 고양이, and pet owners shorten the word to the cute 냥이 or write the cat-sound 야옹 online. There is no separate male/female word the way English has none either, so 고양이 covers them all. The pitfall for English speakers is the existence verb: you must say 고양이가 있어요 ('there is a cat'), because 있다 takes the subject particle 가/이 — English 'I have a cat' tempts learners to reach for an object and say the ungrammatical 고양이를 있어요. Also note Korean does not mark plural here: 고양이 두 마리 already means two cats without any -들 ending, and adding 들 to count sounds unnatural.

Counting with 개 as in 고양이 한 개. 개 counts inanimate objects; living animals require 마리, so it must be 고양이 한 마리.
Forcing a plural with 고양이들 두 마리. The counter 마리 already supplies the number, and the extra 들 is redundant and unnatural — just say 고양이 두 마리.

entries.shortExplanation: 새 means "bird" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bird" is 새 (sae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 새가 날아요 ("the bird flies"). Watch the particle attached to 새 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 날다 (to fly) is the signature verb; subject marker 가 after the vowel
counted with the animal counter 마리
지저귀다 is the natural verb for small-bird song, more specific than 노래하다
도 'also' + 둥지 (nest), a frequent collocation

examples.en: There is a bird in the tree.
examples.note: simple: location 에 + existence 있어요 with subject 가

examples.en: Birds chirp every morning.
examples.note: everyday: 마다 'every' + the verb 지저귀다 for birdsong

examples.en: One bird is flying across the sky.
examples.note: real situation: 하늘을 날다 'fly the sky' uses 을, an idiomatic exception

entries.nuance: 새 is the one-syllable umbrella word for any bird, neutral and basic. To name a species Koreans prefix or attach another element — 참새 (sparrow), 까치 (magpie), 비둘기 (pigeon), 독수리 (eagle) — so 새 is the generic, the others are specific, much like 'bird' versus 'sparrow' in English. The big trap is the homophone 새 meaning 'new', which is a pre-noun (관형사) appearing before a noun, as in 새 가방 'new bag'; the bird stands alone as a full noun and can take particles, so 새가 noticeably differs in role from the adjectival 새. One sound point: when you fly somewhere, Korean idiomatically says 하늘을 날다 with the object particle 을 even though English 'fly in the sky' feels locative — treat 하늘을 날다 as a fixed expression rather than translating 'in' as 에서.

Adding 들 in 새들 한 마리. With the counter 마리 the plural marker is unnecessary; say 새 한 마리 (or just 새들 alone when you mean 'birds' generally without counting).

entries.shortExplanation: 물고기 means "fish (live)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 물고기 (mulgogi) = "fish (live)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 물고기가 헤엄쳐요 ("the fish swims") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 물고기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 헤엄치다 (to swim) is the verb for fish/animals in water; subject 가
키우다 'to raise' an aquarium fish, with object 를
living fish are counted with 마리
잡다 'to catch' — the verb of fishing, takes object 를

examples.en: There is a fish in the tank.
examples.note: simple: 어항 (fish tank) + 에 + existence 있어요

examples.en: I keep small fish.
examples.note: everyday: adjective 작은 'small' modifying the object 물고기를

examples.en: We caught a lot of fish in the sea.
examples.note: real situation: 에서 marks the place of action, 잡다 + past 잡았어요

entries.nuance: 물고기 is literally 물 (water) + 고기 (flesh/meat) — a 'water-creature' — and crucially names the fish while it is alive and swimming. The sharp contrast every learner needs is 물고기 versus 생선 (生鮮, 'fresh-raw'): the moment a fish is destined for the table or sits on ice at the market it becomes 생선, so you order 생선 at a restaurant and keep 물고기 in a pond or aquarium. A third word, 회, names raw sliced fish (sashimi). The English-speaker pitfall is using one word 'fish' for all three situations: saying 물고기 주세요 to a waiter sounds like you want a live pet, not a meal — say 생선 주세요. Note also that 물고기 is singular and plural alike; 물고기 세 마리 is 'three fish' with no -들.

Using 개 to count: 물고기 두 개. Fish are animate and must be counted with 마리 — 물고기 두 마리.
Pluralizing as 물고기들 다섯 마리. The counter already gives the number; drop 들 and say 물고기 다섯 마리.

entries.shortExplanation: 토끼 means "rabbit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 토끼 (tokki) means "rabbit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 토끼가 뛰어요 ("the rabbit jumps/hops"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 토끼 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 뛰다 (to run/jump) captures a rabbit's hop; subject 가 after the vowel
키우다 for keeping it as a pet, with object 를
counted with the animal counter 마리
처럼 'like'; a natural simile comparing speed

examples.en: There is a rabbit in the park.
examples.note: simple: 공원 (park) + location 에 + 있어요 with subject 가

examples.en: The child gives grass to the rabbit.
examples.note: everyday: 한테 'to (an animate)' marks the rabbit as recipient

examples.en: They say a rabbit lives in the moon.
examples.note: real situation: the folk image, with 다고 해요 'they say that...'

entries.nuance: 토끼 is the plain noun for a rabbit or hare, learned by Korean children very early through songs and the famous legend of the 달토끼 ('moon rabbit') who pounds rice cakes (떡) on the moon — so the word carries a gentle, fairy-tale warmth. There is no separate everyday word for 'hare' versus 'rabbit'; 토끼 covers both, and a baby is 새끼 토끼. A useful collocation is the simile 토끼처럼 'like a rabbit', evoking either speed or timidity. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not add a plural -들 just because English says 'rabbits' (토끼 두 마리 is already 'two rabbits'), and when the rabbit is the recipient of an action use the animate particle 한테/에게, not the inanimate 에 — say 토끼한테 먹이를 줘요 ('give food to the rabbit'), never 토끼에 줘요.

Adding a plural ending: 토끼들 두 마리. Korean does not require -들 when counting; 토끼 두 마리 already means 'two rabbits'.
Using 에 to mark the rabbit as a recipient: 토끼에 풀을 줘요. Animate recipients take 한테 or 에게, so it must be 토끼한테 풀을 줘요.
Mispronouncing or misspelling the tense consonant as 도끼. 도끼 means 'axe' — keep the tense ㄲ: 토끼.

entries.shortExplanation: 곰 means "bear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bear" is 곰 (gom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 곰이 있어요 ("there is a bear"). Watch the particle attached to 곰 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 곰 ends in a consonant, so the subject marker is 이, not 가
counted with the animal counter 마리
곰 is a stock simile for someone clumsy or dim; 처럼 'like'
인형 (doll/stuffed toy); the standard word for a plush bear

examples.en: There is a bear at the zoo.
examples.note: simple: 곰 takes 이 after its final consonant

examples.en: Bears sleep in winter.
examples.note: everyday: 잠을 자다 'to sleep', with the seasonal 겨울에

examples.en: That person is really like a bear.
examples.note: real situation: 같다 'to be like' — calling someone slow or oblivious

entries.nuance: 곰 is the one-syllable noun for a bear, and it ends in the consonant ㅁ, which decides every particle that follows: the subject marker must be 이 (곰이), the topic 은 (곰은), and the object 을 (곰을) — the vowel-form partners 가/는/를 are wrong here. Culturally 곰 anchors the Dangun foundation myth, where a bear becomes the mother of the Korean nation, and in casual speech calling someone 곰 같다 means they are dense, clumsy, or slow to catch on (the opposite of 여우 'fox', which implies cunning). A teddy bear is 곰 인형. The core English-speaker pitfall is exactly the particle: learners default to 곰가 있어요 by analogy with 고양이가, but a consonant-final noun forces 곰이 있어요.

entries.nuance: 말 (horse) is a one-syllable consonant-final noun, so its particles are the consonant set — subject 이 (말이), topic 은 (말은), object 을 (말을) — and 말을 타다 is the locked collocation for 'ride a horse'. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle default: do not say 말가 있어요 — the consonant ending forces 말이 있어요.

entries.nuance: 돼지 is the everyday noun for the animal pig, and the sharp distinction is that its meat is 돼지고기 (돼지 + 고기 'meat') — Korean systematically names meats this way (소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken), so you keep 돼지 for the living animal and switch to 돼지고기 at the table or butcher. entries.nuance: 강아지 literally means a puppy (the young of 개 'dog'), but in real Korean life it is the warm, default word people use for any beloved pet dog regardless of age — saying 우리 강아지 about a ten-year-old dog is completely normal and conveys affection, much like English 'puppy' or 'doggy' used fondly. entries.nuance: 산 is the plain native word for a mountain or hill — Korea is about 70% mountainous, so 산 shows up constantly and even small wooded hills behind a neighborhood (뒷산, the back-hill) count as 산. The activity of climbing one is 등산(登山, literally 'ascend-mountain'), an enormously popular weekend hobby, so 등산하다/등산 가다 and 산에 올라가다 are everyday collocations. Watch the verb pairing: a mountain is 높다 (high), never 크다/키가 크다, and you climb it with 올라가다 rather than the bare 오르다 in casual speech. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'I go TO the mountain' tempts you toward 에서, but movement-toward always takes 에 (산에 가요); 에서 is reserved for an action performed AT the mountain (산에서 사진을 찍어요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 산에서 가요 to mean 'I go to the mountain'. 에서 marks the place an action happens, not a destination, so for going there you must use 에: 산에 가요.
Calling a tall mountain 큰 산 by translating 'big' literally. Height of a mountain is 높다, so the natural phrase is 높은 산; 큰 산 sounds like it means broad/large in area, not tall.
Using 오르다 by itself in conversation like English 'climb'. Native speech prefers 산에 올라가요 (go up the mountain); bare 오르다 feels bookish.

entries.shortExplanation: 바다 means "sea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sea" is 바다 (bada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 넓은 바다 ("a wide/open sea"). Watch the particle attached to 바다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 바다 is 넓다 (wide) when stressing openness, 깊다 (deep) for depth
에 marks the destination
에서 marks where the swimming happens
take in the view; 바다 구경 = sea-sightseeing

examples.en: The sea is really wide.
examples.note: Simple description; 이/가 makes 바다 the subject under focus.

examples.en: In summer I go to the sea to have fun.
examples.note: Everyday plan: 놀러 가다 = go in order to play/relax; 에 marks destination.

examples.ko: 바다 보면서 회 한 접시 먹으면 최고예요.
examples.romanization: bada bomyeonseo hoe han jeopsi meogeumyeon choegoyeyo.
examples.en: Eating a plate of raw fish while looking at the sea is the best.
examples.note: Real situation: 회(sashimi) + sea view is a beloved Korean coastal treat.

entries.nuance: 바다 is the native word covering both 'sea' and 'ocean' — Korean doesn't routinely split the two, so 바다 does the work of both unless you specifically say 대양 (the technical 'ocean'). It's a top summer destination, tightly bound to 해수욕장 (海水浴場, 'sea-water-bathe-place', a swimming beach) and to 회 (raw fish) eaten by the shore. Describe it as 넓다 (wide) for its openness or 깊다 (deep) for depth, and pair it with 보다 (to look at / take in the view) for the scenic experience. The sharpest pitfall is sound-confusion: 바다 (sea) versus 바닥 (the floor/ground) differ by one final consonant, so 'sit on the floor' (바닥에 앉다) and 'go to the sea' (바다에 가다) are easy to swap — keep the final ㄱ of 바닥 audible. As with all destinations, going there is 바다에 가요 (에), while swimming AT it is 바다에서 수영해요 (에서).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 바다 (sea) with 바닥 (floor/ground). They differ only by the final consonant; 바닥에 앉아요 = sit on the floor, 바다에 가요 = go to the sea. Pronounce the ㄱ of 바닥 clearly.
Reaching for 대양 to say 'ocean' in everyday talk. Native speakers just say 바다 for both sea and ocean; 대양 is a technical/geographic term that sounds stiff in conversation.
Writing 바다에서 가요 for 'I go to the sea'. Movement toward a place takes 에, so it must be 바다에 가요; 에서 would wrongly mark it as the site of an action.

entries.shortExplanation: 강 means "river" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 강 (gang) = "river". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 긴 강 ("a long river") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 강, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: a river is 길다 (long); 강물 = the river's water
에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: I take a walk by the river
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the walking happens
건너다 is the set verb for crossing water/roads

examples.en: This river is very long.
examples.note: Simple description; a river's measure is 길다 (long).

examples.en: I take a walk by the river every evening.
examples.note: Everyday routine: 에서 marks the location of the walk, 마다 = every.

examples.ko: 주말에 한강에서 치킨 시켜 먹는 게 국룰이에요.
examples.romanization: jumare hangangeseo chikin sikyeo meongneun ge gungnurieyo.
examples.en: Ordering and eating chicken by the Han River on weekends is the standard thing to do.
examples.note: Real situation: 한강 picnics + delivery chicken; 국룰 = 'national rule', the default.

entries.nuance: 강(江) is the Sino-Korean word for a river, the larger flowing-water term, as opposed to 시내/개울 (a small stream or brook) and 천(川) which names mid-size streams (e.g. 청계천). In Seoul, 강 almost reflexively evokes 한강 (the Han River), the city's iconic riverside park where people picnic, jog, bike, and order delivery food on the grass. A river is described as 길다 (long), its water is 강물, and the set verb for getting to the other side is 강을 건너다 (to cross). For English speakers the recurring trap is the particle contrast you'll meet with every place noun: 강에 가요 (에, going TO the river) versus 강에서 산책해요 (에서, the walk happens AT the river) — translating 'walk by the river' with the destination 에 is a classic slip. Also don't say 큰 강 expecting it to mean 'long'; size and length aren't the same adjective.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 강에서 가요 for 'I go to the river'. 에서 is for an action's location; a destination needs 에, so say 강에 가요. Reserve 에서 for things like 강에서 산책해요.
Using 강 for a tiny stream. A small brook is 개울 or 시내; calling it 강 overstates its size. Match the word to the water's scale.
Translating 'cross the river' with 지나가다. The fixed verb for moving to the far bank is 건너다 — 강을 건너다 — while 지나가다 just means pass by.

entries.shortExplanation: 나무 means "tree" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 나무 (namu) means "tree". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 큰 나무 ("a big tree"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 나무 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a tree IS 크다 (big/tall) — unlike a mountain, here 크다 is correct
existence/quantity stated with 이/가
아래 = under; 나무 밑 is the more casual equivalent
심다 is the dedicated verb for planting

examples.en: That tree is really big/tall.
examples.note: Simple description; a tree, unlike a mountain, takes 크다 for size.

examples.en: I rested for a moment under the tree.
examples.note: Everyday: 아래에서 = at the spot under it; 에서 marks where resting happens.

examples.en: On Arbor Day I planted a tree together with my family.
examples.note: Real situation: 식목일(Arbor Day) tree-planting; 심다 is the proper verb.

entries.nuance: 나무 carries a useful double life: it means a living tree AND wood as a material (lumber), so 나무 책상 is a 'wooden desk' and 나무를 심다 is 'plant a tree' — context alone tells you which. It is the everyday native word; the Sino-Korean 목(木) survives only inside compounds like 목재 (timber) or 식목일 (Arbor Day, 植木日 'plant-tree-day'). A tree is described with 크다 (big/tall) — note the contrast with 산, which must use 높다 — and you 심다 (plant) it rather than any generic verb. The signature English-speaker mistake is treating plants like weather: 비가 와요 ('rain comes') tempts learners to say 나무가 와요, but a tree doesn't 오다; to talk about its growth use 자라다 (나무가 자라요, the tree grows). Also, 'under the tree' is 나무 아래/밑, with the location particle 에 or 에서 depending on whether something simply is there or an action occurs there.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 나무가 와요 by analogy with 비가 와요. Trees don't 'come'; to express growth use 자라다 (나무가 자라요), and for existence use 있다 (나무가 있어요).
Forgetting that 나무 also means 'wood'. A wooden chair is 나무 의자; learners often hunt for a separate word, but the same 나무 covers both the plant and the material.
Using 높다 to say a tree is tall, copying 산. A tree's size is 크다 — 큰 나무 — whereas 높다 fits mountains, buildings, and the sky, not trees.

entries.shortExplanation: 꽃 means "flower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "flower" is 꽃 (kkot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예쁜 꽃 ("a pretty flower"). Watch the particle attached to 꽃 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 꽃 is the prototypical 예쁘다 (pretty) noun
피다 is THE verb for blooming; 펴요 is its 요-form
꽃 takes 을/를 as an object; 꽃다발 = bouquet
also 꽃집; the place that sells flowers

examples.en: This flower is really pretty.
examples.note: Simple compliment; 이/가 makes 꽃 the subject in focus.

examples.en: When spring comes, the flowers bloom fully.
examples.note: Everyday: 활짝 (wide open) is the set adverb with 피다; 펴요 = blooms.

examples.ko: 기념일이라 여자친구한테 꽃 한 다발 사 줬어요.
examples.romanization: ginyeomirira yeojachinguhante kko tan dabal sa jwosseoyo.
examples.en: Since it was our anniversary, I bought my girlfriend a bouquet of flowers.
examples.note: Real situation: 한 다발 = one bunch/bouquet; 한테 ... 사 주다 = buy for someone.

entries.nuance: 꽃 is the native word for a flower or blossom, and the single most important thing to lock in is its verb partner: flowers 피다 (to bloom), so 꽃이 펴요 / 꽃이 피었어요 is how you say they are blooming/have bloomed — often intensified by 활짝 (활짝 피다, 'bloom wide open'). It pairs naturally with 예쁘다 (pretty) and 아름답다 (beautiful), and figures in gift culture: 꽃다발 (a bouquet), 꽃집/꽃 가게 (a flower shop), and giving 꽃을 주다 on anniversaries. The biggest pitfall mirrors the 나무 error — weather verbs don't transfer, so 꽃이 와요 is wrong; flowers don't 'come', they 피다. A second subtlety: the spelling 꽃 ends in ㅊ, and learners often mishear/mispronounce its liaisons — 꽃이 sounds like [꼬치], 꽃을 like [꼬츨] — so the consonant resurfaces before vowels even though final 꽃 alone is pronounced [꼳].
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 꽃이 와요 instead of 꽃이 펴요. Flowers bloom with 피다, not 오다; weather words like 비가 오다 don't carry over to plants.
Pronouncing 꽃이 as [꼬시] or dropping the consonant. The ㅊ links to the vowel, so 꽃이 = [꼬치] and 꽃을 = [꼬츨]; the final consonant only becomes [ㄷ] when 꽃 stands alone.
Treating 꽃 as uncountable like English and skipping a counter. To say a bouquet use 한 다발, for single stems 한 송이 — e.g. 장미 한 송이 (one rose).

entries.shortExplanation: 풀 means "grass" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 풀 (pul) = "grass". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 푸른 풀 ("green grass") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 풀, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 풀 takes 푸르다, the 르 word that means vivid green/blue

usagePhrases.en: there is a lot of grass
usagePhrases.note: quantity/existence with 이/가
풀 + 밭(field); a patch of grass to sit on
뽑다 = pull out; weeding the yard

examples.en: The grass in the yard is green.
examples.note: Simple description; 푸르다 conjugates to 푸르러요 (르 irregular).

examples.en: We sat on the grassy field and ate our packed lunch.
examples.note: Everyday: 풀밭에 앉다 (sit on the lawn); 에 marks the spot of sitting.

examples.ko: 여름엔 풀이 워낙 빨리 자라서 자주 깎아야 해요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen puri wonak ppalli jaraseo jaju kkakkaya haeyo.
examples.en: In summer the grass grows so fast that you have to mow it often.
examples.note: Real situation: 자라다(grow) + 깎다(mow); 워낙 = 'by nature, extremely'.

entries.nuance: 풀 is the native word for grass and, more broadly, low non-woody plants — which means it also covers 'weeds', the unwanted ones you 뽑다 (pull out) from a garden. The handy compound 풀밭 (풀 + 밭, 'grass-field') names a lawn or grassy patch where people sit and picnic. Its signature adjective is 푸르다 (vivid green/blue), a 르-irregular that becomes 푸르러요 (not 푸르어요), and it 자라다 (grows). Two traps await English speakers. First, homophone overload: 풀 also means 'glue/paste' (풀로 붙이다, stick with glue) and is the verb stem of 풀다 (to untie/solve) — only context separates them. Second, don't confuse 풀 (grass) with 숲 (forest): one is the low ground cover, the other the dense stand of trees. English lumps 'grass' as uncountable, so learners forget that for a single blade you'd say 풀 한 포기.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 풀 (grass) with 풀 (glue) or the verb 풀다 (to untie/solve). They are spelled the same; context decides — 풀이 많다 (lots of grass) vs 풀로 붙이다 (stick with glue).
Mixing up 풀 (grass) and 숲 (forest). 풀 is low ground cover you sit on; 숲 is a woods full of trees. They're different scales of nature.
Saying 푸르어요 for the color. 푸르다 is a 르-irregular adjective, so the correct 요-form is 푸르러요 with a doubled ㄹ.

entries.shortExplanation: 돌 means "stone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 돌 (dol) means "stone". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 큰 돌 ("a big stone"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 돌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a stone is sized with 크다; 무겁다 (heavy) is its other key adjective
existence/quantity with 이/가
던지다 = throw; 돌 is the object with 을/를
돌 + 담(wall/fence); traditional village walls

examples.en: This stone is quite heavy.
examples.note: Simple description; 무겁다 (heavy) is the natural adjective for 돌.

examples.en: The child threw a stone into the river.
examples.note: Everyday: 던지다 takes 을/를; 강에 = into the river (destination 에).

examples.ko: 제주도엔 돌담으로 둘러싸인 옛날 집이 많아요.
examples.romanization: jejudoen doldameuro dulleossain yennal jibi manayo.
examples.en: On Jeju Island there are many old houses surrounded by stone walls.
examples.note: Real situation: 돌담(stone wall) culture; 둘러싸이다 = be surrounded.

entries.nuance: 돌 is the native word for a stone or rock — the everyday term, while 석(石) and 암(巖) are Sino-Korean elements living inside compounds like 석탑 (stone pagoda) or 암석 (rock, geological). It builds vivid compounds such as 돌담 (stone wall) and 돌다리 (stone bridge), staples of old Korean villages, and on volcanic Jeju the 돌하르방 (grandfather statues) are carved from it. A stone is described as 크다 (big) and especially 무겁다 (heavy), and you 던지다 (throw) it or 줍다 (pick it up). The notable pitfall is a homonym that's culturally loaded: 돌 also means a baby's first birthday (the 돌잔치, first-birthday party). They're spelled identically, so 돌이 무거워요 (the stone is heavy) and 돌이 지났어요 (the first birthday has passed) rely entirely on context. English speakers also tend to over-distinguish 'stone' from 'rock', but 돌 comfortably covers both the pebble and the rock.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 돌 (stone) with 돌 (a baby's first birthday). Identical spelling; context separates them — 돌을 던지다 (throw a stone) vs 돌잔치 (first-birthday party).
Hunting for separate words for 'stone' and 'rock'. 돌 covers a pebble up to a boulder; you don't need a different headword for each English term.
Using 무겁다 to mean 'hard'. 무겁다 is heavy (weight); if you mean the stone is hard to the touch, that's 단단하다. Don't conflate the two.

entries.shortExplanation: 섬 means "island" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: an island is sized with 작다/크다
에 marks the destination
에서 marks where living happens
들어가다 'enter' is idiomatic for reaching an island

examples.en: That island is very small.
examples.note: Simple description; 이/가 makes 섬 the subject in focus.

examples.en: I went over to the island by boat.
examples.note: Everyday: 배를 타다 (take a boat) + 섬에 들어가다, the natural 'reach an island'.

examples.ko: 할머니는 평생 그 섬에서 혼자 사셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeonineun pyeongsaeng geu seomeseo honja sasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandmother lived alone on that island her whole life.
examples.note: Real situation: 에서 marks where she lived; 사시다 is the honorific of 살다.

entries.nuance: 섬 is the pure native word for an island. Islands are reached 배를 타고 (by boat) and described with 작다/크다. The usual particle pitfall applies — destination 섬에 가요 (에) versus the place of an action 섬에서 살아요 (에서) — and the 'I go TO the island' phrasing in English tempts the wrong 에서. Don't double up by saying '제주도 섬', since 도 already means island; just say 제주도, or 제주 섬 informally.

Using 가다 with no helper verb when boarding for an island and expecting it to sound natural. Koreans idiomatically say 섬에 들어가다 (enter the island); plain 섬에 가다 is fine too but 들어가다 is more vivid.

에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: I ride a boat on the lake
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the boating happens
주변 = surroundings; 호숫가 = the lakeside

examples.en: This lake is really wide.
examples.note: Simple description; surface size of a lake is 넓다 (wide).

examples.ko: 아침에 호수 주변을 한 바퀴 돌았어요.
examples.romanization: achime hosu jubyeoneul han bakwi dorasseoyo.
examples.en: In the morning I walked one loop around the lake.
examples.note: Everyday: 한 바퀴 돌다 = go around once, a common walking phrase.

examples.ko: 가을엔 호수에 물안개가 껴서 진짜 분위기 있어요.
examples.romanization: gaeuren hosue murangaega kkyeoseo jinjja bunwigi isseoyo.
examples.en: In autumn, mist settles on the lake and it's really atmospheric.
examples.note: Real situation: 물안개가 끼다 (mist forms); 분위기 있다 = has a nice mood.

entries.nuance: 호수(湖水) is a Sino-Korean compound literally meaning 'lake-water' (湖 lake + 水 water) — a still, land-enclosed body of water, contrasted with the flowing 강 (river) and the vast 바다 (sea). The key contrast for learners: 호수 is calm and bounded, whereas 강 moves and 바다 is open and salty; choosing among them is about the water's form, not just size. A lake is 넓다 (wide across) or 깊다 (deep), its edge is 호숫가 (the lakeside, note the inserted ㅅ), and people 보트를 타다 (ride a boat) or stroll 호수 주변 (around it). The same destination-vs-location particle rule governs everything: 호수에 가요 (에, going there) but 호수에서 보트를 타요 (에서, the boating happens there). Because 호수 is fully Sino-Korean and a bit formal, in casual speech for a small pond you might instead hear 연못 (a garden pond) — don't call a tiny ornamental pond a 호수.

Calling a small garden pond a 호수. A 호수 is a sizeable lake; a little ornamental or garden pond is 연못. Match the word to the scale.
Mixing up 호수 (lake, still water) with 강 (river, flowing water). They're different bodies of water — a lake is enclosed and calm, a river flows — so they aren't interchangeable.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 숲 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 숲 is 깊다 (deep) when dense, 우거지다 (overgrown) for lushness
에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: I take a walk in the forest
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the walking happens
숲 + 속(inside); the interior of the woods

examples.en: This forest is really deep.
examples.note: Simple description; a dense forest is 깊다 (deep), as if hard to see through.

examples.en: Hearing birdsong in the forest, my mind grew calm.
examples.note: Everyday: 에서 marks where the hearing happens; 새소리 = birdsong.

examples.ko: 요즘 사람들이 힐링하러 숲속 캠핑을 많이 가요.
examples.romanization: yojeum saramdeuri hillinghareo supsok kaempingeul mani gayo.
examples.en: These days many people go forest camping to recharge.
examples.note: Real situation: 힐링(healing/recharge) + 숲속 캠핑; the nature-wellness trend.

entries.nuance: 숲 is the native word for a forest or woods — a stand of many trees thick enough to feel enclosed — and pairs with 깊다 (deep, when dense) or 우거지다 (to grow lush/overgrown). Its essential compound is 숲속 (숲 + 속, 'inside the forest'), meaning the quiet interior where you're surrounded by trees; 숲길 is a forest path. It carries a calm, restorative connotation, riding the popular 힐링(healing) and 숲세권 (living near woods) trends. Two pitfalls: spelling/sound — 숲 ends in ㅍ, so although bare 숲 is pronounced [숩], the consonant resurfaces in 숲이 [수피], 숲에서 [수페서]; and a recurring mix-up with 풀 (grass) — 숲 is the dense woods of tall trees, 풀 is the low grass underfoot, so don't swap them. Scale also matters: a couple of trees is just 나무 몇 그루, not yet a 숲; the word implies a real expanse of woodland.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 숲 (forest) with 풀 (grass). 숲 is a woods full of trees you walk into; 풀 is low grass on the ground. They describe different scales of nature.
Pronouncing 숲에 as [수베] or dropping the consonant. The final ㅍ links to the vowel, so 숲에 = [수페] and 숲이 = [수피]; 숲 alone is [숩].
Calling a few scattered trees a 숲. 숲 implies a real expanse of dense woodland; for just a handful of trees say 나무 몇 그루 (a few trees) instead.

entries.explanation: "star" is 별 (byeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 밝은 별 ("a bright star"). Watch the particle attached to 별 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: a star is 밝다 (bright); also 반짝이다 (twinkle)
뜨다 is the verb; 떠요 / 떴어요 are its forms

usagePhrases.en: there are many stars in the sky
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks location of existence
별 구경 = stargazing

examples.en: Tonight the stars are really bright.
examples.note: Simple description; a star's quality is 밝다 (bright).

examples.en: As night fell, the stars came out in the sky.
examples.note: Everyday: 뜨다 → 떴어요 (came out); 에 marks where they appear.

examples.ko: 시골 가면 별이 쏟아질 듯이 많아서 진짜 장관이에요.
examples.romanization: sigol gamyeon byeori ssodajil deusi manaseo jinjja janggwanieyo.
examples.en: In the countryside there are so many stars it's like they'll pour down — a real spectacle.
examples.note: Real situation: 쏟아질 듯이 (as if pouring); 장관 = magnificent sight.

entries.nuance: 별 is the native word for a star, and its crucial verb partner is 뜨다 (to rise/come out) — the very same verb used for the sun and moon — so 별이 떠요 / 별이 떴어요 means stars appear, and they set with 지다 (별이 지다). It's described as 밝다 (bright) and 반짝이다 (to twinkle), and figures in fixed phrases like 별을 보다 (stargaze) and the metaphor 별 (a 'star' = celebrity, same as English) plus 별점 (star rating). The leading pitfall is verb choice: English 'the stars come out' lures learners into 별이 와요, but stars don't 오다 — and weather-style 비가 와요 doesn't transfer here either; the right verb is 뜨다. Note too the homophone-ish 벌 (a bee / a punishment): 별 with the ㅕ vowel is a star, 벌 with ㅓ is a bee — keep the vowels distinct so 별 받다 doesn't come out as 벌 받다 ('be punished').

Saying 별이 와요 instead of 별이 떠요. Stars 'rise/come out' with 뜨다 (like the sun and moon), and they set with 지다; 오다 doesn't apply to them.
Confusing 별 (star) with 벌 (bee / punishment). The vowels differ — 별 has ㅕ, 벌 has ㅓ — so 벌을 받다 means 'get punished', nothing to do with stars. Keep the vowel clear.
Using 빛나다 and 반짝이다 interchangeably without care. Both relate to shining, but 반짝이다 specifically captures the twinkling/flickering of stars; 빛나다 is a steadier 'glow/shine'.

entries.shortExplanation: 달 means "moon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 달 (dal) = "moon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 밝은 달 ("a bright moon") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 달, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the moon is 밝다 (bright); 둥근 달 = round moon
뜨다 is the verb; 떠요 / 떴어요 are its forms

usagePhrases.en: there is a moon in the sky
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks location of existence
보름(15th, mid-month) + 달; the round full moon

examples.en: The moon is really bright tonight.
examples.note: Simple remark; 밝다 (bright) + the soft observing ending -네요.

examples.en: As evening came, the moon rose in the east.
examples.note: Everyday: 뜨다 → 떴어요; 동쪽에서 = from the east (where it rises).

examples.en: On Chuseok we make a wish while looking at the full moon.
examples.note: Real situation: 추석(harvest festival) + 보름달; 소원을 빌다 = make a wish.

entries.nuance: 달 carries two everyday meanings — the moon AND a calendar month (한 달 = one month, 다음 달 = next month) — so the same syllable is one of Korean's classic double-duty words, disambiguated purely by context. As the celestial moon it 뜨다 (rises) and 지다 (sets), exactly like 해 (sun) and 별 (star), giving 달이 떴어요; it's 밝다 (bright) and 둥글다 (round). Culturally it anchors 보름달 (보름 'the 15th/mid-month' + 달 = full moon), central to 추석 (the harvest festival) when families 소원을 빌다 (make wishes) under it. Pitfalls: first, the verb — don't say 달이 와요 ('the moon comes'); the moon 뜨다, not 오다. Second, beware the month/moon overlap: 달이 떴어요 = 'the moon rose', but 두 달 = 'two months' (counted with the native-number+달), and 한 달 means a month, never 'one moon'. Keep the context cue in mind so the two senses don't collide.

Saying 달이 와요 instead of 달이 떠요. The moon 'rises' with 뜨다 (and sets with 지다); 오다 ('come') isn't used for it, just as with the sun and stars.
Confusing the moon with the month sense. 달 also means a calendar month — 한 달 = one month, 다음 달 = next month — so 두 달 is 'two months', not 'two moons'; context tells which meaning applies.
Reaching for 가득한 달 to say 'full moon'. The fixed word is 보름달 (보름 = the 15th of the lunar month + 달); 가득한 달 is a literal English-style translation that Koreans don't use.

entries.shortExplanation: 셔츠 means "shirt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 셔츠 (syeocheu) means "shirt". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 셔츠를 입어요 ("I wear a shirt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 셔츠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: upper-body clothing always takes 입다
흰 is the modifier form of 희다 placed before the noun

usagePhrases.en: the shirt is a bit big
usagePhrases.note: subject marker 가; 좀 softens the complaint
clothing is counted with 벌, never 개

examples.en: I wear a shirt.
examples.note: Bare basics: the verb for putting on body clothing is 입다.

examples.en: This shirt fits me well.
examples.note: 잘 맞다 = to fit; the size partner-verb is 맞다, not 좋다.

examples.ko: 면접 때문에 깔끔한 셔츠 한 벌 샀어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop ttaemune kkalkkeumhan syeocheu han beol sasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought one neat shirt for the interview.
examples.note: Real situation: 깔끔하다 (neat/crisp) is the go-to adjective for dress shirts.

entries.nuance: 셔츠 is the loanword for a collared upper-body shirt; the general Sino-Korean cover term for any top is 상의 (上衣, 'upper garment'), and a knit pullover is 티셔츠/티. Because a shirt covers the torso it ALWAYS takes 입다 ('put on the body'), the same family of dressing verbs that splits by body zone in Korean: 입다 for trunk and legs, 신다 for feet, 쓰다 for the head/face, 끼다 for hands. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating 'wear' as one verb the way English does — you cannot say 셔츠를 써요 or 셔츠를 신어요. Register is neutral and the word fits any politeness level. Natural collocations: 셔츠를 입다/벗다 (put on/take off), 셔츠를 다리다 (iron a shirt), 셔츠가 (안) 맞다 (it does (not) fit). Note that to take a shirt off you switch to 벗다, not a negated 입다.

Saying 셔츠를 써요 by mapping English 'wear' onto 쓰다 — 쓰다 is only for things on the head/face (hats, glasses); a shirt must use 입다.
Counting with 개 (셔츠 한 개). Clothing uses the counter 벌, so it is 셔츠 한 벌.
Using a negated 입다 for taking it off (셔츠를 안 입어요 to mean 'I take it off'). Removing clothing is its own verb 벗다: 셔츠를 벗어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 바지 means "pants" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "pants" is 바지 (baji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바지를 입어요 ("I wear pants"). Watch the particle attached to 바지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: legs are body clothing, so 입다 (not 신다)
긴 is the adnominal form of 길다 before a noun
subject marker 가; 바지 stays singular
counted with 벌, and treated as one item

examples.en: I wear pants.
examples.note: Even though English is plural, 바지 is grammatically singular in Korean.

examples.en: These pants are too long for me.
examples.note: -한테 marks the person a measurement is judged against ('for me').

examples.en: I had the pants shortened at the tailor's.
examples.note: Real situation: 길이를 줄이다 (shorten the length) is the standard alteration phrase.

entries.nuance: 바지 covers the lower body, so despite English treating 'pants' as plural, Korean treats it as a single uncountable garment: there is no plural ending, no 'a pair' built into the word, and the verb is 입다 just like a shirt. The dividing line with footwear matters — legs use 입다 but the feet that stick out below use 신다, so you 입다 your 바지 but 신다 your 양말. Jeans are 청바지 (靑—, 'blue-color pants'), shorts are 반바지 ('half pants'), and dress slacks are often just called 슬랙스. The classic English-speaker error is the literal plural reflex — saying 바지들이 길어요 sounds as odd as saying 'pantses'. entries.shortExplanation: 치마 means "skirt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 치마 (chima) = "skirt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 치마를 입어요 ("I wear a skirt") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: lower-body clothing takes 입다
짧은 is the adnominal of 짧다 before the noun
어울리다 = to look good on someone
counted with the clothing counter 벌

examples.en: I wear a skirt.
examples.note: Skirts use 입다, exactly like pants — both are lower-body garments.

examples.en: Isn't this skirt a bit short?
examples.note: -지 않아요? turns it into a soft, seeking-agreement question.

examples.ko: 결혼식에 갈 거라서 단정한 치마를 골랐어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsige gal georaseo danjeonghan chimareul gollasseoyo.
examples.en: I picked a tidy skirt because I'm going to a wedding.
examples.note: Real situation: 단정하다 (tidy/proper) is the register word for formal dressing; 고르다 = to pick.

entries.nuance: 치마 is the native Korean word for a skirt and is purely neutral; the English loanword 스커트 exists but 치마 is what people actually say in daily life, and a traditional hanbok skirt is also 치마. Like all lower-body clothing it takes 입다, and to take it off you switch to 벗다 — never a negated 입다. The trap for English speakers is again the one-word-'wear' habit plus assuming a fancier loanword is more polite; here the plain native 치마 is the unmarked, fully appropriate choice in every register. A very useful partner verb is 어울리다 ('to suit/match'), used with the marker -이/가 for the item and -에게/한테 for the person: 그 치마가 너한테 잘 어울려. Natural collocations: 치마를 입다/벗다, 짧은/긴 치마 (short/long skirt), 치마가 어울리다, 치마를 갈아입다. Do not confuse 어울리다 (looks good on) with 맞다 (fits in size) — a skirt can 맞다 yet not 어울리다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 신다 for a skirt because it hangs near the legs/feet. 신다 is strictly for feet; a skirt takes 입다.
Saying 치마가 나를 잘 어울려요. 어울리다 marks the wearer with -에게/한테, not the object marker: 치마가 나한테 잘 어울려요.
Reaching for the loanword 스커트 thinking it is more polite. 치마 is the natural, register-neutral default; the loanword carries no extra politeness.

entries.shortExplanation: 코트 means "coat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 코트 (koteu) means "coat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 코트를 입어요 ("I wear a coat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 코트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: outerwear is still body clothing, so 입다
두꺼운 is the adnominal of 두껍다 (ㅂ-irregular)
subject marker 가; 따뜻하다 describes warmth
counted with 벌 like other clothing

examples.en: I wear a coat.
examples.note: An overcoat is worn on the body, so the verb is 입다, same as a shirt.

examples.en: Since it's cold outside, put your coat on and go out.
examples.note: -고 links 'put on' then 'go'; the sequence verb 입고 means 'having put on'.

examples.ko: 올겨울에 입을 따뜻한 코트를 하나 장만했어요.
examples.romanization: olgyeoure ibeul ttatteutan koteureul hana jangmanhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I got myself one warm coat to wear this winter.
examples.note: Real situation: 장만하다 (acquire/get for oneself) is warmer and more natural than 사다 for a planned purchase.

entries.nuance: 코트 is a loanword for a warm outer layer; the broader native umbrella term for any outerwear is 외투 (外套, 'outer wrap'), and a padded winter jacket is 패딩 or 점퍼. Even though it is the outermost layer, 코트 still takes 입다 because the rule keys off the body zone (trunk), not how many layers are underneath; you put it on with 입다 and take it off with 벗다. The English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation-driven spelling and the 'wear' reflex: 코트 is two clean syllables (ko-teu) and is never said with 쓰다 or 차다. A second subtlety: when you mean 'put a coat ON over other clothes' Koreans often say 코트를 걸치다 ('throw on lightly'), a nuance 입다 alone doesn't carry. Natural collocations: 코트를 입다/벗다, 코트를 걸치다 (drape on), 두꺼운/긴 코트, 코트 단추를 잠그다 (button up the coat). Note 걸치다 implies a casual, partial wearing, unlike the full 입다.

Saying 코트를 써요 or 코트를 차요 from English 'wear'. A coat covers the body, so only 입다 works.
Spelling/saying it as one blurred syllable. It is 코트 (ko-teu), with the 으 vowel fully pronounced.
Assuming 입다 covers the casual 'throw it on' meaning. For draping a coat loosely over the shoulders, Koreans prefer 걸치다: 코트를 어깨에 걸쳤어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 모자 means "hat; cap" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "hat; cap" is 모자 (moja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 모자를 써요 ("I wear a hat"). Watch the particle attached to 모자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: head items take 쓰다, not 입다
빨간 is the adnominal of 빨갛다 (ㅎ-irregular)
어울리다 with the item marked by 가
accessories are commonly counted with 개/하나

examples.en: I wear a hat.
examples.note: Anything on the head uses 쓰다 — the same verb as for glasses.

examples.ko: 햇볕이 강하니까 모자를 쓰는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: haetbyeochi ganghanikka mojareul sseuneun ge joayo.
examples.en: Since the sun is strong, it's good to wear a hat.
examples.note: 쓰는 게 좋다 = 'it's good to wear', a gentle suggestion pattern.

examples.ko: 야구장에서 응원하려고 팀 모자를 하나 샀어요.
examples.romanization: yagujangeseo eungwonharyeogo tim mojareul hana sasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought a team cap to cheer at the ballpark.
examples.note: Real situation: 모자 covers both dress hats and baseball caps; context decides which.

entries.nuance: 모자 (帽子, 'head-cap thing'; the hanja 帽 means cap) covers everything from a baseball cap to a winter beanie to a formal hat — Korean does not split 'hat' vs 'cap' by separate everyday words. The crucial verb is 쓰다 ('place on the head'), which Korean also uses for glasses and umbrellas; it does NOT take 입다. The headline English-speaker pitfall is twofold: the 'wear = 입다' overgeneralization, and the fact that 쓰다 is a notorious homonym — the same 쓰다 means 'to write' and 'to use' and even 'bitter'. So 모자를 써요 ('I wear a hat') and 편지를 써요 ('I write a letter') share a verb; only the object tells them apart. To take a hat off you use 벗다, the same removal verb as for body clothing. Natural collocations: 모자를 쓰다/벗다, 모자를 푹 눌러쓰다 (pull a cap down low), 모자가 어울리다, 모자를 거꾸로 쓰다 (wear a cap backwards). Note 눌러쓰다 fuses 누르다+쓰다 for jamming a cap down.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 모자를 입어요 by defaulting to 입다 for all clothing. Head-worn items take 쓰다: 모자를 써요.
Assuming 쓰다 only means 'to write/use' and avoiding it for hats. The very same 쓰다 is the correct verb for putting things on the head.
Negating 쓰다 to mean 'take off' (모자를 안 써요 for 'I remove my hat'). Removal is 벗다: 모자를 벗어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 양말 means "socks" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 양말 (yangmal) = "socks". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 양말을 신어요 ("I wear socks") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 양말, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: anything on the feet takes 신다
두꺼운 is the adnominal of 두껍다 (ㅂ-irregular)
subject marker 이 after a consonant
paired footwear uses 켤레, not 벌

examples.en: I wear socks.
examples.note: Feet take 신다 — the same verb as shoes, never 입다.

examples.en: My feet were cold so I put on thick socks.
examples.note: 발이 시리다 ('feet feel cold') is the idiomatic way to say cold feet.

examples.ko: 편의점에서 양말 한 켤레만 사 신었어요.
examples.romanization: pyeonuijeomeseo yangmal han kyeolleman sa sineosseoyo.
examples.en: I just bought and put on a pair of socks at the convenience store.
examples.note: Real situation: 사 신다 (buy-and-wear) compounds the purchase with immediate use.

entries.nuance: 양말 (洋襪, literally 'Western foot-wrap' — coined when Western-style knitted socks arrived) goes on the feet, so it takes 신다, the dedicated foot-dressing verb shared with shoes; it never takes 입다. Crucially it is counted with 켤레, the counter for things that come in matched pairs (also used for shoes and gloves), so 'one pair of socks' is 양말 한 켤레, and the English-speaker who reaches for 벌 (clothing) or 개 (generic) will sound off. The 'wear = one verb' habit is again the core trap: feet are their own zone in Korean's dressing system. A second pitfall is the subject particle — after the final consonant ㄹ you need 이, giving 양말이, not 양말가. Natural collocations: 양말을 신다/벗다, 양말 한 켤레, 발목 양말 (ankle socks), 양말에 구멍이 나다 (a hole forms in the sock). Note removal is again 벗다, and 구멍이 나다 ('a hole appears') uses 나다, not 생기다, in this fixed phrase.

Saying 양말을 입어요 by using 입다 for all clothing. Feet take 신다: 양말을 신어요.
Counting socks with 벌 or 개. A matched pair uses 켤레: 양말 한 켤레.
Attaching 가 after the consonant (양말가). The subject particle after ㄹ is 이: 양말이 따뜻해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 장갑 means "gloves" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
