entries.shortExplanation: 얇다 means "thin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 얇다 (yalbda) = "thin". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 얇은 옷 ("thin (light) clothing") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 얇다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: modifier 얇은 (regular: 얇- + 은); summer wear, opposite of 두꺼운 옷
the prototypical flat-and-thin object
adverb 얇게 + 썰다, a common cooking instruction
idiom — literally 'thin ears,' meaning you believe whatever you hear

examples.en: This paper is thin.
examples.note: regular polite form 얇아요 (얇- + 아요)

examples.en: I wore a thin shirt.
examples.note: 얇은 modifies 셔츠 in the noun-modifier shape

examples.en: I sliced the meat thinly and made bulgogi.
examples.note: real-situation use with the adverb 얇게 and -아서

entries.nuance: 얇다 is the opposite of 두껍다: a FLAT thing being thin — paper, fabric, a slice, a thin book or wall. It is a regular adjective: 얇다 → 얇아요 (pronounced [얄바요], the ㅂ of the ㄼ cluster surfaces), 얇은, 얇게(adverb), 얇아서. Two contrasts matter for English speakers. First, parallel to 두껍다 vs 굵다, the opposite of 'thin' for ROUND/cylindrical things is 가늘다, not 얇다: thin string, thin noodles, thin fingers, a thin waist are 가늘다 (가는 실, 가는 면, 가는 허리), so 얇은 실 sounds wrong. Second, a thin PERSON (slim body) is 마르다 (마른 사람) or 날씬하다, never 얇은 사람. Use 얇다 strictly for flat, layered objects. The idiom 귀가 얇다 means 'gullible, easily persuaded.' The pronunciation pitfall: 얇다 is [얄따] and 얇아요 is [얄바요], with the hidden ㅂ appearing before a vowel. Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 얇다 for a slim person. A thin/skinny person is 마른 사람 (from 마르다) or 날씬한 사람, not 얇은 사람.
Using 얇다 for round/cylindrical things. Thin string, thin noodles, or a thin waist are 가늘다 (가는 실, 가는 허리), not 얇다.
Mispronouncing the conjugation: 얇아요 is [얄바요] — the hidden ㅂ in the ㄼ cluster is voiced when a vowel follows, not [얄아요].

entries.shortExplanation: 자주 means "often" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자주 (jaju) means "often". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자주 가요 ("I go often"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자주 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: sits right before the verb
frequency, repeated meetings
habitual eating
goes before the 안 of negation

examples.en: I eat kimchi often.
examples.note: Simple habit: 자주 sits directly before the verb 먹어요.

examples.en: These days I can't meet my friends often.
examples.note: Everyday: with 못, 자주 still comes first — 자주 못 만나요, not 못 자주.

examples.ko: 이 동네는 버스가 자주 안 와서 불편해요.
examples.romanization: i dongneneun beoseuga jaju an waseo bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: In this neighborhood the bus doesn't come often, so it's inconvenient.
examples.note: Real situation: 자주 안 와요 = 'comes rarely'; the adverb hugs the whole negated verb.

entries.nuance: 자주 means 'often / frequently' and describes how many TIMES an action repeats over a period — it answers 얼마나 자주 ('how often'), never how fast or how well. The frequency scale runs 항상(always) > 자주(often) > 가끔(sometimes) > 거의 안(hardly), and 자주 sits high but short of 'always'. Its natural opposite is 가끔; learners confuse 자주 with 빨리(quickly), but 자주 is about count of occurrences while 빨리 is about speed of one action — 빨리 먹어요 means 'eats fast', 자주 먹어요 means 'eats often'. Register-neutral, fine for everyone. The big English-speaker pitfall is word order: English lets you say 'I go there often' with the adverb last, but Korean glues 자주 immediately before the verb (자주 가요), and even before 안/못 in negatives (자주 안 가요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가요 자주 by copying English 'I go often'. Korean adverbs precede the verb, so it must be 자주 가요.
Using 자주 to mean 'quickly', as in trying to say 'eat quickly' with 자주 먹어요 — that actually means 'eat often'. Use 빨리 먹어요 for speed.
Placing the adverb after 안 in negatives: 안 자주 와요 is wrong. The order is 자주 안 와요 ('doesn't come often').

entries.shortExplanation: 가끔 means "sometimes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sometimes" is 가끔 (gakkeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가끔 봐요 ("I see it sometimes"). Watch the particle attached to 가끔 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: low-frequency, before the verb

usagePhrases.en: I go once in a while
usagePhrases.note: occasional outing
spontaneous recollection
sporadic contact

examples.en: I sometimes eat ramyeon.
examples.note: Simple: 가끔 marks a low-frequency habit, sitting before 먹어요.

examples.en: On weekends I sometimes sleep in.
examples.note: Everyday: pairs naturally with 주말에는 to mean 'on some weekends, not all'.

examples.en: I'm busy, but every so often I call my parents.
examples.note: Real situation: 가끔은 (with 은) softly contrasts 'at least sometimes' against the busyness.

entries.nuance: 가끔 means 'sometimes / once in a while / occasionally' — clearly less frequent than 자주 but more than 거의 안(hardly ever): the scale is 항상 > 자주 > 가끔 > 거의 안 > 전혀 안. Its nearest rival is 때때로, which means the same but is more bookish/written; in everyday speech 가끔 is the natural choice, while 때때로 can sound like an essay. You can intensify it as 가끔씩 ('every now and then'), which feels even more sporadic and warm. Register-neutral and safe with anyone. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, word order — it must precede the verb (가끔 가요, not 가요 가끔); second, learners over-reach and use 가끔 for things that are actually frequent, so calibrate it as 'only occasionally', not 'fairly often'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Putting it at the end like English 'I go sometimes': 가요 가끔 is wrong; say 가끔 가요.
Treating 가끔 and 자주 as interchangeable. 가끔 means it happens rarely; if it happens often, you must switch to 자주, or your listener will picture a much lower frequency.
Forcing the formal 때때로 into casual chat. It is grammatically fine but sounds stiff; 가끔 (or 가끔씩) is what people actually say out loud.

entries.shortExplanation: 항상 means "always" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 항상 (hangsang) = "always". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 항상 웃어요 ("you always smile") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 항상, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 100% of the time, before the verb
habitual, no exceptions
standing emotional state
reliable repeated action

examples.en: My older sister always eats breakfast.
examples.note: Simple: 항상 = every single time, with no exception, before 먹어요.

examples.ko: 저는 항상 핸드폰을 손에 들고 다녀요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hangsang haendeuponeul sone deulgo danyeoyo.
examples.en: I always carry my phone in my hand.
examples.note: Everyday: 항상 stresses an unbroken habit; pairs well with 들고 다니다 ('carry around').

examples.en: Stay healthy and always be happy.
examples.note: Real situation: a warm blessing — here 늘 and 항상 are swapped freely; both mean 'always'.

entries.nuance: 항상 (Sino-Korean 恒常, 恒 'constant' + 常 'usual', literally 'constant-usual') means 'always / at all times', marking an action that holds without exception — far stronger than 보통(usually), which allows exceptions. Its near-synonym is 늘, a pure native word with the same meaning; the two are almost always interchangeable, though 늘 feels a touch softer and warmer (common in well-wishes) while 항상 sounds a hair more emphatic and is slightly more frequent in writing. Another cousin, 언제나, leans poetic/literary. All are register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 항상 to mean 'usually' — English 'always' is loose ('I'm always late-ish'), but Korean 항상 is literally 100%, so for a normal-but-not-absolute habit use 보통, and keep the word before the verb (항상 와요, not 와요 항상).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 항상 for something that is merely typical. 항상 = exactly every time; if there are exceptions you mean 보통('usually') instead.
Word-order slip: 와요 항상 copies English. Korean needs 항상 와요, adverb before verb.
Assuming 항상 and 늘 differ in meaning and over-thinking which to pick. They are interchangeable; just keep one register — both are neutral and natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 보통 means "usually" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보통 (botong) means "usually". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보통 가요 ("I usually go"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: general habit, allows exceptions
typical routine
default mode of doing
here 보통 works as a noun/modifier

examples.en: I usually get up at seven.
examples.note: Simple: 보통 = 'as a rule, with exceptions allowed', before 일어나요.

examples.en: I usually eat lunch near the office.
examples.note: Everyday: describes the default choice, not an absolute rule.

examples.ko: 보통은 안 그런데 오늘은 좀 피곤하네요.
examples.romanization: botongeun an geureonde oneureun jom pigonhaneyo.
examples.en: Usually I'm not like this, but today I'm a bit tired.
examples.note: Real situation: 보통은 (with 은) sets up a contrast — 'normally... but today...'.

entries.nuance: 보통 (Sino-Korean 普通, 普 'widespread' + 通 'common', literally 'widely-common') means 'usually / normally / ordinarily' and frames what happens as a rule WHILE leaving room for exceptions — that exception-tolerance is exactly what separates it from 항상(always, no exceptions). Think of the ladder 항상 > 보통 > 자주 > 가끔: 보통 says 'this is my default'. Uniquely among these adverbs, 보통 is also a noun/adjective meaning 'ordinary' (보통 사람 'an average person', 보통이에요 'it's so-so'), so context tells you which use is active. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'usually' as a soft 'always' and over-claiming — if you truly mean every time, use 항상; and as always, keep the adverb before the verb (보통 가요), not after.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Inflating 보통 into 항상. 보통 explicitly permits exceptions ('usually, but not always'); if you mean truly every time, say 항상.
Forgetting that 보통 can be a noun. 그 영화 보통이었어요 means 'that movie was just so-so', not 'usually' — don't read it as the frequency adverb.
English-style placement: 자요 보통 is wrong; the order is 보통 자요.

structuredNuance.t: 보통 means 'usually / normally / ordinarily' and frames what happens as a rule WHILE leaving room for exceptions. Think of the ladder 항상 > 보통 > 자주 > 가끔: 보통 says 'this is my default'. Uniquely among these adverbs, 보통 is also a noun/adjective meaning 'ordinary' (보통 사람 'an average person', 보통이에요 'it's so-so'), so context tells you which use is active. Register-neutral.
Its exception-tolerance is exactly what separates it from 항상(always, no exceptions) — if you truly mean every time, use 항상.

entries.shortExplanation: 일찍 means "early" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "early" is 일찍 (iljjik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일찍 자요 ("I sleep early"). Watch the particle attached to 일찍 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: early in clock time
ahead of the usual hour
arriving before time
before normal start time

examples.en: I usually sleep early.
examples.note: Simple: 일찍 = at an early hour, before 자요.

examples.en: Tomorrow I want to get up early.
examples.note: Everyday: 일찍 + 일어나다 is the standard 'wake up early' collocation.

examples.en: Worried about traffic, I left thirty minutes early.
examples.note: Real situation: 일찍 here means 'ahead of schedule', and 30분 일찍 = 'earlier by 30 min'.

entries.nuance: 일찍 means 'early' in the sense of an EARLY POINT IN TIME — early hour of the day or ahead of a schedule — and is the natural opposite of 늦게(late). The classic confusion is 일찍 vs 빨리: 일찍 is about WHEN on the clock (일찍 일어나요 = 'wake up at an early hour'), while 빨리 is about SPEED/quickness (빨리 일어나요 = 'get up quick!'). So '일찍 오세요' invites someone to arrive at an early time, whereas '빨리 오세요' urges them to hurry. It pairs habitually with 자다, 일어나다, 출근하다, 도착하다, 출발하다. Register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 일찍/빨리 mix-up, since English 'early' and 'fast/quick' feel adjacent but map to two different Korean adverbs; also remember 일찍 is an adverb already, so you never conjugate it like the adjective 이르다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 빨리 when you mean 'at an early hour'. 빨리 자요 means 'sleep quickly'; to say 'sleep early (in the evening)' use 일찍 자요.
Trying to conjugate it as if it were an adjective. 일찍 is the fixed adverb; you don't say 일찍어요. The related adjective is 이르다 ('to be early').
Word order: 와요 일찍 mirrors English; Korean puts the adverb first — 일찍 와요.

entries.shortExplanation: 늦게 means "late" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 늦게 (neutge) = "late". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 늦게 자요 ("I sleep late") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 늦게, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: at a late hour
past the usual time
arriving behind time
늦게 + 까지 = 'until late'

examples.en: I went to bed too late yesterday.
examples.note: Simple: 늦게 = at a late hour, here intensified by 너무.

examples.en: On weekends I sleep in until late.
examples.note: Everyday: 늦게까지 ('until late') is a high-frequency collocation.

examples.en: The meeting ran long, so I worked late yesterday.
examples.note: Real situation: 늦게 describes finishing at a late hour, the opposite of 일찍 끝내다.

entries.nuance: 늦게 means 'late', i.e. at a LATE POINT IN TIME or behind schedule, and is the exact opposite of 일찍(early). It is the adverbial form of the adjective 늦다('to be late'), built by attaching -게 to the stem 늦- (늦- + -게 → 늦게); this -게 ending is the general Korean machine for turning a descriptive verb into an adverb. The everyday combo 늦게까지 means 'until late' (늦게까지 공부해요 'study until late'). Two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) keep the -게 — 늦게 is the adverb, while 늦어요 is the conjugated sentence-ending 'is/am late', and 늦은 is the noun-modifier 'late ~'; dropping the -게 and saying 늦어 자요 is wrong. (2) Don't confuse lateness-in-time with slowness — 늦게 가요 means 'go at a late time', whereas 천천히 가요 means 'go slowly'. Register-neutral.

Saying 늦어 자요 (just conjugating the stem) instead of 늦게 자요. To modify the verb you need the adverb form with -게: 늦게 자요.
Confusing 늦게 (late in time) with 천천히 (slowly). 늦게 와요 = 'arrive late'; 천천히 와요 = 'come slowly / take your time'.
Using the modifier 늦은 where an adverb is needed. 늦은 means 'late ~' before a noun (늦은 밤 'late night'); before a verb you need 늦게.

entries.shortExplanation: 먼저 means "first" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 먼저 (meonjeo) means "first". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 먼저 가요 ("I'll go first / ahead"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 먼저 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: leaving before others

usagePhrases.en: please go ahead / do it first
usagePhrases.note: yielding politely
earlier in a sequence
taking the initiative

examples.en: I'll head off first.
examples.note: Simple: 먼저 = ahead of others in time/order, before 갈게요.

examples.en: Wash your hands first, then eat.
examples.note: Everyday: 먼저 marks step one of a sequence (먼저 A 하고 B).

examples.en: I'll be heading in/out first (leaving before you).
examples.note: Real situation: a polite set phrase to excuse yourself before colleagues — 'I'll go ahead.'

entries.nuance: 먼저 means 'first / beforehand / ahead (of others)' — it ranks one action or person EARLIER in a sequence or in time. The key contrast is 먼저 vs 처음: 먼저 is relative ('before the other thing/person', e.g. 먼저 가요 'go ahead of you'), while 처음 means 'the first time ever / the beginning' (처음 만나요 'meeting for the first time'). So 먼저 봤어요 = 'I saw it first (before you)', but 처음 봤어요 = 'I saw it for the first time'. 먼저 is also a courtesy word: 먼저 가세요 / 먼저 하세요 ('go ahead, you first') is everyday politeness, and 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 들어가겠습니다 softens leaving before others. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping every 'first' to one word — choose 먼저 for order-relative 'first/ahead', but 처음 for 'first-ever/at first', and keep 먼저 before the verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 처음 to mean 'go ahead of someone'. 처음 갈게요 sounds like 'I'll go for the first time'; to mean 'I'll go first (before you)' say 먼저 갈게요.
Conversely, using 먼저 for 'the first time'. 먼저 만나요 means 'meet first (before others)'; 'meet for the first time' is 처음 만나요.
Placing it after the verb. English 'you go first' tempts 가요 먼저; Korean order is 먼저 가요 (or politely 먼저 가세요).

entries.shortExplanation: 벌써 means "already" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "already" is 벌써 (beolsseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌써 왔어요 ("you're here already?!"). Watch the particle attached to 벌써 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: sooner than expected
faster than thought
surprise at completion
time flew by

examples.en: Is it lunchtime already?
examples.note: Simple: 벌써 voices surprise that time passed fast.

examples.en: I've already finished that book.
examples.note: Everyday: with past tense + 다, 벌써 stresses 'done sooner than expected'.

examples.en: The snow has already melted. It must be spring.
examples.note: Real situation: 벌써 + the surprise-marker -네요 conveys mild astonishment.

entries.nuance: 벌써 means 'already', but its core flavor is SURPRISE that something happened sooner than you expected — 'wow, already?'. Compare its near-twin 이미: 이미 is the neutral 'already / by now' that simply reports a completed fact (이미 끝났어요 'it's already finished', stating it), whereas 벌써 adds the emotional jolt (벌써 끝났어요? 'it's done already?!'). So a flat report prefers 이미; an astonished reaction prefers 벌써. It naturally rides with past tense and with 다('all'), and often co-occurs with the exclamatory endings -네요/-군요. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't pair 벌써 with the future — English 'already' can sit oddly with plans, but 벌써 is about something that has ALREADY occurred, so it takes past/completed verbs (벌써 갔어요), not 벌써 갈 거예요. Use 곧/이미 곧 logic for 'soon' instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Attaching 벌써 to future actions: 벌써 갈 거예요 is wrong. 벌써 needs a completed event — 벌써 갔어요 ('already left').
Swapping in 벌써 where you only want a neutral report. To plainly state a fact, 이미 is better; 벌써 injects surprise you may not intend.
Word order: 끝났어요 벌써 follows English; Korean puts it first — 벌써 끝났어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 아직 means "still; yet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아직 (ajik) = "still; yet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아직 자요 ("they're still asleep") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아직, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ongoing state, before verb
아직 + negative = 'not yet'

usagePhrases.en: there's still a long way to go
usagePhrases.note: set phrase, 'not nearly done'
ongoing not-knowing

examples.en: I'm still a student.
examples.note: Simple: with a positive noun-sentence, 아직 = 'still'.

examples.en: I haven't eaten yet.
examples.note: Everyday: 아직 + 안/못 + past = 'not yet'; the most common pattern.

examples.en: Almost done? — No, not yet.
examples.note: Real situation: 아직 can stand alone as 아직이요 ('not yet') in reply.

entries.nuance: 아직 covers both 'still' and 'not yet', and which one surfaces depends on polarity: with a POSITIVE verb it means 'still' (아직 자요 'still sleeping'), and with a NEGATIVE verb it means 'not yet' (아직 안 잤어요 'haven't slept yet'). It is the natural counterpart to 벌써/이미 — 아직 안 끝났어요 ('not finished yet') is the mirror of 벌써 끝났어요 ('already finished'). It often rides with the ongoing form -고 있다 to stress an action in progress (아직 자고 있어요 'still sleeping right now') and shows up in fixed phrases like 아직 멀었어요 ('still a long way off'). Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the 아직/벌써 confusion and the negation logic: because English 'yet' lives in questions/negatives, learners forget that Korean 아직 itself flips meaning with the verb's polarity — pair 아직 with 안/못 to say 'not yet', and use it with a plain positive verb to say 'still'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 아직 with 벌써. 아직 안 왔어요 = 'hasn't come yet'; 벌써 왔어요 = 'already came'. They point in opposite directions.
Trying to say 'not yet' with a positive verb. 아직 먹었어요 reads as 'still ate' and is odd; you need the negative: 아직 안 먹었어요.
Adding -았/었- when the state still holds. For 'I'm still hungry' say 아직 배고파요 (present), not 아직 배고팠어요; the past tense would mean the hunger is already over, which contradicts 아직.

entries.shortExplanation: 또 means "again; also" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 또 (tto) means "again; also". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 또 와요 ("come again"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 또 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: repetition of the action
casual goodbye
exasperation at a repeat
unwanted recurrence

examples.en: Let's meet again tomorrow.
examples.note: Simple: 또 = 'one more time', a friendly repeat before 만나요.

examples.en: Late again? You were late yesterday too.
examples.note: Everyday: 또 here carries a tone of 'yet again', mild reproach.

examples.en: It was delicious. I'll come again next time!
examples.note: Real situation: 또 in a warm farewell; 또 올게요 / 또 봬요 are set goodbyes.

entries.nuance: 또 means 'again / once more', and by extension 'also/additionally'; it marks an action REPEATING. Its near-synonym is 다시, and the dividing line matters: 또 is a plain repetition or recurrence ('one more time', often emotional — delight in 또 봐요 or annoyance in 또?!), while 다시 leans toward 'again, properly / from the start / anew', as in redoing something (다시 하세요 'do it over (correctly)'). So 또 전화할게요 = 'I'll call again (next time)', but 다시 전화할게요 = 'I'll call back / try again'. 또 is the natural word in casual goodbyes (또 봐요, 또 만나요) and in venting (또 그래 'there you go again'). Register-neutral, very colloquial-friendly. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting every 'again' to one word — use 또 for casual recurrence/'see you again', 다시 for 'redo/anew', and keep it before the verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reaching for 다시 in a casual goodbye. 다시 봐요 is understandable but leans 'meet again (to pick things back up)'; the warm, idiomatic 'see you again' Koreans actually say is 또 봐요 / 또 만나요.
Using 또 when you mean 'do it over correctly'. 또 하세요 = 'do it one more time'; to mean 'redo it properly / from scratch' say 다시 하세요.
Word order: 와요 또 echoes English 'come again'; Korean puts the adverb first — 또 와요.

entries.shortExplanation: 너무 means "so, really (also: too much)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "so, really (also: too much)" is 너무 (neomu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 너무 비싸요 ("it's too expensive"). Watch the particle attached to 너무 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: excess, before adjective
너무 modifies the adverb 많이

usagePhrases.en: I love it / it's so good
usagePhrases.note: casual positive 'super'
너무 frozen into a verb

examples.en: These shoes are too small.
examples.note: Simple: classic 'excessive' use — 너무 + adjective = beyond the right amount.

examples.en: I drank too much coffee yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday: 너무 stacks onto 많이 ('a lot') to mean 'too much'.

examples.en: Wow, this cake is so delicious!
examples.note: Real situation: in casual speech 너무 flips positive, meaning 'so/really', not 'excessively'.

entries.nuance: 너무 literally means 'too / excessively' — past the appropriate point, usually a complaint (너무 비싸요 'too expensive', 너무 매워요 'too spicy'). The textbook contrast is 너무 vs 아주: 아주 is a neutral intensifier ('very', no judgment), while 너무 traditionally signals EXCESS (a problem). BUT in modern colloquial Korean, 너무 has drifted into a positive 'so/super' (너무 좋아요 'I love it', 너무 예뻐요 'so pretty') — so tone and context decide whether it's a complaint or enthusiasm. It also fossilizes into the verb 너무하다 ('to be too much / go overboard', e.g. 너무해요 'that's not fair'). Register: the positive sense is casual/spoken; in formal writing keep 너무 for genuine excess and use 매우/아주 for neutral emphasis. The English-speaker pitfall: don't assume 너무 is always negative like English 'too' — in speech 너무 좋다 is a compliment, and for plain neutral 'very' before an adjective, 아주/매우 is safer in formal contexts.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading every 너무 as the negative 'too'. 너무 좋아요 in conversation means 'I really love it', not 'I like it too much'.
Using 너무 for neutral 'very' in formal writing. There 너무 still implies excess; prefer 매우 or 아주 for plain emphasis.
Forgetting 너무하다 is a real verb. 너무해요 means 'that's too much / that's unfair', not a typo — it's 너무 used predicatively.

entries.nuance: 아주 means 'very / quite' — a NEUTRAL degree intensifier that simply turns the dial up without implying anything is excessive. entries.nuance: 위 (Sino-Korean would be 上, but 위 is native Korean) names the top surface of something or the space directly above it, and it must attach to a noun: 책상 위, 머리 위, never standing alone like English 'up'. entries.nuance: 아래 is the native Korean word for the area below or underneath something, and like all position nouns it clings to a noun: 책상 아래, 다리 아래. entries.nuance: 앞 is the native Korean noun for the front side of a thing or the space directly ahead of it, and it attaches to a noun: 집 앞, 역 앞. Crucially, 앞 covers BOTH space ('in front of') and time ('ahead, upcoming') — 앞으로 means 'from now on / going forward', and 앞두다 means an event is just ahead. Compare it with 정면 (the literal 'front face/facade', more formal and architectural) and with 앞쪽 ('the front side/forward direction', vaguer). It is neutral in register. Using 앞 by itself for the motion 'go forward' (앞 가요) — it is a noun, so say 앞으로 가요 with the direction particle and a motion verb.

entries.nuance: 옆 is the native Korean noun for the side of a thing or the spot immediately beside it, and it attaches to a noun: 창문 옆, 은행 옆. It also forms handy compounds: 옆집 (the house next door), 옆자리 (the seat beside you), 옆사람 (the person next to you). Register is neutral and very high-frequency in daily speech. Note 옆 is also written/pronounced carefully: the ㅍ batchim links to following vowels (옆에 sounds like '여페').

entries.nuance: 안 is the native Korean noun for the inside or interior of an enclosed space, attaching to a noun: 가방 안, 방 안. Second, the homograph 안 = 'not' (the negation adverb, 안 가요 = I don't go) — same syllable, totally different word, told apart by position (a negating 안 sits before a verb; the noun 안 follows a noun). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping 안 and using bare 에, so 가방에 넣어요 ('put it to/at the bag') instead of the clearer 가방 안에 넣어요 ('put it inside the bag'); (2) overusing 속 where plain 안 is natural; and (3) saying 안에서 있어요 for existence instead of 안에 있어요.

Using 속 everywhere for 'inside' — 속 implies depth/immersion (마음속, 물속); for a plain enclosed space use 안 (방 안에).

entries.explanation: 밖 (bak) means "outside". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 집 밖에 ("outside the house"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 밖 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 밖 + 에 marks the location
existence verb 있다
action place 에서 + verb
direction 으로 + motion verb

examples.en: There is a parcel outside the door.
examples.note: Basic frame: noun 밖에 + 있다 locates the parcel.

examples.en: The weather is nice, so I eat lunch outside.
examples.note: 에서 because eating is an action done out there.

examples.en: I don't really go out much.
examples.note: 밖에 나가다 is the everyday way to say 'go out / leave the house'.

entries.nuance: 밖 is the native Korean noun for the outside or exterior of a place, attaching to a noun: 집 밖, 문 밖. Beware a crucial homograph: 밖에 also functions as a particle meaning 'only / nothing but', and it then REQUIRES a negative verb — 하나밖에 없어요 = 'there is only one' (literally 'outside of one, none'). So 밖에 has two lives: positional noun 밖 + 에 (집 밖에 있어요 = it's outside the house) versus the limiting particle 밖에 (천 원밖에 없어요 = I only have 1000 won). You disambiguate by the verb: positional 밖에 takes a normal verb, particle 밖에 forces a negative (없어요/안). Contrast also with 바깥 (a near-synonym noun for 'outside/outdoors', slightly more concrete, as in 바깥 공기 = the outside air) and 밖쪽 ('the outer side', vaguer). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) saying 밖에서 있어요 for existence instead of 밖에 있어요; (2) being thrown by the 'only' particle 밖에 and forgetting it needs a negative; and (3) treating 밖 as a verb — 'go outside' is 밖으로 나가다 or 밖에 나가다, not 밖 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 밖에서 있어요 for 'it is outside' — existence uses 에 (밖에 있어요); 에서 marks where an action happens.
Confusing positional 밖에 with the particle 밖에 'only' — the particle demands a negative (만 원밖에 없어요 = only 10,000 won); the position word takes a normal verb (집 밖에 있어요).
Using 밖 alone for the motion 'go out' (밖 가요) — say 밖으로 나가요 or 밖에 나가요; 밖 is a position noun.

entries.shortExplanation: 사이 means "between" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "between" is 사이 (sai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 은행과 카페 사이에 ("between the bank and the cafe"). Watch the particle attached to 사이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: between the bank and the cafe
usagePhrases.note: 사이 + 에 with 과/와 linking both sides
existence verb 있다
action place 에서 + verb
사이 = 'relationship' between people

examples.ko: 은행과 카페 사이에 작은 가게가 있어요.
examples.romanization: eunhaenggwa kape saie jageun gagega isseoyo.
examples.en: There is a small shop between the bank and the cafe.
examples.note: Basic frame: A와/과 B 사이에 + 있다 places the shop between two named things.

examples.en: Wind blows between the buildings.
examples.note: 에서 because the wind blowing is an action occurring in that gap.

examples.en: The two people are growing closer.
examples.note: 사이 also means a human relationship — 사이가 좋다/나쁘다 = get along well/badly.

entries.nuance: 사이 is the native Korean noun for the space, gap, or interval between two things, attaching with the linking particle 와/과 to name both sides: 은행과 카페 사이, 너와 나 사이. It is wonderfully broad — physical gaps (건물 사이), time intervals (방학 사이에 = during the break), and crucially human RELATIONSHIPS (친구 사이 = the bond between friends; 사이가 좋다 = to be close). Compare it with 가운데/중간 ('the middle/center' of a single thing or group, not the gap between two distinct items): the chair in the center of the room is 방 가운데, but the shop wedged between the bank and cafe is 은행과 카페 사이. Register is neutral and idiomatic. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping the 와/과 that grammatically pairs the two sides, so 은행 카페 사이 sounds unfinished — say 은행과 카페 사이; (2) using 사이 for the center of one object where 가운데 belongs; and (3) missing the relationship meaning, so 우리 사이 ('our relationship') gets misread as a physical gap. Colloquially 사이 even contracts to 새 (밤새 = all through the night).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forgetting 와/과 when naming both sides — 'between the bank and the cafe' needs 은행과 카페 사이, not 은행 카페 사이.
Using 사이 for the center of a single space — 'in the middle of the room' is 방 가운데, while 사이 is the gap between two separate things.
Reading 사이 only as physical space — 친구 사이 / 우리 사이 means 'relationship', so 사이가 좋다 = 'to get along', not 'the gap is good'.

entries.shortExplanation: 왼쪽 means "left side" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 왼쪽 (oenjjok) = "left side". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문 왼쪽에 ("to the left of the door") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 왼쪽, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to the left of the door
usagePhrases.note: 왼쪽 + 에 marks the location

usagePhrases.en: it is to the left of the bank
usagePhrases.note: existence verb 있다

usagePhrases.en: I meet on the left of the station
usagePhrases.note: action place 에서 + verb
direction 으로 + motion verb

examples.en: There is a mirror to the left of the door.
examples.note: Basic frame: noun 왼쪽에 + 있다 places the mirror.

examples.en: I catch the bus to the left of the shop.
examples.note: 에서 because catching the bus is an action done at that spot.

examples.en: Turn left at the intersection.
examples.note: 왼쪽으로 with 으로 gives real walking/driving directions.

entries.nuance: 왼쪽 is the native compound noun for the left side or leftward direction, built from 왼- ('left') + 쪽 ('side/direction'); it attaches to a noun (문 왼쪽) or stands with a direction particle for movement (왼쪽으로 = to the left). The -쪽 element is the same one in 위쪽/아래쪽/앞쪽, marking 'the ~ side'. Its direct opposite is 오른쪽 (right), and confusing the two is the single most common error when giving directions — practice the pair until 왼 reliably means left. Note also the more formal/literary 좌 (左, Sino-Korean) seen in 좌회전 (left turn, on road signs) versus everyday spoken 왼쪽. Register: 왼쪽 is the normal conversational word; 좌 appears in fixed/official terms. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 왼쪽에서 있어요 for existence instead of 왼쪽에 있어요; (2) swapping 왼쪽 and 오른쪽 under pressure; and (3) using 왼쪽 alone for 'turn left' (왼쪽 도세요 is incomplete) — you need the direction particle: 왼쪽으로 도세요 / 왼쪽으로 가세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 왼쪽에서 있어요 for 'it is on the left' — existence takes 에 (왼쪽에 있어요); 에서 marks where an action happens.
Swapping 왼쪽 (left) and 오른쪽 (right) when giving directions — drill the pair so 왼 always cues 'left'.
Saying 왼쪽 도세요 for 'turn left' — add the direction particle: 왼쪽으로 도세요 / 왼쪽으로 가세요.

entries.nuance: 오른쪽 is the native compound noun for the right side or rightward direction, from 오른- ('right') + 쪽 ('side/direction'); it attaches to a noun (문 오른쪽) or pairs with a direction particle for motion (오른쪽으로 = to the right). Saying 오른쪽에서 있어요 for 'it is on the right' — existence needs 에 (오른쪽에 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action.

entries.shortExplanation: 근처 means "nearby, vicinity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "nearby, vicinity" is 근처 (geuncheo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 집 근처에 ("near the house"). Watch the particle attached to 근처 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 근처 + 에 marks the area
existence verb 있다
action place 에서 + verb
이 근처 = 'around here'

examples.en: There is a big park near my house.
examples.note: Basic frame: noun 근처에 + 있다 places the park in the area.

examples.en: I meet my friend near the station.
examples.note: 에서 because meeting is an action done in that vicinity.

examples.en: Is there a pharmacy around here?
examples.note: 이 근처 (around here) is the phrase travelers use to ask for nearby places.

entries.nuance: 근처 is a Sino-Korean noun (近處, 近 'near' + 處 'place') meaning the nearby area or vicinity surrounding a place; it attaches to a noun (집 근처) or to 이/그/저 (이 근처 = around here). Unlike the adjacency word 옆 ('right next to', touching distance), 근처 covers a looser radius — a few minutes' walk, the general neighborhood. Two near-synonyms to weigh: 근방 (近方) is a slightly more colloquial 'thereabouts', and 부근 (附近) is a more formal/written 'vicinity' (역 부근 sounds bookish); 근처 is the neutral everyday default. Compare also 가까이 (an adverb, 'nearby/closely', as in 가까이 오세요 = come closer) — 근처 is a place noun, 가까이 modifies a verb. Register: 근처 is comfortably conversational. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 근처에서 있어요 for existence instead of 근처에 있어요; (2) using 근처 when the thing is literally adjacent, where 옆 is sharper; and (3) confusing the noun 근처 with the adverb 가까이 — say 집 근처에 있어요 (noun), but 가까이 사세요? for 'do you live nearby?' with the adverbial feel.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 근처에서 있어요 for 'it is nearby' — existence uses 에 (근처에 있어요); 에서 marks where an action takes place.
Using 근처 for something literally adjacent — 근처 is a loose 'in the area'; for 'right next to it' use 옆 (은행 옆에).
Confusing the noun 근처 with the adverb 가까이 — 'near the house' is 집 근처(에) (noun), while 가까이 modifies a verb (가까이 오세요 = come closer).

entries.shortExplanation: 가운데 means "middle, center" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가운데 (gaunde) = "middle, center". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방 가운데에 ("in the middle of the room") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가운데, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: in the middle of the room
usagePhrases.note: 가운데 + 에 marks the location

usagePhrases.en: it is in the middle of the room
usagePhrases.note: existence verb 있다

usagePhrases.en: I rest in the middle of the park
usagePhrases.note: action place 에서 + verb
가운데 = 'among' a group

examples.en: There is a dining table in the middle of the room.
examples.note: Basic frame: noun 가운데에 + 있다 places the table at the center.

entries.nuance: 가운데 is the native Korean noun for the middle or center point of a space, and figuratively 'among' a group; it attaches to a noun (방 가운데) and can mark selection (셋 가운데 하나 = one among three). Its key confusable is 사이: 가운데 is the center of ONE object or area (방 가운데 = the middle of the room), whereas 사이 is the gap BETWEEN two distinct things (은행과 카페 사이 = between the bank and the cafe) — don't use 가운데 to mean 'between two items'. Compare also 중간 (中間, Sino-Korean 'midpoint/midway'), which overlaps but leans toward the middle of a line, range, or process (중간고사 = midterm exam, 중간에 = midway through), while 가운데 feels more like the spatial center or 'among a set'. And 중심 (中心) is the abstract 'core/focal center'. Register: 가운데 is neutral and common. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using 가운데 for 'between two things' where 사이 is correct; (2) saying 가운데에서 있어요 for existence instead of 가운데에 있어요; and (3) swapping 가운데 and 중간 carelessly — 'midway through the movie' is 영화 중간에, while 'the center of the table' is 식탁 가운데.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가운데 for 'between two things' — that is 사이 (A와 B 사이); 가운데 is the center of a single space (방 가운데).
Saying 가운데에서 있어요 for 'it is in the middle' — existence takes 에 (가운데에 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action.
Treating 가운데 and 중간 as identical — 중간 leans 'midway through' a range/process (영화 중간에), while 가운데 is the spatial center or 'among' a set.

entries.shortExplanation: 운동 means "exercise" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 운동 takes the object marker 을 because 하다 acts on it
subject marker 이 after a consonant
-고 싶어요 attaches to the verb 하-, not to the noun
좋아하다 is a verb 'to like', so its object takes 을/를

examples.en: I exercise every day.
examples.note: the everyday 운동하다 frame for a habit

examples.note: 운동을 시작하다 = take up working out

examples.romanization: helseujangeseo han sigan dongan undonghaetdeoni onmomi ppeogeunhaeyo.
examples.en: After working out at the gym for an hour, my whole body is stiff.
examples.note: real gym talk; 운동하다 contracted, with a result

entries.nuance: 운동 is Sino-Korean, 運動 ('move-motion'), and is the umbrella word for physical exercise; it normally appears as 운동하다 (운동을 해요). Crucially it is NOT counted or pluralized like English 'a workout' — you don't say 운동들 for several sessions; you say 운동을 자주 해요. The nearest relative is 스포츠 (a borrowed word for organized sports as a category, e.g. watching 스포츠 on TV), whereas 운동 is the act of exercising your own body, so '운동선수' = athlete but '스포츠 경기' = a sports match. The very same 運動 also means a social 'movement/campaign' (민주화 운동 the democracy movement), so context decides. Saying 운동을 만들어요 by translating 'do/make exercise' literally — 만들다 means physically craft something; the correct light verb is 하다, so 운동을 해요.
Attaching the want-ending to the noun as 운동 싶어요 — -고 싶다 only fastens to a verb stem, so it must be 운동하고 싶어요 / 운동을 하고 싶어요.

subject marker 가 after a vowel

usagePhrases.en: I want to watch a movie
usagePhrases.note: -고 싶어요 on the verb 보-, with 를 on 영화
films are counted with the counter 편, not 개

examples.en: I watch a movie on the weekend.
examples.note: simple habit with 보다

examples.ko: 넷플릭스로 영화 한 편 보면서 쉬었어요.
examples.romanization: netpeullikseuro yeonghwa han pyeon bomyeonseo swieosseoyo.
examples.en: I relaxed watching a movie on Netflix.
examples.note: 영화 + counter 편 + means-particle (으)로

examples.romanization: i yeonghwa jinjja jaemisseunikka kkok yeonghwagwaneseo bwa.

examples.note: casual 반말; 영화관 = cinema, 재밌다 colloquial

entries.nuance: 영화 is Sino-Korean, 映畵 ('project-picture'), literally a projected image, and it is the standard word for a movie/film. It pairs with 보다 ('see/watch'), never 듣다 ('listen'), because film is something you view. A single film is counted with the bound noun 편 (영화 두 편 = two movies), not 개. Don't confuse 영화 with 드라마: 드라마 is a serialized TV series, while 영화 is a self-contained cinema film, so a Korean TV soap is a 드라마, not a 영화. The cinema building is 영화관 (or the loanword 극장). The classic English-speaker pitfall is letting 'a movie' steer you to the generic counter 개 (영화 한 개 sounds wrong) — use 편; and don't calque 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가다, since you say 영화(를) 보러 가다, 'go in order to watch a movie'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 영화를 들어요 by mixing up senses — you don't 'listen to' a film; the verb is 보다, so 영화를 봐요.
Counting with 개 as in 영화 한 개 — films use the dedicated counter 편: 영화 한 편.
Translating 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가요 — Korean expresses purpose, so it is 영화를 보러 가요 ('go to watch a movie').

좋다 is an adjective; subject marker 이
좋아하다 (verb) governs an object with 을
틀다 = switch on/play a track from a device

examples.en: I listen to music.
examples.note: bare habit, 듣다 → 들어요

examples.ko: 운동할 때 신나는 음악을 들으면 힘이 나요.
examples.romanization: undonghal ttae sinnaneun eumageul deureumyeon himi nayo.
examples.en: When I exercise, listening to upbeat music energizes me.
examples.note: 듣다 conditional 들으면; ㄷ-irregular

examples.ko: 카페에서 잔잔한 음악을 틀어 놓으니 분위기가 좋네요.
examples.romanization: kapeeseo janjanhan eumageul teureo noeuni bunwigiga jonneyo.
examples.en: With soft music playing in the café, the mood is nice.
examples.note: 틀어 놓다 = leave it playing in the background

entries.nuance: 음악 is Sino-Korean, 音樂 ('sound-pleasure/joy'), and is the general word for music. Its everyday partner verb is 듣다 ('hear/listen'), which is a ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel the ㄷ becomes ㄹ, so 듣 + 어요 → 들어요 and 듣 + 으면 → 들으면 — memorize this because beginners often write the wrong ❌들다. Distinguish 음악 from 노래: 노래 is a specific 'song' you can sing (with words and a tune), while 음악 is music as a whole, including instrumental pieces, so background café music is 음악, not 노래. Two near-verbs differ too — 듣다 is to receive sound, but 틀다 is to switch a track on from a device. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 ('watch') because you 'watch a music video' in English; for plain audio say 음악을 들어요, and avoid the false stem 들다 — the dictionary form is 듣다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 음악을 봐요 by analogy with watching videos — pure listening uses 듣다, so 음악을 들어요.
Writing the stem as 들다 and conjugating 들어요 from it — the base verb is the ㄷ-irregular 듣다; the ㄹ only appears before a vowel ending.
Using 만들다 for 'make/play music' on a device — to start a track you 틀다, e.g. 음악을 틀어요.

듣다 → 들어요 for receiving the song
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 부르- → 부를 수 있어요
songs are counted with 곡, not 개

examples.en: I sing well.
examples.note: 부르다 → 불러요 (르-irregular doubling)

examples.ko: 친구 생일이라 다 같이 생일 노래를 불렀어요.
examples.romanization: chingu saengirira da gachi saengil noraereul bulleosseoyo.
examples.en: It was my friend's birthday, so we all sang the birthday song.
examples.note: past 불렀어요; 다 같이 = all together

examples.ko: 노래방에서 한 곡 부르고 나니까 스트레스가 풀렸어요.

examples.en: After singing a song at the karaoke room, my stress melted away.
examples.note: 노래방 culture; counter 곡; -고 나니까

entries.nuance: 노래 is a native Korean word for a 'song' — a tune with lyrics you can perform — counted with the bound noun 곡 (노래 두 곡). The most natural verb is 부르다 ('to sing'), a 르-irregular: the stem doubles the ㄹ before a vowel, so 부르 + 어요 → 불러요 and 부르 + 었어요 → 불렀어요. The casual frame 노래를 하다 ('do a song') exists and means to sing, but 노래를 부르다 is more precise and common. Don't blur 노래 with 음악: 음악 is music in general (including instrumentals), while 노래 specifically has a singer and words. Karaoke is 노래방 ('song room'), a core social ritual. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 말하다 ('say/speak') because we 'say the words of a song' — singing is 부르다, never 말하다; and don't translate 'sing a song' twice over as ❌노래를 노래해요, which is redundant — just 노래를 불러요.

Saying 노래를 말해요 because the song 'has words' — speaking is 말하다, but singing is 부르다, so 노래를 불러요.
Forgetting the 르-irregular and writing 노래를 부러요 — the ㄹ doubles before a vowel: 부르 → 불러요.
Counting songs with 개 (노래 한 개) — the proper counter is 곡: 노래 한 곡.

멋있다 'cool/impressive'; subject marker 이
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 추- → 출 수 있어요
배우다 'to learn' → 배워요

examples.en: I dance well.
examples.note: 추다 → 춰요 (우 + 어 contracts to 워)

examples.ko: 무대에서 아이돌처럼 춤을 추니까 다들 환호했어요.
examples.romanization: mudaeeseo aidolcheoreom chumeul chunikka dadeul hwanhohaesseoyo.
examples.en: When I danced like an idol on stage, everyone cheered.
examples.note: 춤을 추다 in action; -니까 sequence

examples.ko: 요즘 방송댄스 배우는데, 춤 동작이 생각보다 어려워요.

entries.nuance: 춤 is a native noun for 'dance', and Korean uses a cognate-verb construction: the verb 추다 ('to dance') pairs only with 춤, giving 춤을 춰요 (추 + 어요 → 춰요, the 우+어 fuses to 워). This 'cognate object' pattern — noun and verb sharing a root — also appears in 잠을 자다 (sleep a sleep) and 꿈을 꾸다 (dream a dream), so learn it as a set. The dictionary form is 춤추다, written solid. Also, while 춤 covers dancing broadly, a single dance 'piece/move' is better called a 동작 (motion) or a specific genre (발레 ballet, 힙합 hip-hop), so don't try to count individual dances with 개. Note 멋있다 (cool) is the natural compliment, not 예쁘다.

Saying 춤을 해요 with the generic light verb — dance requires its cognate verb 추다, so 춤을 춰요.
Writing the contraction wrong as 추어요 left unfused — colloquial Korean contracts 추 + 어요 to 춰요.

예쁘다 (ㅡ-irregular) → 예뻐요; subject 이
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 그리- → 그릴 수 있어요
flat artworks are counted with 장 (sheets)

examples.en: I draw pictures.
examples.note: cognate pair 그림/그리다

examples.ko: 조카가 크레용으로 그림을 그려서 냉장고에 붙였어요.
examples.romanization: jokaga keureyongeuro geurimeul geuryeoseo naengjanggoe butyeosseoyo.

entries.nuance: 그림 is a native noun covering both a 'drawing' and a 'painting', formed from the verb 그리다 ('to draw/paint') — another cognate noun-verb pair, so 그림을 그리다 literally means 'draw a drawing'. A flat artwork is counted with 장 (sheets): 그림 한 장. Korean does not split 'draw' vs 'paint' lexically the way English does; 그리다 covers both pencil sketches and oil paintings, and you specify the medium (색연필로, 물감으로) if needed. The verb 그리다 also figuratively means to 'picture/long for' something (고향을 그리다, to yearn for home), but the everyday hobby sense is making art. The English-speaker pitfall is using 만들다 ('make') because we say 'make a drawing' — Korean uses the cognate verb 그리다, so say 그림을 그려요. Don't confuse 그림 with 사진 (a photograph): 그림 is hand-made art, 사진 is a photo you 찍다 ('take').

examples.ko: 내년에 유럽으로 배낭여행을 떠나려고 돈을 모으고 있어요.
examples.romanization: naenyeone yureobeuro baenangyeohaengeul tteonaryeogo doneul moeugo isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm saving money to set off backpacking around Europe next year.
examples.note: 떠나다 = set off; 배낭여행 compound

examples.ko: 이번 제주도 여행 정말 좋았어, 다음엔 같이 가자.
examples.romanization: ibeon jejudo yeohaeng jeongmal joasseo, daeumen gachi gaja.

entries.nuance: 여행 is Sino-Korean, 旅行 ('journey-go'), meaning travel or a trip. The single most natural verb is 가다 — 여행을 가다 ('go on a trip') — while 여행하다 (with light verb 하다) also works but feels a touch more formal/written. Distinguish 여행 from 출장: 출장 is a business trip you're sent on for work, whereas 여행 is travel for pleasure or sightseeing, so don't call a work assignment a 여행. A traveler is 여행자/여행객 and an overseas trip is 해외여행. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing 보다 ('see') because tourists 'go sightseeing' — to travel you 가다 or 하다, not 보다 (sightseeing specifically is 구경하다 or 관광하다). Also note destination takes (으)로/에 (제주도로 여행을 가다), and beginners often drop the particle on 여행 itself — keep 여행을 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 여행을 봐요 because travel involves 'seeing places' — the verb is 가다 (or 하다): 여행을 가요; sightseeing alone is 구경하다.
Calling a work trip 여행 — a business trip is 출장; 여행 is leisure travel.
Marking the destination with only 에 and no movement sense, e.g. 부산에 여행이에요 — say 부산으로/에 여행을 가요 to express going there.

entries.explanation: "reading" is 독서 (dokseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 독서를 해요 ("I read"). Watch the particle attached to 독서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-noun + 하다; the standard frame 독서하다
topic-introducing 독서가 ...예요
좋아하다 governs the object 독서를
즐기다 'to enjoy' → 즐겨요, slightly literary

examples.en: I read before going to bed.
examples.note: 독서하다 for a tidy habit statement

examples.ko: 제 취미는 독서라서 주말마다 도서관에 가요.
examples.romanization: je chwimineun dokseoraseo jumalmada doseogwane gayo.
examples.en: My hobby is reading, so I go to the library every weekend.
examples.note: 독서 + 도서관 share the 書/도 imagery

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 바빠서 통 독서를 못 했네요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri bappaseo tong dokseoreul mo taenneyo.
examples.en: I've been so busy with work lately that I've hardly read at all.
examples.note: 통 + 못 했다 = hardly did; reflective tone

entries.nuance: 독서 is Sino-Korean, 讀書 ('read-book'), literally 'reading books', and it is a slightly formal, hobby-survey word — it's what you write when asked 취미가 뭐예요?, answering 독서예요. Because it already contains 書 ('book'), 독서 implies reading books specifically, so for casual everyday speech Koreans usually switch to the plain native verb phrase 책을 읽다 ('read a book') — 책 읽는 거 좋아해요 sounds far more natural in conversation than 독서를 좋아해요, which can feel stiff. It pairs with 하다 (독서하다), not 보다 ('watch'), even though English sometimes blurs 'read' and 'look at'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 (because you 'look at' a page) — reading text is 읽다, and the noun is 독서를 하다. Don't try to give 독서 an object like ❌소설을 독서해요; if you name what you read, drop the Sino-noun and say 소설을 읽어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 독서를 봐요 from 'look at a book' — reading is 읽다; the noun frame is 독서를 해요.
Attaching an object to the Sino-noun, e.g. 신문을 독서해요 — 독서 already means reading books; to name the text use 읽다: 신문을 읽어요.
Using stiff 독서를 해요 in casual chat — among friends the natural phrasing is 책 읽어요 / 책 읽는 거 좋아해요.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 등산, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: destination-style 등산을 가다, very common
light verb 등산하다, the activity itself
-고 싶어요 on 가-; 를 on 등산
힘들다 'be hard/tiring'; subject marker 이

examples.en: I go hiking every weekend.
examples.note: 등산하다 for a routine

examples.en: My dad went hiking up Bukhansan with his friends.
examples.note: honorific 가셨어요; 으로 destination

examples.ko: 정상까지 등산하는 데 세 시간이나 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: jeongsangkkaji deungsanhaneun de se siganina geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took a whole three hours to hike to the summit.
examples.note: 등산하다; -는 데 + 이나 emphasis

entries.nuance: 등산 is Sino-Korean, 登山 ('climb-mountain'), specifically going up a mountain on foot, and it pairs with 가다 (등산을 가다) or 하다 (등산하다). It is culturally huge — weekend 등산 with proper gear is a beloved pastime, especially for middle-aged and older Koreans. Distinguish 등산 from 산책: 산책 is a light, flat stroll (a walk in the park or neighborhood), while 등산 implies real uphill climbing of a mountain, so an evening walk is a 산책, not 등산. Also note 하이킹 (loanword) overlaps but 등산 is the everyday native-feeling choice. The English-speaker pitfall is using 타다 ('ride') because we 'climb' mountains and 타다 can mean 'climb onto' a vehicle — for hiking on your own feet you 가다/하다, never 타다 (you'd only 타다 a cable car, 케이블카를 타다). Mark the mountain as a destination with (으)로/에: 산으로 등산을 가요.

Saying 등산을 타요 because you 'climb' — 타다 is for riding/boarding; hiking on foot is 등산을 가요/해요.
Confusing it with a casual walk — a flat stroll is 산책 (산책해요); 등산 means climbing a mountain.
Dropping the destination particle, e.g. 설악산 등산 가요 with no marker — prefer 설악산으로 등산을 가요.

entries.shortExplanation: 수영 means "swimming" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수영 (suyeong) means "swimming". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수영을 해요 ("I swim"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수영 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-noun + 하다; the standard 수영하다
재미있다 'be fun'; subject marker 이
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on the verb 하-
배우다 'to learn' → 배워요

examples.en: I swim in summer.
examples.note: 수영하다, seasonal habit

examples.ko: 어렸을 때 수영을 배워서 지금도 잘해요.
examples.romanization: eoryeosseul ttae suyeongeul baewoseo jigeumdo jalhaeyo.
examples.en: I learned to swim as a kid, so I'm still good at it.
examples.note: 수영을 배우다 → 배워서; ability

examples.ko: 수영장에서 한 시간 동안 수영하니까 배가 너무 고파요.
examples.romanization: suyeongjangeseo han sigan dongan suyeonghanikka baega neomu gopayo.
examples.en: After swimming for an hour at the pool, I'm so hungry.
examples.note: 수영장; 수영하다; result with -니까

entries.nuance: 수영 is Sino-Korean, 水泳 ('water-swim'), and means swimming as an activity; it pairs with the light verb 하다 (수영하다, 수영을 해요). A swimming pool is 수영장 ('swim-place'). Because 수영 names the whole activity, you don't use it for one isolated stroke — 수영을 해요 covers the act of swimming generally. Don't confuse the partner verbs across water sports: you 수영하다 (swim under your own power) but you 타다 ('ride') a surfboard or jet ski. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that — reaching for 타다 because many water/sport activities in English are 'rides', or because Korean uses 타다 for 스키 (스키를 타다, to ski) and 스케이트 (스케이트를 타다, to skate). Swimming is NOT one of those: it is 수영하다, never ❌수영을 타다. Note the contrast 스키를 타다 vs 수영을 하다 — sports that 'mount/ride' equipment take 타다, but body-only activities like swimming and exercise take 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수영을 타요 by analogy with 스키를 타다 / 스케이트를 타다 — swimming uses no ridden equipment, so it is 수영을 해요.
Using 수영 for a single stroke or lap — 수영 names the whole activity; for laps say 몇 바퀴 돌다 or 몇 미터 수영하다.
Confusing 수영 (the act) with 수영장 (the place) — 'I go to the pool' is 수영장에 가요, while 'I swim' is 수영을 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 취미 means "hobby" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "hobby" is 취미 (chwimi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 취미가 뭐예요? ("what is your hobby?"). Watch the particle attached to 취미 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: existence/identity uses 가, not 를
있다 'to have/exist' takes the subject marker 가

usagePhrases.en: I started it as a hobby
usagePhrases.note: 취미로 = 'as a hobby', means/role particle 로
topic 는 to name your hobby

examples.en: What is your hobby?
examples.note: the standard ice-breaker; 가, not 를

examples.en: My hobby is watching movies.
examples.note: verb → noun with -기: 보다 → 보기

examples.ko: 취미로 시작한 요리가 이제는 거의 직업이 됐어요.
examples.romanization: chwimiro sijakan yoriga ijeneun geoui jigeobi dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Cooking, which I started as a hobby, has now almost become a job.
examples.note: 취미로; relative clause; 이/가 되다

entries.nuance: 취미 is Sino-Korean, 趣味 ('interest-taste'), and means a hobby or personal interest. It famously opens small talk: 취미가 뭐예요? — and note it takes 가 there (existence/identity), so a frequent error is ❌취미를 있어요 instead of 취미가 있어요, because 있다 ('to have/exist') is not a transitive verb taking 을/를. To turn an activity into a named hobby, Korean nominalizes the verb with -기: 보다 → 영화 보기 ('movie-watching'), 모으다 → 우표 모으기 ('stamp-collecting'); answering 제 취미는 영화 보기예요 is the model pattern. Distinguish 취미 from 관심: 관심 is broader 'interest/attention' (관심이 있어요 = I'm interested in it), whereas 취미 is specifically a leisure activity you do for fun. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 있다 into a 'have'-with-object frame (취미를 있어요) — use 취미가 있어요; and don't say ❌취미를 해요 for 'do a hobby' — name the activity itself (영화를 봐요) or say 취미를 즐겨요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 취미를 있어요 by translating 'have a hobby' as object + have — 있다 takes the subject marker, so 취미가 있어요.
Listing a hobby with a bare verb, e.g. 제 취미는 영화 봐요 — nominalize it: 제 취미는 영화 보기예요.
Confusing 취미 with 관심 — 'I'm interested in K-pop' is 케이팝에 관심이 있어요, whereas 취미 is the leisure activity you actually do.

usagePhrases.note: destination-style 낚시를 가다, very idiomatic
light verb 낚시하다 for the activity
-고 싶어요 on 가-; 를 on 낚시
topic-introducing 낚시가 ...예요

examples.en: My father likes fishing.
examples.note: honorific 좋아하세요; 낚시 as hobby

examples.ko: 주말에 바다로 낚시를 가서 광어를 두 마리 잡았어요.
examples.romanization: jumare badaro naksireul gaseo gwangeoreul du mari jabasseoyo.
examples.en: I went sea-fishing at the weekend and caught two flatfish.
examples.note: 낚시를 가다 + 잡다; counter 마리

examples.ko: 밤낚시는 조용해서 좋은데 모기가 너무 많아요.
examples.romanization: bamnaksineun joyonghaeseo joeunde mogiga neomu manayo.
examples.en: Night fishing is nice because it's quiet, but there are way too many mosquitoes.
examples.note: 밤낚시 compound; -는데 contrast

entries.nuance: 낚시 is a native noun meaning fishing (with rod and hook) as a pastime, pairing with 가다 (낚시를 가다) or 하다 (낚시하다). Spelling and sound are tricky: the ㄲ cluster means it is written 낚시 but pronounced [낙씨], and the fish-hook itself is 낚싯바늘 — beginners often misspell it ❌낙시. Distinguish the activity 낚시 from the bare act of catching: 잡다 ('to catch/grab') is what you do to the fish (물고기를 잡다), while 낚시(를 하다) is the whole sport of angling, so 'I caught a fish' is 물고기를 잡았어요, but 'I go fishing (as a hobby)' is 낚시를 가요/해요. The English-speaker pitfall is using 잡다 alone to mean 'go fishing' — 잡다 just means grab/catch and needs an object; for the recreational activity use 낚시를 하다. Mark the spot with (으)로/에서: 바다로 낚시를 가다, 강에서 낚시하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 잡아요 by itself to mean 'go fishing' — 잡다 means catch/grab and needs an object (물고기를 잡다); the hobby is 낚시를 해요/가요.
Misspelling it as 낙시 — it is written 낚시 (with ㄲ), even though it sounds like [낙씨].
Saying 낚시를 봐요 or other wrong verbs — pair 낚시 with 가다 or 하다: 낚시를 가요 / 낚시해요.

examples.en: I stopped by the department store to buy a gift, but it was so expensive I just left.
examples.note: Real situation: -러 (purpose) + -아서 (so/therefore) chained naturally.

entries.nuance: 백화점 is Sino-Korean 百貨店, literally 'hundred-goods-store' (百 hundred + 貨 goods + 店 shop), a multi-floor flagship like Lotte or Shinsegae carrying brand clothing, cosmetics, and a food hall. The dividing line learners must feel is 백화점 vs 마트: a 마트 (대형마트, e.g. 이마트) is a warehouse-style discount store for groceries and household goods, while 백화점 is the upscale, salesclerk-served, higher-priced experience. It is also distinct from 쇼핑몰, an open complex of separate shops. Register is fully neutral, fine for anyone. A frequent English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because you 'shop AT' a store in English, beginners say 백화점에서 가요, but motion verbs like 가다/오다 require 에 (백화점에 가요); use 에서 only when an action happens there (백화점에서 옷을 봐요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 백화점에서 가요 for 'go to the store.' 가다 is motion toward a place, so it takes 에: 백화점에 가요. Reserve 에서 for an action done there, like 백화점에서 사요.
Calling a grocery discount store a 백화점. A budget warehouse store is a 마트; 백화점 specifically implies the upscale, department-by-department building.
Treating 백화점 as a count of departments and saying 백화점들에 instead of just 백화점에; the plural 들 is unnecessary and unnatural here.

entries.explanation: "supermarket" is 슈퍼마켓 (syupeomaket). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가까운 슈퍼마켓 ("nearby supermarket"). Watch the particle attached to 슈퍼마켓 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I bought it at the supermarket
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the buying happens
슈퍼마켓 is usually clipped to 슈퍼 in speech

examples.en: The corner shop is close.
examples.note: Casual clip 슈퍼 + adjective 가까워요 (가깝다, ㅂ-irregular).

examples.note: 에서 marks the place of the action 사다.

examples.note: Real situation: -는데 background + -을게요 'I'll (for you)' promise.

entries.nuance: 슈퍼마켓 is a loanword straight from English 'supermarket', and in everyday speech Koreans almost always clip it to 슈퍼 — saying the full 슈퍼마켓 can sound slightly textbook-stiff. The key contrast is scale: 슈퍼 is the small-to-mid neighborhood grocery you pop into for milk or snacks, whereas a 마트 (대형마트) is the big-box chain like 이마트 or 홈플러스, and a 편의점 is the 24-hour convenience store like GS25 or CU. Many small 슈퍼 today are also called 마트 on their signs, so the boundary is fuzzy in practice. Register is fully casual-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, defaulting to the long form 슈퍼마켓 when natives say 슈퍼; second, the motion-particle trap — 가다 takes 에 (슈퍼에 가요), and 에서 belongs only with an action verb (슈퍼에서 사요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Always saying the full 슈퍼마켓 in conversation. Natives clip it to 슈퍼, so 슈퍼 다녀올게 sounds far more natural than 슈퍼마켓에 다녀올게.
Using 슈퍼마켓 for a giant chain hypermarket. That scale is a 마트 (대형마트); 슈퍼 implies the smaller neighborhood store.
Saying 슈퍼마켓에서 가요 to mean 'go to the shop.' Motion verb 가다 needs 에 (슈퍼에 가요); 에서 only marks where an action occurs.

Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 조용한 is the modifier form of 조용하다
에 marks the destination of 가다
에서 marks where the studying happens
빌리다 = borrow; the verb that pairs with 도서관

examples.en: The library is quiet.
examples.note: Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 조용해요.

examples.en: I borrowed a book at the library.
examples.note: 에서 marks the place of the action 빌리다.

examples.ko: 시험 기간이라 도서관에 자리가 하나도 없더라고요.

entries.nuance: 도서관 is Sino-Korean 圖書館, literally 'pictures-books-building' (圖 picture + 書 writing/book + 館 hall), a public place to read, study, and borrow books where quiet is expected. The sharp contrast learners must hold is 도서관 vs 서점: a 도서관 is a LIBRARY where you borrow (빌리다) for free, while a 서점 is a BOOKSTORE where you buy (사다) — English 'library' and Spanish/French false friends like 'librería' push learners to mix these up. Note also 도서관 (the building) vs 도서 (books as items/collection). Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 도서관에서 공부하다, 책을 빌리다/반납하다, 도서관에 자리가 없다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the library/bookstore mix-up, is the particle split: study or read AT a library is 에서 (도서관에서), but going TO it is 에 (도서관에 가다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도서관 when you mean a place that sells books. A bookstore is a 서점; 도서관 is strictly for borrowing, not buying.
Saying 도서관에서 가요 for 'I go to the library.' Motion verb 가다 needs 에 (도서관에 가요); use 에서 only for studying/reading done there.
Pairing 도서관 with 사다 (buy) for the books inside. At a 도서관 you 빌리다 (borrow) and 반납하다 (return), you do not 사다.

entries.explanation: 박물관 (bangmulgwan) means "museum". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 국립 박물관 ("national museum"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 박물관 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 국립 = state-run; a common fixed modifier
에 marks the destination of 가다

usagePhrases.en: I look around at the museum
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the looking happens
입장료 is the cost to enter a 박물관

examples.en: The museum is famous.
examples.note: Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 유명해요.

examples.en: I saw old objects at the museum.
examples.note: 에서 marks the place of the action 보다.

entries.nuance: 박물관 is Sino-Korean 博物館, literally 'broad-things-building' (博 broad + 物 things + 館 hall) — a place displaying historical relics, artifacts, and natural specimens so visitors learn about the past. The essential contrast is 박물관 vs 미술관: a 박물관 shows HISTORY and objects (pottery, tools, dinosaur bones), while a 미술관 shows ART (paintings, sculpture). English lumps both under 'museum' (we say 'art museum'), which is exactly why learners wrongly call a painting gallery a 박물관. Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 박물관을 구경하다/관람하다, 전시(를) 보다, 입장료를 내다, 국립중앙박물관. The English-speaker pitfall is precisely this 'art museum = 박물관' transfer error, plus the usual motion-particle split: go TO it with 에 (박물관에 가다) but view things THERE with 에서 (박물관에서 보다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an art gallery a 박물관 because English says 'art museum.' Paintings and sculpture go in a 미술관; 박물관 is for historical objects.
Saying 박물관에서 가고 싶어요 for 'I want to go to the museum.' 가다 takes 에 (박물관에 가고 싶어요); 에서 is only for actions done there.
Pairing 박물관 with 읽다 because you 'read about history' there. You 구경하다/관람하다 (look around / view) exhibits; you do not 읽다 the museum itself.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination of 가다

usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the viewing happens

entries.nuance: 미술관 is Sino-Korean 美術館, literally 'beauty-art-building' (美 beauty + 術 skill/art + 館 hall) — a building exhibiting paintings, sculpture, and fine art, frequently rotating special exhibitions (전시). The non-negotiable contrast is 미술관 vs 박물관: 미술관 = ART, 박물관 = HISTORY/objects. Because English collapses both into 'museum,' learners habitually swap them; lock it in with 미술(美術) = fine art. A finer point: a small commercial space selling/showing art for sale is often a 갤러리 (loanword), while 미술관 implies a larger institution for viewing. Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 전시를 보다/관람하다, 그림을 감상하다, 미술관 입장료, 특별전. The English-speaker pitfall is calling it a 박물관 (the 'art museum' transfer trap), plus the motion particle: 에 to go there (미술관에 가다), 에서 to view art there (미술관에서 보다).

Calling a 미술관 a 박물관. 미술관 (美術 = fine art) shows paintings and sculpture; 박물관 shows historical objects.
Saying 미술관에서 갔어요 for 'I went to the gallery.' Motion verb 가다 needs 에 (미술관에 갔어요); 에서 only marks where viewing happens.
Pairing 그림 with 읽다 (read). You 감상하다 or 보다 (appreciate/view) a painting in a 미술관, you do not 읽다 it.

entries.nuance: 교회 is Sino-Korean 敎會, literally 'teach-gather' (敎 teach + 會 assembly/meeting) — specifically a PROTESTANT Christian place of worship and its congregation, busiest on Sunday mornings. The contrasts learners must keep straight: 교회 (Protestant church) vs 성당 (Catholic cathedral/church, 聖堂 'holy hall') vs 절 (Buddhist temple). English just says 'church' for both Protestant and Catholic, so newcomers wrongly call a Catholic 성당 a 교회 — Koreans hear that distinction clearly. Note 교회 also means the community of believers, not only the building. Register is neutral; the natural verb is 다니다 (교회에 다니다 = attend regularly), beyond plain 가다. Collocations: 교회에 다니다, 교회 친구, 새벽 기도. The English-speaker pitfall is the Protestant/Catholic blur (교회 vs 성당) plus saying 교회에서 가요 instead of the motion-correct 교회에 가요.

Saying 교회에서 가요 for 'I go to church.' 가다 (and 다니다) take 에 (교회에 가요 / 교회에 다녀요); 에서 only marks an action done there.

entries.nuance: 절 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) for a BUDDHIST temple, the mountainside complex where monks (스님) live and laypeople come to bow and pray quietly. Its near-synonym is 사찰 (寺刹), the formal/written term you see on signs and in news, while 절 is the everyday spoken word — same place, different register. Crucially, 절 must not be mixed with 교회 (Protestant church) or 성당 (Catholic church). Watch the homonym: 절 also means a deep traditional bow (절을 하다 = to bow), and 절하다 is the verb; only context tells them apart. Natural collocations: 절에 가다, 절에서 기도하다, 산속에 있는 절, 백팔배(108 bows). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for a 'temple = grand building' image and overusing the formal 사찰 in casual talk, plus confusing the place-절 with the bow-절 — and of course the motion particle (절에 가다, not 절에서 가다).

entries.nuance: 주민센터 blends Sino-Korean 住民 (住 reside + 民 people = 'residents') with the loanword 센터 ('center') — the small neighborhood (동 dong) office that issues certificates and handles resident reports. usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination of 가다

usagePhrases.en: I report it to the police
usagePhrases.note: 신고하다 = report to authorities; the verb that pairs with 경찰서

examples.en: The police station is close.
examples.note: Simple description; 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 가까워요.

examples.en: I filed a lost-item report at the police station.
examples.note: 에서 marks the place; 분실 신고 = lost-property report.

entries.nuance: 경찰서 is Sino-Korean 警察署, literally 'guard-inspect-office' (警 alert/guard + 察 examine + 署 government bureau) — the police station where you report crimes, lost items, or accidents. Two contrasts matter: by scale, the small neighborhood post is a 파출소 or 지구대 (local police box) while the larger district headquarters is the 경찰서; and by service, you call 경찰서 (or dial 112) for crime/police but the 소방서 (dial 119) for fires and medical emergencies. The verb 신고하다 (report) is the natural partner. Register is neutral/official. Collocations: 경찰서에 신고하다, 분실 신고를 하다, 112에 전화하다, 가까운 파출소. The English-speaker pitfall is calling 119 for police matters (in Korea police = 112, fire/ambulance = 119) and using the broad word 경찰서 when the place you actually visit is the smaller 파출소 — plus the motion particle (경찰서에 가다, not 경찰서에서 가다).

Calling the 소방서 or dialing 119 for a theft or police matter. Police is 경찰서 / 112; the 소방서 / 119 is for fires and ambulances.
Saying 경찰서에서 갔어요 for 'I went to the police station.' 가다 takes 에 (경찰서에 갔어요); 에서 only marks where an action happens.

usagePhrases.note: 가까운 is the modifier form of 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular)
불이 나면 dial 119, which reaches the 소방서

usagePhrases.en: they get dispatched from the fire station
usagePhrases.note: 출동하다 = mobilize/respond; 에서 marks the starting point
소방 (firefighting) + 차 (vehicle); kept at the 소방서

examples.en: The fire station is close.
examples.note: Simple description; 가깝다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 가까워요.

examples.en: A fire broke out, so I called 119.
examples.note: -아서 = so/therefore; 119 reaches the 소방서.

examples.ko: 옆 건물에서 연기가 나길래 바로 119에 신고했더니 소방차가 금방 왔어요.
examples.romanization: yeop geonmureseo yeongiga nagillae baro 119e singohaetdeoni sobangchaga geumbang wasseoyo.

examples.note: Real situation: -길래 'since (I noticed)' + -았더니 'and then (result)'.

entries.nuance: 소방서 is Sino-Korean 消防署, literally 'extinguish-defend-office' (消 extinguish + 防 prevent/defend + 署 government bureau) — the fire station where firefighters (소방관) and fire trucks (소방차) stand by for fires and rescues. The essential pairing every newcomer must memorize: in Korea you dial 119 for the 소방서 (fires AND ambulance/medical emergencies) but 112 for the 경찰서 (police). So a medical emergency also goes through 119/소방서, not just fires — a point that surprises many foreigners. The natural verb 출동하다 (be dispatched) uses 에서 to mark where responders set out from. The English-speaker pitfall is dialing 911 (the US number — Korea splits it into 119 fire/medical and 112 police) and assuming 소방서 is fire-only when it also covers ambulances — plus the motion particle (소방서에 가다, 소방서에서 출동하다).

에서 marks where the applying happens

examples.en: The embassy is far.
examples.note: Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 멀어요.

examples.en: I got a visa at the embassy.
examples.note: 에서 marks the place of the action 받다.

entries.nuance: 대사관 is Sino-Korean 大使館, literally 'great-envoy-building' (大 great + 使 envoy/messenger + 館 hall) — your home country's main diplomatic mission abroad, which helps citizens with passports, visas, and emergencies. Two contrasts matter: 대사관 (embassy, the main mission, usually one per country in the capital Seoul) vs 영사관 (consulate, 領事館, a branch office in other cities handling consular services); and 대사 (the ambassador, a person) vs 대사관 (the building) — note 대사 is also a homonym for 'line/dialogue' in a script, so context matters. The English-speaker pitfall is going to a Korean 시청 or 주민센터 for passport help — those are Korean local offices, while YOUR passport is handled by YOUR country's 대사관 — plus the motion particle (대사관에 가다 for going, 대사관에서 for actions there).

Saying 대사관에서 가요 for 'I go to the embassy.' 가다 takes 에 (대사관에 가요); 에서 only marks where the applying or issuing happens.
