entries.nuance: 한국 (韓國, 'Han nation') is the short, everyday name South Koreans use for their own country; the full official name is 대한민국 (大韓民國), which you mainly hear in formal contexts, news, and at sporting events ('대한민국!' chants). The key boundary for learners: 한국 by itself almost always means South Korea, NOT the whole peninsula — North Korea is 북한 (北韓, 'north Han') and you must never call it 한국. A second near-synonym is 우리나라 ('our country'), which Koreans use warmly when speaking among themselves to mean 'Korea' from an insider stance — but a foreigner saying 우리나라 sounds odd unless they identify as Korean, so as a learner stick with 한국. The particle trap: with movement verbs, 가다/오다 destinations take 에 (한국에 가요 = go to Korea), while origin and the location of an action take 에서 (한국에서 왔어요 = came from Korea; 한국에서 살아요 is also heard but residence more strictly prefers 한국에 살아요).

Saying 한국에 왔어요 to mean 'I came FROM Korea' — 에 marks a destination, so this means 'I came TO Korea'; for origin use 한국에서 왔어요.

entries.nuance: 미국 (美國, literally 'beautiful country') is the standard Korean name for the United States, and crucially it does NOT come from the English sound 'America' — it is a Sino-Korean reading borrowed via Chinese, where 美 was chosen as a phonetic match for the 'me' in 'America' (the same character also means 'beautiful', so the name is a happy accident, not literal praise). Learners often reach for 아메리카, which Koreans understand but sounds like the continent or a textbook transliteration, not a country; in real speech everyone says 미국. The same 國 ('country') element appears in 한국, 중국, 영국 — recognizing it helps you read country names. Note that 미국 covers the whole nation, so for a specific state you must name it (예: 캘리포니아). Particle-wise it behaves like any country noun: 미국에 가다 (go to), 미국에서 오다/살다 (come from / live in). Don't confuse the country 미국 with the language: Americans speak 영어, not '미국어' — there is no such word, since the language is English.

Saying 아메리카 for the country — Koreans use 미국; 아메리카 sounds like the continent or a stiff transliteration.
Inventing 미국어 for 'American language' — there is no 미국어; the language is 영어 (English).
Using 미국에 왔어요 to mean 'I came from the USA' — that says you came TO the USA; for origin say 미국에서 왔어요.

entries.nuance: 중국 (中國, 'central / middle country') is the everyday Korean name for China — the hanja literally means 'the central kingdom', the name China has historically used for itself. The crucial learner split is country vs. language: 중국 is the country, but the language is 중국어 (中國語, 'China-language') — adding 어 (語, 'language/speech') turns most country names into language names (중국→중국어, 일본→일본어, 프랑스→프랑스어). Particle behavior is the standard country pattern: 중국에 가다 (go to), 중국에서 오다/살다 (come from / live in). Don't confuse 중국 with 중국집, which colloquially means a Korean-Chinese restaurant — a different, food-specific word.

Using 중국에 왔어요 for 'I came from China' — 에 is destination; origin needs 중국에서 왔어요.

The reliable learner split is country vs. language: 일본 is the country, the language is 일본어 (日本語) — add 어 and never say '일본을 공부해요' to mean 'study Japanese' (that means studying the country); say 일본어를 공부해요. entries.nuance: 독일 (獨逸) is the Korean name for Germany and, like the other Sino-Korean country names, it does NOT come from the English 'Germany' — it derives via Chinese from 'Deutsch(land)', with 獨 ('Deu-') as the phonetic anchor (so it sounds nothing like the English word). The hanja are purely phonetic here, not meaningful descriptions. The reliable learner split is country vs. language: 독일 is the country, the language is 독일어 (獨逸語) — never '독일을 배워요' for 'study German' (that means studying the country); say 독일어를 배워요. A German person is 독일 사람 (casual) or 독일인 (formal). The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for an English-derived word like '저먼' or '게르만' — these are wrong for the country (게르만 refers to the Germanic ethnic/linguistic group, not the modern nation); Koreans always say 독일. Particle behavior is the usual country pattern: 독일에 가다/살다 (go to / live in), 독일에서 오다 (come from). When stating a role, note the example uses 엔지니어로 — the particle (으)로 marks 'in the capacity of', a handy pattern with jobs.

Saying 저먼 or 게르만 for the country — Koreans use 독일; 게르만 means the Germanic group, not modern Germany.
Using 독일을 배워요 for 'I learn German' — the language is 독일어; 독일 alone is the country.
Using 독일에 왔어요 to mean 'came from Germany' — 에 marks destination; for origin say 독일에서 왔어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 외국 means "foreign country" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "foreign country" is 외국 (oeguk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 외국 여행 ("trip abroad"). Watch the particle attached to 외국 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 외국 modifies 여행; overseas travel
에서 marks origin when the specific country is unstated
살다 takes location 에 for residence overseas
외국 modifies 친구; can mean a friend from abroad

examples.en: I want to live abroad.
examples.note: Simple; 살다 + 고 싶다 = want to live, 에서 marks the location of living

examples.en: I like foreign food.
examples.note: Everyday; 을 marks the object, 외국 음식 = food from other countries

examples.ko: 외국에 한 번도 안 가 봤어요.
examples.romanization: oeguge han beondo an ga bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I've never been abroad even once.
examples.note: Real-situation; 가 보다 = try going/have the experience, 한 번도 + 안 = not even once

entries.nuance: 외국 (外國, 'outside country') is the general word for 'a foreign country / abroad' — the hanja literally combine 外 ('outside') + 國 ('country'), so it means 'any country outside one's own'. Its meaning is relative and speaker-dependent: for a Korean, Japan is 외국, but for a Japanese person, Korea is 외국 — it always means 'not my country'. The key contrast for learners is generality: use 외국 only when you DON'T name a specific country; the moment you mean a particular nation, switch to its name (미국, 일본, etc.). Saying '외국에서 왔어요' is fine if you're being vague ('I came from abroad'), but if you mean the USA, say 미국에서 왔어요. Two important derivatives share the 外國 root: 외국인 (外國人, 'foreigner' — a foreign person) and 외국어 (外國語, 'foreign language'). English speakers sometimes use 외국 where English would say 'overseas' as an adjective, but in Korean 외국 is a noun, so 'go overseas' is 외국에 가다 (literally 'go to a foreign country'). Particle behavior follows the country pattern: 외국에 가다/살다 (go / live), 외국에서 오다 (come from).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 외국 when you mean a specific named country — 외국 is the vague 'abroad'; if you mean the USA, say 미국, not 외국.
Forgetting the 인/어 derivatives — a foreigner is 외국인 and a foreign language is 외국어; 외국 alone is the place, not the person or language.
Using 외국에 왔어요 to mean 'came from abroad' — 에 marks destination; for origin say 외국에서 왔어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 나라 means "country" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 나라 (nara) = "country". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리나라 ("our country") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 나라, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 + 나라 written as one word; means one's own nation warmly
어느 = which (among a set); the standard question word for nations
나라 modifies 이름; the name of a country

usagePhrases.en: every country / from country to country
usagePhrases.note: 마다 = each/every; common in 나라마다 달라요 'differs by country'

examples.en: Which country are you from?
examples.note: Simple, extremely common question; 어느 나라 + 에서 marks origin

examples.en: Our country has four seasons.
examples.note: Everyday; 우리나라 as one word, 사계절 = four seasons

examples.en: The way of greeting differs from country to country.
examples.note: Real-situation; 마다 = each, 다르다 = be different

entries.nuance: 나라 is the plain NATIVE Korean word for 'country' (not Sino-Korean), and it works for any nation in everyday speech. Its closest synonym is the Sino-Korean 국가 (國家), and the dividing line is register and abstraction: 나라 is warm, everyday, and concrete ('어느 나라?'), while 국가 is formal and institutional, used for the state as a political entity (국가 정책 'national policy', 국가대표 'national team' — note 국가 not 나라 here). So you'd ask a new acquaintance 어느 나라에서 왔어요? but a textbook would write 국가 간의 관계 'relations between states'. The single most important collocation is 우리나라 — written as ONE word (not 우리 나라) when it means 'our country' in the sense of 'Korea, from our shared insider view'. English speakers tend to over-use the literal 'my country' (제 나라), which sounds detached; among Koreans the warm default is 우리나라. Particle behavior is regular: 나라가 많다 (there are many countries), 어느 나라에서 (from which country). Don't reach for 국가 in casual conversation — it sounds stiff and bureaucratic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 나라 in formal institutional phrases — 'national team' is 국가대표, 'national policy' is 국가 정책; 나라 is the casual word, 국가 the formal/abstract one.
Writing 우리 나라 with a space when meaning 'Korea/our nation' — the warm fixed sense is one word, 우리나라.
Saying 제 나라 by default for 'my country' — among Koreans the natural warm form is 우리나라; 제 나라 sounds oddly distancing.

entries.shortExplanation: 한국인 means "Korean person" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 한국인 (hangugin) means "Korean person". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 한국인이에요 ("I am Korean"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 한국인 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 한국인 + 이에요; the copula for stating nationality
한국인 modifies 친구; a friend who is Korean
한국인 modifies 관광객; common in travel/news contexts
contrast term sharing the 人 suffix; 외국 + 인 = foreign person

examples.en: I am Korean.
examples.note: Simple nationality statement; 한국인 + 이에요

examples.en: That person is not Korean.
examples.note: Everyday negation; 이/가 아니다 = is not, 이 marks the subject of the negation

examples.ko: 회사에 한국인 동료가 세 명 있어요.
examples.romanization: hoesae hangugin dongnyoga se myeong isseoyo.
examples.en: There are three Korean colleagues at my company.
examples.note: Real-situation; 한국인 modifies 동료, 세 명 counts people

entries.nuance: 한국인 (韓國人, 'Korea-person') means 'a Korean person', built from 한국 + the Sino-Korean suffix 인 (人, 'person'). Its everyday near-synonym is 한국 사람, which means the same thing but feels warmer and more conversational, while 한국인 is slightly more formal and is the form you see in writing, documents, statistics, and news ('한국인 관광객', '재외 한국인'). Both are polite and acceptable — 한국인 is NOT more respectful, just a different register, so don't think you must use 한국인 to be polite. The 인 (人) suffix is productive: 미국인, 중국인, 외국인 all work the same way, paralleling 사람 (미국 사람 etc.). The key English-speaker pitfall is redundancy: because 인 already means 'person', you must NOT say '한국인 사람' — that doubles 'person-person'; choose either 한국인 OR 한국 사람, never both. A second pitfall is the copula: nationality uses 이에요/예요 attached directly (한국인이에요), and the negative is 한국인이 아니에요, with 이 marking the subject of 아니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한국인 사람 — 인 already means 'person', so this redundantly says 'Korean-person person'; use 한국인 or 한국 사람.
Thinking 한국인 is more polite than 한국 사람 — they're equally polite; 한국인 is just more formal/written register, not a respect upgrade.
Negating with 한국인 아니에요 missing the particle — the correct negative is 한국인이 아니에요, where 이 marks the subject of 아니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 세계 means "world" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "world" is 세계 (segye). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전 세계 ("the whole world"). Watch the particle attached to 세계 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 전 (全, 'all') + 세계; means the entire world, very common
세계 modifies 여행; traveling around the world
세계 modifies 최고; 'best in the world', common in praise/ads
세계 modifies 지도; a map of the world

examples.en: I want to travel the world.
examples.note: Simple; 세계 여행 as a noun phrase, 을 marks the object of 하다

examples.en: This song is famous all over the world.
examples.note: Everyday; 전 세계 = the whole world, 에서 marks the location of the state

examples.ko: 그 회사는 세계 시장에서 경쟁하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesaneun segye sijangeseo gyeongjaenghago isseoyo.
examples.en: That company competes in the world market.
examples.note: Real-situation; 세계 시장 = world market, 에서 marks the arena of the activity

entries.nuance: 세계 (世界, 'world-realm') means 'the world' as the whole earth and all its countries and peoples — a global, geographic scope. Its tricky near-synonym is 세상 (世上, 'world-above'), and the boundary matters: 세계 is the planet / international sphere (전 세계 'the whole world', 세계 지도 'world map', 세계 평화 'world peace'), whereas 세상 is 'the world' in the sense of human life, society, and 'how things are' (세상이 좋아졌어요 'the world/times have gotten better', 세상 물정 'the ways of the world'). So 'world map' is 세계 지도, never '세상 지도'; but '그런 세상에 살고 싶어요' (I want to live in such a world) uses 세상. The most useful collocation is 전 세계 ('the entire world'), where 전 (全) means 'all'. English speakers who learned 'world' as one word tend to overextend 세계 into the 세상 territory of 'life/society', so anchor it: 세계 = the globe and its nations; 세상 = the human world / life. Particle behavior is regular: 세계가 넓다 (the world is wide), 전 세계에서 (all over the world).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 세계 for 'the world' in the sense of life/society — 'the world has changed' (society/times) is 세상이 변했어요, not 세계; 세계 is the global/geographic world.
Saying 세상 지도 for 'world map' — the geographic compound is 세계 지도; 세상 is the human-life sense.
Dropping 전 in 'the whole world' — the idiomatic phrase is 전 세계, with 전 (全) meaning 'all/entire'.

entries.shortExplanation: 고향 means "hometown" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고향 (gohyang) = "hometown". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고향이 어디예요? ("Where is your hometown?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고향, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 고향 + 이 + 어디예요; the standard way to ask someone's hometown
내려가다 ('go down') is idiomatic for returning to a hometown outside Seoul
고향 modifies 친구; a friend from where you grew up
고향 modifies 음식; the food of one's home region

examples.en: My hometown is Busan.
examples.note: Simple; 고향 + 은 topic, 이에요 copula naming the place

examples.en: I go to my hometown for the holidays.
examples.note: Everyday; 명절 = traditional holiday, 에 marks the destination

examples.en: I went down to my hometown after a long time and saw my parents.
examples.note: Real-situation; 내려가다 = go down (to one's hometown), 뵈다 = humble 'see/meet' for elders

entries.nuance: 고향 (故鄕, 'old village') means the place where you were born and grew up — the hanja combine 故 ('old/former') + 鄕 ('village/country home'), so it carries a built-in feeling of warmth, nostalgia, and roots, more emotional than the neutral English 'hometown'. It is NOT the same as 집 ('house/home, where you currently live') or 본가 ('one's parents' home'): you can live in Seoul (집은 서울) while your 고향 is Busan. A 고향 can be a city, a town, or a whole region, and it stays your 고향 even decades after you leave. A culturally important collocation is 고향에 내려가다 ('go DOWN to one's hometown') — because Seoul is the center, returning to a provincial hometown is idiomatically 'going down' (내려가다), and going back to Seoul is 올라가다 ('going up'), regardless of actual geography. English speakers often misuse 고향 for their current home or address; remember 고향 is specifically your place of origin and upbringing. The classic conversation opener is 고향이 어디예요? Particle behavior is regular: 고향에 가다 (go to), 고향에서 자라다 (grow up in).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 고향 to mean your current home — that's 집 (house/home you live in); 고향 is specifically where you were born and raised.
Saying 고향에 올라가요 for going to a provincial hometown — returning to a hometown outside Seoul is idiomatically 고향에 내려가다 ('go down').
Asking 고향이 뭐예요? — for a place you ask 고향이 어디예요? (where), since 뭐 (what) is for things, not locations.

entries.shortExplanation: 병 means "illness; disease" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 병 (byeong) means "illness; disease". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 병이 났어요 ("I got sick"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 병 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = the illness 'came out'; never use 받다 or 가지다 here
심하다, not 크다, describes how severe a condition is
고치다 is the casual verb for fixing illness or objects alike
걸리다 needs 에; this fixed phrase = 'got hooked by' a disease

examples.en: I'm relieved I didn't get sick.
examples.note: Simple: 병이 나다 ('fall ill'), negated as 안 나다; the most basic frame.

examples.en: Grandpa caught a serious disease, so he was hospitalized.
examples.note: Everyday: 큰 병 collocates with 걸리다 + 에, and 입원하다 = be admitted.

examples.ko: 이 병은 약으로 못 고치고 수술을 받아야 해요.
examples.romanization: i byeongeun yageuro mot gochigo susureul badaya haeyo.
examples.en: This disease can't be cured with medicine; you have to get surgery.
examples.note: Real-situation: contrasts 고치다(cure) with 수술을 받다(undergo surgery).

entries.nuance: 병 is the Sino-Korean word 病, the broad term for any illness from a cold to cancer; for a serious one Koreans add 큰 (큰 병) and for a minor one they often switch to 감기 or 몸살 instead. Two patterns split by particle: 병이 나다 (a disease 'breaks out,' using 나다 like 열이 나다 'run a fever') versus 병에 걸리다 ('get hooked by' a disease, requiring 에 exactly as 감기에 걸리다). The big English-speaker trap is forcing 'catch' into 받다 or 가지다 — Korean treats catching a disease as being snagged by it, so 병을 걸리다 (wrong particle) and 병을 받다 both sound broken; the disease is the thing you bump into, marked with 에. 병 is neutral in register and fine in both polite and casual speech, but when speaking about an elder's illness you raise the verb politely (병에 걸리셨어요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 병을 걸렸어요: 걸리다 demands the location/contact particle 에, so it must be 병에 걸렸어요.
Saying 병을 받았어요 by translating 'I caught a disease' literally: 받다 is for handing-over; use 병에 걸렸어요 or 병이 났어요.
Treating 병 like a countable thing you 'have' as in 병을 가지고 있어요: Koreans say 병이 있어요 (state of having an illness), not 가지다.

entries.shortExplanation: 주사 means "injection; shot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "injection; shot" is 주사 (jusa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주사를 맞아요 ("I get a shot"). Watch the particle attached to 주사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 맞다 (lit. 'be struck') is how the patient RECEIVES the injection
아프다 describes the painful sensation of the shot itself
놓다 is the action of the person ADMINISTERING it
무섭다 marks the feared thing with 가, not 를

examples.en: I don't want to get a shot.
examples.note: Simple: patient's side always pairs 주사 with 맞다.

examples.en: My cold was bad, so I got a shot at the clinic.
examples.note: Everyday: 주사 맞다 is the standard clinic experience after a 감기.

examples.ko: 간호사 선생님이 아이 팔에 주사를 놓아 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: ganhosa seonsaengnimi ai pare jusareul noa jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The nurse gave the child a shot in the arm.
examples.note: Real-situation: the giver uses 놓다, and -아 주시다 adds politeness for the nurse.

entries.nuance: 주사 is Sino-Korean 注射, literally 'pour (注) and shoot (射),' a vivid image of forcing fluid in through a needle. The crucial point is that the verb flips depending on who acts: the patient says 주사를 맞다 — and 맞다 literally means 'to be hit/struck,' the same verb as in 비를 맞다 (get rained on) or 매를 맞다 (get beaten), framing the shot as something done TO you — while the nurse who administers it says 주사를 놓다 ('lay/place' the shot). English speakers almost always reach for 받다 ('receive') because 'receive a shot' feels logical, but 주사를 받다 sounds unnatural; 받다 is reserved for treatment as a whole (치료를 받다), not the needle. Note 주사 covers the whole injection event, while the physical needle is 주삿바늘 and the syringe is 주사기.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 주사를 받아요: the patient-side verb is 맞다, so it must be 주사를 맞아요; 받다 collocates with 치료, not 주사.
Using 놓다 for yourself as the patient (주사를 놓았어요 meaning 'I got a shot'): 놓다 is the giver's verb; the patient says 맞았어요.
Saying 주사가 무서워해요 to mean 'I'm scared of shots': 무서워하다 needs a human subject; for the shot itself use 주사가 무서워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 치료 means "treatment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 치료 (chiryo) = "treatment". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 치료를 받아요 ("I get treatment") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 치료, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 = the patient RECEIVES the course of care
끝나다 (intransitive) means the process finished on its own
필요하다 marks what is needed with 가, not 를
시작하다 takes 를 for what you start

examples.en: Please get treatment quickly.
examples.note: Simple: patient + 치료를 받다, the core medical-care frame.

examples.ko: 3주 동안 병원에서 치료를 받고 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: 3ju dongan byeongwoneseo chiryoreul batgo mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I got treatment at the hospital for three weeks and improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 동안 (duration) + 치료를 받다 + 좋아지다 (get better).

examples.ko: 의사 선생님이 환자를 정성껏 치료해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: uisa seonsaengnimi hwanjareul jeongseongkkeot chiryohae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The doctor treated the patient with great care.
examples.note: Real-situation: the doctor's side uses the verb 치료하다, not 받다.

entries.nuance: 치료 is Sino-Korean 治療, where 治 means 'to govern/manage' and 療 means 'to heal,' together 'managing an illness back to health' — broader than a single procedure, it covers the whole healing process (medication, therapy, surgery as a package). Watch the actor split exactly as with 주사: the patient says 치료를 받다 ('receive treatment'), while the doctor says 환자를 치료하다 ('treat the patient'), so 받다 vs the 하다-verb tells you who is acting. The nearest neighbor is 진료 (診療, 'examine + heal'), which is narrower — 진료 is the consultation/seeing-the-doctor part (진료를 받다 = 'see a doctor'), whereas 치료 is the actual curing that follows. English speakers sometimes carry over the 'shot' verb and say 치료를 맞다; that is wrong — 맞다 belongs only to 주사. They also drop the particle in 치료가 필요하다, mistakenly saying 치료를 필요해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 치료를 맞아요: 맞다 is only for 주사; treatment is 치료를 받아요.
Saying 치료를 필요해요: 필요하다 is an adjective taking 가, so it must be 치료가 필요해요.
Confusing 치료 with 진료: for just seeing the doctor say 진료를 받다; reserve 치료 for the actual cure.

entries.shortExplanation: 환자 means "patient" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 환자 (hwanja) means "patient". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환자가 많아요 ("there are many patients"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 많다 takes 가 for what is plentiful
보다 = a doctor examining; never 만나다 here

usagePhrases.en: I take care of a patient
usagePhrases.note: 돌보다 = look after, nurse a patient
회복하다 (回復) for getting well again

examples.en: There aren't many patients today.
examples.note: Simple: 환자가 + existence/quantity verb, the most basic frame.

examples.en: There were many patients in the ER, so I waited a long time.
examples.note: Everyday: 환자가 많다 + 기다리다 in a real hospital scene.

examples.ko: 의사 선생님이 입원 환자들을 한 명씩 봐요.
examples.romanization: uisa seonsaengnimi ibwon hwanjadeureul han myeongssik bwayo.
examples.en: The doctor sees the inpatients one by one.
examples.note: Real-situation: 환자를 보다 (examine) + 입원 환자 (inpatient) + 한 명씩.

entries.nuance: 환자 is Sino-Korean 患者, literally 患 'to suffer/afflict' + 者 'person,' i.e. 'a suffering person' — note that 者 is the same 'person' suffix in 기자(reporter) and 과학자(scientist), so the word is built on the idea of one afflicted by illness. The biggest pitfall is the verb for a doctor's exam: Korean says 환자를 보다, using 보다 ('look at') the way a doctor 'looks over' a case, NOT 만나다 ('meet'); 환자를 만나다 sounds like a casual social encounter, not a medical visit, so a doctor never says it about examining someone. Register-wise 환자 is a neutral clinical noun; when the patient is an elder you may add honorifics elsewhere in the sentence (보호자/분), but 환자 itself stays plain. A near term is 손님 — a pharmacy or clinic might call walk-ins 손님 (customers), but inside a hospital the sick person is specifically 환자.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의사가 환자를 만나요 to mean a doctor examines a patient: that sounds like a social meet-up; use 환자를 봐요.
Saying 환자를 가요 or 환자에 가요 confusing person with place: you go to 병원(hospital), and the doctor 환자를 봐요.
Adding wrong honorific verbs to 환자 reflexively (환자께서): 환자 is a neutral noun; honorifics attach by context, not automatically.

entries.shortExplanation: 체온 means "body temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "body temperature" is 체온 (cheon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 체온을 재요 ("I take (someone's) temperature"). Watch the particle attached to 체온 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 재다 = measure, the same verb as for height/length
높다 (high), not 크다 (big), for a reading
정상 (正常) = normal; ~이에요 after a consonant
확인하다 = verify the reading

examples.en: I take the temperature with a thermometer.
examples.note: Simple: instrument 체온계 + 체온을 재다, the core measuring frame.

examples.en: I had a fever, so I checked and my temperature was 38 degrees.
examples.note: Everyday: 재 보다 (try measuring) + ~도 for degrees Celsius.

examples.ko: 아기 체온이 갑자기 올라가서 병원에 데려갔어요.
examples.romanization: agi cheoni gapjagi ollagaseo byeongwone deryeogasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby's temperature suddenly went up, so I took them to the hospital.
examples.note: Real-situation: 체온이 올라가다 (rises) + 데려가다 (take a person).

entries.nuance: 체온 is Sino-Korean 體溫, literally 體 'body' + 溫 'warmth,' so it specifically means the warmth of the body, distinct from 온도 (溫度, 'temperature-degree'), which is the general word for any temperature — air, water, an oven. Use 체온 only for a person or animal's heat and 온도 for the room or weather; saying 방 체온 (room body-temperature) is wrong, it must be 방 온도. The verb is 재다 ('to measure'), the very same verb used for 키를 재다 (measure height) and 길이를 재다 (measure length), because temperature is a quantity you gauge, not something you 'look at' — so 체온을 보다 sounds off to natives. For a high or low reading Korean uses 높다/낮다, never 크다/작다 (big/small), which is the typical English-speaker slip. A closely related symptom word is 열 (fever): 열이 나다 means 'run a fever,' and you confirm it by 체온을 재다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 방 체온 for room temperature: 체온 is only for bodies; the room's temperature is 방 온도.
Saying 체온이 커요: a reading is 높다/낮다, so it must be 체온이 높아요.
Saying 체온을 봐요 instead of 재요: temperature is measured with an instrument, so the verb is 재다.

entries.shortExplanation: 혈압 means "blood pressure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 혈압 (hyeorap) = "blood pressure". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 혈압을 재요 ("I take (someone's) blood pressure") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 혈압, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 재다 = measure, same verb as 체온/키
높다, never 크다, for the reading
낮다 = low; common cause of dizziness
정상 (正常) = within normal range

examples.en: I take my blood pressure at home every day.
examples.note: Simple: habit + 혈압을 재다, the core measuring frame.

examples.ko: 우리 아버지는 혈압이 높아서 약을 드세요.
examples.romanization: uri abeojineun hyeorabi nopaseo yageul deuseyo.
examples.en: My father has high blood pressure, so he takes medicine.
examples.note: Everyday: 혈압이 높다 + 약을 드시다 (honorific 'take medicine').

examples.ko: 갑자기 일어나면 혈압이 떨어져서 어지러울 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi ireonamyeon hyeorabi tteoreojyeoseo eojireoul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you stand up suddenly, your blood pressure can drop and you may feel dizzy.
examples.note: Real-situation: 혈압이 떨어지다 (drops) + 어지럽다 (dizzy) + ~을 수 있다.

entries.nuance: 혈압 is Sino-Korean 血壓, literally 血 'blood' + 壓 'pressure,' a transparent compound naming the pressure of blood in the vessels. Like 체온, it is something you gauge, so the verb is 재다 ('measure') — the identical verb in 키를 재다 and 체온을 재다 — and high/low readings take 높다/낮다, the persistent English-speaker error being 크다/작다 (big/small), which are for physical size, not measured values. For movement of the reading, Korean uses 오르다/올라가다 (rises) and 떨어지다/내려가다 (drops), not 'go up/down' translated as 가다. Distinguish 혈압 from 맥박 (脈搏, pulse/heart rate): both are vital signs taken at the clinic, but 혈압 is the pressure number and 맥박 is the beats per minute. In casual talk people with chronic hypertension say 고혈압 (高血壓, 'high blood pressure' as a named condition), so 고혈압이 있어요 means 'I have hypertension,' a step beyond a one-time high reading.

Saying 혈압이 커요: a reading is described with 높다/낮다, so it must be 혈압이 높아요.
Saying 혈압을 봐요 instead of 재요: blood pressure is measured, so the verb is 재다.
Confusing 혈압 (pressure) with 맥박 (pulse): if you mean heart rate per minute, say 맥박, not 혈압.

entries.shortExplanation: 상처 means "wound; cut" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상처 (sangcheo) means "wound; cut". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상처가 났어요 ("I got a wound"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상처 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = a wound 'appeared'; physical injury
아프다 for the pain of the cut
낫다 (ㅅ-irregular) = heal/recover
소독하다 (消毒) = sterilize before bandaging

examples.en: I got a small cut on my finger.
examples.note: Simple: body part + 에 + 상처가 나다, the core 'get hurt' frame.

examples.ko: 넘어져서 무릎에 상처가 났는데 피가 났어요.
examples.romanization: neomeojyeoseo mureupe sangcheoga nanneunde piga nasseoyo.
examples.en: I fell and got a wound on my knee, and it bled.
examples.note: Everyday: 넘어지다(fall) + 상처가 나다 + 피가 나다 (bleed).

examples.ko: 연고를 바르고 며칠 지나니까 상처가 깨끗이 나았어요.
examples.romanization: yeongoreul bareugo myeochil jinanikka sangcheoga kkaekkeusi naasseoyo.
examples.en: I applied ointment, and after a few days the wound healed cleanly.
examples.note: Real-situation: 연고를 바르다(apply ointment) + 낫다 for healing.

entries.nuance: 상처 is Sino-Korean 傷處, literally 傷 'injure/wound' + 處 'place/spot,' i.e. 'the injured spot' on the body. Crucially, 상처 has a famous double life: physically it is a cut or wound (상처가 나다), but emotionally it means a hurt feeling, and there the collocation flips to 상처를 받다 ('receive a wound,' = be hurt) or 상처를 주다 ('give a wound,' = hurt someone). So a physical injury uses 나다 (it 'comes out'), while an emotional one uses 받다/주다 — mixing these is the classic trap: 상처를 받았어요 about a knee scrape sounds like your feelings were hurt, not your skin. For healing, use 낫다, an ㅅ-irregular verb that drops the ㅅ before a vowel (낫다 → 나아요, 나았어요), and it doubles as 'recover from illness' (감기가 나았어요). A near-synonym is 흉터 (scar) — 상처 is the fresh open wound, 흉터 is the lasting mark it leaves after it heals.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 상처를 받았어요 about a physical cut: 받다 is for emotional hurt; a bodily wound is 상처가 났어요.
Conjugating 낫다 regularly as 낫아요: it is ㅅ-irregular, so the wound healed = 상처가 나았어요 (나아요).
Confusing 상처 with 흉터: the open wound is 상처; the scar left afterward is 흉터.

A near-synonym is 흉터 (scar) — 상처 is the fresh open wound, 흉터 is the lasting mark it leaves after it heals.

entries.shortExplanation: 기침 means "cough" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "cough" is 기침 (gichim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기침이 나요 ("a cough comes on"). Watch the particle attached to 기침 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = the cough 'comes out' involuntarily
하다 = perform the act of coughing
심하다 for a severe, persistent cough
멈추다 (intransitive) = it ceased

examples.en: My throat is itchy, so I keep coughing.
examples.note: Simple: cause 목이 간지럽다 + 기침이 나다, the involuntary frame.

examples.ko: 회의 중에 자꾸 기침을 해서 미안했어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui junge jakku gichimeul haeseo mianhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I kept coughing during the meeting, so I felt sorry.
examples.note: Everyday: 기침을 하다 (active) + 자꾸 (repeatedly) in a social setting.

examples.ko: 기침이 2주 넘게 안 멈추면 병원에 가 보세요.
examples.romanization: gichimi 2ju neomge an meomchumyeon byeongwone ga boseyo.
examples.en: If a cough doesn't stop for over two weeks, go see a doctor.
examples.note: Real-situation: 안 멈추다 + 가 보다 (go and see), giving health advice.

entries.nuance: 기침 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean), and it works in two equally natural patterns that differ subtly in viewpoint: 기침이 나다 frames the cough as something that 'comes out' on its own — built with 나다, the same verb in 열이 나다(run a fever), 콧물이 나다(runny nose), 재채기가 나다(sneeze) — stressing it's involuntary; whereas 기침을 하다 frames it as an action you perform, useful when you mean someone coughs deliberately or repeatedly. English speakers raised on 'have a cough' often try 기침을 가지다 ('possess a cough'), which is flatly wrong — Korean never 'has' a symptom with 가지다; symptoms either 나다 (come out) or you 하다 (do) them. Don't confuse 기침 with 재채기 (a sneeze): 기침 is a throat/chest cough, 재채기 is the explosive nose sneeze, and they are not interchangeable. For severity use 심하다 (기침이 심하다 = a bad cough), not 크다.

Saying 기침을 가지고 있어요 from English 'I have a cough': symptoms use 나다 or 하다, so say 기침이 나요 / 기침을 해요.
Confusing 기침 with 재채기: a throat cough is 기침; the nose sneeze is 재채기.
Saying 기침이 커요 for a bad cough: severity is 심하다, so it must be 기침이 심해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 콧물 means "runny nose; snot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 콧물 (konmul) = "runny nose; snot". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 콧물이 나요 ("my nose is running") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = the mucus 'comes out'
많다 for a heavy runny nose
닦다 = wipe away with a tissue
멈추다 = the discharge ceased

examples.en: It's cold out, so my nose is running.
examples.note: Simple: cause 춥다 + 콧물이 나다, the core symptom frame.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸려서 콧물하고 기침이 같이 나요.
examples.romanization: gamgie geollyeoseo konmulhago gichimi gachi nayo.
examples.en: I caught a cold, so I have a runny nose and a cough together.
examples.note: Everyday: 콧물 + 기침 both with 나다, listed via 하고.

examples.ko: 휴지로 콧물을 닦고 손을 깨끗이 씻으세요.
examples.romanization: hyujiro konmureul dakgo soneul kkaekkeusi ssiseuseyo.
examples.en: Wipe your nose with a tissue and wash your hands well.
examples.note: Real-situation: 콧물을 닦다 (active wipe) + hygiene advice.

entries.nuance: 콧물 is a native compound: 코 (nose) + the linking ㅅ (사이시옷) + 물 (water), literally 'nose-water' — that inserted ㅅ is why it's spelled 콧물 and pronounced [콘물], a tiny spelling point learners miss. Like other discharges it pairs with 나다 (콧물이 나다, 'snot comes out'), exactly parallel to 눈물이 나다 (tears) and 땀이 나다 (sweat), so the whole family of bodily fluids shares this 나다 frame. The key English-speaker trap is reaching for 코가 아프다 ('my nose hurts') to express a cold — but that means literal nose pain, not a runny nose; a stuffy/congested nose is yet another phrase, 코가 막히다 ('the nose is blocked'). So three different states: 콧물이 나다 (runny), 코가 막히다 (stuffy), 코가 아프다 (painful). When you actively clear it you 닦다 (wipe) or 풀다 (blow: 코를 풀다). Register is fully neutral and used freely in everyday talk and at the clinic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 코가 아파요 to mean a runny nose: that's literal nose pain; a runny nose is 콧물이 나요.
Saying 콧물이 막혔어요 mixing up symptoms: a blocked nose is 코가 막혔어요; running is 콧물이 나요.
Misspelling as 코물 without the 사이시옷: it must be 콧물 (pronounced [콘물]).

entries.shortExplanation: 두통 means "headache" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 두통 (dutong) means "headache". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 두통이 있어요 ("I have a headache"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 두통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 있다 = the standard 'have' for 두통
심하다 for a severe headache
나아지다 = improve (from 낫다)
두통약 = headache pill; 약을 먹다 idiom

examples.en: I've had a headache since yesterday.
examples.note: Simple: ~부터 (since) + 두통이 있다, the core 'have a headache' frame.

examples.ko: 스트레스 때문에 두통이 심해서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
examples.romanization: seuteureseu ttaemune dutongi simhaeseo iljjik toegeunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: My headache was bad from stress, so I left work early.
examples.note: Everyday: 때문에(because) + 두통이 심하다 + 퇴근하다 (leave work).

examples.ko: 두통약을 먹고 한숨 자고 나니까 좀 괜찮아졌어요.
examples.romanization: dutongyageul meokgo hansum jago nanikka jom gwaenchanajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I took a headache pill, slept a bit, and felt somewhat better.
examples.note: Real-situation: 두통약을 먹다 + 자고 나다 + 괜찮아지다 (get better).

entries.nuance: 두통 is Sino-Korean 頭痛, literally 頭 'head' + 痛 'ache/pain' — the same 痛 appears in 복통 (腹痛, stomachache) and 치통 (齒痛, toothache), so once you know 통 = 'ache' the whole pain family opens up. The register split matters: 두통 is the bookish/clinical word you'd write on a pharmacy form or say to a doctor, while in everyday speech Koreans far more often say 머리가 아파요 ('my head hurts') with the native adjective 아프다. Both are correct, but to a friend 머리 아파 sounds natural and 두통이 있어 sounds slightly formal. The number-one English-speaker error is double-marking the pain: since 두통 already contains 痛 ('ache'), saying 두통이 아파요 literally means 'the headache hurts' — redundant and wrong; the noun takes 있다/심하다, not 아프다. Use 아프다 only with the body part (머리가 아프다), never with 두통.

Using 두통 with a friend when 머리가 아파 is more natural: save 두통 for the pharmacy/doctor, use 머리가 아프다 in casual talk.
Saying 두통을 가지고 있어요 from 'have a headache': use the state verb 두통이 있어요, not 가지다.

entries.shortExplanation: 소화 means "digestion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "digestion" is 소화 (sohwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 소화가 잘 돼요 ("I digest well"). Watch the particle attached to 소화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 되다 = digestion 'happens'; 잘 = well
안 되다 = it doesn't happen; the standard 'upset stomach'
돕다 (ㅂ-irregular) = help; subject is a food/drink
소화제 (消化劑) = digestion medicine

examples.ko: 저는 우유를 마시면 소화가 잘 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun uyureul masimyeon sohwaga jal an dwaeyo.
examples.en: When I drink milk, I don't digest it well.
examples.note: Simple: condition + 소화가 안 되다, the core indigestion frame.

examples.ko: 급하게 먹으면 소화가 안 되니까 천천히 드세요.
examples.romanization: geupage meogeumyeon sohwaga an doenikka cheoncheonhi deuseyo.
examples.en: If you eat in a hurry you'll get indigestion, so please eat slowly.
examples.note: Everyday: 급하게(hastily) + 소화가 안 되다 + advice with 드세요.

examples.ko: 체했을 때는 소화제를 먹거나 손을 따 주면 좋아요.
examples.romanization: chehaesseul ttaeneun sohwajereul meokgeona soneul tta jumyeon joayo.
examples.en: When your stomach is upset, taking a digestive or pricking the finger helps.
examples.note: Real-situation: 체하다 (have indigestion) + 소화제 + folk remedy.

entries.nuance: 소화 is Sino-Korean 消化, literally 消 'dissolve/dissipate' + 化 'transform' — food being broken down and changed inside you. The governing verb is 되다 ('to become/happen'), so 소화가 되다 = 'digestion takes place' and 소화가 안 되다 = 'indigestion,' the everyday way to say your stomach is off. The big trap for English speakers is treating digestion as an action you do: 소화를 하다 or 소화를 못 하다 sounds unnatural, because Korean frames digestion as something that happens to/in you (되다), not something you actively perform — so 'I can't digest' is 소화가 안 돼요, never 소화를 못 해요. A close real-life synonym is the native verb 체하다, which is more acute: 소화가 안 되다 is general slow/poor digestion, while 체하다 means you got an actual blockage/upset stomach from eating, often suddenly. The medicine is 소화제 (消化劑, 'digestion-agent'), built with the same 劑 as 해열제 (fever reducer).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 소화를 못 해요 for 'I can't digest': digestion is framed with 되다, so say 소화가 안 돼요.
Saying 소화를 해요 to mean 'I digest': it must be the happening-verb 소화가 잘 돼요, not 소화를 하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 건강 means "health" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 건강 (geongang) = "health". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 건강이 좋아요 ("my health is good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 건강, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다, not 높다, describes good health
나쁘다 for poor health
챙기다 = take care of, mind one's health
set farewell/blessing from 건강하다

examples.en: Health is the most important thing.
examples.note: Simple: 건강이 + adjective, the core 'health is X' frame.

examples.ko: 요즘 운동을 시작해서 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum undongeul sijakaeseo geongangi mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I started exercising lately, so my health has improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 운동을 시작하다 + 건강이 좋아지다 (improve).

examples.en: Grandma, please always stay healthy and live a long, long life.
examples.note: Real-situation: honorific 건강하시다 + 사세요 as a warm blessing.

entries.nuance: 건강 is Sino-Korean 健康, where 健 means 'sturdy/robust' and 康 means 'peaceful/well,' together the sound, robust state of body and mind. It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) — never 높다/낮다 (high/low), which is the typical English-influenced slip from 'high level of health' — and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy'). Its honorific imperative 건강하세요 is a beloved set phrase, a warm farewell/blessing meaning 'stay healthy,' especially said to elders and at New Year. A near-synonym is 컨디션 (a loanword from 'condition') — but 컨디션 is your day-to-day fitness/energy level (오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아 = 'I'm not feeling great today'), whereas 건강 is your overall, long-term state of wellness; don't swap them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 건강이 높아요 for good health: health is 좋다/나쁘다, so it must be 건강이 좋아요.
Confusing 건강 with 컨디션: long-term wellness is 건강; today's energy/feeling is 컨디션.
Saying 건강이세요 instead of 건강하세요: the blessing comes from the adjective 건강하다, giving 건강하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 봄 means "spring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 봄 (bom) means "spring". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 봄에 ("in spring"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 봄 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: season takes time particle 에, never 에서
adjective 따뜻하다 in modifier form 따뜻한
subject with 이; 오다 → 와요
two nouns stack with no particle

examples.en: I like spring.
examples.note: 이/가 marks 봄 as the thing liked, not 을/를

examples.en: Cherry blossoms bloom in spring.
examples.note: 에 = time when; 피다 'bloom' → 펴요

examples.ko: 저는 추운 겨울보다 따뜻한 봄이 더 좋아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun chuun gyeoulboda ttatteutan bomi deo joayo.
examples.en: I prefer warm spring over cold winter.
examples.note: 보다 'than' + 더 'more' to compare seasons

entries.nuance: 봄 is the spring season, roughly March to May, the time of mild warmth (따뜻하다) and blossoms — 벚꽃 cherry blossoms above all. It is a pure native Korean word (no 한자), so unlike 춘하추동 it has no Sino reading you must memorize. The natural collocations are 봄이 오다 'spring comes', 봄이 되다 'it becomes spring', 봄 날씨 'spring weather', and 봄나물 'spring greens'. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you go 'in spring' with 봄에, never 봄에서 — 에서 marks the place an action happens, while 에 marks a point in time, and a season is a time. A second trap is treating 봄 like the subject of 'I like': Koreans say 봄이 좋아요 (spring is good-to-me) with 이/가, not 봄을 좋아요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

The big pitfall is the particle: you go 'in spring' with 봄에, never 봄에서 — 에서 marks the place an action happens, while 에 marks a point in time, and a season is a time. A second trap is treating 봄 like the subject of 'I like': Koreans say 봄이 좋아요 (spring is good-to-me) with 이/가, not 봄을 좋아요.

덥다 is ㅂ-irregular → modifier 더운
subject with 이, adjective 좋다

examples.en: Summer is hot.
examples.note: 덥다 ㅂ-irregular: 덥 + 어요 → 더워요

examples.en: I go to the sea in summer.
examples.note: two 에: first = time, second = destination

examples.en: In summer it rains often so I carry an umbrella.
examples.note: 여름에는 sets the topic; 와서 'because it comes'

entries.nuance: 여름 is summer, about June to August — hot (덥다) and humid, with a rainy stretch called 장마 in mid-summer and a late-summer heat wave called 폭염. It is a native Korean word, so there is no 한자 to parse. Note the adjective for hot weather is 덥다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 덥다 → 더워요), used for air and seasons; do not confuse it with 뜨겁다 'hot to the touch', which you use for soup or a stove, not for summer. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

subject 이 + 오다 → 와요

examples.note: 이/가 marks the liked season

examples.romanization: gaeureun siwonhago haneuri nopaseo sanchaekagi joayo.
examples.en: Autumn is cool and the sky is high, so it's good for walks.
examples.note: 가을은 topic; -기 좋다 'good for ~ing'

entries.nuance: 가을 is autumn, about September to November, prized for crisp cool air (시원하다, not 춥다 'cold' yet) and 단풍, the red-and-gold foliage. It is a native Korean word, so no 한자 applies. Two collocations to lock in: 단풍이 들다 'the leaves take on color' and 가을 하늘이 높다 'the autumn sky is high' — Koreans really do describe the sky as 높다 in fall. examples.en: Winter is cold.
examples.note: 춥다 ㅂ-irregular: 춥 + 어요 → 추워요

entries.nuance: 겨울 is winter, roughly December to February — the coldest season (춥다), dry, with snow (눈). It is a native Korean word, so there is no hanja to break down. The adjective is 춥다, a ㅂ-irregular (춥다 → 추워요) used for cold weather; keep it apart from 차갑다 'cold to the touch', which describes water or an icy hand, not the season — so winter is 추워요, never 차가워요. Snow 'falls' with the verb 오다 (눈이 와요), exactly like rain, not with 내리다 in everyday speech. Standard collocations: 겨울이 오다, 겨울 방학 'winter school break', 겨울옷 / 겨울 옷 'winter clothing', 한겨울 'midwinter'. subject 이 + 바뀌다 'change'

examples.en: What season do you like?
examples.note: verb 좋아하다 takes object 을/를

examples.note: set phrase 사계절이 뚜렷하다

examples.en: When the season changes I buy new clothes.
examples.note: -(으)면 'when/if'; 계절이 as subject

entries.nuance: 계절 is the general word for 'season' (a time of year), the umbrella term under which 봄·여름·가을·겨울 sit. It is Sino-Korean, 季節 — 季 'season/quarter' + 節 'period, node' — so the four together are 사계절 (四季節), and you will constantly hear 사계절이 뚜렷하다 'the four seasons are clear-cut' as a point of pride about Korea. Do not confuse 계절 (a season of the year) with 시기 'a period/phase' or with the English loanword 시즌, which Koreans reserve for sports or TV ('시즌 2'); for the natural cycle of the year, 계절 is the only choice. Common partners: 계절이 바뀌다 'the season turns', 환절기 'the change-of-season period', 제철 'in-season (food)'. Pitfall: 'season' as in 'baseball season' is not 계절 — that is 시즌.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

examples.en: What's the date today?
examples.note: 며칠 for the day of the month, with Sino numbers

examples.en: We set the meeting date.
examples.note: 날짜 as object of 정하다

examples.en: The date isn't decided yet.
examples.note: passive 정해지다; 날짜가 as subject

entries.nuance: 날짜 means a calendar date — a specific day pinned to the month and year. It is a native-Korean compound built on 날 'day' (날 + the bound element -짜), so it is not Sino-Korean and has no hanja, even though the numbers you read inside a date (일·이·삼…) are Sino. Keep three look-alikes apart: 날짜 'date (which day of the month)' vs 요일 'day of the week (Monday…)' vs 날 'a day in general'. To ask a date Koreans say 며칠이에요?, and the answer uses Sino-Korean day numbers (오월 십오일 'May 15th'), not the native 하나·둘 set — that is the classic pitfall. Habitual collocations: 날짜를 정하다 'set a date', 날짜를 잡다 'pin down a date', 날짜를 바꾸다 'change a date', 날짜가 지나다 'the date passes'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이/가 + 언제
day + time particle 에
lit. 'I celebrate your birthday'
noun + noun compound

examples.en: When is your birthday?
examples.note: 이/가 + 언제, the standard way to ask

examples.en: I eat seaweed soup on my birthday.
examples.note: 에 marks the day; 미역국 is the birthday custom

examples.en: Happy birthday! Here's a small gift.
examples.note: set greeting 축하해요 + casual gift-giving

entries.nuance: 생일 is 'birthday', Sino-Korean 生日 — 生 'birth/life' + 日 'day', literally 'birth-day'. The culturally loaded fact is that Koreans eat 미역국 (seaweed soup) on a birthday, because mothers traditionally ate it after giving birth. Register matters sharply here: for grandparents, bosses, or anyone you must honor, the polite word is the honorific 생신 (生辰), and the greeting upgrades to 생신 축하드립니다, not the casual 생일 축하해요 you'd say to a friend. The standard greeting is 생일 축하해요 / 생일 축하합니다, literally 'I celebrate (your) birthday' — note it is the verb 축하하다 plus the noun, not an adjective. Collocations: 생일 파티 'birthday party', 생일 선물 'birthday gift', 생일을 챙기다 'to make a fuss of someone's birthday'. Pitfall: don't say 생일 to or about an elder when respect is due — switch to 생신.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

noun + 이에요 predicate
공(公) 'official' + 휴일

examples.en: I rest at home on a day off.
examples.note: 에 marks the day; 쉬다 'rest'

entries.nuance: 휴일 is a non-working day — a day off or a holiday. It is Sino-Korean 休日, 休 'rest' + 日 'day', literally 'rest-day'. Watch the family of look-alikes built on 休: 휴일 'a day off (any non-work day)', 공휴일 (公休日) 'an official public holiday' marked red on the calendar, and 휴가 (休暇) 'leave/vacation you take from work', e.g. summer 여름휴가. The dividing line that trips English speakers: 휴일/공휴일 is a day that is officially free (a Sunday, 설날), whereas 휴가 is personal leave you request and spend, often traveling. So '연차 휴가' is paid leave, but New Year's Day is a 공휴일, not a 휴가. Collocations: 휴일을 보내다 'spend a day off', 황금연휴 'golden (long) holiday', 빨간 날 'a red day (holiday)' in casual speech. Pitfall: don't say 휴가 when you mean a calendar holiday everyone shares.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

entries.nuance: 새해 means 'the new year' — the turning of the year in general. It is a transparent native compound: 새 'new' + 해 'year/sun', so literally 'new year', and there is no hanja involved. Distinguish it from two neighbors: 설날 is specifically the Lunar New Year holiday (the day you eat 떡국 and bow), and 신정 (新正) vs 구정 (舊正) distinguish the Jan-1 solar New Year from the lunar one; 새해 is the broad notion of the year being new and covers the greeting season around both. The fixed greeting is 새해 복 많이 받으세요, literally 'receive much fortune in the new year' — crucially it ends in the verb 받으세요 'please receive'. Collocations: 새해 인사 'New Year greeting', 새해 결심 'New Year's resolution', 새해 첫날 'the first day of the year', 새해가 밝다 'a new year dawns'. Pitfall: 새해 복 많이 alone is half a sentence — keep 받으세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

examples.note: 설날에는 contrast topic; 모이다 'gather'

entries.nuance: 설날 is the Korean Lunar New Year (음력설), the biggest holiday of the year, when families gather, eat 떡국 'rice-cake soup' (and adding a year of age is tied to eating it), and the young perform 세배, a deep New-Year bow to elders, often receiving 세뱃돈 'New Year money'. 설날 is native Korean (설 'New Year' + 날 'day'); often shortened to just 설. Draw the line from 새해: 새해 is the abstract 'new year' and its greeting, while 설날 is the concrete holiday with its customs and days off (설날 연휴). It is also not 추석 — both are major family holidays, but 설날 is winter's New Year, 추석 is autumn's harvest. Collocations: 설날 연휴 'Seollal long weekend', 설 명절 'the Seollal festival', 차례 'ancestral rite', 한복 'traditional dress'. Pitfall: 'on Seollal' is 설날에, and don't equate it with the solar Jan-1 only.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

entries.shortExplanation: 추석 means "Chuseok" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "Chuseok" is 추석 (chuseok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 추석에 ("on Chuseok"). Watch the particle attached to 추석 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: holiday + time particle 에
연휴 'string of holidays'
noun + 이에요
noun + noun compound

examples.en: I eat songpyeon on Chuseok.
examples.note: 에 marks the day; 송편 = half-moon rice cakes

examples.en: I go down to my hometown for Chuseok.
examples.note: 고향에 내려가다 'go down to one's hometown'

examples.en: On Chuseok we make a wish at the full moon.
examples.note: 추석에는 contrast; 소원을 빌다 'make a wish'

entries.nuance: 추석 is the autumn harvest festival, often glossed as 'Korean Thanksgiving', held on the 15th of the 8th lunar month under the full harvest moon (보름달). The Thanksgiving translation is a loose analogy, not an identity: there is no turkey and the date is lunar. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

entries.shortExplanation: 그릇 means "bowl" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그릇 (geureut) = "bowl". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그릇을 씻다 ("to wash a bowl") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그릇, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Pairs with 씻다 (rinse with water), the default verb for dishes — not 닦다.
그릇 is a productive suffix: 밥그릇 (rice), 국그릇 (soup), 개밥그릇 (dog's bowl).
Use the location particle 에 plus 담다 (to put food in) — the natural pair for filling a bowl.
그릇 is the typical thing you 깨다 (break/smash); 깨진 그릇 = a broken bowl.

examples.en: The bowl is pretty.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + descriptive adjective 예쁘다.

examples.en: Please serve the rice into a bowl.
examples.note: Everyday request: location 에 + 담다, the verb for putting food in.

examples.ko: 설거지할 때 깨지기 쉬운 그릇은 따로 씻으세요.
examples.romanization: seolgeojihal ttae kkaejigi swiun geureuseun ttaro ssiseuseyo.
examples.en: When you do the dishes, wash fragile bowls separately.
examples.note: Real situation: 깨지기 쉽다 (easy to break) modifying 그릇 in a kitchen instruction.

entries.nuance: 그릇 is the broad native-Korean word for a vessel that holds food — most often the deeper, rounded bowl that rice, soup, or 반찬 sit in, but it also works as the generic cover term for 'dishes/dishware' (그릇을 닦다 = do the dishes). The dividing line you must feel is 그릇 vs 접시: 그릇 is deep and holds something pourable or piled, while 접시 is the flat plate you lay food onto. Note the everyday verb is 씻다 (rinse), not the English-driven 닦다 (wipe) — 닦다 is for wiping a surface dry, not washing dishes. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you serve food 그릇에 담다 (into the bowl, location 에), so saying 그릇을 담다 is wrong because 담다 needs the destination, not the food, marked. Common collocations: 그릇을 씻다, 그릇에 담다, 그릇을 깨다, 밥그릇.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 그릇을 닦아요 for washing dishes. 닦다 means to wipe (a table, a window) — washing dishes with water is 그릇을 씻어요 / 설거지를 해요.
Don't say 밥을 그릇을 담아요. The bowl is the destination, so it takes 에: 밥을 그릇에 담아요. Marking the bowl with 을 makes the sentence ungrammatical.
Don't reach for 보울 (a borrowed 'bowl'). Korean uses the native 그릇; the loanword sounds unnatural for a normal eating bowl.

entries.shortExplanation: 접시 means "plate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 접시 (jeopsi) means "plate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 접시에 담다 ("to plate / put onto a plate"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 접시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to plate / put onto a plate
usagePhrases.note: Location 에 + 담다; food lands ON a flat 접시, so 에 is required, never 를.
Flat dishes are counted with 장 (sheet-counter) as well as 개; 종이 한 장 uses the same counter.
앞 (front) + 접시 = the small plate set in front of each diner to take shared food onto.
치우다 (clear away) is the natural verb for taking dirty 접시 off the table after a meal.

examples.en: The plate is dirty.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject 이 + adjective 더럽다.

examples.en: I arranged the fruit nicely on the plate.
examples.note: Everyday: location 에 + 담다 with the adverb 예쁘게.

examples.ko: 손님이 오시니까 앞접시도 함께 놓아 주세요.
examples.romanization: sonnimi osinikka apjeopsido hamkke noa juseyo.
examples.en: Since guests are coming, please also set out individual plates.
examples.note: Real situation: hosting context introducing 앞접시 and honorific 오시다.

entries.nuance: 접시 is a flat, shallow plate — the dish you LAY food onto (fruit, grilled meat, a slice of cake) rather than pour into. The contrast to lock in is 접시 vs 그릇: shape decides it, not the food itself. A flat dish is 접시 even for soup-adjacent food, while anything deep and rounded is 그릇. A useful sub-word is 앞접시, the small personal plate each diner pulls shared dishes onto — a normal part of Korean table manners. Because food sits ON the surface, the particle is 접시에 담다 / 접시에 놓다 (location 에); the classic English-speaker error is 접시를 담다, treating the plate as the object. Note plates can be counted with 장 (the sheet-counter, reflecting their flatness) as well as the all-purpose 개. Habitual collocations: 접시에 담다, 접시를 치우다, 접시를 깨다, 앞접시.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 과일을 접시를 담아요. The plate is where the fruit goes, so use 에: 과일을 접시에 담아요.
Don't assume soup goes on a 접시. Liquid or piled food needs the deeper 그릇; a flat 접시 is for things you lay flat, like meat or fruit.
Don't always default to 개 when counting. Flat plates are often counted with 장 — 접시 두 장 — which sounds more natural to many speakers.

entries.shortExplanation: 컵 means "cup" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "cup" is 컵 (keop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 컵에 따르다 ("to pour into a cup"). Watch the particle attached to 컵 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Location 에 + 따르다 (pour); the liquid's destination is the cup, marked with 에.
컵 compounds freely: 종이컵 (paper), 머그컵 (mug), 텀블러 is separate but related.
When measuring a drink, the counter is 잔 (glass/cupful): 물 한 잔, 커피 두 잔.
헹구다 (rinse out) is the precise verb for quickly washing a drinking cup with water.

examples.en: The cup is clean.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 깨끗하다.

examples.en: Please pour water into the cup.
examples.note: Everyday request: destination 에 + 따르다 for pouring a drink.

examples.en: Since it's hot, I'll give it to you in a mug, not a paper cup.
examples.note: Real situation: contrasting 종이컵/머그컵 with 말고 (not ~ but) and honorific 드리다.

entries.nuance: 컵 is a loanword (from English 'cup') covering both cups and drinking glasses for any beverage — there is no everyday split between 'cup' and 'glass' the way English makes one; a glass tumbler and a coffee cup are both 컵 in normal speech, with 머그컵 (mug) and 종이컵 (paper cup) as specific compounds. Watch the difference between the OBJECT and the MEASURE: 컵 is the physical cup, but when you order or count a serving of a drink you switch to the counter 잔 — 커피 한 잔, not 커피 한 컵 in a café. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with pouring: you pour a drink 컵에 따르다 (into the cup, location 에), so 컵을 따르다 is wrong. Also use 따르다 (pour) rather than the English-shaped 붓다, which sounds like dumping a large amount. Frequent collocations: 컵에 따르다, 컵을 헹구다, 종이컵, 머그컵.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't order 커피 한 컵 in a café. Servings of drinks use the counter 잔: 커피 한 잔. 컵 names the object, not the portion.
Don't say 물을 컵을 따라요. The cup is the destination of the pour, so it takes 에: 물을 컵에 따라요.
Don't worry about 'cup vs glass.' Korean 컵 covers both; you don't need a separate word for a drinking glass in everyday speech.

entries.shortExplanation: 숟가락 means "spoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 숟가락 (sutgarak) = "spoon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 숟가락으로 뜨다 ("to scoop with a spoon") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 숟가락, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 뜨다 (scoop up); the spoon is the tool, so 으로 is required.
숟가락 + 젓가락 together = 수저, the standard table-setting pair Koreans lay out.

usagePhrases.en: to set down / lay out a spoon
usagePhrases.note: 놓다 = set the spoon on the table; idiomatically 숟가락을 놓다 can also mean 'finish eating.'
밥 + 숟가락; also used figuratively for a mouthful, as in 한 숟가락만 더.

examples.en: There's no spoon.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + existence verb 없다.

examples.en: I scoop the soup with a spoon and eat it.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 뜨다, linked to 먹다 with -서.

examples.ko: 밥 다 먹었으면 숟가락 놓고 잠깐 쉬자.
examples.romanization: bap da meogeosseumyeon sutgarang noko jamkkan swija.
examples.en: If you're done eating, put down your spoon and rest a bit.
examples.note: Real situation: casual 반말 with the idiom 숟가락(을) 놓다 = stop eating.

entries.nuance: 숟가락 is the deep-bowled metal spoon at the heart of a Korean table — Koreans eat rice and especially soup/stew with it, unlike many cultures that treat the spoon as secondary to the fork. Pair it with the verb 뜨다 (to scoop up a liquid or rice), the precise partner verb. Crucially, 숟가락 + 젓가락 combine into 수저, the everyday word for the whole utensil set you lay out — if someone says 수저 놓아 줘, they mean set out both. A spelling trap: it's 숟가락 with ㄷ (a historical 술 'spoon' + 가락), even though 젓가락 takes ㅅ — learners often wrongly write 숫가락. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you eat 숟가락으로 (with a spoon, instrument 으로), never 숟가락에. Watch the idiom 숟가락을 놓다 — literally 'put down the spoon,' it commonly means to finish a meal. Collocations: 숟가락으로 뜨다, 숟가락을 놓다, 수저, 밥숟가락.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 숫가락. The correct spelling is 숟가락 with ㄷ; only 젓가락 uses ㅅ. They differ on purpose.
Don't say 숟가락에 먹어요. The spoon is the instrument, so it takes 으로: 숟가락으로 먹어요.
Don't take 숟가락을 놓다 literally every time. Beyond 'set the spoon down,' it idiomatically means 'finish eating,' so context matters.

entries.shortExplanation: 젓가락 means "chopsticks" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 젓가락 (jeotgarak) means "chopsticks". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 젓가락으로 집다 ("to pick up with chopsticks"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 젓가락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 집다 (grasp/pick up) — the precise verb for what chopsticks do.
Noun + 질 (doing-an-action) = handling chopsticks; 젓가락질이 서툴다 = clumsy with chopsticks.
나무 (wood) + 젓가락; the throwaway kind from a 분식집, vs everyday metal ones.
Paired utensils take the counter 벌 (set); 한 짝 = just one stick of the pair.

examples.en: Chopsticks are hard.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 어렵다.

examples.en: I pick up side dishes with chopsticks and eat them.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 집다, chained to 먹다 with -서.

examples.ko: 젓가락질이 아직 서툴러서 면이 자꾸 미끄러져요.
examples.romanization: jeotgarakjiri ajik seotulleoseo myeoni jakku mikkeureojyeoyo.
examples.en: My chopstick skill is still clumsy, so the noodles keep slipping.
examples.note: Real situation: 젓가락질 + 서투르다 (르-irregular), explaining a genuine struggle.

entries.nuance: 젓가락 is chopsticks — and Korean chopsticks are distinctively flat, heavy METAL ones, harder for beginners than the rounded wooden chopsticks of Japan or China. The partner verb is 집다 (to grasp/pick up), the action chopsticks perform; for noodles 면을 집다 is natural. A high-value derived word is 젓가락질, 'the skill/act of using chopsticks' (the 질 suffix = doing an action), so 젓가락질이 서툴다 = to be clumsy with chopsticks. Remember 젓가락 takes ㅅ while its partner 숟가락 takes ㄷ — don't cross them. Together they form 수저, the utensil set. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: the particle is 젓가락으로 (instrument 으로), not 젓가락에; and because the word is already plural in meaning, you don't pluralize it — to count, use 벌 for a pair (한 벌) or 짝 for a single stick. Collocations: 젓가락으로 집다, 젓가락질, 나무젓가락, 젓가락 한 벌.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 젇가락 or 저가락. The standard spelling is 젓가락 with ㅅ; pair it correctly against 숟가락 (ㄷ).
Don't say 젓가락에 먹어요. Chopsticks are the instrument: 젓가락으로 먹어요.
Don't count chopsticks with 개 as if singular. A usable pair is 한 벌; a single stick is 한 짝 — 개 sounds off for paired utensils.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 찍다 (stab/spear) — the signature fork action for fruit or cake.
Loanword counted simply with 개/하나; 포크 하나 주세요 = please give me one fork.
In Western-dining contexts the knife is the loanword 나이프, paired with 포크 (vs native 칼).
일회용 (single-use) + 포크; the plastic kind handed out with takeout food.

examples.en: There's no fork.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + existence verb 없다.

examples.en: I spear the cake with a fork and eat it.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 찍다, the natural verb for forking cake.

examples.ko: 아이는 아직 젓가락이 서툴러서 포크로 먹는 게 편해요.
examples.romanization: aineun ajik jeotgaragi seotulleoseo pokeuro meongneun ge pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The child is still clumsy with chopsticks, so eating with a fork is easier.
examples.note: Real situation: contrasting 젓가락/포크 with the nominalizer -는 게.

entries.nuance: 포크 is a loanword (English 'fork') and in Korea is a SECONDARY, situational utensil — used for cake, fruit, salad, and Western food, while everyday rice and soup go with 숟가락 and 젓가락. Its natural partner verb is 찍다 (to stab/spear), as in 과일을 포크로 찍다; this 찍다 also means 'to stamp/take a photo,' so context disambiguates. In a Western place-setting the fork pairs with the loanword 나이프, whereas the all-purpose Korean kitchen knife is the native 칼 — so 포크와 나이프 (table setting) but 칼 (cooking). The English-speaker pitfall is, as with all tools, the particle: 포크로 먹다 (instrument 으로), never 포크에. Don't over-use 포크 — defaulting to a fork at a Korean meal of rice and 반찬 reads as foreign; reach for 젓가락 instead. Collocations: 포크로 찍다, 포크와 나이프, 일회용 포크, 포크 하나.

Don't say 포크에 먹어요. The fork is the instrument: 포크로 먹어요.
Don't pair 포크 with native 칼 in a table setting. Western place settings say 포크와 나이프; 칼 is the cooking knife.
Don't default to 포크 for a Korean rice meal. Rice and side dishes are eaten with 숟가락/젓가락; a fork there sounds foreign.

entries.shortExplanation: 칼 means "knife" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 칼 (kal) = "knife". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 칼로 썰다 ("to slice with a knife") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 칼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 썰다 (slice into pieces) — the core knife action in cooking.

usagePhrases.en: the knife cuts well / is sharp
usagePhrases.note: Idiom: 들다 here means 'cuts well'; 안 든다 = it's dull. Not the 들다 'to hold.'
과도 (果刀, fruit-knife) is the small knife for peeling fruit, a specific type of 칼.
갈다 (grind/sharpen) is the verb for putting an edge back on a dull blade.

examples.en: The knife is sharp.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 날카롭다 (ㅂ-irregular).

examples.en: I slice the vegetables thinly with a knife.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 썰다 with the adverb 얇게.

examples.ko: 이 칼은 잘 안 드니까 한번 갈아야겠어요.
examples.romanization: i kareun jal an deunikka hanbeon garayagesseoyo.
examples.en: This knife doesn't cut well, so I'd better sharpen it.
examples.note: Real situation: the idiom 안 들다 (dull) + resolve ending -아야겠다.

entries.nuance: 칼 is the native, all-purpose Korean word for a knife — above all the kitchen knife, but the SAME word covers any blade: a pocketknife, a sword, a box cutter, all 칼. So unlike English, you don't switch words by type; you specify with a modifier (부엌칼 kitchen, 과도 fruit knife, 맥가이버 칼 Swiss-army). Two idioms are essential: 칼이 잘 들다 means 'the knife cuts well / is sharp' — here 들다 is NOT 'to hold' but 'to cut/take effect,' so 칼이 안 들어요 = it's dull; and 칼을 갈다 = to sharpen. The partner cutting verbs are 썰다 (slice into pieces) and 자르다 (cut through). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 칼로 썰다 (instrument 으로), never 칼에. Note that in a Western table setting the table knife is the loanword 나이프, not 칼. Collocations: 칼로 썰다, 칼이 들다, 칼을 갈다, 과도.

Don't say 칼에 잘라요. The knife is the instrument: 칼로 잘라요 / 칼로 썰어요.
Don't read 칼이 잘 들어요 as 'the knife holds well.' Here 들다 means 'cuts well / is sharp'; the opposite is 칼이 안 들어요 (dull).
Don't expect a different word for sword vs kitchen knife. Korean uses 칼 for both and adds a modifier (부엌칼, 과도) when the type matters.

entries.shortExplanation: 냄비 means "pot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 냄비 (naembi) means "pot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 냄비에 끓이다 ("to boil/cook in a pot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 냄비 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Location 에 + 끓이다; the cooking happens IN the pot, so 에 marks it, not 를.
받침 (support) — the mat you rest a hot 냄비 on so it doesn't burn the table.
Note: a rice/pressure cooker is 솥, a different (heavier, lidded) vessel from 냄비.

usagePhrases.en: for food to scorch onto the pot
usagePhrases.note: 눌어붙다 = stick-and-burn to the bottom; a common kitchen mishap with 냄비.

examples.en: The pot is hot.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular).

examples.ko: 라면은 작은 냄비에 끓이면 더 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: ramyeoneun jageun naembie kkeurimyeon deo masisseoyo.
examples.en: Ramen tastes better cooked in a small pot.
examples.note: Everyday: location 에 + 끓이다 with the conditional -면.

examples.ko: 냄비가 뜨거우니까 꼭 받침 위에 올려놓으세요.
examples.romanization: naembiga tteugeounikka kkok batchim wie ollyeonoeuseyo.
examples.en: Since the pot is hot, be sure to set it on a trivet.
examples.note: Real situation: reason -니까 + 냄비 받침 in a safety instruction.

entries.nuance: 냄비 is a relatively light cooking pot or saucepan — the everyday vessel for boiling soup, simmering 찌개, or making ramen. Two contrasts matter: 냄비 vs 솥 — 솥 is the heavier, deep, lidded cauldron/cooker (think 가마솥, 압력솥 for rice), so don't call a rice cooker a 냄비; and 냄비 vs 프라이팬 — the flat frying pan is its own loanword. The partner verb is 끓이다 (to boil/cook by boiling), and food that scorches onto the bottom 눌어붙다. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you cook 냄비에 끓이다 (location 에) — saying 냄비를 끓이다 literally means 'boil the pot itself,' which is wrong; the pot is where it happens, the food is the object (라면을 냄비에 끓이다). Culturally note 냄비 근성 ('a pot temperament') — a set phrase for quick-to-boil, quick-to-cool enthusiasm. Collocations: 냄비에 끓이다, 냄비 받침, 냄비가 눌어붙다, 냄비 뚜껑.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 냄비를 끓여요 to mean 'cook in the pot.' That reads as boiling the pot itself; say 냄비에 (라면을) 끓여요 — food is the object, the pot the location.
Don't call a rice cooker a 냄비. A deep lidded cooker is 솥 (압력솥, 전기밥솥); 냄비 is the lighter open saucepan.
Don't use 냄비 for a flat frying pan. That's 프라이팬 — different shape, different word.
