entries.shortExplanation: 식탁 means "dining table" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "dining table" is 식탁 (siktak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식탁에서 먹다 ("to eat at the table"). Watch the particle attached to 식탁 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Action location 에서 + 먹다; an action happens AT the table, so 에서, not 에.
차리다 = lay out a meal/setting; 식탁을 차리다 / 밥상을 차리다 = prepare the table.
위 (top) pins location to the surface: 식탁 위에 그릇이 있다.
식탁 + 보 (cloth wrap) = the cloth spread over the dining table.

examples.en: The dining table is big.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 크다.

examples.en: The family sits around the table and eats.
examples.note: Everyday: 둘러앉다 (sit around) + the action verb 먹다.

examples.ko: 저녁 다 됐으니까 얼른 식탁 좀 차려 줄래?
examples.romanization: jeonyeok da dwaesseunikka eolleun siktak jom charyeo jullae?
examples.en: Dinner's ready, so could you set the table quickly?
examples.note: Real situation: casual request -어 줄래? with 식탁을 차리다.

entries.nuance: 식탁 is Sino-Korean, 食卓 — 食 'eat/food' + 卓 'table,' literally an 'eating-table,' i.e. the dining table. Distinguish it from 책상 (a desk, 冊床 'book-table' for study/work) and from 밥상, the lower, often portable meal-table (and by extension the whole spread of food) of more traditional dining — 밥상 emphasizes the laid meal, 식탁 the piece of furniture. The everyday verb is 식탁을 차리다 (set/lay the table). The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle: an ACTION done at the table uses 에서, so 식탁에서 밥을 먹다 — using 식탁에 먹다 is wrong because 에 marks static location/existence (식탁에 그릇이 있다), while 에서 marks where an action occurs. To pin something to the surface, add 위: 식탁 위에 놓다. Collocations: 식탁에서 먹다, 식탁을 차리다, 식탁 위, 식탁보.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 식탁에 밥을 먹어요. Eating is an action, so it needs 에서: 식탁에서 밥을 먹어요. Reserve 에 for existence: 식탁에 그릇이 있어요.
Don't confuse 식탁 with 책상. 식탁 (食卓) is for meals; 책상 (冊床) is the desk for studying or working.
Don't say 식탁을 만들어요 to mean 'set the table.' Use 차리다: 식탁을 차려요. 만들다 = build the furniture, not lay the meal.

entries.shortExplanation: 주방 means "kitchen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주방 (jubang) = "kitchen". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 주방에서 요리하다 ("to cook in the kitchen") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주방, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Action location 에서 + 요리하다; cooking is an action, so 에서, not 에.
용품 (goods/supplies) — 주방 용품 = the pots, knives, and tools of a kitchen.
Real-estate/café term for a kitchen open to the dining area; 주방 takes many such modifiers.
주방 + 장 (長, head) = the chef in charge of a restaurant kitchen.

examples.en: The kitchen is spacious.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 넓다.

examples.en: Mom is making dinner in the kitchen.
examples.note: Everyday: action location 에서 + honorific progressive -고 계시다.

examples.ko: 식당 주방은 위생이 생명이라 늘 깨끗하게 관리해요.
examples.romanization: sikdang jubangeun wisaengi saengmyeongira neul kkaekkeutage gwallihaeyo.
examples.en: A restaurant kitchen lives or dies by hygiene, so it's always kept clean.
examples.note: Real situation: 주방 in a professional sense with 위생/관리하다.

entries.nuance: 주방 is Sino-Korean, 廚房 — 廚 'kitchen' + 房 'room,' literally the 'kitchen room.' The register contrast you should feel is 주방 vs 부엌: both name the cooking room, but 주방 is the slightly more formal, modern, and PROFESSIONAL-leaning word (a restaurant kitchen, kitchenware ads, 주방장 head chef, an apartment's '오픈 주방'), while 부엌 is the warm, homey native word for the kitchen at home — many speakers use them interchangeably for a home kitchen, but you'd never say a restaurant's 부엌 in a business context. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: cooking is an action, so 주방에서 요리하다 (action location 에서), not 주방에 요리하다 — 에 is only for existence (주방에 냉장고가 있다). Useful derivations: 주방 용품 (kitchenware), 주방장 (head chef). Collocations: 주방에서 요리하다, 주방 용품, 오픈 주방, 주방장.

Don't say 주방에 요리해요. Cooking is an action, so use 에서: 주방에서 요리해요. Keep 에 for existence: 주방에 냉장고가 있어요.
Don't treat 주방 and 부엌 as fully identical. For a home kitchen either works, but a restaurant's cooking area is 주방, not 부엌, in formal/business use.
Don't write the hanja-based word as if native. 주방 (廚房) is Sino-Korean; if you want the cozy home word, that's the native 부엌.

entries.shortExplanation: 도마 means "cutting board" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 도마 (doma) means "cutting board". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도마 위에서 썰다 ("to cut on the cutting board"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to cut on the cutting board
usagePhrases.note: 위 + action location 에서; you cut ON TOP of the board, so 위에서, not bare 에.

usagePhrases.en: to wipe the board with a cloth
usagePhrases.note: Here 닦다 (wipe) is right — wiping the board's surface, vs 씻다 for rinsing it.
나무 (wood) vs 플라스틱 도마 (plastic); material modifiers are common with 도마.

usagePhrases.en: the sound of chopping (on the board)
usagePhrases.note: 도마 소리 evokes the rhythmic knock of cooking; a vivid everyday collocation.

examples.en: The cutting board is clean.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 깨끗하다.

examples.en: I slice the vegetables on the cutting board.
examples.note: Everyday: 도마 위에서 + 썰다, the standard chopping frame.

examples.ko: 고기랑 채소는 도마를 따로 써야 위생적이에요.
examples.romanization: gogirang chaesoneun domareul ttaro sseoya wisaengjeogieyo.
examples.en: It's more hygienic to use separate boards for meat and vegetables.
examples.note: Real situation: 따로 쓰다 (use separately) + 위생적이다 in a kitchen-safety tip.

entries.nuance: 도마 is the cutting board — the flat surface you set food on to chop with a 칼. There isn't a tricky near-synonym; the value is in the GRAMMAR and collocations. Because cutting happens on top of the board's surface, the natural frame is 도마 위에서 썰다 (위 'top' + action-location 에서) — bare 도마에 썰다 sounds incomplete, since 에 marks static existence, not where an action plays out. Note the two cleaning verbs split by sense: 도마를 씻다 = rinse it with water; 도마를 닦다 = wipe its surface — both valid, unlike with dishes where 닦다 was wrong. Korean kitchens commonly keep separate boards (고기용/채소용) for hygiene, so 도마를 따로 쓰다 is a natural phrase. Material modifiers abound: 나무 도마, 플라스틱 도마. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 위에서 and using 도마에, or marking the board as the object of 썰다. Collocations: 도마 위에서 썰다, 나무 도마, 도마를 씻다, 도마 소리.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 도마에 썰어요. Cutting happens on the surface, so use 도마 위에서 썰어요 — 위 + the action particle 에서.
Don't mark the board as the object of cutting: 도마를 썰어요 means 'cut the board.' The food is the object; the board is the place (도마 위에서).
Don't assume one cleaning verb. 도마를 씻다 = rinse with water, 도마를 닦다 = wipe the surface; choose by what you actually do.

structuredNuance.t: 도마 is the cutting board — the flat surface you set food on to chop with a 칼. There isn't a tricky near-synonym; the value is in the GRAMMAR and collocations. Note the two cleaning verbs split by sense: 도마를 씻다 = rinse it with water; 도마를 닦다 = wipe its surface — both valid, unlike with dishes where 닦다 was wrong. Korean kitchens commonly keep separate boards (고기용/채소용) for hygiene, so 도마를 따로 쓰다 is a natural phrase. Material modifiers abound: 나무 도마, 플라스틱 도마.

Because cutting happens on top of the board's surface, the natural frame is 도마 위에서 썰다 (위 'top' + action-location 에서) — bare 도마에 썰다 sounds incomplete, since 에 marks static existence, not where an action plays out. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 위에서 and using 도마에, or marking the board as the object of 썰다. Collocations: 도마 위에서 썰다, 나무 도마, 도마를 씻다, 도마 소리.

entries.shortExplanation: 국자 means "ladle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ladle" is 국자 (gukja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국자로 뜨다 ("to ladle/scoop with a ladle"). Watch the particle attached to 국자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 뜨다 (scoop up liquid) — the exact partner verb for a ladle.

usagePhrases.en: to dish out with a ladle
usagePhrases.note: 푸다 (scoop and serve out) is also natural: 국을 국자로 퍼서 담다.
The chain 뜨다/푸다 → 그릇에 담다 is how you serve soup with 국자.
Counted simply with 개/하나; 국자 하나 주세요 = please give me a ladle.

examples.en: Where's the ladle?
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + location question 어디 있다.

examples.en: I ladle the stew and serve it into a bowl.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 뜨다, chained to 담다 with -서.

examples.ko: 국이 모자라면 국자로 더 퍼서 드세요.
examples.romanization: gugi mojaramyeon gukjaro deo peoseo deuseyo.
examples.en: If there isn't enough soup, ladle out more and help yourself.
examples.note: Real situation: conditional -면 + 푸다 (ㅜ-irregular) with honorific 드시다.

entries.nuance: 국자 is the long-handled ladle for serving soup or stew — native Korean, built transparently from 국 'soup' + 자 (a tool suffix seen in 주걱 'rice paddle' family of kitchen tools). Its dedicated partner verbs are 뜨다 (to scoop up a liquid) and 푸다 (to scoop-and-serve out), so a full serving action is 국을 국자로 떠서/퍼서 그릇에 담다. Don't confuse 국자 with 주걱, the flat rice paddle for scooping cooked rice — different shape, different food. Note 푸다 is a ㅜ-irregular verb: its 요-form is 퍼요 (not 푸어요), a small trap when you describe ladling. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you scoop 국자로 (instrument 으로), never 국자에. Collocations: 국자로 뜨다, 국자로 푸다, 국을 국자로 담다, 국자 하나.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 국자에 떠요. The ladle is the instrument: 국자로 떠요.
Don't confuse 국자 (soup ladle) with 주걱 (flat rice paddle). They scoop different things and look different.
Don't write the verb 푸다 as 푸어요. It's ㅜ-irregular: the form is 퍼요 (국을 퍼요), so ladling out is 국자로 퍼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 비누 means "soap" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 비누 (binu) = "soap". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비누로 손을 씻어요. ("I wash my hands with soap.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 비누, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I wash my hands with soap.
usagePhrases.note: 비누 ends in a vowel, so the means particle is 로 (not 으로)
거품 = bubbles/foam; the lather you work up before rinsing

usagePhrases.en: The soap is all worn down.
usagePhrases.note: 닳다 = to wear away; the natural verb for a bar shrinking with use
a flat bar is counted with 장; a boxed/whole one can also be 개

examples.en: I put soap on my hands.
examples.note: simple: 묻히다 = to get/apply something onto a surface

examples.en: I wash my hands clean with soap.
examples.note: everyday: 로 marks the tool you wash WITH, and 을 marks the hands you wash

examples.ko: 이 비누는 향이 순해서 아기도 써요.
examples.romanization: i binuneun hyangi sunhaeseo agido sseoyo.
examples.en: This soap has a mild scent so even the baby uses it.
examples.note: real-situation: 향이 순하다 (the scent is mild) is the natural review phrase

entries.nuance: 비누 is solid BAR soap for hands or body, and it pairs almost automatically with 씻다 (wash) and 거품을 내다 (work up a lather). The key contrast for a shopper is form, not meaning: liquid body cleanser is 바디워시, hand pump soap is 핸드워시/물비누, and a facial cleanser is 클렌저 or 폼클렌징 — calling all of these 비누 sounds like you mean a hard bar. Note 비누 is a native Korean word with no hanja, so do not try to break it into characters. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you wash WITH soap, so it must be 비누로 손을 씻다 (instrument), never 비누를 씻다, which would literally mean you are washing the soap itself. Also, soap is uncountable in English but in Korean a bar is counted, usually 비누 한 장 or 한 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 비누를 손을 씻어요 — you can't double-mark with 를; the tool takes 로, so it's 비누로 손을 씻어요.
Don't call liquid pump soap 비누; that pictures a hard bar. Use 물비누 or 핸드워시 for the pump bottle.
Don't count it as 비누 한 개만 always — a flat bar is naturally 한 장; 개 sounds fine but less idiomatic for a thin bar.

entries.shortExplanation: 수건 means "towel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수건 (sugeon) means "towel". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수건으로 닦다 ("to dry/wipe off with a towel"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수건 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to dry/wipe off with a towel
usagePhrases.note: 수건 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so the means particle is 으로

usagePhrases.en: to wipe off the moisture with a towel
usagePhrases.note: 물기 = wetness/dampness; the standard thing a towel removes
flat cloth items are counted with 장

usagePhrases.en: to hang up the towel (to dry)
usagePhrases.note: 널다 = to hang laundry out; the verb for drying a wet towel

examples.en: The towel is wet.
examples.note: simple: 젖다 (to get wet) describes the state, with subject 이

examples.en: After a shower I dry off with a towel.
examples.note: everyday: 닦다 here means to dry by wiping, not just to clean a surface

examples.ko: 젖은 수건은 빨래통에 넣고 마른 수건을 꺼내요.
examples.romanization: jeojeun sugeoneun ppallaetonge neoko mareun sugeoneul kkeonaeyo.
examples.en: I put the wet towel in the laundry bin and take out a dry one.
examples.note: real-situation: contrasts 젖은 (wet) vs 마른 (dry) modifiers on the same noun

entries.nuance: 수건 is a cloth TOWEL for drying the body, hands, or hair, and its core collocation is 수건으로 닦다 — note 닦다 covers both 'wipe clean' and 'dry off', so 몸을 닦다 means dry yourself, not scrub. 수건 is Sino-Korean (手巾, 'hand-cloth'), which is why it feels slightly more everyday/native than the loanword 타월(towel); stores label big bath or beach towels 타월/배스타월, but in daily home talk 수건 covers everything. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first the particle — because 수건 ends in a consonant you must use 으로 (수건으로), not 로; second, don't reach for 말리다 here — you 수건으로 닦다 (wipe-dry with a towel), whereas 말리다 is for drying by air or a dryer (머리를 드라이기로 말리다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 수건로 — 수건 ends in a consonant, so it must be 수건으로.
Don't use 씻다 for drying off: 수건으로 씻어요 wrongly means 'wash with a towel.' Use 닦다 (수건으로 닦아요).
Don't count towels with 개 by reflex; a folded cloth towel is naturally 수건 한 장.

entries.shortExplanation: 칫솔 means "toothbrush" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "toothbrush" is 칫솔 (chitsol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 칫솔로 이를 닦다 ("to brush one's teeth with a toothbrush"). Watch the particle attached to 칫솔 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to brush one's teeth with a toothbrush
usagePhrases.note: 칫솔 ends in ㄹ, so the means particle is 로 (ㄹ behaves like a vowel here)
모(毛) = hair/bristle; 칫솔모가 부드럽다 = the bristles are soft
the routine action of swapping an old brush for a new one
counted with the general counter 개

examples.en: It's a new toothbrush.
examples.note: simple: 새 + noun = brand-new; here it just names the item

examples.en: Every morning I brush my teeth with a toothbrush.
examples.note: everyday: the full set phrase 칫솔로 이를 닦다; 마다 = every

examples.en: When the bristles splay out, you should swap in a new one.
examples.note: real-situation: 벌어지다 (to spread apart) is the natural verb for worn bristles

entries.nuance: 칫솔 names the BRUSH itself, and you must keep three related words apart: 칫솔 = the brush, 치약 = the paste, and 양치(질) = the whole act of brushing/rinsing the mouth. The standard sentence is 칫솔로 이를 닦다 ('brush teeth with a toothbrush'); 이를 닦다 literally is 'wipe the teeth,' since 닦다 is the all-purpose verb for cleaning by rubbing. 칫솔 is a hybrid: 치(齒) is the hanja for 'tooth' (the ㅅ is the 사이시옷 inserted between 치 and 솔) and 솔 is native Korean for 'brush.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle after a ㄹ-final noun: ㄹ patterns with vowels, so it's 칫솔로, NOT 칫솔으로 — a very common beginner slip. Also don't say 칫솔질하다 for the daily routine; Koreans say 양치하다 or 이를 닦다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 칫솔으로 — a noun ending in ㄹ takes plain 로, giving 칫솔로.
Don't confuse 칫솔 with 치약; the brush is 칫솔, the paste is 치약. 'Brush with toothbrush' = 칫솔로, 'brush with toothpaste' = 치약으로.
Don't say 칫솔을 닦아요 to mean brushing your teeth; that means cleaning the brush. Say 칫솔로 이를 닦아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 치약 means "toothpaste" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 치약 (chiyak) = "toothpaste". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 치약을 짜다 ("to squeeze out toothpaste") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 치약, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 짜다 = to squeeze; the standard verb for getting paste out of the tube

usagePhrases.en: to brush one's teeth with toothpaste
usagePhrases.note: 치약 ends in ㄱ (consonant), so the means particle is 으로
통 counts tubes/containers; a tube of paste is 한 통

usagePhrases.en: to put toothpaste on the toothbrush
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = to apply onto; the natural verb for loading the brush

examples.en: There's no toothpaste.
examples.note: simple: existence/availability with 없다, subject 이

examples.en: I squeeze just a little toothpaste onto the brush.
examples.note: everyday: 짜다 (squeeze) + 조금만 (just a little); 에 marks where it lands

examples.ko: 이 치약은 시린 이에 좋다고 해서 샀어요.
examples.romanization: i chiyageun sirin ie jotago haeseo sasseoyo.
examples.en: They say this toothpaste is good for sensitive teeth, so I bought it.
examples.note: real-situation: 시린 이 = teeth that ache from cold; a common drugstore reason

entries.nuance: 치약 is the PASTE you squeeze onto a 칫솔, and its signature verb is 짜다 (squeeze), not 누르다. Keep the trio straight: 칫솔 (brush) / 치약 (paste) / 양치 (the act). The hanja is transparent and worth remembering — 치(齒) 'tooth' + 약(藥) 'medicine/agent,' literally 'tooth medicine,' which is why it sounds natural to talk about a 치약 being '좋다' for some dental problem. It's counted by the tube: 치약 한 통 (or 한 개). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle pattern: 치약 ends in the consonant ㄱ, so the means form is 치약으로, never 치약로. A second trap is the verb — English 'put toothpaste on' becomes 치약을 묻히다/짜다, and 'brush with toothpaste' is 치약으로 양치하다; don't say 치약을 닦다, which would mean wiping the paste itself clean.

Don't write 치약로 — it ends in a consonant, so the correct means form is 치약으로.
Don't say 치약을 누르다 for getting paste out; the idiomatic verb is 짜다 (치약을 짜다).
Don't mix up 치약 and 칫솔: 치약 is paste, 칫솔 is the brush. You 칫솔에 치약을 짜다 — put paste ON the brush.

entries.shortExplanation: 샴푸 means "shampoo" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 샴푸 (syampu) means "shampoo". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 샴푸로 머리를 감다 ("to wash one's hair with shampoo"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 샴푸 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to wash one's hair with shampoo
usagePhrases.note: 샴푸 ends in a vowel → 로; and hair takes the special verb 감다, not 씻다
떨어지다 here = to run out/be used up (a stock idiom)
헹구다 = to rinse with water; what you do after lathering
the partner products applied after 샴푸 (note Korean 린스 = English conditioner)

examples.en: The shampoo smells nice.
examples.note: simple: 냄새가 좋다 = smells good; here a noun-phrase comment

examples.en: Every evening I wash my hair with shampoo.
examples.note: everyday: locks in 샴푸로 + 머리를 감다 together

examples.ko: 샴푸가 다 떨어져서 마트에서 새로 사 왔어요.
examples.romanization: syampuga da tteoreojyeoseo mateueseo saero sa wasseoyo.
examples.en: The shampoo ran out, so I went and bought a new one at the mart.
examples.note: real-situation: 다 떨어지다 (completely run out) + 사 오다 (go buy and bring back)

entries.nuance: 샴푸 is a loanword (from English 'shampoo'), so there's no hanja to parse, and it specifically means HAIR cleanser — its non-negotiable partner verb is 감다, the special Korean verb reserved for washing hair (and the head). The crucial contrast for a learner is exactly that verb: you 머리를 감다 (wash hair) but 몸을 씻다 (wash body) and 손을 씻다 (wash hands); using 씻다 with hair (머리를 씻다) sounds clearly off to natives. Watch a vocabulary false-friend too: Korean 린스 means CONDITIONER, not a 'rinse' — to rinse the suds out is the verb 헹구다. Because 샴푸 ends in a vowel, the means particle is 샴푸로 (not 으로). And note 떨어지다 doubles as 'fall' and 'run out,' so 샴푸가 떨어졌어요 means it's used up, not that it fell on the floor.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 머리를 씻다 for washing hair; Korean uses the dedicated verb 감다 — 머리를 감다.
Don't assume 린스 means a water rinse; in Korea 린스 = conditioner. To rinse off, use 헹구다.
Don't write 샴푸으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 샴푸로.

entries.shortExplanation: 거울 means "mirror" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.en: to look at oneself in the mirror
usagePhrases.note: 거울을 보다 = check your appearance, NOT stare at the glass

usagePhrases.en: to be reflected in the mirror
usagePhrases.note: 비치다 = to be reflected; 에 marks the surface showing the reflection
깨지다 = to break (for glass); a natural everyday event verb
전신(全身) = whole body; the tall mirror you check your outfit in

examples.en: The mirror is really big.
examples.note: simple: plain description with adjective 크다 and subject 이

examples.en: In the morning I look in the mirror and comb my hair.
examples.note: everyday: 거울을 보다 = look at yourself, then 머리를 빗다

examples.ko: 나가기 전에 전신 거울로 옷이 괜찮은지 봐요.
examples.romanization: nagagi jeone jeonsin geoullo osi gwaenchaneunji bwayo.
examples.en: Before going out, I check in the full-length mirror whether my outfit is okay.
examples.note: real-situation: 거울로 ... 보다 = use the mirror AS a tool to check; -는지 = whether

entries.nuance: 거울 is a MIRROR, a native Korean word with no hanja to decompose, and its meaning hinges on a particle distinction English speakers miss. 거울을 보다 (object 을) idiomatically means 'look at yourself / check your reflection,' the everyday morning-routine sense — it does not mean staring at the slab of glass. By contrast 거울로 보다 (means 로) means 'use the mirror as a tool to see something,' e.g. checking behind you or your outfit. So the same noun flips sense with 을 vs 로. The reflection itself appears with 에: 거울에 비치다 ('be reflected in the mirror'). The pitfall: don't translate English 'look in the mirror' as 거울 안을 보다 ('look inside the mirror') — that's unnatural; the fixed phrase is simply 거울을 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 거울 안을 봐요 for 'look in the mirror'; the natural fixed phrase is 거울을 봐요.
Don't confuse 거울을 보다 (check yourself) with 거울로 보다 (use it as a tool to see); the particle changes the meaning.
Don't use 보이다 when you mean 'I look at myself' — 거울을 보다 is active (you look); 거울에 비치다/보이다 is the reflection appearing.

entries.shortExplanation: 휴지 means "toilet paper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 휴지 (hyuji) = "toilet paper". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 휴지로 닦다 ("to wipe with tissue/toilet paper") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 휴지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 휴지 ends in a vowel → 로; 닦다 = to wipe clean
칸 = a partition/square; the perforated section you tear off

usagePhrases.en: to completely run out of toilet paper
usagePhrases.note: 떨어지다 = run out; the panic phrase in a stall
휴지 + 통(bin); the small trash can, often beside the toilet

examples.en: Please pass me some tissue.
examples.note: simple: 좀 softens the request; 주세요 = please give

examples.en: There's no toilet paper in the restroom.
examples.note: everyday: existence with 없다, subject 가; the stall-emergency line

examples.en: I wiped my mouth with a tissue and threw it in the trash.
examples.note: real-situation: shows 휴지 as table tissue + 휴지통 (bin) in one breath

entries.nuance: 휴지 is the hanja word 休紙 — literally '休 rest/discard + 紙 paper,' i.e. 'paper to be used up and tossed' — and in real life it covers BOTH rolled toilet paper and the flat table tissue you wipe your mouth with; context tells you which. The contrast to learn is 휴지 vs 티슈 vs 화장지: 티슈 is the soft pop-up/pocket pack you carry, 화장지 is the more formal/printed label for toilet roll, and 휴지 is the broad everyday word. Note 휴지통 ('휴지 + bin') means the wastebasket, so don't picture only paper. The pitfall is the particle and the verb: you wipe WITH it, so 휴지로 닦다 (means 로, vowel-final), never 휴지를 닦다 (which would mean wiping the paper itself). Also 휴지 is uncountable-feeling but a torn square is 한 칸 and a roll is 한 통/한 롤.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 휴지를 닦아요 to mean 'wipe with tissue'; the tool takes 로 — 휴지로 닦아요.
Don't equate 휴지 only with toilet paper; it also means table tissue. The pocket pack you carry is 티슈.
Don't write 휴지으로; 휴지 ends in a vowel, so it's 휴지로.

entries.shortExplanation: 세면대 means "sink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 세면대 (semyeondae) means "sink". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 세면대에서 세수하다 ("to wash one's face at the sink"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 세면대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to wash one's face at the sink
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place where the action happens; 세수 = washing the face
막히다 = to be blocked; water then 안 내려가다 (won't drain)

usagePhrases.en: to wipe down / clean the sink
usagePhrases.note: 닦다 here = clean the surface; 를 marks the object cleaned
수도꼭지 = faucet; the spout fitted on the basin

examples.en: The sink is dirty.
examples.note: simple: plain state with adjective 더럽다, subject 가

examples.en: In the morning I wash my face at the sink.
examples.note: everyday: 에서 = location of the activity; 세수하다 is the set verb

examples.en: The sink is clogged so the water won't drain.
examples.note: real-situation: 막히다 + 안 내려가다 is exactly how Koreans report a blockage

entries.nuance: 세면대 is specifically the BATHROOM wash basin where you clean your face and hands, and the sharpest contrast a learner needs is 세면대 vs 싱크대: 싱크대 is the KITCHEN sink for dishes, so the two are not interchangeable. The hanja is descriptive: 세(洗) 'wash' + 면(面) 'face' + 대(臺) 'stand/platform,' literally a 'face-washing stand' — which neatly explains why its home verb is 세수하다 (洗手, 'wash hands/face'). The natural particle is locational 에서 for the action done AT it (세면대에서 세수하다), and 가 when describing its state (세면대가 막히다). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly the 세면대/싱크대 mix-up, plus using 에 instead of 에서 — since washing is an action carried out there, it must be 세면대에서, not 세면대에.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't call the bathroom basin 싱크대; that's the kitchen sink. The bathroom one is 세면대.
Don't say 세면대에 세수해요; an action done at a place takes 에서 — 세면대에서 세수해요.
Don't use 씻다 for the face by itself; 'wash the face' has its own verb 세수하다 (or 얼굴을 씻다).

entries.shortExplanation: 욕조 means "bathtub" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bathtub" is 욕조 (yokjo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 욕조에 물을 받다 ("to fill the bathtub with water"). Watch the particle attached to 욕조 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to fill the bathtub with water
usagePhrases.note: 받다 here = to draw/collect water; 에 marks where the water goes

usagePhrases.en: to soak (one's body) in the tub
usagePhrases.note: 담그다 = to immerse/soak; the verb for sinking into hot water

usagePhrases.en: to take a bath in the tub
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = location of the activity; 목욕 = a soaking bath
반신(半身)욕 = soaking only the lower half; a common Korean tub habit

examples.en: The bathtub is big.
examples.note: simple: plain description with 크다, subject 가

examples.en: I fill the bathtub with warm water.
examples.note: everyday: 물을 받다 = draw water; 에 marks the destination

examples.ko: 따뜻한 욕조에 몸을 담그면 하루 피로가 풀려요.
examples.romanization: ttatteutan yokjoe momeul damgeumyeon haru piroga pullyeoyo.
examples.en: When I soak in the warm tub, the day's fatigue melts away.
examples.note: real-situation: 몸을 담그다 + 피로가 풀리다 (fatigue is relieved)

entries.nuance: 욕조 is the soaking BATHTUB, and the contrast that matters is the activity word: a long soak in the 욕조 is 목욕(하다), whereas a quick standing rinse is 샤워(하다) — many Korean apartments have only a 샤워 stall with no 욕조 at all, so this is a real cultural distinction, not just vocabulary. The hanja is 욕(浴) 'bathe' + 조(槽) 'tub/trough,' literally a 'bathing trough.' Its core verbs are 물을 받다 (fill it, lit. 'receive water'), 몸을 담그다 (soak/immerse), and the action takes locational 에서 (욕조에서 목욕하다). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping English 'fill the tub' onto the wrong verb — Korean says 욕조에 물을 받다, not 욕조를 채우다 in everyday speech — and confusing 목욕 (soak) with 샤워 (shower); 'take a bath' in a tub is 목욕하다, never 샤워하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 샤워하다 for soaking in a tub; a tub bath is 목욕하다. 샤워 is a standing rinse.
Don't say 욕조를 채워요 in casual speech; the idiomatic phrase is 욕조에 물을 받아요.
Don't use 에 for the action of bathing; 'bathe in the tub' takes 에서 — 욕조에서 목욕해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 빗 means "comb" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 빗 (bit) = "comb". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 빗으로 머리를 빗다 ("to comb one's hair with a comb") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빗, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to comb one's hair with a comb
usagePhrases.note: 빗 ends in a consonant → 으로; the noun 빗 and verb 빗다 share a root
the everyday action verb, even when using a brush
-어 넘기다 = to sweep/push back; styling direction
참빗 = closely set teeth; 얼레빗 = widely set teeth

examples.en: The comb is small.
examples.note: simple: plain description with 작다, subject 이

examples.en: In the morning I comb my hair with a comb.
examples.note: everyday: noun 빗 + verb 빗다 together; note the 으로 after a consonant

examples.ko: 엉킨 머리는 빗으로 천천히 빗어야 안 아파요.
examples.romanization: eongkin meorineun biseuro cheoncheonhi biseoya an apayo.
examples.en: Tangled hair you should comb slowly with a comb so it doesn't hurt.
examples.note: real-situation: 엉키다 (get tangled) + 천천히 빗다 (comb slowly)

entries.nuance: 빗 is a COMB, a native Korean word, and the neat thing learners must notice is that the noun 빗 and its action verb 빗다 (to comb) look and sound nearly identical — 빗으로 머리를 빗다 literally stacks 'comb-with hair comb,' which feels redundant in English but is perfectly natural in Korean. The near-synonym to separate is the tool type: 빗 is a flat comb, while a paddle/round HAIRBRUSH is 머리빗 or the loanword 브러시; in casual speech 빗 covers both, but a true brush is 브러시. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle after a consonant-final noun: it must be 빗으로, NOT 빗로 — and beginners often also drop the verb's irregularity, but 빗다 is regular (빗어요, 빗었어요). Don't say 머리를 솔질하다; the verb is simply 빗다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 빗로 — 빗 ends in a consonant, so the means form is 빗으로.
Don't say 머리를 솔질해요 for combing; the verb is 빗다 — 머리를 빗어요.
Don't confuse the noun 빗 (comb) with 빚 (debt) — same sound, different spelling and meaning.

entries.shortExplanation: 면도기 means "razor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 면도기 (myeondogi) means "razor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 면도기로 면도하다 ("to shave with a razor"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 면도기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 면도기 ends in a vowel → 로; 면도하다 = to shave (the action)
깎다 = to shave/trim; the verb pairing with 수염 (beard)
전기(電氣) + 면도기; the plug-in or rechargeable kind
날 = blade; the sharp part you replace when dull

examples.en: The razor is sharp.
examples.note: simple: state with 날카롭다, subject 가

examples.en: Every morning I shave with a razor.
examples.note: everyday: 면도기로 + 면도하다; 마다 = every

examples.en: The blade got dull, so I switched to a new razor.
examples.note: real-situation: 무뎌지다 (become blunt) + 새것으로 바꾸다

entries.nuance: 면도기 is the shaving TOOL, and the hanja explains its whole family: 면(面) 'face' + 도(刀) 'blade/knife' = 면도 ('face-blading' = shaving), plus 기(器) 'device' = the razor itself. So 면도하다 means 'to shave' and 면도기 is the instrument. The contrast to keep clear is 면도기 (the device) vs 면도 (the act) vs 면도날 (the replaceable blade), and an electric one is 전기면도기. Its partner verbs are 면도하다 (shave) and, with 수염 (beard), 깎다 (수염을 깎다, 'cut/shave the beard'). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle plus a doubled object: you shave WITH the razor, so it's 면도기로 면도하다 (means 로, vowel-final); never 면도기를 면도하다, which would absurdly mean 'shave the razor.' Also 면도기 ends in a vowel, so it's 로, not 으로.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 면도기를 면도해요; you shave WITH it — 면도기로 면도해요 (or 면도기로 수염을 깎아요).
Don't write 면도기으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 면도기로.
Don't confuse 면도기 (the razor) with 면도 (the act of shaving); 'do a shave' is 면도하다, the tool is 면도기.

entries.shortExplanation: 드라이기 means "hair dryer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "hair dryer" is 드라이기 (deuraigi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 드라이기로 머리를 말리다 ("to dry one's hair with a hair dryer"). Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to dry one's hair with a hair dryer
usagePhrases.note: 드라이기 ends in a vowel → 로; 말리다 = to dry (something), transitive

usagePhrases.en: to plug the dryer into the outlet
usagePhrases.note: 꽂다 = to plug/insert; 콘센트 = wall outlet
고장 나다 = to break/malfunction (for appliances)
드라이하다 = to blow-dry (and lightly style) with the dryer

examples.en: The hair dryer is hot.
examples.note: simple: state with 뜨겁다, subject 가

examples.en: After a shower I dry my hair with a hair dryer.
examples.note: everyday: 드라이기로 + 머리를 말리다; note transitive 말리다

examples.ko: 드라이기가 고장 나서 머리가 안 말랐어요.
examples.romanization: deuraigiga gojang naseo meoriga an mallasseoyo.
examples.en: The hair dryer broke, so my hair didn't dry.
examples.note: real-situation: contrasts transitive 말리다 (dry it) with intransitive 마르다 (it dries)

Its essential partner verb is 말리다 (to dry something) — and here lies the single biggest English-speaker pitfall: 말리다 is the TRANSITIVE 'dry X,' while 마르다 is the INTRANSITIVE 'X dries / becomes dry.' So 드라이기로 머리를 말리다 = 'I dry my hair with the dryer,' but 머리가 마르다 = 'the hair dries (on its own).' Mixing them (e.g. 머리를 마르다) is ungrammatical. Because 드라이기 ends in a vowel, the means particle is 로 (드라이기로), not 으로. Don't confuse this with 다리미 (clothes iron) — both involve heat, but 드라이기 is for hair.

Don't say 머리를 마르다; 마르다 is intransitive ('hair dries'). To dry it actively, use 말리다 — 머리를 말려요.
Don't write 드라이기으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 드라이기로.
Don't confuse 드라이기 (hair dryer) with 다리미 (clothes iron); both use heat but serve different jobs.

entries.nuance: 에어컨 is a clipped English loanword (air con(ditioner)) — Korean kept only the first half, which is why it looks shorter than the English source. For switching it on you have two natural verbs: 켜다 'turn on' (general, pairs with 끄다 'turn off') and the very colloquial 틀다 'put on/start running', which Koreans love for the AC, fan and radio (에어컨 좀 틀어 줘 'put the AC on for me'). Note 에어컨 is the cooling appliance; the heating equivalent is 난방 (or a 히터), and central building climate control is 냉난방, so do not stretch 에어컨 to mean 'heater'.

dynamic action 에서 (where the resting happens)

usagePhrases.en: I lie down on the sofa
usagePhrases.note: static location 에 with 눕다

examples.en: There is a sofa in the living room.

entries.nuance: 소파 is the English loanword 'sofa', the Western-style upholstered couch for a living room; the everyday native alternative for a long bench-seat is rarely used, so 소파 is the default word. The sharp grammar point is 에 vs 에서 with this noun: use 에 for the END-POINT of a positioning verb — 소파에 앉다 'sit (down) on the sofa', 소파에 눕다 'lie on the sofa' — but 에서 when an ongoing ACTIVITY happens there — 소파에서 쉬다/책을 읽다 'rest / read on the sofa'. English 'on the sofa' hides this split, so learners wrongly say 소파에서 앉아요. A common collocation is 편한 소파 'a comfy sofa'; a sofa-bed is a 소파베드.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 소파에서 앉아요 for sitting down. Positioning verbs like 앉다/눕다/서다 take 에 for the resulting location, not the action-location 에서 — say 소파에 앉아요.
Using 에 for an activity done on the sofa: 소파에 쉬어요 should be 소파에서 쉬어요, because resting is an ongoing action and its setting takes 에서.

Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + 있다

usagePhrases.en: I put it in the wardrobe
usagePhrases.note: destination 에 (into the wardrobe)

usagePhrases.en: I hang it in the wardrobe
usagePhrases.note: 걸다 'hang' (for clothes on a rod)

usagePhrases.en: I take it out of the wardrobe

entries.nuance: 옷장 combines native 옷 'clothes' + the bound morpheme -장 (from the hanja 欌, 'wooden cabinet/closet'), so it is a clothes-cabinet — the same -장 appears in 책장 'bookshelf' and 찬장 'cupboard'. The near-synonyms to separate: 옷장 is the freestanding wardrobe/closet for clothes; 서랍장 is a chest of drawers; 붙박이장 is a built-in closet; and the small bedside one is a 협탁. Verbs split by how the clothes sit: 넣다 'put in' for folded items, 걸다 'hang' for things on hangers, and 꺼내다 'take out'. The particle pitfall is the same IN/OUT contrast as the fridge: into the wardrobe is 에 (옷장에 넣다), out of it is 에서 (옷장에서 꺼내다).

Saying 옷장에서 옷을 넣어요 for storing clothes. Putting clothes INTO the wardrobe needs the destination 에, while 에서 means 'from' — say 옷장에 옷을 넣어요.
Using 옷장 for a chest of drawers. A drawer unit is 서랍장; reserve 옷장 for the hanging/folding wardrobe.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 서랍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 + 열다 (you do open a drawer)
object 을 + 닫다, opposite of 열다

usagePhrases.en: I put it in the drawer
usagePhrases.note: destination 에 (into the drawer)
relational noun 안 'inside' + 에

examples.en: There are socks in the drawer.
examples.note: simple: 에 location + 있다

examples.en: I opened the drawer and took out scissors.
examples.note: everyday: -아서 'open and then' sequential + 꺼내다

examples.ko: 서랍이 안 열려요. 뭔가 걸린 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: seorabi an yeollyeoyo. mwonga geollin geot gatayo.
examples.en: The drawer won't open. Something seems to be stuck.
examples.note: real-situation: 안 열리다 'won't open' (passive) + 걸리다 'be caught'

entries.nuance: 서랍 is a native Korean word (no hanja) for a single sliding drawer; a piece of furniture made of several stacked drawers is a 서랍장 'chest of drawers'. Unlike powered appliances, a drawer is genuinely opened and closed, so it correctly takes 열다 'open' / 닫다 'close' — the contrast to notice is 열다 (you actively open it) versus the passive 열리다 'be/get opened' used when it won't budge (서랍이 안 열려요 'the drawer won't open'). As the object you act on, 서랍 takes 을/를 (서랍을 열다), but as a destination it takes 에 (서랍에 넣다). A handy collocation is 맨 위 서랍 'the top drawer' / 맨 아래 서랍 'the bottom drawer'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 서랍이 열어요 when you open it. The drawer is the object you open, so it takes 을/를 — say 서랍을 열어요. (서랍이 안 열려요 is different: there the passive 열리다 takes 이/가.)
Saying 서랍에서 양말을 넣어요 for putting socks in. Into the drawer is the destination 에; 에서 means 'from' — say 서랍에 양말을 넣어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 커튼 means "curtain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 커튼 (keoteun) means "curtain". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 커튼을 쳐요 ("I draw the curtains"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 커튼 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: fixed verb 치다 'draw across', object 을
걷다 'gather/pull aside' (open them)
subject 이 + 있다
modifier 암막 'light-blocking'

examples.en: There is a curtain on the window.
examples.note: simple: 에 place + 있다

examples.en: The sunlight was too strong so I drew the curtains.
examples.note: everyday: 세다 'be strong' + -아서 reason, past

examples.ko: 자기 전에 커튼을 치고 불을 꺼요.
examples.romanization: jagi jeone keoteuneul chigo bureul kkeoyo.
examples.en: Before sleeping I draw the curtains and turn off the light.
examples.note: real-situation: -기 전에 'before' + 고 listing two actions

entries.nuance: 커튼 is the English loanword 'curtain', the fabric window cover. The verb pitfall is severe: to close/draw curtains across a window the fixed verb is 치다 (커튼을 치다 'draw the curtains'), and to open them you 걷다 'gather aside' (커튼을 걷다) — note 치다 here means 'spread/draw across', the same 치다 as in 텐트를 치다 'pitch a tent', NOT 치다 'hit'. Do not say 커튼을 해요 'do the curtain', which is incomplete, and be careful that 열다/닫다 'open/close' sound less idiomatic than 걷다/치다 for curtains specifically. Distinguish 커튼 (cloth, on a window/stage) from 블라인드 'blinds' (the slatted kind): a thick light-blocking curtain is an 암막 커튼.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 커튼을 해요 to draw them. 하다 doesn't collocate; the set verb is 치다 — say 커튼을 쳐요 to close them and 커튼을 걷어요 to open them.
Confusing 커튼 with 블라인드. Fabric drapes are 커튼; the horizontal/vertical slat type is 블라인드.

entries.explanation: "bookshelf" is 책장 (chaekjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 책장이 있어요 ("there is a bookshelf"). Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + 있다

usagePhrases.en: I shelve it on the bookshelf
usagePhrases.note: 꽂다 'insert upright' (slot a book in), destination 에

usagePhrases.en: I pull it off the shelf
usagePhrases.note: source 에서 + 빼다 'pull out'
정리하다 'organize', object 을

examples.en: There is a bookshelf in the room.
examples.note: simple: 에 place + 있다

examples.en: I shelve the books I've finished on the bookcase.
examples.note: everyday: 다 읽다 'finish reading' modifier + 꽂다

examples.ko: 책장에 책이 너무 많아서 한 줄 더 쌓았어요.
examples.romanization: chaekjange chaegi neomu manaseo han jul deo ssaasseoyo.
examples.en: There were too many books on the shelf so I stacked another row.
examples.note: real-situation: -아서 reason + 쌓다 'pile up'

entries.nuance: 책장 combines 책 (冊 'book') + -장 (欌 'cabinet/case'), literally a book-cabinet, the same -장 as in 옷장 'wardrobe'. Watch a tricky homograph: 책장 also means 'a page/leaf of a book' (책장을 넘기다 'turn the page'), so context decides between 'bookshelf' and 'page'. The signature verb is 꽂다 'to slot/stand upright' for putting a book in (책을 책장에 꽂다) and 빼다/꺼내다 to take it out — 꽂다 captures sliding the spine into the row, far more natural than 넣다 here. Near-synonym: many people also say 책꽂이 (책+꽂이, from 꽂다) for a bookshelf, often a smaller open rack, whereas 책장 tends to be the larger cabinet-style unit. Into the shelf is 에, off the shelf is 에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 책장에서 책을 꽂아요 for shelving a book. Slotting a book INTO the shelf takes the destination 에; 에서 means 'from' — say 책장에 책을 꽂아요.
Using 넣다 for shelving books. 넣다 'put in' works for drawers, but standing a book upright on a shelf is 꽂다 — say 책을 꽂아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 과목 means "subject" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 과목 (gwamok) = "subject". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과목을 좋아해요 ("like a subject") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과목, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 좋아하다 takes the object marker 을/를, not 이/가
the verb 좋아하다 turns into the modifier 좋아하는 placed before the noun
with 많다 the noun takes the subject marker 이, never 을
두 Sino-Korean nouns stack bare with no particle between them

examples.en: I choose a subject.
examples.note: simple 를 + verb: 과목 is the thing you pick

examples.en: My favorite subject is music.
examples.note: 좋아하는 modifies 과목; 은 marks it as the topic of the sentence

examples.ko: 이번 학기에는 과목이 너무 많아서 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon hakgieneun gwamogi neomu manaseo himdeureoyo.
examples.en: This term there are so many subjects that it is hard.
examples.note: real complaint: 많아서 (so many, therefore) links the cause to 힘들다

entries.nuance: 과목 is a school subject as a field of study — math, science, music — the label on a curriculum, written 科目 (科 'branch/category' + 目 'item'), literally a 'category item'. Do not confuse it with 수업, which is the actual class period or lesson you sit through: you 'like a 과목' (the topic) but you 'have a 수업 at 3 o'clock' (the session). It also differs from 전공, the single 'major' you commit to at university — 과목 is any one of many courses. With descriptive adjectives like 많다 or 어렵다 it must take 이/가 (과목이 어려워요), but with 좋아하다/배우다 it takes 을/를; the English-speaker trap is forcing 'I like science' into 과목을 좋아하다 + a separate noun, when Koreans just name the subject directly (음악을 좋아해요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 과목을 많아요 by copying English 'I have many subjects' — 많다 is descriptive, so the subject takes 이: 과목이 많아요.
Using 과목 for the class hour, e.g. 과목이 세 시예요; the timetable slot is 수업, so say 수업이 세 시에 있어요.
Translating 'my major is...' as 제 과목은...; a university major is 전공, so it should be 제 전공은....

entries.shortExplanation: 수학 means "math" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수학 (suhak) means "math". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수학이 어려워요 ("math is hard"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수학 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 어렵다 is descriptive, so 수학 takes the subject marker 이
배우다 (to learn) takes the object marker 을
수학 + 시간 stack bare to mean the math lesson slot
잘하다 (do well) takes 을; this is the set phrase for a skill

examples.en: There is a lot of math homework.
examples.note: simple: 수학 modifies 숙제, and 많다 takes 이/가

examples.en: We learn math at school.
examples.note: 를 marks what we learn; 에서 marks the place

examples.ko: 저는 수학을 잘 못해서 학원에 다녀요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun suhageul jal motaeseo hagwone danyeoyo.
examples.en: I'm not good at math so I go to an academy.
examples.note: real life: 잘 못하다 = 'not good at', 못해서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 수학 is the school subject mathematics, written 數學 (數 'number' + 學 'study') — literally the 'study of numbers'. The 學 ending is the standard Sino-Korean tag for an academic discipline, the same 학 in 과학, 역사학, 의학, so once you know it you can read whole subject names. Note the contrast between 수학 (the abstract discipline) and 산수, the simple 'arithmetic' little children do — adults studying equations always say 수학. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is the particle on the adjective: 'math is hard for me' feels like math is the object, but 어렵다/쉽다 are descriptive verbs, so math is the grammatical subject and takes 이 — 수학이 어려워요, never 수학을 어려워요. To express skill, use the fixed 수학을 잘하다/못하다 with 을, where the verb (not the adjective) governs the object marker.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수학을 어려워요 because English makes math the object; 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 수학이 어려워요.
Using 산수 (arithmetic) for the secondary-school subject; once it involves algebra say 수학.
Dropping 잘 and saying 수학을 해요 for 'I'm good at math'; you need 수학을 잘해요 to convey skill.

entries.shortExplanation: 과학 means "science" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "science" is 과학 (gwahak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 과학이 재미있어요 ("science is fun"). Watch the particle attached to 과학 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 재미있다 is descriptive, so 과학 takes 이
공부하다 takes the object marker 을
과학 modifies 선생님 with no particle between
과학 + 실험 stack to name the lab activity

examples.en: Science is fun.
examples.note: simple descriptive sentence: 이 marks 과학, 재미있다 follows

examples.en: We did an experiment in science class today.
examples.note: 과학 시간 = the lesson; 실험을 하다 is the set phrase

examples.ko: 저는 커서 과학을 더 공부하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun keoseo gwahageul deo gongbuhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: When I grow up I want to study science more.
examples.note: real goal: 커서 'having grown up', 고 싶다 expresses the wish

entries.nuance: 과학 is the school subject and the broad field of science, written 科學 (科 'branch/discipline' + 學 'study') — the 'study of disciplines', i.e. systematic knowledge. The same 과 appears in 과목 (subject) and 학과 (academic department), so the words cluster naturally. Keep 과학 (the field) separate from 과목 (any subject in general) — science is one 과목 among many; and from 기술, the 'technology/practical-skills' subject sometimes paired with it. usagePhrases.note: 배우다 takes the object marker 를
길다 is descriptive, so 역사 takes 가
country name 한국 modifies 역사 with no particle
좋아하다 takes the object marker 를

examples.en: I like history.
examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 를

examples.en: Korean history is very long.
examples.note: 한국 역사 is the topic (는); 길다 describes it

examples.ko: 역사 시험 때문에 어젯밤에 늦게까지 공부했어요.
examples.romanization: yeoksa siheom ttaemune eojetbame neutgekkaji gongbuhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Because of the history exam I studied late last night.
examples.note: real life: 때문에 = 'because of', 늦게까지 = 'until late'

Adding 의 in 한국의 역사 by reflex; natural everyday Korean stacks them bare as 한국 역사.

entries.shortExplanation: 미술 means "art class" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

미술 + 시간 names the art lesson slot
미술 modifies 선생님 with no particle
좋아하다 takes the object marker 을

examples.en: I like art (class).
examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 을

examples.en: We draw pictures in art class.
examples.note: 그림을 그리다 is the fixed verb-noun pair for drawing

examples.ko: 미술 시간에 만든 작품을 교실에 걸었어요.
examples.romanization: misul sigane mandeun jakpumeul gyosire georeosseoyo.
examples.en: We hung the work we made in art class on the wall.
examples.note: real life: 만든 modifies 작품, 걸다 = 'to hang'

entries.nuance: 미술 is the school subject of visual art — drawing, painting, making things — written 美術 (美 'beauty' + 術 'art/technique, skill'), literally the 'technique of beauty'. That same 술 'technique' appears in 기술 (technology) and 예술 (the arts), which helps you read related words. Crucially, 미술 is the subject/field, while 그림 is a concrete 'picture/drawing' you produce, and 예술 is 'the arts' in the grand sense (music, dance, literature too); a child does 미술 in school but creates a 그림. Note the set collocation 그림을 그리다 ('draw a picture'), where the noun and verb share the root 그리- and must appear together. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 미술을 그리다 ('draw art') — you draw a 그림, and you 'learn/like' 미술 (미술을 배우다/좋아하다).

Using 미술 to mean a single picture; one drawing is 그림, while 미술 is the whole subject.
Confusing 미술 with 예술; 예술 is 'the arts' broadly (incl. music/dance), 미술 is specifically visual art.

체육 + 시간 names the gym-class slot
있다 (to exist) takes the subject marker 이
체육 + 복 (clothes) compound for gym clothes

examples.en: I like PE.
examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 을

examples.en: We played soccer in PE.
examples.note: 체육 시간 = the lesson; 축구를 하다 = play soccer

examples.ko: 내일 체육 시간에는 체육복을 꼭 가져와야 해요.
examples.romanization: naeil cheyuk siganeneun cheyukbogeul kkok gajyeowaya haeyo.
examples.en: Tomorrow for PE you must bring your gym clothes.
examples.note: real life: 가져오다 = 'bring', 아/어야 하다 = 'must'

entries.nuance: 체육 is physical education, the school subject of exercise and sport, written 體育 (體 'body' + 育 'to raise, nurture'), literally 'raising/educating the body' — a neat mirror of 교육 (敎育, 'teaching-education'). Keep 체육 (the curriculum subject) distinct from 운동, the everyday word for 'exercise / a workout / sports' in general: you have a 체육 class at school but you go 운동(을) 하다 at the gym on weekends. The compound 체육복 ('PE + clothes') is the required gym uniform, and the venue is the 체육관 (gymnasium). With 있다 the noun takes 이/가 (체육 시간이 있어요), but with 좋아하다 it takes 을/를. Saying 체육을 있어요 for 'there's PE'; 있다 needs the subject marker: 체육 시간이 있어요.
Translating 'gym clothes' word-by-word; the fixed compound is 체육복, not 체육 옷.

지리 + 시간 names the geography lesson slot
country name 한국 modifies 지리 bare
공부하다 takes the object marker 를

examples.en: I learn geography.
examples.note: simple: 배우다 needs the object marker 를

examples.en: In geography we looked at a world map.
examples.note: note the near-twins: 지리 (the subject) vs 지도 (the map)

examples.ko: 저는 한국 지리는 잘 아는데 세계 지리는 어려워요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hanguk jirineun jal aneunde segye jirineun eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: I know Korean geography well but world geography is hard.
examples.note: real life: 는데 contrasts the two halves

entries.nuance: 지리 is geography, the subject about the earth's land, places, and features, written 地理 (地 'earth/ground' + 理 'principle, pattern'), literally 'the patterns of the land'. The 地 'earth' element ties it to 지도 (地圖, 'earth-map'), 지구 (地球, 'earth-globe'), and 지진 (地震, 'earth-quake'), so the cluster is learnable as a family. The trap pair is 지리 vs 지도: 지리 is the field of study (the knowledge), while 지도 is a physical map you hold or look at — in 지리 class you study a 지도. As a modifier, region names stack bare: 한국 지리, 세계 지리. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping in 지도 for the subject (지도를 배워요, 'learn the map'), or adding 의 (한국의 지리) where bare stacking is more natural.

Adding 의 as in 한국의 지리 by reflex; natural Korean stacks it bare: 한국 지리.
Saying 지리를 어려워요; 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 지리가 어려워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 성적 means "grades" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 성적 (seongjeok) means "grades". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성적이 좋아요 ("grades are good"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 성적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다 is descriptive, so 성적 takes 이
나오다 (come out) takes the subject marker 이
받다 (receive) takes the object marker 을
오르다 (rise) takes the subject marker 이

examples.en: My grades are good.
examples.note: simple descriptive: 좋다 takes the subject marker 이

examples.en: The grades come out next week.
examples.note: 성적이 나오다 = results are released/posted

examples.ko: 이번에 성적이 많이 올라서 부모님이 정말 기뻐하셨어요.
examples.romanization: ibeone seongjeogi mani ollaseo bumonimi jeongmal gippeohasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My grades went up a lot this time so my parents were really pleased.
examples.note: real life: 올라서 gives the reason; 기뻐하시다 (honorific) for parents

entries.nuance: 성적 means academic grades, marks, or results, written 成績 (成 'to accomplish, achieve' + 績 'achievement, merit'), literally 'accomplished achievements' — the outcome of your effort. Distinguish it from 점수, a single numeric 'score' on one test (시험 점수 90점), and from 시험, the 'exam' itself: you take a 시험, get a 점수 on it, and your overall 성적 reflects the term. Note the directional verbs that pair with it: 성적이 나오다 (results 'come out'/are released), 성적을 받다 (you 'receive' them), 성적이 오르다/떨어지다 (they rise/fall). The English-speaker pitfall is using 시험 where you mean the resulting grade ('my exam was good' → say 성적이 좋아요), and choosing the wrong particle: with descriptive 좋다 or motion 나오다/오르다 it's 이/가, only with 받다 is it 을/를.

Saying 시험이 좋아요 to mean 'my grades are good'; 시험 is the exam, the result is 성적, so say 성적이 좋아요.
Saying 성적을 좋아요 by treating grades as an object; 좋다 is descriptive, so use 성적이 좋아요.
Using 점수 for the whole term's standing; 점수 is one test's score, the cumulative record is 성적.

entries.shortExplanation: 학년 means "school year" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "school year" is 학년 (hangnyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 몇 학년이에요 ("what grade are you in"). Watch the particle attached to 학년 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

Sino-Korean number 일 + 학년 (note: 일 not 한)
올라가다 (go up) takes the subject marker 이
같은 (same) modifies 학년 directly

examples.en: I'm in first grade.
examples.note: Sino number 일 + 학년; 이에요 states the fact

examples.en: What grade is your sibling in now?
examples.note: 몇 학년 = 'which grade', the standard question

examples.ko: 내년에 삼 학년이 되면 공부가 더 어려워질 거예요.
examples.romanization: naenyeone sam hangnyeoni doemyeon gongbuga deo eoryeowojil geoyeyo.
examples.en: When I become a third-grader next year, studying will get harder.
examples.note: real life: 이 되면 = 'when (one) becomes', 어려워지다 = 'get harder'

entries.nuance: 학년 means a school grade or year level (1st year, 2nd year), written 學年 (學 'study' + 年 'year'), literally 'study-year'. Two things trip up English speakers. First, 학년 always counts with SINO-Korean numbers — 일 학년, 이 학년, 삼 학년 — never the native set (not 한 학년 for 'first grade'; 한 학년 means 'one grade-level' as in 한 학년 위, 'one year above'). Second, keep 학년 (the grade/year you're in) separate from 학교 (the school building/institution) and from 학기 (學期, the 'semester/term' within a year): you're in 이 학년 at your 학교 during the spring 학기. Confusing 학년 with 학기; the year level is 학년, but a semester is 학기 (e.g. 이번 학기).
Asking 무슨 학년이에요?; the natural question word for a number is 몇, so say 몇 학년이에요?

entries.shortExplanation: 전공 means "major" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전공 (jeongong) = "major". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전공이 뭐예요 ("what is your major") shows how it actually behaves. examples.note: the everyday question to a university student

entries.nuance: 전공 is your academic major — the single specialized field you concentrate on at university — written 專攻 (專 'exclusive, sole' + 攻 'to attack, devote effort to'), literally 'to devote oneself exclusively', i.e. to specialize. It can also act as a verb with 하다: 한국어를 전공하다 ('to major in Korean'). The key contrast is 전공 vs 과목: a 과목 is any one of the many courses on your timetable, whereas 전공 is the one field you commit to — you take many 과목 but have one 전공. It also differs from 학과, the 'academic department' that houses the major. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a major 과목 (제 과목은..., wrong) and forgetting that with the verb form the field takes 을/를: not 한국어 전공해요 but 한국어를 전공해요; as a plain noun, though, 전공이 뭐예요 uses 이/가.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 제 과목은 한국어예요 for 'my major is Korean'; a university major is 전공, so use 제 전공은 한국어예요.
Saying 한국어 전공해요 without a particle; the verb form needs 를: 한국어를 전공해요.
Confusing 전공 with 학과; 전공 is the field you study, 학과 is the department, e.g. 한국어학과.

entries.shortExplanation: 학원 means "private academy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 학원 (hagwon) means "private academy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 학원에 다녀요 ("attend an academy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 학원 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 다니다 (commute/attend) takes the destination marker 에
끝나다 (end) takes the subject marker 이
subject name 영어 modifies 학원 bare
끝나다 + 고 = 'after it ends', then do the next thing

examples.en: I go to an English academy.
examples.note: 학원에 다니다 = attend regularly; 에 marks where you go

examples.en: The academy lets out at nine.
examples.note: 끝나다 takes 이/가; 에 marks the clock time

examples.ko: 학교 끝나고 바로 학원에 가야 해서 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: hakgyo kkeunnago baro hagwone gaya haeseo neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: I have to go straight to the academy after school so I'm exhausted.
examples.note: real life: a very Korean routine; 가야 해서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 학원 is a private after-school academy (cram school) where students pay for extra lessons — English, math, piano, taekwondo — written 學院 (學 'study' + 院 'institution, hall'). The 院 'institution' element links it to 병원 (病院 hospital), 대학원 (大學院 graduate school), and 미용원/미장원, so the family is learnable. Sharply distinguish 학원 (a supplementary private institute) from 학교 (學校, the regular public/formal school) and from 대학원 (graduate school) — a child attends 학교 by day and 학원 in the evening. The verb of choice is 다니다, which implies habitual commuting/membership, with the 에 particle: 학원에 다니다 ('attend an academy regularly'), not the one-off 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 학교 for any place of learning, or marking the destination with 를 (학원를 다녀요, wrong) instead of 에.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a cram school 학교; the formal school is 학교, the private institute is 학원.
Saying 학원을 다녀요; the verb 다니다 takes the 에 particle for the place: 학원에 다녀요.
Using 가다 for habitual attendance; for ongoing enrollment Koreans say 다니다, e.g. 학원에 다녀요.

entries.shortExplanation: 유학 means "studying abroad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "studying abroad" is 유학 (yuhak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 유학을 가요 ("go abroad to study"). Watch the particle attached to 유학 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 유학(을) 가다 is the set phrase; 가다 = go there
고 싶다 attaches to 가다 to express the wish
유학 + 생활 names the study-abroad lifestyle
유학(을) 오다 = come (here) to study, from the host's view

examples.en: I'm going to Japan to study abroad.
examples.note: 으로 marks the direction; 유학(을) 가다 is the fixed phrase

examples.en: My older sister went to America to study abroad.
examples.note: past 갔어요; the destination takes 으로/로

examples.ko: 몇 년 동안 유학을 다녀와서 한국어가 정말 유창해요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon dongan yuhageul danyeowaseo hangugeoga jeongmal yuchanghaeyo.
examples.en: Having spent a few years studying abroad, her Korean is really fluent.
examples.note: real life: 다녀오다 = 'go and come back', 유창하다 = fluent

entries.nuance: 유학 means going abroad to study, usually for a degree or a long course, written 留學 (留 'to stay, remain' + 學 'study'), literally 'to remain (somewhere) and study' — note the 留 'stay', which signals it's a sustained stay, not a quick visit. That 留 distinguishes it from 여행 (旅行 'travel'), a trip for leisure: you go on 여행 for a week but go on 유학 for years. It pairs with directional verbs and the destination particle 으로/로: 유학을 가다 (go away to study), 유학을 오다 (come to study, from the host country's angle), 유학을 다녀오다 (go and return). It can also be a verb: 미국에서 유학하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 여행 for academic study abroad, and marking the country with 에 instead of 으로/로 (일본에 유학을 가요 sounds off; say 일본으로 유학을 가요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 여행 (a trip) for academic study abroad; a degree-length stay is 유학, e.g. 유학을 가다.
Saying 일본에 유학을 가요; the directional particle for a destination here is 으로/로: 일본으로 유학을 가요.
Saying 유학에 가요 instead of the set phrase; it's 유학을 가다 (or just 유학 가다), with 을 on 유학.

entries.shortExplanation: 얼굴 means "face" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 얼굴 (eolgul) = "face". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 얼굴이 예뻐요 ("the face is pretty") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 얼굴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: describing looks; subject particle 이
빨갛다, a ㅎ-irregular, drops ㅎ before -아요
씻다 for water-washing, object particle 을
붓다 ㅅ-irregular → 부었어요 in past

examples.en: My older sister's face is really pretty.
examples.note: describing looks; possessive 언니 얼굴 needs no 의 in speech

examples.en: I get up in the morning and wash my face.
examples.note: note the verb 씻다, never 감다, takes the object 얼굴을

examples.en: I got so embarrassed that my face turned red.
examples.note: 빨개지다 = turn red; 이/가 marks the body part that changes

entries.nuance: 얼굴 is the whole human face — both its looks and its surface you wash — and is the everyday word with no formality issue; you use it equally with friends and elders. Its near-synonym 낯 (as in 낯이 익다 'the face looks familiar', 낯설다 'unfamiliar') is old-fashioned and survives mostly in set idioms, so for plain 'face' always reach for 얼굴. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers. First, hair on the head is 감다 (감다 = wash hair) but the FACE is 씻다, the same verb as for hands and dishes — never say 얼굴을 감다. Second, English 'big face' does not transfer: a flattering 'small face' is 얼굴이 작다 (a real Korean compliment about proportion), and you do not say 얼굴이 커요 to mean handsome. Color uses 빨갛다 (얼굴이 빨개요), and to feel for fever Koreans touch the 이마, not the whole 얼굴.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 얼굴을 감다 to mean 'wash my face' — 감다 is only for washing HAIR; the face takes 씻다, so it must be 얼굴을 씻어요.
Translating 'pretty face' as 얼굴이 이뻐다 with wrong spelling; the standard adjective is 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before -어요).
Using 얼굴이 커요 expecting it to sound flattering — in Korean a large face is unflattering; the compliment is 얼굴이 작다, 'small-faced'.

entries.shortExplanation: 머리카락 means "hair strands" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 머리카락 (meorikarak) means "hair strands". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리카락이 길어요 ("the hair is long"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 머리카락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 길다 describes length; 이 marks the subject
빠지다 = shed/fall out, intransitive, takes 이/가
자르다 르-irregular → 잘라요, object 을
까맣다 ㅎ-irregular → 까매요

examples.en: My hair is too long.
examples.note: describing length; 이 marks the strand as subject of 길다

examples.en: Lately a lot of my hair is falling out.
examples.note: 빠지다 is intransitive — the hair falls by itself, so use 이/가, not 을

examples.en: I got my hair cut short at the salon.
examples.note: 자르다 takes the object 을; 짧게 'short' is the adverb form of 짧다

entries.nuance: 머리카락 names the individual strands or the mass of hair as material, whereas 머리 is a slippery word that means both the head and, loosely, the hair growing on it. The dividing line: when you must be unambiguous that you mean the hair itself — counting it, shedding it, a strand on your food — choose 머리카락; for a haircut or hairstyle, casual 머리 is actually more common (머리 잘랐어 'I got a haircut'). One strand is 머리카락 한 올 (the counter 올 is for thread-like things). English speakers stumble two ways. First, English 'hair' is uncountable, but Korean lets you count strands, so 'a hair fell out' is 머리카락 한 올이 빠졌어요, not a plural. Second, hair falling out is 빠지다 (intransitive) — the hair leaves on its own — so it is 머리카락이 빠지다 with 이/가; learners wrongly force the object 을. And cutting is 자르다; 머리카락을 잘랐어요 means a trim, not amputation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 머리카락을 빠져요 with the object particle — 빠지다 is intransitive (the hair sheds itself), so it must be 머리카락이 빠져요.
Treating 머리 and 머리카락 as fully interchangeable; you cannot say 머리가 한 올 빠졌어요 for a single strand — counting strands needs 머리카락 한 올.
Mispronouncing/misspelling the verb as 자라요 (grow) when you mean 잘라요 (cut); 자르다 is a 르-irregular, so 'cut' becomes 잘라요.

entries.shortExplanation: 이마 means "forehead" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "forehead" is 이마 (ima). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이마가 넓어요 ("the forehead is wide"). Watch the particle attached to 이마 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 넓다 'wide/broad', not 크다; 이 marks the subject
뜨겁다 ㅂ-irregular → 뜨거워요, a fever sign
짚다 = press-check for fever, object 를
부딪히다 = get bumped, takes 를

examples.en: My forehead is a bit wide.
examples.note: 넓다 describes a broad surface — never 크다 for a forehead

examples.en: I have a fever so my forehead is hot.
examples.note: 뜨겁다 → 뜨거워요 (ㅂ-irregular); 나다 collocates with 열 for 'a fever comes'

examples.en: My mom felt my forehead to check.
examples.note: 짚다 is the precise verb for laying a hand to check temperature; 를 marks the spot

entries.nuance: 이마 is the forehead, the flat span above the eyebrows, and culturally it is the spot Koreans touch first to check a fever — so it collocates constantly with 열이 나다 ('a fever comes') and 뜨겁다 ('hot'). Two register-neutral verbs matter: to lay a palm on it to gauge temperature is 짚다 (이마를 짚다), and a wide forehead is 이마가 넓다. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is dimension: a forehead has area, not bulk, so 'a big forehead' must be 이마가 넓다 ('wide'), never 이마가 커요 ('big'), which sounds odd and almost comical to Koreans. A second trap is the fever verb — English 'I have a fever' becomes 열이 나다 (literally 'heat comes out'), so you say 열이 나서 이마가 뜨거워요, not the direct 열을 가지다. Note 뜨겁다 is ㅂ-irregular, giving 뜨거워요, and to feel hot to the touch you generally use 뜨겁다 for objects/skin, while 덥다 is for the weather/air.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이마가 커요 for a large forehead — area is described with 넓다, so the natural phrase is 이마가 넓어요.
Translating 'I have a fever' as 열을 가지고 있어요; Korean says 열이 나다, e.g. 열이 나서 이마가 뜨거워요.
Using 덥다 for a hot forehead — 덥다 is for ambient heat (weather); skin/objects that are hot to the touch take 뜨겁다, so 이마가 뜨거워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 볼 means "cheek" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 볼 (bol) = "cheek". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 볼이 빨개요 ("my cheeks are red") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 볼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 빨갛다 ㅎ-irregular → 빨개요; 이 marks the subject
통통하다 = plump (cute), gentle nuance
꼬집다 = pinch affectionately, object 을
뽀뽀하다 + location 에 for a peck

examples.en: The baby's cheeks are chubby.
examples.note: 통통하다 carries a warm, cute tone reserved for plumpness, not fat

examples.en: It was cold outside so my cheeks turned red.
examples.note: 빨개지다 'turn red'; cold weather reddens cheeks — a very common collocation

examples.en: Grandma gently pinched her grandchild's cheek.
examples.note: 꼬집다 = an affectionate pinch; 볼 (not 뺨) keeps it warm and loving

entries.nuance: 볼 is the soft, fleshy cheek and carries an inherently warm, tender tone — it is the word for chubby baby cheeks (볼이 통통하다), cold-reddened cheeks (볼이 빨개지다), and affectionate pinches (볼을 꼬집다). Its near-synonym 뺨 also means cheek but anatomically/coldly and, crucially, collocates with violence: 뺨을 때리다 / 뺨을 맞다 is 'to slap / be slapped across the face'. So the dividing line is emotional temperature: 볼 is gentle and intimate, 뺨 is clinical or harsh. For everyday loving or descriptive talk always pick 볼. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 뺨 as a neutral dictionary 'cheek' and accidentally importing the slapping connotation; a sentence like 아기 뺨이 통통해요 sounds jarring because 뺨 clashes with the cuteness. Also note color is 빨갛다 (볼이 빨개요), the ㅎ-irregular dropping ㅎ before -아요, and a kiss on the cheek attaches with location 에: 볼에 뽀뽀하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 뺨 as a neutral word for 'cheek' in affectionate contexts — 뺨 leans clinical and is tied to slapping (뺨을 때리다); for warm, everyday cheeks use 볼.
Writing 볼이 빨갛아요 — 빨갛다 is ㅎ-irregular, so before -아요 the ㅎ drops and the vowel contracts to 빨개요.
Attaching the wrong particle for a cheek kiss: it is 볼에 뽀뽀하다 (location 에), not 볼을 뽀뽀하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 턱 means "chin; jaw" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 턱 (teok) means "chin; jaw". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 턱이 아파요 ("my jaw hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 턱 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part

A second trap is the verb for resting the chin: it is 괴다, not 놓다 or 대다, so 'I rest my chin on my hand' is 턱을 괴다.
