usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain, very common complaint
넓다 = broad; a physique compliment for men
결리다 = muscle stiffness/crick, special verb
주무르다 르-irregular → 주물러요, object 를

examples.en: I sat for a long time so my shoulder hurts.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요; sitting too long is a classic cause of 어깨가 아프다

examples.ko: 컴퓨터를 오래 해서 어깨가 너무 결려요.
examples.romanization: keompyuteoreul orae haeseo eokkaega neomu gyeollyeoyo.
examples.en: I used the computer a long time so my shoulder is really stiff.
examples.note: 결리다 is the precise verb for a muscular crick — not 아프다 or 딱딱하다

examples.en: I massaged my mom's shoulders (for her).
examples.note: 주무르다 → 주물러요 (르-irregular); -아/어 드리다 adds humble service to an elder

entries.nuance: 어깨 is the shoulder, and the standout point is its dedicated stiffness verb 결리다: a tight, achy crick from posture or computer work is 어깨가 결리다, distinct from plain pain 어깨가 아프다 and never 어깨가 딱딱하다 (딱딱하다 = physically hard, used for objects). Don't read those literally as physical sensations.

entries.shortExplanation: 팔 means "arm" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 팔 (pal) = "arm". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 팔이 아파요 ("my arm hurts") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 팔, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
들다 = lift up, object 을; ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ
다치다 = get injured, object 을

usagePhrases.en: I cross my arms / link arms
usagePhrases.note: 팔짱 끼다 = fixed phrase

examples.en: I carried a heavy bag so my arm hurts.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요; the cause clause uses -아서 'because'

examples.en: Please slowly raise both arms.
examples.note: 들다 takes the object 팔을; -아 보세요 = 'try ~ing' as a gentle instruction

examples.en: I walked arm in arm with my friend.
examples.note: 팔짱(을) 끼다 is the set phrase for linking arms — not 팔을 끼다

entries.nuance: 팔 is the whole arm, shoulder to wrist, and is most often the OBJECT of an action — you raise it, injure it, or link it. The verb to learn precisely is 들다 ('lift'): 팔을 들다 is the natural way to say 'raise your arm', and 들다 is a ㄹ-stem that drops its ㄹ before certain endings (들어요, 드세요). English speakers often substitute 올리다 ('raise/put up'), but 팔을 올리다 sounds slightly off for the natural gesture; reach for 팔을 들다. A second collocation worth memorizing is 팔짱(을) 끼다 — to cross your arms over your chest OR to link arms with someone, an idiom that does not break down word-for-word from English. Injuring the arm is 팔을 다치다 (다치다 = get hurt, takes 을), and arm pain is 팔이 아프다 with the subject particle because there 팔 is what hurts. Watch the particle flip: 팔이 아프다 (subject, it hurts) vs 팔을 들다 (object, you act on it).

Saying 팔을 올려요 for raising an arm — the natural verb for the gesture is 들다, so it is 팔을 들어요.
Using 팔을 끼다 to mean 'link/cross arms' — the fixed expression is 팔짱(을) 끼다, e.g. 팔짱을 끼고 걸어요.
Mixing the particle: 'my arm hurts' is 팔이 아파요 (subject 이, because the arm is what hurts), not 팔을 아파요.

entries.shortExplanation: 손가락 means "finger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 손가락 (songarak) means "finger". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 손가락이 아파요 ("my finger hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 손가락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
다치다 = get injured, object 을
베다 = slice (a cut), object 을
손가락 + instrumental 으로; 가리키다 = point at

examples.en: My finger got caught in the door so it hurts.
examples.note: 끼다 'get caught/pinched'; 손가락이 (subject) is what hurts

examples.en: I lightly cut my finger on a knife.
examples.note: 베다 = a slicing cut; takes the object 손가락을 — not 자르다

examples.en: Pianists have long fingers.
examples.note: 길다 'long'; describing the finger's length with subject 이

entries.nuance: 손가락 literally compounds 손 ('hand') + 가락 (a counter/word for slender stick-like things, as in 젓가락 'chopsticks', 가락국수 'thin noodles'), so it is transparently 'hand-stick' = finger. The crucial verb contrast is for cuts: a slicing wound from a knife or paper is 베다 (손가락을 베다), which means the skin is sliced, NOT 자르다. 자르다 means to cut something off, so 손가락을 잘랐어요 chillingly implies you severed the finger — a real and alarming mistake English speakers make because English 'cut my finger' uses one verb for both. Another trap is the toe: a toe is not a separate root but 발가락 (발 'foot' + 가락), so don't say 발 손가락. Pointing uses the instrumental: 손가락으로 가리키다. Finger pain where the finger is what hurts takes the subject particle (손가락이 아파요), while injuring it takes the object (손가락을 다치다). Note 아프다 and 베다 conjugate as 아파요 (ㅡ drops) and 베었어요.

Saying 손가락을 잘랐어요 to mean 'I cut my finger' — 자르다 means to cut OFF/sever; a slicing cut to the skin is 베다, so it is 손가락을 베었어요.
Inventing 발 손가락 for 'toe' — a toe has its own compound 발가락; 손가락 is strictly the finger.
Using the wrong particle when pointing: you point 손가락으로 (instrumental 으로), not 손가락을, so it is 손가락으로 가리켜요.

entries.shortExplanation: 무릎 means "knee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "knee" is 무릎 (mureup). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무릎이 아파요 ("my knee hurts"). Watch the particle attached to 무릎 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain, common in older people
다치다 = get injured, object 을
꿇다 = kneel, object 을; only for kneeling
붓다 ㅅ-irregular → 부었어요

examples.en: I climbed a lot of stairs so my knee hurts.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요; stair-climbing straining the knee is a classic collocation

examples.en: I fell and hurt my knee.
examples.note: 다치다 takes the object 무릎을; -아서 links the cause 'fell'

examples.en: I knelt down and apologized sincerely.
examples.note: 꿇다 is the dedicated verb for kneeling; 무릎을 꿇다 = to kneel

entries.nuance: 무릎 is the knee, and 무릎이 아프다 is one of the most common aches, especially for older people and after stairs or squatting. The verb to lock in is 꿇다 — the dedicated word for kneeling, used only here: 무릎을 꿇다 means to drop to your knees, an act loaded with meaning (sincere apology, pleading, submission), so it is culturally weightier than English 'kneel'. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 앉다 ('sit') for kneeling — 무릎을 앉다 is simply wrong; kneeling has its own verb 꿇다. A second point: a swollen knee uses 붓다 ('to swell'), a ㅅ-irregular whose ㅅ drops in conjugation, giving past 부었어요 (무릎이 부었어요) — don't regularize it to 붓었어요. Injuring the knee is 무릎을 다치다 (object 을 because you act on/damage it), whereas the knee hurting takes the subject particle 무릎이 아프다. Note Koreans also say 무릎을 꿇리다 (causative) for forcing someone to kneel.

Saying 무릎을 앉다 to mean 'kneel' — kneeling has a dedicated verb 꿇다, so it is 무릎을 꿇다.
Conjugating 붓다 (swell) as 붓었어요; it is a ㅅ-irregular, so the past is 부었어요 (무릎이 부었어요).
Using the subject particle for injury: 'I hurt my knee' is 무릎을 다쳤어요 (object 을, you damaged it), not 무릎이 다쳤어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 등 means "back" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
긁다 = scratch an itch, object 을
등을 돌리다 = turn away (also figurative)
업다 = piggyback; location 에

examples.ko: 딱딱한 바닥에 오래 누워서 등이 아파요.
examples.romanization: ttakttakan badage orae nuwoseo deungi apayo.
examples.en: I lay on a hard floor for a long time so my back hurts.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요; 등 here is the upper back, distinct from 허리

examples.en: My back was itchy so I scratched it.
examples.note: 긁다 = scratch; 가렵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 가려워서 'because itchy'

examples.en: Mom carried the baby on her back and soothed it.
examples.note: 업다 = piggyback-carry; the baby rides 등에 (location 에)

entries.nuance: 등 is specifically the UPPER back — the broad surface from shoulders to mid-spine — and Korean sharply distinguishes it from 허리, the waist/lower back. This split matters because 'back pain' in English is one phrase, but Koreans pick 등이 아프다 for the upper back and 허리가 아프다 for the lower; most everyday backaches (from sitting, lifting) are actually 허리, so defaulting to 등 mislocates the pain. Also note the itch adjective 가렵다 is ㅂ-irregular (가려워요), and 등이 아프다 takes the subject particle because the back is what hurts.

Conjugating 가렵다 (itchy) as 가렵어요; it is ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 가려워요 (등이 가려워요).
Reading 등을 돌리다 as only the physical act — it also carries the figurative sense 'to turn one's back on / abandon someone'.

entries.shortExplanation: 가슴 means "chest" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.en: my chest hurts / my heart aches
usagePhrases.note: both physical pain and heartache
답답하다 = stifled, physical or emotional
두근거리다 = flutter from nerves/excitement
뭉클하다 = a warm lump of emotion

examples.en: I ran up the stairs so my chest feels tight.
examples.note: 답답하다 here is physical breathlessness; 가슴이 marks the subject

examples.en: When I see the person I like, my heart flutters.
examples.note: 두근거리다 = heart-pounding from emotion; -면 'when/if'

examples.ko: 그 영화의 마지막 장면이 너무 가슴이 아팠어요.
examples.romanization: geu yeonghwaui majimak jangmyeoni neomu gaseumi apasseoyo.
examples.en: The last scene of that movie was so heartbreaking.
examples.note: 가슴이 아프다 here is EMOTIONAL pain, not physical — context decides

entries.nuance: 가슴 means the chest physically, but it is also the seat of FEELINGS — Korean locates emotion in the 가슴 the way English uses 'heart'. entries.shortExplanation: 허리 means "waist; lower back" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "waist; lower back" is 허리 (heori). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 허리가 아파요 ("my lower back hurts"). Watch the particle attached to 허리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain, a top everyday complaint
가늘다 = slender; 이 marks the subject
펴다 = straighten/unbend, object 를
굽히다 = bend the body forward, object 를

examples.ko: 하루 종일 앉아 있어서 허리가 아파요.
examples.romanization: haru jongil anja isseoseo heoriga apayo.
examples.en: I sat all day so my lower back hurts.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요; sitting long strains the 허리, not 등

examples.en: I tweaked my lower back while lifting a heavy box.
examples.note: 삐끗하다 = wrench/tweak; 허리를 takes the object as you injure it

examples.en: Straighten your back fully and sit up properly.
examples.note: 펴다 = unbend; 쭉 'fully/straight'; -(으)세요 polite command

entries.nuance: 허리 spans both the waist (the narrow midsection) and the lower back/lumbar region, so 허리가 아프다 normally means LOWER-back pain — by far one of the most common complaints from sitting, lifting, or aging, and it is the word a doctor and a friend both use. This is the flip side of 등 (upper back): English lumps them as 'back', but Korean assigns lower pain to 허리 and upper to 등, so the key pitfall is saying 등이 아파요 for lumbar pain when you mean 허리가 아파요. On the waist side, 허리가 가늘다 ('slim waist') is a body descriptor, and clothing-wise your 허리 is the waistband measurement. Core posture verbs come in an opposing pair: 허리를 펴다 ('straighten/unbend the back', also figuratively 'stand tall after hardship') vs 허리를 굽히다 ('bend forward'); and a sudden tweak is 허리를 삐끗하다. Note 가늘다 is a ㄹ-stem (가늘어요) and 펴다 conjugates straightforwardly (펴요).

Saying 등이 아파요 for lower-back/lumbar pain — that belongs to 허리, so it is 허리가 아파요; 등 is only the upper back.
Using 얇다 (thin, of flat objects like paper) for a slim waist — a slender waist is 가늘다, so 허리가 가늘어요.
Mixing the particle: posture verbs act on the back, so it is 허리를 펴다 / 허리를 굽히다 (object 를), while pain takes 허리가 아프다 (subject 이).

entries.shortExplanation: 기분 means "mood; feeling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기분 (gibun) = "mood; feeling". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기분이 좋아요 ("I feel good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기분, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기분 takes 이, never 을

usagePhrases.en: I feel bad / I'm in a bad mood
usagePhrases.note: 나쁘다 = bad; describes the mood, not a person

usagePhrases.en: a change of mood / refreshing break
usagePhrases.note: 전환 轉換 = switching; 기분 전환 하다 = lift your spirits

usagePhrases.en: don't make me feel bad / don't offend me
usagePhrases.note: 기분 나쁘다 also means 'feel offended'

examples.en: Today I feel really good.
examples.note: Simple: 기분이 + adjective is the core frame.

examples.en: The weather is gloomy so I'm feeling down.
examples.note: Everyday: -아서 gives the cause; 안 좋다 softer than 나쁘다.

examples.ko: 그 말을 듣고 기분이 좀 상했어요.
examples.romanization: geu mareul deutgo gibuni jom sanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: I felt a bit hurt after hearing that.
examples.note: Real situation: 기분이 상하다 = get one's feelings hurt, common after a remark.

entries.nuance: 기분(氣分, literally 'energy-portion') is your momentary emotional weather — how you feel right now — and it rises and falls with events, weather, sleep, or someone's words. Contrast it with 감정 (emotion as a deeper, named state like anger or love) and especially with 행복 (happiness as a lasting condition): 기분이 좋다 is a passing 'I feel good today,' while 행복하다 is 'I am happy with my life.' It is everyday, neutral register and fine with anyone. The big English-speaker trap is the particle: 기분 is the subject of how-you-feel, so it always takes 이 — say 기분이 좋아요, never the object-marked 기분을 좋아요. A second trap is direction: 기분이 좋다 describes YOUR state, so don't use it to call a thing nice; for that use 좋다 alone (이 영화 좋아요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기분을 좋아요. Wrong particle — 기분 is the thing that is good, i.e. the subject, so it must be 기분이 좋아요.
Translating 'I'm in a good mood' as 행복해요. 행복하다 is lasting life-happiness; for a passing mood say 기분이 좋아요.
Using 느낌 for your inner mood (그 영화 느낌이 좋아요 = the film's vibe). 느낌 is the impression a thing gives off; your own mood is 기분.

entries.shortExplanation: 생각 means "thought" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 생각 (saenggak) means "thought". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 생각을 해요 ("I think (about it)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 생각 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 생각하다 = to think; takes 을 as an object
생각 here = idea, like English 'idea'

usagePhrases.en: it comes to mind / I remember
usagePhrases.note: 나다 = arise; the thought surfaces by itself, so 이
에는 frames 'as for my thought'; set opener

examples.en: A good idea came to me.
examples.note: Simple: 생각이 나다 — the idea pops up, so subject 이.

examples.en: I often think about my family.
examples.note: Everyday: 가족 생각을 하다 = to think of family; object 을.

examples.en: Thinking it over again, I was wrong.
examples.note: Real situation: 생각해 보다 = think it through / reconsider.

entries.nuance: 생각 is a pure native-Korean word covering the whole range of English 'thought,' 'idea,' and 'opinion,' so it is wonderfully flexible: 좋은 생각 = a good idea, 제 생각 = my opinion, 생각하다 = to think. The key is how it pairs with verbs. With 하다 (생각을 하다 / 생각하다) it is deliberate, active thinking that YOU do, so the thought is the object → 을. With 나다 (생각이 나다) the thought arises on its own — it surfaces or you suddenly remember — so it is the subject → 이. Contrast 생각하다 with 기억하다: 생각나다 is the thought spontaneously popping up ('it came to me'), while 기억하다 is the willed act of recalling stored memory. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing these two patterns and saying 생각이 해요; if the verb is 하다, you must mark 생각을.

Saying 생각이 해요. With 하다 the thought is what you actively do — the object — so it is 생각을 해요.
Saying 생각을 나요 for 'I remember.' With 나다 the thought arises by itself (subject), so it must be 생각이 나요.
Using 생각하다 where 'remember' is meant. 어제 일이 생각나요 = it comes to mind; deliberate recall of facts is 기억하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 마음 means "heart; mind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "heart; mind" is 마음 (maeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마음이 따뜻해요 ("has a warm heart"). Watch the particle attached to 마음 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 따뜻하다 = warm; describes character

usagePhrases.en: I like it / it suits me
usagePhrases.note: 에 들다 = enters my heart; fixed idiom

usagePhrases.en: I open my heart / open up
usagePhrases.note: 열다 = open; emotional openness
편하다 = comfortable; inner peace, not the body

examples.en: That person has a warm heart.
examples.note: Simple: 마음이 + adjective describes someone's inner nature.

examples.en: I really like this gift.
examples.note: Everyday: 마음에 들다 is THE verb for liking things/people you encounter.

examples.en: Feeling sorry, I reached out first.
examples.note: Real situation: 마음에 = 'out of (a feeling),' a common motive marker.

entries.nuance: 마음 is the native word for the heart-mind: the seat of feelings, will, intentions, and disposition — never the physical organ (that is 심장 心臟, the pump). Contrast it with 생각 (thought/idea, the cognitive content) and with 기분 (a passing mood): 마음 is the deeper, more stable inner self where kindness, sincerity, and intentions live. It anchors many high-frequency idioms: 마음에 들다 (to like / be pleased by something you meet), 마음을 먹다 (to make up one's mind), 마음이 아프다 (to be heartsick). The classic English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: using 마음 for the body-heart (say 심장이 빨리 뛰어요 for a racing heart), and translating 'I like it' as 좋아해요 when you mean a settled approval of something in front of you — Koreans naturally reach for 마음에 들어요 there, where 좋아하다 is a broader 'I like/am fond of.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 마음 for the physical heart. The organ is 심장 — say 심장이 두근거려요, not 마음이 두근거려요.
Saying 마음에 들어요 about an action you enjoy. 마음에 들다 is for liking a thing/person; for enjoying an activity use 좋아하다 (수영을 좋아해요).
Marking it 마음을 들어요. The fixed idiom is 마음에 들다 with 에 — the thing 'enters into' your heart.

entries.shortExplanation: 꿈 means "dream" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 꿈 (kkum) = "dream". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 꿈을 꿔요 ("I dream / I have a dream (asleep)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 꿈, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I dream / I have a dream (asleep)
usagePhrases.note: 꿈을 꾸다 = the only natural verb for dreaming
있다 = have; subject 이

usagePhrases.en: I make a dream come true
usagePhrases.note: 이루다 = fulfill; 이뤄요 is the 요-form
꿈에 나오다 = show up in a dream

examples.en: Last night I had a good dream.
examples.note: Simple: 꿈을 꾸다 — note the same-root verb, like 'dream a dream.'

examples.en: My dream is to become a doctor.
examples.note: Everyday: 꿈 as a life goal, framed with -는 게 ... 이에요.

examples.en: Don't give up — be sure to make your dream come true.
examples.note: Real situation: 꿈을 이루다 = achieve a dream, encouraging tone.

entries.nuance: 꿈 is a single native word that carries both English senses at once — the images you see while asleep AND a cherished hope or life goal — so 꿈이 있어요 can mean 'I had a dream (last night)' or 'I have a dream (ambition),' resolved by context. Its signature feature is the cognate-object verb 꿈을 꾸다, literally 'to dream a dream,' which is the ONLY natural way to say you dreamt; for goals the partner verb is 꿈을 이루다 (to fulfill a dream). Contrast 꿈 (an inner, often emotional aspiration) with 목표 目標 (a concrete, measurable target you set and tick off) and 희망 希望 (hope as a hopeful attitude). The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the all-purpose 하다 and saying 꿈을 해요 — that is meaningless; dreaming must be 꿈을 꾸다. A second trap: don't use 보다 ('see') for dreams as in some languages; Korean dreams are 'dreamt' (꾸다), and a figure 'comes out' in them (꿈에 나오다).

Saying 꿈을 해요 for 'I dream.' 하다 doesn't work here — the fixed verb is 꿈을 꾸다 (꿈을 꿔요).
Saying 꿈을 봤어요 ('I saw a dream'). Korean dreams are dreamt, not seen — use 꿈을 꿨어요.
Using 목표 for a heartfelt life dream. 목표 is a concrete checkable target; an aspiration is 꿈 (제 꿈은 가수예요).

entries.shortExplanation: 사랑 means "love" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사랑 (sarang) means "love". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사랑해요 ("I love you"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사랑 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 사랑하다, the verb; object marker often dropped
에 빠지다 = fall into; fixed idiom
첫 = first; one written word
사랑을 받다 = be loved, very common

examples.en: I love my family a lot.
examples.note: Simple: 사랑하다 takes the loved one as object (가족을).

examples.en: I fell in love with that person.
examples.note: Everyday: 와/과 ... 사랑에 빠지다 = fall in love WITH someone.

examples.en: I grew up receiving lots of love from my parents.
examples.note: Real situation: 사랑을 받다 + 자라다 = a natural 'raised with love' frame.

entries.nuance: 사랑 is the native word for love across the full range — romantic, familial, and affection for friends or even things — and with 하다 it becomes 사랑하다, the verb whose object is the beloved (가족을 사랑해요). Note the register: 사랑해(요) is a weighty, sincere declaration. Koreans say it warmly to family and partners, but to acquaintances or in casual liking they prefer the lighter 좋아하다 ('I like you / I'm fond of you') — confessing 좋아해요 is in fact the standard first step, with 사랑해요 saved for deeper commitment. The English-speaker pitfall is the all-purpose-하다 error 사랑이 해요 (the loved one is the object → 사랑을 / 사랑해요), and over-using 'I love' — English 'I love pizza' should be 피자를 좋아해요, since 사랑하다 for food sounds melodramatic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사랑이 해요. The beloved is the object — say 사랑을 해요, or more naturally the verb 사랑해요.
Telling a new friend 사랑해요. That's a deep declaration; for liking/affection say 좋아해요.
Using 사랑하다 for casual liking of things. 'I love coffee' = 커피를 좋아해요, not 커피를 사랑해요 (sounds exaggerated).

entries.shortExplanation: 걱정 means "worry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "worry" is 걱정 (geokjeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 걱정을 해요 ("I worry"). Watch the particle attached to 걱정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 걱정하다 = to worry; object 을

usagePhrases.en: I have a lot of worries
usagePhrases.note: 많다 = many; subject 이
the standard comforting phrase
걱정이 되다 = worry arises on its own

examples.en: These days I have a lot of worries.
examples.note: Simple: 걱정이 많다 — worries exist (subject 이).

examples.en: My mom worries about my health.
examples.note: Everyday: 걱정하다 takes what's worried about as object (건강을).

examples.en: Don't worry. Everything will be fine.
examples.note: Real situation: 걱정하지 마세요 + reassurance, very natural comfort.

entries.nuance: 걱정 is care or anxiety about something uncertain — the knot in your stomach over a result, a person's health, or money. It splits across two verbs: active 걱정하다 ('to worry about X,' X = object → 건강을 걱정해요) and spontaneous 걱정이 되다 ('X worries me / I become worried,' the worry arises → subject 이). Contrast 걱정 with 고민 (a problem you are mulling over, more like deliberation/a dilemma you turn in your mind) and with 불안 不安 (free-floating anxiety/unease without a clear object): you 걱정 about a specific thing, you 고민 over a decision, you feel 불안 as a mood. The most useful chunk is 걱정하지 마세요/걱정 마 — the go-to way to comfort someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 particle error 걱정이 해요 (use 걱정을 해요), and saying 걱정에 대해 생각해요 when you simply mean 걱정해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 문제 means "problem" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 문제 (munje) = "problem". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문제가 있어요 ("there is a problem") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 문제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 있다 = exist; subject 이
풀다 = solve/untie; object 를
생기다 = come into being; subject 이
one-word reassurance, very common

examples.en: There's one small problem here.
examples.note: Simple: 문제가 있다 — a problem exists (subject 이).

examples.en: I solved all the math problems.
examples.note: Everyday: 문제를 풀다 also covers test questions; object 를.

examples.en: That's not a problem at all.
examples.note: Real situation: 문제가 되다 / 안 되다 = (not) become an issue.

entries.nuance: 문제(問題, 'ask + topic') has two everyday senses English keeps apart: a trouble or difficulty ('we have a problem') AND a question on a test or exercise ('problem 3'). Crucially, both are solved with the same verb 풀다 (literally 'to untie/loosen') — 문제를 풀다 works for a math item and for a real-life difficulty alike, where English would switch to 'answer' vs 'solve.' Other key partners: 문제가 생기다 (a problem arises), 문제가 되다 (to become an issue), and the handy one-word 문제없어요 ('no problem'). Contrast 문제 with 질문 (a question you ASK someone to get information) — a test 문제 is a problem to solve, but raising your hand to ask is 질문하다, not 문제하다. The English-speaker pitfall is the subject/object split: existence and arising take 이 (문제가 있다/생기다), but solving takes 를 (문제를 풀다) — learners often say 문제가 풀어요.

Saying 문제가 풀어요. Solving is transitive — the problem is the object → 문제를 풀어요.
Using 문제 for a question you ask. To ask someone something is 질문(을) 하다; 문제 is a problem/test item, not an inquiry.
Saying 문제를 있어요. 있다 marks existence with the subject — it must be 문제가 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 이유 means "reason" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이유 (iyu) means "reason". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이유가 있어요 ("there is a reason"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이유 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 있다 = exist; subject 이
말하다 = say; object 를
로 = by/for; asks the cause
없이 = without; fixed adverbial

examples.en: There's a reason I'm late.
examples.note: Simple: 이유가 있다 — a reason exists (subject 이).

examples.en: Please tell me the reason.
examples.note: Everyday: 이유를 말하다 — state the reason; object 를.

examples.en: I just came for no particular reason.
examples.note: Real situation: 이유 없이 = 'for no reason,' with 그냥 ('just').

entries.nuance: 이유(理由, 'principle + cause') is the reason or grounds behind something — the 'why.' Distinguish it from two neighbors: 원인 原因 is the objective CAUSE in a cause-and-effect chain (the cause of a fire, an illness — 화재의 원인), more clinical and used for events, whereas 이유 is the reason/justification a person gives for an action or feeling (늦은 이유). 까닭 is a native near-synonym of 이유 but sounds more literary. Useful frames: 이유가 있다 (there's a reason), 무슨 이유로 (for what reason), and the adverbial 이유 없이 (for no reason). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle split again — stating a reason is transitive (이유를 말하다), so 이유가 말해요 is wrong; and don't translate 'the reason why' with a double marker — Korean just modifies the noun: 제가 온 이유 ('the reason I came'), no 왜 needed inside.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이유가 말해요. Telling the reason is transitive — the reason is the object → 이유를 말해요.
Using 이유 for the cause of an accident/disease. The clinical cause is 원인 (사고의 원인); 이유 is a person's stated reason.
Adding 왜 inside 'the reason why': 'the reason why I came' is just 제가 온 이유 — the modifier clause already means 'why.'

entries.shortExplanation: 방법 means "method; way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "method; way" is 방법 (bangbeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 방법이 있어요 ("there is a way"). Watch the particle attached to 방법 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 있다 = exist; subject 이
찾다 = look for; object 을
으로 = by means of; instrumental
modifier before noun

examples.en: There's an easier way.
examples.note: Simple: 방법이 있다 — a way exists (subject 이).

examples.en: I'm looking for a new method.
examples.note: Everyday: 방법을 찾다 — seek a method; object 을.

examples.en: If you do it this way, it's much faster.
examples.note: Real situation: 방법으로 하다 = do it by/in this way; instrumental 으로.

entries.nuance: 방법(方法, 'direction + rule/law') is the method, means, or how-to of doing something — the practical 'way' to reach a result. Its hallmark particle is 으로 ('by means of'): 이 방법으로 하다 = 'do it this way,' the natural answer to 'how?' Contrast 방법 with 방식 方式, which is a style or manner/mode of doing (한국 방식 = the Korean way of doing things, a habitual pattern), whereas 방법 is a concrete procedure that solves a task; and with 길, which literally means 'road/path' but extends to a metaphorical 'way out' (해결할 길이 없다). Common verbs: 방법을 찾다 (find a way), 방법을 알다/모르다 (know/not know how). The English-speaker pitfall is the existence-vs-action particle (방법이 있다 but 방법을 찾다 — learners say 방법이 찾아요), and reaching for 길 ('way/road') where 방법 is meant: '한국어를 배우는 좋은 방법' not '좋은 길.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 방법이 찾아요. Finding a way is transitive — the way is the object → 방법을 찾아요.
Using 길 for a how-to. '학습 방법' (study method), not '학습 길'; 길 stays for roads or a metaphorical 'way out.'
Marking the means with 로 ... 을: it's 이 방법으로 하다 (instrumental 으로), not 이 방법을 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 계획 means "plan" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계획 (gyehoek) = "plan". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 계획을 세워요 ("I make a plan") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계획, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 세우다 = set up/erect; THE verb for plans
있다 = have; subject 이
대로 = as/per; fixed adverbial
noun + noun compound

examples.en: I'm making a travel plan.
examples.note: Simple: 계획을 세우다 — the fixed verb, lit. 'erect a plan.'

examples.en: Do you have special plans this evening?
examples.note: Everyday: 계획이 있다 — a plan exists (subject 이).

examples.en: Everything went well, just as planned.
examples.note: Real situation: 계획대로 = 'as planned,' a very natural phrase.

entries.nuance: 계획(計劃, 'count/reckon + plan') is a worked-out plan or scheme for the future. Its single most important quirk is the verb: Koreans BUILD a plan with 세우다 (literally 'to erect/stand up') — 계획을 세우다 — not 만들다 ('make') as the English calque suggests. Other partners: 계획이 있다 (have a plan) and the smooth adverb 계획대로 ('as planned'). Distinguish 계획 from 예정 豫定, which is a SCHEDULED arrangement that is already set ('내일 출발할 예정이에요' = I'm scheduled/due to leave tomorrow), and from 약속, a personal commitment/appointment with someone — 계획 is your own roadmap, 예정 is a fixed scheduling, 약속 involves another party. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly 계획을 만들다 (use 세우다), and translating 'plan to do' with 계획 as a verb — Korean uses -(으)려고 하다 or -(으)ㄹ 계획이다: 여행할 계획이에요 ('I plan to travel'), not 여행을 계획해요 in casual speech.

Saying 계획을 만들어요. The idiomatic verb is 세우다 — 계획을 세워요 (lit. 'erect a plan').
Saying 계획이 세워요 for 'I make a plan.' Making a plan is transitive — the plan is the object → 계획을 세워요.
Using 계획 for something already scheduled. 'I'm due to leave tomorrow' = 내일 떠날 예정이에요; 예정 is a fixed schedule, 계획 is a plan you draw up.

entries.shortExplanation: 약속 means "promise; appointment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 약속 (yaksok) means "promise; appointment". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 약속을 해요 ("I make a promise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 약속 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. 있다 = have; subject 이
지키다 = keep/protect; object 을
어기다 = break/violate; the opposite of 지키다

examples.en: We promised to meet tomorrow.
examples.note: Simple: -기로 약속하다 = promise to do something.

examples.en: I have plans with a friend tonight.
examples.note: Everyday: 약속이 있다 — note this means an appointment, not a vow.

examples.en: I'll definitely keep my promise. Don't worry.
examples.note: Real situation: 약속을 지키다 + -ㄹ게요 commitment, reassuring tone.

entries.nuance: 약속(約束, literally 'bind + tie' — a tying-together of words) carries two English senses Koreans treat as one: a PROMISE (a verbal commitment) and an APPOINTMENT/plans to meet someone. So 약속이 있어요 almost always means 'I have plans (to meet a person),' which surprises English speakers expecting 'I have a promise.' The signature collocations come as an opposed pair: 약속을 지키다 (keep a promise, lit. 'protect') vs 약속을 어기다 (break it, lit. 'violate'). Contrast 약속 with 예약 豫約 (a RESERVATION/booking for a restaurant, hotel, or hospital — 식당 예약), which is institutional, and with 계획 (your own plan, no other party). The English-speaker pitfalls: the 하다 particle slip 약속이 해요 (use 약속을 해요); using 약속 for a restaurant booking (that is 예약); and saying 약속을 깨다 — while understood, the idiomatic 'break a promise' is 약속을 어기다, whereas 깨다 ('shatter') fits cancelling an appointment (약속을 깨다 = bail on plans).

Saying 약속이 해요. Making a promise is transitive — say 약속을 해요 (or the verb 약속해요).
Using 약속 for a restaurant/hotel booking. A reservation is 예약 (식당을 예약했어요); 약속 is a promise or plans with a person.
Saying 약속을 안 지켜요 is fine, but the natural antonym verb for breaking a vow is 어기다 — 약속을 어겼어요.

usagePhrases.en: I have a lot of experience
usagePhrases.note: 많다 = many; subject 이
경험하다 = to experience; object 을
쌓다 = pile up; the idiomatic verb
modifier before noun

examples.en: I have a lot of work experience.
examples.note: Simple: 경험이 많다 — experience exists in quantity (subject 이).

examples.en: I had the experience of living abroad.
examples.note: Everyday: 경험을 하다 — go through something; object 을.

examples.en: I built up a lot of experience while interning.
examples.note: Real situation: 경험을 쌓다 = accumulate experience, common on résumés.

entries.nuance: 경험(經驗, 'pass through + test/prove') is experience in both English senses: the accumulated know-how you gain over time AND a single event you live through ('a good experience'). The standout collocation is 경험을 쌓다 ('to pile up experience'), the natural way to say you build/gain experience — more idiomatic than 경험을 얻다. Contrast 경험 with 경력 經歷, which is your formal CAREER record / work history as listed on a résumé (경력 3년 = 3 years' career), whereas 경험 is broader lived experience including non-work events; and with 추억, which is a fond MEMORY you look back on emotionally, not the experience itself. Verbs: active 경험하다/경험을 하다 (object → 을) vs stative 경험이 있다/많다 (subject → 이). The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 particle error 경험이 해요 (use 경험을 해요), and mixing up 경험 with 경력 — when an interviewer asks about your 경력, they want your job history, not a nice trip you took.

Confusing 경험 with 경력. Your résumé work history is 경력 (경력이 3년); 경험 is broader lived experience.
Saying 경험을 만들어요 for gaining experience. The idiom is 경험을 쌓다 ('pile up') — 경험을 쌓아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 여권 means "passport" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 여권 (yeogwon) = "passport". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 여권을 보여주다 ("to show one's passport") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: what you do at immigration
every traveler's nightmare
the strict-rules headshot
the office-issues-it verb

examples.en: Do you have your passport?
examples.note: Bare noun + 있어요? is the everyday way to ask; no particle needed in casual speech.

examples.en: I showed my passport at the airport.
examples.note: 여권을 보여주다 is the fixed collocation for presenting it; 을 marks the object.

examples.en: I lost my passport so I went to the embassy.
examples.note: Real-trip trouble: 잃어버리다 (lost-and-can't-recover) is stronger than plain 잃다.

entries.nuance: 여권 is the official booklet that proves your identity and nationality when you cross a border. The hanja is 旅券 (旅 travel + 券 ticket/certificate), literally a 'travel certificate'. Do not confuse it with 비자 (visa), the separate permission to enter a particular country — you carry one 여권 but may need many 비자 inside it. The habitual partner verbs are 여권을 보여주다 (show), 여권을 발급받다 (get it issued), and the dreaded 여권을 잃어버리다 (lose). The English-speaker pitfall is the sound-alike 여건, which means 'conditions/circumstances' and has nothing to do with travel — keep the ㅝ in 여권 crisp, and remember it never takes a plural -s even when you mean several.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 여권을 만들다 ('make a passport') as if you craft it yourself. You don't make it; the government issues it, so the natural verb is 여권을 발급받다 (have it issued).
Mixing up 여권 and 여건. 여권 = passport, 여건 = conditions/circumstances. They differ by one vowel, so 여건이 안 돼요 means 'conditions don't allow it', not anything about a passport.

structuredNuance.t: 여권 is the official booklet that proves your identity and nationality when you cross a border.

entries.shortExplanation: 관광 means "sightseeing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 관광 (gwangwang) means "sightseeing". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 관광을 하다 ("to go sightseeing"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 관광 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the basic 하다 verb form
touring downtown
a must-see spot
a place built for visitors

examples.en: I sightsaw around Seoul.
examples.note: 관광하다 can take the place directly as object — 서울을 관광하다.

examples.en: I went city sightseeing on the weekend.
examples.note: 시내 관광 is the natural noun chunk; 을 marks it as the object of 하다.

examples.en: This city is famous for tourism.
examples.note: 관광으로 유명하다 is the set phrase for 'famous for tourism', with 으로 = 'by means of'.

entries.nuance: 관광 means going around to enjoy famous places and scenery as a relaxed visitor. The hanja 觀光 literally means 'observe (觀) the light/glory (光)' — an old phrase for admiring a region's fine sights. Contrast it with 여행 (travel), the broader word for any journey: 여행 covers the whole trip including transit and rest, while 관광 zooms in on the act of touring attractions, so a beach vacation is 여행 but circling temples is 관광. Also distinguish 출장, a business trip — never call a work assignment 관광. It pairs as 관광을 하다, 관광 명소, 관광지. The pitfall for English speakers: 관광 is the activity, not the person; the tourist is 관광객 (next entry), so you cannot say '관광 came'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a business trip 관광. 관광 is leisure touring; a trip for work is 출장, so '출장을 갔어요' (I went on a business trip), not '관광을 갔어요'.
Using 관광 to mean the person. 관광 is the activity; the visitor is 관광객. Say '관광객이 많아요' (there are many tourists), never '관광이 많아요' for crowds of people.

entries.shortExplanation: 관광객 means "tourist" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tourist" is 관광객 (gwangwanggaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 관광객이 많다 ("there are many tourists"). Watch the particle attached to 관광객 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: describing a crowded spot
visitor from abroad
crowds pour into a place
packed with visitors

examples.en: There are a lot of tourists here.
examples.note: 관광객이 많다 is the go-to phrase for a busy spot; 이 marks the subject.

examples.en: Foreign tourists are taking photos.
examples.note: 외국인 관광객 (foreign tourist) is more natural than 외국 관광객 in modern speech.

examples.en: When cherry-blossom season comes, tourists flock in.
examples.note: 관광객이 몰리다 paints a vivid 'crowds pour in' image.

entries.nuance: 관광객 is a person visiting a place for sightseeing and fun, not a resident. The hanja 觀光客 adds 客 (guest) to 관광, so it literally reads 'sightseeing guest'. The nearest near-synonyms are 여행객 and 여행자: 관광객 stresses someone touring attractions, 여행객 is the neutral 'traveler' you'd see on signs and transport notices, and 여행자 leans literary/individual ('a traveler' in a story). For people from overseas, modern Korean prefers 외국인 관광객 (foreigner-tourist) over the older 외국 관광객. It collocates with 관광객이 많다, 관광객이 몰리다, 관광객으로 붐비다. English-speaker pitfall: don't drop the 객 and say 관광 for the person — 관광 is only the activity, so the human always needs the 객 suffix.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping 객 and using 관광 for the person. 관광 = the activity, 관광객 = the tourist. For a crowd of people you must say '관광객이 많아요', not '관광이 많아요'.
Saying 외국 관광객 instead of the more natural 외국인 관광객. Adding 인 (person) — 외국인 관광객 — sounds smoother when you mean tourists who are foreign nationals.

entries.shortExplanation: 기념품 means "souvenir" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기념품 (ginyeompum) = "souvenir". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기념품을 사다 ("to buy a souvenir") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기념품, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the standard verb pair
where you stock up
buying it for the purpose of keepsake
make sure to get them

examples.en: Did you buy any souvenirs?
examples.note: Casual question drops 을; 기념품 사다 is the core collocation.

examples.en: I picked out a souvenir to give to my friend.
examples.note: 줄 (to give) + 기념품 shows the typical gift framing.

examples.en: I bought this cup as a souvenir.
examples.note: 기념품으로 = 'as a souvenir'; 으로 marks the role the item plays.

entries.nuance: 기념품 is a small item you buy on a trip to remember the place or hand out to people back home. The hanja 記念品 breaks down as 記 (record) + 念 (think of/remember) + 品 (article) — an 'article for remembering'. Compare 선물 (gift) and 특산품 (local specialty): every 기념품 you bring home can become a 선물, but 선물 is any present given for any reason, while 특산품 names the region's signature product (잠실 호두과자, 제주 감귤). The habitual partners are 기념품을 사다, 기념품 가게, 기념품으로 사다. English-speaker pitfall: don't call every trip purchase a 선물 — if its purpose is to commemorate the trip it's a 기념품, and note that the buying verb is 사다, not 'get', so '기념품을 사다' rather than a literal '얻다'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every trip purchase 선물. A keepsake meant to remember the place is 기념품; 선물 is a present given to someone. The two overlap only when you give a 기념품 as a 선물.
Using 얻다 ('obtain/receive for free') for buying souvenirs. You pay for them, so the verb is 사다 — '기념품을 샀어요', not '기념품을 얻었어요'.

entries.shortExplanation: 짐 means "luggage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 짐 (jim) means "luggage". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 짐을 싸다 ("to pack one's bags"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 짐 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the prep-for-a-trip verb
the opposite of 싸다
hand it over for storage

usagePhrases.en: to have a lot of luggage
usagePhrases.note: describing the load

examples.en: Have you finished packing?
examples.note: 짐을 싸다 'pack'; casual speech drops 을 and adds 다 (all).

examples.en: I left my luggage at the hotel and went out.
examples.note: 짐을 맡기다 = entrust/check bags; 에 marks where they stay.

examples.en: When I moved, I had a ton of stuff.
examples.note: 짐 also covers a household's belongings, not just travel bags.

entries.nuance: 짐 is a pure-Korean word (no hanja) for the bags and belongings you carry when you travel or move — often heavy. Its opposite-pair verbs are key: 짐을 싸다 means 'pack' and 짐을 풀다 means 'unpack', a fixed antonym set worth memorizing together. Compare 수하물, the formal airline/airport term you see on signs ('checked baggage'), versus everyday 짐 you'd say out loud. Note 짐 stretches beyond suitcases to all your household goods during a move, and figuratively to a 'burden' (마음의 짐, a weight on the heart). English-speaker pitfall: 짐 is uncountable like English 'luggage', so never pluralize it; and to 'pack' you say 짐을 싸다 (literally 'wrap the load'), not a literal translation of 'put in'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 짐 as countable like 'bags'. 짐 works like 'luggage' — no plural, no counting it directly. Say '짐이 많다' (there's a lot of luggage), not 'many 짐들'.
Inventing a verb for 'pack' from English. Korean uses the set phrase 짐을 싸다 ('wrap the load'); '짐을 넣다' (put luggage in) is not how you say you packed for a trip.

entries.shortExplanation: 캐리어 means "suitcase" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "suitcase" is 캐리어 (kaerieo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 캐리어를 끌다 ("to pull/wheel a suitcase"). Watch the particle attached to 캐리어 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the rolling-it verb
hand it to the airline
cabin-sized one
fill it before the trip

examples.en: The suitcase is heavy.
examples.note: Adjective 무겁다 + bare noun; everyday spoken style.

examples.en: I checked my suitcase at the airport.
examples.note: 캐리어를 부치다 is the fixed verb for checking baggage in.

examples.en: I boarded with just one carry-on suitcase.
examples.note: 기내용 (for-cabin-use) + 캐리어 names a carry-on precisely.

entries.nuance: 캐리어 is the hard, wheeled suitcase with a pull-up handle that you roll behind you. It is a loanword from English 'carrier', but beware: this is a Konglish narrowing — to an English ear 'carrier' suggests a phone carrier or aircraft carrier, while Korean 캐리어 means specifically the rolling suitcase (English calls it a 'suitcase' or 'roller bag'). Contrast it with 가방, the umbrella word for any bag, and with 여행 가방 (travel bag), which can be soft-sided. Because it has wheels, the signature verb is 캐리어를 끌다 (pull/wheel it), not 들다 (lift) — and for flying you 캐리어를 부치다 (check it). English-speaker pitfall: don't say 캐리어를 들다 unless you're literally lifting it off the ground; rolling it is always 끌다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 들다 ('lift/carry in hand') for moving a suitcase along the floor. Since it has wheels, you 끌다 (pull) it — '캐리어를 끌어요', not '캐리어를 들어요', unless you're hoisting it.
Assuming 캐리어 means any 'carrier' as in English. In Korean it only means the wheeled hard suitcase; a soft bag is 가방 or 여행 가방, not 캐리어.

entries.shortExplanation: 배낭 means "backpack" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배낭 (baenang) = "backpack". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 배낭을 메다 ("to wear/sling a backpack") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배낭, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the on-the-back verb
budget-style travel
load it up
carry a heavy one on the back

examples.en: I'm going with my backpack on.
examples.note: 배낭을 메다 'wear on the back'; -고 links to the next action.

examples.en: I put water and gimbap in the backpack.
examples.note: 에 marks where you put things; 이랑 = casual 'and'.

examples.en: In my college days I went backpacking in Europe.
examples.note: 배낭여행 (one word) is the set term for budget backpacking trips.

entries.nuance: 배낭 is the large bag you carry on your back for hiking or rough-and-ready budget travel. The hanja 背囊 is 背 (back) + 囊 (pouch/sack), literally a 'back-sack' — fitting, since the defining verb is 배낭을 메다, 'sling it on your back'. Compare 가방 (any bag, including a handbag or briefcase) and 책가방 (a school bag): 배낭 specifically sits on both shoulders and implies the outdoors or 배낭여행 (backpacking). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: English 'carry/hold a backpack' tempts learners into 배낭을 들다 (hold in the hand), but anything worn on the back takes 메다 — so 배낭을 메다 for wearing it, 들다 only if you're carrying it by the strap in your hand. Pack-it verbs are 꾸리다 and 싸다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 배낭을 들다 for wearing a backpack. Things worn on the back take 메다 — '배낭을 메요'. 들다 (hold in hand) only fits if you're literally gripping it by the strap.
Writing 배낭 여행 as two words. The trip type is the single fixed compound 배낭여행; spacing it apart looks off, like writing 'back packing'.

entries.shortExplanation: 숙소 means "lodging" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 숙소 (sukso) means "lodging". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 숙소를 잡다 ("to find/book lodging"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 숙소 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: secure a place to stay
book it in advance
lodge there overnight
move to another place

examples.en: Where's your accommodation?
examples.note: Bare noun + 어디예요? — the natural way to ask where someone's staying.

examples.en: I booked the lodging online.
examples.note: 숙소를 예약하다 = reserve a stay; 으로 marks the means (online).

examples.en: I reached my lodging late at night and fell straight asleep.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination; 숙소에 도착하다 = arrive at one's lodging.

entries.nuance: 숙소 is the general word for any place you stay overnight on a trip — hotel, guesthouse, motel, or a friend's spare room. The hanja 宿所 is 宿 (lodge/spend the night) + 所 (place), literally 'a lodging place', which is exactly its scope: it names the function, not the building type. Contrast it with the specific 호텔 (hotel) and with 집 (home), where you actually live — never call your travel stay 집. The natural collocations are 숙소를 잡다 (informally 'snag a place'), 숙소를 예약하다 (reserve), and 숙소에 묵다 (lodge there). English-speaker pitfall: 숙소 is a place, so you go 숙소에 (to it) with the 에 particle, and you 묵다 or 머물다 there — don't borrow the English 'stay' as a noun and try to make 숙소 do a verb's job.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling your travel accommodation 집. 집 is the home you live in; a temporary place to sleep on a trip is 숙소. Say '숙소에 갔어요' (I went to my lodging), not '집에' unless you mean your actual home.
Using 살다 ('live/reside') for a short stay. For lodging a few nights you 묵다 or 머물다 — '숙소에 묵어요'. 살다 implies long-term residence, which sounds wrong for a hotel.

usagePhrases.note: plan out the days
tightly-booked day
fix the timing
plans shift

examples.en: What's today's schedule like?
examples.note: Bare 일정 + 어때요? asks casually about the day's plan.

examples.en: I planned out the travel itinerary in advance.
examples.note: 일정을 짜다 = work out a schedule; 짜다 means 'weave/assemble' a plan.

examples.ko: 회의 때문에 내일 일정이 다 바뀌었어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui ttaemune naeil iljeongi da bakkwieosseoyo.
examples.en: Because of a meeting, tomorrow's whole schedule changed.
examples.note: 일정이 바뀌다 (intransitive) = the plan changes on its own; 이 marks subject.

entries.nuance: 일정 is the planned schedule of where you go and what you do, day by day — for a trip, but equally for work or events. The hanja 日程 is 日 (day) + 程 (journey/measure), an 'apportioning of the days'. Distinguish it from 시간 (time, clock time) and 계획 (plan): 시간 is just the hour on the clock, 계획 is the broad intention ('I plan to save money'), while 일정 is the concrete time-tabled sequence of items. Note the signature verb 짜다 — you 일정을 짜다 (literally 'weave a schedule'), the same verb used for 계획을 짜다. Watch the adjective 빡빡하다 / 바쁘다 for a packed itinerary. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 시간 when you mean the agenda — '오늘 시간이 어때요?' asks if someone is free, but '오늘 일정이 어때요?' asks about the day's plan.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 시간 when you mean the itinerary. 시간 = clock time / availability; 일정 = the planned agenda. '시간 있어요?' means 'are you free?', whereas '일정 어때요?' asks about the schedule.
Pairing 일정 with 만들다. Korean weaves a schedule, so the verb is 짜다 — '일정을 짜다'. '일정을 만들다' (make a schedule) sounds unnatural for trip-planning.

entries.shortExplanation: 출발 means "departure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 출발 (chulbal) = "departure". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 출발하다 ("to depart") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 출발, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the 하다 verb form
when you leave
running behind
ahead of leaving

examples.en: We're leaving now.
examples.note: 출발하다 turns the noun into 'depart'; this is how you announce setting off.

examples.en: I checked the train's departure time.
examples.note: 출발 시간 is the fixed compound for 'departure time'.

examples.ko: 눈 때문에 비행기 출발이 두 시간 늦어졌어요.
examples.romanization: nun ttaemune bihaenggi chulbari du sigan neujeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Because of snow, the plane's departure was delayed two hours.
examples.note: 출발이 늦어지다 = the departure gets pushed back; 이 marks subject.

entries.nuance: 출발 means leaving to begin a journey — the moment a person or vehicle starts moving away. The hanja 出發 is 出 (go out) + 發 (set off/issue), 'going out and setting forth'. Its exact antonym is 도착 (arrival), and the pair is worth learning together: 출발 시간 vs 도착 시간. Contrast 출발 with 떠나다, the native verb 'to leave/depart' that carries more emotional weight (leaving a person, a city, even this world), whereas 출발 is the neutral, often scheduled start of motion you hear in stations and airports. As a noun it pairs with 출발 시간, 출발 전에; as a verb 출발하다 it stands alone. English-speaker pitfall: 출발하다 is intransitive — you don't 'depart something'; say '서울에서 출발했어요' (departed from Seoul) with 에서, not an object particle.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 출발하다 as transitive like English 'depart a place'. It's intransitive — use 에서 for the origin: '공항에서 출발했어요' (departed from the airport), never '공항을 출발하다' in standard speech.
Confusing 출발 with 도착. 출발 = departure (leaving); 도착 = arrival (reaching). Swapping them flips your meaning, so '출발 시간' is when you leave, not when you get there.

entries.shortExplanation: 도착 means "arrival" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 도착 (dochak) means "arrival". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도착하다 ("to arrive"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도착 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the 하다 verb form
when you reach the place
getting in late
reach there without trouble

examples.en: I just arrived.
examples.note: 도착하다 = arrive; 방금 (just now) is its frequent partner.

examples.en: I told my friend the arrival time.
examples.note: 도착 시간 is the set compound; 한테 marks the person you inform.

examples.en: I arrived safely at the hotel late at night.
examples.note: 도착하다 takes the place with 에 — 호텔에 도착하다 — plus 무사히 'safely'.

entries.nuance: 도착 means reaching the place you traveled to — the moment a person or vehicle gets there. The hanja 到着 is 到 (reach) + 着 (attach/land), 'reaching and settling in'. Its exact antonym is 출발 (departure). The crucial grammar point is the particle: you arrive AT a place with 에 (도착하다 takes 에), so '집에 도착했어요' (arrived home). Contrast 도착하다 with 도달하다, a more abstract 'reach/attain' used for goals and figures (목표에 도달하다, reach a target) rather than physically arriving somewhere. It pairs with 도착 시간, 무사히 도착하다, 막 도착하다. English-speaker pitfall: English says 'arrive at/in', and Korean is similar but fixed on 에 — never use 에서 (which marks the location of an action or a starting point) with 도착하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

entries.shortExplanation: 입장권 means "admission ticket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "admission ticket" is 입장권 (ipjanggwon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 입장권을 사다 ("to buy an admission ticket"). Watch the particle attached to 입장권 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: get one to enter
the idiomatic 'cut a ticket' verb
reserve in advance
counting with 장

examples.en: Where do I buy admission tickets?
examples.note: 입장권을 사다 'buy a ticket'; 어디서 + 사요? asks where to get them.

examples.en: I booked museum admission tickets in advance.
examples.note: 입장권을 예매하다 = reserve tickets ahead; common for popular sites.

examples.en: Two admission tickets, please.
examples.note: 장 is the counter for flat tickets; 주세요 'please give' is how you ask at a counter.

entries.nuance: 입장권 is the ticket that lets you ENTER a venue — a museum, park, exhibition, or show. The hanja 入場券 is 入 (enter) + 場 (place/venue) + 券 (ticket), literally an 'enter-the-venue ticket'. Distinguish it sharply from 표 and 티켓: 표 is the everyday word for transport tickets (기차표 train ticket, 버스표), 티켓 (loanword) is common for concerts and movies, while 입장권 specifically grants entry to a place. The natural verbs are 입장권을 사다 and the idiomatic 입장권을 끊다 ('cut a ticket', a fixed expression for buying one), plus 예매하다 to book ahead. Count them with the flat-object counter 장: 입장권 한 장. English-speaker pitfall: don't default to 표 for a museum entry — a train ticket is 표/기차표, but entrance to a venue is the 입장권.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 표 for venue entry. 표 is mainly a transport ticket (기차표, 버스표); to get into a museum or exhibition you need an 입장권. Reserve 표 for trains and buses.
Counting tickets with 개 instead of 장. Flat paper items take the counter 장 — '입장권 두 장' (two tickets), not '입장권 두 개', which sounds off for sheet-like tickets.

entries.shortExplanation: 결혼 means "wedding; marriage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 결혼 (gyeolhon) = "wedding; marriage". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결혼을 하다 ("to get married") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결혼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 결혼 is not a verb by itself; it needs 하다, and 을 marks it as the object
use 결혼식, not 결혼, for the event you physically attend with 에
축하하다 'congratulate' is the standard verb at weddings
결혼 + 생활 'life' = the ongoing state of being married, not the ceremony

examples.en: I am married. / I got married.
examples.note: simple: the 했어요 (past of 하다) covers both the event and the resulting status

examples.en: Next month I'm going to my friend's wedding.
examples.note: everyday: for attending the ceremony switch to 결혼식 + 에, never 결혼에

examples.en: I sincerely congratulate you both on your marriage.
examples.note: real-situation: 축하드립니다 is the humble, formal congratulation you'd say or write at a wedding

entries.nuance: 결혼 (結婚, 結 'tie/bind' + 婚 'marry') is Sino-Korean and covers two ideas at once: the act of getting married and the ongoing married state, which is why English speakers must add 하다 (결혼하다) to make it a verb — 결혼 alone is a noun. The dividing line you must learn: 결혼 is the union/marriage itself, while 결혼식 (式 'ceremony') is the wedding event you attend, so you go 결혼식에 가요, never 결혼에 가요. Compare it to 신혼 'newlywed life' and 청혼 'marriage proposal' — same 婚 root, different stages. Register is fully neutral; everyone from teens to elders uses it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 결혼 like the English verb 'to marry' and producing 결혼을 만들어요 ('make a marriage') or dropping 하다 entirely; another is using 와/과 wrongly — you marry someone with ~와/과 결혼하다 (그 사람과 결혼했어요), not ~를 결혼하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 결혼을 만들어요 ('make a marriage') — 만들다 'make' never collocates here; the only correct light verb is 하다, so say 결혼을 해요/결혼했어요.
Saying 결혼에 가요 for attending a wedding — that points at the abstract marriage, not the event; you attend the ceremony, so use 결혼식에 가요.
Marking the spouse with 를 (그 사람을 결혼했어요) — you marry WITH someone, so use ~와/과: 그 사람과 결혼했어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 파티 means "party" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 파티 (pati) means "party". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 파티에 가다 ("to go to a party"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 파티 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the party as the destination you head toward
열다 'open' is the most natural host verb, slightly fancier than 하다
the invitee takes 를 and the party takes 에: 친구를 파티에 초대해요
파티 is usually preceded by the occasion (생일, 송년, 환영)

examples.en: I'm going to a party today.
examples.note: simple: 에 with a motion verb = the place you move toward

examples.ko: 주말에 우리 집에서 파티를 할 거예요.
examples.romanization: jumare uri jibeseo patireul hal geoyeyo.
examples.en: I'm going to have a party at my place this weekend.
examples.note: everyday: note 집에서 (에서 = where the action happens) vs 파티를 (the object you do)

examples.en: I invited all my friends to the year-end party.
examples.note: real-situation: 송년 파티 'year-end party' is a real December fixture; 초대하다 takes the guests as 를

entries.nuance: 파티 is a loanword from English 'party' and means a festive social gathering, usually private and fun (birthday, year-end, housewarming). Its trickiness is purely particle-based: take 에 to GO to one (파티에 가요) but 를 to HAVE/THROW one (파티를 해요/열어요), and use 에서 only when you name the location where the party happens (집에서 파티를 해요). The nearest rivals are 모임 and 잔치: 파티 is casual, Western-flavored, and fun-centered; 모임 is any get-together including serious ones (a book club is a 모임, not a 파티); 잔치 is a traditional Korean feast tied to a life milestone. Register is casual and youthful — you would not call a solemn ceremony a 파티. The main English-speaker pitfall is overusing 에서 with the motion verb 가다 (파티에서 가요 ✗): 에서 marks where something HAPPENS, so going TO the party needs 에. Also note Koreans rarely say 'party' for a simple dinner with friends — that is just a 모임 or a meal.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 파티에서 가요 for 'going to the party' — 에서 marks where an action occurs, not a destination; with 가다 you need 파티에 가요.
Using 만들다 to host (파티를 만들어요 ✗) — say 파티를 해요 or, more naturally, 파티를 열어요 'open/throw a party'.
Calling any casual meal a 파티 — for an ordinary get-together Koreans say 모임; reserve 파티 for an actual festive event.

entries.shortExplanation: 모임 means "gathering; meeting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "gathering; meeting" is 모임 (moim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 모임에 나가다 ("to attend / show up to a gathering"). Watch the particle attached to 모임 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to attend / show up to a gathering
usagePhrases.note: 나가다 'go out (to)' is the idiomatic verb for joining a regular group meeting

usagePhrases.en: to have a gathering (on the schedule)
usagePhrases.note: 이 marks 모임 as the thing that exists; 오늘 모임이 있어요
unlike 파티, 모임 CAN take 만들다 because you create the standing group itself
the qualifier (가족, 동창, 독서) tells you who gathers

examples.en: I have a gathering today.
examples.note: simple: 있다 + 이 to state that a get-together is on the schedule

examples.ko: 저는 한 달에 한 번 독서 모임에 나가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun han dare han beon dokseo moime nagayo.
examples.en: I attend a book club once a month.
examples.note: everyday: 나가다 is the go-to verb for a recurring 모임; 독서 모임 = reading gathering

examples.en: I started a small group with my friends.
examples.note: real-situation: here 모임 is the standing club you create, so 만들다 'make' is correct

entries.nuance: 모임 is native Korean, built from the verb 모이다 'to gather/come together' plus the noun-forming -ㅁ, so it literally means 'a gathering.' It is the broadest, most neutral word for people coming together for a shared purpose — a club, a reunion, a regular dinner crew — and unlike 파티 it carries no festive or Western flavor. The sharp contrast: 파티 is fun and event-like; 회식 is specifically a work-team meal; 모임 is the umbrella term that can be any of these in a low-key way, including serious or hobby groups (독서 모임 'book club', 동창 모임 'alumni reunion'). Particle logic mirrors other event nouns: 에 to attend (모임에 가요/나가요) and 이 to say one exists (모임이 있어요). The English-speaker pitfall is again 에서 with 가다 (모임에서 가요 ✗) — use 에 for the destination. A subtler point: because 모임 can name the standing group, 모임을 만들다 'form a group' is fine, whereas the same phrase sounds odd with one-off 파티.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 모임에서 가요 to mean 'go to the gathering' — 에서 marks where an action happens; the destination needs 에, so 모임에 가요/나가요.
Forcing the English word 'party' onto every 모임 — a quiet hobby club or reunion is a 모임, not a 파티; choosing 파티 makes it sound like a festive event it isn't.
Using 하다 for joining (모임을 해요 to mean 'I attend') — to attend, use 모임에 나가다/가다; 모임을 하다 means the group itself meets/holds a session.

entries.shortExplanation: 행사 means "event" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 행사 (haengsa) = "event". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 행사에 참여하다 ("to take part in an event") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 행사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to take part in an event
usagePhrases.note: 참여하다 'participate' fits the organized, formal tone of 행사 better than casual verbs
열리다 'be opened/held' is the standard passive for scheduled events; 가 marks the subject
진행하다 'proceed, conduct' is the organizer's verb (an MC 진행해요)
행사 takes a formal qualifier (기념, 개회, 졸업) signaling an official occasion

examples.en: There's an event today.
examples.note: simple: 있다 + 가 to announce a scheduled official event

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 회사에서 큰 행사를 해요.
examples.romanization: ibeon jumare hoesaeseo keun haengsareul haeyo.
examples.en: The company is holding a big event this weekend.
examples.note: everyday: 회사에서 (에서 = the organizer/place) + 행사를 (the object held)

examples.en: Many citizens took part in the commemorative event.
examples.note: real-situation: formal 습니다 register; 참여하다 suits the official, public nature of a 행사

entries.nuance: 행사 (行事, 行 'carry out/conduct' + 事 'affair/matter') is Sino-Korean and literally means 'a conducted affair' — i.e., an organized, often official or public event such as a ceremony, opening, campaign, or company function. Its tone is decidedly more formal and institutional than 파티 (fun, private) or 모임 (casual get-together): a corporate launch, a city festival's opening, a school sports day are all 행사. The near-synonym to separate from is 축제 'festival' — a 축제 is specifically a festive, celebratory event with crowds and entertainment, whereas 행사 is the neutral umbrella for any planned event, festive or solemn. Verbs run formal: 행사를 진행하다 'run an event', 행사가 열리다 'an event is held', 행사에 참여하다 'participate'. Particle pitfall as usual: 행사에 가요 for attending, never 행사에서 가요. English speakers also tend to reach for 'have a party' energy and pick casual verbs; with 행사, prefer 열다/진행하다/참여하다 to match its official register.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 행사에서 가요 for 'go to the event' — the destination particle is 에 (행사에 가요); 에서 would mark where an action happens.
Using 행사 for a private fun party — that mismatches register; a birthday bash is a 파티, while 행사 implies an organized/official function.
Pairing it with overly casual verbs like 놀다 (행사를 놀아요 ✗) — say 행사에 참여하다 'take part' or 행사를 진행하다 'run it'.

entries.shortExplanation: 축제 means "festival" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 축제 (chukje) means "festival". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 축제에 가다 ("to go to a festival"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 축제 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the festival as your destination
즐기다 'enjoy, savor' is the typical experience verb; 를 marks the object
열리다 'be held' with 가; 봄마다 축제가 열려요
축제 commonly takes a place or season qualifier (부산, 벚꽃, 지역)

examples.en: I go to a festival in autumn.
examples.note: simple: 에 destination with the motion verb 가다

examples.en: People enjoy the festival in the streets.
examples.note: everyday: 거리에서 (where it happens) + 축제를 즐기다 (enjoy as object)

examples.ko: 매년 봄에 벚꽃 축제가 열려서 관광객이 많이 와요.
examples.romanization: maenyeon bome beotkkot chukjega yeollyeoseo gwangwanggaegi mani wayo.
examples.en: A cherry-blossom festival is held every spring, so many tourists come.
examples.note: real-situation: 열리다 'be held' + the connector -어서 'so/because' linking cause and result

entries.nuance: 축제 (祝祭, 祝 'celebrate/congratulate' + 祭 'rite/festival') is Sino-Korean, literally 'a celebratory rite,' and names a public festival full of food, music, performances and crowds — university festivals (대학 축제), cherry-blossom festivals, regional seasonal festivals. The key contrast is with 행사: 행사 is the neutral, possibly solemn umbrella for any organized event, while 축제 is specifically festive and joyful, so every 축제 is a kind of 행사 but not vice versa. Don't confuse it with 잔치 either — 잔치 is a private, traditional family feast (a baby's first birthday), whereas 축제 is large, public, and community-scale. Natural collocations: 축제가 열리다 'is held', 축제를 즐기다 'enjoy', 축제에 참가하다 'take part'. Register is neutral and warm. The recurring English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 축제에 가요 to attend, not 축제에서 가요 (에서 marks the spot where an action unfolds, e.g. 축제에서 공연을 봐요 'I watch a show AT the festival').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 축제에서 가요 for 'go to the festival' — use 에 for the destination (축제에 가요); 에서 only marks where an action takes place.
Using 축제 for a small private celebration — a family milestone party is a 잔치 or 파티; 축제 implies a large public event.
Pairing it with 보다 as the default verb (축제를 봐요) — you EXPERIENCE a festival, so 축제를 즐기다 'enjoy' or 축제에 가다 'go to' is more natural (you 보다 a specific 공연 inside it).

entries.shortExplanation: 공연 means "performance; show" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "performance; show" is 공연 (gongyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공연을 보다 ("to watch a performance"). Watch the particle attached to 공연 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: you WATCH a show, so the verb is 보다 with 을, not 듣다

usagePhrases.en: to give / put on a performance
usagePhrases.note: the performer's side uses 하다: 가수가 공연을 해요
시작되다 'be started/begin' with 이; 곧 공연이 시작돼요
공연 + 시간 = the scheduled time or duration of the show

examples.en: I'm watching a show today.
examples.note: simple: 보다 'watch' + 을, the core verb for a live show

examples.ko: 그 가수가 무대에서 멋진 공연을 했어요.
examples.romanization: geu gasuga mudaeeseo meotjin gongyeoneul haesseoyo.
examples.en: That singer gave a great performance on stage.
examples.note: everyday: 무대에서 (on stage, where it happens) + 공연을 하다 (the performer's verb)

examples.ko: 공연이 곧 시작되니까 자리에 앉아 주세요.
examples.romanization: gongyeoni got sijakdoenikka jarie anja juseyo.
examples.en: The performance is about to start, so please take your seat.
examples.note: real-situation: 시작되다 'begin' + -니까 'since/so' giving the reason for the request

entries.nuance: 공연 (公演, 公 'public' + 演 'perform') is Sino-Korean, literally 'a public performance,' and covers live shows on a stage — concerts, plays, musicals, dance. The audience side uses 보다 'watch' (공연을 봐요) because it is something you see live; the performer side uses 하다 (공연을 해요). The near-synonym to separate is 콘서트 'concert,' which is narrower (a music gig), while 공연 is the broad cover term for any staged show; also distinguish 전시 'exhibition,' which you also 보다 but is static art you stroll past, not a timed live act. Useful collocations: 공연이 시작되다/끝나다 'the show starts/ends', 공연장 'performance venue'. Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 듣다 'listen' because a concert is musical (공연을 들어요 ✗) — Korean treats the whole staged event as something you 보다 'watch', not 듣다; you only 듣다 the 음악/노래 inside it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 공연을 들어요 'I listen to the show' — even for a concert the staged event is something you WATCH, so use 공연을 봐요; reserve 듣다 for the 음악/노래 itself.
Mixing up audience and performer verbs — the viewer says 공연을 봐요, the artist says 공연을 해요; using 하다 about yourself wrongly claims you're performing.
Using 콘서트 and 공연 as if identical — 콘서트 is specifically a music concert; for a play, musical, or dance use the broader 공연.
