entries.shortExplanation: 전시 means "exhibition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전시 (jeonsi) = "exhibition". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전시를 보다 ("to see an exhibition") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전시, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: you VIEW it with your eyes, so 보다 + 를
열리다 'be held' with 가; 미술관에서 전시가 열려요
관람하다 'view (formally)' is the polite museum verb, more refined than 보다
전시 takes the content type as a qualifier (사진, 미술, 특별)

examples.en: I see an exhibition on the weekend.
examples.note: simple: 보다 'see' + 를, the everyday verb for an exhibition

examples.en: I saw a photo exhibition at the art museum with a friend.
examples.note: everyday: 미술관에서 (where you view it) + 하고 'with' for the companion

examples.ko: 이번 특별 전시는 관람료가 무료라서 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: ibeon teukbyeol jeonsineun gwallamnyoga muryoraseo sarami manayo.
examples.en: This special exhibition is free of charge, so it's crowded.
examples.note: real-situation: 관람료 'viewing fee' + 무료 'free' + -라서 'because (it is)'

entries.nuance: 전시 (展示, 展 'spread out/display' + 示 'show') is Sino-Korean, literally 'to spread out and show,' meaning a display of art, photos, or objects laid out for people to view. Because it is something you take in with your eyes, the verb is 보다 'see' (전시를 봐요) or the more formal 관람하다 'view'; the full event word is 전시회 (會 'meeting/gathering'), and the place is a 전시장 or 미술관. The sharp contrast is with 공연: both pair with 보다, but a 공연 is a timed live act you sit and watch start-to-finish, while a 전시 is a static collection you wander through at your own pace. Don't confuse it with 박람회 'expo/fair' either, which is a large commercial trade show. Register is neutral. The classic English-speaker pitfall is 듣다 'listen' (전시를 들어요 ✗) — there is nothing to listen to; you 보다 it. A second pitfall is saying 전시에 가요 thinking 전시 is a place; you go to the 전시회 or 미술관, and you 보다 the 전시.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 전시를 들어요 'I listen to the exhibition' — an exhibition is purely visual; use 전시를 봐요/관람해요.
Treating 전시 as a place you go to (전시에 가요) — go to the 전시회/미술관 and then 전시를 보다; 전시 names the display, not the venue.
Confusing 전시 with 공연 because both take 보다 — a 전시 is a static display you stroll through, a 공연 is a timed live act; pick by what you're actually watching.

entries.shortExplanation: 데이트 means "date" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 데이트 (deiteu) means "date". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 데이트를 하다 ("to go on a date"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 데이트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 데이트 needs 하다 to become an action; 를 marks it as the object
신청 'application/request' + 하다 = ask for a date; 데이트 신청을 받았어요 'I was asked out'

usagePhrases.en: to go out on a date
usagePhrases.note: -하러 가다 'go in order to do'; pairs the action with going somewhere
첫 'first' is the most common modifier; the milestone outing

examples.en: I'm going on a date this weekend.
examples.note: simple: 데이트 + 하다 + 를, the basic 'go on a date' frame

examples.en: I went on a date with my boyfriend at the Han River.
examples.note: everyday: the partner takes 하고 'with', the spot takes 에서 'at'

examples.ko: 어제 좋아하는 사람한테 데이트 신청을 했어요.
examples.romanization: eoje joahaneun saramhante deiteu sincheongeul haesseoyo.
examples.en: Yesterday I asked out the person I like.
examples.note: real-situation: 한테 'to (a person)' + 데이트 신청을 하다 'ask out'

entries.nuance: 데이트 is a loanword from English 'date' and means specifically a romantic outing between two people who are dating or interested in each other; like other loanword nouns it needs 하다 to act as a verb (데이트하다). The crucial boundary for English speakers is 데이트 vs 약속: English 'date' can mean a calendar appointment, but 데이트 is ONLY romantic — a business meeting or a plan to meet a friend is an 약속 (約束 'a binding promise'), never a 데이트. The partner is marked with 하고/와/과 'with' and the place with 에서; you do NOT mark the partner with 를. Natural collocations: 데이트 신청 'asking out', 첫 데이트 'first date', 소개팅 (a separate word for a blind date). Register is casual and youthful. The headline pitfall is exactly the false friend: do not say 'I have a date with my client' as 손님하고 데이트가 있어요 — that implies romance; use 약속/미팅 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 데이트 for a business or friend appointment — 데이트 is strictly romantic; for any other plan to meet, use 약속 (or 미팅 for a work meeting).
Using the bare noun 데이트 as if it were a verb (우리 내일 데이트 가요 ✗ to mean 'let's date tomorrow') — 데이트 is only a noun, so it needs 하다: say 데이트해요 or 데이트하러 가요.
Marking the partner with 를 (여자친구를 데이트해요 ✗) — you date WITH someone, so use 하고/와/과: 여자친구하고 데이트해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 회식 means "company dinner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "company dinner" is 회식 (hoesik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 회식에 가다 ("to go to the team dinner"). Watch the particle attached to 회식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to go to the team dinner
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the company dinner as your destination
이 marks 회식 as the thing that exists; 오늘 회식이 있어요
the team's action verb is 하다; 팀이 회식을 해요
자리 'seat/occasion' = the social setting of the dinner (회식 자리에서 'at the team dinner')

examples.en: There's a company dinner today.
examples.note: simple: 있다 + 이 to announce a scheduled work dinner

examples.en: After work I'm going to the team dinner.
examples.note: everyday: 퇴근 후에 'after leaving work' + 회식에 가다 (destination 에)

examples.ko: 요즘은 회식을 강요하지 않는 회사가 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun hoesigeul gangyohaji anhneun hoesaga manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: These days more companies don't force employees to attend team dinners.
examples.note: real-situation: 강요하다 'force' + 많아지다 'become many' — reflects real workplace-culture change

entries.nuance: 회식 (會食, 會 'gather/meet' + 食 'eat') is Sino-Korean, literally 'a gathering to eat,' and means a meal that coworkers share together as a team, usually after work and often with drinks — a defining feature of Korean company culture. The contrast to nail is 회식 vs 모임: a 회식 is specifically a work/organization meal you attend as part of your job, with an implicit hierarchy (your 부장 'department head' is there), whereas a 모임 is any casual social gathering by choice. It is also not a 파티 — a 회식 centers on eating and bonding under workplace norms, not festive celebration. Common collocations: 부서 회식 'department dinner', 회식 자리 'the dinner setting', 1차/2차 (the 'first/second round' of venues a 회식 moves through). Register is neutral but the concept itself is loaded with social obligation. The English-speaker pitfall is the usual particle slip (회식에서 가요 ✗ → 회식에 가요) and assuming it is optional fun; culturally it can carry expectation, though that is changing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 회식에서 가요 to mean 'go to the team dinner' — use 에 for the destination (회식에 가요); 에서 marks where an action happens.
Equating 회식 with a casual 모임 or 파티 — 회식 specifically means a work-team meal with workplace hierarchy, not a freely chosen social party.
Using 먹다 as the framing verb for the event (회식을 먹어요 ✗) — you HOLD/ATTEND the event, so 회식을 하다 / 회식에 가다; you 먹다 the food, not the 회식.

It is also not a 파티 — a 회식 centers on eating and bonding under workplace norms, not festive celebration.
會食: 會 'gather/meet' + 食 'eat'.
The English-speaker pitfall is the usual particle slip (회식에서 가요 ✗ → 회식에 가요) and assuming it is optional fun; culturally it can carry expectation, though that is changing.

entries.shortExplanation: 잔치 means "feast; celebration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the feast as your destination
벌이다 'spread out, throw' is the vivid traditional verb for staging a big feast
열리다 'be held' with 가; 마을에 잔치가 열려요
fixed compound: 돌 'first birthday' + 잔치; a major Korean family celebration

examples.en: I'm going to a feast today.
examples.note: simple: 에 destination with 가다

examples.ko: 할머니 생신에 가족들이 모여 잔치를 했어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoni saengsine gajokdeuri moyeo janchireul haesseoyo.
examples.en: On Grandma's birthday the family gathered and held a feast.
examples.note: everyday: 생신 (honorific 'birthday') + 모이다 'gather' + 잔치를 하다

examples.en: I went to my nephew's first-birthday feast and congratulated him.
examples.note: real-situation: 돌잔치 as a fixed word + -아 주다 'do (for someone)'

entries.nuance: 잔치 is a native Korean word for a traditional feast — a celebratory gathering with plenty of food and invited guests to mark a life milestone (a baby's 돌잔치 'first birthday', a 60th birthday 환갑잔치, a wedding feast). Its flavor is warm, communal, and culturally Korean, distinct from the loanword 파티 (modern, Western, fun-centered) and from 회식 (a work meal). The sharpest contrast is 잔치 vs 축제: a 잔치 is private and family/community-based around a personal milestone, while a 축제 is a large public festival open to strangers. Note the idiom 잔치국수 'banquet noodles', the simple noodle dish historically served at feasts (especially weddings). Verbs lean traditional: 잔치를 벌이다/하다 'throw a feast', 잔치가 열리다 'is held'. Register is neutral and homey. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle (잔치에서 가요 ✗ → 잔치에 가요) and over-reaching for 파티 — calling a grandparent's milestone feast a 파티 misses the traditional, family-honoring tone that 잔치 carries.

Saying 잔치에서 가요 for 'go to the feast' — the destination needs 에 (잔치에 가요); 에서 marks where an action occurs.
Substituting 파티 for any 잔치 — 파티 is a casual Western-style party, while 잔치 implies a traditional family/community feast for a milestone; the nuance is lost.
Treating 돌잔치 as two loose words (돌 잔치를 ...) in writing — it is a fixed compound 돌잔치 referring to the one-year-old's celebration; keep it together.

entries.shortExplanation: 초대 means "invitation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 초대 (chodae) means "invitation". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 초대를 받다 ("to receive an invitation"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 초대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 'receive' is the invitee's verb; 결혼식 초대를 받았어요
the host's verb; the guest takes 를 and the place takes 에: 친구를 집에 초대해요
응하다 'comply/respond to' takes 에; the formal way to say you accept
초대 + 장 (狀 'document') = the physical invitation; 청첩장 is specifically a wedding one

examples.en: Thank you for inviting me.
examples.note: simple: 초대하다 + -아 주다 'do for me' + 고마워요 — a set thank-you for being invited

examples.en: My friend invited me to a birthday party.
examples.note: everyday: guest = 저를 (object 를), event = 파티에 (에) — the standard invite frame

examples.ko: 결혼식 초대를 받았는데 그날 못 갈 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsik chodaereul badanneunde geunal mot gal geot gatayo.
examples.en: I got a wedding invitation, but I probably can't make it that day.
examples.note: real-situation: 초대를 받다 'receive an invite' + -는데 'but/and' setting up the contrast

entries.nuance: 초대 (招待, 招 'beckon/summon' + 待 'treat/host') is Sino-Korean, literally 'to beckon and host,' and means an invitation to an event or one's home, with the implication of hosting the guest warmly. It splits cleanly by viewpoint: the host 초대를 하다/초대하다 'gives/extends' an invitation (guest = 를, place = 에), and the guest 초대를 받다 'receives' one. The near-synonym to separate is 부르다 'to call (someone over)' — 부르다 is casual and direct ('I called my friends over'), while 초대하다 is more formal and implies a proper, hosted occasion. Don't confuse 초대장 'invitation card' with 청첩장, which is specifically a wedding invitation. Register is neutral-polite. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 초대 like a thing you 'go' to (초대를 가요 ✗) — you don't go to an invitation; you 받다 'receive' it, then go to the EVENT. Another slip is dropping the directional logic: the person invited is the object (저를 초대했어요), not the destination.

Saying 초대를 가요 'go to an invitation' — an invitation is something you RECEIVE; say 초대를 받았어요, then go to the actual event.
Marking the place as the object of 초대하다 (집을 초대해요 ✗) — invite the PERSON (을/를) to the place (에): 친구를 집에 초대해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 졸업식 means "graduation ceremony" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "graduation ceremony" is 졸업식 (joreopsik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 졸업식에 참석하다 ("to attend the graduation ceremony"). Watch the particle attached to 졸업식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 참석하다 'attend (formally)' suits a ceremony better than plain 가다; takes 에
이 marks the ceremony as the thing that exists; 내일 졸업식이 있어요
열리다 'be held' with 이; 강당에서 졸업식이 열려요
졸업식 + 사진; the keepsake photo taken at the ceremony

examples.en: I'm going to a graduation tomorrow.
examples.note: simple: 에 destination with 가다

examples.ko: 다음 주에 동생 졸업식에 참석할 거예요.
examples.romanization: daeum jue dongsaeng joreopsige chamseokal geoyeyo.
examples.en: Next week I'll attend my younger sibling's graduation.
examples.note: everyday: 참석하다 'attend' + -ㄹ 거예요 'will' for a planned future

examples.ko: 졸업식이 끝나고 가족들과 사진을 많이 찍었어요.
examples.romanization: joreopsigi kkeunnago gajokdeulgwa sajineul mani jjigeosseoyo.
examples.en: After the graduation, I took lots of photos with my family.
examples.note: real-situation: -고 'and then' sequencing + 사진을 찍다 'take photos'

entries.nuance: 졸업식 (卒業式) breaks down as 졸업 (卒 'finish' + 業 'studies/work') 'graduation' plus 식 (式 'ceremony/rite'), so it literally means 'finishing-studies ceremony' — the formal event held when students complete a school. Keep the two pieces straight: 졸업 is the act/fact of graduating (졸업했어요 'I graduated'), while 졸업식 is the ceremony you attend (졸업식에 가요); the antonym ceremony for starting school is 입학식 (入學式 'entering-school ceremony'). entries.shortExplanation: 쫄깃하다 means "chewy (in a pleasant, springy way)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쫄깃하다 (jjolgitada) = "chewy (in a pleasant, springy way)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 면발이 쫄깃해요 ("The noodles are nice and chewy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쫄깃하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: The noodles are nice and chewy
usagePhrases.note: 면발 = the strands/body of the noodle; the #1 compliment for noodles
식감 (食感) = mouthfeel; this exact phrase is everywhere in food reviews
the doubled mimetic form intensifies it — even bouncier
-게 + cooking verb = cook it so it turns out chewy

examples.en: The rice cake is really chewy.
examples.note: simple praise; -네요 adds a warm 'oh, nice' reaction

examples.en: It's freshly pulled noodles, so it's super chewy.
examples.note: 갓 + V-(으)ㄴ = freshly done; pairs naturally with the doubled form

examples.ko: 사장님, 여기 문어가 안 질기고 쫄깃해서 또 왔어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnim, yeogi muneoga an jilgigo jjolgitaeseo tto wasseoyo.
examples.en: Boss, the octopus here isn't tough but pleasantly chewy, so I came back.
examples.note: real restaurant scene; 쫄깃하다 = good chewy vs 질기다 = bad tough, side by side

entries.nuance: 쫄깃하다 is the GOOD chewy — the bouncy, springy, slightly elastic bite of fresh noodles, 떡 (rice cake), or well-cooked octopus, the kind that resists your teeth just enough and snaps back. The sharp dividing line every learner needs: 쫄깃하다 is praise, while its near-opposite 질기다 is the bad 'tough/rubbery' chewy you can't bite through; an overcooked steak is 질겨요, never 쫄깃해요. It is a 의태어-flavored native (non-Sino) word, so it carries a vivid, sensory, casual feel and is used freely in everyday speech and reviews — saying 면이 쫄깃해요 to a restaurant owner is a genuine compliment about 식감 (texture). It collocates above all with 면, 면발, 떡, 식감, and the cooking adverb 쫄깃하게. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not translate 'chewy gum/tough jerky' with 쫄깃하다 (that drifts into 질기다), and never inflect it like a verb — it is an adjective, so the modifier is 쫄깃한 면, never 쫄깃하는 면.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 쫄깃하다 for tough meat you can't bite through. That negative 'tough/rubbery' sense is a different word, 질기다 — 쫄깃하다 is only the pleasant springy kind, so say 고기가 질겨요 for the bad case.
Saying 쫄깃하는 면. 쫄깃하다 is an adjective, so the present modifier is 쫄깃한 (쫄깃한 면), and you never use the verb-style -는.
Forcing 쫄깃하다 onto crispy fried food. Crispy is 바삭하다; 쫄깃하다 is specifically the elastic, springy texture, so 쫄깃한 치킨 sounds wrong unless you mean a soft, gummy crust.

entries.shortExplanation: 바삭하다 means "crispy, crunchy (light and crisp)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 바삭하다 (basakada) means "crispy, crunchy (light and crisp)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 바삭한 치킨 ("crispy fried chicken"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 바삭하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the single most-used pairing; 바삭한 + fried food
famous abbreviation of 겉은 바삭, 속은 촉촉
doubled mimetic form, intensified and very common
-게 + 튀기다, the standard way to talk about frying

examples.en: The cracker is crispy.
examples.note: simplest possible use; 과자 = snack/cracker

examples.en: The fritters just came out, so they're super crispy.
examples.note: 갓 나오다 = just came out; freshness is what makes it 바삭

examples.ko: 여기 돈까스는 겉이 바삭하고 안은 부드러워서 단골 됐어요.
examples.romanization: yeogi donkkaseuneun geochi basakago aneun budeureowoseo dangol dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The cutlet here is crispy outside and soft inside, so I became a regular.
examples.note: real-life 단골(regular) scene; 겉/안 contrast captures 겉바속촉

entries.nuance: 바삭하다 is the LIGHT, airy crunch of fried chicken, 튀김, fresh toast, crackers, or seaweed — a crisp that shatters cleanly, which is exactly why it is the headline selling point of fried food in Korea and the root of the famous slang 겉바속촉 (crispy outside, moist inside). Keep two boundaries straight: its opposite is 눅눅하다 (gone soft/soggy), so once fries lose their crisp Koreans say 눅눅해졌어요, not 바삭해요; and it must not be confused with 딱딱하다 (hard/stiff/rock-hard) — 바삭하다 breaks with a light snap, while 딱딱하다 means uncomfortably hard. It is a native sound-symbolic word (the doubled 바삭바삭 mimics the crunch), so it feels vivid and casual and pours out in mukbang and reviews. Habitual partners: 치킨, 튀김, 김, the adverb 바삭하게, and the verb 튀기다. The English-speaker pitfall: 'crunchy' in English also covers hard nuts or raw carrots (that firm crunch leans 아삭하다 for crisp veg or 딱딱하다 for hard), and of course never write the verb-style 바삭하는 — it is 바삭한 / 바삭해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using it for soggy leftover fries. Once the crispness is gone, the correct word is the opposite, 눅눅하다 — Koreans say 눅눅해졌어요, never 바삭해요, for limp food.
Applying 바삭하다 to the firm crunch of fresh vegetables. That snap is 아삭하다 (crisp like lettuce, apples, cucumber); 바삭하다 is reserved for dry, fried, baked crispness.

entries.shortExplanation: 새콤하다 means "pleasantly sour, tangy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "pleasantly sour, tangy" is 새콤하다 (saekomhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 새콤한 맛 ("a tangy, pleasantly sour taste"). Watch the particle attached to 새콤하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: appetizing sour, unlike the plain/neutral 시다
set phrase for 탕수육, 귤, gummies — extremely common
무치다 = toss with seasoning, as in 무침 dishes
-아/어지다 = became; vinegar is the prototypical source

examples.en: This tangerine is tangy.
examples.note: simplest form; fruit is the easiest 새콤하다 context

examples.en: The cold-noodle broth is tangy, so it whets my appetite.
examples.note: everyday; 입맛이 돌다 = appetite picks up, a set phrase

examples.en: Spicy mixed noodles are best when mixed tangy, that's the real flavor.
examples.note: real cooking opinion; -게 makes it adverbial 'tangily', 제맛 = the proper taste

entries.nuance: 새콤하다 is the appetizing, refreshing, mouth-watering sour of vinegar, citrus, and 무침/냉면 dishes — the sour that makes you want another bite rather than pucker up. The synonym map is the whole point: plain 시다 is just neutral 'sour' (a lemon 시다 simply reports the fact), while 시큼하다 is a sharper, sometimes off or fermented sour that can signal spoilage; 새콤하다 sits in the pleasant middle and is the only one of the three you use as praise. It is a native sound-symbolic adjective with a small, bright vowel (the 'ㅐ/ㅗ' feel diminutive and cute), which is why it reads as charming and casual and lives in the fixed combo 새콤달콤하다 (sweet-and-sour), plastered across snacks and ads. Habitual partners: 맛, 냄새 is rare here, but 무침, 냉면, 귤/레몬, and 새콤하게 (무치다/비비다) are everywhere. entries.nuance: 매콤하다 is a pleasant, appetizing spiciness — a warm, enjoyable kick — and it is built from the plain adjective 맵다 (hot/spicy) plus the diminutive-softening pattern that turns blunt taste words into cozy ones (맵다 → 매콤하다, just as 짜다 → 짭짤하다, 시다 → 새콤하다). In Korean the particle or ending next to 얼큰하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the signature use — for 찌개/탕/짬뽕
-게 + 끓이다 = simmer it so it comes out 얼큰

usagePhrases.en: warm and spicy in the stomach
usagePhrases.note: 그 따뜻한 느낌 — great for cold days/hangovers
the classic morning-after order

examples.en: The broth is hot and hearty.
examples.note: simplest use; 얼큰하다 almost always sits with 국물

examples.en: On cold days, a hot spicy broth is the best.
examples.note: everyday; -엔 = -에는, the warming-comfort nuance

examples.ko: 어제 많이 마셨는데, 얼큰한 짬뽕으로 해장할래요?
examples.romanization: eoje mani masyeonneunde, eolkeunhan jjamppongeuro haejanghallaeyo?
examples.en: I drank a lot yesterday — shall we cure the hangover with hearty jjamppong?
examples.note: real situation; 해장 = curing a hangover, 얼큰하다's natural home

entries.nuance: 얼큰하다 describes the warming, full-bodied, satisfying spicy heat of red-broth soups — 김치찌개, 짬뽕, 매운탕, 해장국 — and crucially it carries a feeling of comfort and physical warmth (몸이 풀리는 느낌), not just raw heat. The synonym contrast: 매콤하다 frames a light pleasant kick on almost any food, but 얼큰하다 is reserved for hot liquid that warms you from the inside, so the two are not swappable (a 떡볶이 sauce is 매콤하다, a steaming hangover soup is 얼큰하다). It collocates almost exclusively with 국물 / 국 / 탕 / 찌개 and the adverb 얼큰하게 (끓이다), and it is the go-to word for 추운 날 (cold days) and 해장 (curing a hangover). One register note Koreans know: 얼큰하다 also slangily means pleasantly tipsy (술이 얼큰하게 올랐다), but the food sense is the everyday default. The English-speaker pitfall: don't attach it to dry or solid food — *얼큰한 치킨 sounds wrong because there's no broth — and don't confuse it with the totally unrelated 느끼하다 (greasy/cloying); 얼큰하다 is hot-and-hearty, 느끼하다 is oily-and-heavy.

entries.explanation: "pleasantly salty, savory" is 짭짤하다 (jjapjjalhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 짭짤한 맛 ("a nice savory-salty taste"). Watch the particle attached to 짭짤하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: appetizing salty, not over-salted
-니 links cause→result: 'being salty, it's tasty'

usagePhrases.en: savory enough to go with rice
usagePhrases.note: 밥반찬 = a side dish for rice
chips, 쥐포(dried fish), nuts, etc.

examples.en: This snack is nice and salty.
examples.note: simplest use; salty snacks are the easy context

examples.en: Fries taste best when they're a little salty.
examples.note: everyday; 좀 = a little (softener), 짭짤하다 = just-right salty

examples.ko: 국이 짜지 않고 딱 짭짤하게 잘됐네요.
examples.romanization: gugi jjaji anko ttak jjapjjalhage jaldwaenneyo.

entries.nuance: 짭짤하다 is the pleasant, moreish, savory saltiness that makes you keep eating — soy-braised dishes (장조림), fries, dried squid, salty snacks — and it is the diminutive-softened, positive cousin of 짜다 (salty), formed by the same pattern that turns 맵다 → 매콤하다 and 시다 → 새콤하다. That pairing is the essential contrast: 짜다 normally means unpleasantly over-salted (a complaint), while 짭짤하다 means the salt level is just right and tasty (a compliment), so 국이 짜요 says 'too salty' but 국이 짭짤해요 says 'perfectly savory.' It collocates with 맛, 반찬, 간식, 장조림 and is the natural praise for anything you'd call a 밥도둑 (a dish so savory it makes you eat extra rice). A well-known casual bonus: 짭짤하다 also means a side income is 'tidy/decent' (부수입이 짭짤하다). The English-speaker pitfall: never use 짭짤하다 to complain that food is too salty — for that you must switch to 짜다 (짜요), because 짭짤하다 is inherently positive — and it is an adjective, so it's 짭짤한 반찬 / 짭짤해요, never 짭짤하는.

usagePhrases.note: 비린 is the modifier form of 비리다
비린내 = the fishy smell; used as much as the adjective

examples.note: simple, polite complaint about freshness

examples.note: everyday cooking tip; 비린내 (noun) in action

examples.romanization: yeogi hoeneun sinseonhaeseo hanado an biryeoyo. hanbeon deusyeo boseyo.
examples.en: The sashimi here is so fresh it's not fishy at all — give it a try.

entries.nuance: 비리다 is almost always negative: the off, fishy taste or smell of seafood — or even of blood (피 비린내) — that isn't fresh, the odor that turns people off raw fish. The companion noun 비린내 (fishy smell) is used every bit as much as the adjective, and because freshness in Korean food culture is judged largely by the *absence* of this quality, 안 비려요 ('not fishy at all') is genuine high praise for 회/생선. The synonym boundary matters: 비리다 is specific to fishy/raw-seafood odor, so don't stretch it to cover general bad smells — spoiled-rotten is 상한 냄새/쉰내, and a strong unpleasant smell in general is 고약하다. Habitual partners: 맛, 냄새, 비린내(가 나다/난다), 생선, 회, and the cooking fixes 레몬/식초/생강 (which 비린내를 잡다/없애다). The English-speaker pitfall: 비리다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 비린 (비린 맛, 비린내), never the verb-style 비리는 맛; and remember it is overwhelmingly a complaint word — you rarely use it positively except in the negated form 안 비리다.

Using 비리다 for general bad smells. It specifically means fishy / raw-seafood; for spoiled-rotten food use 상한 냄새 or 쉰내, and for a generally foul smell use 고약하다.
Treating 비리다 as a neutral descriptor of any seafood. It is a negative judgment about freshness — fresh seafood is praised as 안 비려요, so don't call good sashimi 비려요.

Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

entries.nuance: 떫다 is the dry, mouth-puckering astringency of unripe persimmons, over-steeped tea, persimmon peel, or tannic wine — the sensation that makes your tongue feel rough and tight (혀가 까끌까끌한 느낌). In Korean it is treated as its own taste category, distinct from the other basics, and 감 (persimmon) is the cultural reference point everyone reaches for. The contrast learners must lock in is 떫다 vs 쓰다 (bitter): coffee, 한약(herbal medicine), and 여주(bitter melon) are 쓰다, while an unripe persimmon or strong tea is 떫다 — they are completely different sensations, not degrees of the same thing. Its softer relative is 떨떠름하다, 'a touch astringent.' Conjugation is fully regular (no irregular stem): 떫어요, 떫은, 떫고, 떫지 않다. Habitual partners: 맛, 감, 차, 와인, and 떫은맛(이 강하다/난다). The English-speaker pitfall: English lumps 'bitter' and 'astringent' loosely, so beginners over-use 쓰다 — reserve 쓰다 for true bitterness and use 떫다 for the puckery, drying sensation — and as an adjective it never takes verb endings, so it's 떫은 감 / 떫어요, never 떫는 감 or 떫는다.

entries.shortExplanation: 깔끔하다 means "clean-tasting, crisp (of flavor); also neat/tidy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "clean-tasting, crisp (of flavor); also neat/tidy" is 깔끔하다 (kkalkkeumhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 맛이 깔끔하다 ("the flavor is clean/crisp"). Watch the particle attached to 깔끔하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: no greasy or heavy aftertaste
clear, refreshing soup — high praise
뒷맛 = aftertaste; 깔끔한 뒷맛 = finishes clean
common in drink/soup reviews

examples.en: The broth is clean-tasting.
examples.note: simplest food use; the most common collocation

examples.en: The beer goes down clean.
examples.note: everyday; 목 넘김 = the way it goes down the throat, a set drink-review phrase

examples.ko: 여기 국밥은 안 느끼하고 깔끔해서 자주 와요.
examples.romanization: yeogi gukbabeun an neukkihago kkalkkeumhaeseo jaju wayo.
examples.en: The gukbap here isn't greasy but clean-tasting, so I come often.
examples.note: real regular-customer scene; 깔끔하다 directly contrasted with 느끼하다

entries.nuance: 깔끔하다 has a literal sense of 'tidy/neat/well-organized' (방이 깔끔하다, 일 처리가 깔끔하다), but in food talk it is a heavyweight review word meaning a clean, crisp, non-greasy flavor that leaves no heavy or oily residue — the precise opposite of 느끼하다 (greasy/cloying). That opposition is the contrast to remember: a clear 국물, a light lager, or a soup that 깔끔하게 떨어진다 earns 깔끔하다, whereas fatty 삼겹살 or cream sauce is 느끼하다, so calling rich greasy food 깔끔하다 is self-contradictory. Note it is broader than 담백하다 (plain, mild, not-rich): 담백하다 emphasizes a gentle, un-strong flavor, while 깔끔하다 emphasizes a clean *finish*; they overlap but aren't identical. entries.shortExplanation: 달콤하다 means "sweet (pleasantly, with a nice sweetness)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 달콤하다 (dalkomhada) = "sweet (pleasantly, with a nice sweetness)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 달콤한 디저트 ("a sweet dessert") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 달콤하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: appetizing sweet, softer than plain 달다
set phrase, extremely common in food talk and ads
also used for smells, not only taste
figurative use: pleasant, blissful

examples.en: This cake is sweet.
examples.note: simplest use; desserts are the core 달콤하다 context

examples.en: The strawberries are sweet-and-sour, so I keep eating them.
examples.note: everyday; -게 되다 = end up doing, and the fixed combo 새콤달콤

examples.ko: 이 와인은 너무 달지 않고 은은하게 달콤해서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i waineun neomu dalji anko euneunhage dalkomhaeseo joayo.
examples.en: This wine isn't too sweet, just subtly sweet, so I like it.
examples.note: real tasting scene; 은은하게 = subtly, 달다 (can imply too-sweet) contrasted with 달콤하다

entries.nuance: 달콤하다 is a pleasant, appealing sweetness — and it is the diminutive-softened, more romantic cousin of the plain adjective 달다 (sweet), built by the same pattern that gives 시다 → 새콤하다 and 짜다 → 짭짤하다. That derivation is exactly the contrast to teach: 달다 is neutral and can carry a 'too sweet / cloying' edge (너무 달아서 못 먹겠어요), while 달콤하다 frames the sweetness as just-right and pleasing, which is why it praises desserts, fruit, and even aromas and lives in the combos 새콤달콤하다 (sweet-sour) and 달콤짭짤하다 (sweet-salty, salted-caramel style). It also has a strong figurative life: 달콤한 휴식 (a blissful rest), 달콤한 말 (sweet/honeyed words), 달콤한 사랑. Habitual partners: 디저트, 향, 케이크, 초콜릿, and the doubled-up combos. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 달콤하다 for sickly, overpowering sweetness — for 'too sweet to eat' you must switch to the base word (너무 달아서 못 먹겠어요), because 달콤하다 is inherently positive — and it is an adjective, so it's 달콤한 / 달콤해요, never 달콤하는.

Saying 달콤해서 못 먹겠어요 for sickly-sweet food. 달콤하다 is positive 'pleasantly sweet'; for 'too sweet to eat' switch to the base adjective: 너무 달아서 못 먹겠어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 시큼하다 means "sharply sour, sour (sometimes off)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 시큼하다 (sikeumhada) means "sharply sour, sour (sometimes off)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 시큼한 냄새 ("a sharp sour smell"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 시큼하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: can hint that food has turned
-맛이 나다 = to have a … taste
well-fermented or over-fermented
doubled mimetic form for emphasis

examples.en: The kimchi is sharply sour.
examples.note: simple; fermented foods are the core context

examples.ko: 우유에서 시큼한 냄새가 나요. 상한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: uyueseo sikeumhan naemsaega nayo. sanghan geot gatayo.
examples.en: The milk smells sour. I think it's gone bad.
examples.note: everyday; 상하다 = to spoil, the warning-sign use

examples.ko: 이 빵 시큼한 거 보니 사워도우인가 봐요.
examples.romanization: i ppang sikeumhan geo boni sawodouinga bwayo.
examples.en: This bread tastes sour, so it must be sourdough.
examples.note: real situation; -나 보다 = must be, here the sour is intentional/positive

entries.nuance: 시큼하다 is a sharper, more piercing sour than the appetizing 새콤하다 — context decides whether it's good or a warning. The three-way map is the whole lesson: plain 시다 is neutral 'sour'; 새콤하다 is the pleasant, mouth-watering tang you praise; and 시큼하다 is the strong, biting sour that can be desirable in well-fermented 묵은지 or sourdough but also flags food starting to spoil (sour milk, off rice). So the same word can be positive (묵은지라 시큼해요 = nicely aged) or a red flag (시큼한 냄새가 나요 = this might be off), and the listener reads it from context. It is a native sound-symbolic adjective; the heavier vowel (ㅣ/ㅡ) versus 새콤하다's bright vowel is itself part of why it feels sharper and edgier. Habitual partners: 냄새, 맛, 김치/묵은지, 우유, and 시큼하게/시큼한. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 시큼하다 for the gentle tang of citrus, dressing, or 무침 — that pleasant sour is 새콤하다 — and as an adjective it's 시큼한 / 시큼해요, never 시큼하는.

Using 시큼하다 when you mean the pleasant tangy sour of citrus or a dressing. That appetizing sour is 새콤하다; 시큼하다 is the sharper, sometimes-off sour.
It's an adjective. Use 시큼한 / 시큼해요, not 시큼하는.

entries.english: tough, chewy in a bad way (hard to chew)
entries.shortExplanation: 질기다 means "tough, chewy in a bad way (hard to chew)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tough, chewy in a bad way (hard to chew)" is 질기다 (jilgida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 고기가 질기다 ("the meat is tough"). Watch the particle attached to 질기다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the single most common complaint use
negative; the opposite of 쫄깃한 식감
씹히다 = to be chewed (passive)
the standard praise for good meat

examples.en: This meat is tough.
examples.note: simplest complaint form

examples.en: I cooked it longer and it actually got tougher.
examples.note: everyday; 오히려 = on the contrary, -아/어지다 = became

examples.ko: 사장님, 죄송한데 이 고기가 너무 질겨서 못 먹겠어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnim, joesonghande i gogiga neomu jilgyeoseo mon meokgesseoyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, sorry, but this meat is so tough I can't eat it.
examples.note: real complaint-to-staff scene; polite framing softens a negative judgment

entries.nuance: 질기다 is the BAD chewy: meat or seafood so tough and rubbery it's hard to bite through — and it is the exact negative counterpart of the praised 쫄깃하다 (pleasantly springy/elastic). Locking this pair down is the priority, because English 'chewy' maps onto both and learners constantly swap them: an overcooked steak or stringy squid is 질겨요, while fresh bouncy noodles or well-cooked octopus are 쫄깃해요 — same English word, opposite verdict. It collocates with 고기, 식감, 오징어/문어, and the contrast 질기지 않고 부드럽다 (not tough but tender). Note the conjugation is regular (있다/먹다-type, not an irregular stem): 질겨요, 질긴, 질기고, and it becomes 질겨지다 ('to get tougher'). Beyond food, 질기다 also describes something stubborn and persistent — 질긴 인연 (a tie that won't break), 목숨이 질기다 (hard to kill / tenacious). The English-speaker pitfall: never use 질기다 as praise the way 'chewy' can be positive in English — if you mean the good springy bite, you must switch to 쫄깃하다 — and it is an adjective, so it's 질긴 고기 / 질겨요, never 질기는.

Swapping 질기다 and 쫄깃하다. 질기다 is the negative 'tough/rubbery,' 쫄깃하다 is the positive 'springy/elastic' — English 'chewy' covers both, so choose by whether it's a complaint or praise.
Treating it as a verb. The forms are 질긴 고기 / 질겨요, not 질기는.
Using 질기다 for the good bouncy bite of noodles or 떡. That springy, pleasant texture is 쫄깃하다 — 질기다 only means it's unpleasantly hard to chew.

entries.shortExplanation: 비자 means "visa" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 비자 (bija) = "visa". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비자 종류 ("type of visa") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 비자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 종류 = category; the first thing every form and officer asks
받다 is the natural verb of receiving, never 가지다
만료(滿了)되다 = run out fully; the word printed at immigration
신청하다 = to apply; what you do before you 받다

examples.en: I'm on a student visa.
examples.note: Simplest form: just name the purpose + 비자 + 예요, no D-codes in daily speech.

examples.en: My visa expires next month.
examples.note: 만료돼요 is the spoken contraction of 만료되어요; note 비자가/는, not 비자를, with 만료되다.

examples.en: What visa did you enter the country on?
examples.note: An officer's question; the particle 로 marks the visa as the means of entry, and 들어오다 = come in.

entries.nuance: 비자 is the everyday English loanword (from 'visa'); the native-style Sino-Korean term 사증(査證, literally 'inspect-certify') exists on official paperwork but nobody says it aloud. The nearest thing learners confuse it with is 여권 (passport): a 여권 is the booklet that proves who you are, while a 비자 is the permission stamped or linked to it that lets you enter and stay — you can hold a 여권 with no valid 비자. In conversation Koreans name the purpose and attach 비자 (워홀 비자, 결혼 비자, 학생 비자) instead of the official D-2/F-6 codes. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb: English 'have a visa' tempts you into 비자를 가지다, but Korean uses 비자를 받다 (receive) to obtain one and 비자가 있다 (exist) to possess one; pair it with officials' words 만료되다 (expire) and 연장하다 (extend).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비자를 가지다 for 'get/have a visa' — this is a direct translation of English 'have'; use 비자를 받다 to obtain it or 비자가 있어요 to say you possess one.
Confusing 비자 (the entry/stay permission) with 여권 (the passport booklet); an officer asking about your 비자 does not want to see only your 여권 photo page.
Calling it 사증 in conversation because a dictionary lists it; 사증 is written-only — say 비자 when you speak.

entries.shortExplanation: 체류 means "stay (legal residence in a country)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 체류 (cheryu) means "stay (legal residence in a country)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 체류 자격 ("status of stay / residence status"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 체류 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: your official visa category; the term officers use
기간 = duration; how long you may legally remain
불법(不法) = unlawful; the status to avoid at all costs
pairs with 연장; the most common foreigner errand

examples.en: What is your residence status?
examples.note: The set polite formula 어떻게 되세요? softens a request for official personal info.

examples.en: I extended my period of stay by six months.
examples.note: 기간 + 연장하다 is the standard pairing; 6개월 marks the added length.

examples.ko: 기간이 지나면 불법 체류가 되니까 꼭 연장하세요.
examples.romanization: gigani jinamyeon bulbeop cheryuga doenikka kkok yeonjanghaseyo.
examples.en: If the period passes it becomes overstaying, so be sure to extend.
examples.note: 되다 = become; this shows 체류 inside the real consequence learners fear.

entries.nuance: 체류(滯留) is built from 滯 'stagnate/linger' + 留 'remain', so it literally paints someone staying put in a place — and it is pure bureaucratic register, almost never used alone but locked into fixed compounds (체류 자격, 체류 기간, 체류 연장). The everyday verb learners reach for is 머무르다 'to stay/linger', and that is exactly the dividing line: you 머무르다 at a hotel or a friend's house for a night, but your legal right to be in the country is your 체류 — an abstract immigration status, not a physical act of lodging. You will meet this word constantly on HiKorea (하이코리아) and at the 출입국 office, and the most important phrase is 체류 자격, your visa type. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the verb 'stay': you cannot say 호텔에서 체류했어요 for 'I stayed at a hotel' (use 묵었어요/머물렀어요); 체류 belongs to paperwork, not to where you slept.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 체류 for a short tourist 'stay at a hotel' — that physical sense is 머무르다/묵다 or the noun 숙박; 체류 is your legal residence status only.
Saying 체류증 for the card — there is no such card; the physical card is the 외국인등록증, while 체류 자격 is the abstract status it certifies.
Dropping the compound and saying just 체류 in a form blank; offices expect 체류 자격 or 체류 기간, since 체류 rarely stands alone.

structuredNuance.t: 체류 is pure bureaucratic register, almost never used alone but locked into fixed compounds (체류 자격, 체류 기간, 체류 연장). It is your legal right to be in the country — an abstract immigration status, not a physical act of lodging. You will meet this word constantly on HiKorea (하이코리아) and at the 출입국 office, and the most important phrase is 체류 자격, your visa type.

The everyday verb learners reach for is 머무르다 'to stay/linger', and that is exactly the dividing line: you 머무르다 at a hotel or a friend's house for a night, but your legal right to be in the country is your 체류.
체류(滯留) is built from 滯 'stagnate/linger' + 留 'remain', so it literally paints someone staying put in a place.
The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the verb 'stay': you cannot say 호텔에서 체류했어요 for 'I stayed at a hotel' (use 묵었어요/머물렀어요); 체류 belongs to paperwork, not to where you slept.

entries.shortExplanation: 연장 means "extension (of a period/deadline)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "extension (of a period/deadline)" is 연장 (yeonjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 연장 신청 ("application for an extension"). Watch the particle attached to 연장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 신청 = applying; the core counter pairing
the reason most foreigners ever use this word
the 하다-verb you say at the desk or type online
same word works for housing leases and jobs

examples.en: I'd like to extend my visa.
examples.note: Simplest counter line: noun + 연장하다 + 고 싶어요, no extra words needed.

examples.en: I extended the contract by one more year.
examples.note: 더 = 'more'; shows 연장 reaching beyond visas into housing leases.

examples.ko: 연장 신청이 거절될 수도 있어서 서류를 잘 준비하세요.
examples.romanization: yeonjang sincheongi geojeoldoel sudo isseoseo seoryureul jal junbihaseyo.
examples.en: The extension application could be rejected, so prepare your documents well.
examples.note: 거절되다 = be rejected; -ㄹ 수도 있다 hedges the real risk.

entries.nuance: 연장(延長) means 延 'prolong' + 長 'long', so it literally stretches the length of something time-bound — visas, lease contracts (계약 연장), library loans, deadlines. The word it is constantly confused with is 갱신(更新) 'renewal': 연장 adds more time onto the same existing thing, whereas 갱신 issues a fresh new one to replace the old (you 갱신 a passport or membership card, you 연장 the period you may stay). For immigration it is almost always 체류 연장 or 비자 연장, and the working verb is 연장하다, what you say at the counter. The English-speaker pitfall is the bare imperative: copying 'extend it, please' as 연장 주세요 sounds broken because 연장 is a noun, not the thing being handed over — say 연장하고 싶어요 ('I want to extend') or 연장 신청하러 왔어요 ('I came to apply for an extension') instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 연장 (adding more time to the same document) with 갱신 (replacing it with a newly issued one) — you 연장 your stay but 갱신 an expired card.
Saying 연장 주세요 at the counter as if 연장 were an object; use the verb 연장하고 싶어요 or 연장 신청하러 왔어요.
Pairing it as 연장을 받다 by analogy with 비자를 받다; you 연장하다 (do the extending) or get 연장 신청 승인 (approval), you do not 'receive an extension'.

entries.shortExplanation: 전입신고 means "move-in report (registering a new address)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전입신고 (jeonipsingo) = "move-in report (registering a new address)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전입신고를 하다 ("to file a move-in report") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전입신고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 is the verb; you 'do' the report
기한 = due date; within 14 days of moving
마치다 = complete; what you confirm afterward

usagePhrases.en: to go file a move-in report
usagePhrases.note: destination is the 주민센터

examples.en: When you move, you have to file a move-in report.
examples.note: Core rule in one line; -으면 = 'when/if', -아야 되다 = obligation.

examples.en: I'm on my way to the community center to file a move-in report.
examples.note: 가는 길이에요 = 'on the way to'; 주민센터 is the place you go.

examples.ko: 전입신고를 해야 확정일자를 받아서 보증금을 지킬 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeonipsingoreul haeya hwakjeongiljareul badaseo bojeunggeumeul jikil su isseoyo.
examples.en: Only after filing the move-in report can you get a fixed-date stamp and protect your deposit.
examples.note: -아야 = 'only if/after'; ties 전입신고 to protecting your 보증금.

entries.nuance: 전입신고(轉入申告) is a four-character compound: 轉 'turn/shift' + 入 'enter' + 申 'state' + 告 'report', literally 'report of shifting-in', i.e. declaring to your new district office that you have moved IN. Learners blur it with its mirror-image 전출(轉出) 'moving OUT': in practice you almost never file 전출 yourself — registering your new address with 전입신고 automatically cancels the old one, so 전입신고 is the action that matters. It is a legal must-do at the local 주민센터 within 14 days of moving, and for renters it unlocks 확정일자, the date-stamp that legally protects your deposit, which is why locals treat it as urgent rather than optional. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: this is a 신고 (a formal report you 하다), so you say 전입신고를 하다, never 전입신고를 쓰다 or 만들다 as if writing a document — and missing the 14-day 기한 can bring a fine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 전입신고 (reporting you moved IN) with 전출 (moving OUT) — you normally only file 전입신고, which auto-cancels your old address.
Treating it as optional paperwork; it is legally required within 14 days and missing the 기한 can incur a fine, plus you lose deposit protection without it.
Saying 전입신고를 쓰다 or 만들다; a 신고 is an act you perform, so the verb is 하다 — 전입신고를 하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 등본 means "certified copy (esp. resident registration extract)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 등본 (deungbon) means "certified copy (esp. resident registration extract)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주민등록등본 ("resident registration extract"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 등본 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the full name; 등본 is everyone's short form
떼다 is THE colloquial verb for official documents
통 = the counter for certificates/documents
발급 = the formal act behind 떼다

examples.en: Please issue me just one copy of the extract.
examples.note: Counter line: 한 통만 = 'just one copy'; staff 떼 주다 it for you.

examples.en: My company says to submit a resident extract.
examples.note: 제출하래요 = contracted 제출하라고 해요, '(they) tell me to submit'.

examples.ko: 등본은 정부24에서 인터넷으로 떼서 출력하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: deungboneun jeongbu24eseo inteoneseuro tteseo chullyeokamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can pull the extract online at Gov24 and just print it.
examples.note: -에서 marks the site; 떼서 출력하다 = issue then print, the modern way.

entries.nuance: 등본(謄本) means 謄 'transcribe/copy out' + 本 'original document', i.e. a certified transcript of an original register; in daily life it is short for 주민등록등본, the household sheet listing everyone registered at your address, demanded constantly for jobs, bank accounts, and contracts. The document people mix it up with is 초본(抄本) 'an excerpt copy' (抄 'extract'): the 등본 shows the whole household at one address, while the 초본 traces one individual's personal history including past addresses — offices specify which one they need, so the difference is not cosmetic. The signature English-speaker pitfall is the verb: you do not 받다 ('receive') a 등본, you 떼다 it — 떼다 literally means 'to peel/detach off', the idiomatic word for pulling an official copy, as in 등본 떼러 가요 ('I'm going to get an extract'). Foreigners get the parallel 외국인등록사실증명, but everyone still says 등본 colloquially.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 받다 ('receive') for getting the document; natives say 등본을 떼다, using 떼다 'detach/pull' for official copies.
Confusing 등본 (the whole household at an address) with 초본 (one person's address history); offices ask for one specifically and the wrong one gets rejected.
Forgetting the counter 통; you ask for 등본 한 통, not 등본 하나, when requesting copies at the counter or kiosk.

entries.shortExplanation: 출입국 means "immigration (office); entry and exit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "immigration (office); entry and exit" is 출입국 (churipguk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 출입국 사무소 ("immigration office"). Watch the particle attached to 출입국 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: full name; people shorten it to 출입국
the office handling visas and registration
심사 = screening at the airport
the older official name still seen on signs

examples.en: Foreigner registration is done at the immigration office.
examples.note: -에서 marks where the action happens; 외국인등록 is the process itself.

examples.en: Book your immigration appointment in advance on HiKorea.
examples.note: 미리 = 'beforehand'; you almost always need a reservation first.

examples.ko: 공항 출입국 심사대 앞에서 여권을 미리 꺼내 두세요.
examples.romanization: gonghang churipguk simsadae apeseo yeogwoneul miri kkeonae duseyo.
examples.en: Have your passport out before the airport passport-control desk.
examples.note: 심사대 = inspection desk; 꺼내 두다 = take out and keep ready.

entries.nuance: 출입국(出入國) literally stacks 出 'exit' + 入 'enter' + 國 'country', so the word itself means 'leaving-and-entering the country' and serves as the everyday short name for the 출입국·외국인청/사무소, where foreigners handle visas, registration, and extensions. The trap is that learners flatten it with its one-directional halves 출국 (出國, departing) and 입국 (入國, arriving): 출입국 is the round-trip concept and, by extension, the office/process, whereas 출국 and 입국 each point one way only — you do 출국 심사 when leaving and 입국 심사 when arriving, but the building is the 출입국. At the airport the same root appears in 출입국 심사 (passport control). The practical English-speaker pitfall is assuming you can simply walk in like a U.S. DMV: most 출입국 civil tasks require a 하이코리아 (HiKorea) online reservation first, so 예약하다 before 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming you can walk in without an appointment — most 출입국 tasks require a 하이코리아 reservation booked in advance.
Confusing 출입국 (the office and the two-way concept) with 출국 (departing) and 입국 (arriving), which are strictly one-directional.
Calling the airport line itself 출입국; the act there is 출입국 심사 (inspection), while plain 출입국 in town means the immigration office.

entries.shortExplanation: 재발급 means "reissuance (of a lost/damaged document)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 재발급 (jaebalgeup) = "reissuance (of a lost/damaged document)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 재발급 신청 ("application for reissuance") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 재발급, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 신청 = applying; the standard pairing
for bank cards, ID cards, transit cards
use 받다 when you are the recipient
what you say to the staff member

examples.en: I lost my card, so I have to get it reissued.
examples.note: 잃어버리다 = lose; 재발급받다 keeps you as the receiver of the action.

examples.en: How many days does debit-card reissuance take?
examples.note: 며칠 걸려요? = 'how many days does it take', the natural timing question.

examples.ko: 외국인등록증을 도난당해서 재발급 신청서를 작성하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: oegugindeungnokjeungeul donandanghaeseo jaebalgeup sincheongseoreul jakseonghago isseoyo.
examples.en: My residence card was stolen, so I'm filling out the reissuance application.
examples.note: 도난당하다 = have something stolen; shows the realistic reason for 재발급.

entries.nuance: 재발급(再發給) prefixes 再 'again' onto 발급 '발(發) issue + 급(給) grant', so it literally means 'issuing-and-granting again' — what you request when a document is lost, stolen, or damaged and a replacement must be produced: bank cards, ID, residence card, transit card. The word it must be told apart from is 갱신(更新) 'renewal': 재발급 replaces a copy that is gone or broken (the underlying right is unchanged), while 갱신 is for something whose validity has simply expired and needs updating — so a stolen card is 재발급 but an expired one is 갱신. The recurring English-speaker pitfall is voice/perspective: the citizen says 재발급받다 ('have it reissued', receiver) or asks staff 재발급해 주세요 ('please reissue it'), but learners over-apply 재발급하다 to themselves, which actually describes the office that does the issuing, not the person receiving it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 재발급 when a document merely expired — that situation is 갱신 (renewal); 재발급 is specifically for lost, stolen, or damaged ones.
Saying 재발급하다 about yourself; the citizen 재발급받다 (receives), while the office 재발급하다 / 재발급해 주다 (issues).
Pairing it as 재발급을 사다 because you pay a fee; you 재발급받다 and separately 수수료를 내다 — the fee is paid, the document is not bought.

entries.shortExplanation: 신청서 means "application form" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 신청서 (sincheongseo) means "application form". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 신청서를 작성하다 ("to fill out an application form"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 신청서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to fill out an application form
usagePhrases.note: 작성하다 is the correct office verb, not 쓰다
제출하다 = hand in; casual equivalent is 내다
양식 = the blank form layout you fill in
부 = the counter for copies of documents

examples.en: Please fill out the application form here.
examples.note: The single most common counter instruction; 작성하다 = fill out formally.

examples.en: Don't forget to sign the application form.
examples.note: -에 marks where you sign; 잊지 마세요 = 'don't forget'.

examples.ko: 작성한 신청서는 저쪽 창구에 내시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: jakseonghan sincheongseoneun jeojjok changgue naesimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can submit the completed form at that window over there.
examples.note: 내다 = the everyday word for 제출하다; 창구 = service window.

entries.nuance: 신청서(申請書) is 申 'state' + 請 'request' + 書 'document', literally a 'document stating a request', i.e. any fill-in application form, from visa extensions to library cards. The piece learners confuse it with is plain 신청 (申請), the act of applying: 신청 is what you DO (online or verbally), while the 신청서 is the physical/PDF sheet you complete — '신청을 했어요' means you applied, '신청서를 작성했어요' means you filled out the form. The natural collocation verb is 작성하다 ('compose/fill out'), which sounds far more correct in offices than the literal 쓰다 'write'. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 쓰다 reflex from 'write a form', plus the handing-in step: staff tell you 내세요 or 제출하세요 to submit it, so the full life cycle is 신청서를 작성하다 → 제출하다, and you will hear 신청서 작성해 주세요 at virtually every Korean counter.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 쓰다 ('write') instead of 작성하다 ('fill out') for completing a form; 작성하다 is the standard, more correct office verb.
Confusing 신청서 (the form you complete) with 신청 (the act of applying) — 신청을 하다 = apply, 신청서를 작성하다 = fill out the form.
Counting forms with 개; documents take the counter 부, so it is 신청서 한 부, not 신청서 한 개.

처(處) = place; where you hand things in
the tracking number you get after applying

usagePhrases.en: for the intake to be processed
usagePhrases.note: passive; your paperwork is now in the system

examples.en: Until what time can documents be submitted?

examples.en: Once the intake is complete, we'll notify you by text.
examples.note: 완료되다 = be completed; 알려 드리다 is the humble 'inform you'.

examples.ko: 병원에 도착하면 먼저 접수처에서 접수하고 기다리세요.
examples.romanization: byeongwone dochakamyeon meonjeo jeopsucheoeseo jeopsuhago gidariseyo.
examples.en: When you reach the hospital, first register at the intake desk and wait.

entries.nuance: 접수(接受) joins 接 'receive/connect' + 受 'accept', literally 'receiving and accepting', the bureaucratic word for an office taking in and logging your application or documents — at a clinic or government window you 접수하다 first, then wait for your number, and 접수가 됐어요 means your paperwork is officially in the system. Register is mildly formal but heard everywhere from hospitals to immigration desks.

Saying 접수받다 when you mean to submit your own documents; the applicant 접수하다 (or 접수시키다), the office 접수받다.

usagePhrases.en: to get issued / to be issued (to me)
usagePhrases.note: use this when you are the recipient
the request you make to staff
즉시 = on the spot; e.g. instant cards at a kiosk
passive; 'it gets issued' on its own

examples.en: The residence card is issued a few days later.
examples.note: 발급되다 = the passive 'gets issued'; 며칠 후에 = 'a few days later'.

examples.en: I'd like to be issued one copy of the certificate.
examples.note: 발급받다 keeps you as the receiver; 한 통 uses the document counter.

examples.ko: 여기서는 임시 카드를 즉시 발급해 드려요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseoneun imsi kadeureul jeuksi balgeupae deuryeoyo.
examples.en: Here we issue a temporary card on the spot.

entries.nuance: 발급(發給) is 發 'send out/issue' + 給 'grant/supply', literally 'issuing and supplying', the official act of producing and handing over a card or certificate — it covers IDs, residence cards, and every kind of 증명서. It sits in a tight family learners scramble: 발급 is issuing a brand-new document, 재발급 is reissuing one that was lost or damaged, and 갱신 is renewing one that expired — three different counter requests, not synonyms. The persistent English-speaker pitfall is voice: like a verb that flips with perspective, the citizen says 발급받다 ('have it issued', receiver) or asks 발급해 주세요, the office says 발급하다 / 발급해 드리다, and the document itself 발급되다 / 발급됩니다 (passive). Saying 제가 발급했어요 to mean 'I got one issued' wrongly casts you as the issuing office. The word is plastered on every Korean kiosk and counter (즉시 발급, 무인 발급).

Saying 발급하다 about yourself; the citizen 발급받다 (receives) while the office 발급하다 / 발급해 주다 (issues).
Mixing up 발급 (issuing a new one), 재발급 (reissuing a lost/damaged one), and 갱신 (renewing an expired one) — they are three distinct requests.
Using the active 발급해요 when describing the document; it gets issued, so use the passive 발급돼요 / 발급됩니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 수수료 means "service/processing fee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수수료 (susuryo) means "service/processing fee". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수수료를 내다 ("to pay the fee"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수수료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 is the verb for paying a charge

usagePhrases.en: for a fee to be incurred
usagePhrases.note: 들다 = to cost/be incurred

usagePhrases.en: for a fee to be added on
usagePhrases.note: 붙다 = to be tacked on (e.g. transfers)
무료(無料) = free of charge

examples.en: How much is the fee?
examples.note: The simplest counter question; 얼마예요? = 'how much is it'.

examples.en: A fee gets tacked on when you transfer money.
examples.note: 붙다 = be added; 좀 softens it to 'a bit'.

examples.ko: 이 신청은 수수료가 따로 없어서 무료예요.
examples.romanization: i sincheongeun susuryoga ttaro eopseoseo muryoyeyo.
examples.en: There's no separate fee for this application, so it's free.
examples.note: 따로 없다 = 'there isn't a separate one'; ties to 무료.

entries.nuance: 수수료(手數料) is a wonderfully literal compound — 手 'hand' + 數 'number/effort' + 料 'fee', i.e. a fee for the hand-labor/effort of processing — the catch-all word for an administrative or service charge on bank transfers, card reissuance, document issuance, and booking platforms. It must be separated from two neighbors: 요금(料金) is a usage charge for consuming a service (fares, electricity, phone bills), and 세금(稅金) is tax paid to the government — so a transfer's processing cost is 수수료, your monthly data plan is 요금, and VAT is 세금. Collocationally you 수수료를 내다 (pay it) and it 붙다 / 들다 (gets added / is incurred). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb 'buy': 'I bought... a fee' makes no sense, so never 수수료를 사다 — fees are paid (내다) or incurred (들다), and many counters proudly advertise 수수료 무료.

Confusing 수수료 (a processing/service charge) with 요금 (a usage charge like fares and bills) or 세금 (tax to the government).
Saying 수수료를 사다 because in English you 'pay for' things; you 수수료를 내다 (pay) or it 든다 (is incurred), never 'buy' it.
Assuming any fee is 수수료; a fine is 벌금 and a fare is 요금 — 수수료 is specifically for processing a service or document.

usagePhrases.note: what staff ask you to do
확인 = checking; announced before a task
지참하다 = bring with you (formal)
the everyday polite question form

examples.en: Could you show me your ID, please?
examples.note: 보여 주시겠어요? is a very polite request; 좀 softens it further.

examples.en: For foreigners, the residence card serves as the ID.
examples.note: Explains the foreigner equivalent; A이/가 B예요 = 'A is B'.

examples.ko: 신분증을 안 가져와서 술을 못 샀어요.

entries.nuance: 신분증(身分證) is 身 'body/person' + 分 'standing/status' + 證 'certificate', literally a 'certificate of one's personal standing', and it is the umbrella term for any government photo ID — 주민등록증, 운전면허증, 여권, or for residents the 외국인등록증. The contrast learners need is that 신분증 is the category, not a specific card: a 주민등록증 (the resident registration card Koreans carry) is one kind of 신분증, but so is your passport, so an officer asking for 신분증 is not demanding a Korean card specifically. You will be asked 신분증 있으세요? at banks, pharmacies, offices, and when buying alcohol or cigarettes, and many counter tasks (접수, 발급) require 신분증 확인 first, so always carry one. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: assuming 신분증 means only the Korean 주민등록증 (your 외국인등록증 or 여권 counts), and confusing the near-homophone 신청서 (application form) with 신분증 (ID) — they sound alike to beginners but are entirely different objects.

entries.shortExplanation: 통장 means "bankbook, bank account" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 통장 (tongjang) = "bankbook, bank account". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 통장을 만들다 ("to open a bank account") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 통장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Korean uses 만들다 (make), not 열다 (open), for accounts

usagePhrases.en: to put money in the account
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the account as the destination of the money
the account your monthly pay lands in; a fixed compound
사본 (寫本) = duplicate copy, often required for paperwork

examples.en: I'd like to open one bank account.
examples.note: 하나 + 만들다 is the plain counter way to say 'open one'

examples.en: My salary came into my account.
examples.note: 들어오다 (come in) is the verb for money arriving

examples.ko: 회사에서 통장 사본을 달라고 했는데 어떻게 뽑아요?
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo tongjang saboneul dallago haenneunde eotteoke ppobayo?
examples.en: My company asked for a copy of my bankbook — how do I print one?
examples.note: real payroll-setup situation; 뽑다 = print out

entries.nuance: 통장 (通帳, 'pass-through ledger') is literally the small paper passbook a bank prints transactions in, but in everyday speech it simply means your bank account — 월급 통장, 통장에 돈이 없어요. Its near-synonym 계좌 (口座) is the formal, technical word that appears on official forms and app menus; the dividing line is register, not meaning, and a crucial split shows up in compounds: the account NUMBER is always 계좌번호, never '통장번호'. Anyone, friend or banker, can say 통장 comfortably. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't pair it with 열다 ('open') as English does — Koreans 만들다 (make) a 통장 — and don't import 어카운트 or 'account number'; reach for 통장 in chat and 계좌번호 when reading out the digits.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 통장 번호 for the account number — that slot belongs to 계좌, so the correct form is 계좌번호.
Using 통장을 열다 by analogy with English 'open an account'; Koreans say 통장을 만들다.
Reaching for English 어카운트; in both casual and formal Korean the native word 통장/계좌 is expected.

entries.shortExplanation: 체크카드 means "debit card (check card)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 체크카드 (chekeukadeu) means "debit card (check card)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 체크카드로 결제하다 ("to pay by debit card"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 체크카드 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 로 marks the card as the means of payment

usagePhrases.en: to be issued a debit card
usagePhrases.note: 발급받다 (發給) is the set verb for being issued a card/document
한도 (限度) here is capped by your balance, not by credit

usagePhrases.en: for the debit card to not work
usagePhrases.note: 안 되다 is the everyday way to say a payment is declined

examples.en: I usually pay with my debit card.
examples.note: 계산하다 (pay/settle) pairs naturally with 카드로

examples.ko: 통장에 돈이 없어서 체크카드가 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: tongjange doni eopseoseo chekeukadeuga an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: My debit card was declined because my account was empty.
examples.note: shows the cause-and-effect: 체크카드 draws straight from the 통장

examples.ko: 외국인등록증만 있으면 체크카드는 바로 발급받을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: oegugindeungnokjeungman isseumyeon chekeukadeuneun baro balgeupbadeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you just have your residence card, you can get a debit card issued on the spot.
examples.note: real bank-counter situation for newcomers; ~만 있으면 = 'as long as you have'

entries.nuance: 체크카드 is a debit card: the instant you pay, the money is pulled straight out of your linked 통장, so you can never spend more than you actually have. Compare it sharply with its partner 신용카드 (credit card), which lets you spend now and pay the bill next month — the dividing line is timing of the money, immediate withdrawal versus deferred billing. The word is a Konglish coinage ('check' + 카드) and is the only natural name; Koreans rarely say 데빗카드. Because issuance only requires a balance and no credit check, banks hand 체크카드 to recent arrivals easily, which is why most foreigners start here. The pitfall for English speakers is assuming any card offers a credit buffer — a 체크카드 has none, so '잔액이 부족하면' it simply declines.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it a 데빗카드 from English 'debit card'; Koreans overwhelmingly say 체크카드.
Expecting a 체크카드 to let you overspend like a 신용카드 — it can only draw what's already in your 통장.
Saying 체크카드를 사다 ('buy a debit card'); a card is 발급받다 (issued), not bought.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 긁다 (scratch) is the casual, slangy verb for paying by card

usagePhrases.en: to apply for a credit card
usagePhrases.note: 신청하다 (申請) = formally apply, because issuance isn't automatic
명세서 (明細書) is the itemized monthly bill
할부 (割賦) = splitting a payment over months, a credit-only feature

examples.en: I'll buy this with a credit card.
examples.note: ~로 살게요 is the simple checkout line

examples.en: The credit card gets charged next month.
examples.note: 결제되다 (be settled) captures the 'pay later' nature

examples.ko: 외국인은 신용 기록이 없어서 신용카드 만들기가 좀 어려워요.

entries.nuance: 신용카드 (信用카드, 'trust-card') literally builds on 신용 — your creditworthiness, the bank's trust that you'll repay. You spend now and the total is 결제 (settled) next month, which is exactly what separates it from a 체크카드: the credit card defers the bill and depends on your 신용 record, while the debit card deducts instantly and needs none. Because that trust takes time to establish, banks routinely decline recent arrivals, so many residents carry a 체크카드 until they build a history. Natural collocations include 신용카드 할부 (installments) and 신용카드 명세서 (statement). The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 크레딧카드 — the native compound 신용카드 is universal — and remember the verb to apply is 신청하다, since unlike a debit card it is never issued on demand.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 신용카드 with 체크카드 — the credit card bills you next month, the debit card deducts from your 통장 instantly.
Saying 크레딧카드 in English; the natural word is 신용카드.
Using 만들다 and assuming approval; a 신용카드 must be 신청하다 (applied for) and can be refused.

entries.shortExplanation: 송금 means "money transfer, remittance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 송금 (songgeum) = "money transfer, remittance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 송금하다 ("to send money") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 송금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 송금 + 하다 forms the verb; the object often takes 을/를 (돈을 송금하다)
해외 (海外) = abroad; the prototypical use of 송금
수수료 (手數料) is the service charge, steep on 해외 송금
안 되다 covers any failure to go through

examples.en: I transferred 100,000 won to my friend.
examples.note: 한테 marks the human recipient of the money

examples.ko: 고향에 돈을 보내려면 해외 송금을 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gohyange doneul bonaeryeomyeon haeoe songgeumeul haeya haeyo.
examples.en: To send money to my hometown, I have to do an overseas remittance.
examples.note: ~려면 = 'in order to'; pairs the casual 보내다 with the formal 송금

examples.ko: 계좌번호만 알려 주시면 오늘 바로 송금해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: gyejwabeonhoman allyeo jusimyeon oneul baro songgeumhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: If you just give me the account number, I'll transfer it to you today.
examples.note: real situation; 송금하다 needs a 계좌번호, and ~해 드릴게요 is polite service speech

entries.nuance: 송금 (送金, literally 'send-money') is the act of sending funds to someone, near or far, and works as a verb with 하다. Its near-synonym is 이체 (account-to-account transfer): the dividing line is focus — 송금 foregrounds sending TO a person (친구한테 송금), while 이체 foregrounds the mechanical move BETWEEN accounts (계좌 이체). In casual domestic chat people often just say 돈 보내다, but 송금 sounds correct for bank wires and is the standard term for anything 해외 (overseas). Collocations: 해외 송금, 송금 수수료, 송금 한도. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing direction — 송금 is money going OUT (you send), whereas 입금 is money coming IN — and overlooking that 해외 송금 normally demands ID and a hefty 수수료.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 송금 (sending money out) with 입금 (money coming into an account).
Forgetting that 해외 송금 usually requires your ID and carries a real 수수료 (fee).
Marking the human recipient with 에 (the place particle); a person takes 에게/한테 — say 친구한테 송금했어요.
