entries.shortExplanation: 이체 means "bank transfer (between accounts)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이체 (iche) means "bank transfer (between accounts)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 계좌 이체 ("account transfer"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이체 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the full set phrase you see on apps and ATMs
이체 + 하다; 계좌에서 계좌로 이체하다
한도 (限度) = the daily cap on how much you can move
완료 (完了) is the confirmation wording inside banking apps

examples.en: I send the rent by bank transfer.
examples.note: 계좌 이체로 + 보내다 is the standard way to describe paying rent

examples.ko: 하루 이체 한도가 넘어서 더는 못 보내요.
examples.romanization: haru iche handoga neomeoseo deoneun mot bonaeyo.
examples.en: I've gone over my daily transfer limit, so I can't send more.
examples.note: 한도가 넘다 = exceed the cap; a very common banking snag

examples.ko: 은행 앱에 로그인하면 바로 이체할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: eunhaeng aebe rogeuinhamyeon baro ichehal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Once you log in to the bank app, you can transfer right away.
examples.note: 이체하다 = to transfer between accounts; simplified to everyday app login

entries.nuance: 이체 (移替, 'shift-replace') means moving money from one account to another and almost always appears as 계좌 이체 on bank apps and ATM screens. It overlaps heavily with 송금, and the sharp dividing line is perspective: 이체 stresses the account-to-account mechanics (the money relocates between 계좌), whereas 송금 stresses the act of remitting TO a person. Both take 하다. Do not, however, blur it with 입금 (depositing money INTO an account) — 이체 is the lateral move, 입금 is the inflow. Common collocations: 계좌 이체, 이체 한도, 자동이체. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'transfer' as one undifferentiated word and forgetting the 이체 한도 — a daily ceiling banks set low on new accounts, which silently blocks a large one-time transfer until you raise it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 이체 and 입금 as identical; 이체 moves money between accounts, 입금 puts money in.
Forgetting the 이체 한도 (daily transfer limit) that blocks large one-time transfers on new accounts.
Saying just 이체 to a person when you mean remitting to them; for a person, 송금/보내다 is more natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 환전 means "currency exchange" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "currency exchange" is 환전 (hwanjeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 환전하다 ("to exchange currency"). Watch the particle attached to 환전 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 환전 + 하다; the thing you swap into takes 로 (달러로 환전하다)
소 (所) = place; the manned booth where you swap cash
수수료 (手數料) varies by booth, so it pays to compare
환율 (換率) is the rate; 좋다/나쁘다 describe a favorable/poor rate

examples.en: I exchanged money before going on the trip.
examples.note: simple time-clause ~기 전에 = 'before doing'

examples.en: If you exchange at the airport, the rate is bad.
examples.note: distinguishes 환전 (the act) from 환율 (the rate) in one breath

examples.ko: 명동 환전소가 은행보다 수수료가 싸다고 해서 거기서 바꿨어요.
examples.romanization: myeongdong hwanjeonsoga eunhaengboda susuryoga ssadago haeseo geogiseo bakkwosseoyo.
examples.en: I heard the Myeongdong booths charge lower fees than banks, so I changed it there.
examples.note: real situation; note casual 바꾸다 standing in for 환전하다

entries.nuance: 환전 (換錢, literally 'exchange-money') is swapping one currency for another — won into dollars before a trip home, say — and takes 하다, with the target currency marked by 로 (달러로 환전하다). Keep three look-alikes apart: 환전 is the ACT of changing currency, 환율 (換率) is the exchange RATE you get, and 환불 (還拂) is a totally separate word meaning a refund. In casual speech 돈을 바꾸다 ('change money') often substitutes for 환전하다. Collocations: 해외 환전, 환전 수수료, 환율이 좋다/나쁘다. The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'exchange' collapse 환전 and 환율 into one — and confusing 환전 with the unrelated 환불 — so anchor 환전 to the action and remember each bank or 환전소 sets its own 수수료, which is why where you exchange genuinely matters.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 환전 (changing currency) with 환불 (getting a refund) — different hanja, different meaning.
Confusing 환전, the act, with 환율, the exchange rate itself.
Marking the target currency with 에 instead of the instrumental 로; it's 달러로 환전하다 ('exchange into dollars').

entries.shortExplanation: 잔액 means "account balance, remaining amount" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잔액 (janaek) = "account balance, remaining amount". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 잔액이 부족하다 ("the balance is insufficient") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 잔액, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 부족하다 (不足) — the exact phrase on decline messages
확인하다 (確認) is the standard verb for checking a figure
the amount sitting in your 통장
조회 (照會) is the menu wording at ATMs and in apps

examples.en: How much is the balance right now?
examples.note: simple 얼마예요 question about an amount

examples.ko: 교통카드 잔액이 천 원밖에 안 남았어요.
examples.romanization: gyotongkadeu janaegi cheon wonbakke an namasseoyo.
examples.en: My transit card only has 1,000 won left.
examples.note: shows 잔액 used for a transit card; ~밖에 + negative = 'only'

examples.ko: 카드 결제가 안 돼요. 통장 잔액이 부족한가 봐요.
examples.romanization: kadeu gyeoljega an dwaeyo. tongjang janaegi bujokanga bwayo.
examples.en: The card won't go through — I guess the account balance is low.
examples.note: real checkout moment; ~(으)ㄴ가 봐요 = 'I guess/it seems'

entries.nuance: 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining-amount') is the money left over — in your 통장, on a credit card, or on a 교통카드 (transit card) — and you'll hear the recorded line 잔액이 부족합니다 constantly when a payment is declined, so learn it by ear. Distinguish it crisply from 잔돈 (殘돈): 잔액 is the balance remaining in an account, while 잔돈 is the loose CHANGE handed back after you pay cash. The casual phrasing 남은 돈 ('money left') exists in speech, but formal banking contexts — ATMs, apps, tellers — expect 잔액. Collocations: 잔액 부족, 잔액 조회, 통장 잔액. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 잔돈 when you mean your account balance, and using conversational 남은 돈 on a form or to a banker where the precise term 잔액 is the natural choice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 잔액 (money remaining in an account) with 잔돈 (the small change you get back in cash).
Using 남은 돈 in formal banking contexts where 잔액 is the expected term.
Saying 잔액이 없다 to mean 'a little low'; 없다 means literally zero — for low-but-not-empty use 부족하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 입금 means "deposit, paying money in" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 입금 (ipgeum) means "deposit, paying money in". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 입금하다 ("to deposit / pay money in"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 입금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 입금 + 하다; you 입금하다 into an account marked with 에
확인 (確認) — sellers ask for this to verify the money landed
무 (無) = without; paying into an account via ATM with no book

usagePhrases.en: for a deposit to go through
usagePhrases.note: 되다 is intransitive — money arrives on its own (입금됐어요)

examples.en: I just made the deposit.
examples.note: 방금 (just now) + the past tense is the quick 'it's done' line

examples.ko: 돈 보냈는데 입금 확인 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: don bonaenneunde ipgeum hwagin jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: I sent the money, so please confirm the deposit.
examples.note: exact phrase buyers say to sellers in online deals

examples.ko: 보증금은 계약하는 날 집주인 계좌로 입금하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: bojeunggeumeun gyeyakaneun nal jipjuin gyejwaro ipgeumhamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can pay the deposit into the landlord's account on the day you sign.
examples.note: real housing situation; 계좌로 입금하다 + ~면 되다 ('it's fine to')

entries.nuance: 입금 (入金, literally 'enter-money') is money going INTO an account, the exact opposite of 출금 (出金, 'exit-money') — picture the 入 character as funds stepping in. It takes 하다 when you do it, but note the key voice split: 입금하다 is what YOU actively do, while 입금되다 (intransitive) is what happens when money arrives on its own. Sellers and landlords constantly request 입금 확인 to verify your payment landed, and 무통장 입금 ('passbook-less deposit') is the normal ATM phrase for paying into someone's account. Collocations: 입금 확인, 무통장 입금, 보증금 입금. The English-speaker pitfall is direction (입금 in vs 출금 out) and, above all, saying 입금받다 — for money simply arriving the natural form is 입금되다 (입금됐어요), reserving 받다 for receiving a physical thing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reversing 입금 (money in) and 출금 (money out) — the 入 vs 出 hanja mark the direction.
Saying 입금받다 for money arriving; the natural intransitive is 입금되다 (입금됐어요).
Marking the account with 한테; an account takes 에/(으)로 — 계좌로 입금하다, not 계좌한테.

entries.shortExplanation: 출금 means "withdrawal, taking money out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "withdrawal, taking money out" is 출금 (chulgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 출금하다 ("to withdraw money"). Watch the particle attached to 출금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 출금 + 하다; you 출금하다 from an account marked with 에서
한도 (限度) — the daily cap, set low on new accounts
현금 (現金) = cash; the most common reason to 출금

usagePhrases.en: for a withdrawal to be blocked
usagePhrases.note: 안 되다 covers limits, fraud holds, or low balance

examples.en: I withdrew 50,000 won from the ATM.
examples.note: ATM에서 marks the source point of the cash

examples.ko: 새 통장은 하루 출금 한도가 정해져 있어요.
examples.romanization: sae tongjangeun haru chulgeum handoga jeonghaejyeo isseoyo.
examples.en: A new account has a set daily withdrawal limit.
examples.note: 정해져 있다 = 'is set'; explains why big withdrawals get blocked

examples.ko: 밤 열한 시에 다른 은행 ATM에서 출금하면 수수료가 붙어요.
examples.romanization: bam yeolhan sie dareun eunhaeng ATMeseo chulgeumhamyeon susuryoga buteoyo.
examples.en: If you withdraw at 11 p.m. from another bank's ATM, a fee is added.
examples.note: real after-hours scenario; 수수료가 붙다 = 'a fee attaches'

entries.nuance: 출금 (出金, literally 'exit-money') is taking money OUT of an account, the natural pair to 입금 (入金, 'enter-money') — the 出 character even pictures funds leaving. It takes 하다, and the source account is marked with 에서 (통장에서 출금하다). It headlines every ATM screen and app menu. Crucially, fraud-protection rules give brand-new accounts a low 출금 한도, so a large withdrawal may be refused until you raise the cap at a branch. Collocations: 현금 출금, 출금 한도, 출금 수수료. The English-speaker pitfall is direction — don't swap 출금 (out) with 입금 (in) — and the particle: you withdraw FROM an account with 에서, not 에. Also budget for the fact that after-hours or rival-bank 출금 routinely '수수료가 붙어요' (adds a fee).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 출금 (taking money out) with 입금 (putting money in) — 出 vs 入 fixes the direction.
Marking the account with 에 for the source; withdrawals take 에서 — 통장에서 출금하다.
Forgetting that after-hours or other-bank 출금 usually attaches a 수수료 (fee).

entries.shortExplanation: 자동이체 means "automatic transfer, direct debit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자동이체 (jadongiche) = "automatic transfer, direct debit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 자동이체를 신청하다 ("to sign up for direct debit") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 자동이체, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to sign up for direct debit
usagePhrases.note: 신청하다 (申請) — you register it once at the bank or in the app

usagePhrases.en: to go out by direct debit
usagePhrases.note: 빠져나가다 (slip out) is the idiomatic verb for money auto-leaving
등록 (登錄) = enrolling the payment instruction
안 되다 here usually means the balance was short on the due date

examples.en: I set the rent on automatic transfer.
examples.note: 자동이체로 설정하다 = 'set it on auto'; great for recurring bills

examples.en: My phone bill goes out by direct debit every month.
examples.note: 매달 (every month) underlines the recurring nature

examples.ko: 통장에 돈이 없어서 어제 자동이체가 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: tongjange doni eopseoseo eoje jadongichega an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: My auto-payment failed yesterday because my account was empty.
examples.note: real consequence; the debit silently fails without enough 잔액

entries.nuance: 자동이체 (自動移替, literally 'self-moving transfer') is a standing instruction that pulls a fixed amount from your account on a set schedule — 월세, phone, utility bills — built from 자동 (自動, automatic) plus 이체 (移替, account transfer). That's the sharp contrast with a plain 이체: an 이체 is a single manual move you trigger each time, whereas 자동이체 runs by itself once registered. The idiomatic verb is 빠져나가다 ('slip out'), as in 자동이체로 빠져나가요. Collocations: 자동이체 신청/등록, 자동이체 설정. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming, as with a Western auto-pay, that the system covers a shortfall — it does not: if your 잔액 is short on the due date, the 자동이체 simply fails (안 됐어요) with no overdraft, so you must keep enough money in the account.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 자동이체 (recurring auto-debit) with a one-time manual 이체 you trigger yourself.
Assuming it overdraws to cover a shortfall; without enough 잔액 on the date it just fails.
Saying 자동이체를 보내다; you don't 'send' it — you 신청하다/설정하다 it, then money 빠져나가다.

entries.shortExplanation: 대출 means "loan" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 대출 (daechul) means "loan". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 대출을 받다 ("to take out a loan"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 대출 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) is the verb for getting a loan, not 빌리다 directly
갚다 is the dedicated verb for repaying a debt
a loan to cover a 전세 housing deposit; the most common kind
이자 (利子) = interest, distinct from a one-off 수수료 fee

examples.en: I took out a loan at the bank.
examples.note: 은행에서 + 대출을 받다 is the basic frame

examples.en: The loan interest is so high it's a burden.
examples.note: 이자가 높다 = 'interest is high'; 부담되다 = 'feels burdensome'

examples.ko: 전세 대출을 받아서 보증금을 마련했고, 매달 조금씩 갚고 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeonse daechureul badaseo bojeunggeumeul maryeonhaetgo, maedal jogeumssik gapgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I took out a jeonse loan to cover the deposit and pay it back bit by bit each month.
examples.note: real housing situation; chains 받다 → 마련하다 → 갚다 across the loan's life

entries.nuance: 대출 (貸出, literally 'lend-out') is a bank loan: you 받다 (receive/take out) one and later 갚다 (pay it back) together with 이자 (利子), the interest. Mind two boundaries. First, against 대여 (貸與): 대출 is specifically borrowing MONEY from a financial institution, whereas 대여 leans toward lending or renting OBJECTS (책 대여, 장비 대여). Second, on the paperwork, keep 이자 (ongoing interest on the principal) apart from 수수료 (a one-time service charge). For residents the headline product is a 전세 대출, a loan covering a housing deposit, which banks advertise heavily. Collocations: 대출을 받다/갚다, 대출 이자, 전세 대출. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: a loan is 받다 (received), and you don't '하다' a 대출 the way English 'take a loan' might tempt you — and never confuse 대출 with the object-renting 대여.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 대출 (borrowing money from a bank) with 대여, which leans toward renting or lending objects.
Mixing up 이자 (ongoing interest) with 수수료 (a one-off service fee) on loan paperwork.
Saying 대출하다 to mean 'take out a loan'; the natural phrase is 대출을 받다.

entries.shortExplanation: 대파 means "green onion (large); leek" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "green onion (large); leek" is 대파 (daepa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 대파를 썰어요 ("I slice green onion"). Watch the particle attached to 대파 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 썰다 is the verb for slicing long things; takes 를
produce sold tied in a bundle is counted with 단, never 개
넣다 = put into a pot; the all-purpose 'add an ingredient' verb
들어가다 describes an ingredient that belongs in the recipe

examples.en: Please add some green onion to the soup.
examples.note: casual cooking request; 좀 softens it to 'a bit'

examples.en: I bought a bunch of green onion at the mart.
examples.note: everyday shopping; counter 단 in action

examples.ko: 대파를 송송 썰어서 국 위에 올렸어요.
examples.romanization: daepareul songsong sseoreoseo guk wie ollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I chopped the green onion into little rounds and put it on top of the soup.
examples.note: real cooking; 송송 썰다 = chop into tiny crosswise rounds

entries.nuance: 대파 is the thick, long, white-and-green scallion that anchors almost every Korean soup, stew, and stir-fry — the 대 means 'large', distinguishing it from the slim 쪽파 (small bunching onion) and the round-bulb 양파 (onion). English speakers reach for 'green onion' and assume one word covers all of them, but at a Korean market 대파, 쪽파, 양파, and 마늘쫑 are four different products in four different spots. The single biggest pitfall is the counter: 대파 is bundled and sold by the 단 (bunch), so '대파 한 단' is natural while '대파 한 개' sounds like you are pointing at one lonely stalk. It pairs habitually with 썰다/넣다 and especially the mimetic 송송 썰다 for chopping it into little rings dropped on top of a dish.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 대파 한 개 — produce tied in a bundle takes 단, so it should be 대파 한 단; 개 makes it sound like a single odd stalk.
Using 대파 when you mean the round onion 양파 — they are different vegetables, and a 직역 of English 'onion' will not tell them apart.
Mixing up 대파 with the thin 쪽파; 쪽파 is for 파전/garnish, while 대파 is the workhorse for soups and stir-fries.

entries.shortExplanation: 고춧가루 means "red pepper powder; chili flakes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고춧가루 (gochutgaru) = "red pepper powder; chili flakes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고춧가루를 넣어요 ("I add red pepper powder") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고춧가루, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 for stirring it into a dish; takes 를
매워요 is from 맵다 (ㅂ-irregular), describing heat
powders are measured by the 스푼 (spoonful), not 개
뿌리다 = scatter on top, as a finishing dusting

examples.en: I added more chili powder to the kimchi stew.
examples.note: simple; 더 = 'more', the everyday way to adjust heat

examples.en: Because there's no chili powder, the color isn't red.
examples.note: everyday cause-and-effect; -아서 links reason to result

examples.ko: 고춧가루를 너무 많이 넣으면 안 매운 사람은 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: gochutgarureul neomu mani neoeumyeon an maeun sarameun mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: If you add too much chili powder, people who can't handle spice won't be able to eat it.
examples.note: real situation; 못 먹다 = physically can't eat it

entries.nuance: 고춧가루 is the dried, ground red-chili powder that gives Korean food its signature red color and heat — literally 고추(chili) + 가루(powder). Do not confuse it with 고추장, the fermented red-chili paste: 가루 is dry and dusty, 장 is a thick sticky paste, and they are not interchangeable in a recipe. The notorious spelling trap is the 사이시옷: because the compound 고추 + 가루 forms a tense [까] sound, Korean inserts ㅅ, giving 고춧가루, NOT 고추가루 — a mistake even some natives make in casual texting. Compared with Western cayenne it is coarser and milder by volume, so Korean recipes pour it in by the 스푼. It collocates with 넣다 (stir in) and 뿌리다 (sprinkle on top), and its heat is described with 맵다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 고추가루 without the ㅅ — the 사이시옷 is required, so the correct spelling is 고춧가루.
Confusing 고춧가루 (dry powder) with 고추장 (thick fermented paste); they behave completely differently in cooking.
Pluralizing or counting it like a countable thing (고춧가루 한 개) — it is a powder, measured with 스푼/그램, e.g. 고춧가루 한 스푼.

entries.shortExplanation: 식용유 means "cooking oil (vegetable oil)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 식용유 (sigyongyu) means "cooking oil (vegetable oil)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 식용유를 둘러요 ("I drizzle cooking oil around the pan"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 식용유 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I drizzle cooking oil around the pan
usagePhrases.note: 두르다 = coat a pan by swirling oil around it
떨어지다 = run out / be used up (stock is gone)
에 marks the medium you fry IN
bottled liquids are counted with 병

examples.en: Coat the pan with cooking oil.
examples.note: simple instruction; 두르다, not 넣다, for greasing a pan

examples.ko: 식용유가 다 떨어져서 사러 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: sigyongyuga da tteoreojyeoseo sareo gaya haeyo.
examples.en: The cooking oil ran out, so I have to go buy some.
examples.note: everyday errand; -아서 reason + 야 하다 obligation

examples.ko: 튀김은 식용유를 많이 써서 기름값이 꽤 들어요.
examples.romanization: twigimeun sigyongyureul mani sseoseo gireumgapsi kkwae deureoyo.
examples.en: Deep-frying uses a lot of oil, so the oil cost adds up quite a bit.
examples.note: real situation; 들다 = (money) is required/spent

entries.nuance: 식용유 is the everyday neutral frying oil (usually soybean or canola) — a Sino-Korean compound 食用油 meaning 'food-use oil', i.e. oil fit for eating, as opposed to industrial oil. The crucial contrast is with the aromatic finishing oils 참기름 (sesame) and 들기름 (perilla): 식용유 is the bland workhorse you cook IN, while 참기름/들기름 are fragrant seasonings you add at the END for flavor — never deep-fry in them. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb. In English you 'put oil in the pan', but Korean uses 두르다 (swirl/coat around) for greasing a pan: '식용유를 두르다' is natural, whereas '식용유를 넣다' sounds like you are pouring it into a soup. It collocates with 두르다 (coat), 튀기다 (deep-fry), and is counted by the 병.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 식용유 when you mean a flavoring oil like 참기름 — 식용유 is for cooking IN, not for the nutty finishing aroma.
Saying 식용유를 넣다 to mean greasing a pan — the idiomatic verb is 두르다 (swirl it around), so 식용유를 두르다.
Assuming it is one specific oil; 식용유 is a generic category (soybean, canola, etc.), the way English 'cooking oil' covers several oils.

structuredNuance.t: 식용유 is the everyday neutral frying oil (usually soybean or canola). It collocates with 두르다 (coat), 튀기다 (deep-fry), and is counted by the 병.

entries.shortExplanation: 들기름 means "perilla oil" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "perilla oil" is 들기름 (deulgireum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 들기름을 넣어요 ("I add perilla oil"). Watch the particle attached to 들기름 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 for adding a small amount; takes 을 after a consonant
냄새가 나다 = a smell comes off / is given off

usagePhrases.en: I dress it with perilla oil
usagePhrases.note: 무치다 = toss/dress a vegetable side dish by hand
tiny liquid amounts are counted with 방울 (drop)

examples.en: I added a little perilla oil to the seasoned greens.
examples.note: simple; 조금 = a little, matching its small-amount use

examples.ko: 들기름은 금방 상하니까 냉장고에 넣어 두세요.
examples.romanization: deulgireumeun geumbang sanghanikka naengjanggoe neoeo duseyo.
examples.en: Perilla oil goes bad quickly, so keep it in the fridge.
examples.note: everyday advice; -아 두다 = do and leave it that way

examples.ko: 할머니가 직접 짠 들기름이라 향이 정말 진해요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga jikjeop jjan deulgireumira hyangi jeongmal jinhaeyo.
examples.en: It's perilla oil my grandmother pressed herself, so the aroma is really deep.
examples.note: real situation; 짜다 = press/extract oil, (이)라 = since it is

entries.nuance: 들기름 is perilla-seed oil — 들(perilla/wild) + 기름(oil) — with a bold, nutty, earthy aroma that defines many 나물 (seasoned greens) and is brushed on 김 (laver). Its constant counterpart is 참기름, sesame oil (참 = 'true/genuine'): both are fragrant finishing oils, but 참기름 is lighter, sweeter, more universal, while 들기름 is heavier, grassier, and more regional/seasonal — a Korean cook chooses between them deliberately. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, treating it like generic 'oil' (식용유) and trying to fry in it — you don't; you add a 방울 at the finish. Second, storing it at room temperature: 들기름 oxidizes and turns rancid fast, so '냉장 보관' is the rule. It collocates with 무치다 (dress greens), 바르다 (brush on), and 향이 진하다 (deep aroma).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 들기름 (perilla, grassy/heavy) with 참기름 (sesame, lighter/sweeter) — Koreans pick one on purpose for each dish.
Storing 들기름 at room temperature; it goes rancid quickly, so it should be refrigerated (냉장 보관).
Using 들기름 as a frying oil like 식용유 — it is a finishing aroma added in drops (한 방울), not a deep-frying medium.

entries.shortExplanation: 깨소금 means "toasted sesame salt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 깨소금 (kkaesogeum) = "toasted sesame salt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 깨소금을 뿌려요 ("I sprinkle sesame salt") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 깨소금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 뿌리다 = scatter on top as a finishing garnish
넣다 for mixing it into a dish; 을 after consonant
조금 = a small amount, the typical quantity
고소하다 = the toasty-nutty flavor of sesame/oil

examples.en: Sprinkle sesame salt at the end.
examples.note: simple step; 마지막에 = at the very end, when it's added

examples.ko: 나물에 깨소금을 솔솔 뿌리니까 더 고소해요.
examples.romanization: namure kkaesogeumeul solsol ppurinikka deo gosohaeyo.
examples.en: Sprinkling sesame salt over the greens makes it nuttier.
examples.note: everyday; 솔솔 = lightly/evenly scattering

examples.en: Just adding sesame salt alone makes a rice side dish taste much better.
examples.note: real situation; -만 …-아도 = even just X is enough

entries.nuance: 깨소금 is toasted sesame seeds ground with a little salt — 깨(sesame) + 소금(salt) — used as a finishing seasoning scattered over 나물, 무침, and other 반찬. The flavor it gives is described by the very Korean word 고소하다 (toasty, nutty, oily-rich), a taste that has no neat English match; it is NOT 'savory' (감칠맛) and not 'salty' (짜다). Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, the name says 소금(salt), so learners assume it is mostly salt, but it is mostly sesame — its job is aroma, not saltiness. Second, timing: 깨소금 is a finishing touch added at the very end (마지막에), because grinding and heat dull the toasty smell. Note that in casual kitchen talk many Koreans also loosely call plain toasted whole sesame seeds 깨소금. It collocates with 뿌리다 and the mimetic 솔솔.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 깨소금 is basically salt because of the 소금 in the name — it is mostly toasted sesame; the point is aroma, not saltiness.
Adding it early in cooking; 깨소금 is a finishing garnish (마지막에 뿌리다), since heat kills the toasty 고소함.
Translating its taste as 'savory'; the right word is 고소하다 (nutty/toasty), which is distinct from 감칠맛 (umami-savory).

structuredNuance.t: 깨소금 is toasted sesame seeds ground with a little salt, used as a finishing seasoning scattered over 나물, 무침, and other 반찬. entries.shortExplanation: 생강 means "ginger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 생강 (saenggang) means "ginger". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 생강을 넣어요 ("I add ginger"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 생강 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 for adding it to a dish; 을 after consonant
알싸하다 = the sharp tingling kick of ginger (not 맵다)
다지다 = finely mince, the usual prep for ginger
생강차 = ginger tea; hot drinks counted with 잔

examples.en: Add just a little ginger.
examples.note: simple; -만 = only/just, fitting its strong flavor

examples.en: Adding ginger gets rid of the meat's gamey smell.
examples.note: everyday tip; 비린내 = fishy/gamey off-smell

examples.ko: 감기 기운이 있어서 생강차를 끓여 마셨어요.
examples.romanization: gamgi giuni isseoseo saenggangchareul kkeuryeo masyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I felt a cold coming on, so I brewed and drank ginger tea.
examples.note: real situation; 감기 기운 = the early hint of a cold

entries.nuance: 생강 is fresh ginger root, prized in Korean kitchens for killing the 비린내 (fishy/gamey smell) of meat and fish and for brewing 생강차 against colds. Its kick is best described by 알싸하다 (a sharp, tingling pungency) rather than 맵다 — 맵다 is the chili-heat of 고추, while ginger's bite is a different, almost numbing sharpness, so saying 생강이 매워요 sounds slightly off to natives. Watch the look-alike trap in recipes: 생강(ginger) sits right next to 마늘(garlic) in nearly every Korean marinade (the famous duo 생강·마늘), and beginners reading fast swap them. Because the flavor is so strong, recipes almost always pair it with 조금/조금만 (just a little) and the verb 다지다 (mince). It is usually peeled and minced, not sliced thick.

Describing ginger as 매워요 (chili-spicy); its sharp tingle is 알싸하다, a different sensation from 고추 heat.
Swapping 생강 (ginger) and 마늘 (garlic) when reading a marinade — they appear together (생강·마늘) but are different roots.
Adding too much because the flavor seems mild raw; recipes call for 조금만, as 생강 quickly overpowers a dish.

entries.shortExplanation: 다시마 means "dried kelp (for broth)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 우리다 = steep/draw flavor out into water
넣다 for dropping it into the pot; takes 를
flat sheet-like things are counted with 장
건지다 = fish/scoop solids out of liquid

examples.en: Put one sheet of kelp in the water.
examples.note: simple; counter 장 for a flat piece of kelp

examples.ko: 다시마는 물이 끓기 전에 건져 주세요.
examples.romanization: dasimaneun muri kkeulki jeone geonjyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Take the kelp out before the water boils.
examples.note: everyday tip; -기 전에 = before (an action)

examples.ko: 멸치하고 다시마를 같이 넣고 우리면 국물이 시원해요.
examples.romanization: myeolchihago dasimareul gachi neoko urimyeon gungmuri siwonhaeyo.
examples.en: If you steep anchovies and kelp together, the broth comes out clean and refreshing.
examples.note: real situation; 시원하다 = clean, bracing (of broth)

entries.nuance: 다시마 is dried kelp, the backbone of Korean soup stock, almost always steeped together with 멸치 (dried anchovies) to build 육수. Do not confuse it with 미역, the other common seaweed: 다시마 is thick, leathery, and used to MAKE broth (then removed), whereas 미역 is thin, slippery, and EATEN in 미역국 (birthday/postpartum seaweed soup). The make-or-break tip — and the spot beginners ruin broth — is timing: pull the 다시마 out right before the water boils (끓기 전에 건지다); boil it too long and the broth turns slimy, cloudy, and bitter. It is counted by the flat 장 (sheet), and collocates with 우리다 (steep), 건지다 (scoop out), and 국물/육수 (broth). The 'good broth' compliment that results is 시원하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 다시마 (kelp, for making broth) with 미역 (wakame, eaten in 미역국) — different seaweeds with different jobs.
Letting 다시마 boil; you should 건지다 it right before boiling (끓기 전에), or the broth becomes slimy and bitter.
Counting it with 개; flat sheets of kelp take 장, so 다시마 한 장.

entries.shortExplanation: 육수 means "broth; stock" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: (육수를) 내다 = produce stock by simmering — the set verb
진하다 = deep, strong, concentrated in flavor
우리다 = extract flavor into the water over time
measured-out liquid counted with 컵

examples.en: I made broth from anchovies.
examples.note: simple; 로 = the means/material you make it from

examples.ko: 이 집은 육수가 진하고 깊어서 인기가 많아요.
examples.romanization: i jibeun yuksuga jinhago gipeoseo ingiga manayo.
examples.en: This place is popular because its broth is rich and deep.
examples.note: everyday praise; 깊다 = deep, layered (of flavor)

examples.ko: 육수가 부족하면 물을 조금 더 부으세요.
examples.romanization: yuksuga bujokamyeon mureul jogeum deo bueuseyo.
examples.en: If the broth runs short, pour in a little more water.
examples.note: real situation; 붓다 (ㅅ-irregular) = pour liquid

entries.nuance: 육수 is the savory simmered stock at the base of soups, stews, and noodle dishes — Sino-Korean 肉水, literally 'meat-water', though in practice it is just as often drawn from 멸치 and 다시마, not only bones. The key contrast for learners is 육수 vs 국물: 육수 is the prepared stock you make on purpose as a base, while 국물 is simply 'the liquid in a dish' as served (the 국물 of your ramen, the 국물 of the kimchi). So you 육수를 내다 in advance, then ladle 국물 at the table. Two pitfalls: the 肉 character tempts English speakers to assume 육수 is always meat stock — it isn't. And the idiomatic verb is 내다/우리다 ('produce/steep' broth), not 만들다, so '육수를 내다' is what a cook says. Koreans judge a soup mainly by its 육수, praising it as 진하다 (rich) or 시원하다 (clean).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 육수 and 국물 as the same word — 육수 is the stock you prepare as a base; 국물 is the liquid already in a finished dish.
Assuming 육수 must be meat stock because of 肉(육) — it is frequently anchovy/kelp stock; the word covers all simmered stocks.
Saying 육수를 만들다; the natural collocation is 육수를 내다 (or 우리다), the set verb for producing stock.

entries.explanation: 두부 (dubu) means "tofu". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 두부를 부쳐요 ("I pan-fry tofu"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 두부 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 부치다 = pan-fry in a film of oil (same verb as for 전)
부드럽다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 부드러워요, 'soft/tender'
a pressed block of tofu is counted with 모
으깨다 = mash/crush (e.g. for fillings)

examples.en: One block of tofu, please.
examples.note: simple shop request; counter 모 in everyday use

examples.ko: 두부를 노릇하게 부쳐서 간장에 찍어 먹어요.
examples.romanization: dubureul noreutage buchyeoseo ganjange jjigeo meogeoyo.
examples.en: I pan-fry tofu golden and eat it dipped in soy sauce.
examples.note: everyday dish; 찍어 먹다 = dip-and-eat

examples.ko: 순두부는 보통 두부보다 훨씬 부드러워서 숟가락으로 떠먹어요.
examples.romanization: sundubuneun botong dububoda hwolssin budeureowoseo sutgarageuro tteomeogeoyo.
examples.en: Soft tofu is much softer than regular tofu, so you scoop it up with a spoon.
examples.note: real situation; 떠먹다 = scoop and eat

entries.nuance: 두부 is tofu, sold in firm pressed blocks counted with the special unit 모 ('두부 한 모', never 한 개). The contrast to internalize is 두부 vs 순두부: regular 두부 is firm enough to slice and pan-fry, while 순두부 ('pure/silken tofu') is barely-set custard eaten with a spoon in 순두부찌개 — calling silken tofu plain 두부 will confuse a Korean cook. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: in English you 'fry' tofu, but Korean distinguishes 부치다 (pan-fry in a thin film of oil, the same verb used for 전/jeon) from 튀기다 (deep-fry in lots of oil); slices of tofu are 부치다, not 튀기다. It collocates with 부치다 (pan-fry), 으깨다 (mash), 부드럽다 (soft), and the stews 된장찌개/순두부찌개. Texture words 부드럽다 and 단단하다 (firm) describe its grades.

Counting 두부 with 개 — a block of tofu takes the counter 모, so 두부 한 모.
Calling silken tofu 두부; the spoonable kind is 순두부, and mixing them up changes the dish entirely.
Using 튀기다 (deep-fry) for slices of tofu — pan-frying them in a little oil is 부치다, the jeon verb.

Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 무치다 = dress/toss greens by hand into a 무침 side dish
삶다 = boil in water until done; takes 을
store-packaged produce counted with 봉지 (bag)
아삭하다 = crisp-crunchy, the prized texture

examples.en: Boil the bean sprouts briefly.
examples.note: simple; 살짝 = lightly/just a bit, key for keeping crunch

examples.en: I drank too much yesterday, so I had bean-sprout soup to cure the hangover.
examples.note: everyday; 해장하다 = eat/drink to recover from drinking

examples.ko: 콩나물은 너무 오래 삶으면 물러지고 비린내가 나요.
examples.romanization: kongnamureun neomu orae salmeumyeon mulleojigo birinnaega nayo.
examples.en: If you boil bean sprouts too long, they go mushy and smell beany-off.
examples.note: real situation; 물러지다 = turn mushy, 비린내 = off-smell

entries.nuance: 콩나물 are soybean sprouts — 콩(soybean) + 나물(edible greens) — the long ones with a yellow bean head, a dirt-cheap staple behind the side dish 콩나물무침 and the hangover soup 콩나물국. The must-know contrast is 콩나물 vs 숙주(나물): 콩나물 grow from soybeans (bigger head, firmer, faintly nutty), while 숙주 grow from mung beans (smaller, more delicate, used in 쌀국수/만두소) — Korean recipes specify one, and they are not swappable. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, lumping both under 'bean sprouts' and grabbing the wrong one. Second, cooking time — the whole point is the 아삭한 (crunchy) texture, so you 살짝 삶다 (boil briefly); overboil and they go mushy (물러지다) and develop a beany 비린내. It collocates with 삶다, 무치다, 아삭하다, and counts by the 봉지.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 콩나물 (soybean sprouts) with 숙주 (mung-bean sprouts) — different beans, different dishes; recipes name a specific one.
Overboiling them; the goal is 아삭함 (crunch), so 살짝 삶다, or they turn mushy (물러지다) and smell off.
Counting with 개; a store bag is 콩나물 한 봉지, the natural unit.

entries.shortExplanation: 노릇노릇 means "golden-brown (nicely cooked)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 노릇노릇 (noreunnoreut) = "golden-brown (nicely cooked)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 노릇노릇 구워요 ("I grill it golden-brown") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: pairs with 굽다 (grill/roast)
노릇노릇하게 = the -하게 adverb form before a verb

usagePhrases.en: it cooked to a golden brown
usagePhrases.note: pairs with 익다 (become cooked/done)
pairs with 튀기다 (deep-fry)

examples.en: Pan-fry the jeon until golden-brown.
examples.note: simple instruction; bare 노릇노릇 before the verb

examples.en: The fish grilled up nicely to a golden brown.
examples.note: everyday result; 구워지다 = get grilled (passive)

examples.ko: 식빵을 노릇노릇하게 구우니까 겉은 바삭하고 속은 촉촉해요.
examples.romanization: sikppangeul noreunnoreutage guunikka geoteun basakago sogeun chokchokaeyo.
examples.en: Toasting the bread golden-brown makes it crispy outside and moist inside.
examples.note: real situation; 바삭하다 crispy, 촉촉하다 moist

entries.nuance: 노릇노릇 is a 의태어 (mimetic word) for the appetizing golden-brown surface of food fried, grilled, or toasted just right — built by reduplicating 노릇 from the color root 노랗다 (yellow). Unlike a neutral color word, it carries a built-in 'cooked to perfection, looks delicious' judgment, so it is almost always positive; its opposite outcome is 타다 (to burn), and you would never call burnt food 노릇노릇. It attaches to cooking verbs in two shapes — bare 노릇노릇 or the adverb 노릇노릇하게 — typically with 굽다, 부치다, 튀기다, 익다, and pairs naturally with texture mimetics like 바삭바삭 (crispy). The English-speaker pitfalls: spell it 노릇노릇 (not 노룻노룻), and don't stretch it to mean simply 'yellow' — 노릇노릇 is specifically the cooked golden of a surface, not the color of a lemon or a shirt.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 노릇노릇 for burnt food; once it's overdone the word is 탔다 (from 타다), since 노릇노릇 is inherently 'just-right' and positive.
Spelling it 노룻노룻 — the correct mimetic is 노릇노릇, tied to 노랗다.
Stretching it to mean plain 'yellow' (a lemon, a shirt); 노릇노릇 specifically describes the golden surface of well-cooked food.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 요가 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

수업 = a class/lesson; 요가 클래스 (loanword) is interchangeable at studios
매트 is the fixed loanword for the mat; 깔개 (a Korean word for 'mat') is wrong here
-원(院) marks a small academy/clinic; same suffix as 학원, 병원

examples.en: I like yoga.
examples.note: the simplest frame: noun + 를 + 좋아하다, treating 요가 as a plain object

examples.ko: 저는 일주일에 두 번 요가를 해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun iljuire du beon yogareul haeyo.
examples.en: I do yoga twice a week.
examples.note: 일주일에 N 번 = N times per week; 에 marks the time-span the count happens within

examples.ko: 회사 근처에 요가원이 새로 생겼길래 등록했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesa geuncheoe yogawoni saero saenggyeotgillae deungnokaesseoyo.
examples.en: A yoga studio newly opened near my office, so I signed up.
examples.note: 생기다 = (a place) comes into being/opens; -길래 = 'since (I noticed)', a casual reason

entries.nuance: 요가 is the universal loanword from English 'yoga' (via Sanskrit); no Korean ever translates it. The reflex error is treating it like exercise and saying 요가 운동을 하다 — that doubles 'exercise/do', so just use 요가를 하다 or, colloquially, 요가하다. Compare it with 스트레칭 (stretching): 요가 is a whole disciplined practice with poses (동작/자세) and breathing, while 스트레칭 is just loosening muscles, so they are not swappable. A studio is a 요가원 or 요가 스튜디오 — never 요가집, because the homey suffix -집 is for eateries and shops, not for a class venue. One session is a 요가 수업 / 요가 클래스, and the gear is a 요가 매트.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
요가 운동을 해요. → 요가를 해요.
Adding 운동(을) 하다 ('to do exercise') after 요가 is redundant because 요가 already names the activity; the bare 요가를 하다 / 요가하다 is what Koreans say.
Drop 운동: 요가를 해요 / 요가해요.
요가집에 다녀요. → 요가원에 다녀요.
The suffix -집 means a shop or eatery (e.g. 빵집, 고깃집), so 요가집 sounds wrong for a class venue; studios use the academy suffix -원.
Use 요가원 or 요가 스튜디오.

entries.explanation: "Pilates" is 필라테스 (pillateseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 필라테스를 하다 ("to do Pilates"). usagePhrases.note: the verb is 하다; 필테 is the chat abbreviation friends actually type
기구(器具) = apparatus; contrasts with 매트 필라테스 done on a mat
등록하다(登錄) = to register; classes are sold as prepaid packages
read 일대일; a private lesson, much pricier than group (그룹) classes

examples.en: I do Pilates.
examples.note: the basic frame, naming the activity with the all-purpose verb 하다

examples.en: I'm doing Pilates these days to fix my posture.
examples.note: 다니다 = to attend regularly; -(으)려고 = 'in order to', stating your goal

examples.en: I bought a 10-session pass but I've already used it all.
examples.note: N회권(回券) = an N-session ticket; 끊다 = to buy (a ticketed pass), not 사다

entries.nuance: 필라테스 transliterates the founder's name 'Pilates' and is abbreviated 필테 in texts; the standard spelling is 필라테스 (not 필테스 or 파일라테스). The big learner trap is contrasting it with 요가: people will ask 매트(예요), 기구(예요)? — 매트 필라테스 is floor work, 기구 필라테스 uses the reformer machine, and 필라테스 generally targets core strength and posture (자세) whereas 요가 emphasizes flexibility and breathing, so don't call one the other. 10회권을 샀어요. → 10회권을 끊었어요.

Say 회권(을) 끊다.
필테스를 해요. → 필라테스를 해요.
The correct transliteration keeps 라: 필라테스. Dropping it (필테스) or adding a vowel (파일라테스) are common spelling slips.

entries.shortExplanation: 클라이밍 means "(rock/sport) climbing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 클라이밍 (keullaiming) = "(rock/sport) climbing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 클라이밍을 하다 ("to go climbing") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 클라이밍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: verb 하다; 클라이밍(을) 가다 ('go climbing') is just as common
실내(室內) = indoors; almost all city climbing is at indoor gyms
the short-wall, no-rope style most 20-30s actually do
-장(場) marks a sports venue/ground; cf. 운동장, 수영장

examples.en: I do climbing.
examples.note: the plain frame; 클라이밍 takes 하다 as its activity verb

examples.en: I go climbing with a friend every weekend.
examples.note: N마다 = every N; V-(으)러 가다 = go for the purpose of doing

examples.en: Is there somewhere that rents out climbing shoes at the gym?
examples.note: 암벽화(巖壁靴) = climbing shoes; 빌려주다 = to lend out (vs 빌리다 = to borrow)

entries.nuance: 클라이밍 is the English loanword 'climbing'; keep all four syllables — 클라밍 (dropping 이) is a frequent misspelling. The crucial distinction for an English speaker is 클라이밍 vs 등산(登山): 등산 is hiking/ascending an actual mountain on trails, while 클라이밍 is sport climbing up walls or rock faces — Koreans never mix them, so 'I went climbing this weekend' on a hiking trail should be 등산했어요. The trendy gym style is 볼더링 (bouldering: low walls, no rope, just 매트 below), done at an indoor 클라이밍장. Counter vocabulary that helps: 암벽화 (climbing shoes, which you can 빌리다) and 초크 (grip chalk). Beginners always confess 손에 힘이 없다 ('no grip strength').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
주말에 클라이밍 갔어요. (meaning a mountain hike) → 주말에 등산 갔어요.
등산 is trail hiking up a mountain; 클라이밍 is technical wall/rock climbing. Using 클라이밍 for a casual mountain walk misdescribes the activity.
Hiking a mountain = 등산; wall/rock climbing = 클라이밍.
클라밍을 해요. → 클라이밍을 해요.
The word transliterates 'climbing' with the 이 kept: 클라이밍. Omitting it is a spelling error.
Keep all syllables: 클라이밍.

entries.shortExplanation: 볼링 means "bowling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 볼링 (bolling) means "bowling". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 볼링을 치다 ("to bowl"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 볼링 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: use 치다 ('to strike'), the verb for ball/cue/racket games, not 하다
-장(場) = venue; a classic group hangout, often with 당구장 nearby
게임 is the counter for a round; you pay per 게임
-화(靴) = shoes (Sino-Korean); rent these at the counter

examples.en: I'm not very good at bowling.
examples.note: the simple frame; note 치다 as the verb and 못 + verb = 'can't (do well)'

examples.en: Want to go bowling later today?
examples.note: 이따가 = later (within today); -(으)ㄹ래? = casual 'shall we / want to?'

examples.en: How much is one game of bowling?
examples.note: N에 얼마예요? = how much per N; 에 distributes the price over each unit

entries.nuance: 볼링 is the loanword 'bowling', but the verb is the native 치다 ('to strike/hit'), shared with 당구를 치다, 테니스를 치다 and other implement-and-ball sports — saying 볼링을 하다 marks you as a foreigner. The mental model is: anything you strike with a hand/cue/racket takes 치다, whereas sports you run/play take 하다 (축구를 하다). A 볼링장 (-장 = venue) is a staple group outing and a softer alternative to a drinking 회식. You pay by the 게임 (the counter for a round), and you must swap into rented 볼링화 — the suffix -화(靴) is the Sino-Korean for 'footwear', the same one in 운동화 (sneakers) and 등산화 (hiking boots).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
볼링을 해요. → 볼링을 쳐요.
Implement-and-ball games collocate with 치다 ('strike'); 하다 is the generic 'do' and sounds unnatural for bowling.
Use 볼링을 치다.
운동화 신고 쳐도 돼요? → 볼링화로 갈아 신어야 해요.
Street/athletic shoes (운동화) damage and aren't allowed on the lane; you must change into rented 볼링화.
Rent and wear 볼링화 on the lane.

entries.shortExplanation: 당구 means "billiards, pool" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "billiards, pool" is 당구 (danggu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 당구를 치다 ("to play billiards"). Watch the particle attached to 당구 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: verb 치다 ('strike'), like other cue/ball games; never 하다
-장(場) = venue; cheap and often open late into the night
the pocketed version; plain 당구 usually means pocketless carom
시간당(時間當) = per hour; the loser often covers the fee

examples.en: I can't play billiards.
examples.note: the basic frame; 못 쳐요 = 'can't play (well)', with the proper verb 치다

examples.en: I went to play billiards with friends.
examples.note: N(이)랑 = casual 'with'; V-(으)러 가다 = go in order to do

examples.en: Billiard halls usually charge by the hour.
examples.note: 시간당 = per hour; 계산하다 = to bill/settle up, also 'to do the math'

entries.nuance: 당구(撞球) is Sino-Korean — 撞 'to strike' + 球 'ball', literally 'strike-ball' — and like other cue sports it takes the verb 치다, not 하다. The classic English-speaker trap is meaning: plain 당구 in Korea usually refers to the pocketless carom games 사구 (four-ball) and 쓰리쿠션 (three-cushion), played by bouncing balls off cushions, NOT the pool you know with six pockets — that pocketed version is specifically 포켓볼. So 'let's play pool' is safest as 당구 치자 only if you mean carom; otherwise specify 포켓볼. A 당구장 (-장 = venue) is a cheap, late-night hangout, traditionally male-coded but now mixed, billed 시간당 (per hour), and the loser customarily pays.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
당구를 해요. → 당구를 쳐요.
Cue games collocate with 치다 ('strike'); 하다 is wrong for 당구 just as it is for 볼링.
Use 당구를 치다.
당구 = pool with pockets (assumed). → 포켓볼 for the pocketed game.
Plain 당구 in Korea defaults to pocketless carom (사구/쓰리쿠션); calling the six-pocket game 당구 without specifying confuses Koreans.
Say 포켓볼 when you mean pocket pool.

entries.shortExplanation: 보드게임 means "board game" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보드게임 (bodeugeim) = "board game". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보드게임을 하다 ("to play a board game") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보드게임, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: games take 하다 (to do/play), never 보다 ('watch')
a pay-by-time cafe stocked with games; locals shorten it to 보드카페
룰 = rules (loanword); staff often explain the game for you
N이서 = '(as a group) of N'; 둘이서, 셋이서, 넷이서 …

examples.en: I like board games.
examples.note: the simple frame; 보드게임 is a plain object of 좋아하다

examples.en: The rules of this board game are a bit complicated.
examples.note: 복잡하다(複雜) = complicated, the descriptive verb here; 좀 softens the complaint

examples.ko: 넷이서 할 수 있는 보드게임 추천해 주세요.
examples.romanization: nesiseo hal su inneun bodeugeim chucheonhae juseyo.
examples.en: Please recommend a board game four people can play.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ 수 있는 = that can be done; 추천하다(推薦) = to recommend

entries.nuance: 보드게임 is 'board game' (보드 + 게임). Like all games it takes the verb 하다 ('do/play'), and the trap for English speakers is the verb 'play': there is no all-purpose 'play' in Korean — you 하다 a board game but you 치다 ball games and 켜다/연주하다 instruments, so reaching for one English verb fails. The cultural anchor is the 보드게임 카페 (commonly shortened 보드카페), where you pay by time and staff teach the 룰. It's a cheap date or rainy-day group activity for 20-30s. Don't confuse the game with its parts: the physical board is a 게임판, while 보드게임 names the whole game, and 보드 alone can also mean a snowboard/skateboard, so keep the full 보드게임.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
보드게임을 봐요. → 보드게임을 해요.
English 'play a game' tempts learners toward 보다 ('watch') or a literal calque; games are done with 하다.
Use 보드게임을 하다.
우리 보드 하자. → 우리 보드게임 하자.
Bare 보드 is ambiguous (it can mean a snowboard/skateboard); say the full 보드게임 for the tabletop game.
Keep the full word 보드게임.

entries.shortExplanation: 방탈출 means "escape room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 방탈출 (bangtalchul) means "escape room". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 방탈출을 하다 ("to do an escape room"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 방탈출 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the activity verb is 하다; you 'do' a room, not 'watch' it
the full venue name; often shortened to 방탈
테마 = each themed room you book; 공포 테마 = a horror room
쓰다 = to use; staff give 힌트 when you're stuck

examples.en: I like escape rooms.
examples.note: the basic frame; 방탈출 as a plain object of 좋아하다

examples.ko: 우리 이번 주말에 방탈출 하러 갈까?
examples.romanization: uri ibeon jumare bangtalchul hareo galkka?
examples.en: Shall we go do an escape room this weekend?
examples.note: V-(으)러 가다 = go to do; -(으)ㄹ까? = soft 'shall we?' to a friend

examples.ko: 이 테마 너무 어려워서 결국 탈출 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: i tema neomu eoryeowoseo gyeolguk talchul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: This room was so hard we couldn't escape in the end.
examples.note: 결국(結局) = in the end; 탈출(脫出)하다 = to escape; -아서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 방탈출 is a transparent compound: 방 'room' + 탈출(脫出) 'escape/break-out' (脫 'shed/escape' + 出 'go out'), i.e. 'room escape'. Write it solid as 방탈출 (the set activity noun), not 방 탈출 with a space, and it's commonly clipped to 방탈. The verb is 하다 — the pitfall is English 'do an escape room' vs the false friend 보다: you never 방탈출을 보다 ('watch'), you 하다 (participate in) it. Inside, each scenario is a 테마 you book ahead; you can request a 힌트 when stuck, and the scary ones are 공포 테마. Don't confuse the noun 탈출 (the act of escaping, used in 탈출하다) with the venue word 방탈출 (the game itself). A staple group outing for young adults.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
방탈출을 봤어요. → 방탈출을 했어요.
It's a participatory game: you 하다 (do) it. 보다 ('watch') treats it like a show, which is wrong.
Use 방탈출을 하다.
방 탈출 하러 가자. → 방탈출 하러 가자.
As the name of the activity it is one set word, 방탈출 (or clipped 방탈); inserting a space reads as the literal phrase 'escape the room'.
Write it solid: 방탈출.

examples.note: the basic frame; 전시회 as object of 보다, with 자주 = 'often'

entries.nuance: 전시회 is Sino-Korean — 展示 'display/exhibit' (展 'spread out' + 示 'show') + 會 'gathering/event' — i.e. a (usually temporary) exhibition event you 보러 가다, a go-to casual outing or date for 20-30s, especially as a 사진전 (photo show) or 미술전 (art show), where -전(展) is the compact suffix. 전시회 입장료가 얼마예요? → 전시회 관람료가 얼마예요?

usagePhrases.en: to go to a karaoke room
usagePhrases.note: the standard outing phrase; the venue takes 가다
a pay-per-song booth, shortened to 코노; cheap and solo-friendly
곡(曲) = the counter for songs; 부르다 = to sing, not 하다
the free minutes staff add at the end if you ask

examples.en: I like karaoke rooms.
examples.note: the simple frame; the place 노래방 as object of 좋아하다

examples.note: 2차(次) = the next stop on a night out; 로 marks 노래방 as the chosen next venue

entries.nuance: 노래방 is a pure Korean compound: 노래 'song' + 방 'room' = 'song room', a private karaoke booth that is core Korean nightlife and the classic 2차 ('second round') after dinner or drinks. 가라오케 가자. → 노래방 가자.

Use 노래방 (or 코노) for the ordinary karaoke room.
노래 한 곡 했어요. → 노래 한 곡 불렀어요.
Songs are sung with 부르다, not done with 하다; 곡 is the counter you pair with 부르다.
Use 노래를 부르다 / 한 곡 부르다.

entries.nuance: 찜질방 is a Korean compound: 찜질 'applying heat/a hot compress' + 방 'room' — a 24-hour heated sauna/spa complex where you change into a 찜질복, sweat in heated 한증막 rooms, snack on 식혜 with 삶은 계란, and can even sleep over in a 수면실. The pitfall is treating it as a synonym of 목욕탕(沐浴湯): a 목욕탕 is a plain public bathhouse for washing/soaking in hot tubs, whereas a 찜질방 adds the dry heated 찜질 rooms, communal lounge areas, food, and overnight sleeping — much bigger in scope. 제 옷 입고 들어가도 돼요? → 찜질복으로 갈아입어야 해요.

동호회를 들어갔어요. → 동호회에 가입했어요.

a real button (외출 = going out) that keeps pipes from freezing while saving gas

examples.en: I turn on the boiler.

entries.nuance: 보일러 is a katakana-route loanword (from English 'boiler') but in a Korean home it means far more than the English word: one 보일러 heats BOTH the 온돌 floor and the hot-water supply, so when it dies you lose heat and hot showers at the same moment. Do not confuse it with 난방 (the heating itself, the warmth) or 히터 (a plug-in space heater) — 보일러 is the gas unit that produces 난방. The habitual verbs are 켜다/끄다 (on/off), 틀다 ('crank on'), and 돌리다 ('run it'), while a breakdown is always 고장 나다. The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 보일러가 죽었어요 ('the boiler died') as a direct translation of an English idiom; Koreans say 보일러가 고장 났어요 or 보일러가 안 돼요. Tenants report a dead 보일러 to the 집주인 (landlord) or 관리사무소 (management office) immediately, since no hot water is an emergency.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Saying 보일러를 열다 ('open the boiler') by translating 'turn on' loosely is wrong; 열다 is for doors/lids. Appliances take 켜다 (or 틀다/돌리다), so it's 보일러를 켜다.
Mixing up 보일러 with 난방: 난방이 고장 났어요 sounds odd because 난방 is the abstract heating. The physical unit that broke is the 보일러, so 보일러가 고장 났어요 is what a repair person expects.

The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 보일러가 죽었어요 ('the boiler died') as a direct translation of an English idiom; Koreans say 보일러가 고장 났어요 or 보일러가 안 돼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 누수 means "water leak" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 = 'come into being'; the neutral verb for a problem showing up
발생하다 (occur) is the formal register you use when filing a 관리사무소 report
신고 = official report; 누수 신고를 하다 = lodge a leak complaint with management
흔적 = mark left behind (a water stain on the ceiling proving past leakage)

examples.en: Water is leaking from the ceiling.
examples.note: casual everyday phrasing: the verb 새다 (to leak), not the noun

examples.ko: 천장에서 물이 떨어져서 누수인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: cheonjangeseo muri tteoreojyeoseo nusuin geot gatayo.
examples.en: Water is dripping from the ceiling, so I think it's a leak.
examples.note: ~인 것 같다 = 'seems to be ~', a soft diagnosis

examples.en: There's a leak from the upstairs unit, so I called the landlord.
examples.note: 누수가 생기다 = a leak occurs; 집주인한테 연락하다 = contact the landlord

entries.nuance: 누수 is Sino-Korean: 漏水, literally 漏 'leak/seep' + 水 'water', i.e. 'leaking water'. Because it is a 한자어 noun it carries a formal, technical tone — it is the word you use when reporting damage to a 관리사무소, 집주인, or repair technician, and it appears on invoices and insurance forms. The dividing line you must learn: 누수 is a NOUN naming the phenomenon, whereas the everyday verb 'to leak' is 새다 (물이 새요). So a native speaker casually says 물이 새요 but writes 누수가 발생했습니다 on a report. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 누수 like a verb and producing 누수해요 — this does not exist; you must say 물이 새요 or 누수가 생겼어요. Also distinguish 누수 (water leaking) from its dangerous lookalike 누전 (漏電, electrical leakage/short circuit), and from 결로 (condensation), which looks like a leak but is just humidity beading on a cold surface. Establishing the source — 윗집 (upstairs) vs. building pipes — decides who pays.

Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the idiomatic verb: mold 'blossoms' like a flower — present 피어요, past 폈어요
슬다 is the native verb for mold/rust forming on a surface; common in speech
제거하다 (formal 'eliminate'); casually 곰팡이를 닦다 (wipe off) or 없애다
냄새 = smell; 곰팡이 냄새가 나다 = it smells musty, a tell-tale of hidden mold

examples.en: There's a lot of mold on the wall.
examples.note: location marked by 에; the simplest description

examples.en: During the rainy season, mold easily grows in the bathroom.
examples.note: 잘 + verb = 'easily/often'; 피어요 is from 피다 (to bloom), the verb mold takes

examples.ko: 곰팡이 때문에 벽지를 다 뜯어내고 새로 도배했어요.
examples.romanization: gompangi ttaemune byeokjireul da tteudeonaego saero dobaehaesseoyo.
examples.en: Because of the mold, I tore out all the wallpaper and re-papered.
examples.note: real consequence; ~때문에 (because of) + 뜯어내다 (rip out)

entries.nuance: 곰팡이 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) for mold/mildew, and it is a constant battle in Korean homes — in humid 욕실 (bathrooms), behind furniture pushed against cold exterior walls, and all through 장마 (the summer rainy season). The crucial collocation is the verb: mold 곰팡이가 피다, literally 'mold blooms', as if it were a flower (present 곰팡이가 피어요, past 곰팡이가 폈어요). A second native verb, 슬다 (곰팡이가 슬다 'mold sets in'), is also fully natural. The sharp pitfall for learners is the verb pair 피다 vs. 펴다: 피다 ('to bloom', intransitive) is what mold does, while 펴다 ('to unfold/spread out', transitive — you 펴 a blanket or an umbrella) is a different verb; never say 곰팡이를 펴다. Serious 곰팡이 is legitimate grounds to ask a 집주인 for repairs.

entries.explanation: 환기 (hwangi) means "ventilation, airing out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환기를 하다 ("to ventilate / air out"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 환기 + 하다 = the everyday verb: open the windows and let air through
시키다 (causative 'make it happen') — 환기를 시키다 stresses you actively cause airflow
잘 되다 = 'works well'; 환기가 잘 돼요 praises a room's airflow

usagePhrases.en: for a cross-breeze to blow through
usagePhrases.note: 맞바람 = cross-draft; opening windows on two sides so 맞바람이 쳐서 환기가 잘 돼요

examples.en: I air out the room.
examples.note: 환기 + 하다, the most basic form

examples.ko: 곰팡이가 안 생기게 매일 환기를 시켜요.
examples.romanization: gompangiga an saenggige maeil hwangireul sikyeoyo.
examples.en: I air it out every day so mold doesn't form.
examples.note: ~게 (so that) + causative 시키다; ties ventilation to mold prevention

examples.ko: 이 방은 창문이 작아서 환기가 잘 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: i bangeun changmuni jagaseo hwangiga jal an dwaeyo.
examples.en: This room has a small window, so it doesn't ventilate well.
examples.note: real flaw to flag when viewing a place; 잘 안 되다 = 'doesn't work well'

entries.nuance: 환기 is Sino-Korean: 換氣, literally 換 'change/exchange' + 氣 'air', i.e. 'changing out the air'. Koreans treat daily 환기 as serious housekeeping, because tightly sealed, well-insulated apartments trap cooking smells, CO2, and the moisture that breeds 곰팡이; you 환기 after cooking, after sleeping, and especially on dry winter days. The word takes BOTH 하다 and 시키다 — 환기하다 and 환기시키다 — and here they are effectively interchangeable, both meaning 'open up and let air through'; 시키다 just foregrounds that you are deliberately causing it. Distinguish 환기 sharply from 통풍 (通風), which is the passive property of air being able to pass through a space (a breezy room has good 통풍), whereas 환기 is the active act of refreshing the air. Also keep it apart from 난방 (heating) and 냉방 (cooling) — those change temperature, 환기 changes the air itself. The English-speaker pitfall: 환기 is a noun, so do not bolt it onto random verbs; pair it only with 하다/시키다, or describe airflow with 환기가 잘 되다/안 되다.

entries.shortExplanation: 수도세 means "water bill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "water bill" is 수도세 (sudose). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 수도세를 내다 ("to pay the water bill"). Watch the particle attached to 수도세 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay (a fee/bill); the standard verb for any 공과금
나오다 (lit. 'comes out') is how Koreans say a bill is issued/lands
포함되다 = be included; the make-or-break rental question 'is it 포함이에요?'
요금 (料金, fee) is the technically correct word; on bills you see 상수도 요금

examples.en: I pay the water bill.
examples.note: object marker 를 + 내다, the core pairing

examples.en: Is the water bill included in the monthly rent?
examples.note: the essential question before signing; 포함되어 있다 = is included

examples.en: I got hit with a huge water bill because of a leak.
examples.note: real shock: 요금 폭탄을 맞다 = 'get hit by a bill bomb'

entries.nuance: 수도세 is one of the 공과금 (utility bills) tenants juggle, and it sits in a funny spot: it ends in 세 (稅, 'tax'), but a water charge is really a usage fee, so the textbook-correct term is 수도 요금 (水道料金) — 水道 'water-way/plumbing' + 料金 'fee'. In daily life, though, everyone says 수도세, just as they say 전기세 and 가스비. The verbs are register-defining: a bill 나오다 ('comes out', is issued) and you 내다 (pay) it — never 사다 (buy). The make-or-break rental question is whether it's 포함 (included) in the rent or paid separately. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers: first, do not buy a bill — 'pay the bill' is 수도세를 내다, and 'the bill was high' is 수도세가 많이 나왔어요, literally 'a lot came out'. Second, do not confuse 수도세 (the monetary bill) with 수돗물 (tap water, the actual H2O) — note the sai-siot ㅅ in 수돗물. The slang 요금 폭탄 ('bill bomb') describes a shockingly high bill, often traced to a hidden 누수.

Saying 수도세를 사요 ('I buy the water bill') because 'buy/pay' blur in the learner's head. Bills are paid: 수도세를 내요. They are issued: 수도세가 나왔어요.
Confusing 수도세 (the bill, the money) with 수돗물 (tap water itself). 수돗물을 마셔요 = 'I drink tap water'; 수도세를 내요 = 'I pay the water bill'.

entries.shortExplanation: 전기세 means "electricity bill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전기세 (jeongise) = "electricity bill". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전기세를 내다 ("to pay the electricity bill") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전기세, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. 나오다 = is issued; 많이 나오다 = comes out high
폭탄 (爆彈, bomb) = a shockingly high bill, the classic summer-AC complaint

examples.en: I pay the electricity bill.
examples.note: 를 + 내다, the base pattern

examples.en: I ran the AC a lot, so I'm scared of the electricity bill.
examples.note: 틀다 = crank on (an appliance); 무섭다 here = 'dreadful to think about'

examples.en: The electricity bill came out double last month's.
examples.note: comparison with 보다 (than) + 나/emphasis ('a whopping two times')

entries.nuance: 전기세 follows the same 세 (稅 'tax') vs. 요금 (料金 'fee') split as 수도세: the formally correct term is 전기 요금 (電氣料金), 電氣 'electricity' + 料金 'fee', because it is a usage charge, not a tax — yet 전기세 is what everyone actually says. What makes 전기세 special is Korea's 누진제 (累進制, progressive rate system): residential electricity is billed in escalating tiers, so heavy summer 에어컨 use can push you into a high bracket and spike the bill dramatically, which is why 전기세 폭탄 ('electricity bill bomb') is a fixed summer complaint. Verbs follow the bill pattern: it 나오다 (comes out/is issued) and you 내다 (pay) it. Second, resist English 'high bill' as 전기세가 높아요; the idiom is 전기세가 많이 나왔어요. Unplugging unused 콘센트 (outlets) is the stereotypical 전기세-saving habit.

usagePhrases.en: the gas bill is a burden
usagePhrases.note: 부담되다 = to weigh on you financially; a natural way to say a cost stings
도시가스 (都市gas, piped city gas) + 요금; the official term on the bill

examples.en: I pay the gas bill.
examples.note: 를 + 내다, the core pattern

examples.ko: 가스비 아끼려고 보일러를 외출 모드로 해 놔요.
examples.romanization: gaseubi akkiryeogo boilleoreul oechul modeuro hae nwayo.
examples.en: To save on gas, I keep the boiler on away mode.
examples.note: ~려고 (in order to) + 해 놓다 (do and leave it that way) — a money-saving habit

examples.ko: 이번 겨울은 가스비가 작년보다 더 비싸게 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon gyeoureun gaseubiga jangnyeonboda deo bissage nawasseoyo.
examples.en: This winter the gas bill came out more expensive than last year.
examples.note: real comparison; 보다 (than) + 비싸게 나오다

entries.nuance: 가스비 is worth noticing for one detail: unlike 전기세 and 수도세, it conventionally ends in 비 (費, 'expense/cost'), not 세 (稅, 'tax') — so the form is 가스비, and the fully formal term is 도시가스 요금 (都市가스料金, 'city-gas charge'). The 가스 part is the English loanword 'gas'. 가스비 spikes in winter for a concrete reason: the 보일러 burns gas to provide both 난방 (floor heating) and hot water, so a cold-weather habit of running the 보일러 hard shows up directly as a high 가스비 — tenants routinely link the two. Verbs follow the bill pattern: it 나오다 (comes out) and you 내다 (pay). Pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not buy a bill — 가스비를 사다 is wrong; it is 가스비를 내다 (pay) or 가스비가 나오다 (is issued). Second, do not confuse 가스비 (the gas bill, the money) with 가스 (the gas itself) or with 가스레인지 (the gas stovetop) — 가스가 떨어졌어요 means 'we ran out of gas', whereas 가스비가 많이 나왔어요 is about the bill. By analogy with 전기세, remember the spelling stays 가스비, never 가스세.

Saying 가스비를 사다 ('buy the gas bill'). Bills are paid (가스비를 내다) or come out (가스비가 나오다); they are never bought.
Writing 가스세 by false analogy with 전기세/수도세. This particular utility uses 비 (expense): the correct form is 가스비.
Confusing 가스비 (the bill) with 가스레인지 (the gas range/stove) or 가스 (the fuel). 가스레인지를 켜다 = light the stove; 가스비를 내다 = pay the bill.

entries.shortExplanation: 도배 means "wallpapering" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "wallpapering" is 도배 (dobae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도배를 하다 ("to wallpaper (a place)"). Watch the particle attached to 도배 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 도배 + 하다 = the verb 'to do wallpapering'; the noun alone is not a verb
새로 = anew; the standard phrase for refreshing walls before move-in
비용 (費用, expense); a key negotiation figure with a landlord
the fixed pair Koreans name together when assessing or renovating a rental

examples.en: I had it freshly wallpapered.
examples.note: 새로 하다 = redo from new; the most common everyday use

examples.ko: 곰팡이 때문에 도배를 다시 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gompangi ttaemune dobaereul dasi haeya haeyo.
examples.en: Because of mold, I have to redo the wallpaper.
examples.note: ~때문에 (because of) + 다시 (again); mold is a classic trigger for re-papering

examples.ko: 집주인이 도배랑 장판을 새로 해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jipjuini dobaerang jangpaneul saero hae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The landlord redid the wallpaper and flooring for me.
examples.note: real perk: ~아 주다 (do a favor) + the 도배랑 장판 pair

entries.nuance: 도배 is Sino-Korean: 塗褙, literally 塗 'to coat/spread' + 褙 'to paper/back', i.e. the act of covering walls with 벽지 (wallpaper). The single most important distinction is 도배 (the ACT of papering, a service you commission) vs. 벽지 (壁紙, the wallpaper MATERIAL itself, the rolls of paper): you 벽지로 도배를 하다 — 'do the papering with wallpaper'. Korea papers walls rather than painting them as the default finish, so 도배 is a routine event whenever someone moves in or prepares a unit to rent, and it is almost always spoken of as a pair with 장판 (the vinyl flooring): 도배랑 장판 새로 해 주세요 is a stock request to a 집주인. The English-speaker pitfall: 도배 is a noun and needs 하다 to become a verb — never use it as a bare action word; 'I wallpapered' is 도배를 했어요, not just 도배. A second pitfall is reaching for paint vocabulary: walls here are usually 도배 (papered), so describing a fresh interior, Koreans say 도배를 새로 했어요, not 페인트를 칠했어요 unless paint truly was used. Stained or peeling 벽지 is a common reason a tenant negotiates for fresh 도배 before signing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도배 as a standalone verb: learners say 어제 도배 ('yesterday wallpaper'). It needs 하다: 어제 도배를 했어요.
Confusing 도배 (the act/service of papering) with 벽지 (the wallpaper material). You buy 벽지 and you do 도배; 벽지가 예뻐요 (the wallpaper is pretty) vs. 도배를 했어요 (I had it papered).
Defaulting to paint vocabulary (페인트를 칠하다) for a freshly finished Korean interior. The standard wall finish is papered, so it's usually 도배를 새로 했어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 장판 means "vinyl floor covering" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 장판 (jangpan) = "vinyl floor covering". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장판을 깔다 ("to lay the flooring") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장판, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 깔다 (to spread/lay down flat) is THE verb for flooring, mats, blankets
들뜨다 = to come unstuck and bulge; the most common 장판 defect
누렇다 (deep yellow) describes aged vinyl; grounds to ask for new 장판
the standard rental-checklist pair, named together for move-in renovation

examples.en: The floor covering is clean.
examples.note: simple description of condition with 깨끗하다

examples.en: When I turn on the boiler, the floor covering gets warm.
examples.note: ~면 (when/if) + 따뜻해지다 (become warm); the 온돌 effect on the vinyl

examples.en: The old flooring was yellowed, so I laid new one.
examples.note: real renovation; 누렇다 → 누래서 (because it's yellowed) + 깔다

entries.nuance: 장판 (often the full 장판지/壯版紙, 'thick-board paper', historically oil-treated floor paper) is the smooth vinyl sheet laid over the heated 온돌 floor in most Korean homes — it is what your bare feet touch and what warms up when the 보일러 runs. The signature collocation is the verb 깔다 ('to spread/lay flat'): you 장판을 깔다, the same verb you use to lay a mat or 이불 (bedding). Keep 장판 distinct from 바닥 (the floor structure itself, the ground you stand on) — 장판 is the covering ON the 바닥 — and from 마루 (wood-plank/parquet flooring) and 타일 (tile); 장판 specifically means the soft vinyl sheet. Like 도배, it is a fixed item on the rental checklist and is almost always paired with it: 도배랑 장판. Defects have set vocabulary worth knowing: 장판이 들뜨다 (lifts/bubbles up), 장판이 누렇다 (has yellowed with age), and water damage from 누수 soaking 장판 밑 (under the flooring). The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the wrong verb: flooring is laid (깔다), never 'worn' or 'put on' — avoid 장판을 입다 or 장판을 놓다; the correct phrase is 장판을 깔다.

Pairing 장판 with the wrong verb, e.g. 장판을 입다 (from 'put on'). Flooring is laid down: 장판을 깔다. 입다 is only for clothing.
Confusing 장판 (the vinyl covering) with 바닥 (the floor itself). 바닥이 차가워요 = the floor is cold; 장판을 새로 깔았어요 = I laid new vinyl flooring.
Calling all flooring 장판. Wood-plank flooring is 마루/원목마루 and tile is 타일; 장판 specifically means the soft vinyl sheet over 온돌.
