entries.shortExplanation: 콘센트 means "electrical outlet, wall socket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 콘센트 (konsenteu) means "electrical outlet, wall socket". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 콘센트에 꽂다 ("to plug into the outlet"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 콘센트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 꽂다 (to insert/stick in) is the verb for putting a plug in
뽑다 (to pull out) is the opposite of 꽂다; the 전기세-saving move
부족하다 = to be insufficient; a stock complaint about older/small rooms
멀티탭 (multi-tap) extends one 콘센트 into many; what you buy when outlets are scarce

examples.en: Where is the outlet?
examples.note: asking location with 어디에 (at where); a daily-life question

examples.en: I plugged the phone charger into the outlet.
examples.note: 에 꽂다 = plug INTO; the destination-marking 에

examples.ko: 외출할 때 안 쓰는 콘센트는 다 뽑아 놔요.
examples.romanization: oechulhal ttae an sseuneun konsenteuneun da ppoba nwayo.
examples.en: When I go out, I unplug everything not in use.
examples.note: ~ㄹ 때 (when) + 뽑아 놓다 (unplug and leave it); a saving habit

entries.nuance: 콘센트 is a sneaky loanword: it comes via Japanese コンセント, itself a clipping of English 'concentric plug', so despite the spelling it has NOTHING to do with English 'consent' — it simply means the wall socket. You must keep three pieces separate: the 콘센트 is the socket in the wall; the 플러그 (plug) is on the end of the appliance cord; and the verbs are 꽂다 (to plug in/insert) and 뽑다 (to pull out/unplug). So 충전기를 콘센트에 꽂다 = 'plug the charger into the outlet'. The number of 콘센트 is a genuine concern in older or small Korean rooms, and the fix is a 멀티탭 (power strip, 'multi-tap'), another Konglish term. Unplugging idle devices at the 콘센트 is the classic 전기세-saving habit. Pitfalls for English speakers: first, never read 콘센트 as 'consent' — it is purely the outlet. Second, do not blur 콘센트 (the wall socket) with 플러그 (the cord's plug); 'plug it in' targets the 콘센트 (꽂다), while the thing you hold is the 플러그. Third, mind the verbs — you 꽂다/뽑다 a plug, you do not '열다/닫다' (open/close) an outlet.

Confusing 콘센트 (the wall socket) with 플러그 (the plug on the appliance cord). You insert the 플러그 into the 콘센트: 콘센트에 플러그를 꽂다.

entries.shortExplanation: 음식물쓰레기 means "food waste" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "food waste" is 음식물쓰레기 (eumsingmulsseuregi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 음식물쓰레기를 버리다 ("to throw out food waste"). Watch the particle attached to 음식물쓰레기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 버리다 = to discard; the core verb, but it must go in the right bin
분리하다 (分離, to separate) from 일반쓰레기 and 재활용; legally required
봉투 = bag; you buy the official 음식물 전용 봉투 to dispose of it
냄새가 나다 = it stinks; the summer problem that forces frequent disposal

examples.en: I throw out the food waste.
examples.note: 를 + 버리다, the base pattern

examples.ko: 음식물쓰레기는 일반 쓰레기랑 따로 버려야 해요.
examples.romanization: eumsingmulsseuregineun ilban sseuregirang ttaro beoryeoya haeyo.
examples.en: Food waste has to be thrown out separately from regular trash.
examples.note: the key residency rule; ~랑 따로 (apart from) + ~아야 하다 (must)

examples.en: Our apartment disposes of food waste by card.
examples.note: real system: RFID smart bins; 카드로 (by card) marks the means

entries.nuance: 음식물쓰레기 is a transparent compound: 음식물 (飮食物, 'food/edibles') + 쓰레기 (native word for 'trash') — so literally 'food trash'. The thing every newcomer must internalize is that Korean law mandates separating garbage into at least three streams: 음식물쓰레기 (food waste), 일반쓰레기 (general non-recyclable trash), and 재활용 (recycling). 음식물쓰레기 goes only into designated bins — often weight-based RFID units in apartments where you tag a 카드 and dump it, or into official 음식물 전용 봉투 (yellow food-waste bags) elsewhere. Getting it wrong can mean a 과태료 (administrative fine) or an irritated 관리사무소, so it is a real survival skill. The verbs: you 버리다 (throw out) it and you 분리하다 / 분리수거하다 (sort it out for collection). Pitfalls: first, do not lump it with general trash — 음식물쓰레기 vs. 일반쓰레기 is a legal line, not a preference. Second, note what does NOT count as 음식물쓰레기 even though it came from food: large bones, eggshells, shellfish/clam shells, onion skins, and tea bags are 일반쓰레기, because the rule is roughly 'can livestock eat it?'. Getting that boundary wrong is the most common foreigner mistake.

Assuming everything food-derived is 음식물쓰레기. Bones, eggshells, clam/shellfish shells, onion skins, and tea bags go in 일반쓰레기 — the test is whether livestock could eat it.

entries.shortExplanation: 관리비 means "maintenance fee (for an apartment/building)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 관리비 (gwallibi) = "maintenance fee (for an apartment/building)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 관리비를 내다 ("to pay the maintenance fee") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 관리비, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay; charged monthly on top of 월세
나오다 = is issued/billed; 많이 나오다 = comes out high

usagePhrases.en: to be included in the maintenance fee
usagePhrases.note: 포함되다 = be included; ask what the 관리비 covers before signing
별도 (別途, separate) = not included in the advertised rent; a listing red flag

examples.en: I pay the maintenance fee.
examples.note: 를 + 내다, the base pattern

examples.en: The maintenance fee includes the water bill and cleaning fee.
examples.note: what it covers; 포함되어 있다 = is included

examples.ko: 겨울에는 난방비 때문에 관리비가 확 올라가요.
examples.romanization: gyeoureneun nanbangbi ttaemune gwallibiga hwak ollagayo.
examples.en: In winter the maintenance fee jumps because of heating costs.
examples.note: real seasonal spike; 확 (sharply, all at once) + 올라가다 (go up)

entries.nuance: 관리비 is Sino-Korean: 管理費, literally 管理 'management' + 費 'expense', i.e. 'management/maintenance fee'. It is the monthly building-upkeep charge covering shared costs — cleaning, security (경비), the elevator (엘리베이터), corridor lighting, and very often part of the utilities (수도세, 난방비, sometimes 인터넷) — and crucially it is billed ON TOP OF 월세 (monthly rent), which blindsides many newcomers. Always ask what the 관리비 covers and whether it's 포함 (included) or 별도 (別途, 'separate'), because a temptingly cheap 월세 can hide a fat 관리비. Like other recurring charges it 나오다 (comes out) and you 내다 (pay) it. Pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not confuse 관리비 (the monthly, non-refundable maintenance fee) with 보증금 (保證金, the large refundable deposit you get back when you leave) — they are completely different money. Second, do not assume rent already includes it the way some Western 'all-bills-included' rents do; in Korea 관리비 is usually a separate line. entries.nuance: 부추 is the flat, soft, strongly garlic-smelling green you fold into 부추전, dress raw as 부추무침, or pack into 만두 — its flavor reads as 'garlicky onion grass', much more pungent than the mild oniony 쪽파 (thin scallion) it's often confused with at the stall. -나물 = a blanched-and-dressed vegetable side; the full proper name of 숙주 itself

entries.nuance: 숙주 (full name 숙주나물) is the slim, headless white sprout from the mung bean, and the single most important thing to lock in is the contrast 숙주 vs 콩나물: 콩나물 is the thicker soybean sprout that keeps its yellow bean head and stays firm even in soup, while 숙주 is thinner, has no visible head, tastes more delicate, and collapses quickly. Over-blanching it until limp — 숙주 needs only a 살짝 (brief) scald; long boiling kills the 아삭한 crunch that is the whole point.

-나물 = blanched then tossed with 참기름, 마늘, 소금; the everyday 반찬
데치다 = quick boil, then plunge into cold water to keep the green color

examples.en: One bunch of spinach, please.
examples.note: graded simple: the bare market request; counter is 단

채 썰다 = to cut into thin matchsticks (for 호박나물/잡채)

entries.nuance: 애호박 is the short, pale-green, tender Korean summer squash — softer, sweeter and thinner-skinned than the dark, firm Western zucchini, which Koreans call 주키니 or 돼지호박. The contrast that matters is 애호박 vs 호박: bare 호박 leans toward pumpkin/winter squash (think 호박죽, 단호박), so if you ask for 호박 at a mart you may not get the green stew squash you pictured — say 애호박 specifically. Using 만들다 for the pancake ('전을 만들다') — the idiomatic verb is 전을 부치다 (to pan-fry 전).

thin white clusters; the go-to mushroom for 전골/hot pot
sold in shrink-wrapped 팩 (packs) at the mart

entries.nuance: 버섯 is the umbrella word 'mushroom', but in a real kitchen or market you almost always name the kind: 표고 (shiitake, deep aroma, meaty), 팽이 (enoki, thin white clusters), 새송이 (king oyster, thick stalk), 느타리 (oyster, frilly). entries.nuance: 깻잎 is the broad, jagged-edged perilla leaf eaten as a 쌈 wrap or marinated into 깻잎장아찌, and its big, polarizing minty-anise aroma is what makes it a genuine 'do you like it?' food among residents. entries.nuance: 상추 is the soft, floppy leaf lettuce used to wrap grilled meat as 쌈 — and the sharp line to draw is 상추 vs 양배추 vs 양상추: 상추 is the tender wrapping lettuce, 양배추 is the round head cabbage, and 양상추 is crunchy iceberg/head lettuce for salads. Register is plain everyday vocabulary; the only social note is the BBQ ritual phrase. The single most useful collocation a resident learns is '상추 좀 더 주세요' — refills of 상추 are free at almost every 고깃집, so this one line earns its keep nightly. English-speaker pitfall: 'lettuce' in English defaults to the crunchy salad iceberg, but 상추 is the soft wrap leaf, so don't expect a Caesar-salad crunch; and English speakers often hesitate to ask for more because in many countries refills cost extra — in Korea, just say 더 주세요. 상추 is a native Korean word, no hanja.

usagePhrases.note: the big white radish is counted with 개; a whole one is large
반 개 = half; a normal amount to buy since a full 무 is big
채 썰다 = to cut into thin strips for 무생채/무채
a clean clear soup, often simmered with a little beef

examples.note: graded simple: 반 개 + 만 'only', a realistic small purchase

examples.note: everyday: 무로 = '(made) out of radish', instrumental 로

examples.ko: 국 끓일 때 무를 넣으면 국물이 시원해요.

entries.nuance: 무 is the fat, white Korean radish (daikon) — milder, juicier and far bigger than the small red Western radish, and it's the backbone of 무국, 깍두기, 동치미, 무생채, and many soup stocks. Because a whole 무 is heavy, '반 개' (half) is a perfectly normal amount to ask for. The flavor word fused to it is 시원하다: when Koreans say a 무 broth is 시원해요, they do NOT mean cold — they mean clean, brisk, and refreshing on the palate, the same 시원하다 used to praise hot soup that clears your head. Register is plain everyday vocabulary. Natural collocations: 무를 썰다/채 썰다/넣다, 무국, 무생채, 깍두기, 뭇국(소고기뭇국). English-speaker pitfall: 'radish' summons the little crunchy red salad globe, which is the wrong picture entirely — 무 is a large white root used cooked or fermented; and the 시원하다 trap is real, so a learner who hears '시원한 국' must not picture a chilled soup. 무 is a native Korean word with no hanja.

Picturing the small red Western salad radish — 무 is the large white daikon used in soups, kimchi, and stews.
Reading 시원한 국 as 'a cold/cool soup' — for broth 시원하다 means a clean, refreshing flavor, and it's said even of piping-hot soup.
Counting it with 단 like a leafy green — the solid root takes 개 (한 개, 반 개), not 단.

-용 = 'for the purpose of'; big ones for stock vs small ones for 볶음
a sweet-savory 밑반찬 made with tiny 볶음용 anchovies
the default Korean stock combo, 멸치 + 다시마 (kelp)

examples.en: I make broth with anchovies.
examples.note: graded simple: 로 = 'with/using'; 육수를 내다 is the set verb for making stock

examples.note: everyday: 밑반찬 = staple sides kept on hand; -으로 'as'

examples.ko: 국물용 멸치는 똥을 떼고 써야 안 써요.

examples.en: For broth anchovies you remove the gut before using or it turns bitter.
examples.note: real-situation: 똥을 떼다 = remove the dark gut; 쓰다(bitter) puns with 쓰다(use)

entries.nuance: 멸치 is the dried anchovy, and the practical key is that it comes in sizes by purpose: big 국물용 (broth) anchovies for making stock, and tiny 볶음용 ones for the sweet-savory 멸치볶음 side dish — the suffix -용 ('for the use of') is what tells them apart on the package. Paired with 다시마 (kelp), 멸치 forms the foundational Korean soup stock, 멸치다시마 육수, the savory base behind 국수, 떡국, 된장국 and more. Note 육수 is Sino-Korean, 肉水, literally 'meat-water' i.e. a meat/seafood stock, distinct from 물 (plain water). Register is plain kitchen vocabulary. Collocations: 육수를 내다, 멸치를 볶다, 똥을 떼다, 멸치다시마 육수. A real resident tip: pull the dark gut (똥) out of large anchovies, or the broth goes bitter. English-speaker pitfall: don't picture the oily, salty anchovy fillets from a pizza — Korean 멸치 are whole dried fish, sweet snack-sized when small and broth-makers when large; and grabbing the little snack anchovies for stock, or boiling them too long, both produce a cloudy, bitter 육수.

Using tiny snack/볶음용 anchovies for stock instead of the large 국물용 — size is matched to purpose, and small ones won't give a clean broth.
Boiling the anchovies too long — long boiling makes the 육수 bitter and fishy; simmer briefly and strain them out.

usagePhrases.note: 근 = a market unit; for meat one 근 is 600 g, not 500
the most popular cut for grilling at the table
a cheaper cut, good for 제육볶음 and stews

entries.nuance: 돼지고기 is the everyday meat of Korea — cheaper than 소고기 (beef) and the heart of 삼겹살, 제육볶음, 김치찌개, and 보쌈. It's a transparent compound, 돼지 (pig) + 고기 (meat), and the whole 'animal + 고기' system is worth internalizing: 소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken, 양고기 lamb. The single most practical fact is the unit: at a 정육점 (butcher) or mart, meat is sold by the 근, and for meat one 근 = 600 g — so '한 근' is noticeably more than a Western pound. (Confusingly, for vegetables/fruit a 근 is often 375 g, but for meat assume 600 g.) Register is plain everyday vocabulary. You must also learn cut names — 삼겹살 (belly), 목살 (collar/neck), 앞다리살 (shoulder), 등심 (loin) — because the butcher needs the cut, not just 'pork'. Collocations: 돼지고기 한 근, 돼지고기를 볶다/굽다/삶다, 돼지고기 다짐육. English-speaker pitfall: English 'pork' hides the animal, so beginners reach for bare 고기 (meat) — but a butcher needs to hear 돼지고기 vs 소고기; and assuming 한 근 = 500 g (or a pound) gets the quantity wrong.

Assuming one 근 of meat is 500 g or a pound — for meat 한 근 = 600 g (vegetables differ), so you'll mis-order the amount.
Saying just 고기 ('meat') at the butcher — they need to know 돼지고기 vs 소고기 vs 닭고기; specify the animal.
Ordering 'pork' without a cut — ask by cut name (삼겹살, 목살, 앞다리살); the cut decides the dish and the price.

single eggs are counted with 알 (counter for small round things)
spoken 계란후라이 is more common, but 프라이 is the standard spelling

examples.note: graded simple: the mart price question; 한 판 = 30 eggs

entries.nuance: 계란 is the everyday word for 'egg' and what you'll see on most cartons, menus and lips; 달걀 is the same thing in a slightly more 'proper'/native-flavored register (often preferred in writing and textbooks), so 계란 vs 달걀 is purely register — same egg, both correct. 계란 is in fact Sino-Korean, 鷄卵, literally 'chicken-egg' (鷄 chicken + 卵 egg), which is why it can feel a touch more clinical than the native 달걀; everyday speech leans 계란. Eggs are sold by the 판 (a tray of 30) in bulk or in smaller packs, and a single egg is counted with 알 (계란 한 알). Worth pairing: 노른자 (yolk), 흰자 (white), and the verbs 풀다 (whisk), 삶다 (boil), 부치다/프라이하다 (fry). Register is fully neutral. English-speaker pitfall: learners often treat 계란 and 달걀 as two different foods or worry which is 'correct' — relax, they're interchangeable; and the counter trips people up, since eggs aren't 개 — buy them by the 판 and count singles with 알. Also note the spoken 후라이 vs written 프라이 split for the fried egg.

Counting eggs with 개 ('계란 두 개') — singles take 알 (계란 한 알), and bulk is by the 판 (tray of 30).
Writing 후라이 because that's how it sounds — the spoken 계란후라이 is normal speech, but the standard spelling is 계란프라이.

entries.nuance: 양배추 is the round, dense Western-style head cabbage — and the line to nail is 양배추 vs 배추: 양배추 is the spherical green cabbage for coleslaw, 양배추쌈, and 볶음, while 배추 (specifically 배추/배추 통배추) is the tall, loose-leafed napa cabbage that becomes 김치. They are different vegetables, and the 양- prefix marks the 'Western/foreign' import (compare 양파 onion, 양상추 iceberg). It's counted with 통 (한 통 = a whole head) and very commonly bought as 반 통, since a full head is heavy. Register is plain everyday vocabulary. The signature collocation every resident meets is 돈가스 + 양배추 채 (the shredded-cabbage side with pork cutlet), plus 양배추를 찌다/볶다/채 썰다 and 양배추쌈. English-speaker pitfall: English just says 'cabbage', collapsing two Korean vegetables, so a beginner may buy round 양배추 expecting to make kimchi (which needs 배추) — getting this wrong derails the recipe; and counting it with 개 instead of 통 sounds off. 양배추 is a native-plus-Sino blend in feel but treated as a plain everyday word; no hanja drill needed.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 양배추 (round head cabbage) with 배추 (tall napa cabbage) — kimchi needs 배추; 양배추 is for coleslaw, 쌈, and 볶음.
Counting it with 개 ('양배추 한 개') — the round head takes 통 (한 통, 반 통).
Assuming the 양- in 양배추/양상추 is just a fancy variant of 배추/상추 — 양- marks a distinct Western vegetable, not the same plant.

entries.shortExplanation: 보고서 means "report (written document)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보고서 (bogoseo) means "report (written document)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보고서를 쓰다 ("to write a report"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보고서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쓰다 is the plain everyday verb coworkers use
작성하다 is the formal register for emails and notices
제출하다 is for officially handing it in
검토하다 is what a superior does to your draft

examples.en: What report is this?
examples.note: simple: 무슨 + noun asks 'what kind of'

examples.en: I have to submit the report by today.
examples.note: everyday: 까지 marks the deadline 'by'

examples.ko: 팀장님이 보고서를 다시 쓰래요. 주말에도 야근이에요.
examples.romanization: timjangnimi bogoseoreul dasi sseuraeyo. jumaredo yageunieyo.
examples.en: The team lead told me to rewrite the report. I'm working late even on the weekend.
examples.note: real situation: 쓰래요 is contracted 쓰라고 해요, reported command

entries.nuance: 보고서 is the standard word for any written work document, from a quick 주간 보고서 (weekly report) to a thick 출장 보고서 (trip report). It is Sino-Korean: 報告書, literally 'report-tell-document', where the 書 ending signals a formal written paper (compare 계획서 plan, 신청서 application form). The dividing line learners must feel is 보고서 (the paper you hand in) vs 발표 (the spoken presentation you give from it) vs 보고 (the act of reporting up): you 보고서를 작성해서 그걸로 발표해요. Register-wise 작성하다 belongs in formal/email speech while plain 쓰다 is fine between coworkers. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') because English says 'make a report' — in Korean 보고서를 만들다 sounds like physically constructing an object; a document is 쓰다 or 작성하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 보고서를 만들다 because English says 'make a report' — Korean treats a document as something you 쓰다/작성하다, not 만들다; 만들다 implies physically crafting an object
Confusing 보고서 (the written document) with 발표 (the spoken presentation) — you write a 보고서 and then give a 발표 about it
Writing 보고서 하다; the noun has no 하다 verb, so use 보고서를 쓰다 or, for the act of reporting, the separate verb 보고하다

entries.shortExplanation: 마감 means "deadline; closing (date)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "deadline; closing (date)" is 마감 (magam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마감이 언제예요? ("when is the deadline?"). Watch the particle attached to 마감 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the default way to ask the due date
지키다 literally 'protect/keep', the set partner verb
다가오다 paints it as nearing you

usagePhrases.en: to be chased by a deadline
usagePhrases.note: 쫓기다 'be chased', the idiom for crunch

examples.en: When's the deadline?
examples.note: simple: 언제 'when' + 예요

examples.en: This time I'll definitely meet the deadline.
examples.note: everyday: ㄹ게요 is a personal promise to the listener

examples.en: Chased by the deadline, I couldn't even eat lunch.
examples.note: real situation: 도 'even' + 못 'couldn't' stacks the hardship

entries.nuance: 마감 is a native Korean noun (from the verb 막다 'to block/close off') meaning the point at which something is sealed shut: a report's due date, an application cutoff, a shop's last order, even a magazine going to press. The near-synonym confusion is with 기한 and 데드라인: 기한 (期限) is the dry, official 'time limit/term' you see on documents (제출 기한), while 마감 feels more like the live moment things close, and 데드라인 is a borrowed buzzword. Its signature collocation is the idiom 마감에 쫓기다 (chased by the deadline), the universal way to describe last-minute panic. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'meet a deadline' onto 만나다 ('meet a person'): you do NOT 마감을 만나다 — you 마감을 지키다 (keep/protect it). Note 지키다 is the same verb used for keeping a promise (약속을 지키다), which is the right mental image.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 마감을 만나다 from English 'meet the deadline' — 만나다 is only for meeting people; the correct collocation is 마감을 지키다 ('protect/keep')
Defaulting to 데드라인 in formal writing — it sounds like office slang; written/official Korean prefers 마감 or 기한
Saying 마감했다 to mean you personally finished your task — 마감하다 means to close/wrap up an operation (a shop, an event); for finishing your own work use 끝냈어요 or 마감을 지켰어요

entries.shortExplanation: 결재 means "approval; sign-off (by a superior)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 결재 (gyeoljae) = "approval; sign-off (by a superior)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결재를 받다 ("to get approval") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결재, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 'receive' — you, the junior, receive it
올리다 'send up', because it goes up the ladder
나다 'be issued', intransitive, it happens to you
who signs and in what order

examples.en: Did this get approved?
examples.note: simple: dropped 를 in casual speech, rising intonation = question

examples.en: I just submitted it for approval, so please take a look.
examples.note: everyday: 부탁드려요 is the polite 'I ask of you'

examples.ko: 부장님 결재가 아직 안 나서 진행을 못 하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim gyeoljaega ajik an naseo jinhaengeul mo tago isseoyo.
examples.en: The manager's sign-off hasn't come through yet, so I can't proceed.
examples.note: real situation: 아서 'because' chains the reason to the result

entries.nuance: 결재 is the formal sign-off a superior puts on a document or expenditure before it can proceed, today usually through groupware (전자결재). It is Sino-Korean 決裁, literally 'decide-judge' — a person with authority decides and cuts a ruling. The make-or-break point for everyone, Koreans included, is the homophone pair 결재 (approval) vs 결제 (決濟, payment) — pronounced almost identically but meaning sign-off vs paying money; mixing the spelling is the single most common Korean office typo, so a learner who gets it right looks sharp. Directionally, 결재 flows up: a junior 결재를 올리다/받다, while the boss 결재를 하다/내주다. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 결재를 하다 about yourself when you're the requester — you don't 'do' the approval, you 받다 (receive) it; only the approver does the 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 결제 — that homophone means paying money (카드 결제 'card payment'); the approval/sign-off word is 결재 (決裁)
Saying 결재를 하다 about yourself when you are the one asking — the approver 결재를 해 주다, but you the junior 결재를 받다/올리다
Treating 결재 as a casual 'okay' from a friend — it specifically means an authorized superior's formal sign-off, not everyday agreement (that's 동의 or just 좋아요)

entries.shortExplanation: 거래처 means "client; business partner (company)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 거래처 (georaecheo) means "client; business partner (company)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 거래처에 가다 ("to go to a client's place"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 거래처 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to go to a client's place
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination you visit
관리하다 'maintain/look after' the account
와 'with', 미팅 is everyday office English
에 marks the party you reach out to

examples.en: There's a call from the client.
examples.note: simple: 에서 marks the source of the call

examples.en: That client always pays late.
examples.note: everyday: note 결제 'payment' here, not 결재

examples.ko: 새 거래처를 뚫어서 이번 분기 매출이 올랐어요.
examples.romanization: sae georaecheoreul ttureoseo ibeon bungi maechuri ollasseoyo.
examples.en: We landed a new account, so revenue rose this quarter.
examples.note: real situation: 뚫다 'break through' = win a new client, slangy and proud

entries.nuance: 거래처 means a company you do business with — depending on context a client, a vendor, or a supplier. It is built from native + Sino parts: 거래 (去來, 'go-come' = transactions/dealings) + 처 (處, 'place'), literally 'the place transactions happen', i.e. your business counterparty. The synonym line to hold: 거래처 is the B2B partner firm, 고객 (顧客) is a 'customer/client' broadly (can be an individual or a company), and 손님 is a face-to-face 'guest/customer' who walks in. A salesperson proudly says 거래처를 뚫다 (literally 'break through a client') to mean they won a new account. The English-speaker pitfall is calling an individual contact your 거래처 — the word denotes the company/account, not the person; for the person you'd say 거래처 담당자 (the contact at the client). Also don't downgrade a business partner to 손님, which sounds like a retail walk-in.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 손님 ('guest/walk-in customer') for a B2B partner firm — a business counterparty is a 거래처; 손님 sounds like someone entering a shop
Calling an individual person your 거래처 — the word means the company/account; the person is the 거래처 담당자 (the contact there)
Mixing 거래처 (your partner company) with 거래 (the transaction itself) — you visit a 거래처 to do a 거래

entries.shortExplanation: 매출 means "sales; revenue" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sales; revenue" is 매출 (maechul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매출이 오르다 ("sales go up"). Watch the particle attached to 매출 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 오르다 intransitive 'rise', sales rise on their own
떨어지다 'fall', the natural opposite
올리다 transitive 'raise', you actively raise it
목표 (目標) 'goal/target', a constant team phrase

examples.en: How are this month's sales?
examples.note: simple: 어때요 'how is it' asks for an assessment

examples.en: During COVID sales dropped by half.
examples.note: everyday: 반으로 '(down) to half', 으로 marks the result

examples.ko: 매출 목표를 못 채워서 팀 전체가 스트레스받고 있어요.
examples.romanization: maechul mokpyoreul mot chaewoseo tim jeonchega seuteureseubatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: We couldn't hit the sales target, so the whole team is stressed.
examples.note: real situation: 채우다 'fill/meet (a quota)' is the set verb with 목표

entries.nuance: 매출 is top-line sales/revenue — the gross money coming in before any costs are subtracted. It is Sino-Korean 賣出, literally 'sell-out', i.e. what you sold out the door. The crucial business-vocabulary contrast is 매출 (revenue, total inflow) vs 이익/수익 (利益/收益, profit = what's left after costs): a company can have huge 매출 but tiny 이익. Its life-partners are the rise/fall pair 오르다/떨어지다 (intransitive) and 올리다/낮추다 (transitive), plus 매출 목표 and 매출을 채우다 (meet the sales quota). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) confusing 'sales/revenue' with 'profit' — keep 매출 ≠ 이익 firmly apart; and (2) describing a big figure with 많다 ('many') as in 매출이 많다 — for a high amount Koreans say 매출이 높다 ('high'), since 매출 is a measured level, not a count of items.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 매출 (revenue, total sales) with 이익 or 수익 (profit after costs) — a firm with high 매출 can still have low 이익
Saying 매출이 많다 for a big figure — use 매출이 높다 ('high'); 많다 is for countable quantities, 높다 for measured levels
Saying 매출을 벌다 ('earn sales') from English habit — you 매출을 올리다/내다 (raise/post sales); 벌다 ('earn') goes with 돈 (돈을 벌다)

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 어느 'which' picks one of several
옮기다 'move (yourself/something) over'
다른 + noun 'a different ~'
회식 = the obligatory team meal-and-drinks

examples.en: I'm in the marketing department.
examples.note: simple: 예요 lets you state your placement without a verb

examples.en: Next month I'm transferring to another department.
examples.note: everyday: 로 marks the destination department

examples.ko: 그건 우리 부서 일이 아니라서 저는 잘 몰라요.
examples.romanization: geugeon uri buseo iri aniraseo jeoneun jal mollayo.

entries.nuance: 부서 is the general word for an organizational unit inside a company — a department or division. It is Sino-Korean 部署, where 部 means 'section/division' (the same 部 in 부장 department head) and 署 'a post/office'. The structural distinction newcomers must internalize: a 부서 is the broad department, a 팀 (team) is usually a smaller working unit inside or alongside it, and 부 alone (영업부, 인사부) is the formal divisional name. Beware the look-alike trap 부서 (the department, a place/unit) vs 부장 (部長, the department HEAD, a person) — one letter apart but unit vs human. New hires hear 어느 부서예요? on loop during introductions, so keep it primed. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 부서 and 팀 as interchangeable the way English flips 'department/team'; in a Korean org chart they sit at different levels, and you transfer between them with 옮기다, not 바꾸다 ('swap/change an object').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 부서 (the department/unit) with 부장 (the department HEAD, a person) — they differ by one syllable but one is a place and one is your boss
Treating 부서 and 팀 as identical — a 팀 is normally a smaller unit within a 부서; Korean org charts keep them at distinct levels
Saying 부서를 바꾸다 for a transfer — 바꾸다 means swapping an object; moving yourself to another department is 부서를 옮기다

structuredNuance.t: The general word for an organizational unit inside a company — a department or division. New hires hear 어느 부서예요? on loop during introductions, so keep it primed.

entries.nuance: 팀장 is the team leader — in many Korean companies your most immediate boss, the person you report to daily. It is Sino-Korean 팀(team) + 長 ('head/chief'), the same 長 that ends every Korean rank title: 부장 (department head), 사장 (company president), 회장 (chairman). Two register rules are non-negotiable: (1) you almost always attach 님 — 팀장님 — when speaking to or about them, and (2) you can use the bare rank 팀장 as a respectful address by itself, but never 팀장씨, because 씨 is a peer-level marker that, attached to a superior's title, sounds rude. Knowing 팀장 anchors the whole ladder (팀장 → 부장 → 이사 → 대표). The English-speaker pitfall is importing the Western habit of first names or a flat 'you' for managers: dropping 님 or using 씨 with a boss is a real status error Koreans notice instantly.

Saying 팀장씨 — 씨 is for peers and juniors; attached to a superior's rank it sounds disrespectful, so use 팀장님
Calling them just 너/당신 ('you') — never use second-person pronouns up the ladder; address a superior by 직급(rank)+님, e.g. 팀장님

entries.nuance: 첨부 means attaching a file to a message, and 첨부 파일 (attached file) is one of the highest-frequency phrases in Korean work email. It is Sino-Korean 添附, literally 'add-attach', both characters meaning to append something extra. The distinction to keep is digital 첨부하다 (attach an email file) vs physical 붙이다 (stick/glue something to a surface) vs 부착하다 (affix a label/poster) — English says 'attach' for all three, but a file is only ever 첨부하다. Its fixed companion line 첨부 파일을 확인해 주세요 is basically email etiquette you can paste anywhere. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond reaching for 붙이다, is spacing: in careful business writing it is two words, 첨부 파일, not 첨부파일 (though the squished form is tolerated in casual chat). Also note 첨부 has no plain past on its own — you write 첨부했어요/첨부했습니다, never 첨부 했어요 with a gap.

Saying 파일을 붙이다 ('stick the file') from English 'attach' — physical sticking is 붙이다, but an email file is 첨부하다
Writing 첨부파일 as one word in formal mail — the standard spacing is 첨부 파일 (two words); the joined form reads as casual
Saying 첨부 파일을 보다 to ask the reader to look — politely you say 확인해 주세요 ('please confirm/check'); plain 보다 sounds like a bare command

entries.nuance: 외근 means working outside the office — visiting clients, sites, or branches during the workday. It is Sino-Korean 外勤, literally 'outside-duty', and its exact mirror is 내근 (內勤, 'inside-duty' = desk/in-office work); the 勤 ('duty/labor') here is the same character in 출근 (going to work) and 야근 (night work). The synonym line learners must draw is 외근 vs 출장 (出張): 외근 is a same-day excursion you return from by evening, while 출장 is a longer trip, often overnight or to another city. Saying 외근 중이에요 is the neat, professional way to explain why a coworker isn't at their seat. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'out of the office' as one bucket: don't use 외근 for going home, taking leave, or a multi-day trip — it specifically means leaving the building on work business and coming back. Use the action verb 나가다 (외근 나가다), not 가다 alone, for heading out.

Confusing 외근 (a same-day off-site excursion) with 출장 (a longer, often overnight business trip to another place) — duration is the divider
Saying 외근 가다 to mean leaving for the day/going home — 외근 is specifically leaving the office for work duties and returning; for going home use 퇴근하다
Mixing 외근 with 내근 (desk work in the office) — they are exact opposites, 外 'outside' vs 內 'inside'

entries.nuance: 재택근무 is the formal term for working from home, very commonly clipped to just 재택 in speech (오늘 재택이에요). It is fully Sino-Korean 在宅勤務, parsing as 在 'be located' + 宅 'home/residence' + 근무 'duty/work' — literally 'home-located work duty'. It exploded into daily vocabulary after COVID, so 재택근무 가능해요? is now a normal thing to ask when job hunting. The synonym field: 재택근무 (at home specifically) sits inside the broader 원격근무 (遠隔, 'remote work' from anywhere), while 외근 (off-site duty) is its near-opposite — leaving to go OUT, not staying in. The English-speaker pitfall is inventing a descriptive phrase like 집에서 근무 or 집에서 일해요 as if it were the term: those describe the activity, but the fixed noun is 재택근무. Also keep it apart from 외근 — both involve not sitting at your assigned office desk, but 재택은 home, 외근 is the field.

Saying 집에서 근무 as if it were the set term — it merely describes the activity; the established noun is 재택근무 (or clipped 재택)
Confusing it with 외근, which means going OUT for work duties — 재택근무 is staying HOME (在宅)
Saying 재택근무를 가다 ('go to WFH') — you don't go anywhere; use 재택근무를 하다 or 오늘 재택이에요

entries.nuance: 야근 specifically means staying at the office working late into the night — the iconic symbol of old-school Korean work culture. It is Sino-Korean 夜勤, literally 'night-duty', sharing the 勤 ('duty/labor') of 외근 and 출근. The contrast to nail: 야근 is overtime that runs LATE/at night, whereas 특근 (特勤, 'special duty') and 추가 근무 cover extra work generally, including daytime, weekends, or holidays — so weekend morning work is 특근, not 야근. Its cultural foil is the slang 칼퇴 ('knife-exit' = leaving on the dot at quitting time), the thing everyone dreams of instead. And the carrot is 야근 수당 (overtime pay), which is 나오다 (paid out), not 받다-only. The English-speaker pitfall is using 야근 as a blanket word for all 'overtime' — keep the time-of-day nuance — and saying 야근을 가다 ('go to overtime'); you don't go to it, you 야근을 하다.

Saying 야근을 가다 ('go to overtime') — you don't travel to it; the verb is 야근을 하다 (or just 야근해요)
Assuming 야근 수당 is automatic — note the natural opposite 칼퇴 (leaving exactly on time); also overtime pay 나오다 (is paid out) only if the company provides it

entries.nuance: 연차 is your annual paid-vacation entitlement, counted and consumed in days. It is Sino-Korean 年次, literally 'year-order/yearly' (short for 연차 휴가, 年次休暇 'annual leave'). The synonym boundary learners blur: 휴가 (休暇) is the broad umbrella 'leave/vacation' of any kind (including 병가 sick leave, 여름 휴가 summer vacation), while 연차 is the specific paid days you accrue per year — so 연차 is one type of 휴가. A vital partner word is 반차 (半次, 'half-day leave') for slipping out for just a morning or afternoon. The verbs are fixed: you 연차를 쓰다 (use) or 연차를 내다 (file/submit), and your balance 남다 (remains). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: treating 연차 and 휴가 as fully interchangeable (휴가 is broader), and reaching for 하다 — there is no 연차를 하다; the leave is something you 쓰다 or 내다, not 'do'.

Saying 연차를 하다 — leave is not 'done'; you 연차를 쓰다 ('use') or 연차를 내다 ('file/submit')
Forgetting 반차 (半次, half-day leave) and saying 반 연차 — the established word for a half day off is 반차

examples.note: 담아 놓다 captures 'saved for later'; very common window-shopping phrasing

examples.ko: 할인 시작하면 바로 사려고 장바구니에 미리 담아 뒀어요.
examples.romanization: harin sijakamyeon baro saryeogo jangbagunie miri dama dwosseoyo.
examples.en: I added it to the cart in advance to buy the moment the sale starts.
examples.note: real-situation: 미리 담아 두다 = pre-load the cart before a sale

entries.nuance: '장바구니'는 마트의 손바구니와 인터넷 쇼핑몰의 카트를 둘 다 가리키는 한 단어라 일상에서 정말 자주 들립니다. 구성은 '장'(market/shopping)+'바구니'(basket)예요. 핵심은 동사 선택: 카트에는 '담다'(put into a container)를 쓰고, '넣다'(put in)도 통하지만 앱 버튼에는 거의 항상 '담기'로 표기됩니다. 영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 'add to cart'를 직역해 '장바구니에 더하다'라고 하거나, 최종 구매 동사 '사다'를 카트 단계에 써 버리는 것 — 담는 것(담다)과 결제하는 것(결제하다)은 분리된 두 단계예요. 비슷해 보이는 '바구니'는 그냥 아무 바구니지만, '장바구니'는 반드시 '쇼핑'을 함의합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 장바구니에 사다 — 사다 is the final purchase; you 담다 (add) to a cart first, then 결제 (check out). The cart stage and the buy stage are separate.
Direct-translating 'add to cart' as 장바구니에 더하다 — 더하다 means mathematical addition; the real verb is 담다.
Confusing it with bare 바구니 — 바구니 is any basket (laundry, picnic), while 장바구니 specifically implies shopping.

structuredNuance.t: '장바구니'는 마트의 손바구니와 인터넷 쇼핑몰의 카트를 둘 다 가리키는 한 단어라 일상에서 정말 자주 들립니다. 핵심은 동사 선택: 카트에는 '담다'(put into a container)를 쓰고, '넣다'(put in)도 통하지만 앱 버튼에는 거의 항상 '담기'로 표기됩니다.
비슷해 보이는 '바구니'는 그냥 아무 바구니지만, '장바구니'는 반드시 '쇼핑'을 함의합니다.
구성은 '장'(market/shopping)+'바구니'(basket)예요.
영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 'add to cart'를 직역해 '장바구니에 더하다'라고 하거나, 최종 구매 동사 '사다'를 카트 단계에 써 버리는 것 — 담는 것(담다)과 결제하는 것(결제하다)은 분리된 두 단계예요.

entries.shortExplanation: 배송 means "delivery / shipping (of an ordered item)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "delivery / shipping (of an ordered item)" is 배송 (baesong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 배송이 빠르다 ("the shipping is fast"). Watch the particle attached to 배송 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 빠르다 (르 irregular) — the #1 thing Koreans praise sellers for
받다 pairs naturally with 배송 for ordered products
조회 = look-up; the menu label for tracking your parcel
늦어지다 = (gradually) becomes late, beyond the promised date

examples.en: The shipping is fast.
examples.note: beginner: 배송 + 빠르다, the single most common review phrase

examples.ko: 주문한 지 이틀 됐는데 아직 배송 안 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jumunhan ji iteul dwaenneunde ajik baesong an wasseoyo.
examples.en: It's been two days since I ordered but the delivery still hasn't come.
examples.note: everyday: 배송이 오다/안 오다 is how spoken Korean treats it, as if it 'comes'

examples.ko: 배송 조회해 보니까 지금 터미널에 있대요.
examples.romanization: baesong johoehae bonikka jigeum teomineore itdaeyo.
examples.en: I checked the tracking and it says it's at the terminal now.
examples.note: real-situation: -대요 reports the tracking screen's info secondhand

entries.nuance: '배송' 配送 은 한자 그대로 '나누어(配) 보내다(送)', 즉 파는 사람 쪽에서 주문품을 보내는 과정 전체를 뜻해요. 가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '택배'(宅配, home-delivery): '배송'은 보내는 행위/서비스 단계를 가리키고, '택배'는 그것을 실어 나르는 운송 서비스나 도착한 물건 자체(예: '택배 왔어요')를 말합니다. 또 음식점·치킨처럼 즉시 가져다주는 건 '배달'(配達)이라 영역이 달라요 — 쇼핑몰 상품엔 '배송', 짜장면엔 '배달'. 회화에서는 '배송이 왔다/안 왔다'처럼 마치 배송이 스스로 오는 것처럼 자연스럽게 쓰고, 후기에서 '배송 빠르다'는 거의 칭찬의 기본값입니다. 발음은 [배ː송].
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배달 instead of 배송 for shopping parcels — 배달 is for food/restaurant delivery (피자 배달), while ordered products from a store use 배송.
Equating 배송 and 택배 — 배송 is the shipping process, 택배 is the courier service or the arrived box itself; '택배 왔어요' (the parcel came) cannot become '배송 왔어요' as naturally for the physical box.
Saying 배송을 보내다 about your own received item — as the buyer you 배송을 받다 (receive); the seller is the one who 배송을 보내다.

structuredNuance.t: '배송'은 파는 사람 쪽에서 주문품을 보내는 과정 전체를 뜻해요. 회화에서는 '배송이 왔다/안 왔다'처럼 마치 배송이 스스로 오는 것처럼 자연스럽게 쓰고, 후기에서 '배송 빠르다'는 거의 칭찬의 기본값입니다. 발음은 [배ː송].
가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '택배'(宅配, home-delivery): '배송'은 보내는 행위/서비스 단계를 가리키고, '택배'는 그것을 실어 나르는 운송 서비스나 도착한 물건 자체(예: '택배 왔어요')를 말합니다. 또 음식점·치킨처럼 즉시 가져다주는 건 '배달'(配達)이라 영역이 달라요 — 쇼핑몰 상품엔 '배송', 짜장면엔 '배달'.
'배송' 配送 은 한자 그대로 '나누어(配) 보내다(送)'예요.

entries.english: waybill / tracking (invoice) number for a parcel
entries.shortExplanation: 송장 means "waybill / tracking (invoice) number for a parcel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 송장 (songjang) = "waybill / tracking (invoice) number for a parcel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 송장 번호 ("tracking (waybill) number") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 송장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: almost always said as a set phrase, not 송장 alone
등록되다 = gets entered, meaning the seller has shipped it
뜨다 = pop up on screen, spoken shorthand for 'it's been issued'
입력 = input; the field label when reporting a return

examples.en: Please tell me the tracking number.
examples.note: beginner: a polite request you send a seller after buying

examples.ko: 판매자가 송장 등록을 안 해서 아직 발송이 안 됐나 봐요.
examples.romanization: panmaejaga songjang deungnogeul an haeseo ajik balsongi an dwaenna bwayo.
examples.en: The seller hasn't registered the waybill, so it seems it hasn't shipped yet.
examples.note: everyday: 송장 등록 = the act that flips a parcel to 'shipped'

examples.ko: 반송할 때 송장 번호를 꼭 사진 찍어 두세요.
examples.romanization: bansonghal ttae songjang beonhoreul kkok sajin jjigeo duseyo.
examples.en: When you send it back, be sure to photograph the waybill number.
examples.note: real-situation: practical return tip; -아 두다 = do it and keep it for safety

entries.nuance: '송장' 送狀 은 한자로 '보내는(送) 문서(狀)', 곧 택배 상자에 붙은 운송장(라벨)과 거기에 적힌 번호를 뜻해요. 가장 가까운 혼동어는 '영수증'인데, '영수증'은 돈을 냈다는 결제 증빙이고 '송장'은 어디로 어떻게 보내는지를 적은 배송 라벨이라 기능이 완전히 다릅니다. 회화에서는 거의 항상 '송장 번호'로 붙여 말하고, '송장 떴어요?'(번호 나왔어요?)처럼 줄여 쓰기도 해요. 영어 화자의 함정은 영어 invoice를 떠올려 '대금 청구서'로 오해하는 것 — 한국 쇼핑 맥락의 송장은 청구서가 아니라 추적용 운송 라벨/번호입니다. 발음은 적힌 그대로 [송장]이고(앞 받침 ㅇ 뒤라 된소리가 나지 않아요), 같은 소리의 동음이의어 '송장'(시체)과는 맥락으로 구별됩니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 송장 with 영수증 — 영수증 is a payment receipt proving you paid; 송장 is the shipping/tracking label proving how it's sent.
Assuming 송장 = invoice (a bill to pay) because of the English cognate — in shopping it's the waybill/tracking number, not a charge.
Over-tensifying it to [송짱] — there is no 경음화 after the ㅇ batchim here, so 송장 is simply read [송장] as written.

structuredNuance.t: '송장'은 택배 상자에 붙은 운송장(라벨)과 거기에 적힌 번호를 뜻해요. 회화에서는 거의 항상 '송장 번호'로 붙여 말하고, '송장 떴어요?'(번호 나왔어요?)처럼 줄여 쓰기도 해요. 발음은 적힌 그대로 [송장]이고(앞 받침 ㅇ 뒤라 된소리가 나지 않아요), 같은 소리의 동음이의어 '송장'(시체)과는 맥락으로 구별됩니다.
가장 가까운 혼동어는 '영수증'인데, '영수증'은 돈을 냈다는 결제 증빙이고 '송장'은 어디로 어떻게 보내는지를 적은 배송 라벨이라 기능이 완전히 다릅니다.
'송장' 送狀 은 한자로 '보내는(送) 문서(狀)'예요.
영어 invoice를 떠올려 '대금 청구서'로 오해하는 것 — 한국 쇼핑 맥락의 송장은 청구서가 아니라 추적용 운송 라벨/번호입니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 적립 means "points accrual / earning reward points" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 적립 (jeongnip) means "points accrual / earning reward points". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 포인트 적립 ("earning points"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 적립 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the most common collocation; 적립 needs an object like 포인트/마일리지
-금 (sum of money) = the spendable balance built up from 적립
되다 frames it as happening automatically at checkout

usagePhrases.en: shall I add the points (to your account)?
usagePhrases.note: -아 드리다 = the humble service form a cashier uses

examples.en: If you enter your phone number, you earn points.
examples.note: beginner: heard at almost every Korean checkout, 입력하다 + 적립되다

examples.en: I had 5,000 won in points so I paid with that.
examples.note: everyday: 적립금 is treated like real currency you can spend

examples.en: They give good points here so I come often.
examples.note: real-situation: 적립이 잘되다 = the point rate is generous

entries.nuance: '적립' 積立 은 한자로 '쌓아(積) 세우다(立)', 즉 결제할 때마다 포인트나 마일리지를 차곡차곡 모으는 걸 말하고, 그렇게 쌓인 돈은 '적립금'이라고 해요. 반드시 구별해야 할 짝은 '할인'입니다 — '할인'은 지금 이 결제에서 값을 즉시 깎아 주는 거고, '적립'은 다음에 쓸 포인트를 모아 두는 거라 시점이 다릅니다(지금 vs 나중). 매장 계산대에서 '적립하시겠어요? 전화번호 뒷자리 불러 주세요'를 거의 매번 듣게 돼요. 영어 화자의 함정은 'save money'의 save를 떠올려 적립을 곧장 '돈 절약'으로 이해하는 것인데, 적립은 절약이 아니라 미래에 쓸 포인트 적립이에요. 또 '적립금을 적립하다'는 겹말이라 어색합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 적립 (accruing points for later) and 할인 (an immediate price cut) — different mechanics and different timing.
Saying 적립금을 적립하다 redundantly — you 포인트를 적립하다 to build the balance, then use 적립금 to pay.
Translating 적립 as plain 'save money' — it is earning reward points, not cutting the price you pay now.

structuredNuance.t: '적립'은 결제할 때마다 포인트나 마일리지를 차곡차곡 모으는 걸 말하고, 그렇게 쌓인 돈은 '적립금'이라고 해요. 매장 계산대에서 '적립하시겠어요? 전화번호 뒷자리 불러 주세요'를 거의 매번 듣게 돼요. 또 '적립금을 적립하다'는 겹말이라 어색합니다.
반드시 구별해야 할 짝은 '할인'입니다 — '할인'은 지금 이 결제에서 값을 즉시 깎아 주는 거고, '적립'은 다음에 쓸 포인트를 모아 두는 거라 시점이 다릅니다(지금 vs 나중).
'적립' 積立 은 한자로 '쌓아(積) 세우다(立)'예요.
'save money'의 save를 떠올려 적립을 곧장 '돈 절약'으로 이해하는 것인데, 적립은 절약이 아니라 미래에 쓸 포인트 적립이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 무료배송 means "free shipping" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "free shipping" is 무료배송 (muryobaesong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무료배송이다 ("to be free shipping"). Watch the particle attached to 무료배송 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: describing a listing; written as one word on product pages
기준 = standard/baseline, the minimum spend to qualify

usagePhrases.en: in order to get free shipping
usagePhrases.note: -으려고 = with the intent to; the motive for adding more
the inverted phrasing; 배송비 = the shipping charge itself

examples.en: This one is free shipping.
examples.note: beginner: noun + 이다, straight off a product page

examples.en: If you spend over 30,000 won it's free shipping.
examples.note: everyday: 넘게 사다 = buy more than (the threshold)

examples.ko: 무료배송 채우려고 안 살 것까지 담았어요.
examples.romanization: muryobaesong chaeuryeogo an sal geotkkaji damasseoyo.
examples.en: I added stuff I didn't even need just to hit free shipping.
examples.note: real-situation: 채우다 = fill up to the threshold; extremely relatable shopper behavior

entries.nuance: '무료배송' 無料配送 은 한자로 '요금(料)이 없는(無) 배송(配送)', 곧 배송비를 안 받는다는 뜻이고 보통 한 단어로 붙여 씁니다. 같은 의미를 '배송비 무료'로 뒤집어 말하기도 해요. 가장 가까운 혼동 개념은 '조건부 무료배송'인데, 한국 쇼핑몰은 대개 'O만 원 이상 무료배송'처럼 최소 구매 '기준'을 두기 때문에 그 금액을 채우려고 물건을 더 담는 게 흔한 풍경입니다. 반대말은 '배송비 별도'(shipping charged separately)예요. 영어 화자의 함정은 두 가지 — (1) '공짜배송'이라고 말하는 것: '공짜'는 너무 구어/낮은말이라 표준 표기는 '무료'입니다. (2) free라는 단어만 보고 모든 배송이 무료라고 가정하는 것인데, 거의 항상 최소 주문 기준이 붙습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 공짜배송 — 공짜 is too casual/colloquial; the standard, neutral term is 무료배송 (or 배송비 무료).
Assuming all shipping is free — most Korean shops require a minimum spend (무료배송 기준), so check the threshold.
Confusing 무료배송 with 배송비 별도 — the latter means the shipping fee is charged on top, the opposite of free.

structuredNuance.t: '무료배송'은 배송비를 안 받는다는 뜻이고 보통 한 단어로 붙여 씁니다. 같은 의미를 '배송비 무료'로 뒤집어 말하기도 해요.
가장 가까운 혼동 개념은 '조건부 무료배송'인데, 한국 쇼핑몰은 대개 'O만 원 이상 무료배송'처럼 최소 구매 '기준'을 두기 때문에 그 금액을 채우려고 물건을 더 담는 게 흔한 풍경입니다. 반대말은 '배송비 별도'(shipping charged separately)예요.
'무료배송' 無料配送 은 한자로 '요금(料)이 없는(無) 배송(配送)'이에요.
함정은 두 가지 — (1) '공짜배송'이라고 말하는 것: '공짜'는 너무 구어/낮은말이라 표준 표기는 '무료'입니다. (2) free라는 단어만 보고 모든 배송이 무료라고 가정하는 것인데, 거의 항상 최소 주문 기준이 붙습니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 당일배송 means "same-day delivery" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 당일배송 (dangilbaesong) = "same-day delivery". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 당일배송 되다 ("to be eligible for same-day delivery") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 당일배송, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to be eligible for same-day delivery
usagePhrases.note: 되다 marks availability for a given item
마감 = closing/deadline; order before it to qualify

usagePhrases.en: to receive it via same-day delivery
usagePhrases.note: -으로 marks the delivery method
-는 걸로 = '(I'll take) the one that...', picking by feature

examples.en: Does this come same-day?
examples.note: beginner: the single question shoppers ask most, 되다 = is it available

examples.ko: 오전에 주문하면 당일배송으로 받을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ojeone jumunhamyeon dangilbaesongeuro badeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you order in the morning you can get it same-day.
examples.note: everyday: -으로 marks the method; a morning cutoff is typical

examples.ko: 당일배송 마감이 2시라서 지금 시키면 내일 와요.
examples.romanization: dangilbaesong magami 2siraseo jigeum sikimyeon naeil wayo.
examples.en: The same-day cutoff is 2 p.m., so if you order now it comes tomorrow.
examples.note: real-situation: shows the 마감(cutoff) logic that actually governs it

entries.nuance: '당일배송' 當日配送 은 한자로 '바로 그날(當日) 배송(配送)', 즉 주문한 그 날 안에 받는 걸 말해요. 한국의 빠른 배송 문화에서 형제 같은 말들과 구별이 중요합니다 — '익일배송'(翌日, next-day)은 다음 날, '새벽배송'(자정~이른 아침 도착)은 밤새 배송해 아침에 받는 것, '로켓배송/총알배송'은 업체 브랜드식 빠른 배송이에요. 핵심 함정은 '마감 시간(cutoff)': 당일배송은 거의 항상 'O시 전 주문 시'라는 조건이 붙어, 그 시간을 넘기면 다음 날로 넘어갑니다. 영어 화자는 same-day를 '아무 때나 주문해도 그날 온다'로 오해하기 쉬운데, 반드시 마감 전 주문이라는 전제를 확인해야 해요. '당일'은 '오늘'보다 문어적·약관적인 어감이라 안내문에 잘 쓰입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 당일배송 (same day) with 익일배송 (next day) or 새벽배송 (overnight/dawn delivery) — they sound similar but land on different days.
Assuming it applies whenever you order — it almost always requires ordering before a cutoff time (마감), or it slips to tomorrow.
Saying 오늘배송 — the fixed, listing-standard term is 당일배송; 당일 is the formal counterpart of 오늘.

structuredNuance.t: '당일배송'은 주문한 그 날 안에 받는 걸 말해요. '당일'은 '오늘'보다 문어적·약관적인 어감이라 안내문에 잘 쓰입니다.

'당일배송' 當日配送 은 한자로 '바로 그날(當日) 배송(配送)'이에요.
핵심 함정은 '마감 시간(cutoff)': 당일배송은 거의 항상 'O시 전 주문 시'라는 조건이 붙어, 그 시간을 넘기면 다음 날로 넘어갑니다. 영어 화자는 same-day를 '아무 때나 주문해도 그날 온다'로 오해하기 쉬운데, 반드시 마감 전 주문이라는 전제를 확인해야 해요.

entries.english: direct (in-person) trade between buyer and seller
entries.shortExplanation: 직거래 means "direct (in-person) trade between buyer and seller" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 직거래 (jikgeorae) means "direct (in-person) trade between buyer and seller". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 직거래 하다 ("to do a direct trade"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 직거래 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 거래 is Sino-Korean, so it takes 하다 to become a verb
가능 = possible; a common tag in secondhand listings

usagePhrases.en: the meetup spot for a direct trade
usagePhrases.note: 장소 = place; usually a subway exit or convenience store
보조사 -만 = only; a seller refusing to ship

examples.en: Is in-person trade also possible?
examples.note: beginner: a buyer's quick yes/no question to a seller

examples.en: I bought a chair through an in-person trade on Karrot.
examples.note: everyday: 직거래로 사다 = buy via meeting up; 당근(마켓) is the dominant app

examples.ko: 택배는 안 하고 직거래만 한다고 하시네요.
examples.romanization: taekbaeneun an hago jikgeoraeman handago hasineyo.
examples.en: They say they don't ship and only do in-person trades.
examples.note: real-situation: -다고 하다 reports the seller's stated rule

entries.nuance: '직거래' 直去來 는 한자로 '곧바로(直) 오가며(去來) 거래한다', 곧 중개나 택배 없이 사는 사람과 파는 사람이 직접 만나 물건과 돈을 주고받는 걸 뜻해요. 헷갈리기 쉬운 짝은 발음이 비슷한 '직구'(直購, 직접 구매)인데, '직구'는 해외 사이트에서 중간상 없이 사들이는 해외 직접구매고, '직거래'는 보통 국내 중고 거래에서 얼굴 보고 만나는 방식이에요 — 하나는 해외 온라인, 하나는 국내 대면이라 방향이 정반대입니다. 또 영어 화자가 자주 빠지는 함정은 'direct'를 '직접 깎아 주는 직거래가니까 싸다'처럼 가격 개념으로 오해하는 것인데, 직거래는 가격이 아니라 '거래 방식'(대면)을 가리킵니다. 안전을 위해 사람 많은 지하철역·편의점 앞에서 만나는 게 보통이고, 멀면 '택배 거래'를 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 직거래 means a discount — it refers to the in-person method, not the price; a 직거래 can cost the same as shipping.
Confusing it with 직구 (직접 구매, overseas direct purchase) — 직구 is buying from foreign sites, 직거래 is local face-to-face trade.
Saying 직거래를 하다 with 을/를 then dropping 하다 — 거래 is a noun that needs 하다 (직거래하다) to act as a verb.

structuredNuance.t: '직거래'는 중개나 택배 없이 사는 사람과 파는 사람이 직접 만나 물건과 돈을 주고받는 걸 뜻해요. 안전을 위해 사람 많은 지하철역·편의점 앞에서 만나는 게 보통이고, 멀면 '택배 거래'를 해요.
헷갈리기 쉬운 짝은 발음이 비슷한 '직구'(直購, 직접 구매)인데, '직구'는 해외 사이트에서 중간상 없이 사들이는 해외 직접구매고, '직거래'는 보통 국내 중고 거래에서 얼굴 보고 만나는 방식이에요 — 하나는 해외 온라인, 하나는 국내 대면이라 방향이 정반대입니다.
'직거래' 直去來 는 한자로 '곧바로(直) 오가며(去來) 거래한다'예요.
영어 화자가 자주 빠지는 함정은 'direct'를 '직접 깎아 주는 직거래가니까 싸다'처럼 가격 개념으로 오해하는 것인데, 직거래는 가격이 아니라 '거래 방식'(대면)을 가리킵니다.

entries.english: (user) review / write-up after using a product
entries.shortExplanation: 후기 means "(user) review / write-up after using a product" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "(user) review / write-up after using a product" is 후기 (hugi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 후기를 보다 ("to read reviews"). Watch the particle attached to 후기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 (read/look at) is the verb for consuming reviews before buying
남기다 (leave behind) is the idiomatic verb for posting one
shorthand for a product being highly rated
솔직 = candid; a buzzword promising no sugar-coating

examples.en: Are the reviews good?
examples.note: beginner: 후기 + 좋다, the fastest way to ask if something's worth buying

examples.en: From the reviews, it runs small.
examples.note: everyday: 후기 보니까 = judging from the reviews; -대요 relays what they say

examples.ko: 후기 남기면 적립금 준대서 하나 썼어요.
examples.romanization: hugi namgimyeon jeongnipgeum jundaeseo hana sseosseoyo.
examples.en: They said they'd give points for a review, so I wrote one.
examples.note: real-situation: 남기다 for posting; -ㄴ대서 = because they said they would

entries.nuance: '후기' 後記 는 한자로 '나중에(後) 적은 글(記)', 곧 직접 써 보고 남기는 사용 후기/리뷰예요. 외래어 '리뷰'와 거의 같은 뜻이지만 '후기'가 더 한국적이고 일상에서 흔하며, 식당·숙소·제품 어디에나 붙습니다. 짝을 이루는 말은 '별점'(star rating)이고, 진정성을 강조하는 '솔직 후기'·'내돈내산 후기'(내 돈으로 내가 산, 협찬 아님) 같은 표현이 인기예요. 핵심 함정은 시점: '후기'의 '후'가 '나중/이후'라서 반드시 경험한 뒤에 쓰는 글이며, 사기 전 기대나 계획을 '후기'라 부르면 안 됩니다(그건 그냥 '후기'가 아니에요). 또 영어 화자는 동사로 '후기를 쓰다'를 떠올리기 쉬운데, 더 자연스러운 짝은 '후기를 남기다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 후기 for a future plan or pre-purchase expectation — the 後(after) in 후기 means it is strictly an after-the-fact write-up.
Defaulting to 후기를 쓰다 — it's understandable, but the idiomatic verb for posting one online is 후기를 남기다 (leave a review).
Treating 후기 and 예고/기대평 as interchangeable — 후기 is the experience report, not a preview or hype before use.

structuredNuance.t: '후기'는 직접 써 보고 남기는 사용 후기/리뷰예요. 짝을 이루는 말은 '별점'(star rating)이고, 진정성을 강조하는 '솔직 후기'·'내돈내산 후기'(내 돈으로 내가 산, 협찬 아님) 같은 표현이 인기예요.
외래어 '리뷰'와 거의 같은 뜻이지만 '후기'가 더 한국적이고 일상에서 흔하며, 식당·숙소·제품 어디에나 붙습니다.
'후기' 後記 는 한자로 '나중에(後) 적은 글(記)'이에요.
핵심 함정은 시점: '후기'의 '후'가 '나중/이후'라서 반드시 경험한 뒤에 쓰는 글이며, 사기 전 기대나 계획을 '후기'라 부르면 안 됩니다. 또 영어 화자는 동사로 '후기를 쓰다'를 떠올리기 쉬운데, 더 자연스러운 짝은 '후기를 남기다'입니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 결제 means "payment / checkout (completing a purchase)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 결제 (gyeolje) = "payment / checkout (completing a purchase)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결제하다 ("to pay / check out") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 결제 is Sino-Korean and takes 하다 to become a verb
안 되다 = fails to process; a frequent checkout error
수단 = means; card, transfer, simple-pay, etc.
간편 = easy; 카카오페이·네이버페이-style PIN payments

examples.en: I've finished paying.
examples.note: beginner: 결제하다 in the past, confirming checkout is done

examples.en: I'm trying to pay by card but an error keeps popping up.
examples.note: everyday: 오류가 뜨다 = an error pops up on screen

examples.ko: 결제는 했는데 아직 배송 준비 중이래요.
examples.romanization: gyeoljeneun haenneunde ajik baesong junbi jungiraeyo.
examples.en: I've paid but they say it's still being prepared for shipping.
examples.note: real-situation: shows the 결제 → 배송 sequence; -대요 relays the status

entries.nuance: '결제' 決濟 는 한자로 '셈을 매듭지어(決) 치르다(濟)', 곧 돈을 실제로 내어 거래를 끝맺는 과정 전체를 말해요. 가장 가까운 혼동어가 둘 있습니다. 첫째 '계산': 오프라인 계산대에서 값을 치를 땐 '계산'을 많이 쓰지만, 온라인·카드·앱 맥락에서는 '결제'가 기본입니다. 둘째이자 더 위험한 것은 동음이의 '결재' 決裁 — 이건 상사가 서류를 '승인/재가'한다는 완전히 다른 단어라, 쇼핑 글에서 '결재'로 쓰면 틀립니다(받침 ㅔ vs ㅐ 주의). 한국에서는 '간편결제'(카카오페이·네이버페이 등)가 거의 필수라 꼭 알아 두세요. 영어 화자의 함정은 pay를 그냥 '내다'로만 옮겨 '돈을 내다'에 머무는 것인데, 체크아웃 단계 전체는 '결제하다'가 가장 정확합니다. 발음은 [결쩨].
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 결재 — 결재 means a manager's sign-off/approval (a document being authorized), a completely different word from 결제 (payment).
Confusing 결제 with 계산 — 계산 leans offline/in-store; for app and card payments use 결제.
Stopping at 돈을 내다 for online checkout — 결제하다 is the precise verb for finalizing a purchase, errors and all.

structuredNuance.t: '결제'는 돈을 실제로 내어 거래를 끝맺는 과정 전체를 말해요. 한국에서는 '간편결제'(카카오페이·네이버페이 등)가 거의 필수라 꼭 알아 두세요. 발음은 [결쩨].
가장 가까운 혼동어가 둘 있습니다. 첫째 '계산': 오프라인 계산대에서 값을 치를 땐 '계산'을 많이 쓰지만, 온라인·카드·앱 맥락에서는 '결제'가 기본입니다. 둘째이자 더 위험한 것은 동음이의 '결재' 決裁 — 이건 상사가 서류를 '승인/재가'한다는 완전히 다른 단어라, 쇼핑 글에서 '결재'로 쓰면 틀립니다(받침 ㅔ vs ㅐ 주의).
'결제' 決濟 는 한자로 '셈을 매듭지어(決) 치르다(濟)'예요.
pay를 그냥 '내다'로만 옮겨 '돈을 내다'에 머무는 것인데, 체크아웃 단계 전체는 '결제하다'가 가장 정확합니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 정품 means "genuine / authentic product (not a fake)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정품 (jeongpum) means "genuine / authentic product (not a fake)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정품이다 ("to be genuine"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정품 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the basic noun + 이다 assertion of authenticity
인증 = certification; proof a brand item is real
맞다 = to be correct/right; the question buyers ask sellers
보장 = guarantee; a seller's promise

examples.en: Is this genuine?
examples.note: beginner: 정품 + 이다 question, the core authenticity check

examples.en: The price is so cheap I doubt it's authentic.
examples.note: everyday: 정품인지 의심되다 = suspect it might not be real

examples.en: I bought it because they said it was genuine, but it turned out to be a fake.
examples.note: real-situation: 정품 vs 짝퉁 contrast; -라길래 = because (they) said it was

entries.nuance: '정품' 正品 은 한자로 '바른(正) 물건(品)', 곧 가짜가 아닌 진짜 정식 제품을 뜻해요. 직접적인 반대말은 '짝퉁'(구어, 가짜)이며 격식체로는 '가품'(假品)·'위조품'이라 합니다. 헷갈리기 쉬운 짝이 둘 있어요. (1) 발음이 비슷한 '정가'(正價, the list/retail price): 하나는 진품 여부, 다른 하나는 정해진 가격이라 뜻이 전혀 다릅니다. (2) '진품'(眞品): '진품'은 주로 미술품·골동품이 진짜라는 맥락에 쓰고, 시중 브랜드 상품의 진위에는 '정품'이 자연스러워요. 명품·전자기기를 중고로 살 때 '정품 맞아요?', '정품 인증해 주세요'를 거의 반드시 묻습니다. 영어 화자의 함정은 genuine을 막연히 '진짜'로만 옮겨 '진짜예요?'라고 묻는 것인데, 상거래에서는 '정품이에요?'가 의도를 더 정확히 전달해요.

Confusing 정품 (authentic product) with 정가 (the fixed retail price) — they sound alike but one is about realness, the other about price.
Using 진품 for retail goods — 진품 fits art/antiques being real; for brand-name market items the natural word is 정품.

entries.shortExplanation: 중고 means "used / secondhand (goods)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "used / secondhand (goods)" is 중고 (junggo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 중고로 사다 ("to buy secondhand"). Watch the particle attached to 중고 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: -로 marks the condition/route the item comes in
거래 = transaction; the whole used-market activity
중고 attaches directly in front of a noun (중고차, 중고폰)

usagePhrases.en: for a used item / considering it's used
usagePhrases.note: -치고 = 'for a ...', sets a lenient standard

examples.en: This is secondhand.
examples.note: beginner: 중고 + 이다, plainly stating the condition

examples.en: New ones are expensive so I bought it secondhand.
examples.note: everyday: 중고로 사다 vs 새것; the core reason people go used

examples.en: For a used item, the condition is really clean.
examples.note: real-situation: 중고치고는 = considering it's used, it exceeds expectations

entries.nuance: '중고' 中古 는 한자로 '가운데쯤(中) 오래된(古)', 곧 한 번 이상 쓰인 물건을 말해요. 명확한 반대말은 '새것/새 상품'이고, 거의 안 쓴 물건은 'S급'이나 '미개봉'(unopened)으로 따로 표시합니다. 핵심 문법 함정은 품사: '중고'는 명사라서 형용사처럼 활용하지 않아요 — '중고하다'(X)는 없고, '중고로 사다'·'중고 물건'·'중고폰'처럼 명사 앞이나 조사 -로와 함께 씁니다. 또 발음·표기가 비슷한 '중간'(中間, middle)과 헷갈리지 마세요. 한국은 당근마켓·중고나라 등 중고 거래 문화가 매우 활발해 '중고 거래'라는 말이 일상적이며, 영어의 'second hand'를 직역해 두 단어로 떼어 쓰거나 '두 번째 손'식으로 풀어 말하면 어색합니다 — 그냥 명사 '중고' 한 단어예요.

Treating 중고 as a verb/adjective that conjugates — it's a noun; say 중고로 사다 or 중고 물건, never 중고하다.
Confusing 중고 (secondhand) with 중간 (middle) — different words despite both starting with 中(중).
Splitting or literalizing 'second hand' — Korean uses the single noun 중고, not a two-word or 'second hand' calque.

entries.shortExplanation: 쿠폰 means "coupon (discount voucher)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쿠폰 (kupon) = "coupon (discount voucher)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쿠폰을 쓰다 ("to use a coupon") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쿠폰, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 쓰다 = apply/use it at the buying moment
적용 = application; the actual checkout step that activates it
the separate first step of getting it to your account
할인 = discount; the most common type of coupon

examples.en: I have a coupon.
examples.note: beginner: 쿠폰 + 있다, the simplest way to say you've got one

examples.en: After applying the coupon it got 5,000 won cheaper.
examples.note: everyday: 쿠폰 적용하다 → 싸지다; -았더니 = once I did X, then Y happened

examples.ko: 쿠폰 다운받는 거 깜빡해서 그냥 결제했어요.
examples.romanization: kupon daunbanneun geo kkamppakaeseo geunyang gyeoljehaesseoyo.
examples.en: I forgot to download the coupon and just checked out.
examples.note: real-situation: a common regret; claiming and applying are separate

entries.nuance: '쿠폰'은 영어 coupon에서 온 외래어로, 가격을 그 자리에서 깎아 주는 할인권이에요. 반드시 구별할 짝은 '적립'(포인트 쌓기): 쿠폰은 지금 결제에서 즉시 값을 깎지만, 적립은 나중에 쓸 포인트를 모아 두는 거라 효과 시점이 정반대입니다. 또 '쿠폰'은 깎아 주는 '권리/수단'이고, 그렇게 실제로 깎인 액수는 '할인'이라 층위가 달라요. 한국 앱의 핵심 함정은 절차가 두 단계라는 점 — 먼저 '쿠폰 다운받기/받기'(claim)로 내 계정에 담고, 결제 화면에서 '쿠폰 적용'(apply)을 눌러야 비로소 깎입니다. 받기만 하고 적용을 깜빡하면 할인이 안 돼요. 영어 화자는 'I have a coupon'처럼 받은 것만으로 끝났다고 생각하기 쉬운데, 적용 버튼까지 눌러야 실제 할인이 들어갑니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forgetting that claiming (받다/다운받다) and applying (적용) a coupon are two separate steps — having it isn't using it.
Mixing up 쿠폰 (instant discount voucher) with 적립금/포인트 (saved-up points for later) — opposite timing of the benefit.
Saying 쿠폰을 적립하다 — you 쿠폰을 받다/적용하다; 적립 is for points, not coupons.

entries.shortExplanation: 내성적이다 means "introverted" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 내성적이다 (naeseongjeogida) means "introverted". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 내성적인 성격 ("an introverted personality"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 내성적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 성격 (personality) is the noun it pairs with most
-(이)라서 gives a reason off a 이다-adjective

usagePhrases.en: I'd say I'm on the introverted side
usagePhrases.note: -(으)ㄴ 편이다 hedges instead of stating it flatly
Habitually chained with 조용하다 in self-descriptions

examples.en: I'm a bit introverted.
examples.note: Add 좀 to soften a self-label; note the form is 내성적이에요, not 내성적해요

examples.ko: 저는 내성적이라서 처음 보는 사람이랑 말하는 게 어려워요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun naeseongjeogiraseo cheoeum boneun saramirang malhaneun ge eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: I'm introverted, so talking to people I'm meeting for the first time is hard.
examples.note: -(이)라서 links the trait to its everyday consequence

examples.ko: 걔는 내성적이지만 친해지면 말이 엄청 많아.
examples.romanization: gyaeneun naeseongjeogijiman chinhaejimyeon mari eomcheong mana.
examples.en: He's introverted, but once you get close he talks a ton.
examples.note: 걔 + banmal among friends; -지만 sets up the contrast

entries.nuance: 내성적이다 is the neutral, textbook word for 'introverted' and is completely safe to say about yourself in interviews or first meetings — Koreans read it as a temperament, not a flaw. It is Sino-Korean: 內省的 (內 inner + 省 to reflect/introspect), literally 'inward-reflecting type', so it points to drawing energy inward rather than to being unfriendly. The key contrast is with 소심하다 (timid), which adds a negative 'holds back out of fear' edge, and with 조용하다 (quiet), which is only about low volume; an introvert can be talkative once comfortable. It collocates with 성격, 사람, and the hedge -(으)ㄴ 편이다. The pitfall for English speakers is the conjugation: because the stem already ends in 이다, you say 내성적이에요 / 내성적인, never the 하다-style 내성적해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 내성적해요 — there is no 하다 here; the stem is 내성적이다, so it conjugates as 내성적이에요 / 내성적인
Treating it as a synonym of 소심하다 — 내성적 is just inward-facing and value-neutral, while 소심하다 implies timid, fearful holding-back
Using it to mean merely 'quiet' (조용하다) — composure and volume are separate; 내성적 is about where you get your energy

entries.shortExplanation: 외향적이다 means "extroverted, outgoing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "extroverted, outgoing" is 외향적이다 (oehyangjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 외향적인 성격 ("an outgoing personality"). Watch the particle attached to 외향적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Direct opposite of 내성적인 성격
-(이)라서 gives the reason off 이다
외향적으로 + 변하다 = change in that direction
-(으)ㄴ 편이다 to hedge rather than declare

examples.en: I'm outgoing.
examples.note: Basic self-intro; the form is 외향적이에요, never 외향적해요

examples.ko: 저는 외향적이라서 새 친구 사귀는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun oehyangjeogiraseo sae chingu sagwineun ge joayo.
examples.en: I'm outgoing, so I enjoy making new friends.
examples.note: 친구를 사귀다 = make friends; -(이)라서 ties trait to behavior

examples.ko: 우리 팀장님은 진짜 외향적이라서 회식 때 분위기를 다 살려요.
examples.romanization: uri timjangnimeun jinjja oehyangjeogiraseo hoesik ttae bunwigireul da sallyeoyo.
examples.en: Our team lead is super outgoing, so they liven up the whole mood at company dinners.
examples.note: 분위기를 살리다 = liven up the mood; a 회식 staple scene

entries.nuance: 외향적이다 is the standard, positive-leaning term for 'extroverted' and is woven into MBTI chat, which is hugely popular in Korea — you will constantly hear 'E야 I야?' (Are you an E or an I?). It is Sino-Korean: 外向的 (外 outside + 向 to face/turn toward), literally 'outward-facing type', describing where someone aims their energy. The sharp contrast is with 활발하다: 외향적이다 names the inner trait, while 활발하다 describes the visible liveliness you can see in a room — an extrovert who happens to be tired won't look 활발한 at that moment. It pairs with 성격, the verb 변하다 (외향적으로 변하다), and the hedge -(으)ㄴ 편이다. The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't add 하다 (it's 외향적이에요 / 외향적인), and don't swap in the noun 외향성 (extroversion) where the adjective belongs — say 외향적이에요, not 외향성이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 외향적해요 — correct forms are 외향적이에요 / 외향적인, because the stem ends in 이다
Using the noun 외향성 (extroversion) as if it were the adjective — to describe a person, use 외향적이다
Equating it with 활발하다 — 외향적 is the trait, 활발 is the observable energy, and they don't always coincide

entries.shortExplanation: 꼼꼼하다 means "meticulous, thorough, detail-oriented" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 꼼꼼하다 (kkomkkomhada) = "meticulous, thorough, detail-oriented". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 꼼꼼하게 확인하다 ("check thoroughly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 꼼꼼하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 꼼꼼하게 = adverb form; collocates strongly with 확인하다
High praise for a coworker's reliability
Frequently listed as a 장점 (strength) in interviews
꼼꼼히 = alternate adverb, a touch more written

examples.en: Did you check this thoroughly?
examples.note: Everyday office question; 꼼꼼하게 modifies 확인하다

examples.ko: 저 사람 일 진짜 꼼꼼하게 해서 실수가 거의 없어.
examples.romanization: jeo saram il jinjja kkomkkomhage haeseo silsuga geoui eopseo.
examples.en: That person works so meticulously they almost never make mistakes.
examples.note: Casual praise; 실수 = mistake

examples.en: Read the menu carefully before you order.
examples.note: Practical everyday advice; 꼼꼼하게 modifies 읽어 보다 ('read and check')

entries.nuance: 꼼꼼하다 is native Korean for being careful, thorough, and reliable with details, and in a work context it is high, almost unambiguous praise — it is one of the safest 'strengths' to claim in a Korean interview. It lives in adverb form a lot: 꼼꼼하게 확인하다, 꼼꼼하게 챙기다. Two boundaries matter. First, don't confuse it with 깔끔하다, which is about being neat/tidy in appearance or finish; you can be 꼼꼼한 (thorough) without being 깔끔한, and vice versa. Second, its negative twin is 까다롭다 (picky/demanding to the point of being hard to satisfy) — when thoroughness tips into slowing everyone down, Koreans switch to 까다롭다. The English-speaker pitfall is the adverb: it is 꼼꼼하게 or 꼼꼼히, and you should not bolt 로 onto it (no 꼼꼼하게로); and as praise it modifies how someone works, so anchor it to a verb like 하다/확인하다 rather than leaving it bare.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for 'neat/clean' — that is 깔끔하다; 꼼꼼하다 is about thoroughness, not tidiness
Adding a particle to the adverb: it's 꼼꼼하게 / 꼼꼼히, never 꼼꼼하게로

entries.shortExplanation: 예민하다 means "sensitive, edgy, on edge" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 예민하다 (yeminhada) means "sensitive, edgy, on edge". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 요즘 예민해 ("I'm on edge these days"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 예민하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Warning others you're stressed; banmal
Neutral-to-slightly-negative about a person
Also used for skin, allergies, stomach, sleep
예민하게 굴다 = act oversensitive

examples.en: I'm a bit on edge lately.
examples.note: A quick, very natural heads-up to a friend; banmal

examples.ko: 시험 기간이라 요즘 예민하니까 이해해 줘.
examples.romanization: siheom giganira yojeum yeminhanikka ihaehae jwo.
examples.en: It's exam season so I'm on edge — please bear with me.
examples.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason for asking forbearance

examples.ko: 저는 잠귀가 예민해서 작은 소리에도 깨요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jamgwiga yeminhaeseo jageun soriedo kkaeyo.
examples.en: I'm a light sleeper, so even small sounds wake me up.
examples.note: 잠귀가 예민하다 = sensitive ears while sleeping; the physical sense

entries.nuance: 예민하다 covers two strands: a person being emotionally on-edge, touchy, or easily set off (usually from stress), and physical sensitivity — 피부 (skin), 잠귀 (sleep), 속/위 (stomach). It is Sino-Korean: 銳敏 (銳 sharp + 敏 quick/keen), literally 'sharply keen', which is why it reaches into both perception and temper. About someone's mood it can sound mildly critical, so people most often apply it to themselves as a pre-emptive warning. Two contrasts to fix: 민감하다 (also 'sensitive', 敏感) overlaps heavily but is the word of choice when an issue, market, or sensor is 'sensitive' (민감한 문제 = a sensitive matter), whereas a person on edge is more naturally 예민한; and 예리하다 (sharp/incisive, of a mind or analysis) is a false friend — it means perceptive, not irritable. The English trap is assuming 'sensitive = caring/tender'; for a gently sensitive, easily-moved heart, Koreans say 섬세하다, not 예민하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reaching for 예민하다 to praise a kind, tender person — that warmer 'sensitive' is 섬세하다; 예민하다 leans toward irritable/on-edge
Swapping it freely with 민감하다 — for sensitive topics/data/markets use 민감하다; for a person's frayed mood use 예민하다
Confusing it with 예리하다 (sharp-minded/incisive); a 예민한 person is touchy, a 예리한 person is perceptive
