entries.shortExplanation: 무뚝뚝하다 means "blunt, curt, gruff (cold-seeming manner)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "blunt, curt, gruff (cold-seeming manner)" is 무뚝뚝하다 (muttukttukada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무뚝뚝하게 말하다 ("speak curtly"). Watch the particle attached to 무뚝뚝하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Describes a flat, short-spoken delivery
Often softened with 그래도 (but still…)
겉으로는 = on the outside, sets up a 'but inside…' turn
-아/어 보이다 = looks/seems

examples.en: My dad is kind of gruff.
examples.note: A stock, affectionate description of Korean fathers; banmal

examples.ko: 사장님이 무뚝뚝하게 대답해서 화난 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi muttukttukage daedapaeseo hwanan jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: The boss answered so curtly that I thought he was angry.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 줄 알았다 = mistakenly thought that…

examples.ko: 우리 아빠는 무뚝뚝하지만 속은 정말 따뜻해요.
examples.romanization: uri appaneun muttukttukajiman sogeun jeongmal ttatteutaeyo.
examples.en: My dad is gruff but really warm on the inside.
examples.note: 속은 따뜻하다 = warm inside; the classic redeeming-turn collocation

entries.nuance: 무뚝뚝하다 is native Korean describing a curt, unexpressive manner — short answers, no small talk, a flat face — without necessarily meaning the person is unkind. It is so reliably paired with 속은 따뜻하다 ('warm inside') that the 'gruff exterior, warm interior' arc is almost a cultural template for dads, older men, and Gyeongsang-do speakers. The crucial contrast is with 차갑다 (cold-hearted): 차갑다 implies the person actually is cold toward you, while 무뚝뚝하다 is only about an undemonstrative style — the feeling underneath may be perfectly warm. It also differs from 무례하다 (rude), which is a breach of manners; a 무뚝뚝한 person follows etiquette, they just don't decorate it with warmth. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spelling (the syllable doubles — 무뚝뚝하다, not 무뚝하다), and resisting the instinct to read curtness as hostility, since Koreans hear it as personality, not an insult.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping a syllable as 무뚝하다 — the word reduplicates: 무뚝뚝하다
Using it to mean 'rude' — that is 무례하다; 무뚝뚝하다 is about flat affect, not bad manners
Equating it with 차갑다 (cold-hearted) — 무뚝뚝하다 is just an unexpressive style and often coexists with real warmth

entries.shortExplanation: 다정하다 means "warm, affectionate, sweet (to others)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다정하다 (dajeonghada) = "warm, affectionate, sweet (to others)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 다정한 사람 ("a warm, affectionate person") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 다정하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: High compliment for a partner or close friend
다정하게 + 대하다 = treat kindly

usagePhrases.en: have a warm way of speaking
usagePhrases.note: 말투 = tone/manner of speech
다정다감 is a common four-syllable expansion

examples.en: You're so sweet.
examples.note: A warm, direct compliment to a friend; banmal

examples.ko: 선생님이 다정하게 말해 줘서 긴장이 풀렸어요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi dajeonghage malhae jwoseo ginjangi pullyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The teacher spoke to me so warmly that my nerves eased.
examples.note: 긴장이 풀리다 = tension eases; 다정하게 modifies how they spoke

examples.ko: 남자친구가 너무 다정해서 친구들이 다 부러워해요.
examples.romanization: namjachinguga neomu dajeonghaeseo chingudeuri da bureowohaeyo.
examples.en: My boyfriend is so sweet that all my friends are jealous.
examples.note: 부러워하다 = be envious; a real-life relationship boast

entries.nuance: 다정하다 means warm, tender, and affectionate toward others — it is about emotional closeness and sweet treatment, which makes it the go-to compliment for partners, dear friends, and beloved teachers. It is Sino-Korean at the root: 多情 (多 many + 情 affection/feeling), literally 'much feeling', i.e. full of warmth. The dividing line that matters is with 친절하다 (kind/polite): 친절하다 is the right word for staff being helpful to a customer or a stranger giving directions — courteous service — whereas 다정하다 implies real, personal warmth, so it sounds slightly off for a one-time formal exchange. The expanded 다정다감하다 is a touch more literary but common in praise. The English trap is mapping 'nice/friendly' onto 다정하다 across the board: a cashier being pleasant is 친절한, not 다정한, and reserving 다정하다 for genuine warmth is what keeps it from sounding strange.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다정하다 for polite service — staff being helpful to customers is 친절하다, not 다정하다
Applying it to a one-time formal stranger — it implies real intimacy, so it rings false there; use 친절하다
Confusing the adverb target: 다정하게 modifies how you treat/speak to someone (다정하게 대하다), so anchor it to a verb

entries.shortExplanation: 까칠하다 means "prickly, snippy, hard to please" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 까칠하다 (kkachilhada) means "prickly, snippy, hard to please". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성격이 까칠하다 ("have a prickly personality"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 까칠하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Mildly negative, but often said affectionately

usagePhrases.en: be snippy today of all days
usagePhrases.note: 오늘따라 = unusually today
까칠하게 굴다 = behave in a prickly way
The original literal sense: rough to the touch

examples.en: Why are you so snippy?
examples.note: Casual concern between friends; banmal

examples.ko: 우리 팀장님 평소엔 괜찮은데 마감 때만 까칠해져요.
examples.romanization: uri timjangnim pyeongsoen gwaenchaneunde magam ttaeman kkachilhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: Our team lead is usually fine but gets prickly only around deadlines.
examples.note: 마감 = deadline; -아/어지다 = become

examples.ko: 그 사람 까칠해 보여도 알고 보면 착해요.
examples.romanization: geu saram kkachilhae boyeodo algo bomyeon chakaeyo.
examples.en: He seems prickly, but once you really get to know him he's nice.
examples.note: 알고 보면 = when you actually get to know

entries.nuance: 까칠하다 literally means 'rough to the touch' (you'll still hear 피부가 까칠하다 for dry, stubbly skin) and figuratively describes someone snippy, easily irritated, or hard to please. Crucially it is fairly light and even playful — friends tease each other with it — so it is nowhere near a serious insult; for genuinely mean or nasty, Koreans say 못됐다. The contrast learners most need is with 까다롭다: 까다롭다 is about high, demanding standards (a 까다로운 손님 sends the dish back because it doesn't meet their bar), while 까칠하다 is about mood and attitude (a 까칠한 사람 is touchy and short with you regardless of standards). It very often appears with -아/어지다 to mark a temporary shift (마감 때 까칠해지다 = gets prickly at deadlines) and with 굴다 (까칠하게 굴다). The English-speaker pitfall is over-reading it as harsh: it's closer to 'a bit prickly/snippy' than to 'mean', so deploying it as a real insult overshoots.

Using it as a serious insult — it's relatively mild and often teasing; for genuinely mean use 못됐다
Confusing it with 까다롭다 — 까다롭다 is demanding about standards, 까칠하다 is about a touchy mood/attitude
Forgetting the 'becomes' nuance — for a temporary state, pair it with -아/어지다: 까칠해지다

entries.shortExplanation: 소심하다 means "timid, easily intimidated, fainthearted" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "timid, easily intimidated, fainthearted" is 소심하다 (sosimhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 소심해요 ("I'm timid"). Watch the particle attached to 소심하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Mildly self-deprecating self-intro
Carries a slightly negative nuance
Encouraging a friend to speak up
Beloved set phrase for small, harmless payback

examples.en: I'm a bit timid.
examples.note: Said with a self-deprecating laugh; the form is 소심해요, not 소심하해요

examples.en: Don't be timid, just ask!
examples.note: A friendly push to be bolder; 굴다 = behave/act

examples.ko: 지각한 동료 자리에 몰래 포스트잇 붙였어. 소심한 복수지.
examples.romanization: jigakan dongnyo jarie mollae poseuteuit butyeosseo. sosimhan boksuji.
examples.en: I secretly stuck a post-it on my late coworker's desk. Petty revenge.
examples.note: 소심한 복수 = the classic playful 'petty revenge' phrase

entries.nuance: 소심하다 means timid, fainthearted, or easily intimidated — and unlike the neutral 내성적이다 ('introverted'), it leans negative, implying you hold back when you really shouldn't (can't send back a wrong dish, can't speak up in a meeting). It is Sino-Korean: 小心 (小 small + 心 heart), literally 'small-hearted'. Beware a false-friend trap here: the Chinese 小心 means 'be careful', but in Korean 소심하다 does NOT mean careful — it means timid; the 'careful/prudent' meaning belongs to 신중하다. The sharp contrast with 내성적이다 is the whole point: an introvert simply recharges alone, while a 소심한 person shrinks back out of fear, so the two are not interchangeable. The much-loved set phrase 소심한 복수 ('petty revenge') is everywhere. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the false friend, is using it as an interview 'strength' — it sounds self-critical, so pick 신중하다 (prudent) instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 소심하다 as a synonym of 내성적이다 — introverts aren't necessarily timid; 소심 implies fear and holding back
Reading 小心 as 'careful' (its Chinese meaning) — in Korean 소심하다 is 'timid'; 'careful/prudent' is 신중하다
Offering it as a strength in an interview — it's self-deprecating; use 신중하다 for the positive 'thinks before acting'

entries.shortExplanation: 느긋하다 means "easygoing, laid-back, unhurried" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 느긋하다 (neugeutada) = "easygoing, laid-back, unhurried". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 성격이 느긋하다 ("have a laid-back personality") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 느긋하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Generally positive

usagePhrases.en: wait in a relaxed, unhurried way
usagePhrases.note: 느긋하게 = without rushing
Pairs with leisure nouns (아침, 휴가)

usagePhrases.en: take it easy, relax one's mind
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase: 마음을 ~게 먹다

examples.en: There's no rush, so take your time.
examples.note: 급하다 = be in a hurry; a reassuring, soothing tone

examples.ko: 저는 성격이 느긋해서 웬만한 일에는 스트레스를 안 받아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun seonggyeogi neugeutaeseo wenmanhan ireneun seuteureseureul an badayo.
examples.en: I'm laid-back, so most things don't stress me out.
examples.note: 웬만한 = most ordinary; 스트레스 받다 = get stressed

examples.ko: 휴가 때는 느긋하게 늦잠도 자고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: hyuga ttaeneun neugeutage neutjamdo jago sipeoyo.
examples.en: On vacation I want to sleep in and just take it easy.
examples.note: 늦잠 자다 = sleep in; 느긋하게 colors the whole leisure scene

entries.nuance: 느긋하다 is native Korean for the positive flavor of 'laid-back' — calm, unbothered, and not easily rushed — and it works both for a person's temperament (성격이 느긋하다) and for relaxed stretches of time (느긋한 아침, 느긋한 주말). Its natural antonym is 급하다 (impatient/hasty), and the two are often set against each other. Two contrasts keep it precise. With 여유롭다 (which overlaps), 느긋하다 is about an unhurried temperament, while 여유롭다 leans toward having actual leeway — of time, space, or means (마음의 여유, 시간 여유); you can feel 느긋한 even when you're not objectively 여유로운. With 게으르다 (lazy), the difference is intent: 느긋하다 is unhurried by choice and still gets things done, whereas 게으르다 is an unwillingness to work — calling a relaxed person 게으른 is an insult, not a description. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that lazy/laid-back slip, plus the conjugation: it's a regular 하다-stem, so 느긋해요 / 느긋한, never 느긋어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 게으르다 (lazy) — 느긋하다 is unhurried by choice and still productive, not unwilling to work
Using it interchangeably with 여유롭다 — 여유롭다 stresses having leeway (time/means); 느긋하다 stresses an unhurried temperament
Mis-conjugating as 느긋어요 — it's a 하다-adjective: 느긋해요 / 느긋한

The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that lazy/laid-back slip, plus the conjugation: it's a regular 하다-stem, so 느긋해요 / 느긋한, never 느긋어요.

usagePhrases.note: Common positive description
활발하게 + 활동하다 in clubs, work
Frequent for children
Also describes a room, class, or chat

examples.en: That kid is really lively.
examples.note: A warm remark watching an energetic child; 활발하다 about visible energy

examples.ko: 새로 온 인턴이 성격이 활발해서 금방 다 친해졌어요.
examples.romanization: saero on inteoni seonggyeogi hwalbalhaeseo geumbang da chinhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The new intern is so lively that everyone got close fast.
examples.note: 금방 = quickly; 친해지다 = get close

examples.ko: 동아리에서 활발하게 활동하면 친구를 많이 사귈 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: dongarieseo hwalbalhage hwaldonghamyeon chingureul mani sagwil su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you're active in a club, you can make lots of friends.
examples.note: 동아리 = club; 활발하게 활동하다 is a fixed pairing

entries.nuance: 활발하다 describes lively, energetic, sociable behavior — it's how you praise someone bright and engaged in groups, and it stretches naturally to atmospheres and activities (활발한 토론 = a lively debate, 분위기가 활발하다 = the vibe is lively). It is Sino-Korean: 活潑 (活 alive + 潑 to splash/be spirited), literally 'alive and splashing', a vivid image of bubbling energy. The contrast that matters is with 외향적이다: 외향적이다 names the inner MBTI-style trait (where you draw energy), while 활발하다 names the observable liveliness in the moment — a true extrovert who's exhausted simply won't look 활발한 right then, and a normally reserved person can be 활발한 at a party they love. It's almost always a compliment about people. The English-speaker pitfall is using it as a flat synonym for 'outgoing/extroverted'; reserve 활발하다 for visible energy and motion, and don't attach it to calm, inanimate things, where it sounds wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a pure synonym for 외향적이다 — 활발하다 is observable energy, not the underlying personality trait
Applying it to calm, inanimate things — it implies motion and liveliness, so it sounds off there
Forgetting it covers atmospheres too — 분위기가 활발하다 / 활발한 토론 are natural, not just people

usagePhrases.note: Positive, mature impression
차분하게 = composedly
-아/어지다 = become
Often praised in high-pressure jobs

examples.en: You have such a calm voice.
examples.note: A polite compliment using honorific -(으)시-; about composure, not volume

examples.ko: 차 한 잔 마시니까 마음이 좀 차분해졌어요.
examples.romanization: cha han jan masinikka maeumi jom chabunhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After a cup of tea my mind calmed down a bit.
examples.note: -(으)니까 marks the natural cause; 차분해지다 = grow calm

examples.ko: 급한 상황에서도 차분하게 대처해서 다들 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: geupan sanghwangeseodo chabunhage daecheohaeseo dadeul nollasseoyo.
examples.en: Even in an urgent situation they handled it calmly, so everyone was impressed.
examples.note: 대처하다 = handle/respond to; a strong interview-worthy trait

entries.nuance: 차분하다 is native Korean for calm, composed, and steady — a person who doesn't get rattled, or a quiet, settled mood. It is a strong compliment, especially for keeping your head under pressure (차분하게 대처하다), which makes it an excellent trait to claim in interviews. It commonly takes -아/어지다 to mark a shift into calm (마음이 차분해지다). The contrast learners need most is with 조용하다 (quiet): 조용하다 is about low sound/volume — a quiet room or a person who simply doesn't talk much — while 차분하다 is about inner composure and temperament; someone can speak up plenty and still be 차분한. It also sits opposite 예민하다 (on-edge) and 급하다 (hasty). The English-speaker pitfalls are mapping 'calm = quiet' onto it (they diverge — composure vs. volume) and the conjugation: it's a regular 하다-adjective, so 차분해요 / 차분한, never the doubled 차분하해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 조용하다 (quiet) — 차분하다 is composure/temperament, not just low volume; a talkative person can still be 차분한
Writing 차분하해요 — the stem is 차분하다, so it's 차분해요 / 차분한
Limiting it to mood — it also describes a steady manner under pressure (차분하게 대처하다), a prime interview strength

entries.shortExplanation: 무심하다 means "indifferent, aloof, inattentive" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무심하다 (musimhada) = "indifferent, aloof, inattentive". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 무심한 성격 ("an aloof, inattentive nature") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무심하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Not noticing details or others' moods
무심하게 = without thinking much of it

usagePhrases.en: look after someone in a low-key way
usagePhrases.note: Trendy phrase: aloof on the surface, caring underneath
남한테 = toward other people

examples.en: My husband is kind of inattentive.
examples.note: An extremely common, half-joking relationship complaint

examples.en: I got hurt by something my friend said offhandedly.
examples.note: 무심하게 던진 말 = a careless, throwaway remark

examples.ko: 그 선배는 무심한 듯 챙겨 줘서 인기가 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu seonbaeneun musimhan deut chaenggyeo jwoseo ingiga manayo.
examples.en: That senior looks aloof but quietly looks out for people, so they're popular.
examples.note: 무심한 듯 챙기다 = the beloved 'cold but caring' type

entries.nuance: 무심하다 means indifferent, aloof, or simply not paying attention to others' feelings and small changes — it's the stock (half-joking) complaint about a partner who never notices a new haircut. It is Sino-Korean: 無心 (無 without + 心 heart/mind), literally 'without mind/heart', i.e. not having one's attention on something. Importantly it is gentler than 차갑다 (cold-hearted): a 무심한 person may genuinely care but just fails to show it or notice, whereas 차갑다 implies real emotional coldness toward you — which is exactly why the trendy praise 무심한 듯 챙기다 ('caring in a seemingly indifferent way') works. The other contrast is 무관심하다 (無關心, 'no interest'), which is stronger and usually aimed at topics or matters (정치에 무관심하다 = uninterested in politics), while 무심하다 is about a person's inattentive disposition toward people. The English-speaker pitfall is sliding to 'cold' or 'doesn't care at all'; 무심하다 is closer to 'doesn't notice / doesn't show it' than to genuine coldness or total disinterest.

Confusing 무심하다 (inattentive/aloof) with 무관심하다 — 무관심하다 is stronger 'totally uninterested', usually about a topic
Equating it with 차갑다 (cold-hearted) — 무심하다 is about not noticing/showing, not about being emotionally cold
Reading it as 'doesn't care at all' — a 무심한 person often does care; they just don't express or register it (hence 무심한 듯 챙기다)

entries.shortExplanation: 진통제 means "painkiller" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 진통제 (jintongje) means "painkiller". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 진통제 주세요 ("Please give me a painkiller"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 진통제 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The standard pharmacy request; add 한 통 for a whole box or 한 알 for a single tablet
Oral meds always pair with 먹다, never 마시다 even though English says 'take'
센 is the natural everyday adjective for potency here; 강한 sounds stiff and technical
효과가 있다 = it works; 효과가 빠르다 = it kicks in fast

examples.en: Please give me one painkiller.
examples.note: Simplest counter form: 한 알 = one tablet, with 알 the counter for pills

examples.en: My head hurts so much, do you have any painkillers?
examples.note: Everyday opener at a 약국; -은데 softly sets up the request

examples.ko: 생리통이 심해서 진통제 두 알 먹었는데도 안 나아요.
examples.romanization: saengnitongi simhaeseo jintongje du al meogeonneundedo an naayo.
examples.en: My cramps are bad so I took two painkillers but it's still not better.
examples.note: Real-situation: -는데도 = 'even though'; 안 나아요 = doesn't get better

entries.nuance: 진통제 is the everyday word for any pain-relief pill — headache, cramps, muscle ache — and a pharmacist understands it instantly. The hanja is 鎭痛劑 'suppress-pain-agent': 鎭 calm/suppress, 痛 pain, 劑 a prepared dose, the same 劑 that marks 해열제 and 소화제. The dividing line you must learn is 진통제 (relieves the pain itself) versus 해열제 (lowers a fever); many products do both, but the words name different jobs, so don't treat them as synonyms. Register is fully neutral — kids, grandparents and pharmacists all use it — though in casual speech people often just say the brand 타이레놀. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the verb: English 'take a pill' tempts learners into 마시다 or even 가지다, but a pill is always 먹다 (literally 'eat'), and you count it with 알, not 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 진통제 마셔요 — a pill is 먹다 (eat/take), not 마시다 (drink), regardless of the English 'take'
Treating 진통제 and 해열제 as the same word — 진통제 targets pain, 해열제 lowers fever; some products combine both but the terms are not interchangeable
Counting with 개: it should be 진통제 한 알, because 알 is the counter for tablets

entries.shortExplanation: 소화제 means "digestive medicine (for indigestion)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "digestive medicine (for indigestion)" is 소화제 (sohwaje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 소화제 주세요 ("Please give me some digestive medicine"). Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me some digestive medicine
usagePhrases.note: The go-to request after a heavy meal
먹다 covers both the chewable tablets and the liquid bottles colloquially

usagePhrases.en: I bought digestive medicine because I couldn't digest
usagePhrases.note: 소화가 안 되다 = to have indigestion, the most natural framing

usagePhrases.en: a digestive medicine like Gas Hwalmyeongsu
usagePhrases.note: Names the famous liquid 소화제 brand pharmacists will recognize

examples.en: Please give me one digestive medicine.
examples.note: Simple counter: 하나 / 한 개 works for a bottle or sachet

examples.en: I overate so I took digestive medicine and lay down.
examples.note: Everyday cause-result: 과식하다 = to overeat

examples.ko: 체했는데 소화제 먹어도 속이 계속 더부룩해요.
examples.romanization: chehaenneunde sohwaje meogeodo sogi gyesok deoburukaeyo.
examples.en: I have an upset stomach and even after digestive medicine my belly still feels bloated.
examples.note: Real-situation: 체하다 = stomach 'blocked'; 더부룩하다 = bloated, the signature 소화제 symptom

entries.nuance: 소화제 is what you ask for after eating too much or when you feel 체했어요 (food 'stuck'), and it covers both chewable tablets and the popular liquid bottles like 까스활명수. The hanja is 消化劑 'dissolve-transform-agent': 消 to dissolve/dispel, 化 to change, 劑 a prepared dose — literally an 'agent that makes food break down'. The sharp contrast to memorize is 소화제 versus 위장약: 소화제 is narrowly for digestion after overeating, while 위장약 is the broader stomach medicine for acid, burning (속쓰림) and gastritis. The register is neutral and all-ages. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, learners invent 소화약 by analogy with 감기약, but the correct, fixed form is 소화제 with the Sino-Korean -제 suffix; second, don't reach for 마시다 just because the liquid type is a drink — Koreans still say 소화제 먹다.

Using 소화제 and 위장약 interchangeably — 소화제 is for digestion after overeating, 위장약 treats acid, burning and gastritis
Using 마시다 for the liquid bottle — even drinkable 소화제 pairs with 먹다 in normal speech

entries.explanation: 해열제 (haeyeolje) = "fever reducer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 해열제 주세요 ("Please give me a fever reducer") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me a fever reducer
usagePhrases.note: The standard pharmacy request when running a fever

usagePhrases.en: to give a fever reducer (to someone)
usagePhrases.note: 먹이다 is the causative 'to feed/administer', used for a child or patient

usagePhrases.en: I had a fever so I took a fever reducer
usagePhrases.note: 열이 나다 = to run a fever, the set phrase
-용 (用) = 'for the use of'; ask this way for kids' doses

examples.en: Please give me a fever reducer.
examples.note: Simplest request; 좀 softens it politely

examples.en: My fever was over 38 degrees so I took a fever reducer.
examples.note: Everyday: Koreans cite 도 (Celsius degrees) for fever

examples.ko: 아이한테 해열제 먹였는데도 열이 안 떨어져요.
examples.romanization: aihante haeyeolje meogyeonneundedo yeori an tteoreojyeoyo.
examples.en: Even after I gave my child a fever reducer the fever won't come down.
examples.note: Real-situation: -한테 먹이다 = give meds to someone; 열이 떨어지다 = the fever drops

entries.nuance: 해열제 is the go-to word when 열이 나요 (you have a fever), and pharmacists grasp it at once. The hanja is 解熱劑 'release-heat-agent': 解 to loosen/release, 熱 heat/fever, 劑 a dose — so literally 'an agent that releases the body's heat'. The contrast to fix in your mind is 해열제 versus 감기약: 해열제 does one job, dropping a fever, while 감기약 is the umbrella cold remedy that bundles fever, runny nose and cough together; they overlap but are not the same word. Register is neutral, used at home and in clinics alike. A key pitfall is the verb shift when you dose someone else: you 먹다 medicine yourself, but you 먹이다 (causative) it to a child — English uses 'give' for both, so learners wrongly say 해열제 줬어요 when they mean they administered it. Also resist inventing 열약; the fixed term is 해열제.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 열약 — the correct, fixed term is 해열제 (解熱劑)
Confusing 해열제 with 감기약 — 해열제 only lowers fever, while 감기약 is the broad cold remedy covering several symptoms
Using 해열제 줬어요 to mean you dosed a child — administering meds to someone is 먹이다 (먹였어요), not just 주다

usagePhrases.en: Please give me some cold medicine
usagePhrases.note: The single most common pharmacy request for newcomers

examples.en: Please give me cold medicine.
examples.note: Simplest form; just name the product so the pharmacist knows what you need

examples.ko: 감기 기운이 있어서 감기약 사러 왔어요.
examples.romanization: gamgi giuni isseoseo gamgiyak sareo wasseoyo.
examples.en: I'm coming down with a cold so I came to buy cold medicine.
examples.note: Everyday: 감기 기운 = the onset/feeling of a cold, a very natural phrase

examples.ko: 일해야 해서 안 졸린 감기약으로 주세요.
examples.romanization: ilhaeya haeseo an jollin gamgiyageuro juseyo.
examples.en: I have to work, so please give me the non-drowsy cold medicine.
examples.note: Real-situation: -(으)로 주세요 = 'give me the one that is...', specifying a variant

entries.nuance: 감기약 is the umbrella term for cold remedies and the single most common thing a newcomer buys at a 약국. Note the formation: 감기 is Sino-Korean 感氣 'catch-air/energy' (the Korean concept of a cold as bad air entering the body), but the medicine takes the native suffix -약 ('medicine'), not the Sino-Korean -제 you see in 진통제·해열제·소화제 — so it is 감기약, never 감기제. The contrast worth knowing is 감기약 versus 해열제: 감기약 bundles several cold symptoms (fever, runny nose, cough) into one product, while 해열제 targets fever alone. Register is completely neutral and essential daily vocabulary. The pitfall: English speakers walk in and ask only for 약 ('medicine'), which tells the pharmacist nothing — always say 감기약 — and they forget that 감기약 varies a lot by symptom, so be ready to name 콧물, 기침 or 목.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 감기제 by over-applying the -제 suffix — cold medicine takes native -약: 감기약
Asking only for 약 — the pharmacist needs 감기약 plus your symptom (콧물/기침/목) to choose correctly
Forgetting the drowsy/non-drowsy distinction — say 안 졸린 감기약 if you must drive or work

entries.shortExplanation: 연고 means "ointment / topical cream" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Watch the particle attached to 연고 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: For cuts, burns, rashes and bites
바르다 'to spread/smear' is the fixed verb for creams and ointments

usagePhrases.en: I put ointment on the wound
usagePhrases.note: The spot takes the particle 에: 상처에 바르다
Name the target: 무좀 (athlete's foot), 안연고 (eye ointment)

examples.en: Please put some ointment on here.
examples.note: Simple request; 발라 주세요 = please apply it (for me)

examples.ko: 이 연고는 하루에 세 번 바르세요.
examples.romanization: i yeongoneun harue se beon bareuseyo.
examples.en: Apply this ointment three times a day.
examples.note: Everyday dosage phrasing: 하루에 세 번 = three times a day

examples.ko: 넘어져서 무릎 까졌는데 바르는 연고 있어요?
examples.romanization: neomeojyeoseo mureup kkajyeonneunde bareuneun yeongo isseoyo?
examples.en: I fell and scraped my knee — do you have an ointment to put on it?
examples.note: Real-situation: 까지다 = to get scraped; 바르는 연고 = the kind you apply

entries.nuance: 연고 covers any medicated cream or salve for the skin — cuts, burns, bug bites, rashes — and is Sino-Korean 軟膏 'soft-paste': 軟 soft, 膏 ointment/grease, so literally 'a soft paste'. The verb is always 바르다 ('spread/smear onto'), which is the same verb you use for sunscreen, lotion and lip balm, and it is what cleanly separates 연고 from 파스 (a patch you 붙이다, stick on) and from oral medicine you 먹다. For a specific area, name it up front: 무좀 연고 (athlete's foot), 안연고 (eye ointment), 화상 연고 (burns). Register is neutral and everyday. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating ointment like a pill — 연고 먹다 is wrong because it is external only — and reaching for 칠하다 ('to paint/coat', used for walls and nails) instead of the correct 바르다 for putting medicine on skin.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 연고 먹다 — ointment is applied to the skin with 바르다, never eaten
Using 칠하다 (paint a surface) instead of 바르다 — medicine and cosmetics on skin always take 바르다
Marking the spot with the wrong particle — it's 상처에 연고를 바르다 (에 for the location), not 상처를

usagePhrases.note: For sore muscles and stiff shoulders

usagePhrases.en: to stick on a pain patch
usagePhrases.note: 붙이다 'to stick/attach' is the verb for patches

usagePhrases.en: I put a patch on my shoulder
usagePhrases.note: The body part takes 에: 어깨에 붙이다
뿌리다 = to spray; the aerosol type of 파스

examples.en: Please stick a patch on here.

examples.en: After working out I put a patch on my calf.

examples.ko: 어깨가 결려서 파스 붙였더니 한결 시원해요.

entries.nuance: 파스 is the everyday word for the medicated patches Koreans slap on sore muscles, stiff necks and tired legs. Unlike the -제 and -약 medicines around it, 파스 is a loanword (from German/Dutch 'pasta'/pleister, via Japanese パス), so it has no hanja and no suffix — just the bare borrowed noun. The verb is 붙이다 ('stick on'), which is exactly what separates it from 연고 (a cream you 바르다, spread) and from any pill you 먹다. People habitually mention the strong menthol 냄새 (smell) and the 시원한 (cooling) feel. Register is casual and extremely common in daily life. The English-speaker pitfall is verb choice driven by the English word 'apply': learners say 파스 바르다, but a patch is stuck on with 붙이다 — only the cream or spray variants use 바르다 / 뿌리다 — and some try to swallow it like a pill, when 파스 is strictly external.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 파스 바르다 — a patch is stuck on with 붙이다; only the cream/spray types use 바르다 or 뿌리다
Treating 파스 as something you swallow — it is external-only, applied to the skin
Expecting a hanja or -제/-약 suffix — 파스 is a bare loanword with neither

entries.shortExplanation: 반창고 means "adhesive bandage / band-aid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반창고 (banchanggo) means "adhesive bandage / band-aid". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 반창고 주세요 ("Please give me a band-aid"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반창고 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: For small cuts and scrapes
붙이다 'to stick' is the verb; the strip adheres to the skin
장 is the counter for flat, sheet-like items
방수 (防水) = waterproof, handy for showering

examples.en: Please give me just one band-aid.
examples.note: Simple request with the counter 장 and 만 (just/only)

examples.en: I cut my hand so I put on a band-aid.
examples.note: Everyday: (손을) 베다 = to cut oneself

examples.ko: 물집이 잡혔는데 반창고 붙이는 게 낫겠죠?
examples.romanization: muljibi japyeonneunde banchanggo buchineun ge natgetjyo?
examples.en: I got a blister — it'd be better to put a band-aid on, right?
examples.note: Real-situation: 물집(이) 잡히다 = to get a blister; -겠죠? seeks light agreement

entries.nuance: 반창고 is the standard word for a small adhesive bandage, and is Sino-Korean 絆瘡膏 'bind-sore-paste' (絆 to bind/tie, 瘡 a sore/wound, 膏 paste) — a vivid old image of a sticky strip that binds a wound shut. In real life many Koreans just say the genericized brand 대일밴드 or simply 밴드, all meaning the same thing. The verb is 붙이다 (stick on) and you count them with 장 (the flat-sheet counter). The contrast you must hold is 반창고 versus 붕대: 반창고 is the small ready-made strip for everyday nicks, while 붕대 is the long gauze roll you 감다 (wind) around a sprain or large wound. Register is fully neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing 'apply a bandage' and saying 반창고 바르다 — a band-aid is stuck on with 붙이다, never spread — and mixing up the counter by saying 한 개 instead of the natural 한 장.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 반창고 바르다 — a band-aid is stuck on with 붙이다, not spread on like a cream
Confusing 반창고 with 붕대 — 반창고 is the small adhesive strip, 붕대 is the long gauze roll you wrap (감다)
Counting with 개 — the natural counter for the flat strip is 장: 반창고 한 장

entries.explanation: "bandage / gauze wrap" is 붕대 (bungdae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 붕대 주세요 ("Please give me a bandage"). Watch the particle attached to 붕대 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: For larger wounds or sprains
감다 'to wind/wrap around' is the dedicated verb

usagePhrases.en: I wrapped a bandage around my ankle
usagePhrases.note: The body part takes 에: 발목에 감다
풀다 = to undo/loosen, the natural opposite of 감다

examples.en: Please give me a bandage.
examples.note: Simplest request; 좀 softens it

examples.en: I sprained my ankle so I wrapped it with a bandage.
examples.note: Everyday: 발목을 삐다 = to sprain one's ankle; -(으)로 = with/using

examples.ko: 붕대를 너무 꽉 감으면 피가 안 통해요.
examples.romanization: bungdaereul neomu kkwak gameumyeon piga an tonghaeyo.
examples.en: If you wrap the bandage too tightly, blood won't circulate.
examples.note: Real-situation: 꽉 = tightly; 피가 통하다 = blood circulates

entries.nuance: 붕대 is the rolled gauze bandage you wind around a sprain or a larger wound, and is Sino-Korean 繃帶 'bind-band' (繃 to bind/stretch tight, 帶 a band/belt) — literally a 'binding band', which is exactly how it behaves. Its signature verb is 감다 ('wind/wrap around'), with 풀다 to undo it, and this is what cleanly separates 붕대 from 반창고: a 붕대 is the long roll you wrap (감다) around an ankle or wrist, while a 반창고 is the small ready-made strip you stick on (붙이다) for a paper-cut. Register is neutral and clinical-but-common. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'put on a bandage' tempts learners into 붕대 붙이다, but you wrap it with 감다, not stick it; and learners blur 붕대 with 반창고, asking for the wrong item — say 붕대 for big areas and sprains, 반창고 for tiny nicks.

Saying 붕대 붙이다 — a gauze roll is wound on with 감다, not stuck on like an adhesive strip
Confusing 붕대 with 반창고 — 붕대 is the long roll for big wounds/sprains, 반창고 is the small adhesive strip
Using 입다 or 끼다 for putting it on — the only correct verb for wrapping a bandage is 감다

Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: For cleaning a cut before dressing it
바르다 (spread on) or 닦다 (wipe) for putting it on a wound

usagePhrases.en: I cleaned the wound with antiseptic
usagePhrases.note: -(으)로 = with/using; 닦다 = to wipe clean
따갑다 = to sting/smart, the classic reaction

examples.en: Please give me some antiseptic.
examples.note: Simplest request at the pharmacy counter

examples.ko: 상처에 소독약 먼저 바르고 연고 바르세요.
examples.romanization: sangcheoe sodogyang meonjeo bareugo yeongo bareuseyo.
examples.en: Put antiseptic on the wound first, then apply ointment.
examples.note: Everyday wound-care order: 소독약 → 연고 → 반창고

examples.ko: 넘어진 데를 소독약으로 닦으니까 엄청 따가워요.

examples.en: When I wipe the spot where I fell with antiseptic, it really stings.

entries.nuance: 소독약 is the everyday term for a wound antiseptic such as 포비돈 (povidone-iodine) or 과산화수소 (hydrogen peroxide), and pharmacists know it on sight. It is built from Sino-Korean 消毒 'dispel-poison' (消 to dissolve/dispel, 毒 poison/germs) plus the native suffix -약, so literally 'germ-dispelling medicine'. There is a real distinction to learn between 소독약 and 소독제: in everyday speech 소독약 leans toward the liquid you put on a cut, while 소독제 is the broader 'disinfectant' for hands, surfaces and equipment — overlapping but not identical. You 바르다 or 닦다 it onto skin, and people reliably note that it 따가워요 (stings). Register is neutral and practical for any home first-aid kit. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like medicine you take: 소독약 먹다 is wrong because it is external-only, and beware confusing it with 소독제 for surfaces.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 소독약 먹다 — antiseptic is for external use on wounds, never swallowed
Blurring 소독약 with 소독제 — 소독약 is the liquid for wounds, 소독제 is the broader disinfectant for hands and surfaces
Using 마시다 because it's a liquid — you 바르다 or 닦다 antiseptic onto the skin, not drink it

entries.shortExplanation: 체온계 means "thermometer (for body temperature)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 체온계 (cheongye) means "thermometer (for body temperature)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 체온계 있어요? ("Do you have a thermometer?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 체온계 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Asking at a pharmacy or checking at home
재다 = to measure (temperature, height, length)
The common digital ear-type; 이마 체온계 = forehead type
체온(體溫) = body temperature; the natural object of 재다

examples.en: Do you have a thermometer?
examples.note: Simplest yes/no question at the counter

examples.en: When I took my temperature with the thermometer it was 38.5 degrees.
examples.note: Everyday: 열을 재다 = to take a temperature; -아 보니까 = upon trying

examples.ko: 아기는 귀에 대는 체온계가 재기 편해요.
examples.romanization: agineun gwie daeneun cheongyega jaegi pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: For a baby, the ear thermometer is the easiest to measure with.
examples.note: Real-situation: 귀에 대다 = to put against the ear; -기 편하다 = easy to (do)

entries.nuance: 체온계 is specifically the device for measuring body temperature, built from Sino-Korean 體溫 'body-warmth' (體 body, 溫 warmth) plus 計 'measuring instrument' — the same 計 in 온도계 (thermometer for air/water), 시계 (clock) and 체중계 (scale). That shared 計 is exactly where the trap lies: 체온계 measures a body, while 온도계 measures the temperature of a room, the water or an oven — do not swap them. The verb pairing is 재다 ('measure'), used with 열을 재다 or 체온을 재다. Since COVID, digital, 귀 (ear) and 이마 (forehead) types are everywhere and any 약국 sells one. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'read the thermometer' or 'check my temperature' lures learners into 보다 ('look') or 읽다 ('read'), but Korean uses 재다 ('measure') — you 열을 재다, not 열을 보다 — and learners reach for the generic 온도계 when they need the body-specific 체온계.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 체온계 with 온도계 — 체온계 is for body temperature, 온도계 is for air, water or an oven
Using 보다 instead of 재다 — you 재다 (measure) temperature with it: 열을 재다, never 열을 보다
Saying 온도를 재다 for a fever — for the body it's 체온/열을 재다; 온도 is for the environment

That shared 計 is exactly where the trap lies: 체온계 measures a body, while 온도계 measures the temperature of a room, the water or an oven — do not swap them.

The pitfall is the verb: 'read the thermometer' or 'check my temperature' lures learners into 보다 ('look') or 읽다 ('read'), but Korean uses 재다 ('measure') — you 열을 재다, not 열을 보다 — and learners reach for the generic 온도계 when they need the body-specific 체온계.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me some stomach medicine
usagePhrases.note: For stomach pain, acid or gastritis
먹다 for tablets and sachets alike

usagePhrases.en: My stomach was burning so I took stomach medicine
usagePhrases.note: 속이 쓰리다 = to have a burning/sour stomach

usagePhrases.en: stomach medicine on an empty stomach
usagePhrases.note: 빈속 = empty stomach; note dosing timing matters

examples.en: Please give me some stomach medicine.
examples.note: Simplest counter request; 좀 softens it

examples.ko: 요즘 속이 자주 쓰려서 위장약 먹고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum sogi jaju sseuryeoseo wijangyang meokgo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days my stomach often burns, so I'm taking stomach medicine.
examples.note: Everyday chronic-complaint phrasing with -고 있다

examples.ko: 술 마시기 전에 위장약 미리 먹는 사람도 많아요.
examples.romanization: sul masigi jeone wijangyang miri meongneun saramdo manayo.

entries.nuance: 위장약 is the broad term for stomach and gut medicine, covering acid, burning (속쓰림), bloating and gastritis. It is Sino-Korean 胃腸 'stomach-intestines' (胃 stomach, 腸 intestines) plus native -약, so literally 'stomach-and-gut medicine' — the wider scope is right there in the two organs named. The contrast you must keep straight is 위장약 versus 소화제: 위장약 treats pain, acid and burning across the digestive tract, whereas 소화제 is the narrow remedy for when food won't go down after overeating. A pharmacist will ask your exact symptom — 속쓰림 (burning), 더부룩함 (bloating), 통증 (pain) — before choosing. Register is neutral and very practical for adults in Korea. The English-speaker pitfall is using 위장약 and 소화제 as if interchangeable, and inventing the clipped 위약 (which actually means 'placebo', 僞藥!) — the correct word is the full 위장약.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 위약 — that means 'placebo' (僞藥); the stomach-medicine word is the full 위장약
Using 위장약 and 소화제 interchangeably — 위장약 treats acid/burning/pain, 소화제 only helps digestion after overeating
Pairing it with the wrong verb for liquids — tablets and sachets of 위장약 are all 먹다, not 마시다

entries.shortExplanation: 알약 means "pill / tablet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 알약, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A common reason to ask for liquid or powder instead
알 is both the noun root and the counter for round small things
가루약 = powdered medicine; 말고 = not (that) but
삼키다 = to swallow, more precise than 먹다 here

examples.en: Please give me one tablet.
examples.note: Simplest form with the counter 알

examples.ko: 이 알약은 하루에 두 알씩 드세요.
examples.romanization: i aryageun harue du alssik deuseyo.
examples.en: Take two of these tablets a day.
examples.note: Everyday dosage: 두 알씩 = two each (per time); 씩 = per/apiece

examples.ko: 저는 알약을 잘 못 삼켜서 물약으로 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: jeoneun aryageul jal mot samkyeoseo muryageuro jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I can't really swallow pills, so could you give me the liquid form?
examples.note: Real-situation: 물약 = liquid medicine; -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요? makes a polite request

entries.nuance: 알약 is the everyday word for a solid pill or tablet, and it is a transparent native compound: 알 (a small round thing — a grain, an egg, a berry) + 약 (medicine), literally a 'pellet medicine'. That same 알 doubles as the counter, so you say 한 알, 두 알 — and using 개 here sounds unnatural. The three-way contrast to learn is 알약 (solid tablet) versus 가루약 (powder) versus 물약 (liquid); pharmacists offer these as alternatives. The verbs are 먹다 (general 'take') or, more precisely, 삼키다 ('swallow'). Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: the counter (it's 한 알, not 한 개), and word order — learners flip the compound into 약알, but the head noun comes last in Korean, so it must be 알약. If swallowing is hard, it's completely normal to ask for 물약 or 가루약.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting with 개 — pills take the counter 알: 알약 한 알, not 한 개
Saying 약알 — Korean compounds put the head noun last, so the correct order is 알약
Assuming only 먹다 works — for emphasis on getting it down, 삼키다 (swallow) is the precise verb

entries.shortExplanation: 메뉴판 means "menu (the physical board/booklet)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 메뉴판 (menyupan) means "menu (the physical board/booklet)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 메뉴판 좀 주세요 ("Can I get a menu, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 메뉴판 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Can I get a menu, please
usagePhrases.note: The single most useful sentence when you sit down; 좀 softens the request
What staff say while handing it over
에 marks the menu as the location where the item is absent

usagePhrases.en: You see the menu by QR code
usagePhrases.note: Many places now have no paper menu, just a QR sticker on the table

examples.en: Please give me the menu.
examples.note: The bare, can't-go-wrong version — learn this first

examples.en: Excuse me, could you bring the menu again?
examples.note: 주시겠어요 is the extra-polite re-request after you've already ordered drinks

examples.ko: 메뉴판이 한국어밖에 없어서 사진 보고 시켰어요.
examples.romanization: menyupani hangugeobakke eopseoseo sajin bogo sikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The menu was only in Korean, so I ordered by looking at the photos.
examples.note: 밖에 + negative = 'only'; a very common newcomer reality

entries.nuance: 메뉴판 is the physical object — the booklet you hold or the board on the wall — built from 메뉴 ('menu') + 판 (板, 'board/plate'). The contrast that trips up English speakers is 메뉴 vs 메뉴판: 메뉴 is abstract (the offerings, or even a single dish, as in '오늘의 메뉴'), so if you say '메뉴 주세요' staff may think you're naming or asking about a dish, not requesting the booklet. When you want the thing physically brought to you, always say 메뉴판. The register is neutral and everyday; '메뉴판 주세요' (or the softer '메뉴판 좀 주세요') is perfectly polite in any restaurant, from a tiny diner to a nice one. It habitually pairs with 주세요 (give me), 보다 (look at), and 있다/없다 (it's on / not on the menu).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '메뉴 주세요' when you mean the physical booklet — 메뉴 can mean a dish, so staff may pause; say '메뉴판 주세요' to clearly ask for the booklet/board.
Pronouncing it as two separate words 'menu pan' — it is one compound noun, 메뉴판, said in one breath.
Adding 을/를 awkwardly in speech ('메뉴판을 주세요') — natural spoken Korean usually drops the object particle here: '메뉴판 주세요'.

entries.shortExplanation: 주문 means "an order (of food/drink)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "an order (of food/drink)" is 주문 (jumun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주문하시겠어요? ("Are you ready to order?"). Watch the particle attached to 주문 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The staff's standard opening question (honorific 하시-)
Polite phrasing staff use when approaching the table
들어가다 ('go in') = the kitchen has received it
취소되다 (be cancelled); useful if you change your mind fast

examples.en: I'd like to order.
examples.note: The simplest way to flag that you're ready

examples.ko: 주문 아직 안 했어요. 조금만 더 볼게요.
examples.romanization: jumun ajik an haesseoyo. jogeumman deo bolgeyo.
examples.en: We haven't ordered yet. We'll look a bit more.
examples.note: Buys time when staff come too early; 아직 = 'not yet'

examples.en: Since it's a big group, the order all went in at once.
examples.note: 한꺼번에 = 'all at once'; links naturally to 단체

entries.nuance: 주문 is the noun 'order', from 注文 (注 'pour/note down' + 文 'writing') — originally 'to write down a request', which fits ordering perfectly. The verb is 주문하다, and a key contrast is 주문하다 vs 시키다: both mean 'to order', but 시키다 is more casual and also means 'to make someone do something', so toward staff the cleaner, slightly more standard choice is 주문하다 (시키다 is fine among friends: '뭐 시킬까?'). Knowing the bare noun unlocks the phrases you hear constantly — '주문 도와드릴게요', '주문 들어갔어요', '주문 확인해 주세요' — where 주문 stands alone. Register is neutral and identical in casual and formal dining. It collocates with 하다, 들어가다 (go in), 받다 (take an order), 확인하다 (confirm), and 취소하다 (cancel).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 주문 (an order) with 주말 (weekend) — they look similar to beginners but are unrelated; mis-saying one for the other changes the meaning entirely.
Defaulting to 시키다 with staff ('이거 시켜 주세요') — understandable but a touch blunt; '이거 주문할게요' or simply '이거 주세요' sounds cleaner to servers.
Treating 주문 as a verb on its own ('주문 주세요') — you need 주문하다, e.g. '주문할게요', or attach 하다.

entries.english: an extra order / addition (more of something)
entries.shortExplanation: 추가 means "an extra order / addition (more of something)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 추가 (chuga) = "an extra order / addition (more of something)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공깃밥 추가요 ("An extra bowl of rice, please") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 추가, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: An extra bowl of rice, please
usagePhrases.note: '추가요' alone is a complete spoken request
추가되다 = 'be addable'; 사리 = extra noodle bundle
추가 + 주문하다 when calling staff for a second round
추가 요금 = surcharge; checks if the add-on costs more

examples.en: An extra bowl of rice, please.
examples.note: Minimal pattern: '[item] 추가요' gets you more and gets it rung up

examples.en: We finished the meat, so we added two more portions.
examples.note: 추가하다 as a verb; classic Korean BBQ move

examples.en: Adding cheese to the ramen is 1,000 won.
examples.note: 에 marks what you add the topping to; shows add-ons can cost money

entries.nuance: 추가 is 追加 (追 'chase/pursue' + 加 'add') — literally 'to add on in pursuit', i.e. an additional order: more rice, more meat, an extra topping, a second drink. The sharp contrast is 추가 vs 리필: 추가 means ordering more and usually paying for it, whereas 리필 ('refill') implies a free top-up of the same item. So for paid extras say 추가, for free soda/coffee/side-dish top-ups say 리필. Attaching -요 ('추가요') turns the bare noun into a full, polite spoken request, which is how locals add items without a whole sentence. Register is casual-but-polite and works everywhere; the verb is 추가하다. It pairs with 주문 (order more), 요금 (extra charge), 사리/공깃밥 (extra noodles/rice), and 인분 (extra portions).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '더 주세요' for paid add-ons — fine for free 반찬, but for chargeable items say '[X] 추가요' so staff actually ring it up instead of just topping you off.
Assuming 추가 is always free — unlike 리필, an 추가 normally costs money; confirm with '추가 요금 있어요?' first.
Using bare 추가 as a verb ('밥 추가 주세요') is understandable but the cleaner forms are '밥 추가요' or '밥 추가해 주세요'.

entries.shortExplanation: 리필 means "a refill (free top-up)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 리필 (ripil) means "a refill (free top-up)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 리필 돼요? ("Can I get a refill?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 리필 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The key question — really asks 'is it free?'
되나요 is slightly softer and very natural
무한(無限) = 'limitless'; common at salad bars and buffets
리필하다 + 드릴까요 — what staff sometimes offer you

examples.en: Can I get a refill?
examples.note: The one phrase to memorize before assuming top-ups are free

examples.en: Can I refill the cola here?
examples.note: 여기 ('here') checks this specific place's policy

examples.en: The coffee refill is free only once.
examples.note: 한 번만 = 'just once'; shows refills can be limited even when offered

entries.nuance: 리필 is a loanword from English 'refill', and it specifically carries the nuance of getting more of the same item for free — drinks, side dishes, coffee, popcorn. The dividing line from its cousin 추가 is exactly cost: 리필 = same thing, no charge; 추가 = more (often a different/larger amount) that you pay for. So '콜라 리필 돼요?' asks whether free refills exist, while '콜라 추가요' means 'add another (paid) cola'. Don't assume 됨; the verb 되다 here means 'is it allowed/available', so '리필 돼요?' literally checks the policy before you walk up to the machine. Register is casual and everyday. The verb is 리필하다, and it collocates with 무한(unlimited), 무료(free), 음료/커피(drink/coffee), and 한 번만(only once).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming every refill is free — many cafes charge or limit it, so ask '리필 돼요?' before refilling.
Mixing up 리필 (free same-item top-up) with 추가 (more, usually paid) — using the wrong one can leave you with an unexpected charge or none at all.
Treating 되다 as 'become' here — in '리필 돼요?' it means 'is it possible/allowed', not 'does it become a refill'.

entries.english: pager / buzzer (that vibrates when food is ready)
entries.shortExplanation: 진동벨 means "pager / buzzer (that vibrates when food is ready)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "pager / buzzer (that vibrates when food is ready)" is 진동벨 (jindongbel). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 진동벨 울리면 오세요 ("Come when the buzzer goes off"). Watch the particle attached to 진동벨 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Come when the buzzer goes off
usagePhrases.note: 울리다 = 'ring/sound'; standard counter instruction
가져가다 = 'take (it) along' as staff hand it over
반납하다(返納) = 'return'; expected after you pick up food

usagePhrases.en: Where do I get the buzzer?
usagePhrases.note: 어디서 = 'where (at)'; useful in busy self-order places

examples.en: Come when the buzzer rings.
examples.note: The core instruction you must understand at the counter

examples.en: The buzzer went off, so I went to get the food.
examples.note: -(으)러 가다 = 'go in order to'; the self-pickup flow

examples.en: The buzzer vibrates and lights up together.
examples.note: 이랑 = casual 'and'; describes how it signals

entries.nuance: 진동벨 literally stitches together 진동 (振動, 'vibration') + 벨 ('bell'), so 'vibration bell' — the pager you're handed at counter-service spots, food courts, and many cafes. Unlike a plain 벨 (a doorbell or a call button you press), the 진동벨 is the thing that buzzes you, signaling that you go fetch the food yourself. Recognizing the word is what matters most: staff will say '진동벨 울리면 오세요' and fully expect you to walk up, not wait to be served. After pickup, you 반납 (return) it. Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 울리다 (ring/buzz), 가져가다 (take along), 반납하다 (return), and 받다 (receive one).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Sitting at the table waiting for table service after being given a 진동벨 — the buzzer means YOU pick up; no one brings it.
Walking off with the 진동벨 — you must 반납 (return) it to the counter when you collect your food.
Confusing 진동벨 (the vibrating pager) with 벨 (a call button you press to summon staff) — they work in opposite directions.

structuredNuance.t: The pager you're handed at counter-service spots, food courts, and many cafes. Recognizing the word is what matters most: staff will say '진동벨 울리면 오세요' and fully expect you to walk up, not wait to be served. After pickup, you 반납 (return) it. Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 울리다 (ring/buzz), 가져가다 (take along), 반납하다 (return), and 받다 (receive one).
Literally stitches together 진동 (振動, 'vibration') + 벨 ('bell'), so 'vibration bell'.
Unlike a plain 벨 (a doorbell or a call button you press), the 진동벨 is the thing that buzzes you, signaling that you go fetch the food yourself.

entries.nuance: 셀프 is the English 'self' borrowed as a noun/adjective, and in eateries it is shorthand for 셀프서비스 — it tells you no one will bring it: water, utensils (수저), side dishes (반찬), or refills are yours to fetch. The natural opposite is having staff bring things, and a near phrase is 직접 ('in person, yourself'), which often appears alongside it ('직접 가져오세요'). When you see '셀프' on a sign or hear '물은 셀프예요', the cue is to stand up and go get it from the dispenser or 셀프 코너. Register is casual and everyday, and the word is ubiquitous in Korean restaurants. It collocates with 물(water), 반찬(side dishes), 코너/바(station/bar), and the verbs 가져오다(bring) and 챙기다(grab/take).

Waiting for staff to pour water when a sign says '물 셀프' — get it yourself from the water dispenser or fridge.
Reading 셀프 as a brand or product name — here it simply means 'self-service'.
Forgetting that 셀프 often extends to utensils and refills, not just water — at a '셀프' spot you grab your own 수저 too.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 곱빼기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

entries.nuance: 곱빼기 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) from 곱 ('multiplied, double') + the suffix -빼기, so it means roughly a double serving. Crucially it is tied to noodle and rice-bowl dishes — 짜장면, 짬뽕, 볶음밥 — and is the local way to get more food for a small surcharge: '[dish] 곱빼기로 주세요'. The contrast learners need is 곱빼기 vs 추가/2인분: 곱빼기 makes the single bowl bigger, while 추가 or 2인분 means ordering an additional separate serving (used for meat, side items, etc.). It does not apply to soups, BBQ meat, or drinks. Register is casual, and you'll mainly hear it at 중국집 (Chinese-Korean restaurants) and noodle houses. It collocates with -로 주세요, 시키다 (order), 얼마예요 (how much), and dish names like 짜장면/짬뽕.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 곱빼기 for soups or BBQ meat — it's tied to noodle/rice bowls; for more meat say '추가' or '2인분'.
Saying '큰 거 주세요' ('give me the big one') for a double noodle portion — understandable, but locals specifically say '곱빼기로 주세요'.
Dropping the particle and saying '곱빼기 주세요' is okay, but '곱빼기로 주세요' (with 로, 'in the double form') is the idiomatic phrasing.

Watch the particle attached to 세트 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. examples.note: The default upgrade line at fast food

examples.ko: 세트로 시키면 음료랑 감자튀김이 같이 나와요.

entries.nuance: 세트 is the English 'set' borrowed to mean a combo — a main plus a drink and/or sides at one bundled price. Its direct opposite, and the contrast you must know, is 단품 (單品, 'single item', i.e. à la carte): '세트로 주세요' bundles everything, '단품으로 주세요' gets just the main. Don't confuse 세트 with 사이드 either — 세트 is the whole bundle, 사이드 is one side item inside or beside it. Asking for '세트로 주세요' is the default at fast food and many casual spots, and the price gap with 단품 is the usual reason people choose it. Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with -로 (해 주세요/할게요), 단품 (à la carte), 메뉴 (combo menu), and numbered orders like 1번 세트.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming the displayed price is the 세트 price — menus often show the 단품 (single-item) price; ask '세트로 얼마예요?'.
Confusing 세트 (the whole combo) with 사이드 (the individual side item) — a 세트 contains sides, but 사이드 alone is just one add-on.
Saying '세트 주세요' without specifying which — at a counter, name it: '불고기버거 세트로 주세요' or '1번 세트요'.

("What side items do you have?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사이드, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: 뭐 있어요 = 'what is there'; asks what add-ons are offered

usagePhrases.en: I'll have fries as a side

entries.nuance: 사이드 is the English 'side', meaning the optional side items on a menu — fries, wings, cheese balls, garlic bread — and the contrast that matters is 사이드 vs 반찬: 사이드 is a paid, ordered add-on (especially at chicken, pizza, and burger places), whereas 반찬 is the free Korean side dishes that come automatically with a meal. So fries you 'order as a 사이드'; kimchi and pickled radish are 반찬 and arrive at no charge. You'll see a labeled '사이드 메뉴' section, heavily used in 배달 (delivery) ordering. The natural pairing is 사이드로 + dish + 주세요/시키다 ('as a side, give me / I'll order'). Register is casual. It collocates with 메뉴 (side menu), -로 (as a side), 추가하다 (add), and 메인 (the main).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 사이드 (a paid menu side you order) with 반찬 (the free Korean side dishes) — asking for '사이드 리필' makes no sense; 반찬 is what gets refilled free.
Expecting 사이드 to be included or free — these are ordered and charged separately from the main.
Using 사이드 for the free banchan at a Korean restaurant — there you'd talk about 반찬, not 사이드.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 코스 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 로 marks the course as how you reserved

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a course menu?
usagePhrases.note: 코스 요리 = course dishes; asking at a sit-down place

usagePhrases.note: 차이 = difference; comparing the tiers

usagePhrases.en: How much is the course per person?
usagePhrases.note: 1인당 = 'per person'; course prices are almost always per head

examples.en: Do you have a course menu?

entries.nuance: 코스 is the English 'course', meaning a multi-dish meal served in sequence (appetizer to dessert) at a fixed per-person price — common for dates, anniversaries, 오마카세, and upscale dining, with tiers often labeled A코스/B코스. The contrast to lock in is 코스 vs 세트: a 코스 is plated dish-by-dish in order at a sit-down place, while a 세트 is a fast-food-style bundle that arrives all at once. Although the situation it appears in is a bit more formal, the word itself is neutral. The single biggest practical point is pricing: it is charged 1인당 (per person), not per table. It collocates with 요리 (course dishes), 예약하다 (reserve), 1인당 (per person), and the tier labels A코스/B코스.

Thinking the 코스 price is for the whole table — it is almost always 1인당 (per person), so a listed number gets multiplied by your party size.
Confusing 코스 (a sequenced sit-down course meal) with 세트 (a fast-food combo served all at once).
Assuming you can order a 코스 solo — many require 2인 이상 (two or more), so check '몇 명부터 돼요?' when booking.

The contrast to feel is 단체 vs 일행: 일행 is simply 'the people I'm with' (even two), while 단체 implies a sizeable organized party, typically five-plus, that restaurants treat specially with 단체 예약, 단체석, or a required unified menu. Register is neutral. The practical takeaway is that large groups usually can't just walk in — you book ahead. It collocates with 예약 (reservation), 석 (group seating), 할인 (group discount), and 손님 (a group of guests).

Assuming a 단체 can always walk in and be seated — big groups normally need '단체 예약' in advance.
Saying '단체 자리' when the set phrase is 단체석 — Koreans compress 단체 + 석(席, seat) into one word for group seating.

entries.nuance: 1인분 is 一人分 (一 'one' + 人 'person' + 分 'portion/share'), the per-person serving unit, used above all for meat at BBQ and for other portioned dishes — it answers 'how many servings', not 'how many pieces'. Assuming you can always order 1인분 at BBQ — many spots require a 2인분 minimum, so ask first.
Using 개 instead of 인분 for meat ('삼겹살 두 개 주세요') — meat servings are counted in 인분, so say '삼겹살 2인분 주세요'.

entries.explanation: 가래 (garae) means "phlegm, mucus (in throat/chest)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가래가 끓다 ("phlegm rattles (in the chest)"). usagePhrases.note: 끓는 물처럼 그르렁 소리가 날 때 — 감기·기관지염 설명의 단골
목에 점액이 들러붙어 답답한 '상태'를 강조
가래는 명사라 뱉는 '행위'는 타동사 '뱉다'를 붙임
색을 말하면 의사가 세균 감염 여부를 판단함

examples.en: Phlegm keeps coming up.
examples.note: 가장 짧고 기본적인 증상 문장 — '나오다'가 가래의 표준 짝꿍 동사

examples.en: Phlegm is stuck in my throat, so I keep hacking.
examples.note: '캑캑거리다'는 가래를 뱉으려 목을 긁는 소리를 흉내 낸 의성어

examples.ko: 누런 가래가 나오면 항생제가 필요할 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: nureon garaega naomyeon hangsaengjega piryohal sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: If you cough up yellow phlegm, you might need antibiotics.
examples.note: 의사·약사가 진료 중에 설명할 때 듣게 되는 실제 표현

entries.nuance: 가래는 목·기관지에서 만들어지는 끈끈한 점액으로, 병원에서 호흡기 증상을 말할 때 거의 필수인 순우리말이다. 핵심 짝꿍 동사가 셋인데, 끓는 소리가 나면 '가래가 끓다', 들러붙어 답답하면 '가래가 끼다', 입 밖으로 뱉으면 '가래를 뱉다'로 나눠 쓴다. 비슷해 보이는 '콧물'과는 부위가 갈리니 주의해야 한다 — 가래는 목·가슴(아래쪽), 콧물은 코(위쪽)에서 나오므로, 코를 풀어 나오면 콧물, 기침해서 올라오면 가래다. 의료 상황에서는 다소 적나라해도 register 부담 없이 그대로 쓰면 된다. 영어 'phlegm'은 셀 수 없는 명사처럼 쓰지만, 한국어 가래도 '가래가 많다/적다'로 양을 말하지 수를 세지 않는다. 영어권 학습자는 'I have phlegm'을 '가래를 가지고 있다'로 직역하기 쉬운데, 한국어에서는 소유 동사 '가지다' 대신 '가래가 나오다/끼다'처럼 자동사로 표현하는 것이 자연스럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
가래를 형용사·동사처럼 '가래하다'로 만드는 것 — 가래는 명사이므로 '가래가 나오다 / 끓다 / 끼다'처럼 짝이 되는 동사를 붙여야 한다.
'I have phlegm'을 직역해 '가래를 가지고 있어요'라고 하는 것 — 한국어는 '목에 가래가 껴요 / 가래가 나와요'처럼 자동사 구문을 쓴다.
콧물(코에서 나오는 것)과 가래를 같은 단어로 뭉뚱그리는 것 — 부위가 코냐 목·가슴이냐로 갈리므로 의사에게는 구분해서 말해야 정확히 전달된다.

entries.shortExplanation: 오한 means "chills (shivering from fever)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "chills (shivering from fever)" is 오한 (ohan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오한이 들다 ("to get the chills"). Watch the particle attached to 오한 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 가장 격식 있고 정확한 짝꿍 동사 — 문진표·진료에서 표준
'들다'보다 살짝 캐주얼하지만 똑같이 자연스러움
오한의 느낌을 풀어 쓰는 의태어 표현, 일상 회화에서 더 흔함
병원 증상 체크리스트에 한 쌍으로 자주 등장

examples.en: I suddenly feel chilly and shivery.
examples.note: 회화에서 가장 흔한 캐주얼 버전 — 의태어로 오한의 느낌만 묘사

examples.ko: 열도 나고 오한도 들어서 몸이 덜덜 떨려요.
examples.romanization: yeoldo nago ohando deureoseo momi deoldeol tteollyeoyo.
examples.en: I have a fever and chills, so I'm shivering.
examples.note: 'A도 ~고 B도 ~다'로 두 증상을 나란히 묶는 전형적 독감 설명

examples.ko: 오한이 심하면 두꺼운 이불을 덮고 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: ohani simhamyeon dukkeoun ibureul deopgo puk swiseyo.
examples.en: If the chills are bad, cover up with a thick blanket and rest well.
examples.note: 약사나 지인이 해 주는 조언 — 명령형 '-세요'로 처방

entries.nuance: 오한(惡寒, '미워할 오' + '찰 한' = 글자 그대로 '싫게 느껴지는 추위')은 열이 오를 때 몸 안에서부터 으슬으슬 춥고 떨리는 증상을 가리키는 한자어다. 한자어라 약간 격식이 있어 병원·문진표에서는 그대로 쓰지만, 친구끼리 일상 대화에서는 '몸이 으슬으슬해요'처럼 의태어로 풀어 말하는 편이 훨씬 자연스럽다. 그냥 '추워요'와의 결정적 차이는 '원인'이다 — 방이 추워서 추운 게 아니라 실내 온도와 무관하게 몸 안에서 오는 떨림일 때만 '오한'이라고 해야 의사가 발열을 의심한다. 짝꿍 동사는 '오한이 들다'와 '오한이 나다'가 둘 다 자연스럽고, '발열·식은땀'과 묶여 한 세트로 나오는 일이 많다. 영어권 학습자는 'I feel chills'를 '오한을 느끼다'로 직역하기 쉬운데, 한국어는 감각 주체가 사람이 아니라 증상이라 '오한이 들다/나다'처럼 자동사로 쓰는 것이 표준이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
실내 온도 때문에 추운 것과 구별하지 않고 그냥 '추워요'라고만 하는 것 — 몸 안에서 오는 떨림이면 '오한이 나요/들어요'라고 해야 의사가 발열을 의심하고 정확히 진단한다.
'I feel chills'를 직역해 '오한을 느껴요'라고 하는 것 — 보통 '오한이 들다 / 오한이 나다'처럼 증상을 주어로 한 자동사 구문을 쓴다.
한자어 '오한'을 모든 일상 대화에 그대로 쓰는 것 — 친구 사이에서는 다소 딱딱하게 들리니 '으슬으슬 추워요'로 바꾸면 더 자연스럽다.

그냥 '추워요'와의 결정적 차이는 '원인'이다 — 방이 추워서 추운 게 아니라 실내 온도와 무관하게 몸 안에서 오는 떨림일 때만 '오한'이라고 해야 의사가 발열을 의심한다.

entries.english: body aches, achiness (from overwork or cold)
entries.shortExplanation: 몸살 means "body aches, achiness (from overwork or cold)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 몸살 (momsal) = "body aches, achiness (from overwork or cold)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 몸살이 나다 ("to come down with body aches") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 몸살, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to come down with body aches
usagePhrases.note: 기본형 — '나다'가 증상의 시작을 나타내는 표준 짝꿍 동사
이미 아픈 상태의 '정도'를 말할 때
'기운'을 붙이면 '아직 본격적이진 않지만 올 것 같은 느낌'
감기와 몸살이 함께 올 때 쓰는 합성어

examples.en: I've come down with body aches.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — '나다'를 과거형으로 써서 '지금 아픈 상태'를 알림

examples.ko: 어제 무리했더니 온몸이 쑤시고 몸살이 났어요.
examples.romanization: eoje murihaetdeoni onmomi ssusigo momsari nasseoyo.
examples.en: I overdid it yesterday, so my whole body aches and I came down with it.
examples.note: '-더니'로 원인(무리함)과 결과(몸살)를 연결한 전형적 표현

examples.ko: 몸살 기운이 있어서 오늘은 일찍 들어가 볼게요.
examples.romanization: momsal giuni isseoseo oneureun iljjik deureoga bolgeyo.
examples.en: I feel achiness coming on, so I'll head home early today.
examples.note: 회사에서 조퇴 양해를 구할 때 자연스러운 '-아서' 이유 구문

entries.nuance: 몸살은 과로나 감기 때문에 온몸이 쑤시고 무겁고 기운 없는 상태를 통째로 가리키는 순우리말이라, 영어에 일대일로 맞는 단어가 없어 'body aches' 또는 'feeling run-down'으로 풀어 설명해야 한다. 단순 근육통(근육통)이 특정 근육 하나가 뻐근한 것이라면, 몸살은 전신의 나른함·오한·미열까지 포함하는 훨씬 넓은 개념이라는 점이 핵심 차이다. 기본형은 '몸살이 나다'이고, 회사에 결근·조퇴 사유로 '몸살 났어요'라고 하면 누구나 바로 알아듣는 매우 일상적인 캐주얼 단어다. 본격적으로 아프기 전 단계는 '몸살 기운이 있다'로 표현하는데, 여기서 '기운'은 '에너지'가 아니라 '~할 것 같은 조짐'이라는 뜻이라 영어권 학습자가 헷갈리기 쉽다. 또 하나 흔한 함정은 '몸살이 아프다'인데, 몸살은 '아픈 상태' 자체를 가리키는 명사라 '아프다'와 겹쳐 어색해지니 '몸살이 났어요 / 몸살이 심해요'라고 해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'몸살이 아파요'라고 하는 것 — 몸살은 이미 '아픈 상태'를 가리키는 명사라 '아프다'가 의미상 겹친다. '몸살이 났어요 / 몸살이 심해요'가 맞다.
단순 근육통과 같은 말로 쓰는 것 — 몸살은 특정 근육이 아니라 전신의 나른함·오한까지 포함하는 더 넓은 개념이라 범위가 다르다.
'몸살 기운'의 '기운'을 'energy(힘)'로 오해하는 것 — 여기서는 '아플 것 같은 조짐'이라는 뜻이라, '몸살 기운이 있다'는 '아직 약하지만 몸살이 오려 한다'는 의미다.

structuredNuance.t: 몸살은 과로나 감기 때문에 온몸이 쑤시고 무겁고 기운 없는 상태를 통째로 가리키는 순우리말이라, 영어에 일대일로 맞는 단어가 없어 'body aches' 또는 'feeling run-down'으로 풀어 설명해야 한다. 기본형은 '몸살이 나다'이고, 회사에 결근·조퇴 사유로 '몸살 났어요'라고 하면 누구나 바로 알아듣는 매우 일상적인 캐주얼 단어다.
단순 근육통이 특정 근육 하나가 뻐근한 것이라면, 몸살은 전신의 나른함·오한·미열까지 포함하는 훨씬 넓은 개념이라는 점이 핵심 차이다.
본격적으로 아프기 전 단계는 '몸살 기운이 있다'로 표현하는데, 여기서 '기운'은 '에너지'가 아니라 '~할 것 같은 조짐'이라는 뜻이라 영어권 학습자가 헷갈리기 쉽다. 또 하나 흔한 함정은 '몸살이 아프다'인데, 몸살은 '아픈 상태' 자체를 가리키는 명사라 '아프다'와 겹쳐 어색해지니 '몸살이 났어요 / 몸살이 심해요'라고 해야 한다.

entries.shortExplanation: 두드러기 means "hives, rash (raised, itchy welts)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 두드러기 (dudeureogi) means "hives, rash (raised, itchy welts)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 두드러기가 나다 ("to break out in hives"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 두드러기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 기본형 — '나다'가 표준 짝꿍 동사
피부에 봉긋 돋아 오르는 느낌을 강조
가려움 증상을 함께 말할 때
원인(알레르기)을 밝혀 설명할 때

examples.en: I broke out in hives on my arm.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — 부위 + '두드러기가 나다'

examples.en: I ate shrimp and hives flared up all over.
examples.note: '-더니'로 음식과 알레르기 반응을 인과로 연결, '올라오다'로 돋는 느낌 강조

examples.ko: 이 약을 먹고 두드러기가 나면 바로 끊으세요.
examples.romanization: i yageul meokgo dudeureogiga namyeon baro kkeuneuseyo.
examples.en: If you break out in hives after taking this, stop it immediately.
examples.note: 약사가 부작용을 설명하는 조건문 '-(으)면' + 명령

entries.nuance: 두드러기는 알레르기나 자극 때문에 피부가 가렵고 붉게 부풀어 오르는 발진으로, 음식·약 알레르기 상황에서 거의 반드시 쓰게 되는 순우리말이다. 표준 짝꿍 동사는 '두드러기가 나다'와 '두드러기가 올라오다'인데, 후자는 피부 위로 봉긋 돋아 오르는 시각적 느낌을 살린다. 더 포괄적인 단어 '발진'이 모든 종류의 피부 트러블을 가리키는 상위어라면, 두드러기는 '가렵고 부어오르는' 특정 유형을 콕 집으므로 알레르기 맥락에서 훨씬 정확하다. 또 흔히 헷갈리는 '여드름'은 피지가 막혀 생기는 trouble이라 원인·모양이 전혀 달라, 두드러기와 절대 바꿔 쓰면 안 된다. 영어권 학습자가 빠지기 쉬운 함정은 영어 'hives'가 복수형이라 한국어에서도 복수로 만들려 하는 것인데, 두드러기는 셀 수 없는 명사처럼 '두드러기가 났다'로 단수로 쓰며 개수를 세지 않는다. 또 '두드러기하다'처럼 동사화하는 것도 비문이니 반드시 '나다 / 올라오다'를 붙여야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'두드러기하다'처럼 동사로 만드는 것 — 명사라서 반드시 '두드러기가 나다 / 올라오다'처럼 짝꿍 동사를 붙여야 한다.
여드름(피지로 막혀 생기는 trouble)과 혼동하는 것 — 두드러기는 알레르기성으로 부어오르는 발진이라 원인과 모양이 전혀 다르다.
영어 복수 'hives'에 끌려 복수로 만들려 하는 것 — 한국어 두드러기는 셀 수 없는 명사처럼 '두드러기가 났다'로 쓰고 개수를 세지 않는다.

entries.shortExplanation: 설사 means "diarrhea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "diarrhea" is 설사 (seolsa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 설사를 하다 ("to have diarrhea"). Watch the particle attached to 설사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 기본형 — 한자어 '설사' + '하다'로 만든 표준 동사구
'하다'보다 살짝 캐주얼하지만 똑같이 자주 씀

usagePhrases.en: have an upset stomach and (so) diarrhea
usagePhrases.note: 원인(배탈) + 증상(설사) 세트 표현
약국에서 곧장 찾는 단어

examples.en: I keep having diarrhea.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — '계속'으로 반복을, '하다'로 표준 표현

examples.ko: 상한 걸 먹었는지 설사가 멈추질 않아요.
examples.romanization: sanghan geol meogeonneunji seolsaga meomchujil anayo.
examples.en: I must have eaten something spoiled — the diarrhea won't stop.
examples.note: '-는지'로 추측을, '상하다(음식이 상함)'로 원인을 짐작

examples.en: Please give me anti-diarrheal medicine. It's watery.
examples.note: 약국에서 직접 쓰는 솔직한 부탁 + 상태 묘사

entries.nuance: 설사(泄瀉, '샐 설' + '쏟을 사' = 글자 그대로 '새어 쏟아짐')는 묽은 변을 자주 보는 증상을 가리키는 한자어로, 일상과 의료 양쪽에서 그대로 쓰는 표준 단어다. 정반대 짝인 '변비'와 한 쌍으로 익혀 두면 좋은데, 설사는 묽게 자주 보는 상태, 변비는 굳어서 못 보는 상태다. 짝꿍 동사는 한자어 명사에 '하다'를 붙인 '설사를 하다'가 기본이고, '설사가 나다'도 흔하다. 약국에서 '설사약 주세요'라고 하면 바로 통하니, 다소 민망해도 register 부담 없이 쓰면 된다. 영어권 학습자가 빠지기 쉬운 함정 두 가지가 있다. 첫째, 영어 'diarrhea'가 명사라 'I have diarrhea'를 '설사를 가지고 있다'로 직역하기 쉬운데, 한국어는 '설사를 해요 / 설사가 나요'처럼 동사로 표현한다. 둘째, '설사 아파요'처럼 형용사를 바로 붙이는 것인데, 아픈 건 '배(설사를 동반한 배)'이지 설사 자체가 아니라서 '배가 아프고 설사를 해요'로 나눠 말해야 자연스럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'설사 아파요'라고 하는 것 — 설사 자체는 '아프다'와 어울리지 않는다. '배가 아프고 설사를 해요 / 설사가 나요'처럼 동사를 붙여 표현한다.
'I have diarrhea'를 직역해 '설사를 가지고 있어요'라고 하는 것 — 한국어는 소유 동사 대신 '설사를 하다 / 설사가 나다'를 쓴다.
정반대인 변비(굳어서 못 봄)와 헷갈리는 것 — 설사는 묽게 자주, 변비는 굳어서 못 보는 정반대 상태라 약을 잘못 사면 증상이 악화된다.
