entries.shortExplanation: 변비 means "constipation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 변비 (byeonbi) = "constipation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 변비가 있다 ("to have constipation") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 변비, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기본형 — 상태를 나타내는 '있다'와 짝
증상의 '정도'를 말할 때
병처럼 '걸리다'를 쓰는 것도 자연스러움
약국에서 찾는 단어

examples.en: I've had constipation lately.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — 상태 동사 '있다'와 결합

examples.en: I've been badly constipated lately and it's really uncomfortable.
examples.note: '-아서'로 변비(원인)와 불편함(결과)을 연결

examples.ko: 물을 많이 마시면 변비에 도움이 돼요.
examples.romanization: mureul mani masimyeon byeonbie doumi dwaeyo.
examples.en: Drinking a lot of water helps with constipation.
examples.note: '-에 도움이 되다'는 '~에 좋다'는 뜻의 흔한 건강 표현

entries.nuance: 변비(便祕, '똥 변' + '막힐 비' = 글자 그대로 '변이 막힘')는 변이 굳어 잘 안 나오는 상태를 가리키는 한자어로, 설사와 짝을 이루는 기본 소화기 증상 단어다. 짝꿍 동사가 셋인데 미묘하게 다르다 — 상태를 말하면 '변비가 있다', 정도를 말하면 '변비가 심하다', 병에 '걸리듯' 새로 생긴 것을 말하면 '변비에 걸리다'를 쓴다. 영어 'constipated'는 형용사라 'I'm constipated'처럼 사람이 주어가 되지만, 한국어 변비는 명사라 'I'm constipated'를 '나는 변비다'로 직역하면 어색하고 '변비가 있어요'라고 해야 한다. '걸리다'를 쓸 때 조사도 함정인데, '변비를 걸리다'가 아니라 '변비에 걸리다'로 조사 '에'를 써야 맞다(감기에 걸리다와 같은 패턴). 일상에서 식습관·스트레스 이야기를 할 때도 자연스럽게 등장하며, 약국에서 '변비약 주세요'라고 그대로 쓴다.

'변비하다'로 동사화하거나 'I'm constipated'를 '나는 변비다'로 직역하는 것 — 명사라서 '변비가 있다 / 생기다 / 심하다'로 풀어 써야 자연스럽다.
'변비를 걸리다'처럼 조사를 잘못 쓰는 것 — '감기에 걸리다'와 같은 패턴으로 '변비에 걸리다'라고 조사 '에'를 써야 맞다.
정반대인 설사(묽게 자주 봄)와 헷갈리는 것 — 변비는 굳어서 못 보는 상태라, 약을 잘못 고르면 증상이 더 나빠진다.

영어 'constipated'는 형용사라 'I'm constipated'처럼 사람이 주어가 되지만, 한국어 변비는 명사라 '나는 변비다'로 직역하면 어색하고 '변비가 있어요'라고 해야 한다. '걸리다'를 쓸 때 조사도 함정인데, '변비를 걸리다'가 아니라 '변비에 걸리다'로 조사 '에'를 써야 맞다(감기에 걸리다와 같은 패턴).

entries.shortExplanation: 멍 means "bruise" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 멍 (meong) means "bruise". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 멍이 들다 ("to get a bruise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 멍 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 거의 굳어진 표준 표현 — '들다'와 한 덩어리
'들다'와 비슷하게 자연스러움
'시-'를 붙여 색을 강하게 강조
색이 옅어져 사라질 때 쓰는 회복 표현

examples.en: I got a bruise on my leg.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — 부위 + '멍이 들다'

examples.en: I fell and got a deep blue bruise on my knee.
examples.note: '시퍼렇게'는 멍의 검푸른 색을 강조하는 부사형

examples.en: A bruise usually fades within a week.
examples.note: '빠지다'로 회복(색이 옅어짐)을 표현하는 흔한 설명

entries.nuance: 멍은 부딪히거나 눌려 피부 아래 모세혈관이 터지면서 생기는 검푸른 자국을 가리키는 순우리말로, '멍이 들다'가 거의 한 단어처럼 굳어진 표준 표현이다(주의: 여기서 '들다'는 '안에 배어들다'의 뜻이지 '손에 들다'가 아니다). 색이 변해 사라질 때는 '멍이 빠지다'라고 한다. 비슷한 부상 단어 '상처'와의 결정적 차이는 '피부가 깨졌느냐'다 — 상처는 베이거나 까져 겉이 터진 것이고, 멍은 겉은 멀쩡한데 속에서 출혈이 번진 것이다. 영어권 학습자가 가장 많이 빠지는 함정은 발음이 같은 '멍하다'와 헷갈리는 것인데, '멍하다 / 멍때리다'는 정신이 나가 넋을 놓은 상태를 뜻해 부상과 전혀 무관하다. 따라서 '멍을 하다 / 멍하다'로 부상을 말하면 완전히 다른 뜻이 되어 버린다. 또 영어 'bruise'는 동사로도 쓰여 'I bruised my leg'가 되지만, 한국어 멍은 명사뿐이라 '멍을 했다'가 아니라 '멍이 들었다'처럼 자동사 구문으로 써야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'멍을 하다 / 멍하다'로 부상을 말하는 것 — '멍하다 / 멍때리다'는 정신이 나간 상태라 전혀 다른 뜻이다. 멍든 상처는 '멍이 들다'.
'I bruised my leg'처럼 동사로 직역해 '다리를 멍했다'라고 하는 것 — 멍은 명사라 '다리에 멍이 들었어요'처럼 자동사 구문을 쓴다.
상처(베이거나 까진 것)와 혼동하는 것 — 멍은 겉이 터지지 않고 피부 안쪽에서 출혈이 번진 자국이라 상처와 구분된다.

structuredNuance.t: 멍은 부딪히거나 눌려 피부 아래 모세혈관이 터지면서 생기는 검푸른 자국을 가리키는 순우리말로, '멍이 들다'가 거의 한 단어처럼 굳어진 표준 표현이다(주의: 여기서 '들다'는 '안에 배어들다'의 뜻이지 '손에 들다'가 아니다). 색이 변해 사라질 때는 '멍이 빠지다'라고 한다.
비슷한 부상 단어 '상처'와의 결정적 차이는 '피부가 깨졌느냐'다 — 상처는 베이거나 까져 겉이 터진 것이고, 멍은 겉은 멀쩡한데 속에서 출혈이 번진 것이다.

가장 많이 빠지는 함정은 발음이 같은 '멍하다'와 헷갈리는 것인데, '멍하다 / 멍때리다'는 정신이 나가 넋을 놓은 상태를 뜻해 부상과 전혀 무관하다. 따라서 '멍을 하다 / 멍하다'로 부상을 말하면 완전히 다른 뜻이 되어 버린다. 또 영어 'bruise'는 동사로도 쓰여 'I bruised my leg'가 되지만, 한국어 멍은 명사뿐이라 '멍을 했다'가 아니라 '멍이 들었다'처럼 자동사 구문으로 써야 한다.

entries.english: to be swollen, to swell up
entries.shortExplanation: 붓다 means "to be swollen, to swell up" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be swollen, to swell up" is 붓다 (butda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 발이 붓다 ("one's feet swell"). Watch the particle attached to 붓다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅅ불규칙 → 부어요, 부었어요
울거나 잠을 못 잤을 때도 씀
'퉁퉁'은 심하게 부은 모양을 그린 의태어
목감기 증상을 설명할 때

examples.en: My eyes are puffy.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — ㅅ이 탈락해 '부었어요'가 됨

examples.ko: 하루 종일 서 있었더니 발이 퉁퉁 부었어요.
examples.romanization: haru jongil seo isseotdeoni bari tungtung bueosseoyo.
examples.en: I stood all day, so my feet got all puffed up.
examples.note: '-더니'로 원인(서 있음)과 결과(부음)를 연결, 의태어 '퉁퉁' 강조

examples.ko: 목감기인지 편도가 붓고 침 삼킬 때 아파요.
examples.romanization: mokgamgiinji pyeondoga butgo chim samkil ttae apayo.
examples.en: Maybe it's a throat cold — my tonsils are swollen and it hurts to swallow.
examples.note: 병원에서 자주 하는 설명, '-(으)ㄴ지'로 추측

entries.nuance: 붓다는 신체 일부가 부풀어 오르는 것을 뜻하는 ㅅ불규칙 용언으로, 받침 ㅅ이 모음 어미 앞에서 탈락해 '부어요, 부었어요, 부으면'으로 활용한다(어간 '붓-'에 '-어요'를 붙이면 '붓어요'가 아니라 '부어요'). 발·눈·편도 등 부위와 묶여 매우 자주 쓰는 필수 단어이고, 심하게 부은 모양은 의태어 '퉁퉁'을 앞에 붙여 강조한다. 영어권 학습자에게 가장 위험한 함정은 철자가 같은 두 동사다. 첫째, 똑같이 생긴 '붓다(물을 붓다, to pour)'도 ㅅ불규칙이라 활용형 '부어요'까지 똑같아, 목적어와 문맥(물을/발이)으로만 구분된다. 둘째, 표기가 한 끗 다른 '붇다(라면이 불어 커지다, 양이 늘다)'와 혼동하기 쉬운데, 이건 ㄷ불규칙이라 '불어요'로 활용해 형태가 달라진다. 영어 'swollen'은 형용사처럼 보이지만 한국어 붓다는 '부어 있다(상태)'와 '붓는다(과정)'를 모두 표현할 수 있는 동사라는 점도 알아 두면 좋다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
ㅅ불규칙을 모르고 '붓어요'라고 활용하는 것 — 받침 ㅅ이 탈락하므로 '부어요, 부었어요'가 올바른 형태다.
철자가 같은 '붓다(물을 붓다, to pour)'와 헷갈리는 것 — 둘 다 ㅅ불규칙이라 활용형(부어요)까지 같으니, 목적어(물을)와 문맥으로 구분해야 한다.
'붇다(라면이 불어 늘다)'와 혼동하는 것 — 이건 ㄷ불규칙이라 '불어요'로 활용해 형태가 다르므로, '발이 부었다'와 '면이 불었다'를 구분해야 한다.

entries.english: to ache, to throb (deep, nagging pain)
entries.shortExplanation: 쑤시다 means "to ache, to throb (deep, nagging pain)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쑤시다 (ssusida) = "to ache, to throb (deep, nagging pain)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 온몸이 쑤시다 ("one's whole body aches") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쑤시다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 몸살 때 가장 흔한 표현
관절·궂은 날씨 이야기에 자주
'욱신욱신'은 맥박처럼 지끈대는 통증을 그린 의태어
어르신들이 관절통을 말할 때 단골

examples.en: My whole body aches.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — 몸살의 핵심 묘사

examples.en: I overdid my workout, so my shoulder is throbbing.
examples.note: '-더니'로 원인·결과 연결, 의태어 '욱신욱신'으로 통증의 결을 표현

examples.en: My grandma says her knees ache whenever it rains.
examples.note: '-(ㄴ)대요'로 남의 말 전달, 관절통의 흔한 표현

entries.nuance: 쑤시다는 근육·관절·뼈 안쪽이 욱신욱신 지끈대며 묵직하게 아픈 통증을 뜻하는 동사로, 몸살·근육통·관절통을 묘사할 때 거의 필수다. 같은 통증 형용사인 '따갑다'와의 결정적 차이는 '깊이'다 — 따갑다가 피부 표면이 따끔 쏘는 느낌이라면, 쑤시다는 그보다 깊은 곳(근육·뼈)에서 묵직하게 욱신대는 느낌이다(따라서 베인 상처는 따갑고, 몸살 난 어깨는 쑤신다). 통증의 결을 살릴 때는 의태어 '욱신욱신'을 앞에 붙인다. 형태상 '쑤시다'는 동사라 현재형 '쑤신다'도 자연스럽지만, 증상을 말할 때는 보통 '쑤셔요'로 상태처럼 쓴다. 영어권 학습자의 함정은 '쑤셔요'를 풀어 '쑤시어요'로 또박또박 쓰는 것인데, 실제 회화에서는 '쑤시어'가 줄어 '쑤셔'가 되는 것이 자연스럽다. 또 영어 'ache'는 명사·동사 양쪽으로 쓰지만 한국어 쑤시다는 동사뿐이라 'I have an ache'를 직역하지 말고 '쑤셔요'로 풀어야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
따갑다(표면이 따끔 쏨)와 혼동하는 것 — 쑤시다는 근육·뼈 안쪽이 묵직하게 욱신대는 통증이라 깊이가 다르다.
'쑤셔요'를 '쑤시어요'로 또박또박 풀어 쓰는 것 — 회화에서는 '쑤시어'가 줄어 '쑤셔요'가 되는 것이 자연스럽다.
'I have an ache'를 명사로 직역하려는 것 — 쑤시다는 동사라 '쑤셔요 / 쑤시고'처럼 동사로 풀어 써야 한다.

structuredNuance.t: 쑤시다는 근육·관절·뼈 안쪽이 욱신욱신 지끈대며 묵직하게 아픈 통증을 뜻하는 동사로, 몸살·근육통·관절통을 묘사할 때 거의 필수다. 통증의 결을 살릴 때는 의태어 '욱신욱신'을 앞에 붙인다.
같은 통증 형용사인 '따갑다'와의 결정적 차이는 '깊이'다 — 따갑다가 피부 표면이 따끔 쏘는 느낌이라면, 쑤시다는 그보다 깊은 곳(근육·뼈)에서 묵직하게 욱신대는 느낌이다(따라서 베인 상처는 따갑고, 몸살 난 어깨는 쑤신다).
'쑤시다'는 동사라 현재형 '쑤신다'도 자연스럽지만, 증상을 말할 때는 보통 '쑤셔요'로 상태처럼 쓴다. '쑤시어요'로 또박또박 풀지 않고, 회화에서는 '쑤시어'가 줄어 '쑤셔'가 되는 것이 자연스럽다.
'쑤셔요'를 풀어 '쑤시어요'로 또박또박 쓰기 쉬운데, 실제 회화에서는 '쑤시어'가 줄어 '쑤셔'가 되는 것이 자연스럽다. 또 영어 'ache'는 명사·동사 양쪽으로 쓰지만 한국어 쑤시다는 동사뿐이라 'I have an ache'를 직역하지 말고 '쑤셔요'로 풀어야 한다.

entries.english: to sting, to be sore/prickly (surface pain)
entries.shortExplanation: 따갑다 means "to sting, to be sore/prickly (surface pain)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 따갑다 (ttagapda) means "to sting, to be sore/prickly (surface pain)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목이 따갑다 ("to have a sore/scratchy throat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 따갑다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ불규칙 → 따가워요; 감기 초기 증상으로 매우 흔함
미세먼지·렌즈 때문에도 씀
소독약을 바를 때의 따끔함
피부를 쏘는 듯한 강한 햇빛

examples.en: My throat is sore.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌어 '따가워요'

examples.en: The fine dust is bad, so my eyes sting and burn.
examples.note: '-아서' 이유 구문 + 한국 생활 필수 표현

examples.en: It stings a lot when I put antiseptic on the wound.
examples.note: '-니까'로 상황 제시, ㅂ불규칙 활용 '따가워요'

entries.nuance: 따갑다는 피부나 점막의 '표면'이 따끔따끔 쏘듯 쓰라린 통증을 뜻하는 ㅂ불규칙 형용사로, 받침 ㅂ이 모음 어미 앞에서 '우'로 바뀌어 '따가워요, 따가웠어요, 따가우면'으로 활용한다(어간 '따갑-'에 '-아요'를 붙이면 '따갑아요'가 아니라 '따가워요'). 감기 초기에 '목이 따갑다', 미세먼지가 심한 날 '눈이 따갑다'처럼 한국 일상에서 자주 쓴다. 깊은 곳이 묵직하게 욱신대는 '쑤시다'와의 결정적 차이는 '표면이 쏘느냐'다 — 따갑다는 겉(목 점막·피부·눈)이 따끔 쏘는 느낌이고, 쑤시다는 근육·뼈 속이 욱신대는 느낌이다. 비슷한 표면 통증어 '따끔하다'와도 미묘하게 다른데, '따끔하다'는 바늘에 콕 찔린 듯 순간적인 한 번을, '따갑다'는 화끈거리듯 지속되는 쓰라림을 가리킨다. 영어권 학습자의 가장 흔한 함정은 ㅂ불규칙을 놓쳐 '따갑어요'라고 하는 것이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
ㅂ불규칙을 놓쳐 '따갑어요'라고 활용하는 것 — 받침 ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌므로 '따가워요'가 올바른 형태다.
쑤시다와 혼동하는 것 — 따갑다는 표면(피부·점막)이 따끔 쏘는 통증, 쑤시다는 근육·뼈 안쪽이 욱신대는 통증이라 깊이가 다르다.
'따끔하다'와 똑같이 쓰는 것 — '따끔하다'는 콕 찔린 듯 순간적인 통증, '따갑다'는 화끈거리듯 지속되는 쓰라림이라 지속성이 다르다.

entries.shortExplanation: 어지럽다 means "to be dizzy, light-headed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be dizzy, light-headed" is 어지럽다 (eojireopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 머리가 어지럽다 ("to feel dizzy (in the head)"). Watch the particle attached to 어지럽다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ불규칙 → 어지러워요
'핑 돌다'는 머리가 핑 도는 순간을 그린 표현
원인을 '때문에'로 밝힐 때
함께 나타나는 증상 묶음

examples.en: I feel dizzy.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌어 '어지러워요'

examples.en: I stood up suddenly and felt dizzy, like the room was spinning.
examples.note: '-더니'로 원인·결과 연결, 기립성 어지럼증의 전형적 묘사

examples.ko: 멀미가 나서 머리가 어지럽고 토할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: meolmiga naseo meoriga eojireopgo tohal geot gatayo.
examples.en: I'm carsick — my head is spinning and I feel like throwing up.
examples.note: '-아서' 이유 + ㅂ불규칙 '어지럽고'

entries.nuance: 어지럽다는 머리가 핑 돌고 중심을 잡기 힘들어 비틀거리는 상태를 뜻하는 ㅂ불규칙 형용사로, 받침 ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌어 '어지러워요, 어지러웠어요, 어지러우면'으로 활용한다(어간 '어지럽-'에 '-어요'를 붙이면 '어지럽어요'가 아니라 '어지러워요'). 빈혈·저혈당·멀미 등 다양한 원인으로 생기며 병원 문진에서도 기본 단어다. 명사형 '어지럼증'으로 바꾸면 '어지럼증이 있다'처럼 증상명으로 쓸 수 있다. 비유적으로 '머리가 어지러울 정도로 복잡하다'처럼 정신적 혼란에도 쓰인다. 영어권 학습자가 가장 많이 빠지는 함정 두 가지가 있다. 첫째, ㅂ불규칙을 놓쳐 '어지럽어요'라고 하는 것. 둘째, 소리가 비슷한 동사 '어지르다(방을 어지르다, to make a mess)'와 헷갈리는 것인데, 이쪽은 르불규칙으로 '어질러요'로 활용하고 '어수선하게 흩뜨리다'라는 전혀 다른 뜻이라 '방이 어지럽다(혼란스럽다)'와 '방을 어지르다(흩뜨리다)'를 구분해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
ㅂ불규칙을 놓쳐 '어지럽어요'라고 활용하는 것 — 받침 ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌므로 '어지러워요'가 올바른 형태다.
동사 '어지르다(어수선하게 흩뜨리다, to make a mess)'와 혼동하는 것 — 이쪽은 르불규칙으로 '어질러요'이며 뜻도 전혀 달라, '머리가 어지럽다'와 '방을 어지르다'를 구분해야 한다.
감각 주체를 잘못 잡아 '나를 어지러워요'처럼 쓰는 것 — '머리가 어지러워요 / (저는) 어지러워요'처럼 증상 부위나 화자를 주어로 한다.

entries.shortExplanation: 메스껍다 means "to feel nauseous, queasy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 메스껍다 (meseukkeopda) = "to feel nauseous, queasy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 속이 메스껍다 ("to feel queasy in the stomach") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 메스껍다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to feel queasy in the stomach
usagePhrases.note: ㅂ불규칙 → 메스꺼워요

usagePhrases.en: queasy and about to throw up
usagePhrases.note: 구토 직전의 느낌
원인을 '때문에'로 밝힐 때
메스꺼움을 묘사하는 비슷한 의태 표현

examples.en: I feel queasy.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 기본 문장 — ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌어 '메스꺼워요'

examples.en: I took medicine on an empty stomach and feel nauseous and dizzy.
examples.note: '-더니'로 원인·결과 연결, 약 부작용 설명

examples.ko: 기름진 냄새만 맡아도 속이 메스꺼워서 못 먹겠어요.
examples.romanization: gireumjin naemsaeman matado sogi meseukkeowoseo mon meokgesseoyo.
examples.en: Just smelling greasy food makes me queasy, so I can't eat.
examples.note: '-아도'로 '~만 해도'를 표현, ㅂ불규칙 '메스꺼워서'

entries.nuance: 메스껍다는 토할 것처럼 속이 울렁대는 상태를 뜻하는 ㅂ불규칙 형용사로, 받침 ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌어 '메스꺼워요, 메스꺼웠어요, 메스꺼우면'으로 활용한다(어간 '메스껍-'에 '-어요'를 붙이면 '메스껍어요'가 아니라 '메스꺼워요'). 멀미·약 부작용·임신 초기 입덧 등에서 자주 쓰며 '속이 메스껍다'가 가장 자연스러운 조합이다. 결정적으로 '토하다(to vomit)'와 구분해야 하는데, 메스껍다는 토하기 '직전의 느낌'이지 실제로 토하는 행위가 아니다 — 영어 'nauseous'(메스꺼운 느낌)와 'vomit'(토함)의 차이와 똑같다. 좀 더 캐주얼하게는 '속이 울렁거리다 / 니글거리다'로 풀어 말하는데, '울렁거리다'는 출렁이듯 메스꺼운 느낌, '니글거리다'는 기름진 것이 얹힌 듯 느끼한 메스꺼움을 가리켜 결이 약간 다르다. 영어권 학습자의 가장 흔한 함정은 ㅂ불규칙을 놓쳐 '메스껍어요'라고 하는 것이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
ㅂ불규칙을 놓쳐 '메스껍어요'라고 활용하는 것 — 받침 ㅂ이 '우'로 바뀌므로 '메스꺼워요'가 올바른 형태다.
'토하다(to vomit)'와 같은 뜻으로 쓰는 것 — 메스껍다는 토하기 직전의 '느낌'이지 실제로 토하는 '행위'가 아니다.
감각 주체를 잘못 잡아 '나를 메스꺼워요'처럼 쓰는 것 — '속이 메스꺼워요'처럼 부위(속)를 주어로 삼는 것이 자연스럽다.

entries.shortExplanation: 보조배터리 means "portable charger, power bank" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보조배터리 (bojobaeteori) means "portable charger, power bank". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보조배터리 있어요? ("Do you have a power bank?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보조배터리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a power bank?
usagePhrases.note: asking to borrow one; just the bare noun + 있어요 carries the whole request
충전하다 = charge; here the bank is the thing being charged, not your phone

usagePhrases.en: I'll lend you my power bank
usagePhrases.note: 빌려주다 = lend; -ㄹ게요 makes it a friendly offer
대용량 = large-capacity, the word you scan for when shopping

examples.en: Do you have a power bank?
examples.note: simplest form: the noun alone + 있다 is a complete, natural question

examples.en: My phone died so I packed a power bank.
examples.note: 챙기다 = grab/pack to bring along; note the object particle 를 on 보조배터리

examples.ko: 혹시 보조배터리 잠깐만 빌릴 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: hoksi bojobaeteori jamkkanman billil su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: Could I maybe borrow your power bank for just a sec?
examples.note: 혹시 + -ㄹ 수 있을까요 = the soft, polite way to ask a stranger a favor

entries.nuance: 보조배터리 is the everyday word for a portable power bank, and it is built transparently from 보조(補助, 'auxiliary/supplementary') + 배터리, literally 'auxiliary battery' — so the name itself tells you it is the spare, not your phone's built-in cell. Almost every Korean in their 20s–30s carries one, so it surfaces constantly in casual talk; unlike many long loan-compounds it is rarely clipped — people just say the full 보조배터리, so as a learner say it in full and you'll be understood everywhere. The English loanword 파워뱅크 (power bank) exists but many people will not recognize it, so default to 보조배터리. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not assume the English term transfers, and watch the particle — 보조배터리를 충전하다 means charging the bank itself, whereas 보조배터리로 충전하다 (with 로, 'by means of') means using it to charge something else.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it '파워뱅크' — that is the English term and many Koreans will not understand it; the standard, safe word is '보조배터리'.
Saying just '배터리' when you mean the portable one — bare '배터리' is heard as the phone's internal battery, so keep the full '보조배터리'.
Mixing up the particles: '보조배터리를 충전해요' (charge the bank) vs '보조배터리로 충전해요' (use the bank to charge) — 를 vs 로 flips the meaning.

entries.shortExplanation: 액정 means "(phone/LCD) screen, display glass" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "(phone/LCD) screen, display glass" is 액정 (aekjeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 액정이 깨지다 ("the screen cracks/shatters"). Watch the particle attached to 액정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 깨지다 = break/shatter; the go-to verb for reporting phone damage
수리(修理) = repair; what you ask for at the counter
교체(交替) = swap/replace; pricier than a 수리

usagePhrases.en: a crack line forms on the screen
usagePhrases.note: 금이 가다 = a hairline crack appears, lighter than fully 깨지다

examples.en: The screen cracked.
examples.note: the core sentence you say first at a repair shop

examples.en: I dropped my phone and the screen is totally shattered.
examples.note: 떨어뜨리다 = drop something; 다 = completely

examples.en: How much does it cost to replace the screen?
examples.note: -는 데 (드는 비용) = the cost it takes to do something

entries.nuance: 액정 is Sino-Korean 液晶(液 'liquid' + 晶 'crystal') — literally 'liquid crystal', i.e. LCD — and in daily speech it means the physical glass display panel of a phone. The sharp contrast a learner must keep is 액정 vs 화면(畫面, 'screen/display'): 화면 leans toward what is shown ON the screen (the picture, the UI, 'the screen went black'), while 액정 is the tangible panel that gets dropped, cracked, repaired and replaced. So damage talk almost always uses 액정 (액정이 깨졌어요), and content talk uses 화면 (화면이 안 보여요). It collocates tightly with 깨지다 / 금이 가다 / 수리 / 교체. Pronunciation pitfall: 액정 is said [액쩡] with a tensed 쩡, and do not confuse the written word with 액체(liquid) — they share 액 but are unrelated in meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '화면이 깨졌어요' for cracked glass — Koreans say '액정이 깨졌어요'; 화면 is for what is displayed, 액정 is the physical panel.
Pronouncing it [액정] flat instead of the tensed [액쩡].
Confusing 액정 with 액체 (liquid) — same first syllable, totally different word.

entries.shortExplanation: 약정 means "contract commitment (phone plan lock-in period)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 약정 (yakjeong) = "contract commitment (phone plan lock-in period)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 약정 기간 ("contract (lock-in) period") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 약정, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기간(期間) = span of time; e.g. 2년 약정 기간
끝나다 = end; the moment you're free to switch carriers
the typical lock-in length when you buy a subsidized phone
위약금(違約金) = breach-of-contract fee charged for leaving early

examples.en: I'm on a 2-year contract.
examples.note: simple noun-이에요 statement of your status

examples.en: I got the phone cheap on a 2-year contract.
examples.note: -으로 = by means of/under (the contract); the carrier subsidizes the price

examples.ko: 약정이 아직 안 끝나서 위약금이 나와요.
examples.romanization: yakjeongi ajik an kkeunnaseo wiyakgeumi nawayo.
examples.en: My contract isn't over yet, so there's a penalty.
examples.note: 위약금이 나오다 = a penalty gets charged; -아서 links cause to result

entries.nuance: 약정 is Sino-Korean 約定(約 'promise/bind' + 定 'fix/settle') — a 'fixed, bound agreement' — and in everyday life it almost always means the carrier lock-in period you accept in exchange for a discounted phone. The boundaries learners blur: 계약(契約) is the broad word for a contract you sign (a lease, a job), while 약정 specifically names the telecom/finance lock-in term; and 약속(約束, a personal promise between people) shares the 約 character but is a completely different register — you keep a 약속 with a friend, you are bound by a 약정 with a company. It collocates with 기간, 끝나다, 남다(be left), 위약금. The pitfall: an English speaker may reach for 계약 or even 약속 to say 'my phone contract', but Koreans say 약정 — '약정이 남았어요?' (Is your contract still running?) is the natural phrasing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using '계약' for the phone lock-in — 계약 is a contract in general, but the carrier commitment period is specifically '약정'.
Confusing it with '약속' — 약속 is a personal promise to a person; 약정 is a binding term in a telecom/financial agreement.
Saying '약정이 끝냈어요' (transitive 끝내다, 'I ended it') when you mean it ended on its own — use the intransitive '약정이 끝났어요'.

entries.shortExplanation: 통신사 means "mobile carrier, telecom provider" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 통신사 (tongsinsa) means "mobile carrier, telecom provider". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 통신사를 바꾸다 ("switch carriers"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 통신사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 바꾸다 = change; what you do when your 약정 ends
매장 = retail store; where you sign up or 개통
discount points and coupons tied to your provider
알뜰 = thrifty; cheaper providers riding the big networks

examples.en: Which carrier do you use?
examples.note: 어느 = which (among a known set); a standard getting-to-know-you question

examples.en: I got a movie-ticket discount with my carrier membership.
examples.note: -으로 = by means of; 할인받다 = receive a discount

examples.ko: 외국인도 통신사 매장에서 바로 개통할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: oegugindo tongsinsa maejangeseo baro gaetonghal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Foreigners can activate a line right at a carrier store too.
examples.note: 개통하다 = activate phone service; 도 = even/too

entries.nuance: 통신사 is Sino-Korean 通信社 — 通信(通 'communicate' + 信 'message/signal') + 社('company') = 'communications company', i.e. a mobile/telecom provider like SKT, KT, or LG U+, plus the cheaper 알뜰폰 MVNOs. The contrast to hold: 통신사 = the network/service provider you pay monthly, whereas 제조사(製造社, the maker — 삼성, 애플) is who built the handset, and 폰 회사 is ambiguous between the two. Because 요금제(plans), 약정, and 멤버십 differ by provider, '어느 통신사 써요?' is a genuinely frequent question. Two pitfalls: 통신사 can also mean a 'news agency' (as in 연합뉴스 같은 통신사) in formal contexts, but in daily phone talk it is the carrier; and English speakers often say '폰 회사' thinking 'phone company', which Koreans hear as the manufacturer — say 통신사 for the carrier.

Reading 통신사 as 'news agency' in everyday conversation — in daily life about phones it means your mobile carrier.
Saying '폰 회사' for the carrier — that sounds like the manufacturer (Samsung/Apple); use '통신사'.
Mixing up 통신사 (the service provider) with 제조사 (the device maker) — they are different companies.

usagePhrases.note: -하다 turns the loanword noun into a verb
the phrasing a notification uses: 새 업데이트가 있어요
자동(自動) = automatic; set-and-forget
-중(中) = in the middle of; shown on the loading screen

entries.nuance: 업데이트 is the English loanword used for refreshing software, an app, or your phone's OS to the latest version. The contrast Koreans actually feel is 업데이트 vs 업그레이드: 업데이트 means getting the newest version/patches (bug fixes, new features), while 업그레이드(upgrade) implies moving up a tier or spec — better hardware, a higher plan, a paid premium level. So a routine version refresh is 업데이트, and 'I upgraded to a better phone/plan' is 업그레이드. It collocates with 하다, 있다, 자동, 중. Two pitfalls for English speakers: do not use 업데이트 and 업그레이드 interchangeably the way casual English sometimes does — Korean keeps them distinct; and because it is a noun, you must attach -하다 to make the verb (업데이트해요), not leave it bare as if it were already a verb.

Using '업그레이드' for a normal version refresh — that implies a tier/spec jump; a version refresh is '업데이트'.
Leaving the noun bare as a verb — say '업데이트해요/업데이트했어요', attaching -하다, not just '업데이트요'.
Forgetting the object particle when needed — '업데이트를 했어요' is cleaner than dropping it in writing, though speech often omits it.

entries.shortExplanation: 용량 means "capacity, storage space" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 용량 (yongnyang) = "capacity, storage space". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 용량이 부족하다 ("storage is running low") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 용량, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 부족하다(不足) = be insufficient; the #1 phrase you'll hear
저장(貯藏) = storage/saving; specifies it's storage, not data/volume
꽉 차다 = be packed full; 꽉 intensifies
늘리다 = expand/increase (transitive)

examples.en: I'm low on storage.
examples.note: the everyday complaint in its simplest form

examples.en: I have too many photos, so I'm low on storage.
examples.note: -아서 = so/because; the classic cause of full storage

examples.ko: 용량이 꽉 차서 앱이 설치가 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: yongnyangi kkwak chaseo aebi seolchiga an dwaeyo.
examples.en: Storage is full so the app won't install.
examples.note: 설치(設置) = installation; 안 되다 = won't work

entries.nuance: 용량 is Sino-Korean 容量(容 'hold/contain' + 量 'amount/quantity') = 'the amount that can be held', so it covers a phone's storage, a file's size, a data amount, and even the volume a bowl or container can hold. In the phone context it almost always means 저장 용량 (storage), and 용량이 부족하다 / 꽉 차다 are the phrases you meet constantly. Watch two boundaries: a mobile data allowance is sometimes called 용량 informally, but it is usually said as 데이터 or in GB, so keep 용량 for storage to be clear; and crucially, 용량 is NOT 'volume' in the loudness sense — sound level is 볼륨(volume) or 소리. The English-speaker trap is hearing 'capacity/volume' and reaching for 볼륨, or expecting 용량 to mean only data — anchor it to physical/storage capacity (256기가 용량 = 256GB of storage).

Using 용량 for sound volume — loudness is '볼륨' or '소리', never 용량.
Defaulting 용량 to mean mobile data — data allowances are usually said as '데이터' or in GB; 용량 mainly means storage capacity.
Confusing transitive/intransitive: '용량이 늘다' (capacity increases on its own) vs '용량을 늘리다' (you increase it) — match the particle to the verb.

entries.shortExplanation: 인증 means "authentication, verification" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 인증 (injeung) means "authentication, verification". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 본인 인증 ("identity verification"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 인증 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 본인(本人) = the person themselves; proving you are you
the one-time SMS code you type in
-하다 makes the noun a verb; complete the verification
verifying your identity via your mobile number

examples.en: The verification code arrived.
examples.note: 오다 = come/arrive; the code 'comes' to you by text

examples.ko: 가입하려면 본인 인증을 먼저 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gaiparyeomyeon bonin injeungeul meonjeo haeya haeyo.
examples.en: To sign up you have to verify your identity first.
examples.note: -려면 = if you intend to; 가입하다 = sign up

examples.en: Can I verify with my alien registration card too?
examples.note: -으로 = using; 인증이 되다 = verification goes through; a key resident question

entries.nuance: 인증 is Sino-Korean 認證(認 'recognize/acknowledge' + 證 'proof/certify') = 'certified recognition', i.e. authentication or verification. In Korea nearly every sign-up, payment, and booking requires 본인 인증, so it is essential vocabulary for foreign residents — typically you receive an 인증번호 by text and enter it, and without it you often cannot use the service at all. The look-alike to separate is 인정(認定, acknowledgement/recognition, as in '인정받다' = to be recognized/credited): 인증 and 인정 share the 認 character and look similar but mean different things. Also keep 인증번호(a one-time verification code) distinct from 비밀번호(your password) — English speakers often call the SMS code a 'password', but Koreans call the disposable code an 인증번호 and the reusable secret a 비밀번호.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 인증 (verification/authentication) with 인정 (acknowledgement/recognition) — they look alike but mean different things.
Calling the SMS one-time code a '비밀번호' (password) — the disposable code is an '인증번호'.
Using the verb wrong — say '인증을 하다 / 인증이 되다' (do/get verified); '인증을 받다' works for receiving certification but for the SMS flow 인증하다/인증되다 is more natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 백업 means "backup (data)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "backup (data)" is 백업 (baegeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 백업하다 ("to back up"). Watch the particle attached to 백업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: -하다 verb; save a copy of your data
받다 here = obtain/create a copy onto storage
자동(自動) = automatic; runs by itself to the cloud
안 되다 = fail/not work; common troubleshooting phrase

examples.en: Did you back it up?
examples.note: loanword + 했어요 question; the first thing asked before a phone swap

examples.ko: 폰 바꾸기 전에 백업부터 해 두세요.
examples.romanization: pon bakkugi jeone baegeopbuteo hae duseyo.
examples.en: Back things up before you switch phones.
examples.note: -기 전에 = before doing; -아/어 두다 = do in advance and leave it done

examples.ko: 백업을 안 해서 연락처가 다 날아갔어요.
examples.romanization: baegeobeul an haeseo yeollakcheoga da naragasseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't back up, so I lost all my contacts.
examples.note: 날아가다 = (data) gets wiped/lost; -아서 links cause to result

entries.nuance: 백업 is the English loanword 'backup' used specifically for copying data — phone backups, cloud backups, contacts and photos. Because Koreans change and reset phones often, 백업 is thoroughly everyday vocabulary; the verb is both 백업하다 and 백업받다, and whether your 자동 백업 to the cloud is on is a frequent topic. The key contrast is 백업 vs 저장(貯藏, 'save'): 저장하다 is saving a file in place (saving a document), while 백업하다 means making a separate spare copy for safety — so they are not interchangeable. The English-speaker pitfall is the other English sense of 'backup' (a substitute person, reinforcements, 'I'll back you up'): that meaning does NOT carry into Korean 백업, which in daily life is almost exclusively the data sense — for human backup you'd use words like 지원/대체 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 백업 for the 'substitute/reinforcement' sense of English backup — in Korean daily use 백업 means a data copy only.
Treating '백업하다' and '저장하다' as the same — 저장 is saving in place, 백업 is making a separate spare copy.
Saying '백업했다' when you only opened the file — you must actually create the copy; otherwise it's just 저장, not 백업.

entries.shortExplanation: 설정 means "settings (menu), configuration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 설정 (seoljeong) = "settings (menu), configuration". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 설정에 들어가다 ("go into settings") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 설정, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 들어가다 = enter; 에 marks the place you go into
알림 = notification; the submenu for alerts
바꾸다 = change; 을 marks the setting as the object
초기(初期) = initial/early stage; first-time configuration

examples.en: Go into Settings.
examples.note: -(으)세요 polite command; 에 = into (the menu)

examples.ko: 언어 설정을 영어로 바꿀 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: eoneo seoljeongeul yeongeoro bakkul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Can I change the language setting to English?
examples.note: -로 = into/to (the result); a very useful new-resident question

examples.en: I can't find where the settings are.
examples.note: -는지 = the embedded question 'where'; 못 찾겠다 = can't manage to find

entries.nuance: 설정 is Sino-Korean 設定(設 'set up/establish' + 定 'fix/determine') = 'to set and fix', the standard word for the configuration menu on a phone or app — it is exactly what sits where English shows 'Settings'. Just knowing 설정에 들어가다(go in) and 설정을 바꾸다(change a setting) lets you follow a shop clerk's or friend's instructions easily. The contrast to note: 설정 is the configurable preference, while 설치(設置, installation) is putting an app on, and 설명(說明, explanation) merely looks similar in writing. Mind two things as an English speaker: you can say 세팅(setting) and be understood, but the on-screen menu is almost always labeled 설정, so learn that form; and do not visually confuse 설정(settings) with 설명(explanation) — they share 설 but differ.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '세팅' and expecting it on the menu — it's understood in speech, but the menu label is '설정'.
Confusing 설정 (settings) with 설명 (explanation) — similar shape, different words.
Mixing 설정 (configure preferences) with 설치 (install an app) — going into 설정 is not the same as 설치하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 기종 means "device model (of a phone)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기종 (gijong) means "device model (of a phone)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 폰 기종 ("phone model"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기종 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 기종 = device type/model; pairs with 뭐예요 to ask which one
같은 = same; e.g. sharing a charger because 같은 기종
구형(舊型) = old-type; opposite of 신형 newer model
변경(變更) = change; switching to a different handset

examples.en: What phone model is it?
examples.note: noun + 이/가 뭐예요 = the basic 'what is X?' question

examples.ko: 이 앱은 구형 기종에서는 안 돌아가요.
examples.romanization: i aebeun guhyeong gijongeseoneun an doragayo.
examples.en: This app doesn't run on older models.
examples.note: -에서는 = on/in (contrast); 돌아가다 = (software) runs

examples.en: It's the same model, so we share a charger.
examples.note: -(이)라 = because it is; 같이 = together

entries.nuance: 기종 is Sino-Korean 機種(機 'machine/device' + 種 'kind/type') = 'kind of machine', i.e. the specific model of a device — phones above all, but also cameras, cars, and appliances. When buying a case or film, getting a repair, or doing a used-resale, '기종이 뭐예요?' is nearly mandatory because accessories must match the exact model. The boundary worth noting: 기종 is the model/type of a device, 모델 is the English loanword that also works and is common in ads, while 기계(機械) is 'machine' in the general sense — so 기종 is more precise than 기계 when you mean which model. The English-speaker pitfalls: 'model' translates fine as 모델, but 기종 often sounds more natural in spoken Korean (especially for phones); and do not let the sound drift toward 기분(mood/feeling) — it is [기종], a different word entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 기계 (machine, general) when you mean which specific model — that's 기종 (or 모델).
Assuming only 모델 is correct — 모델 works, but '기종' is often the more natural spoken choice for phones.
Slipping the pronunciation toward 기분 (mood) — keep it [기종], a distinct word.

entries.shortExplanation: 화면보호필름 means "screen protector film" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "screen protector film" is 화면보호필름 (hwamyeonbohopilleum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 화면보호필름을 붙이다 ("apply a screen protector"). Watch the particle attached to 화면보호필름 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 붙이다 = stick/apply on; the verb for putting film on

usagePhrases.en: the film lifts up at the edges
usagePhrases.note: 들뜨다 = peel/lift away from the surface
강화유리(強化琉璃) = tempered glass; the sturdier kind
교체(交替) = swap/replace; redoing a worn protector

examples.en: Did you put a screen protector on?
examples.note: in real life it's clipped to just '필름'; 붙이다 = apply

examples.en: I bought a new phone and put a protector on first.
examples.note: -부터 = starting with; the customary first step

examples.en: The film cracked, so the screen itself is fine.
examples.note: 멀쩡하다 = perfectly intact; the film did its job

entries.nuance: 화면보호필름 is a transparent compound — 화면(畫面, 'screen/display') + 보호(保護, 'protect') + 필름(film, loanword) = 'screen-protecting film' — but in real speech almost everyone clips it to just 필름. Putting one on is a near-universal first step with a new phone, and shop staff routinely offer '필름도 같이 붙여 드릴까요?' (Shall I put the film on too?). The contrast to register: 화면보호필름/필름 is the thin protective sheet on the glass, distinct from 케이스(the case around the body) and from the 액정 (the actual display panel underneath) — the film sacrifices itself so the 액정 survives. Two English-speaker pitfalls: do not picture photographic film or movie 'film' — in the phone context 필름 is the protector sheet; and keep 붙이다(stick/apply) separate from the similar-sounding 부치다(to mail something, or to pan-fry) — '필름 붙여 주세요' uses 붙이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Picturing camera/movie 'film' — in the phone context 필름 means the screen-protector sheet.
Confusing 붙이다 (stick/apply) with 부치다 (mail/pan-fry) — '필름 붙여 주세요' uses 붙이다.
Mixing up the protector with the panel — 필름 is the sacrificial sheet on top; the 액정 is the screen itself underneath.

entries.shortExplanation: 느려지다 means "to slow down, get laggy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 느려지다 (neuryeojida) = "to slow down, get laggy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 폰이 느려지다 ("the phone slows down") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 느려지다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the prototypical subject; describes a change for the worse
갑자기 = all of a sudden; an abrupt drop
점점 = little by little; a creeping decline
speed dropping over time or under load

examples.en: My phone has gotten slow.
examples.note: past -어졌어요 states the result: it became slow

examples.en: When storage is full, the phone slows down.
examples.note: -(으)면 = whenever/if; a cause-and-effect statement

examples.en: The wifi gets slow every evening.
examples.note: -만 되면 = the moment it just becomes (every time); recurring trigger

entries.nuance: 느려지다 is the inchoative pair of the adjective 느리다(be slow): 느리다 + the -어지다 'become' ending = 'to get/grow slow', so the form itself encodes change. The required conjugation logic shows on the 요-form: 느리다 → stem 느리- + 어지다, and because the stem already ends in 이, it contracts to 느려지다 → 느려져요 (present), 느려졌어요 (past) — the 어 of -어지다 fuses with 이 to give 려. The sharp contrast is exactly 느리다 vs 느려지다: 느리다 describes a steady state ('this phone IS slow'), while 느려지다 describes the transition ('it GOT slow / is getting slower'), which is why complaints about a phone degrading use 느려지다 with 점점/갑자기. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'slow' is one word, so learners say 느려요 for everything, but to express that something has worsened over time you need 느려졌어요; also do not confuse it with the look-alike 늘어지다(stretch/drag out, go limp).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using the state adjective 느리다 (느려요) when you mean it WORSENED — for a change over time, say '느려졌어요' (느려지다).
Confusing 느려지다 with 늘어지다 (stretch/sag/drag out) — similar shape, different meaning.
Misconjugating the -어지다 form — it's '느려져요/느려졌어요' (the 이 + 어 fuse to 려), not '느리어져요'.

structuredNuance.t: 느려지다 is the inchoative pair of the adjective 느리다(be slow): 'to get/grow slow', so the form itself encodes change. Complaints about a phone degrading use 느려지다 with 점점/갑자기.

entries.shortExplanation: 교통카드 means "transit card (T-money etc.)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교통카드 (gyotongkadeu) means "transit card (T-money etc.)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교통카드를 찍어요. ("I tap the transit card."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교통카드 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the verb is 찍다 (to tap/stamp on the reader), never 누르다

usagePhrases.en: I top up the transit card.
usagePhrases.note: 충전(充電) literally 'charge electricity' — reused for adding cash value

usagePhrases.en: The transit card balance is low.
usagePhrases.note: 잔액 = remaining balance; the exact phrase the gate flashes

usagePhrases.en: Can I use a transit card?
usagePhrases.note: 돼요? = 'does it work?', the polite way to ask a cabbie or shop

examples.en: Do you have a transit card?
examples.note: simplest form — just 있다 + the noun

examples.en: I topped up my transit card at the convenience store.
examples.note: 에서 marks where the action happens; CU/GS25 all do it

examples.ko: 요즘은 지갑 없이 휴대폰으로 교통카드를 찍어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jigap eopsi hyudaeponeuro gyotongkadeureul jjigeoyo.
examples.en: These days I tap the transit card with my phone instead of a wallet.
examples.note: real mobile-T-money habit; 으로 = by means of the phone

entries.nuance: 교통카드(交通+card) literally welds the Sino-Korean 교통 'traffic/transport' onto the English 'card', and names the rechargeable tap-to-ride card (T머니, 캐시비, or a 후불 credit card) for buses, the subway, and even some taxis. The make-or-break verb is 찍다 'to tap/stamp', never 누르다 'to press a button' — you lay the card flat on the reader, you don't push anything. A prepaid card you 충전 'top up' at convenience stores; the gate beeps your 잔액 'remaining balance'. Don't confuse it with a plain 카드, which to a Korean means a credit/debit card for shopping; the tap-to-ride one is always the full 교통카드. English 'swipe' also misleads — there is no magnetic swipe, only a contactless 찍다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교통카드를 눌러요 for tapping in.
누르다 means to press a button; you tap a card flat on the reader, which is 찍다. → 교통카드를 찍어요.
Using bare 카드 to mean the transit card.
To a Korean 카드 alone = a credit/debit card for buying things. The tap-to-ride card must be the full 교통카드 to be unambiguous.
Saying 교통카드를 채워요 for topping up.
채우다 = fill a physical container; money value on a card is 충전하다. → 교통카드를 충전해요.

English 'swipe' misleads — there is no magnetic swipe, only a contactless 찍다.

entries.shortExplanation: 정기권 means "commuter pass, period pass" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "commuter pass, period pass" is 정기권 (jeonggigwon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정기권을 끊어요. ("I buy a commuter pass."). Watch the particle attached to 정기권 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 끊다 'to cut' is the idiomatic verb for buying a ticket/pass
you reload the same card every period (30 days / 60 rides)

usagePhrases.en: A commuter pass is cheaper than the regular fare.
usagePhrases.note: 보다 = 'than' for the comparison
the standard Seoul Metro period pass — subway only

examples.en: Is a commuter pass cheaper?
examples.note: simple yes/no comparison with 더 'more'

examples.en: Since I take the subway every day, I bought a commuter pass.
examples.note: 니까 gives the reason; 끊다 = buy the pass

examples.ko: 출퇴근만 생각하면 정기권이 이득인데 주말 외출이 많으면 손해예요.
examples.romanization: chultoegeunman saenggakamyeon jeonggigwoni ideuginde jumal oechuri maneumyeon sonhaeyeyo.
examples.en: For just commuting a pass pays off, but if you go out a lot on weekends it's a loss.
examples.note: real cost trade-off; 인데 contrasts the two cases

entries.nuance: 정기권(定期券) is built from 정기 'fixed period' (定 fix + 期 term) plus 권 'ticket/voucher', so literally a 'fixed-term ticket' — a period/commuter pass. The dividing line versus a single 일회용 ticket is repetition: 정기권 only pays off if you ride the same route daily, since Seoul's subway version is a 30-day, 60-trip card. The sharp trap is coverage — the standard subway 정기권 works on the subway ONLY: no buses, and crucially no free 환승 'transfer' to a bus, so a bus-leg commuter loses money. The verb is 끊다 (idiom, literally 'to cut', from tearing a paper ticket) or 충전하다 to reload. Contrast 정기권 (period-based) with 회수권, an older booklet of single fares bought by count, not by time.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming the subway 정기권 covers bus transfers.
The standard period pass is subway-only and gives no free bus 환승, unlike a normal 교통카드. Check your route's bus legs first.
Confusing 정기권 with a one-ride 일회용 ticket.
정기권 is time/count-based for repeat commuting; 일회용 is a single trip. Buying 정기권 for occasional travel wastes money.
Saying 정기권을 사요 and expecting it to sound native.
Korean idiomatically 'cuts' a ticket: 정기권을 끊다. 사다 is understood but 끊다 is what locals say.

structuredNuance.t: A period/commuter pass. It only pays off if you ride the same route daily, since Seoul's subway version is a 30-day, 60-trip card. entries.shortExplanation: 막차 means "last train / last bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 막차 (makcha) = "last train / last bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막차를 놓쳤어요. ("I missed the last train.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막차, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = to miss (let slip) a vehicle you meant to catch
means its DEPARTURE time, not arrival — leave early

usagePhrases.en: I have to catch the last train.
usagePhrases.note: 아야 하다 = obligation 'must'

usagePhrases.en: The last train is gone (service has ended).
usagePhrases.note: 끊기다 = service is cut off for the night

examples.en: What time is the last train?
examples.note: bare schedule question, the survival phrase

examples.en: Let's hurry before the last train is gone.
examples.note: 기 전에 = 'before ~'; classic end-of-night line

examples.ko: 막차 놓쳐서 결국 택시 타고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: makcha notchyeoseo gyeolguk taeksi tago wasseoyo.
examples.en: I missed the last train, so in the end I came by taxi.
examples.note: 아서 = cause→result; 결국 'in the end' adds the resignation

entries.nuance: 막차 fuses the native prefix 막- 'last/final' with 차(車) 'vehicle', literally 'the last vehicle', and it dominates Korean nightlife because the subway stops near midnight and missing it means a pricey taxi. Its exact opposite is 첫차 'first vehicle'. Two collocations are everywhere: 막차 끊기다 'the last service is cut off (gone)' and 막차 놓치다 'miss the last one'. The key pitfall is the English verb 'miss' — Korean uses 놓치다 'let slip', NEVER 잃어버리다 'lose (an object)', so 막차를 잃어버렸어요 sounds like you misplaced a train. Also note 막차 시간 is the DEPARTURE time, so a learner who reads it as an arrival time will stroll up just as the doors close.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 막차를 잃어버렸어요 for missing the last train.
잃어버리다 = lose a physical object. Failing to catch a train is 놓치다. → 막차를 놓쳤어요.
Treating 막차 시간 as the arrival time.
It is the departure time of the final train. Arrive a few minutes early or you literally watch it leave.
Saying 막 차 with a space or as 마지막 차 in casual speech.
The fixed word is one token, 막차. 마지막 차 is grammatical but stilted; locals just say 막차.

structuredNuance.t: 'The last vehicle', and it dominates Korean nightlife because the subway stops near midnight and missing it means a pricey taxi. Two collocations are everywhere: 막차 끊기다 'the last service is cut off (gone)' and 막차 놓치다 'miss the last one'. Also note 막차 시간 is the DEPARTURE time, so a learner who reads it as an arrival time will stroll up just as the doors close.

막차 fuses the native prefix 막- 'last/final' with 차(車) 'vehicle', literally 'the last vehicle'.
The English verb 'miss' — Korean uses 놓치다 'let slip', NEVER 잃어버리다 'lose (an object)', so 막차를 잃어버렸어요 sounds like you misplaced a train.

entries.english: first train / first bus of the day
entries.shortExplanation: 첫차 means "first train / first bus of the day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 첫차 (cheotcha) means "first train / first bus of the day". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 첫차를 타요. ("I take the first train."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 첫차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the earliest departure, ~5:30 a.m. on the subway
when daily service starts

usagePhrases.en: What time is the first train?
usagePhrases.note: asking when service begins

usagePhrases.en: I go on the first train.
usagePhrases.note: (으)로 = by means of / on the first run

examples.en: What time is the first train?
examples.note: simplest schedule question with 몇 시

examples.en: I took the first train to go to the airport.
examples.note: (으)려고 = intention 'in order to'; classic early-flight reason

examples.en: I stayed up all night and just went home on the first train.
examples.note: 밤새우다 'pull an all-nighter'; 으로 marks the means

entries.nuance: 첫차 joins the native prefix 첫- 'first' with 차(車) 'vehicle' — 'the first vehicle' — and is the mirror image of 막차; the subway 첫차 typically rolls around 5:30 a.m. People catch it for early flights or after pulling an all-nighter (밤새우다). The verb 다니다 'to run/operate (regularly)' is the natural partner for when service runs. The English-speaker trap is spacing and a near-homophone: write 첫차 as ONE word (첫 차 with a space reads as 'first car' counting vehicles), and don't mix it up with 첫째 'the first one / firstly', which orders items, not departures. Also resist the calque 'first car' — in transit context 차 here means the scheduled run, not an automobile.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 첫 차 with a space.
Spaced, 첫 차 reads as 'the first car' (counting vehicles). The first scheduled train is the single word 첫차.
Confusing 첫차 with 첫째.
첫째 = 'the first one' / 'firstly' for ordering things or birth order. The day's first departure is 첫차.
Using 첫번 차 to mean the first train.
That is not idiomatic; the established lexical item is 첫차. Just say 첫차.

structuredNuance.t: 'The first vehicle' — the mirror image of 막차; the subway 첫차 typically rolls around 5:30 a.m. People catch it for early flights or after pulling an all-nighter (밤새우다). The verb 다니다 'to run/operate (regularly)' is the natural partner for when service runs.

entries.shortExplanation: 연착 means "delay (of a train, bus, flight)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "delay (of a train, bus, flight)" is 연착 (yeonchak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기차가 연착됐어요. ("The train was delayed."). Watch the particle attached to 연착 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 연착되다 (passive feel) is the most common form
the wording on station/airport notice boards
duration + 연착, no verb needed
이다 lets the noun itself be the predicate

examples.en: The train was delayed.
examples.note: the base sentence; 되다 turns the noun into 'got delayed'

examples.en: It snowed a lot, so the KTX was delayed 30 minutes.
examples.note: 아서 = cause→effect; weather is the usual culprit

examples.en: Because of the delay I almost ended up late to my interview.
examples.note: 때문에 = 'because of'; ㄹ 뻔했다 = 'almost (nearly happened)'

entries.nuance: 연착(延着) is pure Sino-Korean — 延 'delay/extend' + 着 'arrive' — literally 'a delayed arrival', used for trains, buses, and flights, and it's the word on the 연착 안내 'delay notice' board. Standard verb forms are 연착되다 and 연착하다. The crucial contrast is 연착 versus 지각(遲刻): 연착 is a VEHICLE running behind schedule, whereas 지각 is a PERSON arriving late (to work, class). So 'I was late because the train was 연착' needs both words. The pitfall is reaching for plain 늦다 'to be late' for the vehicle — natural for a person, but for a scheduled train/flight the precise transit term is 연착되다. The opposite of 연착 is arriving 정시에 'on time'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using bare 늦다 for a vehicle running behind schedule.
늦다 fits a person; a scheduled train/flight uses 연착되다. → 기차가 연착됐어요, not 기차가 늦었어요 in formal contexts.
Confusing 연착 with 지각.
지각 = a person being late (to work/school). 연착 = a vehicle's delayed arrival. They are not interchangeable.
Saying 연착이 됐다 vs 연착됐다 inconsistently.
Both are heard, but the clean standard is 연착되다 / 연착했다. Avoid dropping the verb entirely except on signage like '10분 연착'.

structuredNuance.t: 'A delayed arrival', used for trains, buses, and flights, and it's the word on the 연착 안내 'delay notice' board. The opposite of 연착 is arriving 정시에 'on time'.

entries.shortExplanation: 급행 means "express (faster service skipping stops)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 급행 (geupaeng) = "express (faster service skipping stops)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 급행을 타요. ("I take the express.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 급행, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the faster train/line that skips minor stops
급행 modifies 열차 'train'

usagePhrases.en: The express is faster than the local.
usagePhrases.note: 보다 = 'than'; 일반 is the all-stops local

usagePhrases.en: The express doesn't stop at this station.
usagePhrases.note: 서다 'to stop/stand' — the make-or-break verb

examples.en: The express is faster.
examples.note: simplest comparison with 더 'more'

examples.en: If you take the express, you get there 20 minutes faster.
examples.note: 면 = 'if/when'; concrete time saved

examples.ko: 이 역엔 급행이 안 서니까 일반 타고 가다가 갈아타세요.
examples.romanization: i yeogen geupaengi an seonikka ilban tago gadaga garataseyo.
examples.en: The express doesn't stop here, so take the local and transfer along the way.
examples.note: platform-level advice; 다가 = switch mid-action

entries.nuance: 급행(急行) is Sino-Korean 急 'urgent/fast' + 行 'go', literally 'fast-going' — express service (Seoul Line 9, the GTX, some Korail lines) that skips smaller stations to save time. Its opposites are 완행(緩行) 'slow-going' or, more commonly today, 일반 'general/local' (all stops). The decisive collocation is 안 서다 'doesn't stop': the 급행 bypasses many stations, so before boarding you must confirm it 서다 'stops' at your destination. The classic English-speaker pitfall is mixing the noun 급행 'express service' with the adjective 급하다 'to be in a hurry/urgent' — same 急 root, but 급하다 describes a person's rush, not a train. People weigh the time saved against the 급행's heavier crowding.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Boarding a 급행 without checking 정차역 (where it stops).
The express skips many stations. If it doesn't 서다 at yours, you overshoot. Confirm first: 급행이 ○○역에 서요?
Confusing 급행 with 급하다.
급행 = express service (a noun). 급하다 = to be in a hurry (an adjective about a person/situation). Don't say 저는 급행해요 for 'I'm in a rush'.
Assuming 급행 is always better.
It's faster but typically far more crowded (Line 9 급행 is infamous). For a short hop or a skipped station, 일반 can be smarter.

entries.shortExplanation: 하차 means "getting off / alighting (from a vehicle)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 하차 (hacha) means "getting off / alighting (from a vehicle)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 하차 벨을 눌러요. ("I press the get-off bell."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 하차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: on a bus; here 누르다 IS right — it's a real button

usagePhrases.en: I get off at the next stop.
usagePhrases.note: 하차하다; 에서 marks the stop

usagePhrases.en: tag-off (tapping your card when getting off)
usagePhrases.note: what unlocks the free bus 환승

usagePhrases.en: Please exit through the back door.
usagePhrases.note: (으)로 = via; standard bus etiquette

examples.en: I'll get off at the next stop.
examples.note: ㄹ게요 = speaker's intention; polite and natural on a bus

examples.ko: 내릴 때 카드를 안 찍으면 하차 처리가 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: naeril ttae kadeureul an jjigeumyeon hacha cheoriga an dwaeyo.
examples.en: If you don't tap your card when getting off, the tag-off doesn't register.
examples.note: 면 = 'if'; why you must tag off

examples.ko: 하차 벨을 미리 눌러야 기사님이 세워 줘요.
examples.romanization: hacha bereul miri nulleoya gisanimi sewo jwoyo.
examples.en: You have to press the bell in advance so the driver stops for you.
examples.note: 아야 = 'only if/must'; 줘요 shows the driver doing it for you

entries.nuance: 하차(下車) is Sino-Korean 下 'down' + 車 'vehicle' — literally 'down from the vehicle' — the formal counterpart to 승차 'boarding'. In everyday speech people just say 내리다 'to get off'; 하차 shows up on signs, announcements, and the bus fare system. It matters most on buses, where a 하차 태그 (tapping your card on exit) is what grants the free 환승 'transfer', and you press the 하차 벨 to signal your stop (note: here 누르다 'press' is correct, because the bell really is a button). Exit norm is the 뒷문 'rear door'. The pitfall: don't over-formalize chatty speech — telling a friend 하차합니다 sounds like a PA announcer; just say 내려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Skipping the 하차 태그 on the bus.
Without tapping off, the system can't compute distance and you lose the 환승 discount (or get charged a max fare). Always tag off.
Confusing 하차 with 승차.
하차 = getting OFF (下 down). 승차 = getting ON (乘 ride). Reversing them sends you the wrong way through the doors.
Saying 하차해요 to a friend in casual chat.
하차 is formal/announcement register. In daily talk use 내리다 → 다음에서 내려요. Save 하차 for signs and the fare system.

structuredNuance.t: 'Down from the vehicle' — getting off. It matters most on buses, where a 하차 태그 (tapping your card on exit) is what grants the free 환승 'transfer', and you press the 하차 벨 to signal your stop (note: here 누르다 'press' is correct, because the bell really is a button). Exit norm is the 뒷문 'rear door'.

entries.shortExplanation: 승차 means "boarding / getting on (a vehicle)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "boarding / getting on (a vehicle)" is 승차 (seungcha). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 승차하세요. ("Please board."). Watch the particle attached to 승차 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 승차하다; announcement/sign register
券 'ticket' — a single-ride ticket, NOT the card

usagePhrases.en: I board through the front door.
usagePhrases.note: (으)로 = via; the bus norm is front-door boarding
the term for a taxi illegally turning you down

examples.en: Please board through the front door.
examples.note: simple instruction; mirrors 뒷문 하차

examples.en: It's convenient to buy your ticket in advance.
examples.note: 아 두다 = do ahead for later; 승차권 = a single fare ticket

examples.en: Last night I got refused a ride by a taxi.
examples.note: 당하다 = suffer/be subjected to; a real late-night frustration

entries.nuance: 승차(乘車) is Sino-Korean 乘 'ride/board' + 車 'vehicle' — literally 'mount the vehicle' — the formal partner of 하차, while casual speech just uses 타다 'to get on/ride'. You meet it in 승차권 'a fare ticket' (券 = ticket) and the well-known 승차 거부 'ride refusal', a taxi illegally declining a passenger (a genuine late-night problem). On buses the rule pairs up as 앞문 승차, 뒷문 하차 'board front, exit rear'. The pitfall is 승차권 vs 교통카드: 승차권 is a single paper/disposable ticket for one trip, whereas the reloadable tap card is a 교통카드 — calling your T-money a 승차권 is wrong. Also keep 승차 (boarding, the act) distinct from 탑승, which Koreans favor for boarding a plane/ship.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a 교통카드 a 승차권.
승차권 = a single-ride fare ticket (券). The rechargeable tap card is a 교통카드. They are different objects.
Confusing 승차 with 하차.
승차 = getting ON (乘 ride). 하차 = getting OFF (下 down). On buses it's 앞문 승차, 뒷문 하차 — don't swap them.
Using 승차 for boarding a plane.
For aircraft/ships Koreans usually say 탑승 (탑승 게이트, 탑승 시간). 승차 is for road/rail 車 vehicles.

structuredNuance.t: 'Mount the vehicle' — boarding. You meet it in 승차권 'a fare ticket' (券 = ticket) and the well-known 승차 거부 'ride refusal', a taxi illegally declining a passenger (a genuine late-night problem). On buses the rule pairs up as 앞문 승차, 뒷문 하차 'board front, exit rear'.
The formal partner of 하차, while casual speech just uses 타다 'to get on/ride'. Also keep 승차 (boarding, the act) distinct from 탑승, which Koreans favor for boarding a plane/ship.

entries.shortExplanation: 개찰구 means "ticket gate, fare gate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 개찰구 (gaechalgu) = "ticket gate, fare gate". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 개찰구를 통과해요. ("I go through the fare gate.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 개찰구, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I go through the fare gate.
usagePhrases.note: 통과하다 = pass through

usagePhrases.en: I tap my card at the gate.
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place of the action
usually a low-balance or read error

usagePhrases.en: Let's meet in front of the gate.
usagePhrases.note: a default meet-up spot in any station

examples.en: See you in front of the fare gate.
examples.note: the everyday meet-up line; 보다 here = 'meet/see'

examples.en: The gate wouldn't open because my balance was too low.
examples.note: 아서 = cause; the classic gate failure

examples.en: Once you pass through the fare gate, the platform is right there.
examples.note: 면 = 'once/when'; 승강장 = the platform

entries.nuance: 개찰구(改札口) is Sino-Korean 改 'check/examine' + 札 'ticket' + 口 'opening/gate' — literally a 'ticket-checking opening' — the subway/train fare gate where you 찍다 'tap' your 교통카드 to enter AND exit. If your 잔액 'balance' is too low it won't open and beeps at you, and it's one of the most common rendezvous points ('개찰구 앞에서 봐'). The platform beyond it is the 승강장. Two pitfalls: don't mix 개찰구 (the in-station fare gate) with 출입구 'a building's entrance/exit' (出入口) — both end in 口, but 출입구 is just a doorway with no fare. And remember to tap at BOTH the entry and exit gate; tap-in only can trigger a max-fare penalty.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 개찰구 with 출입구.
개찰구 = the fare gate inside a station (you tap to pass). 출입구 = a plain entrance/exit of a building. Different things despite the shared 口.
Tapping only when entering, not when exiting.
Distance-based fares need both taps. Skipping the exit tap at the 개찰구 can charge you the maximum fare. Tap in AND out.
Calling it a 게이트 and expecting full clarity.
게이트 is understood (esp. airport 탑승 게이트), but the standard subway word is 개찰구. Use 개찰구 for the fare gate.

structuredNuance.t: The subway/train fare gate where you 찍다 'tap' your 교통카드 to enter AND exit. If your 잔액 'balance' is too low it won't open and beeps at you, and it's one of the most common rendezvous points ('개찰구 앞에서 봐'). The platform beyond it is the 승강장. entries.shortExplanation: 노선 means "route, (transit) line" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 노선 (noseon) means "route, (transit) line". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노선도를 봐요. ("I look at the route map."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노선 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I look at the route map.
usagePhrases.note: 노선도 = route map (圖 'diagram'), the colored subway map
which streets/stops the bus follows
다니다 = run/operate regularly; 이제 = 'now/anymore'
바뀌다 = (intransitive) get changed; route revisions happen

examples.ko: 이 버스 노선이 우리 집 앞을 지나가요.
examples.romanization: i beoseu noseoni uri jip apeul jinagayo.
examples.en: This bus route passes in front of my house.
examples.note: 지나가다 = pass by; a convenient route

examples.ko: 처음 왔을 때 지하철 노선도가 너무 복잡해 보였어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum wasseul ttae jihacheol noseondoga neomu bokjapae boyeosseoyo.
examples.en: When I first arrived, the subway route map looked so complicated.
examples.note: 아 보이다 = 'looks/seems'; the newcomer feeling

examples.ko: 앱에서 노선이랑 막차 시간까지 다 확인할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: aebeseo noseonirang makcha sigankkaji da hwaginhal su isseoyo.
examples.en: In the app you can check everything, even the route and the last-train time.
examples.note: 이랑 = casual 'and'; 까지 = 'even/up to'

entries.nuance: 노선(路線) is Sino-Korean 路 'road' + 線 'line' — literally a 'road-line' — meaning a transit route/line for both buses and subways; the famous 노선도(路線圖) 'route map' (圖 = diagram) is the colored subway map newcomers squint at. The key usage split: for a specific subway line Koreans say the number + 호선 (2호선 'Line 2'), while 노선 is the general word for a route's path, used heavily for buses (버스 노선). Pitfalls: don't conflate 노선 'the route itself' with 노선도 'the map of routes' — one is the line, the other the diagram. And don't say 2노선 for Line 2; the counter is 호선. Apps like 카카오맵/네이버지도 list every 노선 and timetable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 2노선 for 'Line 2'.
Subway lines use the counter 호선: 2호선, 9호선. 노선 is the generic 'route' word, mainly for buses. → 2호선.
Confusing 노선 with 노선도.
노선 = the route/line itself. 노선도 = the printed/onscreen map of routes (圖 diagram). Asking for a 노선 when you want the map gets you the wrong thing.
Using 길 for a bus route.
길 = a street/road or a way to walk. A scheduled transit route is 노선 (버스 노선), not 길.

entries.shortExplanation: 환승역 means "transfer station (where lines connect)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "transfer station (where lines connect)" is 환승역 (hwanseungyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 환승역에서 갈아타요. ("I change lines at the transfer station."). Watch the particle attached to 환승역 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I change lines at the transfer station.
usagePhrases.note: 갈아타다 = transfer/switch vehicles

usagePhrases.en: The next stop is a transfer station.
usagePhrases.note: 이다 statement
늘 = always; rush-hour reality

usagePhrases.en: I get off at the transfer station.
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = at; then you switch lines

examples.en: Sadang is a transfer station.
examples.note: simplest A는 B예요 statement

examples.en: Transfer to Line 2 at Sadang.
examples.note: (으)로 = the target line; giving directions

examples.ko: 환승역은 걷는 거리가 길어서 갈아타는 데 시간이 좀 걸려요.
examples.romanization: hwanseungyeogeun geonneun georiga gireoseo garataneun de sigani jom geollyeoyo.
examples.en: Transfer stations have long walking distances, so changing lines takes a while.
examples.note: 아서 = cause; 는 데 = 'in doing ~ it takes...'

entries.nuance: 환승역(換乘驛) stacks three Sino-Korean roots — 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride' + 驛 'station' — literally a 'ride-exchange station', a stop where two or more subway lines meet so you can 갈아타다 'transfer'. Big ones (사당, 신도림, 왕십리) are notoriously crowded with long underground walks. The sharp contrast is 환승역 vs 환승: 환승역 is the PLACE, while 환승 is the ACT/system of transferring — and a free subway↔bus 환승 depends on tapping your 교통카드 within the time limit, not merely on standing in a 환승역. Pitfalls: don't assume any station lets you switch lines (only a 환승역 does), and don't confuse 환승역 with 종점 'the terminal/last stop'. Note the native verb 갈아타다, not a borrowing, is what you actually 'do' here.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming you can change lines at any station.
Only a 환승역 connects multiple lines. At a normal 역 you can't switch lines without exiting. Check that it's a 환승역.
Confusing 환승역 (place) with 환승 (act/system).
환승역 = the transfer STATION. 환승 = the transfer itself / the discount system. A free bus transfer needs a timely card tap, not just being in a 환승역.
Confusing 환승역 with 종점.
환승역 = a mid-route junction of lines. 종점 = the end-of-line terminal. They sit at very different points of a route.

structuredNuance.t: A 'ride-exchange station', a stop where two or more subway lines meet so you can 갈아타다 'transfer'. Big ones (사당, 신도림, 왕십리) are notoriously crowded with long underground walks. Note the native verb 갈아타다, not a borrowing, is what you actually 'do' here.
