entries.english: terminal, last stop (end of the line)
entries.shortExplanation: 종점 means "terminal, last stop (end of the line)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 종점 (jongjeom) = "terminal, last stop (end of the line)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 종점에서 내려요. ("I get off at the last stop.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 종점, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I get off at the last stop.
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = at; everyone alights here
the driver's end-of-line announcement
where a city bus route ends

usagePhrases.en: I go all the way to the terminal.
usagePhrases.note: 까지 = up to/all the way to

examples.en: Is this the last stop?
examples.note: simple confirmation question to the driver

examples.en: I dozed off and ended up riding all the way to the last stop.
examples.note: 다가 = mid-action switch; 아 버리다 = regret it's done

examples.en: The bus heads into the depot from the last stop, so everyone please get off.
examples.note: 니까 = reason; the end-of-line notice

entries.nuance: 종점(終點) is Sino-Korean 終 'end' + 點 'point' — literally the 'end point' — the final stop where a bus or subway route terminates, the opposite of 첫 정거장 'the first stop' (or 기점 'the origin point'). The driver announces 'here is the 종점, everyone off,' and dozing off to ride 종점까지 'all the way to the end' is a relatable mishap. The pitfall is 종점 vs 터미널: 종점 is the end of a LOCAL route (a city bus's last stop, often by a 차고지 'depot'), whereas a 터미널 (버스 터미널) is the big intercity hub where express coaches depart — calling Seoul's Express Bus 터미널 a 종점 is wrong. Also keep 종점 (end of route) apart from 환승역 (a mid-route junction); they're at opposite ends of the journey.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an intercity bus 터미널 a 종점.
터미널 (버스 터미널/고속터미널) = the large hub where intercity coaches start. 종점 = the last stop of a local route, often near a depot. Don't substitute one for the other.
Confusing 종점 with 환승역.
종점 = the end of the line. 환승역 = a junction mid-route where you switch lines. They are at different points of a route.
Saying 마지막 역 and assuming it always equals 종점.
마지막 역 'the last station' is understood, but the fixed transit term for a route's end is 종점 (esp. for buses). Use 종점 for the end-of-line stop.

structuredNuance.t: The 'end point' — the final stop where a bus or subway route terminates, the opposite of 첫 정거장 'the first stop' (or 기점 'the origin point'). The driver announces 'here is the 종점, everyone off,' and dozing off to ride 종점까지 'all the way to the end' is a relatable mishap.

The pitfall is 종점 vs 터미널: 종점 is the end of a LOCAL route (a city bus's last stop, often by a 차고지 'depot'), whereas a 터미널 (버스 터미널) is the big intercity hub where express coaches depart — calling Seoul's Express Bus 터미널 a 종점 is wrong. Also keep 종점 (end of route) apart from 환승역 (a mid-route junction); they're at opposite ends of the journey.
종점(終點) is Sino-Korean 終 'end' + 點 'point' — literally the 'end point'.

entries.shortExplanation: 점점 means "gradually, more and more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 점점 (jeomjeom) means "gradually, more and more". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 날씨가 점점 추워져요 ("The weather is gradually getting colder"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 점점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: The weather is gradually getting colder
usagePhrases.note: Pairs naturally with -아/어지다 verbs that show change over time
Common with progressive -고 있다 to stress an ongoing trend

usagePhrases.en: My Korean is improving more and more
usagePhrases.note: Everyday way to describe steady skill growth
점점 더 stacks for extra emphasis on the increase

examples.en: Prices keep gradually rising these days, so it's a burden.
examples.note: A very real complaint among residents about cost of living

examples.ko: 운동을 시작하니까 몸이 점점 가벼워지는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: undongeul sijakanikka momi jeomjeom gabyeowojineun geot gatayo.
examples.en: Since I started working out, my body feels gradually lighter.
examples.note: Note 점점 placed right before the change verb 가벼워지다

examples.en: As night fell, the crowd gradually thinned out.
examples.note: Shows 점점 with a decrease verb (줄어들다), not just increases

entries.nuance: 점점 (Sino-Korean 漸漸, literally 'gradual-gradual', the character 漸 'gradual' doubled for emphasis) describes a slow, continuous shift in ONE direction and almost always travels with a change-of-state verb such as 좋아지다, 추워지다, or 늘다 — it cannot modify a static state. Its closest rivals are 점차 and 갈수록: 점차 is the same idea but distinctly more formal/written (you meet it in news and official notices, rarely in chat), while 갈수록 literally means 'as it goes, the more' and feels even more conversational and emphatic. The opposite pole is 갑자기 (suddenly), so never mix them. The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 점점 to mean a plain comparative 'more' — but 'I want more rice' is 더, not 점점; 점점 specifically means 'progressively more over time,' and it needs that unfolding verb beside it. 점점 더 simply doubles the emphasis ('more and more').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 점점 with a static verb like 점점 있어요 — 점점 needs a change verb, so say 점점 많아져요 ('gradually become many')
Reaching for 점점 to translate a simple comparative 'more,' e.g. 점점 주세요 for 'give me more'; that should be 더 주세요, since 점점 only means a gradual increase over time
Confusing it with 갑자기 (suddenly); 점점 is always gradual, never abrupt

entries.shortExplanation: 갑자기 means "suddenly, all of a sudden" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "suddenly, all of a sudden" is 갑자기 (gapjagi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갑자기 비가 왔어요 ("It suddenly started raining"). Watch the particle attached to 갑자기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Classic weather use; the change is abrupt and unexpected

usagePhrases.en: Why are you acting like this all of a sudden?
usagePhrases.note: Mild way to question an out-of-nowhere change in someone
Useful for describing a sudden physical symptom
Very common when you abruptly remember something

examples.ko: 회사에서 갑자기 회식하자고 해서 약속을 취소했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo gapjagi hoesikajago haeseo yaksogeul chwisohaesseoyo.
examples.en: Work suddenly called a team dinner, so I canceled my plans.
examples.note: 갑자기 + an unexpected demand that forces a change of plans

examples.en: My laptop, which was totally fine, suddenly shut off.
examples.note: Pairs 갑자기 with 멀쩡하던 to sharpen the 'out of nowhere' feel

examples.ko: 친구가 갑자기 연락이 안 돼서 걱정했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga gapjagi yeollagi an dwaeseo geokjeonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend suddenly became unreachable, so I was worried.
examples.note: Sudden break in an expected pattern

entries.nuance: 갑자기 marks something abrupt, unplanned, and usually unexpected, often coloured with surprise or disruption — it is the direct semantic opposite of 점점. Compare it with 갑작스럽게 and 별안간: 갑작스럽게 is the adverb form of the adjective 갑작스럽다 and sounds a touch more written/formal, while 별안간 (瞥眼間, literally 'in the blink of an eye') is a vivid literary near-synonym you'll meet in stories more than in speech. In conversation 갑자기 왜 이래요/그래요 can sound slightly accusatory or alarmed depending on tone, so mind the situation. A frequent English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: it is 갑자기, never the tempting 갑짜기, even though the second syllable is pronounced tense. Also resist using it for slow change — 'it's gradually getting cold' is 점점 추워져요, not 갑자기 추워져요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 갑짜기; the second syllable sounds tense but the correct written form is 갑자기
Using it for slow changes where 점점 is needed, e.g. 갑자기 추워져요 wrongly implies an instant drop rather than a gradual cooldown
Forcing 갑자기 onto a planned event; if something was scheduled it isn't 'sudden,' so 갑자기 회의가 있어요 sounds odd when the meeting was on the calendar

entries.shortExplanation: 드디어 means "finally, at last" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 드디어 (deudieo) = "finally, at last". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 드디어 끝났어요 ("It's finally over") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 드디어, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Expresses relief after a long wait or effort
A staple Friday-afternoon expression
Used after a long or tiring trip
Celebrating a result that took real effort

examples.ko: 반년을 기다린 콘서트 표를 드디어 구했어요.
examples.romanization: bannyeoneul gidarin konseoteu pyoreul deudieo guhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I finally got the concert ticket I'd waited half a year for.
examples.note: 드디어 + a long-awaited outcome the speaker genuinely wanted

examples.en: My visa finally came through, so I feel relieved.
examples.note: Note how 드디어 leads naturally into 마음이 놓이다 (feel relieved)

examples.en: Overtime is over and I'm finally going home.
examples.note: Everyday relief after a hard day

entries.nuance: 드디어 carries a strong charge of relief, anticipation paid off, or triumph after a long wait, so it only fits results the speaker actually hoped for — say 드디어! by itself and it means 'at last!' / 'I've been waiting for this!' The sharp dividing line is against 결국 (結局, 'in the end / as a final result'): 결국 is neutral and can even be negative (결국 헤어졌어요, 'they ended up breaking up'), whereas 드디어 needs a payoff worth celebrating — 드디어 헤어졌어요 would oddly sound like the breakup was a happy goal. A second pitfall is the English word 'finally' used to list steps ('and finally, add salt'); that sequencing 'finally/lastly' is 마지막으로, never 드디어. Collocations cluster around achievements and arrivals: 드디어 끝나다, 드디어 도착하다, 드디어 합격하다, 드디어 만나다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 드디어 for unwanted or neutral endings, e.g. 드디어 비가 와요 for unwelcome rain; a plain or negative conclusion takes 결국, since 드디어 implies a hoped-for payoff
Treating it as 'finally' in the sense of listing steps (lastly), e.g. 드디어 소금을 넣으세요; that sequencing meaning is 마지막으로, not 드디어
Pairing it with something trivial and unawaited; 드디어 implies a real wait, so using it for a five-minute errand sounds melodramatic

entries.shortExplanation: 역시 means "as expected, sure enough; also/too" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 역시 (yeoksi) means "as expected, sure enough; also/too". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 역시 맛있네요 ("As expected, it's delicious"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 역시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Confirming that something lived up to its reputation

usagePhrases.en: It's you, as I figured / you're the best
usagePhrases.note: Warm praise meaning someone came through just like you knew
역시 can also mean 'also', similar to 또한

usagePhrases.en: It's not working, just as I feared
usagePhrases.note: Confirms a negative expectation

examples.en: This place's kimchi stew is the best, as expected.
examples.note: 역시 confirming a favorite spot stayed as good as you knew

examples.ko: 역시 출근 시간이라 지하철이 사람으로 꽉 찼어요.
examples.romanization: yeoksi chulgeun siganira jihacheori sarameuro kkwak chasseoyo.
examples.en: Sure enough, it's rush hour, so the subway is packed.
examples.note: Confirming an anticipated situation rather than praising it

examples.ko: 고민하다가 역시 원래 계획대로 하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: gominhadaga yeoksi wollae gyehoekdaero hagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: After agonizing, I decided to go with the original plan after all.
examples.note: 역시 marking a return to what felt right all along

entries.nuance: 역시 (亦是, the hanja literally meaning 'also/likewise this') has two everyday senses learners must keep apart. The dominant one is 'sure enough / just as I expected' — reality matched your prediction, as in 역시 맛있다 ('delicious, exactly as I figured'); on its own, 역시! is an exclamation of 'I knew it!' or admiring 'that's so you.' The second, more formal sense is the original 'also/too,' overlapping with 또한, but in casual speech native speakers far prefer the particle 도 for 'also' (나도, not 나 역시). Do not confuse 역시 with 다시 or 또 ('again') — they share no meaning despite the look. The 'as expected' 역시 frequently fronts a sentence (역시 ~네요/구나) and carries a warm, satisfied tone, often functioning as a compliment that someone or something lived up to its reputation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Overusing the 'also' meaning in casual talk, e.g. 저 역시 가요 for 'I'm going too'; conversationally 저도 가요 (the particle 도) is far more natural, with 역시/또한 reserved for formal speech
Expecting 역시 to mean 'again'; that is 다시 or 또, not 역시
Using 역시 when there was no prior expectation; the 'sure enough' sense needs a belief it confirms, so it sounds empty after a genuine surprise

entries.english: rather, on the contrary, if anything
entries.shortExplanation: 오히려 means "rather, on the contrary, if anything" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rather, on the contrary, if anything" is 오히려 (ohiryeo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오히려 잘됐어요 ("Actually it worked out better that way"). Watch the particle attached to 오히려 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Actually it worked out better that way
usagePhrases.note: Reframes a seeming setback as a good thing

usagePhrases.en: I apologized but instead they got angry
usagePhrases.note: Marks a reaction opposite to what you'd expect

usagePhrases.en: The expensive one is, if anything, worse
usagePhrases.note: Contradicts the assumption that pricier means better

usagePhrases.en: It's I who should be thanking you, rather
usagePhrases.note: Politely flips a thank-you back onto yourself

examples.ko: 지하철이 막힐 줄 알았는데 오히려 더 빨랐어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheori makil jul aranneunde ohiryeo deo ppallasseoyo.
examples.en: I thought the subway would be jammed, but it was actually faster.
examples.note: 오히려 introducing the opposite of an expectation set up by -는데

examples.ko: 쉬려고 누웠는데 오히려 잠이 안 와요.
examples.romanization: swiryeogo nuwonneunde ohiryeo jami an wayo.
examples.en: I lay down to rest, but instead I can't fall asleep.
examples.note: Outcome contrary to the intended effect

examples.ko: 혼날 줄 알았는데 사장님이 오히려 칭찬해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: honnal jul aranneunde sajangnimi ohiryeo chingchanhae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I expected to get in trouble, but the boss praised me instead.
examples.note: A surprising reversal in a workplace setting

entries.nuance: 오히려 signals that the result runs counter to what the speaker or listener would naturally assume — often to a surprising or ironic degree, as in 'if anything, the opposite is true.' It leans on a setup clause, typically ending in -는데 or -지만 or a '~ㄹ 줄 알았는데' ('I thought it'd be X, but…'), and then 오히려 flips it. The key contrast for learners is against 대신(에): 대신에 is a neutral 'instead' for swapping one option/action for another (커피 대신 차, 'tea instead of coffee'), with no element of surprise, whereas 오히려 specifically means 'contrary to expectation.' A near-synonym is 도리어, which is essentially the same but more bookish/literary. The English-speaker pitfall is translating every 'instead' as 오히려 and dropping the contrast: 오히려 needs a prior assumption to overturn, so without that setup it sounds incomplete.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a plain 'instead' for swapping options, e.g. 물 오히려 주스 주세요 for 'juice instead of water'; that neutral substitution is 대신에 (물 대신 주스), since 오히려 means 'contrary to expectation'
Forgetting the setup clause, so the contrast 오히려 needs has nothing to push against — pair it with a -는데 or '~줄 알았는데' that states what you expected
Treating it as 'on the other hand' for balanced comparison; that listing function is 반면(에), whereas 오히려 marks a surprising reversal

entries.english: when it actually comes to it, in reality, faced with it
entries.shortExplanation: 막상 means "when it actually comes to it, in reality, faced with it" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 막상 (maksang) = "when it actually comes to it, in reality, faced with it". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막상 해 보니까 쉬웠어요 ("When I actually tried it, it was easy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막상, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: When I actually tried it, it was easy
usagePhrases.note: Reality turning out different from what you imagined

usagePhrases.en: Now that it's actually time to go, I can't be bothered
usagePhrases.note: The moment of doing it changes how you feel

usagePhrases.en: When it actually comes down to it, you end up doing it all
usagePhrases.note: A common reassurance about rising to the occasion

usagePhrases.en: I wanted to buy it, but seeing it in person, it's not great
usagePhrases.note: Anticipation not matching the real thing

examples.en: I wanted to switch jobs, but now that I'm actually about to quit, I hesitate.
examples.note: 막상 + -려니까 marks the moment of facing the real decision

examples.en: I was worried about the presentation, but once I actually started, it was fine.
examples.note: 막상 + 시작하니까 showing the gap between dread and reality

examples.ko: 월급날만 기다렸는데 막상 받으니까 카드값으로 다 나갔어요.
examples.romanization: wolgeumnalman gidaryeonneunde maksang badeunikka kadeugapseuro da nagasseoyo.
examples.en: I only waited for payday, but when I actually got paid, it all went to the credit card bill.
examples.note: 막상 marking a letdown when the awaited moment arrives

entries.nuance: 막상 sets up a contrast between what you expected, planned, imagined, or wished for and what you actually feel or find once you face the real situation — 'in theory I thought X, but when it came to it, Y.' It is grammatically tied to that confronting moment, so it overwhelmingly pairs with -(으)니까 or the about-to-act ending -(으)려니까 (막상 하려니까, 막상 가려니까). Crucially, do not equate 막상 with 사실 or 정말: 사실 means 'in fact / to tell the truth' about a state of affairs, and 정말 is 'really/truly' as an intensifier — neither carries 막상's specific 'at the actual moment of doing it, against my prior expectation' meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is using 막상 as a generic 'actually': it only works when there is a prior plan, wish, or assumption for the real moment to defy, so without that setup it falls flat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a plain 'actually/really' fact, e.g. 막상 비싸요 to mean 'it's actually expensive'; a factual 'actually' is 사실, while 막상 means specifically 'when faced with the real moment'
Dropping the setup, so there is no expectation for 막상 to contradict; it needs a prior assumption or plan, typically a clause like '~고 싶었는데' before it
Pairing it with the wrong ending; 막상 wants the confronting-the-moment forms -(으)니까/-(으)려니까, so 막상 했어요 alone sounds unfinished without that 'when I actually…' frame

entries.english: anyway, in any case, either way
entries.shortExplanation: 어차피 means "anyway, in any case, either way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 어차피 (eochapi) means "anyway, in any case, either way". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어차피 늦었어요 ("We're late anyway"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어차피 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Accepting a fixed reality as the basis for what follows

usagePhrases.en: It's something I have to do either way
usagePhrases.note: Frames a task as unavoidable regardless of choice
States a settled outcome that won't change

usagePhrases.en: It's the same in any case
usagePhrases.note: Dismisses a distinction as ultimately irrelevant

examples.ko: 어차피 집에 가는 길이니까 같이 가요.
examples.romanization: eochapi jibe ganeun girinikka gachi gayo.
examples.en: I'm headed home anyway, so let's go together.
examples.note: 어차피 presenting a fixed fact that makes the suggestion easy

examples.ko: 어차피 환불도 안 되는데 그냥 써야죠.
examples.romanization: eochapi hwanbuldo an doeneunde geunyang sseoyajyo.
examples.en: It's non-refundable anyway, so I'll just use it.
examples.note: 어차피 + -는데 connecting an unchangeable condition to resignation

examples.en: No matter how much I worry, the result won't change either way.
examples.note: 어차피 stressing that effort won't alter a fixed outcome

entries.nuance: 어차피 (於此彼, roughly 'whether this way or that') sets up a premise that is already decided or unavoidable and reasons from it: since X is fixed anyway, Y follows — it carries a distinct tone of resignation or pragmatic acceptance, sometimes a shrug. It pairs naturally with -니까 or -는데 to link the settled fact to the conclusion drawn from it. The dividing line learners must watch is against the conversational fillers 아무튼 and 어쨌든: those mean 'anyway' in the sense of dropping a tangent and moving on ('anyway, where were we'), and they can start a fresh topic, whereas 어차피 is never a topic-changer — it always asserts that an outcome is already inevitable. So the English 'anyway' splits in Korean by function: settled-outcome 'anyway' is 어차피, but 'anyway, let's get back to it' is 아무튼/어쨌든. Using 어차피 where the result is still genuinely open will sound contradictory.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a topic-changing 'anyway' that just drops a tangent, e.g. 어차피, 우리 뭐 먹을까요?; that filler is 아무튼 or 어쨌든, not 어차피
Placing it where the outcome is still open, e.g. 어차피 합격할 수도 있어요; 어차피 assumes the result is already settled, so it clashes with 'might'
Mistaking its tone as cheerful; 어차피 leans resigned/pragmatic, so using it for happy news can sound oddly defeatist

entries.english: (not) particularly, go out of one's way to, deliberately
entries.shortExplanation: 굳이 means "(not) particularly, go out of one's way to, deliberately" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "(not) particularly, go out of one's way to, deliberately" is 굳이 (guji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 굳이 안 해도 돼요 ("You don't have to go out of your way to do it"). Watch the particle attached to 굳이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: You don't have to go out of your way to do it
usagePhrases.note: Most common use, telling someone not to bother
Questions why someone is making unnecessary effort

usagePhrases.en: If I had to pick / strictly speaking
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase for reluctantly choosing when pressed

usagePhrases.en: I went all the way out there (when I didn't need to)
usagePhrases.note: Highlights effort that wasn't really necessary

examples.ko: 굳이 비싼 데 가지 말고 그냥 편의점에서 사 먹어요.
examples.romanization: guji bissan de gaji malgo geunyang pyeonuijeomeseo sa meogeoyo.
examples.en: Let's not bother going somewhere expensive; let's just grab something at the convenience store.
examples.note: 굳이 + a negative, discouraging needless effort

examples.ko: 바쁘면 굳이 안 와도 되니까 부담 갖지 마세요.
examples.romanization: bappeumyeon guji an wado doenikka budam gatji maseyo.
examples.en: If you're busy, you don't have to come, so don't feel pressured.
examples.note: Polite, considerate use telling someone not to overextend

examples.ko: 굳이 따지자면 저는 매운 음식이 더 좋아요.
examples.romanization: guji ttajijamyeon jeoneun maeun eumsigi deo joayo.
examples.en: If I had to choose, I prefer spicy food.
examples.note: The fixed phrase 굳이 따지자면 for a forced preference

entries.nuance: 굳이 conveys 'going out of one's way' for something not strictly necessary, and it lives most naturally in negative or rhetorical sentences — 굳이 안 해도 돼 ('no need to bother'), 굳이 왜 ('why even bother'). Used in a positive clause it implies someone insisted on doing the unnecessary thing anyway (굳이 멀리까지 갔어요). The contrast learners most need is against 꼭 and 반드시, which mean 'definitely/without fail' and frame an action as necessary or strongly willed — the near-opposite of 굳이's 'not really worth the trouble.' Note too that 굳이 is the adverb; do not confuse it with the verb 굳다 ('to harden') or write it 구지 (a common misspelling driven by the pronunciation [구지]). Among younger speakers, a one-word 굳이? functions as a dry reaction meaning 'is that really necessary?' The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it to 'definitely' or 'deliberately' as a strong positive; its core feeling is the un-necessity of the effort.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it as plain 'definitely,' e.g. 굳이 갈게요 for 'I'll definitely go'; that is 꼭/반드시 (꼭 갈게요), whereas 굳이 implies unneeded effort and would oddly suggest 'I'll go even though there's no point'
Spelling it 구지; the pronunciation is [구지] but the correct written form is 굳이 (with ㄷ palatalizing to ㅈ)
Forgetting that its most natural home is negative sentences, e.g. preferring 굳이 안 사도 돼요 ('no need to buy it') over a forced positive use

entries.english: by nature, originally so much, inherently
entries.shortExplanation: 워낙 means "by nature, originally so much, inherently" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 워낙 (wonak) = "by nature, originally so much, inherently". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 워낙 바빠서 ("Since (they're) so inherently busy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 워낙, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Gives an underlying reason rooted in a stable trait

usagePhrases.en: It's an inherently very famous place
usagePhrases.note: Stresses a well-established reputation

usagePhrases.en: I just can't handle spicy food at all
usagePhrases.note: Describes a long-standing personal trait

usagePhrases.en: Because there are just so many people (as usual)
usagePhrases.note: Explains a situation by an inherent, baseline condition

examples.ko: 그 식당은 워낙 줄이 길어서 예약하는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun wonak juri gireoseo yeyakaneun ge naayo.
examples.en: That restaurant inherently has such long lines that it's better to reserve.
examples.note: 워낙 + -아서 giving the baseline reason behind advice

examples.ko: 제 룸메이트는 워낙 조용해서 집에 있는지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: je rummeiteuneun wonak joyonghaeseo jibe inneunjido mollayo.
examples.en: My roommate is so quiet by nature that I can't even tell if they're home.
examples.note: 워낙 describing an ingrained personality trait

examples.ko: 요즘 워낙 물가가 비싸서 외식을 줄였어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum wonang mulgaga bissaseo oesigeul juryeosseoyo.
examples.en: Prices are just so high these days that I've cut back on eating out.
examples.note: 워낙 framing a stable condition as the cause of a consequence

entries.nuance: 워낙 (also heard as 원체) emphasizes that something is the way it is by its fundamental, baseline nature, or holds to an inherently high degree — and it characteristically leads into a reason with -아서/어서, explaining why a predictable outcome follows (워낙 바빠서…, 워낙 유명해서…). The contrast learners need is against 너무 and the intensifier sense of 정말/진짜: 너무 marks a degree, often a momentary 'too much' feeling ('it's too hot right now'), whereas 워낙 points to a stable, long-standing truth ('inherently/originally so'), so it feels more grounded and explanatory than emotional. A useful near-synonym is 원래 ('originally/by default'), though 원래 simply states the default state while 워낙 stresses the high degree of that default. The English-speaker pitfall is using 워낙 as a free-standing intensifier like 'very' — it normally must be followed by a result or reason clause, not left to modify an adjective on its own at the end of a sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it for 너무 to mean a temporary 'too much,' e.g. 오늘 워낙 더워요 for a one-day heat spike; 너무 더워요 fits a momentary feeling, since 워낙 implies an inherent, ongoing degree
Using it without a follow-up reason or result, e.g. ending a sentence on 그 집 워낙 유명해요; 워낙 normally leads into an explanation like 워낙 유명해서 예약이 힘들어요
Confusing its scope with 원래 (the plain default state); 워낙 specifically stresses a high degree, not just 'originally'

entries.shortExplanation: 자꾸 means "repeatedly, keep (doing), over and over" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자꾸 (jakku) means "repeatedly, keep (doing), over and over". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자꾸 까먹어요 ("I keep forgetting"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자꾸 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Describes an annoying repeated lapse

usagePhrases.en: Why do you keep doing that?
usagePhrases.note: Expresses mild irritation at repeated behavior

usagePhrases.en: They keep contacting me over and over
usagePhrases.note: Repeated, often unwanted, occurrences

usagePhrases.en: If you keep seeing it, it grows on you
usagePhrases.note: A common saying about repeated exposure

examples.en: The internet keeps cutting out, so I called the provider.
examples.note: 자꾸 + a recurring problem that finally prompts action

examples.en: I'm on a diet, but I keep thinking about late-night snacks.
examples.note: 자꾸 for a repeated urge you can't shake

examples.ko: 옆집에서 자꾸 시끄럽게 해서 스트레스를 받아요.
examples.romanization: yeopjibeseo jakku sikkeureopge haeseo seuteureseureul badayo.
examples.en: The neighbors keep being noisy, so it stresses me out.
examples.note: Repeated nuisance from others, carrying clear annoyance

entries.nuance: 자꾸 means something happens again and again, and the heart of it is an exasperated, slightly negative nuance — the repetition is bothersome, involuntary, or beyond the speaker's control, which is why it's the go-to word for gentle complaints (자꾸 까먹어요, 자꾸 그래요). The crucial contrast is against 자주 ('often'), which is a neutral frequency word with no emotional colour: 자주 운동해요 ('I exercise often') is a clean, positive routine, but 자꾸 운동해요 sounds odd because 자꾸 implies a pesky, repeated compulsion. There's also 계속 ('continuously / nonstop'), which stresses unbroken continuation rather than recurring instances. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping both 'often' and 'keep ~ing' onto one word: planned, neutral regularity is 자주/규칙적으로, while only the annoyed 'keeps happening to me' sense is 자꾸. It naturally precedes verbs of habit, glitches, or recurring trouble.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as a neutral 'often,' e.g. 운동을 자꾸 해요 for a healthy routine; plain frequency is 자주, since 자꾸 implies pesky, unwanted repetition
Using it for scheduled regular events, e.g. 자꾸 회의가 있어요 for a standing meeting; 규칙적으로 or 정기적으로 fits planned routines, while 자꾸 sounds like the meetings are an irritation
Confusing it with 계속 (nonstop continuation); 자꾸 is recurring separate instances, whereas 계속 means one unbroken stretch

entries.english: for a long while, quite a while
entries.shortExplanation: 한참 means "for a long while, quite a while" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "for a long while, quite a while" is 한참 (hancham). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한참 기다렸어요 ("I waited for a good while"). Watch the particle attached to 한참 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I waited for a good while
usagePhrases.note: The single most common collocation

usagePhrases.en: I haven't seen (them) for quite a while
usagePhrases.note: 한참 동안 stresses the long stretch of time

usagePhrases.en: It's still a long way off
usagePhrases.note: Used for distance or 'far from done'
Marks a sizable gap before the next event

examples.ko: 버스가 안 와서 정류장에서 한참 기다렸어요.
examples.romanization: beoseuga an waseo jeongnyujangeseo hancham gidaryeosseoyo.
examples.en: The bus didn't come, so I waited at the stop for a good while.
examples.note: 한참 describing a long, somewhat tedious wait

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만난 친구랑 한참 수다를 떨었어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane mannan chingurang hancham sudareul tteoreosseoyo.
examples.en: I chatted for ages with a friend I hadn't seen in a long time.
examples.note: 한참 for an extended, enjoyable activity, not always tedious

examples.ko: 이거 다 하려면 아직 한참 멀었어요.
examples.romanization: igeo da haryeomyeon aji kancham meoreosseoyo.
examples.en: There's still a long way to go before this is all done.
examples.note: 한참 멀었다 meaning far from finished, about progress not distance

entries.nuance: 한참 refers to a fairly long but indefinite stretch of time, and it feels vivid and conversational where 오래 is plainer and more neutral — both mean 'a long time,' but 한참 evokes a tangible 'good while' you actually sat through, so it's the natural pick for waiting, talking, or walking that drags on (한참 기다리다, 한참 걸리다, 한참 동안). In the set phrase 한참 멀었다 it shifts to mean 'far away' or 'nowhere near done,' covering both physical distance and progress. The headline English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, do not use 한참 for an exact duration — it is deliberately vague, so '한 시간 기다렸어요' (one hour) is precise while 한참 is impressionistic; second, never confuse the spelling with 한창 (한창, 'in full swing / at the peak'), as in 한창 바쁠 때 ('right when things are busiest'). They look almost identical but mean completely different things — 한참 is duration, 한창 is peak intensity.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as an exact duration, e.g. 한참 두 시간 기다렸어요; 한참 is deliberately vague, so for a precise length say 두 시간 기다렸어요 without 한참
Confusing 한참 (a long while) with 한창 (in full swing / at the peak), e.g. writing 한참 바쁠 때 when you mean 'when it's busiest' (한창 바쁠 때); they look alike but mean different things
Assuming it always implies tedium; 한참 can describe a pleasant long stretch too, as in 한참 수다를 떨었어요

entries.shortExplanation: 꽤 means "quite, fairly, pretty (much)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 꽤 (kkwae) = "quite, fairly, pretty (much)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 꽤 비싸요 ("It's quite expensive") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 꽤, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Adds a 'more than expected' nuance to the adjective
Mild positive surprise about quality
Modifies a degree higher than anticipated

usagePhrases.en: There are quite a lot of people
usagePhrases.note: Remarking that a number is notably high

examples.ko: 이 동네는 생각보다 꽤 조용하고 살기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i dongneneun saenggakboda kkwae joyonghago salgi joayo.
examples.en: This neighborhood is quite a bit quieter and nicer to live in than I expected.
examples.note: 꽤 + 생각보다 stressing it exceeded expectations

examples.ko: 이번 시험이 꽤 어려웠지만 그래도 잘 봤어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon siheomi kkwae eoryeowotjiman geuraedo jal bwasseoyo.
examples.en: The exam this time was fairly tough, but I still did well.
examples.note: 꽤 setting a moderately high degree before a -지만 contrast

examples.ko: 새로 생긴 카페가 꽤 인기가 많더라고요.
examples.romanization: saero saenggin kapega kkwae ingiga manteoragoyo.
examples.en: The newly opened cafe turned out to be quite popular.
examples.note: 꽤 noting a higher-than-assumed degree with -더라고요

entries.nuance: 꽤 means 'quite' or 'fairly' and very often implies the degree turned out higher than the speaker had expected, lending a faint note of pleasant surprise (꽤 괜찮네요 — 'oh, it's actually pretty good'). On the intensity scale it sits in the middle: stronger than 좀 ('a little / somewhat') but clearly softer than 너무 or 정말/진짜 ('too / really'). The contrast learners should hold is exactly that against 너무: 너무 means an excessive 'too much,' often with a negative edge (너무 비싸요 = 'too expensive, off-puttingly so'), whereas 꽤 비싸요 just notes 'fairly/notably expensive' without the complaint. The emphatic variant 꽤나 adds force, and 꽤 lives comfortably in casual everyday speech. The English-speaker pitfall is using 꽤 in negative sentences the way English allows 'not quite' — 꽤 안 좋아요 sounds off; for 'not that good' Korean prefers 별로 좋지 않아요 or just 별로예요. Keep 꽤 in affirmative statements about a notable degree.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as 'too much,' e.g. 꽤 비싸서 못 샀어요 to mean it was prohibitively pricey; that excessive sense is 너무, while 꽤 stays at a moderate-to-notable level without the complaint
Using it with negatives oddly, e.g. 꽤 안 좋아요; for 'not that good' prefer 별로 좋지 않아요 or 별로예요, since 꽤 sits naturally in affirmative statements
Stacking it as a top-level intensifier; for 'really/extremely' use 정말/너무, as 꽤 deliberately signals a mid, somewhat-surprising degree rather than the maximum

The emphatic variant 꽤나 adds force, and 꽤 lives comfortably in casual everyday speech.

The pitfall is using 꽤 in negative sentences the way English allows 'not quite' — 꽤 안 좋아요 sounds off; for 'not that good' Korean prefers 별로 좋지 않아요 or just 별로예요. Keep 꽤 in affirmative statements about a notable degree.

entries.shortExplanation: 혹시 means "by any chance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 혹시 (hoksi) means "by any chance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 혹시 시간 있어요? ("Do you have time, by any chance?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 혹시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Do you have time, by any chance?
usagePhrases.note: softens a request to a near-stranger

usagePhrases.en: Where is the restroom, by chance?
usagePhrases.note: polite question opener to staff

usagePhrases.en: Are you Korean, by any chance?
usagePhrases.note: a careful guess, not an assumption
fixed phrase, stands on its own

examples.en: How much is this, by any chance?
examples.note: Drop 혹시 at the very front; it instantly makes a blunt question gentle.

examples.ko: 혹시 영어 할 수 있는 분 계세요?
examples.romanization: hoksi yeongeo hal su inneun bun gyeseyo?
examples.en: Is there anyone who can speak English, by chance?
examples.note: 계세요 (honorific of 있어요) plus 혹시 makes this a soft, respectful ask to a room.

examples.en: Bring an umbrella, just in case.
examples.note: Here 혹시 모르니까 = 'because you never know' — the just-in-case use, not a question.

entries.nuance: 혹시 is the Sino-Korean 或是 (或 'perhaps' + 是 'be so') and lives at the FRONT of a question to soften it, exactly like English 'by any chance' or 'do you happen to': it signals you are unsure and refuse to assume, so requests and guesses land politely rather than pushily. Do not confuse it with 만약 (萬若, 'if / supposing'): 만약 sets up a conditional clause and pairs with -면 (만약 비가 오면 = if it rains), whereas 혹시 colors a whole question with tentativeness and does NOT need -면. The big English-speaker trap is dropping 혹시 into a flat statement; it belongs with a question or with the set phrase 혹시 몰라서 / 혹시 모르니까 ('just in case'). It also collocates with 혹시나 (an even softer, more anxious variant) and with 혹시 ~ 거 아니에요? for a worried hunch.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 혹시 (by any chance, in a question) with 만약 (if/supposing) — 만약 needs a -면 conditional (만약 늦으면), while 혹시 just softens a question and takes no -면.
Putting 혹시 in a plain statement like 혹시 비가 와요 to mean 'maybe it's raining' — for a guessing statement use 아마 or -ㄹ지도 몰라요; 혹시 fronts a QUESTION (혹시 비 와요?).
Forgetting the set phrase form: 'just in case' is 혹시 몰라서 / 혹시 모르니까, not a bare 혹시 tacked onto the end.

entries.shortExplanation: 설마 means "surely not; no way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "surely not; no way" is 설마 (seolma). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 설마요 ("no way / you're kidding"). Watch the particle attached to 설마 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: one-word reply of disbelief
disbelief framed as a question
worried, accusing doubt
pairs with 그럴 리가 없다

examples.en: No way, is it already sold out?
examples.note: Front-loaded 설마 turns a plain question into 'don't tell me...' disbelief.

examples.ko: 설마 비 오는데 안 가는 건 아니죠?
examples.romanization: seolma bi oneunde an ganeun geon anijyo?
examples.en: Surely you're not skipping it just because it's raining?
examples.note: 설마 ... 아니죠? is the classic frame: it fishes for the answer 'no, of course not'.

examples.en: I figured it couldn't be, but it was true.
examples.note: 설마 했는데 = 'I thought surely not, and yet' — the let-down twist.

entries.nuance: 설마 expresses strong disbelief that something bad or shocking could actually be true — 'surely not', 'you've got to be kidding', 'don't tell me'. Crucially it ANTICIPATES a denial: the speaker wants the answer to be no, which is why it loves the frames 설마 ~ 아니죠? and 설마 그럴 리가 없다. Contrast it sharply with 아마 (probably): 아마 is a neutral, fairly confident guess that something IS so (아마 올 거예요 = he'll probably come), whereas 설마 leans the opposite way, hoping it is NOT so. The English-speaker pitfall is using 설마 for ordinary 'maybe', or for guesses you actually expect to be true — that is 아마 or 어쩌면. Also remember 설마 carries emotion (alarm, dread, incredulity), so it is out of place in a calm, factual statement. The frozen reply 설마요 alone means 'no way, really?'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 설마 for a neutral 'probably' — 설마 hopes the thing is FALSE (설마 그게 사실이에요?), while a confident guess that it's true is 아마 (아마 사실일 거예요).
Forgetting that 설마 fishes for a denial — pairing it with a cheerful 'yes' answer feels wrong; it expects 아니에요 or 그럴 리가 없다.
Dropping it into a flat factual sentence — 설마 needs the emotional charge of doubt/alarm and usually a questioning or 그럴 리 없다 ending, not a plain declaration.

entries.shortExplanation: 제발 means "please (I beg you)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 제발 (jebal) = "please (I beg you)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 제발 그만해요 ("please stop") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 제발, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: heartfelt pleading
pairs with 부탁
제발 + 좀 doubles the urgency

usagePhrases.en: please, I hope it's not today
usagePhrases.note: with a -았으면 wish

examples.en: Please be quiet, I'm begging you.
examples.note: Said when 조용히 해 주세요 alone isn't strong enough — 제발 adds real desperation.

examples.en: I really hope it doesn't rain.
examples.note: 제발 + the -았/었으면 좋겠다 wish frame: pleading with fate, not a person.

examples.en: Please let it slide just this once.
examples.note: 봐주다 = 'go easy / let off'; 제발 한 번만 is the earnest 'just this once' plea.

entries.nuance: 제발 is a heartfelt, emotionally loaded 'please' used when you are genuinely pleading or desperate — far stronger than the bare polite ending -주세요, which is just normal courtesy. Think of -주세요 as everyday 'please pass the salt', and 제발 as 'I am begging you'. Because it carries real feeling, Koreans reserve it for moments that truly matter (제발 살려 주세요, 제발 그만해), and it can sound melodramatic or even rude if sprinkled on trivial requests. It pairs naturally with 좀 (제발 좀...) to intensify, with 부탁이다 ('it's a request'), and with wish endings -았으면 좋겠다 when you are pleading with circumstances rather than a person. The English-speaker trap is treating 제발 like the all-purpose English 'please' that politely tags every request — in Korean that politeness job is done by -주세요 / -ㄹ게요, and overusing 제발 makes you sound frantic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 제발 for routine polite requests where -주세요 already covers 'please' — 제발 means 'I beg you' and sounds desperate on a casual 'pass me the water'.
Treating 제발 as the English filler 'please' in every sentence — Korean handles ordinary politeness with -주세요/-ㄹ게요; reserve 제발 for genuine pleading.
Pairing 제발 with a cold command and no softening — it usually goes with -주세요, 좀, or a wish ending (제발 ~았으면 좋겠어요), matching its emotional tone.

entries.english: just in time; as it happens
entries.shortExplanation: 마침 means "just in time; as it happens" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 마침 (machim) means "just in time; as it happens". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 마침 잘 왔어요 ("you came at just the right time"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 마침 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: you came at just the right time
usagePhrases.note: welcomes lucky timing

usagePhrases.en: as it happens, I have time
usagePhrases.note: a convenient coincidence

usagePhrases.en: I happen to be going that way too
usagePhrases.note: fortunate overlap
pairs with 잘되다

examples.en: The bus came just then, so I didn't wait.
examples.note: Basic use: 마침 marks the happy 'right at that moment' timing before the verb.

examples.en: It happened to be on sale, so I bought one.
examples.note: 마침 + -길래 ('since it happened to...') is a very natural cause frame for lucky chance.

examples.en: I was about to call, and just then they reached out.
examples.note: -던 참인데 + 마침 stacks two 'right at that instant' cues for a perfect coincidence.

entries.nuance: 마침 marks a lucky, convenient coincidence — 'just in time', 'as it happens', 'right then' — framing an event as a happy accident that fell into place rather than something planned. Do NOT confuse it with 드디어 ('finally / at last'), which is about a long-awaited thing arriving after waiting (드디어 끝났다 = it's finally over); 마침 has no sense of waiting, only of fortunate timing. Its true opposite is 하필, the ANNOYING coincidence: where 마침 is good luck, 하필 is bad luck, so never use 마침 for an unfortunate clash. It collocates with 마침 잘됐다 ('that worked out perfectly'), 마침 잘 왔다 ('you came at the right time'), and the cause endings -길래 / -아서. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'finally' (드디어) when you mean 'as luck would have it', or using 마침 for a bad coincidence that should be 하필.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 마침 (luckily, right then) with 드디어 (finally, after long waiting) — 드디어 implies anticipation (드디어 도착했다), while 마침 is pure fortunate timing with no waiting.
Using 마침 for a BAD coincidence — an unlucky clash is 하필 (하필 그날 비가 왔다); 마침 is reserved for timing that helps you.
Treating 마침 as 'exactly/precisely' for measurements — that is 정확히/딱; 마침 specifically frames a convenient coincidence of timing.

entries.english: of all times; why this one
entries.shortExplanation: 하필 means "of all times; why this one" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "of all times; why this one" is 하필 (hapil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 하필 오늘 ("of all days, today"). Watch the particle attached to 하필 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: sits in front of a noun

usagePhrases.en: why right now of all times?
usagePhrases.note: exasperated question

usagePhrases.en: of all days it rained that day
usagePhrases.note: unlucky timing

usagePhrases.en: of all things / of all people
usagePhrases.note: the emphatic form

examples.en: Of all days, I got sick on the day of the plans.
examples.note: 하필 + 날 spotlights the cruel timing — the worst possible day.

examples.en: Why me, of all people?
examples.note: 왜 하필 나... is the set complaint: 'out of everyone, why ME?'

examples.ko: 하필이면 비 오는 날 우산을 안 가져왔어요.
examples.romanization: hapirimyeon bi oneun nal usaneul an gajyeowasseoyo.
examples.en: Of all days, I forgot my umbrella the day it rained.
examples.note: 하필이면 (emphatic) drives home just how unlucky the choice of day was.

entries.nuance: 하필 voices frustration at unlucky, badly chosen timing or circumstance — 'of all times', 'why this one in particular', 'just my luck'. It is the negative twin of 마침: 마침 is the lucky coincidence, 하필 is the maddening one, so they are not interchangeable. It is built on the Sino-Korean 何必 (何 'what' + 必 'necessarily') — literally 'why must it be (this)?' — which is exactly the grumbling rhetorical question it carries, and the emphatic 하필이면 stresses how rotten the choice of time, place, or person feels. It collocates with question words (왜 하필...?) and with bad-luck nouns (하필 그날, 하필 시험 날). The English-speaker pitfall is using 하필 for good fortune (that is 마침), or stripping out its complaining, put-upon tone and treating it as neutral 'just then' — 하필 always grumbles.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 하필 for GOOD luck — fortunate timing is 마침 (마침 자리가 있었다); 하필 only marks an unwelcome, ill-timed coincidence.
Flattening its tone to a neutral 'at that time' — 하필 inherently complains ('of all times!'); without that grumble it sounds wrong.
Misreading the 何必 origin as a real 'why must' question needing an answer — here it is a rhetorical sigh of bad luck, usually with no expected reply.

entries.english: after a long while; for once
entries.shortExplanation: 모처럼 means "after a long while; for once" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 모처럼 (mocheoreom) = "after a long while; for once". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 모처럼 쉬는 날 ("a rare day off") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 모처럼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: sits in front of a noun

usagePhrases.en: we met after a long time
usagePhrases.note: a precious occasion
with a reason ending -는데
모처럼 + 의 + noun

examples.en: I was thrilled to see my friend after so long.
examples.note: 모처럼 frames the reunion as rare and therefore special.

examples.en: It's a rare day off, but it's raining.
examples.note: The very common bittersweet use: a precious chance spoiled by 비가 와요.

examples.en: Since we're out for once, let's eat something good.
examples.note: 모처럼 ... -으니까 = 'since this is a rare chance, let's make the most of it'.

entries.nuance: 모처럼 marks something that happens rarely and is therefore precious — 'after a long while', 'for once', 'on this rare occasion' — adding the feeling 'this doesn't come often, so let's value it', and it very often sets up a slight let-down (a rare day off that gets rained out). Compare it with 오랜만에, which also means 'after a long time' but is purely neutral about elapsed time (오랜만에 비가 온다 = it's been a while since it rained — could be good OR bad); 모처럼 carries an extra warmth and the sense of a welcome, scarce opportunity, so 모처럼 비가 온다 would sound odd unless the rain is genuinely wished-for. It collocates with 모처럼의 + noun (모처럼의 휴가 = a rare vacation) and with reason endings -는데 / -으니까 to justify seizing the moment. The English-speaker pitfall is using 모처럼 for ordinary, routine happenings, or treating it as a flat synonym of 오랜만에 — 모처럼 always implies the event is rare AND treasured.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 모처럼 for everyday routine events — it specifically marks something RARE and welcome (모처럼 쉬는 날), not your daily commute.
Treating 모처럼 as identical to 오랜만에 — 오랜만에 is neutral 'after a while' (good or bad), while 모처럼 adds 'precious, long-awaited', so it resists negative events.
Forgetting the 의 when modifying a noun directly — 'a rare opportunity' is 모처럼의 기회, not 모처럼 기회.

entries.shortExplanation: 그나마 means "at least; even that much" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그나마 (geunama) means "at least; even that much". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그나마 다행이에요 ("at least that's a relief"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그나마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the classic silver-lining phrase
the least-bad option

usagePhrases.en: this is the little that's left
usagePhrases.note: a scant remainder
그나마 + 도 for emphasis

examples.en: I was late, but at least I caught the last train.
examples.note: 그나마 flags the one redeeming part of an otherwise bad situation.

examples.en: The pay is low, but at least there's no overtime.
examples.note: Sets a downside (적지만) against a small consolation introduced by 그나마.

examples.en: At least I have you, thank goodness.
examples.note: 그나마 ... 다행이다 — relief that, amid hardship, this one good thing remains.

entries.nuance: 그나마 points to a small consolation inside an otherwise bad or limited situation — 'at least', 'even that little bit', 'if nothing else, there's this'. It quietly admits things are not good while spotlighting the single redeeming scrap, so it pairs constantly with 다행이다 (그나마 다행이에요 = 'at least that's a relief'). Contrast it with 그래도 ('still / even so / nevertheless'): 그래도 concedes a point and pushes on regardless (비싸지만 그래도 살래요 = it's pricey but I'll buy it anyway), whereas 그나마 specifically picks out a meager upside as the best of a poor lot. There is also 그것도 vs 그나마도: 그나마도 없다 means 'not even that little bit is left', the bottom of the barrel. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그나마 when the situation is actually fully positive — it requires a backdrop of hardship or scarcity; on genuinely good news it sounds grudging and wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그나마 when things are fully positive — it needs a bad/limited backdrop (그나마 살아남았다); on pure good news it sounds oddly grudging.
Mixing it up with 그래도 (still/even so) — 그래도 concedes and continues anyway (그래도 갈게요), while 그나마 isolates a small silver lining in a poor situation.
Forgetting the emphatic 그나마도 — 'not even that much' is 그나마도 없어요, with 도 stressing that the last small bit is gone too.

structuredNuance.t: 그나마 points to a small consolation inside an otherwise bad or limited situation — 'at least', 'even that little bit', 'if nothing else, there's this'. It quietly admits things are not good while spotlighting the single redeeming scrap, so it pairs constantly with 다행이다 (그나마 다행이에요 = 'at least that's a relief'). There is also 그것도 vs 그나마도: 그나마도 없다 means 'not even that little bit is left', the bottom of the barrel.

Contrast it with 그래도 ('still / even so / nevertheless'): 그래도 concedes a point and pushes on regardless (비싸지만 그래도 살래요 = it's pricey but I'll buy it anyway), whereas 그나마 specifically picks out a meager upside as the best of a poor lot.
The English-speaker pitfall is using 그나마 when the situation is actually fully positive — it requires a backdrop of hardship or scarcity; on genuinely good news it sounds grudging and wrong.

entries.shortExplanation: 어쩌면 means "maybe; possibly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "maybe; possibly" is 어쩌면 (eojjeomyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어쩌면 올지도 몰라요 ("maybe they'll come"). Watch the particle attached to 어쩌면 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: with -ㄹ지도 모르다
a tentative admission
a soft suggestion
a hedged outcome with -ㄹ 수도 있다

examples.ko: 어쩌면 이번 주말에 시간이 날 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: eojjeomyeon ibeon jumare sigani nal sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe I'll have some free time this weekend.
examples.note: 어쩌면 + -ㄹ 수도 있다 keeps the possibility open and uncommitted.

examples.ko: 어쩌면 우리 전에 만난 적 있을지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: eojjeomyeon uri jeone mannan jeok isseuljido mollayo.
examples.en: Maybe we've met somewhere before.
examples.note: 어쩌면 floats a half-formed hunch; -ㄹ지도 몰라요 is its natural partner ending.

examples.ko: 어쩌면 그 사람 말이 맞을지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: eojjeomyeon geu saram mari majeuljido mollayo.
examples.en: Maybe that person is right after all.
examples.note: Signals genuine openness to being wrong — a reconsidering 'maybe'.

entries.nuance: 어쩌면 means 'maybe / possibly' and opens a genuine but uncertain possibility, often one the speaker had not fully considered until now — there's a reflective, 'come to think of it, perhaps...' flavor. It is grammatically drawn to the guessing endings -ㄹ지도 모르다 and -ㄹ 수도 있다, which carry the uncertainty through to the verb. Contrast it with 아마 ('probably'): 아마 is a fairly confident lean toward yes (아마 맞을 거예요 = it's probably right), while 어쩌면 is more open-ended and less committed, weighing a real but not-likely chance, and it can even introduce a surprising or contrary idea. (Note 어쩌면 also has a separate exclamatory use, '어쩌면 이렇게...!' = 'how on earth so...!', but the adverb of possibility is the core meaning here.) The English-speaker pitfall is treating 어쩌면 as confidently as 아마, or pairing it with a flat assertion — it needs a hedging ending, not a bare statement of fact.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 어쩌면 as confidently as 아마 (probably) — 아마 leans toward 'yes, likely' (아마 올 거예요), while 어쩌면 stays open and uncommitted ('maybe, who knows').
Pairing 어쩌면 with a flat assertion (어쩌면 비가 와요) — it needs a guessing ending: 어쩌면 비가 올지도 몰라요 / 올 수도 있어요.
Forgetting its reflective 'come to think of it' nuance — it often raises a possibility newly considered, not a settled prediction.

entries.english: as many as; no less than
entries.shortExplanation: 무려 means "as many as; no less than" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무려 (muryeo) = "as many as; no less than". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 무려 백만 원 ("a whopping million won") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무려, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: sits right before a number
emphasizes a large amount

usagePhrases.en: for no less than ten years
usagePhrases.note: before a duration
a striking comparison

examples.en: That bag costs a whopping three million won.
examples.note: 무려 right before the figure signals 'shockingly, that much'.

examples.en: I stood in line for a full two hours.
examples.note: 무려 ... -이나 doubles the emphasis on the surprisingly large quantity.

examples.ko: 이 영화를 무려 천만 명이 봤어요.
examples.romanization: i yeonghwareul muryeo cheonman myeongi bwasseoyo.
examples.en: No less than ten million people saw this movie.
examples.note: Pairs a big round number with 무려 to stress an impressive scale.

entries.nuance: 무려 goes directly before a number or quantity to stress that the amount is surprisingly, impressively large — 'a whopping', 'no less than', 'as many as' — broadcasting that the speaker finds the figure striking or hard to believe. It works ONLY with quantities (money, counts, durations, multiples), never with a general statement, and it loves to combine with the emphatic particle -이나/나 on the number (무려 두 시간이나). Contrast it with 약 (約, 'approximately / about'), which does the opposite job — softening a number into a rough estimate (약 백 명 = about a hundred); 무려 amplifies and dramatizes, 약 hedges and rounds. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving out the number (무려 비싸요 is wrong — say 무려 삼백만 원이에요), or confusing the amplifying 무려 with the estimating 약. If you want plain 'about', reach for 약 or 대략; if you want 'can you believe how much', that's 무려.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 무려 with no number after it — 무려 must front a quantity (무려 백만 원); 무려 비싸요 is wrong, say 무려 백만 원이에요 or just 정말 비싸요.
Confusing 무려 (amplifies: 'a whopping') with 약 (softens: 'about, approximately') — 약 백 명 = roughly 100, but 무려 백 명 = a whopping 100.
Treating 무려 as plain emphasis like 정말 for adjectives — 무려 specifically dramatizes a NUMBER, not a quality (not 무려 예뻐요).

entries.shortExplanation: 심지어 means "even; on top of that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 심지어 (simjieo) means "even; on top of that". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 심지어 무료예요 ("it's even free"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 심지어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: tacks on a surprising bonus
an extreme example with 도
piling on a worse fact
escalates to the extreme case

examples.ko: 그 식당은 맛있고, 심지어 가격도 싸요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun masitgo, simjieo gagyeokdo ssayo.
examples.en: That restaurant is tasty, and on top of that it's cheap.
examples.note: 심지어 adds an extra, almost too-good point; note 도 on 가격.

examples.en: It was raining, and I didn't even have an umbrella.
examples.note: Escalates from bad to worse; 심지어 + 우산도 = 'didn't even have'.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 심지어 내 이름도 기억 못 해요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun simjieo nae ireumdo gieong mo taeyo.
examples.en: That person doesn't even remember my name.
examples.note: Pushes to an extreme case — of all things, not even the name.

entries.nuance: 심지어 introduces an extreme or surprising addition that pushes a point further than you'd expect — 'even', 'on top of that', 'and get this'. It escalates, whether the extra fact is good (맛있고, 심지어 싸다) or bad (춥고, 심지어 비까지 온다), and it characteristically triggers the particle 도 ('also/even') on the following item. Contrast it with 게다가 ('moreover / what's more'): 게다가 simply adds another point on the same level, fairly neutrally, while 심지어 signals that the next fact is the surprising, over-the-top extreme — the one that makes you raise your eyebrows. Compare also 조차/마저 (particles meaning 'even', stressing the least-expected case); 심지어 often works alongside them. The English-speaker pitfall is using 심지어 as a flat 'also' (that's 또/그리고) or swapping it for neutral 게다가, and forgetting the 도 that naturally follows — 심지어 사과도 안 했어요, not 심지어 사과 안 했어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 심지어 as a plain 'also/and' — that is 또/그리고; 심지어 specifically escalates to a SURPRISING, extreme addition.
Swapping it for neutral 게다가 (moreover) — 게다가 just adds another point, while 심지어 flags the most unexpected, eyebrow-raising one.
Dropping the 도 that usually follows — say 심지어 인사도 안 했어요 (even the greeting); leaving out 도 weakens the 'even' force.

entries.shortExplanation: 도저히 means "(cannot) possibly; no matter what" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "(cannot) possibly; no matter what" is 도저히 (dojeohi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도저히 못 하겠어요 ("I just can't do it"). Watch the particle attached to 도저히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: always with a negative
strong refusal with 안

usagePhrases.en: I can't understand it at all
usagePhrases.note: with 이해가 안 되다
with -ㄹ 수 없다

examples.en: I can't figure out this problem no matter what.
examples.note: 도저히 + 모르겠어요 = total inability after real effort.

examples.en: It's so spicy I just can't eat it.
examples.note: 도저히 + 못 ...겠어요 conveys giving up despite trying.

examples.en: There's just no way I can make time.
examples.note: 도저히 + -ㄹ 수가 없다 = flat impossibility, however hard one tries.

entries.nuance: 도저히 means 'by no means / no matter how hard one tries', and it MUST be paired with a negative — 못, 안, 모르다, or -ㄹ 수 없다 — because its whole job is to intensify an impossibility reached after genuine effort: not just 'I can't', but 'I've tried and there is simply no way'. Without a negative the sentence is ungrammatical (도저히 할 수 있어요 is wrong). Contrast it with 절대 ('never / absolutely (not)'): 절대 can negate too, but it sounds like a firm vow or prohibition about will or principle (절대 안 해 = I absolutely won't, by choice), whereas 도저히 is about practical impossibility despite trying (도저히 못 해 = I genuinely can't manage it). It collocates with 도저히 ~ 수 없다, 도저히 못 ~겠다, 도저히 안 되다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 도저히 in a positive sentence, or reaching for it to mean a willful 'never' where 절대 fits better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도저히 in a positive sentence — it REQUIRES a negative (도저히 못 해요 / 안 돼요 / 이해가 안 돼요); 도저히 돼요 is ungrammatical.
Swapping it for 절대 (never, by will) — 절대 안 해 is a vow of refusal, while 도저히 못 해 is practical inability after trying; the nuance differs.
Forgetting the 'after real effort' meaning — 도저히 implies you genuinely tried and it's impossible, not a casual 'I don't feel like it'.

entries.shortExplanation: 차라리 means "rather; would sooner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 차라리 (charari) = "rather; would sooner". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 차라리 안 가는 게 나아요 ("I'd rather not go") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 차라리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: with -는 게 낫다
preferring one option with -ㄹ래요
choosing the lesser hassle
comparing two bad options

examples.en: Rather than wait, walking would be faster.
examples.note: -느니 차라리 = 'rather than (doing X)' — the core comparison frame.

examples.ko: 복잡한 데 가느니 차라리 집에서 쉴래요.
examples.romanization: bokjapan de ganeuni charari jibeseo swillaeyo.
examples.en: I'd sooner rest at home than go somewhere crowded.
examples.note: Sets a disliked option (가느니) against the preferred-but-still-not-ideal one.

examples.ko: 택시비 낼 바엔 차라리 일찍 나올게요.
examples.romanization: taeksibi nael baen charari iljjing naolgeyo.
examples.en: Rather than pay for a taxi, I'll just leave early.
examples.note: -ㄹ 바엔 차라리 = 'if it comes to (X), I'd rather' — choosing the lesser cost.

entries.nuance: 차라리 picks the lesser of two undesirable options — 'I'd rather', 'I'd sooner', 'better to... instead' — when NEITHER choice is good and you're settling for the more bearable one. The tone is resigned, not enthusiastic: it's a grudging preference, often implying 'this still isn't great, but it beats the alternative'. It characteristically follows the patterns -느니 (차라리) and -ㄹ 바에(는)/-ㄹ 바엔 차라리, both meaning 'rather than doing X', which set up the worse option being rejected. Contrast it with a plain 더 좋다 ('like better'): 더 좋다 is a positive preference between two acceptable things, while 차라리 specifically chooses between two bad-ish things. The English-speaker pitfall is using 차라리 for an option you genuinely want and feel good about — that implies you're happy, which clashes with 차라리's 'lesser evil' resignation; and forgetting that it normally compares against a worse alternative, so it rarely stands alone without that contrast in mind.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 차라리 for an option you actually want and enjoy — it implies neither choice is good (차라리 굶을래 = I'd rather starve); for a happy preference use 더 좋다/더 낫다 plainly.
Forgetting it compares against a WORSE alternative — 차라리 normally answers an unspoken 'rather than that bad option', often with -느니 or -ㄹ 바엔.
Treating it as 'instead' for neutral swaps — '대신' handles plain substitution (커피 대신 차), while 차라리 carries the resigned 'lesser of two evils' choice.
