entries.shortExplanation: 스킨 means "toner (skin)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스킨 (seukin) means "toner (skin)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스킨 발랐어요? ("Did you put on toner?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스킨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 항상 바르다; 스킨 하다는 어색해요
두 단어를 붙여 말하면 한국의 기본 2단계 스킨케어를 가리켜요
올리브영 직원에게 하는 전형적인 부탁 표현
남성 라인은 보통 남성용·남자로 표시되고 올인원이 많아요

examples.en: After washing my face, I apply toner first.
examples.note: 부터 = '먼저, ~부터 시작해서'; 스킨 → 로션 순서를 강조해요

examples.ko: 이 스킨은 향이 거의 없어서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i seukineun hyangi geoui eopseoseo joayo.
examples.en: I like this toner because it has almost no scent.
examples.note: 거의 없다 = '거의 ~ 않다'; 무향이면 fragrance-free예요

examples.ko: 피부가 건성이라 자기 전에 스킨을 두 번 덧발라요.
examples.romanization: pibuga geonseongira jagi jeone seukineul du beon deotballayo.
examples.en: My skin is dry, so I layer toner twice before bed.
examples.note: 덧바르다 = 위에 한 번 더 바르다; 건성↔지성 짝으로 외우세요

entries.nuance: 한국어 '스킨'은 영어 skin(피부)이 아니라 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 토너를 가리키는 화장품 이름이에요. 같은 제품을 '토너'라고도 부르지만, 일상 대화에서는 거의 항상 '스킨'이라고 해요. 영어 단어를 그대로 가져온 콩글리시이기 때문에 영어권 학습자가 '피부'라는 뜻으로 오해하기 쉬운 대표적 함정이에요. 바르는 동작에는 반드시 '바르다'를 쓰고 '스킨 하다'나 '스킨 칠하다'는 어색해요. 보통 '스킨 로션 발랐어?'처럼 로션과 한 세트로 묶여 다니고, '향이 없다', '촉촉하다' 같은 표현과 자주 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
스킨을 '피부(skin)'라는 뜻으로 쓰는 것 — 신체 부위는 '피부'라고 해야 하고, '스킨'은 토너 제품이에요
'스킨 크림'이라고 묶어 부르는 것 — 그런 짝은 없고 기본 세트는 '스킨 + 로션'이에요
'스킨 하다'로 동사화하는 것 — 화장품을 바르는 동작은 '바르다'를 써서 '스킨 발라요'라고 해요

structuredNuance.t: 한국어 '스킨'은 영어 skin(피부)이 아니라 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 토너를 가리키는 화장품 이름이에요. 같은 제품을 '토너'라고도 부르지만, 일상 대화에서는 거의 항상 '스킨'이라고 해요. 보통 '스킨 로션 발랐어?'처럼 로션과 한 세트로 묶여 다니고, '향이 없다', '촉촉하다' 같은 표현과 자주 어울려요.
바르는 동작에는 반드시 '바르다'를 쓰고 '스킨 하다'나 '스킨 칠하다'는 어색해요.
영어 단어를 그대로 가져온 콩글리시이기 때문에 영어권 학습자가 '피부'라는 뜻으로 오해하기 쉬운 대표적 함정이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 로션 means "lotion, moisturizer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "lotion, moisturizer" is 로션 (rosyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 로션 발라요 ("I apply lotion"). Watch the particle attached to 로션 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 스킨 다음에 오는 두 번째 보습 단계
얼굴용은 그냥 로션, 몸은 바디로 구분해요
친구·룸메이트 사이의 반말 부탁
수분 = 촉촉함; 제품 라벨에 흔한 말이에요

examples.en: In winter you have to apply a lot of lotion.
examples.note: 건조한 한국 겨울에 아주 공감되는 문장이에요

examples.en: I like this lotion because it isn't sticky.
examples.note: 끈적거리다 = 끈끈하게 들러붙다; 로션 고를 때 핵심 포인트

examples.ko: 샤워하고 나서 다리에 바디로션을 듬뿍 발랐어요.
examples.romanization: syawohago naseo darie badirosyeoneul deumppuk ballasseoyo.
examples.en: After showering, I slathered body lotion on my legs.
examples.note: 듬뿍 = 아주 넉넉히; 바디로션은 몸 전용임을 보여줘요

entries.nuance: 로션은 스킨 다음에 발라 수분을 채우고 가두는 보습 단계예요. 가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '크림'인데, 로션은 묽고 가벼워 흡수가 빠르고, 크림은 더 되고 진해서 강한 보습이 필요할 때 써요. 또 하나 주의할 점은 그냥 '로션'은 얼굴용을 뜻하고, 몸에 바르는 건 반드시 '바디로션'이라고 한다는 거예요. 영어 lotion은 몸·얼굴을 안 가리지만 한국어에서는 '바디'를 붙이지 않으면 자동으로 얼굴용으로 받아들여요. 동사는 '바르다'이고, '끈적거리다', '흡수가 빠르다', '촉촉하다' 같은 말과 잘 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
로션과 크림을 같은 것으로 보는 것 — 크림이 더 진하고 무거우며, 로션은 가볍고 묽어요
몸에 바르는데 그냥 '로션'이라고만 하는 것 — 바디용은 '바디로션'이라고 해야 얼굴용과 구분돼요
'로션 칠하다'라고 하는 것 — 자연스러운 동사는 '바르다'예요

structuredNuance.t: 로션은 스킨 다음에 발라 수분을 채우고 가두는 보습 단계예요. '끈적거리다', '흡수가 빠르다', '촉촉하다' 같은 말과 잘 어울려요.
가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '크림'인데, 로션은 묽고 가벼워 흡수가 빠르고, 크림은 더 되고 진해서 강한 보습이 필요할 때 써요. 또 그냥 '로션'은 얼굴용을 뜻하고, 몸에 바르는 건 반드시 '바디로션'이라고 해요.
동사는 '바르다'를 써요.
영어 lotion은 몸·얼굴을 안 가리지만 한국어에서는 '바디'를 붙이지 않으면 자동으로 얼굴용으로 받아들여요.

entries.shortExplanation: 선크림 means "sunscreen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 선크림 (seonkeurim) = "sunscreen". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 선크림 발랐어? ("Did you put on sunscreen?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 선크림, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 특히 여름에 아주 흔한 확인·잔소리 표현
꼭 = 빠짐없이; 조언할 때 써요
떨어지다 = 다 써서 없어지다
SPF는 '에스피에프'로 읽어요

examples.ko: 나가기 전에 선크림 바르는 거 잊지 마세요.
examples.romanization: nagagi jeone seonkeurim bareuneun geo itji maseyo.
examples.en: Don't forget to put on sunscreen before going out.
examples.note: 잊지 마세요 = '잊다'의 금지 명령형

examples.ko: 이 선크림은 백탁 현상이 없어서 데일리로 써요.
examples.romanization: i seonkeurimeun baekta kyeonsangi eopseoseo deilliro sseoyo.
examples.en: This sunscreen leaves no white cast, so I use it daily.
examples.note: 백탁 = 하얗게 뜨는 막; 선크림 후기에 꼭 나오는 말

examples.ko: 햇볕이 강한 날은 두세 시간마다 선크림을 덧발라요.
examples.romanization: haetbyeochi ganghan nareun duse siganmada seonkeurimeul deotballayo.
examples.en: On strong-sun days I reapply sunscreen every few hours.
examples.note: 덧바르다 = 위에 다시 바르다; 재도포를 뜻해요

entries.nuance: 선크림은 자외선을 막아 주는 제품으로, 영어 sunscreen에 한국어 '크림'을 붙여 만든 콩글리시 합성어예요. 한국에서는 여름뿐 아니라 사계절 내내 챙기는 필수품으로 여겨요. 비슷한 말로 '선블록(sunblock)'이 있지만 일상에서는 선크림이 압도적으로 흔하고, 영어처럼 'sunblock'을 말로 쓰면 살짝 번역투로 들려요. 표기에서 가장 자주 틀리는 부분이 첫 글자인데, 된소리 '썬'이 아니라 '선'이 표준이에요(브랜드명에만 '썬'을 써요). 고를 때는 'SPF가 높다', '백탁이 없다', '꾸덕하지 않다' 같은 표현으로 따지고, 동사는 '바르다·덧바르다'를 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'썬크림'처럼 된소리로 적는 것 — 표준 표기는 '선크림'이에요(상표가 아니면 '선'으로 써요)
말할 때 영어 'sunblock'을 쓰는 것 — 한국 사람은 거의 항상 '선크림'이라고 해요
한 번 바르고 끝낸다고 표현하는 것 — 실제로는 '덧바르다(재도포)'가 핵심이라 그 표현을 같이 익혀야 해요

structuredNuance.t: 선크림은 자외선을 막아 주는 제품이에요. 한국에서는 여름뿐 아니라 사계절 내내 챙기는 필수품으로 여겨요. 고를 때는 'SPF가 높다', '백탁이 없다', '꾸덕하지 않다' 같은 표현으로 따져요.
비슷한 말로 '선블록(sunblock)'이 있지만 일상에서는 선크림이 압도적으로 흔하고, 영어처럼 'sunblock'을 말로 쓰면 살짝 번역투로 들려요.
영어 sunscreen에 한국어 '크림'을 붙여 만든 콩글리시 합성어예요. 표기에서 가장 자주 틀리는 부분이 첫 글자인데, 된소리 '썬'이 아니라 '선'이 표준이에요(브랜드명에만 '썬'을 써요).
동사는 '바르다·덧바르다'를 써요.

entries.shortExplanation: 파운데이션 means "foundation (makeup)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 파운데이션 (paundeisyeon) means "foundation (makeup)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 파운데이션 추천 ("foundation recommendation"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 파운데이션 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 검색어로도, 직원에게 하는 부탁으로도 흔해요
젊은 층이 아주 자주 쓰는 줄임말이에요
커버력 = 가리는 힘; 핵심 스펙이에요
펴 바르는 메이크업이라 동사는 바르다

examples.en: I prefer a natural foundation over high coverage.
examples.note: A보다 B = A보다 B를 더; 비교 조사 '보다'를 익혀요

examples.ko: 파데 색이 너무 밝아서 얼굴이 둥둥 떠요.
examples.romanization: pade saegi neomu balgaseo eolguri dungdung tteoyo.
examples.en: The foundation shade is too light, so my face looks washed out.
examples.note: (얼굴이) 뜨다 = 색이 안 맞아 따로 논다는 관용 표현

examples.ko: 여름엔 무겁지 않고 가벼운 파운데이션을 새로 샀어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen mugeopji anko gabyeoun paundeisyeoneul saero sasseoyo.
examples.en: For summer I bought a new lightweight foundation.
examples.note: 가볍다 = 발림·커버가 산뜻함; 계절별 선택을 보여줘요

entries.nuance: 파운데이션은 피부톤을 고르게 펴 발라 메이크업의 바탕을 만드는 베이스 화장품으로, 영어 foundation을 그대로 옮긴 외래어예요. 젊은 사람들은 거의 '파데'라고 줄여 말하니 둘 다 알아 두면 좋아요. 비슷한 베이스 제품인 'BB크림·쿠션'과 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 파운데이션은 액체·크림 타입으로 손이나 브러시로 펴 바르고, 쿠션은 퍼프에 묻혀 두드리는 휴대용 형태라는 점이 달라요. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 '칠하다(paint)'를 쓰는 것인데, 화장품은 '바르다'가 맞아요. 고를 때는 '커버력이 좋다', '호수(색번호)가 맞다', '들뜨지 않는다' 같은 표현과 함께 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'칠하다(to paint)'를 쓰는 것 — 파운데이션을 펴 바르는 동작은 '바르다'예요
자기 톤보다 너무 밝은 호수를 고르는 것 — 한국에서는 얼굴이 '둥둥 떠요'라고 표현하며 부자연스럽다고 봐요
파운데이션과 쿠션을 같은 말로 쓰는 것 — 쿠션은 퍼프로 두드리는 휴대형이라 따로 불러요

structuredNuance.t: 파운데이션은 피부톤을 고르게 펴 발라 메이크업의 바탕을 만드는 베이스 화장품이에요. 젊은 사람들은 거의 '파데'라고 줄여 말하니 둘 다 알아 두면 좋아요. 고를 때는 '커버력이 좋다', '호수(색번호)가 맞다', '들뜨지 않는다' 같은 표현과 함께 써요.
비슷한 베이스 제품인 'BB크림·쿠션'과 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 파운데이션은 액체·크림 타입으로 손이나 브러시로 펴 바르고, 쿠션은 퍼프에 묻혀 두드리는 휴대용 형태라는 점이 달라요.
영어 foundation을 그대로 옮긴 외래어예요.
펴 바르는 메이크업이라 동사는 '바르다'가 맞아요.
영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 '칠하다(paint)'를 쓰는 것인데, 화장품은 '바르다'가 맞아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 립스틱 means "lipstick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "lipstick" is 립스틱 (ripseutik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 립스틱 바르다 ("to put on lipstick"). Watch the particle attached to 립스틱 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 바르다
빨간 = 빨갛다의 관형형, '빨간색'도 가능
색 = 컬러; '무슨 색?'으로 물어요
지워지다 = 닦여 없어지다

examples.en: Today I put on red lipstick.
examples.note: 오늘의 메이크업을 설명하는 기본 문장

examples.ko: 이 립스틱은 잘 안 지워져서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i ripseutigeun jal an jiwojyeoseo joayo.
examples.en: I like this lipstick because it doesn't come off easily.
examples.note: 잘 안 ~지다 = 쉽게 ~되지 않다; 지속력을 칭찬해요

examples.ko: 밥 먹다가 컵에 립스틱이 묻어서 다시 발랐어요.
examples.romanization: bam meokdaga keobe ripseutigi mudeoseo dasi ballasseoyo.
examples.en: Lipstick rubbed onto my cup at lunch, so I reapplied.
examples.note: 묻다 = (색·얼룩이) 옮아 붙다; 자동사예요

entries.nuance: 립스틱은 입술에 색을 입히는 색조 화장품으로, 영어 lipstick을 그대로 가져온 외래어예요. 가장 자주 헷갈리는 짝이 '틴트'인데, 립스틱은 막대형으로 발색이 진하고 매트하거나 촉촉한 막을 입히는 느낌이라면, 틴트는 입술에 색이 '물드는(스며드는)' 가볍고 자연스러운 제형이에요. 그래서 '립스틱은 발랐다는 게 티 나고, 틴트는 자연스럽다'고 흔히 말해요. 동사는 '바르다'가 맞고 '칠하다'는 어색해요. 또 '묻다(색이 옮다)'는 자동사라 '컵에 립스틱이 묻었어요'처럼 색이 주어가 되는 점을 익혀 두면 좋아요. '발색이 좋다', '잘 안 지워진다', '색이 진하다' 같은 말과 자주 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
립스틱과 틴트를 같은 것으로 보는 것 — 틴트는 가볍게 물드는 타입, 립스틱은 진하고 막을 입히는 타입이에요
'립스틱 칠하다'라고 하는 것 — 자연스러운 동사는 '바르다'예요
'묻다'에 목적격 '을/를'을 붙여 '컵에 립스틱을 묻었어요'라고 하는 것 — '묻다'는 자동사라 색이 주어가 되어 '컵에 립스틱이 묻었어요'가 맞아요(일부러 묻힐 때만 타동사 '묻히다'를 써요)

structuredNuance.t: 립스틱은 입술에 색을 입히는 색조 화장품이에요. '발색이 좋다', '잘 안 지워진다', '색이 진하다' 같은 말과 자주 어울려요.
가장 자주 헷갈리는 짝이 '틴트'인데, 립스틱은 막대형으로 발색이 진하고 매트하거나 촉촉한 막을 입히는 느낌이라면, 틴트는 입술에 색이 '물드는(스며드는)' 가볍고 자연스러운 제형이에요. 그래서 '립스틱은 발랐다는 게 티 나고, 틴트는 자연스럽다'고 흔히 말해요.
영어 lipstick을 그대로 가져온 외래어예요.
동사는 '바르다'가 맞고 '칠하다'는 어색해요. 또 '묻다(색이 옮다)'는 자동사라 '컵에 립스틱이 묻었어요'처럼 색이 주어가 되는 점을 익혀 두면 좋아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 마스카라 means "mascara" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 마스카라 (maseukara) = "mascara". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마스카라 하다 ("to do/apply mascara") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 마스카라, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 눈 화장은 하다·바르다 둘 다 자연스러워요
워터프루프 = 방수; 흔한 라벨이에요
번지다 = 경계를 넘어 퍼지다
물만으로는 안 지워져 클렌징이 필요해요

examples.en: I teared up, so my mascara smudged everywhere.
examples.note: 번지다 = 퍼져 흐르다; 자동사로 마스카라가 주어예요

examples.ko: 여름엔 땀에 강한 워터프루프 마스카라를 써요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen ttame ganghan woteopeurupeu maseukarareul sseoyo.
examples.en: In summer I use sweat-proof waterproof mascara.
examples.note: 에 강하다 = ~에 잘 견디다; 선택 이유를 말해요

examples.ko: 워터프루프는 클렌징 오일로 살살 녹여서 지워야 해요.
examples.romanization: woteopeurupeuneun keullenjing oillo salsal nogyeoseo jiwoya haeyo.
examples.en: Waterproof mascara needs to be melted off gently with cleansing oil.
examples.note: 살살 = 부드럽게; 제거 방법을 설명해요

entries.nuance: 마스카라는 속눈썹에 발라 길고 진하게 보이게 하는 눈 화장품으로, 영어 mascara를 옮긴 외래어예요. 비슷한 눈 화장품인 '아이라이너'와 헷갈리면 안 되는데, 마스카라는 속눈썹 자체에 바르는 것이고 아이라이너는 눈가에 선을 그리는 것이라 부위와 도구가 달라요. 동사는 '바르다'와 '하다'를 모두 쓸 수 있어요. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 부분은 '번지다'를 타동사로 오해하는 건데, '번지다'는 자동사라 '마스카라가 번졌어요'처럼 마스카라가 주어가 돼요. 또 워터프루프 타입은 물세수로 안 지워지므로 반드시 클렌징 제품으로 지워야 하고, 잘못 지우면 눈가에 번져 이른바 '판다 눈'이 된다고 표현해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
워터프루프 마스카라를 물·폼클렌저만으로 지우려는 것 — 오일 클렌징이 있어야 깨끗이 지워져요
마스카라(속눈썹)와 아이라이너(눈가 선)를 섞어 쓰는 것 — 부위가 다른 별개 제품이에요
'번지다'를 타동사로 쓰는 것 — '내가 마스카라를 번졌다'가 아니라 '마스카라가 번졌다'가 맞아요

structuredNuance.t: 마스카라는 속눈썹에 발라 길고 진하게 보이게 하는 눈 화장품이에요. 워터프루프 타입은 물세수로 안 지워지므로 반드시 클렌징 제품으로 지워야 하고, 잘못 지우면 눈가에 번져 이른바 '판다 눈'이 된다고 표현해요.
비슷한 눈 화장품인 '아이라이너'와 헷갈리면 안 되는데, 마스카라는 속눈썹 자체에 바르는 것이고 아이라이너는 눈가에 선을 그리는 것이라 부위와 도구가 달라요.
영어 mascara를 옮긴 외래어예요.
동사는 '바르다'와 '하다'를 모두 쓸 수 있어요. '번지다'는 자동사라 '마스카라가 번졌어요'처럼 마스카라가 주어가 돼요.
영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 부분은 '번지다'를 타동사로 오해하는 건데, '번지다'는 자동사라 '마스카라가 번졌어요'처럼 마스카라가 주어가 돼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 클렌징 means "cleansing (makeup removal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 클렌징 (keullenjing) means "cleansing (makeup removal)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 클렌징 오일 ("cleansing oil"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 클렌징 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 오일 타입; 진한 화장에 잘 맞아요

usagePhrases.en: to do one's cleansing / remove makeup
usagePhrases.note: 하다를 붙이면 동사가 돼요
클렌징(1차) + 폼클렌저(2차)를 잇는 루틴
워터 타입; 순하고 빨라요

examples.ko: 화장을 진하게 했으면 클렌징을 꼼꼼히 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: hwajangeul jinhage haesseumyeon keullenjingeul kkomkkomhi haeya haeyo.
examples.en: If you wore heavy makeup, you have to cleanse thoroughly.
examples.note: 꼼꼼히 = 빈틈없이; -았/었으면 조건과 함께 써요

examples.ko: 저는 보통 클렌징 오일로 화장을 지워요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun botong keullenjing oillo hwajangeul jiwoyo.
examples.en: I usually remove my makeup with cleansing oil.
examples.note: (으)로 = 수단·도구 조사; 무엇으로 지우는지 표현

examples.ko: 클렌징을 건너뛰고 그냥 자면 다음 날 피부가 뒤집어져요.
examples.romanization: keullenjingeul geonneottwigo geunyang jamyeon daeum nal pibuga dwijibeojyeoyo.
examples.en: If I skip cleansing and just sleep, my skin breaks out the next day.
examples.note: 뒤집어지다 = 피부가 확 안 좋아지다(구어)

entries.nuance: 클렌징은 화장과 노폐물을 녹여 지우는 세안 단계를 통틀어 가리키는 외래어로, '클렌징 하다'처럼 '하다'를 붙여 동사로 써요. 핵심 구분은 그냥 물로 씻는 '세수'와의 차이예요. 세수는 물·비누로 얼굴을 씻는 일반 동작이고, 클렌징은 메이크업까지 전용 제품으로 '녹여서' 지운다는 점이 달라요. 그래서 물세수(물만으로 씻기)는 클렌징으로 치지 않아요. 오일·밤·워터 등 제형이 다양하고, 화장이 진한 날은 클렌징 후 폼클렌저로 한 번 더 씻는 '이중 세안'을 권해요. '꼼꼼히 하다', '화장을 지우다', '건너뛰다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
물세수(물만으로 씻기)를 클렌징으로 여기는 것 — 메이크업은 전용 클렌징 제품으로 녹여 지워야 해요
'클렌징'과 '세수'를 같은 말로 쓰는 것 — 세수는 기본 세안, 클렌징은 화장 제거 단계예요
클렌징을 영어 발음 'cleansing'으로만 떠올려 동사화를 빼먹는 것 — 한국어에서는 '클렌징 하다'로 써요

structuredNuance.t: 클렌징은 화장과 노폐물을 녹여 지우는 세안 단계를 통틀어 가리켜요. 오일·밤·워터 등 제형이 다양하고, 화장이 진한 날은 클렌징 후 폼클렌저로 한 번 더 씻는 '이중 세안'을 권해요. '꼼꼼히 하다', '화장을 지우다', '건너뛰다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
핵심 구분은 그냥 물로 씻는 '세수'와의 차이예요. 세수는 물·비누로 얼굴을 씻는 일반 동작이고, 클렌징은 메이크업까지 전용 제품으로 '녹여서' 지운다는 점이 달라요. 그래서 물세수(물만으로 씻기)는 클렌징으로 치지 않아요.
외래어(cleansing)예요.
'클렌징 하다'처럼 '하다'를 붙여 동사로 써요.

entries.shortExplanation: 토너 means "toner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "toner" is 토너 (toneo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 토너 패드 ("toner pads"). Watch the particle attached to 토너 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 미리 적셔 둔 패드; 한국에서 아주 인기예요
각질을 부드럽게 정리해 주는 토너
스킨과 같은 단계, 동사는 바르다
진정 = 자극을 가라앉힘; 민감 피부용 라벨

examples.ko: 세안 후에 토너로 피부 결을 정돈해요.
examples.romanization: sean hue toneoro pibu gyeoreul jeongdonhaeyo.
examples.en: After washing, I smooth my skin's texture with toner.
examples.note: 결 = 표면 무늬·질감; 정돈하다 = 가지런히 하다

examples.en: Toner pads are really popular these days.
examples.note: 패드 타입은 최근 한국 뷰티 트렌드예요

examples.ko: 각질이 잘 일어나서 일주일에 두 번만 각질 토너를 써요.
examples.romanization: gakjiri jal ireonaseo iljuire du beonman gakjil toneoreul sseoyo.
examples.en: My skin flakes easily, so I use exfoliating toner only twice a week.
examples.note: 만 = 한정 조사; 과한 사용 주의를 보여줘요

entries.nuance: 토너는 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 제품으로, 사실상 '스킨'과 같은 단계를 가리키는 외래어(toner)예요. 둘의 분담을 알아 두면 좋은데, 일상 회화에서는 '스킨'이, 제품 설명·마케팅이나 기능을 강조할 때는 '토너'가 더 흔하게 쓰이는 느낌이에요. 그래서 같은 병을 두고 친구끼리는 '스킨 발랐어?'라고 하고, 광고에서는 '○○ 토너'라고 부르는 식이에요. 특히 '토너 패드', '각질 토너', '진정 토너'처럼 합성어로 자주 등장해요. 영어 화자가 두 단어를 다른 제품으로 오해하기 쉬운데 본질은 같은 단계라는 점이 핵심이고, 동사는 '바르다'를 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
토너와 스킨을 서로 다른 제품으로 생각하는 것 — 본질적으로 같은 첫 단계예요(이름·뉘앙스만 달라요)
각질 토너를 매일 쓰는 것 — 자주 쓰면 오히려 피부가 예민해질 수 있어요
토너에 '하다'를 붙여 '토너 하다'라고 하는 것 — 바르는 제품이라 '토너 바르다'가 맞아요

structuredNuance.t: 토너는 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 제품으로, 사실상 '스킨'과 같은 단계를 가리켜요. 특히 '토너 패드', '각질 토너', '진정 토너'처럼 합성어로 자주 등장해요.
'스킨'과의 분담을 알아 두면 좋은데, 일상 회화에서는 '스킨'이, 제품 설명·마케팅이나 기능을 강조할 때는 '토너'가 더 흔하게 쓰이는 느낌이에요. 그래서 같은 병을 두고 친구끼리는 '스킨 발랐어?'라고 하고, 광고에서는 '○○ 토너'라고 부르는 식이에요.
외래어(toner)예요.
동사는 '바르다'를 써요.
영어 화자가 토너와 스킨 두 단어를 다른 제품으로 오해하기 쉬운데, 본질은 같은 단계라는 점이 핵심이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 향수 means "perfume" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 향수 (hyangsu) = "perfume". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 향수 뿌리다 ("to spray perfume") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 향수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 바르다가 아니라 뿌리다예요
향 = 냄새·향기; '향이 좋다'처럼 써요
매장·온라인에서 흔한 요청
은은하다 = 진하지 않고 잔잔하다, 칭찬이에요

examples.en: Don't spray on too much perfume.
examples.note: 사무실·지하철 예절과 관련된 부탁

examples.ko: 이 향수는 향이 은은해서 부담이 없어요.
examples.romanization: i hyangsuneun hyangi euneunhaeseo budami eopseoyo.
examples.en: This perfume is subtle, so it isn't overpowering.
examples.note: 부담이 없다 = 거슬리지 않다; 향수 평에 흔해요

examples.ko: 면접 보러 갈 때는 향수를 안 뿌리는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop boreo gal ttaeneun hyangsureul an ppurineun ge joayo.
examples.en: It's better not to wear perfume when going to a job interview.
examples.note: 면접 = 면접 시험; 거주자에게 실용적인 조언

entries.nuance: 향수(香水)는 한자 그대로 '향기 향(香)' + '물 수(水)', 즉 '향기 나는 물'이라는 뜻의 한자어예요. 핵심 포인트는 동사인데, 향수는 분사형이라 '바르다'가 아니라 '뿌리다'와 함께 써요. 영어 'put on/wear perfume'을 직역해 '향수 바르다'라고 하면 어색하니 주의하세요. 비슷한 향 제품과도 구분되는데, 농도가 옅고 가벼운 건 보통 '향수' 안에서 오 드 뚜왈렛 등으로 나뉘고, 더 넓게는 '바디미스트'처럼 따로 부르는 제품도 있어요. 한국에서는 좁은 지하철·사무실을 의식해 '은은한' 향을 선호하는 분위기가 강하고, 너무 강하면 '향이 세다'며 다소 부정적으로 봐요. '향이 좋다·은은하다·오래간다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'향수 바르다'라고 하는 것 — 향수는 뿌리는 제품이라 동사 '뿌리다'를 써요
향을 너무 진하게 쓰는 것 — 한국의 사무실·대중교통 예절은 '은은한' 향을 선호해요
'향'과 '향수'를 섞어 쓰는 것 — '향'은 냄새 자체, '향수'는 그 향을 내는 제품이에요

structuredNuance.t: 향수는 '향기 나는 물'을 뜻해요. 한국에서는 좁은 지하철·사무실을 의식해 '은은한' 향을 선호하는 분위기가 강하고, 너무 강하면 '향이 세다'며 다소 부정적으로 봐요. '향이 좋다·은은하다·오래간다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
비슷한 향 제품과도 구분되는데, 농도가 옅고 가벼운 건 보통 '향수' 안에서 오 드 뚜왈렛 등으로 나뉘고, 더 넓게는 '바디미스트'처럼 따로 부르는 제품도 있어요.
향수(香水)는 한자 그대로 '향기 향(香)' + '물 수(水)', 즉 '향기 나는 물'이라는 뜻의 한자어예요.
핵심 포인트는 동사인데, 향수는 분사형이라 '바르다'가 아니라 '뿌리다'와 함께 써요.
영어 'put on/wear perfume'을 직역해 '향수 바르다'라고 하면 어색하니 주의하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 매니큐어 means "nail polish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매니큐어 (maenikyueo) means "nail polish". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 매니큐어 바르다 ("to apply nail polish"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 매니큐어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 바르다
리무버(remover)가 있어야 지워져요
색 = 컬러; 원하는 색을 골라요
젤네일은 더 오래가는 살롱 시술이에요

examples.en: I painted my nails at home over the weekend.
examples.note: 집에서 직접 하는 셀프 네일 상황

examples.en: My polish chipped, so I removed it with remover.
examples.note: 벗겨지다 = (막이) 떨어져 나가다; 자동사예요

examples.ko: 젤네일은 매니큐어보다 훨씬 오래가서 자주 안 해도 돼요.
examples.romanization: jelneireun maenikyueoboda hwolssin oraegaseo jaju an haedo dwaeyo.
examples.en: Gel lasts much longer than regular polish, so I redo it less often.
examples.note: 보다 = 비교 조사; 살롱 젤 vs 셀프 매니큐어 대비

entries.nuance: 한국어 '매니큐어'는 영어 manicure와 뜻이 어긋나는 대표적 함정 단어예요. 영어 manicure는 '손톱·손 관리 서비스 전체'를 뜻하지만, 한국어 매니큐어는 손톱에 바르는 색깔 있는 액체, 즉 영어로는 nail polish를 가리켜요. 그래서 손 관리 서비스를 말하려면 '네일(아트)', '네일 케어'라고 해야 해요. 더 오래가는 살롱 시술은 '젤네일'이라 따로 부르는데, 젤네일은 전용 램프에 굳혀 2~3주 가는 반면 매니큐어는 며칠이면 벗겨지는 차이가 있어요. 동사는 '바르다'이고, 지울 때는 '리무버'가 필요해요. '벗겨지다(막이 떨어지다)'는 자동사라 '매니큐어가 벗겨졌어요'처럼 매니큐어가 주어가 돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
매니큐어를 '손 관리 서비스(manicure)'라는 뜻으로 쓰는 것 — 한국어에서는 바르는 '네일 폴리시'를 뜻하고, 서비스는 '네일'이라고 해요
리무버 없이 매니큐어를 지우려는 것 — 전용 리무버가 있어야 지워져요
저절로 벗겨진 걸 말하면서 '매니큐어를 벗겨졌어요'처럼 '을/를'을 붙이는 것 — '벗겨지다'는 자동사라 '매니큐어가 벗겨졌어요'가 맞아요(내가 일부러 떼어 낼 때만 타동사 '벗기다'를 써요)

entries.shortExplanation: 각질 means "dead skin, flaky skin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "dead skin, flaky skin" is 각질 (gakjil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 각질 제거 ("exfoliation (dead-skin removal)"). Watch the particle attached to 각질 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 제거 = 없앰; 흔한 제품·시술 이름
일어나다 = (살갗이) 들떠 일어나다
관리 = 꾸준히 돌봄
제거제 = 없애 주는 제품

examples.en: It's winter, so my face is getting flaky.
examples.note: 일어나다 = 살갗이 들뜨다; 자동사예요

examples.ko: 저는 일주일에 한 번만 각질을 제거해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun iljuire han beonman gakjireul jegeohaeyo.
examples.en: I exfoliate just once a week.
examples.note: 만 = 한정; 과하지 않게 한다는 뉘앙스

examples.ko: 각질이 많으면 화장이 잘 안 먹어서 들떠 보여요.
examples.romanization: gakjiri maneumyeon hwajangi jal an meogeoseo deultteo boyeoyo.
examples.en: With lots of dead skin, makeup doesn't take well and looks patchy.
examples.note: 화장이 안 먹다 = 화장이 잘 안 받다(관용구)

entries.nuance: 각질(角質)은 한자로 '뿔 각(角)' + '바탕 질(質)', 곧 피부 표면의 단단해진 죽은 세포층을 뜻하는 한자어로, 영어의 dead skin·keratin에 해당해요. 일상에서는 얼굴이나 몸에서 하얗게 들뜨거나 벗겨지는 살갗을 가리켜요. 헷갈리기 쉬운 피부 고민인 '여드름'과는 달라요 — 여드름은 모공이 막혀 생기는 뾰루지이고, 각질은 표면의 묵은 살갗이에요. 각질이 많으면 '화장이 안 먹는다(잘 받지 않는다)'는 관용 표현과 함께 자주 쓰여요. 동사 짝으로 '각질이 일어나다(들뜨다)'는 자동사라 각질이 주어가 되고, 없앨 때는 '각질을 제거하다'처럼 타동사로 써요. 다만 너무 자주 제거하면 피부가 오히려 예민해질 수 있어요.

각질(묵은 살갗)과 여드름(뾰루지)을 같은 문제로 보는 것 — 원인과 관리법이 달라요
각질을 너무 자주 제거하는 것 — 피부 장벽이 약해져 오히려 예민해져요
'일어나다'를 사람 주어로 오해하는 것 — '각질이 일어나다'에서 일어나는 주체는 사람이 아니라 각질이에요

entries.shortExplanation: 화장솜 means "cotton pad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 화장솜 (hwajangsom) = "cotton pad". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 화장솜에 토너 묻히다 ("to dab toner on a cotton pad") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 화장솜, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to dab toner on a cotton pad
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = 적셔서 배게 하다(타동사)

usagePhrases.en: to wipe with a cotton pad
usagePhrases.note: 닦다 = 문질러 깨끗이 하다
단위는 장(얇고 납작한 것)
매니큐어 지울 때도 써요

examples.en: I soak a cotton pad with toner and wipe my face.
examples.note: 묻히다(타동사) + 닦다; 토너 사용법을 보여줘요

examples.ko: 매니큐어 지울 때 화장솜에 리무버를 적셔서 써요.
examples.romanization: maenikyueo jiul ttae hwajangsome rimubeoreul jeoksyeoseo sseoyo.
examples.en: When removing polish, I soak a cotton pad with remover.
examples.note: 적시다 = 액체에 젖게 하다; 묻히다와 비슷해요

examples.ko: 화장솜이 다 떨어져서 다이소에서 한 통 샀어요.
examples.romanization: hwajangsomi da tteoreojyeoseo daisoeseo han tong sasseoyo.
examples.en: I ran out of cotton pads, so I bought a tub at Daiso.
examples.note: 통 = 통째 용기 단위; 자취 생필품 느낌

entries.nuance: 화장솜은 '화장(化粧)' + 순우리말 '솜(cotton wool)'이 합쳐진 말로, 스킨이나 리무버를 묻혀 얼굴·손톱을 닦는 동그란 화장용 솜을 뜻해요. 발음이 비슷한 '화장지(化粧紙, 휴지·tissue)'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 화장솜은 액체를 머금는 두툼한 솜이고 화장지는 코를 풀거나 닦는 얇은 종이라 완전히 다른 물건이에요. 다이소·올리브영에서 싸게 사는 생필품이라 자취생이 자주 사요. 세는 단위로는 '개'가 아니라 얇고 납작한 것을 세는 '장'을 쓰는 게 자연스러워요. 자주 어울리는 동사는 '(토너를) 묻히다·적시다', '(얼굴을) 닦다'이고, '한 장 뽑다', '다 떨어지다' 같은 표현과도 함께 쓰여요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
화장솜을 '화장지(tissue)'나 '휴지'와 혼동하는 것 — 화장솜은 액체를 머금는 화장용 솜이에요
단위를 잘못 쓰는 것 — 화장솜은 '개'가 아니라 얇고 납작한 것을 세는 '장'으로 세요
'묻다'와 '묻히다'를 헷갈리는 것 — 솜에 토너를 적실 때는 타동사 '묻히다'를 써서 '토너를 묻혀요'라고 해요

화장솜은 '화장(化粧)' + 순우리말 '솜(cotton wool)'이 합쳐진 말이에요.
자주 어울리는 동사는 '(토너를) 묻히다·적시다', '(얼굴을) 닦다'예요.

entries.shortExplanation: 니트 means "knit top / sweater" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 니트 (niteu) means "knit top / sweater". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 니트를 입다 ("to wear a knit top"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 니트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: any upper-body garment takes 입다, never 신다/쓰다
따갑다 (prickly) is the #1 wool complaint; don't say 가렵다, which is 'my skin itches'
clothing is counted with the counter 벌, not the generic 개
Koreans size up a sweater by thickness, so 얇다·두껍다 are the habitual adjectives

examples.en: It's a bit chilly today so I wore a knit.
examples.note: simplest frame: weather reason + 입다 in casual 해요체

examples.ko: 이 니트 목 부분이 따가운데 다른 색도 있어요?
examples.romanization: i niteu mok bubuni ttagaunde dareun saekdo isseoyo?
examples.en: The neck of this knit is itchy — do you have other colors too?
examples.note: real in-store line; 따갑다 describes the prickly wool sensation, not skin itch

examples.ko: 캐시미어 니트는 보풀이 잘 생겨서 손빨래해야 해요.
examples.romanization: kaesimieo niteuneun bopuri jal saenggyeoseo sonppallaehaeya haeyo.
examples.en: Cashmere knits pill easily so you have to hand-wash them.
examples.note: care talk: 보풀이 생기다 = to pill, 손빨래 = hand-wash

entries.nuance: 니트 comes from English 'knit', but in everyday Korean it has narrowed to mean one specific thing: a sweater-type pullover top, the fall/winter staple — NOT 'any knitted item' as in English. Its near-synonym 스웨터 exists but sounds slightly dated or textbook-ish; a real Korean shopper says 니트 far more often, and the two are interchangeable when they do appear. The dividing line worth knowing is 니트 (a finished sweater garment) versus 가디건 (an open-front knit you button up): both are knitwear, but 니트 closes over the head while 가디건 opens at the front. Register is fully neutral — you can say 니트 to anyone. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the verb: because you put it on the body you must use 입다, and saying 니트를 신다 (that's for shoes) or 쓰다 (hats/glasses) sounds badly wrong. Also resist the literal logic 'knit = anything knitted'; in Korean it is the garment, and the prickly complaint is 따갑다, distinct from 가렵다 (skin itching).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 니트를 신다 or 니트를 쓰다 — those verbs are for footwear and headwear; a sweater goes on the torso, so it must be 니트를 입다.
Assuming 니트 covers any knitted object (scarf, hat, blanket) like English 'knit' does — in daily Korean it specifically means a sweater-type top, so use 모자/목도리 for the others.
Describing the itch as 니트가 가려워요 — 가렵다 means your skin itches; the prickly-fabric feeling Koreans name is 따갑다, so say 니트가 따가워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 패딩 means "padded (down) winter jacket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "padded (down) winter jacket" is 패딩 (paeding). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 패딩을 입다 ("to wear a padded jacket"). Watch the particle attached to 패딩 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: outerwear still uses 입다, the universal 'wear-on-body' verb
the two lengths Koreans almost always specify by name
warmth is the whole selling point, so 따뜻하다 is the default praise
counted with the clothing counter 벌, not 개

examples.en: I'm thinking of buying a padded jacket for winter.
examples.note: simple intent: -려고요 (planning to), neutral 해요체

examples.en: They say short padding is trendier than long padding this year.
examples.note: trend talk: 유행이다 = to be in style, -래요 = I heard

examples.ko: 이 패딩 거위털이라서 가벼운데도 진짜 따뜻해요.
examples.romanization: i paeding geowiteoriraseo gabyeoundedo jinjja ttatteutaeyo.
examples.en: This one's goose down, so it's light yet really warm.
examples.note: spec talk: 거위털 = goose down vs 오리털 = duck down vs 솜 = synthetic

entries.nuance: 패딩 is a Konglish clipping of 'padded (jacket)' and names the quilted, down- or fiber-filled puffer that is Korea's winter essential. The key contrast for a learner is 패딩 vs 코트: a 코트 is a wool/dressy overcoat, while 패딩 is the puffy insulated one — calling every winter coat 코트 is the most common slip, because to Koreans they are different categories of garment. You will rarely hear 패딩 used bare; people specify length, 롱패딩 (below the knee, once almost a school uniform among students) or 숏패딩 (hip-length), and the fill (거위털 goose down / 오리털 duck down / 솜 synthetic) which drives both warmth and price. Register is neutral and everyday. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: use 입다 (not 신다/쓰다) since it's body clothing, and don't default to 코트 for a puffer — and remember Koreans treat 'down jacket' as one fixed word 패딩 rather than translating 'down' (오리털/거위털) into the name.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every winter coat 코트 — a puffy down jacket is specifically 패딩, whereas 코트 is a wool dress overcoat; mixing them makes a shopkeeper picture the wrong garment.
Forgetting to specify 롱/숏 — Koreans almost always say which length, so just 패딩 주세요 sounds vague; say 롱패딩 / 숏패딩.
Using 신다 or 쓰다 because it's bulky outerwear — it still sits on the torso, so the verb is 입다.

entries.shortExplanation: 후드티 means "hoodie (hooded sweatshirt)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: it's a top, so the verb is 입다
걸치다 = casually layer/throw on, looser than 입다
기모 = brushed inner fleece, the key warmth keyword in winter listings

entries.nuance: 후드티 is a homegrown Korean coinage stitching English 'hood' onto 티 (from 티셔츠, T-shirt) — literally 'hood-tee' — and means a pullover hooded sweatshirt; think of it as a 맨투맨 (crewneck sweatshirt) with a hood added. The sharp near-synonym contrast is 후드티 (pullover, goes over the head) vs 후드집업 (the zip-up hooded jacket, 집업 from 'zip-up'): Koreans name these as two distinct products, so a learner who lumps them together will ask for the wrong rack. Note also that the bare English word 'hoodie' would be transliterated 후디, but the standard, natural Korean is 후드티 — write and say that. Register is casual and youthful but totally acceptable in everyday speech. Pitfalls: use 입다 (or the breezier 걸치다 for 'throw on'), not 신다/쓰다; and don't import the English spelling 후디. The warmth keyword to recognize when shopping is 기모, the brushed fleece lining.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing or saying 후디 from the English word — the standard Korean form is 후드티; 후디 sounds like raw English transliteration.
Confusing 후드티 (pullover hoodie) with 후드집업 (the zip-up version) — the zip one has its own fixed name, so asking for 후드티 won't get you a zipper.
Using 쓰다 because it has a hood you put over your head — the garment as a whole is worn on the body, so it's 후드티를 입다 (the hood being up is 모자를 쓰다 separately).

Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

entries.nuance: 부츠 is straightforwardly English 'boots' and covers footwear rising above the ankle. The single most important thing for an English speaker is the verb: shoes and boots take 신다 (put on the feet), and 입다 — the verb for body clothing — is simply wrong here, a mistake learners make constantly because English uses one word 'wear' for everything. Korean also splits the counter: clothing is 벌 but footwear is 켤레 (a pair), so 부츠 한 켤레, never 부츠 한 개. Lengths get named — 발목 부츠 (ankle boots, also 앵클부츠) vs 롱부츠 (tall boots) — and winter shearling ones are 털부츠 (털 = fur). One more practical trap: Korean shoe sizes are millimeters (245 means 245 mm), so quote the number, not a US/EU size. Register is neutral; say 부츠 to anyone.

Counting boots with 개 instead of the pair-counter 켤레 — say 부츠 한 켤레, since 개 is for generic objects and undercounts a pair.
Giving a US/EU shoe size — Korean sizing is in mm, so 'size 8' means nothing in store; say the number like 245 or 250.

entries.nuance: 맨투맨 looks like English but is pure Konglish: it literally reads 'man-to-man', yet it means a crewneck sweatshirt — a round-necked, hood-less pullover. Translating it word-for-word is the signature pitfall; there is no 'man to man' meaning, and an English speaker hearing it for the first time will guess wrong. The decisive near-synonym contrast is 맨투맨 (no hood) vs 후드티 (hood added): they are the same body of garment differing only by the hood, and Koreans pick the word precisely, so mixing them up sends you to the wrong product. (English 'sweatshirt' is the closest gloss, but Koreans default to 맨투맨.) Register is casual-everyday and fine for all ages. Use 입다, not 신다/쓰다. A bonus you'll hear endlessly: 맨투맨에 청바지 ('a sweatshirt with jeans') is the stock example of a 무난한 (safe, can't-go-wrong) outfit in Korean fashion chatter.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 맨투맨 literally as 'man to man' — it's Konglish for a crewneck sweatshirt and has nothing to do with one-on-one; just learn it as a fixed clothing word.
Mixing it up with 후드티 — 맨투맨 has NO hood while 후드티 does, so asking for 맨투맨 won't get you a hood and vice versa.
Using 쓰다/신다 — it's a torso top, so the verb is 입다.

entries.nuance: 가디건 is the open-front knit layer you close with buttons or a zip — English 'cardigan'. There is a spelling fork worth flagging: the prescriptive standard is 카디건, but in real life and in online shops almost everyone writes and says 가디건, so that's the form you'll actually encounter. The sharp contrast a learner needs is 가디건 (opens at the front, often worn loose) vs 니트 (a closed pullover you put over the head): both are knitwear, but only the cardigan unbuttons, which is why it pairs naturally with 걸치다 ('drape/throw on') as well as 입다. Register is neutral. Pitfalls: don't insist on 카디건 in conversation when you mean to be understood and find it in a search bar — say 가디건; and use 입다/걸치다, not 신다/쓰다. A very Korean collocation: people 챙기다 (bring) a thin 가디건 against fierce office air-conditioning.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 가디건 (open-front, buttons/zip) with 니트 (a closed pullover) — if it opens at the front it's a 가디건, so asking for a 니트 gets you something you can't unbutton.
Insisting on the textbook 카디건 in speech and searches — most Koreans say and type 가디건, so you'll communicate and find results better with that form.
Using 신다/쓰다 — it's body clothing, so 입다 (or 걸치다 for loosely draping it on).

entries.nuance: 레깅스 is English 'leggings' — the stretchy, skin-tight bottoms that double as activewear and everyday athleisure. Two grammar facts trip up English speakers. First, even though they look like tights and English calls socks/tights items you might 'put on your legs', in Korean leggings are body clothing for the lower half, so the verb is 입다 and the counter is 벌 — using 신다 or counting them 한 켤레 (the shoe/sock pair-counter) is wrong. Second, English forces the plural 'leggings', but Korean treats 레깅스 as a single grammatical unit: 레깅스를 입다, never any plural marking. Worth distinguishing from 스타킹 (sheer stockings/tights) and 타이츠 (thicker tights), which are different garments. Register is neutral and casual. The collocation every buyer checks is 비침/비치다 — whether they go see-through when you bend or sit — so you'll see it all over reviews.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting leggings with 켤레 — that pair-counter is for shoes and socks; leggings are clothing worn with 입다, so the counter is 벌.
Using 신다 because they sheath the legs like tights — in Korean they're lower-body clothing, so 레깅스를 입다.
Treating 레깅스 as a plural like English 'leggings' and over-marking it — Korean keeps it singular and unmarked: 레깅스를 입다.

entries.nuance: 슬리퍼 (English 'slipper') in Korea covers open-backed slides worn both as indoor 실내화 and for quick neighborhood errands — broader than the cozy house-slipper the English word suggests. Being footwear, it strictly takes 신다 and is counted with 켤레; the recurring English-speaker error is 슬리퍼를 입다, since English 'wear' hides the verb distinction Korean enforces. The crucial near-synonym line is 슬리퍼 vs 쪼리: the thong type with a strap between the toes is its own word 쪼리 (flip-flops), so calling those 슬리퍼 is imprecise — slides are 슬리퍼, thongs are 쪼리. Culturally, the two-strap 삼선 슬리퍼 ('three-stripe slides') is practically a badge of the broke-but-comfy university/자취 (living-alone) student, so you'll hear it referenced affectionately. Register is casual. Bonus contrast: indoor 실내화 vs outdoor wearing is just context, same word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 입다 for slippers — they go on the feet, so the verb is 신다, like all footwear.
Calling flip-flops 슬리퍼 — the toe-thong type is specifically 쪼리; reserve 슬리퍼 for open-backed slides.
Counting them 한 개 — footwear pairs are counted with 켤레, so 슬리퍼 한 켤레.

entries.nuance: 조끼 is a native Korean word (not a loanword) for a sleeveless top layer — it covers the torso while leaving the arms free. The near-synonym to know is the loanword 베스트 (from English 'vest'), which tends to be used for the dressy waistcoat in a suit, whereas plain 조끼 is the all-purpose everyday/outdoor sleeveless layer; both can mean 'vest', but a Korean reaches for 조끼 for the casual or padded kind. The hugely popular variant is 패딩 조끼 (puffer vest), a go-to for 환절기/간절기 (the changing seasons), and the arm-freedom makes 조끼 a favorite for hiking and outdoor work. The main contrast students confuse is 조끼 (sleeveless) vs 가디건 (sleeved open-front knit) — if it has sleeves it isn't a 조끼. Register is neutral. Use 입다, not 신다/쓰다; it's body clothing despite covering only the trunk.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 조끼 (sleeveless) with 가디건 (a sleeved open-front knit) — a vest has no sleeves, so the two are different garments.
Using 신다 or 쓰다 — it's worn on the torso, so the verb is 입다.
Assuming 조끼 always means a formal waistcoat — the dressy suit version is often called 베스트; plain 조끼 is the casual/padded all-rounder.

The near-synonym to know is the loanword 베스트 (from English 'vest'), which tends to be used for the dressy waistcoat in a suit, whereas plain 조끼 is the all-purpose everyday/outdoor sleeveless layer; both can mean 'vest', but a Korean reaches for 조끼 for the casual or padded kind. The main contrast students confuse is 조끼 (sleeveless) vs 가디건 (sleeved open-front knit) — if it has sleeves it isn't a 조끼.
Use 입다, not 신다/쓰다; it's body clothing despite covering only the trunk.

entries.shortExplanation: 스카프 means "scarf (light/fashion, often silk)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스카프 (seukapeu) means "scarf (light/fashion, often silk)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스카프를 하다 ("to wear a scarf"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스카프 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: neck accessories commonly take the light verb 하다
두르다 = to wrap/drape around, very natural for neck/shoulders
the typical material; silk ones are popular gifts
a thin flat cloth is counted with 장 (the sheet-counter)

examples.en: I wore a scarf today.
examples.note: simplest frame showing the accessory verb 하다, not 입다

examples.ko: 목에 스카프 하나 두르면 분위기가 확 달라져요.
examples.romanization: moge seukapeu hana dureumyeon bunwigiga hwak dallajyeoyo.
examples.en: Wrapping a scarf around your neck totally changes the vibe.
examples.note: fashion talk: 두르다 = to wrap, 분위기 = mood/vibe, 확 = dramatically

examples.en: I bought a silk scarf as a gift.
examples.note: 선물용 = for gifting; flat cloth, so counted 한 장

entries.nuance: 스카프 (English 'scarf') in Korean specifically means the LIGHT, decorative cloth — often silk — you tie around the neck, head, or even a bag handle, worn for style rather than warmth. The essential near-synonym contrast is 스카프 vs 목도리/머플러: 목도리 (native word) and 머플러 (from 'muffler') are the thick, warm winter neck-wraps, while 스카프 is the thin fashion piece — confusing them means wearing the wrong thing for the wrong purpose. The verb is its own pitfall: accessories like this take 하다 ('스카프를 하다') or 두르다 ('wrap'), and the body-clothing verb 입다 is wrong here, just as it would be for 모자 (which takes 쓰다). Because it's a thin flat sheet, the counter is 장, not the clothing counter 벌. Register is neutral. A current collocation: tying a 스카프 onto a 가방 (bag) is a popular styling trick.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 스카프 and 목도리 as the same thing — 스카프 is a light fashion cloth, while 목도리/머플러 is a thick warm winter muffler; pick the right one for warmth vs style.
Using 입다 for a scarf — neck accessories take 하다 or 두르다, so say 스카프를 하다 / 스카프를 두르다.
Counting it with the clothing counter 벌 — a thin flat cloth uses 장, so 스카프 한 장.

entries.shortExplanation: 백팩 means "backpack" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "backpack" is 백팩 (baekpaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 백팩을 메다 ("to carry a backpack (on the back/shoulder)"). Watch the particle attached to 백팩 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to carry a backpack (on the back/shoulder)
usagePhrases.note: shoulder- and back-worn bags use 메다, not 들다
bags are counted with the generic counter 개
the commuter/student staple; 노트북 수납 = laptop storage is a top spec
weight is a leading buying factor, so 가볍다 recurs in reviews

examples.en: I usually carry a backpack around.
examples.note: simplest frame: habit + 메다, anchoring the bag verb

examples.ko: 출퇴근할 때 노트북 넣을 백팩이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: chultoegeunhal ttae noteubung neoeul baekpaegi piryohaeyo.
examples.en: I need a backpack to put my laptop in for commuting.
examples.note: real need: 출퇴근 = commute, 넣을 = relative form 'to put in'

examples.ko: 이 백팩은 수납공간이 많아서 마음에 들어요.
examples.romanization: i baekpaegeun sunapgonggani manaseo maeume deureoyo.
examples.en: I like this backpack because it has lots of storage.
examples.note: feature praise: 수납공간 = storage compartments, 마음에 들다 = to like

entries.nuance: 백팩 is English 'backpack' and names the two-shoulder bag carried on the back. The verb is the heart of the matter: bags worn on the shoulder or back take 메다, while 들다 means to carry by hand (a tote, a paper bag) and is wrong for a backpack — English's single 'carry' hides this, so 백팩을 들다 is a classic slip when you mean wearing it on your back. The useful near-synonym contrast is 백팩 vs 배낭 (Sino-Korean 背囊, literally 'back-bag'): 배낭 carries a strong hiking/trekking, outdoorsy flavor (think 배낭여행 = backpacking trip), whereas 백팩 is the everyday, commuter, fashion-bag word — they overlap but feel different, so reaching for 배낭 to describe a sleek office bag sounds slightly off. Bags are counted with the generic 개 (한 개), not the clothing counter 벌. Register is neutral. The features Koreans scrutinize most are 노트북 수납 (laptop storage) and weight (가볍다).

Using 들다 (carry by hand) for a backpack — back/shoulder bags take 메다, so it's 백팩을 메다; 들다 implies you're holding it in your hand.
Assuming 백팩 and 배낭 feel identical — 배낭 sounds hiking/outdoors (as in 배낭여행), while 백팩 is the everyday commuter word, so they aren't freely swappable.
Counting bags with the clothing counter 벌 — a bag is a generic object, so use 개: 백팩 한 개.

entries.shortExplanation: 운동복 means "workout clothes / activewear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 운동복 (undongbok) = "workout clothes / activewear". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 운동복을 입다 ("to wear workout clothes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 운동복, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: clothing, so 입다
갈아입다 = to change (one outfit) into (another); -으로 marks the result
벌 here counts a top-and-bottom set, not a single piece
편하다 = comfortable, the number-one criterion

examples.en: I wear workout clothes when I exercise.
examples.note: simplest frame: activity + 입다, neutral 해요체

examples.en: Before the gym I change into workout clothes.
examples.note: routine: 헬스장 = gym, 갈아입다 = change into, -기 전에 = before ~ing

examples.ko: 땀 잘 마르는 운동복으로 하나 사려고요.
examples.romanization: ttam jal mareuneun undongbogeuro hana saryeogoyo.
examples.en: I'm planning to buy activewear that dries sweat fast.
examples.note: real spec: 땀이 마르다 = sweat dries; -려고요 = planning to

entries.nuance: 운동복 is a transparent Sino-Korean + native compound: 운동 (運動, 'exercise/movement') + 복 (服, 'clothing') = literally 'exercise-clothes', the umbrella term for activewear, both top and bottom. Because the hanja 복 means 'clothing/garment' generally, you'll meet it across many words (교복 school uniform, 한복 traditional dress, 수영복 swimsuit), which makes 운동복 easy to decode once you know the building block. The near-synonym to weigh is 트레이닝복 (from 'training'): that leans toward the matching tracksuit/sweats set (casually 츄리닝), while 운동복 spans gym, yoga, and running gear more broadly — overlapping but not identical. A subtle point for English speakers: 운동복 normally denotes a top-and-bottom SET, so it's counted 한 벌 and 'wear' is 입다, not 신다/쓰다. With athleisure now everywhere, people 평소에도 (even normally) wear 운동복, so it surfaces well beyond the gym. Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 신다/쓰다 — workout clothes are body clothing, so the verb is 입다 (and the swap action is 갈아입다).
Treating 운동복 as one single garment — it usually means a top-and-bottom set, so it's counted with 벌: 운동복 한 벌.
Assuming 운동복 and 트레이닝복 are identical — 트레이닝복 specifically suggests a tracksuit/sweats set, while 운동복 broadly covers all exercise wear.

entries.shortExplanation: 잔 means "glass; cup (counter for drinks)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잔 (jan) means "glass; cup (counter for drinks)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 커피 한 잔 ("one cup of coffee"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday default: 잔 covers any served drink — coffee, tea, water, beer, soju.
Bar shorthand for another round; you'll hear this constantly while drinking together.
Written as ONE word, this is a verb meaning 'go have a (casual) drink', not literally one glass.
Spacing matters: number + space + 잔 (세 잔), never 세잔.

examples.en: One glass of water, please.
examples.note: Simplest form: [noun] + [native number] + 잔. The counter comes AFTER the number, before the verb.

examples.ko: 저는 하루에 커피를 세 잔씩 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun harue keopireul se janssing masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink three cups of coffee each day.
examples.note: Note 씩 ('each/per') after the counter — '세 잔씩' = three cups apiece per day, a natural habit phrase.

examples.ko: 딱 한 잔만 더 하고 갈게요.
examples.romanization: tta kan janman deo hago galgeyo.
examples.en: I'll have just one more drink and then go.
examples.note: Real bar line: 딱...만 = 'just exactly one', and 한 잔 하다 here means 'have a drink', not eat.

entries.nuance: 잔 is the counter for a serving of liquid held in a cup or glass — it counts the POURED drink, not the container itself. Its near-rivals are 병 (a whole bottle) and 컵 (the physical cup as an object), and the dividing line is what you're measuring: 맥주 한 병 is a full bottle, 맥주 한 잔 is one glass poured from it. The hanja is 盞 ('small cup'), though it feels fully native in use and always takes native-Korean numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean 일/이. Watch two traps: 한잔하다 written together is a VERB ('go for a drink') and is idiomatic, so don't read it as a literal count; and English 'a cup of coffee' tempts learners to reach for 컵, but the natural measure word for the drink itself is 잔.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 일 잔, 이 잔 with Sino-Korean numbers. Counters of servings take native numbers: 한 잔, 두 잔, 세 잔.
Using 잔 to count bottles. A sealed/whole bottle is 병 (맥주 두 병); 잔 is only the glass poured out.
Writing the drink-verb as two words '한 잔 하다' when you mean the idiom 'grab a drink' — the set verb is 한잔하다, one word.

entries.shortExplanation: 켤레 means "pair (counter for shoes, socks, gloves)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "pair (counter for shoes, socks, gloves)" is 켤레 (kyeolle). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신발 한 켤레 ("one pair of shoes"). Watch the particle attached to 켤레 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 켤레 counts things worn as a matching two-of-a-kind: shoes, socks, gloves.
Native numbers only: 한, 두, 세 켤레 — never 일 켤레.
The go-to question form when buying footwear or socks.
Gloves arrive as a set of two, so 켤레, not 개.

examples.en: I want to buy a pair of sneakers.
examples.note: Basic shape: [item] + 한 켤레. One 켤레 = the whole pair, both shoes together.

examples.en: Three pairs of socks are 5,000 won.
examples.note: Market pricing pattern: [quantity]에 [price]. 세 켤레에 = 'for three pairs'.

examples.ko: 등산하려고 두꺼운 양말 두 켤레를 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: deungsanharyeogo dukkeoun yangmal du kyeollereul chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I packed two pairs of thick socks to go hiking.
examples.note: 두 켤레를 marks the object; -려고 ('in order to') gives the purpose.

entries.nuance: 켤레 is the dedicated counter for items that come and are worn as a matched pair — shoes, sneakers, boots, socks, and gloves. The key conceptual point is that ONE 켤레 already means BOTH pieces together (the left and the right), so it functions like English 'a pair'; its near-synonym 짝, by contrast, isolates a SINGLE one of the two, as in 양말 한 짝 ('one sock' — implying its partner is missing). 켤레 is a native Korean word (no hanja) and always pairs with native numbers (한, 두, 세 켤레). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 because English counts 'a pair of shoes' as one set of objects — but footwear and hand/foot-wear that come in twos must take 켤레; another is calling a single lost shoe 한 켤레, when one of the pair is 한 짝.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting shoes with 개. 개 is the all-purpose counter for generic objects; matched footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레).
Saying 두 켤레 for one pair. A single pair (both shoes) is 한 켤레; 두 켤레 means two complete pairs.
Calling one sock 한 켤레. A lone single of the pair is 한 짝 (양말 한 짝); 켤레 always means both.

entries.shortExplanation: 벌 means "counter for sets of clothing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 벌 (beol) = "counter for sets of clothing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 옷 한 벌 ("one outfit/set of clothes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 벌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 벌 counts a complete garment or coordinated set: a suit, a dress, pajamas, hanbok.
A suit (jacket + trousers) counts as a single 벌 — one set.
Asks the count of garments or sets.
Native numbers go before 벌: 한, 두, 세 벌.

examples.en: I'm planning to buy a set of pajamas.
examples.note: Simple: [clothing] + 한 벌. Pajamas (top + bottom) are one 벌, not two.

examples.ko: 출근용 정장을 한 벌 새로 맞췄어요.
examples.romanization: chulgeunyong jeongjangeul han beol saero matchwosseoyo.
examples.en: I had a new work suit custom-made.
examples.note: 맞추다 = 'have tailor-made'; 출근용 = 'for commuting/work'. The whole suit = 한 벌.

examples.ko: 이번 여행에는 갈아입을 옷을 세 벌만 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeohaengeneun garaibeul oseul se beolman chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: For this trip I packed only three changes of clothes.
examples.note: 세 벌만 = 'just three sets'; 갈아입다 = 'to change clothes'.

entries.nuance: 벌 counts clothing as a COMPLETE garment or a coordinated outfit, so a suit, dress, hanbok, or pajama set is 한 벌 even though it physically has several pieces — the counter measures the whole worn unit, not the parts. Its near-synonyms split by what they measure: 벌 is the full set, while 장 counts a single flat piece (티셔츠 한 장 — one tee) and 개 is the casual generic count. 벌 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. The biggest English-speaker trap is logic-counting the pieces: a two-piece suit feels like 'two items', but the matching set is 한 벌, not 두 벌. A second trap is genre confusion — clothes are 벌, but the shoes that complete the look are 켤레, so don't say 신발 한 벌.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting a two-piece suit as 두 벌. The jacket-and-trousers set together is 한 벌 (one set).
Using 벌 for shoes. Footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레); clothing takes 벌.
Counting a single T-shirt as 한 벌 in casual speech. A flat single top is more naturally 티셔츠 한 장 or 한 개; 벌 leans toward full sets.

entries.shortExplanation: 권 means "counter for books and volumes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 권 (gwon) means "counter for books and volumes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 책 한 권 ("one book"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 권 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 권 counts bound things: books, notebooks, magazines, comic volumes.
Native numbers go before 권: 한, 두, 세 권.
The standard quantity question for anything bound.
Each volume of a series is counted separately as a 권.

examples.en: One notebook, please.
examples.note: Basic: [bound item] + 한 권. Notebooks count with 권 just like books.

examples.ko: 한 달에 책을 두 권 정도 읽어요.
examples.romanization: han dare chaegeul du gwon jeongdo ilgeoyo.
examples.en: I read about two books a month.
examples.note: 두 권 정도 = 'about two'; 정도 turns an exact count into an estimate.

examples.ko: 도서관에서 빌린 책 세 권을 오늘 반납해야 해요.
examples.romanization: doseogwaneseo billin chaek se gwoneul oneul bannapaeya haeyo.
examples.en: I have to return the three library books I borrowed today.
examples.note: 세 권을 marks the books as the object; 반납하다 = 'to return (borrowed items)'.

entries.nuance: 권 is the counter for anything BOUND into a spine — novels, textbooks, notebooks, magazines, and each separate volume of a multi-volume series. Its critical contrast is with 장, which counts a single loose SHEET: 종이 한 장 is one sheet of paper, but the whole bound book made of many sheets is 책 한 권. The hanja is 卷, originally 'a scroll/roll', which is why it now measures a complete bound work. It always takes native-Korean numbers and is among the most frequent counters when you talk about reading or studying. entries.shortExplanation: 장 means "counter for flat/thin sheets (paper, tickets)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 장 counts flat, thin things: paper, tickets, photos, cards, banknotes.
Movie, concert, and transport tickets are counted with 장.
The quantity question for sheets, tickets, or photos.
Thin flat foods (김, a cheese slice) also use 장.

examples.en: Two movie tickets, please.
examples.note: Counter-window basic: [ticket] + 두 장 + 주세요. Tickets are flat, so 장.

examples.en: Could you give me just ten sheets of copy paper?
examples.note: 열 장만 = 'just ten sheets'; 만 caps the amount, and -시겠어요 makes it polite.

examples.ko: 가족사진을 한 장 인화하려고 사진관에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: gajoksajineul han jang inhwaharyeogo sajingwane gasseoyo.
examples.en: I went to a photo studio to print one family photo.
examples.note: 한 장 counts the photo; 인화하다 = 'to develop/print a photograph'.

entries.nuance: 장 counts flat, thin items — sheets of paper, tickets, photographs, banknotes, stickers, postcards, and even thin foods like a sheet of dried seaweed (김) or a slice of cheese. Mixing up 장 with 잔 (a glass of drink). They are different words and counters — 종이 한 장 vs 커피 한 잔.

entries.shortExplanation: 대 means "counter for vehicles and machines" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 대, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 대 counts vehicles and machines: cars, bikes, phones, computers, ACs.
Native numbers go before 대: 한, 두, 세 대.
The quantity question for vehicles or appliances.
Home appliances and electronics count with 대.

examples.ko: 우리 집에 차가 한 대 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jibe chaga han dae isseoyo.
examples.en: There's one car in our household.
examples.note: Basic existence: [thing]이/가 한 대 있어요. 차가 한 대 있어요 = 'have one car'.

examples.en: There are as many as five computers in the office.
examples.note: 다섯 대나 — the 나 after the counter adds the surprised nuance 'as many as'.

examples.ko: 오래된 에어컨을 한 대 더 설치하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraedoen eeokeoneul han dae deo seolchihagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We decided to install one more old air conditioner.
examples.note: 한 대 더 = 'one more unit'; -기로 하다 = 'decide to'. Appliances take 대.

entries.nuance: 대 is the all-purpose counter for machines and vehicles — cars, motorcycles, bicycles, computers, phones, cameras, TVs, washing machines, and air conditioners — basically anything mechanical or electronic, so a resident reaches for it constantly when talking about appliances. The hanja is 臺 ('platform/stand'), historically the base a machine sat on, which is why it measures equipment. It contrasts with 채 (whole buildings) and 명 (people): the vehicle is 대, the people riding inside it are 명. It always takes native-Korean numbers. The main English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the generic 개 ('차 두 개') because English just says 'two cars'; machines and vehicles specifically take 대. A subtler trap is counting passengers with 대 — only the machine is 대, while the humans in it are counted with 명.

Using 개 for cars, computers, or appliances. Machines and vehicles specifically take 대 (차 한 대, 노트북 한 대).
Counting the people riding in a vehicle with 대. People are 명 (세 명); only the vehicle itself is 대.
Saying 일 대, 이 대 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 대, 두 대, 세 대.

entries.shortExplanation: 채 means "counter for houses and buildings" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 채 (chae) means "counter for houses and buildings". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 집 한 채 ("one house"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 채 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 채 counts whole houses and freestanding buildings.
Native numbers go before 채: 한, 두, 세 채.
The quantity question for houses or buildings.
채 is used when counting an apartment unit as an owned property.

examples.ko: 우리 동네에 집이 한 채 비어 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri dongnee jibi han chae bieo isseoyo.
examples.en: There's one empty house in our neighborhood.
examples.note: Basic: [building]이/가 한 채. 비어 있다 = 'be (standing) empty'.

examples.ko: 할머니는 시골에 집을 한 채 가지고 계세요.
examples.romanization: halmeonineun sigore jibeul han chae gajigo gyeseyo.
examples.en: My grandmother owns a house in the countryside.
examples.note: 한 채 counts the house; 계세요 is the honorific of 있다 ('has/owns'), respecting grandmother.

examples.ko: 이 일대에 새 아파트가 두 채나 들어섰어요.
examples.romanization: i ildaee sae apateuga du chaena deureoseosseoyo.
examples.en: As many as two new apartment buildings went up in this area.
examples.note: 두 채나 — 나 stresses the surprising number; 들어서다 = '(a building) goes up/is established'.

entries.nuance: 채 counts entire dwellings and sizeable standalone buildings — houses, traditional homes (한옥), and apartment buildings or units treated as whole properties — and it always refers to the STRUCTURE as a complete unit, not the rooms inside. Its near-synonym 동 is the counter used for numbered apartment BLOCKS in a complex (101동), while 채 counts the home as one property; rooms within, meanwhile, are 개 (방 두 개). 채 is a native Korean word (no hanja) and takes native numbers. You meet it most in real-estate talk and neighborhood descriptions. The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 ('집 두 개') because English says 'two houses'; whole buildings specifically take 채. Another trap is using 대 (the machine counter) for a building by analogy — buildings are never 대.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting rooms inside a home with 채. Individual rooms are 개 (방 한 개); the whole house/building is 채.
Using 대 for a building. 대 is for machines and vehicles; a house or building takes 채.
Defaulting to 개 for houses. A whole dwelling takes 채 (집 한 채), not the generic 개.

entries.english: counter for flowers and clustered fruit
entries.shortExplanation: 송이 means "counter for flowers and clustered fruit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "counter for flowers and clustered fruit" is 송이 (songi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 장미 한 송이 ("one rose"). Watch the particle attached to 송이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 송이 counts a single blossom or a naturally clustered bunch.
Native numbers go before 송이: 한, 두, 세 송이.
Fruit that grows in clusters (grapes, bananas) is counted with 송이.
The quantity question for flowers or grape bunches.

examples.en: Just one rose, please.
examples.note: Flower-shop basic: [flower] + 한 송이. 만 = 'just', softening to a single bloom.

examples.en: One bunch of grapes is 10,000 won.
examples.note: 송이 counts the grape cluster; [quantity]에 [price] is fruit-stand pricing.

examples.ko: 졸업식 날 여자친구에게 꽃을 한 송이 건넸어요.
examples.romanization: joreopsing nal yeojachinguege kkocheul han songi geonnesseoyo.
examples.en: On graduation day I handed my girlfriend a single flower.
examples.note: 한 송이 counts the bloom; 건네다 = 'to hand over', and 에게 = 'to (a person)'.

entries.nuance: 송이 counts a single blossom on its stem or a naturally formed cluster of produce — one rose, one tulip, a bunch of grapes, a hand of bananas. Its essential contrast is with 다발: 송이 is ONE separate bloom or cluster, whereas 다발 is a tied BUNDLE of many (꽃 한 다발 = a bouquet, 꽃 한 송이 = a single flower). 송이 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It surfaces whenever you buy flowers or cluster-fruit. The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 ('장미 두 개') because English says 'two roses'; a flower naturally takes 송이. A subtler trap is calling a wrapped bouquet 한 송이 — a gift bouquet is 한 다발, while 송이 stays reserved for each individual stem or cluster.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 for a single flower. A bloom naturally takes 송이 (장미 한 송이), not the generic 개.
Calling a wrapped bouquet 한 송이. A bound bouquet is 한 다발; 송이 is one individual flower or cluster.
Counting loose individual grapes with 송이. The whole hanging cluster is 한 송이; single berries are 알 (포도 한 알).

entries.english: counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)
entries.shortExplanation: 줄 means "counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 줄 (jul) = "counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 김밥 한 줄 ("one roll of gimbap") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 줄, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 줄 counts long line-shaped things: a gimbap roll, a row, a line of text.
Native numbers go before 줄: 한, 두, 세 줄.

usagePhrases.en: to line up in a single row
usagePhrases.note: 한 줄로 + 서다 is a fixed phrase for forming one queue.
The quantity question for lines of text or rows.

examples.en: One roll of gimbap, please.
examples.note: Snack-shop basic: 김밥 + 한 줄. The whole uncut roll is 한 줄, not the slices.

examples.en: Please line up in a single line here.
examples.note: 한 줄로 = 'into one line'; the 로 marks the resulting arrangement. Common queue instruction.

examples.ko: 이 긴 글을 두 줄로 짧게 요약해 봤어요.
examples.romanization: i gin geureul du jullo jjalbge yoyakae bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I summarized this long text into two short lines.
examples.note: 두 줄로 = 'into two lines'; 줄 counts written lines as well as physical rows.

entries.nuance: 줄 counts things stretched out in a long line — a roll of gimbap (a long tube of rice and fillings), a row of seats, a queue of people, and lines of written text. As a plain noun 줄 also means 'a line/string/rope', and the counter inherits that 'long linear thing' image. Its everyday rivals split by shape: 줄 is the whole long line, but once gimbap is sliced, each round piece becomes 개 (김밥 한 개 = one slice). 줄 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers; note the set phrase 한 줄로 서다 ('stand in a single line'), heard constantly in queues. The English-speaker pitfall is counting cut gimbap pieces with 줄 — the uncut roll is 한 줄, individual slices are 개; another is using 개 for a row or queue when the natural counter is 줄.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting sliced gimbap pieces with 줄. The whole uncut roll is 한 줄; each cut slice is 개.
Using 개 for a queue or a row. A line of people or a row is 줄 (한 줄), not the generic 개.
Forgetting the 로 in the line-up phrase. The natural instruction is 한 줄로 서다 ('line up into one row'), with 로.

entries.shortExplanation: 마리 means "counter for animals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 마리 (mari) means "counter for animals". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 강아지 한 마리 ("one puppy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 마리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 마리 counts every kind of animal: pets, fish, birds, insects, livestock.
Native numbers go before 마리: 한, 두, 세 마리.
The quantity question for any creature.
A whole (cooked) chicken is counted with 마리 too.

examples.en: I want to raise one puppy.
examples.note: Basic: [animal] + 한 마리. 키우다 = 'to raise/keep (a pet)'.

examples.ko: 우리 집 어항에는 금붕어가 세 마리 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jip eohangeneun geumbungeoga se mari isseoyo.
examples.en: There are three goldfish in our fish tank.
examples.note: 세 마리 counts the fish; even tiny creatures take 마리, regardless of size.

examples.ko: 배고픈데 치킨 한 마리 시켜 먹을까요?
examples.romanization: baegopeunde chikin han mari sikyeo meogeulkkayo?
examples.en: I'm hungry — shall we order a whole chicken?
examples.note: 한 마리 counts the chicken; 시켜 먹다 = 'order in and eat'. Classic fried-chicken line.

entries.nuance: 마리 is the universal counter for animals — dogs, cats, fish, birds, insects, livestock, and even a whole cooked chicken or fish on the table. Crucially it is size-independent: the same word counts an ant (개미 한 마리) and an elephant (코끼리 한 마리). 마리 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. Its single most important contrast is with 명, the counter for PEOPLE: animals are 마리, humans are 명, and crossing that line matters socially. 마리 is also distinct from 분, the honorific people-counter. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 마리 for people because English says 'two' for both — but calling a person 한 마리 is insulting or mocking (treating them like an animal); always use 명 (or honorific 분) for humans. A second slip is the generic 개 for animals, which sounds wrong — creatures take 마리.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting people with 마리. People take 명 (or honorific 분); 마리 for a human is rude or mocking.
Using 개 for animals. Living creatures take 마리 (강아지 한 마리), not the generic object counter 개.
Saying 일 마리, 이 마리 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리, 세 마리.

마리 is native Korean (no hanja).

entries.shortExplanation: 끼 means "counter for meals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "counter for meals" is 끼 (kki). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 하루 세 끼 ("three meals a day"). Watch the particle attached to 끼 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS: breakfast, lunch, dinner as sittings.
Native numbers go before 끼: 한, 두, 세 끼.
The quantity question for meal sittings.

usagePhrases.en: to make do with a quick meal
usagePhrases.note: 한 끼 + 때우다 is a set phrase for grabbing a quick bite to get by.

examples.en: I eat two meals a day.
examples.note: Basic habit: 하루에 [number] 끼 먹다. 끼 counts the sittings, not the dishes.

examples.ko: 오늘 너무 바빠서 한 끼밖에 못 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: oneul neomu bappaseo han kkibakke mon meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was so busy today I only ate one meal.
examples.note: 한 끼밖에 + 못 — 밖에 ('only') REQUIRES a negative verb, here 못 먹었어요.

examples.ko: 다이어트 중이라 저녁 한 끼는 가볍게 먹으려고 해요.
examples.romanization: daieoteu jungira jeonyeo kan kkineun gabyeopge meogeuryeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I'm dieting, so I try to eat one light dinner.
examples.note: 한 끼는 topic-marks the meal; -려고 하다 = 'try/intend to'. 중이라 = 'because I'm in the middle of'.

entries.nuance: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS — one sitting of breakfast, lunch, or dinner is 한 끼 — so it measures the eating event, not the individual dishes on the table. This is its key contrast with 그릇 (a bowl/serving of food) and 개 (a single dish): 밥 한 끼 is one whole meal, while 밥 한 그릇 is one bowl of rice within it. 끼 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It's the natural way to talk about eating habits, skipping meals, and meal plans (하루 세 끼). Note the set phrase 한 끼 때우다 ('grab a quick bite to get by'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 끼 to count plates or dishes because English loosely says 'a meal' for food generally — but 끼 is the whole sitting; a single dish is 개 or 그릇. A second slip is Sino-Korean numbers (일 끼), when only native 한 끼, 두 끼 work.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting individual dishes or plates with 끼. A dish/serving is 개 or 그릇; 끼 is a whole meal sitting.
Using Sino-Korean numbers like 일 끼, 삼 끼. Meal occasions take native numbers: 한 끼, 세 끼.
Pairing 밖에 ('only') with a positive verb. 한 끼밖에 demands a negative: 한 끼밖에 못 먹었어요, not 먹었어요.

structuredNuance.t: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS — one sitting of breakfast, lunch, or dinner is 한 끼 — so it measures the eating event, not the individual dishes on the table. It takes native numbers and is the natural way to talk about eating habits, skipping meals, and meal plans (하루 세 끼). Note the set phrase 한 끼 때우다 ('grab a quick bite to get by').
This is its key contrast with 그릇 (a bowl/serving of food) and 개 (a single dish): 밥 한 끼 is one whole meal, while 밥 한 그릇 is one bowl of rice within it.
끼 is native Korean (no hanja).

The English-speaker pitfall is using 끼 to count plates or dishes because English loosely says 'a meal' for food generally — but 끼 is the whole sitting; a single dish is 개 or 그릇. A second slip is Sino-Korean numbers (일 끼), when only native 한 끼, 두 끼 work.

entries.shortExplanation: 군데 means "counter for places/spots" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 군데 (gunde) = "counter for places/spots". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 한 군데 ("one place/spot") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 군데, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 군데 counts locations or spots: shops, sites, even sore spots on the body.
Native numbers go before 군데: 한, 두, 세 군데.
Extremely common: 몇 군데 = 'how many spots/places'.
여러 군데 = 'in several spots/places', for scattered locations or pains.

examples.ko: 여기 근처에 카페가 몇 군데 있어요?
examples.romanization: yeogi geuncheoe kapega myeot gunde isseoyo?
examples.en: How many cafés are there near here?
examples.note: Basic: [place] + 몇 군데. 군데 counts the locations being asked about.

examples.en: I even went to as many as three different hospitals.
examples.note: 세 군데나 — the 나 stresses 'as many as three'; 다니다 = 'go around/attend (repeatedly)'.

examples.en: I fell, so I ache in several spots on my body.
examples.note: 여러 군데 = 'in several places'; 군데 counts sore spots too, not just shops.

entries.nuance: 군데 counts locations or spots — shops you visited, apartments you toured, websites you checked, or places on the body that hurt — and it works equally for distinct establishments and for scattered points. Its near-synonym is 곳, which also means 'place', but 곳 is a fuller noun ('a place') and can stand alone or sound slightly more formal/written, whereas 군데 is specifically the conversational COUNTER you attach to a number (세 군데, 여러 군데). 군데 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It pairs constantly with 몇 군데 ('how many places') and 여러 군데 ('several places'). The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 for places because English says 'three places'; locations naturally take 군데 (or 곳). A separate, embarrassing trap is mixing 군데 (a spot) with the look-alike 군대 ('the military/army') — wholly different words.

Confusing 군데 with 군대. 군데 = 'spot/place (counter)'; 군대 = 'the army/military' — a totally different word.
Treating 곳 and 군데 as identical. 곳 is a standalone noun ('a place'); 군데 is the counter you put after a number.
