entries.shortExplanation: 모퉁이 means "corner (of a street or building)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 모퉁이 (motungi) means "corner (of a street or building)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 모퉁이를 돌다 ("to turn the corner"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 모퉁이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 돌다 is the natural verb; 모퉁이를 돌면 = once you round the corner
pointing it out when giving directions
a common landmark in directions
narrow side-street corner, not a big intersection

examples.en: There's a mailbox on the corner.
examples.note: 모퉁이에 = at the corner; the simplest 'corner as a spot' use

examples.en: If you round that corner, you'll see a convenience store.
examples.note: the everyday direction formula: 모퉁이를 돌면 + landmark 보이다

examples.en: Turn right at the next corner.
examples.note: 꺾다 = to make a sharp turn; what a local says guiding you on foot

entries.nuance: 모퉁이 is the corner where a road bends or a building's wall turns — the spot you physically round while walking, pictured from the outside. The near-synonym is 모서리, but the dividing line matters: 모서리 is the sharp edge or corner of a solid object (책상 모서리 = the corner of a desk, 모서리에 부딪히다 = to bump into an edge), while 모퉁이 is a place in the street you move around. It is plain, everyday speech with no register issue, said freely to anyone. It collocates above all with 돌다 (모퉁이를 돌다) and appears as 모퉁이 가게 / 골목 모퉁이 as a landmark. The English-speaker pitfall: English uses one word 'corner' for both the street corner and a table corner, so learners reach for 모퉁이 when they bump a desk — but that edge is 모서리. Also note Koreans say 모퉁이를 돌다 with the object particle 를, not 'turn at the corner' word-for-word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 모퉁이 for a big four-way car intersection — that crossing is 사거리 or 교차로; 모퉁이 is the smaller, pedestrian bend you round
Saying 모서리 for a street corner — 모서리 is the sharp edge of an object (책상 모서리), so 'the shop on the 모서리' sounds like a shop glued to a desk edge
Dropping the verb 돌다: to 'turn the corner' is 모퉁이를 돌다, not just 모퉁이 가다 — without 돌다 the rounding motion is lost

entries.english: the opposite side (right across, facing you)
entries.shortExplanation: 맞은편 means "the opposite side (right across, facing you)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "the opposite side (right across, facing you)" is 맞은편 (majeunpyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 맞은편에 있다 ("to be on the opposite side"). Watch the particle attached to 맞은편 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be on the opposite side
usagePhrases.note: right across, facing the speaker
바로 stresses it is straight across
a facing landmark
very common location phrase

examples.en: The bank is across from the convenience store.
examples.note: the core pattern: [landmark] 맞은편에 있다, with 에 marking location

examples.en: Sit across from me.
examples.note: 제 맞은편 = the side facing me; 맞은편 works for a person opposite you, not just buildings (note: 저랑 here would wrongly mean 'together with me')

examples.ko: 식당이 우리 회사 바로 맞은편이라서 점심때 자주 가요.
examples.romanization: sikdangi uri hoesa baro majeunpyeoniraseo jeomsimttae jaju gayo.
examples.en: The restaurant is right across from our office, so I go there a lot at lunch.
examples.note: 바로 = directly; real-life reason clause showing 맞은편 as a familiar spot

entries.nuance: 맞은편 is the side that directly faces you, built from 맞다 ('to face / to fit') + 편 ('side'), so the image is two spots looking straight at each other across a road, a river, or a table. The near-synonym is 건너편, and the dividing line is subtle but real: 맞은편 stresses facing (it can describe the person seated opposite you), while 건너편 stresses the crossing you do to get there. In daily speech they overlap heavily and either is usually fine. Register is neutral — fine with anyone. It collocates as 바로 맞은편, 맞은편 건물, 역 맞은편. The English-speaker pitfall: 'opposite' in English also means 'contrary / reverse' (the opposite is true), but 맞은편 is strictly spatial — for the abstract opposite you need 반대 (반대로). Another trap is the particle: a place 'is on the opposite side' is 맞은편에 있어요, never 맞은편 있어요 with the 에 dropped.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 맞은편 with 옆 (next to) — 맞은편 is across and facing you, 옆 is beside you; 'next to the bank' is 은행 옆, not 은행 맞은편
Using 맞은편 for the abstract 'opposite' (the opposite is true) — that is 반대; 맞은편 only means the physically facing side
Forgetting the location particle 에 — say 맞은편에 있어요, not 맞은편 있어요; Korean needs 에 to mark where something sits

entries.english: the other side (across the road or river)
entries.shortExplanation: 건너편 means "the other side (across the road or river)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 건너편 (geonneopyeon) = "the other side (across the road or river)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 길 건너편 ("across the street") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 건너편, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the most common collocation

usagePhrases.en: to go to the other side
usagePhrases.note: 으로 = toward

usagePhrases.en: to see from the other side
usagePhrases.note: viewpoint across

usagePhrases.en: the far side of the river
usagePhrases.note: across a river or wide road

examples.en: There's a pharmacy across the street.
examples.note: 길 건너편 = across the road, the single most common pairing

examples.en: To get to the other side, cross at the crosswalk.
examples.note: 으로 = toward; the verb 건너다 echoes the 건너 in 건너편

examples.ko: 아까 강 건너편에서 불꽃놀이를 봤는데 진짜 예뻤어요.
examples.romanization: akka gang geonneopyeoneseo bulkkonnorireul bwanneunde jinjja yeppeosseoyo.
examples.en: Earlier I watched the fireworks from the far side of the river, and it was really pretty.
examples.note: 에서 = from that side; a lived-in scene showing the 'across a river' sense

entries.nuance: 건너편 comes from the verb 건너다 ('to cross') + 편 ('side'), so it literally means 'the cross-over side' — the side you reach by crossing something: a road, a river, the tracks. That built-in crossing is what separates it from its near-synonym 맞은편: 건너편 foregrounds the act of getting across, while 맞은편 simply foregrounds facing you. For directions involving a 횡단보도 (crosswalk) or a wide road, locals reach for 건너편 first, and it pairs naturally with 건너다 (건너편으로 건너가다). Register is neutral. Common collocations: 길 건너편, 강 건너편, 건너편으로 가다. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'the other side' is vaguer than 건너편 — 'the other side of the room' is not 건너편 (use 반대쪽 for the far end of an enclosed space); 건너편 specifically implies a barrier you cross. Also do not confuse it with 다음 ('the next one along') — 건너편 is across from you, not the next building in a row.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 건너편 when the place is on your own side of the road — it must be across something you cross; if no crossing is involved, use 옆 or 근처
Mixing it up with 다음 (next) — 건너편 is the facing side across the street, 다음 is the next one further along your own side
Saying 건너편 for the far end of a single room — that is 반대쪽 or 끝; 건너편 implies crossing a road, river, or tracks

entries.shortExplanation: 지름길 means "shortcut" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 지름길 (jireumgil) means "shortcut". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지름길로 가다 ("to go by the shortcut"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 지름길 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 로 = by way of
handy local knowledge
offering a faster route

usagePhrases.en: to cut through via the shortcut
usagePhrases.note: 질러가다 = to cut across

examples.en: This road is a shortcut.
examples.note: the simplest framing: [road] 이/가 지름길이다

examples.en: If you know the shortcut, it's a good ten minutes faster.
examples.note: 은 here softly emphasizes the amount; pairs the word with a time saving

examples.en: I think there's no shortcut to success.
examples.note: the figurative 'fast track' sense — 성공의 지름길 is a set phrase

entries.nuance: 지름길 is a native Korean compound, not Sino-Korean: from the verb 지르다 ('to cut straight across / take a direct line') + 길 ('road'), so it pictures the path that slices straight through instead of going the long way around. It means a shorter, faster route — often through alleys or back streets a local knows — and just as commonly it is figurative: 성공의 지름길 = 'the shortcut to success', a fast track to a goal. Its natural opposite is 돌아가다 ('to go the long way round'), and it pairs with the verb 질러가다 ('to cut across'), which shares the same 지르다 root. Register is neutral and everyday. The English-speaker pitfall: do not confuse 지름길 with 골목길 (alley) — an alley can serve as a shortcut, but 골목길 names the narrow street itself while 지름길 names the shorter route, whatever street it uses. Spelling also traps learners: it is 지름길, pronounced [지름낄], so people mishear and write 지름낄.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 지름낄 or 지름킬 from the pronunciation — the correct written form is 지름길 (the 길 just sounds tensed after ㅁ)
Confusing it with 골목길 (alley) — 골목길 is the narrow street itself; 지름길 is the shorter route, which may or may not run through an alley
Pairing it with the wrong verb for 'take': you 지름길로 가다 / 지름길로 질러가다 (go BY the shortcut), not 지름길을 가다 as if walking the shortcut as an object

entries.shortExplanation: 갈림길 means "fork in the road / crossroads" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "fork in the road / crossroads" is 갈림길 (gallimgil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갈림길에서 ("at the fork in the road"). Watch the particle attached to 갈림길 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: at the fork in the road
usagePhrases.note: where the road splits
나오다 = to come up ahead
counting the branches
figurative, very common

examples.en: At the fork, go left.
examples.note: 에서 marks the split point where the choice happens

examples.en: If you go a little further, a fork comes up.
examples.note: 나오다 = (a feature) appears ahead, the natural verb for terrain coming into view

examples.ko: 지금 인생의 갈림길에 서 있는 기분이에요.
examples.romanization: jigeum insaengui gallimgire seo inneun gibunieyo.
examples.en: I feel like I'm standing at a crossroads in life right now.
examples.note: the figurative use Koreans love — a big decision point, 인생의 갈림길

entries.nuance: 갈림길 is a native compound from 갈리다 ('to be divided / to split') + 길 ('road'), so the picture is one path branching apart into two or more, the moment you must choose a direction. Literally it guides walking or driving (갈림길에서 오른쪽으로), but Koreans use it just as readily for life's decision points (인생의 갈림길 = a crossroads in life). Its key contrast is with 사거리 (a four-way intersection): a 갈림길 splits one road into branches like a Y, whereas a 사거리 is where two roads cross like a plus sign — splitting versus crossing. It pairs with 나오다 ('to come up ahead') and the locative 갈림길에서. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'crossroads' covers both the literal X-crossing and the figurative dilemma, so learners over-extend 갈림길 to a true intersection — but a road that crosses, not branches, is 교차로 or 사거리; reserve 갈림길 for a fork.

Confusing 갈림길 (a fork that splits one road into branches) with 사거리 (a four-way intersection where two roads cross) — splitting is not the same as crossing
Spelling it 갈림낄 from the pronunciation — the written form is 갈림길
Treating it as only literal — Koreans very often mean the figurative 'crossroads of life' (인생의 갈림길), so don't assume it's always a physical road

entries.shortExplanation: 보도 means "sidewalk / pavement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보도 (bodo) = "sidewalk / pavement". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보도로 걷다 ("to walk on the sidewalk") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 로 = along/by
위 = on top of/along
describing it
the tiled blocks underfoot

examples.en: Walk on the sidewalk.
examples.note: the simplest safety instruction; 로 = along/by way of

examples.en: The sidewalk was narrow, so we walked single file.
examples.note: 아서 = because; a real everyday observation about Korean sidewalks

examples.en: A bike was riding on the sidewalk, so it was almost dangerous.
examples.note: ㄹ 뻔했다 = nearly happened; the live issue of bikes on 보도

entries.nuance: 보도 is Sino-Korean, 步道, literally 'step-road' (步 walk + 道 road) — the formal name for the pedestrian walkway beside a street, identical in meaning to 인도 (人道, 'person-road'). The dividing line between the two is register and channel: 보도 dominates official signage and traffic law (보도 침범 = encroaching on the sidewalk), while 인도 is what people more often say in casual speech; both are correct. Its true opposite is 차도 (車道, 'car-road', the roadway). The everyday compound 보도블록 (the tiled paving blocks) comes up constantly in complaints about uneven sidewalks. The big English-speaker pitfall is a homograph collision: another 보도 means 'news report' (報道, as in 언론 보도 = press coverage) — same hangul, different hanja — so a sentence about 보도 could be about pavement or the press, and only context tells them apart. entries.nuance: 육교 is Sino-Korean, 陸橋, literally 'land-bridge' (陸 land + 橋 bridge) — a footbridge that carries pedestrians up and over a busy road. Its clean opposite is 지하도 (地下道), the underground passage you go down into; the memory hook is direction — 육교 you climb UP, 지하도 you go DOWN. Distinguish it sharply from 다리 (a plain bridge): a 다리 spans a river and usually carries cars (한강 다리), whereas a 육교 is specifically for people crossing over a road. Older 육교 have many stairs (육교 계단) and no elevator, so travelers with luggage or strollers grumble. It pairs with 건너다, 올라가다, 이용하다. The English-speaker pitfall: 'overpass' in English often means a road flyover for cars, but 육교 is for pedestrians — a car overpass over a road is 고가도로. So don't call the highway flyover a 육교, and don't call a river bridge a 육교 either.

Calling a car flyover a 육교 — a road-over-road bridge for vehicles is 고가도로; 육교 is specifically the pedestrian footbridge
Calling a river bridge a 육교 — a bridge spanning a river (한강 다리) is 다리; 육교 only spans a road for people on foot

entries.nuance: 지하도 is Sino-Korean, 地下道, literally 'under-ground road' (地 ground + 下 below + 道 road) — the passage that takes pedestrians beneath a busy road or intersection. Its mirror image is 육교 (陸橋): 지하도 you go DOWN into, 육교 you climb UP over, same crossing by opposite directions. The trap synonym is 지하철 (地下鐵, 'underground iron' = subway): they share 지하 (underground) but 지하도 is a walking tunnel while 지하철 is the train — a 지하도 may connect to a 지하철역 but is not the same thing. Many large 지하도 double as 지하도 상가 (underground shopping arcades), so locals duck in both to cross and to browse. It pairs with 내려가다, 건너다, 출구. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'underground' alone is ambiguous (passage vs. subway), so learners say 지하 when they mean the passage — be specific: the walkway is 지하도, the subway is 지하철. Also use 내려가다 (go down), not 들어가다, to capture the descent.

차선 = lane
at a traffic light

examples.note: the clipped noun form a passenger says to a driver

entries.nuance: 우회전 is Sino-Korean, 右回轉, literally 'right-rotate-turn' (右 right + 回轉 rotation) — the driving and navigation term for a right turn, and the exact mirror of 좌회전 (左回轉, left turn). You hear it constantly from GPS apps like 카카오내비 and 티맵, and as a passenger you direct a taxi with 여기서 우회전해 주세요. The crucial register/usage line is car versus foot: 우회전 belongs to driving, while on foot Koreans simply say 오른쪽으로 가세요 ('go to the right') — using 우회전 for a walking route sounds oddly like you're steering a vehicle. It pairs with 하다 to become a verb (우회전하다) and with 차선, 신호. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'turn right' is one phrase for cars and pedestrians alike, so learners over-apply 우회전 to walking — keep 우회전 for vehicles and 오른쪽으로 for on foot. Also note the hanja 右 (right) versus 左 (left) is the only difference from 좌회전, so don't swap them.

Swapping 우회전 (右, right) and 좌회전 (左, left) — the only difference is the first hanja, so it's easy to flip; 우 = right
Forgetting 우회전 is a noun that needs 하다 to act — 'turn right' is 우회전하다, not 우회전 가다

entries.nuance: 좌회전 is Sino-Korean, 左回轉, literally 'left-rotate-turn' (左 left + 回轉 rotation) — the left-turn mirror of 우회전 (右回轉), and core driving and GPS vocabulary. Worth knowing is 비보호 좌회전 (非保護 左回轉, 'unprotected left turn'): you turn left on a plain green light, without a dedicated green arrow, yielding to oncoming cars — it appears on real signs and trips up new and foreign drivers. The register line mirrors 우회전: 좌회전 is for vehicles, whereas on foot you just say 왼쪽으로 가세요 ('go left'). It pairs with 하다 (좌회전하다), 신호, 차선. The English-speaker pitfall is the same over-extension — don't use 좌회전 for walking; reserve it for cars. entries.nuance: 직진 is Sino-Korean, 直進, literally 'straight-advance' (直 straight + 進 to go forward) — proceeding straight ahead without turning, the third member of the navigation trio with 우회전 and 좌회전. Spoken GPS commands chain them: 직진하다가 좌회전 ('go straight, then turn left'). Its everyday spoken cousins on foot are 쭉 가세요 or 똑바로 가세요 ('go straight on'), so like its turn-siblings, 직진 itself leans toward driving and GPS speech; saying 직진하세요 to someone walking sounds a little mechanical. usagePhrases.note: 도로 = road

entries.nuance: 일방통행 is Sino-Korean, 一方通行, literally 'one-direction pass-go' (一 one + 方 direction + 通行 passage), describing a road where traffic may legally flow in only one direction — a constant feature of Korea's older, narrow neighborhood streets. Its conceptual opposite is two-way traffic, but be careful with the term: the standard word is 양방향 통행 (兩方向, 'both-directions') or simply 양방향, not the made-up 양방통행. Related is 역주행 (逆走行, driving against the flow), the violation you commit if you miss the sign. 일방통행 pairs with 도로, 길, 표지판, and the consequence verb 돌아가다 ('to go around the long way'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't model the antonym on the word and say 양방통행 — Koreans say 양방향. Also, 일방통행 governs the road itself, so it binds cyclists and motorbikes too, not just cars; and figuratively 일방통행 can describe a one-sided relationship (그 사랑은 일방통행이었다), a nuance worth recognizing.

Don't model the antonym on the word and say 양방통행 — Koreans say 양방향.

entries.shortExplanation: 찌개 means "jjigae; thick stew" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 찌개 (jjigae) means "jjigae; thick stew". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 찌개를 끓이다 ("to make/cook a jjigae"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 찌개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 끓이다 'boil (something)' is the standard verb for making stew, not 만들다

usagePhrases.en: the stew comes to a boil
usagePhrases.note: intransitive 끓다 — the pot bubbles on its own
name + 주세요 is how you order any stew
그릇 is the counter for a bowl/portion of stew or rice

examples.en: I like kimchi jjigae.
examples.note: simple statement of taste — 를 marks the object

examples.en: The stew is still boiling, so be careful.
examples.note: everyday warning at the table; -고 있다 = ongoing action

examples.en: We'll share one doenjang jjigae between the two of us.
examples.note: real ordering line — 찌개 is communal, eaten from one pot

entries.nuance: 찌개 is a thick, salty, intensely flavored stew with just enough liquid to spoon over rice, simmered and served bubbling in one earthenware pot that everyone at the table dips into together. The key contrast is 찌개 vs 국: a 국 is a clear, light, soup-like broth you can drink by the bowl (each person gets their own), while a 찌개 is denser, saltier, packed with solid ingredients, and meant to be shared. It is named after its base — 김치찌개, 된장찌개, 부대찌개 — and habitually pairs with 끓이다 'to boil/cook' and 끓다 'to come to a boil'. The big pitfall for English speakers is the verb: you 먹다 'eat' a 찌개, never 마시다 'drink' it (you only 마시다 a thin broth), and you cook it with 끓이다, not 만들다. Do not call it 'soup' on a menu either — that flattens the whole distinction Koreans care about.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 찌개를 마셔요 'I drink the stew' — 찌개 is thick and full of ingredients, so it takes 먹다 'eat'; only a thin 국 or 국물 broth can take 마시다.
Calling 찌개 a 'soup' and lumping it with 국 — a 국 is light and individually served, while 찌개 is dense, salty, and shared from one pot.
Using 만들다 'make' for cooking it; Koreans specifically say 찌개를 끓이다 'boil up a stew', because the cooking method is defined by simmering.

entries.shortExplanation: 국밥 means "gukbap; soup with rice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "gukbap; soup with rice" is 국밥 (gukbap). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국밥을 먹다 ("to eat gukbap"). Watch the particle attached to 국밥 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 'eat', not 마시다 — even though it's soupy, the rice makes it a meal you eat
뜨겁다 = hot to the touch/temperature, the typical comment on a steaming bowl
그릇 counts a bowl/serving
돼지 'pig' + 국밥; the Busan specialty

examples.en: One bowl of gukbap, please.
examples.note: simplest ordering line; 그릇 is the natural counter

examples.ko: 술 마신 다음 날엔 국밥이 최고예요.
examples.romanization: sul masin daeum naren gukbabi choegoyeyo.
examples.en: The day after drinking, gukbap is the best.
examples.note: everyday hangover context — 해장 culture

examples.en: Mix the rice into the broth and eat.
examples.note: real server's tip; 말다 'to put rice into soup' is the exact verb

entries.nuance: 국밥 is literally 국 'soup' + 밥 'rice' — a hot bowl in which rice is either pre-mixed into the broth (토렴) or served alongside to add yourself, eaten fast and cheap as a complete one-bowl meal. It differs from a plain 국 in that 국밥 is a whole meal (rice included), whereas 국 is just the soup component of a larger spread. The defining verb to learn is 말다 'to put/swirl rice into soup' — 밥을 국에 말다 — which has no clean English equivalent and trips learners up. 국밥 is the classic 해장 'hangover-cure' food, and Busan's 돼지국밥 (pork) is nationally famous. Pitfall: even though it looks like soup, you say 국밥을 먹다 'eat gukbap', not 마시다 'drink', because the rice makes it food, not a beverage — and don't forget the counter 그릇 when ordering a single bowl.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 국밥 as just soup and forgetting the 밥 'rice' — the word literally bundles rice and soup into one complete meal.
Saying 국밥을 마셔요 'I drink gukbap' — the rice content means it takes 먹다 'eat'; 마시다 is only for pure liquid.
Ordering '국밥 하나' and stopping there in a sit-down place; the natural, polite phrasing uses the bowl counter: 국밥 한 그릇 주세요.

entries.english: deopbap; rice topped with a dish
entries.shortExplanation: 덮밥 means "deopbap; rice topped with a dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 덮밥 (deopbap) = "deopbap; rice topped with a dish". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 덮밥을 시키다 ("to order deopbap") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 덮밥, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 시키다 'order (food)' — the casual verb diners actually use
맛있다 'be delicious' is an adjective; no 'be' verb needed
제육 'seasoned pork' + 덮밥
하나 'one (thing)' works as a quick counter when ordering

examples.en: When I'm busy I often eat deopbap.
examples.note: simple habit; one-bowl food = fast

examples.en: Squid deopbap is popular because it's spicy.
examples.note: everyday reason with -아서 'because'

examples.en: Please pour the sauce over the rice too.
examples.note: real request; 위에 'on top of' captures the 'covered' image

entries.nuance: 덮밥 comes from the verb 덮다 'to cover' + 밥 'rice' — literally 'covered rice' — a single bowl where a saucy cooked topping (spicy pork, squid, egg, etc.) is laid over white rice and eaten together. The sharp contrast to master is 덮밥 vs 비빔밥: in a 덮밥 the topping sits ON the rice and you eat down through the layers, while in a 비빔밥 'mixed rice' everything is vigorously stirred together (비비다 'to mix') before eating. Common members are 제육덮밥, 오징어덮밥, and 규동-style 소고기덮밥. Two pitfalls hit English speakers: first, do not add a plural -들 because English says 'toppings' — Korean nouns stay unmarked for number; second, do not stir a 덮밥 like a 비빔밥 unless you want to blur the very distinction the name encodes. Order it casually with 시키다, the everyday verb for ordering dishes.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 덮밥 (topping laid over rice) with 비빔밥 (everything stirred together) — the names literally mean 'covered' vs 'mixed', and Koreans eat them differently.
Adding a plural ending like 토핑들 because English pluralizes 'toppings'; Korean leaves the noun unmarked — 덮밥 위의 재료 is fine.
Using only 만들다 'make' when ordering out — diners say 덮밥을 시키다 'order a deopbap', since 시키다 is the verb for ordering prepared food.

entries.shortExplanation: 볶음밥 means "bokkeumbap; fried rice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 볶음밥 (bokkeumbap) means "bokkeumbap; fried rice". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 볶음밥을 볶다 ("to fry up the fried rice"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 볶음밥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to fry up the fried rice
usagePhrases.note: 볶다 'to stir-fry' is the root verb and the one cooks use
만들다 'make' for the general home-cooking sense
김치 + 볶음밥; the most common kind
인분 counts servings/portions per person

examples.en: I make fried rice with leftover rice.
examples.note: simple home use; 하다 stands in for 만들다 casually

examples.en: I eat kimchi fried rice with a fried egg on top.
examples.note: everyday combo; 올리다 'to put on top'

examples.ko: 고기 다 먹고 볶음밥 볶아 주세요.
examples.romanization: gogi da meokgo bokkeumbap bokka juseyo.
examples.en: After the meat, please fry up some rice for us.
examples.note: real BBQ-restaurant line; staff fry it on the grill

entries.nuance: 볶음밥 is 볶음 'stir-frying' (from 볶다 'to stir-fry') + 밥 'rice' — rice tossed in a hot oiled pan with bits of kimchi, vegetables, or meat until it's separated and a little toasty. The contrast learners need is 볶음밥 vs 비빔밥: 볶음밥 is cooked WITH heat — the rice is fried — whereas 비빔밥 is raw-assembled and just stirred cold, no pan. The signature collocation is the cognate-verb pair 볶음밥을 볶다 'stir-fry the fried rice', and at Korean BBQ places staff famously 볶다 it right on the grill at the end of the meal. 김치볶음밥 is the everyday home version. Pitfall: English speakers reach only for 만들다 'make', but a Korean cook will say 볶다 'stir-fry' for the actual action — and watch the spelling/spacing, it is one word 볶음밥, not 볶음 밥.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 볶음밥 (fried in a pan with heat) with 비빔밥 (cold-mixed, no cooking) — only 볶음밥 involves the stir-fry verb 볶다.
Saying only 볶음밥을 만들어요 and never 볶아요; locals use the cognate verb 볶다 'stir-fry' for the cooking action itself.
Writing it as two words 볶음 밥; it is a single fixed compound, 볶음밥, with no space.

entries.shortExplanation: 볶음 means "bokkeum; stir-fried dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bokkeum; stir-fried dish" is 볶음 (bokkeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오징어볶음 주세요 ("stir-fried squid, please"). Watch the particle attached to 볶음 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ingredient + 볶음 names the dish
맵다 'be spicy' — many 볶음 dishes are red-pepper based
볶음 + 반찬; small 볶음 dishes serve as sides
볶음 + 요리 'cuisine/dish' as a category

examples.en: I like stir-fried squid.
examples.note: simple preference statement

examples.en: Stir-fried pork is best eaten with rice.
examples.note: everyday pairing; -아야 'only if/must'

examples.ko: 엄마가 반찬으로 멸치볶음을 자주 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: eommaga banchaneuro myeolchibokkeumeul jaju hae juseyo.
examples.en: Mom often makes anchovy stir-fry as a side dish.
examples.note: real home context; small 볶음 = banchan

entries.nuance: 볶음 is the noun made from 볶다 'to stir-fry' (the -(으)ㅁ ending turns a verb into 'the act/result of'), so it names any dish defined by stir-frying and almost always rides on the main ingredient: 오징어볶음, 제육볶음, 낙지볶음, 멸치볶음. Contrast it with 무침 'a dressed/tossed dish', which is seasoned raw without heat, and with 조림 'a braised dish', which is simmered long in sauce — all three are cooking-method suffixes, and 볶음 specifically means 'pan-fried in oil over high heat'. Big 볶음 dishes (제육볶음) are mains; tiny ones (멸치볶음) are everyday 반찬 side dishes. Pitfall: 볶음 rarely stands alone in speech — saying just '볶음 주세요' sounds incomplete; you almost always front it with the ingredient. And keep the noun 볶음 distinct from the verb 볶다 you conjugate (볶아요/볶았어요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 볶음 when you mean a specific dish — it normally needs the ingredient in front, e.g. 제육볶음, 오징어볶음; bare 볶음 sounds unfinished.
Confusing the dish-noun 볶음 with the cooking verb 볶다; you order a 볶음 but you 볶다 (볶아요) the food.
Assuming 볶음 means raw or tossed — that's 무침; 볶음 is specifically stir-fried in oil over heat.

entries.shortExplanation: 무침 means "muchim; seasoned dressed dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무침 (muchim) = "muchim; seasoned dressed dish". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 콩나물무침 주세요 ("seasoned bean sprouts, please") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무침, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ingredient + 무침 names the dish
새콤하다 'pleasantly sour' — many 무침 use vinegar
cognate verb 무치다 'to dress by hand'
무침 + 반찬; classic cold banchan

examples.en: Today's side dish is seasoned spinach.
examples.note: simple banchan statement

examples.en: The tangy cucumber muchim revives my appetite.
examples.note: everyday taste comment; -아서 'because'

examples.en: Mom dresses the bean sprouts by hand, kneading them.
examples.note: real cooking scene; 조물조물 mimetic for hand-tossing

entries.nuance: 무침 comes from 무치다 'to dress/toss (food) by hand with seasonings', so a 무침 is vegetables or seafood mixed with salt, sesame oil, vinegar, garlic, or chili — by hand, usually with no cooking — and served cool as a 반찬 side dish: 콩나물무침, 시금치무침, 오이무침. The crucial contrast is 무침 vs 볶음: a 무침 is dressed RAW (or with just-blanched veg) and eaten cold, while a 볶음 is stir-fried in oil over heat. The signature cognate phrase is 무침을 무치다 'to dress the muchim by hand', often with the mimetic 조물조물 'kneading lightly'. Pitfall for English speakers: 무침 is normally served at room temperature or cold, so don't expect a hot dish — and the action is 무치다 'toss/dress by hand', not 섞다 'stir/mix with a tool'; the hands-on kneading is the point.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting 무침 to arrive hot — it's dressed and served cool or at room temperature, unlike the stir-fried, heated 볶음.
Confusing 무침 (raw, hand-dressed) with 볶음 (stir-fried in oil) — 무친다 means tossing by hand, no pan involved.
Using 섞다 'mix with a spoon' for the action; the precise verb is 무치다 'dress/toss by hand', often described as 조물조물 kneading.

entries.shortExplanation: 조림 means "jorim; braised dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조림 (jorim) means "jorim; braised dish". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 감자조림 주세요 ("braised potatoes, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조림 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: ingredient + 조림 names the dish
짭짤하다 'pleasantly salty' — the typical 조림 flavor
cognate verb 조리다 'simmer down in sauce'

examples.en: Braised potatoes came as a side dish.

entries.nuance: 조림 is from 조리다 'to braise/simmer down', a dish cooked low and slow in a seasoned (usually soy-sauce-based) liquid until the sauce reduces and the flavor soaks deep into the food: 감자조림, 장조림 (soy-braised beef), 생선조림. The contrast pair is 조림 vs 찌개/전골: a 조림 ends up nearly dry with a thick, concentrated, salty glaze (you don't drink it), whereas stews keep plenty of broth. It's also distinct from 무침 (tossed raw, no heat). Because the soy seasoning is strong and reduced, 조림 is a salty, long-keeping 반찬. Beware a spelling trap: the cooking verb is 조리다 'braise down' (단모음 ㅗ), which Koreans themselves often misspell as 졸이다 — and note 졸이다 also separately means 'to fret/be anxious' (마음을 졸이다). Pitfall for learners: don't expect a soupy result; a finished 조림 has almost no liquid left.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting a soupy bowl — a finished 조림 is nearly dry with a thick reduced glaze, unlike broth-rich 찌개 or 전골.
Confusing 조림 (braised in reducing sauce, with heat) with 무침 (tossed raw by hand, no heat).
Mixing up the verb 조리다 'braise down' with its near-twin 졸이다; 졸이다 separately means 'to be anxious' (마음을 졸이다), a totally different meaning.

조림 is from 조리다 'to braise/simmer down'.

entries.nuance: 구이 is from 굽다 'to grill/roast' and names any dish defined by grilling over heat, attaching to the food: 생선구이, 고등어구이, 삼겹살구이, 더덕구이. It labels the cooking METHOD, in contrast to plain ingredient words like 고기 'meat' or 생선 'fish' (which say nothing about how it's cooked), and against 볶음 (stir-fried in a pan with oil and stirring) — 구이 is grilled/roasted, often with little or no oil and not constantly stirred. The signature golden-done word is 노릇하다 'golden-brown'. A key verb note: 굽다 'to grill' is a ㅂ-irregular verb, so the stem ㅂ becomes 우 — 굽다 → 구워요, 구웠어요, 구워서 — which is exactly where the noun 구이 comes from. Conjugating 굽다 'grill' as a regular verb (구버요); it's ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 구워요/구웠어요/구워서.

entries.nuance: 전골 is a communal hot pot — neatly arranged raw meat, vegetables, mushrooms, and broth set over a portable burner and simmered right at your table so you eat as it cooks. The contrast to nail is 전골 vs 찌개: a 전골 has MORE broth, is laid out raw and cooked in front of the group on a flame, and is built for sharing among several people, whereas a 찌개 is thicker, saltier, and usually arrives already cooked. Because it's inherently group food, it's a staple of 회식 'company dinners'. Collocations: 끓이다/끓다 'boil', plus 사리 추가 'add a noodle/dumpling refill' at the end. Pitfall for English speakers: don't order 전골 for one — it's portioned for two or more (이 인분부터), and unlike a 찌개 it's not delivered pre-made; the cooking happens at the table, so expect to wait and watch it bubble before digging in.

Ordering 전골 for a single person — it's made and portioned for groups (typically 이 인분 and up) to share from one pot.
Confusing 전골 (raw ingredients cooked at your table, broth-rich) with 찌개 (thicker, saltier, usually brought already cooked).
Expecting it to arrive ready to eat; a 전골 simmers in front of you, so you wait for it to 끓다 'boil' first.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 부침개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: cognate verb 부치다 'to pan-fry (in oil)'
바삭하다 'be crispy' — the prized texture
장 counts flat/sheet-like things
ingredient + 부침개

examples.en: On rainy days I pan-fry savory pancakes.
examples.note: simple rainy-day habit; cognate verb in action

examples.en: The pancake is crispy outside and moist inside.
examples.note: everyday texture description; 겉/속 'outside/inside'

examples.en: A savory pancake with a glass of makgeolli — truly the best.
examples.note: real casual invite; the classic pairing

entries.nuance: 부침개 is from 부치다 'to pan-fry (food in a thin layer of oil)' + the -개 noun suffix, so it's the umbrella word for savory flour-batter pancakes: 파전 (green onion), 김치전, 해물파전 (seafood). The near-synonym question is 부침개 vs 전: in everyday speech they overlap heavily, but 부침개 is the broad native cover term, while 전 (Sino-Korean 煎 'pan-fry') often implies smaller, neater individually-battered pieces (호박전, 동그랑땡) and is the more formal/holiday word. The signature cognate phrase is 부침개를 부치다 'pan-fry a pancake', the texture word is 바삭하다 'crispy', and culturally it's rainy-day comfort food eaten with 막걸리 (rice wine). Two pitfalls: count flat pancakes with 장 (the sheet counter), not the generic 개; and never think 'pancake' = sweet — 부침개 is savory, oily, and salty, nothing like a breakfast pancake.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it with the generic 개 — flat, sheet-like 부침개 takes the counter 장: 부침개 한 장.
Assuming 'pancake' means sweet/dessert; 부침개 is savory and pan-fried in oil, eaten as food or a drinking snack, not breakfast.
Using 만들다 only; the idiomatic verb is the cognate 부치다 'pan-fry', as in 부침개를 부치다 — Koreans 부치다 a pancake, they don't just 만들다 it.

Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 주세요 — you just order 'the baekban'; the kitchen decides the sides
푸짐하다 'plentiful' — praise for big portions

place noun: -집 'house/shop'

examples.en: I often eat a baekban set for lunch.
examples.note: simple everyday-lunch habit

examples.romanization: i jibeun banchani manaseo baekbani pujimhaeyo.

examples.note: everyday praise; -아서 'because'

examples.en: Ma'am, one baekban set, please.
examples.note: real ordering line in a neighborhood eatery

entries.nuance: 백반 is Sino-Korean 白飯 — 白 'white' + 飯 'cooked rice' — literally 'white rice', but as a menu word it means the whole cheap home-style set: a bowl of rice with soup and a generous spread of small 반찬 side dishes, all decided by the kitchen. The contrast to learn is 백반 vs 정식: a 백반 is humble, side-dish-driven, and has no single fixed 'main' (you just get whatever the kitchen made that day), whereas a 정식 'set meal' is built around a named main dish (불고기정식) at a set price and feels more put-together. It evokes a Korean home-cooked tray, served in small neighborhood 식당 'eateries'. Count the whole spread with 상 'table setting'. Pitfall: don't take the literal 白飯 'white rice' meaning — ordering 백반 does NOT get you a plain bowl of rice; it gets you a full meal — and don't expect to choose your sides, since 백반 comes pre-set by the cook.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 백반 literally as 白飯 'plain white rice' — on a menu it means a full home-style meal of rice, soup, and many side dishes, not a bare rice bowl.
Expecting to pick your own dishes; 백반 is set by the kitchen, so you take what comes that day.
Confusing 백반 (sides-focused, no fixed main) with 정식 (built around one named main dish at a fixed price).

usagePhrases.en: the set meal comes out well/generously
usagePhrases.note: 잘 나오다 'be well served' — praise for a complete tray

entries.nuance: 정식 is Sino-Korean 定食 — 定 'fixed/set' + 食 'meal' — a set meal organized around one named main dish and served at a fixed price with rice, soup, and side dishes: 불고기정식, 생선구이정식, 한정식 (a full Korean banquet set). The contrast pair is 정식 vs 백반: a 정식 leads with and is priced around a specific main (the name tells you the star dish), and feels more composed and a notch pricier, whereas 백반 is the humbler, side-dish-driven home set with no fixed main. The whole tray is counted with 상, and you choose the set option with -(으)로: 정식으로 주세요. Pitfall: because 정식 already bundles in the rice, soup, and banchan, don't order those sides separately as if à la carte — they're included; and the same 한자 정 定 'fixed' is why a 정식 always comes at one set price, not pick-and-pay.

Confusing 정식 (built around one named main dish, more composed) with 백반 (humble, side-dish-focused home set, no fixed main).
Forgetting the choosing particle when picking the set option; Koreans say 정식으로 할게요/주세요 '-으로' to mean 'go with the set meal version'.

entries.shortExplanation: 자격증 means "certificate; license (qualification)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자격증 (jagyeokjeung) means "certificate; license (qualification)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자격증을 따다 ("to get a certificate"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자격증 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 따다 (literally 'pluck/win') is the default verb for earning a credential through effort; 받다 only fits the moment it is physically handed to you.
The test you sit to earn the credential; 자격증 시험을 보다 = take that exam.

Name the field first: 요리 자격증, 컴퓨터 자격증, 한식조리 자격증. The field word slots directly in front, no particle. (A driver's license, though, is just 운전면허 — 면허 already means 'license', so 운전면허 자격증 is redundant.)

usagePhrases.en: to be equipped with a certificate
usagePhrases.note: 갖추다 = to have in place as a prepared requirement; common on résumés and job postings (자격증을 갖춘 사람).

examples.en: I have one certificate.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 자격증이 있다 = to have one. Use 이 because 자격증 ends in a consonant.

examples.ko: 이직하려고 자격증을 하나 더 따고 있어요.
examples.romanization: ijikaryeogo jagyeokjeungeul hana deo ttago isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm getting one more certificate to change jobs.
examples.note: 이직하다 = change jobs; -으려고 marks the goal. 따고 있다 = in the process of earning.

examples.ko: 그 회사는 토익 점수보다 자격증을 더 봐요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesaneun toik jeomsuboda jagyeokjeungeul deo bwayo.

examples.note: Here 보다 means 'to weigh/consider' when evaluating applicants — not 'to look at' literally.

entries.nuance: 자격증 (資格證, '資格 qualification' + '證 proof-document') is the umbrella term for any official credential certifying a skill — cooking, computing, bookkeeping, forklift operation. Korean adults collect them relentlessly to pad a résumé, so it surfaces in every career-and-self-improvement chat (스펙 쌓기 'building specs'). The dividing line you must keep straight is 자격증 vs 증명서: 자격증 proves you are *qualified to do* something, while 증명서 (證明書) is a plain proof paper like a transcript (성적 증명서) or residence certificate. The trap for English speakers is the verb: in English you 'get' or even casually 'have' a certificate, but Korean reserves 따다 ('win it through effort') for earning one — never 사다 ('buy'), which sounds like a forged document, and only 받다 at the instant of conferral. Habitual partners: 자격증을 따다, 자격증을 갖추다, 자격증 시험.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 자격증을 사다 — 사다 means 'buy', implying you purchased a fake. You *earn* it: 자격증을 따다.
Using 받다 for the whole journey of qualifying. 받다 only fits the conferral moment; the effort of qualifying is 따다.
Confusing 자격증 (proof you are *qualified*) with 증명서 (a factual proof paper like a transcript). A 성적 증명서 is not a 자격증.

entries.shortExplanation: 인강 means "online lecture; recorded class (slang)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 결제하다 = to settle payment; these courses are paid subscriptions, so 결제 (not just 사다) is the natural verb.

examples.en: Instead of going to an academy, I study with online lectures.
examples.note: Shows the classic trade-off: in-person 학원 vs streamed 인강. -으로 = the method.

examples.ko: 그 인강 배속으로 들으면 시간이 진짜 절약돼요.
examples.romanization: geu ingang baesogeuro deureumyeon sigani jinjja jeoryakdwaeyo.
examples.en: If you watch that lecture at higher speed, you really save time.
examples.note: 배속(倍速) = playback speed; 1.5배속/2배속 is a real Korean study habit. 절약되다 = gets saved.

entries.nuance: 인강 is a clipped blend of 인터넷 강의 (인터넷 'internet' + 강의 講義 'lecture'), so it is casual, spoken slang — fine among students and friends, but you would write 인터넷 강의 in a formal report. It means specifically a *pre-recorded, streamed* video course, the backbone of Korean exam prep and self-study. Hold the line against two near terms: 인강 is recorded and on-demand, whereas 화상 수업 / 줌 수업 is a *live* online class you join in real time, and 강의 is the neutral umbrella for any lecture. The pitfall for English speakers is the verb. Because it is video, learners instinctively reach for 보다 ('watch'), but Koreans say 인강을 듣다 ('listen to') — 듣다 is idiomatically locked to lectures regardless of the medium, exactly as you '듣다' a 수업 or 강의. Habitual partners: 인강을 듣다, 인강을 결제하다, 배속으로 듣다, 인강 강사.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 인강의 by analogy with 인터넷 강의 — the clipped form drops everything after 인강; it is just 인강.
Defaulting to 보다 because it is video. The idiom is 인강을 듣다 ('listen'), the same verb used for any lecture.
Using 인강 in a formal essay or e-mail. It is colloquial; switch to 인터넷 강의 or 온라인 강의 in writing.

entries.shortExplanation: 과외 means "private tutoring (one-on-one)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 과외 (gwaoe) = "private tutoring (one-on-one)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과외를 받다 ("to receive private tutoring") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과외, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 when *you are the student* being taught — you receive the lessons.
하다 when *you are the tutor* — a classic college part-time job. Same noun, role decided by the verb.
시키다 = make/arrange-for; parents 시키다 과외 for their kids — they neither receive nor give it.
Subject goes in front: 영어 과외, 수학 과외, 피아노 과외 — no particle between.

examples.en: I take private English lessons.
examples.note: Student's view = 받다. Subject 영어 sits directly before 과외.

examples.ko: 대학생 때 수학 과외를 해서 용돈을 벌었어요.
examples.romanization: daehaksaeng ttae suhak gwaoereul haeseo yongdoneul beoreosseoyo.
examples.en: I earned pocket money tutoring math in college.
examples.note: Tutor's view = 하다. 용돈 = spending money; the archetypal Korean student side job.

examples.en: I'm wondering whether to get my kid a tutor.
examples.note: Parent's view = 시키다, with -한테 marking the child who receives it. 고민 중 = mulling it over.

entries.nuance: 과외 (課外, '課 lesson/coursework' + '外 outside' = 'outside the regular curriculum') is private, typically one-on-one tutoring, usually at the student's home, and it sits in a clear three-way contrast you should master: 과외 is personalized and premium (one tutor, one or a few students), 학원 (學院) is a commercial academy with class-sized groups, and 인강 is a recorded video course. The word's defining grammar is that one noun takes three different verbs depending on who you are: the learner 받다 (receives) it, the tutor 하다 (does/gives) it, and the parent 시키다 (arranges) it — getting these backwards is the #1 English-speaker error, since English flattens all three into 'tutor'/'get tutoring'. Note too that 과외 is not only for children: adults take 과외 for languages, instruments, or golf. Habitual partners: 과외를 받다/하다/시키다, 영어 과외, 그룹 과외.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 받다 and 하다. The student *receives* (과외를 받다); the tutor *does* it (과외를 하다). They are not interchangeable.
Using 받다 or 하다 when a parent sets it up. Parents 시키다 — they arrange it for the child (아이에게 과외를 시키다).
Assuming 과외 means kids only. Adults get 과외 for languages and hobbies too; it is defined by being private, not by age.

structuredNuance.t: 과외 is private, typically one-on-one tutoring, usually at the student's home. Note too that it is not only for children: adults take 과외 for languages, instruments, or golf.

entries.shortExplanation: 수능 means "Korean college entrance exam (CSAT)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수능 (suneung) means "Korean college entrance exam (CSAT)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수능을 보다 ("to take the CSAT"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수능 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 is the fixed verb for sitting an exam in Korean; 시험을 보다 is the parent pattern.
치다 (or formal 치르다) = to undergo a formal exam; slightly more formal/regional than 보다.
A near-national holiday in feel: stock market opens late, planes pause for the listening test.
수능 끝나고 ('after the CSAT') is a landmark phrase marking a senior's release into freedom.

examples.en: Tomorrow is the CSAT.
examples.note: Simple identity sentence: 수능이다 = 'it is the CSAT.' 이에요 because 수능 ends in a consonant.

examples.ko: 조카가 올해 수능을 봐서 온 가족이 긴장했어요.
examples.romanization: jokaga olhae suneungeul bwaseo on gajogi ginjanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: My niece sat the CSAT this year, so the whole family was on edge.
examples.note: 수능을 보다 + family stress — shows how nation-wide the event feels. 긴장하다 = to be tense.

examples.ko: 수능 날에는 영어 듣기 시간에 비행기도 잠깐 멈춰요.
examples.romanization: suneung nareneun yeongeo deutgi sigane bihaenggido jamkkan meomchwoyo.
examples.en: On CSAT day, even planes pause during the English listening section.
examples.note: A true cultural fact; 듣기 = listening test. Great for sounding locally informed.

entries.nuance: 수능 is the clipped form of 대학수학능력시험 (大學修學能力試驗, literally 'university study-ability test') — the single nationwide university-entrance exam held once a year, on a Thursday in mid-November. It is not a generic final; that is precisely the distinction English speakers must keep: 기말고사 is a school's term-end exam, 모의고사 is a practice rehearsal, but 수능 is *the* one-shot national gatekeeper, and calling any big test '수능' sounds wrong to Koreans. As a resident you will feel its weight directly — altered traffic, delayed work start times, hushed neighborhoods, and the famous flight pause during the listening section. The verb is 수능을 보다 ('sit/take'), with 치다/치르다 as a more formal alternative; never 하다, because in Korean you do not 'do' an exam, you 보다 it. Habitual partners: 수능을 보다, 수능 점수, 수능 날, 수능 끝나고.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수능을 하다. Exams are 보다 (or 치르다), never 하다 — 하다 collocates with activities, not with sitting a test.
Treating 수능 as 'the final exam.' It is specifically the once-a-year *national* college-entrance test; a school term exam is 기말고사.
Confusing 수능 (the entrance exam itself) with 입시 (the whole admissions *process* that the 수능 is one part of).

entries.shortExplanation: 모의고사 means "mock exam; practice test" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "mock exam; practice test" is 모의고사 (mouigosa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 모의고사를 보다 ("to take a mock exam"). Watch the particle attached to 모의고사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 = to sit the test, treating the mock like a real exam session.

usagePhrases.en: to work through a practice test
usagePhrases.note: 풀다 ('to solve/loosen') focuses on actually doing the problems, often alone for practice.
성적 = academic results/score; used to forecast real-exam performance and pick target schools.
Mocks are scheduled and named by month (6월/9월 모평); the month carries real predictive weight.

examples.en: I'm taking a mock exam tomorrow.
examples.note: 모의고사 + 보다, the sit-it sense. Simple scheduled-future use of the present tense.

examples.en: After working through the practice test, I analyzed my weak points.
examples.note: 풀다 = do the problems; 약점 분석 (weakness analysis) is the standard follow-up routine.

examples.en: This mock came out harder than usual.
examples.note: 나오다 ('come out') is the idiomatic verb for how a test 'turned out.' 평소보다 = than usual.

entries.nuance: 모의고사 (模擬考査, '模擬 imitation/simulation' + '考査 examination' = 'a simulated exam') is a full-dress rehearsal designed to mimic the real thing, above all the 수능; the high-school version run by education offices is also called 모의평가, clipped to 모평. Students sit them repeatedly to track progress and tame exam nerves. The key boundary for learners is 모의고사 vs 중간/기말고사: a 모의고사 is an ungraded *rehearsal* that predicts performance, while 중간고사 (midterm) and 기말고사 (final) are real school exams that go on your transcript — mixing them up misstates how seriously the result counts. Two verbs split the meaning: 보다 for sitting it as an exam event, 풀다 for the act of solving the questions. The English-speaker pitfall, as with all exams, is reaching for 하다; you 보다 or 풀다 a 모의고사, never 하다 it. Habitual partners: 모의고사를 보다/풀다, 모의고사 성적, 모의고사가 어렵게 나오다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 모의고사 with 중간고사/기말고사. A 모의고사 is a non-graded rehearsal; midterms and finals are real exams that count toward your grade.
Saying 모의고사를 하다 instead of 보다 (to sit it) or 풀다 (to solve it). Exams never take 하다.
Using 풀다 when you mean the formal exam *session*. 풀다 = solve the problems; for the act of sitting it under exam conditions use 보다.

structuredNuance.t: 모의고사 is a full-dress rehearsal designed to mimic the real thing, above all the 수능; the high-school version run by education offices is also called 모의평가, clipped to 모평. Students sit them repeatedly to track progress and tame exam nerves.

entries.shortExplanation: 논술 means "essay exam; argumentative writing test" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 논술 (nonsul) = "essay exam; argumentative writing test". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 논술을 준비하다 ("to prepare for the essay exam") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 논술, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to prepare for the essay exam
usagePhrases.note: 준비하다 = to prepare; 논술 demands dedicated, sustained practice, not last-minute review.
Marks it as a written, open-response test as opposed to 객관식 (multiple-choice).
전형(銓衡) = an admissions screening method; 논술 전형 is one defined route into university.
쓰다 ('write') for the act of producing the essay itself during the exam.

examples.en: I find essay exams hard.
examples.note: Basic 논술이 어렵다 ('the essay exam is hard'); 이/가 marks the subject of the descriptive 어렵다.

examples.ko: 논술은 정답이 하나가 아니라서 더 까다로워요.
examples.romanization: nonsureun jeongdabi hanaga aniraseo deo kkadarowoyo.
examples.en: Essay exams are trickier because there isn't one right answer.
examples.note: Captures the open-ended core of 논술. 정답이 하나가 아니다 = there's no single answer.

examples.en: I got into university through the essay-based track.
examples.note: -으로 marks the admissions route; 합격하다 = to pass/be admitted. Shows 논술 as a real pathway.

entries.nuance: 논술 (論述, '論 to argue/reason' + '述 to state/narrate') is a structured *argumentative essay exam* that tests logical reasoning and disciplined writing, used by Korean universities as one admissions route (논술 전형) alongside grades and the 수능. The sharp contrast learners need is 논술 vs 작문/에세이: 작문 (作文) and the loanword 에세이 mean general composition or a personal/free essay, whereas 논술 is specifically a reasoned, thesis-driven argument graded on logic and structure — so a casual diary entry is 작문, never 논술. Because there is no single correct answer, whole academies (논술 학원) exist just to coach it. Watch the verbs: you 준비하다 it (prepare), 쓰다 it (write the answer), and pass via 논술 전형 — but you would not 보다 it the way you 보다 a multiple-choice 시험, since 논술 emphasizes producing text. Habitual partners: 논술을 준비하다, 논술을 쓰다, 논술 시험, 논술 전형.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 논술 (a reasoned argumentative exam) with 작문/에세이 (general or personal composition). Logic and structure define 논술.
Calling any writing assignment 논술. It means specifically a structured, argument-based exam, not free writing or a report (보고서).
Reaching for 하다: 논술을 하다 is off. Use 논술을 준비하다 (prepare) or 논술을 쓰다 (write the essay).

structuredNuance.t: 논술 is a structured argumentative essay exam that tests logical reasoning and disciplined writing, used by Korean universities as one admissions route (논술 전형) alongside grades and the 수능. Because there is no single correct answer, whole academies (논술 학원) exist just to coach it.

論述 = 論 to argue/reason + 述 to state/narrate.

entries.shortExplanation: 학위 means "academic degree" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 학위 (hagwi) means "academic degree". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 학위를 받다 ("to receive a degree"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 학위 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 = to be conferred — the formal moment the university grants it to you.
따다 ('win/pluck') foregrounds the years of effort behind obtaining it; warmer, more colloquial than 받다.
Hierarchy: 학사(學士) bachelor's, 석사(碩士) master's, 박사(博士) doctorate — each + 학위.
과정(課程) = course/program of study; 석사 학위 과정 = a master's program.

examples.en: I have a bachelor's degree.
examples.note: 학위가 있다 = to hold a degree. 학사 = bachelor's; the level word sits before 학위.

examples.ko: 한국에서 석사 학위를 따려고 유학 왔어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseo seoksa hagwireul ttaryeogo yuhak wasseoyo.
examples.en: I came to Korea to earn a master's.
examples.note: 유학 오다 = come abroad to study; -으려고 marks the purpose. 따다 stresses the effort.

examples.ko: 그 자리는 관련 학위가 있어야 지원할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: geu jarineun gwallyeon hagwiga isseoya jiwonhal su isseoyo.
examples.en: You need a relevant degree to apply for that position.
examples.note: -아야 = the requirement 'must have'; practical for job-hunting talk. 지원하다 = to apply.

entries.nuance: 학위 (學位, '學 learning' + '位 rank/position' = 'a rank in learning') is your formal academic degree: 학사 (bachelor's), 석사 (master's), or 박사 (doctorate). The contrast you must not blur is 학위 vs 학력: 학위 is a specific *degree title* you were granted, while 학력 (學歷) is your overall *level of schooling completed* (e.g. 고졸 'high-school graduate', 대졸 'college graduate') — a job form asking 학력 wants your education level, not a degree certificate. Two verbs serve it with a nuance gap: 받다 marks the conferral ('the degree was awarded to me'), 따다 foregrounds the grind of earning it; pick by which you want to stress. Pair it with 과정 to talk about the program itself (학위 과정). In Korea 학위 matters for both employment and certain visa categories, so it is genuinely practical for residents. The English-speaker pitfall is the all-purpose 하다: you 받다 or 따다 a degree, never 학위를 하다. Habitual partners: 학위를 받다/따다, 석사 학위, 학위 과정.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 학위 (a degree title like 석사) with 학력 (overall education level like 고졸/대졸). Forms asking 학력 want the level, not the degree.
Saying 학위를 하다. A degree is received (받다) or earned (따다); 하다 does not collocate with 학위.
Treating 받다 and 따다 as identical. 받다 = the conferral moment; 따다 = the effortful achievement. Choose by emphasis.

structuredNuance.t: 학위 is your formal academic degree: 학사 (bachelor's), 석사 (master's), or 박사 (doctorate). In Korea 학위 matters for both employment and certain visa categories, so it is genuinely practical for residents.

學位 = 學 learning + 位 rank/position = 'a rank in learning'.

entries.shortExplanation: 입시 means "entrance-exam process; admissions" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "entrance-exam process; admissions" is 입시 (ipsi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 입시를 준비하다 ("to prepare for admissions"). Watch the particle attached to 입시 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 준비하다 over a multi-year span — 입시 is a process, not a single test day.

usagePhrases.en: to go through the admissions process
usagePhrases.note: 치르다 = to undergo a formal ordeal/exam; the right verb for living through the whole 입시.
By far the most common collocation; 대학 입시 = the university-entrance race specifically.
경쟁(競爭) = competition; 입시 is almost inseparable from 치열한 경쟁 (fierce competition).

examples.en: Korean college admissions are really cutthroat.
examples.note: 치열하다 = fierce/cutthroat, the defining adjective for 입시. Simple descriptive sentence.

examples.ko: 입시 때문에 고등학생들이 스트레스를 많이 받아요.
examples.romanization: ipsi ttaemune godeunghaksaengdeuri seuteureseureul mani badayo.
examples.en: High schoolers get a lot of stress because of admissions.
examples.note: 때문에 = because of; 스트레스를 받다 (not 가지다) = to get stressed. A go-to social-commentary line.

examples.ko: 요즘은 입시 제도가 자주 바뀌어서 학부모들이 헷갈려해요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun ipsi jedoga jaju bakkwieoseo hakbumodeuri hetgallyeohaeyo.
examples.en: These days the admissions system changes so often that parents get confused.
examples.note: 제도 = system; 헷갈려하다 = to find confusing. Reflects a real, recurring Korean complaint.

entries.nuance: 입시 (入試, '入 to enter' + '試 examination' = a clip of 입학시험 'entrance exam') refers to the *entire* entrance-examination and admissions enterprise — application strategy, the 수능, 논술, interviews, the whole multi-year campaign — not one exam. This is the precise trap for English speakers: 입시 is the umbrella *process*, whereas 수능 is a single test that happens to sit inside it, and 입학 (入學) is the actual act of *enrolling* once you are admitted; conflating 입시 with 수능 misses that the word names the entire race. It carries heavy cultural freight of brutal competition and is a perennial topic in Korean news and family life (사교육 'private education', 입시 지옥 'admissions hell'). Distinguish it also from 취업 (就業 'getting a job'): 입시 is entering *school*, 취업 is entering the *workforce*. Habitual partners: 대학 입시, 입시 준비, 입시 학원, 입시 경쟁, 입시 제도.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 입시 with a single test. It is the whole admissions process — the 수능, 논술, interviews and applications all fall under 입시.
Confusing 입시 (the entrance/admissions process) with 입학 (actually enrolling) or 취업 (entering the workforce). Different stages entirely.
Saying 스트레스를 가지다 in these sentences. Korean idiom is 스트레스를 받다 — you 'receive' stress, you don't 'have' it.

entries.shortExplanation: 출석 means "attendance (being present)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 출석 (chulseok) = "attendance (being present)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 출석을 부르다 ("to call the roll") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 출석, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 부르다 = to call out (names); what the teacher does at the start of class to check who is present.
출석 체크 is the everyday phrase; 체크하다 = to check off the present students.
인정(認定) = to recognize/grant; a sick day or official absence still 'counted' as 출석.
-률(率) turns it into a rate/percentage: 출석률이 높다 = the attendance rate is high.

examples.en: (The teacher) is calling the roll.
examples.note: Core collocation 출석을 부르다. The act that opens many Korean classes.

examples.en: The professor calls roll every single class.
examples.note: 매 수업마다 = every class without exception; -마다 = each/every. Shows how attendance is policed.

examples.en: Just by completing attendance you can raise your grade.
examples.note: 채우다 = to fill/meet a quota; 학점 = course credit/grade. Reflects attendance counting toward marks.

entries.nuance: 출석 (出席, '出 to go out/appear' + '席 seat' = 'to take one's seat') is the noun for being present, the base of everyday phrases like 출석 체크 and 출석을 부르다. In Korean universities and academies, 출석 frequently feeds directly into your grade, so it is a genuinely practical word; its antonym is 결석 (缺席 'absence'). Two distinctions trip English speakers. First, register-of-place: 출석 is showing up to *class*, 출근 (出勤) is showing up to *work*, and 참석 (參席) is attending an *event/meeting* — so you 출근하다 to the office but 참석하다 a wedding, and using 출석 for either sounds school-bound. Second, 출석 as a verb (출석하다) means 'be present at class/roll call,' so do not stretch it to events; for a ceremony or meeting say 참석하다. Habitual partners: 출석을 부르다, 출석 체크, 출석률, 출석을 인정하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 출석 for showing up to work. That is 출근(하다); 출석 is specifically class attendance.
Saying 출석하다 for attending an event or meeting. For ceremonies and meetings use 참석하다 (to attend/participate).
Confusing 출석 (present) with 결석 (absent). They are opposites — 무단 결석 = an unexcused absence, the thing 출석 prevents.

entries.shortExplanation: 벼락치기 means "cramming (last-minute studying)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 벼락치기 (byeorakchigi) means "cramming (last-minute studying)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 벼락치기를 하다 ("to cram"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 벼락치기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The whole word is a noun; 하다 turns it into the action 'to do cramming.'
-로 marks cramming as the *method*: study by way of last-minute effort.

usagePhrases.en: to take an exam having crammed
usagePhrases.note: -로 again marks the means; describes facing a test on cram-only prep.
밤새(다) = stay up all night; the prototypical 벼락치기 scenario.

examples.en: I cram a lot.
examples.note: Bare frame with 하다. 자주 = often; a rueful self-description many students relate to.

examples.en: It's hard to get a good score by cramming.
examples.note: -로는 = 'by means of, as for'; 받기 힘들다 = hard to get. Standard cautionary advice.

examples.en: The exam's tomorrow and it's cramming again.
examples.note: Casual -야 ending (반말); 또 = yet again. A relatable, self-deprecating student grumble.

entries.nuance: 벼락치기 is a vivid native (non-Sino) compound: 벼락 ('a bolt of lightning') + 치기 (the noun form of 치다 'to strike') — literally 'striking like lightning,' i.e. frantic, all-at-once last-minute studying right before a test. It is colloquial and self-aware; students and recent grads use it about themselves with a wry, slightly guilty tone, so keep it out of academic writing — in a formal context you would rephrase it neutrally, e.g. 단기간에 몰아서 공부하다 ('study intensively in a short period'). The natural contrast is with 꾸준히 공부하다 (studying steadily over time): 벼락치기 is the short, panicked burst, the opposite of sustained effort. Two grammar points carry the English-speaker pitfalls: because it *names an activity*, it takes 하다 (벼락치기를 하다), never 보다 — you don't 'see' cramming — and to mark it as your study *method* you attach -로 (벼락치기로 공부하다). Habitual partners: 벼락치기를 하다, 벼락치기로 공부하다, 밤새 벼락치기, 시험 전날 벼락치기.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 벼락치기를 보다. Cramming is an activity you *do*: 벼락치기를 하다. 보다 (see/take-exam) does not fit.
Using it in formal or academic writing. 벼락치기 is colloquial and self-deprecating; rephrase to something neutral in essays.
Marking the method with the wrong particle. 'Study by cramming' is 벼락치기로 공부하다 (-로 = means), not 벼락치기에 or 벼락치기를 공부하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 까다롭다 means "tricky; demanding; picky (hard to satisfy)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tricky; demanding; picky (hard to satisfy)" is 까다롭다 (kkadaropda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 문제가 까다롭다 ("the questions are tricky"). Watch the particle attached to 까다롭다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Go-to phrase for finicky, hard-to-crack exam questions; not just hard, but fiddly.
ㅂ-irregular before a noun: 까다롭 + 은 → 까다로운, never 까다롭은.
Used for hard-to-meet requirements — scholarships, visas, applications.
입맛(taste) + 까다롭다 = fussy about food; a very common collocation about people.

examples.en: This question is a bit tricky.
examples.note: Plain present 까다로워요 shows the ㅂ-irregular (-롭다 → -로워요). 좀 softens it.

examples.ko: 그 교수님은 채점이 까다로워서 학점 받기 어려워요.
examples.romanization: geu gyosunimeun chaejeomi kkadarowoseo hakjeom batgi eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: That professor grades strictly, so it's hard to score well.
examples.note: 채점(grading) + 까다롭다 is natural. -아서 links cause→result. Past would be 까다로웠어요.

examples.en: The scholarship requirements are pickier than I expected.
examples.note: 조건이 까다롭다 = fussy conditions; 생각보다 = more than expected. Practical for residents seeking aid.

entries.nuance: 까다롭다 describes something *tricky and hard to satisfy* — fiddly exam questions, fussy requirements, or a finicky, hard-to-please person. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the final ㅂ turns to 우 before a vowel, giving 까다로워요 (present), 까다로웠어요 (past), and 까다로운 (before a noun) — memorize these because regularizing to 까다롭아요 is the single most common learner error. The crucial meaning contrast is 까다롭다 vs 어렵다: 어렵다 is plainly 'difficult/hard' in a neutral way, but 까다롭다 adds a layer of *finickiness* — picky, particular, full of fiddly conditions. So a math problem can be 어렵다 (just hard) or 까다롭다 (sneaky, full of traps); a person who is 까다롭다 is hard to please, which 어렵다 can't convey. Applied to people it leans negative (demanding, fussy), so use care describing someone's character. Habitual partners: 문제가 까다롭다, 조건이 까다롭다, 입맛이 까다롭다, 까다로운 교수님.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Regularizing the ㅂ-irregular: it is 까다로워요 / 까다로웠어요 / 까다로운, never 까다롭아요 or 까다롭은.
Using it as a plain synonym for 'difficult.' 어렵다 = simply hard; 까다롭다 adds finicky/picky/fiddly nuance, especially for conditions and people.
Casually calling a person 까다로워요 to their face. Of people it means 'fussy/hard to please' and can sound critical; soften or rephrase.

entries.shortExplanation: 꾸준히 means "steadily; consistently (without giving up)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 꾸준히 (kkujunhi) = "steadily; consistently (without giving up)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 꾸준히 공부하다 ("to study consistently") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 꾸준히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing in a study context — keep at it day after day.
For languages, instruments, sports; emphasizes regular repetition over time.
Praises sustained persistence rather than one big push.
늘다 = to grow/improve; 꾸준히 늘다 = get better bit by bit, continuously.

examples.en: I do it steadily every day.
examples.note: 꾸준히 + 하다, the most generic form of encouragement to keep going. 매일 reinforces the regularity.

examples.en: Studying steadily beats cramming.
examples.note: Direct contrast with 벼락치기. -보다 = than; -는 게 낫다 = it's better to. The classic study moral.

examples.en: If you keep at Korean consistently, you'll improve fast.
examples.note: -면 = if/when; 금방 = quickly; 늘다 = improve. Encouragement aimed straight at the learner.

entries.nuance: 꾸준히 means doing something *steadily and consistently over time, without quitting* — it is the warm praise-word Koreans reach for to describe sustainable, unglamorous, day-after-day effort. The contrast you must internalize is 꾸준히 vs 열심히: 열심히 means 'hard, with intensity/diligence' and can describe a single burst (오늘 열심히 공부했어요 = I studied hard today), whereas 꾸준히 is inherently about *continuity* across time — you cannot be 꾸준히 for one day, because the word means you kept it up. So an all-nighter is 열심히, never 꾸준히; daily practice for a year is 꾸준히. In a self-improvement context it is the natural opposite of cramming (벼락치기) or giving up. The grammar pitfall for English speakers is part of speech: 꾸준히 is an *adverb* that modifies verbs (꾸준히 공부하다), so you cannot use it to describe a noun directly — for that you need the adjective 꾸준하다 (e.g. 꾸준한 노력 'steady effort'). Habitual partners: 꾸준히 공부하다, 꾸준히 연습하다, 꾸준히 노력하다, 꾸준히 늘다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 꾸준히 (consistently, over time) with 열심히 (hard, with intensity). You can be 열심히 for one day; 꾸준히 means you kept it up continuously.
Using 꾸준히 to modify a noun. It is an adverb; for a noun use the adjective form: 꾸준한 노력 ('steady effort'), not 꾸준히 노력.
Pairing it with one-off actions. 꾸준히 implies repetition over time, so 'I studied 꾸준히 last night' is contradictory — that's 열심히.
