entries.shortExplanation: 설렘 means "flutter of excitement; butterflies" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 설렘 (seollem) means "flutter of excitement; butterflies". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 설렘 ("a flutter of excitement"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 설렘 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: native noun made from the verb 설레다 + the nominalizing -ㅁ, like 슬프다→슬픔; the sweet nervous buzz before something good
설렘 가득(한) drops the particle for a snappy, ad-like feel: 설렘 가득한 첫날

usagePhrases.en: to feel one's heart pound with anticipation
usagePhrases.note: the verb almost always travels with the mimetic 두근두근 (heart-thump)

usagePhrases.en: the excitement of a first day at work
usagePhrases.note: N + 의 + 설렘 names what the flutter is about; 여행의 설렘, 첫사랑의 설렘

examples.en: Tomorrow's the picnic, so I'm full of excitement.
examples.note: Simple A-is-B frame: 설렘 가득이에요 packages the whole feeling into one noun phrase.

examples.ko: 첫 데이트 전날이라 설렘 때문에 잠이 안 와요.
examples.romanization: cheot deiteu jeonnarira seollem ttaemune jami an wayo.
examples.en: It's the night before my first date, so I can't sleep from the butterflies.
examples.note: 설렘 때문에 = 'because of the flutter'; 때문에 attaches the cause to the noun, not a verb.

examples.ko: 새집으로 이사 가는 날, 설렘 반 걱정 반이었어요.
examples.romanization: saejibeuro isa ganeun nal, seollem ban geokjeong banieosseoyo.
examples.en: On moving day to the new place, I was half excited and half anxious.
examples.note: 설렘 반 걱정 반 = the set 'half X, half Y' rhythm Koreans use for mixed feelings.

entries.nuance: 설렘 is a warm, *positive* nervousness, the soft flutter before a date, a trip, or a new beginning, never fear or dread. It is native Korean (verb 설레다 + nominalizer -ㅁ, so spelled 설렘, not 설레임, the famous brand-name misspelling). The dividing line vs 신남/신나다 is anticipation vs the thing itself: 설렘 is the sweet buzzing *before* something, while 신나다 is the loud fun *during* it (a game, a party). It pairs constantly with the mimetic 두근두근 and the frame 설렘 반 걱정 반. The English-speaker trap is twofold: writing 설레임 (wrong) instead of 설렘, and conjugating the verb as 설레여요 when the correct present is 설레요 (stem 설레- + -어요 fuses to -레요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 설레임 instead of 설렘. The verb is 설레다, so the noun is 설레-+-ㅁ = 설렘. 설레임 is a popular ice-cream brand spelling, but it is not standard Korean.
Conjugating the verb as 설레여요. The stem is 설레-, and 설레- + -어요 contracts to 설레요, never 설레여요.
Using 설렘 for general thrill like an exciting match. That energetic fun is 신나다/짜릿하다; 설렘 is specifically the soft anticipatory flutter beforehand.

entries.shortExplanation: 여유 means "leeway; breathing room; composure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "leeway; breathing room; composure" is 여유 (yeoyu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시간 여유 ("time to spare"). Watch the particle attached to 여유 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 여유 attaches to a domain word: 시간 여유, 돈 여유, 마음의 여유

usagePhrases.en: to have no leeway / be stretched thin
usagePhrases.note: the go-to soft refusal: covers money, time, OR emotional bandwidth

usagePhrases.en: peace of mind / mental breathing room
usagePhrases.note: literally 'leeway of the heart'; the most quoted collocation
the adjective made from 여유; 여유 자체 is a noun, not 여유하다

examples.en: I have a little time to spare today.
examples.note: Simple existence frame 여유가 있다/없다; here 여유 just means slack in the schedule.

examples.ko: 주말엔 여유 있게 천천히 쉬고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jumaren yeoyu itge cheoncheonhi swigo sipeoyo.
examples.en: On weekends I want to rest slowly, with some breathing room.
examples.note: 여유 있게 = 'in an unhurried way'; the adverbial -게 turns the state into how you do something.

examples.ko: 월급 받아서 통장에 좀 여유가 생기면 여행 가려고요.
examples.romanization: wolgeup badaseo tongjange jom yeoyuga saenggimyeon yeohaeng garyeogoyo.
examples.en: Once payday gives my account some room to breathe, I plan to travel.
examples.note: 여유가 생기다 = 'leeway comes into being'; 생기다 is the natural verb for slack appearing.

entries.nuance: 여유 is one of the most useful daily nouns precisely because it stretches across three domains at once: spare *time*, spare *money*, and emotional *composure*. It is Sino-Korean 餘裕 (餘 'surplus/remainder' + 裕 'abundance'), literally 'left-over abundance', so picture margin or slack rather than emptiness. Koreans prize 마음의 여유 (room in the heart), so 여유가 없어요 is a gentle, relatable way to decline plans or admit stress without oversharing. The contrast to watch is 여유 (a noun = the slack itself) vs 여유롭다 (the adjective = being in a relaxed state); the English-speaker trap is inventing 여유하다, which does not exist. Use 여유가 있다/없다/생기다 for the noun, and 여유롭다 or 여유 있게 when you want the relaxed quality.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 여유하다 for 'to be relaxed.' 여유 is a noun, so use 여유가 있다 or the real adjective 여유롭다. There is no verb 여유하다.
Limiting it to feelings only. 여유 equally covers 시간 여유 (spare time) and 돈 여유 (spare money), so 여유가 없어요 can mean broke, busy, OR frazzled depending on context.
Confusing it with 여가 (leisure time / free time for hobbies). 여가 is a block of free time; 여유 is the felt slack or margin, which is broader.

entries.shortExplanation: 후회 means "regret" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 후회 (huhoe) = "regret". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 후회하다 ("to regret") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 후회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the verb; 후회 itself is the noun, so for the action use 후회하다
the feeling wells up on its own; slightly passive, less self-blaming than 후회하다
the motto phrase: 후회 없이 살자, 후회 없이 도전하다
set idiom (lit. 'beat the ground and regret') for deep, too-late regret

examples.ko: 지금 안 사면 나중에 후회할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jigeum an samyeon najunge huhoehal geot gatayo.
examples.en: If I don't buy it now, I think I'll regret it later.
examples.note: Simple future hunch: 후회하다 + -ㄹ 것 같다 = 'I think I'll regret'; points forward to a choice not yet made.

examples.ko: 그때 그 집 계약 안 한 게 두고두고 후회예요.
examples.romanization: geuttae geu jip gyeyak an han ge dugodugo huhoeyeyo.
examples.en: I keep regretting not signing the lease on that place back then.
examples.note: Noun-as-predicate 후회예요; 두고두고 = 'over and over, lingeringly,' a perfect partner for regret.

examples.en: I want to give it a real try, with no regrets.
examples.note: 후회 없이 = the regret-free mindset phrase young Koreans love as a life motto.

entries.nuance: 후회 is regret aimed squarely *backward* at a choice you already made, with a sting of self-blame. It is Sino-Korean 後悔 (後 'after/behind' + 悔 'to repent'), literally 'after-regret', the regret that comes *after* the deed. The verb 후회하다 is everyday, but the noun surfaces in lines like 후회예요 or 후회가 남아요, and the motto 후회 없이 (without regret) is hugely popular among 20-30s. The key synonym contrast is 후회 vs 아쉬움: 후회 blames *your own* decision ('I shouldn't have done that'), while 아쉬움 is a softer, fate-tinged 'aw, what a shame it didn't work out' with little self-blame. The English-speaker trap is mapping 'I regret it' straight to 후회해요 when you actually want the noun-predicate 후회예요 ('it's a regret'), and reaching for 후회 when the gentle 아쉬움 is what the situation calls for.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 후회 with 아쉬움. 후회 carries self-blame over a choice you made; 아쉬움 is the gentler 'too bad / what a shame' with no blame. Telling a friend 후회되겠다 can sound like you're saying it was their fault.
Saying 후회해요 when you mean 'it's a regret.' For the noun-predicate use 후회예요 (or 후회가 돼요); 후회해요 is the verb 'I (actively) regret.'
Using 후회 for forward-looking worry. Regret only looks back at the past; for 'I'm worried it might go wrong' use 걱정 instead.

entries.shortExplanation: 부담 means "burden; pressure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부담 (budam) means "burden; pressure". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부담이 되다 ("to become a burden"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부담 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the core collocation for both money and expectations: 월세가 부담이 돼요
adjective; the key word for politely declining an overly generous gesture
ultra-common host phrase that puts a guest at ease
pairs with its mirror 부담을 느끼다 (to feel the pressure)

examples.en: The monthly rent is a bit of a burden.
examples.note: Simple 부담이 되다 with money; here 부담 is plainly financial weight.

examples.en: Don't feel any pressure, just come and relax.
examples.note: 부담 갖지 말고 = the set host phrase; 갖지 말다 = 'don't hold (it).'

examples.ko: 이렇게 비싼 선물은 부담스러워서 못 받겠어요.
examples.romanization: ireoke bissan seonmureun budamseureowoseo mot batgesseoyo.
examples.en: A gift this expensive feels like too much, so I really can't accept it.
examples.note: 부담스럽다 in real social give-and-take = graceful refusal, not rudeness.

entries.nuance: 부담 is essential for navigating Korean social give-and-take, where accepting too much puts you in someone's debt. It is Sino-Korean 負擔 (負 'to carry on the back' + 擔 'to shoulder'), literally 'a load you shoulder', and it covers both a *financial* weight (rent, a pricey gift) and an *emotional* one (expectations, obligation). When a host says 부담 갖지 마세요, they are pre-emptively lifting that load off you; when you call a gesture 부담스러워요, you are politely signaling 'this is too generous, I'd feel indebted.' The contrast to learn is 부담 (mental/social pressure or weight) vs 짐 (a literal piece of luggage, or a metaphorical 'I'm a burden to you' = 짐이 되다). The English-speaker trap is translating it only as 'burden' and missing the warm 'please don't trouble yourself' social move, and confusing the formal verb 부담하다 (to bear a *cost*, as in 비용을 부담하다) with feeling pressure, for which you want 부담스럽다 or 부담이 되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it only as 'burden' and missing the social layer. 부담스러워요 is often a courteous 'this is too much for me,' and 부담 갖지 마세요 means 'relax, no strings attached' — pure Korean social grease.
Using 부담하다 when you mean 'to feel pressured.' 부담하다 = to bear a cost formally (비용을 부담하다). For feelings, use 부담스럽다 or 부담이 되다.
Saying 부담이 많다 for heavy pressure. The natural verb is 부담이 되다 or 부담이 크다, not 많다.

entries.shortExplanation: 배려 means "consideration; thoughtfulness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "consideration; thoughtfulness" is 배려 (baeryeo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 배려하다 ("to be considerate (toward)"). Watch the particle attached to 배려 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: verb form; 상대를 배려하다 = to consider the other person's situation
배려 + 心 = the trait; 배려심이 깊다 = deeply considerate
lit. 'consideration seat'; you'll literally read this on subway seats for the elderly/pregnant
graceful thank-you for someone easing your situation

examples.en: Thank you for being so considerate.
examples.note: Simple gratitude with 배려하다 + 주다 (do-for-me); the -아/어 주다 marks the kindness was for your benefit.

examples.ko: 임산부 배려석은 비워 두는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: imsanbu baeryeoseogeun biwo duneun ge joayo.
examples.en: It's best to keep the priority seats free for pregnant passengers.
examples.note: 배려석 = a real word on Seoul subways; 비워 두다 = 'leave it emptied.'

examples.ko: 그 친구는 배려심이 깊어서 모두가 편하게 느껴요.
examples.romanization: geu chinguneun baeryeosimi gipeoseo moduga pyeonhage neukkyeoyo.
examples.en: That friend is so deeply considerate that everyone feels at ease around them.
examples.note: 배려심이 깊다 = the fixed praise; 깊다 ('deep'), not 많다, is the natural partner.

entries.nuance: 배려 is consideration shown through *action*, anticipating someone's needs and quietly easing their discomfort before they have to ask. It is Sino-Korean 配慮 (配 'to arrange/allot' + 慮 'to think over'), literally 'arranging your thinking around others', and it is one of the most praised qualities in Korea, so visible that subway seats are labeled 배려석 (consideration seats). The synonym contrast is 배려 vs 친절(親切): 친절 is surface-level *niceness/kindness* in the moment (a friendly clerk), while 배려 is the deeper, proactive reading of someone's situation and adjusting for it. The English-speaker trap is treating it as plain 'being nice' (that's 친절) and mixing up 배려 (an act / the behavior) with 배려심 (the inner *trait*): you thank someone for their 배려, but you describe a person as 배려심이 깊다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 배려 with 친절. 친절 is being pleasant and kind on the surface; 배려 is proactively considering someone's circumstances and acting to ease them. A rude-but-thoughtful person can still show 배려.
Mixing up 배려 and 배려심. Use 배려 for the act ('thank you for your 배려') and 배려심 for the personality trait ('she has deep 배려심').
Saying 배려가 많다 about a person. For the trait prefer 배려심이 깊다/많다; 배려 alone refers to the considerate act itself.

structuredNuance.t: 배려 is consideration shown through action — anticipating someone's needs and quietly easing their discomfort before they have to ask. It is one of the most praised qualities in Korea, so visible that subway seats are labeled 배려석 (consideration seats).

entries.shortExplanation: 자존심 means "pride; ego (sense of dignity)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자존심 (jajonsim) = "pride; ego (sense of dignity)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 자존심이 상하다 ("to have one's pride hurt") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 자존심, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: THE collocation; the verb is 상하다 (to be spoiled/hurt), never 아프다

usagePhrases.en: to have strong pride / be hard-headed about ego
usagePhrases.note: 세다 'strong' describes a prideful, won't-back-down person

usagePhrases.en: to be stubborn out of pride
usagePhrases.note: negative: refusing to bend just to save face
lit. 'bend one's pride,' as in apologizing first

examples.en: That remark hurt my pride a little.
examples.note: Core frame 자존심이 상하다; note 상하다, the same verb used for food going bad — your pride 'spoils.'

examples.ko: 걔는 자존심이 세서 먼저 연락 안 해요.
examples.romanization: gyaeneun jajonsimi seseo meonjeo yeollak an haeyo.
examples.en: They've got such strong pride that they never reach out first.
examples.note: 자존심이 세다 paints a stubborn, face-saving personality; 세다 = 'strong/tough.'

examples.ko: 사과하기 싫어서 자존심 부리다가 친구랑 멀어졌어요.
examples.romanization: sagwahagi sireoseo jajonsim buridaga chingurang meoreojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I let my stubborn pride win instead of apologizing, and drifted from my friend.
examples.note: 자존심 부리다 = acting out of ego; -다가 marks the action that led to a bad turn.

entries.nuance: 자존심 is pride in the sense of the *ego you defend in front of others* — easily wounded, sometimes a flaw. It is Sino-Korean 自尊心 (自 'self' + 尊 'to honor' + 心 'heart'), literally 'self-honoring heart,' but in real use it leans outward and competitive. The crucial synonym contrast is 자존심 vs 자존감(自尊感): 자존심 looks *outward* (how others see you; it gets 상하다 'hurt' and you can 부리다 'wield' it stubbornly), whereas 자존감 is healthy *inner* self-worth that doesn't depend on winning face. This pair comes up constantly in relationship talk among 20-30s ('너 자존심 때문에 그래 vs 자존감을 키워'). The English-speaker trap is mapping the single English word 'pride' onto both, and choosing the wrong verb: pride does not 아프다 (ache) — it 상하다 (spoils/gets hurt).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 자존심 with 자존감. 자존심 = outward ego you protect from others (can be a flaw); 자존감 = inner self-worth (healthy). Telling someone 자존감이 세다 sounds off — it's 자존심이 세다 for stubborn pride.
Saying 자존심이 아프다. The fixed verb is 자존심이 상하다 (or 자존심을 다치다). 아프다 is for physical aches, not wounded pride.
Using 자존심 for proud-of-an-achievement pride. That positive 'I'm proud of you' is 자랑스럽다, a different word entirely.

structuredNuance.t: 자존심 is pride in the sense of the ego you defend in front of others — easily wounded, sometimes a flaw. In real use it leans outward and competitive.

entries.shortExplanation: 자신감 means "self-confidence" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자신감 (jasingam) means "self-confidence". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자신감이 생기다 ("to gain confidence"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자신감 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 = 'comes into being'; the natural verb for confidence forming after a small win
positive image of confidence overflowing
떨어지다 'to drop'; the mirror of 생기다
adverbial 있게 = the manner; 자신감 있게 발표하다 = present with confidence

examples.en: The interview went well, so I gained confidence.
examples.note: Simple cause→effect with 자신감이 생기다; 면접을 보다 = 'to sit/take an interview.'

examples.ko: 한국어로 말할 때 아직 자신감이 좀 부족해요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoro malhal ttae ajik jasingami jom bujokaeyo.
examples.en: I still lack a bit of confidence when speaking Korean.
examples.note: 자신감이 부족하다 = 'confidence is insufficient,' the everyday way to admit you feel unsure.

examples.en: I presented with confidence, and as a result I got praised.
examples.note: 자신감 있게 = the adverbial phrase; -았더니 reports the result of doing so.

entries.nuance: 자신감 is confidence in *what you can do* — a skill, a task, a performance — and it is the everyday word for it. It is Sino-Korean 自信感 (自 'self' + 信 'to trust/believe' + 感 'feeling'), literally 'the feeling of trusting oneself.' Watch the close pair 자신 vs 자신감: 자신 (自信) is used predicatively as 자신 있어요 ('I'm sure I can do it') about a specific challenge, while 자신감 is the noun naming confidence as a *standing quality* (자신감이 있다/없다/생기다). The other contrast is 자신감 vs 자만심(自慢心): 자만심 is *over*confidence/conceit, the bad kind. The English-speaker trap is two-fold: inventing the verb 자신감하다 (impossible — it's a noun, so pair it with 있다/없다/생기다/넘치다), and over-claiming with 자신감 where a modest Korean would soften to 자신감이 좀 부족해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 자신감하다. It is a noun, so combine it with 있다/없다/생기다/떨어지다, never with 하다.
Confusing 자신감 with 자만심. 자신감 is healthy self-confidence; 자만심 (自慢心) is arrogance/overconfidence. Calling a humble achiever 자만심이 넘친다 is an insult.
Mixing 자신 and 자신감. For a specific task say 자신 있어요 ('I'm confident I can'); for the general quality say 자신감이 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 책임감 means "sense of responsibility" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sense of responsibility" is 책임감 (chaegimgam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 책임감이 강하다 ("to have a strong sense of responsibility"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to have a strong sense of responsibility
usagePhrases.note: 강하다 'strong' is the fixed partner; a top compliment at work
the plain existence form; 책임감이 없다 = irresponsible
adverbial; 책임감 있게 일하다 = to work responsibly

usagePhrases.en: to take responsibility / take the blame
usagePhrases.note: the verb (책임 + 지다 'to bear'); the action, not the feeling

examples.en: That person has a strong sense of responsibility.
examples.note: Simple trait statement; 책임감이 강하다 is the stock phrase, far more natural than 책임감이 많다.

examples.en: If you're going to raise a pet, a sense of responsibility is essential.
examples.note: 책임감이 필요하다 = 'responsibility is needed'; -으려면 = 'if you intend to.'

examples.ko: 맡은 일은 책임감 있게 끝까지 해낼게요.
examples.romanization: mateun ireun chaegimgam itge kkeutkkaji haenaelgeyo.
examples.en: I'll see the work I was given through to the end, responsibly.
examples.note: 책임감 있게 = adverbial; this is the line interviewers love to hear.

entries.nuance: 책임감 is the *inner trait* of taking your duties seriously and owning the outcome, one of the most prized qualities in Korean workplaces. It is Sino-Korean 責任感 (責 'to hold accountable' + 任 'duty/charge' + 感 'feeling'), literally 'the feeling of accountability for one's duty,' so 책임감이 강하다 is a go-to compliment in references, interviews, and self-introductions. Saying 책임감이 많다. The idiomatic verb is 책임감이 강하다 (strong), not 많다 (many).

entries.shortExplanation: 인내심 means "patience; perseverance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 강하다/많다 are the natural partners for the trait
the situation-needs-it frame: 공부엔 인내심이 필요해요
vivid: 바닥나다 'to hit bottom,' patience all used up
가지고 = 'holding,' i.e. patiently keep at it

examples.en: Studying Korean really takes patience.
examples.note: Simple 인내심이 필요하다 (patience is needed); great for talking about long-haul learning.

examples.en: To teach kids, you need a lot of patience.
examples.note: 인내심이 많다 + -아야 하다 ('must have'); -으려면 sets up the goal.

examples.en: The line was so long that I ran clean out of patience.
examples.note: 인내심이 바닥나다 = the colorful 'patience hit rock bottom,' perfect for venting.

entries.nuance: 인내심 is patience as the *strength to endure* hardship and long waits, a character trait, somewhat more formal and dignified than the everyday verb 참다 (to put up with / hold it in). It is Sino-Korean 忍耐心 (忍 'to endure' + 耐 'to withstand' + 心 'heart'), literally 'an enduring heart.' You describe people with 인내심이 강하다/많다 and confess 인내심이 바닥났어요 when you've had it. Reaching for 인내심 in casual venting. For 'ugh, I just put up with it' the everyday 참았어요 sounds natural; 인내심 is more about the lasting trait or virtue.

entries.shortExplanation: 호기심 means "curiosity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 호기심 (hogisim) means "curiosity". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 호기심이 생기다 ("to become curious"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호기심 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 생기다/들다 are the verbs; N에 호기심이 생기다 = curious about N
warm compliment about an eager, open personality

usagePhrases.en: out of curiosity / on a whim
usagePhrases.note: handy reason-marker: 호기심에 한번 해 봤어요
자극하다 'to stimulate'; ads and teasers 호기심을 자극하다

examples.en: I'm a very curious person.
examples.note: Simple trait line; 호기심이 많다 is the set phrase, a gentle compliment if said of others.

examples.ko: 새로 생긴 카페에 호기심이 생겨서 가 봤어요.
examples.romanization: saero saenggin kapee hogisimi saenggyeoseo ga bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I got curious about the newly-opened cafe, so I went and checked it out.
examples.note: N에 호기심이 생기다 — the target of curiosity takes 에, not 을/를.

examples.ko: 호기심에 한국 예능을 봤다가 푹 빠졌어요.
examples.romanization: hogisime hanguk yeneungeul bwatdaga puk ppajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Out of curiosity I watched a Korean variety show, and ended up totally hooked.
examples.note: 호기심에 = 'on a whim'; -다가 marks the shift from a casual try to getting absorbed.

entries.nuance: 호기심 is curiosity, the itch to *find out* or *try* something new, and 호기심이 많다 is a warm compliment about an open, eager mind. entries.shortExplanation: 죄책감 means "guilt; guilty conscience" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "guilt; guilty conscience" is 죄책감 (joechaekgam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 죄책감이 들다 ("to feel guilty"). Watch the particle attached to 죄책감 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 들다 'to arise' is the standard everyday partner
느끼다; a touch more formal/deliberate than 들다
시달리다 'to be harassed by'; for heavy, lingering guilt
남다 'to remain'; the guilt that stays with you afterward

examples.en: I ate a late-night snack, so I feel guilty.
examples.note: Light, everyday 죄책감이 들다 — Koreans use it even for diet slip-ups, not just serious wrongs.

examples.ko: 바쁘다고 부모님께 자주 연락 못 해서 죄책감이 좀 있어요.
examples.romanization: bappeudago bumonimkke jaju yeollang mo taeseo joechaekgami jom isseoyo.
examples.en: I feel a little guilty for not calling my parents often, using being busy as an excuse.
examples.note: 죄책감이 있다 = 'to carry guilt'; …다고 reports the excuse you're making.

examples.ko: 그때 거짓말한 게 계속 죄책감으로 남았어요.
examples.romanization: geuttae geojinmalhan ge gyesok joechaekgameuro namasseoyo.
examples.en: The lie I told back then stayed with me as guilt.
examples.note: 죄책감으로 남다 = the guilt that lingers; 거짓말한 게 = 'the fact that I lied' as the subject.

entries.nuance: 죄책감 is the *inward* feeling of guilt over something you did wrong — the weight on your own conscience. It is Sino-Korean 罪責感 (罪 'sin/wrong' + 責 'blame/accountability' + 感 'feeling'), literally 'the feeling of being to blame for a wrong,' and it pairs most naturally with 들다 (죄책감이 들어요). Notice 20-30s use it *lightly* too — about late-night snacks or skipping the gym — not only grave offenses. The essential synonym contrast is 죄책감 vs 미안함: 죄책감 is the *internal* guilt toward yourself/your conscience, while 미안함 is the feeling of being *sorry toward another person* (and 미안하다 is what you actually say to them). The English-speaker trap is inventing 죄책감하다 (it's a noun — use 들다/느끼다), and using 죄책감 where you really mean apologizing to someone, which calls for 미안하다/미안함.

entries.shortExplanation: 보람 means "sense of reward; fulfillment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보람 (boram) = "sense of reward; fulfillment". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보람을 느끼다 ("to feel fulfilled") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보람, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the standard collocation; 느끼다 'to feel' is the natural verb
보람이 있다/없다 judges whether effort paid off
the adjective from 보람; 보람찬 하루 = a fulfilling day
describes a job that gives a sense of meaning

examples.ko: 오늘 할 일을 다 끝내서 보람이 있었어요.
examples.romanization: oneul hal ireul da kkeunnaeseo borami isseosseoyo.
examples.en: I finished everything I had to do today, so it felt worthwhile.
examples.note: Simple 보람이 있다 = 'there was a sense of reward'; the payoff of a productive day.

examples.ko: 힘들었지만 일을 마치고 나니 보람을 느꼈어요.
examples.romanization: himdeureotjiman ireul machigo nani borameul neukkyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It was hard, but once I wrapped up the work, I felt a real sense of fulfillment.
examples.note: 보람을 느끼다 after effort; -고 나니 = 'after doing, I found that…'

examples.ko: 가르치던 학생이 시험에 합격해서 정말 보람찬 하루였어요.
examples.romanization: gareuchideon haksaengi siheome hapgyeokaeseo jeongmal boramchan haruyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A student I'd been teaching passed the exam, so it was a truly fulfilling day.
examples.note: 보람차다 → 보람찬 (modifier form) + 하루; the fixed phrase 보람찬 하루.

entries.nuance: 보람 is the warm payoff feeling when your effort proves *worthwhile* — the quiet reward of seeing hard work bear fruit. It is a *native* Korean word (no hanja), which is part of why it has no clean one-word English equivalent; 'fulfillment / sense of reward / worthwhileness' all circle it. Koreans use it about jobs, study, volunteering, and parenting: 보람을 느끼다 (to feel fulfilled), 보람이 있다 (it was worth it), and the adjective 보람차다 (보람찬 하루 = a fulfilling day). The synonym contrast is 보람 vs 만족(滿足): 만족 is general *satisfaction* with any outcome (a good meal, a fair price), while 보람 specifically requires that your *effort/contribution* made it meaningful — you earned it. The English-speaker trap is reducing it to a material 'reward' (a prize or money is 상/보상, not 보람), and inventing 보람하다 — use 보람을 느끼다, 보람이 있다, or the adjective 보람차다.

entries.shortExplanation: 세금 means "tax" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 세금 (segeum) means "tax". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 세금을 내다 ("to pay tax"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 세금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 is the standard verb for paying out taxes, bills and fees; never 사다 or 주다
붙다 (to stick) is how Koreans say a tax or fee gets tacked onto a price
신고 申告 = official declaration; 종합소득세 신고 is the yearly income-tax filing
환급 還給 = money returned to you, e.g. the 연말정산 환급 at year-end

examples.en: Tax comes out of my paycheck automatically.
examples.note: 에서 marks the source it leaves from; 빠지다 here = to be deducted

examples.en: Is tax included in this price?
examples.note: 포함되다 = to be included; ask this when a quote looks suspiciously low

examples.en: Freelancers have to file taxes themselves.
examples.note: 직접 = in person/by yourself; relevant for 3.3% 사업소득 work

entries.nuance: 세금 is Sino-Korean 稅金, literally 'tax-money', the umbrella term covering income tax (소득세), VAT (부가세), property tax and the rest. The near-synonym to keep separate is 요금 料金, a usage charge or fare: your phone, gas and subway are 요금, while money owed to the government is 세금. Register is neutral and everyday; you 세금을 내다 (pay), and a tax can 붙다 (get stuck onto a price). The classic English-speaker trap is the verb: English 'buy' tempts learners into 세금을 사다, which is nonsense — tax is something you 내다, never 사다 or 주다. Also note 세금이 비싸다 sounds odd; Koreans say 세금이 많다/높다.

Saying 세금을 사다 because English uses no special verb — you 내다 (pay out) tax, never 사다 (buy) or 주다 (give).
Calling your phone or electricity bill 세금 — a usage charge is 요금; 세금 is specifically money owed to the state.
Saying 세금이 비싸다 — prices are 비싸다, but a tax amount is described with 많다 or 높다: 세금이 많아요.

entries.nuance: 연금 is Sino-Korean 年金, literally 'year-money' — income paid out yearly/regularly in retirement. usagePhrases.note: 오르다 is the default verb; 물가가 올랐어요 is everyday small talk

usagePhrases.en: the cost of living is high
usagePhrases.note: Koreans treat overall prices as one thing that can be 비싸다
상승 上昇 = a rise; you'll see 물가 상승률 (inflation rate) in the news
안정되다 安定 = to become stable, the opposite of runaway inflation

entries.nuance: 물가 is Sino-Korean 物價, literally 'thing-price' — the general price level of goods and services across the economy, not the tag on one item. That is exactly where it splits from its near-synonyms 가격 價格 and 값: 가격/값 is the price of a single product, while 물가 is the aggregate cost of living. So '이 물가가 비싸요' about one coffee is wrong; you mean 가격 or 값. When friends gripe about inflation they say 물가가 올랐다, never 가격이 다 올랐다. Register is fully casual and it is one of the most-used money words in Korea right now. Pronunciation trap: the 가 is tensed (sounds like mulkka) but is still spelled 가, so don't write 물까.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이 물가가 비싸요 about a single product — use 가격 or 값 for one item's price; 물가 is only the overall price level.
Spelling it 물까 or 물카 because of the tense pronunciation — it is always 물가.
Using 물가 for an exchange rate or stock — 물가 is consumer prices; market quotes are 시세 and rates are 환율/금리.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 환율 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: When 환율 rises the won is weaker — costlier to buy dollars, but good for incoming foreign cash
확인하다 確認 — what you do before remitting or exchanging cash
좋다 here means favorable for you specifically, not high
우대 優待 = a discount on the spread your bank or app offers

examples.en: The rate was good today so I sent money home.
examples.note: 송금 = remittance; -아서 links the good rate to the action

examples.en: Overseas online shopping got expensive because of the exchange rate.
examples.note: 때문에 = because of; 해외 직구 = direct overseas purchase

examples.en: The dollar exchange rate passed 1,400 won.
examples.note: 넘다 = to exceed; numbers like this come up constantly in 2020s Korea

entries.nuance: 환율 is Sino-Korean 換率, literally 'exchange-rate' (換 swap + 率 ratio) — the price of one currency in terms of another, central to anyone who remits money or shops abroad. The crucial near-synonym to separate is 환전 換錢, 'exchanging the actual cash': 환율 is the rate, 환전 is the act of swapping money at that rate, so you 환전하다 at a given 환율. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls bite English speakers: first, 환율이 좋다 means favorable-for-you, not numerically high; second, English makes 'the rate went up' sound positive, but 환율이 올랐다 means the foreign currency got more expensive in won, so sending money home actually costs you more. Watch for 환율 우대 (rate discount) on bank and Wise/Toss apps.

Confusing 환율 (the exchange rate) with 환전 (the act of changing cash) — you 환전하다 your money at a 환율; the rate itself is never 환전.
Assuming 환율이 올랐다 is good news — a higher won-per-dollar rate means dollars cost more, so remittances and overseas shopping get pricier.
Reading 환율이 좋다 as 'high' — it means favorable to you, which for a buyer of foreign currency is actually a lower rate.

entries.shortExplanation: 이자 means "interest (on money)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 붙다 (to stick) is the natural verb — your savings earn 이자가 붙어요
내다 when you owe it, e.g. on a loan: 대출 이자를 내다
율 率 = rate; the more formal/news word is 금리 金利
높다/낮다 describe the amount — great for savings, painful for loans

examples.en: This installment savings account has relatively high interest.
examples.note: 적금 = installment savings; -은 편이다 = on the higher side

examples.en: The loan interest goes out every month and it's a burden.
examples.note: 부담되다 = to feel like a financial burden; 나가다 = to go out (be paid)

examples.en: Rates went up lately so the interest increased.
examples.note: Note 금리 (the rate) drives 이자 (the actual money); 늘다 = to increase

entries.nuance: 이자 is Sino-Korean 利子, literally 'profit-child' — money that 'breeds' from a sum, i.e. the actual won your savings earn or that you owe on a loan. The line to draw is 이자 (the money) versus 이자율 / 금리 (the rate, a percentage): 금리가 3%면 이자가 3만 원 — the rate produces the interest. Register is everyday. Whether 이자 is welcome depends entirely on your side of the table: 예금 이자 (deposit interest) is income you 받다, while 대출 이자 (loan interest) is a cost you 내다. The English-speaker pitfall is double: don't use 이자 for the percentage (that's 이자율/금리), and don't say 이자를 받다 about a loan you owe — you only 받다 interest on your own deposits; on a loan you 내다.

Using 이자 for the percentage rate — the rate is 이자율 or 금리; 이자 is the actual won amount that results from it.
Saying 이자를 받다 about a loan you took out — you 내다 (pay) loan interest; you 받다 (receive) interest only on your own savings.
Treating 이자 and 금리 as fully interchangeable — 금리 is the abstract rate (used in news/policy), 이자 is the concrete money on your account.

usagePhrases.note: 갚다 = to pay back a debt; loan repayment is 원금 + 이자
보장 保障 = guarantee; the key phrase separating safe from risky products
손실 損失 = loss; the risk warning on funds and stocks
The two parts of any loan or deposit payout

examples.en: This product guarantees your principal.
examples.note: 보장되다 = to be guaranteed; reassuring for cautious savers

examples.en: Stocks carry the risk of losing your principal.
examples.note: 위험이 있다 = there is a risk; standard disclaimer for new investors

examples.romanization: maedal wongeumirang ijareul gachi gapgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm repaying the principal and interest together every month.
examples.note: -이랑 = casual 'and'; 같이 = together

entries.nuance: 원금 is Sino-Korean 元金, literally 'origin-money' — the original sum you deposited or borrowed, kept separate from the 이자 (interest) layered on top. The pairing 원금 vs 이자 is the backbone of every loan and savings calculation. Beware the look-alike 현금 現金 (cash on hand): they share 金 but 원금 is a principal balance, not physical money. Register is neutral, common in bank apps and contracts. The most damaging English-speaker misreading is 원금 보장 (principal protected): it guarantees only that you won't lose your initial amount — it does NOT promise any profit. So a 펀드 that is not 원금 보장 can drop below what you put in (원금 손실), which is precisely the warning attached to 주식 and 펀드.

Confusing 원금 (the principal balance) with 현금 (physical cash) — they share the character 金 but mean different things.
Reading 원금 보장 as 'profit guaranteed' — it only means you won't lose your initial amount; gains are never guaranteed by that phrase.
Saying 원금을 내다 for repaying a loan — you 갚다 (pay back) the principal of a debt; 내다 fits taxes and fees, not loan principal.

usagePhrases.en: to sign up for a fund
usagePhrases.note: 가입하다 + 에 — the verb for buying into a fund at a bank/app
투자하다 投資 = to invest; the general action, also takes 에
수익률 收益率 = rate of return; what you check to see if you're up or down
적립식 積立式 = paying a fixed amount monthly, popular for beginners

examples.en: The bank recommended a fund but I'm a bit torn.

examples.romanization: jeoneun maedal jogeumssik peondeue neoko isseoyo.

entries.nuance: 펀드 is a loanword from English 'fund' (write 펀드, never 펀트), meaning a pooled investment product — a mutual fund you buy through a bank app or securities account. The defining contrast is with 예금/적금 (bank deposit/installment savings): those are 원금 보장 with fixed 이자, whereas a 펀드 has no guaranteed return and your 원금 is genuinely at risk. Note also 펀드 vs 주식 株式 (individual stocks): a 펀드 is a managed basket, 주식 is buying one company directly. Register is neutral, very common among 20–30s who start with an 적립식 펀드 before moving to 주식/ETF on apps like 토스증권 or 키움. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming a 펀드 behaves like a savings account — it does not; returns can be negative, so you 잃다 (lose), not just earn.

Spelling it 펀트 — the loanword is 펀드, from English 'fund' with a final ㄷ.
Assuming a 펀드 works like a savings account — it is not 원금 보장, so the value can drop below what you paid in.
Treating 펀드 and 주식 as the same — 펀드 is a managed pool of many assets, 주식 is buying shares of one company yourself.

usagePhrases.note: 모으다 = to gather/save up over time, bit by bit

entries.nuance: 비상금 is Sino-Korean 非常金, literally 'non-ordinary money' (非常 emergency + 金 money) — cash set aside for the unexpected: a sudden 병원비, job loss, a broken phone. It carries a fun second life too: secret stash money hidden from a spouse, a staple gag in dramas and memes. The contrast to nail is 비상금 vs 용돈 (allowance / spending money): 용돈 is for everyday spending and is meant to be used up, while 비상금 stays untouched until a real emergency. Register is casual. In Korean the particle or ending next to 소득 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 늘다/줄다 for income going up or down; not 오르다 for income itself
세 稅 = tax; the tax levied specifically on your 소득
증명 證明 = proof; 소득 증명서 is needed for visas, loans, leases
고정 固定 = fixed; a regular salary vs. irregular freelance income

examples.en: You need proof of income to take out a loan.
examples.note: -(으)려면 = if you want to; also required for some visa renewals

examples.en: I increased my income a bit with a side job.
examples.note: 부업 = side job; -(으)로 = by means of; the side-hustle trend is big

examples.en: My income isn't steady so saving is hard.
examples.note: 일정하다 = to be regular/consistent; -지 않다 = negation

entries.nuance: 소득 is Sino-Korean 所得, literally 'that which is obtained' (所 that-which + 得 gain) — the formal word for income or earnings used in official contexts: taxes (소득세), loan and visa paperwork (소득 증명), statistics. It covers ALL earnings, not just salary — freelance, rental and investment income are equally 소득. The near-synonyms to separate are 월급 月給 (your monthly paycheck, what people say in casual chat) and 수익 收益 (profit/return on something invested): 소득 is your total earned income, while 수익 implies a gain produced by an investment. entries.shortExplanation: 지출 means "spending / expenditure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "spending / expenditure" is 지출 (jichul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 지출을 줄이다 ("to cut spending"). Watch the particle attached to 지출 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 줄이다 = to reduce; the core money-saving move
고정 固定 = fixed; rent, 관리비, subscriptions that recur each month
많다/적다 to describe how much you spend, not 비싸다
내역 內譯 = itemized record, what a 가계부 app shows you

examples.en: I spent way too much this month.
examples.note: 이번 달 = this month; 많다 describes the amount of spending

examples.en: Try cutting your fixed expenses first.
examples.note: -부터 = starting from; -어 보다 = give it a try

examples.en: I compared my income and spending.
examples.note: 수입과 지출 (income and spending) is the very common fixed pairing

entries.nuance: 지출 is Sino-Korean 支出, literally 'pay-out' (支 disburse + 出 go-out) — money flowing out, your spending or expenses, and the natural opposite of 소득/수입. Register is mildly formal but completely normal in money conversations; it feels a notch more precise than just 돈을 쓰다. The English-speaker pitfall is describing it with 비싸다 — spending is 많다/적다 (high/low in amount), never 비싸다.

Pairing it as 소득과 지출 in casual speech — the natural everyday pairing is 수입과 지출; 소득 is the documentary/tax word.

usagePhrases.note: Add 하다 to make it a verb; 전기를 절약하다 = save electricity
Seen on appliances and public-campaign signs; 절약 isn't only about money
정신 精神 = spirit/mindset; praising someone's frugal habits
절약 covers time too — 시간 절약 = time-saving

examples.ko: 요즘 돈을 아끼려고 외식을 줄이고 절약하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum doneul akkiryeogo oesigeul jurigo jeoryakago isseoyo.
examples.en: Lately I'm cutting eating out and economizing to save money.
examples.note: 아끼다 = to use sparingly; -(으)려고 = in order to

examples.en: If you save electricity, your maintenance fee goes down.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if; 관리비 = building maintenance fee

examples.ko: 대중교통을 이용하면 교통비를 절약할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: daejunggyotongeul iyonghamyeon gyotongbireul jeoryakal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Using public transport lets you save on transport costs.
examples.note: 교통비 = transport expenses; -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = to be able to

Second, 절약 vs 인색 吝嗇 (stinginess): 절약 is admirable thrift, but 인색하다 or 짠돌이 is the negative 'cheapskate' sense. Register is positive and everyday; it pairs with 아끼다 (use sparingly) and is the goal behind keeping a 가계부. The English-speaker pitfall is using 절약 to mean 'stingy' — that crosses into 인색, a different, unflattering word.

Using 절약 to call someone stingy — 절약 is praise for sensible thrift; the negative 'cheapskate' meaning is 인색하다 or 짠돌이.
Saying 절약을 하다 about money you simply didn't have to spend — 절약 implies a deliberate choice to economize, not an accidental non-expense.

entries.shortExplanation: 회계사 means "accountant (certified)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 회계사 (hoegyesa) means "accountant (certified)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저는 회계사예요. ("I'm an accountant."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회계사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 attaches after the vowel-final 사

usagePhrases.en: to leave it to an accountant
usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the person you hand a task to
자격증 (資格證) = qualification certificate
the big firm a 회계사 works at, not the person

examples.en: I'm an accountant.
examples.note: the plain self-introduction; note 예요, never 이에요, after 사

examples.en: It's easier to leave the year-end tax settlement to an accountant.
examples.note: 맡기다 = entrust; 한테 marks the recipient of the work

examples.ko: 회계사 시험은 합격률이 낮아서 몇 년씩 준비해요.
examples.romanization: hoegyesa siheomeun hapgyeongnyuri najaseo myeon nyeonssik junbihaeyo.
examples.en: The CPA exam has a low pass rate, so people prep for years.
examples.note: 합격률 = pass rate; 몇 년씩 = years on end, real exam-talk

Keep the person (회계사) distinct from the activity 회계 'accounting' and the firm 회계 법인 — English lets 'accounting/accountant' blur, Korean does not. The biggest English-speaker trap is the copula: because 회계사 ends in a vowel it is 회계사예요, and 회계사이에요 is wrong; also resist saying 회계사를 만나다 for a professional appointment when 회계사한테 맡기다/물어보다 (entrust/ask) is what Koreans actually say.

사무실 = office; where you go to file

usagePhrases.en: to leave it to a tax accountant
usagePhrases.note: 에게 = the writing-style equivalent of 한테

examples.en: I asked a tax accountant.
examples.note: 한테 marks the person; 물어보다 = ask and see

examples.en: Being self-employed, I leave the income-tax return to a tax accountant.
examples.note: 맡기다 = entrust; 종합소득세 = the comprehensive income tax freelancers file

examples.ko: 세무사 비용이 생각보다 안 비싸서 그냥 맡겼어요.
examples.romanization: semusa biyongi saenggakboda an bissaseo geunyang matgyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The tax accountant's fee was cheaper than expected, so I just handed it over.
examples.note: 비용 = fee; ~서 그냥 ~했다 is natural 'so I just went ahead and'

entries.nuance: 세무사 (稅務士) is built from 稅務 'tax affairs' (稅 tax + 務 duty/affairs) plus the professional 士, so it literally means 'tax-affairs certified professional' — the licensed expert who prepares and files returns and advises on tax. In today's tech workplaces 개발자 has decisively replaced the older 프로그래머 'programmer', which now sounds slightly dated or narrowly code-only; people almost always pin down the field with a modifier — 앱 개발자, 웹 개발자, 백엔드/프론트엔드 개발자. usagePhrases.note: 전향하다 = convert one's career path

entries.nuance: 프리랜서 is a direct loanword from English 'freelancer' (한국식 외래어), so unlike the Sino-Korean job titles here it has no 한자 and no ~사/~자 suffix — that very form tells you it names modern, flexible, often creative work (designers, writers, translators, photographers, developers) rather than a licensed profession. usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 자
많다 = be many/numerous

usagePhrases.en: business is slow / not doing well
usagePhrases.note: the verb 자영업자 use for a bad stretch
운영하다 = operate/manage a business

examples.note: vowel-final stem → 자영업자예요

examples.note: 경기 = the economy/business cycle; ~들 pluralizes the group — common news framing

entries.nuance: 자영업자 (自營業者) reads transparently from its hanja: 自 'self' + 營 'manage/operate' + 業 'business' + 者 'person' — literally 'a person who self-operates a business', i.e. an owner-operator. usagePhrases.en: to work as a delivery rider
usagePhrases.note: 으로 (after consonant ㄴ) marks the role

examples.romanization: baedarwoni eumsigeul mun ape noko gasseoyo.
examples.en: The delivery worker left the food at the door and went.
examples.note: 놓고 가다 = set down and leave — the contactless-delivery norm

examples.ko: 비 오는 날엔 배달원이 정말 고생해요.
examples.romanization: bi oneun naren baedarwoni jeongmal gosaenghaeyo.
examples.en: On rainy days delivery riders really have it rough.
examples.note: 고생하다 = toil/struggle; ~엔 = ~에는 contracted (on ~ days)

examples.ko: 요즘 퇴근하고 배달원으로 부업하는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum toegeunhago baedarwoneuro bueopaneun sarami manayo.

examples.note: 부업 = side job; 으로 marks capacity — reflects Korea's gig culture

entries.nuance: 배달원 (配達員) combines the Sino-root 배달 (配達) 'delivery' (配 distribute + 達 reach/deliver) with the suffix ~원 (員) 'staff member/worker', the same ~원 in 회사원 office worker or 점원 shop clerk — so it is the neutral, descriptive label for someone whose job is delivering food or parcels, usually by motorcycle. Register matters a lot here: 배달원 is fine for describing the role in writing or in the third person, but to or about the actual person Koreans say the more respectful 배달 기사님 (driver + honorific 님), and app-based riders are widely called 라이더 (from 'rider'). The dated 배달부 (with ~부, an old male-laborer suffix) now sounds condescending — avoid it. Contrast with 택배 기사님: 배달원 leans toward hot-food delivery (배달의민족-style), while 택배 is courier parcels. Habitual phrases: 음식 배달원, 문 앞에 놓다 'leave at the door', 비대면 배달 'contactless delivery'. English-speaker pitfall: don't say 배달 'the delivery (service)' when you mean the person — 배달이 친절했어요 should be 배달원이/기사님이 친절했어요.

실적 (實績) = performance figures, the rep's lifeline

examples.en: I'm a salesperson.
examples.note: consonant-final 사원, so 이에요 — a key exception in this set

examples.en: For a salesperson, the numbers really matter.
examples.note: 실적 = sales performance; ~은 marks the topic 'as for'

examples.ko: 친절한 영업사원 덕분에 차를 좋은 조건으로 샀어요.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 사
name the subject in front: 영어/요가/헬스 강사
로 marks the role

usagePhrases.en: to give a lecture / teach a class
usagePhrases.note: 강의 (講義) = the lecture a 강사 delivers

examples.en: I'm an instructor.
examples.note: vowel-final stem → 강사예요

examples.en: I'm an instructor who teaches English at an academy.
examples.note: 학원 = private academy; ~는 + 강사 relative clause 'an instructor who...'

examples.en: It's been three years working as a yoga instructor.
examples.note: ~ㄴ 지 N년 됐다 = it's been N years since — a key duration pattern

entries.nuance: 강사 (講師) joins 講 'lecture/expound' with the professional 師 'teacher/master' (the dignified 師 also in 의사 doctor, 교사 schoolteacher) — literally 'a lecture-master', i.e. someone who teaches courses. The sharp boundary is the venue and status: 강사 teaches at a 학원 (cram school/academy), gym, or culture center and is hired class-by-class or on contract, whereas 선생님 is the warm catch-all for a schoolteacher you address directly, and 교수(님) is specifically a tenured-track university professor — calling a professor merely 강사 can sound dismissive, since at universities 시간강사 (part-time lecturer) is a precarious lower rank. Subject + 강사 is the default frame: 영어 강사, 수학 강사, 요가 강사, 헬스 강사. Verbs: 강의를 하다 'give a lecture', 가르치다 'teach', 강사로 일하다. usagePhrases.note: 받다 from the client's side

usagePhrases.en: to give counseling / hold a session
usagePhrases.note: 하다 from the counselor's side

examples.en: I'm a counselor.
examples.note: vowel-final stem → 상담사예요

examples.ko: 힘들 때 상담사와 이야기하면 도움이 돼요.

entries.nuance: 상담사 (相談士) builds on 상담 (相談) 'consultation' (相 mutual + 談 talk — literally 'talking things over together') plus the certified ~사 士, so it spans a wide range set by the word in front: 심리 상담사 mental-health counselor, 진로 상담사 career counselor, and the everyday 전화 상담사 / 고객 상담사 (call-center agent). That breadth is the trap — English 'counselor' may evoke only therapy, but Korean 상담사 routinely means the customer-service rep on the phone, so context decides. Distinguish the side of the desk with the verb: the client 상담을 받다 'receives counseling', the counselor 상담을 하다 'does counseling'; and keep the person 상담사 apart from the session 상담 itself (상담이 도움이 됐어요 vs 상담사가 친절했어요). For a clinically licensed therapist the fuller 상담 심리사 or 임상심리사 is used. Also note 상담사 the helper vs 상담원, a near-identical word that leans specifically toward call-center/service agents. English-speaker pitfall: vowel ending means 상담사예요, never 상담사이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 상담사 always means a therapist — it commonly denotes a 전화/고객 상담사 (call-center agent) too; let the modifier (심리/고객) tell you which.
Confusing 상담 (the consultation/session) with 상담사 (the person): 상담이 친절했어요 should be 상담사가 친절했어요.
Saying 상담사이에요 instead of the contracted 상담사예요 required by the vowel ending.

entries.shortExplanation: 공인중개사 means "licensed real estate agent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 공인중개사 (gonginjunggaesa) means "licensed real estate agent". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 공인중개사한테 묻다 ("to ask a licensed agent"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 공인중개사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the person you direct the question to

usagePhrases.en: to go to the real estate office
usagePhrases.note: casually 부동산 = the office, where the 공인중개사 sits

usagePhrases.en: to look for a place to live
usagePhrases.note: 구하다 = seek/secure a home — the core errand
the two lease types the agent arranges

examples.ko: 집 구할 때 공인중개사한테 도움을 많이 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jip guhal ttae gonginjunggaesahante doumeul mani badasseoyo.
examples.en: I got a lot of help from a licensed agent when finding a place.
examples.note: 집을 구하다 = find a home; 한테 도움을 받다 = get help from

examples.en: We did the contract at the real estate office together with the agent.
examples.note: 계약서를 쓰다 = sign a contract; 랑 = casual 'with'

examples.ko: 요즘 공인중개사 시험을 준비하는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gonginjunggaesa siheomeul junbihaneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: Lots of people are prepping for the realtor licensing exam these days.
examples.note: 준비하다 = prepare; reflects its popularity as a 자격증

entries.nuance: 공인중개사 (公認仲介士) is a long but transparent compound: 公認 'officially recognized' (公 public + 認 acknowledge) + 仲介 'mediation/brokerage' (仲 go-between + 介 intermediary) + 士 certified professional — so literally 'an officially-licensed brokerage professional', the agent who arranges 전세, 월세, and home sales, and the person you inevitably deal with when renting in Korea. The number-one English-speaker confusion is place vs person: 부동산 (不動産, lit. 'immovable property') colloquially names the agent's office or the property itself, so 부동산에 가다 = 'go to the agent's office', but the human is the 공인중개사 — never call the person 부동산. The 공인 'officially licensed' prefix matters in formal/contractual contexts; dropping it to just 중개사 is loose. In everyday speech people also warmly say 중개사님 or 사장님 to the agent's face. Collocations: 공인중개사 사무소 'realtor office', 공인중개사 자격증 'realtor license', 집을 구하다 'find a home'. Note 공인중개사 ends in a vowel, so it would be 공인중개사예요, not 공인중개사이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the person 부동산 — 부동산 is the office/property; the licensed human is the 공인중개사 (or politely 중개사님/사장님 to their face).
Dropping 공인 to say just 중개사 in formal or contract settings — the official title is 공인중개사; 중개사 alone is loose.
Saying 공인중개사이에요 instead of the contracted 공인중개사예요, which the vowel ending requires.

entries.shortExplanation: 약사 means "pharmacist" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "pharmacist" is 약사 (yaksa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 약사예요. ("I'm a pharmacist."). Watch the particle attached to 약사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 사
한테 marks the person; the normal first step for minor symptoms
약국 (藥局) = the pharmacy where the 약사 works
짓다 = compound medicine — the verb for filling 처방

examples.en: I'm a pharmacist.
examples.note: vowel-final stem → 약사예요

examples.en: I got a headache medicine recommended by the pharmacist.
examples.note: 추천받다 = be recommended; 한테 marks the source — note pharmacists actively advise

examples.ko: 감기 기운이 있어서 약국에서 약사한테 약을 지어 왔어요.
examples.romanization: gamgi giuni isseoseo yakgugeseo yaksahante yageul jieo wasseoyo.
examples.en: I felt a cold coming on, so I had the pharmacist fill some medicine.
examples.note: 감기 기운 = a touch of a cold; 약을 짓다 = fill/compound medicine

entries.nuance: 약사 (藥師) combines 藥 'medicine/drug' with the professional 師 'master' (the same dignified 師 in 의사 doctor, 교사 teacher) — literally 'a medicine-master', the licensed pharmacist who dispenses drugs and counsels on dosage at a 약국 (藥局, 'medicine bureau'). A culturally important point for English speakers: in Korea the 약사 actively recommends over-the-counter remedies, so walking into a 약국 and asking the 약사 directly is a normal first move for a headache, cold, or upset stomach — you don't always need a doctor. Keep the obvious pairs straight: 의사 (醫師) diagnoses and writes the 처방전 'prescription', then the 약사 fills it; both share 師 but they are different jobs. Also distinguish the person 약사 from 약 'medicine' and 약국 'pharmacy'. Habitual verbs: 약을 짓다 'fill/compound medicine', 약을 추천받다 'get a medicine recommended', 약사한테 물어보다. English-speaker pitfall: the vowel-final stem takes 약사예요, not 약사이에요; and don't say 약사를 만나다 for routine advice — 약사한테 물어보다 (ask the pharmacist) is the natural collocation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 약사이에요 — the vowel-final stem contracts to 약사예요; 이에요 follows consonants only.
Confusing 약사 (pharmacist) with 의사 (doctor): the 의사 diagnoses and prescribes, the 약사 dispenses; they aren't interchangeable.
Mixing up the person and the place — 약사 is the pharmacist, 약국 is the pharmacy: 약국한테 물어봤어요 should be 약사한테 물어봤어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 사회복지사 means "social worker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사회복지사 (sahoebokjisa) = "social worker". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 저는 사회복지사예요. ("I'm a social worker.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사회복지사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 사

usagePhrases.en: to work as a social worker
usagePhrases.note: 로 marks the role
따다 = obtain (a certificate) — 사회복지사 is a licensed job

usagePhrases.en: to work at a welfare center
usagePhrases.note: 복지관 (福祉館) = community welfare center

examples.en: I'm a social worker.
examples.note: vowel-final stem → 사회복지사예요

examples.en: I'm a social worker at a welfare center.
examples.note: 에서 marks the workplace; ~는 relative clause 'who works at...'

examples.ko: 사회복지사 자격증을 따려고 야간 대학에 다녀요.
examples.romanization: sahoebokjisa jagyeokjeungeul ttaryeogo yagan daehage danyeoyo.
examples.en: I attend night classes to earn the social-worker license.
examples.note: 자격증을 따다 = get a license; ~려고 = in order to — a real career-change route

entries.nuance: 사회복지사 (社會福祉士) is a four-part Sino-Korean compound: 社會 'society' + 福祉 'welfare' (福 blessing + 祉 happiness) + 士 certified professional — literally 'a society-welfare certified professional', the licensed worker who supports vulnerable people (the elderly, children, the disabled, low-income families) at a 복지관 'welfare center' or public office. Because it is a 자격증-based occupation, Koreans naturally talk about 자격증을 따다 'earning the license' as the gateway, and many enter mid-career via night or cyber universities. Don't shorten it: 복지사 alone is loose/incomplete in formal contexts — the standard title is the full 사회복지사. Nearby words to keep separate: 자원봉사자 is an unpaid 'volunteer', not a professional 사회복지사; and 요양보호사 (caregiver for the elderly/ill) is a different, more hands-on care license. Collocations: 사회복지사로 일하다, 어르신을 돕다/도와드리다 'help the elderly' (use the humble 도와드리다 for elders), 복지관에서 근무하다. English-speaker pitfall: the vowel ending requires 사회복지사예요, not 사회복지사이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Shortening it to 복지사 in formal contexts — the full, standard title is 사회복지사; 복지사 alone is loose.
Confusing 사회복지사 (a paid, licensed professional) with 자원봉사자 (an unpaid volunteer) — they are different roles.
Saying 사회복지사이에요 instead of the contracted 사회복지사예요 that the vowel ending requires.

entries.shortExplanation: 분실 means "loss (of a personal item)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 분실 (bunsil) means "loss (of a personal item)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 분실 신고 ("lost-item report"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 분실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: What you file at a police station, station office, or on LOST112 when something goes missing.
Verb form (분실 + 하다); the written/official counterpart of spoken 잃어버리다.
物 'object', so 분실물 = the lost thing; 분실물 센터 / 보관소 = lost-and-found.
Noun-before-분실 pattern; you can swap in 지갑·여권·카드 분실 the same way.

examples.en: I lost my bag.
examples.note: Simplest frame: object + 을/를 + 분실했어요, the formal 'I lost ~'.

examples.en: I lost my wallet on the subway, so I came to report it.
examples.note: -아서 links the loss to the reason you're at the counter.

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the lost-and-found here?
examples.note: 혹시 + the signage word 보관소 is exactly how you'd ask staff at a big station.

entries.nuance: 분실 is the Sino-Korean noun (紛失, 'scatter-lose') that officialdom uses on forms, kiosks, and signs like 분실물 보관소; it frames the loss as YOUR own carelessness, not someone else's act. The sharp contrast to learn is 분실 vs 도난: 분실 = you misplaced it yourself (no suspect, police just log it), whereas 도난 = it was stolen (a crime, police investigate). In speech most people still say the warmer 잃어버렸어요; reserve 분실하다 for reporting, writing, or reading signage, where it sounds appropriately crisp and formal. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 분실 like a verb you can attach to a person — you cannot say 사람을 분실했어요 for 'I lost a person'; 분실 only takes inanimate items, and even then you must add 하다 (분실하다) rather than saying bare 분실해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 분실 (you misplaced it) with 도난 (it was stolen) — police log a 분실 but open a criminal case for a 도난, so the wrong word sends your report down the wrong track.
분실 is a noun; to verb it you must add 하다 (지갑을 분실했어요), and never use it about a person — 친구를 분실했어요 is wrong; for missing people Koreans say 실종.
In everyday conversation jumping straight to 분실했어요 can sound stiff; with friends 잃어버렸어요 is far more natural, and 분실 is saved for the official channel.

entries.shortExplanation: 도난 means "theft (having something stolen)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "theft (having something stolen)" is 도난 (donan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도난 신고 ("theft report"). Watch the particle attached to 도난 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Filed when an item was taken by someone — the criminal counterpart of a 분실 신고.
당하다 ('to suffer/undergo') marks YOU as the victim of the theft, not the thief.
Often seen in apartment-complex notices warning residents to lock up.
防止 'block-stop'; printed on locks, tags, and security stickers.

examples.en: My bike got stolen.
examples.note: Core frame: object + 을/를 + 도난당했어요, the victim-marking form.

examples.en: My parcel was stolen, so I reported it to the police.
examples.note: -아서 ties the theft to the action you took next.

examples.ko: 요즘 이 동네에 택배 도난이 많대요.
examples.romanization: yojeum i dongnee taekbae donani mantaeyo.
examples.en: They say there's a lot of parcel theft in this neighborhood lately.
examples.note: -대요 reports hearsay; 도난 stands alone here as a plain noun (no 하다).

entries.nuance: 도난 (盜難, 'theft-calamity') means someone deliberately took your property, so the police open a criminal case instead of merely logging a missing item — that legal weight is the whole reason it contrasts with 분실 (you simply misplaced it). The grammar trap that catches every English speaker is the verb: you must say 도난당하다, where 당하다 marks you as the one who SUFFERED the theft; plain 도난했어요 literally reads 'I committed the theft' and accidentally confesses to the crime. Register-wise 도난 is the formal, report-and-signage word; in casual storytelling Koreans say 누가 훔쳐 갔어요 ('someone stole it and left'). Habitual partners are 도난 신고, 도난 방지, and 도난당하다, and you'll meet the noun on building notices long before you ever need to file the report yourself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Never say 도난했어요 to mean 'I was robbed' — 하다 makes you the actor, so it reads 'I committed theft'; the victim form is 도난당했어요.
도난 (stolen by someone) is not 분실 (you misplaced it); choosing wrong decides whether police investigate a crime or just file a lost report.
Don't attach 도난 to a person as the stolen object — it applies to your belongings; for a kidnapped person the word is entirely different (납치).

entries.shortExplanation: 사고 means "accident" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사고 (sago) = "accident". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교통사고 ("traffic accident") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common compound; written as one solid word, 交通事故.
나다 is the intransitive 'occur' — nobody is blamed, it just happened.
내다 (transitive 'bring about') marks the subject as the one at fault.
現場 'present-spot' = the exact place it happened; police seal it off.

examples.en: There's an accident up ahead.
examples.note: Bare frame: 사고가 나다, the neutral 'an accident occurred', nobody blamed yet.

examples.en: I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
examples.note: 사고를 내다 openly admits fault; the 가/를 swap is the whole meaning.

examples.en: If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
examples.note: 112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance — memorize both.

entries.nuance: 사고 (事故, 'matter-incident') covers any sudden harmful event — car crashes, workplace mishaps, falls — and is the umbrella word a 교통사고 or 산업재해 sits under. The make-or-break contrast is purely grammatical and Koreans listen for it: 사고가 나다 (with 가) means the accident merely HAPPENED, assigning no blame, while 사고를 내다 (with 를) means the subject CAUSED it and is therefore liable — get the particle wrong and you may accidentally confess fault at the scene. Compare also 사건, which is an 'incident/case' in the investigative or criminal sense (a 살인 사건 is a murder CASE), whereas 사고 leans toward unintended mishap. Natural partners are 교통사고, 사고가 나다/내다, 사고 현장, and the everyday 접촉사고 (a minor fender-bender).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the 를 version admits liability and your insurer will treat it differently.
사고 is the EVENT, not the people; the injured person is a 피해자 and the at-fault driver a 가해자 — never call a person a 사고.
Don't reach for 사건 when you mean an everyday crash; 사건 implies a criminal/investigative 'case', while a road bump is a 사고 (or 접촉사고).

entries.shortExplanation: 합의 means "settlement / mutual agreement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 합의 (habui) means "settlement / mutual agreement". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 합의하다 ("to reach a settlement"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 합의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Used for accidents, disputes, and out-of-court deals between two parties.
金 'money' — the sum paid to settle, especially after an accident or assault.
書 'written document' that both sides sign to make the deal binding.
보다 here means 'work out/settle' — the colloquial verb of choice.

examples.en: I reached a settlement with the other party.
examples.note: 합의를 보다 is the everyday spoken phrasing; 상대방 = the other party.

examples.en: We agreed I'd receive one million won as a settlement.
examples.note: -기로 하다 marks the agreed-upon terms; 합의금 is the payout.

examples.en: We filled out the settlement agreement at the police station and the case wrapped up.
examples.note: 합의서 + 작성하다 is the set phrase; settling often closes a minor case.

entries.nuance: 합의 (合意, 'unite-intention', literally 'minds joined') is enormous in Korean accident and minor-crime culture: reaching 합의 with the victim — usually with 합의금 changing hands and a signed 합의서 — frequently reduces a sentence or makes the prosecutor drop the case entirely. The boundary learners blur is 합의 vs 동의: 합의 is a two-way deal where both parties negotiate and CONCEDE to a middle ground (often money, often legal), whereas 동의 is one-sided AGREEMENT that you accept someone's opinion or request ('I agree, that's fine'). It also differs from 약속, an everyday promise about plans. Register is formal-to-neutral, at home in police stations, insurance calls, and contracts. The English-speaker pitfall is using 합의했어요 for casually agreeing on dinner plans — that needs 동의했어요 or 그러기로 했어요; 합의 implies a negotiated, often compensated settlement.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
합의 (a negotiated, usually compensated settlement) is not 동의 (agreeing with an opinion) — 'I agree with you' is 동의해요, never 합의해요.
Saying 합의했어요 implies the deal is final and concluded; if you're still bargaining, say 합의 중이에요 (we're in the middle of settling).
Don't use 합의 for casual plan-making ('let's agree to meet at six') — that's 약속하다 or 그러기로 하다; 합의 carries legal/financial weight.

entries.shortExplanation: 벌금 means "fine (criminal penalty)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "fine (criminal penalty)" is 벌금 (beolgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌금을 내다 ("to pay a fine"). Watch the particle attached to 벌금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 is the verb for paying penalties and fees; never 주다.
刑 'sentence' — a 벌금형 is a criminal sentence served by paying money rather than jail.
State the amount right after 벌금, no particle needed.
告知書 'notification document' = the official payment slip mailed to you.

examples.en: I paid a fine.
examples.note: Bare frame: 벌금을 내다; 내다 (not 주다) is the only natural verb for paying penalties.

examples.en: I got a heavy fine for drunk driving.
examples.note: -(으)로 gives the cause; 나오다 = (a charge) is issued/comes out.

examples.ko: 벌금 고지서가 집으로 와서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: beolgeum gojiseoga jibeuro waseo kkamjjang nollasseoyo.
examples.en: The fine notice came to my house and gave me a fright.
examples.note: 고지서 arrives by mail; -아서 links the surprise to receiving it.

entries.nuance: 벌금 (罰金, 'punishment-money') is a criminal-court fine imposed after a court finds you committed an actual offense, so it rides a completely different legal track from 과태료, the administrative penalty for petty rule-breaking. Koreans draw this line sharply: a 벌금 leaves a record that you were criminally penalized (a 벌금형 is literally a criminal sentence), while a 과태료 — like an illegal-parking charge — carries no such stain. The fixed verb is 벌금을 내다 ('pay'); the English-speaker trap is 벌금을 주다, which uses 'give' and makes it sound like you're handing over money as a gift or donation. Note too that 벌금 is the specific monetary penalty, whereas 처벌 is the broader concept of punishment (jail, suspension, fine) that a 벌금 is just one instance of. You'll most often hear it paired with 내다, 나오다 (it 'came out' = was issued), and 고지서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap 벌금 (criminal court fine) with 과태료 (administrative penalty like illegal parking) — a 벌금 means a court found you guilty, so the wrong word overstates the offense.
Use 벌금을 내다, not 벌금을 주다; 주다 ('give') makes it sound like a voluntary gift rather than a penalty you owe.
벌금 (a specific money fine) is not 처벌 (punishment in general); a 벌금 is one TYPE of 처벌, so don't treat the two as interchangeable.

entries.shortExplanation: 과태료 means "administrative fine (minor penalty)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 과태료 (gwataeryo) = "administrative fine (minor penalty)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과태료를 내다 ("to pay an administrative fine") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과태료, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Standard verb is 내다, the same as for any fee or penalty.
駐車 'parking'; the most common reason a city resident ever gets one.
賦課 'levy-charge' = the act of officially charging it to you.
The slip mailed to you stating the amount and deadline.

examples.en: I got hit with a fine.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 과태료가 나오다 = a fine is issued/comes out against you.

examples.en: I paid a fine for illegal parking.
examples.note: -(으)로 marks the cause; 과태료를 내다 is the set verb phrase.

examples.ko: 기한 안에 내면 과태료가 좀 깎여요.
examples.romanization: gihan ane naemyeon gwataeryoga jom kkakkyeoyo.
examples.en: If you pay within the deadline, the fine gets reduced a bit.
examples.note: Early payment usually earns a discount; 깎이다 = to be cut/reduced.

entries.nuance: 과태료 (過怠料, 'excess-negligence-fee') is a LIGHT administrative penalty for breaking minor non-criminal rules — illegal parking, a late 전입신고, missed reporting deadlines — and crucially it does NOT make you a criminal or leave a criminal record. That is the entire dividing line versus 벌금: a 벌금 is a court fine for an actual offense, whereas a 과태료 is just an administrative charge an office levies on you. Residents bump into 과태료 most often through parking tickets and late move-in registration, and many can be paid online with an early-payment discount. The verb is 과태료를 내다 (or it 나오다, 'comes out'). Two pitfalls: English speakers over-dramatize it by translating it as 'fine' and equating it with 벌금, and the spelling trips people up — it is 과태료 with 태 in the middle, NOT 과대료; the syllable is 怠 'negligence', not 大 'big'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
과태료 (administrative penalty) is not 벌금 (criminal court fine); confusing them makes a parking ticket sound like a criminal conviction.
It's 과태료, not 과대료 — the middle syllable is 태 (怠, negligence), and learners constantly misspell and mispronounce it as 대.
Don't say 과태료를 주다 ('give a fine'); like all penalties it takes 내다 (pay) or 나오다 (be issued).
