entries.shortExplanation: 삼겹살 means "pork belly (grilled)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal) means "pork belly (grilled)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 삼겹살 2인분 주세요 ("Two servings of pork belly, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 삼겹살 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Two servings of pork belly, please
usagePhrases.note: Meat is ordered by 인분 (serving), never by piece — this is the core ordering phrase.

usagePhrases.en: Pork belly with a shot of soju
usagePhrases.note: 에 here marks the food you pair a drink with; the most iconic Korean food-and-drink combo.

usagePhrases.en: We grill and eat pork belly
usagePhrases.note: 굽다 → 구워 (ㅂ-irregular); you cook it yourself at the table-top grill.

usagePhrases.en: The fat renders right out, which is great
usagePhrases.note: 쫙 빠지다 is the set phrase Koreans use to praise well-grilled 삼겹살.

examples.en: Want to go eat pork belly?
examples.note: The everyday casual invite; 먹으러 가다 = go in order to eat.

examples.en: Is the pork belly fully cooked?
examples.note: 익다 = (food) to be cooked through; ask before you pick a piece off the grill.

examples.en: Pork belly only tastes right wrapped in a lettuce leaf.
examples.note: 쌈 = the lettuce/perilla wrap; -아야 제맛이다 = 'it's only truly good when…', a very natural food cliché.

entries.nuance: 삼겹살 literally breaks down as 삼(三, three) + 겹(layer) + 살(flesh) — 'three-layered meat' — naming the alternating stripes of fat and lean in pork belly, and it is the single most iconic Korean BBQ cut and a default casual group meal. Don't confuse it with 목살 (pork neck/collar, leaner) or 오겹살 (a five-layer belly cut with the skin on); waiters list these as separate menu lines. Register-wise the word itself is neutral, but the situation is firmly casual — friends, 회식 work dinners, late nights with soju — never a formal banquet. The pitfall for English speakers is the counter: 'a piece of pork belly' tempts you into 삼겹살 한 개, but you must order by 인분 (삼겹살 2인분), and you say 구워 먹다 (grill-and-eat) rather than the English 'have a barbecue,' because here you do the grilling yourself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 삼겹살 한 개 — meat is counted by 인분 (serving), so the correct order is 삼겹살 1인분 / 2인분.
Calling any grilled pork 삼겹살 — 삼겹살 is specifically the belly cut; 목살 (neck) and 항정살 (jowl) are different lines on the menu.
Using 만들다 ('make') for grilling at the table — Koreans say 삼겹살 구워 먹다 (grill and eat), not 삼겹살 만들다.

entries.shortExplanation: 갈비 means "ribs (beef or pork)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ribs (beef or pork)" is 갈비 (galbi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 돼지갈비 vs 소갈비 ("Pork ribs vs. beef ribs"). Watch the particle attached to 갈비 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 갈비 alone is ambiguous, so the species prefix 돼지/소 is almost always attached.
양념 = seasoning/marinade; -로 주세요 picks one option among several.
Grilled 갈비 is counted by 인분; ~이요 is the quick spoken order form.

usagePhrases.en: One bowl of rib soup, please
usagePhrases.note: 갈비탕 is a soup dish counted by 그릇 (bowl), not 인분 — a different format from grilled 갈비.

examples.en: This place is famous for its marinated ribs.
examples.note: 은/는 here flags 양념갈비 as the topic/specialty being contrasted.

examples.ko: 갈비는 좀 비싸지만 가끔 먹을 만해요.
examples.romanization: galbineun jom bissajiman gakkeum meogeul manhaeyo.
examples.en: Ribs are a bit pricey, but worth it once in a while.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 만하다 = 'worth doing'; beef 갈비 especially reads as a splurge.

examples.en: Shall we go for rib soup at lunch?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ까요? softly proposes a plan; 갈비탕 is a comforting everyday lunch.

entries.nuance: 갈비 means the rib cut, and it heads a whole family of dishes: grilled plain 생갈비, sweet-marinated 양념갈비, the braised 갈비찜, and the soup 갈비탕. The crucial ambiguity for a learner is species — 갈비 can be beef or pork, so Koreans say 소갈비 or 돼지갈비 to be clear, and at many casual BBQ joints an unqualified '갈비' defaults to the cheaper 돼지갈비, while 소갈비 reads as a costly, special-occasion meal. Note the cut sits next to 삼겹살 and 등심 as a grilling option but, unlike them, has a famous sweet marinade tradition (soy, sugar, pear, garlic). The English-speaker trap is treating 갈비 as automatically 'beef ribs' and then conflating the grilled cut with the soup: 갈비 is the rib itself, whereas 갈비탕 (-탕 = clear soup) is a boiled dish — ordering one expecting the other is a common mix-up.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 갈비 always means beef — at many BBQ spots an unmarked 갈비 defaults to pork (돼지갈비); specify 소갈비 for beef.
Treating 갈비 and 갈비탕 as the same thing — 갈비 is the grilled rib; 갈비탕 (-탕 soup) is a boiled broth dish.
Counting 갈비탕 by 인분 — soups are counted by 그릇 (bowl): 갈비탕 한 그릇, while grilled 갈비 uses 인분.

entries.shortExplanation: 등심 means "sirloin / loin (cut of beef)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 등심 (deungsim) = "sirloin / loin (cut of beef)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 등심 1인분 주세요 ("One serving of sirloin, please") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 등심, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A leaner premium beef cut at 소고기 (beef) restaurants, counted by 인분.
부드럽다 (ㅂ-irregular → 부드러워요) is the key praise word for a good cut.

usagePhrases.en: Between sirloin and tenderloin, which is better?
usagePhrases.note: N하고 N 중에 = 'among A and B'; the two cuts are constantly compared.

usagePhrases.en: I'll have the ribeye (marbled sirloin), please
usagePhrases.note: 꽃등심 = the marbled 'flower' upgrade of 등심, a prized higher-grade cut.

examples.en: At a beef restaurant, sirloin is the standard order.
examples.note: 기본 = the default/basic choice; -에서는 sets the location as the frame.

examples.en: Ribeye has good marbling, so it costs more.
examples.note: -아서 links cause→result; 마블링 (marbling) is the price driver for beef.

examples.en: If you overcook sirloin, it turns tough.
examples.note: 익히다 = to cook (transitive); 질겨지다 = to become chewy/tough — lean cuts dry out.

entries.nuance: 등심 is the loin/sirloin, the workhorse grilling cut at beef-focused restaurants — relatively lean yet tender, and the cut people mean by default when they say 'let's get 소고기.' It is a native Korean compound, 등 (back) + 심 (the core/inner flesh), not a Sino-Korean word, so don't go looking for a 한자 reading. The synonym boundary to nail is 등심 vs 안심: both are premium, but 등심 (sirloin, from the back) has a touch more fat and bite, while 안심 (tenderloin) is leaner and softer; menus list them side by side, and the marbled upgrade 꽃등심 ('flower sirloin' = ribeye) is the splurge tier above plain 등심. Collocations cluster around texture and grade: 등심이 부드럽다 (tender), 마블링이 좋다 (well-marbled), 질겨지다 (gets tough). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'sirloin/loin' loosely and ordering 등심 expecting cheap pork — it is almost always higher-priced beef — and overcooking it the way you might a steak, when Koreans grill these cuts only briefly to keep them 부드럽다.

Confusing 등심 (sirloin, slightly fattier, more bite) with 안심 (tenderloin, leaner and softer) — they are adjacent but distinct menu cuts.
Ordering 등심 expecting cheap pork — it is almost always a higher-priced beef cut at a 소고깃집.
Grilling 등심 long like a well-done steak — overcooking makes it 질겨지다 (tough); Koreans sear it briefly.

entries.shortExplanation: 안심 means "tenderloin (cut of meat)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 안심 (ansim) means "tenderloin (cut of meat)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 안심 스테이크로 주세요 ("I'll have the tenderloin steak"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 안심 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 안심 is the leanest, most tender cut and the classic steak choice; -로 picks the option.

usagePhrases.en: Tenderloin is more tender than sirloin
usagePhrases.note: N보다 = 'than N'; the standard comparison that defines 안심.
Counted by 인분 at beef restaurants, like other grilling cuts.
안심 exists for pork too and is the lean cut used in 돈가스 (cutlet).

examples.en: Tenderloin is low in fat, so it's clean and mild.
examples.note: 기름기 = fattiness; 담백하다 = mild, non-greasy — the signature flavor note for lean cuts.

examples.en: I ordered the steak as tenderloin.
examples.note: -(으)로 marks the material/choice the steak is made from.

examples.en: Because it was tenderloin, it was a bit pricier.
examples.note: N(이)라서 = 'because it is N'; 안심 is a premium lean cut.

entries.nuance: 안심 is the tenderloin — the leanest, softest muscle (it does little work), which is why it is the go-to for 스테이크 and why people praise it as 담백하다 (mild and clean, not greasy) and 부드럽다 (tender). The headache here is the homonym: 안심 the cut is spelled identically to the verb 안심하다 (安心하다, 'to feel relieved / at ease', literally 'settle the heart'), so 안심하세요 means 'don't worry,' not anything about meat — only context (a menu vs. a conversation) disambiguates. Assuming 안심 is fattier than 등심 — it is the opposite: 안심 (tenderloin) is the leaner, more 담백한 cut.
Describing 안심 as 느끼해요 (greasy) — lean cuts are 담백해요; 느끼하다 fits fatty foods, not tenderloin.

entries.shortExplanation: 닭다리 means "chicken leg / drumstick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "chicken leg / drumstick" is 닭다리 (dalkdari). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 닭다리 하나 주세요 ("Give me one chicken drumstick, please"). Watch the particle attached to 닭다리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Give me one chicken drumstick, please
usagePhrases.note: It's a discrete piece, so it's counted with 하나/개, not 인분.
살 = the flesh; 닭다리살 is the de-boned thigh/leg meat used in bowls and lunchboxes.

usagePhrases.en: Drumsticks are juicier than chicken breast
usagePhrases.note: 촉촉하다 = moist/juicy; the standard leg-vs-breast contrast.

usagePhrases.en: I go for the drumstick first
usagePhrases.note: N부터 = 'starting from N'; signals the leg is your favorite piece.

examples.ko: 치킨 시키면 저는 닭다리 먼저 먹어요.
examples.romanization: chikin sikimyeon jeoneun dalkdari meonjeo meogeoyo.
examples.en: When we order fried chicken, I eat the drumstick first.
examples.note: 시키다 = to order (food); 먼저 = first — the popular piece everyone reaches for.

examples.en: This is a lunchbox made with boneless chicken-leg meat.
examples.note: -(으)로 만들다 = 'made with'; 닭다리살 (de-boned) is common in 도시락.

examples.en: Kids usually like the drumsticks more.
examples.note: 보통 = usually; the leg is the easy-to-hold, kid-friendly piece.

entries.nuance: 닭다리 is a transparent compound, 닭(chicken) + 다리(leg), meaning the drumstick/leg — widely considered the juiciest, most flavorful part and often the most fought-over piece when a group shares 치킨 (fried chicken). The useful derived form is 닭다리살, the boneless leg/thigh meat (살 = flesh) that fills 도시락 lunchboxes and rice bowls; contrast it with 닭가슴살 (breast meat), the leaner, drier cut that dieters and gym-goers eat. Texture words pair naturally: 닭다리는 촉촉하다 (juicy/moist) versus 닭가슴살은 퍽퍽하다 (dry/mealy). The counting pitfall matters: because 닭다리 is one bone-in piece, count it with 개/하나 (닭다리 하나), never 인분, which is for table-grilled meat by the portion. A second English-speaker trap is treating leg and breast as interchangeable 'chicken' — Koreans care about the cut, so 닭다리 vs 닭가슴살 is a real menu-and-preference distinction, not a throwaway detail.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting 닭다리 with 인분 — it's a single piece, so use 개 or 하나 (닭다리 하나, 닭다리 두 개).
Treating 닭다리 (leg, juicy) and 닭가슴살 (breast, lean/dry) as the same 'chicken' — they differ a lot in fat and texture.
Saying 닭다리가 말랐어요 for 'the leg is dry' — use 퍽퍽하다 for dry meat; 마르다 means a body/object is thin or dried out.

entries.shortExplanation: 새우 means "shrimp / prawn" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 새우 (saeu) = "shrimp / prawn". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 새우 알레르기 있어요 ("I'm allergic to shrimp") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 새우, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: N 알레르기(가) 있다 = 'have an N allergy'; a safety-critical phrase when ordering.
튀김 = deep-fried dish; one of the most common 새우 preparations.
빼다 = to remove/omit; -아 주세요 politely requests it be taken out.

usagePhrases.en: Does this have shrimp in it?
usagePhrases.note: 들어가다 here = (an ingredient) to be included; the go-to question for allergies.

examples.en: Do you like shrimp?
examples.note: A simple everyday preference question with the bare noun.

examples.en: Does this fried rice have shrimp in it?
examples.note: 들어가다 asks whether an ingredient is inside — essential for checking allergens.

examples.ko: 새우 알레르기가 있어서 새우는 꼭 빼 주세요.
examples.romanization: saeu allereugiga isseoseo saeuneun kkok ppae juseyo.
examples.en: I have a shrimp allergy, so please be sure to leave the shrimp out.
examples.note: Chain allergy + 꼭(definitely) + 빼 주세요 to order safely in a real situation.

entries.nuance: 새우 (shrimp/prawn) is one of the most ubiquitous proteins in Korean cooking — fried as 새우튀김, in 볶음밥 (fried rice), in stews, in 깐쇼새우 — so the words around it are practical survival vocabulary, especially 새우 알레르기 있어요 and 새우 빼 주세요 for anyone with a shellfish allergy. Watch the verb 들어가다 ('to go in', here 'to be an ingredient'): 새우 들어가요? literally 'does shrimp go in?' is exactly how you ask whether a dish contains it. Keep 새우 distinct from neighboring shellfish — 게 (crab), 가재 (crayfish/lobster), 조개 (clam) — since 'seafood' in English blurs them but Korean menus name each. The big English-speaker pitfall is the omission phrase: learners reach for 새우 없어요 ('there's no shrimp') to mean 'I can't eat shrimp,' which only states a fact about availability; to make a request you must say 새우 빼 주세요 (remove the shrimp) or state the allergy outright.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 새우 없어요 to mean 'I can't have shrimp' — that just means 'there is no shrimp'; request it with 새우 빼 주세요 or state 새우 알레르기 있어요.
Lumping 새우 with 게 (crab) or 가재 (crayfish) as one 'seafood' — Korean names each shellfish separately on menus.
Using 있다/없다 to ask if a dish contains shrimp — the natural verb is 들어가다: 새우 들어가요?

entries.shortExplanation: 오징어 means "squid / cuttlefish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 오징어 (ojingeo) means "squid / cuttlefish". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오징어볶음 ("Spicy stir-fried squid"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오징어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 볶음 = stir-fry; a popular spicy dish eaten with rice.
질기다 = tough/chewy; squid turns rubbery when overcooked.
마르다 → 마른 (modifier); a classic 안주 (drinking snack) and beer companion.
Whole animals/seafood are counted with 마리, not 개.

examples.en: Do you like squid?
examples.note: Polite everyday preference question with -세요.

examples.ko: 오징어볶음은 밥이랑 같이 먹으면 진짜 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: ojingeobokkeumeun babirang gachi meogeumyeon jinjja masisseoyo.
examples.en: Spicy stir-fried squid is really good eaten with rice.
examples.note: N(이)랑 같이 = 'together with N'; a staple rice-pairing dish.

examples.en: If you cook squid too long, it gets rubbery.
examples.note: 익히다 = to cook (transitive); 질겨지다 = to turn tough — cook squid only briefly.

entries.nuance: 오징어 (squid) is a native everyday word that shows up across the menu: the spicy stir-fry 오징어볶음 eaten over rice, grilled 오징어구이, and especially the dried 마른 오징어, a quintessential 안주 (drinking snack) sold in every convenience store. The texture vocabulary is central — 질기다 (chewy/rubbery) and its change form 질겨지다 (to become tough) — because Koreans know squid must be cooked briefly or it turns rubbery, the opposite of beef which can simmer. The counting pitfall is real: a whole squid is 한 마리 (마리 counts animals and seafood), never 한 개. The other English-speaker trap is lumping cephalopods together: 오징어 (squid), 문어 (octopus), and 낙지 (small/long-arm octopus) are three distinct items with different dishes and prices, so calling all of them 'squid' will get you the wrong thing — for example 낙지볶음 and 오징어볶음 are separate menu lines.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting 오징어 with 개 — whole seafood takes 마리: 오징어 한 마리, 두 마리.
Calling 문어 (octopus) or 낙지 (small octopus) '오징어' — they are different animals and different dishes on the menu.
Using 딱딱하다 (hard, like a rock) for overcooked squid — the right word is 질기다 (chewy/rubbery).

entries.shortExplanation: 조개 means "clam / shellfish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "clam / shellfish" is 조개 (jogae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조개구이 ("Grilled clams/shellfish"). Watch the particle attached to 조개 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 구이 = grilled dish; a popular seaside meal where you grill them at the table.
탕 = clear soup; clams give it a clean, savory broth.
Unopened clams during cooking are dead beforehand and shouldn't be eaten.

usagePhrases.en: The broth is clean and refreshing
usagePhrases.note: 시원하다 of soup = savory and clean-tasting, NOT temperature-cold.

examples.en: We had grilled clams at the seaside.
examples.note: -에서 marks the place of the action; 조개구이 is a classic coastal order.

examples.ko: 이 칼국수는 조개를 많이 넣어서 국물이 시원해요.
examples.romanization: i kalguksuneun jogaereul mani neoeoseo gungmuri siwonhaeyo.
examples.en: This noodle soup has lots of clams, so the broth is clean and savory.
examples.note: -아서 links cause→result; 시원하다 praises a clear, umami broth (not cold).

examples.ko: 조개는 모래가 있을 수 있으니까 잘 씻어요.
examples.romanization: jogaeneun moraega isseul su isseunikka jal ssiseoyo.
examples.en: Clams can have sand, so wash them well.
examples.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason; 해감 (purging sand) is a real prep step before cooking.

entries.nuance: 조개 is the general native word for clams and bivalve shellfish, and it heads dishes like 조개구이 (grilled clams) and 조개탕 (-탕, clear soup). Because it is a category word, when a recipe or menu needs a specific shellfish you switch to the precise name — 바지락 (manila clam), 홍합 (mussel), 가리비 (scallop), 꼬막 (cockle) — so calling all of them just 조개 can be too vague. The flavor cliché to internalize is 국물이 시원하다: with seafood broth, 시원하다 does NOT mean 'cold' but 'clean, brisk, savory' — a deeply Korean way to praise soup, and the classic English-speaker mistranslation. A second pitfall is the safety note baked into 조개가 안 열렸어요: an unopened clam after cooking should be discarded, and Koreans routinely 해감 (soak to purge sand) before cooking, so 모래 (sand) and 씻다 (wash) are common partner words.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 국물이 시원해요 as 'the broth is cold' — with seafood soup 시원하다 means clean, brisk, and savory, not low-temperature.
Using 조개 when the dish needs a specific shellfish — say 바지락 (manila clam), 홍합 (mussel), or 가리비 (scallop) by name.
Eating clams that 안 열렸어요 (didn't open) during cooking — those should be thrown out, not forced open.

entries.shortExplanation: 고등어 means "mackerel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고등어 (godeungeo) = "mackerel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고등어구이 ("Grilled mackerel") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고등어, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 구이 = grilled; a staple home-style and 백반 set-meal fish dish.
조림 = simmered in seasoned (often spicy) sauce, classically with radish (무).
비리다 = the specific fishy smell/taste of seafood, common with oily fish.
손 = a market counter meaning two fish sold as a set.

examples.en: Grilled mackerel often comes out at home-style set-meal places.
examples.note: 나오다 = (a dish) to be served/come out; 백반 meals frequently include 고등어구이.

examples.en: Braised mackerel is delicious simmered together with radish.
examples.note: N(이)랑 같이 = with N; 무 (radish) is the classic 조림 partner.

examples.ko: 고등어는 구울 때 냄새가 좀 나요.
examples.romanization: godeungeoneun guul ttae naemsaega jom nayo.
examples.en: Mackerel gives off a bit of a smell when grilling.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when ~ing'; 냄새가 나다 = a smell arises — oily fish are aromatic while cooking.

entries.nuance: 고등어 (mackerel) is an everyday, cheap, oily fish that anchors home cooking and 백반 (home-style set-meal) tables as 고등어구이 (grilled) or 고등어조림 (braised with radish). The flavor word to learn precisely is 비리다 — the particular 'fishy' smell/taste of not-fresh seafood — which is its own adjective, distinct from generic 냄새가 나다 (to give off a smell): you say 고등어가 비려요, not 고등어 냄새 나빠요, which sounds unnatural. A practical market detail is the counter 손: fish like mackerel are often sold 한 손, meaning a pair (two fish), so 고등어 한 손 ≠ one fish. Keep 고등어 distinct from other common fish on a 생선 (fish) menu — 갈치 (hairtail), 삼치 (Spanish mackerel), 꽁치 (saury) — since a recipe asking for mackerel specifically won't accept a generic 생선. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'bad smell' vocabulary when the precise, non-judgmental word 비리다 is what Koreans actually use for seafood.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 고등어 냄새가 나빠요 for the fishy smell — the natural, specific word is 비리다: 고등어가 비려요.
Assuming 고등어 한 손 = one fish — 손 is a counter meaning a pair (two fish) at the market.
Substituting a generic 생선 when a dish names 고등어 — mackerel's oily flavor differs from 갈치 (hairtail) or 삼치 (Spanish mackerel).

entries.shortExplanation: 연어 means "salmon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연어 (yeoneo) means "salmon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 연어 초밥 ("Salmon sushi"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 초밥 = vinegared-rice sushi; 연어 is one of the most popular toppings in Korea.
덮밥 = a bowl of rice covered with toppings; an easy everyday lunch.
회 = sliced raw fish; 연어회 is hugely popular, often all-you-can-eat (무한리필).
신선하다 = fresh; the key quality word for anything served raw.

examples.ko: 저는 회 중에서 연어를 제일 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hoe jungeseo yeoneoreul jeil joahaeyo.
examples.en: Among sashimi options, I like salmon the most.
examples.note: N 중에서 = 'among N'; 제일 = the most — 연어 is a top 회 pick.

examples.en: One salmon rice bowl and a miso soup, please.
examples.note: N 하나랑 N = 'one N and N'; a very common lunch order.

examples.en: Salmon is also delicious grilled.
examples.note: -아도 = 'even if / also'; 연어 works raw or cooked as 연어구이.

entries.nuance: 연어 (鰱魚, salmon) has surged in popularity in Korea, especially raw as 연어회 and 연어 초밥 and in 연어 덮밥 rice bowls, and it's a trendy, mild, fatty option that newcomers gravitate to before tackling more traditional fish. The contrast worth knowing is 연어 (salmon) vs 송어 (trout): they look similar and both appear raw, but they're different fish, and what budget all-you-can-eat 'salmon' spots serve is sometimes 송어 — so the names aren't interchangeable. Quality vocabulary centers on 신선하다 (fresh), essential since it's eaten raw. A cultural pitfall for English speakers: don't assume every traditional 횟집 (sashimi restaurant) features 연어 — long-established 횟집 often specialize in lean white fish like 광어 (flatfish) and 우럭 (rockfish), and 연어 is more a feature of modern, casual, or 무한리필 (all-you-can-eat) places. Also note 연어 is mild, so the 비리다 (fishy) complaint applies less to it than to oily fish like 고등어.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 연어 (salmon) with 송어 (trout) — they look alike and both appear raw, but they're different fish (some cheap buffets serve 송어).
Assuming every 횟집 serves 연어 — traditional sashimi houses often focus on white fish like 광어 (flatfish) and 우럭 (rockfish).
Calling raw salmon 초밥 — plain sliced raw salmon is 연어회; 초밥 specifically has the vinegared rice underneath.

entries.shortExplanation: 곱창 means "grilled beef/pork intestines" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "grilled beef/pork intestines" is 곱창 (gopchang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 곱창 1인분 주세요 ("One serving of grilled intestines, please"). Watch the particle attached to 곱창 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: One serving of grilled intestines, please
usagePhrases.note: Ordered by 인분 at a 곱창집; one serving is fairly small and pricey.

usagePhrases.en: Intestines with a shot of soju
usagePhrases.note: 에 pairs the food with the drink; a beloved late-night 술안주 combo.
곱창 = small intestine; 막창 (last stomach) and 대창 (large intestine) are distinct cuts.

usagePhrases.en: Fried rice at the end, please
usagePhrases.note: 볶음밥 fried in the leftover 곱창 pan is the traditional finish to the meal.

examples.en: How about grilled intestines and soju tonight?
examples.note: N 어때요? = 'how about N?'; 곱창 is a classic 술안주 (drinking food).

examples.en: People are pretty divided on grilled intestines.
examples.note: 호불호가 갈리다 = opinions split (love-it-or-hate-it); a very natural set phrase.

examples.ko: 곱창 다 먹고 마지막에 볶음밥 꼭 먹어요.
examples.romanization: gopchang da meokgo majimage bokkeumbap kkong meogeoyo.
examples.en: After finishing the intestines, we always get fried rice at the end.
examples.note: 다 먹다 = eat it all up; the pan-fried 볶음밥 finale is a must.

entries.nuance: 곱창 is grilled small intestine (most often beef, but 돼지곱창 / pork is common and cheaper), a beloved but polarizing 술안주 (drinking food) eaten late at night with soju, and the meal traditionally ends with 볶음밥 fried in the rich leftover-fat pan. Register is firmly casual and nighttime — you wouldn't propose 곱창 for a formal lunch. Expecting 곱창 to be cheap because it's offal — per serving it's often pricier than 삼겹살; it's a treat, not a budget food.

entries.shortExplanation: 회 means "sliced raw fish (sashimi)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 회 (hoe) = "sliced raw fish (sashimi)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회 먹으러 가요 ("Let's go eat raw fish") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: 회 = sliced raw fish, eaten at a 횟집; -(으)러 가다 = go in order to do.
모둠 = assorted; a mixed platter of several fish, great when undecided.
Sashimi is counted by 접시 (plate), reflecting how it's served.

usagePhrases.en: I'm not great with raw fish
usagePhrases.note: 잘 못 먹다 = can't really eat / am not good with — a soft, polite decline.

examples.en: Do you like sashimi?
examples.note: Polite preference question with -세요; a common ice-breaker by the coast.

examples.en: If you order the assorted platter, several kinds come out.
examples.note: 시키다 = to order; 나오다 = to be served — 모둠회 covers indecision.

examples.ko: 저는 익힌 게 좋아서 회는 잘 안 먹어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun ikin ge joaseo hoeneun jal an meogeoyo.
examples.en: I prefer cooked food, so I don't really eat raw fish.
examples.note: 익힌 거 = cooked thing; a natural, non-awkward way to opt out of 회.

entries.nuance: 회 (膾, sliced raw fish) is the centerpiece of Korean coastal dining, served at a 횟집 (sashimi restaurant) and typically shared as a 모둠회 (assorted) platter with banchan and a follow-up 매운탕 (spicy fish stew) made from the bones. The boundary that trips up English speakers is 회 vs 초밥 (sushi): 회 is JUST the sliced raw fish — no rice — whereas 초밥 is the vinegared-rice nigiri; so '연어회' is plain salmon slices while '연어 초밥' sits on rice. Korean overwhelmingly borrows Japanese 'sashimi/sushi' concepts but keeps its own words and rituals (eaten with 초장 chili-vinegar sauce or 쌈, lots of soju). Counting is by 접시 (plate), not 인분. Register: 회 먹으러 가요 is a casual, social, often celebratory or seaside-trip invitation. The other pitfall is the homonym field — 회 also lives inside 회사 (company), 회의 (meeting), 회식 (work dinner) — but standalone 회 in a food/restaurant context unambiguously means the raw fish; context, especially the word 횟집, makes it clear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 회 (raw sliced fish, no rice) with 초밥 (sushi on vinegared rice) — 회 is the fish alone; 초밥 includes the rice.
Counting 회 by 인분 — sashimi is served and counted by 접시 (plate): 회 한 접시.
Reading standalone food-context 회 as 회사/회의 (company/meeting) — in a 횟집 it unambiguously means raw fish.

entries.shortExplanation: 폭염 means "heat wave" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 폭염 (pogyeom) means "heat wave". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 폭염이 계속되다 ("the heat wave continues"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 폭염 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject takes 이/가, verb 계속되다 not 오다
official top-level alert; 주의보 is the lighter advisory
에 marks the condition you brace against
fixed news collocation with 기록적이다

examples.en: It's a heat wave again today.
examples.note: simplest form: noun + 이에요 to state the weather

examples.en: Because of the heat wave it's hard to go outside.
examples.note: 폭염 때문에 = the heat wave as the cause of trouble

examples.ko: 폭염 경보가 내려서 야외 활동을 자제하라고 해요.
examples.romanization: pogyeom gyeongboga naeryeoseo yaoe hwaldongeul jajeharago haeyo.
examples.en: A heat wave warning was issued, so they're telling us to limit outdoor activity.
examples.note: 경보가 내리다 = a warning is issued; reacting to an official alert

entries.nuance: 폭염 is Sino-Korean, 暴炎 'violent + blaze', and means an extreme, dangerous spell of summer heat — the warning-level word you hear on the news and in the emergency text alerts (재난문자) that buzz your phone from late July. The dividing line from everyday 더위 is intensity and register: 더위 is the plain native noun for ordinary 'heat' you grumble about ('이 더위 좀 봐'), while 폭염 is official and severe, so you would not use 폭염 in light small talk. It naturally collocates with 경보/주의보 (warning/advisory), 계속되다, 기승을 부리다, and 기록적인. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is the verb: do not say 폭염이 와요 by analogy with 'a heat wave comes' — Koreans say 폭염이 계속돼요, 폭염이 심해요, or 폭염이 기승을 부려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 폭염 in casual small talk about a merely warm day — it is a severe, alert-level word, so for ordinary heat say 더위 or just 더워요.
Saying 폭염이 와요 ('the heat wave comes'), a direct translation of English. The natural verbs are 계속되다 (continues) or 심하다 (is severe): 폭염이 계속돼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 한파 means "cold wave" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "cold wave" is 한파 (hanpa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한파가 몰려오다 ("a cold wave sweeps in"). Watch the particle attached to 한파 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 몰려오다 = surge in en masse, vivid news verb
top alert level; 한파 주의보 is the milder advisory
닥치다 = befall suddenly, set phrase for disasters
fixed collocation with 기록적이다

examples.en: Tomorrow there's a cold wave.
examples.note: simplest form: noun + 예요 to forecast

examples.en: The water pipes froze because of the cold wave.
examples.note: 한파 때문에 = cold wave as cause; 얼다 = to freeze

examples.ko: 한파가 닥쳐서 외출을 줄이는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: hanpaga dakchyeoseo oechureul jurineun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: A cold wave has hit, so it'd be better to go out less.
examples.note: 닥치다 collocation + advice with -는 게 좋다

entries.nuance: 한파 is Sino-Korean, 寒波 'cold + wave', literally a 'wave of cold', and is the winter twin of 폭염: a sudden, severe, alert-level cold snap announced on the news and by emergency text. The line against everyday 추위 is the same intensity gap as 폭염 vs 더위 — 추위 is the plain native noun for ordinary 'the cold' ('이 추위에 어딜 가'), while 한파 implies a sharp, warning-grade plunge that freezes pipes and disrupts transit. It collocates with 경보/주의보, 몰려오다, 닥치다, and 기승을 부리다. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: 'a cold front comes down' tempts 한파가 내려와요, but the idiomatic options are 한파가 와요, 한파가 닥쳐요, or 한파가 몰려와요 — and reserve 한파 for genuinely severe cold, not a slightly chilly afternoon.

Calling an ordinary chilly day a 한파. It is a severe, warning-level word — for everyday cold just say 추워요 or 추위.
Saying 한파가 내려요 ('the cold wave falls/comes down'), copying English. Use 한파가 와요, 한파가 닥쳐요, or 한파가 몰려와요.
Mixing it up with 추위. 추위 is the general native noun for cold weather; 한파 is the specific Sino-Korean term for an extreme cold snap reported in the news.

entries.shortExplanation: 황사 means "yellow dust" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 황사 (hwangsa) = "yellow dust". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 황사가 심하다 ("the yellow dust is severe") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 황사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: describe intensity with 심하다, not 많다
compound for the protective mask people wear
불어오다 = blow in on the wind, natural verb
official alert term

examples.en: The yellow dust is severe today.
examples.note: simplest form: 심하다 to rate the conditions

examples.en: Every spring the yellow dust blows in from China.
examples.note: -마다 = every; explaining the seasonal source

examples.en: Because of the yellow dust I don't think I can open the window.
examples.note: 황사 때문에 + -겠어요 to soften to a judgement

entries.nuance: 황사 is Sino-Korean, 黃沙 'yellow + sand', and names the seasonal haze of desert sand carried on the wind from China and Mongolia, peaking in spring. The crucial contrast is with 미세먼지 ('fine dust', fine particulate air pollution): 황사 is coarse natural desert sand, a centuries-old phenomenon, whereas 미세먼지 is man-made fine pollution measured as PM10/PM2.5 — news reports list them together but they are different things, and conflating them is the classic learner error. Note also that 황사 is described with 심하다 (severe) and the wind verb 불다/불어오다, not with 많다 or 오다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the 황사/미세먼지 mix-up, is reaching for 황사가 와요; in news-register Korean 황사가 심해요 or 황사가 불어와요 sounds far more natural.

Treating 황사 and 미세먼지 as synonyms. 황사 is coarse desert sand blown in seasonally; 미세먼지 is fine man-made particulate pollution measured year-round — they are different phenomena.
Saying 황사가 많아요. Intensity of dust/haze is rated with 심하다: 황사가 심해요.
Saying 황사가 와요 in a forecast. Because it rides the wind, the natural verb is 불다: 황사가 불어와요, or simply 황사가 심해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 소나기 means "sudden shower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 소나기 (sonagi) means "sudden shower". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 소나기가 내리다 ("a sudden shower falls"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 소나기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: standard rain verb 내리다 (or 오다)
만나다 idiomatically = run into the rain
그치다 = stop (of rain), not 끝나다
emphasizes the surprise element

examples.en: A sudden shower is coming out of nowhere.
examples.note: simplest form: 갑자기 + 오다 for rain

examples.en: In summer, sudden showers often fall in the afternoon.
examples.note: 자주 = often; describing the seasonal pattern

examples.en: A sudden shower lets up quickly, so just wait a bit.
examples.note: 그치다 + -니까 reasoning; reassuring someone

entries.nuance: 소나기 is a pure native Korean word for a brief, intense burst of rain that arrives and departs suddenly — the classic summer-afternoon downpour. The dividing line from plain 비 is duration and character: 비 is rain in general (steady, all-day, or light), while 소나기 is specifically short-lived and abrupt, so Koreans typically wait it out under an awning rather than buy an umbrella. It contrasts too with 장맛비 (the long monsoon rains) and 이슬비 (drizzle). Natural partners are 내리다/오다, 그치다 (the proper verb for rain stopping — not 끝나다), and 만나다 ('get caught in'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 소나기 for any rain: it must be brief and sudden, and remember it takes the ordinary rain verbs 오다/내리다, with no special verb of its own.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 소나기 for long, steady rain. It specifically means a short, sudden burst; for general or all-day rain say 비.
Saying 소나기가 끝났어요 when the rain stops. Rain 'lets up' with 그치다: 소나기가 그쳤어요.
Forgetting it takes the normal rain verbs. There is no exotic verb — say 소나기가 와요 / 소나기가 내려요, just like 비.

entries.shortExplanation: 천둥 means "thunder" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "thunder" is 천둥 (cheondung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 천둥이 치다 ("thunder strikes/crashes"). Watch the particle attached to 천둥 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the verb is 치다, never 오다
compound; the boom itself
fixed binomial pair, said in this order
울리다 = resound, for a rolling boom

examples.en: It's thundering.
examples.note: simplest form: the fixed verb 치다

examples.en: The thunderclap was so loud it startled me.
examples.note: -어서 cause; 깜짝 놀라다 = be startled

examples.ko: 천둥이 칠 때는 우산보다 건물 안이 안전해요.
examples.romanization: cheondungi chil ttaeneun usanboda geonmul ani anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: When it thunders, a building is safer than an umbrella.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 = when; giving safety advice

entries.nuance: 천둥 is the native Korean word for thunder — the sound, the boom — and it is locked to the verb 치다 (천둥이 쳐요) or, for a longer rumble, 울리다. The key contrast every learner must nail is 천둥 vs 번개: 천둥 is what you HEAR (the crash), 번개 is what you SEE (the flash). They form the inseparable set phrase 천둥 번개, always in that order, the way English fixes 'thunder and lightning'. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, never say 천둥이 와요 — thunder 'strikes' with 치다, it does not 'come'; second, do not let English 'thunderstorm' blur the two words — when you mean the bright flash, you need 번개, not 천둥. Collocations: 천둥소리, 천둥 번개가 치다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 천둥이 와요, copying 'thunder comes'. Thunder 'strikes': the fixed verb is 치다 — 천둥이 쳐요.
Confusing 천둥 with 번개. 천둥 is the sound you hear; 번개 is the flash you see. They pair as 천둥 번개 but are not interchangeable.
Calling the flash 천둥. If you point at the bright bolt in the sky, that is 번개; 천둥 is only the boom that follows.

usagePhrases.note: same verb 치다 as 천둥
mimetic 번쩍 = a sudden flash
fixed binomial pair
common simile with -처럼

examples.en: Lightning flashed.
examples.note: simplest form: mimetic 번쩍 + 하다

examples.ko: 천둥 번개가 칠 때는 밖에 나가지 마세요.

entries.nuance: 번개 is the native word for the flash of lightning — what you SEE — and like 천둥 it takes the verb 치다 (번개가 쳐요), often spiced with the mimetic 번쩍하다 for that split-second flash. Confusing 번개 (the flash you see) with 천둥 (the boom you hear). Point at the sky-bolt and it is 번개.
Saying 번개가 와요. Like thunder, lightning 'strikes': the verb is 치다 — 번개가 쳐요.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 서리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the verb is 내리다, as if it descends
seasonal compound marking late autumn
끼다 = to settle/coat, as on a windshield
된- intensifier; also figurative 'harsh blow'

examples.en: Frost formed at dawn.
examples.note: simplest form: 내리다 in past tense

examples.en: The first frost has already fallen.
examples.note: 벌써 = already; 첫서리 marks the season turning

examples.en: On a day when frost has formed, the roads are slippery.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 날 = a day when; practical caution

entries.nuance: 서리 is the native word for frost — the thin white crystal coating that forms on cold autumn and early-winter mornings — and it pairs with the verb 내리다 ('to descend'), as Korean pictures frost as settling down from above (서리가 내려요). Distinguish it from neighbours: 얼음 is solid ice, 눈 is snow, 이슬 is dew (the same kind of overnight moisture but liquid, in warm weather) — 서리 is specifically dew that has frozen into white crystals. The seasonal marker 첫서리 (first frost) is something Koreans note when the cold abruptly deepens, and 된서리 means a hard frost (and figuratively a harsh setback). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: do not say 서리가 와요; frost 'descends' (내리다) or 'coats' a surface (끼다) — 창문에 서리가 꼈어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 서리 (frost, white crystals) with 얼음 (solid ice), 눈 (snow), or 이슬 (liquid dew). 서리 is frozen dew on cold mornings.
Saying 서리가 와요. The fixed verb is 내리다 (서리가 내려요), or 끼다 when it coats a surface like a window.
Forgetting 첫서리/된서리 as set words. The first frost is 첫서리 (not 첫 서리 loosely), a recognized seasonal milestone.

entries.shortExplanation: 폭설 means "heavy snow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: standard snow verb 내리다 (or 오다)
top alert level; 대설 경보 is the official term

usagePhrases.en: roads get blocked by heavy snow
usagePhrases.note: -로 marks the cause/means
fixed news collocation

examples.en: Heavy snow fell all night.
examples.note: simplest form: 밤새 = all night + 내리다

examples.en: The roads all got blocked by the heavy snow.
examples.note: -로 cause; 막히다 = be blocked

examples.en: When heavy snow comes, use public transport.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 = when; practical advice

entries.nuance: 폭설 is Sino-Korean, 暴雪 'violent + snow', and means heavy, disruptive snowfall — the snow counterpart of 폭우 (暴雨) and 폭염 (暴炎), all sharing the 暴 'violent/sudden' element that flags danger. The contrast with neutral 눈 (native 'snow', for any ordinary or pretty snowfall) is intensity and register: 폭설 is enough snow to bury roads and cancel flights, paired with 경보 in alerts (the meteorological office's own term is 대설, 大雪). Natural partners: 내리다/오다, 막히다, 쌓이다 (pile up), 기록적인, -로 침수/마비. The English-speaker pitfall is reserving the right word — don't call a light, scenic snow 폭설 — and the verb: 폭설이 와요 is fine in speech, but 폭설이 내려요 reads more naturally in writing and on the news.

Calling light or pretty snowfall 폭설. It means heavy, road-blocking snow; for ordinary snow say 눈.
Writing 폭설이 와요 in formal text. In news/written register 폭설이 내려요 is the natural choice.
Saying 폭설 때문에 길이 막혔어요 is fine, but for 'by means of' the cause, 폭설로 길이 막혔어요 with -로 is the crisp news collocation.

entries.shortExplanation: 일교차 means "daily temperature range" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 일교차 (ilgyocha) = "daily temperature range". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 일교차가 크다 ("the daily temperature range is big") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 일교차, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: the daily temperature range is big
usagePhrases.note: measured with 크다/작다, never 높다/낮다
심하다 stresses how punishing the swing is
벌어지다 = a gap opens up
줄어들다 = shrink, the opposite movement

examples.en: The day-night temperature gap is big these days.
examples.note: simplest form: 크다 to size the range

examples.en: In spring and autumn the temperature gap is severe.
examples.note: listing the seasons; 심하다 for a harsh swing

examples.en: Since the temperature swing is big, take an outer layer.
examples.note: -니까 reason; 챙기다 = pack/bring along

entries.nuance: 일교차 is Sino-Korean, 日較差 'day + compare + difference', i.e. the measured difference between the day's high and low temperature — a phrase Koreans use constantly in spring and autumn forecasts. The make-or-break point is the adjective: a RANGE or GAP is 크다/작다 (big/small), so it is 일교차가 커요, never 일교차가 높아요 — only the temperature itself (기온/온도) is 높다/낮다 (high/low). Keep 일교차 (the gap between high and low) distinct from 기온 (the actual temperature) and 온도차 (any temperature difference, e.g. indoor vs outdoor). It almost always travels with health and clothing advice (감기 조심, 겉옷 챙기다). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 크다-vs-높다 confusion, since English says a 'high temperature range' — in Korean a gap is 'big', not 'high'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 일교차가 높아요. A gap/range takes 크다/작다, not 높다/낮다 — say 일교차가 커요. Only 기온/온도 can be 높다.
Confusing 일교차 with 기온. 일교차 is the gap between the high and low; 기온 is the temperature itself.
Using 일교차 for an indoor-vs-outdoor difference. That is 온도차; 일교차 specifically means the day-to-night swing.

entries.explanation: 열대야 (yeoldaeya) means "tropical night". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 열대야가 계속되다 ("tropical nights continue"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 열대야 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이/가 + 계속되다, not 오다

usagePhrases.en: sleep badly because of the tropical night
usagePhrases.note: 잠을 설치다 = sleep fitfully, set phrase
기승을 부리다 = run rampant, news collocation
연일 = day after day, emphatic

examples.en: Tonight is a tropical night again.
examples.note: simplest form: noun + 예요 about the night

examples.en: I couldn't sleep because of the tropical night.
examples.note: 열대야 때문에 = the sleepless heat as cause

examples.en: Tropical nights keep on, so I sleep with the AC on.
examples.note: -어서 cause; 켜고 자다 = sleep with it on

entries.nuance: 열대야 is Sino-Korean, 熱帶夜 'tropical-zone + night', and names a specific phenomenon: a summer night where the temperature never drops below 25°C, so the air stays oppressive and sleep is wretched. The contrast to draw is that 열대야 is strictly about the NIGHT not cooling down, whereas 폭염 is about extreme DAYTIME heat — a single hot spell can bring both, but they are not the same word. It is a fixture of Korean summer news and small talk, almost always glued to complaints about not sleeping (잠을 못 자다, 잠을 설치다) and running the 에어컨. It takes 계속되다 and 기승을 부리다, not 오다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 열대야 loosely for any hot day; it specifically means a hot, sleepless NIGHT, so a sweltering afternoon is 폭염 or just 더워요, not 열대야.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 열대야 for a hot daytime. It means specifically a hot, sleepless night (temperature staying above 25°C); a hot day is 폭염 or 더워요.
Saying 열대야가 와요. The natural verbs are 계속되다 (continues) or 기승을 부리다 (rages) — 열대야가 계속돼요.
Misspelling it. It is 열대야 (熱帶夜), not 열데야 or 열대얄 — three syllables, ending in 야.

entries.shortExplanation: 습도 means "humidity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "humidity" is 습도 (seupdo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 습도가 높다 ("the humidity is high"). Watch the particle attached to 습도 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: takes 높다/낮다, like a percentage reading
the opposite pole, also 낮다
끈적이다 = be sticky/clammy

examples.en: The humidity is high today.
examples.note: simplest form: 높다 to read the level

examples.en: When the humidity is low, laundry dries fast.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if/when; everyday effect

examples.ko: 장마철에는 습도 때문에 곰팡이가 잘 생겨요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoreneun seupdo ttaemune gompangiga jal saenggyeoyo.
examples.en: In the rainy season, mold forms easily from the humidity.
examples.note: 습도 때문에 cause; 곰팡이가 생기다 = mold appears

entries.nuance: 습도 is Sino-Korean, 濕度 'moisture/damp + degree', i.e. the measured DEGREE of moisture in the air — a percentage reading, which is why, unlike most weather nouns, it takes 높다 (high) and 낮다 (low), exactly like a gauge. The -도 (度 'degree') ending is the same one in 온도 (temperature), 속도 (speed), 강도 (intensity), so anything ending in -도 is a measured level and pairs with 높다/낮다. Keep 습도 (humidity) apart from 온도 (temperature) and from 습기 (濕氣, the dampness/moisture you can feel or that clings to a wall) — 습도 is the number, 습기 is the felt damp. Koreans cite it constantly in muggy summers to explain why heat feels worse, tying into mold, laundry, and 제습기. The English-speaker pitfall is 습도가 많아요 — moisture feels like 'a lot', but a measured degree is high/low: 습도가 높아요.

Confusing 습도 (humidity, the percentage) with 온도 (temperature). Both end in -도 and take 높다/낮다, but they measure different things.
Mixing 습도 with 습기. 습도 is the numerical humidity level; 습기 is the felt dampness/moisture (e.g. 벽에 습기가 차다, dampness builds on the wall).

usagePhrases.note: vivid verb 쏟아지다, stronger than 내리다
alert term; 호우 경보 is the official wording
-로 cause; 침수되다 = be submerged
fixed news collocation

examples.en: Heavy rain is suddenly pouring down.
examples.note: simplest form: 갑자기 + the vivid 쏟아지다

examples.en: The subway stopped because of the heavy rain.

entries.nuance: 폭우 is Sino-Korean, 暴雨 'violent + rain', a torrential downpour heavy enough to flood streets — the rain member of the 暴 family alongside 폭염 (暴炎), 폭설 (暴雪), all flagging sudden violence. The contrast scale runs 이슬비 (drizzle) → 비 (ordinary rain) → 소나기 (a brief sudden burst) → 폭우 (dangerous torrent); the meteorological office's own term is 호우 (豪雨). 폭우 loves the vivid verb 쏟아지다 ('to pour/gush down') and appears with 경보, 침수, 마비, 기록적인, so it carries danger and disruption. Saying 폭우 때문에 침수됐어요 is fine, but the tight news phrasing for the cause is 폭우로 침수됐어요 with -로.
