entries.shortExplanation: 보건소 means "public health center" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보건소 (bogeonso) = "public health center". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보건소에 가다 ("go to the public health center") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보건소, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: go to the public health center
usagePhrases.note: 보건소 is a government-run clinic, typically one per district

usagePhrases.en: get tested at the health center
usagePhrases.note: 검사받다 'undergo a test'; common for free or low-cost screenings and STI tests

usagePhrases.en: get a vaccination / get a shot
usagePhrases.note: the shot itself: 주사를 맞다 (lit. 'be struck by a shot') — never 주사를 받다

usagePhrases.en: the health center for your area
usagePhrases.note: 관할 (管轄) is the one assigned to your district; it matters for some free programs

examples.en: I'm going to the health center to get a flu shot.
examples.note: 주사를 맞다 is the fixed verb for receiving an injection; 맞으러 가다 'go in order to get (a shot)'

examples.ko: 보건소에서 무료로 건강검진을 받을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: bogeonsoeseo muryoro geonganggeomjineul badeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can get a free health check-up at the public health center.
examples.note: 건강검진을 받다 'receive a health screening'; eligibility varies but basic ones are often free

examples.ko: 독감 예방접종은 동네 보건소가 병원보다 훨씬 싸요.
examples.romanization: dokgam yebangjeopjongeun dongne bogeonsoga byeongwonboda hwolssin ssayo.
examples.en: The flu shot is much cheaper at the local health center than at a hospital.
examples.note: 보건소 vs 병원 — the budget motive; 보다 here marks the comparison standard ('than')

entries.nuance: 보건소 (保健所, 保 'protect' + 健 'health' + 所 'office/station', literally a 'health-protection station') is the district-run public health center offering vaccinations, screenings, and basic care at little or no cost. The synonym line to learn is 보건소 vs 병원: a 병원 is a private hospital/clinic for diagnosis and treatment, while 보건소 is a public-budget facility for prevention and low-cost routine care — for a flu shot or travel vaccine you go to the 보건소, for a broken arm or surgery you go to a 병원. Its habitual partners are 예방접종, 건강검진, 무료, 검사. The register is neutral-administrative. Two pitfalls: (1) the shot collocation is 주사를 맞다 (passive 'be hit by an injection'), so the English 'get/receive a shot' must not become 주사를 받다; (2) don't confuse the local 보건소 with the national 보건복지부 (Health Ministry) — the ministry sets policy, the 보건소 is where you actually roll up your sleeve.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 주사를 받다 for 'get a shot'; the set phrase is 주사를 맞다 (the body 'is struck' by the needle). 받다 ('receive') is wrong here even though English uses 'get/receive'.
Treating 보건소 like an ER for emergencies; for urgent care you go to a 병원 or 응급실 — the 보건소 keeps office hours and focuses on prevention.
Confusing 보건소 (local public health center) with 보건복지부 (the national Health & Welfare Ministry); the latter is a policy body, not a place you visit for shots.

structuredNuance.t: 보건소 is the district-run public health center offering vaccinations, screenings, and basic care at little or no cost. Its habitual partners are 예방접종, 건강검진, 무료, 검사. The register is neutral-administrative.

保健所: 保 'protect' + 健 'health' + 所 'office/station' — literally a 'health-protection station'.

Two pitfalls: (1) the shot collocation is 주사를 맞다 (passive 'be hit by an injection'), so the English 'get/receive a shot' must not become 주사를 받다; (2) don't confuse the local 보건소 with the national 보건복지부 (Health Ministry) — the ministry sets policy, the 보건소 is where you actually roll up your sleeve.

entries.shortExplanation: 세무서 means "tax office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 세무서 (semuseo) means "tax office". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 세무서에 가다 ("go to the tax office"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 세무서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 세무서 is the local branch of the national tax service (국세청)

usagePhrases.en: file (a return) at the tax office
usagePhrases.note: 신고하다 (申告) 'declare/report' is the verb for income or a business registration; 에 marks where you report
your 관할 세무서 is decided by your business or home address
세금을 내다 'pay tax' vs 신고하다 'declare it' — declaring and paying are two separate steps

examples.en: Do you know where the tax office is?
examples.note: embedded question -는지; a gentle way to ask directions to the office

examples.en: I got my business registration certificate from the tax office.
examples.note: starting any business or side gig requires 사업자등록 at the 세무서; 발급받다 = receive (an issued doc)

examples.en: Freelancers must file comprehensive income tax at the tax office in May.
examples.note: May is 종합소득세 season; 신고하다 not 내다 — first you declare, then any tax due is paid

entries.nuance: 세무서 (稅務署, 稅 'tax' + 務 'affairs' + 署 'bureau') is the local tax office, the branch of the national 국세청 where you do 사업자등록 and file income tax. The most dangerous confusion is the near-homophone pair 세무서 vs 세무사 (稅務士): 세무서 is the government office, 세무사 is a licensed private tax accountant you hire — one letter changes a public building into a paid professional. A second line is 신고하다 vs 내다: 신고 means to *declare/report* your income, while 내다 means to *pay* the resulting tax; you can 신고 without immediately 내다. Habitual partners: 종합소득세, 부가세, 사업자등록, 홈택스. Pitfall for English speakers: 'file taxes' should be 세금을 신고하다, but learners often borrow 'pay' for everything and say 세금을 내다 even when they only mean to submit the return. Also, don't go to the 구청 to register a business — that is squarely the 세무서's job.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 세무서 (tax office) with 세무사 (a private tax accountant you hire); the office is government and free to visit, the 세무사 is a paid professional. The single-syllable difference 서/사 matters.
Using 세금을 내다 ('pay tax') when you mean 신고하다 ('declare/file'); filing a return and paying the bill are distinct steps in Korean.
Going to the 구청 to register a business or file taxes; residency and buildings are the 구청's domain, but taxes belong to the 세무서.

structuredNuance.t: 세무서 is the local tax office, the branch of the national 국세청 where you do 사업자등록 and file income tax. Habitual partners: 종합소득세, 부가세, 사업자등록, 홈택스.

'File taxes' should be 세금을 신고하다, but learners often borrow 'pay' for everything and say 세금을 내다 even when they only mean to submit the return. Also, don't go to the 구청 to register a business — that is squarely the 세무서's job.

entries.shortExplanation: 파출소 means "local police box / substation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "local police box / substation" is 파출소 (pachulso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 파출소에 가다 ("go to the police box"). Watch the particle attached to 파출소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 파출소 is the small neighborhood police post for minor matters
신고하다 'report (a crime/incident)'; for small incidents, lost items, or disputes
가깝다 → 가까운; they dot the neighborhoods, so one is usually close

usagePhrases.en: hand (something) in at the police box
usagePhrases.note: 맡기다 'entrust/leave with' is the verb for turning in a found wallet

examples.en: If you get lost, go to the police box and ask.
examples.note: simple safety advice; 파출소 doubles as a place to ask directions

examples.en: I found a wallet and handed it in at the nearby police box.
examples.note: 줍다 (ㅂ-irregular: 주워서) 'pick up'; 맡기다 'leave in someone's care' — the standard lost-and-found frame

examples.en: A drunk person was being loud at night, so I called the police box.
examples.note: for non-emergency neighborhood trouble; -아서 gives the reason

entries.nuance: 파출소 (派出所, 派 'dispatch' + 出 'send out' + 所 'post', literally a 'dispatch post' from which officers are sent into the neighborhood) is the small local police box you use for minor incidents, lost-and-found, and neighborhood disputes. The contrast to fix is 파출소 vs 경찰서 (警察署): the 파출소 is the tiny front-line post for everyday small matters, while the 경찰서 is the full district police station that investigates and processes formal cases — and for a genuine emergency you skip both and dial 112. A further wrinkle is that many 파출소 have been merged into larger 지구대 (地區隊) units, so older speakers say 파출소 where the sign now reads 지구대. Natural partners: 신고하다, 맡기다, 분실물, 순찰. Pitfall: English speakers treat 'go to the police' as one phrase, but Korean distinguishes the small 파출소 (walk-in, minor) from the big 경찰서 (formal cases) — and reporting urgent danger should be a phone call to 112, not a walk to the 파출소.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Going to the 파출소 in a real emergency instead of calling 112; the phone line dispatches help far faster than walking to a post.
Confusing 파출소 (small neighborhood police box) with 경찰서 (the district police station that handles formal investigations and cases).
Saying 지갑을 파출소에 주다 ('give the wallet to the police box'); the correct verb is 맡기다 ('entrust/leave in their care'), since you are not gifting it.

entries.shortExplanation: 법원 means "court (of law)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 법원 (beobwon) = "court (of law)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 법원에 가다 ("go to court") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 법원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 법원 is the courthouse where legal cases are heard
소송을 내다 'put forth a suit' is the everyday phrase; 제기하다 is the formal twin
판결 (判決) is the formal decision a judge issues; cf. 선고하다 'to hand down'
which 법원 hears your case depends on the address or contract terms

examples.ko: 그 사건은 지금 법원에서 재판 중이에요.
examples.romanization: geu sageoneun jigeum beobwoneseo jaepan jungieyo.
examples.en: That case is currently on trial at the court.
examples.note: 재판 중 'in the middle of trial'; 에서 marks where the proceeding happens

examples.ko: 소액 사건은 법원에서 비교적 빨리 처리돼요.
examples.romanization: soaek sageoneun beobwoneseo bigyojeok ppalli cheoridwaeyo.
examples.en: Small-claims cases are handled relatively quickly by the court.
examples.note: 소액심판 is a simpler track; 처리되다 (passive) 'get processed'

examples.ko: 집주인이 보증금을 안 줘서 법원에 소송을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: jipjuini bojeunggeumeul an jwoseo beobwone sosongeul naesseoyo.
examples.en: The landlord wouldn't return the deposit, so I filed a lawsuit in court.
examples.note: deposit (보증금) disputes are a common reason renters use the 법원; 소송을 내다 = file suit

entries.nuance: 법원 (法院, 法 'law' + 院 'institution/hall') is the courthouse where civil and criminal cases are decided by judges. For an ordinary resident the realistic contact is a civil matter — most often recovering an unreturned 전세 or 월세 보증금 through a small-claims (소액심판) filing. The contrast to keep straight is 법원 vs 경찰서: the 경찰 (police) *investigate* and gather evidence, while the 법원 *judges* and rules — police never issue a 판결. Note also that 법원's product is a 판결 (ruling), not the same as a 합의 (private settlement). Habitual partners: 소송을 내다, 판결, 재판, 출석, 기한. A real pitfall: court documents carry strict deadlines (기한), and the English instinct to 'deal with it later' is dangerous — ignoring a 법원 letter can mean losing 'by default' (궐석/무변론 패소). Also use 에 for going (법원에 가다) but 에서 for the trial happening there (법원에서 재판하다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 법원 (court) with 경찰서 (police station); the police investigate and arrest, the court judges and rules — they are different stages and different buildings.
Ignoring a deadline (기한) on a 법원 notice; missing it can mean an automatic loss in your case, unlike a casual letter you can answer whenever.
Saying 판결 for any decision; 판결 is specifically a judge's formal ruling. A privately agreed settlement is 합의, not 판결.

entries.shortExplanation: 체육관 means "gymnasium / sports hall" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 체육관 (cheyukgwan) means "gymnasium / sports hall". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 체육관에 가다 ("go to the gym/sports hall"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 체육관 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 체육관 is an indoor sports hall, often public and run by the district
구민 (區民) 'district residents'; these public halls are cheap to use
빌리다 'borrow' for casual use; 대관하다 (貸館) is the formal 'reserve the venue'
racket/court sports take 치다 'hit'; 운동을 하다 for exercise generally

examples.en: I work out at the sports hall every weekend.
examples.note: 마다 'every'; 에서 marks where the activity happens — a simple habit sentence

examples.en: I play badminton with friends at the sports hall.
examples.note: 배드민턴/탁구/농구 take 치다; 이랑 'with' is the casual companion particle

examples.ko: 구청에서 운영하는 체육관이라 이용료가 정말 싸요.
examples.romanization: gucheongeseo unyeonghaneun cheyukgwanira iyongnyoga jeongmal ssayo.
examples.en: It's run by the district office, so the fee is really cheap.
examples.note: public 체육관 vs private 헬스장 — the budget point; -(이)라(서) gives the reason

entries.nuance: 체육관 (體育館, 體育 'physical education' + 館 'hall/large building') is an indoor gymnasium or sports hall, usually a public facility run by the 구청 or city, used for court sports, swimming, and group classes. The synonym you must separate is 체육관 vs 헬스장: a 체육관 is the *building/hall* for badminton, basketball, volleyball or a pool, whereas a 헬스장 (or 피트니스) is a private *weights-and-treadmill gym* — the English word 'gym' covers both, which is exactly the trap. The 館 ending marks a sizeable public hall (cf. 도서관 library, 박물관 museum), reinforcing that it is a venue, not a membership fitness room. Natural partners: 구민체육관, 실내, 대관, 예약, 이용료. Two pitfalls: (1) calling your weights gym a 체육관 sounds like a school sports hall — say 헬스장; (2) court sports use 치다 (배드민턴을 치다), not 하다, so 'do badminton' as 배드민턴을 하다 is understandable but less idiomatic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 체육관 for a private weights gym; that is a 헬스장 or 피트니스. English 'gym' merges the two, but 체육관 specifically means a sports hall/venue.
Saying 배드민턴을 하다 instead of 배드민턴을 치다; racket and ball-court sports (배드민턴, 탁구, 농구) take 치다 'hit'.

entries.shortExplanation: 민원실 means "civil-service / public help desk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "civil-service / public help desk" is 민원실 (minwonsil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 민원실에 가다 ("go to the public help desk"). Watch the particle attached to 민원실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: go to the public help desk
usagePhrases.note: 민원실 is the front-desk office for residents' requests inside a public building
민원을 넣다 'put in a civil request' is the everyday phrase; 제기하다 is formal
창구 (窓口) 'wicket/counter' is where you're served after taking a 번호표
처리하다 'process'; the office 처리하다, the citizen 넣다/제기하다

examples.en: What floor is the help desk on?
examples.note: 층 'floor' with the question word 몇; a basic in-building direction question

examples.ko: 서류 발급은 1층 민원실에서 번호표 뽑고 기다리세요.
examples.romanization: seoryu balgeubeun 1cheung minwonsireseo beonhopyo ppopgo gidariseyo.
examples.en: For document issuance, take a number at the first-floor help desk and wait.
examples.note: 번호표를 뽑다 'pull a number ticket' is the standard 민원실 routine

examples.ko: 주차 문제는 구청 민원실에 민원을 넣었어요.
examples.romanization: jucha munjeneun gucheong minwonsire minwoneul neoeosseoyo.
examples.en: I filed a complaint about parking with the district office help desk.
examples.note: 민원 covers complaints, not just document requests; 민원을 넣다 = lodge a request

entries.nuance: 민원실 (民願室, 民 'people' + 願 'wish/petition' + 室 'room', literally the 'room for citizens' petitions') is the public-service desk inside a government building — the 구청, 동사무소, 세무서 etc. — where residents request documents or file complaints. The key insight is the root word 민원: it means a citizen's *formal request or grievance* to a public office, covering both neutral asks (issuing a certificate) and complaints (noisy construction). So the contrast to draw is 민원실 vs the building itself: 구청/동사무소 is the whole agency, while 민원실 is merely the 室 ('room') inside it where the public is served — it is a desk/floor, not a standalone building. The collocation engine: 민원을 넣다/제기하다 (lodge), 처리하다 (the office processes), 번호표를 뽑다, 창구. Pitfall: English speakers narrow 민원 to 'complaint', but a request for a 등본 is also a 민원; and don't say 민원실에 가다 expecting a separate address — it lives inside a larger 관공서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 민원실 as a standalone building; it is the 室 ('room/desk') for public service located inside a larger government building like a 구청.
Using 민원 only for complaints; it equally covers neutral requests such as getting a certificate issued — both are 민원 you 넣다 at the 민원실.
Mixing up who does what: the citizen 민원을 넣다/제기하다 (lodges), while the office 민원을 처리하다 (processes it). Saying you 처리하다 your own 민원 sounds like you work there.

entries.shortExplanation: 등기소 means "registry office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 등기소 (deunggiso) = "registry office". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 등기소에 가다 ("go to the registry office") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 등기소, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 등기소 handles official property and corporate registrations
떼다 is the everyday verb; 등기부등본 shows ownership and any 근저당 (mortgage liens)
등기 (登記) is the legal record of who owns a property
which 등기소 you use depends on the property's location

examples.en: The registry office is usually near the courthouse.
examples.note: true in practice (등기소 are tied to the court system); a simple location fact

examples.ko: 요즘은 등기소에 안 가도 인터넷등기소에서 열람할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun deunggisoe an gado inteonetdeunggisoeseo yeollamhal su isseoyo.
examples.en: These days you can view records on the internet registry without going to the office.
examples.note: 인터넷등기소 is the online portal; 열람하다 'inspect/browse (records)'

examples.ko: 전세 계약 전에 등기부등본을 꼭 확인하세요.
examples.romanization: jeonse gyeyak jeone deunggibudeungboneul kko kwaginhaseyo.
examples.en: Be sure to check the property register before signing a jeonse contract.
examples.note: checking 등기부등본 reveals hidden mortgages before you pay a deposit; -기 전에 'before V-ing'

entries.nuance: 등기소 (登記所, 登 'record/enter' + 記 'write down' + 所 'office', literally the 'recording office') is the registry that keeps official records of property ownership and company registration, administratively tied to the court (法院) system. Its single most practical product for a renter is the 등기부등본 — the property register you must read before signing a 전세 or 월세 contract to confirm the landlord truly owns the place and to spot existing loans (근저당권). The confusion to kill is the shared syllable 등기: 등기소/등기부 (property *registration*) is unrelated to 등기우편 (*registered* mail at the post office) — same 登記 'to record' but completely different services. Habitual partners: 등기부등본, 부동산 등기, 열람, 인터넷등기소, 근저당. Pitfall: English speakers skip the 등기부등본 check because 'the landlord seems nice', but verifying the register is the one concrete step that exposes a property already heavily mortgaged. Most people now 열람 online rather than visiting in person.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Skipping the 등기부등본 check before a lease; it is the key way to spot a property already heavily mortgaged (근저당) and protect your deposit.
Confusing 등기소/등기 (property registry) with 등기우편 (registered mail at the post office); they share 등기 'to record' but are unrelated services.
Using 발급하다 about yourself for the extract; the office 발급하다 (issues) the 등기부등본 — you 떼다 or 발급받다 (receive) it.

entries.shortExplanation: 출입국사무소 means "immigration office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 출입국사무소 (churipguksamuso) means "immigration office". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 출입국사무소에 가다 ("go to the immigration office"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 출입국사무소 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 출입국사무소 handles visas and foreign-resident registration
체류 (滯留) 'stay/sojourn'; 연장하다 (延長) 'extend' — the core renewal phrase

usagePhrases.en: get one's foreign resident card issued
usagePhrases.note: 외국인등록증 (ARC) is issued here; 발급받다 = receive (an issued doc)

usagePhrases.en: the immigration office for your area
usagePhrases.note: your 관할 office is set by where you live; reservations via 하이코리아

examples.en: You have to make a reservation before going to the immigration office.
examples.note: 예약하고 가다 'reserve and (then) go'; walk-ins are limited

examples.en: If your address changes you must report it to the immigration office too.
examples.note: 체류지 변경 신고 is required of foreign residents; 에도 'also to (there)' marks the extra place

examples.ko: 비자 연장은 출입국사무소에 미리 예약하고 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: bija yeonjangeun churipguksamusoe miri yeyakago gaya haeyo.
examples.en: For a visa extension you must book an appointment at the immigration office in advance.
examples.note: walk-ins are hard; 하이코리아 reservations are expected; 미리 'in advance'

entries.nuance: 출입국사무소 (出入國事務所, 出 'exit' + 入 'enter' + 國 'country' + 事務所 'office', literally the 'country-exit-and-entry affairs office') is the immigration office — the single most important 관공서 for a foreign resident. It issues the 외국인등록증 (ARC/foreign resident card), processes 비자 연장 (visa extensions) and changes of status, and records 체류지 변경 (address updates). Its formal current name is 출입국·외국인청 (the 廳-level seat), but the everyday term stays 출입국사무소. A useful pairing to know is 출입국사무소 vs 동사무소: when a foreign resident moves, the 동사무소 alone is not enough — the move must *also* be reported to 출입국, which is why Koreans say 출입국사무소'에도' 신고하다. Habitual partners: 예약, 하이코리아, 체류 연장, 외국인등록증, 발급받다. Pitfall: English speakers expect to walk in like at a US DMV, but most offices now require an online 하이코리아 reservation and may turn away walk-ins; and 비자 'visa' takes 연장하다 ('extend'), not the English-flavored 'renew' rendered literally.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reporting an address change only at the 동사무소; foreign residents must ALSO report it to the 출입국사무소 (체류지 변경 신고) — hence 출입국사무소에도 신고하다.

Saying 외국인등록증을 발급하다 about yourself; the office 발급하다 (issues) the card, while you 발급받다 (receive) it.

entries.shortExplanation: 우편함 means "mailbox / letterbox" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "mailbox / letterbox" is 우편함 (upyeonham). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우편함을 확인하다 ("check the mailbox"). Watch the particle attached to 우편함 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 우편함 is the box at your building where incoming mail lands

usagePhrases.en: be slipped into / arrive in the mailbox
usagePhrases.note: 꽂히다 (passive) 'be stuck in' describes mail tucked into the slot
apartment lobbies have a wall of 공동 우편함, one slot per unit
many building 우편함 have a small dial/number lock

examples.en: A letter came in the mailbox.
examples.note: 오다 'come' is natural for mail arriving; 에 marks the location it landed in

examples.en: The maintenance-fee bill comes to the mailbox every month.
examples.note: 우편함으로 오다 '(come) by way of the mailbox' — 으로 marks the route/channel; 고지서 = bills

examples.ko: 등기우편은 우편함에 안 넣고 직접 받아야 해요.
examples.romanization: deunggiupyeoneun upyeonhame an neoko jikjeop badaya haeyo.
examples.en: Registered mail isn't left in the mailbox; you have to receive it in person.
examples.note: 등기 requires a signature, unlike regular mail; -지 않고 → 안 넣고 'without putting it in'

entries.nuance: 우편함 (郵便函, 郵便 'mail/post' + 函 'box/case') is the *incoming* mailbox where letters and official notices are delivered, usually a locked unit in an apartment lobby. The crucial contrast is 우편함 vs 우체통 (郵遞筒): the 우편함 is your private *receiving* box at home, while the red 우체통 on the street is the public *outgoing* box you drop letters into — confusing them is the classic learner slip because English 'mailbox' covers both directions. (And 우체국 is the post office building itself.) Note 函 means a case/box, distinct from 통 'cylinder/bin'. Habitual partners: 확인하다, 고지서, 등기우편, 공동 우편함, 비밀번호; mail 'comes' to it via 우편함으로 오다. Pitfall: check it regularly, because 고지서 (bills), tax notices, and government letters with deadlines arrive here — and don't expect 등기우편 (registered mail) in the box, since registered items need an in-person signature and are otherwise re-delivered (재배송).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 우편함 (your incoming home mailbox) with 우체통 (the red public postbox for outgoing letters); English 'mailbox' hides this in/out distinction.
Expecting 등기우편 to be left in the 우편함; registered mail requires an in-person handoff with a signature, or it is re-delivered.
Using 통 instead of 함: a home receiving box is 우편함 (函 'case'), while 우체통 (筒 'cylinder') is the street postbox — they are not interchangeable.

entries.shortExplanation: 관공서 means "government office / public agency" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 관공서 (gwangongseo) = "government office / public agency". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 관공서에 가다 ("go to a government office") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 관공서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 관공서 is the umbrella term for any public office (구청, 세무서, etc.)
업무 시간 (業務時間) usually weekdays 9 to 6, closed weekends and holidays
문을 닫다 'close (its) door' = be shut, esp. on 공휴일

usagePhrases.en: official paperwork from a public office
usagePhrases.note: documents issued or required by a 관공서

examples.en: Government offices are closed on weekends.
examples.note: 문을 닫다 'shut the door' = be closed; a basic, high-frequency fact for newcomers

examples.en: On public holidays all government offices are closed.
examples.note: 공휴일 (public holiday) closures catch newcomers off guard; 다 'all'

examples.en: Government offices only open on weekdays, so I run over during lunch.
examples.note: 평일에만 'only on weekdays'; 다녀오다 'go and come back' for a quick errand

entries.nuance: 관공서 (官公署, 官 'government/officialdom' + 公 'public' + 署 'bureau') is the general cover term for all government and public offices — the category that includes the 구청, 세무서, 동사무소, 보건소 and so on. The contrast to grasp is scope: 관공서 is the *umbrella word*, while 구청/세무서 are specific *instances* of it, so you use 관공서 when you mean 'public offices in general' (their hours, their closures) and the specific name when you mean one place. The practical knowledge baked into the word is the schedule: weekdays only, standard daytime hours (보통 9시–6시), and shut on 공휴일 — the set phrase being 관공서가 문을 닫다 ('the offices close their doors'). Habitual partners: 업무 시간, 공휴일, 휴무, 평일, 서류. Pitfall: English speakers assume offices keep bank-ATM-like evening or weekend access, but 관공서 generally close at 6 on weekdays and entirely on holidays — plan errands for a weekday morning, and use online services (정부24, 홈택스) when the office is shut.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 관공서 keep evening or weekend hours like a bank's ATM; they generally close at 6 on weekdays and are shut on weekends.
Trying to visit on a 공휴일 (public holiday); nearly all 관공서 문을 닫다 (are closed) and you'll need online services like 정부24 instead.
Using 관공서 when you mean one specific office; 관공서 is the umbrella category — for a particular errand name the actual office (구청, 세무서).

entries.shortExplanation: 무척 means "very, really (strong, warm)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무척 (mucheok) means "very, really (strong, warm)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무척 좋아요 ("I like it a lot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무척 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Warmer and more heartfelt than 아주; natural when talking about people or feelings
Adds genuine emotional weight; sounds sincere, not exaggerated
Works for weather and physical states; more expressive than a flat 아주
The -이나 suffix adds extra emphasis and a slightly literary, emotional tone

examples.en: That person is really kind.
examples.note: Simple subject + 무척 + adjective; notice 무척 sits right before the describing word

examples.en: Korean food really suits my taste.
examples.note: 입에 맞다 (lit. 'fit the mouth') is the set phrase for food agreeing with you

examples.en: I was really surprised to hear that news.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with emotion verbs like 놀라다, 기뻐하다, 슬퍼하다

entries.nuance: 무척 means 'very/really,' but unlike the neutral, almost clinical 아주, it carries a warm emotional undertone, so it gravitates toward feelings, people, and personal reactions rather than dry measurements. The dividing line with 아주: you would say 아주 정확하다 (very precise — a cool fact) but 무척 그립다 (miss someone terribly — a feeling). Register is soft and slightly literary, fully standard and never rude, so it works in heartfelt speech and writing alike; in fast texting younger Koreans swap in 너무 or 진짜. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for negation: English 'not very' does NOT become 무척 안 — Korean wants 그다지 안 or 별로 안 there, because 무척 only intensifies upward.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 무척 안 좋아요 for 'not very good' — 무척 only pushes a degree higher, so for 'not very' you need 별로 안 좋아요 or 그다지 좋지 않아요.
Treating 무척 as slang to avoid in polite settings; it is fully standard and soft/literary, so it never sounds rude or too casual even with a boss.
Forcing it onto cold technical facts (무척 정확하다); the emotional flavor clashes, and 아주/매우 정확하다 sounds far more natural there.

entries.shortExplanation: 굉장히 means "incredibly, extremely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "incredibly, extremely" is 굉장히 (goengjanghi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 굉장히 맛있어요 ("It's incredibly delicious"). Watch the particle attached to 굉장히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday strong intensifier, a clear notch above 아주
Loves words of size, scale, amount, or impressiveness
Expresses genuine surprise at a high degree
The base adjective stands alone: 우와, 굉장하다! = Wow, amazing!

examples.en: This bag is incredibly light.
examples.note: Simple form; 굉장히 directly modifies the adjective 가볍다

examples.en: I prepared incredibly hard for the interview.
examples.note: Here it stacks onto the adverb 열심히 to stress effort

examples.en: The subway is extremely crowded today.
examples.note: 붐비다 = to be crowded; a natural commuter remark with -네요 surprise

entries.nuance: 굉장히 is one of the most accessible STRONG intensifiers in everyday Korean and sounds natural in both casual chat and polite speech, even work emails. It comes from the hanja 宏壯 (굉장: 宏 'vast' + 壯 'magnificent') plus the adverbial -히, so at its root it paints something as grand or imposing — which is why it shines on scale and impressiveness (굉장히 크다/많다/대단하다). The synonym line: it overlaps with the breezier, more colloquial 엄청, but 굉장히 is a touch more composed and presentable, while 엄청 is punchier and more slang-leaning. Two English-speaker pitfalls: spelling (it is 굉장히 with 히, never 굉장이), and proportion — slapping 굉장히 on a trivial thing sounds like overstatement, where 꽤 or 좀 fits better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 굉장이 — the adverb is always 굉장히 (adjective stem 굉장 + -히); 굉장이 is simply a misspelling.
Overusing it on minor things (굉장히 for a tiny inconvenience); that reads as exaggeration, and 꽤 or 좀 would sound calmer and more natural.
Assuming the hanja meaning 'grand' lets it modify nouns like 상당한 does; 굉장히 is purely an adverb, so before a noun you must use the adjective form 굉장한 (굉장한 인기).

entries.shortExplanation: 상당히 means "considerably, quite" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상당히 (sangdanghi) = "considerably, quite". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 상당히 비싸요 ("It's quite expensive") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상당히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Measured and slightly formal; common in reviews and reports
Polished tone, good for feedback and workplace talk
Implies a notable, fact-like degree
Adnominal form 상당한: 상당한 시간 = a considerable amount of time

examples.en: This restaurant's prices are quite reasonable.
examples.note: Everyday-but-composed; 상당히 keeps the tone objective

examples.ko: 그 동네는 월세가 상당히 높은 편이에요.
examples.romanization: geu dongneneun wolsega sangdanghi nopeun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: Rents in that neighborhood are considerably high.
examples.note: -은 편이다 = 'tends to be,' softening the claim into a measured observation

examples.en: This project was considerably tricky.
examples.note: Sounds professional and controlled in a work debrief

entries.nuance: 상당히 marks a notable, MEASURED degree and carries a composed, semi-formal tone, so it lives in reviews, reports, and adult conversation. Its hanja 相當 (相 'mutual' + 當 'corresponding/befitting') literally means 'matching/befitting an amount' — i.e. 'amounting to a fair bit,' which is exactly why it feels objective, like you are reporting a fact rather than emoting. Synonym contrast: against the emotional 무척 or the casual 되게, 상당히 sounds understated and analytical; against 꽤 (also 'quite'), 상당히 is a touch stronger and more written-sounding. The key English-speaker pitfall is the adverb-vs-adnominal split: use 상당히 directly before a verb/adjective (상당히 어렵다), but switch to 상당한 directly before a noun (상당한 노력) — you cannot say 상당히 노력 as a noun phrase.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it in very casual chat with close friends, where it sounds stiff and bookish — 되게 or 엄청 land far more naturally there.
Confusing the adverb 상당히 with the adnominal 상당한; before a noun you must say 상당한 (상당한 시간/노력), not 상당히 시간.
Reading it as purely emotional 'very'; 상당히 signals an objective, fair-sized degree, so pairing it with gushing feelings (상당히 사랑해요) sounds oddly detached.

entries.shortExplanation: 제법 means "fairly, quite (better than expected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 제법 (jebeop) means "fairly, quite (better than expected)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제법 잘하네요 ("You're pretty good (better than I expected)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 제법 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: You're pretty good (better than I expected)
usagePhrases.note: Carries mild, pleasant surprise
Notes that something has actually reached a real degree
Implies it exceeded low expectations
Stands alone as praise: 오, 제법인데? = Oh, not bad!

examples.en: Oh, you can actually cook pretty well!
examples.note: Casual 반말; 제법 carries the 'I didn't expect this' surprise

examples.en: It's gotten fairly chilly morning and evening.
examples.note: 쌀쌀하다 = chilly; classic autumn small talk with -아졌어요 'has become'

examples.ko: 이 식당, 가격은 싼데 맛은 제법이에요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang, gagyeogeun ssande maseun jebeobieyo.
examples.en: This place is cheap but the food is actually quite good.
examples.note: Shows the core nuance: the result beats the low price expectation

entries.nuance: 제법 means 'fairly/quite,' but its defining flavor is that something turned out BETTER or MORE than you expected, usually with a dash of admiration. That expectation gap is the whole point: 제법 잘하네요 is a warm compliment ('better than I thought!'), whereas a flat 잘하네요 is neutral praise, and a strong 아주 잘하네요 just rates a high level with no surprise. Synonym contrast: 꽤 also means 'quite/fairly' but is emotionally neutral about expectation, while 제법 specifically encodes 'pleasantly surprising.' Register is friendly and conversational. The English-speaker pitfall is social: because it implies 'I didn't expect you to be this good,' aiming 제법 at a clear expert or a respected senior can sound faintly patronizing — praise them with 정말/아주 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 제법 toward a clearly skilled senior or acknowledged expert; the 'surprisingly good' nuance reads as condescending — switch to 정말 잘하시네요.
Treating it as a plain synonym for 아주; 제법 specifically signals 'more/better than expected,' not just a high degree, so it cannot replace a neutral intensifier.
Applying it to things you always knew would be good (제법 맛있는 유명 맛집); with no surprise gap the word loses its point and sounds off.

entries.shortExplanation: 다소 means "somewhat, rather (formal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "somewhat, rather (formal)" is 다소 (daso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 다소 늦어질 수 있어요 ("It may be somewhat delayed"). Watch the particle attached to 다소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Formal softening tone for notices and emails
Politely understates a negative reaction
Common in reports and official announcements
Diplomatic way to express mild disappointment

examples.en: Today the wind will be somewhat strong.
examples.note: Pure weather-forecast register; the -겠습니다 ending matches the formal tone

examples.en: We apologize that the delivery is somewhat delayed.
examples.note: Standard wording in shop and delivery notices; softens the bad news

examples.ko: 설명이 다소 복잡하니 천천히 읽어 주세요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongi daso bokjapani cheoncheonhi ilgeo juseyo.
examples.en: The explanation is rather complex, so please read it slowly.
examples.note: A polite hedge inside instructions, lowering the alarm

entries.nuance: 다소 means 'somewhat / a little,' but it belongs squarely to FORMAL written and broadcast Korean — notices, weather reports, customer messages, official statements — not chatting with friends. Its hanja 多少 (多 'many' + 少 'few') literally pairs 'more-or-less,' giving it the cool, hedging feel of English 'somewhat,' and it gravitates to mildly negative partners (다소 지연/부족/아쉽다) to soften the blow politely. Synonym contrast: 다소 and 약간 both mean 'slightly,' but 약간 is everyday-neutral and 다소 is buttoned-up and bureaucratic; in casual speech Koreans simply say 좀 or 약간. The English-speaker pitfall is register mismatch and over-stacking: dropping 다소 into friendly chat sounds stiff, and because it means a SMALL-to-moderate degree, combining it with a strong word (다소 엄청) is self-contradictory.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다소 in casual conversation with friends; it sounds oddly formal and newscaster-like — use 좀 or 약간 instead.
Pairing it with strong intensifiers (다소 엄청 / 다소 매우); 다소 caps the degree at small-to-moderate, so it contradicts a 'very' word.
Assuming it carries warmth like English 'a bit'; 다소 is detached and official, so for soft, friendly understatement 살짝 or 좀 fits better.

Its hanja 多少 (多 'many' + 少 'few') literally pairs 'more-or-less,' giving it the cool, hedging feel of English 'somewhat.'

entries.shortExplanation: 살짝 means "slightly, lightly, just a touch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 살짝 (saljjak) = "slightly, lightly, just a touch". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 살짝 매워요 ("It's a little spicy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 살짝, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Very common for taste, temperature, and feelings
Cooking instruction: only briefly in hot water

usagePhrases.en: Please open the door just a bit
usagePhrases.note: Describes a small, gentle physical action
Softens an emotion in a cute, casual way

examples.en: The soup is slightly bland.
examples.note: 싱겁다 = bland; the simplest taste use, 살짝 + adjective

examples.en: Could you move over just a little here?
examples.note: 살짝 makes the request gentle and low-pressure for an action verb

examples.en: The price is a touch burdensome, honestly.
examples.note: 살짝 softens the complaint; -긴 하다 adds 'admittedly'

entries.nuance: 살짝 means 'slightly,' but with a light, gentle, often cute texture, and crucially it modifies ACTIONS as much as states — doing something briefly, softly, or by a small amount (살짝 만지다 'touch lightly,' 살짝 웃다 'smile faintly'). It is hugely common in casual speech and cooking. Synonym contrast with 약간: 약간 is the neutral, measurable 'a little' (약간 차이가 난다), whereas 살짝 is vivid, conversational, and tactile — 'just a touch,' often implying a quick, delicate motion. The big English-speaker pitfall is mentally filing it under 'somewhat' only and forgetting the action sense: English 'slightly' rarely describes how you do something, but 살짝 happily does (살짝 닫다 = close gently), so do not restrict it to adjectives. It also only ever means SMALL — never use it for big degrees.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 살짝 for large or serious degrees (살짝 위험해요 for a real danger); it only marks small, light amounts, so a true high degree needs 꽤/많이.
Forgetting it modifies actions, not just adjectives; 살짝 만지다 means 'touch lightly' and 살짝 열다 'open a crack' — it is not purely a 'somewhat' word.
Swapping in the formal 다소 in friendly chat to mean the same thing; 살짝 is warm and casual, while 다소 sounds like a press release.

structuredNuance.t: 살짝 means 'slightly,' but with a light, gentle, often cute texture, and crucially it modifies ACTIONS as much as states — doing something briefly, softly, or by a small amount (살짝 만지다 'touch lightly,' 살짝 웃다 'smile faintly'). entries.shortExplanation: 도무지 means "(not) at all, simply (can't)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 도무지 (domuji) means "(not) at all, simply (can't)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도무지 모르겠어요 ("I simply have no idea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도무지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Must pair with a negative; stresses total inability

usagePhrases.en: I just can't understand it at all
usagePhrases.note: 이해가 안 가다 = it doesn't make sense to me

usagePhrases.en: It just won't work no matter what
usagePhrases.note: Conveys frustration after repeated trying
잠이 안 오다 = sleep won't come

examples.en: I simply can't tell what this even means.
examples.note: Basic frame: 도무지 ... 모르겠다, the textbook 'can't grasp it' use

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 많아서 도무지 시간이 안 나요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri manaseo domuji sigani an nayo.
examples.en: I'm so busy lately that I just can't find any time.
examples.note: 시간이 나다 = to have time free; the 안 is what 도무지 leans on

examples.ko: 몇 번을 봐도 도무지 답을 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: myeot beoneul bwado domuji dabeul moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: No matter how many times I look, I just can't get the answer.
examples.note: 몇 번을 봐도 = 'however many times I look,' amplifying the helplessness

entries.nuance: 도무지 means 'not at all / simply (cannot)' and is a NEGATIVE-POLARITY adverb: it must be answered later in the sentence by a negative (안, 못, 모르다, -지 않다), and it adds a strong color of frustration and total impossibility, very often about failing to understand or grasp something. Synonym contrast: it is nearly interchangeable with 도저히, but 도저히 leans 'there is no way / it can't be done however hard I try' (도저히 못 참겠다), while 도무지 leans 'I simply can't make sense of it,' tilting toward confusion. Do NOT confuse it with the look-alike 도대체, which is an interrogative intensifier meaning 'what on earth?' (도대체 왜?) and questions rather than negates. The headline English-speaker pitfall: because English 'simply' can be positive, learners write 도무지 좋아요, which is impossible — 도무지 cannot appear in an affirmative sentence at all.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도무지 in a positive sentence (도무지 좋아요); it is negative-polarity and requires 안/못/모르다/-지 않다 to complete it.
Confusing it with 도대체 ('what on earth'); 도대체 questions or expresses exasperation (도대체 왜 그래요?), while 도무지 emphasizes flat inability.
Swapping it freely with 전혀; 전혀 is a neutral 'not at all' for any negated fact (전혀 안 맵다), whereas 도무지 specifically adds frustrated 'no matter what I do' inability.

structuredNuance.t: 도무지 means 'not at all / simply (cannot)' and is a NEGATIVE-POLARITY adverb: it must be answered later in the sentence by a negative (안, 못, 모르다, -지 않다), and it adds a strong color of frustration and total impossibility, very often about failing to understand or grasp something.

entries.shortExplanation: 훨씬 means "much, far (more) — comparative" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "much, far (more) — comparative" is 훨씬 (hwolssin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 훨씬 더 좋아요 ("It's much better"). Watch the particle attached to 훨씬 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Almost always with a comparison; frequently sits before 더
Stresses a big gap between two things
버스보다 훨씬 빨라요 = much faster than the bus
낫다 → 나아요; common when comparing conditions or states

examples.en: This is far cheaper than that one.
examples.note: The bare A보다 B 훨씬 frame; 훨씬 marks how big the price gap is

examples.en: After taking the medicine, I feel much better.
examples.note: 괜찮아지다 = to get better; comparison is implied between before and after

examples.ko: 이 집이 전에 살던 곳보다 훨씬 넓어요.
examples.romanization: i jibi jeone saldeon gotboda hwolssin neolbeoyo.
examples.en: This place is far more spacious than where I lived before.
examples.note: 보다 names the thing compared; 훨씬 says the difference is large

entries.nuance: 훨씬 is the go-to word for emphasizing a LARGE gap in a comparison — 'much/far more' — and it implies the difference is significant, not slight. It pairs naturally with 더 (훨씬 더 빠르다) and with the 보다 comparative structure (택시보다 훨씬). The crucial contrast is with general intensifiers: 아주/너무 just rate one thing's degree on its own ('very fast'), but 훨씬 is inherently RELATIVE and needs a second thing to measure against ('much faster than X'). It also differs from 더 alone, which says merely 'more' with no claim about size, while 훨씬 insists the gap is big. The English-speaker pitfall: 'much better' tempts you to say 훨씬 좋아요 in isolation, but with no expressed or implied 'than what?' it sounds incomplete — Korean expects a comparison target, even if context supplies it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 훨씬 with no comparison at all (훨씬 좋아요 out of nowhere); it is comparative, so there must be an expressed or clearly implied 'than X.'
Replacing 아주/너무 with 훨씬 for a simple high degree; 훨씬 specifically means 'by a large margin more,' not a general 'very.'
Dropping 더 where the meaning is 'more' and expecting 훨씬 alone to carry it in subtle cases; 훨씬 더 is the safe, natural pairing for 'much more.'

entries.shortExplanation: 되게 means "really, so (casual spoken)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 되게 (doege) = "really, so (casual spoken)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 되게 맛있어요 ("It's so good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 되게, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Super common in casual speech, like a spoken 'really'
Everyday complaint about distance or effort
Friendly compliment in relaxed conversation
Mainly spoken; in writing people prefer 정말/아주

examples.en: It's so hot today.
examples.note: The simplest pattern: 되게 + adjective in casual 해요-speech

examples.ko: 여기 분위기 되게 좋다, 자주 오자.
examples.romanization: yeogi bunwigi doege jota, jaju oja.
examples.en: This place has a really nice vibe, let's come often.
examples.note: 분위기 = vibe; pure 반말 among friends, where 되게 thrives

examples.en: The roads are really jammed today.
examples.note: 막히다 = to be congested; an everyday gripe with -네요

entries.nuance: 되게 is a very common CASUAL intensifier meaning 'really/so,' used almost exclusively in spoken Korean among friends, peers, and people you are comfortable with. It feels lively and effortless in conversation but looks out of place in formal writing or business email, where 아주, 매우, or 정말 belong. Synonym contrast: it sits right beside 엄청 and 진짜 as spoken boosters, but 되게 is the most conversational and a bit softer than the punchy 엄청; meaning-wise it just means 'very,' with none of the 'large amount' flavor 엄청 can carry. Two English-speaker pitfalls: spelling and register. Spelling — it is 되게 (from 되다), never 됬게 or 돼게, since 되 + 게 takes no extra ㅆ. Register — because it is so casual, using it in anything written or official instantly sounds too chatty.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 되게 in formal documents, emails, or reports, where it reads as too casual; use 매우/정말/아주 in those registers.
Spelling it 됬게 or 돼게; the correct form is 되게 (stem 되- + -게), with no doubled ㅆ and no 돼.
Assuming it means 'a lot/a ton' like 엄청 can for quantity; 되게 only intensifies a quality ('very'), so 되게 많이 is fine but 되게 alone won't carry 'a huge amount.'

entries.shortExplanation: 엄청 means "super, a ton, tremendously" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 엄청 (eomcheong) means "super, a ton, tremendously". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 엄청 많아요 ("There's a ton"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 엄청 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Strong and casual; great for amounts and intensity alike
Common spoken intensifier across all ages
Adjective form: 효과가 엄청나요 = the effect is huge
Fuller adverb form: 엄청나게 노력했어요

examples.en: There are a ton of people.
examples.note: Quantity use; 엄청 + 많다 is the most natural high-amount pairing

examples.ko: 이번 시험 공부를 엄청 했는데 떨려요.
examples.romanization: ibeon siheom gongbureul eomcheong haenneunde tteollyeoyo.
examples.en: I studied a ton for this exam but I'm nervous.
examples.note: 떨리다 = to feel nervous/shaky; 엄청 here measures the effort

examples.en: The delivery came incredibly fast.
examples.note: 엄청 stacks onto the adverb 빨리; a classic food-delivery comment

entries.nuance: 엄청 is a punchy, casual way to say 'super / a ton,' and it is unusual among these adverbs in handling both QUANTITY (엄청 많다 'a ton') and INTENSITY (엄청 덥다 'super hot') with equal ease. Register is colloquial — extremely frequent in speech and texting across all ages, a step less formal than 굉장히 and far less formal than 매우/대단히. Synonym contrast: against 굉장히, 엄청 is breezier and more slang-flavored while 굉장히 sounds more presentable; against 되게, 엄청 hits harder and can carry the 'huge amount' sense that 되게 cannot. A handy feature is the adjective spin-off 엄청나다 ('to be tremendous') and its adverb 엄청나게, letting you say 효과가 엄청나요. The English-speaker pitfall is degree: like all strong boosters it means a genuinely LARGE amount, so using it for something small (엄청 for a tiny bit) is wrong — reach for 살짝/약간 there.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 엄청 in formal writing where it reads as too casual; choose 매우/대단히/굉장히 for documents and official messages.
Saying 엄청 for tiny degrees (엄청 조금); it implies a genuinely large amount or high intensity, contradicting 'a little' — use 살짝/약간 instead.
Mixing up the bare adverb 엄청 with 엄청나다; before a noun you need the adjective form 엄청난 (엄청난 효과), not 엄청 효과.

structuredNuance.t: 엄청 is a punchy, casual way to say 'super / a ton,' and it is unusual among these adverbs in handling both QUANTITY (엄청 많다 'a ton') and INTENSITY (엄청 덥다 'super hot') with equal ease. entries.shortExplanation: 한층 means "even more, a level more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "even more, a level more" is 한층 (hancheung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한층 더 좋아졌어요 ("It's gotten even better"). Watch the particle attached to 한층 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Often paired with 더; pictures stepping up one level
Common in product and service descriptions
Slightly formal; used for improvement and progress
Nice for relationships deepening one notch

examples.en: Now that it's spring, the days have gotten even warmer.
examples.note: 한층 + 더 implied; the 'one step up from before' feel is built in

examples.ko: 연습을 꾸준히 했더니 실력이 한층 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: yeonseubeul kkujunhi haetdeoni sillyeogi hancheung neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Since I practiced steadily, my skills improved even further.
examples.note: 한층 stresses a clear step up from an existing level

examples.en: Now that it's autumn, the foliage is even more beautiful.
examples.note: 단풍 = autumn leaves; the slightly literary tone suits 한층

entries.nuance: 한층 means 'even more / a level higher,' and it literally pictures improvement as climbing one more 층 (層, 'floor/story/layer') above an already-good state — that built-in 'from an existing baseline, step up one' is its core. Because of that, it almost always implies a POSITIVE upgrade and frequently appears as 한층 더 for extra force. Register is polished and a little written-sounding, so it suits reviews, product copy, and thoughtful speech more than rapid 반말. Synonym contrast: against plain 더 ('more,' no baseline assumption) 한층 insists there was already a good level you are now exceeding; against 훨씬 ('much more,' comparing two separate things by a big margin) 한층 is about one thing rising another step over its former self, and the rise can be modest. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 한층 for a first-time, baseline-less degree (it needs a prior state to step up from), and in casual chat a simple 더 or 훨씬 usually sounds more natural.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 한층 for a first-time degree with no prior baseline; it means going 'one level further' from an existing state, so without that earlier level it sounds wrong.
Treating it as fully casual; in chatty 반말 a plain 더 or 훨씬 sounds more natural, while 한층 leans formal and slightly literary.
Confusing it with 훨씬; 훨씬 compares two different things by a large margin (A보다 훨씬), whereas 한층 raises one thing a step above its own former state.

entries.shortExplanation: 부쩍 means "markedly, noticeably (more)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부쩍 (bujjeok) = "markedly, noticeably (more)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부쩍 늘었어요 ("It increased noticeably") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부쩍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Implies a sudden, visible rise over a short time
Common for sudden weather changes
Notes a marked change in someone's appearance
부쩍 자주 보이네요 = I see you around a lot more lately

examples.en: I've been noticeably more tired lately.
examples.note: 요즘 + 부쩍 is the textbook pairing for a recent, striking change

examples.ko: 환절기라 그런지 감기 환자가 부쩍 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgira geureonji gamgi hwanjaga bujjeong neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe because of the season change, cold patients have increased markedly.
examples.note: 환절기 = change of seasons; 늘다 is the change verb 부쩍 loves

examples.ko: 조카가 못 본 사이에 부쩍 컸어요.
examples.romanization: jokaga mot bon saie bujjeok keosseoyo.
examples.en: My niece/nephew has grown so much since I last saw them.
examples.note: 못 본 사이에 = 'while I wasn't seeing them'; stresses the jump you suddenly notice

entries.nuance: 부쩍 describes a MARKED, noticeable change that happened over a relatively short stretch — 'suddenly a lot more' — and it is a native Korean (non-Sino) word with a vivid, observational feel. Grammatically it craves VERBS OF CHANGE (늘다, 줄다, 커지다, 추워지다, 늙다) rather than static adjectives, and it pairs constantly with 요즘 to mean 'lately, and you can really tell.' The key synonym contrast is with 점점 and 차츰: those describe GRADUAL, step-by-step change ('more and more, slowly'), whereas 부쩍 stresses that the jump was striking and easy to notice, almost abrupt. The English-speaker pitfall: because English 'noticeably' attaches happily to adjectives ('noticeably pretty'), learners try 부쩍 예쁘다, which sounds odd — Korean wants the change form 부쩍 예뻐졌다 ('got noticeably prettier'), since 부쩍 is about movement to a new state, not a static quality.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 부쩍 with static adjectives (부쩍 예쁘다, 부쩍 크다); it needs verbs of change, so say 부쩍 예뻐졌다 or 부쩍 컸다.
Confusing it with the gradual 점점/차츰; those mean slow, steady change, while 부쩍 implies a sharp, noticeable jump in a short period.
Stretching it to long, slow trends; 부쩍 fits a recent, surprising surge (요즘 부쩍...), not a change spread evenly over many years.

structuredNuance.t: 부쩍 describes a MARKED, noticeable change that happened over a relatively short stretch — 'suddenly a lot more' — and it is a native Korean (non-Sino) word with a vivid, observational feel. entries.shortExplanation: 후련하다 means "relieved (after a burden lifts); refreshed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 후련하다 (huryeonhada) means "relieved (after a burden lifts); refreshed". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후련해요 ("I feel relieved"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후련하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective, so 하 + 여요 contracts to 해요 — the most common spoken form

usagePhrases.en: to feel a weight off one's chest
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; literally 'the insides feel clear' — say this after venting or finishing something
adverb form (하다→하게), e.g. 후련하게 울다 to have a good cleansing cry
-아/어지다 attaches to the 해 stem and shows the shift from heavy to light

examples.en: I'm relieved the exam is over.
examples.note: simple 해요 form; use it when a stressful thing is done, not just when you're happy

examples.ko: 할 말을 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련하네요.
examples.romanization: hal mareul da hago nanikka sogi huryeonhaneyo.
examples.en: Now that I've said everything I wanted to, I feel so relieved.
examples.note: -고 나니까 'now that I've finished ~' frames the classic after-venting context

examples.ko: 몇 년 묵은 고민을 털어놓고 나니까 가슴이 다 후련하더라고요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon mugeun gomineul teoreonoko nanikka gaseumi da huryeonhadeoragoyo.
examples.en: After finally pouring out a worry I'd carried for years, my chest felt completely clear.
examples.note: real-situation; 다 here is intensifier 'completely', and -더라고요 reports the felt experience

entries.nuance: 후련하다 names the clean, lightened sensation right after a burden or pent-up stress is released — finishing exams, finally venting, crying it out. Its near-synonym is 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broader word that also covers physical coolness (시원한 바람, a cool breeze) and refreshing drinks, while 후련하다 is reserved almost entirely for emotional/internal release, so '속이 후련하다' and '속이 시원하다' overlap but 바람이 후련하다 is wrong. It is NOT general happiness (기쁘다/행복하다) — it strictly presupposes something heavy was weighing on you and is now gone. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 후련해요 / 후련했어요 / 후련해서, and it collocates above all with 속이, 가슴이, and the adverb 후련하게. English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for it as a synonym of 'happy', but if there was no preceding pressure to discharge, a Korean ear hears it as odd — 'I'm 후련해' out of plain good cheer sounds like a non sequitur.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 후련하다 for plain happiness ('생일이라 후련해요') is wrong — it requires a preceding burden or stress that has just been lifted; for general joy use 기쁘다/행복하다.
Treating it as interchangeable with 시원하다 for physical coolness ('날씨가 후련해요') is wrong; 후련하다 is emotional/internal release only — say 시원하다 for a cool breeze or cold drink.
Saying '후련 있어요' (treating it like a noun) is wrong; it is an adjective, so conjugate it directly: 후련해요, 후련했어요.

entries.english: uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling
entries.shortExplanation: 찝찝하다 means "uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling" is 찝찝하다 (jjipjjipada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 찝찝해요 ("I feel uneasy about it"). Watch the particle attached to 찝찝하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective contracting to 해요 — common after an awkward or unresolved moment
뭔가 ('somehow/something') is the habitual partner adverb that triggers this word
attributive form (하다→한) modifying 기분/느낌
adverb form, e.g. 찝찝하게 헤어졌어요 we parted on an unsettled note

examples.en: Something just feels off.
examples.note: the bare, high-frequency form; 뭔가 sets up the vague unease

examples.en: I got an apology, but something still feels off.
examples.note: -는데 contrasts the apology with the lingering residue; use when a resolution doesn't fully satisfy

examples.ko: 계약서에 도장 찍긴 했는데 조건이 영 찝찝해서 다시 읽어 봤어요.
examples.romanization: gyeyakseoe dojang jjikgin haenneunde jogeoni yeong jjipjjipaeseo dasi ilgeo bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I did stamp the contract, but the terms left me so uneasy that I reread it.
examples.note: real-situation; 영 'utterly' + 찝찝해서 'because it felt off' gives the cause that drove an action

entries.nuance: 찝찝하다 is the nagging, not-quite-resolved discomfort that sticks to you — a conversation that ended badly, a decision you can't fully trust, even a slightly unclean feeling on your skin. Contrast it sharply with 불안하다: 불안하다 is forward-looking anxiety about what might happen, whereas 찝찝하다 is the backward-looking residue of something that already occurred and didn't settle cleanly. It is milder than 죄책감 (guilt) — more 'this won't sit right' than 'I did wrong'. It lives in casual speech and pairs constantly with 뭔가, 영, and 기분/느낌. Note the spelling: the standard dictionary form is 찜찜하다, but 찝찝하다 is the more emphatic, far more common everyday variant. English-speaker pitfall: learners map it to 'uncomfortable' and then misuse it for physical pain (a sore back is 아프다/불편하다, not 찝찝하다); 찝찝하다 is psychological/residual unease, or at most a faint 'icky, not-clean' feeling.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 불안하다 ('내일 시험이 찝찝해요') is wrong — for anxiety about a future event use 불안하다; 찝찝하다 is the lingering residue of something already past.
Using it in formal writing or a business report reads as too casual/slangy; in those registers prefer 꺼림칙하다 or 마음에 걸리다.
Applying it to physical pain ('허리가 찝찝해요') is wrong; for bodily discomfort say 불편하다 or 아프다 — 찝찝하다 is a mental/residual feeling (or a faint not-clean sensation).

entries.english: overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle
entries.shortExplanation: 벅차다 means "overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 벅차다 (beokchada) = "overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 벅차요 ("it's overwhelming / I'm overcome") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 벅차다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; stem 벅차- already ends in ㅏ so it just adds 요 — context decides positive vs negative
set phrase; with 가슴이 it is the moved/overcome-by-joy sense
attributive form (차다→찬); common with 감동, 행복, 순간
adverb form, e.g. 벅차게 다가오다 to hit one overwhelmingly

examples.en: The work is a bit too much for me.
examples.note: simple form, practical sense: a load exceeds your capacity

examples.en: Getting my first paycheck, my heart just swells.
examples.note: the positive 'overcome with emotion' sense; 가슴이 is the tell

examples.ko: 혼자 부모님 병간호까지 하려니 솔직히 벅차서 동생한테 도움을 청했어요.
examples.romanization: honja bumonim byeongganhokkaji haryeoni soljiki beokchaseo dongsaenghante doumeul cheonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: Caring for my parents alone on top of everything was honestly too much, so I asked my younger sibling for help.
examples.note: real-situation; -려니 'when I try to' + 벅차서 gives the reason for an action

entries.nuance: 벅차다 carries two flavors that share one root idea — 'more than the vessel can hold'. One is the heart-swelling kind: overcome with joy, pride, or gratitude (가슴이 벅차다). The other is the practical kind: a workload or responsibility that exceeds your capacity (일이 벅차다). The 가슴이 + 벅차다 frame is almost always the warm, positive reading; a task as subject flips it to the stressful 'I can't cope' reading. Contrast it with 바쁘다: 바쁘다 only means you have a lot to do (busy), while 벅차다 says the amount is beyond what you can manage — you could be 안 바쁘다 yet still find one hard task 벅차다. Note 벅차다 is its own adjective, not a 하다-word, so the stem is 벅차- (벅차요, 벅찼어요, 벅차서, 벅찬). English-speaker pitfall: assuming it is always positive because of its frequent use in emotional moments — '일이 벅차다' is a genuine cry that something is too much.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 벅차다 is always positive is wrong — '이 일은 벅차요' means the task is overwhelming in a can't-cope, stressful way, not joyful.
Equating it with 바쁘다 ('요즘 벅차요' meaning merely 'busy') is imprecise; 바쁘다 = a lot to do, 벅차다 = the amount exceeds your capacity. Use 바쁘다 for ordinary busyness.
Writing 벅차해요 (adding -해요 as if it were a 하다-word) is wrong; the correct polite form is simply 벅차요.

entries.english: empty; feeling a void; missing something
entries.shortExplanation: 허전하다 means "empty; feeling a void; missing something" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 허전하다 (heojeonhada) means "empty; feeling a void; missing something". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 허전해요 ("I feel empty / something's missing"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 허전하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, for emotional emptiness

usagePhrases.en: to feel a void in one's heart
usagePhrases.note: set phrase for loneliness or loss; 마음이 is the default subject
attributive form (하다→한) modifying 마음/기분
adverb form, e.g. 집이 허전하게 느껴져요 the house feels empty

examples.en: Being alone, I feel a bit empty.
examples.note: simple form; the basic 'a void is here' use

examples.ko: 룸메이트가 이사 가니까 집이 너무 허전해요.
examples.romanization: rummeiteuga isa ganikka jibi neomu heojeonhaeyo.
examples.en: Now that my roommate moved out, the place feels so empty.
examples.note: the void left when someone is gone; subject can be a place, not just a person's heart

examples.ko: 20년 키운 강아지를 떠나보내고 나니 집안 곳곳이 허전해서 한동안 적응이 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: 20nyeon kiun gangajireul tteonabonaego nani jiban gotgosi heojeonhaeseo handongan jeogeungi an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: After saying goodbye to the dog I'd raised for 20 years, every corner of the house felt so empty that I couldn't adjust for a while.
examples.note: real-situation; 곳곳이 'in every corner' + 허전해서 conveys pervasive absence

entries.nuance: 허전하다 is the quiet, wistful emptiness left behind when something or someone familiar is missing — a friend moves away, a long routine ends, a pet passes, or you just feel a vague hollow. Contrast it with 외롭다: 외롭다 specifically means lonely/alone (a person without company), whereas 허전하다 is about a felt absence or void that can apply even in a crowd when something expected is gone — you can be surrounded by people and still 허전하다 because a particular presence is missing. It is gentler than 슬프다 (active sorrow); 허전하다 is hollowness, not crying. Notably it attaches not only to 마음/가슴 but to places (집이 허전하다) and even body parts (목이 허전하다 after a haircut, 손이 허전하다 without a ring). English-speaker pitfall: translating 'I miss you' as '당신이 허전해요' — that is wrong; 허전하다 describes the void you feel, not the act of missing a person. For 'I miss you' use 보고 싶어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating it with 슬프다 ('영화가 허전했어요' for a sad film) is wrong — 허전하다 is about absence/a hollow feeling, not tears or sorrow; use 슬프다 for active sadness.
Using 허전하다 to translate 'I miss you' ('네가 허전해' ) is wrong; that idea is 보고 싶어. 허전하다 names the void, not the missing.
Restricting it to people only is too narrow; remember it works for places and even a bare neck/finger (머리 자르니까 목이 허전해요).

entries.shortExplanation: 든든하다 means "reassured; reliable; pleasantly full" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "reassured; reliable; pleasantly full" is 든든하다 (deundeunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 든든해요 ("I feel reassured / it's reassuring"). Watch the particle attached to 든든하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a very common compliment-adjacent word
set phrase; you feel backed-up and safe, 마음이 as subject
attributive form (하다→한); high praise for a friend or colleague
adverb form, e.g. 든든하게 먹다 to eat a hearty, filling meal

examples.en: Having you here, I feel reassured.
examples.note: casual 반말; warm thing to say to a close friend

examples.en: I had a hearty breakfast before heading out.
examples.note: the 'pleasantly full and fueled' sense; 든든하게 + 먹다 collocation

examples.ko: 보험까지 들어 두니 무슨 일이 생겨도 마음이 든든해서 발 뻗고 자게 돼요.
examples.romanization: boheomkkaji deureo duni museun iri saenggyeodo maeumi deundeunhaeseo bal ppeotgo jage dwaeyo.
examples.en: Now that I've even taken out insurance, I feel so secure that I can sleep soundly whatever happens.
examples.note: real-situation; the safety-net sense, with 발 뻗고 자다 'sleep with legs stretched = at ease'

entries.nuance: 든든하다 is the warm feeling of being backed up and secure — a dependable person at your side, a financial safety net, or a filling meal that fuels you for the day. Contrast it with 안심하다: 안심하다 is a verb meaning 'to feel relieved / set one's mind at ease' about a specific worry that has resolved, while 든든하다 is the standing, ongoing sense of having reliable support behind you (a backbone, not a resolved worry). Calling a person 든든하다 (그 사람 참 든든해요) is genuine praise for reliability. With food it means satisfyingly full and energized — more than 배부르다 (merely full): 든든하다 adds 'well-prepared, set up to go'. As a 하다-adjective it gives 든든해요 / 든든했어요 / 든든해서, and collocates with 마음이, 사람, and 든든하게 먹다. English-speaker pitfall: saying '저는 든든해요' to mean 'I am a reliable person' — Korean uses it for the reassurance you feel from something/someone, so frame it as 마음이 든든해요 or 그 사람이 든든해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배부르다 when you mean a hearty, fueling meal misses the nuance — 든든하게 먹다 implies being well-prepared and energized, not just 'no longer hungry'.

Saying '저는 든든한 사람이에요' to boast that you yourself are dependable sounds odd; let others call you 든든하다. Describe the feeling you give: '제가 있으면 든든하시죠?' is more natural, or just say 믿음직하다 of yourself sparingly.
Treating it as identical to 안심하다 is imprecise: 안심하다 (verb) = a worry resolved; 든든하다 (adjective) = ongoing backing/support behind you.
