entries.english: light and unburdened; free of a load
entries.shortExplanation: 홀가분하다 means "light and unburdened; free of a load" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 홀가분하다 (holgabunhada) = "light and unburdened; free of a load". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 홀가분해요 ("I feel unburdened") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 홀가분하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, said when a responsibility ends
set phrase; the weight-off-your-shoulders feeling
attributive form (하다→한) modifying 마음/기분
adverb form, e.g. 홀가분하게 떠나다 to leave unburdened

examples.en: Work's done, so I feel light and free.
examples.note: simple form; the relief of shedding a task

examples.ko: 짐 다 부치고 홀가분하게 여행 다녔어요.
examples.romanization: jim da buchigo holgabunhage yeohaeng danyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I shipped all my luggage and traveled light and carefree.
examples.note: literal lightness blending into emotional lightness; 홀가분하게 + 다니다

examples.ko: 오래 끌던 소송이 끝나니 어깨에 얹혔던 짐을 내려놓은 듯 홀가분하더라고요.
examples.romanization: orae kkeuldeon sosongi kkeunnani eokkaee eonjhyeotdeon jimeul naeryeonoeun deu tolgabunhadeoragoyo.
examples.en: When the long-dragging lawsuit ended, I felt as unburdened as if I'd set down a load on my shoulders.
examples.note: real-situation; the 듯 simile spells out the 'weight set down for good' core meaning

entries.nuance: 홀가분하다 is the buoyant lightness you feel after putting down a long-carried load — finishing a major project, paying off debt, ending an obligation. Contrast it carefully with its closest neighbor 후련하다: 후련하다 emphasizes the cathartic discharge of pent-up stress (the release), whereas 홀가분하다 emphasizes the resulting freedom and mobility (the lightness that remains) — after finally telling someone off you are 후련하다 (it came out), but after a years-long duty finally ends you are 홀가분하다 (you're free now). It implies a relatively lasting relief, not a fleeting one, and pairs above all with 마음이, 어깨, and 홀가분하게 떠나다/다니다. As a 하다-adjective: 홀가분해요 / 홀가분했어요 / 홀가분해서. English-speaker pitfall: using it for a momentary 'phew' — 홀가분하다 should mark a real burden that has been set down for good, so for a quick instant of relief 후련하다 or 다행이다 fits better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for momentary relief ('버스 놓칠 뻔했다가 타서 홀가분해요') is wrong — that's 다행이다/후련하다; 홀가분하다 implies a lasting burden finally set down.
Treating it as identical to 후련하다 blurs a real line: 후련하다 = the cathartic release of stress; 홀가분하다 = the resulting freedom and lightness. Pick by which you mean.
Spelling or saying it 홀가뿐하다 / 홀가분 있어요 is wrong; it is the adjective 홀가분하다, conjugated 홀가분해요, 홀가분했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 홀가분하다 is the buoyant lightness you feel after putting down a long-carried load — finishing a major project, paying off debt, ending an obligation. It implies a relatively lasting relief, not a fleeting one, and pairs above all with 마음이, 어깨, and 홀가분하게 떠나다/다니다.

Contrast it carefully with its closest neighbor 후련하다: 후련하다 emphasizes the cathartic discharge of pent-up stress (the release), whereas 홀가분하다 emphasizes the resulting freedom and mobility (the lightness that remains) — after finally telling someone off you are 후련하다 (it came out), but after a years-long duty finally ends you are 홀가분하다 (you're free now).
As a 하다-adjective: 홀가분해요 / 홀가분했어요 / 홀가분해서.
Using it for a momentary 'phew' is off — 홀가분하다 should mark a real burden that has been set down for good, so for a quick instant of relief 후련하다 or 다행이다 fits better.

entries.shortExplanation: 서먹하다 means "awkward/distant (between people not yet close)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 서먹하다 (seomeokada) means "awkward/distant (between people not yet close)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서먹해요 ("things feel awkward (between us)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서먹하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, describes the relationship's distance
reduplicated form that intensifies and softens the awkwardness, very common in speech
attributive form (하다→한); 사이 = the relationship between people
adverb form, e.g. 서먹하게 인사하다 to greet stiffly

examples.en: We're still a little distant with each other.
examples.note: simple form; states the relationship is not yet close

examples.en: We're on the same team, but it's still awkward between us.
examples.note: -지만 contrast frames not-yet-close coworkers

examples.ko: 10년 만에 만난 동창들과 처음엔 서먹했는데 술 한잔하니 금세 옛날로 돌아갔어요.
examples.romanization: 10nyeon mane mannan dongchangdeulgwa cheoeumen seomeokaenneunde sul hanjanhani geumse yennallo doragasseoyo.
examples.en: With classmates I met after 10 years it was awkward at first, but after a drink we quickly went back to the old days.
examples.note: real-situation; shows 서먹하다 as the dissolvable distance of a long gap

entries.nuance: 서먹하다 describes the awkward, not-yet-comfortable distance BETWEEN people who aren't close — new coworkers, friends after a long gap, two people after a quarrel. It is fundamentally relational. Contrast it with 어색하다 and 멋쩍다, the words learners confuse it with: 어색하다 covers awkwardness in general including situations and one's own self-consciousness (어색한 분위기, an awkward vibe; 어색한 미소, a forced smile), and 멋쩍다 is purely your own sheepish embarrassment — but 서먹하다 specifically names the coolness of a relationship, the gap of unfamiliarity between two parties. The reduplicated 서먹서먹하다 is idiomatic and a touch more vivid. As a 하다-adjective: 서먹해요 / 서먹했어요 / 서먹해서, and it pairs with 사이, 둘이, 분위기. English-speaker pitfall: using 서먹하다 for your own embarrassment ('칭찬받아서 서먹했어요') is wrong — that personal sheepishness is 멋쩍다/어색하다; 서먹하다 needs two parties and a relationship.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for self-conscious embarrassment ('실수해서 서먹했어요') is wrong — that's 어색하다/멋쩍다; 서먹하다 is the distance between two parties, not a feeling inside one person.
Saying you are 서먹하다 by yourself ('저 혼자 서먹해요') is wrong; it always needs a relationship — frame it as 둘이 서먹하다 or 사이가 서먹하다.
Confusing it with 낯설다 ('이 동네가 서먹해요') is wrong; for an unfamiliar place/thing use 낯설다, reserve 서먹하다 for the coolness between people.

entries.english: displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving
entries.shortExplanation: 못마땅하다 means "displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving" is 못마땅하다 (monmattanghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 못마땅해요 ("I'm displeased / I disapprove"). Watch the particle attached to 못마땅하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, expresses disapproval of something
attributive form (하다→한); very common with 표정/얼굴/눈빛
set phrase; 여기다 = to regard/consider
adverb form, e.g. 못마땅하게 쳐다보다 to glare disapprovingly

examples.en: I'm not happy with that decision.
examples.note: casual 반말; the basic 'it doesn't sit right with me' use

examples.en: Mom had a disapproving look about my decision.
examples.note: the classic 못마땅한 표정 collocation; note the senior-reacts-to-junior pattern

examples.ko: 부장님은 신입의 복장이 영 못마땅하신지 회의 내내 인상을 쓰고 계셨어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimeun sinibui bokjangi yeong monmattanghasinji hoeui naenae insangeul sseugo gyesyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The manager, apparently quite displeased with the new hire's outfit, kept frowning throughout the meeting.
examples.note: real-situation; 못마땅하신지 'seemingly displeased' + honorific 시 shows third-person disapproval shown by face

entries.nuance: 못마땅하다 means something does not sit right with you — you disapprove of or find it unsatisfactory. The word transparently builds from 마땅하다 ('to be proper/fitting') negated by 못, so it literally reads 'not as it ought to be', which is exactly its flavor: a falling-short of your standard. It is typically shown through the face (못마땅한 표정/눈빛) rather than declared, and very often features a senior reacting to a junior's choice. Contrast it with 화나다: 화나다 is active anger that flares, whereas 못마땅하다 is quiet, simmering disapproval/dissatisfaction — you can be 못마땅하다 for days without ever being 화나다. Crucially, because it is an adjective of feeling, describing a THIRD person's displeasure requires 못마땅해하다 (부장님이 못마땅해하셨어요), not bare 못마땅하다. English-speaker pitfall: saying '엄마가 못마땅해요' to mean 'Mom is displeased' — that wrongly says 'I am displeased with Mom'; switch to 엄마가 못마땅해하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Describing someone else's displeasure with bare 못마땅하다 ('아빠가 못마땅해요') is wrong/ambiguous — Korean feeling-adjectives need -아/어하다 for third person: 아빠가 못마땅해하세요.
Confusing it with 화나다 ('너무 못마땅해서 소리쳤어요' for an outburst) overshoots; 못마땅하다 is quiet disapproval, not active anger. For flaring anger use 화나다.
Using it for disliking food/taste ('이 음식이 못마땅해요') is off; for plain dislike use 별로예요/마음에 안 들어요 — 못마땅하다 leans toward disapproving of conduct, choices, or attitudes.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; the ㅎ of the ㄶ batchim is silent, so it's pronounced [언짜나요]

usagePhrases.en: to be in a sour mood
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; 기분이 is the usual subject
attributive form (ㄶ stem + 은 → 언짢은); 기색 = a visible sign of a feeling
adverb form, e.g. 언짢게 듣다 to take something the wrong way

examples.en: That remark put me in a bit of a sour mood.
examples.note: simple past; reacting to something mildly offensive

examples.ko: 혹시 제 말 때문에 기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송해요.
examples.romanization: hoksi je mal ttaemune gibun eonjjaneusyeotdamyeon joesonghaeyo.
examples.en: If what I said happened to put you in a bad mood, I'm sorry.
examples.note: the very common polite apology frame 기분 언짢으셨다면

examples.ko: 사장님이 아침부터 무슨 일이 있으셨는지 종일 언짢은 기색이라 다들 눈치만 봤어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi achimbuteo museun iri isseusyeonneunji jongil eonjjaneun gisaegira dadeul nunchiman bwasseoyo.
examples.en: The boss had a displeased air all day as if something had happened in the morning, so everyone just read the room.
examples.note: real-situation; 언짢은 기색 + 눈치 보다 paints reading a superior's sour mood

entries.nuance: 언짢다 describes being in a displeased, slightly offended, sour mood — how you feel when something rubs you the wrong way but you're not full-blown angry. Contrast it with two neighbors: 못마땅하다 points outward at a specific thing you disapprove of (a choice, conduct), while 언짢다 points inward at your own soured emotional state/mood; and 화나다 is hot, flaring anger, whereas 언짢다 is a cooler, lower-grade displeasure. It appears constantly in courteous apologies — '기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송합니다' is a fixed politeness formula. Watch the pronunciation: the ㄶ batchim keeps its spelling but the ㅎ is not separately pronounced, so 언짢아요 sounds like [언짜나요] and 언짢다 like [언짠타]. English-speaker pitfall: respelling it phonetically as 언잖다 or 언짠다 because the ㅎ is inaudible — the correct spelling is always 언짢다 with ㄶ.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 언잖다 or 언짠다 is wrong — the standard spelling is 언짢다 with the ㄶ batchim, even though the ㅎ is not clearly heard.
Using it for real anger ('너무 언짢아서 소리쳤어요' for shouting) overshoots; 언짢다 is a soured mood or mild offense — for strong anger use 화나다.
Pointing it outward at a thing like 못마땅하다 ('그 결정이 언짢아요') is awkward; 언짢다 describes your mood (기분이 언짢다), while disapproval of the decision itself is 그 결정이 못마땅해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 흐뭇하다 means "warmly pleased; contented (often watching others)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 흐뭇하다 (heumutada) means "warmly pleased; contented (often watching others)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 흐뭇해요 ("I feel warmly pleased"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 흐뭇하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a gentle, satisfied warmth
attributive form (하다→한); very common with 미소/표정
set phrase; the prototypical action that goes with this feeling
adverb form modifying verbs like 보다, 웃다

examples.en: Hearing that news, I feel warm and pleased.
examples.note: simple form; quiet pleasure at a good outcome

examples.en: Watching the kids play, I feel so warm inside.
examples.note: the classic context: contentment watching others do well

examples.ko: 손주가 의젓하게 인사하는 모습을 할머니가 흐뭇한 미소로 바라보셨어요.
examples.romanization: sonjuga uijeotage insahaneun moseubeul halmeoniga heumutan misoro barabosyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandmother watched with a contented smile as her grandchild greeted everyone so maturely.
examples.note: real-situation; 흐뭇한 미소 + 바라보다, the signature 'wear it on your face' pairing

entries.nuance: 흐뭇하다 is a warm, gentle contentment — the soft, slightly proud satisfaction of seeing something turn out well, especially OTHERS doing well (kids at play, a junior succeeding, a grandchild behaving). Contrast it with 뿌듯하다 and 자랑스럽다, the words learners blur it with: 뿌듯하다 is the chest-filling pride you feel about your OWN achievement or close stake (시험에 붙어서 뿌듯해요), and 자랑스럽다 is 'proud (of)' often said outward; but 흐뭇하다 is the mellow, observing warmth of an onlooker pleased by a heartwarming scene, calmer and more tender than excited pride. Because it is often worn on the face, it pairs idiomatically with 미소, 표정, and 바라보다. As a 하다-adjective: 흐뭇해요 / 흐뭇했어요 / 흐뭇해서; for a third person's contentment use 흐뭇해하다 (부모님이 흐뭇해하셨어요). English-speaker pitfall: reaching for it about your own big win — '시험 붙어서 흐뭇해요' sounds detached; for personal achievement say 뿌듯하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for your own exciting achievement ('우승해서 흐뭇해요') is off — that calls for 뿌듯하다/기쁘다; 흐뭇하다 is calm, warm satisfaction usually directed at others or a pleasing outcome you witness.
Describing a third person's contentment with bare 흐뭇하다 ('할아버지가 흐뭇해요') is wrong; use 흐뭇해하다: 할아버지가 흐뭇해하셨어요.
Treating it as strong/excited happiness misreads the register; 흐뭇하다 is mellow and tender, so don't swap it for 신나다/너무 행복하다 when describing a thrill.

entries.english: deeply moved; choked up with emotion
entries.shortExplanation: 뭉클하다 means "deeply moved; choked up with emotion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "deeply moved; choked up with emotion" is 뭉클하다 (mungkeulhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 뭉클해요 ("I'm moved / it's touching"). set phrase; the most common frame, 가슴이 as subject

usagePhrases.en: to get choked up (the nose tingles)
usagePhrases.note: vivid set phrase for that nearly-tearing-up moment
adverb form, e.g. 뭉클하게 다가오다 to hit one emotionally

examples.en: That scene was moving.
examples.note: simple past; the basic 'it touched me' use

examples.en: Reading my parents' letter, I got all choked up.
examples.note: the prototypical heartfelt context; 가슴이 뭉클하다

examples.ko: 참전 용사들이 서로 끌어안는 장면에서 나도 모르게 코끝이 뭉클해지더라고요.
examples.romanization: chamjeon yongsadeuri seoro kkeureoanneun jangmyeoneseo nado moreuge kokkeuchi mungkeulhaejideoragoyo.
examples.en: At the scene where the war veterans embraced, my nose tingled with tears before I knew it.
examples.note: real-situation; 코끝이 뭉클해지다 + 나도 모르게 'without realizing' captures the involuntary surge

entries.nuance: 뭉클하다 is the sudden lump-in-the-throat, heart-swelling rush of being deeply moved — a heartfelt letter, a reunion, a touching scene. The word is mimetic: 뭉클 evokes a soft mass welling up and pressing, so it captures the PHYSICAL sensation of emotion rising. Contrast it with 감동하다 (a verb, 'to be touched/impressed'): 감동하다 is the broader, more general statement that you were moved or impressed (even intellectually), whereas 뭉클하다 zeroes in on the warm, almost-teary bodily welling-up in a single instant — you can be 감동했어요 by an admirable feat without being 뭉클; 뭉클 needs the throat-tightening tenderness. It pairs idiomatically with 가슴이 and the very evocative 코끝이. As a 하다-adjective: 뭉클해요 / 뭉클했어요 / 뭉클해서. English-speaker pitfall: using it for cool intellectual admiration ('그 논문이 뭉클해요') is wrong — that is 인상적이다/감동적이다; 뭉클하다 is the momentary emotional, near-teary reaction, not 'impressive'.

Using it for intellectual admiration ('발표가 뭉클했어요' meaning 'impressive') is wrong — 뭉클하다 is the emotional, almost-teary welling-up; for 'impressive' use 인상적이다/감동적이다.
Treating it as a lasting state ('요즘 계속 뭉클해요') is off; it names a momentary surge in a touching instant that then passes, so it fits a specific moment, not an ongoing mood.

examples.en: Getting praised makes me feel a bit sheepish.
examples.note: simple form; the classic trigger — praise you don't know how to take

examples.en: I had nothing to say, so I just laughed sheepishly.
examples.note: the awkward-laugh reflex; 멋쩍게 웃다 is the go-to collocation

examples.ko: 사람들 앞에서 발표하다 이름을 까먹어서 머리만 긁으며 멋쩍게 서 있었어요.
examples.romanization: saramdeul apeseo balpyohada ireumeul kkameogeoseo meoriman geulgeumyeo meotjjeokge seo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: I forgot the name mid-presentation in front of everyone and just stood there sheepishly scratching my head.
examples.note: real-situation; mild public embarrassment plus the head-scratch gesture, not deep shame

entries.nuance: 멋쩍다 is that mild, sheepish self-consciousness — being complimented, caught in a small slip, or left with nothing to say, so you give an awkward little laugh. Contrast it with 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: 부끄럽다 covers shyness or genuine shame, and 창피하다 is stronger 'embarrassing/mortifying' (a real loss of face), whereas 멋쩍다 is the lightest of the three — a momentary, almost endearing social awkwardness with no real shame, the feeling behind a bashful grin. Note it is NOT a 하다-adjective: the stem is 멋쩍- (멋쩍어요, 멋쩍었어요, 멋쩍어서, 멋쩍은), and the ㄱ batchim takes 어 not 해. It collocates above all with 웃음 and 웃다 (멋쩍은 웃음, 멋쩍게 웃다). English-speaker pitfall: confusing it with 서먹하다 — 멋쩍다 is your OWN in-the-moment sheepishness, while 서먹하다 is the distance BETWEEN two people, so they are not swappable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 멋적다 is wrong — the standard spelling is 멋쩍다 with ㅉ.
Conjugating it as a 하다-word ('멋쩍해요') is wrong; it is not 하다-based, so the correct forms are 멋쩍어요, 멋쩍었어요, 멋쩍어서.
Swapping it with 서먹하다 ('칭찬받아서 서먹했어요') is wrong; 멋쩍다 is your own sheepishness in the moment, whereas 서먹하다 is the distance between two people.

structuredNuance.t: 멋쩍다 is that mild, sheepish self-consciousness — being complimented, caught in a small slip, or left with nothing to say, so you give an awkward little laugh. It is the lightest of its family — a momentary, almost endearing social awkwardness with no real shame, the feeling behind a bashful grin. It collocates above all with 웃음 and 웃다 (멋쩍은 웃음, 멋쩍게 웃다).

entries.shortExplanation: 안방 means "master bedroom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 안방 (anbang) means "master bedroom". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 안방 ("the master bedroom"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 안방 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 안 (inner) + 방 (room, 房); the biggest/main bedroom, traditionally the household head's room
차지하다 = to take/occupy; the natural verb when someone grabs the best room
an attached bathroom is a big selling point, so this phrase shows up in listings
the standard pair Koreans use to divide bedrooms among family or roommates

examples.en: This is the master bedroom.
examples.note: Pointing it out on a flat tour; 여기가 X-이에요 is the bare 'this is X' frame

examples.ko: 저는 안방 쓰고, 동생은 작은방 써요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun anbang sseugo, dongsaengeun jageunbang sseoyo.
examples.en: I use the master bedroom and my younger sibling uses the small room.
examples.note: 쓰다 ('use') is the everyday verb for occupying a room, not 살다

examples.ko: 집 보러 갔는데 안방이 생각보다 넓더라고요.
examples.romanization: jip boreo ganneunde anbangi saenggakboda neolbdeoragoyo.
examples.en: I went to see the place and the master bedroom was bigger than I'd expected.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports something you personally noticed on the spot, perfect for a viewing

entries.nuance: 안방 is literally 안 ('inner') + 방 ('room', from the hanja 房), so it points not to size first but to the 'innermost, main' bedroom — culturally the room of the household head, historically where the senior couple slept. The near-synonym trap is 큰방: 큰방 just means 'the big room' by floor area, while 안방 carries the 'master / main' status even in a flat where it isn't literally the largest. Don't confuse it with 거실 (the shared living room) — 안방 is private sleeping space. English speakers often over-extend it and call every bedroom 안방; only the one main room is 안방, the rest are 작은방 or plain 방. It pairs naturally with 안방 화장실 (en-suite) and the contrast set 안방 vs 작은방 when splitting rooms.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling any bedroom 안방. WHY: 안방 specifically means the one main/master room; the others are 작은방 or 방. FIX: reserve 안방 for the principal bedroom only.
Confusing 안방 with 거실 (living room). WHY: they look similar to a beginner but 안방 is a private bedroom while 거실 is the shared lounge. FIX: use 거실 for the open family area, 안방 for the couple's room.
Saying 큰방 when you mean the 'master' room. WHY: 큰방 only describes size, not status. FIX: use 안방 when you mean the main bedroom regardless of which is physically biggest.

structuredNuance.t: 안 ('inner') + 방 ('room') points not to size first but to the 'innermost, main' bedroom — culturally the room of the household head, historically where the senior couple slept. It is private sleeping space, and pairs naturally with 안방 화장실 (en-suite) and the contrast set 안방 vs 작은방 when splitting rooms.

entries.shortExplanation: 다용도실 means "utility room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "utility room" is 다용도실 (dayongdosil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 다용도실 ("utility room"). Watch the particle attached to 다용도실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 다용도 多用途 ('many-use', i.e. multi-purpose) + 실 室 ('room'); the back room off the kitchen

usagePhrases.en: to keep (it) in the utility room
usagePhrases.note: 두다 = to keep/store; what you do with the washer, kimchi fridge, bulky stuff

usagePhrases.en: to have a separate utility room
usagePhrases.note: 따로 있다 = to exist separately; a common plus point in a listing
정리 整理 = sorting out; it clutters fast, so this is a recurring chore

examples.en: The washing machine is in the utility room.
examples.note: Basic location sentence; 에 marks where a thing sits

examples.en: We keep the kimchi fridge in the utility room.
examples.note: 두다 ('keep/store') is the habitual-storage verb, more natural here than 있다

examples.ko: 이 집은 다용도실이 따로 있어서 마음에 들어요.
examples.romanization: i jibeun dayongdosiri ttaro isseoseo maeume deureoyo.
examples.en: I like this place because it has a separate utility room.
examples.note: 다용도실이 따로 있다 is the set phrase house-hunters use as a selling point

entries.nuance: 다용도실 is a Sino-Korean compound: 다용도 多用途 literally 'many + use + purpose' = multi-purpose, plus 실 室 'room'. It's the small enclosed back space off the kitchen (often behind the 베란다) where the washing machine, 김치냉장고, cleaning supplies and recycling live — a near-universal feature of Korean apartments. The synonym to keep apart is 창고 倉庫 ('storehouse'): a 창고 is dead storage, while a 다용도실 is an active work-and-store space you use daily. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't assume laundry happens in the bathroom as in many Western homes — in Korea the washer lives in the 다용도실 (or 베란다); second, don't translate it as 'laundry room', because it does far more than laundry. It collocates with 세탁기, 김치냉장고, and 따로 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming laundry is done in the bathroom. WHY: Korean homes put the washer in the 다용도실 or 베란다, not the bathroom. FIX: locate the 세탁기 in the 다용도실.
Calling it 창고 (storehouse). WHY: 창고 is passive dead storage; 다용도실 is an active, in-home utility space. FIX: use 다용도실 for the working back room, 창고 for a true storeroom.
Rendering it 'laundry room'. WHY: it handles storage, the kimchi fridge and recycling too, not just laundry. FIX: say 'utility room' and let 세탁실 be the narrow 'laundry-only' term.

structuredNuance.t: The small enclosed back space off the kitchen (often behind the 베란다) where the washing machine, 김치냉장고, cleaning supplies and recycling live — a near-universal feature of Korean apartments. It collocates with 세탁기, 김치냉장고, and 따로 있다.

entries.shortExplanation: 신발장 means "shoe cabinet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 신발장 (sinbaljang) = "shoe cabinet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 신발장 ("shoe cabinet") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 신발장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 신발 (shoes) + 장 (cabinet, 欌); the built-in cabinet at the 현관 where shoes are stored

usagePhrases.en: to put into the shoe cabinet
usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = to put inside; the action right after you take your shoes off
꽉 차다 = packed full; a constant complaint for shoe lovers

usagePhrases.en: on top of the shoe cabinet
usagePhrases.note: the flat top is a handy drop spot for keys, masks and deliveries

examples.en: Please put your shoes in the shoe cabinet.
examples.note: Polite request to a guest; 넣다 + 에 = 'put into' a place

examples.ko: 신발장이 꽉 차서 새 운동화 둘 데가 없어요.
examples.romanization: sinbaljangi kkwak chaseo sae undonghwa dul dega eopseoyo.
examples.en: The shoe cabinet is full, so there's nowhere to put my new sneakers.
examples.note: 둘 데가 없다 ('no place to keep it') is a very natural everyday grumble

examples.ko: 택배는 신발장 위에 올려 두시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: taekbaeneun sinbaljang wie ollyeo dusimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can just leave the parcel on top of the shoe cabinet.
examples.note: 위에 올려 두다 = 'set on top and leave'; a typical instruction to a courier

entries.nuance: 신발장 is 신발 ('shoes') + 장 (the native-reading of the hanja 欌, 'cabinet/wardrobe') — the same 장 you see in 옷장, 책장, 거실장, so once you learn it you can decode a whole family of furniture words. It sits at the 현관 (entryway) and is bound up with the absolute Korean rule that shoes come off the instant you step inside and go straight in. The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 신발 박스 / 신발 상자, but a 박스/상자 is a cardboard box you'd carry a single pair in — the built-in furniture piece is always 신발장. A second trap is thinking the shoe-removal is optional; saying 신발장에 넣어 주세요 to a guest is itself a polite way of signalling 'shoes off, please'. It collocates with 넣다, 꽉 차다, and 위에 올려 두다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it 신발 박스 or 신발 상자. WHY: 박스/상자 is a cardboard box, not the entryway furniture. FIX: use 신발장 for the built-in cabinet.
Walking in without using it. WHY: the cultural norm is shoes off and into the 신발장 at the door. FIX: take shoes off at the 현관 and place them in the 신발장.
Mixing up the 장 ('cabinet') in 신발장 with 장 ('market', 場/장). WHY: same syllable, different word. FIX: read the 장 in furniture words as 'cabinet' (欌), as in 옷장 and 책장.

structuredNuance.t: 신발 ('shoes') + 장 ('cabinet/wardrobe') — the built-in cabinet that sits at the 현관 (entryway), bound up with the absolute Korean rule that shoes come off the instant you step inside and go straight in. It collocates with 넣다, 꽉 차다, and 위에 올려 두다.
장 is the native-reading of the hanja 欌 ('cabinet/wardrobe') — the same 장 you see in 옷장, 책장, 거실장, so once you learn it you can decode a whole family of furniture words.

entries.shortExplanation: 선반 means "shelf" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 선반 (seonban) means "shelf". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 선반 ("shelf"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 선반 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a single flat board fixed to a wall or inside a cabinet to set things on

usagePhrases.en: to set up on a shelf
usagePhrases.note: 올려 두다 = to place up and leave; the typical 'put it on the shelf' action
달다 = to mount/install; what you do with a drill, bracket, or adhesive
벽 (wall, 壁) + 선반; the wall-mounted type prized in tiny flats to save floor space

examples.en: Just set the books on the shelf.
examples.note: 올려 두다 = 'place on top and leave it'; the default verb for putting things on a shelf

examples.ko: 화장실에 선반 하나 달았더니 훨씬 깔끔해졌어요.
examples.romanization: hwajangsire seonban hana daratdeoni hwolssin kkalkkeumhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After I put up one shelf in the bathroom, it got much tidier.
examples.note: -았더니 reports the result you observed after doing something — common for a small home upgrade

examples.ko: 선반이 높아서 발판 없이는 손이 안 닿아요.
examples.romanization: seonbani nopaseo balpan eopsineun soni an daayo.
examples.en: The shelf is so high I can't reach it without a step stool.
examples.note: 손이 안 닿다 ('the hand doesn't reach') is the set everyday phrase for 'can't reach'

entries.nuance: 선반 is one single flat shelf board — a ledge — not a whole storage unit. The synonym contrast learners most need: 선반 is one board, whereas 책장 is a standing bookcase (a piece of furniture with many shelves), and 선반 is also not a 서랍 (a pull-out drawer): a 선반 is open and you set things on top, a 서랍 slides out and you put things inside. Note the verb pairing — you 달다 ('mount/install') a 선반 onto a wall, not 만들다, and you 올려 두다 things onto it. In cramped officetels and 원룸, wall-mounted 선반 are a go-to space saver sold cheaply at 다이소 and IKEA, used for kitchen, bathroom and entryway storage alike. The English-speaker pitfall is using 선반 for a full 'bookshelf' unit — in English 'shelf' and 'bookshelf' blur, but in Korean the unit is 책장 and only the board is 선반.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 선반 for a full bookcase. WHY: 선반 is a single board; a standing multi-shelf unit is 책장. FIX: say 책장 for the furniture, 선반 for one ledge.
Confusing 선반 (shelf) with 서랍 (drawer). WHY: a 선반 is open and you put things on it; a 서랍 slides out and you put things in it. FIX: 선반 = open ledge, 서랍 = pull-out drawer.
Saying 선반을 만들다 for installing one. WHY: the natural verb for mounting a shelf is 달다. FIX: use 선반을 달다 ('put up / install a shelf').

structuredNuance.t: One single flat shelf board — a ledge — not a whole storage unit. Note the verb pairing — you 달다 ('mount/install') a 선반 onto a wall, not 만들다, and you 올려 두다 things onto it. In cramped officetels and 원룸, wall-mounted 선반 are a go-to space saver sold cheaply at 다이소 and IKEA, used for kitchen, bathroom and entryway storage alike.

entries.shortExplanation: 거실장 means "TV stand / living-room cabinet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "TV stand / living-room cabinet" is 거실장 (geosiljang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 거실장 ("living-room cabinet (TV stand)"). Watch the particle attached to 거실장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 거실 居室 (living room) + 장 欌 (cabinet); the long low unit the TV sits on

usagePhrases.en: to set on top of the TV stand
usagePhrases.note: 올려놓다 = to place on top; where the TV and remote usually go
장만하다 = to acquire (a sizeable purchase); natural for buying furniture
거실장 typically has drawers for remotes, cables, and odds and ends

examples.en: The TV is on top of the living-room cabinet.
examples.note: Basic location sentence; 티비 is the casual everyday word for TV

examples.en: When I moved, I got myself a TV stand.
examples.note: 장만하다 carries a 'finally acquired something substantial' feel that 사다 lacks

examples.ko: 리모컨은 거실장 서랍 안에 있을 거예요.
examples.romanization: rimokeoneun geosiljang seorap ane isseul geoyeyo.
examples.en: The remote's probably in the drawer of the TV stand.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 makes it a guess; 서랍 안에 = 'inside the drawer'

entries.nuance: 거실장 is 거실 (living room, Sino-Korean 居室 'dwelling-room') + 장 (cabinet, 欌) — the low, wide cabinet that anchors a Korean living room, with the TV on top and remotes, cables and clutter hidden in its drawers and doors. The key contrast for learners is 거실장 vs 거실: 거실장 is the furniture, 거실 is the room itself — same first two syllables, different things. The English-speaker pitfall is inventing 티비 책상 or 티비 테이블 by direct translation of 'TV table' — those aren't the standard term; native speakers say 거실장 (and informally 티비 다이, from Japanese-via-loan 'dai'). It's one of the first large pieces people buy or inherit when furnishing a home, so it surfaces constantly in moving and shopping talk, where it pairs with 장만하다 ('acquire') and 위에 올려놓다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it 티비 책상 or 티비 테이블. WHY: those are literal calques, not the real term. FIX: say 거실장 (or informally 티비 다이).
Confusing 거실장 with 거실. WHY: 거실장 is the cabinet, 거실 is the living room. FIX: add 장 only when you mean the furniture piece.
Using 사다 where 장만하다 fits better. WHY: for a notable furniture purchase, 장만하다 sounds more natural and warmer. FIX: 거실장을 장만했어요 for 'I got myself a TV stand'.

entries.shortExplanation: 화장대 means "vanity / dressing table" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 화장대 (hwajangdae) = "vanity / dressing table". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 화장대 ("vanity / dressing table") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 화장대, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 화장 化粧 (makeup) + 대 臺 (stand/table); the mirrored table for getting ready
앞에 앉다 = sit in front of; where you do makeup or skincare
거울 (mirror) is the defining feature that makes a table a 화장대
정리 整理 = sorting out; cosmetics pile up, so this is a regular chore

examples.en: The vanity mirror is really big.
examples.note: Simple description; 거울 is the part that defines the piece

examples.en: I have so much makeup that my vanity is always messy.
examples.note: 지저분하다 = cluttered/messy; the natural adjective for a crowded surface

examples.ko: 원룸이라 화장대 놓을 자리가 없어서 그냥 거울만 붙였어요.
examples.romanization: wollumira hwajangdae noeul jariga eopseoseo geunyang geoulman butyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Since it's a one-room, there's no space for a vanity, so I just stuck a mirror up.
examples.note: 놓을 자리가 없다 ('no place to set it') captures small-apartment reality

entries.nuance: 화장대 breaks down as 화장 化粧 ('makeup', literally 'transform-adorn') + 대 臺 ('stand/platform'), so it is the dedicated mirrored table where you do makeup and skincare. The dangerous near-twin is 화장실: both start with 화장 化粧, but 화장대 is the dressing table while 화장실 化粧室 is the bathroom/toilet — confusing them in front of a host is a real and embarrassing mix-up. Also keep it apart from 책상 (a work desk): a makeup table specifically is a 화장대, and the 거울 is what distinguishes the two. In small Korean flats it's a coveted but space-hungry item, so many renters skip it for a wall mirror — hence 화장대 놓을 자리가 없다 is a stock phrase. The word signals 'getting-ready space' generally and isn't gendered: men use 화장대 for grooming setups too. It collocates with 거울, 정리, and 앞에 앉다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 화장대 (vanity) with 화장실 (bathroom). WHY: they share 화장 化粧 but mean a dressing table vs a toilet. FIX: 대 臺 = table → 화장대; 실 室 = room → 화장실.
Calling it 책상 (desk). WHY: a 책상 is for studying/working; the mirrored makeup table is a 화장대. FIX: use 화장대 when there's a mirror for getting ready.
Assuming it's women-only. WHY: 화장대 just means a grooming table, used by anyone. FIX: it's fine to say a man has a 화장대.

entries.shortExplanation: 옷걸이 means "clothes hanger / coat rack" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 옷걸이 (otgeori) means "clothes hanger / coat rack". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 옷걸이 ("hanger / coat rack"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 옷걸이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 옷 (clothes) + 걸이 (a thing to hang on, from 걸다); both the small hanger and a standing rack
걸다 = to hang; the core verb built right into the word 옷걸이
a useful request at a store, hotel, or to a roommate
스탠드 (stand) + 옷걸이; the freestanding pole type common in 원룸

examples.en: Hang your coat on the hanger.
examples.note: 거세요 is the polite form of 걸다 ('hang'); 에 marks where you hang it

examples.en: I don't have enough hangers, so clothes keep piling up.
examples.note: 모자라다 = to fall short / be insufficient; an everyday frustration

examples.ko: 원룸엔 붙박이장이 없어서 스탠드 옷걸이 하나 샀어요.
examples.romanization: wollumen butbagijangi eopseoseo seutaendeu otgeori hana sasseoyo.
examples.en: My one-room has no built-in closet, so I bought a standing coat rack.
examples.note: ties to 붙박이장; the classic renter workaround when there's no closet

entries.nuance: 옷걸이 is a transparent native compound: 옷 ('clothes') + 걸이, a noun made from the verb 걸다 ('to hang') plus the thing-noun suffix -이 — so it literally means 'the clothes-hanging thing'. That single word covers both the individual coat hanger and a standing or wall-mounted coat rack; context tells you which (스탠드 옷걸이 forces the 'rack' reading). The synonym to separate it from is 옷장: 옷걸이 is the open hanging tool/rack, while 옷장 is the closed cabinet/wardrobe you shut the doors on. The English-speaker pitfall is treating the act and the object as the same — 옷 걸기 (or 옷을 거는 것) is the act of hanging clothes, but the object is 옷걸이; don't say 옷 걸기 when you want the hanger. Because compact rentals often lack a proper 옷장 or 붙박이장, a 스탠드 옷걸이 is the default. It's an everyday word at home, in shops, and in hotels, pairing with 걸다, 모자라다, and 하나 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 옷걸이 (hanger) with 옷장 (wardrobe). WHY: 옷걸이 is the open hanging tool/rack; 옷장 is the closed cabinet. FIX: 걸이 = hanging thing → 옷걸이; 장 = cabinet → 옷장.
Saying 옷 걸기 for the object. WHY: 걸기 names the action of hanging, not the thing. FIX: the noun is 옷걸이.

Reaching for 행거 only. WHY: 행거 ('hanger', a loanword) usually means the big rolling clothes rack, while the plain hanger and pole rack are 옷걸이 / 스탠드 옷걸이. FIX: default to 옷걸이 unless you specifically mean the large rolling rail.

entries.shortExplanation: 붙박이장 means "built-in closet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "built-in closet" is 붙박이장 (butbagijang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 붙박이장 ("built-in closet"). Watch the particle attached to 붙박이장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 붙박이 (a fixed/built-in thing, from 붙박다) + 장 欌 (cabinet); a wardrobe fixed into the wall
a major plus when renting; it removes the need to buy an 옷장

usagePhrases.en: to put into the built-in closet
usagePhrases.note: where you stash seasonal clothes, bedding, and suitcases
옵션 (option) = a built-in feature agents list as a selling point

examples.en: This place has a built-in closet.
examples.note: A plain 'it has X' selling point; 있다 = to exist/have

examples.ko: 붙박이장이 커서 이불이랑 캐리어까지 다 들어가요.
examples.romanization: butbagijangi keoseo iburirang kaerieokkaji da deureogayo.
examples.en: The built-in closet is big, so even the bedding and the suitcase fit inside.
examples.note: ties to 이불; -까지 ('even') stresses how much it holds

examples.ko: 전에 살던 집은 붙박이장이 없어서 너무 불편했어요.
examples.romanization: jeone saldeon jibeun butbagijangi eopseoseo neomu bulpyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: My previous place had no built-in closet, so it was really inconvenient.
examples.note: 전에 살던 집 = 'the place I used to live'; the natural way to compare past housing

entries.nuance: 붙박이장 is 붙박이 + 장 (cabinet, 欌). 붙박이 comes from the verb 붙박다 ('to fix firmly in place'), so the word literally means a 'fixed-in-place cabinet' — a wall-mounted, immovable wardrobe that comes with the apartment. That immovability is the whole point and the key contrast with 옷장: an 옷장 is a free-standing wardrobe you buy and can move out with you, whereas a 붙박이장 is structurally attached and stays. For renters it's hugely practical because it removes the cost and hassle of buying and hauling an 옷장. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 붙박이장 as movable furniture — by definition it isn't; if you can carry it out, it's an 옷장, not a 붙박이장. The other trap is spelling: keep the ㅌ and the double structure — it's 붙박이장, not 붓박이장 or 붙바기장. Real-estate listings flag it as a prized 옵션, so you'll hear it constantly while flat-hunting, alongside 있다 and -까지 다 들어가다.

Treating 붙박이장 as movable furniture. WHY: it's fixed to the wall and stays with the unit. FIX: a free-standing one you can move is an 옷장, not a 붙박이장.
Misspelling it 붓박이장 or 붙바기장. WHY: it derives from 붙박다, keeping the ㅌ patchim. FIX: the correct spelling is 붙박이장.
Confusing 붙박이장 with 신발장. WHY: both end in 장 but one holds clothes (in the room) and one holds shoes (at the 현관). FIX: 옷 → 붙박이장/옷장; 신발 → 신발장.

entries.shortExplanation: 베개 means "pillow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 베개 (begae) = "pillow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 베개 ("pillow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 베개, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the head pillow you sleep on; correctly spelled 베개, not 배개

usagePhrases.en: to rest your head on a pillow
usagePhrases.note: 베다 is the dedicated verb; 베개 literally is 'the thing you 베다 on'
커버 (cover); the washable cloth case you launder regularly
height and firmness are what people care about most

examples.en: The pillow is too high.
examples.note: Simple 'too X' description; 높다 ('high') is the usual pillow gripe

examples.ko: 새 베개로 바꿨더니 잠이 훨씬 잘 와요.
examples.romanization: sae begaero bakkwotdeoni jami hwolssin jal wayo.
examples.en: After I switched to a new pillow, I sleep much better.
examples.note: 잠이 잘 오다 ('sleep comes well') is the idiomatic way to say you fall asleep easily

examples.ko: 베개 커버는 일주일에 한 번씩 빨아요.
examples.romanization: begae keobeoneun iljuire han beonssik pparayo.
examples.en: I wash the pillowcase once a week.
examples.note: 일주일에 한 번씩 = 'once per week each'; 에 marks the time unit for frequency

entries.nuance: 베개 is specifically the pillow you sleep on, and it comes paired with its own unique verb 베다 ('to lay your head on something') — 베개 is essentially 'the thing you 베다 on', so 베개를 베다 ('to pillow your head') is the set collocation, not 베개를 쓰다. Koreans care a lot about a pillow's 높이 (height) and firmness, which spawns follow-up words like 목베개 ('neck pillow') and 메모리폼 ('memory foam'). The biggest English-speaker pitfall is spelling: it is 베개 (tied to the verb 베다), not the very commonly mis-typed 배개 — the ㅔ/ㅐ contrast is easy to get wrong by ear. The second pitfall is meaning: 베개 is only the sleeping pillow; a decorative throw pillow on a sofa is a 쿠션, and a sit-on floor cushion is a 방석. It collocates with 베다, 커버, and 높다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 배개. WHY: it derives from the verb 베다, so the vowel is ㅔ. FIX: the correct form is 베개.
Using 베개 for a sofa throw pillow. WHY: 베개 is for sleeping; a decorative cushion is a 쿠션. FIX: say 쿠션 for couch throw pillows.
Saying 베개를 쓰다 ('use a pillow'). WHY: the idiomatic verb is the special 베다. FIX: use 베개를 베다 for resting your head on it.

entries.shortExplanation: 이불 means "blanket / duvet (bedding)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이불 (ibul) means "blanket / duvet (bedding)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이불 ("blanket / duvet"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이불 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the main bed covering you sleep under; covers comforters and floor-bedding alike

usagePhrases.en: to pull the blanket over yourself
usagePhrases.note: 덮다 = to cover; the verb that pairs with 이불 when you go to sleep
개다 = to fold; a morning habit, especially with floor bedding
bulky wash you often take to a coin laundromat (빨래방)

examples.en: Cover yourself with the blanket and sleep.
examples.note: Casual 반말 command to family/a friend; 덮다 is the verb for pulling covers over you

examples.ko: 겨울 이불은 너무 두꺼워서 세탁기에 안 들어가요.
examples.romanization: gyeoul ibureun neomu dukkeowoseo setakgie an deureogayo.
examples.en: The winter duvet is so thick it won't fit in the washing machine.
examples.note: links to 다용도실/세탁기; 안 들어가다 = 'doesn't go in / won't fit'

examples.en: Every weekend I wash the bedding and dry it in the sun.
examples.note: 햇볕에 말리다 = 'sun-dry'; a common habit out on the 베란다

entries.nuance: 이불 is the all-purpose native word for the blanket / duvet / comforter you sleep under — crucially, it works whether you sleep on a bed or lay bedding directly on the heated floor (the whole floor-bedding set is 이부자리). Its dedicated verb is 덮다 ('to cover'): you 이불을 덮다 to go to sleep and 이불을 개다 ('fold') in the morning. The synonym to separate it from is 담요: a 담요 is a small lap/throw blanket (the thing you drape over your knees), while the main bed covering is 이불 — don't use 담요 for the whole duvet. Also keep 이불 (the covering) apart from 베개 (pillow) and 침대 (bed); 이불 is only what you pull over yourself. The word is bound to seasonal swaps (여름 이불 vs 겨울 이불) and to the chore of washing bulky bedding, which often means a trip to a 빨래방; a thin summer one is a 홑이불. It collocates with 덮다, 개다, and 빨래.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 담요 for the whole duvet. WHY: 담요 is a small lap/throw blanket; the main bed covering is 이불. FIX: say 이불 for the duvet/comforter, 담요 for a small throw.
Confusing 이불 with 베개 (pillow) or 침대 (bed). WHY: 이불 is only the covering you sleep under. FIX: 이불 = blanket, 베개 = pillow, 침대 = bed.
Saying 이불을 쓰다 for going to sleep under it. WHY: the natural verb is 덮다 ('cover'). FIX: use 이불을 덮다.

entries.shortExplanation: 방석 means "floor cushion / seat cushion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "floor cushion / seat cushion" is 방석 (bangseok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 방석 ("floor/seat cushion"). Watch the particle attached to 방석 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 방석 方席 (square + seat/mat); the flat cushion you sit on, on the floor or a hard chair
깔다 = to spread/lay down; what you do before sitting on the floor
앉다 = to sit; the natural pair verb for 방석
모자라다 = to run short; a realistic worry when guests come over

examples.en: Please sit on the cushion.
examples.note: Polite seating offer; 에 앉다 = 'sit on/at' a spot

examples.en: The chair was hard, so I put a cushion on it.
examples.note: 딱딱하다 = hard; 깔다 ('lay down') also covers padding a hard chair

examples.ko: 손님 오면 방석이 모자랄 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: sonnim omyeon bangseogi mojaral geot gatayo.
examples.en: When guests come, I think we'll be short on cushions.
examples.note: 모자라다 = to run short; -ㄹ 것 같다 softens it to a prediction

entries.nuance: 방석 is Sino-Korean 方席 — 方 ('square') + 席 ('seat/mat') — literally a 'square sitting mat', the flat sit-on cushion central to Korea's floor-sitting (좌식) culture; you'll see stacks of them at floor-seating restaurants, set out for guests, and laid on hard dining chairs. Its verbs are 깔다 ('lay it out') and 앉다 ('sit on it'). The crucial contrast is with 쿠션 and 베개: a 쿠션 is a soft decorative/back cushion you lean against, a 베개 is the pillow you sleep on, and a 방석 is the firm flat one you sit on — three different cushions, three different words. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: don't lump them all under 'cushion', and don't be misled by the spelling into linking 방석 to 방 ('room', 房) — the 방 here is 方 ('square'), unrelated to rooms. Pulling out a 방석 for a visitor is a small but genuine act of hospitality. It collocates with 깔다, 앉다, and 모자라다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Lumping 방석 in with 쿠션 or 베개. WHY: 방석 = sit-on floor cushion, 쿠션 = soft back/throw cushion, 베개 = sleeping pillow. FIX: pick by function — sitting → 방석.
Linking 방석 to 방 ('room'). WHY: the 방 in 방석 is 方 ('square'), not 房 ('room'). FIX: read 방석 as 'square seat-mat', a seating item.
Saying 방석을 놓다 only. WHY: the idiomatic verb for setting one out to sit on is 깔다 ('spread/lay down'). FIX: use 방석을 깔다.

entries.shortExplanation: 매트리스 means "mattress" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매트리스 (maeteuriseu) = "mattress". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매트리스 ("mattress") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: loanword from English 'mattress'; the padded sleeping surface itself
푹신하다 = soft and cushiony; firmness is the main buying factor
만 (only); renters often skip the frame and buy this alone
옮기다 = to move/shift; it's heavy and awkward, especially on moving day

examples.en: The mattress is soft.
examples.note: Plain description; 푹신하다 is the go-to adjective for a plush mattress

examples.en: The mattress is so firm my back gets sore.
examples.note: 배기다 = (a hard surface) digs into you; the natural complaint about firm bedding

examples.ko: 저는 프레임 없이 매트리스만 바닥에 깔고 자요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun peureim eopsi maeteuriseuman badage kkalgo jayo.
examples.en: I sleep with just a mattress on the floor, no frame.
examples.note: 프레임 없이 = 'without a frame'; a very common budget / one-room setup

entries.nuance: 매트리스 is a straight loanword (외래어) from English 'mattress', and it refers to the padded sleeping pad alone — which is exactly where the synonym contrast bites: 침대 is the whole bed (frame + mattress together), while 매트리스 is only the pad on top. This matters in real life because many Korean renters deliberately buy a 매트리스 by itself and put it straight on the floor or a low platform, skipping a full 침대 frame to save money and space — so 침대 사다 and 매트리스만 사다 describe genuinely different purchases. The everyday talk around it is firmness: 딱딱하다 ('firm/hard') vs 푹신하다 ('plush/soft'), plus the verb 배기다 for when a hard surface digs into your back. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) saying 침대 when you mean only the mattress, and (2) the loanword spelling — it's 매트리스, not 매트레스 or 메트리스. It collocates with 푹신하다, 딱딱하다, and 옮기다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 매트리스 with 침대. WHY: 침대 is the full bed (frame + mattress); 매트리스 is only the pad. FIX: use 매트리스 for just the sleeping pad.
Misspelling it 매트레스 or 메트리스. WHY: the standard 외래어 form follows 'mattress' as 매트리스. FIX: write 매트리스.
Saying 매트리스가 딱딱하다 to mean 'comfortable'. WHY: 딱딱하다 means literally 'hard/firm', often a complaint, not praise. FIX: use 푹신하다 for a pleasantly soft mattress.

entries.shortExplanation: 장염 means "enteritis, stomach flu (gut infection/inflammation)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 장염 (jangyeom) means "enteritis, stomach flu (gut infection/inflammation)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 장염에 걸리다 ("to come down with enteritis / a stomach bug"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 장염 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to come down with enteritis / a stomach bug
usagePhrases.note: 병명에는 '나다'가 아니라 '걸리다'를 쓰는 것이 원칙
병원에서 듣는 정식 진단명, '급성(急性)'은 갑자기 심하게

usagePhrases.en: to have diarrhea because of enteritis
usagePhrases.note: 원인 '때문에' + 증상으로 이어지는 세트 표현

usagePhrases.en: food that's good for an upset stomach
usagePhrases.note: 회복식(죽 등)을 물어볼 때 자주 나옴

examples.en: I've got a stomach bug.
examples.note: 가장 기본형 — 병명+'에 걸리다'를 그대로 익히세요

examples.ko: 어제 회를 먹었는데 장염에 걸렸나 봐요.
examples.romanization: eoje hoereul meogeonneunde jangyeome geollyeonna bwayo.
examples.en: I ate raw fish yesterday and I think I got a stomach bug.
examples.note: '-나 보다'로 스스로 추측 — 내과에서 흔한 설명

examples.en: It was enteritis, so I only ate rice porridge for a few days.
examples.note: 회복 상황 묘사 — '죽만'의 '만'은 '오직 ~만'

entries.nuance: 장염(腸炎)은 글자 그대로 '창자 장(腸) + 염증 염(炎)', 곧 장에 염증이 생겨 복통·구토·설사가 함께 오는 흔한 병으로 영어의 'stomach flu'에 가깝다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃 단어는 '배탈'인데, 배탈은 과식·체함으로 잠깐 배가 불편한 가벼운 상태인 반면 장염은 바이러스·세균 감염으로 며칠씩 가고 발열까지 동반하는 더 무거운 병이다. 병명이므로 영어 'have'를 직역한 '장염이 있다'나 '장염이 나다'가 아니라 '장염에 걸리다'가 표준이고, 악화되면 '장염이 심하다'라고 한다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 지점은 조사로, 'I have enteritis'를 '장염을 가지고 있다'로 옮기면 어색하니 동사 '걸리다'와 조사 '에'를 한 덩어리로 외워 두는 것이 안전하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'장염이 나다 / 장염이 아프다'라고 하는 것 — 병명이라 동사 선택이 틀린 경우다. '장염에 걸리다, 장염이 심하다, 장염 때문에 아프다'로 고쳐야 자연스럽다.
단순 '배탈'과 같다고 보는 것 — 배탈은 잠깐 체한 가벼운 상태, 장염은 감염성 염증이라 구토·발열까지 동반하는 더 심한 병이다. 가벼우면 '배탈 났어요', 심하면 '장염에 걸렸어요'로 구분한다.
'장염을 걸리다'처럼 조사 '을/를'을 쓰는 것 — '걸리다'는 '~에 걸리다'로 장소·대상 조사 '에'를 취한다. '장염에 걸리다'가 맞다.

structuredNuance.t: 장염(腸炎)은 글자 그대로 '창자 장(腸) + 염증 염(炎)', 곧 장에 염증이 생겨 복통·구토·설사가 함께 오는 흔한 병으로 영어의 'stomach flu'에 가깝다. 병명이므로 '장염에 걸리다'가 표준이고, 악화되면 '장염이 심하다'라고 한다.
가장 헷갈리는 이웃 단어는 '배탈'인데, 배탈은 과식·체함으로 잠깐 배가 불편한 가벼운 상태인 반면 장염은 바이러스·세균 감염으로 며칠씩 가고 발열까지 동반하는 더 무거운 병이다.
글자 그대로 '창자 장(腸) + 염증 염(炎)', 곧 장에 염증이 생긴 병이라는 뜻이다.
영어 'have'를 직역한 '장염이 있다'나 '장염이 나다'는 표준이 아니다. 'I have enteritis'를 '장염을 가지고 있다'로 옮기면 어색하니, 동사 '걸리다'와 조사 '에'를 한 덩어리로 외워 두는 것이 안전하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 비염 means "rhinitis (chronic stuffy/runny nose, often allergic)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rhinitis (chronic stuffy/runny nose, often allergic)" is 비염 (biyeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비염이 있다 ("to have rhinitis"). Watch the particle attached to 비염 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 만성 질환은 소유처럼 '있다'로 표현
한국에서 가장 흔한 형태, '-성(性)'은 '~의 성질'
잠잠하던 게 다시 심해질 때 쓰는 구어
약국에서 바로 통하는 표현

examples.en: I have rhinitis.
examples.note: 기본형 — 체질·만성 질환은 '있다'로 소개

examples.ko: 환절기라 비염이 심해져서 재채기가 멈추질 않아요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgira biyeomi simhaejyeoseo jaechaegiga meomchujil anayo.
examples.en: It's the change of seasons, so my rhinitis flared up and I can't stop sneezing.
examples.note: 이비인후과에서 흔한 설명 — '멈추질'은 '멈추지를'의 준말

examples.ko: 비염 때문에 코를 너무 풀어서 코끝이 헐었어요.
examples.romanization: biyeom ttaemune koreul neomu pureoseo kokkeuchi heoreosseoyo.
examples.en: I blew my nose so much from rhinitis that the tip got raw.
examples.note: '코를 풀다'(to blow one's nose)를 꼭 익히세요

entries.nuance: 비염(鼻炎)은 '코 비(鼻) + 염증 염(炎)', 곧 코 점막에 염증이 생겨 코막힘·콧물·재채기가 반복되는 만성 질환으로, 미세먼지·꽃가루가 심한 한국에서는 '알레르기성 비염'을 달고 사는 사람이 정말 많다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '감기'인데, 감기는 바이러스로 잠깐 앓고 낫는 일시적 감염이고 비염은 체질·알레르기로 계속 반복되는 상태라 영어로 치면 cold가 아니라 chronic/allergic rhinitis다. 그래서 일시적 병에 쓰는 '걸리다'보다 소유의 '비염이 있다'로 말하고, 환절기마다 나빠지면 '비염이 도지다/심해지다'라고 한다. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 콧물·코막힘만 보고 'I have a cold'처럼 감기로 뭉뚱그리는 것인데, 한국에서는 만성이면 '비염', 며칠짜리면 '감기'로 분명히 갈라 말한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
감기와 같다고 보고 '감기 걸렸어요'로 말하는 것 — 감기는 일시적 감염, 비염은 알레르기·체질로 반복되는 만성 질환이다. 봄마다 코가 막히면 '비염이 있어요'가 정확하다.
'비염에 걸리다'를 단발성처럼만 쓰는 것 — 이미 가진 체질은 '비염이 있다', 증상이 나빠질 때는 '비염이 심해지다/도지다'가 자연스럽다.
'코가 막다'라고 하는 것 — 코는 스스로 막는 게 아니라 막히는 것이므로 자동사 '코가 막히다'가 맞다.

structuredNuance.t: 비염(鼻炎)은 '코 비(鼻) + 염증 염(炎)', 곧 코 점막에 염증이 생겨 코막힘·콧물·재채기가 반복되는 만성 질환이다. 미세먼지·꽃가루가 심한 한국에서는 '알레르기성 비염'을 달고 사는 사람이 정말 많다. 만성이라 소유의 '비염이 있다'로 말하고, 환절기마다 나빠지면 '비염이 도지다/심해지다'라고 한다.

'코 비(鼻) + 염증 염(炎)', 곧 코에 생긴 염증이라는 뜻이다.
영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 콧물·코막힘만 보고 'I have a cold'처럼 감기로 뭉뚱그리는 것인데, 한국에서는 만성이면 '비염', 며칠짜리면 '감기'로 분명히 갈라 말한다.

entries.shortExplanation: 축농증 means "sinusitis (sinus infection, blocked sinuses)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 축농증 (chungnongjeung) = "sinusitis (sinus infection, blocked sinuses)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 축농증이 있다 ("to have sinusitis") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 축농증, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 오래된·만성 상태를 말할 때
감기 끝에 옮겨 붙는 경과를 말함

usagePhrases.en: to have thick yellow nasal discharge
usagePhrases.note: 축농증의 대표 증상
심한 경우의 치료, '수술을 받다'

examples.en: I have sinusitis.
examples.note: 기본형 — 만성 상태라 '있다'로 표현

examples.en: My cold dragged on and turned into sinusitis.
examples.note: '-더니'로 '계속 그러다가 결국' 경과를 설명

examples.en: If sinusitis is bad, you sometimes get antibiotics prescribed.
examples.note: '처방받다'(to get prescribed)는 병원 필수 동사

entries.nuance: 축농증(蓄膿症)은 '쌓을 축(蓄) + 고름 농(膿) + 증세 증(症)', 곧 '고름이 차는 증세'라는 뜻으로, 코 옆 빈 공간인 부비동에 고름이 고여 누런 콧물·코막힘·두통·냄새 둔감이 생기는 병이다. 의학 용어로는 '부비동염(副鼻洞炎)'이지만 일상에서는 한자어 '축농증'을 압도적으로 많이 쓰니 이비인후과에서 그대로 말하면 된다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '비염'인데, 비염은 코 점막 표면의 염증이고 축농증은 그 안쪽 부비동에 고름이 차는 것이라 부위가 다르며, 흔히 비염·감기 끝에 '축농증으로 번지다'라고 한 단계 악화로 이어진다. 영어 화자의 함정은 둘 다 'sinus problem'으로 뭉뚱그리는 것인데, 맑은 콧물·재채기 위주면 비염, 누렇고 끈끈한 콧물·얼굴 압박감이면 축농증으로 구분하면 정확하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
비염과 같다고 보는 것 — 비염은 코 점막 염증, 축농증은 부비동에 고름이 차는 것이라 부위와 증상이 다르다. 누런 콧물·얼굴 통증이면 축농증 쪽이다.
'축농증이 아프다'라고 하는 것 — 병명이라 '축농증이 있다/심하다, 축농증 때문에 (머리가) 아프다'처럼 써야 한다.
콧물 색을 '노란'으로만 말하는 것 — 한국에서 진한 콧물은 관용적으로 '누런 콧물'이라고 한다. '누렇다'를 함께 익히면 증상 설명이 자연스럽다.

'쌓을 축(蓄) + 고름 농(膿) + 증세 증(症)', 곧 '고름이 차는 증세'라는 뜻이다.
영어 화자의 함정은 비염과 축농증을 둘 다 'sinus problem'으로 뭉뚱그리는 것인데, 맑은 콧물·재채기 위주면 비염, 누렇고 끈끈한 콧물·얼굴 압박감이면 축농증으로 구분하면 정확하다.

usagePhrases.note: 가장 기본 표현, 병명+'걸리다'

usagePhrases.en: to get food poisoning from spoiled food
usagePhrases.note: 원인 '상한 음식' + 결과 세트
구토·설사·복통·발열을 가리킴

usagePhrases.note: 더울 때 뉴스·공지에 자주 나오는 당부

examples.en: I must have eaten something spoiled — I got food poisoning.

examples.ko: 회사 회식 후에 다 같이 식중독에 걸렸어요.

examples.note: 집단 발병 — '다 같이'(all together)가 핵심

examples.ko: 여름엔 음식을 상온에 두면 식중독에 걸리기 쉬워요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen eumsigeul sangone dumyeon sikjungdoge geolligi swiwoyo.
examples.en: In summer, leaving food at room temperature easily causes food poisoning.
examples.note: 예방 조언 — '-기 쉽다'는 '~하기 쉽다'

entries.nuance: 식중독(食中毒)은 '먹을 식(食) + 가운데 중(中) + 독 독(毒)', 곧 '먹어서 독에 맞다(중독되다)'는 뜻으로, 상하거나 오염된 음식을 먹고 구토·설사·복통·발열이 갑자기 나는 급성 질환이다. 한국에서는 특히 여름철 단골 뉴스 단어이고, 병이므로 '식중독에 걸리다'가 표준이다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '체하다(소화불량)'와 '장염'인데, 체한 것은 위가 잠깐 막힌 가벼운 상태이고, 장염은 원인이 꼭 음식만은 아닌 장의 감염성 염증인 반면, 식중독은 '나쁜 음식'이라는 원인이 분명하고 한 끼 잘못 먹고 갑자기 심해진다는 점이 특징이다. 영어 화자의 함정은 'food poisoning'을 직역해 '음식 독'처럼 말하거나 '식중독이 나다'라고 하는 것인데, 한국어는 반드시 동사 '걸리다'와 묶어 '식중독에 걸리다'로 쓴다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'식중독이 나다 / 식중독을 걸리다'라고 하는 것 — 표준은 '식중독에 걸리다'다. 조사 '에' + 동사 '걸리다'를 한 덩어리로 외운다.
단순 소화불량(체함)과 혼동하는 것 — 식중독은 오염된 음식으로 인한 중독성 증상이라 구토·발열이 동반되고 훨씬 급격하다. 가벼우면 '체했어요', 심하면 '식중독에 걸렸어요'.
원인을 말할 때 '상한 음식으로'를 '상한 음식 때문에 먹고'처럼 어순을 꼬는 것 — '상한 음식을 먹고 식중독에 걸렸어요'처럼 '먹고'로 원인 행위를 자연스럽게 잇는다.

entries.shortExplanation: 빈혈 means "anemia (low iron/blood, causing dizziness)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "anemia (low iron/blood, causing dizziness)" is 빈혈 (binhyeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빈혈이 있다 ("to have anemia"). Watch the particle attached to 빈혈 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 체질·만성 상태를 말할 때
정도를 말할 때 '심하다'

usagePhrases.en: to be dizzy because of anemia
usagePhrases.note: 원인 → 증상 설명의 핵심 짝
'(으)로'는 '~때문에'의 원인 조사

examples.en: I have a bit of anemia.
examples.note: 기본형 — '좀'으로 정도를 부드럽게

examples.ko: 저는 빈혈이 있어서 갑자기 일어나면 핑 돌아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun binhyeori isseoseo gapjagi ireonamyeon ping dorayo.
examples.en: I have anemia, so I get dizzy if I stand up suddenly.
examples.note: '핑 돌다'는 핑 도는 어지럼증의 생생한 구어

examples.ko: 빈혈이 심해서 철분제를 챙겨 먹고 있어요.
examples.romanization: binhyeori simhaeseo cheolbunjereul chaenggyeo meokgo isseoyo.
examples.en: My anemia is bad, so I'm taking iron supplements regularly.
examples.note: '철분제'(iron supplement), '챙겨 먹다'(take regularly)

entries.nuance: 빈혈(貧血)은 '가난할 빈(貧) + 피 혈(血)', 곧 '피가 모자라다'는 뜻으로, 적혈구나 철분이 부족해 어지럽고 쉽게 피곤하며 얼굴이 창백해지는 상태다. 특히 여성에게 흔하고, 보통 체질처럼 오래가므로 '빈혈이 있다'라고 소유로 말한다. 영어 화자가 가장 많이 혼동하는 이웃은 '저혈압(低血壓, low blood pressure)'인데, 빈혈은 '피의 양·질(적혈구·철분)' 문제이고 저혈압은 '혈압 수치'의 문제라 원인이 전혀 다르다. 또 하나 헷갈리는 것은 '어지럼증(현기증)'으로, 어지럼증은 빙빙 도는 증상 자체를 가리키는 반면 빈혈은 그 증상을 일으키는 혈액의 원인이다. 함정은 'anemia'를 일시적 병처럼 '빈혈에 걸리다'로 쓰는 것인데, 만성이라 '빈혈이 있다/생기다'가 자연스럽고, 핑 도는 순간만 따로 '어지럽다, 핑 돌다'로 표현한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
저혈압과 혼동하는 것 — 빈혈은 혈액 속 적혈구·철분 부족, 저혈압은 혈압이 낮은 것이라 원인이 다르다. 병원에서는 둘을 구별해 말해야 한다.
'빈혈에 걸리다'를 일회성 병처럼 쓰는 것 — 보통 만성·체질이라 '빈혈이 있다/생기다'가 더 자연스럽다.
어지럼 증상을 '빈혈이 와요'로만 뭉뚱그리는 것 — 순간적으로 핑 도는 느낌은 '어지러워요, 핑 돌아요'로, 진단명은 '빈혈이 있어요'로 분리하면 더 정확하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 고혈압 means "high blood pressure, hypertension" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고혈압 (gohyeorap) = "high blood pressure, hypertension". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고혈압이 있다 ("to have high blood pressure") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고혈압, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 만성 질환은 '있다'로
매일 복용하는 약, 구어로 '약을 먹다'
수치를 풀어 말하는 일상 표현
검진·병원에서 결과를 들을 때

examples.en: I have a bit of high blood pressure.
examples.note: 기본형 — 만성 질환은 '있다'로 소개

examples.ko: 아버지가 고혈압이 있으셔서 매일 약을 드세요.
examples.romanization: abeojiga gohyeorabi isseusyeoseo maeil yageul deuseyo.
examples.en: My father has high blood pressure, so he takes medicine every day.
examples.note: 높임 — '있으셔서, 드세요'로 어른을 존대

examples.en: The checkup showed high blood pressure, so I got medication prescribed.
examples.note: '건강검진'(health checkup), '나오다'(results show)

entries.nuance: 고혈압(高血壓)은 '높을 고(高) + 피 혈(血) + 누를 압(壓)', 곧 '혈압이 높다'는 뜻 그대로의 만성 질환으로, 한국 중장년층에게 매우 흔해 건강검진·병원에서 늘 듣는 단어다. 평생 관리하는 병이라 '고혈압이 있다, 고혈압 약을 먹다'처럼 소유·복용으로 표현하고, 진단 시점은 '고혈압 진단을 받다'라고 한다. 일상에서는 한자어 진단명 대신 '혈압이 높다'로 풀어 말해도 똑같이 통한다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '당뇨'인데, 둘 다 흔한 성인병이고 함께 관리하는 일이 많아 묶어 생각하기 쉽지만 고혈압은 '혈압', 당뇨는 '혈당(혈액 속 당)' 문제로 별개의 병이다. 영어 화자의 함정은 'I got high blood pressure'를 '고혈압에 걸렸어요'로 옮기는 것인데, 감기처럼 걸리는 병이 아니라서 '고혈압이 있어요/생겼어요/진단받았어요'가 자연스럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'고혈압에 걸리다'를 감기처럼 쓰는 것 — 만성 질환이라 '고혈압이 있다/생기다, 고혈압 진단을 받다'가 자연스럽다.
당뇨와 묶어 같은 병으로 보는 것 — 고혈압은 혈압, 당뇨는 혈당 문제라 서로 다른 질환이다(함께 관리하는 경우는 많다).
어른의 병을 말할 때 평어로 '고혈압이 있어서'라고만 하는 것 — 윗사람이면 '고혈압이 있으셔서 약을 드세요'처럼 '-시-'로 높여야 예의에 맞다.

'높을 고(高) + 피 혈(血) + 누를 압(壓)', 곧 '혈압이 높다'는 뜻이다.

entries.shortExplanation: 당뇨 means "diabetes (high blood sugar)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 당뇨 (dangnyo) means "diabetes (high blood sugar)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 당뇨가 있다 ("to have diabetes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당뇨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 구어에서 가장 흔한 형태
격식 있는 문서·진단명에서는 '-병'을 붙임
'재다'(to measure)는 혈당·혈압·체온에 두루 씀
식단 이야기에 자주 등장

examples.ko: 저 당뇨가 있어서 단 거 잘 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: jeo dangnyoga isseoseo dan geo jal mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: I have diabetes, so I can't really eat sweet things.
examples.note: 기본형 — 모임에서 음식 제한을 알리는 실전 문장

examples.ko: 할머니가 당뇨가 있으셔서 단 걸 못 드세요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga dangnyoga isseusyeoseo dan geol mot deuseyo.
examples.en: My grandmother has diabetes, so she can't eat sweets.
examples.note: 높임 — '있으셔서, 드세요'로 어른을 존대

examples.ko: 요즘 살이 빠지고 목이 자주 말라서 당뇨 검사를 받았어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum sari ppajigo mogi jaju mallaseo dangnyo geomsareul badasseoyo.
examples.en: I've been losing weight and feeling thirsty a lot, so I got tested for diabetes.
examples.note: 증상 → 검사 흐름, '목이 마르다'(to be thirsty)

entries.nuance: 당뇨(糖尿)는 '엿/사탕 당(糖) + 오줌 뇨(尿)', 곧 '소변에 당이 섞여 나온다'는 뜻에서 온 말로, 혈당이 높아지는 만성 질환이다. 정식 명칭은 '당뇨병(糖尿病)'이지만 일상에서는 '-병'을 떼고 '당뇨'라고 훨씬 많이 쓴다. 평생 식단·혈당을 관리하는 병이라 '당뇨가 있다'라고 소유처럼 말하고, '저 당뇨라서 단 거 못 먹어요'처럼 식당·모임에서 음식 제한을 알리는 대단히 실용적인 단어다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '고혈압'으로, 둘 다 흔한 성인병이라 한데 묶기 쉽지만 당뇨는 '혈당', 고혈압은 '혈압'의 문제라 별개다. 영어 화자의 함정은 'I have diabetes'를 '당뇨에 걸렸어요'로 옮기는 것인데, 감기처럼 걸리는 병이 아니므로 '당뇨가 있어요, 당뇨 진단을 받았어요'가 자연스럽고, 수치를 잴 때는 '혈당을 재다'를 쓴다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
고혈압과 같은 병으로 묶는 것 — 당뇨는 혈당, 고혈압은 혈압 문제로 서로 다르다.
'당뇨에 걸리다'를 일시적 병처럼 쓰는 것 — 만성 질환이라 '당뇨가 있다, 당뇨 진단을 받다'가 자연스럽다.
'혈당을 측정하다'만 떠올려 일상에서 어색하게 말하는 것 — 구어에서는 체온·혈압·혈당 모두 '재다'를 써서 '혈당을 재다'가 가장 자연스럽다.

가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '고혈압'으로, 둘 다 흔한 성인병이라 한데 묶기 쉽지만 당뇨는 '혈당', 고혈압은 '혈압'의 문제라 별개다.
'엿/사탕 당(糖) + 오줌 뇨(尿)', 곧 '소변에 당이 섞여 나온다'는 뜻에서 온 말이다.
영어 화자의 함정은 'I have diabetes'를 '당뇨에 걸렸어요'로 옮기는 것인데, 감기처럼 걸리는 병이 아니므로 '당뇨가 있어요, 당뇨 진단을 받았어요'가 자연스럽고, 수치를 잴 때는 '혈당을 재다'를 쓴다.

entries.shortExplanation: 천식 means "asthma" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "asthma" is 천식 (cheonsik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 천식이 있다 ("to have asthma"). Watch the particle attached to 천식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 만성 질환은 '있다'로
갑자기 숨이 막히는 급성 순간, '발작(發作)'
천식 증상을 설명하는 핵심 표현
응급 시 대처, '흡입기'(inhaler)

examples.en: I have asthma.
examples.note: 기본형 — 만성 질환은 '있다'로 소개

examples.ko: 미세먼지가 심한 날엔 천식 때문에 숨쉬기가 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: misemeonjiga simhan naren cheonsik ttaemune sumswigiga himdeureoyo.
examples.en: On days with heavy fine dust, it's hard to breathe because of my asthma.
examples.note: 한국 생활 밀착 표현 — '숨쉬기가 힘들다'

examples.ko: 갑자기 숨이 막히면 천식 발작일 수 있으니 흡입기를 쓰세요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi sumi makimyeon cheonsik baljagil su isseuni heubipgireul sseuseyo.
examples.en: If you suddenly can't breathe, it could be an asthma attack, so use your inhaler.
examples.note: 응급 안내 — '-(으)니'로 이유를 들어 권유

entries.nuance: 천식(喘息)은 '헐떡일 천(喘) + 숨쉴 식(息)', 곧 '헐떡이며 숨 쉰다'는 뜻으로, 기관지가 좁아져 숨이 차고 쌕쌕거리는 만성 호흡기 질환이다. 미세먼지가 심한 한국에서는 특히 신경 쓰이는 병이고, 평생 관리하는 상태라 '천식이 있다'로 말한다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 '기관지염'과 그냥 '기침감기'인데, 기침감기는 잠깐 앓고 낫는 일시적 감염인 반면 천식은 만성적으로 기관지가 과민해져 호흡 곤란이 핵심이라는 점이 다르다. 갑자기 심해져 숨이 콱 막히는 순간은 따로 '천식 발작'이라고 한다. 영어 화자의 함정은 'short of breath'를 '숨이 짧다'로 직역하는 것인데, 한국어는 '숨이 차다(가쁘다), 숨이 막히다, 쌕쌕거리다'를 쓴다. 또 만성이라 '천식에 걸리다'보다 '천식이 있다'가 자연스럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
단순 기침·감기와 같다고 보는 것 — 천식은 기관지가 좁아지는 만성 질환이라 호흡 곤란이 핵심이다. 며칠짜리 기침이면 '기침감기', 평소 숨이 차면 '천식'.
'숨이 짧다'라고 직역하는 것 — 영어 'short of breath'와 달리 한국어는 '숨이 차다, 숨이 가쁘다, 숨쉬기가 힘들다'로 표현한다.
'천식에 걸리다'를 일시적으로만 쓰는 것 — 만성 질환이라 '천식이 있다'가 자연스럽고, 악화 시 '천식이 심해지다'라고 한다.
