entries.shortExplanation: 폭포 means "waterfall" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "waterfall" is 폭포 (pokpo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 폭포 ("waterfall"). Watch the particle attached to 폭포 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Neutral noun for any falls, tiny drop to famous tourist one
수(水) added; stresses the falling water, not the cliff
떨어지다 (to fall) is the natural verb for the water dropping
소리 = sound; the most-mentioned appeal of a falls

examples.en: Can you hear the waterfall over there?
examples.note: 들리다 = to be audible; simple yes/no question

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와서 폭포 물줄기가 엄청 세요.
examples.romanization: biga mani waseo pokpo muljulgiga eomcheong seyo.
examples.en: It rained a lot, so the waterfall's flow is really strong.
examples.note: 물줄기 = jet/stream of water; 세다 = to be powerful

examples.ko: 폭포 앞에서 사진 찍으면 진짜 시원해 보여요.
examples.romanization: pokpo apeseo sajin jjigeumyeon jinjja siwonhae boyeoyo.
examples.en: Photos taken in front of a waterfall really look refreshing.
examples.note: 찍으면 = if/when you take (a photo); 보이다 = to look/appear

entries.nuance: 폭포 (瀑布, 'gushing-spread water') is the plain, neutral word for a waterfall of any size — a small drop tucked in a 계곡 or a famous tourist landmark alike — and it habitually travels with 소리 (sound) and 시원하다 (refreshing) when people explain why they like it. Unlike 계곡 (the ravine/stream you walk into) a 폭포 is the vertical fall itself, so the two often appear together: 계곡 따라 올라가면 폭포가 나와요. The near-synonym to know is 폭포수: 폭포 is the structure/place, while 폭포수 isolates the cascading water (the 수 is hanja 水, water). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb — in English a waterfall 'falls' but learners reach for 내리다; Korean specifically uses 떨어지다 (폭포가 떨어지다), and the water is 세다 (strong), never 빠르다 (fast).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Misspelling it 포포 or 폭보: the word is 폭포 — first syllable ends in ㄱ batchim, second begins with ㅍ.
Using 내리다 for the falling water (an English 'comes down' transfer) — the natural verb is 폭포가 떨어지다.
Forcing 폭포수 in casual speech: for everyday 'let's go see a waterfall,' plain 폭포 is right; 폭포수 narrowly means the falling water itself.

entries.shortExplanation: 동굴 means "cave" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동굴 (donggul) = "cave". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 동굴 ("cave") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동굴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Natural rock cave; also figurative for a dark cozy hideout
탐험(探險) = adventurous exploring; standard for tourist caves
안 = the interior; 동굴 안은 시원해요
에 + 들어가다 for entering an enclosed space

examples.en: Inside the cave it's cool even in summer.
examples.note: 안은 = inside (as topic); caves stay cold year-round

examples.en: I checked out a lava cave in Jeju.
examples.note: 용암 = lava; 구경하다 is the go-to verb for sightseeing a place

examples.ko: 동굴이 너무 어두워서 손전등이 꼭 필요해요.
examples.romanization: dongguri neomu eoduwoseo sonjeondeungi kkok piryohaeyo.
examples.en: The cave is so dark that a flashlight is essential.
examples.note: 어둡다 → 어두워서 (ㅂ-irregular); 손전등 = flashlight

entries.nuance: 동굴 (洞窟, 'hollow-cavern') is the standard word for a natural cave, including Korea's famous limestone caverns and Jeju's UNESCO lava tubes that headline day trips, and it pairs almost reflexively with 구경하다 (to look around) or 탐험 (exploration). The synonym to separate it from is bare 굴: 굴 can mean 'cave/hole' but in food contexts means 'oyster,' so 굴 구경 is ambiguous while 동굴 구경 is unmistakably the cave. Register is neutral, and there's a warm figurative use — 동굴 같은 방 (a cave-like room) for a dark, snug space, or 동굴에 들어가다 jokingly for hiding away. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'enter the cave' tempts 동굴로 들어가다, but for going INTO an enclosed space you want 동굴에 들어가다; 로 would imply the route/direction you took, not the entering itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Shortening to bare 굴 in travel talk: 굴 also means 'oyster,' so 굴 보러 가자 is confusing — use 동굴 to mean cave clearly.
Saying 동굴로 들어가다 for simply entering: use 동굴에 들어가다 (에), since 로 signals the direction/path rather than the act of going in.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular in 어둡다: 'because it's dark' is 어두워서, not 어둡어서.

entries.shortExplanation: 절벽 means "cliff" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 절벽 (jeolbyeok) means "cliff". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 절벽 ("cliff"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 절벽 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sheer vertical rock face; also figurative for a dead end / crisis
끝 = edge/end; 절벽 끝에 서다 = stand at the edge
위 = top; sea views are described from 절벽 위
에서 marks the source point of the fall

examples.en: This cliff here is really tall.
examples.note: 높다 = tall/high; the basic adjective for a cliff

examples.ko: 위험하니까 절벽 끝에 너무 가까이 가지 마세요.
examples.romanization: wiheomhanikka jeolbyeok kkeute neomu gakkai gaji maseyo.
examples.en: It's dangerous, so don't go too close to the cliff edge.
examples.note: 가까이 = closely (adverb); -지 마세요 = polite 'please don't'

examples.ko: 저 해안 절벽이 사진 명소라서 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: jeo haean jeolbyeogi sajin myeongsoraseo sarami manayo.
examples.en: Those coastal cliffs are a famous photo spot, so it's crowded.
examples.note: 해안 = coast; 명소(名所) = famous/scenic spot

entries.nuance: 절벽 (絶壁, literally 'cut-off wall') is a sheer, vertical cliff or rock face — the 絶 ('to sever') captures how the ground just drops away, common along Korea's coastlines and hiking ridges where signs warn you to stay back. The contrast learners blur is 절벽 vs 언덕: an 언덕 is a gentle, walkable hill, whereas a 절벽 is a vertical drop you could fall off, so they are opposites in steepness, not synonyms. Register is neutral, but 절벽 carries a vivid figurative life — 절벽 끝에 몰리다 (driven to the cliff's edge) means pushed to the brink, and 재정 절벽 is the 'fiscal cliff.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle of falling: you fall 절벽에서 떨어지다 (에서, the source) — using 에 there would wrongly point to a destination, and don't confuse the scenic 해안 절벽 with a soft 'bluff,' which Korean would not call 절벽.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a gentle slope a 절벽: an 언덕 is a small hill you walk up, while 절벽 is a vertical drop — mixing them misstates how dangerous the place is.
Spelling it 절뼉 or 절벅: the correct form is 절벽 with ㄹ batchim on the first syllable.
Saying 절벽에 떨어지다 for falling off: use 절벽에서 떨어지다 (에서 = from the cliff), since 에 would suggest landing onto it.

entries.shortExplanation: 갯벌 means "tidal flat, mudflat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tidal flat, mudflat" is 갯벌 (gaetbeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갯벌 ("tidal flat / mudflat"). Watch the particle attached to 갯벌 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Coastal mud exposed at low tide; a west-coast specialty
체험(體驗) = hands-on experience; a popular family activity

usagePhrases.en: dig for clams in the mudflat
usagePhrases.note: 캐다 = to dig up; the classic mudflat activity
드러나다 = to be revealed, as the tide goes out

examples.en: This is that famous mudflat.
examples.note: Simple identification; 이에요 = polite 'it is'

examples.en: At low tide the mudflat gets fully exposed.
examples.note: 썰물 = ebb/low tide; 쫙 = mimetic for spreading wide open

examples.ko: 갯벌은 미끄러우니까 꼭 장화 신고 가세요.
examples.romanization: gaetbeoreun mikkeureounikka kkok janghwa singo gaseyo.
examples.en: Mudflats are slippery, so be sure to wear rubber boots.
examples.note: 미끄럽다 → 미끄러우니까 (ㅂ-irregular); 장화 = rubber boots

entries.nuance: 갯벌 is the soft, muddy tidal flat that emerges at low tide — a defining feature of Korea's West and South coasts and a beloved hands-on 체험 where families go 조개 캐기 (clam digging). It's a pure native-Korean compound, 개 ('seaside/inlet') + 벌 ('open flat'), joined with a 사이시옷 that adds the ㅅ batchim → 갯벌, which is why the spelling matters. The contrast to nail is 갯벌 vs 해변/모래사장: a 해변 is a firm sandy beach you sunbathe on, while a 갯벌 is wet mud that only exists when the tide is OUT and is tied to 썰물 (low tide) and 밀물 (high tide). The English-speaker pitfall is treating any shoreline as 갯벌 — it specifically means the mud-at-low-tide zone, so don't use it for a regular sandy 해변; also note Korea's 갯벌 are UNESCO-listed, so locals say it with pride, not as 'just mud.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 개벌 or 갯펄: standard spelling keeps the 사이시옷 ㅅ batchim → 갯벌.
Calling a sandy beach 갯벌: 갯벌 is mud exposed at low tide, while a firm sandy shore is 해변 / 모래사장 — they are different terrains.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular in 미끄럽다: 'because it's slippery' is 미끄러우니까, not 미끄럽으니까.

entries.shortExplanation: 등대 means "lighthouse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 등대 (deungdae) = "lighthouse". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 등대 ("lighthouse") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 등대, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Coastal light tower; a very common seaside photo landmark
Ports pair a red and a white one to mark the channel
불빛 = emitted light; what guides ships at night
구경 = casual sightseeing; everyday trip phrasing

examples.en: Can you see the red lighthouse over there?
examples.note: 보이다 = to be visible; simple pointing-out question

examples.en: At night the lighthouse beam is visible from far away.
examples.note: 멀리까지 = all the way far; 까지 = up to/as far as

examples.ko: 빨간 등대 쪽으로 산책하면 노을이 진짜 예뻐요.
examples.romanization: ppalgan deungdae jjogeuro sanchaekamyeon noeuri jinjja yeppeoyo.
examples.en: If you stroll toward the red lighthouse, the sunset is really pretty.
examples.note: 쪽으로 = in the direction of; 노을 = sunset glow

entries.nuance: 등대 (燈臺, 'lamp-platform/tower') is a lighthouse, and on Korean harbor breakwaters you'll famously see a 빨간 등대 (red) and a 하얀/하얀색 등대 (white) marking which side of the channel is which — a beloved backdrop for seaside walks, sunset photos and dates. The hanja 燈 ('lamp') links it to a family of light words, which is exactly the trap: don't confuse 등대 with 등 (a lamp/light) or with the unrelated 등산 (hiking) just because they share 등 sounds. Register is fully neutral and casual, and 등대 also carries a warm figurative sense of a guiding beacon (희망의 등대). The English-speaker pitfall is location particles: for 'meet at the lighthouse' Koreans say 등대 앞에서 / 등대 쪽에서 만나자, because 등대에서 만나자 sounds like meeting literally at its base; and the light it casts is 불빛, not just 빛.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 등대 (lighthouse) with 등 (lamp) or 등산 (hiking): they share the 등 sound but are entirely different words.
Saying 등대에서 만나자 for a meetup point: more natural is 등대 앞에서 / 등대 쪽에서 만나자, since people gather near it, not at its base.
Using 빛 alone for the beam: the lighthouse's glow is 등대 불빛, the standard collocation.

entries.shortExplanation: 항구 means "harbor, port" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 항구 (hanggu) means "harbor, port". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 항구 ("harbor / port"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 항구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The whole working waterfront where boats dock
도시 = city; a proud set phrase (Busan is the classic)

usagePhrases.en: a ship comes into the harbor
usagePhrases.note: 에 + 들어오다 = to come in toward you

usagePhrases.en: a sashimi place near the harbor
usagePhrases.note: 횟집 = raw-fish restaurant; ports mean fresh seafood

examples.en: Busan is a big harbor.
examples.note: Simple statement; 항구예요 = polite 'is a harbor'

examples.ko: 저녁이 되면 항구에 배들이 하나둘 들어와요.
examples.romanization: jeonyeogi doemyeon hanggue baedeuri hanadul deureowayo.
examples.en: Come evening, ships come into the harbor one by one.
examples.note: 하나둘 = one by one; 들어오다 = come in

examples.ko: 항구 앞에서 갓 잡은 생선을 바로 팔아요.
examples.romanization: hanggu apeseo gat jabeun saengseoneul baro parayo.
examples.en: Right by the harbor they sell freshly caught fish on the spot.
examples.note: 갓 잡은 = freshly caught; 바로 = right away/right there

entries.nuance: 항구 (港口, 'port-mouth') is the harbor as a whole — the entire working waterfront of docks, boats and fish markets — strongly tied to Korea's seafood cities like 부산, 속초 and 통영, so it surfaces constantly in 회 (sashimi) trip talk, and 항구 도시 (port city) is a set phrase locals use with pride. The key synonym contrast is 항구 vs 부두: 항구 is the broad harbor area, while 부두 is the specific built pier/wharf where a ship actually ties up — 항구에 도착해서 부두에서 내렸다 shows both. The shared hanja 港 also links it to 공항(空港, airport), the second trap: same character, but 공항 is 'empty-port' = airport, totally different place. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: don't use 항구 for the single pier you board from (that's 부두), and remember a ship 항구에 들어오다/들어가다 (에), since the harbor is the enclosed destination.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 항구 for a single pier: 항구 is the whole harbor, while the specific docking structure is 부두 — keep the two distinct.
Confusing 항구 (harbor) with 공항 (airport): both contain 港, but 공항 means airport — context and the 공(空, sky) make the difference.
Forgetting the verb pairing: a ship 항구에 들어오다 (에 marks the harbor it enters), not 항구를 들어오다.

entries.shortExplanation: 부두 means "pier, wharf, dock" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "pier, wharf, dock" is 부두 (budu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 부두 ("pier / wharf"). Watch the particle attached to 부두 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The built structure where ships tie up and load
정박하다(碇泊) = to dock/anchor (slightly formal)
따라 = along; common stroll/date phrasing
여객선 = passenger ship; where island ferries leave

examples.en: You catch the boat at that pier.
examples.note: 타다 = to board; 에서 marks where you get on

examples.en: We looked at the sea while walking along the pier.
examples.note: 걸으면서 = while walking (ㄷ-irregular 걷다 → 걸으면서)

examples.ko: 섬에 가는 배는 저쪽 여객선 부두에서 출발해요.
examples.romanization: seome ganeun baeneun jeojjok yeogaekseon budueseo chulbalhaeyo.
examples.en: The boat to the island leaves from that passenger pier over there.
examples.note: 여객선 부두 = ferry terminal; 출발하다 = to depart

entries.nuance: 부두 (埠頭, 'wharf-head') is the concrete pier or wharf where boats physically tie up, load and unload — the built edge of the water, as opposed to 항구 (the whole harbor that surrounds it). You'll reach for it most when catching island ferries (여객선 부두) or strolling a photogenic waterfront, and it collocates with 정박하다 (to moor) and 따라 걷다 (walk along). The synonym line to hold is precisely 부두 vs 항구: 부두 is one specific structure, 항구 is the entire harbor district — slightly more concrete/technical, but still everyday. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't swap 부두 and 항구 freely (English 'dock' blurs them, Korean doesn't), and watch the spelling — 부두, not 부뚜, because 부뚜막 is the ledge of a traditional stove, a completely unrelated word; and to board, you say 부두에서 타다 (에서, the place you board from).

Using 부두 and 항구 interchangeably: 부두 is the pier structure, 항구 is the whole harbor — English 'dock' collapses them, Korean keeps them apart.
Spelling it 부뚜: the word is 부두; 부뚜(막) is a stove ledge, an entirely different thing.
Saying 부두에 타다 for boarding: the natural form is 부두에서 (배를) 타다, since 에서 marks the place the action departs from.

entries.shortExplanation: 들판 means "field, open plain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 들판 (deulpan) = "field, open plain". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 들판 ("field / open plain") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 들판, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Wide open grassy or farm land in the countryside
넓다 → 넓은; the most natural pairing
펼쳐지다 = to spread open, used of scenery
가로지르다 = to cross/traverse

examples.en: I can see a wide open field outside the window.
examples.note: 창밖 = outside the window; 보이다 = to be seen

examples.en: When autumn comes, the fields turn yellow.
examples.note: 노랗게 = yellowly (ㅎ-irregular 노랗다); ripening rice

examples.ko: 탁 트인 들판에서 자전거 타니까 진짜 시원했어요.
examples.romanization: tak teuin deulpaneseo jajeongeo tanikka jinjja siwonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Riding a bike across the wide-open field felt so refreshing.
examples.note: 탁 트이다 = to be wide open; 시원하다 here = liberating

entries.nuance: 들판 is a wide open field or plain — farmland, grassland, the scenery rolling past a countryside train window — and it carries a calm, spacious, rural mood, surfacing especially in 가을 (autumn) when the rice fields turn gold. It's a native compound, 들 ('open country/wild field') + 판 ('flat expanse'). The synonym to separate is 들판 vs 밭: a 밭 is a specific cultivated crop plot (a vegetable field you tend), whereas 들판 is the broad, scenic open expanse — so 밭에서 일하다 (work the field) but 들판이 펼쳐지다 (fields spread out before you). Register is neutral, slightly literary/scenic. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'field' is too broad: a sports field is 운동장, a single crop field is 밭, an academic 'field' is 분야 — reach for 들판 only for the open rural plain, and pair it with 펼쳐지다 or 넓다 rather than translating 'a field of...' literally.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 들판 for a cultivated plot: a tended crop field is 밭, while 들판 is the broad open plain — 밭 is for working, 들판 is for the scenic sweep.
Translating every English 'field' as 들판: a sports field is 운동장 and an area of study is 분야 — 들판 is only the rural open expanse.
Spelling it 들빤 or 들반: the correct form is 들판 (ㄹ batchim + 판).

entries.shortExplanation: 언덕 means "hill, slope" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 언덕 (eondeok) means "hill, slope". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 언덕 ("hill / gentle slope"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 언덕 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A small rise, far smaller than a 산 (mountain)
위 = top; 언덕 위 카페 = a hilltop cafe
오르다 = to go up; also 언덕을 올라가다
가파르다 = steep; common for tiring uphill streets

examples.en: There's a house up on that hill.
examples.note: 위에 = on top of; 있다 = there is

examples.ko: 집까지 가는 길이 언덕이라서 좀 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: jipkkaji ganeun giri eondeogiraseo jom himdeureoyo.
examples.en: The way home is uphill, so it's a bit tiring.
examples.note: 언덕이라서 = because it's a slope; 힘들다 = to be tough

examples.en: In spring the hill blooms with tons of flowers.
examples.note: 잔뜩 = a whole lot; 피다 → 펴요 (to bloom)

entries.nuance: 언덕 is a hill or gentle slope — a small rise, far smaller than a 산 (mountain), but enough to make you huff on the walk home — and in Korean cities the hillside neighborhood and the 언덕 위 카페 (hilltop cafe with a view) are a real cultural thing. It's native Korean, and beyond a literal hill it doubles for the tiring incline of a street: 우리 집은 언덕에 있어요 means 'my place is up a slope.' The synonym/scale contrast is the heart of it — don't call a real mountain an 언덕; use 산 for anything you'd actually hike, 언덕 for the small walkable rise (and a steep paved one is 가파른 언덕 or 비탈/비탈길). Register is neutral, often a touch nostalgic. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'hill' and 'mountain' overlap loosely, but Korean draws a firmer line: misusing 언덕 for 설악산 sounds comically small, while calling a neighborhood slope a 산 sounds overdramatic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a real mountain an 언덕: anything you hike is 산; 언덕 is reserved for small hills and slopes, so the scale would sound wrong.
Spelling it 언떡 or 언덬: the correct form is 언덕 (ㄴ batchim + 덕).
Reaching for 산 to describe a steep street: a tiring paved incline is an 언덕 (or 비탈길), not a 산.

entries.shortExplanation: 봉우리 means "peak, summit (of a mountain)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "peak, summit (of a mountain)" is 봉우리 (bonguri). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 봉우리 ("peak / summit"). Watch the particle attached to 봉우리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: An individual mountain peak; a range has several
산 prefixed; a very common combined form
오르다 = to ascend; 정상까지 오르다 is similar
뾰족하다 = pointy; describes sharp summits

examples.en: That peak over there is the highest.
examples.note: 제일 높다 = the highest; simple comparison

examples.ko: 저 멀리 눈 덮인 봉우리가 보여요.
examples.romanization: jeo meolli nun deopin bonguriga boyeoyo.
examples.en: Off in the distance you can see a snow-covered peak.
examples.note: 눈 덮인 = snow-covered; 보이다 = to be visible

examples.ko: 가장 높은 봉우리까지 두 시간쯤 걸려요.
examples.romanization: gajang nopeun bongurikkaji du siganjjeum geollyeoyo.
examples.en: It takes about two hours to reach the highest peak.
examples.note: 가장 높은 = the highest; 걸리다 = to take (time)

entries.nuance: 봉우리 (the 봉 from hanja 峰, 'mountain peak,' plus a native ending) is a single peak or summit, and a ridge or range is understood as several 봉우리 strung together — hikers use it constantly for mountains like 설악산 and 지리산, and the combined 산봉우리 is equally common. The synonym contrast that trips people up is 봉우리 vs 정상: 봉우리 is any one peak among several, while 정상(頂上) is THE very top/highest point you're aiming for — so a mountain can have many 봉우리 but one 정상, and trail talk pairs them (이 봉우리 지나면 정상이에요). Register is neutral, common in hiking and scenery description. The two English-speaker pitfalls: don't equate 봉우리 with 정상 (peak-as-one-of-many vs the single summit), and crucially don't spell it 봉오리 — that's a flower bud, a completely different word, so 산 봉오리 would absurdly mean 'mountain flower-bud.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 봉우리 and 정상 as identical: 봉우리 is one peak among several, while 정상 is the single highest top — a range has many 봉우리 but one 정상.
Spelling it 봉오리: 봉오리 means a flower bud, so the mountain peak must be 봉우리 — a one-vowel slip changes the meaning entirely.
Dropping 산 when context is unclear: in mixed talk 산봉우리 makes 'mountain peak' explicit and avoids ambiguity.

entries.shortExplanation: 해변 means "beach, seashore" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 해변 (haebyeon) = "beach, seashore". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 해변 ("beach / seashore") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 해변, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The sandy shore zone; more 'beach' than the open 바다
산책 = stroll; a very common seaside activity
에서 marks where the activity happens
가 (edge) added; 해변가 카페 = a beachfront cafe

examples.en: In summer I went to Gangneung beach.
examples.note: 강릉 = Gangneung; 에 가다 = go to (a place)

examples.ko: 해변을 따라 걸으니까 노을이 너무 예뻤어요.
examples.romanization: haebyeoneul ttara georeunikka noeuri neomu yeppeosseoyo.
examples.en: Walking along the beach, the sunset was so pretty.
examples.note: 따라 = along; 노을 = sunset glow

examples.en: There weren't many people on the beach, so it was quiet.
examples.note: 별로 + 없다 = not many; 조용하다 = to be quiet

entries.nuance: 해변 (海邊, 'sea-edge') is specifically the sandy beach/shore strip, while 바다 is the sea itself — the distinction is concrete: you lay your towel and stroll on the 해변, but you swim in the 바다, so 해변에서 수영하다 sounds slightly off (you're on the sand, not in the water). East-coast spots like 강릉 and 속초 are the go-to 해변, and it collocates with 산책 (stroll) and 노을 (sunset). The other near-synonym is 해수욕장(海水浴場, 'sea-water-bathing place'): 해변 is the natural shore generally, whereas 해수욕장 is a designated, facility-equipped swimming beach (lifeguards, showers, the official summer-open kind) — overlapping but not identical. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 바다/해변 split: English 'go to the beach' covers both lying out and swimming, but in Korean you 해변에 가다 to be on the shore and 바다에 들어가다 to get in the water.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 해변 (the shore) for 바다 (the sea): 해변에서 수영하다 sounds off because you swim in the water — say 바다에서 수영하다.
Treating 해변 and 해수욕장 as the same: 해수욕장 specifically means a designated swimming beach with facilities, while 해변 is the shore in general.
Carrying over English 'go to the beach' wholesale: Korean splits it into 해변에 가다 (be on the shore) vs 바다에 들어가다 (enter the water).

East-coast spots like 강릉 and 속초 are the go-to 해변, and it collocates with 산책 (stroll) and 노을 (sunset). Register is neutral.

The other near-synonym is 해수욕장(海水浴場, 'sea-water-bathing place'): 해변 is the natural shore generally, whereas 해수욕장 is a designated, facility-equipped swimming beach (lifeguards, showers, the official summer-open kind) — overlapping but not identical.
From 海邊, 'sea-edge.'
The pitfall is exactly that 바다/해변 split: English 'go to the beach' covers both lying out and swimming, but in Korean you 해변에 가다 to be on the shore and 바다에 들어가다 to get in the water.

entries.shortExplanation: 깜짝 means "with a start; suddenly (startled)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 깜짝 (kkamjjak) means "with a start; suddenly (startled)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 깜짝 놀라다 ("to be startled / get a shock"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 깜짝 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to be startled / get a shock
usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing. 깜짝 almost always attaches to 놀라다 — treat them as one chunk.
A reflex exclamation when something startles you. Often stretched to 아이 깜짝이야 or 깜짝 놀랐잖아.
깜짝 + noun = 'surprise ~'. Also 깜짝 파티 (surprise party), 깜짝 방문 (surprise visit), 깜짝 발표 (surprise announcement).
Doubled 깜짝깜짝 means repeatedly flinching, e.g. from loud noises or being on edge.

examples.en: You startled me / I got a shock.
examples.note: The bare-minimum sentence; memorize 깜짝 놀라다 as one unit before anything else.

examples.en: You called me from behind so suddenly that I got startled.
examples.note: Note 불러서 (because you called) gives the cause; 깜짝 sits right before the verb it intensifies.

examples.ko: 뒤에서 친구가 '왁!' 하는 바람에 깜짝이야, 하고 소리를 질렀어요.
examples.romanization: dwieseo chinguga 'wak!' haneun barame kkamjjagiya, hago sorireul jilleosseoyo.
examples.en: My friend went 'Boo!' behind me, and I yelped 'You scared me!'
examples.note: Real-situation: 깜짝이야 used as the live spoken reaction inside a story (반말 narration).

entries.nuance: 깜짝 captures the split-second jolt of being startled, not a gradual surprise — it is the body's flinch the instant something pops up. Compare it with 갑자기 'suddenly': 갑자기 only marks that an event happened without warning (timing), while 깜짝 names the startle reaction itself, so they often appear together (갑자기 ~해서 깜짝 놀랐다). The dividing line vs 놀라다 alone is intensity-of-onset: 깜짝 forces the 'jump' reading. Its strongest collocation is 깜짝 놀라다, and the standalone 깜짝이야! is something you will say constantly. As a noun-modifier it means 'surprise ~' (깜짝 세일, 깜짝 방문). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 깜짝 as a verb: there is no 깜짝하다 — 깜짝 is an adverb and always needs 놀라다 (or another verb) behind it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 깜짝했어요 as if 깜짝 were a verb. 깜짝하다 is not a real word; you must say 깜짝 놀랐어요 — the adverb 깜짝 plus the verb 놀라다.
Using 깜짝 to mean 'suddenly' in a neutral sentence like '갑자기 비가 왔어요'. 깜짝 carries the startle/jump nuance, so for plain unexpected timing you need 갑자기, not 깜짝.
Reaching for 놀라운 (amazing/remarkable) when you mean the jolt. 놀랍다 describes something impressive; 깜짝 놀라다 is the physical flinch — don't swap them.

entries.shortExplanation: 두근두근 means "heart pounding (with excitement or nerves)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "heart pounding (with excitement or nerves)" is 두근두근 (dugeundugeun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가슴이 두근두근하다 ("one's heart goes thump-thump"). Watch the particle attached to 두근두근 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The textbook frame. The subject is 가슴 (chest/heart), and 두근두근 describes how it beats.
Pairs with 설레다 (to be thrilled) for positive anticipation — crushes, trips, first days.
Pairs with 떨리다 (to tremble/be nervous) for the anxious side — auditions, results, exams.
The single-action verb 두근거리다 is the more literary, write-it-down equivalent of 두근두근하다.

examples.en: My heart is pounding.
examples.note: The core sentence — note 가슴이 (heart, as subject) + 두근두근하다 as a descriptive verb.

examples.en: When I meet the person I like, my heart pounds.
examples.note: Everyday romantic context; 만나면 (when/if I meet) sets up the trigger for the flutter.

examples.en: It was my first day at work, so from the morning I was both fluttery and nervous.
examples.note: Real-situation: shows 두근두근 layered with 긴장되다, the mixed excited-anxious feeling a newcomer knows.

entries.nuance: 두근두근 is the sound-feeling of a fast heartbeat (의태어/의성어) and works for BOTH happy anticipation and anxious nerves — context and the partner verb decide which. The key contrast is with 긴장되다 'to be tense/nervous': 긴장되다 is flatly negative stress, whereas 두근두근 is warmer and bodily, often carrying 설렘 (sweet excitement), so a crush or a trip is 두근두근 but rarely just 긴장돼요. It is also distinct from 떨리다 (to physically tremble): 떨려요 can be visible shaking, while 두근두근 is specifically the heart's thumping. Use it adverbially (두근두근 떨려요) or as 두근두근하다. The pitfall for English speakers is mapping it to a pounding heart from physical exertion — after running, Koreans say 숨차다 or 헐떡거리다, not 두근두근, which is reserved for emotional racing. Also remember the subject is usually 가슴/심장, not 'I'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a heart pounding from running or stairs. Exertion is 숨차다 / 헐떡거리다; 두근두근 is the emotional racing of excitement or nerves only.
Assuming it is only fear. 두근두근 strongly implies 설렘 (excitement), so 'I'm scared' alone is 무서워요 — 두근두근 adds the thrilled-anticipation color.
Saying 나는 두근두근해요 with yourself as subject when you really want the heart as subject. The natural frame is 가슴이/심장이 두근두근해요; the heart does the pounding.

entries.shortExplanation: 반짝반짝 means "sparkling; twinkling; shiny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반짝반짝 (banjjakbanjjak) = "sparkling; twinkling; shiny". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 반짝반짝 빛나다 ("to shine/sparkle brightly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 반짝반짝, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The core collocation, for stars, polished surfaces, jewelry, and eager eyes.
Descriptive verb form: 청소했더니 바닥이 반짝반짝해요 (after cleaning, the floor is sparkling).
Describes bright, eager eyes — a child's, or someone lit up with excitement.
Single 반짝 = a brief one-off flash, hence 반짝 세일 (a short, sudden sale) and 반짝 인기 (a brief fad).

examples.en: The stars are twinkling.
examples.note: The simplest frame — 반짝반짝 directly modifies 빛나다.

examples.en: After I finished the dishes, the bowls are sparkling clean.
examples.note: Everyday context; here 반짝반짝하다 works as a stand-alone descriptive verb, no 빛나다 needed.

examples.ko: 선물을 받은 아이가 눈을 반짝반짝하면서 좋아했어요.
examples.romanization: seonmureul badeun aiga nuneul banjjakbanjjakamyeonseo joahaesseoyo.
examples.en: The child who got a present was thrilled, eyes sparkling.
examples.note: Real-situation: 눈이 반짝반짝 for the 'lit-up, eager' look rather than literal shine.

entries.nuance: 반짝반짝 evokes light bouncing off something repeatedly — stars, a just-mopped floor, jewelry, or wide eager eyes. It is famously the opening of the Korean 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' (반짝반짝 작은 별), so it instantly sounds storybook-warm. Two contrasts matter. First, single 반짝 means a brief, one-time flash (반짝 세일, 반짝 스타), whereas doubled 반짝반짝 means continuous glittering. Second, do not confuse it with 번쩍: 반짝 is small, cute, decorative sparkle, while 번쩍 (its 'big brother' with the heavier 어 vowel) is a sudden powerful flash — lightning 번쩍, or 정신이 번쩍 들다 'to snap wide awake'. Korean's vowel symbolism (bright ㅏ/ㅗ = small & cute, dark ㅓ/ㅜ = big & strong) is doing real work here. The English-speaker pitfall is using 반짝반짝 for steady brightness like a lamp; plain brightness is 밝다, and 반짝반짝 specifically requires the glitter/twinkle of reflected, intermittent light.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for steady, non-glittering brightness like a lit lamp or a bright room. Plain brightness is 밝다; 반짝반짝 requires sparkle/twinkle, not constant glow.
Mixing up 반짝 (small cute sparkle) with 번쩍 (a big sudden flash like lightning). The darker vowel in 번쩍 signals something larger and more startling.
Treating 반짝반짝 and single 반짝 as identical. Doubled = ongoing twinkling; single 반짝 = one brief flash, as in 반짝 세일 (flash sale).

entries.shortExplanation: 주룩주룩 means "pouring (rain) steadily; streaming down" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주룩주룩 (jurukjuruk) means "pouring (rain) steadily; streaming down". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비가 주룩주룩 내리다 ("rain pours down steadily"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주룩주룩 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The default frame. 비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the full natural phrase for heavy streaming rain.
For tears running down the face in lines — pairs with 흐르다 (to flow).
For sweat streaming in the heat — 등에 땀이 주룩주룩 (sweat pouring down one's back).
Pairs with 쏟아지다 (to gush) to stress sheer volume of rain.

examples.en: It's pouring (rain).
examples.note: The base weather sentence; 내리다 is the most natural verb for falling rain.

examples.ko: 아침부터 비가 주룩주룩 내려서 우산을 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: achimbuteo biga jurukjurung naeryeoseo usaneul chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It's been pouring since morning, so I grabbed an umbrella.
examples.note: Everyday cause-effect: -아서 (because) links the rain to grabbing the umbrella.

examples.ko: 퇴근길에 갑자기 비가 주룩주룩 쏟아져서 옷이 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: toegeungire gapjagi biga jurukjuruk ssodajyeoseo osi da jeojeosseoyo.
examples.en: On the way home from work, rain suddenly poured down and my clothes got soaked.
examples.note: Real-situation: 주룩주룩 쏟아지다 emphasizing a heavy downpour that drenches you.

entries.nuance: 주룩주룩 describes liquid running down in steady, continuous streams — most often heavy rain, but equally tears and sweat. It is genuinely heavy and unbroken, which is what separates it from the soft drizzle words 부슬부슬 / 보슬보슬 (a fine misty rain you barely need an umbrella for). It also differs from 후두둑, the brief pattering of the first fat drops, and from 주르륵, a single quick run-down (one tear, water down a window); 주룩주룩 is the sustained, repeated version. The natural verb is 내리다 for rain and 흐르다 for tears/sweat. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 주룩주룩 with 오다 by analogy to 'rain comes' — 비가 주룩주룩 와요 is acceptable, but 내리다 sounds cleaner, and crucially you should NOT use 주룩주룩 for light rain at all. During Korea's 장마 (monsoon) season this is the word you'll see in every weather chat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for light rain or drizzle. A fine misty rain is 부슬부슬 / 보슬보슬; 주룩주룩 is genuinely heavy, streaming rain and sounds wrong for a sprinkle.
Defaulting to 비가 주룩주룩 와요. It is not wrong, but 비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the more natural pairing native speakers prefer.
Pairing 주룩주룩 with snow. Snow doesn't 'stream down' — heavy snow is 펑펑 (눈이 펑펑 와요), so reserve 주룩주룩 for rain, tears, and sweat.

entries.shortExplanation: 펑펑 means "(crying) hard; (snowing) heavily; (spending) lavishly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "(crying) hard; (snowing) heavily; (spending) lavishly" is 펑펑 (peongpeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 펑펑 울다 ("to cry one's eyes out"). Watch the particle attached to 펑펑 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Very common: hard, body-shaking sobbing, not a few tears.
Big, fast snowfall in fat flakes. 눈이 펑펑 와요 / 펑펑 내려요.
To splurge / blow money freely, usually with a faintly disapproving tone.
Single 펑 is the actual burst sound — a balloon, a firework, a cork.

examples.en: I cried my eyes out.
examples.note: The base sentence; 펑펑 signals serious sobbing, far stronger than 조금 울었어요.

examples.ko: 밤새 눈이 펑펑 와서 길이 하얘졌어요.
examples.romanization: bamsae nuni peongpeong waseo giri hayaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It snowed heavily all night, so the roads turned white.
examples.note: Everyday weather; 펑펑 with 눈 specifically means thick, fast snowfall.

examples.ko: 월급 받자마자 돈을 펑펑 쓰더니 월말에 카드값 때문에 후회하더라고요.
examples.romanization: wolgeup batjamaja doneul peongpeong sseudeoni wolmare kadeugaps ttaemune huhoehadeoragoyo.
examples.en: She blew money the moment she got paid, then regretted it at month-end over the card bill.
examples.note: Real-situation: 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 with the disapproving 'splurge-then-regret' arc.

entries.nuance: 펑펑 has three everyday senses tied together by the image of something bursting out in abundance: crying hard (펑펑 울다), heavy snowfall (눈이 펑펑 와요), and splurging money (돈을 펑펑 쓰다). Context makes the meaning instantly clear, because each sense has a fixed partner verb (울다 / 오다·내리다 / 쓰다). Two contrasts to lock in. For crying, compare 엉엉 울다 (loud wailing, mouth open) — 펑펑 stresses the gushing flow of tears, 엉엉 the loud sound; both mean hard crying and often interchange. For snow, 펑펑 means big abundant flakes, unlike the rain word 주룩주룩, which never describes snow. The single 펑 is the literal 'pop/bang' of a burst (a vowel-darker, bigger cousin of 팡). The English-speaker pitfall is using 펑펑 for rain — heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 쏟아지다, and 펑펑 with weather means snow only.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 펑펑 for rain. Heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 비가 쏟아지다; with weather, 펑펑 specifically means snow (눈이 펑펑).
Assuming 펑펑 울다 is mild crying. It means serious, hard sobbing — for just a couple of tears use 살짝 울다 or 눈물이 났어요.
Treating 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 as neutral 'spending'. It carries a wasteful/reckless tone; plain spending is just 돈을 쓰다, so don't use 펑펑 unless you mean to imply splurging.

entries.shortExplanation: 살금살금 means "stealthily; tiptoeing quietly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 살금살금 (salgeumsalgeum) = "stealthily; tiptoeing quietly". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 살금살금 걷다 ("to walk stealthily / tiptoe") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 살금살금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core usage: moving quietly on soft feet so as not to be noticed.
Approaching quietly, often to surprise someone or like a cat stalking prey.
Entering quietly, e.g. coming home late and not wanting to wake anyone.
Leaving a room/place without being noticed.

examples.en: I walked on tiptoe / I crept along.
examples.note: The base frame: 살금살금 directly modifies a verb of motion.

examples.ko: 아기가 자고 있어서 살금살금 걸어 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: agiga jago isseoseo salgeumsalgeum georeo nawasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby was sleeping, so I tiptoed out.
examples.note: Everyday considerate movement; -아서 gives the reason for being quiet.

examples.ko: 고양이가 참새를 향해 살금살금 다가가다가 결국 들켜서 참새가 날아가 버렸어요.
examples.romanization: goyangiga chamsaereul hyanghae salgeumsalgeum dagagadaga gyeolguk deulkyeoseo chamsaega naraga beoryeosseoyo.
examples.en: The cat crept toward the sparrow but got spotted in the end, and the sparrow flew off.
examples.note: Real-situation: stalking with 다가가다, the most natural verb for closing in quietly.

entries.nuance: 살금살금 describes moving deliberately and softly so you won't be heard or seen — tiptoeing past a sleeping roommate, a cat stalking a bird, sneaking home late. It carries a slightly playful, cautious feel and pairs with verbs of motion (걷다, 다가가다, 들어가다, 나오다). The sharp contrast to memorize is 슬금슬금: 슬금슬금 means edging away gradually and sheepishly, usually to dodge blame or slip out of a situation (혼날까 봐 슬금슬금 도망쳤다), so it foregrounds 'sneaking off to avoid something', while 살금살금 foregrounds 'quiet footsteps so as not to make noise'. It also differs from 슬며시/슬쩍, which mean doing something subtly or on the sly (slipping a note, a quiet smile) rather than literal quiet walking. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for fast quiet movement: stealthy-but-quick is 후다닥 or 잽싸게, whereas 살금살금 is inherently slow and careful.

Confusing it with 슬금슬금. 슬금슬금 implies edging away sheepishly to avoid blame; 살금살금 is about quiet, careful footsteps so as not to be heard.
Using it for fast quiet movement. Quick-and-quiet is 후다닥 / 잽싸게; 살금살금 is deliberately slow and tiptoeing.
Pairing it with non-motion verbs. 살금살금 needs a verb of moving (걷다, 다가가다); you can't say 살금살금 말하다 for whispering — that's 소곤소곤 / 속삭이다.

entries.shortExplanation: 후다닥 means "hurriedly; in a quick dash" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 후다닥 (hudadak) means "hurriedly; in a quick dash". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후다닥 일어나다 ("to jump up quickly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후다닥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Springing up in a flustered burst, e.g. when you oversleep and bolt out of bed.

usagePhrases.en: to get ready in a rush
usagePhrases.note: Throwing yourself together fast and a little frantically.
Eating very fast, gulping it down before running off.
Running off suddenly, often half in a panic.

examples.en: I jumped up in a flash.
examples.note: The base frame: 후다닥 + a quick action verb.

examples.en: I overslept, so I got ready in a mad rush and left.
examples.note: Everyday morning scramble; -아서 links oversleeping to the frantic prep.

examples.ko: 바퀴벌레가 갑자기 나타나는 바람에 다들 비명을 지르며 후다닥 도망갔어요.
examples.romanization: bakwibeollega gapjagi natananeun barame dadeul bimyeongeul jireumyeo hudadak domanggasseoyo.
examples.en: A cockroach suddenly appeared, so everyone screamed and bolted.
examples.note: Real-situation: 후다닥 도망가다 for a sudden, slightly comic panic-dash.

entries.nuance: 후다닥 conveys doing something in a fast, slightly frantic burst — jumping up, scrambling to get ready, dashing off. The defining flavor is speed PLUS commotion or fluster, which is exactly what separates it from the neutral 빨리 'quickly' and from 잽싸게 'nimbly/deftly': 빨리 is plain speed and 잽싸게 implies smooth, skillful quickness, whereas 후다닥 implies a flustered scramble, often with noise or panic. It is also distinct from 허둥지둥, which stresses being flustered and disorganized (flailing, losing things in your haste); 후다닥 keeps the focus on the quick burst of action itself. Note 후다닥 has the heavy ㅜ/ㅏ vowels of a bigger, more energetic motion, versus the lighter 호다닥. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is pairing it with calm, careful, or slow actions — it clashes with 천천히 and with deliberate tasks, so use it only when there's a hurried, scrambling feel.

Using it for calm, smooth speed. Efficient quickness is 빨리 or 잽싸게; 후다닥 implies a flustered, noisy scramble.
Pairing it with slow or careful actions. 후다닥 천천히 or 후다닥 + a meticulous task is contradictory — the word demands a hurried burst.
Confusing it with 허둥지둥. 허둥지둥 stresses panicky disorganization (flailing about); 후다닥 stresses the quick, sudden burst of the action.

entries.shortExplanation: 빙글빙글 means "round and round; spinning" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "round and round; spinning" is 빙글빙글 (binggeulbinggeul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빙글빙글 돌다 ("to spin round and round"). Watch the particle attached to 빙글빙글 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: turning continuously in circles (intransitive).
The everyday way to say you feel dizzy: 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요.
Transitive: spinning an object, e.g. twirling a pen or a hula hoop.
Shorter 빙빙 is a near-synonym with a slightly faster, looser feel.

examples.en: The top spins round and round.
examples.note: The base frame: 빙글빙글 directly modifies 돌다.

examples.en: I stood up suddenly and my head started spinning.
examples.note: Everyday dizziness; -았더니 (did X, and as a result) links standing up to the dizzy spell.

examples.ko: 회전목마를 너무 오래 탔는지 내려서도 세상이 빙글빙글 도는 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: hoejeonmongmareul neomu orae tanneunji naeryeoseodo sesangi binggeulbinggeul doneun geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe I rode the carousel too long — even after getting off, the world seemed to spin.
examples.note: Real-situation: 빙글빙글 돌다 extended to a lingering whirling sensation.

entries.nuance: 빙글빙글 describes smooth, continuous rotation in place — a spinning top, a carousel, or a dizzy head whirling. For dizziness, 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요 is the natural everyday phrase you'd give a doctor or friend, and 어지러워요 (I'm dizzy) is its plain companion. The crucial contrast is with 데굴데굴: 빙글빙글 is rotating on the spot, while 데굴데굴 is a round object ROLLING ALONG the ground (a ball, a dropped tangerine) — same idea of turning, totally different path. Within the spinning family, the shorter 빙빙 is interchangeable in most cases but feels a touch quicker and is common in 빙빙 돌리다 / 빙빙 돌려 말하다 (to beat around the bush), whereas the darker-vowel 뱅뱅 suggests tighter, smaller circles. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is using 빙글빙글 for a single half-turn: one turn is just 돌다, and 빙글빙글 requires repeated, ongoing rotation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a single turn or half-turn. One turn is 돌다 by itself; 빙글빙글 implies continuous, repeated rotation.
Confusing it with 데굴데굴. 빙글빙글 is spinning in place; 데굴데굴 is rolling along the ground like a ball.
Saying 나는 빙글빙글 돌아요 to mean 'I'm dizzy'. The natural frame puts the head as subject: 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요, or simply 어지러워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 콜록콜록 means "cough-cough (sound of coughing)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 콜록콜록 (kollokkollok) = "cough-cough (sound of coughing)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 콜록콜록 기침하다 ("to cough repeatedly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 콜록콜록, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core pairing with 기침하다 (to cough); the two go together naturally.
Verb form for ongoing coughing fits, written as one word.
Light spoken form, often about a child. 아이가 콜록콜록해요.
Single 콜록 is one cough sound; doubling it = repeated coughing.

examples.en: I'm coughing (cough-cough).
examples.note: The base frame: 콜록콜록 directly modifies 기침하다.

examples.en: I caught a cold and coughed all night long.
examples.note: Everyday clinic/pharmacy line; 감기에 걸리다 (to catch a cold) is the standard collocation.

examples.ko: 옆자리 사람이 마스크도 안 쓰고 콜록콜록거려서 자리를 옮겼어요.
examples.romanization: yeopjari sarami maseukeudo an sseugo kollokkollokgeoryeoseo jarireul olmgyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The person next to me kept coughing without even a mask, so I moved seats.
examples.note: Real-situation: 콜록콜록거리다 in a slightly annoyed observation about someone else.

entries.nuance: 콜록콜록 is the onomatopoeia for repeated coughing and pairs naturally with 기침하다, or stands alone as 콜록콜록거리다 / 콜록콜록하다. It is the word you'll actually use to describe cold symptoms to a 약사 (pharmacist) or 의사 (doctor), alongside 기침이 나요 (I have a cough). A single dry cough is 콜록; the doubled form signals ongoing coughing fits. Two distinctions help. First, 콜록콜록 vs 쿨럭쿨럭: both exist, but the darker-vowel 쿨럭 suggests a deeper, heavier chest cough, while 콜록 is the lighter, standard form you should default to. Second, do not confuse coughing with sneezing — a sneeze is 에취 (the sound) or 재채기 (the noun/act), never 콜록콜록. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja; note that the related noun 기침 and verb 기침하다 are the clinical words, and 콜록콜록 is the vivid sound layered on top. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the rhythm of English 'cough' and writing 콜럭 or mixing spellings; the standard, safe spelling is 콜록콜록.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 콜록콜록 for a sneeze. A sneeze is 에취 / 재채기; 콜록콜록 is specifically the sound of coughing.
Treating 콜록콜록 as a verb on its own. To make it a verb, add an ending: 콜록콜록거리다 / 콜록콜록하다, or pair it with 기침하다.
Switching to heavier-vowel 쿨럭쿨럭 by default. 쿨럭 implies a deeper, heavier cough; the standard everyday form is 콜록콜록.

entries.shortExplanation: 쿨쿨 means "(sleeping) soundly; zzz" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쿨쿨 (kulkul) means "(sleeping) soundly; zzz". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 쿨쿨 자다 ("to sleep soundly / snooze away"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쿨쿨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: deep, sound sleep. 쿨쿨 almost always attaches to 자다.
Dropping into deep sleep (잠들다 = to fall asleep).
Progressive: someone is sound asleep right now.

usagePhrases.en: to snooze / breathe heavily in sleep
usagePhrases.note: Verb form, sometimes implying soft, audible sleeping breaths.

examples.en: (He) is sleeping soundly / zzz.
examples.note: The base frame: 쿨쿨 directly modifies 자다.

examples.en: On weekends I want to sleep in soundly until late.
examples.note: Everyday wish; -고 싶다 (want to) attaches to the verb after 쿨쿨.

examples.ko: 남편은 옆에서 아기가 우는데도 모르고 쿨쿨 자고 있더라고요.
examples.romanization: nampyeoneun yeopeseo agiga uneundedo moreugo kulkul jago itdeoragoyo.
examples.en: My husband was fast asleep, oblivious, even though the baby was crying right next to him.
examples.note: Real-situation: 쿨쿨 자다 with a fond-but-exasperated tone about dead-to-the-world sleep.

entries.nuance: 쿨쿨 is the cozy onomatopoeia for sleeping deeply and soundly — the Korean equivalent of 'zzz'. It pairs almost exclusively with 자다 / 잠들다 and carries a warm, slightly cute tone, so you'd use it for a tired roommate napping or a pet snoozing, not for a clinical sleep report (수면 / 숙면 are the formal words). Two contrasts sharpen it. First, 쿨쿨 means genuinely deep sleep, unlike 꾸벅꾸벅 졸다, which is nodding off / dozing while basically awake (on the subway, in a meeting). Second, do not equate it with snoring: heavy snoring is 드르렁드르렁 or the verb 코를 골다, whereas 쿨쿨 is peaceful, gentle sleeping — at most softly audible breathing, not a sawing snore. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 쿨쿨 to mean any kind of resting; for a quick nap-while-sitting you want 졸다, and for 'go to bed/sleep' in a neutral sense you simply use 자다 — 쿨쿨 specifically adds the 'out cold, sound asleep' picture.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for dozing or nodding off while awake. A light doze is 꾸벅꾸벅 졸다; 쿨쿨 means genuinely deep, sound sleep.
Equating 쿨쿨 with snoring. Loud snoring is 드르렁드르렁 / 코를 골다; 쿨쿨 is peaceful sleeping, not a snore.
Using 쿨쿨 in a formal or medical context. For clinical 'sleep' use 자다 / 수면; 쿨쿨 is casual and a bit cute.

entries.shortExplanation: 데굴데굴 means "rolling (along the ground)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rolling (along the ground)" is 데굴데굴 (deguldegul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 데굴데굴 구르다 ("to roll along / tumble"). Watch the particle attached to 데굴데굴 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: a round thing rolling on the ground (구르다 = to roll).
Rolling off in a direction, away from you.

usagePhrases.en: to roll around on the floor
usagePhrases.note: Often used jokingly for laughing hard or writhing in pain on the floor.
Tense/emphatic variant 떼굴떼굴 for heavier, bigger, more forceful rolling.

examples.en: The ball is rolling away.
examples.note: The base frame: 데굴데굴 + 굴러가다 for a thing rolling off.

examples.en: The ball fell off the desk and rolled away.
examples.note: Everyday object mishap; -아서 chains 'fell off' to 'rolled away'.

examples.ko: 그 개그가 너무 웃겨서 다 같이 바닥에서 데굴데굴 굴렀어요.
examples.romanization: geu gaegeuga neomu utgyeoseo da gachi badageseo deguldegul gulleosseoyo.
examples.en: That joke was so funny we all rolled on the floor laughing.
examples.note: Real-situation: the idiomatic 'ROFL' use, 바닥에서 데굴데굴 구르다.

entries.nuance: 데굴데굴 describes a round object rolling along a surface — a ball, a dropped tangerine, a marble — and by extension a person 'rolling on the floor' laughing hard or doubled over in pain (바닥에서 데굴데굴 구르다, the Korean ROFL). The defining feature is travel along the ground, which is exactly the line against 빙글빙글: 빙글빙글 spins IN PLACE (a top, a dizzy head), while 데굴데굴 always moves the object ALONG. Size matters too: for tiny things rolling — a bead, a single tear, a marble down a slope — 또르르 is the natural choice, whereas 데굴데굴 fits ball-sized objects; and the tenser 떼굴떼굴 amps up the weight/force. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja, but notice the bright ㅔ/ㅜ vowels give it a rounder, friendlier feel than its heavier cousin 떼굴떼굴. The English-speaker pitfall is using 데굴데굴 for spinning in place; if nothing travels across the floor, you want 빙글빙글, not 데굴데굴.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 빙글빙글 (spinning in place). 데굴데굴 always involves a round thing moving along the ground.
Using it for tiny objects. For small things like beads or marbles rolling, 또르르 is more natural; 데굴데굴 fits ball-sized objects.
Forgetting the partner verb. 데굴데굴 needs 구르다 / 굴러가다; saying 데굴데굴 alone without the rolling verb sounds incomplete.

entries.explanation: 두리번두리번 (duribeonduribeon) = "looking around (searchingly)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 두리번두리번 둘러보다 ("to look all around") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 두리번두리번, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: scanning the surroundings (둘러보다 = to look around).
The 거리다 form, just as common as the doubled adverb in speech and writing.
Descriptive verb form: looking this way and that.
Pairs with 주위 / 사방 (surroundings, all directions).

examples.en: I looked all around.
examples.note: The base frame: 두리번두리번 + 둘러보다.

examples.en: I looked around the cafe searching for my friend.
examples.note: Everyday searching; -느라 (busy doing X) gives the reason for scanning.

examples.ko: 처음 와 본 동네라 출구가 어디인지 두리번거리다가 결국 지나가는 분께 길을 물었어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum wa bon dongnera chulguga eodiinji duribeongeoridaga gyeolguk jinaganeun bunkke gireul mureosseoyo.
examples.en: It was my first time in the area, so I looked around for the exit and finally asked a passerby for directions.
examples.note: Real-situation: 두리번거리다 for a lost newcomer getting their bearings.

entries.nuance: 두리번두리번 captures turning your head this way and that to take in your surroundings — searching for someone, getting your bearings when lost, or wide-eyed in a new place. It implies a slightly anxious or curious, restless scanning, and the 거리다 form 두리번거리다 is every bit as common as the doubled adverb. Two contrasts pin it down. Against a single glance: one quick look is 흘끗/힐끗 보다 or 쳐다보다, whereas 두리번두리번 is repeated looking in multiple directions. Against 기웃거리다 (기웃기웃): 기웃거리다 is craning to PEEK INTO a specific spot — a shop window, someone's doorway, often a bit nosy — while 두리번두리번 is broad, all-around scanning of open space. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja; note that the verb pair 둘러보다 'to look around' is the neutral action and 두리번두리번 adds the vivid restless-scanning picture. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for a single directed look; reserve 두리번두리번 for head-turning in several directions.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a single glance. One look is 흘끗/힐끗 보다 or 쳐다보다; 두리번두리번 means repeated looking in multiple directions.
Confusing it with 기웃거리다 (peeking into a place). 두리번두리번 is broad all-around scanning; 기웃거리다 is craning to peek into one spot, often nosily.
Pairing it with a fixed-stare verb like 노려보다 (to glare). 두리번두리번 implies the eyes/head keep moving, so it clashes with steady-stare verbs.

entries.shortExplanation: 단순하다 means "to be simple, plain, uncomplicated" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 단순하다 (dansunhada) means "to be simple, plain, uncomplicated". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 디자인이 단순해요 ("The design is simple"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단순하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: praising a clean, minimal look; 하다-adjective, so 단순하 + 여요 → 단순해요
noun-modifying form is 단순한 + N, never 단순하는
단순한 = 'mere/plain', softening the error as not deep or malicious

usagePhrases.en: Don't think about it too simply
usagePhrases.note: 단순하게 = adverb; casual 반말 warning not to oversimplify

examples.en: This app's screen is simple.
examples.note: plain statement; 단순하다 praises an uncluttered interface

examples.ko: 저는 성격이 단순한 편이라 뒤끝이 없어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun seonggyeogi dansunhan pyeonira dwikkeuchi eopseoyo.
examples.en: I have a pretty simple personality, so I don't hold grudges.
examples.note: 단순한 + 편이다 = 'on the simple side'; describes an easygoing, low-drama nature, not low intelligence

examples.en: The cause was simpler than expected, so I fixed it quickly.
examples.note: 단순해서 = 아서/어서 reason; real troubleshooting reassurance

entries.nuance: 단순(單純) literally combines 單 'single' + 純 'pure', so the core image is 'one pure thing, nothing extra'. It means simple, plain, or uncomplicated in structure or design and is normally positive or neutral. The near-synonym to keep apart is 간단하다(簡單): 간단하다 stresses that a task is quick and brief to do (간단한 점심, 간단히 설명하다), while 단순하다 stresses that a thing's makeup is plain with few parts (단순한 구조). It is a 하다-adjective, so the 요-form is 단순해요 and the modifier is 단순한. Applied to a person, 단순하다 means easygoing and uncomplicated, NOT dumb. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the English insult 'he's simple' to mean stupid: 단순한 사람 actually sounds like a refreshingly drama-free person; for 'dumb' Koreans add words and say 머리가 단순하다 or 단순무식하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Swapping 간단하다 and 단순하다 freely. 간단한 식사 (a quick, light meal) cannot become 단순한 식사 without sounding odd, because 단순하다 describes plain structure, not brevity of effort. Use 간단하다 for quick/brief, 단순하다 for plain/uncomplicated.
Saying 단순한 사람 to call someone stupid. To a Korean ear it praises an easygoing, grudge-free personality. For 'dumb' you must say 머리가 단순하다 or 단순무식하다.
Conjugating it like a verb (단순하다고 생각하는 사람 is fine, but 단순하는 구조 is wrong). As an adjective the present modifier is 단순한, never 단순하는.

entries.english: to be dense, finely-spaced, tightly woven
entries.shortExplanation: 촘촘하다 means "to be dense, finely-spaced, tightly woven" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be dense, finely-spaced, tightly woven" is 촘촘하다 (chomchomhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 촘촘한 빗 ("a fine-toothed comb"). Watch the particle attached to 촘촘하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 촘촘한 + N; the teeth sit very close with tiny gaps
촘촘하게 = adverb; habitual partner of 짜다(weave/knit)
small even gaps between threads; nothing slips through
figurative: a thorough plan with no loose gaps

examples.en: The mosquito net's holes are fine.
examples.note: plain description; tiny, evenly spaced gaps

examples.en: This knit is densely woven, so it's warm.
examples.note: 촘촘하게 짜이다 = passive 'to be woven tightly'; classic clothing comment

examples.ko: 계획을 너무 촘촘하게 세웠더니 쉴 틈이 없었어요.
examples.romanization: gyehoegeul neomu chomchomhage sewotdeoni swil teumi eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: I planned things so tightly that there was no room to rest.
examples.note: figurative; -았더니 reports the consequence of an over-detailed plan

entries.nuance: 촘촘하다 is a native Korean (고유어) word, often felt as the doubled 촘촘 'close-close', describing units packed very near each other with tiny, EVEN gaps: comb teeth, mesh, knit stitches, dotted print, or a finely detailed plan. Its tone is usually positive, carrying a sense of fineness and thoroughness. The synonym to contrast is 빽빽하다: 빽빽하다 stresses crowded fullness with no room to breathe and is often slightly negative (빽빽한 지하철), whereas 촘촘하다 stresses small regular spacing and craftsmanship (촘촘한 그물). The opposite is 성기다 / 듬성듬성하다 (sparse, gappy). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'dense' and landing on 빽빽하다 for everything: a fine-toothed comb or tightly knit fabric is 촘촘하다, not 빽빽하다, and big things crammed together (a packed train) are 빽빽하다, not 촘촘하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 촘촘하다 for large objects crowded together, e.g. 사람이 촘촘하다 for a packed crowd. People packed in are 빽빽하다; 촘촘하다 fits small repeated units like teeth, threads, stitches, dots.
Treating 촘촘하다 and 빽빽하다 as identical. 촘촘하다 = fine, even, often praised spacing; 빽빽하다 = crammed with no room, often a complaint. A tightly knit sweater is 촘촘한 니트, not 빽빽한 니트.
Pairing it with the wrong verb. The natural collocation is 촘촘하게 짜다/심다 (weave/plant densely); 촘촘하게 많다 is unnatural.

entries.shortExplanation: 헐렁하다 means "to be loose, baggy, slack (clothing/fit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 헐렁하다 (heolleonghada) = "to be loose, baggy, slack (clothing/fit)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 바지가 헐렁해요 ("The pants are baggy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 헐렁하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the fit is too loose around the body
헐렁한 + N; can be an intentional oversized style
헐렁하게 = adverb; a deliberate relaxed styling choice
non-clothing use for a fitting that has worked loose

examples.en: This T-shirt is a bit loose.
examples.note: plain fit comment while trying clothes on

examples.en: I lost weight, so my jeans got baggy.
examples.note: 헐렁해지다 = 'became loose'; -아지다 marks the change of state, not a permanent trait

examples.ko: 문고리가 헐렁해서 곧 빠질 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: mungoriga heolleonghaeseo got ppajil geot gatayo.
examples.en: The door handle is loose, so it looks like it'll fall off soon.
examples.note: 헐렁해서 = reason; shows the hardware sense beyond clothes

entries.nuance: 헐렁하다 is a native Korean word for loose, baggy, or slack — mainly clothes that hang away from the body, but also screws, handles, or fittings that have lost their grip. It is the opposite of 꽉 끼다 (skin-tight) and 빡빡하다 (stiff/resistant). The synonym worth separating is 넉넉하다: 넉넉한 옷 is pleasantly roomy with comfortable margin (a compliment), while 헐렁한 옷 leans toward too-loose, sloppy, or oversized. Figuratively 헐렁하다 can paint a person as lax and careless (성격이 헐렁하다 = laid-back to the point of unreliable). The big English-speaker pitfall is using 넓다 for loose clothing because English 'wide/loose' blur together: 넓다 means wide in AREA (a wide road, a wide room), so 바지가 넓다 sounds like the trousers cover a large floor area; loose FIT is 헐렁하다. Also remember 헐렁해지다 for 'became loose' — bare 헐렁했다 implies it was always baggy.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 넓다 for loose clothes (바지가 넓어요). 넓다 = wide in area; loose in fit = 헐렁하다. A baggy shirt is 헐렁한 셔츠, never 넓은 셔츠.
Dropping the change-of-state -아지다. Saying 청바지가 헐렁했다 to mean 'got loose' actually reads as 'the jeans were (always) baggy'; for 'became baggy' you need 헐렁해졌다.
Treating 헐렁하다 as a pure compliment. For a flattering 'nicely roomy' fit, Koreans prefer 넉넉하다; 헐렁하다 often implies it's looser than ideal.

entries.english: to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic
entries.shortExplanation: 빡빡하다 means "to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 빡빡하다 (ppakppakada) means "to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일정이 빡빡해요 ("The schedule is tight"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 빡빡하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the most common figurative use: no spare time

usagePhrases.en: the door is stiff (hard to open)
usagePhrases.note: physical resistance when you push or slide it
빡빡한 + N; back-to-back with no breaks
barely enough money to cover everything

examples.en: The drawer is stiff, so it doesn't open well.
examples.note: physical sense; 빡빡해서 = reason for the resistance

examples.en: I have lots of meetings today, so my schedule is packed.
examples.note: the everyday office use; 일정이 빡빡하다 is a fixed collocation

examples.en: After paying rent, my living budget is tight.
examples.note: money sense; -고 나면 = 'once I've done'; very relatable for residents

entries.nuance: 빡빡하다 is a colloquial native word built on the tense, forceful sound 빡, and it splits into two everyday senses: physically tight and stiff (a drawer, screw, or door that RESISTS moving) and figuratively tight (a packed schedule or a barely-sufficient budget). In both, the core image is zero slack, no breathing room. The synonym to separate is 빠듯하다: 빠듯하다 leans on 'only just enough, cutting it close' (시간이 빠듯하다 = we'll barely make it), while 빡빡하다 adds a feeling of pressure, stiffness, and friction. Don't confuse it with the slang 빡세다, which means an activity is physically or mentally grueling/hardcore (운동이 빡세다), not 'tightly packed'. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'tight schedule' onto 좁다: 좁다 is narrow in physical SPACE (a narrow alley), so 일정이 좁다 is wrong; a tight schedule is 일정이 빡빡하다. Likewise a tight budget is 예산이 빡빡하다, not 예산이 좁다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 좁다 for a tight schedule or budget (일정이 좁아요 / 예산이 좁아요). 좁다 = narrow in space; tight in time/money = 빡빡하다 (or 빠듯하다).
Mixing up 빡빡하다 and 빡세다. 빡세다 (slang) = grueling/hardcore (알바가 빡세다); 빡빡하다 = tight with no slack (스케줄이 빡빡하다). They are not interchangeable.
Overusing it in very formal writing. 빡빡하다 is casual-to-neutral spoken Korean; in a stiff report you might prefer 빠듯하다 or 여유가 없다.

entries.shortExplanation: 매끄럽다 means "to be smooth, sleek, slick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be smooth, sleek, slick" is 매끄럽다 (maekkeureopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 피부가 매끄러워요 ("The skin is smooth"). Watch the particle attached to 매끄럽다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: 매끄럽 + 어요 → 매끄러워요
매끄러운 + N; ㅂ → 우 before the modifier 운
figurative: deal with something without friction or conflict
of an event or process running without hitches

examples.en: This paper has a smooth surface.
examples.note: plain touch description; note 매끄러워요, not 매끄럽어요

examples.en: After I put on lotion, my skin became smooth.
examples.note: 매끄러워지다 = change of state, still ㅂ-irregular; -았더니 reports the result

examples.en: I'm relieved the presentation ended smoothly.
examples.note: figurative: a polished, hitch-free flow; 매끄럽게 = adverb

entries.nuance: 매끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the ㅂ becomes 우/워, giving 매끄러워요, 매끄러운, 매끄러우니까, 매끄러워서 — memorize the 요-form 매끄러워요 and the rest follows. It means smooth and frictionless to the touch (skin, paper, fabric, a polished floor) and figuratively a process or speech that flows without awkward bumps. The crucial synonym contrast is 미끄럽다: both come from the same 'slip' family, but 매끄럽다 is the pleasant, sleek 'smooth to the touch' (a compliment for skin), while 미끄럽다 is the dangerous 'slippery, slip-prone' (a warning about a wet floor). Saying the bathroom floor is 매끄러워요 sounds like you admire its sleek finish; to warn someone they might slip you must say 미끄러워요. The English-speaker pitfall is the regular conjugation 매끄럽어요 — wrong; it must be 매끄러워요, because all ㅂ-irregular adjectives like 춥다→추워요 and 무겁다→무거워요 behave this way.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 매끄럽어요 / 매끄럽은. As a ㅂ-irregular it is 매끄러워요 and 매끄러운, exactly like 춥다 → 추워요 → 추운.
Confusing 매끄럽다 with 미끄럽다. 매끄럽다 = sleek/smooth to the touch (good); 미끄럽다 = slippery/slip-prone (danger). For 'careful, it's slippery' say 미끄러워요, not 매끄러워요.
Using it only for physical surfaces. 매끄럽다 also describes a smooth process or delivery — 일을 매끄럽게 처리하다, 발표가 매끄럽다.

Saying the bathroom floor is 매끄러워요 sounds like you admire its sleek finish; to warn someone they might slip you must say 미끄러워요.

The pitfall is the regular conjugation 매끄럽어요 — wrong; it must be 매끄러워요, because all ㅂ-irregular adjectives like 춥다→추워요 and 무겁다→무거워요 behave this way.

entries.shortExplanation: 거칠다 means "to be rough, coarse; (manner) harsh" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 거칠다 (geochilda) = "to be rough, coarse; (manner) harsh". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 손이 거칠어요 ("The hands are rough") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 거칠다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㄹ-stem: 거칠 + 어요 → 거칠어요 (ㄹ kept before 어)
거친 + N; the ㄹ DROPS before ㄴ → 거친, not 거칠은

usagePhrases.en: the way of speaking is harsh
usagePhrases.note: figurative: blunt, rough manner of speech
거칠어지다 = change of state from smooth to rough

examples.en: This towel is a bit coarse.
examples.note: plain texture comment; not soft against the skin

examples.ko: 겨울이라 손이 거칠어져서 핸드크림을 자주 발라요.
examples.romanization: gyeourira soni geochireojyeoseo haendeukeurimeul jaju ballayo.
examples.en: It's winter, so my hands get rough and I use hand cream often.
examples.note: 거칠어지다 = becomes rough; -아서/어서 chains the reason

examples.ko: 그 사람은 말투가 거칠지만 마음은 따뜻해요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun maltuga geochiljiman maeumeun ttatteutaeyo.
examples.en: That person speaks harshly, but has a warm heart.
examples.note: figurative; -지만 contrasts the rough manner with the kind nature

entries.nuance: 거칠다 is a native ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) adjective meaning rough or coarse to the touch (skin, towels, unfinished surfaces) and, figuratively, harsh or rough in manner (말투가 거칠다, 운전이 거칠다, 숨이 거칠다). It is the antonym of 매끄럽다 and 부드럽다. The synonym to contrast is 까칠하다: 까칠하다 is a smaller, prickly roughness — slightly stubbly skin, OR a person who is touchy and prickly in temperament (성격이 까칠하다) — whereas 거칠다 is broader and rougher, covering coarse texture and genuinely harsh, wild behavior. The grammar pitfall English speakers hit is the ㄹ-stem rule: the ㄹ DROPS before ㄴ, so the present modifier is 거친 손, never 거칠은 손; but it STAYS before 어, giving 거칠어요. A second pitfall is limiting it to texture — in English 'rough' splits into many words, but 거칠다 naturally also covers harsh speech and aggressive, reckless driving (난폭운전).

Writing the modifier as 거칠은 (e.g. 거칠은 손). As a ㄹ-stem the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, so it must be 거친 손, like 길다 → 긴, 멀다 → 먼.

Confusing 거칠다 with 까칠하다 for personality. 까칠하다 = touchy, prickly, hard to please; 거칠다 = harsh, wild, rough-mannered. They paint different characters.
