entries.shortExplanation: 끈적하다 means "to be sticky, tacky, gooey" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 끈적하다 (kkeunjeokada) means "to be sticky, tacky, gooey". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 손이 끈적해요 ("My hands are sticky"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 끈적하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: typically after touching something sugary or sweaty
끈적한 + N; tacky residue underfoot
끈적하게 = adverb; partner of 남다(remain)
humid, clammy summer air clinging to the skin

examples.en: I spilled a drink, so the table is sticky.
examples.note: everyday cleanup scene; 끈적해서 also works for the reason

examples.en: In summer it's humid, so my body feels sticky.
examples.note: 끈적하다 for sweaty, clammy skin — a core Korean-summer word

examples.ko: 이 로션은 발라도 안 끈적해서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i rosyeoneun ballado an kkeunjeokaeseo joayo.
examples.en: This lotion isn't sticky even after applying, so it's nice.
examples.note: -아도 = 'even if'; a standard cosmetic-review point

entries.nuance: 끈적하다 (and its lively variants 끈적거리다, 끈적이다, 끈적끈적하다) is a native word for a sticky, tacky, clinging feel: spilled drinks drying on a table, sweat on a humid day, gooey residue, or honey on the fingers. For Korea's muggy summers it perfectly captures clammy skin and 끈적한 날씨. The doubled 끈적끈적하다 amps up to a heavier, syrupy stickiness. The key synonym contrast is with 미끄럽다 (slippery): they are near-opposites in physics — 끈적하다 GRIPS and clings so things stick together, while 미끄럽다 is frictionless so things slide apart. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing texture with taste: English 'sweet and sticky' bundles them, but in Korean 끈적하다 is purely the sticky TEXTURE, and 달다 is the sweet TASTE — a honey-coated table is 끈적하다, the honey itself is 달다. Figuratively 끈적한 시선/관계 can also mean an uncomfortably clingy gaze or relationship.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 끈적하다 with 미끄럽다. 끈적하다 clings and grips (sticky honey); 미끄럽다 slides away (slippery ice). They describe opposite surface behavior.
Using 달다 (sweet) when you mean the sticky feel. Texture = 끈적하다; taste = 달다. Don't say 이 바닥이 달아요 for a sticky floor.
Forgetting the colloquial -거리다/-이다 forms. In speech Koreans often say 손이 끈적거려요 / 끈적여요 for an ongoing sticky sensation; sticking only to 끈적하다 sounds a little flat.

entries.english: to be densely packed, crammed, dense
entries.shortExplanation: 빽빽하다 means "to be densely packed, crammed, dense" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be densely packed, crammed, dense" is 빽빽하다 (ppaekppaekada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사람이 빽빽해요 ("It's packed with people"). Watch the particle attached to 빽빽하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: crammed so there's no room to move
빽빽한 + N; trees standing close together
tightly written with little spacing between lines
빽빽하게 = adverb; fixed pair with 들어차다(be filled)

examples.en: The subway at commute time is packed with people.
examples.note: a very relatable Seoul commute; 사람이 빽빽하다 is a set phrase

examples.en: The planner is crammed full of appointments.
examples.note: 빽빽하게 적히다 = densely written; figurative packed schedule

examples.ko: 나무가 빽빽해서 햇빛이 잘 안 들어와요.
examples.romanization: namuga ppaekppaekaeseo haetbichi jal an deureowayo.
examples.en: The trees are dense, so sunlight barely gets in.
examples.note: 빽빽해서 = reason; nature/forest sense

entries.nuance: 빽빽하다 is a native word, felt through the tight, stuffed sound 빽, meaning crammed full with almost no gaps: a packed subway, a dense forest, lines of tiny text squeezed onto a page. Its emphasis is crowdedness and lack of room, and it often carries a slightly oppressive, uncomfortable tone. Contrast it carefully with 촘촘하다 and 복잡하다. Versus 촘촘하다: 촘촘하다 admires fine, even, deliberate spacing (a finely woven net), while 빽빽하다 just stresses 'stuffed full, no space' (a forest you can't walk through). Versus 복잡하다(複雜): 복잡하다 means complicated or chaotically busy in arrangement (복잡한 절차, 복잡한 길), whereas 빽빽하다 is specifically about physical density. The opposite is 한산하다 (deserted, sparse) or 듬성듬성하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using bare 많다 for a crowd: 사람이 많다 just says 'there are many people', while 빽빽하다 adds the crucial nuance of being packed in with no breathing space.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 빽빽하다 with 복잡하다. 복잡하다 = complicated/chaotic (복잡한 신청 절차); 빽빽하다 = physically densely packed (사람이 빽빽한 지하철). A crowded train is 빽빽하다; a confusing procedure is 복잡하다.
Using 많다 alone where you need density. 사람이 많아요 = 'there are lots of people'; for 'packed tight with no room' add 빽빽해요.
Applying 빽빽하다 to fine even spacing. A tightly knit fabric or fine-toothed comb is 촘촘하다; 빽빽하다 is for crowded fullness, not delicate spacing.

entries.english: to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide
entries.shortExplanation: 널찍하다 means "to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 널찍하다 (neoljjikada) = "to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방이 널찍해요 ("The room is spacious") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 널찍하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: pleasantly roomy, with a positive feel
널찍한 + N; sounds inviting and comfortable

usagePhrases.en: to settle into a roomy spot
usagePhrases.note: 널찍하게 = adverb; spreading out comfortably
easy to park because there's plenty of space

examples.en: This cafe has roomy seating.
examples.note: plain praise; a popular cafe-hunting criterion in Korea

examples.en: For a studio, the bathroom is quite spacious.
examples.note: N치고 = 'considering it's a ~'; a house-hunting compliment

examples.ko: 거실이 널찍해서 가구를 더 놓을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: geosiri neoljjikaeseo gagureul deo noeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: The living room is roomy, so I can fit more furniture.
examples.note: 널찍해서 = reason; -을 수 있다 shows the practical payoff

entries.nuance: 널찍하다 is a native word derived from 넓다 (wide) plus the suffix -찍하다, which adds a warm, satisfied 'pleasantly so' nuance — so it means not just wide but comfortably, generously roomy, almost always a compliment. The synonym to keep distinct is plain 넓다: 넓다 is the neutral, measurable 'wide/large in area' (운동장이 넓다), while 널찍하다 layers on the feeling that the space is enjoyably spacious and comfortable. You'd use 널찍하다 when house- or seat-hunting to say a place feels nice and open, not merely big. Its direct opposite is 비좁다 (cramped). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 넓다 for everything because English 'spacious' and 'wide' overlap: if you want the cozy, appreciative 'nice and roomy', 널찍하다 carries it, whereas 넓다 can sound flatly factual. Watch the spelling too — it is 널찍하다, not the common misspelling 넓직하다, even though it comes from 넓다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using plain 넓다 when you want the warm 'pleasantly roomy' nuance. 방이 넓어요 just states it's large; 방이 널찍해요 conveys it feels comfortably spacious — a nicer compliment when viewing a place.
Misspelling it as 넓직하다 because it derives from 넓다. The standard spelling is 널찍하다 (the ㄼ is not written out).
Applying it to abstract bigness. 널찍하다 is for physical, walk-around space (rooms, lots, seating); for a wide range of options or broad knowledge you'd use 넓다 (선택의 폭이 넓다), not 널찍하다.

entries.english: to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space
entries.shortExplanation: 비좁다 means "to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 비좁다 (bijopda) means "to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 방이 비좁아요 ("The room is cramped"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 비좁다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: feels too small for what it's used for
비좁은 + N; barely room to pass
비좁게 = adverb; squeezed into too little space
uncomfortably tight, e.g. on a bus or plane

examples.en: The elevator is cramped.
examples.note: plain complaint; everyday apartment-building scene

examples.en: I have a lot of stuff, so the studio feels really cramped.
examples.note: 비좁다 stresses 'uncomfortably tight', stronger than plain 좁다

examples.en: The restaurant was so cramped I bumped into the person next to me.
examples.note: 비좁아서 = reason; concrete tight-space frustration

entries.nuance: 비좁다 is a native word: the intensifying prefix 비- attaches to 좁다 (narrow) and pushes it to 'so narrow it's uncomfortable', i.e. cramped. It is stronger and more clearly negative than plain 좁다, which can be a neutral statement of size (좁은 방 = a small room). Use 비좁다 for rooms stuffed with belongings, packed elevators, tight restaurant tables, or cramped seats. It is the direct antonym of 널찍하다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold. First, treating 비좁다 and 좁다 as identical: 좁다 just says 'narrow/small', while 비좁다 adds 'too tight for comfort', so a tiny but tidy room can be 좁다 yet only an over-stuffed, uncomfortable one is really 비좁다. Second, borrowing the English metaphor 'narrow-minded' onto this word: a narrow-minded person is 속이 좁다 / 마음이 좁다, never 비좁다 — 비좁다 is strictly about physical space.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 비좁다 as identical to 좁다. 좁다 = narrow/small (can be neutral); 비좁다 = cramped, too tight to be comfortable. A cozy small room is 좁다; a suffocatingly packed one is 비좁다.
Using 비좁다 for a person being narrow-minded. That sense is 속이 좁다 or 마음이 좁다; 비좁다 only describes physical space.
Applying it to a narrow long shape that isn't uncomfortable. A slim margin or thin strip is 좁다; reserve 비좁다 for spaces that feel oppressively tight to be in.

entries.shortExplanation: 푹신하다 means "to be soft, fluffy, cushiony" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be soft, fluffy, cushiony" is 푹신하다 (puksinhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 침대가 푹신해요 ("The bed is soft/cushiony"). Watch the particle attached to 푹신하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: comfortable to sink into with a springy give
푹신한 + N; soft and inviting to sit on
doubled form intensifies to extra-soft and bouncy
soft sole that absorbs impact when walking

examples.en: The hotel pillow is fluffy.
examples.note: plain comfort comment; soft with pleasant give

examples.ko: 이 운동화는 밑창이 푹신해서 발이 편해요.
examples.romanization: i undonghwaneun mitchangi puksinhaeseo bari pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: These sneakers have a cushiony sole, so my feet are comfortable.
examples.note: 밑창(sole) + 푹신하다; -아서 chains the reason — a common shoe-shopping line

examples.ko: 새로 산 매트리스가 너무 푹신해서 허리가 좀 아파요.
examples.romanization: saero san maeteuriseuga neomu puksinhaeseo heoriga jom apayo.
examples.en: The new mattress is too soft, so my back hurts a bit.
examples.note: 너무 푹신하다 shows over-softness can be a downside, not always praise

entries.nuance: 푹신하다 (often doubled to 푹신푹신하다 for emphasis) is a native word built on the soft, sinking sound 푹, describing a soft, springy, cushiony feel with pleasant GIVE when you press it: beds, sofas, pillows, thick cushions, padded shoe soles, fluffy bread. Its opposite is 딱딱하다 (hard/firm). The synonym to separate is 부드럽다: 부드럽다 is smooth and gentle to the touch — about surface softness (부드러운 천, 부드러운 머릿결) — whereas 푹신하다 is about volumetric springiness, how something cushions and bounces back when compressed. A silk scarf is 부드럽다 (smooth) but not 푹신하다; a marshmallow pillow is both. For Koreans shopping for furniture, bedding, or shoes, 푹신하다 is a go-to comfort word. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'soft = always good': a mattress described as 너무 푹신하다 (too soft) is a complaint, because excessive softness lacks support and can hurt your back — Koreans often prefer something 적당히 단단한 (moderately firm).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 푹신하다 with 부드럽다. 부드럽다 = smooth/gentle to the touch (a soft fabric, smooth hair); 푹신하다 = springy and cushiony with give (a plush sofa). A smooth-but-firm leather seat is 부드럽다, not 푹신하다.
Assuming 푹신하다 is always positive. 너무 푹신한 매트리스 is a criticism — too soft, no support, sore back. Context decides whether it's praise.
Using it for a flat, firm surface. A thin yoga mat or hardwood floor is not 푹신하다; the word needs noticeable cushioning and bounce-back.

entries.english: to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture
entries.shortExplanation: 눅눅하다 means "to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 눅눅하다 (nungnukada) = "to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과자가 눅눅해요 ("The snack has gone soggy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 눅눅하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: lost its crispness after absorbing humidity
눅눅한 + N; not fully dried, still clammy
humid, clammy air that clings
눅눅해지다 = change of state from crisp/dry to damp

examples.en: The crackers have gone soggy.
examples.note: plain statement; the crunch is gone

examples.en: I didn't seal the snack bag, so it went soggy.
examples.note: 눅눅해지다 = 'became soggy'; -아서 chains the cause

examples.ko: 장마철엔 빨래가 눅눅해서 잘 안 말라요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren ppallaega nungnukaeseo jal an mallayo.
examples.en: During the rainy season, laundry stays damp and won't dry well.
examples.note: 장마철 context; 눅눅해서 = reason — a classic Korean monsoon problem

entries.nuance: 눅눅하다 is a native word for things that have absorbed moisture and turned damp, soggy, or limp: crackers and seaweed (김) that lost their crunch, laundry that stubbornly won't dry, a humid basement room, a 장마철 (rainy-season) apartment. It is essential vocabulary for Korea's sticky summers. Its opposite is the crisp/dry 바삭하다 (crispy) for food and 보송보송하다 (dry and fluffy) for textiles. The synonym English speakers most often confuse it with is 축축하다: 축축하다 is actively WET to the touch — there is visible or palpable water, like a wet towel or rain-soaked socks — whereas 눅눅하다 is the subtler, stale 'humidity-soaked, limp, no longer crisp' state where nothing is dripping but everything feels clammy and soft. A second pitfall is reaching for 젖다 (to get wet): soggy-from-humidity crackers are 눅눅해졌다, not 젖었다, because 젖다 implies they got splashed or soaked in liquid, not slowly softened by moist air.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 눅눅하다 with 축축하다. 축축하다 = wet/moist to the touch (a wet towel, damp socks); 눅눅하다 = damp-soggy and stale from humidity (limp crackers, a muggy room). Nothing drips when it's merely 눅눅하다.
Using 젖다 for soggy snacks. 젖다 = to get wet/soaked in liquid; humidity-softened food is 눅눅해지다, not 젖다. 과자가 젖었어요 sounds like water spilled on it.
Applying 눅눅하다 to pleasant softness. It is negative — limp, stale, clammy. A nice springy pillow is 푹신하다, never 눅눅하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 볼펜 means "ballpoint pen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 볼펜 (bolpen) means "ballpoint pen". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 볼펜 좀 빌려주세요 ("Lend me a pen, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 볼펜 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday request at a desk or counter; 좀 softens it into a polite favor

usagePhrases.en: Please write with a black pen
usagePhrases.note: Banks and offices often require 검은색 (black); 으로 marks the pen as the tool you write with
안 나오다 (won't come out) is THE idiom for a dead pen — the ink won't flow
Casual workplace ask; in speech Koreans drop the 이/가 subject marker after 볼펜

examples.en: Can I just borrow one pen?
examples.note: Simplest favor; 하나만 = just one, -아/어도 돼요? asks permission gently

examples.en: You can write your name here with a pen
examples.note: -으로 marks the tool you write with

examples.ko: 회의 때 쓸 볼펜이 한 자루도 없네요.
examples.romanization: hoeui ttae sseul bolpeni han jarudo eopsneyo.
examples.en: There isn't a single pen to use in the meeting.
examples.note: Real frustration; 자루 counts pens, and 한 자루도 없다 = not even one

entries.nuance: 볼펜 is a loanword shortened from English 'ball pen' and means specifically a ballpoint, the cheap everyday pen, whereas plain 펜 is the umbrella word for any pen and would also cover a 만년필 (fountain pen) or 사인펜 (felt-tip marker). Calling a felt-tip 사인펜 a signing pen by false-friend logic — 사인펜 is a marker; you actually sign with a 볼펜
Counting pens with the generic 개 in writing; the natural counter is 자루, as in 볼펜 한 자루

usagePhrases.en: Jot it down in your notebook
usagePhrases.note: 적어 두다 = write it down and keep it; the go-to phrase for taking a note for later

usagePhrases.en: Can you show me your notes?
usagePhrases.note: 필기 = handwritten class/meeting notes; -ㄹ래? is a casual peer request
권 is the book counter and the natural one for a bound notebook
정리 = organizing; a common compliment about tidy, well-kept notes

examples.en: Please write your name in the notebook.
examples.note: Simple classroom line; 에 marks the notebook as where the writing lands

examples.en: I wrote down everything from the meeting in my notebook.
examples.note: Everyday work use; 다 적다 = jot it all down

examples.ko: 디지털 노트보다 종이 노트가 더 편해요.
examples.romanization: dijiteol noteuboda jongi noteuga deo pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: I find a paper notebook more comfortable than a digital one.

entries.nuance: 노트 is a loanword from English 'note(book)' but in Korean it means the physical bound pad you write in, NOT an abstract 'note' or 'memo' (that idea is 메모). Using 노트 to translate an abstract 'a note to self'; that idea is 메모, and 노트 is the physical book
Counting notebooks with 개; the natural counter is 권, as in 노트 한 권

usagePhrases.note: 로 marks tape as the tool; 붙이다 = to stick something on
박스테이프 = the wide brown box tape, the one everyone hunts for when moving

usagePhrases.en: The tape won't come off easily
usagePhrases.note: 떨어지다 here = come off; a common complaint when tape over-sticks

usagePhrases.en: I fixed it with clear tape
usagePhrases.note: 투명 = transparent; 고정하다 = to fasten in place

examples.en: Please tape it up for me.
examples.note: Simplest request; 좀 softens it and 붙이다 carries the 'stick' meaning

examples.en: I sealed the delivery box tightly with tape.
examples.note: Everyday shipping/moving; 단단히 = firmly, securely

examples.ko: 양면테이프가 일반 테이프보다 훨씬 잘 붙어요.
examples.romanization: yangmyeonteipeuga ilban teipeuboda hwolssin jal buteoyo.
examples.en: Double-sided tape sticks much better than regular tape.
examples.note: Real comparison; 훨씬 = far/much more, and here 붙다 = (it) sticks

entries.nuance: 테이프 is a loanword from English 'tape' and covers most sticky tapes, but Koreans habitually name the type: 박스테이프 (packing tape), 투명 테이프 or 스카치테이프 (clear desk tape, from the Scotch brand), and 양면테이프 (double-sided). The crucial English-speaker trap is transitivity: to stick something on, use the transitive 붙이다 (테이프로 붙이다 = stick it with tape); the intransitive 붙다 means '(it) sticks/is stuck' and can't take an object, so 테이프를 붙다 is wrong. Note the pair flips by viewpoint — 테이프로 종이를 붙이다 (I stick the paper) vs 테이프가 잘 붙다 (the tape sticks well). Don't import the English verb 'tape' as 테이프하다 either; the action is always carried by 붙이다.

Using 테이프하다 like English 'to tape something'; there is no such verb — the action verb is 붙이다
Calling clear desk tape 박스테이프; the wide brown tape is only for boxes, while desk tape is 투명 테이프/스카치테이프

entries.shortExplanation: 스테이플러 means "stapler" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스테이플러 (seuteipeulleo) means "stapler". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스테이플러로 찍어 주세요 ("Please staple it together"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스테이플러 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 찍다 (to stamp/punch) is the verb for stapling; 로 marks the stapler as the tool
심 = the staple refills; 떨어지다 = run out of a supply
장 counts sheets of paper; -ㄹ게요 = I'll do it (announcing your action)
Polite borrowing in a shared office; -아/어도 돼요? asks permission

examples.en: Could you staple it for me?
examples.note: Short favor; the core collocation 스테이플러로 찍다 in a casual -ㄹ래요? request

examples.en: I printed the report and stapled it.
examples.note: Typical office flow; 출력하다 = print out, then staple

examples.ko: 스테이플러가 자꾸 걸려서 잘 안 찍혀요.
examples.romanization: seuteipeulleoga jakku geollyeoseo jal an jjikyeoyo.
examples.en: The stapler keeps jamming, so it doesn't staple well.
examples.note: Real annoyance; 걸리다 = jam/catch, 찍히다 = get stapled (passive)

entries.nuance: 스테이플러 is a loanword from English 'stapler', but the action is pure native Korean: you 찍다 it — a verb whose base sense is to stamp, punch, or press down — so '스테이플러로 찍다' is the only natural collocation and there is NO verb 스테이플러하다. This 찍다 is the same one used for stamping a seal (도장을 찍다) and taking a photo (사진을 찍다), all sharing the 'press down to make a mark' image. The metal staples loaded inside are called 심 — the very same word for pencil 'lead' and mechanical-pencil refills — so 스테이플러 심 다 떨어졌어요 means the staples ran out. English speakers also confuse the device with what it makes: the machine is the 스테이플러, but the individual fastener it leaves is a 스테이플 / 침; in everyday speech the refills are just 심.

Saying 스테이플러하다 as a verb — no such word exists; the action is always 스테이플러로 찍다 using native 찍다
Calling the refills 스테이플 in casual speech; Koreans say 심 (the same word as pencil lead), e.g. 스테이플러 심
Reaching for an English-style verb like 찍기 doesn't help — keep 찍다 and let 로 mark the stapler as the tool

entries.shortExplanation: 포스트잇 means "Post-it (sticky note)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.en: Can you give me one Post-it?
usagePhrases.note: 장 counts the sheets; casual -ㄹ래요? request

usagePhrases.en: Don't stick Post-its on the monitor
usagePhrases.note: A real security rule in many offices; -지 마세요 = please don't

usagePhrases.en: I marked it with a Post-it
usagePhrases.note: 표시하다 = to flag/mark; 으로 marks the Post-it as the means

examples.note: Simplest task; 한 장 = one sheet, 붙이다 = stick it on

examples.ko: 할 일을 포스트잇에 적어서 책상에 붙여요.

entries.nuance: 포스트잇 became the everyday Korean word for a sticky note even though it began as the 3M brand 'Post-it' — a genericized trademark exactly like 'Post-it' or 'Kleenex' in English. examples.ko: 페이지가 많아서 클립 대신 스테이플러를 썼어요.
examples.romanization: peijiga manaseo keullip daesin seuteipeulleoreul sseosseoyo.
examples.en: There were many pages, so I used a stapler instead of a clip.
examples.note: Real decision; 대신 = instead of

entries.nuance: 클립 is a loanword from English 'clip', but on its own it means specifically the small bent-wire paper clip (you can spell it out as 종이 클립). The bigger black fold-back clip with two metal arms is a different object that English calls a 'binder clip'; in Korean that is 집게 ('pincer/tongs') or 더블클립, so you must specify when you need the strong one — 집게 grips far harder than a flimsy 클립. As with other tools there is no verb 클립하다; pair the noun with native verbs instead: 클립으로 묶다 (bind with a clip) or 클립을 끼우다 (slip a clip on). Note the everyday gripe 클립이 서로 달라붙다 (the clips cling to each other) — 달라붙다 = stick together — and remember that to remove one you 빼다 it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 클립 for the big black fold-back clip; that one is 집게 or 더블클립, while plain 클립 is only the small wire paper clip
Saying 클립하다 as a verb — there is none; use 클립으로 묶다 or 클립을 끼우다
Forgetting to specify the type when you need a strong grip; ask for a 집게, since a thin 클립 won't hold thick stacks

entries.shortExplanation: 파일 means "file / folder (for papers)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 파일 (pail) means "file / folder (for papers)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서류를 파일에 정리했어요 ("I organized the documents in a folder"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 파일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I organized the documents in a folder
usagePhrases.note: 정리하다 = sort/organize; 에 marks the folder as the destination
끼우다 = insert between; 두다 = leave it there for later

usagePhrases.en: Give me one clear file, please
usagePhrases.note: 클리어파일 = the clear-sleeve folder, the most common office kind

usagePhrases.en: The file has gotten too thick
usagePhrases.note: 두꺼워지다 = become thick; it's stuffed full of papers

examples.en: Please put the documents in this folder.
examples.note: Simple instruction; 넣다 = put in, 에 = into

examples.ko: 중요한 서류를 파일에 넣어서 책장에 꽂아 뒀어요.
examples.romanization: jungyohan seoryureul paire neoeoseo chaekjange kkoja dwosseoyo.
examples.en: I put the important papers in a file and shelved them
examples.note: 파일에 넣다 = put into a folder/file

examples.ko: 서류가 많으면 파일로 정리하는 게 편해요.
examples.romanization: seoryuga maneumyeon paillo jeongnihaneun ge pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: If you have lots of documents, organizing them in files is convenient.
examples.note: Advice; -는 게 편하다 = it's convenient to ~

entries.nuance: 파일 is a loanword from English 'file' and is a true homonym: it means both a physical document folder AND a computer file, so only context tells them apart — 파일에 끼우다 (slip into a folder) is clearly the paper kind, while 파일을 저장하다 (save the file) is clearly digital. Within the physical sense, Koreans distinguish sub-types you should not blur: a 클리어파일 is the thin transparent sleeve folder most desks use, whereas a 바인더 is the thick ring binder that snaps open, and a plain 폴더 often refers to the cardboard folder. The English-speaker trap is assuming 파일 defaults to 'computer file' and calling the clear sleeve a 바인더 — but 바인더 specifically has rings. Pair it with 넣다 (put in), 끼우다 (insert), 정리하다 (organize), and 꽂다 (shelve).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 파일 always means a computer file; physically it is a document folder, and context decides which sense applies
Calling the thin clear-sleeve folder a 바인더; 바인더 is specifically the thick ring binder, while the sleeve is a 클리어파일
Saying 파일하다 for filing; the action is 파일에 정리하다 / 파일에 넣다 using native verbs

entries.shortExplanation: 스캐너 means "scanner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "scanner" is 스캐너 (seukaeneo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스캐너로 스캔해 주세요 ("Please scan it with the scanner"). Watch the particle attached to 스캐너 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Please scan it with the scanner
usagePhrases.note: 스캔하다 = to scan; 로 marks the scanner as the device
Locating shared office equipment; 에 marks the location

usagePhrases.en: Can you scan the document for me?
usagePhrases.note: 뜨다 ('lift/take off') is colloquial office slang for scanning a copy
연결이 안 되다 = fails to connect; a typical tech complaint

examples.en: Please scan this with the scanner.
examples.note: Plainest request; 이거 = this one, plus the core pair 스캐너로 스캔하다

examples.en: I scanned the document with the scanner and emailed it
examples.note: 스캐너로 스캔하다 = scan with a scanner

examples.ko: 요즘은 스캐너 대신 휴대폰 앱으로 스캔해요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun seukaeneo daesin hyudaepon aebeuro seukaenhaeyo.
examples.en: These days I scan with a phone app instead of a scanner.
examples.note: Modern habit; 대신 = instead of

entries.nuance: 스캐너 is a loanword from English 'scanner' and names the device, while the action is the loan-verb 스캔하다 (스캔 + 하다 = to scan) — so '스캐너로 스캔하다' is the textbook pair, and there is NO verb 스캐너하다. In spoken office Korean people also use the native 뜨다 ('서류를 떠 주세요'), the same 뜨다 used for 'lifting off' a copy. The key conceptual contrast English speakers blur is 스캐너 vs 복사기: a 스캐너 turns paper into a digital file you can email, whereas a 복사기 (copier) turns paper into more paper — different output entirely. Muddying this further, most modern offices have a 복합기 (複合機, all-in-one) that prints, copies, AND scans, so colleagues may say 복합기로 스캔하다 instead of naming a standalone 스캐너. Pair the action with 로 (the tool particle).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스캐너하다 — the verb is 스캔하다 (from English 'scan'), used as 스캐너로 스캔하다
Confusing 스캐너 with 복사기; scanning produces a digital file, copying produces more paper
Forgetting that the office machine is often a 복합기 (all-in-one), so people say 복합기로 스캔하다 rather than 스캐너

entries.shortExplanation: 복사기 means "copier (copy machine)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 복사기 (boksagi) = "copier (copy machine)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 복사기로 복사해 주세요 ("Please make a copy on the copier") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 복사기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Please make a copy on the copier
usagePhrases.note: 복사하다 = to copy; 로 marks the machine as the means
고장 나다 = break down; frequent office bad news
채우다 = to fill; the paper tray ran empty
양면 (兩面, both sides) = double-sided; a common print setting

examples.en: Please copy this on the copier.
examples.note: Plainest request; the core pair 복사기로 복사하다

examples.en: I made 30 copies of the meeting materials on the copier.
examples.note: Everyday office task; 부 counts copies/issues of a document

examples.en: The paper jammed in the copier and I struggled for a while.
examples.note: Real annoyance; 걸리다 = jam, 헤매다 = flounder

entries.nuance: 복사기 is Sino-Korean: 복사 (複寫, 'duplicate-copy') + 기 (機, 'machine'), literally 'duplicating machine', and 복사하다 is the matching verb (복사기로 복사하다). The output is paper — a physical copy — which is exactly what separates it from the near neighbors English speakers mix up: a 프린터 prints digital files onto paper, a 스캐너 turns paper into a digital file, and a 복사기 turns paper into more paper. In practice most offices now run a 복합기 (複合機, 'combined machine', the all-in-one), yet people still say 복사기 out of habit when they just want copies. Two natural-counter points: finished copies take 부 (30부 = 30 copies, the same counter as for newspaper/book issues), and double-sided is 양면 (兩面). Watch the supply words too — when 토너 (toner) runs out it prints 흐리게 (faintly).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 복사기 (copier — makes more paper) with 프린터 (prints digital files) or 스캐너 (makes a digital file from paper)
Counting copies with 개; the natural counter is 부, as in 30부
Assuming the office machine is a standalone 복사기; it's usually a 복합기 all-in-one that also prints and scans

entries.shortExplanation: 형광펜 means "highlighter" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 형광펜 (hyeonggwangpen) means "highlighter". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 중요한 데 형광펜으로 표시했어요 ("I highlighted the important parts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 형광펜 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 표시하다 = to mark/flag; 데 here = spot/part; 으로 marks the pen as the means
Polite borrowing with -아/어도 돼요? (may I ~?)

usagePhrases.en: The yellow highlighter is the most visible
usagePhrases.note: 잘 보이다 = easy to see; yellow reads clearest on white

usagePhrases.en: Please underline it with a highlighter
usagePhrases.note: 줄 긋다 = draw a line; used like underlining

examples.en: Please highlight here with a highlighter.
examples.note: Plain request; 칠하다 = color over a spot

examples.en: I highlighted the exam scope.
examples.note: Study habit; 칠해 놓다 = color it in and leave it marked

examples.en: The highlighter smudged and I can't read the text.
examples.note: Real mishap; 번지다 = bleed/smudge through

entries.nuance: 형광펜 is Sino-Korean plus a loanword: 형광 (螢光, 'firefly-light' = fluorescent/luminous) + 펜 (pen), literally a 'fluorescent pen', which is the standard everyday word for a highlighter — there is no separate native term. Keep it apart from a 색연필 (colored pencil) and a 사인펜 (felt-tip marker): only the 형광펜 lays down that see-through neon wash you read text through. The natural verbs are 칠하다 (color over a stretch) and 표시하다 (mark/flag), and you can also 줄을 긋다 (draw a line) with it, the way English 'underlines'; but note Korean treats highlighting as 칠하다/표시하다, not a verb 형광펜하다, which does not exist. Watch the verb 번지다 (to bleed/smudge) — wet ink 번져서 makes text unreadable. Yellow (노란색) is prized because it 잘 보여요 yet doesn't darken the words.

Calling it a 색연필 (colored pencil) or 사인펜 (felt-tip marker) — those are different tools; the see-through neon one is a 형광펜
Saying 형광펜하다 as a verb; the action is 형광펜으로 칠하다 or 형광펜으로 표시하다
Misusing the smudge verb — say 형광펜이 번지다 (the ink bleeds), not a literal translation of 'smudge'

entries.shortExplanation: 가위 means "scissors" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "scissors" is 가위 (gawi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가위로 잘라 주세요 ("Please cut it with scissors"). Watch the particle attached to 가위 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 자르다 = to cut; 로 marks the scissors as the tool

usagePhrases.en: Can you bring me the scissors?
usagePhrases.note: 갖다주다 = bring over to someone; casual -ㄹ래요? ask
가위질 = the act/motion of cutting with scissors (가위 + 질)
잘 안 들다 = doesn't cut well; the standard idiom for 'dull'

examples.en: Please cut this with scissors.
examples.note: Plainest request; 이거 = this one, plus the core pair 가위로 자르다

examples.en: I cut the tape cleanly with scissors.
examples.note: Everyday desk task; 깔끔하게 = neatly, cleanly

examples.en: I bought a pair of office scissors at the stationery shop.
examples.note: Real shopping; 사무용 = for office use, counted with 하나

entries.nuance: 가위 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) and, crucially for English speakers, it is grammatically singular — Korean has no 'a pair of scissors' construction, so 가위 하나 / 가위 한 개 already means one whole pair, and you never pluralize it. (The very same word 가위 also names the folk 'sleep paralysis' demon in 가위에 눌리다, but as a stationery item it is simply scissors.) The big idiom trap is sharpness: Koreans say the blades 잘 들다 (cut well) or 안 들다 / 무디다 (don't cut / are dull), and they do NOT use the literal 날카롭다 ('sharp-edged') or 'not sharp' to mean a dull pair — 가위가 안 들어요 is how you complain. Pair it with 자르다 (cut) or the action noun 가위질 (가위 + the activity suffix 질, as in 걸레질, 부채질), and note the passive 잘리다 (종이가 잘 안 잘려요 = the paper won't cut).

Trying to pluralize like English 'scissors'; 가위 stays singular — one pair is 가위 하나 / 가위 한 개, never a plural form
Saying 가위가 날카롭지 않다 for 'dull'; natives say 가위가 안 들어요 or 가위가 무뎌요, because sharpness is expressed with 들다, not 날카롭다
Using 자르다 as the only cut-word and forgetting the passive 잘리다 (종이가 안 잘려요 = the paper won't cut)

entries.shortExplanation: 메모지 means "memo pad / notepaper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 메모지 (memoji) = "memo pad / notepaper". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 메모지에 적어 둘게요 ("I'll jot it on a notepad") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 메모지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I'll jot it on a notepad
usagePhrases.note: 적어 두다 = write it down and keep it; -ㄹ게요 announces your action

usagePhrases.en: Just give me one sheet of notepaper
usagePhrases.note: 장 counts flat sheets; 만 = only/just one

usagePhrases.en: Did you see the note on the desk?
usagePhrases.note: Referring to a memo someone left; 위 = on top of

usagePhrases.en: I left the phone number on a notepad
usagePhrases.note: 남기다 = to leave (a message/note) behind

examples.en: Please jot your name on the notepaper.
examples.note: Simple request; 적다 = jot, 에 marks where it goes

examples.ko: 전화 메시지를 메모지에 적어서 전해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jeonhwa mesijireul memojie jeogeoseo jeonhae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I wrote the phone message on notepaper and passed it along.
examples.note: Office message-taking; 전하다 = relay to someone

examples.en: The notepaper ran out, so I wrote on a Post-it.
examples.note: Real moment; 떨어지다 = run out, contrasting 메모지 vs 포스트잇

entries.nuance: 메모지 is a hybrid: 메모 (a loanword from English 'memo') + 지 (紙, 'paper'), literally 'memo paper' — a small pad or loose sheets for quick jottings. Pin down its boundaries against three neighbors English speakers blur: 메모지 is plain loose notepaper that does NOT stick (unlike a 포스트잇, which self-adheres); it is loose sheets rather than a bound 노트 (notebook); and 메모 alone is the abstract act/content of a note, while 메모지 is the physical paper it's written on. So 메모하다 = to jot a memo, and 메모지에 메모하다 = to jot it on notepaper. Count single sheets with 장 (the flat-sheet counter), not 개, and pair it with 적다 / 메모하다 (write), 남기다 (leave behind), or 전하다 (relay). Don't confuse 메모지 with 메모장, which usually means a memo notebook/notepad app.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 메모지 (plain notepaper that doesn't stick) with 포스트잇 (the self-stick kind) — only the 포스트잇 has adhesive
Mixing up 메모 (the note's content/act) and 메모지 (the physical paper); you 메모하다 onto 메모지
Counting sheets with 개; the natural counter is 장, as in 메모지 한 장

structuredNuance.t: 메모지 is a small pad or loose sheets for quick jottings. So 메모하다 = to jot a memo, and 메모지에 메모하다 = to jot it on notepaper. Count single sheets with 장 (the flat-sheet counter), not 개, and pair it with 적다 / 메모하다 (write), 남기다 (leave behind), or 전하다 (relay).

Pin down its boundaries against three neighbors English speakers blur: 메모지 is plain loose notepaper that does NOT stick (unlike a 포스트잇, which self-adheres); it is loose sheets rather than a bound 노트 (notebook); and 메모 alone is the abstract act/content of a note, while 메모지 is the physical paper it's written on. Don't confuse 메모지 with 메모장, which usually means a memo notebook/notepad app.
메모지 is a hybrid: 메모 (a loanword from English 'memo') + 지 (紙, 'paper'), literally 'memo paper'.

entries.english: in advance, ahead of time, beforehand
entries.shortExplanation: 미리 means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 미리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The single most useful collocation for residents; pairs with 식당, 호텔, 병원

usagePhrases.en: to say ahead of time / give notice
usagePhrases.note: Used for advance notice; 미리 말해 주세요 = please tell me beforehand
The default verb after 미리; 서류를 미리 준비하다 = prep documents early

usagePhrases.en: well in advance, in good time
usagePhrases.note: Doubled form stressing 'nice and early, with margin to spare'

examples.en: I bought the tickets in advance.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 미리 + buy, the early-action core meaning

examples.ko: 인기 식당은 미리 예약하지 않으면 자리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: ingi sikdangeun miri yeyakaji aneumyeon jariga eopseoyo.
examples.en: Popular restaurants have no seats unless you reserve in advance.
examples.note: Everyday: 미리 + 예약하다 in a -지 않으면 conditional, a real dining reality

examples.ko: 다음 주에 휴가 쓸 거니까 팀장님께 미리 말씀드렸어요.
examples.romanization: daeum jue hyuga sseul geonikka timjangnimkke miri malsseumdeuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: I'll take leave next week, so I gave my team lead a heads-up in advance.
examples.note: Real situation: 미리 + 말씀드리다 (humble form) for workplace advance notice

entries.nuance: 미리 means doing something ahead of the relevant moment so you're ready when it arrives — its whole focus is the timing being early relative to a deadline or event. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing it with 우선 / 먼저 / 일단: 먼저 and 우선 mean 'first in a sequence or in priority' (do A before B), while 미리 means 'before the due time' (do it now so it's done early). 'I paid first' = 먼저 냈어요 (before others), but 'I paid in advance' = 미리 냈어요 (before the due date) — different ideas entirely. 미리 is native Korean, not Sino-Korean, and it glues onto preparation verbs: 미리 예약하다, 미리 준비하다, 미리 확인하다, 미리 알리다. Register is neutral and works in both polite and casual speech. Note the affectionate doubled 미리미리, which nags 'do it good and early.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 미리 for 'firstly in a sequence': 미리 이거부터 해요 is odd; for ordering steps you want 우선/먼저 이거부터 해요. 미리 only means 'ahead of the due time.'
Dropping it where the early timing is the point: 예약했어요 alone just says 'I booked'; 미리 예약했어요 adds the crucial 'ahead of time' nuance.
Saying 미리 전에 (advance + before) as a redundant pair under the influence of English 'beforehand in advance'; 미리 already contains 'before,' so just 미리 준비했어요.

entries.english: first of all, first and foremost, to begin with
entries.shortExplanation: 우선 means "first of all, first and foremost, to begin with" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "first of all, first and foremost, to begin with" is 우선 (useon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우선 ~부터 ("first of all, starting with ~"). Watch the particle attached to 우선 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 우선 loves -부터; 우선 이것부터 = let's start with this above all
Key noun built on 우선; 우선순위를 정하다 = set priorities
Polite way to settle someone before getting down to business
최 (most) + 우선; 안전이 최우선이에요 = safety is the top priority

examples.en: Have a glass of water first.
examples.note: Simple: 우선 settling an immediate small thing before the rest

examples.ko: 문제가 많지만 우선 급한 것부터 처리할게요.
examples.romanization: munjega manchiman useon geupan geotbuteo cheorihalgeyo.
examples.en: There are many issues, but I'll handle the urgent ones first.
examples.note: Everyday: 우선 + -부터 ordering tasks by priority at work

examples.ko: 이사 오면 우선 전입신고부터 하셔야 해요.
examples.romanization: isa omyeon useon jeonipsingobuteo hasyeoya haeyo.
examples.en: When you move in, you must do the move-in report first of all.
examples.note: Real situation: 우선 fronting the single most important admin step for residents

entries.nuance: 우선 (優先, 優 'superior' + 先 'first') literally means 'take precedence,' so it marks what should come before everything else in importance, not merely in time. Compare 먼저 vs 우선: 먼저 is neutral sequence ('I'll go first / do this first'), while 우선 adds the flavor of priority and deliberate ranking ('first and foremost, before anything else'). Compare 우선 vs 일단: 일단 is 'for now, provisionally, then we'll see,' whereas 우선 ranks by importance. Compare 우선 vs 미리: 미리 is 'ahead of the deadline,' a totally different axis. The Sino-Korean root surfaces everywhere in daily life — 우선순위 (priority), 최우선 (top priority), 우선적으로 (preferentially) — so learning 우선 unlocks a whole word family. It pairs habitually with -부터 to pin the starting point. Register is neutral-to-formal and very common in workplace speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 미리: 우선 is about order/priority ('do this above all, first'), not doing something before a deadline (that's 미리).
Using 우선 for plain 'then / next' steps in a list: 우선 ... 우선 ... sounds wrong; after the first item switch to 그다음에 / 그러고 나서.
Forgetting 우선 strongly prefers -부터: bare 우선 이거 해요 is weaker than the natural 우선 이거부터 해요.

entries.english: for now, first (before deciding the rest), once
entries.shortExplanation: 일단 means "for now, first (before deciding the rest), once" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 일단 (ildan) = "for now, first (before deciding the rest), once". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 일단 ~하고 보다 ("just do ~ first and see") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 일단, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The signature pattern; 일단 해 보고 결정하자 = let's just try it and then decide
일단 밥부터 먹자 = let's just eat first, sort the rest out later
Tentative acknowledgment that leaves room to revisit
일단 시작하면 = once you actually get started

examples.en: Let's just sit down first and talk.
examples.note: Simple: 일단 settling one immediate step before the discussion

examples.ko: 고민은 나중에 하고 일단 신청서부터 내요.
examples.romanization: gomineun najunge hago ildan sincheongseobuteo naeyo.
examples.en: Worry about it later; for now, just submit the application first.
examples.note: Everyday: 일단 deferring the deciding while taking one provisional action

examples.ko: 집은 일단 계약했는데 이사 날짜는 아직 안 정했어요.
examples.romanization: jibeun ildan gyeyakaenneunde isa naljjaneun ajik an jeonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: I went ahead and signed for the place for now, but haven't set the move date yet.
examples.note: Real situation: 일단 = one thing settled provisionally while the rest stays open

entries.nuance: 일단 (一旦, 一 'one' + 旦 'daybreak/moment') means 'for the moment, as a first provisional move' — you commit to one step now and leave the rest to be sorted out later. The defining flavor is tentativeness, which is the sharp line against 우선 and 미리. 우선 ranks by importance ('this matters most, do it first'); 일단 just says 'let's do something for now and see' with no claim about priority. 미리 means 'ahead of the deadline'; 일단 has nothing to do with deadlines. Its signature construction is 일단 ~하고 보자 / ~하고 보다 ('just do X first and see how it goes'), pure spoken Korean for deferring decisions. A second sense is conditional 'once': 일단 시작하면 끝까지 해야죠 ('once you start, you should finish'). Register is casual-to-neutral and extremely high-frequency in everyday speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating it exactly with 우선: 일단 leans 'provisionally, for now,' while 우선 stresses priority/importance. 일단 해 보자 ≠ 우선 해 보자 in feel.
Expecting it to mean 'in advance': that nuance belongs to 미리, never 일단.
Missing the 'once' sense and over-translating: 일단 도착하면 연락해 means 'once you arrive, contact me,' not 'for now arrive.'

entries.shortExplanation: 곧 means "soon, shortly, before long" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 곧 (got) means "soon, shortly, before long". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 곧 도착하다 ("to arrive soon"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 곧 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Classic 'on my way' text; 곧 도착해요 = I'll be there shortly
Announcing an event about to begin; 공연이 곧 시작합니다

usagePhrases.en: to end soon / be over shortly
usagePhrases.note: Reassurance; 거의 다 했어요, 곧 끝나요
Set adverb (esp. broadcasts/announcements): 곧이어 다음 순서입니다

examples.en: Spring is coming soon.
examples.note: Simple: 곧 + a near-future event, forward-looking only

examples.ko: 거의 다 왔어요, 곧 도착하니까 조금만 기다려요.
examples.romanization: geoui da wasseoyo, got dochakanikka jogeumman gidaryeoyo.
examples.en: I'm almost there; I'll arrive soon, so wait just a bit.
examples.note: Everyday: 곧 + 도착하다, the most relatable 'almost there' message

examples.ko: 탑승을 곧 시작하겠습니다. 잠시만 기다려 주십시오.
examples.romanization: tapseungeul got sijakagetseumnida. jamsiman gidaryeo jusipsio.
examples.en: Boarding will begin shortly. Please wait a moment.
examples.note: Real situation: 곧 in a formal announcement register at the airport/station

entries.nuance: 곧 means 'soon,' signaling that something will happen within a short time from the present. It strictly looks forward — 곧 can never describe the past. The key contrast is 곧 vs 금방: 금방 ('in a jiffy') is very casual and works both ways in time (it can even mean 'a moment ago' as in 금방 왔어요), while 곧 is cleaner, slightly more written/formal, and future-only, which is why station and airport announcements favor 곧. A second native-speaker pitfall is mixing 곧 (soon) with 이따가 (later today): 곧 means 'very shortly from now,' whereas 이따가 means 'later on, after some hours' — 곧 갈게요 ('I'm coming right away') is very different from 이따가 갈게요 ('I'll come by later'). 곧 is native Korean. The fixed compound 곧이어 ('coming up next') is worth memorizing as a unit.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 곧 for the recent past ('a moment ago'): that is 방금 / 금방, while 곧 is strictly future. 곧 도착했어요 is wrong; say 방금 도착했어요.
Confusing 곧 (soon) with 곳 (place): they look and sound similar but are unrelated — 곧 = soon, 곳 = a place/spot.
Swapping 곧 and 이따가: 곧 = right away/shortly; 이따가 = later (in a few hours). Don't say 곧 만나요 when you mean 'see you later today.'

entries.english: already (it's done and can't be changed)
entries.shortExplanation: 이미 means "already (it's done and can't be changed)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "already (it's done and can't be changed)" is 이미 (imi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이미 끝나다 ("to be already over"). Watch the particle attached to 이미 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: States a finished, irreversible fact; 이미 끝난 일이에요 = it's a done deal
이미 늦었어요 = there's no point now, the moment has passed
이미 알고 있었어요 = I knew it beforehand, this is no news
이미 결정된 상태예요 = it's already (been) decided, fixed now

examples.en: I've already seen that movie.
examples.note: Simple: 이미 + completed action, a settled fact

examples.ko: 전화했을 때는 이미 가게가 문을 닫았더라고요.
examples.romanization: jeonhwahaesseul ttaeneun imi gagega muneul dadatdeoragoyo.
examples.en: By the time I called, the store had already closed.
examples.note: Everyday: 이미 with -더라고요 for a past-perfect 'it was already done' realization

examples.ko: 환불하려고 했는데 이미 배송이 시작돼서 취소가 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: hwanbulharyeogo haenneunde imi baesongi sijakdwaeseo chwisoga an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I tried to get a refund, but shipping had already started, so I couldn't cancel.
examples.note: Real situation: 이미 marking an irreversible point in a process

entries.nuance: 이미 means 'already,' emphasizing that an action or state is completed and now fixed — often colored by 'and there's no changing it now.' The sharp contrast every learner needs is 이미 vs 벌써. Both translate as 'already,' but 이미 is neutral and factual ('it is already done, that's just the situation'), while 벌써 adds emotional surprise that it happened so fast or so soon ('already?! that quick?'). 이미 끝났어요 = a calm statement of fact; 벌써 끝났어요?! = 'it's over already?!' with raised eyebrows. So choose 이미 when calmly noting that the moment/deadline has passed, and 벌써 when reacting to unexpected speed. 이미 is native Korean and is also future-blind: it only describes things already done, never things about to happen. It pairs naturally with completed clauses and with -더라고요, -았/었- past forms.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it freely with 벌써: 이미 is neutral about timing, while 벌써 carries 'so soon?!' surprise. Use 이미 for a flat fact, 벌써 for astonishment.
Using it for the future: 이미 only describes things already done. 'It'll already be finished by then' needs a future-perfect feel like 그때면 끝나 있을 거예요, not 이미 + future.
Forcing English word order: in English 'already' floats around, but Korean 이미 sits before the verb/predicate it modifies — 이미 다 먹었어요, not 다 먹었어요 이미.

entries.shortExplanation: 아까 means "a little while ago, earlier (today)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아까, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 아까 말했잖아요 = I told you earlier (mild reminder)
아까부터 기다렸어요 = I've been waiting since earlier
아까 그 사람 = that person from before; refers back within today

usagePhrases.en: earlier in the day / this morning
usagePhrases.note: Pins 아까 to a rough part of today

examples.en: I ate a little while ago.
examples.note: Simple: 아까 placing an action in the recent past today

examples.ko: 아까 충전해 놨는데 벌써 배터리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: akka chungjeonhae nwanneunde beolsseo baeteoriga eopseoyo.
examples.en: I charged it earlier, but the battery's already dead.
examples.note: Everyday: 아까 contrasting an earlier action with the present state

examples.ko: 아까 회의 때 말씀하신 거 다시 한 번 설명해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: akka hoeui ttae malsseumhasin geo dasi han beon seolmyeonghae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you explain again what you mentioned earlier in the meeting?
examples.note: Real situation: 아까 + 때 referencing a specific earlier moment today, polite register

entries.nuance: 아까 refers to a short while earlier on the same day — broader than 'just now,' but always recent and never beyond today. The contrast learners most need is 아까 vs 방금: 방금 means literally seconds to a couple of minutes ago, while 아까 can stretch back a few hours (anywhere earlier today). 방금 도착했어요 = 'I arrived this second'; 아까 도착했어요 = 'I arrived a while ago (earlier today).' A second contrast is 아까 vs 전에: 전에 ('before / previously') is open-ended and can mean days, months, or years back, while 아까 is locked inside today. So use 아까 그거 ('that thing from earlier') only for something from the same day. 아까 is native Korean, casual-to-neutral in register, and combines productively with -부터 ('since earlier') and 그 + noun ('that ... from before').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for yesterday or longer ago: 아까 stays within today's recent past. For further back use 어제 / 전에 / 지난번에.
Treating it the same as 방금: 방금 = seconds ago, 아까 = a broader 'earlier today.' Don't say 아까 도착했어요 if you literally just walked in — that's 방금.
Pairing 아까 with the future: it is past-only. 'A bit later' is 이따가, not 아까.

아까 is native Korean, casual-to-neutral in register, and combines productively with -부터 ('since earlier') and 그 + noun ('that ... from before').

entries.shortExplanation: 막 means "just (now), right as, recklessly/randomly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 막 (mak) means "just (now), right as, recklessly/randomly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지금 막 ("right this second"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 막 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Reinforces the 'just now' sense; 지금 막 도착했어요
막 나가려던 참이었어요 = I was just on the point of leaving
막 먹다 = eat mindlessly; 막 쓰다 = use/spend carelessly
이제 막 시작했어요 = we've only just started

examples.en: I just woke up (this second).
examples.note: Simple: 지금 막 + past for an action completed an instant ago

examples.en: Right as I was about to close the door, someone came running.
examples.note: Everyday: 막 + -려는데 marking the exact instant before another event

examples.en: When I'm stressed, I just end up eating mindlessly.
examples.note: Real situation: 막 in the 'recklessly, without restraint' sense

entries.nuance: 막 carries two everyday senses that context tells apart. (1) With a past tense or 참이다, it means 'just this very second' — even fresher and more immediate than 방금 — as in 지금 막 도착했어요 ('I arrived literally just now'). (2) In casual speech it also means doing something wildly, randomly, or without restraint, a shortening in feel of 마구: 막 먹다 (eat carelessly/a lot), 막 쓰다 (spend/use recklessly), 막 던지다 (throw all over the place). The pitfall for English speakers is hearing only the 'just' meaning and missing the 'recklessly' one, or vice versa — the following verb and tone decide it: 막 + past = time; 막 + ongoing careless action = manner. 막 is native Korean and very colloquial; the manner sense in particular sounds casual, so go easy on it in formal settings. It frequently teams up with 지금, 이제, and -려던 참이다 for the time reading.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Forgetting it usually leans on 지금 / 이제 or 참이다 for the time sense: bare 막 도착했어요 is fine, but 지금 막 / 이제 막 / 막 ~려던 참 sound more natural and unambiguous.
Using the careless 막 in polite/formal speech: 막 in the 'wildly' sense is colloquial and can sound crude — soften or avoid it when being formal.

usagePhrases.note: 방금 도착했어요 = I got here only seconds ago
방금 뭐라고 했어요? = asking to repeat what was said a second ago
Common variant emphasizing the very recent instant
방금까지 여기 있었어요 = it was right here until seconds ago

examples.en: I arrived just now.
examples.note: Simple: 방금 + past for an action seconds old

examples.en: The drink you just ordered is ready.
examples.note: Everyday: 방금 in a cafe, an order only moments old, polite -습니다 register

examples.ko: 방금까지 옆에 있었는데 잠깐 사이에 어디 갔지?
examples.romanization: banggeumkkaji yeope isseonneunde jamkkan saie eodi gatji?
examples.en: They were right beside me until just now; where'd they go in that instant?
examples.note: Real situation: 방금까지 emphasizing 'up until seconds ago'

entries.nuance: 방금 (方今, 方 'just/at the time' + 今 'now') is the tightest 'recent past' word, pointing to something that happened only seconds to a couple of minutes ago. The contrast learners need most is 방금 vs 아까: 방금 is 'this very moment past,' while 아까 stretches to 'earlier today' (potentially hours back). 방금 나갔어요 = 'they left seconds ago'; 아까 나갔어요 = 'they left a while ago.' Compare also 방금 vs 막: both can mean 'just now,' but 막 emphasizes the instantaneous edge ('right as it happened') and pairs with 지금/참이다, whereas 방금 is a standalone time word and a touch more neutral. Because of its Sino-Korean root, the variant 방금 전(에) ('just a moment before') is common. 방금 is strictly immediate past — never future. Register is neutral and fits both casual and polite speech, which is why staff use it (방금 주문하신…).

entries.english: in the meantime, all this while, during that time
entries.shortExplanation: 그동안 means "in the meantime, all this while, during that time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그동안 (geudongan) = "in the meantime, all this while, during that time". usagePhrases.en: to have been well all this time
usagePhrases.note: 그동안 잘 지냈어요? = standard catch-up greeting after a gap

usagePhrases.en: to be thankful for everything up to now
usagePhrases.note: 그동안 고마웠어요 = gratitude covering a whole past stretch (often a farewell)
그동안의 노력 = the effort (made) over all that time; noun-modifying use
그동안 못 만났네요 = we couldn't meet all this time

examples.en: I was busy all this while.
examples.note: Simple: 그동안 covering an elapsed stretch up to now

examples.en: Long time no see; how have you been all this while?
examples.note: Everyday: 그동안 framing the whole gap since you last met

examples.ko: 그동안 모아 둔 돈으로 드디어 전셋집을 구했어요.
examples.romanization: geudongan moa dun doneuro deudieo jeonsetjibeul guhaesseoyo.
examples.en: With the money I'd saved up all this time, I finally found a jeonse place.
examples.note: Real situation: 그동안 referring to an extended past saving period

entries.nuance: 그동안 (그 'that' + 동안 'duration/while') means 'during that time / all this while,' referring to a stretch of time spanning a known gap and usually leading up to now. It's the backbone of catching-up greetings (그동안 잘 지냈어요?) and farewell thanks (그동안 고마웠어요). The first pitfall is treating it as a single point: 그동안 is always a span, unlike 그때 ('at that time / that moment'). The second is direction — 그동안 vs 당분간: 그동안 looks back over time that has elapsed, while 당분간 ('for the time being') looks forward from now. So 'thanks for everything up to now' = 그동안 고마웠어요, but 'I'll rest for a while going forward' = 당분간 쉴게요. Grammatically 그동안 is flexible: it works as an adverb (그동안 바빴어요) and, with -의, as a noun modifier (그동안의 노력). Register is neutral and warm; the greeting use is everyday-polite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing it with 당분간 (for the time being, forward-looking): 그동안 looks back over elapsed time; 당분간 looks ahead.
Using it where you mean a specific past day: for 'the other day / last time' use 지난번 / 저번에, not 그동안.

entries.english: for the time being, for a while (from now)
entries.shortExplanation: 당분간 means "for the time being, for a while (from now)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 당분간 (dangbungan) means "for the time being, for a while (from now)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 당분간 쉬다 ("to rest for a while (going forward)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당분간 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to rest for a while (going forward)
usagePhrases.note: 당분간 쉬려고요 = I plan to take a break for the time being
당분간 못 만나요 = we can't meet for a while (a temporary inability)
당분간 외식 안 할 거예요 = I won't eat out for the time being

usagePhrases.en: for the time being at least
usagePhrases.note: Softens to 'at least for now'; implies it may change later

examples.en: I'll be busy for the time being.
examples.note: Simple: 당분간 + future, a temporary state ahead

examples.ko: 돈을 모아야 해서 당분간 여행은 안 가려고요.
examples.romanization: doneul moaya haeseo dangbungan yeohaengeun an garyeogoyo.
examples.en: I need to save money, so I'm not going to travel for the time being.
examples.note: Everyday: 당분간 + future restraint a budgeting resident relates to

examples.ko: 이직 준비 때문에 당분간 약속을 좀 줄이려고 해요.
examples.romanization: ijik junbi ttaemune dangbungan yaksogeul jom juriryeogo haeyo.
examples.en: Because I'm prepping for a job change, I'm going to cut back on plans for a while.
examples.note: Real situation: 당분간 marking a temporary phase ahead with -려고 해요

entries.nuance: 당분간 (當分間, roughly 當 'this present' + 分 'portion' + 間 'interval' — 'for this present interval') means 'for the time being': a limited stretch starting now and running into the near future, with a built-in implication that it's temporary and will change. The defining contrast is 당분간 vs 그동안: 당분간 points forward ('from now, for a while'), 그동안 points back over elapsed time. So 'I'll lie low for a while' = 당분간 조용히 지낼게요, but 'thanks for everything until now' = 그동안 고마웠어요. A second pitfall is using it for permanent states: 당분간 inherently signals 'this won't last forever.' It pairs naturally with future-plan endings (-(으)려고요, -ㄹ 거예요) and negatives of restraint (못, 안 ... -ㄹ 거예요), and it's often softened to 당분간은. Register is neutral and very common in everyday explanations of temporary plans.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 그동안: 당분간 points forward ('from now for a while'), while 그동안 points back over time that has passed.
Using it for permanent states: 당분간 implies the situation is temporary and expected to change. For 'forever / from now on for good' use 앞으로 (계속) / 영원히.
Pairing it with a plain past tense: since 당분간 looks forward, it wants future/intention forms — say 당분간 쉴 거예요 / 쉬려고요, not 당분간 쉬었어요.

("did you ~ it all in that short time?"). Watch the particle attached to 그새 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: 그새 다 먹었어요? = you finished it all that fast?! (surprise)
그새 또 비가 오네요 = it's raining again already, in no time

usagePhrases.note: 그새 잊어버렸어요 = it slipped my mind that quickly

usagePhrases.note: Noun use of 그새 (that short interval); 그새를 못 참고 = unable to wait even that bit

examples.en: They've grown so much in no time.
examples.note: Simple: 그새 + change, with built-in 'so fast!' surprise

examples.ko: 잠깐 화장실 다녀왔는데 그새 자리가 없어졌어요.
examples.romanization: jamkkan hwajangsil danyeowanneunde geusae jariga eopseojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I just popped to the restroom, and in that short time my seat was gone.
examples.note: Everyday: 그새 stressing how fast things changed in a brief absence

examples.ko: 분명히 여기 뒀는데 그새 어디 갔지?
examples.romanization: bunmyeonghi yeogi dwonneunde geusae eodi gatji?
examples.en: I clearly put it right here; where'd it go in that instant?
examples.note: Real situation: 그새 marking a baffling change over a brief moment

entries.nuance: 그새 is a contracted, set form of 그 사이 ('that interval/gap') and means 'in that short while' — almost always carrying a tone of surprise that so much changed in so little time. The contrast learners must keep straight is 그새 vs 그동안: 그동안 is a neutral, often longish stretch ('all this while'), while 그새 specifically flags a surprisingly short interval ('that quick?!'). 그동안 잘 지냈어요? is a calm catch-up; 그새 다 먹었어? is astonishment at speed. It can also work as a noun for that brief stretch itself (그새를 못 참다, 'can't even wait that little bit'). 그새 is native Korean and decidedly casual/spoken — great for reacting to quick changes among friends, less so in formal writing, where 그 사이에 / 그 짧은 사이에 reads better. Note the spelling: keep it as the single set word 그새 to carry the 'so fast!' nuance.

entries.english: long ago, sooner (should have done it earlier)

usagePhrases.note: 진작 할걸 = I should've done it long ago (self-regret)
진작 말했어야지 = you should've said so sooner (mild reproach)
Wishing the knowledge had come earlier
Emphatic variant; 진작에 했어야죠 = you really should've done it long ago

examples.en: You should've told me sooner.
examples.note: Simple: 진작 + -지 그랬어요, gentle 'why didn't you earlier' reproach

examples.ko: 이렇게 쉬운 걸 진작 할걸 그랬어요.
examples.romanization: ireoke swiun geol jinja kalgeol geuraesseoyo.
examples.en: I should have done something this easy long ago.
examples.note: Everyday: 진작 + -ㄹ걸 그랬다 expressing regret over delaying

examples.ko: 맛집인 줄 알았으면 진작 와 봤을 텐데.
examples.romanization: matjibin jul arasseumyeon jinjak wa bwasseul tende.
examples.en: If I'd known it was this good, I'd have come sooner.
examples.note: Real situation: 진작 in an -았/었을 텐데 hypothetical regret about timing

entries.nuance: 진작 means 'sooner / long ago,' but — and this is the whole point — it almost always carries regret or mild reproach that something wasn't done earlier than it actually was. It is not a neutral time word. The contrast learners must internalize is 진작 vs 전에 / 이미: 전에 ('before') and 이미 ('already') are neutral statements of fact, whereas 진작 is loaded with hindsight ('ah, if only it had been done earlier'). So 'I told you before' = 전에 말했어요 (neutral), but 'you should've told me sooner!' = 진작 말하지 (regretful). Because of this emotional core, 진작 habitually pairs with regret/counterfactual endings: -ㄹ걸 (그랬다), -았/었어야지, -았/었으면 ... -ㄹ 텐데. The emphatic variant 진작에 piles on the 'way earlier' feeling. 진작 is native-feeling, casual-to-neutral, and lands flat or even rude if you strip the regret framing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a neutral 'before' like 전에: 진작 always carries the 'should have, sooner' regret. For a plain factual 'before,' use 전에 / 미리.
Pairing it with plain statements instead of regret forms: it wants endings like -ㄹ걸, -았/었어야지, -았/었으면 ... -ㄹ 텐데. Bare 진작 했어요 sounds incomplete.
Confusing it with 미리 (in advance, neutral planning): 미리 예약했어요 = 'I booked ahead of time' (good planning); 진작 예약할걸 = 'I should've booked sooner' (regret). Different feelings entirely.

entries.shortExplanation: 고속버스 means "express (intercity) bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고속버스 (gosokbeoseu) means "express (intercity) bus". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고속버스 타고 가요 ("I'm going by express bus"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고속버스 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 고속버스 + 타다 is the default frame; the means of transport you ride takes 을/를 or just 타고, never 으로 here
the building you depart from — 강남, 센트럴시티 등이 유명; buses use 터미널, never 역
우등(優等) = 'superior grade', 3 wide seats per row with more legroom and a higher fare; worth knowing when booking
예매(豫買) 'buy in advance' is the standard word for booking transport tickets ahead, usually on the 코버스 app

examples.en: The express bus is cheaper than the train.
examples.note: simple A보다 B comparison; 보다 attaches to the thing you measure against

examples.en: It's the weekend, so the express bus tickets are all sold out.
examples.note: 매진(賣盡)되다 = to sell out completely; book early on holidays

examples.ko: 우등으로 예매하면 자리가 넓어서 훨씬 편해요.
examples.romanization: udeungeuro yemaehamyeon jariga neolbeoseo hwolssin pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: If you book the premium one, the seats are wide so it's much more comfortable.
examples.note: 우등으로 uses 으로 'in the manner of'; this is why people pay extra

entries.nuance: 고속버스 (高速 'high-speed' + 버스) is the intercity coach that runs city-to-city on the expressway with few or no stops, so Koreans habitually weigh it against three rivals: the KTX (faster, pricier), the cheaper 무궁화호 train, and 시외버스, which makes more stops and reaches smaller towns. The dividing line you must keep straight is 고속버스 vs 시외버스 — 고속버스 means nonstop expressway travel between major cities and leaves from a 고속버스 터미널, while 시외버스 zig-zags through provincial towns from a different window. It is neutral everyday vocabulary anyone uses, collocating with 타다, 예매하다, 표/자리, and 우등. The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 고속버스역: buses board at a 터미널, and 역 belongs to trains and subways only; a second trap is reaching for 으로 ('by bus') when the natural pattern is simply 고속버스(를) 타다 or 타고 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 고속버스역 — buses use 터미널, not 역 (역 is strictly for trains and subways), so it's 고속버스 터미널.
Confusing 고속버스 with 시외버스 — 고속버스 is nonstop expressway travel between major cities, while 시외버스 makes many stops and reaches smaller towns.

entries.shortExplanation: 시외버스 means "intercity bus (with stops)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "intercity bus (with stops)" is 시외버스 (sioebeoseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시외버스 타다 ("to take an intercity bus"). Watch the particle attached to 시외버스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: used for trips to smaller cities or towns a 고속버스 doesn't reach
often shares a building with the 고속버스 terminal but has a separate ticket window
시간표 'time-table' = schedule; rural departures are sparse, so check it first
완행(緩行) 'slow-going' stops at many towns; its opposite is 직행(直行) 'direct'

examples.en: You get to that village by intercity bus.
examples.note: simple statement; the route a 고속버스 skips

examples.ko: 시외버스는 정류장에 자주 서서 시간이 더 걸려요.
examples.romanization: sioebeoseuneun jeongnyujange jaju seoseo sigani deo geollyeoyo.
examples.en: The intercity bus stops at stations often, so it takes more time.
examples.note: 서다 here = to stop/pull over; this is the trade-off vs 고속버스

examples.en: The last intercity bus is at 8, so we have to hurry.
examples.note: 막차 (last bus) is a survival word; rural lines end early in the evening

entries.nuance: 시외버스 (市外 'outside-the-city' + 버스) is the regional coach that covers shorter routes and makes multiple stops, so it reaches the provincial towns a 고속버스 deliberately skips. The synonym line learners must internalize is 시외버스 vs 고속버스: both are intercity buses, but 고속버스 means nonstop expressway runs between big cities, whereas 시외버스 threads through smaller places and is therefore slower — they even sell from different windows in the same terminal. Within 시외버스 there is a further split, 완행 (all-stops) vs 직행 (express/few-stops), so 직행 시외버스 can be nearly as quick as a 고속버스. It is plain, neutral vocabulary that collocates with 타다, 시간표, 막차, and 정류장. The big English-speaker pitfall is assuming buses run frequently the way they do in a city: rural 시외버스 lines may depart only a handful of times a day, so you must check the 시간표 and never count on a late return.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 시외버스 and 고속버스 as interchangeable — they leave from different windows and serve different route types (provincial-with-stops vs nonstop-expressway).
Assuming frequent departures — rural 시외버스 lines may run only a few times a day, so always check the 시간표 and the 막차 time.
Saying 시외버스역 — like all buses these board at a 터미널/정류장, not a 역.

市外 'outside-the-city' + 버스 — the bus serving routes beyond the city limits.

entries.shortExplanation: KTX means "KTX (high-speed train)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: KTX (KTX) = "KTX (high-speed train)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: KTX 타다 ("to take the KTX") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside KTX, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning.
