entries.explanation: 그러면 (geureomyeon) means "then, in that case, if so". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그러면 이렇게 해요 ("Then let's do it this way"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그러면 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Then let's do it this way
usagePhrases.note: Drawing a next step from what was just said

usagePhrases.note: 그러면 안 되다 is a fixed 'that's not allowed' phrase
Settling a plan based on the prior point
Asking for the next move given the situation

examples.en: You're hungry? Then I'll make ramyeon.
examples.note: Simple condition-then-action; reacts to what the other person said

examples.ko: 이 서류가 필요해요. 그러면 먼저 주민센터에 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: i seoryuga piryohaeyo. geureomyeon meonjeo juminsenteoe gaya haeyo.

entries.nuance: 그러면 means 'then / in that case' and links a conclusion or next step to a condition that was just stated, with the logic 'if that's the situation, then this.' It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + -면 ('if'), so literally it is 'if it is so' — keeping that origin in mind explains why it always reacts to a premise. In fast speech it contracts to 그럼, which is identical in meaning and is what you'll actually hear most of the time. The key contrast for learners is against 그리고: 그러면 responds to a CONDITION ('if so, then...'), whereas 그리고 simply lists the NEXT EVENT in time ('and then'). So 'I woke up and then ate' is 일어났어요. 그리고 먹었어요 — using 그러면 there is wrong because nothing is conditional. Note too that the lookalike 그러면서 ('while doing so') is a different word and not a contraction of this one.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 그리고; 그러면 means 'in that case (conditional)' and reacts to a premise, while 그리고 means 'and then (time sequence)'
Forgetting that the natural spoken contraction is 그럼, not the full 그러면, in everyday talk
Mixing it up with 그러면서 ('while/as one does that'); that is a separate connector, not a casual form of 그러면

It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + -면 ('if'), so literally it is 'if it is so' — keeping that origin in mind explains why it always reacts to a premise.

examples.ko: 주말엔 사람이 많아요. 그러니까 평일에 가는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: jumaren sarami manayo. geureonikka pyeongire ganeun ge naayo.
examples.en: Weekends are crowded. That's why going on a weekday is better.
examples.note: Gives the reasoning behind a recommendation

examples.ko: 그러니까 제 말은, 지금 결정하지 말자는 거예요.
examples.romanization: geureonikka je mareun, jigeum gyeoljeonghaji maljaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: What I mean is, let's not decide right now.
examples.note: 그러니까 제 말은 restates and clarifies your own point

entries.nuance: 그러니까 means 'so / that's why' and presents what follows as the reason-driven result of what came before. It comes from 그렇다 + -(으)니까 ('because it is so'), and that -니까 root is the key to its flavor: -니까 is the 'because' that naturally leads into commands, requests, and urging, which is exactly why 그러니까 pairs so well with advice (일찍 자요) and 'I-told-you-so' lines. This is the sharp dividing line from near-synonym 그래서: 그래서 (from 그렇다 + -아서) merely REPORTS a result neutrally ('so, as a result'), and crucially 그래서 cannot head a command, while 그러니까 actively REASONS and PERSUADES and happily does. Beyond logic, 그러니까 is a heavy conversational filler — 그러니까 내 말이 means 'exactly, that's my point!' (strong agreement), and a trailing 그러니까... works like English 'I mean...' when you restate yourself. English speakers who treat it as a plain synonym of 그래서 miss both the urging nuance and these idiomatic uses.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 그래서; 그러니까 reasons/urges and can introduce a command (그러니까 일찍 자요), while 그래서 only reports a result and cannot head an order
Missing the agreement idiom 그러니까 내 말이, which means 'exactly!' not a literal 'so my words'
Overusing it to start every sentence; as a filler it's fine in speech but looks sloppy if it opens written sentences repeatedly

entries.english: on top of that, moreover, what's more
entries.shortExplanation: 게다가 means "on top of that, moreover, what's more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 게다가 (gedaga) = "on top of that, moreover, what's more". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 게다가 비싸요 ("And on top of that, it's expensive") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 게다가, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: And on top of that, it's expensive
usagePhrases.note: Piling on one more (often negative) point

usagePhrases.en: What's more, even the weather is bad
usagePhrases.note: 게다가 ~까지 stacks an extra burden

usagePhrases.en: On top of that, it's free
usagePhrases.note: Adding a further positive selling point

usagePhrases.en: Plus, the place is close too
usagePhrases.note: 게다가 ~도 tacks on another advantage

examples.en: This restaurant is tasty. On top of that, it's cheap.
examples.note: Simple: stacks a second perk in the same positive direction

examples.en: I worked overtime. On top of that, I even missed the last train.
examples.note: 게다가 ~까지 piling on a worse second misfortune

examples.ko: 방이 넓어요. 게다가 월세도 싸서 바로 계약했어요.
examples.romanization: bangi neolbeoyo. gedaga wolsedo ssaseo baro gyeyakaesseoyo.
examples.en: The room is spacious. Plus the rent is cheap too, so I signed right away.
examples.note: 게다가 ~도 reinforcing a decision with an added reason

entries.nuance: 게다가 means 'on top of that / moreover / what's more,' adding a second point that pushes in the SAME direction as the first — two good things or two bad things stacking up to intensify the overall impression. Its defining contrast is with neutral 그리고 ('and'): 그리고 simply lists items with no emotional slope ('A and B'), while 게다가 conveys 'and as if that weren't enough, also B,' so swapping in a flat 그리고 throws away the cumulative punch. It habitually teams up with the particles 까지 ('even') and 도 ('also') on the added item — 게다가 비까지 와요 ('and on top of that it's even raining'), 게다가 집도 가까워요 — and learning that 게다가 ... 까지/도 frame is the fastest way to sound natural. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 게다가 to add a CONTRASTING point ('it's expensive, however...'); 게다가 cannot pivot, so a contrast needs 하지만 or 그런데 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it to add a contrasting point; 게다가 only stacks same-direction points, so a reversal needs 하지만 or 그런데
Swapping it for a neutral 그리고; 게다가 specifically means 'and what's more', adding cumulative emphasis, not just listing
Forgetting the partner particles; natural 게다가 sentences usually carry 까지 or 도 on the added element (게다가 날씨까지 안 좋아요)

entries.shortExplanation: 따라서 means "therefore, accordingly, thus (formal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 따라서 (ttaraseo) means "therefore, accordingly, thus (formal)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 따라서 결론은 ("Therefore, the conclusion is"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 따라서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Leads into a formal conclusion
Draws a formal consequence in a notice (with -ㅂ니다)
Common in official announcements

usagePhrases.en: Therefore, it may be subject to change
usagePhrases.note: Notice-style logical follow-up

examples.ko: 오늘은 휴일입니다. 따라서 은행은 문을 닫습니다.
examples.romanization: oneureun hyuirimnida. ttaraseo eunhaengeun muneul datseumnida.
examples.en: Today is a holiday. Therefore the bank is closed.
examples.note: Simple formal cause-effect, paired with -ㅂ니다 style

examples.en: The documents are incomplete. Accordingly, we cannot accept the application.
examples.note: Administrative, official register

examples.ko: 규정이 바뀌었습니다. 따라서 모두 다시 신청하셔야 합니다.
examples.romanization: gyujeongi bakkwieotseumnida. ttaraseo modu dasi sincheonghasyeoya hamnida.
examples.en: The rules have changed. Therefore, everyone must reapply.
examples.note: Announcing a required consequence in a notice

entries.nuance: 따라서 means 'therefore / accordingly / thus' and is the formal, logical 'so' of reports, public notices, instructions, contracts, and academic writing. It states a conclusion that follows STRICTLY and objectively from the prior statement, with a more official, impersonal tone than either 그래서 (plain spoken 'so') or 그러니까 (reasoning/urging 'so'). The dividing line: 그래서 and 그러니까 belong to everyday speech and can carry personal feeling or persuasion, whereas 따라서 is detached and rule-like, so in casual conversation it sounds like you're reading a press release. It pairs naturally with the formal -ㅂ니다 ending and with 다음과 같이 ('as follows'). The classic English-speaker trap is mixing this connector up with the homograph verb form 따라서 from 따르다 ('to follow') — as in 규칙을 따라서 ('following the rule'). The connector stands ALONE at the head of a sentence with no object; the verb form has something being followed in front of it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it in casual chat where it sounds like an official notice; in speech use 그래서 or 그러니까 instead
Confusing it with the verb 따르다 ('to follow'): the connector 따라서 stands alone sentence-initially, while 규칙을 따라서 means 'following the rule'
Pairing it with the casual 요-ending; 따라서 belongs to the formal -ㅂ니다 register (따라서 주의가 필요합니다)

entries.english: on the other hand, whereas, by contrast
entries.shortExplanation: 반면에 means "on the other hand, whereas, by contrast" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "on the other hand, whereas, by contrast" is 반면에 (banmyeone). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 반면에 단점도 있어요 ("On the other hand, there are downsides too"). Watch the particle attached to 반면에 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: On the other hand, there are downsides too
usagePhrases.note: Introducing the opposite side of a point

usagePhrases.en: By contrast, the price is high
usagePhrases.note: Weighing a drawback against an upside
Contrasting two places or options
As a clause ending -는/은 반면에, attached directly to a verb/adjective

examples.ko: 형은 키가 커요. 반면에 저는 작아요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeun kiga keoyo. banmyeone jeoneun jagayo.
examples.en: My older brother is tall. By contrast, I'm short.
examples.note: Simple A-vs-B contrast of two clearly stated sides

examples.ko: 도시는 편리해요. 반면에 집값이 너무 비싸요.
examples.romanization: dosineun pyeollihaeyo. banmyeone jipgapsi neomu bissayo.
examples.en: Cities are convenient. On the other hand, housing is way too expensive.
examples.note: Balancing one pro against one con

examples.ko: 월급은 늘어난 반면에 일은 훨씬 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: wolgeubeun neureonan banmyeone ireun hwolssin manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: While the salary went up, the workload grew much more.
examples.note: Shows the bound form -ㄴ 반면에 joining the two sides in one sentence

entries.nuance: 반면에 means 'on the other hand / whereas / by contrast' and explicitly sets two distinct sides, options, or qualities against each other. It comes from the Sino-Korean noun 반면 (反面, literally 'opposite + face/side,' i.e. 'the reverse side') plus the location particle 에 — so its very composition is 'on the opposite side,' which is why it demands a clear A and a clear B to weigh. This is its dividing line from 그런데/근데: those handle a single-topic surprise or twist ('I went out, but it was closed'), whereas 반면에 is analytical and comparative, ideal for pros-and-cons and 'A is X, B is Y' contrasts. It also differs from 한편 in being a sharper head-to-head contrast rather than a loose scene-shift. Note it has two shapes: as a free adverb starting a sentence (반면에 단점도 있어요) and as a bound clause ending -는/은 반면에 attached to the previous verb/adjective (비싼 반면에 'while it's expensive'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping it onto a one-sided remark where there's no real B to contrast — without two sides, 반면에 has nothing to balance and sounds incomplete.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a single-situation surprise; that twist needs 그런데/근데, while 반면에 specifically compares two separate sides
Stating only one side; 반면에 needs a clear A and B, or the contrast has nothing to balance
Confusing the two forms; the standalone adverb is 반면에 (new sentence), but inside one sentence it attaches as -는/은 반면에 (비싼 반면에)

entries.english: that is, in other words, namely
entries.shortExplanation: 즉 means "that is, in other words, namely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 즉 (jeuk) = "that is, in other words, namely". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 즉, 다시 말하면 ("That is, to put it another way") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 즉, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: That is, to put it another way
usagePhrases.note: Signals a restatement is coming

usagePhrases.en: In other words, it means it's free
usagePhrases.note: 즉 ...라는 거예요 spells out what something amounts to
Cutting straight to the core point
즉 ...뜻이에요 states the real meaning

examples.ko: 이건 보증금이에요. 즉, 나중에 돌려받는 돈이에요.
examples.romanization: igeon bojeunggeumieyo. jeuk, najunge dollyeobanneun donieyo.
examples.en: This is a deposit. That is, money you get back later.
examples.note: Restates a term in plainer words; note the comma after 즉

examples.ko: 오늘은 공휴일이에요. 즉, 관공서는 다 쉬어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun gonghyuirieyo. jeuk, gwangongseoneun da swieoyo.
examples.en: Today is a public holiday. In other words, all government offices are closed.
examples.note: Draws the practical implication of a fact

examples.ko: 계약이 끝났어요. 즉, 이제 다른 집을 구해야 한다는 거죠.
examples.romanization: gyeyagi kkeunnasseoyo. jeuk, ije dareun jibeul guhaeya handaneun geojyo.
examples.en: The contract ended. That is, it means I now have to find another place.
examples.note: 즉 ...라는 거죠 reframing a fact as its real consequence

entries.nuance: 즉 means 'that is / in other words / namely' and introduces a RESTATEMENT or precise clarification of what you just said — never new information, only the same point re-expressed more sharply or simply. It is a single Sino-Korean syllable from the hanja 卽 ('namely, that is to say'), and that one-syllable crispness gives it a slightly formal, definitional ring that suits writing, explanations, legal/technical text, and definitions. The contrast to watch: do not confuse 즉 with 그리고 ('and'), which ADDS a separate item; 즉 re-explains, so if what follows is genuinely new content, 즉 is wrong. It overlaps heavily with 다시 말해 ('in other words'), but 즉 is terser and more bookish while 다시 말해 feels more conversational. Punctuation-wise it almost always takes a comma right after it (즉,) and pairs naturally with the nominalizing tails ...라는 거예요 / ...뜻이에요. In very casual chat it can feel clipped, where 그러니까 or 말하자면 sound friendlier.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it to add new information; 즉 only re-explains the same point, so anything genuinely new needs 그리고 instead
Overusing it in very casual speech; in chat 그러니까 or 말하자면 sound more natural than the bookish 즉
Dropping the comma; standard style writes 즉, with a comma before the restatement

entries.english: in other words, to put it differently
entries.shortExplanation: 다시 말해 means "in other words, to put it differently" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다시 말해 (dasi malhae) means "in other words, to put it differently". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다시 말해, 안 된다는 거예요 ("In other words, it means no"). usagePhrases.en: In other words, it means no
usagePhrases.note: Rephrasing to make the point unmistakable
다시 말해서 is the equally common longer form

usagePhrases.en: In other words, it means there's no money
usagePhrases.note: Boiling a situation down bluntly

usagePhrases.en: Put differently, it means there isn't enough time
usagePhrases.note: Restating the real issue

examples.ko: 보증금이 비싸요. 다시 말해, 초기 비용이 많이 들어요.
examples.romanization: bojeunggeumi bissayo. dasi malhae, chogi biyongi mani deureoyo.
examples.en: The deposit is high. In other words, the upfront cost is large.
examples.note: Reframes the point in clearer everyday terms

examples.ko: 답장이 없어요. 다시 말해, 거절이라는 뜻이죠.
examples.romanization: dapjangi eopseoyo. dasi malhae, geojeoriraneun tteusijyo.
examples.en: There's no reply. In other words, it means a rejection.
examples.note: Interprets the real meaning behind a fact

examples.ko: 예약이 다 찼어요. 다시 말해서 오늘은 자리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: yeyagi da chasseoyo. dasi malhaeseo oneureun jariga eopseoyo.
examples.en: Reservations are full. To put it another way, there are no seats today.
examples.note: Shows the interchangeable longer form 다시 말해서

entries.nuance: 다시 말해 literally breaks down as 다시 ('again') + 말해 (the connective form of 말하다, 'to speak'), so its bones say 'speaking again,' working exactly like English 'in other words.' It introduces a clearer, blunter, or more interpretive rephrasing of what you just said, and the fuller form 다시 말해서 is just as common and fully interchangeable. Its near-twin is 즉: both restate, but 다시 말해 is a touch more conversational and explanatory in feel, whereas 즉 is terser and more bookish — so when softly walking a listener through a confusing point, 다시 말해 sounds warmer. The pitfall for English speakers is the surface resemblance to the plain verb phrase 다시 말하다 meaning 'to say (it) again' i.e. to literally repeat the same words; 다시 말해 as a connector does NOT mean verbatim repetition — it signals a reworded explanation, the same idea recast, not the identical sentence said twice.

Confusing it with literal 다시 말하다 ('to repeat the same words'); the connector 다시 말해 introduces a reworded explanation, not a verbatim repeat
Adding brand-new information after it; like 즉, it must restate the same idea, just more clearly
Writing it as one word 다시말해; standard spacing keeps 다시 말해 (and 다시 말해서) as two words

entries.shortExplanation: 예를 들어 means "for example, for instance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "for example, for instance" is 예를 들어 (yereul deureo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예를 들어 김치찌개요 ("For example, kimchi stew"). usagePhrases.note: Giving a concrete instance of a category
예를 들어서 is the equally natural longer form
예를 들면 is a common interchangeable variant
예를 들다 used as a full verb, 'to raise an example'

examples.ko: 한국 음식 좋아해요. 예를 들어 떡볶이요.
examples.romanization: hanguk eumsik joahaeyo. yereul deureo tteokbokkiyo.
examples.en: I like Korean food. For example, tteokbokki.
examples.note: Simple: one concrete instance of a stated preference

examples.ko: 서류가 좀 필요해요. 예를 들어 외국인등록증 같은 거요.
examples.romanization: seoryuga jom piryohaeyo. yereul deureo oegugindeungnokjeung gateun geoyo.
examples.en: You need some documents. For example, things like your residence card.
examples.note: 예를 들어 ... 같은 거 clarifies a vague category with a sample

examples.ko: 취미가 많아요. 예를 들어 등산도 하고 사진도 찍어요.
examples.romanization: chwimiga manayo. yereul deureo deungsando hago sajindo jjigeoyo.
examples.en: I have many hobbies. For example, I hike and take photos.
examples.note: Introducing illustrative activities, here with 도 ... 도

entries.nuance: 예를 들어 means 'for example / for instance' and is the everyday way to introduce a concrete case of a general statement. It is built from the Sino-Korean noun 예 (例, 'example') plus the verb 들다 here meaning 'to raise/cite,' so it literally reads 'raising an example' — the same 들다 as in 손을 들다 ('raise one's hand'). Because it is genuinely a verb phrase, you can flex it: 예를 들어 볼게요 ('let me give an example'), 예를 들어서 (longer connective form), or 예를 들면 ('if one takes an example'), all natural and interchangeable. It works in every register, from chat to academic writing, which makes it one of the most reliable connectors for explaining yourself. The English-speaker pitfalls are two spelling traps: never close up the space (the standard is 예를 들어, not 예를들어), and never blend the variant endings into the non-word 예를 들어면 — the valid forms are 예를 들어 / 예를 들어서 / 예를 들면 only.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing it with no space as 예를들어; the standard spacing is 예를 들어 (and 예를 들어서)
Blending the endings into the incorrect 예를 들어면; the valid forms are 예를 들어, 예를 들어서, and 예를 들면
Pluralizing it like English 'examples'; Korean keeps the singular 예 here, e.g. 예를 들어, not 예들을 들어

entries.shortExplanation: 그럼에도 means "even so, nevertheless, despite that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그럼에도 (geureomedo) = "even so, nevertheless, despite that". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그럼에도 불구하고 ("in spite of that, nevertheless") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그럼에도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 그럼에도 불구하고 is the set, emphatic full form

usagePhrases.en: Even so, I didn't give up
usagePhrases.note: Pressing on despite an obstacle
Sticking to a decision against the odds

usagePhrases.en: Even so, the result was good
usagePhrases.note: An unexpected upside after difficulty

examples.en: It was hard. Even so, I finished it to the end.
examples.note: Simple: persistence despite a stated difficulty

examples.ko: 월급이 적어요. 그럼에도 이 일을 계속하는 이유가 있어요.
examples.romanization: wolgeubi jeogeoyo. geureomedo i ireul gyesokaneun iyuga isseoyo.
examples.en: The pay is low. Nevertheless, there's a reason I keep this job.
examples.note: Introduces a clause that defies expectation

examples.ko: 몸이 안 좋았어요. 그럼에도 불구하고 행사를 진행했어요.
examples.romanization: momi an joasseoyo. geureomedo bulguhago haengsareul jinhaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: I wasn't feeling well. In spite of that, I went ahead with the event.
examples.note: The full emphatic 그럼에도 불구하고 in a weightier register

entries.nuance: 그럼에도 means 'even so / nevertheless / despite that' and signals that what follows happens AGAINST the obstacle just mentioned. It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + the concessive ending -ㅁ에도 ('even though it is'), so structurally it is 'even though it is so.' It is most often heard in its set full form 그럼에도 불구하고 ('in spite of that' — 불구하고 from 不拘, 'not being bound by'), which adds gravity and is common in speeches, editorials, and formal writing. The dividing line to learn is against everyday 그래도: 그래도 is the casual, neutral 'still / even so' you use with friends, while 그럼에도 carries an elevated, determined, slightly dramatic tone — choosing 그럼에도 in a light chat sounds like you've suddenly switched to a TED talk. So the English-speaker pitfall is register mismatch: reach for 그래도 in conversation and reserve 그럼에도 (불구하고) for emphatic or written contexts. Also memorize the fixed spelling 불구하고 — not the common mishearing 불구하구.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for light casual contrast where 그래도 fits; 그럼에도 sounds formal, weighty, and determined
Misspelling the set phrase as 그럼에도 불구하구; the correct form is 그럼에도 불구하고
Treating 불구하고 as optional filler; it specifically means 'in spite of (not bound by)', so 그럼에도 불구하고 is the deliberate emphatic form, not a redundancy

entries.english: meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part
entries.shortExplanation: 한편 means "meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 한편 (hanpyeon) means "meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 한편, 다른 곳에서는 ("Meanwhile, elsewhere"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 한편 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Shifting the scene to a parallel situation
한편으로는 introduces one of two mixed feelings

usagePhrases.en: At the same time, I was also worried
usagePhrases.note: Adding a coexisting, contrasting feeling

usagePhrases.en: on one hand ~ on the other hand
usagePhrases.note: The paired frame for two simultaneous sides

examples.en: I was excited. Meanwhile, my parents were worried.
examples.note: Simple: shifts to a parallel, contrasting reaction

examples.en: On one hand I'm happy, and on the other I'm a little sad.
examples.note: The doubled 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는 frame for mixed feelings

examples.ko: 회사는 채용을 줄였어요. 한편 업무량은 더 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaneun chaeyongeul juryeosseoyo. hanpyeon eommuryangeun deo neureosseoyo.
examples.en: The company cut hiring. Meanwhile, the workload only grew.
examples.note: News-style topic shift to a parallel development

entries.nuance: 한편 means 'meanwhile / on the other hand / for one's part' and shifts attention to a PARALLEL or co-existing situation rather than flatly contradicting the first. It is Sino-Korean, 한 (一, 'one') + 편 (便/篇, 'side'), literally 'one side' — so it frames the next thing as 'one side of the picture,' which is why it can introduce a simultaneous scene, not just an opposite. In news writing, a bare 한편, ... is the standard way to switch topics ('In other news, ...'). Its near-synonym is 반면에, and the dividing line matters: 반면에 (反面, 'opposite side') is a SHARP head-to-head A-vs-B contrast for weighing pros and cons, whereas 한편 is looser and more reportorial, often just panning the camera to a parallel event or adding a coexisting angle. Its most useful conversational life is the doubled frame 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는 (또는 다른 한편으로는), meaning 'part of me... but part of me...,' for mixed feelings. The English pitfall is treating 한편 as a plain 'but'; it does not negate the first clause, it sets a second view beside it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as a flat 'but'; 한편 sets a parallel or coexisting view beside the first, it doesn't contradict it (use 하지만 for negation)
Confusing it with 반면에; 반면에 is a sharp A-vs-B contrast, while 한편 is a looser scene-shift or added angle
Forgetting the mixed-feelings frame 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는, which is its most natural conversational use

entries.english: in the end, eventually, after all
entries.shortExplanation: 결국 means "in the end, eventually, after all" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "in the end, eventually, after all" is 결국 (gyeolguk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 결국 못 갔어요 ("In the end, I couldn't go"). Watch the particle attached to 결국 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: In the end, I couldn't go
usagePhrases.note: Reporting how things finally turned out

usagePhrases.en: It ended up like this after all
usagePhrases.note: Summing up a drawn-out outcome

usagePhrases.en: In the end it'll all work out
usagePhrases.note: 결국엔 adds 은 to stress the final outcome
A final result reached after a struggle

examples.en: I kept hesitating and in the end didn't buy it.
examples.note: Simple: marks the final decision after wavering

examples.en: I held out for days, but I eventually went to the hospital.
examples.note: Outcome reached after resistance; note the lead-in -지만

examples.ko: 다들 말렸는데 결국 제 뜻대로 했어요.
examples.romanization: dadeul mallyeonneunde gyeolguk je tteutdaero haesseoyo.
examples.en: Everyone tried to stop me, but in the end I did it my way.
examples.note: Stresses the eventual result despite opposition, with -는데

entries.nuance: 결국 means 'in the end / eventually / after all' and sums up the FINAL outcome reached after a process, delay, or struggle. It is Sino-Korean, 결 (結, 'to conclude/tie up') + 국 (局, 'situation/end stage'), literally 'the concluding stage' — so it inherently looks back over a whole drawn-out affair to its settling point. The dividing line from near-synonym 드디어 is important: 드디어 celebrates a happy, long-awaited result with relief and excitement ('finally, at last!'), whereas 결국 is emotionally NEUTRAL and frequently tinged with resignation or a sense that the outcome was inevitable ('it came to this after all'). A second contrast English speakers stumble on: 결국 is NOT the 'finally/lastly' that orders items in a list — that ordinal sense ('firstly... finally...') is 마지막으로. 결국 is about how a story RESOLVED, not where an item sits in a sequence. It commonly follows a lead-in clause with -지만 or -는데 sketching the struggle, and the variant 결국엔 (with topic 은) adds extra weight to the final beat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it for 드디어; 결국 is neutral or resigned ('after all'), while 드디어 carries relief and celebration ('finally, at last!')
Using it for ordinal 'finally/lastly' in a list; that sequencing sense is 마지막으로, not 결국
Expecting it to mean a positive result; 결국 often hints the outcome was inevitable or disappointing, so pair it with context that fits

entries.shortExplanation: 이온음료 means "sports drink, electrolyte drink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이온음료 (ioneumnyo) = "sports drink, electrolyte drink". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이온음료 ("sports drink") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이온음료, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 포카리스웨트, 파워에이드 등이 대표 브랜드
편의점에서 주문할 때; 음료는 병/캔이라 보통 '하나'로 셈

usagePhrases.en: When you sweat, a sports drink is good
usagePhrases.note: 운동 후·아플 때 흔히 권하는 말; -으면 = '~하면'

usagePhrases.en: For a hangover it's gotta be a sports drink
usagePhrases.note: 숙취 宿醉 '묵은 취기'(밤새 남은 술기운); -지가 '당연하지' 하는 아는 척 어감을 더함

examples.en: I drank a sports drink after working out.
examples.note: -고 나서 = '~한 뒤에'; 동작 순서를 분명히 함

examples.ko: 몸살 났을 때 물보다 이온음료가 더 나아요.
examples.romanization: momsal nasseul ttae mulboda ioneumnyoga deo naayo.
examples.en: When you have body aches, a sports drink is better than water.
examples.note: 비교의 '보다'는 더 좋은 쪽 앞이 아니라 '물보다'처럼 기준 뒤에 붙음

examples.ko: 편의점에서 이온음료 한 병 사 왔어.
examples.romanization: pyeonuijeomeseo ioneumnyo han byeong sa wasseo.
examples.en: I grabbed a bottle of sports drink from the convenience store.
examples.note: 한 병 = 한 단위의 병; 반말 '사 왔어'는 친구 사이

entries.nuance: 이온음료(ion飮料, '이온+마실 거리')는 땀으로 빠진 전해질을 보충하는 스포츠 음료로 포카리스웨트가 대표격이다. 영어 화자는 보통 'Gatorade'라는 상표명으로 뭉뚱그리지만 한국에서는 운동뿐 아니라 숙취·몸살에도 일상적으로 마신다는 점이 다르다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃 단어는 에너지음료(핫식스·레드불)인데, 이온음료는 카페인이 거의 없고 '각성'이 아니라 '수분·전해질 보충'이 목적이라는 게 결정적 경계선이다. 또 비슷해 보이는 음료수는 '마시는 음료 전반'을 뜻하는 더 넓은 말이라, 이온음료가 음료수의 한 종류다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '이온음료를 마시다 / 이온음료 한 병', 그리고 '땀 흘리고 ~, 숙취엔 ~'. 영어식으로 'ion drink'라고 직역하면 한국에선 통해도 영어권에선 안 통하니, 영어로 옮길 땐 sports/electrolyte drink로 바꿔야 한다.

에너지음료(레드불·핫식스)와 혼동하면 안 됨 — 이온음료는 카페인으로 각성시키는 게 아니라 수분·전해질을 채우는 음료라 목적이 정반대다.

마실 때 동사는 '먹다'보다 '마시다'가 자연스럽다 — '이온음료를 마시다'.

entries.shortExplanation: 매실차 means "green plum tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매실차 (maesilcha) means "green plum tea". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 매실차 ("green plum tea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 매실차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 매실청(매실 시럽)을 물에 타서 만든, 새콤달콤한 차
따뜻하게 = '따뜻한 상태로'; 가게에서 온도를 지정하는 표현

usagePhrases.ko: 소화 안 될 때 매실차 마셔
usagePhrases.romanization: sohwa an doel ttae maesilcha masyeo
usagePhrases.en: Drink plum tea when your digestion is off
usagePhrases.note: 매실은 소화에 좋다는 민간 통념; 반말 권유

usagePhrases.en: Plum tea is sweet and sour
usagePhrases.note: 새콤달콤 = 신맛+단맛이 어우러진 맛을 한 단어로

examples.en: My stomach was upset so I drank plum tea.
examples.note: 속 = 배 속·위장; -아서가 이유('속이 안 좋아서')를 이음

examples.en: This restaurant serves plum tea as a dessert drink.
examples.note: 후식(後食) '뒤에 먹는 것' = 디저트; 식당에서 흔함

examples.en: In summer I make plum tea cold (with the syrup).
examples.note: 타 먹다 = (가루·시럽을) 물에 풀어 마시다

entries.nuance: 매실차(梅實차, '매화나무 열매+차')는 매실청을 뜨거운 물이나 찬물에 타서 마시는 새콤달콤한 음료다. 영어 화자가 'tea'라는 말에 끌려 우려내는 허브티를 떠올리기 쉬운데, 매실차는 잎을 우리는 게 아니라 시럽을 희석한 것이라 본질이 다르다. 가장 가까운 이웃은 유자차로, 둘 다 '청(시럽)을 물에 타는 차'라는 점은 같지만 매실차는 새콤한 매실 맛에 소화제 이미지가 강하고 유자차는 달고 진한 감귤향에 감기 이미지가 강하다는 게 경계선이다. 재료인 매실 한 단어는 '열매' 자체를, 매실청은 '설탕에 절인 시럽'을, 매실차는 '그 시럽을 탄 음료'를 가리키므로 셋을 구분해야 한다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '매실차를 타다/마시다', '소화 안 될 때 ~', '후식으로 ~'. 푸짐한 식사 뒤 주인이 소화에 좋다며 내주기도 하고, 전통찻집 메뉴에서도 흔히 보인다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
매실(열매)과 매실차(음료)를 섞어 쓰면 안 됨 — 'I drank 매실'은 틀리고 마시는 것은 '매실차'다.
티백을 우리는 차로 오해하면 안 된다. 잎을 우린 게 아니라 시럽을 푼 것이라 단맛이 기본이다.
재료를 말할 땐 매실청(시럽), 마실 것을 말할 땐 매실차로 구별해서 써야 한다.

entries.shortExplanation: 유자차 means "yuzu (citron) tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "yuzu (citron) tea" is 유자차 (yujacha). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 유자차 ("citron tea"). Watch the particle attached to 유자차 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 유자청(유자 마멀레이드)을 뜨거운 물에 풀어 만든 차

usagePhrases.ko: 감기 기운 있을 때 유자차 마셔요
usagePhrases.romanization: gamgi giun isseul ttae yujacha masyeoyo
usagePhrases.en: Drink citron tea when you feel a cold coming on
usagePhrases.note: 감기 기운 = 감기 조짐; 비타민C가 많아 감기에 좋다는 통념
한 잔 = 컵·찻잔 단위; 따뜻한 음료는 보통 '잔'으로 셈

usagePhrases.en: Citron tea is good for a sore throat
usagePhrases.note: 목 = 목구멍; '목 아프다'는 인후통의 일상 표현

examples.en: My throat was scratchy so I made some citron tea.
examples.note: 칼칼하다 = 목이 까끌하고 따끔한 느낌

examples.en: In winter, warm citron tea is the best.
examples.note: 최고예요 = '제일 좋다'를 강조; 겨울 단골 음료

examples.ko: 마트에서 유자청 사면 집에서 유자차 만들 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: mateueseo yujacheong samyeon jibeseo yujacha mandeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you buy citron marmalade at the mart, you can make citron tea at home.
examples.note: 유자청 = 유자 마멀레이드/시럽; -으면 조건

entries.nuance: 유자차(柚子차, '유자 열매+차')는 유자청을 한 숟갈 떠서 뜨거운 물에 풀어 마시는, 걸쭉하고 단 겨울 음료다. 영어로 yuzu/citron tea라 하지만 잎을 우리는 차가 아니라 시럽·껍질을 물에 푼 것이라 컵 안에 유자 껍질 조각이 그대로 떠 있는 게 특징이다. 가장 가까운 이웃은 매실차로, 둘 다 '청을 물에 타는 차'지만 유자차는 달고 진한 감귤향에 감기·목 통증 이미지가, 매실차는 새콤한 맛에 소화 이미지가 강하다는 점이 갈린다. 또 재료인 유자청과 음료인 유자차를 구별해야 한다 — 냉장고에 유자청 한 병을 두고 떠 마시는 집이 많다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '유자차를 타다/마시다', '감기 기운 있을 때 ~', '목 아플 때 ~', '따뜻한 ~'. 추운 날 손을 녹이며 마시는 위안의 음료라는 정서가 단어에 배어 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
잎을 우린 차로 오해하면 안 됨 — 유자청(시럽·껍질)을 푼 것이라 컵 안에 껍질 건더기가 떠 있고 단맛이 기본이다.
헤드워드는 한 단어 '유자차'다. '유자 차'처럼 띄우면 어색하다.
재료는 유자청, 마실 것은 유자차로 구분 — '유자차를 사서 탄다'가 아니라 '유자청을 사서 유자차를 탄다'.

structuredNuance.t: 유자청을 한 숟갈 떠서 뜨거운 물에 풀어 마시는, 걸쭉하고 단 겨울 음료다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '유자차를 타다/마시다', '감기 기운 있을 때 ~', '목 아플 때 ~', '따뜻한 ~'. 추운 날 손을 녹이며 마시는 위안의 음료라는 정서가 단어에 배어 있다.

entries.shortExplanation: 에이드 means "ade (fruit soda drink)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 에이드 (eideu) = "ade (fruit soda drink)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 에이드 ("ade") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 에이드, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 카페의 탄산 과일 음료: 레몬에이드, 자몽에이드, 청포도에이드
과일 이름+에이드로 종류를 말함; 자몽 = 그레이프프루트
탄산(炭酸) = 이산화탄소가 든 '거품/톡 쏘는' 성분

usagePhrases.en: I'll have an ade instead of coffee
usagePhrases.note: 말고 = '~이 아니라'; 비커피 음료를 고르는 흔한 표현

examples.en: It was hot so I ordered a cold lemon ade.
examples.note: 시키다 = (음식·음료를) 주문하다

examples.en: The green-grape ade here is really good.
examples.note: 청포도 = 푸른 포도; 가게의 추천 메뉴를 말할 때

examples.en: When I go to a cafe, I only drink ade.
examples.note: -만 = '오직 ~만'; 커피를 안 마시는 사람의 말

entries.nuance: 에이드는 영어 접미사 '-ade(레몬에이드 등)'에서 온 외래어로, 카페에서 시럽과 탄산수를 섞어 얼음과 함께 내는 새콤달콤한 탄산 과일 음료를 통칭한다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 주스인데, 결정적 차이는 '탄산'이다 — 에이드는 톡 쏘는 거품이 있고 주스는 거품 없는 과즙 음료라, 탄산이 싫으면 에이드가 아니라 주스를 시켜야 한다. 또 모양이 비슷한 스무디와도 다르다: 스무디는 과일을 갈아 걸쭉한 반면 에이드는 맑은 탄산 음료다. 커피·차를 빼면 가장 인기 있는 선택지라, 커피를 못 마시는 사람이 카페에서 무난히 고르는 게 에이드다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '에이드를 시키다/마시다', '레몬·자몽·청포도+에이드', '시원한 ~'. 영어 화자가 'lemonade'를 떠올려 무탄산 레모네이드를 기대하면 어긋날 수 있는데, 한국 카페의 에이드는 대개 탄산이 든 점을 기억해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
철자는 그냥 '에이드'다 — '에이드음료'나 '에이드주스'처럼 군더더기를 붙이면 어색하다.
탄산 음료라는 점을 놓치면 안 됨 — 거품 없는 과일 음료를 원하면 에이드가 아니라 주스를 시켜야 한다.
영어 'lemonade' 감각으로 무탄산을 기대하면 안 된다 — 한국의 에이드는 보통 탄산이 들어간다.

structuredNuance.t: 카페에서 시럽과 탄산수를 섞어 얼음과 함께 내는 새콤달콤한 탄산 과일 음료를 통칭한다. 커피·차를 빼면 가장 인기 있는 선택지라, 커피를 못 마시는 사람이 카페에서 무난히 고르는 게 에이드다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '에이드를 시키다/마시다', '레몬·자몽·청포도+에이드', '시원한 ~'.

영어 화자가 'lemonade'를 떠올려 무탄산 레모네이드를 기대하면 어긋날 수 있는데, 한국 카페의 에이드는 대개 탄산이 든 점을 기억해야 한다.

entries.shortExplanation: 스무디 means "smoothie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스무디 (seumudi) means "smoothie". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스무디 ("smoothie"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스무디 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 과일을 얼음과 갈아 만든 걸쭉한 카페 음료
하나요 = '하나 주세요'의 가벼운 줄임; 과일+스무디
갈다 = (믹서로) 갈다; -아서가 방법을 이음

usagePhrases.en: A smoothie and a frappuccino are different
usagePhrases.note: 랑 = '~와'; 스무디는 과일 베이스, 커피 없음

examples.ko: 과일 스무디 한 잔이면 아침 대신 돼요.
examples.romanization: gwail seumudi han janimyeon achim daesin dwaeyo.
examples.en: One fruit smoothie works as a breakfast replacement.
examples.note: 대신 되다 = 대체가 되다; -이면 조건

examples.en: The mango smoothie is the most popular here.
examples.note: 인기(人氣) '사람들의 좋아함' = 인기; 제일이 최상급

examples.en: The smoothie was so cold it gave me brain freeze.
examples.note: 머리가 띵하다 = 머리가 멍하게 얼얼하다(brain freeze)

entries.nuance: 스무디는 영어 smoothie를 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 과일을 얼음과 함께 믹서에 갈아 만든 걸쭉하고 차가운 음료다. 보통 과일 이름이 앞에 붙고(딸기 스무디, 망고 스무디) 띄어 쓰거나 붙여 써도 된다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 셰이크인데, 스무디는 과일이 주재료이고 셰이크는 아이스크림·우유로 만든 더 진한 디저트 음료라는 점이 경계선이다. 또 모양은 비슷해도 커피를 간 음료는 스무디라 부르지 않고 프라푸치노·블렌디드라고 부르며, 맑은 탄산 과일 음료인 에이드와도 질감이 전혀 다르다. 카페에서 '건강한 느낌'으로 고르는 비커피 음료의 대표 격이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '스무디를 갈다/마시다', '딸기·망고+스무디', '한 잔'. 영어 화자가 'smoothie'를 부드러운 음료로 떠올려 우유 셰이크와 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 한국에서 스무디는 기본적으로 과일을 간 음료라는 점을 구분해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
커피를 간 블렌디드 음료를 스무디라 부르면 안 됨 — 그건 프라푸치노/블렌디드이고 스무디는 과일 베이스다.
고정 철자는 '스무디'다 — 체인 이름이 'Smoothie's'라 해도 '스무디스'라고 쓰지 않는다.
셰이크와 혼동 금물 — 셰이크는 아이스크림·우유 기반이라 스무디보다 훨씬 진하고 달다.

영어 smoothie를 그대로 들여온 외래어다.
영어 화자가 'smoothie'를 부드러운 음료로 떠올려 우유 셰이크와 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 한국에서 스무디는 기본적으로 과일을 간 음료라는 점을 구분해야 한다.

Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뽀얗고 살짝 탄산이 있는 발효 쌀 술, 약 6도
병(甁) 단위로 팖; 식당·주점에서 주문

usagePhrases.en: On rainy days it's makgeolli with green-onion pancake
usagePhrases.note: 막걸리에 파전 = 비 오는 날의 단골 조합; -지 어감
가라앉으니 흔든 뒤 따름; -아서가 순서를 이음

examples.ko: 전 부치는 날엔 꼭 막걸리를 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeon buchineun naren kkong makgeollireul masyeoyo.
examples.en: On days we make jeon (pancakes), we always drink makgeolli.
examples.note: 전(煎) = 기름에 부친 부침개; 꼭 = 반드시

examples.en: This makgeolli isn't sweet and tastes clean.
examples.note: 깔끔하다 = (뒷맛이) 개운하고 산뜻하다

examples.ko: 막걸리를 너무 많이 마시면 머리가 아파요.
examples.romanization: makgeollireul neomu mani masimyeon meoriga apayo.
examples.en: If you drink too much makgeolli, you get a headache.
examples.note: 막걸리 숙취에 대한 흔한 경고; -으면 조건

entries.nuance: 막걸리는 뽀얀 빛깔에 약한 탄산이 도는 6도가량의 발효 쌀 술로, 전통적으로 사발에 따라 마시고 비 오는 날 파전과 짝을 이루는 정서가 강하다. 같은 한국 술이라도 소주는 맑고 도수가 높은 증류주, 맥주는 톡 쏘는 곡물 술인 데 비해 막걸리는 탁하고 도수가 낮으며 푸근하고 서민적인 느낌이라는 점이 경계선이다. 비슷해 보이는 동동주는 막걸리의 위쪽 맑은 부분에 가깝지만 일반적으로 막걸리보다 덜 거르고 단맛이 더 도는 술로 구별된다. 병 속에서 앙금이 가라앉으므로 따르기 전에 흔들거나 저어야 끝까지 뽀얀 술이 나온다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '막걸리 한 병/한 사발', '막걸리에 파전', '막걸리를 흔들다/따르다'. 영어 화자가 'rice beer'로 옮기기 쉬운데 맥주처럼 끓여 발효한 술이 아니므로 표준 영어는 makgeolli 또는 rice wine이라는 점을 기억해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
가볍게 탄산이 있고 앙금이 가라앉으니 흔들지 않으면 끝에 뿌연 찌꺼기만 따르게 된다 — 따르기 전에 흔들어야 한다.
'rice beer'로 직역하면 안 됨 — 끓여 만든 맥주가 아니라 발효 쌀 술이라, 영어로는 makgeolli/rice wine이 맞다.
단위는 병/사발이다 — 막걸리는 보통 병이나 사발로 세지 '잔'으로만 세지 않는다.

usagePhrases.note: 요즘 유행하는 하이볼의 기주(베이스 술)
한 잔 = 한 잔; 술을 권하는 표현

usagePhrases.en: I drink whiskey on the rocks
usagePhrases.note: 얼음에 = 얼음을 넣어 / 온더록스로

usagePhrases.en: Whiskey bars are popular these days
usagePhrases.note: 위스키 바 = 위스키 전문 바; 최근 유행

examples.en: Whiskey is strong so I drink it little by little.
examples.note: 독하다 = 도수가 높아 술기운이 세다; -아서가 이유

examples.en: If you mix whiskey with sparkling water, it becomes a highball.
examples.note: 타다 = (액체에) 섞다; -으면 조건, -이 되다 결과

examples.en: I got a bottle of whiskey as a gift.
examples.note: 선물로 = 선물 자격으로; 흔한 선물 품목

entries.nuance: 위스키는 영어 whiskey를 들여온 외래어로, 곡물을 증류해 오크통에 숙성한 독한 술이다. 최근 하이볼 열풍과 위스키 바 유행을 타고 한국에서 급격히 대중화되어, 스트레이트로, 얼음을 넣어(온더록스), 또는 탄산수를 타 하이볼로 마신다. 도수를 묘사할 때는 '독하다'가 자연스러운 짝이다 — 여기서 핵심 구분은 '독하다'와 '진하다'다: 술의 높은 알코올 도수에는 독하다를, 커피·국물 같은 맛의 농도에는 진하다를 쓰므로 위스키에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다가 맞다. 또 같은 양주라도 위스키는 곡물 증류주, 브랜디는 과일(포도) 증류주라는 점이 경계선이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '위스키 한 잔/한 병', '위스키를 마시다/타다', '얼음에/탄산수에'. 영어 화자가 'whiskey liquor'처럼 술을 한 번 더 붙이려 할 수 있는데, 위스키 자체가 술 이름이라 '위스키 술'은 군더더기다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
철자는 '위스키'다 — '위스키주'나 '위스끼'는 틀린 표기다.
'위스키 술'은 겹말이라 어색 — 위스키가 이미 술 이름이므로 술을 덧붙이지 않는다.
도수를 말할 땐 '독하다'를 쓴다 — '위스키가 진하다'는 맛 농도 표현이라 어색하고, 센 술기운은 '독하다'가 맞다.

영어 whiskey를 들여온 외래어다.

entries.shortExplanation: 아메리카노 means "americano (the default Korean coffee order)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아메리카노 (amerikano) means "americano (the default Korean coffee order)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 아메리카노 ("americano"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 아메리카노 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에스프레소+물; 한국에서 가장 많이 시키는 카페 음료
아이스 아메리카노 = 차가운 아메리카노, 국민 기본 메뉴
커피 주문 시 점원이 묻는 정해진 질문; 거 = 것
아아 = 아이스 아메리카노; 뜨아 = 뜨거운 아메리카노

examples.en: I drink an americano every morning.
examples.note: 매일 아침 = 날마다 아침; 일상 커피

examples.en: I drink only iced americanos even in winter.
examples.note: -에도 = '~인데도'; '얼어 죽어도 아이스' 정서

examples.en: Two americanos to go, please.
examples.note: 포장(包裝) '싸서 가져감' = 테이크아웃

entries.nuance: 아메리카노는 에스프레소에 뜨거운 물이나 얼음물을 더한 커피로, 한국 카페에서 압도적인 기본 주문이다. 특히 아이스 아메리카노는 한겨울에도 마시는 사람이 많아 '얼어 죽어도 아이스'라는 농담이 생겼고, 줄임말 아아(아이스)·뜨아(뜨거운)를 알면 현지인처럼 들린다. 핵심 구분은 막연한 '커피'와의 차이다 — 카페에서 그냥 '커피 주세요' 하면 어떤 음료인지 되묻게 되므로 아메리카노처럼 구체 메뉴로 말해야 하고, 그중 무난한 기본값이 아메리카노다. 또 라떼는 우유가 들어가 부드럽고 고소한 반면 아메리카노는 우유 없이 물로 희석해 깔끔하고 쌉쌀하다는 점이 경계선이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '아메리카노 한 잔/두 잔', '아이스/따뜻한 ~', '~ 포장해 주세요'. 주문하면 점원이 으레 '따뜻한 거요, 아이스요?'라고 물으니 이 질문에 답할 준비를 해 두면 좋다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
카페에서 그냥 '커피'만 달라고 하면 안 됨 — 구체 메뉴가 필요하고, 무난한 기본값은 아메리카노다.
아아는 '아이스 아메리카노'만 가리킨다 — 아무 아이스 커피나 아아라고 부르지 않는다.
라떼와 혼동 금물 — 우유가 들어가면 라떼이고, 물로만 희석한 것이 아메리카노다.

entries.shortExplanation: 생맥주 means "draft beer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "draft beer" is 생맥주 (saengmaekju). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 생맥주 ("draft beer"). Watch the particle attached to 생맥주 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 흔히 '생맥'으로 줄임; 잔이나 피처 단위로 팖
잔 = 잔 단위; 주점에서 주문
오백 = 500cc 잔; 천 = 1000cc; 개로도 흔히 셈

usagePhrases.en: Shall we order a pitcher of draft?
usagePhrases.note: 피처 = 여럿이 나눠 마시는 큰 잔; -ㄹ까요? 제안

examples.en: With fried chicken, cold draft beer is the best.
examples.note: 치맥 = 치킨+맥주 문화; -엔 = '~에는'

examples.en: After work we went for a draft beer.

examples.en: The draft here is cheaper than bottled beer.

entries.nuance: 생맥주(生麥酒, '날것의 보리 술')는 통에서 바로 따르는 드래프트 맥주로, 글자 그대로 가열·살균을 덜 한 '신선한' 맥주를 뜻한다. 한국 주점의 기본 술이며 특히 치킨과 짝지어 치맥 문화의 중심에 있다. 핵심 구분은 담는 방식이다 — 생맥주는 통에서 따르는 것, 병맥주는 병에 든 것, 캔맥주는 캔에 든 것이라 같은 맥주라도 서로 다른 말로 부른다. 크기는 오백(500cc)·천(1000cc)으로 부르고 여럿이 마실 땐 피처로 시키며, 입말에서는 '생맥'으로 줄여 쓰는 일이 아주 흔하다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '생맥주 한 잔/두 잔', '오백/천', '피처로', '치킨에 ~'. 영어 화자가 용량을 '500밀리리터'처럼 말하기 쉬운데, 주점에서는 '오백/천'이라고 해야 자연스럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
담는 방식으로 구분 — 통에서 따르면 생맥주, 병이면 병맥주, 캔이면 캔맥주이니 섞어 쓰면 안 된다.
크기를 주문할 땐 '오백/천'으로 말한다 — '500밀리리터'는 주점에서 어색하다.
마실 때는 '먹다'보다 '마시다'나 관용구 '한잔하다'가 자연스럽다 — '생맥주 한잔하다'.

structuredNuance.t: 통에서 바로 따르는 드래프트 맥주로, 글자 그대로 가열·살균을 덜 한 '신선한' 맥주를 뜻한다. 한국 주점의 기본 술이며 특히 치킨과 짝지어 치맥 문화의 중심에 있다. 크기는 오백(500cc)·천(1000cc)으로 부르고 여럿이 마실 땐 피처로 시키며, 입말에서는 '생맥'으로 줄여 쓰는 일이 아주 흔하다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '생맥주 한 잔/두 잔', '오백/천', '피처로', '치킨에 ~'.
핵심 구분은 담는 방식이다 — 생맥주는 통에서 따르는 것, 병맥주는 병에 든 것, 캔맥주는 캔에 든 것이라 같은 맥주라도 서로 다른 말로 부른다.
생맥주(生麥酒)는 '날것의 보리 술'로 이루어진 말이다.
영어 화자가 용량을 '500밀리리터'처럼 말하기 쉬운데, 주점에서는 '오백/천'이라고 해야 자연스럽다.

entries.shortExplanation: 하이볼 means "highball (whiskey + soda)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 하이볼 (haibol) = "highball (whiskey + soda)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 하이볼 ("highball") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 하이볼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 위스키+탄산수+얼음; 지금 매우 유행하는 술
한 잔 = 한 잔; 바·이자카야의 기본 주문
레몬 하이볼 = 레몬을 더한 변형; -로 선택

usagePhrases.en: A highball is low-proof so it's easy to drink
usagePhrases.note: 도수(度數) = 술의 알코올 세기; -아서 이유

examples.ko: 요즘 회식 때 하이볼 많이 마셔요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hoesik ttae haibol mani masyeoyo.
examples.en: These days we drink a lot of highballs at company dinners.
examples.note: 회식(會食) '모여서 먹음' = 회식; 소주를 일부 대체

examples.en: They sell canned highballs even at convenience stores.
examples.note: -에서도 = '~에서조차'; 캔으로 나온 즉석 버전

examples.en: Highballs are smoother than soju, so I like them.
examples.note: 부드럽다 = (목넘김이) 순하다; 보다 비교

entries.nuance: 하이볼은 영어 highball에서 온 외래어로, 위스키에 탄산수를 붓고 얼음을 넣어 만든 술이다. 도수가 낮고 청량해 이자카야·바는 물론 편의점 캔 음료로도 나오며, 요즘 한국에서 가장 유행하는 술 중 하나로 젊은 층이 소주 대신 고르는 경우가 많다. 핵심 구분은 술이냐 아니냐다 — 하이볼은 위스키가 든 '술'이고, 이름이 비슷해 보이는 에이드는 카페의 무알코올 탄산 과일 음료라 마시는 자리와 대상이 전혀 다르다. 또 같은 위스키 음료라도 위스키는 기주(원래 술), 하이볼은 그것을 탄산수로 희석한 칵테일이라는 점이 경계선이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '하이볼 한 잔', '레몬 하이볼', '캔 하이볼', '하이볼을 마시다/타다'. 완전히 굳은 외래어이므로 '하이볼을'을 어색하게 '하이볼-어'처럼 끊어 발음하지 말고 자연스럽게 이어 읽으면 된다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
하이볼은 위스키가 든 술이다 — 무알코올 과일 탄산 음료인 에이드와 혼동하면 안 된다.
위스키와 하이볼을 같은 것으로 보면 안 됨 — 위스키는 원래 술, 하이볼은 탄산수로 희석한 칵테일이다.
완전한 외래어이니 '하이볼을'을 '하이볼-어'처럼 끊지 말고 자연스럽게 이어 발음한다.

structuredNuance.t: 위스키에 탄산수를 붓고 얼음을 넣어 만든 술이다. 도수가 낮고 청량해 이자카야·바는 물론 편의점 캔 음료로도 나오며, 요즘 한국에서 가장 유행하는 술 중 하나로 젊은 층이 소주 대신 고르는 경우가 많다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '하이볼 한 잔', '레몬 하이볼', '캔 하이볼', '하이볼을 마시다/타다'.

영어 highball에서 온 외래어다.
완전히 굳은 외래어이므로 '하이볼을'을 어색하게 '하이볼-어'처럼 끊어 발음하지 말고 자연스럽게 이어 읽으면 된다.

entries.shortExplanation: 진하다 means "strong, rich, concentrated (of a drink/flavor)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 진하다 (jinhada) means "strong, rich, concentrated (of a drink/flavor)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 진하다 ("to be strong/rich"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 진하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 커피·차·국물·우유 등 농도가 짙은 맛
진하게 = 진한 상태로; 샷 추가 느낌을 요청
국물 = 탕·찌개의 액체; 맛의 농도에도 씀
진한+명사 = 진한 ___; 관형형

examples.en: I like strong coffee.
examples.note: 진한 = 진하다의 관형형(명사 앞 형태)

examples.ko: 이 녹차는 너무 진해서 좀 써요.
examples.romanization: i nokchaneun neomu jinhaeseo jom sseoyo.
examples.en: This green tea is so strong it's a bit bitter.
examples.note: -아서가 이유를 이음; 진하다→쓰다로 이어짐

examples.en: If you add less milk, it gets stronger.
examples.note: 진해지다 = 진하게 변하다; -으면 조건

entries.nuance: 진하다는 색·맛·농도가 짙다는 형용사로, 음료에 쓰면 진한 커피, 짙은 차, 우러난 국물, 고소한 우유처럼 '농도가 높은' 상태를 가리킨다. 형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '진한 커피'처럼 -ㄴ 관형형을, 부사처럼 쓸 땐 '진하게 해 주세요'를, 변화에는 '진해지다'를 쓴다. 가장 중요한 구분은 세 갈래다: ① 맛이 진한 데는 진하다를 쓰지 강하다(주로 힘·세기의 강함)는 쓰지 않고, ② 술의 높은 도수에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다를 쓰며, ③ 반대말은 묽고 약한 맛을 뜻하는 연하다다. 즉 진한 아메리카노↔연한 아메리카노, 독한 위스키(도수)↔진한 국물(맛 농도)로 갈래가 다르다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '진한 커피/라떼', '국물이 진하다', '진하게 (해 주세요)', '진해지다'. 영어 'strong'을 그대로 옮겨 술의 도수에까지 진하다를 쓰면 어색하니, 도수에는 독하다, 맛 농도에는 진하다로 갈라 써야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
맛이 진한 음료에는 진하다를 쓴다 — 강하다(힘·세기의 강함)는 맛 농도에 어색하다.
술의 높은 도수에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다 — 진하다는 도수가 아니라 맛의 농도를 가리킨다.
반대말은 연하다(묽다·약하다)다 — '안 진하다'보다 '연하다'가 자연스러운 짝이다.

structuredNuance.t: 색·맛·농도가 짙다는 형용사로, 음료에 쓰면 진한 커피, 짙은 차, 우러난 국물, 고소한 우유처럼 '농도가 높은' 상태를 가리킨다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '진한 커피/라떼', '국물이 진하다', '진하게 (해 주세요)', '진해지다'.

entries.shortExplanation: 미지근하다 means "to be lukewarm, tepid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be lukewarm, tepid" is 미지근하다 (mijigeunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 미지근하다 ("to be lukewarm"). Watch the particle attached to 미지근하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뜨겁지도 차갑지도 않은; 음료에 대한 불평으로 자주 씀
얼음이 녹았을 때 흔히 하는 말
차갑지 않은 물을 원할 때(약 먹을 때 등) 유용
미지근해지다 = 미지근하게 변하다

examples.en: The beer is lukewarm so it tastes bad.
examples.note: -아서가 이유; 미지근한 맥주는 흔한 불평거리

examples.en: Take the medicine with lukewarm water.
examples.note: 이랑 = '~와 함께'; 약사·건강 조언에서 흔함

examples.en: The americano had cooled off and was lukewarm.
examples.note: 식다 = (음식·음료가) 차게 식다

entries.nuance: 미지근하다는 뜨겁지도 차갑지도 않은 '미적지근한' 온도를 뜻하는 형용사로, 뜨거워야 할 커피가 식었거나 차가워야 할 맥주가 미적지근해진 상태에 쓴다. 핵심 구분은 따뜻하다와의 차이다 — 따뜻하다는 마시기 좋게 기분 좋은 온기를 뜻하는 긍정어인 반면, 미지근하다는 마땅한 온도(뜨겁거나 차가워야 함)에 못 미친 상태라 대개 가벼운 불평의 어감을 띤다. 그래서 '커피가 따뜻해요'는 칭찬에 가깝지만 '커피가 미지근해요'는 식었다는 불만이다. 다만 약을 먹거나 속이 예민할 때 '미지근한 물'을 일부러 청하는 긍정적 쓰임도 있다. 형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '미지근한 물', 변화에는 '미지근해지다'를 쓴다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '물·커피·맥주가 미지근하다', '미지근한 물', '미지근해지다'. 액체·물건의 온도에 쓰는 말이라 날씨에는 어울리지 않으니, 포근한 날씨에는 미지근하다가 아니라 포근하다/따뜻하다를 써야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
미지근하다(미적지근함)와 따뜻하다(기분 좋은 온기)는 다르다 — 뜨거워야 할 음료가 식은 건 따뜻하다가 아니라 미지근하다(불평)다.
날씨에는 쓰지 않는다 — 공기 온도가 아니라 주로 액체·물건에 쓰며, 포근한 날씨는 포근하다/따뜻하다다.
형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '미지근한 물'처럼 -ㄴ 관형형을 써야 한다 — '미지근 물'은 틀리다.

structuredNuance.t: 뜨겁지도 차갑지도 않은 '미적지근한' 온도를 뜻하는 형용사로, 뜨거워야 할 커피가 식었거나 차가워야 할 맥주가 미적지근해진 상태에 쓴다. 대개 가벼운 불평의 어감을 띠지만, 약을 먹거나 속이 예민할 때 '미지근한 물'을 일부러 청하는 긍정적 쓰임도 있다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '물·커피·맥주가 미지근하다', '미지근한 물', '미지근해지다'.
핵심 구분은 따뜻하다와의 차이다 — 따뜻하다는 마시기 좋게 기분 좋은 온기를 뜻하는 긍정어인 반면, 미지근하다는 마땅한 온도(뜨겁거나 차가워야 함)에 못 미친 상태라 대개 가벼운 불평의 어감을 띤다. 그래서 '커피가 따뜻해요'는 칭찬에 가깝지만 '커피가 미지근해요'는 식었다는 불만이다.
형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '미지근한 물', 변화에는 '미지근해지다'를 쓴다.
액체·물건의 온도에 쓰는 말이라 날씨에는 어울리지 않으니, 포근한 날씨에는 미지근하다가 아니라 포근하다/따뜻하다를 써야 한다.

entries.shortExplanation: 신기하다 means "amazing, fascinating, novel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 신기하다 (singihada) = "amazing, fascinating, novel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 신기하다 ("to be fascinating / amazing") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 신기하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: everyday word for 'wow, cool!' when something is new or surprising in a good way
adverbial 신기하다 + 게도; opens a sentence: 신기하게도 비가 딱 그쳤어 = amazingly the rain stopped right then
polite -네요 of fresh discovery; mild wonder at something you just learned or saw
신기한 (modifier) + 거(것); 신기한 거 봤어 = I saw something cool

examples.en: This flower is really cool.
examples.note: shortest 반말 form; just point and react, no object particle needed

examples.ko: 한국 지하철은 환승이 잘 돼 있어서 신기해요.
examples.romanization: hanguk jihacheoreun hwanseungi jal dwae isseoseo singihaeyo.
examples.en: The Korean subway transfers are so well-organized, it's amazing.
examples.note: -아서 reason + 신기해요; everyday remark foreigners share with Korean friends

examples.ko: 눈을 처음 봤을 때 너무 신기했어.
examples.romanization: nuneul cheoeum bwasseul ttae neomu singihaesseo.
examples.en: When I saw snow for the first time it was so amazing.
examples.note: past 신기했어 recalling a first experience; object 눈을 marks what amazed you

entries.nuance: 신기하다 is the go-to word for delighted, almost childlike wonder at something new, clever, or unexpected — a smart gadget, your first snow, a magic trick. The connotation is warm and positive. The Sino-Korean root is 神奇 (신기), literally 'divine + marvelous', so the feeling is that something is marvelously beyond the ordinary. The sharpest contrast is with 이상하다 ('weird/off'): both react to the unfamiliar, but 신기하다 is good-surprised ('cool!') while 이상하다 is bad-surprised ('something's wrong'). It also differs from 놀랍다 ('astonishing', more shock than charm). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like 'strange' — saying 신기하다 about a creepy noise sounds like you enjoyed it. As an adjective it never takes 를; you say 이게 신기해, not 이걸 신기해.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for creepy/bad weirdness ('a strange smell') — that negative 'weird' is 이상하다; 신기하다 is positive wonder, so it implies you liked it.
Writing the verbish 신기다 or conjugating 신기다 — the dictionary form keeps 하: 신기하다, 신기해요, 신기한.
Adding 를 as if it were a verb: 이걸 신기해(X). It is descriptive, so the thing that amazes you takes 이/가: 이게 신기해(O).

structuredNuance.t: 신기하다 is the go-to word for delighted, almost childlike wonder at something new, clever, or unexpected — a smart gadget, your first snow, a magic trick. The connotation is warm and positive.

The sharpest contrast is with 이상하다 ('weird/off'): both react to the unfamiliar, but 신기하다 is good-surprised ('cool!') while 이상하다 is bad-surprised ('something's wrong'). It also differs from 놀랍다 ('astonishing', more shock than charm).
The Sino-Korean root is 神奇 (신기), literally 'divine + marvelous', so the feeling is that something is marvelously beyond the ordinary.

반말, said softly while taking something gorgeous in

황홀하다 + -ㄹ 정도로 = so beautiful that...; 황홀할 정도로 아름다웠어

examples.en: The sunset is truly mesmerizing.
examples.note: simple subject + 황홀해요; 노을(sunset) is the textbook trigger

examples.en: Walking the cherry blossom path, it was just breathtaking.
examples.note: -더라 reporting a vivid first-hand impression to a friend

examples.ko: 공연이 너무 황홀해서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
examples.romanization: gongyeoni neomu hwangholhaeseo sigan ganeun jul mollasseo.
examples.en: The show was so enchanting I lost track of time.
examples.note: -아서 cause chained to the set phrase 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어

entries.nuance: 황홀하다 describes beauty so intense it nearly sweeps you out of yourself — reserved for sunsets, night views, sublime music, a magical moment, never an everyday 'pretty'. The Sino-Korean 恍惚 (황홀) literally means 'dazed/entranced', so the word names the spellbound state of the viewer as much as the beauty itself, and it sounds literary and heightened. Contrast it with 아름답다 ('beautiful', the neutral aesthetic word) and 예쁘다 ('pretty', casual and small-scale): dropping 황홀하다 on a so-so cafe latte sounds theatrical. It also differs from 행복하다 ('happy'), which is general well-being, not being dazzled by beauty. The pitfall for English speakers is using it as a synonym for 'lovely/nice'; in Korean it implies near-overwhelm, so save it for genuinely stunning sights and pair it with 진짜/정말 or -할 정도로 for emphasis.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Overusing it for mildly nice things ('the coffee was 황홀해') — 황홀하다 implies almost overwhelming beauty; for ordinary nice use 좋다/예쁘다/멋지다.
Confusing it with 행복하다 (general happiness) — 황홀하다 is specifically about being entranced by beauty or a sublime moment, not everyday contentment.
Applying it to a person's looks bluntly ('너 황홀해') — it sounds odd/over-the-top about a person; for that use 예쁘다/멋지다, and reserve 황홀하다 for scenes and experiences.

entries.shortExplanation: 아찔하다 means "dizzying, heart-stopping, scary-close" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "dizzying, heart-stopping, scary-close" is 아찔하다 (ajjilhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아찔하다 ("to be dizzying / heart-stopping"). Watch the particle attached to 아찔하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the rush when you almost got hurt or look down from a height
반말 reaction right after a near-miss
past tense, retelling a scary moment that already passed

usagePhrases.en: it's dizzying just to think about it
usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase 생각만 해도 + 아찔하다 = I shudder to imagine

examples.en: Looking down, I feel dizzy.
examples.note: bare 반말; height-induced vertigo in the moment

examples.en: A car cut in suddenly and it was really heart-stopping.
examples.note: -아서 cause + past; the near-accident-on-the-road use, extremely common

examples.en: I almost lost my wallet. That was scary-close.
examples.note: set frame 하마터면 …-ㄹ 뻔했어, then 아찔해 as the aftershock

entries.nuance: 아찔하다 captures the dizzy, stomach-dropping jolt of a near-miss or a dangerous height — the physical wave of 'whew, that was close'. It is at once literal vertigo and the split-second emotional shock of almost-disaster, which is why Koreans say it constantly after close calls in traffic. It is an onomatopoeic/mimetic adjective (from 아찔, the lurch of light-headedness), so there is no 한자. The key contrast is with 무섭다 ('scary'), which is steady, ongoing fear, whereas 아찔하다 is one instantaneous lurch; and with 짜릿하다 ('thrilling'), which is the pleasant tingle of excitement. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'dizzy = 어지럽다': 어지럽다 is plain medical dizziness (low blood sugar, spinning room), while 아찔하다 adds the danger/shock element. It habitually pairs with 하마터면…뻔하다 and 생각만 해도.

Using it for ongoing fear ('I'm 아찔해 about the exam') — 아찔하다 is a momentary dizzy jolt; sustained fear is 무섭다/긴장되다.
Saying 아찔하다 for a happy thrill (a roller-coaster you enjoyed) — it implies danger or vertigo, not fun excitement; that pleasant rush is 짜릿하다.
Swapping in plain 어지럽다 for a near-miss — 어지럽다 is just physical dizziness; 아찔하다 carries the 'that was dangerously close' shock.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 섬뜩하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the cold shiver when something is eerie or menacing
반말, reacting to a horror scene or unsettling sight
past tense, retelling an eerie moment after the fact
섬뜩한 (modifier) + noun; common with 느낌, 분위기, 눈빛

examples.en: That painting is kind of creepy.
examples.note: short 반말 + softener 좀; reacting to an unsettling image

examples.ko: 밤에 혼자 그 골목을 지나가는데 섬뜩했어.
examples.romanization: bame honja geu golmogeul jinaganeunde seomtteukaesseo.
examples.en: Walking through that alley alone at night was creepy.
examples.note: -는데 background + past; the lone-dark-alley scene

examples.en: That person's stare was really chilling.
examples.note: -더라 reporting a vivid impression of someone; 눈빛(gaze) is a stock partner

entries.nuance: 섬뜩하다 is the cold-spine, hair-raising creepiness of something eerie or sinister — a dark alley, an unsettling stare, a disturbing news story. It names the sudden chill that runs down your back, sharper and colder than the general fear of 무섭다. It is a native Korean mimetic word (from 섬뜩, the feel of a cold jolt), so there is no 한자. Compare it with three neighbors: 무섭다 ('scary', broad ongoing fear, even of exams); 소름 끼치다 ('to get goosebumps', very close and often interchangeable, focusing on the skin reaction); and 으스스하다 ('spooky/chilly', a milder ambient creepiness). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'creepy' loosely the way English does for a mildly off person ('he's a bit creepy'); in Korean that everyday 'off/sketchy' nuance is closer to 좀 이상하다, and 섬뜩하다 should be saved for a genuinely spine-chilling jolt. It pairs naturally with 눈빛, 분위기, 느낌, 사건.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for ordinary fear of, say, exams or a dog — 섬뜩하다 implies eerie, spine-chilling dread; everyday fear is 무섭다.
Confusing it with 신기하다 — 섬뜩하다 is negative and creepy; 신기하다 is positive fascination, the opposite reaction.
Calling a merely sketchy person 섬뜩하다 the way English says 'creepy guy' — that mild 'off' sense is 좀 이상하다; reserve 섬뜩하다 for a real chill.

entries.explanation: 거북하다 (geobukada) means "uncomfortable, awkward, queasy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 거북하다 ("to feel uncomfortable / queasy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 거북하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: covers both an awkward mood and an upset, heavy stomach

usagePhrases.en: to feel queasy in the stomach
usagePhrases.note: fixed collocation; 속(insides) + 이 + 거북하다 = bloated/uneasy stomach

usagePhrases.en: this feels awkward / my stomach's off
usagePhrases.note: 반말; meaning flips with context (people vs. 속이)
V-기 거북하다 pattern = uncomfortable/awkward to do something

examples.en: My stomach feels a bit off.
examples.note: the core stomach use; 속이 + 거북해, softened with 좀

examples.en: I overate, so my stomach feels queasy.
examples.note: -았더니 (I did X and as a result) + the 속이 거북하다 collocation

examples.en: Honestly, that question was awkward to answer.
examples.note: V-기 거북하다 (대답하기 거북하다) for a question you'd rather not field

entries.nuance: 거북하다 has two everyday lives: a queasy, heavy, ill-sitting stomach (속이 거북하다) and an awkward, uneasy social feeling (분위기가 거북하다, 마주치기 거북하다). Both share the core image of something not sitting right — physically or emotionally. The sharpest contrast is with 불편하다: 불편하다 covers broad 'inconvenient/uncomfortable', including practical inconvenience (불편한 의자 = an uncomfortable chair, 교통이 불편하다 = bad transit), whereas 거북하다 is the more inward, visceral 'this doesn't sit well with me' and is the natural word for an upset stomach. For a hard chair or bad transit you must use 불편하다, not 거북하다. It also overlaps with 어색하다 ('awkward, unfamiliar between people'), but 거북하다 adds a note of mild distaste or discomfort, not just unfamiliarity. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping all of 'uncomfortable' onto one word; remember 거북하다 for queasy stomachs and for situations you find off-putting, and 불편하다 for physical/practical discomfort.

Using it for physical inconvenience like a hard chair or far-away store — that is 불편하다; 거북하다 is queasy or socially ill-at-ease, not 'inconvenient'.
Forgetting the stomach sense — 속이 거북하다 is an extremely common natural collocation after a big meal; learners often only learn the 'awkward' meaning.
Using it for first-meeting shyness ('I felt 거북해 meeting new people') — pure unfamiliar awkwardness is 어색하다; 거북하다 implies it actively bothers you.

entries.shortExplanation: 야속하다 means "heartless (toward me), disappointing, cold" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "heartless (toward me), disappointing, cold" is 야속하다 (yasokada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 야속하다 ("to feel let down by someone's coldness"). Watch the particle attached to 야속하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to feel let down by someone's coldness
usagePhrases.note: soft resentment when someone you care about is unkind or distant
반말, gentle reproach to a close person
-더라 recalling a moment you personally felt slighted
야속한 (modifier) + noun; mild blame, not strong condemnation

examples.en: You're really being cold.
examples.note: bare 반말 reproach said straight to the person who let you down

examples.ko: 힘들 때 연락 한 번 없어서 좀 야속했어.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae yeolla kan beon eopseoseo jom yasokaesseo.
examples.en: You didn't reach out once when I was struggling, it felt cold.
examples.note: -아서 reason + softener 좀; classic complaint toward a friend

examples.en: Even the weather is being cruel — it's raining.
examples.note: playful extension to fate/circumstance with 야속하게 + 까지

entries.nuance: 야속하다 is the soft, wounded resentment you feel when someone close lets you down or seems cold — less anger than quiet hurt. It carries an implicit 'I expected warmth from you and didn't get it', so there is affection tucked underneath the complaint, and it is most natural toward family, close friends, a partner, or even personified fate/weather. The nearest synonym is 섭섭하다 ('hurt/let down'), and the dividing line matters: 섭섭하다 is the broad ache of disappointment ('I'm sad you forgot my birthday'), while 야속하다 specifically blames the other side's apparent heartlessness ('how could you be so cold to me'). It is gentler and more inward than 매정하다 ('cold-hearted', a flatter description of someone) and far softer than 화나다 ('angry'). The English-speaker pitfall is reading it as real anger or using it about strangers and institutions; with strangers there is no prior warmth to betray, so it rings false — use 차갑다/매정하다 instead, and save 야속하다 for people (or fate) you feel close enough to gently reproach.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for strangers or companies ('the bank was 야속해') — 야속하다 implies you expected kindness from a close relationship; for strangers use 차갑다/매정하다.
Treating it as strong anger — it is gentle, hurt reproach with affection underneath, not 화나다; raising your voice with 야속해 mismatches the tone.
Swapping it freely with 섭섭하다 — 섭섭하다 is general disappointment, while 야속하다 specifically points at the other person's coldness toward you.

entries.shortExplanation: 정겹다 means "warm-hearted, cozy, full of affection" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정겹다 (jeonggyeopda) = "warm-hearted, cozy, full of affection". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 정겹다 ("to be warm and heartfelt") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the cozy warmth of a homey scene or close relationship
반말; ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 정겹다 → 정겨워
정겨운 (ㅂ-irregular modifier) + noun; 정겹 + 은 → 정겨운
adverb form; 정겹게 인사하다 = greet warmly

examples.en: My neighborhood is really cozy and warm.
examples.note: shortest 반말; note the ㅂ-irregular 정겹다 → 정겨워, not 정겹어

examples.ko: 할머니 댁은 늘 정겨운 냄새가 나.

examples.en: Grandma's house always has a cozy, homey smell.
examples.note: 정겨운 (modifier) + 냄새; the ㅂ-irregular -은 form 정겨운

examples.en: We hadn't met in ages and they hugged me warmly.
examples.note: 정겹게 (adverb) + 안아주다; warmth expressed through an action

entries.nuance: 정겹다 carries the uniquely Korean feeling of 정(情) — deep, accumulated affectionate warmth between people — so it names the cozy, homey heart you get from a traditional market, an old neighborhood, or a close-knit gathering. The headword is 정(情, 'affection/bond') + 겹다 ('to be full of / overflowing with'), so it literally means 'brimming with 정'. It is about human warmth and connection, not mere physical comfort or temperature, which sets it apart from 따뜻하다 ('warm') — 따뜻하다 can be literal heat or a warm personality, while 정겹다 is specifically that 정-soaked, nostalgic homeyness, and it leans gentle and a touch literary. It also differs from 포근하다 ('soft, snug, cozy'), which is about physical/emotional softness rather than the people-bond of 정. Grammatically the trap is huge: 정겹다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so it becomes 정겨워(요), 정겨운, 정겨우니까 — never the regular 정겹어요/정겹은. English speakers also over-apply it to cute objects; it is about heartfelt human warmth, not cuteness (그건 귀여워, not 정겨워).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 정겹어요/정겹은 — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ turns to 우/워: 정겨워요, 정겨운, 정겨우면.
Using it for cute objects or animals — 정겹다 is heartfelt human/communal warmth (정), not cuteness; for cute use 귀엽다.
Reducing it to plain 'warm temperature' like 따뜻하다 — 정겹다 specifically means brimming with affectionate 정 and nostalgia, not literal or merely figurative warmth.

usagePhrases.note: the aching fondness of longing or cherished love
반말, reacting to a touching story or memory
애틋한 (modifier) + 사이; common for couples or family
애틋한 + 마음; the set phrase for deep affectionate feeling

examples.en: The two of them are so tenderly fond of each other.
examples.note: short 반말 about a couple's bond; subject + 애틋해

examples.en: Being far apart makes the feeling even more tender.
examples.note: -니까 reason + 더; distance intensifying tenderness, a core context

examples.ko: 부모님 사진을 보면 애틋한 마음이 들어요.

examples.en: Looking at my parents' photo brings a tender, longing feeling.
examples.note: 애틋한 마음 + 들다 — feelings 'arise' (들다), not 'come'

entries.nuance: 애틋하다 is a tender, bittersweet fondness — the ache of cherishing someone you miss or love deeply, usually tinged with longing, distance, or the knowledge that the moment is precious and fragile. It is gentler and far more wistful than plain 좋아하다/사랑하다, adding a thread of melancholy, which is why it suits first loves, family far away, or a bond you hold close. The nearest neighbor is 애절하다 ('sorrowfully yearning'), but 애절하다 is more openly sad/desperate, while 애틋하다 keeps a warm, cherishing softness under the ache. It also contrasts with 안타깝다 ('it's a pity / I feel for their misfortune'): 안타깝다 is sympathy for an unfortunate situation, whereas 애틋하다 centers on tender longing toward a person or memory. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for casual liking the way 'fond of pizza' works in English — 애틋하다 is reserved for deep, bittersweet, person-directed tenderness, so for light liking use 좋아하다. A grammar note: feelings here arise with 들다 (마음이 들다), and the verb-ified 애틋해지다 means 'to grow tender'.

Using it for casual liking ('I'm 애틋해 about coffee') — 애틋하다 is deep, bittersweet tenderness toward a person or memory; light liking is 좋아하다.
Confusing it with 안타깝다 — 안타깝다 is pity for someone's misfortune, while 애틋하다 centers on tender, longing affection.
Saying 애틋한 마음이 와요 — feelings arise with 들다, so it is 애틋한 마음이 들어요, not 오다.

entries.shortExplanation: 아련하다 means "hazy, faint, wistfully distant" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "hazy, faint, wistfully distant" is 아련하다 (aryeonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아련하다 ("to be hazy / faintly nostalgic"). Watch the particle attached to 아련하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: for blurry distant memories or a dreamy, faint impression
반말, about a faded memory
아련한 (modifier) + 추억; the single most common partner noun
adverb; 아련하게 떠오르다/생각나다 = come faintly to mind

examples.en: My childhood memories are kind of hazy.
examples.note: short 반말; 기억(memory) as subject, softened with 좀

examples.ko: 그 노래를 들으면 옛날 생각이 아련하게 나.
examples.romanization: geu noraereul deureumyeon yennal saenggagi aryeonhage na.
examples.en: When I hear that song, old memories come back faintly.
examples.note: 아련하게 (adverb) + 생각이 나다 — the memory-surfacing collocation

examples.ko: 사진 속 풍경이 아련해서 더 그리웠어요.
examples.romanization: sajin sok punggyeongi aryeonhaeseo deo geuriwosseoyo.
examples.en: The scenery in the photo was hazy, making me miss it more.
examples.note: -아서 linking 아련하다 to 그립다, the longing it triggers

entries.nuance: 아련하다 describes something faint and hazy — above all distant memories that blur at the edges, leaving a soft, wistful longing behind. It fuses 'dim/indistinct' with gentle nostalgia, so in practice it almost always pairs with 추억(memories), 기억, or 생각, and with the adverb 아련하게 + 떠오르다/생각나다. The crucial contrast is with 흐릿하다 ('blurry/unclear'): 흐릿하다 is plain physical fuzziness — out-of-focus eyesight, a smudged photo, dim letters — with no emotion, while 아련하다 is dreamier and carries that bittersweet pull of the past. It also brushes against 어렴풋하다 ('vague, only faintly recalled'), which is closer to a neutral 'I can barely remember', whereas 아련하다 adds the warm, longing color. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto 'blurry/hazy vision' or any literal fuzz; if your eyes are blurry or a window is foggy, that is 흐릿하다/뿌옇다, not 아련하다. Reserve 아련하다 for faded, emotionally tinged memories, not clear or recent events.

Using it for physically blurry vision or a foggy window ('내 눈이 아련해') — literal fuzziness is 흐릿하다/뿌옇다; 아련하다 carries nostalgia.
Applying it to clear, recent events ('오늘 점심이 아련해') — 아련하다 needs that faded, distant, time-worn quality.
Using it for a neutral 'I can barely recall' fact — that flat vagueness is 어렴풋하다; 아련하다 implies a warm, wistful longing alongside the haze.

entries.shortExplanation: 뿌듯하다 means "proud, fulfilled, heart-swelling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뿌듯하다 (ppudeutada) = "proud, fulfilled, heart-swelling". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 뿌듯하다 ("to feel proud and fulfilled") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 뿌듯하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the chest-swelling satisfaction after an accomplishment
반말, the warm glow after doing something well
past tense, recalling a satisfying moment
뿌듯한 (modifier) + 마음; the stock collocation

examples.en: I got through my whole workout today, so I feel fulfilled.
examples.note: -아서 reason + 뿌듯해; the small-daily-win use, very common

examples.ko: 드디어 한국어로 주문에 성공해서 너무 뿌듯했어요.
examples.romanization: deudieo hangugeoro jumune seonggonghaeseo neomu ppudeutaesseoyo.
examples.en: I finally managed to order in Korean, I felt so proud.
examples.note: 강조 너무 + past; a relatable learner win in Korea

examples.ko: 방 청소를 다 하고 나니까 뿌듯해.
examples.romanization: bang cheongsoreul da hago nanikka ppudeutae.
examples.en: After finishing cleaning my room, I feel fulfilled.
examples.note: -고 나니까 (after doing X, then I felt…) leading into 뿌듯해

entries.nuance: 뿌듯하다 is the warm, chest-swelling pride and fulfillment you feel after accomplishing something — finishing a task, hitting a goal, even doing a small thing well. It is inward, modest satisfaction (the chest literally feeling 'full'), not bragging, so it shows up constantly in everyday self-talk. The native word comes from the mimetic sense of being filled to the brim. The key contrast is with 자랑스럽다 ('proud of'): 자랑스럽다 is typically outward and directed at a person or achievement you want to show off — 아들이 자랑스러워(I'm proud of my son), 한국인인 게 자랑스럽다 — and can imply boasting, while 뿌듯하다 is the quiet inner glow you feel for yourself and rarely takes an external object. It also differs from 만족하다 ('to be satisfied'), which is cooler and more evaluative ('the result meets my standard') versus the heart-warm emotion of 뿌듯하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 뿌듯하다 to mean 'proud of someone else' the way English 'proud' covers both; for that you generally want 자랑스럽다. Watch the spelling too: it is the tense ㅃ, 뿌듯하다, not 부듯하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it to mean 'proud of someone else' ('아들이 뿌듯해') — that outward pride is 자랑스럽다; 뿌듯하다 is your own inner fulfillment.
Spelling it 부듯하다 — it begins with the tense consonant ㅃ: 뿌듯하다, 뿌듯해요.
Equating it with cool 만족하다 — 만족하다 is evaluative satisfaction ('it meets the standard'), while 뿌듯하다 is the warm, emotional heart-swell.
