entries.shortExplanation: 겸연쩍다 means "sheepish, embarrassed, awkwardly self-conscious" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 겸연쩍다 (gyeomyeonjjeokda) means "sheepish, embarrassed, awkwardly self-conscious". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 겸연쩍다 ("to feel sheepish / awkward"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 겸연쩍다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the bashful awkwardness after a small misstep or being caught
반말; the awkward-laugh moment
adverb; 겸연쩍게 웃다 = laugh awkwardly (the signature collocation)
겸연쩍은 (modifier) + noun; common with 표정, 미소

examples.en: I called the wrong name, so I felt sheepish.
examples.note: -아서 cause + past; a minor social slip-up, the prototypical trigger

examples.en: When I got complimented I laughed sheepishly.
examples.note: 겸연쩍게 (adverb) + 웃다; bashful reaction to praise

examples.ko: 혼자 김칫국 마신 게 좀 겸연쩍더라.
examples.romanization: honja gimchitgung masin ge jom gyeomyeonjjeokdeora.
examples.en: Getting my hopes up for nothing felt a bit embarrassing.
examples.note: -더라 + the idiom 김칫국(을) 마시다 (count chickens too early)

entries.nuance: 겸연쩍다 is that mild, sheepish embarrassment when you have made a small slip or feel awkwardly self-conscious — the apologetic, bashful smile after being caught or praised. The -쩍다 ending is a productive suffix meaning 'giving the feeling of' (compare 멋쩍다, 객쩍다, 수상쩍다), and the 겸연(慊然) root adds a shade of feeling slightly ill-at-ease and apologetic. The contrast that matters most is with 창피하다 ('embarrassed/ashamed'), which is full, sometimes face-burning embarrassment over something genuinely mortifying, while 겸연쩍다 is light and bashful, often with a guilty/apologetic tinge. It overlaps heavily with 멋쩍다 ('awkward, at a loss for how to react'), the difference being that 멋쩍다 leans toward 'I don't know how to act' whereas 겸연쩍다 leans toward 'I feel a bit guilty/apologetic'. It is milder still than 부끄럽다 ('shy/ashamed'). The English-speaker pitfall is using it for deep shame or serious embarrassment; in Korean that is 창피하다. Its signature collocation is 겸연쩍게 웃다, the awkward little laugh.

Using it for deep shame or a mortifying public blunder — 겸연쩍다 is mild sheepishness; strong embarrassment is 창피하다.
Spelling it 겸연적다 — the ending is the tense 쩍다: 겸연쩍다, 겸연쩍어, 겸연쩍게.
Treating it as identical to 멋쩍다 — both are awkward, but 겸연쩍다 carries a guilty/apologetic shade, while 멋쩍다 is more 'not knowing how to react'.

entries.english: having a clear conscience, upright, unashamed
entries.shortExplanation: 떳떳하다 means "having a clear conscience, upright, unashamed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "having a clear conscience, upright, unashamed" is 떳떳하다 (tteottteotada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 떳떳하다 ("to be upright / have a clear conscience"). Watch the particle attached to 떳떳하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be upright / have a clear conscience
usagePhrases.note: confident you've done nothing wrong, nothing to hide
반말, standing by what you did
adverb; 떳떳하게 살다 = live honestly, head held high

usagePhrases.en: to feel guilty / unable to hold one's head up
usagePhrases.note: negative form for a guilty conscience

examples.en: I didn't do anything wrong, so my conscience is clear.
examples.note: -니까 reason + 떳떳해; standing your ground in 반말

examples.en: It's money I earned through honest work.
examples.note: 떳떳하게 (adverb) + 일하다; the 'earned honestly' collocation

examples.en: I had told a lie, so I couldn't feel at ease.
examples.note: negative 떳떳하지 못하다 expressing a guilty conscience

entries.nuance: 떳떳하다 means having a clear conscience — being able to hold your head up because you have done nothing shameful or dishonest. It is about moral confidence and integrity, and it lives especially in the adverb 떳떳하게 ('openly, honestly') and the negative 떳떳하지 못하다 ('to feel guilty, unable to look others in the eye'). It is a native Korean word (no 한자), built on the mimetic 떳떳 of standing firm and aboveboard. The sharpest contrast is with 당당하다: both translate loosely as 'confident', but 당당하다 is about bold, self-assured bearing and presence (어깨를 펴고 당당하게 = standing tall and confident) regardless of right or wrong, while 떳떳하다 specifically grounds that confidence in a clean conscience and having nothing to hide. It is not the same as 자신 있다 ('to be confident in one's ability') either — that is about competence, not morality. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'proud' or 'confident'; 떳떳하다 is narrower, meaning 'in the moral clear'. Watch the spelling: doubled ㄸ and patchim ㅅ, 떳떳하다, and keep the 하 — 떳떳해요, 떳떳하게.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 당당하다 — 떳떳하다 stresses a clean conscience (nothing to hide), while 당당하다 stresses bold, self-assured bearing regardless of right or wrong.
Using it to mean 'confident in my skills' — that is 자신 있다; 떳떳하다 is specifically about being morally in the clear.
Spelling it 떳떳다 or 떠떠하다 — keep the doubled ㄸ, the ㅅ patchim, and the 하: 떳떳하다, 떳떳해요, 떳떳하게.

entries.shortExplanation: 명절 means "traditional holiday (Seollal / Chuseok)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 명절 (myeongjeol) = "traditional holiday (Seollal / Chuseok)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 명절 ("traditional holiday") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 명절, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Refers specifically to the big lunar holidays 설날 and 추석, not just any day off.
The standard greeting you say to coworkers and neighbors before the break; pairs with 보내다, never 지내다 here.
명절 plus 연휴; the multi-day stretch most people get off work.
증후군 = syndrome; the real exhaustion (especially for women cooking) that the news discusses every year.

examples.en: Are you going to your hometown this holiday?
examples.note: 내려가다 = to go down (to one's hometown); a classic holiday small-talk opener.

examples.en: Whenever a holiday comes around the highways are completely jammed.
examples.note: -만 되면 = every single time it becomes; the famous 명절 gridlock.

examples.ko: 저는 명절에 일하는 대신 평일에 쉬어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun myeongjeore ilhaneun daesin pyeongire swieoyo.
examples.en: Instead of working on the holiday I take weekdays off.
examples.note: -는 대신(에) = in exchange for / instead of; common for service-industry workers.

entries.nuance: 명절 (漢字 名節, 'name-occasion / notable festival') is the word reserved for Korea's two great lunar-calendar reunions, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (the harvest festival), when the whole country travels home to family — so it carries a heavy weight of family duty, ancestral rites, and obligatory cooking that a neutral day off never has. The sharp contrast to learn is 명절 vs 공휴일 (公休日, 'public-rest-day'): every 명절 is a 공휴일, but most 공휴일 (광복절, 현충일, a single Monday off) are NOT 명절. It also differs from 기념일 (記念日), an 'anniversary / commemorative day' like a wedding anniversary. Register is everyday-polite; asking 명절 잘 보내셨어요? is warm, slightly personal small talk. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 명절 like the generic word 'holiday' and stretching it over Christmas or a random vacation day — and saying 명절 축하해요, since Koreans bless the holiday with 잘 보내세요, not 'congratulations.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 명절 for every public holiday: a single day off like 광복절 or 어린이날 is a 공휴일, while 명절 means specifically the big lunar reunions 설날 and 추석.
Saying 명절 축하해요 sounds off because 축하 ('congratulations') is for achievements; for a holiday you wish 명절 잘 보내세요 (spend the holiday well).
English 'holiday' = any vacation, but 명절 ≠ 휴가 (personal leave) or 방학 (school break); a beach trip in July is 휴가, not 명절.

entries.shortExplanation: 한가위 means "Chuseok, the harvest moon festival" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 한가위 (hangawi) means "Chuseok, the harvest moon festival". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 한가위 ("Chuseok (warm native name)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 한가위 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A softer, purely-Korean name for 추석; favored in greetings and on cards.
The set holiday greeting you'll get by text from companies and friends.

usagePhrases.en: may it always be as good as Chuseok
usagePhrases.note: From the proverb 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라 ('no more, no less, just like Chuseok').
풍성하다 = plentiful/bountiful; a fixed warm collocation for the harvest holiday.

examples.en: Have a happy Chuseok!
examples.note: The most common holiday-greeting text you'll send and receive.

examples.en: On Chuseok people make a wish while looking at the full moon.
examples.note: 보름달 = full moon; 소원을 빌다 = to make a wish, the fixed verb pairing.

examples.en: Hangawi is the heart-warming native-Korean name for Chuseok.
examples.note: 정겹다 = warm/fond; explains the relationship between the two words.

entries.nuance: 한가위 is the warm, indigenous (순우리말, NOT Sino-Korean) name for 추석 (秋夕, 'autumn-evening'), the harvest festival on the 15th of the eighth lunar month. The pieces are 한 ('big / great,' as in 한길, 한복판) plus 가위, an old word tied to 가운데 ('middle') — so it evokes 'the great middle (full-moon) day' of autumn. The key contrast is purely one of register, not meaning: 한가위 and 추석 are the same day, but 한가위 sounds friendlier and more lyrical, so 행복한 한가위 보내세요 feels gentler than the plain 추석 잘 보내세요. You'll meet it most in greetings, cards, and the proverb 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라, a wish that life were always this bountiful. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming it is a separate holiday from 추석 (it is the very same one) and mis-spelling the final syllable as 의 — it is 위, the same shape as 위 'above.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
한가위 and 추석 are one and the same holiday; 한가위 is just the softer native name, so don't schedule them as two different days.
It's spelled 한가위 (ending in 위), not 한가의 — the last syllable is the vowel 위, not 의.
Because 한가위 is native Korean, don't try to write it in 한자; only 추석 (秋夕) has a hanja form.

entries.shortExplanation: 연휴 means "consecutive holidays, a long weekend" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "consecutive holidays, a long weekend" is 연휴 (yeonhyu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 연휴 ("string of holidays / long weekend"). Watch the particle attached to 연휴 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Several days off in a row; the thing everyone plans trips around.
황금 = golden; an extra-long break when holidays line up with the weekend.
계획 = plan; a standard topic of conversation before the break.
징검다리 = stepping stones; when a workday sits between two days off, often taken as leave to bridge them.

examples.en: This Chuseok the long weekend is nice and long.
examples.note: -아서 좋다 = good because; people love when 연휴 stretches out.

examples.en: Because it's a long weekend the plane tickets are all sold out.
examples.note: -(이)라(서) = because it is; 매진되다 = to sell out, demand spikes during 연휴.

examples.en: Enjoy the long weekend (and come back well).
examples.note: A natural send-off to coworkers before the break; -고 오다 = do it and come back.

entries.nuance: 연휴 (漢字 連休, literally 連 'connect / link' + 休 'rest' — 'linked-up rest days') means a run of consecutive days off, the practical block of time Koreans actually organize trips around rather than a single ceremonial holiday. The crucial trio to keep apart: 연휴 = multiple days off in a row on everyone's calendar; 휴일 (休日) = a single day off; and 휴가 (休暇) = your personal, individually-taken vacation leave. So 'I'm taking 연휴 next week' is wrong if you simply mean private time off — that's 휴가. When a 명절 or public holiday connects to a weekend it becomes a 황금연휴 (golden long weekend), and people often burn a vacation day on a 징검다리 (stepping-stone) workday to bridge the gap. Flights and KTX seats sell out fast, so locals book early. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 연휴 onto 'a holiday' (singular event) — 연휴 is fundamentally about the unbroken stretch of days, not the holiday's meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
연휴 specifically means several days off in a row; for one single day off use 휴일, not 연휴.
Don't confuse 연휴 (consecutive days off, fixed on the public calendar) with 휴가 (your personal vacation leave that you request).
Avoid the 직역 'long weekend' when the break is mid-week: 연휴 just means 'consecutive days off' and needn't include a Saturday or Sunday.

entries.shortExplanation: 차례 means "ancestral rite held on holidays" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 차례 (charye) = "ancestral rite held on holidays". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 차례 ("holiday ancestral rite") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 차례, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The morning ceremony honoring ancestors held on 설날 and 추석.
지내다 is the fixed verb for holding the ceremony, never 하다.
상 = table/spread; the array of food set out for the 차례.
The dishes (전, 나물, 송편/떡국, fruit) prepared specifically for the ceremony.

examples.ko: 설날 아침에 차례를 지내고 떡국을 먹어요.
examples.romanization: seolnal achime charyereul jinaego tteokgugeul meogeoyo.
examples.en: On Seollal morning we hold the ancestral rite and then eat tteokguk.
examples.note: The standard sequence of a Lunar New Year morning; -고 links the two steps.

examples.ko: 요즘은 차례를 간소하게 지내는 집도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun charyereul gansohage jinaeneun jipdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many households hold the rite in a simplified way.
examples.note: 간소하게 = simply/plainly; reflects a real modern trend.

examples.ko: 저희 집은 차례를 안 지내고 여행을 가요.
examples.romanization: jeohui jibeun charyereul an jinaego yeohaengeul gayo.
examples.en: Our family doesn't do the rite and travels instead.
examples.note: 저희 = humble 'our'; increasingly common among younger families.

entries.nuance: 차례 (漢字 茶禮, literally 茶 'tea' + 禮 'rite' — historically a simple 'tea offering') is the streamlined ancestral memorial held on the morning of the two 명절, 설날 and 추석, where the family sets out a 차례상 of food and bows to honor all the ancestors together. The single most important contrast is 차례 vs 제사 (祭祀): 제사 is the solemn rite held at night on the death-anniversary (기일) of one specific ancestor, while 차례 is the lighter, daytime, holiday rite for the ancestors collectively — so they are not interchangeable. The locked-in verb is 지내다 (차례를 지내다 / 제사를 지내다); 차례를 하다 sounds wrong to natives. Register is neutral-descriptive, but the topic is culturally weighty. Increasingly, younger households 차례를 간소하게 지내다 (simplify it) or skip it to travel, which is now broadly accepted. The English-speaker pitfall: do not gloss 차례 as a generic 'ceremony' or pair it with 하다 — and do not confuse this homograph with the other 차례 meaning 'turn / sequence' (as in 차례차례, '목차/table of contents'), which is a different word entirely.

차례 (holiday rite, all ancestors, morning) and 제사 (祭祀, death-anniversary rite, one ancestor, evening) are not the same; use 제사 for the yearly memorial of a specific person.
The verb is 차례를 지내다 (hold the rite), not 차례를 하다 — 지내다 is the fixed pairing.

entries.english: New Year's deep bow to elders
entries.shortExplanation: 세배 means "New Year's deep bow to elders" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 세배 (sebae) means "New Year's deep bow to elders". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 세배 ("New Year's bow to elders"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 세배 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The formal full bow children and juniors make on 설날.

usagePhrases.en: to make the New Year's bow
usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb; what you do toward grandparents and parents on Seollal.
Cash elders give after receiving a 세배; note the 사이시옷 and read it '세배똔'.

usagePhrases.en: Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)
usagePhrases.note: The set line you say while performing the 세배.

examples.en: On Seollal I made the deep bow to my grandmother.
examples.note: 께 is the honorific 'to' (raising 할머니); bowing to elders is the core ritual.

examples.en: When you do the New Year's bow, the elders give you money.
examples.note: -(으)면 = when/if; the cause-and-effect kids look forward to most.

examples.ko: 세배할 때 '새해 복 많이 받으세요'라고 말해요.
examples.romanization: sebaehal ttae 'saehae bong mani badeuseyo'rago malhaeyo.
examples.en: While bowing you say 'Happy New Year.'
examples.note: -라고 말하다 = to say (direct quote); the standard accompanying line.

entries.nuance: 세배 (漢字 歲拜, literally 歲 'year / age' + 拜 'to bow' — 'the year-bow') is the deep, formal 큰절 that younger people offer to elders on the morning of 설날 to wish them well for the year, performed together with 새해 복 많이 받으세요. The contrast to fix in mind is 세배 vs the everyday 인사 (人事, 'greeting') and the plain verb 절(을) 하다 ('to bow'): a 세배 is one specific kneeling New-Year bow, not any nod or hello, and it is distinct from a 묵념 (silent tribute) or a funeral bow. The fixed verb is 세배(를) 하다; you make it 'to' an elder with the honorific particle 께, and the elder receives it (세배를 받다). In return they give 덕담 (words of blessing) and 세뱃돈 (New Year's cash). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) don't confuse 세배 (the bow) with 세뱃돈 (the money that follows) — related but different words; (2) note the 사이시옷 in 세뱃돈, pronounced '세배똔'; and (3) since 세배 already contains 절 (a bow), saying 세배를 절하다 is redundant.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 세배 (the bow) with 세뱃돈 (the money received afterward) — they're related but different words, and 세뱃돈 carries a 사이시옷.
세배 is the proper kneeling 큰절 to elders, not a casual nod; performing it carelessly reads as disrespectful.
Use the honorific 께 ('to an elder'), not 에게/한테: 할머니께 세배를 했어요, because you are raising the recipient's status.

entries.shortExplanation: 덕담 means "words of blessing / good wishes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "words of blessing / good wishes" is 덕담 (deokdam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 덕담 ("words of blessing"). Watch the particle attached to 덕담 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Kind, encouraging wishes elders give, especially at New Year.
하다 verb; what an elder does after receiving your 세배.
나누다 = to share; people trade 덕담 around the holiday table.
한마디 = a word/remark; 'say a few kind words' on a happy occasion.

examples.ko: 세배를 하면 어른들이 덕담을 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: sebaereul hamyeon eoreundeuri deokdameul hae juseyo.
examples.en: After you bow, the elders offer words of blessing.
examples.note: 해 주다 = do (for someone); the elder's half of the 세배 exchange.

examples.en: For the new year I heard lots of wishes to stay healthy.
examples.note: 건강하라는 = the quoted wish 'be healthy'; typical New Year 덕담.

examples.ko: 결혼식에서 어른이 덕담 한마디 해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsigeseo eoreuni deokdam hanmadi hae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: At the wedding an elder said a few words of blessing.
examples.note: 해 주시다 (honorific); 덕담 isn't only for New Year — it fits any happy occasion.

entries.nuance: 덕담 (漢字 德談, literally 德 'virtue / goodness' + 談 'talk' — 'virtuous, goodness-bringing speech') means the warm, forward-looking words of blessing an elder gives to younger people, most famously right after receiving a 세배 on 설날 (건강해라, 시험 잘 봐라, 좋은 사람 만나라). The contrast to internalize is 덕담 vs 충고 (忠告, 'frank advice') and 잔소리 ('nagging'): 덕담 is purely positive, well-wishing, and uplifting, whereas 충고 points out what to fix and 잔소리 scolds — so an elder telling you to study harder in a critical tone is NOT giving 덕담. It also differs from 칭찬 (praise for something already done), since 덕담 wishes good things for the future. The fixed verbs are 덕담을 하다 / 나누다 / 건네다; 덕담을 말하다 sounds unnatural. Register: spoken by a senior to a junior, or exchanged among peers at celebrations. The English-speaker pitfall is using 덕담 for any 'good word' including constructive criticism — if it stings or corrects, it isn't 덕담 — and pairing it with 말하다 instead of 하다/나누다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
덕담 is exclusively positive, blessing-type talk for happy occasions — it's never used for advice that scolds or criticizes (that's 충고 or 잔소리).
The verb is 덕담을 하다 / 나누다 / 건네다, not 덕담을 말하다; pair it with 하다 or 나누다 to sound natural.
Don't confuse 덕담 (good wishes for the future) with 칭찬 (praise for a past deed); 덕담 looks forward, 칭찬 looks back.

entries.english: rice-cake soup eaten on New Year
entries.shortExplanation: 떡국 means "rice-cake soup eaten on New Year" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 떡국 (tteokguk) = "rice-cake soup eaten on New Year". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 떡국 ("tteokguk, rice-cake soup") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 떡국, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Thinly sliced rice cakes in clear broth; the must-eat dish on 설날 morning.
Eating a bowl on New Year symbolically adds a year to your age.
그릇 = bowl (the counter); also the joking 'unit' of aging one year.
A popular variant with 만두 (dumplings) added to the same broth.

examples.en: On Seollal morning we always eat tteokguk.
examples.note: 꼭 = without fail; the defining New Year food custom.

examples.ko: 떡국 한 그릇 먹으면 한 살 더 먹는 거예요.
examples.romanization: tteokgu kan geureun meogeumyeon han sal deo meongneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: Eating a bowl of tteokguk means you turn a year older.
examples.note: 한 살 더 먹다 = to gain a year; -는 거예요 explains the custom.

examples.en: I like rice-cake-and-dumpling soup more than plain tteokguk.
examples.note: -보다 더 = more than; comparing the two versions.

entries.nuance: 떡국 is a 합성어 (compound) of pure-Korean 떡 ('rice cake') + 국 ('soup'), so it literally means 'rice-cake soup' — thin oval slices of 가래떡 simmered in a clear beef or anchovy broth, eaten on the morning of 설날. The long-running joke 떡국 한 그릇 = 한 살 ('one bowl, one year older') ties it to the lunar tradition where everyone aged together at New Year, so people still tease 떡국 몇 그릇 먹었어? to ask, half-jokingly, how old you are. Contrast it with two other 떡 dishes: 떡볶이 (spicy stir-fried rice-cake snack — savory-sweet, a totally different cylinder of 떡) and 떡만둣국 (the heartier 떡국 + 만두 variant). The verb is simply 떡국을 먹다 / 끓이다. The English-speaker pitfall: don't conflate 떡국 with 떡볶이 just because both contain 떡, and remember the 'aging' line is folklore — since Korea's 2023 switch to international 만 나이, eating 떡국 has no bearing on your legal age.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 떡국 (savory clear rice-cake soup) with 떡볶이 (spicy stir-fried rice-cake snack) — different dishes despite both using 떡.
The New Year 'aging' line is folklore about 떡국; eating it doesn't change your legal age, especially since Korea adopted 만 나이 in 2023.
The rice cake in 떡국 (sliced 가래떡) isn't the same as the chewy cylinders in 떡볶이; 떡 is a broad category, so naming the dish, not just '떡,' avoids confusion.

entries.explanation: 송편 (songpyeon) means "half-moon rice cakes for Chuseok". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 송편 ("songpyeon (half-moon rice cake)"). Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Stuffed, pine-steamed rice cakes; the signature 추석 food.
빚다 is the special verb for forming dough (and pottery) by hand.
깨 = sesame; a common filling, alongside 콩 (beans), 밤 (chestnut), 팥 (red bean).
솔잎 = pine needles; 송편 is steamed over them, which gives it its scent.

examples.ko: 추석에는 온 가족이 모여서 송편을 빚어요.
examples.romanization: chuseogeneun on gajogi moyeoseo songpyeoneul bijeoyo.
examples.en: On Chuseok the whole family gathers to make songpyeon.
examples.note: 온 가족 = the whole family; making them together is the tradition.

examples.ko: 송편을 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는대요.
examples.romanization: songpyeoneul yeppeuge bijeumyeon yeppeun ttareul nanneundaeyo.
examples.en: They say if you shape songpyeon prettily you'll have a pretty daughter.
examples.note: -(ㄴ/는)대요 = they say (reported); a well-known playful old saying.

examples.en: Sesame songpyeon is the tastiest to me.
examples.note: 제일 = most/best; naming a favorite filling.

entries.nuance: 송편 (the 송 is 漢字 松 'pine,' + native 편/떡 for the cake, so roughly 'pine(-steamed) rice cake') are small half-moon-shaped 떡 stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut and steamed over a layer of 솔잎 (pine needles), eaten at 추석 / 한가위. The verb to lock in is 빚다 — the special hand-forming verb also used for shaping pottery and brewing rice wine — so traditionally you say 송편을 빚다, not the plain 송편을 만들다 (which natives understand but find flatter). Contrast 송편 with the New-Year rice cake in 떡국 (sliced 가래떡, savory, in soup) and with generic 떡: 송편 is one specific shaped, filled, sweet-ish, pine-steamed variety tied to autumn, the half-moon shape echoing the harvest moon. A charming saying claims neatly-made 송편 foretells a pretty daughter. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 만들다 for the verb and treating 송편 as interchangeable with any 떡 — it is the 추석 cake specifically, just as 떡국's slices belong to 설날.

송편 is the 추석 rice cake; don't confuse it with 떡국's sliced 가래떡 or generic 떡 — it's a specific shaped, filled, pine-steamed variety.
It's eaten at 추석, not 설날: pairing 송편 with the New Year (where 떡국 belongs) mixes up the two holidays' signature foods.

entries.shortExplanation: 성묘 means "visiting and tending ancestral graves" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "visiting and tending ancestral graves" is 성묘 (seongmyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 성묘 ("grave visit / grave-tending"). Watch the particle attached to 성묘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Visiting ancestors' graves to pay respects, especially at 추석 and 설날.
가다 verb; the family outing to the gravesite during the holiday.
벌초 = cutting the overgrown grass on the mound, usually done before 추석.
산소 = the burial mound you visit; the respectful word for a grave.

examples.en: I went to visit the family graves with relatives for Chuseok.
examples.note: 다녀오다 = go and come back; 이랑 = casual 'with' (spoken).

examples.en: Before the grave visit we did the grass-cutting first.
examples.note: -기 전에 = before doing; -부터 = starting with, 벌초 precedes 성묘.

examples.ko: 요즘은 성묘 대신 납골당에 가는 사람도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun seongmyo daesin napgoldange ganeun saramdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many people go to a columbarium instead of tending graves.
examples.note: 납골당 = charnel house/columbarium; reflects changing burial customs.

entries.nuance: 성묘 (漢字 省墓, literally 省 'to look in on / examine' + 墓 'grave' — 'to look in on the grave') is the custom of visiting ancestors' burial mounds to tidy them and bow in respect, done above all at 추석 and 설날. Distinguish three linked terms: 성묘 is the whole respectful visit; 벌초 (伐草, 'cut the grass') is the specific chore of clearing weeds off the 산소 (山所), usually done a week or two before the holiday; and 차례 is the food-table rite performed back at home — so 성묘 (at the grave) and 차례 (at home) are different parts of the holiday, not synonyms. The verb is 성묘(를) 가다 / 다녀오다. Note 산소 vs 무덤: 무덤 is the plain word 'grave,' while 산소 is the polite, respectful term used for one's own ancestors. As cremation has become the norm, families increasingly visit a 납골당 (columbarium) instead, yet 성묘 still covers paying these respects. The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing 성묘 / 벌초 / 차례 into one 'grave ceremony' — they are distinct steps — and using 무덤 where the respectful 산소 is expected for your own family.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
성묘 is going to the grave; 차례 is the food-table rite at home — they're separate parts of the holiday, not synonyms.
Don't confuse 성묘 (the whole respectful visit) with 벌초 (the specific task of cutting the grass); 벌초 is one step that precedes a 성묘 trip.
For your own ancestors use the respectful 산소, not the plain 무덤; calling a family grave 무덤 can sound blunt.

entries.english: the 15th of the lunar month; full-moon day
entries.shortExplanation: 보름 means "the 15th of the lunar month; full-moon day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보름 (boreum) = "the 15th of the lunar month; full-moon day". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보름 ("the 15th (full-moon day)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보름, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The midpoint of a lunar month, when the moon is full.

usagePhrases.en: the first full moon of the year
usagePhrases.note: 정월 = first lunar month; a traditional holiday on its 15th.
달 = moon; the round moon seen on a 보름 night.
동안 = during; 보름 also colloquially means a span of roughly 15 days.

examples.en: On the first full moon we crack and eat nuts (burum).
examples.note: 부럼 = nuts cracked for health; 깨 먹다 = crack and eat, a 대보름 custom.

examples.ko: 오늘 밤 보름달이 정말 크고 밝아요.
examples.romanization: oneul bam boreumdari jeongmal keugo balgayo.
examples.en: Tonight's full moon is really big and bright.
examples.note: 보름달 = full moon; a natural everyday remark.

examples.ko: 여행 간 지 벌써 보름이 지났어요.
examples.romanization: yeohaeng gan ji beolsseo boreumi jinasseoyo.
examples.en: It's already been about half a month since the trip.
examples.note: -(ㄴ) 지 ... 지나다 = it's been (time) since; 보름 here = ~15 days.

entries.nuance: 보름 is a pure-Korean word (NOT Sino-Korean) marking the 15th day of the lunar month — the night of the full moon — and by natural extension a casual span of 'about half a month.' Contrast the components in the holiday name 정월대보름 (正月大보름): 정월 (正月) = the first lunar month, 대 (大) = 'great,' so it's 'the great full moon of the first month,' when people crack 부럼 nuts and eat 오곡밥 (five-grain rice) and 나물 for health and luck. Keep three things separate: 보름 (the 15th / full-moon day or a ~15-day span), 보름달 (the full moon you see in the sky), and 정월대보름 (the actual holiday) — so don't shorten the holiday to just '보름.' Also distinguish the duration sense: 보름 ≈ 15 days, whereas 'two weeks' is 2주(일) = 14 days, so they aren't identical. In everyday speech you'll hear it most as 보름달. The English-speaker pitfall is reading 보름 as exactly 14 days like 'a fortnight,' and treating 보름달 (the moon) as if it were the holiday.

보름 by itself is the 15th / full-moon day; the holiday is 정월대보름, so don't shorten the holiday's name to just 보름.
When 보름 means a duration it's roughly 15 days, not exactly two weeks (14 days); don't equate it with 2주.
보름달 is the full moon in the sky, not the holiday or the day itself; keep 보름 (day), 보름달 (moon), and 정월대보름 (holiday) distinct.

entries.english: the dog days of summer (hottest days)
entries.shortExplanation: 복날 means "the dog days of summer (hottest days)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 복날 (bongnal) means "the dog days of summer (hottest days)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 복날 ("dog days (peak-summer days)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 복날 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The three hottest marked days of summer: 초복, 중복, 말복.
삼복 = the three bok days; 더위 = heat — the fiercest stretch of summer.

usagePhrases.en: eat samgyetang on a bok day
usagePhrases.note: The custom of eating hot ginseng-chicken soup to fight heat with heat.
The three 복날 spread across mid-to-late summer, about ten days apart.

examples.en: It's a bok day so the line in front of the samgyetang place is long.
examples.note: -(이)라 = because it's; eating 삼계탕 on 복날 causes famous lunchtime queues.

examples.en: Today's the first bok day — shall we go eat some restorative food?
examples.note: 보양식 = stamina food; -(으)러 가다 = go in order to, -ㄹ까요 invites.

examples.en: During the peak-bok heat I don't even want to go outside.
examples.note: -기도 싫다 = don't even want to; conveys the brutal heat.

entries.nuance: 복날 is a hybrid word: the 복 is 漢字 伏 ('to lie low / crouch,' the same 伏 in 복병 'ambush'), evoking heat so heavy that even the autumn 'metal' energy lies prostrate before it, plus native 날 ('day') — so '복날' is 'the crouching-heat day.' There are three each summer — 초복 (初伏, first), 중복 (中伏, mid), 말복 (末伏, last) — set ~10 days apart and collectively called 삼복 (三伏), the time of 삼복더위 (peak heat). The custom is 이열치열 (以熱治熱, 'fight heat with heat'): eat a steaming 보양식 (補養食, restorative dish) like 삼계탕 or 추어탕, which is why famous soup shops get long lunchtime lines. Two cautions: 복날 is NOT a single fixed date but three separate days, so name 초복/중복/말복 when you mean one; and this 복 (伏 'crouch') is unrelated to the 복 (福 'fortune') in 새해 복 — same sound, different hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming peak-heat days call for cold food: the 복날 tradition is deliberately hot soup, so 'I'll eat 냉면 to celebrate 복날' misses the 이열치열 logic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
복날 isn't one fixed day; it's three separate days (초복, 중복, 말복) spread through summer, so name the specific one you mean.
Despite the heat, the 복날 custom is piping-hot soup (이열치열), not cold food — saying you'll eat 냉면 to 'celebrate' 복날 misses the point.
The 복 in 복날 is 伏 ('crouch/lie low'), not the 福 ('fortune/luck') in 복 많이 받으세요; don't read 복날 as a 'lucky day.'

entries.shortExplanation: 한복 means "hanbok, traditional Korean dress" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "hanbok, traditional Korean dress" is 한복 (hanbok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한복 ("hanbok (traditional dress)"). Watch the particle attached to 한복 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Worn on 명절, at weddings and first-birthdays, and now for photos at palaces.
입다 = to wear (clothes on the body); the verb for putting on the outfit.
대여 = rental; you rent 한복 to enter Seoul's palaces free.
생활 = daily living; a modernized, casual version made for daily wear.

examples.en: On Seollal I wore hanbok and did the New Year's bow.
examples.note: -고 = and (sequence); wearing 한복 for the 명절 rite is the classic occasion.

examples.en: Gyeongbokgung is free admission if you wear hanbok.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if; 무료 = free, a popular reason young people rent 한복.

examples.ko: 요즘은 생활한복을 평소에 입는 사람도 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun saenghwalhanbogeul pyeongsoe imneun saramdo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days some people wear modern hanbok in everyday life.
examples.note: 평소에 = normally/usually; reflects the 생활한복 trend.

entries.nuance: 한복 (漢字 韓服, literally 韓 'Korea / Korean' + 服 'clothing' — 'Korean dress'; the 服 is the same character in 교복 'school uniform,' 양복 'Western suit') is traditional Korean clothing — for women the 저고리 (jacket) and 치마 (skirt), for men 저고리 and 바지 — worn most on 명절, at weddings, and at 돌 (first-birthday) parties. The verb is firmly 입다, the body-clothing 'wear' verb, which contrasts with Korean's other 'wear' verbs: 쓰다 (hats, glasses — 모자를 쓰다), 신다 (shoes, socks — 신발을 신다), and 차다 (a watch — 시계를 차다). So 한복을 쓰다 or 한복을 신다 is wrong. Compare 한복 (Korean) with 양복 (洋服, a Western men's suit) and 교복 (校服, school uniform) — all share 服. For young people and tourists, 한복 대여 near palaces like 경복궁 is popular because wearing it gives free admission and great photos, and a modernized 생활한복 is rising as casual daily wear. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing English 'wear' (one verb for everything) and reaching for 쓰다/신다, plus dismissing 한복 as a museum costume when rental and 생활한복 culture is thriving among 20–30s.

한복 takes 입다 (wear on the body like clothes), not 쓰다 or 신다 — those are for hats/glasses and shoes/socks respectively.
한복 isn't only a museum costume; treating it as purely old-fashioned ignores the trendy palace rental and 생활한복 culture among 20–30s.
Don't mix up 한복 (韓服, Korean dress) with 양복 (洋服, a Western suit) or 교복 (校服, school uniform); they share 服 but name very different clothes.

entries.shortExplanation: 복숭아 means "peach" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 복숭아 (boksunga) = "peach". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 복숭아 한 알에 얼마예요? ("How much is one peach?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 복숭아, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 알 is the natural market counter for round fruit; 한 알 sounds more grocer-like than 한 개.
A genuinely common allergy here; memorize this exact phrase for restaurants and friends' homes.

usagePhrases.en: Do you buy soft peaches or firm ones?
usagePhrases.note: 물복(물렁한 복숭아) vs 딱복(딱딱한 복숭아) — the camp question Koreans really ask each other.
Adjective 무르다 → past 물렀다; peaches bruise and over-soften fast, so this comes up often.

examples.en: Do you like peaches?
examples.note: Simplest frame — just the noun + 좋아하다, no counter or particle traps yet.

examples.en: When summer comes, peaches are really delicious.
examples.note: 되면 = 'when it becomes'; marks 복숭아 as a signature summer fruit.

examples.en: I'm not big on firm peaches; I like the soft juicy ones.
examples.note: Real preference talk: 별로다 (not great) contrasted with 좋다, using the slang short forms.

entries.nuance: 복숭아 is a native Korean word (no hanja) for one of the country's most beloved summer fruits, and it carries real cultural weight: people genuinely split into two camps, 물복 (soft, juicy 물렁복숭아) versus 딱복 (firm, crunchy 딱딱한 복숭아), and asking which someone prefers is small talk. The nearest confusion for learners is texture verbs: when a peach over-softens you say 물렀어요 (from 무르다, to go soft), NOT 썩었어요 (rotten) — mixing those up makes a perfectly good peach sound spoiled. It is also one of Korea's most common food allergies, so 복숭아 알레르기 있어요 is a high-value safety phrase. English speakers often reach for 개 as the counter, but at a fruit stand 한 알 (for one round piece) is far more natural; 개 isn't wrong, just less grocer-like.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting 복숭아 with 개 at a market — for round fruit a vendor expects 한 알; 개 sounds like you're counting generic objects, not produce.
Saying 복숭아가 썩었어요 (rotten) when you only mean it's overripe and soft — the correct word is 물렀어요, from the adjective 무르다.
Treating 물복/딱복 as childish slang to avoid — they're the standard everyday terms; using 물렁한 복숭아 every time sounds stiff.

structuredNuance.t: 복숭아 is a native Korean word for one of the country's most beloved summer fruits, and it carries real cultural weight: people genuinely split into two camps, 물복 (soft, juicy 물렁복숭아) versus 딱복 (firm, crunchy 딱딱한 복숭아), and asking which someone prefers is small talk. It is also one of Korea's most common food allergies, so 복숭아 알레르기 있어요 is a high-value safety phrase.
The nearest confusion is texture verbs: when a peach over-softens you say 물렀어요 (from 무르다, to go soft), NOT 썩었어요 (rotten) — mixing those up makes a perfectly good peach sound spoiled.
It is a native Korean word with no hanja.
English speakers often reach for 개 as the counter, but at a fruit stand 한 알 (for one round piece) is far more natural; 개 isn't wrong, just less grocer-like.

entries.shortExplanation: 참외 means "Korean melon (chamoe)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 참외 (chamoe) means "Korean melon (chamoe)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 참외 한 봉지 주세요 ("One bag of Korean melons, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 참외 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: One bag of Korean melons, please
usagePhrases.note: Often priced by the 봉지 (mesh bag) at markets and marts, not by the single piece.

usagePhrases.en: We peel and eat Korean melon
usagePhrases.note: 깎다 = to peel/pare with a knife; the yellow skin comes off first.

usagePhrases.en: Seongju chamoe is the most famous
usagePhrases.note: 성주 (a county in 경북) is the gold-standard growing region, like a brand of origin.

usagePhrases.en: The yellow ones are the tasty ones
usagePhrases.note: 게 = 것이; ripe 참외 turns bright yellow with pale ridged stripes.

examples.en: I'm seeing chamoe for the first time.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 처음 보다 = to see for the first time, perfect for this very local fruit.

examples.ko: 여름에 참외 깎아서 냉장고에 넣어 두면 시원해요.
examples.romanization: yeoreume chamoe kkakkaseo naengjanggoe neoeo dumyeon siwonhaeyo.
examples.en: In summer, peel chamoe and chill it in the fridge.
examples.note: 넣어 두다 = put it in and leave it; -아 두다 means doing something in advance for later.

examples.ko: 이 참외 진짜 달다, 한번 먹어 봐.
examples.romanization: i chamoe jinjja dalda, hanbeon meogeo bwa.
examples.en: This chamoe is really sweet, try a piece.
examples.note: Casual 반말: plain 달다 + the offer 먹어 봐 (try eating), how you'd talk to a close friend.

entries.nuance: 참외 is the bright-yellow oriental melon that is almost unknown outside Korea, which makes it a delightfully local word to own. Etymology helps it stick: 참 means 'true/real' (as in 참기름 'real sesame oil') and 외 is the old word for melon/gourd, so 참외 is literally 'the genuine melon.' The single biggest learner trap is translating it as 'melon' and saying 멜론 — but 멜론 in Korean means the imported netted cantaloupe/honeydew, a totally different fruit; 참외 is its own category and should stay 참외. Unlike a watermelon you slice into wedges, 참외 is 깎아 먹는 (peeled) fruit: you pare off the yellow skin, and many people scoop out the soft seedy core too. The 성주 region functions like an origin label the way certain places are famous for specific produce, so '성주 참외' signals premium.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 참외 as 멜론 — 멜론 means the imported netted melon (cantaloupe/honeydew); 참외 is a separate fruit and keeps its own name.
Eating 참외 with the peel on — Koreans pare off the yellow skin first (깎아 먹다); leaving it on reads as not knowing how to eat it.
Saying 참외 한 개 at a market when it's bagged — it's commonly sold and counted by the 봉지 (bag), so 한 봉지 fits the real buying unit.

entries.shortExplanation: 자두 means "plum" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "plum" is 자두 (jadu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 자두 한 알 먹을래? ("Want to eat one plum?"). Watch the particle attached to 자두 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Counted with 알 like other small round fruit; -ㄹ래? is a casual offer/invitation.
새콤하다 = pleasantly, refreshingly sour — a positive word, unlike harsh 시다.

usagePhrases.en: Plums are in season right now
usagePhrases.note: 제철 (제 + 철, 'its own season') = peak season, roughly June–July.
씨 = seed/pit; you bite the flesh around the hard central stone.

examples.en: Plums are tart.
examples.note: Two-word frame fixing the core flavor adjective 새콤하다 to the fruit.

examples.en: Just wash the plums and eat them whole.
examples.note: 통째로 = whole/in one piece; -으면 돼요 = 'it's fine if you just…', the easy default.

examples.ko: 마트에 자두 나온 거 보니까 여름 다 됐네.
examples.romanization: mateue jadu naon geo bonikka yeoreum da dwaenne.
examples.en: Seeing plums out at the mart, summer's basically here.
examples.note: -(으)니까 here = 'now that I see…, I realize'; 보니까 (from 보다) frames seasonal fruit as a season signal.

entries.nuance: 자두 is a small, tart-sweet stone fruit (native Korean word, no hanja) piled high at markets from around June, and the flavor Koreans reach for is 새콤달콤 — a fixed pair meaning 'pleasantly sour-and-sweet.' Note the synonym line in that word: 새콤하다 is the GOOD kind of sour (refreshing, appetizing), whereas plain 시다 is just 'sour' and can sound like a complaint, and 떫다 is the puckery astringency of unripe persimmon — don't swap them. Unlike 복숭아, you normally eat 자두 통째로 (whole, skin on), just biting around the hard central 씨 (pit), so peeling it like a peach marks you as unfamiliar with it. The classic learner mix-up is sound-based: 자두 (plum) vs 자몽 (grapefruit) — one syllable apart but entirely different fruit, so listen for the 두/몽 ending.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 자두 (plum) with 자몽 (grapefruit) — they sound alike but are unrelated; the second syllable (두 vs 몽) is the whole difference.
Peeling 자두 like a peach — the thin skin is eaten as-is; you simply wash it and eat it 통째로 (whole), biting around the pit.
Using 시다 for the nice tang — for ripe plum say 새콤하다 (appetizingly sour); 시다 alone can sound like the fruit is too sour to enjoy.

entries.shortExplanation: 감 means "persimmon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 감 (gam) = "persimmon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 단감 줄까, 홍시 줄까? ("Want a firm persimmon or a soft one?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 감, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Want a firm persimmon or a soft one?
usagePhrases.note: 단감 (crunchy, eaten like an apple) vs 홍시 (soft, jelly-like, spooned) — name the type, not just 감.
떫다 = puckery/mouth-drying — the signature word for an underripe 감, not 'bitter.'
곶감 = peeled, dried persimmon; a chewy, very sweet winter treat eaten as a snack.
Counted with 개; 따다 = to pick from the tree, since 감 grows on backyard trees.

examples.en: In autumn persimmons are sweet.
examples.note: Short seasonal frame: 가을엔 (in autumn) + 달다 (sweet).

examples.en: I prefer the firm, crunchy persimmon.
examples.note: 더 좋아하다 = to prefer (like more); 단감 is the apple-crisp variety.

examples.ko: 덜 익은 감은 떫어서 입에 못 대요.
examples.romanization: deol igeun gameun tteolbeoseo ibe mot daeyo.
examples.en: Unripe persimmons are so astringent I can't touch them.
examples.note: 입에 대다 = to put to one's mouth/taste; 못 대다 = can't even try it, vivid spoken phrasing.

entries.nuance: 감 is the quintessential autumn fruit (native Korean, no hanja), and crucially it is an umbrella word that splits into named forms: 단감 (literally 'sweet 감,' the firm crunchy kind eaten sliced like an apple), 홍시 (紅枾 'red persimmon,' the soft jelly-like ripe one you scoop with a spoon), and 곶감 (peeled and dried into a chewy sweet for winter). At a market, saying just 감 is vague — sellers and friends specify which. The flavor word every learner must nail is 떫다 (astringent): an unripe persimmon dries out your whole mouth, and English speakers wrongly call this 써요 (bitter) — but 쓰다 is coffee-bitter, while 떫다 is the puckery tannin sensation, a different word entirely. So 감이 떫어요, never 감이 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using bare 감 when you mean a specific kind — at a market specify 단감 (firm) or 홍시 (soft); 감 alone is ambiguous about texture.
Saying 감이 써요 (bitter) for an unripe one — the correct sensation is 떫다 (astringent); 쓰다 means bitter like coffee, a different taste.
Assuming 곶감 is just 'dried fruit' — it specifically means peeled-and-dried persimmon and is treated as a sweet/snack, not a substitute for fresh 감.

entries.shortExplanation: 망고 means "mango" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 망고 (manggo) means "mango". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 망고 빙수 먹으러 가자 ("Let's go eat mango bingsu"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 망고 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 망고 빙수 (mango shaved ice) is the flagship summer café dessert; -으러 가다 = go in order to.
익다 = to ripen; a ripe 망고 is soft to the touch and fragrant.
냉동 (冷凍 'cold-freeze') = frozen; the budget way to buy it, sold in bags for smoothies.

usagePhrases.en: Apple mango is a bit pricey
usagePhrases.note: 애플망고 = the small, deep-orange premium variety, sold and priced apart from regular 망고.

examples.en: Do you like mango?
examples.note: Plain noun + 좋아하다, the simplest opener.

examples.ko: 망고는 좀 비싸지만 가끔 사 먹어요.
examples.romanization: manggoneun jom bissajiman gakkeum sa meogeoyo.
examples.en: Mango's a bit pricey, but I buy it once in a while.
examples.note: -지만 = 'but' (concession); 사 먹다 = buy-and-eat, the natural verb for treating yourself.

examples.ko: 여름에 카페에서 망고 빙수 한 그릇 먹으면 천국이에요.
examples.romanization: yeoreume kapeeseo manggo bingsu han geureun meogeumyeon cheongugieyo.
examples.en: A bowl of mango bingsu at a café in summer is heaven.
examples.note: 그릇 = bowl-counter for 빙수; -으면 …이에요 frames the payoff.

entries.nuance: 망고 is a loanword (from English 'mango') and, importantly, it carries a 'special imported treat' connotation that the English word lacks — because it's pricier and not locally grown, it reads as an occasional indulgence rather than an everyday fruit like 사과 or 귤. Its single most famous form is 망고 빙수 (mango shaved ice), the dessert that defines summer café menus, so the collocation is worth memorizing as a unit. The key distinction learners miss: 망고 and 애플망고 are NOT interchangeable — 애플망고 is the smaller, sweeter, deep-orange premium type, separately labeled and noticeably more expensive, so don't expect them at the same price. For home use, 냉동 망고 (frozen, 冷凍) is the affordable everyday option people blend into smoothies, while fresh 망고 stays a small luxury.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 망고 is cheap and year-round like apples — fresh mango is imported, pricier, and reads as an occasional treat, which changes how you'd talk about buying it.
Using 애플망고 and 망고 interchangeably — 애플망고 is a distinct, sweeter premium variety sold separately and at a higher price.
Saying 망고 빙수 만들어요 to mean ordering it out — for café desserts you 먹으러 가다 (go to eat) or 시키다 (order); 만들다 implies making it yourself at home.

entries.shortExplanation: 블루베리 means "blueberry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "blueberry" is 블루베리 (beulluberi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 블루베리 한 팩 주세요 ("One pack of blueberries, please"). Watch the particle attached to 블루베리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sold in small 팩 (plastic punnets), never loose — so the buying unit is 한 팩, not 한 개.
냉동 (冷凍) = frozen; the cheaper, year-round option versus pricey fresh 생블루베리.

usagePhrases.en: Blueberries are good for your eyes
usagePhrases.note: 눈에 좋다 = good for the eyes; a near-universal health belief you'll hear repeated constantly.
A staple flavor for the yogurt bowls and smoothies popular with health-minded 20–30s.

examples.en: I bought some blueberries.
examples.note: 사 오다 = buy-and-bring(-back); the everyday 'I picked some up' verb.

examples.en: In the morning I add blueberries to my yogurt.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination (into the yogurt); 넣어 먹다 = add-and-eat, a habitual breakfast.

examples.en: Fresh blueberries are pricey, so I just buy frozen.
examples.note: 생- prefix = raw/fresh (생블루베리); -아서 gives the reason for the practical choice.

entries.nuance: 블루베리 is a loanword (from English 'blueberry') that in Korea is framed above all as a health food, not just a fruit — you will constantly hear 블루베리가 눈에 좋아요 ('good for your eyes'), and it anchors the yogurt-bowl-and-smoothie routine of health-conscious 20–30s. Two practical things shape how you talk about it. First, the counter: it's bought in small pricey 팩 (punnets), so the unit is 한 팩, and counting the whole container with 개 sounds off. Second, the fresh-vs-frozen split: 생블루베리 (생- = raw/fresh) is expensive, so many default to cheaper 냉동 (冷凍, frozen) bags — naming which one you mean matters at the store. Spelling pitfall for English speakers: the standard transliteration is 블루베리, NOT 블루배리 — the third syllable is 베, mirroring 'berry,' even though Korean ㅔ/ㅐ sound nearly identical.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting the container with 개 — buy it as 한 팩 (one punnet); 개 would mean individual berries, which isn't how it's sold.
Spelling it 블루배리 — the correct loanword is 블루베리 (베, not 배); the ㅔ/ㅐ contrast is silent in speech but fixed in writing.
Assuming fresh is the norm — many people buy 냉동 (frozen) because 생블루베리 is expensive, so specify 생 vs 냉동 when it matters.

entries.shortExplanation: 키위 means "kiwi (fruit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 키위 (kiwi) = "kiwi (fruit)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 골드키위가 더 달아요 ("Gold kiwi is sweeter") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 키위, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 골드키위 (sweeter, premium) vs 그린키위 (tarter) — labeled and priced separately at the mart.
Counted with 개; 깎다 = to pare off the fuzzy brown skin with a knife.

usagePhrases.en: Scooping kiwi out is the easy way
usagePhrases.note: 떠먹다 (뜨다 'scoop' + 먹다) = halve it and spoon out the flesh — a very common local habit.
시큼하다 = sharply sour; green kiwi that isn't ripe yet has a real tang.

examples.en: Kiwi is tasty.
examples.note: Bare noun + 맛있다 — the no-frills starter sentence.

examples.en: I halve the kiwi and scoop it with a spoon.
examples.note: 반으로 자르다 = cut in half; -아서 chains the steps (cut, then scoop).

examples.ko: 골드키위는 비싼데 그래도 그게 더 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: goldeukiwineun bissande geuraedo geuge deo masisseoyo.
examples.en: Gold kiwi's pricey, but still, it tastes better.
examples.note: -는데 sets up contrast; 그게 = 그것이, pointing back to the gold one.

entries.nuance: 키위 is a loanword (from English 'kiwi') and an everyday, affordable fruit in Korea, but learners need to know it isn't one uniform thing: it splits into 골드키위 (gold, sweeter, premium, smoother-skinned) and 그린키위 (green, tarter), and these are shelved and priced as distinct items — assuming they taste the same is a real mistake. Two eating habits shape the vocabulary. You can 깎아 먹다 (peel and eat) like other fruit, but a signature Korean move is to halve it and 떠먹다 — 뜨다 'to scoop' + 먹다 — spooning the flesh straight out of the skin cup. The fuzzy brown skin is never eaten; reaching to eat it whole, skin and all, marks unfamiliarity. For flavor, underripe green kiwi is 시큼하다 (sharply sour) — distinguish this from 새콤하다, which is the pleasant refreshing sourness of ripe fruit.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Eating the fuzzy brown skin — Koreans always 깎다 (peel) it or 떠먹다 (scoop the inside out); the skin isn't eaten.
Assuming all 키위 taste the same — 골드키위 (sweet) and 그린키위 (tart) are noticeably different and sold as separate, separately-priced products.
Using 시다 flatly for unripe kiwi — 시큼하다 captures the sharp tang better; and don't confuse it with 새콤하다, the agreeable sourness of ripe fruit.

entries.shortExplanation: 브로콜리 means "broccoli" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 브로콜리 (beurokolli) means "broccoli". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 브로콜리 데쳐 먹어요 ("We blanch and eat broccoli"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 브로콜리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 데치다 = to blanch briefly in boiling water (not fully boil) — the standard prep here.

usagePhrases.en: I buy one head of broccoli
usagePhrases.note: 송이 = the counter for a head/cluster/floret bunch; 개 doesn't fit a whole head.
살짝 = lightly/just a touch; keeps the broccoli green and crunchy instead of mushy.

usagePhrases.en: We dip broccoli in chili-vinegar paste
usagePhrases.note: 초고추장 (초 醋 'vinegar' + 고추장) = the sweet-tangy red dip standard for blanched veg.

examples.en: I don't like broccoli.
examples.note: Negation 안 + 좋아하다 — the simplest way to state a dislike.

examples.ko: 브로콜리는 살짝 데쳐서 초고추장에 찍어 먹어요.
examples.romanization: beurokollineun saljjak dechyeoseo chogochujange jjigeo meogeoyo.
examples.en: Blanch broccoli lightly and dip it in chili-vinegar sauce.
examples.note: 데치다 + 초고추장 is the classic combo; -아서 chains blanch → dip → eat.

examples.en: If you boil broccoli too long, it gets mushy.
examples.note: 삶다 (full boil) contrasts with 데치다 (blanch); 물러지다 = to turn soft/mushy.

entries.nuance: 브로콜리 is a loanword (from English 'broccoli') firmly tied to healthy and diet eating in Korea — it's a fixture on 닭가슴살 (chicken-breast) diet plates and 'clean eating' bowls, so the connotation leans 'health food,' not 'ordinary vegetable.' The most Korean way to serve it is 살짝 데친 (lightly blanched) and dipped in 초고추장, the sweet chili-vinegar paste; serving it raw and plain looks under-prepared by local norms. A crucial cooking-verb contrast for learners: 데치다 means to blanch briefly (just dunk it), while 삶다 means to fully boil — overdoing it (삶다 too long) makes the broccoli 물러지다 (go mushy), losing the crunch Koreans want. The counter trips people up too: a whole head is 한 송이 (the cluster counter), not 한 개, which would sound like you're tallying generic objects.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it with 개 — a whole head is 한 송이; 송이 is the counter for a cluster/bunch like broccoli or flowers.
Serving 브로콜리 raw and plain — the expected style is 데친 (blanched) and dipped in 초고추장; raw looks under-prepared.
Confusing 데치다 with 삶다 — 데치다 is a quick blanch to keep it crunchy, while 삶다 (long boil) makes it 물러지다 (mushy).

The most Korean way to serve it is 살짝 데친 (lightly blanched) and dipped in 초고추장, the sweet chili-vinegar paste; serving it raw and plain looks under-prepared by local norms. The counter also trips people up: a whole head is 한 송이 (the cluster counter), not 한 개.

브로콜리 is a loanword from English 'broccoli'; 초고추장 combines 초 醋 'vinegar' + 고추장.

Counting it with 한 개 would sound like you're tallying generic objects; a whole head is 한 송이. And serving it raw and plain looks under-prepared by local norms — the expected style is blanched and dipped.

entries.shortExplanation: 파프리카 means "bell pepper (paprika)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bell pepper (paprika)" is 파프리카 (papeurika). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빨간 파프리카 주세요 ("Red bell pepper, please"). Watch the particle attached to 파프리카 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sold in red, yellow, orange, and green; red is the sweetest, green the least sweet.
Counted with 개; 썰다 = to slice — it's firm and glossy, easy to cut into strips.
The headline fact: unlike 고추 (hot chili), 파프리카 is sweet and crunchy, zero heat.

usagePhrases.en: I add bell pepper to salad
usagePhrases.note: 에 넣다 = add into; raw 파프리카 is a standard colorful, crunchy salad component.

examples.en: Bell peppers aren't spicy.
examples.note: Short reassurance frame fixing the single most important fact about 파프리카.

examples.ko: 저는 파프리카 생으로 썰어서 그냥 먹어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun papeurika saengeuro sseoreoseo geunyang meogeoyo.
examples.en: I just slice bell peppers and eat them raw.
examples.note: 생으로 = raw/uncooked; -아서 chains slice → eat; 그냥 = 'just (as is).'

examples.ko: 볶음 요리에 파프리카 넣으면 색깔이 예뻐요.
examples.romanization: bokkeum yorie papeurika neoeumyeon saekkkari yeppeoyo.
examples.en: Adding bell pepper to a stir-fry makes the colors pretty.
examples.note: 볶음 요리 = stir-fry dish; often added for color and crunch as much as flavor.

entries.nuance: 파프리카 is a loanword — but from Dutch 'paprika' (Korea imports the seeds/produce heavily from the Netherlands), which is why it isn't the English 'bell pepper.' The number-one thing for English speakers: 파프리카 is the sweet, NON-spicy bell pepper, totally distinct from 고추, the hot chili — assuming 'pepper = spicy' leads to real confusion at the table. There's a second, finer distinction Koreans make that learners flatten: 파프리카 vs 피망. 파프리카 is the large, thick-walled, sweet, glossy one in bright colors; 피망 (from French/Japanese 'piment') is the smaller, thinner, slightly bitter green pepper used in stir-fries — they're sold as separate items, so calling everything 파프리카 will occasionally be wrong. It's a major Korean export crop, so it's everywhere, affordable, and eaten 생으로 (raw) in salads or as crunchy snack strips, as well as added to stir-fries for color.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 파프리카 is spicy because it's a 'pepper' — it has zero heat; the spicy one is 고추, an entirely different word and food.
Calling every bell pepper 파프리카 — the smaller, thinner, slightly bitter green type is 피망, sold separately; the two aren't interchangeable.
Spelling/saying it like English 'paprika' the spice — in Korean 파프리카 means the fresh sweet bell pepper, not the dried red powder (that's 파프리카 가루 or 고춧가루 depending).

entries.shortExplanation: 가지 means "eggplant / aubergine" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가지 (gaji) = "eggplant / aubergine". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가지볶음 해 먹어요 ("We make and eat stir-fried eggplant") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: We make and eat stir-fried eggplant
usagePhrases.note: 볶음 = stir-fry; 가지볶음 is a common 반찬 (side dish), 해 먹다 = make-and-eat at home.
나물 = steamed-then-seasoned vegetable side; 가지나물 is soft, savory, sesame-dressed.
Counted with 개; Korean 가지 is the long, slender purple kind, not the round Western one.
물컹하다 = soft and squishy — the cooked texture that decides who likes it.

examples.en: I can't eat eggplant.
examples.note: 못 먹다 = can't eat (it's not for me) — a very common kid-and-adult line about 가지.

examples.en: When you stir-fry eggplant in oil, it gets tender.
examples.note: 기름에 볶다 = stir-fry in oil; -아지다 on 부드럽다 = 'becomes soft.'

examples.en: Seasoned eggplant is a love-it-or-hate-it dish.
examples.note: 호불호가 갈리다 (好不好, 'like/dislike divides') = opinions split — a set idiom for polarizing foods.

entries.nuance: 가지 in Korea means the long, slender, deep-purple eggplant, not the bulbous Western globe type, so picture a thinner shape. It's a native Korean word — and here's the pitfall that genuinely trips learners: 가지 is a homonym. The same 가지 also means 'kind/type/sort,' as in 한 가지 ('one kind'), 여러 가지 ('various kinds'), and it's even a noun for a tree branch — so context alone tells you whether someone means the vegetable or 'a type of.' As food, it lives mostly as two side dishes: 가지나물 (steamed then seasoned, soft) and 가지볶음 (stir-fried). Its soft 물컹한 texture makes it a textbook 호불호 (好不好, like-or-dislike) food, especially for kids, so it surfaces constantly in 'what foods do you hate?' conversations. Texture note: 물컹하다 (unpleasantly squishy) vs 부드럽다 (pleasantly tender) — same softness, opposite attitude, so choose by whether you mean it kindly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forgetting 가지 is a homonym — it also means 'kind/type' (한 가지, 여러 가지) and 'branch'; context, not the word alone, signals the vegetable.
Picturing a round Western eggplant — Korean 가지 is long and thin, which is why it's sliced into rounds or strips for 볶음 and 나물.
Describing it only as 물컹하다 (squishy, negative) when you actually like it — say 부드럽다 (tender) for the pleasant version of the same softness.

entries.shortExplanation: 고구마 means "sweet potato" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고구마 (goguma) means "sweet potato". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 군고구마 사 먹자 ("Let's buy roasted sweet potato"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고구마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 군- (from 굽다 'to roast') = roasted; 군고구마 is the iconic winter street snack.

usagePhrases.en: Give me one sweet potato, please
usagePhrases.note: Counted with 개 or 하나; a everyday request at a stall or mart.

usagePhrases.en: This drama is so frustrating (lit. 'so sweet-potato')
usagePhrases.note: Slang: 고구마 = a stifling, no-payoff situation, like choking on dry sweet potato.
꿀- ('honey') = the moister, extra-sweet variety, versus the drier 밤고구마 ('chestnut').

examples.en: I like sweet potatoes.
examples.note: Plain noun + 좋아하다 — and a word you'll hear daily in winter.

examples.ko: 고구마는 다이어트할 때 밥 대신 먹기도 해요.
examples.romanization: gogumaneun daieoteuhal ttae bap daesin meokgido haeyo.
examples.en: People sometimes eat sweet potato instead of rice when dieting.
examples.note: 밥 대신 = instead of rice; -기도 하다 = 'also (sometimes) do.'

examples.ko: 그 드라마 너무 고구마라서 보다가 껐어.
examples.romanization: geu deurama neomu gogumaraseo bodaga kkeosseo.
examples.en: That drama was so 'sweet potato' I turned it off mid-watch.
examples.note: Slang in action: 고구마 + -라서 (because it's…); 보다가 껐어 = was watching, then shut it off.

entries.nuance: 고구마 (native Korean word) is two things at once, and you need both. Literally it's the sweet potato — beloved as winter 군고구마 (군- 'roasted', from 굽다), and a favorite diet carb eaten 밥 대신 (instead of rice). Figuratively it's living slang: calling a drama, story, or situation 고구마 means it's frustrating and STIFLING — the image is choking on dry sweet potato with no water. Its built-in antonym is 사이다 (lit. cider/soda), the refreshing 'satisfying, cathartic' payoff; 20–30s constantly contrast a 고구마 (maddening) stretch with a 사이다 (gratifying) moment. Two pitfalls: don't confuse 고구마 with 감자 (regular potato) — different food and different slang weight (감자 has no such meaning); and don't take 고구마 같다 literally as being about food — it's an emotion word meaning 'so frustrating I could scream.' Variety note: 꿀고구마 (honey, moist-sweet) vs 밤고구마 (chestnut, drier-fluffy) are the two types people actually choose between.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 고구마 (sweet potato) with 감자 (regular white potato) — different foods, and only 고구마 carries the 'frustrating' slang.
Taking 고구마 같다 literally — it isn't about food; it means a situation/story is stifling and frustrating, opposite of 사이다 (satisfying).
Treating all sweet potato as one — 꿀고구마 (moist, very sweet) and 밤고구마 (drier, fluffier like chestnut) are the named varieties Koreans pick between.

entries.shortExplanation: 옥수수 means "corn" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "corn" is 옥수수 (oksusu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 찐 옥수수 하나 사 먹어요 ("I buy one steamed corn (on the cob)"). Watch the particle attached to 옥수수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I buy one steamed corn (on the cob)
usagePhrases.note: 찌다 → 찐 (steamed); 찐 옥수수 is a popular warm-weather street snack.
Counted with 개 for a cob — NOT 송이; 개 is the right counter here.
통조림 (통 'can' + 조림) = canned goods; canned corn goes in salads, on pizza, in 김밥.
옥수수차 = roasted-corn tea, a free table drink served hot or cold like 보리차.

examples.en: Corn is tasty.
examples.note: Bare noun + 맛있다 — the minimal starter sentence.

examples.ko: 여름에 길에서 찐 옥수수 사 먹어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreume gireseo jjin oksusu sa meogeoyo.
examples.en: In summer I buy steamed corn from street stalls.
examples.note: 길에서 = on the street; 사 먹다 = buy-and-eat, the habitual snacking verb.

examples.en: Here they give corn tea instead of water.
examples.note: 물 대신 = instead of water; -네요 = mild noticing/remark about the free table tea.

entries.nuance: 옥수수 (native Korean word) is corn, and the key for learners is that it reaches everyday life in three quite different forms, each with its own collocation: 찐 옥수수 (steamed on the cob, from 찌다 'to steam') as a summer street snack; 옥수수 통조림 (canned corn) sprinkled on salads, pizza, and into 김밥; and 옥수수차 (roasted-corn tea), poured free at many restaurants. That last one is the biggest trap: 옥수수차 is a brewed tea like 보리차 (barley tea), NOT a drink full of corn kernels — expecting kernels in your cup is the classic newcomer surprise. The counter also catches people: a cob is 한 개, never 한 송이 (송이 is for clusters/heads like broccoli or grapes), because a single cob counts as one object. So recognizing 찐 옥수수 / 옥수수 통조림 / 옥수수차 covers essentially everywhere you'll actually meet the word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting 옥수수 with 송이 — a cob is 한 개; 송이 is for clusters/heads (broccoli, grapes), which a corn cob isn't.
Expecting kernels in 옥수수차 — it's a roasted-grain brew like 보리차 (barley tea), a clear table drink, not a corn drink with bits in it.
Saying 삶은 옥수수 vs 찐 옥수수 carelessly — both exist (boiled vs steamed), but the street-snack default people name is 찐 옥수수 (steamed).
