entries.shortExplanation: 아이디 means "ID, username" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아이디 (aidi) = "ID, username". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아이디 ("ID, username") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아이디, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: From English 'ID'; the login name you type, always paired with 비밀번호
입력하다 = to input/type in; the standard verb on every login screen
찾다 here = recover, not search; sites have an '아이디 찾기' button
만들다 = to make; casual way to say create a username, vs the fuller 계정을 만들다

examples.en: My ID is 'star'.
examples.note: Simple A는 B예요 frame; note 아이디 takes 는 as the topic when you state it

examples.en: I can't remember my ID.
examples.note: 기억이 안 나다 = can't recall (it won't come to mind); the subject is 아이디, marked 가

examples.en: This ID is already in use.
examples.note: 사용 중 = in use; the exact error you see when your desired username is taken

entries.nuance: '아이디'는 로그인할 때 입력하는 사용자 이름이에요. 영어 'ID'를 그대로 읽은 외래어라 발음도 [아이디]로 거의 같아요. 비밀번호(password)와 한 쌍으로 거의 항상 같이 나오는데, 둘을 헷갈리면 안 돼요. 아이디는 남에게 보여도 되는 '내 이름표'이고 비밀번호는 절대 알려주면 안 되는 '열쇠'라고 생각하면 쉬워요. 또 '아이디'와 '계정(account)'을 같은 말로 쓰는 영어 화자가 많은데, 아이디는 계정을 이루는 한 요소일 뿐이에요. 영어처럼 'my ID is...'를 직역해 조사를 빼고 '아이디 star'처럼 말하기 쉬운데, 한국어에서는 '아이디는 star예요'처럼 조사 '는/가'를 꼭 붙여야 자연스러워요. 요즘은 이메일 주소를 아이디로 쓰는 사이트도 많아요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 아이디 (username, shareable) with 비밀번호 (password, secret) — they are two separate fields and only one is private.
English speakers say 'my ID is star' and drop the particle, e.g. '아이디 star'. Korean needs the topic particle: 아이디는 star예요.
It's 아이디, not 아이드 or the slangy 아디 — write all three syllables in formal or written contexts.

structuredNuance.t: '아이디'는 로그인할 때 입력하는 사용자 이름이에요. 영어 'ID'를 그대로 읽은 외래어라 발음도 [아이디]로 거의 같아요. 비밀번호(password)와 한 쌍으로 거의 항상 같이 나오는데, 둘을 헷갈리면 안 돼요. 아이디는 남에게 보여도 되는 '내 이름표'이고 비밀번호는 절대 알려주면 안 되는 '열쇠'라고 생각하면 쉬워요. 요즘은 이메일 주소를 아이디로 쓰는 사이트도 많아요.
'아이디'와 '계정(account)'을 같은 말로 쓰는 영어 화자가 많은데, 아이디는 계정을 이루는 한 요소일 뿐이에요.
영어처럼 'my ID is...'를 직역해 조사를 빼고 '아이디 star'처럼 말하기 쉬운데, 한국어에서는 '아이디는 star예요'처럼 조사 '는/가'를 꼭 붙여야 자연스러워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 계정 means "account" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계정 (gyejeong) means "account". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 계정 ("account"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 계정 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Your registered account on a service (Google, 네이버, Instagram); broader than 아이디
만들다 = to make; covers the whole account, more complete than 아이디를 만들다
삭제하다 = to delete (data); what you do to close an account permanently
정지되다 = to be suspended/frozen (passive); e.g. banned for spam

examples.en: I have two accounts.
examples.note: Simple counting with 개; 계정 is the subject marked 이

examples.en: I'll log in with my Google account.
examples.note: N으로 로그인하다 = log in with/via N; the everyday 'Sign in with Google'

examples.ko: 회사 계정이라 개인 메일은 못 봐요.
examples.romanization: hoesa gyejeongira gaein meireun mot bwayo.
examples.en: It's a work account, so I can't check personal mail.
examples.note: N이라(서) = because it's N; shows the work-vs-personal account distinction

entries.nuance: '계정'은 한자어 計定으로, 원래 회계에서 '셈을 정해 둔 항목'을 뜻하던 말이 온라인 '계정(account)'으로 확장됐어요. 아이디보다 큰 개념이라, 아이디·비밀번호·설정·데이터를 모두 포함하는 '계정' 전체를 가리켜요. 즉 아이디는 계정의 일부예요. 영어 'account'와 거의 1:1로 대응되지만, 영어의 'account'가 은행 계좌도 뜻하는 것과 달리 한국어는 은행은 '계좌(計座)', 온라인 서비스는 '계정(計定)'으로 단어를 나눠 써요. 발음이 비슷한 이 둘을 섞으면 '은행 계정 만들었어요'처럼 어색해지니, 돈은 계좌, 로그인은 계정으로 구분하세요. 동사는 '계정을 만들다/삭제하다'처럼 쓰고, 정지·해킹 같은 일을 당할 때는 '계정이 정지되다/털리다'처럼 피동으로 말해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 계정 (online account) with 계좌 (bank account). English 'account' covers both, but Korean splits them: money = 계좌, login = 계정.
계정 is broader than 아이디. A 계정 contains your 아이디, 비밀번호, and settings, so they aren't interchangeable.
When an account gets banned, say the passive 계정이 정지됐어요, not the active 계정을 정지했어요 (that would mean you suspended it).

structuredNuance.t: 아이디보다 큰 개념이라, 아이디·비밀번호·설정·데이터를 모두 포함하는 '계정' 전체를 가리켜요. 즉 아이디는 계정의 일부예요. 동사는 '계정을 만들다/삭제하다'처럼 쓰고, 정지·해킹 같은 일을 당할 때는 '계정이 정지되다/털리다'처럼 피동으로 말해요.
영어 'account'와 거의 1:1로 대응되지만, 영어의 'account'가 은행 계좌도 뜻하는 것과 달리 한국어는 은행은 '계좌(計座)', 온라인 서비스는 '계정(計定)'으로 단어를 나눠 써요. 발음이 비슷한 이 둘을 섞으면 '은행 계정 만들었어요'처럼 어색해지니, 돈은 계좌, 로그인은 계정으로 구분하세요.
'계정'은 한자어 計定으로, 원래 회계에서 '셈을 정해 둔 항목'을 뜻하던 말이 온라인 '계정(account)'으로 확장됐어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 로그인 means "login, signing in" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "login, signing in" is 로그인 (rogeuin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 로그인 ("login"). Watch the particle attached to 로그인 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The noun for the act of signing in; from English 'login'
Add 하다 to make it a verb — the standard way Koreans verbify loanwords

usagePhrases.en: login won't work / can't log in
usagePhrases.note: 안 되다 = doesn't work (no fault implied); the classic complaint when a site fails
자동 = automatic; the 'remember me / keep me logged in' checkbox

examples.en: Log in here.
examples.note: Simple command: 로그인 + 하세요; note no object particle is needed

examples.en: I keep getting logged out.
examples.note: 풀리다 = to come undone; the natural way to say a session keeps dropping you

examples.en: I checked 'stay logged in'.
examples.note: 상태 유지 = keep status; the literal label of the stay-signed-in box

entries.nuance: '로그인'은 영어 'log in'을 그대로 들여온 외래어예요. 명사로 쓰다가 '하다'를 붙이면 '로그인하다'라는 동사가 되는데, 이렇게 외래어+하다로 동사를 만드는 건 한국어의 핵심 패턴이에요(클릭하다, 다운로드하다처럼요). 비슷한 말로 '접속하다'가 있는데, '접속(接續)'은 단순히 사이트에 '연결·접근'하는 것이고 '로그인'은 아이디·비밀번호를 넣어 '본인 확인 후 들어가는' 것이라 더 좁아요. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 동사로 써야 할 자리에 명사 '로그인'만 덜렁 쓰는 거예요. '나 로그인'이 아니라 '나 로그인했어'처럼 '하다'를 꼭 붙이세요. 한국 사이트는 본인인증 단계가 많아 로그인 절차가 영어권보다 복잡할 때가 많고, IT 도움을 청할 때 '로그인이 안 돼요'는 가장 많이 쓰는 문장 중 하나예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
To say 'I logged in', use 로그인했어요. Don't use the bare noun 로그인 as if it were a verb (로그인했다 needs 하다).
Don't overuse 접속하다 for 'log in'. 접속하다 just means connect/access; 로그인하다 means you entered credentials to authenticate.
The opposite is 로그아웃, not 로그오프 — 로그오프 is almost never used in Korea.

structuredNuance.t: '로그인'은 영어 'log in'을 그대로 들여온 외래어예요. 한국 사이트는 본인인증 단계가 많아 로그인 절차가 영어권보다 복잡할 때가 많고, IT 도움을 청할 때 '로그인이 안 돼요'는 가장 많이 쓰는 문장 중 하나예요.
비슷한 말로 '접속하다'가 있는데, '접속(接續)'은 단순히 사이트에 '연결·접근'하는 것이고 '로그인'은 아이디·비밀번호를 넣어 '본인 확인 후 들어가는' 것이라 더 좁아요.
명사로 쓰다가 '하다'를 붙이면 '로그인하다'라는 동사가 되는데, 이렇게 외래어+하다로 동사를 만드는 건 한국어의 핵심 패턴이에요(클릭하다, 다운로드하다처럼요).
영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 동사로 써야 할 자리에 명사 '로그인'만 덜렁 쓰는 거예요. '나 로그인'이 아니라 '나 로그인했어'처럼 '하다'를 꼭 붙이세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 로그아웃 means "logout, signing out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 로그아웃 (rogeuaut) = "logout, signing out". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 로그아웃 ("logout") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 로그아웃, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The noun for the act of signing out; from English 'logout'
Add 하다 to verbify; pairs with 로그인하다 and implies you did it yourself
되다 = passive; used when the system signs you out automatically
자동 = automatic; the timed sign-out common on banking/government apps

examples.en: I logged out.
examples.note: Simple past with 하다; you performed the action yourself

examples.en: Always log out on shared computers.
examples.note: 꼭 ~하세요 = be sure to ~; the security reminder you see at a PC방

examples.en: It logs out automatically after a while.
examples.note: 일정 시간 = a set time; here the passive 로그아웃되다 shows the system did it

entries.nuance: '로그아웃'은 영어 'log out'에서 온 외래어로, 로그인의 반대예요. 계정에서 빠져나오는 것을 말하죠. 핵심은 '하다'와 '되다'의 구분이에요. 내가 직접 버튼을 눌러 나오면 능동의 '로그아웃하다', 보안 때문에 시스템이 나를 강제로 내보내면 피동의 '로그아웃되다'라고 해요. 영어는 'I got logged out'과 'I logged out'을 모두 'log out'으로 비슷하게 표현하지만, 한국어는 이 능동/피동을 동사 어미로 분명히 갈라서 말해야 자연스러워요. 또 '로그오프(log off)'라는 말은 한국에서 거의 안 쓰니 '로그아웃'으로 통일하세요. 한국 은행·관공서 사이트는 보안상 몇 분만 가만히 있어도 자동으로 로그아웃되는 경우가 많으니, 갑자기 풀려도 당황하지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Korea uses 로그아웃, not 로그오프 (log off). Stick with 로그아웃 in every register.
For the automatic version say the passive 로그아웃됐어요. Using 로그아웃했어요 wrongly implies you chose to sign out.
Don't say 로그아웃이 풀렸어요 — a session being dropped is itself 로그아웃되다; 풀리다 pairs with 로그인 (로그인이 풀리다).

structuredNuance.t: '로그아웃'은 영어 'log out'에서 온 외래어로, 로그인의 반대예요. 계정에서 빠져나오는 것을 말하죠. 한국 은행·관공서 사이트는 보안상 몇 분만 가만히 있어도 자동으로 로그아웃되는 경우가 많으니, 갑자기 풀려도 당황하지 마세요.
'로그오프(log off)'라는 말은 한국에서 거의 안 쓰니 '로그아웃'으로 통일하세요.
핵심은 '하다'와 '되다'의 구분이에요. 내가 직접 버튼을 눌러 나오면 능동의 '로그아웃하다', 보안 때문에 시스템이 나를 강제로 내보내면 피동의 '로그아웃되다'라고 해요.
영어는 'I got logged out'과 'I logged out'을 모두 'log out'으로 비슷하게 표현하지만, 한국어는 이 능동/피동을 동사 어미로 분명히 갈라서 말해야 자연스러워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 회원가입 means "sign-up, membership registration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 회원가입 (hoewongaip) means "sign-up, membership registration". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회원가입 ("sign-up"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회원가입 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 회원 (member) + 가입 (joining); registering as a member, the 'Sign up' button
Add 하다 to verbify; the full process of becoming a registered member
절차 = procedure/steps; Korean signups often have many
간편 = simple/easy; signing up via Kakao/Naver instead of a full form

examples.en: I signed up.
examples.note: Simple past with 하다; the whole account-creation done

examples.en: You have to sign up first before you can order.
examples.note: N부터 해야 = have to do N first; typical of Korean shopping sites

examples.en: You need phone verification when signing up.
examples.note: ~할 때 = when ~ing; 휴대폰 인증 is near-universal in Korea

entries.nuance: '회원가입'은 한자어 회원(會員, 'meeting-member' = member of a group) + 가입(加入, 'add-enter' = join)으로 이뤄진 말이에요. 글자 그대로 '회원으로 들어가 더해지는 것', 곧 멤버 등록이에요. 비슷해 보이는 '로그인'과는 시점이 달라요. '회원가입'은 처음 한 번 계정을 '만드는' 절차이고, '로그인'은 그 뒤로 매번 그 계정에 '들어가는' 행위예요. 영어로는 'sign up'과 'sign in'이 한 글자(up/in)만 달라 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 한국어는 단어 자체가 달라 오히려 구분이 쉬워요. 영어 화자가 자주 틀리는 건 어순으로, '가입회원'이라고 거꾸로 쓰면 틀린 말이 돼요(회원가입이 맞아요). 한국 사이트는 거의 다 회원가입을 해야 제대로 쓸 수 있고 본인인증·약관 동의 단계가 많아 번거로운데, 요즘은 카카오·네이버로 하는 '간편 가입'이 대세라 훨씬 빨라요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't reverse the order to 가입회원 — the correct compound is 회원가입 (member + join).
회원가입 is signing up (creating the account, done once); 로그인 is signing in afterward (done each visit). Don't confuse the two.
Say 회원가입했어요 for 'I signed up'; the bare noun 회원가입 can't stand in for the verb without 하다.

structuredNuance.t: 글자 그대로 '회원으로 들어가 더해지는 것', 곧 멤버 등록이에요. 한국 사이트는 거의 다 회원가입을 해야 제대로 쓸 수 있고 본인인증·약관 동의 단계가 많아 번거로운데, 요즘은 카카오·네이버로 하는 '간편 가입'이 대세라 훨씬 빨라요.
비슷해 보이는 '로그인'과는 시점이 달라요. '회원가입'은 처음 한 번 계정을 '만드는' 절차이고, '로그인'은 그 뒤로 매번 그 계정에 '들어가는' 행위예요.
'회원가입'은 한자어 회원(會員, 'meeting-member' = member of a group) + 가입(加入, 'add-enter' = join)으로 이뤄진 말이에요.
영어로는 'sign up'과 'sign in'이 한 글자(up/in)만 달라 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 한국어는 단어 자체가 달라 오히려 구분이 쉬워요. 영어 화자가 자주 틀리는 건 어순으로, '가입회원'이라고 거꾸로 쓰면 틀린 말이 돼요(회원가입이 맞아요).

entries.shortExplanation: 즐겨찾기 means "bookmark, favorites" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bookmark, favorites" is 즐겨찾기 (jeulgyeochatgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 즐겨찾기 ("bookmark/favorites"). Watch the particle attached to 즐겨찾기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Native Korean: 즐겨 (enjoyably/often) + 찾기 (visiting); browser bookmarks
추가하다 = to add; the star/right-click menu action, note the 에 (destination)
등록하다 = to register; slightly more formal than 추가하다
목록 = list; your saved collection of sites

examples.en: This site is one of my bookmarks.
examples.note: Simple A는 B예요; 즐겨찾기 used as a plain noun

examples.ko: 자주 가는 사이트는 즐겨찾기에 추가해 두세요.
examples.romanization: jaju ganeun saiteuneun jeulgyeochatgie chugahae duseyo.
examples.en: Bookmark the sites you visit often.
examples.note: ~해 두다 = do ~ in advance for later; perfect for saving things

examples.en: I have too many bookmarks, so I can't find it.
examples.note: 못 찾겠다 = can't manage to find; a relatable clutter problem

entries.nuance: '즐겨찾기'는 영어 'bookmark/favorites'에 해당하는 순우리말이에요. '즐겨(즐기다에서 온, 자주·기꺼이)'와 '찾기(찾다의 명사형, 방문하기)'가 합쳐져 '자주 찾아가는 곳'이라는 뜻이 됐어요. 한국 브라우저 메뉴에는 거의 항상 '즐겨찾기'로 표시돼요. 영어식으로 '북마크'라고 해도 뜻은 통하지만, 메뉴 용어로는 '즐겨찾기'가 표준이니 익혀 두는 게 좋아요. 자주 헷갈리는 점 두 가지: 첫째, 띄어쓰기예요. 한 단어이므로 '즐겨 찾기'처럼 띄우면 안 돼요. 둘째, 조사예요. 영어 'add to favorites'의 to를 생각해 '즐겨찾기를 추가'라고 하기 쉬운데, 추가되는 '곳'을 가리키는 '에'를 써서 '즐겨찾기에 추가하다'가 맞아요. 동사처럼 쓸 때는 '하다'를 붙여 '그 글 즐겨찾기 해 놨어요'라고 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
즐겨찾기 is one word — don't split it as 즐겨 찾기 with a space.
Use the particle 에, not 를, for where you save it: 즐겨찾기에 추가하다 (add to favorites), not 즐겨찾기를 추가하다.
Although 북마크 is understood, Korean browser menus label it 즐겨찾기 — prefer the native term when reading the UI.

entries.shortExplanation: 새로고침 means "refresh, reload" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 새로고침 (saerogochim) = "refresh, reload". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 새로고침 ("refresh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 새로고침, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Native Korean: 새로 (anew) + 고침 (fixing/renewing); reloading a page
Add 하다 to verbify; reload the current page
안 되다 = doesn't work; when F5 does nothing
화면 = screen; the common full phrasing with object 을

examples.en: Try refreshing once.
examples.note: 한번 ~해 보세요 = give ~ a try; the gentlest piece of tech advice

examples.en: If the page doesn't load, refresh.
examples.note: 뜨다 = to come up/appear (of a page); conditional ~으면 + command

examples.en: It's the same no matter how much I refresh.
examples.note: 계속 ~해도 = even if I keep ~ing; venting that nothing changes

entries.nuance: '새로고침'은 페이지를 다시 불러오는 것을 뜻하는 순우리말이에요. '새로(newly, 부사)'와 '고침(고치다의 명사형, 고쳐 바꿈)'이 합쳐져 '새로 고쳐 바꿈'이라는 뜻이에요. 영어 'refresh'를 '리프레시'라고 외래어로 쓰는 일은 거의 없고, 화면이든 F5 키든 거의 항상 '새로고침'이라고 해요. 비슷한 말 '새로고침'과 '다시 불러오기(reload)'는 사실상 같은 동작을 가리키지만, 일상 대화와 브라우저 버튼에서는 '새로고침'이 압도적으로 흔해요. 주의할 점은 두 가지예요. 첫째, '새로고침'은 붙여 쓰는 한 단어라서 '새로 고침'처럼 띄우면 안 돼요. 둘째, 영어 화자는 'refresh'를 'fresh(신선한)'와 연결해 '신선하게 하다'로 오해하기 쉬운데, 여기서 '고침'은 '신선함'이 아니라 '고쳐 새로 함'이라는 뜻이에요. 동사로는 '하다'를 붙여 '새로고침했더니 장바구니가 비었어요'처럼 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
새로고침 is one word — don't write 새로 고침 with a space.
Don't say 리프레시 for refreshing a page; Koreans almost always use the native 새로고침.
It is not built from 신선하다 (fresh). The 고침 part means 'fix/renew', so don't translate it as 'make fresh'.

entries.shortExplanation: 다운로드 means "download" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다운로드 (daullodeu) means "download". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다운로드 ("download"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다운로드 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: From English; saving a file from the internet to your device
Full form with 하다; in speech usually shortened to 다운받다
받다 = to receive; the everyday spoken form, very natural
안 되다 = doesn't work; when a file refuses to save

examples.en: Did you download this?
examples.note: 다운받다 = casual download; 받다 makes it sound natural in speech

examples.en: You have to download the app first.
examples.note: ~아야 되다 = have to ~; 먼저 marks the order of steps

examples.en: The download is slow because the internet is slow.
examples.note: 오래 걸리다 = to take a long time; written 다운로드 fits the explanatory tone

entries.nuance: '다운로드'는 영어 'download'를 그대로 옮긴 외래어로, 인터넷에서 내 기기로 파일을 '내려받는' 것을 뜻해요. 재미있는 점은 한국어가 영어의 down(아래)을 '받다(receive)'로 풀어 '다운받다'라는 반(半)외래어 동사를 만들어 쓴다는 거예요. 글·메뉴에서는 '다운로드(하다)'라고 정식으로 쓰지만, 말할 때는 '다운받다'나 더 줄여 '다운'이라고 하는 게 훨씬 자연스러워요. 예를 들어 '이거 다운받았어?'처럼요. 비슷한 말로 순우리말 '내려받다'가 있는데, 뜻은 똑같지만 공공기관 안내문 같은 격식 있는 글에서 주로 보이고 일상 회화에서는 잘 안 써요. 반대말은 '업로드/올리다'예요. 영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 회화에서까지 '다운로드하다'를 고집하는 것인데, 친구끼리는 '다운받다'가 훨씬 자연스럽게 들려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
In casual speech 다운받다 (or just 다운) is far more natural than the full 다운로드하다 — use 받다 with friends.
Don't confuse 다운로드 (saving onto your device) with 업로드 (sending a file out). They are opposite directions.
다운받다 already contains '받다 (receive)', so don't add another receiving verb — say 다운받았어, not 다운로드를 받았어.

structuredNuance.t: '다운로드'는 영어 'download'를 그대로 옮긴 외래어로, 인터넷에서 내 기기로 파일을 '내려받는' 것을 뜻해요. 반대말은 '업로드/올리다'예요.
비슷한 말로 순우리말 '내려받다'가 있는데, 뜻은 똑같지만 공공기관 안내문 같은 격식 있는 글에서 주로 보이고 일상 회화에서는 잘 안 써요.
재미있는 점은 한국어가 영어의 down(아래)을 '받다(receive)'로 풀어 '다운받다'라는 반(半)외래어 동사를 만들어 쓴다는 거예요. 글·메뉴에서는 '다운로드(하다)'라고 정식으로 쓰지만, 말할 때는 '다운받다'나 더 줄여 '다운'이라고 하는 게 훨씬 자연스러워요. 예를 들어 '이거 다운받았어?'처럼요.
영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 회화에서까지 '다운로드하다'를 고집하는 것인데, 친구끼리는 '다운받다'가 훨씬 자연스럽게 들려요.

entries.shortExplanation: 업로드 means "upload" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "upload" is 업로드 (eomnodeu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 업로드 ("upload"). Watch the particle attached to 업로드 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: From English; sending a file from your device out to the internet
Full form with 하다; sending up a photo, document, etc.
Native verb 'to put up'; the most natural way to say upload in speech
안 되다 = doesn't work; when a file won't go up

examples.en: I uploaded the photo.
examples.note: 올리다 = to put up; the everyday verb for posting/uploading

examples.en: You can just upload the file here.
examples.note: ~하면 돼요 = you just have to ~; note 에 marks the upload destination

examples.en: The file's too big, so it won't upload.
examples.note: 용량이 크다 = large file size; a frequent blocker

entries.nuance: '업로드'는 영어 'upload'에서 온 외래어로, 내 기기의 파일을 인터넷으로 '올려 보내는' 것을 뜻해요. 명사로 쓰고 '하다'를 붙여 '업로드하다'라는 동사를 만들 수 있지만, 일상 대화에서는 순우리말 '올리다'를 쓰는 게 훨씬 흔해요. '인스타에 사진 올렸어', '글 올렸어요'처럼요. 여기서 '업로드하다'와 '올리다'의 미묘한 차이를 알면 좋아요. '올리다'는 SNS·게시판에 글·사진을 '게시'한다는 느낌이 강하고, '업로드하다'는 서버·드라이브에 파일을 '전송'한다는 기술적 느낌이 더 강해요. 그래서 클라우드에 자료를 넣을 때는 '업로드하다'가, 인스타에 일상 사진을 공유할 때는 '올리다'가 더 어울려요. 반대말은 '다운로드/다운받다'예요. 영어 화자는 'upload'를 늘 '업로드하다'로 직역하기 쉬운데, 사진·글이라면 '올리다'가 한국어답게 들려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
In everyday speech, prefer the native 올리다 over 업로드하다 for photos and posts (인스타에 올렸어, not 인스타에 업로드했어).
업로드 (sending up/out) and 다운로드 (bringing down/in) are opposites — don't swap them.
Use 에 for the place you upload to: 여기에 업로드하다 (upload here), not 여기를 업로드하다.

'업로드하다'와 '올리다'의 미묘한 차이를 알면 좋아요. '올리다'는 SNS·게시판에 글·사진을 '게시'한다는 느낌이 강하고, '업로드하다'는 서버·드라이브에 파일을 '전송'한다는 기술적 느낌이 더 강해요. 그래서 클라우드에 자료를 넣을 때는 '업로드하다'가, 인스타에 일상 사진을 공유할 때는 '올리다'가 더 어울려요.

entries.shortExplanation: 캡처 means "screenshot, screen capture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 캡처 (kaepcheo) = "screenshot, screen capture". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 캡처 ("screenshot") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 캡처, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: From English 'capture'; an image of your screen (standard spelling, not 캡쳐)
Add 하다 to verbify; capture what's on screen
화면 = screen; the fuller, clearer phrasing
~해서 보내다 = capture then send; the typical action chain

examples.en: I took a screenshot of this.
examples.note: Simple past with 하다; 캡처 functions as the verb stem

examples.en: I'll screenshot this and send it to you.
examples.note: ~해서 보내다 = do then send; the most common screenshot use

examples.en: The screenshot came out blurry.
examples.note: 흐릿하게 나오다 = to turn out blurry; an image-quality complaint

entries.nuance: '캡처'는 영어 'capture'에서 온 외래어로, 화면을 사진처럼 찍어 저장하는 것을 뜻해요. 정식 표기는 '캡처'이고, 사람들이 흔히 쓰는 '캡쳐'는 틀린 표기예요(외래어 표기법상 '쳐'가 아니라 '처'). 비슷한 말 '캡처'와 '스크린샷(screenshot)'은 둘 다 통하지만, 한국 일상에서는 '캡처'가 훨씬 입에 붙고 짧아서 더 자주 써요. 중요한 구분은 '캡처(screen capture)'와 '사진 찍다(take a real-world photo)'예요. 캡처는 휴대폰·컴퓨터 '화면 속 내용'을 그대로 저장하는 것이고, 카메라로 바깥 풍경을 담는 건 '사진(을) 찍다'예요. 영어 화자가 'take a screenshot'의 take를 생각해 '캡처를 찍다'라고 말하기 쉬운데, '캡처하다' 자체에 이미 '찍어 저장한다'는 뜻이 있어서 '찍다'를 또 붙일 필요가 없어요. 한국에서는 정보·증거를 공유할 때 캡처를 정말 많이 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Standard spelling is 캡처, not 캡쳐 — even though you'll see 캡쳐 everywhere online, write 캡처.
캡처 is capturing the screen's contents; don't confuse it with 사진 찍다 (taking a photo of the real world with a camera).
Don't say 캡처를 찍다. 캡처하다 already means 'take/save a screenshot', so adding 찍다 is redundant.

structuredNuance.t: '캡처'는 영어 'capture'에서 온 외래어로, 화면을 사진처럼 찍어 저장하는 것을 뜻해요. 정식 표기는 '캡처'이고, 사람들이 흔히 쓰는 '캡쳐'는 틀린 표기예요(외래어 표기법상 '쳐'가 아니라 '처'). 한국에서는 정보·증거를 공유할 때 캡처를 정말 많이 써요.

비슷한 말 '캡처'와 '스크린샷(screenshot)'은 둘 다 통하지만, 한국 일상에서는 '캡처'가 훨씬 입에 붙고 짧아서 더 자주 써요. 또 중요한 구분은 '캡처(screen capture)'와 '사진 찍다(take a real-world photo)'예요. 캡처는 휴대폰·컴퓨터 '화면 속 내용'을 그대로 저장하는 것이고, 카메라로 바깥 풍경을 담는 건 '사진(을) 찍다'예요.
영어 화자가 'take a screenshot'의 take를 생각해 '캡처를 찍다'라고 말하기 쉬운데, '캡처하다' 자체에 이미 '찍어 저장한다'는 뜻이 있어서 '찍다'를 또 붙일 필요가 없어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 첨부파일 means "attachment, attached file" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 첨부파일 (cheombupail) means "attachment, attached file". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 첨부파일 ("attachment"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 첨부파일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 첨부 (attaching) + 파일 (file); a file attached to an email/message
보내다 = to send; the basic email action
확인하다 = to check; what you ask a recipient to do
첨부하다 = to attach (the verb of the action), vs the noun 첨부파일

examples.en: I sent the attachment.
examples.note: Simple past with 보내다; 첨부파일 is the object

examples.en: The attachment won't open.
examples.note: 안 열리다 = won't open (intransitive); a frequent email problem

examples.en: I'll send it to you as an attachment.
examples.note: N으로 보내다 = send as/in the form of N; polite business phrasing

entries.nuance: '첨부파일'은 한자어 첨부(添附, '더해 붙이다')와 외래어 파일(file)이 합쳐진 말로, 이메일·메신저에 함께 딸려 보내는 파일을 뜻해요. 회사 생활에서 정말 자주 쓰는 단어예요. 핵심은 명사와 동사의 구분이에요. '첨부파일'은 붙여 보낸 '파일 그 자체(명사)'이고, 파일을 붙이는 '행위'는 '첨부하다(동사)'예요. 그래서 '파일을 첨부했어요(I attached the file)'와 '첨부파일을 보냈어요(I sent the attachment)'를 상황에 맞게 갈라 써야 해요. 비슷한 말로 그냥 '파일'이 있지만, '파일'은 모든 파일을 가리키는 넓은 말이고 '첨부파일'은 '메일·메시지에 붙여 보낸' 파일로 한정돼요. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 'attach a file'의 어순대로 '파일 첨부하다'에서 조사를 빠뜨리는 거예요. 목적어 조사 '을/를'을 넣어 '파일을 첨부하다'가 맞아요. '첨부파일 빠뜨렸어요(forgot the attachment)'는 직장에서 흔한 실수 표현이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
첨부파일 is the file itself (a noun); the action of attaching is 첨부하다 (a verb). Use 파일을 첨부하다 for the action, 첨부파일을 보내다 for the thing.
Don't drop the object particle: say 파일을 첨부하다, not 파일 첨부하다, when you mean the act of attaching.
Don't space the compound noun as 첨부 파일 in normal use; 첨부파일 is written as one word.

entries.shortExplanation: 링크 means "link, URL" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "link, URL" is 링크 (ringkeu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 링크 ("link"). Watch the particle attached to 링크 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: From English; a clickable URL to a page/file (standard spelling, not 린크)
보내다 = to send; sharing a URL in chat
누르다 = to press; how Koreans usually say 'click', especially on mobile
복사하다 = to copy; the 'copy link' share option

examples.en: Please send me the link.
examples.note: Simple request: 보내다 + 주세요; the object particle 를 can drop in casual speech

examples.en: Nothing comes up even when I tap the link.
examples.note: 아무것도 안 뜨다 = nothing appears; a broken-link complaint using 누르다

examples.ko: 모르는 사람이 보낸 링크는 누르지 마세요.
examples.romanization: moreuneun sarami bonael lingkeuneun nureuji maseyo.
examples.en: Don't click links from people you don't know.
examples.note: 누르지 마세요 = don't press; basic phishing safety advice

entries.nuance: '링크'는 영어 'link'를 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 인터넷 주소(URL)나 누르면 다른 페이지로 가는 연결을 가리켜요. 표준 표기는 '링크'이고 '린크'는 틀려요. 한국어에서 흥미로운 점은 'click'을 옮기는 방식이에요. 컴퓨터 마우스 환경에서는 '클릭하다'도 쓰지만, 스마트폰이 일상인 한국에서는 손으로 '누르는' 동작이라 '누르다'를 훨씬 자주 써요. 그래서 '링크 클릭해 보세요'보다 '링크 눌러 보세요'가 더 자연스럽게 들려요. 비슷한 말로 '주소(URL)'가 있는데, '주소'는 'https://...' 같은 글자 형태의 인터넷 주소를 가리키고, '링크'는 그 주소를 담아 '누르면 이동하는' 연결 전체를 뜻해 약간 더 넓어요. 또 '링크를 걸다'라는 표현은 글이나 메시지에 링크를 삽입한다는 뜻으로 자주 써요. 모르는 사람이 보낸 링크는 피싱일 수 있으니 누르지 말라는 안전 안내도 자주 들어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
On mobile, Koreans say 링크를 누르다 (press/tap) far more than 클릭하다 (click) — 누르다 sounds more natural in speech.
Don't write 린크 — the standard spelling is 링크.
Don't equate 링크 exactly with 주소. 주소 is the text URL itself; 링크 is the clickable connection that carries you to it.

entries.shortExplanation: 결혼식 means "wedding (ceremony)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 결혼식 (gyeolhonsik) = "wedding (ceremony)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결혼식에 가다 ("go to a wedding") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결혼식, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Take the particle 에 (destination/event), never 을 — you go TO the event
Set idiom for the couple having their ceremony; 올리다 (lit. 'raise/offer up') sounds more elevated than 하다
Add 場 (-장, 'place') for the building; 예식장 (禮式場) is the equally common synonym
You receive a 청첩장 (invitation); 초대받다 = 'be invited' in passive

examples.en: There's a wedding next week.
examples.note: Simple 있다 existence sentence — note 결혼식이, the subject marker, not 결혼식을

examples.en: There are so many weddings every weekend that it's a bit of a financial burden.
examples.note: 마다 = 'every'; weekend weddings + 축의금 are a real money pressure Koreans joke about

examples.ko: 부장님 딸 결혼식이라 회사 사람들이 다 같이 갔어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim ttal gyeolhonsigira hoesa saramdeuri da gachi gasseoyo.
examples.en: It was our manager's daughter's wedding, so everyone from the office went together.
examples.note: Shows the workplace-obligation register: attending a boss's family wedding is near-mandatory

entries.nuance: 결혼식 is the wedding CEREMONY (식 = 式 'ceremony/rite'), as opposed to 결혼 (結婚, 'tie + marry'), which is the marriage or the act of getting married — so 결혼했어요 means 'I got married,' while 결혼식에 갔어요 means 'I attended a wedding.' That 결혼/결혼식 split is the #1 trap for English speakers, since English 'wedding' blurs both. Compared with the everyday synonym 예식 (禮式, 'ceremony of courtesy'), 결혼식 is the plain default and 예식 sounds slightly more formal/venue-flavored (hence 예식장). The ceremony itself is famously short (30–60 minutes); the socially weighty part is the buffet meal afterward, which your cash gift 축의금 helps cover. Habitual collocations: 결혼식에 가다/참석하다, 결혼식을 올리다, 결혼식장. Take 에 for attendance — 결혼식을 가다 is a common particle error.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't confuse 결혼식 (the ceremony you attend) with 결혼 (the marriage): '결혼했어요' means YOU got married, so saying it when you only went to a friend's wedding wrongly announces your own marriage. Use 결혼식에 갔어요.
Avoid 결혼식을 가다 — 'go' targets a destination, so the natural particle is 에: 결혼식에 가다. The 을/를 here sounds like you're somehow 'doing' the wedding.
Don't say 결혼식을 하다 for the couple holding it; the idiomatic verb is 올리다 (결혼식을 올리다) or simply 결혼하다.

structuredNuance.t: 결혼식 is the wedding CEREMONY (식 = 式 'ceremony/rite'). The ceremony itself is famously short (30–60 minutes); the socially weighty part is the buffet meal afterward, which your cash gift 축의금 helps cover. Habitual collocations: 결혼식에 가다/참석하다, 결혼식을 올리다, 결혼식장.

결혼 (結婚, 'tie + marry') is the marriage or the act of getting married — 결혼했어요 means 'I got married,' while 결혼식에 갔어요 means 'I attended a wedding.' Compared with the everyday synonym 예식 (禮式, 'ceremony of courtesy'), 결혼식 is the plain default and 예식 sounds slightly more formal/venue-flavored (hence 예식장).
식 = 式 'ceremony/rite'; 결혼 = 結婚 'tie + marry'; 예식 = 禮式 'ceremony of courtesy.'
The 결혼/결혼식 split is the #1 trap for English speakers, since English 'wedding' blurs both. Take 에 for attendance — 결혼식을 가다 is a common particle error.

entries.shortExplanation: 장례식 means "funeral" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 장례식 (jangnyesik) means "funeral". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 장례식에 가다 ("go to a funeral"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 장례식 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Particle 에 for attendance; you go to pay respects (조문하다)
장례식장 (場) is the building, often inside a hospital; 빈소 (殯所) is the specific mourning room
參席 'take part'; more formal than 가다, standard in workplace announcements
Said of the bereaved family holding it; drop 식 and use 치르다 ('go through / carry out')

examples.en: I wore black clothes to the funeral.
examples.note: Basic 입고 가다 ('wear and go'); dark, plain clothing is expected

examples.ko: 부장님 아버님 장례식이라 부서 사람들이 다 조문하러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim abeonim jangnyesigira buseo saramdeuri da jomunhareo gasseoyo.
examples.en: It was our manager's father's funeral, so the whole team went to pay respects.
examples.note: 조문하러 가다 = 'go in order to pay condolences'; teaches the -러 purpose ending in a real obligation context

examples.en: It was such sudden news that I rushed straight to the funeral hall.
examples.note: Real-situation register; 달려가다 ('run/rush to') conveys urgency and closeness to the bereaved

entries.nuance: 장례식 is a funeral — 葬 'bury' + 禮 'rite' + 式 'ceremony,' literally the 'burial-rite ceremony.' Distinguish it from the act-focused 장례 (葬禮, the funeral proceedings the family 치르다 'carries out') and from 조문/문상 (弔問/問喪), which is what a GUEST does — paying condolences. So the family 장례를 치르다, while you 장례식에 가서 조문하다. Korean funerals typically run three days at a 장례식장 frequently attached to a hospital, with the 빈소 (殯所, wake room) as the core space. Attending a colleague's or friend's family wake is a heavy social duty; you bring 조의금 in a plain white envelope and wear muted dark clothing. English speakers wrongly carry over 'congratulations'-type warmth — the funeral register is solemn and understated, and bright clothing or cheerful words badly misfire.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't say or bring anything 축하 (congratulatory): the correct sentiment is 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ('I humbly pray for the deceased's peace') or a quiet word of condolence. 축하 at a funeral is a severe register error.
Don't confuse the white-envelope 조의금 (funeral) with the wedding 축의금; using the wrong word or a colored envelope is a serious faux pas.
Don't mix up 장례식 (the ceremony/event) with 장례 (the family's act of holding it): a guest goes to the 장례식, but it's the family that 장례를 치르다.

entries.shortExplanation: 돌잔치 means "first-birthday party (for a baby)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "first-birthday party (for a baby)" is 돌잔치 (doljanchi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 돌잔치를 하다 ("hold a first-birthday party"). Watch the particle attached to 돌잔치 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Said of the parents throwing it; 하다 is natural here
Coworkers/friends with a baby invite you; implies a gift or cash
The highlight: the baby grabs an object said to foretell its future
答禮 'gift in return'; parents give guests 떡, towels, etc. in thanks

examples.en: My niece's first-birthday party is next month.
examples.note: Simple 있다 sentence; 돌잔치 takes the subject marker 가

examples.en: At the doljanchi the baby grabbed the microphone in the doljabi.
examples.note: 에서 marks the location of the action; guests cheer whichever object the baby picks

examples.ko: 요즘은 돌잔치를 작게 가족끼리만 하는 집도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun doljanchireul jakge gajokkkiriman haneun jipdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many families hold the doljanchi small, just among relatives.
examples.note: 끼리 = 'among (only)'; reflects the real shift from lavish halls to intimate gatherings

entries.nuance: 돌잔치 = 돌 (native Korean for a baby's first birthday) + 잔치 (native Korean for 'feast/celebration'), so unlike most life-event words here it is NOT Sino-Korean — there's no hanja. 돌 historically marked surviving the dangerous first year when infant mortality was high, which is why it's celebrated rather than treated like an ordinary 생일. Keep that contrast sharp: 돌잔치 is ONLY the first birthday; every later birthday is 생일, and the polite/honorific 생신 is for elders. The signature ritual is 돌잡이, where the baby grabs an object (money, thread, pencil, mic…) believed to predict its future. As a guest you give cash or a baby gift and may receive a 답례품 in return. Watch the spelling: 돌잔치 is one word, not 돌 잔치.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
돌잔치 is specifically the FIRST birthday — don't use it for a 5th or 30th birthday. Any ordinary birthday is 생일 (and 생신 for an elder).
Write it as one word, 돌잔치, not 돌 잔치 with a space; 잔치 ('feast') is fused onto 돌.
Don't call it 첫 번째 생일 파티 as a literal translation of 'first birthday party' — Koreans have the dedicated word 돌잔치, and the calque sounds foreign.

structuredNuance.t: 돌잔치 is a baby's first-birthday celebration. 돌 historically marked surviving the dangerous first year when infant mortality was high, which is why it's celebrated rather than treated like an ordinary 생일. The signature ritual is 돌잡이, where the baby grabs an object (money, thread, pencil, mic…) believed to predict its future. As a guest you give cash or a baby gift and may receive a 답례품 in return.
Keep the contrast sharp: 돌잔치 is ONLY the first birthday; every later birthday is 생일, and the polite/honorific 생신 is for elders.
돌잔치 = 돌 (native Korean for a baby's first birthday) + 잔치 (native Korean for 'feast/celebration'), so unlike most life-event words here it is NOT Sino-Korean — there's no hanja.
Watch the spelling: 돌잔치 is one word, not 돌 잔치.

entries.shortExplanation: 환갑 means "60th birthday (hwangap)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 환갑 (hwangap) = "60th birthday (hwangap)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 환갑을 맞다 ("reach one's 60th birthday") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 환갑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 맞다 = 'greet/meet' a milestone date; 환갑을 맞이하다 is the fuller form
Add 잔치 ('feast'); the traditional celebration party
Use 시 honorific because it concerns an elder
進甲; the year after 환갑, sometimes also marked

examples.en: My father turns 60 this year.
examples.note: Honorific 이세요 because it's about a parent — never the plain 환갑이에요 for an elder

examples.ko: 예전에는 환갑잔치를 크게 했는데 요즘은 잘 안 해요.
examples.romanization: yejeoneneun hwangapjanchireul keuge haenneunde yojeumeun jal an haeyo.
examples.en: People used to hold big 60th banquets, but these days they often don't.
examples.note: -는데 sets up the past-vs-now contrast; longer lifespans made 60 less momentous

examples.ko: 할머니 환갑이라 온 가족이 호텔에서 식사를 했어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoni hwangabira on gajogi hotereseo siksareul haesseoyo.
examples.en: It was grandmother's 60th, so the whole family had a meal at a hotel.
examples.note: Real-situation use; shows the modern trend of a family meal/trip replacing a banquet

entries.nuance: 환갑 (還甲, 'return + sexagenary-cycle') literally means the 갑(甲) has come full circle: traditional Korea counts years on a 60-term zodiac cycle (干支), so turning 60 'returns' you to the cycle's start — hence also written 회갑 (回甲, 'revolve + cycle'), the more formal variant. Don't confuse it with the milestone above it, 칠순/고희 (70th, 古稀 'rare since old times'), or with 진갑 (進甲, the 61st). Because life expectancy was once short, reaching 환갑 was a rare achievement worthy of a big 환갑잔치; today, with people routinely living far longer, families more often mark it with a trip or gift than a banquet. Crucial register point: 환갑 always concerns an elder, so use honorifics — 환갑이세요, 환갑을 맞으셨어요 — and pair it with 생신 (not 생일) when naming the birthday itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Because it concerns an elder, use honorific forms: 환갑이세요 / 환갑이시다, not the plain 환갑이에요. Dropping the 시 honorific about a parent or grandparent sounds disrespectful.
Don't equate 환갑 with simply 'turning 60' in a Western sense — it's tied to the 60-year 干支 cycle and Korean age reckoning, so the cultural weight (and sometimes the exact year) differs.
Don't reach for 생일 when speaking of the elder's day; pair 환갑 with the honorific 생신 (e.g. 환갑 생신).

entries.shortExplanation: 청첩장 means "wedding invitation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 청첩장 (cheongcheopjang) means "wedding invitation". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 청첩장을 주다 / 받다 ("give / receive a wedding invitation"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 청첩장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 implies a soft obligation to attend or send 축의금
Sent as a KakaoTalk link; now the default, bundling a map and account number
돌리다 ('send around') = casually handing them to friends and coworkers
文句 'phrasing'; the formal text announcing the couple and date

examples.en: I received a wedding invitation yesterday.
examples.note: Basic 받다 sentence; 청첩장 takes 을 as the object

examples.ko: 친구가 청첩장 주려고 일부러 만나자고 했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga cheongcheopjang juryeogo ilbureo mannajago haesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend asked to meet up on purpose just to give me the invitation.
examples.note: -(으)려고 = 'in order to'; handing a paper 청첩장 in person is a courteous gesture

examples.ko: 모바일 청첩장에 계좌번호랑 오시는 길이 다 들어 있더라고요.
examples.romanization: mobail cheongcheopjange gyejwabeonhorang osineun giri da deureo itdeoragoyo.
examples.en: The mobile invitation had the bank account number and directions all included.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a fresh discovery; reflects how digital invites bundle 축의금 transfer info

entries.nuance: 청첩장 (請牒狀) breaks down as 請 'request/invite' + 牒 'official note' + 狀 'document/letter' — a 'letter requesting your presence,' specifically for a WEDDING. Keep it apart from the general 초대장 (招待狀, any invitation card to a party/event): every 청첩장 is a 초대장, but you only call it 청첩장 for a wedding. Increasingly it arrives as a 모바일 청첩장, a KakaoTalk link that bundles a map, schedule, and the couple's bank account number for transferring 축의금. Receiving one carries a quiet obligation: you're expected either to attend or to send the cash gift, and ignoring a close friend's or coworker's 청첩장 can genuinely strain the relationship. Habitual verbs: 청첩장을 주다/받다/돌리다. The hanja is opaque even to many Koreans, so just learn it as a fixed word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't substitute 초대장 (general invitation card) for 청첩장: 초대장 covers any party/event, while 청첩장 is the wedding-specific term. Calling a wedding invite a 초대장 sounds slightly off.
Don't treat a received 청첩장 as optional info — from a close friend or coworker it's a soft social obligation; silence (no attendance and no 축의금) can damage the relationship.
Don't say 청첩장을 보내다 only for paper — these days 청첩장을 보내다 most often means sending the KakaoTalk 모바일 청첩장 link, so don't picture an envelope by default.

entries.shortExplanation: 축의금 means "congratulatory cash gift (at weddings)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "congratulatory cash gift (at weddings)" is 축의금 (chuguigeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 축의금을 내다 ("give/pay the cash gift"). Watch the particle attached to 축의금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 ('hand in / pay') is the standard verb at the 접수처 (reception desk)
보내다 = transfer it to their account when you can't attend
封套 'envelope'; a white envelope you sign your name on at the desk
Common baseline amounts; closer relationships and elders give more

examples.en: I gave 50,000 won as the gift.
examples.note: (으)로 = 'as/by means of'; 5만 원 is the common baseline amount

examples.ko: 접수처에서 봉투에 이름 적고 축의금을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: jeopsucheoeseo bongtue ireum jeokgo chuguigeumeul naesseoyo.
examples.en: I wrote my name on the envelope at the reception desk and handed in the gift.
examples.note: You sign so the couple can record who gave what — teaches the desk routine

examples.ko: 결혼식에 못 가서 축의금만 계좌로 보냈어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsige mot gaseo chuguigeumman gyejwaro bonaesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't make the wedding, so I just sent the gift to their account.
examples.note: Real situation; -만 ('only') + 계좌로 ('by account') shows transfer is fully acceptable

entries.nuance: 축의금 (祝儀金) = 祝 'congratulate' + 儀 'ceremony/propriety' + 金 'money' — literally 'money for a congratulatory ceremony,' the cash you give at HAPPY events, above all weddings. Its exact mirror image is 조의금 (弔儀金, 'condolence-ceremony money') for funerals: same 儀金 ending, opposite first character (祝 'congratulate' vs 弔 'mourn'), and opposite occasions — confusing the two, or reusing the wrong envelope, is a real and embarrassing error. You place 축의금 in a WHITE envelope, sign it, and hand it in at the 접수처 (reception desk) so the couple can record who gave it. Amounts start around 50,000 won and rise with closeness, traditionally in odd denominations (5/7/10만). The English word 'gift' misleads here — this is specifically cash, not a wrapped present, and a 선물 (a physical gift) is a different thing you generally don't substitute.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't mix up 축의금 (weddings / happy events, 祝) with 조의금 (funerals, 弔): the first characters are opposites, and using the wrong word or a white-vs-decorated envelope at the wrong event is a serious social mistake.
Don't give even-numbered amounts like 60,000 or 80,000 won; odd numbers (50,000 / 70,000 / 100,000) are customary, as even amounts traditionally suggest 'splitting.'
Don't translate it as a 선물 ('gift/present') — 축의금 is specifically cash in an envelope; bringing a wrapped object instead can look like you missed the custom.

structuredNuance.t: 축의금 is literally 'money for a congratulatory ceremony,' the cash you give at HAPPY events, above all weddings. entries.shortExplanation: 조의금 means "condolence money (at funerals)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조의금 (jouigeum) = "condolence money (at funerals)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 조의금을 내다 ("give condolence money") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 조의금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 ('hand in') at the 장례식장 reception desk
Plain undecorated white envelope, often with 부의 written on it
전하다 ('convey/deliver') sounds respectful and appropriately solemn
賻儀金; used interchangeably with 조의금, and 부의 is what you write on the envelope

examples.en: I gave condolence money.
examples.note: Basic 내다 sentence; the solemn counterpart to 축의금을 내다

examples.en: On the condolence envelope you usually write '부의.'
examples.note: Teaches the fixed envelope wording, unlike a wedding envelope

examples.ko: 멀어서 못 가고 조의금만 동료 편에 보냈어요.
examples.romanization: meoreoseo mot gago jouigeumman dongnyo pyeone bonaesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't go because it was far, so I sent the condolence money with a coworker.
examples.note: 편에 = 'by way of (a person)'; sending it with someone attending is common when you can't go

entries.nuance: 조의금 (弔儀金) = 弔 'mourn/condole' + 儀 'ceremony/propriety' + 金 'money,' the cash given to a bereaved family — the exact dark twin of 축의금 (祝儀金), which swaps in 祝 'congratulate.' The freely interchangeable synonym is 부의금 (賻儀金, 賻 = 'goods given to help with a funeral'), and confusingly the word you actually write on the envelope is usually 부의 or 조의, not 조의금. It goes in a PLAIN WHITE, undecorated envelope handed in at the 장례식장 reception desk, and like 축의금 it's a near-obligatory courtesy for a coworker's family funeral. Because the occasion is solemn, every cue stays understated — no color, no flourish, quiet delivery (전하다). The cardinal English-speaker error is treating any envelope of money as interchangeable; the 祝/弔 distinction and the white envelope are non-negotiable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Never reuse a colorful or wedding-style envelope: 조의금 requires a plain white one. A decorated envelope at a funeral reads as a painful mistake.
Don't confuse 조의금 (funerals, 弔) with 축의금 (weddings, 祝); the occasions are opposite and the error is serious. Remember 弔 = mourn vs 祝 = congratulate.
Don't write 조의금 ON the envelope — the conventional wording is 부의 (賻儀) or 조의, written vertically on the front.

entries.shortExplanation: 신혼여행 means "honeymoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 신혼여행 (sinhonyeohaeng) means "honeymoon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 신혼여행을 가다 ("go on a honeymoon"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 신혼여행 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Standard verb; particle 을 for the trip you take, 에 for the destination

usagePhrases.en: go and come back from a honeymoon
usagePhrases.note: 다녀오다 = 'go and return'; implies the round trip is complete
Add 地 (-지, 'place/land'); e.g. 하와이, 발리, 몰디브
신혼 + 집; the place the couple sets up after marrying

examples.en: Where are you going for your honeymoon?
examples.note: 어디로 ('to where') with directional 로; a natural question to a couple

examples.en: We went to Bali for our honeymoon.
examples.note: (으)로 = 'as/for'; Southeast Asian beach resorts are typical 신혼여행지

examples.ko: 결혼식 끝나고 바로 신혼여행 다녀와서 집들이를 했어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsik kkeunnago baro sinhonyeohaeng danyeowaseo jipdeurireul haesseoyo.
examples.en: Right after the wedding we went on the honeymoon and then held a housewarming.
examples.note: Real timeline chaining 결혼식 → 신혼여행 → 집들이, three life-event words in sequence

entries.nuance: 신혼여행 (新婚旅行) = 新 'new' + 婚 'marriage' + 旅行 'travel,' literally the 'new-marriage trip,' i.e. the honeymoon taken right after the 결혼식. The root 신혼 (新婚, 'newlywed') names the broader early-married phase and lives in compounds like 신혼집 (first home) and 신혼부부 (newlywed couple). Don't reduce it to plain 여행 (旅行, any trip) — that loses the 'newlywed' meaning entirely, the way English 'trip' wouldn't tell anyone it's a honeymoon. Typical 신혼여행지 are Southeast-Asian beach resorts (발리, 다낭) and longer-haul spots (하와이, 유럽). Note the verb pair: 신혼여행을 가다 to go, 신혼여행을 다녀오다 / 갔다 오다 once you're back. Watch the spacing — 신혼여행 is one word, not 신혼 여행.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't shorten it to plain 여행 when you mean the honeymoon specifically: 여행 is any trip, so '여행 갔다 왔어요' just means you traveled, losing the newlywed meaning.
Write it as one word, 신혼여행, not 신혼 여행 with a space; the 신혼 + 여행 compound is fused.
Don't say 허니문 reflexively just because English does — while 허니문 exists as a loanword, the natural everyday word is 신혼여행.

entries.shortExplanation: 약혼 means "engagement (to be married)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "engagement (to be married)" is 약혼 (yakon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 약혼하다 ("get engaged"). Watch the particle attached to 약혼 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Verb form; 약혼했어요 = 'got engaged'
者 'person'; your engaged partner, gender-neutral (no separate male/female word)
반지 = 'ring'; the ring exchanged at engagement
破婚 'break + marriage'; the antonym verb worth knowing

examples.en: My older sister got engaged.
examples.note: 약혼하다 as a plain past-tense announcement; the most natural way to report it

examples.en: I'm preparing the family meeting together with my fiancé.
examples.note: 랑 = casual 'with'; links naturally to 상견례, the families' first meal

examples.ko: 요즘은 약혼식을 따로 안 하고 바로 결혼 준비하는 사람도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun yakonsigeul ttaro an hago baro gyeolhon junbihaneun saramdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many people skip a separate engagement ceremony and go straight into wedding prep.
examples.note: Real-situation contrast; reflects that formal 약혼식 ceremonies are fading

entries.nuance: 약혼 (約婚) = 約 'promise/pledge' + 婚 'marriage,' literally 'pledging to marry' — the formal engagement, with verb 약혼하다 and partner 약혼자 (約婚者, gender-neutral, so no fiancé/fiancée split to memorize). Keep it firmly distinct from 결혼 (結婚, 'tie + marry'): 약혼한 사이 means 'an engaged couple,' NOT married, and the English speaker's instinct to treat engagement as nearly-married can mislead. The 約 here is the same 約 as in 약속 (約束, 'bind a promise'), a useful memory hook. Its opposite is 파혼 (破婚, 'break the marriage-pledge'), to call the engagement off. In modern Korea a standalone 약혼식 (engagement ceremony) is increasingly skipped; couples often go from agreeing to marry straight into the 상견례 and wedding prep, so 약혼 today is often a status more than an event.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 약혼 (engagement, 約 'pledge') with 결혼 (marriage, 結 'tie'): 약혼한 사이 means engaged, not married. Treating an engaged couple as already married is a meaning error.
Don't hunt for a separate feminine word — 약혼자 covers both fiancé and fiancée; Korean doesn't gender it.
Don't assume there's always an 약혼식 to attend; many couples skip the ceremony entirely, so 약혼 may be just an announced status.

entries.english: formal meeting of the two families (before marriage)
entries.shortExplanation: 상견례 means "formal meeting of the two families (before marriage)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상견례 (sanggyeollye) = "formal meeting of the two families (before marriage)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 상견례를 하다 ("hold the family meeting") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상견례, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Said of the two families formally meeting
자리 ('seat/occasion') = the formal gathering itself
場所 'place'; usually a quiet, refined restaurant
兩家 'both houses'; the people 상견례 brings together

examples.en: The family meeting is next week.
examples.note: Simple 있다 sentence; 상견례 takes the subject marker 가

examples.en: We held the family meeting at a quiet Korean set-menu restaurant.
examples.note: 에서 marks the location of the event; calm upscale restaurants are the norm

examples.ko: 상견례 때 너무 긴장돼서 말을 거의 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: sanggyeollye ttae neomu ginjangdwaeseo mareul geoui mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I was so nervous at the family meeting that I could barely speak.
examples.note: 때 = 'at the time of'; conveys the genuinely formal, tense register of the occasion

entries.nuance: 상견례 (相見禮) = 相 'mutually' + 見 'see/meet' + 禮 'rite/courtesy,' literally 'the courtesy of meeting one another' — specifically the formal first meeting of the two families (양가, 兩家) before a wedding, usually over a meal. Don't generalize it: despite the literal 'mutual meeting,' it does NOT mean any first introduction between strangers — that's just 첫 만남 or 인사. It also isn't 맞선/소개팅 (a matchmaking date between the would-be couple themselves); 상견례 is the PARENTS being introduced once marriage is essentially decided. It's a significant, somewhat stiff milestone held at a quiet, refined restaurant (often a 한정식집), where things going smoothly signals both families approve. Because it's formal, dress and speech stay polite (존댓말 throughout) — treating it casually can offend the in-laws-to-be.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 상견례 for any general first meeting of two people: it specifically means the two FAMILIES meeting before a marriage, not a casual or business first encounter (that's 첫 만남 / 첫 대면).
Don't confuse it with 맞선 or 소개팅 (a setup date between the prospective couple); 상견례 is about the parents/families, after the couple has decided to marry.

entries.shortExplanation: 집들이 means "housewarming party" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 집들이 (jipdeuri) means "housewarming party". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 집들이를 하다 ("have a housewarming"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 집들이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Said of the host throwing the party
Particle 에 for the event; you attend as a guest
Classic choices: 휴지 (toilet paper) and 세제 (detergent)
The host inviting friends over to the new place

examples.en: There's a housewarming this weekend.
examples.note: Basic 있다 sentence; 집들이 takes the subject marker 가

examples.ko: 집들이에 갈 때 보통 휴지나 세제를 사 가요.
examples.romanization: jipdeurie gal ttae botong hyujina sejereul sa gayo.
examples.en: When going to a housewarming, people usually buy toilet paper or detergent to bring.
examples.note: 사 가다 = 'buy and bring'; these gifts carry traditional good-luck meaning

examples.ko: 이사하고 친구들 불러서 집들이를 했는데 분위기가 정말 좋았어요.
examples.romanization: isahago chingudeul bulleoseo jipdeurireul haenneunde bunwigiga jeongmal joasseoyo.
examples.en: After moving I invited friends over for a housewarming, and the mood was really nice.
examples.note: Real situation; -는데 links the setup to the warm, casual atmosphere of the event

entries.nuance: 집들이 is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja): 집 'house' + 들이 (from 들이다, 'to bring/take in'), so it literally evokes 'bringing people into the house' — the housewarming party thrown after an 이사 (移徙, moving). Don't confuse the event with the move itself: you do 이사 first (the act of relocating), THEN 집들이 (the celebration). Also distinguish it from 집들이 선물 vs a generic 선물 — the classic gifts are pointed: 휴지 (toilet paper), because it 'unrolls smoothly' (everything in the new home going smoothly), and 세제 (laundry detergent), whose bubbles symbolize prosperity 'bubbling up.' These are warm, traditional choices, not cheap ones — an English speaker may misread practical household items as an awkward gift. It's a relaxed gathering where the host usually cooks or orders in for friends.

Don't read 휴지 or 세제 as a cheap or odd gift — they're traditional, well-wishing choices (smooth unrolling / bubbling prosperity), and bringing them is the thoughtful, expected move.
Don't confuse 집들이 (the party) with 이사 (the act of moving): the sequence is 이사 first, then 집들이. Saying 집들이 when you mean the move itself is wrong.
Don't take the particle 을 for attendance — you 집들이에 가다 (go TO it); 집들이를 하다 is only for the host throwing it.

entries.shortExplanation: 부고 means "death notice / obituary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "death notice / obituary" is 부고 (bugo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 부고를 받다 ("receive a death notice"). Watch the particle attached to 부고 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 ('receive'); often arrives via KakaoTalk or a workplace message
전하다 ('convey') sounds appropriately solemn and respectful
The text giving the deceased's name, 빈소, and funeral times
오다 ('come') as an intransitive arrival; used when one is received

examples.en: I received a death notice.
examples.note: Basic 받다 sentence; note the solemn register the word carries

examples.ko: 부고 문자에 장례식장 위치가 적혀 있었어요.
examples.romanization: bugo munjae jangnyesikjang wichiga jeokyeo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The death-notice text had the funeral hall's location written on it.
examples.note: 적혀 있다 = 'is written (and remains so)'; the message bundles 빈소 location and visiting hours

examples.ko: 부고를 듣고 바로 조의금을 준비해서 조문하러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: bugoreul deutgo baro jouigeumeul junbihaeseo jomunhareo gasseoyo.
examples.en: On hearing of the death I prepared condolence money right away and went to pay respects.
examples.note: Real timeline -고 ('and then'); a 부고 prompts 조의금 and a visit if you're close

entries.nuance: 부고 (訃告) = 訃 'announcement of a death' + 告 'tell/notify,' literally 'notifying of a death' — the formal notice that someone has died, not the funeral itself. Distinguish it sharply from 장례식 (葬禮式, the funeral ceremony) and 빈소 (殯所, the wake room): you first RECEIVE a 부고, which then leads you to attend the 장례식 at the 빈소. The near-synonym 부음 (訃音, 'news of a death') means the same message but sounds more literary; 부고 is the everyday word, today usually circulated as a 부고 문자 listing the deceased, the 빈소, and visiting times. In a workplace, getting a colleague's family 부고 effectively signals that attending and giving 조의금 is expected. Both word and tone are solemn — the English habit of a quick 'thanks for letting me know' reply misfires; respond soberly with condolences, never an emoji or light remark.

Don't use 부고 for the funeral itself — 부고 is the death NOTICE (訃告), while the funeral is 장례식. You receive a 부고, then attend the 장례식.
Don't respond to a 부고 lightly: no emoji or breezy replies in the KakaoTalk thread. A sober condolence message (e.g. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다) is the correct register.
Don't say 부고를 하다; the natural verbs are 부고를 받다/전하다 or 부고가 오다 — 부고 is something received or conveyed, not 'done.'

entries.shortExplanation: 조용히 means "quietly, calmly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조용히 (joyonghi) = "quietly, calmly". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 조용히 해 주세요 ("please be quiet") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 조용히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request for quiet in a library, cafe, or meeting; 해 주세요 softens it
Lower your voice so others aren't disturbed; contrast 작게 말하다 (low volume)
조용히 지내요 = I'm keeping a calm, low-key life these days
Casual and slightly sharp; 좀 here adds mild irritation, not politeness

examples.en: Be quiet, please.
examples.note: Blunt 반말 between close friends or to a noisy kid; 좀 nudges it toward a plea

examples.en: The baby's sleeping, so come in quietly.
examples.note: 조용히 attaches to the action verb 들어오다 — it modifies HOW you enter

examples.ko: 요즘은 그냥 집에서 조용히 쉬고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun geunyang jibeseo joyonghi swigo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days I'm just resting quietly at home.
examples.note: Here 조용히 = low-key / peacefully, not literal silence

entries.nuance: 조용히 is the adverb of the adjective 조용하다 and stretches from literal silence ('be quiet') to a calm, low-key MANNER of doing things ('live quietly, rest peacefully'), so it's far more useful in speech than the adjective alone. The dividing line with its neighbors matters: 작게 means low in VOLUME, 가만히 means without MOVING, and 몰래 means in SECRET — only 조용히 covers undisturbing quietness. It collocates with 하다, 말하다, 지내다, 들어오다. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as the adjective: you cannot say '조용히 사람' for 'a quiet person' — that needs the adjective form 조용한 사람, while 조용히 only modifies a verb. Also mind the spelling: it ends in 히, not 이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 조용이; the standard adverb form is 조용히 with 히 (the 이/히 choice is fixed per word and just has to be memorized).
Using 조용히 to mean 'secretly / on the sly' — that idea is 몰래 (몰래 나가다 = sneak out). 조용히 only means without noise or fuss.
Saying 조용히 사람 for 'a quiet person'; 조용히 modifies verbs only, so a noun needs the adjective 조용한 (조용한 사람).

entries.shortExplanation: 깨끗이 means "cleanly, thoroughly (clean)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 깨끗이 (kkaekkeusi) means "cleanly, thoroughly (clean)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 깨끗이 씻다 ("to wash thoroughly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 깨끗이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing — hands, dishes, vegetables, fruit
Stresses cleaning all the way, leaving nothing dirty
For wiping a surface until no dirt or smudge remains
깨끗이 비웠어요 = I cleaned my plate / left nothing

examples.en: Wash your hands well.
examples.note: Bare everyday hygiene reminder; 깨끗이 tells you to wash THOROUGHLY, not just briefly

examples.ko: 이사 가기 전에 집을 깨끗이 치웠어요.
examples.romanization: isa gagi jeone jibeul kkaekkeusi chiwosseoyo.
examples.en: I cleaned the place up thoroughly before moving out.
examples.note: The move-out / deposit context where 깨끗이 = leave it spotless

examples.en: I've cleanly put the past behind me.
examples.note: Figurative: 깨끗이 잊다 = forget completely, with no residue of feeling

entries.nuance: 깨끗이 is the adverb of 깨끗하다 and crucially means doing something so the RESULT is clean and complete, not merely 'in a clean manner' — the focus is thoroughness. It's the natural partner of 씻다, 닦다, 청소하다, 치우다, and it extends figuratively to 깨끗이 잊다 (forget cleanly) or 깨끗이 인정하다 (admit it cleanly, with no excuses). Compare 깔끔하게, which describes a tidy, neat appearance/finish (깔끔하게 정리하다), whereas 깨끗이 emphasizes the absence of dirt or residue. The notorious trap is spelling: despite all its 히-ending siblings here, this word ends in 이 — 깨끗이, never 깨끗히. Roughly, when the stem ends in a ㅅ-type sound the adverb often takes 이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 깨끗히; the correct adverb is 깨끗이 with 이. This is one of the most common spelling errors even for native speakers.
Limiting it to physical surfaces — it also means finishing/resolving something completely, as in 깨끗이 잊다 or 깨끗이 포기하다 (give up cleanly).
Reaching for 깨끗이 when you mean a neat, stylish finish; that nuance is 깔끔하게 (깔끔하게 차려입다 = dress neatly), not 깨끗이.

entries.shortExplanation: 가만히 means "still, motionless; just (leave be)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "still, motionless; just (leave be)" is 가만히 (gamanhi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가만히 있어 ("stay still / stay put"). Watch the particle attached to 가만히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Telling someone not to move or fidget; also 'stay out of it'
Asking someone to stop touching or meddling; 좀 adds exasperation

usagePhrases.en: now that I think it over quietly
usagePhrases.note: Sets up a reflective realization
Threat form; the same 가만히 turns menacing here

examples.en: Stay still.
examples.note: Bare command — to a wriggling child or someone about to make things worse

examples.ko: 가만히 좀 있어 봐, 내가 해 줄게.
examples.romanization: gamanhi jom isseo bwa, naega hae julge.
examples.en: Hold still a sec, I'll do it for you.
examples.note: Gentle 반말; 가만히 + 있다 = don't move, vs 가만히 + 두다 = don't touch

examples.en: Thinking it over quietly, I realized I'd messed up.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a realization you came to; 가만히 = calmly, taking a moment

entries.nuance: 가만히 carries two everyday senses that English splits apart: physically staying STILL (가만히 있어 = don't move) and letting something BE / not interfering (가만히 둬 = leave it alone). Note the meaning rides on the verb — 가만히 있다 is about your own body, 가만히 두다 is about not touching another thing. Don't confuse it with 조용히 (without noise): you can sit 가만히 yet keep talking. There's also a buried threat: 가만 안 둬 / 가만히 안 있을 거야 means 'I won't let this go,' so the same word can sound soothing or menacing purely by context. It frequently shortens to 가만 in speech (가만, 이게 뭐지? = 'wait, what's this?').

Translating it only as 'quietly'; 가만히 usually means 'without moving' or 'leave it be', not silence — that's 조용히.
Confusing 가만히 두다 (leave alone) with 가만히 있다 (stay still); the verb decides the meaning, so swapping them changes who/what is acting.
Missing the warning tone in 가만 안 둬 — beginners read it literally, but it's an idiom for 'you'll pay for this / I won't let it slide.'

entries.shortExplanation: 꼼꼼히 means "thoroughly, meticulously" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 꼼꼼히 (kkomkkomhi) = "thoroughly, meticulously". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 꼼꼼히 확인하다 ("to check carefully") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 꼼꼼히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The most common pairing — documents, orders, contracts, bills
Reading every line and detail rather than skimming
Making sure absolutely nothing is left out
Weighing every detail before deciding or paying

examples.en: Look it over slowly and carefully.
examples.note: Bare advice; 꼼꼼히 pairs naturally with 천천히 — careful work isn't rushed

examples.ko: 짐을 꼼꼼히 챙겼는데도 우산을 두고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jimeul kkomkkomhi chaenggyeonneundedo usaneul dugo wasseoyo.
examples.en: Even though I packed carefully, I left my umbrella behind.
examples.note: -는데도 = even though; shows 꼼꼼히 = leaving nothing out

examples.en: The boss taught me the work thoroughly.
examples.note: A compliment — being called 꼼꼼하다 is high praise at a Korean workplace

entries.nuance: 꼼꼼히 is the adverb of 꼼꼼하다 and describes doing something with careful, detail-by-detail attention, never skipping or rushing. In Korea being 꼼꼼하다 is a strong virtue — it's a top answer when describing your work strengths in an interview. The fine line with 자세히 is the key thing for learners: 자세히 is about the DEPTH of detail covered (자세히 설명하다 = explain in full detail), while 꼼꼼히 is about the CAREFULNESS of the doer (꼼꼼히 확인하다 = check meticulously so nothing is missed). It naturally attaches to 확인하다, 읽다, 챙기다, 따지다, and it ends in 히. The pitfall is pairing it with speed: 꼼꼼히 is inherently unhurried, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 jars — thoroughness and haste pull against each other.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 꼼꼼이; the standard adverb is 꼼꼼히 with 히.
Swapping it with 자세히 — 꼼꼼히 stresses the careful manner of the doer, 자세히 stresses the amount of detail, so '꼼꼼히 설명하다' sounds odd where '자세히 설명하다' is natural.
Combining it with speed words; 꼼꼼히 implies taking your time, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 하다 is self-contradictory.

entries.shortExplanation: 충분히 means "enough, sufficiently, plenty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 충분히 (chungbunhi) means "enough, sufficiently, plenty". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 충분히 자다 ("to sleep enough"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 충분히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 충분히 잤어요 = I slept plenty / got enough sleep
Reassuring someone you completely get it
Confirming something is well within reach
Sympathizing — 'anyone could react that way'

examples.en: There's plenty of time.
examples.note: Bare reassurance to take the pressure off; 충분히 = enough and to spare

examples.en: Cook the meat thoroughly before eating.
examples.note: 익히다 = cook through; here 충분히 = to a sufficient degree

examples.en: I completely understand how you feel.
examples.note: Warm, empathetic; spoken 충분히 softens into 'completely/totally'

entries.nuance: 충분히 comes from 充分 (充 'to fill' + 分 'portion/share', literally 'a full portion') and means a quantity or degree has been fully met — enough sleep, enough time, enough understanding. The key contrast for learners is with 완전히 (完全, 'complete'): 충분히 means 'enough for the purpose', not necessarily 100%, so 충분히 익히다 = cook it ENOUGH, while 완전히 익히다 = cook it ALL the way through. In conversation 충분히 also broadens into 'easily / readily' (충분히 그럴 수 있어요 = that could easily happen), which surprises learners expecting a literal amount. It's polite and supportive, which is why it floods comforting speech: 충분히 잘했어요, 충분히 이해해요.

Confusing 충분히 (sufficiently / enough) with 완전히 (completely / entirely); 충분히 means 'enough for the need', not 'totally'.
Forgetting the 'easily / readily' sense in 충분히 그럴 수 있어요 — it's not about a measured amount but about something being entirely plausible.

entries.shortExplanation: 분명히 means "clearly, surely, definitely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "clearly, surely, definitely" is 분명히 (bunmyeonghi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분명히 말하다 ("to say clearly / state plainly"). Watch the particle attached to 분명히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Making your point unmistakable, leaving no room for doubt
분명히 기억나요 = I remember it for certain
Insisting something is so, often against pushback
분명히 올 거예요 = they'll definitely come

examples.en: I definitely put it right here…
examples.note: Bare, half to yourself, when something's gone missing — the classic 분명히 moment

examples.en: Please tell me clearly from now on.
examples.note: 분명히 = unambiguously; a polite request for plain communication

examples.en: You clearly said it'd be done by yesterday.
examples.note: -잖아요 reminds the listener of a shared fact; 분명히 adds insistence

entries.nuance: 분명히 comes from 分明 (分 'divide' + 明 'bright/clear', i.e. 'distinctly clear') and links two senses: stating something plainly ('clearly say'), and asserting strong certainty ('surely, definitely'). The second floods spoken Korean, especially the exasperated 분명히 …했는데 ('I definitely did X, but…') when reality contradicts you. The sharp contrast to learn is with 확실히 (確實): 분명히 leans on the SPEAKER'S own conviction and memory ('I'm sure I did'), while 확실히 points to OBJECTIVE, checkable fact ('it's confirmed'). So 분명히 그 사람이었어 = I'm certain it was him; 확실히 그 사람이었어 leans toward 'it's been verified'. Because 분명히 voices real confidence, it clashes with a hedge — pair guesses with 아마 (probably) instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 분명히 and 확실히 as identical; 분명히 expresses your own subjective certainty, 확실히 reports objective, verifiable certainty.
Using 분명히 for a mere guess; it claims genuine confidence, so an unsure statement needs 아마 (아마 올 거예요 = they'll probably come).
Forgetting the plain 'clearly/distinctly' meaning — 분명히 말하다 is about clarity of statement, not just certainty.

entries.shortExplanation: 확실히 means "certainly, for sure, noticeably" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 확실히 (hwaksilhi) = "certainly, for sure, noticeably". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 확실히 알다 ("to know for sure") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 확실히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 확실히 알아보고 알려줄게요 = I'll check for certain and let you know
Noting an obvious, observable difference
Pinning something down so there's no doubt later
One-word agreement: 확실히. = Definitely.

examples.en: After the medicine I'm noticeably better.
examples.note: Bare remark; here 확실히 = 'you can clearly tell' the difference

examples.ko: 이건 확실히 해 둬야 나중에 문제가 없어요.
examples.romanization: igeon hwaksilhi hae dwoya najunge munjega eopseoyo.
examples.en: We should settle this clearly so there's no problem later.
examples.note: 확실히 해 두다 = nail it down / make sure

examples.en: The new phone is definitely faster, I'll give it that.
examples.note: -긴 하다 concedes a point; 확실히 confirms an observed fact

entries.nuance: 확실히 comes from 確實 (確 'firm/certain' + 實 'real/solid', i.e. 'firmly real') and means 'certainly, for sure' — but its most useful everyday flavor is 'noticeably', when you can plainly OBSERVE a difference: 확실히 빠르다 (clearly faster), 확실히 낫다 (clearly better). Set against 분명히, the divide is subjective vs objective: 분명히 voices the speaker's inner conviction, whereas 확실히 points to verifiable, demonstrable fact. The fixed phrase 확실히 하다 / 확실히 해 두다 ('make it definite / settle it for sure') is everywhere at work and in agreements. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 'noticeably' reading — learners hear 확실히 다르다 as 'surely different' when a Korean means 'you can clearly SEE it's different.'

Treating 확실히 and 분명히 as interchangeable; 확실히 emphasizes objective, checkable certainty, 분명히 your personal conviction.
Overlooking the 'noticeably' sense — 확실히 다르다 / 확실히 좋아지다 means a difference you can plainly observe, not merely 'surely'.
Saying 확실히 사람 etc.; like all these -히 words it modifies a verb or adjective, never a noun directly (a noun needs 확실한).
