entries.shortExplanation: 간단히 means "simply, briefly, lightly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 간단히 (gandanhi) means "simply, briefly, lightly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 간단히 설명하다 ("to explain briefly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 간단히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Giving a short, no-frills explanation
간단히 먹읍시다 = let's just eat something light
Connector that sets up a concise summary
Finishing without fuss or ceremony

examples.en: I just had gimbap for a quick lunch.
examples.note: 간단히 + 먹다 is THE phrase for a light, fast meal

examples.en: I'll keep the meeting short.
examples.note: A polite promise at work to not drag things out

examples.en: Simply put, the point is there isn't enough money.
examples.note: 간단히 말하면 = in short / to sum up

entries.nuance: 간단히 comes from 簡單 (簡 'brief/simple' + 單 'single', i.e. 'plain and single') and means doing something in a simple, brief, light way — a quick meal, a short explanation, a no-fuss finish. The crucial contrast is with 쉽게 (easily): 간단히 describes a small SCALE or effort, while 쉽게 describes low DIFFICULTY, so a task can be done 간단히 (quickly, lightly) yet still not be 쉽게 (it might be hard but short). The connector 간단히 말하면 ('in short') is a handy summarizing tool. The English-speaker trap is using it for a lavish meal or event — 간단히 inherently implies modest and light, so '간단히 잔치' (a simple feast) is a contradiction; for that you'd describe scale differently.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 간단히 (simply / lightly / briefly) with 쉽게 (easily); 간단히 is about small scale or low fuss, 쉽게 is about low difficulty.
Using 간단히 for a big, elaborate meal or event — it implies something light and quick, never a full spread.
Forgetting 간단히 먹다 is idiomatic for a fast, light meal; learners over-literally say 빨리 먹다 ('eat fast'), which is about speed, not lightness.

entries.shortExplanation: 자세히 means "in detail, closely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "in detail, closely" is 자세히 (jasehi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 자세히 설명하다 ("to explain in detail"). Watch the particle attached to 자세히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Asking for or giving a full, detailed explanation
Examining something up close and carefully
Researching all the details before deciding
Polite request for more specifics

examples.en: Tell me in a bit more detail.
examples.note: Bare 반말 request; 자세히 = with more specifics, not louder or faster

examples.en: I asked about the contract terms in detail.
examples.note: A smart move before signing anything in Korea

examples.en: When I looked closely, there was a scratch.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a discovery; 자세히 보다 = inspect up close

entries.nuance: 자세히 comes from 仔細 (仔 'careful' + 細 'fine/minute', i.e. 'down to the fine details') and means 'in detail / closely' — the natural opposite of 간단히. It pairs with 설명하다, 보다, 알아보다, 묻다 whenever you want full information rather than a quick gloss, and 자세히 설명해 주세요 is a survival phrase for getting specifics on contracts, services, and instructions in Korea. Two contrasts sharpen it: against 정확히 (正確, 'accurately'), 자세히 is about AMOUNT of detail while 정확히 is about CORRECTNESS — a long explanation can be 자세히 yet still wrong, hence not 정확히. And against 꼼꼼히, 자세히 describes the detail delivered, 꼼꼼히 the careful manner of the doer. It never describes a quantity of things, only thoroughness of explanation or observation.

Mixing up 자세히 (in detail) with 정확히 (accurately / exactly); detailed is not the same as precise — you can explain at length yet inaccurately.
Using 자세히 about an amount of items; it describes thoroughness of explaining or looking, not how much there is (use 많이 for quantity).
Confusing it with 꼼꼼히; 자세히 설명하다 (give lots of detail) is natural, while 꼼꼼히 fits checking/handling (꼼꼼히 확인하다).

entries.shortExplanation: 무심코 means "absentmindedly, without thinking" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무심코 (musimko) = "absentmindedly, without thinking". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 무심코 말하다 ("to say without thinking") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무심코, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Letting something slip with no intent
A careless comment, often unexpectedly hurtful
Tapping a button on autopilot
Something done without conscious thought

examples.en: It was just something I said without thinking.
examples.note: Bare apology/excuse; signals there was no bad intent

examples.en: I pressed the button without thinking, then canceled.
examples.note: -았다가 = did it, then reversed; 무심코 = on autopilot

examples.en: It was a thoughtless act, but it caused a misunderstanding.
examples.note: 오해를 사다 = to invite a misunderstanding

entries.nuance: 무심코 means doing or saying something absentmindedly, with no conscious intent, and it almost always sets up an UNINTENDED consequence — that's why it lives in apologies and reflections (무심코 한 말 = 'something I said without thinking'). It's built on 無心 (無 'without' + 心 'heart/mind', i.e. 'no mind/attention') plus the native suffix -코. The contrast to keep straight is the pair 무심코 vs 일부러 (on purpose): they're direct opposites, so 무심코 is your go-to when disclaiming intent. Don't confuse it with 무심하게, which means coldly/indifferently (a personality), whereas 무심코 means a one-off lapse of attention. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for anything planned — by definition 무심코 cannot describe a deliberate act.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 무심코 (without thinking) with 일부러 (on purpose); they are direct opposites, so they can't describe the same act.
Using 무심코 for a planned action; it specifically means there was no intention, so it clashes with anything deliberate.
Mixing it up with 무심하게 (coldly / indifferently) — 무심코 is a momentary lapse of attention, not a cold attitude.

entries.english: on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)
entries.shortExplanation: 일부러 means "on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 일부러 (ilbureo) means "on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일부러 그런 거 아니에요 ("I didn't do it on purpose"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 일부러 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I didn't do it on purpose
usagePhrases.note: The standard defense / apology after an accident
Going out of your way to see someone
Deliberately setting time aside for someone
Choosing not to do something on purpose

examples.en: I didn't do it on purpose.
examples.note: Bare, high-frequency apology; the #1 use of 일부러

examples.ko: 바쁠 텐데 일부러 와 줘서 고마워요.
examples.romanization: bappeul tende ilbureo wa jwoseo gomawoyo.
examples.en: Thanks for coming all this way even though you're busy.
examples.note: The warm 'went out of your way' sense — a sincere thank-you

examples.ko: 일부러 매운 걸 골랐어요, 스트레스 풀려고.
examples.romanization: ilbureo maeun geol gollasseoyo, seuteureseu pullyeogo.
examples.en: I picked something spicy on purpose, to relieve stress.
examples.note: Shows clear 'deliberately' intent toward a goal

entries.nuance: 일부러 (native Korean, no hanja) holds two everyday meanings English keeps apart: 'on purpose / intentionally', and 'going out of one's way / specially' to do a kindness. The first lives in apologies (일부러 그런 거 아니에요 = I didn't mean to), the second in thanks (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요 = thanks for making the special trip); both share the core of DELIBERATE effort, which makes it the opposite of 무심코. The contrast learners need is with 억지로 (reluctantly / by force): both involve doing something, but 일부러 is willing and intentional while 억지로 is against your will — 일부러 먹다 (eat on purpose, maybe for a reason) vs 억지로 먹다 (force yourself to eat). The pitfall is missing the warm 'special trip' reading and hearing only blame.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 일부러 (on purpose, willingly) with 억지로 (reluctantly / forcibly); intent is not the same as being forced — 억지로 means against your will.
Missing the warm 'going out of your way' sense, which is very common in thank-yous (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요).
Over-using it for routine choices; for a plain decision Koreans often just state the action, reserving 일부러 for genuinely deliberate or out-of-the-way acts.

entries.english: to one's heart's content, as much as you like
entries.shortExplanation: 마음껏 means "to one's heart's content, as much as you like" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to one's heart's content, as much as you like" is 마음껏 (maeumkkeot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마음껏 드세요 ("eat as much as you like"). Watch the particle attached to 마음껏 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: eat as much as you like
usagePhrases.note: Gracious host phrase at a meal
Telling someone to have a great time without holding back

usagePhrases.en: to rest as much as you want
usagePhrases.note: Encouraging full, guilt-free rest
Inviting a totally free choice

examples.en: I made a lot, so please help yourself.
examples.note: 차리다 = set out food; warm 존댓말 hospitality

examples.en: The exam's over, so let's have all the fun we want today.
examples.note: 마음껏 놀다 = hang out / play with no restraint (반말)

examples.en: I rested as much as I wanted over the vacation.
examples.note: A satisfied way to describe a good, unhurried break

entries.nuance: 마음껏 means doing something fully and freely, to your heart's content, with no need to hold back — a generous, warm word that shines in hosting (마음껏 드세요) and in urging someone to enjoy or rest without restraint. It's 마음 ('heart/mind') + the native suffix -껏 ('to the very limit of'), the same -껏 you meet in 힘껏 (with all one's strength) and 정성껏 (with all one's care), so think of it as 'heart-to-the-max'. The contrast worth noting is with 실컷 (to one's fill / as much as one wants): the two overlap heavily, but 실컷 is more casual and often tied to satisfying an appetite or urge (실컷 자다 = sleep all you want), while 마음껏 sounds a touch warmer and more giving. The pitfall: it specifically means WITHOUT limits, so it clashes with any cap.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing it as two words 마음 껏; the suffix -껏 attaches directly to form one word, 마음껏.
Using 마음껏 where a limit applies — it means freely and without holding back, so it contradicts any restriction (e.g. 'pick one only').
Assuming 마음껏 and 실컷 are identical; they're close, but 실컷 is more casual and appetite-focused, while 마음껏 feels warmer and more generous.

entries.shortExplanation: 면 means "cotton (fabric)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Reads exactly like this on a Korean clothing tag; spoken as '면 백 퍼센트'.
순(純, pure) + 면; the label word on bedding, towels, and baby clothes.
면 + item is the normal way to say what a thing is made of — no 으로 needed.
소재 = material/fabric; staff lean on this word when describing what clothes are made from.

examples.en: Is this cotton?
examples.note: The shortest, most useful tag-check question; 이거 + 명사 + 이에요? identifies a material.

examples.en: In summer cotton material is nice because it's cool.
examples.note: 시원하다 pairs naturally with breathable fabric; -아서 here gives the reason you like it.

examples.ko: 면 100%라서 빨면 좀 줄어들 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: myeon 100%raseo ppalmyeon jom jureodeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: It's 100% cotton, so it may shrink a bit when you wash it.
examples.note: 줄어들다 (shrink) is the real warning shop staff give about cotton; -라서 links the cause.

entries.nuance: 면 is the Sino-Korean word for cotton fabric (한자 綿, 'cotton/silk-floss'), and it papers Korean clothing, bedding, and towel tags. Register is neutral; everyone from shop staff to friends just says 면. The big English-speaker pitfall is the homophones: 면 also means 'noodles' (麵) and 'side/aspect' (面), so only the shopping-vs-food context separates them. Another trap is over-marking the material — beginners say 면으로 만든 티셔츠, but natural Korean is simply 면 티셔츠, sticking the material straight onto the noun.

entries.shortExplanation: 가죽 means "leather" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가죽 (gajuk) means "leather". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 진짜 가죽 ("real / genuine leather"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가죽 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: What you ask for when you don't want fake; 진짜 = real, the everyday opposite of 가짜.
인조(人造, man-made) + 가죽; the formal label term, more precise than the casual 가짜 가죽.
소(cow) + 가죽; the most common leather for bags and shoes, named by animal.
가죽 + item is the standard pattern for naming a leather thing.

examples.en: Is this real leather?
examples.note: The single most useful market question; 진짜 in front flags that you doubt it's genuine.

examples.ko: 가죽 제품은 비 오는 날 조심해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gajuk jepumeun bi oneun nal josimhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: You have to be careful with leather products on rainy days.
examples.note: 조심하다 + -아야 하다 gives practical 'you must' care advice you'll actually hear.

examples.en: For real leather, the price is awfully cheap, isn't it?
examples.note: N치고 = 'for / considering a N'; -ㄴ데요 softly voices polite suspicion about a too-good deal.

entries.nuance: 가죽 is a native Korean word covering all animal leather, and shops split it into 진짜 가죽 (real) versus 인조가죽 or 합성피혁 (synthetic) on the tag. The synonym line that trips up English speakers is 피부 vs 가죽: both can translate as 'skin,' but 피부 is living human/animal skin and skincare, whereas 가죽 is the tanned material made from a hide — you have nice 피부, but you buy a 가죽 가방. entries.shortExplanation: 울 means "wool" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "wool" is 울 (ul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 울 100% ("100% wool"). Watch the particle attached to 울 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Reads on sweater and coat tags; pronounced '울 백 퍼센트'.
울 + item; the warm winter coat people line up to buy for Korean winters.
양(sheep, 羊) + 모(hair, 毛); the technical word printed on care labels, not used in chat.
니트 (knit) + 울 to pin down the material of the sweater.

examples.en: Is this coat wool?
examples.note: Basic material check; 명사 + 이에요? is your all-purpose 'is this made of ___?' question.

examples.en: Wool is warm, but you mustn't machine-/water-wash it.
examples.note: -지만 contrasts the upside with the catch; 물세탁하면 안 되다 = washing with water is not allowed.

examples.ko: 울 스웨터는 드라이클리닝 맡기는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: ul seuweteoneun deuraikeullining matgineun ge joayo.
examples.en: It's best to take wool sweaters to the dry cleaner.
examples.note: 맡기다 = to entrust/drop off; V-는 게 좋다 = 'it's best to' for recommended care.

entries.nuance: 울 is the loanword for wool (straight from English 'wool'), and it dominates Korean winter-clothing tags. Its register-twin is 양모 (羊毛, literally 'sheep-hair'): same material, but 양모 is the bookish label word on care tags while 울 is what anyone says out loud — call a sweater 양모 니트 in conversation and it sounds like you read it off a box. A second contrast worth knowing is 캐시미어 (cashmere), a pricier, softer goat fiber often blended with 울; a tag reading 울 70 캐시미어 30 is a blend, which is why asking 울 몇 퍼센트예요? signals you know quality. The classic English-speaker pitfall is spelling/sound: 울 (wool) versus 월 (month, as in 1월) — one vowel apart and totally different, so don't write 월 코트.

Writing 월 (month) for 울 (wool). They look and sound close but 월 is the calendar word (예: 12월), while the fabric is 울. A '월 코트' makes no sense.
Calling 양모 in everyday conversation. 양모 (羊毛) is the formal label term; spoken Korean uses 울. Save 양모 for reading care tags.
Machine-washing 울 because you skipped the label — real wool felts and shrinks, so it needs 드라이클리닝 or gentle hand washing, never a hot wash.

entries.shortExplanation: 실크 means "silk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 실크 (silkeu) = "silk". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 실크 스카프 ("silk scarf") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 실크, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 실크 + item; scarves are the most common silk buy, often as a gift.
On the tag of nicer blouses and scarves; spoken '실크 백 퍼센트'.
Native term you meet around 한복 (hanbok) and traditional craft goods.
같다 (to be like) turns it into a texture description rather than the actual material.

examples.en: Is this scarf silk?
examples.note: Quick material check; the most natural opener before you ask the price or feel it.

examples.en: Since it's silk, only hand-washing is possible.
examples.note: -라서 gives the reason; 손세탁만 가능하다 = the standard care limit for delicate silk.

examples.ko: 선물용으로 실크 스카프 하나 살까 해요.
examples.romanization: seonmuryongeuro silkeu seukapeu hana salkka haeyo.
examples.en: I'm thinking of buying a silk scarf as a gift.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ까 하다 = 'thinking of doing'; 선물용 = for-gift purpose, a useful shopping word.

entries.nuance: 실크 is the everyday loanword for silk and rules modern speech and department-store tags. Its synonym is the native 비단, but the line is register and setting, not meaning: 비단 carries a traditional, almost literary flavor and lives around 한복, 보자기, and craft fairs, so saying 비단 스카프 at a glossy mall sounds quaint even though staff understand it — there they expect 실크. The texture that sells it is 부드럽다 (soft) and a smooth 촉감 (feel/touch), and a near-miss word is 새틴/satin, a weave that can be silk or polyester, so 실크 같다 ('silk-like') is how you hedge when you're unsure it's the real fiber. The pitfall for English speakers is care: 'silk' feels washable in English, but real 실크 almost always needs 손세탁 (hand washing) or dry cleaning, never a machine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비단 in a modern department store. Staff get it, but 비단 (native, traditional) belongs with 한복 and crafts; for a mall blouse everyone says 실크.
Expecting to machine-wash 실크. Real silk needs 손세탁 or 드라이클리닝; tossing it in the washer ruins the fiber and the shine.
Confusing 실크 (the actual fiber) with 실크 같다 ('silky'). The 같다 form only describes texture — a 실크 같은 블라우스 may really be polyester.

entries.shortExplanation: 플라스틱 means "plastic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 플라스틱 (peullaseutik) means "plastic". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 플라스틱 용기 ("plastic container"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 플라스틱 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 용기 = container; the everyday word for tupperware-type food boxes.
플라스틱 + item to state what it is made of.
전자레인지 + 용(用, for-use); the spec to check before microwaving a container.
쓰레기 = trash; relevant because Korea's recycling sorting is strict.

examples.en: Is this plastic?
examples.note: Fast material check; 이거 + 명사 + 이에요? works for any 'what's this made of?' moment.

examples.en: Can I microwave this container?
examples.note: 돌리다 (to run/spin) is the casual verb for 'microwave it'; -아도 돼요? asks permission.

examples.ko: 저렴한 건 플라스틱이고 비싼 건 유리예요.
examples.romanization: jeoryeomhan geon peullaseutigigo bissan geon yuriyeyo.
examples.en: The cheap ones are plastic and the expensive ones are glass.
examples.note: -는 ... -고 ... contrasts two product tiers by price, a common in-store comparison.

entries.nuance: 플라스틱 is the all-purpose loanword for plastic, covering containers, chairs, and packaging — there is no everyday native synonym, so this borrowed word does all the work. Two contrasts matter when shopping: against 유리 (glass), where 플라스틱 is light and unbreakable but seen as less hygienic and not always microwave-safe; and against 비닐, which English lumps in as 'plastic' too but Korean keeps separate — 비닐 is thin film/sheeting (the 비닐봉지 plastic bag, plastic wrap), while 플라스틱 is rigid molded plastic (the box, the chair). Because Korea enforces 분리수거 (waste sorting) strictly, this word matters beyond the store. The English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation: it is not the two-beat English 'plastic' but a clean four-syllable 플·라·스·틱, and calling a 비닐봉지 a 플라스틱 봉지 will get a puzzled look.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a plastic bag a 플라스틱 봉지. Thin film bags and wrap are 비닐 (비닐봉지, 비닐); 플라스틱 is rigid molded plastic like a box or chair.
Microwaving any 플라스틱 without checking. Only 전자레인지용 (microwave-safe) plastic is rated for heat — ask 전자레인지에 돌려도 돼요? first.

entries.shortExplanation: 유리 means "glass (material)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "glass (material)" is 유리 (yuri). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 유리컵 ("glass cup"). Watch the particle attached to 유리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 컵 = cup; the standard drinking glass, written as one word.
Marketed as heat-safe and more hygienic than plastic ones.
강화(强化, strengthened) + 유리; what you buy as a phone screen protector or tough cookware.
(으)로 되다 = 'be made of'; a natural way to state material — 유리로 된 컵.

examples.en: Is this cup glass?
examples.note: Plain material check; 명사 + 이에요? is the all-purpose 'is this ___?' question.

examples.en: Since it's glass, I'm worried it might break.
examples.note: 깨지다 + V-(으)ㄹ까 봐 = worry that something might happen; -라서 supplies the reason.

examples.en: I'm planning to put a tempered glass on my phone.
examples.note: 붙이다 = to stick on; -(으)려고요 states your shopping intention politely.

entries.nuance: 유리 is glass as a material (Sino-Korean 琉璃, originally a word for colored glass/lapis), used for cups, containers, windows, and 강화유리 (tempered glass) screen protectors. The synonym confusions for English speakers are two: 거울 (mirror) is a separate word — a mirror is made from 유리 but you call it a 거울, not 유리; and 잔, which is the counter/word for a glass-as-a-serving (a 와인 잔, '한 잔 더' = one more glass to drink) rather than the substance. Common collocations are 유리컵, 유리병, 유리 용기, 강화유리, and 유리가 깨지다 (the glass breaks). Using 유리 for 'a glass' you drink from. The serving/counter word is 잔 (한 잔 더 주세요); 유리 is the raw material, 유리컵 is the physical cup.
Forgetting 유리 doubles as a girl's name. '유리가 예뻐요' could praise the glass or the person named Yuri — context decides.

entries.shortExplanation: 금속 means "metal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 금속 (geumsok) = "metal". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 금속 알레르기 ("metal allergy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 금속, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The single most practical phrase — say it before buying earrings, watches, or belts.
재질(材質) = material/composition; staff use it when describing what a product is made of.
프레임 (frame) for glasses, beds, or furniture.
(으)로 되다 = 'be made of'; 금속으로 된 부분 = the metal part.

examples.en: Is this metal?
examples.note: Quick material check; useful for jewelry where you may react to certain metals.

examples.ko: 저 금속 알레르기 있어서 다른 거 없어요?
examples.romanization: jeo geumsok allereugi isseoseo dareun geo eopseoyo?
examples.en: I have a metal allergy, so don't you have something else?
examples.note: 있어서 (-아서, 'because I have') chains the reason to a polite request for an alternative.

examples.ko: 금속 부분이 녹스니까 물기를 닦아 주세요.
examples.romanization: geumsok bubuni nokseunikka mulgireul dakka juseyo.
examples.en: The metal part rusts, so please wipe off the moisture.
examples.note: 녹슬다 = to rust; -니까 gives the reason for the -아 주세요 request to wipe it dry.

entries.nuance: 금속 is the general category word for metal (Sino-Korean 金屬, 金 'gold/metal' + 屬 'belong to,' i.e. 'things in the metal family'). It is the umbrella; for a specific metal Koreans name it directly — 금 (gold, 金), 은 (silver, 銀), 철 (iron/steel, 鐵), 스테인리스 (stainless), 알루미늄 (aluminum) — so the key contrast to internalize is 금속 ≠ 금: 금속 is metal-in-general, while 금 is specifically gold (and a single character of the very same compound). The most useful real-life collocation is 금속 알레르기 (metal allergy), exactly what you say when earrings or a watch make your skin react. Other natural partners: 금속 재질, 금속 프레임, 금속이 녹슬다 (metal rusts). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 금 ('metal' sounds gold-ish) when you mean any metal, or using 철 (iron specifically) as if it meant metal generally.

Saying 금 when you mean metal in general. 금 is gold specifically; the category is 금속. '금 알레르기' would mean a gold allergy, not a general metal allergy.
Using 철 (iron/steel) as a catch-all for metal. 철 is one specific metal; if you don't know which one, say 금속.
Treating 금속 like a brand of metal. It is just the category — to specify, name it: 스테인리스, 알루미늄, 은, etc.

entries.shortExplanation: 고무 means "rubber" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고무 (gomu) means "rubber". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고무장갑 ("rubber gloves"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고무 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 고무 + 장갑; the dishwashing/cleaning gloves in every Korean kitchen.
고무 + 줄(string); also the stretchy elastic in a waistband.
밑창 = sole of a shoe; non-slip rubber soles are a selling point.
재질 = material; how staff describe what something is made of.

examples.ko: 설거지할 때 고무장갑 끼는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: seolgeojihal ttae gomujanggap kkineun ge joayo.
examples.en: It's good to wear rubber gloves when washing dishes.
examples.note: 끼다 = to put on (gloves); V-는 게 좋다 = 'it's good to,' the most common use of 고무.

examples.ko: 이 신발 밑창이 고무라서 안 미끄러워요.
examples.romanization: i sinbal mitchangi gomuraseo an mikkeureowoyo.
examples.en: This shoe's sole is rubber, so it isn't slippery.
examples.note: 미끄럽다 = slippery; -라서 ties the rubber sole to the non-slip result.

examples.en: The waist of these pants is elastic, so it's really comfy.
examples.note: 고무줄 here = the waistband elastic; -(이)라 gives the casual reason, 편하다 = comfortable.

entries.nuance: 고무 means rubber and feels fully native even though it entered Korean as a loanword (via Dutch/Japanese 'gom'). It shows up most in 고무장갑 (rubber gloves), an absolute staple you'll grab at any 마트 or 다이소, and in 고무줄, which usefully covers both a 'rubber band' and the stretchy 'elastic' in clothing waistbands — context decides which. The synonym/pitfall to watch is footwear: rubber rain boots are 장화, not 고무 신발, even though they're literally rubber, because Korean names them by function, not material. Likewise the bouncy 'rubber' of a tire is just 타이어, and a rubber eraser is 지우개 — you rarely say 고무 for these finished objects. Natural collocations: 고무장갑 끼다, 고무 밑창, 고무줄로 묶다 (tie with a rubber band), 고무가 늘어나다 (the rubber stretches).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling rain boots 고무 신발. Rubber rain boots are 장화 — Korean names them by use, not by the rubber they're made of.
Forgetting 고무줄 has two senses. It is both a 'rubber band' (고무줄로 묶다) and clothing 'elastic' (고무줄 바지); only context tells them apart.
Using 고무 for an eraser. A pencil eraser is 지우개, not 고무, even though older Korean and Japanese link the two.

entries.shortExplanation: 도자기 means "ceramic / pottery" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ceramic / pottery" is 도자기 (dojagi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도자기 그릇 ("ceramic dish/bowl"). Watch the particle attached to 도자기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 그릇 = bowl/dish; the typical ceramic tableware.
컵 + 도자기 to pin down the material.
전통(傳統) = traditional; sold as Korean craft and souvenir pieces.
제품 = product; a category sign you'll see at homeware shops.

examples.en: Is this dish ceramic?
examples.note: Quick material check; matters because it affects price, weight, and microwave-safety.

examples.en: Ceramic breaks right away if you drop it.
examples.note: 떨어뜨리다 = to drop; -면 ... 바로 = 'as soon as / right away,' the fragility warning.

examples.ko: 인사동에서 예쁜 도자기 컵을 하나 샀어요.
examples.romanization: insadongeseo yeppeun dojagi keobeul hana sasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought a pretty ceramic cup in Insadong.
examples.note: Insadong is the go-to spot for traditional 도자기; 하나 = 'one (of them)' counts the item.

entries.nuance: 도자기 is the word for ceramics/pottery, a Sino-Korean compound (陶瓷器: 陶 'earthenware' + 瓷 'porcelain' + 器 'vessel') that literally bundles the two fired-clay families into 'fired-clay ware.' It runs from everyday dishes to prized craft pieces sold in places like Insadong, often labeled 전통 도자기. The synonym map is worth knowing: 도자기 is the umbrella, while 도기 (陶器) is coarser earthenware and 자기 (瓷器) is fine porcelain/china; for traditional Korean wares you'll also hear 백자 (white porcelain) and 청자 (celadon) as named subtypes. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: don't confuse glossy 도자기 with 유리 (glass) just because both shine — they're different materials and break differently; and don't microwave 도자기 that has gold or silver trim, because the metallic paint can spark. Common collocations: 도자기 그릇, 도자기 컵, 도자기가 깨지다, 도자기를 굽다 (to fire pottery).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 도자기 (ceramic/pottery) with 유리 (glass). Both can look glossy, but they're different materials — tap them and ceramic is dull, glass rings.
Microwaving 도자기 with gold or silver trim. The metallic decoration can spark; only plain, untrimmed ceramic is reliably microwave-safe.
Treating 도자기 as fragile-proof because it's solid. It chips and shatters easily when dropped — 떨어뜨리면 바로 깨져요.

entries.shortExplanation: 스테인리스 means "stainless steel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스테인리스 (seuteilliseu) = "stainless steel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 스테인리스 텀블러 ("stainless steel tumbler") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 스테인리스, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 텀블러 = tumbler; the insulated bottle everyone carries.
냄비 = pot; a common upgrade from coated pans because nothing peels.
Very common spoken contraction of 스테인리스 — you'll hear it shouted at markets.
식기(食器) = tableware; the metal bowls and spoons used in many homes.

examples.en: Is this tumbler stainless?
examples.note: Material check; matters for heat retention and whether it'll rust.

examples.en: Since it's stainless, it keeps heat well.
examples.note: 보온(保溫) = heat retention; -라서 links the material to its main selling point.

examples.en: Ma'am, is this stainless?
examples.note: 스뎅 is the natural spoken form you'd actually use at a market stall; 아주머니 addresses the vendor.

entries.nuance: 스테인리스 is the loanword for stainless steel, everywhere in Korean kitchens — 텀블러, 냄비, bowls, spoons. Two register notes are essential. First, the full English 'stainless steel' gets trimmed: Korean drops 스틸 and says just 스테인리스, and in casual market speech it contracts even further to 스뎅, so recognizing 스뎅 is genuinely useful when an 아주머니 uses it. Second, the synonym/pitfall is other shiny metals: not every gleaming pan is 스테인리스 — much lighter cookware is 알루미늄 (aluminum), and coated nonstick pans look metallic but their coating (코팅) peels, which is the very durability argument that sells 스테인리스. Natural collocations: 스테인리스 냄비/텀블러/식기, 보온이 잘 되다, 코팅이 안 벗겨지다 (the coating doesn't peel), 녹이 안 슬다 (it doesn't rust). The pitfall for English speakers is over-spelling it as 스테인리스 스틸 and not recognizing the slang 스뎅.

Writing the full 스테인리스 스틸. Korean drops 스틸 — it's just 스테인리스, or 스뎅 in casual speech.
Assuming every shiny pan is 스테인리스. Lighter ones are 알루미늄 (aluminum), and metallic-looking nonstick pans are coated (코팅) — heft and the label tell them apart.
Not recognizing 스뎅. At markets a vendor will say 스뎅이에요, the colloquial clip of 스테인리스 — it means the same thing.

entries.shortExplanation: 천 means "fabric / cloth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 천 (cheon) means "fabric / cloth". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 천 가방 ("cloth / tote bag"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 천 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The fabric tote you use instead of plastic; very common in Korea.
소파 = sofa; the in-store either/or against a 가죽 (leather) sofa.
(으)로 되다 = 'be made of'; 천으로 된 가방 = a fabric bag.
부드럽다 = soft; describing texture while you shop.

examples.en: Is this sofa fabric or leather?
examples.note: A standard either/or question when furniture shopping; 천 vs 가죽 is the core split.

examples.ko: 천 가방은 가벼워서 장 볼 때 좋아요.
examples.romanization: cheon gabangeun gabyeowoseo jang bol ttae joayo.
examples.en: A cloth bag is light, so it's good for grocery shopping.
examples.note: 장(을) 보다 = to do grocery shopping; -아서 gives the reason it's handy.

examples.ko: 천이 얇아서 비치는데 다른 색 없어요?
examples.romanization: cheoni yalbaseo bichineunde dareun saek eopseoyo?
examples.en: The fabric is thin and see-through; don't you have another color?
examples.note: 얇다 = thin; 비치다 = to show through, a real clothing complaint, -는데 softens the request.

entries.nuance: 천 is the native general word for cloth/fabric — any soft woven textile, as opposed to 가죽 (leather), 플라스틱, or 금속. It's the everyday way to ask what something is made of: 천이에요, 가죽이에요? The synonym layer to sort out: 천 is the broadest term, 옷감 specifically means dressmaking fabric/'material for clothes,' and 원단 is the trade/industry word for bolt fabric you'd hear at a fabric market like Dongdaemun — so 천 is what you say in normal life, 원단 is shoptalk. Crucially, 천 is the umbrella, while 면 (cotton), 울 (wool), and 실크 (silk) are specific kinds of 천, so don't say 천 when you actually mean cotton. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the homophone: 천 is also the number 1,000 (千), spelled and pronounced identically — '천 원' is a thousand won, '천으로 된 가방' is a cloth bag, and only context separates them. Collocations: 천 가방, 천 소파, 천이 얇다/두껍다, 천을 자르다 (cut fabric).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 천 (cloth) with 천 (1,000). Same sound and spelling; '천 원' = a thousand won, '천 가방' = a cloth bag — context is your only guide.
Saying 천 when you specifically mean cotton. Cotton is 면; 천 is fabric in general, and 면/울/실크 are particular kinds of 천.
Using 원단 in casual talk. 원단 is the trade word for bolt fabric at a fabric market; in everyday speech just say 천.

entries.shortExplanation: 합성섬유 means "synthetic fiber" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "synthetic fiber" is 합성섬유 (hapseongseomyu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 합성섬유 100% ("100% synthetic fiber"). Watch the particle attached to 합성섬유 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: On the tags of cheaper clothing and sportswear; spoken '합성섬유 백 퍼센트'.
The most common specific 합성섬유 actually named on labels.
천연(天然) = natural; the opposite category — cotton, wool, silk.
소재 = material; how the fabric type is described on a spec line.

examples.en: Is this garment synthetic fiber?
examples.note: Material check; tells you how it'll wash, breathe, and wrinkle.

examples.en: Since it's synthetic, it doesn't wrinkle easily.
examples.note: 구겨지다 = to get wrinkled; -라서 ties wrinkle-resistance to the synthetic material.

examples.en: Do you prefer natural fibers or synthetic ones?
examples.note: The basic fabric either/or when shopping; parallel A가 좋아요, B가 좋아요? offers a choice.

entries.nuance: 합성섬유 is the umbrella term for man-made fabrics — a Sino-Korean compound (合成纖維: 合成 'synthesized/combined' + 纖維 'fiber'), literally 'synthesized fiber.' On labels its named members are things like 폴리에스터 (polyester), 나일론 (nylon), and 아크릴 (acrylic), so 폴리에스터 is a specific kind of 합성섬유, not a different category. The sharp contrast to lock in is 합성섬유 ↔ 천연섬유 (天然纖維, 'natural fiber'): they sit on opposite sides of the care label, with 면/울/실크 in the 천연 column. The practical trade-off — and the reason this word is worth knowing in humid Korea — is that 합성섬유 resists wrinkles and dries fast but breathes poorly, so summer wear in it can feel sticky while sportswear uses it on purpose for stretch and quick-dry. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 합성섬유 as automatically 'bad/cheap'; it's a neutral category, and registering it as the opposite of 천연섬유 (rather than as an insult) keeps your tag-reading accurate.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 합성섬유 (synthetic) and 천연섬유 (natural). They're opposite columns on the care label — 면/울/실크 are 천연섬유, polyester/nylon are 합성섬유.
Thinking 폴리에스터 is separate from 합성섬유. Polyester is a kind of 합성섬유; the tag may name the specific fiber instead of the category.
Assuming 합성섬유 is always bad. It's neutral — sportswear is deliberately synthetic for stretch and quick-dry; the downside is mainly breathability in heat.

entries.shortExplanation: 사물함 means "locker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사물함 (samulham) = "locker". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사물함 비밀번호 ("locker combination/PIN") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사물함, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 비밀번호(秘密番號) = secret number; 다이얼식이면 '자물쇠 번호'라고도 함
조사 -에 = the destination you put something INTO, not -에서
안 열리다 = won't open (자동사 부정); 고장 났을 때 단골 표현
정리(整理) = sorting/clearing; 학기 말에 꼭 하는 일

examples.en: Where are the lockers?
examples.note: 위치를 묻는 가장 기본 문장; 장소 명사 + 이/가 어디예요?

examples.en: Textbooks are heavy, so I keep them in my locker.
examples.note: 두고 다니다 = leave it (there) and go about — 두다 'place' + -고 다니다 'habitually'

examples.ko: 사물함 번호가 기억이 안 나서 한참 헤맸어요.
examples.romanization: samulham beonhoga gieogi an naseo hancham hemaesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't recall my locker number, so I fumbled for a while.
examples.note: 기억이 안 나다 = (a memory) doesn't come — 나다는 저절로 떠오를 때, '안 기억하다'는 비문

entries.nuance: 사물함은 한자 私物函(사물·함)으로 '개인 물건을 넣는 상자', 즉 학교·헬스장·수영장·지하철역에 있는 개인 보관함을 두루 가리킵니다. 영어 locker를 옮긴 외래어 '라커/락커'는 헬스장·스키장에선 들리지만 학교 맥락에서는 거의 안 쓰고 사물함이 표준이에요. 비슷한 말로 '보관함'은 짐을 잠시 맡기는 코인 라커(물품보관함) 느낌이 강하고, 사물함은 한 사람이 학기 내내 전용으로 쓰는 칸이라는 점이 갈림선입니다. 자주 어울리는 말은 '사물함에 넣다/두다, 사물함을 열다, 사물함 비밀번호, 사물함 정리'. 영어식 함정은 두 가지인데, locker를 '연다'고 할 때 전원 켜는 켜다를 쓰면 안 되고(자물쇠는 열다/잠그다), 또 '사물함에서 넣다'처럼 -에서를 쓰면 틀립니다 — 넣는 방향은 -에, 꺼내는 출발점만 -에서예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'사물함을 켜다'는 틀려요. 켜다는 전등·전원을 켤 때만 쓰고, 잠금장치는 '열다/잠그다'를 씁니다.
'사물함에서 책을 넣었어요'는 조사 오류예요. 넣는 방향은 도착점 -에(사물함에 넣다)이고, -에서는 꺼낼 때(사물함에서 꺼내다) 씁니다.
학교에서 'locker'를 그대로 '락커'라고만 하면 어색합니다. 록 음악 하는 사람(rocker)과도 헷갈리니 학교에선 사물함이라고 하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 교무실 means "teachers' office, faculty room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교무실 (gyomusil) means "teachers' office, faculty room". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교무실에 가다 ("go to the teachers' office"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교무실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 선생님을 찾아갈 때; 도착지 -에

usagePhrases.en: please come to the teachers' office
usagePhrases.note: -로 = direction the listener should head toward

usagePhrases.en: wait in front of the faculty room
usagePhrases.note: 위치 명사 + 앞에서; 자주 만나는 장소 표현

usagePhrases.en: get called (in) to the teachers' office
usagePhrases.note: 불려가다 = be summoned (피동); 혼나는 뉘앙스

examples.en: Which floor is the faculty room on?
examples.note: 층 = floor counter; 길 찾을 때 기본 문장

examples.en: I went to the teachers' office during break and asked a question.
examples.note: 쉬는 시간 = the break between classes (쉬다 'rest' + -는 + 시간)

examples.ko: 담임 선생님이 교무실에 안 계셔서 메모를 남겼어요.
examples.romanization: damim seonsaengnimi gyomusire an gyesyeoseo memoreul namgyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My homeroom teacher wasn't in the faculty room, so I left a note.
examples.note: 계시다 = honorific 있다 — 선생님이 주어라 반드시 높임

entries.nuance: 교무실은 한자 敎務室(교무·실), 글자 그대로 '가르치는 업무(敎務)를 보는 방'으로, 선생님들이 함께 쓰는 사무 공간이에요. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃 단어가 '사무실'인데, 사무실(事務室)은 일반 회사·관공서의 업무 공간을 뜻하고 학교 선생님들의 방은 콕 집어 교무실이라 부릅니다(학교 행정·돈 처리는 따로 '행정실'). 학생에게는 칭찬보다 지적받으러 가는 약간 긴장되는 장소라 '교무실에 불려가다, 교무실로 따라와'처럼 혼나는 상황과 자주 묶입니다. 자연스러운 짝은 '교무실에 가다/들르다, 교무실 앞, 교무실로 오세요'. 영어식 함정은 office를 무조건 '사무실'로 직역하는 것 — teachers' office는 교무실이라야 자연스럽고, 또 그 안의 선생님은 주체 높임이라 '있어요'가 아니라 '계세요'를 써야 합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'사무실'과 혼동하지 마세요. 학교 선생님들의 방은 교무실, 일반 회사·관공서의 방은 사무실입니다.
선생님이 주어일 땐 높임을 쓰세요. '선생님이 교무실에 있어요'는 어색하고 '계세요'가 맞습니다.
학교의 돈·서류 처리하는 곳까지 교무실이라 하면 부정확해요. 그쪽은 보통 '행정실'이라고 부릅니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 담임 means "homeroom teacher" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "homeroom teacher" is 담임 (damim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 담임 선생님 ("homeroom teacher"). Watch the particle attached to 담임 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 부를 때는 반드시 뒤에 '선생님'을 붙임
친구끼리 3인칭으로 가리킬 때 줄여 부름

usagePhrases.en: take charge of a homeroom class
usagePhrases.note: 맡다 = take on (a duty); 선생님 입장의 표현

usagePhrases.en: a meeting with the homeroom teacher
usagePhrases.note: 면담(面談) = face-to-face talk; 상담 신청할 때

examples.en: Who is our homeroom teacher?
examples.note: 사람을 묻는 기본 문장; 담임 뒤에 선생님을 붙인 정중형

examples.ko: 우리 담임 선생님은 진짜 잘 챙겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: uri damim seonsaengnimeun jinjja jal chaenggyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Our homeroom teacher really looks out for us.
examples.note: 챙겨 주다 = look after — 챙기다 'see to' + -아 주다 '(do) for someone'

examples.en: I requested a career counseling session with my homeroom teacher.
examples.note: 께 = honorific of -에게 (to a respected person)

entries.nuance: 담임은 한자 擔任(담·임), '맡아서(擔) 책임진다(任)'는 뜻으로, 한 반을 1년간 전담해 출결·생활지도·상담까지 책임지는 선생님이에요. 영어엔 딱 떨어지는 말이 없어 homeroom teacher로 옮기지만, 한국의 담임은 단순히 조회시간만 맡는 게 아니라 학생 생활 전반을 챙긴다는 점이 더 강합니다. 비슷해 보이는 '교과 선생님(과목만 가르치는 분)'과 달리 담임은 '우리 반을 책임지는 한 분'이라는 게 갈림선이고, 회사의 '팀장'에 비유되기도 하지만 그 말과 섞어 쓰진 않아요. 핵심 주의점: 담임은 직책 이름이자 사람을 가리키므로 친구끼리 '우리 담임 바뀌었어'처럼 3인칭으로는 줄여 써도, 선생님을 직접 부르거나 그분 앞에서는 반드시 '담임 선생님'이라고 해야 예의에 맞습니다. '담임!'이라고만 부르면 무례하게 들려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
선생님을 직접 부를 때 '담임!'이라고만 하면 무례합니다. 호칭은 꼭 '담임 선생님'이라고 하세요.
담임은 사람·직책을 가리키므로 '담임 수업, 담임 과목'처럼 과목 뜻으로 쓰면 안 됩니다. 그건 '교과/과목 선생님'입니다.
'우리 담임 선생님이 가르쳐요'에서 선생님이 주어면 높임을 챙기세요 — '가르쳐 주세요/가르치세요'가 자연스럽습니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 반장 means "class president, class leader" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반장 (banjang) = "class president, class leader". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 반장 선거 ("class president election") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 반장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 선거(選擧) = election; 학기 초에 반에서 뽑음
뽑다 = pick/elect (by vote)
되다 takes -이/가 for the resulting role
부-(副) = vice/deputy; 반장을 돕는 자리

examples.en: Are you the class president?
examples.note: 이다 의문형; 가장 단순한 확인 문장

examples.en: Minsu became class president this semester.
examples.note: 되다 앞 주어는 -이/가(민수가 되다), 결과 신분은 보어

examples.en: Since I'm the class president, the responsibility feels heavy.
examples.note: -라서 = because (이다 + -아서, 명사 뒤 이유)

entries.nuance: 반장은 한자 班長(반·장), '반(班)의 우두머리(長)'로, 반을 대표하고 선생님과 학생 사이를 잇는 학생 리더예요(보좌역은 부반장, 副班長). 끝 글자 -長은 회장(會長)·팀장·반장처럼 '~의 장(長), 우두머리'를 만드는 한자라, 회사의 팀장이나 군대의 분대장과 같은 계열이지만 학급 대표는 학교 맥락의 반장으로 못박아 씁니다. 비슷한 '회장(會長)'은 전교를 대표하는 전교회장처럼 더 큰 조직을 이끌 때 쓰니 한 반의 대표는 반장이 맞아요. 보통 학기 초 투표(반장 선거)로 뽑고 책임감 있는 역할로 여겨집니다. 영어식 함정은 조사 생략 — '반장 되다'처럼 -이를 빼면 어색하고 '반장이 되다'라야 하며, become을 옮길 때 결과 신분에 -이/가가 붙는 한국어 특유의 구조('의사가 되다, 반장이 되다')를 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'반장 되다'처럼 조사를 빼면 어색합니다. 결과 신분에는 -이/가를 붙여 '반장이 되다'라고 하세요.
회사 직책 '팀장'이나 군대 '분대장'과 섞어 쓰지 마세요. 학급 대표는 학교 맥락의 반장입니다.
한 반의 대표를 '회장'이라 하면 과해요. 회장은 전교회장처럼 더 큰 조직의 대표에게 씁니다.

structuredNuance.t: 한자 班長(반·장), '반(班)의 우두머리(長)'로, 반을 대표하고 선생님과 학생 사이를 잇는 학생 리더예요(보좌역은 부반장, 副班長). 보통 학기 초 투표(반장 선거)로 뽑고 책임감 있는 역할로 여겨집니다.

영어식 함정은 조사 생략 — '반장 되다'처럼 -이를 빼면 어색하고 '반장이 되다'라야 하며, become을 옮길 때 결과 신분에 -이/가가 붙는 한국어 특유의 구조('의사가 되다, 반장이 되다')를 기억하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 조퇴 means "leaving school (or work) early" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조퇴 (jotoe) means "leaving school (or work) early". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조퇴하다 ("leave early (before the day ends)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조퇴 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 명사 + 하다 동사화
신청(申請) = application; 담임·보건실에 함
가장 흔한 사유; -아서 = reason

usagePhrases.en: logging it as an early dismissal
usagePhrases.note: 처리(處理) = handling; 출결에 기록될 때

examples.en: I'm leaving early today.
examples.note: 가장 짧은 통보형; 명사 + 하다 현재형

examples.en: I had a fever, so I left early during third period.
examples.note: 교시(校時) = the period counter (1교시, 2교시…)

examples.ko: 조퇴하려면 담임 선생님 허락을 받아야 해요.
examples.romanization: jotoeharyeomyeon damim seonsaengnim heorageul badaya haeyo.
examples.en: To leave early, you need the homeroom teacher's permission.
examples.note: -(으)려면 = if you intend to (do); 의도+조건

entries.nuance: 조퇴는 한자 早退(조·퇴), '이를 조(早) + 물러날 퇴(退)' = 정해진 시간보다 일찍 자리를 뜨는 것으로, 학교든 회사든 다 씁니다. 단순한 '일찍 가다/먼저 가다'와의 결정적 차이는, 조퇴는 정당한 사유(아픔·일정)와 허락이 있어야 하고 출결에 기록되는 공식 행위라는 점이에요 — 그래서 결석·지각·조퇴가 한 묶음으로 다닙니다. 반대 방향(늦게 옴)은 지각(遲刻)이고, 아예 안 옴은 결석(缺席)이니 세트로 외우면 좋아요. 자연스러운 짝은 '조퇴하다, 조퇴(를) 신청하다, 조퇴 처리, 몸이 안 좋아서 조퇴'. 영어식 함정 둘: leave early를 직역해 '조퇴를 가다'라고 하면 비문이라 '조퇴하다/조퇴 신청을 하다'로 써야 하고, 친구랑 그냥 일찍 놀러 나갈 땐 조퇴가 아니라 '먼저 갈게/일찍 나갈게'라고 합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'조퇴를 가다'는 틀려요. 동사화는 '조퇴하다', 절차를 말하면 '조퇴 신청을 하다'입니다.
그냥 '일찍 가다'와 다릅니다. 조퇴는 허락·기록이 따르는 공식 표현이라, 친구와 일찍 놀러 갈 땐 안 씁니다.
늦게 오는 것까지 조퇴라 하면 틀려요. 늦게 오는 건 '지각', 안 오는 건 '결석'으로 구분하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 결석 means "absence (from school)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "absence (from school)" is 결석 (gyeolseok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 결석하다 ("be absent"). Watch the particle attached to 결석 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 명사 + 하다; 주어가 빠지는 행위
무단(無斷) = without permission; 허락 없이 빠짐
병결(病缺) = 병으로 인한 결석의 줄임말
사유(事由) = grounds/reason; 출결 처리 때 묻는 말

examples.en: One person is absent today.
examples.note: 명 = counter for people; 출석 확인 기본 문장

examples.en: My cold was bad, so I was absent yesterday.
examples.note: 심하다 = be severe; -아서로 이유 연결

examples.ko: 개근상을 받으려면 결석이 한 번도 없어야 해요.
examples.romanization: gaegeunsangeul badeuryeomyeon gyeolseogi han beondo eopseoya haeyo.
examples.en: To get the perfect-attendance award, you must have zero absences.
examples.note: 개근상(皆勤賞) = the award for never missing a day

entries.nuance: 결석은 한자 缺席(결·석), '빌 결(缺) + 자리 석(席)' = '자리가 비다', 즉 수업에 나오지 않는 것으로 출석(出席)의 정반대예요. 같은 缺을 회사에 쓰면 결근(缺勤)이 되는데, 이게 가장 중요한 갈림선입니다 — 결석은 학교 수업, 결근은 직장 근무에 빠질 때라 섞으면 안 돼요. 사유에 따라 병결(아파서)·무단결석(허락 없이)으로 나뉘고, 특히 무단결석은 부정적으로 여겨져 생활기록부나 성적에 영향을 줄 수 있는 무거운 말입니다. 같은 출결 식구로 지각(늦게 옴)·조퇴(일찍 감)가 함께 다녀요. 영어식 함정: be absent를 옮길 때 '결석을 가다/결석을 하러 가다'처럼 쓰면 비문이고 '결석하다'가 맞으며, 직장에 안 나간 걸 결석이라 하면 어색하니 그땐 결근을 쓰세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'결석을 가다'는 틀려요. '결석하다'로 동사화하거나 '결석을 하다'로 씁니다.
직장에 안 나가는 것을 결석이라 하면 어색합니다. 회사 결근, 학교 결석으로 구분하세요.
무단결석을 가벼운 말로 여기지 마세요. 생활기록부에 남는 부정적 표현이라 단순 '안 갔다'와 무게가 다릅니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 소풍 means "school outing, picnic, field trip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 소풍 (sopung) = "school outing, picnic, field trip". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 소풍을 가다 ("go on an outing") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 소풍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 '하다'가 아니라 '가다'와 어울림
기다려지는 날; 날 = day
보통 봄·가을에 감

usagePhrases.en: the packed lunch for the outing
usagePhrases.note: 도시락 = boxed lunch; 소풍의 핵심

examples.en: We're going on an outing tomorrow.
examples.note: 가장 단순한 예고; 소풍 + 가다

examples.en: We went on the outing and ate gimbap with friends.
examples.note: -이랑 = casual 와/과 (and/with), 받침 뒤

examples.en: The outing got postponed to next week due to rain.
examples.note: 미뤄지다 = get postponed (미루다의 피동); 우천(雨天)=rainy weather

entries.nuance: 소풍은 학생들이 학교 밖 공원·산으로 나가 도시락을 먹고 노는 가벼운 하루 나들이로, 한자는 보통 逍風/消風(거닐며 바람을 쐬다)로 풀이됩니다(다만 일상에선 한자 없이 순우리말처럼 씁니다). 같은 학교 행사라도 갈림선이 분명한데, 박물관·유적지처럼 학습 목적이 강하면 '현장학습', 며칠 묵으며 멀리 가면 '수학여행', 그냥 즐겁게 노는 당일치기가 소풍이에요. 일반 어른의 주말 나들이는 소풍 대신 '나들이/피크닉'을 더 쓰고, 소풍은 학창 시절의 설레는 행사라는 색이 짙습니다. 자연스러운 짝은 '소풍을 가다, 소풍 날, 소풍 도시락, 봄/가을 소풍'. 영어식 함정 둘: picnic이 동사로 쓰인다고 '소풍하다'라고 하면 어색하고 반드시 '소풍(을) 가다'이며, day trip이라도 며칠짜리 여행을 소풍이라 부르면 안 됩니다 — 그건 수학여행이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'소풍하다'는 어색해요. 동사는 '소풍(을) 가다/다녀오다'와 어울립니다.
여러 날 멀리 가는 여행은 소풍이 아니라 '수학여행'입니다. 소풍은 보통 하루짜리예요.
교육 목적이 뚜렷한 견학은 '현장학습'이라 부르는 게 더 정확합니다. 노는 데 초점이면 소풍입니다.

한자는 보통 逍風/消風(거닐며 바람을 쐬다)로 풀이됩니다(다만 일상에선 한자 없이 순우리말처럼 씁니다).
영어식 함정 둘: picnic이 동사로 쓰인다고 '소풍하다'라고 하면 어색하고 반드시 '소풍(을) 가다'이며, day trip이라도 며칠짜리 여행을 소풍이라 부르면 안 됩니다 — 그건 수학여행이에요.

entries.english: deskmate, the person you sit next to
entries.shortExplanation: 짝꿍 means "deskmate, the person you sit next to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 짝꿍 (jjakkkung) means "deskmate, the person you sit next to". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 짝꿍이 되다 ("become deskmates"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 짝꿍 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 자리 배치로 결정; 되다 + -이/가
자리를 바꿨을 때
떠들다 = make noise/chatter; 수업 중 흔한 일
자리 바꾸기(자리 배치 변경)

examples.en: Who's your deskmate?
examples.note: 반말 의문; 친구끼리 쓰는 가장 흔한 문장

examples.en: My deskmate lent me an eraser.
examples.note: 빌려주다 = lend (빌리다 'borrow'와 방향 반대!)

examples.en: I went to eat the school lunch with my deskmate.
examples.note: -(으)러 가다 = go in order to (do); 급식 = school-provided meal

entries.nuance: 짝꿍은 한자어가 아니라 순우리말로, '짝(둘이 한 쌍을 이룸)'에 친근한 접미사 '-꿍'이 붙어 만들어진 다정한 애칭이에요 — 교실에서 같은 책상에 나란히 앉는 옆자리 친구를 부르는 말입니다. 중립적인 '짝'이나 설명조의 '옆자리 친구'와의 차이는 온도예요. 짝꿍은 어린 학생들이 특히 즐겨 쓰는 귀엽고 친밀한 말이라, 어른들 사이에선 아주 가까운 단짝이나 부부를 장난스럽게 '내 짝꿍'이라 부르기도 합니다. 자연스러운 짝은 '짝꿍이 되다, 새 짝꿍, 짝꿍이랑 ~하다, 짝꿍을 바꾸다'. 영어식 함정: deskmate를 격식 있는 글이나 공식 문서에 그대로 짝꿍으로 옮기면 너무 구어적이라 어색하니 그땐 '옆자리 친구/같은 분단 학생'이라 하고, 또 혼자 앉는 1인 책상에는 짝꿍이 없습니다 — 둘이 나란히 앉을 때만 성립하는 말이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
짝꿍은 구어체 애칭이라 공식 문서·보고서엔 어울리지 않아요. 격식 있는 상황에선 '옆자리 친구'라고 하세요.
혼자 앉는 자리엔 짝꿍이 없습니다. 두 명이 나란히 앉을 때 성립하는 말이에요.
'짝꿍이 빌렸어요'로 lent를 말하면 방향이 반대예요. 남이 내게 빌려준 것이면 '빌려줬어요(빌려주다)'입니다.

중립적인 '짝'이나 설명조의 '옆자리 친구'와의 차이는 온도예요. 짝꿍은 더 귀엽고 친밀한 색을 띱니다.
deskmate를 격식 있는 글이나 공식 문서에 그대로 짝꿍으로 옮기면 너무 구어적이라 어색하니 그땐 '옆자리 친구/같은 분단 학생'이라 하고, 또 혼자 앉는 1인 책상에는 짝꿍이 없습니다 — 둘이 나란히 앉을 때만 성립하는 말이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 받아쓰기 means "dictation, spelling test" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "dictation, spelling test" is 받아쓰기 (badasseugi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 받아쓰기 시험 ("dictation test"). Watch the particle attached to 받아쓰기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 시험(試驗) = test; 초등 저학년에서 자주 봄
명사화된 동작 + 하다
점(點) = point/mark; 만점을 받았을 때
연습(練習) = practice; 집에서 미리 함

examples.en: Is there a dictation today?
examples.note: 있다 의문; 일정 확인하는 기본 문장

examples.en: I got two wrong on yesterday's dictation.
examples.note: 틀리다 = get (it) wrong (맞다 'be correct'의 반대)

examples.ko: 선생님이 천천히 불러 주셔서 다 받아썼어요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi cheoncheonhi bulleo jusyeoseo da badasseosseoyo.
examples.en: The teacher read it out slowly, so I wrote it all down.
examples.note: 불러 주다 = read aloud for someone (부르다 + -아 주다)

entries.nuance: 받아쓰기는 순우리말 합성어로, '받아(받다 '받아 적다'의 받아)' + '쓰기(쓰다의 명사형)' = 선생님이 불러 주는 말을 귀로 받아 정확한 맞춤법으로 적는 연습이자 시험이에요. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃이 '필기'와 '베끼기'인데, 받아쓰기는 칠판을 안 보고 '듣고' 적는 것이고, 칠판·교재를 보고 옮겨 적으면 그건 필기(筆記)나 베끼기라 갈림선이 분명합니다(영어로도 dictation은 '듣고 쓰기'). 주로 초등학교 저학년에서 한글 맞춤법을 익히려고 하지만, 외국어 학습에서도 듣기·철자 훈련으로 흔히 활용돼요. 자연스러운 짝은 '받아쓰기 시험, 받아쓰기를 하다, 받아쓰기 100점, 받아쓰기 연습'. 영어식 함정: 동사로 쓸 땐 한 단어 '받아쓰다(받아써요/받아썼어요)'를 쓰고, '받아쓰기하다'보다 '받아쓰기를 하다'가 더 자연스럽다는 점을 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
받아쓰기는 '듣고 적는' 것이에요. 칠판이나 책을 보고 옮겨 적는 건 받아쓰기가 아니라 '필기/베끼기'입니다.
동사로 쓸 땐 '받아쓰다'로 한 단어예요. '받아쓰기하다'보다 '받아쓰기를 하다'가 자연스럽습니다.
'받아적기'라고도 쓸 수 있지만, 학교 시험을 가리키는 표준 명칭은 '받아쓰기'입니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 가정통신문 means "school-to-home notice, parent newsletter" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가정통신문 (gajeongtongsinmun) = "school-to-home notice, parent newsletter". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가정통신문을 받다 ("receive a school notice") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가정통신문, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보통 학생 편에 전달됨
확인(確認) = checking; 부모가 읽고 서명

usagePhrases.en: the reply slip for the school notice
usagePhrases.note: 회신(回信) = reply; 통신문에 딸려 잘라 보내는 답신 종이
-에 적혀 있다 = (info) is written in (상태)

examples.en: Did a school notice come (home)?
examples.note: 오다 의문; 부모가 자주 묻는 기본 문장

examples.ko: 엄마, 가정통신문에 사인 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: eomma, gajeongtongsinmune sain jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: Mom, please sign the school notice.
examples.note: 사인하다 = to sign (loanword, casual); '서명하다'가 더 격식

examples.ko: 가정통신문을 안 내서 선생님이 다시 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: gajeongtongsinmuneul an naeseo seonsaengnimi dasi jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't turn the notice in, so the teacher gave me another.
examples.note: 내다 = hand in / submit

entries.nuance: 가정통신문은 한자 家庭通信文(가정·통신·문), 글자 그대로 '가정(家庭)에 보내는 통신(通信)의 글(文)'로, 학교가 학부모에게 행사·준비물·일정을 알리려고 학생 편에 보내는 안내문이에요(요즘은 앱 알림으로도 옴). 일반 회사의 '공지(公知)'나 안내문과의 결정적 차이는 방향과 대상이에요 — 공지는 조직 안 구성원에게 두루 알리는 것이고, 가정통신문은 학교에서 '가정(부모)으로' 콕 집어 보내는 문서라 보통 부모가 읽고 서명하거나 회신서를 돌려보내야 합니다. 그래서 한국에서 아이를 키우는 사람이 꼭 알아야 하는 생활 단어예요. 자연스러운 짝은 '가정통신문을 받다/내다, 가정통신문 확인, 가정통신문에 서명하다, 회신서를 보내다'. 영어식 함정: notice를 그냥 '공지'로 옮기면 학교→가정 방향이 안 살고, 또 '받기만 하면 끝'이 아니라 서명·회신이 따르는 경우가 많으니 '확인하다'와 한 세트로 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
회사 '공지'와 혼동하지 마세요. 가정통신문은 학교가 '가정(부모)으로' 보내는 안내문입니다.
받는 걸로 끝나지 않을 때가 많아요. 서명·회신서가 필요한 경우가 흔하니 '확인하다'와 함께 기억하세요.
공식 서류엔 '사인'보다 '서명'이 적절해요. '사인'은 구어이고 학교 양식엔 '서명'을 씁니다.

entries.english: school snack shop, tuck shop, kiosk
entries.shortExplanation: 매점 means "school snack shop, tuck shop, kiosk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매점 (maejeom) means "school snack shop, tuck shop, kiosk". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 매점에 가다 ("go to the snack shop"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 매점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쉬는 시간·점심시간에
인기 간식의 대명사
붐비다 = be crowded; 쉬는 시간엔 줄이 긺
운영하시는 분을 친근히 부르는 호칭

examples.en: Where is the snack shop?
examples.note: 위치 묻기; 장소 + 어디 있어요?

examples.en: At lunch I bought bread and milk at the snack shop.
examples.note: -에서 = the place where an action happens (구입 장소)

examples.ko: 쉬는 시간이 짧아서 매점은 늘 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: swineun sigani jjalbaseo maejeomeun neul sarami manayo.
examples.en: Because break is short, the snack shop is always crowded.
examples.note: 늘 = always; -아서로 이유 연결

entries.nuance: 매점은 한자 賣店(매·점), '팔 매(賣) + 가게 점(店)' = 학교·회사·병원·역 구내에 있는 작은 판매소로, 빵·음료·과자 같은 간단한 먹거리를 파는 곳이에요. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃이 '편의점'과 '가게'인데, 갈림선이 둘입니다 — 첫째, 매점은 보통 시설 '안(구내)'에 있고 거리의 독립 점포는 그냥 '가게/상점'이라 부르며, 둘째, 매점은 운영 시간(학교라면 수업 시간대)에만 열고 24시간·체인인 편의점(便宜店)과 규모·운영이 달라요. 학생에게는 쉬는 시간의 작은 즐거움이라 '매점 빵, 매점 가다'가 입에 붙습니다. 자연스러운 짝은 '매점에 가다, 매점에서 사다, 매점이 붐비다, 매점 아주머니'. 영어식 함정: store/shop을 무조건 매점이라 옮기면 안 돼요 — 길거리 상점은 가게, 동네 24시간 점포는 편의점이고, 매점은 어디까지나 시설 구내의 작은 판매소를 가리킵니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
거리의 일반 상점은 매점이 아니에요. 매점은 학교·회사·병원 등 시설 '안(구내)'의 작은 판매소입니다.
편의점과 혼동하지 마세요. 매점은 24시간 체인이 아니고 시설 운영 시간에만 엽니다.
물건을 사는 장소엔 -에서를 쓰세요. '매점에 빵 샀어요'가 아니라 '매점에서 빵 샀어요'가 맞습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 한자 賣店(매·점), '팔 매(賣) + 가게 점(店)' = 학교·회사·병원·역 구내에 있는 작은 판매소로, 빵·음료·과자 같은 간단한 먹거리를 파는 곳이에요. 학생에게는 쉬는 시간의 작은 즐거움이라 '매점 빵, 매점 가다'가 입에 붙습니다. 자연스러운 짝은 '매점에 가다, 매점에서 사다, 매점이 붐비다, 매점 아주머니'.

store/shop을 무조건 매점이라 옮기면 안 돼요 — 길거리 상점은 가게, 동네 24시간 점포는 편의점이고, 매점은 어디까지나 시설 구내의 작은 판매소를 가리킵니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 등교 means "going to school, attending school" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "going to school, attending school" is 등교 (deunggyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 등교하다 ("go to school (in the morning)"). Watch the particle attached to 등교 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 명사 + 하다 동사화
보통 아침 8시 반쯤
준비(準備) = preparation; 아침 루틴
거부(拒否) = refusal; 학교 가기를 거부하는 (심각한) 상태

examples.en: What time do you go to school?
examples.note: 시간 묻기 기본 문장; 명사 + 하다 의문형

examples.en: I usually go to school around eight.
examples.note: -쯤 = approximately (시간·수량 뒤)

examples.ko: 눈이 많이 와서 등교 시간이 한 시간 늦춰졌어요.
examples.romanization: nuni mani waseo deunggyo sigani han sigan neutchwojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It snowed a lot, so the school start time got pushed back an hour.
examples.note: 늦춰지다 = be delayed (늦추다의 피동)

entries.nuance: 등교는 한자 登校(등·교), '오를 등(登) + 학교 교(校)' = 아침에 학교로 가는 것이고, 짝이 되는 반대말은 수업이 끝나 집으로 가는 하교(下校, '내려갈 하')예요 — 登/下가 출근·퇴근의 出/退처럼 한 쌍을 이룹니다. 바로 이 점이 가장 중요한 갈림선인데, 회사에 가는 건 출근(出勤), 학교에 가는 건 등교라 대상이 다릅니다(학생판 출근이라고 생각하면 쉬워요). 한국에서는 등교 시간·등교 복장(교복) 같은 규칙이 꽤 엄격한 편이라 이 단어가 생활 속에 자주 등장합니다. 자연스러운 짝은 '등교하다, 등교 시간, 등교 준비, 등교 거부'. 영어식 함정 둘: go to school을 옮기며 '학교에 등교하다'라고 하면 등교에 이미 '학교(校)'가 들어 있어 의미가 겹치니 그냥 '등교하다'면 충분하고, 직장에 가는 것을 등교라 하면 어색하므로 그땐 출근을 쓰세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'학교에 등교하다'는 의미가 겹쳐 어색합니다. 등(登)과 교(校)에 이미 '학교에 감'이 들어 있으니 '등교하다'면 충분해요.
회사에 가는 것은 '출근'입니다. 학교에 가는 등교와 대상을 구분하세요.
집으로 돌아가는 것을 등교라 하면 틀려요. 반대 방향은 '하교(下校)'입니다.

영어식 함정 둘: go to school을 옮기며 '학교에 등교하다'라고 하면 등교에 이미 '학교(校)'가 들어 있어 의미가 겹치니 그냥 '등교하다'면 충분하고, 직장에 가는 것을 등교라 하면 어색하므로 그땐 출근을 쓰세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 사탕 means "candy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사탕 (satang) = "candy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사탕 하나 주세요 ("One candy, please") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사탕, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Count small candies with 하나/한 개; 하나 is the natural default at a counter.
까다 is the verb for peeling off a wrapper — never 열다 (open) for candy.
막대(stick) + 사탕, a fixed compound written as one word.

usagePhrases.en: to hold a candy in one's mouth
usagePhrases.note: 물다 (to hold in the mouth) fits hard candy you suck on, not chew.

examples.en: Do you like candy?
examples.note: Drop the subject in casual talk; context supplies 'you'.

examples.en: I bought a bag of candy at the convenience store.
examples.note: 봉지 is the counter for a bag/packet of snacks.

examples.ko: 목 아플 때 사탕 하나 입에 물고 있으면 좀 나아요.
examples.romanization: mok apeul ttae satang hana ibe mulgo isseumyeon jom naayo.
examples.en: When my throat hurts, keeping a candy in my mouth helps a bit.
examples.note: Throat-soothing candy is treated as a mild everyday remedy; 물고 있다 = keep held in the mouth.

entries.nuance: 사탕 means hard, sugar-based candy and lollipops — the kind you suck, not the chewy gummies (those are strictly 젤리) or 초콜릿. It is Sino-Korean, 砂糖 'sand-sugar' (the same 糖 'sugar' element in 설탕 table sugar and 당분 sugar content), which is why it sits in the sweets family rather than being a generic 'sweet treat'. Register is fully neutral: a child or an adult says it the same way. The pitfall for English speakers is the verb: you do not 열다 (open) a candy, you 까다 (peel/unwrap) it, and you 물다 or 빨다 (hold/suck) rather than 먹다 when sucking it. Seasonally it carries a faint romance: on White Day (3/14) men give 사탕 to answer the 초콜릿 women give on Valentine's Day.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling gummy candies 사탕 — soft chewy ones are 젤리, a separate category Koreans never merge with 사탕.
Saying 사탕을 열다 for 'unwrap a candy'; the correct verb is 사탕을 까다.
Using 먹다 for sucking a hard candy — when it stays in the mouth, 물다/빨다 is more accurate than 먹다.

entries.shortExplanation: 초콜릿 means "chocolate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 초콜릿 (chokollit) means "chocolate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 초콜릿 한 개 ("one piece of chocolate"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 초콜릿 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 개 counts a single piece; a whole bar is 한 판.
녹다 (to melt) is the verb you hear in summer or in a warm hand.
Loanword modifiers 다크/밀크/화이트 sit directly before 초콜릿.
줄이다 = to reduce; standard health-talk phrasing.

examples.en: Do you like chocolate?
examples.note: Plain everyday question; subject dropped.

examples.ko: 피곤할 때 초콜릿 먹으면 기분이 좀 좋아져요.
examples.romanization: pigonhal ttae chokollin meogeumyeon gibuni jom joajyeoyo.
examples.en: When I'm tired, eating chocolate lifts my mood a bit.
examples.note: 기분이 좋아지다 = one's mood improves; -아지다 marks the gradual change.

examples.ko: 밸런타인데이에 좋아하는 사람한테 초콜릿 주려고 직접 만들었어요.
examples.romanization: baelleontaindeie joahaneun saramhante chokollit juryeogo jikjeom mandeureosseoyo.
examples.en: I made chocolate by hand to give to my crush on Valentine's Day.
examples.note: Handmade (직접 만든) 초콜릿 on Feb 14 is the big Korean custom; 주려고 = intending to give.

entries.nuance: 초콜릿 is a direct loanword from English 'chocolate', and the single most important thing to learn is the spelling: 초콜릿 is standard, while 초콜렛 is a widespread misspelling even among natives — write the former. Unlike the native-word sweets here, it takes loanword flavor modifiers (다크/밀크/화이트) placed before it. Counting trips people up: a flat bar is counted with 판 (한 판), individual squares or wrapped pieces with 개 (한 개), so 'one chocolate' is ambiguous until you pick the counter that matches the shape. Culturally it is the default Valentine's gift from women to men, mirrored by 사탕 on White Day. Pitfall: English lets 'chocolate' be a mass noun ('some chocolate'), but in Korean you still attach a counter, so 초콜릿 좀 (some) or 초콜릿 한 개 (one piece) rather than a bare count.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 초콜렛 instead of the standard 초콜릿 — the second is correct even though both are heard.
Using 판 for a single square — a whole bar is 한 판, one piece is 한 개.
Treating it as an uncountable mass like English 'chocolate'; Korean still needs a counter, e.g. 초콜릿 한 조각/한 개.

entries.shortExplanation: 젤리 means "gummy candy, jelly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "gummy candy, jelly" is 젤리 (jelli). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 젤리 한 봉지 ("a bag of gummies"). Watch the particle attached to 젤리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sold by the 봉지 at convenience stores.
곰(bear) + 젤리; by far the most popular type.
쫄깃하다 describes the springy chew people love in 젤리.
씹다 (to chew) suits 젤리 — unlike hard 사탕, which you suck.

examples.en: Can I have more gummies?
examples.note: Casual permission: -아/어도 돼요? shortened to 돼?

examples.ko: 젤리는 충치 생기기 쉬우니까 조금만 먹어.
examples.romanization: jellineun chungchi saenggigi swiunikka jogeumman meogeo.
examples.en: Gummies cause cavities easily, so eat just a little.
examples.note: 생기기 쉽다 = easy to develop; 조금만 = just a little.

examples.ko: 요즘 편의점엔 마라맛 젤리 같은 신기한 맛까지 있어서 한참 골랐어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum pyeonuijeomen maramat jelli gateun singihan matkkaji isseoseo hancham gollasseoyo.
examples.en: These days convenience stores even have novelty flavors like mala gummies, so I spent ages choosing.
examples.note: 마라맛 is a recent trend; 신기하다 = novel; 한참 = a good while; 고르다 = to pick.

entries.nuance: 젤리 (a loanword from English 'jelly') is the catch-all for chewy gummy sweets — gummy bears, fruit gummies, sour gummies — and is firmly a separate category from hard 사탕 and from 초콜릿; Koreans never file 젤리 under 사탕. The word can also name a wobbly dessert jelly, but in everyday snack talk it almost always means gummies. The defining texture word is 쫄깃하다/쫀득하다 (springy-chewy), and the natural verb is 씹다 (chew), contrasting with the 빨다/물다 (suck) you use for 사탕. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing 젤리 with 잼 (jam, the bread spread) because both come from 'jelly/jam' — they are completely different foods. Convenience stores carry an enormous, constantly rotating gummy wall, so 젤리 is genuinely high-frequency vocabulary.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 젤리 (gummy) with 잼 (jam/spread) — they sound related in English but are entirely different foods in Korean.
Calling 젤리 a kind of 사탕; Koreans keep gummies and hard candy as separate categories.
Using 빨다/물다 (suck) with 젤리 — gummies are chewed, so the verb is 씹다.

entries.shortExplanation: 과자 means "snacks, chips, crackers" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 과자 (gwaja) = "snacks, chips, crackers". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과자 한 봉지 ("a bag of snacks") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 봉지 is the go-to counter for bagged snacks.
부스러기 = crumbs; handy when cleaning up.
눅눅하다 describes chips that lost their crunch; opposite of 바삭하다.

usagePhrases.en: to tear open the snack bag
usagePhrases.note: 뜯다 (to tear) is how you open a sealed 과자 봉지.

examples.en: Wanna go buy some snacks?
examples.note: -(으)러 가다 = go in order to do; 갈래? is a casual invite.

examples.ko: 영화 볼 때 과자랑 음료수는 필수예요.
examples.romanization: yeonghwa bol ttae gwajarang eumnyosuneun pilsuyeyo.
examples.en: Snacks and a drink are a must when watching a movie.
examples.note: 필수예요 = it's essential; 랑 links the pair casually.

examples.ko: 이 과자는 봉지를 뜯으면 생각보다 절반이 공기예요.
examples.romanization: i gwajaneun bongjireul tteudeumyeon saenggakboda jeolbani gonggiyeyo.
examples.en: When you open this snack bag, half of it is air, more than you'd expect.
examples.note: A common joke about 질소과자 (nitrogen-filled bags); 뜯다 = to tear open.

entries.nuance: 과자 is Sino-Korean, 菓子 (菓 'confection/fruit' + 子 a noun suffix), and works as the umbrella term for crunchy packaged snacks — chips, crackers, biscuits, corn puffs, basically the salty-or-sweet bagged stuff in the snack aisle. It deliberately excludes the other categories on this list: gummies are 젤리, hard candy is 사탕, chocolate is 초콜릿. The boundary that trips learners is 과자 vs 쿠키: a freshly baked café cookie is 쿠키, while 과자 leans toward mass-produced, packaged snacks, so calling an artisan cookie 과자 sounds slightly off. Counting is by 봉지 (bag), not by piece, because these come bagged; you 뜯다 (tear) the bag open. Texture is 바삭하다 (crispy) when fresh, 눅눅하다 (soggy) when stale. Koreans love joking about 질소과자 — bags that feel mostly full of nitrogen gas rather than chips.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 과자 for a bakery/café cookie you'd call 쿠키 — 과자 implies packaged, mass-market snacks.
Counting bagged snacks by piece; the natural counter is 봉지 (한 봉지).
Lumping 사탕/젤리/초콜릿 under 과자 — 과자 is the crunchy salty/biscuit category, not candy.

entries.shortExplanation: 팝콘 means "popcorn" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 팝콘 (papkon) means "popcorn". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 팝콘 한 통 ("one tub of popcorn"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 팝콘 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 통 (tub/bucket) is the cinema counter for popcorn.
Flavor sits before 팝콘; 카라멜/치즈 are the most common.
튀기다 (to pop/fry) is the standard verb for making it.
Cinemas let you split two flavors; 반반 = half-half.

examples.en: I made microwave popcorn at home.
examples.note: 돌리다 = to run (the microwave); home popcorn comes by the 봉지.

examples.ko: 영화관에서 팝콘 큰 거 하나 시켰어요.
examples.romanization: yeonghwagwaneseo papkon keun geo hana sikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ordered one large popcorn at the cinema.
examples.note: 큰 거 = the big one; 시키다 = to order.

examples.ko: 고소한 팝콘 냄새 때문에 안 사고는 못 배겨요.
examples.romanization: gosohan papkon naemsae ttaemune an sagoneun mot baegyeoyo.
examples.en: The savory popcorn smell makes it impossible not to buy some.
examples.note: 고소하다 = nutty-savory; idiomatic 못 배기다 = can't resist.

entries.nuance: 팝콘 is a loanword from English 'popcorn' and in Korea is strongly bound to the cinema: the defaults are 카라멜 (caramel) and 치즈 (cheese), often ordered 반반 (half-and-half) and bundled with a drink as a 콤보 set. This is a key culture point — plain buttered popcorn is the mental default in English, but in Korea sweet/cheese flavors dominate, so just saying 팝콘 at a 영화관 may get you a flavored tub. Counters differ by context: the cinema tub is 통 (한 통), while microwave popcorn at home is counted by 봉지. The smell word is the classic 고소하다 (the warm, nutty, slightly savory aroma), a flavor adjective with no neat English equivalent. The verb to make it is 튀기다 (pop/fry), the same verb behind 튀김.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Ordering popcorn by 개 — at a cinema you ask for 한 통 (one tub).
Assuming plain butter is the default; in Korea caramel/cheese (and 반반) are the norm, so specify if you want it plain.
Describing the smell as 맛있는 냄새 only — the precise word Koreans use is 고소하다.
