entries.shortExplanation: 호떡 means "hotteok (sweet filled griddle pancake)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "hotteok (sweet filled griddle pancake)" is 호떡 (hotteok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 호떡 하나 주세요 ("One hotteok, please"). Watch the particle attached to 호떡 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Count with 개; 하나 is the easy default at a stall.
씨앗(seeds) + 호떡, a popular nut-and-seed version from Busan.
굽다 here means griddle/pan-fry, not bake; it is a ㅂ-irregular (구워요).
The molten sugar filling is famously scalding; warn 천천히 먹어.

examples.en: Two hotteok, please.
examples.note: At a busy stall, drop the verb; 개 + 요 is enough to order.

examples.ko: 겨울에 길거리에서 따뜻한 호떡 먹는 게 최고예요.
examples.romanization: gyeoure gilgeorieseo ttatteutan hotteong meongneun ge choegoyeyo.
examples.en: Eating warm hotteok on the street in winter is the best.
examples.note: Quintessential winter street food; -는 게 최고예요 = ...is the best.

examples.ko: 호떡 한 입 베어 물자마자 흑설탕이 흘러나와서 입천장을 데었어요.
examples.romanization: hotteo kan ip beeo muljamaja heukseoltangi heulleonawaseo ipcheonjangeul deeosseoyo.
examples.en: The moment I bit into the hotteok, the brown sugar oozed out and I burned the roof of my mouth.
examples.note: 베어 물다 = to bite into; -자마자 = as soon as; 흑설탕 = brown sugar.

entries.nuance: 호떡 is a chewy, griddle-fried wheat-flour pancake with a molten brown-sugar-and-cinnamon center, sold piping hot from winter street carts. The 호 in 호떡 is the 한자 胡, historically 'foreign/Chinese', marking its origin as an introduced food, attached to native 떡 — but here is the crucial distinction: although the name ends in 떡, 호떡 is NOT a rice cake. Real 떡 is made from pounded rice; 호떡 is a flour dough that is pan-fried, so do not assume the texture or ingredients of 떡. The second pitfall is taste: English speakers often expect a savory pancake, but the classic filling is sweet brown sugar (savory 야채 호떡 exists but is the exception). The verb is 굽다 (griddle), a ㅂ-irregular giving 구워요. The filling is dangerously hot, so locals genuinely warn 천천히 먹어 (eat slowly); trendy 씨앗 호떡 stuffed with seeds and nuts is a market favorite, famously around Busan's BIFF square.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting 호떡 to be savory — the classic filling is sweet brown sugar and cinnamon.
Assuming 호떡 is a rice cake because of the 떡 in its name; it is a fried wheat-flour pancake, not pounded-rice 떡.
Conjugating 굽다 regularly as 굽어요 — it is a ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 구워요.

Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 붕어빵 세 개 주세요 ("Three bungeoppang, please") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 붕어빵, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Sold by count (개); often cheaper as a 묶음 (bundle).
Standard street-stall pricing question.
슈크림 fillings now rival the classic 팥(red bean).

usagePhrases.en: the red bean is packed all the way to the tail
usagePhrases.note: 꽉 차다 = packed full; locals judge a stall by this.

examples.en: Do you eat bungeoppang head-first or tail-first?
examples.note: A playful national debate; 머리부터 = starting from the head.

examples.ko: 요즘은 붕어빵 파는 데 찾기가 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun bungeoppang paneun de chatgiga himdeureoyo.
examples.en: These days it's hard to find a place selling bungeoppang.
examples.note: Stalls have grown scarce; -기가 힘들다 = it's hard to...

examples.ko: 추운 날 갓 구운 붕어빵을 봉지째 들고 호호 불면서 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: chuun nal gat guun bungeoppangeul bongjijjae deulgo hoho bulmyeonseo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: On a cold day I ate freshly griddled bungeoppang straight from the bag, blowing on it to cool it.
examples.note: 갓 구운 = just griddled; 봉지째 = bag and all; 호호 불다 = to blow to cool.

entries.nuance: 붕어빵 is a fish-shaped pastry of waffle-like batter filled with sweet red-bean paste, the iconic Korean winter street snack that pairs with 호떡 and 군고구마. The name is 붕어 (crucian carp) + 빵 (bread, itself a loanword via Portuguese pão), and the single biggest trap for English speakers is taking the fish part literally: 붕어빵 contains no fish whatsoever — it is named purely for the fish-shaped mold. Because of that shape, learners reach for the animal counter 마리, but pastries take 개 (세 개), never 마리. The classic filling is 팥 (red bean); 슈크림 (custard) and even pizza versions now compete. Figuratively, 붕어빵 also means 'identical/spitting image' (e.g. 붕어빵처럼 똑같다) because they all come out of the same mold. Stalls have become rare enough that fans share locations via a 붕어빵 지도 app, and people fondly argue over eating head-first vs. tail-first.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 붕어빵 contains fish — it's named only for its fish shape; the classic filling is red bean.
Counting it with 마리 (the animal counter) because of the fish shape; pastries use 개.
Missing the idiom — 붕어빵 also means 'a spitting image' (붕어빵처럼 닮다), since they're all molded identically.

structuredNuance.t: 붕어빵 is a fish-shaped pastry of waffle-like batter filled with sweet red-bean paste, the iconic Korean winter street snack that pairs with 호떡 and 군고구마. Figuratively, 붕어빵 also means 'identical/spitting image' (e.g. 붕어빵처럼 똑같다) because they all come out of the same mold. Stalls have become rare enough that fans share locations via a 붕어빵 지도 app, and people fondly argue over eating head-first vs. tail-first.
The name is 붕어 (crucian carp) + 빵 (bread, itself a loanword via Portuguese pão).

entries.shortExplanation: 군고구마 means "roasted sweet potato" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 군고구마 (gungoguma) means "roasted sweet potato". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 군고구마 하나 주세요 ("One roasted sweet potato, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 군고구마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sold by the piece (개) or by weight.

usagePhrases.en: the roasted sweet potato is warm
usagePhrases.note: Warmth is the whole appeal in winter; ask 따뜻해요?

usagePhrases.en: to peel the skin off and eat
usagePhrases.note: 껍질 = skin; 까다 = to peel.
꿀(honey) + 고구마: the extra-sweet, moist variety people request.

examples.en: Now that it's winter, I really crave roasted sweet potato.
examples.note: 생각이 간절하다 = to crave intensely; -니까 = now that/because.

examples.en: These days they even sell roasted sweet potatoes at convenience stores.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a mildly surprising thing you observed.

examples.ko: 군고구마는 호일에 싸여 있어서 손이 안 뜨거워서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gungogumaneun hoire ssayeo isseoseo soni an tteugeowoseo joayo.
examples.en: Roasted sweet potato comes wrapped in foil, so your hands don't get hot — I like that.
examples.note: 호일에 싸이다 = to be wrapped in foil; -아서 chains reason to result.

entries.nuance: 군고구마 is a fixed compound, 군 (the past-modifier of 굽다, 'roasted/grilled') + 고구마 (sweet potato), so it literally means 'roasted sweet potato' — and that frozen form matters: when ordering you say the one word 군고구마, not the spelled-out 구운 고구마, which sounds like a description rather than the named street snack. It's a beloved winter food traditionally sold from a barrel-drum roaster on a cart, now also stocked warm at convenience stores, completing the winter trio with 호떡 and 붕어빵. The key vocabulary contrast for learners is 고구마 (sweet potato) vs 감자 (potato): they are different vegetables, and mixing them up changes the dish entirely. People prize the 꿀고구마 variety for its sticky, honey-like sweetness. (Note that 고구마 also has a slang sense — a frustrating, stifling situation — but 군고구마 stays literal.)

Mis-segmenting the word as 군 + 고구마 meaning something else — 군 here is simply 굽다's modifier form 'roasted'.

entries.shortExplanation: 순대 means "sundae (Korean blood sausage)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sundae (Korean blood sausage)" is 순대 (sundae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 순대 일 인분 주세요 ("One portion of sundae, please"). Watch the particle attached to 순대 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sold by 인분 (portion) at 분식 stalls, not by the piece.

usagePhrases.en: to dip it in salt to eat
usagePhrases.note: 찍다 = to dip; many eat 순대 with plain salt.

usagePhrases.en: Do you eat the organ meats too?
usagePhrases.note: 내장 (liver, lung) comes mixed in; some skip it.

usagePhrases.en: to dip the sundae in tteokbokki sauce
usagePhrases.note: A classic 분식 move; 국물 = the broth/sauce.

examples.en: I ordered sundae and fritters together at the snack shop.
examples.note: 분식집 = snack/street-food shop; 같이 시키다 = order together.

examples.ko: 순대는 소금이랑 먹을지 양념장이랑 먹을지 늘 고민돼요.
examples.romanization: sundaeneun sogeumirang meogeulji yangnyeomjangirang meogeulji neul gomindwaeyo.
examples.en: I always agonize over eating sundae with salt or with seasoned sauce.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ지 ...-(으)ㄹ지 = whether to do A or B; regional tastes differ.

examples.ko: 속초 가면 일반 순대보다 훨씬 큰 아바이순대를 꼭 먹어 봐요.
examples.romanization: sokcho gamyeon ilban sundaeboda hwolssin keun abaisundaereul kkong meogeo bwayo.
examples.en: When I go to Sokcho I always try abai-sundae, which is much bigger than regular sundae.
examples.note: 아바이순대 is a famous Sokcho specialty; -아 보다 = try doing.

entries.nuance: 순대 is a steamed sausage made from pig intestine stuffed with 당면 (glass noodles), blood, and other fillings — a pillar of 분식 (snack-shop) culture alongside 떡볶이 and 튀김. The first thing for an English speaker to lock in is the false friend: the English dessert 'sundae' (ice cream) is completely unrelated; that is 선데이 or just 아이스크림 in Korean, while 순대 is a savory blood sausage. The nearest savory cousin is 소시지 (Western sausage), but 순대 is its own traditional category, not a type of 소시지. There is a genuine regional split — some dip it in plain 소금 (salt), others in 양념장 (seasoned sauce) — and it is sold by 인분 (portion), not by 개. The organ meats (내장) usually come on the side, and ordering without them is fine. A famous regional kind is 아바이순대 from Sokcho.

Confusing 순대 with an ice-cream sundae — the English word is a false friend; this is a savory blood sausage (the dessert is 선데이/아이스크림).
Ordering by 개 — 순대 is sold by 인분 (portion).
Calling 순대 a kind of 소시지 — it overlaps in shape but is its own traditional food, not Western sausage.

entries.shortExplanation: 어묵 means "fish cake" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 어묵 (eomuk) = "fish cake". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어묵 한 꼬치 ("one skewer of fish cake") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 어묵, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 꼬치 = skewer; the street form is folded onto a stick.
The hot 국물 (broth) is free and beloved in winter.
오뎅 is the very common colloquial (Japanese-origin) term.
셀프 = self-service; refill your own paper cup for free.

examples.ko: 어묵 꼬치 다섯 개 먹고 국물도 두 컵 마셨어요.
examples.romanization: eomuk kkochi daseot gae meokgo gungmuldo du keom masyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ate five fish-cake skewers and drank two cups of broth too.
examples.note: Count 꼬치 (skewers) and 컵 (cups); 도 = also.

examples.ko: 추운 날 포장마차에서 어묵 국물 마시면 몸이 녹아요.
examples.romanization: chuun nal pojangmachaeseo eomuk gungmul masimyeon momi nogayo.
examples.en: Drinking fish-cake broth at a street tent on a cold day warms you right up.
examples.note: 포장마차 = street food tent; 몸이 녹다 = to thaw/warm up.

examples.ko: 부산 어묵이 워낙 유명해서 갈 때마다 선물로 사 와요.
examples.romanization: busan eomugi wonak yumyeonghaeseo gal ttaemada seonmullo sa wayo.
examples.en: Busan fish cake is so famous that I buy some as a gift every time I go.
examples.note: 워낙 = (so) by nature/famously; -ㄹ 때마다 = every time.

entries.nuance: 어묵 is the standard word for fish cake — ground fish paste shaped and cooked — and the register issue is the heart of this entry. In everyday speech most people, including at stalls, casually say 오뎅 (from Japanese おでん); 어묵 is the 'proper', recommended-Korean term you should default to in writing and polite contexts, while recognizing 오뎅 when you hear it. The 한자 is 魚 'fish' (어) + native 묵 (a set jelly/curd, as in 도토리묵 acorn jelly), so the word literally frames it as a 'fish curd'. The street form is folded onto a skewer (꼬치) and comes with an endlessly refilled, free hot 국물 in winter — and that broth is 셀프 (self-serve), so you do not pay per cup, a frequent point of confusion for visitors. Busan (부산어묵) is the celebrated home of it, and packaged 어묵 is both a soup ingredient and a common gift.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 오뎅 is simply wrong — it is extremely common in speech, just non-standard; 어묵 is the recommended term.
Forgetting the 국물 is self-serve and free; you refill your own cup rather than paying per serving.
Treating 어묵 and 묵 as the same thing — 묵 (e.g. 도토리묵) is a different set-jelly food; 어묵 is the fish version.

entries.shortExplanation: 튀김 means "deep-fried snacks, fritters (tempura-style)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 튀김 (twigim) means "deep-fried snacks, fritters (tempura-style)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 튀김 모둠 주세요 ("An assorted fritter plate, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 튀김 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 모둠 = an assortment of mixed pieces.
Ingredient + 튀김 names each fritter; 오징어/새우/고구마.
바삭하다 = crispy, the key quality marker; opposite 눅눅하다.

usagePhrases.en: to dip the fritters in tteokbokki sauce
usagePhrases.note: The quintessential 분식 way to eat them.

examples.ko: 분식집에서 튀김이랑 순대 시켜서 나눠 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: bunsikjibeseo twigimirang sundae sikyeoseo nanwo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: We ordered fritters and sundae at the snack shop and shared.
examples.note: 나눠 먹다 = to share food; -아서 chains the actions.

examples.ko: 갓 튀긴 튀김이 제일 바삭하고 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: gat twigin twigimi jeil basakago masisseoyo.
examples.en: Freshly fried fritters are the crispiest and tastiest.
examples.note: 갓 튀긴 = just-fried; note 튀긴 (verb) modifying 튀김 (noun).

examples.ko: 김말이 튀김은 겉은 바삭한데 안에 당면이 가득 들어 있어요.
examples.romanization: gimmari twigimeun geoteun basakande ane dangmyeoni gadeuk deureo isseoyo.
examples.en: Gimmari fritters are crispy outside but packed with glass noodles inside.
examples.note: 김말이 = seaweed-rolled fritter; -는데 contrasts outside vs inside.

entries.nuance: 튀김 is a native noun built from the verb 튀기다 (to deep-fry) plus the nominalizing -ㅁ, literally 'a frying / a fried thing', and it means battered deep-fried snacks in the Korean tempura tradition — fried squid, shrimp, sweet potato, and 김말이 (seaweed-and-noodle rolls) — sold at 분식 stalls beside 떡볶이 and 순대. Because it comes from a verb, the number-one pitfall is mixing up 튀김 (the noun: the fried food) with 튀기다/튀긴 (the verb: to fry / fried), as in 갓 튀긴 튀김 'just-fried fritters', where both appear. A second trap is scope: a bare 튀김 usually implies a mixed assortment (모둠), so to order one specific kind you must name the ingredient — 오징어 튀김, 새우 튀김 — rather than just 튀김. The whole point is 바삭함 (crispiness), best 갓 튀긴 (just fried) and ruined when 눅눅하다 (soggy); dunking them in spicy 떡볶이 국물 is the classic move.

Using the verb 튀기다 (to fry) when you mean the noun 튀김 (the fried food) — they share a root but aren't interchangeable.
Expecting one item from a bare 튀김 — it usually means an assortment; specify the ingredient (오징어 튀김 etc.) to order one kind.
Describing stale fritters with the wrong adjective — lost crunch is 눅눅하다, the opposite of 바삭하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 약과 means "yakgwa (honey fried cookie)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "yakgwa (honey fried cookie)" is 약과 (yakgwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 약과 하나 먹을래요? ("Want to have a yakgwa?"). Watch the particle attached to 약과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Counted by 개; traditionally offered with tea.
Bite-size 미니 약과 became a huge trend snack.
It is honey-soaked; 달다 (sweet) is a ㄹ-final adjective (달아요).
Packaged mini versions sell by the 봉지.

examples.en: Yakgwa is chewy outside and soft inside.
examples.note: 쫀득하다 = pleasantly chewy; -고 links two qualities.

examples.ko: 약과는 명절에 차례상에 꼭 올라가는 한과예요.
examples.romanization: yakgwaneun myeongjeore charyesange kkok ollaganeun hangwayeyo.
examples.en: Yakgwa is a traditional sweet that always goes on the holiday ritual table.
examples.note: 한과 = traditional confection; 차례상 = ancestral-rite table; 올라가다 = to be placed on.

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 사람들 사이에서 약과가 다시 유행이라 카페에서도 약과 디저트를 팔아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun saramdeul saieseo yakgwaga dasi yuhaengira kapeeseodo yakgwa dijeoteureul parayo.
examples.en: Yakgwa is trendy again among young people, so cafés even sell yakgwa desserts now.
examples.note: Part of the 할매니얼 (grandma + millennial) retro-snack craze; -이라 = because it is.

entries.nuance: 약과 is a traditional Korean confection (한과): a wheat-flour dough that is deep-fried and then steeped in honey or grain syrup, historically reserved for holidays and ritual tables. Its 한자 is the key insight — 藥菓, literally 'medicine-confection', because in old Korea honey was considered medicinal (藥 'medicine' is the same character as in 약 'medicine' and 한약 herbal medicine; 菓 'confection' is the same as in 과자). So the standout English-speaker pitfall is assuming the name means it contains medicine: it does not — it is simply a honey cookie whose historical luxury ingredient earned the 'medicine' label. The other boundary to keep straight is 약과 (a specific 한과) vs the broad 과자 (mass-market packaged snacks): 약과 is not a 과자, even though both share the 菓 character. Texture is 쫀득하다 (chewy-sticky) and it is quite sweet (달다). It has surged back into fashion among people in their 20s-30s as part of the 할매니얼 retro-snack trend, with cafés selling 미니 약과 and yakgwa-topped desserts.

Conjugating 달다 as 달어요 — it is a ㄹ-final adjective, so 'it's sweet' is 달아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 축구 means "soccer, football" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 축구 (chukgu) = "soccer, football". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 축구 좋아해요? ("Do you like soccer?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 축구, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: By far the most common sport to open small talk with Korean coworkers and friends.

usagePhrases.en: Let's play a round of soccer
usagePhrases.note: 판 is the casual counter for a round/match; 한 판 하다 = 'play a round', breezier than 경기.

usagePhrases.en: Want to go watch a soccer game?
usagePhrases.note: 보러 가다 = 'go in order to watch'; the 러 attaches to the verb stem of the purpose.
조기(早起, 'rising early') 축구 is a fixed term for the weekend dawn matches older men famously play.

examples.en: I play soccer with my friends every weekend.
examples.note: 마다 = 'every'; in speech 축구(를) 하다 drops the 를, and 이랑 is the casual 'with'.

examples.ko: 어젯밤에 손흥민 나오는 축구 경기 봤어요?
examples.romanization: eojetbame sonheungmin naoneun chukgu gyeonggi bwasseoyo?
examples.en: Did you watch the soccer match Son Heung-min was in last night?
examples.note: 나오다 = 'appear/be featured'; EPL games with 손흥민 are huge water-cooler talk.

examples.ko: 한국이 일본을 이겨서 축구 팬들이 다 난리 났어요.
examples.romanization: hangugi ilboneul igyeoseo chukgu paendeuri da nalli nasseoyo.
examples.en: Korea beat Japan, so all the soccer fans went wild.
examples.note: 난리 나다 = 'go into an uproar'; -아서 here marks the cause leading to the reaction.

entries.nuance: 축구 (蹴球, literally 'kick(蹴)-ball(球)') is the default national sport for casual conversation, and dropping a name like 손흥민 buys instant rapport, especially in men's chat. The verb splits by activity: 축구(를) 하다 for playing versus 축구(를) 보다 for watching — never one verb for both, and in speech the 를 is usually dropped. The big English-speaker pitfall is the word itself: do NOT say 풋볼, which Koreans hear as American football, nor 사커; the only natural word is 축구. A second trap is calling a real match 축구 게임 — for a broadcast or pro fixture it is 축구 경기, while 게임 sounds like a casual pickup kickabout. Recognize the cultural compound 조기 축구, the dawn amateur soccer older men play on weekends.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 풋볼 or 사커 — Koreans always say 축구, and 풋볼 specifically sounds like American football to them.
Using 게임 for a real match: a pro or broadcast match is 축구 경기, not 축구 게임 (게임 implies casual pickup).
Saying 축구를 보다 and 축구를 하다 interchangeably — you watch (보다) a match but play (하다) the sport; the verbs are not swappable.

entries.shortExplanation: 야구 means "baseball" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 야구 (yagu) means "baseball". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 야구 좋아해요? ("Do you like baseball?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 야구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Korea's most-attended pro sport (KBO); a safe, friendly small-talk opener.

usagePhrases.en: Which team do you root for?
usagePhrases.note: 응원하다 = 'cheer for'; asking someone's KBO team is a classic bonding move.

usagePhrases.en: Let's go to a baseball game
usagePhrases.note: 보러 가다 again; KBO stadiums are famous for loud, organized fan chants.
시즌 is the everyday loanword; the KBO season runs spring through fall.

examples.ko: 주말에 잠실 가서 야구 볼 거예요.
examples.romanization: jumare jamsil gaseo yagu bol geoyeyo.
examples.en: I'm going to Jamsil this weekend to watch baseball.
examples.note: Locals name the venue: 잠실 가다 rather than 야구장 가다; -ㄹ 거예요 = future plan.

examples.en: When you go to a baseball stadium, chicken and beer are a must.
examples.note: 치킨에 맥주 = 'chicken plus beer' (the 에 means 'added to'); 필수 = 'a must'.

examples.en: Our team came from behind in the 9th, it was such a thrill.
examples.note: 역전(逆轉)하다 = 'reverse the lead'; 9회 = the 9th inning, 에 marks the time point.

entries.nuance: 야구 (野球, literally 'field(野)-ball(球)') is arguably the sport Koreans are most passionate about attending in person — the stadium chants, team songs, and bringing your own 치맥 (치킨+맥주) form a whole culture. The verb pattern mirrors 축구: 야구(를) 하다 for playing, 야구(를) 보다 for watching. Asking 어느 팀 응원해요? signals you want to connect socially. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, for a pro game Koreans usually name the stadium (잠실 가다, 고척 가다) — saying 야구장 가다 sounds like a generic or amateur field. Second, 회 here is the inning counter (1회, 9회), a homophone of 회 'raw fish'; the number and context disambiguate, so 9회 unambiguously means the ninth inning, never sashimi.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For a pro game, saying 야구장 가다 instead of naming the venue (잠실 가다) — 야구장 sounds like a generic/amateur field.
Using 게임 for a KBO match — say 야구 경기; 게임 implies a casual or backyard game.
Reading 9회 as anything but the inning — 회 (inning) here is a counter, not 회 'raw fish'; the number marks it as the 9th inning.

entries.shortExplanation: 농구 means "basketball" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "basketball" is 농구 (nonggu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 농구 할 줄 알아요? ("Do you know how to play basketball?"). Watch the particle attached to 농구 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Do you know how to play basketball?
usagePhrases.note: 할 줄 알다 = 'know how to do'; the natural way to propose a pickup game.

usagePhrases.en: Let's play a game of basketball
usagePhrases.note: 게임 works for pickup hoops; 한 게임 = 'one game', unlike pro soccer where you'd want 경기.
골대 = the hoop/goal post; you'll see them at parks and schoolyards.
Many younger Koreans follow the NBA; the acronym is spelled out in English letters.

examples.en: After work I go play basketball with coworkers.
examples.note: 하러 가다 = 'go in order to play'; 퇴근하고 = 'after clocking out'.

examples.ko: 키 크면 농구 잘할 것 같다는 말 많이 들어요.
examples.romanization: ki keumyeon nonggu jalhal geot gatdaneun mal mani deureoyo.
examples.en: People often tell me I'd be good at basketball since I'm tall.
examples.note: 잘하다 = 'be good at'; -다는 말 듣다 = 'hear people say that...'.

examples.en: I played a game with strangers at the neighborhood court.
examples.note: 농구장 = 'basketball court'; pickup games (픽업 게임) with strangers are common.

entries.nuance: 농구 (籠球, literally 'basket(籠)-ball(球)') had a huge cultural moment in the 90s through the drama '마지막 승부' and the 'Slam Dunk' generation, and pickup games at neighborhood 농구장 remain popular among younger men. The verb is 농구(를) 하다 for playing, 농구(를) 보다 for watching. A useful register note for English speakers: unlike pro soccer, with basketball you can freely say 농구 게임 for a casual pickup game (한 게임 하자), though 농구 경기 is still the word for a formal or broadcast match — so 게임 here is not a mistake the way it would be for a pro 축구 fixture. The two pitfalls are the loanword 바스켓볼 (never used; only 농구) and calling the hoop 농구 문 ('basketball door') instead of the correct 골대.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 바스켓볼 — Koreans only say 농구.
Saying 농구 문 ('basketball door') for the hoop; the correct word is 골대 (or 농구 골대).
Forcing 경기 onto every casual game — for pickup hoops, 농구 한 게임 하자 is perfectly natural, unlike with pro soccer.

entries.shortExplanation: 배구 means "volleyball" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배구 (baegu) = "volleyball". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 배구 좋아해요? ("Do you like volleyball?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배구, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Women's pro volleyball (V-리그) has a strong, growing fanbase in Korea.

usagePhrases.en: Did you watch the volleyball match?
usagePhrases.note: 경기 is the standard word for a formal match in any sport.
국가대표(國家代表) = 'national team', often heard around 김연경 and the Olympics.
배구 was a staple P.E. and 체육대회 (sports day) game for many Koreans.

examples.ko: 김연경 선수 덕분에 배구 팬이 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: gimyeongyeong seonsu deokbune baegu paeni manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to Kim Yeon-koung, volleyball gained a lot of fans.
examples.note: 덕분에 = 'thanks to' (positive cause only); 선수 = 'athlete', a respectful tag after a name.

examples.ko: 우리 회사 체육대회 때 배구 시합 했어요.
examples.romanization: uri hoesa cheyukdaehoe ttae baegu siha paesseoyo.
examples.en: We had a volleyball match at our company sports day.
examples.note: 시합 = match/contest, interchangeable with 경기 in casual use; 때 = 'at the time of'.

examples.ko: 배구는 키가 큰 선수들이 유리한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: baeguneun kiga keun seonsudeuri yurihan geot gatayo.
examples.en: It seems taller players have an advantage in volleyball.
examples.note: 유리하다 = 'be advantageous'; -ㄴ 것 같다 softens it to 'it seems'.

entries.nuance: 배구 (排球, literally 'push/arrange(排)-ball(球)', capturing how the ball is set and pushed over the net) surged in popularity through women's pro volleyball and especially 김연경 (Kim Yeon-koung), making it a warmer small-talk topic than before. It is also a nostalgic schoolyard and company sports-day (체육대회) game. For a match you can use 경기 or the slightly more casual, contest-flavored 시합 (試合) — the dividing line is that 시합 emphasizes the head-to-head contest while 경기 is the neutral all-purpose term. The pitfall for English speakers is the loanword 발리볼, which sounds foreign and is never used; say 배구. Also note 배구 is a clear two-syllable word, so it never gets confused in practice with the bare 배 (boat/stomach/pear).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 발리볼 — the Korean word is 배구.
Assuming 시합 and 경기 are different things — they overlap heavily; 시합 just leans toward 'contest/bout' while 경기 is neutral.
Dropping a syllable to 배 — the sport is always the full 배구; 배 alone means boat/stomach/pear.

entries.shortExplanation: 탁구 means "table tennis, ping-pong" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 탁구 (takgu) means "table tennis, ping-pong". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 탁구 칠 줄 알아요? ("Can you play table tennis?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 탁구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Note the verb: 탁구는 치다 ('hit'), not 하다 — like other paddle/racket sports.

usagePhrases.en: Shall we play a round of ping-pong?
usagePhrases.note: 치다 + 판; -ㄹ까요 makes it a soft 'shall we?' suggestion at a community center.
Dedicated 탁구장 are common in neighborhoods and apartment complexes.
The paddle is 라켓; the table itself is 탁구대.

examples.en: During lunch we play ping-pong in the office lounge.
examples.note: 휴게실 = 'break room'; note 탁구 쳐요 (from 치다), and 에서 marks the location of the action.

examples.ko: 탁구는 운동도 되고 재미도 있어서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: takguneun undongdo doego jaemido isseoseo joayo.
examples.en: Table tennis is good because it's both exercise and fun.
examples.note: 운동이 되다 = 'count as exercise'; -도...-도 = 'both...and'.

examples.ko: 아파트 주민센터에 탁구대가 있어서 자주 쳐요.
examples.romanization: apateu juminsenteoe takgudaega isseoseo jaju chyeoyo.
examples.en: There's a table tennis table at the apartment center, so I play often.
examples.note: 있어서 = 'there is, so'; the object 탁구 is dropped before 쳐요 because it's understood.

entries.nuance: 탁구 (卓球, literally 'table(卓)-ball(球)') is crucial for one reason English speakers stumble on: it takes the verb 치다 ('to hit/strike'), NOT 하다 — you say 탁구를 치다. This 치다 is the same verb used for hitting a ball with an implement (tennis, golf, drums), the dividing line from 하다, which is for sports you do with your whole body or feet (축구를 하다). It is an accessible, low-cost way to socialize, found in 탁구장, apartment community rooms, and office break rooms. Vocabulary to keep straight: the table is 탁구대 and the paddle is 라켓. A register pitfall: calling it 핑퐁 in conversation sounds childish or cutesy; adults say 탁구.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 탁구 하다 instead of the natural 탁구 치다 — paddle sports take 치다.
Calling it 핑퐁 in adult conversation — that sounds childish; say 탁구.
Mixing up 탁구대 (the table) and 라켓 (the paddle) — they are different pieces of equipment.

The verb is the thing English speakers stumble on: it is 치다, not 하다. A register pitfall: calling it 핑퐁 in conversation sounds childish or cutesy; adults say 탁구.

entries.shortExplanation: 테니스 means "tennis" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "tennis" is 테니스 (teniseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 테니스 쳐요? ("Do you play tennis?"). Watch the particle attached to 테니스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Like table tennis, tennis takes 치다 (to hit), not 하다.
-고 있다 = ongoing; 테니스 has boomed as a trendy lesson-based hobby for 20-30s.
예약하다 = 'reserve'; public 테니스장 fill up fast and are booked by app.
레슨 is the standard word; beginners often start with a 강습/레슨 package.

examples.ko: 요즘 테니스 배우는 사람 진짜 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum teniseu baeuneun saram jinjja manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: These days way more people are learning tennis.
examples.note: 많아지다 = 'become many/increase'; 요즘 sets the recent-trend frame.

examples.ko: 주말에 테니스장 잡기가 하늘의 별 따기예요.
examples.romanization: jumare teniseujang japgiga haneurui byeol ttagiyeyo.
examples.en: Booking a court on weekends is like picking a star from the sky.
examples.note: 하늘의 별 따기 = idiom for 'nearly impossible'; 잡다 here = 'secure/book'.

examples.ko: 테니스 치고 나면 온몸이 다 쑤셔요.
examples.romanization: teniseu chigo namyeon onmomi da ssusyeoyo.
examples.en: After playing tennis my whole body aches.
examples.note: -고 나면 = 'after (completing)'; 온몸이 쑤시다 = 'whole body aches'.

entries.nuance: 테니스 is a loanword (no hanja), and the key thing English speakers get wrong is the verb: it is 치다 ('to hit'), exactly like 탁구 and 골프, because you strike a ball with a racket — never 테니스를 하다. In recent years it has become a fashionable lifestyle hobby for Koreans in their 20s-30s, complete with 테니스 룩 (tennis outfits) for social media, so the word now signals a trendy, active social circle. Court booking (테니스장 예약) is genuinely competitive on weekends. One vocabulary contrast worth knowing: the older term 정구 refers specifically to soft tennis and sounds dated, so for the modern racket sport always say 테니스.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 하다 instead of 치다 — racket sports take 치다, so it is 테니스를 치다.
Saying 정구 for modern tennis — 정구 is the older soft-tennis term and sounds dated; say 테니스.
Translating 'book a court' word-for-word — Koreans say 테니스장 예약하다, with 예약 ('reservation'), not a literal rendering of 'book'.

entries.shortExplanation: 골프 means "golf" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 골프 (golpeu) = "golf". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 골프 쳐요? ("Do you play golf?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 골프, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Golf also takes 치다; a common question among professionals and older colleagues.
스크린 골프 (indoor simulator golf) is hugely popular and affordable in Korea.

usagePhrases.en: I'm in the middle of learning golf
usagePhrases.note: -는 중이다 = 'in the process of'; golf lessons have spread to younger people.
골프장 = the course; 'going out to the course' = 필드 나가다.

examples.ko: 주말에 친구들이랑 스크린 골프 치러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jumare chingudeurirang seukeurin golpeu chireo gasseoyo.
examples.en: On the weekend I went to play screen golf with friends.
examples.note: 치러 가다 = 'go in order to play (hit)'; 스크린 골프 is social and often paired with drinks.

examples.en: Golf is daunting to start because the equipment is expensive.
examples.note: 부담되다 = 'feel burdensome'; -기 turns 시작하다 into the noun 'starting'.

examples.ko: 부장님이 주말마다 골프 치러 필드 나가세요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimi jumalmada golpeu chireo pildeu nagaseyo.
examples.en: My boss goes out to the course to play golf every weekend.
examples.note: 필드 나가다 = 'go out to the real course'; -세요 is the honorific for the senior 부장님.

entries.nuance: 골프 is a loanword (no hanja), and like the other racket/club sports it takes 치다 ('to hit') — 골프를 치다, never 골프를 하다, because you strike the ball with a club. Socially it carries a slightly upscale, business-networking image, but 스크린 골프 (screen/simulator golf) has made it casual and accessible — a common night out with friends and coworkers. Two insider words English speakers should learn: the real outdoor course is called 필드 ('field'), and 필드 나가다 means 'go play on an actual course' (as opposed to the screen). In casual speech, plain 골프 치러 가자 often actually means 스크린 골프, so don't assume every mention implies an expensive outdoor round.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 골프 하다 instead of 골프 치다 — club-and-ball sports take 치다.
Assuming 골프 always means an expensive outdoor round — in casual speech it often means 스크린 골프.
Not knowing 필드 — Koreans call the real course 필드 and say 필드 나가다 for playing outdoors; 골프장 is the formal term.

structuredNuance.t: A loanword (no hanja). Socially it carries a slightly upscale, business-networking image, but 스크린 골프 (screen/simulator golf) has made it casual and accessible — a common night out with friends and coworkers. Two insider words to learn: the real outdoor course is called 필드 ('field'), and 필드 나가다 means 'go play on an actual course' (as opposed to the screen).
Like the other racket/club sports it takes 치다 ('to hit') — 골프를 치다, never 골프를 하다, because you strike the ball with a club.
Do not say 골프를 하다 — it is 치다. And in casual speech, plain 골프 치러 가자 often actually means 스크린 골프, so don't assume every mention implies an expensive outdoor round.

entries.shortExplanation: 스키 means "skiing, ski" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스키 (seuki) means "skiing, ski". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스키 탈 줄 알아요? ("Do you know how to ski?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스키 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Do you know how to ski?
usagePhrases.note: Crucial verb: 스키는 타다 ('ride'), used for gear you stand on and ride.
타러 가다 = 'go in order to ride/do'; winter resort trips are common.
스키장 covers the whole resort; the major ones are in 강원도.
빌리다 = 'borrow/rent'; renting (대여) gear at the resort is normal for casual skiers.

examples.ko: 겨울에 강원도로 스키 타러 갈 거예요.
examples.romanization: gyeoure gangwondoro seuki tareo gal geoyeyo.
examples.en: This winter I'm going to Gangwon-do to ski.
examples.note: -로 marks direction toward 강원도; 타러 가다 = 'go to ski'.

examples.en: It was my first time skiing, so I rode the beginner course.
examples.note: 처음이라 = 'since it's the first time'; 초보자 코스 = 'beginner course'.

examples.ko: 스키 탈 때 넘어지면 진짜 아파요.
examples.romanization: seuki tal ttae neomeojimyeon jinjja apayo.
examples.en: When you fall while skiing, it really hurts.
examples.note: 넘어지다 = 'fall down'; -ㄹ 때 = 'when/while doing'.

entries.nuance: 스키 is a loanword (no hanja), and the verb is the whole lesson here: it takes 타다 ('to ride'), never 하다 — 스키를 타다. 타다 is the verb for anything you mount, board, or stand on to move (bus, bike, ski, skateboard), which is exactly why ski, snowboard, and skates all use it rather than 하다. Winter ski trips to 강원도 resorts are a popular group outing, often combined with 보드 (snowboarding) at the same place. The resort and slopes together are 스키장, and gear rental (대여/빌리다) is the norm for casual participants. The pitfall, besides 스키 하다, is conflating 스키 with 보드/스노보드 — they are different activities done at the same 스키장.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스키 하다 — the correct verb is 스키 타다 (you ride skis).
Confusing 스키 (skiing) with 보드/스노보드 (snowboarding) — different sports at the same 스키장.
Using 하다 for board sports too — snowboarding is also 보드(를) 타다, not 하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 스케이트 means "skating, ice skating" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "skating, ice skating" is 스케이트 (seukeiteu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스케이트 탈 줄 알아요? ("Can you skate?"). Watch the particle attached to 스케이트 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Like 스키, skating takes 타다, since you stand on the blades and ride.
타러 가자 = casual 'let's go to skate'; a popular winter date activity.
스케이트장 = the ice rink; seasonal outdoor rinks pop up in winter.
스케이트화 = the boots themselves (화 = 'footwear'); rented at the rink.

examples.en: In winter I went skating at an outdoor rink.
examples.note: 야외 = 'outdoor'; seasonal rinks at city plazas are popular dates.

examples.ko: 스케이트 처음 타는 사람은 벽 잡고 타요.
examples.romanization: seukeiteu cheoeum taneun sarameun byeok japgo tayo.
examples.en: First-timers skate while holding onto the wall.
examples.note: 벽 잡고 = 'gripping the wall'; -고 links the two simultaneous actions.

examples.ko: 김연아 덕분에 피겨 스케이트 인기가 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: gimyeona deokbune pigyeo seukeiteu ingiga manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to Kim Yu-na, figure skating became very popular.
examples.note: 피겨 스케이트 = 'figure skating'; 덕분에 marks the positive cause.

entries.nuance: 스케이트 is a loanword (no hanja) and, like 스키, takes 타다 ('to ride') — 스케이트를 타다 — because you stand on the blades and glide; 하다 is wrong. Korea has a strong skating culture thanks to short-track and figure stars like 김연아 (Kim Yu-na), and seasonal outdoor 스케이트장 are a classic winter date spot. The vocabulary to keep distinct trips up English speakers: 스케이트장 is the rink (place), while 스케이트화 is the boots (화 = footwear), and bare 스케이트 can mean the activity or loosely the gear. Also distinguish ice 스케이트 from 인라인/롤러 (inline/roller skating), which likewise take 타다 but happen on wheels, not ice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스케이트 하다 instead of 스케이트 타다 — you ride skates, so it's 타다.
Mixing 스케이트장 (the rink) with 스케이트화 (the boots) — one is the place, one is the footwear.
Assuming 스케이트 means roller skating — that's 인라인/롤러; plain 스케이트 defaults to ice skating.

entries.shortExplanation: 마라톤 means "marathon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 마라톤 (maraton) = "marathon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마라톤 뛰어요? ("Do you run marathons?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 마라톤, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Marathons take the verb 뛰다 (to run); 달리다 also works.
대회(大會) = 'tournament/event'; weekend city marathons are common.
하프(half) 마라톤 — many beginners start here before a 풀코스 (full course).

usagePhrases.en: I signed up for a marathon
usagePhrases.note: 신청하다 = 'apply/register'; entries open online and fill up fast.

examples.ko: 이번 가을에 처음으로 하프 마라톤 뛰어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon gaeure cheoeumeuro hapeu maraton ttwieoyo.
examples.en: This fall I'm running my first half marathon.
examples.note: 처음으로 = 'for the first time'; the present tense here states a fixed near plan.

examples.en: If you finish the marathon, they give you a medal.
examples.note: 완주(完走)하다 = 'run the full course'; -면 = 'if/when', 줘요 has an unstated 'they'.

examples.ko: 요즘 러닝이 유행이라 마라톤 대회마다 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum neoningi yuhaengira maraton daehoemada sarami manayo.
examples.en: Running is trendy lately, so every marathon event is packed.
examples.note: 유행이라 = 'since it's a trend'; 마다 = 'every (single)'.

entries.nuance: 마라톤 is a loanword (no hanja) and fits the current 러닝 (running) boom among Koreans in their 20s-30s, where running crews and weekend 마라톤 대회 are genuinely trendy social scenes. The verb is 뛰다 or 달리다 ('to run') — not 하다; the fine distinction is that 뛰다 is the everyday word that also means 'jump/sprint', while 달리다 is a touch more squarely 'run/dash', and for marathons the two are interchangeable. Useful related words: 완주 (完走, 'complete the run') means finishing the full distance, and many start with a 하프 마라톤 before attempting the 풀코스. The pitfall for English speakers is assuming 마라톤 always means the full 42.195km; in casual use it loosely covers any race distance run at a 마라톤 대회.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 마라톤 하다 — natural Korean is 마라톤(을) 뛰다 or 마라톤(을) 달리다.
Assuming 마라톤 always means the full 42.195km — casually it can mean any race distance at a 마라톤 대회.
Forgetting 완주 — 'finishing' a marathon is 완주하다, a specific word, not just 끝내다 ('end it').

entries.shortExplanation: 경기 means "match, game (sporting event)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 경기 (gyeonggi) means "match, game (sporting event)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 경기 봤어요? ("Did you watch the game?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 경기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 경기 is the standard word for a sports match in any sport.
시작하다 = 'begin'; said the moment a match kicks off.
결과(結果) = 'result'; 경기 결과 is how you ask the final score/outcome.
있다 = 'there is'; a common check before planning to watch.

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 중요한 축구 경기가 있어요.
examples.romanization: oneul jeonyeoge jungyohan chukgu gyeonggiga isseoyo.
examples.en: There's an important soccer match this evening.
examples.note: Attach 경기 after the sport: 축구 경기, 야구 경기; 이/가 있다 = 'there is'.

examples.ko: 경기가 너무 박빙이라 끝까지 손에 땀을 쥐었어요.
examples.romanization: gyeonggiga neomu bakbingira kkeutkkaji sone ttameul jwieosseoyo.
examples.en: The game was so close I was on edge until the end.
examples.note: 박빙 = 'neck and neck'; 손에 땀을 쥐다 = idiom 'be on the edge of your seat'.

examples.en: The game was canceled today because of rain.
examples.note: 취소되다 = 'be canceled' (passive); 비 와서 = 'because it rained'.

entries.nuance: 경기 (競技, literally 'compete(競)-skill(技)', i.e. a contest of skill) is the all-purpose word for a sporting match and pairs with any sport (축구 경기, 야구 경기). The key contrast for English speakers is register: 경기 is the neutral, formal-friendly term for pro and broadcast sports, whereas the loanword 게임 fits casual pickup play — so defaulting to 게임 for a real match sounds off. A close synonym is 시합 (試合), which leans slightly toward 'contest/bout' and is common in spoken, head-to-head contexts; 경기 stays the safe neutral choice. The classic trap is the homophone: 경기 also means 'the economy' (경기가 안 좋다 = 'the economy is bad'), an unrelated word with different hanja (景氣) — only context tells them apart, but in a sports conversation 경기 is always the match.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Defaulting to 게임 for a pro match — use 경기 for real sporting events; 게임 implies casual play.
Treating 경기 and 시합 as totally separate — they overlap; 시합 just emphasizes the contest, 경기 is neutral.
Confusing 경기 (競技, sports match) with the homophone 경기 (景氣, the economy), as in 경기가 안 좋다 — different word, context disambiguates.

競技, literally 'compete(競)-skill(技)', i.e. a contest of skill.

entries.shortExplanation: 심판 means "referee, umpire" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "referee, umpire" is 심판 (simpan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 심판이 휘슬 불었어요 ("The referee blew the whistle"). Watch the particle attached to 심판 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 휘슬(을) 불다 = 'blow the whistle'; signals a foul or stoppage.
판정(判定) = 'ruling/decision'; 심판 판정 often sparks fan complaints.
A heated shout at a bad call; 똑바로 = 'properly', 봐 is blunt 반말.
오심(誤審) = a refereeing error; a very common sports-news word.

examples.ko: 심판이 우리 팀한테만 불리하게 판정하는 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: simpani uri timhanteman bullihage panjeonghaneun geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: It felt like the ref was ruling unfairly against only our team.
examples.note: 한테만 = 'only against'; 불리하게 = 'disadvantageously'.

examples.en: Anyone can see that play was a wrong call.
examples.note: 누가 봐도 = 'no matter who looks / obviously'; 오심 = 'bad call'.

examples.ko: 요즘은 비디오 판독으로 심판 오심을 줄여요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun bidio pandogeuro simpan osimeul juryeoyo.
examples.en: These days they reduce referee errors with video review.
examples.note: 비디오 판독 = 'video review (VAR-style)'; -으로 = 'by means of'.

entries.nuance: 심판 (審判, literally 'examine(審)-judge(判)') is the referee/umpire across all sports, and it doubles as both the official (person) and the act of officiating. To follow sports talk you need its companions: 판정 (判定, 'ruling/decision'), 오심 (誤審, 'erroneous judgment' = a wrong call), and 비디오 판독 (video review), since fans endlessly grumble about 심판 판정. The whistle collocation is 휘슬을 불다. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not say 레퍼리 — the natural word is 심판, the loanword sounds out of place. Second, 심판 has a heavier non-sports sense of divine 'judgment' (최후의 심판 = 'the Last Judgment'); in a sports context it strictly means the on-field official, so context keeps the two apart.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 레퍼리 — Koreans say 심판, not the English loanword.
Confusing 심판 (referee) with the judgment/verdict sense (최후의 심판 'the Last Judgment') — in sports it's strictly the official.
Saying 심판 실수 for a bad call when the precise term exists — a misjudged call is 오심 (誤審), the standard sports-news word.

entries.shortExplanation: 망치 means "hammer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 망치 (mangchi) = "hammer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 망치 ("hammer") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 망치, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday tool for driving nails; a basic item in any 공구함.

usagePhrases.en: to drive a nail in with a hammer
usagePhrases.note: 못을 박다 = drive a nail in; the tool takes the (으)로 particle, not 을/를.
Noun + 질 turns the tool into the activity; 망치질하다 = to hammer.
고무(rubber) + 망치; soft head for furniture so it leaves no marks.

examples.en: This is a hammer.
examples.note: Plain naming sentence; 망치 ends in a vowel so it takes 예요, not 이에요.

examples.ko: 벽에 액자 걸려고 망치로 못을 박았어요.
examples.romanization: byeoge aekja geollyeogo mangchiro moseul bagasseoyo.
examples.en: I hammered a nail into the wall to hang a frame.
examples.note: 걸려고 = in order to hang; the action verb is 박다, and 망치로 marks the instrument.

examples.ko: 고무망치는 가구 조립할 때 흠집 안 나서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gomumangchineun gagu joripal ttae heumjip an naseo joayo.
examples.en: A rubber mallet is good for assembling furniture since it doesn't leave marks.
examples.note: 흠집(이) 나다 = a scratch forms; this is the register a Korean uses while doing IKEA-style assembly.

entries.nuance: 망치는 못이나 핀을 두드려 박을 때 쓰는 가장 기본적인 손공구입니다. 영어 'hammer'는 명사이자 동사이지만, 한국어 '망치'는 순수 명사라서 '망치하다'라는 동사는 없고, 반드시 '망치로 못을 박다(drive a nail with a hammer)'처럼 도구(으)로 + 동작 동사 구조로 풀어 써야 합니다. 이것이 영어 화자가 가장 자주 빠지는 직역 함정입니다. 두드리는 행위 자체는 '망치질'이라 하고, 비슷한 도구인 '망치(claw hammer)'와 '고무망치(rubber mallet)'는 머리 재질로 구분합니다. 흔히 '못을 박다, 망치질을 하다, 망치로 두드리다'처럼 어울려 쓰며, 도구를 나타낼 때 '망치를'이 아니라 '망치로'를 쓰는 점을 꼭 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 망치를 치다 or 망치하다 — Korean has no verb form of the tool; the natural phrase is 망치로 못을 박다 (drive the nail), with 망치 marked by 로.
Marking the hammer with 을/를 as if it were the object: 망치를 박다 is wrong. You drive the 못(nail) and the hammer is the instrument → 망치로.
Confusing 망치 (hammer) with 못 (nail); the hammer is what hits, the 못 is what gets hit.

structuredNuance.t: 망치는 못이나 핀을 두드려 박을 때 쓰는 가장 기본적인 손공구입니다. 두드리는 행위 자체는 '망치질'이라 하고, 흔히 '못을 박다, 망치질을 하다, 망치로 두드리다'처럼 어울려 씁니다.
비슷한 도구인 '망치(claw hammer)'와 '고무망치(rubber mallet)'는 머리 재질로 구분합니다.

영어 'hammer'는 명사이자 동사이지만, 한국어 '망치'는 순수 명사라서 '망치하다'라는 동사는 없고, 반드시 '망치로 못을 박다(drive a nail with a hammer)'처럼 도구(으)로 + 동작 동사 구조로 풀어 써야 합니다. 이것이 영어 화자가 가장 자주 빠지는 직역 함정입니다. 도구를 나타낼 때 '망치를'이 아니라 '망치로'를 쓰는 점을 꼭 기억하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 못 means "nail (for hammering)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 못 (mot) means "nail (for hammering)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 못 ("nail"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 못 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The metal nail you hammer in; written the same as 못 'cannot' but a separate word.
박다 = drive/embed; the standard verb that pairs with 못, never 넣다.
빼다 = pull out; use pliers (펜치) or the claw of a hammer.
The dent or hole left in the wall; too many can mean a deposit deduction.

examples.en: There's a nail here.
examples.note: 못 ends in a consonant, so the subject form is 못이, not 못가.

examples.ko: 전셋집이라 못 박는 거 조심해야 돼요.
examples.romanization: jeonsetjibira mot bangneun geo josimhaeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: It's a jeonse place, so I have to be careful about hammering nails.
examples.note: Here 못 is the noun object of 박다; landlords may deduct from the deposit for wall damage.

examples.ko: 벽에 못 자국 남으면 보증금에서 깎일 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: byeoge mot jagung nameumyeon bojeunggeumeseo kkakkil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: If nail marks are left on the wall, it could be deducted from the deposit.
examples.note: 못 자국 = nail marks; 깎이다 = get docked — a real concern in Korean rentals.

entries.nuance: 못은 망치로 벽이나 나무에 두드려 박는 금속 핀입니다. 같은 도구류라도 '못'은 두드려서 고정하고 '나사(screw)'는 돌려서 고정한다는 점이 핵심 차이라, 못에는 '박다/빼다', 나사에는 '조이다/풀다'를 씁니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 'put a nail in'을 직역해 '못을 넣다'라고 하기 쉬운데, 못은 '넣다(put in)'가 아니라 '박다(drive in)'와 어울립니다. 둘째, 부정 부사 '못'(못 가요 = can't go)과 글자가 똑같아 헷갈리지만, 명사 못은 '못이, 못을'처럼 조사가 붙고 부사 못은 동사 앞에 홀로 옵니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '못을 박다, 못을 빼다, 못 자국, 못이 박히다(get driven in, 피동)'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up the noun 못 (nail) with the adverb 못 used for inability (못 해요 = can't do). The noun takes particles (못을), the adverb sits bare before a verb.
Using 넣다 from English 'put a nail in' — a nail is 박다 (driven in) with force, not just 넣다 (placed in).
Saying 못을 치다 for hammering a nail; the verb is 못을 박다 (the hammer does the 치다, the nail gets 박다).

structuredNuance.t: 못은 망치로 벽이나 나무에 두드려 박는 금속 핀입니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '못을 박다, 못을 빼다, 못 자국, 못이 박히다(get driven in, 피동)'입니다.
같은 도구류라도 '못'은 두드려서 고정하고 '나사(screw)'는 돌려서 고정한다는 점이 핵심 차이라, 못에는 '박다/빼다', 나사에는 '조이다/풀다'를 씁니다.

영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 'put a nail in'을 직역해 '못을 넣다'라고 하기 쉬운데, 못은 '넣다(put in)'가 아니라 '박다(drive in)'와 어울립니다. 둘째, 부정 부사 '못'(못 가요 = can't go)과 글자가 똑같아 헷갈리지만, 명사 못은 '못이, 못을'처럼 조사가 붙고 부사 못은 동사 앞에 홀로 옵니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 드라이버 means "screwdriver" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "screwdriver" is 드라이버 (deuraibeo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 드라이버 ("screwdriver"). Watch the particle attached to 드라이버 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The hand tool for screws; the same loanword also means a golf 'driver', so context matters.
십자(十字) = cross-shaped; the type you need most often at home.
일자(一字) = straight-line shape; for slotted screws.

usagePhrases.en: to loosen a screw with a screwdriver
usagePhrases.note: 풀다 = loosen/undo; 조이다 = tighten — the verb pair to learn together.

examples.en: Please hand me the screwdriver.
examples.note: Simple request; 드라이버 ends in a vowel so 주세요 attaches cleanly with no extra particle needed in casual speech.

examples.ko: 콘센트 커버 갈려면 십자드라이버 있어야 돼요.
examples.romanization: konsenteu keobeo gallyeomyeon sipjadeuraibeo isseoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: To change the outlet cover, you need a Phillips screwdriver.
examples.note: 갈다 = replace; here 십자 specifies the cross head so the listener brings the right one.

examples.ko: 안경 나사 풀렸는데 정밀 드라이버 있어요?
examples.romanization: angyeong nasa pullyeonneunde jeongmil deuraibeo isseoyo?
examples.en: My glasses screw came loose — do you have a precision screwdriver?
examples.note: 정밀(精密) 드라이버 = the tiny screwdriver for glasses/electronics; note the polite 있어요? for asking to borrow.

entries.nuance: 드라이버는 나사를 돌려 풀고 조이는 손공구입니다. 이름 그대로 영어 'driver'를 빌린 외래어인데, 한국어에서는 같은 발음이 골프채 '드라이버'와 운전자 'driver(기사·드라이버)' 뜻으로도 쓰여서 철물점·공구 맥락이 아니면 오해할 수 있습니다. 영어로는 'screwdriver'지만 한국어에서는 'screw'에 해당하는 부분을 빼고 그냥 '드라이버'라고만 하므로, '스크루드라이버'라고 말하면 어색합니다. 머리 모양에 따라 '십자(十字, cross-shaped)드라이버=Phillips'와 '일자(一字, single-line)드라이버=flathead'로 나뉘고, 작은 것은 '정밀 드라이버'라 합니다. 늘 나사와 함께 '나사를 풀다(loosen)/조이다(tighten)' 동사를 짝지어 외우면 자연스럽습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스크루드라이버 — Korean drops the 'screw' part; it is simply 드라이버. Saying the full English compound sounds unnatural.
Assuming 드라이버 always means a golf club or a chauffeur — at the hardware store or for repairs it means a screwdriver; context disambiguates.
Mixing up 십자(Phillips) and 일자(flat) heads when asking for one; the wrong head won't fit the screw slot.

structuredNuance.t: 드라이버는 나사를 돌려 풀고 조이는 손공구입니다. 머리 모양에 따라 '십자(十字, cross-shaped)드라이버=Phillips'와 '일자(一字, single-line)드라이버=flathead'로 나뉘고, 작은 것은 '정밀 드라이버'라 합니다. 늘 나사와 함께 '나사를 풀다(loosen)/조이다(tighten)' 동사를 짝지어 외우면 자연스럽습니다.
이름 그대로 영어 'driver'를 빌린 외래어인데, 한국어에서는 같은 발음이 골프채 '드라이버'와 운전자 'driver(기사·드라이버)' 뜻으로도 쓰여서 철물점·공구 맥락이 아니면 오해할 수 있습니다.
영어로는 'screwdriver'지만 한국어에서는 'screw'에 해당하는 부분을 빼고 그냥 '드라이버'라고만 하므로, '스크루드라이버'라고 말하면 어색합니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 나사 means "screw" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 나사 (nasa) = "screw". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 나사 ("screw") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 나사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The threaded fastener you turn with a 드라이버, as opposed to a hammered 못.
조이다 = tighten; the key verb to memorize with 나사.
풀다 = loosen; the opposite of 조이다.

usagePhrases.en: for a screw to come loose / fall out
usagePhrases.note: Also a slang idiom: 나사(가) 빠졌다 = to be spaced out / off one's game.

examples.en: The screw is small.
examples.note: Basic description; 나사 ends in a vowel so the subject marker is 나사가.

examples.en: The chair was wobbly, so I retightened the screws.
examples.note: 흔들거리다 = wobble; 다시 조이다 = tighten again — the everyday fix for loose furniture.

examples.ko: 나사 하나 모자라서 가구 조립을 못 끝냈어요.
examples.romanization: nasa hana mojaraseo gagu joribeul mot kkeunnaesseoyo.
examples.en: I was one screw short, so I couldn't finish assembling the furniture.
examples.note: 모자라다 = be short of; a common frustration with flat-pack furniture (note 못 끝내다 = couldn't finish).

entries.nuance: 나사는 드라이버로 돌려 박아 고정하는 나선형 부품으로, 영어 'screw'에 해당합니다. 핵심 구분은 옆 단어 '못(nail)'입니다. 못은 망치로 두드려 박고 동사 '박다/빼다'와 쓰지만, 나사는 돌려서 고정하므로 '조이다(tighten)/풀다(loosen)'와 어울립니다. 따라서 영어 'put in a screw'를 '나사를 박다'로 직역하면 어색하고, '나사를 조이다'가 자연스럽습니다. 비슷한 부품으로 끝이 뾰족하지 않고 너트와 짝을 이루는 '볼트(bolt)'가 따로 있으니 혼동하지 마세요. 또 일상에서 '나사(가) 빠졌다'는 실제 나사가 풀렸다는 뜻 외에 '사람이 정신이 좀 없다·멍하다'는 농담조 관용구로도 자주 쓰입니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '나사를 조이다/풀다, 나사가 헐거워지다, 나사가 빠지다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 박다 for screws from English 'put in' — you 조이다/풀다 (turn) a 나사, you don't 박다 (drive) it like a nail.
Confusing 나사 (screw, turned in) with 못 (nail, hammered in); the fastening method decides the word.
Calling a bolt a 나사 in technical contexts — a 볼트(bolt) pairs with a nut and is distinct, though casual speech blurs them.

structuredNuance.t: 나사는 드라이버로 돌려 박아 고정하는 나선형 부품으로, 영어 'screw'에 해당합니다. 일상에서 '나사(가) 빠졌다'는 실제 나사가 풀렸다는 뜻 외에 '사람이 정신이 좀 없다·멍하다'는 농담조 관용구로도 자주 쓰입니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '나사를 조이다/풀다, 나사가 헐거워지다, 나사가 빠지다'입니다.
핵심 구분은 옆 단어 '못(nail)'입니다. 못은 망치로 두드려 박고 동사 '박다/빼다'와 쓰지만, 나사는 돌려서 고정하므로 '조이다(tighten)/풀다(loosen)'와 어울립니다. 비슷한 부품으로 끝이 뾰족하지 않고 너트와 짝을 이루는 '볼트(bolt)'가 따로 있으니 혼동하지 마세요.
영어 'put in a screw'를 '나사를 박다'로 직역하면 어색하고, '나사를 조이다'가 자연스럽습니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 줄자 means "tape measure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 줄자 (julja) means "tape measure". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 줄자 ("tape measure"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 줄자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The retractable measuring tape; 줄(line/cord) + 자(ruler).

usagePhrases.en: to measure with a tape measure
usagePhrases.note: 재다 = measure; the verb that pairs with any measuring tool, marked by 로.
치수 = dimensions; what you check before buying furniture.
Set phrase for sizing a space: 가로(width, horizontal) 세로(length, vertical).

examples.en: Try measuring it with a tape measure.
examples.note: 재 보다 = give measuring a try; the tool takes 로 (줄자로), not 을.

examples.ko: 냉장고 들어갈 자리 줄자로 먼저 재 보세요.
examples.romanization: naengjanggo deureogal jari juljaro meonjeo jae boseyo.
examples.en: Measure the spot where the fridge will go with a tape measure first.
examples.note: 들어갈 자리 = the spot it'll fit into; 먼저 = first, stressing you measure before buying.

examples.ko: 이 책상 가로세로 좀 재 줄래? 새 방에 들어갈지 봐야 돼.
examples.romanization: i chaeksang garosero jom jae jullae? sae bange deureogalji bwaya dwae.
examples.en: Can you measure this desk's width and length? I need to see if it fits the new room.
examples.note: 들어갈지 = whether it'll fit; casual 재 줄래? asks a friend for the favor.

entries.nuance: 줄자는 둘둘 말리는 띠로 길이나 공간의 치수를 잴 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 이름은 '줄(line/cord)' + '자(ruler)'가 합쳐진 말이라, 빳빳한 막대 모양의 '자(straight ruler)'와 구분됩니다. 곧고 짧은 길이는 '자'로 재고, 가구·가전이 들어갈 큰 공간은 휘어지며 길게 늘어나는 '줄자'로 잽니다. 동사는 영어 'measure'에 해당하는 '재다'를 쓰는데, 영어 화자는 'see/check the length'를 직역해 '길이를 보다'라고 하기 쉽습니다. 길이는 '보다(look)'가 아니라 '재다(measure)'와 어울립니다. 공간을 잴 때는 '가로(width)세로(length)'를 함께 말하는 게 자연스럽고, 도구는 '줄자를'이 아니라 '줄자로 재다'처럼 (으)로로 표시합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '치수를 재다, 길이를 재다, 줄자로 재다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 자 alone for the flexible tape — a plain 자 is a rigid straight ruler; the retractable one is specifically 줄자.
Saying 길이를 보다 from English 'check the length' — you 재다 (measure) a length, you don't 보다 (look at) it.
Marking the tool with 을/를: 줄자를 재다 is wrong; the instrument takes 로 → 줄자로 재다.

structuredNuance.t: 줄자는 둘둘 말리는 띠로 길이나 공간의 치수를 잴 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 동사는 영어 'measure'에 해당하는 '재다'를 씁니다. 공간을 잴 때는 '가로(width)세로(length)'를 함께 말하는 게 자연스럽고, 도구는 '줄자를'이 아니라 '줄자로 재다'처럼 (으)로로 표시합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '치수를 재다, 길이를 재다, 줄자로 재다'입니다.
이름은 '줄(line/cord)' + '자(ruler)'가 합쳐진 말이라, 빳빳한 막대 모양의 '자(straight ruler)'와 구분됩니다. 곧고 짧은 길이는 '자'로 재고, 가구·가전이 들어갈 큰 공간은 휘어지며 길게 늘어나는 '줄자'로 잽니다.
영어 화자는 'see/check the length'를 직역해 '길이를 보다'라고 하기 쉽습니다. 길이는 '보다(look)'가 아니라 '재다(measure)'와 어울립니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 사다리 means "ladder" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ladder" is 사다리 (sadari). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사다리 ("ladder"). Watch the particle attached to 사다리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: For reaching high places; a folding step ladder is common at home.
올라가다 = go up; 에 marks the thing you climb onto, not 를.
사다리 + 차(車, vehicle); the truck-mounted lift used on Korean moving days.
A popular way to decide who pays/loses by drawing ladder lines.

examples.en: The ladder is tall.
examples.note: Simple description; 사다리 ends in a vowel so the subject form is 사다리가.

examples.ko: 전등 갈아야 하는데 사다리 좀 잡아 줄래?
examples.romanization: jeondeung garaya haneunde sadari jom jaba jullae?
examples.en: I have to change the light — can you hold the ladder for me?
examples.note: 잡아 주다 = hold (for someone's safety); a very common everyday request.

examples.en: When moving, it was the 5th floor, so we called a ladder lift truck.
examples.note: 사다리차(를) 부르다 = call a ladder truck; reflects how high-floor Korean moves actually work.

entries.nuance: 사다리는 디딤대를 밟고 높은 곳에 올라갈 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 비슷해 보이는 '계단(stairs)'과 꼭 구분해야 하는데, 계단은 건물에 붙박이로 설치된 층계이고 사다리는 옮길 수 있는 도구라는 점이 다릅니다. 그래서 천장 전등을 갈 때는 '사다리에 올라가다'라고 하지 '계단에 올라가다'라고 하지 않습니다. 영어와 다른 점은 조사인데, 'climb up the ladder'를 직역해 '사다리를 올라가다'라고 하기 쉽지만, 올라가 닿는 대상은 '에/위에'로 표시해 '사다리에 올라가다'가 자연스럽습니다. 한국 생활에서는 이사 때 높은 층으로 짐을 올리는 '사다리차(ladder lift truck)'와, 커피 내기처럼 순서를 정하는 놀이 '사다리 타기'도 함께 알아 두면 좋습니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '사다리에 올라가다, 사다리를 놓다(set up), 사다리를 잡다(hold)'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계단 (stairs) for 사다리 — 계단 is built-in steps in a building; a portable ladder is 사다리.
Marking with 를: 사다리를 올라가다 from English 'climb the ladder' is awkward; the destination takes 에 → 사다리에 올라가다.
Forgetting 사다리차 on moving day — high-floor moves in Korea rely on the ladder lift truck, a distinct word.

entries.shortExplanation: 페인트 means "paint" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 페인트 (peinteu) = "paint". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 페인트 ("paint") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 페인트, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Wall/furniture coating paint; a loanword from English 'paint'.
칠하다 = coat/apply; the standard verb with 페인트, not 그리다.
페인트 + 칠(漆, lacquer/coating); 페인트칠하다 = to do the painting.
묻다 = get smeared on; warn people about wet paint with this verb.

examples.en: The paint isn't dry yet.
examples.note: 마르다 → 말랐어요 (르-irregular: 르 doubles to ㄹㄹ); 아직 안 ~ = not yet.

examples.ko: 방 분위기 바꾸려고 한쪽 벽에 페인트 칠했어요.
examples.romanization: bang bunwigi bakkuryeogo hanjjok byeoge peinteu chilhaesseoyo.
examples.en: To change the room's mood, I painted one wall.
examples.note: 분위기 = mood/vibe; accent-wall DIY is popular, and 칠하다 is the verb, not 그리다.

examples.en: I bought a roller and masking tape to paint it myself.
examples.note: 셀프 = DIY/by oneself; 롤러 = paint roller — the real-situation register of a weekend project.

entries.nuance: 페인트는 벽이나 가구에 발라 색과 보호막을 입히는 도료로, 영어 'paint'를 그대로 빌린 외래어입니다. 가장 중요한 동사 구분은 '칠하다 vs 그리다'입니다. 한국어에서 '그리다(draw/paint a picture)'는 그림이나 형상을 그릴 때 쓰고, 벽을 색칠하는 것은 반드시 '칠하다(coat)'를 씁니다. 영어 'paint the wall'과 'paint a picture'가 같은 동사라서 영어 화자는 '벽을 그리다'라고 잘못 말하기 쉬운데, 벽에는 '페인트를 칠하다'가 맞습니다. 또 화장품이나 연고를 '바르다(apply/spread)'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 넓은 면을 도료로 덮는 작업은 '바르다'보다 '칠하다'가 자연스럽습니다. 행위 자체는 한자 漆(칠)이 붙은 '페인트칠'이라 하고, 옷에 묻으면 '페인트가 묻다'라고 합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '페인트를 칠하다, 페인트가 마르다, 페인트가 묻다, 셀프 페인트칠'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 벽을 그리다 from English 'paint the wall' — 그리다 is for drawing a picture; coating a wall is 페인트를 칠하다.
Using 바르다 by default — 바르다 fits creams/ointments on a small area; for walls the idiomatic verb is 칠하다.
Forgetting 마스킹테이프 to mask the edges; without it the paint lines come out messy (a practical, not grammatical, slip).

structuredNuance.t: 페인트는 벽이나 가구에 발라 색과 보호막을 입히는 도료로, 영어 'paint'를 그대로 빌린 외래어입니다. 옷에 묻으면 '페인트가 묻다'라고 합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '페인트를 칠하다, 페인트가 마르다, 페인트가 묻다, 셀프 페인트칠'입니다.

행위 자체는 한자 漆(칠)이 붙은 '페인트칠'이라 합니다.
영어 'paint the wall'과 'paint a picture'가 같은 동사라서 영어 화자는 '벽을 그리다'라고 잘못 말하기 쉬운데, 벽에는 '페인트를 칠하다'가 맞습니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 전동드릴 means "power drill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전동드릴 (jeondongdeuril) means "power drill". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전동드릴 ("electric/power drill"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 전동드릴 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 전동(電動) = motor-driven; for boring holes or driving screws fast.
구멍을 뚫다 = bore a hole through; the core phrase for drilling.
충전(充電) = recharge; the cordless kind most people buy now.
비트 = the swappable tip; you swap bits for screws vs. holes.

examples.en: This is a power drill.
examples.note: 전동드릴 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), so the copula is 이에요, not 예요.

examples.ko: 선반 달려고 전동드릴로 벽에 구멍 뚫었어요.
examples.romanization: seonban dallyeogo jeondongdeurillo byeoge gumeong ttureosseoyo.
examples.en: To put up a shelf, I drilled holes in the wall with a power drill.
examples.note: 달다 = mount/hang; 뚫다 = bore through, and the tool takes 로 → 전동드릴로.

examples.ko: 콘크리트 벽은 일반 드릴로는 안 뚫려요.
examples.romanization: konkeuriteu byeogeun ilban deurilloneun an ttulhnyeoyo.
examples.en: You can't drill into a concrete wall with a regular drill.
examples.note: 안 뚫리다 = won't bore through (passive); concrete needs a hammer drill — a real DIY caution.

entries.nuance: 전동드릴은 한자 電動(전동, 'electric-motion' = motor-driven)이 붙은 말로, 모터 힘으로 구멍을 뚫거나 나사를 빠르게 박는 전동 공구입니다. 사람이 손으로 돌리는 '수동 드릴'이나 '드라이버'와 달리 전기로 돌아간다는 점이 핵심이라, 가구를 자주 조립하면 작업 속도가 훨씬 빨라집니다. 영어 화자가 가장 잘 틀리는 부분은 동사입니다. 'drill a hole'을 직역하면 '구멍을 파다'가 떠오르지만, '파다(dig)'는 흙·땅을 팔 때 쓰고, 단단한 벽이나 나무를 관통해 구멍을 낼 때는 '뚫다(bore/pierce through)'를 씁니다. 그래서 '벽에 구멍을 뚫다'가 맞습니다. 요즘은 선 없는 '충전(充電) 드릴'이 대세이고, 용도에 따라 끝의 '드릴 비트(drill bit)'를 갈아 끼웁니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '구멍을 뚫다, 나사를 박다, 드릴로 뚫다, 비트를 끼우다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 구멍을 파다 from English 'drill a hole' — 파다 (dig) is for soil/ground; piercing a wall or wood is 구멍을 뚫다 (bore through).
Marking the tool with 을/를: 전동드릴을 뚫다 is wrong; the instrument takes 로 → 전동드릴로 뚫다.
Expecting a basic 전동드릴 to pierce concrete; concrete needs a 해머드릴/임팩트 드릴 (hammer/impact drill).

structuredNuance.t: 전동드릴은 모터 힘으로 구멍을 뚫거나 나사를 빠르게 박는 전동 공구입니다. 요즘은 선 없는 '충전(充電) 드릴'이 대세이고, 용도에 따라 끝의 '드릴 비트(drill bit)'를 갈아 끼웁니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '구멍을 뚫다, 나사를 박다, 드릴로 뚫다, 비트를 끼우다'입니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 케이블타이 means "cable tie / zip tie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "cable tie / zip tie" is 케이블타이 (keibeultai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 케이블타이 ("cable tie / zip tie"). Watch the particle attached to 케이블타이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Plastic strap for bundling cords; also called 케이블 타이 / 타이밴드.

usagePhrases.en: to bundle with a cable tie
usagePhrases.note: 묶다 = tie/bind; the verb that goes with it, marked by 로.
선 정리 = cable management, the main reason people buy these.

usagePhrases.en: to cut the cable tie off
usagePhrases.note: 자르다 = cut; once tightened a standard one only comes off by cutting.

examples.en: I bundled it with a cable tie.
examples.note: 묶다 → 묶었어요; the tool takes 로 (케이블타이로), the cords are the unstated object.

examples.ko: 책상 밑에 선 너무 지저분해서 케이블타이로 묶었어요.
examples.romanization: chaeksang mite seon neomu jijeobunhaeseo keibeultairo mukkeosseoyo.
examples.en: The cords under the desk were so messy that I bundled them with cable ties.
examples.note: 지저분하다 = messy; classic desk cable-management situation.

examples.ko: 케이블타이는 한 번 조이면 자르기 전엔 못 풀어요.
examples.romanization: keibeultaineun han beon joimyeon jareugi jeonen mot pureoyo.
examples.en: Once you tighten a zip tie, you can't undo it without cutting.
examples.note: 조이다 = tighten; 못 풀다 = can't undo — they're one-way unless you buy reusable ones.

entries.nuance: 케이블타이는 영어 'cable tie'를 그대로 빌린 외래어로, 어지러운 전선을 한데 묶어 정리하는 플라스틱 끈입니다. 한국에서는 '선 정리(cable management)'의 필수품으로, 책상 밑이나 TV 뒤 전선을 깔끔히 묶을 때 자주 씁니다. 묶는 도구라는 점에서 옆 단원의 '노끈(twine)'과 헷갈릴 수 있는데, 노끈은 풀었다 다시 묶을 수 있는 천·종이 끈이고, 케이블타이는 톱니로 한 방향만 조여지는 일회용 플라스틱이라 한 번 조이면 가위로 '잘라야(cut)' 풀린다는 점이 결정적으로 다릅니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 그냥 '끈/줄(string/cord)'이라고 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데 일방향 플라스틱 타이는 구체적으로 '케이블타이'입니다. 둘째, 다시 풀어 쓰려 하지만 일반 제품은 'reusable(재사용)' 표시가 없으면 잘라서만 제거됩니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '케이블타이로 묶다, 선을 정리하다, 케이블타이를 조이다/자르다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it just 끈/줄 (string/cord) — the one-way plastic tie is specifically 케이블타이; the generic word loses the meaning.
Marking the tool with 을/를: 케이블타이를 묶다 means tying the tie itself; you bundle cords with it → 케이블타이로 묶다.
Expecting to reuse a standard one; unless labeled 재사용(reusable), it must be cut (자르다) to release.

structuredNuance.t: 케이블타이는 영어 'cable tie'를 그대로 빌린 외래어로, 어지러운 전선을 한데 묶어 정리하는 플라스틱 끈입니다. 한국에서는 '선 정리(cable management)'의 필수품으로, 책상 밑이나 TV 뒤 전선을 깔끔히 묶을 때 자주 씁니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '케이블타이로 묶다, 선을 정리하다, 케이블타이를 조이다/자르다'입니다.

영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 그냥 '끈/줄(string/cord)'이라고 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데 일방향 플라스틱 타이는 구체적으로 '케이블타이'입니다. 둘째, 다시 풀어 쓰려 하지만 일반 제품은 'reusable(재사용)' 표시가 없으면 잘라서만 제거됩니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 손전등 means "flashlight / torch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 손전등 (sonjeondeung) = "flashlight / torch". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 손전등 ("flashlight") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 손전등, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 손(hand) + 전등(電燈, electric lamp); the casual loanword 후레쉬/플래시 is also common.
비추다 = shine/cast light onto; the verb that pairs with it.
켜다 = switch on; 끄다 = switch off — the on/off pair.
Most people just use the phone's built-in light day to day.

examples.en: I turn on the flashlight.
examples.note: 켜다 (turn on a light/device) is the verb for lights; its opposite is 끄다.

examples.ko: 어두운데 핸드폰 손전등 좀 켜 줄래?
examples.romanization: eoduunde haendeupon sonjeondeung jom kyeo jullae?
examples.en: It's dark — can you turn on your phone flashlight?
examples.note: Everyday request; the phone light is most people's default 손전등 these days.

examples.en: The power went out, so I found the breaker box with a flashlight.
examples.note: 정전(停電) = blackout; 두꺼비집 = breaker box (colloquial), and the tool takes 으로.

entries.nuance: 손전등은 한자 電燈(전등, 'electric lamp')에 '손(hand)'이 붙은 말로, 손에 들고 빛을 비추는 휴대용 조명입니다. 반드시 구분할 단어가 '전등'입니다. '전등'은 방이나 천장에 붙은 일반 조명(room/ceiling light)을 뜻하므로, 손에 드는 것은 '손'을 붙여 '손전등'이라 해야 합니다. 일상 회화에서는 외래어 '후레쉬(flash)'나 '플래시'를 더 자주 쓰고, 요즘은 대부분 휴대폰 내장 '손전등' 기능으로 해결합니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 동사입니다. 영어 'shine the light'를 직역할 때 비슷한 발음의 '비치다'를 쓰기 쉬운데, '비치다'는 빛이 저절로 비쳐 든다는 자동사(피동)이고, 내가 손전등으로 어딘가를 비출 때는 타동사 '비추다(shine onto)'를 써야 합니다. 또 불은 '켜다(turn on)/끄다(turn off)'와 짝을 이룹니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '손전등을 켜다/끄다, 손전등을 비추다, 손전등으로 비추다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 전등 alone — a plain 전등 is a room/ceiling lamp; the handheld one must be 손전등 (with 손).
Saying 손전등을 비치다 — 비치다 is intransitive (light shines through by itself); to aim a flashlight you use the transitive 비추다.
Marking the instrument with 을 instead of 으로: you light an area 손전등으로 (with the flashlight), not 손전등을.
