entries.shortExplanation: 공구함 means "toolbox" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 공구함 (gongguham) means "toolbox". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 공구함 ("toolbox"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 공구함 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 공구(工具, tools) + 함(函, case/box); where you keep your hand tools.
넣어 두다 = put away and store; the location takes 에.
A boxed set of basic tools; a handy single purchase for a new home.
The essentials: 망치, 드라이버, 줄자, 펜치 and the like.

examples.en: The toolbox is heavy.
examples.note: 공구함 ends in a consonant (ㅁ), so the subject marker is 공구함이.

examples.en: Put the screwdriver back in the toolbox.
examples.note: 다시 넣어 두다 = put it back and store it; 에 marks the destination, plain 둬 is casual.

examples.en: When I moved, I got myself a basic toolbox.
examples.note: 장만하다 = acquire/get (deliberately, for oneself); the natural verb for setting up a home.

entries.nuance: 공구함은 한자 工具(공구, 'work-tool')에 函(함, 'case/box')이 붙은 합성어로, 망치·드라이버·줄자 같은 손공구를 한데 모아 두는 상자입니다. 어휘 선택에서 두 가지를 구분하면 좋습니다. 첫째, 그릇이나 통은 한국어로 '상자/박스'라고 뭉뚱그리기 쉽지만, 공구 전용 케이스는 한자 '함(函)'을 쓴 '공구함'이 자연스럽습니다(같은 '함'이 '사물함=locker, 우편함=mailbox'에도 쓰입니다). 둘째, 영어 'tool'은 한국어에서 '공구(工具)'와 '도구(道具)' 둘로 나뉘는데, 망치·드릴 같은 철물·연장은 '공구'가 자연스럽고, '도구'는 더 넓게 '수단·기구'를 뜻해 'a tool for learning(학습 도구)'처럼 추상적으로도 씁니다. 그래서 철물점 맥락에서는 '도구함'보다 '공구함'이 맞습니다. 자취·이사 때 기본 '공구 세트'를 하나 '장만해' 두면 간단한 수리나 가구 조립을 직접 할 수 있어 편리합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '공구함에 넣어 두다, 공구 세트를 장만하다, 기본 공구를 갖추다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 상자/박스 generically — those mean any box; the dedicated tool case uses the 함(函) suffix → 공구함.
Saying 도구함 for a hardware toolbox — for physical tools 공구(工具) is the natural word; 도구(道具) leans abstract/general.
Marking with 를: 공구함을 넣다 means putting the box itself somewhere; to store tools inside, the box takes 에 → 공구함에 넣다.

entries.shortExplanation: 노끈 means "string / twine / cord" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "string / twine / cord" is 노끈 (nokkeun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 노끈 ("string/twine"). Watch the particle attached to 노끈 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Thin cord for tying things; thicker than thread, thinner than rope.
묶다 = tie/bind; the core verb with 노끈, marked by 로.
Common for bundling cardboard for 분리수거 (sorted recycling).
풀다 = undo/untie; the opposite of 묶다.

examples.en: I tied it with twine.
examples.note: 묶다 → 묶었어요; the twine is the instrument, so 노끈으로, with the object understood.

examples.en: Tie the newspapers with twine and put them out for recycling.
examples.note: 내놓다 = put out (for collection); a core chore in Korean apartment life.

examples.ko: 노끈이 약해서 무거운 거 묶으면 끊어져요.
examples.romanization: nokkeuni yakaeseo mugeoun geo mukkeumyeon kkeuneojyeoyo.
examples.en: The twine is weak, so it snaps if you tie heavy things.
examples.note: 끊어지다 = snap/break (intransitive); use stronger 밧줄 (rope) for heavy loads.

entries.nuance: 노끈은 물건을 묶을 때 쓰는 가는 끈으로, 굵기로 비슷한 말들을 가르는 게 핵심입니다. 바느질용 '실(thread)'보다는 굵고, 짐을 옮기거나 매는 '밧줄(rope)'보다는 가늘어서, 가벼운 물건을 묶기에 알맞습니다. 한국에서는 특히 종이박스나 신문지를 모아 '분리수거(sorted recycling)'로 내놓을 때 노끈으로 묶는 모습을 흔히 봅니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 영어 'string'을 떠올려 바느질 '실'과 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 박스를 묶는 끈은 '실'이 아니라 '노끈'입니다. 둘째, 동사 짝을 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 묶는 것은 '묶다(tie/bind)', 푸는 것은 '풀다(untie)', 끈이 저절로 끊기는 것은 자동사 '끊어지다'를 씁니다. 무거운 것을 묶으면 끊어질 수 있으니 그럴 땐 더 튼튼한 '밧줄'을 쓰는 게 좋습니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '노끈으로 묶다, 박스를 묶다, 노끈을 풀다, 노끈이 끊어지다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 실 (thread) from English 'string' — 실 is fine sewing thread; bundling cord for boxes is 노끈.
Expecting 노끈 to hold heavy loads; for that you need a thicker 밧줄 (rope) — the words differ by thickness/strength.
Marking with 을/를: 노끈을 묶다 means tying the twine itself; you bind the box with twine → 노끈으로 (박스를) 묶다.

entries.shortExplanation: 후텁지근하다 means "muggy, hot and humid (sticky)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 후텁지근하다 (huteopjigeunhada) = "muggy, hot and humid (sticky)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 후텁지근하다 ("to be muggy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 후텁지근하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Korean summer's sticky heat that clings to your skin; the go-to July–August complaint
polite present; say it when you step outside and the air feels like a wet towel
modifier -ㄴ attaches to the stem before a noun; describes the kind of day
-아/어서 reason form; natural lead-in to '에어컨 켰어요 (I turned on the AC)'

examples.en: It's a bit muggy today.
examples.note: the bare minimum small-talk line; -네요 reacts to what you feel right now

examples.ko: 장마철이라 그런지 방 안이 너무 후텁지근해요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheorira geureonji bang ani neomu huteopjigeunhaeyo.
examples.en: Maybe because it's monsoon season, the room is so muggy.
examples.note: 장마철 (rainy season) is the prime context; -(이)라 그런지 = 'maybe because'

examples.ko: 밖에 나가자마자 후텁지근해서 바로 다시 들어왔어.
examples.romanization: bakke nagajamaja huteopjigeunhaeseo baro dasi deureowasseo.
examples.en: The second I stepped outside it was so muggy I came right back in.
examples.note: casual 반말; -자마자 = 'the moment that', capturing the wall-of-humidity feeling

entries.nuance: 후텁지근하다 names heat AND humidity together — the heavy, steamy, clothes-sticking-to-skin air of a Korean summer night, not just a high number on the thermometer. The sharp contrast is with plain 덥다 (simply 'hot', could be dry desert heat) and with 무덥다 (also oppressive but a touch more formal/written); 후텁지근하다 is the spoken, sensory, slightly whiny word you use when the muggy air actually bothers you. It collocates with 날씨, 방 안, 공기, and especially 장마철. The English-speaker trap is reaching for it whenever it's 'hot' — if there's no stickiness, it must be 덥다, because the whole point of this word is the wet, suffocating quality. Also watch the spelling: standard is 후텁지근하다 (not 후덥지근하다), even though it relates to 덥다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for dry heat: a sunny but dry 28°C day is 덥다, not 후텁지근하다 — this word requires humidity, so reserve it for sticky, sweaty air.
Spelling it 후덥지근하다 by analogy with 덥다; the dictionary-standard form is 후텁지근하다 with ㅌ.
Saying '나는 후텁지근해요' to mean 'I feel hot/sweaty' — the subject is the air or the weather, not a person; for yourself say 덥다 or 땀나다.

entries.shortExplanation: 쌀쌀하다 means "chilly, nippy (cool air)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쌀쌀하다 (ssalssalhada) means "chilly, nippy (cool air)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 쌀쌀하다 ("to be chilly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쌀쌀하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the brisk cool of early morning or late autumn; not freezing, just jacket-weather
polite present; the default spring/fall weather small talk
modifier -ㄴ before a noun; also 쌀쌀한 바람 (a chilly wind)
set phrase for the daily temperature swing (일교차)

examples.en: It's a bit chilly today.
examples.note: the simplest version; 좀 softens it to 'a little'

examples.en: These days it's chilly morning and evening, so take a jacket.
examples.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason for advice; classic seasonal line you'll hear constantly

examples.en: With the wind blowing too, it's way chillier than I expected.
examples.note: -까지 ('even/on top of that') stacks the wind onto the cold; -네요 for in-the-moment reaction

entries.nuance: 쌀쌀하다 is a mild, brisk chill — the kind that makes you reach for a light jacket or cardigan, the signature feeling of spring mornings and autumn evenings. The dividing line you must learn: 쌀쌀하다 (cool, jacket weather) < 싸늘하다 (genuinely cold, often eerie) < 춥다 (cold, the all-purpose word) < 매섭다 (painfully biting winter cold). So if your teeth chatter, it's already past 쌀쌀하다. A second, equally common use is about people: 쌀쌀하다 / 쌀쌀맞다 / 쌀쌀하게 대하다 describe a cold, aloof, standoffish attitude — context (weather vs. a person) tells you which. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as 'cold'; it is deliberately understated, closer to 'a bit nippy', and overusing it for real cold sounds off.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for deep winter cold: when it actually hurts, switch to 춥다 or 매섭다 — 쌀쌀하다 only covers the mild, jacket-level chill.
Treating it as a synonym of 싸늘하다; 싸늘하다 is colder and can feel eerie/tense, whereas 쌀쌀하다 is just pleasantly brisk.
Forgetting the personality meaning: '그 사람 좀 쌀쌀해' means 'that person is a bit cold/distant', not that they feel cool to the touch.

entries.shortExplanation: 포근하다 means "mild and cozy (unusually warm)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "mild and cozy (unusually warm)" is 포근하다 (pogeunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 포근하다 ("to be mild/cozy"). Watch the particle attached to 포근하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: gently warm — a winter day milder than usual, or a soft, snug feeling
polite present; said with relief when winter cold eases
modifier -ㄴ before a noun; also 포근한 이불 (a cozy blanket)
날(이) + adjective is a very natural weather frame

examples.en: It's a bit mild today.
examples.note: the basic line; perfect when a cold spell suddenly softens

examples.en: Even though it's midwinter, the day's so mild I came out for a walk.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ데도 = 'even though'; the textbook context of a surprisingly warm winter day

examples.en: The blanket's so cozy I just can't get up.
examples.note: 반말; shows the 'soft & snug' object sense — 도저히 + 못 = 'no way can I'

entries.nuance: 포근하다 carries warmth wrapped in comfort — most often a winter day that turns out gentler than expected, or soft, snuggly things like 이불 (blankets), 옷, and a mother's hug. The key contrast is with 따뜻하다, which is the neutral, all-temperature 'warm'; 포근하다 adds emotion — you say it with relief, contentment, or affection, never about plain heat. It pairs with 날씨, 날, 이불, 분위기, 품 (embrace). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, do not use it for summer warmth or any strong heat — it is reserved for gentle, mild warmth, so a hot day is 덥다, never 포근하다. Second, do not limit it to weather: '이불이 포근하다' (the blanket is cozy) is just as natural and very common.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for hot weather: 포근하다 is gentle, mild warmth only — a sweltering summer day is 덥다/무덥다, and calling it 포근하다 sounds wrong.
Assuming it equals 따뜻하다: 따뜻하다 is the neutral 'warm', while 포근하다 always adds a cozy, emotionally positive feeling.
Limiting it to weather and missing the object use; '포근한 스웨터/이불' (a cozy sweater/blanket) is an everyday, natural collocation.

structuredNuance.t: 포근하다 carries warmth wrapped in comfort — most often a winter day that turns out gentler than expected, or soft, snuggly things like 이불 (blankets), 옷, and a mother's hug. You say it with relief, contentment, or affection, never about plain heat. It pairs with 날씨, 날, 이불, 분위기, 품 (embrace).
The key contrast is with 따뜻하다, which is the neutral, all-temperature 'warm'; 포근하다 adds emotion — relief, contentment, or affection.

entries.shortExplanation: 무덥다 means "sweltering, hot and stifling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무덥다 (mudeopda) = "sweltering, hot and stifling". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 무덥다 ("to be sweltering") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무덥다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: intense, oppressive, usually humid summer heat; ㅂ-irregular stem
polite present: 무덥 + 어요 → 무더워요 (ㅂ→우)
무더운 before a noun (ㅂ-irregular modifier)
the forecast staple: 무더위가 계속되다 (the heat wave continues)

examples.en: It's really sweltering today.
examples.note: the simple reaction line; 진짜 adds 'really'

examples.ko: 무더운 날에는 수분 섭취가 정말 중요해요.
examples.romanization: mudeoun nareneun subun seopchwiga jeongmal jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: On sweltering days, staying hydrated is really important.
examples.note: newscast-style advice; 무더운 날 = a sweltering day

examples.ko: 밤에도 안 식어서 무더운 열대야가 계속되고 있어요.
examples.romanization: bamedo an sigeoseo mudeoun yeoldaeyaga gyesokdoego isseoyo.
examples.en: It doesn't even cool down at night, so the sweltering tropical nights keep going.
examples.note: 열대야 ('tropical night') pairs naturally with 무덥다; -고 있다 for an ongoing stretch

entries.nuance: 무덥다 is heat with weight — heavy, stifling, energy-draining, almost always with humidity behind it, a clear step above plain 덥다. The 무- here is the intensifying/heavy 'mu-', so think 'heavily hot'. Contrast: 덥다 = neutral 'hot' (any hot), 무덥다 = oppressively, stiflingly hot, and the spoken/sensory cousin 후텁지근하다 leans on the sticky muggy feel while 무덥다 sounds a notch more standard and is the form used in forecasts and writing. Its noun 무더위 appears all over summer weather reports (무더위 특보, 무더위가 기승을 부리다). The two pitfalls: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — it is 무더워요/무더운/무더위, never 무덥어요/무덥은; (2) don't downgrade it to mild warmth — 무덥다 is reserved for genuinely draining heat, so a pleasantly warm day is 따뜻하다, not 무덥다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 무덥어요/무덥은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct forms are 무더워요 and 무더운.
Using it for mild or pleasant warmth: 무덥다 is intense, stifling heat — a nice warm day is 따뜻하다, and a merely hot day is 덥다.
Forgetting the high-frequency noun 무더위; in forecasts you'll hear 무더위가 계속되다/기승을 부리다 far more than the adjective.

structuredNuance.t: 무덥다 is heat with weight — heavy, stifling, energy-draining, almost always with humidity behind it, a clear step above plain 덥다. Its noun 무더위 appears all over summer weather reports (무더위 특보, 무더위가 기승을 부리다).

It is ㅂ-irregular — 무덥 + 어요 → 무더워요, modifier 무더운, noun 무더위, never 무덥어요/무덥은.
Don't downgrade it to mild warmth — 무덥다 is reserved for genuinely draining heat, so a pleasantly warm day is 따뜻하다, not 무덥다.

entries.shortExplanation: 선선하다 means "pleasantly cool, refreshing (air)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 선선하다 (seonseonhada) means "pleasantly cool, refreshing (air)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 선선하다 ("to be pleasantly cool"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 선선하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: comfortable coolness, especially early autumn after the summer heat breaks
polite present; said with relief as the weather turns nice
선선한 most often pairs with 바람 (breeze) or 날씨/공기
-아/어지다 for the seasonal change: '날씨가 선선해졌어요'

examples.en: It's pleasantly cool now.
examples.note: the basic line; 이제 ('now') signals the season has turned

examples.ko: 아침 공기가 선선해서 산책하기 딱 좋아요.
examples.romanization: achim gonggiga seonseonhaeseo sanchaekagi ttak joayo.
examples.en: The morning air is so cool that it's just right for a walk.
examples.note: 딱 좋다 = 'just right'; -기 좋다 = 'good for ~ing'

examples.en: The heat has eased off and it's finally turned cool.
examples.note: 한풀 꺾이다 = '(heat) to die down', a very Korean expression; 드디어 = 'finally'

entries.nuance: 선선하다 is pleasant, refreshing coolness — the welcome relief when summer finally lets go and early autumn arrives, the temperature where you feel comfortable without a jacket. It is always positive, which is exactly the dividing line from its neighbors: 선선하다 (nice, comfortable cool) → 쌀쌀하다 (chilly enough to want a jacket) → 싸늘하다 (uncomfortably, sharply cold). So once you actually feel cold, you have left 선선하다 behind. It collocates with 바람, 날씨, 공기, 가을 and very often appears as 선선해지다 to mark the change of season, or with 한풀 꺾이다 (the heat dying down). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'cool' too literally and applying it to genuinely cold weather, or pairing it with ongoing summer heat — 선선하다 inherently implies the heat has already passed and what's left feels good.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it when it's actually cold: 선선하다 means comfortable, refreshing cool — if you need a jacket, that's 쌀쌀하다, not 선선하다.
Pairing it with peak summer: saying '여름이 선선해요' clashes, because 선선하다 implies the heat has already eased; use it for early autumn or cool evenings.
Confusing it with 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broad 'refreshing/cool' (drinks, AC, relief), while 선선하다 is specifically the pleasant coolness of the air/weather.

structuredNuance.t: 선선하다 is pleasant, refreshing coolness — the welcome relief when summer finally lets go and early autumn arrives, the temperature where you feel comfortable without a jacket. It is always positive. It collocates with 바람, 날씨, 공기, 가을 and very often appears as 선선해지다 to mark the change of season, or with 한풀 꺾이다 (the heat dying down).

Being always positive is exactly the dividing line from its neighbors: 선선하다 (nice, comfortable cool) → 쌀쌀하다 (chilly enough to want a jacket) → 싸늘하다 (uncomfortably, sharply cold). So once you actually feel cold, you have left 선선하다 behind.

entries.shortExplanation: 화창하다 means "sunny and clear (bright, fine weather)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sunny and clear (bright, fine weather)" is 화창하다 (hwachanghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 화창하다 ("to be sunny and clear"). Watch the particle attached to 화창하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: bright, beautiful blue-sky weather; the ideal day to go out
polite present; a cheerful weather report
화창한 + 날씨/봄날 are the typical pairings
standard weather-subject frame

examples.en: The weather's lovely and sunny today.
examples.note: the simple delighted reaction; note 날씨(가) often drops 가 in speech

examples.ko: 날씨가 화창해서 한강 가기 딱 좋아요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga hwachanghaeseo hangang gagi ttak joayo.
examples.en: The weather's so nice and sunny it's perfect for going to the Han River.
examples.note: -아서 reason + -기 좋다; 화창한 날 is when everyone heads to 한강

examples.ko: 내일은 미세먼지도 없고 하늘이 화창할 거래요.
examples.romanization: naeireun misemeonjido eopsgo haneuri hwachanghal georaeyo.
examples.en: They say tomorrow there'll be no fine dust and the sky will be clear and sunny.
examples.note: -(이)래요 reports a forecast; 미세먼지 (fine dust) is a real daily concern in Korea

entries.nuance: 화창하다 describes bright, clear, beautiful weather — sunny skies, fresh air, the kind of day that lifts your mood, classically a spring or autumn 'perfect day'. It is Sino-Korean: 和 (hwa, 'harmonious/gentle') + 暢 (chang, 'flowing freely/unobstructed'), so the image is of mild, freely bright, unblocked weather. The contrast to learn: 맑다 just means 'clear' (sky, water, even sound) and is purely about clarity, while 화창하다 adds warmth, brightness and a pleasant mood — a clear but bitterly cold winter sky is 맑다, not 화창하다. It pairs with 날씨, 봄날, 하늘, 가을. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use it merely for 'not raining' — cloudy-but-dry is not 화창하다; and it describes daytime brightness, so it doesn't fit a clear night sky (for that, 맑다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for 'just not raining': a gray, dry, overcast day is not 화창하다 — the word requires genuine bright, pleasant sunshine.
Treating it as identical to 맑다: 맑다 is plain clarity (it can be clear but freezing), whereas 화창하다 adds warm, cheerful brightness, so a cold clear day is 맑다.
Applying it to night: 화창하다 is about daytime brightness; a clear night sky is 하늘이 맑다, not 화창하다.

structuredNuance.t: 화창하다 describes bright, clear, beautiful weather — sunny skies, fresh air, the kind of day that lifts your mood, classically a spring or autumn 'perfect day'. It pairs with 날씨, 봄날, 하늘, 가을.

The contrast to learn: 맑다 just means 'clear' (sky, water, even sound) and is purely about clarity, while 화창하다 adds warmth, brightness and a pleasant mood — a clear but bitterly cold winter sky is 맑다, not 화창하다.
It is Sino-Korean: 和 (hwa, 'harmonious/gentle') + 暢 (chang, 'flowing freely/unobstructed'), so the image is of mild, freely bright, unblocked weather.

entries.shortExplanation: 습하다 means "humid, damp" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 습하다 (seupada) = "humid, damp". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 습하다 ("to be humid/damp") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 습하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: high moisture in the air; the defining feature of Korean summer and the rainy season
polite present; also said of a damp room or basement
습한 before a noun; also 습한 공기 (damp air)
습하다 + 덥다 is the classic Korean-summer combo

examples.en: It's a bit humid today.
examples.note: the bare small-talk line; you'll feel it before you see it

examples.ko: 장마철엔 너무 습해서 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren neomu seupaeseo ppallaega jal an mallayo.
examples.en: During the rainy season it's so humid the laundry won't dry well.
examples.note: a very real apartment-life problem; -아서 links cause to result

examples.ko: 방이 습한 것 같아서 제습기를 틀었어.
examples.romanization: bangi seupan geot gataseo jeseupgireul teureosseo.
examples.en: The room felt damp so I turned on the dehumidifier.
examples.note: 반말; 제습기 (dehumidifier) is a summer essential — -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 = 'seems'

entries.nuance: 습하다 is about moisture in the air, deliberately separate from temperature — you can have a 습한 but cool, clammy day (a damp basement, a rainy spring). It is Sino-Korean from 濕 ('wet/damp'), and its exact opposite is 건조하다 (dry, from 乾燥). In Korea it is the word behind summer misery: 빨래가 안 마르다 (laundry won't dry), 곰팡이 (mold), and the constant hum of the 제습기 (dehumidifier). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is collapsing it into 'hot': 습하다 means humid, not hot — they merely co-occur in summer, so a cool damp day is still 습하다, and a dry hot desert day is 덥다 but absolutely not 습하다. Keep the pair straight: 습하다 (humid) ↔ 건조하다 (dry), and pair 습하다 with 덥다 only when both are true.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 덥다 ('hot'): 습하다 is purely about moisture, so you can be 습한데 안 더워요 (humid but not hot) — don't use it to mean heat.
Using it for dry conditions: the opposite of 습하다 is 건조하다, so a dry winter day is 건조하다, never 습하다.
Forgetting the indoor/room use: '방/지하실이 습하다' (the room/basement is damp) is just as common as talking about the weather.

structuredNuance.t: 습하다 is about moisture in the air, deliberately separate from temperature — you can have a 습한 but cool, clammy day (a damp basement, a rainy spring). In Korea it is the word behind summer misery: 빨래가 안 마르다 (laundry won't dry), 곰팡이 (mold), and the constant hum of the 제습기 (dehumidifier).
Its exact opposite is 건조하다 (dry). Keep the pair straight: 습하다 (humid) ↔ 건조하다 (dry), and pair 습하다 with 덥다 only when both are true.

entries.shortExplanation: 건조하다 means "dry (air, skin)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 건조하다 (geonjohada) means "dry (air, skin)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 건조하다 ("to be dry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 건조하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: low humidity in the air; the hallmark of Korean winter and spring
polite present; also used for dry skin (피부가 건조해요)
건조한 before a noun; also 건조한 공기/피부
a real fire-risk warning issued in dry seasons (건조주의보가 내려지다)

examples.en: It's so dry these days.
examples.note: the simple seasonal complaint, peak winter

examples.en: The weather's so dry my lips keep chapping.
examples.note: 트다 = (skin/lips) to chap; -아서 cause, -네요 reaction

examples.ko: 피부가 건조할 땐 자기 전에 로션을 꼭 발라요.
examples.romanization: pibuga geonjohal ttaen jagi jeone rosyeoneul kkok ballayo.
examples.en: When my skin is dry, I always put on lotion before bed.
examples.note: shows the skin use; -(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when', 꼭 = 'without fail'

entries.nuance: 건조하다 is the dryness of low-humidity air — the exact opposite of 습하다 — typical of Korean winter and the spring fire-warning season, when 가습기 (humidifiers) come out and 건조주의보 (dry-weather advisories) get issued. It is Sino-Korean: 乾 (geon, 'dry/heaven') + 燥 (jo, 'parched'), literally 'dried and parched'. Its range is wide: equally natural for skin (피부가 건조하다, 입술이 트다) and even for a person's manner or a piece of writing — 건조한 말투/문체 means a dry, flat, emotionless tone. The two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) don't mix it up with 습하다 — they are antonyms, 건조하다 = dry, 습하다 = humid; (2) don't box it into weather only, since 'my skin is dry' (피부가 건조해요) is one of its most everyday uses, and the metaphorical 'dry/dull' sense is common too.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing it up with 습하다: they are opposites — 건조하다 means dry (low humidity), 습하다 means humid, so don't swap them.
Limiting it to weather: 피부가 건조하다 (dry skin) and 입술이 건조하다/트다 (chapped lips) are extremely common, everyday uses.
Missing the figurative sense: 건조한 말투/분위기 means a dry, flat, unfeeling tone or mood — context tells you it's not about humidity.

structuredNuance.t: 건조하다 is the dryness of low-humidity air, typical of Korean winter and the spring fire-warning season, when 가습기 (humidifiers) come out and 건조주의보 (dry-weather advisories) get issued. Its range is wide: equally natural for skin (피부가 건조하다, 입술이 트다) and even for a person's manner or a piece of writing — 건조한 말투/문체 means a dry, flat, emotionless tone.

entries.shortExplanation: 매섭다 means "bitterly cold, biting (wind, cold)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bitterly cold, biting (wind, cold)" is 매섭다 (maeseopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매섭다 ("to be biting/fierce"). Watch the particle attached to 매섭다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: piercing winter cold or a sharp, cutting wind; ㅂ-irregular stem
polite present: 매섭 + 어요 → 매서워요 (ㅂ→우)
매서운 + 바람/추위 are the standard pairings
매섭게 (adverb) intensifies 춥다

examples.en: The wind is really biting today.
examples.note: the simple reaction; 진짜 adds force, -네요 reacts on the spot

examples.ko: 추위가 매서우니까 패딩 단단히 입고 나가세요.
examples.romanization: chuwiga maeseounikka paeding dandanhi ipgo nagaseyo.
examples.en: The cold is biting, so bundle up well in your padded coat before you go.
examples.note: -(으)니까 reason for advice; 패딩 (padded coat) is the Korean winter uniform

examples.ko: 한파에 칼바람까지 매섭게 불어서 귀가 다 얼었어.
examples.romanization: hanpae kalbaramkkaji maeseopge bureoseo gwiga da eoreosseo.
examples.en: On top of the cold wave, a knife-sharp wind blew bitterly and my ears froze solid.
examples.note: 반말; 칼바람 (knife wind) + 매섭다 is very natural, -까지 stacks the wind on the cold wave

entries.nuance: 매섭다 describes a fierce, piercing, almost painful quality — most often a biting winter wind or a sharp cold that hurts exposed skin, the harshest end of the cold scale (쌀쌀하다 → 싸늘하다 → 춥다 → 매섭다). Its core sense isn't temperature but 'cutting/severe', which is why it transfers to people: 매서운 눈빛 (a piercing, fierce stare), 매섭게 몰아붙이다 (to scold/press sharply). It collocates with 바람, 추위, 한파, 칼바람, 눈빛. Two things trip English speakers up: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — it is 매서워요/매서운/매섭게, never 매섭어요/매섭은; (2) don't use it for ordinary cold — 매섭다 is reserved for harsh, biting, painful cold or wind, so a merely cold day is 춥다 and a mildly chilly one is 쌀쌀하다, with 매섭다 saved for when the wind actually stings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 매섭어요/매섭은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct forms are 매서워요 and 매서운.
Using it for mild cold: 매섭다 is harsh, painful, biting cold — a normal cold day is 춥다, and a light chill is 쌀쌀하다.
Missing the figurative use: 매서운 눈빛/말투 means a fierce, sharp gaze or tone, reflecting the word's core sense of 'cutting/severe'.

structuredNuance.t: 매섭다 describes a fierce, piercing, almost painful quality — most often a biting winter wind or a sharp cold that hurts exposed skin. Its core sense isn't temperature but 'cutting/severe', which is why it transfers to people: 매서운 눈빛 (a piercing, fierce stare), 매섭게 몰아붙이다 (to scold/press sharply). It collocates with 바람, 추위, 한파, 칼바람, 눈빛.
It is the harshest end of the cold scale: 쌀쌀하다 → 싸늘하다 → 춥다 → 매섭다.
It is ㅂ-irregular — 매섭 + 어요 → 매서워요, modifier 매서운, adverb 매섭게, never 매섭어요/매섭은.

entries.shortExplanation: 따사롭다 means "warm and gentle (sunlight)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 따사롭다 (ttasaropda) = "warm and gentle (sunlight)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 따사롭다 ("to be warm and gentle") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 따사롭다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the soft, comforting warmth of sunshine; ㅂ-irregular stem
polite present: 따사롭 + 어요 → 따사로워요 (ㅂ→우)
the most common pairing: 햇살/햇볕 (sunshine)
the natural subject is sunlight, not air temperature

examples.en: The sunshine is so warm and gentle.
examples.note: the simple admiring line; 참 = 'truly', a soft intensifier

examples.ko: 봄 햇살이 따사로워서 벤치에 한참 앉아 있었어요.
examples.romanization: bom haetsari ttasarowoseo benchie hancham anja isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The spring sunshine was so gentle and warm that I sat on the bench for a long while.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 한참 = 'for a good while', the cozy basking feeling

examples.ko: 겨울인데도 창으로 따사로운 볕이 들어와서 마음까지 포근해졌어.
examples.romanization: gyeourindedo changeuro ttasaroun byeochi deureowaseo maeumkkaji pogeunhaejyeosseo.
examples.en: Even in winter, gentle sun came through the window and even my heart felt cozy.
examples.note: 반말; 볕이 들다 = 'sun shines in', -까지 extends the warmth to the heart

entries.nuance: 따사롭다 is the softer, more poetic cousin of 따뜻하다, used almost exclusively for sunlight (햇살, 햇볕, 볕) and, by extension, warm-hearted feelings (따사로운 미소, 따사로운 정). Where 따뜻하다 is the everyday, all-purpose 'warm' (warm water, a warm room, a warm person), 따사롭다 specifically evokes a gentle, soothing, slightly literary warmth and a peaceful mood — which is why you meet it in captions, lyrics, essays, and heartfelt speech far more than in plain weather chat. It collocates above all with 햇살/햇볕/볕, and with 미소, 정, 손길. Two pitfalls: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — 따사로워요/따사로운, never 따사롭어요/따사롭은; (2) don't use it for general air temperature or to describe how warm a room or drink is — for that you want 따뜻하다, because 따사롭다 is tied to the gentle warmth of sunshine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 따사롭어요/따사롭은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so use 따사로워요 and 따사로운.
Using it for air temperature or objects: a warm room or warm coffee is 따뜻하다 — 따사롭다 is mainly for sunlight (and warm feelings), not general warmth.
Treating it as fully interchangeable with 따뜻하다: 따사롭다 is softer, more poetic, and sunshine-centered, so it sounds odd in blunt, everyday statements where 따뜻하다 fits.

entries.shortExplanation: 싸늘하다 means "cold and chilly (and often eerie/tense)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 싸늘하다 (ssaneulhada) means "cold and chilly (and often eerie/tense)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 싸늘하다 ("to be cold/chilly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 싸늘하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a sharper, colder chill than 쌀쌀하다; air that's gone genuinely cold
polite present; said when the temperature has clearly dropped
싸늘한 + 공기/날씨; also 싸늘한 분위기 (a tense, frosty mood)
-아/어지다; weather or a mood suddenly going cold

examples.en: It's a bit cold at night.
examples.note: the simple line; the chill that comes after dark

examples.en: Once the sun set, the air suddenly turned cold.
examples.note: -(으)니까 cause-then-effect; -아지다 marks the change to cold

examples.en: One joke from me and the mood turned ice-cold.
examples.note: 반말; the very common figurative use — a frozen, awkward atmosphere after a flat joke

entries.nuance: 싸늘하다 is colder and sharper than 쌀쌀하다, frequently with an unsettling or tense edge — think air that has gone abruptly cold after sunset, or the chill of a too-quiet room. Placed on the cold scale it sits 쌀쌀하다 (mild, jacket weather) < 싸늘하다 (genuinely cold, often eerie) < 춥다/매섭다. But its most useful everyday life is figurative: 분위기가 싸늘하다 / 싸늘해지다 describes a room going awkwardly silent, frosty, or hostile — the classic case being right after someone tells a joke that bombs (썰렁하다 is the lighter 'lame/cringe' version; 싸늘하다 is the heavier 'frozen, hostile' one). It pairs with 공기, 날씨, 새벽, 시선, 반응, 분위기. The pitfalls: don't equate it with 쌀쌀하다 (싸늘하다 is colder and tenser), and don't miss the atmosphere meaning, which natives use constantly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 쌀쌀하다: 싸늘하다 is noticeably colder and often carries an eerie or tense feeling, while 쌀쌀하다 is just mildly brisk.
Missing the figurative 'cold atmosphere' use: 분위기/반응이 싸늘하다 (a frosty mood/reaction) is extremely common in daily conversation, not just weather.
Confusing it with 썰렁하다: after a bad joke, 썰렁하다 = 'lame/cringe', whereas 싸늘하다 = the heavier 'frozen, hostile' silence.

entries.shortExplanation: 푹푹 찌다 means "to be boiling/scorching (oppressively hot)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be boiling/scorching (oppressively hot)" is 푹푹 찌다 (pukpuk jjida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 푹푹 찌다 ("to be sweltering/boiling"). Watch the particle attached to 푹푹 찌다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: vivid idiom: heat so heavy the air feels steamed; standard spacing is 푹푹 찌다
polite present: 찌 + 어요 → 쪄요
찌는 (present modifier) before a noun
pairs with 더위 (heat) for peak-summer days

examples.en: It's totally boiling outside.
examples.note: the everyday exaggeration; 완전 ('totally') is casual intensifier slang

examples.ko: 에어컨 없이는 푹푹 찌는 여름을 도저히 못 버텨요.
examples.romanization: eeokeon eopsineun pukpuk jjineun yeoreumeul dojeohi mot beotyeoyo.
examples.en: Without AC, there's no way I can survive the sweltering summer.
examples.note: 버티다 = to endure; 찌는 modifies 여름, 도저히 + 못 = 'simply can't'

examples.en: Maybe because it's the dog days of summer, it's been sweltering since morning.
examples.note: 반말; 삼복더위 = the hottest stretch (복날), -아서 그런지 = 'maybe because'

entries.nuance: 푹푹 찌다 literally means '(the heat) steams you' — 찌다 is the verb 'to steam', and the mimetic 푹푹 paints heat pressing down in thick waves, so the whole phrase is an idiomatic, highly colloquial way to say it's brutally, oppressively hot. It outranks even 무덥다 in vividness and feeling, and unlike the other items here it is a verb phrase, not a single adjective, so it conjugates on 찌다 (쪄요, 찌는, 쪘어요). You'll hear it everywhere in a Korean heat wave, paired with 더위, 날씨, 여름. Two real pitfalls: (1) 찌다 is a homophone minefield — the same 찌다 means 'to gain weight' (살이 찌다) and 'to steam food' (만두를 찌다), so only the weather context (날씨/더위/밖) tells you it's 'sweltering'; (2) spacing — the standard written form keeps a space, 푹푹 찌다, not 푹푹찌다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing this 찌다 with 찌다 'to gain weight' (살이 찌다) or 'to steam food' (만두를 찌다); only the weather context makes it 'sweltering'.
Writing it as one word 푹푹찌다; the standard form spaces the mimetic adverb: 푹푹 찌다.
Treating it as an adjective and saying 푹푹 쪄서 날씨 → it's a verb phrase, so conjugate on 찌다 (푹푹 쪄요, 푹푹 찌는 날씨).

entries.shortExplanation: 친절하다 means "to be kind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 친절하다 (chinjeolhada) = "to be kind". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 친절해요 ("someone is kind") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 친절하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요, never 친절하요
modifier 친절한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
adverb 친절하게 + verb

examples.en: That person is kind.
examples.note: Plain 반말 친절해; drop 요 with close friends.

examples.en: The staff here is really kind.
examples.note: -들이 marks plural staff; 친절하다 describes how they treat customers.

examples.ko: 길을 몰랐는데 어떤 분이 친절하게 가르쳐 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: gireul mollanneunde eotteon buni chinjeolhage gareuchyeo jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't know the way, but someone kindly showed me.
examples.note: 친절하게 (adverb) + 주시다 honorific = a kind favor done for you.

entries.nuance: 친절하다 is 'kind' in the sense of warm, attentive, service-minded behavior toward others — the word you reach for about staff, neighbors, or strangers who go out of their way for you. It is Sino-Korean 親切 (친 'close/intimate' + 절 'earnest/keen'), literally 'intimately earnest'. Compare 착하다, which is about an inherently good, gentle heart (a moral quality), whereas 친절하다 is about outward considerate treatment in a given moment — a cold person can still be 친절한 at work. It also differs from 다정하다 (affectionate, emotionally close). It follows the regular 하다 conjugation, so 하다 becomes 해요 (친절해요), and the adverb 친절하게 ('kindly') pairs naturally with verbs like 가르쳐 주다 or 설명하다. The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 친절하요 (the 하 must fuse to 해), and don't use it for an object or food — 'kind' as in 'a kind gesture' is fine, but you can't call coffee 친절한.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 친절하요 — the 하다 ending must contract to 해요, so it is 친절해요, never 친절하요.
Using 친절하다 to mean 'good-hearted' in general (e.g. '그는 친절한 사람이라 거짓말을 안 해요'). For inner goodness use 착하다; 친절하다 specifically describes considerate outward behavior.
Treating it like a verb and saying 친절했다 to mean 'acted kindly once' while expecting a do-form — it is an adjective, so to say someone 'was kind to me' you often add the action: 친절하게 대해 줬어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 똑똑하다 means "to be smart" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 똑똑하다 (ttokttokada) means "to be smart". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 똑똑해요 ("someone is smart"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 똑똑하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 똑똑한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
머리(head) + 똑똑하다 collocation

examples.en: Our puppy is really smart.
examples.note: 반말 똑똑해; 똑똑하다 works for clever animals too.

examples.en: That student was smart from a young age.
examples.note: Past 똑똑했어요; -서부터 = 'starting from'.

examples.en: If you act smart(ly), you won't lose out.
examples.note: Adverb 똑똑하게 = 'cleverly/shrewdly', not just 'intelligently'.

entries.nuance: 똑똑하다 is native Korean (not Sino-Korean), and it means 'smart' in the everyday sense of being quick, sharp, and able to understand and judge well — equally natural for a bright child, a clever student, or a clever pet. The nearest rivals are 영리하다 (clever/shrewd, slightly more about cunning and cute cleverness, often for kids and animals) and 똑똑하다's bookish cousin 지능이 높다 ('high IQ'); 똑똑하다 is the warm spoken word, while 우수하다 (excellent) or 유능하다 (competent/capable) describe proven performance and ability at work rather than raw brains. The adverb 똑똑하게 can drift toward 'shrewdly, without being fooled', as in 똑똑하게 소비하다 ('shop smart'). It takes the regular 하다 conjugation (똑똑해요). The English-speaker pitfall: 'smart' in English also means stylish/well-dressed, but 똑똑하다 NEVER means fashionable — for that you need 멋있다 or 옷을 잘 입다 — and beginners often misfire by saying 똑똑하요 instead of the contracted 똑똑해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 똑똑하요 instead of 똑똑해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 똑똑하다 for 'smart' meaning well-dressed/sharp-looking (e.g. '오늘 정말 똑똑해 보여요' to mean a sharp outfit). That English sense doesn't transfer; use 멋있다 or 깔끔하다 for appearance.
Overusing 똑똑하다 about an adult's job performance. To praise a capable colleague Koreans more often say 일을 잘하다 or 유능하다; calling a senior 똑똑하다 to their face can sound like judging a child.

entries.shortExplanation: 게으르다 means "to be lazy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be lazy" is 게으르다 (geeureuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 게을러요 ("someone is lazy"). Watch the particle attached to 게으르다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 르 irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ
modifier 게으른 (regular)
subject takes 이/가
noun 게으름 + 피우다 set phrase

examples.en: I'm really lazy on weekends.
examples.note: 반말 게을러; 르 irregular gives 게을러.

examples.ko: 동생이 너무 게을러서 방 청소를 안 해요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi neomu geeulleoseo bang cheongsoreul an haeyo.
examples.en: My sibling is so lazy that they don't clean their room.
examples.note: 게을러서 (르 irregular + 서) = 'because lazy'.

examples.ko: 요즘 좀 게을러져서 운동을 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jom geeulleojyeoseo undongeul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I've gotten a bit lazy lately so I couldn't work out.
examples.note: 게을러지다 = 'become lazy' (게으르다 + 어지다).

entries.nuance: 게으르다 means 'lazy/idle', describing someone who avoids effort and puts things off; it is native Korean (not Sino-Korean) and carries a clearly negative, faintly scolding tone, so it is something you say about yourself jokingly or about a close family member, but rarely to a senior's face. Its mirror opposite is 부지런하다 (diligent), and its near-neighbor 느리다 means 'slow' (about speed), which is different — a fast worker can still be 게으른 if they dodge work, and a 게으른 person isn't necessarily 느린. Conjugation is the key lesson: 게으르다 is a 르-irregular verb, so before 어요 the 르 doubles the ㄹ and the vowel becomes 어 → 게을러요 (the stem 게으르- → 게을러-); but the modifier and dictionary-style forms stay regular (게으른 사람, 게으릅니다). Watch the set noun phrase 게으름을 피우다 ('to slack off'). The English-speaker pitfall is conjugating it like a regular ㅡ-vowel verb and saying 게으러요 — you must apply the 르 rule to get 게을러요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 게으러요 — this is a 르 irregular, so the ㄹ doubles: the correct form is 게을러요.
Confusing it with 느리다. 게으르다 = unwilling to work (laziness); 느리다 = slow in speed. '동작이 게으르다' to mean physically slow is wrong; say 동작이 느리다.
Using 게으르다 bluntly about a boss or elder. It is judgmental; soften with humor about yourself (저 오늘 좀 게을렀어요) rather than labeling a superior.

Its mirror opposite is 부지런하다 (diligent), and its near-neighbor 느리다 means 'slow' (about speed), which is different — a fast worker can still be 게으른 if they dodge work, and a 게으른 person isn't necessarily 느린.

게으르다 is a 르-irregular verb, so before 어요 the 르 doubles the ㄹ and the vowel becomes 어 → 게을러요 (the stem 게으르- → 게을러-); but the modifier and dictionary-style forms stay regular (게으른 사람, 게으릅니다).
The pitfall is conjugating it like a regular ㅡ-vowel verb and saying 게으러요 — you must apply the 르 rule to get 게을러요.

entries.shortExplanation: 부지런하다 means "to be diligent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부지런하다 (bujireonhada) = "to be diligent". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부지런해요 ("someone is diligent") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 부지런한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
adverb 부지런히 + verb

examples.en: My mom is really diligent.
examples.note: 반말 부지런해; about a hardworking habit.

examples.en: Diligent people get up early in the morning.
examples.note: Modifier 부지런한 + 사람.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 부지런히 공부해서 시험에 붙었어요.
examples.romanization: geu chinguneun bujireonhi gongbuhaeseo siheome buteosseoyo.
examples.en: That friend studied diligently and passed the exam.
examples.note: Adverb 부지런히 = 'diligently/busily'; note the -히 form.

entries.nuance: 부지런하다 means 'diligent, industrious, hardworking by habit', the warm-praise opposite of 게으르다. The 부지런 part is native Korean (not a hanja compound), joined to 하다. The dividing line with near-synonyms matters: 성실하다 (Sino 誠實, 'sincere/faithful') praises a conscientious, reliable, earnest character — about attitude and trustworthiness — while 부지런하다 emphasizes physically keeping busy, not being idle, getting up early and getting things done; 열심히 하다 ('do hard') describes effort on a specific task in the moment, whereas 부지런하다 is a standing trait. The adverb is irregular in spelling — 부지런히 (not 부지런하게 in everyday use) — as in 부지런히 일하다. It conjugates regularly as a 하다 adjective (부지런해요). The English-speaker pitfall: 'diligent' in English often modifies effort on one job, so learners try to plug 부지런하다 into a single action ('I studied diligently') as a verb; for that, use the adverb 부지런히 + verb, and avoid the beginner error 부지런하요 (it must contract to 부지런해요).

Saying 부지런하요 instead of 부지런해요 — the 하다 ending contracts to 해요.
Forgetting the adverb is 부지런히, not 부지런하게, in natural speech: say 부지런히 일해요, not the clunky 부지런하게 일해요.
Equating it exactly with 성실하다. 부지런하다 = actively busy/not idle; 성실하다 = sincere and reliable in attitude. For 'a faithful, conscientious worker' 성실하다 fits better than 부지런하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 솔직하다 means "to be honest" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 솔직하다 (soljikada) means "to be honest". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 솔직해요 ("someone is honest"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 솔직하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 솔직한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
adverb 솔직히 as a discourse opener

examples.en: Honestly, I didn't really like that.
examples.note: 솔직히 = 'honestly' opener; 별로 = 'not great'.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 너무 솔직해서 가끔 상처를 줘요.
examples.romanization: geu chinguneun neomu soljikaeseo gakkeum sangcheoreul jwoyo.
examples.en: That friend is so frank that they sometimes hurt people.
examples.note: 솔직해서 (하다 + 서) shows the blunt-honesty edge.

examples.en: Thank you for the honest feedback.
examples.note: Modifier 솔직한 + 피드백; common at work.

entries.nuance: 솔직하다 means 'honest, frank, candid' — speaking your real thoughts and feelings openly without hiding or sugar-coating. It is Sino-Korean 率直 (솔/率 'frank, straightforward' + 직/直 'straight'), literally 'frank and straight'. The crucial contrast is with 정직하다 (Sino 正直 'upright-straight'), which is moral honesty — not lying, not cheating, being truthful as an ethical quality; 솔직하다 is about emotional candor, saying what you really feel, even bluntly, so 솔직하다 can sometimes mean 'too blunt', while 정직하다 is unambiguously praise. The adverb 솔직히 ('honestly, to be frank') is one of the most common conversation openers in Korean (솔직히 말하면…). It follows the regular 하다 conjugation (솔직해요). English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 솔직하다 when you mean morally honest/trustworthy (use 정직하다), and never say 솔직하요 — it contracts to 솔직해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 솔직하요 instead of 솔직해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 솔직하다 for 'honest' in the moral sense of not stealing or not lying (e.g. '그는 돈에 솔직해요'). For ethical honesty use 정직하다; 솔직하다 is about openly expressing real feelings.
Forgetting the discourse adverb 솔직히. To say 'honestly speaking' Koreans say 솔직히 말해서 / 솔직히 말하면, not 솔직하게 말하면 in casual speech.

entries.shortExplanation: 착하다 means "to be nice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be nice" is 착하다 (chakada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 착해요 ("someone is nice"). Watch the particle attached to 착하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 착한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
idiomatic: 'a kind price' = good value

examples.en: My classmate is good-natured.
examples.note: 반말 착해; describes a gentle heart.

examples.en: A well-behaved child greets adults well.
examples.note: Modifier 착한; -께 honorific for adults.

examples.ko: 이 식당은 양도 많은데 가격도 착해요.
examples.romanization: i sikdangeun yangdo maneunde gagyeokdo chakaeyo.
examples.en: This restaurant has big portions and the price is nice (cheap) too.
examples.note: Idiom 가격이 착하다 = 'reasonably cheap'.

entries.nuance: 착하다 is native Korean and describes an inherently good, gentle, kind-hearted, obedient nature — the goodness is a character trait, a soft and well-meaning heart, often used of children, students, and pets. The key contrast is with 친절하다: 착하다 is about who someone IS inside (good-hearted, won't hurt you, does the right thing), while 친절하다 is about considerate outward treatment in a moment; a shop clerk can be 친절한 at work while a child is 착한 by nature. Note a cultural nuance: calling an adult 착하다 can faintly imply 'naive/pushover' or sound like praising a child, so among grown-ups it is gentle but mild praise. A very common modern idiom is 가격이 착하다 / 착한 가격 ('a kind price' = pleasantly cheap, good value). It conjugates regularly (착해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'nice' in English is a catch-all (nice weather, nice food), but 착하다 applies almost only to a person's (or animal's) moral character — you cannot say 날씨가 착해요 for 'nice weather' (use 좋다), and beginners must contract 착하 + 요 to 착해요, never 착하요.

Saying 착하요 instead of 착해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 착하다 as a general 'nice' for things, weather, or food (e.g. '날씨가 착해요'). 착하다 is about good-hearted character; for pleasant things use 좋다.
Praising a respected adult or boss with 착하다 expecting strong praise — it can sound like calling them a naive pushover or talking down to them. For an admirable adult, 좋은 분이에요 or 인품이 훌륭하다 is safer.

entries.shortExplanation: 나쁘다 means "to be bad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 나쁘다 (nappeuda) = "to be bad". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 나빠요 ("something is bad") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 나쁘다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㅡ drops before 아 → 나빠
modifier 나쁜 + noun
subject takes 이/가

usagePhrases.en: to be bad for the body
usagePhrases.note: -에 나쁘다 = 'bad for ~'

examples.en: I'm in a bit of a bad mood.
examples.note: 반말 나빠; 기분이 나쁘다 = mood is bad.

examples.en: Cigarettes are bad for your health.
examples.note: -에 나쁘다 = 'bad for'; note 에, not 을.

examples.en: I heard bad news, so my heart feels heavy.
examples.note: Modifier 나쁜 + 소식; 들어서 = 'because heard'.

entries.nuance: 나쁘다 is native Korean and is the all-purpose opposite of 좋다, covering 'bad, poor, harmful, unpleasant' — bad weather, a bad mood, a bad habit, bad news, bad for your health. Near-synonyms split by domain: 나쁘다 is the broad evaluative 'bad', while 못되다 means 'wicked, ill-natured' (a morally bad, mean person, stronger and more accusatory), and 안 좋다 ('not good') is a softer, more polite way to say something is bad without the harsh punch of 나쁘다. The conjugation lesson is the ㅡ (으) drop: the stem 나쁘- loses its ㅡ before an ending starting with a vowel, and since the preceding vowel is the bright ㅏ, you add 아 → 나빠요 (past 나빴어요). Useful frame: X에 나쁘다 = 'bad for X' (몸에 나쁘다). English-speaker pitfalls: don't say 나쁘어요 — the ㅡ must drop to give 나빠요; and 'I feel bad' meaning sorry/guilty is NOT 기분이 나빠요 (that means you're in a bad/annoyed mood) — use 미안하다 for apology or 마음이 안 좋다 for feeling bad about something.

Saying 나쁘어요 instead of 나빠요 — 나쁘다 is a ㅡ-irregular: drop ㅡ and add 아 → 나빠요.
Translating English 'I feel bad (guilty/sorry)' as 기분이 나빠요. That means 'I'm in a bad/offended mood'. Use 미안해요 to apologize or 마음이 안 좋아요 to feel bad about something.
Using 나쁘다 for a morally wicked, malicious person and expecting full force — 나쁜 사람 is fine for 'bad person', but for 'mean/ill-natured' 못된 사람 is stronger and more precise.

entries.shortExplanation: 이상하다 means "to be strange" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이상하다 (isanghada) means "to be strange". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이상해요 ("something is strange"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이상하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 이상한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
좀 softens the judgment

examples.en: Something feels a bit off.
examples.note: 반말 이상해; 뭔가 = 'something'.

examples.en: The smell was off, so I didn't eat it.
examples.note: 이상해서 = 'because strange'; food going bad.

examples.ko: 오늘 그 사람 행동이 좀 이상했어요.
examples.romanization: oneul geu saram haengdongi jom isanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: That person's behavior was a bit strange today.
examples.note: Past 이상했어요; 행동이 이상하다 = odd behavior.

entries.nuance: 이상하다 means 'strange, odd, weird, off' — something that doesn't seem normal or feels not-right, from a funny smell to peculiar behavior to a glitchy phone. It is Sino-Korean 異常 (이/異 'different' + 상/常 'normal, usual'), literally 'departing from the usual', which captures the feel exactly: deviating from the expected. The nearest contrast is 신기하다 (Sino 神奇), which is 'strange' in the GOOD sense of fascinating, novel, wondrous — eyes-wide curiosity — whereas 이상하다 leans negative or uneasy ('that's weird/off'); also distinguish 이상하다 from 특이하다 ('distinctive, unusual' in a more neutral, noteworthy way). It conjugates regularly (이상해요). English-speaker pitfall: English 'strange' can be admiring ('a strange and beautiful film'), but if you mean wonderfully novel use 신기하다, not 이상하다 — and saying 음식이 이상해요 implies it has gone bad or tastes wrong, a real complaint. Don't say 이상하요; it contracts to 이상해요.

Saying 이상하요 instead of 이상해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 이상하다 to mean 'amazing/fascinatingly strange'. For wonder and novelty use 신기하다; 이상하다 signals something feels off, unsettling, or wrong.
Casually calling a person 이상한 사람 to mean 'an interesting eccentric'. To Koreans 이상한 사람 strongly implies 'a creepy/weird person', which is insulting; use 독특하다 or 특이하다 for a neutral 'unusual person'.

examples.note: 반말 + 이야; 특별한 + 날.

examples.note: -한테 = 'to me'; emotional value.

examples.note: Adverb 특별히 = 'specially/particularly'.

entries.nuance: 특별하다 means 'special, particular, out of the ordinary' — a day, gift, person, or place that stands apart and carries extra value or meaning. Watch the contrast with 특이하다 (Sino 特異, 'distinctive/peculiar'): 특별하다 = special and usually precious/valued (a special day, a special someone), while 특이하다 = unusual/peculiar in a more neutral or even slightly odd way (a peculiar habit); calling food 특이한 맛 means 'an unusual taste', not 'a wonderful taste'. Also note 특별하다 (adjective, 'is special') vs the adverb 특별히 ('specially, in particular'), which modifies verbs (특별히 신경 쓰다). It conjugates regularly (특별해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'special' in English can mean 'specialized/dedicated' (a special tool, special forces), but for that meaning Korean uses the prefix 특수 (특수 장비, 특수 부대), not 특별하다; and don't say 특별하요 — it must contract to 특별해요.

examples.note: Modifier 중요한 + 회의; -아서 'so'.

examples.en: I value my family the most.
examples.note: 중요하게 생각하다 = 'to regard as important / value'.

entries.nuance: 중요하다 means 'important, significant, crucial' — carrying weight, mattering a great deal. It is Sino-Korean 重要 (중/重 'heavy' + 요/要 'essential, vital'), a vivid literal image of 'heavy and essential', i.e. weighty and indispensable. The sharp contrast is with 필요하다 ('necessary/needed'): 중요하다 ranks how much something MATTERS in significance, while 필요하다 says something is REQUIRED to get a result — an exam can be 중요한 (it matters a lot) and a pencil 필요한 (you need it to take the test); they are not interchangeable. Also distinguish 소중하다 ('precious, dear'), which is emotional preciousness rather than functional weight. The collocation 중요하게 생각하다 / 중요하게 여기다 means 'to value, to prioritize'. It conjugates regularly (중요해요). English-speaker pitfall: learners blur 'important' and 'necessary' — for 'I need it' use 필요하다, reserving 중요하다 for 'it matters'; and never say 중요하요 (contract to 중요해요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 중요하요 instead of 중요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 중요하다 with 필요하다. 중요하다 = matters/significant; 필요하다 = needed/required. '연필이 중요해요' (the pencil is important) usually should be '연필이 필요해요' (I need a pencil).
Using 중요하다 for emotionally precious things. For 'my family is precious to me' Koreans say 소중하다 (가족이 소중해요); 중요하다 sounds more like ranking by significance.

entries.shortExplanation: 필요하다 means "to be necessary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 필요하다 (piryohada) means "to be necessary". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 필요해요 ("something is necessary"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 필요하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 필요한 + noun
the needed thing takes 이/가
verb + ㄹ 필요가 있다

examples.en: I need your help right now.
examples.note: 반말 필요해; the needed thing (도움) takes 이/가.

examples.ko: 이 일을 끝내려면 시간이 더 필요해요.
examples.romanization: i ireul kkeunnaeryeomyeon sigani deo piryohaeyo.
examples.en: To finish this work I need more time.
examples.note: -려면 = 'in order to'; 시간이 필요하다.

examples.en: There's no need to worry that much.
examples.note: ~ㄹ 필요(가) 없다 = 'no need to ~'.

entries.nuance: 필요하다 means 'to be necessary / to be needed', and it is the standard Korean way to say 'I need something'. It is Sino-Korean 必要 (필/必 'must, inevitably' + 요/要 'essential'), literally 'must-have, essential'. The grammar is the heart of the lesson and the main pitfall: Korean treats the needed thing as the GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT with 이/가, not as an object — so 'I need money' is 돈이 필요해요 (lit. 'money is necessary'), and the person who needs it is marked 한테/에게 (저한테 돈이 필요해요), never 돈을 필요해요. Contrast 필요하다 with 중요하다 ('important/matters'): needed vs. significant. The pattern -(으)ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다 means 'there is/isn't a need to ~' (걱정할 필요 없어요). It conjugates regularly (필요해요). English-speaker pitfall: because English 'need' is a transitive verb taking an object, learners wrongly say 나는 물을 필요해요; the correct, natural Korean is 나는 물이 필요해요 — and don't say 필요하요 (contract to 필요해요).

Saying 필요하요 instead of 필요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 필요하다 with 중요하다. 필요하다 = required/needed to achieve something; 중요하다 = significant/matters. '시간이 중요해요' (time matters) and '시간이 필요해요' (I need time) say different things.

entries.shortExplanation: 비슷하다 means "to be similar" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be similar" is 비슷하다 (biseutada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비슷해요 ("things are similar"). Watch the particle attached to 비슷하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 비슷한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
compare-target takes 와/과 or 랑

examples.en: The two of us have kind of similar personalities.
examples.note: 반말 비슷해; 둘이 = 'the two'.

examples.en: This bag is similar to that bag.
examples.note: -(이)랑 비슷하다 = 'similar to' (casual).

examples.ko: 맛이 비슷해서 두 개를 자꾸 헷갈려요.
examples.romanization: masi biseutaeseo du gaereul jakku hetgallyeoyo.
examples.en: The tastes are similar, so I keep mixing the two up.
examples.note: 비슷해서 = 'because similar'; 자꾸 = 'keep ~ing'.

entries.nuance: 비슷하다 means 'similar, alike, resembling' — two things that are close but not identical. It is native Korean (not a hanja word). The crucial contrast is with 같다 ('same/identical'): 비슷하다 says they RESEMBLE each other (close, comparable, but with differences), while 같다 says they are THE SAME; '가격이 비슷해요' = the prices are similar/comparable, but '가격이 같아요' = the prices are exactly the same — mixing these up changes the fact. Note the comparison particle: the thing you compare against takes 와/과 (formal) or 랑/이랑 (casual) plus 비슷하다 (A는 B와 비슷하다). Useful collocations: 성격이 비슷하다, 분위기가 비슷하다, 비슷한 또래 ('similar-aged peers'). It conjugates regularly (비슷해요). English-speaker pitfall: English says 'similar TO', so learners reach for 에/에게, but Korean uses 와/과/랑 — say 이거랑 비슷해요, not 이거에 비슷해요; and don't say 비슷하요 (contract to 비슷해요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the compared thing with 에: 'B에 비슷하다' is wrong. Use 와/과 or 랑/이랑 — 'B와 비슷하다 / B랑 비슷하다'.
Saying 비슷하요 instead of 비슷해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 빨갛다 means "to be red" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 빨갛다 (ppalgata) = "to be red". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사과가 빨개요 ("The apple is red") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빨갛다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, not 을/를
빨간색 = the noun 'red color'
빨개지다 = become red, change of state
빨간 = the modifier that sits before a noun

examples.en: This apple is red
examples.note: the most basic 요-form: 빨갛다 → 빨개요

examples.en: The evening sky was dyed red
examples.note: 빨갛게 = the adverb 'redly', + 물들다 'to be dyed'

examples.en: I got embarrassed so my face turned red
examples.note: 빨개지다 captures the change, not just the state

entries.nuance: 빨갛다 is the vivid, pure 'red' of an apple, a stop light, or a blushing face. Among red words, contrast it with 붉다, which is the more literary, darker 'reddish/crimson' used for blood, sunsets, and emotion (붉은 노을), while 빨갛다 is the bright everyday red a child would point at. As an adjective it describes a STATE, so the thing that is red takes 이/가 (얼굴이 빨개요), never 을/를. The biggest trap for English speakers is the ㅎ-irregular: the stem-final ㅎ vanishes AND the vowel fuses, so it is never 빨갛아요 but 빨개요, and the noun-modifying form is 빨간 (빨간 사과), not 빨갛은. To say something 'turns red,' use 빨개지다, because 빨갛다 alone is a static quality, not a change. Note 빨간색 is the noun 'the color red.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using the modifier 빨갛은 사과 — drop the ㅎ for the modifier too: it is 빨간 사과.
Saying 사과를 빨개요 with 을/를 — a color is a state, so use 이/가: 사과가 빨개요.

entries.shortExplanation: 파랗다 means "to be blue" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 파랗다 (parata) means "to be blue". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 하늘이 파래요 ("The sky is blue"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 파랗다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the classic blue thing, state with 이/가
파란색 = the noun 'blue', sits before another noun
파랗게 = adverb 'bluely' + 칠하다 'paint'
새- prefix intensifies the shade

examples.en: The sky is blue today
examples.note: basic 요-form: 파랗다 → 파래요

examples.en: The sea is really blue, isn't it
examples.note: -네요 adds a tone of fresh observation

examples.en: My lips went blue (from cold/fear)
examples.note: 파랗게 질리다 is a set phrase for going pale/blue

entries.nuance: 파랗다 is the bright blue of a clear sky and the sea, and in Korean it famously also covers what English calls 'green' for traffic lights and fresh leaves (파란불 'the green light,' 파란 잔디 'green grass') — a real surprise for learners. The neighboring word 푸르다 is more poetic and leans 'verdant/azure,' used for 푸른 산 'green mountains' and 푸른 하늘 in songs, while 파랗다 is the plain everyday blue. Being an adjective, the blue thing takes 이/가 (하늘이 파래요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular is the key pitfall: never 파랗아요 but 파래요, and the modifier is 파란 (파란 바다), not 파랗은. Use 파래지다 for 'turn blue,' and 파란색 for the noun 'the color blue.'

Saying 파랗아요 — the ㅎ deletes and the vowel fuses, giving 파래요 as the polite form.
Forming the modifier as 파랗은 바다 — it must be 파란 바다 with the ㅎ dropped.
Assuming 파랗다 only means 'blue' — for a traffic 'go' light Koreans say 파란불, so it can map to English 'green.'

entries.shortExplanation: 노랗다 means "to be yellow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be yellow" is 노랗다 (norata). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바나나가 노래요 ("The banana is yellow"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a fruit
노란색 = noun 'yellow' before another noun
노랗게 = adverb + 익다 'ripen', a natural pair
샛- prefix intensifies the yellow

examples.en: This banana is yellow
examples.note: basic 요-form: 노랗다 → 노래요

examples.en: In autumn the ginkgo leaves turn yellow
examples.note: 노랗게 물들다 = 'be dyed yellow'

examples.en: After starving for days my vision went yellow (I felt faint)
examples.note: 눈앞이 노래지다 is an idiom for dizziness/despair

entries.nuance: 노랗다 is the cheerful pure yellow of a banana, a chick, or a school bus. Korean color adjectives like this come in a 'bright vs dark' vowel-harmony pair: 노랗다 (bright, with ㅗ/ㅏ) feels light and vivid, while its darker partner 누렇다 (with ㅜ/ㅓ) means a dull, dingy, faded yellow like old paper or unhealthy skin — choosing the wrong one changes the whole feeling. As an adjective it takes 이/가 on the yellow thing (잎이 노래요), not 을/를. Watch the ㅎ-irregular: it is 노래요, never 노랗아요, and the modifier is 노란 (노란 우산), not 노랗은. There is also a vivid set phrase 눈앞이 노래지다 'to feel faint/hopeless,' literally 'the front of the eyes turns yellow.' The noun is 노란색.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 노랗아요 — ㅎ drops and the vowel fuses to 노래요 for the polite form.
Writing the modifier as 노랗은 우산 — the correct modifier is 노란 우산.
Mixing up 노랗다 and 누렇다 — 노랗다 is bright/fresh yellow, 누렇다 is dull/sickly yellow, so they are not interchangeable.

entries.explanation: 까맣다 (kkamata) = "to be black". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 머리가 까매요 ("The hair is black") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 까맣다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing hair
까만색 = noun 'black' before another noun
까맣게 + 타다, a very common pair
idiom: 'forget blackly' = forget utterly

examples.en: The cat is black
examples.note: basic 요-form: 까맣다 → 까매요

examples.en: My face got tanned dark in summer
examples.note: 까맣게 타다 = 'get burnt/tanned black'

examples.en: I had completely forgotten the appointment
examples.note: 까맣게 잊다 = forget utterly, a fixed expression

entries.nuance: 까맣다 is everyday black — black hair, a black cat, a dark night sky, or skin tanned by the sun. It is the 'bright/casual' vowel-harmony partner of 꺼멓다 (darker, grimier black) and is closely related to the Sino-flavored noun 검은색; the near-synonym adjective 검다 is slightly more formal/neutral ('to be black/dark'), while 까맣다 sounds more vivid and conversational. As a state adjective the black thing takes 이/가 (머리가 까매요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular trap applies: it is 까매요, never 까맣아요, and the modifier is 까만 (까만 신발), not 까맣은. Korean also uses 까맣게 figuratively — 까맣게 잊다 'to forget completely' and 까맣게 타다 'to get a deep tan' — which do not translate word-for-word into English. The noun is 까만색 (or 검은색).

Saying 까맣아요 — the ㅎ-irregular gives 까매요 as the polite form.
Using the modifier 까맣은 신발 — it should be 까만 신발 with ㅎ dropped.
Translating 까맣게 잊다 literally as 'forget black' — it is an idiom meaning 'to forget completely.'

하얀색 = noun 'white' before another noun
하얗게 + 변하다, change of color
새- prefix = brilliant, spotless white

examples.en: This paper is white
examples.note: basic 요-form: 하얗다 → 하얘요

examples.en: It snowed and the whole world turned white
examples.note: 하얘지다 = the change 'become white'

examples.en: She was so shocked her face went white
examples.note: 하얗게 질리다 = go pale, a set phrase

entries.nuance: 하얗다 is bright, clean white — fresh snow, white paper, clouds, a crisp white shirt. It is the casual, vivid counterpart of the more neutral 희다 'to be white' (희다 sounds slightly bookish, e.g. 흰 눈 in writing), and the darker harmony partner 허옇다 means a dull, pale, washed-out white. As a state adjective the white thing takes 이/가 (눈이 하얘요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular is the core pitfall: it is 하얘요, never 하얗아요, and the noun-modifier is 하얀 (하얀 셔츠), not 하얗은 — though note the related stem 희다 gives the very common modifier 흰 (흰색, 흰 눈). Use 하얘지다 for 'turn white' and the idiom 얼굴이 하얗게 질리다 'to go pale with shock.' The noun is 하얀색 (or 흰색).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 하얗아요 — the ㅎ-irregular produces 하얘요 for the polite form.
Forming the modifier as 하얗은 셔츠 — it is 하얀 셔츠 (or 흰 셔츠 from 희다).
Confusing 하얗다 and 노랗다-style endings — remember 하얗다 fuses to 얘 (하얘요), giving the distinctive ㅒ vowel.

entries.shortExplanation: 동그랗다 means "to be round" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be round" is 동그랗다 (donggeurata). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 달이 동그래요 ("The moon is round"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a shape
동그란 = the modifier before a noun
동그랗게 뜨다, a vivid set phrase
the related noun built from the same root

examples.en: This mirror is round
examples.note: basic 요-form: 동그랗다 → 동그래요

examples.en: The child opened her eyes wide
examples.note: 동그랗게 뜨다 shows surprise

examples.en: Please shape the dough into rounds
examples.note: 동그랗게 빚다 = 'mold into a round shape'

entries.nuance: 동그랗다 describes a small, neat, circular roundness — a coin, a plate, the full moon, wide-open eyes. Distinguish it from 둥글다, which is the broader, more neutral 'round/spherical' (a round table, a globe, a rounded character), and from 동그랗다's own darker harmony partner 둥그렇다 (a bigger, looser round). The diminutive 동- root makes 동그랗다 feel cute and compact, so it pairs naturally with 동그라미 'a (drawn) circle.' As a shape adjective the round thing takes 이/가 (달이 동그래요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular is the trap: it is 동그래요, never 동그랗아요, and the modifier is 동그란 (동그란 접시), not 동그랗은. A favorite collocation is 눈을 동그랗게 뜨다 'to open the eyes wide (in surprise),' where 동그랗게 is the adverb form.

Saying 동그랗아요 — the ㅎ-irregular yields 동그래요 as the polite form.
Using the modifier 동그랗은 접시 — the correct form is 동그란 접시.
Treating 동그랗다 and 둥글다 as identical — 동그랗다 is small/cute round, 둥글다 is general round/spherical.

entries.shortExplanation: 귀엽다 means "to be cute" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 귀엽다 (gwiyeopda) = "to be cute". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 강아지가 귀여워요 ("The puppy is cute") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 귀엽다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing an animal
귀여운 = the modifier before a noun
귀엽게 = adverb form + 웃다
귀여워 + 죽겠다, a strong casual reaction

examples.en: This cat is cute
examples.note: basic 요-form via ㅂ-irregular: 귀엽다 → 귀여워요

examples.en: The baby is really cute(-looking)
examples.note: 귀엽게 생기다 = 'be cute in looks'

examples.ko: 강아지가 너무 귀여워서 계속 보게 돼요
examples.romanization: gangajiga neomu gwiyeowoseo gyesok boge dwaeyo
examples.en: The puppy is so cute I keep looking
examples.note: -아서 links 'cute' to the result

entries.nuance: 귀엽다 means 'cute, adorable, endearing' — the small-and-lovable charm of babies, animals, and round little objects, and it can also describe an older person's behavior as 'charmingly sweet.' Crucially it is NOT the same as 예쁘다 'pretty/beautiful': 귀엽다 is about lovable charm (a chubby puppy), while 예쁘다 is about visual prettiness (an elegant dress), so calling a grown adult only 귀엽다 can imply 'cute like a kid' rather than 'gorgeous.' As a state adjective the cute thing takes 이/가 (아기가 귀여워요), not 을/를. The grammar pitfall is the ㅂ-irregular: the stem-final ㅂ turns into 우/워 before a vowel, so it is 귀여워요, never 귀엽어요, and the modifier is 귀여운 (귀여운 인형), not 귀엽은. The past is 귀여웠어요. Beware: not every ㅂ word is irregular (좁다 → 좁아요), but 귀엽다 is.

Saying 귀엽어요 — 귀엽다 is ㅂ-irregular, so ㅂ becomes 워 and the polite form is 귀여워요.
Using the modifier 귀엽은 인형 — the ㅂ becomes 운, giving 귀여운 인형.
Calling an adult 귀여워요 to mean 'beautiful' — that conveys 'cute/endearing'; for 'pretty' use 예뻐요 instead.

entries.shortExplanation: 멋지다 means "to be cool" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 멋지다 (meotjida) means "to be cool". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저 차가 멋져요 ("That car is cool"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 멋지다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing an object
멋진 = the modifier before a noun
멋지게 = adverb form + 차려입다

usagePhrases.en: to be told one is cool
usagePhrases.note: 멋지다 + quotative, a common compliment

examples.en: This building is cool
examples.note: basic 요-form: 멋지다 → 멋져요

examples.en: You dressed really sharply today
examples.note: 멋지게 차려입다 = dress stylishly

examples.en: Behaving so maturely — that's really cool
examples.note: 멋지다 here praises character, not looks

entries.nuance: 멋지다 means 'cool, stylish, splendid, impressive,' praising not just looks but admirable style or character — a sharp outfit, a stunning view, or someone who acts with class. Built from the native noun 멋 'style/flair/taste,' it is warmer and more sincere than the English loanword 쿨하다, which means 'cool' in the sense of laid-back/unbothered, not 'awesome.' Compare also 멋있다, a near-twin: 멋있다 and 멋지다 are nearly interchangeable, with 멋지다 sounding a touch more exclamatory/admiring. As a state adjective the impressive thing takes 이/가 (경치가 멋져요), not 을/를. Although it ends in 지, it is a fully REGULAR adjective: the stem 멋지- + 어 contracts to 멋져요 (never 멋지어요). The pitfall is leaving it bare as 멋지요 — that drops the required 어, so always use 멋져요; the modifier is 멋진 (멋진 옷) and the past is 멋졌어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 멋지요 for the polite form — the stem needs 어, contracting to 멋져요.
Writing 멋지어요 in full — 지 + 어 contracts, so the natural form is 멋져요.
Using 쿨하다 to mean 'awesome' — 쿨하다 means 'laid-back/unbothered'; for 'cool/impressive' use 멋지다.
