entries.shortExplanation: 날씬하다 means "to be slim" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be slim" is 날씬하다 (nalssinhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 언니가 날씬해요 ("My older sister is slim"). Watch the particle attached to 날씬하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a person
날씬한 = the modifier before a noun
날씬하게 = adverb + 보이다 'appear'
common body-part collocation

examples.en: That actor is slim
examples.note: basic 하다-form: 날씬하다 → 날씬해요

examples.en: I exercised so my legs got slimmer
examples.note: 날씬해지다 = the change 'become slim'

examples.ko: 이 옷을 입으면 더 날씬해 보여요
examples.romanization: i oseul ibeumyeon deo nalssinhae boyeoyo
examples.en: You look slimmer in these clothes
examples.note: 날씬해 보이다 = 'appear slim'

entries.nuance: 날씬하다 is a flattering 'slim, slender, trim' — a fit, attractive thinness people aspire to, often paired with 몸매 'figure' (날씬한 몸매). It is firmly positive, unlike the plain near-synonym 마르다 'to be thin,' which is neutral-to-negative and can imply 'skinny/scrawny' or even unhealthily underweight (너무 말랐어요 'too skinny'); so complimenting someone, choose 날씬하다, not 마르다. Note 마르다 is also a르-irregular verb-like form, whereas 날씬하다 is a clean 하다 adjective. As a state adjective the slim person/part takes 이/가 (다리가 날씬해요), not 을/를. The 하다 pitfall: never 날씬하요 — the 하다 ending becomes 해요 (하 + 여 → 해), so it is 날씬해요. The modifier is 날씬한 (날씬한 모델), the adverb 날씬하게, and 'get slimmer' is 날씬해지다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 날씬하요 — every 하다 adjective conjugates to 해요, so it is 날씬해요.
Using 마르다 as a compliment — 마르다 can sound 'too skinny'; for an admiring 'slim' use 날씬하다.
Marking the body part with 을/를 (다리를 날씬해요) — it is a state, so use 이/가: 다리가 날씬해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 뚱뚱하다 means "to be fat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뚱뚱하다 (ttungttunghada) = "to be fat". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고양이가 뚱뚱해요 ("The cat is fat") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 뚱뚱하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, gentler on an animal
뚱뚱한 = the modifier before a noun
뚱뚱해 + 보이다, often a worry about clothes
뚱뚱한 + 체형, describing body type

examples.en: This penguin is fat
examples.note: basic 하다-form: 뚱뚱하다 → 뚱뚱해요

examples.en: I gained weight lately so I got a bit fat
examples.note: 뚱뚱해지다 = the change; 살이 찌다 = gain weight

examples.en: Will I look fat in these clothes?
examples.note: 뚱뚱해 보이다, a typical self-conscious question

entries.nuance: 뚱뚱하다 is the blunt, plain word for 'fat/chubby,' and like English 'fat' it is sensitive: said straight to or about a person it sounds rude, so Koreans soften it about people and use it freely only for animals or stuffed toys. For people, the polite alternatives are 통통하다 'pleasantly plump/chubby' (cute, kind) and the gentle euphemism 살이 좀 있다 'to have a bit of weight'; the opposite is 날씬하다 'slim.' Note 뚱뚱하다 describes the standing state, while the verb 살이 찌다 'to gain weight' describes the process. As a state adjective the heavy thing takes 이/가 (배가 뚱뚱해요), not 을/를. The 하다 trap: never 뚱뚱하요 — it conjugates to 뚱뚱해요. The modifier is 뚱뚱한 (뚱뚱한 강아지), the adverb 뚱뚱하게, and 'get fat' is 뚱뚱해지다.

Saying 뚱뚱하요 — the 하다 ending becomes 해요, so the polite form is 뚱뚱해요.
Calling a person 뚱뚱해요 to their face — it sounds harsh; soften with 통통하다 or 살이 좀 있다.
Confusing the state with the action — 뚱뚱하다 is 'to be fat,' but 'to gain weight' is the verb 살이 찌다.

entries.shortExplanation: 건강하다 means "to be healthy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 건강하다 (geonganghada) means "to be healthy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 할머니가 건강해요 ("My grandmother is healthy"). usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a person
건강한 = the modifier before a noun
건강하게 + 지내다, a warm farewell phrase

usagePhrases.en: to take care of one's health
usagePhrases.note: the noun 건강 + 챙기다

examples.en: My father is healthy
examples.note: basic 하다-form: 건강하다 → 건강해요

examples.en: I eat lots of vegetables so I got healthier
examples.note: 건강해지다 = the change 'become healthy'

entries.nuance: 건강하다 means 'to be healthy, in good physical condition' — strong, well, free of illness — for a person, a body, or by extension healthy food and habits. It is Sino-Korean: 健康 (健 'sturdy/robust' + 康 'at ease/well'), literally 'robust and well,' which is why the noun 건강 'health' shows up everywhere (건강 검진 'health checkup,' 건강을 챙기다 'mind one's health'). Distinguish it from 튼튼하다 'sturdy/robust,' which stresses physical toughness and durability and also describes objects (튼튼한 책상 'a sturdy desk'), whereas 건강하다 is about wellness and is normally for living things. As a state adjective the healthy one takes 이/가 (몸이 건강해요), not 을/를. The 하다 pitfall: never 건강하요 — it becomes 건강해요. The modifier is 건강한 (건강한 습관), and 건강하게 지내세요 is a standard 'take care / be well' wish.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 건강하요 — the 하다 ending conjugates to 해요, giving 건강해요.
Using 건강하다 for an object — for a sturdy thing like a desk use 튼튼하다; 건강하다 is for living bodies.
Saying 몸을 건강해요 with 을/를 — it is a state, so use 이/가: 몸이 건강해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 어떻다 means "to be how" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be how" is 어떻다 (eotteota). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 날씨가 어때요? ("How is the weather?"). usagePhrases.note: asking about a state with 이/가
어떤 = the modifier 'what kind of'
어떻게 = the adverb 'how/in what way'
어떻게 해 contracted, a panicked reaction

examples.en: How's this outfit? / What do you think?
examples.note: 어때요 also means 'how about it?' to suggest

examples.en: How was the movie yesterday?

entries.nuance: 어떻다 is the question-adjective 'to be how / to be what-like,' the root behind a whole family Koreans use constantly. Learn its three faces: 어때(요)? = 'How is it? / How about it?' (asking a state or making a soft suggestion — 이거 어때요?), 어떤 = the modifier 'what kind of' before a noun (어떤 음악 'what kind of music'), and 어떻게 = the adverb 'how / in what way' for asking method (어떻게 해요? 'how do you do it?'). Do not confuse 어떻다 with 어떡하다, the contraction of 어떻게 하다 'to do how,' which gives the very common cry 어떡해! 'what do I do?!' As an irregular ㅎ adjective, the polite/question form is 어때요, never 어떻아요, and the past is 어땠어요. The single most frequent learner error is choosing the wrong family member — using 어떤 where 어떻게 is needed, or vice versa.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 어떻아요 — 어떻다 is ㅎ-irregular, so the question form is 어때요 (past 어땠어요).
Mixing 어떤 and 어떻게 — 어떤 + noun = 'what kind of' (어떤 색), but 어떻게 + verb = 'how' (어떻게 가요).
Writing 어떻해 for 'what do I do' — the set phrase is 어떡해 (from 어떻게 해), not 어떻해.

entries.shortExplanation: 달다 means "to be sweet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 달다 (dalda) = "to be sweet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 달콤하다 ("to be sweet and lovely") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 달다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: softer, more poetic cousin of 달다, used for desserts and even romance
the noun 단맛 (sweet + taste) is how you name the flavor itself
꿀처럼 is the go-to simile for intense sweetness

usagePhrases.en: to be tasty / to keep saying
usagePhrases.note: idiom: food is delicious, or a word is 'always on your lips'

examples.en: This candy is really sweet.
examples.note: plain statement with 정말 for emphasis; note the subject takes 이

examples.en: The strawberries were sweeter than expected, so I was surprised.
examples.note: -아서 links the taste to your reaction

examples.ko: 손님, 단거 좋아하시면 이 케이크 추천드려요.
examples.romanization: sonnim, dangeo joahasimyeon i keikeu chucheondeuryeoyo.
examples.en: If you like sweet things, sir, I recommend this cake.
examples.note: shop register: 단거 = 단 것 (sweet thing), 추천드리다 is humble

entries.nuance: 달다 is the basic word for sugary, honey-like sweetness, and the dividing line you must learn is 달다 vs 달콤하다: 달다 is the flat, factual report ('this is sweet, maybe too sweet'), while 달콤하다 adds a warm, pleasant, almost romantic glow ('sweet and lovely') and is preferred for desserts, perfume, even 달콤한 사랑. As an adjective 달다 takes 이/가 on the thing tasted (커피가 달아요), never 을/를. Watch the irregular conjugation: the stem ends in ㄹ, which drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ — so the formal form is 답니다 (not 달습니다) and the modifier is 단 (단 음식), yet 달아요 keeps the ㄹ. The English-speaker trap is twofold: do not write 다라요, and remember that to 'add sugar' uses a verb (설탕을 넣다), because English 'sweeten' has no one-word match here. 달다 also coexists with the unrelated verb 달다 meaning 'to hang/attach', so context decides.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '이 커피를 달아요' — 달다 is descriptive, so the tasted item is the subject with 이/가: 이 커피가 달아요.
Writing the polite form as 다라요; the correct contraction keeps the block as 달아요.
Using the formal 달습니다 — because of ㄹ-dropping it must be 답니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 시다 means "to be sour" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 시다 (sida) means "to be sour". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 신맛이 나다 ("to taste sour"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 시다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 신맛 (sour + taste) names the flavor; 나다 means the taste 'comes out'
vivid variant of 시다, hints at a slightly off or fermented sour smell too
the GOOD sour — bright and appetizing, as in 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour)
식초 (vinegar) is the benchmark for sharp sourness

examples.en: The lemon is too sour.
examples.note: basic taste report; 너무 = too (much)

examples.en: The kimchi has fermented, so it's a little sour.
examples.note: -아서 ties fermentation to the sourness; 익다 = to ripen/ferment

examples.ko: 이거 상했나 봐요, 우유에서 신맛이 나요.
examples.romanization: igeo sanghaenna bwayo, uyueseo sinmasi nayo.
examples.en: I think this has gone bad — the milk tastes sour.
examples.note: real situation: sour milk signals spoilage, using 신맛이 나다

entries.nuance: 시다 is the sharp, acidic taste of lemon, vinegar, or over-fermented kimchi, and the key contrast is 시다 vs 새콤하다: 시다 is neutral-to-negative (it can simply mean 'too sour' or even 'spoiled'), whereas 새콤하다 is always the pleasant, refreshing tang you want in 새콤달콤 sweet-and-sour dishes. As a description the sour thing takes 이/가 (레몬이 셔요). The conjugation is the real pitfall: the stem 시- meets the 어요 ending and contracts, so the polite form is 셔요 (시+어요 → 셔요) and the past is 셨어요 — many learners wrongly write the uncontracted 시어요, which sounds bookish and unnatural in speech. Also note Koreans say a sour smell or spoiled food 시다/시큼하다, so when milk goes off you say 신맛이 나다 rather than translating 'gone bad' literally. Keep the subject particle 이/가 and never attach 을/를 to the tasted item.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시어요 in conversation — the natural contracted form is 셔요 (and past 셨어요).
Attaching 을/를: '레몬을 셔요' is wrong; the sour thing is the subject, 레몬이 셔요.
Confusing 시다 with 매콤하다/맵다; 시다 is acidic-sour, not spicy-hot.

entries.shortExplanation: 짜다 means "to be salty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be salty" is 짜다 (jjada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 짠맛이 나다 ("to taste salty"). Watch the particle attached to 짜다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 짠맛 (salty + taste) is the noun for the flavor itself
간 = the salt level of a dish; 간이 짜다/싱겁다 is how cooks judge food
adverb 짜게 + 먹다; doctors warn 짜게 먹지 마세요 (don't eat salty)
소금 (salt) as the obvious benchmark

examples.en: The soup is a bit salty.
examples.note: everyday complaint at the table; 좀 softens it

examples.ko: 라면을 끓일 때 스프를 다 넣으면 짜요.
examples.romanization: ramyeoneul kkeuril ttae seupeureul da neoeumyeon jjayo.
examples.en: If you add the whole seasoning packet when cooking ramen, it gets salty.
examples.note: -(으)면 condition → result

examples.ko: 사장님이 좀 짠 편이라 회식을 잘 안 사요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi jom jjan pyeonira hoesigeul jal an sayo.
examples.en: The boss is a bit stingy, so he rarely treats us to dinner.
examples.note: real-life slang: 짜다 = tightfisted, not about taste

entries.nuance: 짜다 means having a strong salt taste, and the practical contrast for cooking is 짜다 vs 간이 맞다: 짜다 says there is too much salt, while 간이 맞다 means the seasoning is just right (and 싱겁다 means too little). The salty thing takes 이/가 (국이 짜요). Conjugation is regular for an ㅏ-stem: 짜 + 아요 contracts to 짜요 (not 짜아요), past 짰어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, never write 짜아요. Second, 짜다 has a very common figurative meaning — 'stingy / tightfisted' — so 그 사람 진짜 짜 means 'that person is so cheap', nothing to do with food; English 'salty' meaning 'bitter/annoyed' does NOT transfer to Korean 짜다, so do not use it that way. When you want to talk about how salty you eat in general, use the adverb 짜게 (짜게 먹다), which health advice constantly repeats.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 짜아요 for the polite form; the ㅏ-stem contracts to 짜요.
Using 짜다 to mean emotionally 'salty/annoyed' as in English — in Korean that figurative sense is 'stingy', so the English idiom does not carry over.
Saying '이 국을 짜요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 짜요.

entries.shortExplanation: 싱겁다 means "to be bland" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 싱겁다 (singgeopda) = "to be bland". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 간이 싱겁다 ("the seasoning is too weak") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 싱겁다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the standard cook's verdict opposite 간이 짜다
맛이 + 싱겁다 reports a weak overall flavor
adverb 싱겁게 + 먹다; health-conscious eating
figurative: someone whose jokes or actions fall flat

examples.en: The soup is a bit bland.
examples.note: table comment; 좀 keeps it polite

examples.en: I didn't add salt, so the stew is bland.
examples.note: -아서 cause; pairs the missing salt with the result

examples.ko: 병원 밥은 싱겁게 나와서 처음엔 입에 안 맞았어요.
examples.romanization: byeongwon babeun singgeopge nawaseo cheoeumen ibe an majasseoyo.
examples.en: Hospital food comes lightly seasoned, so at first it didn't suit my taste.
examples.note: real situation with 싱겁게 and 입에 맞다

entries.nuance: 싱겁다 is the exact opposite of 짜다: it means a dish lacks salt or has too weak a flavor. The contrast to fix is 싱겁다 vs 담백하다 — both describe mild food, but 싱겁다 is a complaint ('underseasoned, needs salt') while 담백하다 is praise ('cleanly light, refreshing'); never mix them up when complimenting a cook. The bland thing takes 이/가 (국이 싱거워요). This is a ㅂ-irregular: before a vowel ending the ㅂ becomes 우, so 싱겁 + 어요 → 싱거워요, past 싱거웠어요, modifier 싱거운; the formal form keeps ㅂ as 싱겁습니다. The English-speaker trap is writing the regular 싱겁어요 — that form does not exist. Like several taste words it has a figurative use: a person or a story can be 싱겁다, meaning 'anticlimactic, a let-down', as in 그 영화 결말 좀 싱거웠어 ('the ending was a bit flat').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 싱겁어요; because it is ㅂ-irregular the correct form is 싱거워요.
Calling underseasoned food 담백하다 to be polite — 담백하다 is praise, but if it truly lacks salt the honest word is 싱겁다.
Saying '이 국을 싱거워요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 싱거워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 뜨겁다 means "to be hot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뜨겁다 (tteugeopda) means "to be hot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 뜨거운 물 ("hot water"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뜨겁다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the most common modifier pairing; 뜨거운 + noun
김 = steam; you often warn 뜨거우니까 김 조심하세요
adverb 뜨겁게 + 데우다 (warm up)
figurative: intense passion or public attention

examples.en: The coffee is still hot.
examples.note: everyday; 아직 = still

examples.ko: 방금 끓여서 국이 너무 뜨거워요, 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: banggeum kkeuryeoseo gugi neomu tteugeowoyo, josimhaseyo.
examples.en: I just boiled it, so the soup is very hot — be careful.
examples.note: -아서 cause + warning 조심하세요

examples.ko: 뜨거운 거 못 드시면 조금 식혀서 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: tteugeoun geo mot deusimyeon jogeum sikyeoseo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: If you can't handle hot things, I'll let it cool a bit before serving.
examples.note: service register: 드시다/드리다 honorifics with 식히다

entries.nuance: 뜨겁다 describes high temperature you feel by touch or in the mouth — hot soup, hot coffee — and the crucial contrast for English speakers is 뜨겁다 vs 맵다: English 'hot' covers both temperature and spice, but Korean splits them, so a fiery chili dish is 맵다 (spicy), never 뜨겁다. Use 뜨겁다 only for heat. The hot thing takes 이/가 (커피가 뜨거워요). It is a ㅂ-irregular verb: 뜨겁 + 어요 → 뜨거워요, past 뜨거웠어요, modifier 뜨거운 (뜨거운 물), but formal 뜨겁습니다 keeps the ㅂ. Compare with 따뜻하다 (pleasantly warm): 뜨겁다 is so hot it can burn, while 따뜻하다 is comfortably warm — choose by degree. Figuratively, 뜨겁다 means passionate or intense (뜨거운 관심, 뜨거운 응원). Avoid the made-up form 뜨겁어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 뜨겁다 for spicy food because English says 'hot' — spicy is 맵다; 뜨겁다 is only temperature.
Writing 뜨겁어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 뜨거워요.
Confusing 뜨겁다 (burning hot) with 따뜻하다 (comfortably warm) — they differ by intensity.

structuredNuance.t: 뜨겁다 describes high temperature you feel by touch or in the mouth — hot soup, hot coffee. Use 뜨겁다 only for heat. The hot thing takes 이/가 (커피가 뜨거워요). Figuratively, 뜨겁다 means passionate or intense (뜨거운 관심, 뜨거운 응원).

entries.shortExplanation: 차갑다 means "to be cold" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be cold" is 차갑다 (chagapda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 차가운 물 ("cold water"). Watch the particle attached to 차갑다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: default modifier pairing; 차가운 + noun
얼음 (ice) as the benchmark for sharp cold
adverb 차갑게 + 식다 (cool down)
figurative: emotionally distant, unfriendly

examples.en: The water is really cold.
examples.note: basic; 정말 emphasizes

examples.ko: 냉장고에 넣어 둬서 주스가 시원하게 차가워요.
examples.romanization: naengjanggoe neoeo dwoseo juseuga siwonhage chagawoyo.
examples.en: I kept it in the fridge, so the juice is refreshingly cold.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 시원하게 nuance

examples.ko: 그 사람 첫인상은 좀 차가웠는데 알고 보니 따뜻한 사람이에요.
examples.romanization: geu saram cheosinsangeun jom chagawonneunde algo boni ttatteutan saramieyo.
examples.en: He seemed a bit cold at first, but he turned out to be warm.
examples.note: figurative contrast 차갑다 vs 따뜻하다 about personality

entries.nuance: 차갑다 describes a cold temperature felt by touch — cold water, an iced drink, cold hands. The contrast to master is 차갑다 vs 시원하다: 차갑다 is plainly, even uncomfortably cold (object-temperature), while 시원하다 is the pleasant, refreshing cool you welcome on a hot day or in a cold drink, and it does not transfer to people. The cold thing takes 이/가 (물이 차가워요). It is a ㅂ-irregular: 차갑 + 어요 → 차가워요, past 차가웠어요, modifier 차가운, but formal 차갑습니다 keeps ㅂ. There is also a near-twin 춥다 (to be cold): use 춥다 only for the weather/air you feel as a person (날씨가 추워요), and 차갑다 for objects you touch (물이 차가워요) — mixing them is the classic learner error. Figuratively 차갑다 means cold-hearted or aloof (차가운 표정, 차가운 말투). Avoid the wrong form 차갑어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 차갑다 for cold weather — air/weather is 춥다 (날씨가 추워요); 차갑다 is for things you touch.
Writing 차갑어요; the ㅂ-irregular polite form is 차가워요.
Replacing 차갑다 with 시원하다 for an unpleasantly cold object — 시원하다 implies it feels good/refreshing.

entries.shortExplanation: 부드럽다 means "to be soft" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부드럽다 (budeureopda) = "to be soft". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부드러운 식감 ("a soft texture (mouthfeel)") shows how it actually behaves. vivid idiom: 입에서 살살 녹아요 (melts in your mouth)
adverb 부드럽게 + 말하다; soft manner of speaking
figurative: easygoing, mild-tempered

examples.en: This bread is really soft.
examples.note: basic food praise

examples.en: I cooked the meat thoroughly, so it's tender.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 푹 익히다 = cook well

examples.en: His voice was soft, so it was easy to listen to.
examples.note: figurative: 부드럽다 about voice/manner

entries.nuance: 부드럽다 covers a smooth, gentle softness — soft bread, tender meat, smooth fabric, even a gentle voice or manner. The contrast you need is 부드럽다 vs 말랑하다: 부드럽다 is broad and refined (smooth, mellow, gentle), while 말랑하다 specifically means squishy-springy to the touch like a marshmallow or 말랑한 젤리; for tender, melt-in-the-mouth food Koreans prefer 부드럽다. Writing 부드럽어요; as a ㅂ-irregular it becomes 부드러워요.
Using 말랑하다 for tender cooked meat — 말랑하다 is bouncy/squishy; tender food is 부드럽다.
Saying '이 빵을 부드러워요' — the food is the subject: 이 빵이 부드러워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 딱딱하다 means "to be hard" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 딱딱하다 (ttakttakada) means "to be hard". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 딱딱하게 굳다 ("to harden solid"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 딱딱하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: adverb 딱딱하게 + 굳다 (set/harden)
돌 (stone) as the benchmark for stale bread, etc.
figurative: tense, overly formal mood
figurative: rigid, unfriendly way of speaking

examples.en: This cracker is too hard.
examples.note: basic texture complaint

examples.en: The bread cooled down and got hard.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 해지다 (become); change of state

examples.ko: 회의 분위기가 너무 딱딱해서 농담 한마디 했어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui bunwigiga neomu ttakttakaeseo nongdam hanmadi haesseoyo.
examples.en: The meeting felt so stiff that I cracked a joke.
examples.note: figurative use about atmosphere

entries.nuance: 딱딱하다 describes a stiff, unyielding hardness — stale bread, a hard chair, frozen-solid food. The contrast to know is 딱딱하다 vs 질기다: 딱딱하다 means rigid and crunchy-hard (it cracks), while 질기다 means tough and chewy (it stretches and resists your teeth, like overcooked squid or gristly meat) — beginners often say 딱딱하다 when they mean 질기다. As a description the hard thing takes 이/가 (과자가 딱딱해요). It follows the regular 하다 pattern: 딱딱하 + 여요 → 딱딱해요, past 딱딱했어요, modifier 딱딱한, formal 딱딱합니다. The opposite for food is 부드럽다. Figuratively 딱딱하다 means stiff or overly formal — 딱딱한 분위기 (a stiff atmosphere), 딱딱한 사람 (an inflexible person) — and the onomatopoeic doubling 딱딱 gives it that hard, knocking feel. Avoid the form 딱딱하요 (the 하다 ending is 해요).

Saying 딱딱하요; 하다-verbs end in 해요, so it is 딱딱해요.
Using 딱딱하다 for chewy/tough food — that is 질기다; 딱딱하다 is rigid and crunchy.
Saying '이 떡을 딱딱해요' — the food is the subject: 이 떡이 딱딱해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 신선하다 means "to be fresh" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be fresh" is 신선하다 (sinseonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신선한 재료 ("fresh ingredients"). Watch the particle attached to 신선하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 재료 = ingredients; a staple cooking/marketing phrase
신선도 (freshness level, 度 = degree) is the measurable noun
adverb 신선하게 + 보관하다 (store)
figurative: a pleasantly surprising, novel impression

examples.en: This milk is fresh.
examples.note: basic; product freshness

examples.en: It came in this morning, so the fish is fresh.
examples.note: -아서 cause; market situation

examples.ko: 발상이 정말 신선하네요, 그런 생각은 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: balsangi jeongmal sinseonhaneyo, geureon saenggageun mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: What a fresh idea — I'd never have thought of that.
examples.note: figurative 신선하다 about ideas, with -네요 admiration

entries.nuance: 신선하다 is Sino-Korean from 新鮮 (新 'new' + 鮮 'fresh/clear'), and it means newly harvested, just-caught, not spoiled — most at home with produce, seafood, and dairy. The contrast to master is 신선하다 vs 싱싱하다: 신선하다 is the broad, slightly formal word (also used figuratively for ideas), while 싱싱하다 is the lively, native-Korean word that specifically evokes plump, vibrant, still-alive freshness — a fish flapping at the market is 싱싱하다 more than 신선하다. The fresh thing takes 이/가 (생선이 신선해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 신선해요, past 신선했어요, modifier 신선한, formal 신선합니다. The big English-speaker pitfall: 'fresh' in English also means cheeky/impertinent and cool weather — neither transfers; Korean 신선하다 is purely about freshness/novelty. For a refreshing breeze use 시원하다 instead. Figuratively 신선한 충격 means a pleasantly novel surprise.

Using 신선하다 to mean cheeky or to mean cool weather as English 'fresh' can — those senses don't exist in Korean.
Saying 신선하요; the 하다 ending is 해요, so it is 신선해요.
Choosing 신선하다 when you want the vivid 'plump and lively' image of market seafood — that's 싱싱하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 고소하다 means "to be nutty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고소하다 (gosohada) = "to be nutty". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고소한 맛 ("a nutty, roasted flavor") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고소하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the core descriptor for sesame/nut taste
고소하다 describes aroma as well as taste
adverb 고소하게 + 볶다 (stir-fry/roast)
figurative slang: smug pleasure at someone's misfortune

examples.en: This bread has a nutty flavor.
examples.note: basic; 맛이 나다 for 'taste comes out'

examples.en: I drizzled a little sesame oil, so it's even nuttier.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 참기름 is the prototypical 고소한 oil

examples.en: It was kind of satisfying to see that annoying person get scolded.
examples.note: figurative/slang 고소하다 = schadenfreude, with -더라

entries.nuance: 고소하다 names a flavor English barely has a single word for: the warm, toasty, savory taste/aroma of roasted sesame, peanuts, perilla, nuts, and grains — think 참기름, 들기름, 콩가루. The contrast to learn is 고소하다 vs 구수하다: 고소하다 is the bright, light roasted-sesame note, while 구수하다 is a deeper, earthier roasted warmth (well-brewed 숭늉/누룽지, soybean paste 된장, barley tea) — they overlap but 구수하다 feels heartier and more rustic. There is no Sino-Korean root; it is native Korean. The tasty thing takes 이/가 (빵이 고소해요) or you say X에서 고소한 맛이 나다. Regular 하다 conjugation: 고소해요, past 고소했어요, modifier 고소한, formal 고소합니다. English-speaker pitfall: 'nutty' is only an approximation — do not restrict 고소하다 to literal nuts, and beware its common slang meaning 'serves you right / I'm secretly glad', a sense pure English 'nutty' never carries.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Limiting 고소하다 to literal nuts — it covers roasted sesame, oils, and grains, and even describes a savory aroma.
Saying 고소하요; as a 하다-adjective it is 고소해요.
Missing the slang sense: 고소하다 can mean smug satisfaction at someone's misfortune, not just flavor.

entries.shortExplanation: 느끼하다 means "to be greasy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 느끼하다 (neukkihada) means "to be greasy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 느끼한 음식 ("greasy/heavy food"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 느끼하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

속 (stomach) + 느끼하다: the heavy, sickly feeling
느끼함 (the greasiness) + 잡다; e.g. 김치가 느끼함을 잡아줘요
figurative: an over-the-top flirty or corny remark

examples.en: This pizza is a bit greasy.
examples.note: basic; 좀 softens the complaint

examples.ko: 기름진 고기를 많이 먹어서 속이 느끼해요.
examples.romanization: gireumjin gogireul mani meogeoseo sogi neukkihaeyo.
examples.en: I ate a lot of fatty meat, so I feel queasy.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 속이 느끼하다 = stomach feels heavy

examples.ko: 그 사람 자꾸 느끼한 말 해서 좀 부담스러웠어요.
examples.romanization: geu saram jakku neukkihan mal haeseo jom budamseureowosseoyo.
examples.en: He kept saying cheesy lines, so it felt a bit much.
examples.note: figurative 느끼하다 = corny/cringey, with 부담스럽다

entries.nuance: 느끼하다 describes the heavy, oily, cloying feeling of fatty food — pizza, cream pasta, deep-fried meat — and crucially also the queasy after-feeling in your stomach (속이 느끼하다). The contrast to fix is 느끼하다 vs 기름지다: 기름지다 neutrally states a dish is oily/rich (it can even be appetizing), while 느끼하다 carries the negative 'too rich, makes me want something to cut it' nuance — that's why Koreans say 느끼할 때 김치/콜라가 필요해. Its opposite is 담백하다 (cleanly light). The greasy thing takes 이/가 (피자가 느끼해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 느끼해요, past 느끼했어요, modifier 느끼한, formal 느끼합니다. Big English-speaker pitfall: 'greasy' is only half the meaning — 느끼하다 is also the standard way to call a person or their words 'cheesy / corny / smarmy' (느끼한 멘트, 느끼한 남자), so a slick flirt is 느끼하다, which surprises learners expecting only a food word.

Saying 느끼하요; the 하다 form is 느끼해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 담백하다 means "to be light" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the praise phrase for non-greasy taste
기름기 (oiliness) + 없다; what makes food 담백하다
adverb 담백하게 + 조리하다 (cook/prepare)
figurative: plain-spoken, without affectation

examples.en: This tofu dish is light and clean.
examples.note: basic praise for mild food

examples.en: It's made without oil, so it's light and clean-tasting.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 담백하다 + 깔끔하다 pairing

examples.ko: 그 배우는 인터뷰에서 늘 담백하게 말해서 호감이에요.
examples.romanization: geu baeuneun inteobyueseo neul dambaekage malhaeseo hogamieyo.
examples.en: That actor always speaks plainly in interviews, which makes him likeable.
examples.note: figurative 담백하다 about a frank manner

entries.nuance: 담백하다 is Sino-Korean from 淡白 (淡 'thin/light in taste' + 白 'plain/white'), and it is the praise-word for food that tastes clean and mild without grease or heavy seasoning — white fish, tofu, chicken breast, clear broth. It is the deliberate opposite of 느끼하다 (cloyingly greasy). The contrast to master is 담백하다 vs 싱겁다: both describe non-strong flavor, but 담백하다 is a compliment ('refreshingly clean, light'), while 싱겁다 is a complaint ('underseasoned, needs salt') — so call good light food 담백하다, never 싱겁다. English-speaker pitfall: do not translate with plain 'light' as in low-calorie or pale-colored — 담백하다 is specifically about a clean, non-greasy taste. Translating 담백하다 as 'light' in the sense of low-calorie or pale — it means clean, non-greasy taste.
Saying 담백하요; the 하다 form is 담백해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 매우 means "very" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매우 (maeu) = "very". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매우 좋아요. ("It is very good.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매우, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Sits directly in front of the adjective it boosts
Pairs naturally with formal 합니다-style endings

usagePhrases.en: It is a very important issue.
usagePhrases.note: Modifying an adjective inside a noun phrase (중요한)
Can boost an adverb like 빠르게, not only adjectives

examples.en: This book is very difficult.
examples.note: Basic: 매우 placed right before the adjective stem

examples.en: I was very disappointed with the meeting result.
examples.note: Everyday-formal: pairs with 합니다체 in a work setting

examples.ko: 조사 결과 안전성이 매우 높은 것으로 나타났습니다.
examples.romanization: josa gyeolgwa anjeonseongi maeu nopeun geoseuro natanatseumnida.
examples.en: The survey showed the safety level to be very high.
examples.note: Real situation: 매우 in a report/news register where 진짜 would feel wrong

entries.nuance: 매우 means 'very/highly' and signals a high degree, but it lives mostly in the written and formal-spoken register — reports, news, lectures, business email — so a Korean rarely blurts 매우 to a friend. Its nearest neighbors are 정말 and 너무: 정말 carries personal sincerity/surprise ('I really mean it'), 너무 originally meant 'excessively/too much' and now also means 'so' in casual speech, while 매우 is the cool, objective booster with no emotional color. It habitually pairs with 합니다-style endings and abstract adjectives (매우 중요하다, 매우 높다, 매우 만족하다). The English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for 매우 in chat because the textbook glossed it first, which sounds stiff and bookish — like writing 'most assuredly' to a buddy. Also, like all degree adverbs it goes BEFORE the word it modifies (매우 좋다), never after the verb the way English can append 'a lot'.

Placing it after the predicate as in '좋아요 매우' by analogy with English 'good, very much'; Korean degree adverbs must precede the adjective: 매우 좋아요.
Using 매우 with a verb of quantity to mean 'a lot' (e.g. 매우 먹었어요 for 'ate a lot'); for amount use 많이, and reserve 매우 for adjectives/states.

entries.shortExplanation: 정말 means "really" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정말 (jeongmal) means "really". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정말 맛있어요. ("It is really delicious."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정말 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Boosting an adjective with genuine feeling
Adds heartfelt sincerity to 고맙다
As a one-word reaction expressing surprise
Strengthens an apology to sound earnest

examples.en: I am really happy today.
examples.note: Basic: 정말 conveys 'I sincerely feel this'

examples.en: That movie was really sad.
examples.note: Everyday: spoken reaction to a shared experience

examples.en: Thank you so very much for coming despite being busy.
examples.note: Real situation: 정말 + 감사합니다 layers warmth onto a formal thank-you

entries.nuance: 정말 comes from the Sino-Korean 正(정, correct/true)+ 말(speech) — literally 'true words' — so at its core it asserts truth and sincerity, which is why it feels heartfelt rather than merely intensifying. Contrast with 진짜 ('real thing', 眞), which is the casual street twin and can sound slightly more exclamatory or skeptical; and with 너무, which stresses sheer degree ('so/too') without the truth-claim. So 정말 좋아요 = 'I genuinely like it' while 너무 좋아요 = 'I like it SO much.' It is the safe all-register intensifier — fine with both 해요체 and 합니다체 — and stacks beautifully on emotion words (정말 고맙다, 정말 미안하다, 정말 다행이다). As a standalone 정말? / 정말요? it means 'Really?!' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'really' is a one-size-fits-all booster, so learners pour 정말 into sentences that actually want 너무 for sheer degree (정말 추워요 just affirms 'it really is cold,' while 너무 추워요 conveys 'it's unbearably cold') — match the feeling, not just the word. A second trap is reaching for the punchier 진짜 in formal thanks or apologies where 정말 is the safer, more polished choice (정말 감사합니다, not 진짜 감사합니다 to a boss). Note the spelling: it is 정말, not 정말로 unless you deliberately add the adverbial -로 for extra emphasis.

Using 정말 where the emotion calls for 너무; 정말 just affirms truth ('it really is hot'), whereas 너무 더워요 carries the 'unbearably/so hot' intensity English speakers usually intend.
Saying 정말로 everywhere thinking it is the only correct form; bare 정말 is the normal adverb, and 정말로 is a heavier, more emphatic variant used sparingly.
Forcing English word order like '좋아요 정말'; place 정말 before the adjective or verb it intensifies: 정말 좋아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 진짜 means "really" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "really" is 진짜 (jinjja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 진짜 재미있어요. ("It is really fun."). Watch the particle attached to 진짜 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Casual booster, very common among friends
One-word reaction of surprise or doubt
In 반말, questioning authenticity
Exclamation with the plain 다 ending

examples.en: This coffee is really hot.
examples.note: Basic: 진짜 before an adjective in friendly 해요체

examples.en: I was seriously so startled.
examples.note: Everyday 반말: 진짜 amps up a casual story

examples.ko: 그 가게 음식이 진짜 진짜 맛있어서 또 갔어.
examples.romanization: geu gage eumsigi jinjja jinjja masisseoseo tto gasseo.
examples.en: The food there was so so good that I went again.
examples.note: Real situation: doubling 진짜 for playful emphasis in speech

entries.nuance: 진짜 is built on the Sino-Korean 眞(진, true/genuine) + 짜 and literally names 'the real thing/genuine article,' so as a noun it means 'the real one' (가짜 = fake is its antonym) and as an adverb it became the everyday casual 'really.' Its near-twin is 정말 (正말, 'true words'): both mean 'really,' but 진짜 is more colloquial, more exclamatory, and slightly punchier, so friends and younger speakers prefer it, while 정말 sounds a touch more polished and works better in formal thanks/apologies. Compared with 너무 ('so/too'), 진짜 still leans on a truth-flavor ('I'm not kidding') rather than pure degree. It collocates with surprise and strong reactions (진짜 놀랐다, 진짜 대박, 진짜 좋다) and is frequently doubled (진짜 진짜) in speech. The English-speaker pitfall: because it sounds fun, learners drop it into formal writing, emails, or speeches where it reads as slangy — there, switch to 정말 or 매우. Also note 진짜 vs 가짜: as an adverb it is 'really,' but as a noun it is 'a real/authentic thing,' so 이거 진짜야? can mean either 'Is this for real?' or 'Is this genuine?' depending on context.

Using 진짜 in formal writing, business email, or a speech where it sounds slangy; replace with 정말 or 매우 in those registers.
Assuming 진짜 only intensifies; as a noun it means 'the genuine article' (opposite 가짜), so 진짜 명품 = 'an authentic luxury item,' not 'really luxury.'
Pronouncing or writing it 진자; the word is 진짜 with the tense ㅉ, and the spelling matters for being understood.

entries.shortExplanation: 잘 means "well" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잘 (jal) = "well". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 잘 자요. ("Sleep well.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 잘, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 잘 + verb describing the manner of an action
Fuses with 하다 to mean 'be good at'
잘 softens into 'not quite' when negated

usagePhrases.en: I look forward to working with you.
usagePhrases.note: Set greeting; literally 'please treat me well'

examples.en: That person sings well.
examples.note: Basic: 잘하다 = to be skilled at something

examples.en: I'm not good at exercising.
examples.note: Everyday: 잘 못하다 = 'cannot do well / be bad at'

examples.en: Sir, I'll be in your care from now on.
examples.note: Real situation: fixed humble greeting on joining a team

entries.nuance: 잘 means 'well/skillfully/properly,' and unlike English 'well' (which trails the verb: 'sleep well'), Korean 잘 sits directly BEFORE the verb: 잘 자다, 잘 먹다, 잘 하다. Its opposite pair is 못 ('cannot/poorly'), so 잘하다 vs 못하다 is the core skill axis. Watch the spacing rule, which trips everyone up: when it means 'be good at,' it fuses into one word 잘하다 (잘해요), but when it just modifies an action it stays separate 잘 자다, 잘 듣다. A near-synonym for the 'properly' sense is 제대로 ('correctly, as it should be'); 잘 is broader and warmer while 제대로 stresses 'done right, no shortcuts.' 잘 also has idiomatic softening uses: 잘 모르겠어요 isn't 'I know well-not' but a polite 'I'm not quite sure,' and 잘 부탁드립니다 ('please look after me well') is an essential set greeting. The English-speaker pitfall: do not put 잘 before an adjective — you cannot say 잘 예뻐요 for 'pretty well'; 잘 modifies verbs/actions, while degree on adjectives uses 매우/정말/너무. Also remember the negation splits: 잘 못해요 (separate) for ability, and the position of 못 right before the verb.

Placing 잘 before an adjective (예: 잘 예뻐요) to mean 'quite pretty'; 잘 only modifies verbs/actions — use 매우/정말 for adjectives.
Writing the skill meaning as two words (잘 해요) when you mean 'be good at'; that meaning is one word 잘하다 → 잘해요, while the manner meaning stays split (잘 듣다).
Copying English order and saying '자요 잘' for 'sleep well'; the adverb precedes the verb in Korean: 잘 자요.

entries.shortExplanation: 더 means "more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 더 (deo) means "more". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 더 주세요. ("Please give me more."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 더 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 더 before a verb to request a greater amount
더 + adjective forms the comparative
Pairs with 조금 to soften the increase
Set phrase 더 이상 + negative = 'no longer'

examples.en: This bag is more expensive.
examples.note: Basic: 더 + adjective makes the comparison

examples.en: I want to eat a little more.
examples.note: Everyday: 조금 더 softens 'more' politely

examples.en: Today is much hotter than yesterday.
examples.note: Real situation: 보다 marks the standard, 훨씬 stacks before 더 for 'much more'

entries.nuance: 더 is the basic comparative marker meaning 'more,' and crucially Korean has no '-er/more...than' suffix — you simply put 더 before the adjective and (optionally) mark the standard of comparison with the particle 보다: A가 B보다 더 크다 = 'A is bigger than B.' Its direct antonym is 덜 ('less'). A common booster is 훨씬 ('by far, much'), which stacks in front: 훨씬 더 좋다 = 'much better.' Watch two set phrases: 더 이상 + negative = 'no longer / not anymore' (더 이상 못 참아 = 'I can't take it anymore'), and 더 ~ -ㄹ수록 patterns for 'the more...'. The English-speaker pitfall: learners often drop 더 entirely because they expect the adjective itself to change form ('big' → 'bigger'), but 크다 never inflects for comparison — without 더 the sentence just says 'is big,' not 'is bigger.' Another trap is the 보다 direction: 보다 attaches to the thing you compare AGAINST (the 'than' item), so '내가 너보다 커' = 'I'm taller than you,' which feels backwards to English ears. Also don't confuse spoken 더 with the homophone-ish 덜; they are opposites.

Omitting 더 and expecting the adjective to inflect like English 'bigger'; 크다 doesn't change form — you must add 더: 더 커요.
Attaching 보다 to the wrong noun; 보다 marks the standard you compare against ('than X'), so put it on X: 사과가 배보다 더 싸요 = 'apples are cheaper than pears.'
Confusing 더 (more) with 덜 (less) in fast speech; they are exact opposites, so 덜 비싸요 = 'less expensive,' the reverse of 더 비싸요.

entries.shortExplanation: 덜 means "less" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "less" is 덜 (deol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 덜 매워요. ("It is less spicy."). usagePhrases.note: 덜 + adjective lowers the degree

usagePhrases.en: I'm tired because I slept less.
usagePhrases.note: 덜 + verb reduces the amount of an action

usagePhrases.note: Contrasts a partial decrease

entries.nuance: 덜 means 'less / not fully / to a smaller degree,' and it is the exact mirror image of 더 ('more'): wherever you could add 더 to raise the degree, 덜 lowers it (덜 비싸다 = 'less expensive'). Beyond pure comparison it carries a very useful 'not all the way / incompletely' sense that English splits into different words: 덜 익다 = 'underdone/unripe,' 덜 마르다 = 'not fully dry,' 덜 깨다 = 'still half-asleep.' Contrast it with the flat negation 안 ('not at all') and with 별로 ('not particularly'): 덜 좋다 still means it IS somewhat good, just less so, whereas 안 좋다 means 'not good.' Like other degree adverbs it stands before the adjective or verb (덜 자다, 덜 짜다). The English-speaker pitfall: learners try to translate 'less' with 적게 ('in small quantity') for everything, but 적게 is about countable/measurable amount of an action (소금을 적게 넣다 = 'add little salt'), while 덜 scales the degree or completeness (덜 짜게 = 'less salty'). Also do not mix up 덜 with 더 in listening — one syllable flips the meaning entirely. Note: with a negative, 덜 안 ... is unusual; 덜 already lowers, so you rarely negate it.

entries.shortExplanation: 가장 means "most" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가장 (gajang) = "most". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가장 좋아요. ("It is the best.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 가장 + adjective forms the superlative
Modifying an adjective inside a noun phrase

usagePhrases.en: the highest mountain in the world
usagePhrases.note: 가장 with 에서 marking the field of comparison
가장 can mark 'most/first' with adverbs too

examples.en: This mountain is the highest.
examples.note: Basic: pick one out of many with 가장

examples.ko: 저는 사계절 중에 봄을 가장 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun sagyejeol junge bomeul gajang joahaeyo.
examples.en: Of the four seasons, I like spring the most.
examples.note: Everyday: 중에 ('among') sets the group 가장 selects from

examples.en: It is the most trusted product in our company.
examples.note: Real situation: 가장 in a formal/written superlative claim

entries.nuance: 가장 marks the superlative — 'the most / -est' — singling out the top item from a group of three or more (이 중에서 가장 = 'the most among these'). It is the slightly more formal, written-leaning twin of 제일 (which comes from Sino-Korean 第一, 'number one'); the meaning is identical, but 가장 sounds a touch more refined and is preferred in writing, signage, and careful speech, while 제일 is the everyday spoken default. Both stand before the adjective (가장 크다 / 제일 크다). To name the field you compare within, Korean uses 중에(서) ('among') or 에서 ('in'): 셋 중에 가장, 세계에서 가장. The English-speaker pitfall is using a superlative for only two items: English loosely says 'the best of the two,' but Korean superlatives 가장/제일 want three-plus; for exactly two, prefer the comparative 더 ('A가 B보다 더 좋다'). A second trap is forgetting that 가장 modifies the adjective, not the noun, so 'the highest mountain' is 가장 높은 산 (가장 → 높은), never 가장 산. Also note 가장 is unrelated to the homograph 가장(假裝, 'pretense/disguise'); context and usually a following adjective disambiguate.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가장 to compare only two things; superlatives need a group of three or more — for two, use the comparative 더 (둘 중 이게 더 좋아요).
Attaching 가장 to the noun instead of the adjective; 'the tallest building' is 가장 높은 건물, with 가장 modifying 높은, not 가장 건물.
Forgetting to mark the comparison field; to say 'the best in Korea' include 에서/중에: 한국에서 가장 좋아요, otherwise the scope is unclear.

entries.shortExplanation: 제일 means "most" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 제일 (jeil) means "most". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제일 좋아요. ("It is the best."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 제일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Casual everyday superlative
제일 + 좋아하다 in a relative clause
Singling out one spot from several
제일 used like a noun: 'the number one'

examples.en: I like summer the most.
examples.note: Basic: 제일 + 좋아하다 for a favorite

examples.en: I'm the tallest in our class.
examples.note: Everyday: 에서 sets the group 제일 selects from

examples.en: Say what you will, health is what matters most.
examples.note: Real situation: idiomatic 제일이다 = 'is the top priority'

entries.nuance: 제일 means 'the most / number one' and is the casual, high-frequency spoken twin of 가장. It is Sino-Korean 第一 — literally 'order-one,' i.e. 'first/foremost' — which is why besides modifying adjectives (제일 크다) it can also stand alone like a noun meaning 'the best/top': 건강이 제일이다 = 'health comes first,' 네가 제일이야 = 'you're number one.' 가장 is its near-perfect synonym for the adverb use, the difference being register only: 제일 dominates everyday conversation while 가장 feels a bit more formal/written. Both pick the top of a group of three or more, with the field marked by 중에/에서. The English-speaker pitfall: as with 가장, don't use a superlative for just two items (use 더 instead), and don't glue 제일 onto the noun — 'the cheapest restaurant' is 제일 싼 식당, with 제일 modifying 싼. A further nuance learners miss: because 제일 can be nominal (第一 = 'the first/best'), set expressions like 제일이다 and 제일가다 ('to be foremost') exist, so 그게 제일이야 = 'that's the best option,' not literally 'that is most.' entries.shortExplanation: 별로 means "not really" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "not really" is 별로 (byeollo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 별로 안 좋아요. ("It is not really good."). Watch the particle attached to 별로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 별로 must be answered by a negative later
별로 + 안 + adjective softens the negation
Standalone lukewarm verdict

usagePhrases.en: I don't really want to go.
usagePhrases.note: Pairs with the -지 않다 negative

examples.en: That movie wasn't really fun.
examples.note: Basic: 별로 leans on 재미없다 (already negative)

examples.en: It's not really cold today.
examples.note: Everyday: 별로 + 안 softens the cold

examples.en: Honestly, that restaurant was kind of meh.
examples.note: Real situation: 별로이다 as a polite way to say 'underwhelming'

entries.nuance: 별로 means 'not particularly / not really,' a soft, hedged negative, and its defining grammatical rule is that it MUST be completed by a negative form somewhere in the clause — 별로 안 ~, 별로 ~지 않다, or an inherently negative word like 재미없다/모르다. So 별로 좋아요 is ungrammatical; it has to be 별로 안 좋아요. It descends from Sino-Korean 別(별, 'separate/special') + 로, roughly 'in a special way,' which in the negative frame became 'not especially.' The standalone 별로예요/별로였어요 is an extremely common, face-saving way to say something was 'meh, nothing special' without being harshly critical. Contrast it with 전혀 ('not at all'), which is total denial, versus 별로 which is partial/mild ('not so much'); and with 그다지, a more formal/literary synonym of 별로 that follows the same negative-required rule. The big English-speaker pitfall is positive use: learners say 별로 좋아요 thinking 'pretty good,' but 별로 only points downward and needs a negative — 'pretty good' would be 꽤 좋아요 or 제법 좋아요. Also, because 별로 implies a polite letdown, dropping it as a one-word reply (별로...) signals you're unimpressed, so use it carefully about someone's cooking or gift.

Pairing 별로 with the wrong polarity, like 별로 매워요; it must be 별로 안 매워요 or 별로 맵지 않아요.
Confusing 별로 (mild 'not really') with 전혀 (absolute 'not at all'); 별로 안 매워요 = 'not very spicy,' while 전혀 안 매워요 = 'not spicy in the slightest.'

entries.shortExplanation: 거의 means "almost" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 거의 (geoui) = "almost". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 거의 다 왔어요. ("We've almost arrived.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 거의, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 거의 + 다 = 'almost all the way'
거의 before a verb marking near-completion
거의 + negative = 'almost never / hardly'
거의 before a time/frequency word

examples.en: I've almost finished the homework.
examples.note: Basic: 거의 다 = 'nearly all done'

examples.en: I hardly ever watch TV.
examples.note: Everyday: 거의 + 안 = 'almost never'

examples.ko: 공사가 거의 마무리되어 다음 주에 문을 엽니다.
examples.romanization: gongsaga geoui mamuridoeeo daeum jue muneul yeomnida.
examples.en: Construction is nearly wrapped up, so it opens next week.
examples.note: Real situation: 거의 with a verb in an announcement register

entries.nuance: 거의 means 'almost / nearly / practically,' marking that something falls just short of 100% (거의 다 = 'almost all'). Its standout feature for learners is the flip with negatives: 거의 + 안/없다 doesn't mean 'almost not' but renders English 'hardly / scarcely / almost never' — 거의 안 자요 = 'I barely sleep,' 거의 없어요 = 'there's hardly any.' A close synonym is 대부분 ('mostly, for the most part'), but 대부분 is more about the majority portion of a group while 거의 is about proximity to a full degree or completion; and 약 / 대략 ('approximately') are for rounding numbers, whereas 거의 says 'not quite reaching.' It collocates heavily with 다 (거의 다 됐어요), with completion verbs (거의 끝나다, 거의 도착하다), and with frequency words (거의 매일/매번). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 거의 for an exact figure — 'almost exactly 3 o'clock' isn't 거의 세 시 정각; for 'about/approximately' a number, use 약/대략 or '거의 ~ 가까이.' Another trap is forgetting that 거의 안 = 'hardly,' so beginners read 거의 안 봐요 as 'almost watch' when it means 'barely watch.' Place 거의 before the verb, adverb, or quantity it scopes (거의 한 시간, 거의 다 왔다).

Using 거의 for an approximate exact number; for 'about three o'clock' say 세 시쯤 or 약 세 시, not 거의 세 시.

entries.shortExplanation: 전혀 means "not at all" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전혀 (jeonhyeo) means "not at all". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전혀 안 매워요. ("It's not spicy at all."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 전혀 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 전혀 demands a negative ending

usagePhrases.en: I had no idea at all.
usagePhrases.note: 전혀 + 모르다 for total ignorance
전혀 + 없다 = 'not a single one'
Set phrase for complete indifference

examples.en: I don't know that person at all.
examples.note: Basic: 전혀 + 모르다, total denial

examples.ko: 걱정 마, 나 전혀 안 아파.
examples.romanization: geokjeong ma, na jeonhyeo an apa.
examples.en: Don't worry, I'm not hurt in the slightest.
examples.note: Everyday 반말: 전혀 + 안 for full reassurance

examples.en: That rumor is not true in the slightest.
examples.note: Real situation: formal flat denial in 합니다체

entries.nuance: 전혀 means 'not at all / not in the slightest,' the strongest, most absolute negative degree adverb, and like 별로 it is grammatically bound to a negative — 전혀 안 ~, 전혀 ~지 않다, 전혀 없다, 전혀 아니다. It comes from Sino-Korean 全(전, 'whole/entire'), so the image is 'wholly (not),' i.e. zero across the board. The key contrast is intensity: 전혀 = 0% (total denial) while 별로 = 'not so much' (partial), and 그다지 sits with 별로 as a milder 'not particularly'; so 전혀 안 좋아요 = 'not good at ALL' versus 별로 안 좋아요 = 'not that good.' It collocates with 모르다, 없다, 아니다, 상관없다 and reassurances (전혀 안 아파요, 전혀 문제없어요). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 전혀 in a positive sentence — you cannot say 전혀 좋아요 for 'totally good'; 전혀 only points to zero and needs a negative. Note that in casual modern speech some younger speakers jokingly attach 전혀 to a positive ('전혀 괜찮아 = totally fine'), but this is colloquial and best avoided by learners. Also keep it before the predicate, and don't confuse 전혀 with 전부 (全部, 'all/everything'), which is the positive 'entirely.'

Using 전혀 in a positive sentence (전혀 좋아요) for 'totally good'; standard 전혀 must be completed by a negative — 전혀 안 좋아요 (= not good at all).
Confusing 전혀 (entirely-NOT) with 전부 (全部, 'all/everything', positive); 전부 먹었어요 = 'I ate it all,' a completely different claim.
Treating 전혀 like the milder 별로; 전혀 안 매워요 is an absolute 'not spicy at all,' stronger than 별로 안 매워요 ('not very spicy').

entries.shortExplanation: 아마 means "probably" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "probably" is 아마 (ama). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아마 올 거예요. ("They'll probably come."). Watch the particle attached to 아마 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 아마 pairs with the -ㄹ 거예요 guess ending
아마도 is a slightly softer/heavier variant
아마 with the casual conjecture -ㄹ걸요
아마 over a negated guess

examples.en: That person is probably a student.
examples.note: Basic: 아마 + 일 거예요 (noun guess)

examples.ko: 내일은 아마 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: naeireun ama biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow, I think.
examples.note: Everyday: 아마 reinforced by -ㄹ 것 같다

examples.en: Even if we leave now, we'll probably be late.
examples.note: Real situation: 아마 framing a resigned prediction

entries.nuance: 아마 means 'probably / perhaps,' expressing the speaker's reasonable guess, and its grammar is almost inseparable: it is normally completed by a conjecture ending — most often -ㄹ/을 거예요 ('will probably'), or -ㄹ 것 같다, -겠-, -ㄹ걸요. The bare statement 아마 비가 와요 sounds unfinished; you want 아마 비가 올 거예요. A near-synonym is 아마도, which is just a softer, slightly more deliberative version of 아마 (interchangeable; 아마도 can feel a touch more written or musing). Distinguish the certainty scale: 아마 is a fairly confident guess (~maybe 70-80%), 어쩌면/혹시 lean toward 'possibly, by any chance' (lower, more tentative), and 분명히/틀림없이 mean 'surely/definitely' (high certainty). The English-speaker pitfall is using 아마 with a flat present/past as if it were the English adverb that can float anywhere ('he's probably home'): in Korean the verb itself must carry the guessing form, so 'he's probably home' = 아마 집에 있을 거예요, not 아마 집에 있어요. Also avoid 아마 with established facts — 아마 물은 H2O일 거예요 sounds odd because you're hedging a certainty. Place 아마 near the front of the clause, and let the sentence-final ending do the conjecture work.

Pairing 아마 with a plain present/past tense; the predicate must take a guess ending — 아마 올 거예요, not 아마 와요, for 'will probably come.'
Using 아마 about a known fact or certainty; for 'definitely/surely' switch to 분명히/틀림없이, e.g. 분명히 맞아요, since 아마 hedges.
Confusing 아마 ('probably,' fairly confident) with 혹시/어쩌면 ('possibly, by any chance,' tentative); 혹시 시간 있어요? = 'do you by any chance have time?', a softer probe than a 아마 prediction.

entries.explanation: 같다 (gatda) = "to be the same". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: N하고 같다 ("to be the same as N") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 같다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to be the same as N
usagePhrases.note: 하고 = casual 'with/as'; 와/과 is the written equivalent

usagePhrases.en: to seem like N / to be like N
usagePhrases.note: no 하고 here — this means 'resembles', a different sense
똑 intensifies 같다 to 'identical'
lit. 'hearts are the same'

examples.en: Our bags are the same.
examples.note: subject takes 이/가; the two items being equated

examples.en: We're the same age.
examples.note: the compared-to person takes 하고, the matching trait takes 가

examples.en: Your thinking is exactly like mine, so I was startled.
examples.note: real reaction; 랑 = casual 하고, 똑같다 raises the emphasis

entries.nuance: 같다 says two or more things match or are identical — 'A and B are the same'. To compare, the yardstick noun takes 하고/와·과 and the matching trait takes 이/가: 저하고 키가 같아요 ('our height is the same as mine'). Watch the sharp split from 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 means literally no difference, while 비슷하다 allows a gap — friends who 'look alike but aren't twins' are 비슷하다, not 같다. A second trap is the homophone-feeling N 같다 ('seems like N', as in 학생 같아요 'seems to be a student'), which drops 하고 and shifts meaning entirely; 같이 (together / -like) shares the root but is an adverb. English speakers also over-apply 'the same as' with 처럼 — but 처럼 means 'like/as', not 'identical', so keep 같다 for true equality.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 같다 for things that merely resemble each other — for 'similar but not identical' use 비슷하다; 같다 claims zero difference.
Dropping the particle: native Korean is 'A하고 B가 같아요', not 'A B 같아요'. The yardstick needs 하고/와, the trait needs 이/가.
Confusing 같아요 ('is the same') with N 같아요 ('seems like N') — 학생 같아요 means 'seems to be a student', not 'is the same as a student'.

entries.nuance: 다르다 is the antonym of 같다 and conjugates as a 르-irregular: the stem 다르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ and drops 으 to give 달라요 (never 다라요); past is 달랐어요. The pre-noun form 다른 is one of the most-used words in Korean and covers both 'different' and 'another' (다른 색 = 'a different/another colour'). The dangerous trap for English speakers is 틀리다, which means 'to be wrong / incorrect' — even native speakers loosely say 틀리다 for 'different' in speech, but in correct Korean 답이 틀리다 = 'the answer is wrong' while 답이 다르다 = 'the answer is different'. Mixing them can imply someone is mistaken when you only meant they differ, which can sound rude. Pair 다르다 with 하고/와 for the thing compared: 작년하고 달라요 ('it's different from last year').

Using 틀리다 ('to be wrong') to mean 'different' — standard Korean keeps them separate; 다르다 = different, 틀리다 = incorrect, and confusing them can sound like you're calling something a mistake.
Conjugating it as 다라요 — it's a 르-irregular, so the correct present form is 달라요 (and past 달랐어요).
Forgetting the comparison particle: say '이거하고 달라요', not '이거 달라요'.

entries.english: to be exactly the same / identical

entries.explanation: "to be exactly the same / identical" is 똑같다 (ttokgatda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like N하고 똑같다 ("to be identical to N"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하고 marks the thing compared
pre-noun form, e.g. 똑같은 옷 'identical clothes'
adverb — handy for ordering or copying
맨날 'every day' adds a fed-up nuance

examples.en: It's exactly the same as this one.
examples.note: pointing while comparing; 하고 on the reference item

examples.en: The two have identical faces.
examples.note: 둘이 = 'the two of them'; said of twins/look-alikes

entries.nuance: 똑같다 is the emphatic cousin of 같다: the prefix-like 똑 (a mimetic 'precisely / spot-on') pushes 'the same' all the way to 'identical, no difference whatsoever'. Where 같다 can be a calm statement of equality, 똑같다 adds feeling — surprise at a resemblance, or, with words like 맨날 ('every day'), boredom that nothing changes. It dominates everyday speech far more than its formal feel suggests. The adverb 똑같이 ('identically / the same way') is genuinely useful for service situations ('make mine 똑같이'). Beware the same particle trap as 같다: the reference noun needs 하고/와, so 저거하고 똑같아요, not 저거 똑같아요. And don't reach for 똑같다 when things are only roughly alike — that gap is 비슷하다 territory; 똑같다 insists they are indistinguishable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 똑같다 when things are merely similar — 똑같다 claims they are indistinguishable, so for 'kind of alike' use 비슷하다.
Dropping the particle: say '저거하고 똑같아요', not '저거 똑같아요' — the compared item takes 하고/와.
Forgetting the adverb form when modifying a verb: to copy an action say '똑같이 하세요', not '똑같다 하세요'.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아름답다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

adverb form, e.g. 아름답게 꾸미다 'decorate beautifully'
praises inner character, not looks

examples.en: The sea is beautiful.
examples.note: scenery is the prototypical subject; note ㅂ-irregular 아름다워요

examples.note: pre-noun 아름다운 before the noun

entries.nuance: 아름답다 is the 'proper', somewhat literary word for beautiful, reserved most often for scenery, nature, music, art, a person's heart, or a moving moment rather than everyday cuteness. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the final ㅂ turns to 우 before a vowel, giving 아름다워요 / 아름다운 / 아름다워서 (never 아름답어요). The key boundary for learners is 예쁘다: in casual speech, a pretty face, a cute café, or a nice dress is 예쁘다, while 아름답다 sounds more elevated and emotional — calling a snack 아름답다 sounds odd, but a mountain view is 아름답다. 예쁘다 leans 'pretty/cute', 아름답다 leans 'beautiful/sublime'. Note also 곱다 (refined, graceful beauty, often of older speech), which is gentler and more old-fashioned. Use 아름답다 to admire the grand or heartfelt, and don't force it onto small, cute, or tasty things.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as '아름답어요' — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the form is '아름다워요' (pre-noun 아름다운).
Using 아름답다 for food or small cute objects; 예쁘다 ('pretty/cute') or 맛있다 ('tasty') fits those, while 아름답다 suits scenery, art, and heartfelt beauty.
Saying 아름답은 N for the pre-noun form — the ㅂ-irregular gives 아름다운 N.

entries.explanation: 훌륭하다 (hullyunghada) means "to be excellent / splendid". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 훌륭한 N ("an excellent N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 훌륭하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 훌륭한 작품 'an excellent work'
adverb, e.g. 훌륭하게 해내다 'pull it off splendidly'
common praise of a person's integrity
참 adds warm, sincere praise

examples.en: The food is truly excellent.
examples.note: praising a meal a notch above 맛있어요

examples.en: She's an excellent teacher.
examples.note: pre-noun form praising ability and character

examples.en: You've grown up so admirably for your age.
examples.note: real compliment to a young person; adverb 훌륭하게

entries.nuance: 훌륭하다 is high, somewhat formal praise for quality, ability, or moral character — 'excellent, admirable, fine, splendid'. It sits clearly above 좋다 ('good'): 좋다 is everyday and broad, while 훌륭하다 implies something genuinely impressive and worthy of respect, so it shines in reviews, classrooms, and sincere compliments about work, skill, or a person's integrity (인격이 훌륭하다). Compare it with 대단하다: 대단하다 is a hot, spoken 'wow, impressive!' reaction to an achievement, whereas 훌륭하다 is a calmer, more considered verdict on worth — a child's drawing earns 대단하다 in the moment but a master's life work earns 훌륭하다. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates regularly (훌륭해요 / 훌륭했어요) and, being descriptive, takes the pre-noun -ㄴ: 훌륭한 사람, never 훌륭하는 사람. Don't sprinkle it on trivial 'nice' situations, where it can sound grandiose.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 훌륭하다 for casual 'nice/good' situations where 좋다 is enough — it can sound overly grand and formal.
Forming the pre-noun as 훌륭하는 N — adjectives use -ㄴ/은, so it's 훌륭한 N (the -는 form is for verbs).
Treating 훌륭하다 and 대단하다 as interchangeable; 훌륭하다 is a measured judgement of worth, while 대단하다 is a spontaneous 'wow' reaction.

Watch the particle attached to 대단하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 대단한 실력 'amazing skill'

usagePhrases.en: a big deal / a serious matter
usagePhrases.note: flat-tone sense = 'considerable', not praise
진짜 = casual 'really', very common in reactions

usagePhrases.en: it's not that big a deal
usagePhrases.note: modest deflection set phrase

examples.en: Wow, that's really amazing!
examples.note: spontaneous admiration; 와 sets the reaction tone

examples.en: That's an amazing skill.
examples.note: 실력 = skill/ability, a classic partner noun

examples.ko: 혼자 그걸 다 했다고요? 진짜 대단해요!
examples.romanization: honja geugeol da haetdagoyo? jinjja daedanhaeyo!
examples.en: You did all that by yourself? You're really amazing!

entries.nuance: 대단하다 is the everyday go-to compliment — 'impressive, amazing, remarkable' — usually aimed at a person's achievement, effort, or ability, and it carries warm, spoken energy (often opened with 와 or 진짜). Set against 훌륭하다, 대단하다 is the hotter, more emotional in-the-moment reaction ('wow, you're amazing!'), while 훌륭하다 is a cooler verdict on worth; you'd gush 대단하다 at someone who just aced a race, but reserve 훌륭하다 for praising their character or a polished body of work. A second sense surfaces with a flat tone: 대단한 일 = 'a big/serious matter', and the modest deflection 별로 대단한 일 아니에요 means 'it's no big deal'. Watch the adverb 대단히 ('very, greatly', as in 대단히 감사합니다) — it modifies other words and is not the same as the adjective. Also, aim 대단하다 at others; using it on your own success sounds boastful.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 대단하다 about your own achievement — it sounds boastful; Koreans use it to praise others and deflect their own with 별거 아니에요.
Confusing the adjective 대단하다 with the adverb 대단히 ('very/greatly') — 대단히 감사합니다 modifies 'thanks', it doesn't mean 'amazing'.
Using 대단하다 for a measured judgement of quality where 훌륭하다 fits — 대단하다 is a spontaneous reaction, not a formal evaluation.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 평범하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. 지극히 'extremely' is the idiomatic intensifier here

examples.en: I'm an ordinary student.
examples.note: modest self-description, a very natural use

examples.note: honest, mild review; 좀 softens it

entries.nuance: 평범하다 (平凡, 平 'flat/level' + 凡 'ordinary') means 'ordinary, average, nothing special', and it is essentially neutral, not an insult — Koreans use it modestly about themselves or their routines, and 'I want a 평범한 life' is a sincere, even wistful wish. Its sharp antonym is 특별하다 ('special'), and it overlaps with 흔하다 ('common') but from a different angle: 평범하다 judges character/quality ('unremarkable, run-of-the-mill'), while 흔하다 judges frequency ('found everywhere'). So a name can be 흔하다 (lots of people have it) and a person 평범하다 (an average sort) — they aren't swappable. Tone decides the colour: said warmly it's humble; said with a sigh it edges toward 'mediocre/disappointing'. As a 하다-adjective it takes the pre-noun -ㄴ (평범한 사람, not 평범하는 사람) and the adverb 평범하게.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 평범하다 as purely negative — it usually just means 'normal/unremarkable' and is often a modest or even fond description.
Swapping it with 흔하다: 평범하다 rates how ordinary something's quality is, while 흔하다 rates how frequently it occurs — a 흔한 이름 is a common name, a 평범한 사람 is an average person.
Making the pre-noun 평범하는 사람 — adjectives use -ㄴ, so it's 평범한 사람.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 흔하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 흔한 이름 'a common name'
negated, a frequent way to say 'rare'
adverb, e.g. 흔히 쓰는 말 'a commonly used phrase'

usagePhrases.en: to be dirt-common / a dime a dozen
usagePhrases.note: 흔해 빠지다 adds a dismissive nuance

examples.en: That name is very common.
examples.note: talking about frequency of a name

examples.en: It's a common thing around here.

entries.nuance: 흔하다 means something is common, plentiful, easily found, or seen everywhere — its core is frequency/availability. Its direct antonym is 드물다 ('rare, scarce'), and the negated 흔하지 않다 is a natural way to say 'uncommon'. The line to draw is against 평범하다: 흔하다 = 'occurs a lot / is everywhere' (a 흔한 성씨, a common surname), whereas 평범하다 = 'is unremarkable in quality' (a 평범한 영화, an average movie); a thing can be one without the other. Tone gives 흔하다 two flavours: neutrally it just means 'widely available' (마트에서 흔하게 팔아요), but about taste or style it can turn faintly negative — 'too common, unoriginal', as in 흔한 디자인. The adverb is 흔히 ('commonly, often'), as in 흔히 볼 수 있어요. English speakers sometimes reach for 흔하다 to describe a plain personality — but a person's ordinariness is 평범하다, not 흔하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 흔하다 (common/frequent) with the look-alike 흔들다 (to shake) — unrelated words that just resemble each other.
Using 흔하다 for a person's character; for 'an ordinary/unremarkable person' say 평범한 사람 — 흔하다 is about how often something occurs, not personality.
Saying the adverb as 흔하게 when the idiomatic choice is 흔히 (e.g. 흔히 쓰는 표현 'a commonly used expression').

structuredNuance.t: 흔하다 means something is common, plentiful, easily found, or seen everywhere — its core is frequency/availability. Tone gives it two flavours: neutrally it just means 'widely available' (마트에서 흔하게 팔아요), but about taste or style it can turn faintly negative — 'too common, unoriginal', as in 흔한 디자인. The adverb is 흔히 ('commonly, often'), as in 흔히 볼 수 있어요.

Its direct antonym is 드물다 ('rare, scarce'), and the negated 흔하지 않다 is a natural way to say 'uncommon'. English speakers sometimes reach for 흔하다 to describe a plain personality — but a person's ordinariness is 평범하다, not 흔하다.

Watch the particle attached to 소중하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

소중히 + 하다 = 'treat as precious'
여기다 'to consider' is a natural partner

usagePhrases.en: to be precious above all else
usagePhrases.note: 무엇보다 'more than anything' intensifies

examples.en: Family is the most precious.
examples.note: 제일 = most; emotional value, not price

examples.en: She's a precious friend.
examples.note: pre-noun form on a relationship

examples.ko: 네가 준 편지, 아직도 소중하게 간직하고 있어.
examples.romanization: nega jun pyeonji, ajikdo sojunghage ganjikago isseo.
examples.en: I still treasure the letter you gave me.
examples.note: real heartfelt line; 소중하게 + 간직하다 'keep dear'

entries.nuance: 소중하다 (所重, 'that which is weighty/important') describes something dear and treasured — people, time, memories, relationships, a meaningful gift — measuring worth to the heart, not price in money. Keep it apart from two neighbours: 비싸다 is about cost ('expensive'), and 귀하다 is closer but leans 'rare/precious because scarce or noble' (귀한 손님 'an honoured guest'), while 소중하다 is the emotional 'dear to me'. So a cheap toy from a late grandparent is 소중하다 even though it's not 비싸다. It carries warm, sincere feeling, which makes it a lovely word for cards, letters, and heartfelt moments (시간이 소중하다 'time is precious'; 너는 나에게 소중한 사람이야 'you're precious to me'). The adverb 소중히/소중하게 pairs with verbs like 간직하다 ('keep dear') and 여기다 ('regard'). As a 하다-adjective the pre-noun is 소중한, never 소중하는.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 소중하다 for monetary cost — for 'expensive' say 비싸다; 소중하다 is emotional worth, not a price tag.
Confusing it with 귀하다: 귀하다 leans 'rare/precious because scarce or honoured', while 소중하다 means 'dear to my heart'.
Forming the pre-noun as 소중하는 N — adjectives take -ㄴ, so it's 소중한 N (소중한 사람).
