entries.english: a little, a bit, a few
entries.shortExplanation: 조금 means "a little, a bit, a few" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조금 (jogeum) means "a little, a bit, a few". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조금 주세요 ("Please give me a little"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The exact opposite of 많이; requests a small amount
Before an adjective it softens the degree to 'a bit'
조금만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just a moment; 만 ('only') caps it small
A fixed time phrase meaning 'a moment ago'

examples.en: I speak a little Korean.
examples.note: The perfect modest answer for a beginner; 조금 lowers the claim

examples.en: I drank a little water.
examples.note: 조금 before the verb marks a small quantity of the object

examples.en: I'm a little tired today.
examples.note: 조금 softens 피곤하다 so you don't overstate it

entries.nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. Its closest relative is its own contracted form 좀: 조금 is the full, slightly more careful version you can write and say, while 좀 is the quick spoken reduction (조금만요 ↔ 좀만요 are the same idea). Compared with the noun-ish 약간 ('slightly', a touch more formal/written), 조금 is the warm conversational choice. It naturally collocates with quantities and gentle states — 조금 더 ('a little more'), 조금 있다가 ('in a little while') — and its softness makes it ideal for modest answers and polite requests. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 좀 in speech and not realizing it is just 조금 reduced, and over-stacking it with big-amount words: 조금 많이 is self-contradictory because 조금 only ever points to a small degree.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Not recognizing that 조금 usually contracts to 좀 in casual speech; both are correct, but learners who only study 조금 get lost when they hear 좀.
Pairing 조금 with large amounts: 조금 많이 contradicts itself; 조금 is strictly a small degree, so use 많이 or 너무 for big quantities.
Confusing 조금 with 잠깐/잠시 for time: 조금만 means a small amount, while 잠깐만 specifically means 'for a short moment' of time.

structuredNuance.t: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. entries.shortExplanation: 좀 means "a bit, a little (casual); please" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "a bit, a little (casual); please" is 좀 (jom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 좀 비싸요 ("It's a bit pricey"). Watch the particle attached to 좀 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The short, spoken reduction of 조금
Here 좀 is a softener, not really an amount, like a gentle 'please'
Extremely common when ordering or asking for things at a shop
잠깐만요 buys a moment of time; pairs naturally with 좀 in requests

examples.en: It's a bit cold in here.
examples.note: 좀 makes the comment sound soft and offhand rather than a complaint

examples.en: Some water, please.
examples.note: Slipping in 좀 makes the request friendlier and more natural than 물 주세요

examples.en: I'm a little busy today.
examples.note: 좀 cushions a refusal so it lands gently

entries.nuance: 좀 is the contracted, spoken form of 조금 and is everywhere in daily conversation. Its key second life — the part that trips up English speakers — is as a request softener: in 물 좀 주세요 or 좀 도와주세요, 좀 is not measuring a 'little' amount at all but functioning like 'please/if you would', taking the bluntness off a command. So 물 주세요 is grammatically fine but can feel abrupt, whereas 물 좀 주세요 sounds warm and natural. Compared with the full 조금, 좀 is purely conversational and a touch more casual; in formal writing or stiff announcements you revert to 조금 or a fuller polite request form. Collocates constantly with request verbs (좀 주세요, 좀 해 주세요, 좀 보여 주세요) and with mild complaints (좀 춥다, 좀 그렇다). The pitfall is over-literal reading: don't try to translate the 'softener' 좀 as 'a little', and don't drop it from requests — Koreans add it precisely to sound polite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 좀 always means 'a little': in 좀 도와주세요 it works as a politeness softener ('please'), not a quantity. Translating it as 'help me a little' misses the tone.
Dropping 좀 from requests to be 'cleaner': bare commands like 물 주세요 can sound blunt; native speakers add 좀 (물 좀 주세요) to soften them.
Using 좀 in formal writing or speeches, where it reads as too casual; switch to 조금 or a full polite form there.

entries.shortExplanation: 다 means "all, everything, completely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다 (da) = "all, everything, completely". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 다 먹었어요 ("I ate it all") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Right before the verb; signals the action is complete or the whole thing covered

usagePhrases.en: Everything is fine / I'm good with all of it
usagePhrases.note: Means 'all of it' is acceptable

usagePhrases.en: I did it all / I'm done
usagePhrases.note: The natural way to report finishing a task
거의 다 왔어요 = we're almost there; 거의 ('nearly') tempers 다

examples.en: I finished all my homework.
examples.note: 다 + 했어요 says the whole thing is complete

examples.en: I ate all my food.
examples.note: What you say when your plate is empty

examples.en: All my friends came.
examples.note: Here 다 covers 'all of them', the people, not completion

entries.nuance: 다 is a small but powerful native word meaning 'all / everything / completely', placed directly before the verb. It carries two senses that context separates: completion of an action (다 했어요 = 'all done', the task is finished) and total coverage of a group (다 왔어요 = 'everyone came'). Its near-synonym is the fuller 모두; 다 is the short, ultra-frequent spoken default, while 모두 is a touch more deliberate and can also stand alone as a noun ('everyone'). A subtle bonus sense is 'about to be used up/finished' — 시간 다 됐어요 ('time's up'). The classic English-speaker pitfalls are mixing the look-alike one-syllable adverbs (다 'all' vs 또 'again' vs 더 'more'), and English word order: 다 must precede the verb (다 먹었어요), never follow it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the short adverbs by shape: 다 (all), 또 (again), and 더 (more) are all one syllable but mean different things — 다 먹었어요 ('ate it all') vs 또 먹었어요 ('ate again').
Placing 다 after the verb: it goes before, so 다 먹었어요, not 먹었어요 다.
Reading every 다 as 'completely' when it often means 'all of them (people/things)': 친구들이 다 왔어요 is about everyone, not about thoroughness.

entries.shortExplanation: 모두 means "all, everyone, altogether" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 모두 (modu) means "all, everyone, altogether". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 모두 모였어요 ("Everyone gathered"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 모두 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A clearer, fuller 'all/everyone' than the terse 다
모두 합쳐서 얼마예요? = how much for everything together?
여러분 모두 환영해요 = welcome, everyone; 모두 trails the noun as 'all'
Stacking 모두 + 다 adds emphasis: 'all of it, the whole lot'

examples.en: There are four of us in my family.
examples.note: 모두 sums up a total head count, 'in all'

examples.en: Hello, everyone!
examples.note: 모두 as a noun addressing the whole group

examples.en: All my friends are Korean.
examples.note: 모두 here covers 'all of them' as an adverb

entries.nuance: 모두 means 'all / everyone / in total' and feels a notch fuller, clearer, and slightly more formal than the very short native 다. Its distinctive trait — and the reason to learn it alongside 다 — is its flexibility of part of speech: it can be a noun ('everyone': 모두 환영해요, 모두의 꿈 'everyone's dream') or an adverb ('all': 모두 모였어요), whereas 다 leans adverbial. Near-synonyms split by feel: 다 is the quick everyday choice, 모두 is the cleaner one for counting or addressing a whole group, and 전부 ('the entirety/the whole') stresses 'every last bit' and pairs well with things and totals. It collocates with gatherings, totals, and greetings (모두 모이다, 모두 합쳐서, 여러분 모두). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 모두 is only an adverb and only for people; it also stands as a noun and freely covers things and sums (모두 합쳐서).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 모두 is only an adverb: it can stand as a noun meaning 'everyone' (모두 안녕하세요, 모두의 의견 'everyone's opinion').
Restricting 모두 to people: it equally covers things and totals, as in 모두 합쳐서 ('all together in total') or 짐을 모두 챙겼어요 ('I packed all the bags').
Treating 모두 and 다 as identical in register: 다 is the casual spoken default, while 모두 sounds a touch fuller and fits writing or addressing a crowd.

structuredNuance.t: 모두 means 'all / everyone / in total' and feels a notch fuller, clearer, and slightly more formal than the very short native 다. Its distinctive trait is its flexibility of part of speech: it can be a noun ('everyone': 모두 환영해요, 모두의 꿈 'everyone's dream') or an adverb ('all': 모두 모였어요), whereas 다 leans adverbial. It collocates with gatherings, totals, and greetings (모두 모이다, 모두 합쳐서, 여러분 모두).

entries.shortExplanation: 함께 means "together, along with" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "together, along with" is 함께 (hamkke). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 함께 가요 ("Let's go together"). Watch the particle attached to 함께 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A clear, slightly polished way to say 'together'
A common, warm invitation to share a meal
친구와 함께 = together with a friend; needs the 와/과 particle
다 함께 노래해요 = let's all sing together; 다 + 함께 = everyone, together

examples.en: Let's watch a movie together this weekend.
examples.note: 함께 before the verb means 'do it together'

examples.en: I had dinner with my family.
examples.note: The pattern is N과 함께 = 'together with N'

examples.en: Let's study together.
examples.note: A friendly suggestion to a classmate; 함께 sounds inclusive and warm

entries.nuance: 함께 means 'together / along with' and is the slightly warmer, more polished sibling of the everyday 같이. The two overlap almost completely in meaning, but they differ in feel and grammar habits: 같이 is the casual spoken default and also doubles as 'like/as' with 처럼-style nouns (눈같이 'like snow'), whereas 함께 is purely 'together', sounds a touch softer and more heartfelt, and shows up in invitations, slogans, and announcements (함께 가요, 함께 만들어요 'let's build it together'). Both commonly take the particle 와/과 (or casual 하고/랑) to name the companion: 친구와 함께, 가족과 함께. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping that particle — 'with my friend' must be 친구와 함께, not 친구 함께 — and assuming 함께 and 같이 are sharply different when they are really register twins, with 함께 just sounding a shade more polished.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 함께 and 같이 as sharply different words: they overlap closely; 함께 just sounds a bit softer and more polished, 같이 a bit more casual.
Omitting the particle 와/과 before 함께 when naming the companion: it is 친구와 함께, not 친구 함께.
Forgetting 같이 has an extra 'like/as' meaning that 함께 lacks: 별같이 빛나다 ('shine like a star') cannot use 함께.

entries.english: just, simply, for no special reason
entries.shortExplanation: 그냥 means "just, simply, for no special reason" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그냥 (geunyang) = "just, simply, for no special reason". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그냥 집에 있어요 ("I'm just staying home") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그냥, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Means 'simply' doing something, nothing special going on

usagePhrases.en: I just feel kind of off
usagePhrases.note: A vague, soft way to avoid a full explanation
Here it means 'plain / without changes / as-is'
그냥 standing alone answers 'just because'

examples.en: I just want to rest today.
examples.note: 그냥 softens it to 'simply rest, nothing planned'

examples.en: I just asked, no special reason.
examples.note: A very common casual cushion for a question

examples.en: For coffee, just a plain americano, please.
examples.note: 그냥 = 'just the basic/default one'

entries.nuance: 그냥 means 'just / simply / for no particular reason' and is one of the most useful filler-style words in casual Korean, prized because it lets you decline to over-explain. Its sense flexes with context: 'simply, with no agenda' (그냥 집에 있어요), 'plain / as it is, unchanged' (그냥 주세요, 그냥 아메리카노), and the stand-alone 'no reason' reply (왜? 그냥). Its near-neighbor 그저 ('merely, simply') is more literary and emphatic, while 막 ('just, randomly/recklessly') is rougher and busier — so 그냥 is the gentle, neutral middle. It collocates with low-key states and soft hedges (그냥 좀 그래요, 그냥 그래요 'it's so-so', 그냥 한번 'just once for the heck of it'). The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for one fixed translation — 'just' won't always fit — and over-using it in formal or business contexts, where its vagueness can read as evasive or unpolished.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pinning 그냥 to one English word: it slides between 'just', 'plain/as-is', and 'no reason' depending on context — 그냥 주세요 ('as is') vs 그냥 물어봤어요 ('no special reason').
Over-using 그냥 in formal or business settings: it is casual and its vagueness can sound evasive; a fuller explanation fits there.
Confusing 그냥 with 그래서 ('so/therefore') because both start with 그: they are unrelated — 그냥 means 'just', 그래서 links cause and result.

entries.shortExplanation: 꼭 means "definitely, surely, without fail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 꼭 (kkok) means "definitely, surely, without fail". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 꼭 갈게요 ("I'll definitely go"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 꼭 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Adds a firm, sincere promise to the verb
A warm but insistent invitation
Stresses that something is genuinely essential
Standard in reminders and instructions

examples.en: I'll be sure to call tomorrow.
examples.note: 꼭 makes the promise sound committed, not casual

examples.en: Make sure to take your medicine.
examples.note: A caring reminder; 꼭 = without fail

examples.en: Let's definitely go together next time.
examples.note: Sincere, friendly suggestion

entries.nuance: 꼭 means 'definitely / for sure / without fail' and injects strong intention or a firm request into a sentence: with promises it sounds sincere and committed (꼭 갈게요), and with requests it makes them warm but insistent (꼭 오세요). Its near-synonym 반드시 carries the same 'without fail' core but is more formal, rule-like, and written (regulations and warnings favor 반드시 …해야 한다), whereas 꼭 is the warmer, more personal everyday choice; 절대 is its negative-side cousin ('absolutely not', 절대 안 돼요). 꼭 also has a secondary 'exactly/just like' sense (꼭 엄마 같아요 'just like Mom'), though learners use the 'for sure' meaning most. The English-speaker pitfall is the look-alike/sound-alike 곧 ('soon'): 꼭 갈게요 ('I'll definitely go') is a promise of certainty, while 곧 갈게요 ('I'll go soon') is about timing — keep the tense 꼭 distinct from the timing 곧.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 꼭 (for sure) with 곧 (soon): they look and sound close but differ — 꼭 갈게요 is certainty, 곧 갈게요 is timing.
Using 꼭 for casual maybes: it asserts real certainty or a firm wish, so it clashes with '아마' ('probably') — say 아마 갈 거예요 for a tentative plan.
Reaching for 꼭 in stiff regulations: rules and official warnings prefer the formal 반드시 (반드시 착용해야 합니다), while 꼭 stays personal and warm.

entries.shortExplanation: 바로 means "right away; exactly, right (there)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "right away; exactly, right (there)" is 바로 (baro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바로 가요 ("I'll go right away"). Watch the particle attached to 바로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The time sense: immediately, with no delay
The location sense: points to an exact spot
바로 앞에 있어요 = it's right in front; 바로 pins the position
Confirms 'yes, precisely that one'

examples.en: I'll go right now.
examples.note: 지금 바로 = right this very moment, no waiting

examples.en: The school is right next to my house.
examples.note: 바로 옆 = directly beside

examples.en: Let's leave right away.
examples.note: 바로 before the verb signals immediacy

entries.nuance: 바로 carries two everyday senses split by context: 'right away / immediately' with actions (바로 가요, 바로 출발해요) and 'exactly / right (there)' with places and identifications (바로 여기, 바로 앞, 바로 그거예요). For the time sense, its near-synonym 곧 means 'soon / shortly' — a small gap remains — while 바로 means truly 'this instant, with zero delay', so 바로 가요 is more immediate than 곧 가요. For the location/identification sense, 바로 tightens 'next to/in front of' into 'directly, precisely' and has no single English twin; it behaves like 'right' in 'right next to'. It collocates tightly with position words (바로 옆/앞/뒤/위) and with emphatic confirmations (바로 그거, 바로 너 'you, exactly'). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 바로 only means 'immediately' and missing its 'exactly/right-there' use, plus stranding it from the word it marks — keep 바로 hugging the verb or noun (바로 앞, not 앞 바로).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 바로 only means 'immediately': it equally means 'exactly/right (there)' for places and things, as in 바로 여기 and 바로 그거예요.
Separating 바로 from the word it modifies: it must hug the verb or noun — 바로 앞, not 앞 바로; 바로 가요, not 가요 바로.
Swapping 바로 and 곧 for the time sense: 바로 가요 ('go this instant') is more immediate than 곧 가요 ('go soon'), which leaves a short gap.

entries.shortExplanation: 빨리 means "quickly, fast, hurry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 빨리 (ppalli) = "quickly, fast, hurry". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 빨리 가요 ("Let's go quickly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빨리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The default word for doing an action fast
Doubled for emphasis; a famous shorthand for the Korean pace of life
Politely urging someone to hurry
더 빨리 해 주세요 = please do it faster; 더 ('more') raises the speed

examples.en: Hurry up, the bus is coming!
examples.note: Everyday urging when you're in a rush

examples.en: I ate quickly.
examples.note: 빨리 before the verb describes the speed of the action

examples.en: Get well soon.
examples.note: A caring set phrase to someone who is sick; 낫다 ('heal') is ㅅ-irregular

entries.nuance: 빨리 means 'quickly / fast', the adverb derived from the adjective 빠르다 ('to be fast'), and is among the first action adverbs a beginner needs. Doubled as 빨리빨리, it famously captures the Korean 'hurry, hurry' tempo and adds real urgency. Watch the synonym line with 일찍: 빨리 is about speed ('do it fast'), while 일찍 is about an early point in time ('early'), so 빨리 일어났어요 means 'I got up fast' but 일찍 일어났어요 means 'I got up early' — English 'quick/early' blurs this. The deeper pitfall is the adverb-vs-adjective split: from the stem 빠르- you use the adverb 빨리 before a verb (빨리 먹어요), but to describe a noun you must switch to the adjective form 빠른 (빠른 차 'a fast car') — never 빨리 차. 빠르다 is a 르-irregular, so its polite form is 빨라요. It collocates with motion and effort verbs (빨리 가다/오다/하다) and warm wishes (빨리 나으세요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up the adverb 빨리 (quickly) with the adjective 빠르다 (to be fast): before a verb use 빨리 (빨리 먹어요); as a sentence predicate use 빨라요 (차가 빨라요).
Using 빨리 to describe a noun: 'a fast car' is 빠른 차, never 빨리 차 — noun-modifying needs the adjective form 빠른.
Confusing 빨리 (fast, speed) with 일찍 (early, time): 빨리 와요 ('come quickly') is about pace, 일찍 와요 ('come early') is about the hour.

entries.shortExplanation: 더욱 means "even more, all the more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 더욱 (deouk) means "even more, all the more". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 더욱 좋아요 ("It's even better"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 더욱 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Fuller and warmer than the plain 더
A staple of sincere promises
Doubling to 더욱더 pushes the increase strongly
A kind, slightly formal good wish

examples.en: I'll work even harder from now on.
examples.note: A polished, sincere commitment

examples.ko: 날씨가 더우니까 물을 더욱 많이 마셔요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga deounikka mureul deoung mani masyeoyo.
examples.en: Since it's hot, drink even more water.
examples.note: 더욱 강조 = stresses 'even more so'

examples.en: After practicing, it got even better.
examples.note: 더욱 marks a further step up from before

entries.nuance: 더욱 means 'even more / all the more' and is the fuller, warmer, slightly more formal cousin of the basic comparative adverb 더 ('more'). The two share a core, but they split by register and rhythm: 더 is the plain everyday workhorse (더 주세요 'give me more'), while 더욱 adds a literary, heartfelt lift and shows up in earnest statements, speeches, and good wishes (더욱 노력할게요, 더욱 건강하세요), with the reduplicated 더욱더 cranking the emphasis higher still. A neighboring word, 한층 ('a notch more'), is similarly elevated and written. 더욱 collocates with effort, improvement, and wishes (더욱 열심히, 더욱 좋아지다, 더욱 발전하다). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 더욱 in casual chat or texting, where it sounds stiff — there you just say 더 — and assuming it is a wholly separate word from 더 rather than its more polished register-partner.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 더욱 is unrelated to 더: they share the 'more' meaning; 더욱 is just fuller and more formal, 더 is the plain everyday form.
Using 더욱 in casual texting or chit-chat: it sounds stiff and literary there — say 더 instead (더 좋아 rather than 더욱 좋아).
Forgetting 더욱 leans toward earnest, positive contexts: it fits 더욱 발전하다 / 더욱 건강하세요, but a neutral 'a bit more please' is just 더 주세요, not 더욱 주세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 참 means "really, truly, quite" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "really, truly, quite" is 참 (cham). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 참 좋아요 ("It's really nice"). Watch the particle attached to 참 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A warm, gentle 'really', softer than 너무
A sincere compliment with a kind tone
Everyday warm praise for food
참 standing alone flags a sudden 'oh, that reminds me'

examples.en: The weather is really lovely today.
examples.note: 참 lends a soft, sincere, almost admiring feeling

examples.en: Your Korean pronunciation is really good.
examples.note: A warm, genuine compliment; pairs well with 네요

examples.en: Oh, by the way, are you free tomorrow?
examples.note: 참 as a 'that just reminded me' opener

entries.nuance: 참 means 'really / truly / quite' but with a gentle, sincere, faintly admiring warmth that makes it lovely for heartfelt compliments (참 좋아요, 참 예뻐요, 참 착하다 'so kind'). Its register is the dividing line against its near-synonyms: 너무 is strong and can tip into 'too much', 정말/진짜 are emphatic 'really!', while 참 is the soft, warm, slightly old-fashioned 'really' that sounds caring rather than intense — elders use it often. A completely separate, very common use is the stand-alone interjection 참! meaning 'oh, that reminds me!' when something pops into your head mid-conversation. It collocates with gentle praise and pleasant states (참 좋다, 참 예쁘다, 참 잘했어요 'well done'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting 참 to hit hard like 너무 and being puzzled by its softness, and reading the interjection 참! as an intensifier when it actually signals a sudden memory.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading every 참 as an intensifier: standing alone, 참! means 'oh, that reminds me!', a discourse marker, not 'really'.
Expecting 참 to sound strong: it is a soft, warm 'really' (참 좋아요), unlike the heavier 너무 or emphatic 진짜/정말.
Confusing 참 with 잘 ('well'): 참 잘했어요 stacks both — 참 ('really') intensifies 잘 ('well') — so they are not the same word.

entries.shortExplanation: 가득 means "fully, full (to the brim)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가득 (gadeuk) = "fully, full (to the brim)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가득 채우다 ("to fill it full") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가득, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Describes filling a container right to the top
방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 = the room is packed with people
가득 담아 주세요 = please fill it right up
Standard at a gas station: 가득이요 = full tank

examples.en: I poured the cup full of water.
examples.note: 가득 = right up to the brim

examples.en: The mart is packed with people.
examples.note: 가득하다 = to be full/packed; 가득 + 하다

examples.en: Please fill it all the way.
examples.note: Useful at a gas station or when asking for a full serving

entries.nuance: 가득 means 'fully / full to the brim' and specifically describes a container, space, or even a feeling being filled completely — its meaning is about capacity reached, not just quantity. This is the key line against its near-synonym 많이: 많이 marks 'a large amount' in general (많이 먹어요 'eat a lot'), while 가득 says 'filled to the limit', so 컵에 물이 가득 means the cup is brimming, not merely that there is much water around. It pairs habitually with filling verbs — 채우다 ('fill'), 차다 ('become full'), 담다 ('put in'), 넣다 ('insert') — and the bound form 가득하다 means 'to be full/packed' (사람으로 가득하다). It also extends to emotion (행복이 가득하다 'full of happiness'). A handy real-life anchor is the gas station, where 가득이요 means 'fill the tank'. entries.shortExplanation: 푹 means "deeply, soundly (rest/sleep); thoroughly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 푹 (puk) means "deeply, soundly (rest/sleep); thoroughly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 푹 쉬다 ("to rest fully"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 푹 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 푹 쉬세요 = rest up well, a caring set phrase
푹 잤어요 = I slept deeply and well
In cooking: boil slowly until soft and rich
드라마에 푹 빠졌어요 = I'm totally hooked on the drama

examples.en: Please rest up well at home today.
examples.note: A warm thing to say to someone who's tired or unwell

examples.en: I slept soundly yesterday, so I feel refreshed.
examples.note: 푹 자다 = sleep deeply; pairs with feeling 개운하다

examples.en: For a cold, resting well is best.
examples.note: Standard caring advice

entries.nuance: 푹 is a vivid native mimetic adverb (의태어) meaning doing something deeply, soundly, and thoroughly, and it lives most in the caring collocations 푹 쉬다 ('rest well') and 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly'), which beginners hear constantly as warm wishes. Unlike a general intensifier such as 많이 ('a lot') or 잘 ('well'), 푹 adds a specific texture of 'completely, comfortably, all the way down' — 푹 자다 isn't just sleeping much, it's sleeping deep and restoring. It splits into a few homes: rest/sleep (푹 쉬다/자다), slow cooking ('simmer until tender', 푹 끓이다/삶다), and the figurative 푹 빠지다 ('be totally absorbed/hooked'). It also describes sinking softly into something (소파에 푹 파묻히다). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 푹 as an all-purpose 'very'; it is not — it specifically means 'deeply/soundly/thoroughly' and only suits resting, sleeping, simmering, and being absorbed. Above all, memorize the everyday set phrase 푹 쉬세요, the natural way to tell someone to rest up.

Forgetting the high-frequency set phrase 푹 쉬세요: this is the natural caring way to tell someone to rest, and learners often reach for a clunkier phrase instead.
Swapping 푹 for 잘 carelessly: 잘 자요 ('sleep well') is the everyday goodnight, while 푹 자다 stresses deep, sound sleep — close but 푹 adds the 'all the way down' texture.

entries.shortExplanation: 매일 means "every day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "every day" is 매일 (maeil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매일 아침 ("every morning"). Watch the particle attached to 매일 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 매(每) 'each' stacks before a time word: 매일 아침, 매일 밤, 매주 월요일.

usagePhrases.en: day after day, every single day
usagePhrases.note: Reduplicating it adds warmth/emphasis, common in songs and encouragement.
거의 (almost) is the natural softener when it isn't literally 100% of days.
Write it closed (매일같이, not 매일 같이) — it stresses how relentlessly often, sometimes with mild complaint.

examples.en: I study Korean every day.
examples.note: Core habit pattern; 매일 sits right before the verb phrase.

examples.en: I get up at seven every morning.
examples.note: Here the clock time takes 에 (일곱 시에), but 매일 itself never does.

examples.ko: 요즘 거의 매일 비가 와서 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum geoui maeil biga waseo himdeureoyo.
examples.en: Lately it rains almost every day, so it's tough.
examples.note: 거의 매일 + a real complaint; shows the word in a fuller, lived-in sentence.

entries.nuance: 매일 means 'every day' and is the default word for habits and routines. The 매 is Sino-Korean 每 'each/every', and 일 is 日 'day', so it literally reads 'each-day'; swap the second half for 매주 每週 'every week', 매월/매달 'every month', 매년 每年 'every year'. Crucially 매일 is an adverb of frequency, so unlike clock times it takes NO 에 — say 매일 운동해요, never 매일에. English speakers also confuse it with 하루, which is the counter 'one day / a day' (하루 종일 'all day long'); 매일 is the recurring habit, 하루 is a single day. A near rival is 날마다 'each day', which is interchangeable in meaning but feels a touch more literary/measured, while 매일 is the plain everyday choice. It almost always comes before the verb and pairs happily with 거의, 아침/밤, and the emphatic 매일같이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 매일에 공부해요 — frequency adverbs take no particle. Drop 에: 매일 공부해요. (The 에 belongs only on the clock time, e.g. 일곱 시에.)
Using 하루 where you mean a repeated habit, e.g. ✗ 하루 운동해요 for 'I exercise every day'. 하루 = one single day; the habit is 매일 운동해요.
Writing the verb 늘다-style 매일다 or treating it as a noun with 을/를. 매일 is purely an adverb — it modifies the verb directly.

entries.shortExplanation: 나중에 means "later" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 나중에 (najunge) = "later". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 나중에 봐요 ("see you later") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 나중에, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Standard friendly sign-off when you'll meet again at no fixed time.
Polite way to defer without committing to when; 연락하다 = to get in touch.
Frequently paired with 다시 (again) for 'I'll try again later'.
Common warning frame: 나중에 + a future consequence.

examples.en: Let's talk about that later.
examples.note: Gently deferring a topic right now; 나중에 before the verb.

examples.en: I'm busy now, so I'll call back later.
examples.note: Pairs 지금 (now) against 나중에 (later) — the contrast that defines the word.

examples.ko: 이거 지금 안 하면 나중에 후회할 거예요.
examples.romanization: igeo jigeum an hamyeon najunge huhoehal geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you don't do this now, you'll regret it later.
examples.note: Real-situation warning; shows 나중에 reaching into an indefinite future.

entries.nuance: 나중에 means 'later' at some vague, unspecified future point — possibly today, possibly next week, the time is deliberately left open. That open-endedness is exactly why it's so handy for politely putting things off (나중에 할게요 'I'll do it later'). The sharp contrast to learn is 나중에 vs 이따가: 이따가 means 'a little later but still TODAY', whereas 나중에 carries no same-day promise and can mean any future time. Don't reach for English 'after' here — 나중에 is a standalone time adverb, not the connector '-(으)ㄴ 후에/다음에' you use to say 'after doing X'. Note the fixed 에 is baked in: the word is 나중에, and bare 나중 sounds incomplete in speech. It naturally collocates with 봐요, 연락하다, 다시, and 후회하다, and its opposite pole is 먼저/지금 (first/now).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 나중에 for 'in a little while today', e.g. ✗ 나중에 점심 먹어요 meaning soon. For same-day soon use 이따가 점심 먹어요.
Dropping the 에 and saying just 나중 — the adverb is 나중에. Bare 나중 only survives in compounds like 나중 일 (a later matter).
Translating English 'after' with 나중에, e.g. ✗ 밥을 먹고 나중에 for 'after eating'. 'After doing X' is 밥을 먹은 후에 / 먹고 나서; 나중에 is just 'later' on its own.

entries.shortExplanation: 이따가 means "in a bit (later today)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이따가 (ittaga) means "in a bit (later today)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이따 봐요 ("see you in a bit"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이따가 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 이따 is the everyday clipped form of 이따가; both are fine in speech.

usagePhrases.en: I'll call you in a bit
usagePhrases.note: Promising a call soon, still within today.
Same-day plan that's close but not right now.
봬요 (from 뵈다) lifts the register when speaking to someone you respect.

examples.en: Let's have lunch together in a bit.
examples.note: Simple same-day near-future plan; 이따가 up front.

examples.en: I'm in a meeting now, so I'll reply a bit later.
examples.note: Contrasts 지금 (now) with 이따가 (soon, today) — the heart of the word.

examples.en: Let's meet at the cafe around five later.
examples.note: Real plan: 이따가 sets 'later today' and 다섯 시쯤에 pins the rough clock time.

entries.nuance: 이따가 means 'a little later, but still today' — a short gap measured in hours, never days. The defining contrast is 이따가 vs 나중에: 나중에 is open-ended 'later' (maybe another day), while 이따가 firmly stays within the current day, so 이따가 봐요 implies you'll genuinely see them again today. It's casual, conversational, and in fast speech almost always clipped to 이따 (이따 봐요). The notorious English-speaker trap is the homophone 있다가, which sounds identical but is 있다 'to stay/be' + '-다가' and means 'after staying/being a while' (여기 좀 있다가 가요 'stay here a bit then go'); the time adverb meaning 'in a bit' is spelled 이따가 with ㅇ, not 있다가. Like other frequency/time adverbs it takes no particle, sits before the verb, and collocates with 봐요, 전화하다, 만나요, and a soft 쯤에 clock time.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이따가 for next week or 'someday', e.g. ✗ 이따가 여행 가요 for a trip days away. Beyond today use 나중에.
Spelling it 있다가 when you mean 'in a bit'. 있다가 = 'after staying'; the time word is 이따가. Same sound, different word and meaning.
Saying 이따가에 — no particle. Just 이따가, or add a real clock time like 이따가 세 시에.

entries.shortExplanation: 늘 means "always" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "always" is 늘 (neul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 늘 그래요 ("it's always like that"). Watch the particle attached to 늘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Set phrase for a constant pattern; resigned or matter-of-fact.
늘 shines in warm wishes — softer and kinder than a flat 항상.
Conveys ongoing, heartfelt gratitude rather than a one-time thanks.
언제나 ('whenever it is, always') overlaps fully; pick by rhythm/feel.

examples.en: I always eat breakfast.
examples.note: Plain habit; 늘 sits right before the verb, no particle.

examples.en: That restaurant always has a lot of people.
examples.note: Describes a constant state, not a one-off.

examples.en: Thank you for your help. Please always stay healthy.
examples.note: Real closing wish — the warm register where 늘 outshines 항상.

entries.nuance: 늘 means 'always / all the time' and is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja), which gives it a softer, warmer color than its Sino-Korean twin 항상 恒常 'constant-ever'. In meaning they're interchangeable and both sit right before the verb, but 늘 feels gentle and affectionate, so it's the natural pick in heartfelt wishes like 늘 행복하세요 / 늘 건강하세요, while 항상 leans slightly more neutral or formal. A third near-synonym, 언제나, literally 'whenever-it-is' and so 'always', is also swappable. The big spelling pitfall for English speakers: 늘 (the adverb) versus 늘다 (the verb 'to increase/grow'), e.g. 실력이 늘다 'one's skill improves' — never tack a verb ending onto the adverb. And like all such adverbs it refuses particles: write 늘 웃어요, never 늘에 or 늘은. It collocates with state verbs and warm imperatives (그래요, 고마워요, 건강하세요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 늘다 or 늘어요 for the adverb. 늘다 is a separate verb 'to increase' (살이 늘다 'to gain weight'). The frequency adverb is just 늘.
Adding a particle: ✗ 늘은 / ✗ 늘에. Adverbs like 늘 attach to nothing — 늘 + verb directly.
Reaching for stiff 항상 in a tender wish. 항상 행복하세요 isn't wrong, but native speakers more often warm it to 늘 행복하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 이제 means "now, from now on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이제 (ije) = "now, from now on". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이제 괜찮아요 ("I'm okay now") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Implies 'not before, but now' — the recovery is the point.
Marks that the moment to leave has finally arrived.
Add 부터 'starting from' for a fresh-start resolution.
Set phrase: enough of what was happening up to this point.

examples.en: I'm going home now.
examples.note: Signals the turning point — time to wrap up and leave.

examples.ko: 한국어를 일 년 배워서 이제 조금 알아요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul il nyeon baewoseo ije jogeum arayo.
examples.en: I studied Korean a year, so now I know a little.
examples.note: The 'now, unlike before' change is explicit — perfect home for 이제, not 지금.

examples.en: From now on I'll exercise every day.
examples.note: Real resolution; 이제부터 draws a line between the old me and the new.

entries.nuance: 이제 means 'now', but with a built-in sense of CHANGE from a previous state — 'not until now, but now'. That's the whole game: the sharp contrast is 이제 vs 지금. 지금 is a neutral pointer at the present moment ('right now', as on a clock: 지금 몇 시예요?), whereas 이제 frames the present against a different past, so 이제 알아요 means 'now I get it (I didn't before)'. Choose 이제 whenever something has finally turned a corner, and 지금 for a plain timestamp. Add 부터 for 이제부터 'from now on', the go-to phrase for resolutions, and note the fixed expressions 이제 그만 ('enough now') and 이제야 ('only now, at last'). English 'now' covers both Korean words, which is exactly why learners overuse 지금 where the feeling of change calls for 이제. As an adverb it takes no particle (✗ 이제에) and sits before the verb; it commonly pairs with 괜찮다, 가다, 그만, and 부터.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 이제 and 지금 as identical. 지금 = neutral 'right now' (clock time); 이제 = 'now, in contrast to before'. Say 지금 몇 시예요?, but 이제 다 나았어요 ('I'm all better now').
Saying 이제에 — no particle. Use bare 이제, or 이제부터 for 'from now on'.
Using 지금부터 when you mean a life-change resolution. 지금부터 is fine for 'starting this second', but the 'turn over a new leaf' feel is 이제부터.

entries.shortExplanation: 매번 means "every time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매번 (maebeon) means "every time". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 매번 고마워요 ("thank you every time"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 매번 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Warm appreciation for help that keeps recurring.
Describes a recurring pattern, often with a sigh.
거의 softens it when it isn't literally every single occasion.
Common complaint frame: 똑같다 'be identical' + the repetition.

examples.en: Sorry for being late every time.
examples.note: Apologizing for a repeated occasion, not a calendar day.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 갈 때마다 매번 줄을 서야 해요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun gal ttaemada maebeon jureul seoya haeyo.
examples.en: Every time I go to that restaurant, I have to line up.
examples.note: Pairs 갈 때마다 ('each time I go') with 매번 — both stress the recurring occasion.

examples.en: You always help me — honestly, thank you every time.
examples.note: Real thanks; 매번 ties the gratitude to each separate instance of help.

entries.nuance: 매번 means 'every time / each time an occasion arises', and the key is that it counts OCCASIONS, not calendar days. The 매 is Sino-Korean 每 'each/every' (same as in 매일), and 번 is 番 'a time/turn' (as in 한 번 'once', 두 번 'twice'), so it literally reads 'each-turn'. That's the dividing line from 매일 每日 'each-day': use 매일 for things tied to the daily calendar (매일 운동해요), but 매번 when something recurs every time a particular situation comes up (그 사람은 매번 늦어요 'he's late every time'). A close cousin is the suffix '-(으)ㄹ 때마다' '(each) time when', often used right alongside it for emphasis (갈 때마다 매번). English 'every time' as a sentence connector ('every time I see her...') is usually that '-(으)ㄹ 때마다', not bare 매번 — 매번 is the standalone adverb. No particle (✗ 매번에), placed before the verb; it collocates with 고맙다, 그래요, 똑같다, and 늦다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 매번 to mean 'every day' on the calendar, e.g. ✗ 매번 운동해요 for a daily habit. Calendar 'every day' is 매일; 매번 is 'each occasion'.
Adding a particle: ✗ 매번에. None is needed — 매번 + verb directly.
Rendering the connector 'every time I (do)…' as just 매번, e.g. ✗ 매번 그 사람을 봐요 for 'every time I see him'. Use 그 사람을 볼 때마다 (optionally 볼 때마다 매번).

entries.shortExplanation: 금방 means "in a moment; just now" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "in a moment; just now" is 금방 (geumbang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 금방 올게요 ("I'll be right back"). Watch the particle attached to 금방 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Future use: promising a very quick return.

usagePhrases.en: it'll be done in no time
usagePhrases.note: Reassuring someone the wait is short.
Past use: it happened a moment ago.
On the phone, 'I'll be there in a sec'.

examples.en: I'll be there in a moment.
examples.note: Simple future 'soon'; reassuring you'll arrive quickly.

examples.en: Ramyeon cooks fast, so just wait a little.
examples.note: 금방 + 되다 ('be ready') — the everyday 'ready in no time' collocation.

examples.en: The person who just called left a moment ago.
examples.note: Past 금방 = 'just now'; note 방금 nearby — both can be past, but only 금방 also reaches forward.

entries.nuance: 금방 is a two-faced time word: with a FUTURE verb it means 'in a moment / very soon' (금방 올게요 'I'll be right back'), and with a PAST verb it means 'just now / a moment ago' (금방 갔어요 'left just now'). The tense of the verb decides which reading you get, so the same word swings both ways around the present — that's the thing to internalize. The sharp contrast is 금방 vs 방금: 방금 'just now' is strictly PAST (방금 도착했어요 'I just arrived') and cannot mean 'soon', whereas 금방 covers both directions. Origin-wise 금방 is Sino-Korean 今方 'now-just', and it's thoroughly casual, everyday speech. The classic English-speaker error is forcing 방금 into a future sentence or assuming 금방 only means 'soon' and missing its 'a moment ago' use. It takes no particle, sits before the verb, and habitually pairs with 오다/가다, 되다 ('be ready'), and 끝나다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방금 for the future, e.g. ✗ 방금 갈게요 for 'I'll go soon'. 방금 is past-only; the forward-looking 'soon' is 금방 갈게요.
Assuming 금방 only means 'soon' and missing its past sense. With a past verb, 금방 왔어요 = 'I just got here a moment ago', not 'I'll come soon'.
Adding 에: ✗ 금방에. No particle — 금방 attaches straight to the verb.

entries.shortExplanation: 계속 means "continuously, keep ~ing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계속 (gyesok) = "continuously, keep ~ing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 계속하세요 ("please continue") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계속, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 계속 + 하다 fused as a verb; common when telling someone to carry on.
Connected -아서 form for 'keep on (doing)' without a break.
An ongoing, unchanging situation.
Useful in directions: 계속 직진하세요 'keep going straight'.

examples.en: It keeps raining.
examples.note: Ongoing, unbroken action; 계속 before the verb.

examples.en: If you keep going straight here, you'll reach the subway station.
examples.note: 계속 + 직진하다 in real directions — 'continuously, without turning'.

examples.ko: 아기가 자꾸 깨서 밤새 계속 안아 줬어요.
examples.romanization: agiga jakku kkaeseo bamsae gyesok ana jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The baby kept waking up, so I held her all night long.
examples.note: Contrasts 자꾸 (over and over, intermittently) with 계속 (the whole time, unbroken).

entries.nuance: 계속 means an action or state keeps going WITHOUT a break — 'continuously / the whole time / keep ~ing'. It's Sino-Korean 繼續 'connect-continue', which is exactly the image: things joined end to end with no gap. It can fuse with 하다 into the verb 계속하다 'to continue (something)' and appears as the connector 계속해서 'on and on'. The contrast to nail is 계속 vs 자꾸: 계속 is unbroken duration (비가 계속 와요 'it rains nonstop'), while 자꾸 is 'again and again, repeatedly' with gaps between tries, and usually carries a tinge of annoyance (자꾸 전화가 와요 'calls keep coming, ugh'). So 'the baby cried the whole time' is 계속 울었어요, but 'the baby kept waking up (on and off)' leans 자꾸 깼어요. Also distinguish the durative '-고 있다' (in progress right now) — 계속 stresses unbroken continuation over a stretch. No particle, before the verb; collocates with 오다, 가다, 하다, and direction verbs like 직진하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계속 (nonstop, unbroken) when you mean 'over and over' with mild irritation, e.g. on-and-off pestering. That intermittent, annoyed nuance is 자꾸: 자꾸 물어봐요 'they keep asking (and it's bugging me)'.
Saying 계속에 — no particle. Use bare 계속, or the verb 계속하다 / connector 계속해서.
Forgetting 계속 can take an object via 계속하다, e.g. 'continue the meeting' is 회의를 계속하다, not ✗ 회의를 계속 (adverb alone needs a following verb).

entries.shortExplanation: 평소 means "usually, normally" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 평소 (pyeongso) means "usually, normally". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 평소에 ("usually, in normal times"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 평소 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The natural adverbial form — 평소 almost always wears 에 here.
처럼 'like' + 평소 = behaving the same as on an ordinary day.
보다 'than' makes it a comparison against your normal baseline.
Used attributively before a noun: 평소 실력대로 'as per usual form'.

examples.en: I usually go to bed early.
examples.note: Plain habit; the 에 is essential here for the 'usually' sense.

examples.en: Today there are far more people than usual.
examples.note: 평소보다 comparison; 오늘 (today) is implicitly measured against the normal baseline.

examples.en: I was nervous but presented calmly, as usual.
examples.note: Real situation; 평소처럼 means 'the same way I normally do'.

entries.nuance: 평소 is a Sino-Korean noun, 平素 'level-plain / ordinary times', meaning your normal, everyday baseline — the way things usually are when nothing special is going on. Because it's fundamentally a noun, it leans on particles: in conversation it's overwhelmingly 평소에 'usually', or comparative 평소보다 'than usual', or 평소처럼 'as usual'. Its job is to set a default against which you contrast today (평소보다 많아요 'more than usual'). The near-synonym 보통 普通 also means 'usually/ordinarily' and overlaps heavily; the subtle feel is that 평소 points to 'one's ordinary times/baseline' while 보통 states 'as a general rule', so 평소에 운동해요 and 보통 운동해요 are both fine. The English-speaker trap is treating 평소 like a bare adverb such as 항상 and dropping the particle — 'I usually...' wants 평소에, not lonely 평소. It's also not a verb, so never conjugate it; pair it with 에, 보다, 처럼, and attributive nouns (실력, 생활).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the particle for 'usually', e.g. ✗ 평소 일찍 자요. The idiomatic adverbial is 평소에 일찍 자요. (Bare 평소 survives mainly before a noun, like 평소 생활.)
Treating 평소 as a verb or conjugating it (✗ 평소해요). It's a noun/time word; the action comes from a separate verb after 평소에.
Forcing a 평소보다 comparison without the thing compared, e.g. ✗ 평소보다요 alone. You need both sides: 평소보다 사람이 많아요 ('more people than usual').

entries.shortExplanation: 어서 means "quickly; please go ahead" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "quickly; please go ahead" is 어서 (eoseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어서 오세요 ("welcome (come on in)"). Watch the particle attached to 어서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The standard shop/host greeting — you'll hear it everywhere in Korea.
Warmly urging a guest to start their meal.
Inviting someone inside with welcoming haste.
Standalone, softened with 요 when nudging someone to proceed.

examples.en: Welcome! / Come on in.
examples.note: The all-purpose greeting in every store and restaurant.

examples.en: It's cold, so please come on in.
examples.note: 어서 + a caring reason; the urging is warm, not bossy.

examples.en: We're out of time, please hurry up.
examples.note: Even when rushing, 어서 keeps a polite tone — paired with 서두르다 'to hurry'.

entries.nuance: 어서 urges someone to do something soon, but its color is WARM and welcoming rather than the brusque 'hurry up!' of English. That register is everything: it lives almost entirely with polite imperatives, above all the ubiquitous 어서 오세요 'welcome', plus 어서 드세요 / 어서 들어오세요. The sharp contrast is 어서 vs 빨리: 빨리 is plain, neutral-to-blunt 'fast/quickly' and can sound impatient or commanding (빨리 와! 'come fast!'), whereas 어서 hospitably invites and would feel odd shouted in irritation. So a host says 어서 오세요, but a stressed coach barks 빨리빨리. A close, even gentler relative is 어여/얼른 in casual speech ('quick, come on'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 어서 as a sharp command or sticking it on blunt forms — keep it with warm 세요-imperatives. It takes no particle and stands before the verb; alone it softens to 어서요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 어서 as an impatient 'hurry up!', e.g. snapping ✗ 어서! at someone you're annoyed with. For blunt urgency use 빨리; 어서 is welcoming, not scolding.
Pairing it with a cold command form, e.g. ✗ 어서 가 (blunt). It belongs with polite imperatives: 어서 가세요 / 어서 오세요.
Confusing the adverb 어서 with the connector ending '-아서/어서' (because/and-then). 어서 'go ahead, quickly' is one word; 먹어서 'because (I) ate' is a verb stem + ending — totally different.

entries.shortExplanation: 잠깐 means "for a moment, briefly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잠깐 (jamkkan) = "for a moment, briefly". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 잠깐만요 ("just a moment, please") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 잠깐, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Super useful for asking someone to hold on a sec; 만 'just' + 요.
Same idea among friends — 'wait a sec'.
Polite opener when you want a brief word with someone.
동안 'during' frames the short span of time.

examples.en: Please wait a moment.
examples.note: Everyday polite request; 잠깐 sets the short duration.

examples.en: Hold on a sec — I didn't bring my wallet.
examples.note: 잠깐만요 as a real-life 'wait!' interjection mid-situation.

examples.en: Let's rest here a bit before we go.
examples.note: 잠깐 + 쉬다 ('rest'); the natural way to suggest a quick breather.

entries.nuance: 잠깐 means 'for a short moment / briefly', a span felt in seconds to a few minutes — never a long stretch. It's everyday, conversational, and the derived 잠깐만요 is one of the single most useful phrases a learner can own: it's how you say 'wait a sec / excuse me, hold on' to stop someone politely. The near-twin to contrast is 잠시: 잠시 means the same 'briefly' but sounds a touch more formal and refined, so you hear 잠시 후에 ('shortly') and 잠시만 기다려 주세요 in announcements, whereas 잠깐 dominates casual speech. Both are essentially native-flavored time words taking no particle. The English-speaker pitfall is stretching 잠깐 to cover a genuinely long wait ('I waited a while' that lasted an hour isn't 잠깐) and adding 에 (✗ 잠깐에). Place it before the verb; it collocates with 기다리다, 쉬다, 시간 있다, and the attention-getting 잠깐만(요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 잠깐 for a long wait, e.g. ✗ 한 시간 잠깐 기다렸어요. 잠깐 means a very short moment; an hour is 한참/오래, not 잠깐.
Adding a particle: ✗ 잠깐에. None needed — 잠깐 + verb, or 잠깐 동안 for 'for a brief while'.
Reaching for stiff 잠시 with close friends. 잠시만요 isn't wrong but can sound formal; among friends 잠깐만 is more natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 잠시 means "for a moment, briefly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잠시 (jamsi) means "for a moment, briefly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 잠시만요 ("one moment, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잠시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Polite 'hold on'; a notch more formal than 잠깐만요.
Stock announcement phrase: 잠시 후에 출발합니다.
동안 'during' marks the brief span.
Polite set phrase for stepping away briefly.

examples.en: Please wait just a moment.
examples.note: Polite and slightly formal; common at counters and on the phone.

examples.en: The train will arrive shortly.
examples.note: 잠시 후에 in its natural habitat — public announcements.

examples.en: Excuse me for a moment during the meeting.
examples.note: Formal register; 잠시 + 실례하다 to step out politely.

entries.nuance: 잠시 means 'for a brief moment', essentially the same duration as 잠깐, but the register is the whole difference: 잠시 is more formal, polished, and public, which is why it owns announcements and signage — 잠시 후에 도착합니다 ('arriving shortly'), 잠시만 기다려 주세요. The contrast to learn is exactly 잠시 vs 잠깐: identical meaning, but 잠깐 is casual everyday talk while 잠시 is the refined, written-or-announced choice (think 'one moment' on a PA system vs 'hold on a sec' to a friend). 잠시 is Sino-Korean 暫時 'briefly-time', which fits its tidier feel. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming the two words differ in length of time — they don't; only the politeness/formality differs — and as usual not adding 에 to the bare adverb (✗ 잠시에; instead 잠시 후에 / 잠시 동안). Place it before the verb; it collocates with 기다리다, 후에, 동안, and formal 실례하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 잠시 and 잠깐 differ in actual duration. They mean the same brief span; the difference is register — 잠시 formal, 잠깐 casual.
Saying 잠시에 — no particle on the bare adverb. Use 잠시 후에 ('shortly') or 잠시 동안 ('for a short while').
Using formal 잠시 in very casual chat where 잠깐 fits better, e.g. to a close friend 잠깐만! sounds more natural than a stiff 잠시만.

structuredNuance.t: 잠시 means 'for a brief moment', and the register is the whole difference: 잠시 is more formal, polished, and public, which is why it owns announcements and signage — 잠시 후에 도착합니다 ('arriving shortly'), 잠시만 기다려 주세요. Place it before the verb; it collocates with 기다리다, 후에, 동안, and formal 실례하다.

The contrast to learn is exactly 잠시 vs 잠깐: essentially the same duration and identical meaning, but 잠깐 is casual everyday talk while 잠시 is the refined, written-or-announced choice (think 'one moment' on a PA system vs 'hold on a sec' to a friend).
잠시 is Sino-Korean 暫時 'briefly-time', which fits its tidier feel.

The English-speaker pitfall is assuming the two words differ in length of time — they don't; only the politeness/formality differs — and as usual not adding 에 to the bare adverb (✗ 잠시에; instead 잠시 후에 / 잠시 동안).

entries.english: at first; for the first time
entries.shortExplanation: 처음 means "at first; for the first time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "at first; for the first time" is 처음 (cheoeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 처음에 ("at first, in the beginning"). Watch the particle attached to 처음 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: With 에 for 'at the start', usually setting up a later contrast.
으로 marks the 'firstness' of an experience.
Fixed formal greeting the very first time you meet someone.
부터 'from' = right from the start, often 'do it over from scratch'.

examples.en: I came to Korea for the first time.
examples.note: Plain first-experience sentence; 처음 right before the verb.

examples.en: At first it was hard, but now it's fine.
examples.note: 처음에 sets up the classic 'at first... but now' contrast with 지금.

examples.en: Glad to meet you. It's the first time meeting you.
examples.note: Real-situation set phrase for a first introduction — memorize as a unit.

entries.nuance: 처음 means 'the first time' or 'the beginning', and it flexibly works as both a noun and a time adverb. As a time word it most often appears as 처음에 'at first' — typically to contrast the early state with how things turn out later (처음에는 어려웠어요 'at first it was hard') — or as 처음으로 'for the first time' for a brand-new experience. Its opposite is 마지막 'the last/final'. The sharp contrast to master is 처음 vs 먼저: 처음 is 'the first TIME / the beginning' (a point in time), whereas 먼저 is 'first in ORDER / ahead of others, beforehand' (먼저 가세요 'go ahead first', 먼저 손을 씻으세요 'wash your hands first'). So 'I'll do this first (before that)' is 먼저, but 'I did this for the first time' is 처음. English 'first' blurs both, which is the trap. You'll meet 처음 early in the set greeting 처음 뵙겠습니다. It pairs with 에, 으로, 부터, and 뵙다/오다/먹다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 처음 (first time / at first) with 먼저 (first in order, beforehand). 'Go ahead first' is 먼저 가세요, NOT ✗ 처음 가세요.
Forgetting 에 when you mean 'at first', e.g. ✗ 처음 어려웠어요 for the contrastive 'at first'. Use 처음에(는) 어려웠어요.
Breaking up the fixed greeting, e.g. ✗ 처음에 뵙겠습니다. It's the set phrase 처음 뵙겠습니다 — learn it whole, no particle.

English 'first' blurs both 처음 and 먼저, which is the trap.

entries.shortExplanation: 그리고 means "and; and then" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그리고 (geurigo) = "and; and then". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그리고 ("and / and then") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그리고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Sentence-initial connector; never glues two nouns together.

usagePhrases.en: I eat. And then I sleep.
usagePhrases.note: Lists two actions in the order they happen.
Tiny prompt that asks the speaker to keep going.
If you want 'and then after that', the verb-anchored form is 그러고 나서, not 그리고 나서.

examples.en: I'm a student. And I'm learning Korean.
examples.note: Two plain 요-form sentences simply stacked.

examples.ko: 아침에 운동하고 샤워해요. 그리고 회사에 가요.
examples.romanization: achime undonghago syawohaeyo. geurigo hoesae gayo.
examples.en: I work out and shower in the morning. And then I go to work.
examples.note: Note: inside one clause use connective -고; 그리고 starts the next sentence.

examples.en: Coffee and bread, please. And water too.
examples.note: Real café add-on; 랑 joins the nouns, 그리고 adds a whole new request.

entries.nuance: 그리고 is the plainest sentence-level 'and / and then', used to add a second thought or line up actions in sequence. The trap for English speakers is that English 'and' does double duty — it joins nouns ('coffee and tea') AND clauses ('I sat and ate') — but Korean splits those jobs. For nouns you must use 와/과, 하고, or 랑 (커피하고 차), and for two verbs inside one breath you use the connective ending -고 (먹고 자요). 그리고 belongs only at the head of a NEW sentence, like a fresh 'And then…'. Compare it with 그러고 나서 (after finishing that, then), which stresses that the first action is fully done before the next; 그리고 just adds, while 그러고 나서 sequences. Beginners lean on it heavily, which is fine, but stringing five sentences with 그리고…그리고…그리고 sounds childish — vary it with -고, 그다음에, or 그래서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 커피 그리고 차 to mean 'coffee and tea'. 그리고 cannot bind two nouns; the natural forms are 커피하고 차, 커피와 차, or 커피랑 차.
Writing 밥을 먹어요 그리고 자요 as one run-on. 그리고 starts a fresh sentence, so it should be 밥을 먹어요. 그리고 자요 (or simply 밥을 먹고 자요).
Spelling the sequencing form 그리고 나서. The verb-derived form is 그러고 나서 (from 그러다); 그리고 나서 is a very common but incorrect mix-up.

entries.shortExplanation: 그래서 means "so; therefore" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그래서 (geuraeseo) means "so; therefore". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그래서 ("so / that's why"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그래서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Points back to the previous sentence and names its result.

usagePhrases.en: I'm tired. So I sleep early.
usagePhrases.note: Reason first, natural consequence second.
Casual nudge for the speaker to get to the point.

usagePhrases.en: So how did it turn out?
usagePhrases.note: Stock follow-up that asks for the outcome of a story.

examples.en: It's raining. So I'm taking an umbrella.
examples.note: Plain cause → everyday result.

examples.ko: 어제 늦게 잤어요. 그래서 오늘 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: eoje neutge jasseoyo. geuraeseo oneul neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: I went to bed late yesterday. So I'm exhausted today.
examples.note: Past reason leading to a present state — both verbs carry their own tense.

examples.ko: 길이 막혔어요. 그래서 회의에 늦었어요. 죄송합니다.
examples.romanization: giri makyeosseoyo. geuraeseo hoeuie neujeosseoyo. joesonghamnida.
examples.en: Traffic was jammed. So I was late to the meeting. I'm sorry.
examples.note: Real apology context — 그래서 supplies the excuse.

entries.nuance: 그래서 links a cause to its natural result — 'so / that's why' — and is the first cause-effect connector a beginner must own. It is the sentence-starting cousin of the clause ending -아서/-어서 (피곤해서 일찍 자요 = 피곤해요. 그래서 일찍 자요). The sharp boundary to learn is 그래서 vs 그러니까: both can mean 'so', but 그래서 reports a plain consequence, while 그러니까 pushes a conclusion onto the listener and is what you use before a command or suggestion (피곤하지? 그러니까 일찍 자 = so go to bed). Two real pitfalls: first, 그래서 cannot head an imperative or a let's-form — 그래서 일찍 자세요 sounds off, so switch to 그러니까. Second, English 'so' can also mean 'very' ('so tired'); that meaning is 너무/정말, never 그래서. Keep 그래서 strictly for result.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그래서 before a command: 비가 와요. 그래서 우산 가져가세요. Result-into-an-order needs 그러니까 — 비가 와요. 그러니까 우산 가져가세요.
Mixing it up with 그런데 (but / by the way). 그래서 = result; 그런데 = mild contrast or topic shift. They are not interchangeable.
Translating 'so tired' as 그래서 피곤해요. There 'so' means 'very', so it should be 너무 피곤해요; 그래서 only means 'therefore'.

entries.shortExplanation: 그런데 means "but; by the way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "but; by the way" is 그런데 (geureonde). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그런데 ("but / by the way"). Watch the particle attached to 그런데 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Soft contrast OR a gentle pivot to a new topic.

usagePhrases.en: It's nice. But it's a bit pricey.
usagePhrases.note: Mild 'but' that softens the bad news.

usagePhrases.en: by the way, here's the thing…
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase that eases you into a new subject.
In speech almost everyone shortens it to 근데.

examples.ko: 이 식당 맛있어요. 그런데 사람이 너무 많아요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang masisseoyo. geureonde sarami neomu manayo.
examples.en: This place is tasty. But there are way too many people.
examples.note: Two facts, gently set against each other.

examples.ko: 잘 지냈어요? 그런데 그 얘기 들었어요?
examples.romanization: jal jinaesseoyo? geureonde geu yaegi deureosseoyo?
examples.en: Have you been well? By the way, did you hear that news?
examples.note: Here it isn't 'but' at all — it just changes the subject.

examples.en: I'd like to order — but is this spicy?
examples.note: Real ordering moment; softens straight into a question.

entries.nuance: 그런데 (spoken: 근데) is the soft, all-purpose 'but' that also works as 'by the way' to glide into a new topic — this double life surprises English speakers most. As contrast it is far gentler than 하지만 or 그렇지만; it doesn't slam two ideas together, it just notes that something slightly different follows. As a topic-changer it carries no contrast at all: 그런데, 우리 언제 만나요? simply means 'So/Anyway, when shall we meet?'. It is closely tied to the mid-sentence ending -는데, which sets background before a turn (비싼데 살까? = it's pricey, but shall I buy it?). The everyday pitfall is over-translating it as a strong 'however'; if you mean a firm, contrastive 'however', reach for 하지만. And don't write the long form in chat — Koreans type 근데.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 그런데 always means 'but'. Very often it just means 'by the way / so' and introduces zero contrast, as in 그런데 이거 얼마예요? (By the way, how much is this?).
Using 그런데 where you need a strong, clear 'however'. For a firm contrast 하지만/그렇지만 is stronger; 그런데 stays soft.
Saying 그런데 in fast casual speech. It's not wrong, but it sounds bookish — natural spoken Korean contracts it to 근데.

entries.shortExplanation: 하지만 means "but; however" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 하지만 (hajiman) = "but; however". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 하지만 ("but / however") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 하지만, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Clean, direct contrast at the start of a sentence.
Plain head-on contrast.
Walks back a previous negative.
Interchangeable with 그렇지만 in almost every beginner sentence.

examples.en: Korean is hard. But it's really fun.
examples.note: The classic learner contrast sentence.

examples.ko: 저도 가고 싶었어요. 하지만 시간이 없었어요.
examples.romanization: jeodo gago sipeosseoyo. hajiman sigani eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: I wanted to go too. But I didn't have the time.
examples.note: Past wish vs past reality; both clauses keep their tense.

examples.ko: 발표는 떨렸어요. 하지만 끝까지 잘 해냈습니다.
examples.romanization: balpyoneun tteollyeosseoyo. hajiman kkeutkkaji jal haenaetseumnida.
examples.en: The presentation was nerve-wracking. However, I saw it through well.
examples.note: A notch more formal — fits a 합니다-style report.

entries.nuance: 하지만 is the standard, clear-cut 'but / however' for contrasting two full sentences, and it reads a touch more formal and decisive than 그런데/근데. The crucial contrast to internalize is 하지만 vs 그런데: 하지만 is purely contrastive — it never means 'by the way' and never changes the topic, whereas 그런데 is soft and frequently just pivots subjects. So if you only mean a plain 'but', 하지만 is the safe pick; if you're easing into a new question, you want 그런데. It is essentially the sentence-initial sibling of the connective -지만 (어렵지만 재미있어요 = 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요). The pitfalls: never drop it into the middle of one sentence — it heads the contrasting sentence — and don't use it to mean 'by the way', which is 그런데's job, not 하지만's.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 하지만 to mean 'by the way' / to change topics. That nuance belongs only to 그런데; 하지만 is contrast and nothing else.
Splicing it mid-sentence: 맛있어요 하지만 비싸요. It must open the contrasting sentence — 맛있어요. 하지만 비싸요 (or one clause: 맛있지만 비싸요).
Stacking 하지만 with the clause ending -지만 at once: 어렵지만 하지만 재미있어요 is doubled-up. Pick one — either 어렵지만 재미있어요 or 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 또는 means "or" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 또는 (ttoneun) means "or". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 또는 ("or"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 또는 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Offers an alternative; clean and slightly formal.
Sits cleanly between two nouns.
Two options; the particle 로 attaches to the whole choice.
In speech Koreans usually say 아니면 instead.

examples.en: Shall I give you juice or water?
examples.note: Polite either/or offer with nouns.

examples.en: Choose between black or white.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 중에서 ('among') when picking from a set.

examples.en: Payment is possible by cash or card.
examples.note: Exactly the formal register you see on signs and notices.

entries.nuance: 또는 means 'or' and presents a choice between alternatives, most often nouns. It reads clean and a bit formal — the 'or' of written notices, menus, and instructions (현금 또는 카드 = cash or card). Two near-synonyms mark its boundaries: in everyday speech Koreans far more often say 아니면 ('or else / or'), which is the conversational default, while 혹은 is a near-twin of 또는 that is also written and even a shade more literary. The pitfall that trips English speakers is the false friend 또: 또는 = 'or', but 또 on its own means 'again' or 'also' (또 왔어요 = you came again). They look almost identical, so confusing them flips the meaning entirely. Also note 또는 is not used for 'either…or…' emphasis the way English doubles it up; Korean simply lists A 또는 B, or in casual speech A 아니면 B.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 또는 (or) with 또 (again / also): 또 오세요 means 'come again', not 'or come'. Dropping the 는 changes the word completely.
Forcing 또는 into casual chat: 밥 또는 라면 먹을래? sounds stiff. Spoken Korean prefers 밥 아니면 라면 먹을래?
Trying to mirror English 'either…or…' with a doubled 또는. Korean just says A 또는 B (or 둘 중 하나 for 'one of the two'); there is no paired 'either' word.
