entries.shortExplanation: 왜냐하면 means "because; the reason is" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "because; the reason is" is 왜냐하면 (waenyahamyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 왜냐하면 ("because / the reason is"). Watch the particle attached to 왜냐하면 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Opens the explaining sentence; loves a 거든요/때문이에요 ending.
Pairs with 거든요 to share a reason conversationally.
Pairs with 때문이에요 for a tidy 'it is because'.
Always begins a brand-new sentence after the result.

examples.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 왜냐하면 좀 아프거든요.
examples.romanization: oneureun mot gayo. waenyahamyeon jom apeugeodeunyo.
examples.en: I can't go today. Because, you see, I'm a bit sick.
examples.note: The natural 거든요 partner ending.

examples.ko: 저는 여름을 좋아해요. 왜냐하면 바다에 갈 수 있기 때문이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun yeoreumeul joahaeyo. waenyahamyeon badae gal su itgi ttaemunieyo.
examples.en: I love summer. Because I can go to the sea.
examples.note: Reason clause closes with -기 때문이에요.

examples.ko: 환불해 주세요. 왜냐하면 제품에 문제가 있어서요.
examples.romanization: hwanbulhae juseyo. waenyahamyeon jepume munjega isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Please refund this. Because there's a problem with the product.
examples.note: Real complaint; the reason trails off with -어서요.

entries.nuance: 왜냐하면 is built from 왜 ('why') + 냐 (question) + 하면 ('if one asks') — literally 'if you ask why' — so it answers an implied 'why?' by starting the sentence that gives the reason. Its defining feature is that it is bookended: it opens the explanation and almost always closes it with a reason ending such as 거든요, -기 때문이에요, or -어서(요). Leaving that ending off feels unfinished to Korean ears. The key contrast is structural, not lexical: English 'because' can sit mid-sentence and join one clause (I left because I was tired), but 왜냐하면 heads a SEPARATE second sentence after the result is already stated. The plain clause-internal 'because' is -아서/-어서 or -니까 (아파서 못 가요). So use those endings to fuse one sentence, and reserve 왜냐하면 for 'I'll tell you why:' as a fresh sentence — and remember to land the matching ending.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 왜냐하면 like English mid-sentence 'because': 저는 못 가요 왜냐하면 아파요. It must start a new sentence — 저는 못 가요. 왜냐하면 아프거든요 — or just fuse it: 아파서 못 가요.
Dropping the reason ending: 왜냐하면 비싸요 sounds cut off. Natural Korean closes it with 비싸거든요 or 비싸기 때문이에요.
Pairing it with 그래서: 왜냐하면 … 그래서 …. 그래서 means 'so/therefore' (result), the opposite direction, so it clashes with a 'because' clause.

entries.shortExplanation: 그래도 means "still; even so; but still" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그래도 (geuraedo) = "still; even so; but still". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그래도 ("still / even so") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그래도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Grants the prior fact, then does the unexpected anyway.

usagePhrases.en: It's expensive. Even so, I'll buy it.
usagePhrases.note: Buying despite the price — perseverance.

usagePhrases.en: It's hard. But still, it's okay.
usagePhrases.note: Accepts the difficulty without giving up.
Polite thanks despite whatever just happened.

examples.en: It's cold out. Even so, I want to take a walk.
examples.note: Doing it anyway against expectation.

examples.ko: 많이 혼났어요. 그래도 후회는 안 해요.
examples.romanization: mani honnasseoyo. geuraedo huhoeneun an haeyo.
examples.en: I got scolded a lot. But still, I don't regret it.
examples.note: Concedes the cost, holds the stance.

examples.en: Even when I'm busy, I still always work out.
examples.note: Reinforces the concessive ending -아도/-어도 with 그래도.

entries.nuance: 그래도 means 'even so / but still' — you fully accept the previous fact, yet what follows defies what that fact would predict, carrying a flavor of perseverance or resolve. It is the sentence-initial partner of the concessive ending -아도/-어도 ('even if'); 비싸요. 그래도 사요 mirrors 비싸도 사요. The dangerous look-alike is 그래서 ('so / therefore'): one letter apart, opposite meaning — 그래서 follows the expected result, 그래도 goes AGAINST it. So 피곤해요. 그래서 자요 (tired, so I sleep) vs 피곤해요. 그래도 안 자요 (tired, but still I won't sleep). It also differs from plain contrast words like 하지만: 하지만 just sets two ideas side by side, while 그래도 specifically concedes 'granting all that…' and pushes through. Don't use it where there's no 'expected-vs-actual' gap; without that tension it sounds illogical.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 그래서: 피곤해요. 그래서 안 자요 is contradictory (tired, so I won't sleep?). To mean 'tired but still won't sleep' use 그래도 안 자요.
Using 그래도 with no real contrast: 맛있어요. 그래도 또 먹어요 makes no sense (no concession). It needs an 'against expectation' gap — e.g. 배불러요. 그래도 또 먹어요.
Stacking it redundantly with -아도: 추워도 그래도… is acceptable for emphasis but learners often double it wrongly. Either 추워도 산책해요 or 추워요. 그래도 산책해요 is cleaner.

entries.shortExplanation: 그러므로 means "therefore; thus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그러므로 (geureomeuro) means "therefore; thus". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그러므로 ("therefore / thus"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그러므로 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Formal cause→conclusion; lives in writing and speeches.
Leads into a logical, deliberate conclusion.

usagePhrases.en: It is raining. Therefore the event is canceled.
usagePhrases.note: Notice the formal 합니다 ending it pairs with.
Draws a careful, official conclusion.

examples.ko: 증거가 부족합니다. 그러므로 이 결론은 받아들이기 어렵습니다.
examples.romanization: jeunggeoga bujokamnida. geureomeuro i gyeolloneun badadeurigi eoryeopseumnida.
examples.en: The evidence is insufficient. Therefore this conclusion is hard to accept.
examples.note: Essay / argument register.

examples.ko: 모든 인간은 죽는다. 그러므로 소크라테스도 죽는다.
examples.romanization: modeun inganeun jungneunda. geureomeuro sokeurateseudo jungneunda.
examples.en: All humans die. Therefore Socrates also dies.
examples.note: Textbook logical syllogism — its home turf.

examples.ko: 예산이 삭감되었습니다. 그러므로 사업을 축소하기로 결정했습니다.
examples.romanization: yesani sakgamdoeeotseumnida. geureomeuro saeobeul chuksohagiro gyeoljeonghaetseumnida.
examples.en: The budget was cut. Therefore we decided to scale the project down.
examples.note: Formal announcement of a decision.

entries.nuance: 그러므로 means 'therefore / thus' and is the formal, written, logical cousin of everyday 그래서. It frames a deliberate conclusion drawn from a premise, so it belongs to essays, reports, legal text, announcements, and speeches — pair it with 합니다/습니다 endings, never with casual 요 chat. It is the sentence-level twin of the bookish ending -(으)므로 (비가 오므로 = since it rains). Three near-relatives mark its edges: 그래서 is the neutral spoken 'so'; 따라서 ('accordingly / hence') is its closest formal synonym and often interchangeable in writing; and watch the look-alike 그러면 ('in that case / then'), which sets up a CONDITION-driven response, not a logical conclusion. The pitfall is register clash: drop 그러므로 into a chat with a friend and you sound like a courtroom — for everyday speech downgrade to 그래서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그러므로 in casual conversation: 배고파. 그러므로 밥 먹자 sounds absurdly stiff. With friends say 배고파. 그래서 밥 먹자.
Confusing it with 그러면 (then / in that case). 그러므로 = logical conclusion; 그러면 = response to a condition. 'If it's cheap, then I'll buy it' is 싸면 그러면 살게, not 그러므로.
Pairing 그러므로 with a casual 요 ending: 그러므로 가요 mismatches register. Keep it with formal 그러므로 가야 합니다 / 갑니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 그렇지만 means "but; however; nevertheless" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "but; however; nevertheless" is 그렇지만 (geureochiman). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그렇지만 ("but / however"). Watch the particle attached to 그렇지만 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Clear contrast, a touch more formal than 하지만.
Head-on, slightly weighty contrast.
Softens with reassurance after a downside.
Nearly interchangeable; 그렇지만 carries a faint 'that may be so, but…'

examples.ko: 한국어 시험이 어려웠어요. 그렇지만 끝까지 포기하지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo siheomi eoryeowosseoyo. geureochiman kkeutkkaji pogihaji anasseoyo.
examples.en: The Korean exam was hard. Nevertheless, I didn't give up to the end.
examples.note: Effort holding firm against difficulty.

examples.en: I appreciate the offer. However, I'll decline this time.
examples.note: Polite, formal refusal — register fits a workplace.

examples.ko: 증상은 가벼웠어요. 그렇지만 병원에 가 보기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jeungsangeun gabyeowosseoyo. geureochiman byeongwone ga bogiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The symptoms were mild. But still, I decided to see a doctor.
examples.note: Acknowledges one fact, takes a cautious turn.

entries.nuance: 그렇지만 means 'but / however / nevertheless' and is the close sibling of 하지만 — in most beginner sentences they swap freely. It is literally 그렇- ('be so') + -지만 ('but'), so it carries a faint undertone of 'that may be true, but…', conceding the prior point a hair more than the flat 하지만. Register-wise it leans slightly more formal and polished, comfortable in writing or careful, polite speech (감사합니다. 그렇지만 사양하겠습니다). Set it against two neighbors: 그런데/근데 is the soft, casual 'but' that can also mean 'by the way', which 그렇지만 never does; and 그래도 is 'even so', a concessive 'I'll do it anyway' rather than a neutral 'however'. The pitfall is the same as for any of these connectors — it heads the contrasting sentence, so never bury it in the middle of one clause.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Burying it mid-sentence: 좋아요 그렇지만 비싸요. It opens the contrasting sentence — 좋아요. 그렇지만 비싸요 (or fuse to one clause: 좋지만 비싸요).
Expecting it to mean 'by the way' like 그런데. 그렇지만 is contrast only; for a topic change you need 그런데/근데.
Doubling it with -지만: 어렵지만 그렇지만 재미있어요 repeats the same 'but'. Use either 어렵지만 재미있어요 or 어려워요. 그렇지만 재미있어요.

The pitfall is the same as for any of these connectors — it heads the contrasting sentence, so never bury it in the middle of one clause.

entries.english: if so; in that case; then
entries.shortExplanation: 그렇다면 means "if so; in that case; then" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그렇다면 (geureotamyeon) = "if so; in that case; then". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그렇다면 ("if so / in that case") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그렇다면, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Takes a just-stated premise and builds a conclusion on it.
Accepts the condition and reacts to it.

usagePhrases.en: In that case, what do I do?
usagePhrases.note: Asks for a next step given the premise.
In speech this shrinks to the breezy 그럼.

examples.en: You're out of time? In that case, take a taxi.
examples.note: Advice keyed to a stated situation.

examples.ko: 다들 반대하시는군요. 그렇다면 다시 생각해 보겠습니다.
examples.romanization: dadeul bandaehasineungunyo. geureotamyeon dasi saenggakae bogetseumnida.
examples.en: So everyone's against it. In that case, I'll reconsider.
examples.note: Formal meeting register; responds to the room.

examples.ko: 이게 더 싸요? 그렇다면 이걸로 할게요.
examples.romanization: ige deo ssayo? geureotamyeon igeollo halgeyo.
examples.en: This one's cheaper? Then I'll take this one.
examples.note: Real shop decision built on new info.

entries.nuance: 그렇다면 means 'if that's the case / then', taking something just said or asked and setting up the conclusion that follows from it — 'given that, here's what I'll do'. It is the more deliberate, slightly formal counterpart of casual 그럼/그러면 (which contracts further to 그럼 in chat). The boundary to nail is 그렇다면 vs 그래도: both react to a prior statement, but 그렇다면 ACCEPTS the premise and acts on it ('it's cheaper? then I'll take it'), whereas 그래도 CONTRASTS it ('it's pricey, but I'll take it anyway'). It also differs from 그러므로: 그러므로 draws a fixed logical conclusion in writing, while 그렇다면 responds in real time to a condition or supposition, often a hypothetical ('if so'). The pitfall is using it with nothing to respond to — 그렇다면 needs a preceding 'given that' premise; dropped in cold, it sounds like an answer to a question nobody asked.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 그렇다면 (if so → act on it) with 그래도 (even so → act against it). 'It's cheaper, then I'll buy it' is 그렇다면 살게요; 그래도 would mean 'pricey, but I'll buy it anyway'.
Using it with no premise to respond to. 그렇다면 must follow a stated condition or supposition; starting a topic cold with it sounds unanchored.
Mixing it with 그러므로 in a logical proof. 그렇다면 is conditional/hypothetical response; a firm written conclusion wants 그러므로/따라서.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇다면 means 'if that's the case / then', taking something just said or asked and setting up the conclusion that follows from it — 'given that, here's what I'll do'. It is the more deliberate, slightly formal counterpart of casual 그럼/그러면 (which contracts further to 그럼 in chat).

The boundary to nail is 그렇다면 vs 그래도: both react to a prior statement, but 그렇다면 ACCEPTS the premise and acts on it ('it's cheaper? then I'll take it'), whereas 그래도 CONTRASTS it ('it's pricey, but I'll take it anyway'). entries.shortExplanation: 그러자 means "and then; thereupon (just then)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그러자 (geureoja) means "and then; thereupon (just then)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그러자 ("and then / thereupon"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그러자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Storytelling connector for the very next thing that happened.

usagePhrases.en: I opened the door. Thereupon a cat came out.
usagePhrases.note: Second clause is something ELSE's reaction.

usagePhrases.en: I called out. And then my friend turned around.
usagePhrases.note: Immediate response by another party.
Both clauses are past-tense narration; never present/future.

examples.ko: 비가 쏟아졌어요. 그러자 사람들이 일제히 우산을 폈어요.
examples.romanization: biga ssodajyeosseoyo. geureoja saramdeuri iljehi usaneul pyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Rain poured down. Thereupon everyone opened umbrellas at once.
examples.note: The crowd reacts right after the trigger.

examples.ko: 제가 먼저 인사했어요. 그러자 그분도 환하게 웃었어요.
examples.romanization: jega meonjeo insahaesseoyo. geureoja geubundo hwanhage useosseoyo.
examples.en: I greeted them first. And then they too smiled brightly.
examples.note: A response triggered by the speaker's action.

examples.en: The moment I pressed the button, the door slid open.
examples.note: Shows the fused clause ending -자 that 그러자 is built from.

entries.nuance: 그러자 means 'and then / thereupon (just then)' and is a narrative connector: in a past-tense story it marks the event that occurred immediately after the previous one, where the second event is typically someone or something ELSE's reaction to the first (I called → 그러자 my friend turned). It is the sentence-level form of the clause ending -자 ('as soon as / upon'); 버튼을 누르자 문이 열렸다 = 버튼을 눌렀다. 그러자 문이 열렸다. The decisive contrast is 그러자 vs 그래서: 그래서 states a logical CAUSE ('so/therefore'), while 그러자 marks pure TIMING and reaction with no claim of causation — just 'and right then, this happened'. It also differs from 그러고 나서, which sequences two actions by the SAME subject who finishes one then does the next; 그러자's second clause usually has a different subject reacting. Big pitfall: it is locked to past-tense storytelling — pairing it with present or future is ungrammatical.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그러자 with present or future: 문을 열어요. 그러자 고양이가 나와요 is wrong. It is past-tense narration only — 문을 열었어요. 그러자 고양이가 나왔어요.
Treating it as 'so/therefore' like 그래서. 그러자 marks timing and reaction, not cause: 'I was tired, so I slept' is 그래서 잤어요, never 그러자 잤어요.
Giving both clauses the same subject doing a planned next step. For 'I did X, then I did Y myself' use 그러고 나서; 그러자 expects a (usually different-subject) reaction.

It is the sentence-level form of the clause ending -자 ('as soon as / upon'); 버튼을 누르자 문이 열렸다 = 버튼을 눌렀다. 그러자 문이 열렸다.

The decisive contrast is 그러자 vs 그래서: 그래서 states a logical CAUSE ('so/therefore'), while 그러자 marks pure TIMING and reaction with no claim of causation — just 'and right then, this happened'. It also differs from 그러고 나서, which sequences two actions by the SAME subject who finishes one then does the next; 그러자's second clause usually has a different subject reacting.
Big pitfall: it is locked to past-tense storytelling — pairing it with present or future is ungrammatical.

entries.shortExplanation: 그러고 나서 means "after that; and then" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "after that; and then" is 그러고 나서 (geureogo naseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그러고 나서 ("after that / and then"). Watch the particle attached to 그러고 나서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: First action fully finishes, THEN the next begins.

usagePhrases.ko: 밥을 먹어요. 그러고 나서 이를 닦아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: babeul meogeoyo. geureogo naseo ireul dakkayo.
usagePhrases.en: I eat. After that, I brush my teeth.
usagePhrases.note: Strict, explicit time order.

usagePhrases.en: I clean. And then I rest a bit.
usagePhrases.note: Two steps, clearly sequenced.
It comes from 그러다, so it's 그러고, never 그리고.

examples.ko: 아침에 가볍게 운동해요. 그러고 나서 샤워해요.
examples.romanization: achime gabyeopge undonghaeyo. geureogo naseo syawohaeyo.
examples.en: I exercise lightly in the morning. After that, I shower.
examples.note: Routine in finish-then-start order.

examples.ko: 숙제를 다 끝냈어요. 그러고 나서 게임을 했어요.
examples.romanization: sukjereul da kkeunnaesseoyo. geureogo naseo geimeul haesseoyo.
examples.en: I finished all my homework. And then I played games.
examples.note: The -고 나서 ('after doing') logic, made explicit.

examples.ko: 서류에 서명하세요. 그러고 나서 여기 도장을 찍으시면 됩니다.
examples.romanization: seoryue seomyeonghaseyo. geureogo naseo yeogi dojangeul jjigeusimyeon doemnida.
examples.en: Please sign the document. After that, just stamp it here.
examples.note: Step-by-step instructions at an office counter.

entries.nuance: 그러고 나서 means 'after doing that, then' and makes the sequence explicit: action one is COMPLETED, and only then does action two start. It is stronger about ordering than plain 그리고, which merely adds ('and') without insisting the first thing is done. It is the sentence-level form of the ending -고 나서 ('after doing'), built on the verb 그러다 ('to do so') — which is exactly why the spelling is 그러고, and the rampant 그리고 나서 is wrong. Contrast it with 그러자: 그러고 나서 sequences two actions by the SAME person who finishes one and then does the next deliberately, while 그러자 marks an immediate reaction, usually by someone else, in past narration. Use 그러고 나서 to lay out routines or instructions step by step. The pitfall is reaching for it when two actions happen simultaneously — that's 그러면서, not 그러고 나서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 그리고 나서. The form derives from 그러다, so the only correct version is 그러고 나서; 그리고 나서 is a widespread error.
Using it for simultaneous actions: 'I eat while watching TV' is 그러면서, not 그러고 나서. 그러고 나서 strictly means one finishes before the next starts.
Confusing it with 그러자. 그러고 나서 = same subject, planned next step; 그러자 = immediate (often other-subject) reaction in past-tense storytelling.

entries.shortExplanation: 그리하여 means "and so; thus; consequently" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그리하여 (geurihayeo) = "and so; thus; consequently". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그리하여 ("and so / thus") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그리하여, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Formal, literary connector that leads into an outcome.
Ushers in the result at the end of a narrative.

usagePhrases.ko: 그는 열심히 공부했다. 그리하여 마침내 합격했다.
usagePhrases.romanization: geuneun yeolsimhi gongbuhaetda. geurihayeo machimnae hapgyeokaetda.
usagePhrases.en: He studied hard. And so he finally passed.
usagePhrases.note: Outcome of sustained effort, in the literary 했다 register it belongs to.
Same direction as 그래서 but storybook/speech register.

examples.ko: 두 나라는 오랫동안 협상했다. 그리하여 마침내 조약을 맺었다.
examples.romanization: du naraneun oraetdongan hyeopsanghaetda. geurihayeo machimnae joyageul maejeotda.
examples.en: The two nations negotiated for a long time. Thus they finally concluded a treaty.
examples.note: Historical / written narration.

examples.ko: 그는 밤낮으로 노력했다. 그리하여 꿈을 이루었다.
examples.romanization: geuneun bamnajeuro noryeokaetda. geurihayeo kkumeul irueotda.
examples.en: He strove day and night. And so he achieved his dream.
examples.note: Literary biography tone.

examples.ko: 사람들은 힘을 합쳤습니다. 그리하여 마을을 다시 일으켜 세웠습니다.
examples.romanization: saramdeureun himeul hapchyeotseumnida. geurihayeo maeureul dasi ireukyeo sewotseumnida.
examples.en: The people joined forces. Consequently, they rebuilt the village.
examples.note: Formal speech / address register.

entries.nuance: 그리하여 means 'and so / thus / consequently' and is a formal, literary way to lead into a result, typically at the climax of a story, essay, history, or speech. It belongs to written and oratorical Korean and pairs with 한다/했다 or 합니다/했습니다 endings — never with casual 요 chatter. It is the elevated relative of everyday 그래서 ('so'): same forward, cause-to-result direction, just a far more bookish register, often coupled with 마침내 ('at last') for a sense of culmination. Distinguish it carefully from the look-alike 그러나, which means 'but / however' (contrast) — 그리하여 gives a RESULT, the opposite job. Two other formal result words sit nearby: 그러므로/따라서 ('therefore'), which feel logical and argumentative, versus 그리하여, which feels narrative and unfolding ('and thus it came to pass'). The pitfall is pure register: in normal conversation 그리하여 sounds antiquated, almost fairy-tale — downgrade to 그래서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그리하여 in casual speech: 배고팠어. 그리하여 라면 먹었어 sounds like a storybook. Everyday Korean wants 배고파서 라면 먹었어 / 그래서 라면 먹었어.
Confusing it with 그러나 (but / however). 그리하여 leads to a result; 그러나 introduces a contrast — opposite functions despite the similar shape.
Pairing 그리하여 with a 요-form ending: 그리하여 갔어요 clashes in register. Keep it formal/literary — 그리하여 갔다 / 그리하여 갔습니다.

entries.english: while doing so; and at the same time
entries.shortExplanation: 그러면서 means "while doing so; and at the same time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그러면서 (geureomyeonseo) means "while doing so; and at the same time". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그러면서 ("while doing so / and meanwhile"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그러면서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Two actions overlap, usually by the same person.

usagePhrases.en: She smiles. And at the same time waves.
usagePhrases.note: Simultaneous actions, one subject.

usagePhrases.en: I eat. And meanwhile I watch TV.
usagePhrases.note: Doing two things at once.
The 서 makes it 'while'; 그러면 alone means 'if/then'.

examples.en: I listen to music. And at the same time I study.
examples.note: Two overlapping activities.

examples.ko: 그분은 고맙다고 했어요. 그러면서 슬쩍 봉투를 건넸어요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun gomapdago haesseoyo. geureomyeonseo seuljjeok bongtureul geonnesseoyo.
examples.en: They said thanks. And while doing so, quietly handed over an envelope.
examples.note: Says one thing while doing another — a very common nuance.

examples.ko: 자긴 안 한다면서, 그러면서 자기도 다 하더라고요.
examples.romanization: jagin an handamyeonseo, geureomyeonseo jagido da hadeoragoyo.
examples.en: They said they wouldn't, yet meanwhile they did it all too.
examples.note: Carries a hint of 'and yet contradictorily' criticism.

entries.nuance: 그러면서 means 'while doing that / and at the same time' and ties two actions that overlap, usually performed by the same person (eats 그러면서 watches TV). Beyond plain simultaneity it often layers on a remark or gesture made DURING an action ('thanks,' they said, 그러면서 handing over an envelope), and in pointed speech it can imply a contradiction — 'they said they wouldn't, and yet meanwhile they did' — a flavor close to 'all the while'. It is the sentence-level form of the connective -(으)면서 ('while'); 먹으면서 봐요 = 먹어요. 그러면서 봐요. Two boundaries matter: against 그러고 나서, which is strictly sequential (finish one, then the next), 그러면서 is concurrent (both at once); and against the look-alike 그러면 ('in that case / then'), the extra 서 is everything — it converts 'if/then' into 'while'. The pitfall is dropping that 서 and accidentally setting a condition.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그러면서 for actions in sequence: for 'I ate, then brushed my teeth' use 그러고 나서. 그러면서 means the two happen at the same time.
Confusing it with 그러면 (in that case / then). The 서 is decisive: 그러면 = 'if so, then'; 그러면서 = 'while doing so'. Dropping 서 flips the meaning.
Missing its contradictory nuance in speech. 안 먹는다고 하면서, 그러면서 다 먹어요 isn't neutral — it pointedly means 'says they won't, yet eats it all', a mild reproach.

entries.shortExplanation: 아프다 means "to hurt; to be sick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to hurt; to be sick" is 아프다 (apeuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아파요 ("it hurts / I'm sick"). Watch the particle attached to 아프다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅡ drops → 아파요
body part + 이/가 + 아파요
많이 (a lot) intensifies degree
어디가 asks the spot, the doctor's opener

examples.en: I'm a little sick today.
examples.note: 좀 softens it to 'a bit' — telling someone you feel off

examples.en: My stomach hurt so I couldn't go to school.
examples.note: 아파서 = the reason; pairs naturally with 못 갔어요

examples.ko: 많이 아프시면 병원에 꼭 가 보세요.
examples.romanization: mani apeusimyeon byeongwone kkok ga boseyo.
examples.en: If it hurts a lot, please be sure to see a doctor.
examples.note: 아프시면 adds 시 to respect the listener's body

entries.nuance: 아프다 covers both a specific body part hurting (배가 아파요 = my stomach hurts) and the whole-body state of being unwell/sick. The crucial point for English speakers: it is a descriptive adjective, not an action verb, so you describe yourself as 아파요, never 아파해요 — that -해요 ending belongs to verbs like 좋아해요. To say WHAT hurts, the hurting part takes the subject particle 이/가, not 을/를: 머리가 아파요, never 머리를 아파요, because nothing is doing an action to the head; the head simply is in a hurting state. The stem 아프- is ㅡ-irregular: before the -아/어 ending the bare ㅡ drops and, because the remaining vowel ㅏ is bright, 아 is chosen, giving 아 + 아 → 아파요 (not 아프어요). Compare 아프다 with 슬프다 (sad): both are emotional/physical states ending in -프다 and both drop ㅡ the same way (슬퍼요), so once you master 아파요 the pattern transfers. Note the polite/respectful form for an elder is 편찮으세요, a separate honorific word you would use instead of 아프세요 for grandparents.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 아파해요 — 아프다 is an adjective, so the plain polite form is 아파요. -해요 only attaches to verbs, so 아파해요 sounds like you are 'doing' hurt, which is wrong.
Marking the body part with 을/를, e.g. 머리를 아파요. The hurting part is the subject of the state, so it must be 머리가 아파요 with 이/가.
Writing 아프어요 by adding the ending mechanically. The ㅡ of 아프- drops before -아/어, and the bright vowel rule gives 아파요.

entries.shortExplanation: 더럽다 means "to be dirty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 더럽다 (deoreopda) = "to be dirty". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 더러워요 ("it's dirty") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 더럽다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 → 더러워요
the dirty thing takes 이/가
너무 marks an over-the-line degree
modifier form 더러운 + noun

examples.en: Your hands are dirty. Go wash them.
examples.note: everyday hygiene reminder; note 더러워요 not 더럽어요

examples.en: The floor was dirty so I cleaned it.
examples.note: 더러워서 gives the cause, leading to the action 청소했어요

examples.ko: 이 컵은 더러우니까 다른 거 주세요.
examples.romanization: i keobeun deoreounikka dareun geo juseyo.
examples.en: This cup is dirty, so please give me another one.
examples.note: 더러우니까 = 'since it's dirty', justifying a request

entries.nuance: 더럽다 is the everyday word for physically dirty/filthy — a smudged hand, a grimy floor, an unwashed cup. Its clean opposite is 깨끗하다 (clean), and the near-synonym to keep apart is 지저분하다: 더럽다 stresses actual filth/grime (sticky, stained, germy), while 지저분하다 leans toward 'messy/cluttered/untidy' — a desk piled with papers is 지저분해요 even if nothing is grimy, whereas a toilet is 더러워요. 더럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before a vowel ending the final ㅂ of the stem changes to 우, so 더럽- + -어요 → 더러워요, and the noun-modifying form is 더러운 N (더러운 옷), never 더럽은. Beyond the literal sense, Koreans also use 더럽다 figuratively for a 'foul/rotten' temper or situation — 성격이 더럽다 means someone has a nasty disposition — so context decides whether it is hygiene or attitude. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like a regular stem and producing 더럽어요/더럽은; the ㅂ MUST soften to 우. Compare with 춥다 (cold) and 무겁다 (heavy), which conjugate identically (추워요, 무거워요), so the whole ㅂ-irregular family follows one rule.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 더럽어요 — 더럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ becomes 우 and the form is 더러워요.
Using the modifier 더럽은 N. The correct noun-modifying form is 더러운 N, e.g. 더러운 옷.
Reaching for 더럽다 when you mean cluttered/messy. A room strewn with stuff but not grimy is better described as 지저분하다; reserve 더럽다 for genuine filth.

entries.shortExplanation: 재미있다 means "to be fun; interesting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 재미있다 (jaemiitda) means "to be fun; interesting". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 재미있어요 ("it's fun / interesting"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 재미있다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: conjugates like 있다 → 재미있어요
정말 (really) boosts the degree
있다-type modifier is 재미있는, not 재미있은
하나도 + 안 = 'not even a bit'

examples.en: This game is really fun!
examples.note: casual reaction; 진짜 = 'for real' in speech

examples.en: Studying Korean is fun.
examples.note: the thing judged fun takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: The movie I saw yesterday was fun.
examples.note: past tense 재미있었어요 from 재미있- + -었어요

entries.nuance: 재미있다 is literally 재미 (fun, enjoyment) + 있다 (to exist) — 'fun exists [in it]' — which is exactly why it conjugates like 있다 and gives 재미있어요, and why the noun-modifying form is the 있다-style 재미있는 N (재미있는 영화), never 재미있은. It spans both English 'fun' and 'interesting': a party, a game, or a class can all be 재미있어요, so let context choose the English. The near-synonym to separate is 재미있다 vs 흥미롭다: 재미있다 is the warm, everyday 'enjoyable/entertaining' you say about a movie or a friend, while 흥미롭다 is a cooler, more bookish 'intriguing/of interest' you might use for a research finding or a phenomenon — calling a thrilling roller coaster 흥미로워요 sounds oddly academic. Its direct opposite is the single word 재미없다 (재미 + 없다, 'fun does not exist') = boring; do not say 안 재미있다 as your default negative — 재미없어요 is the natural 'it's boring', and 안 재미있어요 reads more like 'it's not [particularly] fun'. The big English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation: because the headword ends in 있다, learners over-apply -하다 or vowel rules and produce 재미있다요 or 재미있아요; the only correct polite form is 재미있어요, with past 재미있었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 재미있다요 or 재미있아요 — it inherits 있다's pattern, so the polite form is 재미있어요 and the past is 재미있었어요.
Forming the modifier as 재미있은 N. 있다-type stems take -는, so it is 재미있는 영화.
Defaulting to 안 재미있어요 for 'it's boring'. The natural, idiomatic word is the opposite 재미없어요; 안 재미있어요 is weaker and less common.

entries.shortExplanation: 나이 means "age" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "age" is 나이 (nai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 나이가 어떻게 되세요? ("how old are you? (polite)"). Watch the particle attached to 나이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the safe, respectful way to ask an adult's age
age uses 많다/적다, never 크다
나이 + 같다 to compare peers
나이 + 차이 (difference)

examples.en: May I ask how old you are?
examples.note: polite question to an adult or stranger

examples.ko: 우리는 나이가 같아서 말 편하게 해요.
examples.romanization: urineun naiga gataseo mal pyeonhage haeyo.
examples.en: We're the same age, so we speak casually.
examples.note: same age (나이가 같다) often licenses 반말

examples.en: You look younger than your age.
examples.note: 나이보다 = 'than [your] age', a common compliment

entries.nuance: 나이 is the native Korean word for a person's age, and it sits at the center of Korean social life because age sets who speaks formally to whom. Register is everything: to an adult, an elder, or a stranger you ask 나이가 어떻게 되세요? (or even more deferential 연세가 어떻게 되세요?, using the honorific 연세 for grandparents), while the blunt 몇 살이에요? is reserved for children or close friends — asking your boss 몇 살이에요? sounds rude. The near-synonym pair is 나이 vs 연세: same meaning, but 연세 (年歲, Sino-Korean) is the respectful 'years' you grant to someone older, so you raise the register by swapping the word, not by adding an ending. Crucially, age is measured with 많다/적다, not size words: 나이가 많아요 = 'is old', 나이가 적어요 = 'is young' — never 나이가 커요, a direct-translation trap from English 'big'. When you state an actual number, age takes NATIVE numbers + the counter 살: 스무 살 (20), 서른 살 (30) — saying 이십 살 with Sino-Korean numbers is a classic beginner error. One more pitfall: the verb is 되세요 (from 되다, 'to become/amount to'), so 어떻게 되세요? literally asks 'how does it come to be?' — treat the whole phrase as a fixed polite formula rather than translating it word by word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Asking an elder or superior 몇 살이에요? — it sounds blunt or childish. Use 나이가 어떻게 되세요?, or 연세가 어떻게 되세요? for someone clearly older.
Saying 나이가 커요 to mean 'old'. Age pairs with 많다/적다, so it must be 나이가 많아요 (old) / 나이가 적어요 (young).
Counting age with Sino-Korean numbers, e.g. 이십 살. Korean age uses native numbers + 살: 스무 살, 서른 살.

entries.shortExplanation: 몸 means "body" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 몸 (mom) = "body". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 몸이 아파요 ("I feel sick (lit. my body hurts)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 몸, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I feel sick (lit. my body hurts)
usagePhrases.note: the default way to say you're unwell; note the particle 이, not 을
softer/vaguer than 아파요; good for general malaise or even feeling low
set farewell when it's cold or someone's sick; 몸 + 조심하다 fused

usagePhrases.en: I feel sluggish (lit. my body is heavy)
usagePhrases.note: tiredness/heaviness, not literal weight; contrast 살이 쪘어요 for weight

examples.en: I'm a bit tired today.
examples.note: simple: 몸이 + adjective is the basic frame for how your body feels

examples.en: I was sick, so I couldn't go to work.
examples.note: everyday: 아파서 (A-아서) gives the reason; pair with 못 가다

examples.ko: 요즘 무리해서 그런지 몸이 자꾸 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum murihaeseo geureonji momi jakku an joayo.
examples.en: Maybe because I've been overdoing it, I keep feeling under the weather lately.
examples.note: real-life: 안 좋다 for ongoing vague unwellness, 자꾸 = keeps happening

entries.nuance: 몸 is the physical body taken as a whole, and crucially it's also the word Koreans reach for to describe how they FEEL: 몸이 아파요 (sick) and 몸이 안 좋아요 (off/unwell) are the everyday health phrases. The near-synonym is the Sino-Korean 신체(身體, 'body-substance'), but 신체 is clinical/official — 신체검사 (physical exam), 신체 활동 (physical activity) — and sounds stiff if you use it about yourself, so say 몸. Habitual collocations: 몸이 아프다, 몸이 안 좋다, 몸이 피곤하다, 몸이 무겁다, 몸조심하다, 몸이 약하다 (to have a weak constitution). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the verb: you say 몸이 아프다 ('the body is sick'), so the body is the SUBJECT (이/가) — never 몸을 아파요. Also don't directly translate 'my body is heavy' as a weight statement; 몸이 무겁다 means you feel sluggish/lethargic, not that you weigh a lot.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 몸을 아파요 with the object particle 을. 아프다 is an adjective-like stative verb, so the body is the subject: 몸이 아파요.
Using 신체 in casual speech, e.g. 신체가 아파요. That sounds like a medical chart; everyday Korean is 몸이 아파요.
Reading 몸이 무거워요 as 'I'm overweight.' It means you feel heavy/sluggish; weight gain is 살이 쪘어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 살 means "flesh; body fat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 살 (sal) means "flesh; body fat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 살이 쪘어요 ("I gained weight"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 살 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the standard line; 살이 찌다, subject particle 이, never 살을 쪘어요
intransitive 빠지다 = it fell off on its own
transitive 빼다 = you actively remove it; takes 을
compound 배(belly) + 살; also 옆구리살 love handles, 허벅지살 thigh fat

examples.en: I've gained a little weight lately.
examples.note: simple: 살이 찌다 is the core intransitive frame

examples.en: I want to lose weight before summer.
examples.note: everyday: 살을 빼다 (transitive, deliberate) + -고 싶다

examples.ko: 다이어트를 해도 살이 잘 안 빠져서 스트레스예요.
examples.romanization: daieoteureul haedo sari jal an ppajyeoseo seuteureseuyeyo.
examples.en: Even though I diet, the weight just won't come off, so it's stressful.
examples.note: real-life: 살이 빠지다 (it comes off by itself) vs 살을 빼다 (you remove it)

entries.nuance: 살 is the soft flesh of the body, and in daily life it's the word for body fat / weight: 살이 찌다 (put on weight) and its pair 살이 빠지다 / 살을 빼다 (lose weight). The synonym contrast that trips learners is 살 vs the Sino-Korean 체중(體重, 'body-weight'): 체중 is the number on the scale (체중을 재다 = to measure one's weight, 체중 50kg), while 살 is the fat itself that you gain, lose, or pinch — in conversation Koreans overwhelmingly say 살, not 체중. Note also 살 ≠ 피부: 살 is the fleshy substance, 피부 is the skin's surface. Watch the transitivity pair: 빠지다 is intransitive ('fat falls off' — 살이 빠지다, subject 이) but 빼다 is transitive ('you take the fat off' — 살을 빼다, object 을); mixing the particles is the classic mistake. Common collocations: 살이 찌다/빠지다, 살을 빼다, 살이 많다, 뱃살, 살이 쪄서. (Same syllable 살 also means 'years of age' as a counter, and homophone-adjacent 쌀 is uncooked rice — different tense ㅆ.)
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 살이 컸어요 for 'gained weight.' 크다 (grow big) is wrong; weight gain is 살이 쪘어요 (from 찌다).
Particle swap with the verb pair: 살을 빠졌어요 or 살이 뺐어요. It's 살이 빠지다 (intransitive, 이) but 살을 빼다 (transitive, 을).
Using 체중 in casual chat: 체중이 쪘어요. Say 살이 쪘어요; 체중 is the formal scale-number word.

entries.shortExplanation: 피 means "blood" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "blood" is 피 (pi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 피가 나요 ("I'm bleeding (lit. blood is coming out)"). Watch the particle attached to 피 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I'm bleeding (lit. blood is coming out)
usagePhrases.note: the must-know phrase; verb is 나다, particle 이/가
멈추다 = to stop; the natural pair to 피가 나다
코(nose) + 피; 코피가 나다 = to get a nosebleed
흘리다 = to spill; more dramatic/literary than 피가 나다

examples.en: My hand is bleeding.
examples.note: simple: location + 에서 (out of) + 피가 나다

examples.en: I fell and my knee bled.
examples.note: everyday: past 났어요; 에서 marks where blood emerges

examples.ko: 피만 봐도 어지러워서 주사를 잘 못 맞아요.
examples.romanization: piman bwado eojireowoseo jusareul jal mon majayo.
examples.en: Just the sight of blood makes me dizzy, so I'm bad with shots.
examples.note: real-life: 피만 봐도 (even just seeing blood) + 어지럽다

entries.nuance: 피 is the plain, native everyday word for blood — what you say the instant you cut yourself: 피가 나요 (I'm bleeding) is the single most useful phrase here. The synonym contrast is with the Sino-Korean 혈액(血液, 'blood-fluid'): 혈액 is the technical/medical register you see on forms and signs — 혈액형 (blood type), 헌혈 (blood donation, 獻血), 혈액 검사 (blood test) — whereas in speech about a scrape you always use 피. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'blood comes out' uses 나다 (to come out/occur), so 피가 나다 — not 피가 오다 (오다 is 'come [toward me]' and is wrong here). Mark where the blood emerges with 에서 (from a place): 코에서 피가 나요. Also note 피 is normally uncountable — don't pluralize it. Handy collocations: 피가 나다, 피가 멈추다, 피를 흘리다, 코피가 나다, 피를 뽑다 (to draw blood, at a clinic).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 피가 와요 for 'I'm bleeding.' The verb is 나다 (come out/occur): 피가 나요. 오다 (come toward) doesn't fit.
Using 혈액 in casual speech about a cut: 혈액이 나요. That's medical-form language; say 피가 나요.
Marking the body part with 에 instead of 에서: 무릎에 피가 나요. Use 에서 for where the blood comes out: 무릎에서 피가 나요.

entries.shortExplanation: 입술 means "lips" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 입술 (ipsul) = "lips". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 입술이 텄어요 ("my lips are chapped/cracked") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 입술, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 트다 → 텄어요; the seasonal winter complaint
the dictionary form; same 트다 used for chapped hands
깨물다 = to bite down; gesture of enduring or nervousness
바르다 = to spread on; 립밤을 바르다

examples.en: My lips get dry easily in winter.
examples.note: simple: 입술이 마르다 (to go dry); 잘 = easily/often

examples.en: My lips were chapped, so I put on lip balm.
examples.note: everyday: 터서 (트다 + 아서, reason) + 바르다

examples.en: When I'm nervous I bite my lip without realizing it.
examples.note: real-life: habit + 저도 모르게 (without even knowing it)

entries.nuance: 입술 means the lips, and it's transparently built from 입 (mouth/opening) + 술 — but the contrast to nail down is 입 vs 입술: 입 is the whole mouth (you eat, speak, and open your 입), while 입술 is specifically the two lip rims (you apply balm to, bite, or chap your 입술). It surfaces constantly in two contexts: winter skin (입술이 마르다 / 입술이 트다, chapped lips) and cosmetics (입술에 립스틱/립밤을 바르다). A frequent learner error is reaching for 입 when you mean the lips — 입이 텄어요 sounds odd; chapping happens to the 입술. Lips are inherently a pair, so Korean leaves them singular: say 입술, not 입술들. Useful collocations: 입술이 마르다, 입술이 트다, 입술을 깨물다, 입술을 바르다, 입술이 부르트다 (to blister, e.g. a cold sore).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 입 where you mean the lips: 입에 립밤을 발라요. Balm goes on the 입술 — 입술에 립밤을 발라요. 입 is the whole mouth.
Pluralizing as 입술들. Lips are treated as a single paired item; just say 입술.
Saying 입술을 깨물었다 vs 깨물다 confusion aside, learners often pick 물다 alone (to bite/hold in mouth). For the lip-biting gesture it's 깨물다 (bite down).

entries.shortExplanation: 혀 means "tongue" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 혀 (hyeo) means "tongue". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 혀를 데다 ("to burn one's tongue"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 혀 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 데다 = to get burned/scalded; 뜨거운 거에 혀를 데다
깨물다 = to bite down; accidental while eating or talking
꼬이다 = to twist; when drunk or nervous, 발음이 새다 nearby
차다 here = to click; gesture of disapproval/pity

examples.en: We taste with our tongue.
examples.note: simple: 혀로 (with the tongue, instrument 로) + 맛 (taste)

examples.en: I burned my tongue eating hot soup.
examples.note: everyday: V-다가 (mid-action) + 혀를 데다

examples.en: The pronunciation is hard, so my tongue keeps getting twisted.
examples.note: real-life: idiomatic 혀가 꼬이다 for fumbling speech

entries.nuance: 혀 is the tongue — the organ you taste, swallow, and articulate sounds with. The key contrast for learners is 혀 (the physical organ) vs 맛 (taste, the sensation): you taste WITH your 혀, but the act 'to taste/sample food' is 맛을 보다, never 혀를 보다. Most common beginner sentences: 혀를 데었어요 (I burned my tongue) and 혀를 깨물었어요 (I bit my tongue), both very real mishaps. It also lives in vivid idioms — 혀가 꼬이다 (slur your words, e.g. when drunk) and 혀를 차다 (click your tongue in disapproval, 'tsk'). Pronunciation pitfall for English speakers: 혀 is one syllable with the vowel 여 (roughly 'hyŏ'/'hyuh'), a y-glide + ŏ — don't flatten it to 'ha' or stretch it into two beats; and keep it distinct from 햐/혜. Mark the instrument with 로/으로: 혀로 핥다 (to lick with the tongue). Collocations: 혀를 데다, 혀를 깨물다, 혀로 핥다, 혀가 꼬이다, 혀를 차다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 혀를 봐요 for 'I taste it.' The body part isn't the verb's object here; tasting food is 맛을 봐요. 혀 is the organ, 맛 is the taste.
Pronouncing 혀 like 'ha' or as two syllables. It's a single 여 (hyŏ) — a y-glide plus ŏ.
Using 자르다 (to cut) for biting the tongue: 혀를 잘랐어요. Accidentally biting it is 혀를 깨물었어요 (bit down).

entries.shortExplanation: 손톱 means "fingernail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "fingernail" is 손톱 (sontop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 손톱을 깎다 ("to cut/clip one's nails"). Watch the particle attached to 손톱 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 깎다 is the idiomatic verb (also for peeling, haircuts); not 자르다
자라다 = to grow; 손톱이 빨리 자라요
발(foot) + 톱; the sibling word, also clipped with 깎다
물어뜯다 = to gnaw; the nervous-habit verb

examples.en: My nails were long, so I clipped them.
examples.note: simple: 손톱이 길다 + 깎다 (clip)

examples.en: I painted my nails.
examples.note: everyday: 손톱에 (on the nails, 에) + 바르다

examples.en: I hit it on the door and my nail broke.
examples.note: real-life: 부러지다 (snap, for rigid things) for a cracked nail

entries.nuance: 손톱 is a fingernail — 손 (hand) + 톱 — and you should bank it together with its mirror word 발톱 (toenail). The verb to memorize is 깎다 (to shave/clip), the very same verb Koreans use for peeling an apple (사과를 깎다) and getting a haircut (머리를 깎다); for trimming nails it's 손톱을 깎다, and learners who reach for 자르다 (to cut [in two]) sound off — 자르다 suggests cutting something through, while 깎다 means shaving a thin layer. To paint nails you 'spread' polish on them: 손톱에 매니큐어를 바르다 (note 에 for the surface). A broken nail uses 부러지다 (to snap), the verb for rigid things. Don't confuse 손톱 (fingernail) with 발톱 (toenail) — only the 손/발 (hand/foot) differs — and keep it one word with no space (손톱, not 손 톱). The 톱 here is unrelated in meaning to 톱 'a saw'; just treat 손톱/발톱 as fixed words. Collocations: 손톱을 깎다, 손톱이 자라다, 손톱이 부러지다, 손톱을 물어뜯다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 자르다 to trim nails: 손톱을 잘라요. The idiomatic verb is 깎다 (shave/clip) — 손톱을 깎아요.
Mixing 손톱 and 발톱: calling a toenail 손톱. 손 = hand, 발 = foot, so toenail = 발톱.
Writing it with a space (손 톱) or as 손톰. It's one solid word, 손톱.

entries.shortExplanation: 눈썹 means "eyebrow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 눈썹 (nunsseop) = "eyebrow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 눈썹이 진하다 ("for eyebrows to be thick/dark") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 눈썹, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 진하다 = dense/dark (also of coffee, makeup); opposite 연하다 light
그리다 = to draw; the standard makeup verb
속(inner) + 눈썹; 속눈썹이 길다 = long lashes
다듬다 = to neaten/groom

examples.en: Your eyebrows are dark and pretty.
examples.note: simple: 눈썹이 + 진하다 (dark/thick)

examples.en: I filled in my eyebrows looking in the mirror.
examples.note: everyday: -면서 (while) + 눈썹을 그리다

examples.ko: 눈썹 위에 작은 점이 하나 있어요.
examples.romanization: nunsseop wie jageun jeomi hana isseoyo.
examples.en: I have a little mole above my eyebrow.
examples.note: real-life: 눈썹 위에 (above, position 위 + 에) + 점이 있다

entries.nuance: 눈썹 is the eyebrow — 눈 (eye) + 썹 — and the must-pair word is 속눈썹 (eyelashes), where 속 means 'inner/inside,' so the lashes are framed as the 'inner brow.' Keep three things separate: 눈 (the eye itself), 눈썹 (the brow ridge of hair above), and 속눈썹 (the lashes on the lid) — calling lashes 눈썹 is the usual slip. The describing adjective is 진하다 (dark/dense, opposite 연하다 'light'), the same word for strong coffee or heavy makeup, so 눈썹이 진하다 = thick, dark brows. In makeup talk the verb is 그리다 (to draw) — 눈썹을 그리다 means to pencil/fill them in, and 눈썹을 다듬다 means to trim/shape them. To place a feature relative to the brow, use a position noun + 에: 눈썹 위에 (above the brow). Eyebrows aren't pluralized with 들. Collocations: 눈썹이 진하다, 눈썹을 그리다, 눈썹을 다듬다, 속눈썹이 길다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling eyelashes 눈썹. Lashes are 속눈썹 (속 = inner); 눈썹 alone is the brow.
Confusing 눈 and 눈썹: using 눈 for the brow. 눈 is the eye; the hairy ridge above is 눈썹.
Saying 눈썹이 검다 (black) when you mean thick/striking. For dark, dense brows Koreans say 눈썹이 진하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 키 means "height (of a person)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 키 (ki) means "height (of a person)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 키가 크다 ("to be tall (lit. height is big)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 키 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to be tall (lit. height is big)
usagePhrases.note: uses 크다 not 길다; 키가 커요
작다 (small), the opposite; never 짧다 for a person's height
casual; more formal 키가 어떻게 되세요?
past 컸다 = grew; 키가 많이 컸어요 = grew a lot

examples.en: My friend is tall.
examples.note: simple: 키가 크다, the core 'tall' frame

examples.en: I'm on the shorter side.
examples.note: everyday: -은 편이다 (tend toward) softens the statement

examples.en: My younger sibling grew a lot taller in a year.
examples.note: real-life: 키가 크다 in past = grew; 사이에 = in the span of

entries.nuance: 키 is a person's height/stature, and the make-or-break point is which adjective it takes: Korean treats height as BIG vs SMALL, so it's 키가 크다 (tall) and 키가 작다 (short) — never 키가 길다 ('long') or 키가 짧다 ('short [in length]'), which are the natural-but-wrong direct translations from English. The same 크다 in the past tense doubles as 'grew': 키가 컸어요 means 'grew taller,' so context decides between 'is tall' and 'grew.' To ask height, casual speech is 키가 몇이에요? and polite is 키가 어떻게 되세요?. This 키 (height) is a separate word from the loanword 키 ('key') and from 키 'rudder/oar' — same spelling, told apart by context. Note height is the subject (키가...), with the person marked by 은/는 (저는 키가 커요 = 'as for me, height is big'). Collocations: 키가 크다, 키가 작다, 키가 크다=grow, 키를 재다 (to measure height), 키 순서 (height order).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 키가 길어요 for 'tall.' Height uses 크다/작다, not 길다/짧다: 키가 커요 / 키가 작아요.
Using 짧다 for short stature: 키가 짧아요. A short person is 키가 작아요 (small), not short-in-length.
Forgetting the double sense of 컸다: 키가 컸어요 can mean 'grew taller,' not only 'is/was tall' — let context guide you.

entries.shortExplanation: 목소리 means "voice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "voice" is 목소리 (moksori). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 목소리가 좋다 ("to have a nice voice"). Watch the particle attached to 목소리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: common compliment; 목소리(가) 좋으시네요
크다 = big/loud (volume), not 높다 (pitch)
lit. 'voice doesn't come out'; from a cold or shouting
낮추다 = to lower (volume or pitch); 목소리를 높이다 = raise it

examples.en: That singer has a really nice voice.
examples.note: simple: 목소리가 좋다, the basic compliment frame

examples.en: I have a cold, so I've lost my voice.
examples.note: everyday: 감기에 걸리다 (catch a cold) + 목소리가 안 나오다

examples.ko: 여기 도서관이니까 목소리 좀 낮춰 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi doseogwaninikka moksori jom natchwo juseyo.
examples.en: This is a library, so please lower your voice.
examples.note: real-life: -니까 (reason) + 목소리를 낮추다 as a polite request

entries.nuance: 목소리 is the (human) voice, transparently 목 (throat/neck) + 소리 (sound) — literally 'throat-sound.' The synonym contrast is 목소리 vs plain 소리: 소리 is ANY sound (a noise, a bang, music), whereas 목소리 is specifically a person's vocal sound, so 'I like her voice' must be 목소리가 좋다, not 소리가 좋다. It serves both compliments (목소리가 좋다) and health (감기 때문에 목소리가 안 나와요 = losing your voice). The sharp learner pitfall is loud vs high: volume is 크다/작다 (목소리가 크다 = loud), but PITCH is 높다/낮다 (목소리가 높다 = high-pitched). English 'a loud voice' tempts people into 목소리가 높아요, which actually says 'high-pitched' — use 목소리가 커요 for loud. To adjust volume, 목소리를 높이다/낮추다 (raise/lower). Collocations: 목소리가 좋다, 목소리가 크다/작다, 목소리가 안 나오다, 목소리를 낮추다, 목소리가 잠기다 (to go hoarse).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 소리 for a person's voice: 그 사람 소리가 좋아요. 소리 = any sound; a voice is 목소리.
Saying 목소리가 높아요 to mean 'loud.' 높다 = high pitch; loud is 목소리가 커요.
Calling a lost voice 목소리가 없어요. Losing your voice is 목소리가 안 나와요 ('won't come out'), not 'have no voice.'

entries.shortExplanation: 배꼽 means "belly button; navel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배꼽 (baekkop) = "belly button; navel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 배꼽이 보이다 ("for the navel to show") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배꼽, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보이다 = to be visible; 옷이 짧아서 배꼽이 보여요
idiom: 'laugh till your navel falls out'; 빠지게 = to the point of falling out
배꼽 + 티(셔츠); everyday fashion word
playful: your belly 'knows' it's mealtime

examples.en: The baby's belly button is really small and cute.
examples.note: simple: 배꼽이 + adjective, plain description

examples.en: The top is short, so my belly button shows a little.
examples.note: everyday: 짧아서 (reason) + 배꼽이 보이다, 살짝 = slightly

examples.ko: 어제 그 영상 보고 배꼽 빠지게 웃었어요.
examples.romanization: eoje geu yeongsang bogo baekkop ppajige useosseoyo.
examples.en: I laughed so hard at that video yesterday.
examples.note: real-life: the 배꼽 빠지게 웃다 idiom in casual past speech

entries.nuance: 배꼽 is the belly button/navel, the small point sitting on the 배 (belly/stomach) — so don't blur 배꼽 (just the navel) with 배 (the whole abdomen): 배가 아파요 is a stomachache, but 배꼽이 아파요 would specifically be the navel. It's a friendly, concrete word that powers some very common expressions: the idiom 배꼽(이) 빠지게 웃다 (to laugh so hard 'your navel falls out' — i.e. split your sides), the fashion word 배꼽티 (crop top), and the joke 배꼽시계 (your stomach 'clock' announcing it's mealtime). Spelling pitfall for learners: it ends in a tense ㄲ — 배꼽, not 배곱 — and it's one word. Because it's a single point, it isn't pluralized. Useful collocations: 배꼽이 보이다, 배꼽이 나오다 (an 'outie'/protruding navel), 배꼽 빠지게 웃다, 배꼽티를 입다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 배꼽 with 배: using 배꼽이 아파요 for a stomachache. A stomachache is 배가 아파요; 배꼽 is only the navel point.
Spelling it 배곱. The tense ㄲ is required: 배꼽.
Translating the idiom literally and stopping at 배꼽이 빠졌어요. The set phrase is 배꼽(이) 빠지게 웃다 — 'laugh till your navel falls out' = laugh extremely hard.

entries.shortExplanation: 주먹 means "fist" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주먹 (jumeok) means "fist". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주먹을 쥐다 ("to clench one's fist"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주먹 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쥐다 = to grip/close the hand; not 잡다 (grab an object)
주먹(fist) + 밥(rice); hand-pressed, a lunchbox staple
size comparison; 사과가 주먹만 해요
날리다 = to send flying; informal/violent register

examples.en: The apple is about the size of a fist.
examples.note: simple: 주먹만 하다 as a size yardstick

examples.en: I got angry and clenched my fist tight.
examples.note: everyday: 꽉 (tightly) + 주먹을 쥐다

examples.en: I made tuna rice balls for lunch.
examples.note: real-life: the compound 주먹밥 in a cooking context

entries.nuance: 주먹 is a clenched fist — the closed hand, as opposed to 손, the hand in general (open or whole). The verb that goes with it is 쥐다 (to grip / close the hand around): 주먹을 쥐다 = to make a fist, often intensified by 꽉 (tightly). Learners often substitute 잡다 (to grab/hold an object), but 잡다 needs a thing to grab — for closing your own hand into a fist it's 쥐다, not 잡다. 주먹 doubles as a vivid size unit (주먹만 하다 = 'as big as a fist'), and it builds the very common food word 주먹밥 (hand-pressed rice ball — 주먹 + 밥). In rougher, informal contexts it heads fight vocabulary: 주먹을 날리다 (throw a punch), 주먹다짐 (a fistfight), and figuratively 주먹구구 (rough/sloppy estimation). Collocations: 주먹을 쥐다, 주먹을 꽉 쥐다, 주먹만 하다, 주먹밥, 주먹을 날리다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 잡다 to make a fist: 주먹을 잡았어요. 잡다 = grab an object; clenching your own hand is 주먹을 쥐다.
Equating 주먹 with 손: saying 주먹 for any hand. 주먹 is specifically the closed/clenched hand; the general hand is 손.
Saying 주먹처럼 커요 for fist-sized. The idiomatic size phrase is 주먹만 하다 — 사과가 주먹만 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 손등 means "back of the hand" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "back of the hand" is 손등 (sondeung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 손바닥 ("palm"). Watch the particle attached to 손등 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 손(hand) + 바닥(flat bottom surface); the opposite side of 손등

usagePhrases.en: for the back of the hand to be dry
usagePhrases.note: 건조하다 = dry (skin/air); winter skincare talk

usagePhrases.en: to apply on the back of the hand
usagePhrases.note: 바르다 = to spread on; 핸드크림을 바르다

usagePhrases.en: to wipe with the back of the hand
usagePhrases.note: instrument 으로; 땀을/입을 닦다

examples.en: The backs of my hands are so dry in winter.
examples.note: simple: 손등이 + 건조하다

examples.en: I put hand cream on the back of my hand.
examples.note: everyday: 손등에 (on, surface 에) + 바르다

examples.ko: 땀이 나서 손등으로 이마를 쓱 닦았어요.
examples.romanization: ttami naseo sondeungeuro imareul sseuk dakkasseoyo.
examples.en: I was sweating, so I quickly wiped my forehead with the back of my hand.
examples.note: real-life: 손등으로 (instrument 으로) + 닦다; 쓱 = with a swipe

entries.nuance: 손등 is the back of the hand, a compound of 손 (hand) + 등 (back) — the very same 등 that means the back of the body, so it literally reads 'hand-back.' Its anatomical opposite, which you should learn as a pair, is 손바닥 (palm), from 손 + 바닥 ('flat bottom/floor surface'); the two name the two faces of the hand and learners often mix them up. Notice how Korean builds body parts with 등 and 바닥: 발등 (top of the foot) and 발바닥 (sole) work identically — a neat pattern to lock in together. Grammar-wise, things sit ON the 손등 with 에 (손등에 크림을 바르다), but when the back of the hand is the TOOL you act with, use 으로 (손등으로 닦다, wipe with it). It's a single word — write 손등, not 손 등. Collocations: 손등이 건조하다, 손등에 바르다, 손등으로 닦다, 손등에 핏줄이 보이다 (veins showing on the back of the hand).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 손등 and 손바닥: using 손등 for palm. 손등 = back of the hand; the palm is 손바닥.
Writing a space: 손 등. It's one solid compound, 손등.
Wrong particle for using it as a tool: 손등에 닦다. To wipe WITH the back of the hand it's 손등으로 닦다 (instrument 으로).

entries.shortExplanation: 목구멍 means "throat (the inside passage)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 목구멍 (mokgumeong) = "throat (the inside passage)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 목이 아프다 ("to have a sore throat") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 목구멍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the short, far more common everyday version

usagePhrases.en: for the throat to sting/be raw
usagePhrases.note: 따갑다 = to sting/prickle; that scratchy cold feeling

usagePhrases.en: to get stuck in the throat
usagePhrases.note: 걸리다 = to get caught; 가시가 목구멍에 걸렸어요
붓다 (ㅅ-irregular) = to swell; 목이 부었어요

examples.en: I caught a cold and my throat hurts.
examples.note: simple: the everyday short form 목이 아프다

examples.en: My throat was raw, so I drank warm water.
examples.note: everyday: 목구멍이 따갑다 + reason -아서

examples.ko: 생선 가시가 목구멍에 걸려서 병원에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: saengseon gasiga mokgumeonge geollyeoseo byeongwone gasseoyo.
examples.en: A fish bone got stuck in my throat, so I went to the clinic.
examples.note: real-life: 목구멍에 걸리다; precise inner-passage sense

entries.nuance: 목구멍 is the throat as the inner passage/gullet, literally 목 (neck/throat) + 구멍 (hole) — 'throat-hole.' The crucial register/synonym point is 목 vs 목구멍: 목 covers both the neck (the outside) AND the throat, and in everyday speech a sore throat is almost always the short 목이 아파요 — people rarely say 목구멍이 아파요 in casual talk. You reach for 목구멍 when you need to specify the inside cavity: something lodged in it (가시가 목구멍에 걸리다), or a raw, stinging sensation deep inside (목구멍이 따갑다). At the clinic the formal term is the Sino-Korean 인후(咽喉), as in 인후염 (pharyngitis) or 이비인후과 (ENT clinic, 'ear-nose-throat dept'). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 목구멍 every time you'd say 'throat' — default to 목 for sore throats and save 목구멍 for the literal inner passage. Spelling: keep the ㅁ — 목구멍, not 목구머. Collocations: 목구멍이 따갑다, 목구멍에 걸리다, 목이 아프다, 목이 붓다, 목이 잠기다 (to go hoarse).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Defaulting to 목구멍이 아파요 for an ordinary sore throat. Everyday Korean is 목이 아파요; 목구멍 is for the specific inner passage.
Forgetting 목 also means 'neck,' so 목 alone is ambiguous — use 목구멍 only when you must specify the inside throat.
Dropping the final consonant: writing 목구머. It's 목구멍 (with ㅁ).

entries.shortExplanation: 뇌 means "brain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뇌 (noe) means "brain". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리가 좋다 ("to be smart (lit. head is good)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뇌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to be smart (lit. head is good)
usagePhrases.note: casual mental ability uses 머리, not 뇌
쓰다 = to use; can be literal or jokingly 'think hard'
informal: 머릿속이 하얘지다 nearby; blanking out
뇌(腦) + 세포(細胞); 뇌세포가 죽다 = brain cells dying, joking

examples.en: The human brain is really fascinating.
examples.note: simple: 뇌 as the literal organ + 신기하다

examples.en: While you sleep, your brain rests too.
examples.note: everyday: -는 동안 (during) + 뇌가 쉬다

examples.ko: 시험 때 너무 긴장하면 뇌가 멈추는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: siheom ttae neomu ginjanghamyeon noega meomchuneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: When I'm too nervous during an exam, it's like my brain freezes.
examples.note: real-life: informal 뇌가 멈추다 for going blank

entries.nuance: 뇌 is the brain as the physical organ — Sino-Korean 腦 ('brain') — and it's the right word for anatomy, health, and science: 뇌 수술 (brain surgery), 뇌세포 (brain cells), 뇌가 손상되다 (the brain is damaged). The key contrast for learners is 뇌 vs 머리: for everyday talk about intelligence, thinking, or memory, Koreans say 머리 (head/mind), NOT 뇌 — 'she's smart' is 머리가 좋다, you 'rack your brain' as 머리를 쓰다, and an idea pops into 머릿속 (inside the head). So reserve 뇌 for the literal organ and use 머리 for mental ability; saying 뇌가 좋다 for 'smart' sounds like a textbook mistranslation. Pronunciation pitfall: 뇌 is a single syllable, the diphthong 외 — roughly 'nö'/'nwe' (close to French eu or a quick 'nweh') — so don't split it into two beats ('no-i') or say 'noy.' Collocations (organ sense): 뇌가 쉬다, 뇌를 쓰다, 뇌 수술, 뇌세포, 뇌가 활성화되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 뇌가 좋다 for 'smart.' Casual intelligence is 머리가 좋다; 뇌 is the physical organ.
Using 뇌 for 'in my mind/head' (an idea, a memory): 뇌에 떠올랐어요. Everyday Korean is 머릿속에 떠올랐어요.
Pronouncing 뇌 as two syllables ('no-i') or 'noy.' It's one syllable with the vowel 외 (≈ 'nö/nwe').

entries.shortExplanation: 남자 means "man, male" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "man, male" is 남자 (namja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 남자 ("man, male"). Watch the particle attached to 남자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the plain, neutral noun for a male person
noun + 이에요/예요; 남자 ends in a vowel, so the contracted 예요
남자 used as a modifier in front of another noun, no particle needed
with a space it is a friend who happens to be male; 남자친구 written solid means boyfriend

examples.en: That person is a man.
examples.note: the simplest A는 B예요 identity sentence

examples.en: The men's restroom is on the second floor.
examples.note: 남자 glued to 화장실 acts like an adjective 'men's'

examples.en: The tall man is my older brother.
examples.note: real situation: a modifier clause 키 큰 plus subject 남자가

entries.nuance: 남자 (Sino-Korean 男子, literally 'male-person') is the flat, everyday noun for a man or male, with no warmth or rudeness built in — it simply states the category, the way 'male' does on a form. Its mirror word is 여자 (woman), and the dividing line you must keep straight is 남자 = any male in general versus 남편 (husband, 男便) = the specific man a woman is married to; an English speaker who reaches for 'my man' and says 내 남자 sounds like a song lyric, not 'my husband'. As a noun it takes 이에요/예요 and the subject marker 가 because it ends in a vowel (남자예요, 남자가), and it loves to sit in front of other nouns with no particle at all: 남자 화장실, 남자 옷, 남자 목소리. The notorious trap is spacing — 남자 친구 with a space is just a friend who is male, while 남자친구 squeezed into one word is a romantic boyfriend, so a stray space can change your whole sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 남자이에요 — because 남자 ends in the vowel ㅏ, the 이에요 contracts and the correct form is 남자예요.
Calling a husband 남자; a husband is 남편, and 남자 alone just means 'a male', so 우리 남자 for 'my husband' sounds wrong.
Writing 남자친구 (solid) when you only mean a buddy who is male — that solid form reads as 'boyfriend'; keep the space: 남자 친구.

entries.shortExplanation: 여자 means "woman, female" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 여자 (yeoja) = "woman, female". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 여자 ("woman, female") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 여자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the plain, neutral noun for a female person
noun + 예요 because 여자 ends in a vowel
여자 used as a modifier before another noun
with a space, a friend who is female; 여자친구 solid means girlfriend

examples.en: That person is a woman.
examples.note: the basic identity pattern A는 B예요

examples.en: The women's clothing store is on the first floor.
examples.note: 여자 stacked in front of 옷 to mean 'women's'

examples.ko: 빨간 옷을 입은 여자가 제 친구예요.
examples.romanization: ppalgan oseul ibeun yeojaga je chinguyeyo.
examples.en: The woman in red is my friend.
examples.note: real situation: a modifier clause describing which 여자

entries.nuance: 여자 (Sino-Korean 女子, literally 'female-person') is the neutral, all-purpose noun for a woman or female and is the exact counterpart of 남자 (man); like 남자 it carries no built-in politeness or insult, it just names the category. The boundary to memorize is 여자 = any female in general versus 아내 (wife) = the specific woman a man is married to, so saying 내 여자 for 'my wife' sounds like a possessive movie line rather than 아내. Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (여자예요, 여자가), and it pairs effortlessly as a modifier: 여자 화장실, 여자 목소리, 여자 옷. Two spacing pitfalls follow the same rule as 남자: 여자 친구 with a space is a platonic friend who is female, but 여자친구 written solid is a girlfriend — and unlike English, you cannot stick 'a' or 'the' in front; the bare noun already covers both.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 여자이에요 instead of 여자예요 — after the vowel ㅏ the copula contracts.
Using 여자 to mean 'wife'; a wife is 아내 (or 와이프 in casual speech), while 여자 alone just means 'a female'.
Saying 여자친구 (solid) for a casual female friend — that reads as 'girlfriend'; keep the space for a plain friend: 여자 친구.

entries.shortExplanation: 어른 means "adult, grown-up" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 어른 (eoreun) means "adult, grown-up". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어른 ("adult, grown-up"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어른 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a fully grown person; also one's elders
noun + 이에요 after the final consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 because 어른 ends in a consonant
plural with 들, often the seniors you must respect

examples.en: I am an adult now.
examples.note: 어른 + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ

examples.en: We use polite speech to adults/elders.
examples.note: everyday: shows the respect sense, 어른 = elder

examples.en: The grown-ups helped the child.
examples.note: real situation: 어른 contrasted directly with 아이 (child)

entries.nuance: 어른 is a native Korean word (no hanja) that covers two linked ideas: an adult as opposed to 아이 (child), and, just as importantly, one's elders — the older people a Korean is socially obliged to treat with respect. That second sense is where English speakers slip: 'adult' in English is a neutral age category, but 어른 often means 'a senior I must bow and use 존댓말 to', so 어른을 공경하다 (respect your elders) is a core phrase. Compare it with three neighbors — 성인 (成人, the legal/clinical 'adult' on documents and age ratings, e.g. 성인 영화), 노인 (an elderly person), and 아이 (child): 어른 is the warm, relational everyday word, 성인 is the bureaucratic one. It ends in the consonant ㄴ, so it takes 이에요 and 이 (어른이에요, 어른이). The adjective 어른스럽다 (to be mature, grown-up in manner) is built straight from it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 어른예요 — because 어른 ends in the consonant ㄴ, the full form 어른이에요 is required.
Treating 어른 as a pure age label like English 'adult'; on official forms and age ratings the word is 성인 (e.g. 성인 인증), while 어른 carries the 'respect your elders' nuance.
Confusing 어른 with 노인 — every 노인 is an 어른, but most 어른 are not 노인 (elderly); don't call a 30-year-old 노인.
