entries.shortExplanation: 아기 means "baby, infant" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "baby, infant" is 아기 (agi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아기 ("baby, infant"). Watch the particle attached to 아기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: a very young child; also a term of endearment
noun + 예요 because 아기 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
아기 modifying 옷 with no particle

examples.en: The baby is sleeping.
examples.note: simplest 아기 + 가 + verb

examples.en: The baby is really cute.
examples.note: everyday: pairs with the adjective 귀엽다

examples.en: Our baby is one year old now.
examples.note: real situation: 돌 = first birthday; 우리 아기 as endearment

entries.nuance: 아기 is a native, affectionate word for a baby or infant — soft and warm in a way the clinical term 아이(아이 = child, broader and older) is not. The boundary to hold: 아기 is roughly 'baby/infant' (newborn up to toddler), 아이 covers any child up through about pre-teen, and 어린이 (children) is the formal/institutional word you see on signs (어린이 보호구역 = school zone). In casual speech 아기 is very often softened to 애기, and shortened further to 애 in fast talk, though 아기 is the textbook spelling. The endearment use matters culturally: parents say 우리 아기 ('our baby') even to a grown child the way English speakers say 'my baby'. Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (아기예요, 아기가), and as a modifier it needs no particle: 아기 옷, 아기 침대, 아기 손.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 아기이에요 instead of 아기예요 — after the vowel ㅣ the copula contracts to 예요.
Treating 아기 and 아이 as interchangeable; 아기 is a baby/infant, while 아이 is a child of a much wider age range.
Assuming 애기 is wrong — it is the very common spoken form, but in writing the standard spelling is 아기.

entries.nuance: 노인 (Sino-Korean 老人, literally 'old-person') is the standard, neutral word for an elderly person in writing and statistics — 노인 복지 (elderly welfare), 노인 인구 (elderly population), 노인정 (senior center). noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
집 (house) + 주인, written solid as one word

examples.en: The owner of this shop is kind.
examples.note: 가게 주인 = shop owner, simple A 주인 pattern

examples.note: everyday: asking whose something is, 주인 + 이

entries.nuance: 주인 (Sino-Korean 主人, literally 'master/main-person') means the owner of a thing or the person running a place — 가게 주인 (shop owner), 식당 주인 (restaurant owner) — and by extension a 'host' or a master to a pet (강아지가 주인을 따라가요 = the dog follows its owner). The combination you must know is 집 + 주인 → 집주인, the standard word for a landlord, written solid as one word; leaving a space (집 주인) reads literally as 'the owner of the house' and feels off for the rental sense. Distinguish 주인 from 사장(님) (社長, the boss/CEO you address staff-side, common for any shop boss) and from 손님 (a guest/customer — the opposite role to 주인-as-host). It ends in ㄴ, so 이에요 and 이 (주인이에요, 주인이). Note the proverb-like phrase 주인 의식 ('ownership mindset'), where 주인 means taking responsibility as if you owned it.

Saying 주인예요 — after the consonant ㄴ the form is 주인이에요.
Writing 집 주인 with a space for 'landlord'; the established word is the solid 집주인 — a space makes it read as 'the house's owner' generically.
Using 주인 where Korean expects 사장님; to a shop boss you usually say 사장님, reserving 주인 for describing who owns the place.

noun + 예요 because 부부 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel

entries.nuance: 부부 (Sino-Korean 夫婦, literally 'husband-wife') means specifically a married couple — the husband and wife taken together as one social unit. The boundary English speakers must respect is 부부 (married) versus 커플 (a loanword from 'couple', a dating pair who may not be married at all); calling your boyfriend-and-yourself 부부 implies you are actually married. It is a dignified, neutral word that combines readily: 신혼부부 (newlyweds), 노부부 (an elderly couple), 잉꼬부부 (a lovebird couple who get along beautifully), 부부 싸움 (a marital spat). Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (부부예요, 부부가). One more nuance: 부부 names the relationship/unit, not the individuals, so you don't use it to point at one person — for that you'd say 남편 (husband) or 아내 (wife).

Writing 부부이에요 instead of 부부예요 — after the vowel ㅜ the copula contracts.
Using 부부 for a dating couple; an unmarried pair is 커플, while 부부 specifically implies marriage.
Applying 부부 to one individual; 부부 is the pair as a unit — a single spouse is 남편 (husband) or 아내 (wife).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 본인 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
ubiquitous on forms; also 본인 서명 (one's own signature)

examples.en: The person must come in person.
examples.note: 본인 + 이; classic counter/office phrasing

examples.note: everyday: 본인 modifying 이름 = 'your own'

entries.nuance: 본인 (Sino-Korean 本人, literally 'origin/root-person', i.e. the actual person concerned) is a formal-leaning word meaning 'oneself' or 'the very person in question'. Its natural home is officialdom — counters, banks, forms, hospitals: 본인 확인 (identity check), 본인 서명 (sign it yourself), 본인 부담금 (the portion the patient pays). The trap for English speakers is two-fold. First, register: in friendly conversation 본인 sounds stiff and bureaucratic, so for 'myself' say 저/나 and for 'yourself' use the person's name or title — overusing 본인 with friends is like saying 'the undersigned' at a coffee shop. Second, reference: 본인 always points back to the relevant person, not necessarily the speaker, so 본인이 오세요 means 'have the person themselves come', whereas to volunteer yourself you'd say 제가 갈게요. Compare 자기 (a casual 'oneself', and also a sweetheart's 'honey') and 스스로 (an adverb, 'by oneself / of one's own accord'). Ending in ㄴ, it takes 이에요 and 이.

Using 본인 to mean 'I' in casual chat; it sounds stiff and official — say 저 or 나 among friends, and use names for 'you'.
Assuming 본인 always means the speaker; it means 'the person concerned', so 본인이 직접 means 'that very person in person', not automatically 'I'.

usagePhrases.note: an unspecified, unknown person (a statement word)
누군가 + 가; the subject marker is commonly added
누군가 + 를 as the object of a verb
누군가 + 에게, the person something is directed to

examples.en: Someone is outside.
examples.note: 누군가 can stand bare before 있어요

examples.en: Someone knocked on the door.
examples.note: everyday: 누군가가 with the subject marker for clarity

examples.note: real situation: 누군가에게 = 'on/to someone'

entries.nuance: 누군가 is a native indefinite pronoun meaning 'someone / somebody' — an unknown or unspecified person. It is built from 누구 ('who') plus the bound 가, and the single most important fact about it is that, unlike bare 누구, it is a STATEMENT word, not a question; 누군가 왔어요 is 'someone came', never 'who came?'. This is exactly the trap for English speakers, because English 'who' and the indefinite blur together — in Korean you must switch words: question → 누구 (누구예요? = who is it?), indefinite → 누군가 (someone). Although the 가 inside it looks like a subject marker, it is fused into the word, so you still add fresh particles freely: 누군가가 (someone, subject), 누군가를 (someone, object), 누군가에게/한테 (to someone). Compare its relatives 아무 ('anyone', needs 도/나) and 어떤 사람 ('a certain person'); 누군가 is the warm, vague 'somebody out there' of songs and wishes.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 누군가 to ask a question; for 'who?' use 누구 (누구예요? / 누가 왔어요?), since 누군가 only states 'someone'.
Thinking the built-in 가 is the subject marker and refusing to add particles; you still say 누군가가 (subj.) and 누군가를 (obj.) normally.
Confusing 누군가 with 아무; 누군가 = 'some specific-but-unknown person', while 아무(나/도) = 'any/no person' and needs 나 or 도.

entries.shortExplanation: 아무 means "anyone, any (person)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아무, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: almost never stands alone — needs 도 or 나
아무 + 도; always paired with a NEGATIVE verb
아무 + 나; 'anyone will do', with a positive verb

examples.en: There's no one at home.
examples.note: 아무도 with the negative 없어요 = 'nobody'

examples.en: Anyone can do this.
examples.note: everyday: 아무나 + positive = 'anyone at all'

entries.nuance: 아무 is a native word meaning 'any (person/thing)', but its defining feature is that it almost never stands alone — it lives only with a partner particle, and which partner you choose flips the meaning, which is the core hurdle for English speakers used to one word 'any'. With 도 plus a NEGATIVE verb it means nobody/nothing: 아무도 없어요 ('no one is here'), 아무것도 몰라요 ('I know nothing'). With 나 plus a POSITIVE verb it means 'anyone/anything at all, no preference': 아무나 와도 돼요 ('anyone may come'), 아무거나 주세요 ('give me anything'). So the polarity of the verb must match the particle: 도 ↔ negative, 나 ↔ positive. Memorize the family as fixed sets — 아무도 (nobody), 아무나 (anybody), 아무것도/아무거나 (nothing/anything), 아무 데도/아무 데나 (nowhere/anywhere), 아무 때나 (anytime). Compare 누군가 ('a certain someone'), which is positive and specific-ish, against 아무 which is sweepingly general.

Using 아무도 with a positive verb; 아무도 must pair with a negative — 아무도 없어요 / 아무도 안 와요, never 아무도 있어요.
Saying 아무 alone to mean 'anyone'; it is incomplete — you need 아무나 (anyone) or 아무도 (no one) to finish the meaning.
Mixing the particles: 'anyone CAN come' is 아무나 와도 돼요 (positive→나), not 아무도, which would force a negative and mean 'no one'.

With 도 plus a NEGATIVE verb it means nobody/nothing: 아무도 없어요 ('no one is here'), 아무것도 몰라요 ('I know nothing'). With 나 plus a POSITIVE verb it means 'anyone/anything at all, no preference': 아무나 와도 돼요 ('anyone may come'), 아무거나 주세요 ('give me anything'). So the polarity of the verb must match the particle: 도 ↔ negative, 나 ↔ positive.

entries.shortExplanation: 아저씨 means "middle-aged man, mister" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아저씨 (ajeossi) means "middle-aged man, mister". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 아저씨 ("middle-aged man, mister"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 아저씨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: an adult/older man; also a way to address one
noun + 예요 because 아저씨 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
calling out to a male worker, driver, or older man

examples.en: That man showed me the way.
examples.note: 아저씨 + 가, describing an older man

examples.en: Mister, how much is this?
examples.note: everyday: 아저씨 as a direct form of address to a vendor

examples.en: The taxi driver was very kind.
examples.note: real situation: 택시 아저씨 = the (male) taxi driver

entries.nuance: 아저씨 is a native word for a middle-aged or grown man, and it does double duty as a friendly way to flag down a male stranger — a shopkeeper, a taxi driver, a delivery man — much like English 'mister' or 'sir', but warmer and more casual. The cultural pitfall for English speakers is age sensitivity: because 아저씨 implies 'middle-aged', calling a man in his twenties or early thirties 아저씨 can sting, since you're effectively saying he looks past his youth; for a younger-looking man people hedge with 저기요 ('excuse me') or 선생님. Its female counterpart is 아주머니 (and casual 아줌마), and the younger-male equivalents are 오빠/형 (for someone close) or 청년 in formal description. It ends in a vowel, so it takes 예요 and 가 (아저씨예요, 아저씨가). Note that 아저씨 is informal — in a business or polite setting you'd upgrade to 선생님 or 사장님 rather than 아저씨.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 아저씨이에요 instead of 아저씨예요 — after the vowel ㅣ the copula contracts.
Calling a young man 아저씨; it implies he looks middle-aged and can offend — use 저기요 or 선생님 for a younger-looking man.
Using 아저씨 in a formal/business setting; there it sounds too casual — switch to 선생님 or 사장님.

usagePhrases.note: an adult/older woman; also a way to address one
noun + 예요 because it ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
the shortened, blunter spoken form of 아주머니

examples.en: That lady is our neighbor.
examples.note: 아주머니 + 가, describing an older woman

examples.en: Ma'am, could I get some water?
examples.note: everyday: 아주머니 as polite direct address

examples.en: The restaurant lady kindly gave us more side dishes.
examples.note: real situation: 식당 아주머니 with honorific 께서/주셨어요

entries.nuance: 아주머니 is a native word for a middle-aged woman and the polite, standard way to address a female stranger or worker — a restaurant server, a shop owner, a neighbor — roughly 'ma'am'. Its shortened form 아줌마 is extremely common in speech but distinctly more casual and can sound blunt or even slightly stereotyped (the brash-auntie image), so 아주머니 is the safer, more respectful choice with someone you don't know. The same age caution as 아저씨 applies and trips up English speakers: labelling a young woman 아주머니/아줌마 implies she looks middle-aged and may offend — for a younger-looking woman use 저기요 ('excuse me') or 선생님. In polite reference you can raise it with 께서 and honorific verbs, as in the example.

Defaulting to 아줌마 with a stranger; the clipped form is casual and can sound rude — the polite full form is 아주머니.

entries.shortExplanation: 이웃 means "neighbor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이웃 (iut) = "neighbor". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이웃 ("neighbor") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이웃, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: a person living nearby; also neighbors collectively
noun + 이에요 after the final consonant ㅅ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
옆집 (the house next door) + 이웃; cf. 이웃 사람 (a neighbor)

examples.en: Our neighbor is very kind.
examples.note: 이웃 + 은 as topic; can be one person or 'the neighbors'

examples.en: A neighbor shared rice cakes with us.
examples.note: everyday: note the liaison — 이웃이 sounds like 이우시

examples.en: I get along well with my next-door neighbor.
examples.note: real situation: 이웃과 = 'with the neighbor', 사이가 좋다 idiom

entries.nuance: 이웃 is a native word (no hanja) for a neighbor — someone who lives close by — and it flexibly means either one specific neighbor or neighbors as a group, depending on context: 좋은 이웃 (a good neighbor), 이웃 사람 (the people next door), 이웃 나라 (a neighboring country). Two practical points for English speakers. First, pronunciation: the final ㅅ is unreleased and sounds like a ㄷ-stop when alone (이웃 ≈ '이욷'), but before a vowel-initial particle it links and softens, so 이웃이 comes out like '이우시' and 이웃을 like '이우슬' — getting this liaison right is what makes it sound natural. Second, it ends in a consonant, so it takes 이에요 and 이 (이웃이에요, 이웃이), not 예요. Culturally, the phrase 이웃사촌 ('a neighbor as close as a cousin') captures how a good 이웃 is valued, and greeting your 옆집 (next door) when you move in is a normal courtesy.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이웃예요 — after the final consonant ㅅ it must be 이웃이에요.
Pronouncing the final ㅅ as a clear English 's'; alone it is a stopped 'ㄷ' sound, and before a vowel it links — 이웃이 → '이우시'.
Forcing a plural 's'; 이웃 already serves for one neighbor or many, so 우리 이웃 can mean 'our neighbor(s)' without 들.

entries.shortExplanation: 주변 means "surroundings, area nearby" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주변 (jubyeon) means "surroundings, area nearby". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주변에 ("in the area, nearby"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주변 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks where things exist; pairs with 있다/많다
N + 주변 = the surroundings of N, no 의 needed
을 marks what you scan with your eyes
주변 also covers the people in one's circle

examples.en: There are many restaurants around the hotel.
examples.note: the everyday frame: N 주변에 + 있어요/많아요

examples.en: I took a walk around the area near the station.
examples.note: 주변을 둘러보다 = scan/look around, object particle 을

examples.ko: 여기 주변에 환전할 데가 있는지 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: yeogi jubyeone hwanjeonhal dega inneunji jom allyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you tell me if there's somewhere to exchange money nearby?
examples.note: real travel ask — note polite 주시겠어요? softens the request

entries.nuance: 주변 is Sino-Korean 周邊 ('encircling edge'), the zone wrapping around a fixed point — 'the area around X'. The near-synonym is 근처 (近處 'near place'): 근처 just means 'somewhere close by, in the vicinity', while 주변 implies the full ring of surroundings on every side, so 호텔 주변 feels like the whole neighborhood and 호텔 근처 feels like 'a spot near the hotel'. 주변 also stretches to people (주변 사람들 = those around you, your circle), which 근처 cannot do. It is neutral in register, fine in both speech and signage. The English-speaker trap is dropping the particle: 'restaurants around the hotel' tempts you to say 주변 식당 있어요, but to state existence you need 주변에 식당이 있어요 (에 = location). Also do not visually confuse it with 주말 (weekend) — same 주 but unrelated.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 주변 식당이 있어요 (no 에). To say things exist in the surroundings you mark location with 에: 주변에 식당이 있어요.
Using 주변 for one nearby spot. If you mean 'a place close by', 근처 is more natural (근처에 카페 있어요?); 주변 leans toward the whole encircling area.
Reading 주변 as 주말 (weekend) because both start with 주 — they share no meaning; 주변 = surroundings, 주말 = weekend.

entries.shortExplanation: 끝 means "end, tip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "end, tip" is 끝 (kkeut). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 끝에 ("at the end"). Watch the particle attached to 끝 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the end-point as a location
N + 끝 = the far end/tip of N
맨 = 'the very/outermost', intensifies 끝

usagePhrases.en: all the way to the end
usagePhrases.note: 까지 = up to; 'to the very end' in space or effort

examples.en: There's a convenience store at the end of the road.
examples.note: 길 끝에 = at the road's end, location 에

examples.ko: 이 줄 맨 끝에 서시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: i jul maen kkeute seosimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can stand at the very end of this line.
examples.note: 맨 끝 = the absolute end; -면 돼요 = 'it's fine if you...'

examples.en: Go all the way to the end of the hallway and turn right.
examples.note: 끝까지 가다 + 오른쪽으로 돌다 = a real direction-giving line

entries.nuance: 끝 is the native-Korean noun for the terminal point of something — the far tip of a line, road, or hallway, and by extension the end of a period of time (방학 끝, 여행 끝). Distinguish it from 가장자리 (the outer rim/edge of a flat thing like a table or page) and from 구석 (an inside corner where two walls meet): 끝 is the end of something long or linear, not a rim or a nook. Register is neutral and everyday. Two pitfalls for English speakers: spelling and the noun/verb split. The word ends in a single ㅌ (끝), often miswritten 끋 or 끝ㅌ; before a vowel that ㅌ links, so 끝에 sounds like 'kkeu-te'. And 끝 is only the noun 'the end' — to say something 'finishes/ends' you need the verb 끝나다 (영화가 끝났어요), not the bare noun. Handy collocations: 길 끝, 맨 끝, 끝까지.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 끋 or 끝ㅌ. The correct form is 끝 with one final ㅌ, and it links to a following vowel (끝에 → 'kkeu-te').
Using the noun 끝 where you need the verb. 'The movie ended' is 영화가 끝났어요 (verb 끝나다), not 영화가 끝이에요 unless you mean 'this is the final part'.
Saying 길 끝 있어요 without 에. To place something at the end, mark location: 길 끝에 편의점이 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 쪽 means "side, direction, way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쪽 (jjok) = "side, direction, way". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이쪽 / 저쪽 ("this way / that way") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쪽, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 이·그·저·어느 + 쪽, written as one word

usagePhrases.en: the right side / the left side
usagePhrases.note: 오른·왼 + 쪽 for left and right
으로 = toward, the direction particle
어느 + 쪽 for asking direction

examples.en: The restroom is over that way.
examples.note: 저쪽이에요 = 'it's that way', a bare location answer

examples.en: If you keep going this way, you'll reach the exit.
examples.note: 이쪽으로 = in this direction; 으로 with movement

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 시청은 어느 쪽으로 가야 돼요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande, sicheongeun eoneu jjogeuro gaya dwaeyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, which way do I go for City Hall?
examples.note: 어느 쪽으로 + 가야 돼요 = real 'which way' question

entries.nuance: 쪽 is a native dependent noun meaning 'side / direction' and is the workhorse of everyday directions. It attaches to demonstratives (이쪽/그쪽/저쪽/어느 쪽) and to 오른/왼 (오른쪽, 왼쪽). The key contrast is 쪽 vs 방향 (方向): 쪽 is concrete and deictic — a side you can point at right here ('over there, this way') — while 방향 is the more abstract heading of travel ('the opposite direction', 'the right direction'); you point 이쪽 but you check 방향이 맞아요?. 쪽 can also politely mean 'your side/end' (그쪽 = 'you' softly). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: write 이쪽/저쪽/오른쪽 as ONE word (이 쪽 with a space is wrong), and use the direction particle 으로 for movement — 이쪽으로 가요 ('go this way'), not 이쪽에 가요 (에 marks a static spot, not a heading).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 이 쪽 / 오른 쪽 with a space. 이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽, 왼쪽 are single words.
Saying 이쪽에 가요 for movement. Direction toward something takes 으로: 이쪽으로 가요 / 오른쪽으로 도세요.
Using 쪽 for an abstract heading like 'the wrong direction'. For that, 방향 is more natural (반대 방향), since 쪽 points at a concrete side.

entries.shortExplanation: 곳 means "place, spot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 곳 (got) means "place, spot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이곳 / 그곳 / 저곳 ("this place / that place"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 곳 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 이·그·저 + 곳, written as one word
adjective + 곳; a frequent modifier pattern
에서 marks the spot of an action
여러 + 곳; counting locations

examples.en: This is a famous place.
examples.note: 유명한 곳이에요 = 'it's a famous place', noun + 이에요

examples.en: I want to rest somewhere quiet.
examples.note: 곳에서 = at the place where you rest; action particle 에서

examples.ko: 여행하면서 가 보고 싶은 곳을 미리 적어 뒀어요.
examples.romanization: yeohaenghamyeonseo ga bogo sipeun goseul miri jeogeo dwosseoyo.
examples.en: I wrote down in advance the places I want to visit on the trip.
examples.note: 가 보고 싶은 곳 = clause + 곳; 적어 두다 = note down for later

entries.nuance: 곳 is a native dependent noun meaning 'place/spot', and it almost always rides on a modifier — an adjective or a relative clause (조용한 곳, 가 본 곳, 이곳). The near-synonym is 데, and the dividing line is register: 곳 is the slightly more formal, written-feeling word (you see it in guidebooks, reviews, signs), while 데 is the casual, spoken word. There is also a grammar difference — 곳 can pair with demonstratives to stand a bit more independently (이곳/그곳), whereas 데 leans even harder on a preceding modifier. Compare 위치 too: 위치 (位置) is the abstract coordinates 'where something sits', but 곳 is a place you go to or are in. Pronunciation pitfall: the final ㅅ is an unreleased 't' stop, so 곳 alone sounds like 'got' with the t held; before a vowel it surfaces, so 곳에 → 'go-se'. And don't drop the particle: say 곳에서 쉬어요, not 곳 쉬어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pronouncing 곳 as a fully released 'got'. The final ㅅ is a held 't' stop; it only releases before a vowel (곳에 → 'go-se').
Dropping the particle. An action 'at a place' needs 에서: 조용한 곳에서 쉬어요, not 조용한 곳 쉬어요.
Using 곳 for abstract position. If you mean 'its location/position is good', use 위치 (위치가 좋아요), not 곳.

entries.shortExplanation: 데 means "place, spot (casual)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "place, spot (casual)" is 데 (de). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 갈 데 ("a place to go"). Watch the particle attached to 데 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: V-(으)ㄹ + 데 = a place to do V
adjective + 데, spoken-feeling
데 also = the part/spot (of the body) that…
another V-(으)ㄹ + 데 collocation travelers use

examples.en: I have no place to go.
examples.note: 갈 데 = a place to go; the modifier is obligatory

examples.ko: 이 근처에 조용한 데 좀 아세요?
examples.romanization: i geuncheoe joyonghan de jom aseyo?
examples.en: Do you know somewhere quiet around here?
examples.note: 조용한 데 = a quiet spot; casual, friendly ask

examples.en: If anywhere hurts, please tell me.
examples.note: 아픈 데 = the spot that hurts; 데 = the affected part

entries.nuance: 데 is the casual, conversational dependent noun for 'place/spot', and it is grammatically bound: it can never stand alone the way 곳 sometimes can — it must follow a modifier (갈 데, 먹을 데, 조용한 데, 아픈 데). The contrast with 곳 is purely register and feel: in speech Koreans reach for 데 (갈 데 없어요), while writing, reviews, and formal signage prefer 곳 (방문할 곳). 데 also has a special sense English speakers love once they see it — 'the spot/part that…', as in 아픈 데 (the place that hurts) or 불편한 데 (the part that's uncomfortable), which 곳 does not naturally cover. The big trap is homonym confusion: this place-noun 데 is unrelated to the sentence connector -는데/-은데 ('and/but/background'), even though they look identical; 갈 데가 없어요 (noun) vs 가고 싶은데 표가 없어요 (connector). Keep a modifier in front and you'll always read it as the place-noun.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 데 with no modifier (데가 있어요 ✗). It must follow a modifier: 갈 데가 있어요 / 조용한 데가 있어요.
Confusing the place-noun 데 with the connector -는데. 갈 데가 없어요 (place) vs 가고 싶은데 (but…) are different grammar despite the same shape.
Forcing 데 into formal writing. A review or sign prefers 곳 (가 볼 만한 곳); 데 sounds too casual there.

entries.shortExplanation: 자리 means "seat, spot, place" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 창가 = by the window; a top travel collocation
빈 (empty) + 자리, written together
에 marks where you sit; pairs with 앉다
잡다 = secure a seat or spot

examples.en: A window seat, please.
examples.note: 자리로 주세요 = 'give me the ~ seat'; 로 picks the option

examples.en: Is there an empty seat here?
examples.note: 빈자리 있어요? = the standard 'seat free here?' ask

examples.ko: 일행이 자리 잡는 동안 제가 주문할게요.
examples.romanization: ilhaengi jari jamneun dongan jega jumunhalgeyo.
examples.en: While my group grabs a table, I'll order.
examples.note: 자리(를) 잡다 = secure seats; 동안 = 'during/while'

entries.nuance: 자리 is the native everyday noun for a seat or a spot you occupy — a seat on a train, a table at a restaurant, a place in a line, even a 'position' in life (좋은 자리 = a good job/standing). The crucial contrast is 자리 vs 의자: 의자 (椅子) is the physical chair as an object, while 자리 is the seat/spot as a space you take or reserve — so you ask 자리 있어요? ('is there a seat/spot?'), not 의자 있어요? (which sounds like 'do you have a chair to sell?'). 자리 collocates richly: 창가 자리 (window seat), 빈자리 (empty seat), 자리에 앉다 (sit down), 자리를 잡다/맡다 (grab/save a spot), 자리를 비우다 (step away from one's seat). Register is neutral and friendly. English-speaker pitfall: with 앉다 ('sit') use the location particle 에 — 자리에 앉아요, not 자리 앉아요; and to choose a seat type use 로/으로 (창가 자리로).

Saying 의자 when you mean a seat/spot. 의자 is a physical chair; a seat you take or reserve is 자리 (빈자리 있어요?).
Dropping 에 with 앉다. 'Sit in the seat' is 자리에 앉아요; 자리 앉아요 is missing the particle.
Using 있다 wrong for a free seat. Ask 빈자리 있어요? ('is there an empty seat?'); 자리가 비었어요? is also fine but means 'is the seat vacated?'.

entries.shortExplanation: 구석 means "corner (inside)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 구석 (guseok) means "corner (inside)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 구석에 ("in the corner"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 구석 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the inside corner as a location
N + 구석 = the inside corner of N
구석 + 자리, a quiet nook seat
reduplicated = 'all over, thoroughly'

examples.en: The bag is in the corner of the room.
examples.note: 구석에 있어요 = sits in the inside corner; location 에

examples.en: Shall we sit at the corner table?
examples.note: 구석 자리 = a tucked-away corner seat; -ㄹ까요? suggests

examples.en: While cleaning I wiped every nook of the house.
examples.note: 구석구석 = thoroughly, all over; vivid native usage

entries.nuance: 구석 is a native noun for an inside corner — the nook where two walls of a room or the inner edges of a box meet — and figuratively a tucked-away, out-of-the-way spot. The sharp contrast is 구석 vs 모퉁이: 모퉁이 is the OUTSIDE corner of a street or building, the bend you turn at (모퉁이를 돌다 = turn the corner), whereas 구석 is an INSIDE nook you tuck into; you can sit in a 구석 but you turn a 모퉁이. There is also the lovely reduplicated form 구석구석 ('every nook and cranny, thoroughly'). Register is neutral, slightly cozy/colloquial. Note 구석 can carry a faintly negative shade (a 'neglected back corner'), so a hotel 'corner room' marketed positively might be called 코너 instead. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 구석 for a street corner — that's 모퉁이; and keep the particle — 구석에 있어요 for location, 구석에서 for an action done there.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 구석 for a street corner you turn. The bend of a street/building is 모퉁이 (모퉁이를 도세요); 구석 is an inside nook.
Dropping the particle. Location takes 에 (구석에 있어요); an action done there takes 에서 (구석에서 사진을 찍었어요).
Treating 구석 as always neutral. It can imply a 'back, neglected' corner, so for a flatteringly described corner room Koreans often say 코너 instead.

Watch the particle attached to 속 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: N + 속 = the interior/depths of N
에 marks the inner location
물 + 속, written together; submerged
figurative 'inside' — within the image

examples.en: My passport is inside the bag.
examples.note: 가방 속에 = down inside the bag; location 에

examples.en: I found a coin inside my pocket.
examples.note: 속에서 = inside (where the finding happened); action 에서

examples.ko: 사진 속 그 골목이 아직도 기억나요.
examples.romanization: sajin sok geu golmogi ajikdo gieongnayo.
examples.en: I still remember that alley in the photo.
examples.note: 사진 속 = within the picture; figurative 속

entries.nuance: 속 is a native noun for the inside, interior, or depths of something — especially a filled, enclosed, or three-dimensional thing (가방 속, 물속, 숲속), and figuratively the inside of an image or a heart (사진 속, 마음속 = deep in one's heart). The essential contrast is 속 vs 안: 안 marks being within a boundary or enclosure (방 안 = inside the room, 건물 안 = inside the building), neutral and structural, while 속 stresses being embedded in the substance or down in the depths (물속 = under the water, 가방 속 = buried in the bag). So 방 안 is natural but 방 속 sounds odd; 물속 is natural but 물 안 sounds odd. 속 also has bodily/emotional senses (속이 안 좋다 = upset stomach; 속상하다 = heartsick) that 안 lacks. Register neutral. English-speaker pitfall: don't reflexively map 'inside' to whichever you learned first — use 안 for rooms/buildings/bounded areas and 속 for filled or deep spaces; and keep 에: 가방 속에 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 속 and 안 by habit. Rooms and buildings take 안 (방 안, 건물 안); filled or deep spaces take 속 (물속, 가방 속).
Forgetting the particle. Location 'inside' needs 에: 가방 속에 있어요, not 가방 속 있어요.
Saying 물 안 for being submerged. 'In the water' is 물속 (written together); 물 안 is unnatural.

entries.shortExplanation: 바깥 means "outside, the outdoors" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 바깥 (bakkat) = "outside, the outdoors". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 바깥에 ("outside (location)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 바깥, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the outdoor location
바깥 + N = the outside/outdoor N
으로 = toward outside; pairs with 나가다
common collocation: 바깥 공기 좀 쐬다

examples.en: There are many people outside.
examples.note: 바깥에 = outside as a location; existence 에

examples.en: The weather outside is colder than expected.
examples.note: 바깥 날씨 = the outdoor weather; 생각보다 = 'than I thought'

examples.ko: 바람도 쐴 겸 바깥으로 잠깐 나갈까요?
examples.romanization: baramdo ssoel gyeom bakkateuro jamkkan nagalkkayo?
examples.en: Shall we step outside for a bit to get some air?
examples.note: 바깥으로 나가다 = go out; -ㄹ 겸 = 'also so as to…'

entries.nuance: 바깥 is a native noun meaning the outside / the outdoors, the natural opposite of 안 (inside). Its near-synonym is 밖: the two are largely interchangeable for 'outside' (바깥에/밖에, 바깥 날씨/바깥 = 'out there'), but 바깥 feels a touch more concrete and substantial — 'the outdoors as a place' — while 밖 is the lighter, more frequent 'outside' and also forms compounds like 창밖 (outside the window) and 문밖 (outside the door). Be very careful: the string 밖에 doubles as the grammar particle '밖에' meaning 'only/nothing but' (천 원밖에 없어요 = 'I have only 1,000 won'), so when you want the location 'outside' it is safer and clearer to say 바깥에. Register is neutral; there's also a dated sense 바깥양반/바깥일 ('the husband / outside affairs'). English-speaker pitfalls: spell it with final ㅌ — 바깥 (not 바깟/바같), and that ㅌ links to vowels so 바깥에 sounds like 'ba-kka-te'; for going out use direction 으로 (바깥으로 나가요).

Misspelling as 바깟 or 바같. The word ends in ㅌ: 바깥, and it links to a following vowel (바깥에 → 'ba-kka-te').
Confusing 바깥에 (outside, location) with the particle 밖에 ('only'). 밖에 + negative = 'only' (물밖에 없어요); for 'outside' prefer 바깥에.
Using 에 for going out. Movement outward takes 으로: 바깥으로 나가요, not 바깥에 나가요.

entries.shortExplanation: 양쪽 means "both sides" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 양쪽 (yangjjok) means "both sides". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 양쪽에 ("on both sides"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 양쪽 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the location on both sides
N + 양쪽 = the two sides of N
다 = all/both; 'both alike'
양쪽 + 끝 = the two far ends

examples.en: There are shops on both sides of the road.
examples.note: 양쪽에 = on both sides; location 에

examples.en: Either one is fine with me.
examples.note: 양쪽 다 = both/either; common when choosing

examples.ko: 다리 양쪽 끝에 경비가 서 있더라고요.
examples.romanization: dari yangjjok kkeute gyeongbiga seo itdeoragoyo.
examples.en: There were guards standing at both ends of the bridge.
examples.note: 양쪽 끝 = the two far ends; -더라고요 = 'I noticed that…'

entries.nuance: 양쪽 is 양 (兩 'two/both', the Sino-Korean root also in 양손 'both hands', 양면 'both sides') plus the native 쪽 ('side'), literally 'both sides'. It names the two opposing sides of something — a road, a door, a choice between two options. Compare 양쪽 vs 양옆: 양쪽 is the general 'both sides', while 양옆 specifically means 'both flanks / the two sides beside' something (양옆에 앉다 = sit on either side of). And contrast it with 둘 다 / 양쪽 다 ('both of them' when choosing): 양쪽 다 괜찮아요 = 'either is fine'. Register neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: it is built from the bound root 양, not from a counting word, so 'both sides' is 양쪽, never 둘쪽 or 두 쪽 (두 쪽 would mean 'two pieces/slices'); and because 양 inherently means exactly two, do not use 양쪽 for three or more sides — for 'all sides/all around' use 사방 (四方) or 곳곳. Keep the particle: 양쪽에 for location.

Using 양쪽 for three or more directions. 양 means exactly two; for 'all around / every side' use 사방 or 곳곳.
Dropping 에 for location. 'Shops on both sides' is 양쪽에 가게가 있어요, not 양쪽 가게가 있어요.

examples.ko: 지금 제 위치 보내 드릴 테니까 그쪽으로 와 주세요.
examples.romanization: jigeum je wichi bonae deuril tenikka geujjogeuro wa juseyo.
examples.en: I'll send you my location now, so please come there.
examples.note: 위치를 보내다 = share location; -ㄹ 테니까 = 'I'll…, so…'

entries.nuance: 위치 is Sino-Korean 位置 (位 'position/rank' + 置 'to place'), literally 'where something is set' — the abstract location or position of a thing. It is the natural word in maps, GPS, apps, and reviews: 위치가 좋다 (good location), 현재 위치 (current location), 위치를 공유하다/보내다 (share/send location). The key contrast is 위치 vs 곳/데: 곳 and 데 are 'a place you go to or are in' (조용한 곳, 갈 데), whereas 위치 is the coordinate/position 'where it sits' relative to other things — you don't 'go to a 위치', you check or describe one. Compare also 장소 (場所), which is a concrete venue/site for an event (모임 장소 = meeting place); 위치 is more abstract than 장소. Register is neutral-to-formal, common in writing and signage. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 위치 to mean 'a nice place to visit' — say 곳/데; and pronounce 치 as 'chi' (위치 = 'wi-chi'), not 'wi-ti'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 위치 for 'a place to go'. A destination is 곳 or 데 (좋은 곳, 갈 데); 위치 is the abstract position of something.
Mispronouncing 치 as 'ti'. 위치 is 'wi-chi'.
Confusing 위치 with 장소. An event venue is 장소 (모임 장소); 위치 is the more abstract 'where it sits'.

entries.shortExplanation: 방향 means "direction" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 방향 (banghyang) = "direction". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방향이 맞다 ("the direction is right") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방향, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 가/이 + 맞다 = 'is correct'
반대 (反對) = opposite
으로 = toward; pairs with 가다
어느 + 방향 for asking a heading

examples.en: Is this the right direction?
examples.note: 방향이 맞다 = the heading is correct; basic check

examples.en: I took a bus going the opposite direction.
examples.note: 반대 방향으로 = the opposite way; 으로 with 가다

examples.ko: 서울역은 지금 어느 방향으로 가야 하는지 잘 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: seouryeogeun jigeum eoneu banghyangeuro gaya haneunji jal moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: I'm not sure which direction I should head for Seoul Station.
examples.note: 어느 방향으로 가야 하다 = which way to head; real lost-traveler line

entries.nuance: 방향 is Sino-Korean 方向 (方 'direction/region' + 向 'to face/head toward'), the abstract heading or orientation of movement. The central contrast is 방향 vs 쪽: 쪽 is the concrete, point-at-it 'side/way' right in front of you (이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽), while 방향 is the abstract course of travel you reason about — 'the opposite direction', 'the right direction', 'which way leads there'. So you point 이쪽 ('this way, here') but you verify 방향이 맞아요? ('am I heading right?') and warn 반대 방향이에요 ('that's the wrong way'). Compare 위치 too: 위치 is where something is (static position), 방향 is which way it faces or you move. Register neutral, fine in speech and signs (e.g., 부산 방향 on a road sign = 'toward Busan'). English-speaker pitfalls: for movement use 으로 (반대 방향으로 가요), not 에 (방향에 가요 is wrong); and don't confuse 방향 with the look-alike 방학 (school vacation) — same 방, unrelated meanings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 방향에 가요 for movement. A heading takes 으로: 반대 방향으로 가요.
Using 방향 where 쪽 fits better. To point at a concrete side say 이쪽/저쪽; 방향 is the abstract course of travel.
Confusing 방향 (direction) with 방학 (school vacation). They share 방 but mean entirely different things.

entries.explanation: 정면 (jeongmyeon) means "the front, directly in front". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정면에 ("at the front, directly in front"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정면 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: at the front, directly in front
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the front-facing spot
N + 정면 = the front face of N
으로 = straight in that direction
에서 = the front as where an action happens

examples.en: There's a big door at the front of the building.
examples.note: 정면에 = on the front face; location 에

examples.en: Just go straight ahead from here.
examples.note: 정면으로 쭉 가다 = head straight on; direction 으로

examples.ko: 역 정면에서 만나는 게 제일 찾기 쉬울 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: yeok jeongmyeoneseo mannaneun ge jeil chatgi swiul geot gatayo.
examples.en: Meeting right in front of the station seems easiest to find.
examples.note: 정면에서 만나다 = meet at the front; 에서 for the meeting spot

entries.nuance: 정면 is Sino-Korean 正面 (正 'straight/correct' + 面 'face/surface'), literally 'the straight face' — the front-facing side of something or the space directly ahead of you. The key contrast is 정면 vs 앞: 앞 is the general, everyday 'front / in front of' (집 앞 = in front of the house) and is what casual speech uses; 정면 is more specific and emphatic, the face that looks straight at you or the line dead-ahead — a building's façade (건물 정면) or 'straight in front' (정면으로 가다). So everyday 'in front of me' is 제 앞, but 'the front of the building / head-on' is where 정면 shines. It also appears in 정면충돌 (head-on collision) and 정면으로 보다 (face head-on). Register neutral-to-formal. English-speaker pitfalls: don't reach for 정면 in casual 'in front of' situations — use 앞; and keep particles straight — 정면에 for a static location, 정면으로 for the straight-ahead direction, 정면에서 for an action done at the front.

Using 정면 for casual 'in front of me'. Everyday speech uses 앞 (제 앞, 집 앞); 정면 stresses the front face / dead-ahead.
Mixing up the particles. Location is 정면에, direction is 정면으로, action-spot is 정면에서.
Treating 정면 as just 'front side' of any object. It implies the main front-facing face (a façade or head-on line), not a random side.

entries.shortExplanation: 가장자리 means "edge, rim" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "edge, rim" is 가장자리 (gajangjari). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가장자리에 ("at the edge"). Watch the particle attached to 가장자리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the rim as a location
N + 가장자리 = the outer rim of N
를 따라 = following the rim
으로 = in the direction of the rim

examples.en: I set the cup at the edge of the table.
examples.note: 가장자리에 = on the rim; location 에

examples.en: I walked slowly along the edge of the lake.
examples.note: 가장자리를 따라 걷다 = walk along the rim

examples.ko: 컵을 가장자리에 너무 가까이 두면 떨어질 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: keobeul gajangjarie neomu gakkai dumyeon tteoreojil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: If you leave the cup too close to the edge, it might fall.
examples.note: 가장자리에 가까이 = close to the rim; -ㄹ 수도 있다 = 'might'

entries.nuance: 가장자리 is a native noun for the outer edge or rim of a flat or bounded thing — a table, a page, a lake, a field. It contrasts sharply with three neighbors: 끝 is the end/tip of something long or linear (길 끝 = the road's end), 구석 is an inside corner where two walls meet (방 구석), and 모퉁이 is the outside corner of a street you turn at (모퉁이를 돌다) — so a tabletop has a 가장자리 (rim) but a hallway has a 끝 (end) and a room has a 구석 (nook). A close synonym is 끄트머리 ('the very edge/tip', more colloquial), and 테두리 means specifically a border/frame line around something. Register is neutral, everyday. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 가장자리 for the end of a road or hallway (that's 끝), and don't confuse the noun 가장자리 (edge) with the unrelated superlative adverb 가장 ('most / -est', as in 가장 큰 = biggest) — they merely share the first two syllables. Keep the particle: 가장자리에 for location, 가장자리를 따라 for 'along'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가장자리 for the end of a road or hallway. That linear end is 끝 (길 끝); 가장자리 is the rim of a flat/bounded thing.
Confusing 가장자리 (edge) with 가장 (most/-est). 가장 is a superlative adverb (가장 큰 = biggest), unrelated to the noun.
Dropping the particle. Location is 가장자리에; 'along the edge' is 가장자리를 따라, not bare 가장자리 따라.

entries.shortExplanation: 물건 means "thing, object, item" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 물건 (mulgeon) = "thing, object, item". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 물건이 있어요 ("There is a thing / I have something") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 물건, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: There is a thing / I have something
usagePhrases.note: 물건 + 이/가 있어요
이/그/저 + 물건
물건 + 을/를 + verb

usagePhrases.en: There are a lot of things
usagePhrases.note: 물건 + 이/가 많다

examples.en: What is this thing?
examples.note: Pointing at an unknown physical object

examples.en: There are too many things in the bag.
examples.note: 에 marks the container; 물건이 많다 = lots of stuff

examples.ko: 손님, 이 물건은 환불이 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: sonnim, i mulgeoneun hwanburi an dwaeyo.
examples.en: Sir/Ma'am, this item can't be refunded.
examples.note: Shop register: 물건 = the merchandise itself

entries.nuance: 물건 is the Sino-Korean 物件 (物 'thing' + 件 'item/case'), the catch-all word for a tangible, hold-in-your-hand object when you don't know or don't need its specific name, and in a store it shifts to mean the merchandise/goods. The sharp contrast is with 것 (and its spoken form 거): 것 is a grammatical 'thing' that can stand for anything at all, even abstractions or whole situations (좋은 것 = a good thing/one), whereas 물건 is strictly a concrete physical item you could pick up — you would never call an idea, a plan, or a feeling a 물건. It is neutral in register and safe with anyone. Common collocations: 물건을 사다/팔다 (buy/sell goods), 물건이 좋다 (the goods are good quality), 물건을 고르다 (pick out an item). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 물건 every time you'd say 'thing' in English; for 'I have a lot of things to do' you need 일 (work/matter), not 물건, and to count items you say 물건 다섯 개, never '다섯 물건'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 할 물건이 많아요 for 'I have many things to do' — 물건 is only physical objects, so this must be 할 일이 많아요 (using 일 = task/matter).
Using 물건 as a counter, e.g. 한 물건 — 물건 is a noun, not a measure word, so count with 개: 물건 한 개, 물건 두 개.
Calling an abstract 'thing' like a good idea 좋은 물건 — for non-physical 'things' use 것: 좋은 것이에요 (it's a good thing).

entries.shortExplanation: 상자 means "box" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상자 (sangja) means "box". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상자가 있어요 ("There is a box"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 상자 + 이/가 있어요
상자 + 안에 (interior location)
상자 + 를 + 열다
adjective (큰) + 상자

examples.en: What's inside the box?
examples.note: 안에 = inside; asking about contents

examples.ko: 이 상자는 너무 무거워서 못 들겠어요.
examples.romanization: i sangjaneun neomu mugeowoseo mot deulgesseoyo.
examples.en: This box is too heavy, I can't lift it.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 들다 = lift

examples.en: I cut open the delivery box with a knife.
examples.note: 택배 = parcel; 뜯다 = rip/tear open

entries.nuance: 상자 is the Sino-Korean 箱子 (箱 'box/chest' + the noun-forming 子), the standard word for a rigid box or carton — cardboard moving boxes, gift boxes, shipping cartons. Its everyday rival is the loanword 박스 (from English 'box'); the two overlap heavily and a Korean might say 박스 하나 just as readily, but 상자 sounds a touch more proper/written while 박스 is breezier and dominates for things like a 'case' of bottled water (생수 한 박스). Contrast it with the soft containers it is NOT: 봉투 (a flat envelope or paper bag) and 봉지 (a flimsy plastic/paper sack) collapse and have no rigid walls. Count boxes with the generic 개 (상자 한 개) or, for full-box quantities, the loan counter 박스. The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 상자 for a tiny rigid case — a jewelry or glasses case is usually 케이스 or 갑, not 상자.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a plastic shopping bag a 상자 — a bag that collapses is 봉지 (plastic) or 봉투 (paper/envelope); 상자 has rigid walls.
Using 상자 for a small hard case like a ring box or pencil case — Koreans say 케이스 or 갑 (반지 케이스, 필통), reserving 상자 for larger cartons.
Opening a sealed cardboard box with 열다 only — 열다 works for a lid, but to slit packing tape you naturally say 뜯다 (tear/cut open): 상자를 뜯다.

entries.explanation: "paper" is 종이 (jongi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 종이가 있어요 ("There is paper"). Watch the particle attached to 종이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 종이 + 이/가 있어요
종이 + 장 (counter for flat things)
종이 + 에 + 쓰다
종이 + 를 + 접다

examples.en: Just give me one sheet of paper, please.
examples.note: 장 counts flat sheets; 만 = just/only

examples.ko: 여기 종이에 이름하고 전화번호를 써 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi jongie ireumhago jeonhwabeonhoreul sseo juseyo.
examples.en: Please write your name and phone number on this paper here.
examples.note: 종이에 = onto the paper, filling a form

examples.en: The printer is out of paper.
examples.note: 다 떨어지다 = run out completely

entries.nuance: 종이 is a pure native Korean word for paper, both as the material (made from 나무/pulp) and as a sheet of it. The crucial point is its counter: flat, thin things are counted with 장 (종이 한 장, 두 장) — the same 장 used for tickets (표 한 장), photos (사진 한 장), and pizza slices, so learning 종이 anchors the whole 'flat-sheet' counter family. Distinguish the raw material 종이 from finished paper products that have their own names: a 신문 (newspaper), a 책 (book), a 공책/노트 (notebook), and a filled-out 서류 (document) are all made of 종이 but are never just called 종이. Useful collocations: 종이에 쓰다/적다 (write on paper), 종이를 접다 (fold paper), 종이를 자르다/찢다 (cut/tear paper). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: defaulting to 개 instead of 장 to count sheets, and using 종이 for a form you must complete — that is 서류 (paperwork) or the document's specific name.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting sheets with 개 — say 종이 한 장 (one sheet), not 종이 한 개; flat things take the counter 장.
Calling a form or official document 종이 — the paper you fill in is 서류 (paperwork) or the named form; 종이 is the blank material.
Writing 'on paper' with the wrong particle, e.g. 종이를 써요 for 'write on paper' — use the surface particle 에: 종이에 써요 (종이를 쓰다 would mean 'use up paper').

entries.nuance: 비닐봉지 stitches together 비닐 (from English 'vinyl', here meaning thin plastic film) + 봉지 (a flimsy sack/pouch), i.e. the thin film bag you get at shops and markets. The contrast to nail down is the container family: 비닐봉지/봉지 is thin and flimsy, 봉투 is a paper bag or an envelope, and 가방 is a sturdy reusable bag/backpack you own. Because Korean stores charge for bags and supermarkets have largely stopped offering single-use ones, 비닐봉지 주세요 / 봉투 필요하세요? are bread-and-butter checkout lines. The big pitfall is the word 비닐 itself: it does NOT mean English 'vinyl' as in vinyl records (that's LP/레코드) or vinyl flooring siding — in Korean 비닐 just means cheap plastic sheeting/film. The verb that goes with it is 담다 — to load/put things into an open vessel — which is exactly the contrast to remember: you 담다 into a 바구니 (open) but you might 넣다 (insert) into a closed 상자 or 봉지. entries.nuance: 양동이 is a bucket or pail — a deep, usually handled vessel for carrying or holding water, typical of cleaning and chores. It is one indivisible native word: do NOT split it into 양 + 동이. The verbs that pair with water-into-bucket are 담다 (put/load in) and 받다 (catch/collect running water): 양동이에 물을 받다. Contrast it with smaller open vessels: a 그릇 is a bowl/dish for food, a 대야 is the wide shallow basin you wash your face or feet in, and a 양동이 is the tall bucket for hauling water. Pitfall: English 'a bucket of X' tempts a 의 ('of'), but Korean simply juxtaposes — 물 한 양동이 (one bucket of water), counting with the noun itself.

Forcing 의 for 'a bucket of water' — Korean stacks the nouns: 물 한 양동이 or 양동이 한가득 (a bucketful), not 물의 양동이.

entries.nuance: 깡통 is a metal can or tin — a food tin, a paint can, an old biscuit tin. The verb to open it is 따다 (to pop/pull open), the very same verb used for opening a bottle or popping a drink can, which is the key collocation to lock in: 깡통을 따다, 병을 따다, 캔을 따다. Here is the register/usage split learners miss: for a beverage can specifically (soda, beer, coffee), Koreans overwhelmingly say the loanword 캔 — 콜라 캔, 맥주 한 캔, 음료수 캔 — and 캔 is also the recycling category, while 깡통 leans toward food/industrial tins and can carry a slightly humble or old-timey flavor (깡통차 = a beat-up old car). So 캔 and 깡통 overlap but aren't identical: order a drink and it's a 캔; describe a dented food tin and it's a 깡통. Count both with 개 or 캔 (콜라 두 캔). Pitfall: opening a can with 열다 sounds off — 열다 is for doors, lids, and books; a sealed can is 따다.

Treating 깡통 and 캔 as fully interchangeable in recycling — the bin/category is the 캔 (cans) section; saying 깡통 분리수거 is understood but 캔 is the standard label.

entries.nuance: 자물쇠 is the physical lock device itself — a padlock or hasp lock — the native-Korean counterpart that forms a matched pair with 열쇠 (key): the 자물쇠 is what you lock, the 열쇠 is what opens it. entries.nuance: 손잡이 is a transparent native compound — 손 (hand) + 잡이 (a holder/gripping part, from 잡다 'to grasp') — literally 'the hand-grab', i.e. any handle, knob, grip, or hold you take hold of: a door handle, a drawer knob, a mug's handle, a kettle grip, the strap/rail you hang onto in a bus or subway. Because it's built from 잡다, the natural partner verb is 잡다 (hold/grab) — 손잡이를 잡다 — and for a turning knob, 돌리다 (turn): 손잡이를 돌리다. It is extremely productive in compounds: 문 손잡이 (door handle), 컵 손잡이 (cup handle), 가방 손잡이 (bag handle), so you rarely need a separate word per object. Two contrasts help: 손잡이 is the grip you hold, whereas 자물쇠/도어록 is the lock mechanism, and 버튼 is a press-button — different parts of the same door. Pitfall: don't reach for 들다 ('lift the whole object') when you only mean grabbing the grip; you 잡다 a 손잡이. Also, the strap you hold standing on the subway is exactly 손잡이, not a borrowed English word.

entries.nuance: 끈 is a one-syllable native word (note the double-consonant ㄲ onset and the ㄴ batchim) covering flexible string, cord, strap, or lace — anything you tie or carry with: shoelaces (신발 끈), bag straps (가방 끈), apron ties (앞치마 끈), a drawstring (끈). It sits in the middle of a thickness scale that learners should sort out: 실 is fine sewing thread, 끈 is a string/cord/strap you bind and fasten with, and 줄 is a thicker line/rope (and 줄 also means a 'line/queue' of people). Its bread-and-butter verbs are 묶다 (tie/bind) and 풀다 (untie/loosen), with 풀리다 as the 'comes undone by itself' intransitive. Useful collocations: 끈을 매다 (tie/do up a lace), 끈을 조이다 (tighten a cord), 끈을 묶다/풀다. Pitfall: English uses 'tie' for shoelaces, but watch the active/passive split — you 끈을 묶다 (you tie it), yet when it loosens on its own you say 끈이 풀렸다 (it came untied), not 끈을 풀었다 (which means you deliberately untied it).

entries.nuance: 바늘 is a native word for a needle — the thin, sharp implement used with 실 (thread) for sewing; 바늘과 실 (needle and thread) is a set phrase, like English. Crucially, 바늘 stretches by metaphor to two other 'needle-shaped' things English keeps separate: the hands of a clock (시계 바늘 — the 긴 바늘 minute hand, 짧은 바늘 hour hand) and a hypodermic needle (주삿바늘), so the one Korean word spans sewing needle, clock hand, and syringe. The verb you must pair correctly is 꿰다 — to pass thread through the eye — 바늘에 실을 꿰다 (thread is threaded into the needle, marked with 에). Because it's sharp, it collocates with 뾰족하다 (pointy) and 찌르다 (prick/stab): 바늘에 찔리다 (get pricked by a needle). Pitfall: don't use 묶다 (tie) for threading — you 꿰다 the thread through; and English 'thread the needle' inverts the Korean direction, where the needle takes the 에 particle (into the needle) and the thread is the object.

entries.nuance: 실 is the native word for thread or yarn — the fine strand used for sewing and knitting, the lifelong partner of 바늘 in the set phrase 바늘과 실. The single most useful fact is its dedicated counter: a strand of thread is counted with 가닥 (실 한 가닥, 두 가닥), the same 가닥 used for a strand of hair (머리카락 한 가닥), so 실 teaches you a counter, not just a word. Sort it firmly from its thicker cousins: 실 is fine thread/yarn, 끈 is a string/cord/strap for tying, and 줄 is a rope or line — a gradient from thinnest to thickest. Natural collocations: 실을 꿰다 (thread it through a needle), 실이 엉키다/풀리다 (the thread tangles/unravels), 실이 끊어지다 (the thread snaps), and the compound 실타래 (a skein of yarn). Two pitfalls: first, don't borrow 끈 for sewing thread — that's too thick. Second, beware the homophone trap — the syllable 실 also appears as a Sino-Korean prefix 實 'real/actual' (실시간 'real-time', 실제 'actual') and as 室 'room' (교실 'classroom'); as a free-standing noun, though, 실 means 'thread'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 끈 (string/strap) where you mean sewing thread — sewing/knitting strand is 실; 끈 is thicker cord for tying.
Counting thread with 개 — a single strand takes 가닥: 실 한 가닥, not 실 한 개.
Confusing the noun 실 (thread) with the bound morphemes 實 'real' (실제, 실시간) or 室 'room' (교실) — those only exist inside other words; alone, 실 = thread.

entries.nuance: 단추 is specifically a clothing button — the disc you fasten on a shirt, blouse, or coat. The verbs are a tidy set worth memorizing together: 채우다 (or 잠그다) to button up, 풀다 to unbutton, and 달다 to sew a button on (with 떨어지다 for one falling off). The contrast that trips up every English speaker is 단추 vs 버튼: English uses 'button' for both clothing fasteners AND press-buttons on machines, but Korean splits them — a button on a remote, elevator, keyboard, or website is 버튼 (loanword), reserved for the press kind, while 단추 is strictly the sew-on clothing kind. So you press the 버튼 on the 엘리베이터 but fasten the 단추 on your 셔츠. (There is also the idiom 첫 단추를 잘못 끼우다 — 'fasten the first button wrong' = get off on the wrong foot, where buttoning is 끼우다.) Pitfall: never say 단추 for a device button (that's 버튼), and don't use 묶다 (tie) to button — buttons are 채우다/잠그다, not tied.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a press-button on a remote, elevator, or app a 단추 — that is 버튼; 단추 is only a clothing fastener.
Buttoning up with 묶다 (tie) — use 채우다 or 잠그다 (단추를 채우다); 풀다 to unbutton.
Saying 단추를 떨어뜨렸어요 when a button simply fell off — for it dropping off by itself use the intransitive 단추가 떨어졌어요; the transitive 떨어뜨리다 means you dropped it.

entries.nuance: 우산 is Sino-Korean 雨傘, literally 雨 'rain' + 傘 'umbrella/parasol' — so the word transparently means 'rain-umbrella', which is your built-in reminder it's for rain. The verb is the deceptively busy 쓰다: to put up/use an umbrella is 우산을 쓰다, the same 쓰다 that covers wearing a hat (모자를 쓰다) and glasses (안경을 쓰다) — Korean groups 'things over your head/face' under 쓰다, distinct from 입다 (clothes on the torso/legs) and 신다 (footwear). The contrast to file away is 우산 vs 양산: both are 傘, but 우산 (雨傘) is the rain umbrella while 양산 (陽傘, 'sun-shade') is a parasol against sunlight — different words for different weather. Useful collocations: 우산을 쓰다/접다/펴다 (put up / fold / open an umbrella), 우산을 챙기다 (remember to grab an umbrella), 우산을 깜빡하다 (forget the umbrella). A folding umbrella is 접는 우산 or 3단 우산, a long one 장우산. Pitfall: English 'wear/carry an umbrella' must become 쓰다 (use over the head), never 입다, and don't reuse 우산 for a sun parasol — that's 양산.

entries.nuance: 정오 is Sino-Korean 正午 ('exact' 正 + 'the horse hour' 午, the old zodiac slot for midday), so it literally pins down 12:00 in the daytime with a crisp, official feel. The everyday spoken equivalent is 낮 12시, which is what friends actually say; 정오 belongs to schedules, broadcasts, train timetables and writing. Do not confuse it with plain 낮, which is the whole bright part of the day, not the single instant — 정오 is one point, 낮 is a span. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the clock reading and tacking on 시: there is no 정오 시. Just say 정오 by itself, or switch to 낮 12시 if you want the casual register. Its mirror-image partner is 자정 (midnight, 12 a.m.).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 정오 시 — 정오 already means 12:00, so adding 시 is redundant; use 정오 alone or 낮 12시.
Confusing 정오 (noon, 12 p.m.) with 자정 (midnight, 12 a.m.) — they share the 正/正 'exact' feel but mark opposite ends of the day.
Using 정오 for the whole afternoon — it is one instant; for the daytime span say 낮.

entries.nuance: 자정 is Sino-Korean 子正 ('the rat hour' 子, the zodiac slot straddling midnight + 'exact' 正), naming the precise instant the date flips from one day to the next. It is the clean single-word counterpart of 정오 (noon); together they form the noon/midnight pair. In casual speech people say 밤 12시, but for cut-offs, deadlines and announcements 자정 is the standard term. entries.nuance: 새벽 is a native Korean word for the dark stretch from roughly 1 a.m. to just before sunrise, the slot that comes after 자정 (midnight) and before 아침 (morning proper, after the sun is up). Contrast it with 아침: 아침 7시 feels like the start of a normal day, whereas 새벽 5시 feels strikingly early or like you never slept. entries.nuance: 한낮 is native Korean: the intensifier 한- ('the very peak of', the same 한 in 한가운데 'dead center') fused with 낮 ('daytime'), so it means the very middle of the day, around noon, when the sun is highest and strongest. entries.nuance: 한밤중 stacks the peak-intensifier 한- onto 밤중 ('the thick of the night'), so it means the deepest, darkest stretch of night around midnight — the exact mirror of 한낮 (high noon). entries.nuance: 올해 is the native Korean word for the present calendar year and slots straight in front of a verb, normally WITHOUT 에: 올해 졸업해요 (I graduate this year), not 올해에. It anchors the three-year set 작년 (last year) – 올해 (this year) – 내년 (next year). There is a Sino-Korean synonym 금년 (今年, 'present year'), but it is stiff and limited to formal writing or speeches; in conversation 올해 is the only natural choice. Two English-speaker pitfalls stand out. First, the 에 habit: because English says 'in this year' learners over-add 에, but native usage drops it after 올해. Second, the look-alike trap with 오늘 ('today') — both start with 오, yet 올해 is a whole year and 오늘 is a single day, so 'I'm twenty this year' is 올해 스무 살이에요, never 오늘.

Adding 에 — 올해 갔어요 is natural, 올해에 갔어요 sounds off; 올해 normally takes no particle before the verb.

Reaching for 금년 in speech — it is formal-written; say 올해 when talking.

entries.nuance: 작년 is Sino-Korean 昨年 ('past/previous' 昨, the same 昨 in 작일 'yesterday' + 'year' 年), so it literally means 'the previous year'. entries.nuance: 하루 is the native Korean word for a single 24-hour day and lives inside several fixed phrases you should memorise as chunks: 하루 종일 (all day long), 하루에 ... 번 (... times a day), and the doubled 하루하루 (day by day, one day at a time). Second, do not let 하루 drift into meaning 'today'; 하루 is 'a day' as a length or an unspecified day ('one day...'), whereas 'today' is the separate word 오늘. So 'I worked all day today' combines both: 오늘 하루 종일 일했어요.

entries.nuance: 며칠 carries two everyday senses decided purely by context: the indefinite 'a few days' (며칠 동안 쉬었어요 = I rested for a few days) and the question 'what date' (오늘 며칠이에요? = what's today's date?). 부터 = starting from that point

entries.nuance: 그때 is the demonstrative 그 ('that', the listener-known one) fused with 때 ('time, occasion'), so it points at a specific moment both speakers can already identify — looking back ('back then') or to a plan just arranged ('see you then'). Write it solid as 그때; the spaced 그 때 is non-standard. Mind the demonstrative trio that mirrors 이/그/저: 이때 = this moment / now in the flow of events, 그때 = that known moment, and the question 언제 = 'when?'. The key English-speaker pitfall is the 'that' default: because English freely says 'that time' for brand-new information, learners reach for 그때 even when the listener has no idea which moment is meant. But 그때 presupposes shared knowledge — if the time is new to your listener you must first establish it (give the date or event), and only then can 그때 refer back to it.

Confusing 그때 (that known time) with 이때 (this/now) or 언제 (when?) — the 이/그/저 logic still applies.

entries.nuance: 나중 is the native noun for a later, unspecified time, and in practice it is almost fused with its particle: you will hear 나중에 ('later, afterward') far more than bare 나중. It is the go-to word for gently postponing things — 나중에 이야기해요 (let's talk later), 나중에 봐요 (see you later). The crucial dividing lines are with two near-synonyms. 이따가 means 'in a little while', but specifically LATER THE SAME DAY, a short wait; 나중에 is open-ended and can be days, months, or a vague someday. 다음에 means 'next time', tied to the next occasion or meeting rather than just elapsed time. So 'see you later today' leans 이따가 봐요, 'see you next time' is 다음에 봐요, and the all-purpose vague 'later' is 나중에 봐요. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the particle (bare 나중 sounds incomplete) and over-using 나중에 for the same-day 'in a bit', where 이따가 is more precise.

Using bare 나중 as an adverb — say 나중에; 나중 almost always needs its 에.
Using 나중에 for 'in a little while (today)' — that short same-day wait is 이따가.
Confusing 나중에 (vague later) with 다음에 (next time/occasion) — time elapsed vs the next meeting.

Like the low numbers, 스물 has a special pre-counter shape: it loses its final ㄹ to become 스무 directly before any counter (스무 살, 스무 개, 스무 명), which is the single biggest trap here. entries.nuance: 아흔 is the native-Korean ninety and the final member of the native tens chain (스물·서른·마흔·쉰·예순·일흔·여든·아흔) — there is NO native word for one hundred, so counting flips to Sino-Korean 백 right after it, a hard stop learners must memorize. entries.shortExplanation: 한 means "one (before a counter)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 한 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the bound pre-counter form of 하나; never used alone
개 is the all-purpose counter for objects
명 is the neutral-polite counter for people
the clock HOUR uses native numbers, so 한 시 not 일 시

examples.en: One cup of coffee, please.
examples.note: 잔 counts cups/glasses; 하나 → 한 before it

examples.en: One person came.
examples.note: 명 is the counter; the number sits as 한, not 하나

examples.en: Let's meet at one o'clock.
examples.note: hours take native numbers, hence 한 시 (minutes would be Sino-Korean)

entries.nuance: 한 is the special bound form of 하나 (one) that appears immediately before a counter (한 개, 한 명, 한 잔, 한 시) — it cannot stand alone the way 하나 can ('얼마예요?'-'하나요', never '한요'). Korean is a classifier language: a number almost always needs a counter, and the moment a counter follows, 하나 contracts to 한, mirroring 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. A subtle point for clocks: the HOUR is native (한 시, 두 시) but the MINUTE is Sino-Korean (일 분, 이 분), so '1:01' is 한 시 일 분 — mixing systems in one phrase. Beyond counting, 한 also means 'about/around' before some words (한 시간쯤, 한 십 분), and appears in 한번 'once', but those senses grow from this same 'one'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '하나 개' before a counter; it must contract to 한 개, 한 명, 한 잔.
Dropping the counter, e.g. '커피 한' — Korean needs '커피 한 잔'.
Using Sino-Korean 일 for the clock hour ('일 시'); the hour is native, so 한 시.

usagePhrases.note: the bound pre-counter form of 둘; not used standalone

examples.en: Two bottles of water, please.
examples.note: 병 counts bottles; 둘 → 두 before it

entries.nuance: 두 is the bound form of 둘 (two) used directly before a counter (두 개, 두 명, 두 병, 두 시). The rule is mechanical: when a counter follows, 둘 always becomes 두 — there is no exception in standard speech — paralleling 하나→한, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. The biggest English-speaker slip is system-mixing on the clock: hours are native (두 시) but minutes are Sino-Korean (이십 분), so '2:20' is 두 시 이십 분. Note also that 둘 is the standalone form ('둘 다' both, '둘이서' the two of us) and you cannot swap them: '두 다' or '둘 개' both sound wrong to a native ear. Practice 두 with high-frequency counters — 개, 명, 잔, 병, 시 — since these dominate ordering and scheduling.

Saying '둘 개', '둘 명' before a counter; the bound form is 두 개, 두 명.
Using Sino-Korean 이 for the clock hour ('이 시') instead of native 두 시.
Writing 'both' as '두 다'; the standalone form is required, so 둘 다.

entries.nuance: 세 is the bound form of 셋 (three) that appears right before a counter (세 개, 세 명, 세 잔, 세 시). Remember 한·두·세·네 as one block, because all four low numbers contract before counters and they saturate everyday speech — ordering food, counting people, telling the hour. Watch the homophone risk: this 세 sounds like 새 'new', 세 (貰) 'rent/lease', and the verb stem 세- 'to count/to be strong', so meaning rides entirely on context and the following counter. As always, 셋 is the standalone form ('셋 다' all three, '셋이서' the three of us); you cannot say '세 다' or '셋 개'. For the clock, hours stay native (세 시) while minutes go Sino-Korean (삼십 분), giving '3:30' = 세 시 삼십 분.

Saying 'all three' as '세 다'; the standalone form is needed, so 셋 다.

스물 → 스무 before 살, the most common use
개 counts objects; never 스물 개

examples.en: I'm twenty.
examples.note: age + 살; 스물 contracts to 스무

examples.note: the counter 개 forces 스무, not 스물 개

entries.nuance: 스무 is the bound, pre-counter shape of 스물 (twenty) — it drops the final ㄹ exactly the way 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네 lose or change their ending before a counter. The headline fact: among the native TENS, 스물 is the sole survivor of this contraction — 서른·마흔·쉰·예순·일흔·여든·아흔 all keep their full shape (서른 살, 마흔 개), so '스무' is special and not a pattern to over-apply. Use it before any counter (스무 살, 스무 개, 스무 명, 스무 시간), but the instant no counter follows you snap back to 스물 ('스물이 넘어요', counting '…열아홉, 스물'). The twin English-speaker errors are forgetting to contract ('스물 살') and over-contracting the higher tens (there is no '서르 살').

entries.explanation: "how many; a few" is 몇 (myeot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 몇 ("how many / a few"). usagePhrases.note: interrogative quantifier; sits in a number's slot before a counter
개 counts objects; 몇 + 개 asks a quantity
명 counts people
literally 'how many o'clock'; the hour uses native counting

examples.en: What time is it now?
examples.note: 몇 시 is the standard way to ask the hour

examples.en: How many people are in your family?
examples.note: 몇 + 명 asks number of people

entries.nuance: 몇 means 'how many' and, grammatically, behaves like a number: it drops straight into the slot before a counter (몇 개, 몇 명, 몇 시, 몇 잔), and since it pairs with the native-number counters, it inherits their world (몇 시 'what time', 몇 살 'how old'). A defining subtlety is that the SAME 몇 also means 'a few / several' when it is not a question — '몇 개 샀어요' can be 'I bought a few' depending on intonation and context. Two boundaries trip English speakers: (1) 몇 almost always needs a counter, so 'how many?' about countable things is 몇 개/몇 명, not bare 몇; (2) don't confuse 몇 시 (what TIME, native + 시) with 며칠 (what DATE/how many days, which behaves on the Sino-Korean date system) — different question, different number family. Compare also 얼마나 'how much/to what extent', which asks degree rather than a countable number.

examples.note: 첫째 opens a list, pairing with 둘째 next

entries.nuance: 첫째 is the native-Korean ordinal 'first', built from 첫 (the bound 'first' form of 하나) + the ordinal suffix -째; the rest of the family runs 둘째, 셋째, 넷째 'second/third/fourth'. It does three jobs: it names the eldest child (저는 첫째예요), it labels the first item in a sequence (첫째 날, 첫째 주 'first week'), and it works like 'firstly/first of all' to organize spoken or written points, almost always followed by 둘째. Don't confuse the ORDINAL system (첫째, 둘째 — order/rank) with the CARDINAL-plus-번/번째 way of listing (일 번, 1번째 'item no. 1'); 첫째 ranks, 일 번 labels. Also note the bound adjective 첫 'first' (첫사랑 first love, 첫날 first day, 첫인상 first impression) — same root, but 첫 attaches to a noun while 첫째 stands as the ordinal itself. A common slip is using the plain number 하나 to mean 'first'; ordering requires 첫째, never 하나.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using plain 하나 to mean 'first'; the ordinal is 첫째 (하나 is just the count 'one').
Mixing the ordinal 첫째 with the Sino-Korean label 일 번/1번 in a list — they aren't interchangeable.
Saying '첫 아이' and '첫째 아이' as if identical; both occur, but for birth-order 'the eldest' the noun is 첫째.
