entries.shortExplanation: 농담 means "joke" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 농담 (nongdam) = "joke". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 농담을 하다 ("to make a joke, to kid") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 농담, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to make a joke, to kid
usagePhrases.note: 농담 is a noun; 'to joke' = 농담하다 / 농담을 하다
set phrase to defuse a remark and show you didn't mean it
-(으)로 marks manner: 'in a joking way,' often 농담으로 한 말 'something said in jest'
fixed idiom for a remark that's partly a real hint

examples.en: I'm joking, don't be upset.
examples.note: tacking on 농담이에요 instantly softens what you just said

examples.en: He took the joke as if I meant it seriously.
examples.note: 진담 = serious talk; the pair 농담 vs 진담 is the key contrast

examples.ko: 농담 반 진담 반으로 같이 가자고 했어요.
examples.romanization: nongdam ban jindam baneuro gachi gajago haesseoyo.
examples.en: Half joking, half serious, I suggested we go together.
examples.note: 농담 반 진담 반 hints the speaker partly means it

entries.nuance: 농담(弄談) is Sino-Korean — 弄 'to play with, tease' + 談 'talk' — literally 'playful talk,' i.e. a joke meant to amuse, not to wound. Its built-in opposite is 진담(眞談) 'earnest/serious talk' (眞 'true' + 談 'talk'), and Koreans lean on the pair constantly: 농담이야, 진담이야? 'Are you kidding or serious?' Distinguish it from 거짓말 'a lie': a 농담 is openly non-serious fun that listeners are meant to recognize, while a 거짓말 is meant to deceive. Also separate it from 장난 'a prank/mischief (often an action),' versus 농담 which is verbal wit. Natural collocations: 농담을 하다, 농담으로 한 말, 농담이 심하다 'the joke goes too far,' 농담 반 진담 반. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 농담 as a verb on its own — say 농담하다; and 'You're joking!' as an exclamation is usually 거짓말! or 진짜?, not 농담!, since 농담이에요 is what YOU say about YOUR OWN remark to signal you weren't serious.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying bare 농담 for 'to joke' — use 농담을 하다 / 농담하다.
Confusing 농담 (harmless joke meant to be seen through) with 거짓말 (a lie meant to deceive).
Mixing up 농담 (verbal wit) with 장난 (a prank or physical mischief) — 장난치다 is 'to mess around,' not 'to joke.'

entries.shortExplanation: 연락 means "contact, getting in touch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연락 (yeollak) means "contact, getting in touch". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 연락을 하다 ("to contact, to get in touch"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to contact, to get in touch
usagePhrases.note: 연락 is a noun; 'to contact' = 연락하다 / 연락을 하다

usagePhrases.en: to hear from someone (lit. contact comes)
usagePhrases.note: 오다, not 을 오다 — the contact is the subject that 'comes to' you: 연락이 오다
되다 here = 'manages to connect'; 연락이 안 돼요 = 'I can't reach them'
연락 + 처(處) 'place/point' → the point at which to reach you = phone/contact info

examples.en: I'll get in touch later.
examples.note: -ㄹ게요 = a casual promise about your own action

examples.en: I heard from my friend.
examples.note: 한테서 = 'from (a person)'; 연락이 오다 takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: I can't reach them by call or text.
examples.note: 연락이 되다/안 되다 = to (not) get through; note 도…도 'neither…nor'

entries.nuance: 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean — 連 'connect/link' + 絡 'tie, network' — literally 'to link up,' and it covers ANY channel of reaching a person: a call, a text, a message, an email. The near-synonym to contrast is 소식: 연락 is the ACT/CHANNEL of getting in touch ('drop me a line'), while 소식 is the CONTENT/word about how someone is. Compare 통화(通話) 'a phone call (specifically)' — narrower than 연락. The crucial grammar quirk for English speakers: 연락 flips between particles. When YOU reach out it's 연락을 하다 / 연락하다 (object 를), but when contact COMES to you it's 연락이 오다 and reachability is 연락이 되다 (subject 이/가) — saying 연락을 오다 is a classic error. Also, English 'contact someone' has a direct object, so learners drop the person-marking 한테/에게: it should be 친구한테 연락하다, and incoming contact is 친구한테서/에게서 연락이 오다. 연락처 (with 처) means your number/details, not the verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 연락을 오다 for incoming contact — it must be 연락이 오다 (이/가), since the contact is what 'comes.'
Dropping the person particle: 'contact me' is 저한테 연락하세요, not 저를 연락하세요.
Confusing 연락 (the act of getting in touch) with 소식 (the news/word itself) — 연락이 없다 = 'they haven't reached out'; 소식이 없다 = 'no word on how they are.'

entries.shortExplanation: 부탁 means "favor, request" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "favor, request" is 부탁 (butak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 부탁을 하다 ("to ask a favor"). Watch the particle attached to 부탁 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 부탁 is a noun; 'to make a request' = 부탁하다 / 부탁을 하다

usagePhrases.en: I have a favor to ask
usagePhrases.note: softly opens a request; 있다 marks 'there is a favor (on my side)'

usagePhrases.en: I look forward to working with you (lit. I kindly entrust this)
usagePhrases.note: humble 드리다 form; the standard polite phrase at introductions/handovers
들어주다 = to grant/heed a request; 좀 softens it

examples.en: I have one favor to ask.
examples.note: 하나 'one' makes the ask feel small and polite

examples.en: Could you take care of this for me?
examples.note: 좀 softens; 부탁해요 here = 'I'm entrusting this to you'

examples.en: I look forward to working with you from now on.
examples.note: the go-to humble greeting when joining a team or starting a project

entries.nuance: 부탁(付託) is Sino-Korean — 付 'hand over/entrust' + 託 'commit, consign' — literally 'to entrust (a matter) to someone,' i.e. to ask a favor. The near-synonym to separate is 요청(要請) 'a (formal) request/demand': 요청 is businesslike and official (a 요청서 is a request form, 협조를 요청하다 'request cooperation'), whereas 부탁 is personal and softens the asker into the lower, indebted position. Compare 부탁 with 명령 'an order/command,' its opposite in power. Register is the heart of this word: among equals 부탁해요, but upward or formally you switch to the humble verb 드리다 → 부탁드립니다 / 잘 부탁드립니다, a set phrase at introductions, handovers, and emails meaning roughly 'please look kindly on me/this.' Collocations: 부탁을 들어주다 'grant a favor,' 부탁을 거절하다 'refuse,' 어려운 부탁. The English-speaker pitfall: 'ask someone a favor' makes learners say 누구를 부탁하다, but the person takes 한테/에게 (친구한테 부탁하다), and bare 부탁 can't be the verb — you need 부탁하다 or the humble 부탁드리다 in polite settings.

Using bare 부탁 as a verb; 'to request' is 부탁을 하다 / 부탁하다 (humble: 부탁드리다).
Saying 잘 부탁해요 to a superior or in formal writing — the expected humble form is 잘 부탁드립니다.
Confusing 부탁 (a personal favor) with 요청 (a formal/official request) — you 요청하다 cooperation from an institution, but 부탁하다 a friend.

entries.shortExplanation: 편지 means "letter" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 편지 (pyeonji) = "letter". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 편지를 쓰다 ("to write a letter") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 편지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: always 쓰다 (write), never 만들다 (make); you 'write,' not 'make,' a letter
보내다 = to send; its pair is 받다 'to receive'
부치다 specifically = drop in the mail; narrower than 보내다
손 'hand' + 편지; carries a warm, heartfelt nuance vs typed mail

examples.en: I write a letter to my mom.
examples.note: 한테 = 'to (a person)'; the recipient takes 한테/에게

examples.en: I received a handwritten letter from my friend.
examples.note: 한테서 = 'from'; 손편지 stresses it was warmly handwritten

examples.en: I mailed the letter at the post office.
examples.note: 부치다 (post) is more precise than 보내다 for physical mail

entries.nuance: 편지(便紙/片紙) is Sino-Korean — commonly written 便紙, with 紙 'paper' — denoting a paper letter you write by hand and send by post. The contrast to draw is with newer media words: 이메일 (email), 문자 (a text message), 메시지/카톡 (an instant message). 편지 specifically evokes paper and ink, so a 손편지 (handwritten letter) feels especially sincere and personal in Korean culture. Note the verbs differ from English instincts: you 쓰다 (write) a letter, 보내다/부치다 (send/post) it, and 받다 (receive) it — and 부치다 is the precise 'put in the mail.' Collocations: 편지를 쓰다/보내다/받다, 답장 'a reply.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'make a card/letter' tempts 편지를 만들다, but a letter is written (쓰다), not made; and don't let 편지 blur into 편의점 (convenience store) — they merely look alike. Recipients are marked with 한테/에게 (또는 honorific 께), senders with 한테서/에게서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 편지를 만들다 ('make a letter') — a letter is written: 편지를 쓰다.
Confusing 편지 (a paper letter) with 이메일/문자 — for email say 이메일, for a text say 문자.
Mis-marking people: write 'to' someone with 한테/에게/께 (엄마한테 편지를 쓰다), and 'from' with 한테서/에게서.

entries.shortExplanation: 답장 means "reply (to a letter or message)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 답장 (dapjang) means "reply (to a letter or message)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 답장을 하다 ("to write back, to reply"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 답장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 답장 is a noun; 'to reply (in writing)' = 답장하다 / 답장을 하다
보내다 = to send; you send a written 답장 back
the standard way to say someone hasn't written back
기다리다 = to wait; common at the end of emails/letters

examples.en: I replied to the text.
examples.note: 에 marks the message you reply 'to'; 답장하다 acts as one verb

examples.en: Please send a reply soon.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 = 'please do (for me)'; 빨리 = quickly

examples.en: I sent an email but there's still no reply.
examples.note: 답장이 없다 = haven't heard back; 아직 = 'still, yet'

entries.nuance: 답장(答狀) is Sino-Korean — 答 'to answer' + 狀 'a written document/letter' — literally 'an answering document,' i.e. a written reply to a letter, text, or email. The sharp contrast every learner needs is with 대답(對答) 'a (spoken) answer/response': you give a 대답 out loud to a question someone asks face-to-face, but you write a 답장 back to a message. A third neighbor is 회신(回信) 'a reply,' the stiff, formal/business word used in official correspondence. So a casual text-back is 답장, answering a teacher's spoken question is 대답, and a corporate email response is often 회신. Collocations: 답장을 하다/보내다/받다, 답장이 늦다 'reply is late,' 답장이 없다. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'answer/reply' is one word, so learners use 대답 for everything — but if it's written, it's 답장; and bare 답장 isn't a verb, so 'to reply' must be 답장하다 / 답장을 하다. The thing you reply to is marked with 에 (문자에 답장하다).

Saying bare 답장 for 'to reply' — use 답장하다 / 답장을 하다.
Mis-marking the target: you reply 'to' a message with 에 (문자에/이메일에 답장하다), not 를.

entries.shortExplanation: 단어 means "word (vocabulary)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "word (vocabulary)" is 단어 (daneo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 단어를 외우다 ("to memorize a word"). Watch the particle attached to 단어 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 외우다 = to memorize by heart; the core study collocation
뜻 = meaning; 단어의 뜻이 뭐예요? 'what does the word mean?'
찾다 = to search/find; 사전에서 단어를 찾다 'look it up in a dictionary'
단어 with the pre-noun 새 'new'; 단어가 새롭다 would put it after

examples.en: I learn new words today.
examples.note: 배우다 → 배워요 (요-form); 새 'new' sits right before the noun

examples.en: What does this word mean?
examples.note: 뜻 'meaning' + 뭐예요? 'what is it?' is the natural way to ask

examples.en: I look up words I don't know in a dictionary.
examples.note: 모르는 단어 = words one doesn't know; 사전에서 찾다 = look up in a dictionary

entries.nuance: 단어(單語) is Sino-Korean — 單 'single' + 語 'word/language' — literally 'a single word,' the discrete vocabulary item you study, memorize, and look up. Contrast it with 말 'words/speech/language' in the broad native sense (말이 빠르다 'speaks fast,' 한국말 'Korean'), and with 어휘(語彙) 'vocabulary' as a whole body of words (어휘가 풍부하다 'has a rich vocabulary'). So one item = 단어, the total stock = 어휘, speech in general = 말. The verbs are telling: you 외우다 (memorize) and 찾다 (look up) a 단어, and ask its 뜻 (meaning). Collocations: 새 단어, 단어를 외우다/찾다, 단어 시험 'vocab quiz,' 단어장 'wordbook.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'word' also means 'news/a message' ('send word,' 'have a word'), but those senses are NOT 단어 — 'word from someone' is 소식, and 'have a word/talk' is 이야기/말; 단어 is strictly the linguistic unit you study. Also keep it apart from look-alikes like 단원 'a unit/chapter.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 단어 for the English 'word' meaning 'news/message' — that is 소식 (word from someone) or 이야기 (a word/talk), not 단어.
Confusing 단어 (one vocabulary item) with 어휘 (one's whole vocabulary) — 어휘가 많다, not 단어가 많다, for 'has a large vocabulary.'
Mixing up 말 (speech/language broadly) and 단어 (a single lexical item): 'Korean (the language)' is 한국말/한국어, never 한국단어.

단어(單語) is Sino-Korean — 單 'single' + 語 'word/language' — literally 'a single word.'

English 'word' also means 'news/a message' ('send word,' 'have a word'), but those senses are NOT 단어 — 'word from someone' is 소식, and 'have a word/talk' is 이야기/말; 단어 is strictly the linguistic unit you study.

entries.shortExplanation: 발음 means "pronunciation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 발음 (bareum) = "pronunciation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 발음이 좋다 ("to have good pronunciation") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 발음, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the quality takes 이/가: 발음이 좋다, NOT 발음을 좋다
연습하다 takes the object 을/를; here you act on 발음
어렵다 is an adjective describing 발음, so again 이/가

usagePhrases.en: to pronounce accurately (lit. pronunciation is exact)
usagePhrases.note: 정확하다 = precise/accurate; a common compliment for learners

examples.en: Your pronunciation is really good.
examples.note: 발음이 좋다 with 이 — the pronunciation is the subject being good

examples.en: This word is hard to pronounce.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular 어렵다 → 어려워요; 발음이 어렵다 keeps 이/가

examples.en: I practice the final-consonant sounds every day.
examples.note: 받침 = a syllable-final consonant; 발음을 연습하다 takes 을 because you act on it

entries.nuance: 발음(發音) is Sino-Korean — 發 'to emit/produce' + 音 'sound' — literally 'to produce sound,' i.e. pronunciation, how a word is sounded out. Distinguish it from 억양(抑揚) 'intonation' (the rise and fall of pitch across a sentence) and 발성 'voice production/projection' — 발음 is specifically the articulation of individual sounds and syllables. As a noun it becomes a verb with 하다: 발음하다 'to pronounce.' Collocations: 발음이 좋다/나쁘다/어렵다/정확하다, 발음을 연습하다, 발음 연습 'pronunciation drill,' 받침 발음 'final-consonant pronunciation.' The headline English-speaker pitfall is PARTICLES: 발음 is the SUBJECT of descriptive adjectives, so it's 발음이 좋다/어렵다 (이/가), but the OBJECT of action verbs, so 발음을 연습하다/하다 (을/를). Saying 발음을 좋다 is ungrammatical because 좋다 'to be good' is a stative adjective that can't take a direct object. Also, English 'pronounce' as a verb tempts bare 발음 — you must say 발음하다.

Using bare 발음 for the verb 'pronounce' — say 발음하다 (e.g. 이 글자를 어떻게 발음해요?).
Confusing 발음 (articulation of sounds) with 억양 (sentence intonation) — flat or sing-song pitch is 억양, not 발음.

entries.shortExplanation: 칭찬 means "praise, compliment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 칭찬 (chingchan) means "praise, compliment". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 칭찬을 하다 ("to praise, to compliment"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 칭찬 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 칭찬 is a noun; 'to praise' = 칭찬하다 / 칭찬을 하다; the person praised takes 을/를

usagePhrases.en: to be praised, to receive praise
usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) is the natural passive-sense pair: 칭찬을 받다, not 가지다

usagePhrases.en: to get a compliment (lit. hear praise)
usagePhrases.note: 듣다 = to hear; praise reaches your ears, so 칭찬을 듣다

usagePhrases.en: to be a sucker for praise (lit. weak to praise)
usagePhrases.note: -에 약하다 = to have a soft spot for; idiomatic

examples.en: The teacher praised me.
examples.note: the praised person takes 를; -아/어 주시다 adds warmth + honors the teacher

examples.en: Getting a compliment makes me feel good.
examples.note: -(으)니까 'because'; 칭찬을 듣다 = to hear/receive praise

examples.en: That person is stingy with praise.
examples.note: 칭찬에 인색하다 = sparing with compliments; -에 marks what they're stingy about

entries.nuance: 칭찬(稱讚) is Sino-Korean — 稱 'to call/state' + 讚 'to praise, extol' — literally 'to speak praise,' i.e. to compliment someone's good action or quality. Its clear opposite pair is 비난(非難) 'criticism/blame' (and the everyday 야단/꾸중 'a scolding'), so the axis is praise ↔ blame. Don't confuse 칭찬 with 자랑 'bragging/showing off,' which is praising ONESELF or one's own things, not another person. Collocations: 칭찬을 하다/받다/듣다, 칭찬을 아끼지 않다 'not spare praise,' 칭찬에 인색하다 'stingy with praise,' the proverb 칭찬은 고래도 춤추게 한다 'praise makes even a whale dance.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'give a compliment' tempts 칭찬을 주다, but Korean RECEIVES praise — 칭찬을 받다/듣다 — so 'I got a compliment' is 칭찬을 받았어요/들었어요, never 칭찬을 가졌어요. Also bare 칭찬 isn't a verb; 'to compliment her' is 그녀를 칭찬하다, marking the person with 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 칭찬을 가지다/주다 for 'get/give a compliment' — Korean uses 칭찬을 받다 / 듣다 (receive/hear).
Using bare 칭찬 as a verb; 'to praise someone' is 누구를 칭찬하다 (person marked with 을/를).
Confusing 칭찬 (praising another) with 자랑 (boasting about oneself) — 자기 자랑 is bragging, not 칭찬.

entries.shortExplanation: 설명 means "explanation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "explanation" is 설명 (seolmyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 설명을 하다 ("to explain, to give an explanation"). Watch the particle attached to 설명 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to explain, to give an explanation
usagePhrases.note: 설명 is a noun; 'to explain' = 설명하다 / 설명을 하다
-아/어 주세요 frames it as a favor; the polite way to ask for an explanation
자세한 'detailed' before the noun; 설명이 자세하다 puts it after
덧붙이다 = to append/add on; common in writing or talks

examples.en: Teacher, please explain it.
examples.note: 설명하다 + 주세요 = 'please explain (for me)'; softens the request

examples.en: Could you explain it one more time?
examples.note: -아/어 주시겠어요? is extra-polite; 한 번 더 = once more

examples.en: This part is a bit short on explanation.
examples.note: 설명이 부족하다 = the explanation is lacking; here 설명 is the subject (이/가)

entries.nuance: 설명(說明) is Sino-Korean — 說 'to tell/speak' + 明 'clear, bright' — literally 'to make clear by telling,' i.e. an explanation of how or why something works. Distinguish it from 설득(說得) 'persuasion' (talking someone INTO agreeing, sharing the 說 root) and from 묘사(描寫) 'description' (depicting what something looks/feels like); 설명 is about clarifying and informing, not convincing or portraying. As a noun it becomes the verb with 하다: 설명하다, very often softened to 설명해 주세요/주시겠어요 'please explain for me.' Collocations: 설명을 하다/듣다, 자세한 설명, 설명이 부족하다/이해가 안 되다, 설명서 'instruction manual.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'explain to me' tempts learners to mark the listener with 를 (저를 설명하다 ✗, which would mean 'explain ME'); the listener takes 한테/에게 (저한테 설명해 주세요), and what you explain takes 을/를. Bare 설명 can't be the verb — use 설명하다. Don't confuse 설명 with the look-alike 설탕 'sugar.'

Marking the listener with 를: 'explain to me' is 저한테 설명해 주세요, not 저를 설명하다 (that means 'explain me').
Using bare 설명 for 'to explain' — say 설명하다 / 설명을 하다.
Confusing 설명 (clarifying/informing) with 설득 (persuading someone) — convincing a person is 설득하다, not 설명하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 안부 means "regards, well-wishes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 안부 (anbu) = "regards, well-wishes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 안부를 전하다 ("to send/pass on one's regards") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 안부, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 전하다 (convey) relays your regards to a third person, often via someone else

usagePhrases.en: to ask after someone (how they're doing)
usagePhrases.note: 묻다 (ask) — ㄷ-irregular: 물어요, 물었어요; you inquire about their well-being
안부 + 인사 'greeting'; the set phrase for asking/sending how-are-yous
to a superior, 묻다 becomes humble 여쭙다: 부모님께 안부를 여쭙다

examples.en: Please give my regards to your parents.
examples.note: 께 = honorific 'to'; 전하다 passes your greeting along to them

examples.en: Meeting after a long time, we asked after each other.
examples.note: 서로 = each other; 안부를 묻다 (ㄷ-irregular 물었어요)

examples.en: Please pass along my regards to the teacher.
examples.note: 여쭙다 = humble 'ask/convey'; used when the person is of higher status

entries.nuance: 안부(安否) is Sino-Korean — 安 'safe, well' + 否 'or not' — literally 'whether (one is) well or not,' i.e. an inquiry into someone's welfare, hence 'regards, well-wishes.' It is not a standalone greeting word like 인사 'a greeting' but the CONTENT of caring after someone, so it lives almost entirely inside two collocations: 안부를 묻다 'ask how someone is' and 안부를 전하다 'send/pass on regards (to a third party).' Contrast 안부 (asking after well-being, often about an absent person) with 인사 (the act/words of greeting someone present) and with 연락 (the channel of contact) — you might 연락해서 안부를 묻다 'get in touch to ask how they are.' Register matters: to elders the verbs go humble — 안부를 여쭙다 (for 묻다) and 안부를 전해 드리다. The English-speaker pitfall: don't attach plain 하다 — there is no natural 안부하다; you must pick 전하다 or 묻다. Also, 안부를 전하다 means relaying regards TO someone else, while asking the person directly is 안부를 묻다 — mixing these reverses who the well-wishing is aimed at.

Saying 안부하다 — there's no such verb; use 안부를 전하다 (send regards) or 안부를 묻다 (ask after someone).
Swapping the two collocations: 안부를 전하다 relays regards to a third party, but to ask the person in front of you it's 안부를 묻다.
Forgetting honorifics with elders — 묻다 becomes 여쭙다 and 전하다 becomes 전해 드리다: 부모님께 안부 여쭤/전해 주세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 월요일 means "Monday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 월요일 (woryoil) means "Monday". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 월요일에 ("on Monday"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 월요일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Time particle 에 marks the day an event happens; this is the form you reach for most.
부터 marks the starting point of a stretch of time (vs 까지 for the end).
Korean prefers 다음 주 월요일 (next week's Monday); bare 다음 월요일 sounds incomplete.
The day comes first, then the time-of-day word: 월요일 아침, 월요일 저녁.

examples.en: Today is Monday.
examples.note: 이에요 simply states what day it is; 오늘 (today) needs no 에.

examples.en: I go to school on Monday.
examples.note: Both 월요일 (when) and 학교 (where) take 에 — 에 covers time and destination.

examples.en: It looks like I'll get busy again from Monday.
examples.note: Real-life grumble: 부터 sets the day the busy stretch starts.

entries.nuance: 월요일 is the start of the Korean work and school week, just as in English, and it carries the same slightly heavy 'back to the grind' feeling captured in 월요병 ('Monday sickness,' the Monday blues). It is Sino-Korean: 月 (moon/month) + 曜 (the celestial-body element shared by all weekday names) + 日 (day) — the seven days are literally named after the moon, fire, water, wood, metal, earth, and sun. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is the preposition: English 'on Monday' makes you want a word, but Korean glues the time particle 에 to the noun (월요일에), and dropping it (월요일 가요) sounds broken. Note also that days are NOT capitalized concepts in Korean and never take a plural — '월요일은' with topic 은 is how you say 'Mondays (as a rule)'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '월요일 가요' without the particle. A specific day of the week needs the time marker, so it must be 월요일에 가요.
Writing it as two words '월 요일'. It is one fused noun, 월요일, with no space.
Saying '다음 월요일' for 'next Monday'. Koreans normally say 다음 주 월요일 (next week's Monday).

entries.shortExplanation: 화요일 means "Tuesday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "Tuesday" is 화요일 (hwayoil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 화요일에 ("on Tuesday"). Watch the particle attached to 화요일 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Attach 에 to state the day something is scheduled.
까지 marks an end point or deadline (the partner of 부터).
Pair the day with 지난주 to point back into the past week.
매주 ('every week') + the day expresses a weekly routine.

examples.en: Tomorrow is Tuesday.
examples.note: 이에요 states the day; 내일 (tomorrow) takes no 에.

examples.en: I have plans on Tuesday.
examples.note: 약속 here means a set appointment with someone, very common with days.

examples.en: I have Korean class every Tuesday.
examples.note: 마다 ('each') stacks with 매주 화요일 to stress a recurring slot.

entries.nuance: 화요일 is the second day of the week, the day after 월요일. The 화 is Sino-Korean 火 'fire' (the same 화 in 화산 'volcano' and 화재 'fire/blaze'), following the East Asian seven-luminaries naming system; you don't need the hanja to use the word, but knowing it helps you keep the order straight. As with every weekday, English speakers tend to omit the particle; 'on Tuesday' must become 화요일에, and 'until Tuesday' is 화요일까지, not a separate preposition word.

Dropping the particle: it should be 화요일에 와요, not 화요일 와요.
Saying '화요일에까지'. Stack only one particle — for a deadline it is just 화요일까지.

Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the day of the event — the default form.
Day first, then 오후 (afternoon); good for pinning down a meeting time.
이번 주 + the day specifies which Wednesday you mean.
쯤 ('about') softens it to an approximate day.

examples.en: Is today Wednesday?
examples.note: 이에요? turns it into a question; subject 이 (오늘이) checks the fact.

examples.en: Do you have time on Wednesday?
examples.note: A natural way to propose meeting; 시간 있어요? = 'are you free?'

examples.en: I'll get in touch again around Wednesday.
examples.note: 쯤 + 에 keeps the day vague; 연락할게요 promises future action.

entries.nuance: 수요일 sits in the middle of the work week, between 화요일 and 목요일, so it often feels like the 'hump' or halfway mark of a busy week. Mixing up 수요일 (Wed) and 목요일 (Thu). The fixed order is 수 (water) before 목 (wood).
Saying '수요일이 있어요' to mean 'on Wednesday'. The time marker is 에, so it is 수요일에 있어요.
Treating 수요일 as a verb-like word; it is a plain noun, so events attach with 에, not by conjugating the day.

Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

Day + 저녁; 저녁 covers both 'evening' and the evening meal.
Use 다음 주 목요일 rather than bare 다음 목요일.
까지 sets Thursday as the deadline.

examples.en: The day after tomorrow is Thursday.
examples.note: 모레가 ... 이에요 identifies the day; no 에 on 모레.

examples.en: I'm meeting a friend on Thursday.
examples.note: 만나다 takes the object marker 를 (친구를) — you meet a person, not 'with' one here.

examples.en: I have to finish the report by Thursday.
examples.note: Workplace reality: 까지 = the hard deadline, 해야 해요 = obligation.

entries.nuance: 목요일 is the fourth day of the week, right before 금요일, and people often start eyeing the weekend from here (the cheerful '불목' — 'fire Thursday,' a night out — plays on this). Forgetting the particle: it is 목요일에 만나요, not 목요일 만나요.

entries.shortExplanation: 금요일 means "Friday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "Friday" is 금요일 (geumyoil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 금요일에 ("on Friday"). Watch the particle attached to 금요일 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks when; the most common form.
Day + 밤; 금요일 밤 is the prime time for going out.
이번 주 + the day pins down which Friday.
Slang clipping of 불타는 금요일 ('burning Friday'); casual speech only.

examples.en: Today is Friday.
examples.note: 이에요 states the day; the topic 은 frames 오늘.

examples.en: I'm watching a movie on Friday.
examples.note: 보다 here means 'watch'; 영화를 보다 is the set collocation for seeing a film.

examples.en: Finally Friday! Today's a wild Friday.
examples.note: 드디어 ('finally') + ~네요 (realization) capture the relief; 불금 is friendly slang.

entries.nuance: 금요일 is the last workday before the weekend, so it carries a light, celebratory mood — Koreans cheer 불금 (from 불타는 금요일, 'burning Friday') the way English says TGIF, but keep that slang for friends, not your boss. The 금 is Sino-Korean 金 'metal/gold' (the same 금 in 금메달 'gold medal' and 황금 'gold'), continuing the fixed weekday order. The recurring English-speaker mistake stays the same: 'on Friday' is 금요일에, never a bare 금요일 before the verb, and 'this Friday' is more naturally 이번 주 금요일 than 이번 금요일.

Using 불금 in formal or work settings. It is casual slang; in polite contexts just say 금요일.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 토요일, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks when something happens.
Day + 아침; 아침 also means breakfast, so context decides.
이번 주 + the day to specify which Saturday.
하고 ('and') links the two weekend days in speech.

examples.en: Tomorrow is Saturday.
examples.note: 이에요 states the day; 내일 needs no 에.

examples.en: I rest at home on Saturday.
examples.note: Place uses 에서 (집에서) for an action's location, while the day uses 에.

examples.en: On Saturdays I usually sleep in.
examples.note: Topic 은 = 'as for Saturdays'; 늦잠을 자다 is the set phrase for sleeping late.

entries.nuance: 토요일 is the first day of the Korean weekend (주말 = Saturday + Sunday), so most people are off work or school and it reads as a relaxed, do-something day. The 토 is Sino-Korean 土 'earth/soil' (the same 토 in 토지 'land' and 영토 'territory'), the sixth of the seven luminaries. A subtle trap here is that the DAY of an action takes 에 (토요일에) but the PLACE of the action takes 에서 (집에서 쉬어요) — English 'at home on Saturday' uses one preposition each, but Korean splits time vs. dynamic location across two particles. Beginners also mix 토요일 (Sat) with 일요일 (Sun); fix it as 토 (earth) before 일 (sun).

Mixing up 토요일 (Sat) and 일요일 (Sun). The order is 토 (earth) before 일 (sun).
Dropping the particle: it should be 토요일에 쉬어요, not 토요일 쉬어요.
Using 에 for the place of an action: rest happens 집에서, not 집에 — 'rest at home' is 집에서 쉬어요.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 일요일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks when something happens.
오전 (a.m./forenoon) is the clock-based partner of 오후 (p.m.).
이번 주 + the day to make clear which Sunday.
마다 ('each') turns the day into a weekly habit.

examples.en: Is today Sunday?
examples.note: 이에요? asks; subject 이 (오늘이) checks the fact of the day.

examples.en: I go to church on Sunday.
examples.note: 교회 takes 에 as a destination — same particle as the day, different role.

examples.en: I spend time with my family every Sunday.
examples.note: 가족하고 = 'with family'; 시간을 보내다 is the set phrase 'spend time.'

entries.nuance: 일요일 is the last day of the weekend, a rest-and-recharge day before the new week, and on most Korean calendars it sits in the first column printed in red as a public holiday. The 일 is Sino-Korean 日 'sun/day' (the same 日 that ends every weekday name and appears in 일기 'diary'), so 일요일 literally reads 'sun-day' — a neat parallel to English. Don't confuse the standalone word 요일, which only means 'day of the week' (used in the question 무슨 요일이에요? 'what day is it?'), with 일요일 'Sunday'. As always for English speakers, 'on Sunday' is 일요일에, and 'spend time WITH family' is 가족하고/가족과 시간을 보내요, where 하고 carries the 'with.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 일요일 (Sunday) with the bare word 요일, which just means 'day of the week.'
Saying '일요일 가요' without the particle. Use 일요일에 가요.
Forgetting the 'with' particle: it is 가족하고 시간을 보내요, not 가족 시간을 보내요.

entries.shortExplanation: 공휴일 means "public holiday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "public holiday" is 공휴일 (gonghyuil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공휴일에 ("on a public holiday"). Watch the particle attached to 공휴일 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the day off when something happens (or doesn't).
이라서 ('because it is') gives the reason offices are closed.
법정 ('legally fixed') stresses it is an official, mandated day off.
대체 ('replacement') — a make-up day off when a holiday falls on a weekend.

examples.en: Tomorrow is a public holiday.
examples.note: 이에요 states the fact; 내일 needs no 에.

examples.en: On public holidays, banks are closed.
examples.note: 에는 = 에 + 는, adding a 'as for that day' contrast; 문을 닫다 = 'close (shop).'

examples.en: Today is a holiday, so I don't go to school.
examples.note: 이라서 links cause to result; 안 가요 negates the verb.

entries.nuance: 공휴일 is an official, calendar-fixed day off when offices, banks, schools, and public services close for everyone at once — think 설날 (Lunar New Year) or 추석 (Chuseok). It is fully Sino-Korean: 公 'public' + 休 'rest' + 日 'day,' literally 'public rest day.' The key contrast for learners is 공휴일 vs. 휴가: 휴가 (休暇) is YOUR personal leave/vacation that you request and take individually, whereas 공휴일 is a national day off no one schedules. Also distinguish 휴일 (any non-work day, including weekends) from 공휴일 (specifically an official public holiday). The usual English-speaker pitfall returns with the particle — 'on a holiday' is 공휴일에 (often 공휴일에는 for contrast), and 'closed' is the idiom 문을 닫다, not a literal translation of 'be closed.'

Confusing 공휴일 (official national holiday) with 휴가 (your personal vacation/leave). You take 휴가; everyone shares a 공휴일.
Saying '공휴일 닫아요' without the particle. Use 공휴일에 닫아요 (or 공휴일에는).
Translating 'is closed' word for word. Korean says 문을 닫아요 ('closes its door'), not a passive 'be closed.'

entries.shortExplanation: 이번 주 means "this week" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에 to mark the time frame of an event.
이번 + 주말 (weekend); note 주말 is one word.
이번 주 + a specific day narrows it down.

usagePhrases.en: all this week / the whole week
usagePhrases.note: 내내 ('throughout') stresses the entire span.

examples.en: I have an exam this week.
examples.note: 이번 주 + 에 sets the time; 시험이 있다 = 'there is an exam.'

examples.en: This week is so busy.
examples.note: Topic 는 frames the week; 바쁘다 is a descriptive verb (adjective), so no object.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 시간 괜찮으면 같이 밥 먹어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon jumare sigan gwaenchaneumyeon gachi bam meogeoyo.
examples.en: If you're free this weekend, let's eat together.
examples.note: 이번 주말에 + a soft invitation; 밥 먹다 ('eat a meal') doubles as 'grab food.'

entries.nuance: 이번 주 means the week we are currently in, the now-frame for plans and schedules. 이번 is native-Korean-style 'this (time/occasion)' and 주 is Sino-Korean 週 'week,' so the phrase is a hybrid 'this week.' It belongs to a tidy set: 지난주 (last week), 이번 주 (this week), 다음 주 (next week). The spacing trips up nearly every learner: 이번 주 and 다음 주 are written as TWO words (a space before 주), but 지난주 is fused into ONE word — a real inconsistency you simply memorize. As with all time nouns, 'this week' as a when-phrase takes 에 (이번 주에), and note that 바쁘다 ('busy') is an adjective-type verb, so you say 이번 주는 바빠요, never add an object to it.

Writing 이번주 as one word. The standard spelling is 이번 주 with a space before 주.
Forgetting the particle: say 이번 주에 있어요, not 이번 주 있어요.
Mismatching the set: 지난주 is one word but 이번 주 / 다음 주 take a space — don't apply one rule to all three.

entries.shortExplanation: 다음 주 means "next week" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다음 주 (daeum ju) means "next week". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다음 주에 ("next week"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다음 주 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에 to mark the future time frame.
다음 + 주말 (weekend), written as one word 주말.
다음 주 + a specific day — the natural way to say 'next Monday.'
쯤 ('about') leaves the timing approximate.

examples.en: I'm going on a trip next week.
examples.note: 다음 주 + 에 sets future time; 여행을 가다 = 'go on a trip.'

examples.en: Next week is a bit free.
examples.note: Topic 는 frames the week; 한가하다 ('be free/relaxed') is descriptive.

examples.ko: 다음 주 월요일에 다시 회의하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: daeum ju woryoire dasi hoeuihagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We decided to meet again next Monday.
examples.note: 다음 주 월요일에 + ~기로 하다 ('decide to') for a settled plan.

entries.nuance: 다음 주 means the week that follows this one, so it naturally pairs with future plans and future-leaning verbs. 다음 ('next') + 주 (週 'week') mirrors the structure of 이번 주, and the trio 지난주 / 이번 주 / 다음 주 should be learned together. Spacing again matters — 다음 주 takes a space like 이번 주, while only 지난주 is written solid. And the time particle holds: a when-phrase is 다음 주에, so 'I'm going next week' is 다음 주에 가요, never bare 다음 주 가요.

Saying '다음 월요일' for 'next Monday'. The natural phrase is 다음 주 월요일.

structuredNuance.t: 다음 주 means the week that follows this one, so it naturally pairs with future plans and future-leaning verbs.
다음 ('next') + 주 (週 'week') mirrors the structure of 이번 주, and the trio 지난주 / 이번 주 / 다음 주 should be learned together.

The contrast to watch is 다음 ('next in a sequence') versus 내년·내일 style words: for weeks you use 다음 주, not a single fused word, and 'next Monday' is idiomatically 다음 주 월요일, not 다음 월요일. Spacing again matters — 다음 주 takes a space like 이번 주, while only 지난주 is written solid.
The time particle holds: a when-phrase is 다음 주에, so 'I'm going next week' is 다음 주에 가요, never bare 다음 주 가요.

entries.shortExplanation: 지난주 means "last week" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "last week" is 지난주 (jinanju). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 지난주에 ("last week"). Watch the particle attached to 지난주 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에 to mark when; almost always with past tense.
Here 지난 + 주말 takes a space (지난 주말), unlike solid 지난주.
지난주 + a specific day points back into the past week.
내내 ('throughout') stresses the whole past span.

examples.en: I went to Busan last week.
examples.note: 지난주 + 에 with past 갔어요 — 지난주 forces past tense.

examples.en: Last week was really hard.
examples.note: Topic 는 frames it; 힘들다 ('be tough') in past 힘들었어요.

examples.en: I met a friend last Friday.
examples.note: 지난주 금요일에 + past 만났어요; 친구를 만나다 takes object 를.

entries.nuance: 지난주 means the week that just ended, so it lives in the past and pulls past-tense verbs with it (갔어요, 만났어요). 지난 is the adnominal form of 지나다 'to pass,' literally 'the week that has passed,' and 주 is 週 'week.' It is the past member of the set 지난주 / 이번 주 / 다음 주. The most notorious detail is spacing: 지난주 ('last week') is written as ONE word, but 이번 주 and 다음 주 take a space — and confusingly, 지난 주말 ('last weekend') splits back into two words because 주말 is its own noun. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: keep the time particle (지난주에) and don't use present tense — 'I went last week' must be 지난주에 갔어요, not 지난주에 가요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing it as two words '지난 주'. For 'last week' the standard spelling is one solid word, 지난주.
Using present tense. 지난주 refers to the past, so it pairs with past tense: 지난주에 갔어요.
Spelling 'last weekend' as 지난주말. It is 지난 주말 (two words), because 주말 is a separate noun.

entries.shortExplanation: 모레 means "the day after tomorrow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 모레 (more) = "the day after tomorrow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 모레 ("the day after tomorrow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 모레, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A pure adverbial time word; usually stands alone with no particle.
까지 attaches for a deadline (one of the few particles 모레 takes).

usagePhrases.en: the morning of the day after tomorrow
usagePhrases.note: 모레 + 아침 stacks the time-of-day after the day word.
When 모레 is the subject of an 'is' sentence, use 가: 모레가 토요일이에요.

examples.en: I have an exam the day after tomorrow.
examples.note: 모레 sits bare as the time; no 에 needed.

examples.en: The day after tomorrow is Saturday.
examples.note: Here 모레 is the subject, so it takes 가, then 이에요 names the day.

examples.en: I absolutely have to hand in the homework by the day after tomorrow.
examples.note: 모레까지 = the deadline; 꼭 ('for sure') + 내야 해요 stresses obligation.

entries.nuance: 모레 means two days from today, one step past 내일 (tomorrow): the sequence runs 어제 (yesterday) → 오늘 (today) → 내일 (tomorrow) → 모레 → 글피 (three days out). Unlike the Sino-Korean day-of-week names, 모레 is a native Korean word and a bare time adverb. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the particle: relative time words like 모레, 내일, 오늘, 어제 normally take NO 에 — 'I'll meet you the day after tomorrow' is 모레 만나요, and adding 에 (모레에) sounds wrong. The exceptions are clear: deadline 까지 (모레까지) and subject 가 (모레가 토요일이에요) do attach. Don't confuse 모레 with 내일 (only one day off) or stretch it to mean any vague 'in a couple of days' — it is exactly the day after tomorrow.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding 에: say 모레 만나요, not 모레에 만나요. Relative time words like 모레/내일/오늘 skip 에.
Confusing 모레 (the day after tomorrow) with 내일 (tomorrow). 모레 is one day further out.
Using 모레 loosely for 'in a few days'. It means exactly two days from now; for three days out use 글피.

entries.shortExplanation: 할머니 means "grandmother" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 할머니 (halmeoni) means "grandmother". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 할머니 ("my (our) grandmother"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 할머니 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Koreans say 우리 (our), not 제 (my), for close family
noun + 예요 because 니 ends in a vowel
께 replaces 에게/한테 to honor an elder
께서 is the honorific of 가, raising the elder

examples.en: Grandmother, sleep well (good night).
examples.note: 안녕히 주무세요 is the honorific bedtime greeting to an elder

examples.en: My grandmother lives in the countryside.
examples.note: the honorific verb ending 사세요 (not 살아요) raises the grandmother

examples.en: Grandmother made the kimchi herself.
examples.note: 께서 + the honorific past 담그셨어요 mark deep respect

entries.nuance: 할머니 is your grandmother on either side, and in plain conversation Koreans use it for both the father's and the mother's mother; add 외- (외할머니) or 친- (친할머니) only when you must mark the side. It is built from 할- (an old prefix meaning a generation above) + 어머니 'mother', and it doubles as a warm, respectful way to address ANY elderly woman you feel close to, much like English 'grandma' for a kindly neighbor. The big trap for English speakers is grammar of respect, not vocabulary: a grandmother is a high-status elder, so the verb itself must be honorific — say 할머니는 사세요 / 주무세요 / 드세요, never the flat 살아요 / 자요 / 먹어요. Pair it with 우리 할머니 ('our grandmother'), not 제 할머니, because Korean treats family as shared. Compared with the polite stranger-address 아주머니/아주머님 (a middle-aged woman), 할머니 implies real old age, so misjudging the age can sting.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 할머니이에요. After a vowel (니) the copula contracts to 할머니예요; 이에요 is only for nouns ending in a consonant.
Saying 할머니가 집에 있어요 about your own grandmother. For an elder you should raise the verb: 할머니께서 집에 계세요 (계세요, the honorific of 있어요).
Calling a middle-aged woman 할머니 to be polite. It signals old age and can offend; use 아주머니 unless she is genuinely elderly.

entries.shortExplanation: 할아버지 means "grandfather" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "grandfather" is 할아버지 (harabeoji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 할아버지 ("my (our) grandfather"). Watch the particle attached to 할아버지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: use 우리, the inclusive 'our', for family
noun + 예요 because 지 ends in a vowel
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테 for an elder
께서 honors the elder as the subject

examples.en: Grandfather, please eat (your meal).
examples.note: 진지 is the honorific word for 밥, and 드세요 honors the eating

examples.en: Grandfather reads the newspaper.
examples.note: the honorific 읽으세요 (not 읽어요) raises the grandfather

examples.en: Grandfather told me old stories.
examples.note: 께서 + 주셨어요 (honorific of 줬어요) show layered respect

entries.nuance: 할아버지 is your grandfather on either side, and casual speech uses it for both the father's and the mother's father; 외할아버지 (maternal) or 친할아버지 (paternal) pin down the side when it matters. It is 할- (a prefix for the generation above) + 아버지 'father', and like 할머니 it can respectfully address any elderly man you know. The spelling trips beginners because of the liaison: it is one solid word, 할아버지, written together — never 할 아버지 — and the ㄹ slides onto the next syllable so it sounds like 하라버지. The deeper pitfall for English speakers is honorifics: a grandfather outranks you, so the verb climbs to the honorific level (읽으세요, 주무세요, 진지 드세요), and 밥 politely becomes 진지. Say 우리 할아버지, mirroring 우리 할머니, rather than the textbook-literal 제 할아버지.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 할아버지이에요. After the vowel 지 it must contract to 할아버지예요.
Splitting it as 할 아버지. Grandfather is a single lexical word, 할아버지, and the liaison even makes it sound like 하라버지.
Saying 할아버지가 밥을 먹어요 for your own grandfather. Raise it: 할아버지께서 진지를 드세요 — honorific subject 께서, honorific noun 진지, honorific verb 드세요.

It is 할- (a prefix for the generation above) + 아버지 'father'.

Say 우리 할아버지, mirroring 우리 할머니, rather than the textbook-literal 제 할아버지.

entries.shortExplanation: 외할머니 means "maternal grandmother (mother's mother)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 외할머니 (oehalmeoni) = "maternal grandmother (mother's mother)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 외할머니 댁 ("maternal grandmother's house") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 외할머니, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 댁 is the honorific word for an elder's home
noun + 예요 because 니 ends in a vowel
께 honors the elder as the recipient
께서 raises the elder as subject

examples.en: My maternal grandmother lives in Busan.
examples.note: honorific 사세요 (not 살아요) raises the grandmother

examples.en: My maternal grandmother gave me pocket money.
examples.note: 께서 + 주셨어요 mark her as an honored giver

examples.en: I visited my maternal grandmother's place during the break.
examples.note: 외할머니 댁 (honorific 'home') + 다녀왔어요 'went and came back'

entries.nuance: 외할머니 is specifically your mother's mother, and the prefix 외 (Sino-Korean 外, literally 'outside') is the key: traditional Korean kinship treated the mother's lineage as the 'outside' family, so 외- consistently marks the maternal side (외할아버지, 외삼촌, 외가). The contrast with plain 할머니 is one of precision, not a different person: 할머니 covers either grandmother loosely, while 외할머니 removes any doubt, and 친할머니 (친 親 'related by blood/paternal line') would name the father's mother. Because she is an elder, the same honorific rules apply — 사세요, 주무세요, 께서, and 댁 for her home — so do not flatten the verbs. The English-speaker pitfall is reading 외 as some negative 'outsider' label; it is just the historical word for the mother's side and carries no coldness at all. Note also 외할머니 is one word; do not insert a space.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 외할머니이에요. After the vowel 니 it contracts to 외할머니예요.
Calling your father's mother 외할머니. The maternal side is 외-; the paternal side is plain 할머니 (or 친할머니).
Reading 외 (外, 'outside') as an insult. It only names the mother's lineage and is completely neutral and affectionate in practice.

structuredNuance.t: 외할머니 is specifically your mother's mother. Because she is an elder, the same honorific rules apply — 사세요, 주무세요, 께서, and 댁 for her home — so do not flatten the verbs.

entries.shortExplanation: 외할아버지 means "maternal grandfather (mother's father)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 외할아버지 (oeharabeoji) means "maternal grandfather (mother's father)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 외할아버지 댁 ("maternal grandfather's house"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 외할아버지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 댁 is the honorific word for an elder's home
noun + 예요 because 지 ends in a vowel
께 honors the elder as the recipient

usagePhrases.en: to take after one's maternal grandfather
usagePhrases.note: 닮다 'resemble' takes the object marker 을/를, not 와

examples.en: My maternal grandfather likes fishing.
examples.note: honorific 좋아하세요 (not 좋아해요) raises the grandfather

examples.en: My maternal grandfather told me old stories.
examples.note: 께서 + 주셨어요 show layered respect

examples.en: I take after my maternal grandfather a lot.
examples.note: 닮다 uses 를: 외할아버지를 닮다, never 외할아버지와 닮다

entries.nuance: 외할아버지 is your mother's father, where 외 (Sino-Korean 外 'outside') marks the maternal lineage, exactly mirroring 외할머니, 외삼촌, and 외가. Against plain 할아버지 the difference is precision: 할아버지 can mean either grandfather casually, 외할아버지 fixes the mother's side, and 친할아버지 (親) would name the father's father. He is an elder, so honorifics are obligatory — 좋아하세요, 주무세요, 께서, 진지, 댁 — and beginners who keep the flat 좋아해요/먹어요 sound disrespectful. Two specific English-speaker pitfalls: first, the verb 닮다 ('resemble, take after') is transitive in Korean and takes 을/를 (외할아버지를 닮다), so the English 'I look like HIM' tempts a wrong 와/하고; second, 외 (外) is not a slur — it simply means the mother's family line. Keep 외할아버지 written as one unbroken word.

Writing 외할아버지이에요. After the vowel 지 it must be 외할아버지예요.
Saying 외할아버지와 닮았어요. 닮다 takes an object: 외할아버지를 닮았어요 ('I take after my maternal grandfather').
Using 외할아버지 for your father's father. That is plain 할아버지 (or 친할아버지); 외- is the mother's side only.

entries.shortExplanation: 삼촌 means "uncle (father's brother)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "uncle (father's brother)" is 삼촌 (samchon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 큰삼촌 / 작은삼촌 ("oldest uncle / younger uncle"). Watch the particle attached to 삼촌 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 큰 'big' = elder, 작은 'small' = younger brother of your father
noun + 이에요 because 촌 ends in the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
외 (外) marks the maternal side

examples.en: Uncle, I'm here!
examples.note: 삼촌 used directly as a friendly address term

examples.en: My uncle gave me a birthday present.
examples.note: for an adult uncle the honorific 주셨어요 is natural

examples.ko: 저는 삼촌하고 같이 축구를 자주 해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun samchonhago gachi chukgureul jaju haeyo.
examples.en: I often play soccer with my uncle.
examples.note: 삼촌하고 'with my uncle'; 하고 is the casual 'with/and'

entries.nuance: 삼촌 (Sino-Korean 三寸, literally 'three degrees/joints') names a relative three kinship 'nodes' away, and in everyday use it means your father's brother, especially an UNMARRIED one; once he marries, many families switch to 큰아버지 (father's older brother) or 작은아버지 (father's younger brother). It is also the go-to friendly word a child uses for any close adult man. The sharp contrast is side-of-family: your father's brother is 삼촌, but your mother's brother is 외삼촌 (외 外 'maternal'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'uncle' as one undivided word — Korean splits it four ways (삼촌/외삼촌 for blood uncles, 고모부/이모부 for aunts' husbands), so you must know whose sibling he is before choosing. Grammatically, because 촌 ends in ㄴ, the copula is 삼촌이에요, and the subject marker is 이, not 가.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 삼촌예요. After the consonant ㄴ it must be 삼촌이에요; 예요 only follows a vowel.
Using 삼촌 for your mother's brother. He is 외삼촌 (외 = maternal); 삼촌 alone defaults to the father's side.
Calling your father's MARRIED older brother 삼촌. Many families expect 큰아버지 / 작은아버지 once he is married, reserving 삼촌 for the unmarried uncle.

entries.nuance: 이모 (Sino-Korean 姨母, 'mother's-sister mother') is specifically your mother's sister, and it is one of the warmest kinship words — so warm that it stretches to your mother's close female friends and, famously, to a friendly woman serving food in a casual restaurant (이모! or politely 이모님!). examples.note: 고모 used directly as an address term to your father's sister

entries.nuance: 고모 (Sino-Korean 姑母, 'father's-sister mother') is specifically your father's sister, the exact mirror of 이모 (your mother's sister). This paternal-versus-maternal split is the heart of Korean kinship: English flattens both into 'aunt', but Korean fixes the side, so 고모 and 이모 are never interchangeable — pick by whose sibling she is. The English-speaker pitfall is the single-word 'aunt' reflex, and also the verb 만나다 ('meet'): it is transitive and takes 를 (고모를 만나다), so 'I meet WITH my aunt' must not become 고모와 만나다 in basic sentences. noun + 이에요 because 촌 ends in the consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 after a consonant

usagePhrases.en: older male cousin / older female cousin (for a girl)
usagePhrases.note: the sibling term encodes both age and the speaker's gender

examples.note: 놀러 오다 'come to hang out'; 사촌이 marks the subject

entries.nuance: 사촌 (Sino-Korean 四寸, literally 'four degrees') is the child of your aunt or uncle on either side; the number 사 'four' reflects the traditional kinship-distance count where siblings are 二寸 and aunts/uncles 三寸. Unlike the gender-neutral, age-neutral English 'cousin', plain 사촌 feels incomplete in speech, so Koreans normally graft on a sibling word to show age and (for older ones) the speaker's own gender: 사촌 동생 (younger), or 사촌 형/오빠/누나/언니 (older). The near rival is 친척, but that is the broad word for relatives in general, whereas 사촌 is the precise 'first cousin'. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: leaving 사촌 bare when context needs the age word, and the copula — because 촌 ends in ㄴ it is 사촌이에요 with subject marker 이, not 가.

Saying 사촌예요. After the consonant ㄴ it must be 사촌이에요.

noun + 예요 because 카 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
한테 'to (a person)', the casual form of 에게

examples.en: My niece/nephew is five years old now.
examples.note: native-number 다섯 + counter 살 for age

examples.note: 사 주다 'buy for someone'; recipient takes 한테

examples.romanization: jokaga neomu gwiyeowoseo jaju ana jwoyo.

entries.nuance: 조카 means your sibling's child and is gender-neutral, covering both nephew and niece with one word; if you truly must specify you can add 남자 조카 / 여자 조카, but bare 조카 is by far the norm. Beginners expect a male-only word because English has separate 'nephew/niece', and that mismatch is the main pitfall — 조카 is neither inherently male nor female. From the child's side, your relationship label flips to 삼촌, 외삼촌, 고모, or 이모 depending on which sibling and which side you are. A useful nearby distinction: 조카 is your sibling's child, whereas your own child's child is 손자/손녀 (grandchild) — different generations, different words. Grammar-wise, the vowel ending 카 gives 조카예요 and the subject marker 가; people you act upon take 한테 (조카한테 사 주다).

Thinking 조카 means only 'nephew'. It is gender-neutral and means 'niece' just as well; specify only with 남자 조카 / 여자 조카 if needed.

noun + 이에요 because 척 ends in the consonant ㄱ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
친척 modifies 집 directly, with no particle between

examples.en: I have many relatives.
examples.note: 친척이 많다 'have many relatives'; 이 marks the thing that exists

examples.en: All the relatives gather on the holidays.
examples.note: 친척들 adds the plural 들; 모이다 'gather' (intransitive)

examples.note: 친척 집 + 다녀오다 'go and come back'

entries.nuance: 친척 (Sino-Korean 親戚, where 親 is the close/paternal blood line and 戚 the relatives by marriage) is the umbrella term for your extended relatives — aunts, uncles, cousins, and more distant kin together. Its near rival is 가족, and the dividing line is closeness: 가족 is your immediate household (parents, siblings, spouse, children), while 친척 is the wider circle beyond it; saying 친척 for your own parents sounds oddly distant. A close synonym 친지 exists but is more formal/literary, so in speech 친척 is the everyday choice. Culturally these are the people you meet at 명절 (the big holidays 설날 and 추석). The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'relatives' blur into 'family', and the grammar: 척 ends in ㄱ, so the copula is 친척이에요 with subject marker 이, never 가.

Using 친척 for your parents and siblings. Immediate household is 가족; 친척 is the wider extended family.
Treating 친척 as exactly equal to 가족. They overlap but differ in scope — 가족 is close/immediate, 친척 is extended.

examples.note: 있다 for possession; 한 명 'one (person)'

Grammatically, because 들 ends in ㄹ (a consonant), the copula is 아들이에요 and the subject marker is 이.

entries.nuance: 손자 (Sino-Korean 孫子, 孫 'descendant' + 子 'child/son') is your grandchild who is a boy — the son of your son or daughter — and its pair is 손녀 (孫女) for a granddaughter. The two combine as 손자 손녀 'grandchildren', and when the gender is unknown or mixed, Koreans use the softer collective 손주 (note: 손주, not the common misspelling 손자, for the gender-neutral sense). The key contrast for learners is generation: 손자 is your CHILD's son, whereas 조카 is your SIBLING's child — both can be young boys, so it is easy to confuse, but they sit one generation apart. The English-speaker pitfall is using 손자 as a unisex 'grandchild'; it is male-specific, so a granddaughter must be 손녀. Grammatically the vowel ending 자 gives 손자예요 and the subject marker 가.

Confusing 손자 with 조카. 손자 is your child's son (one generation down twice); 조카 is your sibling's child.

entries.shortExplanation: 외삼촌 means "uncle (mother's brother)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 외삼촌 (oesamchon) = "uncle (mother's brother)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 외삼촌 ("my uncle (mom's brother)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 외삼촌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Koreans say 우리 ('our'), not 제 ('my'), for family members
댁 is the honorific word for an elder's home, replacing 집
닮다 takes 을/를; 외삼촌을 닮았어요 = I take after him
오시다 adds 시 because an uncle outranks you

examples.en: I have two maternal uncles.
examples.note: 분 counts people respectfully and 계세요 is the honorific 'there are'

examples.en: On the holidays I go to my maternal uncle's house.
examples.note: 명절 = traditional holiday; the particle 에 marks both time and destination

examples.en: My maternal uncle chipped in for my college tuition.
examples.note: 보태 주시다 = kindly help pay; 주시다 shows the favor came from an elder

entries.nuance: 외삼촌 is specifically your mother's brother. It is built from 한자 外 (oe, 'outside/maternal') + 삼촌 三寸 ('three degrees of kinship'), so it literally frames the mother's side as the 'outside' line — a window into how traditional Korean families centered on the father. The sharp contrast to learn is the pair 삼촌 vs 외삼촌: bare 삼촌 defaults to your FATHER's (unmarried) brother, while the 외 prefix swings it to the maternal side, and that same 외 reappears in 외할머니, 외할아버지, 외사촌. English collapses all of this into one word 'uncle,' which is the core pitfall — you cannot translate 'my uncle' into Korean without first deciding whose side and, often, married or not. Register is neutral and used constantly in everyday family talk; just remember to pair it with honorific verbs (계시다, 오시다, 주시다) and with 우리 rather than 제, since Koreans treat relatives as collectively 'ours.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping 외 and saying 삼촌 for your mom's brother — bare 삼촌 points to your father's side, so you have named the wrong uncle entirely.
Translating 'my uncle' as 제 외삼촌 — for family Koreans almost always say 우리 외삼촌, and 제 sounds oddly detached.
Confusing 외삼촌 (mom's brother) with 외숙모, who is his WIFE; the man himself is never 외숙모.

entries.shortExplanation: 며느리 means "daughter-in-law" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 며느리 (myeoneuri) means "daughter-in-law". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 며느리 ("my daughter-in-law"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 며느리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: said only by the husband's parents about their son's wife
들어오다 ('come in') is the set image of marrying into a household
보다 here means 'acquire (in-law)', not 'see'; said when a son marries
맏 ('eldest') marks the daughter-in-law with the heaviest family duties

examples.en: This is my daughter-in-law.
examples.note: spoken by the in-laws when introducing her; 예요 follows a vowel

examples.en: My daughter-in-law makes kimchi from scratch herself.
examples.note: 직접 = in person/by oneself; 담그다 is the verb for making fermented food

examples.en: This year we finally gained a daughter-in-law.
examples.note: 보다 = acquire an in-law; 드디어 ('finally') hints the son married at last

entries.nuance: 며느리 is the word a husband's parents use for their son's wife; it is a pure-Korean (고유어) kinship term, not Sino-Korean. The crucial thing English speakers miss is that it is defined from ONE direction only — the in-laws' side — so a woman never calls herself 며느리 when chatting with her own friends; she would say 결혼했어요 or 시댁(her husband's family). Contrast it sharply with its mirror term 사위 (the daughter's husband): 며느리 = son's wife, 사위 = daughter's husband, and mixing them up is the classic beginner slip. Note the idiom 며느리를 보다, where 보다 does NOT mean 'see' but 'gain an in-law' — the natural way to announce that a son has married. Culturally the word carries weight: the 며느리, especially the 맏며느리 (eldest son's wife), traditionally shoulders cooking and ancestral-rite duties, so the term often appears in talk about holidays and family obligation. Register is ordinary spoken Korean.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 며느리 (son's wife) with 사위 (daughter's husband) — they are opposite in-laws, so swapping them reverses who married whom.
Saying 며느리 about yourself as the wife — it is strictly how the husband's parents refer to her, not a self-description.
Reading 며느리를 보다 as 'to see the daughter-in-law' — here 보다 idiomatically means 'to acquire an in-law', i.e. the son got married.

usagePhrases.note: said only by the wife's parents about their daughter's husband
보다 = acquire an in-law, not 'see'; said when a daughter marries

an idiom: a 사위 is forever treated like an honored guest

examples.en: This is my son-in-law.
examples.note: spoken by the wife's parents introducing him; 예요 after a vowel

examples.en: My son-in-law brought my father-in-law along (respectfully).
examples.note: 모시고 오다 = escort an elder; 장인어른 = wife's father

examples.note: 둘째 = the second (daughter's husband); 보다 = acquire an in-law

entries.nuance: 사위 is the word a wife's parents use for their daughter's husband — the exact male mirror of 며느리. It is a native Korean term, and like 며느리 it is anchored to one viewpoint (the in-laws'), so a man does not introduce himself as 사위 in casual conversation; from his side those people are his 처가 (wife's family). The dividing line to drill is 사위 vs 며느리: 사위 = daughter's husband, 며느리 = son's wife. Watch the idiom 사위를 보다, where 보다 means 'gain an in-law,' not 'see' — the natural way to say a daughter has married. Culturally a 사위 is famously pampered: the saying 사위는 백년손님 ('a son-in-law is a hundred-year guest') means the wife's family treats him with lasting hospitality, the opposite of the duty-laden image attached to a 며느리. The English pitfall is that 'son-in-law' is symmetrical in English, but Korean forces you to know which spouse's parents are speaking before you can pick 사위 or 며느리.

Taking 사위를 보다 literally as 'to see the son-in-law' — the idiom means a daughter got married and the family acquired him as an in-law.

entries.shortExplanation: 지인 means "acquaintance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 지인 (jiin) = "acquaintance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지인을 통해 ("through an acquaintance") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 지인, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 통하다 = go via; the go-to phrase for how introductions or news travel
소개 = introduction; 으로 marks the means by which something happened
가깝다 = close; narrows 지인 to someone you actually know well
업계 = the trade/field; common in work and networking talk

examples.en: I have a few acquaintances (here).
examples.note: 좀 softens the statement; 있다 = have/exist

examples.en: I joined my current company through an acquaintance's introduction.
examples.note: 소개로 = by introduction; 들어오다 = enter/join (a company)

examples.en: That's just something I heard from an acquaintance.
examples.note: 한테 = from (a person); marks 지인 as the distant, unnamed source

entries.nuance: 지인 means an acquaintance — someone you know but who is not a close 친구. It is Sino-Korean, 한자 知人, literally 知 ('know') + 人 ('person'), i.e. 'a known person,' and that bookish origin is why it sounds a notch more formal than everyday speech. The key contrast is 지인 vs 친구: a 친구 implies warmth, shared time, and usually rough age-equality, whereas 지인 deliberately keeps a polite, neutral distance and says nothing about closeness or age — perfect for a colleague-of-a-colleague or a business contact. You will see it most in writing, news, and careful polite speech, especially in the fixed phrases 지인을 통해 and 지인의 소개로 (how Koreans describe getting jobs, apartments, or tips through personal networks). Two pitfalls for English speakers: do not stretch 'acquaintance' to mean a real friend (use 친구 for that), and resist treating 지인 as casual chit-chat vocabulary — it is the slightly elevated, written-leaning choice, where 아는 사람 ('someone I know') is the plainer spoken equivalent.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 지인 for a genuinely close friend — that warmth belongs to 친구; 지인 signals distance, not friendship.
Treating 지인 as breezy slang — it leans formal/written, so in very casual speech 아는 사람 often fits better.
Saying 지인 친구 to mean 'a friend who is an acquaintance' — it is redundant and contradictory; pick one word for the actual closeness.

entries.english: worry; concern; something on your mind
entries.shortExplanation: 고민 means "worry; concern; something on your mind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고민 (gomin) means "worry; concern; something on your mind". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고민이 있어요 ("I have something on my mind"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고민 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I have something on my mind
usagePhrases.note: 고민 + 이 있어요; the worry 'exists,' so use 있다, not 해요

usagePhrases.en: I have a lot on my mind
usagePhrases.note: 많다 = to be many; the default way to say you are stressed about several things

usagePhrases.en: to mull over; to agonize over a choice
usagePhrases.note: 고민 + 하다 turns the noun into a verb of active deliberation
warm, caring way to check on a friend who looks down

examples.en: I have a lot on my mind these days.
examples.note: 요즘 + 고민이 많다 is an extremely common everyday complaint

examples.en: I poured out my worries to a friend.
examples.note: 털어놓다 = to unload feelings; 한테 marks the person you confide in

examples.en: I'm agonizing over which company to join.
examples.note: real decision context: -ㄹ지 고민하다 = wrestle with a choice

entries.nuance: 고민 (苦悶, 苦 'bitter/suffering' + 悶 'anguish') is a problem you keep turning over in your head, usually a personal dilemma or decision you cannot resolve. The dividing line from 걱정 matters: 걱정 is anxious worry about a bad outcome you cannot control ('I'm worried it'll rain'), while 고민 is active mental wrestling over a choice you must make ('I'm torn over which job to take'). Register is neutral and everyday; you say 고민이 있어요 to a friend or 고민입니다 in a formal email. It habitually pairs with 많다, 깊다 (deep), 털어놓다 (unload), and 들어주다 (listen to someone's). The English-speaker trap: 고민 is a noun, so 'I worry' is 고민이 있어요 or 고민해요, never the non-word 고민다; and do not reach for 걱정 every time you would say 'worry' in English, because a decision dilemma is 고민, not 걱정.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 고민다 as a verb. 고민 is a noun; the verb is 고민하다, or you say 고민이 있어요 / 고민이 돼요.
Don't use 걱정 for a choice you're weighing. 'I'm torn over which one' is 고민이에요, not 걱정이에요 — 걱정 is dread about an outcome, 고민 is deliberation.
Don't translate 'have a worry' as 고민을 가지고 있어요. Korean prefers existence: 고민이 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 관심 means "interest; attention; care about something" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the topic ALWAYS takes 에, never 을/를
없다 = to not have; flat, common way to decline

usagePhrases.en: please pay attention / show you care
usagePhrases.note: asking for caring attention, not romantic interest

examples.note: 에 marks the thing you're interested in — lock this particle in

entries.nuance: 관심 (關心, 關 'connect/concern' + 心 'heart') is interest or attention directed toward something or someone — your heart 'connecting' to a topic. The nearest rival is 흥미: 흥미 is the fun, curious spark you get from a hobby or story ('this novel is 흥미롭다'), while 관심 is broader, covering both intellectual interest and caring, watchful attention toward a person. Register is neutral. Watch the two-faced particle behavior, which is the classic English-speaker pitfall: with 있다/없다/많다 the topic takes 에 (음악에 관심이 있어요), but with the verb 가지다 the word 관심 itself becomes the object and takes 을 (관심을 가지다). Saying 음악을 관심이 있어요 is the single most common error. Also note 관심 toward a person can imply romantic interest, so 그 사람한테 관심 있어요 often means 'I like them' — choose your words around people carefully.

Don't say 관심해요 as if it were a verb. Use 관심이 있어요 or the verb 관심을 가지다.

entries.shortExplanation: 인내 means "patience; endurance; perseverance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 인내 (innae) = "patience; endurance; perseverance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 인내가 필요해요 ("patience is needed") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 인내, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 필요하다 = to be needed; the most natural frame for abstract 인내
인내 + 심(心) 'heart'; the everyday word for someone's patience
강하다 = strong; the natural collocation, not 많다
기르다 = to cultivate; patience as something you train

examples.en: Studying Korean takes patience.
examples.note: X에는 인내가 필요하다 = X requires patience

examples.en: I'm a bit on the impatient side.
examples.note: -는 편이다 = tend to be; softer than a flat statement

examples.en: By enduring to the end, I succeeded.
examples.note: 참다 + 인내하다 stacked for emphasis on perseverance

entries.nuance: 인내 (忍耐, 忍 'endure' + 耐 'bear/withstand') is the abstract virtue of patient endurance, the capacity to bear hardship without giving up. It is weighty and somewhat literary, the language of mottos, self-help, and graduation speeches. Three relatives sort out by everyday-ness: bare 인내 is the abstract concept; 인내심 (adding 心 'heart') is patience as a person's character trait and is what you use to describe someone; and 참다 is the plain native verb 'to put up with / hold back' you actually use in daily life ('I held back my anger' = 화를 참았어요). The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 인내가 많아요 to mean 'I'm patient' — patience as a trait is 인내심이 많다/강하다, and for ordinary 'be patient / hang in there' Koreans say 참아요 or 참으세요, reserving 인내하다 for serious perseverance.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't describe a person with bare 인내. Patience as a trait is 인내심: 인내심이 강해요, not 인내가 강해요.
For everyday 'put up with it / be patient,' use 참다 (참으세요), not the heavy 인내하다.
Make the verb with 하다: 인내하다, never 인내다.
