entries.shortExplanation: 자신 means "confidence (in oneself); oneself" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자신 (jasin) means "confidence (in oneself); oneself". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N에 자신이 있어요 ("I'm confident about N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자신 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the skill area takes 에; 자신 'exists,' so use 있다
없다 = to lack; the everyday way to admit self-doubt
자신 + 감(感) 'feeling'; the buoyant emotional state
생기다 = to arise; confidence as something that grows in you

examples.en: I'm confident about cooking.
examples.note: 에 marks the area you're sure you can do well

examples.en: Honestly, I'm not confident about this exam.
examples.note: 솔직히 = honestly; natural hedge before admitting doubt

examples.ko: 발표를 잘 끝내고 나니 자신감이 생겼어요.
examples.romanization: balpyoreul jal kkeunnaego nani jasingami saenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After finishing the presentation well, I gained confidence.
examples.note: -고 나니 = after doing, I found that...; the 자신감 'feeling' word fits here

entries.nuance: 자신 (自身, 自 'self' + 身 'body') literally means 'one's own self,' and in 자신이 있다/없다 it has come to mean confidence in your own ability. Distinguish the two close forms: 자신이 있다 is being sure you CAN do a specific thing ('I'm confident about the test'), task-focused, while 자신감 (adding 感 'feeling') names confidence as an inner emotional state you carry around ('she radiates confidence'). The plain meaning 'oneself' survives in 자기 자신 (one's very own self) and reflexive uses. Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: the area of confidence takes 에 (운동에 자신이 있어요), not 을/를; and don't translate 'I am confident' as 자신이에요 — 자신 is a noun, so it's 자신이 있어요. Beginners also confuse 자신 with 자신감; if you can replace it with 'a feeling of confidence,' use 자신감.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mark the skill area with 에: 운동에 자신이 있어요, not 운동을 자신이 있어요.
Don't say 자신이에요 for 'I'm confident.' Confidence is 자신이 있어요; 자신 alone as a predicate means 'oneself.'
Don't blur 자신 and 자신감. Use 자신감 for the ongoing feeling (자신감이 생기다), 자신이 있다 for being sure about one task.

entries.shortExplanation: 행복 means "happiness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "happiness" is 행복 (haengbok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 행복하다 ("to be happy"). Watch the particle attached to 행복 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 행복 + 하다 = the adjective; this is how you SAY you're happy
polite present of 행복하다; 하다 → 해요
느끼다 = to feel; treats 행복 as an emotion you sense
행복한 가정 (happy home), 행복한 하루 (happy day) — the modifier form

examples.en: I'm really happy right now.
examples.note: adjective 행복하다 → 행복해요; no 이에요 needed

examples.en: I find happiness even in small things.
examples.note: 에서(도) marks where the feeling comes from; 도 = even

examples.en: Have a happy day!
examples.note: 행복한 + noun is a warm everyday send-off

entries.nuance: 행복 (幸福, 幸 'good fortune' + 福 'blessing') is happiness as a deep, lasting state of well-being and contentment with one's life — bigger and more enduring than a passing good mood. Contrast it sharply with 기쁨/기쁘다 and with 기분이 좋다: 기쁘다 is the bright spike of joy from a specific event ('I'm glad I passed!'), whereas 행복하다 is the settled background sense that life is good. So winning a prize makes you 기쁘다 in the moment, but a loving family makes you 행복하다 over years. Register is warm and neutral, common in wishes like 행복하세요 and 행복한 하루. The core English-speaker pitfall: 행복 is a noun, so 'I'm happy' is the ADJECTIVE 행복해요, never 행복이에요 (which would oddly mean 'it is happiness'). Also resist using 행복하다 for momentary delight — for 'I'm so glad / happy about this news,' 기뻐요 is the natural choice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 행복이에요 for 'I'm happy.' Use the adjective 행복해요; the noun-predicate 행복이에요 means 'it is happiness.'
Don't use 행복하다 for momentary delight over one event. That's 기쁘다 (기뻐요); 행복하다 is lasting well-being.
Don't add an object marker to the adjective. 'I'm happy' is just 행복해요, not 행복을 해요.

幸福 — 幸 'good fortune' + 福 'blessing'.

entries.shortExplanation: 불안 means "anxiety; unease; restlessness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 불안 (buran) = "anxiety; unease; restlessness". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 불안하다 ("to be anxious / uneasy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 불안, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 불안 + 하다 = the adjective; the everyday way to express it
polite present of 불안하다
느끼다 = to feel; treats 불안 as a sensed emotion
마음이 불안하다 is a fixed, very natural phrase

examples.en: Before a test I always feel uneasy.
examples.note: 전에 = before; 늘 = always — a routine state

examples.en: Walking alone at night, I feel a little anxious.
examples.note: everyday situation; 좀 softens it to 'a bit'

examples.ko: 그 소식을 듣고 막연한 불안을 느꼈어요.
examples.romanization: geu sosigeul deutgo magyeonhan buraneul neukkyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After that news I felt a vague unease.
examples.note: 막연한 불안 = vague, formless anxiety — a natural pairing

entries.nuance: 불안 (不安, 不 'not' + 安 'peace/safe') literally means 'not at peace' — an unsettled, restless anxiety, the felt opposite of 안심 (relief/security). Separate it from 걱정: 걱정 is worry pointed at a specific thing you can name ('I'm worried about the rent'), often with a thought you could voice, while 불안 is a more diffuse, bodily sense of dread that may have no clear object ('I just feel uneasy'). 불안 is heavier and more clinical-leaning — 불안 장애 is 'anxiety disorder.' Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: 불안 is a noun, so 'I'm anxious' is the adjective 불안해요, not 불안이에요; and don't default to 걱정 for every English 'anxious,' because a free-floating jittery feeling is 불안하다, whereas fretting over a known problem is 걱정하다. The set phrase 마음이 불안하다 is your reliable way to say your heart won't settle.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 불안이에요 for 'I'm anxious.' Use the adjective 불안해요.
Don't use 걱정 for free-floating dread. Nameless unease is 불안하다; fretting over a specific problem is 걱정하다 / 걱정이에요.
Don't omit 마음이 in the idiom. 'My heart is uneasy' is 마음이 불안해요, a set collocation.

entries.shortExplanation: 기대 means "expectation; anticipation; looking forward to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기대 (gidae) means "expectation; anticipation; looking forward to". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N이/가 기대돼요 ("I'm looking forward to N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 기대 + 되다; the THING takes 이/가, not 을/를 — key pattern
기대 + 하다 is the active verb and takes 을/를
크다 = big; the natural collocation, not 높다
부응하다 = to meet; formal but very common set phrase

examples.en: I can't wait for tomorrow's trip!
examples.note: 기대되다 with 이/가; the excited, can't-wait sense

examples.en: I'm really looking forward to the new movie.
examples.note: 기대하고 있다 = actively anticipating; here it takes 를

examples.en: If your expectations are too high, it's easy to be let down.
examples.note: 기대가 크다 + 실망하다 — the natural pairing of hope and letdown

entries.nuance: 기대 (期待, 期 'appointed time/expect' + 待 'wait') is the forward-leaning feeling of waiting for something good, or the hopes you place on a person. The 되다/하다 split is the heart of this word: 기대되다 is the involuntary 'it makes me excited / I can't wait,' so the source takes 이/가 (여행이 기대돼요); 기대하다 is the active 'I expect/anticipate it,' which takes 을/를 (여행을 기대해요). A near-synonym is 설레다 (to flutter with excitement) — but 설레다 is purely the heart-fluttering emotion, while 기대 also carries cognitive expectation about an outcome ('high expectations'). Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall: by analogy with English 'I look forward to it,' learners say 여행을 기대돼요 — but 되다 is intransitive, so it must be 여행이 기대돼요. Also, 기대 cuts both ways: 기대가 크다 sets you up for 실망 (disappointment), a pairing Koreans use constantly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
With 기대되다 use 이/가, not 을/를: 여행이 기대돼요, never 여행을 기대돼요 (되다 can't take an object).
Keep 기대하다 and 기대되다 distinct: 기대해요 = 'I expect/anticipate it' (active), 기대돼요 = 'it excites me' (it happens to me).
Say 기대가 크다 for high expectations, not 기대가 높다 — 크다 is the standard collocation.

entries.shortExplanation: 자유 means "freedom; liberty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "freedom; liberty" is 자유 (jayu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 자유롭다 ("to be free / unrestricted"). Watch the particle attached to 자유 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 자유 + 롭다 = adjective; ㅂ-irregular, so 자유로워요
자유롭다 conjugates with ㅂ-irregular: 롭다 → 로워요
자유 + 시간 written as two words; super useful daily phrase
N의 자유 = the freedom to/of N; common in serious topics

examples.en: I have a lot of free time on weekends.
examples.note: 자유 시간 as a fixed two-word noun

examples.en: Traveling alone, I feel so free.
examples.note: 자유롭다 → 자유로워요 (ㅂ-irregular in action)

examples.en: Everyone has freedom of expression.
examples.note: N의 자유 in the abstract civic sense

entries.nuance: 자유 (自由, 自 'self' + 由 'follow from / on one's own') means freedom — both the grand civic idea (자유와 평등, freedom and equality) and the everyday feeling of doing as you please. The adjective 자유롭다 describes a person or situation as unconstrained; a near rival is 편하다, but 편하다 is comfort/ease ('this chair is comfy'), whereas 자유롭다 is specifically the absence of restriction or obligation ('I'm free to do what I want'). Register is neutral. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the adjective is 자유롭다, NOT 자유하다 — and because 롭다 follows the ㅂ-irregular pattern, the polite form is 자유로워요, not the regular-looking 자유롭어요. Second, 자유 시간 is conventionally written as two separate words; learners often jam it together as 자유시간. To say someone simply 'is free / available,' note Koreans often say 시간이 있어요 (have time) rather than forcing 자유 in.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
The adjective is 자유롭다, not 자유하다, and it's ㅂ-irregular: 자유로워요, never 자유롭어요.
Write 자유 시간 as two words (free time), not the run-together 자유시간.
Don't overuse 자유 for 'I'm free this weekend.' That's usually 시간 있어요; 자유 is freedom/liberty, not mere availability.

structuredNuance.t: Freedom — both the grand civic idea (자유와 평등, freedom and equality) and the everyday feeling of doing as you please. The adjective 자유롭다 describes a person or situation as unconstrained. Register is neutral.
A near rival is 편하다, but 편하다 is comfort/ease ('this chair is comfy'), whereas 자유롭다 is specifically the absence of restriction or obligation ('I'm free to do what I want').
自由 — 自 'self' + 由 'follow from / on one's own'.

entries.english: greed; desire to have more; ambition
entries.shortExplanation: 욕심 means "greed; desire to have more; ambition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 욕심 (yoksim) = "greed; desire to have more; ambition". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 욕심이 나다 ("to feel a craving (to have it)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 욕심, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to feel a craving (to have it)
usagePhrases.note: 나다 = to arise; the urge wells up in you — use 나다, not 하다
많다 = many; describes a person's greedy character
부리다 = to act out (a trait); fixed idiom for greedy behavior

usagePhrases.en: to go for more; to set one's sights high
usagePhrases.note: 내다 = to put forth; can be positive drive or negative grabbing

examples.en: Seeing that bag, I really want it.
examples.note: 보니까 ... 욕심이 나다 = the sight triggers the craving

examples.en: That person is way too greedy.
examples.note: 욕심이 많다 paints a character flaw

examples.en: Don't be greedy — just pick one.
examples.note: 욕심부리다 as advice; warm but firm

entries.nuance: 욕심 (慾心, 慾 'desire/lust' + 心 'heart') is the heart's craving to have or get more than you need — it spans harmless 'ooh, I want that' all the way to real, ugly greed. Set it against neutral 원하다 (to want): 원하다 is plainly wanting something, no judgment, while 욕심 always carries a tinge of 'more than your share / too much.' It can flip positive as drive: 공부 욕심이 많다 means 'eager and ambitious about studying,' admirable. The grammar pitfall is the verb of 'arising': the craving comes with 나다 — 욕심이 나요 — not 욕심을 해요, which is not Korean. To describe a greedy person use 욕심이 많다; for the act of behaving greedily use the idiom 욕심을 부리다. English-speaker note: don't reach for 욕심 whenever you'd say 'want' — neutral wanting is 원하다/-고 싶다; 욕심 specifically flags excess or covetousness.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 나다 for the urge: 욕심이 나요, not the non-word 욕심을 해요.
Don't use 욕심 for neutral wanting. 'I want water' is 물을 원해요 / 마시고 싶어요, not 욕심 — 욕심 implies 'too much.'
Describe a greedy person with 욕심이 많다, and greedy behavior with 욕심을 부리다 — don't swap these collocations.

structuredNuance.t: The heart's craving to have or get more than you need — it spans harmless 'ooh, I want that' all the way to real, ugly greed. It can flip positive as drive: 공부 욕심이 많다 means 'eager and ambitious about studying,' admirable. To describe a greedy person use 욕심이 많다; for the act of behaving greedily use the idiom 욕심을 부리다.
Set it against neutral 원하다 (to want): 원하다 is plainly wanting something, no judgment, while 욕심 always carries a tinge of 'more than your share / too much.'
慾心 — 慾 'desire/lust' + 心 'heart'.

The grammar trap is the verb of 'arising': the craving comes with 나다 — 욕심이 나요 — not 욕심을 해요, which is not Korean. Also don't reach for 욕심 whenever you'd say 'want' — neutral wanting is 원하다/-고 싶다; 욕심 specifically flags excess or covetousness.

entries.shortExplanation: 정성 means "sincerity; heartfelt effort; devotion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 정성 (jeongseong) means "sincerity; heartfelt effort; devotion". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정성껏 ("wholeheartedly; with all one's care"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정성 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 정성 + 껏 'to the fullest'; an adverb already — don't add 하게

usagePhrases.en: to put in one's whole heart
usagePhrases.note: 다하다 = to do fully; the standard set phrase

usagePhrases.en: to be filled with heartfelt care
usagePhrases.note: 담기다 = to be contained; said of gifts, food, letters
정성 + 스럽다 = the adjective describing caring effort

examples.en: Mom lovingly prepared a meal for me.
examples.note: 정성껏 + 차리다; 주셨어요 honors mom doing it for me

examples.ko: 이 선물에는 정성이 가득 담겨 있어요.
examples.romanization: i seonmureneun jeongseongi gadeuk damgyeo isseoyo.
examples.en: This gift is full of heartfelt care.
examples.note: 정성이 담기다, intensified with 가득 (brimming)

examples.en: I served the guests with all my heart.
examples.note: 정성을 다하다 + 대접하다 — the language of hospitality

entries.nuance: 정성 (精誠, 精 'refined/pure' + 誠 'sincerity') is the warm, painstaking care and sincerity you pour into doing something for someone — cooking a meal, choosing a gift, writing by hand. The key contrast is with 노력 (努力, effort): 노력 is neutral exertion toward a goal ('I worked hard for the exam'), measured by output, while 정성 is heart-warmth and devotion, valued for the caring intent itself regardless of result. Koreans prize 정성 deeply: a humble homemade dish made 정성껏 outranks an expensive store-bought one. Register is warm and slightly elevated, common in thanks and hospitality. The English-speaker pitfall: 정성껏 is already a complete adverb (= 'with full sincerity'), so don't tack on 하게 to make 정성껏하게 — just say 정성껏 요리하다. Also, you GIVE 정성 to others; don't use it for cold, goal-driven effort, which is 노력.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
정성껏 is already an adverb. Say 정성껏 만들었어요, never 정성껏하게.
Don't substitute 노력 for 정성. 노력 = goal-directed effort; 정성 = heartfelt devotion and care for someone.
The adjective is 정성스럽다 (정성스러운 선물). Don't say 정성하다 — there is no such verb.

structuredNuance.t: The warm, painstaking care and sincerity you pour into doing something for someone — cooking a meal, choosing a gift, writing by hand. Koreans prize 정성 deeply: a humble homemade dish made 정성껏 outranks an expensive store-bought one. Register is warm and slightly elevated, common in thanks and hospitality.

精誠 — 精 'refined/pure' + 誠 'sincerity'.

entries.shortExplanation: 위로 means "comfort; consolation; words of encouragement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "comfort; consolation; words of encouragement" is 위로 (wiro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 위로가 되다 ("to be a comfort"). Watch the particle attached to 위로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 되다 = to become; the THING that comforts takes 이/가
위로 + 하다; the person you console takes 을/를
받다 = to receive; you receive comfort from someone
의 links the nouns; said at funerals and hard times

examples.ko: 친구의 말 한마디가 큰 위로가 됐어요.
examples.romanization: chinguui mal hanmadiga keun wiroga dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: A single word from my friend was a big comfort.
examples.note: 말 한마디 + 위로가 되다; the thing comforts → 이/가

examples.en: I comforted my struggling friend.
examples.note: 위로하다 takes the person as object; 줬어요 = did it for them

examples.ko: 따뜻한 차 한 잔이 큰 위로가 돼요.
examples.romanization: ttatteutan cha han jani keun wiroga dwaeyo.
examples.en: A warm cup of tea is a great comfort.
examples.note: even an object can 위로가 되다 — 'be comforting'

entries.nuance: 위로 (慰勞, 慰 'console/soothe' + 勞 'toil/weariness') is comfort given to someone who is sad, grieving, or worn out — soothing their hardship. A near relative is 격려 (激勵, encouragement): 격려 cheers you ON toward a future effort ('you can do it, keep going!'), while 위로 soothes present pain and sorrow ('I'm so sorry, it must be hard'). So you 격려 someone before an exam but 위로 them after a loss. Register is gentle and caring. The central English-speaker pitfall is the 되다/하다 split tied to who does what: 위로가 되다 means something IS a comfort, with the comforting thing as subject (네 말이 위로가 됐어 = 'your words comforted me'); 위로하다 means a person actively comforts ANOTHER person, who takes 을/를 (친구를 위로했어요). Saying 위로해요 when you mean 'it comforts me' is wrong — that says 'I comfort someone.' To receive comfort, use 위로를 받다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For 'it is comforting,' use 위로가 돼요, not 위로해요 — 위로하다 means 'I comfort someone else.'
Mark the person you console with 을/를: 친구를 위로해요, not 친구에게 위로해요.
Don't mix up 위로 and 격려: comfort after sorrow is 위로, cheering someone on toward a goal is 격려.

structuredNuance.t: Comfort given to someone who is sad, grieving, or worn out — soothing their hardship. Register is gentle and caring. To receive comfort, use 위로를 받다.

A near relative is 격려 (激勵, encouragement): 격려 cheers you ON toward a future effort ('you can do it, keep going!'), while 위로 soothes present pain and sorrow ('I'm so sorry, it must be hard'). So you 격려 someone before an exam but 위로 them after a loss.
慰勞 — 慰 'console/soothe' + 勞 'toil/weariness'.

Saying 위로해요 when you mean 'it comforts me' is wrong — that says 'I comfort someone.' For 'it is comforting,' use 위로가 돼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 자랑 means "pride; boasting; showing off" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자랑 (jarang) = "pride; boasting; showing off". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: N을/를 자랑하다 ("to show off / boast about N") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 자랑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to show off / boast about N
usagePhrases.note: 를 marks the thing flaunted; can sound braggy
자랑 + 스럽다 = adjective; purely positive, warm pride
자랑 + 거리 'material'; a source of pride

usagePhrases.en: to be the pride of N
usagePhrases.note: 그 학교의 자랑 = the pride of that school

examples.en: My friend showed off a new car.
examples.note: 자랑하다 takes 를; here it leans 'bragging'

examples.en: I'm really proud of my family.
examples.note: 자랑스럽다 = warm pride; the source takes 이/가

examples.en: That athlete is the pride of the whole nation.
examples.note: N의 자랑이다 = to be the pride of N

entries.nuance: 자랑 (native Korean, not Sino-Korean) covers a spectrum from honest pride to boastful showing-off, and context decides the tone. The verb 자랑하다 usually leans negative — 'to brag, to flaunt' — so calling someone's talk 자랑 hints they're full of themselves. By contrast, the adjective 자랑스럽다 is purely warm and positive: 'proud of' (아들이 자랑스러워요). Keep this split from 뽐내다 (to flaunt/preen), which is even more openly show-offy and vain. Register is neutral, though 자랑하다 can sting. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'I'm proud of you' tempts learners to build it from 자랑하다, but 자랑하다 means 'brag,' so 'I'm proud of you' must use the adjective 자랑스러워요 (or 네가 자랑스러워). With 자랑스럽다 the object of pride takes 이/가 (가족이 자랑스러워요), not 을/를; only the verb 자랑하다 (to show off) takes 을/를 (사진을 자랑하다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For 'I'm proud of you' use the adjective 자랑스러워요, not 자랑해요 — 자랑하다 means 'to brag.'
With 자랑스럽다 mark the source of pride with 이/가: 가족이 자랑스러워요, not 가족을 자랑스러워요.
Only 자랑하다 (show off) takes 를: 실력을 자랑하다. Don't put 를 on the adjective 자랑스럽다.

Native Korean, not Sino-Korean — no 한자 backing.

entries.shortExplanation: 평화 means "peace; calm" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 평화 (pyeonghwa) means "peace; calm". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 평화롭다 ("to be peaceful / serene"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 평화 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 평화 + 롭다 = adjective; ㅂ-irregular → 평화로워요
평화롭다 conjugates ㅂ-irregular: 롭다 → 로워요
의 links the nouns; inner calm
지키다 = to guard; the civic-scale collocation

examples.en: The countryside is so peaceful.
examples.note: 평화롭다 → 평화로워요 (ㅂ-irregular)

examples.en: Meditating brings me peace of mind.
examples.note: 마음의 평화 + 얻다 (to gain) — inner calm

examples.en: The whole world hopes for peace.
examples.note: 평화를 바라다 = to wish for peace, the large-scale sense

entries.nuance: 평화 (平和, 平 'level/even' + 和 'harmony') is peace — both the large sense of harmony without conflict (세계 평화, world peace) and the everyday feeling of tranquil calm. The adjective 평화롭다 paints a serene, untroubled scene; the near rival is 조용하다 (quiet), but 조용하다 only means 'low in sound,' while 평화롭다 adds a settled, contented harmony beyond mere silence — a busy family picnic can be 평화롭다 without being 조용하다. The lovely phrase 마음의 평화 names inner peace. Register is neutral and a touch elevated. English-speaker pitfalls. First, the adjective is 평화롭다, NOT 평화하다, and it follows the ㅂ-irregular, so the polite form is 평화로워요, not 평화롭어요. Second, beginners eye-confuse 평화 (peace) with 평소 (平素, 'usual times / ordinarily') because both start with 평 — keep them apart: 평소에 운동해요 means 'I usually exercise,' nothing to do with peace.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
The adjective is 평화롭다, not 평화하다, and it's ㅂ-irregular: 평화로워요, never 평화롭어요.
Don't confuse 평화 (peace) with 평소 (usually / ordinarily) — same first syllable, unrelated meaning.
Don't equate 평화롭다 with 조용하다. 조용하다 is just 'quiet'; 평화롭다 is serene harmony, which can include lively scenes.

structuredNuance.t: Peace — both the large sense of harmony without conflict (세계 평화, world peace) and the everyday feeling of tranquil calm. The adjective 평화롭다 paints a serene, untroubled scene. The lovely phrase 마음의 평화 names inner peace. Register is neutral and a touch elevated.

平和 — 平 'level/even' + 和 'harmony'.

entries.shortExplanation: 전등 means "light, lamp (ceiling/room light)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "light, lamp (ceiling/room light)" is 전등 (jeondeung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전등을 켜다 ("to turn on the light"). Watch the particle attached to 전등 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 전등 + 을 + 켜다; 켜다 is the on-verb for any light/device
전등 + 을 + 끄다; 끄다 is the matching off-verb
전등/전구 + 이/가 + 나가다 = stops working
전등 + 을 + 갈다; 갈다 = swap an old one for new

examples.en: The room is dark. I'll turn on the light.
examples.note: Basic cause→action: 어둡다 (dark) leads to 켜다 (turn on).

examples.en: Please turn off the light when you go out.
examples.note: 꺼 주세요 = polite request; in casual speech 불 꺼 is even more common.

examples.ko: 거실 전등이 자꾸 깜빡거려서 새것으로 갈았어요.
examples.romanization: geosil jeondeungi jakku kkamppakgeoryeoseo saegeoseuro garasseoyo.
examples.en: The living-room light kept flickering, so I replaced it with a new one.
examples.note: 깜빡거리다 = flicker; real-life maintenance situation.

entries.nuance: 전등 is Sino-Korean: 電 (electric) + 燈 (lamp), literally 'electric lamp' — the fixed electric light of a room, typically the ceiling light. The crucial register point: 전등 is the technical/written word, but in real conversation Koreans almost always just say 불 ('fire/light'), as in 불 켜 / 불 꺼. Saying 전등을 켜 주세요 is understood but sounds stiff; 불 좀 켜 줄래? is how people actually talk. Contrast with 조명, which means lighting as a concept or mood (무대 조명 'stage lighting', 조명이 예뻐요 'the lighting is pretty'), whereas 전등 is the physical fixture. The English pitfall is reaching for 열다/닫다 (open/close) because English says 'turn the light on'; lights take 켜다/끄다, never 열다. Also note 전등 is the whole light fixture, not the bulb (전구) that screws inside it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Turning a light on with 열다 ('open') is wrong — that verb is only for doors/windows/lids. Lights always use 켜다 (on) and 끄다 (off).
Over-using 전등 in conversation sounds textbook-stiff. For everyday 'turn the light on/off', native speakers say 불 켜다 / 불 끄다.
Confusing 전등 (the fixture/lamp) with 전구 (the bulb inside it). You replace a burnt-out 전구, not the whole 전등, when only the bulb dies.

structuredNuance.t: 전등 is the fixed electric light of a room, typically the ceiling light — the physical light fixture itself (not the bulb 전구 that screws inside it). It uses the universal light verbs 켜다 (on) and 끄다 (off).

Contrast with 조명, which means lighting as a concept or mood (무대 조명 'stage lighting', 조명이 예뻐요 'the lighting is pretty'), whereas 전등 is the physical fixture. Note also that 전등 is the whole fixture, not the bulb (전구) inside it.
전등 is Sino-Korean: 電 (electric) + 燈 (lamp), literally 'electric lamp'.

And don't reach for 열다/닫다 (open/close) because English says 'turn the light on' — lights take 켜다/끄다, never 열다.

entries.shortExplanation: 전구 means "light bulb" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전구 (jeongu) = "light bulb". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전구가 나가다 ("the bulb burns out / dies") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전구, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 전구 + 이/가 + 나가다 = stops working
전구 + 를 + 갈다; the standard verb for swapping a bulb

usagePhrases.en: to screw in / fit the bulb
usagePhrases.note: 전구 + 를 + 끼우다 = insert into the socket
전구 + 한 개; count bulbs with the general counter 개

examples.en: The light bulb burned out.
examples.note: Simple state result: 나가다 here = stop working, not 'go outside'.

examples.en: The bulb died, so I changed it for a new one.
examples.note: 나가서 (because it died) + 갈다 (replace) — the everyday repair phrasing.

examples.ko: 이 스탠드는 전구를 돌려서 끼우면 돼요.
examples.romanization: i seutaendeuneun jeongureul dollyeoseo kkiumyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: For this lamp, you just screw the bulb in by turning it.
examples.note: 돌려서 끼우다 = turn-and-fit; real instruction-giving register.

entries.nuance: 전구 is Sino-Korean 電 (electric) + 球 (ball/globe), literally 'electric globe' — named for the round glass shape, and it means specifically the screw-in bulb, not the whole fixture (전등). The key idiom learners must memorize is 전구가 나갔어요 for 'the bulb burned out': 나가다 literally means 'go out', and Korean treats a dead bulb as the light having 'gone out', much like English 'the light went out'. To install a fresh one you 갈다 (replace) or 끼우다 (fit/insert). The English-speaker pitfall is saying 전구가 죽었어요 ('the bulb died') by direct-translating English slang — Koreans don't use 죽다 for bulbs; it sounds odd and even slightly comic. Also don't use 깨지다 (shatter) unless the glass actually broke; a simply non-working bulb 나갔어요 even though it looks intact.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 전구가 죽었어요 ('the bulb died') is a direct translation of English that Koreans don't use. The natural verb is 나가다: 전구가 나갔어요.
Mixing up 전구 (the bulb) and 전등 (the lamp/fixture). When the light won't turn on, you usually replace the 전구, not the 전등.
Using 부서지다/깨지다 (break/shatter) for a dead bulb. Those mean the glass physically broke; a burnt-out but intact bulb is 나갔어요.

전구 is the bulb only, distinct from 전등, the whole fixture it screws into.

entries.shortExplanation: 스탠드 means "desk lamp, stand lamp" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스탠드 (seutaendeu) means "desk lamp, stand lamp". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스탠드를 켜다 ("to turn on the desk lamp"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스탠드 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.en: to turn on the desk lamp

entries.nuance: 스탠드 is a 'Konglish' loanword from English 'stand', but its meaning has narrowed in Korean to one thing: a desk or table lamp for reading and studying. This is a false-friend trap — an English speaker hears 'stand' and pictures a rack, a stadium stand, or a place to stand, but in a Korean home 스탠드 means the small reading lamp. Contrast it with 전등, which is the fixed ceiling light of the whole room: you switch off the 전등 and leave just the 스탠드 on for cozy late-night light. Forgetting it takes the same light verbs as everything else: turn it on/off with 켜다/끄다, not 틀다 (which suits TVs, water, and music more than lamps).
Confusing 스탠드 with 전등: the 전등 is the room's main ceiling light, while the 스탠드 is the small movable desk lamp.

usagePhrases.note: 달력 + 을 + 보다, the default verb for consulting it

usagePhrases.note: 달력 + 에 + 표시하다; 에 = the location of the mark

usagePhrases.en: to flip the calendar (to the next month)

entries.nuance: 달력 is a hybrid word — native 달 (month/moon) plus Sino-Korean 曆 (력, calendar/almanac) — and it means the physical printed calendar: the grid of dates you hang on the wall (벽걸이 달력) or stand on a desk (탁상 달력). The sharp distinction English speakers miss is calendar-the-object vs schedule-the-plan. 달력 is only the dated paper grid; your personal plans, appointments, and agenda live in your 일정 (schedule) or 다이어리/플래너 (planner), and on your phone in a 캘린더 app. So 'add it to my calendar' meaning your appointments is 일정에 추가하다, NOT 달력에 추가하다. You 보다 (look at) a 달력 to check a date, 표시하다 to mark a day, and 넘기다 to flip to the next month. Beware also of the bare syllable 달, which alone means 'the moon' or 'a month' — 달력 is the printed object, never the moon.

Using 달력 for your personal schedule/agenda. 'Put it on my calendar' (your plans) is 일정에 넣다 or 다이어리에 적다 — 달력 is just the dated wall/desk grid.
Confusing the syllable 달 (moon / a month) with 달력 (the calendar object). They share 달 but are different words.
Saying 달력을 읽다 ('read the calendar'). You 보다 (look at) a calendar to check a date; 읽다 (read) suits text, not a date grid.

usagePhrases.note: 사진 + 을 + 액자 + 에 + 넣다; 에 = into where
사진(photo) + 액자, names what it holds

usagePhrases.note: 액자 + 에 + 끼우다 = fit snugly in

entries.nuance: 액자 is Sino-Korean 額 (frame/tablet) + 子 (a noun-forming suffix), and it means the frame that holds a photo or picture — the kind you stand on a shelf or hang on a wall. The essential separation for learners is container vs content: the 액자 is the empty frame, while the 사진 (photo) or 그림 (picture/painting) is what goes inside it. So you 넣다 (put) or 끼우다 (fit) a 사진 into an 액자, and you 걸다 (hang) the 액자 on the wall. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb for hanging: use 걸다, not 붙이다. 붙이다 means to stick/affix something flat and adhesive (a poster, a sticker, tape), whereas a framed picture hangs from a hook, which is 걸다 — and its resting state is 걸려 있다 ('is hanging'). Don't confuse 액자 with 틀, the generic word for a frame/mold/framework; 액자 is specifically the decorative picture frame.

Hanging a frame with 붙이다 ('stick on'). A framed picture hangs from a hook → 걸다 (and 걸려 있다 for 'is hanging'). 붙이다 is for posters/stickers.
Swapping 액자 (the frame) and 사진 (the photo inside). You put the 사진 into the 액자 — they are not the same word.
Saying 액자를 만들다 to mean 'take/frame a photo'. To frame a picture you 사진을 액자에 넣다; 만들다 would literally mean to build the frame from scratch.

화분 + 을 + 키우다 = raise/tend it

examples.en: There's a potted plant by the window.
examples.note: Basic location; 창가 = the windowside.

examples.note: Reminder register; 물 주다 = water, ~는 거 nominalizes the action.

entries.nuance: 화분 is Sino-Korean 花 (flower) + 盆 (basin/pot), literally 'flower basin', and it refers to the planter together with whatever grows in it — both the pot and the potted plant as a set. Learners must keep three words apart: 꽃 is the flower (the bloom), 식물 is a plant in general, and 화분 is specifically the potted container-plant. The signature collocation is 화분에 물을 주다 — note Korean 'gives water TO the pot' (화분에... 주다), so the pot takes the particle 에 as the recipient/destination of the water. The English-speaker pitfall is the watering verb: never say 화분이 물을 마시다 ('the pot drinks water'). 마시다 (drink) is only for living beings consuming liquid by mouth; you 주다 (give) water to plants. Another natural verb is 키우다 (to raise/grow), the same verb used for pets and children, reflecting that you 'tend' a plant. To rearrange them you 옮기다 (move).

Using 화분 when you mean a single cut flower. A flower is 꽃; 화분 is the whole potted plant in its container.
Choosing 만들다/만지다 for tending a plant. To grow/keep one you 키우다 (raise), the same verb as for pets — 화분을 키워요.

소파(sofa) + 쿠션, names where it lives

usagePhrases.note: 쿠션 + 이/가 + 푹신하다, the signature texture word

entries.nuance: 쿠션 is a loanword from English 'cushion' and means a soft throw cushion or decorative pillow you put on a sofa, bed, or chair to lean on, hug, or prop yourself up. The boundary learners must draw is against two near-neighbors. First, 베개 is specifically the pillow you sleep on with your head — a 쿠션 is for sitting and leaning, a 베개 is for sleeping, even though both are soft and stuffed. Second, 방석 is the flat floor cushion you sit ON (traditional in Korean homes for sitting on the heated floor), whereas a 쿠션 is something you hold or lean against. The defining adjective is 푹신하다 (soft-and-fluffy), the texture word that pairs with cushions and good mattresses; you 안다 (hug) a cushion or 기대다 (lean on) it. The pitfall is reaching for 베개 because English loosely calls both 'pillow' — keep 쿠션 (throw cushion) and 베개 (sleeping pillow) distinct.

Calling a 쿠션 a 베개. 베개 is strictly the pillow you sleep on under your head; a sofa throw cushion is 쿠션, even if English says 'pillow' for both.
Confusing 쿠션 with 방석 (a flat floor seat cushion). You sit ON a 방석; you hug or lean against a 쿠션.
Describing it as 부드럽다 only. 부드럽다 means smooth/soft to the touch (skin, fabric); the springy 'fluffy' feel of a cushion is 푹신하다.

usagePhrases.en: to cover oneself with a blanket
usagePhrases.note: (몸에) 담요 + 를 + 덮다; drape it over you
담요 + 를 + 개다; 개다 = fold bedding/cloth neatly
무릎(knee/lap) + 담요, names where you use it
담요 + 를 + 덮어 + 주다 = cover someone as a kindness

examples.en: It was cold, so I covered up with a blanket.
examples.note: Basic cause→action; 추워서 = because it's cold.

entries.nuance: 담요 is a light blanket or throw — the thinner cover you drape over your lap, shoulders, or knees when you feel chilly (on a sofa, a plane, at a desk). The contrast every learner needs is 담요 vs 이불: 이불 is the thick quilt/duvet/comforter you sleep under in bed at night, while 담요 is the lighter, smaller throw for warmth while awake. So you 'snuggle under the 이불' to sleep but 'put a 담요 over your lap' while watching TV. Two verb pitfalls stand out. For putting it over yourself, use 덮다 (to cover over) — not 입다 (wear), since a blanket isn't clothing. For tidying it away, use 개다, the specific verb for folding bedding and laundry, NOT 접다. 접다 is for folding paper, a map, or an umbrella along creases; soft bedding is 개다. To cover someone else kindly, the giving form 담요를 덮어 주다 adds the nuance of doing it for them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Folding a blanket with 접다. 접다 is for paper/maps/umbrellas; soft bedding and laundry are folded with 개다 → 담요를 개다.
Confusing 담요 (light throw, used while awake) with 이불 (thick sleeping quilt/duvet). You sleep under an 이불; you drape a 담요 over your lap.
Saying 담요를 입다 ('wear the blanket'). A blanket isn't clothing; you 덮다 (cover) yourself with it → 담요를 덮어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 쓰레기통 means "trash can, wastebasket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쓰레기통 (sseuregitong) means "trash can, wastebasket". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 쓰레기통에 버리다 ("to throw it in the trash can"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쓰레기통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to throw it in the trash can
usagePhrases.note: 쓰레기 + 를 + 쓰레기통 + 에 + 버리다; 에 = into where
쓰레기통 + 을 + 비우다 = make it empty
쓰레기통 + 이/가 + 가득 차다 = filled to the brim
음식물(food matter) + 쓰레기통, a sorted-waste type

examples.en: Where's the trash can?
examples.note: Basic location question; very common phrase.

examples.en: Please throw the tissue in the trash can.
examples.note: 버리다 = throw away; ~에 marks the destination.

examples.note: 가득 차다 (be full) + 비우다 (empty) — the natural pair.

entries.nuance: 쓰레기통 is a transparent compound: 쓰레기 (trash/garbage) + 통 (bin/barrel/container), so 'trash container' = wastebasket/trash can. The verb you must lock in is 버리다 (throw away/discard), and the trash can takes 에 as the destination: 쓰레기통에 버리다 ('throw into the trash can'). The big English-speaker pitfall is 던지다: English 'throw it in the trash' makes learners pick 던지다, but 던지다 means to hurl/toss something through the air (a ball, a stone). Discarding garbage is 버리다, an act of disposal, not a throwing motion. A culturally important note: Korea strictly sorts waste, so beyond the general 쓰레기통 you'll meet 음식물 쓰레기통 (food waste), 재활용(품) / 분리수거함 (recycling bins), and 일반 쓰레기 (general waste) — putting things in the right bin matters. Finally, 쓰레기통 is written as one word with no internal space, and you 비우다 (empty) it when it 가득 차다 (gets full).

Using 던지다 to mean 'throw it in the trash'. 던지다 = hurl through the air (a ball). Discarding garbage is 버리다 → 쓰레기통에 버려요.
Putting a space inside 쓰레기통. It is one word: 쓰레기통 (not 쓰레기 통).
Treating Korean trash as one bin. Waste is sorted: 일반 쓰레기, 음식물 쓰레기통, and 재활용/분리수거함 — use the matching bin.

The verb to lock in is 버리다 (throw away/discard), and the trash can takes 에 as the destination: 쓰레기통에 버리다 ('throw into the trash can'). You 비우다 (empty) it when it 가득 차다 (gets full). 쓰레기통 is a transparent compound: 쓰레기 (trash/garbage) + 통 (bin/barrel/container). It is written as one word with no internal space.

usagePhrases.note: 빗자루 + 로 + 쓸다; 로 = with/using the tool

usagePhrases.en: to sweep the floor with a broom
usagePhrases.note: 바닥(floor) + 을 + 쓸다, the typical target
빗자루 + 질(act of) + 하다 = the act of broom-using
빗자루 + 와 + 쓰레받기, the standard pairing

examples.en: I sweep the floor with a broom.
examples.note: Core sentence; note the 로(with) + 을(object) frame.

examples.en: Could you bring me the broom and dustpan?
examples.note: Real request; 빗자루 almost always teams with 쓰레받기.

examples.ko: 마당에 낙엽이 많아서 빗자루로 싹 쓸었어요.
examples.romanization: madange nagyeobi manaseo bitjaruro ssak sseureosseoyo.
examples.en: There were lots of leaves in the yard, so I swept them all up with a broom.
examples.note: 싹 = clean/completely (sweeping adverb); 마당 = yard.

entries.nuance: 빗자루 is the broom you sweep floors and yards with, and its inseparable verb is 쓸다 (to sweep), with the tool marked by 로/으로: 빗자루로 쓸다 ('sweep with a broom'). It naturally travels with its partner 쓰레받기 (dustpan) — you sweep the dust into the dustpan. The central English-speaker pitfall is mixing up cleaning verbs: 쓸다 (sweep, with a broom) versus 닦다 (wipe, with a cloth) versus 쓸다's lookalike tasks. Sweeping loose dirt/dust off a floor is 쓸다; wiping a surface clean with a rag is 닦다 — don't say 빗자루로 닦다. A second trap is the near-homonym 빗 (a hair comb) and 빗다 (to comb one's hair): 빗자루 (broom) and 빗 (comb) share the 빗 syllable and even the brushing image, but they are different objects — you 빗으로 머리를 빗다 (comb hair with a comb) but 빗자루로 바닥을 쓸다 (sweep the floor with a broom). The act of sweeping can also be nominalized as 빗자루질 / 비질.

Pairing 빗자루 with 닦다 ('wipe'). A broom sweeps → 쓸다 (빗자루로 쓸다); wiping a surface with a cloth is 닦다 (걸레로 닦다).

걸레 + 를 + 빨다; 빨다 = wash cloth/laundry
걸레 + 질(act of) + 하다 = do floor-wiping
걸레 + 를 + 짜다 = squeeze water out

examples.en: I wipe the floor with a rag.
examples.note: Core sentence; 로(with) + 을(object) again.

examples.en: The rag was dirty, so I washed and wrung it out.
examples.note: 빨다(wash) → 짜다(wring), the natural sequence with ~서.

examples.ko: 물 쏟았으니까 걸레로 좀 닦아 줄래?
examples.romanization: mul ssodasseunikka geollero jom dakka jullae?
examples.en: I spilled water, so could you wipe it up with a rag?
examples.note: Casual request; 쏟다 = spill — a real trigger for grabbing a 걸레.

entries.nuance: 걸레 is the cleaning rag or floor cloth used for the dirty work of wiping floors and surfaces, paired with the verb 닦다 (to wipe) and the tool particle 로: 걸레로 닦다. The act of mopping/wiping the floor with it is 걸레질. Two contrasts are essential. By cloth-type: a 걸레 is a grubby floor/cleaning rag (low-status, gets filthy), 행주 is a clean dishcloth for wiping the kitchen counter and dishes, and 수건 is a towel for drying your body — Koreans keep these strictly separate, and calling a kitchen cloth a 걸레 sounds unhygienic. (Note: 걸레 is also a strong insult when applied to a person, so use it only for the object.) The big verb pitfall is washing it: a dirty rag is cleaned with 빨다 (the verb for washing cloth and laundry), NOT 씻다. 씻다 is for washing your body or rinsing dishes/produce; fabric is 빨다. After washing you 짜다 (wring) it. Don't confuse the wiping verb either: 걸레로 닦다 (wipe), not 쓸다 (which needs a broom).

Washing a rag with 씻다. Cloth and laundry are washed with 빨다 → 걸레를 빨다. 씻다 is for the body, hands, dishes, or fruit.
Calling a kitchen dishcloth a 걸레. The clean cloth for counters/dishes is 행주; a 걸레 is the grubby floor rag (and 걸레 is also an insult for a person).
Using 쓸다 ('sweep') with 걸레. A cloth wipes → 닦다 (걸레로 닦다); sweeping needs a broom (빗자루로 쓸다).

usagePhrases.note: 다리미 + 로 + 다리다; tool 로 + the verb 다리다
셔츠(shirt) + 를 + 다리다, a typical target
다리미 + 이/가 + 뜨겁다, the key safety adjective
다리미 + 를 + 켜다 = switch it on to heat

examples.en: I iron the shirt with the iron.
examples.note: Core sentence; note tool 다리미로 + verb 다리다.

examples.en: The iron's hot, so be careful.
examples.note: 뜨겁다(hot) + 조심하다(be careful) — the standard warning.

examples.ko: 면 셔츠는 주름이 잘 가서 매번 다리미로 다려야 해요.
examples.romanization: myeon syeocheuneun jureumi jal gaseo maebeon darimiro daryeoya haeyo.
examples.en: Cotton shirts wrinkle easily, so I have to iron them every time.
examples.note: 주름이 가다 = get wrinkles; ~아야 하다 = have to.

entries.nuance: 다리미 is the clothes iron — the appliance — and it derives from the verb 다리다 (to iron) plus the instrument-forming suffix -이, so it literally means 'the thing for ironing'. This built-in relationship is exactly the trap: the noun 다리미 (the iron) and the verb 다리다 (to iron) look and sound nearly identical, and learners constantly blur them. Lock the pattern as 다리미로 다리다 — 'iron WITH the iron', tool marked by 로, action by the verb 다리다. A second, classic homophone-style pitfall is 다리, which is a completely different word meaning 'leg' or 'bridge' (and the verb 달이다 'to brew/decoct medicine' sounds close too) — only 다리미/다리다 concern clothes. Note the irregular-looking conjugation of the verb: 다리다 → 다려요 (the 이+어 contracts to 여). The iron's defining adjective is 뜨겁다 (hot), and you 켜다 (turn on) the iron to heat it; the ironing board it sits on is a separate item, 다리미판.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Blurring the noun and verb: 다리미 is the iron (the tool), and 다리다 is the action 'to iron'. Say 다리미로 옷을 다려요.
Mixing 다리미 (iron) with 다리 (leg / bridge). They share the 다리 sound but are unrelated words.
Conjugating the verb as 다리어요. 다리다 contracts to 다려요 in the polite present (이 + 어 → 여).

entries.shortExplanation: 벽시계 means "wall clock" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "wall clock" is 벽시계 (byeoksigye). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벽시계를 걸다 ("to hang the wall clock"). Watch the particle attached to 벽시계 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 벽시계 + 를 + 걸다, since it hangs on a wall

usagePhrases.en: a wall clock is hanging on the wall
usagePhrases.note: 벽 + 에 + 걸려 있다 = is in a hung state
벽시계 + 이/가 + 멈추다, often when the battery dies

usagePhrases.en: to change the wall clock's battery
usagePhrases.note: 건전지(battery) + 를 + 갈다 = replace

examples.en: There's a wall clock in the living room.
examples.note: Basic existence + location.

examples.en: Looking at the wall clock, it's already three o'clock.
examples.note: 보니까 = upon looking; ~네요 = mild realization.

examples.en: The wall clock stopped, so I changed the battery.
examples.note: 멈추다(stop) → 건전지 갈다(change battery): the typical fix.

entries.nuance: 벽시계 is a transparent compound, 벽 (wall) + 시계 (clock/watch), so 'wall clock'. The base 시계 is itself Sino-Korean (時計, 'time-measure') and is the family root for a whole set of timepieces: 손목시계 (wrist + clock = wristwatch), 알람시계 / 자명종 (alarm clock), 탁상시계 (desk clock), 모래시계 (sand clock = hourglass), and 해시계 (sun clock = sundial). The English-speaker pitfall is that English splits 'clock' (on a wall/desk) from 'watch' (on the wrist), but Korean uses one word 시계 for both and just prefixes the location: a watch is literally a 'wrist-clock', 손목시계. As an object that hangs, a 벽시계 takes 걸다 (hang) and rests as 걸려 있다 ('is hanging'), exactly like a 액자 or 달력. When it 멈추다 (stops), the usual cause is a dead 건전지 (battery), which you 갈다 (replace). To 'check the time', you 시계를 보다 (look at the clock).

Looking for a separate word for 'watch' vs 'clock'. Korean uses 시계 for both; a wristwatch is just 손목시계 (wrist-clock), a wall clock is 벽시계.
Hanging the clock with 붙이다 ('stick'). It hangs from a hook → 걸다 / 걸려 있다, like a picture frame, not 붙이다.
Saying 벽시계가 죽었어요 for a stopped clock. Use 멈추다: 벽시계가 멈췄어요 — usually the 건전지(battery) needs replacing.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매트, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to lay down / spread out a mat
usagePhrases.note: 매트 + 를 + 깔다; 깔다 = spread flat on a surface
매트 + 위에서 + 운동하다; 위에서 = on top of (action)
요가(yoga) + 매트, names its use
현관(entryway) + 매트, names where it lies

examples.en: I laid a mat on the floor.
examples.note: Core sentence; 깔다 is THE verb for spreading a flat thing down.

examples.en: The baby crawls around on the mat.
examples.note: 위에서 = on top of (with motion); 기어 다니다 = crawl about.

examples.en: Since I'm going to work out, I laid out the yoga mat first.
examples.note: Real prep sequence; ~부터 = (starting) with, ~ㄹ 거라서 = because I'm going to.

entries.nuance: 매트 is a loanword from English 'mat' and covers the family of flat floor mats: 요가 매트 (yoga mat), 현관 매트 (doormat), a baby's play mat, a bath mat, a camping mat. Its signature verb is 깔다, the specific motion of spreading something flat across a surface — you 매트를 깔다 (lay/spread a mat), the same verb used for spreading out bedding (이불을 깔다) or a picnic blanket. The English-speaker pitfall here is verb choice: don't say 매트를 놓다. 놓다 means to set/place a discrete object down on a surface (a cup, a book), whereas a flat sheet that you spread out is 깔다. A second trap is the near-loanword 매트리스 (mattress): a thin floor mat is 매트, but the thick sprung bed you sleep on is 매트리스 — close in sound, different objects. When marking where action happens on the mat, use 위에서 (on top of, for an activity like exercising or playing); plain 위에 marks static location ('on the mat').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Laying a mat with 놓다 ('place'). A flat mat is spread out → 깔다 (매트를 깔다). 놓다 is for setting down a solid object like a cup or book.
Confusing 매트 (a thin flat mat) with 매트리스 (a thick bed mattress). Similar sound, different things.
Using 매트 위에 for an activity done on it. For exercising/playing ON the mat use the action-location 위에서: 매트 위에서 운동해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 부엌 means "kitchen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부엌 (bueok) means "kitchen". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부엌에서 요리하다 ("cook in the kitchen"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부엌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 부엌 takes 에서 because cooking is a dynamic action done there
describing the room itself uses 이/가 + descriptive verb
common chore collocation; 치우다 = clear away/tidy
살림 = household goods & housekeeping; a very natural pairing

examples.en: Where is the kitchen?
examples.note: Simplest form: noun + 이 + 어디예요? to ask location

examples.en: Mom is making kimchi stew in the kitchen.
examples.note: Everyday scene: 에서 for the action + 을/를 for what she cooks

examples.ko: 이사 온 집은 부엌이 좁아서 조금 불편해요.
examples.romanization: isa on jibeun bueoki jobaseo jogeum bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The place we moved into has a small kitchen, so it's a bit inconvenient.
examples.note: Real-life complaint: 부엌이 좁아서 (cause) leads into a reaction

entries.nuance: 부엌 is the warm, native-Korean everyday word for the room where you cook and wash dishes — the heart of the home where the smell of food lives. Its nearest synonym is the Sino-Korean 주방 (廚房, 'cooking-room'): 주방 is the neutral, technical label you see on apartment floor plans, restaurant signs, and in compounds like 주방용품 (kitchen goods), whereas 부엌 carries a homier, more personal feeling — 우리 집 부엌 sounds natural, 우리 집 주방 sounds like a brochure. Both are everyday and polite; there's no status caution. It collocates with 요리하다, 치우다, and 부엌 살림. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the final consonant: it ends in ㅋ (부엌), so the spelling is fixed even though it's pronounced [부억] before a pause — never write 부억. The second trap is particle choice: use 부엌에서 for an action happening there, but 부엌에 for where something simply sits (부엌에 냉장고가 있어요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 부억 instead of 부엌 — it is pronounced [부억] before a pause, but the correct final letter is always ㅋ, so the spelling never changes.
Saying 부엌에 요리해요 for the action of cooking — an action done in a place needs 에서, so it must be 부엌에서 요리해요; 에 only marks where something exists.
Calling a restaurant or floor-plan kitchen 부엌 in a formal label — there the neutral word 주방 (주방용품, 공용 주방) is expected; 부엌 sounds like a cozy home kitchen.

entries.nuance: 욕실 (浴室, 'bathing-room') is the Sino-Korean word for the home room you wash and shower in, the part with the tub, sink, and showerhead. Its constant point of confusion is 화장실 (化粧室, literally 'makeup-room'): 화장실 foregrounds the toilet and is the word you actually say when you need to 'go to the restroom' or ask for one in public, while 욕실 foregrounds the bathing function of a private home. Using 에 for the washing action (욕실에 샤워해요) — an action done there needs 에서, so it must be 욕실에서 샤워해요.

entries.nuance: 서재 (書齋, 書 'book/writing' + 齋 'studio/room') is a private room inside a home set aside for reading, studying, and desk work, usually lined with bookshelves and quietly personal in feel — historically the scholar's room. Two synonyms get confused with it. 도서관 (圖書館, 'library') is a public building where anyone borrows books, the opposite of private; 교실 (敎室, 'classroom') is where a class is taught at school. 서재 is none of these — it is your own room at home. It is neutral and polite, often introduced by whose it is (아빠 서재, 할아버지 서재). It collocates with 책을 읽다, 책이 가득하다, and 서재를 꾸미다. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'study' onto 공부 (the activity of studying): 서재 is the physical room, never the act, so 'I have to study' is 공부해야 해요, not anything with 서재. A second pitfall is reaching for 서재 to mean a public library — that is 도서관.

Using 서재 to mean a public library — that is 도서관; 서재 is strictly a private room inside someone's home.
Saying 서재해요 to mean 'I study' — 서재 is a room, not an action; the verb 'to study' is 공부하다 (공부해요).
Using 에 for the action of reading (서재에 책을 읽어요) — reading is done there, so it needs 에서: 서재에서 책을 읽어요. Use 에 only for where things are (서재에 있어요).

entries.nuance: 지하 (地下, 地 'earth/ground' + 下 'below') literally means 'below the ground' and covers both a home's basement and the underground levels of any building. Its exact antonym is 지상 (地上, 'above ground'); together they split a building, and the boundary syllable 지 is shared, so keep 지하/지상 straight by the 下(below)/上(above) ending. A near-synonym for a home cellar is 지하실 (地下室, the basement room itself): 지하 names the underground zone or floor, while 지하실 names a specific room — say 지하실에서 빨래해요 for the laundry room, but 지하 2층 for floor B2. 지하 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 지하 주차장, 지하 1층, and 지하철 (the 'underground-iron-road,' i.e. subway). The English-speaker pitfall is floor order: floors going down are 지하 + number + 층 (지하 1층 = B1), with 지하 first — never 1층 지하. A second trap is using 'basement' for any low floor; 1층 (the ground floor) is above ground, not 지하.

Saying 1층 지하 for B1 — the fixed order is 지하 + number + 층, so it must be 지하 1층; the 지하 always comes first.
Calling the ground floor 지하 — 1층 is above ground (지상); 지하 begins at 지하 1층, one level below the entrance floor.
Mixing up 지하 and 지하실 — 지하 is the underground zone/floor (지하 2층), while 지하실 is the specific basement room you actually stand in (지하실에 있어요).

entries.nuance: 다락방 is the small, cozy room tucked directly under the sloped roof, with a low ceiling — the kind of hideaway kids love and families fill with seasonal boxes and old keepsakes. It's a native Korean compound: 다락 (the loft space under a roof) + 방 (room), so 다락방 specifically stresses that the loft is a usable room, while plain 다락 names the storage loft as a space (다락에 넣다 = stash it in the loft). It is warm and everyday, never formal, and pairs with 올라가다, 아늑하다, and storage verbs like 넣어 두다 / 올려놓다. The clearest English-speaker pitfall is direction particles: when you go up to it, the goal takes 에 (다락방에 올라가요), but the activity done inside takes 에서 (다락방에서 놀아요) — English 'in the attic' hides this split. A second trap is confusing the up/down spaces: 다락방 is under the roof at the top, the opposite of 지하 (the basement below the house).

Using 에서 for the act of going up (다락방에서 올라가요) — movement toward a goal takes 에, so it is 다락방에 올라가요; 에서 marks where an activity happens, not the destination.
Mixing up 다락방 (attic, under the roof) and 지하 (basement, below the house) — they are at opposite ends of the home; 다락방은 맨 위, 지하는 맨 아래.
Dropping 방 and using 다락 when you mean an inhabited room — 다락 is the loft as storage space, while 다락방 is the room you actually go up into and use.

entries.nuance: 창고 (倉庫, 倉 'granary' + 庫 'storehouse') is any space for keeping things — it scales from a small home storeroom to an outdoor shed to a full industrial warehouse, so context sets the size. At home it's where boxes, tools, and off-season items live. Its dangerous look-alike and near-homophone is 차고 (車庫, garage): they differ by a single ㅇ batchim — 창고 (storage) vs 차고 (car-garage) — and even share the 庫(storehouse) hanja, so learners constantly swap them; remember 창고 has the extra ㅇ for 'th-ings,' while 차(car)고 holds a car. 창고 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 넣다, 쌓아 두다, 정리하다, and 가득 차다. The key English-speaker pitfall is the particle with 넣다: putting something in takes the destination marker 에 (창고에 넣어요), not 에서 — 에서 would wrongly say the putting-action 'happens out of' the storeroom. A second pitfall is using 창고 for a car space; that specific meaning is 차고.

Saying 창고에서 넣어요 for putting something away — 넣다 marks the destination with 에, so it must be 창고에 넣어요; 에서 marks where an action takes place, not where the thing ends up.
Confusing 창고 (storeroom) with 차고 (garage) — they differ by one ㅇ and both contain 庫; 차고 holds a car, 창고 holds things.
Using 창고 for a big shipping/industrial sense without realizing the same word covers home storage too — size comes only from context, so 우리 집 창고 (small) and 물류 창고 (warehouse) are both correct.

Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: put the car in the garage
usagePhrases.note: 에 (destination) + 넣다; the everyday way to say 'park inside'
주차하다 (park) is the more formal verb for the same act
차고 + 문 compound; the up-and-over door

entries.nuance: 차고 (車庫, 車 'vehicle' + 庫 'storehouse', literally 'car-storehouse') is the home structure built to shelter a car, like a garage attached to a house. Two words sit close to it. The near-homophone 창고 (storeroom) differs by only an ㅇ batchim and shares the 庫 hanja, so they're endlessly mixed up: 차(car)고 holds a car, 창고 holds things. The functional near-synonym is 주차장 (駐車場, 'parking lot') — but that's the shared, often open lot for an apartment building or a public area, whereas 차고 is your own private, usually enclosed home garage; you'd say 아파트 주차장 but 우리 집 차고. 차고 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 차를 넣다/빼다, 주차하다, and 차고 문. The English-speaker pitfall is particle direction with the same noun: parking in takes 에 (차고에 넣어요), but taking the car out takes 에서 (차고에서 빼요) — 에 is the goal, 에서 is the source. A second trap is using 차고 for an apartment's communal lot; that is 주차장.

Confusing 차고 (garage, for a car) with 창고 (storeroom) — they differ by one ㅇ; if you say 창고에 차를 넣어요 you've parked the car in the junk room.
Calling an apartment's shared parking area 차고 — a communal or public lot is 주차장; 차고 is specifically your own private home garage.

entries.nuance: 정원 (庭園, 庭 'courtyard' + 園 'garden/park') is a deliberately planted, landscaped garden — flowers, lawn, ornamental trees — carrying a tidy, designed, somewhat refined feeling. A second neighbor is 텃밭, a kitchen vegetable patch grown for food, not for looks. 정원 is neutral and slightly elevated in tone. It collocates with 가꾸다, 꽃을 키우다, 잡초를 뽑다, and 정원이 딸린 집. A second trap is the particle: gardening actions take 에서 (정원에서 키워요), while where a plant sits takes 에 (정원에 나무가 있어요).

entries.nuance: 뒷마당 is the open yard behind a house — a casual, everyday space for kids, pets, chores, and weekend barbecues. The spelling hides a key rule: a 사이시옷 (linking ㅅ) is inserted because 마당 starts with a tense-able sound, so it's 뒷마당, pronounced [뒨마당], never 뒤마당. Its near-synonym tension is with 정원 (a planted, landscaped garden): 마당/뒷마당 is plain living ground, 정원 is cultivated greenery, so kids play in the 뒷마당 but flowers are grown in the 정원. 뒷마당 is casual and homey. Mixing up 뒷마당 (back) and 앞마당 (front) — 뒤 is behind the house and 앞 is in front; getting them backwards reverses the location.
Using 뒷마당 to mean a manicured flower garden — that planted, landscaped sense is 정원; 뒷마당 is just plain open back-of-house ground.

entries.nuance: 발코니 is a loanword (from English 'balcony') for an outdoor platform projecting from a room, fenced by a railing, where you can stand outside the building wall. In everyday Korean apartment talk people very often say 베란다 (also a loanword, 'veranda') for the similar covered service space off the living room — technically a 발코니 cantilevers out and a 베란다 sits on a setback below an upper floor, but in casual speech the two blur and 베란다 is heard more for the laundry/storage strip in apartments. Both are neutral, everyday words. 발코니 collocates with 커피를 마시다, 빨래를 널다, 화분 (flowerpots), and 난간. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling of the loanword: it's 발코니 (ㅂ-ㅏ-ㄹ), not 빌코니 or 발코니아 — follow the fixed Korean transcription. A second pitfall is assuming 발코니 and 베란다 are interchangeable in every register; they overlap heavily in speech but aren't strictly identical, and floor-plan documents distinguish them. Particle-wise, actions take 에서, position takes 에.

Assuming 발코니 and 베란다 are perfectly interchangeable — in casual speech they overlap, but strictly a 발코니 juts out while a 베란다 sits on a setback, and floor plans keep them separate.

Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

이/가 + adjective; describing the boundary wall
쌓다 = stack up, the verb for building a wall
너머 = the far side past a barrier

examples.en: The wall is high.
examples.note: Simple description: 이 + adjective 높다

examples.en: The cat is creeping along the top of the wall.
examples.note: Everyday scene: 담장 위 (top of the wall) + 살금살금 (stealthily)

examples.ko: 옆집과 우리 집 사이에 낮은 담장이 있어요.

examples.note: Real-life: 사이에 (between) shows 담장 as a property boundary

entries.nuance: 담장 is the outer wall or fence that encloses a house or its yard, marking the edge of the property — what you'd peek over to talk to a neighbor. Its plain synonym is 담, which means exactly the same boundary wall; 담장 just sounds slightly more substantial and concrete, and the two are freely interchangeable (담을 넘다 = 담장을 넘다). The crucial contrast is with 벽 (壁): 벽 is an interior or structural wall of a room or building (방 벽에 액자를 걸다, hang a frame on the room's wall), whereas 담/담장 is the outdoor perimeter wall — so a learner who says 담장에 그림을 걸어요 has hung a picture on the outside boundary wall, which sounds odd. 담장 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 넘다, 쌓다, 높다, and 담장 너머. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'wall' covers both indoor and outdoor: you must split it into 벽 (inside) vs 담/담장 (the fence around the yard). A second point: 넘다 ('go over') takes the object marker 을/를, so it's 담장을 넘다, not 담장에 넘다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 담장 for a room's inside wall — an interior or building wall is 벽; 담장 is only the outdoor boundary wall around a house or yard.
Saying 담장에 넘어요 for climbing over it — 넘다 takes the object marker, so it must be 담장을 넘어요; the thing you cross is a direct object, not a location with 에.
Thinking 담 and 담장 mean different things — they're the same boundary wall and interchangeable; 담장 just feels a touch more concrete.

entries.nuance: 마루 is the raised, open, wood-floored space in a traditional Korean house (the 대청마루), where the family sits, rests, and gathers — cool underfoot in summer because it's bare wood, not heated 온돌 floor. Its modern functional successor is 거실 (居室), the apartment living room: people in apartments overwhelmingly say 거실, while 마루 evokes an older hanok-style home, so describing your modern flat you'd say 거실에서 TV 봐요, not 마루에서. (Note 마루 can also just mean the wooden flooring/board itself, e.g. 마룻바닥.) It's a native word, neutral and a bit nostalgic. Because people sit and lie directly on it, 마루 pairs naturally with 앉다, 눕다, 시원하다, and 닦다. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with 앉다: the spot where you sit takes 에 (마루에 앉아요), not 에서 — 에서 is for a broader activity (마루에서 쉬어요), but the precise location of sitting/lying is 에. A second trap is calling a modern living room 마루; that's 거실.

Using 에서 with 앉다 for the sitting spot (마루에서 앉아요) — the exact place you sit takes 에: 마루에 앉아요. Reserve 에서 for a broader activity like 마루에서 쉬어요.
Assuming 마루 only means a 'room' — it also names the wooden flooring itself (마룻바닥), so context decides whether it's the hall or the floorboards.

에 + 걸리다 (get caught); the spot you snag your foot
이/가 + 높다; literally and also figuratively 'hard to access'

entries.nuance: 문턱 is the small raised step or sill at the bottom of a doorway that you step over when passing through. It's a native compound: 문 ('door') + 턱 ('ledge/step'), so it literally means 'the door's ledge.' Don't confuse it with the whole 문 (the door itself) or with 문지방 (a close synonym: the structural doorsill beam — 문지방 is the carpentry member, 문턱 the everyday word for the step you feel underfoot, and in daily speech 문턱 is far more common). Because it's a classic spot to stub a toe, it pairs with warnings (조심하다, 걸리다, 넘어지다). It also has a vivid idiom: 문턱이 높다 means figuratively 'the barrier to entry is high / it feels intimidating to go in' (그 회사는 문턱이 높다), and 문턱이 닳도록 드나들다 means 'visit so often you wear the doorsill down.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with 넘다: the sill is a direct object, so it's 문턱을 넘다, not 문턱에 넘다 — but 'trip ON it' uses 에 with 걸리다 (문턱에 걸리다). A second pitfall is taking 문턱이 높다 literally when a Korean means it figuratively.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 문턱에 넘어요 for stepping over it — 넘다 takes the object marker, so it is 문턱을 넘어요; the sill is what you cross, not a location with 에.
Confusing 문턱 (the doorsill you step over) with 문 (the whole door) — they aren't the same part; 문턱 is only the raised step at the bottom of the doorway.
Reading 문턱이 높다 literally when it's used figuratively — besides 'the sill is high,' it idiomatically means 'the barrier to entry is high / it feels intimidating to go in.'

structuredNuance.t: 문턱 is the small raised step or sill at the bottom of a doorway that you step over when passing through. It also has a vivid idiom: 문턱이 높다 means figuratively 'the barrier to entry is high / it feels intimidating to go in' (그 회사는 문턱이 높다), and 문턱이 닳도록 드나들다 means 'visit so often you wear the doorsill down.'

entries.nuance: 채소 (菜蔬, literally 'greens-vegetables') is the standard, slightly more formal/written word for vegetables you cook or eat. Its everyday spoken twin is 야채 (野菜 'field vegetable'); they overlap almost completely, but signs, recipes, nutrition labels and polite speech lean 채소, while casual conversation often says 야채. Do not confuse it with 과일 'fruit' — Korean draws the vegetable/fruit line just like English. The natural partners are 신선하다 (fresh), 먹다, and the prep verbs 씻다/다듬다. English-speaker pitfall: 채소 is normally treated as an uncountable mass like the English plural, so you say 채소를 많이 먹어요 ('eat a lot'), not a counted '*three vegetables'; reach for a specific name plus a counter when you must count.

Saying 채소들 with the plural -들 the way English forces 'vegetables' plural — Korean treats it as a mass noun, so plain 채소 already covers many; add 많이 for 'a lot' instead.
Mixing up 채소 with 과일 'fruit' — a tomato or cucumber dish is 채소, an apple is 과일; they are separate categories, not interchangeable.
Writing 채속 — the word ends in 소 (the 菜蔬 reading), so the spelling is 채소.

entries.nuance: 식빵 (食빵, the Sino-Korean 食 'to eat/food' + the loanword 빵 'bread' from Portuguese 'pão') is specifically the plain rectangular sandwich loaf you slice for toast — white, soft, unsweetened. It contrasts sharply with 빵, the umbrella word for all bread and pastry: every 식빵 is 빵, but a sweet cream bun or croissant is 빵 and never 식빵. Its habitual partners are 굽다 (toast), 바르다 (spread butter/jam), and the counters 봉지 (a bagged loaf) or 장 (one slice). English-speaker pitfall: don't stretch 식빵 to mean 'bread' in general — order a baguette or a bun and you want 빵, not 식빵; and remember a single slice is counted with 장, not the all-purpose 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 식빵 for every kind of bread — it means only the plain square sandwich loaf; a bakery bun, baguette, or croissant is just 빵.
Counting slices with 개 ('식빵 두 개') — a flat slice takes 장 (식빵 두 장); 봉지 is the whole bagged loaf.
Assuming 식빵 is sweet like dessert bread — it is intentionally plain and is the toast/sandwich base, with sweetness coming from the jam or honey you add.

entries.nuance: 쌀 is the raw, uncooked grain — the dry kernels you buy, store, rinse, and load into the cooker. The moment it is cooked it becomes 밥, a completely different word: you never serve a bowl of '쌀' or eat '쌀' off your plate, you eat 밥. (English collapses both into 'rice', which is exactly the trap.) Going further back, the rice plant in the field is 벼, so Korean uses three words — 벼 (growing) → 쌀 (harvested grain) → 밥 (cooked) — where English uses one. Natural partners: 씻다 (rinse), 짓다/하다 (cook), 떨어지다 (run out). Pitfall: saying '쌀을 먹어요' for a meal sounds like you're eating dry grain; for 'I eat rice (a meal)' say 밥을 먹어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling cooked rice on your plate 쌀 — once it's cooked it is 밥; 쌀 is only the raw grain.
Saying 쌀을 먹어요 to mean 'I eat rice (a meal)' — use 밥을 먹어요; 쌀 here implies raw kernels.
Confusing 쌀 with the look-alike 쌀쌀하다 'be chilly' — unrelated; one is a grain, the other describes cold weather.

entries.nuance: 떡 is dense, chewy cake made by steaming and pounding rice (usually 쌀 or glutinous 찹쌀), not baked or sweet-fluffy. The trap for English speakers is the word 'cake': 떡 is nothing like Western 케이크 (sponge/birthday cake) — it is firm and 쫄깃 (springy-chewy), and Koreans clearly separate 떡, 빵 (baked bread), and 케이크. Its defining texture word is 쫄깃하다; it is 빚다 (shaped) and traditionally 돌리다 (shared with neighbors at a 집들이 housewarming) or eaten as 떡국 at 설날. Pitfall: expecting it to be soft/sweet — many learners are surprised it's chewy and only mildly sweet, and some 떡 (like 가래떡) is barely sweet at all.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting 떡 to be soft and sweet like a Western cake — it is firm and 쫄깃 (chewy); 'rice cake' is a loose translation, not a sponge cake.
Confusing 떡 with 빵 (baked bread) or 케이크 (sponge/birthday cake) — Korean keeps these three clearly apart by how they're made.
Counting it with 개 only — a cut slab takes 조각 (떡 한 조각); 개 fits a whole shaped piece but 조각 is the natural 'a piece of'.

entries.nuance: 국수 is thin wheat-flour noodles, classically served warm in a light broth (잔치국수, 멸치국수) as a humble, comforting everyday meal. Contrast it with 라면, the instant ramyeon eaten from a packet, and with 면 — 면 (麵) is the abstract 'noodle' element inside compounds (라면, 냉면, 짜장면), whereas 국수 is the standalone homey dish; you order a bowl of 국수, but you'd say 면 사리 'an extra portion of noodles'. Watch the look-alike 국 'soup': 국수 is noodles, 국 is the soup itself — one letter apart. Partners: 삶다 (boil), 말다 (drop into broth), counter 그릇. The famous idiom 국수 먹다/먹이다 means 'to get married', since wedding guests were traditionally served 국수.

Mixing up 국수 'noodles' and 국 'soup' — they look almost identical but 국 is the broth/soup and 국수 is the noodles in it.
Calling instant ramyeon 국수 — packet ramyeon is 라면; 국수 is fresh/dried wheat noodles in broth.
Counting it with 개 — a served portion is 한 그릇 (one bowl); use 개 only for, say, packaged bundles.

entries.nuance: 김 is the thin, crisp sheets of dried laver, lightly oiled and salted, eaten as a side (반찬) by wrapping a bite of 밥 — the everyday backbone of many Korean meals and lunchboxes. Confusing edible 김 with the homonym 김 'steam/vapor' (김이 나다 'it's steaming') — same syllable, totally different meaning, sorted out by context.
Counting sheets with 개 — a flat sheet is 한 장 (김 한 장); 개 is wrong for thin flat items.

entries.nuance: 치즈 is the loanword for cheese (from English), most often the individually wrapped square 슬라이스 치즈 that Koreans melt onto ramyeon, toast, rice, and 떡볶이 to make them milder and richer. Because it's a borrowed word it has no synonym to confuse it with, but learners do mix up the verbs: the cheese melts on its own with 녹다 (치즈가 녹았어요), while you melt something else with the causative 녹이다 — keep the pair straight. A flat slice is counted with 장 (치즈 한 장), not 개; a whole block could take 덩어리. Pitfall: don't write it 치스 — the long vowel is 즈, so it's 치-즈, and the natural taste word Koreans pair with melted 치즈 is 고소하다 ('savory/nutty'), not the English 'creamy'.

Counting a slice with 개 ('치즈 한 개') — a flat slice is 한 장 (치즈 한 장); 개 suits a whole lump or item.
Using the active 녹이다 for the cheese itself ('치즈를 녹았어요') — the cheese melts intransitively: 치즈가 녹았어요; you use 녹이다 only when you melt something.

usagePhrases.en: I spread butter on the bread
usagePhrases.note: 바르다 'spread' (르-irregular → 발라요) with 에 for the surface
녹이다 'melt (something)' — the causative, you melt it in a pan
조각 'piece' for a cut block of butter
에 marks the butter as the medium you cook in

examples.en: I spread butter on the bread.
examples.note: simple past action

examples.en: I melt butter in the pan and fry an egg.
examples.note: 녹이다 then 부치다 'pan-fry', joined by -고

examples.ko: 이 빵은 버터를 듬뿍 넣어서 향이 진해요.
examples.romanization: i ppangeun beoteoreul deumppung neoeoseo hyangi jinhaeyo.
examples.en: This bread has lots of butter, so the aroma is rich.
examples.note: reason -아서 + 진하다 'rich/strong'

entries.nuance: 버터 is the loanword for butter (from English), used both as a spread on warm 식빵 and as a cooking fat that makes dishes richer (버터 with garlic, butter-fried eggs). As a borrowing it has no native synonym, but learners blur the melt-verbs just like with cheese: you actively melt butter with 녹이다 (버터를 녹여요), whereas it melts by itself with 녹다 (버터가 녹았어요) — same root, transitive vs intransitive. Spreading is 바르다, which is 르-irregular, so 'I spread' is 발라요, not '*바르어요' — a classic conjugation slip. A cut block is counted with 조각. Pitfall: spelling it 버타; the correct ending is 터, giving 버-터. Don't confuse it with 치즈 either — both are dairy, but 버터 is fat you spread/cook with, 치즈 is the cheese you melt on top.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 버타 — the final syllable is 터, so it's 버터; 버타 mis-hears the vowel.
Conjugating 바르다 as '*바르어요' — it's 르-irregular, so 'spread' is 발라요 (버터를 발라요).
Confusing 버터 with 치즈 — 버터 is the fat you spread on toast or fry with; 치즈 is cheese you slice and melt.

entries.explanation: 잼 (jaem) means "jam". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 식빵에 잼을 발라요 ("I spread jam on the bread"). usagePhrases.en: I spread jam on the bread
usagePhrases.note: 바르다 'spread' (르-irregular → 발라요), 에 for the surface
딸기 'strawberry' + 잼; the most common flavor, noun-noun compound
달다 'be sweet' is the defining taste; note 달다 is ㄹ-irregular (단 잼)
