entries.shortExplanation: 연말 means "end of the year" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연말 (yeonmal) means "end of the year". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 연말에 ("at the end of the year"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연말 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: at the end of the year
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the time point; the default way to say 'late in the year'
Set four-character phrase 年末年始 covering late Dec through early Jan
모임(gathering) — December is packed with these
정산 — the annual income-tax reconciliation every worker dreads/awaits

examples.en: It's already the end of the year.
examples.note: 연말 ends in a consonant, so 이에요; 벌써(already) fits the surprised tone

examples.en: I'm going on a trip with my family at the end of the year.
examples.note: 에 marks the time; 이랑 = casual 'with'

examples.ko: 연말이라 약속이 너무 많아서 정신이 없어요.
examples.romanization: yeonmarira yaksogi neomu manaseo jeongsini eopseoyo.
examples.en: It's year-end, so I have way too many plans and I'm swamped.
examples.note: Real-life: -이라(서) 'because it's', 정신이 없다 = to be frazzled

entries.nuance: 연말 is Sino-Korean 年末, literally 'year-end', meaning roughly December and the closing of the year; its opposite is 연초 年初 'year-beginning' (early January), and the two pair up just like 월초/월말 do. The 말(末) here is the very same 'end/closing' element found in 월말(month-end), 주말(weekend) and 학기말(end of term) — a reliable building block. A frequent confusion is 연말 vs 월말: 연(年) is 'year' and 월(月) is 'month', so 연말 = end of the YEAR while 월말 = end of the MONTH; mixing the hanja flips the scale entirely. Culturally, 연말 evokes a busy, festive rush — 송년회 'year-end parties', 모임, gift-giving — captured in the set phrase 연말연시 年末年始 'year-end and new-year', and in the workplace 연말정산 'year-end tax settlement'. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't say 끝 ('연끝' is not a word — 말 is the fixed bound morpheme for time-spans), use 연말에 with 에 for 'at year-end', and since 연말 ends in a consonant the copula is 이에요, not 예요.

Confusing 연말(end of YEAR, 年) with 월말(end of MONTH, 月) — the first hanja sets the scale.
Saying 연끝 — the fixed word is 연말; 끝 doesn't attach to time-spans the way 말 does.
Saying 연말예요 — it ends in a consonant, so the natural copula is 연말이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 밥그릇 means "rice bowl" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "rice bowl" is 밥그릇 (bapgeureut). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 밥그릇에 밥을 담다 ("to put rice in the rice bowl"). Watch the particle attached to 밥그릇 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to put rice in the rice bowl
usagePhrases.note: 담다 = to put/serve food into a container; pairs with 에 (location into which)
비우다 = to empty, here meaning to finish eating all the rice
Korean rice bowls are small and deep, not wide like a Western bowl
native counter 개 for individual bowls; 그릇 itself can also count servings

examples.en: The rice bowl is small.
examples.note: Subject marker 이 after the consonant-final 그릇; a plain descriptive sentence.

examples.en: Please fill the rice bowl with rice.
examples.note: 에 marks the bowl as the destination; 가득 (full) is the natural adverb with 담다.

examples.ko: 밥그릇은 들지 말고 식탁에 둔 채로 드세요.
examples.romanization: bapgeureuseun deulji malgo siktage dun chaero deuseyo.
examples.en: Don't lift the rice bowl; eat with it left on the table.
examples.note: Real table manners: 들다 = to lift, and -ㄴ 채로 means 'in the state of' leaving it down.

entries.nuance: 밥그릇은 밥(rice) + 그릇(vessel/bowl)이 합쳐진 순우리말로, 밥을 담는 작고 깊은 그릇을 가리켜요. 영어의 'bowl'은 샐러드볼처럼 넓은 것까지 다 포함하지만, 한국의 밥그릇은 한 사람 분량의 밥이 딱 들어가는 작은 크기라는 점이 달라요. 가장 가까운 말인 '공기(밥공기)'와 거의 같은 뜻이지만, 공기는 식당에서 밥의 단위로 더 자주 쓰여요(예: 공기밥 추가). 결정적인 문화 차이는, 일본과 달리 한국에서는 밥그릇을 손에 들지 않고 식탁에 둔 채 숟가락으로 떠먹는다는 점이에요. 영어식으로 그릇을 입가에 들고 먹으면 예의 없어 보이니 주의하세요. 또 'bowl of rice'를 직역해 '밥의 그릇'이라고 하면 어색하고, 한국어는 두 명사를 그냥 붙여 '밥그릇'이라고 합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Lifting the 밥그릇 to your mouth the way you would a Japanese rice bowl or a Western mug — in Korea you leave it on the table and use a spoon, so raising it reads as bad manners.
Translating 'a bowl of rice' word-for-word as 밥의 그릇 with 의; the natural compound is simply 밥그릇 (two nouns stuck together, no particle).
Mixing up 밥그릇 (rice bowl) and 국그릇 (soup bowl) — 밥그릇 is the smaller, deeper one and sits on the left in a standard place setting.

entries.shortExplanation: 국그릇 means "soup bowl" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 국그릇 (gukgeureut) = "soup bowl". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 국그릇에 국을 담다 ("to ladle soup into the soup bowl") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 국그릇, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to ladle soup into the soup bowl
usagePhrases.note: 담다 here = to ladle/serve; the soup is the object, the bowl takes 에
뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 뜨거워요; the metal/ceramic bowl heats up from the soup

usagePhrases.en: to place the soup bowl on the right
usagePhrases.note: standard Korean place setting puts 국그릇 to the right of 밥그릇
counter 개; wider and shallower than a 밥그릇

examples.en: The soup bowl is hot.
examples.note: 뜨겁다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so 뜨겁 + 어요 → 뜨거워요 — careful, the ㅂ becomes 우.

examples.en: Please ladle the soup into the soup bowl.
examples.note: 에 marks the bowl; 담다 covers both 'put in' and 'ladle' depending on the food.

examples.en: The rice bowl goes on the left, the soup bowl on the right.
examples.note: Contrast with the topic marker 은 on each item, showing the standard 상차림 layout.

entries.nuance: 국그릇은 국(soup) + 그릇이 결합한 순우리말로, 국이나 찌개를 담는, 밥그릇보다 넓고 큰 그릇이에요. 영어 'soup bowl'과 거의 일대일로 대응하지만, 한국 식탁에서는 국그릇의 '위치'가 중요해요 — 밥그릇은 왼쪽, 국그릇은 오른쪽에 놓는 것이 기본 상차림이라, 자리만 봐도 무엇을 담는 그릇인지 알 수 있어요. 비슷한 말로 '대접'이 있는데, 대접은 국보다 더 큰 음식(비빔밥, 칼국수)을 담는 한층 큰 그릇을 가리키니 크기로 구분하세요. 뜨거운 국이 담기므로 그릇 자체가 뜨거워지는데, 이때 쓰는 형용사 '뜨겁다'는 ㅂ불규칙이라 '뜨거워요'로 바뀌는 점을 같이 익혀 두면 좋아요. 영어 화자는 'hot'을 무조건 더운 날씨의 '덥다'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 사물·음식이 뜨거울 때는 반드시 '뜨겁다'를 써야 합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 국그릇 to mean a rice bowl or putting it on the left — by convention 국그릇 is wider and sits on the right, while the smaller 밥그릇 sits on the left.
Saying 국그릇이 더워요 for 'the bowl is hot'; 덥다 is only for weather/feeling warm, so a hot object or hot soup must be 뜨겁다 → 뜨거워요.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular: writing 뜨겁어요 instead of 뜨거워요. The ㅂ changes to 우 before a vowel ending.

structuredNuance.t: 국이나 찌개를 담는, 밥그릇보다 넓고 큰 그릇이에요. 영어 'soup bowl'과 거의 일대일로 대응하지만, 한국 식탁에서는 국그릇의 '위치'가 중요해요 — 밥그릇은 왼쪽, 국그릇은 오른쪽에 놓는 것이 기본 상차림이라, 자리만 봐도 무엇을 담는 그릇인지 알 수 있어요.

영어 화자는 'hot'을 무조건 더운 날씨의 '덥다'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 사물·음식이 뜨거울 때는 반드시 '뜨겁다'를 써야 합니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 물잔 means "water glass" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 물잔 (muljan) means "water glass". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 물잔에 물을 따르다 ("to pour water into the glass"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 물잔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to pour water into the glass
usagePhrases.note: 따르다 (르-irregular) → 따라요; the glass takes 에, the water is the object
비다 = to be empty (intransitive); 비우다 would be 'to empty (it)'
채우다 = to fill up; common when a host refills your glass
counter 개; 잔 also works as a counter for drinks (물 한 잔 = one glass of water)

examples.en: The water glass is empty.
examples.note: 비다 → 비었어요 (past); a gentle way to hint you'd like a refill.

examples.en: Please pour some water into the glass.
examples.note: 따르다 is 르-irregular → 따라요; 좀 softens the request politely.

examples.ko: 식당에서는 보통 물이랑 물잔이 셀프 코너에 있어요.
examples.romanization: sikdangeseoneun botong murirang muljani selpeu koneoe isseoyo.
examples.en: At restaurants the water and glasses are usually at the self-serve corner.
examples.note: Cultural note: 이랑 ('and', casual) links the two nouns; many Korean eateries are self-serve for water.

entries.nuance: 물잔은 물(water) + 잔(盞, a small cup for drinks)이 합쳐진 말이에요. 여기서 '잔'은 한자 盞에서 온 글자로, 본래 술이나 차를 따라 마시는 작은 잔을 뜻해서 술잔·찻잔처럼 마시는 그릇에 두루 붙어요. 가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '물컵'인데, 둘 다 통하지만 '컵(cup)'은 영어 외래어로 손잡이 있는 머그까지 폭넓게 가리키고, '잔'은 더 전통적이고 마시는 행위에 초점이 있어 물을 마실 때는 '물잔'이 한결 자연스러워요. 결정적인 영어식 실수는 'drink the glass'를 직역해 '물잔을 마시다'라고 하는 것 — 마시는 대상은 그릇이 아니라 내용물이므로 반드시 '(물잔에 든) 물을 마시다'라고 해야 해요. 또 물을 세는 단위로 쓸 때는 '물 한 잔'처럼 잔이 분류사가 된다는 점도 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 물잔을 마시다 ('drink the glass') by directly translating English — you drink the contents, so it must be 물을 마시다; the glass only holds it.
Assuming 물잔 and 물컵 are identical in feel; 컵 (from English 'cup') is broader and can mean a mug, while 잔 carries a more traditional 'drinking vessel' nuance and sounds natural for water and tea.
Forgetting 따르다 is 르-irregular: writing 따르어요 instead of 따라요 when pouring water.

structuredNuance.t: 물을 따라 마시는 잔이에요. 물을 세는 단위로 쓸 때는 '물 한 잔'처럼 잔이 분류사가 된다는 점도 기억하세요.
가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '물컵'인데, 둘 다 통하지만 '컵(cup)'은 영어 외래어로 손잡이 있는 머그까지 폭넓게 가리키고, '잔'은 더 전통적이고 마시는 행위에 초점이 있어 물을 마실 때는 '물잔'이 한결 자연스러워요.
물잔은 물(water) + 잔(盞, a small cup for drinks)이 합쳐진 말이에요. 여기서 '잔'은 한자 盞에서 온 글자로, 본래 술이나 차를 따라 마시는 작은 잔을 뜻해서 술잔·찻잔처럼 마시는 그릇에 두루 붙어요.
결정적인 영어식 실수는 'drink the glass'를 직역해 '물잔을 마시다'라고 하는 것 — 마시는 대상은 그릇이 아니라 내용물이므로 반드시 '(물잔에 든) 물을 마시다'라고 해야 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 앞접시 means "small individual plate (for sharing)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "small individual plate (for sharing)" is 앞접시 (apjeopsi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 앞접시에 덜다 ("to dish food onto your own small plate"). Watch the particle attached to 앞접시 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to dish food onto your own small plate
usagePhrases.note: 덜다 = to portion out some of a shared dish; 에 marks your plate as destination
one of the most-used restaurant phrases in Korea
하나 더 = one more; add 주세요 to make it a request

usagePhrases.en: to take a portion onto your plate and eat
usagePhrases.note: 덜어 먹다 = to serve yourself a portion and eat — the polite sharing manner

examples.en: Please give me a small plate.
examples.note: The single most common way to ask for a sharing plate; 주세요 = please give.

examples.en: Take the side dishes onto your own plate and eat.
examples.note: -어서 connects 'portion out' then 'eat'; this is standard table etiquette for shared food.

examples.en: Could you give me one more small plate?
examples.note: -시겠어요? is an extra-polite request form, nice when flagging down restaurant staff.

entries.nuance: 앞접시는 앞(front, 'in front of you') + 접시(plate)가 결합한 말로, 여럿이 함께 먹을 때 큰 그릇에서 음식을 각자 덜어 먹는 개인용 작은 접시를 가리켜요. 그냥 '접시'는 음식을 담는 접시 일반을 뜻하지만, '앞접시'는 '내 앞에 두고 덜어 먹는 개인 접시'라는 기능이 핵심이라는 점에서 갈려요. 비슷하게 음식을 나눌 때 쓰는 '덜다'(to portion out)와 한 세트로 외워 두면 좋아요. 한국 식당에서 "앞접시 주세요"는 거의 자동으로 나오는 필수 표현이라, 이 한마디만 익혀도 공유 음식 문화에 자연스럽게 낄 수 있어요. 영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 큰 공유 접시(찌개·고기)에서 바로 자기 입으로 가져가는 것인데, 한국에서는 일단 앞접시에 덜어서 먹는 것이 예의예요. 또 'small plate'를 작은 크기로만 이해해 '작은 접시'라고 하면 뜻이 흐려지니, 공유 상황에서는 '앞접시'라고 콕 집어 말하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Eating straight from the shared pot or platter — in Korea you first 덜다 (portion out) onto your 앞접시, so reaching in with your own chopsticks looks impolite.
Calling it 작은 접시 ('small plate') thinking size is the point; the meaning is functional — it's the personal plate in front of you for shared food, hence 앞(front)접시.
Confusing 앞접시 with the big serving 접시; the serving plate holds the communal dish, while the 앞접시 is your individual one.

structuredNuance.t: 여럿이 함께 먹을 때 큰 그릇에서 음식을 각자 덜어 먹는 개인용 작은 접시를 가리켜요. 한국 식당에서 "앞접시 주세요"는 거의 자동으로 나오는 필수 표현이라, 이 한마디만 익혀도 공유 음식 문화에 자연스럽게 낄 수 있어요. 비슷하게 음식을 나눌 때 쓰는 '덜다'(to portion out)와 한 세트로 외워 두면 좋아요.
그냥 '접시'는 음식을 담는 접시 일반을 뜻하지만, '앞접시'는 '내 앞에 두고 덜어 먹는 개인 접시'라는 기능이 핵심이라는 점에서 갈려요.
앞접시는 앞(front, 'in front of you') + 접시(plate)가 결합한 말이에요.
영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 큰 공유 접시(찌개·고기)에서 바로 자기 입으로 가져가는 것인데, 한국에서는 일단 앞접시에 덜어서 먹는 것이 예의예요. 또 'small plate'를 작은 크기로만 이해해 '작은 접시'라고 하면 뜻이 흐려지니, 공유 상황에서는 '앞접시'라고 콕 집어 말하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 쟁반 means "tray" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쟁반 (jaengban) = "tray". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쟁반에 놓다 ("to place on the tray") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쟁반, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the tray as the surface; 놓다 = to set down
들다 = to lift/carry by hand; what you do to move a loaded tray

usagePhrases.en: to serve resting on a tray
usagePhrases.note: 받치다 = to support underneath; the polite way to bring drinks to a guest
counter 개 also works (쟁반 한 개); 쟁반 itself is a flat carrying board

examples.en: The tray is heavy.
examples.note: Simple descriptive sentence; subject marker 이 after consonant-final 쟁반.

examples.en: I put the cups on a tray and brought them over.
examples.note: -어서 links 'load onto the tray' and 'bring'; 올리다 = to place on top.

examples.en: I served the guest tea resting on a tray.
examples.note: 받치다 (to support from below) shows the courteous serving manner; 에게 marks the guest as recipient.

entries.nuance: 쟁반은 그릇·컵 여러 개를 한꺼번에 옮길 때 쓰는 납작한 운반 도구예요. 핵심은 '담는 그릇'이 아니라 '나르는 판'이라는 점이라, 영어 'tray'와 잘 맞아요. 가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '식판'인데, 식판은 칸이 나뉘어 음식을 직접 담아 먹는 구내식당용 식기인 반면, 쟁반은 음식을 직접 담지 않고 그릇째 받쳐 옮기는 평평한 판이라는 점이 결정적 차이예요. 또 '접시'(plate)와도 다른데, 접시는 음식을 담아 먹는 식기이고 쟁반은 그 접시들을 얹어 나르는 도구예요. 집에서 손님에게 차나 음료를 낼 때 잔을 쟁반에 받쳐 내면 정중해 보이고, 이때 '받치다'(아래에서 받쳐 주다)라는 동사와 함께 자주 쓰여요. 영어 화자는 'a tray of food'를 떠올려 쟁반에 음식을 바로 담는다고 생각하기 쉬운데, 한국에서는 그릇에 담은 뒤 그 그릇을 쟁반에 올려 옮긴다고 이해하는 것이 자연스러워요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 쟁반 to mean a plate you eat from; 쟁반 is for carrying dishes, not for holding food directly — that's a 접시 (plate) or 식판 (meal tray).
Confusing 쟁반 (flat carrying tray) with 식판 (sectioned cafeteria tray you eat from). If it has molded compartments and you eat off it, it's a 식판, not a 쟁반.
Saying 쟁반에 음식을 담다 as if you serve food straight onto the tray; you put food in bowls/plates first, then 쟁반에 올리다 (place them on the tray) to carry.

structuredNuance.t: 그릇·컵 여러 개를 한꺼번에 옮길 때 쓰는 납작한 운반 도구예요. 핵심은 '담는 그릇'이 아니라 '나르는 판'이라는 점이라, 영어 'tray'와 잘 맞아요. 집에서 손님에게 차나 음료를 낼 때 잔을 쟁반에 받쳐 내면 정중해 보이고, 이때 '받치다'(아래에서 받쳐 주다)라는 동사와 함께 자주 쓰여요.
가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '식판'인데, 식판은 칸이 나뉘어 음식을 직접 담아 먹는 구내식당용 식기인 반면, 쟁반은 음식을 직접 담지 않고 그릇째 받쳐 옮기는 평평한 판이라는 점이 결정적 차이예요. 또 '접시'(plate)와도 다른데, 접시는 음식을 담아 먹는 식기이고 쟁반은 그 접시들을 얹어 나르는 도구예요.
영어 화자는 'a tray of food'를 떠올려 쟁반에 음식을 바로 담는다고 생각하기 쉬운데, 한국에서는 그릇에 담은 뒤 그 그릇을 쟁반에 올려 옮긴다고 이해하는 것이 자연스러워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 식판 means "cafeteria meal tray" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 식판 (sikpan) means "cafeteria meal tray". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 식판에 받다 ("to get food served onto your tray"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 식판 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to get food served onto your tray
usagePhrases.note: 받다 = to receive (get served); used as you go down the canteen line
들다 = to hold/carry; you carry your own 식판 to your seat
반납(返納) = to give back; you bus your own 식판 at the return window
반납구 = the slot/window where you hand in the used tray

examples.en: I got rice and soup on my tray.
examples.note: 받다 = to be served; 이랑 casually links the two foods as you go through the line.

examples.en: After eating, I returned the tray.
examples.note: Sequence with -고; 반납하다 (Sino-Korean 返納 'return') is the set verb for handing back the tray.

examples.ko: 식판은 한 판에 칸이 나뉘어 있어요.
examples.romanization: sikpaneun han pane kani nanwieo isseoyo.
examples.en: A meal tray has compartments divided into one board.
examples.note: Topic 은 introduces the defining feature — sectioned compartments — that distinguishes 식판 from 쟁반.

entries.nuance: 식판은 식(食, 'eat/food') + 판(板, 'board/plate')이 결합한 한자어로, 학교·군대·회사 구내식당에서 쓰는, 한 판에 칸이 나뉜 식기예요. 밥·국·반찬을 칸칸이 담아 한 번에 먹고, 다 먹으면 보통 반납구에 직접 갖다 놓는 것이 한국식 셀프 문화예요. 가장 흔한 혼동은 '쟁반'과의 구분인데, 쟁반은 그릇을 얹어 나르는 평평한 판일 뿐 음식을 직접 담지 않지만, 식판은 칸에 음식을 직접 담아 그대로 먹는 식기라는 점이 결정적으로 달라요. 또 식판과 함께 거의 항상 등장하는 한자어 '반납(返納, return)'을 세트로 외워 두면 좋은데, '돌려준다'는 뜻이라 도서관 책 반납처럼 다른 데도 쓰여요. 영어 화자는 'tray'라는 한 단어 안에 쟁반과 식판을 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 칸이 나뉘어 그 위에서 바로 먹으면 '식판', 그릇을 얹어 옮기기만 하면 '쟁반'으로 갈라 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a 식판 a 쟁반 (or vice versa) — if it has molded compartments and you eat directly off it, it's a 식판; a 쟁반 is the flat board you only carry dishes on.
Forgetting the self-service 반납 (return): in Korean canteens you usually carry your 식판 to the 반납구 yourself, rather than leaving it for staff to clear.
Treating 식판 as a Western 'plate' and trying to use 접시 instead; 접시 is a single round plate, while a 식판 is the one-piece sectioned tray specific to cafeterias.

structuredNuance.t: 학교·군대·회사 구내식당에서 쓰는, 한 판에 칸이 나뉜 식기예요. 밥·국·반찬을 칸칸이 담아 한 번에 먹고, 다 먹으면 보통 반납구에 직접 갖다 놓는 것이 한국식 셀프 문화예요.

영어 화자는 'tray'라는 한 단어 안에 쟁반과 식판을 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 칸이 나뉘어 그 위에서 바로 먹으면 '식판', 그릇을 얹어 옮기기만 하면 '쟁반'으로 갈라 기억하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 그릇뚜껑 means "bowl lid / dish cover" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bowl lid / dish cover" is 그릇뚜껑 (geureutttukkeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그릇뚜껑을 덮다 ("to put the lid on the bowl"). Watch the particle attached to 그릇뚜껑 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to put the lid on the bowl
usagePhrases.note: 덮다 = to cover; the lid goes over the bowl's opening
열다 = to open; here lifting off the cover
맞다 = to fit/match; used about whether the lid is the right size

usagePhrases.en: to close the bowl with its lid
usagePhrases.note: 닫다 = to close; common for sealing leftovers

examples.en: The bowl lid doesn't fit.
examples.note: 맞다 = to fit; 안 makes it negative — a frequent kitchen complaint about mismatched lids.

examples.en: Put the lid on the leftover food (and leave it).
examples.note: -어 두다 = do and leave in that state; 덮다 is the verb for covering with a lid.

examples.en: It's hot, so open the bowl lid carefully.
examples.note: -니까 gives the reason; 열다 → 여세요 (the ㄹ drops before 세요) when opening.

entries.nuance: 그릇뚜껑은 그릇(bowl/vessel) + 뚜껑(lid)이 합쳐진 순우리말로, 그릇 위에 덮는 뚜껑을 가리켜요. 음식을 따뜻하게 보관하거나 남은 음식을 덮어 둘 때 써요. 핵심 동사 짝은 '덮다(cover)'와 '열다(open)'인데, 한국어는 뚜껑을 '덮다/열다'라고 하지 영어 'close/open'을 그대로 옮겨 '닫다'만 쓰면 어색할 때가 있어요(덮다가 더 자연스러움). 그냥 '뚜껑'이라고만 해도 대개 통하지만, 냄비뚜껑·병뚜껑처럼 무엇의 뚜껑인지 분명히 하고 싶을 때 앞에 명사를 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 해요. 가장 가까운 혼동은 '냄비뚜껑(pot lid)'으로, 둘 다 뚜껑이지만 받치는 대상이 그릇이냐 냄비냐로 갈려요. 영어 화자는 'a lid for the bowl'을 직역해 '그릇을 위한 뚜껑'이라고 하기 쉬운데, 한국어는 두 명사를 그대로 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 한다는 점을 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 뚜껑 when it's unclear which lid you mean; if a pot lid and a bowl lid are both around, specify 그릇뚜껑 vs 냄비뚜껑 by attaching the noun in front.
Translating 'a lid for the bowl' as 그릇을 위한 뚜껑 with 위한; Korean just compounds the nouns → 그릇뚜껑.
Using 닫다 ('close') for putting a lid on; Koreans more naturally say 뚜껑을 덮다 (cover with the lid) and 뚜껑을 열다 (open it).

structuredNuance.t: 그릇 위에 덮는 뚜껑을 가리켜요. 음식을 따뜻하게 보관하거나 남은 음식을 덮어 둘 때 써요. 핵심 동사 짝은 '덮다(cover)'와 '열다(open)'인데, 한국어는 뚜껑을 '덮다/열다'라고 하지 영어 'close/open'을 그대로 옮겨 '닫다'만 쓰면 어색할 때가 있어요(덮다가 더 자연스러움). 그냥 '뚜껑'이라고만 해도 대개 통하지만, 냄비뚜껑·병뚜껑처럼 무엇의 뚜껑인지 분명히 하고 싶을 때 앞에 명사를 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 해요.
가장 가까운 혼동은 '냄비뚜껑(pot lid)'으로, 둘 다 뚜껑이지만 받치는 대상이 그릇이냐 냄비냐로 갈려요.
그릇뚜껑은 그릇(bowl/vessel) + 뚜껑(lid)이 합쳐진 순우리말이에요.
영어 화자는 'a lid for the bowl'을 직역해 '그릇을 위한 뚜껑'이라고 하기 쉬운데, 한국어는 두 명사를 그대로 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 한다는 점을 기억하세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 받침 means "saucer / coaster (stand under something)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 받침 (batchim) = "saucer / coaster (stand under something)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 받침에 놓다 ("to set on the saucer/stand") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 받침, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the stand as the surface; 놓다 = to put down
받치다 = to support from below — the verb the noun comes from
있다 expresses existence; 받침 없이 = without a stand
받침 compounds: 컵받침 (coaster), 냄비받침 (trivet) — '받침' = the thing underneath

examples.en: There's no saucer.
examples.note: 있다/없다 existence; a quick way to point out a missing stand under your cup.

examples.en: Put the hot cup on the saucer.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination; the saucer protects the table from the hot cup.

examples.en: Without a stand the cup slides around.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if/when; explains why the 받침 underneath is useful.

entries.nuance: 받침은 동사 '받치다(아래에서 받쳐 주다, to support from underneath)'에서 나온 명사로, 컵이나 그릇 '아래에' 받쳐 두는 작은 판을 두루 가리켜요. 그래서 핵심 의미는 '무엇의 아래에 두어 받쳐 주는 것'이고, 영어처럼 용도별로 saucer/coaster/trivet으로 쪼개지 않고 한 단어로 폭넓게 써요. 가장 가까운 짝은 '컵받침'인데, 받침이 일반적인 '아래 받치는 것' 전체를 뜻한다면 컵받침은 '컵 전용 받침'으로 범위가 좁아요 — 즉 컵받침은 받침의 한 종류예요. 같은 원리로 냄비받침(trivet)도 만들어져요. 영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 받침을 음식을 담아 먹는 접시로 오해하는 것인데, 받침은 먹는 그릇이 아니라 다른 것을 받쳐 두는 '바닥 판'이에요. 또 한국어 받침은 글자에서 자음이 아래에 받치는 부분(예: '강'의 ㅇ)도 가리키니, 식기 맥락인지 한글 맥락인지 문맥으로 구별하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 받침 is a plate you eat from; it's a stand placed underneath something (a cup, a pot), not a serving dish — the word literally comes from 받치다 'to support from below'.
Assuming 받침 only means a cup coaster; it's the general word for 'the thing underneath', so a trivet under a pot is 냄비받침 and a coaster under a cup is 컵받침.
Forgetting that 받침 also means the bottom consonant of a Korean syllable block; in a tableware context it's the physical stand, but learners sometimes mix the two senses.

structuredNuance.t: 컵이나 그릇 '아래에' 받쳐 두는 작은 판을 두루 가리켜요. 그래서 핵심 의미는 '무엇의 아래에 두어 받쳐 주는 것'이고, 영어처럼 용도별로 saucer/coaster/trivet으로 쪼개지 않고 한 단어로 폭넓게 써요.
가장 가까운 짝은 '컵받침'인데, 받침이 일반적인 '아래 받치는 것' 전체를 뜻한다면 컵받침은 '컵 전용 받침'으로 범위가 좁아요 — 즉 컵받침은 받침의 한 종류예요. 같은 원리로 냄비받침(trivet)도 만들어져요.
받침은 동사 '받치다(아래에서 받쳐 주다, to support from underneath)'에서 나온 명사예요. 또 한국어 받침은 글자에서 자음이 아래에 받치는 부분(예: '강'의 ㅇ)도 가리키니, 식기 맥락인지 한글 맥락인지 문맥으로 구별하세요.
영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 받침을 음식을 담아 먹는 접시로 오해하는 것인데, 받침은 먹는 그릇이 아니라 다른 것을 받쳐 두는 '바닥 판'이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 컵받침 means "coaster (for a cup)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 컵받침 (keopbatchim) means "coaster (for a cup)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 컵받침에 놓다 ("to put on the coaster"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 컵받침 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the coaster as the surface for the cup
깔다 = to spread/lay flat; what you do before setting the cup
받치다 = to support from below; 컵 아래에 컵받침을 받치다
counter 개; 컵받침 = 컵(cup) + 받침(stand)

examples.en: The coaster is pretty.
examples.note: Simple descriptive sentence; subject marker 이 after consonant-final 컵받침.

examples.en: Please put the cup on the coaster.
examples.note: 위에 = on top of; spells out that the cup sits above the coaster.

examples.en: I laid a coaster under the coffee cup.
examples.note: 밑에 = underneath; 깔다 → 깔았어요 is the natural verb for laying a flat coaster down.

entries.nuance: 컵받침은 컵(cup) + 받침(아래에 받치는 것)이 결합한 말로, 컵 아래에 까는 작은 받침을 뜻해요. 물방울이나 뜨거운 자국이 책상·식탁에 남지 않게 해 주는 것이 주된 쓰임이라 영어 'coaster'와 잘 맞아요. 상위 개념인 '받침'이 아래에 받치는 것 일반을 가리킨다면, 컵받침은 '컵 전용'으로 콕 집은 말이라는 점에서 갈려요. 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '냅킨'인데, 컵받침은 컵을 받쳐 자국을 막는 단단한 받침이고 냅킨은 입·손을 닦는 종이라 기능이 전혀 다르니 섞지 마세요. 격식을 갖춘 찻잔 세트의 받침 접시는 '컵받침'보다 '받침 접시'나 외래어 '소서(saucer)'라고도 하지만, 일상 카페에서는 '컵받침'이 가장 흔해요. 함께 쓰는 동사 '깔다(to lay flat)'도 익혀 두면 좋은데, 컵받침을 '깔다/놓다'라고 자연스럽게 말합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 컵받침 (a firm coaster the cup rests on) with 냅킨 (a paper napkin for your mouth/hands); their functions are completely different.
Using 컵받침 for any saucer; it specifically means a cup coaster, so a formal teacup's plate is better called 받침 접시 or 소서.
Saying 컵받침을 놓다 only and never 깔다; for laying a flat coaster down, Koreans naturally use 깔다 (깔았어요) as well as 놓다.

structuredNuance.t: 컵 아래에 까는 작은 받침을 뜻해요. 물방울이나 뜨거운 자국이 책상·식탁에 남지 않게 해 주는 것이 주된 쓰임이라 영어 'coaster'와 잘 맞아요. 함께 쓰는 동사 '깔다(to lay flat)'도 익혀 두면 좋은데, 컵받침을 '깔다/놓다'라고 자연스럽게 말합니다.

상위 개념인 '받침'이 아래에 받치는 것 일반을 가리킨다면, 컵받침은 '컵 전용'으로 콕 집은 말이라는 점에서 갈려요. 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '냅킨'인데, 컵받침은 컵을 받쳐 자국을 막는 단단한 받침이고 냅킨은 입·손을 닦는 종이라 기능이 전혀 다르니 섞지 마세요. 격식을 갖춘 찻잔 세트의 받침 접시는 '컵받침'보다 '받침 접시'나 외래어 '소서(saucer)'라고도 하지만, 일상 카페에서는 '컵받침'이 가장 흔해요.
컵받침은 컵(cup) + 받침(아래에 받치는 것)이 결합한 말이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 냅킨 means "napkin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "napkin" is 냅킨 (naepkin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 냅킨으로 닦다 ("to wipe with a napkin"). Watch the particle attached to 냅킨 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 = with (tool/means); 닦다 = to wipe
a constant restaurant request; 주세요 = please give
뽑다 = to pull out; you pull napkins from the 냅킨통 (dispenser)
counter 장 for thin flat sheets — not 개

examples.en: Just one more napkin, please.
examples.note: Counter 장 for flat paper; 만 = just, 더 = more — a precise, polite ask.

examples.en: I wiped my mouth with a napkin.
examples.note: 으로 marks the napkin as the tool; the typical after-eating action.

examples.ko: 냅킨은 식탁 위 통에서 뽑아 쓰면 돼요.
examples.romanization: naepkineun siktak wi tongeseo ppoba sseumyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can just pull napkins from the holder on the table.
examples.note: -(으)면 되다 = it's fine to / you may; describes the self-serve 냅킨통 setup.

entries.nuance: 냅킨은 영어 'napkin'을 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 입이나 손을 닦는 종이(또는 천)를 가리켜요. 한국 일상에서는 거의 항상 식당 식탁 위 '냅킨통'에 든 종이 냅킨을 뽑아 쓰는 일회용을 떠올려요. 가장 중요한 구분은 '휴지'와의 차이인데, 휴지는 코를 풀거나 화장실에서 쓰는 두루마리·갑 티슈 같은 일반 화장지를 뜻하고, 냅킨은 식사 중 입·손을 닦는 용도로 식탁에 두는 것이라 쓰임과 장소가 달라요. 식당에서 코를 닦을 종이가 필요할 때 무심코 '휴지'를 달라고 하면 다른 것을 가져올 수 있으니 상황에 맞게 골라 쓰세요. 가장 흔한 문법 실수는 분류사인데, 냅킨은 얇고 납작한 종이라 '개'가 아니라 '장(sheet)'으로 세요 — 냅킨 한 장이 맞고 냅킨 한 개는 어색해요. 또 닦는 도구임을 나타낼 때는 조사 '으로(with)'를 붙여 '냅킨으로 닦다'라고 합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting napkins with 개 instead of the flat-sheet counter 장; thin paper like napkins, tickets, and paper takes 장 (냅킨 한 장, not 한 개).
Confusing 냅킨 (for wiping mouth/hands at the table) with 휴지 (general tissue/toilet paper for your nose or the bathroom); asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong paper.
Dropping the 으로 particle and saying 냅킨 닦다; to mark the napkin as the means you wipe with, use 냅킨으로 닦다.

냅킨은 영어 'napkin'을 그대로 들여온 외래어예요.
가장 흔한 문법 실수는 분류사인데, 냅킨은 얇고 납작한 종이라 '개'가 아니라 '장(sheet)'으로 세요 — 냅킨 한 장이 맞고 냅킨 한 개는 어색해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 이쑤시개 means "toothpick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이쑤시개 (issusigae) = "toothpick". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이쑤시개로 이를 쑤시다 ("to pick one's teeth with a toothpick") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이쑤시개, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to pick one's teeth with a toothpick
usagePhrases.note: 으로 = with; 쑤시다 = to poke/pick at (between the teeth)
있다 question to ask staff; very common after a meal

usagePhrases.en: to use it while covering with one hand
usagePhrases.note: -고 links 'cover' then 'use'; the polite manner is to shield your mouth
counter 개; small stick taken from a holder near the register

examples.en: Do you have a toothpick?
examples.note: 있다 to check availability; the natural thing to ask the cashier after eating.

examples.en: I used a toothpick after eating.
examples.note: Sequence with -고; 쓰다 (to use) → 썼어요 for a one-off past action.

examples.ko: 이쑤시개는 한 손으로 입을 가리고 쓰는 게 예의예요.
examples.romanization: issusigaeneun han soneuro ibeul garigo sseuneun ge yeuiyeyo.
examples.en: It's polite to use a toothpick while covering your mouth with one hand.
examples.note: 가리다 = to cover/shield; -는 게 예의다 frames it as the courteous etiquette.

entries.nuance: 이쑤시개는 이(teeth) + 쑤시개(쑤시다 'to poke at'의 명사형)가 합쳐진 순우리말로, 글자 그대로 '이를 쑤시는 도구'예요. 그래서 이름만 봐도 용도가 보이고, 핵심 동사 '쑤시다(틈을 후비다)'와 한 세트로 외우면 좋아요. 영어 'toothpick'과 일대일로 대응하지만, 쓰임의 문화 규칙이 달라요 — 한국에서는 보통 한 손으로 입을 가리고 조심스럽게 써야 예의 바르게 보여요. 영어 화자가 흔히 범하는 실수는 칵테일 음식이나 과일을 콕 찍어 먹는 데 쓰는 'cocktail pick(꼬치/픽)'과 혼동하는 것인데, 이쑤시개는 어디까지나 이 사이를 청소하는 용도이지 음식을 찍어 먹는 도구가 아니에요(그건 보통 '꼬치'나 '포크'를 써요). 또 '있어요?'로 물을 때 조사 없이 '이쑤시개 있어요?'라고 자연스럽게 말하고, 도구임을 강조할 때만 '이쑤시개로'처럼 으로를 붙입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Picking your teeth out in the open without shielding your mouth; in Korea the polite way is to cover with one hand (한 손으로 가리고), so doing it openly looks rude.
Using an 이쑤시개 to spear fruit or appetizers as if it were a cocktail pick; it's meant for cleaning between teeth, while food is speared with a 꼬치 (skewer/pick) or 포크 (fork).
Adding the wrong particle in 이쑤시개를 있어요; existence with 있다 takes 이/가 or no particle (이쑤시개 있어요?), and 으로 only when marking it as the tool you use.

structuredNuance.t: 글자 그대로 '이를 쑤시는 도구'예요. 그래서 이름만 봐도 용도가 보이고, 핵심 동사 '쑤시다(틈을 후비다)'와 한 세트로 외우면 좋아요. 영어 'toothpick'과 일대일로 대응하지만, 쓰임의 문화 규칙이 달라요 — 한국에서는 보통 한 손으로 입을 가리고 조심스럽게 써야 예의 바르게 보여요. 또 '있어요?'로 물을 때 조사 없이 '이쑤시개 있어요?'라고 자연스럽게 말하고, 도구임을 강조할 때만 '이쑤시개로'처럼 으로를 붙입니다.
이쑤시개는 이(teeth) + 쑤시개(쑤시다 'to poke at'의 명사형)가 합쳐진 순우리말이에요.
영어 화자가 흔히 범하는 실수는 칵테일 음식이나 과일을 콕 찍어 먹는 데 쓰는 'cocktail pick(꼬치/픽)'과 혼동하는 것인데, 이쑤시개는 어디까지나 이 사이를 청소하는 용도이지 음식을 찍어 먹는 도구가 아니에요(그건 보통 '꼬치'나 '포크'를 써요).

entries.shortExplanation: 빨대 means "(drinking) straw" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 빨대 (ppaldae) means "(drinking) straw". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 빨대로 마시다 ("to drink with/through a straw"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 빨대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 = with (means); 마시다 takes the drink as object, not the straw
꽂다 = to insert/stick into; what you do to a juice pouch or cup
종이(paper) + 빨대; the eco-friendly type many cafes now use
counter 개; 빨대 = from 빨다 (to suck) + 대 (rod/stick)

examples.en: I drank juice through a straw.
examples.note: 으로 marks the straw as the means; the object you drink is 주스, not the straw.

examples.en: Please stick a straw in for me.
examples.note: 꽂다 = to insert; 좀 softens the request to put the straw into the drink.

examples.ko: 요즘은 카페에서 종이 빨대를 많이 줘요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun kapeeseo jongi ppaldaereul mani jwoyo.
examples.en: These days cafes often give paper straws.
examples.note: Trend note; 종이 빨대 (paper straw) contrasts with the older 플라스틱 빨대.

entries.nuance: 빨대는 '빨다(to suck)' + '대(가느다란 막대·줄기를 뜻하는 순우리말 명사, 막대기·낚싯대의 그 '대')'가 합쳐진 말로, 음료를 빨아 마시는 가느다란 관이에요. 이름에 동사 '빨다'가 들어 있어 쓰임이 바로 드러나는 점이 외우기 쉬워요. 가장 중요한 문법 포인트는, 영어 'drink the straw'식으로 '빨대를 마시다'라고 하면 틀린다는 거예요 — 마시는 대상은 음료이고 빨대는 수단이므로 '빨대로 (주스를) 마시다'처럼 조사 '으로'를 써야 해요. 발음·철자에서 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '빨래(laundry)'인데, 빨대(straw)와 빨래(washing)는 둘 다 '빨다'에서 왔지만 뜻이 전혀 다르니 받침과 끝소리에 주의하세요. 요즘 카페에서는 환경을 위해 플라스틱 대신 '종이 빨대'를 주는 곳이 많아, '종이 빨대'라는 합성도 자주 들려요. 빨대를 컵·팩에 꽂을 때는 동사 '꽂다(to insert)'와 함께 씁니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 빨대를 마시다 ('drink the straw') by copying English; you drink the beverage, so it's 빨대로 마시다 — the straw takes 으로 as the means.
Mixing up 빨대 (straw) and 빨래 (laundry) because they sound alike and both come from 빨다; watch the ending — 대 vs 래.
Using 넣다 ('put in') for inserting a straw when the precise verb is 꽂다 (to stick/insert into), as in 빨대를 꽂다.

structuredNuance.t: 음료를 빨아 마시는 가느다란 관이에요. 이름에 동사 '빨다'가 들어 있어 쓰임이 바로 드러나는 점이 외우기 쉬워요. 요즘 카페에서는 환경을 위해 플라스틱 대신 '종이 빨대'를 주는 곳이 많아, '종이 빨대'라는 합성도 자주 들려요. 빨대를 컵·팩에 꽂을 때는 동사 '꽂다(to insert)'와 함께 씁니다.
발음·철자에서 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '빨래(laundry)'인데, 빨대(straw)와 빨래(washing)는 둘 다 '빨다'에서 왔지만 뜻이 전혀 다르니 받침과 끝소리에 주의하세요.
빨대는 '빨다(to suck)' + '대(가느다란 막대·줄기를 뜻하는 순우리말 명사, 막대기·낚싯대의 그 '대')'가 합쳐진 말이에요.
가장 중요한 문법 포인트는, 영어 'drink the straw'식으로 '빨대를 마시다'라고 하면 틀린다는 거예요 — 마시는 대상은 음료이고 빨대는 수단이므로 '빨대로 (주스를) 마시다'처럼 조사 '으로'를 써야 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 종이컵 means "paper cup" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "paper cup" is 종이컵 (jongikeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 종이컵에 따르다 ("to pour into a paper cup"). Watch the particle attached to 종이컵 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to pour into a paper cup
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the cup; 따르다 (르-irregular) → 따라요

usagePhrases.en: to get water in a paper cup
usagePhrases.note: 받다 = to receive/catch (water from a dispenser) into the cup
일회용(一回用) = single-use; stresses that it's used once and tossed
counter 개; 종이(paper) + 컵(cup, from English)

examples.en: I got water in a paper cup and drank it.
examples.note: 받다 = to catch/receive water; -아 links filling then drinking.

examples.en: Please give me a paper cup.
examples.note: A quick, polite request; 하나 = one, 주세요 = please give.

examples.en: At work dinners people use a lot of paper cups.
examples.note: 때 = at the time of; practical setting where disposables get used.

entries.nuance: 종이컵은 종이(paper) + 컵(cup, 영어 외래어)이 합쳐진 말로, 한 번 쓰고 버리는 일회용 종이 컵이에요. 정수기 옆, 사무실, 행사장에서 흔히 보여요. 핵심 의미는 '일회용(一回用, single-use)'이라는 점이라, 여러 번 쓰는 '유리컵(glass)'이나 '머그컵(mug)'과 정반대 개념으로 묶여요 — 재질(종이)과 일회성이 동시에 강조되는 단어예요. 영어 화자가 그냥 'cup'을 떠올려 '컵 주세요'라고만 하면 어떤 컵인지 모호하니, 일회용 종이 컵이 필요할 때는 콕 집어 '종이컵'이라고 해야 해요. 함께 알아 둘 동사로, 정수기에서 물을 담을 때는 '따르다(pour)'보다 '받다(receive/catch)'를 더 자연스럽게 써서 '종이컵에 물을 받다'라고 합니다(물이 위에서 떨어지는 것을 받는 느낌). 또 따르다는 르불규칙이라 '따라요'로 활용되는 점도 함께 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reusing a 종이컵 many times like a normal cup; by definition it's 일회용 (single-use), so for a reusable one you'd want a 유리컵 or 머그컵.
Just saying 컵 when you specifically need a disposable paper one; 컵 alone is ambiguous, so specify 종이컵.
Using 따르다 (pour) for filling a cup at a water dispenser when 받다 (to catch/receive the falling water) is the natural verb: 종이컵에 물을 받다.

structuredNuance.t: 한 번 쓰고 버리는 일회용 종이 컵이에요. 정수기 옆, 사무실, 행사장에서 흔히 보여요. 핵심 의미는 '일회용(一回用, single-use)'이라는 점이라, 여러 번 쓰는 '유리컵(glass)'이나 '머그컵(mug)'과 정반대 개념으로 묶여요 — 재질(종이)과 일회성이 동시에 강조되는 단어예요. 함께 알아 둘 동사로, 정수기에서 물을 담을 때는 '따르다(pour)'보다 '받다(receive/catch)'를 더 자연스럽게 써서 '종이컵에 물을 받다'라고 합니다(물이 위에서 떨어지는 것을 받는 느낌).
종이컵은 종이(paper) + 컵(cup, 영어 외래어)이 합쳐진 말이에요.
따르다는 르불규칙이라 '따라요'로 활용되는 점도 함께 기억하세요.
영어 화자가 그냥 'cup'을 떠올려 '컵 주세요'라고만 하면 어떤 컵인지 모호하니, 일회용 종이 컵이 필요할 때는 콕 집어 '종이컵'이라고 해야 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 수저통 means "cutlery holder (for spoons and chopsticks)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수저통 (sujeotong) = "cutlery holder (for spoons and chopsticks)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수저통에서 꺼내다 ("to take out of the cutlery holder") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수저통, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to take out of the cutlery holder
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = out of (source); 꺼내다 = to take out

usagePhrases.en: the holder is on the table
usagePhrases.note: 위에 있다 = is on top of; where the holder usually sits
열다 = to open; some holders have a lid you lift

usagePhrases.en: one set of spoon and chopsticks
usagePhrases.note: counter 벌 for sets; 수저 = 숟가락(spoon) + 젓가락(chopsticks)

examples.en: I took a spoon and chopsticks out of the holder.
examples.note: 에서 marks the source; 이랑 casually links the two utensils you pull out.

examples.en: The cutlery holder is on the table.
examples.note: 위에 있다 locates it; this is where you self-serve utensils at a Korean eatery.

examples.ko: 수저는 수저통에서 직접 꺼내 쓰면 돼요.
examples.romanization: sujeoneun sujeotongeseo jikjeop kkeonae sseumyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can just take the utensils from the holder yourself.
examples.note: -(으)면 되다 = it's fine to; 직접 = personally, highlighting the self-serve custom.

entries.nuance: 수저통은 수저(숟가락+젓가락) + 통(桶, case/bin)이 결합한 말이에요. 여기서 가장 중요한 어휘 포인트는 '수저'인데, 영어로는 보통 'spoon' 하나로 옮기기 쉽지만 한국어 '수저'는 '숟가락(spoon)과 젓가락(chopsticks)을 함께 부르는 말'이라는 점이에요 — 그래서 수저통에는 숟가락과 젓가락이 같이 들어 있어요. 한국 식당에서는 보통 식탁 위나 서랍 속 수저통에 수저가 들어 있어, 종업원을 기다리지 말고 손님이 직접 꺼내 쓰는 셀프 문화가 일반적이에요. 함께 쓰는 동사로 '꺼내다(to take out)'와 출발점을 나타내는 조사 '에서(from/out of)'를 묶어 '수저통에서 꺼내다'로 외우면 좋아요. 또 수저를 셀 때는 한 벌, 두 벌처럼 분류사 '벌(set)'을 써서 숟가락과 젓가락 한 쌍을 한 벌로 센다는 점도 알아 두세요. 통(桶)이라는 한자는 김치통·반찬통처럼 '무언가를 담는 통'에 두루 쓰입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 수저 means only a spoon; 수저 is the cover term for spoon + chopsticks together, which is why a 수저통 holds both 숟가락 and 젓가락.
Waiting for staff to set your utensils; in Korea they're usually in the 수저통 on the table or in a drawer, so you self-serve by 수저통에서 꺼내다.
Counting a spoon-and-chopstick set with 개 instead of 벌; a matched set is 한 벌 (one set), since 수저 comes as a pair.

entries.shortExplanation: 도로 means "road" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 도로 (doro) means "road". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고속도로 ("highway / expressway"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도로 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 고속 (high speed) + 도로 = the big inter-city expressway
fixed traffic phrase; 막히다 (be blocked) is intransitive, so use 가/이 not 을/를
공사 工事 = construction work; the sign you see when a lane is closed

usagePhrases.en: go by this road / take this road
usagePhrases.note: route-marking 로/으로, not 에서; tells which road you travel along

examples.en: This road is wide.
examples.note: simplest description; 넓다 (wide) takes the subject with 은/는 here

examples.en: It's rush hour, so the road is really jammed.
examples.note: everyday complaint; 막히다 stays intransitive, so 도로'가' not 도로'를'

examples.en: The GPS told me to take this road.
examples.note: real driving situation; route particle 로 + indirect command 가라고 하다

entries.nuance: 도로 道路 (道 way + 路 path) is the neutral, infrastructure word for a paved road that cars drive on — what an engineer or a traffic report means by 'road'. The sharp contrast is with 거리: 도로 stresses the vehicle surface (도로가 막히다, 도로 공사), while 거리 is a shopping/walking street you stroll down; you would never say 거리가 막히다 about car traffic. It is also broader than 골목(길) (a narrow alley) and 차도 (the car-only carriageway as opposed to 인도, the sidewalk). Register is plain and works everywhere from signs to news. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle when you mean a route: 'go by this road' is 이 도로'로' 가요 (route-marking 로/으로), not 도로'에서' 가요, because 에서 marks where an action happens, while 로 marks the path you move along.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 도로를 막혀요 — 막히다 (to be jammed/blocked) is intransitive, so the road is the subject: 도로'가' 막혀요.
Using 도로 for a lively shopping street: a street you walk and browse is 거리 (e.g. 가로수길 같은 거리), whereas 도로 sounds like an asphalt traffic artery.
Marking the route with 에서: to express 'let's take this road' say 이 도로'로' 가요, not 이 도로에서 가요 (에서 would mean an action performed on the road).

structuredNuance.t: 도로 is the neutral, infrastructure word for a paved road that cars drive on — what an engineer or a traffic report means by 'road'. Register is plain and works everywhere from signs to news.

道路 = 道 (way) + 路 (path).

entries.shortExplanation: 주유소 means "gas station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "gas station" is 주유소 (juyuso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주유소에 가다 ("go to the gas station"). Watch the particle attached to 주유소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: destination 에 + 가다; 주유소 is a place you head to
the verb is 넣다 (put in); the object is 기름 (oil/fuel), not 주유소
셀프 (self) + 주유소; you pump it yourself, very common in Korea
기름값 = fuel price; describe the station's prices, not the station 'being cheap'

examples.en: Is there a gas station nearby?
examples.note: simple existence question; 있다 takes the subject with 가

examples.en: I filled the tank all the way up at the gas station.
examples.note: everyday refueling; 에서 marks where the action happens, 가득 = full

examples.en: It's a self-service station, so you have to pump it yourself.
examples.note: real situation; -아야 하다 (have to) + 직접 (in person/oneself)

entries.nuance: 주유소 注油所 literally stacks 注 (pour) + 油 (oil) + 所 (place) = 'a place where you pour oil', i.e. a fuel station. Because the 油 is 'oil/fuel', Koreans say 기름(을) 넣다 ('put in oil') even for gasoline — 기름 covers gasoline, diesel, everything in the tank. The natural verb is 넣다 (put in), so the object is 기름, never the station itself. As a 소(所) place-noun it behaves like other locations: 에 for going there (주유소에 가요), 에서 for the action done there (주유소에서 넣어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is importing 'gas': do not say 가스 — 가스 in Korean means cooking/LPG gas, and a fuel stop is 주유소. A second trap is making the station the grammatical object: you fill the car with 기름, so it's 기름을 넣다, not 주유소를 넣다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it a 가스 station — 가스 means household/LPG gas in Korean; the place to refuel a car is 주유소.
Saying 주유소를 넣어요 — the thing you put in is fuel, so it must be 주유소'에서' 기름'을' 넣어요.
Saying 주유소가 싸요 to mean fuel is cheap — describe the price: 그 주유소는 기름값이 싸요 (its gas price is cheap).

structuredNuance.t: 주유소 is a fuel station. Because the 油 is 'oil/fuel', Koreans say 기름(을) 넣다 ('put in oil') even for gasoline — 기름 covers gasoline, diesel, everything in the tank. The natural verb is 넣다 (put in), so the object is 기름, never the station itself. As a 소(所) place-noun it behaves like other locations: 에 for going there (주유소에 가요), 에서 for the action done there (주유소에서 넣어요).

entries.shortExplanation: 좌석 means "seat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 좌석 (jwaseok) = "seat". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 창가 좌석 ("window seat") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 좌석, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 창가 (window side) + 좌석; opposite is 통로 좌석 (aisle seat)
번호 番號 = number; the figure printed on your ticket
예약하다 (book in advance); 좌석 is the object with 을
등급 = class (e.g. 일반실/특실 on the KTX)

examples.en: Where is my seat?
examples.note: simple question on a train or plane; 은/는 marks 'my seat' as topic

examples.en: A window seat, please.
examples.note: everyday booking line; 으로 = 'as/in the form of', i.e. choosing among options

examples.ko: 예매한 좌석에 다른 사람이 앉아 있었어요.
examples.romanization: yemaehan jwaseoge dareun sarami anja isseosseoyo.
examples.en: Someone else was sitting in the seat I'd reserved.
examples.note: real-trip trouble; 예매하다 (book a ticket) + 에 앉다 (sit in/at)

entries.nuance: 좌석 座席 (座 a seat + 席 a mat/place) is the formal, ticketed word for a numbered seat on a bus, train, plane, or in a theater. Its everyday near-synonym is 자리, and the dividing line is register and specificity: 자리 is the casual catch-all ('a spot/place to sit', also 'a vacant spot'), while 좌석 is what appears on tickets, signboards, and reservation screens — you reserve a 좌석, but you save someone a 자리. Natural partners are 창가/통로 좌석 (window/aisle), 좌석 번호, 좌석 예약. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: first, pick the verb by the surface — you 앉다 'on/at' a seat with 에 (좌석에 앉다), not 좌석을 앉다; second, watch the spelling, since 자석 (磁石) means 'magnet' and 좌석 is the seat — the ㅗ vs ㅏ vowel is the whole difference.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 좌석 in casual chat where 자리 fits — for 'save me a spot' say 자리 좀 맡아 줘, not 좌석; 좌석 sounds like a booked transport seat.
Saying 좌석을 앉아요 — you sit at a seat: 좌석'에' 앉아요 (place particle 에).
Misspelling it 자석 — that is 磁石 'magnet'; the seat is 좌석 with the ㅗ vowel.

structuredNuance.t: 좌석 is the formal, ticketed word for a numbered seat on a bus, train, plane, or in a theater. Natural partners are 창가/통로 좌석 (window/aisle), 좌석 번호, 좌석 예약.

Its everyday near-synonym is 자리, and the dividing line is register and specificity: 자리 is the casual catch-all ('a spot/place to sit', also 'a vacant spot'), while 좌석 is what appears on tickets, signboards, and reservation screens — you reserve a 좌석, but you save someone a 자리.
座席 = 座 (a seat) + 席 (a mat/place).

entries.shortExplanation: 목적지 means "destination" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 목적지 (mokjeokji) means "destination". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목적지에 도착하다 ("arrive at the destination"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목적지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: goal-marking 에 + 도착하다; 에 is required, never 를
최종 最終 (final) + 목적지; the last stop when you have transfers
입력하다 (input) into a GPS; here 목적지 is the object with 를

usagePhrases.en: all the way to the destination
usagePhrases.note: 까지 = up to/as far as; marks the end point of the route

examples.en: Where are you headed?
examples.note: simple; a taxi driver's opening question, subject marked with 가

examples.en: It takes about an hour to the destination.
examples.note: everyday travel time; 까지 (up to) + 걸리다 (take time)

examples.en: I entered the destination into the GPS.
examples.note: real driving step; here 목적지 is the object you type in, so 를

entries.nuance: 목적지 目的地 stacks 目 (eye/aim) + 的 (target) + 地 (place/ground) = 'the targeted place', the spot you are traveling toward. The instructive contrast is with 도착지 and 출발지: 목적지 highlights intention ('where I aim to go'), 도착지 is the neutral 'arrival point', and its true opposite is 출발지 (departure point) — pairing 목적지 with 출발지 is the standard map/app framing. Do not confuse 목적지 (place) with 목적 alone (目的 = a purpose/aim, abstract), nor with 목표 (a goal you strive for). It is a slightly formal travel word used by taxi drivers and navigation apps. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you arrive 'at' it with 에 — 목적지'에' 도착하다 — never 목적지를 도착하다, because 도착하다 is intransitive; but when you type it into a GPS the verb is transitive, so it flips to 목적지'를' 입력하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 목적지를 도착해요 — 도착하다 (to arrive) is intransitive and needs the goal particle: 목적지'에' 도착해요.
Confusing 목적지 (the place) with 목적 (the purpose) — 'my destination is Busan' is 목적지는 부산이에요, not 목적은 부산이에요 (that would mean 'my purpose is Busan').
Using 목적지 for a starting point — that is 출발지; 목적지 is only the place you are going to.

entries.shortExplanation: 거리 means "street" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "street" is 거리 (geori). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 거리를 걷다 ("walk along the street"). Watch the particle attached to 거리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 거리 + 를 + 걷다; the path you walk takes 를 here
복잡하다 (complicated/crowded) describing foot traffic and bustle
공연 公演 = performance; the kind done on a pedestrian street

usagePhrases.en: there are many people on the street
usagePhrases.note: location 에 + 있다-type existence; pedestrians, not cars

examples.en: This street is busy with people.
examples.note: simple description; topic 은/는 on the street, 많다 about people

examples.en: It's the weekend, so the street is packed with people.
examples.note: everyday scene; 로 = 'with (filled by)' + 복잡하다 (crowded)

examples.en: I watched a busking performance on the street.
examples.note: real outing; 에서 marks where the watching happened

entries.nuance: 거리 (street) is a native Korean word — note it is NOT the Sino-Korean 距離 'distance', even though the two are spelled and written identically and are told apart only by context. As 'street' it means a public way lined with shops, cafes, and pedestrians that you stroll and browse (think 명동 거리, 가로수길). The sharp contrast is with 도로 道路: 거리 centers on people and street life (거리 공연, 거리가 복잡하다), while 도로 centers on the car surface (도로가 막히다) — Koreans say 도로가 막히다 for a traffic jam but never 거리가 막히다 in that sense. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this homonym: 'the distance is far' is 거리가 멀다, but 'the street is busy' is 거리가 복잡하다 — same word, and only the predicate and situation tell you whether someone means a road you walk or a span you measure.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 거리 for a car-jammed highway — a traffic artery is 도로; 거리 evokes a walkable shopping street, so a jam is 도로가 막히다, not 거리가 막히다.
Forgetting the distance/street homonym — 거리가 멀어요 means 'the distance is far', not 'the street is far'; let context (멀다 vs 복잡하다) disambiguate.
Saying 거리를 걸어가요 vs 거리에서 — to 'walk along' the street the path can take 를 (거리를 걷다); 에서 is for an action located on the street (거리에서 공연을 보다).

structuredNuance.t: 거리 (street) is a native Korean word. As 'street' it means a public way lined with shops, cafes, and pedestrians that you stroll and browse (think 명동 거리, 가로수길).

The sharp contrast is with 도로 道路: 거리 centers on people and street life (거리 공연, 거리가 복잡하다), while 도로 centers on the car surface (도로가 막히다) — Koreans say 도로가 막히다 for a traffic jam but never 거리가 막히다 in that sense.
Note it is NOT the Sino-Korean 距離 'distance', even though the two are spelled and written identically and are told apart only by context.

The trap is exactly this homonym: 'the distance is far' is 거리가 멀다, but 'the street is busy' is 거리가 복잡하다 — same word, and only the predicate and situation tell you whether someone means a road you walk or a span you measure.

entries.shortExplanation: 승강장 means "platform" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 승강장 (seunggangjang) = "platform". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 승강장에서 기다리다 ("wait on the platform") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 승강장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 + 기다리다; the place where the waiting happens
number + 번 (counter) + 승강장; matches station signage
direction 으로 + 가다; head toward the platform
안전선 安全線 = safety line; '승강장 안전선 안쪽으로' is the classic announcement

examples.en: I'm waiting for the train on the platform.
examples.note: simple; 에서 marks the location of waiting

examples.en: Please go to platform 3.
examples.note: everyday direction; 으로 (toward) + 가세요 (polite go)

examples.en: Please step back behind the platform safety line.
examples.note: real announcement you'll actually hear; 안쪽으로 (toward the inside) + 물러나다 (step back)

entries.nuance: 승강장 乘降場 stacks 乘 (board/get on) + 降 (alight/get off) + 場 (place/field) = 'the place where you board and get off', i.e. the platform along the tracks. It is the formal term on signage and in announcements; the everyday spoken equivalent is 플랫폼 (the English loanword), and 타는 곳 ('boarding place') is the plain-Korean label posted in many stations — all three point to the same spot. The crucial contrast is with 정류장 停留場 (a bus/tram STOP at the roadside) and 역 (the whole STATION building): the 승강장 is the specific edge where you stand beside the train, inside the 역. As a 場 place-noun it takes 에서 for waiting (승강장에서 기다려요) and 으로 for moving toward it (승강장으로 가요). The English-speaker pitfall is treating the platform as something you wait 'for': you wait for the TRAIN on the platform, so it's 승강장에서 기차를 기다려요, never 승강장을 기다려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 승강장을 기다려요 — you don't wait for the platform; you wait for the train there: 승강장'에서' 기차'를' 기다려요.
Mixing up 승강장 with 정류장 — 승강장 is the train/subway platform inside a station, while 정류장 is a roadside bus stop.
Confusing 승강장 with 역 — 역 is the entire station; the 승강장 is only the boarding strip beside the tracks.

entries.shortExplanation: 안전벨트 means "seatbelt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 안전벨트 (anjeonbelteu) means "seatbelt". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 안전벨트를 매다 ("fasten the seatbelt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 안전벨트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the verb is 매다 (to tie/fasten), as with a tie or belt
풀다 (to loosen/undo); the natural opposite of 매다
착용 着用 = wearing/putting on; the formal word on signs and laws

usagePhrases.en: if you don't wear a seatbelt
usagePhrases.note: negation 안 + 매다 + 면 (if); used for warnings and fines

examples.en: Please fasten your seatbelt.
examples.note: simple polite command; the standard taxi/airplane line

examples.ko: 차가 출발하기 전에 안전벨트를 꼭 매요.
examples.romanization: chaga chulbalhagi jeone anjeonbelteureul kkong maeyo.
examples.en: I always buckle up before the car starts moving.
examples.note: everyday habit; -기 전에 (before) + 꼭 (without fail)

examples.ko: 신호 대기 중이니까 잠깐 안전벨트를 풀어도 돼요.
examples.romanization: sinho daegi junginikka jamkkan anjeonbelteureul pureodo dwaeyo.
examples.en: We're stopped at the light, so you can unbuckle for a sec.
examples.note: real moment; -아도 되다 (it's okay to) + 풀다 (undo)

entries.nuance: 안전벨트 is a hybrid: Sino-Korean 안전 安全 (安 peace/safe + 全 complete) = 'safety' + the loanword 벨트 (belt) — so literally a 'safety belt'. A common everyday synonym is just 벨트 ('안전벨트 매', often shortened to '벨트 매'), and on signs/laws you meet 착용 (着用 'wearing'). The make-or-break point is the verb: Korean fastens a belt with 매다 (to tie/fasten, the same verb as a necktie) and undoes it with 풀다 (to loosen) — NOT 입다/벗다, which are for clothing you put on the body. That is the central English-speaker pitfall: English 'wear/put on a seatbelt' tempts learners toward 입다, but 안전벨트를 입다 is wrong; it must be 안전벨트를 매다. Likewise 'take it off' is 풀다 (undo), not 벗다 (which is for shoes/clothes/hats).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 안전벨트를 입다 — clothing verbs don't apply; a belt is fastened: 안전벨트를 '매다'.
Saying 안전벨트를 벗다 to take it off — 벗다 is for clothes/shoes; undo a belt with 안전벨트를 '풀다'.
Mixing up 매다 (fasten) with 메다 — 메다 means to sling a bag over the shoulder; the seatbelt verb is 매다.

entries.shortExplanation: 헬멧 means "helmet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "helmet" is 헬멧 (helmet). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 헬멧을 쓰다 ("put on a helmet"). Watch the particle attached to 헬멧 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: head-gear verb 쓰다 (wear on the head), same as a hat/glasses
벗다 (take off); the opposite of 쓰다 for head items
자전거 (bicycle) + 헬멧; also 오토바이 헬멧 for motorcycles
착용 着用 (wearing) + 의무 義務 (duty); legal phrasing for kickboards/bikes

examples.en: I wear a helmet when I ride a bike.
examples.note: simple habit; -ㄹ 때 (when) + 쓰다 for head gear

examples.ko: 킥보드 탈 때도 헬멧을 꼭 써야 해요.
examples.romanization: kikbodeu tal ttaedo helmeseul kkok sseoya haeyo.
examples.en: You have to wear a helmet on a kickboard too.
examples.note: everyday rule; 꼭 (definitely) + -아야 하다 (must)

examples.ko: 헬멧이 좀 작아서 머리가 꽉 껴요.
examples.romanization: helmesi jom jagaseo meoriga kkwak kkyeoyo.
examples.en: The helmet's a bit small, so it squeezes my head.
examples.note: real fitting issue; 꽉 (tightly) + 끼다 (be wedged/snug)

entries.nuance: 헬멧 is a straight loanword from English 'helmet', with no hanja, used for the protective head shell worn on bikes, motorcycles, and especially 전동킥보드 (electric kickboards). A close native-ish synonym is 안전모 安全帽 (安全 safety + 帽 hat/cap), but 안전모 leans toward construction/industrial hard hats, while 헬멧 is the everyday sports/riding word — both can appear in safety rules. The decisive grammar point is the verb family for things worn on the HEAD: Korean uses 쓰다 to put on a helmet, hat, or glasses, and 벗다 to take them off. This is the key English-speaker pitfall — 'wear a helmet' invites 입다 (clothing) or even 풀다 (undo, from belts), but neither fits: it must be 헬멧을 쓰다 and 헬멧을 벗다. Note 쓰다 is a busy homonym (also 'to write', 'to use', 'to be bitter'), so context, not the verb alone, tells you it means 'wear on the head' here.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 헬멧을 입다 — 입다 is for body clothing; head gear uses 헬멧을 '쓰다'.
Saying 헬멧을 풀다 to remove it — 풀다 is for undoing belts/knots; take off head gear with 헬멧을 '벗다'.
Assuming 안전모 and 헬멧 are interchangeable — 안전모 sounds like an industrial hard hat, while a riding/cycling helmet is 헬멧.

entries.shortExplanation: 출발역 means "departure station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 출발역 (chulbaryeok) = "departure station". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 출발역에서 타다 ("board at the departure station") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 출발역, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 + 타다; the action of getting on happens there
the natural pair; 과/와 links the two endpoints
출발 出發 + 시각 時刻 (point in time); the time on your ticket
existence/identity question with 이/가

examples.en: The departure station is Seoul Station.
examples.note: simple identity sentence; 이에요 (it is)

examples.en: I picked up the ticket in advance at the departure station.
examples.note: everyday step; 미리 (beforehand) + 에서 for the place of the action

examples.ko: 출발역을 잘못 알아서 다른 역으로 갔어요.
examples.romanization: chulbaryeogeul jalmot araseo dareun yeogeuro gasseoyo.
examples.en: I had the wrong departure station, so I went to a different one.
examples.note: real mistake; here 출발역 is the object of 알다 (know), so it takes 을

entries.nuance: 출발역 出發驛 stacks 出 (go out) + 發 (set off/emit) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you set off from', the origin of a train trip. Its built-in opposite is 도착역 (arrival station, 到着驛), and the two are the standard pair on tickets and booking screens. Note the difference between 출발역 (the origin STATION) and 출발 (出發, the act of departing) and 출발지 (a more general 'departure point', not necessarily a rail station): for trains and subways you want 출발역. Register is plain and travel-flavored. The English-speaker pitfall is the boarding particle: you get on a train AT the station, so it's 출발역'에서' 타다 (action-location 에서), never 출발역을 타다 — 타다 takes the vehicle as its object (기차를 타다), while the station is just where that happens.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 출발역을 타요 — you board the train, not the station: 출발역'에서' 기차'를' 타요.
Confusing 출발역 with 도착역 — 출발역 is where you start/board, 도착역 is where you end/get off; don't swap them on a booking.
Using 출발 (the departure event) where you need the station — 'my departure station is Seoul Station' is 출발역이 서울역이에요, not 출발이 서울역이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 도착역 means "arrival station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 도착역 (dochagyeok) means "arrival station". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도착역에서 내리다 ("get off at the arrival station"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도착역 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: get off at the arrival station
usagePhrases.note: 에서 + 내리다; the action of alighting happens there

usagePhrases.en: this stop is the arrival station
usagePhrases.note: 이번 역 (this stop) is the announcement framing for 'we're here'
도착 到着 + 시각 時刻; the ETA on your ticket

usagePhrases.en: all the way to the arrival station
usagePhrases.note: 까지 = up to; marks the trip's end point

examples.en: I get off at the arrival station.
examples.note: simple; 에서 marks where the getting-off happens

examples.en: The arrival station is Busan Station, so I ride to the very end.
examples.note: everyday; 이라서 (because it is) + 끝까지 (to the end)

examples.en: This stop is your arrival station, so gather your things.
examples.note: real announcement tone; -니까 (since) + 챙기다 (gather/pack up)

entries.nuance: 도착역 到着驛 stacks 到 (reach) + 着 (attach/land) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you arrive at', the endpoint of a train trip. Its mirror-image partner is 출발역 (departure station), and the pair frames every ticket. Distinguish 도착역 (the arrival STATION) from 도착 (到着, the act/fact of arriving) and from 목적지 (your overall destination, which may be reached after leaving the station): on the train itself, the stop where you alight is your 도착역. The contrast with 종착역 (終着驛, the train's final terminus) also matters — your 도착역 is where YOU get off, which may come before the line's 종착역. The English-speaker pitfall is the alighting particle: you get off AT the station, so 도착역'에서' 내리다 (action-location 에서), not 도착역을 내리다 — 내리다 is intransitive here, taking the place with 에서, not the station as an object.

Saying 도착역을 내려요 — 내리다 (get off) takes the place with 에서: 도착역'에서' 내려요.
Confusing 도착역 with 출발역 — 도착역 is where you get off at the end; 출발역 is where you boarded.
Assuming 도착역 equals the line's last stop — your 도착역 is where you personally alight; the train's final terminus is 종착역.

entries.shortExplanation: 비행기표 means "plane ticket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "plane ticket" is 비행기표 (bihaenggipyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비행기표를 사다 ("buy a plane ticket"). Watch the particle attached to 비행기표 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 사다 (buy); the ticket is the object with 를, verb is not 하다

usagePhrases.en: book a plane ticket in advance
usagePhrases.note: 예매하다 豫買 = reserve-and-buy ahead, the natural word for flights/trains
왕복 往復 (going and returning) ↔ 편도 (one way)
비싸다 (expensive) describes the fare with 가/이

examples.en: I bought a plane ticket.
examples.note: simple past of 사다; ticket as object with 를

examples.en: It's peak season, so plane tickets are way too expensive.
examples.note: everyday gripe; 성수기 (high season) + 비싸다 about the fare

examples.en: I booked a round-trip plane ticket in advance.
examples.note: real planning; 왕복 (round trip) + 예매하다 (book ahead)

entries.nuance: 비행기표 is a transparent compound: 비행기 飛行機 (飛 fly + 行 go + 機 machine = 'flying machine', airplane) + 표 票 (ticket) = 'plane ticket'. A common synonym is 항공권 航空券 (航空 aviation + 券 ticket/voucher), which is the formal/written term you see on booking sites and itineraries, whereas 비행기표 is the everyday spoken version — same thing, different register. The bare 표 means any ticket (train, movie, concert), so 비행기 is what specifies a flight. The verbs are 사다 (buy) and especially 예매하다 (book ahead), with 예약하다 (reserve) also fine. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 'do/get a ticket' does not translate — you 'buy' or 'book' it, so say 비행기표를 사다 / 예매하다, not 비행기표를 하다. A second trap is dropping 비행기 and saying only 표, which is too vague when a flight is meant.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비행기표를 해요 — you don't 'do' a ticket; you 비행기표를 '사요' (buy) or '예매해요' (book).
Using bare 표 for a flight — 표 alone could be any ticket; specify with 비행기표 (or 항공권) for a plane.
Treating 항공권 and 비행기표 as different things — they're the same; 항공권 is just the formal/written term you meet on booking sites.

entries.shortExplanation: 해 means "sun" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 해 (hae) = "sun". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 해가 떠요 ("the sun rises") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 해, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: the motion verb 뜨다, not 오다
지다 = sink/go down, same verb as for flowers wilting

examples.en: The sun rises in the morning.
examples.note: 해가 떠요 is the fixed beginner phrase for sunrise; 떠요 comes from 뜨다.

examples.en: The rain stopped and the sun came out.
examples.note: 해가 나다 specifically means the sun reappears after bad weather.

examples.en: The sun is blazing today.
examples.note: 쨍쨍 is the sound-feel adverb Koreans use for a strong, glaring sun.

entries.nuance: 해 is the pure-Korean word for the sun as the physical disk in the sky, and it is also the everyday word for 'a day' (오늘 하루, 해가 바뀌다 = the year turns). Its near-synonym 태양(太陽) is the Sino-Korean, more scientific or literary word — you say 태양계 (solar system) and 태양이 빛나다 in writing, but in casual speech you almost always say 해. The dividing line: 해 = warm, daily, spoken; 태양 = grand, formal, written. 해 takes the motion verbs 뜨다 (rise) and 지다 (set), so the trap for English speakers is reaching for 오다/가다 by analogy with 'the sun comes up' — 해가 와요 is wrong; it must be 해가 떠요. A second pitfall is confusing 해 (the sun itself) with 햇빛 (sunlight you see) and 햇볕 (sun-warmth you feel on your skin): you do not 'look at the 해' to mean basking — that is 햇볕을 쬐다.

Saying 해가 와요 because English says 'the sun comes up.' Korean uses the rising verb: 해가 떠요 (from 뜨다). 오다 never describes the sun.

entries.shortExplanation: 햇볕 means "sunshine" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 햇볕 (haetbyeot) means "sunshine". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 햇볕이 따뜻해요 ("the sunshine is warm"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 햇볕 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 따뜻하다 pairs with the felt warmth of 햇볕
강하다 for intensity; 따갑다 if it stings the skin
쬐다 is the dedicated verb for soaking up sun/heat
들다 = light enters a room, 볕이 잘 드는 집 = a sunny house

examples.en: The sun is really warm today.
examples.note: Classic small talk; 햇볕 + 따뜻하다 is the natural warmth collocation.

examples.en: The sun stung, so I wore a hat.
examples.note: 따갑다 (prickly/stinging) fits strong 햇볕 better than just 강하다.

examples.en: This room gets good sunlight.
examples.note: Real-estate phrase: 볕이 잘 들다 = a bright, sun-filled room.

entries.nuance: 햇볕 is the sun's warmth and rays as you physically feel them on your skin — the heat, not the brightness. Its crucial near-synonym is 햇빛 (sun + 빛 light), which is the visible light you see with your eyes. The dividing line is touch vs. sight: you warm up in 햇볕 (햇볕이 따뜻하다, 햇볕을 쬐다) but you squint at 햇빛 (햇빛이 눈부시다 = the light is dazzling). 햇볕 is a compound of 해(sun) + 볕(sunlight/ray, with the ㅅ inserted as a 사이시옷), which is why the spelling ends in ㅌ — a very common spelling trap. 햇볕 takes the special verb 쬐다 (to bask/soak up), so the English-speaker pitfall is translating 'get some sun' as 햇볕을 봐요 (literally 'look at the sunshine'), which is wrong; the natural verb is 햇볕을 쬐다. Note Koreans also drop the 해 and just say 볕 (볕이 좋다).

Spelling it 햇빛 when you mean warmth. Warmth on your skin is 햇볕(felt); the light you see is 햇빛(seen). They are different words, not spelling variants.
Writing the final consonant wrong: 햇볃 or 햇빛 instead of 햇볕. The correct ending is ㅌ (받침 티읕), pronounced [핻뼏].
Saying 햇볕을 봐요 for sunbathing. You don't 'see' the warmth; you absorb it: 햇볕을 쬐어요 (verb 쬐다).

entries.shortExplanation: 노을 means "sunset glow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sunset glow" is 노을 (noeul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 노을이 지다 ("the glow spreads at sunset"). Watch the particle attached to 노을 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 지다 — the same setting verb as for the sun
붉다 (deep red) is the signature color of 노을
fixed compound; 아침노을 exists but is far rarer

usagePhrases.en: the sky is dyed with the glow
usagePhrases.note: 물들다 = to be stained/dyed with color, very poetic

examples.en: The sunset glow is really pretty in the evening.
examples.note: Everyday compliment for a beautiful sky; 노을 + 예쁘다.

examples.en: The sky was dyed red with the sunset glow.
examples.note: 물들다 paints the whole sky — a step up in vividness from 지다.

examples.en: We went to the beach to watch the sunset glow.
examples.note: 노을 보러 가다 = go specifically to see the sunset, a real outing.

entries.nuance: 노을 is the red-orange glow that paints the sky at sunrise or (usually) sunset — the colored light on the clouds, not the sun itself. Do not confuse it with 일몰(日沒), which is the technical event of the sun sinking below the horizon (a forecast/almanac word), nor with 석양(夕陽), the Sino-Korean 'evening sun' that refers to the low sun itself rather than the painted sky. The dividing line: 노을 = the colors in the sky (pure-Korean, warm, everyday); 석양 = the setting sun disk (literary); 일몰 = the timed event (technical). 노을 takes 지다 (the same verb as 해가 지다), so 노을이 지다 = the glow comes out as the sun sets — an English speaker easily mis-hears this as 'the glow disappears,' but here 지다 means the sunset is happening, not fading. The pitfall is using 오다 (노을이 와요 ✗); the right verbs are 지다, 붉다, or the lovely 물들다 (to be dyed).

Saying 노을이 와요 by analogy with 'the sunset comes.' Korean uses the setting verb: 노을이 져요 (from 지다), or describe it with 물들다/붉다.
Confusing 노을 (the colored sky) with 석양 (the low evening sun) or 일몰 (the timed sunset event). 노을 is about the colors, not the sun or the clock.
Mishearing 노을이 지다 as 'the glow is fading.' Here 지다 marks the sunset happening — the glow is at its peak, not disappearing.

entries.shortExplanation: 폭풍 means "storm" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 폭풍 (pokpung) = "storm". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 폭풍이 몰아치다 ("a storm rages") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 폭풍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 몰아치다 = beat down violently, the strong verb for 폭풍
불다 because 폭풍 is fundamentally about wind
지나가다 = pass through, used once it clears
fixed idiom for tense calm before trouble

examples.en: They say a storm is coming tonight.
examples.note: -대요 reports a forecast you heard; 폭풍이 오다 is fine for 'a storm comes.'

examples.en: The storm blew and trees fell over.
examples.note: 폭풍 + 불다 (blow) shows it is wind-driven; -어서 gives the cause.

examples.en: The storm raged so the ship couldn't leave.
examples.note: 몰아치다 conveys a violent, battering storm — stronger than 불다.

entries.nuance: 폭풍(暴風) is Sino-Korean, literally 暴 'violent' + 風 'wind' — a violent windstorm, with heavy rain implied. Its near-synonyms split by what dominates: 태풍(颱風) is a named typhoon (a specific tropical cyclone with a forecast track), 비바람 is pure-Korean 'rain-and-wind' for an ordinary nasty day, and 폭풍우(暴風雨) adds 雨 'rain' to stress the downpour. The dividing line: 폭풍 = a fierce wind event (can be metaphorical), 태풍 = the meteorological typhoon, 비바람 = everyday wet-and-windy weather. Because 風 means wind, 폭풍 naturally takes 불다 (to blow) or the intensive 몰아치다 (to rage), while 오다 also works for 'a storm comes.' The English-speaker pitfall is 폭풍이 해요 — 'storm' is a noun, never a 하다 verb. Also note 폭풍 is used metaphorically (폭풍 성장 = explosive growth, 폭풍 오열 = sobbing one's heart out), a flavor English 'storm' doesn't carry the same way.

Saying 폭풍이 해요. 폭풍 is a noun; it cannot take 하다. Use 폭풍이 와요 / 불어요 / 몰아쳐요.
Confusing 폭풍 with 태풍. 태풍 is a specific named typhoon with a forecast; 폭풍 is any violent windstorm (and 폭염 is a heat wave — a totally different word).
Forgetting that 폭풍 takes wind verbs. Because 風 = wind, the natural pairings are 불다 (blow) and 몰아치다 (rage), not just generic 오다.

entries.shortExplanation: 우박 means "hail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 우박 (ubak) means "hail". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우박이 내리다 ("hail falls"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 우박 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내리다 is the standard precipitation verb
쏟아지다 for a sudden heavy burst
떨어지다 stresses individual stones hitting
굵다 (thick/coarse) is the natural size word, not 크다

examples.en: Hail is suddenly falling.
examples.note: 갑자기 (suddenly) is almost a fixed partner — hail is abrupt; 내리다 is the core verb.

examples.en: Hail poured down and cracked the car window.
examples.note: 쏟아지다 captures a violent burst; -어서 links cause to result.

examples.en: Hailstones the size of fists fell.
examples.note: 주먹만 하다 (fist-sized) is how Koreans dramatize big hail; verb 떨어지다.

entries.nuance: 우박 is hail — the balls of ice that fall during a storm. Do not confuse it with three look-alike winter words: 진눈깨비 is sleet (rain mixed with wet snow), 싸락눈/싸라기눈 is tiny grain-snow (much smaller, softer, and it is snow not ice), and 서리 is frost that forms on the ground. The dividing line: 우박 = hard ice balls falling from storm clouds (any season, often summer); 진눈깨비 = mushy half-rain-half-snow; 싸락눈 = fine dry snow pellets. 우박 takes 내리다 (fall), the intensive 쏟아지다 (pour), or 떨어지다 (drop), and casual 오다 works too (우박이 와요, parallel to 비가 와요). The key collocation learners miss: hail size is 굵다/굵은 우박 (coarse), not 큰 우박. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the wind verb 불다 — hail doesn't 'blow,' it falls: 우박이 불어요 ✗, 우박이 내려요 ✓.
