Saying 우박이 불어요 with the wind verb. Hail falls, it doesn't blow: 우박이 내려요 / 와요 / 쏟아져요.
Confusing 우박 (ice balls) with 진눈깨비 (sleet, slushy rain+snow) or 싸락눈 (tiny snow pellets). 우박 is hard ice; the others are snow-based.
Saying 큰 우박 for big hail. The idiomatic size word is 굵다: 우박이 굵다 / 굵은 우박이 내리다.

entries.shortExplanation: 보름달 means "full moon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "full moon" is 보름달 (boreumdal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 보름달이 뜨다 ("the full moon rises"). Watch the particle attached to 보름달 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뜨다, the same rising verb as 해 and 달

usagePhrases.en: the full moon is brilliantly bright
usagePhrases.note: 휘영청 is the set adverb for a dazzling full moon
둥글다 for the round shape; 동그랗다 for small round things

usagePhrases.en: make a wish on the full moon
usagePhrases.note: fixed cultural collocation, esp. at 정월대보름

examples.en: The full moon rose tonight.
examples.note: 보름달이 뜨다 is the base phrase; 뜨다 covers all rising sky bodies.

examples.en: The full moon is brilliantly bright.
examples.note: 휘영청 밝다 is a near-set phrase — the poetic way to say a full moon is dazzling.

examples.en: I made a wish while looking at the full moon.
examples.note: 소원을 빌다 (make a wish) is the Chuseok/대보름 custom learners should know.

entries.nuance: 보름달 is the full moon — a pure-Korean compound of 보름 (the 15th day of the lunar month, i.e. mid-month) + 달 (moon). Its opposite is 초승달 (crescent moon), and its plain superordinate is just 달 (moon). The cultural weight matters: the full moon is tied to 추석 (Chuseok, the harvest festival) and especially 정월대보름 (the first full moon of the lunar year), when Koreans make wishes — so 보름달 carries warm festive connotations a bare 'full moon' lacks in English. It takes 뜨다 (rise) like all sky bodies, and its signature description is 휘영청 밝다 (brilliantly bright). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) reaching for 오다 — 보름달이 와요 ✗, it must be 보름달이 떠요; (2) assuming 'full' is a separate adjective — there is no 가득한 달; the fullness is baked into the single word 보름달.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 보름달이 와요. The moon rises, so use 뜨다: 보름달이 떠요. 오다 doesn't apply to moons.
Confusing 보름달 (full moon) with 초승달 (crescent). 보름(mid-month, round) vs 초승(start of the lunar month, thin sliver) are opposites.
Trying to build 'full moon' from an adjective + 달 (e.g. 가득한 달). It is one fixed word, 보름달, where 보름 already means the 15th/full phase.

entries.shortExplanation: 초승달 means "crescent moon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 초승달 (choseungdal) = "crescent moon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 초승달이 뜨다 ("the crescent moon rises") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 초승달, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 뜨다, the standard rising verb
가늘다 (slender) for the thin sliver shape
눈썹 같다 is the classic shape metaphor
걸리다 = to be hung/caught, poetic for a sliver moon

examples.en: A crescent moon rose in the sky.
examples.note: Base sentence; 초승달 + 뜨다 just like any moon.

examples.en: The crescent moon is thin like an eyebrow.
examples.note: 눈썹처럼 가늘다 — the standard simile Koreans use for a slim crescent.

examples.en: A crescent moon hangs in the western sky.
examples.note: 걸려 있다 (is hanging) gives a still, picturesque image.

entries.nuance: 초승달 is the thin crescent moon seen just after the new moon — a pure-Korean compound from 초승 (the very start of the lunar month) + 달 (moon). It is the direct opposite of 보름달 (full moon). Be careful with two relatives: 그믐달 is also a crescent but the waning one seen at the END of the lunar month (just before the new moon), and the shapes face opposite ways; 반달 is the half moon, a separate phase in between. The dividing line: 초승달 = waxing sliver at the month's start; 그믐달 = waning sliver at the month's end; 반달 = half; 보름달 = full. It takes 뜨다 (rise) and is described with 가늘다 (thin) — the trademark image is 눈썹 같은 초승달 (eyebrow-shaped crescent). English-speaker pitfalls: using 오다 (초승달이 와요 ✗ → 떠요 ✓), and assuming any thin crescent is 초승달 when a waning one is properly 그믐달.

Calling every crescent 초승달. The waxing sliver at the month's start is 초승달; the waning sliver at the month's end is 그믐달 (and they curve in opposite directions).
Using 크다/작다 for its shape. A crescent's defining trait is thinness — describe it with 가늘다 (가는 초승달), not size words.

The dividing line: 초승달 = waxing sliver at the month's start; 그믐달 = waning sliver at the month's end; 반달 = half; 보름달 = full.
초승달 is a pure-Korean compound from 초승 (the very start of the lunar month) + 달 (moon).
English-speaker pitfalls: using 오다 (초승달이 와요 ✗ → 떠요 ✓), and assuming any thin crescent is 초승달 when a waning one is properly 그믐달.

entries.shortExplanation: 별빛 means "starlight" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 별빛 (byeolbit) means "starlight". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 별빛이 반짝이다 ("the starlight twinkles"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 별빛 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 반짝이다 is the signature twinkle verb
쏟아지다 paints a sky overflowing with stars
아래 = beneath; a set romantic/poetic phrase
물들다 = to be steeped/dyed in the light, literary

examples.en: Starlight twinkles in the night sky.
examples.note: 별빛 + 반짝이다 is the core, must-know pairing for twinkling light.

examples.en: Out in the countryside, starlight pours down.
examples.note: 쏟아지다 conveys a dazzling, dense field of stars — far from city lights.

examples.en: We talked under the starlight.
examples.note: 별빛 아래(서) is a fixed atmospheric phrase for a romantic night scene.

entries.nuance: 별빛 is starlight — a transparent compound of 별 (star) + 빛 (light), where the ㅅ is a 사이시옷 inserted between the two nouns (so it is written 별빛, pronounced [별삗]). Distinguish it cleanly from its sibling 달빛 (moonlight) and from plain 별 (the star itself): 별 is the body you point at, 별빛 is the light it casts. Because 빛 means light, the natural verbs are 반짝이다 (twinkle), 빛나다 (shine), and the vivid 쏟아지다 (pour), and the most idiomatic location phrase is 별빛 아래 (under the starlight). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb 오다: light does not 'come' in Korean, so 별빛이 와요 ✗; light 반짝여요/비쳐요/쏟아져요. A second pitfall is using 별빛 when you simply mean stars — 'I saw the stars' is 별을 봤어요 (별), not 별빛을 봤어요; you watch 별, you bask in 별빛.

Confusing 별빛 (starlight) with 달빛 (moonlight). 별=star, 달=moon; both add 빛 (light), but they are different sources.
Using 별빛 when you mean the stars themselves. To say you looked at the stars, use 별 (별을 봤어요). 별빛 is the light they emit, not the dots.

entries.shortExplanation: 달빛 means "moonlight" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "moonlight" is 달빛 (dalbit). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 달빛이 비치다 ("moonlight shines (onto something)"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 비치다 = to shine/be reflected onto a surface

usagePhrases.en: the moonlight is soft and mellow
usagePhrases.note: 은은하다 is the trademark adjective for gentle moonlight
환하다 (brightly lit) for a bright moonlit night
set phrase for a calm, romantic night

examples.en: The moonlight is bright tonight.
examples.note: 환하다 fits a clear, well-lit moonlit night; 달빛 + 환하다.

examples.en: Moonlight shines in through the window.
examples.note: 비치다 needs a surface/opening the light falls on — here 창문으로(through the window).

examples.en: The moonlight shines softly and mellow.
examples.note: 은은하다, the signature 'soft glow' word, distinguishes gentle moonlight from harsh light.

entries.nuance: 달빛 is moonlight — a compound of 달 (moon) + 빛 (light) with the same 사이시옷 as 별빛 (written 달빛, pronounced [달삗]). entries.shortExplanation: 함박눈 means "large snowflakes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 함박눈 (hambangnun) = "large snowflakes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 함박눈이 내리다 ("big snowflakes fall") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 함박눈, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 내리다, the formal precipitation verb

usagePhrases.en: snow comes down in big thick flakes
usagePhrases.note: 펑펑 is the set adverb for heavy fluffy snow
쏟아지다 for a sudden, abundant snowfall
소복이 쌓이다 = accumulate in a soft mound

examples.en: Big snowflakes are falling outside.
examples.note: 함박눈 + 오다, exactly parallel to 비가 와요/눈이 와요.

examples.en: Big fluffy snowflakes are coming down thickly.
examples.note: 펑펑 내리다 is the near-fixed phrase for heavy, fat-flake snow.

examples.en: Overnight, big snowflakes piled up in a soft mound.
examples.note: 소복이 쌓이다 describes the gentle, deep accumulation 함박눈 is loved for.

entries.nuance: 함박눈 is big, fluffy snowflakes that fall thick and slow — the picturesque snow Koreans adore. Its key contrast is 싸락눈 (or 싸라기눈), the fine dry snow pellets that fall in very cold, hard weather: 함박눈 = large soft flakes (often near 0°C, sticks and piles up beautifully); 싸락눈 = tiny gritty grains (bitter cold, doesn't stick well). Also distinguish 진눈깨비 (sleet — wet, slushy rain mixed with snow, which Koreans dislike). The name comes from 함박 (a big wooden bowl / the large 함박꽃 peony blossom), so 함박눈 literally evokes 'bowl-big / peony-big snow' — the same 함박 in 함박웃음 (a big beaming smile). It takes the snow verbs 오다 (casual) and 내리다 (standard), and its trademark adverb is 펑펑 (펑펑 내리다 = pouring down in fat flakes). English-speaker pitfalls: using the wind verb 불다 (함박눈이 불어요 ✗ → 와요/내려요 ✓), and treating 함박 as if it described size with 큰 (don't say 큰 눈; the single word 함박눈 already means 'big-flake snow').

Saying 함박눈이 불어요 with the wind verb. Snow falls: 함박눈이 와요 / 내려요. 불다 is for wind (바람이 불다).

entries.shortExplanation: 먹구름 means "dark rain cloud" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 먹구름 (meokgureum) means "dark rain cloud". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 먹구름이 끼다 ("dark clouds gather/set in"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 먹구름 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 끼다 is the dedicated verb for clouds/fog covering the sky
몰려오다 = surge in as a mass, for an approaching storm
짙다 (dense, deep-colored) for heavy cloud cover
드리우다 = to hang/cast over, also metaphorical for gloom

examples.en: Dark clouds gathered in the sky.
examples.note: 먹구름 + 끼다 is the core pairing; 꼈어요 is the past of 끼다.

examples.ko: 먹구름이 몰려와서 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: meokgureumi mollyeowaseo got biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: Dark clouds rolled in, so it looks like rain soon.
examples.note: 몰려오다 shows the clouds advancing as a front; -ㄹ 것 같다 makes a guess.

examples.en: Dark clouds loomed over the company's future.
examples.note: Metaphorical use: 먹구름이 드리우다 = trouble/gloom looms — a flavor English shares.

entries.nuance: 먹구름 is a dark, gray-black rain cloud — a pure-Korean compound of 먹 (ink, the black inkstick used in calligraphy) + 구름 (cloud), so literally 'ink cloud.' Contrast it with plain 구름 (any cloud, neutral) and with 뭉게구름 (big white fluffy cumulus, a fair-weather cloud): 먹구름 specifically signals rain or a storm is coming, while 뭉게구름 signals a nice day. The defining verb is 끼다 — the special verb for clouds, fog, or haze settling over the sky (구름이 끼다, 안개가 끼다), so the sky 'wears' clouds rather than having them 'come.' It also takes 몰려오다 (roll in) and 드리우다 (loom), and 먹구름 is freely metaphorical for impending bad news (앞날에 먹구름이 끼다). The main English-speaker pitfall is 먹구름이 와요 (by analogy with 비가 와요 'rain comes') — clouds don't 'come,' they gather: 먹구름이 껴요 ✓. Don't strip it to plain 구름 when you mean ominous clouds; the darkness and warning are in the 먹.

Using plain 구름 for storm clouds. 구름 is any cloud; the dark, rain-bearing kind is 먹구름. And fluffy white fair-weather clouds are 뭉게구름.
Forgetting the cloud-specific verb 끼다. Clouds, fog, and haze all 끼다 (끼었다 → 꼈다). It's not 있다 or 오다 for settling-in cover.

entries.shortExplanation: 온도 means "temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "temperature" is 온도 (ondo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 온도가 높다 / 낮다 ("the temperature is high / low"). Watch the particle attached to 온도 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 높다·낮다, never 크다·작다, for temperature
올라가다·내려가다 for the reading moving
재다 = to measure (with a thermometer)
맞추다 for setting an AC, oven, or bath to a target

examples.en: The room temperature is just right.
examples.note: 딱 좋다 (just right) is the everyday comfort phrase; 온도 covers a room.

examples.en: I set the AC to 26 degrees.
examples.note: 온도를 맞추다 = set a device's temperature — a very common daily action.

examples.en: I took the baby's temperature.
examples.note: 온도 also covers body temperature; 온도를 재다 = to measure/take a temperature

entries.nuance: 온도(溫度) is Sino-Korean — 溫 'warm' + 度 'degree' — the general word for temperature of air, water, a room, an oven, anything you can read on a thermometer. Its near-synonyms are narrower: 기온(氣溫, 'air-temperature') is specifically the outdoor air temperature in a weather report, and 체온(體溫, 'body-temperature') is body heat. The dividing line: use 온도 broadly (방 온도, 물 온도), but switch to 기온 for the weather forecast (오늘 기온이 영하예요) and 체온 for a fever (체온이 38도예요). Because it is measured in degrees on a scale, the correct adjectives are 높다/낮다 (high/low), and it moves with 올라가다/내려가다. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is 온도가 커요/작아요 — English says 'high/low temperature,' and Korean agrees: it must be 온도가 높아요/낮아요, never 크다/작다. A second is using 온도 for the outdoor weather when 기온 is what newscasters say.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 온도가 커요 / 작아요. Temperature is high or low, so use 높다/낮다: 온도가 높아요. 크다/작다 is for physical size.
Using 온도 for the outdoor weather temperature. The precise forecast word is 기온 (기온이 높다). 온도 is the general term for any measured temperature.
Confusing 온도 with 체온. Your body temperature / fever is 체온 (체온을 재다); 온도 alone usually means the temperature of a room, water, or the air around you.

entries.shortExplanation: 영하 means "below zero" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 영하 (yeongha) = "below zero". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영하 5도 ("minus five degrees") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 영하, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 영하 comes BEFORE the number
떨어지다 (plunge) is more vivid than 내려가다 for crossing zero
영하 + -의 + noun to modify
-권 (zone/range) for 'down in the minuses'

examples.en: This morning it's minus five degrees.
examples.note: Word order to memorize: 영하 + number + 도. Never 5도 영하.

examples.en: The temperature dropped below zero.
examples.note: 영하로 떨어지다 = the reading plunges past zero; 로 marks the endpoint.

examples.en: Subzero cold is coming tomorrow.
examples.note: 영하권 (the subzero zone) is how forecasters frame a cold snap.

entries.nuance: 영하(零下) is Sino-Korean — 零 'zero' + 下 'below' — meaning below 0°C. Its exact opposite is 영상(零上, 'above zero'), used for plus temperatures (영상 3도 = +3°C). The crucial structural fact, opposite to English, is word order: the marker comes BEFORE the number, so 'minus five degrees' is 영하 5도 (literally 'below-zero five degrees'), never 5도 영하. English speakers also say 'negative five' / 'minus five,' but Korean does not use 마이너스 in weather speech — it is always 영하. 영하 most often appears in winter forecasts and pairs with 떨어지다 (plunge below) and 내려가다 (drop), plus the handy forecaster word 영하권 (the subzero range). The pitfalls: (1) putting the number first (5도 영하 ✗); (2) confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero) — they look and sound similar but are opposites; (3) saying 마이너스 5도 in everyday weather talk, which sounds like a math/English calque rather than natural 영하 5도.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Putting the number before 영하, e.g. 5도 영하. Korean states the zone first: 영하 5도 (below-zero, five degrees).
Confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero). 하=below, 상=above. They are direct opposites, easy to mix up by sound.
Saying 마이너스 5도 for the weather. That's an English-style calque; natural Korean weather speech is 영하 5도.

entries.shortExplanation: 가뭄 means "drought" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가뭄 (gamum) means "drought". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가뭄이 들다 ("a drought sets in"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가뭄 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 들다, the set verb (as for sickness/famine 'setting in')
심하다 for severity/intensity
계속되다 for a prolonged dry spell
풀리다 = to be relieved/loosened, when rain finally comes

examples.en: The drought is severe this year.
examples.note: 가뭄 + 심하다, the everyday way to say a bad drought.

examples.en: A drought set in because it didn't rain.
examples.note: 가뭄이 들다 (a drought sets in) — note 들다, not 오다; -어서 gives the cause.

examples.en: A welcome rain fell and the drought broke.
examples.note: 가뭄이 풀리다 = the drought lifts; 단비(welcome rain) is its natural rescuer.

entries.nuance: 가뭄 is a drought — a pure-Korean noun for a long stretch with little or no rain. It is the direct opposite of 장마 (the summer monsoon rainy season), and learners often pair the two. The defining verb is 들다, which here means 'to set in / take hold' — the same 들다 used when an illness or a famine grips (병이 들다, 흉년이 들다) — so 가뭄이 들다 frames the drought as something that settles over the land, not something that 'arrives.' It is described with 심하다 (severe) and 계속되다 (continues), and lifts with 풀리다 (가뭄이 풀리다 = the drought breaks), often thanks to 단비 (a welcome, much-needed rain). The English-speaker pitfall is 가뭄이 와요 (by analogy with 'a drought comes' / 비가 와요) — a drought doesn't 'come,' it 들어요. Also keep 가뭄 (no rain, dryness) distinct from 장마 (too much rain): they are opposite weather problems, and mixing the verbs (가뭄이 오다 / 장마가 들다) sounds wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가뭄이 와요. A drought sets in, it doesn't come: 가뭄이 들어요 (verb 들다). Compare 비가 와요, but weather conditions like drought take 들다.
Confusing 가뭄 (drought, too little rain) with 장마 (the monsoon rainy season, too much rain). They are opposite situations.
Using the wrong verb when the rain finally comes. The drought 'breaks' is 가뭄이 풀리다 (loosen/relieve), not 가뭄이 끝나 오다 or similar.

entries.shortExplanation: 직업 means "job; occupation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "job; occupation" is 직업 (jigeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 직업이 뭐예요? ("What's your job?"). Watch the particle attached to 직업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The standard polite way to ask someone's occupation; note the particle is 이, not 가.
바꾸다 = swap one thing for another; use it for switching careers, not just today's task.
전문 (專門, specialty) marks a skilled profession like doctor or lawyer.
없다, not 안 있다; this is the natural way to say 'unemployed' softly.

examples.en: What is your job?
examples.note: The go-to first-meeting question; the verb is hidden inside 뭐예요.

examples.en: My job is a nurse.
examples.note: Topic 직업은 + the profession + 예요; you name the job, you don't 'do' it.

examples.en: I want to have a good occupation.
examples.note: 갖다(가지다) 'to hold/have' pairs with 직업 when talking about aspirations.

entries.nuance: 직업 (職業, 'duty-work') is the abstract category of one's profession or line of work — the answer to 'what do you do for a living,' not the daily grind itself. The dividing line you must feel: 직업 is the occupation as an identity (간호사, 교사), 직장 is the specific company you belong to, and 일/업무 is the actual work you perform. So 직업이 뭐예요? asks WHAT you are, while 무슨 일 해요? asks more casually what work you do day to day. Register is neutral-to-formal, perfect for a first meeting; among close friends 무슨 일 해? feels warmer. The classic English-speaker trap is 직업을 해요 to mean 'I work' — Korean never 'does' an occupation; you simply state it with 이에요/예요 (선생님이에요), and the particle after 직업 is 이 (직업이), since the word ends in a consonant.

Confusing 직업 (the profession/identity) with 직장 (the workplace/company). '회사가 멀어요' uses 직장, but '의사예요' is your 직업.
Using 가 after 직업 (직업가) — because 직업 ends in a consonant, the subject particle is 이: 직업이 뭐예요?

entries.shortExplanation: 직원 means "employee; staff member" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 직원 (jigwon) = "employee; staff member". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회사 직원 ("a company employee") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 직원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 sits in front as a noun modifier; no particle needed between them.
한테 marks the human recipient of the question; 에게 is its formal twin.
Place + 직원 names the staff of a specific business.
뽑다 literally 'to pull/pick out' is the everyday verb for hiring.

examples.en: I am a bank employee.
examples.note: Workplace + 직원 + 이에요 states your role simply.

examples.en: Please ask a staff member.
examples.note: You hear this constantly in shops; 한테 + 물어보다 = ask (a person).

examples.en: The staff at this shop are kind.
examples.note: 직원이 + adjective; Korean keeps it singular even for 'the staff' collectively.

entries.nuance: 직원 (職員, 'duty-personnel') is the plain, everyday word for anyone who works at a company, shop, bank, or office — the person on the other side of the counter helping you. The synonym contrast to nail: 직원 is generic 'staff' regardless of rank, while 사원 (社員) specifically names the entry-level rung on the corporate ladder, and 종업원 sounds older/more clerical (waitstaff, hired help). In daily life 직원 is overwhelmingly the natural choice — 직원한테 물어보세요 (ask a staff member) is a sentence you'll use weekly. Register is neutral and safe for everyone. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't call the customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the one who WORKS there, not the visitor (that's 손님); second, English says 'I asked the staff' with no particle, but Korean must mark the person with 한테/에게: 직원에게 물어봤어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the worker; the customer is a 손님. Mixing these reverses who serves whom.
Dropping the particle: 직원 물어봤어요 is wrong. You must mark the person you asked with 한테/에게 → 직원한테 물어봤어요.
Assuming 직원 means a high-ranked person. It's rank-neutral; the boss is 사장 or 상사, not just 직원.

entries.shortExplanation: 직장 means "workplace; one's job" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 직장 (jikjang) means "workplace; one's job". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 직장에 다니다 ("to be employed; to go to work regularly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 직장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to be employed; to go to work regularly
usagePhrases.note: 다니다 'attend regularly' is the set verb; this whole phrase means 'have a job.'
직장 + 동료 (同僚, fellow worker) — your colleague at the same company.

usagePhrases.en: to look for / find a job
usagePhrases.note: 구하다 'to seek/obtain' is the natural verb for job-hunting.

usagePhrases.en: work life; life as an employee
usagePhrases.note: 생활 (生活, daily life) added to mean the whole experience of being employed.

examples.en: I have a job (I go to work).
examples.note: 직장에 다니다 = be employed; the 에 marks the place you regularly attend.

examples.en: My workplace is far from home.
examples.note: 직장이 + 멀다; here 직장 means the physical workplace.

examples.en: I'm looking for a new job.
examples.note: 새 (new) directly modifies 직장; 구하다 = seek/find.

entries.nuance: 직장 (職場, 'duty-place') literally means the 'place of one's work' and covers both the physical workplace and the broader fact of being employed. The crucial contrast: 직업 is your profession/identity (what you are — a teacher), while 직장 is the specific organization you belong to (where you work — Samsung). So 직장에 다니다, literally 'attend a workplace,' is THE idiomatic way to say 'I have a job,' built with 다니다 (to go regularly), the same verb used for 학교에 다니다 (attend school). A salaried worker is a 직장인. Register is neutral and extremely common. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb: don't say 직장에 가다 to mean 'I'm employed' — 가다 only describes today's single trip to the office, whereas 다니다 captures the ongoing state of holding a job. Also resist the literal 'I have a job' = 직장을 가지다; Koreans say 직장에 다녀요 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 직장에 가다 to mean 'I have a job.' 가다 = today's trip; the state of being employed is 직장에 다니다.
Swapping 직장 (where you work) and 직업 (what you do). '의사예요' is 직업; '병원에 다녀요' is 직장.
Saying 직장을 가지다 ('have a workplace') by translating English literally. Natural Korean is 직장에 다녀요.

entries.shortExplanation: 사원 means "staff member; rank-and-file employee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "staff member; rank-and-file employee" is 사원 (sawon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신입 사원 ("a new employee; new hire"). Watch the particle attached to 사원 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 신입 (新入, newly entered) + 사원 — the fresh recruit, hired every spring.

usagePhrases.en: to join as an entry-level employee
usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the rank you enter AT; 입사하다 = enter a company.
정규 (正規, regular) contrasts with 계약직 (contract worker).
평 (平, plain/flat) stresses 'just a regular worker,' no title.

examples.en: I am a new employee.
examples.note: 신입 사원 is a fixed compound; + 이에요 states your level.

examples.en: I joined as an entry-level employee.
examples.note: 으로 marks the entering rank; 입사하다 = enter the company, past 입사했어요.

examples.en: Before being promoted to 대리, I was a 사원.
examples.note: Shows the rank ladder: 사원 → 대리; 이었어요 = was.

entries.nuance: 사원 (社員, 'company-member') is specifically the BOTTOM formal rung on the Korean corporate title ladder — the rank a fresh hire holds before climbing to 대리 → 과장 → 차장 → 부장. The contrast you must internalize: 직원 is the generic, everyday word for 'staff' at any rank, whereas 사원 is a precise rank-title used mostly in HR and on org charts. So every 사원 is a 직원, but a 부장 (department head) is a 직원 and NOT a 사원. You'll hear 신입 사원 (new recruit) everywhere during 공채 (open hiring season). Register is formal/official. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 사원 just because you mean 'an employee' in casual conversation — say 직원. And note the particle 으로 in 사원으로 입사하다 marks the rank you enter as, an 'as/in the capacity of' meaning English drops entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사원 for any worker in casual speech. For generic 'staff' say 직원; 사원 is the specific entry rank.
Thinking a manager (부장/과장) is a 사원. Those are higher ranks; 사원 is the lowest rung only.
Saying 사원에 입사하다. The rank you enter AS takes 으로: 사원으로 입사했어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 업무 means "work; task; duties" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 업무 (eommu) = "work; task; duties". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 업무를 보다 ("to attend to / handle one's work") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 업무, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to attend to / handle one's work
usagePhrases.note: 보다 'to see/handle' is the set verb for processing duties, esp. office/admin work.
업무 + 시간; the time block during which work or service is done.
많다 describes the volume of duties; 바쁘다 describes you being busy.

usagePhrases.en: to take charge of a task
usagePhrases.note: 맡다 'to be entrusted with' = be assigned a duty or responsibility.

examples.en: I have a lot of work today.
examples.note: 업무가 + 많다; describes the amount of work, not your feelings.

examples.en: Working hours are from 9 to 6.
examples.note: 업무 시간 + 부터...까지 frames the start and end of the workday.

examples.en: I've been assigned a new task.
examples.note: 맡다 + 게 되다 = ended up being entrusted with; sounds natural for new duties.

entries.nuance: 업무 (業務, 'occupation-affairs') is the formal word for the specific duties, tasks, and functions tied to a job — the work content itself, especially in office and administrative settings. The synonym contrast to feel: 일 is the broad, native, casual word for 'work/thing/matter' you'd use with friends (일이 많아 = so much to do), while 업무 is its Sino-Korean, businesslike counterpart used in emails, reports, and with superiors (업무 협조 부탁드립니다). They overlap, but 업무 carries an official, structured tone; you would not say 업무 for chores at home. The fixed verb 업무를 보다 ('handle work') mirrors 일을 보다 and 볼일을 보다 (run an errand). The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 업무를 가다 — you 업무를 보다/하다 (handle/do work), never 'go' work; and in relaxed conversation reaching for 업무 instead of 일 can sound stiff and over-formal, like saying 'attend to my duties' to a buddy.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 업무를 가다 to mean 'go to work.' You 업무를 보다/하다; 'going to work' is 출근하다 or 회사에 가다.
Using 업무 in casual chat where 일 fits. To a friend say 일이 많아, not 업무가 많아 — the latter sounds like a memo.
Confusing 업무 (the tasks/duties) with 직업 (the profession). Your 업무 is what you do daily; your 직업 is what you are.

entries.shortExplanation: 회의실 means "meeting room; conference room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 회의실 (hoeuisil) means "meeting room; conference room". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회의실에서 ("in the meeting room"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회의실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the LOCATION where an action takes place (a meeting happens there).
예약하다 (豫約, reserve in advance) — the verb for booking rooms, tables, tickets.
비다 'be empty' + 어 있다 (resultant state) = currently available.
대 (大, big) prefixed; contrast 소회의실 (小, small room).

examples.en: There is a meeting in the meeting room.
examples.note: 회의실에서 + 있다; the meeting (회의) happens IN the room (회의실).

examples.en: I booked the meeting room.
examples.note: 회의실을 + 예약하다, past 예약했어요; 을 marks the room as the object reserved.

examples.en: Is the meeting room free right now?
examples.note: 비어 있다 = is (currently) empty/available — a natural way to check.

entries.nuance: 회의실 (會議室, 'meeting-room') is built transparently from 회의 (a meeting) + 실 (room) — and that 실 is a powerful building block: once you know it, you recognize 사무실 (office), 화장실 (restroom), 교실 (classroom), and 연구실 (lab/study). The key contrast learners blur is 회의 vs 회의실: 회의 is the EVENT (the meeting), 회의실 is the PLACE (the room) — 회의실에서 회의를 해요 means 'we hold a meeting in the meeting room,' two different words. A near-synonym is 미팅룸 (a borrowed English term used in some modern offices), but 회의실 is the standard, safe word. Register is neutral/workplace. The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the particle: an action OCCURS at 회의실에서 (dynamic location), not 회의실에 (static existence/destination). 회의실에 있어요 = 'it is IN the meeting room'; 회의실에서 일해요 = 'I work IN the meeting room.' Choosing 에 vs 에서 wrong is the classic beginner slip.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 회의 (the meeting event) with 회의실 (the meeting room). You attend a 회의 that takes place in a 회의실.
Using 에 for an action: 회의실에 회의해요 is wrong. Actions happen at 회의실에서; 에 is only for existence/destination.
Forgetting the 실 = room logic and inventing words. The pattern 회의+실, 사무+실, 화장+실 is consistent — lean on it.

structuredNuance.t: 회의실 is built transparently from 회의 (a meeting) + 실 (room). A near-synonym is 미팅룸 (a borrowed English term used in some modern offices), but 회의실 is the standard, safe word. Register is neutral/workplace.
The key contrast learners blur is 회의 vs 회의실: 회의 is the EVENT (the meeting), 회의실 is the PLACE (the room) — 회의실에서 회의를 해요 means 'we hold a meeting in the meeting room,' two different words.
회의실 = 會議室, 'meeting-room.' That 실 (room) is a powerful building block: once you know it, you recognize 사무실 (office), 화장실 (restroom), 교실 (classroom), and 연구실 (lab/study).

The sharpest pitfall is the particle: an action OCCURS at 회의실에서 (dynamic location), not 회의실에 (static existence/destination). 회의실에 있어요 = 'it is IN the meeting room'; 회의실에서 일해요 = 'I work IN the meeting room.' Choosing 에 vs 에서 wrong is the classic beginner slip.

entries.shortExplanation: 상사 means "boss; one's superior" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "boss; one's superior" is 상사 (sangsa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 직장 상사 ("a workplace superior"). Watch the particle attached to 상사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 직장 (workplace) + 상사; specifies a boss in the work context.
보고하다 (報告, report) + 한테 marking the person you report TO.
직속 (直屬, directly attached) = the boss right above you in the chain.
지시 (指示, directive); 의 links the superior to their command.

examples.en: My boss is really kind.
examples.note: 상사는 + adjective; used when TALKING ABOUT the boss, not addressing them.

examples.en: I have to report to my boss first.
examples.note: 상사한테 + 보고하다; 한테 = to (a person); 야 하다 = have to.

examples.en: A new boss has arrived.
examples.note: Honorific 오시다→오셨어요 shows respect for the superior's action.

entries.nuance: 상사 (上司, 'upper-office/superior') is the general, descriptive term for anyone who outranks you at work, whatever their specific title. The vital register caution: 상사 is a word you use ABOUT your boss when describing them to others (우리 상사는…), almost never TO their face — addressing them directly, you must use their title + 님: 부장님, 팀장님, 과장님. Calling someone '상사님' to their face sounds odd, like addressing a teacher as 'Superior.' The opposite pole is 부하 ((部下), a subordinate), and a near-synonym 윗사람 ('person above') is softer/more general and can extend beyond work to any senior. Contrast also with 선배, who joined before you but isn't necessarily your boss. The English-speaker pitfall: English freely says 'my boss' and even addresses them by first name, but Korean hierarchy forbids both — you neither say 상사님 nor use their bare name; you use title + 님. Also mark the person you report to with 한테/에게, not just a bare noun.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Addressing your boss as '상사님' to their face. Use their title + 님 instead: 부장님, 팀장님. 상사 is for describing them to others.
Calling your boss by their first name like in English. Korean requires title + 님; using the bare name is rude across rank.
Confusing 상사 (a superior person) with 회사 (the company). They sound similar but mean boss vs. corporation.

entries.shortExplanation: 선배 means "senior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 선배 (seonbae) = "senior (colleague or schoolmate)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회사 선배 ("a senior at work") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 선배, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 (company) + 선배 — someone who joined before you, not necessarily your boss.
Add 님 to address a 선배 respectfully to their face.
한테 marks the source you learn FROM; 배우다 = learn.
대학 (university) + 선배 — an older schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: A senior at work helped me a lot.
examples.note: 선배가 + 도와주다 (help, with benefit); past 도와줬어요.

examples.en: Senior, please show me this.
examples.note: Direct address 선배님 + 알려 주세요 (kindly tell/show me).

examples.en: I really respect that senior.
examples.note: 선배를 + 존경하다 (respect); 를 marks the object of respect.

entries.nuance: 선배 (先輩, 'earlier-generation/fellow') means someone senior to you who entered the same school, university, company, or field BEFORE you — a relationship that structures enormous amounts of Korean social life. The sharp contrast: a 선배 is defined by entering EARLIER, while a 상사 is defined by RANK — your 선배 may or may not be your boss, and your boss may not be your 선배 if they transferred in. Also distinguish 선배 from 어른 (an elder/adult by age generally). Unlike 상사, you CAN and do address a 선배 directly, adding 님 for politeness: 선배님. A 선배 traditionally looks after their 후배 (junior), often picking up the meal tab. Register: warm but respectful, deeply tied to hierarchy. The English-speaker pitfall: English has no real equivalent and learners default to 'senior' = 'boss' — but 선배 is about timing, not authority; treating every 선배 as a 상사 (or vice versa) misreads the relationship. Mark whom you learn from with 한테/에게.

Equating 선배 with 'boss.' A 선배 joined before you but may hold no authority; a boss with power is a 상사.
Confusing 선배 (joined before you) with 후배 (joined after you). They are mirror opposites — get the direction right.
Dropping 님 when speaking TO a senior. To their face it's 선배님; bare 선배 in direct address can sound too casual.

entries.shortExplanation: 후배 means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 후배 (hubae) means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회사 후배 ("a junior at work"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후배 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 + 후배 — someone who joined the company after you.
가르치다 = teach; seniors often guide their 후배.

usagePhrases.en: to treat a junior (buy for them)
usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the receiver; 사 주다 = buy (for someone's benefit).
대학 + 후배 — a younger schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: I have one junior.
examples.note: 후배가 + 한 명 (one person) + 있다; 명 is the counter for people.

examples.en: I bought my junior a coffee.
examples.note: 후배한테 + 사 주다, past 사 줬어요; the 줬 shows you did it FOR them.

examples.en: That junior is really good at their work.
examples.note: 후배는 + 일을 잘하다 (be good at work).

entries.nuance: 후배 (後輩, 'later-generation/fellow') is the mirror image of 선배: someone who entered the same school, company, or field AFTER you, regardless of their age in some cases (entry timing usually outweighs age). The contrast to keep straight is purely directional — 선배 = earlier, 후배 = later — and neither word is about workplace RANK (that's 상사 vs 부하). Within Korea's senior-junior culture, the 선배 is expected to look after the 후배: guiding them at work, answering questions, and famously treating them to meals or coffee (후배한테 밥 사 주다). Register: friendly and caring, but still hierarchy-aware. The key English-speaker pitfall is honorifics: you do NOT attach 님 to 후배 — 님 elevates seniors, so '후배님' is unnatural; you address a junior by name or with 씨. Many learners over-apply 님 to everyone out of caution, which actually misfires here. Also, don't assume a 후배 is younger or lower-ranked — they're simply LATER to the group.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding 님 to 후배 ('후배님'). 님 honors seniors; a junior is addressed by name or with ~씨, not 님.
Mixing up 후배 (joined after you) and 선배 (joined before you). They are exact opposites — direction matters.
Assuming 후배 means 'younger.' It marks LATER entry to the group, not necessarily a younger age.

entries.shortExplanation: 출장 means "business trip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "business trip" is 출장 (chuljang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 출장을 가다 ("to go on a business trip"). Watch the particle attached to 출장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to go on a business trip
usagePhrases.note: 가다 is the set verb; you GO on a 출장, you don't 'do' one.
중 (中, in the middle of) + 이다 = currently on the trip.
해외 (海外, overseas) + 출장 — a trip abroad for work.

usagePhrases.en: to return from a business trip
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place you come back FROM; 돌아오다 = come back.

examples.en: I'm going to Busan on a business trip tomorrow.
examples.note: Place + 으로 (toward) + 출장을 가다; 으로 marks the direction.

examples.en: The manager is away on business now.
examples.note: 출장 중 + honorific 이세요 to respect the superior.

examples.en: This business trip has a tight schedule.
examples.note: 일정 (schedule) + 빡빡하다 (tight/packed) — a real coworker's complaint.

entries.nuance: 출장 (出張, 'go-out-stretch/dispatch') means being sent away from your usual workplace to do work elsewhere — typically a trip to another city or country, often with an overnight stay. The synonym contrast that matters: 출장 is travel FOR WORK, sharply distinct from 여행 (a leisure trip) — never call a vacation a 출장. Within work travel, contrast 출장 (a farther/longer dispatch, often overnight) with 외근 (外勤, off-site work done and returned within the same day, like visiting a client across town). The set verb is 가다 (출장을 가다, go on a trip) and the status phrase is 출장 중이에요 (away on business). Register: standard workplace vocabulary. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — learners say 출장을 하다 ('do a business trip') by analogy with English 'take/do,' but Korean uses 가다 (go); and direction takes 으로 (부산으로 출장 가요), not just 에. Also don't confuse the noun-internal 장 here (dispatch) with the 장 in 직장/공장 (place).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 출장을 하다. The natural verb is 가다: 출장을 가다 (go on a business trip).
Confusing 출장 (work travel) with 여행 (leisure travel). A vacation is never a 출장.
Marking the destination with 에: 부산에 출장 가요 is awkward. Use 으로 for direction → 부산으로 출장 가요.

entries.shortExplanation: 면접 means "job interview" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 면접 (myeonjeop) = "job interview". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 면접을 보다 ("to have a job interview") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 면접, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 'to see' is the FIXED verb here, exactly like 시험을 보다 (take an exam).
합격하다 (合格, pass) + 에 marking the interview you pass; opposite is 떨어지다 (fail).
면접 + 준비 (準備, preparation) — getting ready for the interview.
1차 (1次, first round); Korean hiring often has 1차, 2차 면접 stages.

examples.en: I have a job interview tomorrow.
examples.note: 면접을 보다 → present 봐요; literally 'see an interview' = have one.

examples.en: I prepared hard for the interview.
examples.note: 면접 준비 + 하다, past 했어요; 열심히 = diligently.

examples.en: I'm so happy I passed the interview.
examples.note: 면접에 합격하다 + ~아서 (reason) + 기쁘다 (glad).

entries.nuance: 면접 (面接, 'face-contact/meet') literally means meeting face-to-face, and refers to the job interview where you sit before evaluators. The most important thing to lock in is the FIXED verb: 면접을 보다, literally 'to see an interview,' which uses the same 보다 as 시험을 보다 (take a test) — Korean treats undergoing an evaluation as 'seeing' it. The synonym contrast: 면접 is the oral, face-to-face interview, while 시험 (試驗) is a written test/exam, and 면담 (面談) is a softer counseling-style talk (e.g., with a professor), not a hiring screen. After a 면접 you hope to 합격하다 (pass) rather than 떨어지다 (fall/fail) or 불합격하다. Register: neutral, used in any job-search context. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 면접을 하다 sounds off from the candidate's side — you 면접을 보다 (take it); the company that conducts it may 면접을 진행하다. Also note you pass 면접에 (with 에), patterning like 시험에 합격하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 면접을 하다 as the candidate. The fixed verb is 면접을 보다 (just like 시험을 보다).
Confusing 면접 (oral, face-to-face interview) with 시험 (a written exam). Different formats, different prep.
Using 를 with 합격: 면접을 합격하다 is wrong. You pass INTO it with 에 → 면접에 합격하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 이력서 means "resume; CV" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이력서 (iryeokseo) means "resume; CV". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이력서를 쓰다 ("to write a resume"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이력서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쓰다 'to write' is the natural verb; you write a resume, you don't 'make' it.
내다 'to put/hand out' = submit; 이력서를 제출하다 is its formal twin.
에 marks WHERE you write; 적다 = jot/note down onto the document.
이력서 + 사진 — the ID-style photo traditionally attached in Korea.

examples.en: I'm writing my resume.
examples.note: 이력서를 + 쓰다 + 고 있다 (ongoing) → 쓰고 있어요.

examples.en: I submitted my resume to the company.
examples.note: 회사에 (to the company) + 이력서를 내다, past 냈어요.

examples.en: I wrote my work experience on the resume in detail.
examples.note: 이력서에 + 경력 (career) + 적다, past 적었어요.

entries.nuance: 이력서 (履歷書, 'tread-history-document') literally means a 'record-of-what-you've-walked' document — the page listing your education, work history, and qualifications when applying for a job. The key contrast to draw: 이력서 is the structured factual resume (dates, schools, jobs in fields), whereas 자기소개서 (自己紹介書), often shortened to 자소서, is the separate, longer SELF-INTRODUCTION essay where you narrate your motivation and personality — Korean applications almost always require BOTH, so never use them interchangeably. The verbs are 쓰다 (write it) then 내다/제출하다 (submit it). A culturally specific point: a traditional Korean 이력서 includes a small formal 이력서 사진 (ID photo). Register: neutral job-search vocabulary. The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 이력서를 만들다 ('make/craft a resume') — Korean uses 쓰다 (write), because a resume is conceived as written text, not a manufactured object; and remember that what English calls a 'cover letter' maps roughly onto 자기소개서, not 이력서.

Saying 이력서를 만들다 ('make' a resume). The natural verb is 쓰다 (write); a resume is written, not crafted.
Confusing 이력서 (the factual resume) with 자기소개서/자소서 (the self-introduction essay). Korean jobs need both, separately.
Using 에서 instead of 에 for where you write: you write entries 이력서에 적다 (onto the resume), not 이력서에서.

entries.shortExplanation: 연봉 means "annual salary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "annual salary" is 연봉 (yeonbong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 연봉이 높다 ("to have a high (annual) salary"). Watch the particle attached to 연봉 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 높다 'be high' is the adjective for salary level — NOT 비싸다 (expensive).
올리다 'to raise' (transitive); the intransitive 'salary rises' is 연봉이 오르다.
협상 (協商, negotiation) — the talk where you settle your yearly pay.

usagePhrases.en: How much is the annual salary?
usagePhrases.note: 얼마 asks the amount; a direct (somewhat blunt) money question.

examples.en: This company's salary is high.
examples.note: 연봉이 + 높다; salary takes 높다/낮다 (high/low), not 비싸다.

examples.en: My salary went up a little this year.
examples.note: 연봉이 + 오르다 (rise, intransitive), past 올랐어요.

examples.en: I negotiated my salary when I joined.
examples.note: 입사할 때 (when joining) + 연봉 협상을 하다, past 했어요.

entries.nuance: 연봉 (年俸, 'year-stipend') is your pay expressed as a YEARLY total — and crucially, this is the default unit Koreans use to discuss and compare pay (연봉 3천 = 30 million won a year), unlike the English habit of quoting an hourly or monthly figure. The essential contrast: 연봉 is the annual gross figure used in offers and negotiations, while 월급 (月給, 'month-pay') is the monthly paycheck you actually take home each month — mixing them up distorts the numbers twelvefold. Related: 시급 (時給) is hourly wage (for part-timers), and 보너스/성과급 are bonuses on top. A new hire goes through 연봉 협상 (salary negotiation). Register: neutral, though asking 연봉이 얼마예요? directly can feel intrusive with someone you don't know well. The big English-speaker pitfall is the adjective: a high salary is 연봉이 높다 (high), and a low one 낮다 (low) — NEVER 연봉이 비싸다 ('expensive'), because 비싸다 is for the price of goods, not for amounts of money like wages.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 연봉이 비싸다 for a high salary. Use 높다 (high); 비싸다 (expensive) describes prices of things, not pay.
Confusing 연봉 (yearly salary) with 월급 (monthly paycheck). The figures differ by a factor of twelve.
Assuming Koreans quote monthly pay by default. Salaries are normally discussed as 연봉 (annual), so state the yearly amount.

entries.shortExplanation: 승진 means "promotion (at work)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 승진 (seungjin) = "promotion (at work)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 승진을 하다 ("to get a promotion") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 승진, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 turns the noun into the event; or just 승진하다 as one verb.

usagePhrases.en: to be promoted to department head
usagePhrases.note: Rank + 으로 (to/as) + 승진하다 marks the rank you rise TO.
빠르다 'be fast' describes the pace of climbing the ladder.
축하하다 (祝賀, congratulate); a set phrase when a coworker moves up.

examples.en: I got promoted this time.
examples.note: 승진을 하다, past 했어요; 이번에 = this time/round.

examples.en: I was promoted to section chief.
examples.note: Rank 과장 + 으로 + 승진하다, past 승진했어요.

examples.en: Congratulations on your promotion!
examples.note: Fixed congratulation; just 승진 + 축하해요, no particle needed.

entries.nuance: 승진 (昇進, 'rise-advance') means moving UP to a higher rank or title at work — climbing the corporate ladder from 사원 to 대리 to 과장 and beyond. The contrasts to keep distinct: 승진 is rising in RANK within a workplace, different from 합격 (passing an exam or interview to get IN), from 취직/취업 (landing a job in the first place), and from 이직 (changing to a different company). The verb is 승진하다, and to name the rank you rose to, use rank + 으로: 부장으로 승진했어요 (promoted to department head), where 으로 carries an 'into/as' meaning. When a colleague is promoted, the ready-made phrase is 승진 축하해요. Register: neutral, congratulatory. The English-speaker pitfall: English says 'I GOT a promotion,' tempting learners into 승진을 받다 ('receive a promotion') — but Korean treats it as something you DO/achieve: 승진을 하다 or simply 승진하다, not 받다. Also don't mark the new rank with 에 (부장에 승진 is wrong); the directional 으로 is required.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 승진을 받다 ('receive a promotion') from English 'got a promotion.' Korean uses 승진을 하다 / 승진하다.
Confusing 승진 (rising in rank) with 합격 (passing an exam/interview) or 취직 (getting hired). Different stages entirely.
Marking the new rank with 에: 부장에 승진했어요 is wrong. Use 으로 → 부장으로 승진했어요.

usagePhrases.note: life as a lived routine

examples.note: 생활 focuses on everyday rhythm, not one event.

commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

usagePhrases.note: Plain first-person pronoun used down or sideways: to close friends, younger people, or family. Never up to elders.
나 + 가 fuses to 내가, never '나가.' This shape change is irregular and must be memorized.
나 + 는 marks the topic ('as for me'); shortened to 난 in fast speech and texting.
나 + 도 ('also'); the everyday way to say 'me too' among friends, e.g. 나도 갈래.

examples.en: I'm hungry.
examples.note: Pure 반말: bare 나 with no particle, the most casual register among close friends.

examples.en: Can you give this to me?
examples.note: 나 here is the recipient ('to me'); the bare pronoun stands in for 나한테 in relaxed speech.

examples.en: I'll get everything ready.
examples.note: Real-situation promise: 나 must become 내 before 가, giving the subject 내가.

entries.nuance: 나 is the plain, intimate word for 'I/me' — the counterpart of the humble 저. Choosing between them is not about meaning but about RELATIONSHIP and DIRECTION: 나 points downward or sideways (to friends, juniors, family), while 저 lowers you toward someone you respect; saying 나 to a boss or stranger sounds blunt or rude. 나 carries a warm, unguarded feel, so it dominates 반말 and shows up constantly in 나도 (me too), 나는 (as for me), 내 거 (mine). The classic English-speaker pitfall is the subject form: English keeps 'I' fixed, but Korean fuses 나 + 가 into 내가 — '나가' actually reads as the verb 'go out,' so it is not just wrong but confusing. Also resist supplying a pronoun for every English 'I'; Koreans drop it whenever context is clear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '나가' for 'I (subject)' — that string means 'go out'; the fused subject form is 내가.
Using 나 with a boss, teacher, or stranger; it sounds rude there, so switch to the humble 저.
Forcing 나 into every sentence to match English 'I' — Korean omits the pronoun once it is obvious who is speaking.

structuredNuance.t: 나 is the plain, intimate word for 'I/me' — the counterpart of the humble 저. It carries a warm, unguarded feel, so it dominates 반말 and shows up constantly in 나도 (me too), 나는 (as for me), 내 거 (mine).

usagePhrases.note: Plain second-person pronoun, safe only with close friends and people clearly younger than you.
너 + 가 becomes written 네가, but almost everyone says 니가 out loud to avoid clashing with 내가.
너 + 는 ('as for you'); contracts to 넌 in speech, e.g. 넌 어때?
너 + 도; the casual 'you too,' as in 너도 올래? (Want to come too?).

examples.en: Where are you?
examples.note: Bare 너 in 반말; texting a close friend, no politeness ending at all.

examples.en: Do you like this too?
examples.note: 너 + 도 ('you too') checking a shared taste between friends.

examples.en: You speak first.
examples.note: Real exchange: subject form 네가 (said 니가) telling a friend to go ahead.

entries.nuance: 너 is the plain 'you,' the partner of 나, and is genuinely usable only downward or among intimates — close friends, a younger sibling, a child. The crucial difference from English is that Korean has no neutral, all-purpose 'you': to elders, strangers, coworkers, or anyone you respect, 너 sounds disrespectful or even hostile, so Koreans switch to the person's name + 씨/님, a role word (선생님, 사장님), or simply drop 'you' entirely. The big pitfall is mapping English 'you' straight onto 너 — pointing 너 at a waiter or a senior is a real social error; default to a name or title and let context carry the rest.

Writing '너가' for the subject; the standard written form is 네가 (commonly said 니가).

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Humble first-person pronoun; the safe default with elders, strangers, customers, and in formal settings.
저 + 가 fuses to 제가, never '저가.' Use it to volunteer or take responsibility politely.
저 + 는; the standard opener for introducing yourself: 저는 ...이에요/입니다.
humble 'we'; 저희 회사, 저희 집 politely lowers your own group toward the listener.

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: Simple self-introduction; 저 + 는 paired with the polite 요-form.

examples.en: I'll help you.
examples.note: Everyday offer at work: subject 제가 plus the humble 도와드리다 to lift the listener.

examples.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Kim Minsu.
examples.note: Real first meeting in 격식체 (formal -ㅂ니다); 저 is obligatory here.

entries.nuance: 저 is the humble 'I/me,' the polite counterpart of 나. It does not mean something different from 나 — it encodes DEFERENCE, lowering yourself to raise the listener, so it is the correct choice with elders, strangers, customers, and any formal moment, and it sits naturally with 요-form and -ㅂ니다 speech. Like 나 it has an irregular subject form: 저 + 가 fuses to 제가, not '저가.' Two traps for English speakers: first, the homograph — this 저 (I) is spelled identically to the demonstrative 저 'that (over there),' but sentence position keeps them apart; second, the humble plural 저희 ('we/our'), which has no English equivalent and which learners forget, defaulting to plain 우리 even when politely referring to their own company or family. When in doubt about register, 저 is the safer pronoun.

Saying '저가' for the subject — the fused humble form is 제가.

Using plain 우리 where humility is expected — politely lower your own group with 저희 (저희 회사, 저희 집).

entries.shortExplanation: 당신 means "you (distant/formal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 당신 (dangsin) = "you (distant/formal)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 당신 ("you (formal/distant)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 당신, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-Korean 當身; a 'high' you that, said to a stranger's face, often reads as cold or confrontational.
당신 + 이 (consonant ending takes 이, not 가); appears in lyrics, vows, and between spouses.
당신 + 은; common in ads and self-help writing that address 'you, the reader.'
당신 + 을; literary and romantic, as in 당신을 사랑해요.

examples.en: I love you.
examples.note: Affectionate spousal use; in songs and marriage 당신 is warm, not cold.

examples.en: You are a precious person.
examples.note: Ad / writing voice addressing an unseen reader as 당신.

examples.en: Who are you to talk to me like that?
examples.note: Real argument: the same 당신 turns sharp and confrontational toward a stranger.

entries.nuance: 당신 is a formal 'you' from the Sino-Korean 當身 (當 'this/that', 身 'body/self'), and it is one of the most misleading words for learners. Unlike a flat English 'you,' 당신 has split lives: warm and intimate between spouses ('dear/honey'), poetic in lyrics and prayer, and reader-facing in ads or essays — yet aimed at a stranger's face in conversation it sounds cold, distancing, or like the opening of a fight (it is a staple of street arguments). So although dictionaries gloss it as 'you,' it is NOT the everyday polite 'you'; the honest truth is Korean has no neutral spoken 'you' at all. The pitfall is reaching for 당신 to a clerk, a senior, or a new acquaintance the way you'd say 'you' in English — instead use the person's name + 씨/님, a title (선생님, 사장님, 손님), or drop the word entirely. Reserve 당신 for writing, lyrics, or your own spouse.

Treating 당신 as the polite everyday 'you'; spoken Korean usually omits 'you' or replaces it with a name/role.
Writing '당신가' for the subject — 당신 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이: 당신이.

entries.shortExplanation: 아버지 means "father" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 아버지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The standard, respectful word for one's father, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 지 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 아버지예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 아버지 + 님; used for another person's father or one's father-in-law.

examples.en: My father is an office worker.
examples.note: Note 우리 ('our') for 'my' family member — Koreans rarely say 내 아버지.

examples.en: I respect my father.
examples.note: 아버지 as object with 를; pairs with the humble self-pronoun 저.

examples.en: My father is reading the newspaper.
examples.note: Full honorific chain: subject 께서 + the honorific verb ending -으세요.

entries.nuance: 아버지 is the respectful, neutral word for 'father,' used in polite conversation, in writing, and whenever you speak about your dad to others. Its near-synonym 아빠 is the warm home word ('dad/daddy'): children and many adults call him 아빠 to his face, while 아버지 sounds more grown-up, dignified, or formal — the gap is exactly the English 'dad' vs 'father.' One step higher is 아버님, reserved for someone else's father or your father-in-law. Because a father is an elder, 아버지 naturally pulls honorific machinery: the subject marker 께서, the dative 께, and -(으)시- verb endings (읽으세요, 주무세요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: the copula is 아버지예요 (vowel-final 지 → 예요, not '아버지이에요'); and possession uses 우리 아버지 ('our father'), since 내 아버지 sounds oddly cold to Korean ears.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '아버지이에요' — after the vowel 지 the copula contracts to 아버지예요.
Using casual 아빠 in formal, business, or written contexts where the respectful 아버지 is expected.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The standard, respectful word for one's mother, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 니 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 어머니예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 어머니 + 님; for another person's mother or one's mother-in-law.

examples.en: My mother is a teacher.
examples.note: Again 우리 ('our') for one's own mother, the natural choice over 내 어머니.

examples.en: I gave my mother a present.
examples.note: Honorific dative 께 (not 한테) plus the humble give-verb 드리다.

examples.en: My mother is cooking.
examples.note: Real scene: subject 께서 + honorific 하세요 to respect the elder.

entries.nuance: 어머니 is the respectful, neutral word for 'mother,' used in polite speech, in writing, and when talking about your mom to others. Its near-synonym 엄마 is the affectionate home word ('mom/mommy') that people usually call her directly at home, while 어머니 carries more formality and respect — the same distance as English 'mom' vs 'mother.' The higher honorific 어머님 is for someone else's mother or your mother-in-law. As an elder, 어머니 routinely takes honorific particles and endings: 께서 for the subject, 께 for 'to,' and -(으)시- verbs (하세요, 주무세요). Watch two English-speaker traps: the copula contracts to 어머니예요 after the vowel 니 (not '어머니이에요'); and you give things to her with the honorific 어머니께 ... 드리다, not the plain 어머니한테 ... 줘요. Possession is likewise 우리 어머니, since 내 어머니 sounds unnaturally distant.

Saying '어머니한테 줘요' to an elder; politely it is 어머니께 드려요 (honorific 께 + humble 드리다).

entries.shortExplanation: 낮 means "daytime, day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 낮 (nat) = "daytime, day". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 낮 ("daytime") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 낮, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The bright part of the day, the opposite of 밤 (night).
낮 + 에 marks the time-when; pronounced '나제' from the ㅈ liaison.
낮 + 잠 (sleep) = a daytime sleep; pairs with the verb 자다 (낮잠을 자다).
한 ('full/peak') + 낮 = the hottest, brightest middle of the day.

examples.en: It's warm during the day.
examples.note: 낮 + 에 + 는 sets a daytime topic, implying a contrast with night.

examples.en: I take a nap on weekends.
examples.note: Everyday habit: the compound 낮잠 with its set verb 자다.

examples.en: I work in the daytime and study at night.
examples.note: Real routine contrasting 낮 with its antonym 밤 across one sentence.

entries.nuance: 낮 means the daytime — the bright stretch between morning and evening — and lives as the natural antonym of 밤 (night). It is a pure native Korean noun (not Sino-Korean), and its key feature is pronunciation: the final ㅈ links onto a following vowel, so 낮에 sounds like '나제' and 낮이 like '나지'; before a consonant or pause the ㅈ neutralizes to a 't' sound ('낟'). Its near-synonym 오후 'afternoon' is narrower and Sino-Korean (the clock-time after noon), whereas 낮 is the whole bright span and feels more everyday. The headline English-speaker pitfall is a cluster of look-alikes that differ by one final consonant: 낮 (daytime), 낯 (face, as in 낯설다 'unfamiliar'), and 낫 (a sickle; also 낫다 'to be better / to recover'). They sound nearly identical in isolation, so rely on meaning and the liaison to keep them straight, and pair 낮 with 에 to say 'during the day.'

Forgetting the liaison: 낮에 is pronounced '나제,' not a clipped 'nat-e.'
Treating 낮 and 오후 as identical — 오후 is specifically 'afternoon' (post-noon), while 낮 is the whole bright daytime.

entries.shortExplanation: 색깔 means "color" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 색깔 (saekkkal) means "color". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 색깔 ("color"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 색깔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday standalone word for color; feels fuller and warmer than the bare 색.
무슨 + 색깔 asks which color something is: 무슨 색깔이에요?
색깔 + 이 as subject with an adjective; 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular (예뻐요).
set collocation; 진하다 (deep) vs 연하다 (light) describe color intensity.

examples.en: What color is it?
examples.note: Simplest color question; 색깔 stands alone naturally as the subject.

examples.en: This bag has a pretty color.
examples.note: Double-subject pattern: 가방은 (topic) ... 색깔이 (subject) ... 예뻐요.

examples.en: My favorite color is blue.
examples.note: Real answer: 색깔 as topic, but a specific shade uses 색 inside 파란색.

entries.nuance: 색깔 is the everyday, standalone word for 'color,' built on the Sino-Korean root 색 (色 'color') plus a native suffix that makes it feel fuller and more conversational. Its near-synonym is just 색: the dividing line is grammatical, not meaning — 색깔 stands on its own (색깔이 예뻐요, 무슨 색깔?), while 색 is the building block that fuses to a specific shade name (파란색 blue, 빨간색 red, 노란색 yellow). A more formal, technical synonym is 색상, common in design and shopping ('color option'). The main English-speaker pitfall is over-using 색깔 by sticking it onto shade names — '파란색깔' is wrong; the named colors take 색, giving 파란색. Also, to ask 'what color,' the natural question word is 무슨 색깔, not 어떤 색깔 (which leans toward 'what kind/sort of color').

Asking '어떤 색깔' for 'what color' when 무슨 색깔 is the natural phrasing.
Forgetting 색깔 is for color only — for a person's complexion or facial expression use 안색 / 얼굴색, not 색깔.

entries.shortExplanation: 초록색 means "green" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "green" is 초록색 (choroksaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 초록색 ("green"). Watch the particle attached to 초록색 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The standard color noun for green (草綠色); 초록 alone is also common.
color noun + noun, the basic modifier pattern (no extra particle).

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the green one, please
usagePhrases.note: instrumental 으로 ('in the form of') for choosing a color at a store.
a fresh, pale spring green; a distinct shade, not just 'light 초록.'

examples.en: I like green.
examples.note: Naming a favorite color; 초록색 + 을 좋아하다.

examples.en: Do you have a green umbrella?
examples.note: Shopping: 초록색 directly modifies 우산 with no particle.

examples.en: Now that spring has come, the leaves are green.
examples.note: Real scene: 초록색 + 이에요 describing fresh leaves.

entries.nuance: 초록색 is the standard word for 'green' — the green of leaves and grass. usagePhrases.note: The standard color noun for white; 하얀색 is an equally common synonym.
color noun + clothing item, a very common pairing (no particle).
흰색 + 이에요 to state a color (consonant-final 색 → 이에요).

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the white one, please
usagePhrases.note: instrumental 으로 for picking the white option at a store.

examples.en: This shirt is white.
examples.note: Simple statement of color; 흰색 + 이에요.

examples.en: I bought white sneakers.
examples.note: 흰색 directly modifies 운동화; everyday shopping past tense.

examples.ko: 흰색하고 검은색 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요?
examples.romanization: huinsaekago geomeunsaek junge mwoga deo joayo?
examples.en: Between white and black, which do you prefer?
examples.note: Real choice: 흰색 contrasted with its opposite 검은색 (black).

entries.shortExplanation: 술 means "alcohol, alcoholic drink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: General native word for any alcoholic drink (소주, 맥주, 막걸리...).
술 + 을 with 마시다 (drink), the standard verb — not 먹다.
술 + 집 (house) = a drinking place; the everyday word for a bar.
literally 'do one glass of alcohol'; a warm invitation to drink together.

examples.en: I don't drink.
examples.note: Simple statement; 술 + 을 + the standard verb 마시다, negated with 안.

examples.en: Let's grab a drink together today.
examples.note: Set phrase 술 한잔하다 as a friendly invitation; 잔 is the glass/cup counter.

examples.en: You have to drive, so please don't drink.
examples.note: Real caution: 술은 (contrast topic) + polite prohibition -지 마세요.

entries.nuance: 술 is the general native word for any alcoholic drink — the umbrella over 소주, 맥주, 막걸리, 와인, and more. There is also etiquette baked into the word: you pour for others, not yourself, and a junior turns slightly away when drinking before an elder. The big English-speaker pitfall is reflexively pairing 'drink' with 먹다 (which means 'eat'); in careful Korean alcohol is 마시다. Also keep 술 (alcohol) distinct from 물 (water) — they differ by a single vowel.

entries.shortExplanation: 시 means "o'clock (hour)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "o'clock (hour)" is 시 (si). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한 시 ("one o'clock"). Watch the particle attached to 시 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: NATIVE number 하나 → 한 before 시. Hours always use native numbers.
NATIVE 둘 → 두 + 시, never '이 시.'
몇 + 시 asks the hour: 몇 시예요? (What time is it?).
the HOUR (시) takes native numbers, the MINUTES (분) take Sino numbers.

examples.en: What time is it now?
examples.note: Core question; 몇 시 + 예요 asks for the hour.

examples.en: I get up at seven o'clock.
examples.note: Native 일곱 + 시 + 에 ('at'); 에 marks clock time.

examples.ko: 수업이 세 시 삼십 분에 끝나요.
examples.romanization: sueobi se si samsip bune kkeunnayo.
examples.en: Class ends at 3:30.
examples.note: Mixed systems in one clause: NATIVE 세 시 for the hour, SINO 삼십 분 for the minutes.

entries.nuance: 시 is the counter for the o'clock HOUR (from 時 'time/hour'), and it is one of the great beginner traps because Korean splits its two number systems across the clock: the HOUR uses NATIVE numbers (한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시, 다섯 시...), while the MINUTES counter 분 uses SINO-Korean numbers (일 분, 십 분, 삼십 분). Don't confuse the noun 시 'o'clock' with its homophones 시 'poem' (詩) or the city suffix 시 (市, as in 부산시) — the counter use is always preceded by a native number.

Using Sino numbers for the hour, e.g. '삼 시' for three o'clock; it must be the native 세 시.
Using native numbers for minutes — 분 takes Sino numbers, so say 삼십 분, never '서른 분' or '세십 분.'
Forgetting the pre-시 shape change: 둘 → 두 시, 셋 → 세 시, not '둘 시' / '셋 시.'

entries.shortExplanation: 소 means "cow, ox" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 소 (so) = "cow, ox". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 소가 있어요 ("There is a cow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 소, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 소 + 가 because 소 ends in a vowel
all animals are counted with 마리, never 개
키우다 = to raise/keep an animal, takes 를
풀 = grass; everyday subject-object sentence

examples.en: There's a cow over there.
examples.note: Simple existence: 소 + 가 + 있어요.

examples.en: My grandfather raises two cows.
examples.note: Counter 마리 sits after the number, before 를.

examples.en: The cow goes 'moo'.
examples.note: Animal cries use 울다; 음매 is the Korean 'moo'.

entries.nuance: 소 is the live animal — a cow or ox grazing in a field. The crucial trap for English speakers is that the meat is a completely different word: 소고기 (소 'cow' + 고기 'meat'), so ordering '소' at a restaurant sounds like you want a whole live animal. Compare 소 with the loanword 우유 territory — milk is 우유 (牛乳, 'cow-milk'), not 소 something. 소 is one syllable ending in a vowel, so it always takes the subject marker 가 (소가), and like every animal it is counted with 마리, never 개 (which is for inanimate objects). A second pitfall: the verb for the cow's sound is 울다 'to cry', the same verb used for nearly all animal noises, so 소가 울어요 is natural even though English would never say a cow 'cries'.

Saying 소 주세요 to mean 'beef, please' — 소 is the live animal; the meat is 소고기, so say 소고기 주세요.
Counting cows with 개 (소 한 개). 개 is for objects; animals always take 마리, so say 소 한 마리.
Using 만들다 'make' for raising a cow. To keep/raise a live animal the verb is 키우다, so 소를 키워요.
