entries.shortExplanation: 쥐 means "mouse, rat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쥐 (jwi) means "mouse, rat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 쥐가 있어요 ("There is a mouse"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쥐 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쥐 + 가 because 쥐 ends in a vowel
animals take the counter 마리
잡다 = to catch/trap, takes 를
작다 = small; describes size

examples.en: There's a mouse in the kitchen!
examples.note: Existence at a place: 부엌에 + 쥐가.

examples.en: The cat caught the mouse.
examples.note: Past tense 잡다 → 잡았어요; 쥐 is the object.

examples.ko: 쥐 한 마리가 벽 뒤로 숨었어요.
examples.romanization: jwi han mariga byeok dwiro sumeosseoyo.
examples.en: A mouse hid behind the wall.
examples.note: 숨다 = to hide; 마리 counts the one animal.

entries.nuance: 쥐 covers both 'mouse' and 'rat' — Korean does not lexically split the small one from the big one the way English does, so context (or 큰 쥐 'big rat') carries the difference. The number-one pitfall is the computer device: a computer mouse is the loanword 마우스, never 쥐, so 쥐 클릭 would baffle a listener. Culturally 쥐 carries a negative, dirty, sneaky image (it is also the first animal of the zodiac, 쥐띠 'born in the year of the Rat'). It is one syllable ending in a vowel, so it takes 가 (쥐가), and as an animal it is counted with 마리. Note the verb pairing: you 잡다 'catch/trap' a 쥐, and a cat 잡다 it too — the same verb works for the hunter and the trap.

Calling a computer mouse 쥐. The device is the English loanword 마우스; 쥐 only means the live rodent.
Counting mice with 개 (쥐 한 개). Animals take 마리, so say 쥐 한 마리.
Trying to distinguish 'rat' with a separate base word. There is no everyday separate word — 쥐 is both; add 큰 'big' if size matters: 큰 쥐.

entries.shortExplanation: 뱀 means "snake" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "snake" is 뱀 (baem). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 뱀이 있어요 ("There is a snake"). Watch the particle attached to 뱀 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뱀 + 이 because 뱀 ends in the consonant ㅁ
animals take the counter 마리
무섭다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 무서워요
뱀 + 을 because it ends in a consonant

examples.en: Whoa, a snake!
examples.note: Plain-form exclamation 이다 → 이다! after a consonant.

examples.en: I saw a snake on the mountain.
examples.note: Object 뱀을; 한 마리 can float before the verb.

examples.en: The snake slithered through the grass.
examples.note: 지나가다 = pass through; 스르르 mimics slithering.

entries.nuance: 뱀 is a snake, and for learners it is a perfect drill word for the consonant-ending particle rule: because 뱀 ends in ㅁ, the subject marker is 이 (뱀이, never 뱀가) and the object marker is 을 (뱀을, never 뱀를). Watch the adjective 무섭다 'scary': it is ㅂ-irregular, so 'snakes are scary' becomes 뱀이 무서워요 (the ㅂ turns into 워), not 무섭어요. Counting snakes with 개. Animals take 마리, so say 뱀 한 마리.

entries.shortExplanation: 개구리 means "frog" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 개구리 (gaeguri) = "frog". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 개구리가 있어요 ("There is a frog") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 개구리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 개구리 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
animals take the counter 마리
animal sounds use 울다, not 노래하다
뛰다 = to jump/leap

examples.en: The frog hops.
examples.note: 폴짝 is the mimetic word for a light hop.

examples.en: There are two frogs in the rice paddy.
examples.note: 논 = rice paddy; 마리 counts them.

examples.en: When it rains the frogs go 'ribbit'.
examples.note: 개굴개굴 is the Korean frog sound + 울다.

entries.nuance: 개구리 is a frog, a four-syllable native word that learners must keep whole — dropping the final 리 to say 개구 is a common slip. The big pitfall is the verb for its sound: Korean uses 울다 'to cry' for almost every animal noise, so a frog 'croaks' as 개구리가 울어요, never 노래하다 'sing' and never 말하다. The onomatopoeia is 개굴개굴 (the English 'ribbit'). Distinguish the life stages: a tadpole is a separate word, 올챙이, and there is even a proverb 개구리 올챙이 적 생각 못 한다 ('the frog forgets its tadpole days', i.e. people forget their humble beginnings). It ends in a vowel so it takes 가 (개구리가), and it is counted with 마리.

Saying 개구리가 노래해요 for the sound it makes. Animal cries use 울다, so 개구리가 울어요.
Dropping a syllable and writing 개구 instead of the full 개구리.

examples.note: Existence at a place: 방에 + 벌레가.

entries.nuance: 벌레 is the everyday, slightly negative catch-all for a creepy-crawly — a bug, insect, or worm you would rather not see. The sharp contrast learners need is 벌레 vs 곤충: 곤충 (昆蟲, the Sino-Korean term for 'insect') is the neutral, scientific six-legged classification you meet in textbooks and museums, while 벌레 is the casual spoken word loaded with a faint 'yuck'. Counting bugs with 개 (벌레 한 개). Small creatures still take 마리: 벌레 한 마리.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 모기 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
small creatures take 마리

usagePhrases.en: I got bitten by a mosquito
usagePhrases.note: passive 물리다 + agent particle 에
active 물다 = to bite; 모기 + 가

examples.en: There are lots of mosquitoes in summer.
examples.note: Topic 여름에는 sets the season; 모기가 많다.

examples.en: I got a mosquito bite so it's really itchy.
examples.note: 물리다 + -어서 + 가렵다 cause chain.

examples.ko: 밤새 모기 한 마리가 윙윙거려서 못 잤어요.
examples.romanization: bamsae mogi han mariga wingwinggeoryeoseo mot jasseoyo.
examples.en: One mosquito buzzed all night so I couldn't sleep.
examples.note: 윙윙거리다 = to buzz; 마리 counts it.

entries.nuance: 모기 is a mosquito, and the must-learn point is the bite construction. English says 'a mosquito bit me' (mosquito = subject), but the natural Korean is the passive: 모기에 물렸어요 'I was bitten by a mosquito', where 물리다 is the passive of 물다 'to bite' and the biter is marked with 에, not 가. Saying 모기가 물렸어요 wrongly makes the mosquito the one bitten. If you want the mosquito as the actor you must use active 물다: 모기가 나를 물었어요. The itch that follows is 가렵다 'itchy' (an adjective), and the buzzing is 윙윙. 모기 ends in a vowel, taking 가, and is counted with 마리. It is a constant Korean summer complaint, so this passive bite phrase is extremely high-frequency.

Saying 모기가 물렸어요 to mean 'a mosquito bit me'. That literally means the mosquito got bitten. Use the passive with 에: 모기에 물렸어요.
Treating 가렵다 'itchy' like a verb. It is an adjective, so 'it itches' is 가려워요 (ㅂ-irregular), not 가렵어요.
Counting mosquitoes with 개. They take 마리: 모기 한 마리.

usagePhrases.note: 나비 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
small creatures take 마리
날다 (ㄹ-irregular) → 날아요

usagePhrases.en: the butterfly perched on the flower
usagePhrases.note: 앉다 = to perch/land; modifies 나비

examples.en: The butterfly flutters by.
examples.note: 훨훨 mimics light fluttering flight.

examples.ko: 꽃에 나비 한 마리가 살포시 앉았어요.
examples.romanization: kkoche nabi han mariga salposi anjasseoyo.
examples.en: A butterfly gently landed on the flower.
examples.note: 앉다 for landing; 살포시 = softly.

examples.en: Now that it's spring, there are more butterflies in the garden.
examples.note: -아지다 'become more' → 많아지다.

entries.nuance: 나비 is a butterfly — a pretty, positive native word, unlike most bug vocabulary. Two distinctions matter. First, a moth is 나방, a different (and far less charming) creature, so do not let the similar shapes 나비/나방 blur. The flying verb 날다 is ㄹ-irregular, so 'it flies' is 날아요. 나비 ends in a vowel, taking 가, and is counted with 마리. The onomatopoeia for its flight is 훨훨. 나비 is also a beloved cat name in Korea, roughly the equivalent of 'Whiskers' or 'Kitty'.

small creatures take 마리
무섭다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 무서워요
거미줄 = web; the set verb is 치다, not 만들다

examples.en: There's a spider on the ceiling.
examples.note: 천장 = ceiling; 거미 + 가 + 있어요.

examples.en: The spider spun a web in the corner.
examples.note: 거미줄 + 치다 is the natural pairing.

examples.en: A spider crept down.
examples.note: 내려오다 = come down; 스르르 = smoothly.

entries.nuance: 거미 is a spider, a native word ending in a vowel, so it takes 가 (거미가). Note that, strictly, a spider is an arachnid, not a 곤충 'insect', but in everyday speech Koreans lump it in with 벌레 'bugs' anyway. It is counted with 마리. The adjective 무섭다 'scary' is ㅂ-irregular, so 거미가 무서워요, not 무섭어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the web 거미. The spider is 거미; its web is the compound 거미줄.
Saying 거미줄을 만들어요 'make a web'. The idiomatic verb is 치다: 거미줄을 쳐요.
Counting spiders with 개. They take 마리: 거미 한 마리.

entries.shortExplanation: 땅 means "ground, land, earth (soil)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ground, land, earth (soil)" is 땅 (ttang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 땅이 넓어요 ("The land is wide"). Watch the particle attached to 땅 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 땅 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅇ
땅 + 에 marks the location of resting
땅 + 을 + 파다 'to dig'
real-estate sense; 땅 + 을 + 사다

examples.en: The child sat on the ground.
examples.note: 땅에 marks where they sat.

examples.en: The land here is really wide.
examples.note: 땅이 = subject; 넓다 'spacious'.

examples.en: I dug the ground and planted a small tree.
examples.note: 파다 + -아서 + 심다 'plant'.

entries.nuance: 땅 is the native word for the ground, land, or soil under our feet, and it stretches from the physical dirt you 파다 'dig' to the legal land you 사다 'buy'. The biggest English-speaker trap is 'Earth': the planet is 지구 (地球, 'earth-sphere'), never 땅, so '지구가 둥글다' (the Earth is round), not 땅. Distinguish three near-neighbors: 땅 = ground/land in general; 흙 = the soil/dirt as a substance you hold in your hand; 토지 (土地) = land as a formal real-estate/legal term. 땅 ends in the consonant ㅇ, so it takes 이 (땅이, never 땅가) and the object 을 (땅을). To sit or fall 'on' the ground, mark the spot with 에: 땅에 앉다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 땅 for the planet Earth. The planet is 지구; 땅 is only ground/land/soil here below.
Saying 땅가 넓어요. After the final consonant ㅇ you must use 이: 땅이 넓어요.
Blurring 땅 and 흙. 땅 is the ground/land; 흙 is the soil substance itself — you plant a seed 흙에 (in the soil) but you fall 땅에 (onto the ground).

entries.shortExplanation: 불 means "fire; light (lamp)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 불 (bul) = "fire; light (lamp)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 불이 나다 ("for a fire to break out") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 불, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.en: for a fire to break out
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; 불 + 이 + 나다, never 불이 시작하다

usagePhrases.en: to put out a fire / turn off a light
usagePhrases.note: 불 + 을 + 끄다 (ㅡ-irregular) → 꺼요

usagePhrases.en: to light a fire / turn on a light
usagePhrases.note: 불 + 을 + 켜다 = switch on
불 + 이; 뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 뜨거워요

examples.en: Please turn off the light.
examples.note: 끄다 → 꺼; 좀 softens the request.

examples.en: The room is dark. I'll turn on the light.
examples.note: 켜다 → 켤게요 'I'll switch it on'.

examples.en: A fire broke out in the neighbor's kitchen.
examples.note: 불이 나다 → 났어요, the fixed 'fire starts' phrase.

entries.nuance: 불 is a single native word covering two ideas English keeps apart: 'fire' (flames) and the 'light' of a lamp. So 불을 켜다 / 불을 끄다 means both 'light/extinguish a fire' and 'switch a light on/off' — context decides. The verb pair to memorize is 켜다 (on) / 끄다 (off); never use 열다 'open' / 닫다 'close' for lights, the way some learners do by analogy with English 'open the light'. For a fire breaking out, the fixed phrase is 불이 나다 'a fire occurs' (with 나다 'to come out'), not 불이 시작하다. 불 ends in ㄹ, so it takes 이 (불이, never 불가). Watch the irregulars: 끄다 is ㅡ-irregular (끄다 → 꺼요) and 뜨겁다 'hot' is ㅂ-irregular (뜨거워요). Related: 불꽃 = flame/spark, 모닥불 = campfire.

Saying 불가 났어요. After ㄹ the subject marker is 이: 불이 났어요.
Saying 불이 시작했어요 for a fire breaking out. The set phrase is 불이 나다: 불이 났어요.

맑다 → 맑은 modifies 공기

examples.note: 산 공기 = mountain air; 맑다 'clear'.

examples.note: 마시다 used for inhaling air.

entries.nuance: 공기 is the air we breathe, a Sino-Korean word: 空氣 ('empty-energy/vapor'), the same 氣 'qi/energy' seen in 기분 'mood' and 날씨-adjacent 일기. Two boundaries matter. First, do not confuse 공기 'air' with 날씨 'weather' or 기후 'climate' — they are different concepts, and '오늘 공기 좋다' (good air today) is not the same as '오늘 날씨 좋다' (good weather today). (Beware a homophone: 공기 also names a children's game of jacks and a bowl of rice — context separates them.)

entries.nuance: 오렌지 is the imported orange, written as a loanword straight from English. The taste vocabulary that pairs with it is 새콤달콤하다 'sweet and tangy' and 달다 'sweet'.

Confusing 오렌지 (imported orange) with 귤 (Korean tangerine/mandarin). They are different fruits; 귤 is the small winter one eaten at home.
Counting fruit with 마리 (오렌지 한 마리). 마리 is only for animals; whole fruit takes 개: 오렌지 한 개.
Misspelling the loanword as 오린지 or 오랜지. The standard form is 오렌지.

structuredNuance.t: 오렌지 is the imported orange, written as a loanword straight from English. As a loanword its spelling is fixed — 오렌지, not 오린지 or 오랜지. entries.shortExplanation: 고추 means "chili pepper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고추 (gochu) = "chili pepper". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고추가 맵다 ("the chili pepper is spicy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고추, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 고추 + 가; 맵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 매워요
vegetables are counted with 개
고추 + 를 + 넣다 'put in'
고추 + 가루 with 사이시옷 (inserted ㅅ)

examples.en: This chili is really spicy.
examples.note: 맵다 → 매워요; 진짜 'really' is casual.

examples.en: I sliced chili and added it to the stew.
examples.note: 썰다 'slice' + 넣다; 송송 = finely.

examples.en: You need plenty of chili powder for kimchi to turn red.
examples.note: 고춧가루; 빨갛다 → 빨개요.

entries.nuance: 고추 is the chili pepper, the backbone of Korean spice, and it spawns a small family you should keep straight: ground it becomes 고춧가루 'chili powder' (note the 사이시옷 — an inserted ㅅ for the compound, so 고춧가루, not 고추가루); the fermented red paste is 고추장; a fresh green chili is 풋고추. The sharpest pitfall is 고추 vs 후추: 후추 is black pepper, a totally different seasoning, so swapping them ruins a recipe. The adjective for its heat is 맵다 'spicy', which is ㅂ-irregular (맵다 → 매워요), not 매웠다-style regular. Inanimate, it is counted with 개. Culturally 고추 is loaded — its red color symbolized a baby boy, and it is also slang for a little boy's genitals, so the word carries a knowing double meaning adults will recognize.

Writing the powder as 고추가루. The compound takes 사이시옷: the standard spelling is 고춧가루.
Confusing 고추 (chili pepper) with 후추 (black pepper). They are different seasonings.
Conjugating 맵다 as 맵어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 맵다 → 매워요, so 고추가 매워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 극장 means "theater, cinema" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 극장 (geukjang) means "theater, cinema". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 극장에 가다 ("to go to the theater"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 극장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 극장 + 에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: to watch a movie at the cinema
usagePhrases.note: 극장 + 에서 marks where the action happens
극장 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅇ

usagePhrases.en: to meet in front of the theater
usagePhrases.note: 극장 앞 = place word + 에서

examples.en: I go to the cinema on weekends.
examples.note: 극장에 = where you go (destination).

examples.en: I watched a movie at the theater.
examples.note: 극장에서 = where the watching happened.

examples.en: Let's meet in front of the theater at 7.
examples.note: 극장 앞 + 에서 marks the meeting spot.

entries.nuance: 극장 is a place to watch a show — historically a live theater, today most often a movie cinema. It is Sino-Korean: 劇場 ('drama-place', 劇 'play/drama' + 場 'place/arena', the same 場 in 시장 'market' and 운동장 'sports field'). The register/usage contrast to know is 극장 vs 영화관: 영화관 (映畵館, 'movie-hall') specifically means a film cinema and sounds a touch more modern, while 극장 is the older, broader word that still covers cinemas and is universally understood — a multiplex like CGV is fine to call either. The grammar drill here is the 에 vs 에서 split: use 에 for the destination you go to (극장에 가다) but 에서 for the location where an action occurs (극장에서 영화를 보다). Because 극장 ends in ㅇ, it takes 이 (극장이, never 극장가).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 극장에서 가요 for 'I go to the theater'. Movement-toward takes 에: 극장에 가요. Use 에서 only for an action done there.
Saying 극장가 커요. After the final consonant ㅇ the subject marker is 이: 극장이 커요.
Assuming 극장 means only a live-play theater. In everyday Korean it usually means the movie cinema; the live-stage nuance is context-dependent.

entries.shortExplanation: 서점 means "bookstore" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bookstore" is 서점 (seojeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 서점에 가다 ("to go to the bookstore"). Watch the particle attached to 서점 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 서점 + 에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: to buy a book at the bookstore
usagePhrases.note: 서점 + 에서 marks where you buy
서점 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅁ
크다 → 큰 modifies 서점

examples.en: I bought a book at the bookstore.
examples.note: 권 counts books; 서점에서 = where you bought.

examples.en: There's a bookstore near the school.
examples.note: 서점이 = subject of 있다.

examples.en: Want to go to the bookstore together this weekend?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ래요? casual invitation.

entries.nuance: 서점 is a bookstore, where you buy books. It is Sino-Korean: 書店 ('book-shop', 書 'book/writing' + 店 'store', the same 店 in 편의점 'convenience store' and 음식점 'restaurant'). The contrast every beginner must lock in is 서점 vs 도서관: a 서점 is a shop where you pay and own the book, whereas 도서관 (圖書館, 'library') is where you borrow and return — confusing them produces sentences like 'I bought a book at the library'. A nearly synonymous word is 책방, a warmer, more old-fashioned native-flavored term for a (often small) bookshop. The grammar point is the same 에/에서 contrast: 서점에 가다 (go to) but 서점에서 책을 사다 (buy at). Since 서점 ends in ㅁ, it takes 이 (서점이, never 서점가); books inside are counted with 권.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 서점 (bookstore — you buy) with 도서관 (library — you borrow). They are different places.
Saying 서점가 있어요. After the final consonant ㅁ the subject marker is 이: 서점이 있어요.
Counting books with 개. Books take the bound-volume counter 권: 책 한 권.

entries.shortExplanation: 미용실 means "hair salon, beauty salon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 미용실 (miyongsil) = "hair salon, beauty salon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 미용실에 가다 ("to go to the hair salon") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 미용실, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to go to the hair salon
usagePhrases.note: 미용실 + 에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: to get a haircut at the salon
usagePhrases.note: 머리를 자르다 = cut one's hair
미용실 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㄹ
미용실 + 을 + 예약하다 'reserve'

examples.en: I'm going to the hair salon tomorrow.
examples.note: 미용실에 = destination.

examples.en: I got my hair cut short at the salon.
examples.note: 짧게 'short(ly)' + 자르다 → 잘랐어요.

examples.en: I booked the salon — I'm going to get a perm.
examples.note: 파마하다 'to perm'; -려고요 states intent.

entries.nuance: 미용실 is a hair/beauty salon where you cut, dye, or perm your hair. It is Sino-Korean: 美容室 ('beauty-grooming-room', 美 'beauty' + 容 'appearance/grooming' + 室 'room', the same 室 in 교실 'classroom' and 화장실 'restroom'). The contrast to know is 미용실 vs 이발소: an 이발소 (理髮所, 'barbershop') is the traditional men's barber — think the spinning pole — and now sounds old-fashioned, while 미용실 serves everyone and is the default modern word; younger speakers also say the loanword 헤어숍 or just 미용실. The key collocation is 머리를 자르다 'to cut one's hair' (literally 'cut the head'), with 자르다 → 잘랐어요 in the past. Note 머리 here means 'hair', not 'head', in this context. Since 미용실 ends in ㄹ, it takes 이 (미용실이, never 미용실가).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 미용실 (modern unisex hair salon) with 이발소 (traditional men's barbershop). 미용실 is the everyday default.
Saying 미용실가 있어요. After the final consonant ㄹ the subject marker is 이: 미용실이 있어요.
Saying 머리를 깎다 vs 자르다 incorrectly. For a normal salon haircut Koreans say 머리를 자르다; 깎다 sounds like shaving/clippers, more for very short or buzzed cuts.

structuredNuance.t: 미용실 is a hair/beauty salon where you cut, dye, or perm your hair. The key collocation is 머리를 자르다 'to cut one's hair' (literally 'cut the head'), with 자르다 → 잘랐어요 in the past. entries.shortExplanation: 구체적이다 means "to be concrete, specific, detailed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 구체적이다 (guchejeogida) means "to be concrete, specific, detailed". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 구체적인 예 ("a concrete example"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 구체적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing; 구체적인 예를 들어 주세요 = 'give a concrete example.'
구체적으로 말씀해 주세요 is how you politely ask someone to stop being vague.
Implies real dates, numbers, steps — not just a vague intention.

usagePhrases.en: to be a bit more specific
usagePhrases.note: 좀 더 구체적이었으면 좋겠어요 = 'I wish it were a bit more specific.'

examples.en: The plan isn't concrete yet.
examples.note: Predicate use: 구체적이다 → 구체적이지 않다 for the negative.

examples.ko: 면접에서는 구체적인 경험을 이야기하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseoneun guchejeogin gyeongheomeul iyagihaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: In an interview it's good to talk about specific experiences.
examples.note: 구체적인 + noun describes detailed, real content.

examples.ko: '열심히 하겠다'보다 구체적으로 어떻게 할 건지 말해 주세요.
examples.romanization: 'yeolsimhi hagetda'boda guchejeogeuro eotteoke hal geonji malhae juseyo.
examples.en: Rather than 'I'll work hard,' tell me concretely how you'll do it.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 구체적으로 demands actionable detail over slogans.

entries.nuance: 구체적이다 (具體的 — 具 'equip/possess' + 體 'body/form,' literally 'having a fleshed-out body') is the everyday word for ideas that come with real detail, examples, and numbers, and it is the exact antonym of 추상적이다. Compare it with 자세하다: 자세하다 means 'detailed/thorough' about information already given (자세한 설명 = a thorough explanation), whereas 구체적이다 is about whether something has tangible substance at all (vague plan vs concrete plan). In speech you will hear the adverb 구체적으로 far more than the bare adjective, above all in 구체적으로 말해 주세요. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers: do not drop the 적 (there is no 구체하다; it is always 구체적이다 / 구체적으로), and do not borrow English 'concrete' for physical solidity — for a hard, firm object you need 단단하다, not 구체적이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 구체하다 — the word always keeps 적: it is 구체적이다 as the adjective and 구체적으로 as the adverb. (구체화하다 exists, but that means 'to give shape to / flesh out.')
Using 구체적이다 for physical hardness because English 'concrete' is also a building material — for a solid, firm object use 단단하다; 구체적이다 is only about detail/specificity.
Writing the connective as 구체적이여서; the correct form from the 이다 stem is 구체적이어서 ('because it is concrete').

structuredNuance.t: The everyday word for ideas that come with real detail, examples, and numbers; the exact antonym of 추상적이다. In speech you hear the adverb 구체적으로 far more than the bare adjective, above all in 구체적으로 말해 주세요.

Compare it with 자세하다: 자세하다 means 'detailed/thorough' about information already given (자세한 설명 = a thorough explanation), whereas 구체적이다 is about whether something has tangible substance at all (vague plan vs concrete plan).

entries.shortExplanation: 추상적이다 means "to be abstract" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be abstract" is 추상적이다 (chusangjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 추상적인 개념 ("an abstract concept"). Watch the particle attached to 추상적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 추상적인 개념 is the textbook collocation; e.g. 사랑, 자유 같은 추상적인 개념.
Usually a complaint: 설명이 너무 추상적이에요 = 'the explanation is too abstract.'
추상적으로만 설명하지 마세요 = 'don't explain only in the abstract.'
Vague, non-concrete phrasing that leaves the listener unsure.

examples.en: That statement is a bit abstract.
examples.note: Simple predicate: 추상적이다 → 추상적이에요 in the polite present.

examples.ko: 사랑 같은 추상적인 개념은 말로 설명하기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: sarang gateun chusangjeogin gaenyeomeun mallo seolmyeonghagi himdeureoyo.
examples.en: Abstract concepts like love are hard to put into words.
examples.note: 추상적인 + 개념 is a very frequent pairing.

examples.ko: 너무 추상적으로 말하지 말고 예를 하나 들어 주세요.
examples.romanization: neomu chusangjeogeuro malhaji malgo yereul hana deureo juseyo.
examples.en: Don't speak so abstractly — give me one example.
examples.note: Real-situation use: people push back on 추상적 talk by asking for an example.

entries.nuance: 추상적이다 (抽象的 — 抽 'draw out' + 象 'image,' i.e. an idea 'drawn out' from concrete things) describes what exists only as a concept, with no tangible detail, and is the direct opposite of 구체적이다. In conversation it usually carries a mildly negative tone: calling someone's explanation 추상적 implies it is too vague to be useful, so it works almost as a soft request for specifics. Do not confuse it with 막연하다, which means 'vague/hazy' in the sense of unclear and uncertain (막연한 불안 = a vague unease); 추상적 is specifically about being conceptual rather than concrete. The main English-speaker pitfall is the connective spelling: write 추상적이어서, never 추상적이여서, and memorize the chunk 추상적이어서 이해하기 어렵다 ('so abstract it's hard to understand').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 추상적이여서 — the 이다 stem gives 추상적이어서 ('because it is abstract'); the 여 spelling is wrong.
Confusing 추상 with 추억 ('memory') because they share 추 — they are unrelated; the noun for a memory is 추억, while 추상 means abstraction.
Treating 추상적이다 as purely negative — it is also neutral/technical, e.g. 추상적인 사고 ('abstract thinking') is a valued cognitive skill, not an insult.

entries.shortExplanation: 객관적이다 means "to be objective" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 객관적이다 (gaekgwanjeogida) = "to be objective". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 객관적으로 보면 ("objectively speaking / looking at it objectively") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 객관적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.en: objectively speaking / looking at it objectively
usagePhrases.note: A set discourse opener that signals you're giving a fair, feelings-aside view.
객관적인 사실만 전하다 = 'report only the objective facts' (news register).
The natural adverb + verb pairing for fair decision-making.
Uses the noun 객관성; formal/academic register.

examples.en: That assessment is objective.
examples.note: Simple predicate use of 객관적이다.

examples.ko: 기사에는 객관적인 사실만 담겨 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: gisaeneun gaekgwanjeogin sasilman damgyeo isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: An article should contain only objective facts.
examples.note: 객관적인 + 사실 is a high-frequency newsroom pairing.

examples.ko: 감정을 빼고 객관적으로 한번 판단해 보세요.
examples.romanization: gamjeongeul ppaego gaekgwanjeogeuro hanbeon pandanhae boseyo.
examples.en: Set emotion aside and try judging it objectively for once.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 객관적으로 is invoked precisely to counter 감정적 reactions.

entries.nuance: 객관적이다 (客觀的 — 客 'guest/outsider' + 觀 'view,' i.e. seeing as an outside observer would) means 'grounded in facts rather than personal feeling,' and is the standard antonym of 주관적이다. Keep the 客 'outsider' image: the objective view is the one a neutral third party would share. Korean speakers routinely launch an opinion with 객관적으로 보면 ('objectively speaking') to frame it as fair, so the phrase is as much a politeness/credibility move as a literal claim. Do not confuse it with 공정하다 ('fair/just'), which is about even-handed treatment and ethics, whereas 객관적 is about fact-based, feelings-free perception. The recurring pitfall for English speakers is the adverb form: it is 객관적으로 (the 적 + 으로 suffix), never 객관적게 — Sino-Korean 적 adjectives form adverbs with 으로, not the native 게.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 객관적 (objective) and 주관적 (subjective) by accident — they are exact opposites; anchor them with 客 (outside) vs 主 (self).
Forming the adverb as 객관적게 — Sino-Korean -적 words take 으로, so it must be 객관적으로.
Using 객관적이다 to mean 'fair/just' — for fair treatment use 공정하다; 객관적 is specifically fact-based and emotion-free.

entries.shortExplanation: 주관적이다 means "to be subjective" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주관적이다 (jugwanjeogida) means "to be subjective". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주관적인 의견 ("a subjective opinion"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주관적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A polite hedge: 이건 제 주관적인 의견인데요 = 'this is just my subjective opinion, but…'
맛 평가는 주관적일 수밖에 없어요 = 'taste judgments are inevitably subjective.'

usagePhrases.en: to speak subjectively / from one's own view
usagePhrases.note: 주관적으로 말하면… frames a personal take.
Uses the noun 주관; this one is a compliment, not a criticism.

examples.en: That's too subjective.
examples.note: Simple predicate; often a gentle pushback on someone's claim.

examples.en: That's not a fact but a subjective opinion.
examples.note: Routinely contrasted with 사실/객관적.

examples.ko: 너무 주관적으로만 보지 말고 다른 관점도 들어 보세요.
examples.romanization: neomu jugwanjeogeuroman boji malgo dareun gwanjeomdo deureo boseyo.
examples.en: Don't view it only subjectively — hear out other perspectives too.
examples.note: Real-situation use: paired with the implied antonym 객관적으로.

entries.nuance: 주관적이다 (主觀的 — 主 'self/main' + 觀 'view,' i.e. seeing from one's own standpoint) describes something shaped by personal feeling, taste, or viewpoint, and is the opposite of 객관적이다 (anchored by 主 'self' vs 客 'outsider'). It is most useful as a soft hedge: tagging a statement 주관적인 의견 signals 'this is only my take, not a fact,' which softens assertions politely. Be careful not to use it for 'biased/prejudiced' in a strong moral sense — for prejudice you need 편견 (편견을 가지다 = 'to hold a prejudice'); 주관적 merely means personal, not bigoted. Also distinguish the noun 주관 in 주관이 뚜렷하다, which praises someone for having clear, independent views — there 주관 is a positive trait, the opposite flavor from the cautious 주관적인 의견.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 객관적이다 — remember 주(主, self) vs 객(客, guest/outside) to keep the pair straight.
Using 주관적이다 to mean 'biased/prejudiced' — that strong negative sense needs 편견(을 가지다); 주관적 only means 'personal/viewpoint-based.'
Forming the adverb as 주관적게 — it must be 주관적으로 (-적 + 으로).

主觀的 — 主 'self/main' + 觀 'view,' i.e. seeing from one's own standpoint.

entries.shortExplanation: 일반적이다 means "to be general, common, usual" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be general, common, usual" is 일반적이다 (ilbanjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일반적으로 ("generally, as a rule"). Watch the particle attached to 일반적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A top-tier discourse opener: 일반적으로 한국에서는… states a norm.
일반적인 경우에는 = 'in the usual case'; sets up a default before exceptions.
What most people assume, often before you challenge it.
그건 아주 일반적인 일이에요 = 'that's a totally ordinary thing.'

examples.en: That kind of reaction is common.
examples.note: Simple predicate: reassuring someone their response is normal.

examples.ko: 그건 아주 일반적인 반응이니까 걱정하지 마세요.
examples.romanization: geugeon aju ilbanjeogin baneunginikka geokjeonghaji maseyo.
examples.en: That's a very common reaction, so don't worry.
examples.note: 일반적인 + noun = typical/ordinary.

examples.ko: 일반적으로 한국에서는 신발을 벗고 집에 들어가요.
examples.romanization: ilbanjeogeuro hangugeseoneun sinbareul beotgo jibe deureogayo.
examples.en: Generally in Korea you take your shoes off before entering a home.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 일반적으로 introduces a cultural norm/general rule.

entries.nuance: 일반적이다 (一般的 — 一 'one' + 般 'sort/kind,' i.e. 'of one common sort') means 'typical, common, what is usually the case,' and the adverb 일반적으로 is one of the most useful words for stating a general rule in explanations and writing. Compare it with 보통: 보통 is the casual, everyday word for 'usually' and works in any conversation (보통 7시에 일어나요), whereas 일반적으로 is more formal and explanatory, the kind of phrase you use to lay down a norm or generalization. Watch the meaning shift when you drop 적: 일반 on its own means 'general public / ordinary (non-specialist)' and appears in compounds like 일반인 ('ordinary person'), 일반석 ('regular seat'), 일반실 — so keep the 적 when you mean 'common/typical.' The English speaker's pitfall is reaching for 일반적으로 in casual chat where a Korean would simply say 보통.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 일반적으로 in casual conversation where 보통 is more natural — 보통 = everyday 'usually,' 일반적으로 = formal 'generally/as a rule.'
Dropping the 적: 일반이다 / 일반 shifts to 'general public / non-specialist' (일반인, 일반석), so 'common/typical' must stay 일반적이다.
Forming the adverb as 일반적게 — Sino-Korean -적 takes 으로, giving 일반적으로.

entries.shortExplanation: 합리적이다 means "to be rational, reasonable" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 합리적이다 (hamnijeogida) = "to be rational, reasonable". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 합리적인 가격 ("a reasonable/fair price") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 합리적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Very common in shopping: 가격이 합리적이에요 = 'the price is fair/justified.'
합리적으로 생각해 보세요 = 'think about it rationally.'
Frames a decision as logical rather than emotional or impulsive.
The antonym, built with the prefix 비-(非).

examples.en: That decision is reasonable.
examples.note: Simple predicate; a positive evaluation of a choice.

examples.ko: 이 가격이면 정말 합리적인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i gagyeogimyeon jeongmal hamnijeogin geot gatayo.
examples.en: At this price it really seems reasonable.
examples.note: 합리적인 가격 = a fair, justified price (not merely cheap).

examples.ko: 감정적으로 말고 합리적으로 한번 판단해 봅시다.
examples.romanization: gamjeongjeogeuro malgo hamnijeogeuro hanbeon pandanhae bopsida.
examples.en: Let's judge rationally rather than emotionally for once.
examples.note: Real-situation use: explicitly set against 감정적으로.

entries.nuance: 합리적이다 (合理的 — 合 'fit/accord' + 理 'reason/principle,' i.e. 'in accord with reason') spans two English ideas at once: 'logical/rational' (합리적으로 생각하다 = think logically) and 'reasonable/fair' (합리적인 가격 = a fair price). It almost always carries positive evaluation. Distinguish it from 합당하다, which means 'fitting/warranted/deserved' for a specific case (합당한 처벌 = a fitting punishment) — 합리적 is about overall logic and good sense, not case-by-case appropriateness. The key pitfall: 합리적인 가격 does NOT mean 'cheap'; it means a price that is justified for what you get, so a high price can still be 합리적. And form the opposite with the Sino prefix — 'irrational' is 비합리적이다, not 안 합리적이다 in any careful or written register.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 합리적인 가격 as 'a cheap price' — it means a fair, justified price; something expensive can still be 합리적.
Saying 안 합리적이다 for 'irrational' — the standard form uses the prefix 비-: 비합리적이다.
Confusing 합리적 with 합당하다 — 합당하다 = 'fitting/warranted' for a particular case, while 합리적 = 'logical/reasonable' in general.

structuredNuance.t: Spans two English ideas at once: 'logical/rational' (합리적으로 생각하다 = think logically) and 'reasonable/fair' (합리적인 가격 = a fair price). It almost always carries positive evaluation.
Distinguish it from 합당하다, which means 'fitting/warranted/deserved' for a specific case (합당한 처벌 = a fitting punishment) — 합리적 is about overall logic and good sense, not case-by-case appropriateness.
合理的 — 合 'fit/accord' + 理 'reason/principle,' i.e. 'in accord with reason.'

entries.shortExplanation: 현실적이다 means "to be realistic, practical" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 현실적이다 (hyeonsiljeogida) means "to be realistic, practical". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 현실적으로 ("realistically, in practical terms"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 현실적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 현실적으로 가능할까요? = 'is it realistically possible?'
Contrasts an attainable aim with a pie-in-the-sky 이상적인 목표.
Used when an idea is rejected for being too idealistic.
The antonym with 비-(非); 비현실적인 기대 = unrealistic expectations.

examples.en: That goal is realistic.
examples.note: Simple predicate; says an aim is actually attainable.

examples.ko: 꿈도 좋지만 좀 더 현실적인 목표를 세워 보세요.
examples.romanization: kkumdo jochiman jom deo hyeonsiljeogin mokpyoreul sewo boseyo.
examples.en: Dreams are fine, but try setting a more realistic goal.
examples.note: 현실적인 목표 = an achievable, down-to-earth goal.

examples.ko: 현실적으로 생각하면 그 계획은 시간이 너무 부족해요.
examples.romanization: hyeonsiljeogeuro saenggakamyeon geu gyehoegeun sigani neomu bujokaeyo.
examples.en: Realistically, that plan just doesn't have enough time.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 현실적으로 생각하면 pulls a discussion back to feasibility.

entries.nuance: 현실적이다 (現實的 — 現 'present/appear' + 實 'real/actual,' i.e. 'of present reality') describes something grounded in reality and actually feasible, and is the natural foil to 이상적이다 ('ideal'). Applied to a person it usually means practical and down-to-earth (그 사람은 현실적이에요), which is generally a compliment, not a put-down. Crucially, do not confuse it with 사실적이다 (寫實的, 'lifelike/realistic') — 사실적 is an art-and-description word for vividly true-to-life depiction (사실적인 묘사 = a lifelike portrayal), whereas 현실적 is about practicality and what can really be done. The adverb 현실적으로 is the go-to phrase for steering a conversation toward what is actually possible. Pitfall: don't call a practical person 현실 — 현실 alone is the noun 'reality'; the adjective must be 현실적이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 현실적이다 (realistic/feasible) with 사실적이다 (lifelike/true-to-life) — the latter is for art and vivid description, e.g. 사실적인 그림.
Calling a down-to-earth person 현실 — 현실 is the noun 'reality'; the adjective is 현실적이다.
Forming the opposite as 안 현실적이다 — use the prefix form 비현실적이다 ('unrealistic').

entries.shortExplanation: 이상적이다 means "to be ideal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be ideal" is 이상적이다 (isangjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이상적인 직장 ("an ideal job/workplace"). Watch the particle attached to 이상적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 이상적인 + noun = perfect for its purpose: 이상적인 조건, 이상적인 환경.
이상적으로는 좋지만… sets up the 'but in reality' turn.
Often gently critical: 'a nice idea, but unrealistic.'
Uses the noun 이상; describes someone aspirational (neutral-to-positive).

examples.en: That environment is truly ideal.
examples.note: Simple predicate; high praise for near-perfect conditions.

examples.ko: 집에서 가깝고 월급도 좋으니 이상적인 직장이네요.
examples.romanization: jibeseo gakkapgo wolgeupdo joeuni isangjeogin jikjangineyo.
examples.en: It's close to home and pays well, so it's an ideal job.
examples.note: 이상적인 + noun = ideal/perfect for a purpose.

examples.ko: 이상적으로는 다 같이 가면 좋지만 현실은 좀 달라요.
examples.romanization: isangjeogeuroneun da gachi gamyeon jochiman hyeonsireun jom dallayo.
examples.en: Ideally we'd all go together, but reality's a bit different.
examples.note: Real-situation use: the 이상적으로는 …, 현실은 … contrast is everywhere in speech.

entries.nuance: 이상적이다 (理想的 — 理 'reason/principle' + 想 'thought,' i.e. an idea conceived as perfect) means 'ideal, perfect in theory,' and pairs naturally as the opposite of 현실적이다. The set frame 이상적으로는 …, 현실은 … ('ideally …, but in reality …') is one of the most common rhetorical moves in everyday Korean, so learn it as a unit. Note that, depending on tone, 이상적인 생각 can tip into mild criticism ('too idealistic / not feasible'), much like English 'that's idealistic.' Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not confuse this 이상(理想, 'ideal') with the identical-sounding 이상(異常) in 이상하다 ('strange/odd') — same syllables, opposite feel, different hanja. Second, don't overuse 이상적이다 for ordinary 'good'; reserve it for something close to perfect, and use 좋다 for everyday approval.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing 이상적이다 (ideal, 理想) with 이상하다 (strange, 異常) — identical 이상 sound but different hanja and opposite feel.
Overusing 이상적이다 for plain 'good' — reserve it for near-perfect; for ordinary approval say 좋다.
Forming the opposite as 안 이상적이다 — there's no common 비이상적; instead say 현실적이지 않다 or 비현실적이다 to express the realistic counterpoint.

entries.shortExplanation: 전통적이다 means "to be traditional" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전통적이다 (jeontongjeogida) = "to be traditional". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전통적인 음식 ("traditional food") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전통적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 전통적인 + noun for culturally inherited things: 전통적인 결혼식, 전통적인 방식.
전통적으로 명절에는 가족이 모여요 — introduces a long-standing practice.
Often set against modern/younger-generation attitudes.
Uses the noun 전통; also 전통문화, 전통시장.

examples.en: That method is rather traditional.
examples.note: Simple predicate; can be neutral or hint at 'old-school.'

examples.ko: 설날에는 전통적인 한복을 입는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: seolnareneun jeontongjeogin hanbogeul imneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: On Lunar New Year, many people wear traditional hanbok.
examples.note: 전통적인 + noun describes culturally inherited things.

examples.ko: 전통적으로 한국에서는 어른께 먼저 인사를 드려요.
examples.romanization: jeontongjeogeuro hangugeseoneun eoreunkke meonjeo insareul deuryeoyo.
examples.en: Traditionally in Korea, you greet your elders first.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 전통적으로 + honorific 드리다 introduces a respected custom.

entries.nuance: 전통적이다 (傳統的 — 傳 'pass down' + 統 'lineage/system,' i.e. 'of a handed-down lineage') means 'in keeping with long-standing tradition,' and is the natural adjective for food, clothing, ceremonies, and values passed down over generations; the noun 전통 saturates compounds like 전통문화, 전통시장, 전통혼례. It carries a respectful, valued tone. Do not let English 'traditional = old-fashioned' bleed in: when you mean outdated or behind-the-times, use 구식이다 (구식 휴대폰 = an outdated phone), which is slightly negative, whereas 전통적이다 honors heritage. Also keep 전통(傳統, 'tradition') apart from the near-homophone 정통(正統, 'orthodox/authentic-lineage,' as in 정통 이탈리아 요리 = authentic Italian cuisine) — one syllable apart, clearly different meaning. The adverb is 전통적으로, never 전통적게.

Using 전통적이다 for 'old-fashioned/outdated' — that nuance is 구식이다; 전통적이다 is respectful about heritage, not a criticism.
Confusing 전통 (tradition, 傳統) with 정통 (orthodox/authentic, 正統) — similar sound, different hanja and meaning.
Forming the adverb as 전통적게 — it must be 전통적으로.

傳統的 — 傳 'pass down' + 統 'lineage/system,' i.e. 'of a handed-down lineage.' Keep 전통(傳統, 'tradition') apart from the near-homophone 정통(正統, 'orthodox/authentic-lineage,' as in 정통 이탈리아 요리 = authentic Italian cuisine) — one syllable apart, clearly different meaning.
The adverb is 전통적으로, never 전통적게.

entries.english: to be representative, the most typical example
entries.shortExplanation: 대표적이다 means "to be representative, the most typical example" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 대표적이다 (daepyojeogida) means "to be representative, the most typical example". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 대표적인 음식 ("a representative/iconic food"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 대표적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The dominant pattern: 한국의 대표적인 음식 = Korea's signature food.
대표적으로 김치를 들 수 있어요 = 'kimchi is a prime example.'
Introduces the clearest illustration of a category.
이 작가의 대표적인 작품 = this author's defining work.

examples.en: Kimchi is a representative food of Korea.
examples.note: 대표적인 + noun = the most iconic example of a category.

examples.en: As prime examples, Busan and Jeju are popular travel spots.
examples.note: 대표적으로 opens a list with its leading members.

examples.ko: 한국의 대표적인 명절이라고 하면 보통 설날과 추석을 꼽아요.
examples.romanization: hangugui daepyojeogin myeongjeorirago hamyeon botong seolnalgwa chuseogeul kkobayo.
examples.en: Asked for Korea's representative holidays, people usually name Seollal and Chuseok.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 대표적인 + noun + 꼽다 = to single out as the top example.

entries.nuance: 대표적이다 (代表的 — 代 'on behalf of' + 表 'show/express,' i.e. 'standing in to represent') means 'serving as the most typical or famous example' of a category, and in practice you meet it almost only as 대표적인 + noun or as the list-opener 대표적으로 — the bare predicate 이건 대표적이에요 sounds incomplete and unnatural. Compare it with 유명하다 ('famous'): something can be 유명하다 simply by being widely known, but 대표적 specifically frames it as the standard-bearer that typifies a whole group (대표적인 한식 = the dish that represents Korean food as a category). The root 대표 also lives on its own meaning 'representative/leader' (회사 대표 = company head, 학급 대표 = class rep), so context tells you whether it is the noun 'representative' or this adjective sense. Pitfall: avoid using 대표적이다 as a stand-alone predicate — attach a noun.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 대표적이다 as a bare predicate (이건 대표적이에요) — it sounds incomplete; say 대표적인 음식이에요 or 대표적인 예예요.
Treating 대표적 as a synonym for 유명하다 — 유명하다 just means 'famous,' while 대표적 means 'typifying/standing for a whole category.'
Forming the adverb as 대표적게 — it must be 대표적으로 ('as a prime example').

Avoid using 대표적이다 as a stand-alone predicate — attach a noun.

entries.shortExplanation: 직접적이다 means "to be direct" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be direct" is 직접적이다 (jikjeopjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 직접적인 영향 ("a direct effect/influence"). Watch the particle attached to 직접적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 직접적인 영향을 주다/받다 = to have/receive a direct effect.
Contrasts with 간접적인 원인 (an indirect/contributing cause).
직접적으로 말하기는 좀 그래요 = 'saying it directly is a bit awkward.'
Wording that states things head-on, sometimes too bluntly for comfort.

examples.en: That expression is too direct.
examples.note: Simple predicate; flags wording as overly blunt.

examples.en: Stress has a direct effect on health.
examples.note: 직접적인 영향/원인 are core collocations.

examples.ko: 한국에서는 거절을 직접적으로 말하지 않는 경우가 많아요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseoneun geojeoreul jikjeopjeogeuro malhaji anhneun gyeonguga manayo.
examples.en: In Korea, refusals are often not stated directly.
examples.note: Real-situation use: a cultural point — direct refusal can feel rude.

entries.nuance: 직접적이다 (直接的 — 直 'straight' + 接 'connect,' i.e. 'straight-connected, nothing in between') describes something direct, with no intermediary: 직접적인 원인 (direct cause), 직접적인 영향 (direct impact), a blunt 직접적인 표현. Its antonym is 간접적이다. The big trap for English speakers is that the bare root 직접 is a high-frequency adverb meaning 'in person / by oneself' (직접 만들다 = to make it yourself, 직접 가다 = to go in person) — that 직접 is NOT interchangeable with the adjective-derived 직접적으로, which means 'directly = bluntly/without an intermediary.' So 직접 가다 ('go in person') and 직접적으로 말하다 ('speak bluntly') are different ideas; never swap them. Register note: because Korean often favors indirectness, calling speech 직접적 can carry a faint 'too blunt' overtone. And the connective is 직접적이어서, not 직접적이여서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the adverb 직접 ('in person/oneself,' 직접 가다) with 직접적으로 ('bluntly/without intermediary') — 직접 가다 ≠ 직접적으로 가다.
Writing the connective as 직접적이여서 — the 이다 stem gives 직접적이어서.
Assuming 직접적이다 is always neutral — about speech it can imply 'too blunt'; the polite, softened option is often 간접적인 표현.

entries.shortExplanation: 간접적이다 means "to be indirect" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 간접적이다 (ganjeopjeogida) = "to be indirect". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 간접적으로 듣다 ("to hear (something) secondhand/indirectly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 간접적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 친구를 통해 간접적으로 들었어요 = 'I heard it indirectly through a friend.'
The polite alternative to a blunt 직접적인 표현.
An effect transmitted through something else, not first-hand.
A fixed compound using the root 간접; literally 'indirect smoking.'

examples.en: That approach is a bit indirect.
examples.note: Simple predicate; notes that something goes the roundabout way.

examples.ko: 그 소식은 친구를 통해 간접적으로 들었어요.
examples.romanization: geu sosigeun chingureul tonghae ganjeopjeogeuro deureosseoyo.
examples.en: I heard that news indirectly through a friend.
examples.note: 간접적으로 듣다/알다 = to learn secondhand.

examples.ko: 한국 사람들은 부탁을 거절할 때 간접적인 표현을 더 선호해요.
examples.romanization: hanguk saramdeureun butageul geojeolhal ttae ganjeopjeogin pyohyeoneul deo seonhohaeyo.
examples.en: Koreans tend to prefer indirect expressions when refusing a request.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 간접적인 표현 is the culturally softer, more polite choice.

entries.nuance: 간접적이다 (間接的 — 間 'gap/between' + 接 'connect,' i.e. 'connected through a gap/intermediary') is the exact antonym of 직접적이다 and describes anything done or learned via a go-between: 간접적으로 듣다 (hear secondhand), 간접적인 영향 (a knock-on effect), 간접적인 표현 (a softened, roundabout way of putting something). Learning the 직접/간접 pair together pays off, and the root 간접 anchors fixed compounds like 간접흡연 (secondhand smoke) and 간접 경험 (vicarious experience). Register note: in Korean culture 간접적인 표현 is often the polite, face-saving option, so 'indirect' here is frequently a positive — quite unlike the slightly evasive ring of English 'indirect.' Pitfalls: keep 간접 (indirect) and 직접 (direct) straight, and write the connective as 간접적이어서, never 간접적이여서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 간접 (indirect, 間接) and 직접 (direct, 直接) — they are exact opposites; anchor on 間 'gap/between.'
Writing the connective as 간접적이여서 — the correct form is 간접적이어서.
Reading 간접적인 표현 as evasive/negative — in Korean it's often the polite, considerate choice, not a dodge.

structuredNuance.t: The exact antonym of 직접적이다; describes anything done or learned via a go-between: 간접적으로 듣다 (hear secondhand), 간접적인 영향 (a knock-on effect), 간접적인 표현 (a softened, roundabout way of putting something). entries.shortExplanation: 적극적이다 means "to be active, proactive, enthusiastic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 적극적이다 (jeokgeukjeogida) means "to be active, proactive, enthusiastic". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 적극적으로 참여하다 ("to participate actively"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 적극적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 적극적으로 참여해 주세요 = 'please take part actively' (events, meetings).
A common workplace/school compliment about willingness and drive.

usagePhrases.en: to step up / take the initiative
usagePhrases.note: Describes someone volunteering or pushing things forward.
The antonym; learn the pair 적극적/소극적 together.

examples.en: That person is really proactive.
examples.note: Simple predicate; a warm compliment about someone's drive.

examples.ko: 적극적인 태도 덕분에 좋은 평가를 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jeokgeukjeogin taedo deokbune joeun pyeonggareul badasseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to a proactive attitude, they got a good evaluation.
examples.note: 적극적인 태도 is a stock workplace phrase.

examples.ko: 새 직원이 회의에서 아주 적극적으로 의견을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: sae jigwoni hoeuieseo aju jeokgeukjeogeuro uigyeoneul naesseoyo.
examples.en: The new employee gave opinions very actively in the meeting.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 적극적으로 + 동사 describes eager, take-charge participation.

entries.nuance: 적극적이다 (積極的 — 積 'accumulate' + 極 'utmost,' i.e. pushing to the fullest extent) describes an energetic, take-initiative attitude and is a strong compliment in workplace and school settings (적극적인 참여, 적극적으로 나서다); its direct antonym is 소극적이다 (消極的, 'passive/timid'), and Koreans habitually use the pair to characterize personality. Distinguish it carefully from 긍정적이다 ('positive/optimistic'): 긍정적 is about outlook and mood (긍정적인 사람 = an upbeat person), while 적극적 is about action and initiative — someone can be cheerful (긍정적) yet still hang back (소극적). Two pitfalls: the opposite of 적극적이다 is 소극적이다, NOT 부정적이다 (which is the antonym of 긍정적, 'negative'); and form the adverb as 적극적으로, never 적극적게. Memorize 적극적 / 소극적 as a matched set, since they are the standard vocabulary for describing how forward someone is.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 적극적이다 (proactive/take-initiative) with 긍정적이다 (positive/optimistic) — one is about action, the other about outlook; they don't always go together.
Thinking the antonym is 부정적이다 — that's the opposite of 긍정적; the true antonym of 적극적이다 is 소극적이다 (passive).
Forming the adverb as 적극적게 — it must be 적극적으로 ('actively/proactively').

entries.shortExplanation: 결과 means "result, outcome" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "result, outcome" is 결과 (gyeolgwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시험 결과 ("exam results"). Watch the particle attached to 결과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 결과 + noun: the result OF something; the modifier comes first, no 의 needed
the verb of 'being released' is 나오다 with 이/가, never 를
attaches to a past-tense verb stem: 노력한 결과 = as a result of having tried
sentence-initial discourse connector linking a cause sentence to its outcome

examples.en: How are your exam results?
examples.note: Simple: 결과 as a plain noun taking 이/가 — note Korean has no plural -s

examples.ko: 검사 결과가 아직 안 나와서 기다리고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geomsa gyeolgwaga ajik an nawaseo gidarigo isseoyo.
examples.en: The test results haven't come out yet, so I'm waiting.
examples.note: Everyday: the fixed collocation 결과가 나오다 for results being released

examples.ko: 일 년 동안 열심히 운동한 결과 몸무게가 십 킬로그램이나 줄었어요.
examples.romanization: il nyeon dongan yeolsimhi undonghan gyeolgwa mommugega sip killogeuraemina jureosseoyo.
examples.en: As a result of exercising hard for a year, my weight dropped by a full 10 kg.
examples.note: Real situation: -(으)ㄴ 결과 turns the whole first clause into the cause of the second

entries.nuance: 결과 (結果, literally '結 form/bear + 果 fruit', i.e. the fruit that an action bears) is the end outcome of an action or event, and it almost always pairs with 나오다 (come out) or 나타나다 (appear) rather than any verb of 'making'. Its built-in partner is 과정 (the process leading up to it) and its mirror image is 원인 (the cause behind it), so Koreans constantly say 과정도 중요하고 결과도 중요하다. Register is neutral — fine in a doctor's office (검사 결과), a classroom (시험 결과), or a news report. The big English-speaker trap is twofold: first, you do not 'get' a result with a transitive verb the way English does — the result 나오다 (comes out) on its own and takes 이/가, so 결과를 나오다 is wrong; second, do not confuse the outcome 결과 with the reason 원인/이유 — 결과 is what happened at the end, never why.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 결과를 나오다 — 나오다 ('come out') is intransitive, so the result takes 이/가: 결과가 나오다.
결과 is the outcome, not the cause; for 'the reason/cause' use 원인 (objective cause) or 이유 (personal reason), e.g. 사고의 원인, not 사고의 결과, when you mean what triggered it.
Don't force an English plural — there is no 결과들 in 'exam results'; 시험 결과 already covers singular and plural.

entries.shortExplanation: 원인 means "cause" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 원인 (wonin) = "cause". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사고의 원인 ("the cause of the accident") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 원인, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 원인 names the objective, usually negative, source of a problem; 의 links the two nouns
the investigative collocation; also 원인을 밝히다 = uncover/clarify the cause
X이/가 원인이 되다 = X causes/leads to; subject takes 이/가, not 을/를
habitually modified by 근본적(인) 'fundamental' when discussing deep causes

examples.en: What's the cause of a cold?
examples.note: Simple: 원인 as a plain noun with 의 joining it to 감기

examples.ko: 스트레스가 여러 질병의 원인이 될 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: seuteureseuga yeoreo jilbyeongui wonini doel su isseoyo.
examples.en: Stress can become the cause of various illnesses.
examples.note: Everyday: the X이/가 원인이 되다 pattern, where the cause is the subject

examples.ko: 화재의 정확한 원인은 경찰이 아직 조사하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: hwajaeui jeonghwakan wonineun gyeongchari ajik josahago isseoyo.
examples.en: The police are still investigating the exact cause of the fire.
examples.note: Real situation: 원인 with 조사하다/밝히다 in a serious, investigative register

entries.nuance: 원인 (原因, '原 origin + 因 reason/factor', the originating factor) is the objective, analytical cause of a result — typically a problem, accident, illness, or phenomenon — and it locks together with 결과 as the textbook 원인과 결과 (cause and effect). The crucial dividing line for English speakers is 원인 vs 이유: 이유 is the personal reason or justification a person gives ('the reason I was late'), something you 말하다/대다 (state/offer), whereas 원인 is an impersonal cause you 찾다/밝히다/조사하다 (find/uncover/investigate). So '왜 늦었어요?' is answered with an 이유, never an 원인. Register is neutral-to-formal, common in news, medicine, and engineering. Watch the particle: the cause is the subject of 되다, so it is 원인이 되다, and you say 'X가 Y의 원인이다' (X is the cause of Y), not the reverse.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 원인 for a personal reason like 'the reason I'm late' — that is 이유 (지각한 이유). 원인 sounds clinical and wrong for human motives.
Say 원인이 되다 ('becomes a cause'), not 원인을 되다 — 되다 takes 이/가 on the thing it turns into.
Don't reverse the of-relation: 'the cause of the accident' is 사고의 원인, not 원인의 사고.

entries.shortExplanation: 목적 means "purpose, goal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 목적 (mokjeok) means "purpose, goal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 여행 목적 ("purpose of travel"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase on immigration/visa forms; also 방문 목적 = purpose of visit
the right verb is 이루다 (accomplish) or 달성하다, never 하다
describes an intended aim behind an action; 뚜렷한 목적이 있다 = have a clear aim
Verb-는 것이 목적이다 states what the aim is

examples.en: What's the purpose of this gathering?
examples.note: Simple: asking for the aim of an event with 의 + 목적

examples.ko: 이 프로그램의 목적은 외국인을 돕는 것이에요.
examples.romanization: i peurogeuraemui mokjeogeun oegugineul domneun geosieyo.
examples.en: The purpose of this program is to help foreigners.
examples.note: Everyday: the N의 목적은 -는 것이다 framing that defines a purpose

examples.ko: 친구가 모임 목적이 뭐냐고 물어봐서 '그냥 같이 밥 먹는 거'라고 대답했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga moim mokjeogi mwonyago mureobwaseo 'geunyang gachi bam meongneun geo'rago daedapaesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend asked what the purpose of the gathering was, so I answered 'just to eat together'.
examples.note: 방문 목적, 여행 목적 — '~ 목적' asks the aim/reason

entries.nuance: 목적 (目的, '目 eye + 的 target' — the target your eye is fixed on) is the conscious aim or intention behind an action, more deliberate and goal-directed than 이유 (the reason behind it) or 원인 (the cause that produced it). Compare the near-synonym 목표: 목표 is a concrete, often measurable target you aim to hit (this month's sales 목표, a finish-line 목표), while 목적 is the underlying purpose or 'what it is for' — a company's 목적 may be 'to help people' but its 목표 is 'sell 1000 units'. Register leans formal/written: it dominates immigration forms (방문 목적), reports, and mission statements. Two pitfalls: do not pair it with 하다 (you 이루다/달성하다 a 목적, you never 목적을 하다), and do not confuse 목적 (purpose) with 목적지 (目的地, 'purpose-place' — the destination, an actual place).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 목적 (purpose, abstract) with 목적지 (destination, a physical place you travel to) — adding 지(地, 'place') changes the meaning entirely.
Use 이루다/달성하다 with 목적, not 하다: 목적을 이루다 ('achieve a purpose'), never 목적을 하다.
Don't use 목적 where 목표 fits: a numeric/concrete target ('my goal is to lose 5 kg') is 목표, while 목적 is the broader 'what it is for'.

entries.shortExplanation: 과정 means "process, course" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "process, course" is 과정 (gwajeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 성장 과정 ("the growth process"). Watch the particle attached to 과정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 과정 follows a noun to name a developmental process over time
Verb-는 과정에서 = while/during the process of; highlights events along the way
the dedicated verb is 거치다 (pass through stages), not 가다
also a formal program: 박사 과정 = a doctoral program

examples.en: The cooking process is fun.
examples.note: Simple: -는 과정 nominalizing 'the process of cooking'

examples.ko: 한국어를 배우는 과정에서 실수를 많이 했어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul baeuneun gwajeongeseo silsureul mani haesseoyo.
examples.en: I made a lot of mistakes in the course of learning Korean.
examples.note: Everyday: -는 과정에서 framing events that happen along the way

examples.ko: 이 신청은 서류 심사, 면접, 최종 발표까지 여러 과정을 거쳐야 해요.
examples.romanization: i sincheongeun seoryu simsa, myeonjeop, choejong balpyokkaji yeoreo gwajeongeul geochyeoya haeyo.
examples.en: This application has to go through several stages: document screening, an interview, and the final announcement.
examples.note: Real situation: 과정을 거치다 listing concrete bureaucratic stages

entries.nuance: 과정 (過程, '過 pass through + 程 a stage/measured stretch') is the unfolding process — the sequence of stages something passes through over time — and it also doubles as a formal 'course' of study (교육 과정, 박사 과정, 정규 과정). Its natural opposite is 결과 (the final outcome), which is why Koreans pair them: 결과보다 과정이 중요하다. A close relative is 절차, but 절차 is the fixed set of official procedures/steps you must follow (a legal 절차, an application 절차), while 과정 is the broader, more organic course of how things actually develop. The standout pattern is -는 과정에서 'in the course of doing', perfect for describing side-events that occur while a bigger thing happens. Pitfalls: use 거치다 (not 가다) for 'go through stages', and beware the homophone-ish 과장 (誇張 exaggeration, or 課長 a section chief) — a single jamo separates them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 과장 (exaggeration / section chief) when you mean 과정 (process) — they are different words with different hanja.
Use 거치다 with 과정 for 'go through stages' (과정을 거치다), not 가다 — 가다 means physically 'go', not 'pass through a process'.
Don't substitute 과정 for 절차 when you mean fixed official steps: an application's required steps is 신청 절차, while 과정 is the looser overall course.

entries.shortExplanation: 관계 means "relationship, relation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 관계 (gwangye) = "relationship, relation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 인간관계 ("interpersonal relationships") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 관계, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: very common compound (人間關係) for one's web of social ties; written as one word
관계가 좋다/나쁘다 describes the quality of a relationship; subject takes 이/가
이웃과의 관계 = relationship with neighbors; 와/과 marks the other party

usagePhrases.en: be related, have to do with
usagePhrases.note: X와/과 관계가 있다 = is connected to X; 관계없다 = irrelevant

examples.en: I have a good relationship with my friend.
examples.note: Simple: N과의 관계 + 좋다 for relationship quality

examples.ko: 그 일은 저와 아무 관계가 없어요.
examples.romanization: geu ireun jeowa amu gwangyega eopseoyo.
examples.en: That matter has nothing to do with me.
examples.note: Everyday: 관계가 없다 = unrelated, also 'none of my business'

examples.ko: 이번 사건은 그 회사의 자금 문제와 깊은 관계가 있는 것으로 보여요.
examples.romanization: ibeon sageoneun geu hoesaui jageum munjewa gipeun gwangyega inneun geoseuro boyeoyo.
examples.en: This incident appears to be deeply connected to that company's financial troubles.
examples.note: Real situation: abstract 관계가 있다 linking two facts/events in a formal report tone

entries.nuance: 관계 (關係, '關 a barrier-gate that connects + 係 to tie/link' — a binding link) spans two senses: warm personal relationships (인간관계, 친구 관계, 부부 관계) and abstract relations or connections between facts, events, or ideas. With 있다/없다 it shifts toward 'to be related / have to do with', so 관계없다 / 관계가 없다 is the everyday way to say 'irrelevant' or 'none of my business' (relevant-but-blunter than English). Mark the other party with 와/과, and note the formal genitive 와/과의 관계. A near-synonym is 사이 ('the space between' two people), which is more colloquial and intimate — 우리 사이 좋아 ('we're close') feels warmer and chattier than 우리 관계 좋아, which sounds more analytical. The classic English-speaker slips: never say 관계를 있다 (it must be 관계가 있다), and do not confuse 관계 (relationship) with the look-alike 관심 (關心, interest/attention).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 관계를 있다 — existence/relation takes 이/가: 관계가 있다.
Don't mix up 관심 (interest, 'I'm interested in K-pop' = K팝에 관심이 있다) with 관계 (relationship); they share 관 but mean different things.
For casual closeness between friends, 사이 is often more natural than 관계: 우리 사이 좋아 sounds warmer than 우리 관계 좋아.

entries.shortExplanation: 영향 means "influence, effect, impact" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 영향 (yeonghyang) means "influence, effect, impact". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영향을 주다 ("give influence, affect"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영향 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: X이/가 Y에/에게 영향을 주다 = X affects Y; everyday register
X에게서/에서 영향을 받다 = to be affected by X; the receiving side
more formal than 주다; standard in writing and news
modified by 좋은/나쁜/큰 to describe the effect's quality and size

examples.en: The weather affects my mood.
examples.note: Simple: N에 영향을 주다 — the affected target takes 에, not 을/를

examples.ko: 저는 어릴 때 할머니께 많은 영향을 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun eoril ttae halmeonikke maneun yeonghyangeul badasseoyo.
examples.en: I was greatly influenced by my grandmother when I was little.
examples.note: Everyday: 영향을 받다 with 께 for the respected person who influenced you

examples.ko: 이번 정책은 자영업자들에게 큰 영향을 미칠 것으로 보입니다.
examples.romanization: ibeon jeongchaegeun jayeongeopjadeurege keun yeonghyangeul michil geoseuro boimnida.
examples.en: This policy is expected to have a big impact on the self-employed.
examples.note: Real situation: formal 영향을 미치다 in news/report register

entries.nuance: 영향 (影響, '影 shadow + 響 echo' — a shadow-and-echo that one thing casts onto another) is influence or impact, and it crucially works in two opposite directions you must keep straight: the source 영향을 주다 / 미치다 (gives/exerts an effect) while the recipient 영향을 받다 (receives/is affected). 미치다 is the formal, news-and-essay verb for 'exert an effect', whereas 주다 is everyday conversation. The decisive English-speaker trap is the particle: the affected target is marked with 에 (for things — 환경에 영향을 주다) or 에게/께 (for people — 아이들에게/부모님께 영향을 주다), NOT with 을/를, because the actual object slot is already filled by 영향(을). So 'it affects the environment' is 환경에 영향을 줘요, never 환경을 영향을 줘요. Compare 효과 (效果, the resulting effect/efficacy of a measure, e.g. 약의 효과 'the medicine's effect'): 영향 is the act of influencing, 효과 is the beneficial result that comes out.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap the direction: the affecter uses 주다/미치다, the affected uses 받다. '나는 영향을 줬어요' means YOU influenced something, not that you were influenced.
Mark the target with 에 (things) or 에게/께 (people), not 을/를: 환경에 영향을 주다, never 환경을 영향을 주다.
Don't use 영향 for the beneficial 'effect' of a remedy — that is 효과 (약의 효과); 영향 is the broader, often neutral act of influencing.

entries.shortExplanation: 상황 means "situation, circumstances" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "situation, circumstances" is 상황 (sanghwang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 현재 상황 ("the current situation"). Watch the particle attached to 상황 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 상황 follows a noun/modifier naming the state of affairs
상황이 좋다/나쁘다/심각하다 describe how things stand; subject takes 이/가
frames advice or a reaction to a set of conditions
상황에 따라(서) 다르다 = it depends on the situation

examples.en: How's the situation right now?
examples.note: Simple: 상황 with 이/가 asking after the state of things

examples.ko: 이런 상황에서는 어떻게 해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: ireon sanghwangeseoneun eotteoke haeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: In a situation like this, I don't know what I should do.
examples.note: Everyday: 이런 상황에서(는) framing a reaction to circumstances

examples.ko: 회사 사정이 어려워서, 상황에 따라 채용 일정이 바뀔 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: hoesa sajeongi eoryeowoseo, sanghwange ttara chaeyong iljeongi bakkwil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: Since the company is in a tough spot, the hiring schedule may change depending on the situation.
examples.note: Real situation: the hedging phrase 상황에 따라 in a workplace context

entries.nuance: 상황 (狀況, '狀 condition/form + 況 circumstances' — the configuration of circumstances) describes the overall set of conditions surrounding a moment or event, broader than a single 경우 (a specific case or instance — 이런 경우 = 'in this one case', vs 이런 상황 = 'in this whole situation'). The reflexive phrase 상황에 따라(서) 다르다 ('it depends on the situation') is one of the most useful hedges in Korean, and 이런/그런 상황에서 sets up advice or reactions. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls: keep 상황 (the circumstances around an event) distinct from 상태 (狀態, the state/condition of a single thing or body — 건강 상태 'health condition', 배터리 상태 'battery state'); you describe a person's mood with a 상태, but the events around them with a 상황. And use 에 따라 (not 으로) for 'depending on': 상황에 따라, never 상황으로.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 상황 (the situation/circumstances around an event) with 상태 (the state or condition of a thing or body): 건강 상태, not 건강 상황.
Use 에 따라 for 'depending on the situation', not 으로: 상황에 따라(서), never 상황으로.
For one specific instance, 경우 is sharper than 상황: '이런 경우' = 'in this particular case' vs '이런 상황' = 'in this whole situation'.

entries.shortExplanation: 조건 means "condition, requirement, terms" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조건 (jogeon) = "condition, requirement, terms". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 조건이 좋다 ("the terms are good") shows how it actually behaves.
