Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: common for job/contract terms; 조건이 좋다/나쁘다 rates the deal
갖추다 = to be equipped with / fulfill; also 조건을 만족하다
조건 follows a noun naming the relevant terms (계약 조건 = contract terms)
조건에 맞는 사람 = a person who fits the requirements; 에 맞다, not 을 맞다

examples.en: This job has good terms.
examples.note: Simple: 조건이 좋다 rating an offer's terms

examples.ko: 지원하려면 몇 가지 조건을 갖춰야 해요.
examples.romanization: jiwonharyeomyeon myeot gaji jogeoneul gatchwoya haeyo.
examples.en: To apply, you have to meet a few requirements.
examples.note: Everyday: 조건을 갖추다 = fulfill the requirements

examples.ko: 월급은 마음에 드는데 근무 조건이 안 맞아서 고민이에요.
examples.romanization: wolgeubeun maeume deuneunde geunmu jogeoni an majaseo gominieyo.
examples.en: I like the salary, but the working conditions don't suit me, so I'm torn.
examples.note: Real situation: 근무 조건 weighed in a realistic job-decision context

entries.nuance: 조건 (條件, '條 an article/clause + 件 an item' — itemized clauses) means both the requirements that must be satisfied and the terms/conditions of an arrangement (jobs, contracts, deals, even relationships). With 갖추다/만족하다 it means 'fulfill requirements'; with 맞다 it means 'fit/match the conditions'; and a great everyday word is 조건이 좋다 ('the terms are good'). It is more concrete than 상황 (the overall circumstances): 조건 are the specific, often listed terms, not the general state of affairs. The number-one English-speaker trap is grammatical interference: 'if' in the sense of a conditional sentence is the verb ending -(으)면, NOT the noun 조건. You cannot say '조건 you come, ...' — say '오면 ...'. Use 조건 only as the noun 'a condition/requirement'. Also note 조건에 맞다 (fit) takes 에, while 조건을 갖추다 (possess/fulfill) takes 을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use the noun 조건 to translate the conjunction 'if' — a conditional clause is the ending -(으)면 ('if you come' = 오면), not 조건.
Say 조건에 맞다 ('fit the conditions') with 에, not 조건을 맞다.
Don't blur 조건 with 상황: 조건 are the specific terms/requirements, while 상황 is the broader surrounding circumstances.

entries.shortExplanation: 기준 means "standard, criterion, basis" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기준 (gijun) means "standard, criterion, basis". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기준이 높다 ("the standard is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기준 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 기준이 높다/낮다/엄격하다 describe how strict a standard is

usagePhrases.en: based on / using N as the standard
usagePhrases.note: 성적을 기준으로 = on the basis of grades; do not drop 으로
기준에 맞추다 = to align/adjust to the standard
기준 follows a noun naming what the standard is for (채용 기준 = hiring criteria)

examples.en: The standard is too high.
examples.note: Simple: 기준이 높다 describing a strict benchmark

examples.en: We lined up based on age.
examples.note: Everyday: N을/를 기준으로 = using N as the reference point

examples.ko: 이 제품은 정부의 안전 기준을 모두 통과했습니다.
examples.romanization: i jepumeun jeongbuui anjeon gijuneul modu tonggwahaetseumnida.
examples.en: This product passed all the government's safety standards.
examples.note: Real situation: 안전 기준 + 통과하다 in an official/regulatory register

entries.nuance: 기준 (基準, '基 foundation + 準 a level/measuring standard' — a foundational measuring line) is the standard or yardstick against which things are measured, judged, or sorted. The workhorse phrase N을/를 기준으로(하다) means 'taking N as the basis/reference point' and is everywhere when explaining how something is organized or decided (나이를 기준으로, 가격을 기준으로). The key contrast is 기준 vs 조건: 기준 is the measuring criterion itself (the bar you measure against), while 조건 is a requirement that must be met — a job's 채용 기준 (hiring criteria, the yardstick) differ from its 지원 조건 (application requirements you must satisfy). Register is neutral-to-formal, heavy in administration, hiring, and regulations. Pitfalls: never drop the 으로 in the set phrase (it is N을 기준으로, not N을 기준), and mind the vowel — 기준 (standard) is not 기분 (氣分, mood/feeling).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't drop 으로 in the set phrase: it is N을/를 기준으로 ('based on N'), not N을 기준.
Don't confuse 기준 (standard) with 기분 (mood/feeling) — one vowel apart but completely different words.
Don't swap 기준 and 조건: 기준 is the yardstick you measure by, 조건 is a requirement you must meet.

entries.shortExplanation: 정도 means "degree, extent, about" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "degree, extent, about" is 정도 (jeongdo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어느 정도 ("to some degree, roughly how much"). Watch the particle attached to 정도 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to some degree, roughly how much
usagePhrases.note: 어느 정도 알아요 = I know to some extent; also asks 'how much, roughly?'
그 정도면 충분해요 = that much is enough
한 시간 정도 = about an hour; attaches after a quantity
울 정도로 = to the point of crying; shows intensity

examples.en: It takes about an hour.
examples.note: Simple: N 정도 after a quantity = 'approximately'

examples.ko: 한국어를 어느 정도 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul eoneu jeongdo hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can speak Korean to some degree.
examples.note: Everyday: the set phrase 어느 정도 = 'to some extent'

examples.ko: 어제는 말도 못 할 정도로 피곤해서 일찍 잤어요.
examples.romanization: eojeneun maldo mo tal jeongdoro pigonhaeseo iljjik jasseoyo.
examples.en: Yesterday I was tired to the point I couldn't even speak, so I slept early.
examples.note: Real situation: -(으)ㄹ 정도로 conveying how extreme the state was

entries.nuance: 정도 (程度, '程 a stage/measure + 度 a degree' — a measured degree) expresses degree or extent, and after a number it means 'about/approximately', overlapping with 쯤 but slightly broader: 쯤 attaches tightly to points in time/space (세 시쯤 'around 3'), while 정도 also covers amounts and intensity (열 명 정도 'about ten people', 그 정도 'that much'). The set phrases 어느 정도 ('to some extent') and 그 정도 ('that much') are essential intermediate vocabulary, and the grammar -(으)ㄹ 정도로 ('to the extent/point that') is the go-to way to dramatize how strong something is (죽을 정도로 'to death'). Register is fully neutral. The main English-speaker trap is redundancy: because 정도 already means 'about', do not also add 약 ('approximately') — 약 한 시간 정도 doubles up; pick one, normally 한 시간 정도. Also keep 정도 (degree/extent) apart from the look-alike 제도 (制度, a system/institution).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't double up on 'about': 정도 already means 'approximately', so drop the extra 약 — say 한 시간 정도, not 약 한 시간 정도.
Don't confuse 정도 (degree, extent) with 제도 (system, institution) — similar shape, unrelated meanings.
After a number 정도 means 'about'; don't read 세 시 정도 as 'the degree of 3 o'clock' — it just means 'around 3'.

entries.shortExplanation: 변화 means "change" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 변화 (byeonhwa) = "change". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 변화가 생기다 ("a change occurs") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 변화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the natural intransitive way to say a change arises; subject takes 이/가
분위기에 변화를 주다 = add a change to the mood/atmosphere
modified by 급격한/큰/작은 to describe scale and speed
the thing you adapt to takes 에: 변화에 적응하다

examples.en: These days the weather changes a lot.
examples.note: Simple: 변화가 심하다 = the change is severe/big

examples.ko: 기분 전환하려고 머리 스타일에 변화를 줬어요.
examples.romanization: gibun jeonhwanharyeogo meori seutaire byeonhwareul jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I changed up my hairstyle for a change of mood.
examples.note: Everyday: 변화를 주다 = deliberately introduce a change for variety

examples.ko: 새로운 환경의 변화에 적응하는 데 거의 반년이 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: saeroun hwangyeongui byeonhwae jeogeunghaneun de geoui bannyeoni geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took nearly half a year to adapt to the changes of the new environment.
examples.note: Real situation: 변화에 적응하다 over a realistic adjustment period

entries.nuance: 변화 (變化, '變 to alter + 化 to transform' — alteration-and-transformation) is the noun 'change', used for shifts in states, trends, weather, society, technology, or one's life, and it is more abstract and global than the plain verb 변하다/바뀌다 (a specific thing changes). Distinguish 변화를 주다 ('introduce/make a change', usually for freshness or variety) from 변화가 생기다 ('a change occurs' on its own), and mark what you adapt to with 에 (변화에 적응하다). The subtle English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 변화하다 as the verb for everyday change: 변화하다 exists but sounds formal/scientific ('the climate is changing' 기후가 변화하다), so for ordinary 'something changed' use 변하다 or 바뀌다 (전화번호가 바뀌었어요 'my number changed'), and reserve 변화 for the noun. Compare 발전 (發展, development/progress — change specifically in a better, advancing direction), which carries positive growth that neutral 변화 does not.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use the verb 변하다/바뀌다 for ordinary 'something changes'; the noun-verb 변화하다 sounds formal/scientific, so 전화번호가 바뀌었어요, not 전화번호가 변화했어요.
Say 변화를 주다 ('make/introduce a change') in the 'add variety' sense, not 변화를 하다.
Don't use neutral 변화 when you mean improvement: positive, advancing change is 발전 (회사가 발전했어요), while 변화 is direction-neutral.

entries.shortExplanation: 의미 means "meaning, significance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 의미 (uimi) means "meaning, significance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 의미가 있다 ("be meaningful / have a meaning"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 의미 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 의미 있는 일 = a meaningful thing; covers both 'significant' and 'has a meaning'
the everyday way to say something has no point
축하하는 의미에서 = in the spirit of celebrating
결과에 의미를 두다 = to attach significance to the result

examples.en: What does this word mean?
examples.note: Simple: asking a word's meaning — though casual speech often prefers 뜻

examples.en: I prepared a small gift as a token of thanks.
examples.note: Everyday: -는 의미에서 = 'in the sense/spirit of'

examples.ko: 혼자 떠난 여행은 저에게 특별한 의미가 있었어요.
examples.romanization: honja tteonan yeohaengeun jeoege teukbyeolhan uimiga isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The trip I took alone had a special significance for me.
examples.note: Real situation: 의미가 있다 in the deeper 'significance/value' sense

entries.nuance: 의미 (意味, '意 intention/thought + 味 flavor' — the flavor of an intention) covers both the literal 'meaning' of a word and the deeper 'significance/value' of an experience, so 의미가 있다 elegantly straddles 'has a meaning' and 'is meaningful'. Its near-synonym 뜻 overlaps heavily but skews toward literal word-meaning and is the more colloquial choice: when asking 'what does this mean?' in everyday speech Koreans usually say 무슨 뜻이에요?, saving 의미 for writing or for talking about significance (큰 의미가 있다). The pattern -는 의미에서 ('in the sense/spirit of doing') is a handy intermediate connector for spelling out the intention behind an action. Register is neutral; 뜻 just feels a notch warmer and more spoken. Pitfalls: say 의미가 있다, never 의미를 있다; and don't assume 의미 and 뜻 are always interchangeable — 뜻 also means 'one's will/intention' (그 뜻을 따르다 'follow that wish'), a sense 의미 lacks.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For 'what does this word mean?' both work, but casual speech prefers 뜻: 무슨 뜻이에요? sounds more natural than 무슨 의미예요? in conversation.
Don't say 의미를 있다 — it is 의미가 있다.
Don't treat 뜻 and 의미 as perfect twins: 뜻 also means one's will/intention (부모님의 뜻 'parents' wishes'), a meaning 의미 does not carry.

entries.shortExplanation: 역할 means "role, part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "role, part" is 역할 (yeokal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 역할을 하다 ("play a role"). Watch the particle attached to 역할 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 중요한 역할을 하다 = to play an important role; also for the function of a thing
맡다 = to be put in charge of a role/part; stresses being assigned
modified by 중요한/큰/핵심적인 to rate its weight
splitting up who does what within a team

examples.en: Each person has their own role.
examples.note: Simple: 역할이 있다 = to have a role; 각자 = each person

examples.en: Teachers play an important role for students.
examples.note: Everyday: 역할을 하다 = play/serve a role

examples.ko: 이번 연극에서 저는 주인공 역할을 맡게 되었어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeongeugeseo jeoneun juingong yeokareul matge doeeosseoyo.
examples.en: In this play I ended up taking on the lead role.
examples.note: Real situation: 역할을 맡다 for being cast/assigned a part

entries.nuance: 역할 (役割, '役 a duty/service + 割 a portion' — the portion of duty allotted to you) is the role or part a person, factor, or even an object plays, covering family members (가족 안에서의 역할), team assignments, and the function of things or causes. 역할을 하다 means 'to play/serve a role', while 역할을 맡다 emphasizes being assigned or taking the part on (맡다 = be put in charge). Pronunciation is a real trap: 역할 is pronounced [여칼], with the final ㄱ aspirating the following ㅎ, so learners who say [역할] sound off; and the single most common native misspelling is 역활 — even Koreans get it wrong, but the standard form is 역할. A near-synonym is 기능 (機能, function), but 기능 is the mechanical/technical function of a system or device (이 버튼의 기능 'this button's function'), while 역할 implies a part played within a larger whole, often by a person. Use 맡다 (not 잡다) for taking on a role.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 역활 — even many natives slip, but the correct spelling is 역할 (pronounced [여칼]).
Use 맡다 for taking on a role (역할을 맡다), not 잡다 — 잡다 means physically 'grab/catch'.
Don't swap 역할 and 기능: a device's technical 'function' is 기능 (이 앱의 기능), while 역할 is a part played within a larger whole, usually by a person.

entries.shortExplanation: 기회 means "chance; opportunity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기회 (gihoe) = "chance; opportunity". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기회가 있어요 ("there is a chance") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: existence takes 가, never 를: 기회가 있다
잡다 (grab) is the default verb, not 하다
좋은 modifies the noun directly, no 의
set phrase for a soft, open-ended offer

examples.en: Is there a chance?
examples.note: simplest existence frame with 가 있다

examples.ko: 저는 외국에서 일할 기회를 잡고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun oegugeseo ilhal gihoereul japgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to seize a chance to work abroad.
examples.note: a verb + ㄹ 기회 = 'a chance to do X'

examples.ko: 좋은 기회였는데 그때 안 잡아서 지금도 아쉬워요.
examples.romanization: joeun gihoeyeonneunde geuttae an jabaseo jigeumdo aswiwoyo.
examples.en: It was a good opportunity, but I didn't take it then, so I still regret it.
examples.note: real-talk: 기회를 잡다/놓치다 in past reflection

entries.nuance: 기회 (機會, 機 'opportune moment/device' + 會 'meeting') is a window of opportunity that may not come twice, so it carries a faint pressure to act. The key contrast is 기회 vs 기능: 기회 is a chance to do something, while 기능 is a 'function/feature.' Koreans treat 기회 as something you physically handle — 기회를 잡다 (seize), 기회를 놓치다 (miss), 기회를 주다/얻다 (give/get) — so the partner verb is concrete, never 기회를 하다. With existence it is 기회가 있다/없다, and 기회가 되면 is a gentle, non-committal 'if the chance comes up.' Marking existence with 를: 기회를 있다 ✗. Existence always takes 가: 기회가 있다 ✓

entries.shortExplanation: 태도 means "attitude" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 태도 (taedo) means "attitude". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 태도가 좋아요 ("the attitude is good"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 태도 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: describing state takes 가, not 를
바꾸다 (change) takes the object 를
에 대한 = 'toward/about', a fixed frame
신랄한 평가; can sound like a complaint

examples.en: Your attitude is good.
examples.note: simple praise; state-adjective with 가

examples.ko: 그분은 일에 대한 태도가 정말 진지해요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun ire daehan taedoga jeongmal jinjihaeyo.
examples.en: That person's attitude toward work is really serious.
examples.note: 에 대한 태도 = the standard 'attitude toward X' frame

examples.ko: 실수한 뒤에 태도를 싹 바꿔서 다들 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: silsuhan dwie taedoreul ssak bakkwoseo dadeul nollasseoyo.
examples.en: After the mistake he completely changed his attitude, so everyone was surprised.
examples.note: real-situation: 태도를 바꾸다 + adverb 싹 (cleanly/completely)

entries.nuance: 태도 (態度, 態 'state/manner' + 度 'degree') is the disposition someone reveals through behavior — their stance toward work, people, or a situation. Contrast it sharply with 자세: 자세 can be a literal body posture ('sit up straight' = 자세를 바로 하다) and a metaphorical mindset, but 태도 stays in the mental/behavioral lane and never means physical posture. Saying 태도를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 describes a state, so the particle is 가: 태도가 좋다 ✓
Using 태도 for physical posture — that is 자세 (자세를 바로 하다 'straighten your posture')
Dropping the frame in 'attitude toward X' — Korean needs 에 대한 태도, e.g. 공부에 대한 태도

entries.shortExplanation: 내용 means "content; contents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "content; contents" is 내용 (naeyong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 내용이 어려워요 ("the content is hard"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: descriptive adjective takes 이, not 을
이해하다 (understand) takes object 을
정리하다 = organize/sum up neatly
확인하다 = verify; common in work email

examples.en: The content is hard.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 이

examples.en: I summarized the meeting content briefly and sent it.
examples.note: 내용을 정리하다 — staple office collocation

examples.ko: 문자 내용이랑 실제 약속 시간이 달라서 다시 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: munja naeyongirang silje yaksok sigani dallaseo dasi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: The text's content and the actual appointment time differed, so I checked again.
examples.note: real-situation: 내용 = the substance/wording inside a message

entries.nuance: 내용 (內容, 內 'inside' + 容 'contain') is the substance or gist inside something — a book, message, lecture, contract — as opposed to its outer form. The sharp contrast is 내용 (what it says) vs 형식 (the form/format): a report can have weak 내용 but proper 형식. Don't confuse it with a physical container either; the box itself is 상자/봉투, while 내용물 specifically means the physical 'contents' (items) inside a package. Typical partners: 내용을 이해하다/정리하다/확인하다, 내용이 어렵다/풍부하다, 회의 내용, 문자 내용. The English-speaker pitfall is particle choice driven by the adjective: 'the content is hard' becomes 내용이 어렵다 ✓, not 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 를/을 attaches only to action verbs like 이해하다, never to descriptive 어렵다.

Saying 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 이: 내용이 어렵다 ✓
Using 내용 for the physical box/wrapper — that is 상자/봉투; physical contents inside are 내용물
Confusing 내용 (substance) with 형식 (form/format) when contrasting what a text says vs how it looks

entries.shortExplanation: 종류 means "kind; type" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 종류 (jongnyu) = "kind; type". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 종류가 많아요 ("there are many kinds") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 종류, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: quantity adjective takes 가, not 를
needs 의 before the noun it classifies
여러 (several) attaches directly
같은 종류의 X = 'the same type of X'

examples.en: There are many kinds.
examples.note: simplest frame; 많다 takes 가

examples.en: What kind of music do you like?
examples.note: 어떤 종류의 + noun — the 의 is required

examples.ko: 같은 종류의 제품인데 매장마다 가격이 달라요.
examples.romanization: gateun jongnyuui jepuminde maejangmada gagyeogi dallayo.
examples.en: They're the same kind of product, but the price differs from store to store.
examples.note: real-situation: 같은 종류의 for classifying, not counting

entries.nuance: 종류 (種類, 種 'seed/kind' + 類 'category') is the type or category something belongs to, so 종류가 많다 means 'there are many varieties.' The crucial contrast is 종류 vs 가지: 종류 classifies by KIND (어떤 종류의 음악 'what kind of music'), whereas 가지 is a counter for tallying items (세 가지 방법 'three methods'). They overlap loosely in speech, but 종류 cannot replace 가지 as a number-counter, and 가지 cannot ask 'what type.' Habitual partners: 종류가 많다/다양하다, 어떤 종류, 같은/다른 종류, 여러 종류. Saying 종류를 많다 ✗ — 많다 is descriptive, so the particle is 가: 종류가 많다 ✓
Dropping 의 in 어떤 종류의 음악 — the linking 의 is required to classify the following noun
Using 종류 as a number-counter — to count, use 가지 (세 가지 'three kinds/ways')

entries.shortExplanation: 수준 means "level; standard" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수준 (sujun) means "level; standard". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수준이 높아요 ("the level is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수준 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 높다 is descriptive, takes 이
낮다 = low; pair of 높다
noun + 수준 compounds with no particle
높이다 (raise, causative) takes object 을

examples.en: The level is high.
examples.note: state-adjective 높다 with 이

examples.en: My Korean level is still intermediate.
examples.note: noun + 수준: 한국어 수준, no 의 needed

examples.ko: 꾸준히 연습해서 실력 수준을 한 단계 높이고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: kkujunhi yeonseupaeseo sillyeok sujuneul han dangye nopigo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to raise my skill level up one notch by practicing steadily.
examples.note: real-situation: 수준 (overall level) + 단계 (a discrete step)

entries.nuance: 수준 (水準) literally composes 水 'water' + 準 'level' — picture a carpenter's water level, hence an abstract gauge of where ability or quality sits. It measures how HIGH/LOW something is: 수준이 높다/낮다, 수준을 높이다, 생활 수준, 한국어 수준. The sharp contrast is 수준 vs 단계: 수준 is a continuous level on a scale ('the class is high-level'), while 단계 is a discrete step/stage in a sequence ('move to the next stage' = 다음 단계로). You raise your 수준 but advance through 단계. Note a social caution: saying someone's 수준이 낮다 sounds dismissive about their class/quality, so it can land as an insult. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle — 'the level is high' is 수준이 높다 ✓, not 수준을 높다 ✗; 을 appears only with the action verb 높이다 (raise).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수준을 높다 ✗ — 높다 is descriptive, so use 이: 수준이 높다 ✓ (을 only with 높이다 'raise')
Confusing 수준 (a level on a scale) with 단계 (a discrete step/stage in a sequence)
Casually saying someone's 수준이 낮다 — it can sound like an insult about their quality or class

entries.shortExplanation: 상태 means "state; condition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "state; condition" is 상태 (sangtae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 상태가 좋아요 ("the condition is good"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

나쁘다 (bad), ㅂ-irregular → 나빠요
noun + 상태 compound, no particle
확인하다 (verify) takes object 를

examples.en: The condition is good.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 가

examples.ko: 요즘 잠을 못 자서 건강 상태가 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jameul mot jaseo geongang sangtaega an joayo.
examples.en: I haven't slept well lately, so my health condition isn't good.
examples.note: 건강 상태 + 안 좋다 (negated state)

examples.ko: 중고차라서 사기 전에 상태를 꼼꼼히 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: junggocharaseo sagi jeone sangtaereul kkomkkomhi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Since it's a used car, I checked its condition carefully before buying.
examples.note: real-situation: 상태를 확인하다 about a physical object

entries.nuance: 상태 (狀態, 狀 'shape/form' + 態 'condition') is the present condition of one specific thing — a person's health, an object, a system — captured at a moment. The sharp contrast is 상태 vs 상황: 상태 zooms in on the CONDITION of a single entity (건강 상태 'health condition'), while 상황 is the broader CIRCUMSTANCE/situation surrounding events (교통 상황 'traffic situation', 지금 상황이 복잡해요). Habitual partners: 상태가 좋다/나쁘다, 상태를 확인하다, 건강/배터리/도로 상태, ~한 상태 ('in a … state'). A handy grammar use: 술에 취한 상태로 = 'in a drunken state.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the condition is good' is 상태가 좋다 ✓ (좋다 descriptive), never 상태를 좋다 ✗; and don't reach for 상황 when you mean one thing's condition.

Saying 상태를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 describes a state, so the particle is 가: 상태가 좋다 ✓
Using 상황 (broad situation) when you mean the condition of one specific thing → 상태
Forgetting the compound has no particle: it is 건강 상태, not 건강의 상태 in everyday speech

usagePhrases.note: 보이다 (be seen) takes subject 이
a verb + 는 모습 = 'the image of doing'
modifier attaches directly, no 의
떠오르다 = surface/come to mind

examples.en: I can see the figure.
examples.note: 보이다 'be visible' takes 이, intransitive

examples.ko: 오랜만에 친구의 밝은 모습을 봐서 기뻤어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane chinguui balgeun moseubeul bwaseo gippeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was glad to see my friend looking cheerful after so long.
examples.note: 모습을 보다 — here you actively look (보다, takes 를)

examples.ko: 열심히 일하는 부모님의 모습이 아직도 눈에 선해요.
examples.romanization: yeolsimhi ilhaneun bumonimui moseubi ajikdo nune seonhaeyo.
examples.en: The image of my hardworking parents is still vivid in my mind's eye.
examples.note: real-situation: ~하는 모습 + 눈에 선하다 (vividly remembered)

entries.nuance: 모습 is a native Korean word (고유어, not Sino-Korean) for the visible figure, look, or scene of a person or thing — and crucially the whole impression of how someone appears or behaves, e.g. 일하는 모습 'the sight of someone working.' The sharp contrast is 모습 vs 얼굴: 얼굴 is just the face, whereas 모습 takes in the entire silhouette, manner, and even a remembered image. It also differs from 외모, which is narrowly 'physical looks/attractiveness'; 모습 is more about the captured sight or impression, often with emotional warmth. Watch the transitivity pair: with 보이다 (be visible) use 모습이 보이다 (intransitive, 이); with 보다 (look at) use 모습을 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing these — 모습을 보이다 ✗ for 'something is visible'; that should be 모습이 보이다 ✓ (모습을 보이다 instead means 'to show a certain side of oneself').

Saying 모습을 보이다 to mean 'is visible' — use 모습이 보이다 ✓ (이 + intransitive 보이다)
Using 모습 only for the face — that is 얼굴; 모습 covers the whole figure and manner
Confusing 모습 with 외모 (physical looks/attractiveness) when you mean a captured sight or impression

usagePhrases.note: descriptive 좋다 takes 가
띄우다 (lift) takes object 를
바꾸다 = change the vibe
어색하다 describes a tense vibe

examples.en: The atmosphere is nice.
examples.note: simplest vibe sentence with 가

examples.ko: 이 카페는 분위기가 정말 편안해서 자주 와요.
examples.romanization: i kapeneun bunwigiga jeongmal pyeonanhaeseo jaju wayo.
examples.en: This cafe has a really relaxing atmosphere, so I come often.
examples.note: 분위기가 편안하다 — describing a place's vibe

examples.ko: 회식 분위기가 가라앉아서 제가 농담으로 분위기를 띄웠어요.
examples.romanization: hoesik bunwigiga garaanjaseo jega nongdameuro bunwigireul ttuiwosseoyo.
examples.en: The company-dinner mood sank, so I lifted it with a joke.
examples.note: real-situation: 분위기가 가라앉다 vs 분위기를 띄우다 (passive sink / active lift)

entries.nuance: 분위기 (雰圍氣, 雰 'mist/vapor' + 圍 'surround' + 氣 'air/energy') is literally 'the air that surrounds you' — the collective mood of a place, gathering, or moment. The sharp contrast is 분위기 vs 기분: 분위기 is the SHARED vibe in the room (회식 분위기가 좋다), while 기분 is one person's INNER feeling (제 기분이 좋다 'I'm in a good mood'). Mixing them is the classic error: 'I'm in a good mood' is 기분이 좋아요, not 분위기가 좋아요 (which describes the room, not you). Habitual partners: 분위기가 좋다/편안하다/어색하다, 분위기를 띄우다/바꾸다, 분위기가 가라앉다, 분위기를 깨다 ('kill the mood'). 분위기 있다 colloquially means 'has a classy/romantic ambiance.' The English-speaker pitfall, beyond 기분 confusion, is the particle: 분위기를 좋다 ✗ → 분위기가 좋다 ✓.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 분위기 (shared room vibe) with 기분 (your own mood) — 'I feel good' is 기분이 좋아요, not 분위기가 좋아요
Saying 분위기를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 is descriptive, so use 가: 분위기가 좋다 ✓
Forgetting 분위기를 깨다 ('to kill the mood') when describing someone spoiling the vibe

entries.shortExplanation: 범위 means "range; scope" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "range; scope" is 범위 (beomwi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 범위가 넓어요 ("the range is wide"). Watch the particle attached to 범위 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: descriptive 넓다 takes 가
noun + 범위 compound, no particle
정하다 (decide/fix) takes object 를
안에서 = inside the bounds of

examples.en: The exam scope is wide.
examples.note: 시험 범위 + 넓다 (descriptive, 가)

examples.en: I chose furniture within the budget range.
examples.note: 범위 안에서 = 'within the bounds of'

examples.ko: 발표 주제의 범위를 조금 줄이는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: balpyo jujeui beomwireul jogeum jurineun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: It would be better to narrow the scope of the presentation topic a bit.
examples.note: real-situation: 범위를 줄이다/정하다 — actively set bounds

entries.nuance: 범위 (範圍, 範 'pattern/model' + 圍 'enclose') is the bounded extent something covers — an exam syllabus, a budget, a topic. It is measured 넓다/좁다 (wide/narrow): 범위가 넓다, 시험 범위, 예산 범위, 범위 안에서. The sharp contrast is 범위 (the SPAN/extent covered) vs 한계 (the outer LIMIT you can't pass): 시험 범위가 넓다 means 'the exam covers a lot,' while 체력의 한계 means 'the ceiling of one's stamina.' Don't confuse 범위 with 사이 either — 사이 is the gap or relationship between two specific points/people. 범위 leans formal and written, common in study and work. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the range is wide' is 범위가 넓다 ✓, not 범위를 넓다 ✗ (넓다 is descriptive; 를 only with action verbs like 정하다/줄이다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 범위를 넓다 ✗ — 넓다 is descriptive, so use 가: 범위가 넓다 ✓
Confusing 범위 (the span covered) with 한계 (the outer limit you cannot exceed)
Using 범위 for the space between two points/people — that is 사이 (둘 사이)

entries.shortExplanation: 한계 means "limit; boundary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 한계 (hangye) = "limit; boundary". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 한계가 있어요 ("there is a limit") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 한계, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: existence takes 가, never 를
느끼다 (feel) takes object 를
noun + 의 + 한계 = 'the limit of X'
넘다 (cross over) takes object 를

examples.en: There is a limit.
examples.note: existence frame with 가 있다

examples.ko: 혼자서 할 수 있는 일에는 한계가 있어요.
examples.romanization: honjaseo hal su inneun ireneun hangyega isseoyo.
examples.en: There's a limit to what I can do alone.
examples.note: ~에는 한계가 있다 = 'there's a limit to ~'

examples.ko: 야근이 계속되니까 이제 체력의 한계를 느껴요.
examples.romanization: yageuni gyesokdoenikka ije cheryeogui hangyereul neukkyeoyo.
examples.en: Since the overtime keeps going, I now feel the limit of my stamina.
examples.note: real-situation: 체력의 한계를 느끼다 — reaching one's ceiling

entries.nuance: 한계 (限界, 限 'restrict' + 界 'boundary') is the outer ceiling beyond which something can't go — ability, stamina, patience. 한계를 느끼다 means 'to feel you've hit your limit,' and 한계를 넘다/극복하다 means to push past or overcome it. The sharp contrast is 한계 (the LIMIT you cannot exceed) vs 끝 (the plain END point of a thing): a road has an 끝, but human endurance has a 한계 — 끝 is concrete/sequential, 한계 is the abstract maximum. It also differs from 범위 (the SPAN covered, not the ceiling). Habitual partners: 한계가 있다, 한계를 느끼다/넘다/극복하다, 체력의/인내의 한계. The English-speaker pitfall is the existence particle: 'there is a limit' is 한계가 있다 ✓, not 한계를 있다 ✗ — existence always takes 가/이, never 를/을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한계를 있다 ✗ — existence takes 가: 한계가 있다 ✓
Confusing 한계 (the abstract ceiling/limit) with 끝 (the concrete end point of something)
Using 한계 for the span something covers — that breadth is 범위, while 한계 is the outer boundary

entries.english: moreover; on top of that; what's more
entries.shortExplanation: 더구나 means "moreover; on top of that; what's more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 더구나 (deoguna) means "moreover; on top of that; what's more". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 더구나 비까지 왔어요 ("and on top of that it even rained"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 더구나 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: and on top of that it even rained
usagePhrases.note: The particle 까지 ('even') loves to sit on the added item, underlining that it's one burden too many
Frequently follows a -은/는데 clause that has already laid out the first reason

usagePhrases.en: especially at a time like now
usagePhrases.note: Stresses that the surrounding circumstances make the added fact land even harder

usagePhrases.en: and on top of it I'm sick too
usagePhrases.note: The 도 on the new clause signals 'this as well,' the natural partner of 더구나

examples.en: It's raining. On top of that, the wind is blowing too.
examples.note: Simple two-sentence stack; note 도 on the second, added point

examples.ko: 그 식당은 비싸요. 더구나 맛도 별로였어요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun bissayo. deoguna matdo byeolloyeosseoyo.
examples.en: That restaurant is expensive. What's more, the food wasn't even good.
examples.note: Everyday complaint that piles a second negative onto the first

examples.ko: 초보자에게는 어려운 책인데, 더구나 분량까지 많아서 다 못 읽었어요.
examples.romanization: chobojaegeneun eoryeoun chaeginde, deoguna bullyangkkaji manaseo da mot ilgeosseoyo.
examples.en: It's a hard book for beginners, and on top of that it's so long that I couldn't finish it.
examples.note: Real situation: 까지 marks the final straw that produced the outcome

entries.nuance: 더구나 piles an extra fact on top of what you just said, and that extra fact almost always tips the situation further in one direction — usually worse ('and to make matters worse'). Its closest rivals are 게다가 and 더욱이: all three mean 'on top of that,' but 게다가 is the neutral everyday default that happily adds good or bad news, 더욱이 is the most bookish, and 더구나 sits between them, leaning emotional and feeling like the speaker is fed up. It habitually teams up with 도/까지 on the new clause (비도, 사람까지) and trails after a -는데 set-up. It is purely an adverb that opens or links a clause — never a noun. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 더구나 to tack a cheerful, neutral item onto a list ('I bought apples, and moreover bananas'); there 그리고 or 게다가 is right, because 더구나 quietly promises that the addition raises the stakes.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 더구나 to add a positive or purely neutral item ('샀어요, 더구나 바나나도'): it implies the addition intensifies (usually worsens) the situation, so a flat list needs 그리고/게다가 instead.
Treating it as a noun or object ('더구나가 있어요'): it is an adverb that opens or links a clause, so it can never take 이/가 or 을/를.
Forgetting the 도/까지 partner: '비 왔어요. 더구나 추웠어요' feels bare — Koreans naturally say '더구나 춥기까지 했어요' so the 'one more thing' flavor is carried by the particle.

entries.shortExplanation: 특히 means "especially; in particular" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "especially; in particular" is 특히 (teuki). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 특히 N을/를 좋아해요 ("I especially like N"). Watch the particle attached to 특히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Singles out one favorite member from a larger set you just named
Sits directly in front of an adjective to boost that one quality
The set phrase 그중에서도 ('even among those') often leads into 특히 to narrow down
특히나 is a slightly stronger, more colloquial variant of 특히

examples.ko: 저는 과일을 좋아하는데, 특히 딸기를 제일 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun gwaireul joahaneunde, teuki ttalgireul jeil joahaeyo.
examples.en: I like fruit, and I especially like strawberries the most.
examples.note: Simple: state the category, then 특히 zooms to one item

examples.ko: 이번 시험은 특히 듣기 부분이 어려웠어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon siheomeun teuki deutgi bubuni eoryeowosseoyo.
examples.en: This time the exam was especially hard in the listening section.
examples.note: Everyday: 특히 highlights which part stood out from the rest

examples.ko: 주말에는 사람이 많은데, 특히 일요일 오후가 제일 붐벼요.
examples.romanization: jumareneun sarami maneunde, teuki iryoil ohuga jeil bumbyeoyo.
examples.en: It's crowded on weekends, and Sunday afternoons in particular are the most packed.
examples.note: Real situation: narrows a general statement down to the worst case

entries.nuance: 특히 (Sino-Korean 特, 'special/distinct') points at one member of a group and says 'this one stands out from the rest' — exactly English 'especially' or 'in particular.' The word it constantly gets confused with is its sibling 특별히 (特別, 'special-distinct'): 특히 selects the most notable item from a set, while 특별히 says something was done in a special, deliberate way ('특별히 준비했어요' = I went out of my way to prepare it). Picture 특히 as a spotlight that picks one face out of a crowd, and 특별히 as the extra effort behind a gesture. 특히 naturally rides after a general statement and then pinpoints the exception, and it loves the lead-in 그중에서도. The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 특히 to mean 'I did it specially' — that intent meaning belongs to 특별히, not 특히.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 특히 (singling out one from a group) with 특별히 (doing something in a special/deliberate way): '특히 준비했어요' wrongly says 'I prepared it, of all things,' when you mean '특별히 준비했어요' (I made special preparations).
Parking 특히 far from the item it highlights so the listener can't tell what is being singled out: keep it right next to that word — 특히 듣기가, not 특히 ... 듣기가 ... 어려웠어요 with words in between.
Trying to negate with 특히 ('not especially'): the idiomatic 'not particularly' uses 특별히 + 부정 (특별히 어렵지 않아요), so don't say '특히 어렵지 않아요.'

entries.shortExplanation: 주로 means "mainly; mostly; usually" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주로 (juro) = "mainly; mostly; usually". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 주로 V해요 ("I mainly do V") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주로, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: States your dominant habit while leaving room for exceptions
Marks the place where something typically happens
Identifies the chief object, target, or ingredient
Often follows a time frame to describe what usually fills it

examples.en: On weekends I mostly rest at home.
examples.note: Simple: 주로 describes the typical, default pattern

examples.en: Mostly students come to this cafe.
examples.note: Everyday: marks the dominant kind of customer, not 'only'

examples.ko: 점심은 주로 회사 근처에서 간단히 먹는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: jeomsimeun juro hoesa geuncheoeseo gandanhi meongneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: I usually eat lunch simply near the office.
examples.note: Real situation: 주로 + -는 편이다 softens it to 'as a rule, tend to'

entries.nuance: 주로 (Sino-Korean 主, 'main/principal') means 'mainly/mostly' and names the dominant case among several options, leaving the door open for exceptions. It overlaps with 보통 ('usually') and 대부분 ('for the most part'), but the dividing line is what each emphasizes: 보통 is about frequency over time, 대부분 is about proportion/quantity, and 주로 is about which option is the principal one ('주로 버스로 다녀요' = the bus is my main mode, though not the only one). It is the natural word for describing habits, typical locations, and the main type of thing involved. Crucially it is strictly an adverb here, not the noun 주류 ('the mainstream') that shares the 主 root. The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'mostly' slide into 'always': 주로 signals a strong tendency, so if you truly mean 100%, you need 항상 or 늘 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 주로 to mean 'absolutely always': it names a tendency, so for a no-exceptions claim use 항상/늘 — '저는 항상 집에서 쉬어요' is total, '주로' is just usual.
Confusing the adverb 주로 with the noun 주류 ('mainstream/alcoholic beverages'): here it can only modify a verb or adjective, never take a particle like 주로가.
Reaching for 주로 to talk about pure frequency ('I mostly go three times a week'): for counting how often, 보통 fits better, while 주로 is for which option dominates.

entries.shortExplanation: 비교적 means "relatively; comparatively" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 비교적 (bigyojeok) means "relatively; comparatively". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비교적 쉬워요 ("it's relatively easy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 비교적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sits in front of an adjective to soften the claim against an unstated standard
Can name the yardstick explicitly with -에 비해

usagePhrases.en: it's on the relatively small side
usagePhrases.note: Often pairs with -은/는 편이다 to hedge an amount or degree
Modifies time words too: 'fairly recently, as these things go'

examples.en: This neighborhood is relatively quiet.
examples.note: Simple: hedges the claim against other areas you have in mind

examples.ko: 오늘은 비교적 일이 적어서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun bigyojeok iri jeogeoseo iljjik toegeunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Today there was comparatively little work, so I left early.
examples.note: Everyday: implies 'less than usual,' an implicit comparison to normal days

examples.ko: 한국어 발음은 영어에 비해 비교적 규칙적이라서 배우기 쉬워요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo bareumeun yeongeoe bihae bigyojeok gyuchikjeogiraseo baeugi swiwoyo.
examples.en: Korean pronunciation is relatively regular compared to English, so it's easy to learn.
examples.note: Real situation: -에 비해 makes the standard explicit

entries.nuance: 비교적 (Sino-Korean 比較的, literally '比較 comparison' + the 的 '-ish/in-the-manner-of' suffix) means 'relatively/comparatively' and tells the listener that the quality holds only against some standard, not in absolute terms. That hedge makes you sound careful and measured. Set it against 꽤 and 좀: 꽤 means 'quite/considerably' as a plain intensifier with no comparison built in, 좀 just means 'a bit,' while 비교적 specifically invokes a yardstick ('relative to other options'). Unlike 별로, it carries no negative bias — 비교적 can be relatively good or relatively bad. Because of the 的 suffix it stays adverbial and never conjugates: you cannot say 비교적이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that — turning 'relative' into a predicate; in Korean 비교적 only modifies (비교적 쉬워요), and there should always be at least an implied point of comparison behind it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it as a predicate ('이 일은 비교적이에요'): the 的 makes 비교적 adverb-only, so it must modify something — 비교적 쉬워요, 비교적 빨라요.
Using it where there is genuinely nothing to compare against: 비교적 needs a baseline (even unspoken), so for a flat statement with no yardstick, plain 좀/꽤 is better.
Treating 비교적 as a strong intensifier like 'very': it actually tones a claim down to 'relatively,' so '비교적 어려워요' means moderately hard, not extremely hard — for 'very' use 아주/정말.

entries.english: on the whole; generally; for the most part
entries.shortExplanation: 대체로 means "on the whole; generally; for the most part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "on the whole; generally; for the most part" is 대체로 (daechero). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 대체로 만족해요 ("I'm generally satisfied"). Watch the particle attached to 대체로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Extremely common in reviews and overall evaluations
Gives a big-picture verdict that tolerates minor exceptions
Smooths over small differences to state the overall impression
Often sets up a 'mostly good, with one caveat' structure

examples.en: The food at this restaurant is generally good.
examples.note: Simple: an overall verdict, not a claim about every dish

examples.ko: 호텔은 대체로 깨끗했지만 와이파이가 좀 느렸어요.
examples.romanization: hotereun daechero kkaekkeutaetjiman waipaiga jom neuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: The hotel was on the whole clean, though the Wi-Fi was a bit slow.
examples.note: Everyday: -지만 carves out the one exception to the general impression

examples.ko: 설문 결과를 보면 사람들은 대체로 새 정책에 찬성하는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: seolmun gyeolgwareul bomyeon saramdeureun daechero sae jeongchaege chanseonghaneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: Looking at the survey, people seem to generally support the new policy.
examples.note: Real situation: summarizes a broad trend across many responses

entries.nuance: 대체로 (Sino-Korean 大體, 'the 大 large 體 body/substance' → the main gist) delivers an overall, big-picture judgment — 'on the whole' — while quietly admitting that small exceptions exist. It is the natural word for summaries and evaluations and sounds a touch analytical. Compare it with 주로 and 보통: 주로 picks the single dominant case ('주로 학생이 와요' = mainly students), whereas 대체로 averages over the whole situation to state a general tendency ('대체로 만족스러워요' = satisfied overall, weighing everything). It often pairs with -지만 to add the one caveat. Do not confuse 대체로 with the look-alike 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth') used in exasperated questions like '대체 왜?' — same first syllable, unrelated meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is using 대체로 about a single concrete event ('today's lunch was generally good'); it describes overall tendencies across a set, so for one instance you would just say 맛있었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 대체로 for one single, concrete instance ('오늘 점심은 대체로 맛있었어요'): it sums up an overall tendency across many cases, so for a single event just say 맛있었어요.
Confusing it with 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth/in the world') in questions: '대체 왜 그래요?' is exasperation, while 대체로 is 'on the whole' — same syllable, opposite job.
Swapping 대체로 and 주로 freely: 주로 names the dominant option, 대체로 gives an averaged overall verdict, so 'mainly students come' is 주로, while 'the service was good overall' is 대체로.

entries.shortExplanation: 일반적으로 means "generally; in general; typically" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 일반적으로 (ilbanjeogeuro) = "generally; in general; typically". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 일반적으로 A/V ("generally, A/V") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 일반적으로, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: States what is usually true as a rule or principle
A set lead-in that opens a broad generalization
The adjective form 일반적이다 modifies nouns directly
Frequently sets up a norm to be contrasted with exceptions

examples.en: Generally, the weather is warm in spring.
examples.note: Simple: states a rule-of-thumb truth

examples.en: Generally, symptoms like these get better within a few days.
examples.note: Everyday: gives a typical expectation, the explanatory register of a doctor or article

examples.ko: 일반적으로 말하면, 경험이 많을수록 일이 수월해져요.
examples.romanization: ilbanjeogeuro malhamyeon, gyeongheomi maneulsurok iri suwolhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: Generally speaking, the more experience you have, the easier the work becomes.
examples.note: Real situation: 말하면 frames a broad principle before stating it

entries.nuance: 일반적으로 (Sino-Korean 一般, 'one-kind' → ordinary/common, + 的 + the adverbial -으로) introduces a general rule or what is typically the case — 'in general,' 'typically.' It is noticeably more formal and explanatory than the everyday 보통, which is why it dominates writing, explanations, and academic-leaning speech, whereas 보통 fits casual chat ('보통 7시에 일어나요'). Think of 일반적으로 as the voice of a textbook or an expert stating a norm. Its built-in counterpart is 예외적으로 ('as an exception'), and the two often frame a rule-versus-exception contrast. The form matters: the adverbial -으로 is obligatory, so you cannot drop it and use bare 일반적 as an adverb (that stem only lives inside 일반적인 N or 일반적이다). The English-speaker pitfall is using this formal word for personal habits ('I generally wake at seven'); for your own routines 주로/보통 sound far more natural than 일반적으로.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the -으로 and using bare 일반적 as an adverb ('일반적 맞아요'): the adverb form requires -으로, while 일반적 only survives as 일반적인 N or the predicate 일반적이다.
Using formal 일반적으로 for personal habits ('저는 일반적으로 7시에 일어나요'): for your own routine 보통/주로 are natural, and 일반적으로 sounds like you're stating a societal law about yourself.
Forgetting it sets up a norm vs. exception: pairing it with a one-off surprise is odd, since 일반적으로 invites the implicit 'but sometimes 예외적으로…' frame.

entries.shortExplanation: 특별히 means "specially; particularly; (in negatives) not particularly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 특별히 (teukbyeolhi) means "specially; particularly; (in negatives) not particularly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 특별히 V했어요 ("I did V specially/on purpose"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 특별히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Marks a deliberate, out-of-the-ordinary effort
Common collocation: deliberately paying extra attention

usagePhrases.en: there's nothing in particular I want to V
usagePhrases.note: 특별히 + negative is the idiomatic 'not really / nothing special'
특별히 = in a special way; 특히 = singled out from a group

examples.ko: 오늘은 손님이 와서 특별히 음식을 많이 준비했어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun sonnimi waseo teukbyeolhi eumsigeul mani junbihaesseoyo.
examples.en: We have guests today, so I specially prepared a lot of food.
examples.note: Simple: emphasizes deliberate, beyond-the-usual effort

examples.ko: 특별히 가고 싶은 곳은 없어요. 아무 데나 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: teukbyeolhi gago sipeun goseun eopseoyo. amu dena gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: There's no place I particularly want to go. Anywhere is fine.
examples.note: Everyday: the very common 특별히 + 없다 'nothing in particular' pattern

examples.ko: 선생님이 저를 특별히 챙겨 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi jeoreul teukbyeolhi chaenggyeo jusyeoseo jeongmal gamsahaesseoyo.
examples.en: The teacher looked after me especially well, so I was really grateful.
examples.note: Real situation: marks special, individualized treatment toward one person

entries.nuance: 특별히 (Sino-Korean 特別, 'special-distinct') means doing or feeling something in a special, deliberate, out-of-the-ordinary way, and in negative sentences it softens into 'not particularly.' Its constant point of confusion is 특히 ('especially'): 특별히 is about the special manner or intent behind an action ('특별히 만들었어요' = I made it specially, with effort), while 특히 just selects the standout item from a set ('과일 중에 특히 딸기' = strawberries above the other fruits). A useful mental split: 특별히 answers 'in what way?' (specially), 특히 answers 'which one?' (that one). 특별히 strongly favors negative frames — 특별히 ~없어요/않아요 is the everyday way to say 'nothing in particular / not really.' The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: using 특별히 when you mean 'among these, especially X' (that's 특히), and forgetting that the most natural 'not especially' is precisely 특별히 + a negative, not 특히 + a negative.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 특별히 where you mean 'among these, especially X' ('과일 중에 특별히 딸기'): selecting one from a group is 특히 — 특별히 would imply the strawberry was treated in some special way.
Forgetting that 'not particularly / nothing in particular' is idiomatically 특별히 + negative: say '특별히 어렵지 않아요' / '특별히 없어요,' not 특히 어렵지 않아요.
Reading 특별히 as plain 'very': it means 'in a special/deliberate way,' so '특별히 비싸요' implies an unusual, pointed expensiveness, not a generic 'very expensive' (that's 아주 비싸요).

entries.shortExplanation: 무엇보다 means "above all; more than anything" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "above all; more than anything" is 무엇보다 (mueotboda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무엇보다 중요해요 ("it's important above all"). Watch the particle attached to 무엇보다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The signature collocation — flags the single most important point
Adding -도 to 무엇보다 strengthens the 'above absolutely all' feel
A common lead-in that announces your key point
Stresses priority in both order and importance

examples.en: Health is more important than anything.
examples.note: Simple: the textbook 무엇보다 + 중요하다 pairing

examples.ko: 여러 이유가 있지만, 무엇보다 가족과 가까워서 이 동네를 골랐어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo iyuga itjiman, mueotboda gajokgwa gakkawoseo i dongnereul gollasseoyo.
examples.en: There are several reasons, but above all I chose this neighborhood to be near family.
examples.note: Everyday: highlights the decisive reason among many

examples.ko: 새 직장은 무엇보다도 분위기가 좋아서 정말 마음에 들어요.
examples.romanization: sae jikjangeun mueotbodado bunwigiga joaseo jeongmal maeume deureoyo.
examples.en: More than anything, I really like my new workplace because the atmosphere is good.
examples.note: Real situation: 무엇보다도 points to the top factor in a personal judgment

entries.nuance: 무엇보다 (literally 무엇 'what' + 보다 'than') is a fixed expression — 'than anything,' i.e. 'above all / more than anything' — that elevates one point over everything else, not just over one rival. It is the go-to way to mark your top priority or the most decisive factor when several are in play, and it pairs especially naturally with 중요하다. Adding -도 gives 무엇보다도, slightly more emphatic. Compare it with 특히 ('especially'), which merely spotlights a notable member of a group without ranking it first; 무엇보다 actively crowns one thing #1. It works in both speech and writing and feels warm and emphatic. The English-speaker pitfall is taking 보다 literally as a two-item comparison ('better than what?') and trying to name a single rival noun after it — 무엇보다 is frozen as 'above all,' comparing one point against the entire field, so don't parse it as 'than what' or expect a specific 'than X' object.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 무엇보다 as a two-noun comparison and inserting a rival ('커피보다 무엇보다'): it is fixed as 'above all,' ranking one point over the whole field, not against one named thing.
Reading it literally as 'than what': 무엇 here doesn't ask a question — 무엇보다 functions as a set discourse phrase meaning 'above all / most of all.'
Confusing it with 특히: 특히 just spotlights a standout from a group, while 무엇보다 ranks one thing as the single most important, so 'health is #1' needs 무엇보다, not 특히.

entries.english: never; by no means (with a negative)
entries.shortExplanation: 결코 means "never; by no means (with a negative)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 결코 (gyeolko) = "never; by no means (with a negative)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결코 V지 않다 ("never V; by no means V") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결코, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: never V; by no means V
usagePhrases.note: Must be completed by a negative predicate — the core pattern
Very common with adjective + -지 않다 for emphatic denial
Pairs with 아니다 to firmly reject an identity or quality
결코 is more written/formal; 절대로 is the spoken everyday twin

examples.ko: 저는 그 약속을 결코 잊지 않을 거예요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu yaksogeul gyeolko itji aneul geoyeyo.
examples.en: I will never forget that promise.
examples.note: Simple: 결코 demands the negative 잊지 않다 to land

examples.en: This was by no means an easy decision.
examples.note: Everyday: pairs with 아니다 to emphatically deny a quality

examples.ko: 그분은 결코 그런 말을 할 사람이 아니에요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun gyeolko geureon mareul hal sarami anieyo.
examples.en: He is by no means the kind of person who would say that.
examples.note: Real situation: firmly defends someone by rejecting a possibility

entries.nuance: 결코 is an emphatic negative adverb — 'never / by no means / not in the slightest' — and its defining rule is that it MUST co-occur with a negative ending such as -지 않다, 아니다, or 없다. It cannot stand alone or sit with a plain affirmative verb; the sentence feels broken without the negation. Its everyday partner is 절대(로): the two are close in meaning, but 결코 is more formal, written, and declaration-like (oaths, firm statements, editorials), while 절대로 is what you actually say out loud in conversation. 전혀 ('not at all') also negates but answers 'to what degree' (전혀 안 매워요), whereas 결코 conveys resolute 'never under any circumstances.' The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto English 'never,' which can stand in a positive-looking sentence ('I never go') — Korean 결코 cannot float free; you must supply the negative predicate, so 'I will never go' becomes '결코 가지 않을 거예요,' never '결코 갈 거예요.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing 결코 with an affirmative predicate ('결코 갈 거예요'): it structurally requires a negative — -지 않다 / 아니다 / 없다 — so the correct form is '결코 가지 않을 거예요.'
Using formal 결코 in light, casual chat where 절대(로) or 전혀 fits: '결코' in a relaxed conversation sounds stiff or theatrical; spoken Korean prefers '절대 안 그래' / '전혀 안 매워요.'
Assuming 결코 alone already means 'no' like English 'never' can: it only colors a clause that is itself negated, so it can't carry the negation by itself.

entries.english: finally; at last; in the end
entries.shortExplanation: 마침내 means "finally; at last; in the end" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 마침내 (machimnae) means "finally; at last; in the end". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 마침내 V했어요 ("finally, V happened"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 마침내 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Caps a long, drawn-out process with its awaited result

usagePhrases.en: after a long N, at last
usagePhrases.note: Often follows '오랜 ~ 끝에' (after long effort/waiting)
Common with achievement verbs to mark a hard-won success
마침내 is more literary/weighty; 드디어 is more spoken and excited

examples.en: The long-awaited news finally arrived.
examples.note: Simple: 마침내 frames the result as the end of a long wait

examples.ko: 몇 년 동안 준비한 끝에 마침내 시험에 합격했어요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon dongan junbihan kkeute machimnae siheome hapgyeokaesseoyo.
examples.en: After preparing for years, I finally passed the exam.
examples.note: Everyday: '~ 끝에' supplies the long effort that 마침내 caps

examples.ko: 여러 번 실패했지만 마침내 원하던 결과를 얻었어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo beon silpaehaetjiman machimnae wonhadeon gyeolgwareul eodeosseoyo.
examples.en: I failed several times, but in the end I got the result I wanted.
examples.note: Real situation: closes a struggle with the hard-won outcome

entries.nuance: 마침내 (native Korean) means 'finally / at last' and frames an outcome as the culmination of a long process, sustained effort, or anxious wait — it carries the weight of something hard-won. Its everyday twin is 드디어: both mean 'finally,' but 드디어 is warmer, more spoken, and bursts with the speaker's excitement ('드디어 끝났다!'), while 마침내 is more literary, composed, and narrative — the word a novel or news report uses to crown a climax. A third cousin, 결국 ('in the end / after all'), can mark a neutral or even disappointing conclusion, whereas 마침내 implies the end was awaited and welcome. It loves the set-up '오랜 노력 끝에.' Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't use 마침내 for trivial 'and then finally' sequencing (just listing steps) — it promises a significant, awaited result — and don't confuse it with the look-alike 마침 ('as it happens / just in time'), e.g. '마침 너를 만났네,' which is about lucky coincidence, not culmination.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 마침내 for trivial step-sequencing ('먼저 씻고, 마침내 잤어요'): it implies a meaningful, long-awaited result, so plain sequencing wants 그다음에/마지막으로 instead.
Confusing 마침내 ('at last, after a long process') with 마침 ('as it happens / just in time'): '마침 시간이 있었어요' means 'I happened to have time,' a coincidence, not a culmination.
Substituting 마침내 wherever English says 'in the end' even for letdowns: a disappointing or merely neutral conclusion is 결국 ('결국 안 됐어요'), since 마침내 leans toward a welcome, hard-won outcome.

structuredNuance.t: 마침내 means 'finally / at last' and frames an outcome as the culmination of a long process, sustained effort, or anxious wait — it carries the weight of something hard-won. It loves the set-up '오랜 노력 끝에.'

entries.english: on the contrary; conversely; the other way around
entries.shortExplanation: 반대로 means "on the contrary; conversely; the other way around" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "on the contrary; conversely; the other way around" is 반대로 (bandaero). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like A. 반대로 B. ("A. Conversely, B."). Watch the particle attached to 반대로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Links two opposite situations across sentences

usagePhrases.en: to do it the other way around
usagePhrases.note: Concrete physical sense: reversed manner or direction
오히려 strengthens it into 'no — the reverse, against expectation'
The 과/와 marks the specific reference point being reversed

examples.ko: 형은 활발한데, 반대로 동생은 아주 조용해요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeun hwalbalhande, bandaero dongsaengeun aju joyonghaeyo.
examples.en: The older brother is outgoing; conversely, the younger one is very quiet.
examples.note: Simple: contrasts two people directly

examples.ko: 쉬울 거라고 생각했는데 반대로 정말 어려웠어요.
examples.romanization: swiul georago saenggakaenneunde bandaero jeongmal eoryeowosseoyo.
examples.en: I thought it would be easy, but on the contrary it was really hard.
examples.note: Everyday: reverses the speaker's expectation

examples.ko: 설명서와 반대로 조립해서 다시 해야 했어요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongseowa bandaero joripaeseo dasi haeya haesseoyo.
examples.en: I assembled it the opposite way from the manual, so I had to redo it.
examples.note: Real situation: 'in the reverse manner,' with 과/와 naming the reference

entries.nuance: 반대로 (Sino-Korean 反對, '反 anti/reverse + 對 face/oppose' → opposition) means 'the opposite way,' covering both 'on the contrary' (contrasting facts or expectations) and 'the other way around' (reversed manner or direction). Compare it with the connector 반면(에) ('whereas/on the other hand'): 반면(에) calmly sets two differing facts side by side ('도시는 편리한 반면 복잡해요'), while 반대로 points to an actual, literal opposite — a flipped action, a reversed direction, or an outcome contrary to what was expected. So 'the manual said left, I went right' is 반대로, but 'the city is convenient, whereas the countryside is quiet' is more naturally 반면에. When you reverse a specific reference, keep the 과/와: 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 반대로 as a neutral 'on the other hand' clause-linker where 반면(에) belongs — 반대로 specifically signals a true opposite, not merely a different angle.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 반대로 as a neutral 'on the other hand' where two facts merely differ ('도시는 편리하고 반대로 시골은 조용해요'): a calm side-by-side contrast prefers 반면(에); 반대로 implies a true reversal.
Dropping the particle in 'N과/와 반대로' ('설명서 반대로'): when reversing a specific reference, the 과/와 is needed — 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로.
Confusing it with 거꾸로: 거꾸로 is physically upside-down/backwards ('티셔츠를 거꾸로 입었어요'), while 반대로 is the broader 'opposite/conversely,' so 'wore it inside-out' is 거꾸로, not 반대로.

structuredNuance.t: 반대로 means 'the opposite way,' covering both 'on the contrary' (contrasting facts or expectations) and 'the other way around' (reversed manner or direction). When you reverse a specific reference, keep the 과/와: 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로.

entries.shortExplanation: 오로지 means "only; solely; entirely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 오로지 (oroji) = "only; solely; entirely". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 오로지 N만 ("only N (and nothing else)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 오로지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Habitually closes with -만 to seal the exclusivity

usagePhrases.en: solely for the sake of N
usagePhrases.note: Stresses a single dedicated purpose
Pairs with -ㄹ 뿐이다 for 'merely/only'
오로지 conveys single-minded, wholehearted devotion

examples.ko: 그동안 오로지 가족만 생각하며 일해 왔어요.
examples.romanization: geudongan oroji gajongman saenggakamyeo ilhae wasseoyo.
examples.en: All this time I've worked thinking only of my family.
examples.note: Simple: the -만 partner seals 'only family, nothing else'

examples.ko: 이 결과는 오로지 본인의 노력 덕분이에요.
examples.romanization: i gyeolgwaneun oroji boninui noryeok deokbunieyo.
examples.en: This result is entirely thanks to your own effort.
examples.note: Everyday: attributes a cause to one factor alone

examples.ko: 그 선수는 오로지 우승만을 목표로 몇 년을 훈련했어요.
examples.romanization: geu seonsuneun oroji useungmaneul mokpyoro myeon nyeoneul hullyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: That athlete trained for years aiming solely at the championship.
examples.note: Real situation: 오로지 + 만을 marks one exclusive, all-consuming goal

entries.nuance: 오로지 (native Korean) means 'only / solely / entirely' and emphasizes single-minded exclusivity — one purpose, one person, one cause, with everything else shut out. Its near-synonym is 오직, and both mean 'only,' but the dividing line is emotional temperature: 오직 is plainer and more matter-of-fact, while 오로지 carries a warmer, almost devotional weight, suggesting wholehearted dedication ('오로지 너만을 위해'). It naturally leans on -만 or -뿐 to complete the 'and nothing else' meaning. Crucially, 오로지 is about exclusive focus, not about small quantities — it is NOT the 'only/just X items' of counting. The English-speaker pitfall flows from that: English 'only' covers both devotion ('I think only of you') and scarcity ('only three left'), but Korean splits them — use 오로지/오직 for exclusive focus and 단지/겨우 for 'merely/only (so few),' so 'only three remain' is '겨우 세 개 남았어요,' never 오로지 세 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 오로지 for small quantities ('오로지 세 명 왔어요'): scarcity 'only/just' is 단지/겨우, so say '겨우 세 명 왔어요' — 오로지 is exclusive focus, not a low count.
Dropping the supporting -만/-뿐 ('오로지 가족 생각했어요'): the 'only' sense needs the partner particle — '오로지 가족만 생각했어요' completes it.
Treating 오로지 and 오직 as identical in tone: 오직 is neutral and crisp, while 오로지 adds wholehearted, devotional warmth, so an emotional dedication line ('오로지 너를 위해') loses force if flattened to 오직.

entries.english: in a word; in short; to put it simply
entries.shortExplanation: 한마디로 means "in a word; in short; to put it simply" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 한마디로 (hanmadiro) means "in a word; in short; to put it simply". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 한마디로 N이다 ("in a word, it's N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 한마디로 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sums the whole thing up with a single blunt label

usagePhrases.en: to put it in one word
usagePhrases.note: The fuller set form that explicitly announces a summary
Variant lead-in, slightly more 'let me be frank'
한마디로 is punchier, more spoken and opinionated

examples.en: That movie was, in a word, a waste of time.
examples.note: Simple: compresses a whole judgment into one phrase

examples.en: To put it simply, we just weren't prepared enough.
examples.note: Everyday: 말하면 leads into a blunt one-line summary

examples.ko: 새 제도는 복잡해 보여도 한마디로 누구에게나 공평한 제도예요.
examples.romanization: sae jedoneun bokjapae boyeodo hanmadiro nuguegena gongpyeonghan jedoyeyo.
examples.en: The new system may look complex, but in short it's one that's fair to everyone.
examples.note: Real situation: cuts through detail to deliver the bottom line

entries.nuance: 한마디로 (native Korean: 한 'one' + 마디 'a word/segment of speech' + -로 'by/in') means 'in a word / in short' and signals that you are about to condense everything into one blunt summary or label. It is conversational and usually evaluative — you reach for it right before dropping your bottom line, often a verdict ('한마디로 별로예요'). Compare it with the more neutral, businesslike 요약하면 ('to summarize'): 요약하면 sounds like minutes of a meeting, while 한마디로 sounds like a friend cutting to the chase with an opinion. Its fuller forms 한마디로 말하면 / 한마디로 말해서 are equally common. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't follow 한마디로 with a long, multi-clause explanation — it literally promises ONE short takeaway, so keep what comes after crisp — and don't parse it word-for-word as 'with one word said'; it is a frozen discourse marker meaning 'in short / to sum up,' so the listener expects a punchy summary, not a literal single vocabulary word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Following 한마디로 with a sprawling, multi-clause explanation: it promises one short takeaway, so what comes next should be brief — if you need to elaborate at length, use 정리하자면/요약하자면 instead.
Reading it literally as 'with one word' and then giving a literal single noun only: 한마디로 is a set marker for 'in short,' and the summary can be a short clause, not strictly one vocabulary word.
Using punchy, opinionated 한마디로 in a formal neutral report where 요약하면/정리하면 fits: 한마디로 carries an evaluative, conversational tone that can sound too blunt in dry writing.

structuredNuance.t: 한마디로 means 'in a word / in short' and signals that you are about to condense everything into one blunt summary or label. entries.shortExplanation: 사업 means "business; enterprise; venture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "business; enterprise; venture" is 사업 (saeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사업을 하다 ("to run a business"). Watch the particle attached to 사업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 사업하다 is also one verb; once you add the object marker 을 you must split it: 사업을 하다
시작하다 = to begin; 사업을 차리다 (to set up a business) is a more colloquial alternative
잘되다 is one word and intransitive; the opposite is 사업이 안되다 (business is doing badly)
계획 = plan; 사업 모델, 사업 분야, 사업 자금 also use 사업 as a bare modifier (no 의)

examples.en: I want to run a small business.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 사업을 하다 split by 을; 작은 modifies 사업

examples.ko: 요즘 경기가 안 좋아서 사업이 잘 안돼요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gyeonggiga an joaseo saeobi jal andwaeyo.
examples.en: Business isn't going well these days because the economy is bad.
examples.note: 안돼요 = isn't going well; -아서 gives the reason and can't take a past tense before it

examples.ko: 그분은 맨손으로 시작해서 사업으로 크게 성공한 분이에요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun maensoneuro sijakaeseo saeobeuro keuge seonggonghan bunieyo.
examples.en: He started from nothing and made it big in business.
examples.note: 사업으로 = through/in business; 맨손으로 = with bare hands, a real-life success-story phrase

entries.nuance: 사업 (事業, literally 'affair-work') is business as an active undertaking — running a company, launching a commercial project, or being self-employed. The key boundary is against 산업 (産業, industry as a whole sector): 사업 is what one person or firm concretely does, while 산업 is the field that many businesses belong to (자동차 산업 = the auto industry, but 자동차 사업 = a particular auto-related business venture). It is also broader than the English word — a government or non-profit project is a 사업 too (복지 사업 = welfare project), so don't restrict it to 'for-profit'. Register is neutral; everyone from a small shop owner to a CEO uses it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 사업하다 as a fixed block: the moment an object marker appears you must break it apart (사업을 하다, 사업을 시작하다), never 사업하다를. Also resist translating 'do business with someone' word-for-word — Koreans say 거래하다 (to trade/deal) for that, not 사업을 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 사업 (a venture you actively run) with 산업 (an industry sector): say 자동차 산업이 발전했다 for the sector, but 그는 자동차 사업을 한다 for one person's business.
사업하다 is one verb, but adding the object marker forces a split: 사업을 하다, never 사업하다를.
'Do business with a partner' is not 그 사람과 사업을 하다 — Koreans say 그 사람과 거래하다 (to deal/trade with) for an ongoing commercial relationship.

structuredNuance.t: 사업 is business as an active undertaking — running a company, launching a commercial project, or being self-employed.
