entries.shortExplanation: 산업 means "industry (sector of the economy)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 산업 (saneop) = "industry (sector of the economy)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 자동차 산업 ("the automobile industry") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 산업, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 산업 follows the field as a bare modifier: 반도체 산업, 관광 산업, 게임 산업
발전하다 = to develop/advance; 산업이 성장하다 (to grow) is an equally common partner
구조 = structure; describes how an economy's sectors are organized and is heavy news/policy vocabulary
첨단 = cutting-edge; the natural contrast is 전통 산업 (traditional industry) or 사양 산업 (declining industry)

examples.en: Korea's semiconductor industry is well developed.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 발달해 있다 = is in a developed state; V-아/어 있다 marks a resulting condition

examples.ko: 인공지능 관련 산업이 빠르게 성장하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: ingongjineung gwallyeon saneobi ppareuge seongjanghago isseoyo.
examples.en: AI-related industries are growing fast.
examples.note: 관련 = related (attached directly, no 의); -고 있다 here marks an ongoing change/trend

examples.en: This city is famous for its car industry.
examples.note: N으로 유명하다 = to be famous for N; 자동차 산업 is the clearest everyday example of a 산업 (sector).

entries.nuance: 산업 (産業, 'produce-work') is an industry as an entire economic sector — manufacturing, tourism, IT — never a single company. Use it for macro-level talk: news, government reports, and any discussion of how the economy is structured. The sharp dividing line is against 사업 (事業, business venture): many 사업체 (businesses) together make up one 산업. So 산업을 시작하다 is wrong for 'start a business' — a person cannot launch a whole sector; they start a 사업. A related near-synonym is 업종 (業種, line of business / business category), but 업종 is narrower and is used to classify an individual shop ('what 업종 is your store?'), whereas 산업 is the broad sector above it. Register is formal-to-neutral; you will rarely hear 산업 in casual chat about your own job, but constantly in writing. The English-speaker pitfall is letting the romanization blur it with 사업 — the 산(ㄴ받침) vs 사 distinction is the entire meaning, and the two are not interchangeable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
산업 is a sector, so 산업을 시작하다 cannot mean 'start a business' — use 사업을 시작하다; a person starts a venture, not a whole industry.
Don't let the similar sound merge 산업 (industry) and 사업 (business): the ㄴ batchim in 산 carries the entire meaning difference.
To say what field a small shop is in, Koreans usually ask 업종이 뭐예요? (what's the line of business?), not 산업이 뭐예요? — 산업 is too macro for one store.

structuredNuance.t: 산업 is an industry as an entire economic sector — manufacturing, tourism, IT — never a single company. Use it for macro-level talk: news, government reports, and any discussion of how the economy is structured. Register is formal-to-neutral; you will rarely hear 산업 in casual chat about your own job, but constantly in writing.

The sharp dividing line is against 사업 (business venture): many 사업체 (businesses) together make up one 산업. So 산업을 시작하다 is wrong for 'start a business' — a person cannot launch a whole sector; they start a 사업. A related near-synonym is 업종 (line of business / business category), but 업종 is narrower and is used to classify an individual shop ('what 업종 is your store?'), whereas 산업 is the broad sector above it.
産業 means 'produce-work'.
The pitfall is letting the romanization blur it with 사업 — the 산 (ㄴ받침) vs 사 distinction is the entire meaning, and the two are not interchangeable.

entries.shortExplanation: 경력 means "career experience; work history" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 경력 (gyeongnyeok) means "career experience; work history". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 경력이 있다 ("to have (professional) experience"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 경력 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 경력이 없다; this is a track record, not a one-off experience
쌓다 = to pile up/accumulate — the idiomatic verb; 경력을 만들다 sounds wrong
number + 년 directly after 경력 states length; 경력 단절 = a career gap/break
-직 = position/post; the contrast term in hiring is 신입 (new-graduate hire)

examples.en: I don't really have much (work) experience.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 경력이 없다; 별로 + negative = not really/much

examples.ko: 마케팅 분야에서 경력을 더 쌓고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: maketing bunyaeseo gyeongnyeogeul deo ssako sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to build up more experience in the marketing field.
examples.note: 분야에서 = in the field of; 쌓다 is the fixed verb for accumulating a career

examples.ko: 경력이 화려해도 인성이 안 좋으면 뽑지 않아요.
examples.romanization: gyeongnyeogi hwaryeohaedo inseongi an joeumyeon ppopji anayo.
examples.en: Even with a dazzling résumé, we don't hire someone with poor character.
examples.note: 경력이 화려하다 = to have an impressive career; -아도 = even if — a real hiring-panel remark

entries.nuance: 경력 (經歷, 'pass-through + experience', i.e. things you have lived/worked through) means accumulated professional experience or work history — exactly what fills the career section of a résumé. The critical contrast is with 경험 (經驗): 경험 is experience of any kind, including a fun trip, a first kiss, or eating something new, whereas 경력 is specifically a documented work/professional track record. A backpacking trip is a great 경험 but is not 경력; three years at a company is both. Because it is a record, 경력 is counted in years with 년 (경력 3년), not with 번 (times) or 개 (items). High-frequency offshoots dominate Korean hiring: 경력직 (experienced hire) versus 신입 (new graduate), and 경력 단절 (a career break, often used for women returning to work). Register is neutral and shows up on every job posting. The English-speaker pitfall is using 경력 wherever English says 'experience' — for the broad sense ('It was a great experience'), you need 경험, and swapping them sounds odd to a Korean ear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 경력 for general life experience: 'It was a good experience' is 좋은 경험이었어요, not 좋은 경력이었어요 — 경력 is only a professional track record.
경력 is counted in years with 년 (경력 5년), not with 번 (times) or 개 (pieces).
To build a career, use 경력을 쌓다 (accumulate); 경력을 만들다 (make a career) is unnatural in Korean.

entries.shortExplanation: 채용 means "recruitment; hiring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "recruitment; hiring" is 채용 (chaeyong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 직원을 채용하다 ("to hire an employee"). Watch the particle attached to 채용 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 채용하다 is what the company does; the agent is the employer, not the applicant
공고 = public notice; the place openings are announced (채용 공고를 보다 = to see a job ad)
신입 = entry-level; the partner term is 경력 채용 (experienced-hire recruitment)
과정 = process; 채용이 되다 = to get hired (passive); 채용을 취소하다 = to cancel a hire

examples.ko: 그 회사는 올해 신입을 많이 채용해요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesaneun olhae sinibeul mani chaeyonghaeyo.
examples.en: That company is hiring a lot of new graduates this year.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 신입을 채용하다 — the company is the subject

examples.en: I saw the job posting and submitted my application.
examples.note: -고 = and then; 지원서를 내다 = to hand in an application — note the applicant 지원한다, not 채용한다

examples.ko: 요즘은 수시 채용이 늘어서 공채 시즌이 거의 사라졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun susi chaeyongi neureoseo gongchae sijeuni geoui sarajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Open-ended hiring has grown lately, so the mass-recruitment season has nearly vanished.
examples.note: 수시 채용 = rolling/as-needed hiring vs 공채 (公採, scheduled mass recruitment) — current job-market vocabulary

entries.nuance: 채용 (採用, 'pick/gather + use', i.e. to select and put to use) is the formal, institutional word for recruitment and hiring that companies use — it dominates 채용 공고 (job postings) and 채용 과정 (the hiring process). The register contrast is against the everyday verb 뽑다 (to pick/select): a friend might casually say 회사에서 사람 뽑는대 (I hear the company is taking people on), but the official notice says 채용. The directional pitfall trips up English speakers constantly: the employer 채용한다 (hires/recruits), while the applicant 지원한다 (applies) — these are not interchangeable, so '저는 그 회사에 채용했어요' to mean 'I applied' is wrong; you 지원했어요 and were then 채용됐어요 (got hired). Note also that 입사하다 (to enter a company, already in vocab) is the later step of actually joining after the offer. Spelling matters: the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ), not 체. Worth knowing the modern split: 공채 (scheduled mass hiring) versus 수시 채용 (rolling hiring), a frequent news topic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
채용하다 is what the employer does; the applicant 지원하다 (applies). 'I applied to the company' is 그 회사에 지원했어요, never 그 회사에 채용했어요.
Don't write 채용 as 체용 — the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ).
Getting hired is the passive 채용되다 (저는 채용됐어요), not the active 채용하다, which would mean you did the hiring.

entries.shortExplanation: 수입 means "income; revenue (also: imports)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수입 (suip) = "income; revenue (also: imports)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수입이 많다 ("to have a high income") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수입, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 수입이 적다; describes how much money comes in
줄다 = to decrease (intransitive); 수입이 늘다 = income increases
한 달 = one month; 고정 수입 = fixed/steady income, 부수입 = side income
지출 (already in vocab) = outgo; this is the standard budgeting pair (in vs out)

examples.ko: 저는 한 달 수입이 많지 않아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun han dal suibi manchi anayo.
examples.en: My monthly income isn't very high.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 수입이 많다/적다; 많지 않다 = not much

examples.ko: 프리랜서는 매달 수입이 일정하지 않아서 불안해요.
examples.romanization: peuriraenseoneun maedal suibi iljeonghaji anaseo buranhaeyo.
examples.en: A freelancer's income isn't steady month to month, so it's stressful.
examples.note: 일정하다 = to be steady/fixed; -지 않아서 chains the negative reason

examples.ko: 수입보다 지출이 많으면 적자가 나니까 가계부를 써 보세요.
examples.romanization: suipboda jichuri maneumyeon jeokjaga nanikka gagyebureul sseo boseyo.
examples.en: If spending exceeds income you run a deficit, so try keeping a budget book.
examples.note: 적자가 나다 = to go into the red; N보다 = than — a practical money-management line

entries.nuance: 수입 for personal money means income or revenue — the money coming in — and lives in opposition to 지출 (spending going out). Crucially it is a homograph hiding two different hanja: 收入 ('gather + enter') is income, while 輸入 ('transport + enter') is imports, the opposite of 수출 (輸出, exports). Spoken aloud they are identical, so only context tells you whether 수입 means a paycheck or a shipment of foreign goods; in an economics lecture both senses can appear in one paragraph. The near-synonym for the income sense is 소득 (所得, already in vocab): 소득 is the more formal/statistical word (소득세 = income tax, 소득 수준 = income level), whereas 수입 feels closer to everyday earnings, especially 한 달 수입 (monthly take). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'income' maps only to one fixed word and then panicking when 수입 shows up meaning 'imports' — train yourself to read the surrounding sentence. Also note 수입 is a noun describing a state (수입이 많다), so you don't conjugate it like a verb.

Don't confuse 수입 (income/imports, 入 = enter) with 수출 (exports, 出 = exit); they are economic opposites.
For formal or statistical 'income' (income tax, income bracket) Koreans prefer 소득 (소득세, 소득 수준), not 수입.

entries.shortExplanation: 손해 means "loss; damage (financial)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 손해 (sonhae) means "loss; damage (financial)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 손해를 보다 ("to suffer/incur a loss"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 손해 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 here means 'to incur', not 'to see' — the single most important collocation to memorize
입다 = to suffer (slightly more formal); 손해를 끼치다 = to cause a loss to someone else
크다/적다 size the loss; 손해가 막심하다 = the loss is severe (set phrase)
배상 = indemnity; 손해 배상을 청구하다 = to claim damages — legal/business register

examples.en: If we do it that way, I lose out.
examples.note: Beginner frame: noun-as-predicate 손해(이)다 = to be a loss/disadvantage to someone

examples.ko: 지금 팔면 손해를 볼 것 같아서 조금 더 기다리려고요.
examples.romanization: jigeum palmyeon sonhaereul bol geot gataseo jogeum deo gidariryeogoyo.
examples.en: I think I'll take a loss if I sell now, so I'll wait a bit longer.
examples.note: 손해를 보다 = to incur a loss; -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 = it seems — note 보다 is NOT 'see' here

examples.ko: 환불을 안 해 주면 결국 소비자만 손해를 보는 거잖아요.
examples.romanization: hwanbureul an hae jumyeon gyeolguk sobijaman sonhaereul boneun geojanayo.
examples.en: If they won't refund it, in the end it's only the consumer who loses out, right?
examples.note: 결국 = in the end; -잖아요 = appeals to shared knowledge — a real complaint-line

entries.nuance: 손해 (損害, 'damage + harm') is a loss or disadvantage, almost always financial or in terms of coming out worse off — the direct opposite of 이익/이득 (profit/gain). Its make-or-break collocation is 손해를 보다, where 보다 does NOT mean 'to see' but 'to incur/take', so 손해를 보다 = 'to take a loss'; English speakers often mis-hear this and either mistranslate it or wrongly substitute 손해를 하다, which is simply not Korean. The boundary against 피해 (被害, harm/damage suffered) matters: 손해 leans toward monetary or deal-based disadvantage (a bad sale, an unfair trade), while 피해 covers broader harm including physical or disaster damage (태풍 피해 = typhoon damage, 피해자 = victim). For a machine breaking, use 고장 (malfunction), not 손해. Register is neutral and it even works conversationally as a predicate noun: 나만 손해야 (I'm the only one who loses out). The pitfall to drill is the verb pairing — 손해를 보다 / 입다, never 손해를 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 손해를 보다 (보다 = incur, not see) or 손해를 입다 for 'to suffer a loss'; 손해를 하다 is not Korean.
손해 is monetary/disadvantage loss; for broad harm — physical, disaster, victim — use 피해 (태풍 피해, 피해자), and for a device breaking use 고장.
손해 is the opposite of 이익 (profit), so don't mix it up with 손님 (guest/customer), which only looks similar.

entries.shortExplanation: 가치 means "value; worth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "value; worth" is 가치 (gachi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가치가 있다 ("to be worthwhile / have value"). Watch the particle attached to 가치 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 가치가 없다 (worthless); covers both economic and abstract worth
오르다/떨어지다 for value going up/down (property, stocks, currency, a collectible)
예: 볼 가치가 있다 (worth seeing), 도전해 볼 가치가 있다 (worth trying)
-관 (觀) = view; 가치관이 다르다 = to have different values — a very common relationship phrase

examples.en: This really has value / is worthwhile.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 가치가 있다 as a simple predicate of worth

examples.ko: 그 그림은 시간이 지날수록 가치가 올라갔어요.
examples.romanization: geu geurimeun sigani jinalsurok gachiga ollagasseoyo.
examples.en: That painting rose in value as time went by.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ수록 = the more...; 가치가 오르다/올라가다 for appreciating value

examples.ko: 저는 일을 고를 때 연봉보다 그 일의 가치를 더 중요하게 봐요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun ireul goreul ttae yeonbongboda geu irui gachireul deo jungyohage bwayo.
examples.en: When I pick a job, I weigh the meaning of the work over the salary.
examples.note: 고를 때 = when choosing; 중요하게 보다 = to regard as important — a real values-based statement

entries.nuance: 가치 (價値, 'price + value') means value or worth, spanning both economic value (가치가 오르다 = rises in value, of property or stocks) and abstract worth (인생의 가치 = the value of life, 일의 가치 = the worth of one's work). The most useful pattern built on it is V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 ('worth doing': 볼 가치가 있다 = worth seeing), and the derived 가치관 (one's value system/worldview) is extremely high-frequency, especially 가치관이 다르다 when people clash. The dividing line is against the concrete-amount words 가격 (價格, the listed price/price tag) and 값 (the cost/amount you actually pay): 가치 is how much something is truly worth, which may diverge sharply from its 가격 — a cheap gift can have huge 가치 but a low 가격. Register is neutral-to-elevated. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 가치 into the 'worth doing' slot with the wrong verb (가치가 하다 is wrong; it's 가치가 있다), and mixing it up with 가격 when you mean the sticker price rather than intrinsic worth.

Don't confuse 가치 (intrinsic worth/value) with 가격 (the listed price): a discounted item has a low 가격 but can still hold high 가치.
For 'worth doing' use V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 (볼 가치가 있다), never 가치가 하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 품질 means "quality (of a product)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 품질 (pumjil) = "quality (of a product)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 품질이 좋다 ("to be of good quality") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 품질, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the negatives are 품질이 나쁘다 and 품질이 떨어지다 (quality drops/is poor)
높이다 = to raise (transitive); 품질을 관리하다 = to manage/control quality
관리 = management; a standard business term, often abbreviated 품질 관리부 (QC department)
고- (高) / 저- (低) prefixes attach directly to 품질

examples.en: This clothing is good quality.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 품질이 좋다 — 품질 is the subject, 좋다 the descriptive verb

examples.ko: 가격은 조금 비싸지만 품질이 정말 좋아서 만족해요.
examples.romanization: gagyeogeun jogeum bissajiman pumjiri jeongmal joaseo manjokaeyo.
examples.en: It's a bit pricey, but the quality is so good that I'm satisfied.
examples.note: -지만 = but; -아서 chains the reason 'because the quality is good'

examples.ko: 요즘 소비자들은 가격보다 품질을 더 꼼꼼하게 따져요.
examples.romanization: yojeum sobijadeureun gagyeokboda pumjireul deo kkomkkomhage ttajyeoyo.
examples.en: These days consumers scrutinize quality more carefully than price.
examples.note: 따지다 (already in vocab) = to scrutinize; 꼼꼼하게 = meticulously — a market-trend sentence

entries.nuance: 품질 (品質, 'goods + substance/quality') refers specifically to the quality of goods or products — how well-made and reliable something is. It is THE word in commerce and reviews: 품질 관리 (quality control), 품질 보증 (quality guarantee), 품질이 떨어지다 (quality slips). The sharp restriction English speakers must learn is that 품질 only modifies products/goods, not abstract or experiential things: 'quality of life' is 삶의 질, 'quality of sleep' is 수면의 질, 'quality time' is not 품질 시간 — for all of those you drop the 품 and use bare 질 (質, quality/nature). So 품(品) literally pins it to merchandise. The near-synonym to keep separate is 성능 (性能, performance/specs of a device): a phone can have great 성능 (fast chip) but poor 품질 (cheap, breaks easily) — capability versus build quality. Register is neutral. The pitfall: 품질 is a noun naming a state, so you describe it with 좋다/나쁘다 (품질이 좋다), and you never say 품질을 잘하다, which treats it like an action.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 품질 only for products. 'Quality of life' is 삶의 질, not 삶의 품질 — for abstract quality drop 품 and use bare 질.
품질이 좋다/나쁘다 describes the state; 품질을 잘하다 is wrong because 품질 is a noun, not an action you perform.
Don't equate 품질 (build quality) with 성능 (performance/specs): a gadget can have high 성능 but low 품질.

entries.shortExplanation: 생산 means "production; manufacturing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 생산 (saengsan) means "production; manufacturing". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제품을 생산하다 ("to produce products"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 생산 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 생산하다 = to make/manufacture; the factory or firm is the agent
늘다/줄다 (intransitive) for output rising/falling; 생산을 늘리다 = to increase output (transitive)
대량 = large quantity; the contrast is 소량 생산 (small-batch) and 다품종 소량 생산 (high-mix low-volume)
라인, 과정 attach to 생산 as compounds; 생산성 = productivity

examples.en: This factory produces cars.
examples.note: Beginner frame: A를 생산하다; 공장 (factory) as the natural subject

examples.ko: 원자재 가격이 올라서 생산 비용이 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: wonjajae gagyeogi ollaseo saengsan biyongi neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Production costs rose because raw-material prices went up.
examples.note: 원자재 = raw materials; 비용 (already in vocab) = cost — 생산 as a compound modifier

examples.ko: 수요가 갑자기 늘면 생산을 그만큼 늘려야 하는데 공장이 못 따라가요.
examples.romanization: suyoga gapjagi neulmyeon saengsaneul geumankeum neullyeoya haneunde gongjangi mot ttaragayo.
examples.en: If demand suddenly jumps you have to raise output to match, but the factory can't keep up.
examples.note: 수요 = demand; 생산을 늘리다 (transitive); 따라가다 = to keep pace — a real supply-chain bind

entries.nuance: 생산 (生産, 'give birth/bring forth + produce') means production or manufacturing — the making of goods. It is the supply side of the economy and pairs naturally with 소비 (消費, consumption) as a set: 생산과 소비. The agent is a 생산자 (producer), the mirror of 소비자 (consumer). Keep three look-alike Sino-Korean economy words apart: 생산 (making things/output) vs 산업 (産業, the industry sector that does the making) vs 사업 (事業, a specific business venture) — they share syllables but mean output, sector, and enterprise respectively. The most common grammar pitfall is the transitivity pair English flattens into one verb 'increase': 생산이 늘다 is intransitive ('production increases', no object), but to actively raise output you need the transitive 생산을 늘리다 ('increase production'); using 생산을 늘다 is ungrammatical. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in business and news. Note 대량 생산 (mass production) as a fixed term and 생산성 (productivity) as a high-value derivative.

생산 is making/output; don't stretch it to mean 'industry' (use 산업) or 'business venture' (use 사업), even though all three share syllables.
Match transitivity: 생산이 늘다 (production rises, intransitive) vs 생산을 늘리다 (raise production, transitive). 생산을 늘다 is ungrammatical.
The person who produces is 생산자, not 생산가 — the agent suffix here is -자 (者), paralleling 소비자 (consumer).

entries.shortExplanation: 소비 means "consumption; spending" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "consumption; spending" is 소비 (sobi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 돈을 소비하다 ("to spend money"). Watch the particle attached to 소비 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 소비하다 also takes 에너지를/자원을 소비하다 (consume energy/resources)
늘다/줄다 (intransitive) for spending rising or falling; 소비를 줄이다 = to cut spending (transitive)
-자 (者) = person; the mirror of 생산자 (producer); 소비자 보호 = consumer protection
과- (過) = excessive; the positive contrast is 합리적 소비 (sensible consumption)

examples.en: I'm cutting back on spending these days.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 소비를 줄이다 (transitive); -고 있다 for an ongoing effort

examples.en: When the economy worsens, people reduce their spending.
examples.note: 나빠지다 = to get worse; 줄이다 = to reduce — the cause–effect of a downturn

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 세대는 가치 소비를 중요하게 생각해서 비싸도 의미 있는 걸 사요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun sedaeneun gachi sobireul jungyohage saenggakaeseo bissado uimi inneun geol sayo.
examples.en: Young people today value 'ethical/meaningful consumption', so they buy meaningful things even if pricey.
examples.note: 가치 소비 = value-driven consumption; -아도 = even if — a current consumer-culture trend

entries.nuance: 소비 (消費, 'dissolve/use up + spend') means consumption or spending — using up money, goods, or resources — and is the demand-side counterpart to 생산 (production), giving the staple pair 생산과 소비. Its standout derivative 소비자 (consumer) is one of the most useful economy words you can own (소비자 보호 = consumer protection). Two boundaries matter. First, against 지출 (支出, expenditure, already in vocab): 지출 is an accounting outflow — a line item in a budget — while 소비 is the broader economic act of consuming, including consuming non-money resources. Second, and the key value judgment, against 낭비 (浪費, waste): 소비 is neutral and often necessary (you must consume food and electricity), whereas 낭비 is always negative — money or resources thrown away pointlessly. So calling ordinary, reasonable spending 낭비 is an insult the speaker may not intend. Register is neutral. The grammar pitfall mirrors 생산: use the transitive 소비를 줄이다 to 'reduce spending', not the intransitive 소비를 줄다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
소비 (consumption) is neutral and can be necessary; 낭비 (waste) is always negative. Don't label normal spending 낭비 unless you mean it was wasteful.
Match transitivity: 소비를 줄이다 (cut spending, transitive) vs 소비가 줄다 (spending falls, intransitive). 소비를 줄다 is wrong.
소비 is the broad act of consuming; an individual budget outflow/expense entry is 지출 — don't use 소비 where the accounting term 지출 is meant.

entries.shortExplanation: 예산 means "budget" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 예산 (yesan) = "budget". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 예산을 짜다 ("to draw up a budget") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 예산, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 짜다 = to put together/plan; the most natural verb (it's a structured plan you assemble)
부족하다 = to be short; the opposite is 예산이 남다 (budget left over)
세우다 = to set up; 예산을 초과하다 = to exceed the budget
안에서 = inside; the contrast is 예산을 넘다/초과하다 (to go over budget)

examples.en: I'm a bit short on budget for this trip.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 예산이 부족하다; 좀 softens it

examples.ko: 회사에서 내년 마케팅 예산을 줄이기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo naenyeon maketing yesaneul jurigiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The company decided to cut next year's marketing budget.
examples.note: -기로 하다 = to decide to; 예산을 줄이다 = to reduce the budget

examples.ko: 예산을 미리 짜 두면 충동구매를 줄일 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yesaneul miri jja dumyeon chungdonggumaereul juril su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you set a budget in advance, you can curb impulse buying.
examples.note: -아/어 두다 = do in advance and leave it; 충동구매 = impulse purchase — a practical money tip

entries.nuance: 예산 (豫算, 'beforehand + calculate', i.e. money figured out in advance) is a budget — a planned amount of money set aside for a project, household, or organization before it is spent. The idiomatic verb is 예산을 짜다 ('to weave/assemble a budget'), reflecting that a budget is a structured plan you build; 예산을 세우다 (to set up) also works, but 예산을 만들다 (to make) sounds flat and unnatural. The defining contrast is the plan-versus-actual distinction English blurs under 'budget': 예산 is the forward-looking plan, whereas 지출 (expenditure, already in vocab) and 비용 (the cost incurred) are what actually leaves your pocket, and 가계부 is the record of what was spent. So you 예산을 짜다 first, then track your 지출 against it. Register is neutral and identical in households, companies, and government (국가 예산 = the national budget). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 to 'make a budget' and confusing the planned 예산 with already-spent 지출/비용 — keep 'plan' (예산) and 'spent' (지출) firmly apart.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 예산을 짜다 or 예산을 세우다 for 'make a budget'; 예산을 만들다 sounds unnatural to Koreans.
예산 is the planned amount looking forward, not money already spent — that is 지출 (expenditure) or 비용 (cost).
To go over budget say 예산을 초과하다/넘다, not 예산을 지나다 (which means physically pass by).

entries.shortExplanation: 자본 means "capital (money/assets for business)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자본 (jabon) means "capital (money/assets for business)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자본이 부족하다 ("to be short on capital"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자본 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 부족하다 = to lack; the classic startup problem (initial capital shortfall)
투자하다 = to invest; 자본을 모으다 = to raise/gather capital
-금 (金) = money/funds; the registered founding capital of a company
-주의 (主義) = -ism; 외국 자본 = foreign capital, 자본 시장 = capital market

examples.en: To run a business you need capital.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 자본이 필요하다; -(으)려면 = if you intend to

examples.ko: 그들은 적은 자본으로 회사를 크게 키웠어요.
examples.romanization: geudeureun jeogeun jaboneuro hoesareul keuge kiwosseoyo.
examples.en: They grew the company big on little capital.
examples.note: 적은 = small/little; 키우다 = to grow (something) — 자본으로 = with/using capital

examples.ko: 돈을 많이 벌려면 처음에 자본이 좀 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: doneul mani beollyeomyeon cheoeume jaboni jom isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: To make a lot of money, you need some capital at the start.
examples.note: 돈을 벌다 = to make money; 자본이 있다 — the everyday point that you need starting capital first.

entries.nuance: 자본 (資本, 'resources + root/origin', i.e. the foundational resources of an enterprise) is capital in the economic sense — the money and assets used to start or run a business and to generate more wealth. It is more abstract and formal than plain 돈 (money), and it carries a structural, economy-level flavor: 자본주의 (capitalism), 자본 시장 (capital market), 외국 자본 (foreign capital). Two near-synonyms must be separated. 자금 (資金, funds) is money earmarked for a specific concrete purpose — 사업 자금 (operating funds), 자금이 돌다 (cash flows) — more hands-on than the foundational 자본. And 자산 (資産, assets) is the total of what you own (property, savings, stocks), the broadest of the three. So you might have plenty of 자산 (assets) but lack ready 자금 (working funds), while 자본 names the wealth deployed to do business. The key derivative 자본금 (paid-in capital) is the registered founding sum. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 자본 for everyday pocket cash (that's 돈) or for purpose-specific funds (that's 자금), and don't drop the final ㄴ — it is 자본, not 자보.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
자본 is business/economic capital, not everyday cash: for ordinary money use 돈, and for purpose-specific funds (operating money) use 자금.
Don't blur 자본 (capital deployed in business) with 자산 (total assets you own) — you can be asset-rich (자산이 많다) yet short on working capital.
Keep the final consonant: it's 자본 (with ㄴ), not 자보.

entries.shortExplanation: 판매 means "selling; sales (of a product)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "selling; sales (of a product)" is 판매 (panmae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 판매하다 ("to sell"). Watch the particle attached to 판매 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-noun + 하다 makes a formal verb; 이 책을 판매합니다
intransitive 잘되다 takes 판매 as subject with 가, no agent
launching a product; 다음 달부터 판매를 시작해요
판매 takes a bare noun modifier with no 의, like a compound

examples.en: Where do they sell this?
examples.note: simple: 판매하다 in a casual question, more polite/neutral than 팔아요

examples.en: Online sales are doing really well these days.
examples.note: everyday: note 판매가 + 잘되다, the success is the subject, not you

examples.en: After we lowered the price, sales rose 30 percent.
examples.note: real-situation: business report register with a concrete figure

entries.nuance: 판매(販賣) is Sino-Korean, literally '販 sell + 賣 sell', and names the seller's side of a transaction; its mirror image is 구매(購買) 'buy + buy', the buyer's side. The dividing line you must feel is 판매 vs the everyday native verb 팔다: 팔다 is what you say to a friend (이거 팔아요?), whereas 판매(하다) is the dressed-up word for signs, contracts, menus, and reports (판매 중, 판매 종료). A second trap is 판매 vs 매출(賣出): 판매 is the act of selling, but 매출 is the revenue figure that selling produces, so '매출이 늘었다' means money went up while '판매가 늘었다' means units moved. English speakers also reach for 크다/작다 with sales, but Korean wants 판매가 늘다/줄다 or 잘되다/안되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 판매 where a friend expects 팔다: '이거 판매해요?' sounds like a corporate notice; in casual speech say '이거 팔아요?'
Confusing 판매 (the act of selling) with 매출 (sales revenue): say 매출이 올랐다 for money earned, 판매가 늘었다 for units sold
Pairing the wrong adjective: not 판매가 크다 but 판매가 잘되다 / 판매가 늘다 to say sales are strong

entries.shortExplanation: 경쟁 means "competition; rivalry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 경쟁 (gyeongjaeng) = "competition; rivalry". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 경쟁하다 ("to compete") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 경쟁, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: partner marked with 와/과: 그 회사와 경쟁하다, not 를
set collocation; 치열하다 'fierce/heated' almost lives with 경쟁
에서 marks the arena/contest you win within
업체 'business firm'; bare-noun compound, no 의

examples.en: Don't you two compete, do it together.
examples.note: simple: casual 반말-ish advice, 경쟁하다 about people

examples.en: Competition in this market is too fierce.
examples.note: everyday: the fixed pair 경쟁이 치열하다 you will hear constantly

examples.en: It's hard to compete with big firms on a low-price strategy.
examples.note: real-situation: note 대기업과, the rival takes 와/과

entries.nuance: 경쟁(競爭) is '競 vie + 爭 contend', two parties striving for the same prize, and it spans companies fighting for market share, students for grades, or athletes for a medal. The sharpest contrast to keep straight is 경쟁 vs 경기(競技/景氣): with 技 it is a sports match, with 景 it is the economic climate (경기가 나쁘다 'the economy is bad'), so never let English 'competition' drift into 경기. Register is neutral-to-formal; it suits news and business but is also fine in everyday talk. The must-pair word is 경쟁력 (competitiveness, '경쟁 + 力 power'). The classic English-speaker error is the particle: English says 'compete with X' and learners copy 를, but Korean rivalry is marked 와/과 — 경쟁사와 경쟁하다, never 경쟁사를 경쟁하다.

Marking the rival with 를: not '그 회사를 경쟁하다' but '그 회사와 경쟁하다' (rivals take 와/과)
Confusing 경쟁 with 경기: a match or the economy is 경기, not 경쟁; '경기가 안 좋다' = the economy is weak
Saying 경쟁이 크다 for intensity: the natural collocation is 경쟁이 치열하다 (fierce)

entries.shortExplanation: 협력 means "cooperation; collaboration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 협력 (hyeomnyeok) means "cooperation; collaboration". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 협력하다 ("to cooperate"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 협력 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: partner takes 와/과: 두 회사가 협력하다
관계 'relation'; the standing partnership between sides
긴밀하게 'tightly/closely' is the natural adverb here
업체 'firm'; an outside company you work jointly with

examples.en: Let's cooperate and finish this together.
examples.note: simple: 협력해서 (and so) links the means to the result

examples.en: Cooperation between departments is really important.
examples.note: everyday: 부서 간 'between departments', a common workplace frame

examples.ko: 이번 사업은 현지 업체와 긴밀하게 협력해서 진행합니다.
examples.romanization: ibeon saeobeun hyeonji eopchewa ginmilhage hyeomnyeokaeseo jinhaenghamnida.
examples.en: We'll run this project in close cooperation with a local firm.
examples.note: real-situation: formal 합니다 register; partner marked 와

entries.nuance: 협력(協力) is '協 join + 力 strength', literally pooling forces toward a shared goal, and it is structural and often long-term (협력 관계, 협력 업체). The near-synonym you must separate is 협조(協助) 'join + help': 협조 is lending your assistance when asked, usually for one specific request, and it travels with 받다 — 협조를 받다 / 협조를 구하다 (receive / seek cooperation). So a joint venture is 협력, but asking a colleague to help with one form is 협조. Note the grammar split this creates: you 협력하다 *with* a partner (와/과), but you 협조를 받다/하다, so '협력을 받다' sounds wrong — cooperation as a favor you receive is 협조. The natural opposite to pair for memory is 경쟁 (competition). Register is neutral-formal, common in business and official writing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 협력을 받다: you 협력하다 (cooperate with), but you 협조를 받다 (receive cooperation/help)
Blurring 협력 and 협조: a one-off favor is 협조 (협조 부탁드립니다); a sustained joint effort is 협력
Dropping the partner particle: not '그 회사 협력하다' but '그 회사와 협력하다' (와/과)

entries.shortExplanation: 성장 means "growth; development" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "growth; development" is 성장 (seongjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 성장하다 ("to grow"). Watch the particle attached to 성장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: intransitive; subject + 가/이: 회사가 성장하다
빠르게 'fast' is the standard adverb; cf. 급성장
fixed news compound, bare-noun + 성장
가능성 'possibility'; 성장 modifies it as a compound

examples.en: The kids really grow up fast.
examples.note: simple: literal physical growth of a child

examples.en: This field has high growth potential.
examples.note: everyday: 가능성이 높다, potential is 높다 not 크다

examples.en: Our company grew 20 percent year on year.
examples.note: real-situation: 대비 'compared to' is the business framing

entries.nuance: 성장(成長) is '成 accomplish + 長 lengthen/grow', covering both a child literally growing up and a company or economy expanding, so it is wider than English 'growth' which sounds only economic. The boundary to internalize is 성장 vs 발전(發展): 성장 is getting bigger in scale or size (more sales, taller), while 발전 is advancing in quality or sophistication (better, more developed). A startup that doubles revenue 성장했다; a country that modernizes its institutions 발전했다 — they often co-occur but answer different questions (how big? vs how advanced?). For an explosive jump, Korean prefixes 급- to get 급성장 'rapid growth'. The English-speaker pitfall is the adjective: growth is fast or large, so say 성장이 빠르다 / 성장이 크다, never 성장이 많다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing 많다: not 성장이 많다 but 성장이 빠르다 / 성장이 크다 to describe strong growth
Confusing 성장 (bigger in scale) with 발전 (more advanced in quality): a modernized city 발전했다, a richer one 성장했다
Using 높다 for the growth itself: growth is 빠르다/크다; only 가능성/잠재력 (potential) is 높다

entries.shortExplanation: 위기 means "crisis; critical situation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 위기 (wigi) = "crisis; critical situation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 위기에 빠지다 ("to fall into crisis") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 위기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 빠지다 'fall into', the fixed entry phrase
극복하다 'surmount' is the standard partner verb
fixed compound; cf. 금융 위기 financial crisis
관리 'management'; corporate/PR term

examples.en: We're in a bit of a crisis right now, help.
examples.note: simple: 위기예요 as a plain noun + 예요

examples.en: The company fell into a serious crisis.
examples.note: everyday: 위기에 빠지다, the locked-in 'fall into' phrase

examples.en: We overcame that crisis together.
examples.note: real-situation: 위기를 극복하다, the triumphant pairing

entries.nuance: 위기(危機) is '危 danger + 機 moment/opportunity', literally a 'dangerous moment' — the very character 機 hints why Koreans say 위기는 곧 기회 'a crisis is also an opportunity', pairing it with 기회(機會). Distinguish it sharply from 위험(危險) 'danger + steep': 위험 is general danger or risk that something might harm you (위험하다 'is dangerous'), while 위기 is a decisive turning-point situation already underway (경제 위기, 위기에 빠지다). So a slippery floor is 위험, but a company about to go bankrupt is in a 위기. Idiomatic movement is 위기에 빠지다 (fall in) and 위기를 극복하다/넘기다 (overcome/get past); 위기가 오다 'a crisis comes' is fine, but to enter one you don't say 위기에 들다. Register is neutral-formal, heavy in news and business.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 위기 (a critical situation) with 위험 (general danger/risk): a dangerous knife is 위험하다, not 위기
Saying 위기에 들다 to enter a crisis: the correct fixed form is 위기에 빠지다
Forgetting the rescue verb: a crisis is 극복하다 or 넘기다, not just 끝내다

entries.shortExplanation: 효율 means "efficiency" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 효율 (hyoyul) means "efficiency". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 효율이 높다 ("efficiency is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 효율 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 높다/낮다 (high/low), never 크다, is the scale word
높이다, the transitive causative of 높다
업무 'tasks/duties'; the most common workplace compound
-적이다 turns the noun into an adjective; cf. 효율적으로

examples.en: This is far more efficient.
examples.note: simple: 효율이 높다 as a plain comparison

examples.en: We raised work efficiency by cutting meetings.
examples.note: everyday: 효율을 높이다, the transitive 'raise it' phrasing

examples.en: Allocating your time efficiently is the key.
examples.note: real-situation: adverb 효율적으로 modifying how you act

entries.nuance: 효율(效率) is '效 effect + 率 rate', literally the 'rate of effect' — the ratio of useful output to the effort or resources put in, so it is inherently about getting more from less. Keep it apart from 효과(效果) '效 effect + 果 result': 효과 is whether something works at all (이 약은 효과가 있다 'this medicine is effective'), while 효율 is how economically it works (이 방법은 효율이 높다 'this method is efficient'). A drug can have great 효과 yet poor 효율 if it wastes resources. The scale is 높다/낮다, not 크다, and you raise it with 높이다. To use it as a description you must add -적: the adjective is 효율적이다 and the adverb 효율적으로 — bare 효율하다 does not exist. Its opposite is 비효율 (inefficiency). Register: neutral, everywhere at work.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 효율이 크다: efficiency takes 높다/낮다, so 효율이 높다 / 효율이 낮다
Confusing 효율 (output-to-input ratio) with 효과 (whether it works): 효과가 있다 = it works; 효율이 높다 = it works economically
Using 효율 as an adjective directly: there is no 효율하다; use 효율적이다 / 효율적으로

entries.shortExplanation: 성과 means "result; achievement (outcome of effort)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "result; achievement (outcome of effort)" is 성과 (seonggwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 성과를 내다 ("to produce results"). Watch the particle attached to 성과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 'put out' is the everyday partner verb
좋다 judges the quality of the achievement
거두다 'harvest', a more formal, writerly verb
평가 'appraisal'; the year-end HR review

examples.en: I got some results this time.
examples.note: simple: casual 성과 내다, modest self-report

examples.en: Results came out in proportion to my effort, so I'm proud.
examples.note: everyday: -ㄴ 만큼 'as much as', effort-to-payoff framing

examples.en: This year we achieved remarkable results.
examples.note: real-situation: formal 거두다 + 습니다 for a report

entries.nuance: 성과(成果) is '成 accomplish + 果 fruit', literally the 'fruit of accomplishment' — the concrete payoff that effort earns, and it carries a built-in positive, output-focused color. Contrast it with the neutral 결과(結果) '結 tie + 果 fruit', which is simply any outcome, good or bad: a failed exam is a 결과 but not a 성과. So 성과 implies the result is a worthwhile gain, while 결과 just states what happened. The defining verbs differ from English 'have': you don't 'have' a result, you 성과를 내다 (put out) or, more formally, 성과를 거두다 (reap/harvest). The word everyone chases is 성과급 ('성과 + 給 pay'), the performance bonus. Register: neutral-to-formal, very common at work in reviews and reports.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 성과 (a worthwhile achievement) with 결과 (any outcome): a bad ending is a 결과, not a 성과
Saying 성과를 하다: the verbs are 성과를 내다 (casual) or 성과를 거두다 (formal)
Treating 성과 as neutral: it implies a positive payoff, so you can't say 나쁜 성과 for a flat failure — use 결과

entries.shortExplanation: 목표치 means "target figure; target value" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 목표치 (mokpyochi) = "target figure; target value". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 목표치를 정하다 ("to set a target figure") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 목표치, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 정하다 'decide/fix' the number in advance
달성하다 is the formal 'achieve a set goal' verb
넘다 'cross over', i.e. surpass the line
에 미치다 'reach up to'; negated: 미치지 못하다

examples.en: Let's set the target figure a bit low.
examples.note: simple: casual 잡다 'set/peg' a number

examples.en: Sales far exceeded the target figure.
examples.note: everyday: 목표치를 넘다, surpassing the line

examples.en: We still haven't reached the target figure.
examples.note: real-situation: formal shortfall, 에 미치지 못하다

entries.nuance: 목표치(目標値) is 목표 '目 eye + 標 mark = aim/goal' plus the suffix -치(値) 'numerical value', so it specifically means a *quantified* target — a number you aim to hit, not an abstract aspiration. That -치 is a productive ending worth knowing: 수치 'a figure', 최대치 'the maximum', 평균치 'the average value'. The contrast to feel is 목표 vs 목표치: '제 목표는 행복이에요' (my goal is happiness) cannot become 목표치, because happiness has no number; but '올해 매출 목표치는 10억' works because it is measurable. Idiomatically you 달성하다 (attain) or 넘다 (exceed) a 목표치, set it with 정하다/잡다, and fall short as 목표치에 미치지 못하다. The English-speaker trap is treating it like a rival to beat: not 목표치를 이기다 (defeat) but 목표치를 넘다 (exceed). Register: business/data, fairly formal.

Using 목표치 for abstract aims: a life dream takes 목표, not 목표치 (which must be a number)
Saying 목표치를 이기다: you don't 'defeat' a number, you 목표치를 넘다 (exceed) or 달성하다 (attain)
Wrong reach verb for a shortfall: say 목표치에 미치지 못하다, not 목표치를 못 가다

entries.shortExplanation: 전략 means "strategy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전략 (jeollyak) means "strategy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전략을 세우다 ("to devise a strategy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 전략 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 세우다 'erect/set up', the standard formal verb

examples.en: Let's change our strategy a bit.
examples.note: simple: casual suggestion with bare 전략

examples.en: We devised a new marketing strategy.
examples.note: everyday: 전략을 세우다, the go-to collocation

examples.en: Approach that strategically, not emotionally.
examples.note: real-situation: adverb 전략적으로 vs 감정적으로 contrast

entries.nuance: 전략(戰略) is '戰 war + 略 plan', borrowed from military thinking to mean the big-picture plan for reaching a goal. Its essential partner-contrast is 전술(戰術) '戰 war + 術 art/technique': 전략 is the overarching design (where we want to be and broadly how), while 전술 is the concrete short-term moves that execute it. Winning the market is a 전략; the specific discount this weekend is a 전술 — mixing them up is the classic error. The defining verbs are 세우다 (set up) and the breezier 짜다 (assemble/weave); English speakers default to 만들다 'make', which sounds off — say 전략을 세우다, not 전략을 만들다. To describe acting with strategy, add -적: 전략적이다 / 전략적으로. Register spans formal business and ordinary planning chat alike.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 전략 (overall strategy) with 전술 (tactics): the grand plan is 전략, the on-the-ground move is 전술
Saying 전략을 만들다: the natural verbs are 전략을 세우다 or 전략을 짜다
Skipping -적 for the adjective: it is 전략적이다 / 전략적으로, not 전략이다 to mean 'strategic'

entries.shortExplanation: 분야 means "field; area (of work or study)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "field; area (of work or study)" is 분야 (bunya). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전문 분야 ("field of expertise"). Watch the particle attached to 분야 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 전문 'specialty'; one's area of professional depth
다양한 'diverse' is a natural modifier
에서 marks the domain you operate within
관련 'related'; adjacent areas to a given one

examples.en: What field are you interested in?
examples.note: simple: 분야에 관심 있다, casual self-intro question

examples.en: That person is an expert in that field.
examples.note: everyday: 분야의 전문가, the 의-linked 'expert of'

examples.ko: 저는 신재생 에너지 분야에서 일하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun sinjaesaeng eneoji bunyaeseo ilhago isseoyo.
examples.en: I work in the renewable-energy field.
examples.note: real-situation: 분야에서 일하다, domain marked with 에서

entries.nuance: 분야(分野) is '分 divide + 野 field/open ground', a domain carved out of the whole — an area of study, industry, or activity such as finance, design, or medicine. The boundary to lock in is 분야 vs 부서(部署): 분야 is the broad sector regardless of employer (IT 분야 spans all IT companies), whereas 부서 is a department *inside one company* (마케팅 부서, 인사 부서). You can work in the design 분야 while sitting in the planning 부서. The other near-neighbor is 분야 vs 영역(領域) 'territory/domain', which leans more abstract or jurisdictional; for jobs and studies 분야 is the safe default. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you don't '분야를 일하다' but '분야에서 일하다' (work *in* a field, 에서), and an expert is 분야의 전문가 with 의.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 분야 (a whole sector) with 부서 (a department within one company): 마케팅 부서 is inside a firm; 마케팅 분야 is the whole industry
Saying 분야를 일하다: the correct frame is 분야에서 일하다 (work within, 에서)
Dropping 의 for expertise: it is 그 분야의 전문가, not 그 분야 전문가 in careful speech

entries.shortExplanation: 규모 means "scale; size (of an operation)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 규모 (gyumo) = "scale; size (of an operation)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 규모가 크다 ("to be large in scale") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 규모, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 크다/작다, the scale words; not 길다/넓다
대(大) prefix; cf. 소규모 small-scale
키우다 'grow/raise', the transitive verb
bare-noun compound; how big a firm is

examples.en: The event's scale is bigger than I thought.
examples.note: simple: 규모가 크다, plain reaction

examples.en: The company is small, so the vibe is nice.
examples.note: everyday: 규모가 작다 of an organization

examples.en: The government announced a large-scale investment plan.
examples.note: real-situation: 대규모 as a prefix modifier in news

entries.nuance: 규모(規模) is '規 compass/rule + 模 mould/model', the overall magnitude of an undertaking — a business, project, event, or budget. The key contrast is 규모 vs 크기(size): 크기 is the physical dimensions of a concrete object (가방 크기 'bag size', 화면 크기 'screen size'), while 규모 is the abstract scale of an operation (사업 규모, 행사 규모). You would never say 가방 규모 or, for a person's build, 규모 — that is 크기 or 체격. The scale words are 크다/작다, never 많다 or 넓다, and you expand it with 키우다. The prefixed forms 대규모 (large-scale) and 소규모 (small-scale) are extremely productive in news and business. The English-speaker trap is letting 'size' default to 규모 for tangible things; reserve 규모 for the magnitude of activities and use 크기 for objects.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 규모 for a physical object's size: a bag's size is 크기 (가방 크기), not 규모
Saying 규모가 많다 or 규모가 넓다: scale takes 크다/작다, so 규모가 크다 / 규모가 작다
Applying 규모 to a person's body: build is 체격 or 크기, never 규모

entries.shortExplanation: 수요 means "demand (for a product or service)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수요 (suyo) means "demand (for a product or service)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수요가 많다 ("demand is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 많다/높다 collocate; 수요가 크다 is wrong
늘다/줄다 for up/down: 전기차 수요가 늘어요
frozen pair — demand comes FIRST, reverse of English
예측하다 'predict': 내년 수요를 예측해요

examples.en: Demand for electric cars has risen.
examples.note: simple: 수요가 + 늘다, the demand itself is the subject

examples.en: In summer, demand for air conditioners is high.
examples.note: everyday: 높다 (not 크다) for a high level of demand

examples.en: Supply and demand determine the price.
examples.note: real-situation: the fixed economics pair 수요와 공급 as subject

entries.nuance: 수요(需要) is Sino-Korean, literally '需 need + 要 require', and is the economics word for market demand — how much buyers as a whole want a product. Its fixed partner is its opposite 공급(供給) 'supply', frozen as 수요와 공급 (note the order reverses English 'supply and demand', with demand first). The contrast English speakers must feel is 수요 vs 요구(要求): English 'demand' covers both, but 요구 is a demand or request one person presses on another (임금 인상을 요구하다), while 수요 is impersonal market appetite. 수요 is also a 많다/높다 and 늘다/줄다 word, never 크다, and it belongs to formal economic or business writing, rarely casual chat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 수요 for a personal demand/request: to demand a raise is 임금 인상을 요구하다, not 수요 — 수요 is only impersonal market demand
Saying 수요가 크다 — demand takes 많다/높다 (level) or 늘다/줄다 (change), so say 수요가 많아요 / 수요가 높아요
Reversing the set phrase: in Korean it is 수요와 공급 (demand first), the mirror of English 'supply and demand'

entries.shortExplanation: 투자 means "investment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "investment" is 투자 (tuja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 투자하다 ("to invest"). Watch the particle attached to 투자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: target marked with 에: 주식에 투자하다, not 를
받다; a company takes funding from investors
수익 'profit/return'; what investment earns back
과감하게 'boldly/decisively', a frequent adverb

examples.en: I invest in a savings plan every month.
examples.note: simple: 에 투자하다, the target takes 에

examples.en: That startup received a large investment.
examples.note: everyday: 투자를 받다, from the company's receiving side

examples.ko: 교육에 대한 투자는 미래를 위한 것입니다.
examples.romanization: gyoyuge daehan tujaneun miraereul wihan geosimnida.
examples.en: Investment in education is for the future.
examples.note: real-situation: 에 대한 투자 'investment toward', value-statement register

entries.nuance: 투자(投資) is '投 throw + 資 capital/funds', literally 'throwing in capital' — committing money, time, or effort now to gain a return later, so it covers both finance (주식 투자) and effort (시간 투자, 자기 투자). The crucial contrast is 투자 vs 투기(投機) '投 throw + 機 chance': 투자 is reasoned, value-based commitment, while 투기 is speculation — gambling on short-term price swings (부동산 투기 'real-estate speculation') and carries a negative, reckless tone. Calling someone's careful stock plan 투기 is an insult. The defining grammar is the particle 에: you invest *in* something — 주식에 투자하다, 회사에 투자하다 — never 주식을 투자하다, because English 'invest X' misleads learners into 를. From the funded side you 투자를 받다, and the investor is 투자자(投資者). Register: neutral, common in finance and everyday goal-talk.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 투자 (reasoned investment) with 투기 (speculation/gambling): 투기 implies reckless price-betting and is pejorative
Marking the target with 를: not 주식을 투자하다 but 주식에 투자하다 (invest *in*, 에)
Saying 투자를 하다 toward a person: you 투자하다 in a thing with 에, e.g. 그 사업에 투자하다

From the funded side you 투자를 받다, and the investor is 투자자(投資者). Register: neutral, common in finance and everyday goal-talk.
