entries.english: the final stage, the home stretch
entries.shortExplanation: 막바지 means "the final stage, the home stretch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 막바지 (makbaji) means "the final stage, the home stretch". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 막바지에 ("in the final stretch"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 막바지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 막바지에 이르다 = to reach the final stage
막바지 + noun for last-stage tasks
접어들다 = to move into a stage/phase

usagePhrases.en: summer is in its final days
usagePhrases.note: N이/가 막바지다 = N is winding down

examples.en: The construction has now entered its final stage.
examples.note: 막바지에 접어들다 = enter the home stretch

examples.en: Exam prep is in its final stretch, so I'm really busy.
examples.note: N이/가 막바지다 = is in its last phase; -라서 = so/because

examples.en: This year too has reached its final days before we knew it.
examples.note: 막바지에 이르다 collocation; 어느덧 = before one realizes

entries.nuance: 막바지 is native Korean (from 막 'the very last / the end' + 바지, a phase-marking element), meaning the very last stretch of something that has been underway for a while — a season, a project, a year — exactly 'the home stretch' or 'final phase,' usually with a feel of intensity or winding down just before the end. The contrast to master is 막바지 vs 마지막: 마지막 simply means 'the last (one/item)' of a set (마지막 페이지 = the last page), with no sense of process, whereas 막바지 is the final ongoing phase of something that takes time. A close colloquial cousin is 막판 (a more casual 'the last round / final stretch'). The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 막바지 for 'the last one/item' (that is 마지막), and pair it with the right verbs — 막바지에 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 ('reach/enter the home stretch'), not 막바지에 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 막바지 for 'the last item/one' — that's 마지막 (마지막 줄 = the last line); 막바지 is the final ongoing phase of a process.
Pair 막바지 with 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 for 'reach the home stretch,' not 가다 (막바지에 가다 is unnatural).
막바지 implies something has been going on for a while; don't apply it to a brand-new task that just started — there's no 'final phase' yet.

entries.english: in the meantime, during that time
entries.shortExplanation: 그사이 means "in the meantime, during that time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "in the meantime, during that time" is 그사이 (geusai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그사이에 ("in the meantime, meanwhile"). Watch the particle attached to 그사이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: often with 에; marks the interval between two points

usagePhrases.en: change a lot in the meantime
usagePhrases.note: highlights change over the interval

usagePhrases.en: did something happen in the meantime?
usagePhrases.note: asking about events during the gap

usagePhrases.en: can't endure even that short interval
usagePhrases.note: 그사이를 못 참고 = unable to wait even that briefly

examples.ko: 잠깐 나갔다 왔는데 그사이에 비가 왔나 봐요.
examples.romanization: jamkkan nagatda wanneunde geusaie biga wanna bwayo.
examples.en: I just stepped out and back, and it seems it rained in the meantime.
examples.note: 그사이에 = during that short interval; -나 봐요 = it seems

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만났는데 그사이 아이가 많이 컸네요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane mannanneunde geusai aiga mani keonneyo.
examples.en: It's been a while since I saw them, and the child has grown so much in the meantime.
examples.note: 그사이 stressing change over the gap

examples.ko: 제가 자리를 비운 그사이에 무슨 일 있었어요?
examples.romanization: jega jarireul biun geusaie museun il isseosseoyo?
examples.en: Did something happen while I was away?
examples.note: 그사이에 = in the gap when one was absent

entries.nuance: 그사이 (그 'that' + 사이 'gap/interval'; also written spaced as 그 사이) means 'in the meantime / during that interval' — the gap between two moments, typically while someone was away or time quietly slipped past, and it very often appears as 그사이에 alongside a remark about unexpected change. The contrast to lock in is 그사이 vs 그동안: 그동안 covers a longer, continuous stretch ('all this while, over the whole period' — 그동안 잘 지냈어요?), whereas 그사이 zooms in on a shorter in-between gap, often surprisingly eventful for its brevity. The main English-speaker pitfalls: (1) reaching for 그동안 when you mean a brief 'while I was gone' gap (use 그사이) or vice versa; and (2) spelling worry — both 그사이 (one word) and 그 사이 (spaced) are accepted, so just stay consistent within your text rather than agonizing over it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap 그사이 (a short in-between gap) for 그동안 (the whole continuous stretch up to now); '그동안 잘 지냈어요?' asks about the long period, not a brief gap.
그사이 marks an interval between two points, so it needs that two-point framing; using it for an open-ended 'these days' (요즘) is wrong.
Both 그사이 and 그 사이 are accepted spellings; pick one and stay consistent rather than mixing them in the same piece of writing.

entries.english: (the old) days, one's time/era of life
entries.shortExplanation: 시절 means "(the old) days, one's time/era of life" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 시절 (sijeol) = "(the old) days, one's time/era of life". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 학창 시절 ("one's school days") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시절, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the most common collocation, full of nostalgia
어린 시절의 추억 = childhood memories
refers fondly to a remembered period
pairs with 좋은/힘든 to color the remembered period

examples.en: I sometimes miss my school days so much.
examples.note: 학창 시절 = one's school years; 그립다 = to miss/long for

examples.en: In my childhood, I grew up in the countryside.
examples.note: 어린 시절에(는) = during one's young days

examples.en: In those days everyone was poor but happy.
examples.note: 그 시절 evoking a nostalgic era; -지만 = but

entries.nuance: 시절 is Sino-Korean (時節, 時 'time' + 節 'season/segment', literally a 'season of time'), and it names a remembered stage of one's life almost always tinged with nostalgia — 학창 시절 (school days), 어린 시절 (childhood), 그 시절 (those days). The contrast to feel is 시절 vs 시기 and 때: 시기 is a neutral, analytical phase (성장 시기 = the growth period) and 때 is a plain 'time when…,' whereas 시절 is warm, personal and backward-looking, glowing with fondness. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 시절 looks back — you cannot use it for a future or coolly neutral period, so 'a difficult time ahead' is not 어려운 시절 in the future sense; and (2) 시절 almost always rides on a descriptor (학창/어린/그/좋은), so using it bare to mean just 'time' sounds unfinished — you need that modifier to evoke the remembered stage.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
시절 is nostalgic and backward-looking; don't use it for a future or coolly neutral period (use 시기 for a neutral phase, 때 for a plain 'time when').
시절 normally follows a descriptor (학창/어린/그/좋은 시절); using it bare to mean just 'a time' sounds incomplete.
Don't confuse 시절 (a remembered life-stage) with 계절 (季節, the four seasons); they share 節 but 계절 means spring/summer/autumn/winter.

entries.shortExplanation: 사실 means "fact, truth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사실 (sasil) means "fact, truth". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사실은 제가 한국 사람이 아니에요. ("Actually, I am not Korean."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 사실은 at the very front softens an honest reveal, like English 'actually'
사실 + 이에요 asserts something is objectively true
사실대로 = 'as it really is'; the suffix -대로 means 'in accordance with'

usagePhrases.en: I want to know the truth.
usagePhrases.note: 사실 as the object of a verb takes 을

examples.ko: 사실 저는 매운 음식을 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: sasil jeoneun maeun eumsigeul mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: Actually, I cannot eat spicy food.
examples.note: Bare 사실 (no 은) at sentence start = a casual 'to be honest' before a confession

examples.en: This story is not true.
examples.note: 사실이 아니다 is the set phrase for 'is not true / is false'

examples.ko: 사실은 오늘 그 얘기를 하려고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: sasireun oneul geu yaegireul haryeogo wasseoyo.
examples.en: The truth is, I came today to talk about that.
examples.note: 사실은 + a -려고 왔어요 clause reveals a hidden real reason behind an action

entries.nuance: 사실 (事實, 事 'matter' + 實 'real/true') literally means 'the real state of a matter', so it covers both the noun 'fact' and the adverb 'actually/in fact'. Compare it with 진실: 사실 is a neutral, verifiable fact ('it rained yesterday'), while 진실 is the deeper moral 'truth' you uncover behind lies, so a courtroom seeks 진실, but a weather report states a 사실. Also distinguish 진짜, which is the casual spoken 'really/for real' and an intensifier ('진짜 맛있어!'), whereas 사실 introduces information. The phrase 사실은 / 사실 at the head of a sentence is enormously common in conversation as a gentle 'to tell the truth' before a correction or confession. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 사실 to mean 'really' as an intensity word — '진짜 추워요' (it's really cold) is natural, but '사실 추워요' shifts the meaning to 'actually, it's cold (contrary to what you thought)'. Keep 사실 for facts and reveals, not for emphasis.

Using 사실 as an intensifier like English 'really' (e.g. saying 사실 맛있어요 hoping for 'it's really tasty'). That actually means 'in fact it's tasty (surprisingly)'. For pure emphasis use 진짜 or 정말: 정말 맛있어요.
Saying 사실 아니에요 to mean 'that's not true'. The natural set phrase needs the subject particle: 사실이 아니에요. Dropping 이 sounds broken.
Confusing 사실 with 진실 and using 사실 for a profound, hidden truth. A detective uncovers the 진실; a footnote states a 사실.

entries.shortExplanation: 비밀 means "secret" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "secret" is 비밀 (bimil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이것은 비밀이에요. ("This is a secret."). Watch the particle attached to 비밀 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 비밀 + 이에요 labels information as private
비밀을 지키다 = 'protect/guard a secret', the standard collocation
비밀이 없다 with the subject particle states you hide nothing
비밀로 하다 = 'treat it as secret'; -로 marks the resulting state

examples.en: I told my friend a secret.
examples.note: 한테 marks the human recipient you told it to

examples.en: That is a secret just between us.
examples.note: 우리만의 = 'ours only'; -만의 stacks 'only' + possessive

examples.en: This is a secret only you and I know.
examples.note: Casual 반말 register with friends; 너랑 나만 = 'only you and me'

entries.nuance: 비밀 (祕密, 祕 'hidden/mysterious' + 密 'dense/close') paints a secret as something kept tightly closed in. The verb it lives with is 지키다 ('to guard/keep'), giving 비밀을 지키다 — note that English 'keep a secret' tempts learners to reach for 가지다 ('to have/hold'), but 비밀을 가지다 sounds wrong; you 지키다 (guard) a secret, or 비밀로 하다 (make it secret). Contrast 비밀 with 비결: both share 비(祕), but 비결 (祕訣) is a 'secret know-how / the trick to success' (성공의 비결 = the secret to success), not confidential information. So a chef's 비결 is their technique, while their 비밀 might be that they hate cooking. The word is register-neutral and used freely from children's games to government affairs. Pitfall to avoid: 비밀 is a noun only — there is no verb 비밀하다. To say 'keep something secret' you must add a verb: 비밀로 하다 or 비밀을 지키다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 비밀 as a verb: 비밀해요 does not exist. Use 비밀로 해요 (make it secret) or 비밀을 지켜요 (keep the secret).
Saying 비밀을 가지다 by translating 'have/keep a secret' literally. Korean guards a secret: 비밀을 지키다. To say you simply possess secrets, use 비밀이 있다 / 없다.
Mixing up 비밀 (confidential info) and 비결 (the secret trick/know-how). 'The secret to long life' is 장수의 비결, not 장수의 비밀.

entries.shortExplanation: 규칙 means "rule" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 규칙 (gyuchik) = "rule". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 규칙은 아주 중요해요. ("Rules are very important.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 규칙, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 규칙은 sets 'rules' as the topic being discussed
규칙을 지키다 = 'observe/abide by rules', the core collocation
규칙이 많다 describes a place full of rules
규칙을 만들다 = 'create a rule'

examples.en: I follow the school rules well.
examples.note: 규칙 takes a noun modifier directly: 학교 규칙 = school rules

examples.en: Each company has different rules.
examples.note: -마다 = 'each/every'; pairs naturally with 다르다

examples.en: If you break the rule, you have to pay a fine.
examples.note: 규칙을 어기다 = 'break a rule', the antonym of 지키다

entries.nuance: 규칙 (規則, 規 'compass/standard' + 則 'rule') evokes a measured standard you align to, and its life-partner verbs are 지키다 ('keep/observe') and its opposite 어기다 ('break/violate'). The sharp contrast learners need is 규칙 vs 법: 규칙 is a rule set by a group, school, or game (게임 규칙, 교통 규칙), enforceable socially, while 법 (法) is the law of the land, enforced by the state with courts and penalties. Breaking a 규칙 gets you scolded; breaking a 법 gets you arrested. Also distinguish 규칙 from 규정 (規定), which are formal written 'regulations/provisions' in an official document — a workplace handbook lists 규정, but a casual house rule is a 규칙. Collocations: 규칙을 정하다 (set rules), 규칙대로 하다 (do it by the rules). Pitfall: English 'follow the rules' often becomes 규칙을 따라가다 by literal translation, but the idiomatic verb is 지키다 — 규칙을 지키다. Save 따르다/따라가다 for following a person or path.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 규칙을 따라가다 for 'follow the rules' by direct translation. The natural verb is 지키다: 규칙을 지키다. 따라가다 means physically following someone.
Confusing 규칙 (a group/game rule) with 법 (state law). Traffic etiquette taught at school is 교통 규칙; the criminal code is 법.
Saying 규칙을 부수다 ('smash a rule') for 'break a rule'. To violate a rule, use 어기다: 규칙을 어기다. 부수다 is for breaking physical objects.

entries.shortExplanation: 습관 means "habit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 습관 (seupgwan) means "habit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이것은 좋은 습관이에요. ("This is a good habit."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 습관 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 좋은/나쁜 + 습관 describes the quality of a habit

usagePhrases.en: I want to fix a bad habit.
usagePhrases.note: 습관을 고치다 = 'correct/break a habit'; 고치다 = repair
습관이 되다 = 'turn into a habit', now automatic

usagePhrases.en: I have a habit of going to bed early.
usagePhrases.note: verb + -는 + 습관이 있다 = 'have the habit of ~ing'

examples.en: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
examples.note: -는 습관이 있다 is the frame for stating any routine

examples.en: I changed my coffee-drinking habit.
examples.note: 습관을 바꾸다 = 'change a habit' (swap it), milder than 고치다

examples.en: I can't break my nail-biting habit.
examples.note: Here a small bad tic is a 버릇, not 습관 — note the register difference

entries.nuance: 습관 (習慣, 習 'to practice/learn' + 慣 'to grow accustomed') frames a habit as something drilled in until it feels natural, and it leans slightly formal and neutral. The key contrast is 습관 vs 버릇: 습관 is a broad, often deliberate routine (early rising, daily exercise, good study habits), while 버릇 is colloquial and usually a quirky or annoying unconscious tic — nail-biting, leg-shaking, a child's bad manners. Crucially, scolding a child you say 버릇없다 ('has no manners / is rude'), never 습관없다. Both pair with 고치다 ('fix') for breaking them and 들이다/생기다 for forming them (습관을 들이다 = cultivate a habit; 습관이 생기다 = a habit forms). To say you have one, use 습관이 있다. Pitfall: English 'I have a habit of doing X' must use the verb's -는 present-modifier form before 습관: 일찍 자는 습관 (the habit of sleeping early), not 일찍 자기 습관. Also do not use 가지다 here — habits 있다/되다/생기다, they are not 'had' with 가지다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forming 'have a habit of ~ing' wrongly: 운동하기 습관 is broken. Use the -는 modifier: 운동하는 습관이 있어요.
Using 습관 for a child's rudeness. 'That kid is rude/ill-mannered' is 그 아이는 버릇이 없어요, not 습관이 없어요.
Saying 습관을 가지고 있어요 by translating 'have a habit'. The idiomatic verb is 있다 or 되다: 습관이 있어요 / 습관이 됐어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 성격 means "personality" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "personality" is 성격 (seonggyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 제 성격은 조용해요. ("My personality is quiet."). Watch the particle attached to 성격 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 성격은 + adjective describes a fixed trait
성격이 좋다 = 'is good-natured/easygoing', a common compliment
성격이 비슷하다 compares two people's natures
밝다 ('bright') applied to 성격 = cheerful and warm

examples.en: My friend has a very lively personality.
examples.note: 활발하다 ('active, lively') is a stock 성격 adjective

examples.en: Because our personalities differ, we sometimes argue.
examples.note: -아서/어서 links the trait to its consequence

examples.en: I'm impatient by nature.
examples.note: 성격이 급하다 = a fixed temperament; contrast with the mood word 기분

entries.nuance: 성격 (性格, 性 'nature/disposition' + 格 'character/frame') is a person's enduring inborn character — the stable temperament you are born with and keep for life. Contrast it carefully with 기분, which is a passing mood that changes hourly: '오늘 기분이 좋아요' = I'm in a good mood today (temporary), whereas '성격이 좋아요' = he's a good-natured person (permanent). Mixing these is the single most common error: never use 성격 for how you feel right now. The phrase 성격이 좋다 is a warm social compliment meaning kind, tolerant, easy to get along with — broader than English 'good personality'. Note also 성격이 급하다 ('impatient/hot-tempered nature') is an idiomatic fixed expression. Common partner adjectives: 밝다 (cheerful), 활발하다 (lively), 조용하다 (quiet), 까다롭다 (fussy/picky), 무뚝뚝하다 (blunt). Pitfall beyond the 기분 trap: 'I have a ~ personality' is most naturally 성격이 + adjective (성격이 밝아요), not the heavier 저는 ~한 성격을 가지고 있어요 calque, though 급한 성격이에요 is fine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 성격 for a temporary mood: 오늘 성격이 좋아요 wrongly says 'my permanent character is good today'. For mood use 기분: 오늘 기분이 좋아요.
Calquing 'have a good personality' as 성격을 가지고 있어요. Korean states it with an adjective: 성격이 좋아요 or 성격이 밝아요.
Confusing 성격 with 성질. 성질 also means temperament but skews negative/temper-flare ('성질을 내다' = lose one's temper). To neutrally describe character, use 성격.

entries.shortExplanation: 능력 means "ability" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 능력 (neungnyeok) = "ability". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그분은 능력이 있어요. ("That person is capable.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 능력, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 능력이 있다 = 'has ability', i.e. is competent

usagePhrases.en: I want to build up my ability.
usagePhrases.note: 능력을 키우다 = 'grow/develop ability' over time
능력이 부족하다 = a humble admission of falling short
noun + 능력 names a specific competence: 언어 능력 = language ability

examples.en: That person's work ability is outstanding.
examples.note: -는 능력 = 'the ability to ~'; 뛰어나다 = excel

examples.en: I'm building up my Korean ability.
examples.note: Ongoing -고 있다 with the develop verb 키우다

examples.en: Effort matters more than ability.
examples.note: 능력보다 = 'compared to ability'; -보다 marks the standard

entries.nuance: 능력 (能力, 能 'can/be able' + 力 'power/force') is literally 'the power to be able' — innate or acquired capability to actually get things done, broader and more practical than book knowledge. Its verbs are 있다/없다 (have/lack), 키우다 ('raise/develop'), and 기르다 (cultivate). Contrast 능력 with 실력: 실력 is demonstrated skill/proficiency in a specific domain that you trained for (그 선수는 실력이 좋다 = that player is genuinely skilled), while 능력 is overall capacity, including raw potential and the power to handle responsibility. A new hire may have 능력 (capability/potential) but not yet 실력 (proven skill). Also distinguish 가능성 ('possibility'), which is the abstract noun 가능 + 성 — a chance that something happens, not a person's power. Pitfall: English 'I'm able to ~ / I can ~' should not be forced through 능력. To say 'I can swim', use the verb pattern 수영할 수 있어요, not 수영 능력이 있어요 (which sounds like a formal assessment). Reserve 능력 for describing overall competence, not everyday 'can do'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 능력 to express everyday 'I can ~'. '저는 능력이 운전해요' is wrong. Use -ㄹ 수 있다: 운전할 수 있어요. 능력 describes capacity, not a single action.
Confusing 능력 with 가능 / 가능성. 'There's a possibility of rain' is 비가 올 가능성이 있어요, never 능력. 능력 belongs to people's competence.
Mixing 능력 and 실력. To praise proven, trained skill say 실력이 좋다; 능력이 좋다 emphasizes overall capability and potential.

entries.shortExplanation: 실수 means "mistake" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 실수 (silsu) means "mistake". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 실수했어요. ("I made a mistake."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 실수 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 실수하다 = 'to slip up'; the noun + 하다 acts as one verb
실수 + 예요 to own up to an error

usagePhrases.en: I make a lot of mistakes.
usagePhrases.note: 실수가 많다 describes a tendency, not one event
실수를 하다 split out, with the negative command -지 마세요

examples.en: I made a mistake at work today.
examples.note: Everyday accidental slip; 실수를 하다 with location 에서

examples.en: It's a small mistake, so it's fine.
examples.note: -니까 gives the reason for reassurance

examples.ko: 깜빡하고 이름을 잘못 썼어요. 제 실수예요.
examples.romanization: kkamppakago ireumeul jalmot sseosseoyo. je silsuyeyo.
examples.en: I spaced out and wrote the name wrong. My mistake.
examples.note: Real apology context — 실수 fits an honest, blameless slip

entries.nuance: 실수 (失手, 失 'to lose' + 手 'hand') literally means 'to lose control of one's hand' — a slip, a careless unintended error, with no moral blame attached. This is the crucial contrast with 잘못 (잘 'well' + 못 'cannot'), which means a 'wrong/fault' that carries responsibility or wrongdoing: 실수 is 'oops, I tripped on the word', while 잘못 implies 'I did something wrong and it's my fault'. When you bump someone you say 실수예요 ('sorry, my slip'); when you genuinely wronged them you admit 제 잘못이에요. Also distinguish 실패 ('failure'), which is not achieving a goal, versus 실수, a momentary error along the way — you can make a 실수 and still succeed. The verb is 하다 (실수하다), and a frequent collocation is 실수로 ('by accident/mistake': 실수로 전화했어요 = I called by mistake). Pitfall: English speakers say 실수를 만들다 ('make a mistake') by translating 'make' literally — Korean does not 만들다 (build) a mistake, it 하다 (does) one: 실수를 하다 / 실수하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 실수를 만들다 for 'make a mistake', copying English 'make'. The verb is 하다: 실수했어요 or 실수를 했어요.
Using 실수 when you mean genuine fault or wrongdoing. A blameless slip is 실수; an actual wrong you're responsible for is 잘못 — 제 잘못이에요 for a real apology.
Confusing 실수 with 실패. Forgetting one line is a 실수 (a slip); not passing the whole exam is 실패 (a failure). They are not interchangeable.

entries.shortExplanation: 성공 means "success" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "success" is 성공 (seonggong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 성공했어요. ("I succeeded."). Watch the particle attached to 성공 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 성공하다 = 'to succeed'; noun + 하다 forms the verb
성공이 + adjective treats success as the topic
성공하다 + -고 싶다 to state an aspiration
성공하다 takes 에 for the field you succeed IN, not 을

examples.en: After long effort, I finally succeeded.
examples.note: -끝에 = 'at the end of ~'; pairs with effort then success

examples.en: To succeed, you must keep trying.
examples.note: -려면 = 'if you want to ~'; sets up advice

examples.en: I'm so happy I passed the exam.
examples.note: For passing a test Koreans say 합격, not 성공 — note the boundary

entries.nuance: 성공 (成功, 成 'to accomplish' + 功 'achievement/merit') means achieving a goal or making it big in life, and its verb is 하다 (성공하다), the natural antonym of 실패하다 ('to fail'). A grammar point English speakers stumble on: 성공하다 governs the particle 에 (or 에서) for the domain — 사업에 성공하다 ('succeed in business'), 시험에 성공하다 is odd; you say 시험에 합격하다 instead. This is the sharp contrast: 합격 (合格) is specifically 'passing' an exam, audition, or qualification screening, while 성공 is broad life or project success. Passing the bar exam is 합격; building a thriving company is 성공. Both differ from 성취 (成就), the more literary 'accomplishment/attainment' of a personal achievement. Common collocations: 크게 성공하다 (make it big), 성공을 거두다 (achieve success, formal/written). Pitfall: do not pair 성공하다 with the object particle 을/를 for the thing you succeed at — it's 에 (시험에 합격, 사업에 성공). And use 합격, not 성공, the moment you mean passing a test.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시험을 성공했어요 for 'I passed the exam'. Use 합격: 시험에 합격했어요. 성공 is for broad goals/business, not test results.
Marking the domain with 을/를: 사업을 성공했어요 is wrong. 성공하다 takes 에: 사업에 성공했어요.
Treating 성공 as the opposite of 실수. Its true antonym is 실패 (failure). A 실수 is a small slip, not the opposite of success.

entries.shortExplanation: 실패 means "failure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 실패 (silpae) = "failure". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 실패했어요. ("I failed.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 실패, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 실패하다 = 'to fail (at a goal)'; noun + 하다
실패는 as topic, softening the concept
실패를 두려워하다 = 'fear failure'; 두려워하다 takes 를
실패하다 takes 에 for the area you failed in

examples.en: At first I failed, but I challenged it again.
examples.note: -지만 = 'but'; 도전하다 (take on) fits the resilience tone

examples.en: I learned a lot from failure.
examples.note: 실패에서 = 'from failure'; 에서 marks the source

examples.en: It's okay to fail, so give it a try.
examples.note: -아도 괜찮다 ('even if ~, it's fine') is gentle encouragement

entries.nuance: 실패 (失敗, 失 'to lose' + 敗 'defeat') literally 'to lose and be defeated' — the failure to reach a goal, the clean antonym of 성공 (성공 ↔ 실패). Like 성공하다, the verb 실패하다 governs the particle 에 for the domain: 사업에 실패하다 ('fail in business'), 시험에 실패했어요 is possible but Koreans far more often say 시험에 떨어졌어요 ('I fell off the exam' = flunked) for not passing. That is the contrast to master: 실패 is broad, often big-picture failure, while 떨어지다 is the everyday idiom for failing a test or audition (the opposite of 합격). The big distinction for learners is 실패 vs 실수: 실수 (失手) is a small careless slip you make in passing, whereas 실패 is the larger non-achievement of an outcome — you can commit many 실수 and still avoid 실패. Koreans use 실패 warmly in encouragement: 실패는 성공의 어머니 ('failure is the mother of success'). Pitfall: like 성공, do not use 을/를 for the domain — 사업을 실패했어요 is wrong; it's 사업에 실패했어요. And for flunking a test, prefer 떨어지다 over 실패.

Using 을/를 for the area of failure: 사업을 실패했어요 is wrong. The particle is 에: 사업에 실패했어요.
Saying 시험에 실패했어요 for 'I failed the exam'. Far more natural is 시험에 떨어졌어요. Reserve 실패 for broader goals/projects.
Confusing 실패 (a failed outcome) with 실수 (a momentary slip). Forgetting your lines is a 실수; the whole project not working out is a 실패.

entries.shortExplanation: 노력 means "effort" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 노력 (noryeok) means "effort". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노력이 중요해요. ("Effort is important."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노력 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 노력이 + adjective frames effort as the topic

usagePhrases.en: I make an effort every day.
usagePhrases.note: 노력하다 = 'to make an effort/try hard'; noun + 하다

usagePhrases.en: I put in a lot of effort.
usagePhrases.note: 노력을 하다 split out, with 많이 = 'a lot'

usagePhrases.en: If you try hard, you can do well.
usagePhrases.note: 노력하다 + -면 conditional offering encouragement

examples.en: I'm making an effort to learn Korean.
examples.note: -려고 = 'in order to'; the goal you exert effort toward

examples.en: Without effort, there is no success either.
examples.note: 없이는 = 'without ~ (emphatic)'; a common motivational pairing

examples.en: Let's try a little harder.
examples.note: 반말 자기 격려 / friends; 노력해 보다 = 'try making an effort'

entries.nuance: 노력 (努力, 努 'to strive/exert' + 力 'power/strength') is literally 'to put forth strength' — sustained, earnest effort toward a goal, a warm and admired virtue in Korean culture where 노력하는 사람 ('a person who tries hard') is high praise. Its verb is 하다 (노력하다), and the most natural way to say 'try to do X' is verb-려고 노력하다 (배우려고 노력하다 = make an effort to learn). Contrast 노력 with 애 (애쓰다 = 'to take pains/struggle to do something'): 애쓰다 highlights the toil and is used to thank someone — 애쓰셨어요 ('you worked hard / thanks for your trouble') — while 노력 is the neutral noun for effort itself. Do not confuse 노력 with 노동 (勞動), which is physical 'labor/work' as in a job or workforce. Also distinguish 수고 (受苦), the 'trouble/hard work' you acknowledge in others: 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work'). Pitfall: 노력하다 is intransitive toward a goal — to say 'try TO do something' use the -려고 노력하다 frame, not a direct object; '한국어를 노력해요' is incomplete — say 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요 or 한국어 공부를 열심히 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 노력 (effort/striving) with 노동 (manual labor). 'Hard work pays off' is 노력은 배신하지 않아요; a labor union is 노동조합 — never swap them.
Saying 한국어를 노력해요 to mean 'I try at Korean'. 노력하다 needs a goal clause: 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요.
Using 노력하세요 to thank someone for their hard work. To acknowledge effort, say 수고하셨어요 or 애쓰셨어요; 노력하세요 means 'go try hard (a command)'.

entries.shortExplanation: 차이 means "difference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "difference" is 차이 (chai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 차이가 커요. ("The difference is big."). Watch the particle attached to 차이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 차이가 크다 = 'the gap is large'; 차이 pairs with size adjectives
차이가 있다 = 'there is a difference (between)'

usagePhrases.en: I can't really tell the difference.
usagePhrases.note: 차이를 모르다 with -겠- softening to 'I'm not sure'
noun + 차이: 나이 차이 = age difference/gap

examples.en: Korean and Japanese have differences.
examples.note: A와 B는 차이가 있다 is the frame for comparing two things

examples.en: The price difference is too big.
examples.note: 가격 차이 (price gap); 크다 expresses the magnitude

examples.en: The two look similar, but they do differ.
examples.note: 차이가 나다 = 'a difference arises/shows'; 나다 = to occur

entries.nuance: 차이 (差異, 差 'to differ' + 異 'different/unlike') is the noun 'difference/gap' between two or more things, and it lives with two verbs: 있다 ('there is a difference') and 나다 ('a difference arises/shows') — 차이가 있다 and 차이가 나다 are both natural, the latter stressing that a gap becomes apparent. It also pairs with size adjectives: 차이가 크다/적다 (big/small difference). The contrast to learn is the noun 차이 vs the verb 다르다 ('to be different'): 차이 names the gap as a thing ('there is a difference'), while 다르다 is how you actually say two things 'are different' — '한국어는 일본어와 달라요' (Korean is different from Japanese). English speakers often try to turn 차이 into the predicate ('they are difference'), but you need either 차이가 있다 (noun) or 다르다 (adjective-verb). Also distinguish 차이 (the gap itself) from 차이점 (the specific point/respect in which they differ): 두 제품의 차이점을 알려 주세요 = tell me the specific differences. Pitfall: do not say 차이해요 — 차이 has no verb form; use 차이가 나다/있다 or switch to 다르다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Trying to use 차이 as a verb/predicate: 두 개가 차이해요 is wrong. Say 차이가 있어요 / 차이가 나요, or use the adjective 달라요.
Marking what differs FROM with the wrong particle when using 다르다. 'A is different from B' uses 와/과: A는 B와 달라요, not B를 달라요.
Confusing 차이 (the gap) with 차이점 (the specific differing points). 'List the differences' = 차이점을 알려 주세요; '차이가 크다' is about overall magnitude.

entries.shortExplanation: 전부 means "all, everything" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전부 (jeonbu) = "all, everything". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이게 전부예요? ("Is this everything?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전부, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Asking if nothing remains
전부 paired with 다 doubles the emphasis
전부 here works as an adverb 'completely'
전부 = 'entirely', taking the whole blame

examples.en: I'll give you all the snacks.
examples.note: Casual 반말; 전부 as the object 'the whole lot'

examples.en: All the guests left.
examples.note: 전부 covers every single person in the group

examples.en: I will double-check whether all the supplies have been packed.
examples.note: Formal register; 전부 as adverb "all", with everyday vocabulary

entries.nuance: 전부 is the Sino-Korean noun 全部 ('whole' 全 + 'part' 部, literally 'the whole of every part'), meaning the complete quantity with absolutely nothing left out. The nearest rival is the native word 다: 다 is a pure adverb ('all' / 'completely') and never takes a particle, while 전부 is a noun that can be a subject (전부가), an object (전부를), or stand adverbially — and the two are so close that Koreans habitually stack them as 전부 다 for extra force. Watch the dividing line with 모두: 모두 leans toward 'everyone, every person' and is a touch more formal, whereas 전부 leans toward 'the whole amount/thing'. 전부 is neutral and works in both casual speech and formal writing. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the English 'all the' that glues onto a noun: you don't say 전부 책 — you say 책 전부 or 모든 책, because 전부 follows the noun (or stands alone) rather than premodifying it like 모든.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 전부 책 ('all books') by copying English 'all the books': 전부 cannot premodify like English 'all'. Use 책 전부 ('the books, all of them') or 모든 책.
Using 전부 when you mean 대부분 ('most'). 전부 leaves out nothing; if a few are excluded, you must say 대부분.
Forcing a particle where 전부 is acting as an adverb, e.g. 전부를 먹었어요 when you just mean 'I ate it all' — 전부 다 먹었어요 is the natural choice.

structuredNuance.t: 전부 means the complete quantity with absolutely nothing left out. It is neutral and works in both casual speech and formal writing.

entries.shortExplanation: 절반 means "half" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 절반 (jeolban) means "half". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사과를 절반 먹었어요. ("I ate half the apple."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 절반 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 절반 = exactly one of two equal parts
절반 attached to a whole via possessive 의
절반 as a topic-marked subject
절반으로 = 'into halves', the division endpoint

examples.en: I'll split the candy in half for you.
examples.note: Casual; 절반 as the shared portion

examples.en: Half of the students passed the exam.
examples.note: 절반이 = half of a group as subject

examples.ko: 모인 돈의 절반 이상을 기부하기로 했습니다.
examples.romanization: moin donui jeolban isangeul gibuhagiro haetseumnida.
examples.en: We decided to donate more than half of the money we collected.
examples.note: Formal register; 절반 + 이상 = "more than half", with everyday vocabulary

entries.nuance: 절반 is Sino-Korean 折半 ('break/fold' 折 + 'half' 半 = literally 'fold something in two'), so it carries the feel of cleanly dividing a whole into two equal portions. Its everyday twin is the one-syllable 반, which is the plain Sino-Korean reading of that same 半: 반 is shorter, more casual, and used constantly (반만 주세요, 반반), whereas the two-character 절반 sounds more deliberate and precise, favored when you're stressing the exactness of the split or writing a report. Note 반 also forms set time expressions (한 시 반 'half past one') and compound words (반값 'half price') where 절반 cannot substitute. Register is neutral; both are fine in polite speech. The English-speaker pitfall is the 'into halves' construction: to say 'cut it in half' you need the goal particle 으로 — 절반으로 자르다 — not a bare noun; learners often drop 으로 and produce the incomplete 절반 잘라요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 절반 잘랐어요 for 'I cut it in half' without the goal particle. Use 절반으로 잘랐어요 — 으로 marks the resulting state.
Using 절반 for a vague 'about half / roughly half'. 절반 is exactly one half; for a rough amount say 반쯤 or 절반쯤.
Swapping 절반 into fixed 반 expressions, e.g. 한 시 절반 for 'half past one'. The set form is 한 시 반.

structuredNuance.t: 절반 carries the feel of cleanly dividing a whole into two equal portions. Register is neutral; it is fine in polite speech, and the two-character form sounds deliberate and precise, favored when stressing the exactness of the split or writing a report.

entries.shortExplanation: 일부 means "part, a portion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "part, a portion" is 일부 (ilbu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일부 사람만 왔어요. ("Only some people came."). Watch the particle attached to 일부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 일부 directly premodifying a noun, unlike 전부

usagePhrases.en: I paid part of the money.
usagePhrases.note: 일부 linked to the whole by 의
일부 + 뿐 = 'merely a portion'
일부 as a topic-marked subject

examples.en: Just take some of this.
examples.note: Casual; 일부만 = 'only a portion'

examples.en: Some of the members opposed the meeting.
examples.note: 일부가 = a subset acting as subject

examples.en: What was reported is only a fraction of the facts.
examples.note: Formal; 일부에 불과하다 = 'is nothing but a part'

entries.nuance: 일부 is Sino-Korean 一部 ('one' 一 + 'part' 部 = 'one portion'), naming a limited slice of a larger whole. It sits on a spectrum: 일부 (a part) < 절반 (half) < 대부분 (most) < 전부 (all), and its sharpest contrast is with 전부 — 일부 deliberately implies the rest is excluded. Unlike 전부, 일부 CAN stand right before a noun (일부 사람 'some people'), which makes it behave a bit like English 'some'. Distinguish it from 약간: 약간 is about a small degree/amount of something (a little salt), while 일부 is a countable sub-section of a defined whole (some of the members). Register is neutral and slightly bookish; it's everywhere in news and reports. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 일부 to translate 'a few' when you really mean a small number of discrete things — for 'a few people' Koreans more often say 몇몇 사람 or 몇 명; 일부 frames them as 'a faction/portion of the whole' rather than just 'a small number'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 일부 when you mean 전부 ('the whole thing'). 일부 always signals a remainder is left out.
Translating 'a few friends' as 일부 친구 in casual talk. More natural is 몇몇 친구 or 친구 몇 명; 일부 sounds like 'a faction of (a known group of) friends'.
Dropping the 의 that links 일부 to its whole, e.g. 돈 일부를 for 'part of the money' — say 돈의 일부를.

entries.shortExplanation: 대부분 means "most, the majority" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 대부분 (daebubun) = "most, the majority". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 대부분 집에 있어요. ("Most people are at home.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 대부분, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 대부분 used adverbially = 'mostly'

usagePhrases.en: Most of the students are Korean.
usagePhrases.note: 대부분이 = subject 'the majority'

usagePhrases.en: Most of the shops are closed.
usagePhrases.note: 대부분의 + noun = 'most (of the)'

usagePhrases.en: I use most of my time studying.
usagePhrases.note: 대부분을 = object 'the greater part'

examples.en: On weekends I mostly rest at home.
examples.note: Casual; 대부분 as adverb 'usually/mostly'

examples.en: Most of the attendees were in favor.
examples.note: 대부분이 marking the majority as subject

examples.ko: 설문에 응답한 사람의 대부분이 긍정적으로 평가했습니다.
examples.romanization: seolmune eungdapan saramui daebubuni geungjeongjeogeuro pyeonggahaetseumnida.
examples.en: Most of the survey respondents rated it positively.
examples.note: Formal report register; 대부분이 with a quantified group

entries.nuance: 대부분 is Sino-Korean 大部分 ('big' 大 + 'part' 部 + 'portion' 分 = 'the large part'), meaning almost all but stopping just short of everything — a small remainder is always implied. On the quantity ladder it sits between 일부 (a portion) and 전부 (the whole), and its key contrast is exactly with 전부: claim 대부분 and you leave a little room, claim 전부 and you leave none. It doubles as an adverb meaning 'mostly/usually' (주말엔 대부분 쉬어요), which 전부 cannot do. entries.shortExplanation: 약간 means "a little, a bit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 약간 (yakgan) means "a little, a bit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 약간 매워요. ("It is a little spicy."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 약간 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 약간 as a degree adverb before an adjective
약간 = a small amount of an uncountable thing
약간의 + noun, the bookish noun use
약간 softening the strength of the state

examples.en: The soup is a bit salty.
examples.note: Casual; 약간 dialing a quality down a notch

examples.en: Please add just a little sugar to my coffee.
examples.note: 약간만 = 'only a little', polite request

examples.en: Sales rose slightly this quarter.
examples.note: Formal; 약간 = 'slightly' with a change verb

entries.nuance: 약간 is Sino-Korean 若干 (here meaning 'some small amount / a few'), used both as a degree adverb ('a little, slightly') and, with 의, as a noun ('a small quantity of'). Its closest rivals are 조금 and 좀: 조금 is the everyday native word for 'a little' and is interchangeable in many spots, while 좀 is the contracted, very colloquial form that also functions as a softener in requests (좀 도와주세요). 약간 sounds a shade more measured and is the default when describing a slight degree of a quality (약간 맵다, 약간 다르다) or a small change in formal/written contexts (약간 증가하다). Note it covers small DEGREE and small AMOUNT, unlike 일부, which is a sub-portion of a countable whole. The English-speaker pitfall is putting 약간 after the verb or treating it like a quantity noun on its own: it normally comes right before the adjective/verb it scales (약간 추워요), and when it modifies a noun you need 약간의 (약간의 돈), not a bare 약간 돈.

Using 약간 for a large quantity. It always means 'a little/slightly'; for a big amount use 많이 or 상당히.
Writing 약간 돈 for 'a little money'. To modify a noun use 약간의 돈, or rephrase as 돈을 약간 (with a verb).
Confusing it with 일부: 약간 맵다 ('slightly spicy', degree) is fine, but for 'some of the members' you need 일부, not 약간.

entries.shortExplanation: 여러 means "several, various" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "several, various" is 여러 (yeoreo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 여러 사람이 왔어요. ("Several people came."). Watch the particle attached to 여러 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 여러 must sit directly before the noun
여러 + counter 번 = 'several times'
여러 가지 = 'various kinds of'
여러 stressing variety, not just number

examples.en: Several friends came over.
examples.note: Casual; 여러 명 = 'several people' with a counter

examples.en: Several problems came up at once.
examples.note: 여러 + plural noun as subject

examples.ko: 이 사안은 여러 부서가 함께 논의해야 합니다.
examples.romanization: i saaneun yeoreo buseoga hamkke nonuihaeya hamnida.
examples.en: This matter must be discussed jointly by several departments.
examples.note: Formal; 여러 emphasizing multiple distinct parties

entries.nuance: 여러 is a native determiner (관형사) meaning 'several / various / a number of', and its defining trait is that it ONLY ever stands in front of a noun — it can never be a subject, object, or stand alone, and it never takes a particle (no 여러가, no 여러를). Its nearest neighbors are 몇 and 여러 가지: 몇 means 'a few / how many' and asks or implies a small uncertain count (몇 명?), while 여러 asserts 'quite a few, more than two or three' and often adds a flavor of 'various, of different sorts'. For countable people/things you pair it with a counter (여러 명, 여러 번, 여러 개); for 'various kinds' you say 여러 가지. Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall is trying to use 여러 the way you'd use the noun 'several' in 'several came' — Korean cannot say 여러가 왔어요; you must supply a noun, e.g. 여러 사람이 왔어요 or 여러 명이 왔어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 여러 alone as a subject/object, e.g. 여러가 왔어요. 여러 must modify a noun: 여러 사람이 왔어요.
Attaching a particle to 여러 (여러를, 여러가). It's a determiner and takes none; particles go on the noun after it.
Confusing 여러 with 몇: 여러 번 = 'several (many) times' asserts a fair number, while 몇 번 = 'a few / how many times' is small or questioning.

entries.shortExplanation: 수량 means "quantity, amount" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수량 (suryang) = "quantity, amount". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수량이 부족해요. ("The quantity is not enough.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수량, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 수량 as subject in a stock context
수량 = the counted number of items
수량 stated with a number + counter
수량 paired with 많다, not 크다

examples.en: Count the quantity of these for me.
examples.note: Casual; 수량 = how many pieces

examples.ko: 재고 수량이 부족해서 주문할 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: jaego suryangi bujokaeseo jumunhal su eopseoyo.
examples.en: We can't order because the stock quantity is low.
examples.note: 재고 수량 = 'stock quantity', everyday store talk

examples.ko: 주문 수량을 정확히 기재해 주시기 바랍니다.
examples.romanization: jumun suryangeul jeonghwaki gijaehae jusigi baramnida.
examples.en: Please state the order quantity accurately.
examples.note: Formal; 주문 수량 = 'order quantity' on a form

entries.nuance: 수량 is Sino-Korean 數量 ('number' 數 + 'amount' 量 = 'numbered amount'), and it specifically means a COUNTABLE number of discrete items — it lives in shopping, ordering, inventory, and shipping contexts. Compare 양 (量) alone, which means 'amount' in a broader, often uncountable sense (물의 양 'the amount of water', 일의 양 'the amount of work'); you would not say 물의 수량. Compare also 개수 (個數), which narrowly means 'the number of pieces' and is even more strictly about a count, while 수량 can feel a touch more formal/commercial. Because 수량 is about number, it pairs with 많다/적다 ('many/few'), not 크다/작다 ('big/small'). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping the English 'amount' (which English uses for both countable and uncountable) onto 수량 across the board — for liquids, time, work, or emotion you need 양, and for water specifically 물의 수량 sounds wrong; say 물의 양.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 수량 for uncountable things (water, time, work, feelings). Those take 양: 물의 양, 일의 양 — not 수량.
Pairing 수량 with 크다/작다. Since it's a count, use 수량이 많다/적다 ('the quantity is large/small').
Confusing 수량 with 수: bare 수 means 'number' abstractly (학생 수 'number of students'), while 수량 implies a counted stock or order amount.

entries.shortExplanation: 단위 means "unit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 단위 (danwi) means "unit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 단위가 달라요. ("The unit is different."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단위 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 단위 as subject = unit of measure
무게 단위 = 'unit of weight'
단위 naming the measuring standard

usagePhrases.en: It's sold in units of a thousand won.
usagePhrases.note: 단위로 = 'in/by units of'

examples.en: The unit of length is the meter.
examples.note: Casual; 단위 naming a standard measure

examples.ko: 이 약은 한 알 단위로 처방돼요.
examples.romanization: i yageun han al danwiro cheobangdwaeyo.
examples.en: This medicine is prescribed by the pill.
examples.note: 단위로 = 'by the unit of', one pill at a time

examples.ko: 보고서의 금액은 백만 원 단위로 표기되어 있습니다.
examples.romanization: bogoseoui geumaegeun baengman won danwiro pyogidoeeo itseumnida.
examples.en: The figures in the report are shown in units of one million won.
examples.note: Formal; 백만 원 단위 = 'million-won units'

entries.nuance: 단위 is Sino-Korean 單位 ('single' 單 + 'position/rank' 位 = 'a single standard place'), meaning a unit of measurement (meter, kilogram, won) and, by extension, the basic block by which something is counted or grouped (가족 단위 'by household', 학년 단위 'by grade'). Its crucial contrast is with 수량: 단위 is the YARDSTICK (kg, m), while 수량 is the COUNT you get when you measure (열 개, 5킬로그램). Don't confuse it either with 단계 ('stage/step', 段階), which sounds similar but means a phase in a process. A very productive pattern is 단위로 ('in/by units of') — 천 원 단위로, 시간 단위로 ('by the hour'). Register is neutral to formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 단위 for the counted amount itself: English 'a unit of three' tempts learners to say 단위 for the quantity, but the number is 수량/개수 and 단위 only names the measuring standard or grouping.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 단위 (the measuring standard, e.g. kg) with 수량 (the counted amount, e.g. 5 of them).
Mixing up 단위 with 단계 ('stage/step'). They look alike but 단계 is about phases in a process, not measurement.
Dropping the 로 in the 'by units of' pattern, e.g. 천 원 단위 팔아요 — say 천 원 단위로 팔아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 두께 means "thickness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "thickness" is 두께 (dukke). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 두께가 얇아요. ("The thickness is thin."). Watch the particle attached to 두께 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 두께 with 얇다, the matched adjective
두께 = the front-to-back dimension
두께 stated with a value
두께 paired with 두껍다

examples.ko: 이 이불 두께 좀 봐, 엄청 두꺼워.
examples.romanization: i ibul dukke jom bwa, eomcheong dukkeowo.
examples.en: Look how thick this blanket is.
examples.note: Casual; 두께 with 두껍다 for a thick object

examples.ko: 벽의 두께가 두꺼워서 소리가 안 들려요.
examples.romanization: byeogui dukkega dukkeowoseo soriga an deullyeoyo.
examples.en: The wall is so thick that sound doesn't pass through.
examples.note: 두께 explaining a real consequence

examples.en: This glass was made with a thickness of 5 millimeters.
examples.note: Formal; 두께 with a precise measurement

entries.nuance: 두께 is a native noun built from the adjective 두껍다 ('thick') plus the nominalizing suffix -이/-께, and it names the front-to-back dimension of a flat or layered object — paper, a wall, fabric, glass, a steak. Its matched adjectives are 두껍다 ('thick') and 얇다 ('thin'), and a frequent trap is reaching for the wrong 'thick': 두껍다 is for flat/layered things (두꺼운 책), while 굵다 ('thick/stout') is for long round things like rope, fingers, or tree trunks — so a thick rope is 굵은 줄, never 두꺼운 줄. Keep 두께 separate from the other -이 measurement nouns: 길이 (length), 높이 (height), 넓이 (area), 깊이 (depth). Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'thick' covers both flat things and round things, so learners over-apply 두께/두껍다 to ropes, wires, and noodles, where Koreans switch to 굵기/굵다.

Using 두께 for height. 두께 is the thin front-to-back dimension; vertical extent is 높이.
Saying 두꺼운 줄 for a 'thick rope'. Round, long things take 굵다: 굵은 줄, and their measure is 굵기, not 두께.
Pairing 두께 with the wrong scale word — describe it with 두껍다/얇다, e.g. 두께가 얇다, not 두께가 작다.

entries.shortExplanation: 무게 means "weight" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 무게 (muge) = "weight". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 무게가 무거워요. ("The weight is heavy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무게, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 무게 with 무겁다, its matched adjective
무게를 재다 = 'to weigh'
무게 stated with a value
무게 paired with 가볍다

examples.en: This bag's weight is no joke.
examples.note: Casual; 무게 + 무겁다 implied for something heavy

examples.ko: 짐 무게가 기준을 넘어서 추가 요금을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: jim mugega gijuneul neomeoseo chuga yogeumeul naesseoyo.
examples.en: The luggage weight exceeded the limit, so I paid an extra fee.
examples.note: Real situation; 무게 at an airport check-in

examples.en: Parcel fees vary according to weight.
examples.note: Formal; 무게에 따라 = 'depending on weight'

entries.nuance: 무게 is a native noun from the adjective 무겁다 ('heavy') plus the -에/-게 nominalizer, meaning how heavy something is. Its matched adjectives are 무겁다 ('heavy') and 가볍다 ('light'), and the standard verb for measuring it is 재다 (무게를 재다 'to weigh'). Beyond the physical sense, 무게 also carries the figurative meaning of 'gravity, importance, dignity' — 말의 무게 'the weight of one's words', 무게를 잡다 'to put on a serious air'. Keep it distinct from 수량 (how MANY) and from 양 (how much in a general/uncountable sense): a box's 무게 is its heaviness, its 수량 is how many boxes there are. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: English 'weigh' is one word, but Korean splits it — 무게를 재다 means 'to measure the weight (of something)', whereas the intransitive 'it weighs 5 kg' is 5킬로그램이 나가다 (무게가 나가다), so learners wrongly say 무게를 재다 when they mean 'it weighs ~'.

Confusing 무게 (weight) with 수량 (the count of items) — a heavy box vs. how many boxes there are.
Describing weight with the wrong adjective, e.g. 무게가 크다. Use 무게가 무겁다/가볍다 ('heavy/light').

entries.shortExplanation: 길이 means "length" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 길이 (giri) means "length". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 길이가 길어요. ("The length is long."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 길이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 길이 with 길다, its matched adjective
길이를 재다 = 'to measure length'
길이 stated with a value
길이 paired with 짧다

examples.en: This string's length is just right.
examples.note: Casual; 길이 with 좋다 for a fitting length

examples.en: I cut my hair length to the shoulders.
examples.note: Everyday; 길이 in a haircut context

examples.en: The length of this bridge reaches about 1.2 kilometers.
examples.note: Formal; 길이 with a large measured figure

entries.nuance: 길이 is a native noun from the adjective 길다 ('long') plus the -이 nominalizer, naming the end-to-end (usually horizontal) extent of something. Its matched adjectives are 길다 ('long') and 짧다 ('short'), and you measure it with 재다 (길이를 재다). It belongs to a tidy family of -이 measurement nouns you should keep straight: 길이 (length, side to side), 높이 (height, bottom to top), 깊이 (depth, surface to bottom), 넓이 (area), and the odd one out 두께/굵기 for thickness. The sharp contrast is 길이 vs 높이: a desk's 길이 is how long it is across, its 높이 is how tall it stands — confuse them and a Korean will picture the wrong dimension. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is using 길이 for vertical 'how tall', because English loosely says 'the length of the pole' even when standing upright; in Korean a standing object's vertical measure is 높이, and 길이 implies the laid-flat, lengthwise dimension.

Pairing 길이 with the wrong adjective, e.g. 길이가 크다. Use 길이가 길다/짧다 ('long/short').
Mixing up the -이 family: 깊이 (depth) and 넓이 (area) are not interchangeable with 길이 — match the dimension to the word.

usagePhrases.note: 높이 with 높다, its matched adjective
높이를 재다 = 'to measure height'
높이 stated with a value
높이 paired with 낮다

examples.ko: 이 선반 높이 좀 낮춰 줘.
examples.romanization: i seonban nopi jom natchwo jwo.
examples.en: Lower this shelf's height a bit.
examples.note: Casual; 높이 with 낮추다 to adjust it

examples.ko: 책상 높이를 내 키에 맞게 조절했어요.
examples.romanization: chaeksang nopireul nae kie matge jojeolhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I adjusted the desk height to fit my build.
examples.note: Everyday; 높이 조절 for furniture

examples.en: This building's height reaches 123 floors and 555 meters.
examples.note: Formal; 높이 with an impressive figure

entries.nuance: 높이 is a native noun from the adjective 높다 ('high/tall') plus the -이 nominalizer, naming the bottom-to-top (vertical) extent of something — a building, a mountain, a shelf, a jump. entries.shortExplanation: 피부 means "skin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 피부 (pibu) = "skin". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 피부가 좋아요 ("your skin is nice") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 피부, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the default compliment; 좋다 here means clear and healthy, not merely 'good'
건조하다 (乾燥) is the set adjective for dry skin, never 마르다
a borrowed phrase Koreans use for acne and irritation as a noun
note the particle 에 (to/for the skin), the standard frame for skincare claims

examples.en: Your skin is really nice.
examples.note: a stock compliment; mark the topic with 가, the thing praised

examples.ko: 겨울에는 피부가 너무 건조해서 로션을 발라요.
examples.romanization: gyeoureneun pibuga neomu geonjohaeseo rosyeoneul ballayo.
examples.en: In winter my skin gets so dry that I put on lotion.
examples.note: 건조해서 (because dry) links cause to action with -아서

examples.ko: 햇볕에 오래 있었더니 피부가 따갑고 빨개졌어요.
examples.romanization: haetbyeote orae isseotdeoni pibuga ttagapgo ppalgaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After being in the sun a long time my skin stings and turned red.
examples.note: 빨개지다 = 빨갛다 + 지다, 'become red'; the ㅎ-irregular drops in 빨개

entries.nuance: 피부 is the skin as a surface and a beauty concern, so it overwhelmingly turns up in compliments (피부가 좋다 = clear, glowing) and skincare talk (피부에 좋다, 피부 트러블, 피부가 건조하다). The near-synonym 살 also means 'skin/flesh' but refers to the soft fleshy meat under the surface and to body fat (살이 찌다 = gain weight), so 손등 살이 텄어요 is the chapped flesh while 피부 관리 is the cosmetic surface — never swap them. 피부 is Sino-Korean, 皮膚 'hide-skin', which is why it sounds slightly clinical yet is perfectly everyday. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for 마르다 ('dry up, become thin') for dry skin; skin takes the adjective 건조하다 instead, and 'I have sensitive skin' is 피부가 예민해요/민감해요, not a 직역 with 'sensitive' as a noun.

Translating 'skin and bones' or 'get under my skin' literally. Those English idioms don't exist in Korean; describe the meaning instead (e.g. 너무 말랐어요 for very thin).
Using 살 when you mean the cosmetic surface. 얼굴 살이 좋아요 sounds like 'nice facial flesh/cheeks'; for clear complexion say 얼굴 피부가 좋아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 뼈 means "bone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뼈 (ppyeo) means "bone". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 뼈가 부러졌어요 ("my bone broke"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뼈 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 부러지다 is the verb reserved for snapping long rigid things like bones and branches
튼튼하다 = sturdy/robust; the go-to word for healthy bones, not 강하다
note 에 (for the bones); the frame used in food and calcium ads
an idiom for being extremely thin or worn out

examples.en: The puppy likes bones.
examples.note: a simple object sentence; 뼈를 takes the object particle

examples.en: I fell and broke the bone in my arm.
examples.note: 부러지다 is intransitive — the bone breaks 'by itself', so use 가

examples.ko: 나이가 들면 뼈가 약해져서 칼슘을 챙겨 먹어야 해요.
examples.romanization: naiga deulmyeon ppyeoga yakaejyeoseo kalsyumeul chaenggyeo meogeoya haeyo.
examples.en: As you age your bones weaken, so you should take calcium.
examples.note: 약해지다 'become weak' + 챙겨 먹다 'make sure to eat'

entries.nuance: 뼈 is the hard bone inside the body and, by extension, a bone in meat or fish. The crucial collocation is 뼈가 부러지다 'a bone breaks': Korean fusses over WHICH break-verb you use — 부러지다 is for snapping rigid long things (bones, pencils, branches), 깨지다 is for shattering brittle things (glass, plates, a skull as 두개골), and 금이 가다 is a hairline crack/fracture. So a clean break is 부러지다, but a fracture a doctor sees on an X-ray is often 뼈에 금이 갔어요. Native, non-Sino word, so it feels plain and bodily; the formal medical counterpart is 골(骨), seen in compounds like 골절 'fracture' and 골다공증 'osteoporosis'. English speakers misfire by saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 (sounds like the bone shattered into pieces) for an ordinary break — use 부러졌어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 for a normal broken bone. 깨지다 implies shattering brittle objects; a snapped bone is 부러졌어요. Reserve 금이 갔어요 for a hairline fracture.
Using 강하다 for strong bones. 강하다 fits force or personality; healthy sturdy bones take 튼튼하다, so say 뼈가 튼튼해요.
Forgetting 부러지다 is intransitive and adding 를. Don't say 뼈를 부러뜨렸어요 unless you mean someone actively broke it; for 'my bone broke' say 뼈가 부러졌어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 근육 means "muscle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "muscle" is 근육 (geunyuk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 근육이 뭉쳤어요 ("my muscle is knotted up"). Watch the particle attached to 근육 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뭉치다 'to clump/lump together' is the set verb for a stiff, knotted muscle
생기다 'come into being'; the natural way to say muscle has appeared
풀다 'to release/undo'; used for stretching out tension, opposite of 뭉치다
근육통 (筋肉痛) is the noun for the soreness after a workout

examples.en: That person has a lot of muscle.
examples.note: describing build; 많다 'be many/much' takes 가 on the thing

examples.ko: 어제 운동을 무리해서 오늘 온몸 근육이 아파요.
examples.romanization: eoje undongeul murihaeseo oneul onmom geunyugi apayo.
examples.en: I overdid the workout yesterday so today my muscles ache all over.
examples.note: 무리하다 'to overdo it' + 온몸 'whole body'

examples.ko: 오래 앉아 있었더니 어깨 근육이 뭉쳐서 좀 풀어 줬어요.
examples.romanization: orae anja isseotdeoni eokkae geunyugi mungchyeoseo jom pureo jwosseoyo.
examples.en: After sitting a long time my shoulder muscles knotted up, so I worked them loose.
examples.note: 뭉치다 ↔ 풀다 pairing; 줬어요 here adds a gentle 'did for it' nuance

entries.nuance: 근육 is muscle tissue, the body part you build at the gym and the thing that gets sore or knotted. It is Sino-Korean, 筋肉 'sinew-flesh', which is why the soreness noun is 근육통 (筋肉痛, lit. muscle-pain). The signature collocation is 근육이 뭉치다 'the muscle clumps up' — 뭉치다 literally means to lump together (rice 뭉치다 into a ball), and a stiff knotted muscle is pictured the same way; its natural opposite is 근육을 풀다 'release the muscle' by stretching. Don't confuse 근육 (the tissue) with 힘 (strength/power, the force it produces): 힘이 세다 = strong, but 근육이 많다 = muscular. The English-speaker pitfall is describing a knot as 딱딱하다 'hard' — that just states a texture; the idiomatic medical-feeling phrase Koreans actually say is 근육이 뭉쳤어요.

Saying 근육이 딱딱해요 for a knotted muscle. 딱딱하다 only states it feels hard; the natural phrase for a tense knot is 근육이 뭉쳤어요.
Mixing up 근육 and 힘. 근육이 세요 is wrong; for 'I'm strong' say 힘이 세요, and reserve 근육이 많아요 for being muscular.
Saying 근육을 키워요 expecting it to mean a quick 'flex'. 키우다 means to grow/raise muscle over time (training); to flex a muscle right now is 힘을 줘요 or 알통을 만들어요.

usagePhrases.note: 뛰다 'to run/leap' doubles as 'to beat' for the heart
두근거리다 is the onomatopoeic verb for a fast, fluttering heartbeat
약하다 'be weak'; a standard medical description
심장마비 (心臟痲痺) lit. 'heart paralysis', the medical term

examples.en: People have one heart.
examples.note: a simple fact sentence; 하나 'one' + 예요

examples.ko: 갑자기 뒤에서 불러서 심장이 멎는 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi dwieseo bulleoseo simjangi meonneun jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: Someone suddenly called from behind and I thought my heart would stop.
examples.note: 멎다 'to stop/cease'; -는 줄 알았다 'I thought it would'

examples.ko: 계단을 뛰어 올라왔더니 심장이 터질 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: gyedaneul ttwieo ollawatdeoni simjangi teojil geot gatayo.
examples.en: I ran up the stairs and now my heart feels like it'll burst.
examples.note: 터지다 'to burst'; vivid but everyday exaggeration for racing

entries.nuance: 심장 is the physical heart organ — the muscle that beats — and it is Sino-Korean, 心臟 'heart-organ'. The key boundary for English speakers: in Korean the SEAT OF EMOTION is not 심장. Love, sincerity and feelings live in 마음 (the mind-heart, 마음이 아프다 = heartbroken) or 가슴 (the chest, 가슴이 뛰다/벅차다 for excitement and emotion). 심장 stays literal and medical: it 뛰다 (beats), 두근거리다 (pounds with adrenaline or fear), or 멎다/터지다 in vivid shock. Note 심장 vs 가슴: a doctor checks your 심장, but you clutch your 가슴 (chest) in feeling. The classic 직역 trap is writing 'my heart aches (emotionally)' as 심장이 아파요 — that sounds like cardiac pain; for emotional hurt say 마음이 아파요.

Confusing 심장 with 가슴. To say your chest feels tight or fluttery with emotion, Koreans say 가슴이 답답해요 / 가슴이 뛰어요, not 심장이.
Translating 'from the bottom of my heart' as 심장. The idiom is 진심으로 or 마음 깊은 곳에서, never with 심장.

혈액형 (血液型) lit. 'blood-type'; the everyday word even in casual chat
뽑다 'to pull out/draw'; the verb for drawing blood or pulling teeth
순환 (循環) 'circulation'; common in health talk, e.g. 혈액 순환이 잘 돼요

examples.en: My blood type is A.
examples.note: the one casual spot 혈액 appears daily; 혈액형 + 이에요

examples.en: They drew blood at my health checkup.
examples.note: 건강 검진 'health screening'; 뽑다 for the draw

examples.ko: 손발이 찬 건 혈액 순환이 잘 안 돼서 그래요.
examples.romanization: sonbari chan geon hyeoraek sunhwani jal an dwaeseo geuraeyo.
examples.en: Cold hands and feet happen because circulation isn't good.
examples.note: 혈액 순환이 안 되다 'circulation doesn't work well'

entries.nuance: 혈액 is the formal, clinical word for blood — Sino-Korean 血液 'blood-fluid' — so it lives in hospital and health vocabulary: 혈액 검사 (blood test), 혈액형 (blood type), 혈액 순환 (circulation), 혈액 기증 (blood donation). Its everyday counterpart is the native word 피, which is what you say for blood you actually SEE: a bleeding cut is 피가 나요, never 혈액이 나요. So the dividing line is register and visibility — 피 = the red liquid in daily life, 혈액 = the technical substance in medical contexts. The one exception where the Sino word wins in casual speech is 혈액형 'blood type', which almost everyone says over 피의 형. The English-speaker pitfall is using 혈액 for ordinary bleeding (sounds like a lab report) — for a nosebleed or a scrape, say 피.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 혈액이 나요 for a bleeding cut. That sounds like a clinical report; visible bleeding is 피가 나요.
Over-formalizing casual blood-type talk. While 혈액형 is correct, don't say 혈액 for the blood in 'I'm bleeding' — switch to 피.
Mixing up the verbs. You don't 마시다 or 흘리다 혈액 in normal speech; blood is 뽑다 (drawn) or 검사하다 (tested), while you 흘리다 피 (shed blood).

entries.shortExplanation: 침 means "saliva; spit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "saliva; spit" is 침 (chim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 침을 뱉어요 ("I spit"). Watch the particle attached to 침 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뱉다 'to spit out'; the set verb, used literally and in 'spit it out (confess)'
삼키다 'to swallow'; also used for swallowing words/anger
고이다 'to pool/collect'; what your mouth does at a tasty smell
침이 마르다 'mouth goes dry'; idiom for praising someone endlessly

examples.en: The baby is drooling.
examples.note: 흘리다 'to let flow'; simple everyday drooling

examples.en: You mustn't spit on the street.
examples.note: manners; -으면 안 되다 'must not'

examples.ko: 맛있는 냄새를 맡으니까 입에 침이 고여요.
examples.romanization: masinneun naemsaereul mateunikka ibe chimi goyeoyo.
examples.en: Smelling the delicious food makes my mouth water.
examples.note: Korean's exact equivalent of 'mouth waters' = 침이 고이다

entries.nuance: 침 is the saliva in your mouth, and it pairs with a precise set of verbs: 침을 뱉다 (spit out), 침을 삼키다 (swallow), 침을 흘리다 (drool), and 침이 고이다 (pool — the 'mouth waters' image). Beware the homonyms: this same syllable 침 also means an acupuncture needle (침을 맞다 = get acupuncture), a (clock/compass) needle/hand, and 'sting'(벌침 = bee sting) — context fully disambiguates, but it surprises learners. Two vivid idioms ride on it: 침이 마르도록 칭찬하다 'praise until your mouth runs dry' and 군침이 돌다 'mouth waters with craving'. The pitfall is the verb: English 'water' (as in mouth-watering) tempts a 직역 with 물, but Korean says 침이 고이다 (saliva pools), and 'I'm drooling' is 침을 흘려요, not anything with 물.

Confusing the homonyms. 침을 맞다 means 'get acupuncture', not 'get hit with spit'; saliva-침 takes 뱉다/삼키다/흘리다.
Translating 'mouth waters' with 물. The fixed phrase is 입에 침이 고이다 (or 군침이 돌다); never 입에 물이 나요.
Wrong verb for drooling. 침이 나와요 is understandable but flat; natural Korean is 침을 흘려요 for drooling.

entries.shortExplanation: 땀 means "sweat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 땀 (ttam) = "sweat". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 땀을 흘려요 ("I sweat / I work hard") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 땀, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 흘리다 'to shed'; literal sweating AND the idiom for hard effort
나다 'to come out/occur'; the most everyday way to say you're sweating
닦다 'to wipe/clean'; with a towel or sleeve
식은땀 lit. 'cooled sweat'; the sweat of fear, nausea, or close calls

examples.en: It's hot so I'm sweating.
examples.note: the basic frame; 땀이 나다 with 가 on the spontaneous event

examples.en: After exercising I wiped off the sweat with a towel.
examples.note: -고 나서 'after doing'; 닦다 takes 를

examples.en: Right before the presentation I broke out in a cold sweat.
examples.note: 식은땀이 나다 = the fear/nerves version of sweating

entries.nuance: 땀 is sweat, a native word, and the verb choice carries the meaning. 땀이 나다 (sweat occurs) is the neutral everyday 'I'm sweating', while 땀을 흘리다 (shed sweat) both describes heavy sweating AND works as a metaphor for hard work — 땀 흘려 일하다 'to work by the sweat of one's brow', and 노력의 땀 'the sweat of effort'. A key compound is 식은땀 'cold sweat', the clammy sweat of fear, illness, or a near-miss (식은땀이 나다/흐르다). Contrast 땀 with 눈물 (tears) and 침 (saliva): all three are bodily fluids that idiomatically 나다, but only 땀 carries the 'effort/labor' connotation. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'sweat' as a verb and saying 땀을 해요 — Korean has no 'to sweat' verb; you either 흘리다 the sweat or it 나다 on its own.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 땀을 해요 for 'I sweat'. There's no verb 'to sweat'; say 땀이 나요 (it comes) or 땀을 흘려요 (I shed it).
Missing the idiom. 땀을 흘리다 can mean hard work, so 땀 흘려 번 돈 means 'money earned through hard work', not literally sweaty money.
Using plain 땀 for the fear-sweat. The clammy nervous kind is specifically 식은땀, e.g. 식은땀이 났어요, not just 땀이 났어요.
