entries.shortExplanation: 눈물 means "tears" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 눈물 (nunmul) means "tears". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 눈물이 나요 ("tears come / I start to cry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 눈물 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: tears come / I start to cry
usagePhrases.note: 나다 'to come out'; the most natural way to say tears well up
흘리다 'to let flow'; slightly more vivid/literary than 나다
describing a person, not a quantity of liquid
참다 'to endure/hold in'; fighting off crying

examples.en: I'm tearing up because I watched a sad movie.
examples.note: cause + 눈물이 나다; the spontaneous event takes 가

examples.en: I yawned and tears welled up in my eyes.
examples.note: 눈물이 핑 돌다 = tears suddenly well up; 핑 is the swirl mimetic

examples.ko: 울고 싶었지만 사람들 앞이라 눈물을 꾹 참았어요.
examples.romanization: ulgo sipeotjiman saramdeul apira nunmureul kkuk chamasseoyo.
examples.en: I wanted to cry but I held the tears back hard in front of people.
examples.note: 꾹 참다 'endure firmly'; 눈물을 참다 takes the object 를

entries.nuance: 눈물 is tears, a transparent native compound 눈(eye)+물(water). Its default verb is 눈물이 나다 'tears come' — note that 'I cry' is often expressed this way (눈물이 나요 ≈ 'I'm tearing up') rather than only with the verb 울다 'to cry/weep'. 눈물을 흘리다 'shed tears' is a touch more vivid, and 눈물을 참다 means to hold them back. Watch the idiom 눈물이 많다: it does NOT mean you produce a lot of liquid — it means you're a soft-hearted person who cries easily; its opposite 눈물이 없다 means stoic. Vivid set phrases: 눈물이 핑 돌다 (tears suddenly well), 눈물이 그렁그렁하다 (eyes brimming). The pitfall is the 직역 눈물을 울어요 — you can't 'cry tears' in Korean; tears 나다 (come) or you 흘리다 (shed) them, while 울다 stands alone as 'to cry'.

Saying 눈물을 울어요. 울다 already means 'to cry' and takes no object; say 눈물이 나요 (tears come) or just 울어요.
Literalizing 눈물이 많아요 as 'lots of tear liquid'. It describes a tender person who cries easily, like English 'a crybaby/soft-hearted'.
Wrong particle on the spontaneous event. 'Tears came' is 눈물이 났어요 (가), not 눈물을 났어요; the object 를 only fits 흘리다/참다.

entries.shortExplanation: 숨 means "breath" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "breath" is 숨 (sum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 숨을 쉬어요 ("I breathe"). Watch the particle attached to 숨 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 쉬다 — the SAME verb as 'to rest'; 숨을 쉬다 = 'breathe'
차다 'to fill up'; the set phrase for being winded
참다 'to hold in/endure'; also used for holding back emotion

usagePhrases.en: I take a deep breath in
usagePhrases.note: 들이쉬다 'breathe in' vs 내쉬다 'breathe out', built on 쉬다

examples.en: Try breathing slowly.
examples.note: clinic instruction; -아 보세요 'try doing'

examples.en: I ran up the stairs and now I'm out of breath.
examples.note: 숨이 차다 — winded; the event takes 가

examples.en: I held my breath for 30 seconds underwater.
examples.note: 숨을 참다 takes the object 를; 동안 'for (a duration)'

entries.nuance: 숨 is a breath / one's breathing, a native word, and its core verb is 숨을 쉬다 'to breathe' — note that 쉬다 is also the verb 'to rest', a neat overlap (breathing is the body resting). Directional variants build on it: 들이쉬다 (breathe in), 내쉬다 (breathe out), 한숨을 쉬다 (sigh). To say you're winded, Korean uses 숨이 차다 'breath fills up' (the event takes 가), and to hold your breath is 숨을 참다. Compare 숨 with the Sino-Korean 호흡 (呼吸 'exhale-inhale'), which is the technical 'respiration' used in yoga, medicine, and 인공호흡 (CPR) — 숨 is the plain everyday word. Vivid idioms: 숨이 막히다 'be suffocated/overwhelmed', 숨을 거두다 'to pass away (lit. gather one's breath)'. The pitfall is saying 숨을 해요 — there's no 'to breath' verb; you 쉬다 (do/rest) the breath.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 숨을 해요 for 'I breathe'. The verb is 쉬다, so say 숨을 쉬어요 — and note 쉬다 also means 'rest'.
Using 숨 in a yoga/medical setting where 호흡 fits. 'Focus on your breathing' in class is usually 호흡에 집중하세요.
Wrong particle for being winded. 'I'm out of breath' is 숨이 차요 (가); don't say 숨을 차요. Use 를 only with 참다 (hold).

entries.shortExplanation: 수염 means "beard; mustache" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수염 (suyeom) = "beard; mustache". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수염을 길러요 ("I'm growing a beard") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수염, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기르다 'to grow/raise'; the verb for growing hair, beards, pets
깎다 'to shave/pare'; same verb as shaving and sharpening a pencil
나다 'to grow/sprout'; how facial/body hair appears
콧(nose)수염 vs 턱(chin)수염 specify which when it matters

examples.en: Cats have whiskers.
examples.note: 수염 also = animal whiskers; simple 있다 sentence

examples.en: Dad shaves every morning.
examples.note: daily routine; 깎다 takes 를

examples.ko: 한동안 면도를 안 했더니 수염이 덥수룩하게 났어요.
examples.romanization: handongan myeondoreul an haetdeoni suyeomi deopsurukage nasseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't shave for a while so a scruffy beard grew in.
examples.note: 덥수룩하다 'be bushy/scruffy'; 수염이 나다 for it coming in

entries.nuance: 수염 covers all facial hair — beard and mustache together — and also animal whiskers (고양이 수염), so context tells you which; to be specific Koreans add a body part: 콧수염 (mustache, nose-beard), 턱수염 (chin beard), 구레나룻 (sideburns). It's Sino-Korean, 鬚髥. The verbs are the heart of it: you 기르다 (grow) a beard over time, it 나다 (sprouts) on its own, and you 깎다 (shave) it off — 깎다 is the same verb as shaving hair short and sharpening a pencil, picturing paring something down. Note the everyday near-synonym 면도(面刀)하다 'to shave' (lit. 'face-blade'): 면도하다 is the act of shaving, while 수염을 깎다 names the beard as object. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 자르다 'to cut' — you cut hair with scissors (머리를 자르다), but a beard is pared/shaved with 깎다, not 잘라요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수염을 잘라요 for shaving. 자르다 is cutting with scissors (good for hair length); shaving a beard is 수염을 깎아요 or 면도해요.
Forcing 수염 to mean only 'beard'. It also means a mustache and animal whiskers; specify 콧수염/턱수염 if the distinction matters.
Using 자라다 transitively for growing a beard. 자라다 'to grow' is intransitive (수염이 자라요 = it grows); to deliberately grow one say 수염을 길러요.

entries.shortExplanation: 주름 means "wrinkle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주름 (jureum) means "wrinkle". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주름이 생겼어요 ("wrinkles have formed"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주름 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 'to form/appear'; the set verb for wrinkles coming with age
자글자글 is the mimetic word for lots of tiny crinkly wrinkles
펴다 'to unfold/straighten'; for skin or ironing cloth
눈가 'eye area'; the most-mentioned wrinkle spot

examples.en: Grandma has many wrinkles.
examples.note: appearance; 많다 takes 가 on 주름

examples.ko: 웃을 때 눈가에 주름이 살짝 생겨요.
examples.romanization: useul ttae nungae jureumi saljjak saenggyeoyo.
examples.en: When I smile, slight wrinkles form around my eyes.
examples.note: 눈가에 'at the eye area' + 살짝 'slightly'

examples.en: I ironed out the wrinkles in the shirt.
examples.note: same 주름 for cloth creases; 펴다 removes them

entries.nuance: 주름 means a wrinkle on skin AND a fold/crease in fabric or paper — same word for both. It's a native word, and its defining verb is 주름이 생기다 'wrinkles form' (생기다 = come into being), the standard way to talk about aging skin; you smooth them with 주름을 펴다 (unfold/straighten, also used for ironing). Common spots: 눈가 주름 (crow's feet), 이마 주름 (forehead lines), 팔자 주름 (nasolabial folds, named for the 八 shape). A vivid mimetic, 자글자글하다, describes finely crinkled skin. Don't confuse 주름 (a line/fold in a surface) with 흉터 (a scar from a wound) or 점 (a mole) — different skin features entirely. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'wrinkles appear' tempts 주름이 나다 (the 나다 you'd use for pimples or sweat), but wrinkles specifically 생기다 — say 주름이 생겼어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 주름이 나요 for wrinkles. The verb 나다 fits pimples/sweat; wrinkles use 생기다, so say 주름이 생겼어요.
Treating 주름 as skin-only. The same word means cloth creases — 주름이 가다/지다, and 주름치마 is a pleated skirt.
Confusing 주름 with 흉터. A line from aging is 주름; a mark left by a cut or burn is 흉터 (scar).

entries.shortExplanation: 점 means "mole; spot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "mole; spot" is 점 (jeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 점을 빼요 ("I remove the mole"). Watch the particle attached to 점 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 빼다 'to take out/remove'; the set verb for laser mole removal
있다 'to exist'; describing where a mole sits

usagePhrases.en: I draw on a beauty spot
usagePhrases.note: 찍다 'to dot/stamp'; making a point, also photos and dipping sauce
검은 'black/dark'; the common color descriptor

examples.en: I have one mole on my face.
examples.note: appearance; 하나 'one' counts it

examples.ko: 눈 밑에 있는 점을 병원에서 뺐어요.
examples.romanization: nun mite inneun jeomeul byeongwoneseo ppaesseoyo.
examples.en: I had the mole under my eye removed at a clinic.
examples.note: 점을 빼다; 눈 밑 'under the eye'

examples.en: The teacher made a dot on the board.
examples.note: same 점 = 'dot/point'; 찍다 for marking it

entries.nuance: 점 is a mole on the skin, and the very same word means a dot, point, spot, period (punctuation), and even a 'point' as in a score or aspect (좋은 점 = a good point). It's Sino-Korean, 點. For a skin mole the defining collocation is 점을 빼다 'remove the mole' — 빼다 means to take/pull out (also used for 'lose weight', 살을 빼다), reflecting how a mole is extracted by laser. Don't use 지우다 'to erase' (that's for writing, stains, or files) — you 빼다 a mole, not 지워요. Useful relatives: 주근깨 (freckles), 기미 (age/sun spots, melasma). Beware the homonym range: 점심 (點心, lunch) literally 'dot the heart', 점수 (點數, score), 점 보다 (have one's fortune told). The English-speaker pitfall is calling a mole a 'spot' and erasing it — Korean removes (빼다) the 점.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 점을 지워요 to remove a mole. 지우다 is for erasing writing/stains/data; a mole is 점을 빼요 (taken out, often by laser).
Assuming 점 only means 'mole'. It also means a dot, a (score) point, and an aspect — e.g. 좋은 점 'a good point', 점수 'score'.
Using 자르다 for mole removal. You don't 'cut' a mole off in normal speech; the clinic verb is 빼다 (or 제거하다 in formal medical contexts).

entries.shortExplanation: 속옷 means "underwear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 속옷 (sogot) = "underwear". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 속옷을 갈아입어요. ("I change my underwear.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 속옷, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the verb 갈아입다 'change clothes' is the natural partner, not just 입다
underwear is counted with 벌, the counter for clothing sets
면(綿) names the fabric; 면 + garment is a fixed modifier pattern
차림 means 'state of being dressed in', describing what someone has on

examples.en: I change my underwear every day.
examples.note: 갈아입다 (change-into) is the habitual verb; plain 입다 sounds like a first-time action

examples.en: My underwear got all wet.
examples.note: 이/가 marks 속옷 as the thing that got into the wet state — 다 = 'completely'

examples.ko: 새 속옷을 사야 하는데 어디 가지요?
examples.romanization: sae sogoseul saya haneunde eodi gajiyo?
examples.en: I need to buy new underwear, but where should I go?
examples.note: real shopping moment: -는데 sets up the problem, -지요? asks for advice

entries.nuance: 속옷 is the umbrella word for anything worn directly against the body under your outer clothes — it transparently breaks down as 속 'inside, inner part' + 옷 'clothes', so literally 'inner clothes'. It covers both men's and women's items and is the neutral term you'd use shopping or at home; in clinical or marketing contexts you may also meet the Sino-Korean 내의(內衣, 'inner-garment') for thermal underwear specifically. The crucial trap for English speakers is the verb: although you 'wear' underwear in English, the everyday Korean verb is 갈아입다 ('change into') because underwear is something you swap daily, and the counter is 벌 (one 속옷 한 벌), never 개. Do not confuse 속옷 with 잠옷 (pajamas) or 수영복 (swimsuit) — those are worn over the body for a purpose, while 속옷 stays hidden underneath.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 속옷을 신어요 — 신다 is only for things you put on your feet (socks, shoes). Underwear bottoms still take 입다/갈아입다, so say 속옷을 입어요/갈아입어요.
Counting with 개: 속옷 두 개 sounds like two random objects. Use the clothing counter 벌 → 속옷 두 벌 ('two sets of underwear').
Treating 속옷 and 내복 as identical. 내복/내의 specifically means warm thermal long-johns for winter; plain 속옷 is the general everyday term.

entries.shortExplanation: 잠옷 means "pajamas" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잠옷 (jamot) means "pajamas". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 잠옷으로 갈아입어요. ("I change into pajamas."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잠옷 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the result you change into; 갈아입다 is the natural verb at bedtime
바람으로 = 'wearing only ~', stressing you're underdressed to go out
커플 + item is a popular set-phrase for matching outfits
-은 채로 = 'in the unchanged state of', i.e. without taking it off

examples.en: At night I wear pajamas.
examples.note: 은 on 밤에 contrasts night with the daytime; 입다 is fine for the habitual statement

examples.en: The pajamas are so comfy I don't want to take them off.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 벗다 'take off' is the opposite of 입다

examples.en: I ran to the convenience store in my pajamas.
examples.note: 잠옷 차림으로 = 'dressed only in pajamas', a very Korean way to say you went out underdressed

entries.nuance: 잠옷 literally stacks 잠 'sleep' (the noun from 자다 'to sleep') + 옷 'clothes', so 'sleep-clothes' — clothes whose whole job is to be comfortable in bed. It overlaps with the borrowed 파자마 (pajamas) and the broader 실내복 ('indoor wear', 室內服), but 잠옷 specifically frames the garment around sleeping, while 실내복 is any loungewear you'd relax in awake. Register is fully neutral and casual. The English-speaker pitfall is cultural rather than grammatical: in Korea wearing 잠옷 outside the home reads as notably sloppy, so the phrases 잠옷 바람으로 / 잠옷 차림으로 ('in just your pj's') carry a faintly embarrassed nuance. Grammatically remember the opposite of 입다 ('put on') is 벗다 ('take off'), and use the clothing counter 벌, not 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 to count: 잠옷 두 개 is wrong for a garment. Say 잠옷 한 벌 / 두 벌 with the clothing counter 벌.
Saying 잠옷을 신어요 — 신다 is reserved for footwear. Pajamas take 입다 (top and bottom together): 잠옷을 입어요.
Assuming 잠옷 = any home clothes. If you mean general loungewear you stay awake in, 실내복 or 편한 옷 is more accurate; 잠옷 implies you're going to bed.

structuredNuance.t: Clothes whose whole job is to be comfortable in bed. Register is fully neutral and casual.

entries.shortExplanation: 정장 means "suit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "suit" is 정장 (jeongjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정장을 차려입어요. ("I dress up in a suit."). Watch the particle attached to 정장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I dress up in a suit.
usagePhrases.note: 차려입다 ('dress up smartly') is the verb that matches formal wear
a jacket-and-trousers set is counted as 한 벌, since 벌 means a full matching set
차림 = 'the way one is dressed', so 정장 차림 = dressed formally
맞춤 (from 맞추다 'to have made to fit') marks a custom-ordered suit

examples.en: I wore a suit today.
examples.note: basic statement; 을 marks the object, 입다 the verb

examples.en: Since it's a job interview, I dressed up in a suit.
examples.note: -이라서 'because it is' gives the reason; 차려입다 stresses dressing up properly

examples.ko: 검은색 정장에 흰 셔츠가 제일 무난해요.
examples.romanization: geomeunsaek jeongjange huin syeocheuga jeil munanhaeyo.
examples.en: A black suit with a white shirt is the safest choice.
examples.note: A에 B = 'B paired with A'; 무난하다 'safe/unobjectionable' is the go-to word for fail-proof outfits

entries.nuance: 정장 is Sino-Korean 正裝, literally 正 'proper, correct' + 裝 'attire' — 'correct/proper dress', i.e. the formal outfit appropriate for serious occasions (interviews, weddings, funerals, important meetings). It overlaps with 양복(洋服, 'Western clothes'), but there is a real dividing line: 양복 names the Western-style tailored garment as a thing (and skews masculine and slightly old-fashioned), whereas 정장 names the formal register of the outfit and applies equally to men's and women's formal wear. The opposite is 캐주얼 or 평상복 ('everyday clothes'). The English-speaker pitfall is counting and the verb: a suit is one matched set, so 정장 한 벌 (not 한 개), and the natural verb is 입다 or, for the 'dress up' feel, 차려입다 — never 신다, which is only for footwear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting with 개: 정장 한 개 is wrong. A suit is a set → 정장 한 벌.
Using 정장 and 양복 interchangeably for women. 양복 sounds like a man's Western suit; for a woman's formal outfit say 정장.
Saying 정장을 신어요 — 신다 is for shoes/socks only. A suit takes 입다 or 차려입다: 정장을 입어요.

structuredNuance.t: The formal outfit appropriate for serious occasions (interviews, weddings, funerals, important meetings). The opposite is 캐주얼 or 평상복 ('everyday clothes').

entries.shortExplanation: 청바지 means "jeans" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 청바지 (cheongbaji) = "jeans". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 청바지를 입어요. ("I wear jeans.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 청바지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: trousers take 입다 (put on the legs), with 를 as the object marker
borrowed style adjectives like 스키니 sit directly in front of 청바지
딱 맞다 'fit exactly' is the set phrase for a perfect fit
A에 B lists a paired outfit, 'B worn with A'

examples.en: On weekends I wear jeans.
examples.note: 은 on 주말에 contrasts the weekend with workdays; casual register

examples.ko: 청바지가 좀 끼어서 한 치수 큰 걸 샀어요.
examples.romanization: cheongbajiga jom kkieoseo han chisu keun geol sasseoyo.
examples.en: The jeans were a bit tight, so I bought one size up.
examples.note: 끼다 'be tight/snug' is the natural fit complaint; -아서 gives the reason

examples.en: These jeans don't shrink even when washed.
examples.note: -아도 'even if'; 줄어들다 'shrink' is the verb for fabric shrinking

entries.nuance: 청바지 = 청(靑) 'blue/indigo' + 바지 'trousers', literally 'blue trousers' — the 청 element is what specifically marks denim, since plain 바지 just means 'pants' of any kind. It's the standard, completely neutral word for jeans across all ages and is far more common in speech than the English loan 진/데님 (데님 normally refers to the fabric, not the finished garment). Casual register, never formal. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, jeans are grammatically singular in Korean — 청바지 한 벌 / 한 개, never a plural form — so you don't 'wear a pair'; second, the verb is 입다 ('put on the lower body'), and a tight or loose fit is described with 끼다 ('snug/tight') or 헐렁하다 ('loose'), not the English 'tight'. Pair it naturally with 티셔츠 or 운동화 for the default casual look.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating jeans as plural like English. There is no plural; say 청바지 한 벌 ('one pair of jeans'), and 'these jeans' is just 이 청바지.
Saying 청바지를 신어요 — 신다 is for footwear. Trousers take 입다: 청바지를 입어요.
Calling jeans 데님. 데님 is the fabric (denim); the garment is 청바지. 'A denim jacket' would be 청재킷, not 데님.

structuredNuance.t: The standard, completely neutral word for jeans across all ages. Casual register, never formal. Pair it naturally with 티셔츠 or 운동화 for the default casual look.

entries.shortExplanation: 티셔츠 means "t-shirt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 티셔츠 (tisyeocheu) means "t-shirt". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 티셔츠를 입어요. ("I wear a t-shirt."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 티셔츠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: tops take 입다; 를 marks the object
반팔 'half-sleeve' specifies sleeve length, vs 긴팔 'long-sleeve'
thin flat tops are often counted with 장, the counter for flat sheet-like things
A에 B names the classic paired casual outfit

examples.en: In summer I often wear t-shirts.
examples.note: 은 contrasts summer with other seasons; 자주 'often' marks the habit

examples.en: The t-shirt shrank, so I gave it to my younger sibling.
examples.note: 줄어들다 'shrink'; -아서 reason; 주다 'give' takes the recipient with 에게/한테 (here dropped casually)

examples.en: The neckline of this t-shirt has stretched out.
examples.note: 목 here = the collar/neckline; 늘어나다 'stretch out' is the opposite of 줄어들다

entries.nuance: 티셔츠 is a direct loanword from English 'T-shirt' (named for its T shape), and it specifically means a pull-over knit top — most often short-sleeved cotton. The key contrast English speakers miss is 티셔츠 vs 셔츠: in Korean 셔츠 by itself implies a button-up collared shirt (a dress shirt / 와이셔츠), so a casual tee must keep the 티 to stay distinct. Sleeve length is built right into the noun phrase: 반팔 티셔츠 (half-sleeve) vs 긴팔 티셔츠 (long-sleeve). Register is casual and neutral. The pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다, never 신다; (2) thin tees are frequently counted with 장 ('흰 티 한 장' = one plain white tee), though 벌 also works for an outfit; and (3) Koreans clip it to 티 in speech (흰 티, 검은 티), so don't be thrown when the 셔츠 disappears.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 셔츠 for a casual tee. 셔츠 alone suggests a button-up dress shirt; keep 티셔츠 (or 티) for a pull-over t-shirt.
Saying 티셔츠를 신어요 — 신다 is footwear only. A top takes 입다: 티셔츠를 입어요.
Forcing English plural 'two t-shirts' as a plural noun. Say 티셔츠 두 장 / 두 벌 — Korean marks number with a counter, not a plural ending.

entries.shortExplanation: 스웨터 means "sweater" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sweater" is 스웨터 (seuweteo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스웨터를 입어요. ("I wear a sweater."). Watch the particle attached to 스웨터 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: knit tops take 입다; 를 marks the object
목폴라 'turtleneck' specifies the collar type before the noun
보풀이 일어나다 'form lint balls/pills' is the set phrase for knitwear pilling
손빨래(하다) 'hand-wash' — the care verb knitwear usually needs

examples.en: It got cold, so I took out a sweater.
examples.note: -아서 reason; 꺼내다 'take out' (of storage) fits seasonal clothes

examples.en: I layer a shirt under the sweater.
examples.note: 받쳐 입다 'wear underneath as a layer' is the exact verb for layering

examples.en: This sweater is warm but a bit itchy/prickly.
examples.note: -는데 contrasts the two qualities; 따갑다 'prickly' is what wool feels like on skin

entries.nuance: 스웨터 is a loanword from English 'sweater' and names a warm knitted pullover top for cold weather. It sits in a tight cluster of near-synonyms you should separate: 니트 (from 'knit') is the broad fashion word for any knitted top and is currently more trendy in clothing shops; 가디건 (cardigan) is the open-front, button-up knit you wear like a jacket; 스웨터 leans toward the closed pull-over you slip over your head. So a buttoned knit is 가디건, not 스웨터. Register is neutral/casual. Pitfalls for English speakers: (1) the verb is 입다, and layering under it is 받쳐 입다; (2) describe wool's feel with 따갑다 ('prickly') or warmth with 따뜻하다, not a borrowed word; (3) count with 벌, and remember knit care vocabulary like 보풀 (pilling) and 손빨래 (hand-wash) that comes up constantly when shopping for one.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an open button-front knit a 스웨터. That garment is a 가디건; 스웨터 is the closed pull-over type.
Using 개 to count: 스웨터 한 개. A garment takes the set counter 벌 → 스웨터 한 벌.
Saying it's 'warm' as 더워요. 덥다 is for hot weather/feeling hot; a cozy warm sweater is 따뜻하다 → 스웨터가 따뜻해요.

structuredNuance.t: Names a warm knitted pullover top for cold weather; 스웨터 leans toward the closed pull-over you slip over your head. Register is neutral/casual.

entries.shortExplanation: 원피스 means "dress" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 원피스 (wonpiseu) = "dress". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 원피스를 입어요. ("I wear a dress.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 원피스, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: a one-piece garment takes 입다; 를 marks the object
무늬 'pattern' attaches to a noun: 꽃무늬 'flower pattern'
어울리다 'suit/match' is the standard compliment verb for clothes
season + garment is a fixed modifier pattern

examples.en: Today I wore a dress.
examples.note: 은 on 오늘 highlights today as different from usual; simple past with 입다

examples.ko: 이 원피스 너무 예쁜데 좀 비싸요.
examples.romanization: i wonpiseu neomu yeppeunde jom bissayo.
examples.en: This dress is so pretty, but it's a bit pricey.
examples.note: -는데 sets up the 'but'; 예쁘다 is the ㅡ-irregular adjective for 'pretty'

examples.en: I'm going to buy a dress to wear to the wedding.
examples.note: 입을 (future-modifier) + noun = 'a dress to wear'; -려고요 states the intention

entries.nuance: 원피스 is a loanword from English 'one-piece', and that literal sense is the whole point: it's a dress where top and skirt are a single connected garment, as opposed to a 투피스 ('two-piece', a matching top-and-skirt set). The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 원피스 vs 드레스: everyday casual or work dresses are 원피스, while 드레스 in Korean is reserved for a formal gown — a wedding dress (웨딩드레스) or evening gown — so calling your sundress a 드레스 sounds like you're going to a gala. The word is essentially female-coded. Register is neutral. Pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다; (2) compliment the fit with 어울리다 ('it suits you'), the single most useful clothes-shopping verb; (3) count with 벌, and (4) never split a 원피스 into separates — that's literally a 투피스.

Calling a casual dress a 드레스. 드레스 means a formal gown (wedding/evening); an everyday dress is 원피스.
Saying 원피스가 예뻐요 to mean 'it looks good on you'. 예쁘다 describes the dress itself; to say it suits the person use 어울리다 → 원피스가 잘 어울려요.
Using 개 to count: 원피스 한 개. Use the clothing counter 벌 → 원피스 한 벌.

entries.shortExplanation: 반바지 means "shorts" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반바지 (banbaji) means "shorts". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 반바지를 입어요. ("I wear shorts."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반바지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: trousers (short or long) take 입다; 를 marks the object
A에 B names a summery paired outfit
시원하다 'refreshingly cool' is the perfect word for breezy summer clothes
용(用) 'for the purpose of' makes 운동용 'for exercise'

examples.en: When it's hot, I wear shorts.
examples.note: -(으)면 'if/when'; 덥다 ㅂ-irregular → 더우면

examples.en: The shorts are long, reaching down to the knee.
examples.note: -아서 result; 까지 'up to'; 무릎 'knee' is the reference length for shorts

examples.ko: 회사에는 반바지를 입고 가면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeneun banbajireul ipgo gamyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can't wear shorts to the office.
examples.note: -고 가다 'go (while) wearing'; -(으)면 안 되다 'must not' marks the dress-code rule

entries.nuance: 반바지 = 반(半) 'half' + 바지 'trousers' — literally 'half-pants', i.e. trousers cut short, ending around or above the knee, in direct contrast with 긴바지 ('long pants'). It's the standard neutral word for shorts in everyday speech, used for both casual summer wear and athletic shorts. The 반 here is the same Sino-Korean 'half' you meet in 반(half-hour) and 반값(half-price), so the morphology is worth banking. Register is casual; like 청바지 it would read as too informal for an office, which is exactly why dress-code sentences (회사에 반바지는 좀…) come up. Pitfalls for English speakers: (1) shorts are grammatically singular — 반바지 한 벌, never plural and never 'a pair'; (2) the verb is 입다, not 신다; and (3) describe the airy feel with 시원하다 ('cool/breezy'), not 추워요 ('cold'), which would imply the weather, not the comfort.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating shorts as plural like English. No plural form exists; say 반바지 한 벌 and 'these shorts' = 이 반바지.
Saying 반바지를 신어요 — 신다 is footwear only. Shorts take 입다: 반바지를 입어요.
Using 짧은바지 as the normal word. While understandable, the everyday term is the single word 반바지; 긴바지 is its natural opposite.

entries.shortExplanation: 벨트 means "belt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "belt" is 벨트 (belteu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벨트를 매요. ("I fasten a belt."). Watch the particle attached to 벨트 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 매다 'tie/fasten' (or 하다) is the verb for putting on a belt — never 입다
풀다 'undo/loosen' is the natural opposite of 매다
가죽 'leather' as a material modifier sits before the noun
구멍 'hole'; 벨트를 한 칸 줄이다 'take the belt in one notch' is the related phrase

examples.en: I put a belt on my pants.
examples.note: 에 marks where the belt goes; 매다 is the correct verb

examples.ko: 살이 빠져서 벨트를 한 칸 더 조였어요.
examples.romanization: sari ppajyeoseo belteureul han kan deo joyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I lost weight, so I tightened my belt one more notch.
examples.note: 살이 빠지다 'lose weight'; 조이다 'tighten'; 칸 = a notch/slot

examples.en: This belt goes well even with a suit.
examples.note: 에도 'even with'; 어울리다 for matching accessories to an outfit

entries.nuance: 벨트 is a loanword from English 'belt' — the strap worn around the waist to hold up trousers or as an accent, very often leather (가죽). A more traditional native synonym exists, 허리띠 (허리 'waist' + 띠 'band/sash'), which sounds plainer and a touch old-fashioned; in fashion and shopping contexts 벨트 dominates. The single most important point for English speakers is the verb. You do NOT 입다 a belt; you 매다 ('tie/fasten') or, very commonly, 하다 (벨트를 하다 'put a belt on'), and you take it off with 풀다 ('undo'). This 매다/하다 pattern is the same one used for 넥타이 and 스카프 — accessories you fasten rather than slip your body into. Tightening or loosening is counted in 칸 (notches): 벨트를 한 칸 조이다/풀다. Count belts with 개 (벨트 한 개), since they're individual objects, not garment sets.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 벨트를 입어요. 입다 is only for clothes you put your body through. A belt is fastened: 벨트를 매요 / 벨트를 해요.
Using 벗다 to take it off. 벗다 is for taking off worn clothing; for a belt you 풀다 ('undo') → 벨트를 풀어요.
Counting with 벌: 벨트 한 벌. 벌 is for clothing sets; a belt is one object → 벨트 한 개.

entries.shortExplanation: 넥타이 means "necktie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 넥타이 (nektai) = "necktie". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 넥타이를 매요. ("I tie a necktie.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 넥타이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 매다 'tie/knot' (or 하다) is the verb for a tie — never 입다

usagePhrases.en: I loosen / take off the tie.
usagePhrases.note: 풀다 'undo' is the natural opposite of 매다
무늬 'pattern' → 줄무늬 'stripe pattern' modifies the noun
고쳐 매다 'fix and re-tie' = adjust a crooked knot

examples.en: I put on a tie when I go to work.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 'when'; 매다 is the correct verb for tying it

examples.en: The tie has gone a little crooked.
examples.note: 비뚤어지다 'become crooked/askew' is the verb for a knot slipping out of line

examples.ko: 면접 때문에 넥타이를 새로 하나 샀어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop ttaemune nektaireul saero hana sasseoyo.
examples.en: Because of the interview, I bought a new tie.
examples.note: 때문에 'because of'; 하나 'one (item)'; ties are bought for formal occasions

entries.nuance: 넥타이 is a loanword from English 'necktie' — the long strip of cloth knotted at the neck of a dress shirt, standard in business and formal wear and largely male-associated. Korean has no everyday native equivalent, so 넥타이 (often clipped to 타이 in fashion contexts) is simply the word. The decisive thing for English speakers is again the verb: a tie is fastened, so you 매다 ('tie/knot') it or use the catch-all 하다 (넥타이를 하다), and you undo it with 풀다 — using 입다 here is a classic beginner error, because 입다 is strictly for garments you put your torso or legs into. This is the same 매다/하다/풀다 family as 벨트 and 스카프. Adjusting a crooked knot is 고쳐 매다 or describing it as 비뚤어지다 ('go askew'). Count ties with 개 (넥타이 한 개), not the clothing-set counter 벌.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 넥타이를 입어요. A tie isn't put on the body like clothing; it's tied: 넥타이를 매요 / 넥타이를 해요.
Using 벗다 to remove it. Take a tie off with 풀다 ('undo') → 넥타이를 풀어요, the mirror image of 매다.
Counting with 벌. 넥타이 한 벌 is wrong; a single tie is 넥타이 한 개.

entries.shortExplanation: 목걸이 means "necklace" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 목걸이 (mokgeori) means "necklace". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목걸이를 해요. ("I put on a necklace."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목걸이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 is the everyday verb for wearing accessories — not 입다
걸다 'hang' fits literally, since a necklace hangs from the neck
진주 'pearl' names the material before the noun
어울리다 'suit/match' for jewelry paired with an outfit

examples.en: Today I put on a necklace.
examples.note: 은 on 오늘 marks the contrast with usual; 하다 → 했어요 is the natural past

examples.en: I got a necklace from a friend for my birthday.
examples.note: 한테서 'from (a person)'; 받다 'receive' — necklaces are a common gift

examples.en: The necklace chain snapped.
examples.note: 줄 'chain/string'; 끊어지다 'snap/break (of a line)' is the exact verb for a chain breaking

entries.nuance: 목걸이 is, unusually for this list, a pure native Korean word, transparently built from 목 'neck' + 걸이, a noun from 걸다 'to hang' — so literally 'a neck-hanger', the thing you hang around your neck. That etymology is also a memory hook for the verb: you can 걸다 ('hang') a necklace, though the most common everyday verb for putting on any accessory is simply 하다 (목걸이를 하다). The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 입다 ('wear'), which only works for clothing you put your body into; jewelry takes 하다/걸다, removed with 풀다 or 빼다. Register is neutral. Watch the family of related neck/ear words that share 걸이 or a body part: 귀걸이 (ear-ring, 귀 'ear' + 걸이) and 팔찌 (bracelet) all take 하다, not 입다. Count with 개 (목걸이 한 개), and note that the cord is the 줄, which can 끊어지다 ('snap').

Saying 목걸이를 입어요. Jewelry is never 입다; say 목걸이를 해요 (most natural) or 목걸이를 걸어요.
Using 벗다 to take it off. 벗다 is for clothes; remove a necklace with 풀다 or 빼다 → 목걸이를 빼요.
Counting with 벌: 목걸이 한 벌. An accessory is an object → 목걸이 한 개.

entries.shortExplanation: 반지 means "ring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ring" is 반지 (banji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 반지를 껴요. ("I put on a ring."). Watch the particle attached to 반지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: 끼다 'insert (onto a finger)' is the dedicated verb for rings — not 입다 or even 하다
빼다 'pull out/remove' is the natural opposite of 끼다
커플 + item names matching rings worn by a couple

usagePhrases.en: The ring fits the finger perfectly.
usagePhrases.note: 딱 맞다 'fit exactly' for ring sizing

examples.en: I wear a ring on my ring finger.
examples.note: 약지 'ring finger'; 에 marks where; 끼다 is the verb

examples.ko: 반지가 너무 꽉 껴서 안 빠져요.
examples.romanization: banjiga neomu kkwak kkyeoseo an ppajyeoyo.
examples.en: The ring is so tight it won't come off.
examples.note: 꽉 끼다 'fit too tightly'; -아서 reason; 빠지다 'come off/slip out'

examples.en: I gave a ring when I proposed.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 'when'; 주다 'give'; rings carry the engagement meaning here too

entries.nuance: 반지 is the everyday word for a finger ring, a piece of jewelry worn for decoration or as an engagement/couple symbol (커플 반지, 결혼 반지). The verb is the headline for English speakers, and it's special: rings take 끼다 ('to insert/slip onto'), because you slide your finger through them — not 입다 (clothing), not even the general accessory verb 하다 that 목걸이 and 벨트 use. So 반지를 껴요 ('I put on a ring'), removed with 빼다 ('pull out'); a too-tight ring 꽉 끼다 and won't 빠지다 ('come off'). This 끼다 also governs other finger/face items you thread or slot on — 장갑을 끼다 (gloves), 안경을 끼다 (glasses) — so learning it here pays off broadly. Register is neutral. Count rings with 개 (반지 한 개), and place them with 에 on a finger: 손가락에/약지에 반지를 끼다.

Saying 반지를 입어요 or 반지를 해요. A ring uses its own verb 끼다 → 반지를 껴요; 하다 sounds off for rings specifically.
Using 벗다 to remove it. 벗다 is for clothing; pull a ring off with 빼다 → 반지를 빼요.
Saying 반지가 작아요 to mean it's too tight to wear. For the snug fit say 반지가 꽉 껴요 ('the ring fits too tightly'); 작다 just describes the ring's size in the abstract.

entries.shortExplanation: 기쁨 means "joy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기쁨 (gippeum) = "joy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기쁨이 커요 ("The joy is big") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기쁨, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기쁨 ends in a vowel, so the subject marker is 이, not 가
the fixed verb for emotions is 느끼다 'feel', not 가지다 'have'
Koreans 'divide' (나누다) a feeling rather than 'share' it the English way
큰 'big' is the natural adjective for 기쁨, not 높은 'high'

examples.en: I'm really glad
examples.note: the everyday way to express the feeling is the adjective 기쁘다, not the noun 기쁨

examples.en: I felt great joy at the news that I passed
examples.note: 에 marks the trigger of the emotion, like 'at' the news

examples.ko: 아이의 웃음이 부모에게는 가장 큰 기쁨이에요
examples.romanization: aiui useumi bumoegeneun gajang keun gippeumieyo
examples.en: A child's laughter is the greatest joy to parents
examples.note: 에게는 marks the experiencer; this is a heartfelt, almost written register

entries.nuance: 기쁨 is the noun 'joy/gladness', the nominalized form of the adjective 기쁘다 (기쁘 + ㅁ). It names a bright, often momentary delight sparked by a specific good event — passing an exam, a reunion, good news. The near-synonym to separate is 행복 (幸福), 'happiness': 행복 is a broad, lasting state of life ('a happy marriage'), while 기쁨 is the sharp spike of gladness at one happy thing. So you feel 기쁨 about your friend's wedding but wish them lifelong 행복. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the noun in speech: to say 'I'm happy/glad' a Korean almost always uses the adjective 기뻐요, and saves the noun 기쁨 for when it is the subject or object of a sentence (기쁨을 느끼다, 기쁨이 크다). Note too that the verb is 느끼다 'feel', never 가지다 'have'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기쁨이에요 to mean 'I'm glad'. 기쁨 is a noun ('joy'), so that literally says 'It is joy'. To report your own feeling use the adjective: 기뻐요.
Using 행복 and 기쁨 interchangeably. 행복 is a lasting state of well-being; 기쁨 is the burst of gladness at one event. 'I felt 행복 that I passed' sounds odd — use 기쁨 for the moment of good news.

entries.shortExplanation: 슬픔 means "sadness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 슬픔 (seulpeum) means "sadness". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 슬픔이 밀려와요 ("Sadness washes over me"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 슬픔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 슬픔 + 이; 밀려오다 'surge in' is the vivid collocation for waves of feeling
느끼다 'feel' is the fixed verb, not 있다 'have/exist'
슬픔 collocates with 깊은 'deep', mirroring English
에 잠기다 'be submerged in' is an idiom for being lost in an emotion

examples.en: I'm so sad
examples.note: to say you feel sad, use the adjective 슬프다, not the noun

examples.en: I felt great sadness because my pet passed away
examples.note: -아서/어서 gives the cause; 떠나다 'leave' is a gentle euphemism for death

examples.en: That film left a quiet sadness
examples.note: 잔잔한 'calm, gentle' + 슬픔 captures a lingering, bittersweet mood

entries.nuance: 슬픔 is the noun 'sadness/sorrow', built from the adjective 슬프다 (슬프 + ㅁ). It is a heavy, quiet grief that wells up inside — from loss, parting, or disappointment — and it lingers, unlike a flash of irritation. Compare it with 우울 (憂鬱), 'depression/gloom': 우울 is a duller, more clinical low mood with no single cause ('I feel 우울 today for no reason'), whereas 슬픔 is sorrow you can usually point to a reason for. It also differs from 아쉬움, the mild 'too bad / wish it were otherwise' regret. The classic English-speaker mistake is using the noun where the adjective belongs: 'I am sad' is 슬퍼요 (adjective), never 슬픔이에요, which would mean 'It is sadness'. entries.shortExplanation: 분노 means "anger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "anger" is 분노 (bunno). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분노가 치밀다 ("anger surges up"). Watch the particle attached to 분노 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 분노 + 가; 치밀다 'boil/well up' is the set verb for rising rage
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb for the emotion
참다 'endure/suppress' is the habitual partner for restraining 분노
분노 + 의 + noun links the feeling to what shows it

examples.en: I'm so angry
examples.note: in daily speech the everyday phrase is 화가 나다, not the heavy noun 분노

examples.en: I felt anger at the unfair ruling
examples.note: 에 marks the trigger; 분노 suits weighty, public injustices

examples.en: The citizens' anger burst out into the streets
examples.note: this grave, news-style register is exactly where 분노 belongs

entries.nuance: 분노 is the Sino-Korean noun for 'anger/wrath', 분노 憤怒 — 憤 'indignation' + 怒 'rage' — so by its very characters it is righteous, intense fury, not petty annoyance. The crucial contrast for learners is the everyday word 화 (火, literally 'fire'): in conversation Koreans say 화가 나다 'anger arises' or 화를 내다 'show anger' for ordinary irritation, while 분노 is reserved for grave, often moral or collective rage — social injustice, betrayal, public outrage — and shows up in news, speeches, and writing far more than in casual chat. Saying 분노했어요 over a late bus sounds comically overblown; 짜증 났어요 'I got annoyed' or 화가 났어요 fits. The pitfall: English 'angry' is one word covering all intensities, so learners overuse 분노. Match the register — keep 분노 for the heavy stuff and use 화/짜증 for daily friction.

entries.shortExplanation: 두려움 means "fear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 두려움 (duryeoum) = "fear". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 두려움이 밀려와요 ("Fear washes over me") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 두려움 + 이; 밀려오다 conveys fear creeping or surging in
느끼다 'feel' is the standard verb for this inner emotion
이겨내다 'win out over' is the inspiring partner verb
noun + 없이 'without' is the set adverbial phrase

examples.en: I'm scared to sleep alone
examples.note: for plain 'I'm scared' use the adjective 무섭다, not the noun 두려움

examples.en: I felt fear before a new challenge
examples.note: 앞에서 'in front of' frames what you face; 두려움 fits abstract dread

examples.ko: 실패에 대한 두려움이 그를 멈추게 했어요
examples.romanization: silpaee daehan duryeoumi geureul meomchuge haesseoyo
examples.en: Fear of failure made him stop
examples.note: N에 대한 두려움 'fear of/about N' is the standard frame for what is feared

entries.nuance: 두려움 is the noun 'fear/dread', from the adjective 두렵다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 두렵 + 음 → 두려움). Separate two relatives: 무서움/무섭다 is concrete, gut-level scared ('a scary movie', 'the dog is scary'), the word you actually say in conversation, whereas 두려움 is heavier, more abstract and literary, and is the one paired with big life anxieties. A third, 공포 (恐怖), is sheer terror/horror, the genre word for horror films and panic. So a spider triggers 무서움, an uncertain future triggers 두려움, a horror movie deals in 공포. entries.shortExplanation: 외로움 means "loneliness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 외로움 (oeroum) means "loneliness". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 외로움을 타다 ("to be prone to loneliness"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 외로움 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 외로움을 타다 'catch/feel loneliness' is the idiomatic set phrase, like catching a chill
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb
외로움 pairs with 깊은 'deep', as in English
달래다 'comfort/soothe' is the tender partner verb

examples.en: I'm a bit lonely these days
examples.note: for 'I feel lonely' use the adjective 외롭다, not the noun

examples.en: I feel loneliness living away from home
examples.note: 에서 marks the situation that produces the feeling

examples.ko: 사람들 속에서도 외로움을 느낄 때가 있어요
examples.romanization: saramdeul sogeseodo oeroumeul neukkil ttaega isseoyo
examples.en: There are times I feel lonely even amid people
examples.note: 속에서도 'even within' captures the ache of loneliness in a crowd

entries.nuance: 외로움 is the noun 'loneliness', from the adjective 외롭다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 외롭 + 음 → 외로움). It is the empty, aching emotional sense of being cut off from others — a feeling you can have even surrounded by people. The sharp contrast learners need is 혼자 'alone' (just the physical fact of being by oneself, no feeling implied) versus 외로움 (the emotion). You can be 혼자 and perfectly content, or in a crowd and full of 외로움. A subtler neighbor is 고독 (孤獨), 'solitude': 고독 is weightier, often chosen or even noble — the solitude of an artist — while 외로움 is the plain, sad pang of missing connection. A very Korean collocation is 외로움을 타다, literally 'to ride/catch loneliness', meaning someone gets lonely easily. Pitfall: don't equate 외로움 with 혼자 — being alone and feeling lonely are different words, and 'I'm lonely' is the adjective 외로워요, not 외로움이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 그리움 means "longing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "longing" is 그리움 (geurium). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그리움이 사무치다 ("longing pierces deep"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 그리움 + 이; 사무치다 'pierce to the bone' is the literary set verb
느끼다 'feel' is the everyday verb
에 젖다 'be soaked in' is the poetic idiom for being filled with the feeling
그리움 + 의 + noun marks who/what is missed

examples.en: I miss my mom
examples.note: to say 'I miss ___' Koreans use 보고 싶다 'want to see', not the noun 그리움

examples.en: Longing for my hometown washes over me
examples.note: N에 대한 그리움 'longing for N' is the standard frame

examples.ko: 오래된 편지가 그 시절의 그리움을 불러일으켜요
examples.romanization: oraedoen pyeonjiga geu sijeorui geuriumeul bulleoireukyeoyo
examples.en: An old letter stirs up longing for those days
examples.note: 불러일으키다 'stir up/evoke' pairs with deep nostalgic feelings

entries.nuance: 그리움 is the noun 'longing/yearning', from the verb 그리워하다 / adjective 그립다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 그립 + 음 → 그리움). It is a warm, bittersweet ache for someone or somewhere absent — a person far away, a lost time, your hometown — blending sweetness with quiet sorrow, close to English 'nostalgia' when aimed at the past. The key contrast is the everyday verb 보고 싶다, literally 'want to see', which is how Koreans actually say 'I miss you/it' in conversation; 그리움 is the noun naming that emotion and lands more poetic and reflective, common in songs and writing. Save the noun 그리움 for when the feeling itself is the subject or object (그리움이 밀려오다, 그리움을 느끼다), and remember the ㅂ-irregular: 그립다 → 그리워요, 그리움.

entries.shortExplanation: 즐거움 means "enjoyment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 즐거움 (jeulgeoum) = "enjoyment". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 즐거움이 가득하다 ("to be full of enjoyment") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 즐거움, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 즐거움 + 이; 가득하다 'be full' collocates with abundant feeling
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb
누리다 'enjoy, partake of' is the elevated partner verb for pleasures one gets to have
소소한 'small, modest' + 즐거움 is a very common warm collocation

examples.en: I really had fun today
examples.note: for 'it was fun / I had fun' use the adjective 즐겁다, not the noun

examples.en: I felt great enjoyment on the trip
examples.note: 에서 marks the activity that gives the pleasure

examples.ko: 요리는 저에게 소소한 즐거움 중 하나예요
examples.romanization: yorineun jeoege sosohan jeulgeoum jung hanayeyo
examples.en: Cooking is one of my small everyday joys
examples.note: 중 하나 'one among' frames it as a recurring source of pleasure

entries.nuance: 즐거움 is the noun 'enjoyment/fun', from the adjective 즐겁다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 즐겁 + 음 → 즐거움). Draw the line clearly: 기쁨 spikes at a good event (you passed!), while 즐거움 flows from an enjoyable experience (the party was fun). 즐거움 is native Korean, the ㅂ-irregular nominalized form of 즐겁다 (즐겁 + 음 → 즐거움).
Mind the ㅂ-irregular: 즐겁다 → 즐거워요, and the noun is 즐거움, not '즐겁음'.
'Fun' is an adjective in English, so learners say 즐거움이에요 meaning 'it's fun' — but that's the noun ('It is enjoyment'); say 즐거워요 or 재미있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 부끄러움 means "shyness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부끄러움 (bukkeureoum) means "shyness". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부끄러움을 타다 ("to be shy by nature"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부끄러움 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 부끄러움을 타다 'catch shyness' is the idiom for being a shy person
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb
부끄러움이 많다 'have much shyness' describes a bashful personality
도 없이 'without even' intensifies the absence of embarrassment

examples.en: I was so embarrassed when presenting
examples.note: for 'I felt shy/embarrassed' use the adjective 부끄럽다

examples.en: I felt shy at being praised
examples.note: -고 links the cause; blushing-shyness, not moral shame

examples.ko: 그는 부끄러움이 많아서 처음엔 말이 없어요
examples.romanization: geuneun bukkeureoumi manaseo cheoeumen mari eopseoyo
examples.en: He is very shy, so he's quiet at first
examples.note: 부끄러움이 많다 describes a bashful temperament

entries.nuance: 부끄러움 is the noun 'shyness/embarrassment', from the adjective 부끄럽다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽 + 음 → 부끄러움). So a blush at a compliment is 부끄러움, spilling coffee on yourself in front of everyone leans 창피함, and a scandal that destroys your honor is 수치심. A native collocation is 부끄러움을 타다 'to be the shy type', parallel to 외로움을 타다. entries.shortExplanation: 용기 means "courage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "courage" is 용기 (yonggi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 용기가 필요해요 ("Courage is needed"). Watch the particle attached to 용기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 용기 ends in a vowel → 가; 필요하다 'be needed' is the set partner
용기를 내다 'put out courage' is the fixed idiom — not 만들다 'make' or 가지다 'have'
잃다 'lose' is the opposing partner verb
북돋우다 'spur on' is the verb for giving others courage

examples.en: Be brave / Take heart
examples.note: 용기를 내다 is THE everyday phrase for 'work up the nerve'

examples.en: I worked up the courage to confess
examples.note: Verb-ㄹ/을 용기 'the courage to do' modifies 용기 with what you dared

examples.en: Your support gave me courage
examples.note: 용기를 얻다 'gain courage' pairs naturally with encouragement from others

entries.nuance: 용기 is the Sino-Korean noun 'courage/bravery', 용기 勇氣 — 勇 'brave' + 氣 'spirit/energy' — literally 'brave spirit'. Contrast 용기 with 자신감 (自信感) 'confidence/self-assurance': 자신감 is belief in your own ability ('confidence in your English'), built from skill, while 용기 is the nerve to act despite fear, regardless of skill. You also 얻다 'gain' or 잃다 'lose' 용기. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — saying 용기를 가지다 instead of the idiomatic 용기를 내다 — and conflating 'courage' with 'confidence' (자신감), which are distinct in Korean.

Saying 용기를 가지다 or 용기를 만들다 for 'work up courage'. The fixed idiom is 용기를 내다 ('put out courage'), e.g. 용기를 내세요.

Using 용기 for reckless boldness. 용기 is admirable bravery; thoughtless daring is closer to 무모함 ('recklessness'), which is negative.

entries.shortExplanation: 희망 means "hope" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 희망 (huimang) = "hope". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 희망이 있어요 ("There is hope") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 희망, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 희망 + 이; 있다/없다 'there is/isn't' is the core partner
unlike most feelings, 희망 naturally takes 가지다 'have', plus 품다 'cherish'
잃다 'lose' is the standard opposite collocation
희망 + 의 + noun forms set phrases like 희망의 끈 'a thread of hope'

examples.en: There's still hope
examples.note: 있다 'exist' is the everyday verb; 아직 'still' is a frequent companion

examples.en: I hold hope for the future
examples.note: N에 대한 희망 'hope for/about N' is the standard frame for what is hoped for

examples.en: Don't let go of that small thread of hope
examples.note: 희망의 끈 'thread of hope' + 놓다 'let go' is a set encouraging idiom

entries.nuance: 희망 is the Sino-Korean noun 'hope', 희망 希望 — 希 'wish/hope for' + 望 'gaze into the distance, aspire' — so its very characters paint hope as gazing toward something wished for. It is a bright, forward-looking expectation that good things will come, weightier and more enduring than a casual wish, and it gives comfort and strength in hard times. Separate it from two relatives. 소원 (所願) is a specific 'wish' you make — the one wish on a shooting star or a birthday candle — concrete and singular, whereas 희망 is broader, an outlook on the future. 기대 (期待) is 'expectation/anticipation', leaning toward something you fairly confidently await ('I have high 기대 for the movie'), while 희망 keeps the sense of hoping for an uncertain but desired outcome. A notable point of grammar: although feelings usually take 느끼다, 희망 prefers 가지다 'have', 품다 'cherish', or 있다/없다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 희망 for a small, immediate wish where 소원 or the grammar pattern -았으면 좋겠다 'I wish that…' is natural, e.g. for 'I hope it doesn't rain' Koreans say 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요, not a sentence built on 희망.

entries.shortExplanation: 추억 means "memory" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 추억 (chueok) means "memory". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 추억이 떠오르다 ("a memory comes to mind"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 추억 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 추억 + 이; 떠오르다 'float up' is the set verb for memories surfacing
추억을 만들다 'make memories' is the exact, very common collocation
에 잠기다 'be submerged in' is the idiom for reminiscing
추억 + 의 + noun marks a spot tied to fond recollection

examples.en: I have many good memories
examples.note: 추억 collocates with 좋은 'good' and 많다 'be many'

examples.en: We made many memories traveling together
examples.note: 추억을 만들다 'make memories' — the natural verb is 만들다, never 하다

examples.ko: 이 노래를 들으면 학창 시절 추억에 잠겨요
examples.romanization: i noraereul deureumyeon hakchang sijeol chueoge jamgyeoyo
examples.en: When I hear this song I sink into memories of my school days
examples.note: 추억에 잠기다 captures dwelling in fond nostalgia

entries.nuance: 추억 is the Sino-Korean noun for a 'cherished memory', 추억 追憶 — 追 'pursue, trace back' + 憶 'recollect' — so literally 'tracing back a recollection', a warm act of looking fondly on the past. The vital contrast is with 기억 (記憶), 'memory' in the neutral, factual sense: 기억 is your mental record of any information — a phone number, where you parked, what someone said — and can be good or bad, while 추억 is specifically a treasured, emotionally warm past experience you reminisce about. So you 기억하다 'remember' a fact, but you 추억을 만들다 'make memories' on a trip and look back on 좋은 추억 'good memories' from childhood. A signature collocation is 추억을 만들다 'make memories', built with 만들다, not 하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 추억 for ordinary remembering — 'Do you remember his name?' must use 기억 (그 사람 이름 기억나요?), because 추억 implies sentiment and a whole experience, not mere recall.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 추억 for plain factual memory. 'Do you remember the password?' needs 기억 (기억나요?), not 추억, which means a fond, sentimental past experience.
Saying 추억을 하다 for 'make memories'. The fixed verb is 만들다: 추억을 만들다. To reminisce, use 추억에 잠기다 or 추억을 떠올리다.
Calling a bad event a 추억. 추억 carries warmth; an unpleasant thing you recall is just a 기억 (안 좋은 기억) or 일.

entries.shortExplanation: 감정 means "emotion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "emotion" is 감정 (gamjeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 감정이 상하다 ("to get one's feelings hurt"). Watch the particle attached to 감정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 감정이 상하다 'feelings spoil' is the fixed idiom for being hurt/offended
표현하다 'express' is the natural partner verb
숨기다 'hide/conceal' is the common opposite collocation
감정 + 의 + noun links the feeling to its shift

examples.en: My feelings got hurt
examples.note: 감정이 상하다 is THE set phrase for feeling hurt or offended

examples.ko: 저는 감정 표현을 잘 안 해요
examples.romanization: jeoneun gamjeong pyohyeoneul jal an haeyo
examples.en: I don't really express my emotions
examples.note: 감정 표현 'emotional expression' is a common compound noun

examples.en: There are times feeling runs ahead of reason
examples.note: 감정 vs 이성 'reason' is the classic paired contrast

entries.nuance: 감정 is the Sino-Korean cover term for 'emotion/feeling', 감정 感情 — 感 'feel, sense' + 情 'feeling, affection' — the umbrella under which 기쁨, 슬픔, 분노 and the rest all sit, broader than any single mood. Two contrasts matter. Against 기분 (氣分), 'mood/how you feel right now': 기분 is the transient, surface state of the moment — 기분이 좋아요 'I'm in a good mood', 기분 나빠 'that bugs me' — and it is what you use in everyday chat, whereas 감정 is the deeper, more general category of human emotion and sounds more analytical. Against 이성 (理性), 'reason/rationality': 감정 vs 이성 is the standard 'heart vs head' pairing in Korean. The signature idiom is 감정이 상하다, literally 'the feelings spoil', meaning to get hurt or offended — a phrase learners must know. The English-speaker pitfall: for everyday 'I feel good/bad' do not say 감정이 좋아요; the natural sentence is 기분이 좋아요. Reserve 감정 for talking about emotions in general, expressing/hiding them (감정을 표현하다/숨기다), or being hurt (감정이 상하다).

Missing the idiom 감정이 상하다 ('to get hurt/offended') and instead saying 감정이 아프다 ('emotion hurts'), which is unnatural for offense.
Treating 감정 as one specific feeling. 감정 is the umbrella term; to name an actual feeling, use 기쁨, 슬픔, 화 etc. '복잡한 감정' (mixed emotions) is fine, but a single feeling is better named directly.

entries.shortExplanation: 식사 means "meal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 식사 (siksa) = "meal". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 식사를 해요 ("I have a meal") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 식사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 식사하다 is the verb; 를 marks the meal as object
subject 가 — the meal itself is delayed
honorific -시- greeting to elders
준비하다 = prepare; sets the table/cooks

examples.en: Let's eat together.
examples.note: casual invite; 식사하다 fuses noun + 하다

examples.en: Today's meal was really delicious.
examples.note: compliment to the cook; past tense

examples.en: Director, have you eaten yet?
examples.note: standard polite greeting up the hierarchy

entries.nuance: 식사 食事 (literally 'eat-affair') is the dignified, Sino-Korean word for a meal, while 밥 is the plain native word that also literally means cooked rice. The dividing line is register, not meaning: with friends or children you say 밥 먹었어? but to a boss, an elder, or a customer you switch to 식사하셨어요?, which sounds respectful and adult. 식사 pairs naturally with 하다 (식사하다), 준비하다, 대접하다 (treat someone to a meal). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the verb 식사를 먹다; Korean treats 식사 as an activity, so you either say 식사하다 or, more plainly, 밥을 먹다 — never 식사를 먹다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 식사를 먹어요. 식사 already implies eating, so it takes 하다: 식사해요, or use 밥을 먹어요 instead.
Greeting a close friend with 식사하셨어요? — it sounds stiffly formal; with peers say 밥 먹었어?
Treating 식사 as countable like 'three meals'. Koreans count meals with 끼: 하루 세 끼 (three meals a day), not 세 식사.

밥 is the plain native word that also literally means cooked rice. The dividing line is register, not meaning: with friends or children you say 밥 먹었어?, but to a boss, an elder, or a customer you switch to 식사하셨어요?, which sounds respectful and adult.

The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the verb 식사를 먹다. Korean treats 식사 as an activity, so you either say 식사하다 or, more plainly, 밥을 먹다 — never 식사를 먹다.

entries.shortExplanation: 소금 means "salt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 소금 (sogeum) means "salt". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 소금을 넣어요 ("I add salt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 소금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = put in; 을 marks the salt
subject 이 — the food is over-salted
조금 = a little, softens the amount
좀 + 주세요 = soft polite request

examples.en: I add a little salt to the soup.
examples.note: cooking action with 에 (into the soup)

examples.en: This food is a bit salty.
examples.note: describe taste with 짜다, not 소금이 많다

examples.en: If it's bland, add more salt.
examples.note: conditional -으면; 더 = more

entries.nuance: 소금 is plain native-Korean table salt, the baseline seasoning whose taste is 짜다 (salty). Don't confuse the substance with the flavor: the food is described as 짜요 (salty) or 싱거워요 (bland/under-seasoned), while 소금 is the thing you add to fix bland food. Its constant opposite in the kitchen is 설탕 (sugar), and the two look and pour alike, which is exactly the running joke when a cook grabs the wrong jar. 소금 collocates with 넣다, 뿌리다 (sprinkle), 치다 (toss salt on), and 간을 하다 (season to taste). The English-speaker trap is the particle on requests: say 소금 좀 주세요, not 소금을 주세요 with full force — the bare 소금 + 좀 sounds far more natural and polite at a table.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이 음식은 소금이 많아요 to mean 'salty'. Natural Korean uses the adjective: 이 음식은 짜요.
Confusing 소금 (salt) with 설탕 (sugar) — they sit side by side; taste-check before adding.
Using 소금을 주세요 stiffly. At the table, 소금 좀 주세요 is the warm, idiomatic request.

Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = put in; 을 marks the sugar
but for taste prefer the adjective 달다

usagePhrases.en: I add a lot of sugar
usagePhrases.note: 많이 = a lot, adverb before the verb
없이 = without (no particle after it)

examples.en: I add sugar to the coffee.
examples.note: 에 marks the drink it goes into

examples.ko: 저는 단 거 별로 안 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun dan geo byeollo an joahaeyo.
examples.en: I don't really like sweet things.
examples.note: express preference with 단 거, not 설탕

examples.en: This bread is too sweet.
examples.note: describe taste with 달다, not 설탕이 많다

entries.nuance: 설탕 雪糖 (literally 'snow-sugar', for its white crystals) is refined white sugar; the taste it gives is 달다 (sweet). As with salt, separate the substance from the flavor — food is 달아요 (sweet), and 설탕 is what makes it so. Korean savory cooking quietly uses a spoon of 설탕 to round off salty-spicy sauces, so 설탕 is a normal pantry item, not just for dessert. Its kitchen partner-opposite is 소금, and it collocates with 넣다, 뿌리다, and 타다 (dissolve sugar into a drink). A frequent English-speaker pitfall: to say a dish 'is sweet' use 달아요, not 설탕이 많아요, which oddly reports the ingredient amount rather than the taste.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이 빵은 설탕이 많아요 for 'this bread is sweet'. Say 달아요 — describe the taste, not the dose.
Mixing up 설탕 (sugar) with 소금 (salt); both are white powders, so confirm before adding.
Forgetting 없이 takes no particle: it's 설탕 없이, never 설탕을 없이.

entries.shortExplanation: 간장 means "soy sauce" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 간장 (ganjang) = "soy sauce". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 간장을 넣어요 ("I add soy sauce") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 간장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the sauce
subject 이 + adjective 짜다

usagePhrases.en: I dip it in soy sauce
usagePhrases.note: 찍다 = dip; 에 marks the dipping target
붓다 (ㅅ-irregular) → 부어요

examples.en: I dip the dumplings in soy sauce.
examples.note: 찍어 먹다 = dip-and-eat, one motion

examples.en: This soy sauce is a bit salty.
examples.note: describe with 짜다

examples.en: I add a spoonful of soy sauce to the dish.
examples.note: 한 숟갈 = one spoonful

entries.nuance: 간장 (the 간 here is the native root meaning 'saltiness/seasoning', not a hanja for liver) is dark fermented soy sauce that delivers a deep savory saltiness plain 소금 can't reach. Two real types matter in a Korean kitchen: 국간장 (light, for seasoning soups) versus 진간장/양조간장 (darker, for stir-fries and braises and as a dip), so 'soy sauce' is really a small family. It collocates with 찍다 (dip), 넣다, 붓다, 조리다 (braise in soy sauce), and 졸이다. The English-speaker pitfall is the dipping particle: you dip food INTO sauce with 에 — 간장에 찍다 — not 간장을 찍다; and note 붓다 is ㅅ-irregular, dropping the ㅅ to give 부어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 간장을 찍어요 for dipping. The sauce is the destination: 간장에 찍어 먹어요.
Calling 간장 sweet. Its defining taste is salty/savory — 짜다 — though braises add sugar.
Conjugating 붓다 as 붓어요. It is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요 (pour).

entries.shortExplanation: 고추장 means "red chili paste" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 고추장 (gochujang) means "red chili paste". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고추장을 넣어요 ("I add chili paste"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고추장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the paste
맵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 매워요

usagePhrases.en: I mix it with chili paste
usagePhrases.note: 비비다 = mix; 에 marks what you mix into
바르다 (르-irregular) → 발라요

examples.en: I add chili paste to bibimbap.
examples.note: 에 marks the dish it goes into

examples.en: This chili paste is really spicy.
examples.note: 매워요 from ㅂ-irregular 맵다

examples.en: I mix rice with chili paste and eat it.
examples.note: 비벼 먹다 = mix-and-eat

entries.nuance: 고추장 (고추 'chili pepper' + 장 醬 'fermented paste') is thick red fermented chili paste — spicy 맵다 but with an underlying sweetness and fermented depth, so it isn't just 'hot'. Keep it apart from its jar-mate 된장 (brown soybean paste, savory not spicy) and from 고춧가루 (dry chili powder); all three live in Korean cooking but do different jobs. 고추장 collocates with 비비다 (mix into rice), 넣다, 풀다 (dissolve into stew), and 찍다 (dip lettuce/cucumber). Two conjugation traps hide here: the partner verbs 맵다 (→ 매워요, ㅂ-irregular) and 바르다 (→ 발라요, 르-irregular) both shift stems, and you mix rice 고추장에 비벼요 with 에, not 고추장을.

Treating 고추장 and 된장 as the same paste. 고추장 is red and spicy; 된장 is brown, salty-savory soybean paste.
Saying 맵어요. 맵다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 매워요.
Confusing 고추장 (the paste) with 고춧가루 (dry chili powder) — different texture and use.

entries.shortExplanation: 된장 means "soybean paste" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "soybean paste" is 된장 (doenjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 된장을 풀어요 ("I dissolve soybean paste"). Watch the particle attached to 된장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 풀다 = dissolve/loosen into liquid
subject 이 + 짜다
으로 = with/using (instrument)
넣다 = add

examples.en: Mom makes stew with soybean paste.
examples.note: 으로 marks 된장 as the means

examples.en: This soybean paste is a bit salty.
examples.note: taste check with 짜다

examples.en: I dissolve soybean paste into the broth.
examples.note: 풀다 = stir paste until it spreads

entries.nuance: 된장 (된 'thick/stiff' + 장 醬 'fermented paste') is brown fermented soybean paste with a deep, salty, almost cheesy umami; it is the backbone of 된장찌개, perhaps the most everyday Korean stew. The key verb is 풀다 (literally 'loosen'): because the paste is dense, you don't just drop it in, you stir it until it dissolves through the broth — 된장을 물에 풀다. Don't mix it up with red 고추장 (spicy chili paste) or with Japanese-style miso, which is milder and sweeter. 된장 collocates with 풀다, 끓이다, 넣다, and 으로/로 (cook WITH it). The English-speaker pitfall is the instrument particle: 된장으로 끓이다 (because 된장 ends in a consonant it takes 으로, not 로).

Confusing 된장 (brown, savory) with 고추장 (red, spicy). Different color, different taste.
Saying 된장을 넣다 and stopping. For stew you 풀다 — stir it until it dissolves through the broth.
Using 된장로. After a final consonant the instrument particle is 으로: 된장으로 끓여요.

entries.shortExplanation: 식초 means "vinegar" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 식초 (sikcho) = "vinegar". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 식초를 넣어요 ("I add vinegar") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 를 marks the vinegar
시다 → 시어요 (sour)
조금 = a little
섞다 = mix together

examples.en: I add a little vinegar to the cold noodles.
examples.note: 에 marks the dish

examples.en: This vinegar is too sour.
examples.note: describe with 시다

examples.ko: 식초 한 숟가락 넣으면 더 새콤해요.
examples.romanization: sikcho han sutgarang neoeumyeon deo saekomhaeyo.
examples.en: Add one spoon of vinegar and it gets tangier.
examples.note: 새콤하다 = pleasantly tangy

entries.nuance: 식초 食醋 (literally 'food-vinegar') is sour vinegar used to give food a fresh, sharp tang. Its core taste word is 시다 (sour), but Koreans often prefer the softer, appetizing 새콤하다 ('pleasantly tangy'), which carries a positive nuance that plain 시다 lacks — vinegar in cold noodles or pickles is 새콤해요, not merely 셔요. It collocates with 넣다, 섞다, 치다 (splash vinegar on), and the flavor pair 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour). The English-speaker pitfall is conjugating 시다: the 요-form is 시어요/셔요, not 'sieyo' as a literal vowel-by-vowel reading might suggest, and learners often default to 'sour' = 시다 when describing dressed dishes, where 새콤하다 sounds far more natural and tasty.

Expecting 식초 to be sweet. Its defining taste is sour — 시다.
Describing dressed cold noodles only as 셔요. The tastier, idiomatic word is 새콤해요 (pleasantly tangy).
Forgetting 식초 ends in a vowel, so the object particle is 를: 식초를 넣어요, not 식초을.
