entries.shortExplanation: 후추 means "pepper (black pepper)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 후추 (huchu) means "pepper (black pepper)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후추를 뿌려요 ("I sprinkle pepper"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후추 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 뿌리다 = sprinkle/scatter; 를 marks pepper
맵다 → 매워요
조금 = a little
좀 + 주세요 polite request

examples.en: I sprinkle pepper on the meat.
examples.note: 에 marks the surface; 뿌리다 = scatter on top

examples.en: This soup has a strong peppery taste.
examples.note: 후추 맛 = pepper flavor

examples.en: Pass me the pepper, please.
examples.note: at the table; bare noun + 좀

entries.nuance: 후추 (originally from 호초 胡椒, 'foreign/barbarian pepper', reflecting that black pepper came via the Silk Road) is ground black pepper that gives a sharp, warm, slightly numbing pungency. The crucial contrast is 후추 (black pepper) versus 고추 (chili pepper) and 고춧가루 (chili powder): they sound alike to beginners but are botanically unrelated and taste different — 후추 is woody and aromatic, 고추 is fiery red heat. 후추 collocates with 뿌리다 (its signature verb — you sprinkle it on at the end), 넣다, 갈다 (grind), and 후추 맛/향 (pepper taste/aroma). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly the 후추/고추 mix-up, plus reaching for 넣다 when the natural finishing verb is 뿌리다, scattering it over the top.

Confusing 후추 (black pepper) with 고추 (chili pepper). One is a brown ground spice, the other a red hot vegetable.
Saying 후추를 넣어요 for a final sprinkle. The idiomatic verb is 뿌리다 — 후추를 뿌려요.
Using 후추을. 후추 ends in a vowel, so the particle is 를: 후추를.

entries.shortExplanation: 양념 means "seasoning; marinade" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "seasoning; marinade" is 양념 (yangnyeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 양념을 만들어요 ("I make the seasoning"). Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 만들다 = make; 을 marks the seasoning mix
맵다 → 매워요

usagePhrases.en: I marinate it in the seasoning
usagePhrases.note: 재우다 = let marinate; 에 marks the bath
넣다 = add

examples.en: Mom makes the marinade for the meat.
examples.note: 고기 양념 = seasoning for meat

examples.en: This seasoning is a bit spicy.
examples.note: describe with 맵다

examples.en: I marinate the chicken in the seasoning.
examples.note: 재우다 = leave to soak up flavor

entries.nuance: 양념 is the native-Korean word for a whole blend of seasonings — soy sauce, garlic, sesame oil, sugar, chili — mixed to flavor a dish, NOT a single spice. This is the key contrast: one spice is a 향신료 or just its name (소금, 후추), but the prepared mixture you rub or pour on is 양념. The word also signals a style: 양념치킨 is chicken coated in sweet-spicy 양념 sauce, opposite 후라이드 (plain fried). 양념 collocates with 만들다 (make), 무치다 (toss/dress vegetables in it), 재우다 (marinate), 바르다 (brush on), and the verb 양념하다 (to season). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 양념 = one spice; if you only added salt, that's not really 양념 — 양념 implies a composed blend, and you marinate IN it with 에 (양념에 재우다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 양념 means a single spice. It's a blended seasoning/marinade; one spice is its own name (소금, 후추).
Saying 양념을 재워요. You marinate the food IN seasoning: 닭고기를 양념에 재워요.
Forgetting the verb form 양념하다 (to season), distinct from just naming the noun 양념.

The pitfall is assuming 양념 = one spice; if you only added salt, that's not really 양념 — 양념 implies a composed blend, and you marinate IN it with 에 (양념에 재우다).

entries.shortExplanation: 국물 means "broth; soup liquid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 국물 (gungmul) = "broth; soup liquid". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 국물을 마셔요 ("I drink the broth") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 국물, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 마시다 = drink; 을 marks the liquid
뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 뜨거워요
시원하다 here = soothing, not cold
더 = more

examples.en: I drank up all the ramyeon broth.
examples.note: 다 = all the way; 마시다 for liquid

examples.en: This broth is really soothing.
examples.note: hot soup that feels good going down

examples.en: The broth is still hot, so be careful.
examples.note: -니까 = because; warning

entries.nuance: 국물 (국 'soup' + 물 'water') is the liquid part of a soup or stew, as opposed to the 건더기 (the solid pieces) — that pair is the contrast to know. Its most famous quirk is the word 시원하다: applied to a steaming hot broth, 시원해요 does NOT mean cold — it means the hot liquid feels refreshing, clearing, soothing, the way a hot bath or a sip of hot soup makes you exhale 'ahh'. 국물 collocates with 마시다 (drink — you drink broth, you don't 먹다 it), 우러나다 (flavor steeps out), 진하다 (rich/concentrated), and 시원하다/뜨겁다. The headline English-speaker pitfall is hearing 시원한 국물 and translating 'cold broth' — for liquid you actually drink, use 마시다, and read 시원하다 as 'soothing'.

Translating 시원한 국물 as 'cold broth'. For hot soup it means refreshing/soothing as it goes down.
Saying 국물을 먹어요. Broth is a liquid you 마시다 (drink): 국물을 마셔요.
Conjugating 뜨겁다 as 뜨겁어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 뜨거워요.

entries.shortExplanation: 밀가루 means "flour" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 밀가루 (milgaru) means "flour". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 밀가루를 사요 ("I buy flour"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 밀가루 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 사다 = buy; 를 marks flour
하얗다 (ㅎ-irregular) → 하얘요
반죽하다 = make dough
로 = with/from (밀가루 ends in vowel)

examples.en: Bread is made from flour.
examples.note: 로 marks flour as the material

examples.en: I dissolve the flour in water.
examples.note: 풀다 = mix powder into liquid

examples.en: I like flour-based foods.
examples.note: 밀가루 음식 = noodles, bread, dumplings, etc.

entries.nuance: 밀가루 (밀 'wheat' + 가루 'powder') is specifically wheat flour. The compound is transparent — '가루' means any fine powder, so 쌀가루 is rice flour, 콩가루 bean powder, 고춧가루 chili powder — which means 밀가루 by itself always implies WHEAT, and you can't use it generically for 'flour' from other grains. Culturally, 밀가루 음식 (wheat-based food: noodles, bread, fritters) is a whole category often set against 밥 (rice meals). It collocates with 반죽하다 (knead into dough), 풀다 (dissolve into liquid), 묻히다 (coat food in flour), and 로 (made from flour). The English-speaker pitfall is using 밀가루 as a catch-all for 'flour': if it's rice flour you must say 쌀가루, and the material particle after the vowel-final 밀가루 is 로, not 으로.

Using 밀가루 for any flour. It specifically means wheat flour; rice flour is 쌀가루.
Saying 밀가루으로. After the vowel ㅜ the particle is 로: 밀가루로 만들어요.
Conjugating 하얗다 as 하얗아요. It is ㅎ-irregular: 하얘요 (is white).

entries.shortExplanation: 참기름 means "sesame oil" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sesame oil" is 참기름 (chamgireum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 참기름을 넣어요 ("I add sesame oil"). Watch the particle attached to 참기름 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the oil
고소하다 = warm nutty flavor
두르다 (르-irregular) → 둘러요
바르다 (르-irregular) → 발라요

examples.en: I add sesame oil to the bibimbap.
examples.note: finishing touch; 에 marks the dish

examples.en: This seasoned vegetable smells nicely of sesame oil.
examples.note: 참기름 향 = sesame-oil aroma

examples.en: I drizzle a drop of sesame oil on the rice.
examples.note: 한 방울 = one drop; 두르다 = drizzle around

entries.nuance: 참기름 (참 'true/genuine' + 기름 'oil') is fragrant toasted sesame oil, prized for finishing dishes — added at the very end for aroma, not used for high-heat frying. Note the 참 prefix means 'true/real', distinguishing it from 들기름 (perilla oil), its closest cousin: both are nutty finishing oils, but 참기름 is from sesame and rounder, 들기름 from perilla leaves and grassier/sharper. Its signature taste word is 고소하다, that warm toasty-nutty quality English has no single word for. 참기름 collocates with 넣다, 두르다 (drizzle around), 바르다 (brush on seaweed/meat), and the aroma noun 향. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't use 참기름 to deep-fry (it's a finishing oil, and it burns), and both partner verbs 두르다 and 바르다 are 르-irregular, becoming 둘러요 and 발라요.

Using 참기름 to deep-fry. It's a finishing/aroma oil added at the end; use 식용유 for frying.
Confusing 참기름 (sesame oil) with 들기름 (perilla oil) — related nutty oils, but different seeds and flavor.
Conjugating 두르다 as 두르어요. It is 르-irregular: 둘러요 (drizzle around).

entries.shortExplanation: 거실 means "living room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 거실 (geosil) = "living room". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 거실이 넓어요. ("The living room is spacious.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 거실, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 거실 + 이 because the word ends in a consonant; subject of a description

usagePhrases.en: There is a TV in the living room.
usagePhrases.note: static existence uses 에, not 에서

usagePhrases.en: I rest in the living room.
usagePhrases.note: an action happens here, so 에서 replaces 에
거실 as a direct object takes 을

examples.en: This is the living room.
examples.note: simplest 이다 sentence introducing a room to a guest

examples.en: The family gathers in the living room and watches TV.
examples.note: everyday: 거실 collocates with 모이다 (gather) and 텔레비전을 보다

examples.ko: 손님이 오면 거실로 안내해서 소파에 앉으시게 해요.
examples.romanization: sonnimi omyeon geosillo annaehaeseo sopae anjeusige haeyo.
examples.en: When guests come, I show them to the living room and seat them on the sofa.
examples.note: real situation: direction 로 (to the living room) + honorific 앉으시다

entries.nuance: 거실 is the shared 'living/common' room of a Korean home — the social hub where the family relaxes together and where guests are received, almost always centred on a 소파 and a TV. It is Sino-Korean: 居室, literally 居 'to dwell/reside' + 室 'room', so the feel is 'the room you live in (together)'. Contrast it with 응접실 (應接室, a formal parlour for receiving visitors), which sounds old-fashioned and upper-class today, and with 방, the generic word for any closed 'room/bedroom'; 거실 specifically names the open central area. Register is fully neutral — children and adults alike say 거실. The big English-speaker pitfall is location particles: because a TV simply sits there you say 거실에 텔레비전이 있어요 (에 = existence), but because you *do* something there you switch to 거실에서 쉬어요 (에서 = action). Mixing these up (거실에서 텔레비전이 있어요) is the single most common error.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 거실에서 소파가 있어요 to mean 'there is a sofa in the living room'. Existence/location of a thing takes 에 (거실에 소파가 있어요); 에서 only marks the place where an action occurs.
Calling the living room 방. 방 means a closed private room (often a bedroom); the open central area is specifically 거실. Use 거실, not 방, for the family room.
Treating 거실 as 'house' and saying 거실에 가요 for 'I'm going home'. To go home you say 집에 가요; 거실 is just one room inside the 집.

structuredNuance.t: 거실 is the shared 'living/common' room of a Korean home — the social hub where the family relaxes together and where guests are received, almost always centred on a 소파 and a TV. Register is fully neutral — children and adults alike say 거실.

entries.shortExplanation: 침실 means "bedroom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 침실 (chimsil) means "bedroom". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 침실이 조용해요. ("The bedroom is quiet."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 침실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 침실 + 이 as subject of a quality

usagePhrases.en: There is a bed in the bedroom.
usagePhrases.note: existence of furniture uses 에
sleeping is an action, so 에서
침실 as object takes 을

examples.en: This is my parents' bedroom.
examples.note: simple 이다 sentence labelling a room

examples.ko: 저는 보통 밤 열한 시에 침실에 들어가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun botong bam yeolhan sie chimsire deureogayo.
examples.en: I usually go into the bedroom at eleven at night.
examples.note: everyday: 침실에 들어가다 (enter), time with 에

examples.ko: 아기가 깰까 봐 침실에서는 발소리를 죽여요.
examples.romanization: agiga kkaelkka bwa chimsireseoneun balsorireul jugyeoyo.
examples.en: Afraid the baby might wake, I tread silently in the bedroom.
examples.note: real situation: topic-marked 에서는 + 발소리를 죽이다 idiom

entries.nuance: 침실 is the private 'sleeping room', Sino-Korean 寢室 from 寢 'to sleep/lie down' + 室 'room' — so literally 'sleep-room', which makes its core meaning easy to remember. It names the room by its function (sleeping), whereas the everyday word 방 is the neutral term for any room and is what Koreans most often say in casual speech ('내 방' = my room) even when they mean their bedroom; 침실 sounds slightly more formal or descriptive, the word you'd see on a floor plan or in a real-estate ad (안방 = the main/master bedroom). Do not confuse it with 거실 (the shared living room) — 침 vs 거 is the whole difference. The English-speaker pitfall is again the 에 / 에서 split: the bed *is there* (침실에 침대가 있어요, existence → 에) but you *sleep* there (침실에서 자요, action → 에서). Also note Koreans rarely say '내 침실'; 내 방 is far more natural for 'my bedroom'.

Saying 침실에서 침대가 있어요. The bed's existence takes 에 (침실에 침대가 있어요); reserve 에서 for actions like 자다 or 쉬다.
Insisting on 침실 in casual conversation. To say 'I'm going to my room/bed', Koreans say 내 방에 가요, not 내 침실에 가요 — 방 is the natural everyday word.
Confusing 침실 with 거실. They look alike but 침(寢) = sleep and 거(居) = dwell; 침실 is the bedroom, 거실 is the family living room.

entries.shortExplanation: 베란다 means "balcony" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "balcony" is 베란다 (beranda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 베란다가 넓어요. ("The balcony is spacious."). Watch the particle attached to 베란다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 베란다 ends in a vowel, so subject 가

usagePhrases.en: There are flowerpots on the balcony.
usagePhrases.note: existence of objects uses 에

usagePhrases.en: I dry laundry on the balcony.
usagePhrases.note: drying is an action → 에서
베란다 as object takes 를 after a vowel

examples.en: That apartment has a big balcony.
examples.note: simple description with 가

examples.ko: 엄마는 베란다에서 고추를 말리고 화분도 키워요.
examples.romanization: eommaneun berandaeseo gochureul malligo hwabundo kiwoyo.
examples.en: Mum dries chillies and grows potted plants on the balcony.
examples.note: everyday: classic 베란다 uses — drying food and 화분 키우다

examples.ko: 겨울에는 베란다 문을 닫아서 찬 바람이 안 들어오게 해요.
examples.romanization: gyeoureneun beranda muneul dadaseo chan barami an deureooge haeyo.
examples.en: In winter we shut the balcony door so the cold wind can't get in.
examples.note: real situation: 닫다 + causative '~게 하다' for keeping cold out

entries.nuance: 베란다 is a loanword (from English 'veranda'), so there is no hanja — and that loan path creates the main pitfall: in Korean apartments 베란다 actually refers to what English calls a *balcony/utility deck*, the enclosed strip off the living room where families keep 화분 (potted plants), dry 빨래 (laundry) and 고추 (chillies), and store overflow. Technically architects distinguish 발코니 (balcony) from 베란다 and from 테라스 (terrace, a ground-level open deck), but in ordinary speech most Koreans just say 베란다 for that apartment space. Contrast it with 마당, the open *yard/ground* of a detached house — 베란다 hangs off an upper-floor flat, 마당 is earth you stand on. Register is fully neutral. Watch the particles: plants simply sit there (베란다에 화분이 있어요, 에) but laundry is actively dried there (베란다에서 빨래를 말려요, 에서); and because it ends in a vowel the subject marker is 가, not 이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이 after the vowel: writing 베란다이 넓어요. After a vowel use 가 (베란다가 넓어요). The 이/가 choice follows the final sound.
Equating 베란다 with 마당. 베란다 is the deck off an apartment; 마당 is the open ground/yard of a house. They are different spaces — pick by housing type.
Saying 베란다에서 화분이 있어요 for 'there are pots on the balcony'. Existence takes 에 (베란다에 화분이 있어요); 에서 is for the action of drying, watering, etc.

entries.shortExplanation: 현관 means "entrance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 현관 (hyeongwan) = "entrance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 현관이 좁아요. ("The entrance is narrow.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 현관, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 현관 + 이 as subject

usagePhrases.en: There are shoes at the entrance.
usagePhrases.note: shoes exist there → 에

usagePhrases.en: I take off my shoes at the entrance.
usagePhrases.note: taking off is an action → 에서
현관 as object takes 을

examples.en: This is the entryway.
examples.note: simple labelling sentence

examples.ko: 집에 들어올 때는 현관에서 신발을 벗어요.
examples.romanization: jibe deureool ttaeneun hyeongwaneseo sinbareul beoseoyo.
examples.en: When entering the house, we take our shoes off at the entrance.
examples.note: everyday: the core Korean custom, 들어올 때 + 벗다

examples.ko: 택배는 그냥 현관 앞에 놓고 가 주세요.
examples.romanization: taekbaeneun geunyang hyeongwan ape noko ga juseyo.
examples.en: Please just leave the parcel in front of the entrance.
examples.note: real situation: 현관 앞 (in front of) + polite request 놓고 가 주세요

entries.nuance: 현관 is the indoor 'entry hall' of a home — the small sunken or tiled area just inside the door where you step out of your shoes before going up into the living space. It is Sino-Korean 玄關, literally 玄 'dark/profound' + 關 'barrier/gate', a term originally from Zen architecture meaning the threshold into a dwelling. The all-important cultural point: Koreans always remove shoes at the 현관 (현관에서 신발을 벗어요), so this word carries the whole shoes-off custom. Distinguish it sharply from 대문, the *outer gate* opening from the street into the yard: 대문 is outside on the property line, 현관 is the door/hall of the building itself — an apartment has a 현관 but no 대문. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'entrance' as one undifferentiated word and so reaching for 입구 (the entrance *to* a public place like a station or shop); for the entry of a *home* you must use 현관, and remember existence is 에 (신발이 현관에 있어요) but the act of removing shoes is 에서.

Confusing 현관 with 대문. 대문 is the outer street gate of a house; 현관 is the building's own entry door/hall. Apartments have only a 현관.

usagePhrases.note: snow accumulating on a surface → 에

usagePhrases.en: A sound comes from the roof.
usagePhrases.note: the sound originates/occurs there → 에서

examples.note: simple description; ㅎ-irregular adjective in 요-form

examples.en: When it rains, you hear the sound of rain on the roof.

entries.nuance: 지붕 is the *outside* top cover of a building — the slates, tiles or concrete that shed rain, snow and sun. It is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja). English uses 'roof' loosely for both ('the roof of the room'), which is exactly the trap — looking up indoors at the light you must say 천장, never 지붕. 지붕 collocates with weather and damage verbs: 눈이 쌓이다 (snow piles up), 비가 새다 (rain leaks through), 날아가다 (be blown off). commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pointing at the indoor ceiling and saying 지붕. Indoors, the upper surface with the light is 천장; 지붕 is only the outdoor roof. English 'roof' covers both, Korean does not.
Saying 지붕에서 눈이 있어요 for 'there's snow on the roof'. Snow's presence takes 에 (지붕에 눈이 있어요); 에서 marks where an action/sound happens.
Conjugating the colour as 빨갛아요. 빨갛다 is ㅎ-irregular: drop ㅎ and add 요 → 빨개요 (지붕이 빨개요).

usagePhrases.note: thing hanging there → 에

usagePhrases.en: I hang a clock on the wall.
usagePhrases.note: attaching to the wall surface uses 에, not 에서
벽 as object takes 을

examples.en: This wall is a bit thin.
examples.note: simple description with topic 은

examples.en: I've put family photos up on the wall.
examples.note: everyday: 붙이다 + resultative '~아 놓다' (have it stuck up)

examples.en: Sound from next door travels through the wall, which is a bit uncomfortable.
examples.note: real situation: 벽을 타고 (travelling along the wall) + 들리다

entries.nuance: 벽 is a *vertical* dividing surface — the side of a room, the partition between flats, or a freestanding masonry wall — and it is the surface things get hung *on*. It is Sino-Korean 壁. Two contrasts matter. First, 벽 vs 바닥/천장: 벽 is the upright side, 바닥 the floor underfoot, 천장 the surface overhead. Second, 벽 vs 담(장): a 벽 is typically a *building/structural* wall, whereas 담 or 담장 is the *outer boundary wall/fence* around a yard — English 'wall' covers both, so don't say 벽 for the wall enclosing a garden (that's 담). The decisive English-speaker pitfall is the particle for hanging: you hang a picture *on* the wall, but Korean uses 에 (the destination/surface), not 에서 — 벽에 그림을 걸어요, never 벽에서. 벽 collocates with 걸다 (hang), 붙이다 (stick), 기대다 (lean against). Using 벽 for a garden's boundary wall. The outer enclosing wall of a yard is 담 or 담장; 벽 is a structural/room wall.
Conjugating 하얗다 as 하얗아요. It is ㅎ-irregular: 벽이 하얘요 (drop ㅎ, contract to 얘).

usagePhrases.en: There is a bag on the floor.
usagePhrases.note: object resting there → 에
sitting down onto the floor surface → 에

entries.nuance: 바닥 is the *floor* you stand, sit and (with 온돌 under-floor heating) even sleep on — a native-Korean word with no hanja. Its core sense is broader than English 'floor': 바닥 means the *bottom surface* of anything, so it also covers the bed/bottom of a pan, a river or the sea (강 바닥, 바다 바닥), and figuratively 'rock bottom' (가격이 바닥이다 = the price has hit bottom). For the part of a building you must not confuse it with 마루 (a wooden-floored area/hall) or with 층, which means a *storey/level* of a building — '2층' is the second floor *as a level*, but the surface you walk on is 바닥. Because Korean homes are heated through the floor, 바닥 collocates strongly with 따뜻하다/뜨겁다 (warm/hot) and with 앉다 and 닦다. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 층 when you mean the physical surface, and remember sitting *down onto* the floor uses 에 (바닥에 앉아요). The temperature words 차갑다/미끄럽다 are ㅂ-irregular → 차가워요/미끄러워요.

Saying 바닥에서 가방이 있어요. The bag's presence takes 에 (바닥에 가방이 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action.
Conjugating 차갑다 as 차갑아요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 바닥이 차가워요 (ㅂ → 워).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 천장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 천장 + 이 as subject of a quality

usagePhrases.en: There is a light on the ceiling.
usagePhrases.note: fixture mounted there → 에
the dripping happens/originates there → 에서

usagePhrases.en: I look up at the ceiling.
usagePhrases.note: 천장 as object takes 을

examples.en: This room has a high ceiling.
examples.note: simple description; 천장 collocates with 높다/낮다

examples.en: The light hanging from the ceiling is too dim.
examples.note: everyday: 천장에 달리다 (hung from the ceiling) modifying 등

examples.ko: 윗집에서 물이 새는지 천장에 얼룩이 생겼어요.
examples.romanization: witjibeseo muri saeneunji cheonjange eollugi saenggyeosseoyo.

examples.note: real situation: 물이 새다 (leak) + 얼룩이 생기다 (a stain forms)

entries.nuance: 천장 is the *inside* upper surface of a room — what you see when you lie down and look up, with the 등 (light) fixed to it. It is Sino-Korean 天障, literally 天 'sky' + 障 'barrier/screen', i.e. the 'sky-screen' overhead, a nice image for the indoor counterpart of the sky. The essential contrast is 천장 vs 지붕: 천장 is *inside* (ceiling), 지붕 is *outside* (roof). English collapses both into 'roof/ceiling' loosely, which is the main trap — indoors, always 천장. 천장 pairs with 높다/낮다 (high/low), 등이 달리다 (a light is hung), and 물이 새다/얼룩이 생기다 for leak damage. Register is neutral and descriptive. The particle pitfall is the familiar one: the light *is mounted* there (천장에 등이 있어요, 에) but water *drips* there (천장에서 물이 떨어져요, 에서, because dripping is the action/source). Memory hook: 천(天, sky) is up high → ceiling; 지붕 starts with 지 like 지구(earth)'s outer shell.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 지붕 for the indoor ceiling. The inside surface with the light is 천장; 지붕 is the outdoor roof only.
Saying 천장에서 등이 있어요. A mounted light's existence takes 에 (천장에 등이 있어요); reserve 에서 for the dripping/leaking action.
Pronouncing/writing it 천정. The standard form is 천장 (天障); 천정 is a common but non-standard variant — use 천장.

usagePhrases.note: the tree exists there → 에
playing is an action → 에서

entries.nuance: 마당 is the open *ground/yard* belonging to a detached house — bare earth or paving where the family dries crops, sweeps leaves, sets out a 평상, or grills meat in summer. It is a native-Korean word (no hanja) and carries a warm, traditional, single-house feel; an apartment dweller does *not* have a 마당, so the word itself implies a 단독주택 (detached home). Distinguish it sharply from 정원 (庭園), a cultivated ornamental *garden* with planned flowers and lawn — 마당 is plain working ground, 정원 is decorative; and from 베란다, the small deck off an apartment. Figuratively 마당 can even mean an 'occasion/situation' (이 마당에 = 'at this point/in this situation'), though beginners can set that aside. 마당 collocates with 넓다 (spacious), 쓸다 (sweep), 놀다 (play), 나무/꽃이 있다. Register is neutral and homely. Pitfall: don't use 마당 for an apartment's outdoor space (that's 베란다), and keep 에 for existence (마당에 나무가 있어요) versus 에서 for actions (마당에서 놀아요).

Treating 마당 and 정원 as identical. 마당 is plain open yard/ground; 정원 is a planned ornamental garden. Pick by whether it's working ground or decorative planting.
Saying 마당에서 나무가 있어요. A tree's existence takes 에 (마당에 나무가 있어요); 에서 only marks where an action like 놀다 happens.

usagePhrases.note: 울타리 ends in a vowel → subject 가
flowers on the fence surface → 에
leaning against it marks the fence with 에

examples.en: That house has a low fence.

entries.nuance: 울타리 is a light, often see-through *fence/hedge* — wooden slats, wire, or a row of shrubs — that gently marks where a yard or field ends. It is native Korean (no hanja). Its core collocation is 울타리를 치다 ('put up a fence'), and figuratively it means a protective boundary ('가족이라는 울타리' = the shelter of family). Distinguish it sharply by *solidity and material*: a 울타리 is open and low, whereas 담 / 담장 is a *solid masonry wall* (brick or concrete) enclosing a property — English 'fence/wall' blurs these, but a thing you can see through is 울타리, a thing you cannot is 담. Don't confuse it with 벽 either: 벽 is a *building's* wall (a room side or partition), while 울타리 stands outdoors around open ground. Register is neutral, slightly rural/homely. The particle pitfall: leaning against or blooming on the fence uses 에 (울타리에 기대요), and because the word ends in a vowel its subject marker is 가, never 이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이 after the vowel: 울타리이 낮아요. After a vowel use 가 (울타리가 낮아요).
Confusing 울타리 with 담. 담/담장 is a solid masonry boundary wall; 울타리 is a light open fence or hedge. Choose by whether you can see through it.
Using 울타리 for a room's wall. The wall of a building/room is 벽; 울타리 is an outdoor boundary around a yard.

structuredNuance.t: 울타리 is a light, often see-through fence/hedge — wooden slats, wire, or a row of shrubs — that gently marks where a yard or field ends. Its core collocation is 울타리를 치다 ('put up a fence'), and figuratively it means a protective boundary ('가족이라는 울타리' = the shelter of family). Register is neutral, slightly rural/homely.

Distinguish it sharply by solidity and material: a 울타리 is open and low, whereas 담 / 담장 is a solid masonry wall (brick or concrete) enclosing a property — a thing you can see through is 울타리, a thing you cannot is 담. Don't confuse it with 벽 either: 벽 is a building's wall (a room side or partition), while 울타리 stands outdoors around open ground.
It is native Korean (no hanja).

entries.shortExplanation: 대문 means "front gate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 대문 (daemun) means "front gate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 대문이 커요. ("The front gate is big."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 대문 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 대문 + 이 as subject

usagePhrases.en: There is a doorbell on the front gate.
usagePhrases.note: the doorbell is on the gate → 에

usagePhrases.en: I wait at the front gate.
usagePhrases.note: waiting is an action → 에서
대문 as object takes 을; 잠그다 (lock)

examples.en: Our front gate is blue.
examples.note: simple description with 이다

examples.ko: 할머니가 대문 앞에서 저를 기다리고 계셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga daemun apeseo jeoreul gidarigo gyesyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandma was waiting for me in front of the gate.
examples.note: everyday: 대문 앞 + honorific progressive 기다리고 계시다

examples.ko: 밤늦게 들어올 때는 대문을 꼭 잠그고 들어와요.
examples.romanization: bamneutge deureool ttaeneun daemuneul kkok jamgeugo deureowayo.
examples.en: When you come in late at night, be sure to lock the gate behind you.
examples.note: real situation: 잠그고 들어오다 (lock then come in), instruction register

entries.nuance: 대문 is the main *outer gate* of a house — the large door in the boundary wall through which you pass from the street into the 마당. It is Sino-Korean 大門, literally 大 'big' + 門 'gate/door' = 'big gate', which fits its sense as the principal entrance to the property. The crucial contrast is 대문 vs 현관: 대문 is *outside* on the property line (street → yard), while 현관 is the *building's* own entry hall where you take your shoes off (yard → inside); a detached house has both, but an apartment has only a 현관 and no 대문. Also distinguish the generic 문 ('door/gate' of anything) — 대문 specifically names the big front gate. 대문 collocates with 열다/닫다 (open/close), 잠그다 (lock), 두드리다 (knock), and 대문 앞 (in front of the gate). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfall: don't call the apartment building's entry door a 대문 (that's the 현관/공동현관), and keep 에 for what sits on the gate (대문에 자물쇠가 있어요) versus 에서 for actions like waiting (대문에서 기다려요).

Using 대문 for an apartment building's entrance. That shared door is the 공동현관/현관, not 대문 — 대문 belongs to detached houses with a yard.
Saying 대문에서 자물쇠가 있어요. A lock's presence takes 에 (대문에 자물쇠가 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action such as 기다리다.

entries.shortExplanation: 회사원 means "office worker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "office worker" is 회사원 (hoesawon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 회사원이에요. ("I am an office worker."). Watch the particle attached to 회사원 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 이에요 after a final consonant (원)
subject 이 after consonant
평범하다 = ordinary, a very common pairing

usagePhrases.en: I want to become an office worker.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: I'm an office worker.
examples.note: the default polite way to state your job

examples.en: My older brother is an office worker at a bank.
examples.note: 에서 marks the workplace where the action happens

examples.ko: 회사원들은 보통 아침 아홉 시까지 출근해요.
examples.romanization: hoesawondeureun botong achim ahop sikkaji chulgeunhaeyo.
examples.en: Office workers usually clock in by nine in the morning.
examples.note: 출근하다 'go to work' is the verb that lives with 회사원

entries.nuance: 회사원 is 會社員 ('company-member'), literally a member of a company, and it is the neutral catch-all a salaried employee of a private firm gives when asked 무슨 일 하세요? Contrast it with 직장인, which means 'a working person' in general (anyone with a paid job, including teachers or nurses): every 회사원 is a 직장인, but not every 직장인 is a 회사원. Also separate it from 사업가, the owner who runs the business — a 회사원 is employed by someone else. The pitfall for English speakers is twofold: 회사원 ends in a consonant so the copula is 회사원이에요, never 'office worker'-style 회사원예요; and don't translate 'I work at a company' as a job title — to name the job you simply say 회사원이에요 rather than literally rendering the English sentence.

Saying 회사원예요 — wrong, because 원 ends in a consonant you must use 이에요: 회사원이에요.
Using 회사원 for a self-employed shop owner — that person is 자영업자 or 사장님; 회사원 is specifically a salaried employee of someone else's company.
Calling any working adult 회사원 — a nurse or teacher is a 직장인 but not a 회사원; 회사원 implies a typical office/company job.

entries.shortExplanation: 공무원 means "civil servant" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 공무원 (gongmuwon) = "civil servant". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 저는 공무원이에요. ("I am a civil servant.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공무원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 이에요 after the consonant ending 원
subject 이 after consonant
공무원 시험 is a fixed compound; 시험을 보다 = sit an exam

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a civil servant.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 pairs with 이/가

examples.en: I'm a civil servant.
examples.note: stated plainly, like any job

examples.en: My older sister is a civil servant working at city hall.
examples.note: 시청 'city hall' is a typical 공무원 workplace

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 사람들이 공무원 시험을 많이 준비해요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun saramdeuri gongmuwon siheomeul mani junbihaeyo.
examples.en: These days many young people study for the civil-service exam.
examples.note: 준비하다 'prepare for' is the verb that collocates with 시험

entries.nuance: 공무원 is 公務員 ('public-affairs-member'), one who handles 공무, the affairs of the state, so it covers anyone employed by the government — a ward office clerk, a public-school teacher, a tax officer. The key contrast is with 회사원: a 회사원 works for a private 회사, while a 공무원 works for the 나라 (state) and has 정년 (guaranteed tenure to retirement). Don't confuse it with 정치인 (a politician, who is elected) — a 공무원 is hired through the 공무원 시험 and is meant to be politically neutral. For learners the pitfalls are the copula (consonant ending → 공무원이에요, not 공무원예요) and the cultural weight: in Korea 공무원 is prized for 안정성 (stability), so saying 공무원이 되고 싶어요 carries a strong 'I want a secure life' overtone that the bare English 'civil servant' doesn't convey.

Equating 공무원 with 정치인 — a 공무원 is an appointed/hired official, whereas a 정치인 is an elected politician; mixing them sounds confused.
Assuming 공무원 means only office desk staff — public-school teachers and firefighters are also 공무원, so the word is broader than English 'civil servant' feels.

entries.shortExplanation: 주부 means "homemaker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주부 (jubu) means "homemaker". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저는 주부예요. ("I am a homemaker."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주부 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 부
subject 가 after a vowel
전업 'sole occupation' stresses it is full-time work
집안일 'household chores' is the typical object

examples.en: My mom is a homemaker.
examples.note: the most natural everyday sentence with 주부

examples.en: I'm a full-time homemaker raising children.
examples.note: 키우다 'raise (a child)' collocates with 주부

examples.en: These days homemakers also earn money with a side job.
examples.note: 부업 'side work' shows 주부 is treated as real labor

entries.nuance: 주부 is 主婦 ('head-wife'), the person who is the 主 (head, manager) of household affairs; historically it implies a married woman running the home. The sharp modern contrast is 전업주부 (full-time homemaker, no outside job) versus 맞벌이 (a dual-income couple where both work) — and note the rising 주부 covers men too, though many will specify 전업주부 or use 살림하다 'to keep house' for the activity. Don't confuse 주부 (the person) with 가사 / 집안일 (the housework itself). The English-speaker pitfalls: 부 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 주부예요, never 주부이에요; and 'housewife' in English can sound dated, but 주부 in Korean is a perfectly neutral, respectable job answer — pair it warmly, e.g. 부지런한 주부 'a diligent homemaker'.

Saying 주부이에요 — wrong; 부 ends in a vowel, so use 주부예요.
Using 주부 to mean the chores — the chores are 집안일/가사; 주부 is the person who does them.
Assuming 주부 is always female or always married — modern usage allows men, and 전업주부 just marks that homemaking is the person's full-time role.

entries.shortExplanation: 사업가 means "businessperson" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "businessperson" is 사업가 (saeopga). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 사업가예요. ("I am a businessperson."). Watch the particle attached to 사업가 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
subject 가 after a vowel
성공하다 'succeed' is the classic modifier

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a businessperson.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 pairs with 이/가

examples.en: My uncle is a businessperson.
examples.note: stating someone's occupation plainly

examples.en: He's a businessperson who founded a small company.
examples.note: 세우다 'establish (a company)' collocates with 사업가

examples.ko: 성공한 사업가가 되려면 위험을 감수해야 해요.
examples.romanization: seonggonghan saeopgaga doeryeomyeon wiheomeul gamsuhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: To become a successful businessperson you have to take risks.
examples.note: 위험을 감수하다 'bear risk' captures the core of 사업가

entries.nuance: 사업가 is 事業家 ('enterprise-expert'), where 가(家) is the suffix for a person skilled in a field (as in 작가, 화가, 음악가); it pictures someone who builds and runs an 사업 (a business venture) and shoulders its risk. Contrast three near words: 사업가 = the entrepreneur/operator with vision and risk; 사장(님) = the literal 'company president/boss' title you address people by; and 자영업자 = a small self-employed shop owner. So a corner-store owner is rarely called a 사업가 — that word sounds bigger, more ambitious. Don't mix 사업가 (the person) with 사업 (the business itself: 사업을 하다 'run a business'). Pitfalls: 가 ends in a vowel so it's 사업가예요, never 사업가이에요; and don't borrow English 'I do business' literally as a title — to name the job say 사업가예요.

Saying 사업가이에요 — wrong; 가 ends in a vowel, so it must be 사업가예요.
Confusing 사업가 (the owner/person) with 사업 (the business activity) — you run a 사업, you are a 사업가.
Calling a tiny shop owner a 사업가 — that everyday person is usually 자영업자 or 사장님; 사업가 implies a larger, risk-taking venture.

entries.explanation: 디자이너 (dijaineo) = "designer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 저는 디자이너예요. ("I am a designer.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 디자이너, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 너
멋있다 'stylish/cool' fits the creative field
the field word goes in front: 옷/웹/그래픽 디자이너

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a designer.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm a designer.
examples.note: the bare job statement

examples.en: My friend is a designer who makes clothes.
examples.note: the -는 clause 옷을 만드는 specifies the kind of designer

examples.ko: 그 디자이너가 이번 시즌 신상품을 디자인했어요.

entries.nuance: 디자이너 is a direct loanword from English 'designer', written in 외래어 (foreign-loan) spelling, used for anyone who designs — clothes, graphics, web pages, products. Because the bare word is broad, Koreans almost always front a field: 옷 디자이너 (fashion), 웹 디자이너 (web), 그래픽 디자이너 (graphic). Be careful not to confuse 디자이너 with 디자인 (the design itself: 디자인이 예쁘다 'the design is pretty') — one is the person, one is the output. A nearby word is 설계자, but that leans toward technical/architectural 'designer-engineer', so for fashion or visual work stick with 디자이너. Pitfalls for English speakers: 너 ends in a vowel, so it's 디자이너예요, never 디자이너이에요; and the matching verb is 디자인하다, so 'I design clothes' is 옷을 디자인해요, not a literal word-by-word transfer of the English.

Confusing 디자이너 (the person) with 디자인 (the design) — you do 디자인, you are a 디자이너.
Leaving the field off when it matters — 디자이너 alone is vague; specify 옷 디자이너, 웹 디자이너, etc., as Koreans naturally do.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 프로그래머 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 머
subject 가 after a vowel
실력 있다 'have skill' is the natural praise

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a programmer.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm a programmer.
examples.note: the plain job answer

examples.en: My younger sibling is a programmer who makes games.
examples.note: 만들다 'make' describes what they build

examples.en: The programmer writes code late into the night.
examples.note: 코드를 짜다 'write/assemble code' is the insider collocation

entries.nuance: 프로그래머 is the loanword 'programmer', the person who writes computer 프로그램 (programs). The most useful contrast is with 개발자 ('developer', 開發者 'one who develops'): in real Korean tech workplaces 개발자 is now the more common, broader title (covering design, building, and shipping software), while 프로그래머 highlights specifically the coding act and can sound slightly narrower or more old-school. Both are fine to say. Don't confuse 프로그래머 (the person) with 프로그램 (the program) — you make a 프로그램, you are a 프로그래머. The natural verb for the work is 코드를 짜다 or 개발하다, not a literal calque of English 'to program'. Pitfall: 머 ends in a vowel, so it must be 프로그래머예요, never 프로그래머이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 프로그래머이에요 — wrong; 머 ends in a vowel, so use 프로그래머예요.
Confusing 프로그래머 (the person) with 프로그램 (the software) — you build a 프로그램, you are a 프로그래머.
Assuming 프로그래머 is the only modern title — in Korean tech 개발자 'developer' is now more common and often preferred.

entries.nuance: 엔지니어 is the loanword 'engineer', someone who designs, builds, and maintains machines or systems. The instructive contrast is with the Sino-Korean 기술자 (技術者 'skill-person', a technician): 엔지니어 leans toward the degreed, design-and-theory professional, while 기술자 emphasizes a hands-on tradesperson who operates or repairs. So a factory line repairer might be a 기술자, whereas the person who designed the line is an 엔지니어 — though in casual speech they overlap. As with other fields, Koreans front the specialty: 기계 엔지니어, 소프트웨어 엔지니어. Pitfalls: 니어 ends in a vowel, so it's 엔지니어예요, never 엔지니어이에요; and don't reach for 'engineer' to mean a train driver (a false friend from older English) — that person is a 기관사.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 엔지니어이에요 — wrong; the word ends in a vowel, so use 엔지니어예요.
Treating 엔지니어 and 기술자 as identical — 엔지니어 suggests a degreed design professional, 기술자 a hands-on technician.
Using 엔지니어 for a train operator — that is 기관사; the English 'engineer = train driver' sense does not transfer.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 작가, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
유명하다 'famous' is the typical pairing
베스트셀러 'bestseller' fronts the noun

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a writer.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm a writer.
examples.note: the bare job statement

examples.en: She's a writer who writes novels.
examples.note: 쓰다 'write' is the core verb of 작가

examples.ko: 그 작가가 이번에 새 책을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: geu jakgaga ibeone sae chaegeul naesseoyo.
examples.en: That author just put out a new book.

entries.nuance: 작가 is 作家 ('make-house/expert' = one who creates works), used for authors of novels, essays, and also drama or film scripts (a 드라마 작가 is a screenwriter). The crucial contrast for learners is 기자 (記者, a news reporter who reports facts) — both write, but 작가 creates literary/creative work while 기자 gathers and reports news, so never swap them. A wider umbrella is 글쓴이/저자 'author of a specific text', but as a profession 작가 is the word. Note the suffix 가(家) marks 'a master of a field', the same one in 화가, 사업가, 음악가. Pitfalls: 가 ends in a vowel → 작가예요, never 작가이에요; and the idiom for publishing is 책을 내다 (literally 'put out a book'), so don't calque English 'make a book' as 책을 만들다, which sounds like physically manufacturing it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 작가이에요 — wrong; 가 ends in a vowel, so use 작가예요.
Confusing 작가 with 기자 — a 작가 creates literary/creative writing, a 기자 reports the news; they are different jobs.
Saying 책을 만들었어요 for 'published a book' — to release a book the idiom is 책을 냈어요; 만들다 sounds like physically producing the object.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 화가 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
유명하다 'famous' pairs naturally
유명하다 in its modifier form 유명한

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a painter.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.note: naming someone's profession

examples.note: 그리다 'draw/paint' is the verb that lives with 화가

examples.ko: 그 화가가 그린 그림이 비싸게 팔렸어요.
examples.romanization: geu hwagaga geurin geurimi bissage pallyeosseoyo.

entries.nuance: 화가 is 畵家 ('picture-expert'), a fine-art painter whose work is 그림 (pictures/paintings), again with the 가(家) 'master of a field' suffix. The contrast to keep clear: 화가 is one specific kind of 예술가 (藝術家, artist) — 예술가 is the umbrella that also includes musicians (음악가), dancers, and sculptors, so a 화가 is an 예술가 but not vice versa. Also distinguish 화가 (the person) from 그림 (the painting) and from 화백, a respectful term for a renowned master painter. The natural verb is 그림을 그리다 'paint a picture'. Pitfalls: 가 ends in a vowel → 화가예요, never 화가이에요; and don't say 그림을 만들다 for painting — 그리다 is the right verb, while 만들다 'make' would sound like constructing an object rather than painting.

Saying 화가이에요 — wrong; 가 ends in a vowel, so use 화가예요.
Confusing 화가 (the painter) with 그림 (the painting) — the person paints the 그림.
Using 그림을 만들다 for 'to paint' — the correct verb is 그림을 그리다; 만들다 implies building an object, not painting.

Watch the particle attached to 교수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 수; said of oneself
add 님 + honorific 오시다 when speaking about them
께 is the honorific 'to'; 여쭤보다 humbly = ask

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a professor.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm a professor who teaches at a university.
examples.note: about yourself you may drop 님

examples.en: Our professor is really kind.
examples.note: 친절하시다: the honorific -시- because they outrank you

examples.en: The professor asked a hard question today.

entries.nuance: 교수 is 敎授 ('teach-confer'), a university professor who both teaches and researches — note this is higher and narrower than 선생님, the general word for any teacher (and the polite word for a schoolteacher). A 선생님 may teach at any level; a 교수 specifically holds a university post, so don't call a professor 선생님 in a formal setting, nor a kindergarten teacher 교수. The huge register point: in real use you almost always attach 님 → 교수님, and you conjugate verbs about them with honorific -시- (가르치세요, 오셨어요). You may say plain 교수 when stating your own job humbly, but addressing or referring to someone else's professor without 님 sounds blunt to the point of rude. Pitfall: 수 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 교수예요, never 교수이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교수이에요 — wrong; 수 ends in a vowel, so use 교수예요.
Dropping 님 when addressing or referring to someone's professor — say 교수님; bare 교수 there sounds disrespectful.
Using 선생님 and 교수 interchangeably — 교수 is specifically a university professor, while 선생님 is the general/school-level teacher term.

entries.shortExplanation: 통역사 means "interpreter" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 통역사 (tongyeoksa) = "interpreter". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 저는 통역사예요. ("I am an interpreter.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 통역사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 사
필요하다 'be needed' takes 이/가, not 을/를
동시 'simultaneous' marks the real-time specialty

usagePhrases.en: I want to become an interpreter.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm an interpreter.
examples.note: the plain job answer

examples.en: One interpreter came to the meeting.
examples.note: 명 is the counter for people

examples.en: That interpreter interpreted English into Korean.
examples.note: A를 B로 통역하다 'interpret A into B'

entries.nuance: 통역사 is 通譯士 ('through-translate-specialist'), where 士(사) is the dignified suffix for a licensed/qualified professional (also in 변호사 lawyer, 회계사 accountant). It means specifically an interpreter of spoken language in real time. The essential contrast is 번역사 (翻譯士), who translates written text: spoken = 통역, written = 번역, and the people and verbs differ (통역하다 vs 번역하다). Don't blur them — saying 번역사 for a conference interpreter is a clear error to Korean ears. Note also the verb 통역하다 takes the pattern A를 B(으)로 통역하다. Pitfalls: 사 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 통역사예요, never 통역사이에요; and the thing you 'need' takes 이/가 with 필요하다 (통역사가 필요해요), not the 을/를 an English speaker expects from 'need an interpreter'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 통역사이에요 — wrong; 사 ends in a vowel, so use 통역사예요.
Confusing 통역사 (spoken) with 번역사 (written) — 통역 is live spoken interpreting, 번역 is text translation.
Saying 통역사를 필요해요 — 필요하다 marks the needed thing with 이/가, so it is 통역사가 필요해요.

Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 사
the vehicle goes in front: 버스/택시/트럭 운전사
기사 is the more courteous term you call them by

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a driver.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: My father is a truck driver.
examples.note: the vehicle precedes 운전사

examples.ko: 택시 운전사가 길을 정말 잘 알아요.
examples.romanization: taeksi unjeonsaga gireul jeongmal jal arayo.

entries.nuance: 운전사 is 運轉士 ('move-turn-specialist'), a person who drives a vehicle (bus, taxi, truck) for a living, with the professional suffix 士(사). The register point is the most important thing here: 운전사 is a neutral descriptive label, but to a driver's face — a taxi or bus driver — Koreans politely say 기사님 (기사 = 技士, with respectful 님), and 운전기사 is the courteous full form. Calling out 운전사! to address someone would sound curt. Distinguish 운전사 (the person) from 운전 (the act of driving: 운전을 하다 'to drive', 운전을 잘하다 'drive well'). Pitfalls: 사 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 운전사예요, never 운전사이에요; and for the activity 'I can drive' you say 운전할 수 있어요, using the verb 운전하다, not the job noun.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 운전사이에요 — wrong; 사 ends in a vowel, so use 운전사예요.
Addressing a driver as 운전사 — to their face the polite form is 기사님; 운전사 used directly sounds blunt.
Confusing 운전사 (the person) with 운전 (the driving) — you do 운전, you are a 운전사.

examples.en: This intersection is always jammed with traffic.
examples.note: 차가 막히다 = traffic is backed up, a fixed collocation

entries.nuance: 사거리 is literally 四거리 — the Sino-Korean 四 (four) glued to native 거리 (street), so it names a point where four roads cross, the single most useful landmark for directions. Distinguish it from 교차로, which is the formal/technical word on road signs and in traffic news; 사거리 is what people actually say out loud, and it specifies four ways, whereas a three-way fork is 삼거리. English speakers wrongly say 사거리에 가요 for 'turn at the intersection' — 가다 with 에 only means 'go (to) the intersection' as a destination; to describe an action performed there (turn, meet, wait) you must switch to 에서. Note also it is 사거리 in everyday speech, never 사거리길.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사거리에 우회전해요 — 우회전하다 is an action at a place, so it needs 에서: 사거리에서 우회전해요.
Calling every crossing a 사거리 — if only three roads meet it is a 삼거리; 사거리 specifically means four ways.
Using 교차로 in casual speech to a friend — it sounds like a news report; say 사거리 when chatting.

entries.shortExplanation: 골목 means "alley" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 골목 (golmok) = "alley". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 좁은 골목 ("narrow alley") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 골목, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the default image of a 골목 — tight and small
으로 marks the direction you turn into
에서 because playing is an action done there
안 = the inner part, where hidden shops hide

examples.en: The good restaurant is tucked inside the alley.
examples.note: 골목 안 = back in the alley, a very common food-hunting phrase

examples.en: The children play in the alley.
examples.note: 에서 marks the place of the activity

examples.en: Cars can't get into this alley.
examples.note: 못 + verb = physically cannot, fits a tiny lane

entries.nuance: 골목 is a small, narrow back-lane between buildings — think the winding side streets of an old neighborhood, often lined with tiny homes and hidden eateries; the longer 골목길 stresses it as a walkable path. Contrast it sharply with 길, the general word for any road or way: every 골목 is a 길, but you call something a 골목 precisely when it is narrow, branching off a bigger street. It is a native Korean word (no hanja), warm and homey in feeling — 골목 carries nostalgia, which is why 골목 상권 (alley shopping district) and 골목길 are beloved. English speakers misuse 길 for a tiny side street; if a car can barely pass, Koreans feel it as a 골목, not a 길. Avoid the direct-translation trap of 'small road' = 작은 길; the natural phrase is 좁은 골목.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 길 for a tight back lane — Koreans reserve 골목 for narrow branching lanes; 길 sounds too wide.
Saying 작은 길 as a literal 'small road' — the natural collocation is 좁은 골목 (narrow alley).
Putting 에 on an action: 골목에 놀아요 is wrong; playing needs 골목에서 놀아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 광장 means "plaza" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 광장 (gwangjang) means "plaza". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 넓은 광장 ("wide open plaza"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 광장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 넓다 (spacious) is the adjective that defines a 광장
에서 because gathering is an action done there

usagePhrases.en: the plaza is full of people
usagePhrases.note: 에 + 있다/많다 states what is located there

usagePhrases.en: the plaza in front of city hall
usagePhrases.note: a famous Seoul gathering spot

examples.en: I go to the plaza every weekend.
examples.note: 마다 = every, 에 marks the destination

examples.en: People gather at the plaza.
examples.note: 에서 marks where the gathering happens

examples.en: A big event is held in the plaza.
examples.note: 행사가 열리다 = an event is held, set phrase

entries.nuance: 광장 is 廣場 — 廣 (wide) + 場 (place/ground), literally 'wide ground', so it names a large paved public square where crowds gather for rallies, festivals, or rest, like 광화문 광장. Do not confuse it with 공원 (park): a 공원 is green, with trees, grass and benches for leisure, while a 광장 is an open hard-surfaced civic space built for people to assemble. Because 광장 historically hosts demonstrations and ceremonies, it carries a civic, public-life connotation that 공원 lacks. English speakers reach for 공원 when they mean a city square — if it is paved and made for crowds, it is a 광장. Also resist 'big park' = 큰 공원 for a plaza; the right word is simply 광장.

Calling a paved city square 공원 — a 공원 is green and leisure-focused; an open civic square is a 광장.
Translating 'square' as 사각형 — that is the geometric shape; the public square is 광장.
Marking gathering with 에: 광장에 모여요 should be 광장에서 모여요 because gathering is an action.

entries.shortExplanation: 다리 means "bridge" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bridge" is 다리 (dari). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 긴 다리 ("long bridge"). Watch the particle attached to 다리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 길다 describes a span stretching over water
를 because the bridge is the object you cross
위 = on top of, the deck you walk along

usagePhrases.en: a bridge over the Han River
usagePhrases.note: Seoul has many famous ones

examples.en: Please cross that bridge.
examples.note: 건너다 takes 를; -세요 makes it a polite instruction

examples.en: We took photos up on the bridge.
examples.note: 다리 위에서 = on the bridge, 에서 for the action of taking photos

examples.en: This bridge lights up at night.
examples.note: 불이 켜지다 = lights come on, a natural collocation

entries.nuance: 다리 is a native Korean word and a famous homonym: the very same 다리 means 'leg', and context alone tells them apart — 다리가 아프다 is 'my leg hurts', while 다리를 건너다 is 'cross the bridge'. As a structure it lets you pass over a river, road, or valley and is a top landmark in directions. Distinguish it from 육교, which is specifically a pedestrian overpass/footbridge across a road, and 고가도로, an elevated car roadway; plain 다리 is the everyday cover term, especially the great river bridges (한강 다리). The verb that pairs with it is 건너다 (to cross), taking the object particle 를. English speakers sometimes say 다리를 가다 — but you 'cross' a bridge (다리를 건너다), you do not simply 'go' it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 다리를 가요 for 'cross the bridge' — the verb is 건너다: 다리를 건너요.
Forgetting that 다리 also means 'leg' — listen to context; 다리가 아프다 is about your leg, not a bridge.
Using 다리 for a footbridge over a road — that specific one is 육교 (pedestrian overpass).

entries.shortExplanation: 터널 means "tunnel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 터널 (teoneol) = "tunnel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 긴 터널 ("long tunnel") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 터널, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 길다 fits a passage that takes a while to drive through
를 + 지나다 = go through it
에 + 들어가다 marks the point you go into
빠져나오다 = emerge from, natural with terminus

examples.en: The car enters the tunnel.
examples.note: 에 + 들어가다 marks the entry point

examples.en: We passed through a long tunnel.
examples.note: 지나다 takes 를; the whole tunnel is the object

examples.en: Inside the tunnel the radio cuts out.
examples.note: 터널 안 = inside; 안 나오다 = doesn't come through

entries.nuance: 터널 is a direct loanword from English 'tunnel' (written in Hangul), naming a passage bored through a mountain or under ground so cars and trains can pass. There is a pure-Korean-style equivalent 굴, but 굴 leans toward a natural cave or burrow, whereas 터널 is the engineered road/rail structure — so a subway runs through a 터널, while a bear sleeps in a 굴. The verbs that pair with it are 지나다 / 통과하다 (pass through, with 를) and 들어가다 / 나오다 (enter / exit, with 에). English speakers sometimes overuse 다리 for 'a way through a mountain', but a bridge goes over and a 터널 goes through. Resist also the literal 'go in the tunnel' = 터널에 가다; you 'enter' it: 터널에 들어가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다리 for a passage through a mountain — over a gap is 다리, through a mountain is 터널.
Saying 굴 for a highway tunnel — 굴 suggests a natural cave; the engineered road one is 터널.
Saying 터널에 가다 — to go through, use 터널을 지나다 or to enter, 터널에 들어가다.

entries.shortExplanation: 계단 means "stairs" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계단 (gyedan) means "stairs". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가파른 계단 ("steep stairs"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 계단 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 가파르다 (르 irregular) is the typical descriptor
를 + 올라가다, the stairs are the path you ascend
를 + 내려가다 for descending
으로 marks stairs as the means, vs the elevator

examples.en: Go up the stairs slowly.
examples.note: 올라가다 takes 를; 천천히 = slowly

examples.en: Take the stairs instead of the elevator.
examples.note: 으로 = by way of; 대신 = instead of

examples.en: Be careful not to fall on the stairs.
examples.note: 에서 marks where; -지 않게 = so as not to

entries.nuance: 계단 is 階段 — 階 (step/rank) + 段 (level/section), literally 'stepped levels', the fixed set of steps between floors. Distinguish it from 층계 (a more bookish synonym for a flight of steps) and especially from 계단 vs the moving 에스컬레이터: a 계단 is stationary and you climb it under your own power. The natural verbs are 올라가다 (go up) and 내려가다 (go down), each taking 를 because the staircase is the path traversed; to say you choose stairs as your method, use 계단으로 (by the stairs). The classic English-speaker error is 계단을 타다 (ride the stairs) — you ride a vehicle or an escalator, but ordinary stairs you 올라가다/내려가다, not 타다. Also 계단 is the steps; one single step is a 계단 한 칸.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 계단을 타다 — you don't 'ride' fixed stairs; use 계단을 올라가다 / 내려가다.
Marking the means with 를: 계단을 가요 for 'take the stairs' should be 계단으로 가요.
Confusing 계단 with 층 (floor) — 층 is a building level; 계단 is the steps connecting levels.

entries.shortExplanation: 엘리베이터 means "elevator" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "elevator" is 엘리베이터 (ellibeiteo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 엘리베이터를 타다 ("take the elevator"). Watch the particle attached to 엘리베이터 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 를 + 타다, the standard verb for boarding it
를 + 기다리다, wait for it to arrive
에서 + 내리다 marks getting out

usagePhrases.en: the elevator is out of order
usagePhrases.note: 고장 나다 = break down, common notice

examples.en: We take the elevator.
examples.note: 타다 takes 를 — you board it like a vehicle

examples.en: I met a neighbor in the elevator.
examples.note: 에서 marks where the meeting happened

examples.en: The elevator is broken, so I take the stairs.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; note the 계단으로 contrast

entries.nuance: 엘리베이터 is the English loanword 'elevator' in Hangul, the small moving cabin that carries people between floors. A common synonym you will see on signage is 승강기 (昇降機, 'rise-descend machine'), the formal/legal term in building notices, while 엘리베이터 is the everyday spoken word. Crucially it is treated like a ride: the verb is 타다 (to board/ride), taking 를 — the very same 타다 used for buses and taxis — and you 내리다 (get off) with 에서. English speakers wrongly map their 'get in/out' onto 들어가다/나가다, but Korean frames it as boarding: say 엘리베이터를 타다, not 엘리베이터에 들어가다. Do not mix it up with 에스컬레이터 (escalator), which is the open moving staircase; the 엘리베이터 is the enclosed box.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 엘리베이터에 들어가요 for 'get in the elevator' — Korean rides it: 엘리베이터를 타요.
Mixing up 엘리베이터 (the enclosed box) with 에스컬레이터 (the moving stairs).
Using 가다 for boarding: 엘리베이터를 가요 is wrong; the verb is 타다.

entries.shortExplanation: 에스컬레이터 means "escalator" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 에스컬레이터 (eseukeolleiteo) = "escalator". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 에스컬레이터를 타다 ("take the escalator") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 에스컬레이터, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 를 + 타다, you ride the moving steps
길다 fits the deep subway ones

usagePhrases.en: hold the handrail on the escalator
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where, 손잡이를 잡다 = grab the rail
으로 marks it as the means of going up

examples.en: We take the escalator.
examples.note: 타다 takes 를, just like the elevator

examples.en: I hold the handrail on the escalator.
examples.note: 에서 marks where the holding happens

examples.en: It's easier if you go up by escalator.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if; 으로 marks the means

entries.nuance: 에스컬레이터 is the loanword 'escalator' in Hangul — the moving staircase you stand on in subway stations and department stores. The dividing line from 엘리베이터 is movement type: an 에스컬레이터 is an open, continuously moving set of steps you stand on, while an 엘리베이터 is an enclosed cabin that lifts you; English keeps them apart too, but their similar Korean spellings make learners blur them, so anchor 에스컬레이터 = 'stairs that move'. Like other ride-things it pairs with 타다 (to ride, with 를), and to express it as your method you use 에스컬레이터로 (by escalator). A frequent error is treating it as fixed stairs and saying 에스컬레이터를 올라가다 alone — you ride it (타다); if you do walk up while it moves, that is 걸어 올라가다. Mind the spelling: it is 에스컬레이터, not 에스칼레이터.

Saying 에스컬레이터를 올라가다 as if it were fixed stairs — you ride it: 에스컬레이터를 타다.
Misspelling it 에스칼레이터 — the correct form is 에스컬레이터.

entries.shortExplanation: 입구 means "entrance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 입구 (ipgu) means "entrance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 건물 입구 ("building entrance"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 입구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: the most common compound — where you go in
에서 because meeting is an action done there
를 + 찾다, look for the way in
막히다 = get blocked, useful warning

examples.en: See you at the station entrance.
examples.note: 에서 marks where you'll meet

examples.en: Where is the entrance?
examples.note: 어디예요? = where is it, a key question

examples.en: It's crowded so the entrance is hectic.
examples.note: -아서 gives the cause; 복잡하다 = congested

entries.nuance: 입구 is 入口 — 入 (enter) + 口 (mouth/opening), literally the 'mouth you enter through', i.e. the way into a building or area. Its exact opposite is 출구 (出口, 'exit-mouth'), and the two share the 口 'opening' character, so learning them as a 入/出 pair makes both stick. Contrast 입구 with 정문 (正門, 'main gate'), the principal front gate of a campus or large building — a place can have one grand 정문 plus several smaller 입구. For meeting people, the action verb 만나다 takes 에서 (입구에서 만나요), while merely stating something is located there uses 에. English speakers often confuse 입구 and 출구 because both end in 구; remember 입 = in, 출 = out. Avoid the literal 'in-door' = 안 문; the real word is 입구.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 입구 (entrance, 入) with 출구 (exit, 出) — both end in 口, but 입 = enter, 출 = exit.
Marking a meeting with 에: 입구에 만나요 should be 입구에서 만나요 (an action happens there).
Saying 안 문 as a literal 'in-door' — the natural word for entrance is 입구.

entries.shortExplanation: 출구 means "exit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "exit" is 출구 (chulgu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 역 출구 ("station exit"). Watch the particle attached to 출구 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: numbered exits are everywhere in the subway
으로 + 나가다 marks the way out you take
essential phrase for subway meetups
를 + 찾다, look for the way out

examples.en: Go out exit number three.
examples.note: 으로 marks the exit as the path out; 삼 번 = no. 3

examples.en: Where is the exit?
examples.note: the mirror question to 입구가 어디예요?

examples.ko: 저는 칠 번 출구 앞에서 기다릴게요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun chil beon chulgu apeseo gidarilgeyo.
examples.en: I'll wait in front of exit 7.
examples.note: 출구 앞 = in front of the exit; -ㄹ게요 = I will

entries.nuance: 출구 is 出口 — 出 (go out) + 口 (opening), literally the 'exit-mouth', the way you leave a building or station; in the subway each is numbered (몇 번 출구), so 'meet at exit 7' is everyday Korean. It is the exact opposite of 입구 (入口, entrance), and the shared 口 'opening' character ties the 出/入 pair together. Distinguish 출구 from 비상구 (非常口, 'emergency exit'), the marked fire-escape door — a normal way out is a 출구, the emergency one is a 비상구. To leave through it you say 출구로 나가다, where 으로 marks the exit as your route. English speakers blur 출구 and 입구 because both end in 구; fix the memory with 출 = out, 입 = in. And note exits are counted with the native-Sino number + 번 (삼 번 출구), not with English ordinals.

Confusing 출구 (exit, 出) with 입구 (entrance, 入) — both end in 口, but 출 = out, 입 = in.
Saying 출구를 나가요 — to mark the route out, use 출구로 나가요.
Using 출구 for a fire escape — the emergency one is specifically 비상구.

entries.shortExplanation: 복도 means "hallway" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 복도 (bokdo) = "hallway". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 긴 복도 ("long hallway") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 복도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 길다 fits a corridor stretching past many rooms
에서 marks where; 뛰지 마세요 is the school sign
끝 = far end, where the last room sits
를 + 지나다, pass along it

examples.en: The classroom is at the end of the hallway.
examples.note: 복도 끝 = the far end; 에 marks where it is located

examples.en: Don't run in the hallway.
examples.note: 에서 marks where; -지 마세요 = please don't

examples.en: The hallway is quiet.
examples.note: 조용하다 = quiet, a typical descriptor

entries.nuance: 복도 is 複道 — the indoor corridor or passage inside a building that links rooms, offices, and classrooms; picture a school or office hallway. The key boundary is indoor vs outdoor: a 복도 is always inside a building, whereas a 골목 is a narrow lane outside between buildings — so you wait for a friend 복도에서 inside the school, but explore a 골목 out in the neighborhood. Do not stretch 복도 to mean a road; it is strictly an interior walkway. Natural verbs are 지나다 (pass along, 를) and the activity-marking 에서 for things done there (복도에서 기다리다, 복도에서 뛰다). English speakers sometimes reach for 골목 for an inside passage — keep it straight: outside lane = 골목, inside corridor = 복도. Also 복도 is the passage itself, while the entrance hall of a home is rather 현관.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 골목 for an indoor passage — outside it's a 골목, but inside a building it's a 복도.
Marking an activity with 에: 복도에 기다려요 should be 복도에서 기다려요.
Calling a building's entry hall 복도 — the front entry of a home is 현관, not 복도.

entries.shortExplanation: 옥상 means "rooftop" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 옥상 (oksang) means "rooftop". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 건물 옥상 ("building rooftop"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 옥상 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the flat top you can actually stand on
에 + 올라가다 marks the destination up top
에서 because resting is an action done there

usagePhrases.en: see the night view from the rooftop
usagePhrases.note: 야경을 보다 = take in the night scenery

examples.en: Let's go up to the rooftop.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination; 올라가다 = ascend

examples.en: I hang the laundry on the rooftop.
examples.note: 빨래를 널다 = hang washing, a classic 옥상 activity

examples.en: The night view from the rooftop is gorgeous.
examples.note: 에서 marks the vantage point you view from

entries.nuance: 옥상 is 屋上 — 屋 (house/building) + 上 (on top), literally 'on top of the building', meaning the flat, accessible roof terrace where people dry laundry, grow plants, or take in the view. The sharp contrast is with 지붕, the sloped roof of a house that simply covers it and that you do not walk on: a Korean apartment block has an 옥상 you can climb to, a traditional 한옥 has a tiled 지붕 you cannot stand on. Because 옥상 is a usable open space, it pairs with 올라가다 (go up to, with 에) and activity 에서 (옥상에서 쉬다, 빨래를 널다, 야경을 보다). English 'roof' lumps both together, so learners overuse 지붕 — but if you can stand on it, it is an 옥상; if it is the sloping cover, it is a 지붕. Note also 옥상 is the open top of a building, distinct from 다락 (an attic room under the roof).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a flat usable rooftop 지붕 — 지붕 is the sloped cover you can't stand on; the open terrace is 옥상.
Marking resting with 에: 옥상에 쉬어요 should be 옥상에서 쉬어요 (an action happens there).
Confusing 옥상 (open rooftop) with 다락 — 다락 is the attic space tucked under the roof.
