entries.shortExplanation: 점수 means "score" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "score" is 점수 (jeomsu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 점수가 좋아요 ("the score is good"). Watch the particle attached to 점수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: with 좋다 use the subject particle 가, not 를: 점수가 좋다, never 점수를 좋다
when an action verb like 받다 acts on it, the object particle 를 returns
나오다 is intransitive, so the score is the subject (가), not the object
Koreans pair a score with 높다/낮다 (high/low), never 크다/작다 (big/small)

examples.en: The score is good.
examples.note: The simplest frame: just the noun plus 가 and an adjective, the everyday way to comment on a result.

examples.en: I got my Korean test score back.
examples.note: 받다 takes 를 because you actively receive the number that was handed to you.

examples.ko: 선생님, 제 점수가 왜 이렇게 낮아요?
examples.romanization: seonsaengnim, je jeomsuga wae ireoke najayo?
examples.en: Teacher, why is my score so low?
examples.note: A real classroom complaint: 낮다 (low) is the natural opposite of 높다, never 작다.

entries.nuance: 점수 is the numeric points you earn on a test, quiz, or game — the raw figure itself, written 95점 with the counter 점. The hanja is 點數, literally 'dot-number', from 點 (point/dot) plus 數 (number), so it is intrinsically a counted quantity. Do not confuse it with its near-synonym 성적 (成績): 성적 is your broader academic standing or report-card record (overall grades, ranking, a transcript), while 점수 is one concrete number on one item — you can have a good 점수 on a single quiz yet a poor overall 성적. The natural verbs are 점수가 나오다 (the score comes out / is released) and 점수를 받다 (to receive a score); for high or low you must say 점수가 높다/낮다, NOT 크다/작다. The English-speaker trap is the particle: with the descriptive 좋다/높다 the score is the subject and takes 가 (점수가 좋다), so saying 점수를 좋다 by copying English 'I scored a good score' is ungrammatical.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using 성적 and 점수 interchangeably. 성적 is your overall record; for the single number on one test you want 점수, e.g. 시험 점수가 좋아요, not 시험 성적이 좋아요 unless you mean the whole grade.
Marking the score with 를 before 좋다: 점수를 좋아요 is wrong because 좋다 is an adjective taking a subject. Say 점수가 좋아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 교과서 means "textbook" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교과서 (gyogwaseo) = "textbook". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교과서를 펴요 ("open the textbook") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 교과서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 펴다 (spread open) is the standard classroom verb for opening a book to a page, not 열다
나오다 with 에 is how Koreans say content 'comes up' in a book
로 marks the textbook as the tool/means you study by
a subject name directly modifies 교과서 with no particle between them

examples.en: Please open your textbook.
examples.note: The exact phrase a teacher says: 펴다 plus the polite command -세요.

examples.en: The answers are all right there in the textbook.
examples.note: 에 marks the book as the location where the answers appear (나와 있다).

examples.ko: 저는 인터넷 강의보다 교과서로 공부하는 게 편해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun inteonet ganguiboda gyogwaseoro gongbuhaneun ge pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: I find studying with the textbook easier than online lectures.
examples.note: 로 frames the textbook as the means, contrasted with 강의 via 보다.

entries.nuance: 교과서 is the official course book for a specific school subject — the authorized text a class is taught from, often government-approved (국정/검정 교과서). The hanja 敎科書 breaks down as 敎 (teach) + 科 (subject/branch) + 書 (book), literally 'teaching-subject book', which is exactly its job. Keep three near-words apart: a 공책 (空冊, 'empty book') is a blank notebook you write in; a 참고서 (參考書) is a supplementary study/reference guide; and a plain 책 is any book at all — only 교과서 is the core subject text used in lessons. The natural verb is 교과서를 펴다 (open it to a page) rather than 열다 (which suits a door or lid), and you study 교과서로 (by means of the textbook). The English-speaker pitfall is calling any school book a 책 or mixing it with 공책: if you say 교과서에 써요 meaning you write in it, a Korean pictures defacing the printed text — you write 공책에, in your notebook, not in the 교과서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 열다 to open a textbook, as in 교과서를 열어요. 열다 is for doors and lids; to open a book to a page Koreans say 교과서를 펴요.
Confusing 교과서 with 공책. 공책 is a blank notebook for writing; the printed subject book is 교과서. Say 공책에 써요 for writing, 교과서를 봐요 for reading.
Treating 교과서 as any book. A novel or comic is just 책; reserve 교과서 for the official text of a school subject.

entries.shortExplanation: 필통 means "pencil case" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 필통 (piltong) means "pencil case". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 필통에 넣어요 ("put it in the pencil case"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 필통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: put it in the pencil case
usagePhrases.note: 넣다 (put in) naturally pairs with 에 to mark where something goes
existence/possession uses 있다 with the subject particle 이
unlike a book, a case has a lid, so 열다 (open) is correct here
filled pencil cases are typically described with 귀엽다 (cute) by students

examples.en: The pencil case is on the desk.
examples.note: A simple location statement: 위에 (on top) plus 있어요 for where it sits.

examples.en: I put the pencil into the pencil case.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination of 넣다; the pencil (object) takes 를.

examples.ko: 새 필통을 샀는데 연필이랑 지우개가 안 들어가요.
examples.romanization: sae piltongeul sanneunde yeonpirirang jiugaega an deureogayo.
examples.en: I bought a new pencil case but the pencil and eraser don't fit.
examples.note: A real-life grumble: 들어가다 (to fit inside) with the negative 안.

entries.nuance: 필통 is the small case or box that holds your writing implements — pens, pencils, eraser. The word is Sino-Korean 筆筒, from 筆 (writing brush/pen) + 筒 (tube/cylinder), originally a 'brush-tube', a holder for calligraphy brushes that now means any pencil case. Do not confuse the container with its contents: 연필 (鉛筆, 'lead-brush') is the pencil itself, 볼펜 a ballpoint, and 지우개 the eraser — the 필통 is merely the case they live in. Because a case has a lid you 필통을 열다 (open it) and you 연필을 필통에 넣다 (put a pencil in), so the location particle 에 marks where things go. The English-speaker pitfall is naming the part for the whole: a beginner may point at a pencil and say 필통, but 필통 is strictly the case — if you mean the pencil, say 연필. Also avoid the verb 입다/신다 here; you do not 'wear' a 필통, you 열다 it or 가지고 다니다 (carry it around).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the pencil itself 필통. 필통 is only the case; the pencil is 연필. Point at the pencil and say 연필, point at the box and say 필통.
Using 열다 for a textbook by analogy after learning 필통을 열다. The lid case opens (필통을 열다), but a book opens to a page with 펴다 (교과서를 펴다).
Saying 필통에 연필이 있다 when you mean to put it in, then using 있다 instead of 넣다. 있다 states it is already there; the action of inserting is 넣다 (필통에 넣어요).

entries.shortExplanation: 책가방 means "school bag" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "school bag" is 책가방 (chaekgabang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 책가방을 메요 ("carry the school bag (on the back)"). Watch the particle attached to 책가방 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: carry the school bag (on the back)
usagePhrases.note: 메다 is the dedicated verb for shouldering a backpack, not 들다 or 입다

usagePhrases.en: put it in the school bag
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the bag as the place something goes into with 넣다
책가방 is habitually described as 무겁다 (heavy) because of the books inside
싸다 (to pack/wrap) is how Koreans say they get their bag ready

examples.en: The school bag is heavy.
examples.note: The basic complaint frame: subject plus the adjective 무겁다.

examples.en: I put the textbook into my school bag.
examples.note: 에 marks where the textbook goes; 넣다 is the action of putting in.

examples.en: Every morning I put my bag on my back and head to school.
examples.note: 메고 (shouldering, and then…) chains the bag onto the going; -고 links the two actions.

entries.nuance: 책가방 is the bag a student carries books and supplies in — in practice a backpack worn on both shoulders. It is a compound of 책 (冊, book, Sino-Korean) + 가방 (bag, a native-feeling loanword), literally 'book-bag'. The crucial point is the verb: a backpack worn on the back/shoulder takes 메다 (책가방을 메다), whereas a handbag or briefcase carried in the hand takes 들다 (가방을 들다) — choosing the wrong one sounds off, like saying you 'hold' a backpack in your fist. You also 책가방을 싸다 (pack it) the night before and 책가방에 넣다 (put things in). Its near-words: a generic 가방 is any bag, a 백팩 is the English loan 'backpack', and a 핸드백 is a woman's handbag — 책가방 specifically frames it by its school-book purpose. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 입다 (wear) or 들다 (hold) because English says 'wear a backpack' or 'carry a bag'; in Korean a backpack is neither worn like clothes nor held like a purse — it is 메다, shouldered.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 책가방을 입어요 by translating 'wear a backpack'. 입다 is for clothing; a backpack is shouldered, so say 책가방을 메요.
Using 들다 for a backpack. 들다 means to carry in the hand (a handbag, a suitcase). For a bag on your back use 메다: 책가방을 메고 가요.
Marking the bag with 에서 when putting things in. Insertion is a destination, so use 에: 책가방에 넣어요, not 책가방에서 넣어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 운동장 means "playground" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 운동장 (undongjang) = "playground". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 운동장에서 놀아요 ("play at the playground") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 운동장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 활동(놀다) happens AT a place, so the action particle 에서 is required
모이다 marks the field as the end point of movement, so 에
a 운동장 is rated by area with 넓다 (spacious), not 크다

usagePhrases.en: run a lap around the field
usagePhrases.note: 돌다 with 을 treats the track as the path you traverse

examples.en: The playground is spacious.
examples.note: A first sentence: subject 가 plus 넓다, the standard way to size up an area.

examples.en: The students play soccer on the field.
examples.note: 에서 because 축구를 하다 (the activity) happens there; the place hosts an action.

examples.ko: 체육 시간에 운동장에 나가서 줄을 섰어요.
examples.romanization: cheyuk sigane undongjange nagaseo jureul seosseoyo.
examples.en: In PE class we went out to the field and lined up.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination of 나가다 (go out to); then 줄을 서다 (line up) follows.

entries.nuance: 운동장 is the open sports field or grounds of a school where pupils exercise, run, and play — typically a large dirt or turf area with a track, the heart of Korean school PE and 체육대회 (sports day). The hanja is 運動場: 運 (move) + 動 (move) — together 運動 means 'exercise/sports' — plus 場 (place/ground), so the whole is literally 'exercise-grounds'. The make-or-break grammar is 에서 vs 에: use 에서 for what you DO there (운동장에서 뛰다/놀다/축구하다), because 에서 marks the location of an action, but use 에 only for motion toward it (운동장에 가다/나가다/모이다). Its near-word 놀이터 is the little playground with swings and a slide for small children, whereas 운동장 is the big school athletic field — do not mix them. Size is 넓다 (spacious), not 크다. The English-speaker pitfall is using a single 'at' particle for everything: English 'play at the playground' and 'go to the playground' both feel like one preposition, but Korean splits them — 운동장에서 놀다 (play, action) yet 운동장에 가다 (go, destination), and putting 에 where an activity happens (운동장에 놀아요) is a classic error.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 운동장에 놀아요 for playing there. Playing is an action that happens at the place, so it needs 에서: 운동장에서 놀아요. Reserve 에 for going to it (운동장에 가요).
Confusing 운동장 with 놀이터. 놀이터 is a small children's playground with swings; the school sports field is 운동장. A high-schooler plays soccer on the 운동장, not the 놀이터.
Describing the field as 커요. Area is judged by spaciousness, so the natural adjective is 넓다: 운동장이 넓어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 교문 means "school gate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교문 (gyomun) means "school gate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교문 앞에서 만나요 ("meet in front of the gate"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교문 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: meet in front of the gate
usagePhrases.note: 교문 앞 (gate-front) is the usual meeting spot; 에서 marks where you meet
지나다 (pass) takes 을, treating the gate as the point you go past
닫히다 (be closed) is the verb for a gate shutting at curfew time
앞 (front) attaches to 교문 to pinpoint the area before it

examples.en: The school gate is big.
examples.note: Plain description: 교문 as subject with 크다, fine for a physical structure's size.

examples.en: I met my friend in front of the school gate.
examples.note: 에서 marks the spot of the meeting; 교문 앞 is the conventional rendezvous point.

examples.ko: 지각해서 교문이 닫히기 전에 뛰어 들어갔어요.
examples.romanization: jigakaeseo gyomuni datigi jeone ttwieo deureogasseoyo.
examples.en: I was running late, so I dashed in before the gate closed.
examples.note: 닫히기 전에 (before it closes) plus 뛰어 들어가다 (run in) — the real drama of a tardy student.

entries.nuance: 교문 is the main gate at the entrance of a school — the formal threshold students pass through each day, often guarded and shut after the bell. The hanja 校門 is 校 (school) + 門 (gate/door), literally 'school-gate'. Distinguish it from the broader 정문 (正門, 'main/front gate' of any building or institution) and from a plain 문 (any door): 교문 specifically frames the gate as a school's, so a hospital's main entrance is its 정문, not its 교문. Note that 門 in Korea names large gates and named structures (광화문 Gwanghwamun, 동대문 Dongdaemun), so 교문 carries that weightier 'gateway' feel, not a flimsy door. The natural collocations are 교문 앞에서 만나다 (meet in front of the gate — the default student meetup) and 교문을 지나다 (pass through it), and a gate 닫히다 (closes) at curfew. Unlike a sports field judged by 넓다, a gate's size is 크다. The English-speaker pitfall is over-generalizing 'gate/door' to plain 문 — 문을 지나다 sounds like passing some random door; for the school's entrance gate you want 교문을 지나다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 문 instead of 교문 for a school's entrance gate. 문 is any door; the school's main gate is specifically 교문. Say 교문 앞에서 봐요 for meeting at school.

Confusing 교문 with 정문. 정문 is the main front gate of any building (a hospital, a company); only a school's gate is 교문 — though a school's 교문 may also be called its 정문 when contrasting front vs back gates.
Marking the meeting place with 에 instead of 에서. Meeting is an action, so the place takes 에서: 교문 앞에서 만나요, not 교문 앞에 만나요.

entries.shortExplanation: 교복 means "school uniform" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "school uniform" is 교복 (gyobok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 교복을 입어요 ("wear the uniform"). Watch the particle attached to 교복 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 입다 is the verb for putting on upper-body/whole clothing, which a uniform is
어울리다 (to suit) with 가 is how Koreans compliment how clothes look on someone
맞추다 means to have clothes custom-made to your size, common for new uniforms
교복 is typically bought new (새) at the start of a school year

examples.en: The uniform is pretty.
examples.note: Simple appraisal: subject 가 plus 예쁘다, the everyday way to praise its looks.

examples.ko: 저는 매일 교복을 입고 학교에 가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maeil gyobogeul ipgo hakgyoe gayo.
examples.en: I wear my uniform to school every day.
examples.note: 입고 (wearing, and then…) links dressing to going via -고; 를 marks the uniform.

examples.ko: 교복 치마가 너무 짧아서 좀 불편해요.
examples.romanization: gyobok chimaga neomu jjalbaseo jom bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The uniform skirt is so short it's a bit uncomfortable.
examples.note: A real student remark: 치마 (skirt) as a part of the 교복, with 짧다 (short).

entries.nuance: 교복 is the prescribed uniform students wear at a Korean middle or high school — a recognizable set (blazer, shirt, skirt or trousers, often a name tag) that signals which school you attend. The hanja 校服 is 校 (school) + 服 (clothes/garment), literally 'school-clothes'. The 服 element appears in many clothing words — 한복 (Korean dress), 양복 (a Western suit), 교복 — so it reliably means 'attire'. Crucially the verb is 입다 (입다 covers shirts, jackets, dresses, and uniforms — anything worn on the torso or as a full outfit), NOT 신다 (which is only for footwear) and NOT 쓰다 (for hats/glasses): you 교복을 입다. Other natural phrases are 교복을 맞추다 (have it tailored) and 교복이 어울리다 (it suits you). Its near-word 사복 (私服, 'private clothes') means your own casual clothes worn on non-uniform days — a 사복 데이 is a free-dress day. The English-speaker pitfall is treating Korean 'wear' as one word the way English does: English 'wear' covers shoes, hats, and shirts alike, but Korean splits them by body zone, so saying 교복을 신다 (using the shoe verb) is a telltale beginner slip — it must be 교복을 입다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교복을 신어요 by using the single English 'wear'. 신다 is only for footwear; clothing worn on the body uses 입다, so the uniform is 교복을 입어요.
Using 쓰다 for the uniform after learning 모자를 쓰다 (wear a hat). 쓰다 is for things on the head; the uniform garment is 입다.
Confusing 교복 with 사복. 사복 is your own casual clothes; the school's required outfit is 교복. On a free-dress day you wear 사복, not 교복.

entries.shortExplanation: 급식 means "school meal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 급식 (geupsik) = "school meal". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 급식을 먹어요 ("eat the school meal") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 급식, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 (eat) takes 를; 급식 is treated as the food you consume
맛있다 (tasty) with 가 is the universal verdict students pass on the food
급식 directly modifies 시간 to name the scheduled meal slot

usagePhrases.en: the meal is served / comes out
usagePhrases.note: 나오다 describes today's menu 'coming out' on the tray

examples.en: Today's school meal is tasty.
examples.note: The classic lunchroom line: 오늘 (today) plus subject 가 and 맛있다.

examples.en: The students go to the cafeteria to eat lunch.
examples.note: 먹으러 (in order to eat) shows purpose with -(으)러; 를 marks 급식.

examples.ko: 오늘 급식에 제가 제일 좋아하는 닭갈비가 나왔어요!
examples.romanization: oneul geupsige jega jeil joahaneun dalkgalbiga nawasseoyo!
examples.en: My favorite dak-galbi came out in today's school lunch!
examples.note: An excited report: 급식에 ... 나오다 (appear in the meal); 에 marks the meal as where the dish shows up.

entries.nuance: 급식 is the meal supplied institutionally — the school (or workplace) lunch served en masse and eaten together, usually on a divided tray (식판). The hanja 給食 is 給 (give/supply) + 食 (food/meal), literally 'supplied food', which captures that it is provided to a group rather than ordered individually. This is the dividing line from its near-words: 식사 (食事) is the formal/general word for 'a meal' (any meal, politely), 밥 is the casual everyday word for 'a meal' or 'rice', and 점심 names specifically 'lunch' by time of day — but only 급식 carries the sense of a meal institutionally provided to students/staff. So a meal you cook at home or buy at a restaurant is 밥 or 식사, never 급식; 급식 implies the cafeteria system. Natural phrases: 급식을 먹다 (eat it), 급식이 나오다 (today's menu is served), 급식 시간 (lunch period). The English-speaker pitfall is using 급식 for any lunch — if you ate lunch at a café you say 점심을 먹었어요 or 밥을 먹었어요, not 급식을 먹었어요, because 급식 specifically means the provided school/work meal.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 급식 for a meal you made or bought yourself. 급식 is the institutionally provided cafeteria meal; a home or restaurant meal is 밥 or 식사. Say 점심 먹었어요, not 급식 먹었어요, when you ate out.
Treating 급식 and 점심 as the same. 점심 is 'lunch' by time of day; 급식 is the served school meal specifically. You can eat 점심 anywhere, but 급식 only at a school/workplace canteen.
Marking the served dish with 를 in 'a dish came out in the meal'. The dish appears via 나오다 (intransitive), so the meal is the location with 에: 급식에 불고기가 나왔어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 수업료 means "tuition fee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 수업료 (sueomnyo) means "tuition fee". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수업료를 내요 ("pay the tuition"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수업료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: fees are 내다 (pay/hand over to an institution), never 사다 (buy)
price is judged with 비싸다/싸다 (expensive/cheap), with 가 marking the subject
오르다 (rise) is the verb for prices increasing; note the 르 irregular (올라요)
한 달 (one month) modifies 수업료 to specify the period being paid for

examples.en: The tuition is expensive.
examples.note: A plain price judgment: subject 가 with 비싸다, the core way to call something pricey.

examples.en: I pay the academy tuition every month.
examples.note: 매달 (every month) sets the frequency; 내다 takes 를 for the fee you hand over.

examples.ko: 올해 등록금이랑 수업료가 또 올라서 부담이 커요.
examples.romanization: olhae deungnokgeumirang sueomnyoga tto ollaseo budami keoyo.
examples.en: With registration and tuition fees rising again this year, the burden is heavy.
examples.note: A real worry: 오르다 (rise) plus 부담이 크다 (the burden is big), 등록금 vs 수업료 distinguished.

entries.nuance: 수업료 is the fee charged for taking lessons — the money you pay an academy (학원), school, or course for instruction. The hanja 授業料 is 授 (give/confer) + 業 (work/study) — together 授業 means 'a lesson/class', the act of teaching being given — plus 料 (fee/charge), so literally 'lesson-fee'. The element 料 marks fees throughout Korean: 입장료 (admission), 수수료 (commission), 사용료 (usage fee), 수업료 (tuition). Distinguish it from the near-word 등록금 (登錄金, 'registration money'), the lump enrollment fee for a university semester — at a 대학교 you usually pay 등록금, while at a 학원 you pay 수업료 each month; many learners blur them. The essential verb is 내다 (수업료를 내다, to pay/remit a fee), and prices 오르다 (rise) or are 비싸다 (expensive). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사다 (buy) because English can 'pay for' a class as if purchasing it — but in Korean you do not 'buy' a fee; you 내다 (pay/hand over) it: 수업료를 사다 is wrong, 수업료를 내다 is right.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 수업료를 사요 by analogy with 'buying a class'. A fee is paid, not bought; the verb is 내다: 수업료를 내요.

Confusing 수업료 with 등록금. 등록금 is the lump registration/enrollment fee (typical at universities); 수업료 is the per-course/monthly lesson fee (typical at academies). Use the one that matches the institution.
Describing the fee with 커요 for 'high'. A price is 비싸다 (expensive), not 크다: 수업료가 비싸요. Reserve 크다 for physical size.

Distinguish it from the near-word 등록금 (登錄金, 'registration money'), the lump enrollment fee for a university semester — at a 대학교 you usually pay 등록금, while at a 학원 you pay 수업료 each month; many learners blur them.

The hanja 授業料 is 授 (give/confer) + 業 (work/study) — together 授業 means 'a lesson/class', the act of teaching being given — plus 料 (fee/charge), so literally 'lesson-fee'. The element 料 marks fees throughout Korean: 입장료 (admission), 수수료 (commission), 사용료 (usage fee), 수업료 (tuition).
The pitfall is reaching for 사다 (buy) because English can 'pay for' a class as if purchasing it — but in Korean you do not 'buy' a fee; you 내다 (pay/hand over) it: 수업료를 사다 is wrong, 수업료를 내다 is right.

entries.shortExplanation: 장학금 means "scholarship" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "scholarship" is 장학금 (janghakgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 장학금을 받아요 ("receive a scholarship"). Watch the particle attached to 장학금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) takes 를; a scholarship is awarded to you
신청하다 (to apply/request) is the verb for putting in an application
나오다 describes the award money being granted/disbursed
타다 colloquially means to be awarded a prize or scholarship

examples.en: I got a scholarship.
examples.note: The proud one-liner: 받다 plus past -았어요, 를 marking the award.

examples.ko: 성적이 좋아서 이번 학기에 장학금을 신청했어요.
examples.romanization: seongjeogi joaseo ibeon hakgie janghakgeumeul sincheonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: My grades were good, so I applied for a scholarship this term.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason (good grades); 신청하다 is the act of applying.

examples.ko: 전액 장학금을 타서 등록금 걱정이 없어졌어요.
examples.romanization: jeonaek janghakgeumeul taseo deungnokgeum geokjeongi eopseojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I won a full scholarship, so my tuition worries are gone.
examples.note: 전액 (full amount) modifies it; 타다 (win) plus the relief of 걱정이 없어지다.

entries.nuance: 장학금 is the award money granted to a student to support their studies — for merit (성적 장학금), need, or special talent — money you do not repay, unlike a loan. The hanja 奬學金 is 奬 (encourage/reward) + 學 (study/learning) + 金 (money/gold), literally 'study-encouraging money', so the very word frames it as funds that reward and enable learning. Distinguish it sharply from 학자금 (學資金, 'study-capital'), which is the broader pool of money for education and often appears in 학자금 대출 (a student loan you must repay): a 장학금 is given to you, whereas 학자금 대출 is borrowed. Also unlike a plain 돈 (money) or 용돈 (allowance), 장학금 specifically denotes an academic award. The natural verbs are 장학금을 받다 (formally receive) and the colloquial 장학금을 타다 (win/get one), plus 장학금을 신청하다 (apply) and 장학금이 나오다 (it comes through). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it just 돈 — saying 학교에서 돈을 받았어요 to mean a scholarship loses the meaning; the award is 장학금, and confusing it with the repayable 학자금 대출 reverses who gives money to whom.

Confusing 장학금 with 학자금 (대출). A 장학금 is granted and not repaid; 학자금 대출 is a student loan you must pay back. They are opposite directions of obligation.
Using 사다 or 벌다 for getting a scholarship. You neither buy nor earn-by-working a scholarship; you 받다 (receive) or 타다 (win) it: 장학금을 받아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 동아리 means "club" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동아리 (dongari) = "club". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 동아리에 들어가요 ("join a club") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동아리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 들어가다 (enter/go into) with 에 is the set phrase for joining a club
활동하다 (to be active/take part) happens at the club, so 에서
가입하다 (to enroll/become a member) is the more formal 'join'
the activity name (사진) modifies 동아리 directly to name the club's focus

examples.en: I joined a music club.
examples.note: 에 marks the club as what you entered (들어가다); past tense -았어요.

examples.en: Our club meets every Friday.
examples.note: 에서 because 모이다 (the activity of gathering) takes place there; 매주 sets the rhythm.

examples.en: Thanks to club activities I got close with the older students.
examples.note: 덕분에 (thanks to) plus 친해지다 (grow close) — the real social payoff of joining.

entries.nuance: 동아리 is a student club or society — a voluntary group bound by a shared hobby or interest (band, film, basketball, debate) that meets regularly, central to Korean school and university life. Unlike most school vocabulary here, it is a NATIVE Korean word, not Sino-Korean, which is why it has no hanja and a soft, homegrown feel. Distinguish it from its near-words: 동호회 (同好會) is the equivalent club for adults/the general public (a hiking 동호회, a tennis 동호회), 모임 is any informal gathering or get-together (a dinner 모임), and 클럽 the English loan tends to mean a nightclub or a formal organization — only 동아리 specifically names the student-interest club. The set verb is 동아리에 들어가다 (literally 'go into the club' = join) or the formal 가입하다, and you 동아리에서 활동하다 (are active in it), with 에서 marking the place of activity. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: using 모임 (a one-off gathering) for what is really an ongoing 동아리, and reaching for 참가하다/join with a wrong particle — Korean says 동아리에 들어가다 (에, destination of entering), not 동아리를 들어가다.

Using 모임 for a school club. 모임 is a casual one-time gathering (a meal, a meetup); an ongoing student interest group is a 동아리. Say 동아리에 들어갔어요, not 모임에 들어갔어요, for joining a club.
Marking the club with 를 when joining: 동아리를 들어가요 is wrong. 들어가다 here takes the destination particle 에: 동아리에 들어가요.
Confusing 동아리 with 동호회. 동아리 is for students at school/university; 동호회 is the same kind of club for adults in society. A working adult joins a 동호회, a student a 동아리.

entries.shortExplanation: 기숙사 means "dormitory" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기숙사 (gisuksa) means "dormitory". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기숙사에 살아요 ("live in the dormitory"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기숙사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 살다 (live/reside) takes 에 to mark the dwelling place
지내다 (to stay/get by) is an action over time, so the place takes 에서
들어가다 with 에 means to move in / take up residence there
기숙사 modifies 생활 (life) to name the experience of living in one

examples.en: I live in the dormitory.
examples.note: The basic residence statement: 살다 with the location particle 에.

examples.en: I'm staying in the dorm with a roommate.
examples.note: 에서 because 지내다 (the ongoing activity of living) happens there; 룸메이트랑 (with a roommate).

examples.ko: 기숙사는 밤 11시에 통금이라서 일찍 들어가야 해요.
examples.romanization: gisuksaneun bam 11sie tonggeumiraseo iljjik deureogaya haeyo.
examples.en: The dorm has an 11 p.m. curfew, so I have to go in early.
examples.note: A real rule of dorm life: 통금 (curfew) plus -아야 하다 (have to); 들어가다 for going in.

entries.nuance: 기숙사 is a dormitory — a residential building where students or workers live communally near their school or job, typically with shared rooms, rules, and a curfew (통금). The hanja 寄宿舍 is 寄 (lodge/entrust) + 宿 (stay overnight/lodge) + 舍 (house/building), literally a 'lodging house', a place you stay away from home. The 宿 element recurs in lodging words — 숙박 (宿泊, lodging), 합숙 (合宿, a training-camp stay), 숙소 (宿所, the place you stay) — all sharing 宿 'lodge / stay overnight'. Distinguish it from its near-words: 자취방 / 자취 is living alone off-campus in a rented room (자취하다, to live on one's own), 하숙 (下宿) is boarding with a family who provides meals, and 원룸 is a studio flat — only 기숙사 means the institution-run communal dorm. The dual-particle logic matters: use 에 for the state of residing (기숙사에 살다) and motion in (기숙사에 들어가다), but 에서 for activities done there (기숙사에서 공부하다/지내다). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it 집 (home) — your 기숙사 is where you stay, but 집 evokes your family home; a student says 기숙사에 가요 to go back to the dorm, while 집에 가요 means going to their actual home, often a different place entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the dorm 집. 집 is your (family) home; the communal student residence is 기숙사. 'I'm going back to the dorm' is 기숙사에 가요, distinct from 집에 가요 (going to your real home).
Confusing 기숙사 with 자취/하숙. 기숙사 is an institution-run dormitory; 자취 is living alone in a rented place; 하숙 is boarding with a family who feeds you. Pick the one that fits the living arrangement.
Using 에서 for simply residing: 기숙사에서 살아요 is off. The state of living takes 에 (기숙사에 살아요); save 에서 for actions done there (기숙사에서 지내요/공부해요).

entries.shortExplanation: 상점 means "store" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "store" is 상점 (sangjeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 상점에서 옷을 사요. ("I buy clothes at the store."). Watch the particle attached to 상점 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I buy clothes at the store.
usagePhrases.note: place + 에서 marks where an action happens
상점 + 운영하다 is the set phrase for operating a shop
주인 attaches with no particle to mean the shopkeeper
동네 (local area) is the most common modifier

examples.en: There are many stores.
examples.note: simple 이/가 subject statement; 많다 = to be many

examples.en: Let's meet in front of the store.
examples.note: 앞에서 (in front of + at) names a meeting spot

examples.ko: 그 상점은 물건이 좋아서 손님이 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu sangjeomeun mulgeoni joaseo sonnimi manayo.
examples.en: That store has good goods, so it has many customers.
examples.note: real situation: -아서 links cause (good goods) to result (many customers)

entries.nuance: 상점 is the broad, slightly bookish word for a retail shop, built from the hanja 商店 (商 'commerce' + 店 'shop'), so it literally reads 'commerce-shop.' Its everyday rival is 가게, which is the warm, native-feeling word people actually say out loud ('동네 가게', the corner shop); 상점 sounds a notch more formal and is what you see on signs, in textbooks, and in writing. Compare also 매장, which is a brand's sales floor inside a bigger building. The English-speaker pitfall: do not stretch 상점 to cover a restaurant or a café — those are 식당 and 카페, never 상점. And because English says 'at the store,' learners reach for 에, but the location of an action takes 에서 (상점에서 사요), while 에 marks a destination or static existence (상점에 가요 / 상점에 있어요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '상점에 옷을 사요' for 'I buy clothes at the store.' Buying is an action performed there, so it needs the action-location particle: 상점에서 옷을 사요. 에 would only fit a verb of going or existing.
Calling a restaurant a 상점. 상점 sells goods, not meals; a place you eat at is 식당 (or 음식점), and a coffee place is 카페.
Treating 상점 and 가게 as interchangeable in casual speech. They overlap in meaning, but in spoken Korean 가게 is far more natural ('가게 가서 우유 사 와'), while 상점 can sound stiff.

entries.shortExplanation: 매장 means "retail outlet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매장 (maejang) = "retail outlet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매장을 둘러봐요. ("I look around the outlet.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 둘러보다 (look around) takes 매장 as its object with 을
직원 attaches directly to mean the floor employee
오프라인 distinguishes a real shop from an online one
들르다 (stop by) pairs with 에, the destination particle

examples.en: The outlet is spacious.
examples.note: simple description; 넓다 = to be wide/spacious

examples.en: I try on clothes at the outlet.
examples.note: 입어 보다 = 'try wearing'; 에서 marks where you do it

examples.ko: 이 브랜드는 백화점 안에 매장이 있어요.
examples.romanization: i beuraendeuneun baekwajeom ane maejangi isseoyo.
examples.en: This brand has an outlet inside the department store.
examples.note: real situation: 안에 (inside) shows a 매장 nested in a bigger building

entries.nuance: 매장 comes from the hanja 賣場 (賣 'to sell' + 場 'place/floor'), literally 'selling-floor,' and that image is the key: it is the sales space of a brand or company, very often a counter or section housed inside a department store, mall, or large building. The near-synonym 가게 is a standalone little shop someone owns; 매장 is corporate and branch-like — Nike has 매장, your aunt has a 가게. 상점 is the generic textbook word, while 매장 specifically foregrounds the selling area itself. The English-speaker pitfall: 'outlet' in English can mean a discount store, but Korean 매장 has no discount sense at all — a discount mall is 아울렛 (a separate loanword). Also do not call a website a 매장; an online shop is 온라인 쇼핑몰 or just 쇼핑몰.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 매장 for an internet shop because English 'outlet' feels online-friendly. 매장 is a physical selling floor; an online store is 온라인 쇼핑몰 / 인터넷 쇼핑몰.
Assuming 매장 means a bargain/discount store like an English 'outlet.' A Korean discount mall is the loanword 아울렛; plain 매장 carries no cheap-price meaning.
Saying '매장에서 가요' for 'I go to the outlet.' Going is movement toward a destination, so use 에: 매장에 가요. Reserve 에서 for actions done inside it (매장에서 봐요).

structuredNuance.t: 매장 is the sales space of a brand or company, very often a counter or section housed inside a department store, mall, or large building. It specifically foregrounds the selling area itself.

entries.shortExplanation: 영업시간 means "business hours" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 영업시간 (yeongeopsigan) means "business hours". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영업시간을 확인해요. ("I check the business hours."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영업시간 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 확인하다 (check) takes 영업시간 as object with 을
외 (outside of) marks times the shop is closed
끝나다 (to end) pairs with 이; the day's service is over
안내 (guidance/notice) is the posted sign of opening times

examples.en: The business hours are long.
examples.note: simple description with 이 + 길다 (to be long)

examples.en: Weekend business hours differ from weekdays.
examples.note: everyday: 와/과 다르다 = 'differs from'; note 과 after 평일

examples.en: What are your business hours here?
examples.note: real situation: 어떻게 되세요? is the polite set phrase to ask a shop's hours

entries.nuance: 영업시간 is the stretch of time a business is open for service, from 영업 (營業, 'operate a business': 營 'manage' + 業 'enterprise') plus 시간 (時間, 'time-interval': 時 'hour' + 間 'gap'). So the whole word reads 'business-operating time-interval.' Distinguish it from plain 시간, which is just 'time/hours' in general; 영업시간 is specifically the open-for-customers window, and its opposite edge is marked by 영업 종료 ('closing') or 영업 시작 ('opening'). A related sign word is 휴무일, the regular day off when there are no 영업시간 at all. The English-speaker pitfall: to ask the hours, English logic tempts a literal '영업시간이 뭐예요?', but Koreans say 영업시간이 어떻게 되세요? (or 몇 시까지 해요?). Also note 영업시간 is the period; the act of being open is 영업하다 ('to be open for business'), so 'Are you open now?' is 지금 영업해요?, not 지금 영업시간이에요?.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Asking '영업시간이 뭐예요?' for 'What are your hours?' It is grammatical but unnatural; the idiomatic question is 영업시간이 어떻게 되세요? or simply 몇 시까지 해요?.
Using plain 시간 when you mean opening hours, e.g. '이 가게 시간이 어때요?' — that just asks about time vaguely. Specify 영업시간 to mean when the shop is open.

entries.shortExplanation: 정가 means "list price" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "list price" is 정가 (jeongga). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정가로 사다 ("to buy at list price"). Watch the particle attached to 정가 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 정가 + 로 means 'at the full price', no discount
의 links 정가 to 절반 (half) for '50% off' phrasing
정가 + 표 (table/tag) is the posted sheet of fixed prices
적혀 있다 = 'is written (and stays so)' on the tag

examples.en: The list price is expensive.
examples.note: simple 이/가 statement; 비싸다 = to be expensive

examples.en: I bought it cheaper than the list price.
examples.note: everyday: 보다 = 'than'; 싸게 (cheaply) is the adverb form of 싸다

examples.ko: 이 책은 정가가 만 오천 원인데 할인해서 만 원에 샀어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegeun jeonggaga man ocheon woninde harinhaeseo man wone sasseoyo.
examples.en: This book's list price is 15,000 won, but with a discount I bought it for 10,000.
examples.note: real situation: -는데 sets up contrast between 정가 and the price actually paid (에)

entries.nuance: 정가 is the official, fixed, manufacturer-or-seller-set price printed on a product before any markdown — from the hanja 定價 (定 'to fix/decide' + 價 'price'), literally 'decided price.' Its sharp opposite within shopping is 할인가, the 'discount price,' and you will constantly hear them paired: '정가 30,000원 → 할인가 21,000원.' Do not confuse it with 가격, which is the neutral, general word for 'price' of anything; 정가 specifically claims 'this is the standard, undiscounted figure.' Related is 정찰제, a 'fixed-price system' where haggling isn't allowed. The English-speaker pitfall: 'list price' makes learners want to say 정가 is what you pay, but in Korea the figure on the receipt is often the 할인가 or 판매가 (selling price), not the 정가. Also remember to pay 'at' a price uses 로/으로 (정가로 샀어요), not 에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 정가 as the price you actually pay. 정가 is the pre-discount sticker figure; what you hand over may be the 할인가 (discount price) or 판매가 (selling price).
Swapping 정가 for the all-purpose 가격. 가격 just means 'price' in general; choose 정가 only when you specifically mean the fixed, official, undiscounted price.
Saying '정가에서 샀어요' for 'I bought it at list price.' The price you transact at takes 로/으로: 정가로 샀어요. 에서 would wrongly mark a location.

entries.shortExplanation: 상품권 means "gift certificate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상품권 (sangpumgwon) = "gift certificate". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 상품권으로 결제하다 ("to pay with a gift certificate") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상품권, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to pay with a gift certificate
usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the means of payment; 결제하다 = to settle payment
문화 (culture) + 상품권 is the popular book/media voucher brand type

usagePhrases.en: to give a gift certificate as a present
usagePhrases.note: 선물하다 (to gift) takes 상품권 as its object with 을
권 here is the counter-suffix for the bill's face value

examples.en: I have a gift certificate.
examples.note: simple existence with 이 + 있다

examples.en: I paid with the gift certificate.
examples.note: everyday: 으로 = 'by means of'; 계산하다 = to pay/check out

examples.ko: 백화점 상품권은 현금처럼 쓸 수 있어서 선물로 인기가 많아요.
examples.romanization: baekwajeom sangpumgwoneun hyeongeumcheoreom sseul su isseoseo seonmullo ingiga manayo.
examples.en: Department-store gift certificates can be used like cash, so they're popular as gifts.
examples.note: real situation: 처럼 (like) + -ㄹ 수 있다 (can) explain why it's a favored 선물

entries.nuance: 상품권 is a prepaid voucher you spend like cash at shops, from the hanja 商品券 (商品 'merchandise/goods' + 券 'ticket, certificate'), literally 'goods-ticket.' That final 권 (券) is the same 'ticket/coupon' morpheme in 입장권 (admission ticket) and 할인권 (discount coupon), so recognizing it unlocks a whole family of words. Distinguish 상품권 from 쿠폰, a coupon that knocks a percentage or amount off — a 상품권 carries real stored money you redeem, whereas a 쿠폰 just discounts. Culturally, gifting 상품권 (especially 백화점 상품권 and 문화상품권) is extremely common and not seen as impersonal. The English-speaker pitfall: don't confuse it with 영수증 (receipt) or 보증서 (warranty card); only 상품권 holds spendable value. And to pay with one, use 으로 (상품권으로 샀어요), the instrument particle — not 로 after a consonant-final noun mistakenly, since 상품권 ends in ㄴ and correctly takes 으로.

Confusing 상품권 with 쿠폰. A 상품권 is prepaid money you redeem; a 쿠폰 merely discounts a purchase. 'I paid with a gift certificate' is 상품권으로 냈어요, not 쿠폰으로.
Writing '상품권로 샀어요.' Because 상품권 ends in the consonant ㄴ, the instrumental particle is 으로: 상품권으로 샀어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 교환 means "exchange" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 교환 (gyohwan) means "exchange". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교환하다 ("to exchange"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교환 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 교환 + 하다 turns the noun into the verb 'to swap an item'
가능하다 (be possible) pairs with 이; the standard shop phrasing
로 marks what you swap into (the target size)
및 (and, formal) is the set sign wording at counters

examples.en: Can I exchange it?
examples.note: simple: 되다 here means 'is allowed/possible'

examples.ko: 이 옷을 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i oseul keun geollo gyohwanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to exchange this for a bigger one.
examples.note: everyday: 걸로 (= 것으로) marks the replacement; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: You can exchange it only if you have the receipt.
examples.note: real situation: -아야 (only if) states the condition for 교환

entries.nuance: 교환 means swapping a purchased item for a different size, color, or model of the same kind of product, from the hanja 交換 (交 'to cross/mutual' + 換 'to change'), literally 'mutually change.' The crucial shopping contrast is with 반품, a 'return' that gives your money back: 교환 keeps the transaction (you walk out with goods), 반품 undoes it (you walk out with a refund). Counters typically post '교환·반품 안내' together. Note 교환 is also used more broadly than shopping — 의견 교환 (exchanging opinions), 정보 교환 (exchanging information) — so the word isn't shop-only, but here it's the item-swap sense. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'exchange money' tempts a literal 돈을 교환하다, but currency exchange is 환전 (a different word). To swap into the replacement item, use 로/으로 (큰 사이즈로 교환), and remember the verb is 교환하다, so 'I want to exchange' is 교환하고 싶어요, not 교환을 싶어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 교환 (swap for another item) with 반품 (return for a refund). If you want your money back, that's 반품; 교환 means you leave with replacement goods.
Saying 돈을 교환하다 for changing currency. Money exchange is 환전(하다); 교환 is for swapping purchased items or, figuratively, opinions/information.
Marking the replacement with the wrong particle: '큰 사이즈에 교환해요.' Use 로/으로 for what you swap into — 큰 사이즈로 교환해요.

structuredNuance.t: 교환 means swapping a purchased item for a different size, color, or model of the same kind of product. Note it is also used more broadly than shopping — 의견 교환 (exchanging opinions), 정보 교환 (exchanging information) — so the word isn't shop-only, but here it's the item-swap sense.

entries.shortExplanation: 반품 means "return" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "return" is 반품 (banpum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 반품하다 ("to return (an item)"). Watch the particle attached to 반품 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 반품 + 하다 forms the verb 'to send goods back'
가능하다 pairs with 이; the policy-statement phrasing
신청 (application) + 반품 is the online button to start a return

usagePhrases.en: return due to a change of mind
usagePhrases.note: 단순 변심 ('simple change of heart') is the fixed policy term

examples.en: Can I return it?
examples.note: simple: 되다 = 'is allowed', the quick counter question

examples.en: I'd like to return these shoes and get a refund.
examples.note: everyday: -고 chains 반품하다 and 환불받다 (receive a refund)

examples.ko: 택을 떼면 반품이 안 되니까 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: taegeul ttemyeon banpumi an doenikka josimhaseyo.
examples.en: If you remove the tag, a return isn't possible, so be careful.
examples.note: real situation: -니까 gives the reason warning before acting

entries.nuance: 반품 is sending a purchased item back to the seller, normally to undo the sale and get a refund, from the hanja 返品 (返 'to send back/return' + 品 'goods'), literally 'return the goods.' The sharp pair is 교환 (swap for another item, transaction kept) versus 반품 (give it back, transaction reversed) — Korean shops list them side by side as '교환·반품.' Closely linked is 환불 (還拂, 'refund'): you do a 반품 in order to receive a 환불, so they often appear together (반품하고 환불받다). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'return to the store' can make learners think of going back to a place, but 반품 is about returning the goods, not yourself returning somewhere — physically going back is 돌아가다, while handing the item back is 반품하다. Also, 반품하다 already contains 하다, so don't add an extra verb: 'I returned it' is 반품했어요, not 반품을 했어요 in the sense of doing something else.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 반품 (return for refund) and 교환 (swap for a different item). If you want money back, say 반품; 교환 leaves you with replacement goods.
Using 반품 for 'returning to a place.' 반품 means sending goods back; physically going back somewhere is 돌아가다. 'I'm going back to the store' is 가게에 다시 가요, not 가게에 반품해요.
Confusing 반품 with 환불. 반품 is the act of sending the item back; 환불 is getting the money. The sequence is 반품한 뒤에 환불받아요 — you return it, then you're refunded.

structuredNuance.t: 반품 is sending a purchased item back to the seller, normally to undo the sale and get a refund.

entries.shortExplanation: 품절 means "sold out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 품절 (pumjeol) = "sold out". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 품절되다 ("to be/become sold out") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 품절, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 품절 + 되다 makes the passive 'to sell out' (no human agent)
품절 modifies 상품 (product) directly, like an adjective
일시 ('temporarily') softens it — restock expected
임박 ('imminent') is the urgency tag on shopping sites

examples.en: This is sold out.
examples.note: simple 이에요 statement after a consonant-final noun

examples.en: That color is already sold out.
examples.note: everyday: 품절되다 + 벌써 ('already') stresses how fast it went

examples.en: I wanted to buy it, but it was sold out, so I couldn't.
examples.note: real situation: -이라서 ('because it is') gives the reason for 못 사다

entries.nuance: 품절 describes a product that is completely sold out and currently unavailable, from the hanja 品切 (品 'goods' + 切 'cut off/run out'), literally 'goods cut off.' The natural opposites/relatives are 재고 ('stock on hand') and 입고 ('arrival of new stock'); a thing is 품절 precisely when the 재고 hits zero, and it returns when 재입고 (restock) happens. Distinguish 품절 from 매진 (賣盡, 'sold out'), which carries the same idea but is used for tickets and seats (콘서트 매진, a sold-out concert) rather than store merchandise — say 품절 for products, 매진 for tickets. The English-speaker pitfall: 품절 is a noun/state, and Koreans most often state it as 품절이에요 or with the verb 품절되다 (품절됐어요), so avoid forcing the English passive into something like 품절돼졌어요. Also, to say a specific variant is gone, name it as the subject: 이 사이즈는 품절이에요 ('this size is sold out'), not 품절이 이 사이즈예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 품절 for tickets or seats. Sold-out tickets/concerts/seats are 매진 (매진됐어요); reserve 품절 for store products and merchandise.
Over-conjugating into '품절돼졌어요.' The natural forms are the noun statement 품절이에요 or the verb 품절됐어요. 되다 already supplies the passive sense.
Confusing 품절 (sold out, none left) with 재고 (stock available). 재고가 없어요 ('there's no stock') and 품절이에요 overlap, but 재고가 있어요 is the in-stock opposite of 품절.

entries.shortExplanation: 재고 means "stock" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 재고 (jaego) means "stock". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 재고가 있다 ("to have stock / be in stock"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 재고 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to have stock / be in stock
usagePhrases.note: 있다 with 이 is the core 'we have it' phrase
확인하다 takes 재고 as object with 를; the staff's action
떨어지다 ('fall/run out') idiomatically means stock is depleted
정리 ('sorting out') + 세일 names an inventory-clearing sale

examples.en: It's in stock.
examples.note: simple existence: 이 + 있다 = 'there is stock'

examples.en: Is this size still in stock?
examples.note: everyday: 남아 있다 ('remain') is how shoppers ask if any is left

examples.en: There's no stock in the warehouse, so we have to order it.
examples.note: real situation: -아서 gives the reason; -아야 하다 = 'have to'

entries.nuance: 재고 is the quantity of goods a shop currently has on hand to sell, from the hanja 在庫 (在 'to exist/be present' + 庫 'storehouse'), literally 'present in the warehouse.' It is the direct counterpart of 품절: while stock 재고 remains, you can buy; when 재고 runs out, the item becomes 품절. Don't confuse 재고 with 창고 (倉庫, the physical 'warehouse' building) — they share the 庫 'storehouse' character, but 재고 is the inventory inside, 창고 is the room itself. A common collocation is the idiom 재고가 떨어지다 ('stock runs out,' literally 'falls'), the same 떨어지다 used for running out of supplies generally. The English-speaker pitfall: English says 'in stock,' tempting 재고에, but Korean uses existence — 재고가 있어요 ('there is stock') for in stock and 재고가 없어요 for out of stock. To ask a clerk, the idiomatic line is 이거 재고 있어요? rather than a literal translation of 'Do you have this in stock?'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '재고에 있어요' to mean 'it's in stock.' Stock is expressed by existence: 재고가 있어요 (in stock) / 재고가 없어요 (out of stock). 에 would wrongly mark a location.
Confusing 재고 (the inventory) with 창고 (the warehouse building). 'There's no stock' is 재고가 없어요; 'it's in the warehouse' is 창고에 있어요.
Treating 재고 and 품절 as the same word. 재고가 없어요 (no stock) leads to 품절이에요 (sold out). When 재고가 있어요, the item is still buyable — the opposite of 품절.

structuredNuance.t: 재고 is the quantity of goods a shop currently has on hand to sell. A common collocation is the idiom 재고가 떨어지다 ('stock runs out,' literally 'falls'), the same 떨어지다 used for running out of supplies generally.

It is the direct counterpart of 품절: while stock 재고 remains, you can buy; when 재고 runs out, the item becomes 품절. Don't confuse 재고 with 창고 (倉庫, the physical 'warehouse' building) — they share the 庫 'storehouse' character, but 재고 is the inventory inside, 창고 is the room itself.
From the hanja 在庫 (在 'to exist/be present' + 庫 'storehouse'), literally 'present in the warehouse.'

English says 'in stock,' tempting 재고에, but Korean uses existence — 재고가 있어요 ('there is stock') for in stock and 재고가 없어요 for out of stock. To ask a clerk, the idiomatic line is 이거 재고 있어요? rather than a literal translation of 'Do you have this in stock?'.

entries.shortExplanation: 계산서 means "bill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "bill" is 계산서 (gyesanseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 계산서를 주세요. ("Please give me the bill."). Watch the particle attached to 계산서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 를 + 주세요 is the polite 'please give me' request
나오다 ('come out') is how a bill is said to be issued
확인하다 takes 계산서 as object; you verify the amounts
좀 softens the request; 보여 주다 = 'show'

examples.en: The bill, please.
examples.note: simple: drop the particle in casual speech for a quick ask

examples.en: The bill seems a bit off.
examples.note: everyday: 좀 ('a bit') + 이상하다 (be strange) flags a possible error

examples.ko: 계산서를 보니까 음료가 두 번 찍혀 있었어요.
examples.romanization: gyesanseoreul bonikka eumnyoga du beon jjikyeo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: When I looked at the bill, the drink was rung up twice.
examples.note: real situation: -니까 ('upon doing') leads into the discovery

entries.nuance: 계산서 is the itemized statement of what you owe, from 계산 (計算, 'calculation/reckoning': 計 'to count' + 算 'to compute') plus the suffix 서 (書, 'written document'), so it reads 'a written reckoning.' That 서 (書) 'document' morpheme also forms 신청서 (application form) and 보증서 (warranty), a handy pattern to learn. The key contrast is with 영수증 (領收證, 'receipt'): a 계산서 is the request for payment showing the itemized total before/at paying, while 영수증 is the proof you already paid — at a restaurant you get the 계산서 to settle, then the 영수증 afterward. Note 계산서 also has a formal tax sense (세금계산서, 'tax invoice') in business. The English-speaker pitfall: 'bill' in English also means paper money, but Korean 계산서 never means a banknote — a bill/note of money is 지폐. And to ask for the check politely, Koreans say 계산서 주세요 or simply 계산할게요 ('I'll pay'), not a literal 'check, please.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계산서 for paper money because English 'bill' is ambiguous. A banknote is 지폐 (or 돈); 계산서 is only the itemized statement of charges.
Confusing 계산서 (the bill/invoice you pay from) with 영수증 (the receipt proving you paid). Ask for 계산서 before paying; keep the 영수증 after.
Forcing a literal 'check please' as something like '체크 주세요.' At a restaurant, say 계산서 주세요 or 계산할게요 to ask for and settle the bill.

entries.shortExplanation: 봉지 means "bag" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 봉지 (bongji) = "bag". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 봉지에 담다 ("to put into a bag") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 봉지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination; 담다 = to put/pack into a container
비닐 (vinyl) + 봉지 is the everyday convenience-store bag
하나 (one) + 주세요; you often pay extra for it
봉지 doubles as a counter: 'a packet of'

examples.en: A bag, please.
examples.note: simple request; particle dropped in casual speech

examples.en: You have to pay for a plastic bag.
examples.note: everyday: -아야 하다 ('have to') reflects Korea's paid-bag rule

examples.ko: 산 물건을 봉지에 담아서 들고 갔어요.
examples.romanization: san mulgeoneul bongjie damaseo deulgo gasseoyo.
examples.en: I packed what I bought into a bag and carried it out.
examples.note: real situation: 담아서 ('pack and then') chains into 들고 가다 (carry along)

entries.nuance: 봉지 is a thin plastic or paper bag for carrying purchases, and it doubles as a counter for packeted goods (과자 한 봉지, 'a bag of chips'). The most common compound is 비닐봉지 ('vinyl/plastic bag'). Crucially, distinguish 봉지 from 가방: a 가방 is a durable bag you own and reuse — a handbag, backpack, or suitcase — whereas a 봉지 is the flimsy throwaway sack the cashier gives you; calling your backpack a 봉지 sounds odd. Also nearby is 봉투, which is more for envelopes and sturdier paper/shopping bags (종이봉투), with some overlap. Culturally, Korean shops charge for 비닐봉지 by law, so 봉지 드릴까요? ('Shall I give you a bag?') usually implies a small fee. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'bag' covers everything, so learners over-apply 봉지; reserve it for disposable shopping sacks, and use 가방 for personal bags. To pack items 'into' it, use 에 with 담다 (봉지에 담다), the destination particle, not 에서.

Calling a backpack, purse, or suitcase a 봉지. Those reusable personal bags are 가방; 봉지 is the disposable shopping sack the store hands you.
Saying '봉지에서 담아요' for 'I put it in the bag.' 담다 packs into a destination, so use 에: 봉지에 담아요. 에서 marks where an action happens, not where things go in.
Forgetting 봉지 works as a counter and saying '과자 한 개' when you mean a packet. A packaged bag of snacks is 과자 한 봉지; 한 개 would suggest a single piece.

entries.shortExplanation: 거스름돈 means "change" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 거스름돈 (geoseureumdon) means "change". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 거스름돈을 받다 ("to receive change"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 거스름돈 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 takes 거스름돈 as object with 을; you get it back
주다 hands the change to the customer; the everyday verb pairing
됐어요 ('it's fine') politely declines the change
잔돈 is the shorter near-synonym, also meaning loose coins

examples.en: Please give me my change.
examples.note: simple request; particle dropped casually

examples.en: The change is short.
examples.note: everyday: 모자라다 ('be insufficient') flags a shortfall

examples.ko: 만 원을 냈는데 거스름돈을 안 줬어요.
examples.romanization: man woneul naenneunde geoseureumdoneul an jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I paid with 10,000 won, but they didn't give me the change.
examples.note: real situation: -는데 contrasts paying with not receiving change

entries.nuance: 거스름돈 is the money handed back when you pay more than the exact price — pure native Korean, from the verb 거스르다 ('to give change back; to go against the flow') plus 돈 ('money'), so it pictures money 'flowing back' to you. Its close synonym is 잔돈, but the two differ: 거스름돈 is specifically the change returned from a payment, while 잔돈 more broadly means small coins/loose change you carry (잔돈 있어요? = 'Do you have small change?'). From a customer's side it pairs with 받다 (거스름돈을 받다, 'receive change'); from the cashier's side it pairs with 주다 (거스름돈을 줬어요, 'gave the change') — note you say 거스름돈을 주다, not the redundant 거스름돈을 거슬러 주다, since the noun and the verb 거슬러 주다 both come from 거스르다 and stacking them doubles the meaning. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'change' is overloaded, and learners confuse this money sense with 바꾸다 ('to change/alter') or 환전 (currency exchange) — 거스름돈 has nothing to do with those. Also beware 용돈, which sounds vaguely similar but means 'pocket money/allowance,' a completely different word. To say 'keep the change,' don't translate literally; Koreans say 거스름돈은 됐어요 or 그냥 가지세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 거스름돈 (change from a payment) with the verb 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') or 환전 (currency exchange). 거스름돈 is only the cash returned after overpaying.
Mixing up 거스름돈 with 용돈. They sound a little alike, but 용돈 is 'pocket money/allowance,' while 거스름돈 is the change a cashier gives back.
Translating 'keep the change' word-for-word. The natural phrasings are 거스름돈은 됐어요 or 그냥 가지세요 — a literal version sounds unnatural.

entries.shortExplanation: 노트북 means "laptop" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "laptop" is 노트북 (noteubuk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 노트북으로 일해요. ("I work on a laptop."). Watch the particle attached to 노트북 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Tool/means takes -으로 after a consonant: 노트북 ends in ㄱ, so 노트북으로, never 노트북로.
The on/off pair is 켜다/끄다; for booting you also hear 부팅하다, but 켜다 is the everyday word.
가볍다 (light) vs 무겁다 (heavy) is the standard weight pair buyers care about; 가벼워요 is the ㅂ-irregular polite form.
충전(充電) 'fill electricity'; you charge the 배터리, and when it dies you say 배터리가 다 됐어요.

examples.en: This laptop is light.
examples.note: Simple description; 가볍다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so polite form is 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.

examples.en: I watch movies on my laptop too.
examples.note: 도 'also' attaches to the object to add it to other uses; note the means particle 으로 on the device.

examples.en: The company gave me a laptop.
examples.note: Computers and machines are counted with the counter 대, so 한 대 = one (machine).

entries.nuance: 노트북 is the default Korean word for a laptop computer — it comes from English 'notebook' (short for 노트북 컴퓨터), so a beginner's instinct that it means a paper notebook is the classic 직역 trap: a paper notebook is 공책 or just 노트, and only the computer is 노트북. The near-synonym 컴퓨터 is the umbrella term for any computer, while 노트북 specifically marks the portable/foldable kind; a desktop is 데스크톱 or 데스크탑. 랩탑 exists as a transliteration but sounds foreign and is rarely spoken — Koreans say 노트북. Register is fully neutral, fine in any setting. Habitual collocations: 노트북을 켜다/끄다 (turn on/off), 노트북으로 일하다/공부하다 (work/study on it), 노트북이 느리다/빠르다, 가볍다/무겁다, and 노트북을 충전하다 (charge it). The pitfall for English speakers is the particle: 'on a laptop' is 노트북으로 (means), not 노트북에 — 노트북에 would mean physically 'onto/in the laptop' (e.g. saving a file).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 랩탑 because it matches English 'laptop'. It is understood but sounds unnatural — Koreans overwhelmingly say 노트북.
Using 노트북 for a paper notebook. A spiral paper notebook is 공책 or 노트; 노트북 is only the computer. 'I wrote in my 노트북' would sound like you typed into a laptop.
Writing 노트북에서 영화를 봐요 for 'I watch movies on a laptop'. The device as a means takes 으로 (노트북으로 영화를 봐요); 에서 marks a location, so it implies the movie is somewhere inside the device.

entries.shortExplanation: 마우스 means "mouse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 마우스 (mauseu) = "mouse". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마우스로 클릭하다 ("to click with a mouse") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 마우스, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 마우스 ends in a vowel (ㅡ→스), and the rule still gives 마우스로; 클릭하다 borrows 'click' + 하다.
고장 나다 = 'a breakdown occurs', the natural way to say a device stopped working; spaced 고장 나다.
움직이다 is the everyday verb for moving an object slightly; 마우스를 움직여요 in polite speech.
무선(無線) 'no-wire'; the opposite wired is 유선(有線), so 유선 마우스 vs 무선 마우스.

examples.en: The mouse isn't working.
examples.note: 안 되다 'doesn't work/function' is how you report a device problem in casual speech.

examples.en: I even draw pictures with the mouse.
examples.note: 도 adds drawing as an extra use; 그리다 (draw) → 그려요.

examples.en: I bought a new mouse.
examples.note: Small countable items use 하나 (one) naturally; 새 (new) goes directly before the noun.

entries.nuance: 마우스 is purely the computer pointing device — it is a transliteration of English 'mouse' and, crucially, never means the animal. The live animal is 쥐 (which covers both mice and rats; Korean does not split them the way English does), so the English habit of one word for both is exactly the pitfall: '쥐가 고장 났어요' would be absurd, and '마우스가 집에 있어요' sounds like hardware, not a pet. Register is neutral and technical-everyday. Natural collocations: 마우스로 클릭하다 (click), 마우스를 움직이다 (move it), 마우스가 고장 나다 / 안 되다 (it breaks / doesn't work), and the wired/wireless split 유선 마우스 vs 무선 마우스. The means particle is again 으로 — 마우스로 클릭하다, not 마우스에 클릭하다 (English 'click ON' tempts 에/에서, but Korean treats the mouse as the instrument, so 으로).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 마우스 for the animal. The rodent is 쥐; 마우스 only ever means the computer device.
Saying 마우스에 클릭해요 by analogy with 'click ON the mouse'. You click WITH the mouse, so it's the instrument: 마우스로 클릭해요. 클릭하다 itself takes the screen target with 을/를 or just the place you click.
Expecting a separate word for a small mouse vs a big rat in everyday talk — Korean uses 쥐 for both, so don't search for a 마우스/쥐 size distinction the way English has mouse/rat.

entries.shortExplanation: 모니터 means "monitor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 모니터 (moniteo) means "monitor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 모니터로 영화를 보다 ("to watch a movie on a monitor"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 모니터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to watch a movie on a monitor
usagePhrases.note: Means particle 으로 marks the screen you view it through; 보다 (watch) → 봐요.
Size pair 크다 (big) / 작다 (small); 화면(畫面) 'screen' is the display surface, so 화면이 크다 is also common.
연결(連結) 'link-tie'; you 연결하다 (connect) a monitor to a 노트북 with a 케이블.
Borrowed 듀얼 'dual'; two screens side by side, very common phrasing in offices: 모니터 두 대.

examples.en: The monitor is too bright.
examples.note: 너무 'too (much)' before an adjective; 밝다 (bright) → 밝아요.

examples.en: I view photos large on the monitor.
examples.note: 크게 is the adverb form of 크다 'big' → 'largely/in big size'.

examples.ko: 큰 모니터를 한 대 사고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: keun moniteoreul han dae sago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to buy a big monitor.
examples.note: Screens are machines, so counter 대; -고 싶다 expresses the speaker's own desire.

entries.nuance: 모니터 is specifically a computer display screen, distinct from a 텔레비전/TV which is a broadcast set you watch programs on — the dividing line is function, not shape: even an identical-looking panel is a 모니터 if it shows your computer and a 텔레비전 if it receives channels. From English 'monitor', it stays neutral in register. Note the related word 화면 (畫面, 'picture-surface') means the screen/display *content or surface* itself, so '화면이 꺼졌어요' = the display went dark, while '모니터를 샀어요' = I bought the physical unit. Habitual collocations: 모니터를 켜다/끄다, 모니터로 ~를 보다, 모니터를 연결하다 (connect), 모니터가 크다/작다/밝다/어둡다, and 듀얼 모니터 / 모니터 두 대. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a TV a 모니터 (and vice versa), plus reaching for 에서 — you watch 모니터로 (through it as a means), and 모니터에 means onto the monitor (e.g. 모니터에 먼지가 있어요, dust on the monitor).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

structuredNuance.t: 모니터 is specifically a computer display screen. From English 'monitor', it stays neutral in register. Habitual collocations: 모니터를 켜다/끄다, 모니터로 ~를 보다, 모니터를 연결하다 (connect), 모니터가 크다/작다/밝다/어둡다, and 듀얼 모니터 / 모니터 두 대.

entries.shortExplanation: 프린터 means "printer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "printer" is 프린터 (peurinteo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 프린터로 인쇄하다 ("to print with a printer"). Watch the particle attached to 프린터 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The machine is 프린터; the action is 인쇄(印刷)하다 'print'. 프린트하다 (from 'print') also exists colloquially.
고장 나다 for a malfunction; office printers famously 자주 고장 나요 (break down often).

usagePhrases.en: the printer is out of paper
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the container/location here — paper is inside the printer, so 프린터에, not 프린터로.
흑백(黑白) 'black-white'; color is 컬러, so 컬러 프린터 vs 흑백 프린터.

examples.en: I print photos with the printer.
examples.note: 뽑다 'pull out/print out' is the casual verb for getting a printout; means particle 으로.

examples.en: There is a printer at the office.
examples.note: Existence 있다 with location 에; machines counted with 대.

examples.en: The printer ran out of paper.
examples.note: 다 떨어지다 'be all used up'; 에 marks where the paper is (inside the printer).

entries.nuance: 프린터 is the physical printing machine (from English 'printer'), and the key contrast learners must internalize is device vs action: the act of printing is 인쇄하다 (印刷하다, Sino-Korean 'print') or casually 프린트하다 / 뽑다, while a printed handout itself is 프린트 (a 프린트, a printout). So '프린터를 했어요' is wrong — you 인쇄를 했어요 (did the printing) using the 프린터. Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 프린터로 인쇄하다/뽑다, 프린터가 고장 나다, 프린터에 종이가 없다/떨어지다, 프린터로 ~를 출력하다 (출력 出力, the more technical 'output/print'), and 컬러/흑백 프린터. Two particle traps: the means is 프린터로 (print *with* it), but supplies live *in* it, so paper and ink take 에 — 프린터에 종이가 없어요, 프린터에 잉크가 떨어졌어요. English 'print it on the printer' wrongly suggests 에 for the action.

entries.shortExplanation: 스피커 means "speaker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 스피커 (seupikeo) = "speaker". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 스피커로 음악을 듣다 ("to listen to music on a speaker") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 스피커, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to listen to music on a speaker
usagePhrases.note: Means 으로; 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular → 들어요 (the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel).
소리 'sound', 크다 'big/loud'; for sound, 크다/작다 = loud/quiet, so 소리가 커요.
켜다/끄다 on/off; a Bluetooth speaker you 블루투스로 연결하다 (connect via Bluetooth) first.
블루투스 'Bluetooth'; wireless portable ones are everywhere, phrased 블루투스 스피커.

examples.en: The speaker is too loud.
examples.note: Sound volume uses 크다 (loud) / 작다 (quiet), not 시끄럽다 here; 시끄럽다 is 'noisy/annoying'.

examples.en: I play songs on the speaker.
examples.note: 틀다 'turn on/play (audio/video)' is the natural verb for playing music; means particle 으로.

examples.en: I bought a new speaker.
examples.note: 하나 for one small item; 새 directly before the noun for 'new'.

entries.nuance: 스피커 (from English 'speaker') means the audio output device that plays sound — and the trap is that, unlike English, it does NOT mean a person speaking. A speaker at an event/lecture is 발표자 (發表者, 'presenter') or 연사 (演士), and a native speaker of a language is 원어민; calling a presenter a 스피커 is a 직역 mistake. Register is neutral, technical-everyday. Useful contrast: 스피커 outputs sound out loud, whereas 이어폰/헤드폰 send it privately to your ears. Habitual collocations: 스피커로 음악을 듣다/틀다, 스피커를 켜다/끄다, 스피커 소리가 크다/작다, 스피커를 (블루투스로) 연결하다, and 블루투스 스피커. For volume use 소리가 크다/작다 (loud/quiet), and note 음량/볼륨 (volume) is the level you 높이다/낮추다 (raise/lower). The particle pitfall: play music 스피커로 (means), not 스피커에서.
