Using 스피커 for a person who speaks. A presenter is 발표자/연사; a native speaker is 원어민. 스피커 is only the sound device.
Saying 스피커가 시끄러워요 to mean 'the speaker is loud'. 시끄럽다 means 'noisy/bothersome'. For plain loudness say 소리가 커요; use 시끄럽다 only when the sound is annoying.
Saying 스피커에서 음악을 들어요 for listening via the speaker. The device is the means: 스피커로 음악을 들어요. 에서 marks a place and sounds odd here.

entries.shortExplanation: 이어폰 means "earphones" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이어폰 (ieopon) means "earphones". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이어폰으로 음악을 듣다 ("to listen to music with earphones"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이어폰 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to listen to music with earphones
usagePhrases.note: Means 으로 after consonant ㄴ; 이어폰으로. Listening is 듣다 → 들어요 (ㄷ-irregular).
끼다 'insert/wear (snug things)' is the verb for in-ear buds; 끼다/빼다 = put in / take out.
줄 'cord/wire'; 엉키다 'get tangled'. Wired buds are 유선 이어폰.
무선(無線) 'wireless'; the true-wireless buds (like AirPods) are 무선 이어폰 or 블루투스 이어폰.

examples.en: I put in earphones and listen to music.
examples.note: -고 links two actions in sequence; 끼다 is the right verb for in-ear buds (not 쓰다/입다).

examples.en: On the subway I use earphones.
examples.note: Here 쓰다 'use' is fine for the general act of using; 에서는 = at (location) + topic 는.

examples.en: The earphone cord keeps tangling.
examples.note: 자꾸 'repeatedly/keep ~ing' captures the recurring annoyance; 엉키다 → 엉켜요.

entries.nuance: 이어폰 (from 'earphone') are small in-ear listening devices, and the sharp contrast is with 헤드폰 — the bigger over-the-ear cans: don't call headphones 이어폰. Within earbuds, wired ones are 유선 이어폰 and the true-wireless type (AirPods-style) are 무선 이어폰 / 블루투스 이어폰, though many people just say 에어팟 generically. Register is neutral. The verb pitfall is choosing how to 'wear' them: in-ear buds take 끼다 (insert snugly) — 이어폰을 끼다 — while over-ear 헤드폰 take 쓰다 (wear on the head); 입다 (wear clothes) is wrong for both. Habitual collocations: 이어폰을 끼다/빼다, 이어폰으로 음악을/영어를 듣다, 이어폰 줄이 엉키다, and 무선/유선 이어폰. Particle note: listen 이어폰으로 (means), and the cord 줄 takes 이/가 as the subject that tangles (줄이 엉켜요), not 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling over-ear headphones 이어폰. Big over-the-head ones are 헤드폰; 이어폰 are the small in-ear kind.
Saying 이어폰을 입다 or 이어폰을 신다 for putting them in. In-ear buds take 끼다 (이어폰을 끼다). 입다 is for clothing and 신다 is for footwear.
Using 이어폰에서 음악을 들어요. The earphones are the means, so 이어폰으로 음악을 들어요. Reserve 에서 for a location, not a device you listen through.

entries.shortExplanation: 데이터 means "data" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "data" is 데이터 (deiteo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 데이터로 영상을 보다 ("to watch videos using data"). Watch the particle attached to 데이터 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Means 으로; mobile data as the means of connecting. 데이터로 = on (mobile) data.
부족(不足)하다 'be insufficient'; near month-end people say 데이터가 부족해요.

usagePhrases.en: to use up all the data
usagePhrases.note: 다 'all' + 쓰다 'use'; 데이터를 다 썼어요 = the allowance is gone.
무제한(無制限) 'no-limit'; a 데이터 무제한 요금제 is an unlimited-data plan.

examples.en: I'm low on data this month.
examples.note: 이번 달 'this month' sets the time frame; 부족하다 'be insufficient/short'.

examples.en: I use data because there's no wifi.
examples.note: -아서/어서 gives reason; 없어서 'because there isn't', then the result clause.

examples.ko: 데이터를 다 써서 영상이 안 나와요.
examples.romanization: deiteoreul da sseoseo yeongsangi an nawayo.
examples.en: I used up my data, so videos won't play.
examples.note: Chained -아서/어서 for cause; 안 나오다 'won't come out/play' for media not loading.

entries.nuance: 데이터 (from English 'data') in everyday Korean almost always means your mobile-phone data allowance, not abstract research information — that everyday narrowing is the pitfall: a scientist's 'the data shows...' is 자료 (資料, 'reference material') or 데이터 in technical writing, but '데이터가 없어요' to a normal person means your phone's data ran out, not 'there is no information.' The near-synonym is 정보 (情報, 'information'), which is the content/knowledge itself, distinct from the data allowance you buy. Register is neutral and very common when newcomers set up a phone. Habitual collocations: 데이터를 쓰다/다 쓰다, 데이터가 부족하다/남다 (be short / be left over), 데이터로 영상을 보다, 데이터를 켜다/끄다 (toggle mobile data), and 데이터 무제한 (unlimited). Particle pitfall: connect 데이터로 (by means of data), not 데이터에서. Also, 'a lot of data' is 데이터가 많다, and 'out of data' is 데이터가 떨어지다/다 되다.

Equating 데이터 with 정보 in daily talk. To a normal person 데이터 = your phone's data allowance; abstract information is 정보, and research data is 자료.
Saying 데이터에서 영상을 봐요 for watching on mobile data. Data is the means: 데이터로 영상을 봐요. 에서 marks a location and is wrong here.
Using 데이터가 없어요 to mean 'there is no information'. To most listeners that means your mobile data is used up. For 'no information' say 정보가 없어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 요금제 means "phone plan" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 요금제 (yogeumje) = "phone plan". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 새 요금제로 바꾸다 ("to switch to a new plan") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 요금제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to switch to a new plan
usagePhrases.note: 바꾸다 'change/switch'; the target plan takes 으로 (요금제로 바꾸다) = 'change INTO a plan'.
고르다 'pick' is a 르-irregular → 골라요; you compare and 고르다 a 요금제.
비싸다 (expensive) / 싸다 (cheap) is the price pair; 비싸요/싸요 in polite speech.
A 요금제 named by its feature; 무제한(無制限) 'no-limit', a very common plan type.

examples.en: I want to switch to a cheaper plan.
examples.note: Target of 바꾸다 takes 으로; -고 싶다 for the speaker's wish.

examples.en: This plan has a lot of data.
examples.note: Topic 는 introduces the plan, then comments on its data; 많다 'be a lot' → 많아요.

examples.en: Could you recommend a plan?
examples.note: 좀 softens the request; -아/어 주세요 'please do for me'.

entries.nuance: 요금제 (料金制, literally '料金 fee/charge + 制 system' = 'fee system/plan') is a mobile-phone service pricing plan — the package of data, calls, and texts you sign up for — and it is one of the first words a newcomer needs when getting a phone. The crucial contrast is 요금제 (the plan/scheme) vs 요금 (料金, the fee/charge itself): 요금제를 바꿨어요 = I changed my PLAN, but 요금이 많이 나왔어요 = the CHARGE came out high (my bill was big). Confusing them is the main pitfall. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 요금제를 바꾸다/고르다/선택하다, 요금제가 비싸다/싸다, 요금제를 추천하다, and feature names like 데이터 무제한 요금제, 알뜰 요금제 (budget/MVNO plan). Particle note: when switching, the new plan is the destination with 으로 — 새 요금제로 바꾸다, not 요금제를 바꾸다 alone when you mean 'switch TO'. The 알뜰폰 (budget carrier) world is where newcomers often hunt for a cheap 요금제.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 요금제 with 요금. 요금제 = the plan/scheme; 요금 = the actual fee/bill. '요금이 나왔어요' = the charge came; '요금제를 바꿨어요' = I changed plans.
Saying 요금제에 바꿨어요 for 'switched to a plan'. The new plan is the destination, marked 으로: 새 요금제로 바꿨어요. 바꾸다 pairs the old thing (을/를) with the new (으로).
Treating 요금제 as a generic 'price'. It specifically means a telecom service plan, not the price of goods (that's 가격 or 값).

The 알뜰폰 (budget carrier) world is where newcomers often hunt for a cheap 요금제.
The crucial contrast is 요금제 (the plan/scheme) vs 요금 (料金, the fee/charge itself): 요금제를 바꿨어요 = I changed my PLAN, but 요금이 많이 나왔어요 = the CHARGE came out high (my bill was big).
요금제 is 料金制, literally '料金 fee/charge + 制 system' = 'fee system/plan'.
Confusing 요금제 with 요금 is the main pitfall. Particle note: when switching, the new plan is the destination with 으로 — 새 요금제로 바꾸다, not 요금제를 바꾸다 alone when you mean 'switch TO'.

entries.shortExplanation: 문자 means "text message" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 문자 (munja) means "text message". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 문자로 연락하다 ("to contact by text"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 문자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 연락(連絡)하다 'get in touch'; 문자로 = by text. After a vowel the means particle is plain 로, and 문자 ends in the vowel ㅏ, so 문자로, never 문자으로.
오다 'come' is the natural verb for an incoming message; 문자가 왔어요 = a text arrived.
보내다 'send'; the send/receive pair is 보내다 / 받다, and incoming ones 오다.
확인(確認)하다 'confirm/check'; you 확인하다 a message you received.

examples.en: A text came in.
examples.note: Incoming messages use 오다 (come), not 받다, in this announcing sense: 문자가 왔어요.

examples.en: A text came from the bank.
examples.note: 에서 marks the source 'from' (an organization); the bank as origin of the text.

examples.en: Please send the address by text.
examples.note: Means 문자로 'by text'; -아/어 주세요 for a polite request.

entries.nuance: 문자 (文字, 'written character/letter') in daily speech is the everyday word for an SMS text message — short for 문자 메시지. The pitfall is its double life: literally 문자 means written characters/letters (e.g. 한글은 한국의 문자예요, 'Hangul is Korea's writing system'), so context decides. Crucially, 문자 is NOT a paper letter in the mail — that is 편지 (便紙). The near-synonym 카톡 (a KakaoTalk message) is what most people actually send now; 문자 specifically implies the carrier SMS (often bank/official notices), while a casual chat is 카톡 or 메시지. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 문자를 보내다/받다, 문자가 오다, 문자를 확인하다, 문자로 연락하다, and the source pattern 은행/회사에서 문자가 오다. Particle traps: 'by text' is 문자로 (means); the sender/source is marked 에서 for organizations (은행에서) or 한테서/에게서 for people. English speakers often want 'text' as a verb — Korean splits it into 문자를 보내다 (send a text).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 문자 for a posted letter. A physical mailed letter is 편지; 문자 is an SMS text (or, literally, written characters).
Saying 문자를 받았어요 when announcing an arrival. To say 'a text just came', Koreans say 문자가 왔어요 (오다). 받다 is fine for 'I received it', but the natural alert is 왔어요.
Forgetting 문자 needs a verb for 'to text'. There is no single verb; say 문자를 보내다 (send a text) or 문자로 연락하다 (contact by text).

entries.shortExplanation: 영상통화 means "video call" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "video call" is 영상통화 (yeongsangtonghwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 영상통화로 이야기하다 ("to talk over video call"). Watch the particle attached to 영상통화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Means 으로; 영상통화로 = by/over video call. 이야기하다 'talk/chat'.
통화 is a 하다-noun, so the action is 영상통화를 하다 'do a video call', i.e. make one.
끊기다 'be cut off (passive)'; a bad connection 끊겨요. Contrast 끊다 'hang up (on purpose)'.
연결(連結) 'connection'; 안 되다 'fails to work' — a frequent complaint with weak signal.

examples.en: I video-call with my family.
examples.note: 이랑 'with' (casual) marks the other party; the action is 영상통화를 하다.

examples.en: We talk while seeing each other's faces on video call.
examples.note: -면서 'while (doing both)'; the appeal of video is 얼굴을 보다 (see the face).

examples.en: I video-called my parents on the weekend.
examples.note: Time 에 (주말에) + companion 이랑; past 했어요.

entries.nuance: 영상통화 (映像通話, '映像 video-image + 通話 phone-call' = literally 'video phone call') is a phone call with live video — invaluable for newcomers keeping in touch with family abroad. The sharp contrast is with plain 통화 (通話), a voice-only call: 그냥 통화 = a normal voice call, but 영상통화 = with video, so dropping 영상 changes the meaning. Don't say just 통화 when you specifically mean seeing each other's faces. The near-synonym 화상통화 exists (more formal/business, e.g. video conferencing leans 화상 회의), while 영상통화 is the everyday personal term, and people also say 페이스타임/영통 casually. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 영상통화를 하다, 영상통화로 이야기하다/얼굴을 보다, 영상통화가 끊기다, and 영상통화 연결이 안 되다. Particle/verb traps: it is a 하다-noun, so 'make a video call' = 영상통화를 하다 (not 영상통화하다 in writing, though spoken); the other party takes 이랑/하고/와/과 ('with'); 'over video call' is 영상통화로.

Dropping 영상 and saying just 통화 when you mean a video call. 통화 alone is a voice call; keep 영상 (or say 영상통화) for video.
Using 끊다 instead of 끊기다 for a dropped call. 끊다 = you deliberately hang up; 끊기다 = it got cut off by itself (bad signal). '전화가 끊겼어요' = the call dropped.
Marking the other person with 에게/한테 as if calling 'to' them. The companion in a video call takes 와/과/하고/이랑 ('with'): 친구랑 영상통화를 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 배경화면 means "wallpaper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배경화면 (baegyeonghwamyeon) = "wallpaper". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다 ("to make a photo into wallpaper") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배경화면, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to make a photo into wallpaper
usagePhrases.note: Means/material 으로 'with/from (a photo)'; 만들다 'make' → 만들어요.
바꾸다 'change/swap'; the most common action — 배경화면을 자주 바꿔요.
설정(設定)하다 'set/configure'; 으로 marks the role 'as' — 사진을 배경화면으로 설정하다.
Related: 잠금(lock)+화면(screen). The lock screen is 잠금화면, the home/background is 배경화면.

examples.en: The wallpaper is pretty.
examples.note: 예쁘다 (pretty) is a ㅡ-irregular → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before 어).

examples.en: I changed my wallpaper to a dog photo.
examples.note: Material 으로 'with (a dog photo)'; past 바꿨어요.

examples.en: I set this photo as my wallpaper.
examples.note: Role 으로 'as'; 설정하다 is the menu-style verb for 'set/apply'.

entries.nuance: 배경화면 (背景畫面, '背景 background + 畫面 screen-picture' = 'background screen image') is the wallpaper/background image on a phone or computer — and the pitfall is the English word 'wallpaper': this is purely the digital screen background, never the paper you put on a real room wall. Room wallpaper is 벽지 (壁紙, 'wall-paper'), so '방 배경화면을 발랐어요' would be nonsense — you 벽지를 바르다 (paste wallpaper) on a wall. Within screens, contrast 배경화면 (the home/background image) with 잠금화면 (lock screen) and 바탕화면 (the desktop on a computer); they overlap but name different surfaces. The component 화면 (畫面) means 'screen/display', the same 화면 as in 모니터 화면. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 배경화면을 바꾸다/설정하다, 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다, 배경화면이 예쁘다/어둡다, and the pair 배경화면/잠금화면. Particle note: the photo you use is the material/role with 으로 — 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다, 배경화면으로 설정하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배경화면 for real room wallpaper. The digital screen background is 배경화면; physical wall covering is 벽지 (you 벽지를 바르다, paste it).
Saying 배경화면에 사진을 만들어요. The photo is the material you make it FROM, so use 으로: 사진으로 배경화면을 만들어요 / 설정해요.
Conflating 배경화면 with 잠금화면. 배경화면 is the home/background image; 잠금화면 is the lock screen you see before unlocking. They are set separately on a phone.

entries.shortExplanation: 평일 means "weekday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 평일 (pyeongil) means "weekday". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 평일에 ("on a weekday"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 평일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에 for 'on'; 평일에 갔어요 = went on a weekday
No particle: 평일 sticks directly to the next noun to modify it
Common slot for off-peak hours, doctor visits, quiet cafes
After-work time; 평일 저녁에 운동해요 = I work out on weeknights

examples.en: On weekdays I go to school.
examples.note: Topic 은 makes a 'weekdays, as for them' contrast with weekends

examples.en: On weekdays there are fewer people.
examples.note: 에는 = 에(on) + 는(contrast), the natural way to set the scene

examples.en: It's hard to make time on a weekday.
examples.note: Real-life 직장인 complaint: 시간(을) 내다 = to make/spare time

entries.nuance: 평일 is Sino-Korean 平日 (平 'flat/ordinary' + 日 'day'), literally an 'ordinary day' — Monday through Friday, the regular working days, set against 주말 (weekend) and 휴일 (holiday/day off). The dividing line vs 주중 (週中, 'inside the week'): 평일 simply names the ordinary days as a category, while 주중 frames those same days as the span 'during the week' and pairs naturally with 주말 as a matched contrast (주중에는 바쁘고 주말에는 쉬어요). 평일 is neutral and used by everyone in any register, from a weather report to a friend's text. It habitually appears as 평일 + time-of-day (평일 아침/낮/저녁) and with 에/에는. The English-speaker pitfall: 'weekday' in English can mean 'any single working day' OR the whole work portion of the week, but in Korean 평일 leans toward the category of ordinary days, so for a duration like 'during the week I'm busy' Koreans more often say 주중에는 바빠요; also don't write the near-homophone 휴일 (rest day) by mistake.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 평일날 to mean 'on a weekday' is redundant — 일(日) already means 'day', so 날 doubles it; just say 평일에.
Writing 주말 (weekend) when you mean 평일 — they are exact opposites, so 평일에 일해요 (work on weekdays) vs 주말에 쉬어요 (rest on weekends).
Forgetting 에 in time phrases: not 평일 갔어요 but 평일에 갔어요, because a point-in-time noun needs the locative-time particle 에.

Also don't write the near-homophone 휴일 (rest day) by mistake.

entries.shortExplanation: 주중 means "midweek" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "midweek" is 주중 (jujung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주중에 ("during the week"). Watch the particle attached to 주중 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에; the default frame for 'on weekdays as a span'

usagePhrases.en: during the week (as opposed to weekends)
usagePhrases.note: 에는 sets up the 주중 vs 주말 contrast
No particle before the noun it modifies
내내 = 'the whole time'; 주중 내내 바빴어요 = busy the whole week

examples.en: I work during the week.
examples.note: 에는 frames the span and implies 'but on weekends I don't'

examples.en: I have no time during the week.
examples.note: 있다/없다 take 이/가 on the thing possessed: 시간이 없어요

examples.en: I work on weekdays and rest on weekends.
examples.note: Real rhythm-of-life sentence pairing 주중 with 주말

entries.nuance: 주중 is Sino-Korean 週中 (週 'week' + 中 'middle/inside'), literally 'inside the week' — the Monday-to-Friday stretch viewed as a span of time. It overlaps heavily with 평일 (平日), but the dividing line is framing: 평일 names the ordinary days as a category, whereas 주중 emphasizes the duration 'during the week' and is the natural partner of 주말 (週末, 'week-end') in a balanced contrast — Koreans reflexively say 주중에는 ... 주말에는 .... Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 에/에는, with 내내 ('주중 내내', all week long), and with verbs of routine (일하다, 바쁘다). The English-speaker pitfall: 'midweek' in English often means specifically Tuesday–Thursday, but 주중 covers the whole working span, so don't narrow it to just the middle days; and because 주중 is a time-span noun it still needs 에 (주중에 바빠요), unlike a bare adverb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 주중 as 'Wednesday-ish only' the way English 'midweek' can — 주중 means the whole Mon–Fri span, so 주중에 바빠요 = busy all week, not just the middle.
Writing 주말 (weekend) when you mean 주중 — one letter (중 vs 말) flips the meaning to the opposite half of the week.
Dropping 에: not 주중 시간이 없어요 (ambiguous) but 주중에 시간이 없어요, since the time span needs the 에 particle to mean 'during'.

entries.shortExplanation: 매주 means "every week" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 매주 (maeju) = "every week". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매주 월요일 ("every Monday") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매주, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Add a specific day right after: 매주 월요일에 회의해요
Pair with a frequency count; 매주 한 번 청소해요
마다 intensifies 'each and every'; optional but common
꼬박꼬박 = without ever skipping; stresses regularity

examples.en: I exercise every week.
examples.note: 매주 sits right before the verb like an adverb — no particle

examples.en: I go to the library every week.
examples.note: 에 attaches to the place 도서관, not to 매주

examples.en: I take a Korean class every week.
examples.note: 수업을 듣다 = to take/attend a class (literally 'listen to')

entries.nuance: 매주 is Sino-Korean 每週 (每 'each/every' + 週 'week'), literally 'each week' — every week without exception. The 每 prefix is the same building block in 매일 (every day), 매달/매월 (every month), 매년 (every year), so learning it once unlocks the whole set. Unlike a time-point noun, 매주 behaves as a frequency adverb and normally takes NO particle, sitting just before the verb (매주 만나요), though you can add 마다 for emphasis (매주마다). It collocates with a following day (매주 금요일), with counts (매주 두 번), and with 꼬박꼬박/규칙적으로 for 'regularly'. The English-speaker pitfall: learners copy the 'on weekdays → 평일에' habit and wrongly stick 에 onto 매주 (✗매주에); 매주 is already adverbial, so 매주 가요 is complete. Also distinguish 매주 (every week, recurring) from 이번 주 (this week, one specific week) — different concept entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

examples.note: 매달 is adverbial and takes no particle, like 매주

examples.note: 방세를 내다 = to pay rent; classic monthly-bill collocation

매년 생일에 케이크를 먹어요 = cake on each birthday
초 = start; 매년 초에 계획을 세워요
빠짐없이 = 'without omission'; stresses an unbroken streak

examples.en: I travel every year.
examples.note: Adverbial 매년 needs no particle before the verb

examples.note: 에 attaches to 고향(hometown), the destination, not to 매년

examples.note: Real-life 명절(traditional holiday) gathering; 마다 = 'on each'

entries.nuance: 매년 is Sino-Korean 每年 (每 'every' + 年 'year'), literally 'each year' — every year without exception, the time-axis sibling of 매일/매주/매달. entries.shortExplanation: 분 means "minute" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 분 (bun) = "minute". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 오 분만 ("just five minutes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 분, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 만 = 'only'; 오 분만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just five minutes
정도 = 'about/approximately' for a soft estimate

usagePhrases.en: in ten minutes / ten minutes later
usagePhrases.note: 후에 = 'after'; counts forward from now
동안 = 'during/for' a duration of minutes

examples.en: Ten minutes are left.
examples.note: 분 always uses Sino numbers: 십 분, never ✗열 분

examples.en: It takes ten minutes from here.
examples.note: (시간이) 걸리다 = to take (time); the go-to duration verb

examples.en: Let's meet at 3:30.
examples.note: Mixed clock: native 세 시 (3 o'clock) + Sino 삼십 분 (30 min)

entries.nuance: 분 is the time unit 'minute', written with the hanja 分 (to divide/a part) — a minute being a division of the hour. The crucial rule: 분 ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·사·오·...), so it's 오 분, 삼십 분, never the native 하나·둘·셋. This creates Korea's famous mixed clock, where the HOUR uses native numbers + 시 (한 시, 두 시) but the MINUTE uses Sino numbers + 분 (십 분, 삼십 분): 한 시 십 분 = 1:10. Note 분 also means 'a respected person' (한 분 = one person, honorific) and is the honorific counter for people — same syllable, totally different word, disambiguated by context. The English-speaker pitfall: applying the native numbers used for 시 to 분 as well (✗한 분 for one minute — that actually means 'one person, honorific'); the correct 'one minute' is 일 분. Collocates with 후/전 (after/before), 동안 (for), 정도 (about), 만 (only), and 걸리다 (to take).

Carrying the hour pattern into minutes: 한 시 (1 o'clock, native) is right, but 'one minute' is 일 분, not ✗한 분 (which means 'one honored person').
Forgetting the mixed system in a full time: 1:30 is 한 시 삼십 분 — native hour + Sino minute — not all-native or all-Sino.

entries.shortExplanation: 초 means "second" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 초 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 만 = 'only'; 십 초만 기다려요
동안 = 'for' a span; 삼십 초 동안 흔드세요 = shake for 30 sec
후에 = 'after'; 삼 초 후에 출발해요
몇 = 'how many' with counters; 몇 초 걸려요? = how many seconds?

examples.en: Count ten seconds.
examples.note: 초 takes Sino numbers: 십 초, never ✗열 초

examples.en: Ramyeon takes 3 minutes 30 seconds.
examples.note: 초 pairs with 분 for precise durations: 삼 분 삼십 초

examples.en: Answer within ten seconds.
examples.note: (시간) 안에 = 'within' a time limit — quiz/game register

entries.nuance: 초 is the time unit 'second', from the hanja 秒 (a tiny fraction of time). Like 분 (minute), it ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·...), so it's 십 초, 삼십 초, never native 열·서른. It most often appears alongside 분 to give a precise duration (삼 분 삼십 초 = 3:30 of cooking time, lap times, countdowns) and with 동안 (for), 안에 (within), 후/전 (after/before). Beware: the syllable 초 is a homonym jungle — 초 also means 'candle' (촛불 = candlelight), 'vinegar' (식초), and 'the beginning of' a period (월초 = early month, 초반 = early stage); only context tells them apart. The English-speaker pitfall: again, do not import native numbers (✗열 초); and don't confuse the duration 초 (second) with 첫/처음 (first/at first) — 'the first second' is 첫 일 초, while 처음 means 'at first' in a sequence. For everyday speech Koreans round to 분 and rarely specify 초 except in cooking, sports, or countdowns.

Mixing up the homonyms: 초 here is 'second (time)'; 'candle' is also 초 but appears as 촛불/생일 초, and 'vinegar' is 식초 — context decides.
Saying ✗일 초 for 'at first' — that means 'one second'; 'at first/first of all' is 처음(에) or 우선, a different word.

entries.shortExplanation: 시각 means "point in time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "point in time" is 시각 (sigak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 출발 시각 ("departure time"). Watch the particle attached to 시각 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed compound on schedules: 출발 시각을 확인해요
도착 시각이 늦었어요 = the arrival time was late
정확하다 → 정확한; 정확한 시각을 알려 주세요
Formal clock-reading, e.g. on a station display or news

examples.en: I look up the train time.
examples.note: 알아보다 = to look into/check; travel-schedule register

examples.en: The meeting time has changed.
examples.note: 바뀌다 = to change (intransitive); subject takes 이

examples.en: Boarding time is 3 p.m.
examples.note: Airport/announcement tone — 시각 fits formal -습니다 speech

entries.nuance: 시각 is Sino-Korean 時刻 (時 'time' + 刻 'a carved mark/notch') — literally a 'carved mark of time', i.e. one precise point on the clock, like a departure, arrival, or boarding moment. The all-important contrast is with its near-twin 시간 時間 (時 'time' + 間 'interval/space'): 시각 = a single instant ('at what moment'), whereas 시간 = a span/duration OR the general notion of 'time/hours' ('how long'). So 출발 시각 = the departure moment (e.g. 3:00), but 비행 시간 = the flight duration (e.g. 2 hours). 시각 carries a formal, schedule-board, announcement flavor — you meet it on tickets, timetables, and in news ('현재 시각'), but in casual chat people just say 시간 even for a point in time (몇 시에 만나? rather than 몇 시각에). The English-speaker pitfall: 'time' in English covers both, so learners reach for the familiar 시간 everywhere and never use 시각, or worse, swap them — saying ✗시각이 없어요 for 'I have no time' (that should be 시간이 없어요, a duration). Use 시각 only when you mean a pinpoint moment, usually formal.

Using 시각 in casual speech for 'what time' — Koreans say 몇 시에 만나요?, not ✗몇 시각에; reserve 시각 for formal schedules.
Confusing 시각 (point in time) with the homonym 시각(視覺, 'eyesight/visual sense') — same sound, different hanja; context (clock vs senses) tells them apart.

entries.shortExplanation: 기간 means "period" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기간 (gigan) = "period". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험 기간 ("exam period") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기간, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 시험 기간이 길어요 = the exam period is long
방학 기간에 여행해요 = travel during the break
계약 기간은 일 년이에요 = the term is one year
할인 기간을 놓쳤어요 = I missed the sale window

examples.en: The application period ended.
examples.note: Official-notice tone; 접수 = receiving applications

examples.en: I learned a lot in a short period.
examples.note: 짧다 → 짧은; 기간 takes 에 to mean 'within that span'

examples.en: The road is blocked during the construction period.
examples.note: 기간 동안 = 'for the duration of'; everyday signage Korean

entries.nuance: 기간 is Sino-Korean 期間 (期 'a fixed term/appointed time' + 間 'interval') — a defined stretch of time with a clear START and END, such as an exam season, a vacation, a contract term, or a sale window. Contrast it sharply with 시간 時間: 시간 is generic 'time/hours/duration' you measure (세 시간 = three hours), while 기간 is a bounded named span you don't usually count in hours (시험 기간 = the exam period, not '×N hours'). Also distinguish 동안, which is the grammatical word for 'during/for' and attaches to spans (방학 동안), whereas 기간 is the noun naming the span itself (often combined: 방학 기간 동안). 기간 collocates with administrative life — 접수/신청 기간 (application period), 계약/임대 기간 (contract/lease term), 유효 기간 (validity period/expiry), 공사 기간 — and takes 에 ('within') or 동안 ('throughout'). The English-speaker pitfall: translating every 'time' as 시간 and saying ✗시험 시간이 길어요 to mean 'the exam season is long' — that actually reads as 'the exam's duration (one sitting) is long'; the season is 시험 기간.

Confusing 'how long is the period' (기간) with 'how much time' (시간): 유효 기간이 언제까지예요? (until when is it valid) vs 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? (how long does it take).

Translating every 'time' as 시간 and saying ✗시험 시간이 길어요 to mean 'the exam season is long' — that actually reads as 'the exam's duration (one sitting) is long'; the season is 시험 기간.

entries.shortExplanation: 최근 means "recently" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 최근 (choegeun) means "recently". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 최근에 ("recently / lately"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 최근 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 최근에 이사했어요 = I moved recently — 에 needed for the time point
As a modifier, 최근 attaches directly: 최근 뉴스를 봤어요
까지 = 'up to'; 최근까지 일했어요 = worked until lately
Set phrase 들어 = 'entering into'; 최근 들어 부쩍 추워졌어요

examples.en: I've been reading a lot of books lately.
examples.note: 최근에 + present = an ongoing recent habit

examples.en: I met a friend recently.
examples.note: With past tense, 최근에 marks a recent completed event

examples.ko: 최근 몇 년 동안 많이 변했어요.
examples.romanization: choegeun myeon nyeon dongan mani byeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: It has changed a lot over the past few years.
examples.note: 최근 + 몇 년 동안 = 'over the recent few years', written/formal feel

entries.nuance: 최근 is Sino-Korean 最近 (最 'most' + 近 'near') — literally 'most near (in time)', i.e. the recent stretch right up to now. Its near-synonym 요즘 (native, 'these days') overlaps but differs in register and shape: 최근 is more written/formal and works both as a noun-modifier (최근 동향 = recent trends) and, with 에, as a time adverb (최근에 = recently); 요즘 is purely casual-spoken and adverbial (요즘 바빠요), never a noun-modifier (✗요즘 뉴스 sounds off; 최근 뉴스 is right). A subtle nuance gap: 최근 can point to a recent completed event (최근에 갔어요 = I went recently), while 요즘 leans toward the ongoing present situation (요즘 가요 ≈ I go these days). 최근 collocates with 에, 까지, 들어, and number spans (최근 3년/몇 달). The English-speaker pitfall: 'recently' is a bare adverb in English, so learners drop the particle and say ✗최근 갔어요; as a time-point noun 최근 needs 최근에 갔어요. Conversely, when modifying a noun, you DON'T add 에 (최근 소식, not ✗최근에 소식).

Dropping 에 as a time adverb: ✗최근 이사했어요 → ✓최근에 이사했어요, because the recent time point takes the 에 particle.
Using 요즘 as a noun-modifier: ✗요즘 뉴스 → ✓최근 뉴스; 요즘 is adverb-only, while 최근 can sit before a noun.
Over-stretching 최근 to the distant past — 최근 means 'just lately'; for the remote past use 예전(에) or 옛날(에) instead.

entries.shortExplanation: 요즘 means "these days" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "these days" is 요즘 (yojeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 요즘 어때요? ("How are things these days?"). Watch the particle attached to 요즘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Stock friendly opener — no particle on 요즘
들어 = 'coming into'; 요즘 들어 자주 피곤해요 = tired often lately
요즘 같은 시대에 = 'in an age like today's'
요즘 유행이에요 = it's trendy these days (spoken)

examples.en: Are you busy these days?
examples.note: 요즘 needs no particle; it works straight as an adverb

examples.en: I haven't been sleeping well lately.
examples.note: 못 자다 = can't sleep; 요즘 frames an ongoing present state

examples.en: What have you been up to these days?
examples.note: 지내다 = to get along/spend one's days — warm small-talk Korean

entries.nuance: 요즘 is a native Korean word (a contraction of 요사이 → 요즈음 → 요즘) meaning 'around now, these days, lately'. It is one of the single most common small-talk openers in Korean, the natural lead-in to 'how have you been?' Its near-synonym 최근(에) (最近, Sino 'most near') means roughly the same time but differs in register and grammar: 요즘 is warm, casual, spoken, strictly adverbial (요즘 바빠요) and CANNOT modify a noun (✗요즘 소식 → use 최근 소식); 최근 is more formal/written and can both modify nouns and, with 에, act as an adverb. Crucially 요즘 takes NO particle — it stands alone before the clause (요즘 어때요?). It pairs with 들어 ('요즘 들어' = of late), with present-tense verbs for ongoing situations, and with 같은 ('요즘 같은' = like nowadays). The English-speaker pitfall: treating 요즘 like a past-time word and saying ✗요즘 갔어요 ('I went these days'?) — 요즘 describes the ongoing present, so use present tense (요즘 가요 / 요즘 다녀요); for a finished recent event switch to 최근에 갔어요.

Adding a particle: ✗요즘에 바빠요 → ✓요즘 바빠요, because 요즘 is already adverbial and rejects 에.
Pairing 요즘 with a one-off past event: ✗요즘 친구를 만났어요 (sounds like a habit) → for a single recent meeting say 최근에 친구를 만났어요.
Using 요즘 to modify a noun: ✗요즘 뉴스 → ✓요즘 나오는 뉴스 or simply 최근 뉴스; 요즘 can't directly precede a noun.

entries.shortExplanation: 예전 means "the past" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 예전 (yejeon) = "the past". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 예전에 ("in the past / back then") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 예전, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예전에 여기 살았어요 = I used to live here
부터 = 'from/since'; 예전부터 알았어요 = I've known since long ago
보다 = 'than'; 예전보다 좋아졌어요 = better than before
예전 모습 그대로예요 = just like you used to be

examples.en: In the past I had lots of time.
examples.note: 에는 (에+는) adds 'as for back then', contrasting with now

examples.en: I met an old friend again.
examples.note: 예전 modifies 친구 directly — an old/former friend

examples.en: We don't see each other as often as we used to.
examples.note: 예전만큼 = 'as much as before'; nostalgic, real-life tone

entries.nuance: 예전 means 'the (fairly distant) past, the old days, a while back' and carries a gently nostalgic flavor, the feeling of looking back on how things used to be. Its near-synonyms map onto a distance scale: 옛날 (옛날, native 'olden times') is the most remote — fairy-tale 'once upon a time' (옛날 옛적에) or 'the old days' long gone; 예전 is past but within a person's own lived memory ('back when I was younger'); 최근 (最近) is the recent past close to now. So you'd say 예전에 여기 살았어요 (I used to live here, a few years back) but 옛날 사람들 for 'people of old'. 예전 works both as a time adverb with 에 (예전에) and as a noun-modifier (예전 사진 = old photos), and it loves 부터 (since), 보다/만큼 (than/as much as), and 그대로 (just as it was). The English-speaker pitfall: using 예전 for 'a moment ago / just now' — that's 아까 or 방금, not 예전; 예전 implies a meaningful gap of time, often months or years, viewed with hindsight, not 'earlier today'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예전 for the very near past: ✗예전에 전화했어요 for 'I called a moment ago' → use 아까/방금 전화했어요; 예전 implies a long-ago time.
Dropping 에 as an adverb: ✗예전 살았어요 → ✓예전에 살았어요, since the past time point needs the 에 particle.
Treating 예전 and 옛날 as identical — 옛날 is the remote 'once upon a time / olden days', while 예전 is the nearer, personally-remembered past.

entries.shortExplanation: 기온 means "temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 기온 (gion) means "temperature". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기온이 높아요 ("the temperature is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기온 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: air temperature takes 높다/낮다, never 크다
fixed phrase: 기온은 떨어지다/오르다, not 내려가다 in forecasts
일교차 means the daily high-low gap
영하 = below zero, 영상 = above zero

examples.en: The temperature is high today.
examples.note: simplest 이/가 + 높다 frame

examples.en: When night comes the temperature drops a lot.
examples.note: time clause + the set verb 떨어지다

examples.ko: 일교차가 커서 아침저녁으로 기온이 많이 달라요.
examples.romanization: ilgyochaga keoseo achimjeonyeogeuro gioni mani dallayo.
examples.en: The daily temperature range is big, so the temperature differs a lot morning and evening.
examples.note: real forecast register with 일교차

entries.nuance: 기온 is the air temperature expressed as a number of degrees (氣溫, 기 'air/atmosphere' + 온 'warmth'), so it is the measurable reading the forecaster gives, whereas 날씨 is the whole overall feel of the weather (sunny, humid, windy) and 온도 is the neutral word for the temperature of any object or liquid like 물 온도 water temperature or 체온 body temperature. Use 기온 only for outdoor air. It pairs with 높다 high and 낮다 low, and with the motion verbs 오르다 rise and 떨어지다 fall; the big English-speaker trap is reaching for 크다/작다 (big/small) the way English lets you say a 'big' difference, but a temperature itself is 높다/낮다, and only the gap 일교차 or 차이 can be 크다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기온이 커요 to mean a high temperature; size words do not apply, say 기온이 높아요.
Using 온도 for the weather outside (온도가 높아요 about the sky); for outdoor air use 기온, and reserve 온도 for objects or water.
Saying 기온이 내려가요 by translating 'go down'; the idiomatic verb for the reading is 기온이 떨어지다.

entries.shortExplanation: 일기예보 means "weather forecast" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "weather forecast" is 일기예보 (ilgiyebo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일기예보를 보다 ("to check the forecast"). Watch the particle attached to 일기예보 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: forecasts are watched/read with 보다, not 듣다 by default
맞다 = turn out correct; opposite 틀리다
quote source with 에서 + 고 하다
주간 weekly, 오늘/내일 일기예보 for the day

examples.en: I check the weather forecast every morning.
examples.note: habit with 마다 + 보다

examples.en: The forecast was right, so I grabbed an umbrella.
examples.note: 맞다 as result + practical action

examples.en: The forecast said it would snow tomorrow.
examples.note: reported speech with 에서 ... 고 하다

entries.nuance: 일기예보 is the official weather forecast you get from the news or an app (日氣豫報, literally 일기 'the day's air = weather' + 예보 'fore-report'), so it names the prediction itself, not the weather. Contrast it with plain 날씨, which is the actual weather happening now: you say 날씨가 좋아요 for today's nice weather but 일기예보가 좋아요 only when the predicted outlook is good. Koreans habitually 일기예보를 보다 (watch/read it) and judge it as 맞다 right or 틀리다 wrong, and they quote it with 일기예보에서 ~고 했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a verb ('to forecast') — it is a noun, so attach a verb like 보다 or 확인하다, and use 에서 (the source particle) rather than 에 when reporting what it announced.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 듣다 by default (일기예보를 들었어요) because English says 'hear the forecast'; the unmarked verb is 보다 since people watch or read it.
Saying 일기예보를 했어요 as if it were a verb; it is a noun, so say 일기예보를 봤어요/확인했어요.
Marking the source with 에 (일기예보에 ~고 했어요); the quoting source particle is 에서: 일기예보에서 비가 온다고 했어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 장마 means "rainy season" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 장마 (jangma) = "rainy season". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장마가 시작되다 ("the rainy season begins") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장마, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: set inchoative 시작되다 / opposite 끝나다, 물러가다
철 = season; 장마철에 = during the rainy season
전선 = the weather front that brings it
마른장마 = a dry spell with little rain

examples.en: The rainy season begins in summer.
examples.note: season + inchoative 시작되다

examples.en: During the rainy season laundry does not dry well.
examples.note: 철 period + a real everyday consequence

examples.en: This year the rainy season is long, so I am worried about mold.
examples.note: real-life worry: humidity and mold

entries.nuance: 장마 is Korea's long early-summer monsoon, the roughly three-to-four-week stretch around late June and July when a stationary rain front parks over the peninsula and brings steady, humid rain day after day. It is a whole climatic period, not a single rainfall, so it contrasts sharply with 비 (one instance of rain) and with 소나기 (a sudden short downpour): you can have 비 during 장마, but 장마 names the season. The word is treated as native Korean (it is not a hanja compound), and it lives in fixed phrases — 장마가 시작되다/끝나다 and the compound 장마철 'rainy-season time'. The pitfall for English speakers is calling any rainy day 장마; reserve it for the seasonal monsoon, and note that 장마 takes 시작되다/끝나다 rather than the falling verbs 오다/내리다 that plain rain uses.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a single rainy day 장마 (오늘 장마예요 for one wet afternoon); 장마 is the multi-week season — for one rain say 비가 와요.
Saying 장마가 와요 / 장마가 내려요 by analogy with rain; the season 시작되다 begins and 끝나다 ends, while only 비 오다/내리다.
Dropping 철 when you mean 'during the rainy season'; say 장마철에 rather than just 장마에 for the time frame.

entries.shortExplanation: 태풍 means "typhoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 태풍 (taepung) means "typhoon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 태풍이 오다 ("a typhoon comes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 태풍 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 태풍 moves, so it uses 오다/지나가다/북상하다
지나가다 = pass by, leaving calm after
영향권 = the affected zone forecasters mention
strength is 강하다/세다, named 태풍 + name

examples.en: A typhoon is coming tomorrow.
examples.note: basic motion verb 오다

examples.en: Because the typhoon came, all the flights were canceled.
examples.note: cause + a real consequence (결항)

examples.en: As the typhoon moves north it is gradually getting stronger.
examples.note: news register: 북상하다 + 세지다

entries.nuance: 태풍 is a typhoon, the large tropical storm system that strikes Korea mainly in late summer and early autumn (颱風, literally 태 'typhoon' + 풍 'wind'). Even though the second character means wind, 태풍 is conceived as a moving body of weather, so it travels with 오다 come, 지나가다 pass, and the news verb 북상하다 move north — it does not 'blow.' That is the key contrast with plain 바람 wind, which 불다 blows: you must not say 태풍이 불어요. entries.nuance: 무지개 is a rainbow, the arc of color that forms when sunlight passes through droplets after rain. The grammar point that matters is its set verb: a rainbow 뜨다 (rises/appears), exactly like the sun 해가 뜨다 and the moon 달이 뜨다, because Korean treats things that emerge in the sky with 뜨다; you may also hear 무지개가 생기다 it forms. entries.nuance: 안개 is fog or mist — the cloud of tiny water droplets near the ground that cuts visibility. Its defining grammar is the verb 끼다, the same verb used for clouds 구름이 끼다, meaning the haze 'settles in,' so 안개가 끼다 is the standard way to say it gets foggy and 안개가 걷히다 that it lifts. Density is expressed with 짙다 thick and 옅다 thin — never the physical-thickness word 두껍다 — and a thick fog is 짙은 안개. 안개 is a native Korean noun (no hanja), and a close relative is 안개비 'misty drizzle.' The crucial pitfall for English speakers is the verb: do not say 안개가 와요 (treating fog like rain) and do not say 안개가 두꺼워요 by translating 'thick fog' literally; say 안개가 끼다 and 안개가 짙다.

Saying 안개가 와요 because rain 'comes'; fog settles, so the verb is 끼다 — 안개가 꼈어요.
Saying 안개가 두꺼워요 by translating 'thick fog'; physical thickness 두껍다 is wrong here — use 짙다: 안개가 짙어요.
Saying 안개가 가요 for fog clearing; the set verb is 걷히다 or 사라지다 — 안개가 걷혔어요.

들다/비치다 = shine into a space
가리다 = shield, e.g. with a hand or curtain
따갑다 = it stings on the skin

examples.note: basic 이/가 + 강하다

examples.note: 들다 'enter a space' + location 으로

entries.nuance: 햇빛 is sunlight — literally 해 'sun' + 빛 'light,' the visible light streaming from the sun (the ㅅ in the middle is a 사이시옷, so it is written 햇빛 and sounds like '핻삗'). It is close to two cousins you should separate: 햇살 is the same sunlight pictured as soft, slanting rays and feels warmer and more literary (따스한 봄 햇살 'warm spring rays'), while 햇볕 is specifically the sun's warmth/heat you feel on your skin, the thing you sunbathe in (햇볕이 따갑다, 햇볕을 쬐다). So describe brightness/light with 햇빛, gentle poetic rays with 햇살, and felt heat with 햇볕. 햇빛 pairs with 강하다 strong, 들다/비치다 to shine in, and 가리다 to block. The English-speaker pitfall is using 햇빛 for the warmth you bask in — that role belongs to 햇볕 (햇볕을 쬐다 'soak up the sun'), not 햇빛.

usagePhrases.note: static location takes 에서 with action verbs
지다 = (shade) forms, e.g. 나무 그늘이 지다

examples.note: reason + 에서 with the action 쉬다

examples.note: possessive compound + 시원하다

entries.nuance: 그늘 is shade — the cool, dimmer area where an object blocks the sun, and it is the natural opposite of 햇빛/햇볕, prized as a refuge on a hot day (그늘이 시원하다 'the shade is cool'). The contrast every learner must nail is 그늘 vs 그림자: 그늘 is the shaded zone you can stand in and cool off, an area, whereas 그림자 is the dark shape an object casts — your silhouette on the ground (내 그림자가 길다 'my shadow is long'). Calling your cast silhouette 그늘; the shape on the ground is 그림자 — 그림자가 길어요, not 그늘.

entries.shortExplanation: 더위 means "heat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 더위 (deowi) = "heat". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 더위를 타다 ("to be sensitive to heat") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 더위, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. examples.note: basic 이/가 + 심하다

entries.nuance: 더위 is heat as a felt, oppressive condition — the experience of hot weather rather than a number — formed from the adjective 덥다 'to be hot' plus the noun-making ㅟ, so it is the noun counterpart of 덥다 (mirroring 추위 from 춥다). Translating 'I get hot easily' as 더위를 먹어요; that idiom means heatstroke. 'I'm sensitive to heat' is 더위를 타요.
Swapping 더위 and 기온; a high reading is 기온이 높다, while 더위 is the felt heat — 더위가 심하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 추위 means "cold" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

entries.nuance: 첫눈 is the first snowfall of the season (첫 'first' + 눈 'snow'), and in Korea it is wrapped in romantic feeling: there is a widespread sentiment that meeting or confessing love on the day of 첫눈 brings good luck, so the word carries warmth a plain 눈 does not. Grammatically it behaves like the snow it is: it 오다 comes or 내리다 falls (내리다 sounding slightly more written), and you 첫눈을 기다리다 wait for it. Note the homonym trap: 첫눈 also means 'first sight' in the fixed phrase 첫눈에 반하다 'to fall in love at first glance,' where 눈 is the 'eye' — context tells the two apart. The contrast with plain 눈 is purely about that 'first of the season' specialness plus the emotional aura. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing 'the first snow appeared/showed up'; like all snow it simply 오다/내리다 — say 첫눈이 왔어요.

Saying 첫눈이 떴어요 or 나타났어요 ('appeared'); snow falls, so use 오다/내리다 — 첫눈이 왔어요.
Reading 첫눈 only as 'first snow' in 첫눈에 반하다; there it means 'first sight (of the eye)' — 'I fell for them at first sight.'
Treating 첫눈 as just any snow; reserve it for the season's first snowfall — repeated snow is simply 눈이 와요.

entries.shortExplanation: 장화 means "rain boots" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: footwear takes 신다; remove with 벗다
-고 = and then go, the 'put on and...' chain
the classic material; 노란 장화 = yellow boots
비 오는 날 = rainy days call for them

examples.en: It rained, so I put on rain boots.
examples.note: reason + 신다 for footwear

examples.ko: 아이가 노란 장화를 신고 첨벙첨벙 뛰어요.
examples.romanization: aiga noran janghwareul singo cheombeongcheombeong ttwieoyo.
examples.en: The child is splashing around in yellow rain boots.
examples.note: -고 chain + the mimetic 첨벙첨벙

examples.ko: 장마철엔 장화 한 켤레쯤 있으면 편해요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren janghwa han kyeollejjeum isseumyeon pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: In the rainy season it's handy to have a pair of rain boots.
examples.note: real advice + the counter 켤레 for pairs

entries.nuance: 장화 is tall waterproof boots — rain boots or rubber wellies — worn to keep feet dry on wet days (長靴, literally 장 'long' + 화 'shoe/boot,' i.e. 'long boots' reaching up the calf). Because the hanja names height, 장화 implies the tall shaft, distinguishing it from ordinary low 신발/구두 shoes and from 부츠, the borrowed word for fashion boots: 장화 is specifically the practical, often rubber, rain-and-mud boot (고무장화). Like all footwear it takes the verb 신다 to put on and 벗다 to take off, and pairs by the 켤레 (a pair). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 입다 'to wear' the way English uses one verb for all clothing — boots, like shoes and socks, demand 신다 (장화를 신다), never 입다; reserve 입다 for body garments like coats and shirts.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 장화를 입다 because English 'wear' covers everything; footwear takes 신다 — say 장화를 신어요.
Calling fashion boots 장화; stylish boots are 부츠, while 장화 is the rubber rain/mud boot.
Counting them with 개 (장화 두 개); pairs of footwear use 켤레 — 장화 한 켤레 'a pair of rain boots.'

entries.shortExplanation: 하나 means "one (native number)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 하나 (hana) means "one (native number)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 한 개 ("one item"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 하나 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하나 drops its 나 to become 한 right before a counter
the HOUR is always native: 한 시, never 일 시
명 is the plain counter for people; 한 분 is the polite version
the full standalone 하나 takes particles like 만, 도, 를

examples.en: One, two, three!
examples.note: counting out loud (a countdown) uses the bare standalone forms

examples.en: Please give me just one apple.
examples.note: before the counter 개, 하나 must shrink to 한

examples.en: The meeting starts at one in the afternoon.
examples.note: real scheduling: the clock hour is native (한 시) but you would say the minutes in Sino

entries.nuance: 하나 is the native-Korean (고유어) word for "one," the counting system Koreans use for tangible things, people, age, and the clock hour — as opposed to its Sino-Korean twin 일, which rules dates, money, minutes, and phone numbers. The single biggest fact to internalize: when 하나 sits directly in front of a counter (개, 명, 시, 살, 마리), it loses its last syllable and becomes 한 — 한 개, 한 명, 한 시 — while the full 하나 only stands alone (as in counting "하나, 둘" or taking a particle, 하나만). English speakers reliably trip here by saying 하나 개 or, worse, importing the Sino number and saying 일 개; both sound clearly wrong to a Korean ear. There is no hanja because it is purely native, so do not look for one.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 하나 개 — before any counter the form must contract to 한, so it is 한 개. The full 하나 is only used standalone or with a particle.
Using the Sino 일 for the hour or for objects (일 시, 일 개). The clock hour and counting things are native territory, so it must be 한 시, 한 개.
Writing it solid as 한개 — Korean keeps a space between the number-word and the counter: 한 개.

usagePhrases.note: 둘 drops its 받침 ㄹ and becomes 두 before a counter
the hour is native, so 두 시 (never 이 시)

examples.en: Which of the two do you like more?
examples.note: standalone 둘 takes the particle 중에 ('among')

examples.note: the counter for cups is 잔, and 둘 contracts to 두 in front of it

entries.nuance: 둘 is native-Korean "two," used for counting concrete things, people, and the clock hour, in contrast to Sino 이 which handles minutes, money, floors, and dates. The bare 둘 survives only when it stands alone or takes a particle — note the very common 둘 다 ('both') and 둘 중에 ('between the two'). English speakers often forget the contraction and say 둘 개, or reach for the Sino 이 (이 개), both of which sound off; they also tend to say 두 다 by mistake, but the fixed idiom is 둘 다. Saying 두 다 for 'both' — the idiom keeps the full form: it is 둘 다.
Using Sino 이 to count objects or tell the hour (이 시). The hour and tangible things are native: 두 시, 두 개.

entries.nuance: 열 is native-Korean "ten," used for counting things, people, age, and the clock hour, while Sino 십 takes minutes, money, dates, and floors. It does not contract by itself (열 개, 열 시, 열 명), and it is the building block for the native teens: eleven through nineteen are 열 plus the lower number, so 열하나/열한, 열둘/열두, 열셋/열세, and you still say the hour with these (열한 시 = eleven o'clock). Saying 열 한 시 as two separate words — the teen fuses into one word before the counter: 열한 시.
Trying to use native numbers for huge quantities. Native effectively stops near 99; above that switch to Sino.

entries.nuance: 일 is the Sino-Korean (漢字語) number "one," from the hanja 一 (a single horizontal stroke). It governs the abstract/measured world: dates, money (원), minutes, phone numbers, floors, bus and problem numbers, and any count from the hundreds up — the exact opposite of native 하나, which counts tangible things, people, and the clock hour. So one o'clock is 한 시 but one minute is 일 분; one apple is 사과 한 개 but one won is 일 원. English speakers, used to a single set of numbers, constantly blur the line — saying 일 시 for one o'clock or 하나 분 for one minute. A handy memory hook: anything that already feels like a 'code' or a 'measurement' (clock minutes, addresses, prices) is Sino 일.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 일 시 for one o'clock — the hour is native, so it must be 한 시. Sino 일 is for the MINUTES: 일 분.
Using native 하나 for money, minutes, or floors (하나 원, 하나 분). Those are Sino: 일 원, 일 분.
Reading a phone number in native numbers. Each digit is Sino, so 010 is 공일공, not 영하나영.

entries.nuance: 이 is the Sino-Korean number "two," from the hanja 二 (two horizontal strokes). It runs dates, money, minutes, floors, math, and counts in the hundreds and up — versus native 둘/두, which counts physical things, people, and the clock hour. So two o'clock is 두 시 but two minutes is 이 분; two cups is 두 잔 but two won is 이 원. A real trap unique to 이: it is identical in sound to the demonstrative 이 ('this') and the subject/topic particle context around it, so 이 분 can mean either 'two minutes' or 'this person' (분 = honorific 'person') depending on context — listen carefully. English speakers also tend to use native 둘 for prices or floors (둘 층); those are Sino: 이 층. Treat measured, coded things as Sino 이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이 시 for two o'clock — the hour is native, so 두 시. Sino 이 is for minutes: 이 분.
Using native 둘/두 for money or floors (두 원, 두 층). Those are Sino: 이 원, 이 층.
Confusing 이 분 ('two minutes') with 이분 / 이 분 ('this person'). Context and the noun 분 decide; the number reading needs a measured noun like 분(minute).

entries.nuance: 삼 is the Sino-Korean number "three," from the hanja 三 (three horizontal strokes). entries.nuance: 사 is the Sino-Korean number "four," from the hanja 四. It rules dates, money, minutes, floors, math, and larger counts — opposite native 넷/네, which counts physical things, people, and the clock hour. So four o'clock is 네 시 but four minutes is 사 분; four tickets is 네 장 but 4,000 won is 사천 원. The culturally important point: the Sino reading 사 is a homophone of 死 ('death'), so it is mildly taboo — hospitals and some buildings label the fourth floor 'F' instead of 사 층, and people avoid 4 in gift sets. That superstition rides only on Sino 사, not native 넷. The usual learner error is telling the hour with 사 (사 시) or putting native 네 on money (네천 원). Measured contexts stay Sino, 사.

entries.nuance: 만 is the Sino-Korean number "ten thousand," from the hanja 萬. The deep point for English speakers: Korean does NOT group large numbers by thousands the way English does — it groups by 만 (10,000). So 100,000 is 십만 (ten 만), 1,000,000 is 백만 (hundred 만), and 10,000,000 is 천만 (thousand 만). This 만-based grouping is the single hardest mental switch in Korean numbers, because you must constantly divide by ten-thousands rather than thousands. Unlike 백 and 천, the bill 만 원 is commonly said 일만 원 too, especially when writing checks or being precise. The classic mistake is calculating 'a million' as 천천 (thousand-thousand) — it does not exist; a million is 백만. Master the ladder 만 → 십만 → 백만 → 천만 → 억(100,000,000).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Grouping by thousands like English — Korean groups by 만(10,000). So 100,000 is 십만, not '백천'.
Saying 천천 for a million — that does not exist. A million is 백만 (100 × 만).
Forgetting that for the 10,000-won bill, 일만 원 is acceptable and common for clarity, unlike 백/천 where 일 is dropped.

structuredNuance.t: 만 is the Sino-Korean number "ten thousand." The deep point for English speakers: Korean does NOT group large numbers by thousands the way English does — it groups by 만 (10,000). So 100,000 is 십만 (ten 만), 1,000,000 is 백만 (hundred 만), and 10,000,000 is 천만 (thousand 만). This 만-based grouping is the single hardest mental switch in Korean numbers, because you must constantly divide by ten-thousands rather than thousands. Unlike 백 and 천, the bill 만 원 is commonly said 일만 원 too, especially when writing checks or being precise. Master the ladder 만 → 십만 → 백만 → 천만 → 억(100,000,000).
만 is the Sino-Korean number, from the hanja 萬.

entries.nuance: Koreans often give subway directions by line number plus exit number or direction.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 2호선은 5번 출구예요 if you mean the boarding area. Say 2호선 타는 곳은 5번 출구 쪽이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 전개 means "development / pacing (of a story)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 전개 (jeongae) means "development / pacing (of a story)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전개가 느린 것 같아요. ("I think the pacing is slow."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 전개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I think the pacing is slow.
usagePhrases.note: 느리다 is an adjective, so use 느린 것 같아요.

examples.en: The pacing is too slow, you know.
examples.note: -잖아요 reminds the listener of something both viewers just experienced.

entries.nuance: Use 전개 for the flow of a story or argument, not for a person's speed.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not translate pacing literally as 속도 in movie-review sentences when you mean story development. 전개 is more natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 결말 means "ending / conclusion (of a story)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ending / conclusion (of a story)" is 결말 (gyeolmal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 결말이 좀 아쉬운 것 같아요. ("I think the ending is a bit disappointing."). Watch the particle attached to 결말 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I think the ending is a bit disappointing.
usagePhrases.note: 아쉽다 becomes 아쉬운 before 것 같아요.

examples.en: I thought the ending felt a bit rushed.
examples.note: Past impression: 것 같았어요.

entries.nuance: 결말 is about narrative ending; 끝 is more general and less review-like.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not overuse 끝 for movie-review nuance. 결말 sounds more natural for story endings.

entries.shortExplanation: 연기 means "acting / performance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연기 (yeongi) = "acting / performance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연기가 자연스러운 것 같아요. ("I think the acting seems natural.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I think the acting seems natural.
usagePhrases.note: 자연스럽다 is ㅂ-irregular: 자연스러운.

examples.en: The actors' performances were really good, you know.
examples.note: -잖아요 works because both people saw the same acting.

entries.nuance: 연기 is the noun; 연기하다 is the verb 'to act/perform.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 연기 'acting' with 연기 'smoke' in other contexts; movie/drama context makes the meaning clear.

entries.shortExplanation: 주인공 means "main character / protagonist" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 주인공 (juingong) means "main character / protagonist". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주인공 배우가 정말 잘하거든요. ("The lead actor is really good, you see."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주인공 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: The lead actor is really good, you see.
usagePhrases.note: -거든요 gives this as supporting background for the speaker's opinion.

examples.en: I think the main character is too perfect.
examples.note: 완벽하다 becomes 완벽한 before 것 같아요.

entries.nuance: 주인공 can refer to a fictional main character or the lead person in a real event.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 배우 when you mean the character inside the story; use 주인공 for protagonist, 배우 for actor.

entries.shortExplanation: 개인적으로 means "personally / in my personal opinion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "personally / in my personal opinion" is 개인적으로 (gaeinjeogeuro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 개인적으로는 열린 결말을 좋아하거든요. ("Personally, I like open endings, you see."). Watch the particle attached to 개인적으로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Personally, I like open endings, you see.
usagePhrases.note: A natural way to explain a different preference without sounding confrontational.

examples.en: Personally, I think it's a bit disappointing.
examples.note: Double softening: personally + seems.

entries.nuance: 개인적으로 does not mean privately here; it marks a personal opinion.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not combine 개인적으로는 저는 unless you need strong contrast. Usually 개인적으로는 alone is enough.

entries.shortExplanation: 솔직히 means "honestly / frankly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 솔직히 (soljiki) = "honestly / frankly". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 솔직히 좀 아쉬웠거든요. ("Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 솔직히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
usagePhrases.note: -거든요 gives the honest feeling as background.

examples.ko: 솔직히 말하면 결말이 급한 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: soljiki malhamyeon gyeolmari geupan geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: Honestly, I thought the ending felt rushed.
examples.note: 솔직히 말하면 + 것 같았어요 softens a direct critique.

entries.nuance: 솔직히 is more direct than 개인적으로, so pair it with softer grammar when criticizing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 솔직히 as a license to be blunt; Korean still often needs softening after it.

entries.english: to be / to stay (honorific for a person's presence)
entries.shortExplanation: 계시다 means "to be / to stay (honorific for a person's presence)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계시다 (gyesida) means "to be / to stay (honorific for a person's presence)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교수님이 연구실에 계세요. ("The professor is in the office."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 계시다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: The professor is in the office.
usagePhrases.note: A respected person's physical presence uses 계시다.

examples.en: The team lead is not at their desk right now.
examples.note: 안 계세요 is the natural negative for a respected person's location.

entries.nuance: 있으세요 can be used for possessions or states, but 계세요 is the respectful choice for where a person is.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For a teacher or elder's location, say 어디에 계세요? instead of 어디에 있으세요?

entries.shortExplanation: 드리다 means "to give (humble, to someone respected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to give (humble, to someone respected)" is 드리다 (deurida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 부모님께 선물을 드렸어요. ("I gave my parents a gift."). Watch the particle attached to 드리다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I gave my parents a gift.
usagePhrases.note: 께 plus 드리다 marks the respectful direction of the giving.

examples.en: I'll give the materials to the team lead.
examples.note: A useful office sentence that pairs naturally with reported speech.

entries.nuance: 드리다 is about humble direction: I give upward. If the senior person gives to you, use 주시다 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 드리다 just because the sentence is polite; use it when the recipient is someone you honor.

entries.english: to tell / to say (humble, to someone respected)
entries.shortExplanation: 말씀드리다 means "to tell / to say (humble, to someone respected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 말씀드리다 (malsseumdeurida) = "to tell / to say (humble, to someone respected)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교수님께 사정을 말씀드렸어요. ("I explained the situation to the professor.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 말씀드리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I explained the situation to the professor.
usagePhrases.note: This is more natural than 교수님께 말했어요 in a respectful context.

examples.en: I'll tell the team lead that I want to participate.
examples.note: The reported content uses -다고; the speaking verb is humble.

entries.nuance: 말씀드리다 points upward to the listener. 말씀하시다 is used when the respected person speaks.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 제가 말씀하셨어요. Use 제가 말씀드렸어요 for your humble action.

entries.english: to meet / to see (humble, someone respected)
entries.shortExplanation: 뵙다 means "to meet / to see (humble, someone respected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뵙다 (boepda) means "to meet / to see (humble, someone respected)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 내일 교수님을 뵐 수 있을까요? ("Could I meet the professor tomorrow?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뵙다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Could I meet the professor tomorrow?
usagePhrases.note: 뵐 is the future/modifying form of 뵙다.

examples.en: It's nice to meet you for the first time.
examples.note: A fixed formal first-meeting greeting.

entries.nuance: 뵙다 is humble: it lowers your action of meeting so the other person is respected.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For friends, use 만나다 or 보다; 뵙다 is too formal for equal casual relationships.

entries.shortExplanation: 잡수시다 means "to eat (very honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to eat (very honorific)" is 잡수시다 (japsusida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 할머니, 진지 다 잡수셨어요? ("Grandma, have you finished your meal?"). Watch the particle attached to 잡수시다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Grandma, have you finished your meal?
usagePhrases.note: 진지 is also honorific vocabulary for 밥.

examples.en: Grandfather ate breakfast.
examples.note: 께서 plus 잡수셨어요 marks high respect.

entries.nuance: 드시다 is the safer everyday honorific for eating; 잡수시다 sounds very respectful and elder-focused.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 잡수시다 for yourself.

entries.shortExplanation: 하마터면 means "almost / by a narrow margin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 하마터면 (hamateomyeon) = "almost / by a narrow margin". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 하마터면 울 뻔했어요. ("I almost cried.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 하마터면, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하마터면 adds the near-miss alarm feeling.

examples.en: I almost lost my wallet.
examples.note: A common everyday close-call sentence.

entries.nuance: 하마터면 is dramatic but natural when the speaker feels relieved that the event did not happen.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 하마터면 alone; pair it with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요.

entries.english: to tremble / to feel nervous and shaky
entries.shortExplanation: 떨리다 means "to tremble / to feel nervous and shaky" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 떨리다 (tteollida) means "to tremble / to feel nervous and shaky". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 발표할 때 목소리가 떨렸어요. ("My voice shook during the presentation."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 떨리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: My voice shook during the presentation.
usagePhrases.note: A very common presentation/interview sentence.

examples.en: I was so nervous I almost cried.
examples.note: 떨리다 often appears near close-call emotion sentences like 울 뻔했어요.

entries.nuance: 떨리다 can be physical shaking or the nervous feeling behind it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 떨다 for every nervous feeling; 떨리다 is the more natural intransitive form for 'my voice/hands/heart shake.'

entries.shortExplanation: 실력 means "skill level / actual ability" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "skill level / actual ability" is 실력 (sillyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 연습할수록 실력이 늘어요. ("The more you practice, the more your skill improves."). Watch the particle attached to 실력 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: The more you practice, the more your skill improves.
usagePhrases.note: A clean proportional sentence for -(으)ㄹ수록.

examples.en: The more you use Korean, the more your ability improves.
examples.note: 실력이 늘다 is the natural collocation.

entries.nuance: 실력 is not confidence or effort; it is the ability itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Say 실력이 늘어요 for ability improving, not 실력이 커요.

entries.english: because of / as a result of an unexpected problem
entries.shortExplanation: 바람에 means "because of / as a result of an unexpected problem" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
