entries.explanation: 바람에 (barame) = "because of / as a result of an unexpected problem". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비가 오는 바람에 약속이 취소됐어요. ("The appointment got canceled because it rained.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 바람에, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: The appointment got canceled because it rained.
usagePhrases.note: The rain is the disruptive cause.

examples.ko: 갑자기 일이 생기는 바람에 못 갔어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi iri saenggineun barame mot gasseoyo.
examples.en: I could not go because something suddenly came up.
examples.note: A very common excuse/explanation frame.

entries.nuance: 바람에 usually carries a negative or inconvenient result, unlike neutral -아서/어서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 바람에 for happy planned reasons. For purpose, use -기 위해서.

entries.shortExplanation: 취향 means "taste; personal preference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 취향 (chwihyang) means "taste; personal preference". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제 취향이에요. ("It is my taste."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 취향 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A natural way to say something suits your personal preference.
Useful when comparing preferences without arguing.
취향에 맞다 is a very common collocation.

examples.en: Quiet cafes are my taste.
examples.note: Connects preference with a descriptive noun phrase.

examples.en: Our movie tastes are a little different.
examples.note: Common with 영화, 음악, 음식, 옷, and 카페.

entries.nuance: 취향 is subjective. 좋아해요 states a preference, while 취향 names the style or taste behind that preference.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 취향 for every objective choice. For price, distance, or time, use comparison expressions instead.
취향 is usually paired with 이/가 or 에: 취향이 달라요, 취향에 맞아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 추천하다 means "to recommend" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to recommend" is 추천하다 (chucheonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 추천해 주세요. ("Please recommend one."). Watch the particle attached to 추천하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite service or friend request.
The thing recommended takes 을/를.

examples.en: Please recommend another color too.
examples.note: Useful in shopping after trying something on.

entries.nuance: 추천하다 is neutral and practical. In speech, 추천해 주세요 is much more useful than the dictionary form.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 추천하다 alone as a request. Say 추천해 주세요.
The recommended item usually takes 을/를: 식당을 추천하다, 색을 추천하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 한번 means "once; just to try" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 한번 (hanbeon) = "once; just to try". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 한번 해 보세요. ("Give it a try.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 한번, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A soft encouragement, not a hard command.

usagePhrases.en: Should I try it on once?
usagePhrases.note: Natural in clothing shops.

examples.en: Try on these clothes once.
examples.note: 한번 makes the suggestion feel low-pressure.

entries.nuance: 한번 does not always literally mean one time. With -아/어 보다, it often means 'just give it a try.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not over-translate 한번 as exactly one time in every sentence.
For spacing, both 한 번 and 한번 appear, but this course treats the conversational chunk 한번 해 보세요 as one useful expression.

entries.english: to be okay; to be fine
entries.shortExplanation: 괜찮다 means "to be okay; to be fine" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 괜찮다 (gwaenchanta) means "to be okay; to be fine". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 괜찮아요. ("It is okay / I am okay."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 괜찮다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: It is okay / I am okay.
usagePhrases.note: Common response to offers, suggestions, and concern.
Useful when trying or choosing.

examples.en: If the size is okay, I will take this one.
examples.note: Common shop decision frame.

entries.nuance: 괜찮아요 can mean okay, fine, no thanks, or not bad. Context decides.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not assume 괜찮아요 always means yes. After an offer, 아니요, 괜찮아요 can mean no thanks.
For a direct recommendation, use 좋아요 or 추천해요; 괜찮아요 can sound milder, like 'it's okay.'

entries.english: to not matter; to be okay either way
entries.shortExplanation: 상관없다 means "to not matter; to be okay either way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to not matter; to be okay either way" is 상관없다 (sanggwaneopsda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 상관없어요. ("It does not matter."). Watch the particle attached to 상관없다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Common answer when either choice is okay.

usagePhrases.en: It is okay even if it is expensive.
usagePhrases.note: -아/어도 plus 상관없다 is a useful concession frame.

examples.en: It does not matter even if we are a little late.
examples.note: The outcome stays okay despite the condition.

entries.nuance: 상관없다 is neutral and practical. It can sound indifferent, so use 괜찮아요 when you want a warmer tone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 상관없다 when you actually have a strong preference.
The condition often appears with -아/어도: 늦어도 상관없어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 늦다 means "to be late" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 늦다 (neutda) = "to be late". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 조금 늦을 것 같아요. ("I think I will be a little late.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 늦다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I think I will be a little late.
usagePhrases.note: Soft warning before you arrive late.

usagePhrases.en: I guess the reply is late.
usagePhrases.note: Inference from the missing reply.

examples.en: Traffic is heavy, so I might be a bit late.
examples.note: -ㄹ지도 몰라요 leaves the possibility open.

entries.nuance: 늦다 is a descriptive verb, so it behaves like an adjective in Korean. Use 늦게 for the adverb 'late': 늦게 왔어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 늦게 when the sentence needs 'be late': 늦을 것 같아요, not 늦게 것 같아요.
For a delayed reply, 답장이 늦다 is natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 가능성 means "possibility; chance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가능성 (ganeungseong) means "possibility; chance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비 올 가능성이 있어요. ("There is a chance it will rain."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가능성 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: There is a chance it will rain.
usagePhrases.note: A more noun-based way to talk about probability.
Useful when you are not fully ruling something out.

examples.en: There is a chance they will be late, so let's order first.
examples.note: 가능성 gives the reason for a practical decision.

entries.nuance: 가능성 is a noun, so it pairs with 있다, 없다, 높다, and 낮다. It is a little more formal than just saying -ㄹ지도 몰라요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 가능하다 when you mean 'chance' as a noun. Say 가능성이 있어요.
가능성이 높아요 means 'it is likely,' not 'the ability is high.'

entries.shortExplanation: 단서 means "clue" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "clue" is 단서 (danseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 단서가 있어요. ("There is a clue."). Watch the particle attached to 단서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A simple way to say the guess is not random.

usagePhrases.en: We can guess from this clue.
usagePhrases.note: The clue takes 로 when it is the basis or means.

examples.ko: 하늘이 흐린 게 첫 번째 단서예요.
examples.romanization: haneuri heurin ge cheot beonjjae danseoyeyo.
examples.en: The cloudy sky is the first clue.
examples.note: A concrete clue before a weather inference.

entries.nuance: 단서 is more everyday and lighter than 증거 when you are only guessing. 증거 sounds more like evidence or proof.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 단서하다. Use 단서가 있다 or 단서로 추측하다.
Use 증거 when you mean proof; use 단서 when you only have a clue.

entries.shortExplanation: 추측하다 means "to guess; to infer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 추측하다 (chucheukada) = "to guess; to infer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 단서로 추측해요. ("I infer from a clue.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 추측하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 로 marks the basis or means.
A useful hedge when you are not sure.

examples.ko: 우산을 보고 비가 오나 봐요라고 추측했어요.
examples.romanization: usaneul bogo biga ona bwayorago chucheukaesseoyo.
examples.en: I saw the umbrella and guessed, 'It looks like it is raining.'
examples.note: The visible object supports the inference.

entries.nuance: 추측하다 is more explicit than -나 봐요. In conversation, the pattern often does the work, and 추측하다 names the thinking process.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 추측하다 for facts you already know.
In casual speech, 너무 추측했어요 can sound odd; say 그냥 추측이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 그치다 means "to stop; to let up" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그치다 (geuchida) means "to stop; to let up". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비가 그쳤어요. ("The rain stopped."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그치다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The rain is the subject.
A natural weather possibility sentence.

examples.en: I think the rain will stop soon.
examples.note: -ㄹ 것 같아요 makes a soft prediction.

entries.nuance: 그치다 is intransitive: 비가 그쳐요. If you stop doing an action yourself, use 멈추다 or 그만하다 depending on the sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 비를 그쳐요 for 'the rain stops.' The rain takes 이/가: 비가 그쳐요.
그치다 is especially common with rain and snow.

entries.shortExplanation: 중 means "middle; in the middle of" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "middle; in the middle of" is 중 (jung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 회의 중이에요. ("I am in a meeting."). Watch the particle attached to 중 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Noun plus 중 compresses the current activity.
Verb plus -는 중 emphasizes being mid-action.

examples.en: I am on a call, so please wait a moment.
examples.note: 중이라 gives the reason from the current activity.

entries.nuance: 중 feels more immediate than broad -고 있어요. It often sounds like 'right in the middle of it.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not attach 중 directly to adjectives: 바쁜 중이에요 is unnatural for 'I am busy.' Say 바빠요 or 일하는 중이에요.
With verbs, use the modifier: 먹는 중이에요, not 먹다 중이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: 동안 means "during; for a duration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동안 (dongan) = "during; for a duration". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기다리는 동안 책을 읽었어요. ("I read a book while waiting.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동안, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I read a book while waiting.
usagePhrases.note: Two actions overlap during the same span.

usagePhrases.en: I could not see the message during the meeting.
usagePhrases.note: The meeting is the time span.

examples.en: I studied Korean for one hour.
examples.note: A duration noun can come before 동안.

entries.nuance: 동안 is about overlapping time or duration. It does not mean the contrastive English 'while' in sentences like 'while this is cheap, that is expensive.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use V-는 동안, not V-은 동안: 자는 동안, 공부하는 동안.
For a point in time, use 때; for the whole span, use 동안.

entries.shortExplanation: 그다음 means "then; after that; next" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 그다음 (geudaeum) means "then; after that; next". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그다음 뭐 해요? ("What do you do next?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그다음 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Useful when asking about the next step.

usagePhrases.en: First I wash, and then I eat breakfast.
usagePhrases.note: 먼저 and 그다음 make the sequence easy to follow.

examples.ko: 예약을 확인하고 나서 그다음 방으로 올라갔어요.
examples.romanization: yeyageul hwaginhago naseo geudaeum bangeuro ollagasseoyo.
examples.en: After checking the reservation, I went up to the room next.
examples.note: 그다음 names the following step after a completed action.

entries.nuance: 그다음 is conversational and clear. In writing, 그 후 or 이후 can sound more formal.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 그다음 as a noun for 'the next person' unless the context is clear.
For immediate timing, use -자마자 or 바로, not only 그다음.

entries.shortExplanation: 중간에 means "in the middle; midway" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "in the middle; midway" is 중간에 (junggane). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 중간에 계획을 바꿨어요. ("I changed the plan midway."). Watch the particle attached to 중간에 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A direct match for a changed plan.

usagePhrases.en: I got a call midway while going.
usagePhrases.note: Pairs naturally with -다가.

examples.en: I took a short break in the middle of studying.
examples.note: The original action pauses before it is finished.

entries.nuance: 중간에 does not always mean the exact mathematical center. It often means midway or before the process was finished.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 중간에 for a completed first action. If the first action finished, use -고 나서.
For a location physically between two places, 중간 is a noun; this card focuses on timing.

entries.shortExplanation: 열리다 means "to open; to be opened" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 열리다 (yeollida) = "to open; to be opened". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문이 열려 있어요. ("The door is open.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 열리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The open state continues.
The window became open and remains that way.

examples.en: The cafe door is still open.
examples.note: 아직 plus result-state is very natural.

entries.nuance: 열다 needs an actor opening something. 열리다 lets the opened thing become the subject.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 문을 열려 있어요. The thing in the state takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Use 열고 있어요 only when someone is actively opening it right now.

entries.english: to turn on; to be turned on
entries.shortExplanation: 켜지다 means "to turn on; to be turned on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 켜지다 (kyeojida) means "to turn on; to be turned on". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불이 켜져 있어요. ("The light is on."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 켜지다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The on-state continues.
Common for phones and computers.

examples.ko: 방에 불이 켜져 있어서 누가 있는 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: bange buri kyeojyeo isseoseo nuga inneun jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: The light was on in the room, so I thought someone was there.
examples.note: Result-state gives the visual clue.

entries.nuance: 켜다 is the action of turning something on. 켜지다 focuses on the thing becoming or being on.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 불을 켜져 있어요. Say 불이 켜져 있어요.
Use 켜고 있어요 only when someone is in the act of turning it on.

entries.shortExplanation: 취업 means "employment; getting a job" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "employment; getting a job" is 취업 (chwieop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 취업을 위해서 ("for employment / in order to get a job"). Watch the particle attached to 취업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: for employment / in order to get a job
usagePhrases.note: Noun plus 을/를 위해서.
Common compound for preparing to get hired.

usagePhrases.en: to succeed in getting a job
usagePhrases.note: A natural result phrase.

examples.en: I practice Korean every day in order to get a job.
examples.note: Purpose plus daily practice.

examples.ko: 방학 동안 취업 준비를 할 거예요.
examples.romanization: banghak dongan chwieop junbireul hal geoyeyo.
examples.en: I will prepare for job hunting during vacation.
examples.note: Duration plus practical goal.

entries.nuance: 취업 is the process or result of getting employment. 직업 is your occupation or job type, and 회사 is the company. For a purpose sentence, 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서 is natural.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 직업을 위해서 when you mean 'to get a job'. Use 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서.
Do not drop the object particle in the learner frame. Say 취업을 위해서, not 취업 위해서, until the full pattern feels natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 해요체 means "everyday polite speech style" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 해요체 (haeyoche) = "everyday polite speech style". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 발표 끝났어요. ("The presentation is over.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 해요체, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Natural polite everyday style after the formal presentation is done.

usagePhrases.en: May I ask the teacher a question?
usagePhrases.note: Polite, but not rigid.

examples.ko: 친구가 아니면 처음에는 해요체로 말하는 게 안전해요.
examples.romanization: chinguga animyeon cheoeumeneun haeyochero malhaneun ge anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: If they are not a friend, it is safe to speak in haeyo style at first.
examples.note: Practical social rule for learners.

entries.nuance: 해요체 is polite conversation, not formal ceremony language. It sounds warmer and more natural than 합쇼체 in daily life.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 합쇼체 with classmates after class can sound stiff or distant.
Using 반말 with someone you just met can sound rude even if the grammar is simple.

entries.shortExplanation: 합쇼체 means "formal polite speech style" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 합쇼체 (hapsyoche) means "formal polite speech style". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지금부터 발표를 시작하겠습니다. ("I will begin the presentation now."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 합쇼체 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I will begin the presentation now.
usagePhrases.note: Formal presentation opening.
Formal question style.

examples.en: In an interview, speaking in formal polite style sounds natural.
examples.note: A real setting where 합쇼체 fits.

entries.nuance: 합쇼체 overlaps with the name 하십시오체. Learners mainly need to recognize the endings -ㅂ니다/습니다, -ㅂ니까/습니까, and -(으)십시오.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 합쇼체 everywhere because it feels 'more polite'. In everyday talk, it can sound too stiff.
Forgetting that ㄹ drops before ㅂ니다: 살다 becomes 삽니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 반말 means "casual non-polite speech" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "casual non-polite speech" is 반말 (banmal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 반말해도 돼요? ("Can we speak casually to each other?"). Watch the particle attached to 반말 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Can we speak casually to each other?
usagePhrases.note: A common way to ask permission before switching.

usagePhrases.en: I use casual speech with close friends.
usagePhrases.note: Relationship controls the speech level.

examples.ko: 처음 만난 사람에게 반말을 쓰면 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum mannan saramege banmareul sseumyeon muryehage deullil su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you use casual speech with someone you just met, it can sound rude.
examples.note: Social boundary.

entries.nuance: 반말 is not 'bad Korean'. It is the right style in close relationships, but the wrong style in many public or first-meeting settings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 반말 with a teacher or staff member because the learner knows the short form.
Thinking 반말 equals friendly in every situation. Relationship and permission matter.

entries.shortExplanation: 존댓말 means "polite or respectful speech" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 존댓말 (jondaenmal) = "polite or respectful speech". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 처음에는 존댓말로 말하세요. ("At first, speak politely.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 존댓말, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Safe default advice.

usagePhrases.en: I use polite speech with the teacher.
usagePhrases.note: A relationship-based choice.

examples.ko: 존댓말을 써도 상황에 따라 해요체와 합쇼체가 달라져요.
examples.romanization: jondaenmareul sseodo sanghwange ttara haeyochewa hapsyochega dallajyeoyo.
examples.en: Even when using polite speech, haeyo style and formal style differ by situation.
examples.note: Shows that 존댓말 is an umbrella term.

entries.nuance: 존댓말 is about social respect. It does not automatically mean the most formal ending possible.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 존댓말 only with 합니다. 해요체 is also 존댓말.
Using honorific -(으)시- for yourself. Respectful speech and subject honorifics are related but not identical.

entries.shortExplanation: 말투 means "way of speaking; speech tone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 말투 (maltu) means "way of speaking; speech tone". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어떤 말투를 써야 해요? ("What way of speaking should I use?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 말투 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: What way of speaking should I use?
usagePhrases.note: Directly useful in this chapter.
A common feedback sentence.

examples.ko: 발표에서는 말투를 조금 더 격식 있게 바꿔야 해요.
examples.romanization: balpyoeseoneun maltureul jogeum deo gyeoksik itge bakkwoya haeyo.
examples.en: In a presentation, you need to make your tone a little more formal.
examples.note: Speech-level choice as a tone adjustment.

entries.nuance: 말투 can describe grammar level, but also attitude. A sentence can be grammatically polite and still sound cold or awkward.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking only the verb ending matters. Particles, word choice, and directness also affect 말투.

entries.shortExplanation: 격식 means "formality; formal manners" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "formality; formal manners" is 격식 (gyeoksik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 격식 있는 자리 ("a formal setting"). Watch the particle attached to 격식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A key phrase for choosing 합쇼체.
Describes the manner of speaking.

examples.ko: 면접은 격식 있는 자리라서 합쇼체가 자연스러워요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeun gyeoksik inneun jariraseo hapsyochega jayeonseureowoyo.
examples.en: An interview is a formal setting, so formal polite style sounds natural.
examples.note: Connects setting to speech level.

entries.nuance: 격식 is not just politeness. It is the formal frame expected by the setting.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 격식 있는 말투 with close friends can sound distant or theatrical.

entries.shortExplanation: 높임말 means "honorific or respectful language" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 높임말 (nopimmal) = "honorific or respectful language". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 높임말을 쓰다 ("to use honorific language") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 높임말, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: General phrase.
Focuses on manner of speaking.

examples.ko: 선생님에 대해 말할 때는 높임말을 써요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnime daehae malhal ttaeneun nopimmareul sseoyo.
examples.en: When talking about a teacher, I use honorific language.
examples.note: The honored person is the topic of the sentence.

entries.nuance: 높임말 is not only being polite to the listener. It can honor a third person, such as a teacher or parent.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -(으)시- for yourself. Do not say 제가 가세요.
Thinking 존댓말 and 높임말 are always the same. They overlap, but they answer different social questions.

entries.shortExplanation: 께서 means "honorific subject particle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 께서 (kkeseo) means "honorific subject particle". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 선생님께서 오세요. ("The teacher is coming."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 께서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 께서 marks the respected subject.
Particle and verb both carry respect.

examples.en: The boss is in the meeting room.
examples.note: Respected subject plus 계시다.

entries.nuance: 께서 honors the subject. It is not the same as 께, which means 'to' a respected person.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 께서 for yourself: 제가께서 is impossible.
Confusing 께서 with 께. 선생님께서 오세요 but 선생님께 말씀드려요.

entries.shortExplanation: 께 means "to a respected person" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to a respected person" is 께 (kke). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 선생님께 질문해요. ("I ask the teacher a question."). Watch the particle attached to 께 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I ask the teacher a question.
usagePhrases.note: Respectful recipient.
께 and 드리다 work together.

examples.en: I will first guide the customer.
examples.note: Formal service language.

entries.nuance: 께 marks a respected recipient. 께서 marks a respected subject.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 선생님께서 질문해요 when you mean 'I ask the teacher'. Use 선생님께 질문해요.
Using 한테 in formal respectful contexts where 께 is expected.

entries.shortExplanation: 계시다 means "to be; to stay (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계시다 (gyesida) = "to be; to stay (honorific)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 선생님이 교실에 계세요. ("The teacher is in the classroom.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계시다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: The teacher is in the classroom.
usagePhrases.note: Honorific existence/location.

usagePhrases.en: The boss is not here right now.
usagePhrases.note: Common office/service phrase.

examples.en: My parents are at home.
examples.note: Respectful way to talk about parents.

entries.nuance: 계시다 replaces 있다 only for respected people. For things, use 있다: 가방이 있어요, not 가방이 계세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계시다 for objects or animals without a special respectful reason.
Using 있다 for a respected person in a context where honorifics are expected.

entries.shortExplanation: 드시다 means "to eat; to drink (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 드시다 (deusida) means "to eat; to drink (honorific)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 식사하셨어요? ("Have you eaten?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 드시다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Very common respectful greeting-like question.
Honors the teacher as subject.

examples.en: Grandmother is eating.
examples.note: Traditional respectful meal word plus honorific verb.

entries.nuance: 드시다 honors the eater/drinker. It does not honor the food.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 드시다 for your own eating: 제가 드세요 is wrong.
Thinking 드시다 means only 'eat'. It can also be used for drinking.

entries.shortExplanation: 주무시다 means "to sleep (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to sleep (honorific)" is 주무시다 (jumusida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 안녕히 주무세요. ("Good night. / Sleep well."). Watch the particle attached to 주무시다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Respectful bedtime phrase.
Respected subject.

examples.en: My parents usually sleep early.
examples.note: Respectful family sentence.

entries.nuance: 주무시다 is a special honorific verb. Do not build it mechanically from 자다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 자세요 can be understandable, but 주무세요 is the standard respectful form.
Using 주무시다 for yourself.

entries.shortExplanation: 말씀하시다 means "to say; to speak (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 말씀하시다 (malsseumhasida) = "to say; to speak (honorific)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 선생님께서 말씀하셨어요. ("The teacher said it.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 말씀하시다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Respected subject speaks.
Respectful request to the listener.

examples.en: My mother spoke first.
examples.note: Honors mother as subject.

entries.nuance: 말씀하시다 honors the speaker. 말씀드리다 humbles your act of telling someone respected.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 말씀하시다 and 말씀드리다. The direction of respect is different.
Using 말하다 where 말씀하시다 is expected for a respected subject.

entries.english: to give/do for a respected person (humble)
entries.shortExplanation: 드리다 means "to give/do for a respected person (humble)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 드리다 (deurida) means "to give/do for a respected person (humble)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부모님께 연락드릴게요. ("I will contact my parents."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 드리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Respectful recipient.
Humble speech toward the teacher.

examples.en: I will guide the customer again.
examples.note: Service-register humble helper.

entries.nuance: 드리다 respects the recipient, not the subject. It is different from -(으)시-, which honors the subject.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 제가 오시다 or 제가 드세요 to be polite about yourself. Use 드리다 only when your action goes to someone respected.
Forgetting 께 before the respected recipient.

entries.english: but; by the way (casual shortened 그런데)
entries.shortExplanation: 근데 means "but; by the way (casual shortened 그런데)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "but; by the way (casual shortened 그런데)" is 근데 (geunde). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 근데 오늘 시간 돼? ("But / by the way, are you free today?"). Watch the particle attached to 근데 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: But / by the way, are you free today?
usagePhrases.note: Casual topic opener.

usagePhrases.en: But that is a little difficult, though.
usagePhrases.note: Soft pushback with -는데요.

examples.ko: 근데 자료는 언제 보낼 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: geunde jaryoneun eonje bonael su isseoyo?
examples.en: But when can you send the materials?
examples.note: Spoken contrast in a team conversation.

entries.nuance: 근데 is common in speech, but it can sound too casual in a presentation, email, or formal announcement.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 근데 in formal writing where 그런데 is safer.
Using 근데 every sentence; it becomes filler if there is no real contrast or topic shift.

entries.shortExplanation: 사실은 means "actually; to be honest" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사실은 (sasireun) = "actually; to be honest". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사실은 아직 다 못 했어요. ("Actually, I have not finished it yet.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사실은, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Actually, I have not finished it yet.
usagePhrases.note: Softly reveals the real situation.

usagePhrases.ko: 사실은 제가 먼저 말을 꺼내고 싶었어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: sasireun jega meonjeo mareul kkeonaego sipeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Actually, I wanted to bring it up first.
usagePhrases.note: Useful before a sensitive topic.

examples.ko: 사실은 오늘 자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요.
examples.romanization: sasireun oneul jaryoga ajik an kkeunnanneundeyo.
examples.en: Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.
examples.note: Opens bad news with a softer frame.

entries.nuance: 사실은 does not mean every sentence is a dramatic confession. It often simply prepares the listener for background or a correction.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사실은 and then giving information the listener already knows very well. 잖아요 may fit better for shared information.
Translating 'actually' into 사실은 in every English sentence; sometimes 그런데 or 아니면 no marker is more natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 잖아요 means "you know; as you know" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 잖아요 (janayo) means "you know; as you know". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회의 시간이 짧잖아요. ("The meeting time is short, you know."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잖아요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: The meeting time is short, you know.
usagePhrases.note: Shared constraint.
Can sound pointed depending on tone.

examples.en: The team lead is busy now too, you know.
examples.note: Uses shared context to justify a suggestion.

entries.nuance: 잖아요 is for shared information. For new background, use -거든요 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 잖아요 to announce new information. That can sound like 'You should have known this.'
Using it in formal public speech. It is conversational.

entries.shortExplanation: 거든요 means "you see; the thing is" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "you see; the thing is" is 거든요 (geodeunyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어제 갑자기 일이 생겼거든요. ("Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see."). Watch the particle attached to 거든요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.
usagePhrases.note: New background.

usagePhrases.en: That cafe has a nice atmosphere, you see.
usagePhrases.note: Reason for liking or choosing the cafe.

examples.ko: 오늘은 먼저 시작해 주세요. 제가 조금 늦거든요.
examples.romanization: oneureun meonjeo sijakae juseyo. jega jogeum neutgeodeunyo.
examples.en: Please start first today. I am running a little late, you see.
examples.note: Explains a request with new background.

entries.nuance: 거든요 gives new background. It is softer than just dropping a reason, but it can sound defensive if the tone is too clipped.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 거든요 for something everyone already knows. 잖아요 is usually better for shared information.
Treating it as a full replacement for because. It carries conversational background, not just logic.

entries.english: though; you see; soft trailing ending
entries.shortExplanation: 는데요 means "though; you see; soft trailing ending" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 는데요 (neundeyo) = "though; you see; soft trailing ending". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지금 좀 바쁜데요. ("I am a little busy right now, though.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 는데요, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I am a little busy right now, though.
usagePhrases.note: Soft refusal or hesitation.

usagePhrases.en: The materials are not finished yet, though.
usagePhrases.note: Bad news without sounding too blunt.

examples.ko: 그 의견도 좋은데요, 시간이 조금 부족해요.
examples.romanization: geu uigyeondo joeundeyo, sigani jogeum bujokaeyo.
examples.en: That opinion is good too, but we are a little short on time.
examples.note: Soft contrast before disagreement.

entries.nuance: 는데요 is not only 'but'. It often sets up background and hands the next move to the listener.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 는데요 as a random polite ending in every sentence.
Forgetting the adjective form: 바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요.

entries.shortExplanation: 자료 means "materials; data; documents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자료 (jaryo) means "materials; data; documents". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자료를 보내다 ("to send the materials"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Common team or class message.
Slides or handouts for a presentation.

examples.en: I will send the materials before the meeting.
examples.note: Practical work or study-group sentence.

entries.nuance: 자료 can mean data, but in daily work and study talk it often means the file, handout, or slide deck someone needs.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 정보 for every kind of material. 정보 is information; 자료 is often the actual file or reference material.
Confusing 자료 with 의견. 의견 means opinion.

entries.shortExplanation: 배경 means "background; context" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "background; context" is 배경 (baegyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 배경을 설명하다 ("to explain the background"). Watch the particle attached to 배경 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Useful before a proposal or disagreement.
A soft way to introduce context.

examples.en: I will explain the background first.
examples.note: Keeps the conversation organized.

entries.nuance: 배경 is broader than 이유. 이유 is the reason; 배경 is the surrounding context that makes the reason understandable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이유 when the listener needs a fuller context. 배경 may sound more natural.
Overusing 배경 in very casual chat where 그냥 왜냐하면 is enough.

entries.shortExplanation: 상대방 means "the other person; conversation partner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 상대방 (sangdaebang) = "the other person; conversation partner". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 상대방이 모를 때 ("when the other person does not know") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상대방, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: when the other person does not know
usagePhrases.note: Important for choosing 거든요 instead of 잖아요.

usagePhrases.en: to consider the other person's feelings
usagePhrases.note: Conversation strategy.

examples.ko: 상대방이 처음 듣는 내용이면 거든요가 더 자연스러워요.
examples.romanization: sangdaebangi cheoeum deunneun naeyongimyeon geodeunyoga deo jayeonseureowoyo.
examples.en: If the other person is hearing it for the first time, 거든요 is more natural.
examples.note: Explains the usage boundary.

entries.nuance: 상대방 is neutral. It is not necessarily an opponent; it can simply mean the other person in the interaction.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 상대방 always means an enemy or opponent. In conversation study, it usually means the listener.
Ignoring what the 상대방 already knows when choosing 잖아요 or 거든요.

entries.shortExplanation: 부드럽게 means "softly; gently; smoothly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부드럽게 (budeureopge) means "softly; gently; smoothly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부드럽게 말하다 ("to speak gently"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부드럽게 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Tone of delivery.
Useful for polite disagreement.

examples.ko: 그 의견에는 부드럽게 반대하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: geu uigyeoneneun budeureopge bandaehaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: It is better to disagree with that opinion gently.
examples.note: Connects tone with disagreement.

entries.nuance: 부드럽게 is about manner or tone. It does not automatically make the content polite if the sentence itself is too direct.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every polite sentence 부드럽게. The sentence must actually soften the delivery.
Forgetting that tone and grammar work together in Korean.

entries.shortExplanation: 말을 꺼내다 means "to bring up a topic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to bring up a topic" is 말을 꺼내다 (mareul kkeonaeda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 먼저 말을 꺼내다 ("to bring it up first"). Watch the particle attached to 말을 꺼내다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Starting a topic before someone else does.
Used for sensitive topics.

examples.ko: 자료가 늦어진 이야기는 제가 먼저 말을 꺼낼게요.
examples.romanization: jaryoga neujeojin iyagineun jega meonjeo mareul kkeonaelgeyo.
examples.en: I will bring up the delayed materials first.
examples.note: A real meeting or team-project sentence.

entries.nuance: 말을 꺼내다 is about starting a topic, not physically taking words out. It often implies a little hesitation or tact.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 말 as an unrelated animal noun. In this phrase, 말 means words or speech.
Using 말하다 when the point is initiating a difficult topic. 말을 꺼내다 is more precise.

entries.shortExplanation: 보니까 means "when I saw/tried/checked" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 보니까 (bonikka) = "when I saw/tried/checked". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가 보니까 ("when I went and saw / tried going") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보니까, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: when I went and saw / tried going
usagePhrases.note: Useful after visiting a place.
Useful for information you verified.

examples.ko: 그 식당에 가 보니까 생각보다 조용하더라고요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdange ga bonikka saenggakboda joyonghadeoragoyo.
examples.en: When I tried going to that restaurant, it was quieter than I expected.
examples.note: Experience leads to a firsthand observation.

entries.nuance: 보니까 is evidence-based. It sounds odd if you did not actually see, try, or check the thing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 보니까 for pure hearsay. If someone only told you, use a reported-speech form instead.
Forgetting the try/check meaning in 가 보다 or 확인해 보다.

entries.shortExplanation: 더라고요 means "I noticed; it turned out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 더라고요 (deoragoyo) means "I noticed; it turned out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 생각보다 괜찮더라고요. ("It was better than I expected."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 더라고요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: It was better than I expected.
usagePhrases.note: Common review-style observation.

usagePhrases.en: There were a lot of people, I noticed.
usagePhrases.note: Firsthand scene report.

examples.en: These days, the atmosphere has changed a lot, I noticed.
examples.note: Reports a noticed change.

entries.nuance: 더라고요 is not just past tense. It carries the speaker's evidence and realization.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 더라고요 for something you only heard from someone else.
Using it for your own planned action as if you observed yourself from outside.

entries.english: I observed X, and then Y happened
entries.shortExplanation: 더니 means "I observed X, and then Y happened" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "I observed X, and then Y happened" is 더니 (deoni). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 처음에는 조용하더니 ("it was quiet at first, and then..."). Watch the particle attached to 더니 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: it was quiet at first, and then...
usagePhrases.note: Observed state followed by change.
Observed repeated action followed by result.

examples.en: It was quiet at first, and then there were quickly more people.
examples.note: A direct observed change.

entries.nuance: Plain -더니 has an eyewitness feel. For your own action causing a result, -았/었더니 is usually the safer form.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 내가 가더니 for your own neutral action. Use 갔더니 when your own action led to a result.
Using -더니 when there is no change or result after the first observation.

entries.shortExplanation: 생각보다 means "more/less than expected" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 생각보다 (saenggakboda) = "more/less than expected". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 생각보다 괜찮다 ("to be better than expected") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생각보다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Common review phrase.
Often used with 나오다 or 끝나다.

examples.en: The food came out faster than expected, I noticed.
examples.note: Expectation plus firsthand observation.

entries.nuance: 생각보다 naturally pairs with 더라고요 because both talk about what you found after experience.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 생각보다 without saying what was different from expectation.
Confusing 생각보다 with 그냥 생각. 생각보다 is a comparison phrase.

entries.shortExplanation: 처음에는 means "at first" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 처음에는 (cheoeumeneun) means "at first". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 처음에는 조용하다 ("to be quiet at first"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 처음에는 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Early state before a change.
Before later realization.

examples.en: It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded.
examples.note: Natural setup for an observed change.

entries.nuance: 처음에는 points to the first stage. It needs a later stage to feel complete.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 처음에는 without showing what changed afterward.
Confusing 처음에는 with 처음으로, which means 'for the first time.'

entries.shortExplanation: 예전에는 means "in the past; before" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "in the past; before" is 예전에는 (yejeoneneun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예전에는 조용했어요. ("It used to be quiet."). Watch the particle attached to 예전에는 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Past state.

usagePhrases.en: There used to be few people.
usagePhrases.note: Past comparison.

examples.en: It used to be quiet, but these days there are many people, I noticed.
examples.note: Before-now contrast.

entries.nuance: 예전에는 is broader than 어제 or 지난주. It points to an earlier period, not one exact moment.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예전에는 for a single recent event when 어제 or 지난번 is clearer.
Forgetting the contrast when using 예전에는 in a change sentence.

entries.shortExplanation: 요즘은 means "these days; nowadays" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 요즘은 (yojeumeun) = "these days; nowadays". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 요즘은 사람이 많아요. ("These days there are many people.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 요즘은, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: These days there are many people.
usagePhrases.note: Current state.

usagePhrases.en: The atmosphere has changed these days.
usagePhrases.note: Current change.

examples.en: These days, the number of customers has increased a lot, I noticed.
examples.note: Current observation after change.

entries.nuance: 요즘은 is not just today. It means the recent/current period.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 요즘은 for one event that happened only today.
Forgetting that 요즘은 often invites a contrast with before.

entries.english: to come to know; to find out
entries.shortExplanation: 알게 되다 means "to come to know; to find out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 알게 되다 (alge doeda) means "to come to know; to find out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 나중에 알게 되다 ("to find out later"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 알게 되다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Discovery over time.

usagePhrases.en: to come to know through experience
usagePhrases.note: Experience-based realization.

examples.ko: 직접 가 보니까 왜 유명한지 알게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: jikjeop ga bonikka wae yumyeonghanji alge dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: After going there myself, I found out why it is famous.
examples.note: Realization after firsthand experience.

entries.nuance: 알게 되다 emphasizes the process of finding out. 알다 simply states that you know.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 알게 되다 when you already knew the fact all along.
Forgetting that it often pairs with a discovery trigger like 보니까, 듣고 나서, or 경험하면서.

entries.shortExplanation: 관찰하다 means "to observe" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to observe" is 관찰하다 (gwanchalhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 변화를 관찰하다 ("to observe a change"). Watch the particle attached to 관찰하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Careful observation over time.
Watching how someone responds.

examples.ko: 일주일 동안 분위기가 어떻게 변하는지 관찰했어요.
examples.romanization: iljuil dongan bunwigiga eotteoke byeonhaneunji gwanchalhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I observed how the atmosphere changed over a week.
examples.note: Careful observation of change.

entries.nuance: 관찰하다 is useful for deliberate observation. For a casual visit, 가 보니까 or 보니까 often sounds more natural.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 관찰하다 for every casual noticing. It can sound too deliberate or academic.
Forgetting that 더라고요 still needs firsthand evidence, even if the verb 관찰하다 is not used.

entries.shortExplanation: 붐비다 means "to be crowded" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 붐비다 (bumbida) = "to be crowded". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 식당이 붐비다 ("the restaurant is crowded") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 붐비다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Place-focused crowding.
Observed change.

examples.en: It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded, I noticed.
examples.note: A natural restaurant or event observation.

entries.nuance: 붐비다 describes the place or route becoming crowded. 사람이 많다 describes the number of people more directly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 붐비다 for one person being busy. For a busy person, use 바쁘다.
Forgetting that 붐비다 usually needs a place or traffic-like subject.

entries.shortExplanation: 다고 했어요 means "said that..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다고 했어요 (dago haesseoyo) means "said that...". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 금요일에 본다고 했어요. ("They said we will take it on Friday."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다고 했어요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: They said we will take it on Friday.
usagePhrases.note: Reported statement.

usagePhrases.en: They said they are busy today.
usagePhrases.note: Adjective statement.

examples.en: The teacher said the exam is on Friday.
examples.note: Respectful reporting with 하셨어요.

entries.nuance: 다고 했어요 reports a statement, not a question or command. Match the inner ending to the sentence type.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -다고 for questions. A reported question needs -냐고.
Forgetting present action-verb forms like 간다고 and 먹는다고.

entries.shortExplanation: 냐고 물어봤어요 means "asked whether/if..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "asked whether/if..." is 냐고 물어봤어요 (nyago mureobwasseoyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 몇 시에 만나냐고 물어봤어요. ("They asked what time we are meeting."). Watch the particle attached to 냐고 물어봤어요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: They asked what time we are meeting.
usagePhrases.note: Reported wh-question.

usagePhrases.en: They asked whether I submitted the homework.
usagePhrases.note: Reported yes/no question.

examples.en: My friend asked when the exam is.
examples.note: Question content stays question-marked with -냐고.

entries.nuance: 냐고 is for reported questions. Do not switch to -다고 just because the whole sentence now ends like a statement.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 언제 온다고 물어봤어요 when you mean 'asked when they are coming'. Use 언제 오냐고 물어봤어요.
Overusing the formal textbook -느냐고 in everyday conversation when -냐고 is natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 는지 means "whether; what/when/where... inside a sentence" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 는지 (neunji) = "whether; what/when/where... inside a sentence". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험이 언제인지 알아요? ("Do you know when the exam is?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 는지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Do you know when the exam is?
usagePhrases.note: Embedded question with 이다.

usagePhrases.en: Please check what time we are meeting.
usagePhrases.note: Embedded question after 확인하다.

examples.en: Did the teacher also say when the exam is?
examples.note: The question 'when is the exam?' sits inside a larger question.

entries.nuance: 는지 is not reported speech by itself. It embeds a question so verbs like 알다, 모르다, 확인하다, and 궁금하다 can use it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -냐고 when no one asked a question. If you just do not know the answer, use -는지.
Using -는지 for a direct quote instead of an embedded question.

entries.shortExplanation: 라고 하다 means "to tell someone to..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 라고 하다 (rago hada) means "to tell someone to...". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 숙제를 제출하라고 하셨어요. ("They told us to submit the homework."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 라고 하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: They told us to submit the homework.
usagePhrases.note: Reported instruction.

usagePhrases.en: They said to check the message.
usagePhrases.note: Instruction, not statement.

examples.en: The teacher told us to submit the homework by tomorrow.
examples.note: Classroom instruction being passed along.

entries.nuance: 라고 하다 for instructions is separate from noun +(이)라고 하다, as in 학생이라고 했어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -다고 하다 for commands: 제출한다고 하셨어요 means 'said they will submit', not 'told us to submit'.
Confusing reported command -(으)라고 with noun quote -(이)라고.

entries.shortExplanation: 대요 means "they say; I heard that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "they say; I heard that" is 대요 (daeyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 내일 온대요. ("They say they are coming tomorrow."). Watch the particle attached to 대요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: They say they are coming tomorrow.
usagePhrases.note: Contracted reported statement.

usagePhrases.en: They say they are busy today.
usagePhrases.note: Adjective statement contraction.

examples.en: The teacher says the exam is on Friday.
examples.note: Spoken version of 본다고 해요.

entries.nuance: 대요 is common, but first learn what it expands from so you do not mix statements with questions.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 대요 for reported questions. Questions contract to 냬요 in casual speech.
Forgetting the source of the information when using 대요.

entries.english: to ask; to ask and find out
entries.shortExplanation: 물어보다 means "to ask; to ask and find out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 물어보다 (mureoboda) = "to ask; to ask and find out". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 친구한테 물어보다 ("to ask a friend") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 물어보다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday spoken phrase.

usagePhrases.en: to ask what time it is
usagePhrases.note: Embedded question plus 물어보다.

examples.en: My friend asked what time we are meeting.
examples.note: Reported question with the everyday verb 물어보다.

entries.nuance: 묻다 is the dictionary/base verb. 물어보다 is often the natural spoken choice for asking someone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 묻다 forms mechanically when 물어보다 sounds more natural in conversation.
Forgetting the person marker: 친구한테 물어봤어요 or 선생님께 물어봤어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 다시 말하다 means "to say again; to repeat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다시 말하다 (dasi malhada) means "to say again; to repeat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다시 말해 주세요. ("Please say it again."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다시 말하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Polite repeat request.
Restating the point.

examples.ko: 못 들었으면 다시 말해 달라고 해요.
examples.romanization: mot deureosseumyeon dasi malhae dallago haeyo.
examples.en: If you did not hear it, ask them to say it again.
examples.note: Useful repair phrase in reported speech practice.

entries.nuance: 다시 말하다 is not just the adverb 다시. It is a practical repair phrase when reported information is unclear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 다시 말하다 as only the word 다시. The useful chunk is the whole phrase.
Using it when you need 확인하다 instead: 다시 말하다 repeats; 확인하다 checks.

entries.shortExplanation: 올라온 공지 means "a notice that was posted" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "a notice that was posted" is 올라온 공지 (ollaon gongji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어제 올라온 공지 ("the notice posted yesterday"). Watch the particle attached to 올라온 공지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Completed action before the noun.

usagePhrases.en: to check the notice posted today
usagePhrases.note: Common school or app action.

examples.en: I checked the notice posted yesterday again.
examples.note: Unpacks a real portal-notice phrase.

entries.nuance: 올라온 is not a separate full sentence here. It sits before 공지 and tells you which notice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 올라온 as a separate sentence and losing the final noun 공지.
Confusing 올라온 공지 with 올라갈 공지. 올라온 is already posted; 올라갈 is going to be posted.

entries.shortExplanation: 제출할 보고서 means "a report to submit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 제출할 보고서 (jechulhal bogoseo) = "a report to submit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 내일 제출할 보고서 ("the report to submit tomorrow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 제출할 보고서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Future modifier before the noun.

usagePhrases.en: to review the report to submit
usagePhrases.note: Work/study document phrase.

examples.en: I reviewed the report I will submit tomorrow again.
examples.note: Shows future noun modification in a real task.

entries.nuance: 제출할 points forward. It differs from 제출한 보고서, a report that was already submitted.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 제출할 as a standalone future sentence instead of a modifier for 보고서.
Confusing 제출할 보고서 with 제출한 보고서.

entries.english: to be written; to be used
entries.shortExplanation: 쓰이다 means "to be written; to be used" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쓰이다 (sseuida) means "to be written; to be used". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 공지에 쓰인 표현 ("the expression used/written in the notice"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쓰이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: the expression used/written in the notice
usagePhrases.note: Completed passive modifier.

usagePhrases.en: a word that is often used
usagePhrases.note: Present passive modifier.

examples.en: The expression used in the notice was a little difficult.
examples.note: Focuses on the expression, not the writer.

entries.nuance: 쓰이다 focuses on the written/used item. 쓰다 focuses on the person writing or using it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 쓰다 when the sentence subject is the expression or word itself. 공지에 쓰인 표현 is the natural phrase.
Forgetting that 쓰이다 can mean both 'be written' and 'be used.'

entries.english: to have no choice but to
entries.shortExplanation: 수밖에 없다 means "to have no choice but to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to have no choice but to" is 수밖에 없다 (subakke eopsda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 야근할 수밖에 없어요. ("I have no choice but to work late."). Watch the particle attached to 수밖에 없다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I have no choice but to work late.
usagePhrases.note: Deadline pressure.

usagePhrases.en: I have no choice but to check again.
usagePhrases.note: Only realistic next step.

examples.ko: 마감이 오늘이라서 이 방법을 선택할 수밖에 없어요.
examples.romanization: magami oneuriraseo i bangbeobeul seontaekal subakke eopseoyo.
examples.en: The deadline is today, so we have no choice but to choose this method.
examples.note: No-choice situation plus reason.

entries.nuance: 수밖에 없다 is resignation to the only remaining option, not inability.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 할 수 없어요 when you mean 'I have no choice but to do it.' 할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it.
Writing 수 밖에 with a space in this fixed expression. Use 수밖에.

entries.shortExplanation: 리가 없다 means "there is no way that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 리가 없다 (riga eopsda) = "there is no way that". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지금 포기할 리가 없어요. ("There is no way we would give up now.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 리가 없다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: There is no way we would give up now.
usagePhrases.note: Strong disbelief about giving up.

usagePhrases.en: There is no way the data is wrong.
usagePhrases.note: Past possibility is strongly rejected.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 마감을 잊었을 리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: geu sarami magameul ijeosseul liga eopseoyo.
examples.en: There is no way that person forgot the deadline.
examples.note: Strong logical disbelief.

entries.nuance: 리가 없다 carries confidence or emotional conviction. It is not a neutral maybe-not.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방법이 없다 for 'there is no way that.' 방법이 없다 means there is no method.
Using 리가 없다 when you only mean a soft guess. For uncertainty, use -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 or 아마 아닐 거예요.

entries.english: to be only; to be nothing but
entries.shortExplanation: 뿐이다 means "to be only; to be nothing but" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 뿐이다 (ppunida) means "to be only; to be nothing but". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기다릴 뿐이에요. ("I am only waiting."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뿐이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Only this action, nothing more.

usagePhrases.en: The only thing left is this method.
usagePhrases.note: Only remaining option.

examples.ko: 결국 우리가 할 수 있는 건 수정뿐이에요.
examples.romanization: gyeolguk uriga hal su inneun geon sujeongppunieyo.
examples.en: In the end, all we can do is revise it.
examples.note: Limits the choice to one remaining action.

entries.nuance: 뿐이다 closes the scope. It differs from 뿐만 아니라, which opens the sentence to an additional point.
