commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 뿐이다 with 뿐만 아니라. 뿐이다 means only; 뿐만 아니라 means not only but also.
Using 만 when the whole action, not just a noun, needs limiting.

entries.shortExplanation: 걸요 means "probably; I think..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "probably; I think..." is 걸요 (georyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아직 회의 중일걸요. ("They are probably still in a meeting."). Watch the particle attached to 걸요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: They are probably still in a meeting.
usagePhrases.note: Soft but confident guess.
Past guess.

examples.en: They are probably still at the office.
examples.note: Careful workplace guess.

entries.nuance: 걸요 is softer than a plain statement, but it is not as open-ended as 글쎄요. The speaker still has a hunch.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 걸요 for a wish. For wishes, use -(으)면 좋겠어요.
Confusing sentence-final -걸요 with regret -ㄹ걸 그랬어요.

entries.english: I hope; it would be good if...
entries.shortExplanation: 좋겠어요 means "I hope; it would be good if..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 좋겠어요 (jokesseoyo) = "I hope; it would be good if...". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 답장이 빨리 오면 좋겠어요. ("I hope the reply comes quickly.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 좋겠어요, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I hope the reply comes quickly.
usagePhrases.note: Hoped-for outcome.

usagePhrases.en: It would be good to leave a message.
usagePhrases.note: Gentle suggestion.

examples.en: If you are not sure, it would be good to ask first.
examples.note: Careful advice.

entries.nuance: 좋겠어요 is useful when you want to express a hope or suggestion without sounding like an order.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 좋겠어요 as plain 'I like it.' For liking, use 좋아요.
Using it when you need a firm instruction.

entries.shortExplanation: 다면 means "if; supposing that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 다면 (damyeon) means "if; supposing that". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이미 나갔다면 ("if they already left"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다면 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Hypothetical based on uncertainty.

usagePhrases.en: if I were the person in charge
usagePhrases.note: Noun hypothetical.

examples.ko: 혹시 이미 퇴근했다면 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: hoksi imi toegeunhaetdamyeon mesijireul namgyeo dumyeon jokesseoyo.
examples.en: If they already left work, it would be good to leave a message.
examples.note: Hypothetical plus gentle solution.

entries.nuance: 다면 often feels more hypothetical or careful than plain -(으)면.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다면 for every real condition. Plain -(으)면 is often enough for simple real-world conditions.
Forgetting noun form N이라면.

entries.shortExplanation: 것 같아요 means "I think; it seems like" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "I think; it seems like" is 것 같아요 (geot gatayo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 좀 부담스러운 것 같아요. ("I think it feels a bit burdensome."). Watch the particle attached to 것 같아요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I think it feels a bit burdensome.
usagePhrases.note: Soft opinion.
Past inference.

examples.ko: 제 생각에는 먼저 물어보는 게 좋을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: je saenggageneun meonjeo mureoboneun ge joeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: In my opinion, I think it would be good to ask first.
examples.note: Careful opinion instead of a blunt order.

entries.nuance: 것 같아요 is not the same as 같다 meaning 'same.' Here it softens the whole statement.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Linking 것 같아요 to 같다 as 'same' and missing the hedge meaning.
Keeping a full English-style clause before it. Korean turns the idea into a modifier before 것.

entries.english: will; must be; I see (inference/volition marker)
entries.shortExplanation: 겠 means "will; must be; I see (inference/volition marker)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 겠 (get) = "will; must be; I see (inference/volition marker)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 알겠어요. ("I understand.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 겠, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed polite response.
Inference about someone else.

examples.en: I will ask carefully.
examples.note: Formal intention.

entries.nuance: 겠 is not one English word. It can be intention, inference, or a set response depending on context.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating every 겠 as future tense only.
Using 겠어요 too strongly when 것 같아요 would be a softer guess.

entries.shortExplanation: 조심스럽게 means "carefully; cautiously" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 조심스럽게 (josimseureopge) means "carefully; cautiously". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조심스럽게 물어보다 ("to ask carefully"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조심스럽게 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Useful when not sure.
Tone control.

examples.en: Since I am not sure, I will ask carefully.
examples.note: Careful action because the information is uncertain.

entries.nuance: 조심스럽게 is about tone and risk. It is not just physical carefulness.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a noun. It is an adverb: 조심스럽게 말해요.
Thinking grammar alone creates softness. Word choice and tone also matter.

entries.shortExplanation: 선물 means "gift; present" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "gift; present" is 선물 (seonmul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 친구에게 선물을 줬어요. ("I gave a gift to a friend."). Watch the particle attached to 선물 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I gave a gift to a friend.
usagePhrases.note: 에게 marks the receiver.

usagePhrases.en: I also gave a gift to the teacher.
usagePhrases.note: 께 is honorific; 도 means also.

examples.en: It would be good to prepare at least a small gift.
examples.note: 이라도 gives the sense of at least.

entries.nuance: 선물 can be the thing given, received, bought, or prepared. In this chapter, focus on the particle around the person and the particle attached to 선물 itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 에게 with objects instead of people. Say 친구에게 선물을 줬어요, not 선물에게.
Forgetting that 도 and 만 can replace 을/를: 선물도 줬어요, 선물만 샀어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 알레르기 means "allergy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 알레르기 (allereugi) = "allergy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요. ("I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 알레르기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.
usagePhrases.note: 못 marks a real restriction.
있다 marks the presence of the allergy.

examples.ko: 고기는 싫어서 안 먹는 게 아니라 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: gogineun sireoseo an meongneun ge anira allereugiga isseoseo mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: It is not that I avoid meat because I dislike it; I cannot eat it because of an allergy.
examples.note: Contrasts 안 먹다 with 못 먹다.

entries.nuance: 알레르기 gives a concrete outside reason. In Korean this often makes 못 sound appropriate because the limit is physical or medical, not a preference.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 안 먹어요 when the reason is a medical restriction and you need 못 먹어요.
Using 알레르기 like an adjective. Say 알레르기가 있어요 or 우유 알레르기가 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 저희 means "our / my (humble, polite)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 저희 (jeohui) means "our / my (humble, polite)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저희 가족은 네 명이에요. ("There are four people in my family."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 저희 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: There are four people in my family.
usagePhrases.note: Polite family introduction to someone outside the family.
Humble 우리 with respectful family noun 부모님.

examples.ko: 회사 동료에게는 '저희 가족은 네 명이에요'라고 말해요.
examples.romanization: hoesa dongnyoegeneun 'jeohui gajogeun ne myeongieyo'rago malhaeyo.
examples.en: To a coworker, say 'There are four people in my family.'
examples.note: 저희 fits polite outside-the-family introductions.

entries.nuance: 저희 is not colder than 우리; it is socially careful. Use it when the listener is outside your group and the situation is polite. Use 우리 with close friends, family, and many natural everyday phrases like 우리 엄마.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 제 가족은 too mechanically. It is possible, but 저희 가족은 sounds more natural in polite introductions.
Using 저희 for the listener's family. 저희 lowers your own side, not the other person's side.
Forgetting that 저희 pairs naturally with 가족 and 부모님 in formal or semi-formal introductions.

entries.shortExplanation: 식후 means "after meals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "after meals" is 식후 (siku). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식후에 드세요. ("Take it after meals."). Watch the particle attached to 식후 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Common pharmacy instruction.

usagePhrases.ko: 하루 세 번, 식후에 드셔야 해요.
usagePhrases.romanization: haru se beon, sikue deusyeoya haeyo.
usagePhrases.en: You have to take it three times a day after meals.
usagePhrases.note: Combines frequency and timing.

examples.ko: 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드세요.
examples.romanization: yageun sikue haru se beon deuseyo.
examples.en: Take the medicine three times a day after meals.
examples.note: 약 + 식후 + 하루 세 번 is the core pharmacy frame.

entries.nuance: 식후 is concise and label-like. In casual speech you can also say 밥 먹고, but at a clinic or pharmacy 식후 is the expected word. 식후 usually pairs with 에 or a time amount: 식후에, 식후 30분.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 식후 for any after-action meaning. It specifically means after meals.
Confusing 식후 with 식전. 식후 is after meals; 식전 is before meals.
Forgetting 에 in speech: 식후에 드세요 is smoother than just 식후 드세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 원룸 means "studio apartment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 원룸 (wollum) = "studio apartment". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 원룸을 보러 왔어요. ("I came to see a studio apartment.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 원룸, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I came to see a studio apartment.
usagePhrases.note: Real-estate viewing frame.

usagePhrases.en: Is the maintenance fee separate for this studio?
usagePhrases.note: Fee-checking question.

examples.ko: 이 원룸은 보증금 500만 원에 월세 70만 원이에요.
examples.romanization: i wollumeun bojeunggeum 500man wone wolse 70man wonieyo.
examples.en: This studio has a 5 million won deposit and 700,000 won monthly rent.
examples.note: Common listing-price structure.

entries.nuance: 원룸 literally comes from 'one room', but in Korean it is a housing category, not just any one room. It usually means a small self-contained studio with a bathroom and kitchenette.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating every 'room' as 원룸. 방 is a room; 원룸 is a studio apartment.
Forgetting that 원룸 listings are usually quoted with both 보증금 and 월세.
Assuming 관리비 is always included. Always ask 관리비는 따로예요?

entries.shortExplanation: 부동산 means "real estate; real estate office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 부동산 (budongsan) means "real estate; real estate office". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부동산에 원룸을 보러 갔어요. ("I went to a real-estate office to see a studio."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부동산 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I went to a real-estate office to see a studio.
usagePhrases.note: Common newcomer housing scene.

usagePhrases.en: I checked the contract at the real-estate office.
usagePhrases.note: Place of contract handling.

examples.en: I went to a real-estate office to find a place.
examples.note: -기 위해 gives the planned purpose.

entries.nuance: When Koreans say 부동산에 가요, they usually mean the neighborhood office, not an abstract real-estate market. For the person, say 공인중개사 or 중개사.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 부동산 only means property. In conversation it often means the real-estate office.
Calling the agent 부동산 사람 too vaguely when 공인중개사 or 중개사 is clearer.
Forgetting 에/에서: 부동산에 가다, 부동산에서 계약하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 전세 means "large-deposit lease" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "large-deposit lease" is 전세 (jeonse). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전세예요, 월세예요? ("Is it jeonse or monthly rent?"). Watch the particle attached to 전세 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Is it jeonse or monthly rent?
usagePhrases.note: Basic listing question.

usagePhrases.en: The jeonse deposit is too expensive.
usagePhrases.note: 전세 still revolves around a deposit.

examples.ko: 저는 전세보다 월세 원룸을 찾고 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jeonseboda wolse wollumeul chatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I am looking for a monthly-rent studio rather than jeonse.
examples.note: Useful for telling an agent your housing type.

entries.nuance: 전세 is not simply 'deposit'. The deposit itself is 보증금; 전세 is the lease type built around a very large deposit.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 전세 when you mean any deposit. The deposit is 보증금.
Assuming 월세 has no deposit. 월세 often also has 보증금.
Translating 전세 as monthly rent. Monthly rent is 월세.

entries.shortExplanation: 계약서 means "contract document" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계약서 (gyeyakseo) = "contract document". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 계약서를 확인해 두세요. ("Check the contract and keep it prepared.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계약서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Check the contract and keep it prepared.
usagePhrases.note: -아/어 두다 for preparation.

usagePhrases.en: The deposit is written in the contract.
usagePhrases.note: Contract details as written information.

examples.ko: 이사하기 전에 계약서를 다시 확인해야 해요.
examples.romanization: isahagi jeone gyeyakseoreul dasi hwaginhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: Before moving, you have to check the contract again.
examples.note: Practical pre-move task.

entries.nuance: 계약서 is the document, while 계약하다 is the action of making/signing the contract. Do not blur them when asking questions.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 계약해요 when you mean the paper itself. The paper is 계약서.
Not checking whether 관리비 and options are included before signing.
Forgetting the object marker: 계약서를 확인하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 계약하다 means "to sign / make a contract" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계약하다 (gyeyakada) means "to sign / make a contract". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오늘 계약할 수 있어요? ("Can I sign the contract today?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 계약하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Can I sign the contract today?
usagePhrases.note: Possibility question with ㄹ 수 있어요.

usagePhrases.en: Before signing, check the maintenance fee.
usagePhrases.note: Before-contract warning.

examples.ko: 마음에 들면 오늘 계약할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: maeume deulmyeon oneul gyeyakal su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you like it, you can sign the contract today.
examples.note: Real-estate agent line.

entries.nuance: 계약하다 is broader than housing, but in this chapter it should stay tied to real-estate contracts. 계약서를 확인하다 happens before 계약하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예약하다 for signing a lease. 예약하다 is reserve/book; 계약하다 is contract.
Forgetting that 계약하다 is the action and 계약서 is the document.
Saying 계약을 쓰다 is possible in some contexts, but 계약하다 is the safe learner verb.

entries.shortExplanation: 포함되다 means "to be included" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be included" is 포함되다 (pohamdoeda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 관리비에 인터넷이 포함돼 있어요? ("Is internet included in the maintenance fee?"). Watch the particle attached to 포함되다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Is internet included in the maintenance fee?
usagePhrases.note: Fee inclusion question.

usagePhrases.en: The water bill is included in the maintenance fee.
usagePhrases.note: Common rental detail.

examples.ko: 인터넷이 포함돼 있으면 바로 계약할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: inteonesi pohamdwae isseumyeon baro gyeyakal su isseoyo.
examples.en: If internet is included, I can sign right away.
examples.note: Condition tied to a housing decision.

entries.nuance: 포함되다 focuses on what is included in a price or category. Do not use it like English 'include' with the fee as active subject unless you restructure the sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 관리비가 인터넷을 포함해요 too literally. The natural housing question is 인터넷이 관리비에 포함돼 있어요?
Forgetting 에 after 관리비: 관리비에 포함되다.
Confusing 포함되다 with 필요하다. 포함되다 is about inclusion, not need.

entries.shortExplanation: 따로 means "separately" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 따로 (ttaro) = "separately". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 관리비는 따로예요? ("Is the maintenance fee separate?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 따로, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core rental question.

usagePhrases.en: You have to pay the electricity bill separately.
usagePhrases.note: Separate utility fee.

examples.ko: 관리비가 따로면 월세가 더 비싸게 느껴져요.
examples.romanization: gwallibiga ttaromyeon wolsega deo bissage neukkyeojyeoyo.
examples.en: If the maintenance fee is separate, the monthly rent feels more expensive.
examples.note: Condition that changes the decision.

entries.nuance: 따로 is not only about money, but housing learners need it for separate fees and separate payments.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Asking only 월세가 얼마예요? and forgetting 관리비는 따로예요?
Using 따로 as a noun. It works as an adverb or predicate with 이다: 따로 내요, 따로예요.
Missing the hidden total cost when 관리비 or utilities are 따로.

entries.shortExplanation: 사이즈 means "size" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사이즈 (saijeu) means "size". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사이즈가 맞아요. ("The size fits."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사이즈 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 맞다 is about size or correctness, not style.
A direct shop question.

examples.ko: 사이즈가 조금 커서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: saijeuga jogeum keoseo han chisu jageun geotdo boyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: The size is a little big, so could you show me one size smaller too?
examples.note: Combines size judgment with a polite staff request.

entries.nuance: 사이즈 is the size label or fit. Use 맞다 for whether it fits, and 어울리다 for whether it looks good on someone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 어울리다 for size. 사이즈가 맞아요 means it fits; 잘 어울려요 means it suits you.
Asking only 이거 있어요? when you need a size. Say 다른 사이즈 있어요?
Forgetting that shop staff may ask 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? to mean what size would you like?

entries.shortExplanation: 치수 means "size; measurement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "size; measurement" is 치수 (chisu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한 치수 큰 거 ("one size larger"). Watch the particle attached to 치수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 큰 modifies 거 through the adjective modifier form.
작은 is the modifier form of 작다.

examples.ko: 한 치수 작은 것도 입어 봐도 돼요?
examples.romanization: han chisu jageun geotdo ibeo bwado dwaeyo?
examples.en: May I try on one size smaller too?
examples.note: Natural fitting-room sentence.

entries.nuance: 사이즈 is the everyday label; 치수 is the size measurement or one-step comparison used in 한 치수 큰/작은.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 더 작은 사이즈 only every time. 한 치수 작은 거 is compact and natural in clothing stores.
Confusing 치수 with 가격. 치수 is about size or measurement, not price.
Forgetting the modifier: 한 치수 작아요 describes a size, but 한 치수 작은 거 asks for the item.

entries.shortExplanation: 피팅룸 means "fitting room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 피팅룸 (pitingnum) = "fitting room". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 피팅룸이 어디예요? ("Where is the fitting room?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 피팅룸, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A practical store question.

usagePhrases.en: The fitting room is on the right.
usagePhrases.note: Likely staff answer.

examples.ko: 이 셔츠 입어 보고 싶은데 피팅룸이 어디예요?
examples.romanization: i syeocheu ibeo bogo sipeunde pitingnumi eodiyeyo?
examples.en: I want to try on this shirt. Where is the fitting room?
examples.note: Connects trying on with store navigation.

entries.nuance: 피팅룸 is used in many stores, but 탈의실 also means changing room. For clothing shopping, 피팅룸 is natural and easy to understand.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling staff with 피팅룸? alone. Make it a full question: 피팅룸이 어디예요?
Using 입다 without try-on meaning. 입어 봐도 돼요? asks permission to try it on.
Assuming every shop allows try-ons; ask first for cosmetics, innerwear, sale items, or delicate clothing.

entries.shortExplanation: 단정하다 means "to be neat; tidy; presentable" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 단정하다 (danjeonghada) means "to be neat; tidy; presentable". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 단정한 셔츠 ("a neat shirt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단정하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A-ㄴ/은 N modifier form.
Appearance judgment with -아/어 보이다.

examples.ko: 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보여요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeneun i syeocheuboda namsaek syeocheuga deo danjeonghae boyeoyo.
examples.en: For an interview, the navy shirt looks neater than this shirt.
examples.note: Connects interview clothing with comparison and appearance.

entries.nuance: 단정하다 means neat, orderly, and socially appropriate. It is not the same as stylish or trendy; it is often safer for interviews, school, and work.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예쁘다 for every clothing compliment. 예쁘다 is pretty; 단정하다 is neat and appropriate.
Saying 단정 옷. Use the modifier form: 단정한 옷.
Confusing 단정하다 with 깨끗하다. 깨끗하다 is clean; 단정하다 is presentable and orderly.

entries.shortExplanation: 인분 means "serving; portion for one person" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "serving; portion for one person" is 인분 (inbun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 삼겹살 두 인분 주세요. ("Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal."). Watch the particle attached to 인분 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal.
usagePhrases.note: Core barbecue order.

usagePhrases.en: Please give us one more serving.
usagePhrases.note: Common extra order.

examples.ko: 삼겹살 두 인분하고 공기밥 하나 주세요.
examples.romanization: samgyeopsal du inbunhago gonggiba pana juseyo.
examples.en: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal and one bowl of rice.
examples.note: Combines a serving counter and a rice order.

entries.nuance: 명 counts people; 인분 counts portions. 두 명 왔어요 says two people came, but 두 인분 주세요 orders two servings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 명 to order food. Say 삼겹살 두 인분, not 삼겹살 두 명.
Forgetting that some restaurants have a minimum order such as 2인분.
Treating 인분 as exactly the eater count. People can order more or fewer servings than the number of people.

entries.shortExplanation: 공기밥 means "bowl of rice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 공기밥 (gonggibap) = "bowl of rice". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공기밥 하나 주세요. ("Please give me one bowl of rice.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공기밥, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me one bowl of rice.
usagePhrases.note: Simple restaurant request.

usagePhrases.en: We will add a bowl of rice.
usagePhrases.note: Common after ordering meat or stew.

examples.en: The seasoning is spicy, so I eat it with a bowl of rice.
examples.note: Reason plus food pairing.

entries.nuance: 밥 can mean cooked rice or a meal. 공기밥 is the restaurant item, a separate bowl of rice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Ordering 밥 vaguely when the menu item is 공기밥.
Confusing 공기밥 with 볶음밥. 공기밥 is plain rice; 볶음밥 is fried rice.
Forgetting the counter: 공기밥 하나/두 개 is common.

entries.shortExplanation: 밑반찬 means "basic side dishes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 밑반찬 (mitbanchan) means "basic side dishes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 밑반찬 좀 더 주세요. ("Please give us a little more side dishes."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 밑반찬 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Please give us a little more side dishes.
usagePhrases.note: Polite refill request.
Simple restaurant compliment.

examples.en: The side dishes are not enough, so please give us more.
examples.note: Uses -니까 before a request.

entries.nuance: 밑반찬 is not the main dish. It refers to small supporting dishes such as kimchi, vegetables, or pickles served with the meal.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every Korean side dish 밑반찬 in every context. On a menu, 반찬 or 사이드 may also appear.
Forgetting 좀 in refill requests. 밑반찬 좀 더 주세요 sounds softer.
Assuming refills are always unlimited; most ordinary restaurants refill, but special side dishes may not be free.

entries.shortExplanation: 익다 means "to be cooked; to ripen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to be cooked; to ripen" is 익다 (ikda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 고기가 익었어요. ("The meat is cooked."). Watch the particle attached to 익다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Food is the subject.
Useful at a table grill.

examples.en: The meat is cooked now, so please cut it.
examples.note: -니까 gives the reason for the request.

entries.nuance: 익다 is intransitive: 고기가 익어요. 익히다 is transitive: 고기를 익혀요, to cook something through.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 고기를 익어요. Use 고기가 익어요 because the meat becomes cooked.
Confusing 익다 with 굽다. 굽다 is the cooking action; 익다 is the result.
Using 익다 only for fruit. It also works for meat, rice, and other food becoming cooked.

entries.shortExplanation: 쌈장 means "ssamjang; thick sauce for wraps" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 쌈장 (ssamjang) = "ssamjang; thick sauce for wraps". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쌈장 조금만 주세요. ("Please give me just a little ssamjang.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쌈장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me just a little ssamjang.
usagePhrases.note: Useful if the sauce is strong or salty.

usagePhrases.en: The ssamjang is a bit salty.
usagePhrases.note: Taste description.

examples.en: The ssamjang is salty, so put in only a little.
examples.note: Reason plus advice.

entries.nuance: 쌈장 is not the same as 고추장. It is a mixed paste commonly used for wraps with grilled meat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every red sauce 고추장. 쌈장 is a specific wrap sauce.
Using too much without tasting; 쌈장 can be salty.
Forgetting that 쌈장 often goes with 상추, 마늘, and grilled meat.

entries.shortExplanation: 드라마 means "TV drama; series" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 드라마 (deurama) means "TV drama; series". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이 드라마 본 적 있어요? ("Have you watched this drama before?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 드라마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Have you watched this drama before?
usagePhrases.note: Experience question.

usagePhrases.en: What drama are you watching these days?
usagePhrases.note: Natural small-talk question.

examples.en: My friend said this drama is fun.
examples.note: Reported recommendation.

entries.nuance: 드라마 usually means a scripted series, not a one-off movie. 영화 is movie; 예능 is variety show.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 영화 for every streamed show. A series is usually 드라마.
Forgetting 보다: 드라마를 봐요, not 드라마를 들어요.
Using 본 적 있어요 for something you watched yesterday with a time. Use 봤어요 for a dated event.

entries.shortExplanation: 댓글 means "comment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "comment" is 댓글 (daetgeul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 댓글을 달다 ("to leave a comment"). Watch the particle attached to 댓글 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The verb is 달다.
The comment is the subject.

examples.en: The actor is good too, but the comments are more fun, you know.
examples.note: A reason/background sentence for online content.

entries.nuance: 댓글 is online. For a spoken comment or opinion, 말 or 의견 may fit better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 댓글을 쓰다 is understandable, but 댓글을 달다 is the standard collocation.
Using 코멘트 for ordinary social media comments. 댓글 is the everyday word.
Forgetting subject/object particles: 댓글이 재미있어요, 댓글을 달아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 공유하다 means "to share" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 공유하다 (gongyuhada) = "to share". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영상을 공유했어요. ("I shared the video.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공유하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Digital sharing.

usagePhrases.en: I shared it with a friend.
usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the recipient.

examples.en: It was fun, so I shared the video with a friend.
examples.note: Reason plus digital action.

entries.nuance: 공유하다 is broader than sending. 보내다 is to send; 공유하다 emphasizes making content available or passing it along.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 나누다 for social media sharing. Use 공유하다 for links, videos, and files.
Forgetting the object: 영상을 공유했어요, 링크를 공유했어요.
Mixing 공유하다 with 저장하다. Sharing is not saving.

entries.shortExplanation: 자막 means "subtitles; captions" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 자막 (jamak) means "subtitles; captions". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자막이 좋아요. ("The subtitles are good."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자막 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Simple evaluation.
Streaming problem.

examples.en: My friend said the subtitles are good.
examples.note: Reported opinion.

entries.nuance: 자막 can mean subtitles for translation or captions on video. In streaming apps, 자막 설정 is subtitle settings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 자막 with 제목. 자막 is subtitles; 제목 is a title.
Saying 자막을 봐요 when you mean the subtitles show on screen. Use 자막이 나와요.
Forgetting that 자막 takes 이/가 when it appears: 자막이 안 나와요.

entries.shortExplanation: 끊기다 means "to cut out; disconnect; buffer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to cut out; disconnect; buffer" is 끊기다 (kkeunkida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 영상이 계속 끊겨요. ("The video keeps cutting out."). Watch the particle attached to 끊기다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Streaming problem.
Connection problem.

examples.en: The video keeps cutting out, though.
examples.note: -는데요 softly raises the problem.

entries.nuance: 끊기다 is passive/intransitive: the video or connection cuts out. 끊다 is what someone actively cuts or ends.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 끊다 for a video problem. Say 영상이 끊겨요, not 영상을 끊어요.
Confusing 끊기다 with 느리다. 느리다 is slow; 끊기다 is stopping/cutting out.
Forgetting the subject: 영상이 끊겨요, 와이파이가 끊겨요.

entries.shortExplanation: 아이돌 means "idol; K-pop idol" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 아이돌 (aidol) = "idol; K-pop idol". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어떤 아이돌 좋아해요? ("Which idol do you like?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아이돌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Natural entertainment question.

usagePhrases.en: Did you see that idol's stage?
usagePhrases.note: K-pop viewing conversation.

examples.ko: 친구가 그 아이돌 무대가 대박이라고 했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga geu aidol mudaega daebagirago haesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend said that idol's stage was amazing.
examples.note: Reported fan reaction.

entries.nuance: 아이돌 can refer to a solo idol or group member. For the whole group, 그룹 or 아이돌 그룹 is clearer.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가수 for every K-pop idol. 가수 is singer; 아이돌 includes the fandom/performance context.
Forgetting that borrowed words still take Korean particles: 아이돌이, 아이돌을, 아이돌한테.
Using formal fan slang before you understand the fandom context.

entries.shortExplanation: 연결하다 means "to connect" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연결하다 (yeongyeolhada) means "to connect". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 와이파이를 다시 연결해 보세요. ("Try reconnecting the Wi-Fi."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연결하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Natural troubleshooting advice.
General digital setup sentence.

examples.ko: 영상이 계속 끊기면 와이파이를 다시 연결해 보세요.
examples.romanization: yeongsangi gyesok kkeunkimyeon waipaireul dasi yeongyeolhae boseyo.
examples.en: If the video keeps cutting out, try reconnecting the Wi-Fi.
examples.note: Problem plus suggested action.

entries.nuance: 연결하다 is active: you connect something. 연결되다 means something is connected.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 연결하다 when the subject is the Wi-Fi itself. 와이파이가 연결됐어요 is natural for 'the Wi-Fi is connected.'
Confusing 연결하다 with 공유하다. 연결하다 connects; 공유하다 shares content.
Forgetting 을/를 for what you connect: 와이파이를 연결해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 교수님 means "professor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "professor" is 교수님 (gyosunim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 교수님께 물어봐요. ("I ask the professor."). Watch the particle attached to 교수님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 께 is respectful 'to'.
Honorific verb ending for the professor.

examples.en: I decided to ask the professor before the midterm.
examples.note: Decision plus school context.

entries.nuance: Use 선생님 for school teachers or language teachers, and 교수님 for university professors.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a university professor 선생님 is understandable, but 교수님 is more natural.
Using 교수 without 님 when addressing or referring respectfully.
Using 한테 in formal writing to a professor; 께 is more respectful.

entries.shortExplanation: 학기 means "semester; school term" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 학기 (hakgi) = "semester; school term". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이번 학기 ("this semester") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 학기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Common school time phrase.
학기 works naturally with 동안.

examples.ko: 이번 학기 동안 매일 한국어를 공부하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon hakgi dongan maeil hangugeoreul gongbuhagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: I decided to study Korean every day during this semester.
examples.note: 학기 plus 동안.

entries.nuance: 학기 is an academic term; 방학 is vacation/break between terms.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 학기 for a single class period. A class period is 수업 or 시간.
Confusing 학기 with 학년. 학기 is semester; 학년 is grade/year.
Adding 에 before 동안: say 한 학기 동안, not 한 학기에 동안.

entries.shortExplanation: 중간고사 means "midterm exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 중간고사 (junggangosa) means "midterm exam". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 중간고사 전에 ("before the midterm"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 중간고사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Common schedule phrase.
Exam period.

examples.ko: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요.
examples.romanization: junggangosa jeone balpyo gwajereul kkeunnaeya haeyo.
examples.en: We have to finish the presentation assignment before the midterm.
examples.note: Exam deadline plus obligation.

entries.nuance: 중간 means middle; 고사 is exam. In daily student talk, 시험 is more general, while 중간고사 is specifically the midterm.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 중간고사 for every test. Use 시험 for general exams.
Confusing 중간고사 with 기말고사. Midterm comes in the middle; final comes at the end.
Forgetting the timing phrase: 중간고사 전에, 중간고사 동안, 중간고사 끝나고.

entries.shortExplanation: 기말고사 means "final exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "final exam" is 기말고사 (gimalgosa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기말고사 준비 ("final exam preparation"). Watch the particle attached to 기말고사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Noun phrase.
보다 is used for taking exams.

examples.ko: 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받기 위해 매일 공부해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gimalgosaeseo joeun seongjeogeul batgi wihae maeil gongbuhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: I have to study every day in order to get a good grade on the final exam.
examples.note: Purpose plus obligation.

entries.nuance: 기말 means the end of the term. 기말고사 is final exam; 중간고사 is midterm exam.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 기말고사 before the middle of the semester. That is 중간고사.
Saying 시험을 치다/보다 both work for taking an exam; 시험을 만들다 does not mean take an exam.
Using 에 with 기말고사 when the sentence is about results. Say 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받다.

entries.shortExplanation: 과제 means "assignment; homework" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 과제 (gwaje) = "assignment; homework". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과제가 있어요. ("There is an assignment.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Basic class question.
Useful deadline phrase.

examples.ko: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: junggangosa jeone balpyo gwajereul kkeunnaegiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We decided to finish the presentation assignment before the midterm.
examples.note: Decision plus assignment.

entries.nuance: 숙제 is homework, often younger-school or daily work. 과제 sounds more academic and can include reports, presentations, and projects.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 숙제 for every university assignment. 과제 is often more natural.
Forgetting the object marker when needed: 과제를 끝내요.
Confusing 과제 with 문제. 문제 is a question/problem; 과제 is an assigned task.

entries.shortExplanation: 호선 means "subway line number" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 호선 (hoseon) means "subway line number". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 몇 호선이에요? ("Which line is it?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호선 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Natural question when checking a route.
으로 marks the line you change to.

examples.en: Which line do I transfer to if I want to get to Seoul Station?
examples.note: Route question plus transfer.

entries.nuance: 호선 is for subway line labels, not for bus routes. Say 2호선 for Line 2, but 버스 노선 for a bus route.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 2노선 for Line 2. Subway lines use 호선: 2호선.
Using 호선 for bus routes. Use 노선 for buses.
Forgetting 으로/로 with transfers: 1호선으로 갈아타세요.

entries.english: to book or buy a ticket in advance
entries.shortExplanation: 예매하다 means "to book or buy a ticket in advance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to book or buy a ticket in advance" is 예매하다 (yemaehada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like KTX 표를 예매하다 ("to book a KTX ticket"). Watch the particle attached to 예매하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 표 is the object; 예매하다 is the booking action.

usagePhrases.en: I booked it in the app.
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the booking action happened.

examples.ko: 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매하려고 해요.
examples.romanization: busan ganeun KTX pyoreul yemaeharyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I am trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan.
examples.note: Natural ticket-counter or app sentence.

entries.nuance: 예매하다 is ticket-centered and usually means the seat or ticket is secured before departure or showtime. 예약하다 is broader and can mean reserving a restaurant, hotel, appointment, or service.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예약하다 for every ticket situation. It may be understood, but KTX/movie/concert tickets naturally use 예매하다.
Forgetting the object: 표를 예매하다, not just KTX를 예매하다 when you mean the ticket.
Confusing 예매하다 with 사다. 사다 is buy in general; 예매하다 adds advance booking.

entries.shortExplanation: 편도 means "one-way ticket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 편도 (pyeondo) = "one-way ticket". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 편도 한 장 ("one one-way ticket") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 편도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Tickets are counted with 장.
Short counter answer.

examples.en: I will book the ticket to Busan one-way.
examples.note: 으로/로 marks ticket type here.

entries.nuance: 편도 is the opposite of 왕복. It answers the ticket type question, not the destination question.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한쪽 for a one-way ticket. Use 편도.
Confusing 편도 with 편의점. They only sound partly similar.
Forgetting the counter when buying: 편도 한 장 주세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 왕복 means "round trip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 왕복 (wangbok) means "round trip". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 왕복 표 ("round-trip ticket"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 왕복 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The return is included.
으로 marks the ticket type.

examples.en: I booked a round trip from Seoul to Busan.
examples.note: Useful when both directions are fixed.

entries.nuance: 왕복 is the ticket-plan pair of 편도. The question 편도예요, 왕복이에요? is a normal ticket-counter question.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 돌아오는 표 when the counter simply asks ticket type. 왕복 is the compact ticket word.
Confusing 왕복 with 반복. 반복 means repetition.
Buying 왕복 when your return time is not fixed can be inconvenient; 편도 may be safer.

entries.english: sold out for tickets or seats
entries.shortExplanation: 매진 means "sold out for tickets or seats" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "sold out for tickets or seats" is 매진 (maejin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 표가 매진이에요. ("The tickets are sold out."). Watch the particle attached to 매진 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Ticket availability sentence.
되다 makes the sold-out state.

examples.ko: KTX 표가 매진이면 다음 기차로 예매하세요.
examples.romanization: KTX pyoga maejinimyeon daeum gicharo yemaehaseyo.
examples.en: If the KTX tickets are sold out, book the next train.
examples.note: 매진 plus V면 creates the fallback plan.

entries.nuance: 매진 is for tickets and seats. 품절 is for products on a shelf or in an online store.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 품절 for train tickets. Say 매진.
Saying 매진하다 for the customer's action. The ticket is 매진되다 or 매진이에요.
Forgetting that 매진 often needs a fallback sentence: 매진이면 다음 기차로 가요.

entries.shortExplanation: 지연 means "delay" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 지연 (jiyeon) = "delay". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 버스 지연 ("bus delay") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 지연, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Noun compound for the cause.
지연되다 in past tense.

examples.en: I was late to the appointment because of a bus delay.
examples.note: N 때문에 names the cause.

entries.nuance: 지연 sounds more official than 늦다. Use 늦다 for a person being late and 지연 for a service, schedule, or system delay.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사람이 지연됐어요 for a person. Say 사람이 늦었어요.
Using 늦다 when the service delay is the topic. For announcements, 지연되다 is more natural.
Adding a particle before 때문에: say 버스 지연 때문에, not 버스 지연이 때문에.

entries.shortExplanation: 배차 간격 means "interval between buses or trains" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 배차 간격 (baecha gangyeok) means "interval between buses or trains". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 배차 간격이 길어요. ("The interval between buses or trains is long."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 배차 간격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: The interval between buses or trains is long.
usagePhrases.note: Long interval means more waiting.
Useful with transit apps.

examples.ko: 이 노선은 배차 간격이 길어서 택시로 갈게요.
examples.romanization: i noseoneun baecha gangyeogi gireoseo taeksiro galgeyo.
examples.en: This route has a long service interval, so I will go by taxi.
examples.note: Connects route information to a transport choice.

entries.nuance: 배차 간격 is not the travel time. It is the gap between one bus or train and the next one.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 배차 간격 with 소요 시간. 소요 시간 is how long the trip takes.
Using it for one delayed vehicle. 지연 is delay; 배차 간격 is the normal interval.
Forgetting 이/가 with the measured interval: 배차 간격이 길어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 매표소 means "ticket counter / ticket office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ticket counter / ticket office" is 매표소 (maepyoso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매표소에 가다 ("to go to the ticket counter"). Watch the particle attached to 매표소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to go to the ticket counter
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination.

usagePhrases.en: to book at the ticket counter
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the booking happens.

examples.en: I am going to the ticket counter to book a KTX ticket.
examples.note: Purpose plus destination.

entries.nuance: 매표소 is the selling place for tickets. 표 is the ticket itself, and 예매하다 is the booking action.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 매표소 with 표. 매표소 is the place; 표 is the ticket.
Using 에서 when only naming the destination. Say 매표소에 가요, but 매표소에서 예매해요.
Calling every service desk 매표소. It is specifically for ticket sales.

entries.shortExplanation: 동갑 means "same age" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 동갑 (donggap) = "same age". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 동갑이에요. ("We are the same age.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동갑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Common age-discovery sentence.

usagePhrases.en: If we are the same age, can we speak casually?
usagePhrases.note: Age does not automatically remove politeness; you still check.

examples.en: If we are about the same age, can I say we are the same age?
examples.note: Socially careful age question.

entries.nuance: 동갑 is useful because Korean relationships often adjust around age. Still, being 동갑 does not mean you immediately use 반말; closeness and setting matter too.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 동갑 means you can use 반말 immediately. Ask or wait for the other person to suggest it.
Using 친구 only because someone is the same age. 친구 implies relationship, not just age.
Forgetting final consonant pronunciation: 동갑 sounds like dong-gap, with the final ㅂ pronounced clearly before a vowel.

entries.shortExplanation: 호칭 means "form of address / title" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 호칭 (hoching) means "form of address / title". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 호칭을 정하다 ("to decide on a title/form of address"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호칭 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to decide on a title/form of address
usagePhrases.note: Common after age or role is known.
Safe learner question.

examples.ko: 처음엔 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen seonbaenim gateun hochingeul sseuneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: At first, people tend to use a title like seonbaenim.
examples.note: Polite title choice.

entries.nuance: 호칭 is not just a word choice; it signals age, role, closeness, and respect. When unsure, asking 어떤 호칭을 쓰면 될까요? is safer than guessing too casually.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an older coworker by first name without checking. Use a title or ask first.
Using 씨 with everyone. It can be neutral, distant, or awkward depending on workplace hierarchy.
Forgetting 님 in respectful titles such as 선배님, 사장님, 교수님.

entries.shortExplanation: 어르신 means "elder; older person respectfully" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "elder; older person respectfully" is 어르신 (eoreusin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어르신이 계세요. ("An elder is there."). Watch the particle attached to 어르신 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다.
께 and 여쭤보다 both add respect.

examples.en: If elders are there too, I will ask, 'May I help?'
examples.note: Respectful presence plus polite help offer.

entries.nuance: 어르신 is respectful and warm. 어른 simply means adult or grown-up; 어르신 adds social respect for age.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 어른 when you need respectful tone. 어르신 is safer for elders.
Pairing 어르신 with 있다 in polite speech. Use 계시다: 어르신이 계세요.
Using 반말 around elders just because the setting is casual.

entries.shortExplanation: 세제 means "detergent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 세제 (seje) = "detergent". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 세제를 사다 ("to buy detergent") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 세제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Object marker 를.

usagePhrases.en: to bring detergent as a housewarming gift
usagePhrases.note: 선물로 marks the gift role.

examples.en: It is okay to bring detergent as a housewarming gift.
examples.note: Practical gift sentence.

entries.nuance: 세제 is practical rather than fancy. In 집들이 culture, practical household gifts can feel considerate because they help the new home run smoothly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 세제 with 세금. 세제 is detergent; 세금 is tax.
Using it for soap in general. Soap is 비누; detergent is 세제.
Forgetting that gift role uses 로: 선물로 세제를 가져가요.

entries.shortExplanation: 덕분에 means "thanks to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 덕분에 (deokbune) means "thanks to". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 선배님 덕분에 ("thanks to you / thanks to the senior colleague"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 덕분에 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: thanks to you / thanks to the senior colleague
usagePhrases.note: Respectful gratitude.

usagePhrases.en: It went well thanks to you.
usagePhrases.note: Common closing thanks.

examples.en: Thanks to you, the atmosphere became comfortable.
examples.note: Positive cause in a social setting.

entries.nuance: 덕분에 is for welcome causes. 때문에 often sounds neutral or negative, so 선배님 때문에 잘 됐어요 can sound like blame even with a good result.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 때문에 to thank someone. Use 덕분에 for a positive cause.
Forgetting the person before 덕분에: 선배님 덕분에, 친구 덕분에.
Using 덕분에 for a bad result. For bad results, 때문에 is usually natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 재우다 means "to put someone to sleep" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to put someone to sleep" is 재우다 (jaeuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아기를 재우다 ("to put a baby to sleep"). Watch the particle attached to 재우다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to put a baby to sleep
usagePhrases.note: The baby sleeps; someone else causes it.

usagePhrases.en: to put someone to bed early
usagePhrases.note: Common parenting sentence.

examples.en: The mother put the baby to sleep.
examples.note: Causative: the baby sleeps, the mother causes it.

entries.nuance: 자다 is intransitive: 아기가 자요. 재우다 adds a causer: 엄마가 아기를 재워요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 엄마가 아기를 자요. Use 재우다 when the mother puts the baby to sleep.
Forgetting the object/causee: 아기를 재우다.
Treating 재우다 as simply 'sleep.' The subject is not the sleeper.

entries.english: to make someone laugh; to be funny
entries.shortExplanation: 웃기다 means "to make someone laugh; to be funny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 웃기다 (utgida) = "to make someone laugh; to be funny". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사람들을 웃기다 ("to make people laugh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 웃기다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Causative use.
Everyday adjective-like use.

examples.en: That joke made everyone laugh.
examples.note: The joke is the causer.

entries.nuance: 웃다 is what the person does; 웃기다 is what causes the laughing. In speech, 웃기다 also works like 'to be funny.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 웃다 when the subject is the joke. Say 농담이 웃겼어요, not 농담이 웃었어요.
Forgetting that 웃기다 can be casual and colloquial as 'funny.'
Mixing up 웃기다 with 울리다: one causes laughter, the other tears or ringing.

entries.english: to make someone cry; to ring
entries.shortExplanation: 울리다 means "to make someone cry; to ring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 울리다 (ullida) means "to make someone cry; to ring". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사람을 울리다 ("to make someone cry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 울리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Emotional causative.
Sound causative.

examples.en: That movie made me cry.
examples.note: The film causes the crying.

entries.nuance: 울다 is cry or ring by itself; 울리다 makes someone cry or makes a sound ring.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 영화가 울었어요 when the movie made you cry. Say 영화가 저를 울렸어요.
Forgetting the object in emotional causative: 저를/사람들을 울리다.
Confusing 울리다's two uses: emotional 'make cry' and sound 'ring.'

entries.shortExplanation: 낮추다 means "to lower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "to lower" is 낮추다 (natchuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 소리를 낮추다 ("to lower the volume"). Watch the particle attached to 낮추다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Very common daily command.
Business or shopping context.

examples.en: I lowered my voice because we were in a meeting.
examples.note: The subject causes the voice level to become lower.

entries.nuance: 낮다 is an adjective, while 낮추다 is an action verb. Compare 소리가 낮아요 with 소리를 낮춰 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 낮다 as an action: 소리를 낮아요 is wrong. Say 소리를 낮춰요.
Confusing 낮추다 with 내려가다. 내려가다 means go down; 낮추다 means lower something.
Forgetting the object marker: 목소리를 낮추다.

entries.english: to reduce; to cut down on
entries.shortExplanation: 줄이다 means "to reduce; to cut down on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 줄이다 (jurida) = "to reduce; to cut down on". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이다 ("to reduce phone-watching") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 줄이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: -는 것 turns the action into the object being reduced.
A common budget phrase.
Daily command for volume.

examples.ko: 자기 전에 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jagi jeone hyudaepon boneun geoseul jurigiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: I decided to cut down on looking at my phone before sleeping.
examples.note: -는 것 is the habit being reduced; -기로 했어요 reports the decision.

entries.nuance: 줄이다 is transitive: you reduce something. 줄다 is intransitive: something decreases by itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 줄다 for your own action: 지출을 줄어요 is wrong. Say 지출을 줄여요.
Forgetting the object: 휴대폰 보는 것을 줄이다, not just 휴대폰 보다 줄이다.
Confusing 줄이다 with 낮추다. 낮추다 is lowering a level such as price, voice, or volume; 줄이다 is reducing amount or frequency.

entries.english: to be natural; obvious; no wonder
entries.shortExplanation: 당연하다 means "to be natural; obvious; no wonder" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 당연하다 (dangyeonhada) means "to be natural; obvious; no wonder". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 당연하네요 ("No wonder; that makes sense."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당연하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Fresh realization.
More formal acknowledgement.
Adverb form.

examples.ko: 연습을 많이 했으니까 잘하는 게 당연하네요.
examples.romanization: yeonseubeul mani haesseunikka jalhaneun ge dangyeonhaneyo.
examples.en: Since you practiced a lot, no wonder you are good.
examples.note: -네요 shows the speaker is realizing why the result makes sense.

entries.nuance: 당연하다 can sound dismissive if used carelessly. 당연하네요 is softer than 당연해요 because it frames the comment as realization.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 당연하다 to praise directly. For praise, say 잘하시네요; 당연하네요 explains why the result makes sense.
Forgetting that 당연히 is the adverb, while 당연하다 is the adjective.
Overusing 당연하지요 in formal situations; 당연하군요 or 그렇군요 can sound more measured.

entries.shortExplanation: 근거 means "evidence; grounds; basis" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "evidence; grounds; basis" is 근거 (geungeo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 근거가 부족하다 ("the evidence is insufficient"). Watch the particle attached to 근거 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Formal evaluation phrase.
Essay and report collocation.

examples.en: This report lacks evidence.
examples.note: Formal written 평가.

examples.en: Evidence that supports the claim must be presented.
examples.note: 근거를 제시하다 is the basic formal writing frame.

examples.ko: 자료의 출처가 분명해야 근거로 사용할 수 있다.
examples.romanization: jaryoui chulcheoga bunmyeonghaeya geungeoro sayonghal su itda.
examples.en: The source of the material must be clear for it to be used as evidence.
examples.note: 근거로 사용하다 marks the role of the material with 로.

entries.nuance: 근거 is broader than 증거; 증거 often means proof/evidence, while 근거 can mean the basis for reasoning.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이유 when the writing needs evidence. 이유 is a reason; 근거 is supporting basis.
Saying 근거를 부족하다. The noun is subject: 근거가 부족하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 결론 means "conclusion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 결론 (gyeollon) = "conclusion". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결론을 내리다 ("to draw a conclusion") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결론, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Standard academic phrase.
Useful in revisions.

examples.en: Therefore, the conclusion must be reviewed again.
examples.note: 따라서 links evidence to action.

examples.en: After analyzing the material, a conclusion was drawn.
examples.note: 결론을 내리다 is the standard verb phrase.

examples.en: If the evidence is weak, the conclusion also loses persuasiveness.
examples.note: Shows why 결론 depends on 근거 in argument writing.

entries.nuance: 결론 is the end point of reasoning, not simply the ending of a story.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 결말 for essays. 결말 is a story ending; 결론 is an argument conclusion.
Forgetting object marking in 결론을 내리다.

entries.shortExplanation: 핵심 means "core; key point" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 핵심 (haeksim) means "core; key point". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 핵심 주장 ("main claim"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 핵심 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Common essay phrase.
Formal summary frame.

examples.ko: 그러나 핵심 주장은 유지할 수 있습니다.
examples.romanization: geureona haeksim jujangeun yujihal su itseumnida.
examples.en: However, the main claim can be maintained.
examples.note: 그러나 marks contrast while 핵심 narrows the scope.

examples.ko: 이 글의 핵심은 비용 문제가 아니라 안전 문제이다.
examples.romanization: i geurui haeksimeun biyong munjega anira anjeon munjeida.
examples.en: The key point of this piece is not cost but safety.
examples.note: 핵심은 A가 아니라 B이다 is a useful written contrast frame.

examples.ko: 핵심 내용을 먼저 정리한 뒤 사례를 붙인다.
examples.romanization: haeksim naeyongeul meonjeo jeongnihan dwi saryereul buchinda.
examples.en: First organize the key content, then attach examples.
examples.note: 핵심 내용 naturally pairs with summary and outline work.

entries.nuance: 핵심 is more formal and analytical than 중요한 부분.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 핵심 for any detail. It should be central, not incidental.
Mixing 핵심 내용 and 핵심 주장 without deciding whether you mean content or claim.

entries.shortExplanation: 논리 means "logic; reasoning" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "logic; reasoning" is 논리 (nolli). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 논리가 부족하다 ("the reasoning is insufficient"). Watch the particle attached to 논리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Critical writing phrase.
Revision phrase.

examples.en: Ultimately, the core of the report is evidence and reasoning.
examples.note: 결국 sums up the argument.

examples.en: The claim is clear, but there is a leap in the reasoning.
examples.note: 논리에 비약이 있다 is the natural critique, not 논리가 비약하다.

examples.ko: 두 문장 사이의 논리를 더 분명히 해야 한다.
examples.romanization: du munjang saiui nollireul deo bunmyeonghi haeya handa.
examples.en: The reasoning between the two sentences needs to be made clearer.
examples.note: Useful when revising paragraph flow.

entries.nuance: 논리 is the structure of reasoning, not simply an opinion.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 논리 as a vague synonym for 생각. 생각 is thought; 논리 is reasoning.
Forgetting that 논리가 비약하다 is unnatural; say 논리에 비약이 있다.

entries.shortExplanation: 사례 means "case; example" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 사례 (sarye) = "case; example". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사례를 제시하다 ("to present a case/example") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사례, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Formal support phrase.
Report heading phrase.
