examples.en: In contrast, the case analysis needs supplementation.
examples.note: 반면에 contrasts one part of a report with another.

examples.ko: 주장을 뒷받침하려면 구체적인 사례를 제시해야 한다.
examples.romanization: jujangeul dwitbatchimharyeomyeon guchejeogin saryereul jesihaeya handa.
examples.en: To support a claim, concrete cases must be presented.
examples.note: 사례를 제시하다 is the report-writing counterpart to giving examples.

examples.en: Foreign cases and domestic cases were compared.
examples.note: 사례 works well with comparative analysis.

entries.nuance: 사례 is more formal than 예 and often implies a real case or representative example.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예 only in formal reports when 사례 would sound more analytical.
Forgetting object marking in 사례를 제시하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 가설 means "hypothesis" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 가설 (gaseol) means "hypothesis". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가설을 세우다 ("to form a hypothesis"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가설 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Research phrase.
Evidence phrase.

examples.en: The experimental result supported the hypothesis.
examples.note: Plain written -다 style.

examples.ko: 연구자는 먼저 가설을 세운 뒤 자료를 수집했다.
examples.romanization: yeongujaneun meonjeo gaseoreul seun dwi jaryoreul sujipaetda.
examples.en: The researcher first formed a hypothesis and then collected data.
examples.note: 가설을 세우다 is more natural than 가설을 만들다 in research writing.

examples.ko: 새로운 자료는 기존 가설과 맞지 않았다.
examples.romanization: saeroun jaryoneun gijon gaseolgwa matji anatda.
examples.en: The new data did not fit the existing hypothesis.
examples.note: Shows 가설 as something evidence can support or challenge.

entries.nuance: 가설 is not a casual guess; it is a testable proposition.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 추측 when formal research writing needs 가설.
Saying 가설을 만들다 in academic prose; 가설을 세우다 is more standard.

entries.shortExplanation: 이론 means "theory" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "theory" is 이론 (iron). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이론이 유효하다 ("the theory is valid"). Watch the particle attached to 이론 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Formal evaluation phrase.
Academic usage.

examples.ko: 따라서 이 이론은 유효하다고 볼 수 있다.
examples.romanization: ttaraseo i ironeun yuhyohadago bol su itda.
examples.en: Therefore, this theory can be considered valid.
examples.note: Formal conclusion after evidence.

examples.ko: 이 이론은 여러 사례를 설명하는 데 도움이 된다.
examples.romanization: i ironeun yeoreo saryereul seolmyeonghaneun de doumi doenda.
examples.en: This theory helps explain several cases.
examples.note: 이론 explains patterns across cases, not just one opinion.

examples.en: The theory was reviewed through field data.
examples.note: 이론을 검토하다 links naturally to evidence-based writing.

entries.nuance: 이론 is more structured than 생각 or 의견.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이론 for any personal idea. For a personal view, use 의견 or 생각.
Forgetting object marking in 이론을 적용하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 반론 means "counterargument; objection" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 반론 (ballon) = "counterargument; objection". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 반론을 제기하다 ("to raise a counterargument") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 반론, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Formal debate phrase.
Essay revision phrase.

examples.en: However, expected counterarguments must also be reviewed.
examples.note: 그러나 introduces contrast in written prose.

examples.ko: 반론을 예상하지 않으면 글의 설득력이 약해진다.
examples.romanization: balloneul yesanghaji aneumyeon geurui seoldeungnyeogi yakaejinda.
examples.en: If counterarguments are not anticipated, the writing becomes less persuasive.
examples.note: Good argument writing handles objections before the reader raises them.

examples.ko: 학생들은 서로의 주장에 대해 반론을 제기했다.
examples.romanization: haksaengdeureun seoroui jujange daehae balloneul jegihaetda.
examples.en: The students raised counterarguments against each other's claims.
examples.note: 반론을 제기하다 is the standard formal verb phrase.

entries.nuance: 반론 is an argument against a claim; 반대 is broader opposition.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 반대 when the text specifically needs a counterargument.
Forgetting the object marker in 반론을 제기하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 완전 means "totally; really (casual intensifier)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 완전 (wanjeon) means "totally; really (casual intensifier)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 완전 웃겨 ("so funny / totally funny"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 완전 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Casual reaction in chat.
Casual negative evaluation.
Stacked casual emphasis.

examples.en: This comment is so funny lol.
examples.note: 완전 fits casual peer chat.

examples.en: That video is totally legendary.
examples.note: 완전 naturally intensifies slang like 레전드.

examples.ko: 공식 글에서는 완전보다 매우나 상당히가 자연스럽다.
examples.romanization: gongsik geureseoneun wanjeonboda maeuna sangdanghiga jayeonseureopda.
examples.en: In official writing, 매우 or 상당히 is more natural than 완전.
examples.note: The key lesson is register control.

entries.nuance: 완전 literally means complete, but in casual speech it works as a general booster. It can sound youthful, excited, or blunt depending on context.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 완전 in essays or official notices where 매우, 상당히, or 매우 are safer.
Assuming 완전 always means completely in a literal sense; in chat it often just means really.
Stacking too many boosters such as 완전 진짜 너무 in one sentence unless the tone is intentionally playful.

entries.shortExplanation: 레전드 means "legendary; iconic; wildly memorable (slang)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "legendary; iconic; wildly memorable (slang)" is 레전드 (rejeondeu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 레전드 댓글 ("legendary comment"). Watch the particle attached to 레전드 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Comment-section phrase.
Casual reaction after a live stream or show.
Common intensifier plus slang.

examples.en: The reaction to that comment is legendary.
examples.note: Plain exclamatory -다 works in casual online reactions.

examples.en: Today's live chat was legendary.
examples.note: Natural after an especially chaotic or funny stream.

examples.ko: 공식 보고서에는 레전드라는 표현을 쓰지 않는다.
examples.romanization: gongsik bogoseoeneul lejeondeuraneun pyohyeoneul sseuji anhneunda.
examples.en: The expression 레전드 is not used in official reports.
examples.note: Slang recognition includes knowing where not to use it.

entries.nuance: 레전드 can praise something impressive, but it can also be ironic when something is absurd or unbelievably bad.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 레전드 as only positive. Online use can be ironic.
Using 레전드 in formal writing where 유명한 사례, 대표적 사례, or 대단한 would fit better.
Adding honorifics directly to slang to make it formal. 레전드세요 is not a safe formal upgrade.

entries.shortExplanation: 개웃겨 means "hilarious; so funny (very casual slang)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 개웃겨 (gaeutgyeo) = "hilarious; so funny (very casual slang)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 개웃겨 ㅋㅋㅋ ("so funny lolol") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 개웃겨, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Typical short chat reaction.
진짜 boosts the reaction.
Comment-thread use.

examples.en: This comment is hilarious lolol.
examples.note: Natural only in very casual text.

examples.ko: 친구한테는 개웃겨라고 해도 되지만 교수님께는 정말 재미있었습니다라고 해야 한다.
examples.romanization: chinguhanteneun gaeutgyeorago haedo doejiman gyosunimkkeneun jeongmal jaemiisseotseumnidarago haeya handa.
examples.en: You can say 개웃겨 to a friend, but to a professor you should say 정말 재미있었습니다.
examples.note: The same reaction needs a different register.

examples.ko: 단톡방에서는 개웃겨가 자연스럽지만 회사 공지에는 맞지 않는다.
examples.romanization: dantokbangeseoneun gaeutgyeoga jayeonseureopjiman hoesa gongjieneun matji anhneunda.
examples.en: 개웃겨 is natural in a group chat, but it does not fit a company notice.
examples.note: Register boundary.

entries.nuance: 개웃겨 is stronger and rougher than 너무 웃겨 or 진짜 웃겨. It can sound friendly, but it can also sound careless if the relationship is not close.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개웃겨 because it means funny without noticing the rough casual prefix 개-.
Trying to make it polite with 요. 개웃겨요 is possible among close peers but still slangy, not formal.
Using it about sensitive topics; the strong casual tone can sound dismissive.

entries.shortExplanation: 라이브 채팅 means "live chat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 라이브 채팅 (raibeu chaeting) means "live chat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 라이브 채팅에 올라오다 ("to appear in live chat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 라이브 채팅 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: For comments appearing on screen.

usagePhrases.en: the live chat is too fast
usagePhrases.note: Common complaint during streams.
Neutral descriptive phrase.

examples.ko: 라이브 채팅이 너무 빨라서 댓글을 다 못 읽었어.
examples.romanization: raibeu chaetingi neomu ppallaseo daetgeureul da mot ilgeosseo.
examples.en: The live chat was so fast that I couldn't read all the comments.
examples.note: Digital scenario for this chapter.

examples.ko: 라이브 채팅에는 ㅋㅋ와 ㅇㅈ 같은 반응이 자주 올라온다.
examples.romanization: raibeu chaetingeneun kkwa ngj gateun baneungi jaju ollaonda.
examples.en: Reactions like ㅋㅋ and ㅇㅈ often appear in live chat.
examples.note: Connects the digital place to the slang forms.

examples.ko: 공식 문의는 라이브 채팅보다 이메일로 남기는 것이 안전하다.
examples.romanization: gongsing munuineul laibeu chaetingboda imeillo namgineun geosi anjeonhada.
examples.en: For official inquiries, leaving an email is safer than using live chat.
examples.note: Register and channel choice matter.

entries.nuance: 라이브 채팅 is a channel, not a writing style. It invites short reactions, abbreviations, and fast turn-taking.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming live-chat slang transfers to email or official posts.
Using 댓글 for every chat line; 댓글 is a comment, while 라이브 채팅 is the live chat space.
Overusing abbreviations when the chat is customer support or official service chat.

entries.shortExplanation: 입자 means "particle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "particle" is 입자 (ipja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 입자를 확인하다 ("to check the particle"). Watch the particle attached to 입자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Review checklist phrase.
Use 이/가 because 입자 is the subject.
Revision action.

examples.ko: 이 문장은 입자를 다시 확인해야 해요.
examples.romanization: i munjangeun ipjareul dasi hwaginhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: This sentence needs its particles checked again.
examples.note: Useful when reviewing learner output.

examples.ko: 면접 답변에서는 입자 하나도 어색하게 들릴 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop dapbyeoneseoneun ipja hanado eosaekage deullil su isseoyo.
examples.en: In an interview answer, even one particle can sound awkward.
examples.note: Shows why production review matters.

examples.ko: 이유는 맞지만 입자가 틀려서 문장이 부자연스러워요.
examples.romanization: iyuneun matjiman ipjaga teullyeoseo munjangi bujayeonseureowoyo.
examples.en: The reason is right, but the sentence sounds unnatural because the particle is wrong.
examples.note: Meaning and grammar both matter.

entries.nuance: 입자 is the technical grammar term. In class it helps learners talk about the exact small piece that changed the sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Ignoring particles because the main vocabulary is correct.
Using 은/는 and 이/가 as simple English subject markers instead of discourse choices.
Changing a noun without rechecking whether the particle still fits.

entries.shortExplanation: 시제 means "tense" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 시제 (sije) = "tense". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시제를 확인하다 ("to check the tense") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Review checklist phrase.
Production review judgment.
Natural feedback phrase.

examples.ko: 이미 끝난 일이라면 시제를 과거로 바꿔야 해요.
examples.romanization: imi kkeunnan iriramyeon sijereul gwageoro bakkwoya haeyo.
examples.en: If it is something already finished, you need to change the tense to past.
examples.note: Connects time meaning to ending choice.

examples.ko: 이메일을 보내기 전에 시제와 높임말을 같이 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: imeireul bonaegi jeone sijewa nopimmareul gachi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Before sending the email, I checked the tense and honorific language together.
examples.note: Tense and register are reviewed together.

examples.ko: 경험을 말할 때 시제가 흔들리면 답변이 불안정하게 들려요.
examples.romanization: gyeongheomeul malhal ttae sijega heundeullimyeon dapbyeoni buranjeonghage deullyeoyo.
examples.en: When talking about experience, if the tense wavers, the answer sounds unstable.
examples.note: Interview and storytelling context.

entries.nuance: 시제 is not just past, present, and future labels. It is how the listener tracks whether an event happened, is happening, or is planned.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing past and present in one story without reason.
Forgetting that Korean future or intention can use -(으)ㄹ 거예요, -겠습니다, or -(으)려고 하다 depending on register and meaning.
Changing a sentence from casual to formal but leaving the tense or aspect inconsistent.

entries.shortExplanation: 연결어 means "connector; linking word" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 연결어 (yeongyeoreo) means "connector; linking word". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 연결어를 고르다 ("to choose a connector"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연결어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Writing and revision phrase.
Feedback phrase.
Revision action.

examples.ko: 공식 이메일에서는 그래서보다 따라서가 더 자연스러울 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: gongsik imeireseoneun geuraeseoboda ttaraseoga deo jayeonseureoul su isseoyo.
examples.en: In a formal email, 따라서 may be more natural than 그래서.
examples.note: Register affects connector choice.

examples.ko: 반대 내용을 말할 때는 연결어를 그러나로 바꿔 보세요.
examples.romanization: bandae naeyongeul malhal ttaeneun yeongyeoreoreul geureonaro bakkwo boseyo.
examples.en: When saying opposing content, try changing the connector to 그러나.
examples.note: Connector follows the relationship between ideas.

examples.ko: 연결어 하나가 글의 논리를 완전히 바꿀 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yeongyeoreo hanaga geurui nollireul wanjeonhi bakkul su isseoyo.
examples.en: One connector can completely change the logic of the writing.
examples.note: Important synthesis point.

entries.nuance: 연결어 is about logic, not decoration. A connector tells the reader how to understand the next sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그래서 for every result even in formal writing.
Using 즉 when the next sentence adds new information instead of restating the same point.
Choosing connectors by English translation without checking the sentence relationship.

entries.shortExplanation: 문체 means "writing style; register style" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "writing style; register style" is 문체 (munche). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 문체를 맞추다 ("to make the style consistent"). Watch the particle attached to 문체 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Revision phrase.
Common learner issue.
Positive review phrase.

examples.ko: 공식 이메일에서는 문체를 끝까지 격식 있게 맞춰야 해요.
examples.romanization: gongsik imeireseoneun munchereul kkeutkkaji gyeoksik itge matchwoya haeyo.
examples.en: In a formal email, the style should stay formal until the end.
examples.note: Register consistency.

examples.ko: 따라서와 ㅋㅋ가 한 문단에 같이 나오면 문체가 섞여 보여요.
examples.romanization: ttaraseowa kkga han mundane gachi naomyeon munchega seokkyeo boyeoyo.
examples.en: If 따라서 and ㅋㅋ appear in the same paragraph, the style looks mixed.
examples.note: Connects chapters 63 and 64.

examples.ko: 카톡 답장과 면접 답변은 문체부터 달라야 해요.
examples.romanization: katok dapjanggwa myeonjeop dapbyeoneun munchebuteo dallaya haeyo.
examples.en: A KakaoTalk reply and an interview answer need to differ from the style level onward.
examples.note: Final synthesis of register choice.

entries.nuance: 문체 is broader than one polite ending. It covers the whole feel of the text: vocabulary, endings, connectors, and sentence shape.

entries.shortExplanation: 신청 means "application" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

entries.nuance: 신청 is a Sino-Korean noun (申請, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') meaning a formal application or request you put in to an office, bank, or service — you are asking an authority to grant or process something. It overwhelmingly takes 하다 to become the verb 신청하다 ('to apply for'), and 신청서 is the physical form you fill in. Compare it carefully with 지원 (支援/志願): 신청 is the neutral 'put in a request' (카드를 신청하다 = apply for a card), while 지원 is 'apply to/for' a job or school where you are a candidate being selected (회사에 지원하다 = apply to a company). Also distinguish 접수, which is the office's act of RECEIVING and logging your 신청. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in any official or banking setting. The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 지원 for everyday errands (it sounds like job-hunting) and forgetting that 신청 needs 하다 to act as a verb — 신청 by itself is only the noun, so 'I apply' is 신청해요, not bare 신청.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 지원 for everyday requests like 'apply for a card' — 지원하다 implies competing for a job/school; for services and paperwork use 신청하다 (카드를 신청해요).
Saying bare 신청 to mean 'I apply' — 신청 is a noun; you must add 하다 (신청해요) or 을/를 하다 (신청을 해요).
Confusing 신청 (your request) with 접수 (the office logging it) — you 신청하다, then the counter 접수하다; they are two sides of one transaction.

It overwhelmingly takes 하다 to become the verb 신청하다 ('to apply for'), and 신청서 is the physical form you fill in. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in any official or banking setting.

entries.nuance: 신청서 is a Sino-Korean compound (申請書, 신청 'application' + 書 'document/writing') — the actual paper or digital FORM you complete to make a 신청. The 書 suffix is the same 'written document' element in 서류, 계약서 (contract), and 보고서 (report), so recognizing it helps you read official office vocabulary. Distinguish 신청서 (the specific application form) from the broader 서류 (any documents/paperwork) and from 양식 (the blank template/format itself): you grab the 양식, write on it, and it becomes your 신청서, which is one piece of 서류. The verbs that pair with it are formal: 작성하다 (fill out/complete) and 제출하다 (submit), rather than casual 쓰다/내다 — though 쓰다 and 내다 are fine in speech. Register is neutral-formal, standard at counters. The English-speaker pitfall is calling every document a 신청서: it is specifically an APPLICATION form, so a contract is 계약서 and general paperwork is 서류 — and remember the form-filling verb is 작성하다, not 만들다 (make).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling all paperwork 신청서 — it is specifically the application form; use 서류 for documents in general and 계약서 for a contract.
Saying 신청서를 만들다 ('make the form') for filling it in — the correct verb is 작성하다 (complete/fill out) or casual 쓰다.
Confusing 신청서 with 양식 — 양식 is the blank template/format; once you write your details on it, it becomes your 신청서.

examples.note: Everyday errand: 챙기다 (gather/pack) the papers ahead of the 전에 clause.

examples.ko: 여권 사본 같은 필요한 서류를 모두 제출하셔야 합니다.
examples.romanization: yeogwon sabon gateun piryohan seoryureul modu jechulhasyeoya hamnida.
examples.en: You must submit all the required documents, such as a passport copy.
examples.note: Real procedure: 필요한 서류 (required documents) as object of formal obligation 제출하셔야 합니다.

entries.nuance: 서류 is a Sino-Korean noun (書類, 書 'writing/document' + 類 'kind/category') meaning official documents or paperwork as a category — the bundle of forms, copies, and certificates a procedure demands. It is a collective, somewhat abstract term: 서류를 준비하다 = get your paperwork in order, covering many individual papers at once. Contrast it with 문서 (文書), which is 'a document' as a discrete file or record (often electronic or archival, e.g. an internal 문서), while 서류 evokes the practical stack you submit for an application. A single sheet is 종이 (paper) and one specific form is e.g. 신청서; 서류 is the umbrella. Natural collocations are 서류를 준비하다/챙기다/제출하다/접수하다 and 서류 심사 (document review). Register is neutral, ubiquitous at banks, immigration, and government offices. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 서류 as countable like 'a document' — Korean uses it as a mass/collective noun, so you rarely say 한 서류; for one item name the specific form (신청서 한 장) or use 문서 for a discrete record.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it like English 'a document' (한 서류) — 서류 is collective/mass; for one sheet say 신청서 한 장 or 서류 한 부 (one set).
Swapping 서류 and 문서 freely — 서류 is the practical paperwork you submit; 문서 is a discrete document/file, often archival or electronic.
Using 종이 for official papers — 종이 is the physical material 'paper'; the forms and certificates you submit are 서류.

entries.shortExplanation: 신분증 means "ID card" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "ID card" is 신분증 (sinbunjeung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신분증을 제시하다 ("to present one's ID"). Watch the particle attached to 신분증 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 제시하다 = show it for inspection
확인하다 = the staff verifies it
사본 = photocopy/duplicate
지참하다 = carry it with you (formal)

examples.en: Do you have your ID?
examples.note: Simple frame: the everyday counter question, 있다 + honorific 으세요.

examples.en: You need an ID when opening a bankbook.
examples.note: Everyday: 신분증 as subject of 필요하다 inside a 때 (when) clause.

examples.ko: 본인 확인을 위해 신분증을 제시해 주시기 바랍니다.
examples.romanization: bonin hwagineul wihae sinbunjeungeul jesihae jusigi baramnida.
examples.en: Please present your ID for identity verification.
examples.note: Real formal notice: 제시하다 with 위해 (for the purpose of) 본인 확인 (identity check).

entries.nuance: 신분증 is a Sino-Korean compound (身分證, 身分 'social status/identity' + 證 'certificate/proof') — any official photo ID that proves who you are: a 주민등록증 (national ID), 운전면허증 (driver's license), or 여권 (passport) all count as a 신분증. The 證 'proof' suffix recurs in 학생증 (student ID), 자격증 (certificate), and 영수증 (receipt), so it flags 'certifying document'. Note the difference from 신분 alone, which is the abstract 'identity/social standing' (신분을 밝히다 = reveal one's identity), while 신분증 is the physical card. At banks and offices the set verbs are formal: 제시하다 (present) and 지참하다 (bring), with staff doing 확인하다 (verify); in speech 보여 주다 (show) and 가져오다 (bring) are natural. Register is neutral, indispensable for any errand. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 아이디 (a loanword that in Korean means a login USERNAME, not a physical ID) when you mean the card — for a photo identity card always use 신분증, and never confuse it with 카드 alone (which suggests a bank/credit card).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 아이디 for a physical ID card — in Korean 아이디 means a login username; the photo identity card is 신분증.
Using 신분 instead of 신분증 — 신분 is abstract 'identity/status'; the card you hand over is 신분증 (add 證 = the proof document).
Calling it just 카드 — 카드 alone suggests a bank/credit card; specify 신분증 for an identity document.

entries.shortExplanation: 통장 means "bankbook" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 만들다 = the standard verb for opening one
개설하다 = formally establish (an account)
정리 = bringing entries up to date
noun-noun: the account one's pay goes into

examples.en: I want to open a bankbook.
examples.note: Simple frame: 통장 as object of 만들다 with desire 고 싶다.

examples.en: How much money is in the account?
examples.note: Everyday: 통장에 (in the bankbook) as location of 돈 with 있다.

examples.ko: 새 통장을 개설하려면 신분증과 도장이 필요합니다.
examples.romanization: sae tongjangeul gaeseolharyeomyeon sinbunjeunggwa dojangi piryohamnida.
examples.en: To open a new bankbook, you need an ID and a seal.
examples.note: Real bank procedure: formal 개설하다 + intention 려면 listing required items with 과.

entries.nuance: 통장 is a Sino-Korean noun (通帳, 通 'pass through/circulate' + 帳 'ledger/book') — the physical passbook that records deposits and withdrawals, and by extension the everyday word Koreans use for a bank account itself (통장을 만들다 = open an account). Here is the key contrast learners must master: 통장 is the tangible book / the account in casual speech, while 계좌 (計座) is the technical ACCOUNT NUMBER and the formal term used for transfers (계좌이체 = wire transfer, 계좌번호 = account number). So you 'open a 통장' but you 'transfer to a 계좌'. The verb for opening is colloquial 만들다 or formal 개설하다 (establish). Natural collocations: 월급 통장 (salary account), 통장 정리 (update the passbook), 통장 사본 (a copy of the passbook). Register is neutral, fully everyday. The English-speaker pitfall is using 계좌 where 통장 is natural and vice versa: to open the book say 통장을 만들다, but when giving someone your details for a transfer, you give your 계좌번호, not your 통장번호.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계좌 for the physical book/casual 'account' — you 통장을 만들다 (open a bankbook); 계좌 is the formal account/number used for transfers.
Saying 통장번호 for the number you give for a transfer — that is 계좌번호; 통장 is the book itself.
Using 열다 ('open' a door) to mean 'open an account' — the verb is 만들다 (make) or formal 개설하다 (establish).

entries.shortExplanation: 계좌 means "account" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 계좌 (gyejwa) means "account". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 계좌를 개설하다 ("to open an account"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 계좌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 개설하다 = formally establish an account
알려 주다 = tell/inform someone of it
money moved account-to-account
로 marks the destination account

examples.en: Please tell me your account number.
examples.note: Simple frame: 계좌번호 as object of 알려 주다 with polite request.

examples.en: I sent 100,000 won to my friend's account.
examples.note: Everyday: 계좌로 (to the account) as destination of 보내다 (send).

examples.en: Your salary is automatically transferred to the registered account.
examples.note: Real notice: 계좌로 as destination of passive 이체되다 (be transferred), with 등록된 (registered).

entries.nuance: 계좌 is a Sino-Korean noun (計座, 計 'count/reckon' + 座 'seat/position') meaning a bank account in the technical, financial sense — the entity identified by a 계좌번호 (account number) that money moves into and out of. It is the formal counterpart to 통장 (the physical passbook / casual word for account): banks, transfer screens, and official forms all say 계좌 — 계좌이체 (account transfer), 가상계좌 (virtual account), 계좌 개설 (account opening). The distinction is functional: you 통장을 만들다 (open the book) but you 입금하다 / 이체하다 to a 계좌, and you give your 계좌번호 for someone to pay you. The verb is 개설하다 (formal, 'establish') rather than 만들다 in official contexts. Register is neutral-formal, the standard term in any financial transaction. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing 계좌 and 통장: when transferring money or quoting the number, always use 계좌(번호); reserve 통장 for the passbook or casual 'I opened an account'. Also do not confuse 계좌 with 계산 (計算, calculation/paying a bill) — close-looking 한자 but different words.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 통장번호 when you mean the transfer number — the number money is sent to is the 계좌번호.
Saying 계좌를 만들다 in formal contexts — banks say 계좌를 개설하다 (establish); 만들다 pairs more with 통장.
Confusing 계좌 (account) with 계산 (paying/calculating a bill) — similar 한자 but 계산하다 means to settle a bill, not to bank.

entries.shortExplanation: 입금 means "deposit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "deposit" is 입금 (ipgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 입금을 하다 ("to make a deposit"). Watch the particle attached to 입금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 입금 + 하다 = put money in
에 marks the receiving account
확인되다 = it is verified as received
내역 = itemized record of incoming money

examples.en: I deposited 50,000 won into the account.
examples.note: Simple frame: 입금하다 with amount + 계좌에 as destination 에.

examples.en: When you deposit money, a text message comes.
examples.note: Everyday: 입금하다 in a 면 (when/if) clause; deposit triggers an alert.

examples.ko: 입금이 확인되는 대로 상품을 보내 드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: ipgeumi hwagindoeneun daero sangpumeul bonae deurigetseumnida.
examples.en: We will ship the item as soon as the deposit is confirmed.
examples.note: Real transaction: passive 입금이 확인되다 with 는 대로 (as soon as) in formal commerce.

entries.nuance: 입금 is a Sino-Korean noun (入金, 入 'enter' + 金 'money') meaning the act of money coming IN — depositing funds into an account, or money being received. It takes 하다 (입금하다 = to deposit/pay in) and pairs with 에 for the destination: 계좌에 입금하다. Its exact opposite is 출금 (出金, money going out / withdrawal), and the 入/出 pair is worth memorizing together, like 입구/출구 (entrance/exit). Distinguish 입금 from 송금 (送金, 'remitting/sending money', emphasizing the transfer ACROSS to another party) and from 이체 (移替, the account-to-account 'transfer' operation): when you pay a seller, you 입금하다 (the money enters their account) or 송금하다 (you send it); the bank's mechanism is 이체. Natural collocations: 입금 확인 (deposit confirmation), 입금 내역, 무통장 입금 (bankless/cash deposit). Register is neutral, everyday in shopping and banking. The English-speaker pitfall is using 저금 (saving up) or 예금 (a savings deposit/balance) for the act of paying in — those describe SAVING money, while 입금 is the transactional act of putting funds into an account right now.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 입금 (depositing/money in) with 출금 (withdrawing/money out) — they are 入/出 opposites; double-check which direction the money moves.
Using 저금 or 예금 for 'pay this in' — 저금/예금 mean saving money; the act of depositing into an account is 입금하다.
Forgetting the destination particle — it is 계좌에 입금하다 (에 = into); using 로 here sounds off for the receiving account.

entries.shortExplanation: 출금 means "withdrawal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 출금 (chulgeum) = "withdrawal". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 출금을 하다 ("to make a withdrawal") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 출금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 출금 + 하다 = take money out
에서 marks the source account
한도 = the maximum allowed
money drawn out automatically

examples.en: I withdrew some cash.
examples.note: Simple frame: 출금하다 with object 현금 (cash) in past tense.

examples.en: I'm going to withdraw 100,000 won from the account.
examples.note: Everyday: 출금하다 with source 에서 + amount and intention 려고 하다.

examples.ko: 하루 출금 한도는 백만 원으로 제한됩니다.
examples.romanization: haru chulgeum handoneun baengman woneuro jehandoemnida.
examples.en: The daily withdrawal limit is capped at one million won.
examples.note: Real bank rule: 출금 한도 as subject with 으로 제한되다 (be limited to).

entries.nuance: 출금 is a Sino-Korean noun (出金, 出 'exit/go out' + 金 'money') meaning the act of money going OUT — withdrawing funds from an account. It takes 하다 (출금하다 = to withdraw) and, crucially, pairs with 에서 (the source) rather than 에: 계좌에서 출금하다 = withdraw FROM the account. It is the direct opposite of 입금 (入金, depositing), and learners should drill the 入/出 contrast plus the particle switch (입금은 '에', 출금은 '에서'). Near terms: 인출 (引出) is a more formal synonym for cash withdrawal seen on ATM screens and forms, while 출금 is the everyday word; 이체 (transfer) moves money to another account rather than taking it out as cash. Natural collocations: 출금 한도 (withdrawal limit), 자동 출금 (auto-debit), 출금 수수료 (withdrawal fee). Register is neutral, standard at ATMs and banks. The English-speaker pitfall is using 에 instead of 에서 with 출금 (the money LEAVES, so it is the source 에서), and confusing 출금 with 입금 — because the 한자 differ by only one character, mixing them up can send money the wrong way.

Using 에 instead of 에서 — withdrawal is FROM a source, so it is 계좌에서 출금하다 (에서), not 계좌에 출금하다.
Swapping 출금 (money out) and 입금 (money in) — the 한자 differ by one character (出 vs 入); confirm the direction before acting.
Assuming 출금 always means cash — at an ATM yes, but on forms the formal synonym is 인출; a transfer to another account is 이체, not 출금.

examples.ko: 타행 이체 시 건당 오백 원의 수수료가 부과됩니다.
examples.romanization: tahaeng iche si geondang obaek wonui susuryoga bugwadoemnida.
examples.en: A fee of 500 won per transaction is charged for transfers to other banks.
examples.note: Real bank notice: 수수료가 부과되다 (be levied) with 건당 (per case) and 시 (upon/when).

entries.nuance: 수수료 is a Sino-Korean noun (手數料, 手數 'effort/handling' + 料 'charge/fee') meaning a service fee or commission — the charge a bank, agency, or service takes for handling a transaction (transfer fees, ATM fees, brokerage commission). The 料 'fee' suffix recurs in 요금 (utility/usage charge), 입장료 (entrance fee), 수업료 (tuition), so it flags 'a charge for ~'. Distinguish 수수료 from those siblings: 요금 is a usage charge for a service you consume (전기 요금 = electricity bill, 통화 요금 = call charges), 세금 (稅金) is a tax to the government, and 비용 (費用) is general 'cost/expense' — while 수수료 specifically is the HANDLING fee skimmed for processing your transaction. Natural verbs: 수수료가 들다/붙다/부과되다 (a fee is incurred/added/levied) and 수수료를 내다 (pay it). Register is neutral-formal, standard wherever transactions carry charges. The English-speaker pitfall is using 요금 or 비용 for a transaction commission — for the per-transaction handling charge at a bank or service, the precise word is 수수료, and remember it 'attaches' with 붙다 rather than being 'made'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 요금 for a bank commission — 요금 is a usage charge (전기 요금); the per-transaction handling fee is 수수료.
Calling it 세금 — 세금 is a government tax; a service's processing charge is 수수료, not a tax.
Saying 수수료를 만들다 — fees are not 'made'; they 들다/붙다/부과되다 (are incurred/added/levied), and you 내다 (pay) them.

entries.shortExplanation: 등록 means "registration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: 등록 + 하다 = enter oneself/something on a register
되다 = the registration goes through
the open window to register
being enrolled automatically

examples.en: I register my name here.
examples.note: Simple frame: 등록하다 with object 이름 in present tense.

examples.ko: 외국인 등록을 하러 출입국 사무소에 가요.
examples.romanization: oegugin deungnogeul hareo churipguk samusoe gayo.
examples.en: I'm going to the immigration office to do my alien registration.
examples.note: Everyday: 외국인 등록 (alien registration) as object of 하다 with purpose 러.

examples.ko: 수강 신청 후 등록금을 납부해야 등록이 완료됩니다.
examples.romanization: sugang sincheong hu deungnokgeumeul napbuhaeya deungnogi wallyodoemnida.
examples.en: Registration is complete only after you pay tuition following course sign-up.
examples.note: Real procedure: passive 등록이 완료되다 (registration is completed) tied to 납부 (payment) condition.

entries.nuance: 등록 is a Sino-Korean noun (登錄, 登 'record/ascend' + 錄 'register/record') meaning officially entering a person or thing onto a register or roll — enrolling, registering, recording in a system. It takes 하다 (등록하다 = to register) or 되다 (등록되다 = to be registered), and appears in 외국인 등록증 (alien registration card), 주민등록 (resident registration), 등록금 (registration/tuition fee), 등록 번호 (registration number). The contrast learners need is with 신청 and 접수: 신청 is REQUESTING something, 접수 is the office RECEIVING your request, and 등록 is the result of being formally ENTERED onto the official record — often you 신청 first, the desk 접수, and finally you are 등록 in the system. Compare also 가입 (加入, 'joining/subscribing' to a membership, service, or insurance — 보험 가입, 회원 가입), which is about becoming a MEMBER, whereas 등록 is about being recorded in a registry. Register is neutral-formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 등록 for joining a club or signing up for a service (that is 가입) and using 가입 for recording an official entry (that is 등록) — and remembering 등록 needs 하다/되다 to function as a verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 등록 for joining a membership or service — that is 가입 (회원 가입); 등록 is being entered on an official register.
Confusing 등록 with 신청 — you 신청하다 (request) something first; 등록 is the resulting formal entry in the records.
Saying bare 등록 as a verb — add 하다 (등록해요) or 되다 (등록됐어요); 등록 alone is only the noun.

entries.shortExplanation: 접수 means "reception, filing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 접수 (jeopsu) = "reception, filing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 접수를 하다 ("to file/submit (and have it logged)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 접수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 접수 + 하다 = lodge your application at the desk
되다 = the office has logged it
the counter that takes submissions
the number assigned when filed

examples.en: File it here. / Register here.
examples.note: Simple frame: 접수하다 with honorific request at an intake desk.

examples.en: I filed the documents in the morning.
examples.note: Everyday: 접수하다 with object 서류 in past tense — handed in and logged.

examples.ko: 접수가 완료되면 접수 번호를 문자로 보내 드립니다.
examples.romanization: jeopsuga wallyodoemyeon jeopsu beonhoreul munjaro bonae deurimnida.
examples.en: Once your filing is complete, we send the reference number by text.
examples.note: Real procedure: passive 접수가 완료되다 with the assigned 접수 번호 being sent.

entries.nuance: 접수 is a Sino-Korean noun (接受, 接 'receive/connect' + 受 'accept') meaning the RECEIVING and logging of an application or document by an office — both the act of an institution taking your submission in, and (loosely) your act of handing it in at the 접수 창구 (intake window). It takes 하다 and 되다: from your side 서류를 접수하다 can mean 'submit/file', while 접수가 되다 / 접수되다 means 'it has been received/registered by them'. The crucial trio for learners: 신청 (you REQUEST) → 접수 (the office RECEIVES/logs it) → 처리 (處理, they PROCESS it). So 접수 sits in the middle, the moment your paperwork is officially accepted and assigned a 접수 번호. Distinguish it from 제출 (提出, the physical act of 'submitting/handing over' a document) — 제출 is the handing in, 접수 is the institution accepting and registering it. Register is neutral-formal, standard at hospitals, offices, and event desks (병원 접수 = hospital reception/check-in). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 접수 as plain 'submit' (that is 제출) and missing its 'be accepted/logged' meaning — 접수가 됐어요 means your application is now officially in the system, not merely handed over.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 접수 as just 'submit' — 제출 is handing the document over; 접수 is the office RECEIVING and logging it (접수되다 = it's now registered).
Confusing 접수 (intake/logging) with 등록 (being entered on the register) — 접수 comes first at the desk; 등록 is the later formal record.

entries.shortExplanation: 발급 means "issuance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 발급 (balgeup) means "issuance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 발급을 받다 ("to be issued (something)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 발급 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 발급 + 받다 = receive an issued document
하다 = the office issues it
the charge to have it issued
재 + 발급 = issuing a replacement

examples.en: I got a passport issued.
examples.note: Simple frame: 발급받다 (receive issuance) with object 여권 in past tense.

examples.ko: 증명서는 무인 발급기에서 뽑을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeungmyeongseoneun muin balgeupgieseo ppobeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can get the certificate from an automated issuing machine.
examples.note: Everyday: 발급 in the compound 발급기 (issuing kiosk) with 뽑다 (print/pull) + ability.

examples.en: If you have lost your card, you must apply for a reissue.
examples.note: Real procedure: 재발급 as object of 신청하다 under a 다면 (if) condition, formal obligation.

entries.nuance: 발급 is a Sino-Korean noun (發給, 發 'issue/send out' + 給 'give/supply') meaning the official ISSUING of a document, card, or certificate by an authority — passports, ID cards, certificates, bank cards are all 발급. Crucially, it splits by direction: the OFFICE 발급하다 (issues), but YOU 발급받다 (receive the issuance) — so for your own errand the natural verb is 발급받다, not 발급하다 (which would mean you are the issuer). This 받다 pattern mirrors other 'receive an action' verbs. 재발급 (reissue) is the common compound when something is lost. Distinguish 발급 from 신청 and 등록: you 신청 (request) a document, the office 발급 (issues) it, after which you might be 등록 (recorded) somewhere. Compare also 교부 (交付), a more bureaucratic synonym for 'issue/hand over' seen in legal/government text, versus everyday 발급. Register is neutral-formal, standard at banks and government counters. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 발급하다 about getting your OWN document — that wrongly casts you as the issuing authority; to say 'I got X issued', use 발급받다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 발급하다 for getting your own document — that means YOU issue it; to receive one, use 발급받다 (여권을 발급받았어요).
Confusing 발급 (issuing a document) with 신청 (requesting it) — you 신청하다 first, then the office 발급하다; they are different steps.
Forgetting the 재 in 재발급 for replacements — a lost card needs 재발급 (reissue), not a fresh 발급, on the form.

entries.shortExplanation: 의견 means "opinion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "opinion" is 의견 (uigyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 의견을 말하다 ("to state an opinion"). Watch the particle attached to 의견 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 의견 + 을 with 말하다, the default verb for voicing a view
의견 + 이 with 다르다, the set way to say 'we disagree'
의견 + 을 with 듣다, asking for input
의견 stands as a count noun you can put 다른 'other' in front of

examples.en: My opinion is a little different.
examples.note: Simple frame: 의견은 + adjective states where you stand on something.

examples.ko: 이 문제에 대해 여러분의 의견을 듣고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i munjee daehae yeoreobunui uigyeoneul deutgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to hear your opinions on this issue.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~에 대해 (about) + 의견을 듣다, common in class or meetings.

examples.ko: 회의에서 제 의견을 솔직하게 말했지만 받아들여지지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuieseo je uigyeoneul soljikage malhaetjiman badadeuryeojiji anasseoyo.
examples.en: I gave my opinion frankly in the meeting, but it wasn't accepted.
examples.note: Real situation: voicing 의견 at work, with the realistic outcome that it may be rejected.

entries.nuance: 의견 is Sino-Korean (意見, 意 'mind/intention' + 見 'view/seeing'), literally 'how your mind sees something' — a considered position or judgment you can defend, usually about a topic, plan, or issue. The crucial contrast is with 생각: 생각 is the broad word for any 'thought' that crosses your mind, while 의견 is specifically a stance offered for discussion or evaluation, so a meeting asks for 의견 (positions), not just 생각 (musings). It is register-neutral and very common in school and workplace settings; the polite request 의견을 여쭤봐도 될까요? raises it a notch. Natural collocations: 의견을 말하다/내다/제시하다 (state/put forward), 의견이 다르다/같다 (disagree/agree), 의견을 모으다 (gather opinions), 반대 의견 (an opposing view). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 의견 every time you'd say 'I think' — 'I think it's good' is 좋은 것 같아요 or 좋다고 생각해요, NOT 좋은 의견이에요; 의견 is the opinion itself as a thing, not the act of thinking. Also don't say 의견하다 — there is no such verb; you 의견을 말하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의견하다 to mean 'to opine' — 의견 is a noun with no verb form; use 의견을 말하다 / 의견을 내다.
Using 의견 where English 'I think...' just hedges — 'I think it'll rain' is 비가 올 것 같아요, not an 의견; 의견 is a stance offered for discussion.
Confusing 의견 with 생각 — 생각 is any thought; 의견 is a position on a topic, so a survey or meeting collects 의견, while daydreaming is 생각.

entries.shortExplanation: 생각 means "thought, idea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 생각 (saenggak) = "thought, idea". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 생각이 나다 ("to come to mind / remember") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생각, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 생각 + 이 with 나다, an idea or memory pops up by itself
생각 + 이 with 들다, a thought arises in you
생각 + 을 with 하다, the everyday 'to think things over'
생각 + 이다 evaluates a suggestion as good

examples.en: That's a good idea!
examples.note: Simple frame: 생각 + 이에요 to praise a suggestion someone just made.

examples.en: Yesterday's events suddenly came to mind.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 생각나다 (one written verb) = 'to remember / cross one's mind' on its own.

examples.ko: 며칠 동안 곰곰이 생각해 봤는데, 그냥 포기하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: myeochil dongan gomgomi saenggakae bwanneunde, geunyang pogihaneun ge naeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: I thought it over carefully for a few days, and I feel it's better to just give up.
examples.note: Real situation: 생각해 보다 (think it over) leading to a tentative conclusion with ~것 같다.

entries.nuance: 생각 is the native Korean catch-all noun for a 'thought', 'idea', or 'opinion' — anything that happens in the mind: memories, intentions, plans, beliefs, judgments. It is far broader and softer than Sino-Korean 의견 (a defined stance for discussion): 좋은 생각이에요 praises an idea, whereas 의견 frames it as a formal position. It also overlaps with 마음 ('heart/mind' as feeling/will), but 생각 is the cognitive 'thinking' side while 마음 is the emotional/volitional side — 생각이 바뀌다 = I changed my mind (reasoning), 마음이 바뀌다 = my heart changed (feelings). Register-neutral and one of the highest-frequency nouns in the language. Key collocations: 생각이 나다 (come to mind/remember), 생각이 들다 (a thought arises), 생각해 보다 (think it over), ~라고 생각하다 (to think that ~). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb pattern: 'I think that it's true' is 사실이라고 생각해요 with the quotative ~라고, not 사실 생각해요; and 'I remember' is most naturally 생각나요, not a literal translation. Don't confuse 생각나다 (it comes to mind, intransitive) with 생각하다 (to actively think, transitive).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the quotative ~라고: 'I think it's good' is 좋다고 생각해요, not 좋다 생각해요 or 좋은 것 생각해요.
Mixing up 생각나다 and 생각하다 — 생각나다 = it pops into your head (옛날이 생각나요), 생각하다 = you deliberately think (잘 생각하세요).
Using 생각 for a formal 'opinion' in a meeting where 의견 fits better — 생각 sounds casual/personal, 의견 sounds like a position offered for debate.

entries.shortExplanation: 이유 means "reason" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 이유 (iyu) means "reason". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이유가 있다 ("to have a reason"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이유 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 이유 + 이 with 있다, there exists a reason
이유 + 를 with 묻다, to inquire why
이유 + 없이 forms the adverb 'for no reason'
이유 + 로 with 무슨, asking the grounds 'on what reason'

examples.en: There's no special reason.
examples.note: Simple frame: 이유 + 없다 to brush off a 'why' question politely.

examples.en: Please explain the reason you're late.
examples.note: Everyday frame: [modifier]~(으)ㄴ + 이유 packs the reason into a noun phrase.

examples.ko: 회사를 그만둔 이유는 여러 가지가 있지만, 가장 큰 이유는 건강이었어요.
examples.romanization: hoesareul geumandun iyuneun yeoreo gajiga itjiman, gajang keun iyuneun geongangieosseoyo.
examples.en: There are several reasons I quit the company, but the biggest reason was my health.
examples.note: Real situation: layering reasons (여러 가지 이유 / 가장 큰 이유) when explaining a big decision.

entries.nuance: 이유 is Sino-Korean (理由, 理 'principle/logic' + 由 'cause/origin'), the 'reason' or grounds behind something — the answer to 'why?'. Its sharpest contrast is with 원인 (原因, 'cause'): 이유 is the justification or motive a person gives ('the reason I'm late'), often subjective and explainable, while 원인 is the objective, often impersonal cause of a result ('the cause of the fire', 화재의 원인). So you ask a friend 무슨 이유로 늦었어? but an investigator looks for the 원인 of an accident. Also distinguish 까닭, a more native, slightly literary synonym of 이유. Register-neutral and extremely common. Core collocations: 이유가 있다/없다, 이유를 묻다/대다/설명하다, 이유 없이 (for no reason), 그런 이유로 (for that reason), ~는 이유는 (the reason that ~ is). The English-speaker pitfall: don't bolt 이유 onto a 'because' clause redundantly — Korean already has 왜냐하면 ... 때문이에요 / ~기 때문에 to say 'because', so '왜냐하면 그 이유는...' is clunky; pick one. Also, 'the reason is because...' should be ~는 이유는 ... 때문이에요, where the sentence ends in 때문이다, not a second 이유.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 원인 for a personal motive — the reason you skipped class is 이유, while 원인 is an objective cause (사고의 원인 = the cause of the accident).
Doubling up 'because': '왜냐하면 그 이유는 비가 와서요' is redundant; say 왜냐하면 비가 왔기 때문이에요, or simply 비가 와서요.
Forgetting 때문이다 closes a 'the reason is...' sentence: 늦은 이유는 차가 막혔기 때문이에요, not 늦은 이유는 차가 막혔어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 관심 means "interest, attention" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "interest, attention" is 관심 (gwansim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 관심이 있다 ("to be interested"). Watch the particle attached to 관심 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 관심 + 이 with 있다, the standard 'I'm interested'
관심 + 을 with 가지다, to develop interest
~에 marks the target; 관심이 많다 = lots of interest
관심 + 을 with 끌다, to draw interest

examples.en: I'm very interested in Korean music.
examples.note: Simple frame: ~에 관심이 많다/있다 names the topic you're into with ~에.

examples.ko: 요즘 사람들이 환경 문제에 관심을 가지기 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum saramdeuri hwangyeong munjee gwansimeul gajigi sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: People have started taking an interest in environmental issues lately.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 관심을 가지다 = to take/develop an interest, with 시작하다 for 'start to'.

examples.ko: 처음엔 그냥 관심이었는데, 이제는 진지하게 공부하고 싶어졌어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen geunyang gwansimieonneunde, ijeneun jinjihage gongbuhago sipeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: At first it was just curiosity, but now I've come to want to study it seriously.
examples.note: Real situation: 관심 as a starting spark that grows into a serious commitment.

entries.nuance: 관심 is Sino-Korean (關心, 關 'to be connected/concerned' + 心 'heart/mind'), literally 'the heart being connected to something' — interest, concern, or attention directed at a topic, activity, or person. Two contrasts matter. Against 흥미 (興味): 흥미 is the felt 'fun/excitement' kind of interest, a momentary enjoyment (흥미로운 영화 = an interesting/fun movie), whereas 관심 is a steadier, often deliberate concern you choose to 'have' or 'give' (관심을 가지다). Against 호기심 (好奇心, curiosity): 호기심 is the itch to find out, while 관심 is broader attention or care. Note 관심 also means romantic/personal attention — 관심 있어? can imply 'do you like me?' in the right context. Register-neutral, very high frequency. Collocations: ~에 관심이 있다/없다/많다, 관심을 가지다/두다/끌다/받다, 관심 분야 (field of interest), 무관심 (indifference). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the thing you're interested in takes ~에 (or ~에 대해), so it's 음악에 관심이 있어요, NOT 음악을 관심이 있어요 or 음악 관심 있어요. Also 'I'm interested' is a state with 있다 (관심이 있다), not 관심하다 — there is no verb 관심하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the topic with 을/를: it's 영화에 관심이 있어요 (interested IN movies), not 영화를 관심이 있어요 — the target takes ~에 / ~에 대해.
Saying 관심하다 — there's no such verb; use 관심이 있다 (state) or 관심을 가지다 (take interest).
Swapping 관심 and 흥미 — a fun, momentary 'that's interesting!' is 흥미롭다, while 관심 is steady concern/attention you give to a topic or person.

entries.shortExplanation: 복잡하다 means "to be complicated" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 복잡하다 (bokjapada) = "to be complicated". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 복잡해요 ("it is complicated") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 복잡하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 contracts to 해요, never 복잡하요
modifier form 복잡한 + noun

usagePhrases.en: to have a lot on one's mind
usagePhrases.note: 머리가 복잡하다, an idiom for a cluttered, stressed mind
복잡하다 also covers crowded, tangled places

examples.en: This problem is too complicated.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 복잡해요 to call something hard to untangle.

examples.en: Because it was the weekend, downtown was crowded with people.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 복잡하다 = 'crowded/congested' for places, with ~로 'with (people)'.

examples.ko: 설명을 들을수록 더 복잡해져서, 결국 포기하고 싶어졌어요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongeul deureulsurok deo bokjapaejyeoseo, gyeolguk pogihago sipeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The more I listened to the explanation, the more complicated it got, so in the end I felt like giving up.
examples.note: Real situation: 복잡해지다 (become complicated) showing a situation worsening as it's explained.

entries.nuance: 복잡하다 is a Sino-Korean 하다-adjective (複雜 + 하다, 複 'multiple/layered' + 雜 'mixed/miscellaneous'), literally 'many things mixed together', so it spans three English ideas at once: (1) complicated/intricate (복잡한 문제 = a complex problem), (2) crowded/congested (길이 복잡하다 = the road is jammed), and (3) mentally cluttered/troubled (머리가 복잡하다 = my head is a mess). Its opposite is 간단하다 (simple). Contrast it with 어렵다: 어렵다 is 'difficult' (hard to do or understand, possibly even if simple in structure), while 복잡하다 stresses having too many tangled parts — a problem can be 복잡하지만 어렵지 않다 (complicated but not hard). As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 복잡해 → 복잡해요 (never 복잡하요), modifier 복잡한, adverb 복잡하게, and 'become complicated' is 복잡해지다. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 복잡하다 for a task that is merely 'hard' — use 어렵다 for difficulty; and for a crowded café, Koreans naturally say 사람이 많다 or 복잡하다, but never the literal 'busy'. Also avoid 복잡하고 있다 — it's a state (복잡해요), not an ongoing action.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 복잡하요 — 하다 words contract to 해, so it must be 복잡해요; the modifier is 복잡한, not 복잡하는.
Using 복잡하다 for plain 'difficult' — a hard exam question is 어려워요; 복잡하다 means tangled/many-parted (or crowded), e.g. 절차가 복잡해요 (the procedure is complicated).
Treating it as an action verb: 'I am being busy/complicated' is not 복잡하고 있어요; the state is simply 복잡해요 or 머리가 복잡해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 맛 means "taste, flavor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 맛 (mat) means "taste, flavor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 맛이 있다 → 맛있다 ("to be delicious"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 맛 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 맛 + 이 + 있다 fuses into the one word 맛있다
맛 + 이 + 없다 fuses into 맛없다
맛 + 을 with 보다, to sample the flavor
맛 as a count noun: which flavor/taste

examples.en: How does this soup taste?
examples.note: Simple frame: 맛이 어때요? is the standard way to ask 'how does it taste?'

examples.en: I like spicy flavor more than sweet flavor.
examples.note: Everyday frame: flavor compounds 단맛(sweet)/매운맛(spicy)/짠맛(salty) + ~보다 to compare.

examples.ko: 오랫동안 끓였더니 국물에서 깊은 맛이 나기 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: oraetdongan kkeuryeotdeoni gungmureseo gipeun masi nagi sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: After simmering it a long time, a deep flavor began to come out of the broth.
examples.note: Real situation: 맛이 나다 (a flavor comes out) plus 깊은 맛 (deep, rich flavor) in cooking.

entries.nuance: 맛 is the native Korean noun for taste or flavor — both the literal taste on the tongue and, by extension, the 'flavor/charm' of an experience (사는 맛 = the joy of living; 그 영화는 보는 맛이 있다 = that movie is fun to watch). Its most important behavior is fusion: 맛 + 있다 → 맛있다 (delicious) and 맛 + 없다 → 맛없다 (not tasty) are written as single words and are the everyday way to praise or pan food. Contrast 맛 with 향 (香, scent/aroma, from the nose, e.g. 커피 향) and with 식감 (食感, texture/mouthfeel) — Koreans separate flavor (맛), smell (향), and texture (식감). The five basic tastes form compounds: 단맛, 짠맛, 신맛(sour), 쓴맛(bitter), 매운맛(spicy/hot). Register-neutral, extremely high frequency. Collocations: 맛이 있다/없다, 맛을 보다 (taste it), 맛이 나다 (a taste comes out), 맛이 진하다/연하다 (strong/mild), 입맛 (appetite/palate). The English-speaker pitfall: 'this is tasty' is 맛있어요 (one word), not 맛이 좋아요 in casual speech (though 맛이 좋다 exists, it sounds more written/evaluative); and don't say 맛이 나빠요 for 'it tastes bad' — say 맛없어요. To ask 'what does it taste like?', use 무슨 맛이에요? or 맛이 어때요?, not a literal 'how is the taste'.

Writing 맛 있다 / 맛 없다 as two words for 'delicious/not tasty' — they fuse into 맛있다 / 맛없다 (one word, stress shifts).
Saying 맛이 나빠요 for 'it tastes bad' — natural Korean is 맛없어요; 나쁘다 is for general 'bad', not flavor.
Confusing 맛 (taste) with 향 (smell) or 식감 (texture) — 'it smells good' is 향이 좋아요, not 맛이 좋아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 방법 means "method, way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "method, way" is 방법 (bangbeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 방법이 있다 ("there is a way/method"). Watch the particle attached to 방법 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 방법 + 이 with 있다, a way exists
방법 + 을 with 찾다, to look for a solution
adjective + 방법, naming a good approach
방법 + 없다, 'no other choice/method'

examples.en: There's no other way.
examples.note: Simple frame: 방법이 없다 = there's no method/option, a common resigned phrase.

examples.ko: 이 단어를 외우는 좋은 방법이 있어요?
examples.romanization: i daneoreul oeuneun joeun bangbeobi isseoyo?
examples.en: Is there a good way to memorize this word?
examples.note: Everyday frame: [verb]~는 + 방법 = 'a way to do X', the go-to question for tips.

examples.ko: 여러 방법을 다 시도해 봤지만, 결국 가장 단순한 방법이 제일 효과적이었어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo bangbeobeul da sidohae bwatjiman, gyeolguk gajang dansunhan bangbeobi jeil hyogwajeogieosseoyo.
examples.en: I tried all sorts of methods, but in the end the simplest method was the most effective.
examples.note: Real situation: surveying 여러 방법 (various methods) and concluding which worked best.

entries.nuance: 방법 is Sino-Korean (方法, 方 'direction/manner' + 法 'rule/method'), the 'way', 'method', or 'means' of doing something — the procedure or approach to reach a goal. Compare it with 방식 (方式, 'style/mode/manner'): 방법 is the concrete how-to ('a method to fix it'), while 방식 is the overall style or fashion in which something is done (생활 방식 = lifestyle, 사고방식 = way of thinking) — you wouldn't say 사고방법. Also distinguish 수단 (手段, 'means/instrument', often the tool or even an unscrupulous means: 교통수단 = means of transport, 수단과 방법을 가리지 않다 = by any means necessary). Register-neutral, very common. Core collocations: 방법이 있다/없다, 방법을 찾다/알다/모르다/바꾸다, [동사]~는 방법 (a way to do ~), 해결 방법 (solution), 사용 방법 (how to use). The English-speaker pitfall is the 'a way to do X' frame: it's [verb in ~는 form] + 방법, e.g. 'a way to study' is 공부하는 방법, NOT 공부 방법 in spoken contexts (though 공부 방법 as a fixed noun-noun compound is fine for 'study method'). Don't say 방법으로 어떻게 when you just mean 어떻게 ('how') — 방법 is the noun 'method', not the question word 'how'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방법 where the question word 어떻게 ('how') is needed — 'How do I do this?' is 이거 어떻게 해요?, not 이거 무슨 방법으로 해요? unless you truly want to ask which method.
Saying 사고방법 / 생활방법 — fixed terms use 방식: 사고방식 (way of thinking), 생활 방식 (lifestyle); 방법 is the concrete how-to.
Forgetting the ~는 modifier for 'a way to do X': 'a way to get there' is 가는 방법, not 가기 방법 or 가다 방법.

entries.shortExplanation: 장점 means "strength, merit, advantage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 장점 (jangjeom) = "strength, merit, advantage". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장점이 있다 ("to have a merit/strength") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장점, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 장점 + 이 with 있다, an advantage exists
장점 + 이 with 많다, lots of good points
가장 큰 + 장점, ranking the top merit

usagePhrases.en: to make the most of a strength
usagePhrases.note: 장점 + 을 with 살리다, to leverage an advantage

examples.en: This method has many advantages.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 장점이 많다/있다 to list what's good about something.

examples.ko: 온라인 수업의 장점은 시간을 아낄 수 있다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: ollain sueobui jangjeomeun siganeul akkil su itdaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: The advantage of online classes is that you can save time.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~의 장점은 ...라는 것이다, the set 'the advantage of X is that ~' pattern.

examples.ko: 면접에서 자신의 장점과 단점을 솔직하게 말하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseo jasinui jangjeomgwa danjeomeul soljikage malhaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: In an interview, it's good to honestly state your own strengths and weaknesses.
examples.note: Real situation: 장점과 단점 paired in the classic interview question about yourself.

entries.nuance: 장점 is Sino-Korean (長點, 長 'long/superior' + 點 'point'), literally a 'strong point' — a merit, advantage, or strength of a thing, plan, or person. It is almost always used in deliberate contrast with its antonym 단점 (短點, 'short point' = weakness/drawback); the pair 장점과 단점 is a fixed collocation, like English 'pros and cons'. Compare 장점 with 강점 (強點, 'strong point/forte'): 강점 emphasizes a competitive strength relative to others (우리 회사의 강점 = our company's competitive edge), while 장점 is the neutral 'good point' of anything. Also note 좋은 점 (a more colloquial 'the good thing about it'). Register-neutral and common in reviews, interviews, and comparisons. Collocations: 장점이 있다/많다, 장점을 살리다 (leverage), 장점을 살펴보다 (examine the merits), 큰 장점, 최대 장점 (greatest advantage). The English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'advantage' as 이득 or 이점 indiscriminately — 이득 (利得) is material 'gain/profit', and 이점 (利點) is 'an advantageous point/benefit' often in a strategic sense; for the everyday 'good point of X', 장점 is the natural choice. Also, when describing a person's virtue, 장점 (good trait) differs from 매력 (charm/appeal) — a reliable friend has a 장점, a charismatic one has 매력.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing the wrong antonym: the opposite of 장점 is 단점 (장점과 단점 = pros and cons), not 약점 (which is 'a vulnerability/weak spot', e.g. in a fight or argument).
Using 이득 for 'advantage' of a method — 이득 is monetary gain; the merit/strength of a plan is its 장점.
Saying 장점이 좋다 — that's redundant ('the good point is good'); just say 장점이 있다/많다, or 좋은 점이 있다.

entries.shortExplanation: 단점 means "weakness, drawback, shortcoming" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 단점 (danjeom) means "weakness, drawback, shortcoming". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 단점이 있다 ("to have a drawback"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 단점 + 이 with 있다, a weak point exists
단점 + 을 with 고치다, to improve a flaw
가장 큰 + 단점, ranking the worst weakness

usagePhrases.en: to make up for a weakness
usagePhrases.note: 단점 + 을 with 보완하다, to compensate for a flaw

examples.en: This phone has almost no drawbacks.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 단점이 없다/있다 to evaluate the downsides of a product.

examples.ko: 제 단점은 가끔 너무 솔직하다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je danjeomeun gakkeum neomu soljikadaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My weakness is that I'm sometimes too honest.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~의 단점은 ...라는 것이다, the 'my weakness is that ~' interview pattern.

examples.ko: 이 방법의 단점은 시간이 오래 걸린다는 점인데, 그래도 가장 안전해요.
examples.romanization: i bangbeobui danjeomeun sigani orae geollindaneun jeominde, geuraedo gajang anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The drawback of this method is that it takes a long time, but it's still the safest.
examples.note: Real situation: conceding a 단점 (~다는 점) while still recommending the option.

entries.nuance: 단점 is Sino-Korean (短點, 短 'short/lacking' + 點 'point'), literally a 'short point' — a weakness, drawback, flaw, or shortcoming of a thing, plan, or person. It is the fixed antonym of 장점 (長點, merit), and the pair 장점과 단점 functions exactly like English 'pros and cons / strengths and weaknesses'. The key contrast to master is 단점 vs 약점 (弱點, 'weak point/vulnerability'): 단점 is a general flaw or downside that's just part of something (이 차의 단점 = this car's drawback, e.g. poor mileage), while 약점 is an exploitable vulnerability or sensitive spot — a rival attacks your 약점, a coach targets the opponent's 약점, and a personal sore subject is a 약점, not a 단점. Also compare 결점 (缺點, a 'defect/fault', slightly stronger, hints at something missing) and 흠 (a native word for a 'flaw/blemish'). Register-neutral. Collocations: 단점이 있다/없다, 단점을 고치다/보완하다 (fix/compensate), 단점을 인정하다 (admit a flaw), 큰 단점. The English-speaker pitfall: in self-introductions, 'my weakness' should be 단점 (a manageable shortcoming), not 약점 — calling it your 약점 sounds like you're confessing an exploitable vulnerability. And don't say 단점이 나쁘다 ('the drawback is bad') — that's redundant; just 단점이 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying your interview 'weakness' is your 약점 — use 단점 (a shortcoming); 약점 is an exploitable vulnerability/sore spot, which sounds wrong in self-introduction.
Mismatching the antonym: 단점 pairs with 장점 (단점보다 장점이 많다 = more pros than cons), not with 강점.
Adding a redundant evaluation: 단점이 나쁘다 is circular; say 단점이 있다, or name it: 단점은 비싸다는 거예요 (the drawback is that it's expensive).

entries.shortExplanation: 차이 means "difference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: "difference" is 차이 (chai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 차이가 있다 ("there is a difference"). Watch the particle attached to 차이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 차이 + 이 with 있다, a difference exists
차이 + 이 with 나다, a difference appears between things
차이 + 이 with 크다, a large gap
~와 marks the thing compared against; 차이가 있다

examples.en: The two photos have almost no difference.
examples.note: Simple frame: A는/두 N은 + 차이가 없다/있다 to say things are (not) different.

examples.ko: 이 두 단어는 의미에 큰 차이가 있어요.
examples.romanization: i du daneoneun uimie keun chaiga isseoyo.
examples.en: These two words have a big difference in meaning.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~에 차이가 있다 (a difference IN ~), here 의미에 (in meaning).

examples.ko: 가격은 비슷한데 품질에서 차이가 많이 나서, 결국 더 비싼 걸 샀어요.
examples.romanization: gagyeogeun biseutande pumjireseo chaiga mani naseo, gyeolguk deo bissan geol sasseoyo.
examples.en: The prices are similar, but there's a big difference in quality, so in the end I bought the more expensive one.
examples.note: Real situation: 차이가 나다 in 품질에서 (in quality) driving a purchase decision.

entries.nuance: 차이 is Sino-Korean (差異, 差 'discrepancy/gap' + 異 'different'), the 'difference', 'gap', or 'disparity' between two or more things. It pairs with two key verbs: 차이가 있다 (a difference exists, more static) and 차이가 나다 (a difference shows up/emerges, more dynamic, often for a noticeable gap, e.g. 실력 차이가 나다 = a clear skill gap). The thing you compare with takes ~와/과 (A는 B와 차이가 있다), and the dimension of difference takes ~에(서) (의미에 차이가 있다 = a difference in meaning). Contrast 차이 with 다르다, the adjective 'to be different': 다르다 describes that two things are not the same (A와 B는 달라요), while 차이 is the noun naming the gap itself (A와 B는 차이가 있어요) — Koreans often use 다르다 for a qualitative 'different' and 차이 for a measurable/quantifiable gap (나이 차이 = age gap, 온도 차이 = temperature difference). Don't confuse 차이 with 차별 (差別, 'discrimination'), which is unfair treatment based on a difference. Register-neutral, very common. Collocations: 차이가 있다/없다/나다/크다, 차이를 느끼다 (feel a difference), 큰 차이, 별 차이 없다 (no real difference), 나이 차이/시차 (time difference). The English-speaker pitfall: 'A is different from B' is most naturally A는 B와 달라요 (using 다르다 + 와), not A는 B에서 차이예요; reach for the noun 차이 when you mean 'the difference between/in', and the verb 다르다 when you simply mean 'differs'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 차이 like an adjective: 'A is different from B' is A는 B와 달라요 (다르다), not A는 B와 차이예요; 차이 is a noun ('the gap'), so say 차이가 있어요.
Marking the compared item with 을/를: it's A는 B와 차이가 있어요 (differ FROM B with ~와), not B를 차이가 있어요.
Confusing 차이 (a neutral difference/gap) with 차별 (discrimination) — 남녀 차이 = differences between men and women; 남녀 차별 = gender discrimination.

entries.shortExplanation: 태도 means "attitude" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 태도 (taedo) = "attitude". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 태도가 좋다 ("to have a good attitude") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 태도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 태도 + 이 with 좋다, a good manner/disposition
태도 + 이 with 나쁘다, a poor attitude
태도 + 를 with 바꾸다, to shift one's stance/manner
adjective + 태도, describing one's manner

examples.en: That person has a really good attitude.
examples.note: Simple frame: 태도가 좋다/나쁘다 to judge someone's manner or disposition.

examples.ko: 선생님은 항상 학생들에게 친절한 태도로 말해요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimeun hangsang haksaengdeurege chinjeolhan taedoro malhaeyo.
examples.en: The teacher always speaks to students with a kind attitude.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~한 태도로 (with a ~ attitude) describes the manner of an action.

examples.ko: 실력도 중요하지만, 일을 대하는 성실한 태도가 더 중요하다고 생각해요.
examples.romanization: sillyeokdo jungyohajiman, ireul daehaneun seongsilhan taedoga deo jungyohadago saenggakaeyo.
examples.en: Skill matters too, but I think a sincere attitude toward work is more important.
examples.note: Real situation: weighing 태도 (work attitude) against 실력 (skill) in a values statement.

entries.nuance: 태도 is Sino-Korean (態度, 態 'form/manner/bearing' + 度 'degree/measure'), a person's 'attitude', 'manner', 'bearing', or 'stance' — both the outward way they carry and conduct themselves (공손한 태도 = a polite manner) and their inner posture toward something (인생을 대하는 태도 = one's attitude toward life). Contrast it with 자세 (姿勢): 자세 literally means physical 'posture/pose' (바른 자세로 앉다 = sit with good posture) but is also used figuratively for a committed 'attitude/stance', often a praiseworthy, proactive one (배우려는 자세 = a willing-to-learn attitude) — so 자세 leans toward earnest mindset, while 태도 is the broader, more neutral 'manner' that can be good OR bad (태도가 나쁘다 is normal; 자세가 나쁘다 usually means literal bad posture). Also distinguish 입장 (立場, 'position/standpoint' on an issue) and 성격 (性格, 'personality', a stable trait vs. a situational 태도). Register-neutral, common in evaluations of behavior, work, and manners. Collocations: 태도가 좋다/나쁘다, 태도를 바꾸다/취하다 (change/take an attitude), ~에 대한 태도 (attitude toward ~), 근무 태도 (work attitude), 강경한 태도 (a hard-line stance). The English-speaker pitfall: 'attitude' in English can imply a personality trait or even sass, but Korean 태도 is more about manner/conduct in a given context; for a fixed personality trait use 성격, and don't say 태도하다 — there is no such verb; you 태도를 취하다/보이다 (take/show an attitude).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 태도하다 — 태도 is a noun with no verb form; use 태도를 보이다/취하다 (show/take an attitude) or describe with ~한 태도로.
Confusing 태도 (manner/conduct, can be good or bad) with 성격 (personality, a stable trait): 'he has a kind personality' is 성격이 착해요, while 태도가 좋다 judges his behavior in a situation.
Mixing up 태도 and 자세 — 자세 is literal posture (자세를 바르게 하다) or an earnest mindset (적극적인 자세); for a generic, possibly negative 'attitude', use 태도.

entries.shortExplanation: 느낌 means "feeling, impression, vibe" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
entries.explanation: 느낌 (neukkim) means "feeling, impression, vibe". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 느낌이 좋다 ("to have a good feeling/vibe"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 느낌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 느낌 + 이 with 좋다, something feels right
느낌 + 이 with 들다, an impression arises
느낌 + 이 with 오다, intuition kicks in
modifier + 느낌, 'a feeling of being ~'

examples.en: This café has a good vibe.
examples.note: Simple frame: 느낌이 좋다 to say a place/person gives a pleasant impression.

examples.en: I get the feeling something is wrong.
examples.note: Everyday frame: [modifier]~ㄴ + 느낌이 들다 = 'I get a ~ feeling/sense that ~'.

examples.ko: 설명을 들어도 완전히 이해한 느낌이 안 와서, 한 번 더 물어봤어요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongeul deureodo wanjeonhi ihaehan neukkimi an waseo, han beon deo mureobwasseoyo.
examples.en: Even after hearing the explanation, I didn't get the feeling I fully understood, so I asked once more.
examples.note: Real situation: 느낌이 안 오다 (it doesn't click) prompting a follow-up question.

entries.nuance: 느낌 is the native Korean noun from the verb 느끼다 ('to feel'), meaning a 'feeling', 'impression', 'sense', or 'vibe' — the subjective sensation or intuition something gives you, whether physical (차가운 느낌 = a cold feeling) or atmospheric (느낌이 좋은 사람 = someone who gives off a good vibe). The crucial contrast is with 기분 (氣分): 기분 is your own emotional 'mood/spirits' caused by events (기분이 좋다 = I'm in a good mood, 기분 나빠 = I'm upset), whereas 느낌 is the impression/sense you get OF something external (그 사람 느낌이 좋다 = that person gives a good impression — about them, not your mood). Also distinguish 감정 (感情, 'emotion' as a category: love, anger) and 감각 (感覺, 'sense/sensation', the faculty). Register-neutral and hugely frequent in casual speech, where 느낌 also works as a vague 'kind of, sort of, like' filler (약간 매운 느낌? = kind of spicy?). Collocations: 느낌이 좋다/이상하다, 느낌이 들다 (a feeling arises), 느낌이 오다 (it clicks/I get a hunch), 첫 느낌 (first impression), ~는 느낌 (a feeling of ~ing). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 느낌 for your own mood — 'I feel good/happy today' is 오늘 기분이 좋아요, NOT 느낌이 좋아요 (which describes an external thing's vibe). And 'I feel that ~' is naturally ~ㄴ 느낌이 들어요 with 들다, not 느낌해요 (no such verb).

Using 느낌 for your own mood: 'I'm in a good mood' is 기분이 좋아요, while 느낌이 좋아요 means 'it/he gives a good vibe' (an external impression).
Saying 느낌하다 — there's no verb; the natural patterns are 느낌이 들다 / 느낌이 오다, or the source verb 느끼다 ('느꼈어요').
Forgetting the ~ㄴ/는 modifier: 'a warm feeling' is 따뜻한 느낌, and 'I get the feeling it's true' is 사실인 느낌이 들어요, not 사실 느낌.
